article_title: Practitioner's Guide to Integrating Literacy and Science
citation: Practitioner's guide to integrating literacy and science. (2025). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Introduce science vocabulary as the need for words arises, rather than without need or context
description: The guide recommends introducing and defining science vocabulary during discourse when students allude to technical ideas, for example when a student mentions light "bouncing off objects," so words like absorb and reflect are learned in context. It states plainly: "It's important to introduce words as the need arises, rather than introducing words without need or context." This connects vocabulary work to the rich-vocabulary component and to students' own models and questions.
requirements: A classroom discussion context in which students raise ideas that allude to technical terms
target_learners: Elementary students, including emergent multilinguals
target_learning_goals: Science vocabulary development supporting comprehension across subjects
examples: In Lesson 3, students learn definitions of absorb and reflect as they suggest revisions to the classroom model.
key_sources: Practitioner's guide to integrating literacy and science. (2025). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/practitioners-guide-to-integrating-literacy-and-science/

article_title: Practitioner's Guide to Integrating Literacy and Science
citation: Practitioner's guide to integrating literacy and science. (2025). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Build and progressively revise a class consensus model of the phenomenon across the lesson sequence
description: The guide has students sketch initial individual models, then maintain a class consensus model on chart paper that is deliberately incomplete at first — "It's OK if this initial model is inaccurate and/or incomplete" — and revised as observations, experiments, and reading accumulate. By Lesson 8 the final model represents sunlight transferring energy to objects, reflecting off light-colored surfaces and being absorbed by dark ones, with captions, and is used to explain or predict related phenomena.
requirements: Chart paper or similar visible record of student ideas and the consensus model maintained throughout the unit
target_learners: Elementary students in grades K-6
target_learning_goals: Modeling and explaining scientific phenomena
Connecting new ideas to prior ideas across lessons
examples: In Lesson 8, students suggest changes so the consensus model shows sunlight reflecting off light-colored objects but absorbed by dark-colored ones.

article_title: Positionality in Teaching: Implications for Advancing Social Justice
citation: Angelica Paz Ortiz, Beth Tarasawa, Jack Straton, Noelle Al-Mustaifry, Anmarie Trimble. (2019). Positionality in teaching: Implications for advancing social justice. Journal of General Education 67(1), 109-121. https://www.nwea.org
title: Teachers of justice- and equity-focused classes should model vulnerability by demonstrating honest self-assessment of their own relationship to power, privilege, and oppression
description: The article argues that teaching classes concerned with justice and equity requires instructors to model the same vulnerability they ask of students. As the authors state, "we must model justice and equity in all of our work," and "Modeling honest self-assessment allows us to ask students to be reflective about their relationship to power, privilege, and oppression." The approach frames the teacher's own positionality work as a precondition for asking students to do it.
requirements: Instructors must be willing to demonstrate vulnerability themselves before asking students to discuss how society's messages about race, gender, and sexual identity have affected them
target_learners: higher education students in classes concerned with justice and equity
target_learning_goals: reflection on one's relationship to power, privilege, and oppression
examples: The authors report that teaching classes concerned with justice and equity led them to adopt this stance across all of their work
key_sources: Angelica Paz Ortiz, Beth Tarasawa, Jack Straton, Noelle Al-Mustaifry, Anmarie Trimble. (2019). Positionality in teaching: Implications for advancing social justice. Journal of General Education 67(1), 109-121. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/positionality-in-teaching-implications-for-advancing-social-justice/

article_title: The Influence of Rapidly Guessed Item Responses on Teacher Value-Added Estimates: Implications for Policy and Practice
citation: Andrew Rice. (2018). The influence of rapidly guessed item responses on teacher value-added estimates: Implications for policy and practice. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 40(2), 267-284. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+influence+of+rapidly+guessed+item+responses+on+teacher+value-added+estimates
title: Educators should be mindful of rapid guessing when interpreting student test results
description: The article recommends that because rapid guessing occurs frequently on achievement tests, educators should attend to its presence when interpreting what student test scores mean. The authors state that "rapid guessing occurs frequently enough that educators should be mindful of its effect on the interpretations of student test results." This recommendation follows from their finding that the behavior varies across grades, subjects, and teachers, even though it did not substantively change teacher value-added estimates under their specifications.
requirements: Test response-time or rapid-guessing behavior must be observable or estimable for the test results being interpreted.
constraints: The article's own value-added analysis found no substantive effect of rapid guessing on teacher performance estimates under the specifications used, so the recommendation concerns score interpretation rather than teacher accountability estimates.
target_learners: K-12 students taking achievement tests
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of student achievement test results
examples: The study examined rapid guessing prevalence on achievement tests and evaluated its influence on teacher value-added estimates before recommending mindful interpretation.
key_sources: Andrew Rice. (2018). The influence of rapidly guessed item responses on teacher value-added estimates: Implications for policy and practice. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 40(2), 267-284. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+influence+of+rapidly+guessed+item+responses+on+teacher+value-added+estimates

article_title: Are Test and Academic Disengagement Related? Implications for Measurement and Practice
citation: Emily Wolk, Sharon Bi, Tran Keys. (2018). Are test and academic disengagement related? Implications for measurement and practice. Educational Assessment 24(2), 119-134. https://www.nwea.org/research-publications/
title: Use rapid-guessing indicators alongside academic disengagement indicators when interpreting test scores and supporting students
description: Because test disengagement (rapid guessing) is related to academic disengagement (chronic absenteeism, course failures) and to social-emotional factors like poor self-management, educators and assessment programs should treat rapid-guessing behavior as a signal connected to broader disengagement rather than as isolated test noise. The article discusses "implications for measurement and practice" of this connection.
requirements: Response-time or rapid-guessing indicators must be available from test data to identify test disengagement
constraints: The available text reports the relation without effect sizes; the full-text discussion of measurement and practice implications was not examined
target_learners: High school students
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of test scores
Identification of disengaged students for support
examples: The study related chronic absenteeism and course failures to rapid guessing on items and examined social-emotional predictors of rapid guessing
key_sources: Emily Wolk, Sharon Bi, Tran Keys. (2018). Are test and academic disengagement related? Implications for measurement and practice. Educational Assessment 24(2), 119-134. https://www.nwea.org/research-publications/

article_title: Achievement and Growth Norms for Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Foundational Skills
citation: Wei He, NWEA Psychometrics and Analytics. (2026). Achievement and Growth Norms for Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Foundational Skills. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/spanish-map-reading-fluency-technical-report/
title: Use normative results alongside other evidence of student learning, not as the sole basis for placement or instructional decisions
description: The report cautions that although the achievement and growth norms provide context for interpreting student performance at a point in time and growth over time, "decisions about student placement or instructional planning should not rely on norms alone." Educators are advised to consider normative results together with other evidence such as classroom performance and teacher observations, because test scores alone have limited meaning without appropriate context.
requirements: Educators must supplement norm-referenced scores with other evidence of student learning, such as classroom performance and teacher observations
constraints: The norms reflect a norming sample concentrated in the South (particularly Texas) and in early grades, which the report says provides important context for interpretation
target_learners: Students in grades K-3 assessed with Spanish MAP Reading Fluency
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of student achievement and growth in foundational Spanish reading skills
examples: The report's conclusion states the norms offer context for schools, educators, and parents to understand performance relative to peers in the norming sample, supporting more informed evaluation of student outcomes.
key_sources: Wei He, NWEA Psychometrics and Analytics. (2026). Achievement and Growth Norms for Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Foundational Skills. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/achievement-and-growth-norms-for-spanish-map-reading-fluency-foundational-skills-report/

article_title: Behind at the starting line: What Kindergarten test scores tell us about reaching proficiency in 3rd grade
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, Karyn Lewis, Emily Morton. (2026). Behind at the starting line: What Kindergarten test scores tell us about reaching proficiency in 3rd grade. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org/research/publications/behind-at-the-starting-line-what-kindergarten-test-scores-tell-us-about-reaching-proficiency-in-3rd-grade/
title: Use early (Kindergarten) assessment data to identify at-risk students and intervene before third grade
description: The brief recommends that educators use early identification from Kindergarten test data to intervene and influence learning trajectories before students reach third grade. As the description states, "This early identification is key for educators, enabling them to intervene and influence learning trajectories before the next critical milestone: third grade." The principle treats kindergarten assessment as a screening step that triggers support rather than waiting for later milestones.
requirements: Kindergarten test score data must be available and interpreted to flag students at risk of falling further behind
constraints: Grounded in the brief's framing of third grade as the next critical milestone; the supplied text does not print details of which interventions work
target_learners: Kindergarten students in U.S. schools
target_learning_goals: Early academic trajectories in reading and math leading to third-grade proficiency
examples: The brief analyzes Kindergarten scores of more than 400,000 U.S. students to flag students at risk of falling further behind

citation: Megan Kuhfeld, Karyn Lewis, Emily Morton. (2026). Technical Appendix for Behind at the starting line: What Kindergarten test scores tell us about reaching proficiency in 3rd grade. NWEA Research technical brief. https://www.nwea.org

article_title: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Technical Report
citation: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Technical Report. (2026). NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Four-level phonological awareness progression from rhymes and syllables to phoneme manipulation
description: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency structures its Phonological Awareness domain as a research-based developmental progression "with two measures at each of four levels": Level 1 Rhymes and Syllables, Level 2 Syllable Blending and Initial Sounds (a transitional level), Level 3 Phoneme Blending and Segmenting, and Level 4 Syllable and Phoneme Manipulation. Reports also include a Level 0, indicating readiness for Level 1 concepts, and a Level 5, indicating Level 4 concepts can be reinforced. Within-domain adaptivity selects measures based on student performance within this progression.
requirements: Adaptive selection of a subset of measures within the progression during each test event
constraints: Level 2 is transitional, indicating whether students are ready to move on to phoneme blending and segmentation
target_learners: Pre-K through grade 2 students developing Spanish phonological awareness
target_learning_goals: Phonological awareness skills supporting decoding, aligned to CCSS en español foundational skills standards
examples: Rhyme Completion and Counting Syllables at Level 1; Phoneme Substitution and Syllable Addition/Deletion at Level 4, each with printed item specifications and CCSS en español alignments
key_sources: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Technical Report. (2026). NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/spanish-map-reading-fluency-technical-report/

article_title: MAP Growth Spanish Technical Report- Addendum
citation: MAP Growth Technical Report Spanish Addendum for 2024–2025. (2026). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Transadaptation of calibrated English items into culturally and linguistically appropriate Spanish items
description: A structured item-development process in which "The Spanish Math item bank is composed entirely of items that have been transadapted using a careful and highly structured process that starts with calibrated English Math items." Items are adaptations, not only translations: original English content is adapted for cultural and linguistic appropriateness, guided by International Test Commission guidelines, with glossaries, linguistic and content editing, proofreading in generic neutral Spanish for U.S. Spanish speakers, and expert validation that the Spanish item preserves the original construct and quality.
requirements: Selection of English source items with strong content and alignment that are culturally neutral or have adaptable parallel terms
Review stages covering linguistic editing, content editing, and proofreading, followed by subject-matter expert validation and a final quality check
constraints: Some English items are removed from development rather than translated when context or linguistic complexity makes them non-viable candidates
target_learners: Spanish-speaking students in U.S. K–12 assessments
target_learning_goals: Measuring the same mathematical constructs across languages
Preserving item construct and skill targeting when moving between English and Spanish
examples: Each Spanish Math item keeps the same standards alignment as its English counterpart and adopts the same RIT value; Wang and Li (2020) found English- and Spanish-calibrated item parameters were similar enough that separate calibrations were not required
key_sources: MAP Growth Technical Report Spanish Addendum for 2024–2025. (2026). HMH Education Company / NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/map-growth-spanish-technical-report-addendum/

article_title: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency content guide
citation: NWEA. (2025). Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Content Guide. https://www.nwea.org
title: Four-level Spanish phonological awareness progression from rhymes and syllables to manipulation
description: The Phonological Awareness domain is organized as "two measures at each of four levels": Level 1 Rhymes and Syllables, Level 2 Syllable Blending and Initial Sounds, Level 3 Phoneme Blending and Segmenting, and Level 4 Syllable and Phoneme Manipulation. The guide states the measures "are designed to ﬁt this research-based progression," and reports also include a Level 0 (ready for Level 1 concepts) and Level 5 (Level 4 concepts can be reinforced).
requirements: Measures align to CCSS en español foundational skills standards
adaptive within-domain selection points students to a ZPD level in the progression
constraints: In Spanish, syllable awareness figures more prominently than in English, where phonemes are the smaller unit emphasized

target_learning_goals: syllable and phoneme blending, segmenting, and manipulation
examples: Rhyme Completion and Counting Syllables at Level 1; Phoneme Blending and Segment & Count Phonemes at Level 3

article_title: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency content guide
citation: NWEA. (2025). Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Content Guide. https://www.nwea.org
title: Assess oral reading with rate, accuracy, prosody, and comprehension rather than WCPM alone
description: The guide argues one-minute WCPM-only assessment loses the instructional value of accuracy scores and can equate faster reading with better reading. Citing Valencia et al. (2010), it states that "four types of scores each contribute to a best prediction of general passage comprehension: rate, accuracy, prosody, and comprehension," and that "MAP Reading Fluency is modeled by this more robust approach" of reading a complete passage aloud and answering comprehension questions.
requirements: Audio recording and playback so teachers can rate prosody and consider dialect or pronunciation nuances
passage comprehension items accompanying oral reading passages
constraints: With oral reading, complex comprehension tasks are typically a poor fit since they often require revisiting text; the guide instead raises text complexity to gauge growth
target_learners: Primary-grade students still building passage comprehension skills
target_learning_goals: oral reading fluency
passage comprehension
examples: Spanish MAP Reading Fluency scores SWCPM, decoding accuracy, and passage comprehension automatically, with prosody rated by teachers via audio playback
key_sources: NWEA. (2025). Spanish MAP Reading Fluency Content Guide. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/spanish-map-reading-fluency-content-guide/

article_title: English MAP Reading Fluency technical report
citation: NWEA. (2024). English MAP Reading Fluency Technical Report. https://www.nwea.org
title: Report oral reading rate, decoding accuracy, and comprehension separately rather than subsuming accuracy into WCPM alone
description: The report cites research "that accuracy scores are useful in instructional decisions, but that this use is lost when they are subsumed into the WCPM score alone." Following Valencia et al. (2010), it argues that rate, accuracy, prosody, and comprehension each contribute to predicting passage comprehension, and states "MAP Reading Fluency is modeled by this more robust approach." Accordingly, the assessment reports decoding accuracy and comprehension alongside oral reading rate to generate an individualized reader profile of strengths and needs.
requirements: Audio playback is needed for teacher rating of prosody where of interest
constraints: Complex comprehension tasks are typically a poor fit for oral reading administration since they often require revisiting the text for analysis
target_learners: primary-grade students still building passage comprehension skills
target_learning_goals: accurate individualized diagnosis of oral reading strengths and needs
examples: The Oral Reading Fluency report shows SWCPM, decoding accuracy, and passage comprehension scores, and teachers can play back the audio recording for further evaluation
key_sources: NWEA. (2024). English MAP Reading Fluency Technical Report. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/english-map-reading-fluency-technical-report/

article_title: English MAP Reading Fluency technical report
citation: NWEA. (2024). English MAP Reading Fluency Technical Report. https://www.nwea.org
title: ZPD-leveled foundational skills progressions mapped to aligned instructional materials
description: The Phonological Awareness and Phonics & Word Recognition domains each offer within-domain adaptivity along a progression of skills, so reported data point toward a zone of proximal development (ZPD) level within the domain. "Each step in the Phonological Awareness and Phonics & Word Recognition progressions is mapped to best practice instructional materials made available by the Florida Center for Reading Research." This links assessment results directly to instruction at the student's current skill level, from single letters and letter sounds up to word reading and phoneme manipulation.
requirements: Within-domain adaptive administration is needed to locate each student's ZPD level in the progression
target_learners: early readers not yet ready to read passages
target_learning_goals: phonological awareness
phonics and word recognition
examples: ZPD levels are reported for Phonological Awareness and Phonics & Word Recognition with performance expectations by level
key_sources: NWEA. (2024). English MAP Reading Fluency Technical Report. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/english-map-reading-fluency-technical-report/

article_title: Mitigating the Academic Impacts of Proximity to Homicide: The Role of Schools
citation: Johnson, D.W., Hinze-Pifer, R., Orta, D., & Guz, S. (2024). Mitigating the academic impacts of proximity to homicide: The role of schools. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Build trusting educator-student relationships and broadly restorative responses to misconduct to protect students from adversity
description: The report holds that the particular quality of relationships between educators and students is a critically important barometer of success in mitigating the impacts of proximity to homicide. It states that "Efforts to make school systems and structures—particularly how a school responds to student misconduct—broadly restorative are an important part of the broader strategy of focusing on relationship and connectedness." Interviews in mitigating schools highlighted communication, coordination, and trust across the school community.
requirements: Sustained effort building collaborative, trusting relationships among adults in the school
School leaders who help create and sustain responsive school communities
constraints: Responsive, resilient school communities do not emerge from a single initiative and require substantial resources and sustained hard work
target_learners: Students exposed to community violence, particularly students of color in high-poverty communities
target_learning_goals: Academic performance, engagement, and resilience in the aftermath of adverse experiences
examples: Mitigating schools emphasized trusting, connected relationships among students and between students and adults across a range of climate measures

Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/mitigating-the-academic-impacts-of-proximity-to-homicide

article_title: Typical learning for whom? Guidelines for selecting benchmarks to calculate months of learning
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, Melissa Diliberti, Andrew McEachin, Jon Schweig, Louis T. Mariano. (2023). Typical learning for whom? Guidelines for selecting benchmarks to calculate months of learning. Research brief. https://www.nwea.org
title: Select benchmarks for months-of-learning calculations deliberately, guided by the metric's trade-offs
description: The brief's central recommendation, reflected in its title, is that benchmarks of typical learning used to calculate months of learning should be selected deliberately, since the choice of benchmark shapes the resulting months-of-learning figure. The authors write to "inform future uses by researchers and media" and discuss "how to calculate this metric as well as its trade-offs". Because the metric has major downsides despite its accessibility, users should weigh those trade-offs when choosing benchmarks.
requirements: An explicit benchmark of typical learning must be chosen before translating test scores into months of learning
constraints: The translation has major downsides despite its perceived accessibility
target_learners: K-12 students whose achievement is reported in months of learning
target_learning_goals: Accurate communication of student achievement relative to typical learning
examples: The brief provides guidelines for selecting benchmarks to calculate months of learning, aimed at researchers and media
key_sources: Megan Kuhfeld, Melissa Diliberti, Andrew McEachin, Jon Schweig, Louis T. Mariano. (2023). Typical learning for whom? Guidelines for selecting benchmarks to calculate months of learning. Research brief. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/73510/

article_title: Achievement and Growth Norms for Course-Specific MAP Growth Tests
citation: Wei He. (2022). Achievement and Growth Norms for Course-Specific MAP® Growth™ Tests. NWEA Research Report. https://www.nwea.org
title: Update achievement norms periodically with recent data and combine normative information with other evidence for high-stakes decisions
description: The report argues that because the educational ecosystem constantly changes and can exert impacts on student achievements, norms "need to be periodically updated, typically utilizing more recent test event data" so they reflect changes in student achievement in a timely manner. It also cautions that placement or instructional decisions relying solely on normative performance are likely to be less accurate, so normative information should be combined with other evidence about student performance or growth for major decisions.
requirements: A schedule for re-norming using recent test event data (the report describes three-year rolling user norms updated every other fall)
constraints: Placement or instructional decisions that solely rely on the normative performance of students are likely to be less accurate
target_learners: Students in Grades 6–12 taking course-specific assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of achievement and growth scores for placement and instructional decisions
examples: NWEA updated the Algebra 1, Geometry, and Algebra 2 norms using 2019/20–2021/22 test events and plans three-year rolling norms released every other fall
key_sources: Wei He. (2022). Achievement and Growth Norms for Course-Specific MAP® Growth™ Tests. NWEA Research Report. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/achievement-and-growth-norms-for-course-specific-map-growth-tests/

article_title: Measuring student reading comprehension performance: Considerations of accuracy, equity, and engagement by embedding comprehension items within reading passages
citation: Guerreiro, M., & Johnson, J. (2022). Measuring student reading comprehension performance: Considerations of accuracy, equity, and engagement by embedding comprehension items within reading passages. Practical Assessment, Research, and Evaluation, 27.
title: Embed comprehension items throughout reading passages to reduce extraneous measurement barriers
description: This principle holds that reading comprehension assessments should present items throughout a passage rather than only at its conclusion, because end-of-passage formats may inadvertently measure extraneous constructs. The article argues embedding achieves "a more precise measure of reading comprehension by removing barriers for students to demonstrate their understanding."
requirements: Assessment items must remain related to the passage content
constraints: Evidence is limited to reading comprehension assessment contexts
target_learners: K-12 students taking reading comprehension assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of reading comprehension
examples: The study compared embedded-item passages with traditional end-of-passage item placement and found a significant impact on measured achievement.

Measuring student reading comprehension performance: Considerations of accuracy, equity, and engagement by embedding comprehension items within reading passages. article_title: The instructional legacy of COVID-19: Teacher adaptation in response to the pandemic
citation: Connolly, H., Abowd, N., & Chase, C. C. (2022). The instructional legacy of COVID-19: Teacher adaptation in response to the pandemic. Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences – ICLS 2022. https://www.isls.org
title: Treat periods of forced instructional change as opportunities to foster teacher adaptation and transfer of new practices
description: Because the pandemic transition to distance learning led most surveyed teachers to plan transfer of what they learned to in-person teaching, and 30% to plan transformative practices, the article supports treating disruptive change as a lever for professional growth rather than only a disruption to manage. The authors state that "One positive outcome of the pandemic is that it promoted teacher adaptation."
requirements: Teachers must experience a substantial change in teaching conditions that requires adaptation, and their learning during that period should be surfaced and supported
constraints: Evidence comes from a single Spring 2020 survey of 71 K-8 teachers reporting planned, not observed, future practice
target_learners: K-8 teachers
target_learning_goals: Developing adaptive teaching practices that persist beyond the disruptive episode
examples: The study surveyed 71 K-8 teachers during the sudden 2020 shift to distance learning and found most planned to transfer their learning to future in-person teaching
key_sources: Connolly, H., Abowd, N., & Chase, C. C. (2022). The instructional legacy of COVID-19: Teacher adaptation in response to the pandemic. Proceedings of the 16th International Conference of the Learning Sciences – ICLS 2022. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-instructional-legacy-of-covid-19-teacher-adaptation-in-response-to-the-pandemic/

article_title: Achievement and growth norms for English MAP Reading Fluency Foundational Skills
citation: Wei He, NWEA Psychometric Solutions. (2022). Achievement and Growth Norms for English MAP Reading Fluency Foundational Skills. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Combine normative information with other evidence rather than relying on norms alone for placement and major instructional decisions
description: The report cautions that users "should exercise caution about the limited generalizability of the inferences" supported by the 2018-2019 norming data, and that placement or instructional decisions relying solely on normative performance "are likely to be less accurate". It recommends that normative information be combined with other evidence about student performance or growth when making placement or other major instructional decisions.
requirements: Access to additional evidence about student performance or growth beyond the norm-referenced score
constraints: The limitation stems from the norms being based on a single pre-pandemic (2018-2019) administration with limited generalizability
target_learners: Students in Grades K-3 whose scores are interpreted with these norms
target_learning_goals: Accurate placement and instructional decision-making in early reading
examples: The report states NWEA will continue monitoring student achievement as schools recover from pandemic-related learning loss and will update the norms as more appropriate data become available

article_title: Looking beyond vision: Supports for students who are blind or visually impaired in mathematics
citation: Steinbach, S. (2022). Looking beyond vision: Supports for students who are blind or visually impaired in mathematics. NWEA.
title: Provide BVI students with a mixed-representational, multi-sensory approach to mathematical materials
description: The review argues that because there is not a "one size fits all" way of presenting technical information, mathematical materials for BVI students should combine multiple representations and senses — tactile, verbal, tonal, haptic — rather than relying on a single access mode. It cites evidence that combining voiced auditory descriptions with tactile graphics increased braille readers' likelihood of correct answers, and that successful approaches "provide a variety of interfaces for access". Adapted materials act as a bridge from sequential perception to more well-rounded understanding.
requirements: Materials must be adapted for BVI use, since BVI students perceive the world through tactile and acoustic inputs in a sequential way at first
constraints: More research is needed on the effects of a multisensory approach on math task performance and on how to teach BVIs to gather information from multiple sources efficiently
target_learners: Students who are blind or visually impaired in K-12 mathematics
target_learning_goals: Accessing and demonstrating mathematical content knowledge through non-visual and multi-sensory representations
examples: The review cites Ferrell et al. (2017) preliminary results showing braille readers with both voiced auditory descriptions and tactile graphics increased their likelihood of answering items correctly
key_sources: Steinbach, S. (2022). Looking beyond vision: Supports for students who are blind or visually impaired in mathematics. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/looking-beyond-vision-supports-for-students-who-are-blind-or-visually-impaired-in-mathematics/

article_title: Using Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve math accessibility for students with visual impairments
citation: Kang Xue, Elizabeth Barker. (2022). Using Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve math accessibility for students with visual impairments. https://www.nwea.org/resources/using-artificial-intelligence-ai-to-improve-math-accessibility-for-students-with-visual-impairments/
title: Assess item quality for accessible math tests by checking whether items measure achievement equally well for students with and without visual impairments
description: This principle defines item quality for accessible assessments in terms of equitable measurement: a high-quality item is "those that measured achievement for both students with and without VI equally well," while a low-quality item "showed differences between the two groups of students." The article applies this criterion to MAP Growth math items to separate items that work for screen-reader users from those that create barriers, framing accessibility as an equity issue in opportunity to learn math.
requirements: Achievement data from both students with VI taking accessible versions and students without VI taking standard versions
A method for detecting differential measurement between the two groups
constraints: Applied to math assessment items for students with VI who use screen readers; the brief does not claim generalization to other subjects or disability categories
target_learners: students with visual impairments
students without visual impairments
target_learning_goals: equitable measurement of math achievement
identifying assessment barriers for screen-reader users
examples: The study classified MAP Growth math items as high- or low-quality using this equal-measurement criterion across the two student groups

article_title: Changes in school composition during the COVID-19 pandemic: Implications for school-average interim test score use
citation: Jonathan Schweig, Megan Kuhfeld, Andrew McEachin, Melissa Diliberti, Louis Mariano. (2022). Changes in school composition during the COVID-19 pandemic: Implications for school-average interim test score use. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org
title: Exercise caution when comparing school-average interim test scores across pandemic and pre-pandemic periods because school composition may have changed
description: This principle holds that school-aggregate interim test scores used to monitor performance and inform recovery policies should not be taken at face value as indicators of school progress when school composition changes over time. The article motivates it by noting that faulty comparisons arise when "changes in school composition over time" contaminate COVID-19-era aggregate scores. It directs users of school-average scores to consider composition change before interpreting differences as meaningful differences in school performance.
requirements: Users must have access to information about school composition over time to judge whether aggregate-score comparisons are contaminated
constraints: The concern applies to COVID-19-era comparisons with historical and other proximal aggregate scores, per the article's framing
target_learners: K-12 students in schools using interim assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate monitoring of school performance and progress using school-average test scores
examples: The report examines NWEA MAP Growth assessment data used by states and districts during the 2020-2021 school year to investigate this issue
key_sources: Jonathan Schweig, Megan Kuhfeld, Andrew McEachin, Melissa Diliberti, Louis Mariano. (2022). Changes in school composition during the COVID-19 pandemic: Implications for school-average interim test score use. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/changes-in-school-composition-during-the-covid-19-pandemic-implications-for-school-average-interim-test-score-use/

article_title: An investigation of item parameter invariance using focused calibration samples for MAP Growth
citation: Wei He, NWEA Psychometric Solutions. (2021). An Investigation of Item Parameter Invariance Using Focused Calibration Samples for MAP Growth. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Existing MAP Growth item parameter estimates can be reused in new assessments that administer items more closely aligned to student grade level
description: This principle holds that when focused calibration samples produce difficulty estimates comparable to original all-grade estimates, existing item parameters remain appropriate for new grade-aligned test designs. The report concludes that "the existing item parameter estimates are still appropriate if used in the new MAP Growth assessments that intend to administer items more closely aligned to the grade level of the student." Items showing different estimates across samples are routed to further content and psychometric review. The standard calibration procedure's minimum sample size of 1,000 and average of at least 2,000 are cited as likely contributors to the observed invariance.
requirements: Calibration sample sizes should remain large; the report cites the Rasch literature suggesting estimates are similar once sample size reaches 250, and the standard MAP Growth procedure sets a minimum of 1,000
constraints: Items whose estimates differ across calibration samples require further content and psychometric review before reuse
The report notes item parameter estimate accuracy can be affected by various factors beyond sample size, some of which may not be known to practitioners
target_learners: K-12 students taking MAP Growth assessments in math, reading, science, and language usage
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of student achievement on the RIT scale across grade levels
examples: Study 1 recalibrated items using on-grade-only samples; Study 2 used target-grade plus two adjacent grades; both found estimates comparable to the original all-grade calibrations
key_sources: Wei He, NWEA Psychometric Solutions. (2021). An Investigation of Item Parameter Invariance Using Focused Calibration Samples for MAP Growth. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/an-investigation-of-item-parameter-invariance-using-focused-calibration-samples-for-map-growth/

article_title: Proportional relationships decluttered—at last!
citation: James Tanton, Ted Coe, April Ström, Kyle Pearce. (2022). Proportional relationships decluttered—at last! White paper. https://www.nwea.org
title: Six common contexts where proportional relationships arise
description: The paper enumerates the everyday and mathematical settings where, in its words, 'common sense informs us that a proportional relationship is at play': unit conversion and exchange rates, constant rates, percentages, scaled drawings and maps, similar figures in geometry, and ratios. Each context is worked with the same scaling-in-tandem reasoning rather than with cross multiplication.
requirements: Each context must involve two measurable quantities that plausibly scale in tandem
constraints: The paper cautions that constant-rate statements concern changes in quantities, not absolute values: distance from home is not proportional to clock time
target_learners: middle grades and secondary mathematics students
target_learning_goals: recognize proportional structure across varied contexts
examples: The paper works unit conversion (100 inches ↔ 254 cm), a 35-cents-per-dollar tax rate, a 135%-of-a-quantity problem, a 1:500 map scale, judging a friend's face width with fingers, and a 3:5 boy-to-girl class ratio
key_sources: James Tanton, Ted Coe, April Ström, Kyle Pearce. (2022). Proportional relationships decluttered—at last! White paper. https://www.nwea.org

article_title: Proportional relationships decluttered—at last!
citation: James Tanton, Ted Coe, April Ström, Kyle Pearce. (2022). Proportional relationships decluttered—at last! White paper. https://www.nwea.org
title: Teach proportionality by focusing on ways of thinking rather than ways of doing
description: The paper's closing recommendation is that proportionality instruction should begin with the way of thinking of scaling in tandem rather than with standard procedures. It states: 'it makes perfect sense when we begin by focusing on ways of thinking (scaling in tandem), rather than ways of doing,' noting that throughout the article it never needed to 'set up a proportion or cross multiply.'
requirements: Instruction must present covarying measurable quantities and scaling reasoning before or instead of procedural shortcuts
constraints: The paper acknowledges 'There is much more to learn and discuss,' including connections to multiplication and division development and debates about definitions of ratios and rates
target_learners: middle grades and secondary mathematics students
target_learning_goals: develop robust conceptual understanding of proportionality
examples: Throughout the paper every problem, from exchange rates to the cats-and-rats teaser, is solved by scaling quantities directly rather than by cross multiplication

article_title: MAP Growth linking studies: Intended uses, methodology, and recent studies
citation: Ann Hu, NWEA Psychometric Solutions. (2021). MAP Growth Linking Studies: Intended Uses, Methodology, and Recent Studies. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/resource/type/linking-studies/
title: Use fall and winter RIT scores to identify at-risk students early and provide tailored interventions
description: Because linking studies connect RIT scores to state proficiency levels, educators can use students' fall, winter, and early spring RIT scores to predict spring summative performance before the state test is administered. The article states that "educators can identify students who are at risk of not meeting state proficiency standards early in the year and provide tailored educational interventions or place students in the appropriate learning groups based on their entry levels." This supports programs such as Read by Grade 3.
requirements: A current linking study for the state's summative assessment
Fall, winter, or early spring MAP Growth administration
constraints: Partners are encouraged to use the projected performance level in score reports, which reflect district-specific instructional weeks
target_learners: Students in Grades 2–8, including Grade 2 students identified for Read by Grade 3 support
target_learning_goals: Meeting state proficiency standards in ELA and mathematics
examples: Grade 2 ELA linking results help educators identify students behind in reading for Read by Grade 3 programs; special studies derive RIT cuts for grade-retention decisions.
key_sources: Ann Hu, NWEA Psychometric Solutions. (2021). MAP Growth Linking Studies: Intended Uses, Methodology, and Recent Studies. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/resource/type/linking-studies/

article_title: A method for identifying partial test-taking engagement
citation: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld. (2021). A method for identifying partial test-taking engagement. Applied Measurement in Education, 34(2), 150-161. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/a-method-for-identifying-partial-test-taking-engagement/
title: Interpret effort-moderated scores cautiously when test events indicate partial engagement
description: This principle states the article's recommended practice for score interpretation: effort-moderated (E-M) scores estimate what a disengaged test taker would have scored when fully engaged, but retained responses can still "be distorted by disengagement" when engagement is partial. The article directs that when test events indicate partial engagement, such scores should be read as tentative rather than taken at face value. It serves measurement professionals interpreting E-M adjusted results.
requirements: Test events must be available that can indicate the presence of partial engagement, so that the identification method can flag affected scores before interpretation.
constraints: The article states the caution applies when test events indicate the presence of partial engagement; it does not claim E-M scores are generally untrustworthy.
target_learners: K-12 students taking computer-based achievement tests
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of achievement test scores adjusted for test-taking disengagement
examples: The article recommends that when test events indicate the presence of partial engagement, effort-moderated scores should be interpreted cautiously.
key_sources: Steven Wise, Megan Kuhfeld. (2021). A method for identifying partial test-taking engagement. Applied Measurement in Education, 34(2), 150-161. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/a-method-for-identifying-partial-test-taking-engagement/

article_title: Six insights regarding test-taking disengagement
citation: Steven Wise. (2021). Six insights regarding test-taking disengagement. Educational Research and Evaluation, 26(5-6), 328-338. https://www.nwea.org/research/
title: Assessment programs should attend to test-taking disengagement when interpreting scores
description: This principle holds that operators of assessment programs, particularly international assessment programs, should consider disengaged test taking when making and defending inferences from scores. The article's stated purpose is to discuss "six important insights yielded by this research and their implications for assessment programs", grounding the recommendation in evidence that disengagement distorts individual and aggregated scores and therefore the validity of country-level attainment inferences.
requirements: Assessment programs need methods for measuring disengagement to act on it
target_learners: Students in international and large-scale assessment programs
target_learning_goals: Valid interpretation of assessment scores at individual and aggregate levels
examples: The article derives implications for assessment programs from six research insights on disengagement
key_sources: Steven Wise. (2021). Six insights regarding test-taking disengagement. Educational Research and Evaluation, 26(5-6), 328-338. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/six-insights-regarding-test-taking-disengagement/

article_title: Understanding differential growth during school years and summers for students in special education
citation: Angela Johnson, Elizabeth Barker. (2021). Understanding differential growth during school years and summers for students in special education. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org
title: Provide support during school years so students with disabilities can grow as much as or more than peers
description: The brief's research finds that "with support, students with disabilities grow as much or more academically during the school year than their peers without disabilities during some years." This principle holds that adequate school-year support is the condition under which students with disabilities keep pace academically, and that summer loss, not school-year learning capacity, drives widening gaps.
requirements: School-year support for students with disabilities must be in place for growth to match or exceed peers
constraints: The finding applies to grades K-4 and only some school years, per the brief's description
target_learners: Students with disabilities in grades K-4
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement and growth in reading and mathematics
examples: The brief examined academic achievement and growth of students with and without disabilities in grades K-4, comparing school-year and summer growth patterns
key_sources: Angela Johnson, Elizabeth Barker. (2021). Understanding differential growth during school years and summers for students in special education. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/understanding-differential-growth-during-school-years-and-summers-for-students-in-special-education/

article_title: Avoiding bias from sum scores in growth estimates: An examination of IRT-based approaches to scoring longitudinal survey responses
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2020). Avoiding bias from sum scores in growth estimates: An examination of IRT-based approaches to scoring longitudinal survey responses. Psychological Methods. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000367
title: When estimating growth from repeated self-report survey measures, score the items with multidimensional IRT approaches that account for latent variable covariances over time rather than sum scores
description: This principle holds that longitudinal survey growth estimates are less biased when scores come from multidimensional IRT models that account for latent variable covariances over time. The article's simulations and empirical studies show such scores yield "better recovery of growth parameters relative to models using sum scores and other IRT approaches." It applies to researchers scaling psychological and social-emotional constructs across school years.
requirements: A consistent set of self-report survey items administered across multiple school years in a single-cohort repeated measure design
constraints: Advantage demonstrated relative to sum scores and other IRT approaches in the article's simulation and empirical studies; scope is psychological and social-emotional survey constructs
target_learners: elementary and middle school students surveyed on psychological and social-emotional learning constructs
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of student growth on psychological and social-emotional constructs
examples: The authors produced scores in a single-cohort repeated measure design using sum scores and multiple IRT approaches, then compared growth parameter recovery in longitudinal growth models fitted to each set of scores.
key_sources: Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2020). Avoiding bias from sum scores in growth estimates: An examination of IRT-based approaches to scoring longitudinal survey responses. Psychological Methods. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000367

article_title: The learning curve: Revisiting within-year linear growth assumptions
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2021). The learning curve: Revisiting within-year linear growth assumptions. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 14:1, 143-171.
title: Test the linearity of within-year growth assumptions before using growth estimates for policy decisions
description: This principle holds that research and policy uses of achievement growth should first verify the assumption of linear within-year growth, because related research has relied on a "mostly untested assumption: that growth in achievement is linear throughout the entire school year." The article tests this assumption directly with seasonal score data and finds it often unjustified, particularly in reading, so growth estimates for policy should not default to linearity.
requirements: Achievement data collected at multiple within-year time points (fall, winter, spring) to test seasonal growth patterns
constraints: The article reports the assumption is especially problematic in reading
target_learners: Kindergarten through 8th grade students
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of annual learning for policy decisions such as school-year length
examples: The authors examined the assumption using math and reading test scores for over seven million students across three seasonal time points in 2016-17
key_sources: Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2021). The learning curve: Revisiting within-year linear growth assumptions. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 14:1, 143-171. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/35099/

article_title: User guide for interpreting the NWEA state dashboard: Exploring the educational impacts of COVID-19
citation: User guide for interpreting the NWEA state dashboard: Exploring the educational impacts of COVID-19. (2021). NWEA Center for School and Student Progress. https://www.nwea.org
title: Interpret cross-sectional COVID-era achievement differences alongside shifts in the number and composition of students tested
description: The guide advises dashboard users to consider testing-pattern changes when reading term-over-term results. It states that "testing patterns across the country have varied significantly this year within and between schools and observed student attrition is not random," so users must understand shifts in numbers of students tested before interpreting cross-sectional differences in outcomes across terms.
requirements: Access to the dashboard's information on how the number of students tested has potentially changed between terms for the groups and schools of interest
constraints: Cross-sectional samples may include schools that tested in one term but not the other, so samples can differ between terms
target_learners: kindergarten to eighth grade public school students in selected states
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of COVID-era achievement and growth trends in reading and math
examples: The guide quotes the NWEA attrition study finding larger fractions of attriters were minoritized students and students with lower fall 2019 achievement

article_title: Robust IRT scaling: Considerations in constructing item bank from tests across years
citation: Jungnam Kim, Furong Gao, & Dong-In Kim. (2017). Robust IRT Scaling: Considerations in constructing item bank from tests across years. Paper presented at the annual meeting of the National Council on Measurement in Education, San Antonio, TX.
title: When test design changes may introduce multidimensionality, prefer separate calibration with as few equating transformations as possible over concurrent calibration
description: The article recommends considering separate calibration with minimal equating transformations when accumulated tests share overlapping items but blueprint or item-type changes may violate IRT assumptions. It notes that "concurrent calibration is more accurate when the data fit the IRT model" but is "less robust to violations of the IRT assumptions due to multidimensionality," and its results showed the separate-calibration transformations (CH and SM) agreed closely while concurrent calibration diverged. The study operationalized this by transforming multiple tests simultaneously (SM) to minimize equating steps.
requirements: Overlapping common items between tests to anchor transformations
At least 20 common items per test for grouping tests into a simultaneous transformation
constraints: The article's support is one licensure exam context; a single concurrent calibration failed to run for the second block and had to be split into sub-blocks
The authors state a study to investigate why concurrent calibration produced such different results would be necessary
target_learners: examinees of national licensure examinations
target_learning_goals: stable item parameters and comparable scores across years of test administrations
examples: In the study, chain equating added tests one at a time starting from 2014F, choosing at each step the test sharing the highest number of common items with the bank; simultaneous equating equated 19 second-block tests together in a first step and the remaining 15 in a second step
key_sources: Jungnam Kim, Furong Gao, & Dong-In Kim. (2017). Robust IRT Scaling: Considerations in constructing item bank from tests across years. Paper presented at the annual meeting of the National Council on Measurement in Education, San Antonio, TX. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/robust-irt-scaling-considerations-in-constructing-item-bank-from-tests-across-years/

article_title: From through-course summative to adaptive through-year models for large-scale assessment: A literature review
citation: Garron Gianopulos. (2019). From Through-Course Summative to Adaptive Through-Year Models for Large-scale Assessment: A Literature Review. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Match the score aggregation method to a proven model of how students learn the tested material
description: This principle, drawn from Wise's recommendations quoted in the review, holds that methods for combining through-course scores into end-of-year proficiency estimates must rest on validated models of student learning. Wise states that "Methods used for aggregating results from through-course assessments to estimate end of- year proficiency or annual growth should be based on proven models of how students learn the material that is being tested." Otherwise, mid-year results can misestimate end-of-year status and growth.
requirements: Research demonstrating relationships between time of instruction and student mastery of targeted knowledge and skills
constraints: Mid-year results can significantly underestimate or overestimate end-of-year status and growth if the aggregation method is inconsistent with how students actually learn
target_learners: K-12 students assessed through through-year accountability systems
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of end-of-year proficiency and annual growth from interim scores
examples: Wise's End-of-Unit Model uses simple addition when learning is bounded to each period; his Continuous Learning Model uses projection-based weighted averages when learning is continuous
key_sources: Garron Gianopulos. (2019). From Through-Course Summative to Adaptive Through-Year Models for Large-scale Assessment: A Literature Review. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/from-through-course-summative-to-adaptive-through-year-models-for-large-scale-assessment-a-literature-review/

article_title: Arguing about the effectiveness of assessments for the classroom
citation: Garron Gianopulos. (2021). Arguing about the effectiveness of assessments for the classroom. The Journal of Mathematical Behavior, 61. https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/the-journal-of-mathematical-behavior
title: Design and evaluate classroom assessments around the problem, or 'job-to-be-done,' the intended test user needs solved
description: This principle holds that classroom assessment design and evaluation should start from the important problem faced by intended test users, treating score use as part of a potential solution to that problem rather than as an endpoint of validity evidence alone. The article argues that "this lack fails to reflect the ultimate purpose of a test score—to help solve an important problem faced by intended test users" and urges a shift from validity to effectiveness.
requirements: Designers must identify the important problem faced by intended test users and articulate an effectiveness argument linking score use to solving it.
constraints: The article scopes this conceptualization to classroom assessments based on complex constructs, such as learning progressions in math and science.
target_learners: K-12 students assessed through classroom and interim assessments in math and science
target_learning_goals: using interim and classroom assessment scores to support instructional decisions within learning progressions
examples: The article contrasts effectiveness arguments for interim assessments based on a conventional test blueprint versus a test blueprint augmented with learning progressions.

article_title: A longitudinal study of reading growth for students with visual impairments
citation: Boroson, Beth; Barker, Elizabeth; Li, Xueming (Sylvia). (2017). A longitudinal study of reading growth for students with visual impairments. Journal on Technology and Persons with Disabilities, 6, 158–171. https://www.nwea.org
title: Use longitudinal reading-growth data to set expectations for academic growth and inform instructional practices
description: The article argues that tracking students' reading development as they progress through school serves two purposes: it "provides expectations for academic growth and informs instructional practices." Applying this principle means analyzing longitudinal achievement data for a population of interest and using the resulting growth patterns to calibrate expectations and guide instruction, as the authors do for students with visual impairments.
requirements: Requires longitudinal achievement data covering students' progression through school grades
target_learners: Students with visual impairments in grades 3–10
target_learning_goals: Reading achievement and reading growth
examples: The authors analyzed eight years of MAP reading data for 224 students with visual impairments and compared their growth with a nationally normed general-population group

article_title: Spanish MAP Growth Reading technical report
citation: NWEA. (2021). Spanish MAP Growth Reading Technical Report. https://www.nwea.org
title: Transadaptation: adapting English assessment items into culturally and linguistically appropriate Spanish rather than translating them
description: The transadaptation process converts selected English assessment items into Spanish versions that are not translations but adaptations. The report states "The Spanish items are not translations but rather transadaptations of the English items. Original English content was adapted to be culturally and linguistically appropriate in Spanish." Experts consider regionalisms and dialects, cultural differences, grammatical features, and content appropriateness, guided by International Test Commission guidelines, followed by linguistic editing, content editing, and proofreading rounds.
requirements: Subject matter experts and content specialists review candidate items for cultural neutrality or appropriate parallel terms and concepts
Glossaries, style guides, and terminology are compiled for consistency, and items undergo three rounds of review (linguistic editing, content editing, proofreading)
constraints: Some English items are rejected as untranslatable; items with copyright or public domain passages were excluded from transadaptation
target_learners: Spanish-speaking students in United States schools taking Spanish-language reading assessments
target_learning_goals: Parallel measurement of reading skills across English and Spanish language arts constructs
examples: About 1,350 items were transadapted from the English pool, while about 2,250 native Spanish items were developed across Grades K–8 to cover Spanish-only standards such as accents and sound-symbol correspondence
key_sources: NWEA. (2021). Spanish MAP Growth Reading Technical Report. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/spanish-map-growth-reading-technical-report/

article_title: Calibration of Spanish MAP Growth Math tests
citation: Wang, S., & Li, S. (2020). Calibration of Spanish MAP Growth math tests. Portland, OR: NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Calibrate transadapted assessment items in the target language using empirical student responses rather than borrowing source-language item parameters
description: The article argues, on psychometric scaling and validity grounds, that a test's scale and construct can only be made and verified from students' empirical responses, so borrowed English item RITs should be replaced with calibrated Spanish item RITs. Its major finding is that "calibrating Spanish math item parameters using students' empirical responses is a much better approach to constructing the Spanish MAP Growth Math tests according to psychometric scaling and validity theory". The report operationalizes this with fixed-person-score calibration designs and a six-point recommendation list for operational practice.
requirements: Enough student responses collected on the target-language items to calibrate item parameters empirically
constraints: The recommendation rests on the study's evidence of negligible old-new differences for these Spanish math items; the article frames the argument in terms of psychometric scaling and validity theory rather than a measured improvement in student outcomes
target_learners: K-12 students assessed in Spanish
target_learning_goals: Accurate representation of student performance on transadapted assessments
examples: The recommendations list directs NWEA to replace all current English math item parameters in Spanish tests, stop using English parameters in the future, implement routine calibration, review status 12 and 13 items with content experts, keep status 10 items operational, and conduct an annual item parameter drift study
key_sources: Wang, S., & Li, S. (2020). Calibration of Spanish MAP Growth math tests. Portland, OR: NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/calibration-of-spanish-map-growth-math-tests/

article_title: Preparing early learners: Considerations for supporting the kindergarten class of 2021
citation: Beth Tarasawa, Angela Johnson, Christine Yankel. (2021). Preparing early learners: Considerations for supporting the kindergarten class of 2021. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org
title: Prioritize effectively supporting youngest students' learning because early skills are foundational to longer-term outcomes
description: The brief holds that because early academic and nonacademic skills are foundational, educators and leaders must find ways to effectively support young learners' learning, especially given pandemic-related enrollment changes. It states that "finding ways to effectively support our youngest students’ learning is critical for educators and leaders." This principle directs leader attention and resources toward early elementary grades during recovery.
requirements: Educators and leaders need an understanding of pandemic-related changes in kindergarten enrollment and early learning
target_learners: Young learners in preschool and early elementary school, including the kindergarten class of 2021
target_learning_goals: Foundational academic and nonacademic skills predictive of longer-term outcomes
examples: The brief frames its four leader considerations around this priority, noting that understanding enrollment changes and supporting young students' learning is critical
key_sources: Beth Tarasawa, Angela Johnson, Christine Yankel. (2021). Preparing early learners: Considerations for supporting the kindergarten class of 2021. NWEA Research brief. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/preparing-early-learners-considerations-for-supporting-the-kindergarten-class-of-2021/

article_title: Fall 2019 to fall 2020 MAP Growth attrition analysis
citation: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld. (2020). Fall 2019 to fall 2020 MAP Growth attrition analysis. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org
title: Interpret fall 2020 assessment results with considerable caution against prior typical years, checking demographic shifts among tested students
description: The brief recommends that when attrition is systematic, comparisons of post-disruption results to prior years are biased by composition change. It states "considerable caution is warranted when interpreting fall 2020 assessment results, especially in relationship to previous, typical academic years that may include a substantively different group of students." Educational leaders should consider demographic shifts among tested students when planning support and recovery efforts.
requirements: Analysts must compare the demographic composition of students tested in the current period against the prior period before interpreting score trends.
constraints: The recommendation arises specifically from COVID-19-era attrition in MAP Growth data; the brief does not claim it generalizes to all assessment contexts.
target_learners: K-12 students assessed with MAP Growth
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of achievement trends for instructional and recovery decisions
examples: The study compared characteristics of fall 2019 testers who retested in fall 2020 versus those who did not, using data for 5.2 million students.
key_sources: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld. (2020). Fall 2019 to fall 2020 MAP Growth attrition analysis. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/fall-2019-to-fall-2020-map-growth-attrition-analysis/

article_title: A cessation of measurement: Identifying test taker disengagement using response time
citation: Wise, S., & Kuhfeld, M. (2020). A cessation of measurement: Identifying test taker disengagement using response time. In M. Margolis, & R. Feinberg (Eds.), Integrating Timing Considerations to Improve Testing Practices, Routledge. https://www.routledge.com/
title: Decisions to include or exclude rapid guesses during scoring should hinge on the intended purpose of the measurement
description: The chapter recommends that the choice about how to treat rapid guesses in scoring be driven by the test's purpose. As it states, "the choice to include/exclude rapid guesses during scoring hinges primarily on whether measurement is intended to indicate as accurately as possible what the test taker knows and can do or if it represents an achievement hurdle that is considered the test taker's responsibility to clear." When the goal is accurate indication of achievement, disengaged responses should be managed during scoring rather than counted as evidence of low ability.
requirements: A clear decision about whether the test is intended to indicate achievement accurately or to serve as an achievement hurdle the test taker is responsible for clearing
target_learners: test takers on large-scale and interim assessments
target_learning_goals: valid interpretation of achievement scores
examples: The chapter frames scoring decisions for rapid guesses around this purpose distinction rather than prescribing a single uniform rule
