article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology: Educator Guide
citation: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org
title: AI builds learner agency when students have opportunities to set goals and make choices about their learning
description: The guide's agency principle holds that AI should expand, not replace, students' capacities to act: "AI should expand students' capacities to act, think, decide, and connect, not replace them." It states that "AI can build agency among students when students have opportunities to set goals and make choices about their learning," and that AI can increase agency by personalizing content and connecting learning to students' goals, interests, and identities. Teachers are urged to help students identify interests and questions that matter to them.
requirements: Tools should allow students to choose when and how to use the AI, including opting out
Students need opportunities to set goals and make choices about their learning
constraints: When AI tools support personalization, privacy is often a trade-off; discuss with students what information is appropriate to share with an LLM and how their data could be used
target_learners: K-12 classroom students using AI tools
target_learning_goals: Learner agency, purpose, and motivation
examples: The guide recommends building in stop-and-reflect moments about when students should use AI and what decisions they should have the freedom to make, and using AI to weave connections meaningful to students into content to increase relevance.
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology: Educator Guide
citation: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org
title: Design learning so students do the cognitive work themselves when AI tools are in use
description: The guide's metacognition principle states that "AI can support thinking, but it is critical for teachers to design learning so that students do the cognitive work themselves." It warns that when the judgment about the right level of challenge is outsourced to LLMs, student thinking can be undermined, and that research has found some AI tools inhibit productive struggle by reducing cognitive effort. Teachers can foster metacognition by supporting planning, self-monitoring, reflection, and revision.
requirements: Give students space to bring their own thinking and ideas to the table before introducing AI
Build in ample opportunities for human-to-human connection, since relationships, mentorship, and modeling promote productive struggle and metacognition
constraints: Rapid access to large amounts of information may interfere with a learner's ability to notice gaps in their own understanding, an essential process for metacognition and self-regulated learning
target_learners: K-12 classroom students using LLMs
target_learning_goals: Metacognition, productive struggle, and self-regulated learning
examples: The guide suggests stop-and-reflect prompts such as: What thinking are you doing? What thinking is the AI doing? Is AI helping you understand, or helping you avoid thinking?
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology: Educator Guide
citation: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org
title: Use AI accessibility features such as captioning, transcription, and translation to reduce barriers, but not for higher-stakes decisions
description: The guide's accessibility principle says AI's "capacity to support accessibility" is one of its current strengths: "AI can support features such as automatic captioning, transcription, translation, text-to-speech, and more, opening access to materials that were previously out of reach for some students." It also notes AI lets students express ideas across multiple modes, consistent with research that all learners benefit from multiple means of representation and expression. Benefits are not automatic, and the guide sets explicit limits for higher-stakes work.
requirements: Use accessibility features in ways that support access without changing what some students are asked to learn
Follow district policies, especially regarding sensitive and identifiable student information
constraints: The potential to broaden accessibility does not make AI a good fit for higher-stakes work, such as making decisions about accommodations or IEP goals
The theory that people have different learning styles has been debunked; the benefit comes from multiple means of representation, not matching styles
target_learners: Students with diverse access needs, including multilingual learners and students with IEPs
target_learning_goals: Access to content and multiple forms of expression
examples: The guide notes some tools allow learners to move objects around physically as well as write to express their understanding, rather than just using one modality.
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology: Educator Guide
citation: Digital Promise. (2025). Everyone's talking about AI, but what does the research say about how it should be used for learning? https://digitalpromise.org
title: AI erodes critical thinking when outputs are accepted without background knowledge, but sharpens it when outputs are critiqued, compared, or verified
description: The guide's critical-thinking principle is two-sided: "AI can erode critical thinking when students accept AI outputs without background knowledge or the ability to judge the quality of the content." Conversely, "AI can sharpen their thinking skills when they use AI output as an object to critique, compare, or verify." It stresses that critical thinking is taught within meaningful subject matter, not as a generic skill isolated from content, and that AI can generate false but confident outputs.
requirements: Students need sufficient background knowledge and skill to use AI meaningfully and evaluate whether its output is accurate
Teach students basic information about AI before learning with AI, and integrate learning about AI while using AI tools
constraints: Critical thinking should be built into topics of study rather than taught in isolation only when using AI
target_learners: K-12 students using AI in subject-matter coursework
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking and evaluation of AI-generated content
examples: The guide recommends questions that consider multiple perspectives or missing information: What evidence supports this? What might be missing? Whose perspective is absent?

The guide states that "Co-establishing expectations with students, parents, and other caregivers helps to build consistency between the home, school, and classroom environments." description: The panel identifies interaction as pivotal to young children's learning and advises giving children multiple opportunities for group or one-on-one back-and-forth conversations about what they are learning. The guide is direct about the mechanism: "Children learn more from conversing with the teacher than from listening to teachers talk for extended periods." Developmentally appropriate instruction for ages 3-5 uses hands-on activities, short verbal instructions, and no expectation that children sit still more than 10-15 minutes or complete worksheets.

Hands-on instructional activities with short verbal instructions

article_title: Using Research in Ed-Tech: What Does Research-based Product Development Mean?
citation: Digital Promise. (2015). Using Research in Ed Tech: The what, how, and why of research-based product development. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Review learning research broadly and critically before prototyping ed tech products
description: Before building a product, developers should ground design decisions in the learning sciences literature. The guide states: "Before prototyping products, ed tech companies should review research broadly and critically", pointing to tools such as Google Scholar, ERIC and its thesaurus, and Digital Promise's map of education research. It recommends considering research areas including pedagogy/instruction, curriculum studies, psychology, assessment, and cognitive science, and pairing each finding with an application example from companies such as GlassLab Games and BrainPOP.
requirements: Access to scholarly search tools (Google Scholar, ERIC) and to summaries such as review journals and distillation resources like Harvard's Usable Knowledge
constraints: Research findings may not transfer to the product's setting: the guide notes that if research "has only been done in large preschools with teachers, then the findings may not be applicable to your product"
target_learners: ed tech product developers
target_learning_goals: designing products grounded in research on how people learn
examples: GlassLab Games designed Ratio Rancher around research on students' additive-strategy errors with proportions; BrainPOP's Make-a-Map was shaped by research on concept maps and knowledge retrieval
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2015). Using Research in Ed Tech: The what, how, and why of research-based product development. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/f25f7b43-06d9-4732-908b-7409f79b0a91

article_title: Using Research in Ed-Tech: What Does Research-based Product Development Mean?
citation: Digital Promise. (2015). Using Research in Ed Tech: The what, how, and why of research-based product development. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Evaluate research for consensus, responsible use, setting fit, and quality rather than cherry picking supportive findings
description: When reviewing research, developers should apply four considerations the guide names: whether there is agreement or competing theories, whether the research is used responsibly, in what settings it was conducted, and whether the findings are trustworthy. The guide warns: "Avoid selectively “cherry picking” research findings that say what you want to hear", illustrating with a scenario of twenty rigorous studies favoring one strategy versus two mediocre studies favoring another. It also recommends peer-reviewed journals as reliable sources and notes that laboratory-only findings may not generalize to classrooms or homes.
requirements: Access to education review journals and quality-evaluation resources such as the Harvard Family Research Project's ten tips
constraints: Findings from regimented laboratory environments may not hold in real-world environments such as classrooms or home use by parents
target_learners: ed tech product developers
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of learning research for product decisions
examples: The guide's cherry-picking scenario contrasts twenty rigorous trigonometry studies favoring strategy A with two mediocre studies favoring strategy B
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2015). Using Research in Ed Tech: The what, how, and why of research-based product development. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/f25f7b43-06d9-4732-908b-7409f79b0a91

description: The paper identifies five fundamental qualities research has found in effective homework (Carr, 2013): "Purpose: Homework should be meaningful for learning; it should not be 'busy work.'" along with efficiency, ownership, competence, and aesthetic appeal. article_title: Rubrics for Examining Historical Thinking Skills in High School World History Activities and Student Work
citation: Hardy, A., Iwatani, E., Means, B., & Seylar, J. (2023). Rubrics for examining historical thinking skills in high school world history activities and student work. Digital Promise. (Original work published 2021). https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/111
title: Four-level developmental scale from absence to rigorous presence for scoring historical thinking
description: Each rubric dimension uses a common four-level structure: generally 0 indicates the absence of a historical thinking practice in the activity or student work, 1 indicates emergence, 2 indicates presence, and 3 indicates rigorous presence. Level 1 typically captures selecting, listing, or stating; Level 2 brief explanation or analysis; Level 3 extended explanation or analysis. This grain-size makes the rubrics usable to profile opportunities and performance across assignments.
requirements: Scorers judge the complexity rather than length of arguments in student work; in assignments, formative vs. summative purpose, expected evidence, and expected time or length help determine whether a brief or extended response is called for.
constraints: Almost every dimension calls for an extended argument to be scored at the highest level.
target_learners: high school world history students
target_learning_goals: historical thinking skills
examples: A1 Level 3 requires an extended explanation of a claim, reason, or evaluation, such as integrating evidence from multiple sources and addressing counterarguments.
key_sources: Hardy, A., Iwatani, E., Means, B., & Seylar, J. (2023). Rubrics for examining historical thinking skills in high school world history activities and student work. Digital Promise. (Original work published 2021). https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/111

Steps 1 to 3 cover assessing benefits, assessing readiness, and assembling a diverse design team; Steps 4 to 6 cover aligning on rationale and vision, selecting the audience and designing the instrument, and launching; Steps 7 to 9 cover interpreting results, forming actionable steps, and implementing and adjusting actions with feedback loops. Resources including staff time, a secure survey platform, and staff for data cleaning, visualization, and analysis

article_title: Navigating Research Approvals for EdTech Research and Evaluation: A Practical Guide
citation: Younger, J. (2026, September). Navigating research approvals for edtech research and evaluation: A practical guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/318
title: Design the de-identified data architecture before data collection begins
description: Because external evidence goals often emerge after a product ships, the guide urges teams to decide up front whether researchers will ever touch identifiable data. It states that "If there is a realistic possibility that the project will become research, design the data architecture before data collection begins," since de-identifying after analysis is fundamentally different from never granting access. Early architecture decisions preserve the option of an NHSR pathway and avoid costly retrofits.
requirements: Identifiers must be permanently removed or firewalled before researchers can view or analyze data
Role separation between those who link identifiable records and those who analyze research data
constraints: Retrofitting an operational product evaluation into publishable research after collection is described as much harder than designing it appropriately beforehand
target_learners: K-12 students whose platform usage data may support external efficacy evidence
target_learning_goals: Building external evidence and meeting procurement or ESSA evidence-tier standards
examples: The guide contrasts retrospective log analysis with prospective co-designed A/B testing using randomized system-generated IDs and a firewalled analytics interface

article_title: An Initial Logic Model to Guide OpenSciEd Research: Updated Version
citation: McElhaney, K., Baker, A., Chillmon, C., Kasad, Z., Liberman, B., & Roschelle, J. (2022, March). An initial logic model to guide OpenSciEd research: Updated version [White paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/152
title: OpenSciEd's five distinctive instructional principles for student-centered science learning
description: The paper enumerates five distinctive principles reflecting students' intended classroom experience: coherence from the student perspective via storylines motivated by student-generated questions; phenomena-driven learning through iterative cycles of investigating, explaining, modeling, and questioning; evidence-based revision in which "Students seek and use evidence to figure something out as they build and revise their explanations, models, and arguments"; consensus-building routines for scientific argumentation; and embodiment of the Framework's three-dimensional vision. Collectively these principles promote equitable participation by giving students agency and valuing their ideas, experiences, and backgrounds.

constraints: Investigators may emphasize existing principles differently or add additional principles in specific research questions
target_learners: K-12 science students
target_learning_goals: science explanation, modeling, argumentation, and engagement with authentic science practices
examples: Each lesson is motivated by questions students generate to explain a phenomenon or solve a problem; anchoring phenomena are revisited over the course of investigation to test ideas

title: OpenSciEd classroom-level instructional features: facilitator teacher, student questions, navigation routines, practices, problematization, and assessment
description: Figure 2 summarizes six distinctive classroom features: the teacher as facilitator who choreographs learning experiences without prescriptive scripts; instruction driven by student questions supported by driving question boards; lesson-to-lesson enactment with "whole class navigation discussions to maintain coherence from the students' perspective"; practice-based activities engaging science and engineering practices; problematization moments that prompt students to identify gaps in understanding; and assessment opportunities such as consensus models and performance tasks applying concepts to new contexts.
requirements: Materials and teachers must be anticipatory of student questions so activities can respond to them
constraints: Teachers must promote classroom interactions that engage students deeply with the practices; teacher materials identify what needs to be problematized
target_learners: K-12 science students
target_learning_goals: figuring out target science ideas through investigation and collaborative sensemaking
examples: Driving question boards help build a shared mission that a classroom learning community needs to figure out phenomena or solve a design problem

positive youth development

decoding
fluency
comprehension

article_title: FLIGHT (Facilitating Long-term Improvements in Graduation and Higher Education for Tomorrow)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2019). Transition to College intervention report: Facilitating Long-Term Improvements in Graduation and Higher Education for Tomorrow (FLIGHT)/Take Stock in Children (TSIC)®. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: FLIGHT's five-component support model combining scholarships, mentoring, case management, workshops, and student detail reports
description: FLIGHT organizes its services around five components: "The intervention included five components aimed at increasing the likelihood of students applying for, being accepted to, and enrolling in college." These are a pre-paid college scholarship for students who remain in good academic standing, one-on-one mentoring from adult volunteers, intensive case-management services from school staff, academic and college preparation workshops for students and their parents, and a year-end Student Detail Report of grades, attendance, test scores, and intervention status provided to parents, teachers, and guidance counselors. The model extends the TSIC® base with more intensive academic, attendance, and behavioral monitoring and added workshops.
requirements: Trained adult volunteer mentors meeting students a minimum of 15 sessions per year for at least 30 minutes; an assigned student advocate case manager; dedicated school-day space for meetings and workshops.
constraints: Cost information for FLIGHT was not reported in the reviewed study or on the TSIC® website; the WWC could only identify preliminary cost components.
target_learners: eligible low-income middle and high school students in grades 6 through the first three semesters of college
target_learning_goals: college application and enrollment
academic success and graduation on track
examples: Students in grades 7-10 participate in three workshops per year and students in grades 11-12 participate in six workshops per year, each lasting one to four hours; College Access and Success Meetings review progress toward graduation and college enrollment one to four times per year.

article_title: CASEL SEL Framework
citation: Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning (CASEL). (2020). What Is SEL? https://casel.org/fundamentals-of-sel/
title: SAFE: four elements of high-quality SEL instruction
description: SAFE is an acronym for four elements the page says characterize high-quality SEL instruction: "Sequenced – following a coordinated set of training approaches to foster the development of competencies; Active – emphasizing active forms of learning to help students practice and master new skills; Focused – implementing curriculum that intentionally emphasizes the development of SEL competencies; and Explicit – defining and targeting specific skills, attitudes, and knowledge." It functions as a design checklist for SEL curricula.
requirements: Curricula must be sequenced, active, focused, and explicit to count as high-quality SEL instruction
constraints: The page presents SAFE as a program-design feature associated with effective SEL programs, not as a tested manipulation in this source
target_learners: K-12 students in classroom SEL instruction
target_learning_goals: social and emotional competencies
key_sources: Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning (CASEL). (2020). What Is SEL? https://casel.org/fundamentals-of-sel/

article_title: CASEL SEL Framework
citation: Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning (CASEL). (2020). What Is SEL? https://casel.org/fundamentals-of-sel/
title: Weave SEL into all students' educational experiences across classrooms, schools, homes, and communities
description: The page's implementation guidance holds that SEL is most effective when integrated across key settings rather than delivered as isolated lessons. It states, "SEL is most effective when it's woven into all students' educational experiences," and that SEL is "integrated across key settings where students live and learn: classrooms, schools, homes, and communities." This principle guides systemwide SEL implementation.
requirements: Ongoing planning, implementation, evaluation, and continuous improvement by all members of the school community
constraints: SEL efforts both contribute to and depend upon a school climate where all students and adults feel respected, supported, and engaged
target_learners: all students in a school community
target_learning_goals: social and emotional competence developed across the full educational experience
examples: Integrating SEL goals and practices with universal, targeted, and intensive academic and behavioral supports; fostering school culture rooted in students' sense of belonging
key_sources: Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning (CASEL). (2020). What Is SEL? https://casel.org/fundamentals-of-sel/

article_title: National Network of Partnership Schools (NNPS)
citation: Attendance — National Network of Partnership Schools (NNPS). (2001). https://www.nnps.jhucsos.com
title: One-Year Action Plan for Partnerships linking engagement activities to school improvement goals
description: A reusable yearly planning structure in which a school's Action Team for Partnerships writes a One-Year Action Plan that selects and schedules family and community engagement activities across the school year. The activities "must be connected to goals for a welcoming climate and for student success that are included in the School Improvement Plan." The plan focuses on two academic goals, one behavioral goal and one overall goal for a welcoming school climate, and the team evaluates the quality of each activity implemented to continually improve outreach to all families.
requirements: Goals in the Action Plan must be connected to goals already included in the School Improvement Plan.
An Action Team for Partnerships must be assembled to write and carry out the plan.
constraints: The plan covers one school year and is assessed for quality and progress at year's end.
target_learners: All families in the school community, elementary through high school
target_learning_goals: Academic success goals, behavioral goals, and a welcoming school climate
examples: The Ohio NNPS schools used this planning structure to organize partnership activities aimed at improving student engagement, which was associated with increased average daily attendance.

article_title: ParentCorps
citation: ParentCorps program description, New York University Langone Health. (2024). ParentCorps. https://parentcorps.org
title: ParentCorps three-component model: staff professional development, a 14-week parenting program, and a classroom SEL program
description: ParentCorps operates through three coordinated components. First, professional development helps staff "build strong, culturally responsive relationships with families" and reflect on their beliefs about families while learning the science of early childhood development. Second, a group-based 14-week parenting program affirms families' experiences, builds family-to-family connections, and shares evidence-based parenting practices. Third, Friends School is a classroom program developing children's social-emotional skills.
requirements: Delivery through existing pre-K or Head Start staff with ParentCorps training and coaching
target_learners: Pre-kindergarten children
Families of pre-K children
Early childhood educators and school leaders
target_learning_goals: Culturally responsive family relationships
Evidence-based parenting practices
Children's social-emotional skills
examples: Staff training includes reflecting on beliefs about and lived experiences of families; the parenting program runs 14 weeks in groups
key_sources: ParentCorps program description, New York University Langone Health. (2024). ParentCorps. https://parentcorps.org

article_title: Beable One
citation: Beable. (2024). Beable evidence rating: Promising. https://www.beable.com
title: Blended implementation combining independent student practice with teacher-led full-class and small-group instruction
description: The Beable implementation model combines digital independent practice with teacher instruction: it "supports independent student practice with feedback, complemented by teacher-led instruction for both full class and small group settings." Teacher-led and independent learning supplemental materials are aligned with effective instruction, progression of skills, progress monitoring, and measures of success.
requirements: Teachers need orientation or training (onsite or online) and aligned supplemental materials to run the full-class and small-group components

target_learning_goals: reading growth
literacy skill progression with progress monitoring

article_title: SIM: Xtreme Reading — Struggling Readers
citation: Xtreme Reading. (2011). Evidence for ESSA program review. https://www.evidenceforessa.org
title: Successful Xtreme Reading implementation requires leadership support for coaching time and accommodating school schedules
description: The review specifies that implementation depends on leadership that is "willing to support teachers in implementation, provide time for coaching, and willing to create school schedules that accommodate such instruction." This reflects the program's highly structured methods, which need both teacher willingness to follow instructional steps and organizational conditions that protect coaching and scheduling time.
requirements: Teachers willing and able to implement the instructional steps provided by the curriculum
target_learners: Struggling adolescent readers
target_learning_goals: Adolescent reading strategy instruction

article_title: Strategic Instruction Model (SIM)
citation: Strategic Instruction Model (SIM). (2024). University of Kansas Center for Research on Learning. https://sim.ku.edu
title: Content Literacy Continuum: tiered schoolwide literacy structure combining whole-class routines with targeted intensive instruction
description: The Content Literacy Continuum (CLC) organizes schoolwide literacy efforts into tiers: whole class/whole school instruction through CLC routines applied across classes by content and support teachers, and a targeted tier (Xtreme Reading, Learning Strategies Curriculum, Fusion) providing further support and intensive instruction to struggling readers. The review's structure diagram lists "Whole Class/Whole School", "Content Literacy Continuum (CLC)", "Targeted", "Xtreme Reading", "Learning Strategies Curriculum", and "Fusion". Instructional routines and learning strategies are applied across classes, while targeted SIM adds a daily reading period.
requirements: Content and support teachers applying routines and strategies across classes
School schedules accommodating an additional daily reading period for targeted students
target_learners: all students in a secondary school
struggling readers reading two to five years below grade level
target_learning_goals: content-area literacy
reading comprehension
decoding
examples: One of the six qualifying studies evaluated the whole-school CLC while five evaluated targeted SIM forms

article_title: Strategic Instruction Model (SIM)
citation: Strategic Instruction Model (SIM). (2024). University of Kansas Center for Research on Learning. https://sim.ku.edu
title: SIM implementation requires distributed teacher capacity, leadership support, coaching time, and a Literacy Leadership Team over a three-to-five-year adoption
description: The review specifies that successful SIM implementation depends on staffing and organizational conditions: content and support teachers willing and able to implement the routines and strategies, leadership willing to support teachers, provide time for coaching, and create school schedules that accommodate such instruction, plus a Literacy Leadership Team of core content and support teachers and school leadership to guide implementation. Initial adoption takes place over a three-to-five-year period as staff work through planning, implementing, and sustaining phases.
requirements: Leadership must provide time for coaching and create school schedules that accommodate the instruction
A Literacy Leadership Team must be created to guide implementation
constraints: Initial adoption takes place over a three-to five-year period

target_learning_goals: schoolwide adolescent literacy improvement
examples: The review lists staffing requirements including a Literacy Leadership Team created by core content and support teachers and school leadership

article_title: Talent Development High School (TDHS)- Attendance
citation: Talent Development High School. (2005). https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Ninth-grade structure of interdisciplinary learning communities with double-dose courses and freshman seminars
description: This pattern organizes the ninth grade into "small interdisciplinary learning communities within the 9th grade" and pairs it with curricula based on "double dose" English and math courses. Freshman seminars focus on study skills and time management, and the structure is complemented by career academies and cooperative learning, all introduced through professional development.
requirements: Professional development to help schools implement the structure
An additional teacher-level facilitator is required

study skills and time management

article_title: How Individual Plans of Study Can Support Students’ College and Career Readiness and Success
citation: REL Central. (2023). How Individual Plans of Study Can Support Students’ College and Career Readiness and Success. REL Central. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/rel/regions/central/
title: Implement individual learning plans with adult support and regular review
description: This principle holds that personalized education and career plans work best when they are not stand-alone documents: the publication states that benefits are suggested "when IPS are implemented with the support of adults and regularly reviewed". Adults help students develop and use the plans, and periodic review keeps the plan aligned with the student’s evolving interests, skills, and goals throughout secondary school.
requirements: Support of adults during implementation
Plans are regularly reviewed rather than created once and left static
constraints: The publication suggests this practice may support outcomes; it does not report direct evidence of effectiveness
target_learners: middle and high school students
target_learning_goals: college and career readiness
academic engagement
sense of agency
examples: The publication frames IPS as plans that guide and focus students’ efforts throughout middle and high school when supported and reviewed by adults

article_title: Participation in Math Corps Increases College Enrollment
citation: Barbara Harris, Lindsay Fox. (2022). Participation in Math Corps Increases College Enrollment. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/participation-in-math-corps-increases-college-enrollment
title: Pairing intensive math instruction with emotional and social support in a summer program
description: Math Corps pairs an academic component with a relational one: its founders' "primary goal for the camp was to support the emotional and social needs of the students in Detroit," and they used their math-teaching backgrounds to add "high-quality math instruction" to that support. The pattern is an intensive summer camp format in which mentoring and positive influences are delivered alongside substantive instruction in a school subject, rather than as separate programming.
requirements: Staff with subject-matter teaching backgrounds who can deliver high-quality instruction while also attending to students' emotional and social needs.
constraints: The article describes this pattern as implemented in a summer camp for middle school students in a single city; it does not claim the pattern generalizes to other settings or grade levels.
target_learners: middle school students who could benefit from mentoring and positive influences
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
social and emotional development
examples: Math Corps educators leveraged their backgrounds as math teachers to create an intensive summer program providing both emotional and social support and high-quality math instruction.

article_title: Changing the Principal Supervisor Role to Better Support Principals: Evidence from the Principal Supervisor Initiative
citation: Ellen B. Goldring, Melissa A. Clark, Mollie Rubin, Laura K. Rogers, Jason A. Grissom, Brian Gill, Tim Kautz, Moira McCullough, Michael Neel, Alyson Burnett. (2020). Changing the Principal Supervisor Role to Better Support Principals: Evidence from the Principal Supervisor Initiative. Mathematica and Vanderbilt University. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/changing-the-principal-supervisor-role-to-better-support-principals-evidence-from-the-principal-supervisor-initiative
title: Redesign the principal supervisor role from administrative compliance toward developing principals as instructional leaders
description: The PSI demonstrates a design principle for district leadership support: shift the principal supervisor position away from a traditional focus on administration, operations, and compliance toward developing and supporting principals to be effective instructional leaders. Districts that made this shift under the PSI saw principals' perceptions of their supervisors improve, though effects did not extend to teachers' perceptions of principals.

Supervisors redirected toward developing and supporting principals rather than administration, operations, and compliance
constraints: In the PSI evaluation, the redesign did not improve teachers' perceptions of principals' performance

article_title: The Promotion Power Impacts of Louisiana High Schools
citation: Jonah Deutsch, Matthew Johnson, Brian Gill. (2020). The Promotion Power Impacts of Louisiana High Schools. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/the-promotion-power-impacts-of-louisiana-high-schools
title: Five-outcome long-term success framework for school impact measurement
description: The report organizes school effectiveness measurement around five long-term student outcomes: "On-time high school graduation", "Completion of a college or career readiness credential", "College enrollment", "Persistence in college", and "Earnings at age 26". This multi-outcome structure lets a state assess schools' contributions to long-term success rather than short-term test performance alone, and supports comparing school effectiveness across different outcome domains.
requirements: Requires statewide longitudinal data linking students to high school, postsecondary, and workforce records
constraints: Outcome window extends to earnings at age 26, requiring long follow-up periods
target_learners: Public high school students
target_learning_goals: Graduation
College and career readiness
College persistence
Early-career earnings
examples: Louisiana used this framework to become one of the first states to identify its high schools' contributions to students' long-term success separately from other factors.

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Fraction Face-Off!
citation: Fraction Face-Off!. (2021). Evidence for ESSA program description. https://www.evidenceforessa.org/programs/mathematics/fraction-face-off
title: Tutor-introduces-then-cooperative-groups lesson structure with a sports theme
description: Each lesson follows a sequence in which tutors introduce "concepts, skills, problem-solving strategies, and procedures," after which "students work in groups, sharing solutions and helping others." Lessons have a sports theme and "make extensive use of cooperative learning." This structure repeats daily across the 36-day tutoring period.

constraints: Delivered as 35-minute daily small-group sessions

article_title: Developing a Stealth Assessment System Using a Continuous Conjunctive Model
citation: Jiaqi Yu, Wenchao Ma, Jewoong Moon, Andre R. Denham. (2022). Developing a Stealth Assessment System Using a Continuous Conjunctive Model. Journal of Learning Analytics, 9(3), 11–31. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7639
title: Implement evidence-based assessment models at the early stage of educational game development to enable task-specific stealth assessment
description: The article argues that stealth assessment should be built into a game from the start rather than retrofitting analytics onto pre-existing games. It notes it is "hard to track players' mastery of content knowledge due to the lack of task-specific data across the game levels" when using pre-existing games, and that researchers have promoted "implementing evidence-based assessment models at the early stage of game development". The Nomads was designed with task-specific tracking and a CCM so that randomly generated items could yield diagnostic skill profiles.
requirements: Game tasks mapped to skills via a Q-matrix determined by subject experts
An event-based logging system recording each completed item's skills, correctness, timing, and scaffold use
constraints: Building a DGBL application with a learning analytics system from scratch is costly and time-consuming, per the article
target_learners: K-12 students playing educational mathematics games
target_learning_goals: Unobtrusive measurement of skill mastery during gameplay
Diagnostic skill profiles that inform learning support
examples: The study's team designed and developed The Nomads from scratch with nine task types, embedded scaffolds, and log parameters aligned to five attributes before collecting data.

article_title: Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through 8
citation: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Personalize and scaffold problem contexts before problem solving: reword problems into familiar contexts and clarify unfamiliar words in advance
description: The guide recommends that, so students can focus on the mathematics and reasoning, teachers ensure familiarity with a problem's context and language before solving. Concretely, "Teachers can help students by rewording problems, placing them in familiar contexts that better align with students' backgrounds, and clarifying unfamiliar words in advance." It illustrates this by recasting a grocery-shopping fraction problem as a gift-card problem at an electronics store.
requirements: Teachers need advance preparation time to review and reword problems before instruction.
constraints: These strategies are described as especially important for English language learners and students currently struggling with mathematics.
target_learners: Students in grades 4 through 8
English language learners
Students struggling with mathematics
target_learning_goals: Mathematical problem solving in grades 4-8
examples: The guide rewords a Mrs. Sears grocery problem (spent 2/5, then 1/3 of the remainder, $30 left) into a Lee gift-card problem at Gadgets Galore with identical mathematics.
key_sources: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/16

article_title: Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through 8
citation: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Review required mathematics concepts and explicitly teach specialized mathematics vocabulary (including multiple-meaning words) before problem solving
description: The guide advises teachers, when deciding whether to use a problem, to "review with the class the mathematics concepts required to solve it," noting the review is more beneficial the longer it has been since the concepts were addressed and especially for struggling students. It also says it is important "to explicitly teach academic language and review the meaning of specialized mathematics vocabulary, such as divisor or hypotenuse," and to distinguish multiple-meaning words like area, table, root, and volume in mathematical use, which is particularly essential for English language learners.
requirements: Advance problem preparation time to identify the required concepts and specialized vocabulary.
constraints: The benefit of concept review grows with the elapsed time since the underlying concepts were last addressed; explicit vocabulary teaching is described as particularly essential for English language learners.
target_learners: Students in grades 4 through 8
English language learners
Struggling students
target_learning_goals: Readiness to solve mathematical problems requiring known concepts and precise mathematical vocabulary
examples: Reviewing divisor or hypotenuse meanings, and distinguishing mathematical uses of multiple-meaning words such as area, table, root, and volume.
key_sources: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/16

article_title: Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through 8
citation: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Balance routine and non-routine problems in classroom problem solving
description: The guide's final structural recommendation is that "teachers should try to strike a balance between routine and non-routine problems." Routine problems are solvable by familiar step-by-step methods and "can help students strengthen their understanding of an operation or mathematical idea." Non-routine problems lack predictable solution paths and "help students think strategically and apply mathematics in new situations." The pattern pairs the two problem types across instruction.
requirements: A supplementary supply of both routine and non-routine problems, since textbooks may not provide enough of either type.
constraints: What counts as non-routine is relative: what is non-routine for a less experienced problem solver may be routine for more advanced students.
target_learners: Students in grades 4 through 8
target_learning_goals: Strengthening understanding of operations and ideas (routine) and strategic thinking and applying mathematics in new situations (non-routine)
examples: Routine problems may be cognitively demanding and multi-step yet still follow familiar methods; non-routine problems require grappling with new skills and concepts not yet mastered.
key_sources: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/16

article_title: Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through 8
citation: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Make problem solving an active part of classroom instruction and source supplementary problems beyond the textbook
description: The guide's overarching recommendation is that "Problem solving should not be reserved solely for homework and individual practice assignments. It should be an active part of mathematics teachers' classroom instruction." To do this, teachers must allocate preparation time for thoughtful problem selection and "will likely need to explore a variety of supplementary materials to find relevant and appropriate problems to extend the examples provided in their mathematics textbooks."
requirements: Teachers must allocate time during advance preparation to select problems thoughtfully and explore supplementary problem sources.
constraints: The textbook alone is treated as insufficient; problems must be extended with supplementary materials.
target_learners: Students in grades 4 through 8
target_learning_goals: Strengthening skills and deepening understanding of math concepts through meaningful real-world problems
examples: The guide frames meaningful real-world problems as more likely to strengthen skills and deepen conceptual understanding when embedded in daily instruction.
key_sources: Preparing Problems for Classroom Instruction. (2012). Improving Mathematical Problem Solving in Grades 4 Through Overview, U.S. Department of Education funded practice-guide presentation. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/16

citation: Bailey, T., Bashford, J., Boatman, A., Squires, J., Weiss, M., Doyle, W., Valentine, J. C., LaSota, R., Polanin, J. R., Spinney, E., Wilson, W., Yeide, M., & Young, S. H. (2016). Secure faculty and staff buy-in by sharing error-rate research on single-test placement

persistence

title: Offer students performance-based monetary incentives
description: One of the guide's six recommendations is that institutions offer students performance-based monetary incentives, one of the structural interventions the panel identified. The guide includes budgeting guidance and implementation advice for this practice as part of creating conditions that give underprepared students the best chance of realizing their educational goals. citation: Pattenhouse, M.*, Noakes, S.*, Mills, K., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025, November). Framework for Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/275
title: Learner-centered design: promote agency, foster metacognition, and enable accessibility
description: The framework's Learner-Centered principle holds that emerging technology tools "can realize learner variability, helping all students reach their full potential, when they promote agency, foster metacognition and when developers enable accessibility." Practices include personalizing for learners, making learning relevant, grounding in purpose, enabling productive struggle, providing reflection opportunities, assistive technologies, multimodality, and translanguaging, each with safety spotlights on privacy, explainability, and fairness.

constraints: Safety spotlights note privacy, explainability, and fairness must be addressed within each practice

target_learning_goals: Learner agency, metacognition, and equitable access to learning
examples: Strategies include allowing users to opt out of adaptive AI features and aligning content with learners' funds of knowledge

title: Evidence-based design: apply research, use meaningful measures, and leverage relevant expertise
description: The Evidence-Based principle states that "the starting point for developing emerging technology-enabled tools is to apply research and use meaningful measures of learning." Developers should leverage relevant expertise — researchers, subject matter experts, educators, and learners through co-design — throughout development, define learning outcomes measured with validated instruments, and plan iterative product improvements aligned to ESSA's Tiers of Evidence.

title: School-within-a-school career academy structure with sustained student-teacher clusters
description: This pattern organizes a small learning community inside a larger high school. "A small learning community is formed within the larger high school by clustering three to five teachers and 50–75 students per grade." Teachers are drawn from academic and career-related disciplines and remain with students from year to year, with one lead teacher administering the academy and liaising with administrators and employer partners. Students take two to four academy courses a year, with block-scheduled academy classes in the morning followed by regular classes in the afternoon.
