title: Set clear classroom guardrails and restrict high-risk AI applications such as automated grading
description: The brief recommends districts establish comprehensive governance frameworks defining appropriate AI use boundaries through co-designed policies involving educators, learners, and families. It specifies that "high-risk applications including those affecting student assessment, disciplinary decisions, or personal data should not rely solely on AI systems." Policies should be context-driven and flexible across differently resourced districts while maintaining strong safety standards.
requirements: Co-designed responsible use policies defining when AI tools are helpful and where human judgment is essential
Professional learning and safeguards embedded into procurement and adoption processes from the start
constraints: District capacity varies dramatically, from thousands of staff with dedicated tech teams to just a handful of employees
Studies highlight the importance of training teachers to adapt AI use to promote critical thinking and avoid learner overreliance on automated outputs
target_learners: PK16 students, including learners with disabilities and multilingual learners
target_learning_goals: Responsible, equitable, and critical use of AI-enabled classroom technologies
examples: The brief's Appendix 2 catalogs risks including biased facial recognition in test proctoring, AI-generated false content, and educator overdependence on algorithmic recommendations, and recommends a govern-map-measure-manage lifecycle approach

citation: Ruiz, P., Peters Hinton, V., Prado, Y., Noakes, S., Liberman, B., Chillmon, C., Van Nostrand, P., Shell, A., Karim, S., Dallas, D., & Zachariah, I. (2025). Integrating AI-enabled edtech in PK16 education: Five recommendations for state and district leaders. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/273
title: Five EdTech Quality Indicators: Safe, Evidence-Based, Inclusive, Usable, and Interoperable
description: The brief presents the Five Edtech Quality Indicators—developed by 1EdTech, CAST, CoSN, Digital Promise, InnovateEDU, ISTE+ASCD, and SETDA—as core criteria for building AI-enabled edtech evaluation and accountability systems. Each indicator names a requirement: AI-enabled edtech must protect data and be "Safe," grounded in ESSA evidence tiers, "Inclusive" in prioritizing accessibility and equitable design, "Usable" by educators and students, and "Interoperable" through established interoperability standards for secure data exchange. Districts are encouraged to use these frameworks rather than start from scratch.
requirements: Vendors must demonstrate robust data privacy and security, evidence-based design aligned with the ESSA Tiers of Evidence, accessibility, ease of use, and adherence to interoperability standards
constraints: The brief notes many third-party validations still require research on product quality
target_learners: PK16 students and educators affected by district edtech procurement
target_learning_goals: High-quality, responsible evaluation and design of AI-enabled edtech
examples: SETDA's 2025 guide integrates the five indicators into state procurement processes with adaptable model questions

description: Appendix 1 of the brief outlines a four-phase adoption cycle for AI-enabled edtech: vision and planning, implementation, ongoing evaluation, and scaling and sustaining, each with key challenges and recommendations. It states that "Planning for AI-enabled edtech requires districts to move beyond reactive purchasing decisions and establish strategic frameworks that align technology with clear learning objectives and pedagogical goals." AI-enabled tools require specialized evaluation criteria including algorithmic transparency, bias mitigation, and data privacy.

Comprehensive support systems including professional learning, clear usage guidelines, and usage tracking

article_title: Researching Digital Learning Platforms: Foundations, Methods, and Policy Recommendations
citation: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257
title: DLP-as-research-infrastructure: platforms as dynamic environments that shape, capture, and reflect learning
description: The paper's central organizing framework is that digital learning platforms are more than delivery mechanisms: they are evolving into research infrastructure. Whereas most edtech research treats platforms as external interventions, the authors argue platforms provide interaction data—clickstreams, hint requests, response sequences—that can support theory-connected inquiry. As they put it, DLPs are 'evolving into research infrastructures capable of supporting systematic inquiry into learning, design, and fairness at scale.'
requirements: Platforms must provide detailed interaction data such as clickstreams, time-on-task, hint requests, and response sequences, and must permit researcher access and transparency
constraints: Most commercial or institutionally adopted platforms offer limited or inconsistent access to backend data, which restricts reproducibility and secondary analysis
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students using digital learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Understanding learning processes, instructional design effectiveness, and fairness in digital learning environments
examples: ASSISTments, Google Classroom, Khan Academy, MATHia, Moodle, and other platforms are described as providing structured environments plus detailed interaction data used to study engagement, scaffolds, and adaptive feedback
key_sources: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257

article_title: Researching Digital Learning Platforms: Foundations, Methods, and Policy Recommendations
citation: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257
title: Embedded experimental designs: randomized experiments and structured comparisons run inside DLPs during authentic learning
description: This pattern describes embedding interventions directly within platform infrastructure—modifying problem formats, feedback types, or visual scaffolds—and observing effects during authentic learning activities. The paper highlights several variants: RCTs, A/B testing (e.g., E-TRIALS in ASSISTments), factorial designs (Terracotta), and adaptive learning interventions. As the authors state, 'One important affordance of some DLPs is the ability to conduct randomized experiments or structured comparisons at scale.'
requirements: Platform infrastructure must allow content modification or experimental embedding; researchers must assess the platform's flexibility in advance, and fidelity monitoring tools such as teacher dashboards and backend logs are essential
constraints: Not all DLPs permit experimental embedding (e.g., Khan Academy provides limited backend access); IRB and district approvals, implementation fidelity, generalizability across platforms and domains, and logistical coordination with school calendars are stated challenges
target_learners: Middle school, medical, and online learners using DLPs in authentic settings
target_learning_goals: Causal evaluation of instructional design features such as feedback timing, worked examples, and adaptive item selection
examples: The paper cites ASSISTments RCTs (Feng et al., 2023; Smith et al., 2022), a Kahoot! RCT in medical education, ASSISTments E-TRIALS A/B testing, and Terracotta factorial designs
key_sources: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257

article_title: Researching Digital Learning Platforms: Foundations, Methods, and Policy Recommendations
citation: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257
title: Self-Regulated Learning theory as a lens for DLP trace data
description: The paper presents SRL theory as one of three frameworks connected to DLP data. SRL concerns how students actively plan, monitor, and evaluate their learning, and DLPs allow detailed tracking of these behaviors through time-on-task data, hint usage, and problem-solving attempt sequences. The authors note studies citing ASSISTments log data on planning prompts and self-assessment, showing 'SRL scaffolds support not only learning outcomes but also offer researchers a window into students' metacognitive decision-making in real time.'
requirements: DLP environments must log behaviors traceable to SRL phases, such as time-on-task, hint requests, and sequence of problem-solving attempts
constraints: The authors state the examples are illustrative, 'not to validate any of these frameworks as dominant in the field,' and more often theories are applied post hoc rather than built into platform design
target_learners: K-12 and higher education learners using digital platforms
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning behaviors: planning, monitoring, help-seeking, and reflection
examples: The paper cites ASSISTments studies of planning prompts, reflective questions, and self-assessment mechanisms (Inventado et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020)
key_sources: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257

article_title: Researching Digital Learning Platforms: Foundations, Methods, and Policy Recommendations
citation: Wei, X., Roschelle, J., Pautz Stephenson, S. & Wortman, A. (2025). Researching digital learning platforms: Foundations, methods, and policy recommendations. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/257
title: Community of Inquiry framework: three presences for interpreting DLP discourse and feedback data
description: The paper presents the CoI framework as a lens for DLPs that include discussion forums, peer collaboration tools, or reflection prompts. It 'posits that effective online learning environments emerge from the interaction of three core presences: cognitive presence, social presence, and teaching presence.' The authors highlight Li et al. (2022), who used sentiment analysis of Coursera reviews grounded in CoI theory to distinguish knowledge-seeking from skill-seeking MOOCs, illustrating how CoI helps interpret instructional presence beyond log data alone.
requirements: DLPs must include learner discourse or feedback channels—discussion forums, peer collaboration tools, or embedded reflection prompts—for CoI constructs to be applied
constraints: Traditionally applied to higher education and asynchronous online learning; factors like collaborative meaning-making and instructor presence are 'not always visible through log data alone'
target_learners: MOOC learners and online higher education students
target_learning_goals: Understanding cognitive engagement, social presence, and instructional presence in online learning
examples: Li et al. (2022) analyzed thousands of Coursera learner reviews, distinguishing knowledge-seeking courses (content-driven) from skill-seeking courses (instructor-interaction-driven)

title: SEERNet initiative
description: SEERNet is a network funded by the Institute of Education Sciences to support research using data from digital learning platforms. According to the paper, it 'has fostered a shared vision for responsible, inclusive, and theory-driven research by convening and supporting the research community.' SEERNet DLPs, researchers, and partners work on shared data infrastructure, standardized data governance, de-identified well-documented datasets, and research-practice partnership models piloted by SEERNet grantees.
requirements: Continued collective effort across researchers, educators, and platform partners; investment in shared data infrastructure and open analytics tools, especially for publicly funded platforms
constraints: The paper notes most commercial platforms offer limited or inconsistent backend data access, which fragments reproducibility and secondary analysis
target_learners: Students using SEERNet digital learning platforms (e.g., ASSISTments, MATHia)
target_learning_goals: Enabling rigorous, ethical, theory-driven research on learning within platforms
examples: SEERNet grantees and collaborators piloted research-practice partnership models shaped by real classroom needs (Digital Promise, n.d.)

title: Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators (CIRCLS/Digital Promise, 2024)
description: A bilingual reference glossary published on circls.org and shared on informalscience.org, written so that "educators to reference when learning about and using artificial intelligence (AI)". It opens with a definition of AI and then defines AI-related terms in alphabetical order, pairing each English entry with a Spanish translation. It was last updated March 31, 2024, and is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International.
requirements: Intended as a reference for educators who are learning about and using AI; entries are alphabetical, starting from a base definition of AI.
constraints: The authors note it was last updated on March 31, 2024, so definitions reflect the field as of that date.
target_learners: Educators
target_learning_goals: Understanding artificial intelligence terminology for educational practice
examples: Entries include Artificial Intelligence, Algorithm, ChatGPT, Computer Vision, Critical AI, Training Data, Foundation Models, Human-Centered Perspective, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, Adaptive Learning, Interpretable and Explainable Machine Learning, Machine Learning, Neural Networks, Robots, and UX/UI design.

citation: Ruiz, P. & Fusco, J. (2024). Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators. Educator CIRCLS Blog. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: AI built two primary ways: human-given rules versus machine learning
description: The glossary presents AI as "a branch of computer science" in which systems use hardware, algorithms, and data to create "intelligence" to do things like make decisions, discover patterns, and perform actions. It organizes the field by two primary build approaches: rule-based systems where human programmers give the rules, and machine learning algorithms that discover their own rules. This distinction anchors the rest of the glossary, including neural networks, LLMs, and generative AI.
requirements: Understanding the rule-based versus machine-learning distinction is needed to follow related entries such as algorithm, black boxes, and training data.
target_learners: Educators
target_learning_goals: Understanding how AI systems are built and how machine learning differs from rule-based systems
examples: The algorithm entry explains that machine learning algorithms "can discover their own rules ... or be rule-based where human programmers give the rules."

citation: Ruiz, P. & Fusco, J. (2024). Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators. Educator CIRCLS Blog. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Prefer interpretable machine learning over post-hoc explainable machine learning in educational AI
description: The glossary defines interpretable machine learning as the creation of models that are inherently interpretable because "they provide their own explanations for their decisions". It recommends this approach over explainable ML, arguing we should understand what is happening from the beginning in our systems rather than try to explain black boxes after the fact, and notes we cannot know for certain whether an XAI explanation is correct.
requirements: Educators and developers evaluating AI tools should check whether interpretability is built into the model rather than added as an after-the-fact explanation.
constraints: The glossary notes that with XML/XAI "we cannot know for certain whether the explanation we are getting is correct", and presents interpretable models as the researchers' recommended alternative.
target_learners: Educators
Developers of AI-mediated learning tools
target_learning_goals: Evaluating the transparency and trustworthiness of AI systems used in education
examples: The glossary's interpretable machine learning and black boxes entries contrast IML with XAI, describing two primary ways to pull back the curtain on AI black boxes.

citation: Ruiz, P. & Fusco, J. (2024). Glossary of Artificial Intelligence Terms for Educators. Educator CIRCLS Blog. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Adopt a human-centered perspective: AI should augment, not replace, teachers
description: The glossary's human-centered perspective entry frames AI as working with humans and "helping to augment human skills". It states that people should always play a leading role in education and that AI systems should not replace teachers. The related intelligence augmentation entry adds that there is a fine line between augmenting and replacing, so technologies should let humans choose what a system does and when.
requirements: AI in education should be designed so humans retain the leading role and can choose what the system does and when it does it.
target_learners: Educators
target_learning_goals: Making decisions about the role of AI in teaching and learning
examples: The intelligence augmentation entry suggests a teacher might automate redundant classroom tasks to do more of the things only a human can do.

title: Intelligent Tutoring Systems with adaptive learning
description: The glossary defines an Intelligent Tutoring System as "a computer system or digital learning environment that gives instant and custom feedback to students". An ITS may use rule-based AI or machine learning under the hood, and can support adaptive learning, in which material difficulty, pacing, sequence, and type of help are adjusted based on the learner's prior responses.
requirements: An ITS relies on underlying algorithms and code (the 'under the hood' layer), which may be rule-based AI or machine learning.
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students using digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: Receiving instant, customized feedback and adaptive pacing in digital learning
examples: The adaptive learning entry explains that difficulty of material, pacing, sequence, type of help given, or other features can be adapted based on the learner's prior responses.

citation: Kyle Dunbar, Katie Wilczak, Kelly Mills, Nick Mireles, and Alison Shell. (2025). Portraits in Progress: Emerging Future-Ready Skills Assessment Strategies. Digital Promise and Pearson. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Three-component framework for Portrait of a Graduate assessment systems
description: The report defines assessment as the process of gathering, analyzing, and interpreting evidence of student learning, and organizes district activity into three components: collecting evidence, evaluating and analyzing that evidence, and reporting and communicating student growth. District methods are mapped onto this framework in Figure 1 and Table 1, spanning performance tasks, tech-enabled scenarios, defenses of learning, rubrics, self-reflection, report cards, microcredentials, and dashboards.
requirements: Assessment systems must gather, analyze, and interpret evidence in relation to meaningful learning goals
constraints: The framework is drawn from a landscape scan of districts at different stages of Portrait of a Graduate implementation, not from a validated measurement study
target_learners: K-12 students in districts with Portrait of a Graduate frameworks
target_learning_goals: future-ready skills such as critical thinking, communication, collaboration, and creativity
examples: District strategies organized by assessment component observed in the landscape scan, per Figure 1 and Table 1

title: Defense of learning as a Portrait of a Graduate assessment
description: A defense of learning is a presentation in which students use selected artifacts to demonstrate and defend readiness for a next step such as promotion or graduation, scored by a trained panel using a rubric. In Shelby County Public Schools, students defend their learning in 5th, 8th, and 12th grades, and the defense serves as a graduation requirement for seniors. The report describes it as powerful for students, teachers, caregivers, and community members, and notes Shelby holds calibration sessions to increase score reliability.
requirements: Trained panels, rubrics, and calibration sessions to achieve score reliability
constraints: Like performance tasks, defenses of learning face challenges achieving score reliability
target_learners: students in grades 5, 8, and 12 presenting defenses of learning
target_learning_goals: Portrait of a Graduate skills, competencies, and dispositions
examples: Shelby County Public Schools students collect artifacts across time and explain how the collection demonstrates they have met a specific level of competency on each Portrait skill

title: Curriculum-embedded classroom activities and assessments with frequent scoring (Ephrata)
description: Teacher-designed activities embedded in the curriculum can serve as assessments of Portrait of a Graduate skills. In Ephrata Area School District, teachers develop or select six assignments per marking period that elicit evidence of skills and dispositions, rate work as recognizing, understanding, or applying the skill, and enter scores in the student information system. The report states this provides a breadth of data across settings and tasks over time, though assignment variability makes it hard to claim each scored assignment is individually valid.
requirements: Ongoing, teacher-centered professional development and district-developed rubrics
constraints: Variability in the types and quality of assignments teachers use may undermine claims that each scored assignment is individually a valid assessment
target_learners: high school students in Ephrata Area School District
target_learning_goals: Portrait of a Graduate skills and dispositions
examples: Ephrata's system is part of a larger assessment system including cornerstone projects and a Life Ready Graduate Certificate

title: Locally developed, grade-banded rubrics as the shared evaluation method across districts
description: Of the seven districts with assessments in place, all used locally developed, grade-banded rubrics to evaluate student evidence of Portrait of a Graduate skills. Rubrics identify outcomes and evidence representing specific performance levels, are typically developed at district level with educator input, and are accompanied by calibration sessions in which educators collectively score student work samples. Their strength is representing each district's unique context and goals; their challenge is potential wide variability in teachers' scores.
requirements: Calibration sessions where educators review and collectively score student work samples and unpack interpretations of rubric score levels
constraints: Locally-designed rubrics differ across districts, which limits comparability of scores across districts
target_learners: K-12 students assessed with district Portrait of a Graduate rubrics
target_learning_goals: future-ready skills and competencies defined in local Portrait frameworks
examples: Norwalk Public Schools teachers co-designed a critical thinking rubric using the district's learning progression

title: Badging with physical Badge Books and 'I can' statements (South Glens Falls)
description: Badging is a reporting method in which badges—visuals representing specific skills—are awarded when students demonstrate proficiency, physically or digitally. In South Glens Falls, students earn badges in a physical Badge Book of stickers that includes "I can…" statements for each skill, awarded by teachers, principals, and district leaders using district-level criteria. The report notes badges generate student excitement but, without valid measures, may not be awarded consistently and comparably.
requirements: Valid measures and strong systems, plus a process by which students receive an explanation of why they did or did not earn a badge
constraints: Best used as part of a wider system of assessment with careful thought to collecting and evaluating student evidence
target_learners: K-12 students in districts using badging
target_learning_goals: Portrait of a Graduate skills
examples: Three districts interviewed are experimenting with badging as a means of communicating student achievement

title: District-level dashboards aggregating Portrait of a Graduate skill data
description: Dashboards are web-based platforms presenting aggregated and disaggregated data on student Portrait of a Graduate ability, used by two interviewed districts and explored by four more. Shelby County's dashboard aggregates defense of learning data by grade level, school, and demographic, informing professional learning decisions, and is publicly accessible to caregivers and community members. Challenges include the technical skills and resources required, data syncing maintenance, and protecting student privacy.

constraints: Student data and privacy must be maintained while providing transparency of data

citation: Can Student Surveys About Social-Emotional Development and School Climate Reveal Which High Schools Best Support Social-Emotional Development? (2019). Education Next. https://www.educationnext.org
title: Two-domain structure of school social-emotional value-added: social well-being and work habits
description: The article's value-added analysis organizes school effects on social-emotional development into two distinct domains. It reports that "School effects cluster in two domains, social well-being and work habits, and some schools are better at one than the other." This taxonomy means a school can excel at supporting one dimension while lagging on the other, so a single summary rating would obscure meaningful differences among schools. The domains are measured through students' own survey assessments of their development and school climate.
requirements: Annual detailed student survey data about social-emotional development and school climate administered to students in the school system
constraints: Effects are identified for ninth-grade students in Chicago Public Schools high schools via value-added analysis
target_learners: ninth-grade high school students
target_learning_goals: social-emotional development, including social well-being and work habits
examples: The study identifies individual high schools' impacts on ninth-grade students' social-emotional development and test scores through value-added analysis of annual survey results

article_title: Linking Social-Emotional Learning to Long-Term Success
citation: Can Student Surveys About Social-Emotional Development and School Climate Reveal Which High Schools Best Support Social-Emotional Development? (2019). Education Next. https://www.educationnext.org
title: Use social-emotional survey measures alongside traditional indicators like test scores for a more complete picture of school performance
description: The article recommends combining student survey measures of social-emotional development with traditional academic indicators when evaluating how schools prepare students. It states that "these surveys can be used alongside traditional indicators like test scores to provide a more complete picture of how schools prepare students for the future." Because social-emotional value-added is nearly as predictive of schools' test-score impacts as test-score value-added itself, the two kinds of measures capture complementary information about school quality.
requirements: A detailed annual survey about social-emotional development and school climate administered to students, plus value-added analysis to identify school effects
constraints: The authors describe the analysis as an important early step toward understanding how schools influence social-emotional development and how it can be useful for policy
target_learners: ninth-grade high school students
target_learning_goals: social-emotional development and academic preparation for future outcomes
examples: Chicago Public Schools administered a detailed annual survey about social-emotional development and school climate, and the authors used value-added analysis to identify schools' impacts on social-emotional development and test scores

article_title: Supporting School Improvement
citation: Hart, H., Young, C., Chen, A., Zou, A., & Allensworth, E.M. (2020). Supporting school improvement: Early findings from reexamination of the 5Essentials survey. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://www.5-essentials.org/
title: Five Essential Supports framework: five organizational essentials that influence students' learning
description: The framework identifies five key elements of school organization that influence students' learning: Effective Leaders, Collaborative Teachers, Involved Families, Supportive Environment, and Ambitious Instruction. The report states the framework "identified five key elements, or “essential supports,” of a school that influenced its students' learning". Each essential is defined behaviorally: Effective Leaders are "the driver for change"; a Supportive Environment is "safe, nurturing, stimulating, and focused on learning for all students"; Ambitious Instruction "challenges students through well-organized curricula". The 5Essentials Survey operationalizes the framework, and this study revalidates it in elementary and high schools.
requirements: Strength in multiple essentials: in the original validation, schools strong in at least three of the five supports were 10 times more likely to improve reading and math gains than schools weak in three to five supports
constraints: The authors note the framework encompasses more than school climate and prefer to describe schools strong in the essentials as having strong organizations rather than strong climates
target_learners: K-12 students in Chicago Public Schools (elementary and high schools)
target_learning_goals: Student achievement growth (reading and math)
Attendance
GPA
Freshman OnTrack and college enrollment
examples: The framework was crafted with input from the superintendent, principals, teachers, university professors, community activists, and parents during Chicago's 1990s districtwide reform, then studied with qualitative, survey, and administrative data from 1991–2005

citation: Hart, H., Young, C., Chen, A., Zou, A., & Allensworth, E.M. (2020). Supporting school improvement: Early findings from reexamination of the 5Essentials survey. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://www.5-essentials.org/
title: 5Essentials Survey: 22 Rasch-scored measures of school organization for teachers and students
description: The 5Essentials Survey captures the strength of each essential support through items completed by teachers and students; underlying concepts such as Instructional Leadership or Student-Teacher Trust are captured with groups of items called measures. Each survey includes 20 measures, with 22 unique measures across levels. Measures were recalibrated with Rasch analysis on 2014–19 data, and respondent Rasch scores were weighted by precision to compute school-level mean scores. The survey has been administered in more than 6,000 schools and since 2014 counts for 5–10 percent of a CPS school's quality rating.
requirements: Measures must maintain acceptable Rasch reliability and explain sufficient variance at the school level to differentiate schools
constraints: Because school ratings are consequential, the report notes there could be pressure for schools to appear strong, and exaggerated responses would compromise the survey's ability to accurately assess performance
Fourth- and fifth-grade students fully participated for the first time in 2020 and were not included in the analyses

CPS teachers in grades pre-k–12
target_learning_goals: Measuring school organizational strength to guide improvement in student outcomes
examples: In 2014 the survey became part of CPS accountability policy, comprising 5–10 percent of a school's quality rating; results reports have been publicly available since 2013

title: Schools working to improve on 5Essentials measures can expect outcome gains even before reaching strength
description: Because both starting the year strong on 5Essentials measures and improving on measures during the year predicted better student outcomes, schools below the strength threshold still benefit from growth. The report states: "schools that are working to improve in areas, such as Student-Teacher Trust or Teacher Influence, but have not yet reached a point of strength, can still see improvements in their students' outcomes such as GPAs, tests, and attendance." This makes measure growth a usable improvement signal for schools not yet strong on an essential support.

Analyses controlling for prior student achievement to attribute improvement beyond expected growth

article_title: High School GPAs and ACT Scores as Predictors of College Completion
citation: Allensworth, E. (2020). High school GPAs and ACT scores as predictors of college graduation. Educational Researcher, 49(3), 198-211. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Students' efforts to improve HSGPAs have considerable potential leverage for college readiness, unlike efforts to improve ACT scores
description: The article recommends that because HSGPAs relate strongly and consistently to college graduation while ACT signal largely reflects school factors, "students’ efforts to improve their HSGPAs would seem to have considerable potential leverage for improving college readiness." It contrasts this with little evidence that improving ACT scores raises college success.

constraints: The article states there is "little evidence that students will have more college success if they work to improve their ACT score"

target_learning_goals: College readiness and college graduation
examples: The study compared graduation rates of students with the same HSGPA or ACT score across high schools

article_title: High School GPAs and ACT Scores as Predictors of College Completion
citation: Allensworth, E. (2020). High school GPAs and ACT scores as predictors of college graduation. Educational Researcher, 49(3), 198-211. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: HSGPA breadth theory: GPAs' multi-criteria composition makes them strong college-readiness indicators
description: The article proposes an explanatory account of why HSGPAs predict college success despite perceived inconsistency across schools. HSGPAs aggregate "effort over an entire semester in many different types of classes, demonstration of skills through multiple formats, and different teacher expectations." The authors argue this variety "might help to make HSGPAs strong indicators of readiness because they measure a very wide variety of the skills and behaviors that are needed for success in college," where students face widely varying content and expectations.
requirements: HSGPAs must draw on many criteria across different class types and formats, as the article describes
constraints: HSGPAs are perceived to represent inconsistent levels of readiness across high schools, an assumption the study tests
target_learners: High school students
target_learning_goals: College readiness

citation: Bruzgulis, A., Hart, H., & Young, C. (2019). The challenges facing CPS administrators: Roadblocks to school improvement. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Policymakers and district staff should target supports at administrators facing substantial roadblocks in nearly every category, especially the one-third reporting considerable roadblocks
description: The brief's interpretive summary recommends that "policymakers and district staff may want to consider which supports can best address administrators' and schools' needs," with the most pressing group being the one-third of administrators reporting substantial roadblocks in nearly every survey category. article_title: Integrating Social, Emotional, and Academic Development (SEAD)
citation: Integrating Social, Emotional and Academic Development: An Action Guide for School Leadership Teams. (2019). Aspen Institute. https://hthgse.edu/empathy-interviews-learn-about-the-problem-from-a-users-perspective/
title: SEAD integration rests on a three-legged stool: explicit instruction, embedded practice in academics, and a relationship-rich learning environment
description: The guide's central framework holds that integrating social, emotional, and academic development (SEAD) requires three mutually reinforcing components: explicit skill instruction, embedded practice during academic instruction, and a healthy relationship-based environment. The guide states that "Enacting SEAD in practice rests on a three-legged stool" and that schools must address "social, emotional, and academic dimensions of learning together because they are inextricably linked in students' experiences." Integration also means embedding SEAD into overall school improvement rather than treating it as a siloed add-on program.
requirements: School leadership teams treat SEAD as integrated into school improvement strategy rather than a siloed initiative or add-on program
constraints: Each school community must adapt the approach to its own aspirations and values of students, families, faculty, and stakeholders
target_learners: All students pre-K through 12th grade
target_learning_goals: Social-emotional competencies alongside academic development
examples: The guide organizes its five sections (vision, student learning experience, adult learning, climate, asset mapping) around this framework

title: Four learning mindsets—belonging, success expectancy, growth mindset, and value—support academic behaviors and persistence
description: The guide identifies four student mindsets that underpin academic behavior, persistence, and performance, expressed from the student's point of view: "I belong in this learning community," "I can succeed at this," "My ability and competence grow with my effort (also known as a 'growth mindset')," and "This work has value for me." These mindsets are presented as the motivational foundation schools should cultivate through relationships, purposeful learning, and student agency. The guide ties them to the claim that learning is a social process requiring connection to peers, teachers, and adults.
requirements: Students need to feel connected to and supported by peers, teachers, and other adults in the building

target_learning_goals: Academic behaviors, persistence, and performance on academic tasks
examples: Teachers foster purpose by connecting discussions to issues students care about and selecting texts reflecting students' identities, cultures, and interests

title: Use existing staff and time more strategically before adding new SEAD programs or positions
description: The guide's asset-mapping principle holds that schools should inventory and realign all resources—staff, time, technology, space, community assets, and budget—around their vision before purchasing new programs. It argues that traditional add-on approaches are "insufficient because it rarely attends to the classroom teachers that comprise over 80% of a typical school's budget," and that "Identifying opportunities to use existing staff and time more strategically should come before making additional investments." Resource equity means allocating by need rather than giving every student the same thing.
requirements: A full asset map of resources inside and outside the school, including community assets such as after-school care, health centers, and nonprofits
constraints: New positions created through trade-offs may lack content-team colleagues and need district professional-learning support
target_learners: All students, with resource decisions based on need
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to social, emotional, and academic development supports
examples: Rogers' school eliminated teaching assistant positions and hall monitors to fund a floating science teacher and expanded planning time

title: Social-emotional development cannot be color-blind: educators must examine their own identities and biases
description: The guide's equity sections and its Pine View vignette argue that SEL implementation must attend explicitly to race, identity, and bias. The vignette concludes that "SEL cannot be color-blind and it is just as important for adults as it is for children," and the guide recommends educators "do reflective internal work to understand their own identities and how privilege and bias can influence perceptions of and relationships with students." Leaders should create space to discuss equity and power and model leaning into discomfort rather than reaching closure.
requirements: School leaders create space to discuss equity and power; a growth-orientation, non-judgmental process for staff self-reflection
constraints: Staff pushback is anticipated; the vignette reports significant fallout and divisions persisting over time

target_learning_goals: Healthy integrated identity development and equitable social-emotional support
examples: Pine View's leadership team trained on implicit bias, then rolled out staff PD on identifying and addressing bias; one teacher resisted and rallied dissenters to the district

description: The report organizes college choice through the concept of college match: "match schools are colleges where, on average, students who are admitted have comparable qualifications to the student," contrasted with reach schools (a stretch) and safety schools (near-certain admission). article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Practice-driven data: a five-lesson approach to using data for school improvement that has no playbook and no fidelity standard
description: The paper names and organizes an approach to data use in schools called practice-driven data, developed through the University of Chicago's partnership with Chicago Public Schools. It is explicitly not a scripted program: the approach has no playbook, no singular practice, no such thing as fidelity, and is instead rooted in respect for educator professionalism, context, and autonomy. The framework consists of five lessons — prepare (build capacity to facilitate hard conversations), focus (prioritize research-based indicators), make meaning (develop shared ownership over the implications of research), strategize (use the right data at the right time), and disrupt (identify and stop inequity). Together, the authors write, these lessons form an approach that focuses stakeholders on the most important goals and features of an ecosystem of data use with the potential to catalyze systematic improvement in student outcomes.
requirements: Educators and leaders must build capacity to facilitate hard data conversations, with an emphasis on trust, collaboration, and culture
Research-based indicators must be available and integrated into data that reaches schools
constraints: The approach was generated in a place-based partnership with Chicago high schools, and the authors note the high school context differs from K-8 and post-secondary education
The authors state the approach has no playbook and no fidelity standard, so implementation is inherently contextual
target_learners: high school educators and school leaders
district and school system leaders
school support organizations
target_learning_goals: using data to guide instructional and school improvement practice
building educator capacity for data-driven conversations
prioritizing research-based indicators of student success
examples: The paper presents the five lessons in Figure 1 and illustrates each with Chicago high school practice, such as NCS-supported Freshman Success Teams and the To&Through Online Tool

article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Four-stage data strategy cycle — understand, collect, transform, socialize — carried by a data strategist working with a team leader
description: This pattern describes how school-based data work is organized in NCS partner high schools. A data strategist moves through four stages: understand (know the research, the data systems, and which teams need what data), collect (find and download the needed data), transform (clean, merge, and build graphs, rosters, tables, and reports that spur teams to action), and socialize (bring data to teams, plan meetings, and help individuals understand what the data means). The paper stresses that generating the data and driving the conversation are two sides of the same coin, requiring a skilled data strategist and a team leader who collaboratively brings data to life in team meetings. Figure 3 applies the same four stages to attendance data, from reviewing attendance research to supporting the Care Team's follow-up with chronically absent students.
requirements: A data strategist with analytic skills and fluency in data analysis applications, and a team leader skilled in facilitating data-driven discussions
Data strategists benefit from district-provided professional development on school-facing data systems and from professional learning communities for sharing tools
constraints: The paper notes the strategist role varies across contexts and is more often played by an educator already on a team than a stand-alone position
target_learners: school-based data strategists
team leaders and teacher teams
target_learning_goals: analyzing student outcome data to guide practice
planning productive data conversations that lead to action
examples: Figure 3 applies the stages to attendance data: downloading period-level attendance files, merging variables into one spreadsheet, building an attendance-by-on-track graph for the Freshman Success Team, and creating a roster of chronically absent students for the Care Team

title: A predictable set of educator teams — freshman success, instructional leadership, postsecondary leadership, senior leadership, and care — drives improvement in NCS partner high schools
description: The paper describes the teaming structures used to drive improvement in NCS partner high schools, where visiting educators would likely find a predictable set of teams. Table A lays out five common teams with their members, responsibilities, and data: a Freshman Success Team monitoring the transition into high school using GPA, grades, attendance, behavior, and eighth-grade early warning data; an Instructional Leadership Team working on instructional coherence; a Postsecondary Leadership Team supporting college search, application, and enrollment; a Senior Leadership Team setting vision and monitoring high-level data; and a Care Team of specialists intervening with socially vulnerable students. A common collaboration rhythm is a bi-weekly meeting of roughly 45-60 minutes in which teams analyze data, set intervention strategies, and progress monitor. The paper argues distributed leadership and teaming structures are crucial for driving teacher collaboration at scale in large, complex high schools.
requirements: Distributed leadership and teaming structures, with administrator support for each team
Dedicated meeting time in which teams analyze student data and monitor interventions
constraints: Team structures look different across schools, and the paper notes high schools are often large, complex organizations where individual educators have limited time to collaborate
target_learners: high school teacher teams and administrators
freshman success and postsecondary teams
target_learning_goals: monitoring student transitions and academic achievement
organizing school-wide improvement efforts around shared data
examples: Table A specifies, for instance, that the Freshman Success Team uses GPA, course grades, attendance rates, behavioral data, and eighth-grade early warning indicator data to monitor students' transition into high school
key_sources: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/practice-driven-data-lessons-chicagos-approach-research-data-and-practice-education

article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Make data safe: build trust and conditions for hard data conversations rather than punitive judgment
description: This principle holds that data improves practice only when educators can discuss it without defensiveness, so school leaders must invest in making data safe. Many educators have primarily experienced data punitively, as a way to make harsh judgments about individual teachers or students; the goal of approaching data safely is not to make the data palatable, but to build conditions for hard conversations about current practice and improvement strategies. Trust is built through clear mission, shared values, structured protocols that instill a sense of efficacy, and by engaging in difficult data-driven conversations and reflecting on them — the paper states there is no standardized approach and the work is deeply contextual and personal. Principals and administrators must set conditions for teams to keep a lens of improvement and support rather than shame and judgment.
requirements: Strong school leadership that supports a culture of data-driven improvement
Team leaders skilled in facilitating data discussions using norms, protocols, and listening techniques
Time and intention to build social trust within teams and across the school
constraints: The paper states trust cannot be built in an off-site professional learning session and there is no standardized approach to developing it
target_learners: principals and school administrators
teacher teams and professional learning communities
target_learning_goals: using data collaboratively to interrogate and improve practice
building collective responsibility for student outcomes
examples: In high-functioning teams, educators are motivated by commitment to students and collective responsibility as peers rather than an external motivator like a rating system, which the paper links to a remarkably high level of social trust
key_sources: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/practice-driven-data-lessons-chicagos-approach-research-data-and-practice-education

article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Disaggregate outcomes by students' prior achievement so cross-school comparisons highlight differences in practice, not population
description: This principle addresses a chronic failure mode of cross-school data discussions: comparing schools that serve very different populations, which invites defensive excuses. Effective data systems instead show comparisons of indicators and outcomes of similar students across schools, highlighting differences in practice rather than differences in population. The To&Through Online Tool operationalizes this by disaggregating freshman course performance by eighth-grade GPA and attendance — the most powerful predictors of ninth-grade performance — and by providing data on comparison schools whose ninth-graders had similar middle-grades performance. Focusing on students at a particular band of prior achievement allows more rational and fair comparisons, removes quick explanations, and supports a search for promising practices among schools achieving better results with similar students.
requirements: Data systems must be technically designed to disaggregate outcomes by indicators of prior performance and to identify comparison schools
Educators need dedicated time, space, trust, and safety for constructive cross-school conversations, with attention to objectives, norms, and facilitation
constraints: The paper notes school leaders may never fully separate learning from accountability contexts, and that lessons drawn from an outside partner perspective may vary from those of actors inside the system
target_learners: school leaders and educator teams comparing outcomes across schools
data system designers
target_learning_goals: identifying relative strengths and weaknesses against similar schools
sharing promising practices across schools
examples: In Figure 4, only 41 percent of a sample school's high opportunity students — ninth-graders with strong eighth-grade course performance — earned a 3.0 GPA in freshman year, lower than high opportunity students citywide or at similar schools, prompting cross-school practice sharing

article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: To&Through Online Tool: a public-facing data tool disaggregating Chicago high school outcomes by prior achievement
description: The To&Through Online Tool is a public-facing data tool with data on all Chicago public high schools, developed by the To&Through Project using Consortium research on middle-grade indicators. It disaggregates freshman course performance by eighth-grade GPA and attendance — combined into summary measures estimating a student's risk and opportunity for success or struggle in ninth grade — and shows how comparison schools with similar incoming students are faring. Its displays are designed for simplicity and practice use: one graph begins with a question framing the data's purpose, uses a simple stacked line graph, allows disaggregation by student group such as moderately qualified graduates, and integrates high school and college data from different sources to prompt questions about how shifts in practice led to changes in outcomes.
requirements: Underlying Consortium research identifying eighth-grade GPA and attendance as the most powerful predictors of ninth-grade performance
Integration of high school and college data from different sources into one interface
constraints: The paper presents the tool in the Chicago context, where over 90 district-run high schools serve dramatically different populations
target_learners: high school educators and school leaders
district administrators and researchers
target_learning_goals: tracking freshman on-track and college enrollment outcomes
placing school results in context against comparison schools
examples: Figure 6 shows a To&Through graph of college enrollment rates for moderately qualified graduates over time at a sample school, splitting enrollment between 2-year and 4-year colleges

article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Five characteristics of effective indicators: predictiveness, usability and clarity, right-time availability, direct causal linkage, and malleability
description: A Consortium report cited in the paper outlines five characteristics of effective indicators: predictiveness, usability and clarity, real time/right time availability, direct causal linkage to outcomes, and malleability. Predictiveness alone is insufficient — researchers must also show which indicators are less predictive and therefore poor targets — and even rigorously predictive indicators fail if they are not understandable, simple, and applicable in schools, since complexity that becomes a barrier to action undermines use. Indicators should be available in real time or at the right time, should have a direct causal linkage so that improving them changes the ultimate outcome, and must be malleable, meaning educators can move them with known strategies. The paper grounds the framework in the assumption that indicators' predictive power is practical rather than deterministic: indicators estimate likely outcomes to trigger support, with the goal that the predicted outcome does not correspond with the student's actual outcome.
requirements: Researchers must provide evidence of what indicators are and are not predictive of, and attend to how indicators will be incorporated into daily practice
Indicators must be available at the right time for educators to act, not only once a year
constraints: Establishing direct causal linkage is a complicated task, and indicators like eighth-grade test scores cannot be changed by high school educators
target_learners: researchers and analysts developing indicators
school-based educators using indicator data
target_learning_goals: identifying students who need support
focusing school improvement strategies on outcomes that matter
examples: The Freshman Success Team at Sarah E. Goode STEM Academy uses a staged intervention flowchart (Figure 5) that first separates students with extremely low attendance, then uses GPA bands to assign classroom instruction, tutoring, or attendance-team support

Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/practice-driven-data-lessons-chicagos-approach-research-data-and-practice-education

article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Design data systems for practice: streamline data, keep displays simple, consolidate systems, and separate improvement data from accountability reporting
description: The paper gives data system designers four guidelines for focusing and aligning data systems while avoiding common mistakes. First, streamline the amount of data, asking what questions practitioners must answer and providing only the data needed, since educators drown in data when everything is included. Second, show data in ways that are easy to understand — users on the ground prefer something clean and simple, and basic stacked bar and line graphs are often best. Third, consolidate data into one system, because disconnected interfaces force front-line users to integrate data themselves and signal that improvement work is unrelated. Fourth, design data systems for practice, not accountability reporting, since compliance-driven collection creates fatigue and mistrust and often gives educators no mechanism to review the data for their own inquiry.
requirements: Placing the most important practitioner questions at the top of any data set or display
Building data infrastructure that connects data points and products across systems
Clear evidence that a new display format's benefits outweigh the learning curve for practitioners
constraints: The paper notes schools still require flexibility in day-to-day data monitoring to meet immediate practice needs, with simplicity reserved for big-picture views
target_learners: data system designers
school-based educators who use district data systems
target_learning_goals: quickly answering priority questions about student outcomes
moving efficiently from data display to improvement conversation
examples: Figure 6's To&Through graph illustrates the guidelines: it opens with a framing question, uses a simple stacked line graph, disaggregates by moderately qualified graduates, and integrates high school and college data from different sources
key_sources: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. article_title: Are GPAs an Inconsistent Measure of Achievement across High Schools? Examining Assumptions about Grades versus Standardized Test Scores
citation: Allensworth, Elaine M., & Clark, Kallie. (2019). Are GPAs an Inconsistent Measure of College Readiness across High Schools? Examining Assumptions about Grades versus Standardized Test Scores. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Use high school grades, not individual test scores, as the primary formative indicator of college readiness, and rely less heavily on standardized test scores in accountability
description: The article concludes that HSGPAs "perform in a strong and consistent way across high schools as measures of college readiness, while ACT scores do not", and recommends that schools use grades formatively to guide improvement and assess college-readiness programs, while relying much less heavily on test scores. Because individual ACT scores add little beyond HSGPA and vary inconsistently across schools, districts should also track students' actual college performance rather than proxy readiness with test scores alone.
requirements: Longitudinal data systems that allow districts to track students' actual performance in college
Transcript-based (not student-reported) HSGPAs
constraints: The study used only Chicago Public Schools data and public schools; relationships could differ with a more comprehensive sample
HSGPA is not an equivalent measure of readiness across schools; school effects remain
target_learners: High school graduates enrolling in four-year colleges
target_learning_goals: Academic readiness for college persistence and graduation
examples: The authors recommend that states and districts rely less heavily on standardized test scores in accountability systems and that schools measure and publish school effects on postsecondary outcomes

Examining Assumptions about Grades versus Standardized Test Scores. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/are-gpas-inconsistent-measure-achievement-across-high-schools-examining-assumptions

article_title: High School Graduation and College Readiness Indicator Systems
citation: Allensworth, E.M., Nagaoka, J., & Johnson, D.W. (2018). High school graduation and college readiness indicator systems: What we know, what we need to know. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://ncs.uchicago.edu/freshman-on-track-toolkit
title: Early warning and college readiness indicator systems: data organized into advance predictions of attainment to trigger strategic action
description: The report defines an indicator system as more than data: "At its most basic, an indicator provides a prediction of educational attainment (e.g., high school graduation, college graduation) well in advance of the outcome." Predictions are estimates that let practitioners change a student's trajectory, and only strategic use of information within data systems turns a piece of data into an indicator. The report distinguishes early warning indicators, which signal likelihood of high school graduation, from college readiness indicators, which signal likelihood of obtaining a college degree, and describes three uses: identifying students in need of intervention, focusing and assessing school improvement, and holding schools accountable.
requirements: A strong data system that produces setting-level and student-level indicators for schools to use in practice, which almost always requires district and state policymakers to provide resources for technology and personnel
Structures that provide guidance to educators around data use, since having data is not the same as having an indicator system
constraints: Predictions are not certainties; the report states that predicting an outcome is not the same thing as knowing that outcome will occur
The report omits description of system-level indicators, focusing on the school level consistent with the John W. Gardner Center framework
target_learners: High school students, particularly ninth-graders
Middle grades students
target_learning_goals: High school graduation
College readiness and post-secondary enrollment, persistence, and graduation
examples: Chicago issues data reports generally every other week flagging ninth-grade students getting Ds or below in a core course or with low attendance
A student-level example is a list of ninth-graders updated weekly flagging students with low attendance or Ds/Fs; a setting-level example is first quarter attendance rates by period and subject
Figure 1 depicts policymakers, school support organizations, school leadership teams, and teacher and school staff teams all playing roles in effective indicator use

article_title: High School Graduation and College Readiness Indicator Systems
citation: Allensworth, E.M., Nagaoka, J., & Johnson, D.W. (2018). High school graduation and college readiness indicator systems: What we know, what we need to know. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://ncs.uchicago.edu/freshman-on-track-toolkit
title: Choose indicators that are predictive, usable, available in real time, causally linked to attainment, and malleable through school practices
description: The report proposes five ideal properties of indicators, each building on the prior: predictiveness, usability and clarity, real-time/right-time availability, direct causal linkage to educational attainment, and malleability. It states that "Indicators that are known to be malleable through specific practices—and that are strongly and causally linked to educational attainment—provide the greatest opportunity for improving students' outcomes." The properties are offered as selection criteria for deciding which indicators should be the focus of an early warning or college readiness indicator system.
requirements: The decision of which indicators to focus on should be shaped by the plan for how the indicators will be used; indicators are not effective if practitioners do not have strategies to act on them
Indicators must be calculable in a timely way and understandable, since some indicators are difficult to calculate or confusing and difficult to use
constraints: The review states there is insufficient research to evaluate any of the indicators being used along all of these dimensions

The review warns that predictive analytics approaches, while highly predictive, risk replicating and reinforcing previous inequitable or discriminatory patterns because models are based on historical data
target_learners: High school students
Middle grades students
target_learning_goals: High school graduation
College readiness
examples: The review contrasts ninth-grade GPA, which predicted Chicago graduation with 80 percent accuracy, against eighth-grade test scores and background characteristics at 65 percent accuracy
The review notes educators may benefit from multiple indicators if they provide complementary types of information that aid intervention efforts

citation: Allensworth, E., Moore, P., Sartain, L., & de la Torre, M. (2016). The Educational Benefits of Attending Higher-Performing Schools: Evidence from Chicago High Schools. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications
title: Four-tier classification of Chicago high schools by graduation rate and average ACT score
description: The research groups Chicago high schools into four performance tiers using graduation rate and average ACT composite score: selective enrollment, top-tier non-selective, mid-tier non-selective, and low-tier non-selective. Figure 1 prints, for the CPS Class of 2015, a "90.0" four-year graduation rate and "24.5" average ACT for the 10 selective schools, versus "50.6" and "14.8" for the 28 low-tier schools. This tiering is the basis for all outcome comparisons in the summary.
requirements: Schools are classified by graduation rates and ACT scores, with non-selective tiers defined relative to average ACT scores and graduation rates
constraints: Non-selective tiers include neighborhood, charter, and special high schools, so tier differences are not purely selectivity differences

target_learning_goals: high school achievement, student experiences, and college outcomes
examples: Figure 1 reports the CPS Class of 2015 average performance by tier, e.g., top-tier schools with an 82.3 graduation rate and 18.5 average ACT

description: The summary rests on two studies. The first examines "the effects of attending a higher-performing school on students' academic and nonacademic outcomes" using "a propensity score approach with an extensive array of pre-high school characteristics" for CPS cohorts entering high school from 2008-2011. The second compares students just above and just below selective enrollment admission thresholds in a regression discontinuity design for 2010-2013 cohorts, investigating neighborhood socioeconomic differences.

article_title: The Network for College Success
citation: Pitcher, M. A., Duncan, S. J., Nagaoka, J., Moeller, E., Dickerson, L., & Beechum, N. O. (2016). The Network for College Success: A Capacity-Building Model for School Improvement. University of Chicago. https://ncs.uchicago.edu
title: The NCS capacity-building model for school improvement
description: The Network for College Success model is a whole-school improvement framework that builds the systems, structures, and capacity of school staff rather than adopting an external reform package. It is organized around four key elements: "1. Creating Professional Learning Networks; 2. Applying Research-Based Data to Practice; 3. Coaching and Capacity Building; and 4. Distributing Leadership and Building High-Functioning Teams." NCS embeds learning in sustained professional learning communities working toward long-term goals, provides job-embedded coaching to school leaders, and positions principals as primary drivers of change who must distribute leadership across staff. The paper illustrates the model through the Freshman On Track work in Chicago Public Schools.
requirements: Sustained, long-term partnerships rather than one-time professional development, because the paper states one-time drive-by professional development is insufficient for deep and lasting change
constraints: The paper states it is not an evaluation of NCS nor evidence of its efficacy; it documents the model and stakeholder experiences
target_learners: High school principals, teacher leaders, counselors, and data strategists in urban districts
target_learning_goals: School leaders' capacity to use research-based data, lead collaborative improvement, and raise freshman success and graduation rates
examples: NCS facilitated cross-school Collaboratives for principals, counselors, teacher leaders, and data strategists, and provided job-embedded coaching to school leaders in 32 partner schools over 10 years

article_title: The Network for College Success
citation: Pitcher, M. A., Duncan, S. J., Nagaoka, J., Moeller, E., Dickerson, L., & Beechum, N. O. (2016). The Network for College Success: A Capacity-Building Model for School Improvement. University of Chicago. https://ncs.uchicago.edu
title: Freshman On-Track indicator and Individual School Report
description: The Freshman On-Track indicator is a research-based early-warning metric: a student is On-Track if he or she earns at least five full-year course credits and no more than one semester F in a core course in ninth grade. Its simplicity makes it easy to calculate with school-generated data. CPS began providing real-time early-warning data reports in 2008, and the Freshman On Track Individual School Report (ISR) was developed to provide customized data so school leaders can analyze trends and set measurable goals. The paper also notes an accompanying Freshman On-Track Toolkit organized around four components including Developing Capacity & Leadership and Applying Research & Data.
requirements: Real-time data reports and training and resources that help school leaders put the data into practice
constraints: The paper notes concerns arose that On-Track improvements might not represent true changes in performance, which a subsequent Consortium study addressed
target_learners: Ninth-grade students in urban high schools, supported by principals, counselors, and grade-level teacher teams
target_learning_goals: Increasing freshman course passing and On-Track status as a foundation for high school graduation
examples: CPS adapted the year-end metric for point-in-time monitoring throughout the year to flag students in need of interventions

article_title: The Network for College Success
citation: Pitcher, M. A., Duncan, S. J., Nagaoka, J., Moeller, E., Dickerson, L., & Beechum, N. O. (2016). The Network for College Success: A Capacity-Building Model for School Improvement. University of Chicago. https://ncs.uchicago.edu
title: Embed educator learning in sustained professional learning communities rather than one-time professional development
description: The NCS model holds that school improvement requires embedding adult learning in sustained professional learning communities working toward long-term goals. The paper states that "one-time, 'drive-by' professional development is insufficient in creating deep and lasting change." NCS operationalizes this through long-term partnerships and monthly Collaboratives in which school leaders examine research, interrogate data, and share practice in a safe, normed environment. Cross-school sharing of data and practice is built into every session so educators learn from peers facing similar challenges.
requirements: Networks need strong cultures with trusting relationships, norms, and protocols that create a safe space for honest, open problem-solving
constraints: If people perceive that speaking honestly will have negative consequences, the flow of information about problems will be suppressed, making improvement unlikely
target_learners: High school principals, assistant principals, counselors, teacher leaders, and data strategists
target_learning_goals: Leaders' capacity to lead and manage school change and improve student outcomes through collaborative problem-solving
examples: The Principals' Collaborative met monthly in each other's schools to examine problems of practice; practitioners reported that cross-school data sharing pushed them to question their own practices

article_title: The College Match Indicator
citation: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. (2016). The College Match Indicator, in Matching Students to Opportunity. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: College match indicator
description: The college match indicator is a simple measurement tool developed by researchers at the UChicago Consortium to gauge how students fare on the road to college. As the text states, it is "a simple way to measure the extent to which students are struggling on the path to college enrollment." The chapter uses the indicator as an example of how indicators can be used to shape practice, describing its origins, the role of Consortium research in its development, and related efforts in Chicago Public Schools.
requirements: Requires underlying data on students' academic qualifications and college enrollment to identify the extent to which students are struggling on the path to college enrollment
constraints: The chapter itself discusses three limitations of the college match indicator
target_learners: High school students preparing for college enrollment
target_learning_goals: College access and successful matching of students to postsecondary institutions
examples: Used in Chicago Public Schools as an example of how indicators can be used to shape practice

article_title: The Educational Attainment of Chicago Public Schools Students
citation: Nagaoka, J., & Healey, K. (2016). The educational attainment of Chicago Public Schools students: 2015: A focus on four-year college degrees. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. http://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/educational-attainment-chicago-public-schools-students-2015-focus-four-year-college
title: Bachelor's Degree Attainment Index and Direct Bachelor's DAI metrics
description: The UChicago Consortium developed two metrics to estimate students' progression to and through college: the Bachelor's DAI and the Direct Bachelor's DAI. The Direct Bachelor's DAI counts students taking "the straight-forward path of graduating high school in four years, enrolling immediately in a four-year college, and earning a four-year college degree within six years of starting college," estimated at 16 percent for 2015. The Bachelor's DAI additionally counts students who first enroll in a two-year college or delay entry before earning a four-year degree, yielding 18 percent.
requirements: Requires district data on high school graduation, immediate four-year college enrollment, and six-year college graduation rates, plus data on delayed-entry and two-year-entry pathways for the Bachelor's DAI
constraints: The brief notes a national Bachelor's DAI cannot be calculated because comparable data on bachelor's degree completion for students who delay college entry are not available
target_learners: CPS ninth-graders
target_learning_goals: Progression to and through four-year college degree attainment
