article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Quality instruction for English learners supports students to develop a sense of agency, confidence, and determination
description: The brief frames student agency as a core feature of quality instruction for English learners, defining it as the capacity and propensity to take purposeful initiative and noting that agency embraces self-regulated learning. It argues that language is a key resource for learning self-regulation, so teachers should design instruction that builds language and regulation in tandem, with cycles of goal setting, reflection, and revision.
requirements: Students and teachers need time, support, learning opportunities, and grace as they begin to integrate opportunities to develop self-regulation and agency.
target_learners: English learners (multilingual learners) in K-12 classrooms
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning, metacognition, agency, and English language development
examples: The brief suggests students begin by formulating a simple goal such as adding time order words to their writing, then over time define goals with a greater variety of language, supported by sentence frames like "When I first wrote the text, I thought…" "Now I think…".
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673602

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: A four-routine instructional sequence—explicit instruction, modeling, practice opportunities, and feedback—builds student capacity to self-assess
description: The brief describes a series of intentional instructional routines for building student capacity to self-assess. Explicit instruction provides clear, direct guidance as an early-stage strategy; modeling demonstrates self-assessment, including think-alouds and examples of both exemplary and less optimal practices; structured low-stakes practice opportunities allow improvement with regular and repeated practice; and feedback, such as probing questions, supports students reviewing work against success criteria and setting goals.
requirements: Teachers and students benefit from keeping a growth mindset, understanding that they are emergent learners who will improve with regular and repeated practice in low-stakes settings.
target_learners: English learners learning self-assessment practices
target_learning_goals: Self-assessment against success criteria and goal setting
examples: Models can come from other sources, for example, videos of other students using success criteria in their self-assessment.
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673602

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Middle school transition-words writing lesson integrating self-assessment, peer feedback, and personal learning goals
description: A middle school lesson vignette in which English learners and native English-speaking students learn to show relationships between ideas by combining sentences with transition words. Students write personal learning goals based on the success criterion, revise drafts with optional partner brainstorming and sentence stems, exchange peer feedback aligned to the success criteria, rate themselves using a rubric, and set a new personal learning goal for the next lesson.
requirements: The teacher designed the lesson after reviewing students' writing drafts from a previous day, which demonstrated that students needed support creating coherence and fluidity in their writing.
target_learners: Middle school English learners at various proficiency levels and native English-speaking peers
target_learning_goals: Using transition words to show relationships between ideas in writing (time order, place, compare and contrast, cause and effect, importance)
examples: After receiving peer feedback, students assess their own writing based on the success criterion and their personal learning goal, and the teacher plans to review students' self-assessments and personal goals to inform lesson planning.
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673602

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Divergent versus convergent perspectives in formative assessment
description: The brief distinguishes two assessment perspectives teachers bring to interpreting student evidence. A divergent perspective is based on events occurring in real time and oriented toward curiosity and openness toward students' sensemaking; it requires listening to student responses versus listening for how students are responding, and supports uncovering both assets and prior knowledge. A convergent perspective focuses on how closely student thinking corresponds with pre-determined learning expectations, such as end-of-year standards.
requirements: Teachers need to manage the dynamic between the divergent opportunities that unfold through classroom interactions and the opportunities they design to support student learning of predetermined goals, as Cowie states in the brief.
target_learners: Diverse students, including English learners from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Equitable formative assessment that maximizes opportunities for diverse students to demonstrate the breadth of their knowledge and abilities
examples: The brief cites Pryor & Crossouard's finding that when teachers took a divergent perspective, their feedback was exploratory, provisional or provocative, prompting further engagement rather than correcting mistakes.
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673602

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Quality instruction for English learners promotes asset-based teaching, learning, and assessment grounded in funds of knowledge and identity
description: The brief's second feature holds that students' knowledge, experience, and sensibilities are critical assets for gaining new knowledge and skills. Asset-based instruction prioritizes what students can do rather than what they can't yet do, rooted in students' funds of knowledge—abilities passed down through generations—and funds of identity. Teachers build instruction around student-specific funds (interests, talents, passions) and community funds (collective histories, activities, norms, values).
requirements: Teachers must develop an understanding of their students' families, communities, cultures, and interests in ways that establish and sustain relationships.
constraints: The brief notes this sociocultural focus is particularly important for learners from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, who may otherwise experience a sociocultural disconnect from classroom activities and settings.
target_learners: English learners and their non-English learner peers
target_learning_goals: Meaningful, culturally responsive learning that leverages students' rich experiences as a catalyst for developing learning
examples: Teachers can gather evidence by asking students to journal and write stories about their families in their first language and in English, bring in collections of significant items, make videos, take photographs, and draw self-portraits.
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673602

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Middle school biotechnology fermented-drinks lesson demonstrating asset-based instruction and divergent formative assessment
description: A snapshot vignette of a middle school science lesson in which English learners at various proficiency levels work with non-English learner peers to apply biotechnology principles: researching fermented drinks made by family members and neighbors, creating one from an existing family recipe, and developing an original drink for a local target audience. A student's aunt shares her fermentation expertise, and the teacher checks in with groups, asking open-ended questions and providing feedback.
requirements: Each subsequent task in the lesson builds on the prior one to move students toward the learning goal, making learning visible to the teacher and fellow students and providing actionable evidence for formulating next steps.
target_learners: Middle school English learners at various levels of English proficiency and their non-English learner peers
target_learning_goals: Applying principles of biotechnology to real-world situations
examples: After reviewing taste-survey results, students decided to switch their flavor choice to reflect only one target audience; the teacher's open-ended question "How can you find out?" prompted them to draw on peers' research displayed around the room, supporting individual and group agency.
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673602

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/introduction-to-the-extended-thinking-through-discourse-continuum/
title: Two discourse types — exploratory and explanatory — comprise English learners' interactional opportunities
description: The brief organizes collaborative interaction into two discourse types. It states that "Exploratory discourse supports students to speculate, imagine, and conjecture about what might be and to jointly construct new understandings," while explanatory discourse supports sharing what they know, developing arguments, constructing explanations, and providing descriptive accounts. The two types carry different language requirements for vocabulary and sentence structure, so teachers can scaffold disciplinary language, for example by role-playing conversational moves. The brief cites Legare (2014) and Bunch (2014) for this distinction.
requirements: Teachers call attention to and provide scaffolding for how to achieve the purposes of exploratory or explanatory discourse through disciplinary language.
target_learners: English learners in K-12 classrooms
target_learning_goals: Content knowledge and language development through academic discourse
examples: Teachers design regular opportunities for academic discourse based on meaningful prompts and tasks with well-structured routines and appropriate linguistic support.
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/introduction-to-the-extended-thinking-through-discourse-continuum/

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/introduction-to-the-extended-thinking-through-discourse-continuum/
title: Shared regulation and co-regulation are social modes of regulation that emerge when students jointly construct knowledge
description: Drawing on Bailey and Heritage, the brief describes social modes of regulation in interactive learning environments: "group members regulate their collective learning (shared regulation) and students support the regulation of others (co-regulation)." Shared regulation means students collaborate to meet learning goals through projects, discussions, and other engagement — intentional interaction focused on goals, not engagement for its own sake. Co-regulation leverages peers to share knowledge, analyze each other's words and work, and give feedback; in classrooms prioritizing it, greater collective efficacy often arises among students.
requirements: Interaction with peers to move learning forward; intentional student interaction focused on achieving learning goals.
target_learners: English learners and their non-EL classmates
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated and collective progress toward lesson learning goals
examples: Peer feedback is described as the formative assessment practice that supports co-regulation, involving both individual reflection and collaborative discussion.
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/introduction-to-the-extended-thinking-through-discourse-continuum/

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/introduction-to-the-extended-thinking-through-discourse-continuum/
title: Design regular structured opportunities for academic discourse and use them as a major source of evidence of learning
description: To enact quality instruction for English learners, the brief recommends that teachers "design regular opportunities for students to engage in academic discourse based on meaningful prompts and tasks accompanied by well-structured routines and appropriate linguistic support," and "utilize these discourse opportunities as a major source of evidence of learning." Conversations centered on learning deepen content knowledge and language skills, and create ample evidence of students' learning status that peers and teachers can use for meaningful feedback.
requirements: Meaningful prompts and tasks, well-structured routines, and appropriate linguistic support.
constraints: Students' questions or prompts may at times elicit silence in the moment rather than talk as students ponder, wonder, and reflect.
target_learners: English learners, including students with emerging levels of English proficiency
target_learning_goals: Deep learning of content knowledge and language development
examples: In the 2nd-grade fluency lesson, students turn and talk about the learning goal, review success criteria, and use discourse as the basis for peer feedback and self-assessment.
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/introduction-to-the-extended-thinking-through-discourse-continuum/

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Participate in Collaborative Discussions. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://csaa.wested.org/resource/introduction-to-the-extended-thinking-through-discourse-continuum/
title: Build a learning culture with three components — acceptance and trust, accountability, and appreciation — so students take academic risks and support each other's learning
description: The brief states that a supportive learning culture "includes three primary components: acceptance and promotion of trust and academic risk-taking, accountability for one's own and other's learning, and appreciation of each person's unique gifts and perspectives." In such a culture, English learners trust that teacher and peers value mistakes as sources of new learning, take risks with language and ideas, and can access affordances such as anchor charts, task directions, and language supports like formulaic expressions and images.
requirements: Teachers demonstrate and cultivate trust and respect, provide models for risk-taking and mutual support, create a physical environment that enables exploration, and establish and practice norms for listening and responding to each other's ideas.
target_learners: All students (ELs and non-ELs) in a classroom community
target_learning_goals: Open sharing of partial or emergent ideas and effective formative assessment
examples: Using learning goals and success criteria, every member can give descriptive, actionable feedback, which the brief says levels the playing field between peers and lets even emergent learners assume a leadership role.

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Quality instruction for English learners integrates learning of concepts, analytic practices, and language simultaneously
description: The brief argues that language development should not be treated as a separate process from content learning. It defines three disciplinary practices: conceptual understandings, analytic practices, and language practices, and states that "Quality instruction for English learners integrates learning of concepts, analytic practices, and language simultaneously." Teachers plan lessons that create opportunities to use language across the four language domains connected to rigorous, grade-level content.
requirements: Academic content teachers see themselves as teachers of language and develop understanding of the specific language of their discipline
constraints: Not every lesson requires the same level of emphasis on each type of disciplinary practice; teachers strategically decide which to emphasize
target_learners: English learners (multilingual learners) in K-12 content-area classrooms
target_learning_goals: Disciplinary content learning, analytic practices, and discipline-specific language development
examples: Teachers plan lessons with opportunities for students to use language and reflect across reading, writing, speaking, and listening in connection to grade-level content, working together around worthwhile inquiry questions, texts, and topics
key_sources: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673604

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Learning goals and success criteria open the formative assessment process and represent disciplinary practices including language
description: The brief positions learning goals and success criteria as "the first part of the formative assessment process." Learning goals articulate what students are expected to know and do beyond what they can already do autonomously, and success criteria "outline how students will demonstrate that they have met the learning goal and indicate an observable action." Teachers of English learners include the language required to engage in disciplinary content in these goals, and use success criteria as look-fors and listen-fors to interpret evidence during lessons.
requirements: Teachers ground goals and criteria in knowledge of disciplinary learning progressions, language patterns of analytic practices, student assets, and students' current language and content learning
target_learners: English learners across grade levels
target_learning_goals: Content, analytic-practice, and language-focused learning goals
examples: An early elementary science lesson on plants includes the success criterion of using linking words like 'because' and 'then' to explain how plant parts work together
key_sources: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673604

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Five task characteristics for integrated learning and evidence gathering: rigorous, interactive, authentic, language-rich, and multimodal
description: The brief enumerates characteristics tasks should have when teachers plan to gather evidence and frame learning experiences: "they should be rigorous, interactive, authentic, support language, and offer a choice of modality." Rigorous tasks promote deep higher-order thinking; interactive tasks invite collaboration; authentic tasks address students' lived experiences; language-rich tasks integrate the four domains; multimodal tasks offer choices for accessing learning and representing knowledge.
requirements: Tasks must generate visible or audible student learning outputs that teachers can gather as evidence during tasks
target_learners: English learners in content-area classrooms
target_learning_goals: Deep conceptual understanding, disciplinary language use, and demonstration of knowledge through multiple modes
examples: In the 5th-grade vignette, students could complete a graphic organizer in pairs, draw pictures with labels, or give oral explanations, and some English learners paired with peers providing home-language support
key_sources: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673604

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Language development time should connect to grade-level content and disciplinary practices, not isolated grammar or vocabulary drills
description: The brief argues that not all opportunities to use language are equivalent and that lessons are most effective when they engage students in thinking about how specific language achieves a communicative purpose. It warns that "Time spent concentrating on grammatical, lexical, or morphological structures for their own sake should be avoided," giving as counterexamples vocabulary lists, verb conjugation, or translation disconnected from content under study.
requirements: Targeted language development must reflect and connect to current grade-level content learning and disciplinary practices
target_learners: English learners in content-area instruction
target_learning_goals: Linguistic skills and knowledge required to operate independently in content-area classrooms
examples: In math, teachers design activities drawing attention to specialized meanings for common terms like unit or rate in word problems; in science, teachers provide model sentences with linking words such as 'Plants need roots because they bring in nutrients.'
key_sources: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., Blitz, J., & Garcia-Arena, P. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners: Formative Assessment Support for Integrated and Meaningful Language Learning. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673604

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners with Formative Assessment: Introduction
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED531981
title: Ambitious teaching and learning for English learners grounded in sociocultural theory
description: The brief presents "ambitious teaching and learning" as an umbrella concept "grounded in a sociocultural theory", requiring educators to understand students' lived experiences and design learning opportunities for students to co-construct knowledge alongside peers. For English learners it means seeing them as students with promise and value rather than defined by needs and risks. It frames the seven features of high-quality EL instruction.
requirements: Educators must deeply understand who their students are and how their lived experiences and knowledge can contribute to learning
target_learners: English learners (K-12)
target_learning_goals: Simultaneous development of English proficiency, academic content, and analytic practices

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners with Formative Assessment: Introduction
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED531981
title: Seven features of ambitious teaching for English learners
description: The brief enumerates seven features: integrating concepts, analytic practices, and language; drawing attention to how language makes meaning through authentic tasks; scaffolding beyond current knowledge; developing agency; structured collaborative discussion; asset-based teaching and assessment; and a learning culture where all students support each other's learning. Formative assessment undergirds these features.
requirements: Teachers must design and facilitate instruction positioned between students' current and future abilities
target_learners: English learners and non-English learners
target_learning_goals: Conceptual, analytic, and linguistic development
key_sources: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673605

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners with Formative Assessment: Introduction
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED531981
title: Formative assessment as a planned ongoing process and feedback loop
description: The brief defines formative assessment as "a planned ongoing process of inquiry that teachers and students participate in together to understand the current status of learning". It is not a set of stand-alone tools but a sensemaking process of noticing and responding to what students say, do, make, or write. The feedback loop (Figure 1) includes setting learning goals and success criteria, planning evidence-embedding experiences, attending to and making sense of evidence, and responding to advance learning.
requirements: A collaborative and respectful classroom environment embedding clarifying goals, eliciting evidence, self-assessment and peer feedback, actionable feedback, and using evidence to move learning forward
constraints: It is not a set of stand-alone tools, strategies, or tests
target_learners: All students, particularly English learners
target_learning_goals: Self-directed learning and improved understanding of disciplinary learning outcomes
key_sources: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673605

article_title: Accelerate Success for English Learners with Formative Assessment: Introduction
citation: Jones, B., Faulkner-Bond, M., & Blitz, J. (2024). Accelerate Success for English Learners With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED531981
title: Feedback should focus on the work or thinking, not the person, and preserve agency with clues rather than complete solutions
description: The brief recommends quality feedback that "focuses on the work or the thinking, not the traits of the person receiving feedback", e.g., "Your argument may have missed a step." Feedback at the edge of competence should indicate growth areas "without providing a complete solution", using clues or suggestions to preserve the receiver's agency. Student-requested feedback invites follow-up conversations.
requirements: Students must have the opportunity to respond to the feedback they receive
target_learners: All students, particularly English learners
target_learning_goals: Advancing learning while preserving student agency
examples: The brief gives example feedback focused on the work: "Your argument may have missed a step." and "I didn’t understand how you reached that conclusion."

article_title: Rethinking Language in Mathematics for English Learners: Connecting Theory, Research, and Practice
citation: Haiwen Chu, Monique Evans. (2025). Rethinking Language in Mathematics for English Learners: Connecting Theory, Research, and Practice. National Research and Development Center to Improve Education for Secondary English Learners at WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Systemic functional linguistics genre continua (mode, tenor, field) as an account of long-term language development
description: The brief draws on systemic functional linguistics, whose "fundamental premise" is considering "how language use is embedded in social purposes." Genres serve particular purposes and include continua of mode (dialogic-to-monologic organization), tenor (peer-to-authoritative relations), and field (everyday-to-technical topics). The authors use these continua to characterize how learners over time become more monologic, authoritative, and technical, and to interpret RAMPUP student language samples.
requirements: Language growth requires meaningful opportunities over sustained periods of time, per the brief
constraints: The brief applies the continua to secondary mathematics contexts with English Learners
target_learners: secondary English Learners
target_learning_goals: academic language development alongside mathematical concepts

citation: Haiwen Chu, Monique Evans. (2025). Rethinking Language in Mathematics for English Learners: Connecting Theory, Research, and Practice. National Research and Development Center to Improve Education for Secondary English Learners at WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: RAMPUP (Reimagining and Amplifying Mathematics Participation, Understanding, and Practices) summer bridge program
description: RAMPUP is a 3-week summer bridge enrichment course for rising 9th grade students bureaucratically designated as English Learners, designed to engage students with crosscutting mathematical concepts such as patterns and equivalence. Its modules include sorting tasks on real-world photographs, growing-pattern jigsaw activities, and collaborative description writing. Field trials over two summers refined the usability and feasibility of the materials.
requirements: Iterative development with classroom observation to refine usability and feasibility, as the authors report
constraints: Studied as an enrichment summer bridge setting for rising 9th graders, not the regular-year course
target_learners: rising 9th grade English Learners
target_learning_goals: engagement with crosscutting concepts such as patterns and equivalence
examples: Sorting photographs of floor tiles, woven clothing patterns, and sunflowers, then labeling groups with sticky notes

citation: Haiwen Chu, Monique Evans. (2025). Rethinking Language in Mathematics for English Learners: Connecting Theory, Research, and Practice. National Research and Development Center to Improve Education for Secondary English Learners at WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Three pedagogical shifts for designing learning for English Learners: concepts over preteaching, generative expressions over scripts, integrated modes over separate modes
description: The brief organizes its recommendations as a shift table: from preteaching vocabulary to developing concepts and the language to talk about them; from requiring sentence starters as rigid scripts to offering generative formulaic expressions; and from treating reading, writing, listening, and speaking as four separate modes to integrating oracy and literacy in meaningful activities. These shifts are informed by the theory and field-trial examples in the brief.
requirements: Educators must design learning that supports both language learning and rigorous content-area learning
constraints: Addressed to secondary educators working with English Learners in U.S. classrooms

target_learning_goals: ambitious mathematics learning with concurrent language development
examples: Table 2 of the brief lays out the From…To… shifts; Table 3 offers reflection questions and concrete actions for planning

citation: Early Literacy Performance in Massachusetts: Key Findings From 2023/24 School Year Data. (2025). WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Massachusetts DESE statewide K–3 early literacy screening dataset (2023/24)
description: A statewide collection of early literacy screening assessment results from schools and districts participating in targeted state grants, with 2023/24 the first year screening was required for all kindergarten through grade 3 students statewide. The 2023/24 data cover "137,000 students" in "612 schools" across "144 districts", about 53 percent of the state's K–3 students, and screenings are "typically administered two to three times per year" to identify students at risk of reading difficulties and guide early intervention.

constraints: Data cover about half the state's K–3 population because not all schools and districts were required to report.

article_title: Early Literacy Performance in Massachusetts: Results of Ongoing Analysis of Literacy Screening Assessments (2023/24 Data)
citation: Lemke, M., Faulkner-Bond, M., LeBeau, B., Soo Ping Chow, A., & Quesen, S. (2025). Early literacy performance in Massachusetts: Results of ongoing analysis of literacy screening assessments (2023/24 data). WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Screening assessment risk benchmarks are set by three distinct methods (predictive, judgment-based, normative), so there is no common definition of risk across assessments
description: The report organizes how approved Massachusetts screening assessments define their significant-risk cut scores into three approaches: predictive analysis against an external criterion, judgment-based standard setting, and normative percentile cutoffs. It states that "The most common approach across screening assessments is a predictive approach that establishes a risk cut score by using an external criterion," while Star uses the 25th national percentile and i-Ready uses judgment-based standard setting. Because cut scores are derived differently, the report concludes "there is no truly common definition of risk across screening assessments," which complicates cross-assessment and cross-school trend analysis.
requirements: Interpreting risk categories requires knowing which benchmark-setting method each assessment's publisher used, as compiled in the report's Table 2 from technical documentation and publisher communication.
constraints: The report states the lack of a common definition of risk can create challenges for schools, districts, and the state, including inconsistent identification of mobile students and potentially conflicting information for parents.
target_learners: Kindergarten through grade 3 students in Massachusetts public schools
target_learning_goals: Early identification of students at risk of reading difficulty
examples: Table 2 classifies Acadience, DIBELS 8th Edition, MAP Reading Fluency, mCLASS, EarlyBird, and FastBridge as predictive; i-Ready as judgment-based; and Star Early Literacy and Star Reading as normative (below 25th national percentile).
key_sources: Lemke, M., Faulkner-Bond, M., LeBeau, B., Soo Ping Chow, A., & Quesen, S. (2025). Early literacy performance in Massachusetts: Results of ongoing analysis of literacy screening assessments (2023/24 data). WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677571

citation: Lemke, M., Faulkner-Bond, M., LeBeau, B., Soo Ping Chow, A., & Quesen, S. (2025). Early literacy performance in Massachusetts: Results of ongoing analysis of literacy screening assessments (2023/24 data). WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Massachusetts K-3 early literacy screening longitudinal dataset (2020/21-2023/24)
description: A longitudinal analytic file combining early literacy universal screening benchmark scores with SIMS demographic data, MCAS scores, ACCESS for ELLs data, and school- and district-level contextual data, organized as one observation per student, per test period (BOY, MOY, EOY), per assessment, per year. In 2023/24 it includes "388,204 scores" representing "137,159 unique students across 144 districts and 612 schools," about 53 percent of the state's K-3 population, drawn from 13 screening assessments with six assessments accounting for 92 percent of the data. WestEd built and analyzes it for DESE under state grant and screening-regulation data collection.
requirements: Data depend on schools and districts participating in state grants or the statewide screening requirement sharing assessment data with DESE, with publisher data-sharing agreements for some records.
constraints: The sample overrepresents Hispanic students, students from low income backgrounds, and English learners by 6 to 8 percent relative to the state, so the report states findings may slightly underestimate overall state performance and may not be fully generalizable.

target_learning_goals: Monitoring early literacy performance and progress and identifying students at risk of reading difficulty
examples: The 2023/24 data doubled from 2022/23, with mCLASS (37%) and DIBELS 8th Edition (21%) the most commonly used assessments.

article_title: Understanding the At-Risk Indicator: Nevada's Pupil-Centered Funding Plan
citation: Tanner, S., Krausen, K., Garcia, B., & Brown, A. (2025). Understanding the At-risk indicator: Nevada's Pupil-Centered Funding Plan. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Nevada's GRAD score: a machine learning–generated At-risk indicator in a school funding formula
description: The GRAD score is a machine learning output produced within Nevada's Infinite Campus system, described as the first such indicator used in a state funding formula. The report states that "The GRAD score is calculated by a machine learning program from Infinite Campus that analyzes approximately 70 data points about a student in areas including academic performance, attendance, behavior, home, and economic stability." Students in the lowest quintile of GRAD scores are designated At-risk and generate a 0.35 weight above the Statewide Base for their schools, subject to unduplicated counting rules.
requirements: Student data across academic performance, attendance, behavior, home, and economic stability must flow into the Infinite Campus system so the algorithm can score each student
A statewide lowest-quintile cutoff must be computed annually (on or around October 1) to convert scores into At-risk designations
constraints: Students who also qualify for special education or English Learner status are funded in those categories, not as At-risk, due to unduplicated counts
Funding counts come from the prior fiscal year's October 1 validation data, so budgets rely on year-old identifications
target_learners: K-12 public school students in Nevada scoring in the lowest quintile of GRAD scores
target_learning_goals: Identifying students at risk of not graduating with their cohort so additional funding reaches their schools
examples: In fiscal year 2025 the Statewide Base was $9,414 per student, so each At-risk student generated an additional $3,294 for their LEA

article_title: The Impact of the Mindsets Mathematics Program on Student Engagement, Ability to Reason, and Repeated Reasoning
citation: Gage, N. (2025). The impact of the Mindsets mathematics program on student engagement, ability to reason, and repeated reasoning. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Mindsets mathematics program: collaborative, hands-on, challenge-based curriculum aligned to the Standards for Mathematical Practice
description: Mindsets is a mathematics program built around "collaborative, hands-on challenges that immerse students in real-world scenarios." Each multi-hour challenge opens with a compelling real-life context, moves students through increasingly complex problems highlighting a particular SMP, and ends with a culminating hands-on activity such as making pancakes or setting prices for a dog-walking business. Teachers receive targeted professional development and real-time implementation support, and challenges align with the California Mathematics Framework without being California-specific.
requirements: Teachers receive targeted professional development and real-time implementation support to lead the challenges
constraints: In the studied implementation, SMP data were only available for one of the middle challenges and one of the end challenges
target_learners: middle school students in grades 6–8
target_learning_goals: engagement in mathematics
ability to reason abstractly and quantitatively (SMP 2)
repeated reasoning (SMP 8)
examples: In the 2025 summer session, challenges were organized around weekly themes: Building Community, Food Week, Movement, Shark Tank, and The Amazing Race
key_sources: Gage, N. (2025). The impact of the Mindsets mathematics program on student engagement, ability to reason, and repeated reasoning. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677579

citation: Gage, N. (2025). The impact of the Mindsets mathematics program on student engagement, ability to reason, and repeated reasoning. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Embed mathematics reasoning in authentic, real-world collaborative tasks with mixed-grade groupings to support engagement and equitable access
description: The report argues that mathematics learning environments should use context-rich, problem-based tasks rather than deficit-oriented remediation. The Mindsets design situates challenges in real-world contexts, uses mixed-grade groupings so older students revisit foundational content while supporting younger students, and is "intended to allow students to engage meaningfully and reduce the stigma often associated with remediation." The authors state this supports equitable mathematics instruction that rejects remediation models.
requirements: Access to meaningful tasks, high expectations, and supportive teacher facilitation
constraints: Evidence comes from a single 5-week summer implementation in one district; the authors call for broader consideration and replication

target_learning_goals: engagement
mathematical reasoning
equitable access to grade-level content
examples: Most sessions were conducted in mixed-grade groupings, allowing older students to revisit foundational content while supporting younger students' preparation for middle school rigor

article_title: Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons from Innovative State Approaches under ESSA
citation: Mitch Herz, Mel Wylen. (2025). Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons From Innovative State Approaches Under ESSA. White paper.
title: Hierarchy of Purposes of Statewide School Accountability Systems
description: The paper proposes a four-level hierarchical model of statewide school accountability systems, expanding on the National Center for the Improvement of Educational Assessment's four key roles. It argues that "the highest purpose of statewide school accountability systems should be to encourage specific action to improve school-level outcomes." The levels are cumulative: Level 1 identify purpose and vision; Level 2 design the system to serve that vision; Level 3 communicate accountability information to interest holders; Level 4 create linkages between accountability information and action, via horizontal coordination across the SEA and vertical coordination between SEA, districts, and schools.
requirements: States must identify the purpose and vision for the larger education system, often through strategic plans, theories of action, and logic models
Successfully implementing lower levels is necessary for the system to operate at higher levels
constraints: The model is proposed based on literature review and four case studies; the paper notes findings are not intended to be generalizable to all states
target_learners: state education agencies
district and school leaders
policymakers
target_learning_goals: connecting school accountability systems to school improvement and improved student outcomes
examples: The paper illustrates Level 4 with Mississippi's literacy gains, combining horizontal coordination across agencies through the Literacy-Based Promotion Act and vertical collaboration across all levels of the education system
key_sources: Mitch Herz, Mel Wylen. (2025). Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons From Innovative State Approaches Under ESSA. White paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677595

article_title: Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons from Innovative State Approaches under ESSA
citation: Mitch Herz, Mel Wylen. (2025). Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons From Innovative State Approaches Under ESSA. White paper.
title: Four Key Tensions in Implementing Innovative Accountability Approaches
description: From case-study interviews and document review, the paper distills four tensions states navigate when implementing innovative accountability approaches: general versus targeted use of the system; accessible versus complex information; normative versus criterion-based approaches; and statewide requirements versus local flexibilities. The authors state, "Based on our interviews and document review conducted in the case studies, we distilled four key tensions as states attempted to implement innovative accountability approaches." Tensions operate across all levels of the hierarchy and manifest differently at each level.
requirements: Addressing these tensions in meaningful ways moves a system closer to improving integration within the education ecosystem
constraints: The tensions were distilled within the context of the four examined cases; a lack of clarity around these points can create additional challenges in achieving system goals
target_learners: state education agencies
district leaders
policymakers
target_learning_goals: designing and refining statewide accountability systems that support school improvement
examples: Utah's bottom-25-percent indicator is presented as a normative approach example; proficiency measures as the most common criterion-based form; summative school ratings as an accessibility-versus-complexity example

title: Ohio's Early Literacy Indicator within the SQSS Accountability Indicator
description: Ohio's accountability system includes an early literacy indicator tracking how well schools support K-3 students in developing reading skills, situated within the School Quality and Student Success indicator. Per the paper, "The Early Literacy Indicator tracks improvement in three areas: kindergarten readiness, grade 1 and grade 2 literacy improvement, and grade 3 reading proficiency." The accountability component formalizes commitment by tracking proficiency on the grade 3 ELA test, promotion to grade 4, and improvement among students previously off track, and is embedded in a broader ecosystem including the science of reading framework, dyslexia screening law, and mandated teacher PD.

Centralized data systems and infrastructure for data integration
constraints: With multiple state-approved vendors, some districts struggled to align local tools with state reporting expectations; differences in cut scores and timing added confusion

elementary educators
district leaders

citation: Mitch Herz, Mel Wylen. (2025). Refining Statewide School Accountability Systems: Lessons From Innovative State Approaches Under ESSA. White paper.
title: Utah's Lowest Quartile (LQ) Growth Indicator
description: Utah's accountability model includes a growth indicator focused on the lowest performing 25 percent of students in each school, developed under the Next Generation School Accountability initiative and required by state statute (Utah Code 53E-5-205) as a measure of equitable educational opportunity. The paper explains, "Using student growth percentiles (SGPs), the LQ metric captures the share of students in a school's lowest quartile who achieved typical or better growth from one year to the next." This normative approach lets schools be recognized for helping all students progress, not just those near proficiency thresholds.
requirements: Technical metrics like SGPs must be paired with strong communication with interest holders
Multiyear processes of advisory input, technical refinement, and educator engagement
constraints: Reliance on SGPs created interpretation challenges, especially in schools where year-over-year group sizes vary; some parents and educators viewed the term lowest 25 percent as stigmatizing; the indicator is underutilized by community interest holders

school and district leaders
target_learning_goals: academic growth of the lowest quartile of students and equitable educational opportunity
examples: The indicator was piloted and refined through Utah's Next Generation School Accountability vision with input from the Assessment and Accountability Policy Advisory Committee

article_title: Compass Care at Valor Collegiate Academies: Attendance Program Spotlight
citation: Zimiles, J., Nakamoto, J., & Boal, A. (2025). Compass Care at Valor Collegiate Academies: Attendance program spotlight. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Compass Care: a six-phase, family-centered wraparound program model for chronic absenteeism
description: Compass Care is a wraparound support model in which a dedicated Compass Care Team staff member works with chronically absent students and their caregivers over a 10-week cycle. The article describes it as "a family-centered wraparound program that leverages strengths-based practices to address the barriers that prevent students from attending and succeeding in school." The model serves 10 to 15 families per cycle and is consistently composed of six phases—referral, onboarding, engagement, action, transition, and sustainability—while remaining adaptable to school context.
requirements: A staff member from the Compass Care Team assigned to each school, implementing three to four cycles per school year
Families must consent to enrollment after outreach offering the program as support
constraints: The program can be adapted to align with the unique school context, but the six phases are constant
Piloted at a charter network of two middle schools and one high school; generalization evidence pending
target_learners: Students experiencing chronic absenteeism (missing at least 10 percent of school days)
Their caregivers
target_learning_goals: School attendance
Academic achievement
Student social and emotional well-being
Caregiver capacity to support students
examples: At Valor Collegiate Academies, Compass Care staff reviewed chronic-absence lists, solicited school-staff input, and enrolled families through outreach by email and phone

citation: Zimiles, J., Nakamoto, J., & Boal, A. (2025). Compass Care at Valor Collegiate Academies: Attendance program spotlight. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Six-phase program cycle from referral through post-program sustainability

A 10-week cycle during the school year with periodic follow-up in the subsequent three months

article_title: How English Learners Are Screened for Risk of Reading Difficulty: Use of English- and Spanish-Language Screeners in the 2023/24 School Year
citation: Soo Ping Chow, A., Faulkner-Bond, M., Lemke, M., LeBeau, B., & Quesen, S. (2025). How English learners are screened for risk of reading difficulty: Use of English- and Spanish-language screeners in the 2023/24 school year. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Five-cluster typology of English learner language-of-assessment screening practices
description: The brief uses k-modes clustering, a technique for identifying natural groups within categorical data, to sort English learners into five screening-practice clusters based on assessment language at each time of year. The solution that best reflected the sample showed "five primary practices in the screening of English learners": English-only at all periods (90%), both languages at all periods (8%), English all periods with Spanish at MOY/EOY (1%), alternating languages (under 1%), and Spanish all periods with English at EOY (under 1%). Clusters were characterized by program enrollment, native language, years in U.S. schools, and ACCESS performance.
requirements: Requires categorical assessment-taking data at each screening period (BOY, MOY, EOY) to assign students to clusters
constraints: Some students do not fit perfectly within a given cluster; students were assigned to the cluster that most closely aligned with their screening practices
Solutions with more than five clusters had redundant or indistinguishable clusters; fewer than five revealed no new meaningful groups
target_learners: English learners in grades K–3
target_learning_goals: Early literacy screening for risk of reading difficulty
examples: Cluster 1 (21,582 students) was screened only in English; cluster 4 (185 students) alternated Spanish at BOY, English at MOY, Spanish at EOY

article_title: Applying a Partially Nested Regression Model to Evaluate the Impact of ASSISTments on Middle School Students' Math Achievement
citation: Huang, C.-W., Feng, M., & Li, L. (2025). Applying a partially nested regression model to evaluate the impact of ASSISTments on middle school students' math achievement. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Virtual comparison group (VCG) construction via NWEA's matching algorithm
description: The VCG approach creates an equivalent virtual comparison for each treatment student: each treatment student was matched with up to 51 real students from NWEA's national MAP test database based on school locale, school-level FRL percentage, test-taking dates, grade level, and pretest scores; aggregated values were treated as a single virtual comparison student. Each virtual student received a comparison criteria level from 0 to 8, with smaller values indicating a closer match. Approximately 89 percent of virtual comparison students were within level 0 to 2.
requirements: Requires access to NWEA's extensive national MAP test database and its matching algorithm, plus treatment-group baseline scores and covariates (locale, FRL, test dates, grade, pretest).
constraints: Matching quality varies: criteria levels ranged from 0 to 8, with 9 virtual students (0.32%) at the loosest level 8; the approach is a proxy for an experimental control group, not random assignment.
target_learners: middle school students in grades 6-8
target_learning_goals: middle school mathematics achievement
examples: In this study, 1,578 virtual comparison students (55.27%) were exact matches at level 0, and the baseline equivalence effect size between groups was -0.03, which the authors say indicates the matching algorithm performed as expected.
key_sources: Huang, C.-W., Feng, M., & Li, L. (2025). Applying a partially nested regression model to evaluate the impact of ASSISTments on middle school students' math achievement. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677665

article_title: Applying a Partially Nested Regression Model to Evaluate the Impact of ASSISTments on Middle School Students' Math Achievement
citation: Huang, C.-W., Feng, M., & Li, L. (2025). Applying a partially nested regression model to evaluate the impact of ASSISTments on middle school students' math achievement. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Partially nested regression model for matched-comparison designs with treatment-only clustering
description: The partially nested (PN) RCT model of Lohr et al. (2014) handles designs in which treatment students are nested in groups (teachers or intervention clusters) but comparison students are not. Instead of treating the treatment-effect coefficient as fixed, the model treats it as a random effect with an error term, allowing additional variation at the cluster level for the treatment group only. The authors apply it to a quasi-experimental matched comparison design, including pretest scores as a covariate, suppressing the Level 2 random intercept, and modeling independent residual variances that differ by treatment condition.
requirements: Requires creating intervention-cluster (IC) values for the virtual comparison group as singleton clusters via generated markup teacher identification numbers, and fitting via REML with Satterthwaite degrees-of-freedom approximation as recommended by Lohr et al. (2014).
constraints: The model was designed for RCTs with treatment-only nesting; the authors note it can also be applied to a QED, especially a matched comparison group design, following Lohr et al. (2014).
target_learners: middle school students in grades 6-8
target_learning_goals: estimating intervention effects on math achievement in partially nested quasi-experimental designs
examples: The authors fit the model in Stata with a random slope for treat at Level 2, noconstant to suppress the random intercept, and residuals(independent, by(treat)); the estimated IC-level variance was 11.86, with Level 1 residual variances of 71.48 (treatment) and 2.88 (VCG).

title: vPLC-augmented ASSISTments intervention with four-step formative assessment process
description: The intervention combines WPI's ASSISTments online math platform with a virtual professional learning community (vPLC) designed to enhance scalability, reducing travel and scheduling barriers especially for rural districts. middle school math teachers, including those in rural districts

teachers' use of ASSISTments reports to differentiate instruction and adjust teaching

title: ASSISTments platform with the four steps of formative assessment
description: ASSISTments is "a free, web-based formative assessment platform for teachers and students in grades 3 through 12" that delivers immediate feedback, hints, explanations, and step-by-step scaffolds while generating color-coded class- and student-level reports. Its use is standardized into four steps of formative assessment: Assign standards-aligned problem sets, Practice with immediate feedback, Assess reports to identify patterns and errors, and Review selected problems using anonymized projected data. The intervention paired the platform with a virtual professional learning community to train rural middle school teachers.

constraints: Home internet or device access limits out-of-school use, so the study found in-class use more equitable

formative assessment practices

article_title: Scaling Teachers' Professional Development for ASSISTments Companion Report: Implementation Analysis of the ASSISTments Intervention
citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments companion report: Implementation analysis of the ASSISTments intervention. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Virtual professional learning community (vPLC) for ASSISTments teacher training
description: The vPLC is a virtual professional learning model designed to connect rural and geographically isolated teachers with peers and learning opportunities. It consisted of eight 75-minute virtual facilitated sessions during the school year, supplemented by asynchronous activities, led with three core goals: supporting effective ASSISTments use following the four steps, engaging teachers in analysis-of-practice, and modeling NCTM norms of excellent math teaching. Teachers responded positively: most (87%) participated fully, and about half rated the vPLC as comparable to or better than other professional development they had experienced.
requirements: Trained facilitators, a facilitation guide, and session structures such as breakout-room discussions with peer teachers
constraints: Designed for teachers with limited access to in-person PLCs; rural vPLCs are more effective when flexible, interactive, relevant, and ongoing, per the article's cited research
target_learners: rural middle school math teachers and teachers lacking peer networks or in-person professional learning access
target_learning_goals: effective use of ASSISTments and the four steps of formative assessment
data-informed math instruction
professional community building
examples: Session themes included using ASSISTments data and common wrong answers to inform instruction and framing mistakes as part of learning

Students complete regular assignments built from OER curriculum problems (Illustrative Math, EngageNY) and mastery-oriented Skill Builders, receiving "immediate feedback on the correctness of answers"; they "cannot proceed to the next problem until they have correctly solved the current one". Teachers view real-time grid-format reports showing per-question accuracy, common wrong answers, and individual student responses, which they use to target instruction and form groups.

citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., Huang, C.-W., Luttgen, K., Grady, J., Yang, S., Lavine, A., Collins, K., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments: Evaluation final report. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Virtual professional learning community (vPLC): eight 75-minute synchronous sessions with asynchronous Slack activities, facilitated by former teachers
description: The vPLC is a scalable professional learning model designed to support effective ASSISTments implementation, particularly in rural and underresourced settings. "Teachers participated in eight 75-minute virtual sessions, each preceded by thought-provoking asynchronous activities delivered via Slack", facilitated by two former middle school teachers using a facilitation guide. Sessions follow a consistent structure including icebreakers, a Story From the Field, breakout discussions in small groups, a Teachers' Lounge segment, and digital sticky-note reflections.
requirements: Treatment teachers were expected to attend at least seven of eight synchronous vPLC sessions held between September and February and to complete at least four of eight asynchronous activities on Slack.
constraints: The vPLC was designed for rural educators who often lack access to local PLCs or peer networks; an optional ninth and tenth session were provided.
target_learners: Rural middle school math teachers in grades 6-8
target_learning_goals: Effective use of ASSISTments, formative assessment practice, and data-driven instructional decision-making

citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., Huang, C.-W., Luttgen, K., Grady, J., Yang, S., Lavine, A., Collins, K., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments: Evaluation final report. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Four-step formative assessment cycle: create assignments, assist students through immediate feedback, assess class performance, analyze answers together
description: The report organizes the intervention around a "4-step formative assessment process (Heritage & Popham, 2013) that is integrated throughout the ASSISTments platform": (1) create assignments aligned with grade-level standards using OERs or Skill Builders; (2) assist students through immediate feedback, hints, and explanations; (3) assess class performance by reviewing reports to identify needs; and (4) analyze answers together by projecting anonymized reports for whole-class discussion of misconceptions. The vPLC embedded this cycle across its session content.
requirements: Teachers must review performance reports to identify student needs and inform future instruction, and project anonymized reports for whole-class review.
constraints: The cycle's ultimate goal, as stated, is to improve student math achievement; sessions 2 through 6 each highlighted different report features to build teachers' instructional toolkit over time.
target_learners: Middle school math teachers and their grade 6-8 students
target_learning_goals: Formative assessment practice and improved student math achievement
examples: Session 7 focused on the fourth step, analyzing answers together, including strategically sequencing and sharing student work leveraging ASSISTments open responses.

citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., Huang, C.-W., Luttgen, K., Grady, J., Yang, S., Lavine, A., Collins, K., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments: Evaluation final report. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Analysis-of-practice vPLC session pattern: teacher-shared stories, breakout discussion grounded in teachers' own classrooms, and peer-to-peer exchange
description: The vPLC's reusable session pattern is grounded in "the analysis-of-practice model, an evidence-based approach to improving instruction through collaborative reflection (Taylor et al., 2017)". Each session opens with norms and an icebreaker, features a Story From the Field in which a participating teacher shares a real instructional experience, moves through facilitator-led concept introduction or platform demonstration, then small-group discussion referencing teachers' own classrooms, assignments, and student data, and closes with informal peer Q&A and reflection.
requirements: Facilitators experienced in using ASSISTments and a facilitation guide grounded in best practices for professional learning are needed to run the sessions.
constraints: The format is participant-driven and responsive, with teachers actively shaping each session by contributing their own practices and pedagogical insights.
target_learners: Practicing middle school math teachers, including those in rural or professionally isolated settings
target_learning_goals: Collaborative reflection on instruction and integration of ASSISTments into classroom routines

citation: Hannan, M., Rainier, S., & Perry, R. (2026). Beyond curriculum adoption: What district leaders are saying about using Illustrative Mathematics. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: The implementation chain: HQIM implementation as a phased, multi-level, multi-year system process
description: This report frames HQIM implementation through CCSSO's "implementation chain," in which coordinated actions must occur across levels of the education system, where "each level is responsible for creating coherence for the next level" (2025, p. 8). CCSSO's analysis proposes five phases unfolding over 4 or more years: exploration, program installation, initial implementation, consistent implementation, and innovation and sustainability. The report uses this framework to organize district leaders' accounts of IM implementation as an ongoing, cyclical process rather than a one-time adoption event.
requirements: Successful HQIM uptake necessitates coordinated, integrated actions across the levels of the school system
constraints: The report states the duration of the phases is likely variable between contexts and curricula and can vary from school to school within a district
target_learners: Grades 6–8 mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Consistent, coherent use of adopted high-quality instructional materials in mathematics
examples: The report's five interview themes are organized to reflect implementation as a cyclical process, from vision-setting through equity refinement

article_title: Measuring What Matters: Considerations for Measuring the Implementation of High-Quality Instructional Materials in Mathematics
citation: Perry, R., Nucci, D., Walters, K., McKinney, D., Nielsen, S., & Hannan, M. (2026). Measuring what matters: Considerations for measuring the implementation of high-quality instructional materials in mathematics. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Curriculum enactment as a translation process from official curriculum through teacher-intended curriculum to enacted curriculum
description: The report conceptualizes instructional materials as "resources that specify intended teacher and student interactions with mathematics" and frames implementation as a chain of translations: official curriculum, teacher-intended curriculum, and enacted curriculum. Figure 1 depicts a dynamic system with official and operational sections, reciprocal feedback from student outcomes to enacted and intended curricula, and external factors shaping all stages. Teachers add, modify, and omit curricular elements based on attitudes, beliefs, and goals, so the enacted curriculum is a personalized, flexible version of the intended one.
requirements: Understanding enactment requires data from multiple actors in the translation chain, including curriculum developers, district leaders, teachers, and students
constraints: The report notes teachers must make professional decisions in complex, dynamic environments, so intended interactions seldom go as planned
target_learners: middle grades (6–8) mathematics students
target_learning_goals: mathematics learning through standards-aligned core curriculum implementation
examples: The study's four research questions and instruments are organized around capturing each translation stage, from developer intent to student experience
key_sources: Perry, R., Nucci, D., Walters, K., McKinney, D., Nielsen, S., & Hannan, M. (2026). Measuring what matters: Considerations for measuring the implementation of high-quality instructional materials in mathematics. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681340

article_title: Measuring What Matters: Considerations for Measuring the Implementation of High-Quality Instructional Materials in Mathematics
citation: Perry, R., Nucci, D., Walters, K., McKinney, D., Nielsen, S., & Hannan, M. (2026). Measuring what matters: Considerations for measuring the implementation of high-quality instructional materials in mathematics. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Five-dimension framework for operationalizing HQIM implementation fidelity: dosage, adherence, instructional quality, student experience, and support
description: The report defines implementation as "a reduction in the translational difference between the essential, intended design elements of the curriculum and its enactment in classrooms" and operationalizes five dimensions. Dosage captures how much of the official curriculum teachers use; adherence captures following prescribed units, lessons, and sequence; instructional quality captures alignment of instruction with intended interactions; student experience captures students' perceptions of opportunities to learn; and support captures district and school professional learning. The framework treats implementation as contextual, informed by professional learning that shapes teachers' decisions to add, modify, or omit curriculum elements.
requirements: Measuring fidelity requires identifying which dimensions are core to the intervention, and the report notes a minimum fidelity threshold is not always clearly specified
constraints: Classroom-based interventions like HQIM add complexity because teachers make professional decisions in dynamic environments; the framework was designed for middle-grades mathematics and the team did not anticipate generalizing beyond the middle grades
target_learners: middle grades (6–8) mathematics students and their teachers
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of curriculum implementation to attribute student outcomes to programs
examples: Table 1 maps each fidelity dimension to specific teacher-survey items, such as percentage of class time using the core curriculum for dosage and frequency of instructional practices for quality
key_sources: Perry, R., Nucci, D., Walters, K., McKinney, D., Nielsen, S., & Hannan, M. (2026). Measuring what matters: Considerations for measuring the implementation of high-quality instructional materials in mathematics. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED681340

article_title: Measuring What Matters: Considerations for Measuring the Implementation of High-Quality Instructional Materials in Mathematics
citation: Perry, R., Nucci, D., Walters, K., McKinney, D., Nielsen, S., & Hannan, M. (2026). Measuring what matters: Considerations for measuring the implementation of high-quality instructional materials in mathematics. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Tri-annual teacher survey operationalizing dosage, adherence, instructional quality, and support
description: A teacher self-report survey administered "three times annually during the 2024–2027 study period" to all participating grades 6–8 teachers, designed to take no longer than 30 minutes per administration. The team chose self-reporting as "the least burdensome and most reliable strategy" given the logistical and fiscal challenges of direct observation in a national study. Items are drawn where possible from nationally validated surveys and operationalize dosage (units taught, percentage of class time using the core curriculum), adherence (skipping, supplementing, modifying), instructional quality (frequency of teacher and student instructional practices), and support (professional learning hours, usefulness ratings, and planning collaboration).
requirements: Requires teacher self-report items from nationally validated surveys and aggregation of responses to create individual implementation measures comparable across districts using different programs
constraints: The report acknowledges the challenges related to the reliability of self-report data and notes locally gathered fidelity data cannot be relied on because districts use different programs and measures
target_learners: grades 6–8 mathematics teachers in participating districts
target_learning_goals: measuring curriculum dosage, adherence, instructional quality, and professional learning support for impact models
examples: The survey replicates a 2018 National Survey of Science and Mathematics Education adherence question with options from Not at all to To a great extent, used to create a single adherence score with low, moderate, and high cut scores

title: Short student survey measuring mathematical experiences, sense of belonging, and mathematics self-efficacy
description: A student-facing instrument, taking "no longer than 15 minutes to complete," administered at the beginning and end of each school year to triangulate teacher self-reports of implementation. It uses the same construct categories as the teacher survey—coherence, cognitive demand, collaboration and discourse, formative assessment, and differentiation—with items drawn from existing valid and reliable instruments. It includes belonging items, described as a significant predictor of motivation, and "Nine additional survey items were also included to replicate a reliable self-efficacy scale." The team plans exploratory factor analysis and correlation plots to compare teacher and student reports.
requirements: Requires items drawn from existing valid and reliable survey instruments and administration at the beginning and end of each school year
constraints: The report notes classroom practice may not meet a coherence standard for implementation fidelity if teachers' and students' reports differ, which is why student-facing instruments were created

target_learning_goals: capturing student experience of mathematical opportunities to learn and classroom interactions
examples: Illustrative Mathematics provides a Building a Mathematical Community Plan with student prompts and ways to make student thinking visible, an example of curriculum features aimed at belonging and self-efficacy
