article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review
citation: Fronius, Darling-Hammond, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2019). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review. WestEd Justice & Prevention Research Center. http://jprc.wested.org/
title: Integrate restorative justice school- and district-wide rather than as an add-on program to sustain it
description: This principle holds that RJ practices work best when embedded in a school's overall philosophy and formal policy rather than run as a bolt-on program. The review states that "one way to sustain RJ practices is to integrate them across the school and district rather than having RJ be an add-on program," and that such integration is often described as "Whole School Restorative Justice." Oakland research is cited as suggesting integration is more effective across a range of outcomes than reaction-based practices alone.
requirements: District integration of the RJ approach into formal policy and procedures, with decisions about discipline considering multiple stakeholders including teachers, administrators, youth, parents, and community members
constraints: The review notes this implementation information is not backed by rigorous scientific evidence such as randomized controlled trials supporting causal claims about which steps are helpful or essential
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Improved school climate, reduced exclusionary discipline, and sustained restorative practice implementation
examples: The review cites Oakland research (Jain et al., 2014) suggesting integration throughout the school is substantially more effective than limited, reaction-based RJ practices, and a Detroit district leveraging Title I funding to hire a full-time RJ coordinator.
key_sources: Fronius, Darling-Hammond, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2019). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review. WestEd Justice & Prevention Research Center. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED595733

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review
citation: Fronius, Darling-Hammond, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2019). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review. WestEd Justice & Prevention Research Center. http://jprc.wested.org/
title: Reintegrative shaming, procedural justice, and defiance theory as theoretical frameworks underlying restorative justice in schools
description: The review organizes RJ's theoretical grounding around three accounts. Reintegrative shaming theory distinguishes shaming that leads to "reconciliation with and reacceptance of the wrongdoer" from stigmatizing shaming that isolates the offender. Procedural justice holds that giving students voice in decision-making leads them to view institutional power as more legitimate and fair. Defiance theory warns that absent perceived legitimacy and fairness, young people may respond with defiance and future infractions. Together these frameworks support RJ's potential for stronger school community and fewer behavioral issues.
requirements: Educators must be able to recognize how to use shame as a path toward reintegration rather than stigmatization, a line the review notes is fine and easily crossed
constraints: Critics argue reintegrative shaming may have unintended harmful effects in school settings (Vaandering, 2010, as cited in the review)
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Increased student perceptions of fairness and legitimacy of school discipline, greater compliance, and stronger school community
examples: The review describes reintegrative shaming materializing as direct actions such as requiring a student to publicly apologize, or indirect actions such as a teacher expressing disappointment to a student's parent.
key_sources: Fronius, Darling-Hammond, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2019). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review. WestEd Justice & Prevention Research Center. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED595733

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review
citation: Fronius, Darling-Hammond, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2019). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review. WestEd Justice & Prevention Research Center. http://jprc.wested.org/
title: Restorative justice implementation guides and toolkits for schools and districts
description: The review compiles a table of publicly available guides and toolkits that "provide more information on the steps to consider when starting an RJ program in a school or district." These include The Advancement Project's educator guide (2014), the Denver School-Based Restorative Practices Partnership's step-by-step guide (2017), Kidde & Alfred's Alameda County working guide (2011), the Restorative Interventions Implementation Toolkit (Beckman, McMorris, & Gower, 2012), and the Oakland Unified School District whole-school implementation guide (2014), each with a printed source URL.
requirements: Administrators and educators need access to the tools and resources necessary to successfully fund, implement, and evaluate their RJ program
constraints: The review notes the implementation steps these resources describe are not backed by rigorous scientific evidence such as randomized controlled trials
target_learners: K-12 school and district administrators and educators implementing RJ programs
target_learning_goals: Funding, implementing, and sustaining restorative justice programs in schools and districts
examples: The review's Table 1 lists five resources with authors, years, and source URLs, including the Oakland Unified School District Restorative Justice Implementation Guide: A Whole School Approach.
key_sources: Fronius, Darling-Hammond, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2019). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: An Updated Research Review. WestEd Justice & Prevention Research Center. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED595733

article_title: Next Generation Science Standards in Practice: Tools and Processes Used by the California NGSS Early Implementers
citation: Tyler, B., & DiRanna, K. (2018). Next Generation Science Standards in practice: Tools and processes used by the California NGSS Early Implementers. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Criteria for Choosing Phenomena tool with anchoring and investigative phenomena categories
description: The Initiative defines phenomena as "occurrences in the natural and human-made world that can be observed and cause one to wonder and ask questions" and distinguishes two types by scale: anchoring phenomena, which are "larger in scale and are the focus of instructional units (i.e., instruction over multiple weeks)", and investigative phenomena, which serve as foci of multi-day learning sequences. The tool provides guiding questions for instructors choosing phenomena, developed in collaboration with #ProjectPhenomena and the San Diego County Office of Education.
requirements: Phenomena must be selected to match target learning outcomes and spark curiosity, taking into account local context, student ability levels, interests, and previous experiences
constraints: The NGSS do not specify which phenomena to use because phenomena need to be relevant to the students in each community
target_learners: K-8 students in participating California districts
target_learning_goals: Three-dimensional NGSS science understanding: explaining phenomena using SEPs, DCIs, and CCCs
examples: Guiding questions include whether students can observe or investigate the phenomenon firsthand or through someone else's experiences, whether explanations would be grade-level appropriate, and whether the phenomenon is relevant to real-world issues or the students' local environment
key_sources: Tyler, B., & DiRanna, K. (2018). Next Generation Science Standards in practice: Tools and processes used by the California NGSS Early Implementers. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED596757

article_title: Next Generation Science Standards in Practice: Tools and Processes Used by the California NGSS Early Implementers
citation: Tyler, B., & DiRanna, K. (2018). Next Generation Science Standards in practice: Tools and processes used by the California NGSS Early Implementers. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Phenomena-based, three-dimensional conceptual flow for mapping a multi-week NGSS unit storyline
description: The conceptual flow is "a process for graphically mapping the storyline of a three-dimensional (3D) NGSS instructional unit lasting six to eight weeks or longer", carried out collaboratively by same-grade teachers in five steps: identify an anchor phenomenon, individually pre-think needed concepts, create a collaborative cluster map, match SEPs, DCIs, and CCCs to the grade level, and sequence concepts into a coherent graphic. The graphic differs from a concept map by also showing the hierarchy of ideas and the sequence for instruction, and serves as a reference for planning the learning sequences within the unit.
requirements: Collaborative development through conversation with colleagues; the report states much of the value resides in the collaborative experience rather than the product alone
constraints: Development is time-intensive; conceptual flows are often modified over time with a mindset of continuous improvement
target_learners: K-8 students; the pattern is used by teachers of grades K-8
target_learning_goals: Coherent, student-centered NGSS unit design integrating science and engineering practices, disciplinary core ideas, and crosscutting concepts
examples: A Grade 5 conceptual flow for the unit "What's in Our Water?" with the anchor phenomenon that sewage water can be made drinkable, connected investigative phenomena, CCCs, SEPs, and DCIs, with each column representing a learning sequence
key_sources: Tyler, B., & DiRanna, K. (2018). Next Generation Science Standards in practice: Tools and processes used by the California NGSS Early Implementers. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED596757

article_title: Next Generation Science Standards in Practice: Tools and Processes Used by the California NGSS Early Implementers
citation: Tyler, B., & DiRanna, K. (2018). Next Generation Science Standards in practice: Tools and processes used by the California NGSS Early Implementers. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: 5E instructional model (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate) for developing NGSS learning sequences
description: The 5E instructional model, originally developed by BSCS (Bybee et al., 2006), is used by Early Implementers to develop learning sequences of multiple lessons, each based on an investigative phenomenon from the conceptual flow. It is "based on the constructivist approach to learning, which says that learners build new ideas on top of prior knowledge and understanding", and its five stages move from capturing interest and eliciting prior knowledge through exploration, student explanation, application, and evaluation occurring throughout the cycle. Teachers plan each stage with a backwards design recording the 3D concepts, what the teacher does, and what the student does.
requirements: Planning driven by student questioning, experience, and discussion; each stage records a three-dimensional concept including specific DCIs, SEPs, and CCCs
constraints: Because NGSS calls for 3D instruction, a learning sequence is seldom completed in a single class period
target_learners: K-8 students in Early Implementer districts
target_learning_goals: Student-centered, inquiry-based science lessons building deep conceptual understanding rather than memory of facts
examples: Nine grade K-8 NGSS Early Implementer Learning Sequences were created and field tested, such as Kindergarten Pushes and Pulls, 5th Grade What's in Your Water?, and 8th Grade Understanding White Sharks
key_sources: Tyler, B., & DiRanna, K. (2018). Next Generation Science Standards in practice: Tools and processes used by the California NGSS Early Implementers. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED596757

article_title: Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: A Research Review
citation: Fronius, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2016). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: A Research Review. WestEd. http://jprc.wested.org
title: Restorative justice theoretical frameworks: reintegrative shaming, procedural justice, and defiance theory
description: The review organizes RJ's theoretical basis around three accounts. Reintegrative shaming (Braithwaite) shames wrongdoing while reintegrating the offender into the community rather than isolating them; procedural justice (Tyler) holds that giving students voice in decision-making increases perceived legitimacy and compliance; and defiance theory links perceived illegitimacy and unfairness to defiance and future infractions. Together, "The perspectives of reintegrative shaming, procedural justice, and defiance theory all support the potential of RJ in leading to a stronger school community, better climate, and fewer behavioral issues." The review uses these frameworks to explain why RJ might reduce punitive discipline while building relationships.
requirements: Educators must be able to use shame as a path toward reintegration rather than stigmatization, which the review says educators may not always recognize
constraints: Critics argue reintegrative shaming may have unintended harmful effects in school settings (Vaandering, 2010); there is a fine line between supportive and stigmatizing shame
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Building positive school climate, student accountability, and behavioral self-regulation through relationship repair
examples: The review describes reintegrative shaming materializing as direct actions such as requiring a public apology or indirect actions such as a teacher expressing disappointment to a parent
key_sources: Fronius, Persson, Guckenburg, Hurley, & Petrosino. (2016). Restorative Justice in U.S. Schools: A Research Review. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED596786

article_title: What Accelerates a Community of Practice? Inflection Points That Changed the Course of the Math in Common Initiative
citation: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). What accelerates a community of practice? Inflection points that changed the course of the Math in Common Initiative. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/project/math-in-common-evaluation/
title: Four organizing structures built the Math in Common community of practice: district leadership teams, guiding principles with annual improvement plans, in-person learning opportunities, and access to diverse expertise
description: The MiC CoP was built on four primary organizing structures identified in the initiative's first phase: "District MiC leadership teams to engage in the work," a set of guiding principles and annual improvement plans, in-person learning opportunities in a variety of formats, and access to individuals with a broad range of diverse expertise. These structures guided the CoP's five-year work and created opportunities for later inflection points. In-person formats included fall, winter, and spring two-day convenings, expert-led workshops, and site-visit consultancies.
requirements: A convening organization to run meetings, review proposals, and help organize district leadership teams
District-selected MiC coordinators acting as liaisons between districts, the CoP, and partners
constraints: The authors note the four structures are far from a complete set of influences, omitting informal participant-driven connections among members
target_learners: District MiC leadership team members (administrators, math specialists, principals) in K-8 districts implementing CCSS-M
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning about mathematics standards implementation
Cross-district sharing of instructional materials and best practices
examples: Two-day convenings three times per school year served as the primary organizing mechanism for districts' annual cycles of inquiry
Site-visit consultancies, such as Oakland Unified's January 2016 showcase of lesson study, drew participation from teams in eight MiC districts
key_sources: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). What accelerates a community of practice? Inflection points that changed the course of the Math in Common Initiative. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/project/math-in-common-evaluation/

article_title: From the Brink of Closure: Key Factors in One Charter School's Successful Turnaround
citation: Evan, A. (2019). From the brink of closure: Key factors in one charter school's successful turnaround. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://dcpcsb.egnyte.com/dl/hdsUO9pDbh/
title: TenSquare's Data-Driven School Improvement Process
description: A continuous-improvement cycle in which a turnaround partner first conducts a comprehensive school performance audit covering academic, financial, and operational areas, then develops a multi-year redesign plan prioritized by intensity of focus, identifies evidence-based interventions, monitors implementation and impact toward goals, adjusts implementation, and provides ongoing feedback. At Perry Street the process began with an audit "to identify the areas in need of improvement — from academic to financial to operational" and its findings "served as the basis for the creation of a multifaceted five-year redesign plan."
requirements: A comprehensive baseline audit of performance, processes, and resources to set improvement goals
Ongoing progress-monitoring structures at board, leadership, and staff levels
constraints: The report presents this as one school's process; it states no framework should be a magic bullet and decisions should consider each school's needs and context
target_learners: Charter school leaders, board members, and authorizers pursuing school turnaround
target_learning_goals: School-wide organizational improvement and improved student achievement outcomes
examples: TenSquare's five-year engagement at Perry Street from May 2014 through 2018–19, moving from intense daily support to feedback-only consultation
key_sources: Evan, A. (2019). From the brink of closure: Key factors in one charter school's successful turnaround. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://dcpcsb.egnyte.com/dl/hdsUO9pDbh/

article_title: From the Brink of Closure: Key Factors in One Charter School's Successful Turnaround
citation: Evan, A. (2019). From the brink of closure: Key factors in one charter school's successful turnaround. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://dcpcsb.egnyte.com/dl/hdsUO9pDbh/
title: Five-Component Framework for Systemic School Turnaround
description: TenSquare's framework holds that successful turnaround requires transforming five core components in tandem: board and leadership, talent, teaching and learning, culture, and operations and finance. The report states the approach "centered on transforming five core components" and that working on any one component in isolation "results in turnaround efforts that quickly deteriorate." Each component had defined content, e.g., teaching and learning included curriculum and assessment alignment to standards and evidence-based instructional practices.
requirements: Simultaneous attention to all five components rather than isolated improvement efforts
constraints: The report cautions that "No framework should be a magic bullet" and implementation must fit the school's needs and context
target_learners: School leaders, boards, and turnaround partners in low-performing charter schools
target_learning_goals: Comprehensive organizational transformation supporting student achievement
examples: Perry Street overhauled leadership structure, talent systems, curriculum alignment to PARCC, PBIS behavior systems, and budget reallocation
key_sources: Evan, A. (2019). From the brink of closure: Key factors in one charter school's successful turnaround. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://dcpcsb.egnyte.com/dl/hdsUO9pDbh/

article_title: Educators Collaborating to Improve Mathematics: Three Structures That Mattered in Math in Common Districts
citation: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Educators collaborating to improve mathematics: Three structures that mattered in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org/permissions
title: Three key collaborative structures for changing the dynamics of classroom instruction during standards implementation
description: The report proposes that standards implementation in mathematics rests on three collaborative structures: role-diverse sense-making teams, strategic partnerships with technical assistance providers, and empowered site-based leaders. The authors observed that "one important strategy to guide this change comes from diverse groups of educators working together to create coherence and alignment of effort within a district system." The structures share functions: supporting iterative shared understanding, cross-group collaboration, and adult learning practices.
requirements: All educators and staff across the district system must be involved in the learning agenda; the report states no one can be left out
constraints: The framework derives from observations of 10 California districts implementing the CCSS-M under the Math in Common initiative, not from a controlled comparison
target_learners: K-8 teachers and district educators in public school districts
target_learning_goals: Implementing standards-aligned mathematics instruction and shifting classroom instructional dynamics
examples: Math in Common districts developed these structures over five years to interpret the CCSS-M and shift classroom instruction
key_sources: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Educators collaborating to improve mathematics: Three structures that mattered in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org/permissions

article_title: Educators Collaborating to Improve Mathematics: Three Structures That Mattered in Math in Common Districts
citation: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Educators collaborating to improve mathematics: Three structures that mattered in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org/permissions
title: Role-diverse sense-making teams that interpret standards and carry a consistent districtwide message
description: This pattern brings together staff from many roles — teachers, coaches, principals, math department staff, and district administrators — to interpret standards, create implementation visions, and promote them systemwide. The report states these teams "can interpret and make sense of standards, create visions for the standards implementation in the real contexts of the district and its classrooms, and then protect and promote these visions throughout the system." Teams functioned as PLCs or task-focused groups working on instructional materials, observation tools, or parent education.
requirements: Teams must be a diverse and complementary mix of system leaders and educators representing varying roles, perspectives, and expertise from across the district
Collaboration must be intentionally centered on shifting a particular facet of the dynamics of classroom instruction or a specific monitoring structure
constraints: The report notes districts experienced repeated leadership turnover; participating staff served as keepers of the vision amid organizational turmoil
target_learners: District administrators, principals, coaches, and teachers implementing new standards
target_learning_goals: Developing shared understanding of standards and consistent messaging about standards-aligned instruction
examples: Dinuba Unified developed a classroom observation rubric and protocol through a role-diverse team, recalibrating as principals and coaches joined
Oakland used a site-based mini-grant program to incentivize role-diverse teams to write standards-implementation plans
key_sources: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Educators collaborating to improve mathematics: Three structures that mattered in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org/permissions

article_title: Educators Collaborating to Improve Mathematics: Three Structures That Mattered in Math in Common Districts
citation: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Educators collaborating to improve mathematics: Three structures that mattered in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org/permissions
title: Strategic partnerships with technical assistance providers built on collaborative inquiry and district vision
description: This pattern describes district partnerships with external technical assistance providers that are targeted and responsive to local context rather than generic. The report states successful partnerships "frequently started with both parties seeking clarity about the goals of their collaborative work together, and with willingness to engage in an ongoing relationship built on honest communication, inquiry, vulnerability, and trust." Providers supported professional learning, materials review, and districtwide adult learning strategies.
requirements: Districts and providers must seek clarity about shared goals and commit to an ongoing relationship of honest communication and trust
Partnerships often begin with heavier initial district investment in time and resources, moderated as district capacity grows
constraints: The report notes much of this assistance was funded by finite MiC grant funds, and sustainability depended on districts building their own capacity
target_learners: District leaders, coaches, and teachers contracting with external expertise
target_learning_goals: Building internal district capacity for standards-aligned mathematics instruction
examples: Garden Grove partnered with the Irvine Math Project to build TOSA capacity to lead summer institutes, leaning less on the provider over time
key_sources: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Educators collaborating to improve mathematics: Three structures that mattered in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.WestEd.org/permissions

article_title: Roadblocks and Routes: Professional Development in Math in Common Districts
citation: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Roadblocks and routes: Professional development in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/permissions
title: Structuring PLCs with clear purpose and collaborative-work frameworks (High-Leverage Team Actions)
description: Because PLCs without clarity of purpose may drift toward undirected planning or devolve into coffee chats, MiC districts organized PLCs more intentionally over time. Tim Kanold's High-Leverage Team Actions (HLTAs), 10 activities for collaborative work based on NCTM's Principles to Actions, encouraged "a focus on mathematics (with activities organized around a unit of study) and a process for iterative improvement of a PLC's capacity." Dinuba paired HLTAs with coach support, PLC-leader meetings, principal sessions, process maps, and reflection rubrics.
requirements: Structures that guide clarity of purpose for teachers' collaborative time
Support such as coach guidance, leader capacity-building, and monitoring (e.g., PLC team logs, reflection data)
constraints: Research cited in the report notes teachers do not always find PLCs helpful learning structures, and fostering collaboration is difficult to do well and not a guaranteed path to improved outcomes
target_learners: K–8 mathematics teachers in PLC teams
PLC leaders
Site administrators
target_learning_goals: Improving collaborative teacher learning around mathematics instruction, high-cognitive-demand tasks, and formative assessment
examples: Dinuba Unified introduced HLTAs after a 2014 MiC convening, added monthly 90-minute PLC lead huddles in 2017–18, and monitored success via teacher reflection data and PLC team logs
key_sources: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Roadblocks and routes: Professional development in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/permissions

article_title: Roadblocks and Routes: Professional Development in Math in Common Districts
citation: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Roadblocks and routes: Professional development in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/permissions
title: Develop an array of differentiated PD strategies rather than one-size-fits-all PD
description: Based on five years of observations, the report recommends that districts "Develop an array of PD strategies for differentiating in-service support, to enable useful learning for all teachers," following multiple routes rather than one-size-fits-all PD. Because teachers' prior experience and training may not prepare them for standards implementation, districts should organize many different PD formats and experiences reflecting the diverse ways people learn.
requirements: Funding or reallocated resources to support multiple PD formats and teachers' collaborative work
constraints: The report notes large pull-out PD days can default to a sit-and-get model disconnected from daily classroom work, and out-of-contract-time PD suffered sub-optimal attendance
target_learners: K–8 mathematics teachers with diverse prior experience and training
target_learning_goals: Effective implementation of new mathematics standards
examples: MiC districts used summer institutes, after-school trainings, book studies, lesson study, site-based PLCs, online repositories and PD modules, and coaching, differentiating by teacher needs
key_sources: Perry, R., Marple, S., & Reade, F. (2019). Roadblocks and routes: Professional development in Math in Common districts. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/permissions

article_title: A Cross-State Evaluation of MIND Research Institute's ST Math Program and Math Performance
citation: Wendt, S., Rice, J., & Nakamoto, J. (2019). A cross-state evaluation of MIND Research Institute's ST Math program and math performance. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: ST Math: game-based instructional software teaching math through visual puzzles
description: ST Math is a game-based instructional software program for K-12 students created by the MIND Research Institute, whose stated purpose is to boost math comprehension through visual learning. The software "games begin without language or symbol abstractions by posing math problems as purely visual puzzles," with interactive animated manipulatives giving informative feedback and 100 percent puzzle scores required to progress through levels. The games follow JiJi, a cartoon penguin, and the program is integrated into classroom instruction but can also be used in a computer lab or at home.
requirements: Puzzle scores of 100 percent are required for progression through the levels
target_learners: K-12 students
elementary students in grades 3-5 (evaluation population)
target_learning_goals: mathematics comprehension through visual learning
examples: Evaluated across 474 treatment schools in 16 states using state standardized math assessment outcomes for grades 3-5
key_sources: Wendt, S., Rice, J., & Nakamoto, J. (2019). A cross-state evaluation of MIND Research Institute's ST Math program and math performance. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED601907

article_title: Understanding the Experiences of LGBTQ Students in California
citation: Hanson, T., Zhang, G., Cerna, R., Stern, A., & Austin, G. (2019). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ students in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Three fundamental developmental supports — caring adult relationships, high expectations, and meaningful participation — as protective factors in schools
description: The report organizes its school supports domain around three CHKS-measured developmental supports: "caring adult relationships, high expectations for students, and opportunities for meaningful participation in the classroom and school community." It argues these supports meet basic developmental needs, serve as protective factors mitigating risk factors youth experience, and foster psychological safety and school connectedness linked to positive academic, behavioral, and personal outcomes including resiliency. The report argues their implementation by school staff should be a top priority for LGBTQ youth, given evidence that LGBTQ youth experience lower adult support.
requirements: School staff must provide the supports; the report argues teacher training and professional development are important to improving teacher responsiveness to LGBTQ students' needs.
constraints: The report's own evidence for the supports' role in explaining LGBTQ disparities is correlational, based on cross-sectional CHKS data and a particular statistical model.
target_learners: Middle and high school students in California public schools, including LGBTQ students
target_learning_goals: School connectedness, academic motivation, mental health and well-being, academic performance
examples: The CHKS measures the supports with multi-item scales (e.g., Caring Adult Relationships, High Expectations, Opportunities for Meaningful Participation) administered to roughly 800,000 secondary students.
key_sources: Hanson, T., Zhang, G., Cerna, R., Stern, A., & Austin, G. (2019). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ students in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED601909

article_title: Understanding the Experiences of LGBTQ Students in California
citation: Hanson, T., Zhang, G., Cerna, R., Stern, A., & Austin, G. (2019). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ students in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: California Healthy Kids Survey (CHKS)
description: The CHKS is "an anonymous modular assessment for students ages 10 (grade 5) and above" developed in 1998 by WestEd for the California Department of Education. Participation has been voluntary since 2010 except in districts receiving tobacco prevention grants; the CDE minimally requires administration in grades 7 and 9. This study uses pooled 2017-19 data from 2,749 secondary schools, with about 70 percent of California districts administering the survey to more than 1.2 million students in that period. The report calls aggregated CHKS data arguably the nation's largest data source on LGBTQ youth.
requirements: Districts must administer the survey in grades 7 and 9 at minimum to capture comparable statewide data.
constraints: Participation is voluntary since 2010 (except tobacco-grant districts), and students declining to respond to gender identity or sexual orientation questions were omitted from this study's analyses.
target_learners: Students in grade 5 and above; this study covers grades 7, 9, and 11
target_learning_goals: Assessment of school climate, safety, supports, mental health, engagement, and academic performance
examples: The study analyzed responses from 804,683 students on gender identity and 796,079 on sexual orientation across 2,749 secondary schools.
key_sources: Hanson, T., Zhang, G., Cerna, R., Stern, A., & Austin, G. (2019). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ students in California. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED601909

article_title: Balancing Act: State and District Roles in School Improvement under ESSA
citation: Dunn, L., & Ambroso, E. (2019). Balancing act: State and district roles in school improvement under ESSA. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://centeronschoolturnaround.org
title: Six key strategies characterize how SEAs implement SEA and LEA roles in school improvement under ESSA
description: From interviews with school improvement leads in 10 SEAs, the authors identified six strategies present in every SEA's approach: taking on multiple roles with LEAs, balancing support and accountability, differentiating support by district characteristics, building district capacity for sustainable change, prioritizing local contexts and needs, and leveraging ESSA requirements to specify roles. The authors state, "From these interviews, we identified six key strategies that were present in each of the 10 SEAs' approaches to implementing SEA and LEA roles in improvement." They present the set as building "a comprehensive, cohesive, and coherent system of support for school improvement."
requirements: SEAs must work with and through LEAs, which ESSA positions as key levers for school improvement
constraints: Strategies were identified from interviews with 10 purposively selected SEAs chosen for well-established and varied approaches, so breadth beyond these states is not established
target_learners: State education agency and local education agency staff supporting school improvement
target_learning_goals: Improving outcomes in comprehensive support and improvement (CSI) and targeted support and improvement (TSI) schools
examples: Louisiana leverages ESSA to require identified schools to choose high-quality English and math curricula and a professional development vendor, and competitively allocates its 7% school-improvement set-aside
key_sources: Dunn, L., & Ambroso, E. (2019). Balancing act: State and district roles in school improvement under ESSA. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED602966

article_title: Should Schools Be Conducting Lockdown Drills?
citation: Schildkraut, J., Grogan, K., & Nabors, A. (2020). Should schools be conducting lockdown drills? WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/schools-lockdown-drills/
title: Taxonomy distinguishing lockdown drills from active shooter drills and exercises
description: The brief argues that much confusion in the debate over school safety drills stems from muddling terminology. It defines "active shooter" as "one or more individuals actively engaged in killing or attempting to kill people in a populated area", whereas lockdowns are used for "any active threat inside a school or other location". It further distinguishes drills, performed by single entities to test a specific procedure, from exercises, which involve multiple agencies and test interagency cooperation. This taxonomy frames the article's argument that lockdown drills can be incorporated into the school day, whereas active shooter exercises require considerable planning and may be costly.
requirements: The distinction requires schools and districts to use consistent terminology when planning and mandating emergency drills.
constraints: The brief notes drills are often confused with exercises and with active shooter drills in public discussion, so the terms are "typically discussed as if they were one and the same".
target_learners: K-12 students
school faculty and staff
target_learning_goals: emergency preparedness
knowing how to respond during a lockdown
key_sources: Schildkraut, J., Grogan, K., & Nabors, A. (2020). Should schools be conducting lockdown drills? WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/schools-lockdown-drills/

article_title: Should Schools Be Conducting Lockdown Drills?
citation: Schildkraut, J., Grogan, K., & Nabors, A. (2020). Should schools be conducting lockdown drills? WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/schools-lockdown-drills/
title: Follow NASP best practices when conducting lockdown drills: careful planning, announced drills, accommodation of vulnerable students, and debriefing
description: The brief relays the National Association of School Psychologists' guidance for conducting lockdown drills in ways that minimize psychological harm. NASP (2017) "recommends, for example, that drills be carefully planned and that a school safety team be involved in such preparations", that schools consider the needs of students with disabilities or mental health concerns, that drills "never be unannounced", and that participants be debriefed at the conclusion. The brief presents this guidance as the current best-practice standard despite the limited research base.
requirements: Drills should be carefully planned with a school safety team involved; drills should never be unannounced and participants should be debriefed.
constraints: The brief notes research on lockdown drills is sparse, so the guidance rests on expert recommendation rather than a robust evidence base.
target_learners: K-12 students
students with disabilities or mental health concerns
faculty and staff
target_learning_goals: emergency preparedness
responding appropriately during a lockdown
examples: NASP's 2017 guidance recommends planning, school safety team involvement, announced drills, and debriefing; its 2018 guidance adds trauma mitigation such as providing clear information and directions and maintaining a controlled response.
key_sources: Schildkraut, J., Grogan, K., & Nabors, A. (2020). Should schools be conducting lockdown drills? WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/schools-lockdown-drills/

article_title: Mindfulness-Based Practices for Schools
citation: Browning, A., & Romer, N. (2020). Mindfulness-based practices for schools. WestEd. https://californias3.wested.org/wp-content/uploads/Mindfulness-Based-Practices-for-Schools.pdf
title: Mindfulness as attention and self-regulation cultivation complementary to SEL
description: The brief defines mindfulness as "maintaining a moment-by-moment awareness of our thoughts, emotions, bodily sensations, and surrounding environment with openness and curiosity" and frames mindfulness practices as cultivating attention, self-awareness, and self-knowledge of how thoughts and feelings affect actions. It positions mindfulness as complementary to social and emotional learning, since self-awareness and self-management are among CASEL's five core SEL skills, and links it to executive functioning in the prefrontal area of the brain.
requirements: Practices must cultivate attention including self-awareness and self-knowledge of thoughts, feelings, and sensations
target_learners: K-12 students
teachers and educators

article_title: Mindfulness in Education: An Approach to Cultivating Self-Awareness That Can Bolster Kids' Learning
citation: Browning, A. (2020). Mindfulness in education: An approach to cultivating self-awareness that can bolster kids’ learning [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://SELcenter.WestEd.org
title: Mindfulness as cultivated moment-by-moment awareness supporting self-awareness and self-regulation
description: The brief defines mindfulness as “maintaining a moment-by-moment awareness of our thoughts, emotions, bodily sensations, and surrounding environment with openness and curiosity.” It frames mindfulness as the practice of cultivating attention to foster self-awareness and self-knowledge about thoughts, feelings, and sensations and how they affect actions. School-based mindfulness strategies are described as largely drawn from mindfulness-based stress reduction and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, which the brief calls validated strategies for anxiety and stress management.
requirements: Practices are taught as attention-cultivation routines that help learners notice thoughts, feelings, and bodily sensations
constraints: School-based strategies are largely drawn from MBSR and MBCT, per the brief
target_learners: pre-K-12 students
educators and school staff
target_learning_goals: self-awareness
self-regulation
stress management
examples: Educators practice pausing and taking several deep breaths when a strong emotional reaction is triggered

article_title: Mindfulness in Education: An Approach to Cultivating Self-Awareness That Can Bolster Kids' Learning
citation: Browning, A. (2020). Mindfulness in education: An approach to cultivating self-awareness that can bolster kids’ learning [Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd]. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://SELcenter.WestEd.org
title: Mindfulness integrated as an integral component of wider school structures, routines, and curricula
description: The brief recommends embedding mindfulness within existing school structures rather than as a stand-alone add-on, stating that “mindfulness is best taught and learned as an integral component of wider school structures, routines, and curricula.” It emphasizes flexibility: implementation can be slow or fast, one element at a time or comprehensive, led by individual teachers or rolled out school-wide, and does not require a full class period. Figure 1 organizes example practices by setting and audience with learning objectives and benefits.
requirements: Integration into wider school structures, routines, and curricula rather than isolated delivery
constraints: Depending on local school policies, students may have the opportunity to opt in to some practices

educators
target_learning_goals: social and emotional learning
self-regulation
focus and attention

article_title: Lessons Learned about Leading the Implementation of Formative Assessment: A Framework for School Leaders and Leadership Teams
citation: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Five-practice framework for leading formative assessment implementation
description: The brief presents a leadership framework (Exhibit 1) of five synergistic practices for guiding formative assessment implementation: "fostering understanding of formative assessment; communicating a compelling vision...; modeling a culture of learning...; leading site-based professional learning...; and nurturing the conditions necessary for the changes associated with implementing and scaling formative assessment." It was derived from WestEd's site observations and leadership coaching at 12 school campuses in three urban districts during the How I Know project (2017–2020). The practices are described as operating "synergistically to support and strengthen the learning and mindset shifts needed by teachers and their students."
requirements: Leaders must themselves understand formative assessment's grounding principles and the instructional shifts it requires
constraints: Framework derived from one project's observations across 12 campuses in three urban districts
target_learners: school leaders and leadership teams in K-12 sites
target_learning_goals: leading instructional change toward formative assessment practice
examples: WestEd coaches documented five leadership practices that appeared to enhance implementation across 12 school campuses in three districts between 2017 and 2020
key_sources: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606088

article_title: Lessons Learned about Leading the Implementation of Formative Assessment: A Framework for School Leaders and Leadership Teams
citation: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Formative assessment as shared use of evidence of student learning to guide ongoing teaching and learning
description: The brief defines formative assessment as "the educational approach of engendering learning by having teacher and students alike assess students' current knowledge and understanding — based on what students say, do, make, or write — and then use that evidence to guide ongoing teaching and learning efforts." It repositions students as active agents who set goals, create self-oriented feedback loops, and adapt strategies, and notes teachers shift from "delivering" a subject to facilitating learning. Classroom culture changes are described as required for implementation.
requirements: Teachers and students share responsibility for learning; evidence of learning is used as a foundational practice
constraints: Requires changes in classroom culture and in traditional teacher and student roles
target_learners: K-12 teachers and students
target_learning_goals: students learning how to learn; teachers using evidence of learning to guide instruction
examples: Teachers practicing formative assessment listen, observe, question, and review student work to determine what each student needs to move forward
key_sources: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606088

article_title: Lessons Learned about Leading the Implementation of Formative Assessment: A Framework for School Leaders and Leadership Teams
citation: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Leaders should foster shared understanding of what formative assessment is and is not
description: The brief recommends that leaders develop deep knowledge of formative assessment — "what it looks like in the classroom, how it differs from current instructional practice, how to distinguish it from 'just good teaching,' and how to address persistent misinterpretations." Because implementation "is not a simple matter of adhering to a prescribed set of activities" but requires internalizing new principles, leaders who succeeded immersed themselves in learning, developed an anchor definition, and addressed misconceptions as they arose.
requirements: Leaders need deep knowledge of formative assessment and its grounding principles before fostering others' understanding
constraints: Teachers must internalize new principles and examine personal beliefs, so extensive leadership support is needed
target_learners: school leaders and leadership teams
target_learning_goals: building shared staff understanding of formative assessment practice
examples: Observed leaders developed a definition of formative assessment that served as an anchor for teachers and developed routines to visit classrooms and notice emerging practices
key_sources: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606088

article_title: Lessons Learned about Leading the Implementation of Formative Assessment: A Framework for School Leaders and Leadership Teams
citation: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Leaders should communicate a compelling vision highlighting changes in the student role
description: The brief states that a "compelling vision of formative assessment — what it is, what it looks like in practice, and why it is important — provides stakeholders with motivation and clarity." Leaders may frame the vision around metacognition, disciplinary knowledge and learner identity, or motivation and self-efficacy, all of which "contribute to supporting equity goals." When the vision becomes community-wide, "coherence and momentum around this work increase."
requirements: Vision must align with existing site goals and initiatives and be prioritized among competing expectations
constraints: Diverse viewpoints and misconceptions about learning exist across communities that the vision must address
target_learners: teachers, students, parents, and district stakeholders
target_learning_goals: mobilizing commitment to formative assessment implementation
examples: Observed leaders clarified what teachers would see more of and less of as students developed metacognition and agency, and met with superiors to validate formative assessment as a core improvement strategy
key_sources: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606088

article_title: Lessons Learned about Leading the Implementation of Formative Assessment: A Framework for School Leaders and Leadership Teams
citation: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Leaders should model an adult learning culture that mirrors formative assessment norms
description: The brief argues that formative assessment requires a classroom culture where students "take risks, show what they don't know, give and receive feedback, and learn from peers," and that teachers need the same supportive culture. Leaders must therefore "model an adult learning culture that moves away from a tight focus on accountability to building norms that give permission and encourage teachers to identify what they don't yet know," communicating that everyone is a learner.
requirements: Leaders must be transparent about their own learning and engage in inquiry together with teachers and students
constraints: Many schools' existing policies and norms reflect a compliance mindset that differs from the needed culture
target_learners: school leaders, teachers
target_learning_goals: building norms of risk-taking, feedback exchange, and evidence use among adults
examples: Observed leaders were transparent about their own learning related to formative assessment and provided feedback in ways that engender trust, respect, and empathy
key_sources: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606088

article_title: Lessons Learned about Leading the Implementation of Formative Assessment: A Framework for School Leaders and Leadership Teams
citation: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Leaders should apply change-management knowledge and align policies to sustain scaling
description: The brief states that leaders nurturing conditions for scaling should "learn and apply change management models to predict, notice, and respond to stages of individual and systems-level change," citing Coburn's Four Dimensions of Scale as an example. Because formative assessment is typically adopted by small groups of teachers adding others over years, teachers will be at very different stages. Leaders should also review and align building-level policies — "particularly grading and reporting policies, or required assessment practices" — that support or hinder the work.
requirements: Leaders need a range of models and strategies for guiding change and tolerance for messiness
constraints: At any given time, groups of teachers will be at very different stages of understanding; conflicting policies such as teacher evaluation forms can inhibit change
target_learners: school and district leaders managing multi-year implementation
target_learning_goals: sustaining and scaling formative assessment across a site
examples: During the How I Know Project, observed leaders aligned building-level policies to reduce conflicting expectations and supported revision of systems-level practices that inhibited change
key_sources: Gerzon, N., & Jones, B. (2020). Lessons learned about leading the implementation of formative assessment: A framework for school leaders and leadership teams. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606088

article_title: Getting Better at Getting More Equitable: Opportunities and Barriers for Using Continuous Improvement to Advance Educational Equity
citation: Valdez, A., Takahashi, S., Krausen, K., Bowman, A., & Gurrola, E. (2020). Getting better at getting more equitable: Opportunities and barriers for using continuous improvement to advance educational equity. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Equity audits as a continuous improvement practice for seeing systems
description: Equity audits are a promising practice identified in the study for helping educators understand, or "see," their systems with a focus on "inequities in access, opportunity, and outcomes by student groups." TA providers and county offices of education use them to guide the collection and analysis of data, with results then used to inform improvement efforts. Topics vary by provider, from career and college readiness to discipline rates by student groups, and one county leader reported equity audits helped district leaders access in-school, in-classroom data beyond what the state dashboard provides.
requirements: Protocols vary by TA provider and focus area; audits require collecting data on differences in experiences, opportunities, and outcomes across student groups, including interviews with students
constraints: The dashboard alone does not provide the in-school, in-classroom view; audits complement rather than replace dashboard data
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly students of color and underserved student groups in California districts
target_learning_goals: Understanding and dismantling structural inequities in access, opportunity, and outcomes
examples: In 2018, San Rafael City Schools partnered with Education Trust West and the Marin Promise Partnership to conduct an equity audit of students' career and college readiness; one leader noted a reduction in suspension rates in one district
key_sources: Valdez, A., Takahashi, S., Krausen, K., Bowman, A., & Gurrola, E. (2020). Getting better at getting more equitable: Opportunities and barriers for using continuous improvement to advance educational equity. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606089

article_title: Getting Better at Getting More Equitable: Opportunities and Barriers for Using Continuous Improvement to Advance Educational Equity
citation: Valdez, A., Takahashi, S., Krausen, K., Bowman, A., & Gurrola, E. (2020). Getting better at getting more equitable: Opportunities and barriers for using continuous improvement to advance educational equity. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Continuous improvement as an umbrella term for disciplined system-improvement methodologies
description: The report frames continuous improvement as "an umbrella term to capture a range of disciplined system-improvement methodologies, including improvement science, networked improvement communities, Lean, Six Sigma, and Design-Based Implementation Research." These methodologies empirically test changes to a system by improving the interactions of people, processes, materials, and norms, and centrally include the voices of those at the front lines of the system and those who use it. The report applies this framework to examine how California education leaders use such approaches to advance educational equity.
requirements: A data infrastructure that provides feedback tied to organizational outcomes, shared improvement methodology, and leadership practices that build and sustain a continuous-improvement culture
constraints: The report notes current continuous improvement efforts in California are insufficient on their own to address persistent inequities without an intentional equity commitment
target_learners: K-12 students in California education systems, particularly students of color and other underserved student groups
target_learning_goals: Reducing disparities in learning experiences and outcomes through disciplined system improvement
examples: California's statewide system of support uses continuous improvement principles and methods, with county offices of education providing differentiated assistance such as needs assessments and root-cause analyses
key_sources: Valdez, A., Takahashi, S., Krausen, K., Bowman, A., & Gurrola, E. (2020). Getting better at getting more equitable: Opportunities and barriers for using continuous improvement to advance educational equity. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606089

article_title: Strategies for Trauma-Informed Distance Learning
citation: Pate, C. (2020). Strategies for trauma-informed distance learning. Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd. https://SELcenter.WestEd.org
title: Perry's 3 Rs framework (Regulate, Relate, Reason) sequences trauma-informed intervention from regulation to reasoning
description: The brief adopts neuroscientist Bruce Perry's "3 Rs" approach as its organizing framework for trauma-informed education. Educators are told to "closely follow the process of how to reach the 'learning brain' — beginning from the back of the brain and moving to the front": first ensure students are regulated in their hindbrain, feeling "physically and emotionally calm and settled"; then related in the midbrain through safe, supportive relationships; and finally able to reason in the forebrain, ready for formal instruction. The brief argues a child who is unsettled is unlikely to connect with others or have the cognitive capacity for higher-level learning processes.
requirements: Educators must address regulation and relational safety before expecting engagement with formal academic instruction
constraints: The framework is presented as applying to all children but is described as particularly critical for students experiencing adversity and in distance learning contexts
target_learners: K-12 students learning remotely, especially those experiencing adversity or trauma
target_learning_goals: Emotional regulation
social connection
readiness for academic learning
examples: The brief organizes all of its distance-learning strategies under the three headings Regulate, Relate, and Reason
key_sources: Pate, C. (2020). Strategies for trauma-informed distance learning. Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606091

article_title: Strategic Resource Allocation for the 21st Century: How State Leaders Can Address the Silent Recession
citation: Krausen, K., Caparas, R., Ripma, T., & Willis, J. (2020). Strategic resource allocation for the 21st century: How state leaders can address the silent recession. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/strategic-resource-allocation/
title: State funding models should balance targeted funds for student needs with sufficient local flexibility
description: The report argues that state K–12 funding system design matters as much as funding levels: "An effective school funding model should provide targeted funds to ensure that spending aligns with state priorities and serves all students equitably, but should also allow sufficient flexibility for school districts to use funds to meet their local needs." It notes most states use foundation formulas with weighted student formulas, and that states have shifted toward local flexibility over the past decade while some archaic provisions (e.g., obsolete small-district thresholds) work against desired outcomes.
requirements: States control how education funding is structured and distributed through the design of their funding system, so the principle applies at the state policy level
constraints: The report notes evidence suggests foundation formulas tend to be the most effective at ensuring adequacy, but states must also weigh targeting versus flexibility tradeoffs
target_learners: K–12 public school students, including economically disadvantaged students, English learners, and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Equitable allocation of resources to support state goals for student performance
examples: Most states' formulas now distribute additional funds to LEAs based on student characteristics such as low-income and English learner status; high-performing states also account for regional cost differences, district size, and school type
key_sources: Krausen, K., Caparas, R., Ripma, T., & Willis, J. (2020). Strategic resource allocation for the 21st century: How state leaders can address the silent recession. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/strategic-resource-allocation/

article_title: Sound Basic Education for All: An Action Plan for North Carolina
citation: WestEd, Learning Policy Institute, & Friday Institute for Educational Innovation at North Carolina State University. (2019). Sound Basic Education for All: An Action Plan for North Carolina. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: The Leandro sound basic education framework: four constitutional components every North Carolina student is entitled to
description: The framework, affirmed unanimously by the Supreme Court of North Carolina in Leandro v. State (1997), defines a "sound basic education" as one providing at least four components: sufficient ability to read, write, and speak English and knowledge of fundamental mathematics and physical science; fundamental knowledge of geography, history, and basic economic and political systems for informed choices; and sufficient academic and vocational skills to engage in postsecondary education or training and to compete on an equal basis in further education or employment. The action plan uses this definition as the standard against which it assesses state compliance and organizes its recommendations across educators, leaders, funding, early childhood, and assessment and accountability.
requirements: State action must enable every student, including those at risk, an equal opportunity to obtain a sound basic education as defined in Leandro
constraints: The report notes the definition must enable students to function in a complex and rapidly changing society, so the bar for proficiency has been raised as standards were updated
target_learners: All North Carolina K-12 public school students, including at-risk students and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Foundational literacy and mathematics
Informed civic and economic decision-making
Readiness for postsecondary education, vocational training, and gainful employment
examples: Judge Lee's 2018 order charged the independent consultant with recommending actions to provide a competent, certified, well-trained teacher in every classroom, a well-trained competent principal in every school, and the resources necessary for an equal opportunity to a sound basic education
key_sources: WestEd, Learning Policy Institute, & Friday Institute for Educational Innovation at North Carolina State University. (2019). Sound Basic Education for All: An Action Plan for North Carolina. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606141

article_title: Hero Elementary Playlist Pilot Study in After-School Programs
citation: Li, L., Maher, B., Weiser, G., Orenstein, A., Chow, E., & Atienza, S. (2019). Hero Elementary playlist pilot study in after-school programs. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Hero Elementary science playlists for K-2 after-school programs
description: The Hero Elementary playlists are organized sets of K-2 science activities — "interactive games, educational apps, non-fiction e-books, hands-on activities, and a digital science notebook" — each centered on a conceptual theme in K-2 science (e.g., Pushes and Pulls, Changing Motion, Classifying Matter, Solid or Liquid). Five playlists were piloted across eight weeks in after-school programs, with educators completing three to four playlists.
requirements: Tablet access, internet connectivity, and login infrastructure
Educator training and completion of an Educator Action Plan
constraints: Technical glitches (login scanning, connectivity, projector setup, app freezes) impeded implementation; educators perceived content difficulty differently across sites, with one site finding content too easy for all grades
target_learners: Kindergarten, first-grade, second-grade, and mixed-grade after-school students, with emphasis on Latino communities and children with disabilities
target_learning_goals: K-2 science concepts in motion, forces, and properties of matter aligned to Next Generation Science Standards
examples: Playlists such as Solid or Liquid combine digital episodes, games, e-books, notebooks, and hands-on activities like Push, Slide, Bump
key_sources: Li, L., Maher, B., Weiser, G., Orenstein, A., Chow, E., & Atienza, S. (2019). Hero Elementary playlist pilot study in after-school programs. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED608115

article_title: Securing and Protecting Education Funding in California
citation: Hahnel, C., Hough, H., & Willis, J. (2020). Securing and Protecting Education Funding in California. Policy Analysis for California Education. https://edpolicyinca.org
title: New revenues must be paired with system improvements and accountability, including strengthened fiscal transparency so stakeholders understand how money is being used
description: The report's Finding 5 holds that "New Revenues Must be Paired With System Improvements and Accountability," reflecting stakeholder views that more resources are necessary only if the public and policymakers are offered assurances that funds will be spent well. Its fourth recommendation operationalizes this: "The state should strengthen fiscal transparency and analysis so that stakeholders understand how money is being used and see the results of that spending." Several interview participants emphasized efficiency, saying how money is used matters as much as or more than total spending level.
requirements: Fiscal transparency and analysis infrastructure so stakeholders can see how money is used and the results of that spending
constraints: The report notes the state's funding system is complex and opaque, which it says makes transparency and modernization difficult
target_learners: California K–12 public school students
target_learning_goals: Ensuring additional education funding is used effectively to improve student outcomes
examples: Interview participants called for a process toward better outcomes instead of focusing on inputs or adequacy, and the report recommends the state strengthen fiscal transparency and analysis
key_sources: Hahnel, C., Hough, H., & Willis, J. (2020). Securing and Protecting Education Funding in California. Policy Analysis for California Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED609211

article_title: Considerations for Supporting a Successful Start to the 2020-2021 School Year for Students with Disabilities
citation: Considerations for supporting a successful start to the 2020-2021 school year for students with disabilities. (2020). National Center for Systemic Improvement (NCSI), WestEd. https://ncsi.wested.org
title: Use Universal Design for Learning as the instructional foundation for all students in both distance and school-based settings
description: The guidance recommends that Universal Design for Learning (UDL) form the instructional foundation for all students as schools plan for in-person, distance, and blended service delivery. It states that "Universal Design for Learning (UDL) should form instructional foundation for all students" and that educators need support to ensure UDL is in place across settings. SEAs are asked how they are guiding general education teachers to understand and use UDL.
requirements: Educators need support to ensure UDL is in place in distance and school-based settings
target_learners: all students, including students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: access to standards-based instruction across in-person, distance, and blended delivery models
examples: The document pairs the premise with SEA guiding questions on how the agency is guiding general education teachers to understand and use UDL as a foundation for all instruction.

article_title: Considerations for Supporting a Successful Start to the 2020-2021 School Year for Students with Disabilities
citation: Considerations for supporting a successful start to the 2020-2021 school year for students with disabilities. (2020). National Center for Systemic Improvement (NCSI), WestEd. https://ncsi.wested.org
title: Plan inclusive practices intentionally so special and general education teachers partner in virtual and blended models
description: The guidance holds that inclusive practices are achievable in virtual and blended service delivery but require deliberate planning. It states that "Inclusive practices are possible in virtual and blended models and must be intentionally planned" and that special and general education teachers should partner to plan and provide effective instruction. Guiding questions point SEAs toward approaches such as virtual co-teaching and data sharing among IEP team members.
requirements: Special and general education teachers partnering to plan and provide effective instruction
constraints: Inclusion in virtual and blended models must be intentionally planned rather than assumed
target_learners: students with disabilities in general education settings
target_learning_goals: effective instruction through partnered special and general education planning
examples: The document asks what guidance SEAs are providing on virtual co-teaching and on data sharing and instructional planning among IEP team members when not in the same building at the same time.

article_title: Considerations for Supporting a Successful Start to the 2020-2021 School Year for Students with Disabilities
citation: Considerations for supporting a successful start to the 2020-2021 school year for students with disabilities. (2020). National Center for Systemic Improvement (NCSI), WestEd. https://ncsi.wested.org
title: Multi-Tier Systems of Support (MTSS) as a seminal structure for launching the school year supporting quality learning for all students
description: The guidance positions Multi-Tier Systems of Support as an organizing framework through which SEAs can support districts in launching the 2020-2021 school year. It states that "Multi-Tier Systems of Support (MTSS) can provide a seminal structure for launching 2020-2021 in ways that support quality learning for all students." SEA guiding questions cover sustaining and growing district implementation, guidance on data collection, instructional planning including intensive interventions, progress monitoring, and integrated systems attending to both academic and behavioral/social emotional data.

constraints: The framework is offered for the specific context of launching the 2020-2021 school year under varied reopening conditions

target_learning_goals: quality learning supported through integrated academic and behavioral/social emotional systems
examples: The document asks whether the SEA provides guidance for integrated systems of support that attend to both academic and behavioral/social emotional data and planning.

article_title: Considerations for Supporting a Successful Start to the 2020-2021 School Year for Students with Disabilities
citation: Considerations for supporting a successful start to the 2020-2021 school year for students with disabilities. (2020). National Center for Systemic Improvement (NCSI), WestEd. https://ncsi.wested.org
title: Sustain high expectations for students with disabilities through intentional efforts rather than lowering the bar
description: The guidance warns that high expectations for students with disabilities are at risk during pandemic-era planning unless intentional efforts sustain them. It states that "High expectations could be at risk for students with disabilities unless intentional efforts exist to sustain them" and asks SEAs whether they are ensuring they are not lowering the bar through policy decisions on assessment, standards-based instruction, attendance, and grading exemptions.

article_title: Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools, Part 1: The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, lead authors Aimee Evan, Laura Groth, and Hannah Sullivan. (2020). Identifying Indicators of Distress in Charter Schools: Part 1 The Role and Perspective of Charter School Authorizers. Bethesda, MD: Manhattan Strategy Group. https://ncsrc.org
title: Taxonomy of indicators of distress and indicators of failure in charter schools
description: The report distinguishes leading 'indicators of distress' — characteristics occurring early in a school's decline that 'tend to be more difficult to measure and easier to influence than lagging indicators' — from lagging 'indicators of failure,' output data points occurring later that are easier to measure but 'require more substantive interventions to influence.' Distress indicators are organized into seven categories: leadership, governing board, operations, finance, talent, culture, and instruction, derived from a literature review and authorizer perspectives, and categorized using the Four Domains for Rapid School Improvement framework adapted to the charter context.
requirements: Indicators must be locally validated in each authorizing context before use as predictors of distress
constraints: Not all indicators will show up in each struggling school; authorizers' capacity and policy directives limit which indicators they can collect and examine
target_learners: Charter school authorizers and state education agencies
target_learning_goals: Identifying struggling charter schools early enough for manageable intervention
examples: Table 1 lists distress indicators such as mismatched leadership competencies, inability to convene the board, breakdown in compliance, and failure to properly manage finances, alongside failure indicators such as declines in achievement, growth, graduation rates, and financial viability
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, lead authors Aimee Evan, Laura Groth, and Hannah Sullivan. (2020).
