article_title: Supporting Students Experiencing Homelessness: District Approaches to Supports and Funding
citation: Levin, S., Espinoza, D., & Griffith, M. (2022). Supporting students experiencing homelessness: District approaches to supports and funding. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/557.894
title: District homeless programs provide a coordinated web of six support categories: essential items, transportation, academic services, health supports, specialized unaccompanied-youth support, and family supports
description: Across all five study districts, homeless program staff coordinated services provided by the district program, schools, and community-based organizations. The report enumerates the categories: "Essential items. District homeless programs in our study prioritized providing students and their families with basic necessities, including food, hygiene products, clothing, shoes, and school supplies." Transportation to and from school is required by the McKinney-Vento Act; academic services include tutoring, summer programs, and post–high school planning; health supports include physicals, screenings, counseling, and safety classes; unaccompanied youth receive shelter-embedded staff and prepaid cell phones; families receive linkages to child care, counseling, and emergency funding to prevent loss of housing.
requirements: McKinney-Vento-funded liaisons with dedicated time to provide and coordinate supports, plus partnerships with schools, shelters, food banks, medical providers, nonprofits, child welfare agencies, and housing authorities
constraints: Program staff consistently described transportation as a large cost for their programs, and emergency family funding was provided only when resources and need were known
target_learners: k–12 students experiencing homelessness, including unaccompanied youth and their families
target_learning_goals: educational engagement, attendance, and academic success for students in temporary housing
examples: Cincinnati's Project Connect offers an 8-week summer academic and enrichment course plus after-school tutoring; Santa Fe's Adelante Program provides school supplies, clothing, groceries, tutoring, mentorship, and case management in Spanish and English
key_sources: Levin, S., Espinoza, D., & Griffith, M. (2022). Supporting students experiencing homelessness: District approaches to supports and funding. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/557.894

article_title: Supporting Students Experiencing Homelessness: District Approaches to Supports and Funding
citation: Levin, S., Espinoza, D., & Griffith, M. (2022). Supporting students experiencing homelessness: District approaches to supports and funding. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/557.894
title: Whole child approach to supporting students experiencing homelessness, grounded in the science of learning and development
description: The report frames students experiencing homelessness as having interrelated physical, emotional, and academic needs that signal "a need for a whole child approach to supporting them." It holds that "Such an approach is consistent with the science of learning and development, which shows that stability, consistency, trust, and belonging are foundational to effective learning." Under this account, homelessness harms learning through stress, instability, trauma, and school mobility that raise risks to health, social-emotional well-being, engagement, and achievement, so district supports must address nonacademic needs (housing, health, transportation, family stability) alongside academic services.
requirements: Coordination across district homeless programs, schools, and community-based organizations, with referral pathways into existing school-based supports for vulnerable students
constraints: The report states housing instability can negatively affect students even after the period of homelessness ends, and that addressing systemic causes of homelessness lies beyond districts' scope
target_learners: k–12 students experiencing homelessness, including unaccompanied youth
target_learning_goals: educational engagement, achievement, and attainment supported through stability, trust, and belonging
examples: Study districts folded students experiencing homelessness into existing school-based programs for vulnerable students, allowing homeless program staff to make referrals rather than provide all services directly

article_title: State Preschool in a Mixed Delivery System: Lessons from Five States
citation: Garver, K., Weisenfeld, G. G., Connors-Tadros, L., Hodges, K., Melnick, H., & Plasencia, S. (2023). State preschool in a mixed delivery system: Lessons from five states. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/387.446
title: Three governance approaches for mixed delivery preschool: direct state contracting, LEA subcontracting, and intermediary agencies
description: The report organizes state mixed delivery governance into three approaches (Table 2). Alabama "directly contracts with all preschool providers and allows both LEAs and non-LEAs to apply through a statewide grant application process." New Jersey and New York route funding through LEAs, which subcontract with non-LEAs. Michigan and West Virginia "grant funding only to intermediary agencies" — intermediate school districts and county boards of education — which then subcontract with LEAs and non-LEAs. The report uses this typology to analyze how contracting structures shape funding flow, provider support, and oversight.
requirements: A state must decide how much oversight rests at the state versus regional or local level, and which entities may contract directly with providers
constraints: The report states decisions about governance are often highly political and depend on a state's context, such as its size and local governance structures
target_learners: 4-year-old children enrolled in state-funded preschool
3-year-old children enrolled in state-funded preschool
target_learning_goals: Access to high-quality preschool experiences across provider settings
examples: Alabama's statewide grant application process lets the state manage geographic distribution of FCPK seats but requires additional state administrative oversight
West Virginia brings LEA and non-LEA providers together in county collaboratives to map how to serve children across setting types

article_title: State Preschool in a Mixed Delivery System: Lessons from Five States

title: Establish strong program standards aligned across LEA and non-LEA settings so all children receive high-quality preschool experiences
description: The report's first recommendation holds that states operating mixed delivery preschool should set the same quality standards for every provider setting. The case study states "have high quality standards that are aligned across LEAs and non-LEAs to ensure that families have access to quality care in a variety of settings," including shared curriculum, class size, ratio, professional development, and child assessment requirements. The report argues this alignment supports equitable access to quality regardless of setting.

target_learning_goals: Consistent access to high-quality preschool learning environments
examples: All five case study states require an evidence-based curriculum, class size of 20 or less, and at least a 1:10 teacher-to-child ratio in both LEA and non-LEA settings

description: A framework, attributed by the report to the Learning Policy Institute and Turnaround for Children, holding that "schools that optimize student learning, development, and well-being are those that integrate structures and practices that instantiate the Guiding Principles for Equitable Whole Child Design." The five principles are positive developmental relationships; environments of safety and belonging; rich learning experiences and knowledge development; development of social, emotional, and cognitive skills, habits, and mindsets; and integrated support systems, all aimed at healthy development, learning, and thriving. article_title: Federal and State Resources for Students Experiencing Homelessness
citation: Espinoza, D., Griffith, M., Burns, D., & Shields, P. M. (2023). Federal and state resources for students experiencing homelessness. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/546.264
title: McKinney-Vento Act framework of educational rights and district obligations for students experiencing homelessness
description: Title VII, subpart B, of the McKinney-Vento Homeless Assistance Act is the major federal framework establishing services and protections for students experiencing homelessness, requiring that they "have access to the same free, appropriate public education" as other children. It defines eligibility (lacking "a fixed, regular, and adequate nighttime residence") and obligates every LEA, funded or not, to designate a homeless liaison who identifies and enrolls students, ensures full participation, provides transportation, informs communities of rights, and refers families to housing, medical, dental, and mental health services.
requirements: Every LEA must designate a district homeless liaison, regardless of whether it receives McKinney-Vento funding
Liaisons must coordinate with state coordinators and community agencies providing education and related services
constraints: The report states the act is inadequately funded to accomplish its goals, and identification is challenged by stigma, housing instability, and limited district capacity

target_learning_goals: Equal access to free, appropriate public education
School stability and full participation
examples: LEA obligations include providing transportation to and from school regardless of where students are currently residing, and referring them to key resources such as housing and health services

description: The report states that effective SEL programs utilize four practices represented by the acronym SAFE: programs are "Sequenced", "Active", "Focused", and "Explicit", meaning they involve developmentally coordinated activities, active skill learning, intentional development of personal and social skills, and clearly identified, taught, and practiced skills. title: CASEL five-competence-cluster framework for social and emotional learning
description: The report describes the CASEL framework as the most influential SEL framework, organizing immediate SEL outcomes around "five competence clusters": self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills, and responsible decision-making. Each cluster is substantively defined — for example, self-management "requires skills to manage one's emotions, thoughts, and behaviors effectively in different situations". Approximately two thirds of U.S. states with SEL standards base their standards on this framework, and it is embedded in the report's conceptual model (Figure 1) linking competencies to short- and long-term student outcomes.

article_title: Fostering Belonging, Transforming Schools: The Impact of Restorative Practices
citation: Darling-Hammond, S. (2023). Fostering belonging, transforming schools: The impact of restorative practices. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/169.703
title: The program–practice distinction: restorative programs are training systems while restorative practices are the specific actions that drive outcomes
description: The report's central organizing framework distinguishes restorative programs—systems of training designed to encourage community members to use restorative practices—from restorative practices themselves. It states that "Restorative programs offer various kinds of training to staff to help them learn to use restorative practices" while "Restorative practices are the specific actions in which community members might engage in a restorative school." Because programs often fail to shift practices pervasively, prior research evaluating program adoption may miss the effectiveness of practices, the true target of interest. This study is designed to measure the impacts of student exposure to practices directly.
requirements: Evaluating practices rather than programs requires data that track student exposure to restorative practices over time, which the report notes few datasets have allowed
constraints: The report notes programs vary substantially in design and implementation and that there is no established definition of which program model makes a school 'restorative'
target_learners: middle school students
target_learning_goals: conflict resolution skills
school climate
reduction of exclusionary discipline
examples: The report identifies program quality, restorative readiness, and teacher discretion as moderators of whether a program results in student exposure to practices

article_title: Fostering Belonging, Transforming Schools: The Impact of Restorative Practices
citation: Darling-Hammond, S. (2023). Fostering belonging, transforming schools: The impact of restorative practices. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/169.703
title: Typology of restorative practices: repair practices and community-building practices
description: The report subdivides restorative practices into two types, stating "Restorative practices can be roughly subdivided into two types: repair practices and community-building practices." Repair practices (associated with restorative justice) bring together stakeholders—victims, respondents, and facilitators, sometimes including community members—to resolve issues and determine restorative responses such as community service, restitution, apologies, or behavior-change agreements. Community-building practices foster an interconnected school community in which transgressions are less common, and include community-building circles, reentry circles for returning students, and capacity-development activities such as role-playing conflict situations. Restorative programs themselves fall into add-on and whole-school models.
requirements: Whole-school implementation involves providing instruction in restorative concepts and skills to all school personnel and students
constraints: The report calls this a rough subdivision and notes formal conferences may also include community members such as witnesses, friends, and family
target_learners: K-12 students
middle school students
target_learning_goals: conflict repair
relationship building
social and emotional capacity to manage conflict
examples: Community-building circles held regularly (e.g., every Monday morning in homeroom) help students and staff deepen relationships and trust

article_title: The Federal Role in Ending Teacher Shortages
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., DiNapoli, M., Jr., & Kini, T. (2023). The federal role in ending teacher shortages. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/649.892
title: Factory-model school heritage as the root cause of de-professionalized teaching conditions
description: The report argues that 'at the root of the crisis in teaching is the way teaching was conceptualized when our current school structures were designed a century ago' to accommodate compulsory mass education. Scientific managers applied Henry Ford's assembly-line model with 'more tightly prescribed curriculum, more teacher-proof texts, more extensive testing, and more regulations,' adopting age-grading and tracking as sorting mechanisms. Teachers were placed in 'egg-crate' classrooms with no scheduled time for planning, collaboration, or ongoing learning. The report states most schools 'still carry the marks of their industrial origins in the standardized structures, curriculum, and tracking systems; the design of the teaching job; and the lack of time and space for collaboration among teachers and personalization for students.'
requirements: Transformation of school structures toward strong relationships, personalization, and collaborative planning time, as in the report's sixth recommendation area
constraints: The report frames this as a historical-structural account of U.S. teaching conditions, noting today's schools are less regimented than they once were but retain industrial marks
target_learners: K–12 teachers and students in U.S. public schools
target_learning_goals: Understanding how school organizational design shapes teacher effectiveness, retention, and instructional quality
examples: The report contrasts U.S. conditions with high-achieving nations where teachers get 15 to 25 hours a week of planning and collaboration time, and notes only 47% of the U.S. education workforce are classroom teachers versus at least 70% in many other countries

description: The report distills UCLA Community School's approach into six key practices: knowing and building on a community's history, assets, and culture; developing and articulating desired core competencies; nurturing shared leadership and collective agency; creating space for collaborative inquiry, professional autonomy, and teacher development; using data and stories to elevate the school's vision and track progress; and affirming everyone's role. description: The report defines community schools as "a place-based strategy for providing whole child supports deeply rooted in the local context". They leverage partnerships to provide health and social services, expanded learning opportunities, family engagement, community-connected instruction, collaborative leadership, and a culture of belonging, safety, and care, typically coordinated by a community school manager. The report cites an evidence base linking community schools to improved attendance, achievement, graduation, and reduced achievement gaps.

Students in Grades 2-5 take the Reader Identity Self-Assessment (RISA) each fall, analyzing their Spanish and English reading data, setting goals, and reflecting on their "bilingual or multilingual reader selves", then tracking progress in longitudinal bar graphs shared with families.

article_title: State Support for Civic Engagement
citation: Thompson, C. (2023). State support for civic engagement. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/878.726
title: Civic diploma seals as a state pattern for recognizing student civic readiness
description: The report describes a growing state pattern of recognizing civic engagement through seals on students' diplomas. Seven states (Arizona, California, Georgia, Nevada, New York, Ohio, and Virginia) offer such a seal in the 2022-23 school year, and Tennessee offers one for districts or schools. In the seven student-seal states, "all require students to complete service learning, community service, or civic action, combined with course requirements," and LEAs validate requirements, confer seals, and report data to the state education agency. The National Council for the Social Studies has developed a toolkit supporting states interested in developing civic seals.

constraints: Seals are optional additions to a traditional diploma in states such as Arizona and Georgia

target_learning_goals: Civic knowledge

examples: Arizona requires a 3.0 GPA in social studies, passing the Arizona Civics Exam, three civic learning programs, two civic engagement activities, and 75 or more hours of community service

Teachers pair a content objective (the "bricks") with a language objective (the "mortar") in every subject, group students heterogeneously across grades and language backgrounds, and end units with performance-based assessments. The report notes that "by integrating English language objectives into each subject, students practice language skills while building and demonstrating their content knowledge."

article_title: Striving for Relationship-Centered Schools: Insights from a Community-Based Transformation Campaign
citation: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856
title: Three principles of the Relationship Centered Schools campaign
description: The Relationship Centered Schools (RCS) campaign, launched in 2015 by Californians for Justice, is a youth-led school transformation initiative organized around three guiding principles. The report states that the campaign "centers three principles to guide action and school improvement: (1) create space for relationship-building, (2) value student voice, and (3) invest in staff." These principles direct how youth organizers, educators, and district leaders collaborate to restructure secondary schools so that students of color and students from low-income backgrounds are known, supported, and able to reach their potential. The campaign has sought to spur transformation in 11 comprehensive high schools across four California regions.
requirements: A community-based organization with youth chapters or after-school programming at school sites to anchor ongoing youth and organizer engagement
constraints: The campaign's approach to change manifests differently in local settings; in Long Beach it operated primarily at the district level while in Fresno it maintained a school-level focus
target_learners: High school students of color
Students from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Student motivation and engagement
Sense of belonging and being known by a caring adult
Student agency and voice in school decision-making
examples: Since 2016, CFJ youth organizers have collaborated with district officials, school leaders, and educators in Fresno, Long Beach, Oakland, and San José to advance relationship-centered approaches
key_sources: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856

article_title: Striving for Relationship-Centered Schools: Insights from a Community-Based Transformation Campaign
citation: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856
title: Community organizing cycle as a model for school transformation
description: The report describes the community organizing cycle as the change model embodied by the RCS campaign. It explains that this cycle "seeks to build collaborative power in relationship-centered and incremental ways and to elevate the voices of often marginalized groups in change efforts." Key dimensions include a focus on relationship-building, deliberate efforts to ensure diverse actors can share experiences and concerns to identify actionable issues, and leadership development through educational campaigns and training sessions that expand reach and build alliances. This model positions youth, educators, and leaders as co-drivers of equity-oriented continuous improvement rather than recipients of top-down reform.
requirements: Ongoing engagement between youth organizers and school/district staff to build connections, surface common concerns, and inform co-determined action steps
constraints: Because the approach is modeled after the community organizing cycle, relationship-centered transformation manifests differently in local settings
target_learners: Secondary school youth organizers
Youth of color in community organizing chapters
target_learning_goals: Leadership development
Deep listening and effective communication skills
Understanding of systemic racism and education inequity
examples: CFJ chapter or after-school meetings serve as a forum for leadership development, engaging students in discussions of critical issues and opportunities to hone interpersonal and leadership competencies
key_sources: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856

article_title: Striving for Relationship-Centered Schools: Insights from a Community-Based Transformation Campaign
citation: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856
title: Youth-led professional development trainings on racial justice and relationship-centered practices
description: Youth-led professional development opportunities are a primary mechanism through which the RCS campaign has spread relationship-centered practice beyond its core set of actors. Interviewees from all four regions mentioned "the growing presence of youth-led trainings, which were learning opportunities that gathered practitioners and students together to learn how to better advance racial justice at school sites." These trainings were typically open to interested educators and school leaders across the district, structured by topic (including implicit bias and relationship-centered practices), and featured youth leadership, a consistent focus on racial justice, and discussion of culturally responsive and antiracist approaches.
requirements: Youth facilitators prepared through CFJ chapter leadership development
Openness of educators and school leaders to attend sessions facilitated by youth
constraints: Efforts to reach youth, leaders, and educators beyond the core set of involved actors has most often included youth-led professional development opportunities typically open to interested leaders and school staff members
target_learners: Educators and school leaders
Youth facilitators
target_learning_goals: Understanding how racism manifests in school structures and practices
Approaches to interrupt racist practices
Community-building and deep listening
examples: The first biannual Racial Justice, Equity, and Healing Summit, held in Oakland Unified in January 2020, offered youth-facilitated 2-hour workshops including 'An Introduction to Racial Justice, Equity, and Healing' and 'How To Be an Antiracist Educator in Oakland'
key_sources: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856

citation: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856
title: Design teams and student advisory committees for student voice in decision-making
description: As part of increasing student voice in decision-making and strategic-planning forums, Long Beach Unified implemented two participatory structures. The report describes how "Design teams (groups of staff, family members, and students who identify equity challenges and potential solutions) and student advisory committees (students from various pathways who advise their principal on school climate topics) enabled a wide range of students to share their perspectives and take an active role in school improvements." These structures institutionalize diverse student representation in school governance and improvement processes.
requirements: Staff, family members, and students willing to serve together on design teams
Principals open to receiving student advisory input on school climate
target_learners: High school students from various pathways
School principals and staff
target_learning_goals: Student voice in school decision-making
Identifying and addressing equity challenges
examples: Student advisory committees drew students from various pathways to advise principals on school climate topics

article_title: Striving for Relationship-Centered Schools: Insights from a Community-Based Transformation Campaign
citation: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856
title: Biweekly homerooms as relationship-centered small communities
description: McLane High School transformed its homeroom structure as a core RCS effort to build consistent relationships in a large school. The report explains that "Biweekly homeroom periods aimed to form small communities for McLane's large student population and enable consistent, multiyear connections." Through its RCS partnership, McLane refined this pattern by training select students to lead homeroom community-building efforts and providing related professional development to educators, embedding relationship-building into the regular schedule rather than treating it as an add-on.
requirements: Biweekly scheduled homeroom time
Training for select students to lead community-building
Professional development for educators on homeroom practices
target_learners: High school students in a large comprehensive high school
target_learning_goals: Sense of belonging in a small community
Consistent multiyear connections with adults and peers
examples: McLane fine-tuned its homeroom practices by training select students to lead homeroom community-building efforts and providing related professional development to educators

article_title: Engaging First: Supporting Young Learners through Family Engagement
citation: Morgan, I., Gillispie, C., & Waller, A. (2024). Supporting Young Learners Through Family Engagement: Engaging First. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Four facets of meaningful and effective family engagement
description: The report organizes its analysis of effective family engagement around four facets: "communication; shared decision-making; connections, trust, and mutual respect; and cultural inclusiveness." It holds that authentic engagement is a collaboration that "involves shared decision-making, trust, mutual respect, and should be asset based and culturally responsive," and that engagement strategies mainly bringing parents into the school building tend to be less effective than programs linking families to children's learning at home. The report uses these facets to structure its survey findings and recommendations.
requirements: Schools must build relationships and share decision-making, particularly with families from groups marginalized by the education system
constraints: One-off activities such as open houses, conferences, volunteering, and chaperoning are not sufficient to improve outcomes and may conflict with work schedules or pose logistical hurdles
target_learners: families and schools of first and second grade students
target_learning_goals: meaningful family engagement that supports student learning and well-being
examples: The report's Findings section is structured by these facets: communication, shared decision-making, connections with parents and school staff, and cultural inclusiveness
key_sources: Morgan, I., Gillispie, C., & Waller, A. (2024). Supporting Young Learners Through Family Engagement: Engaging First. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED658182

article_title: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families
citation: Levitan, S., & Munyan-Penney, N. (2024). Meaningful Assessment Reporting: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org/
title: Use asset-framing in assessment reports so results acknowledge system responsibility and student strengths rather than deficit labels
description: The brief holds that "asset-based language and beliefs are fundamental to strong assessment reporting." Asset-framed reports explicitly acknowledge system-level responsibility for providing supports, highlight students' strengths and capabilities, and avoid deficit language such as "student cannot" in favor of phrases like "has yet to demonstrate" or "may need support in." The brief illustrates this with Massachusetts' report language assigning the school a role in determining assistance, contrasted with Delaware and Idaho language it says places the onus on the student.
requirements: Reports must emphasize system-level action rather than faulting individual students, and avoid language reinforcing deficit mindsets
constraints: The brief states asset-framing is not about hiding achievement gaps or lowering expectations for students
target_learners: K-12 students and their families, particularly those from historically underserved backgrounds
target_learning_goals: families' accurate understanding of assessment results and appropriate actions to support grade-level learning
examples: Massachusetts' score report states the school, in consultation with the parent/guardian, should determine the coordinated academic assistance the student needs; New Mexico's use of the label "novice" is cited as a stigmatizing counterexample
key_sources: Levitan, S., & Munyan-Penney, N. (2024). Meaningful Assessment Reporting: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED658190

article_title: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families
citation: Levitan, S., & Munyan-Penney, N. (2024). Meaningful Assessment Reporting: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org/
title: Five best practices for designing meaningful individual score reports
description: The brief lays out "five essential best practices" for individual score report design: involving students and families in the design process, using asset-framing, clearly communicating the purpose of assessments, helping users make sense of the data, and providing actionable information. Reports should use a "bottom line up front" design that prominently highlights key takeaways, explain key terminology while minimizing jargon, include narrative explanations, high-quality translations, and guiding questions, and offer next steps such as a helpline and conversation starters. State examples include South Carolina's guiding questions, Texas's multilingual PDF walkthrough, Rhode Island's QR-code video, and Ohio's tailored recommendations.
requirements: A clear theory of action articulating the purpose of statewide assessments should inform draft reports used when engaging with families
Targeted consultation with students and families of color, low-income families, and multilingual families, with compensation and attention to time and meeting location
constraints: Space is limited on reports, so states must carefully decide which data needs additional explanation; including rich explanatory content can make reports text heavy, a trade-off states must balance
target_learners: K-12 students and their families
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of assessment results and use of results to support learning
examples: South Carolina's report includes guiding questions such as what the child's score means; Illinois' report includes questions and prompts for families to use with teachers and suggests actions by readiness level
key_sources: Levitan, S., & Munyan-Penney, N. (2024). Meaningful Assessment Reporting: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED658190

article_title: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families
citation: Levitan, S., & Munyan-Penney, N. (2024). Meaningful Assessment Reporting: Making Assessment Reports More Meaningful for Students & Families. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org/
title: Oregon parent assessment-literacy modules
description: Oregon's Department of Education, working with Behavioral Research & Teaching at the University of Oregon and other partners, "created five modules on topics such as the purpose of statewide assessments, how to make sense of assessment results, and how to support learning at home." Each module includes a fact sheet and video in both English and Spanish and lets users listen in on a conversation between a teacher and a parent or guardian. The brief presents the modules as a promising state strategy for increasing parents' assessment literacy.
requirements: Modules were customized to align with state and district assessment data in comparable efforts, suggesting alignment with local assessment systems is needed
target_learners: parents and guardians of K-12 students in Oregon
target_learning_goals: understanding the purpose of statewide assessments, interpreting results, and supporting learning at home
examples: Each module includes a fact sheet and video in English and Spanish featuring a simulated teacher-parent conversation

article_title: Teacher Residencies: State and Federal Policy to Support Comprehensive Teacher Preparation
citation: Saunders, R., Fitz, J., DiNapoli, M. A., Jr., & Kini, T. (2024). Teacher residencies: State and federal policy to support comprehensive teacher preparation. Learning Policy Institute & EdPrepLab. https://doi.org/10.54300/358.825
title: Common elements of high-quality teacher residencies
description: Research on graduate-level residency programs with demonstrated strong outcomes identifies a set of common design elements that distinguish residencies from traditional and most alternative preparation pathways. Well-designed residencies "consist of strong partnerships between local education agencies and teacher preparation programs," require a full year of residency alongside an accomplished mentor teacher who is the teacher of record, tightly integrate coursework with classroom practice, place cohorts in teaching schools, offer post-residency mentoring, recruit diverse candidates for district needs, and provide financial support in exchange for a multiyear teaching commitment.
requirements: strong partnerships between local education agencies and teacher preparation programs
a full year of residency working alongside an accomplished mentor teacher who is the teacher of record
coursework tightly integrated with classroom practice
financial support for residents, often in exchange for a multiyear district teaching commitment
constraints: These features reflect evidence collected from graduate-level teacher residency programs; newer undergraduate and no-service-requirement variations have yet to be studied, per the report.
target_learners: postbaccalaureate and undergraduate teacher candidates preparing for PK–12 teaching
target_learning_goals: comprehensive clinical teacher preparation
teacher effectiveness and retention in high-need districts and subject areas
examples: State policies in the 12 states studied reflect most or all of these features, and the federal Teacher Quality Partnership grant program incorporates them.
key_sources: Saunders, R., Fitz, J., DiNapoli, M. A., Jr., & Kini, T. (2024). Teacher residencies: State and federal policy to support comprehensive teacher preparation. Learning Policy Institute & EdPrepLab. https://doi.org/10.54300/358.825

article_title: Teacher Residencies: State and Federal Policy to Support Comprehensive Teacher Preparation
citation: Saunders, R., Fitz, J., DiNapoli, M. A., Jr., & Kini, T. (2024). Teacher residencies: State and federal policy to support comprehensive teacher preparation. Learning Policy Institute & EdPrepLab. https://doi.org/10.54300/358.825
title: Pathways Alliance national definition of teacher residencies
description: The Pathways Alliance, a coalition of K–12 and higher education organizations, defines teacher residencies as "preparation pathways that are anchored in partnership" with curricula collaboratively designed by local education agencies and teacher preparation programs. Two goals anchor the definition: ensuring aspiring teachers have affordable, high-quality supports while learning to teach, and supporting the instructional and staffing needs of local schools and districts. In yearlong pre-service clinical practice, residents are not teachers of record; they work alongside accomplished mentor teachers experiencing the breadth of teachers' roles across a year. The report uses this definition to guide its review of state policies.
requirements: partnership between local education agencies and teacher preparation programs with collaboratively designed curriculum
yearlong pre-service clinical practice in which residents are not teachers of record
constraints: The report notes recent state models include undergraduate programs not always tied to a service requirement, variations that have yet to be studied.
target_learners: aspiring PK–12 teachers in residency preparation pathways
target_learning_goals: affordable high-quality preparation for teaching
meeting district instructional and staffing needs
examples: The report highlights 12 states whose policies align with the Pathways Alliance definition, including Montana and West Virginia promoting undergraduate residencies and Arizona, California, Indiana, Mississippi, and New York focusing on postbaccalaureate programs.
key_sources: Saunders, R., Fitz, J., DiNapoli, M. A., Jr., & Kini, T. (2024). Teacher residencies: State and federal policy to support comprehensive teacher preparation. Learning Policy Institute & EdPrepLab. https://doi.org/10.54300/358.825

article_title: Developing Educational Leaders in California: The 21st Century California School Leadership Academy
citation: Fitz, J., Levin, S., & Wechsler, M. E. (2024). Developing educational leaders in California: The 21st Century California School Leadership Academy. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/515.306
title: 21st Century California School Leadership Academy (21CSLA)
description: 21CSLA is a statewide California initiative providing "high-quality professional learning opportunities that are accessible and free of charge to California's PreK–12 educational leaders," including central office, site, and teacher leaders. It is administered by a State Center at UC Berkeley in partnership with UCLA and the California Subject Matter Project, and delivers learning through seven regional academies as a lead agency in California's Statewide System of Support.
requirements: Regional academy offerings must align with the California Professional Standards for Education Leaders and the Quality Professional Learning Standards
constraints: Participation is open to leaders from schools and districts that receive federal Title II funds
target_learners: PreK–12 central office leaders, site leaders, and teacher leaders, with special focus on novice leaders, leaders in high-need settings, and leaders involved in school improvement
target_learning_goals: equity-centered transformational leadership
continuous improvement
leading instruction and school improvement
examples: In the first grant cycle the initiative served approximately 8,300 leaders and its deliverables required at least 12 hours for communities of practice and localized offerings and a minimum of 25 hours of individual coaching
key_sources: Fitz, J., Levin, S., & Wechsler, M. E. (2024). Developing educational leaders in California: The 21st Century California School Leadership Academy. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/515.306

article_title: Developing Educational Leaders in California: The 21st Century California School Leadership Academy
citation: Fitz, J., Levin, S., & Wechsler, M. E. (2024). Developing educational leaders in California: The 21st Century California School Leadership Academy. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/515.306
title: Three synergistic professional learning modalities: communities of practice, localized professional learning, and coaching
description: 21CSLA regional academies deliver professional learning through three primary modalities. According to the report, "Communities of practice allow leaders to participate in collaborative learning. Localized professional learning provides experiences that are problem based and context specific. Coaching enables individualized, tailored support and opportunities for feedback and reflection." The State Center's guidance describes the three modalities as synergistic and complementary, and all activities must occur over an extended duration.
requirements: Communities of practice and localized offerings must involve at least 12 hours of professional learning; coaching must provide a minimum of 25 hours of individual leadership coaching per participant
constraints: Regional academies have flexibility in delivery and content, but implementation is structured by the State Center's guidance document
target_learners: school administrators, teacher leaders, and district administrators in California
target_learning_goals: equity-centered problems of practice
continuous improvement capacity
individualized leadership growth
examples: Year 3 deliverables required a minimum of 12 communities of practice groups, eight localized learning opportunities serving at least 240 participants, and coaching for a minimum of 60 leaders
key_sources: Fitz, J., Levin, S., & Wechsler, M. E. (2024). Developing educational leaders in California: The 21st Century California School Leadership Academy. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/515.306

article_title: Developing Educational Leaders in California: The 21st Century California School Leadership Academy
citation: Fitz, J., Levin, S., & Wechsler, M. E. (2024). Developing educational leaders in California: The 21st Century California School Leadership Academy. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/515.306
title: Design leader professional learning with the research-based characteristics of high-quality principal learning programs
description: The report holds that leader professional learning benefits leaders only when it is high quality, and it enumerates the characteristics research documents for high-quality principal learning programs. It states that "the professional learning provided aligns with research on effective leader development that shows the importance of meaningful and authentic learning opportunities that apply learning in practice; a focus on leading instruction, developing people, creating a collaborative learning organization, and managing change; mentoring or coaching, along with feedback and opportunities for reflection; and cohort or networking structures that create a professional learning community." 21CSLA's design is mapped against these characteristics.
requirements: proactive recruitment and a focus on equity-oriented leadership, in addition to the applied learning, content focus, coaching with feedback and reflection, and cohort structures named above
target_learners: school principals and other PreK–12 educational leaders
target_learning_goals: instructional leadership
developing people
managing change
building collaborative learning organizations
examples: Table 3 of the report maps each research-based characteristic to a 21CSLA practice, such as required needs assessments, CPSEL-aligned curriculum, required coaching and communities of practice structures, and recruitment strategies

article_title: On the Path to Leadership: California's Administrator Induction Programs
citation: Wechsler, M. E., Patrick, S. K., Thompson, C., & Levin, S. (2024). On the path to leadership: California's administrator induction programs. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/636.224
title: California's job-embedded administrator induction model: a two-tier credential system with three required induction elements
description: California's model pairs a two-tier credential structure (Preliminary and Clear Administrative Services Credentials) with a required 2-year induction program. Per the report, "The state's 2-year induction model focuses on job-embedded, individualized support" comprising coaching with a trained coach for at least 40 hours per year, personalized professional development for at least 20 hours per year, and multiple assessments tied to the California Professional Standards for Education Leaders. Assessments include an initial assessment informing an individual induction plan, benchmark assessments, and a summative assessment supporting the clear credential recommendation. The report presents this model as reflecting research-based elements of high-quality administrator learning.
requirements: Programs must be approved by the California Commission on Teacher Credentialing and follow its standards of quality and effectiveness
Participants develop an individual induction plan collaboratively with their coach, grounded in the CPSEL
Coaching must begin within 30 days of program entry and occur primarily in person at the site
constraints: The report notes the model replaced a more traditional, coursework-based induction program and that flexibility within the standards produces considerable variation across programs
target_learners: Newly credentialed school administrators (principals, assistant principals)
District and non-school administrators (e.g., directors of professional development, truancy officers)
target_learning_goals: Development of leadership knowledge and skills aligned with the CPSEL
Professional growth, resilience, and career advancement for early-career administrators
examples: Case study programs included ACSA–Shasta County Office of Education, ACSA–Silicon Valley, CSU Dominguez Hills, Los Angeles Unified School District, National University, and UC Berkeley Leadership Support Program
key_sources: Wechsler, M. E., Patrick, S. K., Thompson, C., & Levin, S. (2024). On the path to leadership: California's administrator induction programs. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/636.224

article_title: State Approaches to Developing Educational Leaders
citation: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572
title: Six-function taxonomy of state leadership development initiatives
description: The report organizes state initiatives by the specific leadership development "functions" they perform beyond generally enhancing leaders' skills: "providing role-specific professional learning," supporting induction of early-career leaders, facilitating career advancement for aspiring leaders, supporting leadership teams, providing differentiated assistance for school improvement, and facilitating training for supervisors. The authors present these categories as "a useful heuristic for understanding important points of variation across states' leadership development initiatives," with Table 2 mapping functions to states (role-specific learning in 21 states; induction 9; career advancement 7; teams 10; differentiated assistance 5; supervisor training 5).

constraints: The authors state the categories are a heuristic; some programs serve a single function while others serve multiple, often overlapping, functions
target_learners: District administrators
Principals
Assistant principals
Teacher leaders
target_learning_goals: Understanding the range of leadership development functions states support
Informing design of statewide leadership initiatives

article_title: State Approaches to Developing Educational Leaders
citation: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572
title: Role-specific professional learning convening role-alike colleagues with applied practice
description: State initiatives frequently provide professional learning designed for particular leadership roles, since "leaders in a particular role may have specific professional learning needs that are not necessarily shared by their colleagues in different roles." These programs bring together role-alike professionals in communities of practice, offer mentorship or coaching, and create opportunities to apply learning at participants' school or district sites. Examples include the Arkansas Leadership Academy's suite of role-differentiated programs (Teacher Leader Program serving 54 participants in 2022–23; Master Principal Program serving 60 across three phases), Delaware's Assistant Principal Academy, and South Carolina's School Leadership Executive Institute serving up to 24 leaders per year.
requirements: Programming must be designed around the substantive distinctions between leadership roles
Programs typically combine role-alike cohorts with mentorship, coaching, or job-embedded application
constraints: The report describes these programs but does not evaluate their quality or outcomes
target_learners: Principals
Assistant principals
Teacher leaders
District administrators
target_learning_goals: Developing role-specific leadership competencies
Connecting with role-alike colleagues
examples: The Arkansas Master Principal Program is a three-phase program over 3 school years in which participants apply learning at their school site, collect evidence of intervention efficacy, and earn the Master Principal designation with bonuses of $25,000 annually for up to 5 years in high-need schools
key_sources: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572

article_title: State Approaches to Developing Educational Leaders
citation: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572
title: Statewide induction support for early-career leaders via mentoring, coaching, and cohort learning
description: Ten states operate initiatives specifically targeting early-career leaders, six focused exclusively on induction into the principalship and four covering other roles such as the assistant principalship. Programs pair new leaders with experienced mentors (e.g., Idaho's twice-monthly calls and two site visits per quarter), provide cohort-based seminars and coaching (Hawaii's 2-year New Principal Academy), and build networks. The report notes 23 states required early-career principal induction as of 2021, and that state programs can supplement or substitute where districts provide none.
requirements: Mentors matched in a similar role or with relevant leadership experience
Structured contact frequency such as regular coaching calls, site visits, or monthly seminars
constraints: In states without induction requirements, participation in these state initiatives is voluntary; the report does not evaluate the outcomes of the described programs
target_learners: Early-career principals
First- and second-year assistant principals
Newly appointed district leaders
target_learning_goals: Acclimating to new leadership roles
Building policy knowledge and professional networks
Coping with role-related stress
examples: The Kansas Educational Leadership Institute served 132 principals and assistant principals, 38 superintendents and assistant superintendents, and 16 special education leaders in 2022–23, with completers earning credits toward license renewal
key_sources: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572

citation: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572
title: Career advancement pathways preparing aspiring leaders for the principalship
description: Seven states have initiatives targeting aspiring leaders, five with programming designed to support their transition into the principalship or other roles, and two welcoming aspiring leaders alongside current leaders. Programs such as Georgia's Aspiring Principal Program use "job-embedded leadership simulations," coaching, and real-world scenarios; Maryland's Promising Principals' Academy combines multi-day convenings with communities of practice guided by leadership coaches. The report cites district-level pipeline evidence suggesting preservice talent development "can be a lever for improving in-service effectiveness."
requirements: Selection or nomination mechanisms (e.g., superintendent recommendation) or open registration
Relevance structures such as coaching, mentorship, or real-world scenarios
constraints: In Arizona and Arkansas, professional learning is not specifically tailored to aspiring leaders' needs, though they may attend alongside current leaders
target_learners: Aspiring principals
Assistant principals
Teacher leaders seeking leadership roles
target_learning_goals: Preparing for transition into the principalship
Developing leadership competencies before appointment
examples: Arkansas's Reach program requires no application, registers participants per event, and engages close to 500 participants yearly through virtual case-study sessions

article_title: State Approaches to Developing Educational Leaders
citation: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572
title: Team-based professional learning engaging school and district leadership teams collaboratively
description: Ten states offer statewide opportunities for school- or district-based teams to learn collaboratively, acknowledging that "leadership within a school or district is distributed, rather than concentrated in singular roles." Team-based professional learning can enhance the quality and effectiveness of team interactions, broaden the stakeholders invested in new practices, and incorporate broader perspectives. Collective improvement of instructional practices

article_title: Strategies to Foster Integration in Early Childhood Education
citation: Plasencia, S., & Melnick, H. (2024). Strategies to foster integration in early childhood education. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/639.507
title: Diversity by design schools combine innovative instructional models, transportation, and a controlled-choice lottery
description: The report describes San Antonio Independent School District's "diversity by design" schools, which enroll students from inside and outside district boundaries starting in preschool. These schools "have three main components to foster and maintain socioeconomic diversity: (1) innovative instructional models that attract diverse families, (2) transportation that allows children to attend schools outside of their neighborhood, and (3) a complex lottery that maintains socioeconomic and linguistic diversity." The pattern pairs a controlled choice enrollment mechanism with features that make the school attractive and accessible across segregated residential areas.

transportation enabling attendance outside the neighborhood
instructional models with broad appeal to diverse families

These actions include culturally responsive environments supported by professional development, recruiting and retaining a diverse staff, and engaging families in ways that meet their needs. The principle holds that diversity alone is insufficient without deliberate inclusiveness.

a diverse staff who can work effectively with diverse children and families
family engagement that meets families' needs

article_title: California's Local Control Funding Formula: Next Steps toward Equity
citation: Kaplan, J. (2025). California's Local Control Funding Formula: Next steps toward equity. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/820.131
title: LCFF three-grant funding structure: base, supplemental, and concentration grants
description: The LCFF is California's K–12 finance framework, distributing "roughly $4 out of every $5 that K–12 schools receive from the state budget and local property tax revenue" through three per-pupil grants. The base grant follows average daily attendance adjusted by grade level and accounts for approximately 80% of LCFF dollars. The supplemental grant provides 20% of the base grant per unduplicated student from low-income families, an English learner, or foster youth. The concentration grant provides 65% of the base grant (initially 50%) for districts enrolling more than 55% such students.
requirements: Student need categories (low-income, English learner, foster youth) must be identified and counted for supplemental and concentration grant allocation
constraints: Approximately 130 basic aid districts with high local property tax revenue are not subject to the LCFF formula
Students categorized in more than one targeted group generate funding only once (unduplicated count)
target_learners: K–12 students in California school districts, county offices of education, and charter schools
target_learning_goals: Equitable allocation of school funding to support students with greater educational needs
examples: The 2021–22 state budget legislation raised the concentration grant from 50% to 65% of the base grant, requiring the increase to fund staff in high-need schools

article_title: Using Data to Improve School Climate: Insights from Three California Schools
citation: Klevan, S., Leung-Gagné, M., & Nakajima, T. M. (2024). Using data to improve school climate: Insights from three California schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/918.411
title: Four-domain framework of positive school climate (Safety, Community, Academics, Institutional Environment)
description: The report adopts a multidimensional conception of school climate organized into four domains drawn from Wang and Degol's review: "In a review of the literature on school climate, Wang and Degol (2016) outline 13 dimensions of school climate, which fall under four domains." Safety covers physical and emotional security and fair discipline; Community covers relationships, connectedness, and respect for diversity; Academics covers leadership, teaching and learning, and professional development; Institutional Environment covers structural features. The three case study schools focused mainly on the Safety and Community domains.

constraints: The case study schools were not focused on the institutional environment domain because features like class size and building quality are not typically under site-level leaders' control

school leaders and educators
target_learning_goals: improving school climate to support student well-being, engagement, and learning
examples: The report's Table 1 defines the three domains and their dimensions, adapted from Wang and Degol (2016), and the report's findings are organized by these domains and dimensions

article_title: Funding Student Needs: A Review of State Funding Policies for English Learners and Students from Low-Income Backgrounds
citation: Griffith, M., & Burns, D. (2025). Funding student needs: A review of state funding policies for English learners and students from low-income backgrounds. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/471.440
title: Taxonomy of state K–12 funding formula models: student-based, resource-based, hybrid, and unique systems
description: The report organizes state school funding systems into a taxonomy of models. "Student-based systems (36 states, including the district of Columbia) provide a base amount of money for each student, with additional weights or funds for specific student groups, such as English learners or students from low-income backgrounds." Resource-based systems (nine states) set amounts based on staffing positions via student-to-position ratios; four states use hybrid systems combining facets of both, and two states (Vermont and Wisconsin) have unique systems. This taxonomy frames the report's comparison of how states allocate supplemental EL and at-risk funding.

constraints: Some states using student-based formulas do not have a set base funding amount, making analysis of additional funding difficult

target_learning_goals: Equitable allocation of educational resources to support student learning needs
examples: Colorado's 2023–24 student-based formula provided a base of $8,076 with an additional 0.08 weight for English learners, translating into an additional $646 per EL student

article_title: Standards-Based Education Reforms: Looking Back to Look Forward
citation: Kirst, M. W. (2024). Standards-based education reforms: Looking back to look forward. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/647.623
title: Loose coupling explains why standards policies disconnect from classroom outcomes
description: Loose coupling is the paper's central explanatory concept: educational organizations tend to disconnect policies from outcomes, so federal and state standards policies only weakly and inconsistently shape classroom teaching. The paper applies it system-wide, from Washington, DC to individual classrooms, arguing that classroom impact will be "highly inconsistent in the absence of thorough, targeted support on standards-aligned teaching methodologies or curriculum construction." It frames effective implementation as requiring buy-in at every level rather than top-down dictates.
requirements: Buy-in at the various levels of the system; policymakers cannot simply dictate from the top down
constraints: Classroom-level instructional impact is highly inconsistent absent thorough, targeted support on standards-aligned teaching or curriculum construction
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. public schools
target_learning_goals: Standards-aligned instruction in core academic content areas

article_title: Standards-Based Education Reforms: Looking Back to Look Forward
citation: Kirst, M. W. (2024). Standards-based education reforms: Looking back to look forward. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/647.623
title: Sticky reforms share new structures, powerful constituencies, and easily accessible evidence of compliance
description: The paper proposes a three-part pattern for judging whether an education reform will persist: new organizational or physical structures, powerful constituencies created by the reform, and easily accessible evidence of compliance. It illustrates the pattern with the Advanced Placement program, which "has caused changes in organizational structure in the form of separate courses," created constituencies among colleges accepting AP credit, and is easily monitored through national standardized tests. Classroom pedagogy reforms, by contrast, are hard to monitor and lack constituencies, so they rarely last.
requirements: Reforms must create structures, constituencies, or monitorable compliance evidence to persist
constraints: Practices within the classroom are difficult to monitor and to change, so pedagogy-focused reforms are unlikely to last without teacher support
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. public schools
target_learning_goals: Sustained implementation of standards-aligned instruction
examples: The Advanced Placement program persists since the mid-1950s because it meets all three stickiness criteria

citation: Kirst, M. W. (2024). Standards-based education reforms: Looking back to look forward. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/647.623
title: Design standards policy so mutually supportive, coherent legislation reaches school internal control systems and secures teacher support
description: The paper distills research-based conditions under which federal and state policies can influence classroom teaching: legislative acts must be mutually supportive and coherent, must reach school internal control systems that influence teaching, must offset countervailing district standard operating procedures, and must be formulated to secure teacher support. It cites the authors' 1985 argument that "decisions about instruction require the active involvement of teachers if they are to be successfully implemented," warning against centrally imposed, universally applied instructional reforms.
requirements: Active involvement of teachers in instructional decisions; local decision-making about allocation and adaptation
constraints: Centrally imposed, universally applied pedagogical reforms have a discouraging implementation history

citation: Kirst, M. W. (2024). Standards-based education reforms: Looking back to look forward. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/647.623
title: A school can never outperform the capacity of its professional educators, so capacity-building must be wide-reaching, thorough, consistent, and sustained
description: The paper's core capacity principle holds that no reform can exceed the capability of a school's educators: "a given school will simply never be better than the capacity of its professional educators to deliver the instruction that best serves its students." Educators' capacity to enact standards-based instruction depends on knowledge, skill, and a broader support system including positive working conditions. Capacity-building must therefore reach far more than a small minority of the workforce and be sustained over time.
requirements: Knowledge, skill, and a broader support system including positive working conditions that enable educators to enact their skills in practice
constraints: Such capacity-building is rarely provided for by federal, state, or local policymakers
target_learners: School leaders and teachers in K-12 systems
target_learning_goals: Enacting standards-based instruction

article_title: Design Principles for Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2024). Design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/111.528
title: Six design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems
description: The report proposes a framework of six principles that state assessment systems should incorporate to have a net positive impact on instruction: Authentic, Curriculum-Anchored, Educative, Developmental and Asset-Oriented, Reflective of and Responsive to Learners, and Useful for Informing Decisions That Impact Instruction. The principles are designed to "Build upon current conceptions of alignment to standards" and to "focus on the most discerning features of assessment system design," triangulating among instructional shifts, key users, and evidence-based behaviors to influence. Each principle is elaborated with rationale and critical features.
requirements: State assessment systems defined as all instruments, supports, and communications from the state education agency about assessment
constraints: The principles are intentionally focused on features of state summative assessments rather than optional local activities
target_learners: K-12 students assessed by state large-scale assessment systems
target_learning_goals: Disciplinary knowledge and practice aligned to state standards
Positive instructional impact of assessment systems
examples: The report details each principle with rationale and critical features, using science assessment examples from states pursuing innovative systems

article_title: Design Principles for Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2024). Design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/111.528
title: Authentic assessment tasks centering disciplinary sensemaking
description: The Authentic principle holds that assessments should "highlight and center the key concepts, modes of inquiry, and ways of learning in the discipline." Systems that center authenticity use tasks representing authentic disciplinary activities, assess sensible bundles of standards contributing to substantive performance, and prioritize depth over breadth, rather than relying on selected-response proxies for performance or superficial contrived contexts. Critical features include high-quality performance tasks, emphasizing sensemaking over covering the breadth of standards, and focusing on the most-needed instructional shifts for the grade band.
requirements: High-quality performance tasks as a component of state assessment systems
constraints: State assessments are described as a relatively blunt instrument to guide change; efforts to do it all have resulted in assessments unsuccessful at compelling instructional change
target_learners: K-12 students, with examples drawn from science assessment
target_learning_goals: Authentic disciplinary sensemaking and problem-solving
Engagement with science and engineering practices and crosscutting concepts
examples: Science assessments foregrounding science and engineering practices, emphasizing using scientific ideas to make sense of data and distinguish validity of claims

article_title: Design Principles for Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2024). Design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/111.528
title: Design state assessments to be connected to and informed by high-quality curriculum
description: The Curriculum-Anchored principle argues against "curriculum agnostic" assessment design. The report states that assessments aligned only to the letter of standards, "without attending to how students developed those ideas and practices, often result in superficial assessments that are not particularly useful to any high-quality curriculum context." Instead, states should design assessments that signal, incentivize, and support high-quality instructional materials, either closely reflecting specific materials or coherently complementing them through extended transfer opportunities.

constraints: Requires states to pay more attention to and support local curriculum decisions, implying a partnership role for state education agencies

target_learning_goals: Deeper learning through coherent curriculum-assessment alignment
Trustworthy assessment results
examples: A growing number of states provide guidance, financial incentives, and requirements for adoption and implementation of high-quality instructional materials

citation: Yun, C., Fitz, J., Nakajima, T., & Mauerman, C. (2025). Educating for equity: Alder Graduate School's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/812.965
title: Alder's high-touch, whole adult support approach to resident success
description: The report describes Alder's organizing approach as a "high-touch, whole adult" model: recognizing that financial precarity and systemic inequities can block candidates' skill development, the program wraps residents in academic, financial, and social supports. An Office of Student Services proactively identified challenges "both through surveys and one-on-one conversations" and connected students with financial, food, housing, health care, academic, social, and hiring supports matched to need. The approach is framed as key to preparing the diverse educator pool Alder recruits.

article_title: Educating for Equity: Alder Graduate School's Teacher Residency
citation: Yun, C., Fitz, J., Nakajima, T., & Mauerman, C. (2025). Educating for equity: Alder Graduate School's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/812.965
title: Yearlong coteaching residency with gradual release into full instructional responsibility
description: Alder's clinical model places residents 4 days per week in selected school sites as coteachers with mentor teachers, using a coteaching and gradual release model. Residents teach at least one component of the school day from the first day of school, share all lesson plans with mentors before leading instruction, complete monthly "takeover days" in fall, and move to full takeover weeks in spring. Gradual release documents for each month suggest activities, responsibilities, and foci for residents, mentors, and clinical directors, and mentors and residents may customize the model.
requirements: School sites selected against Alder criteria (mentor qualifications, school demographics, principal commitment), at least 2 hours per week of Sacred Meeting Time for coplanning and debriefing, and weekly documented mentor observations in SchoolMint Grow
constraints: As of 2022–23 Alder did not yet use a professional development school model hosting a large group of residents at a single site
target_learners: Preservice teacher candidates earning preliminary California credentials
target_learning_goals: Development of instructional practice, professional identity, and full classroom leadership readiness
examples: Takeover days served the dual function of freeing mentors' time to attend Mentor Seminar while scaffolding residents' readiness for full spring takeover weeks
