citation: Gardner, M., Melnick, H., Meloy, B., & Barajas, J. (2019). Promising models for preparing a diverse, high-quality early childhood workforce. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/preparing-diverse-high-quality-early-childhood-workforce
title: EDvance at San Francisco State University: two cohort-based pathways to a B.A. in early childhood education
description: EDvance is an early childhood teacher preparation program at San Francisco State University's Marian Wright Edelman Institute that recruits historically underrepresented students, including Black and Latino/a students, into two pathways: a lower division pathway and the upper division PATH pathway for working early educators. Courses are "cohort-based, are strategically chosen and scheduled, and incorporate a focus on social justice and equity." Lower division students complete a supervised one-day-per-week practicum with a mentor teacher; PATH students work at least 25 hours per week and use videos of their work with children for faculty and peer feedback.
requirements: Dedicated staff and faculty for advising and supports, strong local partnerships and philanthropy, and PATH students working at least part time as early educators
constraints: Supported by philanthropy and local partnerships, which the report notes the programs have relied on for faculty development and continuous improvement
target_learners: Aspiring and current early educators, focusing on Black and Latino/a students historically underrepresented in higher education
target_learning_goals: Bachelor's degree in child and adolescent development, California Child Development Teacher Permit, and socially just early childhood teaching practice
examples: By offering intensive support services and a clearly articulated pathway, EDvance has graduated more than 90% of its PATH students in just 2 years.

citation: Gardner, M., Melnick, H., Meloy, B., & Barajas, J. (2019). Promising models for preparing a diverse, high-quality early childhood workforce. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/preparing-diverse-high-quality-early-childhood-workforce
title: Six common features of promising early educator preparation models
description: Across three case studies targeting different workforce segments, the report identifies shared design features: "Local early educator pipelines and pathways," relationship-building among students, instructors, and staff; "Opportunities for clinical practice in feedback-rich environments"; multifaceted student supports; well-supported and diverse staffs of instructors, advisors, and coaches; and community partnerships and funding to strengthen preparation. The report suggests these features may be developed locally and supported at the state level.
requirements: Dedicated staff who understand their local context, plus partnerships and funding that provide financial supports, student teaching opportunities, and classroom space
constraints: The features were observed in three California case study programs and New Jersey's state-level example; the report presents them as promising rather than proven at scale
target_learners: Diverse current and future early educators of children birth to age 5
target_learning_goals: Effective early childhood teaching practice, credential and degree attainment, and persistence through preparation
examples: All three case study programs create cohorts of students who take coursework and advance through their preparation together.

article_title: The Road to High-Quality Early Learning: Lessons from the States
citation: Wechsler, M., Kirp, D., Tinubu Ali, T., Gardner, M., Maier, A., Melnick, H., & Shields, P. (2016). The road to high-quality early learning: Lessons from the states. Palo Alto: Learning Policy Institute. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/
title: Build early education quality on ten research-based building blocks, from whole-child assessment to quality rating and improvement systems
description: Drawing on its prior report The Building Blocks of High-Quality Early Childhood Education Programs, the report specifies "the key elements of quality" in programs with exemplary results. These include "Using early learning standards and curricula that address noncognitive as well as cognitive dimensions of children's experiences," assessing the whole child, preparing and coaching teachers, attending to varying needs including English language learners, engaging families, providing sufficient learning time, small classes and low ratios, program-level assessments, and a quality rating and improvement system used for improvement and accountability.
requirements: Programs must implement the blocks together: the report states "Quality is the key: If the potential of early education is to be realized, the program has to be of high quality."
target_learners: Preschool-aged children, including low-income children, English language learners, and children with special needs
target_learning_goals: Cognitive and noncognitive development, school readiness, and narrowed achievement gaps
examples: The four case study states mandate curricula grounded in child development principles such as play-based instruction, and favor "unobtrusive observation-based instruments over paper-and-pencil tests."
key_sources: Wechsler, M., Kirp, D., Tinubu Ali, T., Gardner, M., Maier, A., Melnick, H., & Shields, P. (2016). The road to high-quality early learning: Lessons from the states. Palo Alto: Learning Policy Institute. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/

article_title: The Road to High-Quality Early Learning: Lessons from the States
citation: Wechsler, M., Kirp, D., Tinubu Ali, T., Gardner, M., Maier, A., Melnick, H., & Shields, P. (2016). The road to high-quality early learning: Lessons from the states. Palo Alto: Learning Policy Institute. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/
title: Michigan's Great Start Readiness Program (GSRP)
description: GSRP is "Michigan's state-funded preschool program for 4-year-old children who have factors that place them at risk of educational failure." Begun as a $1 million pilot in 1985, it grew to serve 38,213 children in 2014-15, reaching 51% of eligible 4-year-olds, with 80% in full-day programs. It targets families at or below 250% of the federal poverty level, caps class size at 18 with 1:8 or better ratios, requires research-validated curricula, and provides monthly classroom visits from Early Childhood Specialists with an M.A. and five or more years of experience.
requirements: Lead teachers must hold a valid Michigan teaching certificate with an early childhood endorsement or a B.A. in early childhood education or child development; programs must use a research-validated curriculum such as HighScope or Creative Curriculum
constraints: The report notes Michigan's progress "remains fragile": local providers' capacity varies considerably, and the budget appropriation process generates uncertainties
target_learners: At-risk 4-year-old children, prioritized by family income and risk factors
target_learning_goals: Kindergarten readiness, reading and math proficiency, and on-time graduation
examples: GSRP/Head Start blended classrooms combine a part-day GSRP slot with a part-day Head Start slot to create a full-day slot for one child, applying the highest standard from either program.
key_sources: Wechsler, M., Kirp, D., Tinubu Ali, T., Gardner, M., Maier, A., Melnick, H., & Shields, P. (2016). The road to high-quality early learning: Lessons from the states. Palo Alto: Learning Policy Institute. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/

article_title: Does Teaching Experience Increase Teacher Effectiveness? A Review of the Research
citation: Kini, T., & Podolsky, A. (2016). Does Teaching Experience Increase Teacher Effectiveness? A Review of the Research. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/our-work/publications-resources/does-teaching-experience-increase-teacher-effectiveness-review-research
title: Increase stability in teacher job assignments so teachers can refine instruction at a given grade level and subject
description: The review recommends that administrators and policymakers "Increase stability in teacher job assignments so that teachers can refine their instruction at a given grade level and subject," because its review shows repeated experience teaching the same grade level or subject is associated with more rapid improvement in effectiveness. It pairs this with recommendations to build collegial working conditions and to distribute experienced teachers more equitably across schools.
requirements: Teachers must be assigned to and retained in a consistent grade level and subject so repeated experience can accumulate.
constraints: The recommendation rests on the review's synthesis of observational studies using fixed-effects methods, not on an experimental test of assignment stability.
target_learners: K-12 public school students in the United States
target_learning_goals: Improved student achievement through faster growth of teacher effectiveness
examples: The review's policy recommendations section advises increasing stability in teacher job assignments, creating strong collegial relationships among staff, and strengthening equitable distribution of more experienced teachers.

article_title: Social, Emotional, and Academic Development through an Equity Lens
citation: Duchesneau, N. (2020). Social, Emotional, and Academic Development Through an Equity Lens (#ReEnvisionSEL). The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/resource/social-emotional-and-academic-development-through-an-equity-lens/
title: Shift SEL focus from fixing kids to addressing adult beliefs, mindsets, and systemic policies that create learning environments
description: This principle calls for school and district leaders to approach social, emotional, and academic development through an equity lens by shifting focus away from "fixing kids" and toward addressing adult beliefs and mindsets and school/district policies that create the learning environment. The report argues "approaches that fail to acknowledge the influence of the learning environment, or fail to address the processes and structures in schools that disadvantage some students, may do more harm than good." It requires considering societal realities, individual realities, and cultural background.
requirements: Educators must examine their own biases and deficit thinking about students of color
constraints: Telling students of color to believe in their ability will not be effective if adults harbor deficit thinking and haven't addressed their own negative biases
target_learners: students of color
students from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: social-emotional development
academic development
social-emotional well-being
examples: The report cites Chicago Public Schools training educators in restorative justice and the Native American Community Academy integrating Native culture throughout the school

article_title: Social, Emotional, and Academic Development through an Equity Lens
citation: Duchesneau, N. (2020). Social, Emotional, and Academic Development Through an Equity Lens (#ReEnvisionSEL). The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/resource/social-emotional-and-academic-development-through-an-equity-lens/
title: Social, emotional, and academic development (SEAD) through an equity lens framework
description: The report proposes a framework in which students' social-emotional skills, mindset, and academic learning are shaped by three interacting layers: classroom factors (adult beliefs, mindsets, and behaviors), school/district systems and policies, and societal context. It argues "all learning is social and emotional" and that separating social-emotional learning from academic learning allows for problematic implementation focused too narrowly on behavior modification. The framework shifts from a deficit-based to a strength-based mindset, from one-size-fits-all to recognizing cultural and contextual influences, and from allowing bias to targeted efforts to reduce bias.
requirements: Educators and leaders must shift focus away from fixing kids toward addressing environments and systems
constraints: Approaches that ignore context carry significant risks for students already underserved by the education system
target_learners: all students
students of color
students from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: social-emotional development
academic development
holistic student success
examples: The framework envisions learning environments where students feel they belong, are challenged to reach their potential, and receive academic and holistic supports

article_title: "...And They Cared": How to Create Better, Safer Learning Environments for Girls of Color
citation: “...and they cared”: How to create better, safer learning environments for girls of color. (2020). National Women’s Law Center & The Education Trust. https://nwlc.org
title: Restorative justice as a less punitive alternative to zero-tolerance school discipline
description: Restorative justice is described as "a less punitive, more positive alternative to addressing school-based conflicts and violence than the more traditionally used punitive method or zero-tolerance policies." At its core it is about building community, giving space to learn from and correct mistakes, and addressing root causes of behavior through listening, accountability, and healing, using evidence-based practices such as talking circles where all parties discuss what happened, its impact, and how to correct the harm. The guide reports students respond well and that it helps students build trust, respect, and social emotional skills.
requirements: Each school should have a trained restorative justice coordinator on site to support positive discipline practices
It requires follow-up rather than being a quick-fix, one-step process, per students interviewed
Doing so requires financial resources
constraints: Implementation inconsistencies at the school level were reported in Oakland
Students noted that if a conflict is not improved after restorative justice, more steps should be taken
target_learners: K–12 students, especially Black, Latina, and Native girls
target_learning_goals: Social emotional learning
Positive school climate and belonging
examples: Oakland maintains a restorative justice program supported by central office staff, school counselors, and restorative justice facilitators
Chicago’s Culture of Calm program trained schools on peer juries, restorative justice, and counseling
key_sources: “...and they cared”: How to create better, safer learning environments for girls of color. (2020). National Women’s Law Center & The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED607322

article_title: "...And They Cared": How to Create Better, Safer Learning Environments for Girls of Color
citation: “...and they cared”: How to create better, safer learning environments for girls of color. (2020). National Women’s Law Center & The Education Trust. https://nwlc.org
title: District-level reform pattern: data transparency, defiance-suspension bans, and restorative infrastructure
description: The guide identifies a reusable district-level pattern of policy changes: "Oakland has implemented a few practices that other districts across the country can adopt or adapt to improve schools for Latina and Black girls." The pattern includes making discipline data by race and gender publicly available, banning suspensions for willful defiance, prohibiting suspension or police referral for dress code violations, requiring community input, maintaining centrally supported restorative justice programs, providing professional development on classroom management, and investing in school-based health centers. Chicago implements a parallel set including student-led disciplinary proceedings and ending early-grade suspensions.
requirements: Central office support for restorative justice, including coordinators and counselors
Regular review of discipline data with action to address disparities
constraints: Implementation inconsistencies at the school level persisted in Oakland
Chicago kept a $33 million annual school police contract in 2020
target_learners: K–12 students, especially Black, Latina, and Native girls
target_learning_goals: Positive school climate
Equitable discipline
Reduced lost instructional time
examples: Oakland implemented 16 School-based Health Centers as part of a full-service community schools strategy available to nearly all secondary students
In 2020 Oakland’s board voted to eliminate its schools police department and reinvest $2.5 million in student support services

citation: Losen, D. J., & Martinez, P. (2020). Lost opportunities: How disparate school discipline continues to drive differences in the opportunity to learn. Learning Policy Institute; Center for Civil Rights Remedies at the Civil Rights Project, UCLA. http://www.schooldisciplinedata.org
title: Eliminate out-of-school suspensions for minor misconduct and replace punitive exclusion with supportive, educational alternatives
description: The report recommends that policymakers eliminate out-of-school suspensions and expulsions for lower-level offenses and reduce suspension length for other offenses, replacing punitive discipline with responses that serve an educational purpose. It urges educators to "pursue nonpunitive strategies—alternatives that teach responsibility, enhance social and emotional learning, and help students improve their conduct," including trauma-informed, restorative, and culturally responsive practices, supported by teacher training in classroom management.
requirements: Training for teachers to improve classroom management skills aligned with nonpunitive responses
Administrators must be provided training and support to implement discipline reforms with integrity
constraints: The report acknowledges some recommendations may be beyond the scope of the descriptive research presented and are based on the authors' prior studies and broader knowledge of the literature

target_learning_goals: Protecting the opportunity to learn by reducing lost instructional time and improving student conduct and school climate
examples: California's statewide policy changes limiting suspension for minor misconduct, which the report says appear to have reduced suspensions and narrowed the racial divide

article_title: The College Promise Guidebook for California and Beyond

title: Formalize College Promise partnerships early with MOUs signed by the highest-ranking leaders of each partner institution
description: The Guidebook recommends documenting shared commitment through contracts, mission statements, partnership agreements, or MOUs. It advises that "MOUs should be established early in the planning process" and that "The highest-ranking person possible from each partner institution or organization should sign the MOU" to secure executive-level buy-in and empower staff to deliver on commitments. Detail should be enough to make the MOU an effective tool but not so much that minor program changes become difficult.

article_title: The College Promise Guidebook for California and Beyond
citation: Rauner, Lundquist, & Smith. (2019). The College Promise Guidebook for California and Beyond. WestEd. https://californiacollegepromise.wested.org/guidebookresources/
title: College Promise as a comprehensive place-based access and completion model combining financial assistance, student support services, early messaging, and cross-sector collaboration
description: The Guidebook frames College Promise as more than financial aid: "A strong program also provides students and their families with targeted student support services and early messaging about program benefits and requirements." Programs are collaborative, engaging education institutions, nonprofits, local government, and philanthropy, and increasingly serve part-time students, GED completers, and incumbent workers alongside recent high school graduates attending full time. More than 300 programs across 44 states are reported nationwide. The model aligns with California's Vision for Success goals of increasing completion and transfer and reducing equity gaps.

Financial support combined with targeted student support services
constraints: The majority of programs target recent high school graduates attending full time, though eligibility is broadening

target_learning_goals: postsecondary access, persistence, certificate and degree completion, and transfer
examples: California's AB19 allocated $46 million in the 2018–2019 state budget, allowing schools to cover one year of tuition fees for first-time, full-time community college students

article_title: Sustainable Strategies for Funding Teacher Residencies: Lessons from California
citation: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california
title: The "3 R's" framework for sustainable teacher residency funding: reallocate resources, reduce costs, and reinvest savings
description: The report's organizing framework groups residency sustainability strategies into three approaches. Reallocating means integrating residents into existing budget lines such as substitutes, after-school staff, and paraeducators; reducing costs means tapping university and financial aid resources, no-cost materials, and negotiated tuition reductions; reinvesting means "capturing the savings resulting from residency investments in terms of reduced turnover and onboarding costs." As the report states, "Together, these approaches offer “3 R’s” to more sustainably fund residencies: reallocate resources, reduce costs, and reinvest savings."
requirements: Strong partnerships between districts, universities, and other entities with a common vision, since strategies depend on coordinated local resources
constraints: There is no one best model for residency sustainability; local context and trade-offs of different strategies must be considered in each community
target_learners: Teacher residency candidates in high-need shortage areas
target_learning_goals: Well-prepared teachers for shortage areas
Recruitment and retention of teachers of color
examples: Fresno Unified illustrates reallocation via ESSA school improvement funding; Sanger illustrates cost reduction through an integrated two-semester curriculum; the report describes reinvesting turnover savings to fund residencies over time.
key_sources: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california

article_title: Sustainable Strategies for Funding Teacher Residencies: Lessons from California
citation: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california
title: High-quality teacher residency design pattern: district-university partnership, yearlong mentored clinical work, integrated coursework, and financial supports
description: The report identifies a set of common characteristics that research has distinguished for high-quality residencies, setting them apart from traditional and alternative pathways. Programs "consist of strong partnerships between school districts/LEAs, universities, and sometimes other entities," tightly integrate coursework with classroom practice, require a full year alongside an accomplished mentor teacher, recruit diverse candidates for district hiring needs, provide financial support in exchange for a multi-year district commitment, place cohorts in teaching schools, and offer ongoing mentoring for graduates.
requirements: A partnership between a local education agency and an accredited teacher preparation program, with mentor stipends/release time and induction supports for graduates
constraints: Residencies can look very different depending on context; the report notes the highlighted programs share the characteristics to different extents
target_learners: Teacher candidates preparing for high-need shortage areas
target_learning_goals: Clinically oriented, theory-to-practice teacher preparation
Gradual taking on of teaching responsibility under mentor guidance
examples: The five highlighted California programs (Fresno, Humboldt North Coast, Sanger, Kern, San Francisco) all share these characteristics, with resident pay ranging from $3,600 in sub pay to $25,635 plus benefits.

article_title: Sustainable Strategies for Funding Teacher Residencies: Lessons from California
citation: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california
title: North Coast Teacher Residency Consortium: a half-time special education residency that lets paraeducators keep their salaries while training
description: The Humboldt County Office of Education and Humboldt State University launched this residency in fall 2019 to recruit existing special education paraeducators across 32 primarily rural districts. "Paraeducator residents keep their jobs during the residency but are guaranteed to spend at least 50% of every day in a class setting working with a special education mentor teacher." Residents earn salaries of $18,127 to $25,635 plus benefits, receive $10,000 tuition and testing-fee coverage, and attend evening courses, with remotely located residents using distance learning tools.
requirements: Partnership agreements guaranteeing the 50% clinical fieldwork minimum and release time for program requirements, including site-swap systems; a $9,000 supplemental site budget for mentor stipends and substitutes
constraints: The program was in its first year, so results were too early to show; half-time placements are a compromise, as full-time paid placements would be ideal
target_learners: Employed special education paraeducators seeking certification
target_learning_goals: Full special education credential preparation
Co-planning, curriculum design, and whole-class and small-group teaching with mentor support
examples: Eight of the 10 inaugural residents were paraeducators; by year's end, 9 of 10 residents had full-time teaching positions, and the program reported strong demand for the next cohort.
key_sources: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california

article_title: Sustainable Strategies for Funding Teacher Residencies: Lessons from California
citation: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california
title: Sanger STaR integrated two-semester curriculum: eleven courses consolidated into two yearlong integrated courses, saving residents roughly $4,000
description: Fresno State faculty and Sanger Unified leadership redesigned the STaR residency curriculum from three semesters with eleven separate courses into two yearlong integrated courses, one spanning pedagogy content and one covering curriculum and subject-matter instruction. Faculty teams collaborated for over a year, using classroom-based inquiry cycles around "real-time puzzles of practice" as a common structure. "For the 25 STaR residents, the two-semester model was beneficial in more ways than saving an entire semester’s worth of time and roughly $4,000 in tuition," including a free summer to earn money and no-cost course materials.
requirements: Sustained faculty collaboration across expertise areas (literacy, special education, mathematics, science, culturally and linguistically sustaining pedagogy) and alignment with district professional development initiatives
constraints: The redesign responded to Sanger's specific district initiatives, such as earlier introduction of inclusion and differentiation strategies; the report presents it as one local design, not a general model
target_learners: Multiple-subject teacher residency candidates, including those seeking bilingual certification
target_learning_goals: Deeper, more coherent learning through integrated coursework
Modeling integrated lesson planning and teaching for residents' own practice
examples: The previous model's summer, fall, and spring course lists were consolidated so that two yearlong courses replaced eleven separate courses, with clinical work continuing yearlong in the classroom.
key_sources: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california

article_title: Sustainable Strategies for Funding Teacher Residencies: Lessons from California
citation: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california
title: Provide mentor teachers stipends and release time commensurate with the yearlong, intensive mentoring residencies require
description: Because residency mentors host residents 4 to 5 days a week for a full academic year and make significant instructional shifts, the report argues programs must "recognize the skill, time, energy, and specialized professional development required of them by providing mentor stipends and release time." This contrasts with typical student teaching, where mentors host candidates only 10 to 15 weeks with limited hours. Recognizing mentors as central influences on residents' learning also develops teacher leaders within schools and districts.
requirements: Funding streams for mentor stipends and release time, which the report suggests can come from reallocated professional development dollars
constraints: Mentor stipend levels vary by partnership district, as shown in the report's program table (e.g., $1,000 to $3,400)
target_learners: Experienced mentor teachers hosting residency candidates
target_learning_goals: High-quality clinical mentoring across a full academic year
Development of teacher leaders within schools and districts
examples: Highlighted programs pay mentors $1,000–$3,400 or offer course reductions and laptops; Fresno mentor teachers received release time to attend classes with residents and co-design integrated thematic units.
key_sources: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california

article_title: Student Progress before and after California State University's Executive Order 1110
citation: Bracco, K. R., Barrat, V. X., Skjoldhorne, S., & Finkelstein, N. (2021). Student Progress Before and After California State University's Executive Order 1110. WestEd. http://csustudentsuccess.org/multiple-measures
title: Pair entry-level course completion reforms with sustained academic and nonacademic supports, because completing gateway requirements alone does not retain students
description: The report argues that eliminating developmental courses and accelerating first-year GE completion is only a first step: "completion of the A2 and B4 requirements appears to be necessary but not sufficient for long-term retention." It draws on student-success literature and reform examples such as CUNY Start and Georgia State to argue reforms must be intentional and cohesive, support students through their entire college careers, and combine mutually supportive efforts rather than separate initiatives, including advising, tutoring, and financial support.
requirements: Reforms must support students through their entire college careers with mutually supportive efforts rather than separate initiatives, as the report states citing the student-success literature.
constraints: The report states systemwide analyses of academic courses only cannot capture campus-level differences in implementation or the additional supports students receive.
target_learners: First-year CSU students, particularly those placed into supported (Category III/IV) entry-level courses
target_learning_goals: Completion of general education written communication and quantitative reasoning requirements
Retention and progress toward degree completion
examples: The report recommends campus-level analyses examining whether systemwide racial/ethnic differences appear on individual campuses and how supports affect different groups, and suggests campus teams redouble advising for undeclared students.
key_sources: Bracco, K. R., Barrat, V. X., Skjoldhorne, S., & Finkelstein, N. (2021). Student Progress Before and After California State University's Executive Order 1110. WestEd. http://csustudentsuccess.org/multiple-measures

article_title: Student Progress under California State University's Executive Order 1110: A Systemwide Analysis of Outcomes in 2018/19
citation: Bracco, K., Barrat, V., & Finkelstein, N. (2020). Student progress under California State University's Executive Order 1110: A systemwide analysis of outcomes in 2018/19. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: WestEd course categorization scheme for EO 1110 entry-level WC and QR course types
description: A four-category scheme developed by WestEd researchers to classify how CSU campuses provide additional supports to students in entry-level Written Communication and QR courses under EO 1110. The report states that "the research team found four broad categories of courses": traditional single-semester courses; single-semester courses with additional supports (separate one-unit support modules, embedded support with additional hours, or supplemental instruction); multiterm sequences using two-semester stretch or prerequisite models; and small-unit support courses. Researchers used the scheme to examine student paths toward A2 and B4 requirements and completion rates by placement category.
requirements: Course records must be classifiable into one of the four course types using campus course designations
constraints: The report notes course structures and supports are necessarily broad and cannot capture the nuanced differences from campus to campus
target_learners: CSU entering first-year students placed in Written Communication and Mathematics/Quantitative Reasoning Categories II to IV
target_learning_goals: Completion of entry-level General Education A2 (Written Communication) and B4 (Mathematics/Quantitative Reasoning) requirements in the first year
examples: Researchers used the scheme to compare first-semester course-taking paths (Figures 8-10) and completion rates by course type and placement category (Figures 11-12)
key_sources: Bracco, K., Barrat, V., & Finkelstein, N. (2020). Student progress under California State University's Executive Order 1110: A systemwide analysis of outcomes in 2018/19. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED613408

article_title: State Guidance for High-Impact Tutoring
citation: State Guidance for High Impact Tutoring. (2021). https://studentsupportaccelerator.org
title: Research-based guardrails for high-impact tutoring programs: school-day scheduling, at least three sessions weekly, consistent tutors, tutor training and coaching, data use, and aligned materials
description: The brief enumerates seven research-based commonalities of successful high-impact tutoring programs: they occur during the school day, include at least three sessions per week for the school year, use groups of four or fewer students, provide a consistent tutor supported by oversight and coaching, train and coach tutors, use data to inform sessions and assess program effectiveness, and use materials aligned with research and state standards. As the brief states, "For tutoring approaches to be effective, students have to spend a substantial amount of time working with their tutor."
requirements: Programs must provide tutors with pre-service training, oversight, ongoing coaching, and clear lines of accountability
Materials must be aligned with state standards and research on teaching and learning and be engaging for students and easy for tutors to use
constraints: The brief notes leaders must balance what the evidence says is most effective with what is most feasible given resource constraints and local context
target_learners: K12 students disproportionately impacted by the pandemic
students needing the most academic supports
target_learning_goals: accelerated academic recovery in math and English language arts
examples: The brief's guardrail list specifies embedded school-day scheduling, a minimum of three sessions per week for the duration of the school year, and data-informed session planning
key_sources: State Guidance for High Impact Tutoring. (2021). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED614259

article_title: State Guidance for High-Impact Tutoring
citation: State Guidance for High Impact Tutoring. (2021). https://studentsupportaccelerator.org
title: Keep tutoring groups to four or fewer students because tutoring impacts diminish substantially in larger groups
description: The brief recommends capping tutoring groups at four students, grounding the recommendation in the value of individualized instruction. It warns that "the impacts of tutoring diminish substantially in groups larger than four students," and it criticizes state guidance that expands group sizes to reach all students with highly effective teachers, suggesting instead that states widen the tutor pool.
requirements: Individualized instruction is essential to effective tutoring
constraints: The brief acknowledges leaders must balance evidence with feasibility given resource constraints and local context
target_learners: K12 students in high-impact tutoring programs
target_learning_goals: improved math and ELA achievement through individualized instruction
examples: The brief advises states not to expand group sizes but to expand the pool of potential tutors using paraprofessionals or recent college graduates
key_sources: State Guidance for High Impact Tutoring. (2021). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED614259

article_title: State Guidance for High-Impact Tutoring
citation: State Guidance for High Impact Tutoring. (2021). https://studentsupportaccelerator.org
title: Provide tutors with pre-service training, ongoing coaching, and clear accountability; trained non-teachers can be effective tutors
description: The brief recommends that tutors receive pre-service training, oversight, ongoing coaching, and clear lines of accountability. It states that "Certified teachers, paraprofessionals, AmeriCorps members, college students, and other volunteers who receive high-quality training can all be effective tutors," and that students should have a consistent tutor skilled at relationship-building to support academic and non-academic outcomes.
requirements: Tutors need high-quality pre-service training plus ongoing oversight, coaching, and clear lines of accountability
Students should have a consistent tutor skilled at relationship-building
target_learners: K12 students receiving tutoring
target_learning_goals: academic and non-academic outcomes through strong tutor-student relationships
examples: Saga Education publicly released a self-paced basic tutor training including modules on growth mindset, building relationships with students, and lesson planning
key_sources: State Guidance for High Impact Tutoring. (2021). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED614259

article_title: State Guidance for High-Impact Tutoring
citation: State Guidance for High Impact Tutoring. (2021). https://studentsupportaccelerator.org
title: Publicly available tutoring implementation resources: National Student Support Accelerator toolkits, Saga Education tutor training, and Proven Tutoring provider list
description: The brief catalogs three publicly available resources for states and districts implementing high-impact tutoring. The National Student Support Accelerator offers toolkits whose "Tools include guidelines for articulating each aspect of a tutoring program leaders need to determine, a calculator for determining program costs, guidance on aligning tutoring curriculum to school curriculum, and key points to cover when engaging families." Saga Education released a self-paced basic tutor training, and Proven Tutoring at Johns Hopkins University provides a list of tutoring providers with a proven research base.
requirements: States and LEAs must navigate implementation challenges such as program design, cost planning, curriculum alignment, and family engagement
target_learners: K12 students served by state and district tutoring programs
target_learning_goals: effective implementation of high-impact tutoring programs
examples: Saga Education's self-paced training includes modules on growth mindset, building relationships with students, and lesson planning
Proven Tutoring lists existing tutoring providers across the country with a proven research base
key_sources: State Guidance for High Impact Tutoring. (2021). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED614259

article_title: Advancing Integration and Equity through Magnet Schools
citation: George, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2021). Advancing integration and equity through magnet schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/magnet-schools
title: First door and second door components of diverse, effective magnet schools
description: The report organizes the shared features of diverse magnet schools that support positive social and academic outcomes into two categories. "First door" components bring students from different backgrounds to the school: integration embedded in school design and mission, intentional family outreach, inclusive enrollment practices, and free transportation. "Second door" components foster inclusive environments once students arrive: culturally responsive curriculum and instruction for all students, staff prepared for heterogeneous classrooms, ongoing professional development, and nondiscriminatory, restorative discipline practices. The report states these components "help to foster inclusive environments and promote shared success for students of color within diverse magnet schools, without tracking them into separate classes that depress their opportunities for success."
requirements: Magnet schools need support to effectively implement evidence-based components, per the report, including funding and policy support at federal, state, and district levels.
constraints: The report notes magnet schools vary significantly in theme, pedagogy, design, and implementation, making generalized conclusions about effectiveness difficult.
target_learners: students of color
English learners
students from low-income families
white and more affluent students in diverse magnet schools
target_learning_goals: access to rigorous, culturally responsive curriculum for all students
inclusive school climates supporting achievement for students of all backgrounds
examples: The report lists first door components such as "intentional and ongoing family outreach and engagement" and "provision of free transportation," and second door components including "culturally responsive curriculum and instruction" and "nondiscriminatory, restorative discipline practices."
key_sources: George, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2021). Advancing integration and equity through magnet schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/magnet-schools

article_title: Advancing Integration and Equity through Magnet Schools
citation: George, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2021). Advancing integration and equity through magnet schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/magnet-schools
title: Magnet schools: public schools of choice with special curricula designed to achieve voluntary desegregation
description: Magnet schools are public elementary or secondary schools that seek voluntary desegregation through parental choice rather than mandatory student assignment, by offering specialized instruction and innovative academic offerings that draw students from surrounding areas. The federal definition quoted in the report describes "a special curriculum capable of attracting substantial numbers of students of different racial backgrounds." Research cited in the report identifies distinguishing characteristics: "a distinctive school curriculum organized around a specific special theme or method of instruction," voluntary enrollment, and choice across neighborhood and sometimes district boundaries. One of the first magnet schools, McCarther-era McCarver Elementary School in Tacoma, WA, was established in 1968; recent estimates of operating magnet schools range from 3,285 to 4,340, educating over 3.5 million students.
requirements: Enrollment is completely voluntary, and students' ability to choose magnet schools depends on factors including whether the school operates on a regional basis and offers transportation.
constraints: The report notes wide variation in estimates of magnet schools highlights the necessity for a widely agreed upon definition, particularly for policy and research purposes, and that many magnet schools have departed from their integrative missions.
target_learners: families exercising voluntary school choice across attendance zones
students in urban centers and surrounding suburban districts
target_learning_goals: access to specialized, innovative academic programs
reduction of racial isolation through integrated enrollment
examples: The report describes McCarver Elementary School in Tacoma, WA, established in 1968 as part of a controlled choice program, followed in 1969 by the William Monroe Trotter School in Boston and others in Buffalo, Houston, and Minneapolis.
key_sources: George, J., & Darling-Hammond, L. (2021). Advancing integration and equity through magnet schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/magnet-schools

article_title: Building a National Early Childhood Education System That Works
citation: Building a National Early Childhood Education System That Works. (2021). Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org
title: Federally funded ECE programs: Head Start, Early Head Start, CCDBG, IDEA Part C and B-619, and Preschool Development Grant Birth Through 5
description: Appendix 1 of the whitepaper describes the major federally supported ECE programs. Head Start is "a comprehensive early education program for preschool-age children from low-income families, including young children with disabilities," providing health, nutrition, and family engagement services, receiving $10.6 billion in federal funding in 2020. Early Head Start serves pregnant women, infants, and toddlers ($905 million in partnerships funding in 2020). CCDBG provides states funding for child care vouchers for children birth to age 12 ($5.83 billion in 2020, with a minimum 9% quality set-aside). IDEA Part C ($477 million) and Part B-619 ($394 million) fund early intervention and preschool special education, and PDG-B5 ($275 million in 2020) supports state system building.
requirements: Programs must follow program-specific standards such as the Head Start Performance Standards and state-defined eligibility criteria
constraints: Head Start serves families below the federal poverty level or receiving public assistance; CCDBG quality guidance generally gives states discretion to set their own standards
target_learners: children birth through age 5 from low-income families
children with disabilities
migrant and Native American families
target_learning_goals: school readiness and healthy development
early intervention and special education services
parental work support and child development
examples: The appendix notes Head Start programs must ensure at least 10% of children served are those with special needs, and states can transfer up to 30% of TANF funds to CCDBG.
key_sources: Building a National Early Childhood Education System That Works. (2021). Learning Policy Institute. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED614493

article_title: Engine of Inequality: Michigan's Education System
citation: The Education Trust–Midwest. (2021). Engine of Inequality: Michigan's Education System. https://midwest.edtrust.org/advocacy/
title: Four cornerstones of a fair and effective school funding system: adequacy, equity, transparency, and responsibility
description: Developed by EdBuild and summarized in this report, the framework holds that a fair school funding system rests on four cornerstones. "ADEQUACY: The school funding allocated through the state formula should be sufficient to support a rigorous, high-quality education program for all students." EQUITY requires targeting funds to districts according to students' greater needs; TRANSPARENCY requires spending reporting that creates a feedback loop between state decisions and district needs; RESPONSIBILITY treats district and school leaders as accountable, flexible decision-makers. The report uses the framework to evaluate Michigan's system and propose reforms.
requirements: Expenditure reporting is required for general per-pupil funding and for every student need category so spending reflects state intentions and reaches intended students.
constraints: The report presents these as policy cornerstones based on EdBuild national research and lessons from strong funding systems, not as empirically tested interventions.
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly low-income students, English Learners, students with disabilities, and students in high-poverty and rural districts
target_learning_goals: Ensuring sufficient and equitably distributed educational resources so all students can achieve at high levels and access post-secondary opportunity
examples: The report evaluates Michigan against each cornerstone, finding regressive district funding, very low equity weights, weak fiscal transparency, and inadequate accountability for equity-targeted dollars.
key_sources: The Education Trust–Midwest. (2021). Engine of Inequality: Michigan's Education System. https://midwest.edtrust.org/advocacy/

article_title: Engine of Inequality: Michigan's Education System
citation: The Education Trust–Midwest. (2021). Engine of Inequality: Michigan's Education System. https://midwest.edtrust.org/advocacy/
title: Weighted student funding formula with transformative equity weights
description: A funding-formula structure in which a base per-pupil amount (in Michigan, the foundation allowance) is multiplied by weights for student need categories, so "every time there is an increase in adequacy funding, there are also automatic increases to equity funding." The report presents a hypothetical example: a $10,000 base with weights of 75% for English Learners, 90% for low-income students, and 160% for students with disabilities yields $17,500, $19,000, and $26,000 per student respectively, and a base increase to $12,000 raises equity dollars automatically. The report argues this resolves the adequacy-versus-equity tension in budget increases.
requirements: Weights must be set at transformative levels based on research and leading-state practice; if weights are too low, every future adequacy investment compounds inequity.
constraints: Michigan's current system is student-based but not a true weighted formula, using varying mechanisms and dollar allotments that require separate legislative action for equity increases.
target_learners: K-12 students, with priority for low-income students, English Learners, students with disabilities, and students in high-poverty or rural communities
target_learning_goals: Automatically closing opportunity gaps as adequacy funding grows, ensuring vulnerable students receive resources needed to achieve at the same high levels as peers
examples: Massachusetts phases in low-income weights up to 105% more ($8,797.76 per pupil in districts with 80% or more low-income students) versus Michigan's $755.78; Maryland phases in 73% for low-income students and 85% for English Learners by fiscal year 2033.
key_sources: The Education Trust–Midwest. (2021). Engine of Inequality: Michigan's Education System. https://midwest.edtrust.org/advocacy/

article_title: Special Issues Brief: How Region 2 States Are Leveraging Innovative Strategies to Address Critical Shortages of Education Personnel
citation: Dana Chambers and Trang Hoang. (2022). How Region 2 States Are Leveraging Innovative Strategies to Address Critical Shortages of Education Personnel. Special Issues Brief.
title: Region 2 educator pipeline and substitute-training programs (NextGen Educators, Educators Rising, Highlander fast-track substitute training, Warrior Teaching Fellows)
description: The brief profiles state and district programs expanding the educator workforce in Connecticut, New York, and Rhode Island. Connecticut's NextGen Educators Program partners the state education department with Central Connecticut State University to bring cohorts of teacher candidates into K–12 classrooms with professional mentors; in 2020–21 there were 18 CCSU students in the program. Rhode Island's Highlander Institute runs a 10-hour asynchronous training covering online classroom management, lesson planning, and teaching practices for racially and culturally diverse classrooms, plus a help desk for new substitutes.
requirements: Partnerships between state agencies, universities, and community organizations; mentor connections for candidates
constraints: The brief describes these programs descriptively; it reports no outcome evaluations of them
target_learners: K-12 students in Connecticut, New York, and Rhode Island; prospective and substitute teachers
target_learning_goals: Expanding and diversifying the educator workforce in shortage areas
examples: Educators Rising offers curriculum and micro-credentials for high school students; NYC Men Teach began in 2015 with a $16 million budget to recruit 1,000 men of color into teaching; the TA to BA Fellowship covers tuition up to $1,000 for teaching assistants pursuing bachelor's degrees
key_sources: Dana Chambers and Trang Hoang. (2022). How Region 2 States Are Leveraging Innovative Strategies to Address Critical Shortages of Education Personnel. Special Issues Brief. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED619872

article_title: What a Systematic Review of 32 Evaluations Says about the Impact of School-Based Law Enforcement
citation: Fisher, B., & Petrosino, A. (2022). What a systematic review of 32 evaluations says about the impact of school-based law enforcement. WestEd. https://jprc.wested.org
title: Crime-deterrence logic and its hypothesized unintended consequences as competing accounts of SBLE effects
description: The brief frames SBLE evaluation around two competing accounts. The deterrence logic "posits that crime is less likely to occur if a potential offender perceives a high risk that they will be caught," predicting reduced misbehavior, improved safety perceptions, and secondary benefits like attendance and test scores. The unintended-consequences account predicts overuse of the formal justice system for school-resolvable behavior, increased fear, and greater detection of offenses, harming perceptions and learning. The review's findings support the second account for discipline outcomes.
requirements: Quantitative evaluations comparing units with SBLE to units without SBLE, at student or school level, to test the competing predictions
constraints: The brief notes many included studies used designs that do not permit strong causal inferences and no randomized control trial findings were available yet
target_learners: K-12 students in schools with school-based law enforcement
target_learning_goals: School safety and climate
student discipline outcomes
learning outcomes such as achievement and attendance
examples: The review examined over 16,000 reports and included 32 studies with 1,002 effect sizes, estimating student-level and school-level effects separately
key_sources: Fisher, B., & Petrosino, A. (2022). What a systematic review of 32 evaluations says about the impact of school-based law enforcement. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED621156

article_title: What a Systematic Review of 32 Evaluations Says about the Impact of School-Based Law Enforcement
citation: Fisher, B., & Petrosino, A. (2022). What a systematic review of 32 evaluations says about the impact of school-based law enforcement. WestEd. https://jprc.wested.org
title: Do not expect SBLE to improve school safety or learning; expect increased student punishment instead
description: Based on its synthesis, the brief advises that SBLE's documented effect is punitive rather than protective: "SBLE contributes to increased punishment of students without providing improvements in school safety." Decision-makers weighing SBLE adoption or retention should therefore not expect crime prevention or learning gains from officer presence alone, and should weigh the discipline increases against the absence of safety or learning benefits.
requirements: Districts considering SBLE should consult evaluation evidence comparing units with and without SBLE rather than relying on deterrence expectations alone
constraints: The brief cautions that many included studies used designs that do not permit strong causal inferences, and no randomized control trial findings were available yet
target_learners: K-12 students in schools with or considering school-based law enforcement
target_learning_goals: School safety and climate
student discipline outcomes
learning outcomes such as achievement and attendance
examples: The review's synthesis of 32 evaluations found higher exclusionary discipline with SBLE and no significant relationships with learning outcomes or most crime outcomes
key_sources: Fisher, B., & Petrosino, A. (2022). What a systematic review of 32 evaluations says about the impact of school-based law enforcement. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED621156

article_title: Learning from Young People about How Safe and Supportive Conditions at Home Can Inform School Climate
citation: Mosley, J., & Valdez, A. (2022). Learning from young people about how safe and supportive conditions at home can inform school climate. Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd. https://SELcenter.WestEd.org
title: Student voice as a continuum from adult-run feedback activities to student-led action
description: The brief organizes student voice as forms ranging "from adult-run activities, such as soliciting student feedback on a lesson, to adult-supported activities, such as training students to research a problem that affects them through youth participatory action research, to more student-led forms of action, such as student advisory groups and student organizing." All forms involve taking notice of and acting on what students say about school from their point of view. The framework positions students as experts of their own experiences and essential partners in their education.
requirements: Adults take notice and act on what students say about school from their point of view
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those marginalized by the education system
target_learning_goals: School climate improvement; student leadership and co-creation of learning environments
examples: The brief cites youth participatory action research, student advisory groups, and student organizing as progressively more student-led forms
key_sources: Mosley, J., & Valdez, A. (2022). Learning from young people about how safe and supportive conditions at home can inform school climate. Center to Improve Social and Emotional Learning and School Safety at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED621228

article_title: Promising Practices: Smart State Strategies for Building Intensive Tutoring Systems
citation: Promising Practices: Smart State Strategies for Building Intensive Tutoring Systems. (2022). Education Trust, Education Reform Now, and FutureEd. https://www.edtrust.org/
title: Research-based tutoring program design features: small groups, in-school-day sessions, high frequency, consistent tutor, trained tutors
description: The brief distills recurring research-based features that state tutoring laws and guidance require: small tutoring groups (four or fewer students in Colorado; maximum three in elementary and four in middle schools in Tennessee), sessions during the school day, high frequency sustained across the year ("at least 30 minutes of tutoring at least three times per week" in Louisiana), students working "with the same tutor throughout the year," and tutors who "receive training." These features appear as legislative requirements in Colorado and Tennessee and as core-pillar guidelines in Louisiana.
requirements: Tutors receive training
Sessions occur at least two to three times per week for a semester or full year
Group sizes stay at or below three to four students
constraints: Louisiana's core pillars are guidelines rather than requirements, though LDOE works with districts to ensure fidelity
Tennessee does not require tutoring during the school day, only noting it is more effective
target_learners: K-12 students with unfinished learning
Elementary and middle school students
target_learning_goals: Accelerating mastery of grade-level academic content in math and ELA
examples: Colorado's House Bill 21-1234 requires up to $2,200 per participating student for programs meeting the research-based features
Tennessee's TN ALL Corps requires groups of at most three students in elementary schools and four in middle schools, 30-45 minute sessions at least twice per week for at least a full semester
key_sources: Promising Practices: Smart State Strategies for Building Intensive Tutoring Systems. (2022). Education Trust, Education Reform Now, and FutureEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622839

article_title: Promising Practices: Smart State Strategies for Building Intensive Tutoring Systems
citation: Promising Practices: Smart State Strategies for Building Intensive Tutoring Systems. (2022). Education Trust, Education Reform Now, and FutureEd. https://www.edtrust.org/
title: Statewide intensive tutoring programs with dedicated funding and vetted vendor hubs (Accelerate, TN ALL Corps, Vetted Texas Tutor Corps)
description: The brief profiles named statewide tutoring systems built with relief funds: Louisiana's Accelerate program (part of $90 million in academic and social-emotional recovery spending, with a year-long math and ELA tutoring curriculum developed with the teacher-leader community and a vendor guide of state-approved private providers); Tennessee's TN ALL Corps (an estimated $200 million initiative under the Learning Loss Remediation and Student Acceleration Act, with matching grants to LEAs); and Texas's Vetted Texas Tutor Corps, which "provides districts free access to instructional materials for tutoring" and TEA-subsidized tutor training with ongoing technical assistance via Regional Education Service Centers.
requirements: District participation criteria such as Tennessee's requirement that about 500 intervention schools have fully implemented tutoring programs to receive state funding starting fall 2022
Trained tutors and, in Louisiana, use of formative assessment data to inform sessions
constraints: Colorado's CDE has not stated how much of its $58 million set-aside it plans to spend on tutoring and has made no indication it plans structured professional development
Tennessee's math resources are optional for participating districts
target_learners: K-12 students statewide with unfinished learning
Students in districts approved for matching-grant participation
target_learning_goals: Accelerating literacy and math learning through intensive tutoring integrated with state recovery strategies
examples: Louisiana works closely with a cohort of eight LEAs providing extra implementation support while WestEd studies the process and outcomes
New Mexico committed $22 million to targeted intensive tutoring programs and $40 million to a teacher-pipeline program providing tutors
key_sources: Promising Practices: Smart State Strategies for Building Intensive Tutoring Systems. (2022). Education Trust, Education Reform Now, and FutureEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622839

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Louisiana
citation: Educator Diversity State Profile: Louisiana. (2022). EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Make educator diversity data visible and actionable to stakeholders
description: The brief's first strategy holds that "all stakeholders must have access to useful and timely educator workforce data to set goals and chart a path forward." State education agencies, as keepers of state data systems, should publicly share school-level teacher demographics, the racial makeup of candidates entering and completing preparation programs, and retention data disaggregated by race/ethnicity, so stakeholders can make targeted workforce decisions at school, district, and state levels.
requirements: Data should be publicly available and easily accessible, e.g., in dashboards, school report cards, or state-developed reports
constraints: Louisiana was rated as not publicly posting retention data for educators of color disaggregated by race/ethnicity
target_learners: K-12 public and charter school students
target_learning_goals: Equitable access to teachers of color and same-race teachers
examples: Louisiana posts school-level racial demographics through its Educator Workforce Reports and Louisiana School Finder, earning a green rating on that criterion
key_sources: Educator Diversity State Profile: Louisiana. (2022). EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622849

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Massachusetts
citation: Education Trust. (2020). Educator Diversity State Profile: Massachusetts. https://edtrust.org
title: Five-goal state policy framework for increasing educator workforce diversity
description: The brief organizes state policy conditions into five goals: making educator diversity data visible and actionable, setting clear state and district goals, supporting preparation programs to recruit and prepare teachers of color, targeting resources to recruit and hire a diverse workforce, and improving working conditions and growth opportunities for teachers of color. Each goal is scored on a three-level rating scale ("Meets Criteria, Partially Meets Criteria, Does Not Meet Criteria") with printed rating methodologies and exemplar states. The framework is used to profile Massachusetts and guide state-level advocacy.
requirements: State education agencies collect and share educator workforce data so stakeholders can set goals and chart a path forward
constraints: Applies to state-level policy conditions; the brief states districts and schools also struggle to diversify using traditional methods and need targeted state resources
target_learners: P-12 students statewide
target_learning_goals: Increasing student access to strong and diverse educators
examples: Massachusetts is rated against all five goals, earning greens on data dashboards, stakeholder engagement, Grow Your Own grants, and anti-bias training, and reds on completer data, retention data, scholarships, MSI investment, and residency pathways
key_sources: Education Trust. (2020). Educator Diversity State Profile: Massachusetts. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622850

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: North Carolina
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: NORTH CAROLINA. https://edtrust.org
title: Six-strategy state policy framework for increasing educator workforce diversity
description: The brief organizes state policy conditions for increasing the racial diversity of the educator workforce into six strategies: making educator diversity data "visible and actionable to stakeholders"; setting clear state and district goals; investing in educator preparation programs to increase enrollment and improve preparation of teachers of color; targeting resources to districts and schools to recruit and hire a diverse workforce; investing in retention efforts that improve working conditions and provide growth opportunities; and using federal COVID-related relief funds for these strategies. Each strategy is operationalized with criteria and a three-level rating scale applied to North Carolina.
requirements: State education agencies must collect and analyze educator workforce data to lead targeted, data-informed efforts
constraints: Framework is addressed to state-level policymakers, advocates, and educators; ratings reflect one state's status in 2022
target_learners: state policymakers and education advocates
K-12 districts and schools
educator preparation programs
target_learning_goals: increasing the racial and cultural diversity of the educator workforce
improving student access to diverse educators
examples: North Carolina is rated green on sharing program-level candidate demographics, hosting the DRIVE Summit, GYO investment, teacher academies, and induction/mentoring; yellow on data visibility, goals, licensure interrogation, and district partnerships; red on scholarships, program approval standards, MSI investment, hiring-manager training, residencies, and leadership development
key_sources: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: NORTH CAROLINA. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622852

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: North Carolina
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: NORTH CAROLINA. https://edtrust.org
title: EdTrust policy scan rating methodology for state educator-diversity policies
description: A rating instrument the brief uses to score each state's progress on the six diversity strategies. Each criterion is scored on a three-level scale — "Meets all or most of the requirements within the goal," "Meets some of the requirements within the goal," or "Meets one or no requirements within the goal" — with printed rating methodologies listing the evidence thresholds for each level (e.g., publicly available school-level versus district-level versus no demographic data). The brief applies it criterion-by-criterion to North Carolina and names comparison states (Massachusetts, Illinois, Tennessee, Arkansas, New Jersey, Florida, Alabama, Virginia, Oregon, New York, California, Minnesota, Delaware, Ohio, Texas) as examples.
requirements: Publicly available, timely educator workforce data against which criteria can be verified
constraints: Ratings depend on publicly posted state data and agency responses; the brief notes some entries reflect that the state education agency did not respond to questions about investments
target_learners: state education agencies
policy advocates and researchers
target_learning_goals: evaluating state policy conditions for recruiting, preparing, and retaining teachers of color
examples: The data-visibility criterion is rated yellow because North Carolina posts district-level but not school-level racial demographics of the educator workforce

article_title: Educators of Color Make the Case for Teacher Diversity
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Make the Case for Teacher Diversity: Educators of Color. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/
title: Center the voices of teachers of color and their students by giving them a permanent seat at the policy decision-making table
description: The brief argues that when creating and implementing policies affecting classrooms, "it's imperative that students and teachers have a permanent seat at the decision-making table." The three policy levers themselves were developed by more than 100 educators of color at the 2022 Philadelphia convening, demonstrating the principle in action; state leaders are urged to continue centering teachers of color's voices and stories.
requirements: Policymaking processes must include teachers of color and students as ongoing participants, not one-time consultees
target_learners: teachers of color
students
state policymakers
target_learning_goals: designing educator-diversity policies that reflect the experiences of those they affect
examples: More than 100 educators of color from seven states developed state action plans and identified the three top policy levers at the 'Building a Movement' convening.

article_title: Educators of Color Make the Case for Teacher Diversity
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Make the Case for Teacher Diversity: Educators of Color. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/

advocates
researchers
