title: New Mexico community schools grant program and funding structure
description: New Mexico's Community Schools Act (2013, updated 2019) established a state grant program; legislative funding began in 2019 with an initial $2 million and totals $36.9 million allocated through 2025. For 2024-25, "90 schools either received funding for implementation grants or were designated to participate in the Accredit Community Schools pilot program." The program funds full-time community school coordinators, planning, and implementation, supplemented by federal Full-Service Community Schools grants totaling $7.5 million and a $1.8 million congressionally directed technical assistance award.

constraints: The 2024 appropriation was reduced from $10 million to $8 million, with grant awards lowered accordingly

article_title: New Mexico Community School Profile: Los Padillas Elementary School
citation: Germain, E. (2024). New Mexico community school profile: Los Padillas Elementary School. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-school-los-padillas-brief
title: Genius Hour: student-elected enrichment blocks in the extended day with showcase events
description: Genius Hour is Los Padillas's extended-day enrichment structure in which "Students select an extracurricular activity to focus on daily for 6 weeks," with options ranging "from coding, robotics, and circuits to knitting, soccer, martial arts, and mariachi." All teachers are involved, keeping classes small for individualized attention, and academic skills are woven in informally. Each 6-week cycle ends with a Genius Hour Showcase where parents and caregivers observe what students produced, serving also as family engagement.
requirements: Extended day schedule with time built in for enrichment
All teachers involved so classes stay small
constraints: Devised as part of the school redesign and directly tied to community priorities gathered in visioning sessions
target_learners: Elementary students (PreK–5) in a Title I, predominantly Hispanic dual language school
target_learning_goals: Student choice and voice
Academic enrichment
Relationship-building across grades
Family engagement
examples: A former educator attributed a major reduction in bullying, fights, and disciplinary action to Genius Hour, noting cross-grade relationships and belonging as drivers; more than 70 caregivers attended the Genius Hour showcase.
key_sources: Germain, E. (2024). New Mexico community school profile: Los Padillas Elementary School. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-school-los-padillas-brief

title: New Mexico's six key site-level practices of community schools
description: The New Mexico Public Education Department defines a community school as "a whole child, comprehensive strategy to transform schools" where educators, families, community members, and students organize in- and out-of-school resources so young people thrive. PED identifies six key site-level practices grounded in research and practitioner expertise: expanded culturally enriched learning opportunities; rigorous community-connected classroom instruction; a culture of belonging, safety, and care; integrated systems of support; powerful student and family engagement; and collaborative leadership with shared power and voice. Los Padillas's transformation is organized around these practices.

Trusting relationships among school community members
Data-informed and inclusive decision-making

title: Los Padillas Wildlife Sanctuary (5-acre experiential education facility)
description: The Los Padillas Wildlife Sanctuary is a 5-acre experiential education facility on the school campus that was "in disrepair and out of use" in 2017 and revived at community insistence as an outdoor learning space. Fourth-graders completed a project-based pond-restoration unit, researching at ponds across town and learning from experts; Tribal leaders use the sanctuary's tree-stump seating area for storytelling about Native culture and history. APS helps maintain the grounds and arranges visits for every 3rd-grade class across the city.

Native culture and history

article_title: Cultivating Relationships in Secondary Schools: Structures That Matter
citation: Hernández, L., & Darling-Hammond, L. (with Nielsen, N.). (2024). Cultivating relationships in secondary schools: Structures that matter. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/cultivating-relationships-secondary-schools-brief
title: Small learning communities: cohorts/houses, advisory systems, looping, and block scheduling that keep students and staff together in smaller units
description: Small learning communities organize staff and students into 'smaller and closer-knit units' and are described as 'a primary mechanism for promoting personalized relationships in schools.' The brief enumerates four options for large comprehensive secondary schools: cohort/house structures, advisory systems, looping across more than one year, and block scheduling with fewer, longer class periods. In effective advisory systems, each advisor serves a small group of students (usually 15–20), often over 2 to 4 years, meeting regularly and acting as liaison between school, student, and home
Block scheduling fosters relationship-building especially when courses continue for a full year and teachers use longer periods for inquiry, directed practice, and personalized instruction

recently immigrated newcomer students
target_learning_goals: student motivation, engagement, and sense of being known by school adults
academic, social, and emotional development

title: Relationship-centered schooling framework from the science of learning and development
description: This brief organizes school redesign around relationship-centered schooling, drawing on 'Design Principles for Schools: Putting the Science of Learning and Development Into Action.' It holds that 'Connections between students and school adults are at the core of relationship-centered schooling' and that positive relationships should be consistent and individualized, trustful, respectful, and reciprocal, and focused on all aspects of young people's development. article_title: Strategies and Suggestions for Local Education Agencies Using the Four Domains for Rapid School Improvement Framework
citation: The Center for School Turnaround and Improvement. (2025). Strategies and suggestions for local education agencies using the Four Domains for Rapid School Improvement framework. WestEd. https://csti.wested.org/
title: Four Domains framework organizes rapid school improvement into four domains of three practices each
description: The Four Domains for Rapid School Improvement is a systems framework created by WestEd's Center for School Turnaround and Improvement that, per the guide, was built "to outline the critical practices of successful school turnaround in the domains that research and experience suggest are critical to rapid and significant improvement." The framework names four domains — Turnaround Leadership, Talent Development, Instructional Transformation, and Culture Shift — each with three practices (12 practices total), and this guide supplies LEA-level strategies, desired future states, and reflection questions for each practice.
requirements: District and school leadership teams engage in improvement planning using the framework's domain, practice, and survey-item structure
constraints: The guide is a supplement to the framework and CALL survey system, intended for LEA and district leaders rather than classroom-level instruction

article_title: The Landscape of Middle School Career and Technical Education in Nebraska
citation: Torre Gibney, T., Fong, P., Lewis, J., Maduli, D., & Castellano, M. (2024). The landscape of middle school career and technical education in Nebraska. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Two common national models for middle school CTE delivery: career field–specific introductory coursework and stand-alone career exploration courses
description: The report identifies, based on interviews with national CTE experts, two common middle school delivery models: "introductory CTE coursework that puts middle grade students on a pathway to high school CTE programs", whether career field–specific or rotational, and "semester- or year-long career exploration courses focused on self-awareness and career awareness". Nebraska practice reflects both: career field–specific exploratory or introductory courses across six career fields, and generalized career development and exploration courses such as Middle School Career Development. Nationally, experts report no consensus about which model middle grades should offer.
requirements: Middle school introductory CTE courses are not formally part of a sequenced program of study; local contexts use them to recruit students into future high school CTE coursework.
constraints: Across and within states, middle grade CTE and career development programming are very uneven, and there is no consensus about whether middle grades should offer introductory CTE courses or stand-alone career exploration courses.

target_learning_goals: Career awareness and exploration
Connecting academics to career and college possibilities
Self-awareness and informed education and career decision making
examples: Lincoln Public Schools requires semester-long FCS and STS courses in grades 6–7 with grade 8 electives; Elkhorn Public Schools uses six-week exploratory rotations; Omaha and Millard offer exploratory CTE as electives in a six-week rotation.

article_title: Leading Inclusive, Coherent, and Effective Assessment Systems: Closing Opportunity and Outcome Gaps for Students with Disabilities
citation: Arnold, J., Hayes, S., & Zagata, E. (2025). Leading inclusive, coherent, and effective assessment systems: Closing opportunity and outcome gaps for students with disabilities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Leaders should foster a culture of inclusion and high expectations for students with disabilities before or alongside technical assessment improvements
description: The brief argues that technical assessment improvements alone will fail without a culture of inclusion and high expectations. Focus group experts recommended three moves: championing inclusion (students with disabilities are "general education students first"), recognizing intersectional student identities, and employing asset-based approaches such as reframing the IEP "from a deficit-repair tool to a learning resource." Leaders set a shared communitywide vision that explicitly includes students with disabilities.
requirements: Leaders set a shared, communitywide vision for teaching and learning that explicitly includes students with disabilities
constraints: Technical improvements to assessment practices alone will likely not have a positive impact if low-expectation culture persists
target_learners: students with disabilities in K-12 schools and districts
target_learning_goals: ambitious learning goals connected to standards
access to general education curriculum
examples: Focus group experts recommended reframing the IEP from a deficit-repair tool to a learning resource, shifting educators' approaches to intervention, instruction, and assessment.
key_sources: Arnold, J., Hayes, S., & Zagata, E. (2025). Leading inclusive, coherent, and effective assessment systems: Closing opportunity and outcome gaps for students with disabilities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673562

title: Leaders should dismantle structural barriers separating assessment in special and general education contexts
description: The brief's second theme holds that the divide between general and special education creates "a fundamental crack in the foundation of many education systems," affecting assessment decisions. Experts recommended including special education expertise in all assessment-related decision-making, and establishing structures for collaborative data sharing, analysis, and use among general and special educators, administrators, support staff, students, and families.

constraints: Without addressing structural divides, assessment data for students with disabilities cannot be used effectively to promote success in the general education curriculum

target_learning_goals: use of assessment data to improve instruction and supports
examples: Leaders can audit whether intervention data are shared with all educators and whether general and special educators regularly review formative, interim, and summative results together.

title: Leaders should promote effective data use practices: collaborative data teams, role-specific data literacy, and broader data sources
description: The brief's third theme stresses that assessment quality is meaningless if data are not used to improve teaching and learning. Experts recommended dedicating time and structures for collaborative data teams that empower special education teachers, building role-specific data literacy for educators, leaders, students, and families, and broadening data sources to include opportunity-to-learn data, lived experiences, and student and family voices alongside assessment data.

All education partners need data literacy skills relevant to their roles

article_title: Leading Inclusive, Coherent, and Effective Assessment Systems: Closing Opportunity and Outcome Gaps for Students with Disabilities
citation: Arnold, J., Hayes, S., & Zagata, E. (2025). Leading inclusive, coherent, and effective assessment systems: Closing opportunity and outcome gaps for students with disabilities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Leaders should address assessment systemically: align tools with system goals, evaluate quality and appropriateness, invest in assessment literacy, and emphasize continuous improvement
description: The brief's fourth theme urges leaders to treat assessment as "part of a broader, coherent ecosystem that supports student learning" rather than disconnected tools. Leaders establish a shared vision and common definition of mastery, align assessment tools with standards and classroom experiences (including IEP-based scaffolds), evaluate assessment quality and appropriateness for students with disabilities, invest in assessment literacy, and continually audit and evaluate the assessment system.

Professional learning that builds assessment literacy among general and special educators and leaders

article_title: Implementation and Impact of the Project with Curriculum in Juvenile Justice Facilities and Group Homes
citation: Nakamoto, J., Carter, C., & Russo, S. (2025). Implementation and impact of the Project With curriculum in juvenile justice facilities and group homes. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Project With: a 12-lesson literary-based relationship skills and self-management curriculum for justice-involved youth
description: Project With is a sexual health curriculum adapted from The Art of Loving Well in which youth read a literary selection such as a short story or poem, discuss it with peers and a facilitator with lived experience consistent with justice-involved youth, and complete an aligned activity. It comprises 12 lessons delivered in a 6-week, twice-weekly format, with each lesson carrying a "Big Idea" related to relationship skills or self-management. Discussing fictional characters rather than personal experiences provides a sense of safety aligned with trauma-informed practices, and the curriculum can also be characterized as a social and emotional learning program.
requirements: Delivery by a facilitator with lived experience consistent with the experiences of justice-involved youth
Groups of 5 to 10 youth sharing a meal with the facilitator between two lessons in ideal delivery
constraints: Youth who leave their site before lessons end cannot complete the full curriculum
target_learners: Justice-involved youth in juvenile justice facilities and group homes, ages 12 to 21
target_learning_goals: Relationship skills
Self-management and self-regulation
Goal setting and life planning
Sexual risk avoidance
examples: Lesson 1, "Two Wolves," uses a grandfather's short story about a battle between a good wolf and an evil wolf to convey that love and relationships are a journey; activities include sequencing steps of a healthy relationship and a budgeting exercise related to parenting.

article_title: Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems: What Is the Role of Performance Assessments?
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2025). Instructionally relevant assessment systems: What is the role of performance assessments? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/411.469
title: Signaling function of large-scale assessments as a driver of instructional experiences
description: The report describes signaling as the mechanism by which large-scale assessments shape instruction: rich performance tasks provide concrete examples and direct experiences of the kinds of learning opportunities students should have, signaling to educators and leaders the instruction needed to prepare students to complete such tasks. It argues assessment systems frequently make their biggest mark on instruction through this signaling function, influencing what gets taught and what success looks like. The cascade of signals grows as districts adopt predictive interim assessments and item banks mirroring state questions.
requirements: Assessment tasks must model instructional shifts and sophisticated performance expectations for the signal to point toward deeper learning
constraints: The report presents signaling as an authors' interpretation of how assessments influence instruction, not a tested causal result
target_learners: K-12 students in state and district assessment systems
target_learning_goals: deeper learning
disciplinary practices
higher-order thinking and problem-solving
examples: Performance tasks in large-scale programs signal features of effective learning environments and, when curriculum-embedded, provide actual classroom experiences
key_sources: Badrinarayan, A. (2025). Instructionally relevant assessment systems: What is the role of performance assessments? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/411.469

article_title: Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems: What Is the Role of Performance Assessments?
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2025). Instructionally relevant assessment systems: What is the role of performance assessments? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/411.469
title: Constants-and-knobs framework for designing performance assessments by purpose
description: The report frames performance assessment design as governed by constants and knobs. Constants are the non-negotiables true of all high-quality performance assessments: designed for targeted high expectations, open-ended and generative, equitable and accessible to all, requiring authentic sense-making, and including clear evaluation criteria. Knobs are variable features turned based on philosophy, priority, purpose, and goals, including student choice/agency, connection to student identities, disciplinary sophistication, transfer, creativity, collaboration, integration across domains, student reflection, range of evidence, and coverage. No single task attends equally to all knobs; a series of tasks over time can reveal a complete picture of student learning.
requirements: Constants must be present for performance assessments to be trustworthy measures of student learning
constraints: No single performance task will measure all knobs equally; a given assessment may foreground some knobs and background others
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: authentic sense-making
demonstration of knowledge, skills, and abilities
examples: A student portfolio and defense may suit graduation readiness decisions but be less useful as a stand-alone curriculum-embedded task for assessing progress at a point in time
key_sources: Badrinarayan, A. (2025). Instructionally relevant assessment systems: What is the role of performance assessments? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/411.469

article_title: Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems: What Is the Role of Performance Assessments?
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2025). Instructionally relevant assessment systems: What is the role of performance assessments? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/411.469
title: Common tasks and rubrics with calibrated scoring for system-level performance assessment
description: Large-scale systems using performance assessments rely on common tasks or sets of calibrated tasks designed for common rubrics that can be reliably used and scored across classrooms and contexts. Systems may give all students the same task, one of a set of equated tasks, curriculum-embedded tasks, or options for equated assessments connected to the statewide summative. Reliable scoring depends on clear, evidence-based rubrics and trustworthy, calibrated ratings among scorers, often using expert-vetted student work benchmarks to anchor training and calibration.
requirements: Clear, evidence-based rubrics field-tested and validated on a wide range of student work; rater training building shared conceptual understanding and consistent rubric application
constraints: Locally developed tasks lacking these features should not be used within large-scale systems
target_learners: K-12 students in state, district, and national assessment programs
target_learning_goals: comparable and trustworthy measurement of student performance
examples: AP, IB, and NAEP develop rubrics from content-specific research on learning, expert responses, task-based student work, and cognitive labs; some systems use trained local teachers with a central audit of a representative sample of scored work
key_sources: Badrinarayan, A. (2025). Instructionally relevant assessment systems: What is the role of performance assessments? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/411.469

article_title: Why Environmental Justice Is Educational Justice
citation: Kristen Hengtgen and William Rodick. (2025). Why Environmental Justice Is Educational Justice. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Empower students as climate actors through agency, mentorship, and community-partnered learning opportunities
description: The report's first principle holds that students' school experiences should prepare them to be future leaders and "support them to act now on the issues they care about most." It argues the antidote to climate anxiety is empowerment, and that schools enable youth empowerment by listening to students and providing opportunities for action. Recommended system-level changes include professional development building mentorship and leadership into school routines, funding professional learning communities that engage students as researchers, and partnerships with universities and climate-focused organizations.
requirements: Professional development for school leaders and teachers to build mentorship and leadership opportunities into regular school practices
Partnerships with universities, climate-focused organizations, and community groups developing research and civic engagement skills
constraints: Children cannot bear the full responsibility of solving a problem they did not create, per the report
target_learners: P-12 students, particularly students of color and students from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Climate literacy
civic engagement and agency on climate issues
examples: The Tucson Unified School District's 2024 climate action plan was written and researched by the youth-led Arizona Youth Climate Coalition; the Climate READY dual-enrollment program had students generate a community resilience plan presented to local government, and an evaluation found participants improved environmental literacy and felt more prepared, confident, and capable of communicating about climate change.
key_sources: Kristen Hengtgen and William Rodick. (2025). Why Environmental Justice Is Educational Justice. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED674764

article_title: Why Environmental Justice Is Educational Justice
citation: Kristen Hengtgen and William Rodick. (2025). Why Environmental Justice Is Educational Justice. EdTrust. https://edtrust.org
title: Integrate social and emotional learning with academic development to address climate-related distress, including through collective action
description: The report's third principle holds that schools should foster students' social and emotional well-being as essential to academic development, since climate change affects well-being through weather disruptions, degraded developmental conditions, and distress over observable and future threats. It argues students need safe, nurturing environments that intentionally incorporate social and emotional learning rather than behavioral interventions aimed at fixing them, and recommends school-based health professionals who can conduct climate-related distress assessments.
requirements: Professional development helping educators recognize students' social and emotional needs in the context of climate change and racial injustices
Investment in school-based health professionals able to conduct climate-related distress assessments and provide interventions
constraints: Educators are not often clinically trained, per the report
target_learners: P-12 students, especially children near industrial pollution, children of color, and children in concentrated poverty
target_learning_goals: Social-emotional coping skills such as self-regulation, social awareness, communication, and collaboration
examples: NEEF and the Climate Mental Health Network found virtually every middle school teacher reported encountering student emotional reactions to climate change but most felt unequipped to help, prompting a toolkit of teacher-tested, standards-aligned resources; the report states students are less likely to exhibit depression symptoms from climate anxiety if engaged in collective action.
key_sources: Kristen Hengtgen and William Rodick. (2025). Why Environmental Justice Is Educational Justice. EdTrust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED674764

title: Three measurable statewide teacher workforce goals: shortages, equitable access, and diversity
description: The Collaborative proposes three goal areas anchoring statewide planning: addressing teacher shortages by increasing fully prepared teachers in designated shortage areas, improving equitable access so students in highest need schools have access to fully prepared and experienced teachers mirroring lowest need schools, and increasing teacher diversity to mirror the state. Each goal is structured with subgoals and metrics (Appendix A), informed by review of goals in Connecticut, Maryland, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and Texas, and grounded in a long-term vision that "All learners have equitable access to a fully prepared educator workforce that mirrors the diversity of the student population."

increasing teacher workforce diversity

citation: Hernández, L., & Germain, E. (2026). Community schools in rural California: Leveraging shared resources in West Kern County. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/643.620
title: MQI virtual math coaching
description: The consortium adopted Harvard University's Mathematical Quality of Instruction (MQI) coaching, described as "a program that engages math educators in virtual and video-based coaching cycles." A participating teacher films a math lesson, the coach reviews it and provides individualized feedback, and may refer the teacher to the MQI video library. The consortium used it to maximize access to and frequency of math coaching that was previously unavailable and unaffordable to the individual small districts.
requirements: Grant resources to fund access to the external coaching program, which individual districts could not previously afford.
target_learners: K–8 math teachers in small rural districts
target_learning_goals: Mathematics instruction and achievement
examples: Consortium leaders invested in math coaches as a primary means of spurring academic improvement; none of the districts had access to math coaches before receiving community school grants.
key_sources: Hernández, L., & Germain, E. (2026). Community schools in rural California: Leveraging shared resources in West Kern County. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/643.620

article_title: Community Schools in Rural California: Leveraging Shared Resources in West Kern County
citation: Hernández, L., & Germain, E. (2026). Community schools in rural California: Leveraging shared resources in West Kern County. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/643.620
title: Coherent cross-district professional development system for community school personnel
description: The West Kern Consortium built a professional development system for community school coordinators and social workers combining monthly virtual communities of practice, individual coaching from initiative leaders, and site visits to other districts or regions. The report states "these capacity-building opportunities coalesced to create a coherent professional development system, which is a critical systems-level support for high-quality community school implementation." The design enables personnel in similar roles across districts to share best practices and engage in collaborative problem-solving.
requirements: Dedicated community school personnel in each district to participate; initiative leaders with capacity to facilitate communities of practice, coaching, and site visits.
target_learners: Community school coordinators and social workers in small rural districts
target_learning_goals: Professional capacity for family engagement, service connection, and community school implementation
examples: Communities of practice convened virtually each month; CSCs and social workers received individual coaching and engaged in site visits to connect with personnel in other districts or regions.
key_sources: Hernández, L., & Germain, E. (2026). Community schools in rural California: Leveraging shared resources in West Kern County. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/643.620

article_title: Community Schools in Rural California: Leveraging Shared Resources in West Kern County
citation: Hernández, L., & Germain, E. (2026). Community schools in rural California: Leveraging shared resources in West Kern County. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/643.620
title: Small rural districts should pool resources through cross-district consortiums to attain capacity no single district could achieve alone
description: The report's first lesson is "Working Stronger Together": by bringing together small, rural districts, the consortium "amassed and leveraged resources that individual districts likely would not have attained by working independently." These previously unavailable resources provided critical capacity and helped alleviate challenges in connecting students and families with resources—two common issues in rural schools. The principle applies the community schools strategy where economies of scale are unavailable.
requirements: Districts with similar demographics and challenges willing to share ideas and resources; a formal structure for initiative management and collaboration.
constraints: The report notes cross-district consortium formation remains underutilized and understudied.
target_learners: Students in small rural districts
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement, attendance, and access to social and mental health supports
examples: Three founding elementary districts jointly won a 5-year, $2.5 million federal Full-Service Community Schools grant in 2018, later expanding with a $9.5 million state implementation grant.

article_title: Investing in a High-Quality Teacher Workforce: Lessons from Texas Teacher Preparation Programs
citation: Bland, J. A., Ralph, K., Wei, W., Wang, V., Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Investing in a high-quality teacher workforce: Lessons from Texas teacher preparation programs. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/871.327
title: High-quality preparation pattern: practice-based coursework tightly coupled to a full-year, gradual-release clinical experience with trained mentor co-teachers
description: The three profiled programs share a design in which scaffolded, rigorous coursework is linked to "a full year of intensive, gradual-release clinical practice under the guidance of an experienced mentor teacher". Candidates experience the complete school year as co-teachers, take on responsibilities from day one, and follow delineated timelines for progression of responsibilities and co-teaching practices. Assessments shifted from evaluating what candidates know to what they can do, and course content is sequenced to add complexity progressively across preclinical and clinical years.
requirements: Purposefully selected and trained mentor teachers who co-teach, monitor candidates' progression, and provide feedback and coaching
Structures delineating general timelines for candidates' progression of responsibilities throughout the school year
constraints: The report notes some structures are still being enhanced as implemented, and each case study emphasizes different program components to varying degrees
target_learners: Undergraduate and postbaccalaureate teacher candidates at minority-serving institutions
target_learning_goals: Day-one readiness to lead a classroom
Integration of coursework content with clinical teaching practice
examples: UH expanded student teaching from one semester to two and made the yearlong residency the standard for all undergraduate candidates (about 300 per year); UTRGV additionally offers a yearlong clinical experience called STEP UP
key_sources: Bland, J. A., Ralph, K., Wei, W., Wang, V., Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Investing in a high-quality teacher workforce: Lessons from Texas teacher preparation programs. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/871.327

article_title: Investing in a High-Quality Teacher Workforce: Lessons from Texas Teacher Preparation Programs
citation: Bland, J. A., Ralph, K., Wei, W., Wang, V., Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Investing in a high-quality teacher workforce: Lessons from Texas teacher preparation programs. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/871.327
title: Site coordinator role combining field supervision, coaching, seminar teaching, mentor training, and governance facilitation
description: The site coordinator, a role common to US PREP residency transformation sites, fulfills the responsibilities of traditional university field supervisors—"supervising, coaching, and conducting observations for residents during their clinical experience"—while also teaching practicum seminars and methods courses, training and collaborating with mentor teachers, supporting residents emotionally, and facilitating quarterly governance meetings with partner districts. Because site coordinators' work touches many dimensions of candidates' experiences, candidate support structures are well scaffolded and aligned.
requirements: Sufficient staffing to maintain a low ratio of teacher candidates to site coordinators, enabling frequent, meaningful feedback to each candidate
Personnel with both coaching and instructional expertise
constraints: The report recommends recruiting site coordinators from educators nearing retirement, senior teachers, and instructional leaders, implying supply considerations
target_learners: Teacher residents in yearlong clinical placements
target_learning_goals: Clinical skill development through frequent observation, coaching, and feedback
examples: At UH, site coordinators guide residents through scaffolded, graduated teaching responsibilities alongside mentor teachers
key_sources: Bland, J. A., Ralph, K., Wei, W., Wang, V., Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Investing in a high-quality teacher workforce: Lessons from Texas teacher preparation programs. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/871.327

article_title: Teacher Residencies in Texas: Supporting Successful Implementation
citation: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., Ralph, K., Snyder, J., Bland, J. A., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Teacher residencies in Texas: Supporting successful implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/630.675
title: Common elements of high-quality teacher residencies
description: The report enumerates features that prior research identifies as common to effective teacher residencies: strong LEA–preparation program partnerships, a full year of residency "working alongside an accomplished mentor teacher who is the teacher of record," tightly integrated coursework and classroom practice, cohorts in teaching schools, postresidency induction support, recruitment for district needs, and financial support often tied to a teaching commitment. TCLAS required districts and EPPs to adopt such research-based design elements.
requirements: Close partnerships between local education agencies and teacher preparation programs
Yearlong clinical placement with an accomplished, compensated, trained mentor teacher
Coursework tightly integrated with classroom practice
target_learners: Preservice teacher residents in K–12 educator preparation programs
target_learning_goals: Clinical teaching skill development and retention of new teachers in district pipelines
examples: TCLAS required yearlong clinical placements of at least 3 days per week, $20,000 stipends for up to 20 residents per year, and shared EPP–district governance
key_sources: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., Ralph, K., Snyder, J., Bland, J. A., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Teacher residencies in Texas: Supporting successful implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/630.675

article_title: Teacher Residencies in Texas: Supporting Successful Implementation
citation: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., Ralph, K., Snyder, J., Bland, J. A., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Teacher residencies in Texas: Supporting successful implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/630.675
title: Contextualized preparation model of teacher residencies
description: The Texas Education Agency framed the TCLAS residency model as "contextualized preparation": teachers are prepared within the district where they will work, learning from district context and culture, engaged in daily practice-based learning in district classrooms, coached daily by a high-quality mentor teacher, and building relationships within the school community during preparation. The report describes this as a departure from licensure systems premised on teachers being equally ready to work at any school in the state.
requirements: District–EPP partnership with shared ownership over preparation, support, and success of the resident
constraints: Preparation is shaped to the needs and goals of the specific partner district rather than transferable statewide
target_learners: Teacher residents preparing for employment in partner districts
target_learning_goals: District-specific teaching practice, relationships, and school culture knowledge
examples: TEA launch materials asked district leaders to imagine incoming teachers prepared in the district prior to day 1, with daily coaching from a high-quality mentor teacher

article_title: Advancing Achievement through Biliteracy. Brief #2: State Policy Levers to Support a Strong and Sustainable Bilingual Teacher Workforce in California
citation: Grayson, D., & Jacobson, A. (2026). Advancing achievement through biliteracy: Brief #2: State policy levers to support a strong and sustainable bilingual teacher workforce in California. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Kern County regional BLA workforce planning pilot
description: A regional BLA workforce planning pilot that "brought together county, district, and educator preparation program partners in Kern County for a series of planning workshops in 2025 to examine recruitment and retention data and identify workforce strategies." The pilot is presented alongside the EL-WIN initiative as a scalable, replicable proof point demonstrating how districts, counties, and preparation programs can jointly analyze and coordinate supply and demand to address critical workforce needs.
requirements: Partnership among county offices, districts, and educator preparation programs; internal collection of workforce data where state systems do not provide it
constraints: The pilot county office of education collects some data only for some districts, and pilot districts have varied internal collection practices
target_learners: Multilingual Learners in Kern County bilingual instructional programs
target_learning_goals: expanding access to bilingual instructional programs that improve student achievement
examples: The pilot's workshops in 2025 examined recruitment and retention data and produced workforce strategies for strengthening the BLA workforce.

article_title: Community Schools in Lynwood Unified: Building Capacity for Districtwide Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934
title: Conduct a holistic districtwide analysis of existing services and unmet needs to target community schools funding and implementation
description: The principle holds that districts scaling community schools should first analyze what services already exist and what is still needed, using multiple data sources, so that new funds fill genuine gaps rather than duplicating provision. Lynwood leadership used "a combination of referral data tied to the district's health collaborative, climate surveys, and administrative data to pinpoint high areas of need" and gaps in resources, staffing, and partnerships. This analysis drove use of CCSPP funds, such as hiring student support analysts after referral analysis revealed a Tier 3 behavioral support gap.
requirements: Existing service and partnership infrastructure whose use can be traced through data such as referral records, climate surveys, and administrative data
constraints: The report presents this as a lesson from one rapidly scaling district implementing without a prior planning grant; effectiveness evidence is descriptive
target_learners: K-12 students in a high-need, majority low-income district
target_learning_goals: Student well-being, attendance, and access to integrated academic and non-academic supports
examples: Lynwood analyzed health collaborative referrals, climate surveys, and administrative data, then used CCSPP funds to hire four certified student support analysts to address a gap in Tier 3 behavioral supports for general education students without IEPs.
key_sources: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934

article_title: Community Schools in Lynwood Unified: Building Capacity for Districtwide Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934
title: Clearly define the community school coordinator's skills, responsibilities, and position classification before hiring to support selection and onboarding
description: Because the community school coordinator is a role that previously did not exist in most schools, the report recommends defining its skills, disposition, and classification up front. The report states that "Clearly defining the skills, responsibilities, disposition, and position classification for the community school coordinator helped ensure the right people were hired and enabled a smooth onboarding process." Lynwood sought people with commitment to community, familiarity with existing resources, and relationship-building ability, and designated the position as classified management so coordinators could lead on campus without being diverted into certificated duties.
requirements: District vision for the coordinator role; a job description emphasizing relationship-building, assets and needs assessment, and governance committee development; collaboration with principals and unions
constraints: Classification choice (classified management) was made on the recommendation of the Los Angeles County Office of Education and may not transfer to districts with different labor contexts
target_learners: New community school coordinators and the students and families they serve
target_learning_goals: Effective coordination of integrated student supports and community school implementation
examples: Lynwood listed the coordinator position as classified management, onboarded coordinators by meeting with every campus entity to set expectations, and clarified collaboration points with community liaisons.
key_sources: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934

article_title: Community Schools in Lynwood Unified: Building Capacity for Districtwide Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934
title: Community schools as a whole child transformation strategy anchored by a cross-boundary coordinator role
description: The report frames community schools as an evidence-based school transformation strategy that unites students, families, educators, and community partners to improve learning and well-being through a whole child approach. Its central organizing concept is the coordinator: "a school-based staff member not traditionally found in schools, who is charged with organizing access to a range of public and private resources tailored to student and family needs and weaving them into the fabric and daily operations of the school." Coordinators act as cross-boundary leaders and connectors between schools, community partners, and families, and require targeted capacity building because the role is new and distinct from typical school positions.
requirements: Key practices such as expanded learning opportunities, family engagement, integrated systems of support, collaborative leadership, and a culture of belonging; systems-level supports including resources, shared governance, data systems, professional learning, and partnerships
constraints: The report notes quality depends on full implementation and that practitioners in different locations have different tools and resources available
target_learners: K-12 students and their families, particularly in marginalized or high-need communities
target_learning_goals: Improved student learning, well-being, attendance, connectedness, and reduced exclusionary discipline
examples: Lynwood applied the strategy districtwide, embedding coordinators within its Student Services Department alongside SEL specialists, clinical social workers, and community liaisons as a wraparound team.
key_sources: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934

article_title: Cultivating Math Mindsets: Teaching Practices That Enable Equitable Classroom Learning
citation: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406
title: Composite daily math lesson structure with six engagement-oriented components
description: The observed middle school math lessons shared a common structure of six components: a warm-up, direct instruction, group activity, share-out, note-taking, and demonstration of understanding. Each teacher integrated at least five of these six components, whether the class period was 45 or 90 minutes. The structure deliberately builds in social interaction, with "Random assignment to groups; not ability-based grouping" at standing whiteboard stations, and low-stakes warm-ups and checks "with no grade."
requirements: Class time structured so students can move around and socially interact with a variety of classmates
constraints: Documented in 45- to 90-minute middle school periods across five California middle schools
target_learners: middle school math students
target_learning_goals: engaged math learning
mathematical problem-solving
examples: Table 2 describes each component's goal, structure, and teacher and student roles, e.g., the share-out goal to "Celebrate multiple ways to represent and solve math problems."
key_sources: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406

article_title: Cultivating Math Mindsets: Teaching Practices That Enable Equitable Classroom Learning
citation: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406
title: Support math teachers with collaboration time, sustained professional learning, and coaching focused on contextual needs
description: The report identifies organizational practices that enable teachers to improve math classroom conditions: allocating school-day time for collaborative learning such as professional learning communities, shared planning, and peer observation, which can build teachers' efficacy and confidence; enabling access to well-designed professional learning, "particularly when these opportunities align with school goals and involve sustained engagement over an extended period of time"; and providing coaching or expert support focused on teachers' contextual needs. At the school level, teachers valued in-classroom support staff and structured collaboration norms set by leaders.
requirements: Staffing capacity and resources allocated to support organizational priorities
constraints: Findings reflect the supports identified by teachers in three California districts serving majority students of color and students from low-income families
target_learners: middle school math students
target_learning_goals: improved math instruction
positive classroom learning conditions
examples: Teachers from schools with strong PLC collaboration and on-site math coaches described these as key supports; leaders' norms around collaboration time guided improvement-focused conversations between teachers.
key_sources: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406

article_title: Cultivating Math Mindsets: Teaching Practices That Enable Equitable Classroom Learning
citation: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406
title: Four positive classroom conditions framework for engaged math learning
description: The report organizes its findings around four classroom conditions under which, drawing on the science of learning and development and the authors' prior research synthesis, students learn math best: positive relationships with teachers and peers, a strong sense of classroom and mathematics belonging, support in adopting a growth mindset, and opportunities to engage with high-quality instruction. Figure 1 depicts these conditions, together with data access and use and school and district practices, as system factors supporting students' engagement in learning math. The framework holds that these conditions "can occur simultaneously with and reinforce high-quality instruction" and particularly matter for students from historically marginalized groups and during the middle school years.
requirements: System factors—data access and use, and school and district practices—that enable teachers to cultivate the conditions
constraints: Evidence base summarized from neuroscience, psychology, and developmental and learning sciences syntheses; classroom illustrations drawn from 10 case-study teachers
target_learners: middle school math students
students from historically marginalized groups
target_learning_goals: engaged math learning
positive math mindsets
reduced math anxiety
examples: The study documents how 10 teachers fostered each condition, e.g., routines such as welcoming students at the door, structuring daily group work, and creating a space of learning without fear of ridicule or shame.
key_sources: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406

article_title: Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future
citation: Charlotte Pierce. (2026). Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future. EdTrust-Midwest. https://midwest.edtrust.org
title: Talent Together registered teacher apprenticeship
description: Talent Together is a Michigan alternative certification program that "provides a free route to teacher certification and includes a registered apprenticeship to obtain paid work experience." It is a partnership between 56 intermediate school districts and 18 colleges and universities, prioritizes applications from uncertified current school employees in partner districts, and accepted 950 individuals in its first cohort while receiving 2,500 applications for 600 spots in its second cohort year. The report presents it as a promising path for growing and diversifying the teacher workforce.
requirements: Prioritizes applications from current school employees without teacher certifications who work in partner districts
target_learners: Current school employees without teacher certification in partner Michigan districts
target_learning_goals: Obtain teacher certification with paid work experience through a registered apprenticeship
examples: The first cohort was 24% people of color and the second cohort 41%, compared with 11.3% of Michigan teachers overall.

citation: Charlotte Pierce. (2026). Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future. EdTrust-Midwest. https://midwest.edtrust.org
title: On the Rise Academy community-recruitment alternative certification program
description: On the Rise Academy, run by Detroit Public Schools Community District, "recruits new teacher candidates from the local community," with 75% of participants working in DPSCD as paraprofessionals, attendance agents, and academic interventionists. Candidates receive coaching cycles, observations, and intentional school placements under principals committed to their success. In 2021 about 90% of candidates were teachers of color, and DPSCD credits improvement in teacher vacancies partly to the Academy's pipeline of new teachers offsetting retirements and resignations.
requirements: Placements in buildings with principals who understand the model and support candidates
target_learners: Detroit community members and school support staff seeking certification
target_learning_goals: Teacher certification and effective classroom practice in Detroit schools
examples: DPSCD's chief human resources officer describes coaching cycles: candidates are observed and given feedback rather than "thrown into the wilderness."

citation: Charlotte Pierce. (2026). Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future. EdTrust-Midwest. https://midwest.edtrust.org
title: MiCareer Rural Credentialing Hub for rural Michigan educators
description: The Michigan Consortium for Addressing Rural Education Expansion and Retention (MiCareer) Resource Hub is "an innovative partnership between educator preparation institutions and rural school districts that works to increase the number of qualified and credentialed educators in rural classrooms." It engages rural residents who are uncertified but have completed most coursework, hold temporary credentials, or are veteran teachers certified in another state, helping them earn credentials and experience at little to no cost. The report presents it as a response to rural barriers such as housing affordability and recruiting local talent.

target_learners: Rural community members with partial preparation, temporary credentials, or out-of-state certification
target_learning_goals: Earn Michigan teaching credentials and classroom experience

citation: Charlotte Pierce. (2026). Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future. EdTrust-Midwest. https://midwest.edtrust.org
title: Provide strong coaching and continuous support to teacher candidates in alternative certification programs
description: The report states that "Strong coaching and support are essential ingredients for alternative programs to be successful," according to program administrators and teacher candidates. Support appears as intensive summer institutes, classroom observations, frequent professional development throughout the year, on-site coaching when the program is housed in the school building, and intentional candidate placement in supportive buildings. Because alternative-route candidates often work as teachers of record while training, the report says any certification training program should offer robust support and continuous feedback loops.

Support mechanisms such as summer institutes, observations, and professional development sessions

article_title: Trust and interaction design in AI-enabled systems: a systematic literature review
citation: Abramson SL, Sora-Cardenas J, Nandakumar P, Bruce JE, Gopinath N, Zangari LG and Feijóo-García PG (2026). Trust and interaction design in AI-enabled systems: a systematic literature review. Front. Psychol. 17:1932655. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1932655
title: Crampton Smith's four-dimensional framework for operationalizing interaction design factors in AI trust research
description: The review operationalizes interaction design factors—defined as "a design element that can be manipulated to shape how users interact with a system"—using Crampton Smith's four dimensions: Semantics (words, language, tone, linguistic framing), Visual representations (typography, iconography, diagrams, visual hierarchy), Physical embodiment (physical objects and spatial configurations), and Time (dynamic evolution of system behavior during interaction). The framework was chosen for its breadth in accommodating novel AI interaction paradigms, and the nine emergent design factors are interpreted as recurring manifestations within these dimensions rather than an alternative taxonomy.
requirements: Studies must examine how a design-related characteristic of the AI-enabled system or interaction influences trust for a factor to fall within this framework's scope as applied by the review.
constraints: The review notes Nielsen's taxonomy does not treat time as a manipulable design variable, whereas Crampton Smith's inclusion of time is particularly relevant for AI-enabled systems whose outputs may evolve adaptively.
target_learners: users of AI-enabled systems across domains such as healthcare, banking, and education
target_learning_goals: calibrated and appropriate trust in AI-enabled systems
examples: The review mapped its nine inductively coded factors onto the four dimensions, e.g., Semantics: Explainability, Confidence, Transparency; Physical embodiment: Anthropomorphism, Interface; Time: Errors, Perceived Control, Competence, Explainability.
key_sources: Abramson SL, Sora-Cardenas J, Nandakumar P, Bruce JE, Gopinath N, Zangari LG and Feijóo-García PG (2026). Trust and interaction design in AI-enabled systems: a systematic literature review. Front. Psychol. 17:1932655. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1932655

article_title: A Comprehensive Review of the Changing Landscape of Academic Dishonesty in Automated Proctoring in the Era of Artificial Intelligence
citation: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). A comprehensive review of the changing landscape of academic dishonesty in automated proctoring in the era of artificial intelligence. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01275-6
title: Taxonomy of proctoring systems: offline proctoring and online proctoring subdivided into live, semi-automated, and fully automated
description: The review organizes proctoring systems into a classification derived from its literature study. It states that "various proctoring systems have been developed: offline proctoring, online proctoring", with online systems "categorized into live proctoring, semi-automated and automated proctoring systems". Offline proctoring requires a physical invigilator at an exam venue; live proctoring combines a virtual tool with a human proctor monitoring in real time; semi-automated proctoring records video and periodic images; fully automated proctoring uses AI tools without human involvement and generates a report at the end of the exam.
requirements: Fully automated proctoring requires infrastructure such as persistent internet connectivity, authentication, storage facilities, and security, which the review notes incur huge costs.
constraints: The review notes semi-automated proctoring has the drawback of lack of internet connectivity and the infrastructure required for processing images.
target_learners: students in higher education institutions
high school students taking online exams
target_learning_goals: maintaining academic integrity during examinations
preventing cheating in online and offline assessments
examples: The review describes semi-automated image-based proctoring in which "the examinee's photos are taken at specified intervals: at the start of the exam, at the conclusion, and during the answering process, every 30 to 45 s."
key_sources: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). A comprehensive review of the changing landscape of academic dishonesty in automated proctoring in the era of artificial intelligence. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01275-6

citation: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). A comprehensive review of the changing landscape of academic dishonesty in automated proctoring in the era of artificial intelligence. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01275-6
title: Key functionalities of online proctoring systems: eye gaze tracking, head pose estimation, facial recognition, user verification, activity recognition, and authentication
description: The review identifies a set of core functionalities that online proctoring systems implement, stating that "Some key functionalities involved in online proctoring are eye gaze tracking, head pose estimation, facial recognition, user verification, activity recognition, and authentication." These functionalities are typically implemented with camera-based monitoring and browser lockdown components; the review devotes separate sections to the algorithms and datasets used for each functionality and their reported accuracies and limitations.
requirements: Online proctoring commonly incorporates a camera-based monitoring component and a locking control (browser lockdown) that prevents examinees from opening new tabs.
constraints: The review notes that in large exam settings the efficiency of online proctoring systems is hindered by the inability of teachers to invigilate properly.
target_learners: students in higher education institutions
online exam candidates
target_learning_goals: ensuring academic integrity in online examinations
detecting cheating behavior during remote assessments
examples: The review's Fig. 3 presents a classification of key functionalities of online proctoring systems, and Tables 3 and 4 analyze systems for eye gaze estimation and head pose estimation respectively.

article_title: Acceptance of AI-Assisted English Language Learning Tools in Higher Education: Psychological Correlates Across Disciplinary and Proficiency Groups
citation: Wu J, Wang Y, He Y, Yin X, Chen F and Wan B (2026) Acceptance of AI-assisted English language learning tools in higher education: psychological correlates across disciplinary and proficiency groups. Front. Psychol. 17:1806457. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1806457
title: A learner-centered extension of TAM framing psychological resources, affective correlates, and contextual grouping variables alongside baseline acceptance constructs
description: The study retains the Technology Acceptance Model's baseline constructs — perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, behavioral intention, and satisfaction — and adds learner-centered correlates rather than replacing TAM. As the article states, "the present study retains PU, PEOU, BI, and satisfaction as baseline acceptance-related constructs, while examining learning motivation, self-eﬃcacy, anxiety, and risk perception as theoretically informed or exploratory correlates." Motivation (self-determination theory) addresses the value dimension, self-efficacy (social cognitive theory) the capability dimension, while anxiety and risk perception are treated as affective and evaluative correlates whose direction remains an empirical question. Disciplinary affiliation and English proficiency serve as contextual grouping variables for mean-level and subgroup-specific analyses.
requirements: Cross-sectional survey measurement of the four acceptance constructs and the psychological correlates; the framework organizes regression-based association analyses rather than causal or mediation models.
constraints: The article states the framework "does not imply causal ordering, mediation, temporal sequencing, or process-based eﬀects" given the cross-sectional design.
target_learners: Non-English-major undergraduates in higher education English courses
target_learning_goals: Acceptance and sustained use of AI-assisted English language learning tools
examples: The framework was applied to survey data from 210 Chinese undergraduates, with full-sample adjusted regressions, mean-level group comparisons by discipline and CET-4 proficiency, and exploratory subgroup-specific regressions.
key_sources: Wu J, Wang Y, He Y, Yin X, Chen F and Wan B (2026) Acceptance of AI-assisted English language learning tools in higher education: psychological correlates across disciplinary and proficiency groups. Front. Psychol. 17:1806457. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1806457

article_title: Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring
citation: Robinson, Carly D., David Gormley, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring. EdWorkingPaper No. 26-1451, Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai26-1451
title: Spectrum of relational intensity for models of personalized instruction
description: The article proposes a framework placing models of personalized instruction on a spectrum of relational intensity, from tech-led (low relational intensity), where humans oversee AI-student interactions from the backend, to human-led (high relational intensity), where a dedicated tutor uses AI as a supplement to direct instruction. The studied model sits near the midpoint: an in-person tutor supporting engagement, not delivering instruction. The article notes each modality spans a range, not a point, so the ordering is not fixed.
requirements: Comparing models across the spectrum requires accounting for differing personnel, training, and coordination costs the article says more human-intensive models require.
constraints: The article states the ordering is not fixed because each modality spans a range, not a point; for instance an AI-assisted human tutor can reach or even exceed the relational intensity of in-person tutoring.
target_learners: elementary school students
target_learning_goals: literacy/reading engagement with AI-delivered personalized instruction
examples: The studied intervention assigned tutors to small groups of 2-5 students for sessions with a 10-minute check-in, 15 minutes of platform work, and a 2-5 minute reflection.
key_sources: Robinson, Carly D., David Gormley, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring. EdWorkingPaper No. 26-1451, Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai26-1451

article_title: Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring
citation: Robinson, Carly D., David Gormley, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring. EdWorkingPaper No. 26-1451, Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai26-1451
title: Provide human support alongside AI tutoring tools; access alone does not ensure meaningful student engagement
description: The article's central design recommendation is that schools deploying AI-based learning tools should not rely on access alone: providing access to an AI tutor, whether after school or during school hours, did not ensure meaningful engagement. Pairing the platform with an in-person tutor focused on engagement, motivation, and troubleshooting increased both usage and content completion, suggesting that "implementation and student engagement may be equally important determinants of impact" as technology quality. Human support may be especially important for students least likely to persist with AI-based learning on their own.
requirements: Tutors need standardized training designed to help them support students while using the AI platform, and sites need capacity to assign tutors to small groups.
constraints: The article states human-intensive models require additional personnel, training, and coordination; and human support increased engagement but usage remained well below the levels recommended for measurable reading gains.
target_learners: elementary school students, including economically disadvantaged students (>80% of the sample)
target_learning_goals: reading/literacy engagement with AI-delivered personalized instruction
examples: In both districts, treatment students met tutors in small groups of 2-5 for sessions including a 10-minute check-in, 15 minutes on the platform, and a 2-5 minute reflection; tutors did not provide direct reading instruction.

article_title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Policy: A Qualitative UNESCO Framework Analysis
citation: Adarkwah, M. A., Ercan, A. M., Schneider, K., & Bayar, E. (2026). Generative Artificial Intelligence Policy: A Qualitative UNESCO Framework Analysis. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(2). https://doi.org/10.53761/801ryw41
title: UNESCO's eight-component GenAI framework as an evaluation lens for higher education GenAI policy robustness
description: UNESCO's eight-component GenAI framework is an evaluative framework whose components span ethical and governance principles as well as inclusion, equity, and sustainability considerations such as internet access, gender parity in AI, and environmental impact. The study uses it as "a lens for evaluating the robustness of the policies" of thirty highly ranked universities, scoring how fully each institution's GenAI policy covers the framework's elements. Coverage of the components varied widely across countries and institutions.
requirements: Institutional GenAI policy documents available for analysis against the framework's eight components
constraints: The framework was applied to highly ranked universities in the top ten countries for AI preparedness, not to all higher education institutions
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: safe and responsible integration of generative AI
promotion of academic integrity
examples: The study evaluated the GenAI policies of thirty QS-ranked universities across the top ten countries for AI preparedness using the framework's eight components

article_title: Toward Agent-based Educational Science: Rethinking Educational Research in the Age of AI
citation: Zhang, Y., Jiang, J. & Tang, X. (2026). Toward Agent-Based Educational Science: Rethinking Educational Research in the Age of AI. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 113. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10209-5
title: Agent-based educational science: formalizing educational theories as interacting agents and environments for in silico experimentation
description: Agent-based educational science (AES) is a research agenda in which educational theories are formalized as interacting agents and environments, enabling in silico experimentation on developmental processes. The authors frame it as "a coordinated invitation to the research community to reorient its priorities, workflows, data infrastructures, and validation practices around theory-constrained, dynamically updateable, and empirically examinable simulations of learner development." It targets developmental processes that are otherwise slow or infeasible to test empirically.
requirements: Educational theories must be formalized as interacting agents and environments
constraints: Simulations must be theory-constrained, dynamically updateable, and empirically examinable, as the article states
target_learners: learners across educational settings whose development is modeled in simulation
target_learning_goals: theory building in the science of learning
evaluation of pedagogical approaches and AI-driven learning technologies
key_sources: Zhang, Y., Jiang, J. & Tang, X. (2026). Toward Agent-Based Educational Science: Rethinking Educational Research in the Age of AI. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 113. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10209-5

citation: Zhang, Y., Jiang, J. & Tang, X. (2026). Toward Agent-Based Educational Science: Rethinking Educational Research in the Age of AI. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 113. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10209-5
title: Student Development Agents: computational agents generating developmental features under counterfactual educational environments
description: Student Development Agents are the article's concrete instantiation of AES: "computational agents designed to generate developmental features under counterfactual educational environments." They serve as simulated learners whose developmental trajectories can be examined in silico, allowing educational innovations to be evaluated before large-scale implementation. The article presents them as enabled by recent advances in generative artificial intelligence.
requirements: Generative artificial intelligence capabilities, which the article says bring the agenda within practical reach
constraints: The article presents them as a concrete instantiation of a proposed agenda, not as a validated system
target_learners: simulated learners representing students in educational environments
target_learning_goals: generating developmental features under counterfactual educational environments

title: Treat simulation-based prediction as distributional regularities and counterfactual dynamics, not deterministic forecasts of individual trajectories
description: The article sets a scope principle for AES-style prediction: throughout the paper, prediction means "distributional regularities and counterfactual dynamics, not to deterministic forecasts of individual trajectories." The authors state this distinction is made explicitly to address humanistic concerns about flattening learner diversity. Any use of simulated learners for prediction should therefore operate at the level of distributions and counterfactuals rather than individual fate.
requirements: Users of AES-style predictions must interpret them as distributional and counterfactual, not individual forecasts
constraints: The article states this distinction is needed to address humanistic concerns about flattening learner diversity
target_learners: learners whose development is modeled in educational simulations
target_learning_goals: ethical use of prediction in educational research
preserving learner diversity in simulation-based evaluation

article_title: Evolution of AI in Education: Agentic Workflows
citation: Kamalov, F., Santandreu Calonge, D., Smail, L., Azizov, D., Thadani, D. R., Kwong, T., Atif, A. (2025). Evolution of AI in Education: Agentic Workflows. https://github.com/AzizovDilshod/Multi-agent-System-for-Essay-Assessment/tree/main
title: Four-paradigm taxonomy of agentic workflows in education: reflection, planning, tool use, and multi-agent collaboration
description: The article proposes a technological taxonomy that categorizes agentic workflows in education into four major design paradigms. As the article states, "Four major paradigms underpin many current agentic approaches" — 1) reflection, where the agent analyzes past actions to refine future behavior; 2) planning, where the agent creates and follows a sequence of steps or sub-goals; 3) tool use, where the agent leverages external resources such as calculators, code execution, web search, and APIs; and 4) multi-agent collaboration, where multiple specialized agents coordinate toward a common goal. The review applies this framework to map technical capabilities onto pedagogical affordances.
requirements: An LLM-based agent layer that orchestrates reasoning, tools, and coordination around a goal
constraints: The paradigms are distinct but often complementary strategies; implementations vary in degree of agenticness
target_learners: students in AI-supported educational settings
educators and instructional designers building agentic tools
target_learning_goals: designing and evaluating AI-agent-based educational systems
examples: The review dedicates a subsection of Section 4 to each paradigm, synthesizing educational applications, advantages, and challenges
key_sources: Kamalov, F., Santandreu Calonge, D., Smail, L., Azizov, D., Thadani, D. R., Kwong, T., Atif, A. (2025). Evolution of AI in Education: Agentic Workflows. https://github.com/AzizovDilshod/Multi-agent-System-for-Essay-Assessment/tree/main

title: Platforms for building agentic systems: AutoGen, MetaGPT, CrewAI, LangGraph, and Phidata
description: The article catalogs development platforms that "facilitate the development and implementation of agentic systems, such as AutoGen, CrewAI, LangGraph, MetaGPT, and Phidata". Table 2.1 compares their key features, pros, and cons: AutoGen is open-source and highly customizable with a steep learning curve; MetaGPT uses standardized prompt sequences and excels at orchestrating complex agent interactions; CrewAI offers production-oriented, structured role-based delegation but collects anonymized usage data; LangGraph provides graph-based multi-actor workflows with fine-grained state control but requires graph-theory familiarity.
requirements: Framework documentation and technical familiarity appropriate to each platform
constraints: Each platform carries stated cons, e.g., CrewAI's privacy-raising usage-data collection and LangGraph's graph-theory prerequisite
target_learners: educators and researchers building agent-based educational applications
target_learning_goals: implementing agentic AI systems for educational purposes
