article_title: The dark side of AI in education: AI dependency as a mediator linking academic self-efficacy and teacher support to learning burnout among university students
citation: Huang Q, Tu S, Lin J, Lu L and Lv C (2026). The dark side of AI in education: AI dependency as a mediator linking academic self-efficacy and teacher support to learning burnout among university students. Front. Psychol. 17:1889053. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1889053
title: Resource-depletion mediation framework: AI dependency as the mechanism linking personal and contextual resources to learning burnout
description: The article proposes an integrated framework in which academic self-efficacy (a personal psychological resource) and teacher support (a contextual resource) shape AI dependency, which in turn is associated with learning burnout. Grounded in Conservation of Resources, Cognitive Offloading, and Social Cognitive Theory, it treats AI dependency as "a comprehensive psychological phenomenon that encompasses emotional, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions". Dependency may temporarily conserve cognitive resources but gradually deplete internal learning resources such as critical thinking and autonomous learning competence, intensifying burnout.
requirements: Measurement of academic self-efficacy, teacher support, AI dependency, and learning burnout as distinct validated constructs
Theoretical framing in Conservation of Resources, Cognitive Offloading, and Social Cognitive Theory
constraints: The cross-sectional design limits the ability to establish causal relationships among the variables
The proposed model may capture only part of the mechanisms underlying AI dependency, indicating that its explanatory scope is not exhaustive
Reciprocal relationships may exist, such as higher burnout leading to greater AI dependency
target_learners: university students in AI-assisted learning environments
target_learning_goals: reducing learning burnout
promoting responsible and autonomous AI use
examples: The study tested the framework with a cross-sectional survey of 276 university students using PROCESS Model 4 mediation analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples.

article_title: The AI disruption in engineering education: an analysis of changing student norms through cultural historical activity
citation: Tiina Leino Lindell, Christian Stöhr. (2026). The AI disruption in engineering education: an analysis of changing student norms through cultural historical activity theory. Journal of Computing in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12528-025-09488-8
title: Cultural-Historical Activity Theory as a framework for analyzing how GenAI transforms educational activity systems
description: The study adopts Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) as its analytical framework, understanding human action as mediated by tools within an activity system of six interconnected components: rules, tools, subjects, division of labor, community, and object. In CHAT, norms are "implicit rules that regulate activity", and contradictions are historically and culturally situated tensions that arise when new elements such as GenAI disrupt established practices. The article treats these contradictions not as obstacles but as "the driving force of change in activity", using them as analytical entry points to explain how students' GenAI use transforms norms and practices in engineering education.
requirements: Analysis requires identifying contradictions as tensions between components of the activity system, following the recommendations of Sannino and Engeström (2018) and Virtaluoto et al. (2016) as the article states
constraints: The authors call their introduction to CHAT "short and necessary incomplete"
The framework was applied to one technical university in Northern Europe, so the analysis is context-sensitive to that setting
target_learners: Engineering students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Understanding how access to GenAI reshapes implicit rules, norms, and educational practices
examples: The article analyzes students using GenAI to 'enhance idea generation' as a shift from purely human-generated ideas to a hybrid approach, indicating changed division of labor and a new implicit rule about ideation tools

article_title: Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers' intervention and students' engagement in the mathematics classroom
citation: Osama Swidan. (2026). Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers' intervention and students' engagement in the mathematics classroom. ZDM-MathematicsEducation. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01810-7
title: Goldin's engagement structures framework: affect as a representational system integral to mathematical engagement
description: The study draws on DeBellis and Goldin's and Goldin's framework in which affect operates as a representational system alongside cognition during mathematical work. Central to this perspective is the notion of engagement structures, defined in the article as "recurrent yet dynamically evolving conﬁgurations of affect, motiva- tion, behavior, social interaction, and mathematical reason- ing" that shape participation in problem-solving. Each structure is organized around a motivating desire (e.g., Get the Job Done, Help Me, I'm Really into This), and contexts can produce branching, replacement, or stabilization of structures. The article extends the framework to classrooms where AI-generated emotional alerts become elements of the situation that may interact with students' affective pathways.
requirements: Requires analyzing affect, motivation, behavior, social interaction, and mathematical reasoning together during in-the-moment mathematical activity rather than as separate predictors or outcomes.
constraints: The article states that constructs such as affective representations, affective pathways, motivating desires, and engagement structures are theoretically informed analytic interpretations rather than directly observable emotional states.
target_learners: high school mathematics students during problem-solving
target_learning_goals: sustained mathematical engagement during problem-solving
integration of affect with mathematical reasoning
examples: The author coded episodes for engagement processes of activation, stabilization, and branching, and for teacher responses including reframing, reinforcement, collective discussion, inquiry, and non-intervention.

citation: Osama Swidan. (2026). Responding to AI-generated emotional alerts: teachers' intervention and students' engagement in the mathematics classroom. ZDM-MathematicsEducation. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01810-7
title: Dash4Emotion: a teacher-facing AI emotional alert dashboard
description: Dash4Emotion is a research prototype that gives the teacher real-time visual information about students' facially expressed emotions during problem-solving; students neither view nor interact with the interface. It classifies six emotions via a pretrained face-api.js TensorFlow model (about 310 KB, reported 70–80% accuracy on FER-2013), grouped into negative, positive, neutral, and surprise categories. An individual alert appears when a student exhibits a negative emotion continuously for at least six seconds, "displayed as a red-framed rectangle with the student’s name and an emoji"; positive emotions appear every fifteen seconds in green frames, and a class-level time-based histogram summarizes collective emotional states.
requirements: A standard webcam per student capturing facial expressions; the interface is teacher-facing only, with students neither viewing nor interacting with it.
constraints: The article states accuracy may decrease when participants wear glasses, precision in adolescent contexts may be limited because training data consist mainly of adult faces, the model was used as released without retraining or calibration, it cannot capture reflective or delayed states, and alerts served as cues for pedagogical reflection rather than definitive evidence of student emotion.
target_learners: high school students working on technology-supported mathematics tasks
target_learning_goals: making students' moment-to-moment emotional engagement visible to the teacher during independent work
examples: In the study lesson, red-framed individual alerts and the class-level histogram were synchronized with classroom video and used as temporal anchors for identifying analytic episodes.

article_title: Artificial and Emotional Intelligence: Two Key Forces for Teachers' Professional Development in an Era of Uncertainty
citation: Aponte ML, Vargas Sánchez AD, Chiappe A and Martínez-Pérez S. (2026). Artificial and emotional intelligence: two key forces for teachers' professional development in an era of uncertainty. Front. Psychol. 17:1935683. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935683
title: Relational densification as an evaluative criterion for AI-supported teacher socio-emotional development
description: The article distinguishes relational density, the structural and experiential quality of teachers' professional relationships, from relational densification, "the process through which those relational qualities are intentionally expanded, stabilized, and made more accessible within a professional community." Density is characterized by "trust, emotional reciprocity, co-regulation, continuity of support, shared reflection, and collective responsibility for professional care," and explicitly not by interaction frequency alone. Densification serves as a conceptual criterion for judging whether AI-supported initiatives strengthen mentoring, peer support, and psychological safety.
requirements: Evaluation must move beyond platform-centered metrics and examine whether initiatives increase relational conditions through which teacher wellbeing can be sustained
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual criterion and evaluative hypothesis, stating it does not claim relational densification has been empirically demonstrated as a causal outcome of AI-supported teacher training
target_learners: teachers
teacher educators
school and university professional communities
target_learning_goals: teacher wellbeing
socio-emotional competence
professional trust and collaboration
examples: The article operationalises the criterion across individual, dyadic/small-group, and organizational levels, with matched assessment methods including validated scales, mentoring logs, social-network analysis, and policy analysis

title: Taxonomy of five AI-mediated functions in teacher professional development with differentiated ethical and pedagogical risks
description: The article treats educational AI as a heterogeneous family of systems rather than one technology, distinguishing "coordination systems, recommendation tools, analytics, conversational agents, and emotional AI" and examining their differentiated risks. Emotional AI is defined in a restricted sense as systems "that claim to recognize, infer, simulate, respond to, or classify emotions through computational means," deserving particular caution because they intervene directly in the socio-emotional domain. The taxonomy underpins the article's claim that critique should target substitutive, data-extractive uses rather than AI-mediated support in general.
requirements: Risk analysis and governance must be matched to the specific AI-mediated function, since a scheduling tool and an emotion-inference system raise different ethical concerns
constraints: The critique is directed only at uses that individualize wellbeing, replace human relationships, intensify data extraction, infer affective states without safeguards, or connect emotional information to managerial decisions

institutional leaders

target_learning_goals: teacher wellbeing

title: Seven design conditions for AI as relational infrastructure in teacher development, each linked to risks, safeguards, and outcome indicators
description: The article operationalises its thesis through seven design conditions: relational reinvestment of freed time, community as the unit of design, limits on symbolic substitution, affective data governance, critical AI literacy as socio-emotional competence, cultural fragility of algorithmic empathy, and demonstrable relational densification. "Table 1 synthesizes this distinction by linking each design condition with the main risk it addresses, the institutional safeguards required, and possible outcome indicators." Each condition names a failure mode, for example that "AI personalizes support but leaves teachers isolated in individual trajectories."

title: Reinvest AI-freed time relationally through explicit institutional policy, because efficiency gains do not automatically become care
description: The principle holds that automation opens a possibility but does not determine outcomes: "the time recovered through AI must be converted into protected spaces for mentoring, shared pedagogical reflection, peer accompaniment, and the strengthening of communities of practice." Without an explicit institutional rule of relational reinvestment, efficiency is reabsorbed as demand. The article cites intervention evidence that wellbeing efforts yield better results when linked to conditions sustainable over time rather than episodic actions.

constraints: AI gains count as fundamental only when translated into relational practices previously unfeasible for lack of time, not when producing short-term operational relief

institutional policy makers

title: Limit symbolic substitution: conversational systems should route teachers toward human support rather than act as emotional companions
description: The article warns that the deepest harm of socio-emotional AI is not technical error but a pseudo-bond: an interface that resembles a relationship yet displaces it. In teacher development, "conversational and recommendation systems should therefore facilitate conversations among colleagues, route teachers toward mentoring when signs of isolation appear, and promote community spaces that can sustain reflection." The point is not to prohibit conversational interaction but to prevent the interface from occupying the symbolic place of human accompaniment.
requirements: Conversational systems must be designed to refer teachers to human mentoring and community spaces, and must not present themselves as emotional companions
constraints: The article notes people can develop meaningful relationships with social chatbots, including intimacy and attachment, so low-friction simulated bonds may become preferred over real intersubjectivity

target_learning_goals: authentic professional relationships
socio-emotional growth through human interaction

title: Treat critical AI literacy as a socio-emotional competence, taught through reflective and dialogic professional learning rather than technical workshops alone
description: The article argues that "in teacher training, AI literacy is not only a technical competence; it is also a socio-emotional competence," because it affects autonomy, agency, help-seeking, and vulnerability. Without it, teachers over-delegate judgement and naturalize recommendations. Professional development should therefore embed AI literacy in "reflective, dialogic, and ethically oriented professional learning experiences" where teachers examine real scenarios, discuss privacy dilemmas, and collectively define acceptable uses of AI.

article_title: When AI threatens my future career: growth mindset and perceived employability in Chinese college students' career decision making anxiety
citation: Chen H (2026) When AI threatens my future career: growth mindset and perceived employability in Chinese college students' career decision making anxiety. Front. Psychol. 17:1933842. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1933842
title: Cognitive-appraisal-based moderated mediation framework linking AI employment threat, perceived employability, growth mindset, and career decision-making anxiety
description: The article proposes and tests an integrated model drawing primarily on cognitive appraisal theory, in which "AI employment threat perception represents an appraisal of potential career threat, whereas perceived employability reﬂects students' evaluation of whether they possess suﬃcient career resources to respond to that threat." Growth mindset is positioned as a personal resource shaping this appraisal process, so that students who view abilities as developable interpret AI-driven change as opportunity for skill renewal rather than denial of their employment value. The framework integrates threat appraisal, resource appraisal, and a moderator explaining heterogeneity in students' responses.
requirements: Self-report measures of AI employment threat perception, perceived employability, career decision-making anxiety, and growth mindset from students facing AI-related labor market change
constraints: Cross-sectional single-time-point design limits causal and temporal inference
Sample drawn from a single institutional context in China, limiting generalizability
Model emphasizes threat-oriented appraisal and captures only part of the broader response process
target_learners: College students approaching career decisions in an AI-driven labor market
target_learning_goals: Career decision-making confidence
Accurate appraisal of AI-related employment change
Employability development
examples: The author tested the framework with hierarchical regression, bootstrap mediation, moderation, simple slope, and moderated mediation analyses on survey data from 526 students.

article_title: Perceived AI empowerment and threat in relation to university students' dependence on GenAI: the indirect role of trust in AI
citation: Zhu K, Ma Y, Zhang J and Liu J (2026). Perceived AI empowerment and threat in relation to university students' dependence on GenAI: the indirect role of trust in AI. Front. Psychol. 17:1940317. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1940317
title: Dual-appraisal model of GenAI dependence integrating cognitive appraisal theory and trust theory
description: The article proposes a dual-appraisal model in which perceived AI empowerment and perceived AI threat are two relatively independent cognitive appraisals that shape university students' dependence on GenAI, both directly and indirectly through trust in AI. Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory and trust theory, it treats trust as "an important psychological pathway linking students' appraisals of GenAI with their reported reliance on the technology." Empowerment appraisals are associated with greater trust and dependence, threat appraisals with lower trust and dependence, and the two appraisals coexist rather than forming opposite ends of one continuum.
requirements: Measurement of perceived AI empowerment, perceived AI threat, trust in AI, and AI dependence as distinct validated constructs; the article's scales showed Cronbach's α from 0.933 to 0.954 and discriminant validity via Fornell–Larcker and HTMT criteria.
constraints: The study is cross-sectional, single-source self-report, so the model describes associations rather than causal effects; common method bias cannot be ruled out entirely, and the sample was a convenience sample of Chinese university students.
target_learners: University students with prior GenAI experience
target_learning_goals: Understanding and managing students' reliance on generative AI in academic learning, including maintaining independent judgment and verification when using AI support
examples: In the 360-student survey, the model explained 42.7% of variance in trust in AI and 45.9% of variance in AI dependence, with significant direct and indirect paths in both appraisal pathways.

article_title: A study on AI-enabled course development, AI proficiency, and first-year students' academic and psychological adjustment
citation: Zhang J and Yin Y (2026). A study on AI-enabled course development, AI proficiency, and first-year students' academic and psychological adjustment. Front. Psychol. 17:1909803. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1909803
title: Course support–competence transformation–psychological outcomes framework integrating Self-Determination Theory and Control-Value Theory
description: The article constructs an analytical framework integrating Self-Determination Theory and Control-Value Theory to explain how AI-enabled course support relates to first-year students' self-reported psychological adjustment. It proposes that "course support → competence transformation → motivation activation → self-reported psychological outcomes" constitutes a coherent explanatory pathway, with AI proficiency as the mediating competence mechanism and AI usage pressure as a moderating boundary condition. Clear course structures are theorized to raise perceived control, while AI proficiency raises perceived competence.
requirements: Supportive course contexts with clear structures and effective guidance so that perceived control and competence can develop
constraints: The framework was tested only with cross-sectional self-report data, so all pathways are statistical associations rather than causal effects
target_learners: First-year university students
target_learning_goals: Academic adjustment to university learning
Emotional management and stress coping in AI-supported courses
examples: The study tested the framework with hierarchical regression, bootstrap mediation, moderation, moderated mediation, and AMOS structural equation modeling on 551 first-year student responses

citation: Zhang J and Yin Y (2026). A study on AI-enabled course development, AI proficiency, and first-year students' academic and psychological adjustment. Front. Psychol. 17:1909803. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1909803
title: Manage AI-related workload in course design because excessive AI usage pressure attenuates proficiency's psychological benefits
description: Because AI usage pressure significantly attenuated the indirect pathway from course development satisfaction to psychological adjustment, the article recommends that course design attend to students' technological workload, not only tool coverage. The authors advise that "Instructors should control the number of AI-based tasks in course design, clearly define which tasks are suitable for AI use and which must be completed independently, and provide actionable guidelines," warning that excessive monitoring and task overload can turn AI from a learning support into a source of strain.
requirements: Course teams able to define which tasks are suitable for AI use and which must be completed independently
constraints: Derived from cross-sectional self-report associations in one institution; the authors note firm policy recommendations require longitudinal, multi-institution studies
target_learners: First-year university students using AI platforms for coursework
target_learning_goals: Protecting self-reported psychological adjustment while using AI learning tools
Reducing AI-related task pressure and uncertainty
examples: 66.97% of surveyed students reported additional pressure when completing tasks on AI platforms, and the moderated mediation index of −0.051 confirmed attenuation under high pressure

title: HI-AI collaborative flipped classroom framework explained by constructivist learning theory, cognitive load theory, and the technology acceptance model
description: The article proposes a human intelligence (HI)-AI collaborative framework layered on the flipped classroom, in which AI provides "real-time information resources and support for instructional process analysis" while teachers design higher-order tasks and give in-depth feedback. Three complementary theoretical perspectives explain the observed patterns: constructivist learning theory, cognitive load theory, and the technology acceptance model (TAM). AI is positioned as a cognitive scaffold that reduces extraneous load and frees resources for instructor-led higher-order activities.

Instructor guidance rules requiring students to verify and rewrite AI outputs
constraints: Benefits may not be replicable in resource-limited settings where such tools are unavailable
In teacher-centred systems or contexts discouraging AI reliance, implementation requires tailored adaptation and faculty development
Tested only in a single pharmacology course with international students from South and Southeast Asia

target_learning_goals: pharmacological knowledge integration and clinical decision-making
higher-order clinical thinking
self-directed learning
examples: In the 2025 cohort, students used DeepSeek V3.1 and Kimi for information gathering, outline generation, and concept explanation across all three course phases, with AI also supporting instructional process analysis in class.

citation: Chamil Arkhasa Nikko Mazlan, Muhammad Atiullah Othman, Ahmad Rithaudin Md Noor, Surasak Jamnongsarn, Riyan Hidayatullah. (2026). From abstract ethics to situated practice: a bibliometric analysis of AI ethics and professional judgement. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10630-1
title: Three-orientation analytical framework for AI ethics research: normative ethics, applied governance, and practice-based ethics
description: The study develops a conceptual distinction between three orientations of AI ethics research: "normative ethics, referring to abstract principles such as fairness, accountability, and transparency", applied governance referring to regulatory, policy, and institutional frameworks, and "practice-based ethics, referring to situated professional judgement, interpretive decision-making, and context-sensitive ethical reasoning". The framework is informed by social practice theory and accounts of professional judgement and practical wisdom. It is used as an interpretive lens for reading the keyword co-occurrence network and highly cited literature, enabling identification of shifts from abstract principles toward context-sensitive, practice-oriented perspectives.

constraints: The article states the framework "does not alter the bibliometric structure of the dataset but provides a theoretically informed lens for interpreting how ethical discourse is distributed"

professionals working with AI systems

description: The article proposes a holistic framework integrating 20 teacher-perceived ethical tensions into three domains: "authenticity of learning, authority challenge, and collaborative dynamics". Tensions were assigned to domains by the primary locus of ethical concern rather than by method, and the domains are interrelated, with tensions in one area able to produce tensions in another. It operationalizes academic-integrity concerns for AI-mediated online language classrooms.

description: The study's content analysis organizes the feedback that DeepSeek and ChatGPT gave on students' cent-based intonation tables into four dimensions. title: AI-assisted intonation feedback model: Cubase cent measurement analyzed by ChatGPT and DeepSeek without teacher intervention
description: A four-week feedback pipeline in which students' violin performances were recorded with Cubase Pro 8 and the VariAudio module yielded cent-level deviation data for 44 target notes, entered manually into an intonation deviation table. Students presented the table to the models via their own smartphones with a fixed prompt asking the AI to evaluate like a teacher, then planned their individual practice from the weekly feedback.

students' personal smartphones and AI accounts
constraints: No teacher intonation feedback was given during the process; students were asked not to use vibrato; the étude was performed at 40 bpm
target_learners: music teacher candidates (violin majors, ages 19–24)
target_learning_goals: intonation accuracy in violin performance
examples: In the study, 2208 note data points were collected across the four-week application, and feedback texts were collected after each lesson as qualitative data

title: Test discriminant validity and dimensionality before scoring multidimensional acceptance questionnaires with separate subscales
description: The article recommends that researchers who assemble multidimensional acceptance questionnaires verify that the assumed subdimensions are empirically distinct before interpreting subscale scores. It states that "Testing discriminant validity (HTMT) and dimensionality (ECV, ωh) before subscale scoring is therefore advisable", because closely related AI and gamification perceptions may not be empirically distinct even when each subscale is internally reliable. The recommendation generalizes beyond EFL to educational technology research where discriminant validity is rarely reported.

constraints: The article's evidence is structural validity only, from a single-institution, predominantly female sample; criterion validity was not examined
target_learners: EFL learners in higher education
educational technology researchers
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of learners' acceptance of AI-gamified adaptive learning tools
examples: For the 13-item measure, the authors conclude the evidence supports a general total score over separate subscale scores, with perceived gamification as an optional, interpretable facet

article_title: From digital transformation to intelligent classrooms: artificial intelligence, adaptive leadership, and service delivery in global higher education—a systematic literature review
citation: Nyamboga TO (2026) From digital transformation to intelligent classrooms: artificial intelligence, adaptive leadership, and service delivery in global higher education—a systematic literature review. Front. Educ. 11:1899369. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1899369
title: Integrated TOE, socio-technical systems, and adaptive leadership framework for AI-enabled intelligent classrooms and service delivery transformation
description: The review grounds its synthesis in an integrated conceptual framework combining the Technology–Organisation–Environment (TOE) framework, Socio-Technical Systems (STS) theory, and Adaptive Leadership theory. Within it, AI is "the central technological driver enabling the development of intelligent learning environments and automated institutional systems," adaptive leadership is "the organisational mechanism that supports change management, institutional alignment, and stakeholder engagement," and service delivery outcomes are the performance dimension reflecting efficiency, responsiveness, accessibility, and student satisfaction. TOE explains institutional adoption patterns; STS explains alignment between technical infrastructure and social structures; adaptive leadership explains how leaders mobilise institutions to address complex technological challenges.
requirements: Institutional readiness, leadership capacity, digital infrastructure, financial resources, staff competencies, and organisational culture as conditions the framework identifies for AI-driven transformation
constraints: The framework is developed for higher education institutions and its components are shaped by internal organisational conditions and external environmental pressures
Leadership-related findings carry moderate certainty due to contextual variability across regions
target_learners: higher education students
university leaders and administrators
target_learning_goals: institutional digital transformation

adaptive leadership capacity for technological change
examples: The review used the framework to structure its thematic synthesis of 155 studies across five domains: AI integration, adaptive leadership, infrastructure readiness, service delivery transformation, and barriers to sustainability

article_title: Technical and pedagogical limitations of artificial intelligence in undergraduate EFL higher education: a systematic review
citation: Espinoza-Celi V and Vargas-Saritama A (2026) Technical and pedagogical limitations of artificial intelligence in undergraduate EFL higher education: a systematic review. Front. Educ. 11:1948091. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1948091
title: Higher-order analytical framework distinguishing technical from pedagogical limitations of AI in undergraduate EFL instruction
description: The review develops an inductively derived framework that separates system- and infrastructure-related constraints (technical limitations) from instructionally mediated constraints (pedagogical limitations), each grouped into higher-order categories. Technical limitations concern "constraints arising from AI system performance and technological infrastructure", while pedagogical limitations arise from how AI is selected, integrated, mediated, and interpreted in teaching. The categorization "emerged inductively from the synthesis of the included studies and was subsequently interpreted in relation to TPACK", which supplies a conceptual point of reference without serving as an a priori coding scheme.
requirements: Evidence extracted only from Results, Discussion, and Conclusions sections of empirical studies, with each study contributing one occurrence per category to prevent overrepresentation
constraints: The framework was derived from Scopus-indexed studies published 2021–2026 in undergraduate EFL contexts; reliance on a single database limits breadth of evidence retrieval
Technical and pedagogical limitations may co-occur within the same educational context, so the domains are not mutually exclusive
target_learners: Undergraduate EFL students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Identification and management of technical and pedagogical limitations in AI-supported language learning
examples: The framework organized seven technical limitations into two categories and eight pedagogical limitations into five categories across the 54 included studies

title: AI-TPACK as a professional knowledge bridge linking general AI literacy, science teaching self-efficacy, and AI integration intention
description: The study positions AI-TPACK — pre-service science teachers' perceived ability to integrate AI tools, science content, inquiry-based pedagogy, and ethical judgment — as the central construct of a serial mediation model. Rather than a comprehensive measure of AI competence, the article frames it as "a professional knowledge bridge between general AI literacy and AI integration intention". It situates AI-TPACK within TPACK, DPACK, and DiKoLAN AI developments, extending TPACK's proposition that technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge must be integrated contextually to AI-integrated science teaching.
requirements: Requires measuring AI literacy, AI-TPACK, science teaching self-efficacy, and AI integration intention as distinct, empirically distinguishable constructs (HTMT values below 0.85 in this study)
constraints: The article states the AI-TPACK measure reflects perceived AI-integrated pedagogical knowledge and "did not directly encompass the sociocultural consequences of digitality or actual competence in data processing, simulation and modeling, and scientific information evaluation"
target_learners: pre-service science teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: AI-integrated pedagogical competence for inquiry-based science teaching
confidence in using AI to support inquiry, experimentation, data interpretation, and scientific explanation
examples: The study modeled AI-TPACK as a first-order serial mediator between AI literacy and intention in a PLS-SEM analysis of 548 Chinese pre-service science teachers.

article_title: How to Assess AI Literacy: Misalignment Between Self-Reported and Objective-Based Measures
citation: Shan Zhang, Ruiwei Xiao, Anthony F. Botelho, Guanze Liao, Thomas K. F. Chiu, John Stamper, and Kenneth R. Koedinger. 2026. How to Assess AI Literacy: Misalignment Between Self-Reported and Objective-Based Measures. In LAK26: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK 2026). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://doi.org/10.1145/3785022.3785088
title: Paired self-report and objective-based AI literacy assessment instruments for K–12 teachers
description: The study developed two psychometrically validated instruments aligned to Ng et al.'s four AI literacy dimensions: a 25-item scenario-based objective MCQ test and a 15-item (refined to 13) five-point Likert self-report scale adapted from AILS-CCS. Items were "written in a scenario-based format that situates test-takers in realistic pedagogical contexts and requires them to engage with AI to solve educational problems". Both were validated with 288 Taiwanese K–12 teachers and function as diagnostic tools for professional development.
requirements: Items aligned to an established AI literacy framework shared across both measures
Translation and piloting with a local teacher to check wording and cultural nuances
constraints: The objective assessment was not tailored to specific subjects or grade levels
Some existing technical items in related instruments may capture unfamiliarity with technical terminology rather than the capacity to integrate AI into practice
target_learners: K–12 pre-service and in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: AI literacy: knowing and understanding AI, using and applying AI, evaluating and creating AI, and AI ethics
examples: Data were collected in February 2025 from over 2,000 Taiwanese teachers via mailing lists; 358 completed the survey and the final analytic sample was 288

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance
citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: AI learning companions framework: three interrelated design foundations
description: The paper defines AI learning companions as "adaptive, pedagogically informed, LLM-powered agents designed for integration into learning environments" and organises their design into three foundations. The pedagogical foundation addresses how students learn with AI, fostering cognitive engagement, metacognitive awareness, and agency. The adaptive foundation addresses how AI learns about students, modelling cognitive, affective, and behavioural data to tailor feedback and instruction. The responsible design foundation ensures systems remain transparent, accountable, inclusive, and secure, upholding human oversight, equity, and trust.
requirements: Deliberate engineering that prioritises durable learning over short-term performance, rather than repurposing LLMs built for work
constraints: The framework is illustrated through five case studies said to reveal both promise and current limitations of existing tools; the supplied text is truncated before the case studies
target_learners: students across diverse educational contexts and levels
target_learning_goals: durable understanding
metacognitive growth
learner agency
examples: The paper states the framework is illustrated through five case studies spanning diverse educational contexts, levels, and tool designs

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance
citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: Nine-dimension contrast between AI for work and AI for learning
description: Figure 1 formalises the contrast between AI designed for professional productivity and AI designed to support learning across nine dimensions, including purpose, nature of interaction, relationship to cognitive effort, error, measures of success, failure mode, and design principle. In work contexts AI performs the task and success is output quality; in learning contexts AI must "scaffold and challenge the learner to produce their own understanding", interactions are developmental and cumulative, and success is measured by retention, transfer, and metacognitive growth. The key failure mode for learning AI is performance gains masking absent learning.
requirements: Design intent must deliberately withhold direct answers and preserve productive struggle
constraints: The paper frames this as a conceptual contrast, not an empirically tested taxonomy
target_learners: learners in educational environments
target_learning_goals: durable learning
retention
transfer
examples: The paper states AI for work fails when productivity gains mask skill atrophy, while AI for learning fails when task scores improve while knowledge retention declines

title: Four pedagogical principles for AI companion design derived from the HELF
description: Building on the Higher Education Learning Framework, the paper derives four principles for AI companion design: "deep and interactive learning", which prompts learners to actively process and connect new knowledge; "guided scaffolding", delivering adaptive guidance calibrated to the learner's Zone of Proximal Development; "learning to learn and higher-order learning", fostering metacognition, reflection, and autonomy; and "contextual learning", situating learning in authentic contexts for transfer and disciplinary identity. Each principle is elaborated with companion strategies such as prompting generation and retrieval rather than provision, and metacognitive calibration comparing expressed confidence against actual performance.
requirements: Companions must make the student do the thinking rather than remain passive recipients of explanation
constraints: Principles are drawn from the learning sciences literature rather than tested in this paper
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: deep durable understanding
metacognitive skills
transfer
learner autonomy
examples: The paper recommends companions shift fluidly across interactional roles as tutor, peer, or novice to sustain dialogue and perspective-taking

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance
citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: Four-stage adaptive cycle: Capture, Model, Adapt, Evolve
description: The paper's adaptive foundation organises how AI learns about students into a continuous four-stage cycle. "Capture" records learners' digital footprints, including LLM-generated conversational trace data, to gather evidence of engagement and understanding. "Model" builds a multi-dimensional learner model from cognitive, affective, and behavioural data, combining LLM interpretation with algorithms such as knowledge tracing. "Adapt" determines what, how, and when to adjust learning experiences, conceptualised through outer-loop task sequencing and inner-loop within-task support. "Evolve" evaluates the effectiveness of adaptations through design-loop adaptivity and closed-loop evaluation to drive continual improvement.
requirements: Integration of traditional learner-modelling algorithms with LLM interpretation; open learner model interfaces for transparency
constraints: Most current LLM applications remain stateless, making sustained adaptation to individual learners impossible without this foundation
target_learners: learners in digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: personalised feedback
self-regulated learning
adaptive instruction
examples: The paper proposes Reinforcement Learning from Human Learning (RLHL) as a possible route to tutoring systems that continually learn from interactions with students

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance
citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: Responsible design foundation: four commitments of security, transparency, accountability, and inclusion
description: The paper organises responsible practice for AI learning companions around four interwoven commitments unified by trustworthiness. "Security" protects learner privacy, data, and digital wellbeing through lawful data practices, including separating personally identifiable information from interaction data. "Transparency" makes AI processes, reasoning, and data flows visible and explainable, building on Open Learner Models and the XAI-ED framework. "Accountability" retains meaningful human oversight with human-in-the-loop checkpoints for high-stakes inferences such as mastery promotion and at-risk flags. "Inclusion" ensures companions are fair, accessible, and responsive to diverse learners, abilities, languages, and contexts.
requirements: Human oversight and dispute channels for contesting model states; evaluation of companions on retention, transfer, and metacognition, not only output accuracy
constraints: The paper states these commitments apply to any AI application but clarifies how they play out distinctively with learning companions
target_learners: diverse learners across abilities, languages, and contexts
target_learning_goals: trustworthy and equitable AI-supported learning
learner agency
digital wellbeing
examples: The paper recommends modular architectures isolating sensitive processes, privacy-preserving aggregated features, and audit logs linking inputs, model states, actions, and outcomes

citation: Jinwen Tang. (2026). NEW AI-DRIVEN TOOLS FOR ENHANCING CAMPUS WELL-BEING: A PREVENTION AND INTERVENTION APPROACH. Doctoral dissertation, University of Missouri-Columbia. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10804
title: LSDE: a four-dimensional response-quality signal (Length, Self-disclosure, Emotion, Specificity) for adaptive conversational survey control
description: LSDE is the dissertation's multidimensional operationalization of open-ended response quality, capturing "Length, Self-disclosure, Emotion, and Specificity" per exchange. Grounded in survey methodology holding that quality is "multidimensional rather than captured by a single indicator", it yields per-exchange signals suitable for online control in short sessions. AURA uses LSDE as the reward signal that guides within-session selection of follow-up question types.
requirements: Lightweight heuristics or model-based scoring to produce per-exchange quality signals during short 10-15 exchange conversations
constraints: Designed for short sessions of about 10-15 exchanges, which limits the horizon and constrains exploration
target_learners: campus survey respondents (students, faculty, staff, alumni)
target_learning_goals: eliciting deeper, higher-quality open-ended feedback about campus satisfaction and well-being
examples: AURA scores each user response along the four LSDE dimensions and updates expected gains for follow-up question classes such as validate, specify, reflect, and probe

description: The dissertation's proposed framework (Objective 3) unifies the preventive layer (TigerGPT plus AURA) with the intervention layer (PsychoGPT and SMMR). "This design allows insights from survey chatbot's adaptive dialogues, such as emerging student concerns or early signs of distress, to flow directly into specialized models like PsychoGPT or SMMR." By aligning both strategies under one system, administrators can enhance campus-wide satisfaction initiatives while identifying and supporting individuals experiencing psychological challenges.

constraints: The intervention tools were tested on public datasets rather than live campus data; the dissertation states they demonstrate capabilities with potential to be adapted for real campus contexts

article_title: An Activity-Theoretical Approach to Teacher Professional Development in Pedagogical AI Agent Design
citation: Haiyang Xin, Qiannan Niu, Shuang Li, Yimeng Sun, Ching Sing Chai, Lingyun Huang, Gaowei Chen. (2026). An Activity-Theoretical Approach to Teacher Professional Development in Pedagogical AI Agent Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12934
title: CHAT-SDT diagnostic framework for transformative teacher professional development
description: The framework integrates Engeström's Cultural-Historical Activity Theory with Self-Determination Theory as a replicable diagnostic logic for professional development. The study "adopts Engeström's (2001) activity theory to analyze teachers' AI agent creation as an activity system comprising six interrelated elements: subject, object, tools, rules, community, and division of labor." CHAT diagnoses where structural contradictions exist; SDT explains how those contradictions thwart autonomy, competence, and relatedness, mapping each diagnosed need frustration onto concrete redesign choices. The authors offer it as extending beyond AI contexts.
requirements: Diagnosis of activity system contradictions through systematic analysis of behavioral and interview data before intervention redesign
constraints: In this study researchers acted as interventionists diagnosing contradictions within district-mandated PD constraints, rather than participants collectively identifying contradictions as in pure formative interventions
target_learners: K-12 in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: Sustained creation of pedagogical AI agents aligned with instructional goals
Integration of AI tools with pedagogy and content knowledge (AI-TPACK/IPACK)
examples: Cycle 2 mapped autonomy frustration to choice architecture, competence frustration to progressive scaffolding and embedded AI assistants, and relatedness frustration to community sharing and peer consultation channels.

title: CocoFlow AI agent builder platform used by teachers to construct pedagogical agents
description: CocoFlow is an AI agent builder platform developed by the EdTech company COCOROBO Limited, used as the core tool in both workshop cycles. Its "editing interface supports teachers in constructing pedagogical agents through prompt engineering, knowledge base creation via file upload, and workflow design via a visual drag-and-drop canvas." Teachers were expected to independently create at least one deployable AI agent aligned with their instructional subject and learning objectives. Platform behavioral logs over eight weeks provided the engagement data for Cycle 1's clustering analysis.
requirements: Teachers apply prompt engineering, knowledge base construction, and visual workflow design to build deployable agents
constraints: Interviewed teachers reported platform functional limitations and insufficient subject-specific templates as technical barriers

examples: Cycle 1 teachers used CocoFlow during a two-day workshop and retained full platform access during an eight-week naturalistic observation period.

title: Integrate capacity building with need satisfaction simultaneously in teacher professional development rather than sequentially
description: The article's third design principle holds that professional development should build technological capacity and satisfy basic psychological needs at the same time. The authors argue that "sequential approaches produce decoupling," whereas synergistic design in which scaffolds enhance both capability and satisfaction enables sustained engagement. Cycle 2 operationalized this by pairing TPACK-oriented training with autonomy, competence, and relatedness supports, producing synchronized gains in capacity and willingness.

constraints: The authors note interventions succeed when tools match disciplinary needs and autonomy is substantive

target_learning_goals: Sustained AI agent creation practice combining knowledge growth and motivation
examples: Cycle 2 combined progressive scaffolding, embedded AI Q&A assistant, discipline-specific templates, choice of topics and modes, and community sharing within the same two-day workshop.

title: Keep the instructor in the loop when using GenAI-generated course materials
description: The article argues that "GenAI can be effectively leveraged without hurting student experience when the instructor remains in the loop": instructors should review, restyle, and selectively delete GenAI-generated content before classroom use. In the study, the instructor matched GenAI slides to their visual style and deleted content such as learning-objectives slides, adjustments the authors describe as requiring little effort.

citation: Theodora, A., & Tselios, N. (2026). Artificial Intelligence in Lifelong Learning: Opportunities and Challenges in Adult Education Policy.
title: Three paradigms of AI in education: AI-directed, AI-supported, and AI-empowered learning
description: The paper conceptualizes AI in education as part of a broader socio-technical system rather than isolated tools. It states that "Contemporary research suggests that AI can be understood through three main paradigms: AI-directed learning, AI-supported learning, and AI-empowered learning." These paradigms differ in learner autonomy and the degree of AI interaction with human cognition, ranging from automated content delivery to collaborative, learner-centered environments.
requirements: The paradigms are distinguished by the degree of learner autonomy and the extent to which AI interacts with human cognition, so classification requires assessing both dimensions.
constraints: The paper presents this as a conceptual organization drawn from contemporary research, not as an empirically tested taxonomy.
target_learners: adult learners in formal, non-formal, and informal lifelong learning contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding how AI can be positioned in learning environments across a spectrum from automated delivery to learner empowerment

citation: Theodora, A., & Tselios, N. (2026). Artificial Intelligence in Lifelong Learning: Opportunities and Challenges in Adult Education Policy.
title: Hybrid intelligence: human and artificial intelligence complementing one another in adult learning
description: The paper introduces hybrid intelligence as a recent theoretical approach in which "human and artificial intelligence complement one another." In this view AI does not replace human thinking but extends it, supporting decision-making, reflection, and problem-solving. The authors align this with the idea that effective educational systems should combine human judgment with data-driven insights, particularly in complex adult learning contexts.
requirements: Effective educational systems must combine human judgment with data-driven insights rather than delegating decisions wholly to AI.
constraints: The paper presents hybrid intelligence as a theoretical position attributed to recent literature (Cukurova; OECD), not as a tested model.

article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: Instructional intelligence and adaptivity as independent system properties
description: The chapter treats instructional intelligence and adaptivity as two distinct, independent system properties. Instructional intelligence is "a system's capacity to infer learner state and reason about pedagogically appropriate responses", while adaptivity is the ability to "modify instructional actions at runtime" without pausing or rebuilding the system. Because they are independent, a system can be strong on one and weak on the other, and improving one does not automatically improve the other. The chapter uses this two-dimensional framing to organize its historical synthesis and analysis of AI approaches.
requirements: Systems must articulate architectural considerations for both dimensions to integrate AI within established learning and training evaluation frameworks
constraints: The fourth configuration (high intelligence-high adaptivity) "has proven extraordinarily difficult to achieve in practice" due to computational constraints: deep learner modeling required processing time incompatible with real-time interaction
target_learners: Learners and trainees using serious games across healthcare, defense, and education domains
target_learning_goals: Personalized, adaptive learning trajectories in serious games and simulation-based training
examples: Fig. 1 illustrates the two-dimensional intelligence–adaptivity space with representative systems positioned ordinally from each historical phase
key_sources: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962

article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: Six-phase historical arc of adaptive training systems (1969–present)
description: The chapter synthesizes a chronological progression of adaptive training systems through six phases: Phase I (1969–1980s) parameter-control CAI with behaviorist foundations; Phase II (1980s–1990s) model-based intelligent tutoring systems with explicit learner models; Phase III (1990s–2000s) dynamic difficulty adjustment from commercial games; Phase IV (2000s–2010s) structured authoring and modular platforms; Phase V (2010s–2020s) mastery learning and learning analytics; Phase VI (2020–present) AI-enabled runtime adaptivity. The arc reveals that "each phase solved one problem and introduced a new one" and that AI "inherits all unsolved problems simultaneously."
requirements: Understanding the arc requires documenting learner modeling depth, diagnostic specificity, adaptation timescale, and policy sophistication for each phase
constraints: The historical arc reveals "an upper limit on achievable intelligence: an architectural constraint not correctable by better implementation alone" in pre-AI systems
target_learners: Designers and researchers of serious games and adaptive training systems
target_learning_goals: Understanding how computational learning systems have attempted to integrate instructional intelligence and runtime adaptation
examples: Table 1 lists representative systems per phase: PLATO and TICCIT (Phase I); Cognitive Tutors, AutoTutor, SHERLOCK (Phase II); Left 4 Dead AI Director, ALEKS (Phase III); e-Adventure, StoryTec, GIFT (Phase IV); Khan Academy, Duolingo (Phase V); Khanmigo, MATHia with RL, Duolingo Max (Phase VI)

article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: LLMs extend the instructional intelligence axis through semantic understanding without manual knowledge engineering
description: The chapter argues that large language models address the knowledge-engineering bottleneck that historically bounded instructional intelligence. LLMs are "AI systems trained on large collections of text to develop a broad understanding of language, concepts, and their relationships." For serious games this enables four capabilities previously requiring manual authoring: natural language interaction with unstructured learner input, context-sensitive explanation generation, grounded content generation via retrieval-augmented generation, and metacognitive scaffolding through Socratic prompts and worked-example variations.
requirements: Grounded content generation requires retrieval-augmented generation combining LLM language capabilities with access to validated domain sources such as medical protocols and assessment rubrics
constraints: LLMs provide reactive intelligence without proactive pedagogical control: they do not inherently maintain persistent learner models or pursue long-term pedagogical objectives
LLM outputs are sensitive to prompt formulation, creating reproducibility and reliability challenges
LLMs may generate confident, fluent content that is factually incorrect (hallucination risk), particularly serious in high-stakes domains
target_learners: Learners in serious games across healthcare, defense, and education domains
target_learning_goals: Semantic understanding of unstructured learner responses, context-sensitive feedback, and metacognitive scaffolding
examples: In healthcare simulation, LLMs allow virtual patients to respond naturally to open-ended history-taking questions rather than requiring multiple-choice menu selection
key_sources: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962

article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: Reinforcement learning extends the adaptivity axis through learned instructional policies
description: The chapter presents reinforcement learning as replacing hand-authored control logic with policies "learned from experience rather than explicitly programmed." An RL agent observes the learning environment state, selects an instructional action, receives a reward signal, and gradually develops strategies maximizing cumulative reward. For serious games, RL reframes instructional adaptation as sequential decision-making covering task sequencing, difficulty calibration, intervention timing, and scaffolding fading, operating at interaction timescales for genuinely real-time adaptivity.
requirements: Effective RL-based instructional adaptation requires external systems providing cognitive state inference and carefully designed reward functions to optimize pedagogically meaningful objectives
constraints: RL optimizes observables, not cognitive states: it does not inherently address what the learner knows, misunderstands, or needs to develop conceptually
There is no agreed methodology for specifying pedagogically valid reward functions for complex skill domains
target_learners: Learners in serious games requiring real-time instructional adaptation
target_learning_goals: Task sequencing, difficulty calibration, intervention timing, and scaffolding fading optimized from interaction data
examples: RL actions include deciding when to provide hints versus allowing productive struggle, described as the educationally beneficial experience of working through a challenge without immediate assistance
key_sources: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962

article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: Agent-based architectures coordinate intelligence and adaptivity at runtime through modular specialization
description: The chapter presents agent-based architectures as a coordination mechanism for combining LLM intelligence and RL adaptivity within a single system. A multi-agent system distributes instructional responsibility across specialized components—a learner modeling agent, a pedagogical policy agent, a content generation agent, and a safety validation agent—that "can be developed, tested, validated, and updated independently." This extends Phase IV's separation of concerns to intelligent, learned components, enabling runtime coordination where one agent continuously updates a rich learner model while another makes rapid instructional decisions within timescales compatible with interactive gameplay.
requirements: Each agent must have a well-defined interface specifying what information it receives and what it produces
Practical implementations require asynchronous pipelines, with content generation occurring in the background and instructional responses delivered at natural transition points
constraints: Agent-based architectures "remain largely aspirational in fully integrated form" in the current state of the field

Coordination overhead: LLM-based content generation typically requires 500 milliseconds to two seconds, and total multi-agent pipeline response times may exceed what is compatible with moment-to-moment immersive game interaction
Emergent behaviors arising from agent interactions may be harmful and require evaluation methodologies beyond traditional software testing
Transparency and instructor trust require deliberate architectural investment in logging, explanation, and instructor control mechanisms
Validation must assess the decision-making process rather than fixed content, requiring simulation-based evaluation, expert monitoring, and ongoing auditing that does not end at deployment
target_learners: Learners in serious games and immersive simulation-based training
target_learning_goals: Integrated instructional intelligence and real-time adaptivity within unified architectures
examples: Configurations range from a two-agent design pairing learner modeling with policy components to architectures coordinating scenario generation, affective state monitoring, dialogue management, and safety validation simultaneously
key_sources: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962

article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: Instrument serious games for learning analytics from the start, as interaction data becomes the foundation for future adaptive intelligence
description: The chapter derives from Phase V's legacy the principle that every serious game should capture learning analytics data even before AI capabilities are introduced. Historical logs of learner responses accumulated by learning analytics platforms "are precisely what modern reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms train on," using past interaction records to learn which instructional actions tend to produce good outcomes. Early instrumentation ensures the data foundation exists as the system architecture matures toward adaptive intelligence.
requirements: Systems must collect and transmit data about learner interactions, including which questions were answered, how long each took, and how often hints were requested
constraints: Learned policies are only as good as the interaction data they train on (Phase V's data dependency)
target_learners: Learners using serious games that will later integrate AI-driven adaptivity
target_learning_goals: Building the data foundation for reinforcement learning-based instructional adaptation
examples: Phase V platforms such as Khan Academy and Duolingo with Half-Life Regression spaced repetition demonstrated that computational analysis of interaction data could inform instructional improvement
key_sources: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962

article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: Adaptive system optimization targets must be aligned with learning, not just performance
description: The chapter identifies as a lesson carried forward from Phase I through the AI era that "the targets that adaptive systems optimize must be aligned with learning, not just performance." Phase I demonstrated that even simple threshold-based rules improved outcomes compared to one-size-fits-all delivery, but adaptation was driven by observable performance metrics rather than understanding of the learner's underlying knowledge state. Contemporary RL systems face the same risk: they optimize whatever performance signals they are given as targets, and if those signals reflect surface behavior rather than genuine learning, the system may improve measurable outcomes without supporting real understanding.
requirements: Reward functions must be designed to reflect genuine learning and skill transfer rather than surface accuracy or engagement metrics
constraints: There is no agreed methodology for specifying pedagogically valid reward functions for complex skill domains
target_learners: Learners using adaptive training systems across all six historical phases and contemporary AI-enabled systems
target_learning_goals: Durable competence development, skill transfer, and conceptual understanding rather than surface performance
examples: Phase III DDA systems optimized engagement, flow, and player satisfaction rather than durable competence development, demonstrating how engagement optimization can substitute for learning
key_sources: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962

article_title: Defining AI Fatigue in Academic Contexts: Dimensions, Indicators, and a Stage-Based Model Using Grounded Theory
citation: Miranda, J. P. P., Parreño, E. B., & Rivera, J. G. (2026). Defining AI Fatigue in Academic Contexts: Dimensions, Indicators, and a Stage-Based Model Using Grounded Theory. International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research, 25(5), 91–107. https://doi.org/10.26803/ijlter.25.5.5
title: AI Fatigue Model: a six-stage framework describing how AI-related strain accumulates and reinforces itself
description: The AI Fatigue Model is a stage-based conceptual framework explaining how the five dimensions of AI fatigue develop across repeated academic AI interaction. It proposes "six progressively intensifying stages": Initial Effort Reduction, Expansion of AI Roles, Accumulation of Strain, Disruption of Self-Regulation, Fatigue Consolidation, and a Feedback Loop in which continued AI use returns students to earlier stages and intensifies all pressures. The stage sequence was derived from the order in which participants described pressures in their accounts.
requirements: Requires empirical validation; the authors state the model "requires empirical validation before broader application".
constraints: Findings are exploratory, drawn from three universities in one academic region and self-reported data.
target_learners: university students using AI chatbots for academic work
target_learning_goals: recognizing and managing strain from sustained academic AI use
examples: In the Accumulation of Strain stage, students reported pressures across the five dimensions, e.g., "I feel mentally exhausted after checking so many outputs" (n = 72).

article_title: Smaller, Younger, and More Impactful: How AI-Assisted Writing Transforms Research Teams
citation: Haoyang Wang, Mingze Zhang, Yi Bu, Star Xing Zhao, Meijun Liu. (2026). Smaller, Younger, and More Impactful: How AI-Assisted Writing Transforms Research Teams. https://openalex.org/
title: Junior-researcher AI adoption account: diffusion of innovations, publish-or-perish incentives, and displacement of senior writing tasks
description: The article offers a three-part explanation for why AI-assisted writing teams are younger. First, drawing on diffusion of innovations theory, it states that "younger individuals tend to be early adopters of new technologies and more open to novel ideas", suggesting junior researchers are more inclined to adopt AI-assisted writing. Second, junior researchers face intense publish-or-perish pressure with limited time and resources, giving them incentives to use tools that speed up research. Third, AI now performs manuscript preparation, editing, and formatting tasks traditionally handled by senior authors, reducing the need for senior involvement and allowing teams to function with fewer senior authors.
requirements: AI-assisted writing tools must be accessible to junior researchers
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation offered to explain the observed age pattern, not a tested mechanism
target_learners: junior researchers
research teams in science
target_learning_goals: adoption of AI-assisted writing in academic work
career development of early-career scientists
examples: The article cites a large-scale study of over two million scientists in which junior researchers who adopted AI were more likely to become established scientists and saw faster career progression
key_sources: Haoyang Wang, Mingze Zhang, Yi Bu, Star Xing Zhao, Meijun Liu. (2026). Smaller, Younger, and More Impactful: How AI-Assisted Writing Transforms Research Teams. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27404

article_title: Beyond Tool Adoption: A Practical Five-Stage Developmental Continuum for AI Literacy in Higher Education
citation: Liu, J. P., & Levy, R. (2026). Beyond Tool Adoption: A Practical Five-Stage Developmental Continuum for AI Literacy in Higher Education. North Carolina State University.
title: The five-stage AI Literacy Continuum (Stages 0–4) describing developmental orientations toward AI use
description: The article proposes a five-stage developmental continuum: "0) Not Yet Engaged, 1) Uncritical Use, 2) Informed Use, 3) Critical Evaluation, and 4) Improvement". It complements dimensional competency frameworks by providing a diagnostic and instructional pathway describing how learners progress from avoidance or passive consumption toward responsible engagement, analytical judgment, and active contribution to AI systems. Stages are predominant orientations rather than rigid categories, and progression is generally sequential but not strictly linear.
requirements: Educators use observable indicators (Table 1) to diagnose learners' current stage and design instruction matched to it
constraints: The continuum is descriptive rather than normative at the individual level; stage is domain-dependent and learners may regress under unfamiliar conditions
target_learners: higher education students
faculty
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
responsible and critical engagement with AI systems
examples: Table 1 operationalizes each stage with observable indicators and possible assessment evidence, described as practical heuristics rather than psychometrically validated cut scores

citation: Liu, J. P., & Levy, R. (2026). Beyond Tool Adoption: A Practical Five-Stage Developmental Continuum for AI Literacy in Higher Education. North Carolina State University.
title: Target Stages 2–3 as the graduation baseline for AI literacy in higher education
description: The article recommends that institutions treat Stage 2 (Informed Use) as the minimum acceptable level and Stage 3 (Critical Evaluation) as the aspirational target for most degree programs, with Stage 4 reserved for advanced students. Stage 2 means graduates "understand how AI works at a functional level, use AI tools responsibly, and recognize when human judgment is required." The continuum should be interpreted within disciplinary contexts.
requirements: Curricular pathways (general education courses, discipline-embedded assessment, advanced electives) matched to institutional context and student needs
constraints: Stage is domain-dependent; students may exhibit different stages across different domains of practice
target_learners: all university students
target_learning_goals: informed and responsible AI use
critical evaluation of AI outputs
examples: Figure 1 marks Stages 2–3 with a dashed border as the recommended graduation baseline for higher education

citation: Liu, J. P., & Levy, R. (2026). Beyond Tool Adoption: A Practical Five-Stage Developmental Continuum for AI Literacy in Higher Education. North Carolina State University.
title: Two-day intensive training agenda sequenced to move learners from Stage 0 through Stage 4 transitions
description: Table 5 maps each activity of the 2-day hands-on AI/LLM training to the stage transition it facilitates: demystification of platforms moves Stage 0 to 1; hands-on API use, local model deployment, and RAG-based verification move Stage 1 to 2; tool evaluation, fine-tuning concepts, and bias detection move Stage 2 to 3; advanced fine-tuning, auto-coding agents, and building a small language model from scratch move Stage 3 to 4.
