title: AI integration as a tensioned system in which educational value emerges only when pedagogical goals, ethical safeguards, and contextual constraints are addressed together
description: The review's integrative analytical perspective conceptualises AI in mathematics education not as separate domains of innovation and risk but as "a tensioned system in which educational value emerges only when pedagogical goals, ethical safeguards, and contextual constraints are addressed together". This framework explains why technologically advanced solutions may yield uneven or counterproductive results without instructional and institutional adaptation, and it underpins the review's caution that technical performance alone is insufficient evidence of instructional effectiveness.

constraints: The framework is a review-level interpretation, not a directly tested model; the review avoids causal wording unless supported by direct evidence

article_title: Amid an Epistemic Iteration: How AI Methodologies May Transform the Nature of Science Education Research
citation: Paul P. Martin, Marvin Rost, Jenna Koenen, Nicole Graulich. (2026). Amid an Epistemic Iteration: How AI Methodologies May Transform the Nature of Science Education Research. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-026-00789-7
title: Seven-phase framework for reflecting on how AI methodologies may transform science education research
description: The article proposes a framework of seven epistemological phases for AI-based educational research: "(1) problem framing, (2) instrumentation and measurement, (3) experimentation and evidence‑based inference, (4) comparisons and replication, (5) building norms and consensus, (6) implementation and its consequences, and (7) continuous refinement." Each phase is paired with guiding questions and exemplified through both thermometer history and AI analysis of student learning. The framework is intended to help the community interrogate what is analyzed, how analyses acquire meaning, and how practices reshape the field's foundations.
requirements: Researchers use the phases as analytical dimensions paired with guiding questions rather than as a prescribed procedure
constraints: The authors state the phases are "analytical dimensions of epistemic iteration rather than prescribed steps that all research must follow in a fixed order"; phases may repeat, overlap, or be absent
target_learners: science education researchers
target_learning_goals: reflective evaluation of AI-based research methodologies and their epistemic implications
examples: The article pairs each phase with guiding questions (Fig. 1) and illustrates each with a thermometer-history case and a student-learning-analysis case

citation: Paul P. Martin, Marvin Rost, Jenna Koenen, Nicole Graulich. (2026). Amid an Epistemic Iteration: How AI Methodologies May Transform the Nature of Science Education Research. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-026-00789-7
title: Epistemic iteration as a lens on AI's transformation of science education research, with a three-stage analogy to measurement of student learning
description: Drawing on Chang (2004), the article defines epistemic iteration as "successive stages of knowledge that build iteratively on one another to achieve specific epistemic aims." It argues AI methodologies may mark a new stage in science education research's own epistemic iteration, paralleling thermometry's stages. The analogy maps a first stage of personal empiricism, a second of relative comparisons as in classical test theory, and a third of formalized measurement models such as item-response theory and Rasch modeling, with AI offering possible further improvement.
requirements: The analogy is used in Chang's practice-based sense of measurement as an evolving system of practice that renders phenomena observable
constraints: The authors acknowledge the analogy "may fall short in certain respects" because analyzing student learning is context-dependent and AI methodologies are data-analysis methods, not measurement instruments themselves
target_learners: science education researchers
target_learning_goals: understanding methodological change in a research field through history and philosophy of science
examples: The article parallels the replacement of water's boiling point with its steam point to argue AI's usefulness "must be empirically examined" through sustained cycles of testing and comparison

article_title: AI-peer integrated feedback in second language writing classes: exploring students' engagement and writing performance
citation: Liu W (2026) AI-peer integrated feedback in second language writing classes: exploring students' engagement and writing performance. Front. Psychol. 17:1871951. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1871951
title: Sociocultural Theory framing of AI-peer integrated feedback as layered scaffolding within the Zone of Proximal Development
description: The study frames AI-peer integrated feedback through Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory, whose core constructs are the Zone of Proximal Development, mediation, and scaffolding. ZPD is "the gap between students' independent writing ability and the higher level of writing performance they can attain with tailored external support". The intervention operationalizes scaffolding as sequentially layered support: AI-mediated individualized feedback on key writing dimensions first, then peer-driven social mediation in which learners elaborate on and negotiate revision suggestions. Mediation positions feedback, whether from peers or AI, as a mechanism steering learners toward enhanced performance.
requirements: Feedback must be matched to learners' developmental potential within their ZPD
AI feedback precedes peer feedback so peer mediation can elaborate on AI suggestions
constraints: The framework was examined specifically in EFL argumentative writing among Chinese English majors at B2 proficiency
target_learners: tertiary EFL students
English majors in advanced writing courses
target_learning_goals: L2 argumentative writing performance
engagement with writing feedback
examples: The experimental group received AI feedback on four rubric dimensions via standardized prompts, then engaged in 30-minute rubric-based peer evaluation followed by 15-minute small-group discussion across five biweekly writing tasks

title: Five-theme taxonomy of learning outcomes of AI applications in science and chemistry education
description: The review organizes the effects of AI applications in science and chemistry education into five themes: prompt engineering, learning, vocational skills development, active participation, and technology. Each theme aggregates outcomes coded from the 18 included studies, with frequencies of 6, 9, 5, 2, and 3 respectively.

title: Taxonomy of AI-supported lecturer decision-making organized along four interrelated dimensions
description: The review develops an integrated taxonomy organizing AI-supported lecturer decision-making in higher education along four dimensions: lecturer decision types, AI system types, student data, and learning outcomes. As the article states, "the taxonomy organizes the field along four interrelated dimensions: lecturer decision types, AI system types, student data, and learning outcomes." It locates decision-making in the interaction among these dimensions rather than treating AI systems as isolated tools, and serves as a conceptual foundation for identifying dominant patterns and underrepresented areas across the reviewed studies.
requirements: Derived inductively via Mayring's qualitative content analysis from 27 empirical studies in higher education contexts
constraints: Categories were not mutually exclusive; a single study could be coded under multiple AI systems, decision types, data types, learning outcomes, methods, functions, and interfaces

title: Socio-technical mechanisms framework: data visibility, interface mediation, and attentional guidance
description: The review draws on three socio-technical mechanisms to interpret how AI systems support and mediate lecturer decision-making. As the article defines them, "data visibility refers to a system's capacity to render specific aspects of reality observable, accessible, and actionable," interface mediation describes the interactional space where system representations are interpreted, and attentional guidance directs users' limited cognitive resources toward specific indicators. These mechanisms were not predefined coding categories but a theory-informed framework applied after inductive analysis, grounded in socio-technical systems theory and Human-Centered AI.

constraints: The article states the resulting proposition is "a theoretical proposition that guided the interpretation of the review findings rather than a claim tested in the present study"

title: AI-TPACK framework: seven interconnected knowledge domains for AI-supported teaching
description: The AI-TPACK framework extends TPACK to GenAI contexts by conceptualizing AI-related competence as "seven interconnected knowledge domains": CK and PK as disciplinary and pedagogical foundations, AI-TK for knowledge of AI principles and applications, PCK, AI-TCK for AI use within disciplinary contexts, AI-TPK for aligning AI tools with instructional strategies, and integrative AI-TPACK. The article uses it as the core analytical framework, retaining the seven dimensions separately because different domains may contribute differently to innovative practice. It emphasizes evaluating AI-generated content, understanding algorithmic logic, and coordinating human–AI collaboration.

description: The article proposes an integrated model in which AI-based educational technology use relates to critical thinking both directly and indirectly through cognitive load, with self-regulated learning moderating the load-to-critical-thinking path. It extends Cognitive Load Theory and self-regulated learning models, examining "the mediating eﬀect of cognitive load and the moderating eﬀect of self-regulated learning." The model treats cognitive load as the mechanism and self-regulation as the condition altering its strength.

citation: Li Y (2026) Beyond output metrics: reframing AI-assisted vocal pedagogy through human learning and educational value. Front. Psychol. 17:1844841. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844841
title: Three-level framework linking technical adaptation, human learning processes, and educational outcomes in AI-assisted vocal pedagogy
description: The article proposes a framework with three levels: AI-generated evidence (acoustic, performance-related, multimodal indicators), human learning processes through which evidence is interpreted (bodily experience, metacognition, self-regulated practice, motivation, learner beliefs, teacher–student dialogue), and educational outcomes judged by effectiveness, equity, and sustainability. The article states the model "should be read recursively rather than as a one-way pipeline from measurement to outcome": evidence informs interpretation, interpretation shapes practice, and practice changes later evidence. Figure 1 visualizes this dynamic relationship.
requirements: AI-generated evidence must be interpreted through human learning processes and pedagogical mediation before it becomes educationally meaningful
constraints: The article states the framework should be applied as a context-sensitive guide rather than as a universal scoring template, and adapted across vocal genres and learning contexts

target_learning_goals: interpretation and pedagogical use of AI-generated vocal performance evidence
self-regulated vocal practice and expressive development

Each row pairs an evidence and interpretive standard with the educational value addressed and possible empirical uses such as test–retest checks, explanation tasks, practice plans/logs, learner-profile comparison, longitudinal studies, and bias/fairness audits.

target_learning_goals: oral demonstration of subject knowledge, critical thinking, coherence and communication skills in viva voce performance-based assessment

title: Individual Zones of Optimal Functioning: anxiety as facilitative within bounds and detrimental beyond a learner-specific optimal zone
description: The article adopts a multidimensional account of assessment anxiety in which moderate arousal can be facilitative while anxiety beyond an individual's optimal zone triggers threat responses (fight, flight, freeze, fawn) that impair working memory and undermine the validity of oral assessments. It states that "Models such as the Individual Zones of Optimal Functioning (IZOF) highlight that optimal anxiety levels vary considerably between learners, shaped by factors including trait anxiety, prior experiences and emotion regulation capacity". This frames the study's focus on anxiety that exceeds optimal arousal rather than anxiety as inherently harmful.
requirements: Assessment design decisions should be evaluated against individual differences in optimal arousal rather than a single anxiety threshold
constraints: The article notes the point at which anxiety becomes counterproductive is especially variable among learners who experience social anxiety or who are neurodivergent
target_learners: pre-university and higher-education students facing oral performance-based assessments, including socially anxious and neurodivergent learners
target_learning_goals: preserving valid demonstration of competence by keeping assessment anxiety within manageable, facilitative bounds
examples: The study distinguishes facilitative anxiety from excessive anxiety and targets the latter when interpreting AIvaluate's anxiety-reduction results

description: The study uses the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a deductive framework with four constructs — perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, behavioural intention, and actual use — while remaining open to broader influences. citation: AlSheikh MH, Zaini R, ALmulhem MA and Ahmad S (2026). Mapping artificial intelligence integration in higher education: a systematic review using the FACETS and SAMR frameworks. Front. Educ. 11:1871468. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1871468
title: FACETS framework for describing AI innovations in education across six dimensions
description: The FACETS framework, introduced by Gordon et al. in BEME Guide No. 84, offers a structured approach to describe AI innovations in education across six dimensions: Form of AI, AI Use Case, Context, Education Focus, Technology, and SAMR. The review describes it as acting as a "compass" for reporting AI in education, combining details often reported separately into a single description. It was used as the coding schema in this review to classify each included study and enhance comparability across studies.

article_title: The pitfalls of AI detection in academic writing: bias, false positives, and the need for inclusive assessment
citation: Victor Angelier. (2026). The pitfalls of AI detection in academic writing: bias, false positives, and the need for inclusive assessment. AI and Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-026-01376-w
title: AI-text detectors infer machine authorship from statistical properties of submitted text rather than directly observing provenance
description: The paper's conceptual account holds that passive detectors classify from "statistical or learned properties of submitted text, not provenance itself". Predictability-related properties such as low perplexity, reduced variation in local predictability, and formulaic density make both additional-language writing and highly conventional academic prose vulnerable to machine-authorship classification. Information-theoretic work shows that even an optimal detector "cannot obtain information that is absent from the observed text", so classification error cannot be eliminated when human and machine text distributions overlap. The account explains why vendor percentages should not be read as calibrated posterior probabilities of authorship.
requirements: Detectors require textual properties from which machine authorship can be inferred; the composition of proprietary features is not disclosed, so the mechanism of a proprietary score cannot be established externally
constraints: Classification error cannot be eliminated when underlying distributions are insufficiently separable
Benchmark performance may not transfer to multilingual, collaborative, translated, or heavily revised academic writing
Watermarking supports provenance verification only in controlled systems; absence of a watermark cannot establish human authorship
target_learners: higher-education students
postgraduate researchers
scholarly authors
target_learning_goals: academic integrity assessment
academic writing evaluation
examples: The paper's Table 1 lists textual features plausibly associated with elevated flag-risk, such as restricted vocabulary range and conventional formulaic phrases, alongside their legitimate human origins

article_title: It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction
citation: Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Küchemann, David J. Rakestraw, & Patrik Vogt. (2026). It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction.
title: AIRIS: a three-phase framework for cognitively activated AI augmentation in physics instruction
description: AIRIS (Activate – Inquire – Reflect with Intelligent Support) is a three-phase instructional framework that structures student activities before, during, and after AI use in science education. It is not tied to a specific tool and focuses on when and how AI enters the learning process. The authors state: "We propose a simple but powerful three- phase instructional framework for AI -augmented science education that structures student activities before, during, and after AI use". It draws on self-regulated learning, cognitive load, multiple representations, and hybrid intelligence research.
requirements: Requires prior direct instruction establishing the conceptual knowledge students need for meaningful Phase 1 predictions
Requires teachers able to design tasks that resist AI completion and evaluate AI outputs in their domain
constraints: Presented as a design proposal grounded in established learning science principles, not as an empirically validated intervention
Designed for inquiry-based instruction and problem-solving settings; does not replace direct instruction
target_learners: introductory physics students
target_learning_goals: epistemic practices of physics: predicting, evaluating evidence, coordinating representations
examples: The Shard elevator ride task, in which students sketch predicted a-t, v-t, and s-t diagrams before AI use, delegate data visualization and integration to AI, then interpret and reflect on the outputs

article_title: It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction
citation: Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Küchemann, David J. Rakestraw, & Patrik Vogt. (2026). It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction.
title: Three-phase lesson pattern: epistemic grounding before AI, guided delegation during, epistemic responsibility after
description: A reusable lesson-level pattern in which each AI-integrated task passes through three phases. Before AI use, students activate prior knowledge and establish expectations that serve as a reference point; during AI use, computational tasks are delegated while epistemic judgment stays with students; after AI use, learning is consolidated through interpretation and reflection on what the AI contributed. The authors note it "shares the three-phase structure of established inquiry cycles such as 5E1" and is "an AI -specific adaptation of existing inquiry cycles, not a replacement for them".
requirements: Phase 1 tasks must require genuine prior-knowledge activation rather than surface recall
Phase 3 must make the human-AI division of cognitive work explicit, e.g. via a written reflection
constraints: Applies to any phenomenon that can be measured, modelled, and interpreted, such as smartphone recordings of a bouncing ball, rolling cylinder, or pendulum
target_learners: introductory physics students in inquiry-based labs
target_learning_goals: constructing initial mental models
critically evaluating AI-generated representations
coordinating multiple representations
examples: In the elevator task, Phase 1 asks students to sketch expected diagrams and justify expectations; Phase 2 asks them to compare AI-generated diagrams with their sketches; Phase 3 includes a 150–200 word written reflection on what the AI and the student each contributed

title: Make prediction, evaluation, and reflection non-delegable components of every AI-integrated task
description: The principle holds that when AI is integrated into instruction, the epistemic operations of predicting outcomes before AI engagement, evaluating AI outputs against expectations, and reflecting on the division of cognitive work must remain with the learner. The authors state that "AIRIS prevents this by making prediction, evaluation, and reflection non-delegable components of every task", countering a cumulative hollowing-out of epistemic engagement from incremental AI accommodations.
requirements: Tasks must be designed so students generate their own expectations before AI is introduced
Teachers must monitor whether students critically compare AI outputs against their own predictions or simply accept them
constraints: Addresses risk at the level of individual instructional design, not at the level of the education system

target_learning_goals: preserving epistemic engagement and scientific reasoning practices under AI augmentation

article_title: It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction
citation: Jochen Kuhn, Stefan Küchemann, David J. Rakestraw, & Patrik Vogt. (2026). It's Not the Tool, It's the Task: A Framework for Cognitively Activated AI Augmentation in Physics Instruction.
title: Delegate procedural execution to AI but keep prediction, evaluation, and representational coordination as student learning objectives
description: The article proposes a criterion for deciding what may be delegated to AI based on the cognitive level of the operation. It argues that "Procedural execution, running an integration algorithm or generating a standard plot, may legitimately be delegated to AI", by analogy with calculators replacing manual arithmetic. By contrast, predicting what a result should look like, judging whether AI output is physically meaningful, and coordinating representations across modalities are irreducibly human epistemic tasks that cannot be delegated without undermining course learning goals.
requirements: Teachers must judge which operations in a task are procedural versus epistemic before assigning AI support
constraints: The argument is theoretical, grounded in SRL, CTML, MER, and hybrid intelligence research rather than in new empirical data
target_learners: introductory physics students
target_learning_goals: representational competence
physical interpretation of model outputs
epistemic judgment
examples: In the elevator task, numerical integration and curve generation are delegated to AI, while explaining the meaning of slopes and checking physical consistency of the diagrams remain student tasks

article_title: When AI Agents Teach Each Other: Discourse Patterns Resembling Peer Learning in the Moltbook Community
citation: Eason Chen, Ce Guan, A Elshafiey, Zhonghao Zhao, Joshua Zekeri, Afeez Edeifo Shaibu, and Emmanuel Osadebe Prince. (2026). When AI Agents Teach Each Other: Discourse Patterns Resembling Peer Learning in the Moltbook Community. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14477
title: Three-level framework for defining "learning" in AI agent contexts
description: The article proposes distinguishing three levels when asking whether AI agents learn: "discourse-level patterns", where agent outputs structurally resemble peer learning exchanges such as validation, extension, and questioning; "operational adaptation", where agents modify behavior based on interactions, for example saving information to persistent memory; and "cognitive learning", involving genuine understanding or skill acquisition. The framework anchors the study's cautious stance: the analysis operates at level (1), with some evidence of level (2), and makes no claims about level (3). It functions as a scope-defining taxonomy for interpreting AI peer-learning-like discourse.
requirements: Analysis of agent behavior must specify which level it addresses, since discourse resemblance does not establish cognitive learning
constraints: The article makes no claims about level (3), cognitive learning, and warns patterns may be artifacts of LLM training data, prompting strategies, or platform affordances
target_learners: designers and researchers of educational AI systems
target_learning_goals: interpreting whether AI agent behavior constitutes learning

citation: Katy Ilonka Gero, Tao Long, Carly Schnitzler, and Paramveer S. Dhillon. 2026. From Planning to Revision: How AI Writing Support at Different Stages Alters Ownership. In Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS '26), June 13–17, 2026, Singapore, Singapore. ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://doi.org/10.1145/3800645.3813003
title: Materialist and idealist routes to psychological ownership of writing
description: The article frames psychological ownership of writing through two routes drawn from philosophy and writing studies: a materialist route (Locke's labor theory, where mixing labor with resources makes the object one's property) and an idealist route (Hegel's embodiment of will, identity and values). It uses this framing to interpret its experiment, "investigat[ing] the various "routes" towards ownership of a piece of writing by comparing the contribution of ideas (idealist) versus text (materialist) from AI support", while noting that time reduced by AI support underlies both routes.

constraints: The article notes the routes are entangled and "it is not clear whether some routes are more effective at generating psychological ownership than others"

target_learning_goals: Maintaining feelings of ownership, agency, and cognitive engagement during AI-assisted writing
examples: The experiment compared AI support at planning, drafting, and revision stages and measured ownership, attribution of ideas and text, and essay quality

citation: Rose Niousha, Samantha Boatright Smith, Bita Akram, Peter Brusilovsky, Arto Hellas, Juho Leinonen, John DeNero, and Narges Norouzi. (2026). The Missing Evaluation Axis: What 10,000 Student Submissions Reveal About AI Tutor Effectiveness. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05648
title: Engagement-based evaluation framework for AI tutors (RelScore and SuccScore)
description: The framework extends AI tutor evaluation with a behavioral dimension grounded in student interaction data, complementing pedagogical assessment. It quantifies "engagement qualityof tutor feedback by examiningwhetherandhowstudents used the AI tutor's feedback, conditioned on their subsequent code revisions". An LLM judge labels each feedback sentence for relevance (whether it influenced the student's code edit) and success (whether the suggested change was applied correctly), yielding RelScore, the fraction of feedback sentences students engage with, and SuccScore, the fraction of engaged feedback applied correctly.

Logged consecutive submissions per student-problem pair so feedback can be compared against the following revision
LLM-judge annotation with human agreement validation
constraints: Metrics measure immediate feedback uptake, not longer-term learning outcomes

RelScore and SuccScore measure alignment between feedback and code edits rather than direct feedback reading, making revisions not driven by feedback hard to distinguish; large-scale rewrites or partially adopted suggestions complicate attribution

target_learning_goals: effective use of AI tutor feedback in programming problem solving

research readiness

description: The paper distinguishes access equity, whether students and institutions can obtain devices, broadband, software, and support, from impact equity, whether AI-enabled learning produces comparable gains across subgroups. It argues that 'Access without learning gains can reproduce inequality in a more technologically sophisticated form, while learning gains observed only in average outcomes can obscure subgroup harms.' Evaluation should use disaggregated evidence on learning gains, transfer, persistence, and confidence calibration.

article_title: Modeling AI-TPACK in Practice: Insights from Teachers'' Multi-Agent Workflow Design
citation: Sun, Y., Xin, H., Li, S., Niu, Q., Chai, C. S., Huang, L., & Chen, G. (2025). Modeling AI-TPACK in Practice: Insights from Teachers' Multi-Agent Workflow Design. https://cocorobo.cc
title: AI-TPACK framework operationalized as four AI-specific knowledge dimensions for analyzing generative-AI-era teacher design
description: The AI-TPACK framework extends traditional TPACK for AI integration. The article operationalizes it, "as specified for the generative AI context by Ning et al. (2024)", as an a priori coding scheme with four dimensions: "AI-Technological Knowledge (AI-TK), AI-Technological Pedagogical Knowledge (AI-TPK), AI-Technological Content Knowledge (AI-TCK), and the overarching AI-TPACK (Integration)". The framework addresses the gap that traditional TPACK inadequately addresses architectural thinking for coordinating agent logic, because AI agents' generative and conversational nature differs from prior educational technologies. The study used it to code both design artifacts and interview transcripts.
requirements: Requires coding schemes and analyses that capture AI-specific dimensions beyond operational tool proficiency, including prompt engineering and AI affordance understanding
constraints: The article notes traditional TPACK inadequately addresses multi-agent architectural thinking, so the framework is specific to AI integration contexts
target_learners: K-12 in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: Integrating AI technologies, pedagogy, and content knowledge when designing AI-powered instructional tools
examples: The researchers used the four dimensions as the a priori coding scheme for thematic analysis of 15 workflow artifacts and 12 interviews, achieving Cohen's kappa=0.81 on artifact coding

citation: Noviello, Y., Birillo, A., Migut, G. (2026). ANVIL: Analogies and Videos for Lecturers. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16295
title: ANVIL: a three-layer generative pipeline producing analogy-based manim animations with an agentic repair loop
description: ANVIL (ANalogies and VIdeos for Lecturers) is an open-source system that automates end-to-end production of analogy-based instructional animations for CS concepts. It "employs a staged pipeline that generates an analogy (Textual Layer), compiles it into a structured visual screenplay (Screenplay Layer), and generates executable Python manim code". A bounded diagnose-repair-verify loop capped at n=3 iterations recovers from code-generation failures without human intervention, and all intermediate artifacts are saved for inspection and reuse.

Repair is invoked only if errors are detected and the loop is capped at n=3 iterations

target_learning_goals: Understanding of abstract CS concepts through analogy-based visual explanations
examples: For each of nine CS topics, participants were shown the target concept definition, the generated textual analogy, and the corresponding rendered animation

citation: Miina Koyama, Ruiwei Xiao, and John Stamper. (2026). PromptDecipher: Supporting AI Tutor Authoring Through Editable Simulated Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16605
title: PromptDecipher: a web-based system for authoring AI tutoring chatbots through direct correction of bot responses
description: PromptDecipher is a web-based system that "enables educators to author and refine AI tutoring chatbots through direct correction of bot responses, without requiring expertise in prompt engineering." Teachers create a bot, select a foundation model (OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google), optionally upload course materials, and work in a test environment showing a simulated student chat. The primary unit of authoring is the simulated tutoring chat, not the prompt; a live prototype, an anonymized codebase, and an anonymized demo are available.

constraints: The correction-based pipeline is described as a demonstration; deployment and evaluation in an AI for Educators MOOC is scheduled for fall 2026 and has not yet been reported

target_learning_goals: authoring educationally effective AI tutoring chatbots
examples: Attendees at the demonstration author an AI tutoring bot end-to-end: setup, test and correct with a simulated student profile, then iterate and publish, generating a shareable link.

title: Reverse Prompting Pipeline: diff analysis, prompt rewrite, and regression verification triggered by teacher corrections
description: The Reverse Prompting Pipeline is the automated mechanism at the core of PromptDecipher, triggered when a teacher submits an edit to a bot response. It runs three steps: "Diff analysis. An LLM compares the original and corrected responses to infer the teacher's pedagogical intent"; a targeted prompt rewrite proposed for teacher review; and "Regression verification. The revised prompt is automatically evaluated across all previously passed test cases." The test-correct-verify cycle continues until the teacher is satisfied.

constraints: The pipeline is the primary contribution of the demonstration; its effects on testing rates and prompt quality are not yet empirically established

target_learning_goals: translating corrective feedback on bot behavior into system prompt requirements

article_title: Faculty Orientations Shape Adoption of AI in Research and Teaching
citation: T. J. Atherton, I. Descamps, M. Webel, T. R. Holmes, C. L. Vizcarra, N. Sui, J. J. Foley IV. (2026). Faculty Orientations Shape Adoption of AI in Research and Teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18140
title: Proposed model of AI adoption in which epistemic interpretation of AI shapes the relationship between sentiments and practical use
description: The article proposes a model in which faculty adoption of AI is driven not primarily by access, social influence, or perceived utility, but by how instructors interpret AI's role in disciplinary thinking and knowledge production. As the authors state, "We therefore propose a model of AI adoption where epistemic interpretation of AI shapes the relationship between sentiments of AI and its practical use." Faculty differ not in whether they see benefits and risks, but in how they interpret AI's role in disciplinary thinking; those oriented away see AI as potentially undermining careful engagement needed for expertise, while those oriented toward it value delegating ancillary thinking with risks treated as constraints. The construct of AI pedagogical orientation operationalizes this account.
requirements: The model was developed for a targeted population of pedagogically motivated STEM faculty (RCSA Cottrell awardees) surveyed at a particular moment in AI adoption
constraints: The authors note external factors currently not driving adoption may become relevant at later stages as technologies, information, and institutional responses mature
target_learners: STEM faculty in higher education
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting faculty adoption and integration of AI (LLMs) in research and teaching
examples: The model was built from a mixed-methods survey of 90 Cottrell faculty combining EFA, logistic regression, and qualitative coding of open-ended responses

article_title: Design Principles and Observable Indicators for AI-Enabled Pedagogical Accompaniment: Evidence from the Amico Dual-Mode Prototype in Italy and China
citation: Pier Paolo Benedetti. (2026). Design Principles and Observable Indicators for AI-Enabled Pedagogical Accompaniment: Evidence from the Amico Dual-Mode Prototype in Italy and China. Accepted at the 2026 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Education (ICAIE 2026), IEEE.
title: Relational bridge: AI-enabled pedagogical accompaniment as temporary, directional, bounded micro-mediation toward human engagement
description: The framework defines AI-enabled pedagogical accompaniment as "a structured process that supports learners in clarifying goals, articulating questions, and identifying next steps, while consistently orienting interaction toward teachers, peers, and communities of practice." Its core, the relational bridge, is a sequence of micro-mediations with three properties: temporality (interaction limited in scope and duration), directionality (oriented toward concrete next steps involving human actors), and boundedness (constrained by pedagogical purposes and ethical safeguards). Effectiveness is assessed by observable transitions toward participation, agency, and responsibility, not by engagement with the AI itself. The bridge is explicitly designed to be temporary and to avoid open-ended conversational loops.
requirements: Human-in-command governance: adults retain responsibility for educational decisions, relational boundaries, and ethical oversight, with explicit thresholds for escalation or hand-off to human actors.
constraints: The framework explicitly rejects technocentric and substitutionist models; the system is not conceived as an autonomous empathic subject or surrogate for human care, and does not provide curricular instruction, psychological counseling, or affective companionship.
target_learners: Learners in technical and vocational education facing challenges of self-efficacy, orientation, and continuity of engagement
target_learning_goals: Orientation, reflection, and decision-making; articulation of goals and questions; transition toward human educational relationships
examples: A learner reporting post-lesson confusion is asked for a concrete goal, offered 1–3 micro-actions, prompted to select a human target, and given a closure prompt with a next-step plan; a transition attempt is logged when a human target is selected.
key_sources: Pier Paolo Benedetti. (2026). Design Principles and Observable Indicators for AI-Enabled Pedagogical Accompaniment: Evidence from the Amico Dual-Mode Prototype in Italy and China. title: Amico dual-mode prototype (AmicoMio and AmicoTuo) with age-sensitive configuration
description: Amico is an AI-mediated interaction device, developed as a digital agent and where feasible as a social robot, for non-clinical educational contexts, particularly technical and vocational education. AmicoMio emphasizes "precision, step-by-step reasoning, explicit framing of tasks, and concrete suggestions for action," while AmicoTuo prioritizes "maieutic questioning, reformulation, and meaning -making" without a therapeutic stance. The prototype enforces transparency of system identity, bounded sessions, dependency-prevention prompts, and data minimization, and was configured by age band (6–18, 20–40, 40–65 years) via mode-specific instruction sets and fine-tuning of the supportive mode, with per-mode sampling parameters (temperature and top-p) tuned as part of the design surface.
requirements: Operates under non-negotiable constraints: human-in-command governance, transparency of identity and limits, prevention of dependency dynamics, data minimization, and explicit orientation toward teachers, peers, and communities of practice.
constraints: Scope is intentionally limited: it does not provide curricular instruction, psychological counseling, or affective companionship, and does not optimize for content mastery through personalization; success criteria prioritize relational and governance outcomes over learning gains.
target_learners: Technical and vocational education learners across age bands 6–18, 20–40, and 40–65 years, plus adult educational actors such as teachers and parents
target_learning_goals: Task clarification, procedural orientation, reflective meaning-making, and preparation for interaction with teachers or peers
examples: Pilot participants in Italy and China engaged with both modes in structured scenarios covering task clarification, decision-making, reflection on next steps, and preparation for interaction with teachers or peers.

title: Principle-to-indicator mapping as an accountability device for AI-enabled pedagogical systems
description: The framework translates pedagogical design principles into observable indicators using a compact mapping (Table I) from principle to indicator to observation method: transparency of identity and limits (misinterpretation rate via survey/observation), scaffolding toward humans (transition-to-human prompts and follow-through signals via logs/observation), directional micro-mediations (micro-action formulation and completion via logs/rubrics), prevention of dependency (looping and exclusive-use signals via logs), communicative autonomy support (goal/question articulation quality via rubrics), and data minimization (sensitive-data solicitation frequency, which should be near zero). The mapping is treated as an accountability device making the system's pedagogical function testable through concrete traces, structured judgments, and participant perceptions.
requirements: Combines light quantitative traces with qualitative rubrics and facilitator observation so that accompaniment is not reduced to what is easiest to measure; indicators are treated as signals supporting professional judgment, not exhaustive KPIs.
constraints: In the pilot, transition-to-human follow-through could not be systematically verified and was not reported as a quantified metric; facilitator notes and brief post-task items require confirmation with larger samples and validated instruments.
target_learners: Learners and adult educational actors in non-clinical educational settings
target_learning_goals: Pedagogical accountability: assessing whether an AI system supports education or drifts into substitution and dependency dynamics
examples: The relational bridge loop (Table II) operationalizes the mapping in six steps: entry, micro-mediation generating 1–3 micro-actions, directionality toward a human target, exit with closure prompt, accountability checks, and risk-signal response reducing interaction and recommending human contact.

article_title: Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost
citation: Won Ik Cho, Seong-hun Kim, Geunhye Kim. (2026). Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost. Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24688
title: Five-factor moderation framework extending the Gries-Naudé AI productivity model
description: The paper proposes that five human and environmental factors—human resource composition, baseline capability of individuals, learning curve of practitioners, incentives for fair use, and flexibility of objectives—moderate whether AI adoption translates into realized productivity gains. It formalizes these as an organizational effectiveness factor Ω = ωC·ωI, a capability-adjusted productivity term, a learning-curve factor λi(τ), and an endogenous automation threshold, revising the Gries-Naudé partial equilibrium model in which these were exogenous parameters. The authors state: "We identify five key moderating factors: human resource composition, baseline capability of individuals, learning curve of practitioners, incentives for fair use, and flexibility of objectives."
requirements: Requires treating human and environmental factors as endogenous organizational variables that practitioners actively manage, rather than exogenous technological parameters
constraints: The revised production function aggregates over a single organizational subunit such as a team or department, not an entire firm; the influence of each factor depends on the domain and organizational characteristics
target_learners: organizational practitioners adopting AI
students and teachers in educational institutions
target_learning_goals: understanding conditions under which AI adoption yields realized productivity or learning gains
examples: The paper contrasts a flat AI task force where ωC approaches unity with a multi-layer hierarchy where ωC collapses despite high nominal expert availability
key_sources: Won Ik Cho, Seong-hun Kim, Geunhye Kim. (2026). Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost. Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24688

article_title: Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost
citation: Won Ik Cho, Seong-hun Kim, Geunhye Kim. (2026). Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost. Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24688
title: Guarantee fair-use incentives with monitoring mechanisms before expecting AI productivity gains
description: The paper argues that incentives for using AI are only legitimate when practitioners use AI to a similar degree, because heterogeneous use under relative evaluation produces inequality and erodes incentives to develop one's own skills. It claims: "the productivity impact of AI can be maximized if and only if incentives for fair use are strong, accompanied by monitoring mechanisms that detect misuse, given that the costs of unfair use are salient to practitioners." This factor is modeled as the incentive alignment component ωI of the organizational effectiveness modifier.
requirements: Homogeneity among practitioners in degree of AI use
Monitoring mechanisms that detect misuse
Costs of unfair use must be salient to practitioners
constraints: In high-stakes settings such as educational assessment, hiring, or safety-critical applications, verification procedures, human oversight, or usage restrictions may constrain the labor-saving benefits AI could otherwise provide
target_learners: organizational practitioners
students in educational institutions
target_learning_goals: fair and appropriate use of AI tools
preserving incentives to develop one's own skills
examples: The paper notes adopting AI is the dominant strategy for individuals since it brings competitive results in shorter turn-around-time, but is effective only when all participants agree to a similar degree of use
key_sources: Won Ik Cho, Seong-hun Kim, Geunhye Kim. (2026). Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost. Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24688

article_title: Position: Adopting AI in Practice Does Not Guarantee the Productivity Boost

title: Keep organizational objectives flexible enough to incorporate AI-augmented work modes
description: The paper argues that whether AI adoption shows measured productivity gains depends on whether organizational performance indicators correspond to outputs AI can augment. It states: "The productivity impact of AI is maximized when organizational objectives are flexible enough to incorporate AI-augmented work modes, when evaluation criteria appropriately recognize AI-assisted contribution as individuals' own, and when goal-setting processes can adapt as AI capabilities evolve." Rigid objectives are modeled as an effective automation threshold below the technical first-best.
requirements: Evaluation criteria that recognize AI-assisted contribution as individuals' own
Goal-setting processes that can adapt as AI capabilities evolve
constraints: In domains where current AI is weak, such as manufacturing, flexible objectives alone cannot produce gains because AI does not influence the overall organizational goal
target_learners: organizational supervisors and policy managers
educational institutions setting assessment objectives
target_learning_goals: aligning performance evaluation with AI-augmented work modes
examples: The paper contrasts software engineering, where AI is already human-level capable and expected performance is stretched, with manufacturing where AI is weak

title: AI-integrated LMS for middle school with bounded, policy-gated AI assistance embedded in everyday coursework
description: The article proposes a middle-school LMS that couples standard capabilities (course organization, assignments, assessments, communication) with bounded AI features. It states the aim to 'provide structured, safe, and scalable learning support that mirrors and enhances day-to-day classroom practice', adding formative feedback, adaptive practice sequencing, study planning, and teacher-facing analytics. The platform is designed as a complement to classroom instruction, deployable in authentic school settings as routine coursework.

Requires workflows that fit classroom constraints and support variable connectivity and device access

Learning habits such as persistence, planning, and effective help-seeking

title: Learning-context personalization engine: mastery, spacing, and help-seeking signals guide when and how AI assistance is delivered
description: The article's learning-context modeling approach maintains student-level learning state to tailor support and sequencing. The engine 'aggregates signals such as mastery by concept, attempt history, time-on-task, spacing intervals, and help-seeking behavior', and on that basis determines when to recommend review, when to escalate to teacher attention, and what scaffolding type fits the student's current context. This operationalizes feedback, self-regulated help-seeking, and spaced-practice mechanism families from the learning sciences inside the LMS.

Logging of attempts, revisions, hint usage, and AI interaction metadata

target_learning_goals: Skill mastery and retention
Self-regulated learning and effective help-seeking
examples: Spaced review recommendations and reminders based on mastery history and time since last practice; escalation to teacher attention on sustained struggle

title: Give AI assistance under a help-not-answers rule that preserves productive struggle
description: Because answer-giving can short-circuit productive struggle, the article's AI assistance module follows a bounded-support policy: 'It follows a "help, not answers" rule: the goal is to guide students toward the next step with formative feedback and scaffolding, without simply giving away solutions.' Assistance takes the form of targeted hints based on error type, revision-encouraging feedback, reflection prompts, and short conceptual explanations, keeping students doing the thinking rather than supplying solutions.
requirements: Policy constraints such as no direct answers on graded items
Teacher and administrator configurability of AI behavior
Logging of all AI outputs for auditability
constraints: Assistance must be bounded by context (practice vs. assessment), since unrestricted help on graded work would undermine learning and validity of outcomes
target_learners: Middle school students
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding and revision
Productive persistence rather than answer-copying
examples: Practice-mode AI Learning Coach providing guided, stepwise hints with controlled next-hint progression, while AI help is disabled on graded assignments

title: Gate AI assistance for minors through a policy gateway with privacy-first governance and audit logs
description: For deployment with minors, the article treats governance and privacy as first-class architectural requirements. All help requests pass through a policy gateway where 'the gateway evaluates classroom policy and task context, applying rules such as age-appropriate constraints, content filters, and assessment-specific restrictions'; disallowed or violating outputs are blocked and replaced with safe fallbacks. The governance module enforces role-based access control, data minimization, encryption, and retention rules, and logs prompts, responses, and policy decisions for oversight.

Separation of personally identifiable information from de-identified research logs
Continuous safety monitoring of AI outputs with a process for correcting or disabling harmful behaviors

target_learning_goals: Safe, equitable access to AI-supported learning

article_title: AI-Driven Analytics of Team-Teaching Talk: Acoustic Patterns across Experience, Cohorts and the Learning Design
citation: Yuchen Liu, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Riordan Alfredo, Paola Mejia-Domenzain, Dwi Rahayu, and Sadia Nawaz. (2026). AI-Driven Analytics of Team-Teaching Talk: Acoustic Patterns across Experience, Cohorts and the Learning Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09831
title: Spatial pedagogy framework of four classroom space types
description: Spatial pedagogy is a theoretical lens holding that "classroom spaces acquire pedagogical meaning through the discourse enacted at particular physical classroom areas, as well as through teachers' positioning and proximity to students and learning resources". It distinguishes four space types — Authoritative, Interactional, Supervisory, and Personal — characterised through observable spatial pedagogy behaviours. The article applies it to team-teaching contexts, where multiple teachers share and negotiate classroom space, and refines the Interactional type into talk-oriented categories for its coding scheme.
requirements: Requires structured classroom observation of teachers' positioning and movement, and, to capture enactment fully, analysis of how teachers speak within these spaces, since the same spatial configuration can serve different instructional purposes
constraints: The article notes spatial positioning alone is insufficient to fully capture enactment because pedagogical meaning is also shaped by how teachers speak within these spaces
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate university students in team-taught classes
target_learning_goals: understanding and describing the micro-level enactment of teaching in classroom space
examples: The study coded spatial pedagogy behaviours in 36 team-teaching sessions using a scheme adapted from this framework, retaining Instruction, Interaction and Collaboration categories
key_sources: Yuchen Liu, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Riordan Alfredo, Paola Mejia-Domenzain, Dwi Rahayu, and Sadia Nawaz. (2026). AI-Driven Analytics of Team-Teaching Talk: Acoustic Patterns across Experience, Cohorts and the Learning Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09831

article_title: AI-Driven Analytics of Team-Teaching Talk: Acoustic Patterns across Experience, Cohorts and the Learning Design
citation: Yuchen Liu, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Riordan Alfredo, Paola Mejia-Domenzain, Dwi Rahayu, and Sadia Nawaz. (2026). AI-Driven Analytics of Team-Teaching Talk: Acoustic Patterns across Experience, Cohorts and the Learning Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09831
title: AI-based speech processing pipeline for multi-teacher classroom audio
description: An automated pipeline for analysing team-teaching talk: multi-channel headset recordings are processed with a weighted fusion of spectral masking and ECAPA-TDNN speaker-embedding-based masking to reduce cross-channel interference, transcribed with WhisperX, and used to extract 88 acoustic features with openSMILE from fixed 1-second segments. Quality was verified via word error rate: "The WER decreased from158%before cross-talk mitigation to21%after processing, which is considered acceptable". Standardised features were reduced by Varimax-rotated PCA into five rotated components explaining 58% of cumulative variance.
requirements: Wireless headset microphones per instructor for audio capture; cross-talk mitigation before transcription; z-score normalisation of features before dimensionality reduction
constraints: In two of the 36 sessions a microphone placement issue rendered one instructor's audio unusable, so analyses included 34 sessions with complete recordings
target_learners: teachers in team-teaching higher-education classrooms
target_learning_goals: scalable automated analysis of how team teaching is enacted in classroom talk
examples: Applied to 36 recorded undergraduate and postgraduate database-course sessions at Monash University, yielding five rotated components used for group comparisons

title: Six-behaviour spatial pedagogy coding scheme for team teaching
description: An observation coding scheme adapted from prior work that integrates spatial pedagogy space types with team-teaching research. "The final coding scheme distinguished six spatial pedagogy behaviours organised into three broader categories": Instruction (Lecturing), Interaction (Ts-S interaction, T-S interaction, T-Ss interaction), and Collaboration (Assisting, T-T interaction). Supervisory and Personal space behaviours were not retained because they typically involve little or no sustained speech. Inter-rater reliability on a pilot session reached a Cohen's Kappa of 0.75.

constraints: Behaviours associated with Supervisory and Personal space types were excluded from the analytical scheme because they typically involve little or no sustained speech

article_title: The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices
citation: Eimler, S.C., Erle, L., Flood, D., Haiman, A., Häckert, L., Helgert, A., McGinness, L., Yapici, B. (2026). The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11215
title: CodeCarbon: open-source Python package for estimating carbon emissions of local AI workloads
description: CodeCarbon is an open-source, lightweight Python package that measures the power draw of local hardware and estimates carbon intensity using assumptions about the local electricity grid. It queries hardware interfaces to measure instantaneous wattage over the duration of a computational process; when low-level measurements are unavailable it assumes the hardware uses 50% of its Thermal Design Power, falling back to global constants such as 85W for a CPU. The article proposes it be used to report total CO2 estimates with AIED publications.
requirements: Access to local hardware interfaces for power measurement, or hardware detectable via internally stored TDP lookup tables
constraints: Dynamic tracking of hardware usually underestimates total energy consumption by approximately 20% because software tracking cannot profile power supply unit inefficiencies, cooling systems, or peripheral devices
It effectively defaults to a PUE-equivalent of 1.0, so local measurements may not represent the footprint of models deployed in local production environments
target_learners: AIED researchers publishing educational AI systems
target_learning_goals: Transparent reporting of the environmental cost of educational AI research
examples: The article suggests stating a total CO2 estimate after the abstract but before the introduction of a paper, e.g., reporting carbon intensity per minute of tutoring for a tutoring system or per question graded for an automated grading system
key_sources: Eimler, S.C., Erle, L., Flood, D., Haiman, A., Häckert, L., Helgert, A., McGinness, L., Yapici, B. (2026). The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11215

article_title: The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices
citation: Eimler, S.C., Erle, L., Flood, D., Haiman, A., Häckert, L., Helgert, A., McGinness, L., Yapici, B. (2026). The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11215
title: TerraFlops: open-source wrapper integrating hardware emissions data, PUE-equivalent values, and ML performance metrics
description: TerraFlops is an open-source proof-of-concept wrapper for tracking tools such as CodeCarbon that integrates raw hardware emissions data with facility-level PUE variables and ML performance metrics to generate a unified sustainability score. Its cloud mode applies fixed PUE values for providers such as AWS, GCP, or GENERIC to project data-centre deployment costs, while a local_auto mode calculates a dynamic PUE from real-time hardware load, assigning a PUE of 1.60 to workloads under 10% system capacity and scaling down to 1.08 at high utilisation.
requirements: An underlying tracking tool such as CodeCarbon; users may need to adjust the wrapper to reflect their specific hardware
constraints: The local PUE values may still be an under-estimate, as the energy efficiency of consumer-grade GPUs is significantly lower than cloud-based hardware
Refining these benchmarks remains an area for future work
target_learners: AIED researchers training or deploying ML models for educational applications
target_learning_goals: Reporting model accuracy alongside environmental and computational cost
examples: The authors used the TerraFlops wrapper when training a logistic regression model on the Iris and Breast Cancer datasets from the UCI machine learning repository, reporting the resulting sustainability statistics before their own introduction

article_title: The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices
citation: Eimler, S.C., Erle, L., Flood, D., Haiman, A., Häckert, L., Helgert, A., McGinness, L., Yapici, B. (2026). The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11215
title: Theoretical FLOP estimation framework for decoder-only transformer LLMs
description: The article derives theoretical floating-point operation counts for the most common architecture of open source LLMs, the Pre-Layer Normalisation decoder-only transformer, assuming Rotary Position Embeddings, RMS Layer Normalisation, and KV caching. Given the architecture and the numbers of prompt and completion tokens, the total cost of the first token and of subsequent tokens (which are computationally cheaper due to KV-caching) can be calculated from matrix-dimension FLOP rules. A simpler approximation, FLOPs = 2Nn where N is active parameters and n total tokens, was found in previous studies to be accurate within 10%.
requirements: Knowledge of the architecture and the number of prompt and completion tokens; for the full formula, model parameters such as d_model, d_ff, number of heads, layers, and vocabulary size
constraints: Recent DeepSeek versions using Multi-Headed Latent Attention are not considered in the calculations
The authors anticipate the difficulty of finding each required parameter for the full formula could be prohibitive for most users
target_learners: AIED researchers using open source or proprietary LLMs
target_learning_goals: Estimating and reporting the computational cost of LLM-based educational systems
examples: Figure 1 diagrams the decoder-only transformer, with grey arrows indicating matrix dimensions for parameter counts and blue arrows indicating FLOPs required to generate the first token

article_title: The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices
citation: Eimler, S.C., Erle, L., Flood, D., Haiman, A., Häckert, L., Helgert, A., McGinness, L., Yapici, B. (2026). The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11215
title: AIED research should standardize reporting of computational and environmental costs of LLM and ML usage
description: The article argues that awareness of environmental issues should become standardized in AIED through norms for reporting specifics of LLM usage in papers. It presents three recommendations: use CodeCarbon to measure and report carbon intensity for any AIED system run on local or cloud hardware; use the TerraFlops wrapper for ML tasks to report carbon emissions alongside accuracy with PUE-equivalent and composite metrics; and use theoretical FLOP estimations for proprietary LLMs. Making the environmental footprint of LLMs more visible would let the community set standards for sustainable educational AI research.
requirements: Community adoption of shared reporting norms and tools
Tools such as CodeCarbon and TerraFlops tested for non-expert usability
constraints: The current framework does not consider the water consumption of cloud-based GPUs, which has a very significant detrimental effect on some communities
PUE-equivalent baselines could be refined for consumer-grade versus cloud-based GPUs
target_learners: AIED researchers and conference organizers
target_learning_goals: Accountability and transparency regarding the environmental impact of AI in education
examples: The authors report their own paper's sustainability metrics (total corrected carbon intensity, total computational cost, training efficiency) immediately before the introduction as an example of how these metrics could be reported, and suggest future AIED conferences could require sustainability reporting as a condition of submission, similar to anonymity requirements

article_title: AiAWE: An Open-Source LLM Automated Writing Evaluation System Using LoRA-Adapted Instruction-Tuned Models
citation: John Maurice Gayed. (2026). AiAWE: An Open-Source LLM Automated Writing Evaluation System Using LoRA-Adapted Instruction-Tuned Models. A PREPRINT. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12801
title: AiAWE open-source automated writing evaluation platform
description: AiAWE is a Django web application, publicly accessible at https://app.awade.gec.waseda.ac.jp, that serves students and educators with "real-time essay scoring, rubric-referenced qualitative feedback, batch processing, and custom-rubric configuration." It runs llama.cpp inference of a Q4_K_M-quantised LoRA-adapted Gemma-3-27B model on a single RTX 3090, with average inference latency below two seconds per essay. Educator-facing features include batch user creation via Excel upload, batch essay processing (batches of over 1,000 essays in a single run), admin-defined custom rubric configurations with temperature settings, and token-based authentication with per-model daily request quotas. An experimental AWADE mode runs the base Gemma model without a LoRA adapter against instructor-defined rubrics for formative feedback.
requirements: A local workstation with consumer-grade GPU(s) (production uses a single RTX 3090 with 24 GB VRAM) running llama.cpp with the specified Q4_K_M GGUF quantisation and the released LoRA adapter
constraints: The experimental AWADE custom-rubric mode "is not evaluated against any benchmark" and is presented only as a demonstration of extensibility
The article specifies bartowski GGUF files for replication, since quantisation provenance affects quality
target_learners: Adult L2 English learners preparing for TOEFL Independent Writing
University students in argumentative writing courses
target_learning_goals: Rubric-aligned argumentative essay writing proficiency
Formative feedback on argumentative writing
examples: In production the platform has served thousands of scored essays, including individual submissions and batches of several hundred essays, without service degradation

article_title: AiAWE: An Open-Source LLM Automated Writing Evaluation System Using LoRA-Adapted Instruction-Tuned Models
citation: John Maurice Gayed. (2026). AiAWE: An Open-Source LLM Automated Writing Evaluation System Using LoRA-Adapted Instruction-Tuned Models. A PREPRINT. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12801
title: Dual-purpose LoRA adaptation: adapter carries scoring, preserved base model carries feedback generation
description: The article proposes that LoRA adaptation on an instruction-tuned checkpoint can yield one model serving two purposes: because LoRA freezes base weights and learns only a small low-rank update, "the original model’s general-purpose instruction-following and text-generation capabilities are largely preserved during adaptation." The adapter was trained on score-only targets (the bare human score, no feedback), yet at inference the fine-tuned model "produces well-formed feedback despite never having been trained on feedback examples." The authors attribute the scoring behavior to the adapter and the feedback formatting to the preserved instruction-following of the base model. Keeping adapters unmerged at inference is described as a deployment convenience, not a determinant of the dual-purpose behavior.
requirements: Fine-tuning via LoRA (weights frozen, low-rank adapter only) on an instruction-tuned checkpoint, rather than full fine-tuning, so base generative capabilities survive adaptation
constraints: The capacity-preserving effect weakens as rank grows; at higher ranks the adapter can overwrite instruction-following behavior needed for structured output, as observed for LLaMA above rank 64
target_learners: Adult L2 English learners
University writing students
target_learning_goals: Numeric essay scoring against a rubric
Rubric-referenced qualitative writing feedback
examples: The production prompt requests a JSON object with both a score and a structured reasoning field, and the score-only-trained model produces the reasoning field

article_title: AI as a Partner in Learning about, Doing, and Engaging with Science: Vigilance as the Key to Productive Augmentation
citation: Marcus Kubsch. (2026). AI as a Partner in Learning about, Doing, and Engaging with Science: Vigilance as the Key to Productive Augmentation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16822
title: Calibrated epistemic vigilance framework for learning with AI
description: The paper specifies epistemic vigilance—the "evaluation of communicated information from a source"—for the AI case, dividing it into the automatic check, the disposition to honor its signal, and the calibration policy setting how much scrutiny the signal buys. Its mechanism: the check weighs a claim's coherence with prior knowledge and sets processing depth, so vigilance gates whether deep processing, where integrated conceptual knowledge forms, occurs. The AI case is distinctive because optimized fluent, confident surfaces read as trustworthy whether or not the content is, and the source side of evaluation is emptied, forcing evaluation onto content.
requirements: Adequate prior knowledge for the check to run on: checking requires the prior knowledge a claim must cohere with, not the knowledge it teaches.
constraints: The claim is scoped to integrated conceptual knowledge; facts and routine procedures are built by other processes and may genuinely suffice with correction and adoption.
target_learners: K-12 and university science students
scientists working with AI co-scientists
members of the public using AI for decisions
target_learning_goals: integrated conceptual science knowledge
epistemic vigilance as a capacity worth having
examples: The bouncing-ball example: a correct energy-dissipation answer passes the fast check, a plainly wrong one raises the flag, and a terminology-dressed wrong answer requires widening the web of beliefs to catch the contradiction.

description: The effortless bypass dilemma names the challenge that general-purpose AI tools can perform academic tasks across the full cognitive pipeline, so learners can complete standard homework with simple prompts outside any designed learning environment. The author characterizes it as fundamentally a motivation problem: the goal is ensuring learners choose effortful engagement when easier alternatives exist. It frames the paper's renewed AIED research agenda.

article_title: AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge
citation: Brady D. Lund and Zoë Abbie Teel. (2026). AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge. University of North Texas.
title: A three-part framework of AI literacy as epistemic agency: Contextual Use, Critical Interrogation, and Participatory Governance
description: The paper proposes a framework for AI literacy organized around three interlocking dimensions rather than sequential stages. The authors state: "we propose a framework for AI literacy that is organized around three interlocking dimensions: Contextual Use, Critical Interrogation, and Participatory Governance." Each dimension corresponds to a distinct relationship to AI knowledge production: situated user, critical interpreter, and civic participant. The dimensions are cumulative but not hierarchical, mutually reinforcing as a practice rather than a ladder.
requirements: Learners engage with AI as situated users, critical interpreters, and civic participants simultaneously, since the dimensions are mutually reinforcing rather than sequential
constraints: The authors state it is not a complete curriculum or policy prescription but a theoretical frame; considerable work remains to translate it into concrete pedagogical practice and assess its effectiveness
target_learners: Students and adult learners using generative AI systems
target_learning_goals: Epistemic agency: critically evaluating, resisting, and participating in the governance of AI knowledge production
examples: The paper illustrates Contextual Use with a student researching a policy question who accounts for the model's framing assumptions, and Participatory Governance with the EU AI Act public consultation and the Detroit Digital Justice Coalition's data sovereignty work

article_title: AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge
citation: Brady D. Lund and Zoë Abbie Teel. (2026). AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge. University of North Texas.
title: Large language models as apparatuses of power-knowledge that produce structured accounts reflecting distributions of authority in training data
description: Applying Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, the paper argues LLMs are not neutral retrieval tools but systems that are productive of knowledge and constitutive of the subjects who encounter it. The authors state: "Large language models and generative AI technologies are a new apparatus of power-knowledge within this frame." Generated responses produce a probabilistically structured account reflecting the distributions of authority and legitimacy within training data, including the dominance of peer-reviewed, English-language, Western-produced, and formally published sources.
requirements: Users must be equipped to recognize and interrogate the encoding of power in AI outputs, since the question is not whether AI systems encode power but whether users can name what a system cannot or will not represent
constraints: The authors note this is not a claim that AI systems are simply biased in the pejorative sense, but that all knowledge systems are selective and selectivity is always a form of power
target_learners: Users of generative AI systems in education, healthcare, and research
target_learning_goals: Understanding how AI produces what it presents as knowledge and interrogating its structuring assumptions
examples: The paper links inability to recognize what a system cannot represent to Fricker's hermeneutical injustice, which AI systems risk reproducing and scaling

citation: Markus S. Feser & Paul L. Tschisgale. (2026). AI-based scoring systematically underestimates conceptual understanding of linguistically weak students' explanations in physics. Physics Education, Leibniz Institute for Science and Mathematics Education, Kiel. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-8503-0951
title: Language bias in assessing text-based explanations as a task-inherent challenge of inferring conceptual understanding through language
description: The article proposes that language bias — the systematic influence of lexical and syntactic quality on assessments of conceptual understanding — is not merely a flaw of particular assessors. Because explanations "are linguistic representations through which that understanding is communicated", any assessor must identify evidence of understanding within linguistic features, and imprecise vocabulary and syntax can obscure that evidence. The finding that AI-based scoring reproduces the bias previously documented for STEM teachers supports framing the problem as inherent to the scoring task itself, spanning human and AI assessment in STEM education.

constraints: The article's evidence comes from German-language physics explanations of a single task by secondary-school students; generalization to other STEM fields, languages, and formats requires further research

multilingual and international learners
target_learning_goals: scientific explanation of physical phenomena
valid assessment of conceptual understanding
