citation: Yongli Xiang, Zhifang Zhang, Bojun Yang, Ziming Hong, Lei Feng, Miao Xu, Tongliang Liu. (2026). When Agents Learn to Be You: Benchmarking Privacy Leakage, Impersonation Risk, and Defenses in Persona Skills. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03700
title: AntiSkillBench: an end-to-end benchmark for persona-skill privacy and impersonation risks
description: AntiSkillBench is a benchmark that evaluates risks and defenses across the persona-skill pipeline. It comprises "a dataset of 7,500 persona-grounded dialogue traces, constructed from 50 behaviorally rich profiles spanning diverse task scenarios", an evaluation suite measuring skill-level privacy leakage and agent-level attribute disclosure and behavioral impersonation, and a defense evaluation covering online and post-hoc interventions. Profiles are organized into demographics, background, personality, and communication dimensions, with 50 persona-grounded questions per user expanded into three-round dialogues.
requirements: Requires persona-grounded user profiles and simulated multi-turn dialogue traces as input for skill distillation
constraints: Traces are simulated user-assistant dialogues rather than real user histories
target_learners: LLM-based agent systems and their developers
target_learning_goals: Evaluating privacy leakage and impersonation risk in personalized agent skills
examples: 50 user roles each paired with 50 generated questions and expanded into three-round dialogues, yielding 2,500 dialogue traces comprising 7,500 persona-grounded user turns
key_sources: Yongli Xiang, Zhifang Zhang, Bojun Yang, Ziming Hong, Lei Feng, Miao Xu, Tongliang Liu. (2026). When Agents Learn to Be You: Benchmarking Privacy Leakage, Impersonation Risk, and Defenses in Persona Skills. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03700

article_title: When Agents Learn to Be You: Benchmarking Privacy Leakage, Impersonation Risk, and Defenses in Persona Skills
citation: Yongli Xiang, Zhifang Zhang, Bojun Yang, Ziming Hong, Lei Feng, Miao Xu, Tongliang Liu. (2026). When Agents Learn to Be You: Benchmarking Privacy Leakage, Impersonation Risk, and Defenses in Persona Skills. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03700
title: Persona-skill pipeline risk formulation: risk concentration, impact amplification, and defense degradation
description: The article formulates persona-skill safety along a trace-skill-agent pipeline, where a distillation function processes personal traces into a reusable person-grounded artifact that is then equipped to an agent. It identifies three distinctive risks: "Risk concentration", since distillation consolidates fragmented information into artifacts that are easier to inspect, transfer, and misuse; "Impact amplification", since portable artifacts can be deployed across agents without modifying the underlying model; and "Defense degradation", since cross-trace distillation weakens record-level anonymization and retrieval filtering. Risks are operationalized at two levels: skill-level privacy leakage and agent-level impersonation risk.
requirements: A threat model with adversaries acting at either the skill-inspection stage or the agent-interaction stage of the pipeline
constraints: The defender can only intervene on the trace side before distillation, and does not modify the distillation function, the agent, or the deployed skill-use interface
target_learners: LLM-based agent systems and their developers
target_learning_goals: Understanding how personal traces become exposed when distilled into executable persona skills
examples: Skill distillation and skill-equipped generation form the process Tu -> su -> y, with skill-level leakage during distillation and impersonation risk downstream

article_title: AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience
citation: Łucja Biel. (2026). AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience. University of Warsaw. https://uw.edu.pl
title: AI-related risk profile of legal translation: five interrelated risk categories
description: The chapter proposes an analytical framework mapping how AI creates professional risk in legal translation. As printed: "I propose an AI-related risk profile of legal translation comprising five interrelated categories according to the aspect of professional practice they affect: linguistic, technical, legal, ethical and cognitive". Linguistic risks cover terminology, mistranslations and genre conventions; technical risks cover hallucinations and unpredictable performance; legal risks cover data protection, confidentiality, copyright and liability; ethical risks cover algorithmic bias, transparency and access to justice; cognitive risks cover illusions of quality, automation bias, cognitive surrender and deskilling. The framework grounds the argument that legal accountability requires human-centred augmentation.
requirements: Applied for analytical purposes to legal translation's high-risk setting, where translation errors may have severe consequences
constraints: The chapter notes many risks were first identified for NMT but apply equally, and in several respects more acutely, to GenAI
target_learners: legal translators
legal translator trainees
target_learning_goals: risk awareness in AI-assisted legal translation
informed technology choices
examples: Figure 1 presents the five risk categories and their manifestations, from terminology and hallucinations to automation bias and deskilling

article_title: AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience
citation: Łucja Biel. (2026). AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience. University of Warsaw. https://uw.edu.pl
title: AI Literacy Framework for legal translation: four mutually reinforcing dimensions
description: The chapter's central framework adapts general AI literacy models (Ng et al. 2021; Long and Magerko 2020; Krüger 2024) to legal translation. It defines AI literacy for legal translators as the capacity to make informed, critical and ethically responsible decisions about the use and supervision of AI while preserving translation quality, legal certainty and professional accountability. As printed: "AI literacy is conceptualised here as a multidimensional construct comprising four mutually reinforcing dimensions: Foundational, Procedural, Critical and Strategic". Foundational covers understanding AI systems and data literacy; Procedural covers workflow integration and prompt engineering; Critical covers human oversight, verification and automation-bias awareness; Strategic covers professional judgement about whether, when and how AI should be used. The framework is presented as a transversal layer of legal translation competence supporting digital resilience.
requirements: Builds on existing legal translation competence models (strategic, thematic, linguistic/textual, instrumental, professional) rather than replacing them
constraints: The chapter states the framework "requires empirical validation" and that future research should evaluate the effectiveness of pedagogical interventions
target_learners: legal translators
legal translation students
target_learning_goals: critical and responsible AI use
professional judgement about AI use
digital resilience
examples: Figure 2 presents the AI Literacy Pyramid for Legal Translation and Table 1 maps each dimension to its function and knowledge/skills

citation: Łucja Biel. (2026). AI Literacy for Legal Translation: Developing Digital Resilience. University of Warsaw. https://uw.edu.pl
title: Use AI in legal translation as augmentation that preserves human control, not unsupervised automation
description: The chapter argues that legal accountability requires human-centred augmentation rather than unsupervised automation. As printed: "Augmentation refers to the use of AI to support professional judgement while preserving human control over translation decisions". Because legal translation carries professional responsibility and legal accountability, and errors may have severe consequences, automation that replaces human decision-making cannot satisfy these requirements. The principle underpins the AI literacy framework, whose strategic dimension governs whether, when and how AI should be used.
requirements: Translators retain responsibility for the final translation and exercise informed professional judgement over AI output
constraints: The chapter notes attitudes of authorities towards AI use remain inconsistent, and courts have held machine-translated evidence deficient where knowing, voluntary consent could not be guaranteed
target_learners: legal translators
legal translation students
target_learning_goals: responsible AI integration
maintaining professional accountability
examples: The chapter cites US case law (United States v. Cruz-Zamora; United States v. Ramirez-Mendoza) where Google Translate-mediated police interactions were held deficient

article_title: Exploring Fraction Comprehension and Interest in Elementary Education Through AI-Powered Personalized Learning
citation: Holman, Kenneth. (2024). Exploring Fraction Comprehension and Interest in Elementary Education Through AI-Powered Personalized Learning. https://stars.library.ucf.edu/etd2024/32
title: Mathbot's design framework: Constructionism combined with Reinforcement Learning Theory for adaptive AI-driven learning
description: The Mathbot intervention is grounded in a dual theoretical foundation combining Papert's Constructionism and Skinner's Reinforcement Learning Theory. The article states that "The Mathbot intervention draws from both Papert's Constructionism and Skinner's Reinforcement Learning Theory, forming a foundation for adaptive AI-driven learning environments." Constructionism contributes hands-on, active learning through interaction and reflection, with group discussions after sessions reinforcing reflection and peer-to-peer learning. Reinforcement theory contributes immediate feedback: correct answers receive positive reinforcement encouraging repetition of successful strategies, while incorrect answers prompt additional scaffolding and practice guiding students toward mastery. The author describes the two as balancing exploratory learning with behavioral reinforcement.
requirements: Immediate feedback loops that reinforce correct answers and provide scaffolding after incorrect answers
Group discussion opportunities after Mathbot sessions to support reflection and peer-to-peer learning
target_learners: elementary students with mathematical learning challenges
target_learning_goals: fraction comprehension
fraction comparison skills
examples: Students engaged directly with fraction problems in Mathbot, receiving immediate feedback and positive reinforcement, with teachers in both groups following the same fraction-comparison lesson plan over five days

title: Mathbot: an AI-based personalized learning platform integrating student interests into fraction problems
description: Mathbot is an AI-based personalized learning platform for elementary mathematics that dynamically adapts to individual learning patterns and integrates personal interests into fraction problems. The article describes it as exemplifying AI technology "by integrating students' interests into fraction problems, creating an engaging and customized approach to mathematics education." In the evaluated intervention, fourth and fifth graders with mathematical learning challenges used Mathbot during 40-minute sessions across five consecutive school days, receiving adaptive feedback personalized to their learning needs while teachers followed a shared lesson plan on fraction comparison. citation: Udeshi, T., Khazenzon, A., Khan, K., Breen, N., Corwin, R., DiGiano, C., Weatherholtz, K., Zaluski, M. (2026). Methodologies for Improving the Quality of AI Tutoring in K-12 Education. https://sites.google.com/khanacademy.org/aied2026supplementalmaterial/home
title: Theory of action linking AI tutor quality to engagement, skill acquisition, and transfer
description: The article grounds its measurement choices in an explicit causal chain: tutor quality drives cognitively engaged interaction, engagement predicts skill acquisition, and skill acquisition should generalize to standardized assessment performance. Metrics are chosen to span this chain, from proximal engagement measures to distal transfer. The cognitive engagement metric is "grounded in the ICAP framework (Chi and Wylie, 2014), which distinguishes four levels of cognitive engagement—Passive, Active, Constructive, and Interactive—predicting deeper learning as engagement deepens."
requirements: Metrics must be sensitive to change, moving after 1-2 weeks of experimentation as leading indicators of effective tutoring
constraints: The chain is stated as a motivating theory; the article measures proximal engagement and near transfer rather than standardized-assessment outcomes directly
target_learners: K-12 students using Khanmigo on Khan Academy
target_learning_goals: Skill acquisition in exercised skills, measured as near transfer to independently attempted next items
examples: Next-item correctness is described as capturing near transfer on a new item measuring the same underlying skill, counting only items attempted independently without further tutor help

title: Khanmigo AI Component workflow architecture with declarative overrides
description: Each Khanmigo feature is a chat-based workflow with its own system prompt, guardrails, and configurable steps. The lowest-level building block is the AI Component: "a simple, generic function that we expect to have variable output, usually from an LLM call." Components are called through a single entry point providing standardized logging, offline-evaluation compatibility, and declarative dot-notation overrides of inputs such as prompt variables and model attributes. Because the workflow entry point is itself an AI Component, experiments can add, remove, or replace whole workflow steps.

constraints: The platform is primarily written in Go with a small Python service supporting a Math Agent that runs student math in a sandbox with NumPy and SymPy

article_title: Modeling AI Overreliance as a Complex Adaptive System
citation: Ahana Biswas. (2026). Modeling AI Overreliance as a Complex Adaptive System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19616
title: AI reliance as a complex adaptive system: a micro-founded agent-based model of population-level reliance dynamics
description: The article models AI reliance as a population process rather than a one-shot individual judgment. Agents repeatedly choose among solving alone, accepting AI output unverified, or verifying, updating Dirichlet beliefs about AI quality and, when networked, learning from peers through experience-based or opinion-dynamics channels. As the authors put it, "individual learning rules, peer observation, and feedback exposure jointly determine whether a population remains calibrated or enters a self-reinforcing state of unverified reliance." The model is used as a theoretical tool for isolating mechanisms and deriving qualitative comparative statics, not as a point forecast.
requirements: A population of heterogeneous agents facing repeated tasks with the core learning loop, in which "belief→action→outcome→updated belief" drives choice; the cascade results additionally require a networked peer channel and a social-proof feedback term entering the unverified-use utility.
constraints: "AI quality is exogenous and stationary, the network fixed, and verification stylized."
The model is a theoretical tool for isolating mechanisms rather than a point forecast; its implications are qualitative and conditional, doubling as testable hypotheses.
target_learners: professionals repeatedly using AI assistants for information-seeking and decision tasks
target_learning_goals: calibrated reliance on AI assistance — trusting it when right and checking it when wrong
examples: The model's components are mapped to a running example of a professional using an AI assistant who may answer alone, accept the AI's answer, or check it, and who sees colleagues increasingly accept AI answers unchecked.
key_sources: Ahana Biswas. (2026). Modeling AI Overreliance as a Complex Adaptive System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19616

article_title: Modeling AI Overreliance as a Complex Adaptive System
citation: Ahana Biswas. (2026). Modeling AI Overreliance as a Complex Adaptive System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19616
title: Redesign the feedback users see — make verification visible or dampen social proof — rather than only lowering the private cost of checking
description: When unverified AI use is visible to peers, reliance dynamics are governed by a verification-suppression feedback loop, so effective interventions reshape what users see others doing. In the model, "interventions that change what users see others doing are more effective than interventions that only lower the private cost of checking", because cost-only levers leave the social pull toward unverified use intact. The levers are the salience of verification and the structure of exposure, not connectivity.
requirements: The intervention must act on the feedback channel itself — for example, surfacing peers' verification behavior or damping the visibility of unverified use — rather than only changing individual costs.
constraints: Implications are qualitative and conditional rather than quantitative forecasts.
The visibility effect is a counter-cascade above a threshold in sV, not a guaranteed outcome; for smaller sV the recovery is partial.
target_learners: communities of users sharing AI assistants in networked settings
target_learning_goals: maintaining verification behavior and calibrated reliance on AI at the population level
examples: In the simulations, strong verification visibility (sV = 1.0) drove the population to near-complete verification with regret 0.07, while reducing verification friction alone (λV = 0.05) lifted verification only to 0.12 and did not lower regret.

article_title: When Saying No Makes Better Videos: Designing Dual Gatekeeping for Pedagogically Grounded AI Content Creation
citation: Yearim Kim, Injun Baek, and Nojun Kwak. 2026. When Saying No Makes Better Videos: Designing Dual Gatekeeping for Pedagogically Grounded AI Content Creation. In Proceedings of Understanding and Engaging Critical Resistance to AI in Education (CHI '26 Workshop). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19812
title: Principled resistance: theory-grounded, dual-layer gatekeeping of AI-generated educational content
description: The article conceptualizes "principled resistance" as "deliberate, theory-grounded pushback against AI outputs that fail pedagogical standards", taking three concrete forms: rejecting (requesting regeneration), revising (manual editing), and overriding (vetoing automated flags). Rooted in Mayer's CTML, the framework holds that educators and algorithms catch different kinds of problems—humans detect nuanced pedagogical mismatches while algorithms verify structural integrity—so building both checkpoints into one pipeline creates overlapping coverage neither could achieve alone. It reframes pedagogical friction as a site of professional accountability rather than inefficiency.
requirements: Educators must be briefed on the CTML principles the system enforces, as participants in the study were "priorly briefed on the CTML principles"
constraints: The article notes neither layer is exhaustive and the long-term viability of iterative review in daily classroom preparation remains unknown
target_learners: educators creating instructional video content
target_learning_goals: pedagogical quality of AI-generated instructional videos
examples: PedaCo operationalizes the framework with educator script review before rendering and automated metrics after video synthesis

title: PedaCo: a dual gatekeeping human-AI video co-creation system
description: PedaCo (Pedagogical Co-creation) is a human-AI collaborative system that "integrates two complementary gatekeeping mechanisms: reviewing scripts through CTML-informed criteria, and an automated metric evaluating finished videos against computationally measurable CTML dimensions." Layer 1 intervenes before rendering: an LLM generates an initial script, an AI reviewer produces principle-organized feedback identifying potential violations, and the educator decides what to accept, revise, or regenerate. Layer 2 performs post-synthesis evaluation, automating five dimensions: coherence, redundancy, temporal contiguity, modality, and image quality.
requirements: The educator inputs learning content and configures which CTML principles the system should enforce before script generation
constraints: The article states dimensions like Personalization (tone) "require a deep understanding of curricular structures and learner psychology that currently remains the sole domain of the human expert", so only algorithmically feasible dimensions are automated
target_learners: educators creating instructional video content
target_learning_goals: instructional coherence and narrative-visual synchronization in AI-generated videos
examples: The interface visualizes automated metrics at the video level, allowing users to assess alignment between the final video and the learning content

title: Place pedagogical friction at the script stage, where textual revision is efficient and rendered errors are nearly impossible to correct
description: The article argues productive friction should be strategically embedded upstream: "Textual revisions are computationally and laboriously efficient, whereas pedagogical errors baked into a rendered visual narrative are nearly impossible to correct post-synthesis." Placing the human checkpoint at the intermediate script stage makes pedagogical critique economically viable while keeping the system advisory and preserving the educator's authority to say no based on curricular context. The authors also state productive friction is most effective when theoretically grounded and hybridized across human and computational agents.

article_title: AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency
citation: Kuhn, J., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Greene, J. A., Malone, S., Vogt, P., & Fütterer, T. (2026). AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency in Hybrid Human-AI Cognition. https://osf.io/preprints
title: AIRIS: a multi-level control allocation architecture for preserving epistemic agency in hybrid human-AI cognition
description: AIRIS (AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems) is a theoretical framework, not a cognitive architecture like ACT-R, specifying what must remain in place for genAI-supported work to sustain understanding. It rests on three core principles: "human epistemic primacy", "complementary generative engagement", and "event-driven intervention". The article states that "AIRIS is a multi-level control allocation architecture specifying the conditions under which epistemic agency can be preserved in hybrid generative systems," and that "The architecture does not itself improve learning; it specifies what must remain in place for genAI -supported work to sustain understanding." It integrates distributed cognition, cognitive load theory, multimedia learning, and self-regulated learning.
requirements: Regulatory support must be enactable by a teacher, the learner's own internalized regulation, or a future technical implementation; the framework specifies functional regulatory requirements rather than a fixed instructional sequence.
constraints: The article states the architecture does not itself improve learning; it specifies conditions for sustaining understanding.
target_learners: learners using generative AI in educational and knowledge-work contexts
target_learning_goals: preserving epistemic agency and durable understanding during genAI-supported epistemic work
examples: The framework is presented as an episodic control-allocation layer that activates when destabilizing patterns emerge, with a Detect–Diagnose–Act cycle linking behavioral traces to targeted interventions.

article_title: AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency
citation: Kuhn, J., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Greene, J. A., Malone, S., Vogt, P., & Fütterer, T. (2026). AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency in Hybrid Human-AI Cognition. https://osf.io/preprints
title: Seven destabilizing mechanisms of hybrid cognition, from control redistribution to motivational-affective drift
description: AIRIS's diagnostic layer comprises seven mechanisms: control redistribution, germane effort attenuation, calibration drift, delegation drift, representational passivity, dual-threshold instability, and motivational-affective drift. The article frames them as hypotheses: "the following seven mechanisms specify those disturbances as theoretically derived, empirically testable hypotheses, not as established facts, nor as a claim that disturbance is inevitable." The mechanisms "are not independent failure modes but form a self -reinforcing system," interacting so that, for example, delegation drift feeds motivational-affective drift and deepens calibration drift.
requirements: Each mechanism is grounded in existing theoretical frameworks (distributed cognition, CLT/CTML, SRL) and requires empirical testing through the derived propositions.
constraints: The article states the mechanisms describe conditions of potential destabilization, not inevitable outcomes; direct experimental tests of the dual-threshold prediction remain scarce.
target_learners: learners and designers of genAI-integrated learning environments
target_learning_goals: diagnosing where hybrid human-AI cognition loses epistemic equilibrium
examples: Darvishi et al. (2024) is cited for behavioral evidence that students with genAI feedback access showed measurable reductions in independent evaluative reasoning that deepened across repeated interactions.

article_title: AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency
citation: Kuhn, J., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Greene, J. A., Malone, S., Vogt, P., & Fütterer, T. (2026). AI-Augmented Inquiry and Regulation in Hybrid Systems: A Control Allocation Architecture for Preserving Epistemic Agency in Hybrid Human-AI Cognition. https://osf.io/preprints
title: Five regulatory operators (Anticipate, Interrogate, Reflect, Integrate, Synthesize) activated by event-driven triggers
description: AIRIS's regulatory layer specifies five operators that target internal generative engagement at points of emerging instability. The article states: "AIRIS employs five complementary regulatory operators: Anticipate , Interrogate, Reflect, Integrate, and Synthesize." Operators are episodic, triggered by event-driven mechanisms rather than running continuously, and may be enacted as system prompts, instructor interventions, or internalized self-regulation strategies. Three trigger classes are distinguished from interaction traces: calibration discrepancy, delegation dominance, and reflection compression triggers.
requirements: Trigger operationalization requires disentangling genAI-assisted from independent performance, e.g., via brief probe tasks requiring independent knowledge construction without genAI access.
constraints: AIRIS-triggered regulation should be understood as a scaffold, not a substitute, for the learner's own regulatory awareness; the long-term goal is internalization of regulatory competencies.
target_learners: learners in genAI-integrated learning environments, instructors, and system designers
target_learning_goals: restoring equilibrium between human generative engagement and genAI-supported processes
examples: Calibration discrepancy triggers activate when confidence levels diverge strongly from performance outcomes; delegation dominance triggers activate when users consistently consult genAI before articulating their own ideas.

title: Require minimal independent reasoning before genAI consultation (the Anticipate sequencing principle)
description: A core AIRIS design implication, an application of the Anticipate operator: wherever possible, humans should engage in at least minimal independent reasoning before consulting genAI. The article argues this sequencing "ensures that the human agent enters the genAI consultation with a cognitive stake in the outcome, increasing the likelihood that genAI outputs are actively evaluated rather than passively accepted." It is presented as one of AIRIS's most consistent design implications, keeping evaluative authority with the human agent.
requirements: Learners or environments must create an occasion for own reasoning first, so consultation follows rather than precedes independent attempts.
constraints: The principle is derived from the framework and supporting cited evidence; the article presents it as an application of the Anticipate operator rather than a tested prescription of this article itself.
target_learners: learners using genAI in inquiry, writing, and problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: preserving generative engagement and active evaluation of genAI outputs
examples: The article cites Pi et al. (2026): when learners identified errors in their own work before receiving genAI feedback, they achieved substantially larger learning gains than when the genAI identified the errors for them.

article_title: AI as Teammate: Rethinking Task Distribution in Medical Training
citation: Tsim, F., Gutoreva, A., Weiss, A., & Dubosh, N. (2026). AI as Teammate: Rethinking Task Distribution in Medical Training. Correspondence: fenditsim@gmail.com
title: SCAN: a four-subzone task-allocation framework extending Vygotsky's ZPD with metacognition for human-AI task distribution
description: SCAN is a human-centric decision-making framework organizing clinical tasks along four subzones—Substitute, Complement, Aid, and Non-Negotiable—defined by two dimensions: the degree to which AI can appropriately assume cognitive responsibility and the developmental consequences for the learner. The article states that "SCAN is a human-centric, decision-making framework for systematic task allocation between a learner, human experts, and AI." It extends Vygotsky's ZPD by adding a 'known to AI' circle to the zones of actual and potential development, and operates through task identification, processing, and evaluation.
requirements: Adequate learner metacognition: without it, task classification collapses because learners cannot reliably assign tasks to correct subzones
constraints: Developed for cognitively demanding professional domains; the article presents it as a conjectural, testable framework rather than an empirically validated one
target_learners: Medical students and residents in clinical training
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning development
Metacognitive task classification and AI engagement
examples: Figure 1 locates S between 'unknown to learner' and 'known to AI', C between 'known to learner' and 'known to AI', A at the overlap of all three circles, and N as the original ZPD
key_sources: Tsim, F., Gutoreva, A., Weiss, A., & Dubosh, N. (2026). AI as Teammate: Rethinking Task Distribution in Medical Training. Correspondence: fenditsim@gmail.com. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28373

article_title: AI as Teammate: Rethinking Task Distribution in Medical Training
citation: Tsim, F., Gutoreva, A., Weiss, A., & Dubosh, N. (2026). AI as Teammate: Rethinking Task Distribution in Medical Training. Correspondence: fenditsim@gmail.com
title: Two complementary developmental trajectories: Internalization (human-human) and Symbiosis (human-AI) in clinical reasoning formation
description: The article proposes that clinical reasoning development proceeds along two simultaneous trajectories. The Internalization Trajectory preserves Vygotsky's original human-human account through the Non-Negotiable subzone with human more-knowledgeable-others, instantiated historically by apprenticeship. The article states: "SCAN proposes the Symbiosis Trajectory where a learner navigates from Substitute through Aid to Complement, progressively developing task-specific knowledge in collaboration with GenAI." The authors conjecture the two are complementary and that complete clinical formation requires both, with epistemic agency and responsibility increasing progressively in each.
requirements: Both trajectories must be present; neither substitutes for the other, per the authors' conjecture
constraints: The complementarity of the two trajectories is explicitly framed as a conjecture, not a tested result
target_learners: Medical trainees from first-week students to senior residents
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning development
Self-regulation and epistemic responsibility for AI use
examples: In the Symbiosis Trajectory, a first-week student generates a differential with AI (Substitute, other-regulation), a third-year student augments reasoning with AI suggestions (Aid, shared regulation), and a senior resident directs LLMs and takes full epistemic responsibility (Complement, self-regulation)
key_sources: Tsim, F., Gutoreva, A., Weiss, A., & Dubosh, N. (2026). AI as Teammate: Rethinking Task Distribution in Medical Training. Correspondence: fenditsim@gmail.com. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28373

citation: Tsim, F., Gutoreva, A., Weiss, A., & Dubosh, N. (2026). AI as Teammate: Rethinking Task Distribution in Medical Training. Correspondence: fenditsim@gmail.com
title: Respond to inappropriate AI use as a competency deficit warranting instruction, not as misuse warranting enforcement
description: Because misclassification implies a metacognitive competency deficit rather than a norm violation, the article argues the appropriate response is instruction rather than sanctions. It states: "The natural response to misclassification is instruction: explicit teaching of subzone classification as a cognitive skill." A curriculum organized around misuse prevention invests in policy, surveillance, and enforcement, whereas misclassification prevention invests in metacognitive instruction, task design, and supervised practice.
requirements: Curriculum capacity for explicit subzone classification teaching, scaffolded classification practice, and formative feedback on classification accuracy
constraints: The article presents this as an argument about educational coherence and lasting effects, not as a tested comparison of enforcement versus instruction
target_learners: Medical trainees using generative AI in clinical settings
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive evaluation of AI use
Appropriate human-AI task allocation
examples: The article contrasts misuse-prevention curricula investing in policy, surveillance, and enforcement with misclassification-prevention curricula investing in metacognitive instruction, task design, and supervised practice

article_title: AI in Particle Physics Education: Research Problems and Foundational Skills
citation: M. Mikhasenko, M. Stahl, I. Segal, D. Parmar, A. Zimmer, and A. Kazatsky. (2026). AI in Particle Physics Education: Research Problems and Foundational Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05719
title: Research-shaped homework: self-contained undergraduate problems combining multiple methods, data representations, and workflows with AI permitted as a partner
description: A homework design in which assignments are "self-contained pieces" of professional research practice, combining several methods, data representations, and workflows rather than routine applications of one known method. In KT1, ten such sheets covered literature work, modeling, plotting, detector interpretation, derivations, analysis-style measurements, and scientific communication, with AI explicitly allowed and students responsible for verifying results. The instructor tested candidate tasks beforehand and found a single prompt did not reliably yield a complete solution.
requirements: Tasks must be tested so that a single prompt does not reliably yield a complete solution
Students must remain responsible for verifying whether AI output makes physical sense
Assignments need extended time (1.5 weeks per sheet in KT1)
constraints: The article treats resistance to a single prompt as design experience, not a durable property of the assignments, since models improve drastically
target_learners: advanced undergraduate physics students (fifth-semester bachelor students in the KT1 cohort)
target_learning_goals: research practice skills such as modeling, data interpretation, and scientific communication
foundational nuclear and particle physics knowledge
examples: HW2 required extracting published proton-proton collision data, transforming variables, and producing a 3D-printed spherical surface plot; HW8 asked students to design visual characters encoding hadron quantum numbers
key_sources: M. Mikhasenko, M. Stahl, I. Segal, D. Parmar, A. Zimmer, and A. Kazatsky. (2026). AI in Particle Physics Education: Research Problems and Foundational Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05719

article_title: AI in Particle Physics Education: Research Problems and Foundational Skills
citation: M. Mikhasenko, M. Stahl, I. Segal, D. Parmar, A. Zimmer, and A. Kazatsky. (2026). AI in Particle Physics Education: Research Problems and Foundational Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05719
title: Require dedicated unaided practice for foundational knowledge, since assisted performance with AI is not independently retrievable knowledge
description: The article argues that because "assisted performance is not the same as independently retrievable knowledge," AI may act as an effective tutor but students need dedicated unaided practice to obtain foundational knowledge. The prevalent educational criterion should be whether a student can recall and apply knowledge without aid, as in a written examination. The KT1 examination's low, confounded record is offered as a warning supporting this distinction, alongside cited external evidence that unrestricted answer access can decrease long-term learning.
requirements: An assessment format in which students must recall and apply knowledge without aid
Separation of research-shaped exploratory work from foundational-skill assessment
constraints: The KT1 examination record was confounded by incentive structure and format differences, so it serves as a warning rather than a clean measure
target_learners: undergraduate physics students in AI-permitted courses
target_learning_goals: independently retrievable foundational physics knowledge
unaided problem-solving on standard calculations
examples: The revised KT1 plan makes a written examination the focus determining the final grade, with homework counting only toward bonus points and multiple mock examinations offered for unassisted practice

citation: Md. Masudul Islam, Mirza Niaz Morshed, Md. Shafiqul Islam. (2025). Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Sustainable Development: An Ethical Governance and Development Goals Framework. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7643-5420
title: AIRE Taxonomy: a six-level progression from AI awareness to governance foresight
description: The Artificial Intelligence Reasoning and Ethics (AIRE) Taxonomy is a six-tier model extending Bloom's hierarchy with ethical and governance tiers: Recognize, Comprehend, Apply, Analyze, Integrate, and Govern. The article states that "the study introduces a six-tier framework the AIRE Taxonomy that extends Bloom’s hierarchy (Kastberg, 2003) to encompass ethical synthesis and governance foresight." Each tier specifies a learning outcome, a governance competency, and a measurable indicator, and the taxonomy functions as both a pedagogical framework and a policy evaluation instrument across micro, meso, and macro levels.
requirements: Each tier specifies a learning outcome, a governance competency, and a measurable indicator, enabling evaluation across learner, institutional, and policy levels
constraints: In most academic contexts, particularly within undergraduate programs of two to three years, it is not feasible to achieve the full spectrum of competencies outlined in the higher tiers of the taxonomy; the framework should be interpreted as a multi-stage developmental model rather than a linear curriculum
target_learners: learners, educators, policymakers, and institutions engaged in AI education and governance
target_learning_goals: AI literacy progressing from foundational recognition to ethical reasoning and governance capability
examples: Table 1 pairs each AIRE level with illustrative indicators, e.g. percentage of institutions offering AI awareness modules for Level 1 and presence of national AI literacy benchmarks for Level 6

It organizes the goals into People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, and Partnership clusters with AI literacy at the centre, and identifies five analytical dimensions: competency, ethical, governance, innovation, and measurement.

title: MeduAI-SP: a multi-agent LLM standardized-patient training platform with patient, tutor, turn-evaluator, and final-evaluator agents
description: MeduAI-SP is a web-based LLM platform for simulated clinical interview training built from specialized agents: "a patient agent for simulated dialog, a tutor agent providing Socratic prompts for history taking, clinical reasoning, and empathic communication without disclosing diagnostic information, and a turn-level evaluator agent that monitors clinical progress without revealing summative scores." A final evaluator produces post-encounter OSCE-aligned scoring. The platform also supports a structured non-LLM progressive-disclosure control mode and a patient-only examination mode, and logs all interaction data.

clinical reasoning

article_title: AlgoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Theoretical Computer Science Education -- A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for Algorithm Analysis and Complexity Theory
citation: Sushan Adhikari. (2026). AlgoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Theoretical Computer Science Education — A Comprehensive Evaluation Framework for Algorithm Analysis and Complexity Theory. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14572
title: AlgoRAG: a five-stage RAG pipeline for theoretical computer science education
description: AlgoRAG is a retrieval-augmented generation system coupling DeepSeek V3 with a curated TCS knowledge base. Its "five-stage pipeline" performs query analysis with mathematical entity recognition, hybrid dense-and-sparse retrieval, pedagogical re-ranking on educational utility, context-grounded generation with structured prompt templates, and post-processing that normalizes inline mathematics and formats numbered proof steps. It is implemented in Python with sentence-transformers embeddings, ChromaDB vector storage, and a released evaluation harness.

target_learning_goals: algorithm analysis
complexity theory
formal proof techniques and asymptotic reasoning
examples: Evaluated on 179 exam-style questions spanning asymptotic analysis, recurrence relations, dynamic programming, graph algorithms, NP-completeness, sorting, and divide-and-conquer

title: Rubric-based pedagogical quality scoring as a primary evaluation metric for educational AI in formal domains
description: The article defines a composite pedagogical quality score on [0,1] as the mean of six binary criteria applied per response: step-by-step exposition, correct mathematical notation, worked example, query coverage, explanation depth, and proof-step granularity. Because "equivalent mathematical proofs can use substantially different wording", the authors argue this rubric "captures educational value independently of surface wording" and is a more appropriate primary metric than ROUGE or BLEU for mathematical educational AI, offering a reusable benchmark methodology.

article_title: Evaluating AI Tutoring at the Speed of Innovation: Practitioner-Led Micro-Randomised Trials of an AI Tutoring Platform in GCSE Science
citation: Wayne Harrison, Rahil Khowaja, Emma Dobson, Germaine Uwimpuhwe, and Steve Higgins. (2026). Evaluating AI Tutoring at the Speed of Innovation: Practitioner-Led Micro-Randomised Trials of an AI Tutoring Platform in GCSE Science. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14789v1
title: Rapid cumulative micro-RCT evaluation architecture: signal, replication, accumulation
description: An evaluation architecture for rapidly evolving educational AI in which practitioner-led micro-randomised controlled trials are repeated across cohorts, contexts and product versions. Its value lies "not in replacing definitive evaluation with small studies, but in enabling a rapid, cumulative evaluation architecture in which randomised estimates can be generated, replicated and updated". Three linked stages structure the model: an initial trial generates a provisional causal signal; replication tests whether direction and magnitude recur; accumulation characterises the distribution of effects across versions, pedagogy, populations and implementation. Successive estimates are represented through forest plots and cumulative meta-analysis, retaining individual estimates rather than allowing a pooled mean to obscure heterogeneity.
requirements: Random allocation embedded in routine practice, with secure randomisation separating allocation and analysis from teacher judgement
Common protocols, transparent reporting, consistent core outcomes and explicit version documentation across cycles
constraints: Individual micro-RCTs provide only provisional estimates; engagement analytics are post-randomisation and cannot support causal inference
The randomised intention-to-treat contrast should remain the causal centre of the evidence
target_learners: Secondary school students (Year 9 and Year 10) in mainstream English schools
target_learning_goals: GCSE science attainment in extended written answers to curriculum-aligned examination questions
examples: The Medly evaluation embedded three parallel subject-specific micro-RCTs in routine revision practice over four weeks, using the WhatWorked Teachers platform for randomisation and automated ANCOVA reporting.
key_sources: Wayne Harrison, Rahil Khowaja, Emma Dobson, Germaine Uwimpuhwe, and Steve Higgins. (2026). Evaluating AI Tutoring at the Speed of Innovation: Practitioner-Led Micro-Randomised Trials of an AI Tutoring Platform in GCSE Science. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14789

article_title: Evaluating AI Tutoring at the Speed of Innovation: Practitioner-Led Micro-Randomised Trials of an AI Tutoring Platform in GCSE Science
citation: Wayne Harrison, Rahil Khowaja, Emma Dobson, Germaine Uwimpuhwe, and Steve Higgins. (2026). Evaluating AI Tutoring at the Speed of Innovation: Practitioner-Led Micro-Randomised Trials of an AI Tutoring Platform in GCSE Science. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.14789v1
title: The moving intervention: educational AI as a versioned configuration rather than a fixed product
description: A conceptual account of why conventional evaluation lags educational AI: the intervention "may be better understood as a versioned configuration of technological capabilities, pedagogical functions and implementation practices at a particular point in time: a moving intervention rather than a fixed product". Movement comes both from technological change and from implementation, so evaluation requires documenting software version, pedagogical framing and implementation conditions. The authors distinguish technological implementation (interfaces, underlying models, which change quickly), instructional features (adaptive practice, diagnostic feedback, scaffolding, more stable) and pedagogical intention (most stable), arguing cumulative evaluation needs enough version information to identify technological change while documenting pedagogical conditions that permit learning across versions.
requirements: Evaluation must document not only software version but the pedagogical framing and implementation conditions instantiated in the version actually studied
constraints: Evidence can retain high internal validity for the version studied while becoming progressively less informative about the version currently in use
Not every software update creates an entirely new intervention; the three-level distinction between technological implementation, instructional features and pedagogical intention applies
target_learners: Secondary school students using rapidly evolving AI tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Attainment on curriculum-aligned examination questions in school science
examples: The Medly trial evaluated a particular configuration of the platform at a particular point in its development, which the authors treat as precisely the problem their wider argument addresses.

article_title: Evaluating AI Tutoring at the Speed of Innovation: Practitioner-Led Micro-Randomised Trials of an AI Tutoring Platform in GCSE Science

title: Keep the randomised intention-to-treat contrast as the causal centre, using engagement analytics only to generate hypotheses
description: In rapid evaluations of educational AI, platform analytics are immediate and granular, but the article argues that "analysis of post-randomisation usage does not provide causal inference". The randomised intention-to-treat contrast should remain the causal centre of the evidence, with engagement data used to generate hypotheses for subsequent tests. This disciplined limit on interpretation lets rapid cycles stay credible while still exploiting granular usage data.
requirements: Random allocation preserving an intention-to-treat contrast as the primary analysis
Engagement analyses reported as associational, adjusted for baseline attainment
constraints: Post-randomisation engagement may reflect motivation, access, prior capability or other characteristics, so it cannot support causal dose-response claims without an identification strategy such as randomised encouragement
target_learners: Secondary school students in mainstream English schools
target_learning_goals: GCSE science attainment in extended written answers
examples: In the Medly evaluation, the intention-to-treat analysis was confirmatory while the questions-answered association and threshold estimates were labelled exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

article_title: A light-touch AI literacy intervention helps protect against AI political persuasion
citation: Reed Orchinik, David Rand. (2026). A light-touch AI literacy intervention helps protect against AI political persuasion. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16432
title: Light-touch AI literacy warning about LLM persuasion and selective information
description: A brief pre-conversation warning telling users that LLMs "can be 'prompted' to persuade or manipulate" and "may present information in a biased or selective way, emphasizing one side of an issue." The general version was shown identically worded in both studies; Study 2 added a specific version disclosing which direction the model was instructed to argue. It is a minimal, text-only intervention shown before a conversation with an LLM assigned to persuade.
requirements: Delivered before the user converses with an LLM; the conversation must last at least three exchanges in the evaluated design
constraints: Tested only on political attitudes on contested issues with compelling arguments on both sides; the authors state effectiveness may differ in domains involving factual beliefs, e.g. conspiracy theories
target_learners: Adult U.S. online panel participants (CloudResearch Connect)
target_learning_goals: Recognizing that AI systems can be prompted to persuade and may present information selectively, creating resistance to AI persuasion attempts
examples: In both studies participants gave initial attitudes, saw the warning or no warning, held a conversation with an LLM instructed to shift their views, and answered the attitude measures again

article_title: A light-touch AI literacy intervention helps protect against AI political persuasion
citation: Reed Orchinik, David Rand. (2026). A light-touch AI literacy intervention helps protect against AI political persuasion. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16432
title: Inform users of AI's persuasive potential before AI conversations to confer targeted protection without general distrust
description: Because recognizing a counter-party's persuasive intent creates resistance (the article's persuasion knowledge theory motivation), designers should present a brief warning that LLMs can be prompted to persuade and may present information selectively before users converse with AI on contested topics. The article's evidence shows this roughly halves persuasion while leaving general trust in generative AI intact, suggesting protection is targeted rather than blanket skepticism.
requirements: The warning must be shown before or at the start of the AI conversation; wording must convey that models can be prompted to persuade or manipulate
constraints: Does not entirely eliminate AI's persuasive effects; tested on political attitude topics, and the authors state effectiveness may differ for factual beliefs such as conspiracy theories
target_learners: Adult users of conversational AI systems
target_learning_goals: Resistance to manipulative AI persuasion while preserving the benefit of accurate AI
examples: Two experiments randomized U.S. participants to warning or no-warning control before conversations with GPT-4.1 (Study 1) or Grok 4.5 (Study 2) instructed to shift their political views

article_title: AI literacy over tool design: a mixed-methods study of scaffolded versus unrestricted generative AI in programming education
citation: Azimi, S. (2026). AI Literacy over Tool Design: A Mixed-Methods Study of Scaffolded versus Unrestricted Generative AI in Programming Education. Delft University of Technology.
title: AI Study Coach: a notebook-embedded scaffolded AI tutor with two modes and four session constraints
description: The AI Study Coach is an AI tool built into Jupyter-notebook laboratory sessions so students can consult it without leaving the task. It operates in two modes: Explainer mode, in which it "explained analytic outputs and the design choices behind the code", and Debugger mode, which gives stepwise hints from general to specific without generating code. Four constraints apply each session: a 25-hint budget, a fifteen-minute AI-use limit, an end-of-session written reflection, and tagging of AI-sourced code. Together these constituted the scaffold under study.
requirements: Integration into the notebook environment so consultation happens within the laboratory task
Teaching-team visibility of tagged AI-sourced code for the scaffold to be monitorable
constraints: The article's results say nothing about scaffolds in general, only that this particular scaffold did not produce the assumed learning advantage
target_learners: master's-level students in a data analytics and machine learning course with varied prior programming experience
target_learning_goals: data analysis and machine learning practice: understanding analytic outputs, debugging code, and responsible AI use
examples: In the pilot, Coach students used Explainer and Debugger modes under the four constraints, logged every interaction, and completed end-of-session reflections
key_sources: Azimi, S. (2026). AI Literacy over Tool Design: A Mixed-Methods Study of Scaffolded versus Unrestricted Generative AI in Programming Education. Delft University of Technology. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16784

article_title: I code or AI code: A comparative evaluation of AI-rated scores in classroom observations
citation: Fong, Y., Xiang, J., Chan, T.-Y. D., Lee, K., & Lau, E. Y. H. (2026). I Code or AI Code: A Comparative Evaluation of AI-rated Scores in Classroom Observations. The Education University of Hong Kong. https://www.eduhk.hk
title: CLASS Pre-K framework: three domains of teacher-child interaction quality comprising ten rated dimensions
description: The Classroom Assessment Scoring System Pre-K is a standardized observational framework assessing classroom quality through teacher-child interactions. It comprises "three overarching domains derived from observed dimensions": Emotional Support (four dimensions including Positive Climate and Teacher Sensitivity), Classroom Organization (three dimensions including Behavior Management), and Instructional Support (three dimensions including Quality of Feedback). Dimensions are rated on a 7-point Likert scale from low to high quality, and domain scores are aggregated from dimension scores. In this study it served as the common framework against which human and AI ratings were compared.
requirements: Trained, calibrated raters (or an equivalently trained AI model) using the CLASS manual and exemplar videos are needed to produce reliable dimension scores
constraints: Footage of recess or unstructured free-play periods is excluded to maintain consistency with the measure's coding requirements
The CLASS methodology typically requires between four and seven observations per classroom for a representative classroom-level estimate
target_learners: Children aged 3-4 in kindergarten (K1) classrooms
target_learning_goals: Quality of teacher-child interactions supporting children's learning and development
examples: The study applied the full CLASS framework to 87 video-recorded observations from 38 Hong Kong K1 classrooms, with eight trained human raters and a prompt-trained GPT-5.0 model scoring the same transcripts

article_title: AI-written admissions essays are widespread but penalized
citation: Calvin Isley, Johann D. Gaebler, and Sharad Goel. (2026). AI-written admissions essays are widespread but penalized. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22549
title: LLM-based pipeline converting unstructured application materials into structured measures, including a seven-dimension essay quality score validated against expert ratings
description: The authors built an LLM-based pipeline that converts unstructured application materials (transcripts, recommendation letters, resumes, essays) into structured measures, extracting 216 measures designed with admissions officers. Essay quality is scored along seven dimensions—"grammar, style, clarity, prompt responsiveness, voice, commitment to public service, and demonstrated leadership"—each graded on a five-point scale, then combined into a composite score fitted to predict expert ratings from five admissions officers. The automated and expert ratings correlate at 70%. The pipeline also produced 427 covariates used in the causal models.
requirements: Requires LLM scoring prompts with concrete rubric criteria per dimension and expert calibration ratings from admissions officers to fit dimension weights
constraints: The authors state the automated quality measure is an imperfect proxy for expert judgment and may systematically miss dimensions of quality that matter in admissions
target_learners: graduate program applicants
target_learning_goals: accurate structured assessment of applicant writing quality and application materials
examples: Five admissions officers each rated up to 100 essays (50 likely human, 50 likely AI) on a six-point scale to calibrate the composite score; the resulting LLM-based rating correlated 70% with expert ratings (Fig. 2).

article_title: When AI Tutors Speak: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment
citation: Shihao Yang, Marshall Van Alstyne, and Chrysanthos Dellarocas. (2026). When AI Tutors Speak: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23958
title: Attempt-first structured tutoring cycle with Bloom laddering and a transfer capstone
description: The article's treatment is a pedagogical cycle enforced by the tutor's system prompt, not the underlying model. The tutor opens with retrieval warm-up on prior material, draws questions from the week's learning objectives ordered up Bloom's ladder, and "posesone question at a timeand requiresanattemptbeforeitwillexplain;thisistheprompt'scentralrule." On error it scaffolds with a smaller step, graduated hint, or a worked example followed by an isomorphic variant; errors receive targeted feedback written to a persistent blackboard the student can export. A topic is complete only when the student answers an unassisted transfer question, then the session advances one Bloom rung up. The authors map attempt-first questioning to retrieval practice, the Bloom ladder with transfer capstone to the SOLO relational threshold, and required production on every turn to the production and self-explanation channels, operationalizing the interactive tier of the ICAP hierarchy.
requirements: A course-specific knowledge base (weekly readings, lecture notes, problem sets) to ground the tutor
A rule-dense pedagogical prompt the LLM follows reliably on every turn
Structured tool-calling so the tutor can write to the shared blackboard
constraints: The cycle operates identically in both channels, so it isolates pedagogy from delivery modality by design
It was deployed as an optional, ungraded weekly practice layer barred from graded-assessment content
target_learners: Working-professional online MBA students in a quantitative corporate-finance module
target_learning_goals: Quantitative finance problem-solving (NPV, discount rates, cost of capital) with conceptual depth at SOLO relational level or better
examples: The deployed tutor diagnosed before explaining, required an attempt, scaffolded errors with smaller steps rather than answers, consolidated worked results to the blackboard, and closed topics only on unassisted transfer (Figure 3)
key_sources: Shihao Yang, Marshall Van Alstyne, and Chrysanthos Dellarocas. (2026). When AI Tutors Speak: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23958

article_title: When AI Tutors Speak: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment
citation: Shihao Yang, Marshall Van Alstyne, and Chrysanthos Dellarocas. (2026). When AI Tutors Speak: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23958
title: Design AI tutors for pedagogical structure first; humanlike modality is an engagement lever, not a learning lever
description: The article's headline design recommendation is that what makes an AI tutor educational is its pedagogical structure — attempt-first questioning, scaffolding, and production demands — not how humanlike its delivery channel feels. As the authors put it, "Pedagogical structure shapes what students practice, and modality shapes how they interact with the tutor. Making an AI more humanlike does not by itself make it more educational." Voice roughly doubled conversational interaction and was increasingly preferred, yet produced weekly mastery statistically equivalent to text at 2.8× the cost, so programs should treat modality as a purchasable engagement and adoption lever and invest their design effort in the guardrailed tutoring pedagogy that the offloading evidence identifies as protective.
requirements: A structured tutoring prompt that diagnoses before explaining and requires student production on every turn
Assessment instrumentation (engaged-time metering, transcripts, cost accounting) to verify that engagement gains are not mistaken for learning gains
constraints: Voice carried a 2.8× cost premium for equivalent measured mastery in this quantitative, problem-set-driven graduate setting
The modality null is identified within students in one course; the authors note task–technology-fit reasons text may suit stepwise analytical work
target_learners: Working professionals in asynchronous online graduate programs
target_learning_goals: Authentic learning (unassisted exam performance and SOLO-scored reasoning depth) rather than assisted performance
examples: The experiment randomized tutor access against a no-AI holdout and alternated voice and text weekly within AI-arm students, holding pedagogy, model, and knowledge base constant across channels
key_sources: Shihao Yang, Marshall Van Alstyne, and Chrysanthos Dellarocas. (2026). When AI Tutors Speak: Evidence from a Randomized Field Experiment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23958

article_title: AIfred: Augmented Learning through Functional Robotic Embodiment at the Desk
citation: Gregorio Orlando, Milan Groshev, Eduardo Castelló Ferrer. (2026). AIfred: Augmented Learning through Functional Robotic Embodiment at the Desk. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38737
title: AIfred: desk-based robotic arm with end-effector projector delivering spatially co-located generative AI assistance
description: AIfred is a prototype combining a robotic arm with a mini projector at its end-effector, an OptiTrack motion-capture system tracking a desk object, and an overhead camera. It operates through a three-stage spatial assistance pipeline: workspace perception (MediaPipe gesture detection triggering a screenshot), context-aware content generation (Gemini models interpreting the scene under the active interaction mode), and robot-mediated projection onto the indicated desk location. Three interaction modes were programmed: math homework (scaffolding hints rather than answer replacement), generate image, and draw. All code and materials are publicly available in the article's stated repository.
requirements: Requires workspace perception hardware: an overhead camera, a motion-capture system tracking the robot base and a trackable desk object, and an inverse kinematics solver to orient the projector
constraints: The OptiTrack motion-capture tracking limits deployment outside controlled lab settings, per the authors' limitations section
The current design prioritizes functional projection over expressive robot behavior
target_learners: university-campus adult participants across humanistic, social-science, business, and engineering backgrounds
target_learning_goals: math problem solving on quadratic equations
sketch-to-image generation
drawing quality
examples: In the user study, participants completed math assignments, image-generation from sketches, and drawing tasks with AIfred or laptop ChatGPT, including a crossover third drawing task

article_title: AIfred: Augmented Learning through Functional Robotic Embodiment at the Desk
citation: Gregorio Orlando, Milan Groshev, Eduardo Castelló Ferrer. (2026). AIfred: Augmented Learning through Functional Robotic Embodiment at the Desk. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38737
title: Embed AI guidance physically within the learner's workspace when guidance and task share a spatial frame
description: The article recommends delivering AI assistance directly into the physical workspace rather than on a separate screen, because projected guidance keeps digital content aligned with handwritten work and avoids context switching. The authors state that "co-locating guidance matters most when the instructions and the task share a unified spatial frame", and that robot-mediated projection is "not a general-purpose replacement for screen-based assistance, but a targeted one". The principle is instantiated by AIfred's robot-mediated projection of task-relevant guidance next to physical work materials.
requirements: A projection or in-situ display mechanism capable of placing generated guidance at the location of the physical work
Perception of the user's physical task context so generated content is task-relevant
constraints: Symbolic content that can be read from a screen and reproduced on paper gains less from co-location; the benefit concentrates in spatial tasks such as drawing
Screen-based assistance remained faster for repeated revisions in the image-generation task
target_learners: adult learners and creative practitioners doing desk-based work
target_learning_goals: short-term learning transfer of practiced reasoning
drawing and creative output quality
examples: AIfred projected hints, formulas, and reasoning cues next to math work, and projected reference images and tutorials directly onto the learner's paper during drawing

article_title: Artificial intelligence in university physics education: a systematic review of empirical studies
citation: Malikova Z, Ualikhanova B, Turmambekov T, Rakhashev B and Berdaliyev D (2026). Artificial intelligence in university physics education: a systematic review of empirical studies. Front. Educ. 11:1964629. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1964629
title: Five-domain analytical synthesis of AI use in university physics education
description: The review organizes its cross-study synthesis of the 11 included studies into five analytical domains: "feedback and scaffolding; virtual tutoring and learning support; content generation and teacher preparation; collaborative learning and simulation/modeling; and AI literacy, trust, and critical evaluation." For each domain, Table 6 records patterns of AI use, contradictions across studies, and conditions identified as relevant to educational use, such as alignment between AI-supported activities and assessment tasks and support that guides reasoning rather than providing complete answers. Figure 2 provides a conceptual summary of the relationships among these patterns, conditions, contradictions, and outcomes.
requirements: Empirical studies of AI used for pedagogical purposes in university physics education with direct participation of university students, as defined by the review's PICOS criteria.
constraints: The review states the figure "should be interpreted as a conceptual synthesis of the reviewed evidence rather than as a causal model."
target_learners: University physics students
Pre-service physics teachers
target_learning_goals: Physics conceptual understanding and problem solving
AI literacy and critical evaluation of AI outputs
examples: Table 6 maps each domain to patterns, contradictions, and conditions; e.g., in the feedback domain, benefits were stronger when homework and assessment content were closely aligned (Lu et al., 2025).

citation: Chen D, Zeng L, Ou W and Zhong S (2026) ASR technology in college English speaking instruction: the role of feedback internalization and metacognitive strategies. Front. Psychol. 17:1847238. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1847238
title: Integrated model of ASR features, metacognitive strategies, and oral proficiency outcomes with language proficiency as moderator
description: The article proposes "a comprehensive theoretical framework that examines the dynamic relation -ships between ASR technology, learner characteristics, and pedagogical outcomes." It positions four ASR features (recognition accuracy, usage frequency, corrective feedback quality, reflection task design) as inputs, reflective behavior and intrinsic motivation as psychological mediators that transform external feedback into internalized learning, and language proficiency as a moderator of the mediator-to-outcome paths. The framework integrates metacognitive strategies with ASR-assisted second language learning and was tested via structural equation modeling.

undergraduate students in higher education

feedback internalization

citation: Firdausi, H.; Wasis; Sholikah, R. W.; Lemantara, J.; Rosyadi, F. D.; Ginardi, R. V. H.; Pradityo, M. H. A.; Hakim, A. R. (2026). title: FRISCO framework: six criteria of critical thinking (Focus, Reason, Inference, Situation, Clarity, Overview)
description: The FRISCO framework, proposed by Ennis, "outlines six criteria of critical thinking: Focus, Reason, Inference, Situation, Clarity, and Overview." In this study it serves as the multidimensional scoring rubric for physics essays: each of six essay sub-questions on greenhouse-gas impacts maps to one dimension, scored 1–4 with rubric descriptors such as Reason's "detailed explanations supported by relevant evidence when making conclusions." The framework treats critical thinking as a set of separable reasoning components rather than a single holistic score.

target_learning_goals: Critical thinking in scientific reasoning and argumentation about physics content
examples: The dataset instrument consisted of a case description followed by six essay sub-questions, one per FRISCO dimension, scored on a 4-point scale by three raters

title: Hybrid IndoBERT–BiLSTM automated essay scoring architecture with per-dimension classifiers
description: The IB-BiLSTM architecture "combines IndoBERT as a contextual encoder with a two -layer Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) as a sequential classifier." IndoBERT produces token-level embeddings of shape (batch × 128 × 768) fed to the BiLSTM, followed by Dense layers (256 and 128 units, ReLU) and a four-unit softmax for score levels 1–4. Six independent classification models were built, one per FRISCO dimension, rather than a single multi-label classifier, and all IndoBERT parameters were trainable for joint fine-tuning.
requirements: Pretrained IndoBERT (indobert-base-p1) with WordPiece tokenization; balanced class-weighted loss; hyperparameter tuning via 5-fold CV on macro-F1
constraints: Evaluated on a small dataset (83 training / 23 test students); the article reports that accuracy alone is insufficient for ordinal AES evaluation because high-accuracy variants can show majority-class collapse
target_learners: Indonesian high school physics students
target_learning_goals: Automated multidimensional assessment of critical thinking in physics essays
examples: Ten IB-BiLSTM variants (A–J) varying learning rate, dropout, and BiLSTM units were trained; IB-BiLSTM-I won Situation and Clarity, and the best model per dimension was deployed in a web-based system returning per-dimension scores

title: Two-stage data preparation pipeline: rule-based synthetic generation plus LLM paraphrase augmentation without data leakage
description: The pipeline first generates synthetic score-level-1 samples in the training partition only, using "template-based generation (40%), quality degradation (35%), and a combined approach (25%)", including truncation to 20–40% of original length and removal of domain-critical keywords. Second, paraphrase-based augmentation via the Gemini API balances minority classes at scores 2–4 to a uniform 25% per level. Splitting was done once at the student level so each student's responses appear in a single partition, "thereby preventing cross -dimensional data leakage," and the test set stayed locked and unmodified.
requirements: Augmentation and generation confined strictly to the training partition; fixed random seed; target counts set to the majority class size per dimension
constraints: Alternative techniques (back-translation, synonym substitution, EDA) were excluded after preliminary experiments showed lower output quality and inconsistent meaning preservation in the Indonesian physics essay domain; in Overview, augmentation marginally decreased QWK
target_learners: Indonesian high school physics students whose essays form the scored dataset
target_learning_goals: Reliable ordinal automated scoring of critical thinking dimensions despite severe class imbalance
examples: After augmentation, training-set sizes ranged from 148 (Reason) to 212 (Inference) samples per dimension, with the test set fixed at 23 samples throughout

article_title: Ensuring Academic Integrity through Automated Online Exam Proctoring: A Decade-Long Systematic Review
citation: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). Ensuring academic integrity through automated online exam proctoring a decade long systematic review. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01224-3
title: Conceptual multi-layered framework integrating biometric verification, visual/audio analysis, and environmental monitoring
description: The review proposes a conceptual multi-layered framework for automated proctoring that combines biometric verification, visual and audio analysis, and environmental monitoring to improve academic integrity. It is offered as an integrative synthesis of the reviewed ML, DL, IoT, and hybrid techniques, addressing the review's finding that "a clear, unified framework that balances detection accuracy, privacy preservation, and context-aware -ness remains lacking." The framework is a design proposal, not an evaluated system.
requirements: Integration of multimodal behavioral inputs such as keystroke dynamics, gaze tracking, and environmental monitoring in a cost-effective and scalable way, as the review states is currently insufficient
constraints: The review states many existing models are limited by dataset biases, generalization issues across diverse environments, and ethical concerns around intrusive surveillance
target_learners: higher education students in online examinations
target_learning_goals: uphold academic integrity and fair assessment in online examinations
examples: The review's contribution list states it "Proposes a conceptual multi-layered framework integrating biometric verification, visual/audio analysis, and environmental monitoring to improve academic integrity."

article_title: Ensuring Academic Integrity through Automated Online Exam Proctoring: A Decade-Long Systematic Review
citation: Malhotra, M., & Chhabra, I. (2026). Ensuring academic integrity through automated online exam proctoring a decade long systematic review. Discover Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44217-026-01224-3
title: AIPS four-feature integrity taxonomy: authentication, browsing tolerance, remote authorization and control, and report generation
description: The review describes Artificial Intelligence Proctoring Systems as ensuring system integrity through four main features: authentication (e.g., camera-based face verification so only registered students log in), browsing tolerance (restricting computer and internet use during tests), remote authorization and control (letting examiners initiate, stop, resume tests and investigate suspicious activity during live proctoring), and report generation (compiling summaries of student actions from exam recordings). This taxonomy organizes the review's classification of proctoring system functions.
requirements: Front and rear cameras and microphones already present on students' devices, which the review says these systems use to monitor actions
constraints: The review notes these surveillance measures may be perceived as violating privacy, requiring measures that assure users of safety and privacy
target_learners: higher education students in online examinations
target_learning_goals: maintaining academic integrity during online assessment
examples: The review states "AIPS ensures system integrity by looking at four main features: (1) authentication, (2) browsing tolerance, (3) remote authorization and control, and (4) generating reports."
