article_title: From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs
citation: Yi Zhang & Julia Rayz. (2026). From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08009
title: Bloom-aligned framework for measuring educational control in LLMs
description: The framework operationalizes educational control — "the ability to preserve a task's instructional intent while shifting its cognitive demand toward specified learning objectives" — using revised Bloom's Taxonomy as an ordinal scale from Remember (1) to Create (6). It applies two matched intervention settings, general difficulty control and Bloom's control, and two metrics: Observed Cognitive Shift (OCS), the average movement along the taxonomy, and Target Zone Accuracy (TZA), precision of landing in the targeted zone. It is applied to programming tasks in computer science education to study the gap between solving tasks and adapting them for learners.
requirements: An LLM-as-a-judge cognitive-level classifier; the article uses claude-3.5-haiku, validated with Gwet's AC2 of 0.95 against human consensus on a 150-question subset
constraints: The judge is used to compare relative movement across matched intervention conditions rather than to assert that every absolute label is definitive
Bloom's Taxonomy serves as a structural proxy focused on task-level cognitive demand, not multi-turn tutoring dynamics or learner-specific adaptation
target_learners: programming learners in computer science education
target_learning_goals: aligning generated programming tasks with intended Bloom's Taxonomy cognitive levels
examples: Applied to a matched Qwen3-Next general/coder pair across 2,520 tasks from BigCodeBench, LiveCodeBench v5, and SWE-Bench-Verified, with four interventions per task under a shared template and decoding settings
key_sources: Yi Zhang & Julia Rayz. (2026). From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08009

article_title: From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs
citation: Yi Zhang & Julia Rayz. (2026). From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08009
title: Assess LLM educational control beyond execution correctness before deploying models as educational tools
description: The article argues that excelling at execution benchmarks shows a model can be a proficient problem solver without being an effective educator, and that optimizing solely for functionally correct solutions can cause an "illusion of learning". It recommends that "when deploying LLMs as educational tools, we should look beyond valid problem-solving and actively assess whether a model can recognize educational frameworks, adjust cognitive complexity, and intentionally mutate tasks for different learners." The Bloom-aligned framework provides a concrete evaluation for this.
requirements: Evaluation against an established learning-objective taxonomy rather than pass-or-fail execution metrics alone
constraints: Findings establish a comparative baseline on two Qwen3-Next models; broader validation across additional model families, scales, and training recipes remains an important next step
target_learners: novice programming learners
target_learning_goals: keeping AI-generated tasks within learners' zone of proximal development
examples: The framework revealed that both evaluated models readily synthesize additional cognitive complexity but struggle to produce lower-level mutations for novice-oriented learning
key_sources: Yi Zhang & Julia Rayz. (2026). From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08009

citation: V. Švábenský, J. Vykopal, S. Leelaluk, P. Čeleda, F. Okubo, A. Shimada. (2026). Assessment in Team Problem-Solving Exercises in Computing Education. Proceedings of the 56th IEEE Frontiers in Education Conference (FIE '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19209v1
title: INJECT Exercise Platform (IXP) with integrated automated team-assessment methods
description: The IXP is an open-source learning platform for tabletop exercises in which teams interact only with teammates and the platform, which delivers scenario messages and logs each team's activity, e.g., milestone achievements, tool usage, and email responses. In this study the TTXs were conducted in-person using the IXP, instructors role-played actors via email, and the platform recorded the log data that both assessment methods consumed. The IXP team has since incorporated the paper's assessment methods into the latest version of the platform.

constraints: The IXP intentionally provides no immediate feedback on teams' progress; feedback is discussed in the debriefing

article_title: Assessment in Team Problem-Solving Exercises in Computing Education
citation: V. Švábenský, J. Vykopal, S. Leelaluk, P. Čeleda, F. Okubo, A. Shimada. (2026). Assessment in Team Problem-Solving Exercises in Computing Education. Proceedings of the 56th IEEE Frontiers in Education Conference (FIE '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19209v1
title: Five-part scope framework for post-exercise automated team assessment in TTXs
description: The article defines its assessment scope through five grounded characteristics: assessment targets teams rather than individuals, since a team is the fundamental unit and succeeds only when members collectively resolve tasks; it is summative, using milestones as predefined checkpoints that serve as indicators of the learning objectives the team has met; it is exercise-specific, relying only on data collected during the TTX to protect privacy; it is post-exercise, delivering instant results within minutes; and it is fully automated, with manual assessment used only as an evaluation benchmark. This framework organizes the study's two methods and their educational purposes, including grading, hot-wash debriefing, and feedback on deviations from expected procedures.
requirements: Milestones must be predefined in the exercise design so they can indicate met learning objectives
constraints: Individual contributions within a team are explicitly outside the scope; verbal within-team communication is out of scope
target_learners: student teams in higher and formal computing education
target_learning_goals: summative assessment of team problem-solving performance
examples: The framework's post-exercise timing motivated methods that deliver results within minutes instead of hours or days

article_title: The Effect of High-Frequency, Automatically-marked Formative Assessments on Student Outcomes in A-Level Sciences
citation: Matey Yordanov, Mikhail Bychkov, and Andrei Kuchma. (2026). The Effect of High-Frequency, Automatically-marked Formative Assessments on Student Outcomes in A-Level Sciences. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23566
title: Cortex automated handwritten STEM assessment marking platform
description: Cortex is a proprietary automated grading platform for complex handwritten A-Level STEM responses, combining Handwritten Text Recognition fine-tuned on "complex mathematical notation, chemical structures, and physical diagrams" with deterministic mark-scheme-aligned evaluation. It operates through educator, student, and administrator portals; students handwrite solutions on paper, photograph and upload them, and receive grades with granular marginalia within 2 hours. Its defining feature is deterministic Error Carried Forward logic that docks method marks for early errors while awarding ECF marks for valid subsequent logic.
requirements: Handwritten responses must be photographed and uploaded as scans for parsing
Evaluation aligns with formalised A-Level mark schemes such as Edexcel and Cambridge formats
constraints: Images are algorithmically stripped of Personally Identifiable Information before evaluation
The platform was provided free of charge by Cortex Global for this study
target_learners: Upper-secondary A-Level STEM students aged 16-18
target_learning_goals: Procedural fluency and misconception correction in A-Level Mathematics, Further Mathematics, Biology, Chemistry, and Physics
examples: Intervention students submitted weekly or bi-weekly handwritten practice and partial mocks processed with step-by-step annotations within 2 hours of submission

article_title: The Effect of High-Frequency, Automatically-marked Formative Assessments on Student Outcomes in A-Level Sciences
citation: Matey Yordanov, Mikhail Bychkov, and Andrei Kuchma. (2026). The Effect of High-Frequency, Automatically-marked Formative Assessments on Student Outcomes in A-Level Sciences. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23566
title: Deploy automated marking as a high-speed formative loop accelerator to decouple assessment frequency from human grading capacity
description: The article proposes that fully automated marking of complex handwritten STEM work functions as "a high-speed ''formative loop accelerator''": it does not replace the educator but collapses feedback latency from nearly two weeks to under 2 hours and enables a fourfold increase in retrieval practice volume. This decouples assessment frequency from staffing constraints, letting institutions run rigorous mock examination programmes without inflating staff workloads or precipitating teacher burnout.
requirements: An automated grading platform capable of parsing unstructured handwritten STEM notation and applying official mark schemes
Students must handwrite responses on paper to preserve cognitive fidelity of examination conditions
constraints: The study could not isolate the discrete impact of automated feedback quality from the increase in practice volume
Whether high-frequency human feedback would yield identical results remains unknown
target_learners: Upper-secondary A-Level STEM students in international secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Improved final mock examination outcomes and exam readiness in STEM A-Level subjects
examples: The intervention cohort completed weekly or bi-weekly practice exercises and partial mock examinations marked automatically over a 16-week term, while the control cohort completed two human-graded mocks

article_title: Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training
citation: Jiawen Tao, Miao Peng, Yaoming Li, Xiaokun Yuan, Mengzhou Wu, Wenhan Yu, Guoan Wang, Nuo Chen, Tong Yang, Maxm Pan. (2026). Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28109
title: Five-stage retrieval-grounded textbook synthesis pipeline producing 686K source-grounded books (32B tokens)
description: A pipeline that transforms a pre-training corpus into textbook-form training data in two phases: knowledge extraction (query generation, retrieval, chunking, KMeans clustering with relevance filtering) and structured generation (hierarchical TOC planning with a quality gate, then source-grounded section generation and assembly). The article states it "retrieves and clusters source documents, plans hierarchical tables of contents (TOCs) with quality filtering, and assembles source-grounded sections into complete books." It produced 249K TOCs (91.8% passing the gate) and 686K books totaling 32B tokens across 15,387 disciplines, with up to 48 variants per discipline.
requirements: A searchable pre-training corpus index for keyword retrieval, plus LLMs for query generation, TOC planning, quality gating, and section generation
constraints: The pipeline requires a searchable corpus index, which adds preprocessing and retrieval-infrastructure overhead, per the article's limitations
target_learners: language models undergoing mid-training
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge injection and improved downstream benchmark performance
examples: For the running example discipline (Feedforward Neural Networks), 1,346 unique documents were retrieved into 40 clusters; 15 of 16 TOC variants passed the gate, yielding 45 books of 630 sections and 10.5M characters
key_sources: Jiawen Tao, Miao Peng, Yaoming Li, Xiaokun Yuan, Mengzhou Wu, Wenhan Yu, Guoan Wang, Nuo Chen, Tong Yang, Maxm Pan. (2026). Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28109

article_title: Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training
citation: Jiawen Tao, Miao Peng, Yaoming Li, Xiaokun Yuan, Mengzhou Wu, Wenhan Yu, Guoan Wang, Nuo Chen, Tong Yang, Maxm Pan. (2026). Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28109
title: Treat book-level organization as a first-class axis in synthetic pre-training data design, in both construction and training-time packaging
description: The article argues that how synthetic content is organized into coherent books matters beyond the content itself or local rewriting style. On the generation side, a book-level plan provides the scaffold for long, structured text; on the training side, preserving that structure keeps planned adjacent sections in a shared document with continuous positions and shared intra-document attention. The authors state that "organizing related content into coherent books consistently outperforms the alternatives," positioning organization as a first-class data-design axis alongside content and style.
requirements: A retrieval-grounded synthesis pipeline with clustering, hierarchical TOC planning, and book assembly, plus sequence packing with intra-document attention masking at training time
constraints: Each condition is trained once, so training-run variance remains unmeasured; the effect is demonstrated in mid-training settings with an 8% book slice and was not optimized for synthetic-data proportion
target_learners: language models undergoing mid-training or continued pre-training
target_learning_goals: improved downstream knowledge, reasoning, STEM, and code performance
examples: The Full condition retains each TOC-planned textbook as one training document; Split, RandomConcat, and Rephrase controls isolate packaging, length, and rewriting respectively

article_title: WIP: Chat-Debugging: Large Language Model as a Hardware Debugging Assistant
citation: Andrew Ash and John Hu. (2026). WIP: Chat-Debugging: Large Language Model as a Hardware Debugging Assistant. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02420
title: LLM-assisted hardware debugging protocol mapped to the four-step troubleshooting model
description: The paper proposes a protocol following Katz and Anderson's troubleshooting model, in which an LLM-assistant supports each of the four steps: "understanding the system, testing the system, locating the bug, and ﬁxing the bug." The LLM summarizes datasheets and expected component functionality, helps draft test plans, generates multiple potential root causes, and reminds the student of hardware context while fixing and verifying the bug. The student must maintain control by validating the LLM's claims throughout.
requirements: The student must maintain control of the interaction by validating the LLM's claims to ensure it has an accurate understanding of the hardware
The student needs patience and endurance, and must commit to assertively correcting the LLM's misunderstandings
constraints: Prompting strategies will change as LLM models are regularly updated and improved
target_learners: electrical and computer engineering students debugging circuits in labs and projects
target_learning_goals: hardware debugging and troubleshooting skills
debugging confidence
examples: In the study, the LLM provided accurate hardware information during system understanding, helped draft test plans, generated potential root causes from test results, and helped draft functionality tests after the fix

article_title: Chat Debugging: An Exploratory Study of Human-AI Collaboration to Debug Analog Circuits
citation: John Hu and Andrew J. Ash. (2026). Chat Debugging: An Exploratory Study of Human-AI Collaboration to Debug Analog Circuits. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02955
title: Cognitive task analysis of troubleshooting identifies human pain points that human-LLM collaboration is positioned to address
description: The paper builds on cognitive task analysis models that frame debugging as multi-step processes, including Katz's model of understanding the system, testing, locating errors, and repairing errors, and Johnson's model of problem space construction and reduction. It identifies three human pain points: limited hypothesis generation, lack of experience, and working memory overflow during problem space reduction. LLMs are positioned to supply experience recall, hypothesis generation, reasoning, and planning, while humans contribute hands-on measurements. The article states that "a case library that stores relevant past experiences as advice for the learner" is one of Jonassen's three essential components.
requirements: The framework presupposes structured functional or topological system representations for effective selective search of the problem space
constraints: The article notes early cognitive models omitted experience, which Jonassen's architecture was proposed to capture
target_learners: undergraduate electrical and computer engineering students
target_learning_goals: analog circuit debugging and troubleshooting skill
examples: The study maps observed student-LLM chat logs onto these pain points, using the models to interpret where LLMs compensate for novice deficits

article_title: Behaviorally Adaptive Visual Diversion for Inclusive and Resilient Digital Assessment Delivery
citation: Gupta, L. R., Kaur, K., Ram, D. S., & Parani, P. (2026). Behaviorally Adaptive Visual Diversion for Inclusive and Resilient Digital Assessment Delivery. arXiv preprint, under review at IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://arxiv.org
title: BAVD: a behaviourally-adaptive visual diversion model for digital assessment rendering
description: BAVD is a coupled dynamical-systems model in which a synthetic, non-semantic visual field is composited with assessment content and modulated in real time by observed candidate behaviour. The article states that the underlying question content is never altered, reworded, or restructured; only the visual presentation carries an adaptive, low-intensity diversion signal. The model comprises a Diversion Field Generator, a Rendering Tensor, a Behaviour Tensor, a Composite Integrity Functional, and a Multi-dimensional Entropy Functional, with diversion intensity treated as a first-class adaptive variable governed jointly by behavioural evidence and a candidate's declared accessibility profile.
requirements: A per-session secret key delivered to the rendering client over an authenticated channel, since the diversion field is keyed to a per-session secret and its resistance to capture rests on that key rather than on the adversary being unfamiliar with the construction.
constraints: The mechanism addresses screen-capture and screen-sharing adversaries; a compromised client that reads true content before compositing, and an adversary who memorises items, are out of scope and not addressable at the rendering layer.
The paper is a theoretical contribution and reports no platform performance data.
target_learners: higher-education candidates taking high-stakes digital assessments
target_learning_goals: maintaining assessment integrity during digital assessment delivery
examples: The authors describe the framework as a component of the MARS assessment platform, while noting the article reports no platform performance data.
key_sources: Gupta, L. R., Kaur, K., Ram, D. S., & Parani, P. (2026). Behaviorally Adaptive Visual Diversion for Inclusive and Resilient Digital Assessment Delivery. arXiv preprint, under review at IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03531

article_title: Behaviorally Adaptive Visual Diversion for Inclusive and Resilient Digital Assessment Delivery
citation: Gupta, L. R., Kaur, K., Ram, D. S., & Parani, P. (2026). Behaviorally Adaptive Visual Diversion for Inclusive and Resilient Digital Assessment Delivery. arXiv preprint, under review at IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://arxiv.org
title: Treat accessibility attenuation as a first-class part of a security mechanism, with its cost stated rather than assumed away
description: The principle holds that when a security mechanism adds sensory load, accommodation should be incorporated directly into the same adaptation law rather than as a separate opt-out system bolted on afterward, and the security cost of accommodation should be quantified and made visible. The article operationalises this with an accommodation coefficient applied multiplicatively to adapted intensity, so attenuation reduces the visual footprint without exempting the candidate from ordinary integrity evaluation.
requirements: Diversion intensity must already be a dynamic, per-candidate quantity rather than a fixed platform-wide setting, so that accommodation can act on the same adaptation law.
constraints: Attenuation does not preserve capture degradation; at full accommodation the unsynchronised-channel fidelity guarantee fails, so the institution must plan replacement assurance such as reallocated evidence weights or supervised delivery.
target_learners: candidates with registered visual-processing accommodations, photosensitivity, or attention-related conditions
target_learning_goals: equitable access to high-stakes digital assessment without unintended equity burden
examples: The model sets an accommodation coefficient ai in [0,1] through the institution's existing accessibility-declaration process, where ai = 1 fully suppresses the diversion field regardless of behavioural evidence.

article_title: Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education
citation: Adam Coscia, Sujata Duwal, Langdon Holmes, Scott Crossley, and Alex Endert. (2026). Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04006
title: Trustworthiness serves as a structured lens for evaluating LLMs in education, bridging abstract ethical principles and operational technical requirements
description: The article proposes adapting trustworthiness criteria from the ML community as a structured lens for LLM evaluation in education. Trustworthiness functions as an anchor that connects high-level ethical concerns (fairness, safety) to concrete, quantifiable measurements that learning engineers can apply per response. The authors argue this lens helps "bridge the LLM evaluation gap" by providing measurements that help learning engineers align on education-specific challenges and systematically identify potential pedagogical disruptions before deployment.
requirements: Trustworthiness dimensions must be adapted and re-contextualized to the educational deployment context, since which dimensions matter is a property of the deployment
constraints: Ethical frameworks describe principles rather than measurements, leaving open how a learning engineer should check a specific response before it reaches a learner
target_learners: learning engineers
educational technology developers
target_learning_goals: evaluating LLM responses for pedagogical alignment
identifying pedagogical disruptions before deployment
examples: The authors adapted Huang et al.'s eight dimensions of trustworthy LLMs as a starting framework, then filtered and adjusted measures through co-design sessions with learning engineers
key_sources: Adam Coscia, Sujata Duwal, Langdon Holmes, Scott Crossley, and Alex Endert. (2026). Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04006

article_title: Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education
citation: Adam Coscia, Sujata Duwal, Langdon Holmes, Scott Crossley, and Alex Endert. (2026). Calibrating Trustworthiness: Co-Designing Metrics and Visualizations for Evaluating LLMs in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04006
title: Five trustworthiness metrics comprising 20 measures for evaluating LLM trustworthiness in education
description: The article co-constructed a set of five trustworthiness metrics comprising 20 quantitative measures tailored to pedagogical use. Metrics visible in the article include Misinformation, Sycophancy, Diplomacy, Disposition, Learning Method, and Response Quality, each defined by criteria such as "The LLM only generates true, substantiated factual claims" and "The LLM response follows established principles of learning." Measures were sourced from ML trustworthiness literature, education literature on pedagogical prompt patterns, and task-based response quality criteria, then refined through collaborative whiteboarding sessions with learning engineers.
requirements: Measures must automatically compute over every response
Measures must be grounded in the learning context including the textbook passage, learner summary, and preceding dialogue
constraints: Not every ML trustworthiness measure may be needed for education; some require re-contextualization to foreground the relevant pedagogical disruption

K-12 and higher education students using LLM-powered digital textbooks
target_learning_goals: evaluating LLM responses for trustworthiness
detecting pedagogical disruptions in LLM-generated dialogue
examples: The Socratic measure aligns with Knowles' Principles of Adult Learning; the Scaffolding measure incorporates Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development; the SERT measure incorporates self-regulated learning principles

Visualizations map each violation onto the span of the response, the learner's message, or the passage responsible, enabling raters to verify flags against the source text before acting on them.

title: Intelligent digital textbook framework with LLM-powered structured dialogue for reading comprehension support
description: The learning engineer collaborators are developing a framework for intelligent digital textbooks augmented with AI capabilities. Learners write a summary after reading each page, scored by a finetuned ModernBERT model. If below the passing threshold, a structured dialogue sequence triggers: the learner re-reads a selected passage, then the LLM agent Llama3 generates a self-explanation reading training question, followed by a follow-up question and summary revision advice grounded in the passage and dialogue.

summary writing and revision

article_title: Do Assessment Instruments Measure the Same Thing for Humans and LLMs? A Latent Structure Analysis
citation: Alona Strugatski, Licol Zeinfeld, Giora Alexandron. (2026). Do Assessment Instruments Measure the Same Thing for Humans and LLMs? A Latent Structure Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15630
title: A validity-oriented framework for comparing assessment latent structure across humans and LLMs
description: The article introduces a methodological framework that treats similarity of latent factor structure as a necessary, though not sufficient, condition for transferring score interpretations from humans to LLMs. It combines exploratory factor analysis, factor congruence with Hungarian-algorithm factor matching, and repeated resampling against a human-human baseline. As the authors state, it "introduces a validity-oriented framework for comparing the latent structure of assessments across humans and LLMs", demonstrated through two case studies showing instruments "may capture substantially different constructs in humans and LLMs".
requirements: Requires human and LLM response data on the same item set, with preprocessing (removing zero-variance items and unstable tetrachoric correlation estimates) before factor retention and extraction.
Requires a human-human resampling baseline, since within-human similarity is itself variable across resamples.
constraints: The article states it addresses only one aspect of validity, internal structure; generalization to related tasks measuring the same abilities is not examined.
target_learners: Grade 11-12 chemistry students
university entrance exam examinees
LLM systems evaluated on educational assessments
target_learning_goals: construct-level interpretation of assessment scores
validity of LLM capability claims from educational assessments

article_title: Learning to Grade Efficiently: A Bandit-Driven Prompt-Selection Framework for Low-Cost LLM Essay Scoring
citation: Olga Manakina, Igor Bogdanov. (2026). Learning to Grade Efficiently: A Bandit-Driven Prompt-Selection Framework for Low-Cost LLM Essay Scoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23814v1
title: Cost-aware multi-armed bandit framework for adaptive prompt selection in automated essay scoring
description: The framework treats each prompt-model combination as an arm in a multi-armed bandit (MAB) controller that adaptively selects prompting strategies during inference. The agent "observes a reward signal based on the agreement between the LLM's predicted score and the examiner's ground-truth score", using an epsilon-greedy algorithm whose reward incorporates prediction accuracy (negative absolute error) and optionally penalizes token usage. This transforms prompt selection from offline hyperparameter optimization into an online learning task, claimed as the first application of online control mechanisms to AES.

A set of distinct prompt recipes implemented as arms, with a prompt library separating templates from dynamic instantiation
constraints: Implemented and tested with only one LLM (Gemini 2.5) on IELTS Task 2 essays
The epsilon-greedy implementation used a constant exploration rate (ϵ = 0.2), which the authors say could be further refined
target_learners: IELTS Writing Task 2 candidates whose essays are scored
target_learning_goals: Accurate, cost-efficient automated scoring of argumentative essays against official band-score criteria
examples: The system dynamically assembles prompts from a template library, injecting essay question and text, and sequentially generates criterion-specific prompts for multi-step recipes before programmatically calculating the overall score.

article_title: Causal Modelling of Support Interventions for Student Competency Assessment
citation: Francesca Mangili, Alessandro Antonucci, Rafael Cabañas de Paz. (2026). Causal Modelling of Support Interventions for Student Competency Assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24632
title: Partially specified structural causal model (PSCM) protocol for educational assessment
description: The article proposes modelling educational tests as partially specified structural causal models in which observable endogenous variables (answers and hint usage) are generated by latent exogenous variables. As the article states, "endogenous variables — students' answers and hint usage — are the observed variables of our model, generated by the latent exogenous variables skill, luck, and help-seeking". Structural equations are elicited from domain experts in purely logical form, and the resulting graph is acyclic by construction, making the model semi-Markovian and ensuring more tractable inference. The framework explicitly supports interventional and counterfactual reasoning beyond associative probabilistic learner models.
requirements: Structural equations must be elicited from a domain expert for each question, identifying the relevant skills and the logical relation between skills, luck, help and answers
constraints: The protocol requires the structural equations to be elicited from experts; exogenous marginal PMFs are typically unavailable and must be recovered by causal EM back-propagation
target_learners: compulsory school students
target_learning_goals: assessment of student competencies
profiling individual student abilities
evaluating effects of support interventions such as hints
examples: Applied to a CAT battery assessment of algorithmic skills with 12 question nodes, two skills (algorithmic competence and autonomy), hint, luck and propensity variables

article_title: Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks
citation: Paul A. Jewsbury and Steven W. Nydick and Manqian Liao and Siyuan (Marco) Chen. (2026). Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13590v1
title: Consensus calibration: a divide-and-conquer Bayesian procedure that reconstructs the pooled posterior of an evolving IRT item bank from independently calibrated periods
description: Consensus calibration treats recalibration as a divide-and-conquer Bayesian computation: each time period is calibrated independently and the period posteriors are combined without revisiting earlier data. The procedure works in two layers — per-draw robust characteristic-curve linking to a common metric, then precision-weighted aggregation in which the prior contributed by each period is removed and a single consensus prior is reinstated. The article states that "The correction targets the posterior dispersion, not only its location", and that an update's cost scales with the new data rather than the full history.
requirements: Disjoint examinee samples across periods so period likelihoods are conditionally independent
Simple structure: each item loads on a single latent dimension
Aggregate anchor invariance across periods
Gaussian summaries of each period's item posterior, prior contribution, and population-coefficient posterior
constraints: Cross-period conditional independence requires disjoint examinee samples, since substantial overlap would count some responses more than once
The factors combined are plug-in Gaussian summaries of each period's hierarchical posterior, an approximation whose validity was assessed empirically in the benchmark comparison
The aggregation targets each item's marginal posterior; the joint dependence across items induced by shared hyperparameters and common linking constants is not reconstructed
target_learners: language-assessment examinees (e.g., Duolingo English Test test takers)
target_learning_goals: accurate item calibration and test scoring in continuously evolving assessment item banks
examples: Applied to four consecutive quarterly calibration periods of the Duolingo English Test, each with tens of thousands of items and hundreds of thousands of examinees, and compared against a pooled single-run benchmark
key_sources: Paul A. Jewsbury and Steven W. Nydick and Manqian Liao and Siyuan (Marco) Chen. (2026). Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13590

article_title: Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks
citation: Paul A. Jewsbury and Steven W. Nydick and Manqian Liao and Siyuan (Marco) Chen. (2026). Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13590v1
title: Per-draw robust linking: solving a response-count-weighted robust Haebara criterion separately for each posterior draw propagates linking uncertainty into the linked posteriors
description: The linking step maps each independently calibrated period to a common reference metric by minimizing a response-count-weighted pseudo-Huber (robust Haebara) discrepancy between expected-score curves on anchor items. Following Baldwin (2011), the criterion is minimized separately for each posterior draw rather than once at the posterior mean; the article states that "Applying it draw-wise propagates the linking uncertainty, together with its dependence on the item parameters, into the linked posteriors." Weighting anchors by response count lets better-estimated items contribute more to the link, approximating concurrent calibration.
requirements: An anchor set of common items that is invariant in aggregate
A designated reference period defining the metric
Anchor screening by potential scale reduction factor (R-hat at most 1.05) and iterative purification removing top-decile residual anchors
constraints: Each period's fit identifies the latent metric only up to a linear transformation, so linking is required before aggregation
Robust variants suit a partial-invariance context in which a minority of anchor items function differently
target_learners: language-assessment examinees in adaptive testing programs
target_learning_goals: accurate cross-period item calibration with propagated linking uncertainty
examples: In the evaluation, the robust per-draw criterion with the R-hat-and-purification anchor screen was solved for 200 draws of each non-reference period
key_sources: Paul A. Jewsbury and Steven W. Nydick and Manqian Liao and Siyuan (Marco) Chen. (2026). Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13590

Each period was calibrated by a scalable Bayesian explanatory IRT engine with period-specific item posteriors thinned to approximately 1,000 draws. The run comprised four consecutive quarterly calibration periods spanning approximately one year with the third period defining the reference metric.

Consecutive calibration periods with a designated reference period
constraints: Each period included on the order of tens of thousands of items and hundreds of thousands of examinees
The benchmark was fit with a separate ability distribution per period (a multiple-group model) to match the ability structure of the per-period calibrations
target_learners: Duolingo English Test examinees
target_learning_goals: language-proficiency scoring and adaptive item selection in a high-stakes assessment
examples: Linking used the robust per-draw criterion solved for 200 draws of each non-reference period; the consensus Gaussian was sampled to provide 2,000 draws per item

article_title: Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K-12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools
citation: Jacobson, M. J.; Rodriguez-Rivera, G.; Drineas, P.; and Xue, Y. (2026). Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K–12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18072
title: ARC: a hubs-based K–12 AI and robotics education framework with a self-reinforcing mentorship loop
description: ARC organizes hands-on, mentor-led workshop events around regional hubs: primary hubs at colleges train undergraduate mentors via a credit-bearing course and host workshops for nearby K–12 teams, and mature school programs become secondary hubs that host workshops for other nearby schools. The article describes "a self-reinforcing education loop" in which primary hubs train undergraduates, undergraduates teach K–12 students, teams become self-sustaining, and mature teams host their own workshops, giving the framework potential for multiplicative and super-linear growth in mentorship capacity and geographic reach. Workshop content is adapted to age, experience, and competition level, from foundational programming for FLL teams to autonomy, computer vision, and AI for advanced teams.
requirements: Primary hubs require colleges or other STEM institutions able to run the ARC course, train undergraduate mentors, and host workshops; secondary hubs require a mature, self-sustaining school program with enough internal technical knowledge to help nearby teams.
constraints: The trial did not test the full regional system, which would require several years for supported programs to mature and new hubs to form.
target_learners: K–12 students in rural and under-served regions
undergraduate computer science students
target_learning_goals: programming, robotics, and AI literacy
technical mentoring and teaching skills
examples: The trial deployment at one large Indiana university enrolled nine undergraduates, ran weekly two-hour sessions, and supported three new FLL teams from one rural school using LEGO robots and two provided FLL game arenas.
key_sources: Jacobson, M. J.; Rodriguez-Rivera, G.; Drineas, P.; and Xue, Y. (2026). Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K–12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18072

article_title: Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K-12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools
citation: Jacobson, M. J.; Rodriguez-Rivera, G.; Drineas, P.; and Xue, Y. (2026). Teaching AI, Robotics, & Community: A Hubs-Based K–12 Education Framework for Reaching Rural Schools. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18072
title: Spatially-explicit Markov model of ARC regional growth
description: A discrete-time stochastic model with annual transitions representing both school robotics-program development and each school's relationship to the ARC network. Each K–12 school carries two state variables — a FIRST program state (no program, Early, Mature) and an ARC state (Unreachable, Reachable, Supported, secondary Hub) — with nine legal combinations, plus college hub states; geography enters through a fixed relation specifying which schools each hub can serve. The article states "Reachability alone does not alter a school's natural program-development probabilities" and that direct ARC support is what allows different maturation and persistence behavior. It was instantiated for Indiana with 1,925 public K–12 schools and 32 potential college hubs, simulated 40 years over 1,000 Monte Carlo runs across 12 optimism levels, with ablations isolating hub-growth mechanisms.
requirements: A run requires the set of schools, initial valid states, potential primary-hub colleges, the geographic relation, model parameters, and rules for selecting schools when launch or support capacity is limited.
constraints: A mean-field approximation replacing exact geography with regional averages is more analytically tractable but loses spatial clustering, overlapping coverage, and local capacity constraints.
target_learners: K–12 schools in a mixed-rural region being modeled
target_learning_goals: projecting regional growth of robotics program access and mentorship reach
examples: At optimism level 6 the model produced 992 programs and reached 1,415 schools after 40 years, compared with a mean of 161 programs under the ARC-off natural-growth baseline.

citation: Satoshi Takahashi, Atsushi Yoshikawa, Megumi Kose, Kenichi Suzuki, Chieko Inoue, Yumi Watanabe, and Mari Sawada. (2026). Automating Constructive Assessment with Large Language Models: Toward Scalable and Repeated Evaluation of Practical Competence. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25790
title: Hierarchical Diagnostic Reasoning (HDR): a structured constructive assessment of practical judgment
description: HDR is a descriptive assessment proposed by Takahashi et al. (2025) that "diagnoses learners' applied cognitive skills through practical cases containing the misuse of knowledge." It conceptualizes reasoning hierarchically: (1) read and understand the scenario, (2) identify the error, and (3) explain why it is incorrect. Each question combines error selection with a rationale description in a pre-defined frame, so responses converge and the learner's practical judgment and structural understanding are visualized. This study automates the full HDR cycle—problem generation, scoring, and feedback—using ChatGPT prompt design.
requirements: Problems must embed intentional misuses of knowledge aligned with educational intentions, which traditionally requires specialized expertise
Scoring requires unified judgment criteria given to learners (e.g., target only descriptions containing errors; judge based on information within the case)
constraints: Designing problems with intentionally misused knowledge requires specialized expertise
Scoring descriptive answers and creating individual feedback traditionally depend on human resources, making large-scale implementation and immediacy difficult
target_learners: Working adults in business/MBA education
target_learning_goals: Practical judgment and structural understanding of applied knowledge (e.g., STP analysis)
Higher-order cognitive skills such as analysis and evaluation
examples: The original problem was a seven-paragraph STP case study about an electronics manufacturer's sales representative, with three embedded errors identified through interviews with business-education practitioners

citation: Romain Puech, Dewang Kumar Agarwal, Antonio Santamaría Escobar, Dimitris Bertsimas. (2026). Bespoke: Generating MOOC-Quality Industry-Personalized Lecture Videos at Scale. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26540
title: Bespoke: a five-stage pipeline that regenerates a complete industry-personalized lecture video from a seed transcript
description: Bespoke is a directed acyclic pipeline that takes a seed lecture transcript, a learner profile (healthcare, finance, energy, or generic), and a target duration, and compiles a new lecture video with slides, narration, and charts. Its five stages write audience-specific learning objectives, plan the lecture around a retrieved domain paper, write narration, build slides and charts in parallel, and reveal slide elements as they are spoken. Generation used Claude Sonnet 4.6 with GPT-5.2 validating in a bounded refine loop, following backward design and Mayer's multimedia principles. The article describes it as a pipeline that "regenerates a complete lecture video for a stated professional audience from a seed transcript".

A stated learner profile and target duration
A bound of three refinement iterations to keep cost finite
constraints: All videos in the evaluation were generated without instructor intervention at generation time

Mean API cost is about $0.22 per minute of video
target_learners: working professionals in healthcare, finance, and energy seeking upskilling

target_learning_goals: industry-appropriate understanding of technical topics such as decision trees, at audience-calibrated depth and with domain-relevant examples
examples: From 31 graduate seed lectures the pipeline generated over 200 videos across three industries plus a generic audience, at medium (5–15 minutes) and long (up to about 45 minutes) durations

article_title: Argus: Academic Integrity in the Era of Generative AI
citation: David Racovan, Ajay Rawat, Christopher K. May, Jeffrey A. Turkstra. (2026). Argus: Academic Integrity in the Era of Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36073
title: Argus: a static-analysis triage tool for detecting LLM-assisted code development
description: Argus is a static analysis system that processes each student's Git repository commit history, evaluating heuristic indicators in two categories: "Advanced C topics not taught in the course curriculum" and "stylistic patterns inconsistent with course conventions". Weighted indicators, temporal span analysis, and burst detection (commits of at least 30 new lines at 15 or more lines per minute) combine into an aggregate H-score, with dynamic normalization attenuating indicators common in the class. Scores surface through a web interface ranking students for staff review.
requirements: Requires access to the student's working history, such as automatic Git commits on a university-managed server; at institutions without similar infrastructure it may still function on static heuristic indicators alone.
constraints: A high H-score is never treated as evidence of misconduct; benign behaviors such as prior programming experience or drafting in an external editor can produce elevated scores.
target_learners: undergraduate students in large-enrollment introductory C programming (CS2) courses
target_learning_goals: academic integrity enforcement
detecting LLM-assisted code development
examples: In Spring 2026, three course staff reviewed the top 300 students by H-score in roughly 8 hours each, with a median review time of about 1.5 minutes per student.

article_title: Argus: Academic Integrity in the Era of Generative AI
citation: David Racovan, Ajay Rawat, Christopher K. May, Jeffrey A. Turkstra. (2026). Argus: Academic Integrity in the Era of Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36073
title: Pair any automated LLM-detection system with a structured human review process before academic integrity action
description: The article argues that automated detection scores should triage rather than decide cases: "We argue that any automated detection system must be accompanied by a structured process for human review." Because a false accusation carries lasting consequences while a missed case affects only one student's learning, the appropriate standard is whether a tool makes human review fast and structured enough to be feasible in large-enrollment courses. Argus operationalizes this by ranking students by H-score, surfacing individual indicators in code context, and requiring manual review by policy before any integrity action.
requirements: Course staff must review flagged cases manually before any academic integrity action; the tool's purpose is to expedite triage, especially where individual review of every student is infeasible.
constraints: The authors accept a non-zero false negative rate; benign behaviors such as prior programming experience or pasting code drafted in an external editor can produce elevated scores.
target_learners: undergraduate students in large-enrollment programming courses
target_learning_goals: fair academic integrity enforcement
efficient triage of suspected LLM-assisted work
examples: In Spring 2026, staff reviewed the top 300 students by H-score plus top-150 per-assignment students, with three reviewers evaluating independently then reaching consensus, and extreme benefit of the doubt given to avoid false positives.

citation: Elizondo-García ME, Hernández-De la Cerda H, Benavides-García IG, Caratozzolo P and Membrillo-Hernández J (2025) Who is solving the challenge? The use of ChatGPT in mathematics and biology courses using challenge-based learning. Front. Educ. 10:1417642. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2025.1417642
title: UTAUT2-inspired 15-item survey instrument for assessing student perceptions of ChatGPT-assisted activities
description: A concluding survey administered after ChatGPT-assisted activities in both courses, comprising fifteen items: thirteen Likert-scale items (1–10) and two open questions. The Likert items were "inspired by the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2) model" and aligned with critical thinking, instructional design, technology acceptance, and usage, grouped into three dimensions: Acceptance of the AI Tool (Q1–Q5), Instructional Design of the Learning Activity (Q6–Q7), and Critical Thinking (Q8–Q13). Items were filtered and consulted with experts in Psychology and Pedagogical Architects, who recommended them as sequential in analyzing students' perceptions when using ChatGPT.
requirements: Administered upon completion of the ChatGPT-assisted activity in the course
constraints: Items may seem repetitive; the article reports experts recommended them as sequential in analyzing perceptions
target_learners: higher education students in digital general-education STEM courses
target_learning_goals: student perceptions of AI-tool acceptance, instructional design quality, and critical thinking about AI outputs
examples: Used in the February–June 2023 pilot in Fundamentals of Biological Systems and Mathematics and Data Science for Decision Making

title: ChatGPT-as-starting-point with mandatory cross-validation against academic sources
description: A challenge-based learning activity design in which students use ChatGPT as a starting point for research and then verify its outputs. In the biology course activity on gut microbiota, students gained quick insight from ChatGPT and "were tasked with validating the information derived from ChatGPT by cross-checking it with at least two academic, reliable, verifiable, and current sources." article_title: ChatGPT as a Virtual Laboratory Teaching Assistant in Undergraduate Biology
citation: M. Said Doğru & Emily K. Faulconer. (2026). ChatGPT as a Virtual Laboratory Teaching Assistant in Undergraduate Biology. Research in Science Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11165-025-10271-z
title: Sociotechnical Systems Theory frames ChatGPT as a technical support provider interlinked with the social context of the laboratory course
description: The article applies Sociotechnical Systems (STS) Theory, which "gives a systems thinking perspective to an entity where people (with their effectiveness and abilities) work towards goals by following specific processes and using technology." In this framing, ChatGPT is a technical component interlinked with the social components (students, instructors, TAs), supporting laboratory engagement through collaborative questioning and increasing participation in active learning, but not directly managing laboratory experiments. The framework positions ChatGPT as "a technical support provider but not as the primary executor of experimental processes."
requirements: Students should receive instruction on using the technology tool based on its functionality, accuracy, reliability, and user interface.
constraints: The degree of integration and scaffolding of ChatGPT into the existing laboratory course structure is a contextual factor; institutional policies and culture related to AI use can influence the relationships.
target_learners: undergraduate biology laboratory students
target_learning_goals: laboratory concept understanding
active learning through collaborative questioning
examples: The study used the STS framework to explore how students and instructors interact with ChatGPT as a virtual TA in an introductory biology laboratory course.

title: Integrate AI laboratory support with human instructor guidance and a safety net against incorrect information
description: The article recommends that ChatGPT serve as a resource that lifts the burden of answering basic questions from TAs and instructors, while humans remain in the loop. Because "students must understand the error rate provided by the system, and a safety net must be in place to ensure students do not proceed with incorrect information," AI support should be balanced with the guidance of human instructors. Educators should develop a pedagogical approach providing learners strategies for fact-checking AI output.
requirements: Students must understand the error rate of the AI system.
A safety net must be in place to ensure students do not proceed with incorrect information, which could present safety concerns in the biology laboratory.
constraints: The article states replacing human teachers with genAI technology is difficult at this stage of the technology's development.

target_learning_goals: accurate laboratory content knowledge
critical evaluation of AI-generated information
examples: The study evaluated ChatGPT responses to student-generated enzyme laboratory questions and found SMEs considered human TAs more accurate for 5 of 8 questions, motivating the safety-net recommendation.

article_title: Impact of automated scoring on interpreting performance and self-regulated learning: evidence from a pedagogical experiment
citation: Chen C and Liu T (2026) Impact of automated scoring on interpreting performance and self-regulated learning: evidence from a pedagogical experiment. Front. Psychol. 17:1867463. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1867463
title: Align teacher feedback with automated feedback in timing and individuation to support planning and emotional regulation
description: The article recommends that teacher feedback be aligned with automated feedback "in timing and individuation" so that the two sources jointly support the SRL phases automated scoring leaves untouched. Automated scores sustain deliberate practice during execution, but planning and emotional regulation need human scaffolding that is timely and individualized. The recommendation arises from the finding that students rarely analyzed why errors occurred and that emotional responses to scores diverged.
requirements: Instructors must have capacity to provide feedback that matches the immediacy and individualization of automated scores
constraints: The article notes instructor supply limits timely, substantive feedback to every student on every after-class exercise in conventional settings
target_learners: student interpreters (MTI/undergraduate translation and interpreting majors)
target_learning_goals: interpreting performance
self-regulated learning, especially planning and emotional regulation
examples: Over 14 weeks the experimental group used the Yunyi system for after-class tasks while both groups received collective instructor feedback in the following week's class

article_title: Impact of automated scoring on interpreting performance and self-regulated learning: evidence from a pedagogical experiment
citation: Chen C and Liu T (2026) Impact of automated scoring on interpreting performance and self-regulated learning: evidence from a pedagogical experiment. Front. Psychol. 17:1867463. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1867463
title: Zimmerman's three-phase cyclical SRL model as a lens for locating which phases automated feedback reaches
description: The study adopts Zimmerman's (2000, 2002) three-phase model of self-regulated learning — forethought, performance, and self-reflection — as its primary analytical lens, treating each of the system's four feedback dimensions as an input into self-judgment. The model is chosen because it "can accommodate the possibility... that a feedback intervention reaches some phases but not others, instead of treating SRL as a single global capacity". The article's contribution is specifying which phase automated scoring reaches: it reinforced the performance phase, reached self-reflection only in its lower-effort form, and left forethought largely untouched.
requirements: Evaluation of automated feedback tools should be phase-differentiated rather than global, measuring SRL phases individually instead of relying on a single overall score
constraints: Motivational constructs such as self-efficacy are treated as forethought subprocesses rather than a separate phase, following Zimmerman's placement of self-motivation beliefs within forethought
target_learners: student interpreters using automated scoring systems
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning across forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases
examples: The questionnaire's four measurement blocks (Pre-learning Planning, Execution and Monitoring, Evaluation and Reflection, Emotional Motivation) were mapped onto the model's phases

citation: Pei-Hua Chen, Hsin-Yu Lee, Yueh-Min Huang and Ting-Ting Wu. (2026). Unpacking the heterogeneity of pre-service teachers' ChatGPT acceptance: a latent profile analysis across STEM and non-STEM disciplines. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00634-x
title: Integrated TAM–UTAUT2 five-construct framework for person-centered analysis of generative AI acceptance
description: The study integrates the Technology Acceptance Model with UTAUT2 to capture both individual cognition and context. As the article states, "The present study adopts three core TAM constructs (PU, PEOU, AT) and two contextual UTAUT2 constructs (SI, FC)". Performance and effort expectancy are measured with the established TAM scales to avoid redundancy, and consumer-oriented UTAUT2 components are dropped as less relevant to teachers' professional settings. The five constructs serve as LPA indicators, with behavioral intention as a distal outcome.
requirements: Measured via a contextualized questionnaire referencing ChatGPT and teaching-related tasks, validated by expert content review
constraints: The article notes CFA was not conducted, so factorial and discriminant validity evidence (AVE, composite reliability) is absent and future studies should incorporate CFA before LPA
target_learners: pre-service teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: understanding and differentiating pre-service teachers' acceptance of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT
examples: The framework structured the questionnaire (six constructs, five-point Likert items) and the LPA model in which disciplinary background was examined as a moderator of profile distribution

title: Diffusion-of-innovation-based user typology mapping acceptance profiles to adopter categories
description: The study grounds its person-centered user typology in Rogers' diffusion of innovation theory, mapping latent profiles onto adopter categories. As printed: "Technology Pioneers align with early adopters, Pragmatic Evaluators and Environmental Observers reflect the evidence-based and socially driven characteristics of the early and late majorities, respectively, while Resistant Skeptics correspond to the hesitation typically observed among laggards." The typology's practical contribution is guiding differentiated training, since user-type-based differentiated training reportedly yields better outcomes than standardized programs.
requirements: Person-centered analysis (LPA) on multiple acceptance indicators rather than variable-centered average effects
constraints: Profile labels were conceptualized by mapping construct patterns to Rogers' categories, an interpretive step rather than a tested result
target_learners: pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: identifying distinct technology-adopter types to tailor AI literacy training
examples: The four identified profiles were labeled Pragmatic Evaluators, Environmental Observers, Technology Pioneers, and Resistant Skeptics based on construct patterns and disciplinary distribution

article_title: From fear to innovation: A case study of transformative faculty development for ethical AI integration in higher education
citation: John Chick, Laura Morello and Stephanie Staffey. (2026). From fear to innovation: a case study of transformative faculty development for ethical AI integration in higher education. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00225-x
title: UBRIDGE Institute: a six-week synchronous interdisciplinary faculty development program for ethical AI integration
description: The UBRIDGE (Universal design, Bloom's taxonomy, Reflection, Integration, Design thinking, Growth mindset, Ethics) Institute was a six-session synchronous Zoom program, two hours weekly, for interdisciplinary faculty across arts, sciences, education and health professions. It aimed to scaffold AI integration through "inclusive pedagogy, ethical reasoning, and course redesign principles". Sessions combined hands-on AI experimentation, design-thinking worksheets, discussion boards, and capstone AI-integration plans.
requirements: Voluntary participation with sustained six-session duration, active learning, coherence with participant needs, and collective participation, following Darling-Hammond et al. as the article cites
constraints: Self-selection bias: participants volunteered and received modest stipends, limiting generalizability to faculty who might resist such opportunities
target_learners: Higher education faculty and staff across disciplines, from novice to experienced AI users
target_learning_goals: Ethical AI integration in teaching
Inclusive course design
AI-informed pedagogical content knowledge
examples: Participants produced capstone projects ranging from redesigned assignments leveraging AI to departmental policy proposals and research projects examining AI impact

citation: Ciğercci FM and Uygun N (2026). Evaluation of primary school teachers' use and perceptions of artificial intelligence in primary school mathematics instruction: a mixed-methods study. Front. Psychol. 17:1741116. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1741116

description: The study interprets teachers' AI perceptions through two frameworks used as interpretive lenses rather than statistically tested models. TAM holds that "users' beliefs about a technology—particularly its perceived usefulness and ease of use—shape attitudes and behavioral intentions related to adoption," explaining variation in willingness, attitudes, and engagement. TPACK and AI-related extensions interpret how teachers translate engagement into mathematics-specific practice, emphasizing that effective integration depends on the interaction of technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge.

title: Integrity economy: external pressure from regulation, benchmarking and cross-institutional competition to drive academic integrity reform
description: The article argues that internal institutional development alone is insufficient because very little institutional development is likely to pay out without the right kinds of external affordance. It notes there is not yet a flourishing 'integrity economy' in higher education and that "Benchmarking and collaboration thus have essential roles to play, as do pressure from quality and regulatory agencies". Following Heyneman, it proposes generating a reputational economy based on academic ethics rather than research reputation, drawing an analogy with how global research reputation risk indices (rankings) have proven key to reform by stimulating a global reputation race.

Transparency as a change driver in higher education
constraints: Accountability agencies' efforts are likely to have muted impact given the lagging nature of reform, the lack of resonance with academic practice, and the truly global nature of the situation
The world lacks a recognised forum for discussing the intersection of universities, governance and GenAI

article_title: Meta-Cognitive Insights into Cognitive Offloading: Mechanisms, Interventions, and Educational Implications
citation: Yufei Guo & Qun Ye. (2026). Meta-cognitive insights into cognitive offloading: mechanisms, interventions, and educational implications. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06621-5
title: Nelson and Narens's dynamic metacognitive model applied to cognitive offloading: object level and meta level with monitoring and control
description: The review organizes cognitive offloading within Nelson and Narens's (1990) dynamic metacognitive model, in which "the object level involves direct engagement with speciﬁc cognitive operations and task execution" while "the meta-level encompasses processes interacting with the object level, including metacognitive mon- itoring and control." Monitoring provides upward information flow (e.g., perceived difficulty), and control exerts downward influence (e.g., deciding to use a reminder). The review extends this model by distinguishing metacognitive beliefs from metacognitive experiences and by tracing offloading decisions across pre-task anchoring and in-task updating phases.
requirements: The model requires both object-level task execution and meta-level monitoring and control operating in interaction during learning tasks
constraints: The review applies the model specifically to learning contexts where internal and external strategies coexist, such as mental arithmetic versus calculators and spatial memory versus GPS
target_learners: students in educational contexts, including younger learners and learners with mathematical difficulties
target_learning_goals: strategic selection between internal and external cognitive strategies during learning tasks
examples: The review's Fig. 1 adapts the model for offloading contexts, illustrating monitoring of task performance and effort informing meta-level decisions about internal versus external strategies
key_sources: Yufei Guo & Qun Ye. (2026). Meta-cognitive insights into cognitive offloading: mechanisms, interventions, and educational implications. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06621-5

article_title: Meta-Cognitive Insights into Cognitive Offloading: Mechanisms, Interventions, and Educational Implications
citation: Yufei Guo & Qun Ye. (2026). Meta-cognitive insights into cognitive offloading: mechanisms, interventions, and educational implications. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06621-5
title: Beliefs-versus-experiences distinction as a two-component account of metacognition in offloading
description: The review's second organizing axis distinguishes metacognitive beliefs, which "encompass individuals ' general beliefs and knowledge about themselves stored in long-term memory," from metacognitive experiences, which "comprise metacognitive feelings aris- ing from speciﬁc information during the monitoring of of ﬂoading tasks" and are more sensitive to domain-specific and perceptual information. Beliefs dominate pre-task anchoring; experiences dominate in-task updating. The review argues this distinction reconciles contradictory feedback-intervention findings, because feedback targeting beliefs may fail during tasks while trial-by-trial performance feedback modulates experiences effectively.
requirements: Distinguishing which metacognitive component a feedback intervention targets (beliefs versus experiences) to predict its effects
constraints: The framework is argued from existing studies rather than tested directly in this review
target_learners: students using external aids and tools in technology-enhanced learning environments
target_learning_goals: rational timing of cognitive offloading decisions across learning phases
examples: The review interprets Grinschgl et al.'s (2020) unexpected null effect of ranking feedback on offloading as belief-level changes being overridden by authentic task experiences
key_sources: Yufei Guo & Qun Ye. (2026). Meta-cognitive insights into cognitive offloading: mechanisms, interventions, and educational implications. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06621-5

article_title: Meta-Cognitive Insights into Cognitive Offloading: Mechanisms, Interventions, and Educational Implications
citation: Yufei Guo & Qun Ye. (2026). Meta-cognitive insights into cognitive offloading: mechanisms, interventions, and educational implications. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06621-5
title: Match feedback type to metacognitive component and task phase: calibrate beliefs before tasks, provide task-specific feedback during tasks
description: The review proposes that feedback interventions should follow "the principle of timing-component matching for feedback interventions": before task commencement, educators should calibrate metacognitive beliefs with accurate, constructive information about individual abilities; during task execution, they should prioritize immediate, specific, task-related feedback such as real-time accuracy indicators. Matching feedback type to the metacognitive component dominant at each stage is said to maximize feedback's positive effects on rational offloading decisions.
requirements: Feedback must be matched to the dominant metacognitive component at each phase — belief-targeting information pre-task, experience-targeting task-specific information during tasks
constraints: Abstract ranking feedback targeting beliefs may fail to affect in-task offloading decisions dominated by metacognitive experiences, as in Grinschgl et al. (2020)
target_learners: students in technology-enhanced learning environments using external cognitive aids
target_learning_goals: rational cognitive offloading decisions and calibrated metacognitive monitoring
examples: The review derives this principle from reconciling Gilbert et al.'s (2020) advice-feedback benefits with Grinschgl et al.'s (2020) null behavioral effect of ranking feedback

description: The Jordan Chatbot is a human-centred, pedagogical support agent built on the GPT-4o large language model and deployed as a unit-specific conversational agent within the LMS. The article states it "integrates three core components: (1) system instructions defining the chatbot's identity, personality, inclusions, and exclusions; (2) a curated knowledge base containing disciplinary and institutional materials; and (3) an embedded interface within the LMS". Its design draws on situated learning theory and Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, positioning the chatbot as a mediating tool that extends but does not replace teacher guidance, and supports self-regulated learning through immediate personalised feedback.

article_title: The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth — a differentiated framework and testable propositions
citation: Lin J and Al-Hada NM (2026) The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth—a differentiated framework and testable propositions. Front. Psychol. 17:1906070. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906070
title: Differentiated three-level framework mapping AI-integration strategies onto surface, intermediate, and deep cognitive processing
description: The article proposes "a differentiated three-level framework that maps AI-integration strategies onto surface, intermediate, and deep cognitive processing, with a priori classification rules, level-specific AI roles, risks, and boundary conditions". For each level it specifies the cognitive operations involved, the appropriate AI role, primary risks of uncritical use, testable predictions, and preregistered boundary conditions. Surface tasks delegate operations extraneous to the focal objective, so AI serves as an efficiency tool; intermediate tasks require AI as a guided scaffold with metacognitive scaffolds; deep tasks require AI as a dialog partner while cognitive work stays with the learner. Task level must be classified a priori relative to the preregistered learning objective, coded by blind independent raters.
requirements: Task level must be classified a priori in relation to the preregistered learning objective, with the classification rule and examples preregistered and coded by two independent raters blind to condition and predicted direction.
constraints: The framework is presented as a falsifiable interpretation of a heterogeneous literature, not an established pattern; genuine heterogeneity across tasks, populations, and tools remains a rival explanation.
target_learners: learners using generative AI across educational levels, from primary school through university
target_learning_goals: durable, transferable higher-order learning including analysis, evaluation, and critical thinking
examples: Table 1 assigns AI roles per level: efficiency tool for surface retrieval and formatting tasks, guided scaffold for intermediate application tasks, and dialog partner for deep analysis, evaluation, and creative synthesis tasks.

article_title: The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth — a differentiated framework and testable propositions
citation: Lin J and Al-Hada NM (2026) The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth—a differentiated framework and testable propositions. Front. Psychol. 17:1906070. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906070
title: Episodic–habitual offloading distinction and the cognitive-debt construct
description: The article's original extension is "the distinction between episodic offloading—the deliberate, task-specific delegation of an operation while retaining awareness of what is offloaded and why—and habitual offloading—routine, weakly monitored reliance that may recalibrate expected cognitive effort". It adopts "cognitive debt to denote a potential cumulative reduction in metacognitive calibration and/or unaided higher-order cognitive performance that persists beyond a particular AI-assisted episode". A proposed cognitive-debt cycle runs from routine AI use through reduced engagement, weakened calibration practice, and increased reliance, but is explicitly treated as a hypothesis requiring prospective longitudinal tests, not an established sequence.
requirements: For construct validity, cognitive debt must be operationalized as a within-person deterioration from baseline in outcomes measured without AI, after controlling for prior knowledge and practice, separable from offloading frequency and dependency.
constraints: The cognitive-debt cycle is not yet an established longitudinal sequence; the observational paths cited do not establish that routine AI use causes declining engagement.
target_learners: learners and teachers integrating generative AI into study and instruction
target_learning_goals: metacognitive calibration and unaided higher-order cognitive performance
examples: The article hypothesizes three predictors of the transition from episodic to habitual offloading: frequency of unconditioned AI use, low metacognitive monitoring accuracy, and environmental press incentivizing product quality over learning process.

article_title: The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth — a differentiated framework and testable propositions
citation: Lin J and Al-Hada NM (2026) The critical-thinking paradox in generative AI-integrated learning: distinguishing efficiency from cognitive depth—a differentiated framework and testable propositions. Front. Psychol. 17:1906070. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906070
title: Match the AI role to the cognitive-processing level: efficiency tool, scaffold, or dialog partner
description: The framework prescribes level-appropriate AI roles: at surface level AI reduces extraneous load as an efficiency tool; at intermediate level AI should function as a scaffold providing worked examples, guided prompts, and structured feedback, contingent on metacognitive scaffolds; at deep level "AI should function only as a dialog partner: a Socratic interlocutor that poses questions, offers counterarguments, and prompts the learner to justify, refine, and reflect on their reasoning, but does not perform the cognitive work itself". The principle follows from the claim that offloading germane processing impairs learning while offloading extraneous processing can benefit it.
requirements: At the intermediate level, effectiveness is contingent on metacognitive scaffolds—prompts that require learners to explain, elaborate on, or self-explain AI-generated content.
constraints: The article notes preliminary studies are consistent with Socratic dialog supporting deeper engagement but do not establish that a Socratic design is necessary or sufficient across domains.
target_learners: students at all educational levels using generative AI, with roles calibrated to developmental stage and prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: preserving germane cognitive processing and critical-thinking development during AI-integrated tasks
examples: The article cites Lee and Wu's (2025) 15-week randomized controlled trial in which a scaffolded ChatGPT system enhanced cognitive engagement compared with standard ChatGPT, but only when structured prompts guided learners through knowledge integration phases.

title: Six-standard framework for faculty technology integration in higher education: Instructor, Coordinator, Leader, Researcher, Learner, and Contributor
description: The study's final theory of ontological innovation is a framework of six standards covering the three faculty workload areas of teaching, research, and service.
