title: Six-process framework for keeping GenAI policies and guidelines current and relevant
description: A framework of six standalone, non-sequenced processes identified through grounded coding of Delphi responses to ensure GenAI policies and guidelines remain current: creating a dedicated GenAI Committee, conducting regularly scheduled policy reviews, providing ongoing professional development and support, communicating with all stakeholders, evaluating the effectiveness and impact of GenAI, and monitoring external developments. As the article states, the panel coding "identified six key processes to ensure that GenAI policies and guidelines remain current and relevant in HE settings." The six are standalone processes rather than a sequence of action, and Table 2 operationalizes each with concrete actions such as investing in research partnerships and monitoring changes in laws, data privacy standards, and industry standards.

constraints: The order of the six processes does not connote a sequence of action or importance; each is a standalone process

higher education faculty
higher education students

title: Design GenAI policies for equitable access to prevent exacerbating digital divides
description: The panel voiced concern that without deliberate action GenAI could exacerbate digital divides or create new inequities. As one panelist warned, "the digital divide remains a problematic issue and GenAI policies that do not explicitly address access risk furthering the divide along class and other socio-economic lines." The principle calls for institutions to provide access to approved GenAI platforms through campus licenses or shared platforms, avoid assignments requiring paid tools, accommodate students lacking off-campus connectivity, and conduct equity audits of GenAI technologies before adoption to evaluate fairness and accessibility.

constraints: Panelists noted that access without the knowledge and skills to use GenAI can negatively impact students as much as not having the technologies

target_learning_goals: equitable participation in GenAI-enhanced learning

title: Use GenAI to support, not replace, human learning and critical thinking through proactive integration strategy
description: The panel strongly advocated proactive strategic integration of GenAI into teaching and learning, guided by the central principle that "GenAI should be used to "support, not replace" human learning and critical thinking." This means designing curricula and assessments that leverage GenAI to enhance learning while assessing higher-order skills so that simply copying GenAI's answer would not fulfill the task. Panelists advocated in-class, oral, or application-based assessments and process-focused assignments requiring students to document their thinking and GenAI use, while keeping curricula aligned with GenAI-adoption realities in workplaces.
requirements: Curricula and assignments redesigned to test deeper learning and critical thinking, reducing over-reliance on GenAI-generated responses
constraints: Panelists warned against outright bans, favoring proactive integration over prohibition

higher education faculty
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
preparation for a GenAI-enriched workforce
examples: Panelists recommended guidelines that educate students on using GenAI as a support tool for critical thinking and creativity rather than as a shortcut to completing work

article_title: Learning-by-Teaching with ChatGPT: The Effect of a Teachable ChatGPT Agent on Programming Education
citation: Angxuan Chen, Yuang Wei, Huixiao Le, Yan Zhang. (2024). Learning-by-Teaching with ChatGPT: The Effect of Teachable ChatGPT Agent on Programming Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15226
title: Prompt-based teachable ChatGPT agent structured by a five-stage help-seeking model
description: The teachable ChatGPT agent is a prompt-based configuration of gpt-4 that role-plays a help-seeking student learning the eight queens puzzle. The authors "employed a prompt-based design approach that could modify the role of ChatGPT", structuring its responses around Gall's five-stage help-seeking process model, and deliberately "used the original ChatGPT without other augmented techniques" so that its mistakes resemble a beginner and create opportunities for students to teach.
requirements: Learners first watch instructional videos covering the backtracking algorithm and the puzzle
An online judging platform that automatically evaluates whether the generated code solves the puzzle
Learners take an explicit teaching role, guiding the agent only in natural language
constraints: Accuracy of the agent's generated code was not controlled; the authors note ChatGPT may hallucinate wrong content without control
target_learners: university students with a computer-science background and self-reported fundamental C++ coding ability
target_learning_goals: knowledge of the backtracking algorithm and the eight queens puzzle
C++ programming skill for solving the eight queens puzzle
examples: Experimental-group participants helped the agent form correct code within a one-hour supervised session, sharing screens to prevent searching for solutions online
key_sources: Angxuan Chen, Yuang Wei, Huixiao Le, Yan Zhang. (2024). Learning-by-Teaching with ChatGPT: The Effect of Teachable ChatGPT Agent on Programming Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15226

article_title: Learning-by-Teaching with ChatGPT: The Effect of a Teachable ChatGPT Agent on Programming Education
citation: Angxuan Chen, Yuang Wei, Huixiao Le, Yan Zhang. (2024). Learning-by-Teaching with ChatGPT: The Effect of Teachable ChatGPT Agent on Programming Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15226
title: Use natural-language teaching tasks with ChatGPT agents to promote deeper cognitive processing in learning-by-teaching
description: Because teaching an agent through free natural-language dialogue produced knowledge and SRL gains, the article recommends that "educators create tasks requiring students to teach or explain concepts to ChatGPT agents using natural language to promote deeper cognitive processes". Natural dialogue stands in for the human peer that traditional learning-by-teaching requires and avoids the button-clicking and blank-filling interactions of earlier teachable agents.
requirements: A ChatGPT-based teachable agent that accepts free natural-language explanation rather than predefined response options
constraints: Supported so far only in programming education with university students in a short-term task
target_learners: university students learning programming
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of algorithms
deeper explanation and reorganization of knowledge through teaching
examples: Experimental-group participants were required to guide the ChatGPT agent using only natural language, explaining the backtracking algorithm and instructing the agent to follow their reasoning

article_title: CoTAL: Human-in-the-Loop Prompt Engineering for Generalizable Formative Assessment Scoring and Feedback
citation: Cohn, C., Ashwin T S, Mohammed, N., & Biswas, G. (2026). CoTAL: Human-in-the-Loop Prompt Engineering for Generalizable Formative Assessment Scoring and Feedback. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02323
title: CoTAL: a three-phase framework unifying Evidence-Centered Design, human-in-the-loop prompt engineering, chain-of-thought prompting, and active learning for formative assessment scoring
description: CoTAL is an LLM-based approach to formative assessment scoring defined as an approach "that(1)leveragesEvidence-CenteredDesign(ECD)toalignassessments andrubrics with curriculum goals, (2) applieshuman-in-the-loopprompt engineering to automate responsescoring,and(3)incorporateschain-of-thought(CoT)promptingandteacherandstudent feedback to iteratively refine questions, rubrics, and LLM prompts." Phase I is human-driven assessment and rubric development; Phase II co-develops and optimizes prompts via response scoring with inter-rater reliability, prompt development with few-shot CoT exemplars, and active learning against a validation set; Phase III deploys the refined prompt in classrooms and uses teacher and student critique to refine questions, rubrics, and prompts.
requirements: Human consensus scoring with Cohen's κ reaching at least 0.70 before prompt development, with disagreement 'sticking points' documented and used as few-shot exemplars
Few-shot examples balanced across subscores, including at least one positive and one negative instance per subscore (multi-label) or one instance per score (multi-class)
constraints: The authors found the LLM tended to overfit when few-shot instances were numerous or CoT chains too granular, so they insert only a single instance during active learning
Token limitations in GPT-4's context window prohibited active learning in the Debugging Task
target_learners: K-12 STEM+C students (sixth-grade, ages 11-12 in the study)
target_learning_goals: Formative assessment of cross-domain science, computing, and engineering understanding, including conservation of matter, computational modeling, and fair-test engineering reasoning
examples: Teachers and researchers applied ECD to develop the SPICE curriculum's Rules, Debugging, and Engineering formative assessments; prompt patterns used included persona, context manager, template, and meta language creation patterns.
key_sources: Cohn, C., Ashwin T S, Mohammed, N., & Biswas, G. (2026). CoTAL: Human-in-the-Loop Prompt Engineering for Generalizable Formative Assessment Scoring and Feedback. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02323

article_title: CoTAL: Human-in-the-Loop Prompt Engineering for Generalizable Formative Assessment Scoring and Feedback
citation: Cohn, C., Ashwin T S, Mohammed, N., & Biswas, G. (2026). CoTAL: Human-in-the-Loop Prompt Engineering for Generalizable Formative Assessment Scoring and Feedback. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02323
title: SPICE curriculum formative assessments: Rules Task, Debugging Task, and Engineering Task with cross-domain rubrics
description: SPICE (Science Projects Integrating Computing and Engineering) is "a three-week middle school curriculum unit in which students redesign a schoolyard using surface materials that minimize post-rainstorm runoff while satisfyingdesignconstraints(e.g.,cost,accessibility)." Within it, three formative assessments were scored by CoTAL: a Rules Task with a nine-subscore categorical rubric expressing rainfall-absorption-runoff conditionals, a Debugging Task with five subscores for identifying errors in a fictional classmate's block-based code, and an Engineering Task scored 0-4 on recognizing unfair design comparisons due to differing rainfall inputs. Rubrics explicitly tag science (SCI), computing (COM), and engineering (ENG) domains.
requirements: Assessments and rubrics developed through ECD-aligned participatory design between teachers and researchers, targeting NGSS performance expectations
constraints: The Engineering Task rubric is a single 0-4 multi-class score, unlike the multi-label subscore rubrics of the other two tasks
target_learners: Upper elementary and middle school students in Earth science and engineering design
target_learning_goals: Cross-domain conceptual knowledge connecting science, computing, and engineering, including conservation of matter, conditional logic, debugging computational models, and fair tests
examples: In the Rules Task, a response stating 'if rainfall is equal to the absorption limit, then set absorption to rainfall, and set runoff to zero' earns 3 points (R4, R5, R6).

article_title: AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education
citation: Jarosław A. Chudziak and Adam Kostka. (2025). AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12484
title: Multi-agent AI tutoring architecture with an orchestrating Tutor Agent and specialist agents
description: The article proposes a multi-agent architecture implemented on LangGraph in which a central Tutor Agent (GPT-4o) interprets student input and orchestrates other components via a ReAct-style framework. A Memory Dispatcher oversees conversations and controls memory modules, while a pipeline of agents (Research, Planning, Step Handling, Coding) builds courses, and auxiliary tools include a Symbolic Solver, Function Plotter, and Course Graph Drawer. The design prioritizes "deep understanding and independent problem-solving over direct answers" through guided, tool-assisted learning.
requirements: Underlying LLM capabilities: the article states system performance remains fundamentally dependent on underlying LLM capabilities and possible biases
constraints: Personalization currently operates on a basic set of attributes
Pedagogical effectiveness of generated courses is yet to be evaluated empirically
target_learners: students learning mathematics, including exam-preparation students
target_learning_goals: deep conceptual understanding of mathematics topics
independent problem-solving
exam revision and targeted practice
examples: The Tutor Agent uses Socratic questioning instead of solving an equation immediately, dynamically adjusting support based on progress tracked in memory
key_sources: Jarosław A. Chudziak and Adam Kostka. (2025). AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12484

citation: Jarosław A. Chudziak and Adam Kostka. (2025). AI-Powered Math Tutoring: Platform for Personalized and Adaptive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.12484
title: Dual-memory personalization framework (long-term memory and working memory)
description: The platform personalizes tutoring through a dual-memory framework: long-term memory (LTM) stores persistent, student-specific data such as prior knowledge, misconceptions, learning preferences, and goals, while working memory (WM) maintains the context of the current learning session, including topic, problem state, and recent interactions. These modules inform the Tutor Agent and content generation components, enabling proactive support such as targeted hints when a known misconception like difficulty with negative sign distribution occurs, or function plotting for students who prefer visual explanations.
requirements: A Memory Dispatcher to oversee conversations and control the appropriate memory modules
constraints: Current personalization operates on a basic set of attributes, per the authors' stated limitation
target_learners: mathematics students with varying prior knowledge and learning paces
target_learning_goals: individualized tutoring responsive to student misconceptions and preferences
examples: If LTM knows a student usually has difficulty understanding negative sign distribution, the system proactively offers targeted hints or corrective feedback

title: GraphRAG textbook knowledge retrieval for grounded tutoring
description: The system implements Retrieval-Augmented Generation via the GraphRAG framework, in which textbook material is represented as a knowledge graph to provide contextually relevant information to the Tutor Agent and course-generation pipeline. The authors chose GraphRAG over normal vector RAG on the argument that its graph structure better represents educational content relations for contextual tutoring. The Tutor Agent retrieves textbook data to ground its responses, and the course pipeline accesses GraphRAG data when constructing structured learning plans.
requirements: Textbook material represented as a knowledge graph to provide structured educational content
constraints: The article notes future work will explore the potential of different RAG architectures
target_learners: mathematics students using the tutoring platform
target_learning_goals: grounding tutor responses and generated courses in course textbook content
examples: The Tutor Agent retrieves textbook data to ground its responses during guided tutoring interactions

title: DAG-based course generation for structured learning and exam revision
description: The Course component generates an individual Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of relevant topics for structured learning such as exam preparation. The DAG shows prerequisite knowledge, suggests optimal learning paths based on textbook knowledge and dependency analysis, and enables students to monitor their learning progress. A pipeline of agents (Research, Planning, Step Handling, Coding) accesses memory and GraphRAG data to construct the structured DAG, which is stored in a database.
requirements: Access to memory modules and GraphRAG data; a pipeline of Research, Planning, Step Handling, and Coding agents; database storage
constraints: The pedagogical effectiveness of courses generated through GraphRAG for students is yet to be evaluated empirically
target_learners: students preparing for examinations
target_learning_goals: structured revision paths respecting prerequisite dependencies
progress monitoring during exam preparation
examples: A student preparing for an examination may request a revision course, and the system automatically arranges a structured plan individualized to their specific needs

article_title: The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents
citation: Kirk Vanacore, Ryan S. Baker, Avery H. Closser, and Jeremy Roschelle. (2026). The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19303
title: Keep, Change, Center, Study framework for designing conversational AI tutors
description: A four-part design framework for conversational AI tutoring systems. It directs designers to keep evidence-based legacy ITS features (knowledge tracing, behavior and affect detection, knowledge graphs), change delivery by leveraging generative AI for automatic content generation and dialogic feedback, center opportunities unique to conversational tutoring (meaning-making, student agency, diagnosis of reasoning), and study open research questions (efficacy testing, student experience, human-AI collaboration). The article presents it as a research agenda for building tutors that are "scalable, pedagogically effective, and responsive to the social and motivational dimensions of learning".
requirements: Design must integrate legacy ITS learner-model technologies with generative AI rather than replacing them
constraints: The article states there is little evidence that generative AI alone can match the multifaceted nature of high-quality tutoring
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students using conversational AI tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Conceptual learning supported by dialogue-based tutoring, including motivation and self-regulation
examples: Table 1 summarizes the four categories with examples such as knowledge tracing for Keep and automatic content generation for Change
key_sources: Kirk Vanacore, Ryan S. Baker, Avery H. Closser, and Jeremy Roschelle. (2026). The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19303

article_title: The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents
citation: Kirk Vanacore, Ryan S. Baker, Avery H. Closser, and Jeremy Roschelle. (2026). The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19303
title: Inner–outer loop architecture as a legacy ITS design pattern to retain in conversational AI tutors
description: A defining conceptual advance of the legacy ITS era: a dual structure in which the inner loop manages step-level interactions within a single problem (error detection, correctness feedback, graduated hints at impasses) while the outer loop selects which problems to give next, guided by knowledge tracing models and curricular sequencing rules. The article argues this separation "remains one of the most influential design patterns in the ITS tradition" and proposes that in generative AI conversational tutors this architecture could constrain the tutoring session to appropriate content within and between problems.
requirements: The outer loop must be guided by knowledge tracing models and curricular sequencing rules to select appropriate problems
constraints: Legacy ITS were often domain-specific and highly structured, which the article names as a characteristic of the era
target_learners: Students using adaptive tutoring systems in domains such as mathematics and physics
target_learning_goals: Adaptive practice with appropriate problem sequencing and step-level feedback
examples: Systems like Cognitive Tutor, ANDES, and ALEKS provided finely tuned adaptivity both within and across problems using this dual structure

article_title: CODE-GEN: A Human-in-the-Loop RAG-Based Agentic AI System for Multiple-Choice Question Generation
citation: Xiaojing Duan, Frederick Nwanganga, and Chaoli Wang. (2026). CODE-GEN: A Human-in-the-Loop RAG-Based Agentic AI System for Multiple-Choice Question Generation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.03926
title: CODE-GEN dual-agent architecture separating generation from validation
description: CODE-GEN is a human-in-the-loop agentic AI system integrating retrieval-augmented generation with a dual-agent architecture: a Generator agent produces multiple-choice coding comprehension questions grounded in retrieved course context, and a Validator agent independently assesses each question across seven pedagogical dimensions. Both agents are augmented with an Arithmetic Expression Evaluator and a Sandboxed Python Runner. The article states the separation "allows the system to decouple the creative task of question generation from the analytical task of quality evaluation" and treats automated validation as an empirical object of study rather than an assumed capability.

citation: Wei Zhang, Yihang Cheng, Zhirong Ye & Kezhen Huang. (2026). CogEvolution: A Human-like Generative Educational Agent to Simulate Student's Cognitive Evolution. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14786v1
title: CogMath-948 dataset of eighth-grade math interactions with cognitive state annotations
description: CogMath-948 is a dataset the authors constructed from real educational scenarios because suitable open datasets were lacking for fine-grained cognitive evolution research. It "covers real learning data from 1,245 eighth-grade students over six months", with four dimensions per interaction: question and response information, reflective explanations of reasoning or error causes, ICAP-based cognitive engagement labels, and fine-grained misconception classifications for incorrect answers. It serves as the evaluation corpus for all CogEvolution comparisons and ablations.

article_title: CogEvolution: A Human-like Generative Educational Agent to Simulate Student's Cognitive Evolution
citation: Wei Zhang, Yihang Cheng, Zhirong Ye & Kezhen Huang. (2026). CogEvolution: A Human-like Generative Educational Agent to Simulate Student's Cognitive Evolution. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14786v1
title: CogEvolution framework: ICAP perception, IRT-based memory retrieval, and evolutionary cognitive state update
description: CogEvolution is a generative educational agent architecture that shifts from static personas to dynamic cognitive flow. It "consists of three highly coupled components": a Cognitive Adapter for depth perception mapping interaction features to a probability distribution over the four ICAP levels; an IRT-Driven Memory Retrieval Module that scores hybrid semantic and structural (item-characteristic-curve) similarity to decide whether to reuse an old schema or trigger confusion and exploration; and an Evolutionary Cognitive State Update Mechanism using a mutation-selection-update cycle in which LLM-generated cognitive hypotheses are fitness-evaluated under a ZPD constraint and integrated with a step size set by the ICAP-based cognitive evolution rate. The update magnitude depends on cognitive engagement depth: passive participation yields minor mutations while constructive participation allows significant structural restructuring.
requirements: Perceived cognitive conflict (input not fully explained by the current knowledge structure) to trigger mutation
A ZPD-formalized search radius constraining hypothesis fitness, penalizing excessive leaps or stagnation
A memory bank of interaction quadruples and a structural-similarity threshold for schema reuse
constraints: Evaluated on eighth-grade mathematics practice data (CogMath-948); the article's claims are about simulated student cognitive evolution in that setting
target_learners: simulated eighth-grade math students
novice teachers via student simulation
target_learning_goals: modeling knowledge internalization, transfer, and cognitive state transitions during practice
examples: The agent outputs behavioral decisions, mastery confidence probabilities for AUC/RMSE evaluation, and an alignment check marking low-confidence steps when the semantic alignment coefficient falls below the threshold

article_title: Confidence Estimation in Automatic Short Answer Grading with LLMs
citation: Longwei Cong, Sonja Hahn, Sebastian Gombert, Leon Camus, Hendrik Drachsler, and Ulf Kroehne. (2026). Confidence Estimation in Automatic Short Answer Grading with LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.00200
title: Hybrid confidence framework integrating model-based confidence with dataset-derived aleatoric uncertainty via semantic heterogeneity
description: The framework treats LLM grading unreliability as arising from two sources: epistemic uncertainty, estimated from model-based signals (verbalized, latent, and consistency-based confidence), and aleatoric uncertainty, estimated from the dataset. Aleatoric uncertainty is operationalized by embedding student responses with a sentence-transformer model, clustering them with Ward linkage, and computing normalized Shannon entropy of label distributions within each cluster as a heterogeneity proxy. The signals are fused by a Random Forest classifier with Platt scaling into a calibrated hybrid confidence score. The article states it proposes "a hybrid confidence framework that integrates model-based confidence signals with an explicit estimate of dataset-derived aleatoric uncertainty."
requirements: A calibration subset of labeled student responses to estimate cluster label distributions and learn the classifier's calibration mapping
Human-annotated correctness labels for training the fusion classifier
constraints: Evaluated on a binary correct/incorrect scoring setting with one open-weight model (gpt-oss-20b) and one dataset; the authors state generalizability across models, domains, and annotation schemes remains to be assessed
target_learners: students whose short constructed responses are automatically graded in science assessment
target_learning_goals: accurate and reliable automated scoring of short constructed-response answers to support human-in-the-loop assessment
examples: On the SciEntsBank Test_UD split, responses were embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, clustered with agglomerative hierarchical clustering, and cluster entropies assigned to test responses via nearest centroid

citation: Zixin Chen, Peng Liu, Rui Sheng, Haobo Li, Jianhong Tu, Xiaodong Deng, Kashun Shum, Dayiheng Liu, Huamin Qu. (2026). Are Agents Ready to Teach? A Multi-Stage Benchmark for Real-World Teaching Workflows. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14322
title: Teaching-system episode framework: knowing–teaching–acting across three capability surfaces
description: The article proposes that tutor-agent readiness requires three separable capability surfaces: Stage 1 pedagogical judgment (a bounded teacher decision from packaged evidence), Stage 2 situated tutoring (a history-dependent adaptive teaching policy over a multi-turn episode), and Stage 3 end-to-end LMS workflow execution (institutional action). It argues these "separate knowing what a teacher should do, teaching through an evolving interaction, and acting without losing the educational rationale across an institutional workflow." The framework defines an auditable teaching-system episode in which evidence supports a decision, the decision guides interaction or execution, and the learner or course consequence is observable, spanning six teacher-work capabilities: diagnosing, designing, creating, teaching, communicating, and evaluating.

constraints: The three stages are complementary diagnostic surfaces rather than an ordered difficulty scale

target_learning_goals: pedagogical judgment
adaptive multi-turn tutoring
end-to-end LMS teaching-workflow execution

title: TEACHARENA benchmark: 354 audited source-grounded tasks with matched verifiers
description: TEACHARENA is a source-grounded benchmark of "354 audited tasks" spanning three stages and six teacher-work capabilities (diagnosing, designing, creating, teaching, communicating, evaluating). Tasks are built through a pedagogical-insight-driven pipeline: each specifies a target instructional insight, grounds it in transformed educational material, published pedagogy, or deterministic course state, and pairs it with a matched verifier over turn-level responses, tutoring trajectories, or persistent artifacts and environment states. Stage 1 has 117 tasks, Stage 2 has 100 tasks across 13 disciplines with six controlled learner profiles, and Stage 3 has 137 tasks in a deterministic synthetic Canvas-style LMS linking 126 learners, 432 course enrollments, 222 assignment records, 1,058 quiz attempts, and 13 editable presentations. Code and data are available on Hugging Face.

constraints: Stage 2 uses simulated learners and Stage 3 a deterministic synthetic LMS; coverage remains weighted toward STEM

target_learning_goals: evaluating tutor agents on pedagogical judgment, adaptive tutoring, and institutional workflow execution

title: Four hypothesized phases of student perception of intelligence: Hype, Distrust, Trust, and Dependency
description: The article proposes four conceptual lenses for organizing how students' valuation of human versus artificial intelligence shifts as experience with AI deepens: Hype (HI < AI), Distrust (HI > AI), Trust (HI ~ AI), and Dependency (HI >> AI). The phases are explicitly "not proposed as universal or sequential psychological stages, but as conceptual lenses for organizing these shifts, which may overlap or reoccur." In the Trust phase AI serves as a cognitive scaffold while responsibility for evaluation remains with the learner; in Dependency, generation and organization are partially externalized to the system.

title: Human-AI common ground through shared analytics artifacts
description: CLARA is designed around the idea that learners, educators, and AI should reason over the same representations rather than following a generate-and-consume pattern. The article states that "the artifacts sit between the user and the AI, which are visible to both, queryable by both, and interpretable by both", so an educator can point to a concept-map node and the agent can cite a relationship from the same map. This is common ground in a practical sense of shared analytical objects, not full mutual knowledge verified through grounding acts. The framework suggests AI systems should generate representations that become shared working material supporting ongoing inquiry from both sides.
requirements: Artifacts must be visible to, queryable by, and interpretable by both the user and the AI agent
constraints: The article distinguishes this from common ground in the full sense of mutual knowledge verified through grounding acts
target_learners: Learners and educators engaging in collaborative group work
target_learning_goals: Collaboration literacy: interpreting and reflecting on how a group collaborates
examples: In CLARA, a learner or educator viewing a concept map and asking the agent a question works from the same shared reference as the agent, which cites relationships from the same map in its responses
key_sources: Dawei Xie, Khalil Anderson, Tochukwu Eze, Chenghong Lin, Bookyung Shin, and Marcelo Worsley. (2026). CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17259

article_title: CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy
citation: Dawei Xie, Khalil Anderson, Tochukwu Eze, Chenghong Lin, Bookyung Shin, and Marcelo Worsley. (2026). CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17259
title: CLARA agentic analytics system
description: CLARA (Collaboration Literacy through Artifact Reasoning and Augmentation) is an agentic analytics system that transcribes discussions in real time, computes psycholinguistic metrics, and uses GPT-4.1 to generate concept maps and 7C collaboration assessments from transcripts. Artifacts are embedded with text-embedding-3-large and indexed into distinct ChromaDB collections, and a ReAct agent built with LangGraph and GPT-4.1-mini iteratively calls six tools (including search_sessions, get_concept_map, get_assessment, get_speaker_profile) to synthesize responses traceable to stored artifacts. Users can explore artifacts on a dashboard and constrain which artifact types the agent may consult.
requirements: Speech-to-text transcription with speaker attribution; artifacts indexed into separate vector database collections per artifact type
constraints: The collaboration assessment comparison relied on 10 discussions analyzed by human experts, which the authors state is not sufficient for strong generalizations
target_learners: Learners and educators in collaborative group-work settings, from workshops with child participants to college classroom discussions
target_learning_goals: Developing and assessing collaboration literacy
examples: The system was evaluated on a dataset of 12 sessions containing 35 discussions spanning technical debugging, policy analysis, generative AI, and exploratory science conversations
key_sources: Dawei Xie, Khalil Anderson, Tochukwu Eze, Chenghong Lin, Bookyung Shin, and Marcelo Worsley. (2026). CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17259

article_title: CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy
citation: Dawei Xie, Khalil Anderson, Tochukwu Eze, Chenghong Lin, Bookyung Shin, and Marcelo Worsley. (2026). CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17259
title: LLM-generated artifacts serving dual roles as user-facing scaffolds and indexed retrieval infrastructure
description: A design pattern in which a first LLM pass produces structured analytical representations (concept maps, collaboration assessments) that are simultaneously visualized for human interpretation and indexed as the knowledge base a second agentic pass retrieves and reasons over. The article states that "the system is creating its own retrieval infrastructure: the artifacts generated in the first pass become the indexed knowledge that supports reasoning in the second pass". The artifacts offload identifying what matters and distilling it into analytical structures, letting the agent focus on synthesis and interpretation.
requirements: Artifacts must fall within the embedding model's context window (8,192 tokens, so no chunking was needed) and be indexed in collections separated by artifact type
constraints: Whether more open-ended or less formalized representations would provide the same retrieval advantage is stated to be an open question
target_learners: Learners and educators using AI-augmented analytics dashboards
target_learning_goals: Making collaboration visible and discussable; supporting grounded AI reasoning about group work
examples: CLARA indexes each artifact as a single document in its own ChromaDB collection, letting users restrict which representations the agent consults
key_sources: Dawei Xie, Khalil Anderson, Tochukwu Eze, Chenghong Lin, Bookyung Shin, and Marcelo Worsley. (2026). CLARA: An AI-Augmented Analytics Dashboard for Collaboration Literacy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17259

article_title: The Hidden Cost of Contextual Sycophancy: an AI Literacy Intervention in Human-AI Collaboration
citation: Cansu Koyuturk, Sabrina Guidotti, and Dimitri Ognibene. (2026). The Hidden Cost of Contextual Sycophancy: an AI Literacy Intervention in Human–AI Collaboration. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18372
title: Sycophantic dependence: a collaboration pattern in which users' initial errors shape AI feedback that reinforces those errors in final decisions
description: The article names sycophantic dependence as "a collaboration pattern in which users' initial errors shape AI feedback, which in turn reinforces those same errors in users' final decisions". It is grounded in a sociocultural perspective on learning as interaction with a more knowledgeable other: when model responses stop challenging or extending the learner's reasoning, the AI functions not as a better-informed partner but as a feedback mechanism reproducing the learner's misconceptions. The construct organizes the study's measures of user-to-AI dependence, error carryover, and final decision quality.
requirements: Multi-turn human–AI interaction in which the user produces an initial response before receiving AI feedback, as in the study's initial-ranking-then-collaborate-then-revise task structure
constraints: The article notes some apparent sycophantic behavior may stem from general generative biases — repetition of salient context elements shifting the token distribution — rather than explicit agreement or pleasing intent
target_learners: Higher education students and other less knowledgeable users of LLMs in learning and decision-making contexts
target_learning_goals: Analytical reasoning and decision-making under uncertainty; critical engagement with AI feedback
examples: In the experiment, participants' initial rankings contained an average of 2.21 non-gold items, and carryover of these errors significantly reduced both advice quality and final performance
key_sources: Cansu Koyuturk, Sabrina Guidotti, and Dimitri Ognibene. (2026). The Hidden Cost of Contextual Sycophancy: an AI Literacy Intervention in Human–AI Collaboration. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18372

article_title: Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst
citation: Singh, M., Mansi, G., & Riedl, M. O. (2025). Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst. Georgia Institute of Technology. https://www.gatech.edu/
title: Concept Catalyst: an LLM-assisted, teacher-facing tool for generating scaffolding questions for engineering design challenges
description: Concept Catalyst is a web-based tool that assists teachers in analyzing a design challenge and creating scaffolding questions. It uses LLMs to summarize and decompose an engineering design challenge into concepts, lets teachers visually manipulate and link related concepts, and proposes scaffolding questions the teacher can modify or accept. The tool is entirely teacher-facing; students do not interact with the system and only receive printed scaffold questions.
requirements: Teachers supply a paragraph summary of the design challenge or upload a unit map, then highlight key concepts and organize them in a concept graph before question generation
constraints: The article acknowledges that usage of this tool might still face structural issues, like access of AI-supported tools being disproportionate between different socio-economic classes
target_learners: K-12 engineering teachers
target_learning_goals: Supporting students' engagement with the Engineering Design Process through scaffolding questions
examples: Teachers highlight words or phrases in an approved summary to generate concept-buttons, move them into a Concepts Graph, connect them with lines, and attach concepts to question groups that each generate five questions
key_sources: Singh, M., Mansi, G., & Riedl, M. O. (2025). Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst. Georgia Institute of Technology. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20511

article_title: Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst
citation: Singh, M., Mansi, G., & Riedl, M. O. (2025). Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst. Georgia Institute of Technology. https://www.gatech.edu/
title: Three-stage Summarize-Conceptualize-Synthesize workflow for AI-assisted scaffold creation
description: Concept Catalyst organizes scaffold creation into three stages: (1) Summarize, in which the teacher inputs or uploads a challenge summary; (2) Conceptualize, in which the teacher highlights key concepts and visually connects them; and (3) Synthesize, in which scaffolding questions are generated from concept groups. The stages are not linear, allowing an iterative flow that supports teacher reflection as visualization of concepts gradually adds clarity.
requirements: A teacher-approved summary and a teacher-built concept graph must exist before question generation in the Synthesize step
constraints: The workflow is designed for engineering design challenges and the Engineering Design Process, not for general lesson planning
target_learners: K-12 engineering teachers
target_learning_goals: Creating hard scaffolding questions aligned to the stages of the Engineering Design Process
examples: In the Synthesize step the teacher attaches any number of concepts to a question group, clicks Generate questions, and receives five questions addressing the attached concepts
key_sources: Singh, M., Mansi, G., & Riedl, M. O. (2025). Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst. Georgia Institute of Technology. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20511

article_title: Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst
citation: Singh, M., Mansi, G., & Riedl, M. O. (2025). Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst. Georgia Institute of Technology. https://www.gatech.edu/
title: Keep the teacher in control of AI-generated scaffolds to preserve teacher agency
description: The article argues that LLM-based tools should support rather than replace teachers by keeping decision-making with the teacher and using the LLM only as a generator of suggestions. Concept Catalyst avoids the opacity of LLM-based decision making by keeping the decision making task entirely with the teacher: at every point the teacher can accept, reject, or modify any artifact the tool creates, preserving teacher agency while leveraging generative AI.
requirements: The interface must let teachers review, edit, accept, or reject every AI-generated artifact, including summaries, concepts, and questions
constraints: The article notes LLMs may not be reliable enough in a fully automated capacity, so oversight by teachers is required
target_learners: K-12 engineering teachers
target_learning_goals: Maintaining teacher agency and pedagogical judgment when using generative AI for lesson preparation
examples: Generated questions enter a question bank only after the teacher accepts or modifies them, and the final approved questions are printed or exported to PDF
key_sources: Singh, M., Mansi, G., & Riedl, M. O. (2025). Creating Learning Scaffolds for Engineering Design Using Concept Catalyst. Georgia Institute of Technology. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20511

article_title: Combating Harms of Generative AI in CS1 with Code Review Interviews and a Flipped Classroom
citation: Peter Fowles, Erik Falor, Sulove Bhattarai, John Edwards, and Seth Poulsen. (2026). Combating Harms of Generative AI in CS1 with Code Review Interviews and a Flipped Classroom. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21374
title: CS1-CR course structure: unrestricted AI use with mandatory oral code review interviews and a flipped classroom
description: CS1-CR is a CS1 course design in which students may freely use generative AI on coding assignments but must complete "an oral, in-person code review (CR) interview session with a TA or instructor within 48 hours after each submission deadline". Rubric scores count for 30% of the assignment grade and code review performance for 70%, with a zero for missing the session. One of three weekly class days was cancelled for interviews, replaced by a flipped classroom with pre-class lecture videos and in-class coding activities. Eleven TAs were trained via mock interviews and structured per-assignment interview protocols.
requirements: Trained TAs with a structured per-assignment interview protocol
Scheduling infrastructure (tutoring center app) and a free weekly class day for interview sessions
constraints: Adds extra student-TA contact time, making truly controlled studies difficult
Scaling beyond about 100 students with the same number of TAs is untested
target_learners: University introductory computer science (CS1) students
target_learning_goals: Understanding and justifying submitted code
Core programming concepts such as Python syntax, logic, tracing, and functions
examples: In Fall 2025, 96 students completed weekly 15-minute code review interviews after each assignment submission with no restrictions on AI tool usage.
key_sources: Peter Fowles, Erik Falor, Sulove Bhattarai, John Edwards, and Seth Poulsen. (2026). Combating Harms of Generative AI in CS1 with Code Review Interviews and a Flipped Classroom. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21374

article_title: Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction
citation: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23177
title: Asymmetric miscalibration account of cognitive offloading to AI (the speedup illusion framework)
description: The article proposes that offloading decisions require calibration — an accurate mental model of one's own and the tool's capabilities — and that for LLMs this calibration is asymmetric: people are "accurate in their prediction of the completion time" for independent work but systematically underestimate AI-assisted time. Grounded in the metacognitive access argument, it holds that people lack privileged access to an LLM's internal workings, and that effort-time conflation sustains the illusion. The framework positions calibration as both a subject and a mechanism for studying AI use.
requirements: Applies to simple cognitive tasks completable under 5 minutes with current LLM assistants; the article notes the complexity level at which AI genuinely saves time is an open question
constraints: Based on between-subjects aggregates with crowdsourced participants; the prediction and completion samples were not completely disjoint
target_learners: US adult Prolific participants completing simple cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: Accurate calibration of when AI assistance saves time versus effort in cognitive offloading decisions
examples: The study operationalized calibration as the gap between predicted and actual completion times across 24 tasks in four categories of LLM use at two difficulty levels.
key_sources: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23177

article_title: Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction
citation: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23177
title: Evaluate AI productivity in terms of both time and subjective cognitive effort, and treat calibration as an intervention point against overreliance
description: Because AI assistance reduces felt effort even when it saves no time, the article argues that "narratives and reports about AI productivity should also consider a more encompassing notion of cognitive offloading that takes into account the subjective experience". It further positions calibration as "a key intervention point to adjust behavioral outcomes such as overreliance", since miscalibration encouraging AI use can form a feedback loop with cognitive deskilling.
requirements: Users and designers need measures capturing both completion time and subjective effort (e.g., NASA-TLX) when judging AI-assisted efficiency
constraints: The feedback-loop risk is described as preliminary evidence; excessive offloading is cautioned to lead to cognitive deskilling and overreliance
target_learners: Adults deciding whether to offload cognitive tasks to LLM assistants
target_learning_goals: Well-calibrated decisions about when to offload cognition to AI, conserving the intended resource
examples: The article recommends future work examine how incentive structures interact with completion times and reported effort, and when people choose to use AI.
key_sources: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). Cognitive offloading and the speedup illusion in human-AI interaction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23177

article_title: Catching The Correct Answer Trap: Characterising AI Tutor Blind Spots When Analysing Student Reasoning
citation: Moiz Imran and Sahan Bulathwela. (2026). Catching TheCorrectAnswerTrap: Characterising AI Tutor Blind Spots When Analysing Student Reasoning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23925
title: The correct answer trap and coincidental correctness paths as an account of AI reasoning-assessment failure
description: The correct answer trap (CAT) is the paper's named failure mode in AI misconception detection: models under-detect misconceptions when students reach a correct answer via flawed reasoning, because "if a model treats correctness as evidence of understanding, systematic under-detection of misconceptions will prevail". The paper explains item-level vulnerability through a "coincidental correctness path", a form of what Kapur calls "unproductive success", where common flawed procedures happen to produce the correct output for the specific values chosen. The account draws on assessment design theory, including Barton's principle that a diagnostic question should not be answerable correctly while a key misconception is held, and the procedural/conceptual knowledge distinction of Hiebert and Lefevre.
requirements: Detection systems must evaluate student reasoning explanations, not only final answers, for the trap to be assessed at all
constraints: Characterised within mathematics education on the Eedi dataset; whether the trap extends systematically to other domains and populations remains an open question per the authors
target_learners: school mathematics students on the Eedi tutoring platform
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis of student misconceptions in mathematics reasoning
examples: Integer subtraction (−8)−(−5), where the flawed rule 'subtract then make negative' yields the correct answer but fails on (−5)−(−8)
key_sources: Moiz Imran and Sahan Bulathwela. (2026). Catching TheCorrectAnswerTrap: Characterising AI Tutor Blind Spots When Analysing Student Reasoning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23925

article_title: Profiling cognitive offloading in LLM-mediated synthesis writing: Volume vs. content
citation: Poquet, O., Nanduri, M. S., Salinas Loyer, M. X., Stadler, M., Sailer, M., Jovanovic, J. (2026). Profiling Cognitive Offloading in LLM-mediated Synthesis Writing: Volume vs. Content. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10434
title: A Salomon-based dynamic interactionist framework for learner-LLM distributed cognitive systems
description: The article adapts Salomon's dynamic interactionist view of distributed cognition to learner-LLM systems, treating them as comprising "three elements of a distributed cognitive system: (1) individual cognition, (2) the activity that affords distribution, and (3) the distribution of the cognitive process between a learner and a tool". Individual cognition is represented by prior knowledge; the affording activity is comprehension, structured by Kintsch and van Dijk's micro- and macro-levels; and distribution is captured by the learner's role (active/passive) at each comprehension level, reflecting Salomon's distinction between shared activity and division of labour.
requirements: The activity affording distribution must be specified; the article treats comprehension as this activity because it underpins many tasks and requires selection, organisation, and generation of information
constraints: Existing theories were not designed for tools with the range and flexibility of offloading that LLMs enable, motivating this bridging perspective
target_learners: university students using LLMs in writing tasks
target_learning_goals: text comprehension and synthesis writing
examples: In the study, learners read two texts with opposing views on predictive modelling in education and wrote a synthesis essay via a custom interface embedding LLM access
key_sources: Poquet, O., Nanduri, M. S., Salinas Loyer, M. X., Stadler, M., Sailer, M., Jovanovic, J. (2026). Profiling Cognitive Offloading in LLM-mediated Synthesis Writing: Volume vs. Content. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10434

article_title: Profiling cognitive offloading in LLM-mediated synthesis writing: Volume vs. content
citation: Poquet, O., Nanduri, M. S., Salinas Loyer, M. X., Stadler, M., Sailer, M., Jovanovic, J. (2026). Profiling Cognitive Offloading in LLM-mediated Synthesis Writing: Volume vs. Content. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10434
title: Coding framework for the content of LLM offloading prompts (active/passive by local/global comprehension)
description: A four-way coding scheme applied to each of 564 learner prompts, capturing whether the learner "remained somewhat active or was passive during a comprehension activity, and if the comprehension within a prompt was targetting local or global level". Active prompts specify learner direction (clarifying gaps, seeking evaluation or structure); passive prompts leave the LLM to act without learner-specified constraints; local refers to micro-level items and global to whole-text or cross-text structure. Reproducibility was checked against three LLM-based labelling agents, reaching an average kappa of 0.64 (passive/global) and 0.61 (local/global).
requirements: An expert-coded prompt corpus and a coding framework with worked examples; automated agent labelling with framework-rule checking for reproducibility
constraints: The framework was not further fine-tuned to avoid overfitting; the article notes other tasks may require other lenses to represent offloading patterns
target_learners: university students using LLMs in synthesis writing
target_learning_goals: characterising comprehension-related cognitive offloading in learner-LLM interaction
examples: Example codings include 'What does the assumption mean in text A?' as active-local and 'Write me a 300-word synthesis' as passive-global
key_sources: Poquet, O., Nanduri, M. S., Salinas Loyer, M. X., Stadler, M., Sailer, M., Jovanovic, J. (2026). Profiling Cognitive Offloading in LLM-mediated Synthesis Writing: Volume vs. Content. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10434

article_title: Profiling cognitive offloading in LLM-mediated synthesis writing: Volume vs. content
citation: Poquet, O., Nanduri, M. S., Salinas Loyer, M. X., Stadler, M., Sailer, M., Jovanovic, J. (2026). Profiling Cognitive Offloading in LLM-mediated Synthesis Writing: Volume vs. Content. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10434
title: Interventions should attend to what learners delegate to LLMs, not just limit the volume of LLM use
description: Because the same volume of LLM use can describe qualitatively different offloading processes, the article argues that "interventions targeting the volume of LLM use, such as limiting the number of prompts, may be insuffi- cient". More targeted approaches attend to whether learners retain active involvement in structuring and evaluating, or hand off entire segments of the comprehension process. Tools making the distribution of cognitive work visible to learners and instructors could support this, though evaluation is still needed.
requirements: Means of characterising prompt content (who performs the activity, at what comprehension level) so that delegation patterns can be distinguished
constraints: The article states more work is needed to evaluate offloading processes and their differentiated effects, and whether fragmentation patterns predict learning outcomes directly and hold across tasks with different cognitive demands
target_learners: university students using general-purpose LLM chatbots for academic writing
target_learning_goals: retaining active comprehension and knowledge construction during LLM-mediated writing
examples: The study showed Strategic and Full Offloading involved similarly high prompting volumes but very different learner engagement, which volume-based profiling did not convey
key_sources: Poquet, O., Nanduri, M. S., Salinas Loyer, M. X., Stadler, M., Sailer, M., Jovanovic, J. (2026). Profiling Cognitive Offloading in LLM-mediated Synthesis Writing: Volume vs. Content. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10434

article_title: Confident yet Concerned: Inconsistencies in Computing Students'' Attitudes on Cybersecurity
citation: Adama, V., Biddle, R., Arachchilage, N., & Lottridge, D. (2026). Confident yet Concerned: Inconsistencies in Computing Students' Attitudes on Cybersecurity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18541
title: Emerging attitude of resignation toward cybersecurity, analogous to digital resignation and privacy cynicism
description: The article proposes, as future work, an attitude of resignation specific to cybersecurity, drawing on Draper and Turow's "digital resignation" and Hoffmann et al.'s "privacy cynicism", defined as "an attitude of uncertainty, powerlessness and mistrust towards the handling of personal data by online services, rendering privacy protection behaviour subjectively futile". Because the study observed interest in cybersecurity alongside a lack of confidence and self-efficacy, the authors suggest resignation may be emerging for security as it has for privacy.
requirements: Future research to test whether a cybersecurity-specific resignation attitude exists, as the authors state this would be important future work
constraints: The article offers this as a speculative suggestion from one survey, not a tested construct
target_learners: computing university students
young tech-savvy adults
target_learning_goals: cybersecurity awareness and protective behaviour
motivation to learn about cybersecurity
examples: The survey found one cluster less prepared, quite unconfident, and very interested in learning more, which the authors link to possible resignation
key_sources: Adama, V., Biddle, R., Arachchilage, N., & Lottridge, D. (2026). Confident yet Concerned: Inconsistencies in Computing Students' Attitudes on Cybersecurity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18541

article_title: Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations
citation: Naaz Sibia, Jessica Wen, Amber Richardson, Yashika Jain, Khushi Malik, Bogdan Simion, Carolina Nobre, Angela Zavaleta Bernuy, Andrew Petersen, and Michael Liut. 2026. Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations. ICER 2026 Vol. 1. https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811662
title: Three-theme account of selective engagement with multi-representational visualization tools: agency, representational fit, and legitimacy
description: An explanatory account of why learners engage with or resist available visual scaffolds, constructed inductively through reflexive thematic analysis of interviews and think-alouds. The article reports that "three themes were constructed that characterized variation across participants": agency (students' relationship to cognitive effort and control), representational fit (individual differences in what felt helpful versus overwhelming), and legitimacy (concerns about what tool use signaled about academic identity). The framework extends MER/DeFT and cognitive load guidance, which the authors say address cognitive design but say little about affective and social dimensions of engagement.
requirements: Interview and think-aloud accounts from learners using multi-representational tools, interpreted through reflexive thematic analysis within an interpretivist epistemology
constraints: Themes were constructed from 19 undergraduates at one large North American research university who had completed CS1 and CS2; the authors take an interpretive stance rather than seeking a best tool
target_learners: undergraduate novice programmers who have completed CS1 and CS2
target_learning_goals: engaging with multi-representational program visualizations to support reasoning about program execution and abstraction
key_sources: Naaz Sibia, Jessica Wen, Amber Richardson, Yashika Jain, Khushi Malik, Bogdan Simion, Carolina Nobre, Angela Zavaleta Bernuy, Andrew Petersen, and Michael Liut. 2026. Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations. ICER 2026 Vol. 1. https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811662

article_title: Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations
citation: Naaz Sibia, Jessica Wen, Amber Richardson, Yashika Jain, Khushi Malik, Bogdan Simion, Carolina Nobre, Angela Zavaleta Bernuy, Andrew Petersen, and Michael Liut. 2026. Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations. ICER 2026 Vol. 1. https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811662
title: Position visualizations as verification instruments students opt into, with toggleable abstraction levels, rather than as automatically imposed explanation guides
description: The article recommends deploying visualization tools so that learners keep control over when supports appear and how dense they are. The authors state that "friction that learners control can feel productive, while friction that tools impose can feel alienating," and that tools supporting student-chosen reveal timing "may better preserve the sense of active construction that students associate with learning." They further recommend "Toggleable abstraction levels, where students can adjust visual density to their current needs," so one tool can serve students who find metaphors essential and those who find them overwhelming.
requirements: Tools must let students choose when to reveal visual supports rather than presenting them automatically, and must offer adjustable visual density
constraints: The authors note this does not mean abandoning scaffolding, but designing scaffolds students can opt into rather than having imposed on them
target_learners: undergraduate novice programmers in CS1/CS2
target_learning_goals: preserving active reasoning and engagement with program visualizations
examples: In the study, students who engaged most successfully used the MR tool's views to verify reasoning they had traced manually, and experienced students selectively engaged metaphor views in linked-list tasks despite publicly framing them as beneath them
key_sources: Naaz Sibia, Jessica Wen, Amber Richardson, Yashika Jain, Khushi Malik, Bogdan Simion, Carolina Nobre, Angela Zavaleta Bernuy, Andrew Petersen, and Michael Liut. 2026. Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations. ICER 2026 Vol. 1. https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811662

article_title: Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations
citation: Naaz Sibia, Jessica Wen, Amber Richardson, Yashika Jain, Khushi Malik, Bogdan Simion, Carolina Nobre, Angela Zavaleta Bernuy, Andrew Petersen, and Michael Liut. 2026. Code as Anchor, Memory and Metaphor as Support: Learner Experiences with Multi-View Visualizations. ICER 2026 Vol. 1. https://doi.org/10.1145/3765964.3811662
title: Multi-representational program visualization tool with synchronized code, memory, and metaphor views
description: A web-based visualization probe designed for the study, drawing on MER/DeFT and concreteness fading. The article states the authors "designed a visualization tool with multiple views that draws on MER/DeFT and concreteness fading to address limitations of existing program visualization tools." Its interface presents three synchronized panes — Code View with the active line highlighted, Memory View aligned with Python Tutor's representation, and Metaphor View using analogy-based depictions (house for scope, magician's table for while loops, relay race for linked lists) — with brushing and linking across views and step controls. It was refined across three formative feedback cycles with instructors, a visualization researcher, and nine teaching assistants.
requirements: Formative refinement for conceptual fidelity, usability, and alignment with common student misconceptions; synchronized execution across views
constraints: The CS2 configuration steps through execution at function level rather than line by line, which participants criticized as undermining the tool's purpose
target_learners: undergraduate students who have completed CS1 and CS2
target_learning_goals: tracing, explaining, and extending code across scope, while loops, and linked lists
examples: All visualization materials are openly available at the authors' GitHub repository, and reproducible gaze analysis code is available on OSF

article_title: Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models
citation: Fang, L., Zhang, Y., Park, J., Wang, Z., Ma, P., Zhai, X. (2026). Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20264
title: Confidence-aware selective automated scoring framework
description: The framework adapts a pretrained ViT with LoRA and derives a response-level confidence score from the stability of predictions under semantic-preserving test-time perturbations (crops, rotations). The article states that "automated scoring systems must decide not only what score to assign, but also whether that score can be trusted." A Top-η test-time selection step retains only the most decisive perturbed views before aggregating the final prediction and confidence. Varying the threshold τ controls the trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk.
requirements: A pretrained ViT backbone adapted via LoRA, M semantic-preserving test-time perturbations per response, and a confidence threshold τ
constraints: Expert-provided scores were the reference, so systematic tendencies in human scoring may be reflected in model performance
Data from middle school classrooms in one region of the United States
target_learners: middle school science students
target_learning_goals: rubric-based proficiency levels (Beginning, Developing, Proficient) on NGSS-aligned scientific modeling tasks
examples: The framework was evaluated on six NGSS-aligned middle school drawing items with K=3 proficiency levels, using M=20 perturbations and η=0.75.
key_sources: Fang, L., Zhang, Y., Park, J., Wang, Z., Ma, P., Zhai, X. (2026). Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20264

Following the annotation protocol, "each drawing is assigned to one of three ordered proficiency levels:Beginning, Developing, orProficient", scored independently by domain experts. title: Automated scores should carry explicit confidence so low-confidence responses are deferred to human review
description: Automated scoring systems should output not only a predicted score but also a confidence value that signals when the score can be trusted. article_title: CourseBlueprint: A Structured Pipeline for Adaptive Pedagogical Video Generation Grounded in Course Corpora
citation: Md Zabirul Islam, Md Motaleb Hossen Manik, and Ge Wang. (2026). CourseBlueprint: A Structured Pipeline for Adaptive Pedagogical Video Generation Grounded in Course Corpora. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20608
title: BMED 2300 benchmark corpus and evaluation harness for course-grounded pedagogical video generation
description: A reusable benchmark artifact built from the BMED 2300 Bio-Imaging course, packaged with "twenty-three lectures, 1,116 slides, aligned transcripts, a multi-repetition LLM-judge rubric, and regex-grounded objective metrics." Chunks are slide-granular, each embedding preserving a one-to-one link between a textual explanation and its slide image, stored in a flat inner-product FAISS index with 3,072-dimensional vectors. The harness pairs repeated LLM-judge rubric scoring (1-5 scale, n=3 reps) with deterministic metrics such as Flesch reading ease and regex counts of analogies and retrieval prompts.
requirements: Slide-granular chunking so each retrieved record links a textual explanation to a specific slide image
A course corpus with transcripts and slide images so the FAISS index can be rebuilt deterministically
constraints: Out-of-corpus topics fall back to placeholder slides and lose the benefit of course-grounded visual reuse
target_learners: undergraduate biomedical engineering students
target_learning_goals: biomedical imaging concepts such as filtered back projection, MRI relaxation, ultrasound transducers, X-ray attenuation, and CT reconstruction artifacts
examples: The corpus was used to evaluate five in-corpus topics with one learner persona, producing ten videos scored by the judge and objective harnesses
key_sources: Md Zabirul Islam, Md Motaleb Hossen Manik, and Ge Wang. (2026). CourseBlueprint: A Structured Pipeline for Adaptive Pedagogical Video Generation Grounded in Course Corpora. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20608

article_title: CourseBlueprint: A Structured Pipeline for Adaptive Pedagogical Video Generation Grounded in Course Corpora
citation: Md Zabirul Islam, Md Motaleb Hossen Manik, and Ge Wang. (2026). CourseBlueprint: A Structured Pipeline for Adaptive Pedagogical Video Generation Grounded in Course Corpora. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20608
title: CourseBlueprint typed pedagogy pipeline with scaffolding, adaptive style, and engagement modules
description: CourseBlueprint is a retrieval-augmented pipeline that converts a topic and learner persona into a course blueprint rendered as an instructional video. It "replaces prompt chaining with typed intermediate representations": a scaffolding module builds a stage-labeled prerequisite concept graph with deterministic cycle removal, an adaptive controller assigns per-concept style specifications across depth, vocabulary, example density, abstraction, and analogy use, and an engagement generator emits narration following a fixed hook-retrieval-core-analogy-forward template. Each module can be disabled via a Boolean flag, enabling ablations by replacing its typed output with a default object.
requirements: A FAISS retrieval index over a course corpus grounds every pedagogy stage
Closed-enumeration schema validation with balanced fallback for out-of-vocabulary values
constraints: The optional verifier was disabled in reported experiments to control cost, so factual correctness is supported by retrieval but not independently verified
target_learners: undergraduate biomedical engineering students
target_learning_goals: prerequisite-aware sequencing of course concepts
learner-adapted explanation depth and vocabulary
sustained cognitive engagement in asynchronous lecture video
examples: In the filtered-back-projection run, the abstraction field changed from concrete for raw measurements to mixed for back-projection and abstract for filtering

citation: Md Zabirul Islam, Md Motaleb Hossen Manik, and Ge Wang. (2026). CourseBlueprint: A Structured Pipeline for Adaptive Pedagogical Video Generation Grounded in Course Corpora. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20608
title: Implement engagement as an explicit typed contract rather than a global instruction to be more engaging
description: The article recommends that engagement moves in generated instruction be enforced as structured output fields rather than requested in prose. Without "a structured output schema, the model may produce fluent narration while omitting the instructional moves that sustain attention and connect concepts." Casting engagement as a typed contract also makes it measurable, since regex counts of analogies and retrieval prompts can be cross-checked against typed fields, and it makes ablations cleaner because a module is disabled by replacing its typed object.
requirements: Typed output schemas with closed enumerations and post-validators for each narration
Post-validation checks on required fields and word count, with regeneration on failure
constraints: Demonstrated in asynchronous generated lecture video grounded in a course corpus; the reported evidence covers only the engagement module ablation on five in-corpus topics with one persona
target_learners: undergraduate biomedical engineering students
target_learning_goals: sustaining attention through hooks, retrieval prompts, analogies, and forward links in instructional narration
examples: The full pipeline's sinogram narration contained a hook, prior-concept callback, analogy, and forward link, while the ablated variant produced a roughly 31-word glossary fragment with none of these moves

article_title: The Correct Answer Trap: Pedagogically-Grounded Detection and Feedback for Hidden Misconceptions
citation: Moiz Imran, Sahan Bulathwela. (2026). The Correct Answer Trap: Pedagogically-Grounded Detection and Feedback for Hidden Misconceptions. PEAF 2026: Workshop on Pedagogical Evaluation of Automated Feedback. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5878-2143
title: Graduated assessment rubric separating answer correctness from method validity
description: The rubric adapts the mathematical assessment distinction between the answer mark (correct output) and the method mark (valid reasoning) to automated diagnosis. For correct-answer cases it distinguishes four categories: clear reasoning, needs clarification, misconception detected, and wrong answer. The paper argues a binary formulation "collapses Options 2 and 3, either falsely accusing students whose explanations are merely brief, or losing the routing signal that distinguishes unclear from flawed reasoning." It grounds the design in Black and Wiliam's formative assessment steps.
requirements: Requires student responses containing a short written explanation alongside the answer, plus a mark scheme describing the expected reasoning method
constraints: Short explanations (average 16 words) can be genuinely ambiguous, so the rubric treats diagnostic ambiguity as a property of the evidence rather than a failure of the model
target_learners: school mathematics students on the Eedi platform
target_learning_goals: detecting hidden mathematical misconceptions in student reasoning
examples: The paper evaluates the rubric with BERT-base, Gemini 3 Flash, and Gemma 4 26B on 3,702 held-out Eedi responses
key_sources: Moiz Imran, Sahan Bulathwela. (2026). The Correct Answer Trap: Pedagogically-Grounded Detection and Feedback for Hidden Misconceptions. PEAF 2026: Workshop on Pedagogical Evaluation of Automated Feedback. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5878-2143

article_title: The Correct Answer Trap: Pedagogically-Grounded Detection and Feedback for Hidden Misconceptions
citation: Moiz Imran, Sahan Bulathwela. (2026). The Correct Answer Trap: Pedagogically-Grounded Detection and Feedback for Hidden Misconceptions. PEAF 2026: Workshop on Pedagogical Evaluation of Automated Feedback. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5878-2143
title: Detect-verify-escalate pipeline with four pedagogically distinct routes
description: The pipeline routes each student submission through an answer-key check and, for correct-answer cases, an LLM graduated assessment producing four routes: Red (wrong answer, automated correction), Green (clear reasoning, no action), Amber-1 (unclear reasoning, automated diagnostic follow-up question), and Amber-2 (misconception detected, verification then teacher escalation). Figure 1 shows approximate volumes per 1,000 submissions: 736 LLM calls and 64 teacher reviews. The design responds to the paper's findings that fine-tuned models cannot assess method validity and that precision is too low for direct teacher escalation.
requirements: Reasoning-capable model, graduated output preserving the routing signal, and intermediate verification before teacher escalation
constraints: All findings come from 15 mathematics questions on one platform, with TM concentrated in 2 items; the diagnostic follow-up proof of concept generated questions for 7 TM instances with no student responses collected
target_learners: school mathematics students and their teachers
target_learning_goals: routing automated feedback according to reasoning validity and diagnostic certainty
examples: Two deployment configurations are proposed: a teacher dashboard mode where the system filters a review queue, and an autonomous tutor mode where each flag triggers a low-cost formative follow-up question

citation: Yao Lyu, Leonymae Aumentado, Holden Winton, Jared Lee Katzman, Sparkle Berry, Zachary Rowe, Kimberly Sanders, and Tawanna R. Dillahunt. 2026. Co-Designing Community-Centered AI Education for Adults: A Midwestern Case Study. CSCW Companion '26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3785651.3831486
title: Co-designing community AI education through four key decisions: balanced topics, conceptual grounding, local relevance, and dialogical learning
description: This pattern describes the recurring design decisions the research team and community partners made when co-creating the AI education session. Balanced topics covered both positive and negative sides of AI; conceptual grounding used "educational materials suitable for a general audience without prior AI expertise"; local relevance drew on community examples such as deepfakes and local landscapes; and dialogical learning treated members as co-producers of AI understanding rather than recipients of expert knowledge.
requirements: Community partner involvement in feedback and revision rounds on session materials
Content accessible at an 8th-grade reading level with technical terms avoided
constraints: The pattern was developed for adults outside formal educational systems in a community setting rather than academic classrooms
target_learners: Adults outside formal educational systems in a local community
target_learning_goals: Building a comprehensive mental map of AI
Understanding core AI concepts such as data, training, and bias
examples: The session adopted the Code.org activity AI for Oceans and an interactive poll on identifying AI fake images versus real images using local landscapes
