article_title: Co-Designing Community-Centered AI Education for Adults: A Midwestern Case Study
citation: Yao Lyu, Leonymae Aumentado, Holden Winton, Jared Lee Katzman, Sparkle Berry, Zachary Rowe, Kimberly Sanders, and Tawanna R. Dillahunt. 2026. Co-Designing Community-Centered AI Education for Adults: A Midwestern Case Study. CSCW Companion '26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3785651.3831486
title: AI literacy as community capacity rather than individual technical competency
description: The article proposes reconceiving AI literacy through the lens of community capacity, defined by prior work it cites as "the collection and interplay among human, organizational, and social resources that enable a community to recognize and address problems". From its analysis, AI literacy was "less about mastering tools or technical mechanisms, but more about developing the capacity to recognize AI in everyday contexts, critically interpret its outputs, articulate concerns and expectations, and make informed decisions". The theory resists generic, top-down framings and holds that community members themselves should hold the power to define what AI means in their lives.
requirements: Frameworks, measures, and interventions explicitly grounded in specific populations rather than technical skill-centric definitions
Evaluation methods that capture critical awareness, sense-making, and decision-making rather than technical mastery alone
constraints: Developed from a single case study of one co-designed session in a predominantly African American community on the east side of a major Midwestern city
target_learners: Adults outside formal educational systems in local communities
target_learning_goals: Recognizing AI in everyday contexts
Critically interpreting AI outputs and articulating concerns and expectations
Making informed decisions about AI
examples: The session surfaced tensions between utility and risk rather than framing AI as inherently beneficial or harmful, aligning with scholarship critiquing techno-solutionist narratives

title: Clover: an instrumented AI code completion tool with attention checks
description: Clover is a Visual Studio Code extension that uses the Gemini 3 Large Language Model to provide real-time, single-line code suggestions at the cursor position. It logs fine-grained interaction events (generation, acceptance, rejection, revision, execution) with timestamps, and deliberately injects attention checks: suggestions "semantically inconsistent with the student's immediate coding goal" whose acceptance or rejection probes critical engagement. It was designed to mirror GitHub Copilot's interface for ecological validity.

Relies on a single AI model, with significant differences in performance and latency based on model selection

target_learning_goals: Critical evaluation of AI-generated code suggestions during programming tasks

title: Taxonomy of interaction behaviors with AI code suggestions
description: The article synthesizes fragmented prior characterizations of AI code completion interactions into a unified taxonomy of behavioral metrics. It organizes events into suggestion generation events (generate attention check, generate suggestion, suggestion shown), acceptance events (tab accept, slow accept), rejection and revision events (accept then modify, accept then delete, ignore), execution events (run code), and derived and aggregated session metrics such as acceptance rate, failed attention check rate, and average dwell time. The taxonomy operationalizes behaviors previously observed only qualitatively, such as slow accept, backtracking, and accept-and-adapt, so they can be captured quantitatively at scale.
requirements: Fine-grained event-level logging of suggestion generation, display, and user actions with timestamps
constraints: Developed and prototyped in a single CS1 course context with one problem type and one AI model; future work could more extensively interrogate sequential behaviors and interaction over time
target_learners: Novice programmers using AI code completion tools
target_learning_goals: Measuring and interpreting critical engagement with AI-generated code suggestions
examples: Applied to session-level Spearman correlation analysis of 55 students' interaction logs during the rainfall problem

title: No single behavioral metric reliably captures critical engagement with AI code suggestions
description: The article concludes that because interaction metrics were weakly or inconsistently correlated with task performance, while some behaviors such as tab acceptance were strongly associated with failed attention checks, educators and researchers should interpret behavioral metrics as a pattern rather than rely on any one measure. The authors state that "no single metric reliably captures critical engagement" and that metrics may reflect a complex mix of reflective reasoning, over-reliance, or negative expertise.

constraints: Dwell time is ambiguous: it may indicate deliberate reasoning, superficial engagement, or negative expertise where experienced students quickly reject low-quality suggestions
Findings come from a single problem, single model, and a single class at one university

target_learning_goals: Assessing critical engagement with AI-generated code
examples: In the 55-student study, number of runs correlated positively with task performance yet also positively with failed attention checks, showing productive behaviors can coexist with lapses in critical engagement

article_title: Concept Catalyst: Exploring Scrutable Interfaces to Structure K-12 Teacher Interactions with Generative AI
citation: Gennie Mansi, Sunni Newton, Roxanne Moore, Meltem Alemdar, Mark Riedl. (2026). Concept Catalyst: Exploring Scrutable Interfaces to Structure K-12 Teacher Interactions with Generative AI. https://ceismc.gatech.edu
title: Scrutable interfaces for generative AI: manipulable knowledge representations that let users shape outputs without understanding the model
description: Scrutable interfaces use a knowledge representation, such as a concept map, to structure users' interactions with an underlying AI model. Critically, scrutable systems "don’t require users to understand how the underlying AI model works to change the AI system output"; instead the representation supports metacognitive self-monitoring, reflection, and planning. This article broadens the concept in two ways: extending scrutable systems from students to teachers as users, and applying them to black-box generative AI models, where the interface lets users "understand, reflect on, and directly edit the inputs to the GPT model to achieve their desired outcomes".
requirements: A knowledge representation (e.g., a concept map) that users can create, edit, and iterate on, which feeds the AI's inputs
An underlying AI model whose outputs change in response to the representation, so users need not understand the model's internals
constraints: Concept Catalyst does not allow teachers to scrutinize the inner workings of the GPT model; scrutability is limited to editing inputs
Prior scrutable systems targeted students, not teachers, so this extension is exploratory
target_learners: K-12 engineering teachers
target_learning_goals: Reflective practice in curriculum and scaffold design
Effective structuring of generative AI interactions
examples: Concept Catalyst links a teacher-built concept map to a pre-written ChatGPT prompt template; as teachers reflect and edit the map, they alter the selected concepts and thereby the generated scaffolds
key_sources: Gennie Mansi, Sunni Newton, Roxanne Moore, Meltem Alemdar, Mark Riedl. (2026). Concept Catalyst: Exploring Scrutable Interfaces to Structure K-12 Teacher Interactions with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30590

title: Concept Catalyst: a generative AI co-writing tool with a scrutable concept-map interface for engineering teachers

Teachers highlight concepts in a sample paragraph, relate them in an editable concept map, and select concepts that are inserted into "a pre-written prompt for ChatGPT to generate scaffolds". Teachers keep final control: they can save, edit, regenerate, or remove scaffolds and disseminate them as worksheets, discussion questions, or documentation requirements.

article_title: CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education
citation: Alonso-Carracedo, M., Fernandez-Boullon, R., Celard, P., Rodríguez-Martínez, F. J., & Otero-Cerdeira, L. (2026). CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00140
title: CogTax: a four-level cognitive taxonomy integrating cognitive complexity and operational impact via a maximum rule
description: CogTax is a four-level cognitive taxonomy for command-line computing education that integrates two dimensions: cognitive complexity C, derived from Bloom's Revised Taxonomy, and operational impact O, the degree to which commands modify system state and the reversibility of those modifications. The article states that "The taxonomy explicitly considers whether actions are observational (read-only, zero risk), reversible (modifiable, low risk), structural (altering logical organization, moderate risk), or administrative (system-wide impact, high complexity)." The taxonomy level is the maximum of the two dimensions, ensuring both conceptual understanding and operational awareness are addressed. It was developed and validated in a second-year undergraduate Linux system administration course.
requirements: Commands must be classifiable along both a cognitive-complexity dimension and an operational-impact dimension; the framework targets command-line domains such as Linux/bash system administration
constraints: Developed and validated in the context of a second-year undergraduate Linux system administration course; the reviewed literature identifies no prior taxonomy jointly modelling the two dimensions for command-based domains
target_learners: second-year undergraduate Computer Engineering students in an Operating Systems course

title: Sequence command-line instruction so operational safety is established before operational power, consolidating each level's prerequisites before the next
description: The article derives a constructivist curriculum sequencing principle from the taxonomy: each level's prerequisites should be fully consolidated before the next level is introduced, with course units introducing L(k+1) material assuming mastery of all L1...L(k) concepts. It states that "The L= max(C, O) decomposition has a specific implication for introductory courses: operational safety should be established before operational power is introduced." Worked examples should be provided at the ZPD boundary, with the two dimensions separated where possible, introducing conceptually complex but operationally safe commands before operationally impactful ones.
requirements: An explicit ordered complexity taxonomy so material can be placed relative to each learner's current competence; grounding in constructivist scaffolding and Cognitive Load Theory
constraints: Grounded in command-line computing education; the article notes cognitive patterns of some L3 commands (e.g., pipelines) may be conceptually accessible earlier than their operational impact allows
target_learners: undergraduate students learning Linux system administration
target_learning_goals: safe progression from read-only inspection to advanced system management operations
examples: The taxonomy was developed and validated in a second-year undergraduate course spanning basic session management and filesystem navigation through process management including signal handling and compilation

title: 585-command expert-annotated Linux/bash dataset with balanced four-level representation
description: A dataset of Linux/bash commands annotated with CogTax levels by domain experts, combining commands from authentic student assessments with synthetically generated commands. The article states: "The complete dataset consists of 585 Linux/bash commands organized into two partitions: a held-out test partition of 117 commands and a training partition of 468 commands." The training partition was deliberately balanced across levels: L1 (143 commands, 24.4%), L2 (151 commands, 25.8%), L3 (144 commands, 24.6%), and L4 (147 commands, 25.1%). Expert annotators discussed ambiguous cases and established consensus classification rules applied uniformly across the dataset.
requirements: Expert annotation by computer science professors with systems programming instruction experience; consensus rules for ambiguous cases
constraints: The balanced distribution contrasts with naturally skewed educational distributions where introductory-level commands predominate
target_learners: second-year undergraduate Computer Engineering students
target_learning_goals: evaluation of automatic taxonomy-level classification of commands

citation: Alonso-Carracedo, M., Fernandez-Boullon, R., Celard, P., Rodríguez-Martínez, F. J., & Otero-Cerdeira, L. (2026). CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00140
title: AST-based structural command representation using bashlex parse trees, tree metrics, and TF-IDF weighted n-grams
description: A structural representation pipeline that parses Linux/bash commands into abstract syntax trees using bashlex and extracts features from the trees. The article explains that "each command is additionally represented by the multiset of ordered pairs(parent_label, child_label)extracted from the AST," alongside ten numeric tree metrics (node count, depth, max width, leaf count, branching factor, pipelines, operators, redirects, commands, subshells) and TF-IDF weighted n-grams (n = 1 to 4) over the DFS preorder node-kind sequence. This abstracts away lexical content such as file names and arguments, retaining structural relationships that determine command behaviour.
requirements: Valid Linux/bash commands parseable by bashlex; standard scaling of numeric metrics
constraints: Purely syntactic analysis cannot distinguish commands with identical syntax but different operational semantics, such as structurally identical L1 and L2 commands
target_learners: computing education researchers and instructors classifying commands
target_learning_goals: automatic assignment of taxonomy levels from command syntax

title: Embedding-based semantic command representation with four pretrained models and four preprocessing strategies
description: A complementary representation encoding commands as dense vectors in a semantic space. The article defines it as follows: "An embedding model is a neural network trained to map arbitrary text to a fixed-length numeric vector, such that texts with similar meaning are mapped to nearby points in the resulting vector space." Four models are evaluated (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, all-mpnet-base-v2, multilingual-e5-small, BAAI/llm-embedder) under four preprocessing strategies: raw, normalized (replacing literals, paths, and numbers with placeholders), instruction-tuned (prepending a fixed classification prefix), and combined. Embeddings are language-agnostic by construction, supporting cross-language generalization.
requirements: Pretrained embedding models; choice of preprocessing strategy affects representation quality
constraints: Embeddings may miss structural complexity markers that have weak lexical correlates, per the article's framing of the two branches as complementary
target_learners: computing education researchers and instructors classifying commands
target_learning_goals: automatic assignment of taxonomy levels from command semantics

article_title: Constructing Epistemic AI Literacy: Detecting Epistemic Aims and Processes in Student-AI Co-Programming
citation: Menggian Wu. (2026). Constructing Epistemic AI Literacy: Detecting Epistemic Aims and Processes in Student-AI Co-Programming. 2nd International Workshop on AI Literacy Education For All (ALIT4ALL 2026), co-located with AIED 2026, Seoul, Republic of Korea.
title: Epistemic AI Literacy (EAIL): a process-oriented framework for AI literacy grounded in the AIR framework
description: EAIL reframes AI literacy as a process-oriented epistemic phenomenon enacted during human-GenAI interaction, defined as the ability to understand, regulate, and critically engage with AI as cognitive agents, including deciding when to trust, outsource, verify, justify, and override AI judgments. Drawing on the AIR framework of epistemic aims, ideals, and reliable processes, it operationalizes literacy at the level of prompt-response pairs rather than through trait-like self-report scales. The article argues that 'AI literacy is most clearly enacted during direct interaction with AI systems, especially when learners engage in tasks that require higher order thinking.'
requirements: Analysis requires authentic human-AI interaction data, with the prompt-response pair as the unit of analysis
constraints: The study only focuses on detecting and describing epistemic aims and epistemic processes, not all AIR components simultaneously
target_learners: undergraduate programming students using generative AI
target_learning_goals: critical and epistemically productive engagement with AI-generated knowledge
examples: Applied to 200 sampled co-programming chat sessions from the StudyChat corpus to profile students' epistemic performance

title: Seven-code labeling scheme for epistemic AI literacy indicators (inquiry relevance, aims, five strategies)
description: A construct-mapping scheme (Table 1) with seven binary analytic codes: inquiry relevance, mastery-oriented vs non-mastery-oriented aims, and five epistemic strategies (outsourcing, explanation-seeking, verification-seeking, prompt monitoring, epistemic justification). Each code carries a definition, regex-style lexical indicators, and example quotes, e.g., outsourcing as 'Delegating cognitive work without problem framing: pasting code/questions/errors with minimal interpretation or specific inquiry.' The scheme grounds both human annotation and automated LLM labeling.

constraints: Lexical indicators are probabilistic cues with a semantic gap, where context-sensitivity weakens the link between word usage and underlying intent

description: Because robust epistemic engagement rarely emerges without intentional support, AI-supported learning environments should be designed so that task success cannot be achieved through superficial outsourcing. The article warns that 'in unregulated settings, surface-level task success and pseudo-success may become the dominant mode of interaction, as robust epistemic engagement does not reliably emerge without intentional instructional and design support.' This calls for CS curricula prioritizing high-level epistemic engagement over mere task completion.

title: Child-centered AI safety evaluation framework integrating expert guidelines with real-world AI incident data
description: The article introduces an evaluation framework for child safety in generative AI that combines two resources: expert-proposed child safety guidelines and AI incident databases. It first constructs "a taxonomy of child safety risk categories informed by expert guidance," then leverages incident data to build a synthetic test set reflecting realistic harmful scenarios. The framework is designed to be flexible and extensible so it can respond rapidly to real-world AI incidents, addressing the gap that most existing safety benchmarks focus on general adult user populations.

It states: "We coded each extracted student comment on three dimensions: comment type, code expression level, and code construct, assigning one label per dimension." The taxonomy treats comments not as documentation but as "student-written specifications for Copilot" that steer an LLM.

citation: Tam Nguyen, Hung Nguyen, Robert Ogburn. (2026). AI-accelerated End-to-End Framework for Rapid Professional Upskilling. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14044
title: CrewScaler: an end-to-end five-stage AI-accelerated upskilling pipeline
description: CrewScaler organizes rapid upskilling as a pipeline in which AI accelerates production at every stage rather than a single stage. It pairs each AI-acceleration mechanism with a learning-efficiency mechanism and a quality-control check, and its outputs face external validation. The article defines rapid upskilling as "minimizing time-to-competency for professionals acquiring a frontier technical topic", where competency is demonstrated against an external standard rather than self-reported. Humans retain high-judgment roles including blueprint design, SME review, misconception authoring, and item rating.
requirements: Each stage pairs an AI-acceleration mechanism with a learning-efficiency mechanism and a quality-control check, as summarized in the article's Table I
External validation checks independent of the authors are part of the pipeline design
constraints: The authors state the evidence is design, artifacts, and external validation signals, not controlled-comparison evidence
target_learners: Adult professionals upskilling in frontier technical topics
target_learning_goals: Rapid attainment of vendor-scored professional certification competencies
examples: Applied to multi-agent AI systems, the pipeline produced a roughly 3,000-page knowledge base, verified chapters, 16 tutoring protocols, and a 530-question assessment bank tagged to a 10-domain, 53-skill blueprint

citation: Tam Nguyen, Hung Nguyen, Robert Ogburn. (2026). AI-accelerated End-to-End Framework for Rapid Professional Upskilling. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14044
title: CrewScaler 16-protocol AI-tutor coaching library
description: The framework specifies the AI tutor's pedagogy in advance as a library of 16 named protocols drawn from the retrieval-practice, productive-failure, and affect literatures, rather than a single general-purpose prompt. Protocols include direct explanation, Socratic questioning, worked examples, hint escalation, spaced retrieval, productive failure, and "affective support that prioritizes boredom over frustration". A selection layer picks the active protocol each turn by fixed priority: integrity risk first, then affective signals, then group context, then learner intent. Six cross-cutting principles constrain every protocol.
requirements: A selection layer that prioritizes integrity risk, affective signals, group context, and learner intent
Grounded RAG and academic-integrity guardrails as stated quality controls
constraints: The article cites evidence that current LLMs labeled incorrect learner actions no better than chance in a 223-domain testbed, motivating explicit protocol design
target_learners: Adult professionals in frontier technical upskilling programs
target_learning_goals: Reducing time-to-competency through protocolized one-to-one tutoring
examples: The tutor classifies wrong answers as conceptual, procedural, factual, or careless and checks them against a per-chapter misconception catalog so feedback names the specific misconception

title: Misconception-keyed assessment development with blueprint-tagged difficulty distribution
description: The assessment stage engineers distractors from documented misconceptions rather than inventing them at question-writing time, and fixes difficulty distribution in advance at 30% easy, 50% medium, 20% hard. Every item traces to an atomic, ID-tagged knowledge item recording at least two documented misconceptions at extraction time; easy stems test one knowledge item, medium stems two to three, and hard stems three to five. The article states this pattern is consistent with evidence that "explicit difficulty control steers LLM-generated item pools away from trivially easy questions".

article_title: Did Alice Do Wrong? Cross-Cultural Differences in Student Perceptions of Generative AI Use in University Computing Education
citation: Brian Harrington, Irina Zlotnikova, Gayathri Nadarajan, and Samuel Ekundayo. (2025). Did Alice Do Wrong? Cross-Cultural Differences in Student Perceptions of Generative AI Use in University Computing Education. ACM Trans. Comput. Educ. 26, 1, Article 15. https://doi.org/10.1145/3776558
title: Hofstede's cultural dimensions framework as a lens for interpreting cross-cultural differences in GenAI ethical judgments
description: The article uses Hofstede's cultural dimensions theory—power distance, individualism versus collectivism, competitiveness, and uncertainty avoidance—as the theoretical basis for interpreting why Canadian and Korean students judged identical GenAI scenarios differently. Canada is characterized by "low power distance and high individualism," fostering strict anti-plagiarism norms, while Korea's higher power distance and collectivist orientation frame knowledge as communal. The authors argue this model provides "the most precise and contextually appropriate theoretical foundation" for analyzing students' ethical evaluations of GenAI in structured university settings, over alternatives such as Schwartz's values theory or the GLOBE study.
requirements: Application to educational settings requires distinguishing dimensions relevant to authority, rule-following, and uncertainty around emerging technologies
constraints: The authors caution against overgeneralizing cultural patterns, noting misconduct often arises from inadequate institutional support, insufficient training, and language barriers rather than inherent cultural values
target_learners: university computing students
target_learning_goals: ethical reasoning about GenAI use in coursework
academic integrity understanding

article_title: What Does the Credential Still Certify? Cognitive Stewardship for AI-Mediated Education
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). What Does the Credential Still Certify? Cognitive Stewardship for AI-Mediated Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19988
title: Cognitive stewardship framework for AI-mediated assessment
description: Cognitive stewardship is "the institutional practice of governing how cognitive work is divided between humans and AI while preserving understanding, verification, responsibility, access, and contestability." It aligns four elements: the learning claim being certified, the delegation boundary specifying what AI may do, the evidence standard showing what observable work remains, and the safeguards protecting privacy, accessibility, proportionality, equity, and appeal. A policy is under-specified when any element is missing. The framework treats validity as a warrant structure and is applied to institutional policy revision, not to individual competency checklists.
requirements: A policy must state the learning claim, delegation boundary, evidence standard, and safeguards; any missing element makes it under-specified
constraints: The framework is a normative lens; the audit applying it is a diagnostic application, not a framework-neutral test of institutional quality
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: credential validity of certified human capacities under AI-mediated assessment
examples: A first-year writing course redesign distributes evidence across diagnostic work, a source map, an AI-feedback workshop, the final essay, and a revision memo; a programming course splits claims between AI-limited tracing tasks and AI-permitted projects with explanation and defense of choices
key_sources: Kai Yao. (2026). What Does the Credential Still Certify? Cognitive Stewardship for AI-Mediated Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19988

article_title: What Does the Credential Still Certify? Cognitive Stewardship for AI-Mediated Education
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). What Does the Credential Still Certify? Cognitive Stewardship for AI-Mediated Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19988
title: Five delegation types taxonomy
description: The framework uses five recurring delegation types: access support, feedback support, process support, substitution, and output-verification support. As the article states, "Access support enables participation, for example through translation, speech-to-text, or assistive scaffolding. Feedback support offers critique or suggestions while the learner retains judgment." Process support assists planning, drafting, debugging, or workflow; substitution occurs when AI performs the operation being assessed; output-verification support treats checking AI-mediated work as a capability to be taught and assessed. The categories describe the role of assistance in a task and are not moral or fixed tool labels.
requirements: The same use must be re-classified per task, since one use can be access support in one task and substitution in another
constraints: The categories are descriptive roles, not moral labels or fixed tool labels
target_learners: higher education students
university instructors and policy writers
target_learning_goals: classifying AI use relative to the certified learning claim
examples: The scenario stress test applied these five types plus a programming-workflow case to each audited policy package

article_title: ConnectED: A Curriculum-Aligned AI System for Vietnamese Instructional Lesson Planning and Student Learning
citation: Thang Doan Viet, Anh Nguyen Hoang, Tinh Luong Son, Anh Hoang Thi Ngoc, Huyen Giang Thi Thu, Tai Le Quy. (2026). ConnectED: A Curriculum-Aligned AI System for Vietnamese Instructional Lesson Planning and Student Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28647
title: ADDIE-based orchestration framework for curriculum-aligned LLM lesson generation with teacher validation gates
description: ConnectED uses the ADDIE instructional design model as a unifying orchestration layer, using "ADDIE to structure instructional reasoning, decompose pedagogical goals, and control generation flow" rather than treating the LLM as a black-box generator. Each of the five phases produces concrete, evaluable artifacts and serves as a prompt boundary where curriculum compliance can be verified and teacher approval solicited before the next phase begins. The Evaluation phase feeds student learning signals back into Design and Develop, closing the instructional loop.
requirements: Teacher validation checkpoints at each ADDIE phase boundary, with teachers retaining authority to review, revise, or regenerate AI outputs
Structured prompt templates encoding Official Dispatch 5512 requirements, including three-dimensional learning objectives and the mandated four-step activity structure
constraints: The paper acknowledges ADDIE-based orchestration may introduce a degree of rigidity in lesson generation, and experienced teachers may prefer more flexible workflows beyond predefined instructional phases
target_learners: Vietnamese secondary school teachers (grades 6-12)
target_learning_goals: Curriculum-aligned lesson planning compliant with Official Dispatch 5512
examples: In ConnectED, the Analyze phase extracts key concepts and generates objectives, Design produces lesson outlines following the four-step structure, and Develop transforms approved designs into lesson plans, slides, simulations, and Manim animations

article_title: The Tragedy of the Cognitive Commons: How AI Could Disrupt the Regeneration of Professional Expertise
citation: Lovett, N. (2026). The tragedy of the cognitive commons: How AI could disrupt the regeneration of professional expertise. Human Resource Development Review. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/15344843261470602
title: The Cognitive Commons framework
description: The Cognitive Commons is defined as "the collective pool of deep human expertise within a profession that functions as a shared resource whose regeneration can no longer be taken for granted." It exhibits three commons characteristics: collective dependence (a free-rider problem where organizations benefit from a talent pool they avoid paying to develop), non-excludability, and degradability through overexploitation of the regeneration mechanism. Degradation manifests through generational employment patterns rather than visible scarcity, so apparent stock stability can mask regeneration failure. An integrative six-node causal chain (Figure 1) and construct definitions (Table 1) formalize how entry-level position elimination and augmentation-without-internalization erode Internalized Mastery, degrading validation and raising latent systemic risk.
requirements: Applies only when AI substitutes for developmental cognitive labor, the pathways are hard to replicate outside organizational work, and the three commons characteristics co-occur
constraints: Excludes professions facing wholesale disintermediation; assumes AI still requires human oversight; assumes a Western model of professional formation through organizational entry-level employment and credentialing
target_learners: Entry-level professionals in AI-exposed occupations
HRD scholars and workforce policymakers
target_learning_goals: Development of deep, validation-capable professional expertise
Sustained regeneration of profession-wide expert capacity
examples: The paper applies the framework to software engineering, financial analysis, and legal research as higher-vulnerability occupations, with medicine and engineering facing slower dynamics due to regulatory intensity and safety criticality.
key_sources: Lovett, N. (2026). The tragedy of the cognitive commons: How AI could disrupt the regeneration of professional expertise. Human Resource Development Review. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/15344843261470602

article_title: The Tragedy of the Cognitive Commons: How AI Could Disrupt the Regeneration of Professional Expertise
citation: Lovett, N. (2026). The tragedy of the cognitive commons: How AI could disrupt the regeneration of professional expertise. Human Resource Development Review. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/15344843261470602
title: The Validation Tether and the Internalized/Distributed Mastery distinction
description: The framework distinguishes Internalized Mastery (deep domain knowledge built through "sustained cognitive struggle and authentic professional practice across progressive levels of complexity") from Distributed Mastery (proficiency in orchestrating AI systems). The Validation Tether holds that "effective orchestration of opaque AI systems requires independent domain understanding sufficient to recognize when systems operate outside competence boundaries." It separates surface validation (detecting obvious errors and plausibility, attainable without internalized expertise) from substantive validation (detecting domain-specific errors beneath plausible surfaces), which requires Internalized Mastery and an epistemic stance that prompts interrogation of AI outputs. Because commons depletion removes the pathways that build Internalized Mastery, it threatens both expertise forms simultaneously.
requirements: Substantive validation requires internalized domain knowledge that cannot be acquired through observation or AI-assisted performance alone
constraints: Validation Tether refers to a structural relationship between expertise forms, not a trainable disposition; assumes AI outputs remain superficially plausible rather than fully autonomous and reliable
target_learners: Professionals overseeing AI systems in consequential domains
Organizations designing human-AI workflows
target_learning_goals: Substantive validation of AI outputs
Recognizing when AI operates outside its competence boundaries
examples: The paper illustrates the tether with financial analysts assessing flawed assumptions in risk assessments, physicians checking AI diagnostic recommendations against patient-specific factors, and software engineers detecting maintenance problems in executing code.
key_sources: Lovett, N. (2026). The tragedy of the cognitive commons: How AI could disrupt the regeneration of professional expertise. Human Resource Development Review. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/15344843261470602

article_title: The Tragedy of the Cognitive Commons: How AI Could Disrupt the Regeneration of Professional Expertise
citation: Lovett, N. (2026). The tragedy of the cognitive commons: How AI could disrupt the regeneration of professional expertise. Human Resource Development Review. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/15344843261470602
title: Five structural factors determining occupational commons vulnerability
description: The framework states that "The framework identifies five factors that determine an occupation's commons vulnerability": task substitutability (how far AI performs the tasks that historically provided novice developmental experience), regulatory intensity, safety criticality, professional association strength, and work modularization. Professions should show greater disruption where AI exposure is higher, where early-career development was concentrated organizationally rather than educationally, and where the three commons characteristics are most pronounced. The unit of analysis is the occupation, not the national economy, and countervailing dynamics (new AI-era developmental pathways, mixed aggregate labor-market evidence) establish that the depletion mechanism is not universal.
requirements: Vulnerability assessment requires occupation-level analysis of which specific cognitive tasks AI substitutes for
constraints: Applies only to professions meeting the three structural conditions; early empirical evidence is drawn from US, UK, and German labor markets, reflecting the research base rather than a theoretical limitation
target_learners: HRD researchers
Workforce and profession-level governance bodies
target_learning_goals: Prioritizing expertise-regeneration interventions in high-vulnerability occupations
Generating testable predictions about differential commons disruption
examples: The paper places software engineering, financial analysis, and legal research in higher-vulnerability categories, and medicine and engineering in slower-degradation categories due to institutional counterpressures.

article_title: CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities
citation: Arthur Nijdam, Paul Stankovski Wagner, Sara Ramezanian. (2026). CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05910
title: CourseGraph: an LLM-plus-sBERT-plus-Random-Forest pipeline for detecting overlap between university courses
description: CourseGraph is a four-step methodology for automatically assessing whether an external course overlaps with courses in a home curriculum. As the authors describe, "CourseGraph first extracts information such as course titles, descriptions, and learning outcomes from a course's webpage using a Large Language Model (LLM) and a tailored prompt." The extracted fields are embedded with sBERT, cosine similarities are computed between course pairs, and size-independent features (max, min, mean similarity, and fractions above 0.5, 0.6, 0.7) feed a 15-dimensional feature vector into a Random Forest classifier that outputs an overlap/no-overlap decision. Embedding each course component separately supports explainability of which components drive an overlap prediction.
requirements: Course webpages must publicly provide course title, description, prerequisites, learning outcomes, and level for extraction
constraints: The methodology assumes that all course information is publicly available and can be compared between institutions
target_learners: university students in mobility programs such as Erasmus+
target_learning_goals: identifying overlapping educational content when selecting external courses toward a degree
examples: Trained on the TU/e CS overlap matrix (60 positive pairs augmented with 180 negative pairs) and validated on 24 LU Erasmus+ decisions

citation: Arthur Nijdam, Paul Stankovski Wagner, Sara Ramezanian. (2026). CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05910
title: Decision tree used by a curriculum administrator to assess external courses for the Lund C program
description: Based on correspondence with the former program director, the authors constructed a decision tree (Fig. 1) capturing how external courses are assessed for the Lund University Information and Communication Engineering (C) program. "Firstly, the program director decides whether a course is within the scope of the C program, or counted as external." External courses are capped at 15 ECTS; in-scope courses are matched to LU equivalents, assigned a level (G1/G2/A), and possibly counted toward one of five specialization tracks. Partial overlap is credited proportionally: "overlap below 20% (less than 1.5 ECTS) is disregarded; overlap between 20% and 66.7% warrants 2–5 ECTS; and overlap exceeding 66.7% (more than 5 ECTS) is treated as full equivalence." CourseGraph targets the content-overlap decisions in this tree.
requirements: A curriculum administrator's decision process and program metadata (levels, specialization tracks) to ground the assessment rules
constraints: Automatic assignment of course level falls outside the scope of this paper
target_learners: exchange students in the Lund University C program
target_learning_goals: crediting external courses appropriately toward degree requirements
examples: The tree distinguishes external (max 15 ECTS), mandatory-program, and specialization-track outcomes, with five tracks: KS, PVS, PVT, SEC, and ADV

The authors summarize that "the content and level of the course needs to be appropriate for a course to be counted as part of the degree program." citation: Alexei Kaltchenko and Gurnivaj Tiwana. (2026). ChatGPT Solves All Tested Qiskit Homework Assignments. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19707
title: Do not interpret a correct personalized, execution-oriented take-home artifact as evidence of independent understanding; directly assess conceptual understanding instead
description: The article argues that correctness of a take-home artifact, even a personalized and execution-oriented one, is insufficient evidence of independent understanding, since all tested artifacts were produced by direct ChatGPT outsourcing. Instructors should distinguish AI-supported production from verified understanding and directly assess whether students can explain and adapt the result. The authors state their tested measures were recommendations derived from the observed failure mode, not experimentally compared in this study.

article_title: Incorporating Cognitive Load and Knowledge Transfer for Multi-Domain Knowledge Tracing
citation: Haotian Zhang, Shucun Wang, Jinze Wu, Liang Ding, Shuochen Liu, Zhenya Huang, Jing Sha, Shijin Wang, and Qi Liu. (2026). Incorporating Cognitive Load and Knowledge Transfer for Multi-Domain Knowledge Tracing. arXiv:2608.24005. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24005
title: LT-MKT framework: joint modeling of cognitive load and knowledge transfer for multi-domain knowledge tracing
description: LT-MKT is a knowledge tracing framework for multi-domain learning scenarios that jointly models two factors the authors argue are overlooked by single-domain methods: cognitive load and knowledge transfer. It constructs a Multi-domain Hierarchical Graph with LLM-guided reasoning, models cognitive load via "question difficulty, domain transition, and domain coverage", updates knowledge states with a GRU, and applies intraGAT and interGAT layers for prerequisite-based within-domain and cross-domain semantic transfer, followed by state fusion and prediction.

Student interaction sequences spanning multiple domains with response correctness labels

article_title: CogEvol: Towards Efficient and Reliable Learning Environment Generation
citation: CogEvol Team, CogEvol Inc. & Tsinghua University. (2026). CogEvol: Towards Efficient and Reliable Learning Environment Generation. arXiv:2608.30968v2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30968
title: Learning Environment Generation (LEG): formalizing courseware artifact generation as a contract-bound task
description: LEG is the task framework the report introduces: given a course brief, produce in a single pass either a presentation slide as a renderer-valid structured JSON scene graph or a self-contained executable interactive HTML page spanning six educational sub-types (simulations, diagrams, games, code playgrounds, 3D visualizations, structured learning pages). Outputs are scored along four dimensions — fidelity, layout, interactivity, and correctness — with interactivity measured by executing the artifact rather than judged from appearance. The report states that to its knowledge generation of such environments "has not been formalized as a task before".
requirements: A strict output contract: the production renderer hard-fails on unrecognized keys, string-typed coordinates, percentages, or invented element types; an HTML page succeeds only if it runs.
constraints: LEG generates the environment's content — slides and interactive pages — not the platform plumbing such as accounts, analytics, and distribution surrounding them.
target_learners: Learners using interactive courseware and simulation-based materials

article_title: Beyond AI Literacy: A Structured Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis of Measures for Competent Generative-AI Use
citation: Daniele Verí. (2026). Beyond AI Literacy: A Structured Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis of Measures for Competent Generative-AI Use. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15624
title: Four-domain framework for competent generative-AI use measurement: knowledge and use, epistemic oversight, reliance calibration, and operational control of tool-using agents
description: The review organizes validated instruments into four domains ordered by proximity to operational work: knowledge and use, epistemic oversight, reliance calibration, and operational control of tool-using agents. The domains are "complementary measurement targets, not a single proficiency continuum": a person may know much about AI yet rely on it poorly, verify diligently without technical depth, or manage an agent safely through a familiar workflow without explaining model architecture. The framework is cut by measurement claim rather than curricular content, distinguishing it from curricular frameworks such as the AI Literacy Heptagon.
requirements: Training placement needs the distinctions between domains; domains should not be collapsed into one continuum without evidence.
constraints: The coverage map is the author's interpretive classification with no independent duplicate coding or inter-rater agreement; coverage describes measurement target, not validation quality.
target_learners: adults using generative AI in work and education
target_learning_goals: competent generative-AI use including verification, reliance calibration, and supervision of tool-using agents
examples: The review maps 22 focal instruments into Table 1 coverage ratings (Strong, Partial, Weak, None) across the four domains.

title: Conservative taxonomy and definition for classifying hallucinated and erroneous references
description: The article defines a "hallucinated" reference narrowly as one containing "verifiably fabricated bibliographic information", treating incomplete references as non-hallucinations when present information is correct and the work is identifiable. It adapts Li et al.'s citation hallucination taxonomy with letter codes: S (ACM metadata mismatch), H (author-field error), R (valid bibliographic variant), W (working group and task force reports), M (other typos), and A (alternative substitutions for et al.). This taxonomy structures the manual coding of 828 SET A records and provides a starting point for automated checking systems.
requirements: Classification requires inspection of the raw reference, matched metadata, ACM DOI page, source PDF, and where useful external bibliographic records
constraints: The definition is deliberately conservative; incomplete but identifiable references are not hallucinations
Source PDFs must be checked before labelling a case as potentially hallucinated, since apparent errors may reflect ACM metadata discrepancies
target_learners: computing education researchers
reviewers and program committees
target_learning_goals: understanding reference integrity and citation verification in scholarly writing
examples: Two coders classified 828 SET A records using the adapted taxonomy, finding S (229) most common, then H (225) and R (188)

title: Shared responsibility model: authors verify every cited work, venues adopt targeted checks and explicit policies, and publishers improve metadata quality
description: The article proposes a shared responsibility model as the way forward against hallucinated references. Authors should verify every cited work, especially when generative AI was used in writing, and should not cite sources they have not personally checked. Reviewers and program committees should not be expected to manually audit every reference; venues can adopt targeted checks for high-risk cases and make policies explicit at submission. Publishers should improve metadata quality and support post-publication correction and reference-validation tools.
requirements: Authors personally verify every cited work before citing it
Automated tools should be human-in-the-loop systems that highlight suspicious references, explain why a reference was flagged, and return feedback to authors before review
constraints: Many suspicious references turn out to be metadata mismatches, valid variants, or human errors rather than hallucinations, so automated checking is not straightforward
Manual checking of references goes beyond what can be expected from reviewers
target_learners: academic authors
reviewers and program committees
publishers and venue organizers
target_learning_goals: maintaining citation accuracy and research integrity when using generative AI writing tools
examples: The article reports that ACM policy allows retraction for AI-related content-integrity issues, arXiv has proposed bans for fabricated references, and some computing education venues list fabricated references among grounds for desk rejection

article_title: CoLearn: An Agentic Tutor that Learns its Learner in a Human-AI Co-Learning Loop
citation: Kailai He, Zhihao Wu, Linhai Zhang, Runcong Zhao, Yulan He, Jiazheng Li. (2026). CoLearn: An Agentic Tutor that Learns its Learner in a Human–AI Co-Learning Loop. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21154
title: Human–AI co-learning loop: persistent learner-state memory, adaptive question generation, and a transparent evidence view
description: CoLearn operationalises the ideal tutor as a loop in which the learner practises while the agent refines a persistent memory of the learner's mastery and misconceptions. It has "three components: (i) a persistent learner-state memory that updates per-topic mastery with a soft-evidence variant of Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, where a large language model acts as a continuous observation function", (ii) adaptive question generation targeting the weakest topic and recurring misconceptions, and (iii) an evidence view making personalisation visible and testable. Co-learning here is deliberately modest: the question strategy stays fixed while only the agent's memory adapts.
requirements: A persistent per-(learner, subject) memory record so evidence accumulates across sessions rather than per-session logs
An LLM grader emitting continuous mastery_evidence and evidence_strength values in [0,1] as the observation function
constraints: The strategy guideline is a fixed text consulted on every generation; automatic revision from accumulated outcomes is planned but not yet implemented
A rising mastery estimate is evidence that the agent's belief has changed, not proof that the learner has mastered the skill
target_learners: secondary-school science learners (evaluated on Biology and Chemistry curricula)
target_learning_goals: topic-level mastery diagnosis
misconception identification and remediation through targeted practice
examples: In a worked live round, a clearly wrong GCSE Biology answer lowered mastery 0.56→0.23 via competence-gated BKT, stored three misconceptions, and the adaptive engine re-targeted that skill next turn

title: Context prompts: instructor-designed prompts defining role, task, and boundaries of a Gen AI interaction
description: The article's central framework is the context prompt: instructor-designed prompts that establish guidelines for generative AI to follow during student interactions. The authors write that through a context prompt, instructors establish guidelines for Gen AI to follow that can guide students in exploration and reflection activities, and that it is important to provide Gen AI specific guidelines in order to scaffold it to stay on target. The prompt is prioritized at the start of the chat and maintained across the conversation.

constraints: Gen AI models are not equal, and the choice of platform matters

examples: An exploration context prompt instructs the AI to act as a learning guide taking a Socratic approach, break down every step, and suggest resources when appropriate

title: Six fundamental components of prompt engineering, ordered from task and context down to tone
description: The article presents a six-component account of prompt engineering, stating there are six fundamental components to prompt engineering, from most important to least important: 1) task, 2) context, 3) exemplar, 4) persona, 5) format, and 6) tone. Task is the instruction the AI is expected to carry out and is the most critical component; context provides background details; exemplars illustrate desired style; persona, format, and tone shape delivery but are less essential. These principles are reflected in the article's example prompts.

title: StudioCrit research mode with provisional cognitive and architectural classification
description: StudioCrit is an optional board/class mode of Critsly for architecture-studio research. "It classifies sticky notes and critique comments using Bloom's revised taxonomy and architectural evaluation dimensions", exposing visible badges and analytics with metadata such as matched verbs, confidence and ambiguity. Studios can link multiple boards, educators manage classes and invitations, learners contribute to boards, and researcher access supports class analytics and export within role boundaries.

Taxonomy-version metadata so assigned labels remain inspectable
constraints: Classifications are provisional; metadata are not evidence of calibrated probabilities or validated explanations
Multi-verb and multi-topic comments can create ambiguity
No complete classifier specification, thresholds or gold-standard annotation set is provided

target_learning_goals: making critique activity inspectable by cognitive and architectural category for educators and researchers

title: 39-column evidence export schema with machine classification and human-review fields
description: StudioCrit's research workflow exports evidence as a structured CSV snapshot. "The refreshed export schema is reported to contain 39 columns spanning studio/board context, provenance, note content and position, machine classification and human review." Field groups include studio/board identifiers, provenance fields such as research_participant_code, classification fields such as primary_brt_level, confidence and ambiguity_flag, and human-review fields such as manual_override_status and coder_reconciliation_status, so later analysts can distinguish machine output from agreed human codes.

Independent human codes obtained and disagreements reconciled before export

Exports can contain internal user identifiers, note contents and provenance, so participant codes alone do not make records anonymous

title: Critique-to-evidence workflow: snapshot, independent coding, reconciliation, export
description: This pattern connects an evolving design artefact, its critique, an action plan and an inspectable research record. As the report states, "The intended research workflow is to preserve a machine-evidence snapshot, obtain independent human codes, reconcile disagreements and export the reviewed record." Machine-generated cognitive and architectural labels are treated as provisional and are checked against independent human coding before any analytic use, retaining the educator's interpretive role.

Independent human coders and a reconciliation step before export
constraints: No completed human-coder validation or inter-rater reliability analysis is reported in this article
The workflow's educational benefits remain hypotheses for evaluation

description: Before treating machine-assigned cognitive or architectural labels as evidence, the article recommends a human-coder validation study. "A future study should specify a coding manual, define the unit of analysis and have independent coders label an appropriate sample before reconciliation." Agreement should be reported before disagreements are resolved, with Cohen's kappa offered as one established option for nominal labels, and machine-human agreement distinguished from human-human agreement.

Independent coders labelling an appropriate sample before reconciliation
Agreement statistics reported before disagreements are resolved

None of the proposed validation activities is a completed result of this report

article_title: CLARA: Can AI Assess Developmental Appropriateness in Children's Stories?
citation: Sijing Yin, Zirui Wang, Qian Liu, Jiamou Liu. (2026). CLARA: Can AI Assess Developmental Appropriateness in Children's Stories?. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05783
title: Bilingual benchmark of 1107 Chinese-English children's stories with silver developmental references and structured annotations
description: A benchmark resource of 1107 aligned Chinese-English children's stories extracted from storybooks and educational materials in PDF and PPT formats, with normalized silver developmental references and structured COG, LAN, and SEL annotations. The article states: "we construct a bilingual benchmark contain- ing 1107 Chinese–English children's stories col- lected from storybooks and educational materials in PDF and PPT formats." Manual verification of 100 sampled stories found 95% acceptable extraction quality, 93% correct story grouping, and 91% adequate bilingual semantic consistency; 1030 stories are retained for quantitative evaluation.

Normalized silver developmental references mapped to five age groups
Structured annotations across COG, LAN, and SEL dimensions

English narratives are translations, so the design evaluates consistency under translation rather than cross-lingual or cross-cultural generalization
The 0-2 group contains only 30 stories and text-only analysis omits illustrations, repetition, and caregiver interaction

target_learning_goals: Developmental narrative understanding across cognitive, language, and social-emotional dimensions

A cloth-bear story is annotated with COG labels simple cause, action consequence, and routine understanding, with publisher reference 2-5 and CLARA prediction 4-6

article_title: How motivation and roles influence metacognitive engagement in student-GenAI interaction
citation: Cui, Y., Yan, W., Chiu, T. K. F., & Nakajima, T. (2026). How motivation and roles influence metacognitive engagement in student-GenAI interaction. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 23(34). https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00610-z
title: Four-role taxonomy of GenAI roles: instructor, enhancement tool, replacement tool, collaborator
description: The article develops a four-category taxonomy of the functional roles students assign to GenAI in authentic interaction. It extends the tripartite Instructor–Collaborator–Tool taxonomy of Ouyang and Jiao (2021) by splitting the Tool category using Fügener et al.'s augmentation–automation distinction. As the article states, "When GenAI was used to reduce cognitive load, extend the student's capabilities, or assist with tasks the student could not accomplish independently, the role was coded as Enhancement Tool", whereas a Replacement Tool substitutes for the student's own thinking. Roles were coded per interaction log from log content plus retrospective accounts.
requirements: Coding requires access to the stated purpose of each interaction, combining log text with the learner's retrospective account, since roles "could not be reliably inferred from surface text"
constraints: Applied to learning-related undergraduate GenAI use in authentic, self-initiated dialogues; motivation coded as a binary intrinsic-versus-extrinsic contrast rather than finer SDT subtypes
target_learners: Undergraduate students using GenAI for learning
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive regulation of student-GenAI dialogue
Self-directed learning with generative AI
examples: Roles were observed in 120 authentic interaction logs: Instructor 25.0%, Replacement Tool 45.8%, Enhancement Tool 21.7%, Collaborator 7.5% (Table 2)

article_title: Customizing AI for writing pedagogy: a systematic review of pedagogical goals, theoretical principles, and technical design
citation: Luo, Y. (2026). Customizing AI for writing pedagogy: a systematic review of pedagogical goals, theoretical principles, and technical design. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10697-w
title: Five-category taxonomy of pedagogical goals in customized AI writing instruction
description: The review derives five pedagogical goal categories through an iterative mixed inductive–deductive coding process across 23 studies: multi-dimensional feedback and scoring, writing process and metacognition, higher-order academic skills, alternative assessment models, and learner feedback literacy. The review reports that "multi-dimensional feedback and scoring dominated the literature (N = 9), followed by goals related to writing process and metacognition (N = 6) and higher-order academic skills (N = 6)", while alternative assessment models and learner feedback literacy were each represented by only one study, revealing a strong concentration on product- and performance-oriented outcomes.
requirements: Studies must pursue explicit pedagogical goals in customizing AI for writing instruction to be classifiable within the taxonomy
constraints: Derived from 23 empirical studies published between January 2020 and September 2025
target_learners: Higher education L2 academic writing learners
target_learning_goals: Writing competence development through AI-mediated feedback and process support
examples: The review coded studies reporting multiple goals under each applicable category, producing co-occurrence data visualized in Fig. 2

article_title: Assisting the grading of a handwritten general chemistry exam with artificial intelligence
citation: Jan Cvengros and Gerd Kortemeyer. (2026). Assisting the grading of a handwritten general chemistry exam with artificial intelligence. Discover Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44163-026-01606-4
title: Use human-in-the-loop AI grading with confidence-based selective filtering that defers uncertain cases to human graders
description: The article advocates a selective-prediction/deferral workflow in which the AI grades all student-items first and a confidence filter establishes "trust or distrust in these AI-judgements", accepting only reliable decisions and deferring higher-risk cases to humans. Filters include a partial-credit threshold, an IRT-based risk threshold, and exclusion by problem type. The authors argue this is essential because AI scores can exhibit undue confidence in ambiguous cases, and regulatory frameworks such as the EU's high-risk designation for AI in educational assessment mandate human oversight.
requirements: Confidence filter parameters must be adjustable based solely on risk tolerance, with stricter parameters rejecting more item-gradings and increasing human workload
A ground-truth-equivalent human grading workflow must remain available for deferred cases
constraints: The article states previous experiences show multimodal AI often succeeds in reading handwriting but still fails to interpret scientific diagrams and graphs, motivating exclusion of Drawing and Graphing parts
Filtering operates on AI scores alone, since in a production setting the ground truth would be unknown
target_learners: large-enrollment university students in general chemistry courses for non-majors
target_learning_goals: reliable scoring of open-ended handwritten exam responses including reaction equations, derivations, and explanations
examples: The study deployed the workflow in parallel with routine TA grading of a 15-page, 60-point, 46-part handwritten final exam, with students receiving only TA-assigned points
key_sources: Jan Cvengros and Gerd Kortemeyer. (2026). Assisting the grading of a handwritten general chemistry exam with artificial intelligence. Discover Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44163-026-01606-4

article_title: Assisting the grading of a handwritten general chemistry exam with artificial intelligence
citation: Jan Cvengros and Gerd Kortemeyer. (2026). Assisting the grading of a handwritten general chemistry exam with artificial intelligence. Discover Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44163-026-01606-4
title: Argument-based validity and generalizability framing of AI-assigned scores as fallible observations with selective deferral
description: The article grounds AI-assisted grading in test theory and generalizability theory, treating AI-assigned points as "fallible observations with multiple error sources (items, raters/runs, tasks)" that can be estimated and, where appropriate, reduced through aggregation or design. For score interpretation it adopts Kane's argument-based validity perspective, requiring that claims about score meaning be supported by explicit warrants and evidence. The human-in-the-loop setup follows selective-prediction/deferral frameworks, in which the model grades confidently when reliable and defers uncertain cases to humans.
requirements: Explicit warrants and evidence must support claims about score meaning and decisions such as pass/fail cut scores
Error sources at item, rater/run, and task levels must be estimable for reliability analysis
constraints: The framework assumes run-to-run errors are approximately mean-zero and only weakly correlated across items
target_learners: higher-education students in large-enrollment STEM courses
target_learning_goals: valid and reliable automated scoring of open-ended handwritten assessment responses
examples: The study operationalized the framework with ICC(A,1)/ICC(A,k), repeatability Sw and RC, Kendall's W, and Lin's CCC, plus a two-parameter logistic IRT model defining risk as the absolute deviation between AI-assigned and expected scores

title: Align GenAI integration in nursing education with professional standards and codes of ethics to protect core nursing values
description: Participants held that ethical GenAI use is not a purely technical issue but must stay connected to the NMBA Registered Nurse Standards for Practice, the NMBA Code of Conduct and the ICN Code of Ethics, which emphasise "integrity, accountability, critical thinking, and a commitment to lifelong learning". Some proposed formalised expectations, such as academic standards of practice that students sign up to acknowledging their entry into the profession. The article's recommendations call for nursing-specific guidance aligned with these ethical codes and professional standards.

accountability
patient safety

title: Three-theme account of nursing academics' sense-making about GenAI: ambiguity, core-value threats, and ethical development
description: The study's organizing framework groups nursing academics' accounts of GenAI into three major themes with nine minor themes: (1) Navigating the Unknown: Ambiguity in GenAI Use, covering policy ambiguity, divergent attitudes and curriculum adaptation; (2) GenAI Challenging Nursing's Core Values, covering professional identity, overreliance, and misconduct risks; and (3) Developing Ethical Nurses in a Digital Age, covering curricular integration, safeguarding critical thinking, and embedding professional values. undergraduate nursing students

guiding curriculum and assessment redesign

article_title: Artificial intelligence perceptions and career anxiety among health sciences students
citation: Dağ, E., Nal, M., Topuz, İ., Kılınç, H., Demir, Y. & Bektaş, G. (2026). Artificial intelligence perceptions and career anxiety among health sciences students. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-42030-z
title: AI anxiety as a perception-driven appraisal mechanism within the Stress and Coping framework
description: The article frames students' AI anxiety using Lazarus and Folkman's process/interaction model, in which "stress stems not so much from the external threat itself, but rather from the individual's perception of how risky the threat is". AI anxiety is conceptualised as a perception-driven mechanism that converts technological change into career-related stress: students appraise AI as a threat to expected employability (primary appraisal) and judge their coping resources, such as AI literacy and self-efficacy, insufficient (secondary appraisal). The study's main contribution is classifying AI anxiety as a multidimensional stress response specific to the job search process rather than a general fear of technology.
requirements: The framework applies to populations who have not yet entered the labour market, whose assessment is gain- or failure-focused rather than loss-focused
constraints: The article distinguishes students' employability-threat appraisal from working adults' job-loss appraisal; workplace job-insecurity inferences should not be drawn from student findings
target_learners: University health sciences students preparing to enter the labour market
target_learning_goals: Understanding AI-related career stress and employability perceptions
examples: The study interprets its regression findings as showing AI is appraised as a threat because students believe they lack the knowledge, skills and resources to meet AI-related demands

citation: Wei Dai and Cecilia Ka Yuk Chan. (2026). Shaping responsible GenAI use in research through AI literacy-oriented guidelines: insights from postgraduate students. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00609-6
title: Ng et al.'s four-dimensional AI literacy framework as a lens for researchers' responsible GenAI use
description: The study draws on Ng et al.'s framework conceptualising AI literacy as an integrated set of knowledge, practical, evaluative, and ethical capacities: "Know & Understand AI", "Use & Apply AI", "Evaluate & Create AI", and "AI Ethics". In the research context, the dimensions denote awareness of GenAI's capabilities, limitations and risks; appropriate employment across research tasks; judging the accuracy, originality and scholarly value of AI-mediated outputs; and reasoning about authorship, originality, privacy, accountability and over-reliance. The study uses the framework to analyse PGR students' practices and to structure its proposed guidelines.
requirements: Guidelines must address each of the four dimensions across diverse research tasks rather than principles alone.
constraints: The article states AI literacy had not yet been sufficiently defined or contextualised in relation to research practice prior to this study.
target_learners: postgraduate research students (MPhil and PhD)
target_learning_goals: responsible and ethical use of GenAI in research
AI literacy development across knowledge, application, evaluation and ethical dimensions
examples: The study mapped focus-group findings onto the dimensions: capability awareness to Know & Understand, discipline-specific applications to Use & Apply, ethical boundaries to Evaluate & Create, and concerns about accuracy, originality, privacy and skill degradation to AI Ethics.

citation: Dai, Z., Huang, F., Xiong, J., Yang, Y., Zhang, Q., & Peng, X. (2026). International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00631-0
title: Scaffolding-perspective comparison of chatbots and search engines as technological scaffolds for problem posing
description: The article frames chatbots and search engines as two distinct forms of technological scaffolding for problem-based inquiry, taking interaction mode as its entry point. It contrasts them by stating that "chatbots emphasize bidirectional interaction by engaging students in sustained natural language dialogue and adjusting feedback in response to students’ input", whereas search engines center on keyword query input and result selection oriented toward unidirectional information retrieval. From this, chatbots are expected to provide dynamic and contingent cognitive and metacognitive scaffolding, while search engines mainly provide resource-level support with conceptual and procedural attributes. The study uses this framework to motivate its experimental comparison of the two tools.
requirements: Both tools must operate as external digital support within problem-based inquiry activities in STEM inquiry environments
constraints: The framework is applied to primary science problem posing contexts in this study, and the two tools are described as differing in interaction mode, scaffolding form, and resulting cognitive support
target_learners: Primary school students in science classrooms
target_learning_goals: Generating and refining scientific questions during inquiry-based learning
examples: The study operationalized the framework by giving the experimental class a GenAI chatbot for dialogic question generation and refinement and the control class a search engine for text-based retrieval and reading, both on tablets

title: Three-dimensional framework for assessing problem posing ability: number, category, and quality
description: The article operationalizes students’ problem posing ability in science into three coded dimensions, defining them so that "category was used to reflect the breadth of question types and the characteristics of their knowledge sources; and quality was used to reflect the depth of cognitive processing" demonstrated in students’ questions, with number reflecting how many questions were posed. The framework draws on English (1997), Silver and Cai (2005), and Yuan and Sriraman (2011). Number is coded in five levels, category into six question types, and quality into five cognitive levels from the revised Bloom’s taxonomy. The dimensions feed a 10-point total score weighted 3, 2, and 5 points for number, category, and quality.

Coding by trained raters with inter-rater reliability assessed using the Kappa coefficient

citation: Patiño Hernández JF, Chiappe A and Ortega González E (2026). From digital competence to AI-responsive pedagogy: a scoping review of technology-supported teacher education. Front. Educ. 11:1949296. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1949296
title: AI-responsive pedagogy: maintaining pedagogical agency when deciding whether, when and how AI participates in teaching
description: AI-responsive pedagogy is the review's interpretive construct linking teacher digital competence with pedagogical enactment of AI. It denotes "the professional capacity to decide whether, when and how AI should participate in teaching and teacher learning, and to select, interrogate, adapt or constrain AI outputs in relation to pedagogical purposes, disciplinary knowledge, evidence of learning, ethical commitments and contextual conditions". The construct builds on UNESCO's AI Competency Framework for Teachers and extensions of TPACK to AI-related professional knowledge, and is explicitly not a synonym for AI adoption or tool proficiency. Its specific conditions are derived from patterns across the reviewed studies rather than imposed as a normative framework.

constraints: Responsiveness does not mean adapting education to technological change; the review derives its conditions from reviewed study patterns rather than a predetermined normative framework

article_title: Epistemic Dependence in AI-Mediated Learning
citation: Du Y, Yuan Y (2026) Epistemic dependence in AI-mediated learning. AI & SOCIETY. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-026-03294-1
title: Six diagnostic criteria for distinguishing productive epistemic reliance from harmful epistemic dependence
description: The review operationalises the boundary between productive reliance and harmful dependence through a six-criterion diagnostic table: "contestability, recoverability, transfer, traceability, distributed responsibility and epistemic plurality". Each criterion is stated as a contrast — e.g. transfer means capability persists when the system is absent, whereas dependence means performance collapses when AI support is withdrawn. The criteria are offered as diagnostic questions for research, design and pedagogy, not as a psychometric scale.
requirements: Empirical validation: the review states the criteria are not a psychometric scale and need empirical validation
constraints: No single criterion is decisive in every context; the pattern matters, as does the importance of the delegated judgement
target_learners: Learners in AI-mediated educational settings across disciplines
target_learning_goals: Developing epistemic judgement and responsible use of AI for knowledge-related tasks
examples: Table 2 contrasts productive reliance (learner can reconstruct main reasoning with reduced support) with harmful dependence (learner can reproduce a product but cannot explain how the conclusion was reached)

article_title: Epistemic Dependence in AI-Mediated Learning
citation: Du Y, Yuan Y (2026) Epistemic dependence in AI-mediated learning. AI & SOCIETY. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-026-03294-1
title: Four-pathway model linking AI affordances and institutional conditions to configurations of epistemic dependence
description: The review's central analysis specifies four parallel pathways — fluent authority, frictionless delegation, opaque synthesis and institutionalised dependence — linking contextual conditions to configurations of epistemic reliance. A pathway is explicitly not a deterministic causal chain: "Educational consequences are attached only to harmful configurations, while design, pedagogical and governance responses may intervene at more than one point in the model." The framework distinguishes direct educational evidence from adjacent-domain evidence treated as hypotheses.
requirements: Assessment of each pathway configuration through the six diagnostic criteria before attributing educational consequences
constraints: Pathways are plausible relations to be investigated, not established causal effects; adjacent-domain evidence from search, smartphones, medicine or aviation does not prove equivalent educational effects
target_learners: Learners, teachers and institutions using or provisioning generative AI in education
target_learning_goals: Preserving verification, evaluative and disciplinary judgement under AI mediation
examples: Pathway 1 treats fluent authority and personalised social presence; Pathway 2 treats delegation compressed into a single request-response cycle; Pathway 3 treats synthesis that hides evidential structure; Pathway 4 treats institutional procurement and platform integration
key_sources: Du Y, Yuan Y (2026) Epistemic dependence in AI-mediated learning. AI & SOCIETY. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-026-03294-1
