citation: Du Y, Yuan Y (2026) Epistemic dependence in AI-mediated learning. AI & SOCIETY. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-026-03294-1
title: Relational epistemic agency as the normative aim of AI-mediated learning
description: The review proposes relational epistemic agency as the normative orientation of AI-mediated learning: "the capacity to question, verify, compare, justify and know responsibly within relations of interdependence." The norm is compatible with substantial AI use and rejects both technological solutionism and simple anti-dependence positions; the practical objective is to configure dependence rather than eliminate it. It retains an explicit asymmetry: AI may shape reasoning without possessing reciprocal responsibility or legitimate authority.
requirements: Learners retain meaningful capacities to participate in how claims are formed, assessed and accepted, even while exercising agency through social, material and institutional supports
constraints: The review states this aim requires a substantive defence and is not an automatic consequence of using AI or of a discrete design intervention
target_learners: Learners at all levels using AI-mediated tools in education
target_learning_goals: Forming people who can ask questions, assess evidence, revise beliefs, give reasons and respond to challenge
examples: The review's test is functional and developmental: does the relation enlarge the learner's capacity to participate in epistemic practice, or merely deliver a product?

article_title: The impact of AI anxiety on career decisions of college students
citation: Duan, N., Li, L., Lin, G. & Chen, H. (2026). The impact of AI anxiety on career decisions of college students. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-37648-y
title: Integrated mediating-moderating model of AI anxiety and career decisions grounded in Career Construction Theory
description: The article develops a model, grounded in Career Construction Theory, in which AI anxiety affects career decisions through two routes: a direct path and an indirect path via career adaptability, which the article calls "a core psychological resource for individuals to cope with career challenges and uncertainty". Career adaptability is hypothesised to mediate the anxiety-to-decision link via resource depletion, while self-efficacy is hypothesised to moderate only the direct path. The empirical test confirmed mediation but not moderation, which the authors read as showing the adaptability pathway is central to how AI anxiety shapes career construction.

constraints: The article states results are most applicable to undergraduate populations in small and medium-sized cities in western China and should be cautiously generalised elsewhere

article_title: Educating minds with generative AI
citation: Laura Desiree Di Paolo, Andy Clark & Thomas Wachter. (2026). Educating minds with generative AI. Communications Psychology 4:128. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-026-00522-8
title: Education as a hybrid, multi-technological cognitive ecology under the 4E account of cognition
description: The article adopts the 4E account of cognition, in which the mind is embodied, embedded, enacted and sometimes extended, and applies it to schooling. It argues that schools are not neutral settings but hybrid cognitive ecologies: 'schools have always been hybrid, multi-technological cognitive ecologies, in which tools, materials, norms, and routines jointly structure learners'agency and epistemic habits over development'. Educational technologies are therefore never neutral tools but scaffolds that structure how future generations learn, and integrating GenAI means transforming the conditions under which cognition is enacted in schools.
requirements: Analysis of pedagogical impact must consider how learning environments are organised at scale, how agency is distributed, and which forms of knowledge are afforded over time, not only isolated individual outcomes
constraints: The framework is presented as a conceptual Perspective; the authors note emerging evidence on GenAI's cognitive effects 'remain preliminary'
target_learners: school students across developmental stages
target_learning_goals: development of cognition shaped by educational environments and tools

citation: Laura Desiree Di Paolo, Andy Clark & Thomas Wachter. (2026). Educating minds with generative AI. Communications Psychology 4:128. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-026-00522-8
title: GenAI as epistemic infrastructure that organises how knowledge is produced, circulated and legitimised
description: The article conceptualises GenAI as epistemic infrastructure: systems that 'do more than provide access to knowledge: they organise how knowledge is produced, circulated, evaluated, and legitimised'. When institutionalised in education, GenAI may assume this infrastructural role, as with AI-powered teaching management systems that consolidate curriculum planning, instructional support, assessment and progress reporting in one algorithmically mediated environment, imposing participation structures on teachers, administrators and parents and reshaping what counts as legitimate participation in the educational system.
requirements: Sustained and explicit reflection on pedagogical infrastructures and methodologies when GenAI is introduced
constraints: The authors warn that without such reflection, GenAI is likely to amplify values already dominant, such as performance, standardisation, optimisation, and error avoidance

teachers and educational institutions
target_learning_goals: epistemic practices and norms of knowledge production and evaluation

title: Education as a multitechnological cognitive ecology in which AI is one deliberately combined component among many
description: The article's concluding proposal is to conceive of education as a multitechnological cognitive ecology in which 'no single technology dominates: low-tech, embodied, and collaborative tools are combined with digital and AI-based resources according to pedagogical aims rather than market logic'. GenAI is framed not as a ready-made solution but as a diagnostic catalyst and stress test that exposes tensions between efficiency-oriented schooling and broader developmental aims, compelling a redesign guided by embodied, situated, collaborative and materially grounded learning. A principle of deliberate use calls for combining tools by pedagogical affordances and treating AI as one component among many.
requirements: A prepared conceptual and practical vocabulary for transformation; the article states the vision already exists but has lacked institutional will, technological ecology and resources
constraints: AI systems are among the most resource-intensive technologies deployed in education, with substantial energy, water and infrastructural costs, which the article says must be accounted for

target_learning_goals: the full range of human learning and development, including agency, critical judgment, collaboration and meaningful participation
examples: The article cites initiatives such as Learn Your Way, which transforms traditional textbooks into multimedia learning materials including audio lessons, narrated slides, and mind maps tailored to learners' preferences, as pointing toward this ecology.

citation: Li, H. and Zhang, W. (2026). Empowerment over enforcement: unpacking the psychological drivers of AI-assisted deep revision in EFL writing. Front. Psychol. 17:1871022. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1871022
title: SDT-plus-Psychological-Safety integrated model of AI-assisted deep revision, scoped by Cognitive Load Theory
description: The article proposes an integrated framework in which Self-Determination Theory's psychological needs explain deep cognitive engagement with generative AI in EFL writing, complemented by Cognitive Load Theory: APL functions as "a strategic cognitive scaffold" that offloads lower-level linguistic operations, freeing working memory for higher-level reflection, which then supports Perceived Competence, Intrinsic Motivation, and Psychological Safety as parallel pathways to Deep Revision Engagement. article_title: Coach not crutch: Evidence that AI can improve writing skill despite reducing effort
citation: Benjamin Lira, Todd Rogers, Daniel G. Goldstein, Lyle Ungar, and Angela L. Duckworth. (2025). Coach not crutch: Evidence that AI can improve writing skill despite reducing effort. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02880
title: Effort versus learning-environment framework: AI can reduce effort while improving the learning environment, with skill depending on the net effect
description: This framework holds that a practice tool affects skill acquisition through two opposing channels: the effort learners expend and the quality of the learning environment. As the article's Figure 1 caption states, "Relying on AI may cause people to exert less effort but improve the learning environment," and "Post-practice writing skill depends on the net effect of effort and the quality of the learning environment." The article uses this framework to explain why AI practice, despite reducing effort, produced larger skill gains: AI supplies high-quality, just-in-time, personalized examples illustrating otherwise abstract writing principles, consistent with literature on learning by observation.
requirements: A learning tool must improve the quality of examples or feedback available to the learner, not merely reduce effort, for net skill gains to occur
constraints: The article notes it is not clear whether the benefits of AI examples would generalize to other domains like math or computer programming, where a single example may reveal less of the producing process
In the experimental paradigm, participants interacted with AI only once; long-term effects of repeated use remain an open question the authors flag
target_learners: adult learners practicing professional writing skills
target_learning_goals: professional writing skill acquisition
examples: In Study 4, participants who only viewed an AI-generated example improved as much as those who practiced with the AI tool, supporting the examples mechanism
key_sources: Benjamin Lira, Todd Rogers, Daniel G. Goldstein, Lyle Ungar, and Angela L. Duckworth. (2025). Coach not crutch: Evidence that AI can improve writing skill despite reducing effort. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02880

article_title: DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation
citation: Vishal Kumar, Shubhra Mishra, Rebecca Hao, Rizwaan Malik, David Broman, Dorottya Demszky. (2025). DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation. NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: MATH-AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08283
title: 398-item evaluation dataset of teacher-requested geometric diagrams from Coteach
description: The dataset is drawn from real conversations in Coteach, an AI assistant for mathematics educators using the Illustrative Mathematics K-12 Math v.360 curriculum: 6,000 random teacher conversations were pulled and geometric constructions sampled. The article states, "We sampled 398 instances of geometric constructions (i.e. pairs of (teacher's request, generated code))", yielding 208 2D and 190 3D diagrams, with 12 used for calibration and 386 for the test set, enabling evaluation of diagrams used in the wild.
requirements: Grounded in real teacher-LLM interactions from one curriculum (Illustrative Mathematics)
constraints: Dataset is grounded in one curriculum; additional validation on other domains such as physics diagrams is needed per the article
target_learners: K-12 mathematics educators using AI assistants
target_learning_goals: Automatic evaluation of mathematically and spatially sound educational diagrams
examples: 208 2D diagrams (triangles, circles, rectangles) and 190 3D shape diagrams (prisms and cubes) sampled from 6,000 random Coteach conversations
key_sources: Vishal Kumar, Shubhra Mishra, Rebecca Hao, Rizwaan Malik, David Broman, Dorottya Demszky. (2025). DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation. NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: MATH-AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08283

article_title: DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation
citation: Vishal Kumar, Shubhra Mishra, Rebecca Hao, Rizwaan Malik, David Broman, Dorottya Demszky. (2025). DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation. NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: MATH-AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08283
title: DiagramIR back-translation pipeline with intermediate representation and rule-based checks
description: DiagramIR evaluates TikZ-generated diagrams by having an LLM translate the code into a schema-constrained intermediate representation, on which deterministic rule-based checks run (e.g., diagram fully in canvas, outlines closed). The article states that back-translating into an IR lets it "factor out surface form (code formatting, macro usage)", localize errors to explicit types, enable validators that run without a large model, and gain auditability, since checks explain precisely why a diagram passes or fails.
requirements: An LLM performs the semantic analysis (TikZ to IR), while rule-based checks perform the evaluation
constraints: The intermediate representation captures a restricted set of geometric primitives and relations; complex diagrams like multi-step constructions may require iterating on the schema and checks
Back-translation relies on LLMs for parsing TikZ into IRs, which introduced stochastic errors during IR generation
target_learners: K-12 mathematics educators and education-technology developers
target_learning_goals: Scalable automated evaluation of mathematical and spatial correctness of generated diagrams
examples: Rule-based checks include whether the diagram is fully in canvas, whether outlines are closed, and whether labels are associated with correct elements
key_sources: Vishal Kumar, Shubhra Mishra, Rebecca Hao, Rizwaan Malik, David Broman, Dorottya Demszky. (2025). DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation. NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: MATH-AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08283

article_title: DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation
citation: Vishal Kumar, Shubhra Mishra, Rebecca Hao, Rizwaan Malik, David Broman, Dorottya Demszky. (2025). DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation. NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: MATH-AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08283
title: Six-criterion rubric for mathematical and spatial correctness of math diagrams
description: The rubric assesses generated diagrams on two axes, mathematical correctness and spatial correctness, and was mirrored in the automated pipeline. The article says it was built to "capture criteria that (i) correspond to the most frequent failure modes observed in generated diagrams, (ii) are unambiguous, observable, and (iii) compatible with both human and LLM judging", with criteria such as labeled angles matching drawn angles and elements not problematically overlapping.
requirements: Criteria must be unambiguous, observable, and compatible with both human and LLM judging
constraints: Focuses on mathematical and spatial correctness, leaving out pedagogical usefulness, which the article calls a critical but more subjective dimension
target_learners: K-12 mathematics educators using AI assistants
target_learning_goals: Judging whether generated diagrams are mathematically and visually sound
examples: Rubric criteria include: Labeled angles match drawn angles; Diagram is fully in frame; Elements are scaled to be readable; Elements do not problematically overlap
key_sources: Vishal Kumar, Shubhra Mishra, Rebecca Hao, Rizwaan Malik, David Broman, Dorottya Demszky. (2025). DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation. NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: MATH-AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08283

article_title: DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation
citation: Vishal Kumar, Shubhra Mishra, Rebecca Hao, Rizwaan Malik, David Broman, Dorottya Demszky. (2025). DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation. NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: MATH-AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08283
title: Build education-technology evaluation on lightweight, low-cost pipelines that work with smaller models
description: The article argues that equitable education technology requires evaluation methods that run reliably and cheaply at scale, rather than depending on expensive frontier models. It states that "For education technology to be truly equitable, evaluation methods must work reliably with open models and lightweight pipelines that can be deployed at scale at low costs", and that AI education tools "need to be built at the lowest cost possible". Task-specific automated pipelines combining symbolic abstraction with lightweight inference are its proposed route.
requirements: Decoupling perception from verification so that validators can run without a large model
constraints: Closed-source frontier models are costly and impractical for resource-constrained educational deployments, per the article
target_learners: K-12 mathematics educators and their students in resource-constrained settings
target_learning_goals: Reliable automated quality evaluation of AI-generated instructional diagrams
examples: DiagramIR enabled GPT-4.1-Mini to evaluate diagrams comparably to GPT-5 as a judge at 10.3x lower total dataset cost

article_title: EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners
citation: Shenqi Lu and Liangwei Zhang. (2026). EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01196
title: EduSim-LLM, a zero-coding educational platform integrating LLMs with CoppeliaSim robot simulation
description: EduSim-LLM is an educational platform that integrates LLMs with the CoppeliaSim robotics simulator so users can control robots in natural language. Users type instructions and observe simulated robot behaviors, since it provides "a novice-friendly interface" allowing robot operation "without writing any code." It supports direct and autonomous interaction modes, multiple robot configurations including mobile robot teams and manipulators, and multiple LLM backends such as Groq's llama3-70b and Ollama's local llama3.1:8b. Its hierarchical pipeline comprises a natural language interface, an LLM-based instruction planner, a simulation control backend, and a Gradio user interaction frontend.
requirements: Requires an LLM backend (e.g., Groq's llama3-70b versatile or Ollama's local llama3.1:8b), LangChain for prompt administration, and the CoppeliaSim simulator with its remote API
constraints: Validated in simulation environments with YouBot robots; no physical-robot deployment is reported
target_learners: beginners and non-experts in robotics
learners and instructors with limited programming experience
target_learning_goals: natural-language robot control
educational robotics programming
examples: The experiment test platform integrated CoppeliaSim with three YouBot robots: one with a vision sensor, one with a transport box for obstacle removal, and one with a robotic arm for grasping.
key_sources: Shenqi Lu and Liangwei Zhang. (2026). EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01196

article_title: EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners
citation: Shenqi Lu and Liangwei Zhang. (2026). EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01196
title: Four-module architecture for language-driven robot control in educational simulation
description: The article describes a hierarchical instruction processing pipeline in which natural language is translated into executable robot behavior. The architecture "consist of four modules: (1) Natural language interface, (2) LLM-based instruction planner, (3) Simulation control backend, and (4) User interaction frontend." User instructions are sent to an LLM via structured prompts, and the LLM output is converted into Python control code executed in CoppeliaSim through action primitives such as moveForward, moveToXY, and closeGripper. The backend also implements 7-stage progressive deceleration with overshoot detection and maintains trajectory history for navigation.
requirements: A structured prompt template and a pre-constructed control function library are needed so the LLM planner can translate directives into robot-compatible action primitives
constraints: The LLM planner depends on the language-model backend chosen; the backend was evaluated with Groq's llama-3.3-70b-versatile
target_learners: beginner robotics learners
non-expert robot users
target_learning_goals: intuitive natural-language control of robotic systems
understanding language-to-action translation in robotics
examples: The executeActionCode function dynamically parses LLM-generated commands into sequential Python calls executed via CoppeliaSim's remote API.
key_sources: Shenqi Lu and Liangwei Zhang. (2026). EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01196

citation: Shenqi Lu and Liangwei Zhang. (2026). EduSim-LLM: An Educational Platform Integrating Large Language Models and Robotic Simulation for Beginners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.01196
title: Combine structured prompt templates with a pre-constructed robot function library to improve LLM instruction-parsing reliability
description: The principle is to send user instructions to the LLM through a structured prompt template and to execute LLM output against a pre-constructed library of robot action functions, so that natural language is converted into reliable, executable control code. The article reports that "The integration of structured prompts and a pre-constructed function library improves parsing reliability and system responsiveness." This pairing is how EduSim-LLM converts free-form instructions into sequential Python calls in CoppeliaSim.
requirements: A structured prompt template and a pre-constructed library of robot control functions (e.g., moveForward, moveToXY, closeGripper) that the LLM-generated code can call
constraints: Evaluated with Groq's llama-3.3-70b-versatile in CoppeliaSim simulation; the article reports reliability for these settings
target_learners: beginners in robotics
non-expert robot users
target_learning_goals: reliable natural-language control of robots
learning language-to-action translation
examples: EduSim-LLM applies a structured prompt template to convert natural language into Python control code, with executeActionCode parsing LLM-generated commands into sequential Python calls.

article_title: The Aftermath of DrawEduMath: Vision Language Models Underperform with Struggling Students and Misdiagnose Errors
citation: Li Lucy, Albert Zhang, Nathan Anderson, Ryan Knight, Kyle Lo. (2026). The Aftermath of DrawEduMath: Vision Language Models Underperform with Struggling Students and Misdiagnose Errors. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00925
title: DrawEduMath benchmark of teacher-annotated student hand-drawn math responses
description: DrawEduMath is an English-language benchmark pairing 2,030 images of real K-12 students' handwritten responses to math problems with three data types: 2.0k+ free-form teacher captions, 44.4k+ synthetic QA pairs, and 11.6k+ teacher-written QA pairs. It draws from the ASSISTments platform and a taxonomy the paper simplifies into image creation and medium, correctness & errors, and content description question types. The authors describe it as involving "noisy, naturalistic data pulled from an online learning platform," and use it to snapshot 11 VLMs' performance.
requirements: Teacher annotations and QA pairs from experienced teachers
An LLM-as-judge scoring setup (majority vote of Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4o) to binarize answer similarity
constraints: Single English-language benchmark from one platform (ASSISTments); estimated 85% of images from Title I schools; questions reflect what was salient to Teaching Lab annotators
target_learners: K-12 mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Mathematics problem solving and error diagnosis
examples: Evaluation of 11 VLMs released in 2025 across four developers, with a leaderboard continuously updated for a year after release
key_sources: Li Lucy, Albert Zhang, Nathan Anderson, Ryan Knight, Kyle Lo. (2026). The Aftermath of DrawEduMath: Vision Language Models Underperform with Struggling Students and Misdiagnose Errors. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00925

article_title: EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice
citation: Cameron Mohne, Nicholas Vo, Dora Demszky, Chris Piech. (2026). EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11444
title: EducaSim: an LLM-agent simulation environment for teacher role-play practice
description: EducaSim is a web application that simulates a small-group CS1 section so teachers-in-training can practice instruction through role play without live personnel. Users interact by voice or text; a runnable IDE's output is piped into agent memories, and post-session feedback combines talktime statistics, LLM-generated feedback, and self-reflection prompts. It was deployed as an optional preparation tool for 1,300 volunteer teachers serving about 20,000 students, with sessions costing "$0.05 - $0.10 depending on duration".
requirements: Requires course materials (e.g., lecture transcripts) that can be chunked and loaded into agent memories via the admin-side upload interface
constraints: The framework cannot fully represent the diversity of individual human understandings and intentionally omits identity traits such as cultural context or neurodivergence that the authors say cannot be ethically represented using a LLM
target_learners: Novice and pre-service teachers in massive online courses
target_learning_goals: Instructional practice skills such as explaining concepts, engaging students, responding to questions, and noticing gaps in learning
examples: Deployed for three exercises aligned to weeks three, four, and six of an open-access CS1 course; 254 sessions averaging 15 minutes 45 seconds
key_sources: Cameron Mohne, Nicholas Vo, Dora Demszky, Chris Piech. (2026). EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11444

article_title: EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice
citation: Cameron Mohne, Nicholas Vo, Dora Demszky, Chris Piech. (2026). EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11444
title: Behavior-based persona and course-grounded memory architecture for simulated students
description: EducaSim's student-agent architecture synthesizes generative agents with personas and memories, domain-contextualized memories aligned with actual course material, and a classroom dynamic tree using LLM as a judge. Personas are defined by pedagogically relevant behaviors rather than demographic identity traits, including "(1) name, (2) engagement style, and (3) speech style". Course texts are chunked chronologically, tagged with low/medium/high engagement levels, and prepended with strings describing what the student does and does not know; retrieval scores memories by recency, importance, and cosine-similarity, returning the top-k.
requirements: Course materials must be ordered chronologically based on when a student would encounter them so teachers can refer to past material
constraints: Agents are an approximation, not a perfect representation, of student behavior and cannot fully represent the diversity of human understandings or confusions
target_learners: Teachers-in-training practicing instruction
target_learning_goals: Realistic simulated student interactions grounded in actual course content
examples: Memories carry engagement-level strings defining knowledge states; Figure 2 visualizes populated student memories at varying engagement levels
key_sources: Cameron Mohne, Nicholas Vo, Dora Demszky, Chris Piech. (2026). EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11444

article_title: EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice
citation: Cameron Mohne, Nicholas Vo, Dora Demszky, Chris Piech. (2026). EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11444
title: Post-session feedback combining talktime statistics, LLM analysis, and self-reflection prompts
description: EducaSim's feedback pattern layers three components after each session: talktime statistics totaling each speaker's words and silence; LLM-generated feedback identifying instructional behaviors such as teacher uptake, talk proportions, questioning quality, and evidence of student misconceptions; and reflective prompts for teacher self-assessment. A separate LLM infers reasons behind instructional challenges, selects remediation strategies, and highlights what the teacher did well, such as "answering questions, revoicing student understandings, or attempts at engaging students".
requirements: Requires a full session transcript of teacher-student interaction to analyze
constraints: Feedback effectiveness depends on the teacher's uptake; the pattern was designed for CS1 small-group scenarios
target_learners: Teachers-in-training reviewing their practice
target_learning_goals: Improving instructional behaviors such as uptake, questioning, and student engagement
examples: One teacher reported reviewing the feedback and changing her approach, which produced more student replies in her second session
key_sources: Cameron Mohne, Nicholas Vo, Dora Demszky, Chris Piech. (2026). EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11444

article_title: DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring
citation: Bingxi Zhao, Jiahao Zhang, Xubin Ren, Zirui Guo, Tianzhe Chu, Yi Ma, Chao Huang. (2026). DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring. Technical Report, The University of Hong Kong. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26962
title: Hybrid Personalization Engine: closed-loop personalization coupling static knowledge grounding with dynamic learner memory
description: The Hybrid Personalization Engine is DeepTutor's explanatory architecture for personalized tutoring: it "couples static knowledge grounding with dynamic learner memory", pairing Static Knowledge Grounding (dual-index retrieval over course content) with Dynamic Personal Memory that distills multi-turn interactions into an evolving learner profile D=(Ds,Dw,Dr). The closed loop operationalizes formative assessment: "weaknesses diagnosed during problem tutoring propagate to Dw and directly shape which questions are generated next", while practice outcomes refine future explanations. Each completed interaction appends a trace tree and updates the profile, so every interaction personalizes the next.
requirements: requires a structured memory capturing fine-grained interaction histories rather than scalar skill scores
requires modules that share and continuously update the learner memory
constraints: quantitative evaluation covers only the tutoring core; longitudinal evaluation of the extension layers is left for future work
target_learners: university-level students across humanities, sciences, engineering, business, and frontier research domains
target_learning_goals: diagnosing and remediating individual knowledge gaps
difficulty-calibrated practice
citation-grounded explanation
examples: Tutoring proceeds through investigate, guided solving, and iterative writing stages; question generation separates idea selection from critic-guided question–answer–explanation construction.
key_sources: Bingxi Zhao, Jiahao Zhang, Xubin Ren, Zirui Guo, Tianzhe Chu, Yi Ma, Chao Huang. (2026). DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring. Technical Report, The University of Hong Kong. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26962

article_title: DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring
citation: Bingxi Zhao, Jiahao Zhang, Xubin Ren, Zirui Guo, Tianzhe Chu, Yi Ma, Chao Huang. (2026). DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring. Technical Report, The University of Hong Kong. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26962
title: Trace Forest: hierarchical three-level learner memory with programmatic toolkit
description: The Trace Forest is DeepTutor's hierarchical memory in which each tree records one complete tutoring interaction as a multi-resolution, semantically searchable artifact. "Nodes are organized into three levels: Level 1 stores session-level input and a global summary; Level 2 captures intermediate planning units; and Level 3 preserves fine-grained execution records including tool outputs, evidence, and validation outcomes." Every node carries a dense embedding for similarity-based retrieval. A TraceToolkit exposes three operations — SearchTrace, ListTraces, and ReadNodes — letting every agent explore learner history at the resolution it needs.
requirements: every node carries a dense embedding to enable similarity-based retrieval across the forest
target_learners: individual university-level learners in multi-turn tutoring
target_learning_goals: fine-grained learner profiling for gap-aware tutoring and practice generation
examples: Three memory agents actively query the TraceToolkit to compare latest behavior against cross-session patterns before updating the profile.
key_sources: Bingxi Zhao, Jiahao Zhang, Xubin Ren, Zirui Guo, Tianzhe Chu, Yi Ma, Chao Huang. (2026). DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring. Technical Report, The University of Hong Kong. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26962

article_title: DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring
citation: Bingxi Zhao, Jiahao Zhang, Xubin Ren, Zirui Guo, Tianzhe Chu, Yi Ma, Chao Huang. (2026). DeepTutor: Towards Agentic Personalized Tutoring. Technical Report, The University of Hong Kong. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26962
title: TutorBench: student-centric interactive benchmark with source-grounded learner profiles
description: TutorBench is a student-centric benchmark that "couples a detailed learner persona with source-grounded knowledge gaps and an interactive tutoring task". It draws on 30 knowledge bases spanning five broad disciplines, instantiates three learner profiles per knowledge base for 90 profiles, and retains exactly three accepted interactive tasks per profile, yielding 270 tasks. Gaps are typed as misconceptions, incomplete understanding, and missing knowledge, each anchored to specific source pages. Evaluation uses a first-person LLM student simulator and personalized rubrics, with entries checked by human reviewers before release.
requirements: profiles and tasks undergo human review for factual correctness, plausibility, gap–task consistency, and pedagogical naturalness
constraints: relies on LLM-powered student simulators and rubric-based assessors, inheriting a gap between controlled simulation and real learner behavior
target_learners: simulated university-level students at beginner, intermediate, and advanced levels
target_learning_goals: adaptive tutoring behavior across multi-turn dialogue and customized practice generation
examples: Each entry carries three source-grounded knowledge gaps, each anchored to specific pages from the source KB materials.

article_title: EduGage: Methods and Dataset for Sensor-Based Momentary Assessment of Engagement in Self-Guided Video Learning
citation: Zikang Leng, Edan Eyal, Yingtian Shi, Jiaman He, Yaqi Liu, and Thomas Plötz. (2026). EduGage: A Multimodal Dataset and Benchmark for Sensor-Based Momentary Assessment of Engagement in Self-Guided Video Learning. Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Ubiquitous Technol. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01238
title: EduGage dataset: synchronized multimodal sensor streams with minute-level engagement-probe ratings in self-guided video learning
description: The EduGage dataset contains "16 participants, 64 video-viewing sessions, 699 probe-aligned windows, and approximately 12 hours of synchronized multimodal recordings". Each window links the sensor data preceding an engagement probe to its self-report label, video identifier, segment timing, contextual metadata, and quiz responses, released with participant-grouped evaluation splits and study materials on Figshare to support reproducible engagement modeling research.
requirements: Released with fixed participant-grouped splits to avoid participant-level leakage and preserve label coverage across folds; accompanied by preprocessing and benchmark code for reproducing the participant-independent protocol
constraints: The reported label represents a specific attentional aspect of engagement rather than the complete multidimensional engagement construct
target_learners: college students in self-guided asynchronous video learning
target_learning_goals: fine-grained momentary engagement estimation during instructional video viewing
examples: Dataset available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.32145994 with accompanying preprocessing, modeling, and benchmark code in the public GitHub repository

citation: Zikang Leng, Edan Eyal, Yingtian Shi, Jiaman He, Yaqi Liu, and Thomas Plötz. (2026). Wearable Ubiquitous Ubiquitous Technol. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01238
title: Engagement-probe ratings as a pragmatic single-item operationalization of the attentional aspect of momentary engagement
description: The article frames its single-item probe ("How difficult was it to pay attention during the last minute of the lecture?") as a temporally localized reference signal targeting perceived difficulty sustaining attention, explicitly not equivalent to engagement as a whole. The authors write that they use it "as a narrower, engagement-related attentional experience rather than as engagement itself or its direct inverse", recognizing that a learner may remain engaged with demanding material while finding attention hard to sustain.
requirements: Repeated in-situ administration at approximately one-minute intervals placed at natural stopping points in the content, with a short practice phase so participants learn the scale before the main task
constraints: The single-item measure is not intended to reproduce comprehensive multidimensional engagement instruments; its narrower construct coverage is acknowledged as a limitation
target_learners: college students in self-guided video learning
target_learning_goals: momentary perceived difficulty of sustaining attention during instruction
examples: During the study, the video paused at each probe and the screen displayed the abbreviated cue "Report engagement now," with participants responding on the 1–5 scale learned during training

article_title: EduGage: Methods and Dataset for Sensor-Based Momentary Assessment of Engagement in Self-Guided Video Learning
citation: Zikang Leng, Edan Eyal, Yingtian Shi, Jiaman He, Yaqi Liu, and Thomas Plötz. (2026). EduGage: A Multimodal Dataset and Benchmark for Sensor-Based Momentary Assessment of Engagement in Self-Guided Video Learning. Proc. ACM Interact. Mob. Wearable Ubiquitous Ubiquitous Technol. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01238
title: Deploy engagement sensing for broad temporal patterns and support triggers, not for exact point-level prediction of self-reported attention difficulty
description: Because engagement is partially latent and the self-report target is subjective, the article argues wearable sensing can only approximate moment-to-moment dynamics. The authors write that "in practical learning systems, such models may be most useful for identifying broader temporal patterns, such as sustained increases in attention difficulty or video segments where learners may benefit from reflection, review, or support" rather than expecting perfect agreement with self-report.
requirements: Models that capture meaningful temporal structure in attention difficulty, evaluated with participant-independent splits so performance reflects generalization to new learners
constraints: Exact self-reported scores remain difficult to predict; prediction discrepancies are expected because self-reports are subjective and physiological signals are indirect and may reflect fatigue, prior knowledge, video difficulty, movement, or distraction
target_learners: college students in self-guided asynchronous video learning
target_learning_goals: identifying periods of sustained attention difficulty and video segments needing review or support

title: ECNUClaw: an open-source Python framework for learner-profiled intelligent study companions in K-12 education
description: ECNUClaw is an open-source framework for building learner-profiled intelligent study companions in K-12 education. It implements "a five-dimension learner profile—covering cognitive, behavioral, emotional, metacognitive, and contextual dimensions" extracted at each dialogue turn, and feeds profile updates into an adaptive strategy engine. The framework is implemented in Python, supports seven Chinese LLM providers through an OpenAI-compatible adapter layer, and its source code is publicly released on GitHub.

title: Education Brain model: a bio-inspired three-layer architecture for educational AI systems
description: The Education Brain model, proposed by Zhang and Xu, is a computing architecture for educational AI systems modeled after the human nervous system. It divides a system into "three functional layers analogous to the sensory, central, and motor nervous systems": a sensory layer capturing multi-modal educational data, a central layer processing data through AI, knowledge graphs, and learner models to generate pedagogical decisions, and a motor layer outputting interventions. ECNUClaw adopts this as its high-level architectural pattern, mapping signal extraction, profile/strategy generation, and adaptive prompt output to the three layers.
requirements: An educational AI system must separate data capture, pedagogical decision generation, and intervention output into distinct functional layers
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Personalized, adaptive educational support delivered by AI systems
examples: ECNUClaw separates its components into signal extraction (sensory), profile construction and strategy generation (central), and adaptive prompt output (motor) layers

title: Human-AI Collaborative IQ: education should cultivate learners' capacity to collaborate with AI rather than receive answers
description: Human-AI Collaborative IQ is the concept that "a new form of intelligence emerges when humans and AI systems collaborate effectively, and that education should cultivate this collaborative capacity." Under this view, AI should enhance the learner's own thinking and metacognition rather than deliver answers. ECNUClaw encodes the principle in its HEADS prompt templates, which prohibit direct answer-giving and prescribe Socratic questioning, grounded in Vygotsky's zone of proximal development with scaffolding gradually withdrawn as competence grows.
requirements: The companion must guide learners toward self-discovery through questioning rather than providing answers directly
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive development, self-discovery, and skills for collaborating with AI
examples: The HEADS base template includes the constraints "Never give direct answers. Use Socratic questioning to guide self-discovery" and "Help the learner develop skills for collaborating with AI, not dependency on AI"

title: Digital Portrait Three-Layer Framework for dynamic, multi-source learner assessment
description: The Digital Portrait Three-Layer Framework, by Zhang et al., argues that traditional test-score-based evaluation captures only a narrow slice of learner ability. It comprises "an indicator system layer that defines what to measure, a data practice layer that collects and fuses multi-source behavioral and academic data, and a digital portrait layer that constructs a dynamic, visualized learner profile for educational decision-making." The framework motivated ECNUClaw's five-dimension profile structure, which captures behaviors, emotional states, and metacognitive patterns beyond academic performance.

target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Comprehensive, dynamic learner assessment for educational decision-making
examples: ECNUClaw's five-dimension profile—cognitive, behavioral, emotional, metacognitive, contextual—directly implements the framework's call for multi-dimensional profiling

title: Five-dimension learner profile maintained across subject switches from dialogue signals
description: ECNUClaw constructs and maintains a learner profile across five dimensions—cognitive, behavioral, emotional, metacognitive, and contextual—stored as per-dimension JSON fields in a SQLite table. Signals are extracted at every turn via keyword dictionaries and turn counting: Bloom's taxonomy level from question patterns, weak knowledge points from error markers, mood and self-efficacy from sentiment keywords, and reflection and strategy preference from metacognitive markers. All subject companions share a single memory store, so the profile persists across subject switches.
requirements: Each dimension is updated after every interaction via update_profile_from_interaction, which processes accumulated user messages for signals
constraints: The keyword-based signal extraction is the most significant limitation: a student expressing frustration without predefined keywords will not have their profile updated, and Bloom's classification relies on surface-level question patterns rather than semantic understanding
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Personalized guidance informed by cognitive, behavioral, emotional, metacognitive, and contextual learner state
examples: In the paper's example dialogue, a frustration marker triggers a self-efficacy decrement of 0.1 and adds 'fractions' as a weak topic, and the strategy engine steps back to basics with increased encouragement

title: Engagement forecasting as a supervised week-ahead prediction task in ITS
description: Engagement forecasting is framed as a supervised prediction task estimating a learner's next-week engagement from prior ITS interaction traces. The article defines it as "a supervised, week-ahead regression task within an ITS predicting two observable outcomes: minutes practiced (effort) and new skills mastered (progress)". It complements fine-grained EDM tasks (affect detection, wheel-spinning, dropout prediction) by operating at a weekly timescale aligned with instructional rhythms, and its explainability analysis positions forecasts as decision-support signals for tutors and students rather than direct measures of motivation or learning.

article_title: Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks
citation: Enkelejda Kasneci and Gjergji Kasneci. (2026). Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14604
title: Taxonomy of pedagogical sycophancy: frame abandonment distinguished from factual error via CS-SYC, AUTH-SYC, FACE-SYC, and DIR-SYC subtypes
description: The paper defines pedagogical sycophancy as pressure-contingent validation of a misconception after the tutor is pushed to agree, distinguishing it from ordinary factual error. Its core organizing concept is "frame abandonment-a tutoring-specific failure where agreeableness collapses the corrective friction needed for conceptual change". The taxonomy decomposes this into channels: CS-SYC (context-switch frame attack, where a student invokes valid but instructionally inappropriate jargon), AUTH-SYC (deference to notes, textbooks, or instructors), FACE-SYC (social-affective face-saving that overrides corrective duty), and DIR-SYC (direct endorsement), with EVADE as a sixth judge label. A rubric operationalizes the labels for automated judging.
requirements: Judging requires the full four-turn dialogue for context but labels only the post-pressure response T2, using a shared rubric with structured JSON outputs
constraints: The three pressure modes are intended as core tutoring-relevant channels rather than an exhaustive ontology of all possible pedagogical failures
target_learners: students interacting with LLM tutors in math, physics, economics, chemistry, biology, and computer science
target_learning_goals: accurate conceptual understanding resistant to misconception reinforcement under social-epistemic pressure
examples: Figure 2 depicts a student pressure turn inducing misconception validation via the three channels, with the label determined from the tutor's post-pressure response
key_sources: Enkelejda Kasneci and Gjergji Kasneci. (2026). Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14604

article_title: Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks
citation: Enkelejda Kasneci and Gjergji Kasneci. (2026). Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14604
title: EDUFRAMETRAP: a six-domain tutoring sycophancy benchmark of 360 trap families yielding 3,240 confidence-by-pressure instances
description: EDUFRAMETRAP is a controlled pre-deployment benchmark for tutoring robustness under social-epistemic pressure. Its atomic unit is a trap family pairing a misconception wrong in the default instructional setting with a plausible niche framing a student might invoke. The article states "We construct360 trap familiesacross 6 domains (Table 1)" and each family is instantiated by crossing three confidence levels with three pressure modes, so "This yields 9 variants per trap family (3,240 instances total)". Dialogues are four turns (S1-T1-S2-T2) and the post-pressure response T2 is scored. Trap families are generated by a Builder LLM and filtered by a separate Validator LLM, with a leakage-resistant trap-family-level split (108 dev, 252 test).
requirements: Deterministic template selection of student pressure wording per (trap, confidence, mode) ensures exact reproducibility
Two independent LLM judges score each T2, with human adjudication of disagreements
constraints: The benchmark is synthetic by design and a controlled pre-deployment risk signal, not a substitute for naturalistic tutoring studies or longitudinal learning-outcome evaluations
target_learners: LLM tutoring systems serving students in six STEM and social-science domains
target_learning_goals: maintaining kind-but-correct correction of misconceptions under agreement-seeking pressure
examples: Code, data, evaluation scripts, and run-stamped JSONL logs are released at the project GitHub repository for exact re-analysis
key_sources: Enkelejda Kasneci and Gjergji Kasneci. (2026). Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14604

article_title: Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks
citation: Enkelejda Kasneci and Gjergji Kasneci. (2026). Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14604
title: Tutoring evaluations should report pressure-resolved failure rates, confidence-conditioned deference profiles, and judge-disagreement reliability signals
description: The paper recommends that educational LLM evaluations treat pedagogical sycophancy under social-epistemic pressure as a safety failure and measure it explicitly before deployment. It states: "We recommend that evaluations report (i) pressure-specific failure rates, (ii) confidence-conditioned “deference profiles” rather than a single aggregate, and (iii) explicitreliability signals such as judge disagreement and human-validated subsets where feasible." The rationale is that a single aggregate score can hide the most safety-relevant cases, since borderline responses mix correction with reassurance, and warm hedged correction can resemble warm wrong capitulation.
requirements: Two-judge disagreement tracking and human adjudication of ambiguous cases, because polite capitulation can resemble good pedagogy
constraints: Reported rates should be interpreted together with disagreement and audit statistics, not as judge-independent facts
target_learners: benchmark creators, model developers, and deployers of LLM tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: avoiding pressure-contingent validation of learner misconceptions in deployed tutors
examples: The paper's own evaluation reports adjudicated SYC and DISAGREE rates per tutor, per pressure mode, per confidence level, and per domain rather than a single leaderboard score

title: CyberScholar: a rubric-aligned GenAI writing-feedback platform using RAG, rubric agents, and a curated knowledge base
description: CyberScholar is a multimodal, multilingual writing workspace for Grade 4 and above in which students draft in a vertically divided editor with AI and human dialogue tools on the right. Its workflow includes CyberHelper for drafting assistance, CyberReviewer, which "delivers quantitative feedback with qualitative narrative justification from AI rubric agents, peers, teachers, or self-reflection," a Composition Report analyzing AI use via logfile data, teacher-built Rubric Agents using multiple-pass prompt engineering, and a Knowledge Base of "curated, educator-validated domain content stored in a vector database for retrieval -augmented generation." article_title: The efficiency-gain illusion: People underestimate the rate of AI use and overestimate its benefits on simple tasks
citation: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). The efficiency-gain illusion: People underestimate the rate of AI use and overestimate its benefits on simple tasks. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22687
title: Efficiency-gain illusions framework: two distinct miscalibration patterns (time vs. effort) underlying AI-use decisions
description: The article proposes that decisions to use AI rest on a cost-benefit comparison requiring calibration of one's own capabilities and the tool's, and identifies two named illusions: a speedup illusion, where predicted time savings exceed actual savings, and an offloading illusion, where predicted effort reduction exceeds actual reduction. The two follow distinct mechanisms: "for time, people misjudge the efficiency of AI assistance, while for effort, they misevaluate how hard it would be to complete tasks independently." Both miscalibrations push people toward AI use and, via a carryover effect, can form an overreliance feedback loop.
requirements: Applies to cognitively simple tasks completable in under five minutes independently, as studied in the article's task set
constraints: The article states it focuses on human miscalibration rather than AI capability, and AI capabilities change over time
target_learners: Adult AI chatbot users (US adult Prolific samples)
target_learning_goals: Well-calibrated decisions about when to use AI assistance versus completing tasks independently
examples: Study 2 operationalized the illusions formally: the speedup illusion holds when predicted minus predicted-AI time exceeds actual minus actual-AI time, and the offloading illusion analogously for NASA-TLX effort ratings.
key_sources: Sunny Yu, Myra Cheng, Ahmad Jabbar, Ilia Sucholutsky, Katherine M. Collins, Dan Jurafsky, Robert D. Hawkins. (2026). The efficiency-gain illusion: People underestimate the rate of AI use and overestimate its benefits on simple tasks. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22687

title: 24-task set derived from the Taxonomy of User Needs and Actions (TUNA) with easy and difficult variants
description: The article constructed a set of 24 tasks "derived from the Taxonomy of User Needs and Actions (TUNA), a framework of different ways that people use AI based on different degrees of cognitive effort required." The tasks span TUNA's four categories — information seeking, information processing and synthesis, procedural guidance and execution, and content creation and transformation — with three task types per category and an easy and difficult variant per task (e.g., naming one versus five Olympic medalists). All tasks were completable in under five minutes independently and were used across the three studies with a GPT-4o chat interface.

article_title: Practitioner beliefs and behaviors in AI-enhanced education: DOT framework survey evidence
citation: Gibson, D., Azukas, M. E., & Knezek, G. (2025). Practitioner Beliefs and Behaviors in AI-Enhanced Education: DOT Framework Survey Evidence. https://doi.org/10.70725/846858waolmj
title: The DOT Framework: combining Design Thinking and Open Systems theory to guide intentional, human-centered AI-enhanced teaching
description: The DOT Framework combines the iterative logic of Design Thinking (empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test) with the Open Systems Model (environment, input, process, structure, output, feedback) to guide Transformation of teaching through intentional AI enhancement. It positions AI as "a co-intelligent collaborator, an adaptive, semi-autonomous cognitive partner whose contributions are shaped and evaluated through ongoing human guidance." The framework operates at micro-system (classroom) and macro-system (institution) levels simultaneously, situating AI use within a pedagogical and institutional ecosystem that values human judgment, iterative refinement, and systemic coherence. The survey provides preliminary descriptive support for it as a model of practitioner beliefs and practices.

constraints: The article states current empirical support is preliminary and descriptive rather than confirmatory validation, and the framework's link to instructional outcomes remains untested

The pattern links museum field data through student-created materials to intended community outcomes, followed by co-dissemination via open-source release and student co-authorship.

Boundary-spanning events at planned weeks of the course

article_title: Cross-Dataset Bloom Question Classification: Supervised Models and Prompted LLMs
citation: Abdolali Faraji, Mohammadreza Molavi, Zohreh Rasoulkhani, Mohammadreza Tavakoli, and Gábor Kismihók. (2026). Cross-Dataset Bloom Question Classification: Supervised Models and Prompted LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13684
title: Lightweight UI for instructor-driven Bloom classification built on the selected-questions-verbs prompt
description: A lightweight tool built on the article's best-performing prompting strategy. Instructors provide a small set of example questions per Bloom level for their context; the tool "extracts key action verbs from these examples" and uses them with the examples to construct the classification prompt. Users upload question sets in CSV/Excel and receive Bloom-level predictions in structured output. A user study with N=50 Prolific participants reported low workload (NASA-TLX means: mental demand 2.32, effort 2.46, frustration 1.68) and mean SUS of 78.2 (SD 14.07).
requirements: Instructors must supply example questions per Bloom level for their specific course, topic, or learning objectives
constraints: The article notes feedback from real instructors would provide more precise insights for practical deployment, as the UI was tested with pilot users
target_learners: instructors classifying large question banks
target_learning_goals: automatic Bloom-level classification of assessment questions
examples: In the usability study, participants interacted with the UI for 10 minutes for one of their real courses and added Bloom-level examples
key_sources: Abdolali Faraji, Mohammadreza Molavi, Zohreh Rasoulkhani, Mohammadreza Tavakoli, and Gábor Kismihók. (2026). Cross-Dataset Bloom Question Classification: Supervised Models and Prompted LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13684

article_title: Cross-Dataset Bloom Question Classification: Supervised Models and Prompted LLMs
citation: Abdolali Faraji, Mohammadreza Molavi, Zohreh Rasoulkhani, Mohammadreza Tavakoli, and Gábor Kismihók. (2026). Cross-Dataset Bloom Question Classification: Supervised Models and Prompted LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13684
title: Cross-dataset Bloom classification benchmark corpus of five datasets totaling 4,179 questions
description: The study assembled five Bloom's taxonomy–annotated question datasets totaling 4,179 questions, mapped to the revised Bloom cognitive levels for comparability. Four are human-authored sets frequently used in Bloom classification research (Yahya et al. 2012: 600; Sangodiah et al. 2017: 415; Mohammed and Omar 2020: 126; Gani et al. 2023: 1,200 questions), plus an LLM-generated set from Scaria et al. 2024 (1,838 questions) included to reflect the growing prevalence of AI-generated educational content. Code, prompts, and datasets are available in the authors' GitLab repository.
requirements: All labels must be mapped to the revised Bloom taxonomy to ensure consistency across datasets
target_learners: researchers evaluating Bloom question classification methods
target_learning_goals: cross-dataset evaluation of Bloom-level question classification
examples: Each dataset served once as the training source in the cross-dataset evaluation, with the other four treated as unseen test sets

article_title: Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment
citation: Brandon Pardi, Garret Castro, Michael Pisman, Avash Adhikari, and Santosh Chandrasekhar. (2026). Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15572
title: Three-stage methodology combining student surveys, LLM skill extraction, and dynamic preference-aware matching
description: The article proposes a data-driven team-formation framework with three stages: "student surveys to capture detailed and granular skill sets and project preferences; (2) LLM-driven extraction of essential project skills from sponsor-provided descriptions; and (3) a dynamic matching algorithm that iteratively prioritizes currently unfulfilled skills and integrates student preferences during team formation." It is positioned as combining bottom-up student agency with top-down project skill requirements in a single scalable pipeline, addressing gaps in tools like CATME Team-Maker that do not match skills to projects or dynamically integrate preferences.
requirements: Students complete skill and preference surveys at the start of the course, with project summary descriptions available beforehand
A skill list predetermined from prior and anticipated project requirements
LLM-generated skill ratings are manually reviewed before use
constraints: Relies on self-reported skills and preferences, leaving it vulnerable to misrepresentation
The preference weight parameter requires manual tuning
LLM-generated project skills still require manual verification
target_learners: senior-level computer science capstone students
target_learning_goals: effective team formation for project-based learning
student motivation and agency through preference alignment
examples: Validated on UC Merced capstone data from Fall 2023 (16 projects, 68 students) and Spring 2024 (27 projects, 122 students)
key_sources: Brandon Pardi, Garret Castro, Michael Pisman, Avash Adhikari, and Santosh Chandrasekhar. (2026). Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15572

article_title: Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment
citation: Brandon Pardi, Garret Castro, Michael Pisman, Avash Adhikari, and Santosh Chandrasekhar. (2026). Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15572
title: LLM-based project skill extraction workflow using a fine-tuned Llama 3.2 instruct model
description: A component that parses sponsor-provided project descriptions and asks an LLM to rate the necessity of each skill on a 0–5 scale, where "a 5 is given when a skill is realistically indispensable for a project." The implementation "uses a preexisting fine-tuned instruct version of Llama 3.2" and produces "a structured JSON list of skills and their rated necessity, that is then manually reviewed and given minor or no corrections." The prompt includes caveats about multiple possible solution paths (e.g., Pytorch or Tensorflow) so the model considers multiple potential solutions.
requirements: The same skill list given to students is sent to the LLM with each project description
Manual review of the LLM's structured JSON skill ratings
constraints: The article notes LLM-generated project skills still require manual verification
target_learners: senior-level computer science capstone students
target_learning_goals: accurate skill-to-project alignment in team formation
examples: Applied to sponsor-submitted capstone project descriptions at UC Merced
key_sources: Brandon Pardi, Garret Castro, Michael Pisman, Avash Adhikari, and Santosh Chandrasekhar. (2026). Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15572

article_title: Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment
citation: Brandon Pardi, Garret Castro, Michael Pisman, Avash Adhikari, and Santosh Chandrasekhar. (2026). Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15572
title: Greedy student-to-project assignment algorithm with dynamic skill weighting and tunable preference weight
description: The matching system iteratively computes a match score for every student-project pair, combining a student's preference score weighted by an instructor-tunable parameter α with skill self-ratings weighted by a dynamic skill weight β. As the article explains, "as the algorithm progresses, and more students are assigned to the project, the value ofβp(k)for unfulfilled skills will increase leading to a higher match score for students that satisfy those skills." A skill counts as unfulfilled when no assigned student self-rated proficiency of 3 or higher on the survey's 1–5 scale. The greedy process selects the highest match score each round, with ties broken by preference then randomly, and projects with higher average preference receive more capacity up to a fixed team-size limit of five.
requirements: Instructor-defined preference weight α
Student skill and preference survey data
A predetermined skill list shared by surveys and LLM extraction
constraints: The current method can favor projects with many required skills at the expense of those with rare but critical skills
All skills are currently treated equally, with fulfillment based on a single student's intermediate-level rating
target_learners: senior-level computer science capstone students
target_learning_goals: balanced teams with skill coverage and preference alignment
examples: Used to form teams in UC Merced capstone courses with team sizes of three to five students
key_sources: Brandon Pardi, Garret Castro, Michael Pisman, Avash Adhikari, and Santosh Chandrasekhar. (2026). Improving Capstone Team Outcomes through Dynamic Skill Matching and Preference Alignment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15572

article_title: The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization
citation: Seyed Parsa Neshaei, Abhinand Shibu, and Fatma Betül Güres. (2026). The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15902
title: Card-based design-time GenUI paradigm for educational content
description: The paper proposes organizing educational content as bounded, modality-agnostic semantic cards whose learning objective is encoded separately from any interface representation. At authoring time, a GenAI engine produces a defined set of representation variants (interactive, audio, simplified text, low-bandwidth), which the instructor reviews before delivery; approved variants are stored in repositories for deployment without runtime generation. The authors state this "embeds Universal Design for Learning principles into the authoring workflow, and removed per-learner inference costs." The card boundary is presented as what makes generation tractable and keeps a domain-knowledgeable human in the loop.
requirements: Educators define bounded learning units as cards with explicit learning objectives and content fields before any representation is generated
Generated representations are reviewed and approved by the instructor before learners see them
constraints: The assumption that card variants are interchangeable from a learning perspective is stated by the authors as an unvalidated empirical claim
Client may still invoke runtime AI for selected functions such as answering questions or feedback
target_learners: Diverse learners including those needing audio-first, simplified-text, interactive, or low-bandwidth representations
target_learning_goals: Preserving the intended learning objective across multiple interface representations
examples: The paper contrasts a card on the quadratic formula, which encodes objective, prerequisites, examples, misconceptions, and an assessment prompt without specifying presentation form, against a lesson authored as a slide deck that inherits visual-layout assumptions
key_sources: Seyed Parsa Neshaei, Abhinand Shibu, and Fatma Betül Güres. (2026). The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15902

article_title: The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization
citation: Seyed Parsa Neshaei, Abhinand Shibu, and Fatma Betül Güres. (2026). The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15902
title: Card as bounded semantic content unit
description: A card is defined as "thesmallestmeaningfulunitofinstructional content that can be authored, reviewed, sequenced, and delivered independently." It may introduce a concept, explain a procedure, present a worked example, or provide practice, and is characterized by semantic structure rather than visual appearance. Cards are structured objects with fields such as learning objective, concept description, examples, prerequisite knowledge, constraints, assessment item, and source material. Cards also support composition into sequences or graphs with prerequisite relationships, optional branches, remediation paths, and thematic clusters.
requirements: Cards encode what the learner is intended to understand separately from how it will be represented
Fields must bound generation to representations of a specific, instructor-authored unit
target_learners: Educators authoring educational material for diverse learner contexts
target_learning_goals: Authoring at the level of learning intent before representational commitments are made
examples: A card on the quadratic formula would include the learning objective, prerequisite concepts, key explanation, notation, examples, common misconceptions, and perhaps a short assessment prompt
key_sources: Seyed Parsa Neshaei, Abhinand Shibu, and Fatma Betül Güres. (2026). The Missing Layer: Why EdTech Needs Design-Time Generative UI, Not Just Runtime Personalization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15902

title: Card repository of approved representation variants
description: Once cards and their representation variants are approved, they are stored in a card repository, "a reusable collection of semantically structured learning units and their approved representation variants." A repository would contain the semantic card, metadata, approved variants, version history, and deployment constraints. Different clients render the same repository differently: a web client might show the interactive version, a mobile-first client simplified text and audio, and a WhatsApp-based client the low-bandwidth representation. Repositories could support sharing, remixing, localization, and cross-platform deployment while preserving instructor control.
requirements: Instructor approval of representation variants before they enter the repository
Semantic cards must be authored independently of any particular interface representation
target_learners: Learners in varying deployment contexts including low-bandwidth and mobile-first settings
target_learning_goals: Consistent learning content delivered through context-appropriate interface representations
examples: The paper describes a WhatsApp-based client delivering the low-bandwidth representation of the same card a web client renders interactively

article_title: Engagement Intensity as a Learner-Modeling Signal for Adaptive AI Ethics Instruction
citation: Yongkyung Oh, Lynn Talton, Alex Bui. (2026). Engagement Intensity as a Learner-Modeling Signal for Adaptive AI Ethics Instruction. KDD 2026 AI for Education Day, at the ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD '26). https://kdd2026.kdd.org
title: Engagement intensity as a pair of complementary intake features (reported use and self-rated familiarity) for learner modeling
description: The article introduces engagement intensity as a working label for two complementary intake indicators of technology engagement drawn from technology acceptance and AI literacy research: "reported use and self-rated familiarity." It functions as a lightweight learner-modeling signal for intake-level grouping, explicitly scoped to pre-instruction segmentation rather than adaptive sequencing, personalized feedback, or a full intelligent tutoring system. In this framing, behavioral usage frequency is the primary axis and familiarity a secondary, self-perception-based check on perceived readiness.
requirements: Both features must be collected as short pre-instruction survey items before instruction begins
constraints: The article defines adaptive as intake-level learner grouping only, not differentiated materials, adaptive sequencing, personalized feedback, or a full intelligent tutoring system
target_learners: graduate and postdoctoral bioscience trainees in research ethics instruction
target_learning_goals: intake-level learner profiling for adaptive AI ethics instruction
key_sources: Yongkyung Oh, Lynn Talton, Alex Bui. (2026). Engagement Intensity as a Learner-Modeling Signal for Adaptive AI Ethics Instruction. KDD 2026 AI for Education Day, at the ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18548

citation: Yongkyung Oh, Lynn Talton, Alex Bui. (2026). Engagement Intensity as a Learner-Modeling Signal for Adaptive AI Ethics Instruction. KDD 2026 AI for Education Day, at the ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD '26). https://kdd2026.kdd.org
title: Five-item pre-instruction AI perception intake survey
description: A short anonymous online survey (about 10 to 15 minutes, Qualtrics) administered around a required RCR course, in which "Five perception items served as focal outcomes, each on a five-point Likert scale": accuracy trust, distinguishing capability, complex-task trust, critical-thinking risk, and training interest. Items are analyzed as distinct facets rather than pooled, alongside three intake features (usage frequency, familiarity, prior AI education).
requirements: Administered before instruction; respondents may skip items and no identifying information is stored
constraints: Both predictors and outcomes are single-item self-report measures, so common-method variance cannot be excluded and multi-item reliability is unavailable
target_learners: bioscience graduate students and postdoctoral trainees
target_learning_goals: measuring baseline AI perceptions to inform adaptive instruction
examples: Used with 93 UCLA bioscience trainees enrolled in a Spring 2025 Responsible Conduct of Research course
