article_title: Curiosity as Linguistic Intervention: Using LLM Tutoring Dialogues to Influence Exploratory Learning Behavior
citation: Ganganath, G., Bolonghege, P., Lyu, Q., Varakantham, P., & Kandappu, T. (2026). Curiosity as Linguistic Intervention: Using LLM Tutoring Dialogues to Influence Exploratory Learning Behavior. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22349
title: CURIOBOT curiosity-modulated tutoring framework
description: CURIOBOT is an inference-time prompting framework that turns Berlyne's collative variables into five conversational operators — NOVELTY, COMPLEXITY, CONFLICT, UNCERTAINTY, and NEUTRAL — selected adaptively at each tutor turn from interaction signals such as response depth and learner initiative. COMPLEXITY "expands the surrounding conceptual space by exposing additional mechanisms and dependencies" while the intervention modifies only conversational framing, keeping the topic and learning objective unchanged. Both operator selection and response generation are implemented with prompted black-box LLMs without fine-tuning.
requirements: A shared system prompt defining the tutoring role, plus operator-conditioned generation separated from a modulator stage that analyzes dialogue context before each tutor turn
constraints: The Modulator is a prompted LLM agent with a fixed decision rule, leaving the operator-selection policy itself unoptimized, per the article's limitations section
target_learners: Postgraduate students learning topics in STEM, social sciences, and arts & humanities
target_learning_goals: Exploratory questioning, conversational agency, productive struggle, and observable epistemic curiosity during tutoring dialogue
examples: In the 3×3×3 factorial study, each domain was assigned to one tutoring variant (Baseline, CURIOBOT, or study-oriented mode), producing 270 conversations across Claude, Gemini, and GPT
key_sources: Ganganath, G., Bolonghege, P., Lyu, Q., Varakantham, P., & Kandappu, T. (2026). Curiosity as Linguistic Intervention: Using LLM Tutoring Dialogues to Influence Exploratory Learning Behavior. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22349

article_title: Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions
citation: Li Siyan, Kai-Hui Liang, Shopnil Shahriar, Yilin Ye, Shiyoh Goetsu, Wei-Wei Du, Masahiro Yoshida, Tsunayuki Ohwa, Xuhai Xu, and Zhou Yu. (2026). Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26641
title: Clinical Empathy Module for PA coaching chatbots
description: The Clinical Empathy Module is a pipeline attached to the Empathetic chatbot variant that identifies Empathy Opportunities in user messages and generates clinically informed empathetic responses. It consists of three submodules: an "Empathy Opportunity Classifier", a "Strategy Sampler", and an "Instruction Generator". The classifier is a GPT-4o-mini-based model with "a top-three classification accuracy of 85.3%"; the sampler draws from EO-specific strategy distributions built from statistics in Rey Velasco et al.; the generator produces system instructions for GPT-4o describing the chosen strategies. Only the Empathetic chatbot variant has access to this module.
requirements: A GPT-4o base model and WhatsApp/Twilio delivery infrastructure
EO-to-strategy mappings derived from the healthcare-professional response data of Rey Velasco et al.
Check-in questions designed to elicit negative self-disclosure so that naturalistic Empathy Opportunities arise
constraints: The module is not activated in the initial consultation session; it operates only in maintenance sessions
The chatbot does not retain every single past conversation, since summaries are condensed and only the top 3-5 relevant bullets are retrieved
target_learners: Inactive but motivated adults seeking to increase physical activity
target_learning_goals: Sustained physical activity behavior change
Increased intention to follow coaching advice and self-efficacy
examples: In the six-week study, the Empathetic chatbot using this module was associated with faster growth in intention to follow and self-efficacy compared to the Non-Empathetic condition
key_sources: Li Siyan, Kai-Hui Liang, Shopnil Shahriar, Yilin Ye, Shiyoh Goetsu, Wei-Wei Du, Masahiro Yoshida, Tsunayuki Ohwa, Xuhai Xu, and Zhou Yu. (2026). Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26641

article_title: Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions
citation: Li Siyan, Kai-Hui Liang, Shopnil Shahriar, Yilin Ye, Shiyoh Goetsu, Wei-Wei Du, Masahiro Yoshida, Tsunayuki Ohwa, Xuhai Xu, and Zhou Yu. (2026). Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26641
title: Elaboration Likelihood Model peripheral-route account of empathy's invisible impact
description: The article interprets its pattern of results — empathy's effects appearing in behavioral trajectories rather than in users' explicit ratings — through the Elaboration Likelihood Model's peripheral route. The authors state: "We interpret this pattern through the Elaboration Likelihood Model's peripheral route." On this account, empathy acts as a peripheral cue that shapes motivation and trust supporting sustained change, even when "it may be hard for lay users to identify explicitly". This framing explains why perceived-empathy ratings diverge from measured outcomes in their study.
requirements: A multi-session coaching context in which users repeatedly interact with the chatbot over time
Outcome measures that capture behavioral trajectories (e.g., step counts, intention over days) rather than only single-shot perception ratings
constraints: The article offers this as an interpretation of its observed pattern, not as a directly tested mechanism
target_learners: Inactive but motivated adults using digital PA coaching tools
target_learning_goals: Motivation and adherence in physical activity behavior change
Trust in and rapport with a coaching chatbot
examples: The authors use this account to explain why the Empathetic chatbot improved intention and self-efficacy faster while participants could not consciously distinguish the versions

Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26641

article_title: DysLexLens: A Low-Resource LLM Framework for Analysing Dyslexic Learners Insights from Online Forums
citation: Dana Rezazadegan, Atie Kia, Phongpadid Nandavong, Dominique Carlon, Jeremy Nguyen, Abhik Banerjee, James Marshall, Anthony McCosker, Yong-Bin Kang. (2026). DysLexLens: A Low-Resource LLM Framework for Analysing Dyslexic Learners' Insights from Online Forums. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27619
title: DysLexLens: evidence-traceable LLM framework with three-layer architecture and public GitHub release
description: DysLexLens is a low-resource LLM framework that transforms noisy social media posts into a dictionary-driven corpus, performs knowledge-graph-based question reasoning, generates verifiable responses, and evaluates them quantitatively and through human-grounded assessment. It is applied to dyslexia-AI Reddit data with 30 questions, and the article states that "DysLexLens, sample data, questions and evaluation results are available at Github1 to support reproducibility." Responses are generated with gpt-4o-mini and carry inline source-chunk references.
requirements: A reusable knowledge graph is constructed from the filtered corpus before query reasoning and is built once rather than dynamically reconstructed per query.
A concept dictionary aligned with the research objectives is needed for the filtering step.
constraints: Reddit discussions do not represent all dyslexic learners, and LLM-based triple extraction and retrieval may introduce noise; the graph should be treated as an interpretive aid rather than a complete representation of learner experience.
target_learners: Dyslexic learners and related stakeholders in online forum communities
target_learning_goals: Understanding how dyslexic learners use and perceive AI tools for learning support
examples: Applied to Reddit data collected from 50 screened subreddits, filtered from 23,480 posts and comments down to a focused dataset of 319 posts from 27 subreddits using a five-concept dictionary (dyslexia, AI, technology, learning support, perception).
key_sources: Dana Rezazadegan, Atie Kia, Phongpadid Nandavong, Dominique Carlon, Jeremy Nguyen, Abhik Banerjee, James Marshall, Anthony McCosker, Yong-Bin Kang. (2026). DysLexLens: A Low-Resource LLM Framework for Analysing Dyslexic Learners' Insights from Online Forums. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27619

article_title: ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education
citation: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662
title: ELEVATE: a three-stratum framework for locally deployed GenAI avatar tutors
description: ELEVATE (Efficient LLM Education with Virtual Avatar Teaching Engine) is a framework for developing GenAI-driven avatar tutors governed by institutional epistemic infrastructures. It integrates "LLM-driven dialogue with embodied 3D avatars for multimodal interaction" and adopts a local-first execution model. The framework "formalizes a three-stratum design that separates (i) a student-facing virtual avatar interaction layer, (ii) a local GenAI execution and multimodal synthesis core, and (iii) a teacher-facing governance layer", forming a closed loop in which teacher-defined constraints govern engine behavior and the avatar embodies responses.
requirements: Deployment on local or on-premise institutional hardware without cloud dependency
Teacher-defined constraints encoded as system-level specifications governing LLM and retrieval behavior
constraints: The authors adopt a system-level perspective and do not aim to evaluate learning outcomes directly
target_learners: school students across heterogeneous educational levels and subjects
target_learning_goals: personalized tutoring and real-time question answering aligned with curriculum requirements
examples: A working prototype was implemented and deployed in a real-world educational curriculum aligned with curriculum requirements, running on standard PCs and smartphones
key_sources: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662

article_title: ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education
citation: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662
title: Deploy educational GenAI locally first so student data stays within the institutional boundary
description: The article argues that GenAI tutoring in schools should follow a local-first principle: inference runs on institutional hardware rather than cloud services. The authors state the pipeline "can run without external cloud dependencies, which (i) reduces recurring costs, (ii) enables offline operation, and (iii) strengthens privacy-by-design by keeping student interactions within the institutional boundary". This addresses data-sovereignty and compliance concerns that make cloud LLM services difficult for schools to adopt at scale.
requirements: Local or on-premise compute capable of hosting the LLM and TTS models
Institutional governance over configuration and knowledge sources
constraints: Particularly relevant for European educational contexts where data protection constraints and procurement limitations hinder cloud adoption; under-resourced institutions may lack suitable local hardware
target_learners: students in public schools, including under-resourced and rural contexts
target_learning_goals: privacy-preserving, institutionally governed AI-supported tutoring
examples: The prototype's server-side pipeline ran entirely locally without reliance on cloud infrastructure, with speech recognition performed on-device and TTS executed on a local machine
key_sources: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662

article_title: ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education
citation: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662
title: ELEVATE Engine: streaming, queue-based client-server pipeline for low perceived latency
description: The ELEVATE Engine is the framework's technical core, split into a client that renders the avatar and manages interaction and a server that performs LLM inference and speech synthesis. Its central design choice is streaming generation: "Instead of waiting for a full response completion, the server emits partial outputs (e.g., paragraphs or chunks) as soon as they are available." Queue-based orchestration decouples ASR, LLM, and TTS stages so generation proceeds independently of synthesis, avoiding cascaded blocking and supporting incremental delivery with per-segment ordering metadata.
requirements: Explicit client-side coordination for ordering, validation/decryption, and audiovisual synchronization of streamed segments
Queue-based orchestration between pipeline modules
constraints: The reference implementation's interaction boundary is text-based: speech-to-text runs on the client device and the server receives only textual prompts, with no server-side ASR module
target_learners: school students interacting via smartphones, desktop PCs, and immersive 3D environments
target_learning_goals: responsive conversational tutoring with timely feedback and smooth turn-taking
examples: The server pipeline can be horizontally partitioned across multiple low-end consumer nodes, with Orchestrator, LLM inference, and TTS running as separate processes communicating through the same message interface
key_sources: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662

article_title: ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education
citation: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662
title: Teacher Interaction Layer: a web-based configuration surface for pedagogical intent, persona, and role
description: The Teacher Interaction Layer is a lightweight web-based configuration page through which educators shape the virtual tutor's behavior; all settings are injected directly into the LLM system prompt. It exposes personality presets (e.g., Neutral, Friendly, Patient, Verbose, Concise, plus a Custom option), thumbnail-based avatar appearance selection, a knowledge base selector, and teacher type. "The interface specifies the type of teacher through mutually exclusive radio-button options (e.g., professor (replicating lecture content), tutor (providing repeated explanations and scaffolding), and exam trainer", with a save action persisting settings as reproducible configuration artifacts.
requirements: Settings must be persisted as configuration artifacts (templates, rule sets, corpus descriptors) interpreted by the server at runtime for traceability
constraints: Personality presets are deliberately constrained; styles beyond them require additional engineering inputs such as tailored prompt templates or policy rules
target_learners: students in classrooms configured by their teachers
target_learning_goals: consistent, pedagogically framed tutoring behavior matching classroom norms and assessment contexts
examples: Thumbnail-based avatar selection was chosen to keep configuration concrete and low-effort while avoiding value-laden textual descriptors, supporting a gender-respectful workflow
key_sources: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662

article_title: ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education
citation: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662
title: Use embodied, multimodal avatars to make AI tutoring accessible to learners who struggle with text
description: The article argues that AI tutoring interfaces should move beyond text-only chatbots toward embodied multimodal virtual humans. It states that "speaking and gesturing avatars can benefit learners who struggle with text-based communication (e.g., young children or students with reading difficulties)" and can offer accessible modalities such as voice output, lip-reading support, or sign-language-capable avatars. The prototype operationalizes this with captions, adjustable speaking rate, simplified-language toggles, high-contrast UI, and lip-synchronized facial articulation.
requirements: Avatar facial articulation clear enough to avoid degrading comprehension during voice-based tutoring
Accessibility features (captions, speaking-rate control) exposed as first-class configuration options
constraints: The avatar was designed conservatively to remain legible on small screens while avoiding overly realistic features that may increase the risk of discomfort in some learners
target_learners: young children, students with reading difficulties, and learners with impairments
target_learning_goals: comprehensible, inclusive multimodal tutoring dialogue
examples: The client enforces clear turn-taking through listening/thinking/speaking states, and lip-sync is driven directly by the played audio
key_sources: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662

article_title: ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education
citation: Lorenzo Stacchio, Michele Giordano, Daniele Berardini, Primo Zingaretti, Emanuele Frontoni. (2026). ELEVATE: Designing Human-Centered GenAI Virtual Tutors for Scalable and Inclusive Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30662
title: Five-stage game-ready asset production pipeline for a pedagogically controlled 3D Virtual Teacher avatar
description: The prototype's Virtual Teacher avatar was manually authored rather than sourced from a pre-packaged library, to give pedagogical control over appearance and expressive affordances. The pipeline runs through Character Creator, ZBrush sculpt refinement, Substance Painter material authoring, Mixamo auto-rigging and animation, and OBJ export. The authors treat the avatar as part of the interaction channel, in which "facial expressions, turn-taking cues, and lip synchronization are treated as communicative signals that shape how students interpret the tutor's epistemic stance and instructional intent".
requirements: Face mesh must support clear lip articulation to avoid degrading comprehension during voice-based tutoring
Polygon count, texture sizes, and shader complexity must keep the asset computationally tractable on consumer hardware for stable frame rates under concurrency
constraints: Texture resolution was balanced to preserve facial readability while limiting VRAM and bandwidth overhead for mobile and consumer devices
target_learners: school students interacting with the avatar on smartphones and PCs
target_learning_goals: legible embodied communication of tutor state and instructional intent
examples: Mixamo was used to obtain baseline idle and conversational animations, enabling rapid iteration on embodied behaviors without bespoke animation production

article_title: Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2
citation: Margaret Ellis, Nikitha Donekal Chandrashekar, Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Mohammed Farghally, Jake O'Brien, and Naren Ramakrishnan. (2026). Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30908
title: DURA (Demystify-Use-Reflect-Assess): a lightweight framework for incorporating LLMs into courses
description: DURA is the article's four-component framework for updating courses to incorporate AI/LLMs: Demystify how LLMs work and how they affect learning; Use LLMs with guidance and attribution; Reflect on LLM use and problem-solving; and Assess programming assignment skills through proctored assessments with retakes. The authors call it "our lightweight framework for incorporating LLMs into courses" and apply it in a large flipped CS2 course of 442 students. They state its components "deliberately support the learning process, as well as the need for reliable evidence of student learning," with demystification as the foundational component.
requirements: The assess component is course specific and time-intensive, requiring question banks to support retakes, which the authors note was not reliable to generate without oversight
Supporting test review and retakes requires support by the instructional team
constraints: The authors position the changes as manageable initial steps before overhauling labs and projects, and cannot attribute outcomes causally due to lack of a control group
target_learners: undergraduate CS2 (data structures) students
instructors adapting CS courses for LLM use
target_learning_goals: meeting course learning outcomes without LLM assistance
effective and ethical LLM use
metacognition and self-regulation around LLM use
examples: In CS2: a 30-minute week-2 LLM demystification lesson, attribution statements on every code file, reflection assignments in weeks 4, 8, and 13, and reallocation of 20% of the course grade to proctored assessments with retake days one week after each test
key_sources: Margaret Ellis, Nikitha Donekal Chandrashekar, Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Mohammed Farghally, Jake O'Brien, and Naren Ramakrishnan. (2026). Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30908

article_title: Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2
citation: Margaret Ellis, Nikitha Donekal Chandrashekar, Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Mohammed Farghally, Jake O'Brien, and Naren Ramakrishnan. (2026). Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30908
title: 30-minute LLM demystification lesson introducing how LLMs work and research on their learning effects
description: A 30-minute lesson added in the second week of the CS2 course explaining that LLMs are a machine learning model, a Transformer doing next-token prediction, and that LLMs do not think or problem solve. It "highlighted the CS education research on how LLM use can affect student learning" and included a ChatGPT-generated example of risks such as shallow understanding and inhibited debugging skills. The authors state the lesson can be used in a variety of courses.
requirements: Adaptation from an existing introductory-course lesson with more detail on how LLMs work, plus CS education research references
constraints: The demystify lesson itself is broadly reusable, unlike the course-specific assessment changes
target_learners: undergraduate CS students in introductory programming and data structures courses
target_learning_goals: building an informed mental model of LLMs
avoiding over-trust of LLMs and shortcuts to learning
examples: The lesson explained next-token prediction, emphasized LLMs do not think or problem solve, and presented an example of risks for a CS2 student generated by ChatGPT
key_sources: Margaret Ellis, Nikitha Donekal Chandrashekar, Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Mohammed Farghally, Jake O'Brien, and Naren Ramakrishnan. (2026). Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30908

article_title: Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2
citation: Margaret Ellis, Nikitha Donekal Chandrashekar, Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Mohammed Farghally, Jake O'Brien, and Naren Ramakrishnan. (2026). Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30908
title: Allow LLM use with required attribution while increasing the weight of proctored assessments with retakes to guard against over-reliance
description: Rather than banning or unconditionally allowing LLMs, the course permits their use with a required attribution statement on every code file, while grade weight shifts from programming assignments to proctored assessments with retakes. The authors state this approach "allows the use of LLMs but with assessment design to provide guardrails against over-reliance," so students can still meet learning objectives without assistance. The attribution statement's final sentence makes students responsible for completing work unassisted.
requirements: In-class proctored retakes of each test, with question banks of assignment-aligned questions created over a summer with UTA support
Office-hours test review with a TA or instructor after the first attempt
constraints: Assessment alignment with programming assignments is course specific and time-intensive; generating question variations was not reliable without oversight
target_learners: undergraduate CS2 students
instructors of large introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: independent mastery of course learning outcomes
responsible and documented LLM use
independent comprehension of assignment skills
examples: The CS2 course reallocated 20% of the grade from programming assignments (45% to 25%) to proctored assessments (35% to 55%), used two tests each with a retake day one week later, and required per-file attribution statements
key_sources: Margaret Ellis, Nikitha Donekal Chandrashekar, Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Mohammed Farghally, Jake O'Brien, and Naren Ramakrishnan. (2026). Demystify, Use, Reflect, Assess (DURA): An Experience Report on LLM Integration in CS2. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30908

article_title: Data Comics for Education: Evaluating Effectiveness, Benefits, and the Ethics of AI-Assisted Creation
citation: Zirui Shan, Vanessa Echeverria, Yuheng Li, Yi-Shan Tsai, and Roberto Martinez-Maldonado. (2026). Data Comics for Education: Evaluating Effectiveness, Benefits, and the Ethics of AI-Assisted Creation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02361
title: Two-stage data comic creation pattern separating human-led narrative design from human–AI co-creation of visual elements
description: The article describes a two-stage production process for building data comics with GenAI assistance. In Stage 1, a researcher extracts key insights and classifies them into Bach et al.'s content relation categories, mapping them onto panel layouts, with reviewers validating choices. In Stage 2, image elements are generated with DALL-E 3 via ChatGPT-4, integrated into pre-defined panel layouts, and assembled with storytelling elements in Canva. The authors state the process separated "human-led narrative design from the human–AI co-creation of visual elements".
requirements: Researcher expertise in data science, visual analytics, and visualisation or dashboard design to extract insights and review outputs
Established data comic design patterns (Bach et al.) to structure content relation and layout decisions
GenAI text-to-image tooling (DALL-E 3 via ChatGPT-4) and an assembly tool (Canva)
constraints: Comics were created by researchers, not students or teachers, so the process is described for expert-led production
The article does not report effects of the process itself, only of the resulting comics
target_learners: university students from diverse disciplines
target_learning_goals: interpreting and reasoning with visual data
comprehending data-driven insights
examples: Four data comics on climate change data were produced this way and compared against four matched conventional visualisations in a within-subjects study with 60 students
key_sources: Zirui Shan, Vanessa Echeverria, Yuheng Li, Yi-Shan Tsai, and Roberto Martinez-Maldonado. (2026). Data Comics for Education: Evaluating Effectiveness, Benefits, and the Ethics of AI-Assisted Creation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02361

article_title: CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming
citation: H. Chad Lane, Bryson Kageler. (2026). CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming. SLM4ED'26: The 1st Workshop of Small Language Models for Education. https://github.com/InviteInstitute/CSTutorBench
title: CSTutorBench: a 17-question benchmark with an 8-criterion pedagogical rubric for evaluating LLMs as VEX VR block-based programming tutors
description: CSTutorBench is a benchmark for evaluating language models as CS tutors in VEX VR, a block-based robotics simulation for middle school students. It contains 17 scenario-based questions across four types (debugging, debugging_iterative, optimization, conceptual), each scored on an 8-criterion rubric (0–2 points each, 16 points max) with universal and type-specific criteria, plus evaluator notes hidden from the model under test. The rubric "operationalizes established research on tutoring and formative feedback into computable dimensions," and the benchmark, rubric, and full evaluation pipeline are released on GitHub.
requirements: Requires a human-in-the-loop LLM-as-judge evaluation pipeline with per-question hybrid review and calibration notes carried forward across questions
constraints: The evaluation set contains only 17 questions, which the authors state limits the precision of per-criterion comparisons; type-specific criteria are scored on subsets as small as one or two questions
All items are single-turn and do not capture multi-turn tutoring dialogues; models have not been evaluated with actual students, so higher rubric scores may not predict learning outcomes
target_learners: middle school students (grades 6–8) working in block-based programming environments
target_learning_goals: block-based programming in VEX VR, including sequencing, sensor navigation, and algorithmic optimization
examples: The six debugging_iterative entries approximate multi-turn tutoring by presenting 2–3 code snapshots of a student's self-directed fix attempts, such as a student who first tries a repeat-10 loop then switches to repeat-100
key_sources: H. Chad Lane, Bryson Kageler. (2026). CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming. SLM4ED'26: The 1st Workshop of Small Language Models for Education. https://github.com/InviteInstitute/CSTutorBench

article_title: CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming
citation: H. Chad Lane, Bryson Kageler. (2026). CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming. SLM4ED'26: The 1st Workshop of Small Language Models for Education. https://github.com/InviteInstitute/CSTutorBench
title: CSTutorBench rubric operationalizes tutoring and formative-feedback research into eight computable scoring criteria
description: The rubric translates established tutoring and feedback research into eight scored criteria (0–2 points each): seven universal criteria plus one type-specific criterion per question type. Conciseness reflects Shute's finding that "feedback complexity is inversely related to error correction and learning efficiency"; Actionability draws on Hattie and Timperley's model of feedback that reduces the gap between current and desired performance; Targetedness is grounded in expert human tutors who engage with specific contextual factors rather than generic advice. The four type-specific criteria reflect Narciss's interactive tutoring feedback (ITF) model, which holds that no single feedback type is optimal across all tasks and feedback must be calibrated to both the task and the student's state.
requirements: Each criterion includes a stable description across entries plus entry-specific addenda describing correct and incorrect responses, to maintain consistency while capturing domain knowledge
constraints: The type-specific criteria each apply only to their question type (e.g., hint not solution on the 8 debugging questions, acknowledges progression on the 6 iterative debugging questions)
target_learners: middle school students (grades 6–8)
target_learning_goals: receiving effective tutoring and formative feedback in block-based programming
examples: The acknowledges_progression criterion specifically evaluates whether a response recognizes and builds on the student's prior fix attempts provided as context
key_sources: H. Chad Lane, Bryson Kageler. (2026). CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming. SLM4ED'26: The 1st Workshop of Small Language Models for Education. https://github.com/InviteInstitute/CSTutorBench

article_title: DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging
citation: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. Companion Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Systems, Programming, Languages, and Applications: Software for Humanity (SPLASH Companion '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3837729.3840500
title: DebugTracker: a VS Code extension recording lightweight debugging-process evidence for classroom tasks
description: DebugTracker is a Visual Studio Code extension that "records lightweight debugging-process evidence for classroom tasks". It captures test commands, editor and debugger metadata, student checkpoints, source snapshots, and human labels as append-only JSONL events, and exports timeline and Markdown reports for human review. It is largely language-agnostic, capturing evidence through standard VS Code mechanisms rather than language-specific tooling.
requirements: Requires VS Code 1.88 or newer; debugger evidence depends on the relevant VS Code language extension, and test-command detection relies on shell integration or instructor-configured patterns
constraints: The article states debugger evidence "depends on the relevant VS Code language extension", and the optional AI coach is off by default and requires an OpenAI-compatible endpoint when enabled
target_learners: Students debugging programming tasks in classroom courses
target_learning_goals: Systematic debugging process skills: reproducing failures, forming hypotheses, editing fixes, and verifying repairs
examples: The demonstration uses a Python checkout-pricing task with a failing test caused by free-shipping eligibility computed from the original rather than the discounted taxable subtotal; TypeScript and Java variants are also available
key_sources: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. Companion Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Systems, Programming, Languages, and Applications: Software for Humanity (SPLASH Companion '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3837729.3840500

article_title: DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging
citation: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. Companion Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Systems, Programming, Languages, and Applications: Software for Humanity (SPLASH Companion '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3837729.3840500
title: Separating coached practice traces from uncoached assessment traces in process evidence capture
description: DebugTracker structures each recording session into one of two mutually exclusive modes. "Evaluation Mode is uncoached: it disables process prompts, solution hints, and after-session feedback, and marks its reports as assessment traces", while Training Mode provides process prompts and optional AI feedback. This explicit mode boundary keeps coached practice traces separate from assessment evidence so instructors can trust what an assessment trace contains.
requirements: Students must select a mode at session start; the tooling must disable coaching features in assessment mode and label reports accordingly
constraints: The two modes differ only in coaching; the article states the coaching "never reveals the fix or patches the code for the student"
target_learners: Students completing debugging exercises in programming courses
target_learning_goals: Debugging process competence that can be assessed without coaching contamination
examples: In the demonstration the presenter selects the Evaluation Mode path, runs python -m unittest, and the exported report is labeled a Student Summary (Evaluation)
key_sources: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. Companion Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Systems, Programming, Languages, and Applications: Software for Humanity (SPLASH Companion '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3837729.3840500
grain_size: session-level workflow for a single debugging task

article_title: DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging
citation: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. Companion Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Systems, Programming, Languages, and Applications: Software for Humanity (SPLASH Companion '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3837729.3840500
title: Assess the debugging process, not only the final patch, because identical final code can hide different debugging competence
description: Classroom assessment that considers only the submitted code and pass/fail test result creates a process-visibility gap: the intermediate steps of reproducing, narrowing, hypothesizing, and verifying leave no durable record. The article argues that "the final code can look identical even when the underlying debugging competence differs", so feedback that ignores the process misses what the exercise was meant to assess. Recording the reproduce-observe-hypothesize-edit-verify chain makes that process reviewable.
requirements: A lightweight, structured record of the debugging process that is cheap to produce, cheap to read, and bounded to the task at hand
constraints: Screen recording and live observation capture the process faithfully but do not scale to large cohorts, are intrusive, and collect far more data than a review task requires; commit history is too coarse and easily rewritten
target_learners: Novice programmers in classroom debugging exercises
target_learning_goals: Systematic debugging investigation rather than lucky guessing or repeated edit-and-test flailing
examples: The article contrasts two students who both submit a passing solution: one may have followed an evidence-based debugging process while the other edited and tested repeatedly until the suite turned green
key_sources: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. article_title: DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging
citation: Jiatong Liu, Xue Yao, Zehua Zhang, and Yongqiang Tian. (2026). DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging. Companion Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Systems, Programming, Languages, and Applications: Software for Humanity (SPLASH Companion '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3837729.3840500
title: Treat privacy as a capture-policy problem: record task-relevant metadata rather than full interaction replay
description: DebugTracker's privacy stance is to bound capture to the task: "it records task-relevant metadata rather than a full interaction replay". By default it does not store complete terminal output, screen video, mouse movement, or per-keystroke history, and it saves baseline and final source snapshots so instructors can compare the starting bug with the submitted fix. Reports also separate captured evidence from instructor-only interpretation.
requirements: A capture policy that limits storage to task-relevant metadata; workspace-local artifacts such as JSONL logs, Markdown reports, and snapshots
constraints: The article states this design records less than full replay, so it captures what a review task requires rather than everything a student did
target_learners: Students whose debugging sessions are recorded for assessment
target_learning_goals: Process-oriented feedback and assessment of debugging without intrusive surveillance-style capture
examples: Human labels are appended as separate events and instructor-side reports are derived from the log, keeping the student's raw assessment trace distinct from the instructor's interpretation

article_title: Experimental Evidence on the Learning Impact of Generative AI
citation: Zara Contractor and Germán Reyes. (2026). Experimental Evidence on the Learning Impact of Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08849
title: A model of learning with AI in which AI acts as a tutor that raises the return to research effort or as a delegate that replaces the student's own writing
description: The article builds a model in which a student divides cognitive effort between research (reading and searching) and writing, both producing knowledge, with writing also producing the essay. The article states: "We model AI as a technology that gives the student two non-mutually exclusive capabilities" — used as a tutor it raises the return to research effort, and used to write the essay it lets the student delegate, removing the essay-quality reward from the student's own work so effort falls in both activities. The model rationalizes the test-score gain, the time shift from writing toward research, and the enjoyment gain, and predicts that outcomes differ by use type.
requirements: Students choose how to use AI; the model treats delegation as a choice variable whose threshold rises with the value the student places on knowledge
constraints: The model is an organizing framework the authors use to rationalize their experimental results, not an independently estimated structural model in the main text; the complete model is in Appendix D
target_learners: undergraduates completing time-bounded academic assignments on unfamiliar topics
target_learning_goals: factual and conceptual knowledge acquisition and retention
analytical essay writing
examples: The model's prediction that delegated essays' quality advantage should vanish once AI is removed is examined with the Session Two unaided essays
key_sources: Zara Contractor and Germán Reyes. (2026). Experimental Evidence on the Learning Impact of Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08849

article_title: EduGuard: A Safe RAG-Based LLM Tutor for Programming Education
citation: S M Asif Hossain, Ruksat Khan Shayoni, M. F. Mridha, and Jungpil Shin. (2026). EduGuard: A Safe RAG-Based LLM Tutor for Programming Education. arXiv preprint arXiv:2607.15738. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15738
title: EduGuard: a safe response-control pipeline combining retrieval, pedagogical strategy selection, rubric-aware generation, claim-level verification, and overreliance control
description: EduGuard is a safe tutoring architecture in which a student query passes through query understanding, instructor-approved course retrieval, strategy selection, generation, verification, and overreliance control. The article states that "EduGuard analyzes a student query, retrieves instructor-approved evidence, selects a pedagogical strategy, generates a response, verifies generated claims with a separate NLI model, and applies an overreliance-control policy." Its authors frame this as novelty through "a response-control policy rather than merely combining RAG and prompting."
requirements: A course repository of instructor-approved material, a rubric policy labeling assistance levels, and an architecturally separate NLI verifier (DeBERTa-v3-large-MNLI) with an entailment threshold
constraints: The verifier is architecturally separate but not immune to correlated failure modes because both models are trained on broad web data
Not ready for autonomous deployment; student-facing use should include instructor oversight
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: programming concept understanding
debugging skill
academic-integrity-appropriate help seeking
examples: The pipeline classifies intents such as direct-answer seeking, maps them to actions including Socratic hint and refusal-with-guidance, and regenerates responses whose unsupported-claim ratio exceeds a threshold

title: Safe GenAI tutoring requires explicit pedagogical control, evidence verification, and deployment safeguards, not only retrieval or stronger prompting
description: The article argues that grounding and prompting alone cannot ensure safe tutoring because retrieved context may still leak solutions and self-checks share generator failure modes. It concludes that "safe GenAI tutoring requires not only retrieval or strong prompting, but explicit pedagogical control, evidence verification, and deployment safeguards." Deployment safeguards include instructor oversight, opt-out options, de-identification, retention limits, and clear warnings that the system provides formative support rather than grading decisions.
requirements: Explicit pedagogical strategy policy, a claim-level verifier separate from the generator, and instructor oversight during student-facing use
constraints: The authors state the system should not be treated as ready for autonomous deployment
Leakage policy is partly contextual; what is allowed in one course may be disallowed in another
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: safe and integrity-preserving use of AI tutoring support
examples: EduGuard implements the principle by regenerating responses that fail claim verification and returning refusal-with-guidance when a second draft also fails

article_title: Designing for What Cannot Be Seen: Supporting Embodied String Learning for Musicians with Blindness and Low-Vision
citation: Shi Shi, Lingyun Chen, Zitao Zhang, Amanda R. Draper, and Eli Blevis. 2026. Designing for What Cannot Be Seen: Supporting Embodied String Learning for Musicians with Blindness and Low-Vision. The 28th International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18598
title: Perceptual-reference-during-action account of embodied accessibility
description: The article proposes that in embodied skill domains, accessibility is not only about accessing instructions or representations but about accessing ongoing perceptual reference during action. String technique states such as bow path, grip tension, and wrist alignment are conventionally monitored through vision, so learners with BLV must reconfigure technique learning "from seeing to inferring" via proprioception, auditory feedback, kinesthetic memory, and teacher mediation. This account frames the study's breakdown findings and motivates designs that externalize invisible technique states into non-visual, practice-compatible cues.
requirements: Applies to embodied skill domains where technique states are conventionally taught and corrected through visual demonstration or mirror-based self-monitoring.
constraints: Derived from a qualitative study of four upper-string musicians with BLV; the authors note violin and viola offer fewer stable external reference points than floor-anchored instruments.
target_learners: Musicians with blindness and low-vision learning bowed string instruments
target_learning_goals: Embodied instrumental technique such as bow control, hand-arm alignment, and intonation
examples: The study triangulated practice videos, lesson observations, and interviews, identifying breakdowns in right-hand bow control, left-hand coordination, and score-related practice.

title: Augmented bow track with graded friction feedback
description: A speculative clip-on augmentation positioned between the bridge and fingerboard, using two moving tensioners that hold the bow and shift position according to the string being played. Rather than enforcing a fixed path, it makes bow deviation perceptible through graded friction that increases as the bow drifts, aiming to build muscle memory through repeated practice. Envisioned functions include non-visual feedback for drift and contact-point change, continuous low-attention feedback enabling mid-stroke correction, adaptive bow-lane awareness for dynamics, and practice scaffolding with post-practice summaries.
requirements: Must preserve freedom of movement and function as a learning companion rather than define a single correct technique or replace instruction.
constraints: Speculative concept not yet evaluated in deployed contexts; the authors state whether it works in practice remains to be evaluated.
target_learners: Violin and viola learners with blindness and low-vision
target_learning_goals: Straight bow path, contact-point awareness, and bow-lane control for dynamics
examples: Inspired by M1's low-tech rubber band and pencil aid, whose feedback I1 called effective but binary and dependent on teacher supervision.

title: Augmented bow hold aid with finger pressure force mapping
description: A bow-mounted augmentation preserving the geometry of a traditional frog, using thin-film pressure sensors (e.g., Velostat) to produce a spatial force map across finger contact points and an IMU to capture bow orientation and kinematics. By mapping where pressure concentrates and shifts, the system could infer finger placement and over-gripping patterns and provide real-time, low-attention feedback indicating which contact region is too tense and which finger to relax or reposition. It is framed as a temporary, practice-oriented scaffold for habit-building rather than a permanent replacement for conventional bow hold training.
requirements: Must preserve compatibility with existing bows and minimal disruption to established motor habits, per the article's design rationale.
constraints: The enlarged grip volume is a stated tradeoff: prolonged use may lead players to adapt to a larger grip and feel discomfort returning to an unaugmented bow; M2 cautioned the aid might not transfer when removed and could deform correct posture.
target_learners: Violin and viola learners with blindness and low-vision
target_learning_goals: Relaxed bow hold, balanced load distribution across fingers, and reduced over-gripping
examples: M2 rated the concept positively but warned that hand posture with and without the pinky holder is not the same, drawing on prior experience with rubber attachments altering tactile perception.

title: Left-hand alignment wearable with personalized baseline and event-based haptic feedback
description: A lightweight narrow band (approximately 1.5 cm wide) worn around the lower forearm near the wrist, intended to sense wrist alignment and forearm rotation using wearable sensing modalities such as orientation and surface movement. It learns an individualized baseline rather than enforcing a universal correct posture, and provides brief, localized haptic feedback when sustained deviation such as wrist collapse or insufficient arm rotation is detected. Envisioned functions include intonation-related technique support and selective use during warm-ups or drills, removed during musical interpretation to avoid over-reliance.

article_title: Data Annotations as Pedagogical Hints: From Subjective Labels to Critical Thinking
citation: Ralf Raumanns, Theresa Elstner, Louis Ferger-Andrews, Louise M. Carlsen, Martin Potthast, Gerard Schouten, Josien P. W. Pluim, and Veronika Cheplygina. (2026). Data annotations as pedagogical hints: from subjective labels to critical thinking. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20149v2
title: The learning persona: a three-assumption analytical framework tracing student movement from a traditional single-ground-truth mindset to a subjectivity-aware mindset
description: The learning persona is a theoretical construct derived from user-centred design principles representing what students should ideally understand after the annotation task. It rests on three assumptions: students start with a traditional mindset treating disagreement as error, disagreement reflects domain complexity, and students must recognise their own role in constructing biased datasets. The trajectory operationalises five concepts — annotation ambiguity, data quality, bias and fairness, implementation barriers, and pedagogical effectiveness — mapping students from "Single ground truth" to "Multiple valid labels". The authors use it as an analytical guide, not a grading rubric.
requirements: Used as an analytical perspective against which to evaluate quantitative survey data and qualitative feedback, not as a grading rubric
constraints: The article states the learning persona is a theoretical ideal serving as an analytical guide rather than a grading rubric
target_learners: Bachelor data science and machine learning students
target_learning_goals: Understanding subjectivity of data annotation
Understanding how human judgement shapes AI model behaviour
Understanding bias and fairness in AI
examples: Figure 3 summarises the trajectory: students ideally move from a traditional mindset (single ground truth, disagreement = error) to a subjectivity-aware mindset (multiple valid labels, disagreement = signal)

title: Design annotation-based assignments so disagreement is explicitly framed as a learning opportunity, with sufficient interpretive ambiguity, reduced repetitive workload, and mitigated emotional discomfort
description: The article proposes that manual data annotation tasks serve as pedagogical hints teaching students that human judgement influences model behaviour, but only if designed deliberately. Its four stated takeaways for future iterations are to ensure "sufficient interpretive ambiguity", reduce repetitive workload, mitigate emotional discomfort, and explicitly frame disagreement as a learning opportunity rather than a problem to solve. Without such framing, students tend to treat inconsistency as a defect to eliminate rather than a signal of domain complexity.
requirements: The task must involve genuinely subjective annotation (e.g., hair coverage on a 3-point scale) rather than unambiguous labelling
Appropriate framing of medical-image discomfort and of disagreement as signal
constraints: Emotional discomfort from medical imagery risks overshadowing the learning if not framed appropriately
Repetitive labelling and cumbersome tooling can overshadow the learning potential
target_learners: Bachelor data science and machine learning students in university courses
target_learning_goals: Recognising subjectivity in data annotation
Connecting human judgement to model behaviour and AI bias
examples: At both universities, students annotated skin lesion images for hair coverage on a 3-point scale in groups over two weeks, documented decisions, and compared labels with peers to analyse disagreement

title: Two-part skin lesion annotation activity (individual dataset exploration plus group annotation on a 3-point scale) implemented at Fontys and ITU Copenhagen
description: An educational activity integrated into two existing courses: Data Mining (5 ECTS, Fontys) and Projects in Data Science (7.5 ECTS, ITU). The first part is an individual Jupyter-notebook assignment exploring ISIC (or PAD-UFES-20) images including agreement analysis; the second is a group task annotating 100–200 skin lesion images for visible hair on a 3-point ordinal scale (0 = none, 1 = some, 2 = a lot), using Label Studio or a CSV template. article_title: Embodied Inquiry with AI as Facilitator: An Exploratory Case Study
citation: Eugenio Tufino, Paola Damiani. (2026). Embodied inquiry with AI as facilitator: an exploratory case study. https://udlguidelines.cast.org
title: ISLE (Investigative Science Learning Environment): inquiry organized around observational, testing and application experiments
description: ISLE is an approach to physics teaching in which students build and test physics knowledge the way physicists do, starting from phenomena they observe with their own eyes and hands. It is organized around three kinds of experiment: observational experiments where students look for patterns and propose multiple explanations; testing experiments where each explanation is put at risk in hypothetico-deductive form, aiming to falsify; and application experiments where the surviving model solves a practical problem. In this study, the laboratory session on statics of fluids followed the ISLE sequence, with the AI facilitator configured to follow it. It rests on four foundations: the epistemology of physics, findings of cognitive science, theories of learning communities, and universal design.
requirements: Students work through the process in small groups and express ideas in multiple representations: words, diagrams, graphs and equations, and in practice gestures as well
constraints: The structure of ISLE derives from how physics itself produces knowledge, not from a general theory of learning; its family resemblance with Kolb's cycle is a resonance rather than a foundation
target_learners: university students in physics education, many of whom intend to become teachers
target_learning_goals: learning physics by building and testing models like physicists
thinking scientifically through observation, testing and application experiments
examples: Students first explored how pressure grows with depth in water, then used a dynamometer to weigh objects at different depths to construct the buoyant force model F = ρ·g·V
key_sources: Eugenio Tufino, Paola Damiani. (2026). Embodied inquiry with AI as facilitator: an exploratory case study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21349

title: Design AI facilitation in two phases: embodied model-building stays human first, and the AI enters only afterward on the epistemic layer
description: The article proposes a division of labour in which students build the physics model with their own hands, instruments and shared meaning before any AI enters, and a language-based facilitator then facilitates application of the model to a new phenomenon. In the study's words, the embodied inquiry came first and stayed human, and the facilitator entered later on the epistemic layer, where its channel suffices, making the AI a complement to embodied inquiry rather than a substitute for it.
requirements: The boundary of the facilitator must be planned from the start and made visible to the students themselves
constraints: Fragility: under student pressure the facilitator crossed from scaffolding reasoning to inventing data, so fidelity must be checked rather than assumed
target_learners: university students in laboratory physics courses
target_learning_goals: applying and extending a student-built physics model to a new phenomenon while preserving embodied experience
examples: Students built the buoyancy model without AI in phase one; in phase two a custom Gem named “Physics ISLE Lab process” facilitated applying it to floating drink cans

article_title: Embodied Inquiry with AI as Facilitator: An Exploratory Case Study
citation: Eugenio Tufino, Paola Damiani. (2026). Embodied inquiry with AI as facilitator: an exploratory case study. https://udlguidelines.cast.org
title: Bridge between ISLE multiple representations, multimodal resources, and UDL multiple means, read through the interactionist embodiment tradition
description: The authors propose a bridge, offered as an interpretive inference rather than an established equivalence: what physics education research calls multiple representations, and social semiotics calls multimodal resources, is what Universal Design for Learning calls multiple means. Their primary lens is the interactionist tradition of embodiment research, in which meaning is built between people as they talk, gesture and act together, so the meaning of a laboratory activity lives in the interaction rather than inside individual heads or the worksheet. Read this way, the UDL Guidelines 3.0, with their principle of multiple means of action and expression, describe from the side of inclusion what ISLE describes from the side of physics practice: a learning environment that keeps many channels for meaning open.
requirements: A learning environment that keeps many channels for meaning open, rather than privileging the verbal one
constraints: The bridge is an interpretive inference of the authors rather than an established equivalence
target_learners: university students, including those served by inclusive design in higher education
target_learning_goals: becoming fluent in a critical constellation of modes of disciplinary discourse: words, diagrams, graphs, mathematics, apparatus and actions
examples: ISLE group work in the study, where students point, manipulate, sketch and gesture as ways of thinking together

article_title: A didactical-driven teacher assistant for a dimensional modeling course
citation: Laurent Brisson, Maria Teresa Segarra and Gregory Smits. (2026). A didactical-driven teacher assistant for a dimensional modeling course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22598
title: Deterministic pedagogical orchestration architecture with the LLM as linguistic executor
description: The architecture separates pedagogical orchestration from text generation: instructional decisions (intent recognition, concept selection, chunk typing, prompt structure) are handled by deterministic modules, and the LLM is restricted to controlled disambiguation and surface-form generation. The pipeline proceeds through six stages: intent detection, concept detection, constrained retrieval, didactic resolution, prompt construction, and LLM generation. This separation, in the authors' words, "ensures pedagogical traceability (every decision maps to an explicit rule), enforces correctness through deterministic unit-testable logic, and makes the pipeline model-agnostic". It was designed to operate without commercial LLM budget or GPU infrastructure.
requirements: A formalisation of the instructor's own pedagogical reasoning: intents, a domain ontology, and an instructor-authored structured editorial corpus
Detection lexicons calibrated to the course vocabulary and language
constraints: Adapting to a new course requires the instructor to formalise their own pedagogical practice, not merely configure a tool
Courses centred on theorem derivation, algorithmic processes, or code production may require different taxonomies and retrieval strategies
target_learners: University students in a French-language dimensional modelling course
target_learning_goals: Answering conceptual questions in dimensional modelling in line with the instructor's didactic practice
examples: For the query 'Qu'est-ce qu'une clé naturelle ?', the Definition approach retrieves the definition of the concept and, via the is a relation, its parent concept's definition, while the confused with relation injects a disambiguation note into the prompt
key_sources: Laurent Brisson, Maria Teresa Segarra and Gregory Smits. (2026). A didactical-driven teacher assistant for a dimensional modeling course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22598

title: Intent-to-didactic-approach mapping structuring responses by Bloom level and typed chunk selection
description: The system elicited the instructor's actual response practice into a small set of declarative didactic approaches (Definition, Identification, Illustration, Explanation, Comparison, Complex synthesis), each targeting a Bloom level and defining core chunk types that structure the generated response plus an ontology-enrichment strategy. Five pedagogical intents form the exhaustive set: DEFINE, EXPLAIN, ILLUSTRATE, COMPARE, and IDENTIFY, where "IDENTIFY is the inverse of DEFINE". Constrained retrieval selects content by metadata filters on chunk type and concept id rather than unconstrained similarity.
requirements: A knowledge graph of concepts with structural and didactic relations curated by the instructor
An editorial corpus segmented into nine typed chunks with concept-identifier metadata
constraints: If constrained retrieval returns no chunk for a required type, the system returns a static reformulation message rather than silently switching to unconstrained retrieval
target_learners: University students asking conceptual questions about course content
target_learning_goals: Responses structured to the pedagogical intent and Bloom level of the student's question
examples: Each approach in Table 1 defines a required chunk type whose retrieval failure triggers graceful degradation, with other listed types retrieved when available

citation: Laurent Brisson, Maria Teresa Segarra and Gregory Smits. (2026). A didactical-driven teacher assistant for a dimensional modeling course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22598
title: Instructor-curated knowledge graph and dual-readability typed chunk corpus for a dimensional modelling course
description: The course knowledge is represented as a lightweight knowledge graph containing 43 concepts organised into thematic groups, connected through structural relations (is a, part of) and didactic relations (precedes, confused with, mutually exclusive with) curated by the instructor. The course material is authored as structured Markdown revised "for dual readability: human and machine", with each concept on a dedicated page, content segmented into nine chunk types determined by the markup itself, and every chunk indexed in a ChromaDB store with concept id and chunk type as filterable attributes. Every answer is grounded in this instructor-authored material with permalinks to the relevant teaching pages.
requirements: Each new content source must be indexed with concept identifiers and chunk types so constrained retrieval continues to operate on pedagogical role
constraints: The current corpus is mono-authored, originating solely from the instructor's teaching notes
target_learners: University students in the dimensional modelling course
target_learning_goals: Grounding chatbot answers in verified curricular content with permalinks to teaching pages
examples: The vector store acts as a typed metadata index: canonical chunks such as definitions, notations and rules are retrieved by type and concept identifier, not by similarity to the student's question

article_title: EduZone: A Framework for Evaluating LLM Safety for K-12 Students and Teachers
citation: Park, J., Han, J., Yoo, H., Ahn, S.-Y., Yoon, J., & Oh, A. (2026). EduZone: A Framework for Evaluating LLM Safety for K-12 Students and Teachers. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02024
title: EduZone: an automated, extensible framework for evaluating LLM safety in K-12 educational scenarios
description: EduZone is an automated adversarial evaluation framework for LLM safety in education. It builds a multidimensional taxonomy that "combines student- and teacher-facing LLM usage, fine-grained curriculum topics, and both general and education-specific safety risks", transforms these into adversarial interactions under three settings, and classifies responses into four safety levels. The authors release 5.2K adversarial prompts and the framework publicly.

article_title: Once a Response, Always a Response: Detecting LLM-generated Text via Latent Prompt Restoration
citation: Hongrui Bao, Yubing Ren, Jinhan You, Fang Fang, Shi Wang, Yanan Cao. (2026). ONCE A RESPONSE, ALWAYS A RESPONSE: DETECTING LLM-GENERATED TEXT VIA LATENT PROMPT RESTORATION. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05741
title: Latent prompt dependency: machine-generated text retains a detectable assistant-response context after the original prompt is removed
description: The article proposes that instruction-tuned LLMs produce text conditioned on prompts, and that although the original prompt is removed, its influence persists: the text still implicitly remembers it was a response. EchoPrompt operationalizes this by restoring a generic assistant-response context and measuring context-conditioned likelihood gain. The authors state the hidden dependency "can be partially reactivated by prepending a unified generic prefix", making it a discriminative signal between machine and human text.
requirements: Detection requires paired base and instruction-tuned proxy models and a fixed generic assistant-style prefix
constraints: The signal is weaker for non-chat/completion outputs from models that do not rely on instruction-tuned assistant behavior
target_learners: researchers and platform moderators detecting LLM-generated text
target_learning_goals: distinguishing machine-generated from human-written text
examples: EchoPrompt prepends the fixed prefix 'You are a helpful, versatile, and intelligent AI assistant...' to each evaluated passage before dual-model scoring

article_title: Once a Response, Always a Response: Detecting LLM-generated Text via Latent Prompt Restoration
citation: Hongrui Bao, Yubing Ren, Jinhan You, Fang Fang, Shi Wang, Yanan Cao. (2026). ONCE A RESPONSE, ALWAYS A RESPONSE: DETECTING LLM-GENERATED TEXT VIA LATENT PROMPT RESTORATION. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05741
title: EchoPrompt: a training-free zero-shot detector using restored assistant-context calibrated scoring
description: EchoPrompt is a three-step training-free detector: it (1) prepends a unified task-agnostic assistant-style prefix to restore a generic response context, (2) computes token-level log-likelihoods under an instruction-tuned proxy model on the restored sequence and under the base model on the original text, defining a context-calibrated token-level gap averaged into a sequence score, and (3) applies threshold-based detection where a higher score indicates stronger latent prompt dependency. Its score is Score_EchoPrompt(X; cg) = (1/(n-1)) * sum of log P_inst(xt|cg,x<t) - log P_base(xt|x<t).
requirements: an instruction-tuned proxy model paired with its corresponding base model
a fixed generic assistant-style prefix, selected on an independent HC3 development set and fixed across datasets and proxy families
a decision threshold
constraints: non-chat/completion outputs yield lower AUROC (82.50% on RAID)
it may produce false positives and false negatives; the authors do not recommend it as definitive evidence of authorship or the sole basis for consequential decisions
target_learners: researchers
platform moderators
educators screening LLM-generated text
target_learning_goals: zero-shot detection of machine-generated text
examples: Runtime per sample is 0.254s, a middle-range efficiency relative to heavier baselines like LastDE++ (1.529s) and DNA-DetectLLM (0.444s)

description: CyberAGENTS is a layered, ontology-guided multi-agent framework for gamified cybersecurity learning built on the principle of structured autonomy. citation: Chenguang Pan, Airui Meng, and Youmi Suk. (2026). Distilling Black-Box Machine Learning into a Small, Self-Explaining Language Model for Learning Analytics. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.21165
title: Two-stage mentor–mentee distillation pipeline for self-explaining predictive LLMs
description: The pipeline first fits a flexible ML estimator and interprets it with ALE-fANOVA decomposition, then fine-tunes a small open-weight LLM on mentor traces with LoRA. The authors state the design is "estimator-agnostic and paired with a faithfulness-first evaluation framework that audits every narration against the attribution it claims to describe." Unlike prior designs in which the LLM merely restates an explanation another system provides, this mentee produces the estimate, decisions, and explanation itself. Deployment requires only a small model interacting in natural language.
requirements: An upstream fitted estimator that returns an individual-level estimate and a decomposition-based interpretation tool (ALE-fANOVA)
constraints: The pipeline treats the upstream estimator's output as a black box, so errors in the estimator propagate to the distilled model
Requires acceptance-gated validation of mentor traces before training
target_learners: Students, parents, counselors, and classroom-level educational stakeholders
target_learning_goals: Interpreting individual-level predictions and treatment-effect estimates to support educational decision-making
examples: Instantiated on an X-learner causal estimator with the HSLS:09 dataset, producing a fine-tuned Gemma E2B that maps a student's covariate profile to an effect estimate, explanation, and recommended action

citation: Shi, H., Bi, R., Lin, X., & Dai, Y. (2025). Decreasing Digital Distraction in College Students: Associated Online Learning Strategies Identified by Unsupervised Data Mining Approaches. https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/P85S3
title: Embed explicit self-regulation training and self-control tools in online courses to foster lower digital distraction
description: The article recommends that educators build students' capacity to regulate attention in digital environments rather than only removing distractions. Because SRL strategies such as goal setting, environment structuring, and time management co-occurred most consistently with lower distraction, the authors advise that "educators can incorporate explicit training on self-control skills within course structures", including workshops on structured study schedules and self-control tools. This targets college students in online courses and the goal of maintaining focused engagement.
requirements: Educators need course structures that can host explicit training on self-control skills, such as workshops or modules on creating structured study schedules
constraints: The supporting evidence is associative and self-reported from one university sample; the article frames these as preliminary insights for future research, not tested interventions
target_learners: college students in synchronous online courses
target_learning_goals: maintaining focused attention and reducing off-task digital device use during online learning
examples: The article suggests embedding workshops or modules on creating structured study schedules and using online self-control tools like Pomodoro timers, task prioritization apps, and notification blockers, and designing synchronous sessions with real-time polls, Q&A sessions, and personalized communication.

article_title: An Emancipatory Vision for Designing (Generative) AI for Learner Flourishing
citation: Luis P. Prieto, Yannis Dimitriadis. (2026). An emancipatory vision for designing (generative) AI for learner flourishing. International Workshop on Critical and More-than-human Perspectives on AI in Education (at EC-TEL 2026). https://luispprieto.com/
title: Emancipatory vision of AIED oriented to learner flourishing within nested complex systems
description: The paper proposes an alternative vision in which educational AI is designed to foster long-term learning, agency, and flourishing rather than performance alone. It holds that technology deployment is the beginning of appropriation, that systems should intervene only while necessary, that multiple values in tension should be elicited and navigated, and that education is a communal process of socialization into group knowledge and values. The article argues learners using such technologies will be more attuned to evidence-based notions of human flourishing, and expects flourishing learners to lead to more flourishing societies and environment.
requirements: AI systems built specifically for education rather than retrofitted general-purpose workplace technologies
constraints: The vision is described as embrionary and not yet realized; many open questions remain
target_learners: all learners using educational AI technology
target_learning_goals: long-term learning
learner agency
human flourishing
examples: The paper contrasts its vision with the learning-performance paradox and GenAI side effects such as over-reliance and metacognitive laziness
key_sources: Luis P. Prieto, Yannis Dimitriadis. (2026). An emancipatory vision for designing (generative) AI for learner flourishing. International Workshop on Critical and More-than-human Perspectives on AI in Education (at EC-TEL 2026). https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07715

title: Ten tentative design principles for emancipatory AIED (tools not agents, appropriation, fading, exiting the screen, and more)
description: The paper offers an initial catalog of ten design principles for educational AI built on its alternative assumptions: design for multi-level agency (tools and services, not autonomous agents), appropriation and unfolding, fading scaffolding, exiting the screen, emotional detachment (avoiding attachment hacking), theoretical and value syncretism via modular plugin architectures, uncertainty (minimalist flexible designs), learner resourcefulness, metacognition, and socio-technical interoperability. The authors state these are tentative and later discussions and prototypes need to further exemplify them.
requirements: designs should support or be able to integrate with multiple theories of learning and pedagogy
constraints: principles are tentative and not yet exemplified in prototypes
target_learners: learners in classrooms and other educational settings using AIED systems
target_learning_goals: learner autonomy
metacognition
resilience and resourcefulness
social flourishing
examples: Principle 5 states AIED systems should avoid posing as people even while supporting the emotional aspects of learning, to prevent attachment hacking
