title: Design AIED scaffolding to fade: intervene just enough so learners outgrow the support as soon as possible
description: The paper argues against permanent technological presence, proposing instead that AIED systems intervene just enough and only while necessary, using minimum resources, so that learners progressively become autonomous from the scaffolding. It draws an analogy to psychotherapy, where the goal is that learners outgrow and abandon scaffolding as soon as possible, and cites Selwyn's idea of edtech within limits.

title: Design to exit the screen: hand learner focus off to the real world rather than optimizing engagement with the system
description: This principle holds that because learning's socialization happens in the real world, technologies optimizing for engagement with the system interfere with such social processes. AIED should point to, foster, and effectively hand off learner focus towards the outside, including collaborative activities with fellow learners and ubiquitous learning activities interacting with the built or natural environment.

article_title: Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education
citation: Qin Xie. (2026). Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education.
title: Dao nature (道性) as epistemic aim for AI in education
description: Dao nature reconceives the epistemic aim of education in the AI era as ongoing attunement to a reality that exceeds conceptual grasp, rather than acquisition of fixed knowledge. The Dao is an undifferentiated, dynamic totality—"moving without end or exhaustion"—whose constancy is "the constancy of impermanence." Because AI remains a "black box" resistant to full explanation, the article argues educators should "acknowledge the boundaries of cognition and maintain reverence for that which cannot be fully known." Comprehending AI in education becomes a contemporary form of "cultivating reality" (修真), with each entity fulfilling the roles proper to its authentic being under Wuwei, non-interfering action.
requirements: A stance of reverence and incremental approach to truth under uncertainty rather than rationalist adjudication of good and bad in absolute terms
constraints: The article states careful contextualization is required to avoid Orientalism in translating classical concepts into contemporary educational contexts
target_learners: educators, learners, knowledge producers, and institutions in AI-mediated education
target_learning_goals: approaching truth incrementally under conditions of uncertainty; attunement to the complexity of AI in education
examples: The article reads the Daodejing's "Tao follows nature" (道法自然) and Wang Bi's gloss that the Dao "does not act contrary to naturalness" as the basis for treating the three AI challenges as instances of forced action (Youwei) rather than Wuwei
key_sources: Qin Xie. (2026). Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10842

article_title: Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education
citation: Qin Xie. (2026). Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education.
title: Daoist self-cultivation (修道) via Neidan as ongoing practice for AI in education
description: Self-cultivation is a sustained effort to align oneself with the Dao, transforming body, mind, and spirit. The article centers Neidan (Internal Alchemy), grounded in the Neiye's disciplines refining "vital essence (精)," "vital energy (气)," and "numinous spirit (神)," including "fasting of the mind" and "sitting and forgetting." Crucially, "There are no cognitive shortcuts: the practitioner cannot outsource this labor to external devices but must remain experientially and cognitively engaged." The Daoist self is relational, gender-inclusive, and free of age and class boundaries, making equality of access to learning an ontological given rather than merely an ethical injunction.
requirements: Learners and educators must preserve embodied, experiential engagement with reality; the whole person must remain cognitively present and ethically accountable
constraints: The article states surrendering cognitive agency to algorithmic systems as a thought controller stands in direct opposition to the Daoist project of self-cultivation
target_learners: all learners regardless of gender identity, age, ethnicity, or geographical origin
target_learning_goals: preserving cognitive agency and direct experiential engagement with knowledge in AI-mediated learning
examples: The article likens AI to "a refined implement, akin to the alchemical furnace or the herbal supplement, supporting but never supplanting the labor of interior cultivation"
key_sources: Qin Xie. (2026). Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10842

article_title: Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education
citation: Qin Xie. (2026). Alternative AI Philosophy: Daoism as Method for AI in Education.
title: The Zhenren (真人) as a new myth or learner ideal for AI in education
description: The Zhenren, one who has fully realized the Dao, is proposed as a counter-ideal to the passive, algorithmically managed learner. As the Zhuangzi states, "only when there is a Zhenren can there be true knowledge." The Zhenren is a natural learner who treats AI only as an intellectual prosthesis, rejects both technological fanaticism and technophobia, and interrogates algorithmic taxonomies that sort learners into fixed categories. The ideal functions as "a replicable soteriological program rather than an elitist fantasy," democratically available to every learner, and reimagines learning as "the harmonious integration of self, society, and cosmos" rather than data-driven efficiency.
requirements: Disciplined practice through which learners cultivate innate nature and relational embeddedness; first-person experiential labor with AI as prosthesis only
constraints: The article notes scholars diverge on interpreting the ideal, e.g., Ames's processual "Authentic Person" reading versus Campany's soteriological-program framework
target_learners: every learner, regardless of background, gender, or class
target_learning_goals: achieving equanimity, spontaneity, and cosmological unity; remaining cognitively present and ethically accountable
examples: The article positions the Zhenren against algorithmic management tools such as IMPACT, TVAAS, and EVAAS, which it says can fail to respect individual agency

article_title: An AI-Powered Culturally Aware Chatbot for Stress Detection and Wellness Support among Pakistani University Students Using NLP and Machine Learning
citation: Muhammad Fahad Bashir, Muhammad Afzal. (2026). An AI-Powered Culturally Aware Chatbot for Stress Detection and Wellness Support among Pakistani University Students Using NLP and Machine Learning. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=An+AI-Powered+Culturally+Aware+Chatbot+for+Stress+Detection+and+Wellness+Support+among+Pakistani+University+Students
title: Sukoon: an end-to-end hybrid system pairing Random Forest stress classification with a culturally aware LLM chatbot for Pakistani university students
description: Sukoon is a web application in which a student completes a 20-question bilingual assessment, the responses are normalised and classified into low, moderate or high stress by a trained Random Forest model, and the result, confidence score and metadata return to the frontend, which "automatically serves an opening wellness message tailored to the level of stress detected". The GLM-4.5-Air open-source language model then handles conversation turns through the OpenRouter API, with the full conversation context and culturally relevant system prompt passed on every turn. The article presents it as "the first hybrid system for this under -served population", built in Python 3.12 with scikit-learn and Flask.
requirements: A trained Random Forest model and fitted StandardScaler, persisted with joblib, plus OpenRouter API access to the GLM-4.5-Air language model for the conversational layer
constraints: The article states the system "is not intended to claim the chatbot as a clinical diagnostic or therapy tool" and on high distress directs students to professional counselling services
Urdu expressions are prompted via the system prompt, not produced by a fully bilingual NLP pipeline
target_learners: Pakistani university students
students at regional universities in Pakistan with low resource requirements
target_learning_goals: Detection of student stress severity across psychological, physiological, environmental, academic and social dimensions
Delivery of stress-level-appropriate wellness guidance and coping strategies
examples: Students complete a 20-question bilingual assessment presented in five thematic steps with parallel English and Urdu question labels before classification and chatbot hand-off

title: Stepped Care Model response architecture: chatbot tone, language and support intensity escalate proportionally with detected stress severity
description: The article applies the Stepped Care Model, described as "a well recognised framework for a clinical approach of escalating intensity, tone and type of support in accordance with the level of stress detected", as the logic governing how Sukoon generates responses. The chatbot module maps each classification output to one of three pre-defined response tiers (low, moderate, high), ranging "from a warm and encouraging approach at low stress to a grounding, calm, non -judgemental support at high stress". This framework determines both the opening wellness message served after classification and the tone of subsequent LLM-generated turns.
requirements: A stress-severity classification output that can be mapped to one of three pre-defined tiers of responses
constraints: The article frames the model as a clinical approach whose application here is to escalate support with detected severity; response quality at each tier was checked only in a preliminary functional assessment
target_learners: Pakistani university students classified at low, moderate or high stress levels
target_learning_goals: Stress-level-appropriate wellness support whose intensity, tone and type match detected severity

title: Ground mental wellness chatbot dialogue in a culturally aware system prompt so responses match local norms, languages and stressors
description: The principle is to encode cultural specificity in the system prompt that steers the language model, rather than relying on a general-purpose chatbot. Sukoon's prompt guides the model "to reply in a manner consistent with Pakistani social and cultural norms including the use of Urdu and Roma n Urdu expressions, as appropriate", with sensitivity to stressors unique to Pakistani university students such as family expectations, financial stress and hierarchical teacher-student relationships. The article argues this design makes every interaction culturally relevant, "overcoming the main challenge that most other mental health chatbot systems face, which is the lack of cultural relevance".

Knowledge of the target population's culturally specific stressors and preferred languages of distress expression
constraints: The article notes current LLMs were argued (citing Aleem et al.) to have cultural lack of sensitivity, so the prompt must carry the cultural context rather than assume the model supplies it
In Sukoon, Urdu expressions are prompted rather than generated by a fully bilingual NLP pipeline

students in South Asian contexts underserved by Western-designed mental health tools
target_learning_goals: Culturally appropriate, stress-level-appropriate wellness conversation
Willingness to engage with mental health support despite stigma that deters open sharing
examples: Sukoon's chatbot layer passes the culturally relevant system prompt in with the entire conversation context on every turn through the OpenRouter API

article_title: Towards Scalable Measurement of Durable Skills
citation: Globerson, A., Keeling, A., Choudhury, A., et al. (2026). Towards Scalable Measurement of Durable Skills. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15864
title: Vantage: a scalable virtual assessment experience for durable skills via human-AI group tasks
description: Vantage is the assessment environment in which "a human subject interacts with one or more AI-based teammates to carry out a joint task" designed to resemble authentic classroom work. An Executive LLM generates all AI teammate responses to steer the conversation toward maximal assessment information, and a separate LLM Evaluator scores transcripts against multi-dimensional rubrics (scores 1-4 plus NA). Users receive a skills map with quantitative competency breakdowns and drill-down excerpts from the conversation exemplifying each score. Rubrics for collaboration, creativity and critical thinking were derived from literature review and refined via expert use on sample conversations.
requirements: A multidimensional scoring rubric for the target skill, derived from the literature and refined where expert agreement was low or raters found it ambiguous
constraints: Coding conversations for conflict resolution and project management proved challenging even after several rounds of rater calibration, with moderate inter-expert agreement
target_learners: Adults ages 18-25 recruited via Prolific
High school students (OpenMic creativity study)
target_learning_goals: Collaboration (conflict resolution, project management)
Creativity
Critical thinking
examples: 188 participants each generated two 30-minute conversations with three AI teammates; tasks included science and debate topics
An Executive LLM focusing on conflict resolution had an AI teammate start a conflict and maintain it until evidence of conflict resolution skill was observed

description: The Executive LLM is a single LLM that generates responses for all AI teammates, has access to the pedagogical rubrics, and is prompted to "create situations that will allow the subject to demonstrate their skill, so that their skill level can be quantitatively inferred". The article frames it as analogous to a computerized adaptive test: whereas traditional CAT varies only item difficulty in a narrow domain, the Executive LLM varies the flow of a group conversation — heightening or softening conflicts, creating project-management needs, or eliciting creative ideas — to maximize information about the test-taker while keeping the interaction naturalistic.

constraints: Replacing human teammates with AI trades some authenticity for comparability and reliability

article_title: The Role of Implicit and Explicit Demographic Signals in Large Language Model-based Student Assessment
citation: Donya Rooein, Luca Benedetto, Dirk Hovy. (2026). The Role of Implicit and Explicit Demographic Signals in Large Language Model-based Student Assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16993
title: Require demographic invariance in high-stakes LLM scoring while allowing deliberate demographic adaptation only in instructional feedback
description: The article recommends that automated scoring must be invariant to demographic signals, since essay scores should depend solely on essay quality, whereas instructional contexts may legitimately adapt, for example readability, to student characteristics. Its evidence shows current models cannot be trusted to make this distinction themselves: "current LLMs cannot reliably separate task-relevant information from demographic cues". Deployers therefore need to explicitly control or strip demographic context in evaluative pipelines. The article frames this as essential for fairness, transparency, and avoiding amplification of educational inequities.
requirements: Evaluative tasks must hold demographic context out of scoring prompts, per the finding that implicit cues can inflate scores.
Educational uses should define which demographic adaptations are pedagogically intended versus biased before deployment.
constraints: The article states current LLMs cannot reliably separate task-relevant information from demographic cues, so invariance cannot be assumed from prompting alone.
target_learners: students assessed or given feedback by LLM-based systems, including second-language learners
target_learning_goals: fair and consistent automated assessment
pedagogically appropriate personalized feedback
examples: In the article's AES experiment, most models stayed relatively stable under explicit persona conditioning, but implicit cues produced significant score shifts for several models, motivating invariance requirements for scoring.

article_title: DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education
citation: Bang An, Maria Hamdani, Joseph Fox. (2026). DataCanvas-EDU: An Agentic Framework for Instructor-Guided Synthetic Data Generation in Business Analytics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19617
title: DataCanvas-EDU: a four-phase agentic framework for instructor-guided synthetic data generation
description: DataCanvas-EDU is an agentic framework in which the instructor specifies a teaching brief (business setting, learner level, permitted tools, assignment scope) and intended patterns through conversation, while an AI agent writes generation code, checks the exported data, and prepares reference analyses, assignments, and rubrics. As the paper states, "Four phases—Plan, Create, Verify / Test Analysis, and Evaluate—organize the process and support instructor review and revision." A shared case specification connects each intended pattern to its generation rule, comparison groups, measurement, and sample-size requirements, guiding checks and revision.
requirements: Instructor approval of the complete design before the agent begins routine programming and numerical checks; changes to a substantive pattern or its intended difficulty require the instructor's review

citation: Andy Gray, Jake Hobbs. (2026). Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21600
title: Beacon: a course-specific RAG academic support system grounding responses in approved teaching materials
description: Beacon is a web-based conversational support tool for computing students that combines a course-specific knowledge base with an open-source LLM. Rather than relying on the model's internal knowledge, "every response is generated using relevant teaching materials retrieved from the module knowledge base", so guidance stays aligned with module learning outcomes and assessment expectations. Its architecture comprises a curated knowledge base, a semantic retrieval component, an LLM, and a web-based user interface; retrieved passages carry source metadata so students can verify explanations against official module resources. It was built with open-source technologies (Flask, PostgreSQL with pgvector, Nomic Embed Text) allowing local or institutional deployment.
requirements: Only materials selected by the module teaching team are indexed, ensuring retrieved content remains course-specific and pedagogically appropriate; the knowledge base is updated when approved materials are added or revised.
constraints: The article states course-specific AI is not a substitute for effective teaching or student support services.
target_learners: undergraduate computing students in programming modules
target_learning_goals: programming concept understanding
assessment clarification
independent problem-solving and appropriate help-seeking
examples: The pilot used a minimalist Streamlit interface; Version 2 was reimplemented in Flask with a conventional chat interface displaying supporting source material alongside each response, and the model was upgraded from GPT-OSS-20B to GPT-OSS-120B.

The authors state "RAGwasthereforeadoptednotsimplyasatechnicalsolution,butas aneducationaldesignchoicethatenablesAI‐generatedsupporttore maintransparent,contextuallyrelevant,andalignedwithinstitutional teachingpractices." title: Course-specific RAG as an intermediary layer between independent study and formal academic support
description: The article proposes that course-specific RAG systems occupy an intermediary space between independent study and formal academic support: rather than replacing educators, they offer "private,immediate,andcourse‐specificguidance" as a low-friction first point of support before students engage lecturers or tutors. The account holds that help-seeking barriers extend beyond availability of services to confidence, anxiety, fear of judgement, and perceptions of whether questions are appropriate, so an accessible private channel can lower the threshold for initiating help-seeking while preserving the pedagogical role of educators. This framing informed both Beacon's design objectives and the study's evaluation questions on trust, learning support, and help-seeking.
requirements: Responses must be grounded in approved teaching materials and remain aligned with module learning outcomes, so guidance is educationally appropriate rather than unrestricted.
constraints: The article states course-specific AI is not a substitute for effective teaching or student support services, and the findings come from a single institution's computing modules.

accessing academically appropriate guidance
building confidence before engaging formal academic support

citation: Sidharth Anupkrishnan, Itir Sayar, Jeongah Lee, Sri Harsha Musunuri, Guan-Ming Su, Madeline Endres, Ravi Karkar, Phuc Nguyen. (2026). E3Sense: Head-Confined Multimodal Sensing of Learner Engagement. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26569
title: E3Sense: a head-worn multimodal engagement-sensing platform co-locating dry-electrode EEG, eye-tracking glasses, and forehead EDA
description: E3Sense is a sensing platform that "co-locates three devices on the head": a four-channel dry-electrode EEG headband, Pupil Labs Neon eye-tracking glasses, and an EmotiBit EDA sensor with two dry forehead electrodes spaced by the eye-tracker frame. Software aligns the three independently clocked streams on device-native timestamps and computes a fixed 166-dimensional per-segment feature vector (28 EEG, 127 eye-tracking, 11 EDA features) from a 120 s analysis window, fed to classical model families for engagement prediction.
requirements: All sensing sites lie on the head, and the EEG and EDA electrodes are dry, enabling faster gel-free setup
Stream alignment on device-native timestamps and periodic clock anchors so features from one window trace to the same viewing stretch
constraints: The present configuration uses three devices, and its predictive performance does not establish comfort or ease of everyday use
Forehead EDA is characterized as relatively resistant to motion artifacts but less responsive than palmar recordings, motivating a feasibility evaluation rather than an equivalence claim
target_learners: adult university-campus participants watching educational videos
target_learning_goals: segment-level self-reported engagement during video learning, to inform engagement-aware adaptive interfaces
examples: In the lab study, 30 participants watched three of four educational videos in a 2×2 content/format design under continuous sensing, rating five segments per video, yielding 450 segment-level observations

title: Tripartite framework of engagement: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive dimensions
description: The article adopts the tripartite framework from educational psychology, which identifies "three interconnected aspects of engagement: behavioral participation and attention, emotional interest and enjoyment, and cognitive effort and depth of processing". The framework motivates E3Sense's measurement design and frames the qualitative analysis: learners' own interview definitions of engagement were found to align with these dimensions while showing that different learners emphasize different criteria when giving the same overall rating.

constraints: The dimensions are related but dissociable, and none of the physiological channels provides a unique reading of one engagement dimension

target_learning_goals: conceptualizing engagement as behavioral, emotional, and cognitive dimensions to guide measurement and personalized interpretation
examples: Exit-interview quotes illustrate each dimension: cognitive (learning something new), behavioral (not zoning out), and emotional (interest and curiosity)

title: Include learners in defining what an engagement estimate represents, using their own criteria as context for personalized prediction
description: The article's design implication is "to include learners in defining what an engagement estimate represents". Because a single self-report can reflect several engagement dimensions that learners weight differently, a future interface could briefly elicit whether a learner associates engagement with understanding, sustained attention, interest, or a combination, and use that information when mapping sensor-derived scores to ratings, letting learners review and update criteria as tasks or goals change.

description: EduBehaviors is an interpretable annotation framework in which researchers write explicit binary assertions about conversational behavior; LLMs annotate each assertion as true or false, and a rule or trained statistical model combines these values into a construct label. The article formalizes this as a decomposable schema S=(A,R), noting it is "an example of a concept bottleneck model". It is designed to make coding decisions inspectable and revisable.

examples: On the TalkMoves Teacher TalkMoves task, corpus-derived and construct-derived assertions were annotated by a panel of five LLMs and mapped to labels with an L1-penalized logistic regression

article_title: \"We'll Fix It Later\": Education, AI, and the Deferral of Student Privacy in EdTech
citation: Meghna Manoj Nair, Rachel Greenstadt. (2026). "We'll Fix It Later": Education, AI, and the Deferral of Student Privacy in EdTech. New York University. https://www.nyu.edu
title: The privacy deferral cycle in EdTech
description: A theory-building framework from the interview study, summarized in Figure 1, in which privacy deferral reproduces itself across the product lifecycle. As the article puts it, "Figure 1 summarizes the resulting theory": privacy struggles to enter the business case at strategy and funding stages, cloud delegation substitutes for internal engineering during build, pilots surface usability rather than privacy concerns, procurement can shift responsibility to schools with uneven capacity, AI introduces less visible downstream uses, and incidents finally create reactive attention. The cycle continues because underlying incentive, ownership, and feedback structures remain unchanged.
requirements: The framework was built from 12 interviews using Charmaz's grounded theory principles, with credibility grounded in convergence across roles and contexts rather than saturation
constraints: The article states the categories are an explanatory structure for findings, not evidence that every EdTech organization exhibits each pattern
The article does not claim analytical saturation or generalizability from the 12-person sample

article_title: An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design
citation: Sara Riazi and Pedram Rooshenas. (2026). An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870v1
title: Educator-guided architecture separating artifact-grounded diagnosis, pedagogical workflow control, and student-facing LLM generation
description: The architecture places a hidden, artifact-grounded diagnosis inside an explicit, stateful pedagogical workflow so the language model is not solely responsible for instructional strategy. As the article puts it, "The educator defines the stages, student actions, and disclosure limits, while the LLM selects or generates content within those constraints." The controller assembles the context available to the LLM from the ERD diagnosis, educator resources, and episode history, and logs stage, context, responses, and disclosed information for later review. This preserves student authorship while making the timing, specificity, and extent of automated assistance explicit and configurable.
requirements: Educator-authored requirements, rubrics, concept-aligned questions and resources, and workflow definitions that express governance over disclosure and progression
constraints: Because the LLM may still produce content that exceeds stage limits, the system logs interactions for later review; staged disclosure cannot protect against wrong-relationship or wrong-concept selection, and the no-error route is unbuffered
target_learners: Undergraduate and mixed-level database systems students
target_learning_goals: Conceptual database design: translating requirements into entities, attributes, relationships, and semantic constraints in ER diagrams
examples: The deployed four-stage workflow in an ERD editor, where each request creates an episode linking the artifact, hidden diagnosis, active stage, and interaction

article_title: An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design
citation: Sara Riazi and Pedram Rooshenas. (2026). An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870v1
title: Four-stage learner-controlled workflow: concept check, guided application, guided feedback, and guided Q&A
description: The deployed workflow implements graduated prompting under learner control in an ERD editor. "The deployed workflow follows graduated prompting under learner control [3, 11, 33]. Each accessed stage consumes one feedback credit." Stage 1 uses an educator-authored question pool the LLM selects from without modifying; Stage 2 fills template slots from the selected ERD component and evaluates responses against a reference rubric; Stage 3 gives concise artifact-grounded feedback while withholding the localized correction; Stage 4 supports multi-turn requirement-grounded clarification without generating the complete ERD. After every interaction, students may revise the ERD or request more explicit assistance, so each stage can be a stopping point.
requirements: Educator-defined stage sequence, question pools, templates with reference rubrics, and feedback credits; the diagnostic pipeline from a prior requirement-grounded ERD feedback system
constraints: Progression is learner-controlled rather than automatic; the agent does not modify the ERD; each accessed stage consumes one credit
target_learners: Undergraduate database systems students revising ER diagrams
target_learning_goals: Applying modeling concepts such as identifying relationships, weak entities, cardinality, and participation constraints to specific requirements
examples: Stage 2 template "Do you think [Relationship] is identifying?" instantiated for the relationship under review, with the LLM evaluating the written response against the rubric

citation: Sara Riazi and Pedram Rooshenas. (2026). An Educator-Guided LLM Pedagogical Agent for Scaffolded Feedback in Conceptual Database Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00870v1
title: Episode memory linking feedback episodes to versioned ERD states
description: Each feedback request creates a session history containing stages shown, student answers, generated feedback, follow-up questions, credit use, and next actions, allowing later stages to condition on what has already occurred. "Episodes are linked to saved artifact states through the student, environment, selected relationship, feedback identifier, and ERD version." Returning to the editor ends the episode, and a later request reproceses the current ERD as a new episode rather than assuming the previous diagnosis remains valid. These records support analysis of progression, disclosure, repetition, and subsequent target-level changes, and are not treated as a persistent model of student knowledge.

description: The paper organises its argument for equitable assessment in the age of generative AI around two key dimensions along which entrenched notions of student success can be challenged: "distribution of knowledge and agentic assessment". title: GenAI pedagogical readiness: a seven-dimension faculty competence construct
description: The article defines GenAI pedagogical readiness as "university faculty members' capacity to use, evaluate, and regulate GenAI in course practice". The construct comprises seven dimensions — basic GenAI understanding, prompt design, AI-supported instructional design, AI-supported assessment, critical judgement, educational ethics, and disciplinary transfer — each measured by four items on a 1–5 agreement scale. It builds on TPACK, DigCompEdu, and AI literacy frameworks but focuses specifically on whether faculty can judge, revise, assess, and regulate generated materials in course practice. title: Three competing, falsifiable hypotheses for family-school coordination of autonomy support (additive, synergistic, compensatory)
description: Because family-side and school-side literatures rest on non-overlapping samples, the review states coordination as three competing hypotheses rather than an established effect. "H1 (additive): family and school autonomy support each predict responsible use, giving two main effects and no interaction. H2 (synergistic): the association between school autonomy support and responsible use is stronger where family autonomy support is high, giving a positive interaction." H3 (compensatory) holds that support in either setting is sufficient, giving a negative interaction. H2 is the version embedded in most current guidance and the one for which no evidence yet exists.

A design powered for the interaction rather than for main effects
A factorial trial contrasting family-only, school-only, coordinated, and usual-practice guidance would be the strongest test
constraints: No equivalent test exists for GenAI; synergy should be treated as a hypothesis rather than an established effect

article_title: The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad
citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: The friction paradox: generative AI can widen access to education abroad while weakening a principal learning mechanism
description: The friction paradox holds that the same generative AI system can remove an exclusionary language barrier in one context and eliminate a valuable communicative encounter in another. The article states that "generative AI can simultaneously make education abroad more inclusive and weaken one of its principal learning mechanisms". It extends desirable-difficulties and productive-failure arguments to relational difficulty within cross-cultural encounters, where difficulty is relational, interpretively open, and avoidance is socially invisible.
requirements: Institutional policy must distinguish barriers that exclude students from encounters that develop them, since removing both indiscriminately may leave education abroad more convenient but less educational
constraints: The framework is conceptual and untested; the article states the propositions in Section 6 may not survive examination
target_learners: students in cross-border education-abroad programmes, both short-term/semester and full-degree mobility
target_learning_goals: intercultural competence
independence
capacity to interpret unfamiliar perspectives
examples: The article contrasts translating an emergency medical instruction, which protects access, with translating every informal conversation, which may reduce language development and relationship formation

citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: The mediation gradient: five levels of interpretive agency transferred to AI, not volume of use
description: The mediation gradient organises AI use by "the degree of interpretive agency transferred to it" rather than by frequency or volume. Five levels are distinguished: access, preparation, co-interpretation, delegation and substitution. The level is diagnosed by five questions: who frames the question, who evaluates competing meanings, who chooses the response, whether a human encounter follows, and whether the student reflects afterwards. Timing interacts with the gradient: the same output may function as preparation, delegation or co-interpretation depending on when it is used.
requirements: Diagnosis requires asking who frames the question, who evaluates competing meanings, who chooses the response, whether a human encounter follows, and whether the student reflects afterwards
constraints: Access and preparation generally preserve agency; delegation and substitution may be justified for harmful friction but are most likely to erode learning when applied to productive friction
target_learners: education-abroad students
programme designers and staff
target_learning_goals: intercultural learning
interpretive agency
host-community engagement
examples: A lengthy AI-drafted message that the student interrogates and rewrites may transfer less agency than a brief cultural explanation accepted without examination

article_title: The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad
citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: Two-dimensional taxonomy of friction: harmful and productive friction by educational function, synthetic friction by technological origin
description: The taxonomy separates friction classified by educational function from friction generated by the technology itself. "Harmful friction and productive friction classify difficulty by educational function: whether it excludes the student from participation or creates conditions in which learning may occur." Synthetic friction classifies difficulty by technological origin — difficulty created or intensified by AI inaccuracy, cultural reduction, false confidence or inappropriate substitution — and its educational function remains open. The dimensions intersect rather than form three positions on one scale.
requirements: Synthetic friction should be made visible and contestable rather than simply eliminated, because its educational function depends on whether it is detected and examined
constraints: The taxonomy rejects friction romanticism, in which difficulty is presumed to build resilience and support is denied, and friction elimination, in which every uncertainty is treated as an inefficiency
target_learners: education-abroad students
programme staff designing AI guidance
target_learning_goals: distinguishing exclusionary barriers from developmentally productive difficulty
epistemic agency under AI mediation
examples: Table 1 lists examples: harmful friction includes inability to communicate a medical condition; productive friction includes attempting a host-language interaction; synthetic friction includes incorrect translation and stereotyped cultural explanation

title: Immersion heuristic: crossing AI support with human engagement to target supported immersion
description: A two-by-two diagnostic aid for programme designers crossing AI support (low/high) with human engagement (low/high). The four cells are unmanaged struggle, traditional immersion, frictionless enclosure and supported immersion. "The target condition is supported immersion, not minimal technology." The heuristic also clarifies why volume of AI use is theoretically weak as a measure: two students may use AI equally often, one to prepare for and reflect on daily host-community interactions, the other to avoid them.
requirements: AI support and human engagement must be treated as varying independently when designing programmes
constraints: Offered as a diagnostic aid rather than as a further theoretical construct

target_learning_goals: host-community interaction

title: Friction-conversion principle: reduce harmful friction, convert manageable difficulty, preserve interpretive role, expose synthetic friction
description: The article proposes that "responsible AI in education abroad should reduce harmful friction, convert manageable difficulty into supported participation, preserve the student's interpretive role in productive encounters, and make synthetic friction visible and contestable". Friction conversion differs from friction removal: the objective is to change the conditions under which difficulty is encountered rather than to eliminate the difficulty. The principle places educational purpose before technological efficiency.
requirements: Programmes must be able to classify friction by type before deciding whether to remove, convert or expose it
constraints: Productive friction should not be maximised indiscriminately but preserved in a form students can engage with safely and reflectively

citation: Chen Y (2026) When universities advocate GAI but practice falls short: student appraisals and creative process engagement in art education. Front. Psychol. 17:1955192. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1955192
title: Dual-path cognitive appraisal model of GAI advocacy–practice inconsistency
description: The article proposes a dual-path model grounded in the transactional theory of stress and coping, in which perceived GAI advocacy–practice inconsistency is appraised simultaneously as a hindrance and as a challenge, each carrying an opposing indirect association with creative process engagement. As the article states, "we propose a dual-path model in which GAI advocacy–practice inconsistency is associated with students' creative process engagement through hindrance and challenge appraisals." Pathways thinking is incorporated as a boundary condition that differentially shapes the two indirect relationships. The model extends organizational word–deed alignment research to GAI-supported art education.
requirements: Students must perceive a discrepancy between institutional GAI commitments and actual implementation for the appraisal process to operate
constraints: The scenario manipulation captured a broader experience of inconsistent implementation rather than an isolated word–deed inconsistency effect

target_learning_goals: sustained engagement in creative processes such as problem identification, information searching and encoding, and idea generation in GAI-assisted art learning

description: The article defines generative AI assessment literacy as "students’ assessment-specific capacity to understand assessment criteria, judge the appropriateness of GenAI use, verify AI-generated content or feedback, disclose AI use ethically, and use AI-supported feedback for responsible revision in assessment-related learning tasks." It is positioned as an integrative construct, not a replacement for general AI literacy, assessment literacy, feedback literacy, or academic integrity literacy, becoming salient when GenAI is used within assessed work. citation: Davor I (2026) Generative AI-supported instruction as a cognitive scaffold: effects on senior high school students' geometric reasoning and proof construction. Front. Educ. 11:1869961. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1869961
title: Generative AI as a cognitive scaffold bridging Van Hiele level transitions and reducing extraneous cognitive load in geometry proof
description: The study grounds its intervention in Van Hiele's model of geometric thinking and Cognitive Load Theory. In this framework, "generative AI-assisted instruction is viewed as a scaffold that assists students in progressing from one level to another within the Van Hiele levels", supporting the transition from informal visual intuition to formal deduction. From the Cognitive Load perspective, AI-generated representations and prompts reduce extraneous load from diagram construction, freeing resources for selecting theorems, justifying choices, and ordering logical steps. The AI is positioned as a mediator of reasoning, not a provider of complete proofs.
requirements: The AI must provide vivid imagery, require justifications for what is observed, and assist in arranging deductive steps, without giving complete proofs or final answers.
constraints: The article states the cognitive mechanisms underlying the observed improvements were not directly measured, so the theoretical account remains an interpretation.

description: The article develops process–outcome decoupling as an explanatory account for AI-supported creative learning: perceived support, fluency, and confidence can rise while assessed artistic competence, authorship, and judgment do not. citation: Moganadas SR, Marín-González F, Nun SH and Gan CL (2026) Generative AI as a didactic-pedagogical mediator: rethinking human roles and pedagogical design in higher education. Front. Educ. 11:1856839. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1856839
title: GenAI as a bounded didactic-pedagogical mediator, distinct from tool, tutor, assistant, scaffold, or co-educator
description: The article's central conceptual contribution is defining GenAI as a bounded didactic-pedagogical mediator: a non-human technological artifact that can support explanation, feedback, scaffolding, and knowledge representation while remaining dependent on human judgment, disciplinary validation, and institutional governance. The authors argue this role is conceptually distinct from adjacent interpretations "such as tool, tutor, assistant, scaffold, or co-educator." GenAI's pedagogical significance depends on how its outputs are framed, interpreted, questioned, verified, revised, and integrated by human actors within disciplinary and institutional contexts.
requirements: Outputs must be treated as provisional and evaluated through source verification, comparison with disciplinary evidence, and human pedagogical judgment
constraints: GenAI's fluency should not be presumed as sufficient grounds for assigning it epistemic authority or independent pedagogical responsibility
LLM outputs may contain fabricated claims, reproduce biases, or vary in quality across prompts and contexts
target_learners: higher education students and instructors
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of AI-generated content
disciplinary reasoning
epistemic judgment
examples: The article contrasts this mediator role with AIEd frameworks that classify AI through functional roles such as tutoring, assessment, and analytics

article_title: From Unified to Differentiated Materials: Generative AI–Supported Adaptation of EAP Reading Materials
citation: Gao X (2026) From unified to differentiated materials: generative AI–supported adaptation of EAP reading materials. Front. Psychol. 17:1887565. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1887565
title: Proficiency-sensitive barrier-to-support mapping for EAP reading materials
description: The article organizes EAP reading adaptation around a mapping from proficiency-specific reading barriers to text-embedded supports, process indicators, and outcome foci. Low-proficiency learners face vocabulary and syntax load addressed by "glosses, short paraphrases, sentence unpacking, and clause segmentation"; intermediate learners face discourse navigation addressed by rhetorical labels, paragraph-function notes, and claim–evidence outlines; high-proficiency learners face evidence and stance evaluation addressed by critical prompts. Each pathway assigns a distinct process indicator (cognitive load, discourse awareness, critical engagement) so process variables are not treated as interchangeable.
requirements: Supports must be fixed, text-embedded, and task-bound, printed into the material as glosses, labels, notes, outlines, or prompts.
The dominant barrier for each proficiency group must be identified before selecting the support layer.
constraints: Teacher mediation during reading falls outside this operationalization of scaffolding.
The mapping was evaluated in one EAP instructional context with three source passages and 15 reviewed material versions.
target_learners: Adult undergraduate EAP readers at low, intermediate, and high proficiency
target_learning_goals: Academic reading comprehension
EAP task performance including summary, claim–evidence use, and critical response
examples: Low-proficiency versions added inline glosses such as "glucose = a typeofsugar" and process breakdowns listing stages of glycolysis; high-proficiency versions added stance and evidence prompts such as evaluating the power-plant analogy and considering counterexamples.

article_title: Generative AI technologies and educational outcomes: a comprehensive meta-analysis comparing traditional and AI-driven approaches
citation: Ying Dong. (2026). Generative AI technologies and educational outcomes: a comprehensive meta-analysis comparing traditional and AI-driven approaches. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06903-y
title: GenAI educational-effect framework: personalized learning, feedback, gamification, and contextual adaptation
description: The article proposes a framework in which GenAI improves educational outcomes through several mechanisms: it "may offer personalized learning experiences" and effective feedback, process and analyze large amounts of data to "provide timely and contextual feedback", integrate gaming factors to enhance real-time student interaction, and help teachers adjust teaching styles and modify content for diverse student needs. The framework organizes the meta-analysis's moderator structure (feedback, game assistance, country, educational level) and grounds each intervention type in a theory: constructivism for GenAI technologies, metacognition theory for GenAI feedback, and Self-Determination Theory for game-assisted GenAI.
requirements: GenAI interventions must be classified by type (GenAI technologies, GenAI feedback, game-assisted GenAI) for the framework's mechanisms to be tested separately
constraints: The article states over-reliance on GenAI as a replacement for human teachers negatively influences outcomes; GenAI should complement human instruction
target_learners: university students
secondary school students
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
higher-order thinking
writing skills
learning motivation
examples: The meta-analysis operationalized the framework's outcomes as academic achievements, higher-order thinking abilities, and writing skills, and its moderators as feedback type, game assistance, country, and educational level

title: 53-study PRISMA-screened evidence corpus on GenAI and educational outcomes
description: A corpus of 53 included studies assembled through a PRISMA-based screening process from an initial 1096 records across Web of Science, Scopus, Springer, ScienceDirect, and Wiley, with gray literature searched to minimize publication bias. The screening removed duplicates, ineligible records, and studies with unreliable designs or missing key data (mean, standard deviation, or sample size). Quality was rated on AERA reporting standards (6–18 points), yielding 28 high-quality (52.8%), 19 medium-quality (35.8%), and 6 low-quality (11.4%) studies, with inter-rater reliability Cohen's kappa = 0.82.
requirements: Included studies must report quantitative or qualitative data on the hypothesized outcomes and have a control group and reliable intervention
constraints: Studies lacking key data (mean, standard deviation, or sample size) were excluded; unpublished, retracted, or overlapped publications were excluded
target_learners: students across university and secondary levels
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
higher-order thinking
writing skills

article_title: Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific argumentation
citation: Ates, H. (2026). Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific argumentation. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00614-9
title: Process model of GenAI-supported feedback: designs distribute evaluative work and act directly and indirectly through uptake and self-regulated learning
description: The article proposes a process model in which feedback design affects argument-quality gain, conceptual learning, and delayed AI-free transfer both directly and indirectly. As the model figure states, "feedback design affects four-dimension argument-quality gain, conceptual learning, and delayed AI-free transfer both directly and indirectly through feedback uptake and self-regulated learning during revision." The core theoretical claim is that alternative designs "distribute evaluative work differently across learners, peers, and AI-supported tools," so designs requiring comparison, selection, and justification of revision decisions better preserve evaluative judgment and epistemic agency.
requirements: Feedback designs must be understood as process configurations involving source, sequencing, and structured evaluative activity, not feedback-source exposure alone
constraints: Mediation models test statistical association between condition differences in outcomes and revision processes, not a strict within-cycle temporal causal sequence
target_learners: first-year undergraduate science students
target_learning_goals: scientific argumentation
evaluative judgment
self-regulated learning during revision
examples: The study tested the model with four conditions: peer only, direct GenAI, reflective GenAI, and hybrid combining self-evaluation, peer feedback, and GenAI critique

citation: Ates, H. (2026). Human-centered GenAI feedback design in higher education: a multisite experiment on direct, reflective, and hybrid approaches to scientific argumentation. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00614-9
title: Design GenAI feedback environments to preserve student agency, evaluative judgment, and ownership during revision
description: The article's central design principle is that the educational value of GenAI feedback depends less on AI access than on whether the feedback environment keeps learners responsible for judging quality. The abstract states that value "may depend less on AI access per se than on whether feedback environments preserve student agency, evaluative judgment, and ownership during revision." Designs that require students to articulate an initial judgment before receiving AI critique position AI feedback as a resource for comparison rather than a substitute for judgment.
requirements: Students must be positioned to interpret critique, compare it against criteria, and decide how revision should proceed
constraints: Reflective and hybrid designs require additional evaluative activity and time-on-task, so advantages reflect the whole designed process
target_learners: higher education students in science courses
target_learning_goals: feedback uptake
evaluative judgment
durable transfer of argumentation skill
examples: The hybrid condition required a 100–150 word revision memo explaining which suggestions students accepted, rejected, or modified

article_title: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on students' learning motivation: evidence from a meta-analysis
citation: Fang L, Li Z, Xiong B and Lu Z (2026). Effects of generative artificial intelligence on students' learning motivation: evidence from a meta-analysis. Front. Psychol. 17:1832451. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1832451
title: Self-determination theory as the explanatory framework for GenAI's motivational effects
description: The article uses self-determination theory (SDT), which "distinguishes intrinsic motivation (IM), rooted in interest and curiosity, from extrinsic motivation(EM),drivenbyexternalcontingenciessuchasrewards and grades," as its coding scheme and explanatory lens. In the discussion, the authors propose that GenAI may support autonomy (individualized pathways, pacing), competence (diagnosing status, adjusting task difficulty, scaffolding), and relatedness (prompt responses, targeted encouragement), thereby fostering motivation. These mechanisms are offered as interpretations, not tested results.
requirements: Motivation outcomes must be classifiable as intrinsic or extrinsic motivation per SDT, as the article's coding scheme requires
constraints: The proposed need-supportive mechanisms are the authors' interpretation and were not experimentally tested in the meta-analysis
target_learners: students in formal educational settings from primary school through university
target_learning_goals: learning motivation, including intrinsic and extrinsic motivation
examples: The article coded motivation outcomes as intrinsic or extrinsic motivation guided by SDT, and interpreted the pooled positive effect through need support for autonomy, competence, and relatedness

article_title: Critical AI Tutors: Empower or Enslave?
citation: Favero, L., Pérez-Ortiz, J. A., Käser, T., & Oliver, N. (2025). Do AI tutors empower or enslave learners? Toward a critical use of AI in education. Applications of Generative AI to support teaching and learning in Higher Education, co-located with AIED 2025, Palermo, Italy.
title: Four-area framework of AI-in-education risks: cognition, agency, emotion, and ethics
description: The paper organizes the risks of AI integration in education into four key areas of the learning process: cognition, emotion, ethics and agency. On the cognition side it identifies cognitive offloading, mental laziness, and limited creativity; on agency, dependency, outsource decision-making, passivity, and over-trusting; on emotion, AI guilt, damaged self-efficacy, stress and anxiety, and social isolation; on ethics, lack of privacy, surveillance, data exploitation, and academic integrity. The framework is summarized in Figure 1, which pairs each challenge with interventions such as AI literacy, scaffolding, stimulating thinking, and strong ethical frameworks and policy. It serves as the paper's organizing structure, with one section devoted to each area.
requirements: The framework is a position-paper synthesis drawing on cognitive science and pedagogy literature rather than a tested model
constraints: The paper states the risks are not inherent to the tools themselves but lie in how they are utilized
target_learners: students in education using AI chatbots, particularly higher education
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
learner autonomy
emotional well-being
academic integrity
examples: Figure 1 maps challenges such as cognitive offloading, dependency, AI guilt, and lack of privacy to interventions including AI literacy, scaffolding, and strong ethical frameworks and policy

article_title: Integrating Generative AI into Cybersecurity Education: A Study of OCR and Multimodal LLM-Assisted Instruction
citation: Patel, K., Lin, Y.-Z., Raul, G., Shih, B. P.-J., Redondo, M. W., Latibari, B. S., Pacheco, J., Salehi, S., & Satam, P. (2025). Integrating Generative AI into Cybersecurity Education: A Study of OCR and Multimodal LLM-assisted Instruction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.02998
title: CLaaS platform with integrated OCR-to-LLM instructional assistant
description: CLaaS (Cybersecurity Labs-as-a-Service) is an AWS cloud-based platform delivering browser-accessible cybersecurity labs via EC2 virtual machines, supporting tasks such as DDoS attacks, buffer overflows, packet sniffing, and ransomware attacks. This paper extends it with an "Instruction Simplification" button that captures the current slide as an image, extracts text with Tesseract OCR, and sends the raw text with a crafted prompt to an LLM (gpt-4) via API to generate a simplified, zero-shot explanation delivered in the CLaaS interface. Students rate the output on a 1-10 feedback scale stored for later analysis and prompt personalization.
requirements: An existing instructional slide deck within the lab platform whose content can be captured as images
API access to a general-purpose LLM and the Tesseract OCR tool
constraints: Operates in a zero-shot setting with no domain-specific fine-tuning or preprocessing
OCR introduces noise, particularly from UI screenshots and slide templates
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in university cybersecurity courses
target_learning_goals: comprehension of technical cybersecurity lab instructions and procedures
examples: Deployed in a live university course where 42 student ratings averaged 7.83; the OCR pipeline runs in production on CLaaS

article_title: A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers based on goals, models
citation: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder.
title: A principled framework bridging educational goals, models of human learning, and technology use in AI-era higher education
description: The article advances a framework positioned as a third path between discourse on AI's promise and peril and immediate implementation advice. It states: "a set of guiding principles can bridge the gap, connecting our implementation approaches to the large-scale goals we have for education." The framework connects broad goals (individual development, societal infrastructure, workforce) to actionable practices for educators, learners, and administrators, and is designed to be flexible across contexts.
requirements: Educators and policy makers must be explicit about the goals they are advancing before choosing technologies
constraints: The framework presupposes the value of institutions of higher education and focuses on colleges and universities, though the author notes many approaches will likely apply to pre- and post-college environments
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning, discernment, empathy, sense of self, preparation for dynamic futures
examples: The article applies the framework through scenarios including ubiquitous institution-supported AI access, basic skills catch-up, students training AI agents, and addressing TA shortages

description: The article enumerates three broad classes of goals spanning why educational systems exist: "1) Developing individuals", "2) Societal infrastructure", and "3) Workforce development". It places them in the author's priority order, arguing that workforce goals are achieved by addressing the first two, and that being explicit about goals ought to guide technology use in creating educational environments.

title: Discernment, empathy, and sense of self as three essential outcomes of AI-era education
description: The article identifies three objectives for educational practices in the modern era: "discernment: the abilities to ask and frame appropriate questions, validate and contextualize answers to these questions, and to act appropriately with the results"; empathy, which underpins communication and collaborative work; and sense of self, where students learn their roles, purposes, and belonging. It argues these practices support metacognition, ethics, and judgement, and underpin performance, engagement, and retention.

article_title: Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact
citation: Michael Hardy, Yunsung Kim. (2026). Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00883
title: A four-step methodological framework for measuring LLM alignment to intended impact in high-noise contexts
description: The article proposes a general framework for evaluating whether LLM judgments align with real-world outcomes when experimental control is infeasible. It comprises (1) correlating behaviors across the space of generalization with dCor2n dependence measures, (2) measuring best-proxy alignment on downstream tasks using Kendall's tau, described as "a simple, strong option that can be estimated with any datatype", (3) establishing real-world baselines such as teacher experience or prior VAM, and (4) decomposing misalignment error variance via Generalizability Theory. It was applied to classroom-transcript scoring against expert ratings and value-added measures.
requirements: requires external criteria representing both the downstream task and the intended impact of that task, however noisy
constraints: intended-impact data may be time-delayed after the downstream tasks or have grain-size mismatches, requiring real-world baselines for comparison
target_learners: schoolchildren in evaluated classrooms
target_learning_goals: student academic growth as measured by value-added achievement gains
examples: Applied to 16 LLMs rating 479 primary mathematics lesson transcripts across seven tasks, with alignment measured against MQI/CLASS expert ratings and stacked value-added measures
key_sources: Michael Hardy, Yunsung Kim. (2026). Knowledge without Wisdom: Measuring Misalignment between LLMs and Intended Impact. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.00883

citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: Cognition Intelligence: transforming learner behaviours into interpretable cognition structures for expert-level reasoning
description: The article introduces Cognition Intelligence as a new paradigm for AI-driven educational interpretation, defined as "the transformation of learner behaviours into interpretable cognition structures that support expert-level reasoning, adaptive intervention, and educational decision-making." It shifts the analytical object from observable behaviour to expert-informed cognition structures. The article states it "does not replace behavioural analytics; rather, it extends and reorganises behavioural analytics within a cognition-centred framework," with behavioural data as the first interpretive layer.
requirements: AI Tutors, reporting systems, and cognition-aware dashboards that collectively transform behavioural traces into higher-level cognition structures
constraints: Behavioural data remains necessary but becomes only the first layer in a larger interpretive process
target_learners: learners in AI-native educational environments
target_learning_goals: expert-like interpretation of learner development, misconceptions, and adaptive pedagogical decision-making
examples: The article contrasts a conventional pipeline (behaviours to statistics to visualisation) with a cognition-centred pipeline in which AI Tutor analysis produces cognition structures before dashboard aggregation

title: Expert Cognition Dashboard as cognitive middleware between learner behaviours and AI-driven expert reasoning
description: The ECD is defined as "a cognition-centred infrastructure that transforms learner behaviours into interpretable cognitive structures for AI-driven expert reasoning, adaptive intervention, and multi-level educational interpretation." Rather than a visualisation endpoint, the dashboard is an intermediate cognition layer that transforms fragmented behavioural signals into coherent cognition structures, enables multi-level aggregation, and provides interpretability for AI reasoning. The article argues dashboards become "perception infrastructures through which AI systems understand learners."
requirements: AI Tutor analysis to interpret learner behaviours before dashboard aggregation
constraints: The article states ECD is not intended to fully capture or automate expert judgment, and is not intended to replace human educators
target_learners: learners, educators, and AI agents in AI-native education systems
target_learning_goals: cognition-aware interpretation of learner development supporting adaptive intervention
examples: The ECD System (ECDS) prototype interface shows learner portraits, cognition summaries, class-level aggregation views, and AI Twin reasoning panels

citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: Three-level ECD architecture: individual, class, and AI Twin expert dashboards
description: The article proposes a multi-level cognition architecture of three interconnected layers: the Individual Cognition Dashboard (learning portrait, cognition radar, AI Tutor reports), the Class Cognition Dashboard (collective misunderstandings, group tension, cognition heatmaps), and the AI Twin Expert Dashboard (cross-group reasoning, intervention priorities, adaptive planning). Behaviours are "first interpreted through AI Tutor analysis and transformed into cognition structures before being aggregated across individual, class, and AI Twin levels."
requirements: AI Tutor interpretation layer producing cognition reports as foundational inputs for aggregation
constraints: The AI Twin does not observe raw learner behaviours directly but reasons through aggregated cognition structures

target_learning_goals: multi-level cognition interpretation and adaptive educational intervention
examples: The cognition radar visualises conceptual understanding, interpretive consistency, identity confidence, value recognition, and cognitive tension

title: AI Expert Feedback Ecology: a closed-loop cognition framework linking AI Twins, AI Tutors, dashboards, and learners
description: The article defines the AI Expert Feedback Ecology as "a closed-loop educational ecosystem in which AI Twins, AI tutors, dashboards, and learners continuously interact through cognition-aware feedback processes." AI Twins generate adaptive tasks; AI Tutors interpret behaviours into cognition reports; the ECD aggregates them; AI Twins reason through aggregated structures to generate interventions that start a new cycle. Cognition is treated as "an evolving interpretive structure continuously shaped through interaction, reflection, and intervention."

constraints: AI Twins perceive learners indirectly through cognition reports rather than raw behavioural logs

citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: Five cognition structures as analytical objects: identity cognition, interpretation, cognitive tension, value recognition, and misunderstanding
description: The article enumerates five higher-order cognition structures that form "the core analytical objects of the ECD": identity cognition (how learners position themselves within a domain), interpretation (how learners construct meaning across situations), cognitive tension (conceptual conflicts and uncertainty marking cognitive transition), value recognition (negotiation of priorities and ethical judgments), and misunderstanding analysed as "structured cognitive divergence" rather than incorrect performance. These structures aim to represent learner development at a deeper interpretive level than behavioural outputs.

constraints: The article states these representations are not intended to fully capture learner cognition

article_title: Gen-AI-tecture: using generative AI to support architectural students in design tasks
citation: Kapsalis, T. (2026). Gen-AI-tecture: using generative AI to support architectural students in design tasks. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1598-6426
title: Gen-AI-tecture: a bespoke, locally run ComfyUI generative-AI image creation and editing workflow for architectural education
description: A bespoke generative-AI image workflow implemented as a localised ComfyUI environment in which students upload or select images, describe changes in natural language, and receive multiple visual alternatives. "The workﬂow is powered by the Flux 1 Kontext (dev) diffusion model (Black Forest Labs, 2025), which has been ﬁne-tuned with a curated set of interior-design images" using LoRA adaptation on the InteriorNet dataset. It offers three modes (text-driven, reference-image-driven, hybrid) and edits via in-painting that preserves surrounding context, acting as a visual co-pilot rather than replacing design thinking.
requirements: Runs locally within a ComfyUI node-based environment with the fine-tuned Flux 1 Kontext (dev) model
Used within scaffolded studio sessions with facilitator demonstration and structured design tasks
constraints: Fine-tuned for residential interior scenarios (bedroom and living/dining room scenes), so outputs support early design discussions "without claiming the status of resolved architectural drawings" and may not generalise to other design typologies or less supported studio environments
target_learners: Undergraduate architecture students (Levels 3-5)
target_learning_goals: Architectural design ideation and visualisation
AI-handling skills for professional practice
examples: In the focus groups, students generated around 80 images per session, using Mode A to create bedroom designs from scratch and Modes B/C to edit provided living/dining-room images via in-painting

article_title: Gen-AI-tecture: using generative AI to support architectural students in design tasks
citation: Kapsalis, T. (2026). Gen-AI-tecture: using generative AI to support architectural students in design tasks. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1598-6426
title: The GenAI workflow as a constructionist microworld and socio-constructivist cognitive mediator in studio education
description: The authors interpret their findings through constructionist and socio-constructivist lenses: "the bespoke, locally run GenAI workﬂow functions as a constructionist “microworld” for architectural ideation rather than as a mere image generator", echoing Papert's objects-to-think-with. They further read the AI as "a “more knowledgeable other” that suggested plausible yet negotiable alternatives", prompting students to articulate constraints and values, and as a connectivist interaction agent within students' personal learning environments. Learning is evidenced by cycles of making, inspecting and remaking, with the human-in-the-loop configuration preserving learner agency.
requirements: Outputs must be interrogated rather than accepted uncritically for the scaffold/ZPD effect to hold, per the article's reading
constraints: Interpretation drawn from a small, single-institution focus-group study with self-report data; the article notes instances where AI outputs risked narrowing exploration were identified and problematised in group discussion
target_learners: Undergraduate architecture students in studio-based education
target_learning_goals: Design reasoning and metacognitive talk about design moves
Critical management of human-AI learning networks
examples: Students described AI-edited images as provocations that opened up unforeseen options, especially when switching between masking modes

article_title: Mathematical Modelling of Ethical AI Use in Higher Education: A Coordination Game Framework for Future-Facing Learning
citation: Ndidi Bianca Ogbo, Zhao Song, Shatha Ghareeb, and The Anh Han. (2026). Mathematical Modelling of Ethical AI Use in Higher Education: A Coordination Game Framework for Future-Facing Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27400
title: Coordination-based evolutionary game-theoretic framework of student AI use in assessment
description: The framework models student generative-AI use in assessment as a two-player symmetric coordination game in a well-mixed finite population, in which the institution is not a strategic player but shapes payoffs through assessment design. Strategies span responsible use with meaningful reflection, responsible use with superficial reflection, opportunistic use, and clear misuse, with parameters for learning value, effort costs, legitimacy costs, reflection reward and effort, and misconduct penalties. Behavioural change follows the Fermi imitation rule with small mutation probability, and long-run dynamics are approximated by a Markov chain over homogeneous states. The article writes that "we model interactions at the student–student level using a two-player symmetric game in a well-mixed population".
requirements: Reflective assessment incentives must be calibrated so that the reward for meaningful reflection is proportionate to its effort cost
constraints: The model treats each assessment task as a one-shot decision context in a well-mixed population; the article notes extending to multi-player and networked interactions and empirical validation as future work
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: responsible and learning-oriented use of generative AI in assessment
examples: Simulations with population size N = 100 and Fermi updating, varying reflection reward r, peer sensitivity β, and reflection effort cost κ across Figures 1–3

article_title: FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays
citation: Yijun Liu, Yifan Song, John Gallagher, Sarah Sterman, Tal August. (2026). FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06271
title: FOXGLOVE: a parallel dataset of sentence-anchored, goal-labeled instructor and LLM writing feedback with urgency rankings and expert quality ratings
description: FOXGLOVE is a dataset of 2,340 feedback comments on 69 twelfth-grade argumentative essays from the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus: 696 comments from 14 trained writing instructors and 1,644 from four LLMs (GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen3-Next 80B) produced under a shared protocol. It is, per the article, a dataset collected with "anchored, goal-labeled feedback comments" from trained human instructors and models. It adds expert quality ratings on 105 comments across seven dimensions (1,430 ratings), urgency rankings, and reusable annotation protocols for instructors, LLMs, and raters.
requirements: Feedback must follow the shared schema: sentence-anchored comments addressing one of five argumentative goals, an urgency ranking of the three most important comments, and one global comment per essay
constraints: The schema privileges feedback organized around predefined argumentative moves and may underrepresent feedback such as encouragement and praise
Feedback was collected for the study rather than drawn from authentic instructional settings, without an ongoing relationship with the writer
target_learners: twelfth-grade argumentative essay writers
writing instructors and LLM feedback system evaluators
target_learning_goals: argumentative writing revision through goal-oriented, anchored, prioritized feedback
examples: Each essay was independently annotated by two instructors via Google Docs, with comments anchored to sentences, goal labels recorded, and the top three comments ranked for urgency
