article_title: FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays
citation: Yijun Liu, Yifan Song, John Gallagher, Sarah Sterman, Tal August. (2026). FOXGLOVE: Understanding Goal-Oriented and Anchored Writing Feedback from Experts and LLMs on Argumentative Essays. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06271
title: Three-property schema for usable writing feedback: goal-orientation, anchoring, and prioritization
description: The article operationalizes three properties that writing research identifies as making feedback usable for revision: goal-orientation (engaging the rhetorical goal the writer is pursuing), anchoring (pointing to the specific text where revision should occur), and prioritization (ranking the most important revisions). The article states these address distinct revision needs: "what, where, and in what order", and that feedback usable for revision requires all three. In FOXGLOVE every feedback giver produces sentence-level comments labeled with one of five argumentative goals (Position, Claim, Evidence, Counterclaim, Rebuttal), anchors them to contiguous sentences, and ranks the three most urgent comments.
requirements: Feedback must be anchored to one or more contiguous full sentences, address exactly one goal per comment, and include an urgency ranking and a global comment
constraints: The schema encodes one particular view of what good feedback is and is intended as one lens on feedback quality, not a definitive standard
target_learners: high-school and college writing students
target_learning_goals: argumentative writing revision
formative feedback design
examples: Instructors and LLMs both produced feedback under this schema, enabling systematic comparison of where human and model feedback align and diverge

citation: Yifan Liu, Jaime Arguello, Orland Hoeber, Chang Liu, Soo Young Rieh, Luanne Sinnamon, et al. (2026). Report on CHIIR 2026 Workshop on Generative AI and Academic Search (GAI&AS). ACM SIGIR Forum. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08936
title: Three types of metacognitive laziness in academic search: plan-deficit, monitoring-deficit, and regulation-deficit
description: This framework, presented in a lightning talk by Song and Liu, identifies three types of metacognitive laziness during academic search behaviors: "plan-deficit, monitoring-deficit, and regulation-deficit". It characterizes ways learners offload metacognitive processes to GenAI systems, and it grounds two design challenges: evolving GenAI from fact-retrievers to problem-solving scaffolds at the strategy layer, and embedding metacognitive scaffolds to mitigate each type of laziness. The framework is used to foster adaptive collaboration and human-AI symbiosis in creative academic search.

title: GenAI systems should build trust by being transparent about process, purpose, and performance
description: A workshop roundtable principle of good GenAI design holds that "GenAI systems should build trust by being more transparent aboutprocess, purpose, and performance". Regarding process, systems should explain how an answer or output was generated, including which sources informed it; regarding purpose, systems should elicit the user's higher-level purpose to provide appropriate support; regarding performance, systems should convey their level of confidence about the accuracy and completeness of a response. The workshop also called for methodologies to measure the extent to which systems exhibit these principles.

citation: Nicholas Micallef, Olga Petrovska. (2026). Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education. International Symposium on Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Higher Education Symposium (AITHE). https://www.swansea.ac.uk/staff/nicholas.micallef
title: Domain-specific GenAI declaration framework translating an activity taxonomy into task-specific disclosure instruments
description: The framework is a design artefact that translates the Bouvier et al. taxonomy of GenAI-mediated activities (Generate, Interpret, Evaluate, Get Feedback, Refine, Brainstorm, Design, Simulate, Reflect) into assessment-facing declaration categories for Computer Science coursework. It comprises two parallel task-specific structures (writing and coding) in which students indicate whether GenAI was used, its extent (Minor, Moderate, Extensive), and provide explanations with example prompts. The authors position it as operating "at the level of thestudent's declaration", complementing policy-level instruments such as the AI Assessment Scale, which operates at the educator's design-decision level.
requirements: Requires accurate self-reporting by students, accompanied by clear institutional guidance on which tools count as GenAI use
constraints: It does not itself detect misconduct
Transferability to disciplines beyond computing remains an open question
The goal is not a precise measurement instrument but a structured way to describe GenAI use
target_learners: Computer Science higher education students, including school-leavers, international students, career-changers, and degree apprentices
target_learning_goals: Academic integrity and transparent disclosure of GenAI use
Student reflection on their own learning process with GenAI
AI literacy and preparation for professional documentation of GenAI workflows
examples: A writing-focused form organised around six activity categories and a coding-focused form with five activity categories, both using the same Minor/Moderate/Extensive extent scale with explanations and example prompts

title: Writing-focused GenAI declaration structure with six activity categories
description: A declaration form for writing-focused activities (e.g., a short literature review on technology and society) organised around six activity categories: Planning & Structure, Textual Content Generation, Research & Analysis, Revision & Polish, Visual Content, and Evaluation & Feedback. For each category students (1) state whether GenAI was used (Yes/No), (2) specify the extent of use (Minor, Moderate, Extensive), and (3) provide a short explanation with example prompts. As in the writing structure, students indicate whether GenAI was used and to what extent, with a short description and example prompts. title: Frame GenAI declarations as reflective instruments rather than compliance artefacts, using granularity, task specificity, intensity, prompt transparency, and reflection over punishment
description: The framework is guided by five principles that "collectively shift declarations from compliance artefacts to reflective instruments": granularity over a binary yes/no; task specificity; intensity as well as presence (Minor, Moderate, Extensive); prompt-level transparency via brief explanations and example prompts; and reflection over punishment, framing the declaration "as a description of process, not an admission of guilt". The last principle responds directly to empirical evidence that students avoid declaring GenAI use when they perceive the form as a penalty mechanism.
requirements: Declaration forms must offer multiple activity types per assessment, a shared extent scale, and space for explanations and example prompts
constraints: Relies on accurate self-reporting; novice programmers can experience an illusion of competence and misattribute GenAI contributions to their own work
target_learners: Higher education students, particularly in Computer Science
target_learning_goals: Honest self-assessment of GenAI use
Reflection on the learning process
Reducing perceived stigma of disclosure
examples: The framework asks students to indicate both whether and to what extent they used GenAI for each activity type, alongside short explanations and example prompts

title: Reframing the 5% problem as a situated instructional challenge requiring teacher-facing interpretive support
description: The article proposes that the 5% problem — only a small fraction of students engaging at levels sufficient for meaningful learning gains — should be understood not merely as a usage deficit but as a challenge of teacher interpretation. It argues that "the 5% problem extends beyond time-on-task and reflects challenges in interpreting meaningful student effort," and that teacher-facing systems should situate engagement patterns within broader instructional and contextual information rather than only detecting disengagement.

citation: Jordan Gutterman, Ashish Gurung, Lee Branstetter, Kenneth Koedinger, and Vincent Aleven. (2026). Cross-Subject Predictive Validity for Learning Outcomes of Delayed Start Behavior. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25308
title: Session-level behavioral measures as content-independent, practitioner-aligned detectors of self-regulated learning
description: The article proposes that session-level measures like delayed start provide "a new opportunity for content-independent detectors, adding a behavioral component to the traditional usage and progress based on student engagement with content." Because the daily class period in K-12 is a bounded work space, its start and end times serve as behavioral anchors for defining self-regulation measures. The framework holds that detectors built from DLP log data already in use require no new diagnostics and frame results in minutes of delay, matching what educators observe. It bridges education research and classroom practice through interpretable measures.

K-12 class periods with bounded start and end times to anchor delay measurement
constraints: Results derived from one middle-school context with 45-minute class periods and one math platform; thresholds could differ in other contexts, e.g. 60-minute sessions
The raw minutes metric leaves the predictive power of classroom and contextual factors on the table
The work does not identify precisely which construct delayed start best represents

target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning behaviors such as timely task initiation
Standardized math and ELA achievement
examples: The classwork-session inference algorithm classified practice instances with more than five concurrent students from the same class during school hours as classwork sessions, identifying 841 sessions across 26 classes

article_title: From Prompting to Epistemic Proactivity: Temporal Trajectories of Student-AI Interaction in Mathematics Learning
citation: Abdelghani, R., Kaiser, P., Murayama, K. (2026). Changes in Help-Seeking Strategies Predict unaided Performance during AI-based Mathematical Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28472
title: Epistemic proactivity (EP): the extent to which learners retain responsibility for regulating and advancing their own knowledge-building while using AI
description: Epistemic proactivity characterizes "the extent to which learners retain this responsibility to carry out the important process for learning" during AI-supported learning. It concerns what role learners retain — whether they frame problems and originate learning trajectories or merely react to ones imposed by the AI — and goes beyond prompt sophistication or general engagement by focusing on how responsibility for knowledge-building is distributed between learner and AI. The study operationalizes EP through two behavioral dimensions: SRL functions (plan, monitor, request, evaluate) and the epistemic orientation of help-seeking (understanding-oriented versus closure-oriented requests), and treats EP as a developing property of the interaction rather than a fixed learner characteristic.
requirements: Behavioral codes capture only regulatory functions explicitly expressed in dialogue and should not be interpreted as a complete measure of internal self-regulation.
constraints: EP does not assume learners should perform every cognitive or regulatory operation independently; delegation becomes problematic when the learner increasingly relies on the model for determining what to pursue, generating reasoning, and judging understanding.
target_learners: secondary-school students (Grade 9)
target_learning_goals: mathematical modelling with linear and quadratic functions
examples: The study coded 880 substantive student turns for SRL function and help-seeking orientation and related within-session change scores to unaided post-test performance.
key_sources: Abdelghani, R., Kaiser, P., Murayama, K. (2026). Changes in Help-Seeking Strategies Predict unaided Performance during AI-based Mathematical Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28472

article_title: Gaze-Informed Proactive AI Assistance for Children’s Picture Exploration
citation: Zekun Wu, Man Su, Huiyong Li, Tomohiro Nagashima, and Anna Maria Feit. (2026). Gaze-Informed Proactive AI Assistance for Children Exploring Picture Books. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00445
title: Ollie: a gaze-informed LLM storytelling assistant for children's picture-book exploration
description: Ollie is an LLM-based (GPT-4o) proactive assistant that narrates picture-book scenes for children without requiring explicit requests. As the article describes it, "Ollie uses gaze-based attention detection to identify the child's current primary AOI, applies relevance-based AOI selection to choose a related but unassisted secondary AOI, and then prompts the LLM with the two AOIs and the full picture to produce spoken storytelling assistance." Narrations are delivered via text-to-speech, chain prior hooks, and end with an open-ended question to spark curiosity.
requirements: An eye tracker capturing the child's gaze during exploration, with predefined AOIs segmented into meaningful regions of the picture
A 5-second warm-start phase with no state inference to initialize the HMM parameters via batch EM
constraints: In the user study, assistance was limited to three initial instances per image with a minimum three-second interval between triggers, after pilot observations that overly frequent assistance interrupted self-directed exploration
The only parent preferring the baseline raised privacy and security concerns related to eye tracking
target_learners: preschool and early elementary-school children (ages 5-8 in the study)
target_learning_goals: sustaining attention and curiosity during open-ended picture exploration
narrative understanding and visual literacy support during picture-book reading
examples: In the within-subject study, children explored six Wimmelbook-style images, three per condition, with Ollie delivering spoken German narration via Azure text-to-speech
key_sources: Zekun Wu, Man Su, Huiyong Li, Tomohiro Nagashima, and Anna Maria Feit. (2026). Gaze-Informed Proactive AI Assistance for Children Exploring Picture Books. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00445

article_title: From Answer Generators to Reasoning Facilitators: Designing AI Tutors for Mathematical Reasoning in High-Stakes Environments
citation: Harry Feng, Yuan Tian, and Erica Zhao. 2026. From Answer Generators to Reasoning Facilitators: Designing AI Tutors for Mathematical Reasoning in High-Stakes Environments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01692
title: Reasoning-Centered Product Loop: Orient, Visualize, Repair, Retrieve, Verify
description: A five-part design framework the authors propose for educational AI, moving beyond answer delivery. It holds that educational AI "should not hide answers under the guise of preventing cheating" but make answer access an entry point into reasoning; treat text and diagrams as one synchronized reasoning object; use contextual step-specific repair buttons; shift similar-problem recommendations into delayed spaced-retrieval workflows; and expose curriculum-fit signals before asking students to trust output. It emerged from the AITutor field deployment.
requirements: AI output must be decomposable into inspectable steps with curriculum-fit signals exposed before trust is requested
constraints: Evidence currently covers interaction behavior and perceived support, not measured learning gains; validated only in a 12-day deployment with 12 junior-high students in an exam-oriented Chinese context
target_learners: junior-high students preparing for high-stakes exams
target_learning_goals: mathematical reasoning inspection, local repair, and delayed retrieval
examples: AITutor implemented the loop via layered worked examples, step-linked visual grounding, contextual follow-up prompts, and an automated wrong-book review view
key_sources: Harry Feng, Yuan Tian, and Erica Zhao. 2026. From Answer Generators to Reasoning Facilitators: Designing AI Tutors for Mathematical Reasoning in High-Stakes Environments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01692

title: AITutor: an LLM-based iPad tutoring app translating pedagogical mechanisms into UI features
description: AITutor is a React Native/Expo iPad app with a Python/FastAPI backend that orchestrates LLM calls, curriculum-constrained prompting, retrieval over digitized course materials, and telemetry logging. Rather than "treating the AI as an open-ended chatbot, we constrained the interaction, translating pedagogical mechanisms into explicit UI features." Its features are layered worked examples (overview, orientation, explanation, final-answer checkpoint, exam-format layer), step-linked visual grounding, a contextual follow-up dock, and a delayed retrieval/wrong-book loop.
requirements: curriculum-constrained prompting and knowledge tags to keep methods within the junior-high syllabus
fast enough answer access for homework pressure
constraints: evaluated only as a prototype over a 12-day shared field window with a reliability outage on May 20–21
target_learners: junior-high students (Grades 7–9) preparing for the Zhongkao
target_learning_goals: inspectable, repairable mathematical reasoning
examples: deployed with 12 instrumented students producing 7,379 telemetry events across 104 valid sessions

title: GAIDE: A Guiding Framework for AI-Integrated Design for Educators
description: GAIDE is a framework supporting K-12 teachers in creating AI-powered learning technologies through vibe coding. It combines Design Thinking phases with adapted INTERACT design components, bookended by an initial Understand AI phase and a final Reflect on Ethical Application phase. Revisions from the empirical workshop included that "Learning Environment was removed, and Learning Objectives was newly introduced" in the Design phase, and the framework visualizes a non-linear, iterative cycle of collaborative design.

Mentor support during prototyping and testing phases

Developing AI literacy
examples: In the workshop, teachers used Google AI Studio to prototype Math Mysteries, guided through INTERACT design components such as Learning Objectives, Learner Differentiation, and Knowledge Mapping

title: Teacher-mentor-AI collaboration as a distributed expertise system in AI technology creation
description: The article conceptualizes workshop interactions among teachers, mentors, and AI as "a dynamically coordinated system of distributed expertise, grounded in distributed cognition theory". Evidence-based knowledge from mentors, practice-based knowledge from teachers, and generative knowledge from AI are integrated and reconfigured through interaction. AI is treated not merely as a tool but as a mediational artifact that shapes teachers' thinking, as teachers externalize tacit knowledge through prompt writing, prototype demonstration, and output review.

university faculty mentors

Teacher professional learning

description: The article argues that prior co-design models positioned researchers or developers as primary drivers, with teachers contributing only domain expertise or partial participation. GAIDE instead "position[s] teachers as the primary designers, supported by AI-enabled vibe coding", which the authors say grants teachers greater agency and lets them shape technologies directly around their instructional goals. Vibe coding lowers the technical barrier so teachers can carry the full design process themselves.

Structured guidance such as the GAIDE framework
constraints: The article notes the Presidential AI Challenge itself offers limited instructional scaffolding for educators with minimal prior AI design experience

target_learning_goals: Designing classroom-relevant AI-powered tools
Technology integration

citation: Tseng, T., Seoror, L.H., Adda, J., Factor, M., Darabi, R., Matschke, K.R., Fu, T., Lin, A., Maram, A., Sinha, A. (2026). Flowcode: An AI-Powered Programming Environment for Scaffolding Iteration in Creative Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06721
title: Flowcode: an AI-powered creative coding environment integrating a code-structure flowchart with pedagogically constrained LLM explanations
description: Flowcode is a Node-based web application using GPT-4o that supports beginners iterating on found creative coding projects (Anime.js animations using HTML, CSS, and JS). Its interface has four components: code editors, a live preview, an LLM-generated flowchart summarizing project features across two abstraction levels, and an explanation panel producing "fill-in-the-blank code snippets" rather than full solutions. The system was refined across a pilot workshop and a lab study.

Designed for learners new to creative coding working on web-based animation projects
constraints: Evaluated only with a single model (GPT-4o), which the authors note may not represent other LLMs' performance
Studied over short 40-minute iteration periods; longer-term use unexplored

undergraduate and graduate students new to programming with web animation libraries
target_learning_goals: understanding existing code across HTML, CSS, and JS
iterating on found creative coding projects by actively writing code
examples: In the lab study, participants picked from four CodePen animation projects and iterated on them for 40 minutes while thinking aloud

citation: Tseng, T., Seoror, L.H., Adda, J., Factor, M., Darabi, R., Matschke, K.R., Fu, T., Lin, A., Maram, A., Sinha, A. (2026). Flowcode: An AI-Powered Programming Environment for Scaffolding Iteration in Creative Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06721
title: Introduce deliberate friction into AI-generated code assistance to prioritize learning over vibe coding
description: The article argues that code assistants for learning should deliberately slow learners down rather than maximize efficiency. Flowcode instruments friction by "revealing individual explanation steps one at a time and requiring users to directly edit blanks in generated code snippets rather than be given a full solution." The authors see this as distinct from friction arising from LLM misinterpretation, aiming to prioritize deeper learning and direct experimentation.
requirements: An LLM prompted to produce incomplete, fill-in-the-blank code rather than full solutions
An interface that reveals explanations step by step and avoids one-click code transfer
constraints: Friction slows prototyping speed, which the authors present as a trade-off favoring learning
Fill-in-the-blank behavior was not fully reliable even after prompt refinement
target_learners: novice programmers and new creative coders
target_learning_goals: understanding generated and found code
actively writing code rather than pasting AI solutions
examples: Flowcode removed the copy-to-clipboard button, stopped auto-inserting generated code into editors, and required clicking a 'Show Next Step' button to reveal each explanation step

article_title: Adoption-Ready Project-Based Learning for Computing Education: The FORAP Framework and a Multi-Scale Project Portfolio
citation: Suleiman, A. D., DeWaters, J., Shepherd, D. C., Korkmaz, T., Hussain, F., Liu, Y., & Hou, D. (2026). Adoption-Ready Project-Based Learning for Computing Education: The FORAP Framework and a Multi-Scale Project Portfolio. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11129
title: FORAP: a framework organizing computing PjBL projects as coordinated adoption-ready packages
description: FORAP (Framework for Organizing Reusable and Adaptable PjBL Projects) organizes each project as a coordinated package centered on aligned learning objectives, described through project attributes, and supported by three coordinated support packages: instructor, student, and assessment. Project attributes (greenfield vs. brownfield, scope and duration, technical complexity, domain, and optional competency specification such as CC2020 mapping) let instructors judge course fit and plan adaptation. The framework was used to package a 14-project portfolio and is grounded in PjBL principles of authentic, collaborative, and self-directed learning.
requirements: Aligned learning objectives as the organizing anchor for project packaging
Modular, flexible packaging that supports reuse across offerings and adaptation to different course contexts
Support materials addressing instructor adoption barriers and common student technical challenges
Structured milestones, checkpoints, and aligned assessment artifacts for formative and summative assessment
constraints: Successful implementation still depended on instructor preparation, TA readiness, class size, and platform or environment constraints
Materials require ongoing maintenance as dependencies, software versions, platforms, and technologies change
Adoption is not plug-and-play; instructors still make local decisions about scope, pacing, tooling, and support
target_learners: undergraduate computing students
target_learning_goals: computing course learning objectives across software engineering, cybersecurity, machine learning, databases, and related domains
examples: The Touchalytics project package illustrates the framework: four phased tasks, instructor notes and sample solutions, installation guidelines and labs, and phased milestones with transfer-oriented design problems and a detailed rubric
key_sources: Suleiman, A. D., DeWaters, J., Shepherd, D. C., Korkmaz, T., Hussain, F., Liu, Y., & Hou, D. (2026). Adoption-Ready Project-Based Learning for Computing Education: The FORAP Framework and a Multi-Scale Project Portfolio. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11129

title: Multi-scale portfolio of 14 adoption-ready computing PjBL project packages

Table I summarizes attributes and classroom trial counts per project, and the portfolio is available at the project's documentation site.

citation: Dumlao, J. M. Z., Wang, M., Xie, Z., Hu, J., Bar, I., Chaney, G., III, Gold, H., & Teplitskiy, M. (2026). Generative AI Availability, Grades, and Student Satisfaction at a Large University. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21534
title: Human-validated LLM annotation pipeline reconstructing assessment weights from syllabi to measure course GenAI susceptibility
description: The pipeline converts syllabus PDFs to Markdown and uses an LLM through a university-managed API gateway to reconstruct final-grade weights for each assessment category, which feed the continuous GenAI-susceptibility treatment variable. The authors use "reconstruction" rather than extraction because LLMs "generate labels that are likely to match the document". Validation against a stratified human-annotated sample found strong recovery, with susceptibility reconstructed at a mean absolute error of 0.063 on the 0–1 scale.

constraints: Unknown exams are assumed non-susceptible by default; projects with unspecified presentation weightings are split equally between susceptible and non-susceptible
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students at a large U.S. public university
target_learning_goals: measuring course assessment structures to study effects of GenAI availability on grades and satisfaction

title: The GenAI substitution hypothesis: assessment susceptibility to GenAI automation conditions whether AI availability inflates grades without learning
description: The GenAI substitution hypothesis holds that students may substitute GenAI capabilities for their own mastery on assessments that can be completed outside instructor observation, earning satisfactory grades without the cognitive effort that promotes learning. The article defines "GenAI susceptible assessments as those where GenAI tools may directly substitute for student ability, like take-home exams, problem sets, and essays", contrasting them with in-person closed-book exams, presentations, and live demonstrations where full automation is precluded. If true, grades should rise disproportionately in susceptible courses and lose signaling value.
requirements: An assessment structure weighting susceptible (unproctored, take-home, or open) assessments heavily enough that GenAI could substitute for student effort
constraints: Substitution need not be strategic; instructors perceive an 'illusion of competence' when students complete assessments with GenAI, per work the article cites
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: validity of grades as signals of mastery; student learning and satisfaction under GenAI availability
examples: The study operationalizes the hypothesis as a prediction that grades rise disproportionately in high-susceptibility courses after ChatGPT's release, and finds no such differential effect

citation: Sifatul Anindho, Videep Venkatesha, Jaclyn Ocumpaugh, and Nathaniel Blanchard. (2026). Ordered Network Analysis of Epistemic Emotions during Collaborative Problem Solving. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23317
title: Ordered network analysis (ONA) as a method for modeling directional temporal transitions among affective states in small, temporally coarse educational datasets
description: Ordered network analysis extends epistemic network analysis by incorporating temporal ordering into network construction, "allowing edges to represent ordered transitions between codes rather than unordered co-occurrence." The article applies ONA to retrospective cued-recall affect reports from a short situated CPS task, using a moving window of 2 events, groups as units of analysis, and difference networks to compare conditions. This makes ONA suited to modeling affect dynamics where the sequence of states is as informative as their co-presence, even in small datasets where descriptive summaries treat states as independent.
requirements: Timestamped self-report events so that ordered connections between codes appearing within a moving window can be constructed
constraints: Standard ENA collapses temporal order within windows; the article notes simultaneous co-occurring labels require an arbitrary fixed ordering, and small temporally coarse datasets limit what can be modeled
target_learners: adult learners collaborating in person on problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: understanding dynamics of epistemic emotions during collaborative problem solving
examples: The study used the webENA tool with a moving window of 2 events; a sensitivity analysis with window sizes 2, 3, and 4 found consistent network structures

title: Retrospective cued-recall dataset of affective states from 27 participants in 9 groups completing the Weights Task
description: A dataset in which 27 participants in 9 groups of three were video recorded completing the first phase of the Weights Task, a collaborative problem-solving activity adapted from Khebour et al., then individually reviewed their session recording using retrospective cued-recall. Participants reported affective states from a set of seven (Confused, Curious, Frustrated, Disengaged, Optimistic, Surprised, and Conflicted), either voluntarily (self-caught) or after a 60-second inactivity probe (probe-caught), with all reports timestamped. All groups arrived at the correct final solution.

constraints: The authors state the dataset is relatively small with a proportionately large male population and a fixed set of predefined labels, which may limit generalizability; RCR is susceptible to recall bias and temporal imprecision

article_title: From Prompt to Embodied Simulation: Using Generative AI to Create AR Physics Learning Tools
citation: Ofek Levy, Joshua Glazer, Noah D. Finkelstein, and Yossi Ben-Zion. (2026). From Prompt to Embodied Simulation: Using Generative AI to Create AR Physics Learning Tools. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22From+Prompt+to+Embodied+Simulation%22
title: Four-element prompt structure for generating embodied AR physics simulations
description: A reusable prompt template whose fixed elements are the tools (libraries and camera handling), the display (objects drawn over the camera image and what each represents), the hand controls (which finger motion controls which quantity), and optimization requirements that prevent jumps and jitter. The article states "The elements are fixed; only their content changes from one simulation to the next," and shows that "The same four elements produce very different simulations, and in all of them the physics appears in the learner's own environment." Each simulation runs as a single HTML file in an ordinary browser with no installation.
requirements: A common LLM tool with a code-running canvas mode (or copying the code into an .html file), a camera, and the MediaPipe Hands library plus a transparent drawing layer, with Three.js for 3D scenes
constraints: In tools such as ChatGPT and Claude the built-in preview window may not have access to the camera, requiring saving the code as an .html file and opening it in the browser
A first prompt is almost never perfect and AR simulations are sensitive to edge cases, so iterative refinement is expected
target_learners: teachers with no coding background
students in introductory physics courses
target_learning_goals: physics concepts represented spatially, such as amplitude, wavelength, electric fields, and the right-hand rule
examples: The wave-and-lamp simulation, a single charge with its 3D field grid, two charges with a combined field, and the right-hand rule drawn on the student's own hand, all built from the same four elements

title: Hand-controlled AR electromagnetism simulations: fingertip charge with field grid, two-charge combined field, and right-hand rule on the student's own hand
description: Three simulations built from the same four-element prompt, with full prompts given in the online appendix. In the first, "the tip of the index finger is an electric charge, and a three-dimensional grid of arrows, showing the electric field of the charge, fills the space around the student"; arrows are longer near the charge and shorter farther away. In the second, each index finger is a charge of opposite sign and bringing the hands together concentrates the combined field. In the third, "the right-hand rule is drawn on the student's own hand: three arrows, force, velocity, and field, anchored to three fingers and rotating with the hand," displayed without mirroring so handedness is preserved.

constraints: The visualizations are qualitative teaching representations; the wave-and-lamp simulation is explicitly not a quantitative model of an electromagnetic field

teachers of electromagnetism
target_learning_goals: electric fields of point charges
field superposition of two charges
the right-hand rule for the magnetic force F = qv × B
examples: Appendix Prompts A, B, and C give the complete prompts for the single charge, two-charge, and right-hand-rule simulations respectively

article_title: Development and applications of Generative AI in architectural design studios
citation: Leman Figen Gül, Burak Delikanlı, Oğulcan Üneşi, Ertuğrul Ömer Gül. (2025). Development and applications of Generative AI in architectural design studios. ITU A|Z • Vol 22 No 3 • November 2025 • 751-774. https://doi.org/10.58278/0.2025.109
title: Four approaches to leveraging GenAI in the architectural design process: exploring the unknown problem space, solution space enhancement, framing and rephrasing, and design externalization
description: The article organizes students' observed GenAI use into four approaches mapped to Boden's creativity types: 'exploring unknown problem space' for concept development and inspiration in early design, 'solution space enhancement' for generating alternatives, 'framing and rephrasing' where LLMs and prompts become central to the design process, and 'a tool for design externalization' after design decisions, analogous to a rendering engine. The article states "A central limitation shared by these four approaches to leveraging GenAI is the inherently subjective nature of creativity, which resists objective evaluation."
requirements: Students need competencies and discernment to differentiate between GenAI models and use them effectively to avoid design fixation
constraints: The article acknowledges that further research is necessary to substantiate the framing-and-rephrasing approach
creativity is context-dependent and resists objective evaluation
target_learners: third-year architecture design students
target_learning_goals: design creativity
design process exploration and ideation
examples: A student based her entire design methodology on transforming GenAI visuals into virtual spaces, using LLMs to describe spaces, generating 2D images, and converting them into 3D models for plans and sections

description: GAI-A is a user-friendly GenAI interface for architectural design developed for non-programmers, built with React.js frontend and Flask backend. Users create collages in a GUI; the backend generates prompts describing the collage, refines them via ChatGPT, and produces a final 'render' image. Its purpose is to transform image collages into cohesive singular representations of the user's intended theme.

title: Boden's three types of creativity as a framework for GenAI-supported design creativity
description: The article adopts Boden's account of creativity in AI as "the ability to generate novel and valuable ideas" and her three ways new ideas arise: "combinational" creativity generating novel combinations of familiar ideas, "exploratory" creativity delving into overlooked potential of conceptual spaces, and "transformational" creativity transforming dimensions of a conceptual space to generate previously impossible structures. The authors use this triad to interpret students' GenAI-supported design processes in the studios, observing the discovery process as exploring the unknown problem space and a combinatorial analogue as solution space enhancement.

constraints: The article states Boden's triad was observed "to a certain degree" in the students' processes

target_learning_goals: understanding creativity in AI-assisted design processes

article_title: Unanticipated Effects of Generative AI on Expertise Pathways and Performance Perception in System Administration
citation: Rana Abou Khamis, Hala Assal, and Ashraf Matrawy. (2026). Unanticipated Effects of Generative AI on Expertise Pathways and Performance Perception in System Administration. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28650
title: Two-shift account of GenAI's unanticipated socio-technical effects on technical work
description: The article proposes that GenAI's effects on technical professions extend beyond accelerated workflows through two connected shifts. The first is compression of expertise pathways, where "GenAI allows users to skip many foundational, hands-on tasks that once served as the training ground for technical judgment." The second is a performance perception shift, where fast output becomes the expected norm while human validation effort stays invisible. The account is grounded in reflexive thematic analysis of interviews with 14 sysadmins and IT professionals with 2 to 15 years of experience.
requirements: Applies to technical professionals who use GenAI in daily work, as the interviewed sysadmins did
constraints: Findings are within the context of system administration workflows; the authors expect but do not demonstrate the effects in other technical fields
target_learners: System administrators and IT professionals
Novice and early-career technical staff including interns
target_learning_goals: Development of technical intuition, diagnostic judgment, and the expertise needed to validate AI-generated output
examples: The article's interview study with 14 sysadmins identified the two shifts through Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis

article_title: EduClaw-Bench: A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Pedagogical LLM Agents with Simulated Learners
citation: Lee, U.; Lee, S.; Jeong, Y.; Lee, E.; Shin, M.; Kwon, H. (2026). EduClaw-Bench: A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Pedagogical LLM Agents with Simulated Learners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03206
title: EduClaw-Bench: a 30-day LMS-based benchmark for pedagogical LLM agent tutors with KT-grounded simulated learners
description: EduClaw-Bench is a virtual evaluation environment that places an agent tutor in a continuous 30-day relationship with a simulated learner, scoring it on five axes across 55 scenarios. The simulated learner's mastery over knowledge concepts is "estimated by a KT model trained on real students' interaction data", which "both drives its free-response answers and is probed daily for learning gain." The tutor interacts through an LMS with read, write, and messaging APIs, and each scenario pairs one of 11 learner personalities with one of 5 study schedules.

constraints: The simulated learner "remains a simulation rather than a full substitute for classroom learners"; the field tutor validation covers one subject and "validates the instrument rather than any single adapter's score"
target_learners: K-12 elementary mathematics students (grades 5-8 based on XES3G5M persona metadata)
target_learning_goals: Elementary mathematics knowledge-concept mastery
Long-horizon tutoring effectiveness
Curriculum design quality
examples: 10 agent adapters evaluated on 3 base-model tiers (Solar-pro3, Codex-gpt5.5, Qwen3-4B-Thinking) across 8,637 completed runs

citation: Lee, U.; Lee, S.; Jeong, Y.; Lee, E.; Shin, M.; Kwon, H. (2026). EduClaw-Bench: A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Pedagogical LLM Agents with Simulated Learners. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03206
title: KT-grounded simulated learner: coupling an AKT knowledge tracing model with LLM role-play for persistent simulated students
description: The simulated learner couples two components: a knowledge tracing model (AKT) that maintains a per-KC belief map trained on real student interaction data, and an LLM that role-plays the student and generates free-response attempts. The AKT model is "trained on real XES3G5M learners" and "maintains a per-KC belief map" that is updated at each observation. The LLM student generates answers conditioned on the KT belief state, and "graded probe outcomes are fed back into fθ, so KT and LLM stay coupled across D=30 virtual days." This design addresses the known failure of pure LLM-simulated students to reproduce real students' ability distributions, misconception dynamics, or authenticity under tutoring.

Persona seeds pooled from real training students' practice logs with precomputed initial beliefs
An LLM student whose system prompt is composed from ability level, grade band, and weakest/strongest KCs
constraints: The ability level is fixed at 'average' in all reported runs
Multi-seed confidence intervals are left to future work
target_learners: K-12 elementary mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Knowledge-concept mastery tracking
Simulated learning gain measurement
examples: AKT trained on 5,027 sequences with test AUC of 0.80
2,169 persona seeds from real XES3G5M training students
ECE of 0.049 and Brier score of 0.033 over 1.19M item attempts

article_title: Exploring Students' Perceptions of Using Generative AI-Assisted Problem Posing
citation: Lindsay Dawson, N. Sanjay Rebello. (2026). Exploring Students' Perceptions of Using Generative AI-Assisted Problem Posing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12523
title: Horizontal and vertical transfer framework for guiding AI-assisted problem posing
description: The study employs a conceptual framework, adapted from the authors' prior work on transfer of learning and Jonassen's problem-solving framework, in which problem posing proceeds by "horizontal transfer, where the reader takes explicit information from the problem and tries to align it with pre-created knowledge structures, and vertical transfer, where a reader actively recognizes features of a situation, activating and applying prior knowledge". Horizontal transfer changes a problem's representation or context while keeping the approach the same; vertical transfer alters complexity and requires applying concepts more deeply. The framework was taught in the training video to give students a theoretically grounded basis for posing problems with Gen AI as a guide.
requirements: Students receive training that introduces the framework and prompt-engineering techniques before posing problems
constraints: In prior studies students were not trained with a conceptual framework for posing new problems; this study adapts one to fill that gap
target_learners: prospective engineering majors in first-semester calculus-based physics
target_learning_goals: transfer of learning in physics problem solving
problem-posing skills
examples: The 15-minute training video introduced the conceptual framework along with examples of utilizing prompt engineering to pose a physics problem

article_title: Using Gemini and LuaLaTeX to transcribe physics videos into PDF/UA-2 and ISO 32005 math-accessible PDFs
citation: Looney, C. W., & Duston, C. L. (2026). Using Gemini and LuaLaTeX to transcribe physics videos into PDF/UA-2 and ISO 32005 math-accessible PDFs.
title: v6m AI video-transcription workflow (Gemini AI Studio + LuaLaTeX SE tagging + PDFix validation)
description: A mostly automated workflow that transcribes instructional physics videos with substantial mathematical content into math-accessible PDFs using freely available tools. Gemini in AI Studio listens to and watches the uploaded or linked video, sampling one frame per second, and produces LaTeX output under the v6m system instructions; the output is pasted into a prewritten LuaLaTeX preamble shell with automated Structure Element tagging and compiled locally, then validated with PDFix Desktop Lite for PDF/UA-2 and ISO 32005 compliance. The authors state it is "a free, widely available, mostly automated system that can make integrated use of the audio and visual information in a video".
requirements: A local-machine LaTeX installation with a modern TeX distribution compatible with 2026-standard math-SE tagging, since free web-based Overleaf times out on LuaLaTeX SE-tagged compilation
Users must strictly avoid inputting protected, sensitive, or proprietary institutional information into the free AI Studio tier
constraints: Tested primarily on introductory physics videos up to 20 minutes in length produced by two faculty members
No special instructions for English units are provided
target_learners: blind and low-vision students in undergraduate physics and mathematically intensive STEM courses
target_learning_goals: screen-reader-accessible reconstruction of spoken equations and visual arguments from instructional videos
examples: Sixteen test videos spanning lightboard, whiteboard, and screencast formats were transcribed; LaTeX sources and compiled PDFs are released in supplementary folders a-latex-files-v6m and b-pdf-files-v6m

title: Segment-structure transcript format with boldface labels replacing bracketed nonverbal insertions
description: The v6m system instructions organize transcripts into distinct verbal and descriptive segments marked by boldface labels rather than square brackets, with both segment types able to contain math. Early tests showed that closing display math at the end of a square-bracketed descriptive segment caused numerous compilation failures; the authors report that "Abandoning square brackets and adopting the segment structure delivered an immediate and substantial improvement in stability and overall performance". The labels also provide a less-ambiguous transition signal for screen reader users than bracketed text.
requirements: A prewritten LuaLaTeX preamble compatible with the segment structure

constraints: Brief bracketed insertions of nonverbal description cannot be injected directly into the verbal flow

article_title: Evaluation in the Age of AI: Output as Evidence of Learning
citation: Md Zarzees Uddin Shah Chowdhury and Samin Rahman Khan. (2026). Evaluation in the Age of AI: Output as Evidence of Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22660
title: The output-as-evidence model and its collapse: generative AI decouples produced artifacts from the cognitive labor they were meant to certify
description: The article's organizing framework is the 'output-as-evidence' model: the assumption that a student artifact (essay, proof, code) is a direct reflection of cognitive labor, resting on "the assumption of proportional effort". Generative AI collapses the novice-expert production barrier, so the final product no longer signals that mental processes occurred, creating a verification problem existing institutions cannot resolve. The authors call this the proxy crisis and argue the focus on 'cheating' misses a structural misalignment between assessment design and learning outcomes.
requirements: Assessment regimes must treat artifacts as proxies for cognitive processes, which requires that attribution of the artifact to a specific cognitive agent be reliable
constraints: The authors state no surface-level task modification (specificity, realism, multimodal components) reliably distinguishes AI-generated from human-generated responses without rethinking what is assessed
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: genuine understanding, reasoning, and judgment as demonstrated through assessment
examples: The article cites Deans et al.'s comparative analysis in which ChatGPT-generated graduate coursework performed at or above passing levels and even domain experts detected it only marginally better than chance.

title: AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) and FACT framework: tiered taxonomies for bounding and disclosing AI use in assessment
description: The AIAS (AI Assessment Scale) is "a tiered taxonomy that maps different levels of AI involvement onto different assessment contexts", letting faculty design tasks where AI use is explicitly bounded, disclosed, and critically evaluated rather than covert. The FACT (Fundamental, Applied, Conceptual, Thinking) framework similarly supports transparent definitions of ethical tool use. Both treat AI as "a pedagogical variable to be deliberately managed" rather than an adversary, aligning policy with post-graduation professional realities.
requirements: Institutions must invest in training faculty to use the frameworks consistently and build evaluation rubrics capable of assessing process transparency alongside substantive quality

university faculty and assessment designers
target_learning_goals: ethical and transparent AI tool use
process transparency in assessed work
examples: The article presents AIAS as enabling tiered task design where AI involvement is mapped explicitly onto assessment contexts instead of binary bans.

citation: Garrod, O. G. B., Ince, R. A. A., Liu, M., Huti, M., Boos, M., Waldock, A., Andrews, D., Alonso-Kropil, R., & Atherton, P. (2026). Edu-QuRating: Multi-Dimensional Educational Data Curation with Distilled Pairwise Judgements. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09425
title: Edu-QuRating pipeline and released Edu-QuRater scorers, rubrics, code, and models
description: Edu-QuRating is a data-curation pipeline that samples text pairs from an education-rich corpus, obtains soft LLM-judge preference labels under criterion-specific rubrics, and distils them into single-text Edu-QuRater score layers with a neural Bradley–Terry objective. The core model produces six criterion-specific scores per text, with additional student- and teacher-facing foundational-literacy scorers. The article releases rubrics, source code, a nanotron fork, and trained models on Hugging Face, stating the scorers are "deployed for corpus filtering, small-language-model pre-training mixtures, and response-level GRPO rewards."

constraints: The scorers inherit the coverage of the upstream corpus and cannot compensate for missing languages, curricula, or genres
target_learners: primary and secondary school learners
beginning readers in foundational-literacy programmes
teachers and educators in LMIC classrooms
target_learning_goals: educational quality assessment of text
foundational literacy instruction support
curation of learner- and teacher-facing educational materials
examples: Scoring all 322.25M FineWeb-Edu-Fortified rows on 32 H200 GPUs in ~72 hours, and filtering with a conjunctive 50-50-50 percentile rule to retain 51.94M rows

title: Multi-dimensional rubric taxonomy of educational text quality: Core-Ed, FL-Student, and FL-Teacher rubric families
description: The article defines three rubric families totalling 20 output dimensions. The Core-Ed family contains six criteria covering educational level, primary and secondary suitability, factual accuracy, lesson engagement, and pedagogical structure. Two foundational-literacy families, modelled on the GEEAP report's six components of evidence-based reading instruction, score text "through two different lenses": FL-Student evaluates text as practice material a beginning reader could exercise skills on, while FL-Teacher evaluates instructional material addressing the educator, rewarding explicit and systematic teaching practices. constraints: Level and audience dimensions are treated as metadata labels rather than quality signals in the absence of additional context

article_title: Integrating Flipped Learning and Generative AI for Practice-Based Design Education: Evidence from a Knit Yarn Design Course
citation: Hong Qu, Zichao Ling, Yadie Yang. (2026). Integrating Flipped Learning and Generative AI for Practice-Based Design Education: Evidence from a Knit Yarn Design Course. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18505
title: Integrated framework assigning complementary roles to flipped preparation, exemplar calibration, GenAI exploration, and studio refinement
description: The article proposes a pedagogical framework that connects flipped preparation, exemplar reference, GenAI-assisted visual exploration, and studio-based refinement in a practice-based design course. Rather than treating flipped learning and GenAI as separate innovations, the design "assigned them complementary roles: preparing, calibrating, exploring, making, and refining". Pre-class videos and readiness checks support preparation, the gallery provides feasible examples, the GenAI module supports early visual exploration, and instructor feedback with hands-on studio practice supports feasibility judgement and material realization. The authors state the framework helps explain why outcome differences appeared most clearly in creativity, design skills, and problem solving.
requirements: Pre-class activities must be structured and connected to in-class work rather than optional content delivery
GenAI-supported visual prototyping must be connected to clear criteria, reflective comparison, and subsequent physical making
constraints: GenAI outputs cannot reliably represent executable knitting instructions or physically feasible textile outcomes
Empirical support is from one small historical-cohort course implementation
target_learners: third-year undergraduate design students
target_learning_goals: knit yarn design combining visual ideation, material experimentation, and technical development
examples: The course used four lecture sessions and nine studio sessions, with pre-class micro-videos, embedded readiness checks, a curated gallery of thirteen yarn-type categories, and a parameter-guided GenAI ideation module

description: A responsive website developed to support pre-class learning, studio readiness, and early-stage visual ideation in an undergraduate knit yarn design course, accessible on desktop and mobile devices. The Course module delivered eight micro-videos of approximately five minutes with embedded formative readiness checks unlocked after a viewing threshold; the Gallery provided exemplars organized by yarn type across thirteen lab-producible categories plus a Color Thief palette tool; the GenAI module offered parameter-guided prompt scaffolding with optional reference images. The platform also logged learning traces including video watch time, readiness-check records, gallery visits, and image generation frequency.

article_title: Detecting GPT-Assisted Writing Using Interpretable Stylometric Features
citation: Rajesh Kumar, Nabeel Siddiqui, Alexander Fuchsberger. (2026). Detecting GPT-Assisted Writing Using Interpretable Stylometric Features. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26687
title: Sliding-window stylometric detection protocol with disjoint user splits and median aggregation
description: A detection framework in which each document is split into "a pre-specified length of250 words and a stride of125words" windows, nine stylometric features are computed per window, and window-level probabilities are aggregated using a median rule with a 0.50 threshold for document-level classification. Disjoint sets of users are used for training and testing to prevent author-specific style leakage. The protocol was evaluated with eight classifiers on the IIITD-BU (Paraphrased) dataset of 180 samples from 90 participants.
requirements: Requires all windows from a given participant to be kept within the same training, validation, or test set to prevent data leakage
constraints: GPT-assisted in this dataset means responses written by paraphrasing GPT-generated content, not the broader range of AI-assistance practices
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: detecting GPT-assisted academic writing for academic integrity review
examples: The 90 participants were partitioned into 72 training participants (144 samples) and 18 held-out participants (36 samples), producing 722 windows in total

article_title: Who Acts, Who Knows, Who Answers? A Corpus-Assisted Discourse Analysis of Agency, Epistemic Responsibility, and Accountability in Generative AI Higher Education Research
citation: Poudyal, B. (2026). Who Acts, Who Knows, Who Answers? A Corpus-Assisted Discourse Analysis of Agency, Epistemic Responsibility, and Accountability in Generative AI Higher Education Research. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7210-5480
title: Four-part conceptual distinction: grammatical activation, functional agency, epistemic authority, and normative accountability
description: The article proposes a four-part conceptual distinction drawn from its empirical observations: "grammatical activation, functional agency, epistemic authority, and normative accountability". Grammatical activation makes an actor identifiable in a clause; functional agency refers to performance that produces consequences; authority is a warranted capacity to judge and endorse; accountability is an obligation to justify and bear consequences. The categories relate but are not equivalent, and the distinction explains how the literature gives AI functional agency while retaining human answerability without drawing the boundary clearly.
requirements: Users must keep the difference between performing an action, holding authority over an action, and being accountable for an action clearly in view when describing AI in educational writing.
constraints: The distinction was derived from titles and abstracts only, which the article states carry far less information about method and joint authorship than full texts.
target_learners: higher education researchers and scholars writing about GenAI
target_learning_goals: distinguishing functional agency from epistemic authority and normative accountability in discourse about AI in education
examples: The corpus analysis showing AI grammatically active in 447 predicate associations yet never assigned a strictly responsible predicate illustrates the distinction.

title: Operational classification model: policy layers, defaults, and fallbacks produce operational clarity that shapes decision conditions
description: The article proposes a model in which written governance shapes decision conditions through two mechanisms: policy layers allocate authority, and defaults and fallbacks preserve continuity when lower-level instructions remain silent. Together they produce operational clarity, which the article says "structures whether students and educators proceed, disclose, seek approval, modify conduct, or refrain". The model shifts the unit of analysis from an isolated policy to a classification pathway through documents, authorities, and defaults, and separates policy content from policy performance. It distinguishes legitimate governance diversity from operational failure.

constraints: This document study does not test the choices people actually make

citation: Divyansh Chandarana, Sandipan De, Vivek Gupta. (2026). DRAFTTRACE: A Multi-View Analytics Environment for AI-Integrated Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36544
title: Three complementary views of AI-integrated writing: product, process, and interaction
description: The article argues that understanding student writing in AI-mediated settings requires three complementary views: the product view characterizes the final artifact, the process view captures how the artifact develops over time, and the interaction view captures how the student engages with the AI during that process. The authors state that "understanding of writing requires considering three complementary views" and argue existing tools treat these capabilities as separate signals rather than complementary views of the same writing activity. DRAFTTRACE operationalizes this framework by capturing and aligning all three.

constraints: The captured signals do not capture every aspect of the writing process and cannot observe all external resources or activities that may contribute to a response

article_title: Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems
citation: McConvey, K., Zhai, A., Li, R., & Guha, S. (2026). Fairness Theatre: Evaluating Post-Hoc Fairness Interventions in Vendor-Controlled Early Warning Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38552
title: Fairness theatre: dashboard fairness metrics converge while groups' error burdens persist or worsen
description: Fairness theatre names the condition the article develops empirically: post-hoc adjustments that satisfy dashboard-level fairness metrics while the error burdens students and advisors actually experience stay the same or worsen. The article defines it as "post-hoc adjustments that make the metrics on an institution's dashboard look fair while the errors students and advisors actually live with stay the same or get worse." It stresses the pattern "isn't intentional deception" but is what procurement produces when fairness work is confined to vendor-exposed outputs. The concept was developed through evaluating six interventions under simulated procurement constraints.
requirements: A vendor-controlled predictive system whose design decisions are outside the institution's reach, with only calibrated outputs available for adjustment
constraints: The article develops the concept under simulated procurement constraints at a single Ontario college and reads findings as indicative of similar vendor-controlled settings, not settled facts about all of them
target_learners: Higher education students flagged or missed by early warning systems, including small and underrepresented demographic groups
target_learning_goals: Equitable allocation of scarce advising and retention-support resources across student groups
examples: The article's evaluation showed post-hoc adjustments can satisfy dashboard-level fairness metrics while leaving the distribution of error burdens intact or worse

title: Error-type profiling: translating fairness metrics into the errors advisors and students encounter
description: Error-type profiling is the analytic lens the article introduces to judge fairness interventions by how they redistribute false positives and false negatives across groups, rather than only by whether fairness metrics converge. The article introduces it as "a lens that translates fairness metrics into the terms advisors actually encounter: which students appear on caseloads and which are never seen." With predicted-successful as the positive class, a false negative is a successful student predicted at-risk who occupies a scarce advising slot and risks stigmatization, while a false positive is a struggling student predicted successful who never appears on any advisor's caseload.
requirements: Access to group-level error rates (TPR, FPR, positive classification rate) on model outputs, and a defined workflow consequence for each error type
constraints: The article evaluates error redistribution under a single-axis demographic framework that cannot capture compounding disadvantages for intersectional students
target_learners: College students subject to early warning risk flagging, and the advisors acting on flagged caseloads
target_learning_goals: Fair distribution of false positives and false negatives in predictive student-support triage
examples: The article evaluated each of the six interventions by how it redistributes errors across types and groups, asking whether fairness gains reflect genuine improvement or merely shift which students bear which errors

title: Fairness in procured AI as cooperative work negotiated among vendors, institutions, advisors, and students
description: The article reframes post-hoc fairness in procured AI as a problem of cooperative work rather than a property of a model. It states that "fairness is not a property of a model but an outcome negotiated among vendors, institutions, advisors, and students, and procurement contracts restrict the mutual visibility and control this negotiation requires." Vendors hold design knowledge, institutions hold knowledge of student populations and equity obligations, and the contract ensures neither party's knowledge reaches the other's decisions, leaving parties with starkly unequal power to accomplish fairness together.

constraints: Procurement contracts grant vendors authority over the model and leave institutions to govern only outputs, so the negotiation the framework requires is structurally restricted

description: The article built a comparative evaluation testbed simulating an institution's position under vendor procurement: a research replica EWS and six post-hoc fairness methods applied without accessing, modifying, or retraining the underlying model. The replica is "an XGBoost classifier of the same model class the AutoML platform had selected, trained on the same data with SMOTE-NC class balancing and post-hoc calibration." examples: The six methods spanned threshold tuning (GetFair), group-specific calibration (Decoupled), boundary relabeling (Reject Option), prediction flipping (MBS), audit-and-correct pipelines (Bias Mitigation), and quantile thresholding (GBCP)

article_title: Who Thinks First? Designing Productive Friction with Engage-to-Unlock GenAI
citation: Xiaotian Su, Laura Rimell, Jiazheng Li, Amal Rannen-Triki, Ulrich Paquet, Lisa Anne Hendricks, Rida Qadri, Daphne Ippolito and Piotr Mirowski. (2026). Who Thinks First? Designing Productive Friction with Engage-to-Unlock GenAI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01518
title: Engage-to-Unlock: engagement-based access as a productive-friction mechanism for GenAI
description: Engage-to-Unlock is an interaction method in which generative capabilities become available only after users show task-relevant engagement. The article describes it as "a form of productive friction in which access to generative capabilities responds to each writer's engagement rather than elapsed time alone." In argumentative writing, the Tell-me text-generation mode unlocks when the essay contains a complete position and at least one distinct argumentative development linked to that position, detected by an LLM-based discourse classifier (micro-averaged F1 of 91.5%, macro-averaged F1 of 83.6%). Until unlock, users work with a pedagogical Teach-me assistant.
requirements: An LLM-based discourse classifier to detect the required engagement elements (position and argumentative development) in the user's draft
A restricted assistant mode (Teach-me) available before unlock and a generative mode (Tell-me) gated behind the criterion
constraints: In the study, 9 of 107 Engage-to-Unlock participants (8.4%) did not reach the contribution criterion and never unlocked Tell-me
The mechanism was implemented and tested for argumentative writing, where engagement is reflected in a position and supporting rationale
target_learners: Adult crowd workers (Prolific participants) completing argumentative writing tasks
target_learning_goals: Developing one's own position and argumentative rationale before receiving generative AI text generation
Accurate evaluation of AI-generated content for evidence and reasoning errors
examples: In the controlled experiment, Tell-me became available when both a complete position and a supporting claim were detected, each contributing 50% to a circular progress indicator, with partial formulations contributing 25%

article_title: What Makes Something Hard(er)? Explaining Question Difficulty in Natural Language
citation: Peng Cui, Qiaoyuan Zheng, Rudolf Debelak, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). What Makes Something Hard(er)? Explaining Question Difficulty in Natural Language. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01627
title: A three-step framework for generating validated natural-language explanations of question difficulty
description: The article introduces a framework that treats difficulty as "a quantity to be explained" rather than only estimated. It first fits a 1PL IRT model to LLM response matrices to estimate each item's difficulty, then repeatedly samples "contrastive sets of difficult and easy items" and prompts an LLM to propose hypotheses explaining the gap, and finally refines, matches, and selects hypotheses via L1-regularized regression on held-out questions. The output is interpretable natural-language difficulty factors that can be used predictively and causally.
requirements: Requires LLM response records for the question pool to fit the IRT model
Requires a held-out verification set for hypothesis selection via LASSO
constraints: Difficulty estimates depend on the respondent pool of LLMs used to fit the IRT model
target_learners: large language models evaluated on reasoning benchmarks
target_learning_goals: explaining and predicting item difficulty of reasoning questions
examples: Applied to GSM8K, BBH-structured, and WinoGrande with 5,000 or 3,811 LLM respondents per dataset
key_sources: Peng Cui, Qiaoyuan Zheng, Rudolf Debelak, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). What Makes Something Hard(er)? Explaining Question Difficulty in Natural Language. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01627

article_title: Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education
citation: Jorge Fábrega. (2026). Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02731
title: Epistemic ownership: a four-capacity framework for the learner's command over AI-mediated work
description: Epistemic ownership is an interpretive framework for the learner's justificatory command over work produced through distributed cognition with external systems, including generative AI. It comprises four interdependent functions: "direction, integration, evaluation and answerability". The article uses the first three, which can leave observable traces in AI-mediated interaction, to characterize how cognitive work is distributed between learner and system; answerability requires additional elicitation. The framework also names justificatory dispossession, the condition in which strong performance coexists with weak command because an adequate AI contribution is adopted without the learner reconstructing its reasoning.
requirements: Analysis of observable interaction traces requires sequential interaction records in which learner re-entry after an AI contribution can be examined
constraints: The article states epistemic ownership itself cannot be read directly from a chat transcript; absence of a coded behavior does not establish absence of the underlying capacity, and answerability lies beyond the empirical analysis developed here
target_learners: higher-education students in artificial intelligence and computer science courses
target_learning_goals: learner command over AI-mediated cognitive work
justification and evaluation of AI contributions
examples: The article applies the framework's first three dimensions to 150 StudyChat conversations, coding turn-level evidence of Direction, Integration, and Evaluation
key_sources: Jorge Fábrega. (2026). Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02731

article_title: Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education
citation: Jorge Fábrega. (2026). Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02731
title: StudyChat dataset of student–LLM conversations in AI and computer science coursework
description: StudyChat records student interactions with an LLM-based chatbot during Fall 2024 and Spring 2025, with each record containing a student prompt, the LLM response, and conversation, student, assignment, and interaction-order identifiers. The article reports that "The corpus contains 2,214 conversations from 203 students completing 7 course assignments in artificial intelligence and computer science", comprising 16,851 student utterances with a mean of 7.6 student turns per conversation (median = 4). The conversation is the sampling unit and released normalized assignment grades serve as measures of assessed performance.
requirements: Exact semester, student, and assignment identifiers for linking scores to conversations
constraints: Records only activity occurring within the interaction; the computational task environment produces unusually visible feedback, which may make some forms of participation easier to observe than in other domains
target_learners: undergraduate students in artificial intelligence and computer science courses
target_learning_goals: programming
data preprocessing
regression and classification
language-modeling tasks
examples: The article samples 150 conversations proportionally across semester, assignment, and conversation-length strata from this corpus
