article_title: Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education
citation: Jorge Fábrega. (2026). Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02731
title: Coding scheme for observable Direction, Integration, and Evaluation in student–AI interaction traces
description: An exploratory multilabel coding scheme applied to student turns in AI-mediated conversations, with the student turn as coding unit interpreted in relation to its local sequence and the whole conversation. Direction is coded when "the learner exercises task-relevant control over the purpose, constraints, procedure, artifact, or trajectory of the activity"; Integration when a subsequent action connects to uptake, application, transformation, or reuse of a prior AI contribution; Evaluation when the learner participates in judging a contribution through inspection, comparison, testing, discrepancy detection, diagnosis, correction, or criterion-based judgment. Provenance is recorded separately for content, criteria, and judgments, and evidence is classified as explicit or conservatively inferable.
requirements: Development through iterative human-in-the-loop analysis of boundary cases, with the codebook, prompt, and output schema frozen before application to the analytical sample
constraints: The codes describe observable participation, not an additive measure of epistemic ownership; Integration and Evaluation require opportunities for learner re-entry, so short conversations provide few opportunities for these dimensions to appear
target_learners: higher-education students interacting with LLM chatbots on coursework
target_learning_goals: observable cognitive participation in AI-mediated tasks
examples: The protocol was developed on 40 heterogeneous conversations, reaching saturation after 23 cases, tested on a 14-conversation pilot, then applied to 150 conversations using GPT-5.6 Sol with Structured Outputs
key_sources: Jorge Fábrega. (2026). Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02731

article_title: EVOL: Simulator-Guided Evolutionary Expert Synthesis for Deployment-Free Learning Path Recommendation
citation: Geonwoo Bang, Dongho Kim, and Moohong Min. (2026). EVOL: Simulator-Guided Evolutionary Expert Synthesis for Deployment-Free Learning Path Recommendation. arXiv:2610.03273. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03273
title: EVOL: simulator-guided demonstration learning for deployment-free learning path recommendation
description: EVOL adapts the robotics sim-to-real demonstration recipe to educational recommendation: a DKT-based knowledge evolution simulator (KES) both synthesizes per-learner expert paths via evolutionary search and hosts RL fine-tuning, while the deployed actor plans from the initial mastery alone. Per the article, "An asymmetric actor-critic architecture has the actor commit to blind planning from h0 in keeping the inference constraint while the critic exploits the privileged evolving mastery h𝑡 for accurate value targets during training." Training has three stages: evolutionary expert generation, behavioral cloning, and PPO fine-tuning with a warm-started privileged critic. At deployment the actor alone emits the full L-step path with no KES query.
requirements: A trained DKT simulator queryable during training
A combinatorial sequence decision problem with sparse terminal reward
Instance-specific near-optimal sequences that human demonstrations cannot supply
constraints: The deployed policy cannot access the simulator or counterfactual intermediate feedback at inference time
Demonstrations inherit whatever the DKT fails to represent, such as identical dynamics for learners with identical histories regardless of aptitude
target_learners: online learners on tutoring platforms with interaction histories
target_learning_goals: maximizing mastery improvement on target concepts via ordered learning paths
examples: Stage 1 evolves a population of 60 candidate paths over 50 generations inside the KES, selecting the single best path per learner; Stage 2 distills experts via behavioral cloning; Stage 3 refines with asymmetric PPO
key_sources: Geonwoo Bang, Dongho Kim, and Moohong Min. (2026). EVOL: Simulator-Guided Evolutionary Expert Synthesis for Deployment-Free Learning Path Recommendation. arXiv:2610.03273. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03273

article_title: Responsible Institutional Analytics: Interpreting Bias with AI Support
citation: Marques, F., Ortiz-Beltrán, A., Amarasinghe, I., & Hernández-Leo, D. (2026). Responsible Institutional Analytics: Interpreting Bias with AI Support. Journal of Universal Computer Science, 33(6). https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07205
title: FACTRIA: a framework of biasing factors for responsible institutional analytics interpretation
description: FACTRIA (Framework of Factors in the Analytical process and the data Context for Responsible Institutional Analytics) synthesizes fragmented knowledge on factors that hinder responsible interpretation of IA visualizations. As the article states, it is "a framework that organizes potential biasing factors across four areas: the analytics pipeline, institutional context, course-level characteristics, and demographics." It does not prescribe decisions but provides "a structured, evidence-informed scaffold" helping users surface implicit assumptions, question comparability, and recognize factors shaping interpretation. The framework is intended as flexible and extensible, with additional biasing factors to be incorporated as IA practices evolve.
requirements: Users must become familiar with the factors before interpretation; in the study participants read a framework summary before the task
constraints: The article states FACTRIA "remains a framework that may require adaptation across cases and institutional contexts" and does not prescribe how decisions should be made
target_learners: Academic managers
Educators
LMS and teaching-quality support staff in higher education
target_learning_goals: Responsible, bias-aware interpretation of institutional analytics dashboards
examples: The framework was encoded factor-by-factor into a chatbot and used to analyze four authentic IA cases on satisfaction, performance, LMS interaction, and LMS configuration diversity
key_sources: Marques, F., Ortiz-Beltrán, A., Amarasinghe, I., & Hernández-Leo, D. (2026). Responsible Institutional Analytics: Interpreting Bias with AI Support. Journal of Universal Computer Science, 33(6). https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07205

article_title: Responsible Institutional Analytics: Interpreting Bias with AI Support
citation: Marques, F., Ortiz-Beltrán, A., Amarasinghe, I., & Hernández-Leo, D. (2026). Responsible Institutional Analytics: Interpreting Bias with AI Support. Journal of Universal Computer Science, 33(6). https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07205
title: FACTRIA-aware chatbot: a GenAI assistant with retrieval-augmented, framework-bound prompting for IA dashboards
description: A web-based, LLM-powered chatbot integrated into an IA dashboard that supports responsible interpretation of institutional analytics. Its interaction logic "uses a deterministic state machine to connect users' initial interpretations to the framework and emphasize relevant factors," then "cycles through F ACTRIA factors related to the visualization, providing prompts that guide reflection towards the visible data." Rather than offering interpretations or recommending decisions, it prompts users to reflect on data quality, assumptions, comparability, and other biasing factors via FACTRIA-aware retrieval-augmented generation.
requirements: Grounding in the FACTRIA framework through retrieval-augmented generation
Integration with a dashboard visualization so prompts reference the visible data
constraints: The article notes possible automation bias and over-reliance on chatbot guidance; some participants found prompts too generic and preferred more direct guidance
target_learners: Higher education stakeholders interpreting institutional analytics: professors, academic managers, and technical support staff
target_learning_goals: Factor-aware, responsible interpretation of institutional analytics visualizations
examples: In the study, each participant first interpreted a visualization without the chatbot and then the same visualization with FACTRIA-aware chatbot guidance across two of four authentic IA cases

article_title: GenAI literacy and GenAI-assisted self-regulated learning behaviors: the roles of learning agency and challenge emotions
citation: Yang J, Liu X, Zhao W and Wang T (2026). GenAI literacy and GenAI-assisted self-regulated learning behaviors: the roles of learning agency and challenge emotions. Front. Psychol. 17:1902668. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1902668
title: Develop GenAI literacy beyond tool operation by building understanding of capabilities and limitations, critical evaluation of outputs, and informed use decisions
description: The article's practical implication is that GenAI literacy development for special education undergraduates should not stop at operational skills. It states that "Developing GenAI literacy should go beyond teaching students how to operate GenAI tools and should include opportunities to understand their capabilities and limitations, critically evaluate their outputs, and make informed decisions about their use in learning." This rests on the finding that GenAI literacy was positively associated with GenAI-assisted self-regulated learning behaviors.
requirements: Instruction should include opportunities to understand GenAI capabilities and limitations, critically evaluate outputs, and make informed decisions about use in learning, not only tool operation.
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional and limited to special education undergraduates in four Chinese provinces, so causal interpretation and generalizability are limited.
target_learners: special education undergraduates
target_learning_goals: GenAI literacy
self-regulated learning with GenAI support
examples: The survey of 434 special education undergraduates measured GenAI literacy with a 25-item scale across GenAI knowledge, skills, attitudes and values, and ethics dimensions, and found higher literacy associated with more self-regulated learning behaviors when using GenAI.

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence and the transformation of medical education: a scoping review
citation: Zhao J, Yang K, Gao H and Jiang G (2026). Generative artificial intelligence and the transformation of medical education: a scoping review. Front. Educ. 11:1907589. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1907589
title: Conditional effectiveness of GenAI learning activities: benefit depends on bounded tasks, grounding, active engagement, iterative feedback, and faculty oversight
description: The review's central interpretive account is that GenAI's educational value is conditional rather than uniform: "GenAI was neither uniformly superior nor uniformly harmful. Its effects depended on the instructional system in which it was embedded." Across illustrative studies, positive findings tended to co-occur with bounded tasks, curated grounding, active engagement, feedback requiring comparison or revision, and faculty oversight, while null or unfavorable cases involved replaced stronger resources, disrupted team cognition, or unreliable content.
requirements: Task bounded with curated content or structured case grounding
Learners engage actively and feedback requires comparison or revision
Faculty retain oversight of factual and pedagogical quality
constraints: These conditions are hypothesis-generating rather than a tested moderator analysis
The review did not test grounding as a quantitative moderator
target_learners: entry-to-practice medical students, preclinical through clerkship
target_learning_goals: history taking, communication, clinical reasoning, diagnostic performance, and selected knowledge outcomes
examples: The review contrasts controlled simulation gains with trauma-pilot teamwork disruption and fabricated-syndrome self-study as illustrations of the conditional pattern

article_title: Examining the Impact of Generative AI on Student Motivation and Engagement: The Mediating Role of Autonomy-Support and Autonomous Motivation in Education
citation: Ahmed A and Sultan A (2026) Examining the impact of generative AI on student motivation and engagement: the mediating role of autonomy-support and autonomous motivation in education. Front. Psychol. 17:1852265. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1852265
title: Integrated SDT–EVT–TAM framework for student engagement in GenAI-supported learning
description: The article proposes a unified framework combining Self-Determination Theory, Expectancy-Value Theory, and the Technology Acceptance Model to explain engagement in Generative AI-supported learning. It states that the study "extends existing AI-in-education literature by integrating SDT, EVT, and TAM within a unified framework to explain student engagement in Generative AI-supported learning environments." In the model, five perceived needs/value beliefs feed autonomy support for AI use and autonomous motivation for AI use, which drive student motivation and then engagement. The abstract reports that "autonomy support and autonomous motivation significantly increased student motivation, which subsequently emerged as the strongest predictor of student engagement."
requirements: Data from students with direct exposure to Generative AI tools, analysed via PLS-SEM with measurement and structural model evaluation
constraints: Tested in a single institution (King Saud University, Saudi Arabia) with a convenience sample; the article notes empirical evidence from Saudi higher education remains comparatively limited
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: student motivation and engagement in GenAI-supported learning
examples: PLS-SEM test of the integrated model with 297 students, with R² for engagement of 0.700

citation: Ahmed A and Sultan A (2026) Examining the impact of generative AI on student motivation and engagement: the mediating role of autonomy-support and autonomous motivation in education. Front. Psychol. 17:1852265. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1852265
title: 38-item GenAI motivation and engagement survey instrument (nine constructs)
description: A structured questionnaire adapted from previously validated scales in educational psychology, technology acceptance, and AI adoption literature, modified for the Generative AI context. It consists of "38 items distributed across nine latent constructs": perceived autonomy, perceived competence, perceived relatedness, perceived expectancy, perceived value, autonomy-support of AI use, autonomous motivation of AI use, student motivation, and student engagement, all on a five-point Likert scale. A 50-student pilot confirmed clarity and reliability, with all constructs exceeding Cronbach's alpha of 0.70.

The article distinguishes it from self-regulated learning: LOU captures GenAI-specific practices such as concept clarification, feedback interpretation, and output evaluation, whereas SRL captures domain-general planning, monitoring, and adjustment across academic tasks.

article_title: From Enhancement to Over-Reliance: A Mixed-Method Study of Generative AI and Sustainable Learning Performance
citation: Gao L, Sun Y and Khan SU (2026) From enhancement to over-reliance: a mixed-method study of generative AI and sustainable learning performance. Front. Psychol. 17:1847369. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1847369
title: Dual-pathway model of generative AI use and sustainable learning
description: The article integrates three theories — AI literacy, self-regulated learning, and cognitive offloading — into a dual-pathway model in which effective AI use opens both a positive path to sustainable learning performance and a negative path through AI over-reliance. The authors state that "the same behaviors that constitute eﬀective AI use can, under conditions of reduced self-regulation or elevated polychronicity, activate the over-reliance pathway". Polychronicity moderates both pathways as an individual-difference variable. The model is positioned against technology-acceptance approaches that measure intention to use rather than learning outcomes.
requirements: Students must actually engage with generative AI tools in academic work for the pathways to be observed
Measurement of AI literacy, SRL, critical AI evaluation, effective AI use, over-reliance, polychronicity, and sustainable learning performance as distinct constructs
constraints: Developed and tested in Chinese higher education with purposively sampled AI-using students
Sustainable learning performance is measured as perceived, self-reported retention, independence, and transfer
target_learners: university students using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: sustainable knowledge retention
independent application of learning
transfer of understanding across contexts
examples: The model was tested with PLS-SEM on a three-wave time-lagged survey of 623 Chinese university students and elaborated with 15 educator interviews

title: Build students' AI literacy as a protective measure against AI dependence
description: The principle holds that teaching students to understand, interpret, and critically evaluate AI systems protects the quality of their learning when generative AI is available. citation: Xiaoqi Wang, Lawrence Jun Zhang, Yanan Zhang. (2026). Generative artificial intelligence-supported self-regulated learning (GenAI-SRL) in L2 writing: scale development, validation, and short-form construction. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-026-09481-1
title: GenAI-SRL framework: six interacting regulatory dimensions for GenAI-mediated L2 writing
description: The framework reconceptualizes SRL for GenAI-supported L2 writing, consolidating cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, affective, social-behavioral, and environmental regulation. GenAI-SRL is "conceptualized here as a unified process in which the use of GenAI as a compositional resource and the critical governance of that use are mutually constitutive dimensions of regulatory activity." It extends pre-GenAI L2 writing models by adding affective and environmental regulation, the latter covering governance of AI tool use.

title: Extended Social Cognitive Theory framework positioning thoughtless GenAI use within triadic reciprocal determinism
description: The study adopts Social Cognitive Theory—personal factors, behavior, and environment in triadic reciprocal determinism—as its core analytical framework and extends it by inserting TUGA as a behavioral element interacting with SE and MOV and the GenAI environment. The article states that "the present study incorporates the TUGA into the SCT framework to examine the role of this behavior within the triadic interaction system." It argues classical SCT's static view of environment lags behind dynamic, autonomous GenAI features and that SCT needs extension for gender-differentiated pathways.
requirements: Applicable to technology-mediated learning environments where the technology exhibits dynamic, autonomous, and interactive characteristics
constraints: The authors state SCT's traditional framework conceptualizes environment statically and lacks systematic theoretical support for explaining gender-differentiated pathways in GenAI contexts

learning motivation

title: Six-type taxonomy of generative AI systems for STEAM educators
description: The review distinguishes six types of GenAI systems relevant to STEAM classrooms: text-generation, image-generation, audio-generation, video-generation, code-generation, and multimodal systems that integrate two or more functions. It states that "For STEAM educators, it is useful to distinguish six types of GenAI systems", naming examples such as ChatGPT, DALL·E, Runway ML, and GitHub Copilot. Multimodal systems are described as especially relevant to STEAM projects requiring learners to move between words, images, numbers, models, and computational artifacts.

constraints: GenAI should not be equated with all AI in education; predictive analytics, dashboards, automated scoring, and intelligent tutoring are not necessarily generative

article_title: Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics
citation: Zachery Quince and Emily Faulconer. (2026). Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00651-w
title: SAMR as a metric of constructive-alignment depth for GenAI use in assessment
description: The article positions the SAMR framework (Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition) not as a taxonomy of technology use but as a measure of how deeply GenAI integration preserves or bypasses constructive alignment. It states that "the SAMR framework is uniquely appropriate because it focuses on the functional behaviour change in the learning task, distinguishing between use as a passive cognitive shortcut (substitution) or as a cognitive partner for deep inquiry (redefinition)". Constructive alignment provides the baseline for assessment validity, and authentic assessment serves as the design intervention that fosters evaluative judgement so students critically engage with GenAI rather than offload cognitive effort.
requirements: Assessment tasks must be aligned with learning outcomes and activities so that SAMR level can be read as depth of alignment rather than tool frequency
constraints: The article cautions against viewing SAMR as a simple hierarchy; each level can be pedagogically appropriate depending on learning goals, and the mapping is context-dependent across disciplines and assessment types
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students
target_learning_goals: evaluative judgement
authentic demonstration of disciplinary reasoning under GenAI-available conditions
examples: Student declarations were mapped to SAMR levels: Learning and Formatting aligned with substitution/augmentation, Doing Task with modification/redefinition, and Feedback spanned all four levels

title: Four-category functional classification of student GenAI use (Learning, Formatting, Doing Task, Feedback) with SAMR mapping
description: A descriptive coding framework developed inductively from students' mandatory GenAI-use declarations in the physics unit, classifying the "clearly stated pedagogical function of each reported GenAI use" into four themes: Learning (researching, understanding, conceptualising, refining understanding), Formatting (structure, organisation, admin tasks), Doing Task (calculations), and Feedback (clarification, feedback, verification, checking results). Each category was mapped to SAMR levels: Learning to Substitution→Augmentation, Formatting to Substitution, Doing Task to Modification→Redefinition, and Feedback across all levels. Frequencies per assessment provided the primary evidence for evaluating student GenAI use.
requirements: Mandatory student declarations stating tools and purposes of GenAI use
Collaborative coding by two academics with consensus decisions
constraints: The SAMR mapping was interpretive and context-dependent rather than a fixed classification; declarations were self-reported and may be incomplete or strategically framed

title: Design assessments so that task demands, not policy labels, shape which GenAI functions students use
description: The article argues that a purpose-specific or open-use policy label defines what is permitted but cannot determine how students use GenAI; the assessment itself creates the demand. It concludes that "assessment design shapes which GenAI functions become meaningful": tasks rewarding polished communication elicit language and structure uses, while problem-solving tasks elicit checking, clarification, and verification uses. Assessment design that rewards understanding and requires student judgement aligns with the markers of evaluative judgement, keeping constructive alignment intact in the GenAI era.
requirements: Assessment tasks that require application of concepts to real-world scenarios and student judgement
constraints: The study is a single case with limited generalisability and does not establish a causal link between policy and outcomes; confounds include learning progression, tool familiarity, and task complexity

target_learning_goals: maintaining constructive alignment and evaluative judgement when GenAI is available

article_title: The association between generative AI use and university students’ critical thinking: a moderated mediation model of GenAI feedback literacy and reflective thinking
citation: Yan Z, Fang Z and Zou W (2026). The association between generative AI use and university students' critical thinking: a moderated mediation model of GenAI feedback literacy and reflective thinking. Front. Psychol. 17:1939286. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1939286
title: Dual-route pattern: direct association at low reflectivity, feedback-mediated association at high reflectivity
description: The article proposes a dual-route account integrating the extended-mind framework, cognitive load theory and feedback-literacy theory. GenAI can act as a complementary cognitive partner or a substitute depending on use; feedback literacy is the channel converting AI exposure into critical thinking; reflective thinking determines which route dominates. The article states: "We refer to this contrast between a predominantly direct association at low reflectivity and a predominantly feedback-mediated association at high reflectivity as a dual-route pattern." The estimated model supports this structure, with opposite-signed interaction terms.
requirements: Requires measures of GenAI use, GenAI feedback literacy, critical thinking and reflective thinking, modelled in a moderated mediation structure
constraints: All variables were measured concurrently by self-report in a cross-sectional design, so the account describes associations, not demonstrated mechanisms
target_learners: university undergraduates
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
feedback literacy
reflective thinking
examples: The PLS-SEM model with 421 Chinese undergraduates estimated both interaction terms with opposite signs, consistent with the dual-route reasoning.

article_title: Effectiveness of GenAI in Enhancing Writing Performance: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Mark Feng Teng. (2026). Effectiveness of GenAI in enhancing writing performance: a meta-analysis. Asian-Pacific Journal of Second and Foreign Language Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40862-026-00444-2
title: Multilevel conceptualization of moderators in GenAI-mediated writing research (technological, learner, and contextual factors)
description: The article proposes a multilevel framework for understanding variability in GenAI-mediated writing outcomes. It states that "Technological factors (e.g., tool type) determine the nature and depth of available feedback; learner factors (e.g., proficiency, education level) shape the capacity to interpret and internalize that feedback; and contextual factors (e.g., instructional model, sociocultural environment) influence how GenAI is integrated into learning practices." The framework holds that these moderators interact dynamically rather than operating independently, providing a principled basis for synthesizing cross-contextual studies and interpreting empirical variability.
requirements: Moderators must be coded at technological, learner, and contextual levels to interpret cross-study variability in GenAI writing effects
constraints: The article notes the moderators interact dynamically, so single-factor explanations of outcome variability are incomplete

target_learning_goals: L2/EFL writing performance, including linguistic accuracy, lexical sophistication, and text quality
examples: The meta-analysis operationalized the framework by coding intervention duration, education level, instructional model, and sample size as moderators in subgroup and meta-regression analyses

title: Ouyang and Jiao's three paradigms of AI in Education: AI-Directed, AI-Supported, and AI-Enhanced Learning
description: A taxonomy the review adopts to organize how Artificial Intelligence is used in Education, synthesizing three paradigms. In AI-Directed Learning "the student is the direct recipient of the AI system, which provides opportunities for individualized learning and immediate feedback". AI-Supported Learning is cooperative learning involving interaction between student and AI system, and AI-Enhanced Learning treats AI in Education as a complex system involving students, teachers, stakeholders and AI techniques serving as a tool to enrich human intelligence. The review presents this as a synthesis of prior literature rather than an empirically tested model.

title: Lee's Know-Build-Critique (KBC) model for guiding students' conscious use of GAI
description: The review reports that Lee (2023) proposes the Know-Build-Critique (KBC) model "to guide students in the conscious use of GAI". The model emphasizes "understanding the capabilities and limitations of technology, integrating new information critically and responsibly, and ethically evaluating generated information". It responds to the review's argument that adoption of GAI requires training students who not only use, but also actively build and critique knowledge, capable of identifying ethical issues and reflecting on AI's social implications.

constraints: Attributed in the review to Lee (2023); the review does not report empirical evaluation of the model

article_title: GIFT-AI: Teaching the Game and Leveling the Field: Peer and AI Review + Reflection in a Business Writing Course
citation: MacArthur M, Minnillo S, Sperber L, Whithaus C and Stillman N (2025) GIFT-AI: teaching the game and leveling the field: Peer and AI Review + Reflection in a business writing course. Front. Commun. 10:1615752. https://doi.org/10.3389/fcomm.2025.1615752
title: PAIRR: peer review plus criteria-based chatbot feedback with reflection before and after revision
description: PAIRR is a curricular model for writing courses that sequences peer review and AI feedback around a single draft. Teachers scaffold major assignments so students complete peer review of a full draft, then elicit criteria-based chatbot feedback on the same draft, then reflect on and critically assess both kinds of feedback and formulate revision plans, and after revising compose a second reflection on how each kind of feedback influenced their revisions. The article describes it as a model that "integrates GenAI feedback into writing curricula" and reports it is now being implemented at 8 public colleges and universities in California through a 3-year grant project.
requirements: Peer review must use assignment-specific criteria such as a checklist or evaluation rubric
Chatbot prompts assign a supportive peer reviewer role and use the same assignment-specific criteria
Students complete a reflection comparing peer and AI feedback and a revision plan before revising
constraints: Designed for writing courses with major drafted assignments; the article frames it for professional and business writing contexts
target_learners: upper-division undergraduate professional writing students
multilingual international students
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
writing revision and rhetorical awareness
writerly agency and metacognitive understanding of the writing process
examples: In the 2024 Business Writing course, students completed five major assignments, each requiring a rough draft, an audience analysis, formal peer review by 2-3 peers, and revision, with ChatGPT used for AI review with privacy settings activated

title: Offer guided introduction to AI literacy in writing courses to level the playing field for underprepared and multilingual students
description: Because students enter writing courses with different academic preparation, English fluency, and prior AI experience, the authors argue that a guided introduction to AI literacy is an equity measure. They cite evidence that underprepared students appear less likely to use AI and more likely to misuse it, and that students with educated parents tend to be more likely to use chatbots, concluding that "Offering a guided introduction to AI literacy in Business Writing can therefore level the playing field for all students." The PAIRR model operationalizes this by positioning AI neither as a tool to correct deficient writing nor as a way to avoid writing, but as an additional supportive perspective that does not replace human feedback.
requirements: Course-level clarity on acceptable and unacceptable AI uses
Instructor willingness to address AI misuse through supportive conversation and rewrite options rather than plagiarism reports
constraints: Rationale rests partly on cited prior studies rather than on data collected in this article

first-generation, low-income, and multilingual writers
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
educational equity in writing support
academic integrity understanding
examples: When Haoyu over-relied on AI for the first assignment, the instructor spoke with him in office hours about the value of his voice and unique experience, and he rewrote the assignment for a new grade

article_title: Intelligent tutoring in dynamic domains: a graph-based system for comparative analysis of adaptive algorithms
citation: Csépányi-Fürjes, L., & Kovács, L. (2026). Intelligent tutoring in dynamic domains: a graph-based system for comparative analysis of adaptive algorithms with intuitionistic fuzzy logic and forgetting. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10639-6
title: Evolving Knowledge Space Graph (EKSG) model
description: The EKSG model is a graph-structured knowledge representation framework for adaptive intelligent tutoring in fast-changing domains, combining the structural clarity of ontologies with the adaptive potential of Competence-Based Knowledge Space Theory. The article describes it as "a Knowledge Space Theory (KST) based (Doignon & Falmagne, 1985) conceptual framework specifically designed to support adaptive intelligent tutoring in fast-changing domains" that "integrates principles of temporal graph theory to represent dynamically changing domains." In this study it is operationalized in the G4L system, with knowledge units, material units, and test units as graph nodes connected by prerequisite_of edges.
requirements: A graph database to represent and query the prerequisite structure among knowledge units, as implemented in Neo4j
constraints: Before this study there was no publicly available implementation of the model and no empirical studies evaluating its practical feasibility or pedagogical utility
target_learners: university students in fast-evolving domains such as computer science
target_learning_goals: structured domain knowledge acquisition and adaptive learning pathways in dynamic curricula
examples: Operationalized in the Graph4Learn system for the JDBC API subdomain of a Database Systems II course, segmented into 15 knowledge units
key_sources: Csépányi-Fürjes, L., & Kovács, L. (2026). Intelligent tutoring in dynamic domains: a graph-based system for comparative analysis of adaptive algorithms with intuitionistic fuzzy logic and forgetting. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10639-6

citation: Csépányi-Fürjes, L., & Kovács, L. (2026). Intelligent tutoring in dynamic domains: a graph-based system for comparative analysis of adaptive algorithms with intuitionistic fuzzy logic and forgetting. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10639-6
title: Graph4Learn (G4L) intelligent tutoring system
description: G4L is a Python-based web application implementing the EKSG model with real-time knowledge tracking, adaptive content delivery, and detailed analysis of learner activity. The article states that "The EKSG model is realized within a Neo4j graph database" while "learner profiles and activity logs are systematically stored in a MySQL relational database." It comprises learner, teacher, and knowledge retention subsystems; the retention subsystem "performs scheduled updates of learner knowledge states" using "a configurable forgetting simulation algorithm to adjust the learner model accordingly."
requirements: A relational logging database recording all learner actions and system events, and a graph database holding the knowledge structure
constraints: Evaluated in one course subdomain (JDBC API) with 15 knowledge units; three participants remained inactive and provided no interaction data
target_learners: university students in computer science courses
target_learning_goals: adaptive content delivery, knowledge state tracking, and self-regulated learning support
examples: Used in a classroom study where participants were automatically assigned to BN, KST, or WDDI algorithm groups in a randomized but balanced fashion

title: Adapted IFL Interpretation Triangle for knowledge state visualization
description: The adapted Atanassov intuitionistic fuzzy logic triangle visualizes and classifies learner knowledge states per knowledge unit. The horizontal leg represents correct responses and the vertical leg incorrect responses; "The triangle vertices define three epistemic categories: point 'unknown' (origin, marked by '?'), point 'does not know' (top of the vertical leg, marked by 'X'), and point 'knows' (end of the horizontal leg, marked by '✓')." Threshold regions partition the triangle, and the system recommends the units whose estimated states are closest to the 'knows' vertex, prioritizing "units that the learner is most likely to master with minimal effort."
requirements: Measured mastery values per knowledge unit mapped onto the triangle, and predicted states propagated through the knowledge graph by the selected algorithm
constraints: The proximity-based recommendation deliberately deviates from classical KST outer-fringe recommendation, targeting medium to large knowledge units with partial content overlap rather than highly granular structures
target_learners: university students using the G4L system
target_learning_goals: understanding one's own knowledge state and deciding what to study next
examples: The teacher dashboard visualizes system-generated indicators via the adjusted IFL Interpretation Triangle

article_title: Guarded adoption of generative AI in higher education: high-achieving students, successful-student identity
citation: Jason Zagami. (2026). Guarded adoption of generative AI in higher education: high-achieving students, successful-student identity, and epistemic agency in a single-university mixed-methods survey. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education 23:47. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00625-6
title: Guarded adoption: selective, bounded, verification-intensive AI use in defence of epistemic control and successful-student identity
description: Guarded adoption is the paper's proposed interpretation of how high-achieving students relate to generative AI: "a form of selective engagement in which students use AI, but under conditions that seek to preserve epistemic control, intellectual ownership, and the legitimacy of their own learning". It is explicitly not scepticism, technophobia, or refusal; the concern is whether AI "remains subordinate to the learner's judgment". The article offers it as one plausible interpretation of the observed achievement-patterned differences, not a validated construct or general theory of student identity under AI conditions.
requirements: Requires attending to the conditions under which students accept AI use, not just adoption counts or enthusiasm ratings
constraints: The article states it is one plausible interpretation, not a general theory of student identity under artificial intelligence conditions; successful-student identity is used as an integrative analytical label, not an established or previously validated construct
target_learners: higher education students, particularly high-achieving students (self-reported GPA bands of 5.5 or above)
target_learning_goals: maintaining epistemic agency and independent judgment while using generative AI for learning
examples: A student who uses AI as a tutor-like conversational aid "but only while 'confirming accuracy'"; a student who lets AI assist with collecting and organising material but insists synthesis remains "solely my own"

Guarded adoption of generative AI in higher education: high-achieving students, successful-student identity, and epistemic agency in a single-university mixed-methods survey. article_title: Guarded adoption of generative AI in higher education: high-achieving students, successful-student identity
citation: Jason Zagami. (2026). Guarded adoption of generative AI in higher education: high-achieving students, successful-student identity, and epistemic agency in a single-university mixed-methods survey. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education 23:47. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00625-6
title: Epistemic agency as the primary frame for evaluating student AI use: the learner's relation to outputs matters more than amount of use
description: The paper adopts epistemic agency (drawing on Nieminen and Ketonen, 2024) as its strongest primary frame, shifting attention "from tool adoption to knowledge positioning". A student may use AI extensively and still exercise strong epistemic agency by treating outputs as provisional, interrogating warrants, verifying claims, and subordinating them to their own judgment; conversely, light use can be weak if outputs are accepted uncritically. The article concludes that "low AI use is not automatically educationally valuable, and high AI use is not automatically suspect". Supporting concepts include possible selves, identity-based motivation, and self-authorship.
requirements: Attention to how students relate to knowledge, assessment, and responsibility, not merely what they know
constraints: The article states the survey measures are not psychometrically strong enough to test a full motivational model, and it cannot claim to observe self-authorship in a formal developmental sense from brief survey comments
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: exercising judgment over AI outputs; remaining a responsible agent in relation to pre-processed information
examples: The article's distinction between a student who interrogates and verifies AI outputs while using them heavily, and one who uses AI lightly but accepts outputs uncritically

article_title: Transforming Curriculum Design with Generative AI: A Model for Assessing Teacher Digital Competence
citation: Guillén-Gámez, F. D., Tomczyk, Ł., Habibi, A., & Díaz Vargas, B. L. (2026). Transforming curriculum design with generative AI: a model for assessing teacher digital competence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10647-6
title: Extended Technology Acceptance Model for GenAI integration in curriculum planning
description: The article proposes an extended version of Davis's Technology Acceptance Model applied to GenAI tools in curriculum design. "The model included factors such as Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, Perceived Enjoyment, Self-Efficacy, Attitude of Use, and Behavioural Intention, analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM)." Self-efficacy is the only exogenous factor; PU, PEOU, PE, AOU, BI and digital competence are endogenous. The novel contribution is the explicitly modelled path from behavioural intention to pedagogical digital competence, which "in the traditional TAM model... had not previously been explicitly demonstrated".
requirements: Measurement of all seven latent factors as reflective constructs on a 7-point Likert scale, with reliability (α, CR > .70) and convergent validity (AVE > .50) established
constraints: Digital competence is operationalized as self-reported pedagogical competence, "rather than objective performance-based competence"; the model was tested only at the overall sample level in the Dominican Republic
target_learners: In-service teachers across early childhood, primary, secondary and higher education in the Dominican Republic
target_learning_goals: Developing teachers' pedagogical digital competence for planning and integrating GenAI tools (text, image, multimedia, video) into curriculum design
examples: The instrument was validated with 434 in-service teachers using a three-round expert review and PLS-SEM in Smart-PLS 4, with all twelve hypothesised paths supported

citation: Mohammad Hadra, Karleen Cambridge and Mostefa Mesbah. (2026). Evaluating the accuracy and reliability of AI content detectors in academic contexts. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00213-1
title: Balanced 192-text evaluation dataset of EFL, professional, AI-generated, and hybrid texts
description: The study constructed a dataset of 192 texts balanced across four authorship categories, with "Each category comprised 48 texts" spanning authentic EFL Foundation Program coursework written before August 2022, professional texts sampled from the XSum corpus, AI-generated texts from ChatGPT (GPT-4.1) and Claude 3 Opus, and hybrid texts integrating approximately 50% human with 50% AI content. Texts spanned three word-count ranges and two genres, and detector outputs were mapped to Human, Hybrid, or AI categories using established thresholding ranges (0–20%, 21–79%, 80%+).

Ethical approval and anonymization for student coursework use
constraints: EFL student texts cannot be publicly released but may be shared in anonymized and approved form for legitimate research purposes
Hybrid texts used a fixed 50/50 mixture, which the authors note real-world writing uncommonly adheres to
target_learners: EFL undergraduate and pre-undergraduate (Foundation Program) students
target_learning_goals: Academic integrity decision-making about student writing authorship
examples: EFL texts were final coursework submissions from FPES courses at Sultan Qaboos University, written prior to August 2022

article_title: Evaluating the accuracy and reliability of AI content detectors in academic contexts
citation: Mohammad Hadra, Karleen Cambridge and Mostefa Mesbah. (2026). Evaluating the accuracy and reliability of AI content detectors in academic contexts. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00213-1
title: Use AI-content detectors only as supplementary indicators that prompt further inquiry, never as sole evidence of academic misconduct
description: The article concludes that AI-content detectors "should not serve as primary or determinative evidence in academic misconduct investigations" because their accuracy, consistency, and fairness are insufficient, particularly for hybrid texts and EFL writers. Automated detection "should not be interpreted as evidence of misconduct; at best, it signals a need for further review." Institutions should pair detector outputs with informed human judgment and clear policies on acceptable AI use.
requirements: Informed human judgment accompanying detector outputs
Clear institutional policies distinguishing acceptable AI assistance from deceptive practices
Faculty training on interpreting detector outputs cautiously and contextually
constraints: Both evaluated detectors performed poorly on hybrid texts and showed sensitivity to text length and genre, limiting reliability across writing contexts

higher education students generally
target_learning_goals: Fair and equitable academic integrity decision-making
examples: The study's balanced 192-text evaluation showed macro-average F1-scores below 0.55 for both detectors and near-zero Originality recall on hybrid texts

article_title: Is hands-on learning still necessary in the age of AI? A thematic review
citation: Yu J, Liu L and Zhu Q (2026). Is hands-on learning still necessary in the age of AI? A thematic review. Front. Psychol. 17:1897168. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1897168
title: Process-oriented framework of expanded hands-on learning: Embodied Hands-on and Cognitive Hands-on
description: The review proposes that hands-on learning is expanding into two interrelated forms: Embodied Hands-on, based on the body, tools, and materials, and Cognitive Hands-on, based on language, judgement, and human–AI iteration. Both share a cycle of action, feedback, reflection, and refinement but rely on different sources of feedback and are not educationally equivalent. The framework emerged inductively from thematic analysis of 32 studies and is conceptual rather than empirically tested.
requirements: Learners must remain involved in action, feedback, reflection, and refinement for AI-supported activity to acquire the process characteristics of hands-on learning
constraints: The framework is conceptual and has not yet been empirically tested
There is insufficient evidence to show that the two forms can replace one another
target_learners: design students in higher education
target_learning_goals: creative thinking
design judgement
student agency
examples: The review synthesises prompting, generating, comparing, selecting, and revising as Cognitive Hands-on, and sketching, model making, and material experimentation as Embodied Hands-on

article_title: Under surveillance: Mapping remote proctoring practices in the assessment of nursing students — a scoping review
citation: Harerimana A, Mtshali N, Mchunu G. (2026). Under surveillance: mapping remote proctoring practices in the assessment of nursing students— a scoping review. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00229-7
title: Remote proctoring as a spectrum of technologically mediated assessment security strategies
description: The review organizes remote proctoring into a spectrum of modalities rather than a monolithic practice: AI-based automated/recorded systems (Honorlock, Respondus Monitor with LockDown Browser), live human invigilation (ProctorU), webcam/video proctoring with lockdown browsers, mobile-phone-based invigilation (the Invigilator app), and electronic test-center surveillance. It states remote proctoring "constitutes a spectrum of technologically mediated assessment security strategies, each with distinct trade-offs", reflecting disparities in infrastructure, institutional capacity, and assessment context. Context-adapted approaches in resource-constrained settings illustrate pragmatic alternatives to proprietary AI systems.
requirements: Depends on reliable internet connectivity, suitable devices, user-friendly platforms, adequate technical support, and assessment approaches aligned with student expectations
constraints: No single proctoring approach is universally effective; success is highly context-dependent
target_learners: nursing students (undergraduate, graduate, pre-registration)
target_learning_goals: upholding academic integrity in online assessment
examples: Six included studies deployed Honorlock (UK), ProctorU and Respondus Monitor (USA), the Invigilator mobile app (Southern Africa), webcam proctoring with lockdown browser (USA), and electronic test-center surveillance (Egypt)
key_sources: Harerimana A, Mtshali N, Mchunu G. (2026). Under surveillance: mapping remote proctoring practices in the assessment of nursing students— a scoping review. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00229-7

citation: Harerimana A, Mtshali N, Mchunu G. (2026). Under surveillance: mapping remote proctoring practices in the assessment of nursing students— a scoping review. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00229-7
title: Implement context-sensitive, ethically grounded proctoring policies supported by integrity-by-design assessment approaches
description: The review recommends that nursing programs adopt proctoring policies tailored to local context and ethics, rather than assuming a single universally effective approach. It states "Nursing programs must implement context-sensitive, ethically grounded proctoring policies, supported by integrity-by-design assessment approaches that prioritize authentic learning, student well-being, and equity." This follows from its finding that success is highly context-dependent and that proctoring can impose performance penalties, exacerbate inequalities, and normalize intrusive surveillance.
requirements: Balancing exam security with student well-being, fairness, and equitable access to digital tools
constraints: Only six empirical studies met the inclusion criteria, limiting the breadth and generalizability of the findings; most studies relied on self-reported perceptions
target_learners: nursing students in online and hybrid assessment programs
target_learning_goals: academic integrity in online assessment while prioritizing authentic learning, student well-being, and equity
examples: The review recommends future longitudinal, multi-site, and theory-informed designs and more studies from low- and middle-income settings to guide equitable, context-sensitive assessment strategies

citation: Hochberg N and Waitzman R (2026). From information providers to learning designers: heutagogical teaching practices in AI-enhanced education. Front. Educ. 11:1905833. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1905833
title: Five-dimensional typology of AI-enhanced heutagogical teaching practices
description: The article proposes a theory-informed typology in which AI-enhanced heutagogical teaching comprises five interconnected dimensions: designing for learner agency, self-regulated teaching and reflection, AI-supported learning design, designing for capability development, and critical AI literacy. The authors state that "The hybrid analysis generated five interconnected dimensions of AI-enhanced heutagogical teaching," with each dimension's analytic focus, illustrative reported practices, and boundary of inference summarized in Table 1. It functions as a formative design heuristic rather than a validated measurement scale.

constraints: Evidence concerns teacher reports and artifacts, not student outcomes; the typology is explicitly not a validated measurement scale

target_learning_goals: teacher professional learning in AI-supported, heutagogically oriented learning design

article_title: From information providers to learning designers: heutagogical teaching practices in AI-enhanced education
citation: Hochberg N and Waitzman R (2026). From information providers to learning designers: heutagogical teaching practices in AI-enhanced education. Front. Educ. 11:1905833. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1905833
title: Dual-layer relationship: teacher reflective regulation and critical AI literacy mediate learner-facing agency and capability design
description: The article proposes a dual-layer, developmental process in which teacher-level self-regulated reflection and critical AI literacy preserve professional judgment when working with generative systems, and that judgment is then enacted in learning designs intended to support learner agency and capability. The authors write that "At the teacher layer, self-regulated reflection and critical AI literacy help preserve professional judgment in interaction with probabilistic systems." AI-supported design connects the layers but does not guarantee learner self-determination.
requirements: Teachers' developing self-regulation, reflective practice, and design autonomy; explicit testing in future classroom research
constraints: The dual-layer relationship remains a proposition for future testing rather than a demonstrated student outcome
target_learners: in-service teachers participating in AI-focused professional development
target_learning_goals: designing learning environments that support learner self-determination and capability
examples: The article links the proposition to Arvatz et al.'s (2025) finding of parallel progression in teachers' self-regulated learning and students' reflective capacities, while keeping the learner-outcome claim explicitly untested

article_title: Rethinking teachers’ diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis
citation: Hoppe T, Loibl K and Leuders T (2026). Rethinking teachers' diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis. Front. Educ. 11:1857661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1857661
title: Meta-diagnosis: teachers' evaluative and integrative processing of AI-generated and self-generated diagnostic evidence
description: Meta-diagnosis is the cognitive process through which teachers critically evaluate and integrate two qualitatively different types of diagnostic evidence: their own judgments of student learning and AI-generated inferences based on algorithmic interpretation of student data. The article introduces it as the central diagnostic demand of AI-supported formative assessment, illustrated through contrasting case examples of subtraction teaching with and without a learning platform. It is 'not tied to a specific type of AI-supported assessment system but refers to the evaluative and integrative processes required of teachers.'
requirements: Teachers must have access to AI-generated diagnostic inferences that are accessible to them, so that these 'need to be evaluated and integrated into teachers' own diagnostic judgments'.
constraints: When explainable AI insights are limited, teachers must rely more strongly on their own classroom observations and observations of students' interactions with AI-supported learning environments.
target_learners: teachers in AI-supported classrooms
target_learning_goals: formative assessment and adaptive instructional decision-making
examples: In the AI-assisted case example, the teacher weighs a dashboard's place-value error pattern against her own observation of the student's growing frustration before deciding to offer encouragement before addressing the misconception.
key_sources: Hoppe T, Loibl K and Leuders T (2026). Rethinking teachers' diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis. Front. Educ. 11:1857661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1857661

article_title: Rethinking teachers’ diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis
citation: Hoppe T, Loibl K and Leuders T (2026). Rethinking teachers' diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis. Front. Educ. 11:1857661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1857661
title: DiaCoM framework specified for AI-supported formative assessment
description: The DiaCoM framework (Loibl et al., 2020) conceptualizes teachers' diagnosing as information processing: 'when teachers assess students' prerequisites, they perceive and interpret cues (such as verbal explanations or written solutions) and form diagnostic judgments.' The article specifies it for AI-supported settings: situation characteristics now include AI-generated diagnostic inferences as an additional information source, diagnostic behavior includes accepting, rejecting, or modifying AI suggestions, and person characteristics include knowledge about AI systems' functioning and limitations. The AI-related specification of diagnostic thinking is conceptualized as meta-diagnosis.
requirements: The framework distinguishes internal processes (perceiving, interpreting, deciding) from observable external diagnostic behavior, both shaped by person characteristics and situation characteristics.
constraints: The article states the goal is 'not to prescribe how teachers should diagnose more effectively, but to better understand the cognitive processes underlying their diagnostic judgments in AI-supported contexts.'
target_learners: teachers
teacher educators and researchers
target_learning_goals: understanding and developing teachers' diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment
examples: The framework has been used in studies of judgments about task demands, interpretation of ambiguous student responses, and prediction of student errors.

citation: Hoppe T, Loibl K and Leuders T (2026). Rethinking teachers' diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis. Front. Educ. 11:1857661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1857661
title: Develop teachers' AI literacy so they use AI diagnostic tools with appropriately calibrated trust rather than uncritical reliance
description: The article argues teachers require well-developed AI literacy when working with AI-based diagnostic tools: 'AI literacy refers to teachers' ability to recognize potential biases and inaccuracies in AI-generated information, to understand the underlying logic, capabilities, and limitations of AI systems, and to critically evaluate the pedagogical relevance and ethical implications of algorithmic outputs.' Such literacy fosters appropriately calibrated trust instead of automation bias and uncritical reliance on AI recommendations in instructional decision-making.
requirements: Teachers need opportunities to develop understanding of AI systems' logic, capabilities, and limitations, including awareness of automation bias when interacting with algorithmic decision support.
constraints: The article notes empirical evidence for the effectiveness of AI-supported diagnostic systems in educational settings is still limited.
target_learners: teachers
preservice teachers
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of AI-generated diagnostic information
responsible use of AI in formative assessment
examples: The article links AI literacy to recognizing biases and inaccuracies and to evaluating the ethical implications of algorithmic outputs, citing AI-literacy literature.

title: Teacher dashboards visualizing AI-analyzed student learning data in real time
description: Teacher dashboards are a component of AI-supported diagnostic systems that visualize analyses of students' learning processes for teachers. The article states that 'Teacher dashboards visualize this information, providing up-to-date insights into individual learners' progress and task performance,' enabling teachers to keep track of many students at once, identify patterns across the class, and support micro- and macro-level adaptations of instruction. In the case example, a dashboard summary indicates which students show which error patterns, such as a possible place-value misconception.
requirements: Using dashboard information to inform instruction requires teachers to interpret AI-generated analyses in relation to their own classroom observations, contextual knowledge, and instructional goals.
constraints: Dashboard analyses capture the student's conceptual difficulty but, as the case example shows, may not capture emerging frustration or disengagement the teacher observes directly.
target_learners: K-12 teachers
teachers using AI-supported learning platforms
target_learning_goals: class-wide monitoring of learning processes
timely instructional adaptation
examples: In the AI-assisted case example, the integrated system analyses subtraction responses in real time, highlights recurring place-value errors, and suggests follow-up activities via a dashboard summary.

article_title: Psychological predictors of continued ChatGPT use among university students: the roles of AI literacy, trust, and academic self-efficacy
citation: Peichen Hu. (2026). Psychological predictors of continued ChatGPT use among university students: the roles of AI literacy, trust, and academic self-efficacy. Front. Psychol. 17:1900190. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1900190
title: Capability-to-cognition-to-behavior moderated serial mediation model of continued generative AI use
description: The article proposes and tests a model in which AI literacy (capability) relates to continued ChatGPT use through an ordered psychological sequence: literacy to trust in AI, trust to academic self-efficacy, self-efficacy to continued use, with AI anxiety moderating the first link. The authors label this the "capability-to-cognition-to-behavior pattern" and contrast it with parallel-predictor acceptance models (TAM/UTAUT) that enter constructs side by side. In the tested sample the model accounted for 40% of variance in trust and continued use and 38% in self-efficacy.
requirements: Requires measuring AI literacy, trust in AI, academic self-efficacy, and AI anxiety with multi-item scales among learners who already use the tool
constraints: The ordering is a modeling assumption cross-sectional data cannot confirm; the sample comprises existing users only, so the account applies to sustained engagement rather than first-time uptake
target_learners: University students who already use generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: Sustained, productive engagement with generative AI for academic work
examples: Tested with a full latent-variable SEM on survey data from 450 Chinese university students with prior ChatGPT experience, with Monte Carlo confidence intervals (20,000 draws) for indirect effects
key_sources: Peichen Hu. (2026). Psychological predictors of continued ChatGPT use among university students: the roles of AI literacy, trust, and academic self-efficacy. Front. Psychol. 17:1900190. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1900190

article_title: Analyzing Undergraduate Problem-Solving in Physics Through Interaction With an AI Chatbot
citation: Syed Furqan Abbas Hashmi, N. Sanjay Rebello. (2025). Analyzing Undergraduate Problem-Solving in Physics Through Interaction With an AI Chatbot. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14778
title: Custom Socratic AI physics chatbot with dual GPT-4o Instructor and Verifier agents that logs full dialogue transcripts
description: A web-based Socratic tutoring system deployed in an introductory mechanics course. A Django backend deployed on Heroku manages API calls to OpenAI's GPT-4o, using two instances: an Instructor that "is responsible for generating the next question or hint for the student," and a Verifier that evaluates each student answer's correctness and quality. The dialogue is structured as a sequence of steps (conceptual understanding, setting up equations, performing calculations), begins with broad prompts such as "What is your approach?", and logs full transcripts for analytics.
requirements: Students interact individually via a web interface with the problem statement pre-loaded and reviewable at any time
constraints: The article states the fixed question progression and GPT-4o hints limit adaptivity
target_learners: first-year STEM majors in introductory calculus-based physics
target_learning_goals: physics problem solving integrating energy conservation, projectile motion, and kinematics
examples: Students solved a context-rich human-cannonball spring-launch problem adapted from the University of Minnesota PER group, requiring Hooke's law, gravitational potential energy, and projectile motion

article_title: Analyzing Undergraduate Problem-Solving in Physics Through Interaction With an AI Chatbot
citation: Syed Furqan Abbas Hashmi, N. Sanjay Rebello. (2025). Analyzing Undergraduate Problem-Solving in Physics Through Interaction With an AI Chatbot. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14778
title: Use complete AI-tutoring dialogue transcripts as fine-grained analytics linking help-seeking behavior to performance
description: The article argues that Socratic AI systems can serve instruction and research simultaneously by logging full interaction transcripts. The authors state that AI-driven Socratic dialogue "generates fine-grained analytics for physics education research, establishing a scalable dual-purpose tool for instruction and learning analytics." Transcript-based coding of question specificity linked help-seeking behavior to expected grades, a methodological gap the authors say existing studies leave open because they focus on aggregate performance metrics.
requirements: Full dialogue transcripts must be logged and student utterances coded (e.g., broad versus specific questions) for the analytics to be computed
constraints: The article states its binary broad/specific classification is coarse and overlooks nuances, and a finer-grained taxonomy is planned
target_learners: first-year STEM majors in large-enrollment introductory physics courses
target_learning_goals: problem-solving progress and help-seeking behavior in physics
examples: The authors coded each student question in 150 transcripts as broad or specific and related the specificity fraction to self-reported expected course grade

article_title: Systematic Review of Collaborative Learning Activities for Promoting AI Literacy
citation: A Hingle, A Johri. (2024). Systematic Review of Collaborative Learning Activities for Promoting AI Literacy. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6178-1256
title: ICAP framework: Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive hierarchy of learning modes
description: The ICAP framework distinguishes observable states of learning engagement, allowing more effective assessment of educational activities and stable cross-study comparison of collaborative learning. In its hierarchy, "interactive activities that engage learners in instructional settings to co-construct new knowledge yield the best learning outcomes." The interactive mode involves developing knowledge beyond provided materials by asking questions, giving and receiving feedback, and incorporating others' ideas; it is followed by the constructive mode, then active (applying knowledge to similar but non-identical scenarios), then passive activities like listening or reading, which are less effective. The review uses ICAP to classify each included study's CL activity, partners, and modes.
requirements: Activities must be classifiable into the four observable learning modes using the modes' classifying verbs
constraints: Passive activities are less effective because they require similar cues or contexts for recall, per the framework the review cites
target_learners: learners of all ages in AI literacy settings, from children to professionals
target_learning_goals: AI literacy knowledge and skills
collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The review classified each of the nine studies' activities, e.g. a card game where players combine cards creatively (constructive: strategize play; interactive: respond to challenged plays)
key_sources: A Hingle, A Johri. (2024). Systematic Review of Collaborative Learning Activities for Promoting AI Literacy. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6178-1256

article_title: Systematic Review of Collaborative Learning Activities for Promoting AI Literacy
citation: A Hingle, A Johri. (2024). Systematic Review of Collaborative Learning Activities for Promoting AI Literacy. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6178-1256
title: Corpus of nine empirical studies of collaborative learning for AI literacy (2015-2023)
description: A systematically collected corpus of nine studies published between January 2015 and December 2023, identified via PRISMA procedures from ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, SCOPUS, and Web of Science, with an initial yield of 227 studies. Studies span classroom, online community, home, office, and crowdsourced settings and audiences from children (ages 7-12) to educators, families, pathologists, and undergraduate computing students. Inter-rater agreement for inclusion and exclusion criteria was 0.9 (Cohen's kappa). Table 1 summarizes each study's goal, location, activity, and participants.
requirements: Studies had to meet six criteria: 2015-2023 publication, conference or journal venue, English, AI literacy focus, human-human or human-AI collaboration, and an empirical activity or intervention
constraints: ScienceDirect and ProQuest were excluded due to excessive irrelevant studies; the final dataset may potentially exclude relevant studies using different descriptors

educators
families
undergraduate computing students
professionals such as pathologists
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
machine learning literacy
21st century skills
human-AI collaboration competence
technical AI skills
examples: Included studies include Druga et al. 2019 (102 children, workshops across four countries), Lee et al. 2022 (37 educators in an AI book club), and Cai et al. 2019 (21 pathologists in a qualitative laboratory study)

article_title: Generate-Then-Validate: Question Generation for Education
citation: Yumou Wei, John Stamper, and Paulo F. Carvalho. 2026. Generate-Then-Validate: A Novel Question Generation Approach Using Small Language Models. In LAK26: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK 2026), Bergen, Norway. ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://doi.org/10.1145/3785022.3785100
title: Generate-Then-Validate: a Phi-2-based question generation pipeline with expansive generation and selective validation
description: A question generation pipeline that uses the 2.7B-parameter SLM Phi-2 as both generator and validator, requiring no fine-tuning. Its two stages are expansive generation, which builds MCQs through a five-step incremental prompt (seed, stem, choices, answer, explanation), and selective validation via syntactic filtering, answer confidence evaluation, and an LO alignment check based on log-probability relevance. The authors state that "our pipeline first performs expansive generation to create an abundance of candidate questions and refine them through selective validation based on novel probabilistic reasoning". Applied to 41 AP Environmental Science LOs, it produced a final pool of 3,205 MCQs from 8,200 candidates.
requirements: An open-source SLM exposing next-token probabilities (Phi-2 via HuggingFace) so choice-label probabilities and log-probability relevance can be extracted
A set of learning objectives as pipeline input, in action-based or content-based form
constraints: Evaluated for multiple-choice questions; adapting to other question types requires adjusting the generation and validation steps, though the authors state the core idea remains applicable
target_learners: middle-school science students (questions drawn from AP Environmental Science objectives)
target_learning_goals: assessing learning objectives such as explaining the carbon cycle or describing impacts of human activity on wetlands and mangroves
examples: Generated 200 MCQs per LO for 41 AP Environmental Science LOs (8,200 candidates), retaining 3,205 after the three validation steps, with a mean of 78.17 MCQs per LO (SD = 29.05)

article_title: Not All Students Engage Alike: Multi-Institution Patterns in GenAI Tutor Use
citation: Youjie Chen, Xixi Shi, Xinyu Liu, Shuaiguo Wang, Tracy Xiao Liu, Dragan Gašević. (2026). Not All Students Engage Alike: Multi-Institution Patterns in GenAI Tutor Use. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.00447
title: Two-stage learning analytics framework for GenAI Tutor engagement: session-level engagement types plus student-level transition patterns
description: The article proposes a learning analytics framework that first identifies engagement types at the conversation session level through clustering on behavioral, cognitive, and temporal features, then aggregates them into student-level engagement patterns via process mining. The authors state they "propose a learning analytics framework that identifies conversation session-level engagement types and integrates with student-level engagement patterns, which can be applied to other human-AI interaction data." It builds on prior process-mining work that segments logs into sessions and aggregates tactics into strategies.
requirements: Requires student-GenAI interaction logs with prompts, responses, and timestamps, plus engineered behavioral, cognitive, and temporal features
constraints: Emotional engagement was not characterized because the authors lacked approaches to reliably infer emotions from their data logs
target_learners: post-secondary students
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving student engagement with GenAI tutoring tools
examples: Applied to 113,255 conversation sessions from 11,406 students across 200 classes at ten institutions, segmented with a 15-minute threshold plus LLM topic segmentation achieving an F1-score of 0.9
key_sources: Youjie Chen, Xixi Shi, Xinyu Liu, Shuaiguo Wang, Tracy Xiao Liu, Dragan Gašević. (2026). Not All Students Engage Alike: Multi-Institution Patterns in GenAI Tutor Use. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.00447

article_title: Not All Students Engage Alike: Multi-Institution Patterns in GenAI Tutor Use
citation: Youjie Chen, Xixi Shi, Xinyu Liu, Shuaiguo Wang, Tracy Xiao Liu, Dragan Gašević. (2026). Not All Students Engage Alike: Multi-Institution Patterns in GenAI Tutor Use. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.00447
title: Design and scale GenAI Tutors with discipline-sensitive embedding rather than as a one-size-fits-all solution
description: The article argues that productive engagement with GenAI Tutors at scale depends on how tools are embedded in discipline-specific instructional and assessment structures, not only on backend model generalizability. The authors conclude that "GenAI Tutors should not be viewed as a one-size-fits-all solution, but require discipline-sensitive design to support effective use at scale," since engagement patterns differed substantially between STEM and non-STEM courses.
requirements: Attention to disciplinary variation in instructional design and assessment structures when embedding the tutor in courses
constraints: Findings come from classes and institutions with high GenAI Tutor adoption and may not generalize to low-use settings
target_learners: post-secondary students across STEM and non-STEM disciplines
target_learning_goals: productive, learning-supportive engagement with GenAI tutoring tools
examples: STEM courses' weekly closed-ended problems were associated with brief, task-oriented tutor use, while non-STEM open-ended assignments and take-home projects were associated with more iterative, later-semester use
