article_title: SafeTutors: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems
citation: Rima Hazra, Bikram Ghuku, Ilona Marchenko, Yaroslava Tokarieva, Sayan Layek, Somnath Banerjee, Julia Stoyanovich, Mykola Pechenizkiy. (2026). SAFETUTORS: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17373
title: AI Tutor Risk Taxonomy: 11 harm dimensions and 48 sub-risks grounded in learning-science theory
description: The article proposes a taxonomy comprising 11 parent risk categories and 48 sub-risks characterizing how an AI tutor can compromise learning, extending beyond content-level harms like toxicity. It states the taxonomy is "grounded in established learning sciences literature" and defines each category by its underlying learning-science construct, covering cognitive, epistemic, metacognitive, motivational-affective, developmental-equity, instructional alignment, behavioral-inquiry, ethical-epistemic integrity, informational-semantic, reflective-critical, and pedagogical relationship risks.
requirements: Each category is defined in terms of its underlying learning sciences construct and illustrated with representative tutor-learner interactions
constraints: The taxonomy targets tutoring-specific harms in educational interaction rather than conventional content-level LLM safety harms
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students interacting with LLM-based AI tutors in STEM subjects
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding and mastery of mathematics, physics, and chemistry through scaffolded tutoring
examples: The taxonomy grounds categories in cited theories, e.g., cognitive risk in cognitive load and knowledge construction theories, and instructional alignment risk in constructive alignment theory
key_sources: Rima Hazra, Bikram Ghuku, Ilona Marchenko, Yaroslava Tokarieva, Sayan Layek, Somnath Banerjee, Julia Stoyanovich, Mykola Pechenizkiy. (2026). SAFETUTORS: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17373

article_title: SafeTutors: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems
citation: Rima Hazra, Bikram Ghuku, Ilona Marchenko, Yaroslava Tokarieva, Sayan Layek, Somnath Banerjee, Julia Stoyanovich, Mykola Pechenizkiy. (2026). SAFETUTORS: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17373
title: SAFETUTORS benchmark: 3,135 single-turn instances and 2,820 multi-turn tutoring sequences across three STEM domains
description: SAFETUTORS is a benchmark for joint safety and pedagogical evaluation of AI tutors in mathematics, physics, and chemistry. It comprises "3,135 single-turn instances and 2,820 multi-turn tutoring sequences constructed via crescendo-based escalation", with multi-turn conversations spanning 5-8 turns. Data was built from seed questions in MathDial and CAMEL-AI, filtered with GPT-5.2, and validated through three human annotation stages reaching Fleiss' kappa of 0.82, 0.74, and 0.69 across stages, with 91.3% of instances receiving consistent final labels after adjudication.
requirements: Human validation through expert annotation to ensure pedagogical validity, conversational coherence, and alignment with intended risk categories
constraints: Covers three STEM domains only (physics, chemistry, mathematics); automated harm scoring is done by LLM judges with majority voting, verified against human labeling on a stratified sample with Cohen's kappa = 0.76
target_learners: Students in mathematics, physics, and chemistry at varied difficulty levels
target_learning_goals: Scaffolded problem solving, misconception repair, and mastery of STEM learning objectives
examples: Multi-turn conversations begin with a legitimate scientific problem and student utterances progressively steer the tutor toward a specific risk category
key_sources: Rima Hazra, Bikram Ghuku, Ilona Marchenko, Yaroslava Tokarieva, Sayan Layek, Somnath Banerjee, Julia Stoyanovich, Mykola Pechenizkiy. (2026). SAFETUTORS: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17373

article_title: Unpacking Interaction Profiles and Strategies in Human-AI Collaborative Problem Solving: A Cognitive Distribution and Regulation Perspective
citation: Zhanxin Hao, Xiaobo Liu, Jiaxin Fan, Yun Long, Jifan Yu, Wenli Chen, Yu Zhang. (2025). Unpacking Interaction Profiles and Strategies in Human-AI Collaborative Problem Solving: A Cognitive Distribution and Regulation Perspective. https://www.maic.chat
title: HA-CORD: Human-AI Cognitive and Regulatory Distribution model
description: The HA-CORD model integrates distributed cognition theory with regulation-of-learning theories (self-regulation, co-regulation, socially-shared regulation) to explain human-AI collaborative problem solving. The article states: "we propose a more integrated framework for AI-supported collaborative problem solving, one that explains both how cognitive work is distributed and how that distribution is dynamically regulated by human and AI agents." It treats cognitive offloading and scaffolding alongside metacognitive monitoring and model adaptation, and organizes the three empirical profiles (DR, CI, DE) along axes of distributed cognition and distributed regulation.
requirements: Dialogue-level coding of human-AI interaction to observe cognitive distribution and regulatory moves
constraints: The article notes classical distributed cognition pays less explicit attention to metacognitive activities within individual human members, which the regulation layer is intended to address
target_learners: college students collaborating with AI agents
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving
metacognitive regulation of learning
examples: The three identified profiles were mapped onto the model as a spectrum from distributed cognition with metacognitive detachment (DR) to human-centered cognition with deepest regulation (CI), with DE as a transitional middle ground

article_title: Modernizing Ground Truth: Four Shifts Toward Improving Reliability and Validity in AI in Education
citation: Thomas, D.R., Borchers, C., Vanacore, K.P., Koedinger, K.R., & Kizilcec, R.F. (2026). Modernizing Ground Truth: Four Shifts Toward Improving Reliability and Validity in AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29141
title: Four shifts for establishing ground truth in AIED: diagnostic IRR, transparent reporting, LLM risk mitigation, and validity-first evidence
description: The article's central framework proposes four practical shifts for establishing ground truth in AIED labeling: (1) treat IRR as "a diagnostic signal to localize disagreement and refine constructs rather than a mechanical acceptance threshold"; (2) require transparent reporting of rater expertise, codebook development, reconciliation procedures, and segmentation rules; (3) mitigate risks in LLM annotation through bias audits and verification workflows; and (4) complement agreement statistics with validity and effectiveness evidence, including uncertainty-aware labeling, criterion-related checks, and close-the-loop evaluations. The framework is grounded in the distinction between noise and bias and illustrated through multimodal tutoring case studies.
requirements: Reporting must cover rater characteristics, codebook evolution, and conflict resolution for the transparency shift to function as described.
constraints: The framework targets AIED settings with high-inference constructs, skewed label distributions, and temporally segmented multimodal data; the authors state the goal is not to replace established psychometric frameworks but to translate and extend them.
target_learners: AIED researchers and dataset builders annotating educational interaction data
target_learning_goals: Improving reliability and validity of labeled educational datasets used to train and evaluate AI tutoring and assessment systems
examples: The paper uses a running example of multimodal tutoring data in which a student's verbal confusion is paired with visual cues and processed into a transcribed, timestamped interaction.
key_sources: Thomas, D.R., Borchers, C., Vanacore, K.P., Koedinger, K.R., & Kizilcec, R.F. (2026). Modernizing Ground Truth: Four Shifts Toward Improving Reliability and Validity in AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29141

article_title: Interpretable Knowledge Tracing
citation: Shuyan Huang, Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Andrew Lan. (2026). Interpretable Difficulty-Aware Knowledge Tracing in Tutor-Student Dialogues. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01097
title: Interpretable difficulty-aware conversational knowledge tracing framework (knowledge estimator + difficulty estimator + IRT-based predictor)
description: A three-module framework for knowledge tracing in tutor-student dialogues: a knowledge estimator that encodes the original question and dialogue history to produce a scalar ability estimate from LLM logits over GOOD/BAD tokens; a difficulty estimator that jointly considers question text, dialogue context, and the next tutor-posed task to produce a difficulty estimate from HARD/EASY logits; and an IRT-based predictor applying a 1PL (Rasch) model, where "the probability of correctness increases as the positive difference between ability and difficulty grows." The design "aligns model predictions with cognitive theory and improves interpretability."
requirements: An LLM fine-tuned on dialogue-based tutoring data with observed correctness labels, optimized by minimizing binary cross-entropy loss through the IRT prediction layer
constraints: Experiments cover only math dialogues; a learnable vector discrimination parameter led to degraded performance, so a scalar sensitivity parameter is used
target_learners: students in one-on-one math tutoring dialogues
target_learning_goals: predicting student correctness on upcoming tutor-posed tasks and tracking evolving knowledge state during tutoring
examples: The framework was instantiated on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA fine-tuning and evaluated on QATD2k and MathDial against LLMKT and deep learning KT baselines
key_sources: Shuyan Huang, Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Andrew Lan. (2026). Interpretable Difficulty-Aware Knowledge Tracing in Tutor-Student Dialogues. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01097

article_title: ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming
citation: Anahita Golrang, Kshitij Sharma, Simon Dehaen, Olga Viberg. (2026). ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02703
title: ProPACT: forecast-driven dyadic learner modeling treating collaboration as the object of instruction
description: ProPACT is an AI-driven adaptive collaborative tutor that treats collaboration itself, rather than the individual learner, as the object of instruction. It builds a dyadic learner model in which "ProPACT constructs a dyadic learner model based on Joint Visual Attention (JVA) and Joint Mental Effort (JME), alongside individual mental effort (ME)", and uses an XGBoost forecasting model to predict suboptimal collaboration states up to 30 seconds ahead. Predictions drive a hierarchical adaptive policy that orchestrates dialogue prompts, gaze-awareness cues, AI-assisted code suggestions, and task-based hints while fading support during productive collaboration.
requirements: Dual eye-tracking and pupillometry sensing infrastructure to measure JVA, ME, and JME in real time
Empirically validated thresholds from prior DUET and eye-tracking research for discretizing indicators into High, Average, and Low levels
constraints: The study was conducted in a controlled laboratory setting with a relatively small sample size and short-duration debugging tasks
The system relies on specialized sensing infrastructure, including dual eye-tracking and pupillometry, which poses practical and financial constraints for large-scale deployment
target_learners: Undergraduate or master's students in computer science or engineering learning pair programming
target_learning_goals: Collaborative debugging and pair-programming regulation, including attention alignment and cognitive-effort balance
examples: In the evaluation, 26 dyads debugged tasks containing only logical bugs under control and ProPACT feedback conditions with eye trackers individually calibrated
key_sources: Anahita Golrang, Kshitij Sharma, Simon Dehaen, Olga Viberg. (2026). ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02703

article_title: ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming
citation: Anahita Golrang, Kshitij Sharma, Simon Dehaen, Olga Viberg. (2026). ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02703
title: ProPACT Hybrid-AI feedback system with five feedback tools and hierarchical trigger policy
description: The feedback system is a Hybrid-AI framework that "combines data-driven forecasting with rule-based pedagogical decision-making". An XGBoost model predicts JVA, JME, and ME over a 30-second horizon; predictions are discretized against each participant's resting baseline using a ±2SD criterion and mapped against a desired collaboration matrix to predefined trigger conditions. Five feedback tools are integrated: GitHub Copilot autocomplete, dual text selection, a gaze-awareness tool, a dialogue prompt, and a last-resort task-based hint, selected via a top-down hierarchical policy prioritizing minimal intervention.
requirements: A desired collaboration matrix and predefined trigger conditions (e.g., gaze-awareness triggered when JVA = Low, dialogue prompt when JME = Low, task-based hint when both MEs = High)
Per-participant resting baselines for the ±2SD discretization of predicted states
constraints: The task-based hint is used only as a last-resort intervention, triggered when less intrusive scaffolds fail and both collaborators exhibit sustained extreme mental-effort levels
target_learners: Undergraduate or master's computer science and engineering students pair programming on debugging tasks
target_learning_goals: Restoring joint attention and cognitive alignment during collaborative debugging
examples: The gaze-awareness tool visualizes a partner's gaze as a translucent colored rectangle highlighting the current attention region (nine lines of code), triggered when JVA is low

citation: Anahita Golrang, Kshitij Sharma, Simon Dehaen, Olga Viberg. (2026). ProPACT: A Proactive AI-Driven Adaptive Collaborative Tutor for Pair Programming. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02703
title: Escalate collaborative scaffolds from minimally intrusive to directive only after lower-intensity interventions are exhausted
description: ProPACT's adaptive policy prioritizes minimal intervention and escalates support only when forecasted risk of breakdown increases. Its staged design follows the principle that "adaptive support principles that recommend escalating assistance only after lower-intensity interventions are exhausted, particularly under high cognitive load". Less intrusive tools (gaze cues, dialogue prompts, temporary Copilot activation) precede the most directive support, the task-based hint, which is reserved for sustained extreme mental-effort levels indicating cognitive strain or stagnation.
requirements: Real-time forecasts of collaboration states to identify when lower-intensity interventions have failed
constraints: The most directive support (task-based hint) is reserved for cases where both collaborators exhibit sustained extreme mental-effort levels
target_learners: Pair-programming dyads in undergraduate or master's programming education
target_learning_goals: Sustaining productive collaboration and cognitive balance without undermining learner autonomy
examples: ProPACT triggers a dialogue prompt when JME falls below threshold and reserves the task-based hint, which prompts selection of the current task and bug, for when less intrusive scaffolds fail

article_title: A meta-analysis of the effect of generative AI on productivity and learning in programming
citation: Maier, S., Gunzenhäuser, M., Schweisthal, J., Schneider, M., & Feuerriegel, S. (2026). A meta-analysis of the effect of generative AI on productivity and learning in programming. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04779
title: Integrate GenAI into computer science education carefully, emphasizing explanation, reasoning, and critical evaluation rather than code production alone.
description: The article recommends rethinking curricula and GenAI integration by moving beyond code production alone and placing greater emphasis on explanation, reasoning, and critical evaluation, so that students develop the skills required to work safely and effectively with GenAI assistance. This principle responds to the meta-analytic finding that GenAI use does not consistently translate into improved learning or skill development, and that unrestricted access may hinder genuine skill acquisition. The authors argue that banning GenAI tools is neither realistic nor desirable given their growing professional role, making deliberate pedagogical integration essential.
requirements: Curricula must place greater emphasis on explanation, reasoning, and critical evaluation alongside code production.
GenAI integration must be deliberate rather than unrestricted, as unrestricted access may hinder genuine skill acquisition.
constraints: Banning GenAI tools is neither realistic nor desirable given the growing role of GenAI in professional programming practice.
The evidence base for learning outcomes is limited (11 effect sizes from 10 studies) and heterogeneous (I² = 86%).
target_learners: Computer science students at university and pre-university levels
Novice programmers
target_learning_goals: Programming skill acquisition
Code comprehension and reasoning
Critical evaluation of AI-generated code
examples: The article's meta-analysis found significant learning effects only when students retained access to GenAI during the assessment itself, suggesting observed gains reflect tool-augmented performance rather than durable skill acquisition.
The authors note that when students rely on GenAI to generate or repair code, they may bypass critical learning processes such as reasoning through errors and internalizing core concepts.
key_sources: Maier, S., Gunzenhäuser, M., Schweisthal, J., Schneider, M., & Feuerriegel, S. (2026). A meta-analysis of the effect of generative AI on productivity and learning in programming. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04779

article_title: A meta-analysis of the effect of generative AI on productivity and learning in programming
citation: Maier, S., Gunzenhäuser, M., Schweisthal, J., Schneider, M., & Feuerriegel, S. (2026). A meta-analysis of the effect of generative AI on productivity and learning in programming. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04779
title: Cognitive offloading: reliance on GenAI can allow students to bypass core learning processes, reducing active engagement and impairing fundamental programming skill development.
description: Cognitive offloading, as described in this article, is the phenomenon whereby reliance on GenAI tools allows students to bypass core learning processes such as trial-and-error learning, debugging, and iterative refinement when they delegate core tasks to GenAI. The article states this "may reduce active engagement with problem solving, which, in turn, can lead to shallow understanding and ultimately impair the development of fundamental programming skills." As an explanatory framework, it accounts for the meta-analytic finding that GenAI assistance shows no significant pooled learning benefit: students may complete tasks without internalizing underlying reasoning, producing tool-dependent capabilities that fail to persist without AI support.
requirements: Students must have access to GenAI tools during learning phases for offloading to occur.
The framework presupposes that foundational programming skills require active engagement with problem-solving processes.
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretive framework consistent with prior research in other educational domains, not as a mechanism directly tested within the meta-analysis itself.
The article notes that capabilities developed during AI-assisted coding may prove tool-dependent, failing to persist without AI support.
target_learners: Novice programming students
Computer science students at university and pre-university levels
target_learning_goals: Development of fundamental programming skills
Internalizing core concepts through debugging and iterative refinement
examples: The article cites this phenomenon to explain why learning effects emerged only when GenAI was permitted during assessment: students perform better with tools available, but gains may reflect tool-dependent augmentation rather than durable learning.
The article warns that reliance on GenAI tools may backfire when students are required to explain, adapt, or debug AI-generated code.

article_title: Human-AI Co-Mentorship in Project-Based Learning: A Case Study in Financial Forecasting
citation: Freyaa Chawla, Ahan Chawla, Rishi Singh, Joe Germino, Grigorii Khvatskii. (2026). Human-AI Co-Mentorship in Project-Based Learning: A Case Study in Financial Forecasting. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05144
title: Human-AI co-mentorship model with complementary tactical and strategic roles
description: The article proposes a co-mentorship model in which AI tools and human mentors play fundamentally different, complementary roles in project-based learning. AI provides "just-in-time tactical support: generating code scaffolding, suggesting hyperparameter ranges, and offering quick explanations of unfamiliar concepts," while human mentors frame problems, validate architectural decisions, and supply domain intuition and a complete project vision. The article states "The most effective co-mentoring configuration was rathercomplementary: AI handled routine implementation tasks, freeing human mentors to focus on higher-level reasoning, debugging and conceptual explanation."
requirements: Human mentors with domain expertise must remain available for strategic decisions, validation of AI outputs, and conceptual explanation.
constraints: Findings come from a single cohort of high-school and early-undergraduate students at US-style institutions over one summer; the authors caution against extrapolating to other contexts.
Findings are specific to the versions of LLM tools available during the summer of 2025.
target_learners: high-school students
early-undergraduate students
novices with limited domain expertise
target_learning_goals: research and programming skills
conceptual understanding of machine learning and finance
critical evaluation of AI outputs
examples: Daily stand-ups of around 30 minutes focused on problems to be solved, with students pursuing learning exercises between sessions, including dialogues with AI tools.

title: Student-built ETF forecasting pipeline with LLM-scored news sentiment dataset
description: The project's technical artifact is a two-stage predictive system: regression models estimate the magnitude of ETF price deltas and classification models predict direction, with predictions merged by multiplying magnitude and sign. The dataset covers "a historical price dataset for 29 exchange-traded funds (ETFs), covering January 2, 2024 through September 23, 2025" harvested via the Yahoo Finance API, plus 260 scraped NASDAQ news articles scored by gpt-5-mini on a -10 to +10 scale with justifications, aggregated daily by sector. Sentiment coverage was sparse and uneven across ETFs, from 0% to 23.16% as shown in Table 1.
requirements: Mentor intervention was needed for rate limiting, error recovery, and anti-bot scraping measures such as dynamic content loading.
constraints: Sector-level sentiment aggregation may dilute ETF-specific signals; zero-imputation for days without news may introduce bias; LLM scores were not validated against human-coded ground truth.

machine learning model development and validation
web scraping and data engineering

article_title: Distinguishing performance gains from learning when using generative AI
citation: Yan, L., Greiff, S., Lodge, J. M., & Gašević, D. (2025). Distinguishing performance gains from learning when using generative AI. Nature Reviews Psychology, 4, 435–436. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-025-00467-5
title: Performance versus learning distinction: performance during task execution does not imply durable learning
description: The article organizes its argument around a fundamental distinction between performance and learning. Performance refers to observable behaviours during task execution, often influenced by external supports, whereas learning involves enduring changes in knowledge or behaviour characterized by the ability to independently retain and transfer skills. The article applies this distinction to critique generative-AI research that measures only immediate task success.
requirements: Assessment must capture independent retention and transfer, not just in-task performance, for the distinction to be observable
constraints: The article notes the distinction is underexamined in emerging research on generative AI in education
target_learners: tertiary students
K-12 students
target_learning_goals: durable knowledge retention
transfer of skills
examples: The article illustrates the distinction with cramming: a student may achieve high test performance after massed practice yet fail to retain or apply the knowledge later

title: Design generative AI-supported tasks to promote active metacognition and balance efficiency with autonomy
description: The article recommends that educators and designers ensure generative AI-supported tasks promote learning rather than just performance gains. They should promote active metacognition by encouraging learners to critically evaluate AI-generated outputs rather than accepting them passively, and "balance efficiency with autonomy", using generative AI to support, not replace, independent cognitive effort.
requirements: Tasks must create opportunities for learners to critically evaluate AI outputs and for unaided problem-solving alongside AI feedback
constraints: The article warns that excessively offloading cognitive tasks to generative AI risks reducing active cognitive engagement needed for deep encoding, retention and transfer

independent problem-solving

article_title: Faster Completion, Less Learning: Generative AI Reduced Study Time on Math Problems and the Knowledge They Build
citation: Rismanchian, S., Uzun, H., Matayoshi, J., Cosyn, E., & Kurd-Misto, E. (2026). Faster Completion, Less Learning: Generative AI Reduced Study Time on Math Problems and the Knowledge They Build. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21629
title: Cognitive surrender versus cognitive offloading as the explanatory framework for AI-related learning loss
description: The article adopts Shaw & Nave's distinction between cognitive offloading and cognitive surrender. Offloading is "the strategic outsourcing of a narrow task (e.g., a calculator for arithmetic)" while the user retains the structure of reasoning; surrender is "the adoption of an AI-generated output as one's own answer with minimal scrutiny", relinquishing cognitive control of problem-solving. The authors use this framework to explain why earlier tools produced efficiency gains without retention decline, whereas generative AI produces the selective, supervision-sensitive, age-graded behavioral signature and retention loss they document.
requirements: Interpreting the behavioral pattern as surrender requires that the decline be selective to AI-transcribable formats, supervision-sensitive, and age-graded, as the article states
constraints: The article notes the boundary between AI-susceptible and AI-resistant problem formats is a moving target as multimodal and agentic AI capabilities advance
target_learners: Grade 5 through college mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Durable retention of mathematics knowledge
examples: The article contrasts a student using a calculator, who still constructs the solution strategy, with a student who copies a word problem into a chatbot and pastes the returned solution
key_sources: Rismanchian, S., Uzun, H., Matayoshi, J., Cosyn, E., & Kurd-Misto, E. (2026). Faster Completion, Less Learning: Generative AI Reduced Study Time on Math Problems and the Knowledge They Build. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21629

title: ALEKS and ALEKS PPL behavioral trace datasets for studying AI-era learning behavior
description: The study builds on two large log datasets from ALEKS, an adaptive mathematics learning and assessment platform built on knowledge space theory: "3.2 million ALEKS learning interactions for investigating time-on-task, complemented by 12.2 million ALEKS PPL placement-assessment response times for examining proctoring and learning outcomes". The learning panel spans Grade 5 through College Algebra over 2015 Q3–2025 Q3; the PPL panel covers more than 400 US institutions, with proctored and non-proctored sessions and randomly assigned extra retention items.

article_title: Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment
citation: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment.
title: ECD-based framework treating GenAI as a design variable with three sequential governance stances
description: The framework applies Evidence-Centered Design's three models—student, evidence, and task—as sequential decision criteria for GenAI governance in STEM assessment. It analyzes how GenAI reshapes each model and, as the abstract states, "specifies when to restrict, scaffold, or require GenAI use in STEM assessment." Decisions are organized across two branches (AI interaction competency is or is not the target construct) with a construct revision loop, and the authors note that "Governance decisions are not static" and require ongoing reassessment as capabilities evolve.
requirements: Assessment designers must explicitly specify the target construct, the evidence rules linking work products to it, and the task design before choosing a governance mode
constraints: Decisions may shift as GenAI capabilities and task designs evolve, requiring ongoing reassessment
target_learners: STEM students in higher education, particularly introductory physics
target_learning_goals: Disciplinary competence measured under GenAI integration, including disciplinary AI interaction competency
examples: Figure 1 depicts Branch A (AI interaction competency targeted, leading to Require) and Branch B (not targeted, leading to Scaffold or Restrict decisions) with a grey dashed construct-revision path
key_sources: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24837

citation: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment.
title: Choose Restrict, Scaffold, or Require GenAI governance from the construct targeted and whether redesign can restore the inferential chain
description: The article articulates three governance stances grounded in validity: "Restrict is warranted when GenAI would contaminate the inferential link between student work products and targeted unaided proficiency"; "Scaffold is warranted when bounded GenAI support can support peripheral demands without revealing the target construct"; and Require is warranted when the target construct is disciplinary AI interaction competency with tasks eliciting distinguishable process artifacts. The stances are sequential: Restrict applies only after scaffold options fail.
requirements: An explicit ECD analysis of the student, evidence, and task models for the specific assessment before selecting a stance
constraints: Restrict is a last resort, triggered only when neither leveraging GenAI's generative capacity nor guardrailing within a redesigned task can preserve construct validity
target_learners: STEM students in assessment contexts where GenAI is available
target_learning_goals: Preserving assessment validity for targeted disciplinary constructs while preparing students for AI-enabled workflows

citation: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment.
title: Remora Free Body Diagram Require-GenAI task
description: A task deployed in an undergraduate introductory physics course in which students collaborate with GenAI to construct the most accurate free body diagram of a remora fish attached to a shark. The problem meets the accuracy-ceiling criterion because an accurate diagram requires forces specific to remora biology that "GenAI consistently failed to produce correctly without disciplinary guidance from the student." It elicits five categories of process artifact (tool used, prompting summary, final output, critique, assumption reflection), with Q2 evidencing Physics-Driven AI Interaction and Q4 evidencing Physics-Grounded Evaluation.
requirements: Students must document their own reasoning about what GenAI got wrong and why, so cognitive contribution is distinguishable from AI output
constraints: The task does not require students to submit interaction logs directly; Q2 functions as a self-report of the prompting conversation
target_learners: Undergraduate introductory physics students
target_learning_goals: Physics-driven AI interaction and physics-grounded evaluation of AI-generated content
examples: Students who accept GenAI output uncritically are detectable because their FBDs reflect generic force configurations rather than the biologically specific forces the task demands

citation: Gao, Y., Chen, Z., Li, M., & Zhai, X. (2026). Generative AI as a Design Variable: An Evidence-Centered Framework for Principled Governance in STEM Assessment.
title: Water Balloon Physics Image Require-GenAI task
description: A second Require-GenAI task in which GenAI has a dual role: "it is simultaneously the source of the artifact being analyzed and the tool students use to correct it." Students receive a GenAI-generated image of a child swinging a water balloon in horizontal circles, identify physically impossible elements, use GenAI to generate a more accurate image, and ask GenAI to construct a correct free body diagram. A three-way error classification (what GenAI identified, what the student identified independently, what the student believes GenAI misidentified) makes independent judgment directly observable and separable from AI contribution.
requirements: The accuracy-ceiling criterion: GenAI consistently missed at least one expert-anchored error in the image and FBD, as confirmed by the expert answer key
constraints: A student who cannot independently identify errors beyond what GenAI flags produces an artifact that fails the distinguishability condition

target_learning_goals: Independent identification of Newtonian mechanics violations and physics-grounded critique of AI-generated diagrams
examples: The expert answer key identifies string angle, balloon deformation, and spurious centripetal force addition as key errors

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence and the marginalization of minoritized knowledges in higher education
citation: Fatiha TALI OTMANI. (2025). L'intelligence artificielle générative et la marginalisation des savoirs minoritaires dans l'enseignement supérieur. Le cas du handicap. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22marginalisation+des+savoirs+minoritaires+dans+l%27enseignement+sup%C3%A9rieur%22
title: Les quatre modes d'usage de l'IA dans la recherche (Oracle, Surrogate, Quant, Arbiter) et l'« illusion d'exploration scientifique »
description: La revue mobilise la taxonomie de Messeri et Crockett (2024) de quatre modes d'usage de l'IA dans la recherche, « porteurs chacun d'un risque pour la diversité épistémique ». Comme Oracle, l'IA synthétise la littérature mais ne traite que les corpus accessibles, marginalisant les travaux non anglophones ou non textuels ; comme Surrogate, elle produit des données de substitution reconduisant les biais des populations surreprésentées ; comme Quant, elle risque de contourner les cadres théoriques au profit du calcul ; comme Arbiter, elle s'invite dans le peer review. Ces modes convergent pour produire une « illusion d'exploration scientifique » : les chercheurs croient parcourir l'ensemble des questions possibles alors qu'ils n'examinent qu'un sous-ensemble compatible avec les capacités des outils.
requirements: Les quatre modes supposent que les chercheurs reconnaissent que chaque mode ne traite qu'un sous-ensemble des questions et corpus, afin d'éviter l'illusion d'exhaustivité que l'article nomme « illusion d'exploration scientifique ».
constraints: L'article précise que la performance des agents-Surrogate « suppose toutefois que les participants modélisés appartiennent aux populations les mieux documentées » (Park et al., 2024).
target_learners: enseignants-chercheurs et chercheurs en enseignement supérieur
target_learning_goals: maintien de la diversité épistémique dans les pratiques de recherche
usage critique des outils d'IA dans la production scientifique
examples: Park et coll. (2024) : des agents reproduisent à 85 % les réponses humaines à l'Enquête Sociale Générale, performance limitée aux populations les mieux documentées.

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence and the marginalization of minoritized knowledges in higher education
citation: Fatiha TALI OTMANI. (2025). L'intelligence artificielle générative et la marginalisation des savoirs minoritaires dans l'enseignement supérieur. Le cas du handicap. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22marginalisation+des+savoirs+minoritaires+dans+l%27enseignement+sup%C3%A9rieur%22
title: L'« usager universel » : figure normée de l'utilisateur qui exclut structurellement les étudiants en situation de handicap de la conception des outils d'IA
description: La revue mobilise le concept d'« usager universel » (Oudshoorn et al., 2004), via le cadre analytique de Collin et Marceau (2022), pour saisir l'exclusion des étudiants en situation de handicap. Ce concept « désigne la tendance des concepteurs à élaborer leurs outils pour un utilisateur implicitement normé, à savoir jeune, valide, occidental, maîtrisant une langue dominante, disposant d'un accès aisé aux infrastructures numériques ». Les étudiants en situation de handicap se trouvent exclus « non parce que les concepteurs les auraient oubliés délibérément, mais parce que leur situation les rend moins visibles dans les données et moins compatibles avec les catégories préexistantes ». Ce cadre articule les biais des systèmes d'IAG aux inégalités préexistantes.
requirements: Sortir de ce paradigme suppose, selon l'article, une recherche participative « impliquant les personnes concernées dans la conception et l'évaluation des outils d'IA éducative ».
constraints: L'article précise que la représentation des personnes en situation de handicap dans les équipes de conception « reste marginale, ce qui limite la capacité de ces équipes à anticiper les besoins et à éviter les biais d'exclusion ».
target_learners: étudiants en situation de handicap dans l'enseignement supérieur
target_learning_goals: conception d'outils d'IA éducative accessibles et adaptés à la diversité des situations de handicap
examples: Les architectures des outils d'IA sont conçues pour un utilisateur implicitement normé ; les outils conçus pour les utilisateurs « universels » se révèlent peu accessibles aux personnes présentant certains handicaps.

article_title: Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues
citation: Zhangqi Duan, Shuyan Huang, Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Simon Woodhead, Andrew Lan. (2026). Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30051
title: First-of-its-kind real-world dataset of student dialogues and question responses from a math learning platform
description: A dataset built from a real-world online math learning platform where students practice multiple-choice questions and can initiate on-demand chat conversations with human tutors grounded in the question. After processing it "contains 1,775 dialogues and 66,705 question-answering records from 670 students", spanning topics including Algebra, Geometry, and Number. Dialogues average 12.95 turns, 84.8% are tutor-initiated, and turn-level dialogue acts and correctness labels were annotated with GPT-4.1. The authors state they are in the process of publicly releasing it after PII removal.
requirements: Turn-level dialogue act and correctness annotations, produced via GPT-4.1 annotation following prior work
constraints: The data is fully anonymized, so demographic information about individual students and tutors is not available
target_learners: K-12 math students on an online learning platform
target_learning_goals: Mathematics question answering and tutoring dialogue behavior
examples: Questions span Algebra, Geometry, and Number; interactions include 31 tutors and five dialogue-act labels such as Math Answer and Not Understanding
key_sources: Zhangqi Duan, Shuyan Huang, Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Simon Woodhead, Andrew Lan. (2026). Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30051

article_title: Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues
citation: Zhangqi Duan, Shuyan Huang, Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Simon Woodhead, Andrew Lan. (2026). Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30051
title: History-conditioned student simulation: two-component profile-generator-plus-simulator framework
description: The article establishes the task of history-conditioned student simulation, where a model predicts a student's next tutoring-dialogue turn conditioned on their prior question-answering and dialogue history. "We propose a two-component framework in which a profile generator summarizes a student's history and a simulator predicts student turns conditioned on the resulting profile." Both components are trained with reinforcement learning so that profiles are optimized for faithful downstream simulation: the simulator is fine-tuned with SFT then DPO against counterfactual mismatched profiles, and the profile generator is distilled then refined with GRPO using ground-truth turn log-likelihood as reward.
requirements: Student learning histories containing both question-answering records and tutoring dialogues
A compact profile representation because directly conditioning on full histories is often infeasible
constraints: Histories are trimmed heuristically to the most recent 8 QA interactions and 3 dialogues due to context-length and memory limitations
target_learners: Math students practicing on online learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Faithful simulation of student knowledge state and dialogue behavior for tutor evaluation and training
examples: The framework was instantiated as ProfileRL with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct base models trained via LoRA and evaluated on the math platform dataset
key_sources: Zhangqi Duan, Shuyan Huang, Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Simon Woodhead, Andrew Lan. (2026). Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30051

article_title: Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues
citation: Zhangqi Duan, Shuyan Huang, Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Simon Woodhead, Andrew Lan. (2026). Who Am I? History-Aware Profiles for Student Simulation in Tutoring Dialogues. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30051
title: Five-component structured student profile capturing knowledge and dialogue behavior
description: Each generated profile has a fixed structure with five sections: Knowledge State (estimated KC mastery as correct over total attempts), Knowledge Acquisition (how mastery changes over time), Misconception (recurring mathematical errors), Dialogue Behavior (tendencies and common dialogue acts), and Linguistic Style (verbosity, terminology use, fragment versus full explanations). "Each generated profile has a fixed structure with five components, which align with important aspects of student knowledge and behavior identified in (Scarlatos et al., 2026)." Profiles are initialized by prompting a proprietary reasoning LLM, then distilled into a trainable open-source generator.
requirements: A recent window of question-answering and dialogue interactions as input for profile generation
constraints: The profile is a compact summary of a truncated history window, not the student's entire learning history
target_learners: Students with longitudinal histories on a math learning platform
target_learning_goals: Representing student knowledge state, misconceptions, and dialogue behavior for turn-level simulation
examples: In the qualitative case study, the GRPO-refined profile records a concrete misconception on Squares, Cubes, etc. that the GPT profile omitted, plus observable linguistic markers such as "i dont understand"

article_title: Beyond Access: Guided LLM Scaffolding for Independent Learning in Undergraduate Statistics
citation: Mohammad Amanlou, Yasaman Amou-Jafari, Fereshte Bagheri, Fatemeh Boloukazari, Mehrad Liviyan, Elahe Khodaverdi Nadrabadi, Shahab Sherafat, Behnam Bahrak. (2026). Beyond Access: Guided LLM Scaffolding for Independent Learning in Undergraduate Statistics. Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Computers in Education. https://github.com/MohammadAmanlou/Guided-LLM-Scaffolding
title: Six-family guided LLM-use protocol operationalizing scaffolding, help-seeking, self-regulation, and AI-literacy principles
description: The guided-use protocol is a student-facing training and rule set delivered before Topic 2 with weekly reminders, framing the model as "a fallible tutor rather than an answer source" and emphasizing "explanation-seeking, stepwise help , verification, and ethical use." It defines six observable rule families: R1 process-over-answer, R2 concept tutoring, R3 stepwise-hint seeking, R4 active practice and retrieval, R5 verification and calibrated trust, and R6 ethical/no-help use. The authors describe it as translating established learning-science principles into transcript-codeable LLM-use behaviors rather than a generic prompting template.
requirements: Explicit slide-based orientation with examples of productive and unproductive prompts before LLM use begins, plus weekly reminders
constraints: The same LLM platform and model were used in both LLM-access conditions; guidance differed through training and rules rather than a separate model or hard-coded guided mode
target_learners: second-semester Electrical Engineering and Computer Engineering undergraduates
target_learning_goals: probabilistic reasoning including conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, random variables, and distributions
examples: Three raters independently coded 67 student-practice transcripts against the six rule families, reaching Fleiss' κ = .896 before consensus

article_title: Generativism: Toward a Learning Theory for the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Shan Li, Juan Zheng. (2026). Generativism: Toward a Learning Theory for the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://orcid/org/0000-0001-6001-1586
title: Generativism: a learning theory framing learning as iterative co-construction of knowledge between human learners and generative AI systems
description: Generativism is a proposed learning theory for the generative AI age, organized around four constructs — epistemic partnership, distributed agency, generative literacy, and adaptive metacognition — and four principles specifying their relations. The article defines learning as "the deliberate co-construction of knowledge through iterative human-AI interaction", positioning learning as neither purely human nor AI-driven but emergent at the intersection. It reframes AI from "tool" to "cognitive partner" and offers a foundation for rethinking instructional design, learning, assessment, and expertise development.
requirements: Learners must retain responsibility for interpretation and judgment when working with AI, and the four constructs are interdependent: partnership requires agency decisions, agency requires literacy, and literacy requires metacognitive regulation.
constraints: The framework is a theoretical proposal; the article reports that no new data were generated or analyzed in this study.
target_learners: learners in educational settings where generative AI plays an integral role in cognition
target_learning_goals: durable understanding and expertise development through human-AI knowledge co-construction
key_sources: Shan Li, Juan Zheng. (2026). Generativism: Toward a Learning Theory for the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://orcid/org/0000-0001-6001-1586

article_title: Generativism: Toward a Learning Theory for the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Shan Li, Juan Zheng. (2026). Generativism: Toward a Learning Theory for the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://orcid/org/0000-0001-6001-1586
title: Generative literacy: a critical literacy comprising prompt competence, evaluative judgment, epistemic vigilance, and integrative synthesis
description: Generativism defines generative literacy as "a form of critical literacy oriented toward prompting, evaluating, refining, and integrating AI-generated knowledge artifacts". It synthesizes four higher-level capacities: prompt competence (formulating and revising queries), evaluative judgment (assessing accuracy, coherence, relevance, and contextual appropriateness), epistemic vigilance (maintaining critical scrutiny even when output appears fluent or plausible), and integrative synthesis (combining AI content with prior knowledge to produce meaning exceeding the AI output). The article treats it as a condition for meaningful learning, not merely a technical skill.
requirements: Learners need these capacities to transform AI output into understanding rather than consuming it as a replacement for their own thinking; the article states learners cannot make sound delegation decisions without them.
constraints: The article notes existing AI literacy frameworks do not adequately address the unique challenges posed by generative systems, positioning this construct as an extension of prior frameworks such as ED-AI Lit and Long and Magerko's competencies.
target_learners: learners working with generative AI systems in educational settings
target_learning_goals: evaluating, refining, and integrating AI-generated outputs in support of genuine understanding
key_sources: Shan Li, Juan Zheng. (2026). Generativism: Toward a Learning Theory for the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://orcid/org/0000-0001-6001-1586

article_title: Contaminated Collaboration: Measuring Gender Bias Transfer in LLM-Assisted Student Writing
citation: Ariyan Hossain, Kazi Kamruzzaman Rabbi, Farig Sadeque, S M Taiabul Haque. (2026). Contaminated Collaboration: Measuring Gender Bias Transfer in LLM-Assisted Student Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15914
title: Stereotype Congruence Rate (SCR): a free-text occupational stereotyping metric grounded in BLS labor-market gender distributions
description: SCR is a complementary bias metric the article introduces because existing benchmarks "probe model-internal associations via templated inputs and cover only broad occupational categories", which does not suit free-text career recommendations. It is defined as "the proportion of essays in which the recommended occupation matches the biography subject's gender stereotype", with occupations labeled via BLS CPSAAT11 workforce gender shares (over 60% one gender = stereotyped; otherwise neutral). Neutral occupations count in the denominator but not as matches, making the metric conservative.
requirements: Requires extracted occupation strings matchable to BLS CPSAAT11 categories (fuzzy matching threshold ≥85 with manual resolution) and population-level occupational gender distribution data
constraints: The article notes US occupational norms were used because locally grounded labor-market gender data were not publicly accessible in the study's deployment country
target_learners: undergraduate students writing career-plan essays
target_learning_goals: career planning and occupational attribution in AI-assisted writing
examples: Applied to the 123-participant experiment's essays, SCR was 0.714 in the biased condition, 0.450 in control, and 0.390 in neutral; sensitivity analyses at 55% and 65% thresholds preserved the ordering
key_sources: Ariyan Hossain, Kazi Kamruzzaman Rabbi, Farig Sadeque, S M Taiabul Haque. (2026). Contaminated Collaboration: Measuring Gender Bias Transfer in LLM-Assisted Student Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15914

article_title: Contaminated Collaboration: Measuring Gender Bias Transfer in LLM-Assisted Student Writing
citation: Ariyan Hossain, Kazi Kamruzzaman Rabbi, Farig Sadeque, S M Taiabul Haque. (2026). Contaminated Collaboration: Measuring Gender Bias Transfer in LLM-Assisted Student Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15914
title: Design educational AI writing tools to be fairness-aware, since biased assistants propagate gender stereotypes into student-authored text without users noticing
description: The article calls for "fairness-aware design in educational AI tools" after showing that a verifiably gender-biased LLM assistant transferred its bias into students' career-plan essays, suppressing female-target agency and raising gender-stereotypic occupational recommendations. Because biased-condition participants reported no awareness of influence, fairness cannot rely on user vigilance; the assistant's configuration itself must be checked. The article also shows a carefully configured neutral assistant may attenuate baseline stereotyping.
requirements: Verification that the assistant's prompts and outputs exhibit no measurable gender bias before deployment, as the article's validation phase did before the human study
constraints: Debiasing efforts targeting male over-representation would not fix this effect, which the authors say sits on the female side; transfer was demonstrated on a single open-source model (llama-3.3-70b-instruct), so generalization across model families remains untested
target_learners: undergraduate students using LLM writing assistance
target_learning_goals: career planning and written self-presentation free of gender-stereotypic framing
examples: The study's neutral LLM condition, configured to suggest careers based only on demonstrated experiences and skills, produced the lowest stereotype congruence rate of the three conditions
key_sources: Ariyan Hossain, Kazi Kamruzzaman Rabbi, Farig Sadeque, S M Taiabul Haque. (2026). Contaminated Collaboration: Measuring Gender Bias Transfer in LLM-Assisted Student Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15914

article_title: Generative AI Literacy Training Improves Intelligence Analysts’ Discrimination of Real and AI-Generated Images
citation: Negar Kamali, Candice Rockell Gerstner, Jessica Hullman, Matthew Groh. (2026). Generative AI Literacy Training Improves Intelligence Analysts' Discrimination of Real and AI-Generated Images. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28510
title: Five-category artifact taxonomy for evaluating AI-generated images
description: The article organizes visual inspection of AI-generated images around a taxonomy of five artifact categories drawn from a written guide on distinguishing AI-generated images from authentic photographs. The training "was structured around five categories of artifacts": anatomical implausibilities (hands, eyes, teeth, body structure, identity inconsistencies), stylistic artifacts (cinematization, plastic textures, hyper-real detail), functional implausibilities (dysfunctional objects, malformed text and logos), violations of physical constraints (inconsistent lighting, shadows, reflections, perspective), and sociocultural implausibilities (historically or culturally incongruent scenarios). Each category was taught with concise explanations paired with multiple visual examples, and the same taxonomy coded analysts' free-text reasoning in the qualitative analysis.
requirements: Explanations paired with multiple visual examples per category, with visual callouts highlighting regions of interest
Examples drawn from contemporary diffusion models so the taught cues match the artifacts current generators produce
constraints: The article cautions analysts against over-reliance on any single cue, since artifact visibility varies with scene complexity, pose, image resolution, and viewing time
Real photographs can contain non-generative artifacts such as compression and focus inconsistencies, so the presence of an artifact does not by itself imply an image is AI-generated
target_learners: intelligence analysts
professionals whose verification decisions carry operational weight, such as journalists and content moderators
target_learning_goals: distinguishing real photographs from AI-generated images
articulating detection reasoning using specific artifact categories
examples: The 30-minute training consisted of 32 slides with 50 AI-generated images and 7 real images, presenting concise explanations with visual examples for each artifact category
key_sources: Negar Kamali, Candice Rockell Gerstner, Jessica Hullman, Matthew Groh. (2026). Generative AI Literacy Training Improves Intelligence Analysts' Discrimination of Real and AI-Generated Images. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28510

article_title: Generative AI Literacy Training Improves Intelligence Analysts’ Discrimination of Real and AI-Generated Images
citation: Negar Kamali, Candice Rockell Gerstner, Jessica Hullman, Matthew Groh. (2026). Generative AI Literacy Training Improves Intelligence Analysts' Discrimination of Real and AI-Generated Images. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28510
title: Analyst image-detection open code, data, and stimulus release
description: The article releases the study's code, de-identified data, and stimulus images through a public GitHub repository (https://github.com/negarkamali/analyst-image-detection). The release includes "all stimulus images (50 AI-generated images and 47 real photographs)" from the deployed 97-image evaluation set, which was balanced across authenticity, scene complexity, and matched real–fake image-to-text description pairs. The stimulus set was drawn from a larger pool of 149 verified real photographs and 450 photorealistic AI-generated images used in previous deepfake-detection research, making it reusable for training and evaluation studies on human discrimination of diffusion-model imagery.
requirements: Stimulus images balanced with respect to authenticity, scene complexity, and image-to-text descriptions to support controlled experiments
constraints: The study examines photorealistic still images from diffusion models only; it does not examine AI-generated video or audio
target_learners: intelligence analysts
researchers studying human detection of AI-generated media
target_learning_goals: evaluating human ability to distinguish real from AI-generated images
designing and replicating training interventions on artifact-based visual discrimination
examples: The counterbalanced experiment collected 2,544 image-level judgments from 32 intelligence analysts using this stimulus set

article_title: Evaluating Interactivity: Toward Automated Assessment of AI-Generated Explorable Explanations
citation: Xiaozao Wang, Zhewei Wang, Hongyi Wen. (2026). Evaluating Interactivity: Toward Automated Assessment of AI-Generated Explorable Explanations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31012
title: FSM-based representation of interactivity as learner-controllable states and transitions (EE-Eval)
description: The article conceptualizes interactivity as "a finite space of learner-controllable states and transitions", represented as a directed graph G = (V, E, M) where V denotes semantic interaction states, E transitions, and M task-level metadata such as pedagogical intent. Interaction logic is operationalized with a JSON-based schema capturing states, events, transitions, and components, extracted from generated HTML via a few-shot LLM strategy and validated against schema constraints. Evaluation compares extracted FSMs to semi-automatically constructed ideal FSMs using structural (node/edge counts, degree distributions, density), semantic (embedding-based comparison of state labels, actions, events, metadata), and behavioral-coherence (isomorphism score) metrics, weighted 0.4/0.4/0.2 after a constrained grid search.
requirements: Requires extracted FSMs to satisfy schema constraints including state uniqueness, transition consistency, and referential integrity
Requires a pre-defined reference (ideal) FSM encoding pedagogical intent for comparison
constraints: The article states FSMs may not fully capture highly continuous or emergent interaction patterns, potentially simplifying rich user experiences into discrete transitions
Evaluation quality depends on the accuracy of FSM extraction, which may introduce noise or bias
Ideal FSM construction involves domain assumptions that may not generalize across all topics or pedagogical contexts
target_learners: Learners using AI-generated interactive learning materials in computer science education
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of computer science concepts through interactive exploration
examples: The pipeline generated 2497 explorable explanations across 127 concepts with six AI models, extracted FSMs, and computed similarity against ideal FSMs; weights (0.4, 0.4, 0.2) yielded the strongest alignment with human ratings on a validation subset.
key_sources: Xiaozao Wang, Zhewei Wang, Hongyi Wen. (2026). Evaluating Interactivity: Toward Automated Assessment of AI-Generated Explorable Explanations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31012

article_title: The GenAI Skill Bypass: Mapping Divergent Pathways of University Students and Staff AI Literacy
citation: Oliveira, E., English, N., Ryan, T., Misiejuk, K., dal Ponte, C., López-Pernas, S., & Saqr, M. (2026). The GenAI Skill Bypass: Mapping Divergent Pathways of University Students and Staff AI Literacy. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05411
title: Replace one-size-fits-all GenAI curricula with modular, diagnostic-driven interventions differentiated by role
description: The article argues that because students, academics, and professional staff show distinct orders of emergence, institutions should deploy "modular, diagnostic-driven interventions that respect the pragmatic context of each group" rather than uniform curricula. The self-assessment instrument acts as a diagnostic dashboard letting learners visualise their profile and test out of basics they already grasp, aligning with self-determined learning.
requirements: A diagnostic self-assessment instrument capable of mapping each learner's capability profile across skill thresholds
constraints: The study's data come from a single institution, and the authors state future multi-institutional studies are required to confirm whether the trajectories replicate
target_learners: university students
academic staff
professional staff
target_learning_goals: GenAI literacy
self-diagnosis of capability gaps
examples: The host institution operationalised the 28-item framework into modular GenAI training units for academic and professional staff, recording over 5,000 enrolments and over 3,100 module completions within the first nine months of release

article_title: The GenAI Skill Bypass: Mapping Divergent Pathways of University Students and Staff AI Literacy
citation: Oliveira, E., English, N., Ryan, T., Misiejuk, K., dal Ponte, C., López-Pernas, S., & Saqr, M. (2026). The GenAI Skill Bypass: Mapping Divergent Pathways of University Students and Staff AI Literacy. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05411
title: 28-item GenAI Literacy and Fluency self-assessment instrument with hierarchical polytomous items
description: A taxonomy-based self-assessment instrument built on the GenAI Literacy and Fluency framework (Dal Ponte et al., 2025), comprising 7 primary items each with response options coded 0–4 along a hierarchical scale "from emerging to sophisticated guided by Bloom's revised taxonomy", yielding 28 binary criteria thresholds per respondent. It replaces Likert scales with observable, self-assessable behaviours and was used here as a diagnostic probe mapped with Rasch and Guttman analyses.
requirements: Respondents select their own level of competence within the hierarchy of response options; Guttman analysis requires complete response vectors
constraints: It measures self-perceived ability, and the authors caution that perception does not always equate to performance

academic staff
professional staff

examples: Administered online to N=158 respondents at The University of Melbourne between February and August 2025, with responses analysed via the Partial Credit Model in R using the TAM package

article_title: A Comparative Analysis of Institutional and Course Generative AI Policies within Higher Education: Implications for Instruction in Computing Education
citation: Amrita Ganguly, Aditya Johri, Nora McDonald, Areej Ali, Umama Dewan, and Aayushi Hingle Collier. (2026). A Comparative Analysis of Institutional and Course Generative AI Policies within Higher Education: Implications for Instruction in Computing Education.
title: Instructor-centered framework for translating institutional GenAI guidance into course implementation via three mediating factors
description: The authors propose a framework that guides the translation of institutional guidance to course implementation by placing the instructor at the center of the process and considering mediating factors (Figure 3). The first factor is the instructor's current expertise in GenAI use and broader AI literacy, along with the training needed to implement GenAI in instruction; in CS this includes understanding model limitations in code generation and recognizing security vulnerabilities in AI-generated code. The second factor is discipline or domain, since implications of GenAI use differ sharply between theory-heavy courses such as algorithms and applied ones such as software engineering. The third factor is the nature of instruction and required pedagogical knowledge, as GenAI use varies across lecture-based, lab-based and project-based courses.
requirements: Instructor AI literacy and training to implement GenAI in instruction
Accounting for whether the course is theory-heavy or applied
Pedagogical knowledge matched to lecture-based, lab-based, or project-based instruction
constraints: The framework is proposed, not empirically tested in this study; the authors state the transition to productive GenAI use will be an arduous task and substantial revisions to existing CS pedagogical practices will be needed
target_learners: Higher education students in computing courses
target_learning_goals: Responsible and productive GenAI use aligned with course learning outcomes
Preservation of problem-solving skills while supporting technical skill development
examples: The study found increased institutional focus on CS has not translated into clearer direction for CS instructors, leaving them to navigate these decisions largely on their own
key_sources: Amrita Ganguly, Aditya Johri, Nora McDonald, Areej Ali, Umama Dewan, and Aayushi Hingle Collier. (2026). article_title: A Comparative Analysis of Institutional and Course Generative AI Policies within Higher Education: Implications for Instruction in Computing Education
citation: Amrita Ganguly, Aditya Johri, Nora McDonald, Areej Ali, Umama Dewan, and Aayushi Hingle Collier. (2026). A Comparative Analysis of Institutional and Course Generative AI Policies within Higher Education: Implications for Instruction in Computing Education.
title: Linked dataset of institutional GenAI policies and CS course syllabi from U.S. R1 universities
description: A linked two-level dataset built from the Carnegie Classification list of 131 R1 institutions. Researchers searched university websites for GenAI policies from October 9 to November 26, 2023; fourteen institutions had no policy or mention of GenAI, leaving 116 institutions in the analysis with 141 documents collected. Course syllabi were collected from March 4 to May 11, 2024 via Google searches for computer science course syllabi, resulting in 98 syllabi from 54 R1 universities, each treated and coded as a separate unit. The overlap analysis found 47 institutions have both institutional and course-level guidelines.
requirements: Publicly available documents only, collected under Institutional Review Board approval
constraints: Restricted to U.S. R1 institutions and CS syllabi, limiting generalizability to other institution types and disciplines; does not capture how policies are implemented, interpreted, or enforced in practice
target_learners: Higher education instructors and administrators in computing education
target_learning_goals: Understanding alignment between institutional and course-level GenAI guidance
examples: Figure 1 shows among 131 R1 institutes how many have institutional guidelines (116), course level guidelines (54) and both (47)

article_title: Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS)
citation: Hossain, S., & Nawmi, T. A. (2026). Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14301
title: A theory-derived four-type typology of GenAI reliance organized by cognitive governance retained and scope of delegation
description: The typology conceptualizes reliance on generative AI not as a quantity to be calibrated but as "a repertoire of qualitatively distinct behavioral patterns whose consequences for learning differ." It derives from metacognition, critical AI literacy, and approaches-to-learning theory, organized along two dimensions: "the degree of cognitive governance the writer retains" and "the scope of delegation." Strategic reliance denotes metacognitively governed, critically evaluated engagement; Instrumental reliance denotes efficiency-targeted surface-level delegation; Dependent reliance denotes wholesale outsourcing with uncritical acceptance; and Dialogic reliance denotes iterative co-construction with the tool as interlocutor.
requirements: The typology was specified deductively from named theoretical frameworks before item writing, with each facet grounded in a source framework such as metacognitive regulation, critical AI literacy competencies, surface approaches to learning, cognitive offloading, or sociocultural co-construction.
constraints: The typology was developed for extended academic writing contexts, and the article notes each instrument's coverage reflects its task ecology, with Instrumental reliance having no counterpart in problem-solving-domain structures.
target_learners: undergraduate students using generative AI in academic writing
target_learning_goals: identifying qualitatively distinct patterns of reliance on generative AI during academic writing
supporting AI literacy intervention and responsible GenAI use
examples: The GenAI-RTS operationalizes the typology with 20 items: four Deliberate Use items, four Critical Evaluation items, and four items each for Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic reliance, rated on 7-point Likert scales.
key_sources: Hossain, S., & Nawmi, T. A. (2026). Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14301

article_title: Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS)
citation: Hossain, S., & Nawmi, T. A. (2026). Measuring How Students Rely on Generative AI in Academic Writing: Development and Multi-Source Validation of the Generative AI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14301
title: GenAI Reliance Types Scale (GenAI-RTS), a 20-item instrument measuring four reliance types across five facets
description: The GenAI-RTS is a 20-item self-report instrument measuring reliance on generative AI in academic writing, with all items rated on 7-point Likert scales (1 = Strongly Disagree, 7 = Strongly Agree). It operationalizes four theoretically derived types across five measurement facets: "four Deliberate Use items informed by metacognitive awareness theory" and four Critical Evaluation items adapted from critical AI literacy competencies, plus four items each for Instrumental, Dependent, and Dialogic reliance. Subscale scores are item means (range 1–7), and the Strategic composite weights its two facets equally.
requirements: Administration as a self-report survey; the article recommends revising the response format from seven to five points based on Rasch category-functioning results.
constraints: Scores describe reliance profiles rather than assign students to types; no diagnostic cut scores are proposed, and the highest-subscale classification serves research description only.
target_learners: undergraduate students at higher education institutions
target_learning_goals: measuring how students rely on generative AI during academic writing
identifying reliance profiles for research, assessment, and AI literacy intervention
examples: Sample items include "I set clear objectives for using generative AI tools before each writing session" (Deliberate Use) and "I verify facts in text produced by generative AI tools against authoritative sources" (Critical Evaluation).

article_title: Auditing Institutional Heterogeneity for Generative AI in Patient Education: A Large-Scale Study of 102 US Transplant Handbooks
citation: Yubo Li, Rema Padman, Ramayya Krishnan. (2026). Auditing Institutional Heterogeneity for Generative AI in Patient Education: A Large-Scale Study of 102 US Transplant Handbooks. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22606
title: TransplantQA corpus: 102 US transplant handbooks from 23 centers paired with 1,115 patient-derived questions
description: TransplantQA is a benchmark pairing institutional patient-education handbooks with patient-derived questions for auditing retrieval-augmented patient-facing AI. The article states "The TransplantQA corpus contains 102 patient-education handbooks from 23 U.S. solid-organ transplant centers, covering 16 of the 20 largest U.S. programs by procedure volume." Questions were curated from public institutional Q&A pages, community forums, and patient-facing medical organizations, filtered from over 3,000 candidates, and labelled with organ and a 13-topic taxonomy.
requirements: Questions carry organ labels and topic categories from a 13-topic taxonomy; handbooks are grouped by organ and care phase for analyses
constraints: It is a curated public-source benchmark, not a prospective patient survey or a clinician-validated inventory of information needs; topic frequencies reflect source selection rather than population demand
target_learners: transplant patients and families seeking institution-specific education
target_learning_goals: answering patient questions about transplant care from institution-authored education materials
examples: The production run paired the corpus into 48,056 generated answers and 1,772,261 unique within-question handbook pairs
key_sources: Yubo Li, Rema Padman, Ramayya Krishnan. (2026). Auditing Institutional Heterogeneity for Generative AI in Patient Education: A Large-Scale Study of 102 US Transplant Handbooks. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22606

article_title: Auditing Institutional Heterogeneity for Generative AI in Patient Education: A Large-Scale Study of 102 US Transplant Handbooks
citation: Yubo Li, Rema Padman, Ramayya Krishnan. (2026). Auditing Institutional Heterogeneity for Generative AI in Patient Education: A Large-Scale Study of 102 US Transplant Handbooks. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22606
title: HERO-QA pipeline: hierarchical retrieval, answer generation with abstention, and a structured-output LLM judge
description: HERO-QA is the audit pipeline the article uses to generate and compare answers grounded in different institutional handbooks. The article states it "uses hierarchical BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) and dense retrieval (Xiao et al., 2024) with reranking, or the full extracted text for short handbooks (≤80,000 characters)." Qwen3-32B generates answers at temperature 0.1 and can return NOT ADDRESSED when evidence is insufficient; a Qwen3-32B judge with structured JSON output assigns a relationship label (ABSENT, CONSISTENT, COMPLEMENTARY, DIVERGENT, CONTRADICTORY), a divergence topic, and a low/medium/high significance rating.
requirements: Retrieval quality and sufficient handbook text; the judge supplies labels, divergence topics, and significance ratings for disagreements
constraints: The article states these ratings describe potential consequences inferred by the model, not observed patient harm, and do not establish clinical correctness; generation and judging use the same model family
target_learners: health-IT teams auditing patient-facing generative AI systems
target_learning_goals: measuring coverage and disagreement across institutional patient-education corpora before AI deployment
examples: The reference run produced 48,056 generated answers and 1,772,261 unique within-question handbook pairs, with 156,876 pairs receiving non-absent labels
