article_title: Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought
citation: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751v1
title: Maieutic Partner / Generative Refusal framework for Tools for Thought
description: The paper proposes shifting GenAI from a "Co-author" role to a "Maieutic Partner" that facilitates inquiry by strategically withholding text generation. Generative Refusal treats refusal "not as a lack of functionality, but as a core mechanic for Tools for Thought": the AI creates "a structured gap that demands user input, rather than filling that gap with synthetic text", shifting interaction from delegation to activation. The framework draws on desirable difficulties and scaffolding within the Zone of Proximal Development, and is operationalized in Actor's Note, which refuses to generate text and instead asks context-aware questions.
requirements: The domain must be one where the mental effort of articulation and interpretation is central to learning, such as artistic training
constraints: The paper argues the efficiency-first paradigm is detrimental specifically in educational and training contexts, not universally
target_learners: professional and student actors in artistic training
target_learning_goals: internalizing character roles through first-person reflective journaling
critical articulation rather than cognitive offloading
examples: Actor's Note analyzes the uploaded script, role, and performance date to generate three context-specific questions daily, framed in the second person to elicit first-person reflection
key_sources: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751

article_title: Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought
citation: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751v1
title: Adapt AI scaffolding friction to the learner's workflow phase: low-friction prompts early, high-friction challenges later
description: The paper's second design implication holds that learners' cognitive needs shift as work progresses: early on users struggle with inertia and the "blank page" and need low-friction prompts to initiate writing, while later they struggle with fixation on established interpretations and need "high-friction, challenging questions to deepen their understanding". A static tool cannot address both needs, so future TfT systems should adjust scaffolding dynamically based on the user's workflow phase, acting as a pacemaker early and a challenger or devil's advocate later.
requirements: The system must detect the user's workflow phase, via system-driven inference from script metadata or performance date, user-driven self-report, or leader-driven synchronization
constraints: Detecting the workflow phase is described by the authors as a key open design challenge
target_learners: professional and student actors
users of creative Tools for Thought
target_learning_goals: initiating reflective writing
deepening interpretation beyond established interpretations
examples: Actor's Note used the actor's current rehearsal stage as a prompt parameter, focusing on backstory during table work versus emotional continuity during run-throughs

article_title: Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought
citation: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751v1
title: Frame AI reflection tools as non-judgmental spaces to mitigate social evaluation threat, positioned as preparatory sandboxes rather than replacements for human feedback
description: Because deep reflection requires vulnerability and human feedback loops introduce social evaluation threat, the paper recommends explicitly framing AI-based reflection tools as "non-judgmental spaces" where the cost of error is zero. Participants shared raw, unpolished thoughts with the AI that they would hide from human directors or peers, so AI's lack of social agency becomes a functional asset for honest introspection. The paper also warns that the absence of social stakes may reduce extrinsic motivation and performative energy, so such tools should be positioned as preparatory sandboxes, not replacements for the rehearsal floor.
requirements: The tool must be explicitly framed as a non-judgmental space where the cost of error is zero
constraints: The very absence of social stakes that makes AI a safe space might reduce the extrinsic motivation, adrenaline, and performative energy derived from a human audience or director
target_learners: professional and student actors
learners in high-stakes training environments
target_learning_goals: honest introspection and experimentation without self-censorship
deep reflective practice requiring vulnerability
examples: Participants explicitly noted that they shared raw, unpolished thoughts with the AI that they would hide from human directors or peers to maintain their professional image
key_sources: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751

article_title: Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought
citation: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751v1
title: Adopt internalization—performance without the tool—as the primary success metric for Tools for Thought
description: The paper argues that the industry standard of measuring performance with the tool fails to distinguish genuine cognitive augmentation from dependency. Instead, it proposes that the HCI community adopt "Internalization" as a primary success metric: measuring residual, post-tool performance. The study operationalized this by measuring "performance without the tool" and found users applied the internalized questioning patterns independently after the intervention. If a user cannot perform the task better after the tool is removed, the system has served as a prosthetic for production, not a scaffold for thought.
requirements: Evaluation must include an unassisted, post-tool measurement phase to capture residual effects
constraints: The paper notes the field lacks standardized longitudinal metrics or unassisted evaluation protocols for measuring cognitive internalization, posing this as an open workshop question
target_learners: users of generative AI learning tools
professional and student actors
target_learning_goals: distinguishing cognitive augmentation from dependency
lasting independent questioning habits
examples: The 14-day study measured residual effects after AI assistance was removed, finding participants self-generated similar questions (M = 4.87 on a 7-point scale)
key_sources: Sora Kang. (2026). Stop Writing for Me: Generative Refusal in AI Tools for Thought. In Proceedings of CHI 2026 Workshop on Tools for Thought. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24751

article_title: Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes
citation: Ugwuanyi, K., Mair, C., Dovchin, S., Erdocia, I., Kuteeva, M., & Airemionkhale, E. (2025). Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes. https://scholar.google.com
title: Algorithmic colonialingualism: GenAI's standard-English-based algorithmic systems exclude the linguistic repertoires of marginalised speakers
description: Algorithmic colonialingualism is a concept proposed by contributor Sender Dovchin to name how GenAI can re-colonise language: "the algorithmic system of GenAI is based on standard English varieties, while most varieties of world Englishes are not often reflected". The article gives Aboriginal English spoken by First Nations people in Australia as an unreflected example, and notes AI systems are not designed to handle translanguaging, the fluid movement between linguistic and semiotic repertoires. The concept frames GenAI as a double-edged sword that risks excluding marginalised speakers from AI design and functionality.
requirements: Analysis of GenAI's linguistic inclusivity must attend to which varieties are represented in training data and system design
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual framing from one contributor's afterword, not an empirically tested model
target_learners: Academic writers and publishers, especially scholars from Indigenous, migrant, and Global South backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Critical awareness of linguistic bias in GenAI-mediated academic writing
examples: Dovchin's analysis of translanguaging data showing AI systems cannot accommodate flexible hybrid practices
key_sources: Ugwuanyi, K., Mair, C., Dovchin, S., Erdocia, I., Kuteeva, M., & Airemionkhale, E. (2025). Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28505

article_title: Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes
citation: Ugwuanyi, K., Mair, C., Dovchin, S., Erdocia, I., Kuteeva, M., & Airemionkhale, E. (2025). Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes. https://scholar.google.com
title: The standardisation paradox: GenAI makes English simultaneously more homogeneous and more heterogeneous
description: The standardisation paradox is contributor Christian Mair's account of GenAI's dual effect on English: "LLMs confront us with a standardisation paradox, with English becoming more homogeneous and more heterogeneous at the same time". On the homogeneous side, only one dominant written standard (US English) prevails in LLM output, marginalising even British English. On the heterogeneous side, prompting for a Nigerian or Jamaican English version of an American English text yields output full of Nigerian Pidgin or Jamaican Creole, opening space for hybridised forms rather than handbook-described national standards.
requirements: Interpretation of LLM output requires distinguishing national standard varieties from creole and pidgin varieties
constraints: The article leaves open whether the notion of national standard varieties needs revision or whether LLM training data are biassed against them
target_learners: Scholars of World Englishes, linguistics students, academic writers
target_learning_goals: Understanding how GenAI reshapes norms of written English in scholarly communication
examples: Prompting for Nigerian or Jamaican English versions of an American English text producing Pidgin/Creole-heavy output instead of the national standards described in handbooks

article_title: Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes
citation: Ugwuanyi, K., Mair, C., Dovchin, S., Erdocia, I., Kuteeva, M., & Airemionkhale, E. (2025). Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes. https://scholar.google.com
title: Ethical and inclusive GenAI use in academic writing should be guided by reflexivity, accountability, and language awareness
description: The article proposes that ethical GenAI use in academic writing rests on human agency rather than the tool: contributor Esther states that "these three core principles must guide our use of GenAI as writers or reviewers: reﬂexivity, accountability, and language awareness". Writers and reviewers must recognise GenAI's biases and limitations, continually and reflexively examine how they train, prompt or engage with GenAI, and remain committed to inclusive practices in the face of normative language ideologies. Maria adds that legitimacy of diverse Englishes is a human endeavour, secured through correct and nuanced prompts in iterative human-GenAI interaction so scholars' voices are not erased during language correction.
requirements: Users must recognise the biases and limitations of GenAI and reflexively examine their prompting and engagement practices
constraints: The article warns against overrelying on LLMs to write in standard varieties at the expense of epistemic diversity
target_learners: Academic writers, peer reviewers, doctoral researchers
target_learning_goals: Maintaining authorial voice and linguistic identity while using GenAI ethically
examples: A contributor avoids AI-flagged words like 'delve' and 'underscore' to keep a human style, and uses iterative prompting to resist erasure of voice

article_title: Comparative Validation of GPT-4o-mini and Teacher Mean Scores for Automated Scoring of Music Analysis Responses: Single-Pass Deployment, Repeatability, and Strategy-Specific Bias
citation: Baicheng Lin, Lingxi Jin, and Kyung-Seok Min. (2026). Comparative Validation of GPT-4o-mini and Teacher Mean Scores for Automated Scoring of Music Analysis Responses: Single-Pass Deployment, Repeatability, and Strategy-Specific Bias. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01783
title: Use LLM scoring of open-ended music analyses as a supplementary human-in-the-loop tool with strategy-specific calibration and dimension-level validation
description: The article recommends deploying LLM scoring as a supplement, not a replacement, for teacher judgment in music-analysis assessment. It proposes that "The LLM could provide preliminary scores or criterion-referenced feedback and flag responses that require further review," with teachers examining unusual score patterns, uncertain terminology, and large dimension discrepancies. Because prompting strategies produce distinct bias profiles and dimension-specific weaknesses, operational use requires calibration per strategy and validation per rubric dimension.
requirements: Strategy-specific calibration before operational use
Dimension-level validation rather than total-score agreement alone
Continued human oversight of flagged responses
constraints: Findings are from one model (GPT-4o-mini), one music-analysis task, one institutional context, and three runs at temperature 0.9; the article states they may not generalize to other models, tasks, sampling settings, institutions, or high-stakes assessment contexts
target_learners: undergraduate university music students
target_learning_goals: written music analysis covering harmonic analysis, formal structure, reasoning coherence, and music-theoretical terminology
examples: The study scored 300 undergraduate responses to a Mozart piano sonata analysis task with three teachers' mean scores as the reference, comparing Fs+CoT, RAG, and SC prompting strategies across Run1 and three-run aggregation conditions.

article_title: When AI Wears Many Hats: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing Education
citation: Narang, Unnati, Vishal Sachdev, and Ruichun Liu. (2025). When AI Wears Many Hats: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing Education. Journal of Public Policy & Marketing. https://doi.org/10.1177/07439156251328237
title: GAI role framework: tutor, teammate, and tool mapped onto teaching, social, and cognitive presence
description: The article integrates Role Theory with the Community of Inquiry (CoI) model to propose that GAI can assume three roles in marketing education. As a tutor, GAI provides personalized instruction and helps with learning specific concepts and skills; as a teammate, it collaborates by sharing ideas and offering different perspectives; as a tool, it completes assigned tasks efficiently. Each role is posited to influence teaching, social, and cognitive presence differently, shaping learning experience and workplace readiness.
requirements: Learning objectives of the marketing course determine which role GAI should assume
Instructors provide instructions (system prompts) to the GAI chatbot for each role
constraints: The roles often overlap and interact dynamically in practice, particularly in online and hybrid formats
Framework validated only on a convenience sample and should be expanded in future research
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate marketing students
target_learning_goals: marketing concepts and skills
critical thinking
collaboration
workplace readiness
examples: In Principles of Marketing, GAI offers personalized feedback on student projects; in Marketing Research, GAI facilitates brainstorming sessions; in Marketing Analytics, GAI helps apply data analytics techniques and generates code and reports
key_sources: Narang, Unnati, Vishal Sachdev, and Ruichun Liu. (2025). When AI Wears Many Hats: The Role of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing Education. Journal of Public Policy & Marketing. https://doi.org/10.1177/07439156251328237

The review "covered 11 distinct marketing courses taught by the marketing faculty at a large midwestern U.S. public university," followed by "a survey of 14 full-time faculty members" who teach these courses. It extracted learning objectives and topics from syllabi and mapped instructors' reported GAI use to course type and objectives.

title: One assignment, three GAI role implementations: tutor, teammate, and tool modifications
description: The article presents a reusable assignment design pattern in which a single marketing assignment is modified for each GAI role. In a social media marketing assignment on viral campaigns, the tutor version uses a Socratic dialogue with GAI as an expert guide, the teammate version has students collaborate with GAI while maintaining a critical approach, and the tool version restricts GAI to data gathering and analysis while requiring independent recommendations. The pattern advances specific learning objectives within the role framework.

title: Address privacy, equity, academic integrity, transparency, and overreliance when integrating GAI across its roles
description: The article argues that responsible GAI adoption in marketing education requires addressing a set of ethical considerations spanning its three roles. These "encompass privacy, equity, academic integrity, transparency, and potential overreliance on AI systems, each requiring careful attention to ensure responsible implementation." Educators must establish clear data-handling protocols compliant with regulations like FERPA and develop inclusive implementation strategies so all students can benefit regardless of technological or economic circumstances.

target_learning_goals: responsible and equitable use of GAI in learning

description: A distributed edge-cloud system pairing a Meta Quest 3 VR frontend with a GPU-accelerated backend. article_title: Agentic AI-driven Immersive Simulation: A Knowledge-Aware Virtual Training Platform for High Dose Rate (HDR) Brachytherapy
citation: Ronghua Xu, Kepha Barasa, Manoj Kumal, Xinyun Liu, Weihua Zhou, Xin Qian. (2026). Agentic AI-driven Immersive Simulation: A Knowledge-Aware Virtual Training Platform for High Dose Rate (HDR) Brachytherapy. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08163
title: RAG-based cognitive backend grounding assistant responses in HDR brachytherapy guidelines
description: The backend functions as an intelligent tutor built on a RAG pipeline: guideline documents are parsed, split into 512-token chunks with overlap, embedded (nomic-embed-text or MedEmbed), and indexed in a FAISS vector store. At query time a hybrid dense-plus-sparse retrieval performs cosine-similarity search, and retrieved chunks are synthesized by an LLM (e.g., GPT-4o-mini) into actionable instructions delivered via TTS. The article states this grounds responses "strictly grounded in the medical literature," mitigating hallucination risk.
requirements: Authoritative HDR brachytherapy guideline documents for ingestion; an embedding model, FAISS index, STT module (OpenAI Whisper), LLM, and TTS module
constraints: Its ability to provide answers is limited by the quality and number of documents it can reference; the standardized guideline set cannot account for institution-specific protocols, practitioner preferences, or unusual scenarios
target_learners: medical trainees practicing brachytherapy procedures
target_learning_goals: receiving real-time, evidence-based procedural guidance during training
examples: The four-stage RAG pipeline (preprocess, knowledge retrieval, actionable generation, post-process) is implemented with Langchain, PyPDF, FAISS, Ollama, Flask, Whisper, FastAPI, and ngrok in the prototype
key_sources: Ronghua Xu, Kepha Barasa, Manoj Kumal, Xinyun Liu, Weihua Zhou, Xin Qian. (2026). Agentic AI-driven Immersive Simulation: A Knowledge-Aware Virtual Training Platform for High Dose Rate (HDR) Brachytherapy. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08163

article_title: Revisiting the Performance of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Introductory Object-Oriented Programming
citation: Marina Lepp, Joosep Kaimre. (2026). Revisiting the Performance of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Introductory Object-Oriented Programming Assessments: Insights from 2026. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3303-5245
title: Require careful human verification of GenAI-generated solutions for conceptually demanding object-oriented programming tasks
description: The article recommends that while contemporary GenAI systems can effectively support routine code generation, solutions involving more complex object-oriented reasoning need human checking. It states that GenAI systems "can effectively support routine code generation but still require caref ul human verification for conceptually demanding object -oriented programming tasks", because high overall scores do not translate into consistent performance on interfaces, abstract classes, and visual reasoning.
requirements: Instructors or reviewers must check GenAI solutions on conceptually demanding OOP topics such as interfaces, abstract classes, and visual program interpretation before relying on them.
constraints: The recommendation rests on evaluation of one Java-based introductory course's assessments, delivered in Estonian, with single first responses and no prompt engineering; the article notes AI assistants are highly sensitive to task phrasing and format.
target_learners: first-year university students in an introductory Java object-oriented programming course
target_learning_goals: object-oriented programming concepts including classes, inheritance, interfaces, and abstract classes
examples: Across the study's assessments, most models scored above the historical student cohort average, yet interfaces, abstract classes, and graphics-related questions continued to produce recurring errors.
key_sources: Marina Lepp, Joosep Kaimre. (2026). Revisiting the Performance of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Introductory Object-Oriented Programming Assessments: Insights from 2026. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3303-5245

article_title: Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction
citation: Matthew Keenan, Nishant Kheterpal, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Cyrus Omar. (2026). Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23309
title: Eight learner-centered design criteria for classroom proof assistants, organized under learning and usability goals
description: The article proposes a framework of two broad goals — "learning: the tool should help students refine and improve their mathematical proof skills; and usability: the tool should not create unnecessary frictions in writing proofs" — expanded into eight numbered criteria: supporting active exploration, consistent model, requiring engagement, notation similar to written proofs, engagement similar to written proofs, easy setup, minimal training, and minimal tedium. The criteria were synthesized from prior classroom deployments and a workshop survey, and the authors believe they are transferable to classroom proof assistants for other domains.
requirements: The assistant must require genuine cognitive engagement with the mathematical ideas in order to complete exercises, and feedback should be provided for partial proofs, not just once a proof is complete.
constraints: The final two learning criteria apply specifically to settings where students are expected to write proofs on paper, since in many but not all classroom settings transfer to pen-and-paper is expected.
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate programming languages students
target_learning_goals: equational reasoning
structural induction
transfer of proof skills to pen-and-paper
examples: Criterion 5 motivated the major iteration between deployments: students had to explicitly write out evaluation steps instead of simply clicking possibly reducible sub-expressions.
key_sources: Matthew Keenan, Nishant Kheterpal, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Cyrus Omar. (2026). Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23309

article_title: Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction
citation: Matthew Keenan, Nishant Kheterpal, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Cyrus Omar. (2026). Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23309
title: Hazel Prover, a web-based classroom proof assistant for equational and inductive reasoning about typed functional programs
description: Hazel Prover is "implemented as an extension to Hazel, a live typed functional programming environment". Students interleave programs and theorem specifications in the Hazel editor; theorem constructs appear as proof obligations at the bottom of the screen. Students highlight sub-expressions and choose to rewrite or perform an induction, with evaluation steps, algebra steps checked by an external computer algebra checker, and assumption steps. There is no proof-assistant-specific syntax; all proof logic is expressed via a graphical user interface, and proofs are laid out similarly to written proofs.
requirements: Installation and setup should be straightforward, and the tool should require minimal training specific to the tool, per the article's Criteria 6 and 7.
constraints: The algebra solver is given access only to arithmetic and arithmetic operators, leaving Hazel's control flow and list primitives opaque, so students cannot simply rewrite the entire proposition to true.
target_learners: upper-level undergraduate and graduate programming languages students
target_learning_goals: step-by-step equational and inductive reasoning about functional programs
examples: In the second deployment one exercise required students to write their own implementation of Peano multiplication and prove it correct.
key_sources: Matthew Keenan, Nishant Kheterpal, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Cyrus Omar. (2026). Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23309

article_title: Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction
citation: Matthew Keenan, Nishant Kheterpal, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Cyrus Omar. (2026). Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23309
title: Require the tool's engagement pattern to match pen-and-paper proof engagement, since even small automation can cause dramatic transfer failures
description: The article's central design lesson is that a classroom proof assistant must not only force engagement but make the engagement pattern similar enough to pen-and-paper. The authors report "non-obvious lessons about the extent to which even small amounts of seemingly tedium-saving automation can lead to dramatic transfer failures": automating evaluation stepping in the first deployment left students unable to transfer, while requiring students to write out each evaluation step substantially improved transfer. Designers should audit which automated steps replace reasoning students must practice for on-paper assessment.
requirements: The tool must force users to think through all the steps they would need to learn to think through in order to write a proof on paper (Criterion 5).
constraints: This must be balanced against Criterion 8 (Minimal Tedium): the assistant should not obligate proof steps that would be elided on paper or require didactically trivial long tasks.
target_learners: students learning to write proofs independently of the tool
target_learning_goals: transfer of proof skills to pen-and-paper exams
examples: Between deployments, double-clicking green-highlighted reducible sub-expressions was replaced by requiring students to highlight a sub-expression, type what it steps to, and press a check button validating the step.
key_sources: Matthew Keenan, Nishant Kheterpal, Jean-Baptiste Jeannin, Cyrus Omar. (2026). Hazel Prover: A Classroom Proof Assistant for Learning Structural Induction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23309

article_title: A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies
citation: Hingle, A., & Johri, A. (2025). A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies. https://www.google.com/search?q=A+Guided+Inquiry+Approach+to+Students+Co-Designing+Generative+AI+Course+Policies
title: Conceptual model positioning students as co-designers of course policies through guided inquiry, perspectival thinking, and student voice
description: The article's conceptual model (Figure 1) positions students not only as learners but as co-designers of course structures and policies. It integrates guided inquiry as the activity frame with perspectival thinking from situated learning theory and principles of student voice, so that "perspectival thinking, informed by situated learning theory and principles of student voice, helps students examine AI policy guidelines from multiple stakeholder perspectives." The model treats the GenAI policy itself as both an artifact for student engagement and a pedagogical tool, complementing top-down policy analyses by centering student agency.
requirements: A guided inquiry learning environment with curated resources and structured individual-then-collaborative policy design tasks
Instructor and institutional support for multi-stakeholder discussion
constraints: The study reframes policy as a social process rather than a fixed institutional document; co-design does not imply instructors or students alone bear responsibility for policy development
target_learners: undergraduate students in technology ethics coursework
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
perspectival thinking about AI governance
student voice in policy formation
examples: Students completed readings, used GenAI to brainstorm policy ideas, wrote individual policies with at least five justified elements, then collaborated in groups of 4-6 for roughly 45 minutes to craft a collective policy
key_sources: Hingle, A., & Johri, A. (2025). A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies. https://www.google.com/search?q=A+Guided+Inquiry+Approach+to+Students+Co-Designing+Generative+AI+Course+Policies

article_title: A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies
citation: Hingle, A., & Johri, A. (2025). A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies. https://www.google.com/search?q=A+Guided+Inquiry+Approach+to+Students+Co-Designing+Generative+AI+Course+Policies
title: GenAI policy co-design module: guided inquiry activity with curated resources, individual policy design, and group discussion
description: A 3-4-week course module on GenAI in education within an undergraduate course, Technology and the Global Society. Students received curated resources (readings, videos, reports, policies), used GenAI to brainstorm policy ideas, wrote an individual policy detailing at least five justified elements, then joined a group discussion of 4-6 peers lasting approximately 45 minutes to develop a collective policy, followed by written reflection. "The module culminated in a group discussion, with prior activities designed to prepare students for it." Each policy element needed to be justified with evidence.
requirements: Curated starter resources provided in the first week
Individual writing assignment with feedback before group discussion
Reflection debrief and written assignment after discussion
constraints: The module assumed students would have access to GenAI tools; the activity was both a graded assignment and a source of research data, a dual role the authors note may have influenced student responses
target_learners: junior and senior undergraduate information technology and cybersecurity students
target_learning_goals: understanding how GenAI functions
ethical and policy reasoning about AI use
multi-stakeholder policy design
examples: Figure 3 presents an excerpt of a group's designed GenAI course policy; Table 1 lists ten curated resources including peer-reviewed articles, TED talks, and institutional policies

citation: Hingle, A., & Johri, A. (2025). A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies. https://www.google.com/search?q=A+Guided+Inquiry+Approach+to+Students+Co-Designing+Generative+AI+Course+Policies
title: ED-AI Lit framework: six elements of AI literacy used as the analytic framework
description: The study draws on the ED-AI Lit framework (Allen & Kendeou, 2024) as the primary framework for data analysis, situating perspectival thinking and student voice within a structured approach to AI literacy. The framework comprises six elements: Knowledge, Evaluation, Collaboration, Contextualization, Autonomy, and Ethics, spanning understanding how AI works, critically judging AI technologies, collaborating with AI systems and individuals, using AI in real-world settings, self-determination in AI interactions, and recognizing moral issues including fairness, accountability, transparency, and privacy.
requirements: Context-specific approaches aligned with learners' educational levels, disciplinary backgrounds, and goals for engaging with AI
constraints: The article notes AI literacy in practice is often supported through levels of learning progressing from recognizing or understanding basic AI functionality to creating with AI
target_learners: undergraduate students learning about AI
target_learning_goals: AI literacy across knowledge, evaluation, collaboration, contextualization, autonomy, and ethics
examples: The study's Findings section organized its seven themes around the framework's six elements plus a theme on institutional responsibility
key_sources: Hingle, A., & Johri, A. (2025). A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies. https://www.google.com/search?q=A+Guided+Inquiry+Approach+to+Students+Co-Designing+Generative+AI+Course+Policies

article_title: A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies
citation: Hingle, A., & Johri, A. (2025). A Guided Inquiry Approach to Students Co-Designing Generative AI Course Policies. https://www.google.com/search?q=A+Guided+Inquiry+Approach+to+Students+Co-Designing+Generative+AI+Course+Policies
title: Scaffold co-design activities so student input moves from surface-level consultation toward substantive participation in governance
description: The article recommends that policy co-design activities be designed so students genuinely articulate values and negotiate trade-offs rather than merely being consulted. From the student voice literature, the authors conclude that "co-design activities may benefit from additional scaffolding that supports students in moving from surface-level input toward what Hart (1992) describes as 'substantive' participation." Students in the study expressed desire to shape GenAI policy while signaling uncertainty about how to contribute meaningfully, and the authors caution against arrangements where student input is solicited but does not substantively shape outcomes.
requirements: Communication between instructor, administrative, and student roles in policy formation
Scaffolding that supports students in articulating values and negotiating trade-offs
constraints: The authors caution against arrangements in which student input is solicited but does not substantively shape outcomes
target_learners: undergraduate students as primary stakeholders in course policy
target_learning_goals: genuine participation in educational governance decisions
examples: Participants in the study wanted a say in developing and revising course policies, viewing this as essential for building trust between the institution, instructors, and students

article_title: Beyond Generation and Accuracy: Diagnosing and Enhancing Visual Chain-of-Thought for Geometry Problem Solving
citation: Zhitong Dong, Jicai Pan, Yingguo Gao, Jingting Ding, Hao Chen, Jinjie Gu. (2026). Beyond Generation and Accuracy: Diagnosing and Enhancing Visual Chain-of-Thought for Geometry Problem Solving. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12606
title: GeoVAD-Bench: a trajectory-level diagnostic benchmark for visual chain-of-thought geometry solving
description: GeoVAD-Bench is a diagnostic benchmark of "600 geometry problems requiring auxiliary-line constructions", each recast into a trajectory-level evaluation spanning five dimensions: original-diagram perception, auxiliary-diagram quality, auxiliary-diagram utilization, reasoning-process correctness, and final-answer accuracy. It pairs these metrics with three controlled auxiliary conditions (No-Aux, Auto-Aux, GT-Aux) that isolate intermediate error modes, the causal gains of visual aids, and the autonomy gap. Problems are stratified by difficulty, language (Chinese and English), and answer format (multiple-choice and open-ended). The article positions it as the only listed benchmark evaluating all five dimensions with explicit, separately reported metrics.
requirements: Problems must strictly necessitate auxiliary-line constructions, and each instance requires a verifiable answer plus a validated reference construction and corresponding auxiliary diagram.
constraints: Evaluation of the four process metrics relies on Gemini-3.1-Pro as the judge, and non-interleaved models are approximated with an external image-editing pipeline.
target_learners: multimodal reasoning models evaluated on geometry problem solving
target_learning_goals: diagnosing where visual chain-of-thought reasoning fails across perception, construction, utilization, and deduction
examples: The article uses the benchmark to compare closed- and open-source models and to attribute error categories among incorrect solutions for MathCanvas-7B and CodePlot-CoT-32B.
key_sources: Zhitong Dong, Jicai Pan, Yingguo Gao, Jingting Ding, Hao Chen, Jinjie Gu. (2026). Beyond Generation and Accuracy: Diagnosing and Enhancing Visual Chain-of-Thought for Geometry Problem Solving. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12606

article_title: Beyond Generation and Accuracy: Diagnosing and Enhancing Visual Chain-of-Thought for Geometry Problem Solving
citation: Zhitong Dong, Jicai Pan, Yingguo Gao, Jingting Ding, Hao Chen, Jinjie Gu. (2026). Beyond Generation and Accuracy: Diagnosing and Enhancing Visual Chain-of-Thought for Geometry Problem Solving. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12606
title: GeoWeave: a progressive evaluation-to-optimization framework pairing capability-ordered SFT with interleaved RL and step-level credit assignment
description: GeoWeave is a post-training framework that converts diagnostic findings into targeted training. It combines a modular data construction pipeline covering "fine-grained geometric perception, faithful diagram editing, and coherent interleaved reasoning" with a progressive training framework: three SFT stages (perception warmup, auxiliary-diagram editing, unified interleaved solving) that first train separate model branches and then all parameters, followed by Interleave-RL. The RL stage organizes text and image actions in a single rollout, applies group-relative policy optimization to text, retains a velocity-MSE constraint for image generation, and uses step-level credit assignment that localizes erroneous perception and deduction steps and upweights their low-entropy tokens.
requirements: Requires a base multimodal model supporting native interleaved generation, curated perception, editing, and interleaved-reasoning datasets, and verifiable outcome and process rewards.
constraints: The image-generation branch receives no independent policy-gradient update; its effect is reflected indirectly through the updated visual state and final answer.
target_learners: multimodal reasoning models (8B-scale unified multimodal models)
target_learning_goals: planning auxiliary constructions, generating faithful edited diagrams, grounding deduction in updated visual states, and producing correct answers
examples: Applied to SenseNova-U1-8B, the framework produced GeoWeave-8B, trained with three SFT stages (4,000, 10,000, and 6,000 steps) and Interleave-RL on 9K samples.
key_sources: Zhitong Dong, Jicai Pan, Yingguo Gao, Jingting Ding, Hao Chen, Jinjie Gu. (2026). Beyond Generation and Accuracy: Diagnosing and Enhancing Visual Chain-of-Thought for Geometry Problem Solving. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.12606

article_title: Generative AI and Extended Reality in Collaborative Architectural Design Education: An Exploratory Studio Study
citation: Xiao, Y., Chen, M., Li, Y., Powers, N., Wiesenfeld, M., Smith, G., Farzin, S., Liu, S. (2026). Generative AI and Extended Reality in Collaborative Architectural Design Education: An Exploratory Studio Study. arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.13494. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13494
title: GenARch: a GenAI-assisted multi-user XR pipeline for collaborative architectural conceptual design
description: GenARch is a pipeline integrating GenAI-based visual generation with collaborative XR environments, deployed as a technology probe embedded in an existing studio workflow. Its "in-house web and XR clients support structured or free-text/speech prompting, 2D image generation, 2D-to-3D conversion, and sharedreview." Generated assets are stored in a common gallery so students need not remain in-headset during processing, and selected assets are exported to Arkio for tabletop and full-scale inspection, collaborative manipulation, site/context viewing, and lighting-based shadow analysis. Technically it uses synchronized Meta Quest 3 and web clients, a Python/FastAPI backend, DALL·E 3 for text-to-image, Shap-E/TripoSR/Tripo3D for 2D-to-3D reconstruction, and Photon networking with Meta spatial anchors.
requirements: Used primarily during conceptual ideation and collaborative visualization, with students continuing their usual design tools for subsequent development
constraints: The study evaluates the addition of the structured GenARch workflow rather than isolating the effects of GenAI or XR from all other tools
Technical limitations in 2D-to-3D generation, scale fidelity, latency, contextual data, and control were inseparable from the educational experience
target_learners: undergraduate architectural engineering students in a design studio course
target_learning_goals: collaborative architectural conceptual design
visual ideation and representation
spatial evaluation and shared design review
examples: Four teams (N=16) incorporated GenARch into their usual course workflow across a tutorial, a 35-minute ideation session, and an 80-minute immersive collaborative visualization activity, while three teams (N=11) continued the usual workflow
key_sources: Xiao, Y., Chen, M., Li, Y., Powers, N., Wiesenfeld, M., Smith, G., Farzin, S., Liu, S. (2026). Generative AI and Extended Reality in Collaborative Architectural Design Education: An Exploratory Studio Study. arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.13494. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13494

article_title: From Prompts to Physical Laws: A Generative AI Workflow for Engineering Physics Education
citation: Laura B. Alvarado-Cruz, Josep Ll. Suñer, Pedro Yuste, Juan C. Castro-Palacio, Juan A. Monsoriu, and Francisco M. Muñoz-Pérez. (2026). From Prompts to Physical Laws: A Generative AI Workflow for Engineering Physics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19400
title: Four-phase generative-AI physics workflow: video generation, Tracker tracking, Excel Solver curve fitting, parameter validation
description: A replicable instructional workflow combining generative-AI video platforms (PixVerse.ai, Grok Imagine, Pippit), the open-source Tracker video analysis tool, and the Microsoft Excel Solver GRG Nonlinear algorithm. As the article states, "The proposed workflow is organized into four sequential phases: (i) generation of synthetic videos using generative AI, (ii) extraction of kinematic data throug video analysis with software Tracker, (iii) estimation of model parameters by means of non-linear curve fitting, and (iv) identification and validation of the recovered physical parameters." It functions as a virtual laboratory mirroring experimental practice from model construction to quantitative validation.
requirements: Access to generative-AI video platforms, the Tracker open-source video analysis tool, and the Excel Solver add-in with the GRG Nonlinear algorithm
constraints: The agreement achieved is approximate rather than exact, since videos are generated from natural-language descriptions rather than explicit physical equations
target_learners: introductory engineering physics students
target_learning_goals: experimental design
data acquisition
parameter estimation
model evaluation
modelling of physical systems
examples: Three scenarios were generated: a wooden block sliding with constant friction, a silicone rubber sphere falling in glycerin, and a skydiver with deployed parachute, each tracked and fitted to its analytical model
key_sources: Laura B. Alvarado-Cruz, Josep Ll. Suñer, Pedro Yuste, Juan C. Castro-Palacio, Juan A. Monsoriu, and Francisco M. Muñoz-Pérez. (2026). From Prompts to Physical Laws: A Generative AI Workflow for Engineering Physics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19400

article_title: From Prompts to Physical Laws: A Generative AI Workflow for Engineering Physics Education
citation: Laura B. Alvarado-Cruz, Josep Ll. Suñer, Pedro Yuste, Juan C. Castro-Palacio, Juan A. Monsoriu, and Francisco M. Muñoz-Pérez. (2026). From Prompts to Physical Laws: A Generative AI Workflow for Engineering Physics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19400
title: Use AI-generated synthetic experiments as virtual laboratories where physical lab access is limited or unavailable
description: Because generative-AI videos can be tracked and quantitatively validated like real footage, they can substitute for conventional laboratory settings when resources are scarce. The article states the methodology "provides a virtual laboratory framework through which students can perform forms of experimental validation even when access to the corresponding physical setup is limited or unavailable." This supports active, autonomous learning aligned with data-analysis and experimentation skills while removing logistical barriers of a physical laboratory.
requirements: A video tracking tool and a curve-fitting environment must accompany the generated videos so students can extract and validate quantitative data
constraints: None of the platforms used was specifically trained to simulate physical phenomena; coherent motion relies on sufficiently precise verbal description rather than formal physics knowledge in the system
target_learners: introductory engineering physics students in resource-limited or remote contexts
target_learning_goals: data analysis
experimentation skills
model validation
examples: The three generated scenarios served as virtual experiments whose fitted parameters (friction coefficient, viscosity, drag coefficient) matched literature ranges

article_title: Harnessing Generative UI for Education: Tailored Learning Interactives
citation: Alisa Kovshov, Anisha Choudhury, Anna Iurchenko, Amy Keeling, Avinatan Hassidim, Ayelet Shasha Evron, Ayça Çakmakli, Diana Akrong, Femi Olanubi, Gal Elidan, Ian Li, Ido Lerer, Katherine Chou, Lidan Hackmon, Michal Gordon, Nir Kerem, Niv Efron, Preeti Singh, Rena Levitt, Rotem Yulzary, Shlomi Ben Shimon, Sophie Allweis, Tracey Lee-Joe, Tzvika Stein, Yaniv Carmel, Yael Haramaty, Yishay Mor, Yossi Matias and Yuri Lev. (2026). Harnessing Generative UI for Education: Tailored Learning Interactives. Google Research. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20738
title: Four-pillar conceptual framework for tailoring generative UI to learning: curriculum alignment, agency and motivation, guidance and scaffolding, formative feedback
description: The article develops a conceptual framework of four pillars for tailoring generative interfaces to learning: "curriculum alignment; agency and motivation; guidance and scaffolding; formative feedback." Each pillar is mapped to a concrete UX/UI choice in Table 1: articulated teacher-approved learning objectives, progressive difficulty challenges balancing achievement and self-efficacy, AI-generated scaffolding such as multi-tiered hints and real-time context-aware feedback that prompts critical thinking rather than revealing answers, and introspective intros and solvers with worked solutions. The framework grounds the generation pipeline's pedagogical guardrails.
requirements: Each pillar must be implemented via a corresponding UX/UI choice in the generated interactive, as detailed in Table 1
constraints: Off-the-shelf Gen-UI models lack optimization for pedagogical precision, so the pillars must be imposed as guardrails rather than assumed
target_learners: K-12 and undergraduate STEM students across primary, middle school, high school and undergraduate levels
target_learning_goals: STEM conceptual understanding through active inquiry, hypothesis testing, and variable manipulation in simulations and mini-games
examples: Table 1 maps the guidance and scaffolding pillar to introductory walkthroughs, reference toolboxes, multi-tiered hints, and real-time context-aware feedback
key_sources: Alisa Kovshov, Anisha Choudhury, Anna Iurchenko, Amy Keeling, Avinatan Hassidim, Ayelet Shasha Evron, Ayça Çakmakli, Diana Akrong, Femi Olanubi, Gal Elidan, Ian Li, Ido Lerer, Katherine Chou, Lidan Hackmon, Michal Gordon, Nir Kerem, Niv Efron, Preeti Singh, Rena Levitt, Rotem Yulzary, Shlomi Ben Shimon, Sophie Allweis, Tracey Lee-Joe, Tzvika Stein, Yaniv Carmel, Yael Haramaty, Yishay Mor, Yossi Matias and Yuri Lev. article_title: Harnessing Generative UI for Education: Tailored Learning Interactives
citation: Alisa Kovshov, Anisha Choudhury, Anna Iurchenko, Amy Keeling, Avinatan Hassidim, Ayelet Shasha Evron, Ayça Çakmakli, Diana Akrong, Femi Olanubi, Gal Elidan, Ian Li, Ido Lerer, Katherine Chou, Lidan Hackmon, Michal Gordon, Nir Kerem, Niv Efron, Preeti Singh, Rena Levitt, Rotem Yulzary, Shlomi Ben Shimon, Sophie Allweis, Tracey Lee-Joe, Tzvika Stein, Yaniv Carmel, Yael Haramaty, Yishay Mor, Yossi Matias and Yuri Lev. (2026). Harnessing Generative UI for Education: Tailored Learning Interactives. Google Research. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20738
title: Learning interactives generation pipeline: four stages from teacher request to guidance components
description: Learning interactives are generated in four stages (Figure 2): Planning (from a teacher request to learning objectives and a simulation idea), Scaffolding (from objectives to K=5 levelled goals), Gen-UI (from idea and goals to a generated simulation UI), and Guidance (tour, hints, solutions, feedback). The textual planning stage produces entities, relations, telemetry, visual features, knobs and actions; the scaffolding stage iteratively generates and critiques each level's goal; the Gen-UI stage applies generate-then-refine with visual, solution, telemetry and mechanical critiques. A collection of teacher-approved interactives is available at research.google.com/p/learning-interactives.
requirements: An educator-initiated request specifying subject, grade level and query, with teacher review/approval of generated learning objectives
constraints: Single-prompt UI generation satisfying pedagogical requirements succeeds only 3.5% of the time, so iterative critique loops are required

title: Levelled-goal scaffolding pattern: iteratively generated goals meeting concreteness, clarity, growth and scaffolding desiderata
description: Each learning interactive decomposes a complex concept into a sequence of K=5 levelled goals the student must solve. Goals must satisfy four desiderata the article names: "Concreteness", "Clarity", "Growth" (each goal more complex than preceding ones or introducing a new concept), and "Scaffolding" (not significantly more difficult than predecessors). Because attaining these for the full set in a single prompt is highly improbable, each goal is generated given the previous stages' goals, critiqued, and re-created until all K goals are verified.

constraints: The scaffolding stage is negligible in run-time relative to UI generation because goals are short in textual tokens

citation: Erfan Entezami, Andrew Lan, and Madeline Endres. (2026). Generative AI May Reinforce Social Biases in Software Engineering Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28483
title: When deploying LLMs for educational decision-making, explicitly specify decision criteria and minimize unnecessary demographic cues
description: The article's mitigation principle is that prompt design and the information provided to a model substantially influence its biased behavior. It recommends that practitioners "explicitly specify the criteria used to make decisions and minimize unnecessary demographic cues", because seemingly innocuous attributes such as names signaling gender or nationality can affect model outputs. The study's persona experiments show that adding task-relevant skill information reduced but did not eliminate bias, supporting information design as a partial mitigation lever.

constraints: The article shows additional task-relevant information reduced biases but did not fully eliminate them; demographic attributes still influenced decisions when multiple valid options existed.

target_learning_goals: fair and equitable team formation and educational content generation
examples: In the team formation experiments, Skill-based personas containing technical qualifications steered assignments toward ground-truth teams (99.2% on-pair) yet gender still biased the choice between equally valid teams.

title: Four GPT-4o-backed AI TA configurations with pedagogical guardrails on a web-based coding platform
description: The study's artifact is a set of four AI teaching assistants backed by the OpenAI GPT-4o LLM, deployed on a web-based coding platform with a split-screen interface showing the problem statement, submission history, and chatbot beside an embedded editor. The four configurations varied only in system prompts and contextual information: "AI TAs were backed by the OpenAI GPT-4o LLM and returned responses to student queries based on custom prompts" with pedagogical guardrails similar to CodeHelp. Direct conditions gave brief responses without complete code solutions; Socratic conditions guided exclusively through targeted questions.

A web-based coding platform hosting the programming tasks and chat interface
constraints: The four configurations differed only in system prompts and contextual information; the interface was otherwise identical
Guardrails withhold complete code solutions rather than providing them

target_learning_goals: code-writing and debugging tasks involving lists, loops, and conditionals
examples: 132 students were randomly assigned across Direct + Full Context, Direct + No Context, Socratic + Full Context, and Socratic + No Context conditions while completing one code-writing and two debugging tasks

title: Balance pedagogical guidance style and context awareness in AI TA design rather than treating more scaffolding or more context as inherently better
description: The article argues that guardrailed AI teaching assistants are effective only when their pedagogical guidance and contextual awareness fit the task and the student. It reports that "guardrails can become roadblocks when pedagogical guidance and contextual awareness are not well balanced": a Socratic chatbot with limited context demanded high effort, while a rigidly Socratic chatbot with full context was rated least favorably. Educators should configure guidance style according to whether the assignment goal is task completion, conceptual understanding, or productive struggle.

Integration of the tool with the assignment environment combined with deliberate design of how the chatbot uses context pedagogically
constraints: In the studied CS1 setting, the Socratic + Full Context configuration was experienced as least favorable for task completion
Full context alone did not ensure support felt useful or led to stronger understanding
target_learners: introductory programming (CS1) students
target_learning_goals: programming task completion and debugging comprehension

citation: Lili Chen, Gavin Buskes, Yuxin Ren and Chin Tong Leong. (2026). Feedback Without the Wait: Piloting a Generative AI Practice Platform in a Large Maths Class. 37th Annual Conference of the Australasian Association for Engineering Education, UNSW, Sydney. https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/
title: Decouple feedback immediacy from solution verification: keep the human in the loop upstream at answer verification, not at the point of grading
description: This design pattern resolves the tension between feedback immediacy and trustworthy human oversight by relocating human review. As the authors state, "Rather than asking GenAI to grade live submissions, we position human markers as upfront verifiers of answers and use the model only to generate immediate, scaffolded feedback against those human-endorsed solutions." GenAI then generates immediate feedback by reasoning against answers a human has already endorsed, preserving immediacy where it matters pedagogically while retaining oversight where students value it most. The authors argue this is a workable and transferable pattern for trustworthy, scalable formative practice in engineering education.
requirements: An existing, demonstrator-verified solution set for the GenAI to reason against
Staff comfortable with reviewing solutions of AI-generated questions
An institutional environment that permits GenAI for practice
constraints: Positioned as practice rather than assessment; the article does not claim the pattern is validated for graded assessment
target_learners: large undergraduate electrical engineering cohorts
target_learning_goals: formative practice in probability and random models
immediate scaffolded feedback guiding revision
examples: In the pilot, demonstrators verified problem-booklet solutions upfront and the feedback agent generated immediate feedback against those human-endorsed solutions, with prompts designed around the feed-forward principle

title: Conditional mediational framework: AI as scaffold for writing and digital critical thinking only under critical, verificatory, responsibility-oriented interaction
description: The article synthesizes constructivist and sociocultural accounts of mediated learning with process-writing and self-regulation models. Generative AI is conceptualized as a mediational means operating within the learner's zone of proximal development, able to propose outlines, model genre conventions, and surface alternatives. Its central claim is explicitly conditional: "AI applications can act as mediational tools supporting both writing development and digital critical thinking only when instruction structures human–AI interaction to be critical, verificatory, and responsibility-oriented." Learning benefits therefore depend on how learners interact with mediation—questioning, comparing drafts, rejecting or adapting suggestions—rather than on tool access alone.
requirements: Instruction must structure human–AI interaction to be critical, verificatory, and responsibility-oriented
Learners must engage with AI outputs by questioning, comparing drafts, rejecting or adapting suggestions, and justifying compositional choices
constraints: When used without instructional scaffolding as a shortcut to finished text, AI can undermine independent composing, weaken engagement with primary sources, blur authorial boundaries, and introduce integrity risks
target_learners: EFL university students in AI-rich writing environments
target_learning_goals: Writing development
Digital critical thinking and AI literacy
Self-regulated, ethically grounded authorship
examples: The study's intervention operationalized the framework through verification routines, hallucination-detection instruction, and structured ethical self-regulation coupled with ideation and revision support

article_title: A Framework for Institutional Change in the Age of AI
citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A framework for institutional change in the age of AI. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00649-4
title: Six-dimension framework for adapting institutional change models to the AI era
description: The framework identifies six diagnostic dimensions along which prior interactive-engagement (IE) change models must be reconsidered for generative AI: three concerning tools (evidence base, rate of change, scope) and three concerning people (faculty agency, change agent role, student role). It is grounded in sociocultural activity-system models in which tools transform activity. The authors state: "Our framework identifies six dimensions along which existing IE change models must be reconsidered in light of generative AI’s arrival." title: Privilege humble, local inquiries rather than scaling unevidenced AI practices
description: Because the evidence base for AI-based pedagogy does not yet exist, change efforts should surface and document localized uses of AI that show promise, share emerging cases without overclaiming generalizability, and aggregate these efforts to build future evidence. The article states: "Rather than advocating or scaling practices whose effectiveness has not been established, we should seek out and learn from localized uses of AI that show promise". Institutions should provide experimentation resources and access with guardrails without long-lasting commitments.

constraints: Scaling unevidenced practices risks exacerbating existing equity gaps, as learners with greater resources and digital literacy benefit first

article_title: Reimagining mathematics education through intelligent tutoring: evidence, opportunities, and implementation challenges
citation: Ogunsakin IB, Ayanwale MA, Falebita OS and Felemu OJ (2026) Reimagining mathematics education through intelligent tutoring: evidence, opportunities, and implementation challenges. Front. Educ. 11:1943906. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1943906
title: Connectivism as the underpinning theoretical lens for AI-supported mathematics learning
description: The review adopts connectivism, which "conceptualises learning as the formation, navigation, evaluation, and maintenance of connections within distributed knowledge networks". ITSs and adaptive platforms function as technological nodes within learners' knowledge networks, collecting interaction evidence, estimating performance, recommending resources, and providing feedback. Teachers remain central nodes who contextualise content, evaluate AI recommendations, and connect digital activities to curricular objectives. The framework rejects the assumption that AI can independently direct mathematics learning.
requirements: Learning is understood as interaction across human and technological knowledge networks, requiring learners and teachers able to judge the accuracy and relevance of networked information.
constraints: The review notes connectivism does not fully explain how an intelligent system modifies instruction in response to learner performance, so adaptive instruction is added as a complementary mechanism.
target_learners: mathematics learners across educational levels using AI-supported tutoring environments
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding, problem-solving, and use of networked mathematical resources
examples: The review uses connectivism to interpret a learner attempting a problem, receiving an adaptive prompt, examining an alternative representation, revising strategy, and applying revised understanding to a more demanding task.

title: Conceptual model of AI-powered mathematics learning with six interrelated components and four outcome categories
description: Figure 1 presents a conceptual model developed from connectivism and adaptive instruction comprising "six interrelated components: learner participation, learning networks, AI-driven ITSs and adaptive tools, networked learning and problem-solving, AI-enhanced learning progression, and learning outcomes". Outcomes are differentiated into cognitive, achievement, behavioural-affective, and instructional categories that are not treated as interchangeable. Relationships are conceptual and reciprocal, not statistically tested causal pathways. Contextual conditions such as infrastructure, teacher preparedness, and data governance condition all relationships.
requirements: Valid learner modelling, adaptive tasks, diagnostic feedback, appropriately calibrated scaffolding, and meaningful teacher mediation for the model's expected benefits to be realised.
constraints: The model's relationships are conceptual and reciprocal, not statistically tested causal pathways; a system cannot be considered educationally effective if its benefits accrue mainly to learners with reliable digital access.
target_learners: mathematics learners in AI-supported tutoring and adaptive learning settings
target_learning_goals: personalised instruction, real-time feedback, engagement, problem-solving, and teacher-informed differentiation
examples: The review synthesises its 20 retained publications through a mechanism-outcome-context logic mapping mechanisms such as learner modelling and real-time feedback onto the four outcome categories.

citation: Ogunsakin IB, Ayanwale MA, Falebita OS and Felemu OJ (2026) Reimagining mathematics education through intelligent tutoring: evidence, opportunities, and implementation challenges. Front. Educ. 11:1943906. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1943906
title: Deploy ITSs as human-guided instructional resources with teacher mediation, not as autonomous replacements for teachers
description: The review concludes that "ITSs should function as human-guided instructional resources rather than autonomous replacements for teachers". Teachers interpret system-generated evidence against curricular goals, classroom observations, and knowledge of individual learners, because algorithmic recommendations may not reliably distinguish misconceptions, linguistic difficulties, disengagement, and technical interruptions. AI analytics should function as an additional source of formative evidence rather than an authoritative replacement for teachers' professional knowledge.
requirements: Teacher preparedness, pedagogical and curricular alignment, valid assessment, and teachers' capacity to translate system outputs into meaningful instructional action.
constraints: The review states algorithmic classifications may misrepresent learners when models are trained on unrepresentative data or rely on narrow indicators of mathematical competence.
target_learners: mathematics learners in classrooms where teachers mediate ITS use
target_learning_goals: formative assessment, targeted intervention, and differentiated mathematics instruction
examples: The review's synthesis found the most consistent benefits when systems combined valid learner modelling with adaptive tasks, diagnostic feedback, calibrated scaffolding, and meaningful teacher mediation.

title: DMO-GRU hybrid framework: Dwarf Mongoose Optimization tuning of a Gated Recurrent Unit for student performance prediction
description: The DMO-GRU framework combines the Dwarf Mongoose Optimization algorithm with a Gated Recurrent Unit neural network. DMO performs feature selection and automatic hyperparameter tuning (learning rate, dropout, number of hidden units), while the GRU captures temporal patterns in student learning data. The article states that "our hybrid DMO-GRU model makes use of DMO's worldwide search capabilities" to improve GRU's learning process and produce more precise forecasts of student engagement and performance. The authors position the integration as suited to noisy, sparse or irregular educational data and as promoting individualized, adaptive learning.

title: Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) network for modeling sequential student learning behaviour
description: The GRU is a recurrent neural network architecture used in the proposed model to capture temporal patterns in student engagement, quiz performance and content interaction. The article explains that "the Gate Recurrent Unit is a type of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) that focusses on solving the gradient disappearance problem", operating with a reset gate that decides how new input combines with old memories and an update gate that controls how much previous memory is retained at each time step. Its lightweight architecture is described as enabling quicker training and lower computational cost than typical LSTM models, suiting real-time online learning applications.

article_title: Academic integrity in the age of generative AI: A scoping review of research on higher education student voices
citation: Ji Ying. (2026). Academic Integrity in the Age of Generative AI: a Scoping Review of Research on Higher Education Student Voices. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09752-1
title: Students as active ethical agents navigating an ethical grey zone in GenAI use
description: The review's organizing framework positions higher education students not as passive recipients of GenAI technology or institutional policies, nor as culprits who breach integrity without ethical constraints, but as active agents who interpret, adapt, and shape the ethical contours of GenAI use. Drawing on Bandura's notion of ethical agency, it frames students as navigating the 'grey areas' of academic integrity through personal ethical frameworks and reasoning, exercising agency via human-AI collaboration, de facto policymaking, strategic calibration, and resistance to over-reliance. The framework underpins the review's call for students to be treated as partners in developing policies.

academic integrity

citation: Haozhe Jiang, Yixin Li, Ritesh Chugh, Yueyou Xin and Hongyu Cheng. (2026). The AI-powered co-inquirer: a systematic review of ChatGPT for inquiry-based learning in STEAM education. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00628-9
title: Five-role taxonomy of ChatGPT in STEAM inquiry-based learning: tutor, learning tool, domain expert, learning peer, and teaching assistant
description: The review inductively identified five distinct roles ChatGPT assumes in STEAM-related IBL, classified by primary pedagogical function and the nature of interaction with learners or teachers. The tutor role provides instructional scaffolding and corrective feedback; the learning tool role is a practical instrument for searching, question generation, and task completion; the domain expert role supplies disciplinary knowledge and content-specific suggestions; the learning peer role engages learners as a conversational partner for exchanging ideas; and the teaching assistant role supports teachers in lesson preparation, task design, and feedback generation. The review notes these roles are not mutually exclusive and often shift with inquiry phase and instructional design.
requirements: Roles are distinguished analytically by primary pedagogical function and the nature of interaction between ChatGPT and learners or teachers
constraints: Roles were identified from 24 empirical studies in STEAM-related IBL contexts and may shift depending on the inquiry phase and instructional design

examples: Guiding mathematical problem-solving (tutor), assisting question formulation (learning tool), suggesting greener analytical methods in chemistry laboratory learning (domain expert), participating in reflective discussion (learning peer), and supporting scenario-based activity design (teaching assistant)

title: Integrated analytical framework combining the technology-based learning framework with Pedaste et al.'s five-phase inquiry cycle

title: Engineering Design-Based Learning (EDBL) as a six-stage iterative pedagogical framework
description: EDBL is a pedagogical approach grounded in problem-based learning and constructivist theories in which students engage in authentic, iterative design challenges to develop scientific understanding and practical skills. The article describes it as typically involving six core stages: "(1) identifying the problem, (2) researching the problem, (3) proposing possible solutions, (4) selecting and developing the best solution, (5) prototyping and testing, and (6) evaluating and redesigning." In science education it fosters systems thinking, collaboration, and creative problem-solving deemed essential for STEM literacy. The study uses EDBL stages as the primary evaluation framework for rating AI-generated lesson plans.
requirements: Instructional materials that are context-sensitive, cognitively engaging, and pedagogically sequenced
Well-designed lesson plans that guide students through each phase and align with cognitive and affective curriculum goals
target_learners: 6th-grade science students
target_learning_goals: Scientific understanding and practical skills through iterative design challenges
Systems thinking, collaboration, and creative problem-solving for STEM literacy
examples: The study asked both AI platforms to generate an EDBL-based lesson plan for a 6th-grade 'Sustainable Living and Biodiversity' unit and had eleven experts rate each plan against the EDBL stages.
key_sources: Karaismailoglu, F., Surmeli, H., & Yildirim, M. (2026). Suitability of Artificial Intelligence Supported Lesson Plans from the Perspective of Science Education Experts. Journal of Science Education and Technology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-026-10342-4

citation: Karaismailoglu, F., Surmeli, H., & Yildirim, M. (2026). Suitability of Artificial Intelligence Supported Lesson Plans from the Perspective of Science Education Experts. Journal of Science Education and Technology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-026-10342-4
title: Build pedagogical models and learning-science principles into educational AI systems, since domain-specific training improves instructional output quality
description: The article argues that AI developers should integrate established pedagogical models such as EDBL into system design, enabling more coherent and process-oriented instructional outputs. The education-focused platform's stronger performance in supporting EDBL's iterative stages suggests that "pedagogical training in AI systems can yield meaningful improvements, regardless of subject matter or grade level." Developers are advised to prioritize deeper integration of learning science principles and pedagogical models into AI architectures.
requirements: Integration of established pedagogical models such as EDBL into AI system design
constraints: Both platforms still scored lowest in engineering skills, indicating a persistent challenge in simulating complex, process-oriented learning tasks
target_learners: Teachers and students using AI-supported lesson planning in science education
target_learning_goals: Process-oriented, iterative instructional outputs aligned with pedagogical frameworks
examples: The education-focused platform (Teacher's Buddy) outperformed the general-purpose ChatGPT-4 on iterative EDBL stages and on most overall quality criteria in expert ratings.

article_title: Designing an AI-integrated role-rotation pedagogical model to support competence-related learning in pre-service educational psychologists
citation: Kenzhebayeva Z, Matayev B, Sarsembayeva E, Kolyukh O, Assenova N and Ospanova A (2026) Designing an AI-integrated role-rotation pedagogical model to support competence-related learning in pre-service educational psychologists. Front. Educ. 11:1905781. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1905781
title: AI-integrated role-rotation pedagogical model conceptualizing role rotation as a mechanism for structuring critical human-AI interaction
description: The model combines four interconnected components: a digital educational environment, integration of generative AI tools, case-based learning, and collaborative role-based interaction with role rotation. Grounded in socio-constructivist, reflective, and experiential perspectives, it conceptualizes AI as "a mediating cognitive and reflective tool embedded within case-based learning, role rotation, and collaborative reflection." Its novel contribution is treating role rotation "not merely as a participation strategy but as a pedagogical mechanism for structuring critical human-AI interaction in professional learning," requiring students to reconsider AI-generated outputs from analytical, practical, and reflective positions.
requirements: Students rotate through all four professional roles across iterative learning cycles
AI use is embedded in case-based tasks with prompts requiring comparison with theory and contextual adaptation
constraints: Developed and examined in gifted-education coursework for pre-service educational psychologists; findings are context-specific qualitative evidence of engagement, not demonstrated competence gains
target_learners: Undergraduate pre-service educational psychologists
target_learning_goals: Professional reasoning and case analysis
Intervention planning and contextual adaptation
Critical evaluation of AI-generated outputs
Reflective practice
examples: In the eight-week intervention, groups of five students rotated through Case Constructor, Research Analyst, Practitioner-Interventionist, and Reflective Researcher roles on gifted-education cases using ChatGPT-5 with role-specific prompts.
key_sources: Kenzhebayeva Z, Matayev B, Sarsembayeva E, Kolyukh O, Assenova N and Ospanova A (2026) Designing an AI-integrated role-rotation pedagogical model to support competence-related learning in pre-service educational psychologists.
