citation: Kenzhebayeva Z, Matayev B, Sarsembayeva E, Kolyukh O, Assenova N and Ospanova A (2026) Designing an AI-integrated role-rotation pedagogical model to support competence-related learning in pre-service educational psychologists. Front. Educ. 11:1905781. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1905781
title: Four-role rotation cycle: Case Constructor, Research Analyst, Practitioner-Interventionist, and Reflective Researcher
description: The pattern assigns four successive professional roles within each case-based learning cycle. The Case Constructor focuses on "contextual problem framing"; the Research Analyst evaluates evidence and compares AI-generated information with psychological theories; the Practitioner-Interventionist adapts recommendations to specific educational contexts and justifies strategies; and the Reflective Researcher critically examines AI-generated outputs and collaborative decisions. All participants rotated through each role, ensuring every student experienced all role perspectives at least once during the iterative learning cycles.
requirements: Small collaborative groups that remain stable across cycles
Explicit role descriptions and facilitation, since participants reported uncertainty in unfamiliar roles
constraints: The Reflective Researcher role was most frequently described as challenging; the Case Constructor role was generally perceived as more accessible
target_learners: Undergraduate pre-service educational psychologists in professional preparation coursework
target_learning_goals: Perspective-taking across professional roles
Analytical reasoning and evidence evaluation
Intervention planning
Critical reflection on professional decisions
examples: Table 1 presents an illustrative weekly cycle in which a perfectionism/social-anxiety gifted-learner case moves through case construction, AI-comparative analysis, intervention planning, and critical reflective evaluation.

article_title: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
citation: Kestin, G., Miller, K., Klales, A., Milbourne, T. & Ponti, G. (2025). AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting. Scientific Reports 15:17458. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-97652-6
title: PS2 Pal: a custom AI tutor platform engineered around pedagogical best practices
description: PS2 Pal is a GPT-4-based AI tutoring platform built for undergraduate physics lessons. Its system prompt was engineered to "facilitate active engagement, manage cognitive load, and promote a growth mindset," and because a prompt alone could not reliably scaffold multi-part problems, the platform guides students sequentially through each part of each problem. Prompts were enriched with comprehensive step-by-step answers to guard against hallucinations; 83% of students rated its explanations as good as or better than human instructors'.
requirements: A large language model capable of closely following complex prompts
Expert-crafted, question-specific prompts written by instructors experienced with the content
A carefully structured framework designed to scaffold and guide student interactions
High-quality instructional videos
constraints: Accuracy relied on pre-written answers rather than model-generated solutions
Preparation of system prompts and solutions took significant overhead, and the platform software took several months to develop
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory physics
target_learning_goals: physics concepts and problem-solving skills at the understanding, applying, and analyzing levels of Bloom's Taxonomy
examples: Students worked through the lesson handout, asking questions and confirming answers with the AI tutor called PS2 Pal
key_sources: Kestin, G., Miller, K., Klales, A., Milbourne, T. & Ponti, G. (2025). AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting. Scientific Reports 15:17458. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-97652-6

citation: Kestin, G., Miller, K., Klales, A., Milbourne, T. & Ponti, G. (2025). AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting. Scientific Reports 15:17458. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-97652-6
title: Design AI tutoring systems around seven research-based pedagogical best practices
description: The article enumerates best practices that foster learning and applies them to AI tutor design: "(i) facilitating active learning, (ii) managing cognitive load, (iii) promoting a growth mindset, (iv) scaffolding content, (v) ensuring accuracy of information and feedback, (vi) delivering such feedback and information in a targeted and timely fashion, and (vii) allowing for self-pacing." Practices i-v were built via system prompts and platform structure; vi-vii are the personalization advantages AI offers over classrooms.
requirements: Student-AI interactions must be carefully designed to follow research-based best practices
Pedagogical best practices must be explicitly and carefully built into each application
constraints: A system prompt alone could not reliably scaffold problems with multiple parts
LLM hallucinations pose a significant challenge for educational use

target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of science content
examples: The AI platform guided students sequentially through each part of each problem, mirroring the in-class instructor's approach

article_title: Redefining personalized learning in the artificial intelligence era: an updated systematic review from 2019 to 2025
citation: Khalifeh, F., Santiago, R., & Palau, R. (2026). Redefining personalized learning in the artificial intelligence era: an updated systematic review from 2019 to 2025. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00440-6
title: Eight core components of AI-supported personalized learning as a socio-technical system
description: The review synthesizes across included studies that AI-supported personalized learning is best understood as a socio-technical system integrating pedagogical design, algorithmic processes, and ethical governance. It identifies eight essential components: "learner profile, data inputs, content model, instructional model, adaptive engine, interface and user controls, personalization goals, and evaluation and governance." This framework organizes how the review defines personalized learning in AI-rich contexts and guides its comparison of related terms.
requirements: All eight components must be addressed for a comprehensive definition of AI-supported personalized learning
constraints: Derived from synthesis of studies published 2019–2025 in nine high-impact educational technology journals
target_learners: K-12 and higher education learners using AI-supported learning systems
target_learning_goals: Tailoring content, pacing, and support to individual learner needs, characteristics, and goals
examples: The review used this component set to organize findings across its seven research questions on term definitions and interrelationships

article_title: The Intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Instructional Design Practice: A Systematic Review
citation: Pınar Nuhoğlu Kibar & Hale Ilgaz. (2026). The intersection of artificial intelligence and instructional design practice: a systematic review. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10624-z
title: Human–AI collaboration in instructional design: AI as co-worker, collaborator, and partner rather than a mere tool
description: The review synthesizes an emerging conceptualization in which AI is "not only regarded as a tool but was also conceptualised as a co-worker, collaborator, and partner within the instructional design process". It reports that human–AI collaboration leverages complementary strengths, with AI supporting personalization, content generation, feedback, and data-informed decisions, while "pedagogical intent, ethical judgment, and critical reflection remain human-centered responsibilities". The review positions AI predominantly as a collaborative assistant rather than an autonomous agent that augments human judgment and pedagogical reasoning.
requirements: Human expertise must remain central: contextual understanding, factual verification, and pedagogical soundness of AI outputs depend on designers' professional judgment
constraints: The review reports evidence regarding AI's added value in ID as emergent and context dependent, with few long-term, process-focused studies
target_learners: instructional designers
teachers
faculty members
pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: effective integration of AI into instructional design processes
maintaining pedagogical integrity in AI-supported design
examples: The review reports Liu & Xiao (2025) finding teachers used GenAI especially in the Analysis, Design, and Evaluation phases of ADDIE, and Lawrence et al. (2023) studying teachers sharing control with an AI application coordinating learning transitions
key_sources: Pınar Nuhoğlu Kibar & Hale Ilgaz. (2026). The intersection of artificial intelligence and instructional design practice: a systematic review. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10624-z

article_title: The Intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Instructional Design Practice: A Systematic Review
citation: Pınar Nuhoğlu Kibar & Hale Ilgaz. (2026). The intersection of artificial intelligence and instructional design practice: a systematic review. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10624-z
title: Treat AI-generated instructional design outputs as drafts requiring active human review, adaptation, and contextualization rather than using them directly
description: The review's synthesis indicates AI functions most effectively when its outputs are actively mediated by designers and teachers. It reports that "AI is found to function most effectively when AI-generated outputs are actively reviewed, adapted, and contextualized, rather than being used directly", and advocates a "human-in-the-loop" approach in which human cognition and ethical oversight guide GenAI outputs toward pedagogical integrity. GenAI is characterized as an augmentative rather than replacement technology.
requirements: Designers must verify factual accuracy and ensure pedagogical soundness of AI-generated materials
Iterative prompt refinement is needed to produce instructionally meaningful outputs
constraints: The review reports iterative prompting constitutes an additional cognitive and design workload, and AI outputs often lack sensitivity to local instructional conditions
target_learners: instructional designers
teachers
pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: producing pedagogically aligned, contextually appropriate instructional materials with AI support
examples: The review reports Choi et al. (2024) found GenAI-generated course elements often lacked feasibility and accuracy, requiring designers to intervene through revision and fact-checking, and Choi (2025) found pre-service teachers often revised or discarded AI-generated lesson components

article_title: Adult Learners' Perspectives of AI Applications in Supporting Andragogy
citation: Jinhee Kim, Xi Lin, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick. (2026). Adult learners' perspectives of AI applications in supporting andragogy. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10621-2
title: Three learner-derived design principles for AI systems supporting andragogy: human-in-the-loop, emotional design, and adaptability
description: The study distills adult learners' interview perspectives into three design-principle themes with six sub-themes: human-in-the-loop (building shared mental models between humans and AI; enabling human-AI co-creation), emotional design (calibrating an appropriate level of AI reliance; empathetic communication), and adaptability (continuous adaptation; interoperability). Learners wanted AI that keeps "learning about the individual learners it is interacting with," guides skepticism of its own outputs, communicates empathetically, adapts after deployment, and works across platforms.
requirements: AI systems must involve human input, oversight, and decision-making alongside AI, with interpretable explanations of system behavior and learner control over generative processes.
constraints: Findings derive from perceptions of a small sample of degree-seeking adult learners on the East Coast of the US and are inherently subjective; the authors call for empirical measurement of effectiveness in future research.
target_learners: Adult learners (typically 25 years or older) in online learning environments
target_learning_goals: Self-directed, experience-based, problem-centered adult learning aligned with personal and professional goals
examples: Participants designed 11 AI-application scenarios and paper prototypes (e.g., AI tutor, empathetic chatbot, AI simulation, AI-powered career coach) that were reviewed by five faculty experts and used as interview prompts.

article_title: AI Anxiety: A Comprehensive Analysis of Psychological Factors and Interventions
citation: Kim, J.J.H., Soh, J., Kadkol, S., Solomon, I., Yeh, H., Srivatsa, A.V., Nahass, G.R., Choi, J.Y., Lee, S., Nyugen, T., Ajilore, O. (2025). AI Anxiety: a comprehensive analysis of psychological factors and interventions. AI Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00686-9
title: AI Anxiety as a named psychological phenomenon: apprehension or fear stemming from accelerated AI development
description: The article names and defines AI Anxiety as a psychological phenomenon arising from rapid AI advancement. It states that the rapid advancement of AI "has raised significant concerns regarding its impact on human psychology, leading to a phenomenon termed AI Anxiety—feelings of apprehension or fear stemming from the accelerated development of AI technologies." The article positions this construct as under-analysed, stating the current literature lacks a comprehensive analysis, and offers the paper as an attempt to fill that gap by examining psychological factors and proposing solutions. In the wiki this serves as the anchor concept for claims about AI Anxiety's causes and remedies.
requirements: The construct is presented as needing comprehensive analysis, which the article says the current literature lacks
constraints: The accessible text is the abstract; the construct is defined but not empirically measured in the available text
target_learners: Adults and students affected by the spread of AI technologies, including learners in educational settings
target_learning_goals: Understanding psychological responses to AI technologies
Recognising AI Anxiety as a barrier to engagement with AI-enabled learning and work
examples: The article's framing of AI Anxiety as a phenomenon distinct enough to warrant its own comprehensive analysis and intervention set
key_sources: Kim, J.J.H., Soh, J., Kadkol, S., Solomon, I., Yeh, H., Srivatsa, A.V., Nahass, G.R., Choi, J.Y., Lee, S., Nyugen, T., Ajilore, O. (2025). AI Anxiety: a comprehensive analysis of psychological factors and interventions. AI Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00686-9

article_title: AI Anxiety: A Comprehensive Analysis of Psychological Factors and Interventions
citation: Kim, J.J.H., Soh, J., Kadkol, S., Solomon, I., Yeh, H., Srivatsa, A.V., Nahass, G.R., Choi, J.Y., Lee, S., Nyugen, T., Ajilore, O. (2025). AI Anxiety: a comprehensive analysis of psychological factors and interventions. AI Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00686-9
title: A causes taxonomy for AI Anxiety: fear of replacement as primary contributor with four secondary causes
description: The article organises the drivers of AI Anxiety into a primary cause and a set of secondary causes. It states: "We delve into the primary contributor to AI Anxiety—the fear of replacement by AI—and explore secondary causes such as uncontrolled AI growth, privacy concerns, AI-generated misinformation, and AI biases." This yields a two-tier taxonomy: replacement fear at the top, with uncontrolled growth, privacy, misinformation, and bias as secondary branches. The wiki can use this structure to organise interventions targeting each cause.
requirements: Interventions should be matched to the specific cause of anxiety they target, per the article's cause-then-solution structure
constraints: The taxonomy is asserted analytically in the abstract; the accessible text reports no empirical validation of the cause hierarchy
target_learners: Workers, students, and the general public experiencing apprehension about AI technologies
target_learning_goals: Understanding the psychological drivers of AI Anxiety
Distinguishing primary from secondary causes when designing interventions
examples: The article's own structuring of its analysis: primary contributor first, then secondary causes, then multidisciplinary solutions
key_sources: Kim, J.J.H., Soh, J., Kadkol, S., Solomon, I., Yeh, H., Srivatsa, A.V., Nahass, G.R., Choi, J.Y., Lee, S., Nyugen, T., Ajilore, O. (2025). AI Anxiety: a comprehensive analysis of psychological factors and interventions. AI Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00686-9

article_title: AI Anxiety: A Comprehensive Analysis of Psychological Factors and Interventions
citation: Kim, J.J.H., Soh, J., Kadkol, S., Solomon, I., Yeh, H., Srivatsa, A.V., Nahass, G.R., Choi, J.Y., Lee, S., Nyugen, T., Ajilore, O. (2025). AI Anxiety: a comprehensive analysis of psychological factors and interventions. AI Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00686-9
title: Mitigate rising AI Anxiety by first understanding its root causes and then implementing strategic interventions
description: The article closes its abstract with a design principle for anyone responding to AI Anxiety: diagnosis precedes intervention. It states that "Understanding the root causes of AI Anxiety and implementing strategic interventions are critical steps for mitigating its rise as society enters the era of pervasive AI." The principle directs educators and designers to analyse which causes of anxiety operate in their population before selecting interventions, consistent with the article's cause-taxonomy-then-solutions structure. It frames both steps as critical rather than optional.
requirements: Interventions must be preceded by an analysis of the root causes of AI Anxiety in the target population
constraints: The article presents this as a critical step within its broader argument; the accessible text reports no test of the principle's effectiveness
target_learners: Educators, institutions, and policymakers designing responses to AI Anxiety among learners and workers
target_learning_goals: Mitigating AI Anxiety as AI becomes pervasive in learning and work contexts
examples: The article's own sequence: examining psychological factors underlying AI Anxiety before proposing solutions to tackle the problem

article_title: Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications
citation: Jinhee Kim, Xi Lin, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick. (2026). Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications and AI system design principles. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10655-6
title: The Productive Failure framework: two phases of generation/exploration and consolidation/knowledge assembly
description: The article presents a PF framework, extended from Kapur's two-phase model, organizing productive failure into two phases with six subcategories. Phase 1 covers problem exploration, solution generation, and collaborative problem-solving; Phase 2 covers comparison and contrast, knowledge reorganization, and knowledge transfer. The authors state, "The PF model is organized into two phases: (1) Generation and Exploration and (2) Consolidation and Knowledge Assembly." The framework structures both the course design and the thematic analysis of AI support.
requirements: Learners engage with complex, ill-structured problems targeting concepts they have not yet learned before receiving instruction
constraints: The authors note PF is not universally effective and depends on careful implementation, requiring a safe environment, skilled facilitation, and well-chosen problem content
target_learners: adult learners (typically 25 years or older) in higher education
target_learning_goals: deep understanding and long-term knowledge transfer through learning from initial failed attempts
examples: The 15-week COIL course structured team design work by PF phases, from initial brainstorming notes in Weeks 1-2 to final project reports in Weeks 13-15
key_sources: Jinhee Kim, Xi Lin, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick. (2026). Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications and AI system design principles. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10655-6

article_title: Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications
citation: Jinhee Kim, Xi Lin, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick. (2026). Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications and AI system design principles. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10655-6
title: Five learner-informed design principles for AI systems supporting productive-failure-based learning
description: The study synthesizes adult learners' reflections into five design-principle themes with 13 sub-themes: human-AI collaboration (complementary roles, interpretability, human-in-the-loop), usability (accessibility and inclusivity, error handling, visual cues of AI usage, controllability), open knowledge and resource utilization (data interoperability, seamless integration), reflective design (correction mechanisms, follow-up questions), and emotional design (AI personality, AI conversation design). The authors state that "these principles represent learner-derived design intentions that cut across multiple project contexts and design scenarios."
requirements: Principles emerged from storyboards, paper prototypes, and focus group discussions rather than from single, fully specified system designs
constraints: Teams did not develop operational AI systems; principles were not all instantiated as concrete interface features in every prototype
target_learners: adult learners (typically 25 years or older) as primary stakeholders and end-users of adult learning systems
target_learning_goals: preserving productive struggle while offering targeted, non-directive AI support across PF phases
examples: Table 4 lists the 13 sub-themes with exemplary participant quotes, such as learners choosing the level of AI assistance they are comfortable with
key_sources: Jinhee Kim, Xi Lin, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick. (2026). Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications and AI system design principles. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10655-6

article_title: Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications
citation: Jinhee Kim, Xi Lin, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick. (2026). Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications and AI system design principles. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10655-6
title: Design PF-supporting AI to ask questions and foster comparison rather than supply correct solutions
description: This principle holds that AI supporting productive failure should act as a partner rather than a problem-solver, keeping learners at the center while offering support when needed. The article argues that supplying the correct solution short-circuits the PF process; instead, "the AI system should ask questions, motivate learners to explain their reasoning, or foster comparisons between different ideas." The study's teams instantiated this in chatbots that deliberately avoided direct answers and prompted learners to justify assumptions and compare alternatives.
requirements: AI behaviors must preserve learners' ownership of meaning-making and sustain productive struggle during exploration
constraints: Too much scaffolding, especially during early problem generation, may reduce the productive struggle that drives deep learning
target_learners: adult learners engaging in PF-based learning before formal instruction
target_learning_goals: deep understanding through productive struggle, comparison of approaches, and knowledge reorganization
examples: Multiple teams designed AI chatbots that deliberately avoided providing direct answers, instead prompting learners to justify assumptions, compare alternatives, or revisit earlier failures
key_sources: Jinhee Kim, Xi Lin, Seongryeong Yu, Rita Detrick. (2026). Designing AI systems to support a productive-failure-based learning: insights from adult learners on AI applications and AI system design principles. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10655-6

article_title: Know When to Trust: Making AI Scoring More Reliable for Educational Assessment
citation: Organisciak, P., & Acar, S. (2026). Know when to trust: Making AI scoring more reliable for educational assessment. Behavior Research. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03058-1
title: Use self-confidence, weighted probabilistic scoring, and ensembles as drop-in improvements to existing LLM-based educational scoring systems
description: The article recommends adopting its three techniques as drop-in additions to existing LLM scoring pipelines: "All three techniques improve the performance and trustworthiness of automated scoring models, and are compatible as drop-in improvements to existing techniques." It positions them for systems that derive a quantitative measure from text input.
requirements: An existing LLM-based scoring system that derives a quantitative measure from a text input
constraints: The article's evidence base is scoring of divergent thinking responses (the Alternative Uses Test)
target_learners: participants in creativity assessment studies
target_learning_goals: reliable automated scoring of open-ended divergent thinking responses
examples: The techniques were tested on over 20,000 Alternative Uses Test responses from more than 2,000 participants across multiple studies, improving correlation with human judges from r = 0.781 to r = 0.823
key_sources: Organisciak, P., & Acar, S. (2026). Know when to trust: Making AI scoring more reliable for educational assessment. Behavior Research. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03058-1

article_title: Know When to Trust: Making AI Scoring More Reliable for Educational Assessment
citation: Organisciak, P., & Acar, S. (2026). Know when to trust: Making AI scoring more reliable for educational assessment. Behavior Research. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03058-1
title: Ocsai and confidence Python libraries for confidence-aware LLM scoring
description: The authors release two software artifacts. The ocsai library implements "confidence measurement and weighted probabilistic scoring in Python". A standalone library, named confidence, demonstrates "drop-in confidence-aware scoring for the OpenAI and Gemini APIs, as well as HuggingFace transformers, which covers many open weights models", runnable with a single command without local installation, with examples for extracting log probabilities and computing weighted scores.
requirements: Supported backend (OpenAI, Gemini, or HuggingFace transformers) for the confidence library
target_learners: researchers and practitioners scoring open-ended text responses
target_learning_goals: automated scoring of divergent thinking and other text-based measures
examples: The verbal divergent thinking implementation is available in a free web-based tool at https://openscoring.du.edu/scoringllm, shown in Fig. 8

article_title: Beyond prior knowledge: the predictive role of knowledge-building in tutor learning
citation: Fathima Ameen, Tasmia Shahriar, Aditi Mallavarapu, Shiyan Jiang, Noboru Matsuda. (2026). Beyond prior knowledge: the predictive role of knowledge-building in tutor learning. Behaviormetrika. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41237-026-00294-9
title: ExpectAdapt: an expectation-tailored adaptive questioning framework of three stacked LLMs for teachable agents
description: ExpectAdapt (Expectation-tailored Adaptive Questioning Framework) generates adaptive follow-up questions after a tutor answers a static focal question. It consists of "three stacked Large Language Models (LLMs)": an Expected Response Generator, an Alignment Detector, and a Follow-up Question Generator, all using GPT-3.5-turbo via the OpenAI API. The Alignment Detector compares the tutor's response to an expected response and, in the study, "classified 69% of KBR and 63% of KTR as aligned"; the generator targets uncovered conceptual stems, with a maximum of three follow-ups per focal question.
requirements: Requires an expected-response generator supplied with domain-specific conceptual assertions and an expert role prompt to minimize mathematical errors
Requires the follow-up generator to stop once all stems from the expected response have been addressed
constraints: A follow-up question is generated only when the response is classified as aligned, to avoid being out of context or overly corrective
target_learners: middle school students (grades 6–8) learning algebraic equation solving
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge and procedural skill in algebraic equation solving
shifting tutors from knowledge-telling to knowledge-building responses
examples: In the study, ExpectAdapt was integrated into APLUS so SimStudent posed follow-up questions such as "Are all equations with no coefficient done?" after shallow tutor responses

citation: Fathima Ameen, Tasmia Shahriar, Aditi Mallavarapu, Shiyan Jiang, Noboru Matsuda. (2026). Beyond prior knowledge: the predictive role of knowledge-building in tutor learning. Behaviormetrika. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41237-026-00294-9
title: APLUS: a learning-by-teaching environment in which students tutor SimStudent to solve algebraic equations
description: APLUS (Artificial Peer Learning Using SimStudent) is an online learning-by-teaching environment in which students, acting as tutors, "teach a virtual agent named SimStudent to solve algebraic equations through guided problem solving". SimStudent learns production rules via programming by demonstration (inductive logic programming), proposes solution steps, and asks focal questions when the tutor disagrees or lacks a production. Tutors can quiz SimStudent across four quiz levels and access a Problem Bank, Unit Overview, Introduction Video, worked Examples, and a meta-tutor agent, Mr. Williams, who gives voluntary metacognitive hints.
requirements: SimStudent is pre-trained on a small set of one-step equations to establish baseline knowledge before tutoring begins
constraints: In the version used in the study, solution steps allow only four basic math operations: add, subtract, multiply, and divide by a term
target_learners: middle school students (grades 6–8)
target_learning_goals: algebraic equation solving
effective tutoring and self-regulated learning strategies
examples: Mr. Williams might hint, "SimStudent failed on the two-step equation. Teaching similar equations will help him pass that quiz item."

article_title: Layer-Sensitive Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Assisted Writing: Supported Performance and Independent No-AI Outcomes
citation: Chen X (2026) Layer-sensitive cognitive offloading in generative AI-assisted writing: supported performance and independent no-AI outcomes. Front. Psychol. 17:1906199. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906199
title: Layer-sensitive account of cognitive offloading in GenAI-assisted writing
description: The article proposes a four-layer account of cognitive offloading in GenAI-assisted writing, distinguishing surface, structural, idea, and reasoning offloading as "related but non-equivalent dimensions". Surface offloading concerns grammar, vocabulary, and local expression; structural offloading concerns outlines, sequencing, and global organization; idea offloading concerns claims, examples, and content directions; reasoning offloading concerns warrants, counterarguments, evidence interpretation, and argumentative logic. The framework treats frequency of AI use as insufficient, since one reasoning-generation request may matter more than several language requests.
requirements: Primary layer scores derived from coded interaction and revision evidence, with brief self-report used only for triangulation
constraints: The article states the offloading framework showed promising initial structural, reliability, and convergence evidence but requires independent validation
target_learners: Chinese L1 undergraduates writing academic English
target_learning_goals: Independent academic writing quality
Higher-order thinking in argumentative writing
examples: Layer scores were coded from prompts, AI outputs, adoption decisions, and draft–revision records; a four-factor model fit substantially better than a one-factor model (CFI = 0.959 vs 0.585)
key_sources: Chen X (2026) Layer-sensitive cognitive offloading in generative AI-assisted writing: supported performance and independent no-AI outcomes. Front. Psychol. 17:1906199. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906199

article_title: Layer-Sensitive Cognitive Offloading in Generative AI-Assisted Writing: Supported Performance and Independent No-AI Outcomes
citation: Chen X (2026) Layer-sensitive cognitive offloading in generative AI-assisted writing: supported performance and independent no-AI outcomes. Front. Psychol. 17:1906199. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1906199
title: Keep GenAI assistance away from the claim, evidence, and revision operations through which writing competence develops
description: The article's instructional implications recommend designing GenAI-supported writing so that the tool assists without assuming responsibility for core reasoning operations. Recommended practices include that "Students can complete an independent claim–evidence plan before consulting AI", that AI access initially be limited to diagnostic questions, alternatives, reader feedback, and local language clarification, and that students classify each AI-influenced change as accepted, modified, or rejected with a rationale. Rubrics can credit reasoning provenance and revision ownership, and support can then be faded with periodic independent tasks.
requirements: Logging or documentation of adoption decisions so students justify how AI suggestions were accepted, changed, or rejected
constraints: The bounded condition combined delegation restrictions with compulsory reflection, so the design cannot isolate the effect of either component; results are classroom-level associations from six intact classes, not definitive causal effects
target_learners: Undergraduate L2 academic writers
target_learning_goals: Independent writing competence after AI support is removed
Higher-order thinking and revision ownership
examples: In the study, bounded-support students could request brainstorming questions, alternative outline options, reader-response feedback, and language clarification, while requests for complete paragraphs, final thesis statements, or full-text rewriting were prohibited

article_title: 'The LEARN Framework for Responsible Use of Generative AI in Education: A Neuroscience-Informed Model for Problem-Based Learning'
citation: Lorna Uden · Gwo-Jen Hwang. (2026). The LEARN framework for responsible use of generative AI in education: a neuroscience-informed model for problem-based learning. Journal of Computers in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40692-026-00398-x
title: The LEARN framework: five components for neuroscience-informed, PBL-based GAI assessment design
description: The LEARN framework is a conceptual, neuroscience-informed model comprising five interrelated components: Lifelong Learning, Engagement, Active Processing, Reflection, and Neuro-based Design. It synthesises cognitive/educational neuroscience, constructivist and problem-based learning theory, and literature on ethical engagement with GAI, positioning GAI 'as a cognitive scaffold rather than as a cognitive substitute'. Each component is enacted through PBL practices, explained by neurocognitive mechanisms, and operationalised through assessable learning traces such as portfolios and AI-use disclosure.
requirements: Instructional design must align with neurocognitive principles such as cognitive load management, reward-based motivation, and social connectedness
constraints: The framework is conceptual; the authors state that neuroscience principles 'are not presented as empirical outcomes of the LEARN framework itself, but as theoretical foundations'
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: deep, self-directed, and reflective learning
critical evaluation of AI outputs
ethical self-regulation in AI use
examples: An Environmental Science PBL task in which students analyse declining aquatic biodiversity, using GAI in three staged phases with retained prompts, reasoning maps, and reflective commentary
key_sources: Lorna Uden · Gwo-Jen Hwang. (2026). The LEARN framework for responsible use of generative AI in education: a neuroscience-informed model for problem-based learning. Journal of Computers in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40692-026-00398-x

article_title: 'The LEARN Framework for Responsible Use of Generative AI in Education: A Neuroscience-Informed Model for Problem-Based Learning'
citation: Lorna Uden · Gwo-Jen Hwang. (2026). The LEARN framework for responsible use of generative AI in education: a neuroscience-informed model for problem-based learning. Journal of Computers in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40692-026-00398-x
title: Three foundational pillars of LEARN: motivation, scaffolding, and mentoring
description: The LEARN framework rests on three foundational pillars that act as enabling conditions: 'Motivation, Scaffolding and Mentoring'. Motivation is linked to dopaminergic reward pathways and self-determination theory's autonomy, competence, and relatedness; scaffolding breaks down tasks, provides feedback, and gradually reduces support; mentoring provides social and emotional support through trust and modelling, activating brain regions involved in social cognition and emotional regulation. Together the pillars underpin engagement, adaptability, and ethical AI literacy.
requirements: Assessment tasks must be staged with mentoring, feedback cycles, and structured retrieval practice so scaffolding and mentoring can operate
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement and persistence
independence from AI over-reliance
resilience and ethical modelling
examples: Neuro-based Design assessments scaffolded from simple to complex tasks with mentoring, staged feedback cycles, and retrieval practice

citation: Lorna Uden · Gwo-Jen Hwang. (2026). The LEARN framework for responsible use of generative AI in education: a neuroscience-informed model for problem-based learning. Journal of Computers in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40692-026-00398-x
title: LEARN-informed PBL assessment pattern: staged GAI access with process-weighted rubrics and assessable learning traces
description: A reusable assessment pattern situating learning in an authentic, ill-structured PBL problem with three GAI stages (permitted, restricted, permitted-with-justification) and four assessed artefacts: a Problem Analysis Report, a Reasoning Map, an AI Use Log, and a Reflective Commentary of approximately 500 words. The rubric 'prioritises learning processes over final products', weighting scientific reasoning and use of evidence at 40%, critique and refinement of AI outputs at 25%, reflective and metacognitive engagement at 20%, and the final proposal at 15%.
requirements: Students must retain all AI prompts and outputs, and justify which AI suggestions were accepted, modified, or rejected
constraints: The pattern is illustrated in one Environmental Science example; the article reports no empirical evaluation of the task
target_learners: higher education students in PBL courses
target_learning_goals: evidence-based reasoning
critical evaluation of AI outputs
metacognitive reflection on AI use
examples: The aquatic biodiversity consultancy task in which students act as an environmental consultancy team analysing causes and proposing an evidence-based intervention strategy

article_title: Would You Let a Humanoid Play Storytelling With Your Child? A Usability Study on LLM-Powered Narrative Human-Robot Interaction
citation: Maria Lombardi, Carmela Calabrese, Davide Ghiglino, Caterina Foglino, Davide De Tommaso, Giulia Da Lisca, Lorenzo Natale, Agnieszka Wykowska. (2025). Would you let a humanoid play storytelling with your child? A usability study on LLM-powered narrative Human-Robot Interaction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02505
title: iCub LLM-powered narrative HRI system architecture
description: A companion-like social robotic platform in which the iCub humanoid and a human partner co-create a story in turn from pictures on nine soft cubes, each story built on a sequence of three cubes. Perception modules run online from the robot's own eye camera: face recognition (OpenPose, FaceNet embeddings, an SVM classifier), mutual-gaze detection from 19 facial key-points, online-trainable object detection, and zero-shot sticker description via ChatGPT-4o as VLM. Story generation uses ChatGPT-4o as LLM with ad-hoc prompts, plus speech transcription and synthesis, all orchestrated by a finite state machine over the YARP middleware. The article states the design 'allows to change stimuli fast without training the system again, representing a future easily adaptive tool for therapists.'
requirements: A local network connecting the robot to a GPU-equipped workstation and client laptop running the perception and generation modules
Online-trainable perception so the system is not constrained to a pre-trained subset of partners or objects
constraints: All perception uses only RGB frames from iCub's eye, without external sensors
Latency from external services such as ChatGPT and slow motor movement affected perceived efficiency
target_learners: children under 10, including children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (intended end users)
target_learning_goals: communication skills, turn taking, autonomy, and narrative expression through collaborative storytelling
examples: In the validation experiment each adult participant invented three stories with iCub, exchanging cubes in turn while the robot detected stickers, generated story pieces and gave positive feedback.
key_sources: Maria Lombardi, Carmela Calabrese, Davide Ghiglino, Caterina Foglino, Davide De Tommaso, Giulia Da Lisca, Lorenzo Natale, Agnieszka Wykowska. (2025). Would you let a humanoid play storytelling with your child? A usability study on LLM-powered narrative Human-Robot Interaction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02505

article_title: Would You Let a Humanoid Play Storytelling With Your Child? A Usability Study on LLM-Powered Narrative Human-Robot Interaction
citation: Maria Lombardi, Carmela Calabrese, Davide Ghiglino, Caterina Foglino, Davide De Tommaso, Giulia Da Lisca, Lorenzo Natale, Agnieszka Wykowska. (2025). Would you let a humanoid play storytelling with your child? A usability study on LLM-powered narrative Human-Robot Interaction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.02505
title: Six-phase turn-taking narrative interaction protocol for human-robot story co-creation
description: A reusable interaction structure for a joint human-robot storytelling session, organised in six phases: introduction (task explanation and partner detection), iCub turn (robot asks for, grasps and identifies the first cube and starts the story), human turn (participant chooses the second cube and continues the story while listened to), a further iCub turn for the final cube and ending, a wrap-up phase in which iCub recaps the jointly generated story, and a closure phase in which iCub greets the participant, expressing joy. Phases 2-5 repeat for each trial, so the pattern scales to multiple stories per session.
requirements: Perception modules for face recognition, cube detection and sticker identification so the robot can track turns and respond to the chosen image
Speech-to-text and text-to-speech modules so the robot can listen to and narrate story pieces
constraints: The protocol was validated with adult participants as a feasibility step before deployment with children
target_learners: children under 10 in educational and rehabilitation protocols, including autistic children
target_learning_goals: turn taking, collaborative narrative creation, and communication skills
examples: Each participant invented three stories (trials) with iCub, with the phase sequence repeating per trial and a short ad-hoc questionnaire after each story.

article_title: MathBuddy: Affective Math Tutoring
citation: Debanjana Kar, Leopold Böss, Dacia Braca, Sebastian Dennerlein, Nina Hubig, Philipp Wintersberger, and Yufang Hou. (2025). MathBuddy: A Multimodal System for Affective Math Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19993
title: Map detected student affect to pedagogical moves: challenge positive/neutral students, motivate negative-affect students
description: MathBuddy operationalizes affective adaptation with a simple mapping rule: aggregated student emotion is reduced to Positive, Neutral, or Negative, and this state selects the tutor's pedagogical stance. As the authors state, "if the student is in a positive or neutral affective state, the student is challenged by MathBuddy, while a negative affective state causes the system to try to motivate the student." The rule is grounded in educational-psychology work on academic emotions and is delivered to the LLM tutor via system prompts. It turns continuous multimodal affect sensing into an actionable instructional decision at every conversational turn.
requirements: Reliable real-time emotion recognition from at least one modality (text or facial expression), aggregated into a Positive/Neutral/Negative state before each tutor response
constraints: The authors found that emotion information without education-theory grounding misguides smaller tutor models
The aggregation rule suppresses Neutral states, producing low Neutral recall (0.15) in the user study
target_learners: Mathematics learners in one-on-one tutoring with an LLM-based tutor
target_learning_goals: Math problem-solving with scaffolded guidance; maintaining engagement and motivation during tutoring
examples: In MathBuddy, the aggregated emotion from text (fine-tuned BERT classifier) and webcam facial expressions is mapped to primitives and injected into the tutor prompt, switching between challenge and motivate instructions
key_sources: Debanjana Kar, Leopold Böss, Dacia Braca, Sebastian Dennerlein, Nina Hubig, Philipp Wintersberger, and Yufang Hou. (2025). MathBuddy: A Multimodal System for Affective Math Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19993

article_title: MathBuddy: Affective Math Tutoring
citation: Debanjana Kar, Leopold Böss, Dacia Braca, Sebastian Dennerlein, Nina Hubig, Philipp Wintersberger, and Yufang Hou. (2025). MathBuddy: A Multimodal System for Affective Math Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19993
title: MathBuddy: multimodal emotion-aware LLM math tutoring system
description: MathBuddy is an emotionally aware LLM-powered math tutor that, per the authors, "dynamically models the student's emotions and maps them to relevant pedagogical strategies, making the tutor-student conversation a more empathetic one." It captures emotions from conversational text (a fine-tuned DistilBERT classifier) and from webcam facial expressions (face-api.js, reporting 76% accuracy and 71% F1 on its test set), aggregates both modalities into Positive/Neutral/Negative, and prompts the LLM tutor accordingly. The system has a TypeScript frontend with chat interface, webcam input, and visual workspace, and a Python REST backend for inference. Code, dataset, and demo video are publicly released.
requirements: Webcam access and conversational text input for multimodal emotion capture
A backend LLM tutor model (e.g., LearnLM) prompted with the aggregated emotional state
constraints: The authors state the current text- and face-based modalities "may not be informative enough to accurately capture a user's emotional state" in technical education contexts
Handwritten-note submission is reserved for future research owing to implementation constraints
target_learners: Learners solving mathematics problems (study participants aged 15-55)
target_learning_goals: Geometry and probability problem solving with scaffolded, emotionally adaptive tutoring
examples: In the user study, each participant completed two tutoring sessions (one geometry, one probability problem) in Emotion ON and OFF conditions with randomized order, webcam capture, and pre/post multiple-choice tests
key_sources: Debanjana Kar, Leopold Böss, Dacia Braca, Sebastian Dennerlein, Nina Hubig, Philipp Wintersberger, and Yufang Hou. (2025). MathBuddy: A Multimodal System for Affective Math Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19993

article_title: MathBuddy: Affective Math Tutoring
citation: Debanjana Kar, Leopold Böss, Dacia Braca, Sebastian Dennerlein, Nina Hubig, Philipp Wintersberger, and Yufang Hou. (2025). MathBuddy: A Multimodal System for Affective Math Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19993
title: Annotated student-utterance emotion dataset (224 turns) for text-based emotion recognition in math tutoring
description: The authors annotated student turns in the hard version of the MathDial-Bridge dataset to support developing emotion recognition models from text. Emotion extraction was modeled as multi-label classification over three target states — Boredom, Engagement, and Neutral — with a polarity score from 0 to 2 capturing intensity as an arousal indicator. "Finally, 224 unique student turns were annotated ensuring an equal distribution across the labels." The manually annotated set serves as a test set, while a noisy silver-labeled dataset generated with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B serves as training data for fine-tuning BERT-based models.
requirements: Annotated student-tutor conversational data; the authors note the lack of such an annotated dataset was a major bottleneck they addressed by annotating MathDial-Bridge student turns
constraints: The authors state the dataset "currently contains coarse-grain emotion labels for student utterances" and that finer emotion labels capturing micro facial expressions are left for future work
target_learners: Students interacting in text-based math tutoring dialogues
target_learning_goals: Recognition of student affective states (boredom, engagement, neutral) to support emotionally aware tutoring
examples: Four annotators aged 27-38 labeled the data; after an initial round yielding 40% Cohen's Kappa agreement, three annotators adjudicated conflicts, and the best fine-tuned model (DistilBERT) reached 61.8% accuracy and 57.9% F1

article_title: Human Autonomy and Sense of Agency in Human-Robot Interaction: A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Glawe, F., Schmeckel, T., Brauner, P., & Ziefle, M. (2025). Human Autonomy and Sense of Agency in Human-Robot Interaction: A Systematic Literature Review. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22271
title: Five-cluster taxonomy of factors potentially influencing human autonomy and sense of agency in HRI
description: From a thematic synthesis of the 22 included studies, the review organises the factors examined as potentially influencing human autonomy or sense of agency in HRI into five broad clusters: robot adaptiveness, robot communication, robot anthropomorphism, robot exposure, and individual differences. The authors state these "clusters are broad but not exhaustive" and that every article was assigned to at least one cluster, with studies not isolating specific factors placed in an 'Other' category. The taxonomy serves as an initial map of the field's independent variables.
requirements: Applied to studies that measure human autonomy or sense of agency after, during, or for an imagined interaction with an autonomous robot or cobot
constraints: The clusters are described as broad but not exhaustive
target_learners: HRI researchers and designers studying human users of robots
target_learning_goals: Understanding and fostering human autonomy and sense of agency in human-robot interaction
examples: The review assigned each of the 22 included articles to at least one cluster, e.g., robotisation studies to robot exposure and individual differences.

article_title: ISD-Agent-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Instructional Design Agents
citation: YoungHoon Jeon, Suwan Kim, Haein Son, Sookbun Lee, Yeil Jeong, Unggi Lee. (2026). ISD-Agent-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Instructional Design Agents. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10620
title: ISD-Agent-Bench: 25,795-scenario benchmark with multi-judge evaluation for LLM-based ISD agents
description: ISD-Agent-Bench is a large-scale benchmark of instructional-design scenarios built by combining a Context Axis of educational settings with an ISD Axis of 33 ADDIE-based sub-steps. The article states it is "the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM-based ISD agents", constructed "with 25,795 scenarios and 1,202 test cases, featuring stratified sampling across 9 contextual dimensions". Evaluation combines ADDIE rubric assessment (70%) with trajectory evaluation (30%) using a cross-provider multi-judge protocol achieving 0.905 inter-judge reliability.
requirements: Scenarios require LLM-based generation from seed abstracts plus rule-based and LLM-based validation stages to ensure logical consistency
constraints: Seed abstracts show domain concentration, with education-specific (1.9%) and healthcare (0.1%) domains underrepresented
target_learners: Learners across all context-axis categories: teens to adults over 40, K-12 through corporate and vocational settings
target_learning_goals: Instructional systems design across the full ADDIE lifecycle: analysis, design, development, implementation, and evaluation
examples: The dataset includes a representative Hard scenario: designing a game-based business leadership course for corporate professionals in an online synchronous environment with gamification required and 2-4 weeks duration
key_sources: YoungHoon Jeon, Suwan Kim, Haein Son, Sookbun Lee, Yeil Jeong, Unggi Lee. (2026). ISD-Agent-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Instructional Design Agents. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10620

article_title: ISD-Agent-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Instructional Design Agents
citation: YoungHoon Jeon, Suwan Kim, Haein Son, Sookbun Lee, Yeil Jeong, Unggi Lee. (2026). ISD-Agent-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Instructional Design Agents. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10620
title: Four ISD theory-based agents (React-ADDIE, ADDIE-Agent, Dick-Carey-Agent, RPISD-Agent) grounded in classical ISD theories
description: The article develops four LLM agents grounded in classical ISD theories: React-ADDIE "integrates the classical ADDIE framework with ReAct-style reasoning" using 5 phase-level tools; ADDIE-Agent implements the five-phase sequential workflow with 14 specialized tools; Dick-Carey-Agent follows the nine-step systematic design model with explicit dependency tracking and criterion-referenced assessment; and RPISD-Agent implements Rapid Prototyping ISD with K=3 refinement cycles prioritizing early prototype generation over comprehensive upfront analysis.
requirements: Agents require a base LLM (evaluated with Gemini-3-Flash, GPT-5-mini, Solar-Pro3) and tool definitions corresponding to their ISD theory's phases or steps
constraints: RPISD-Agent's approach is optimized for time-constrained scenarios where rapid delivery outweighs exhaustive planning; ADDIE-Agent's fine-grained decomposition incurs higher computational overhead
target_learners: Instructional designers and educational program developers across corporate, higher-education, and K-12 contexts
target_learning_goals: Automating the full instructional systems design lifecycle from needs analysis through evaluation
examples: React-ADDIE generates a thought, executes the phase tool, and observes the result at each ADDIE phase, encapsulating complete reasoning for an entire phase within a single LLM call

article_title: Knowledge-Based Design Requirements for Generative Social Robots in Higher Education
citation: S. Vonschallen, D. Oberle, T. Schmiedel, and F. Eyssel. (2026). Knowledge-Based Design Requirements for Generative Social Robots in Higher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12873
title: Three knowledge types (self-, user-, context-knowledge) as drivers of autonomous GSR behavior
description: The article adopts a knowledge-based design perspective in which a generative social robot's autonomous behavior is driven by three types of agent knowledge. Self-knowledge is "the robot's internal understanding of its role, personality, functionalities, and expected behaviors"; user-knowledge is information about the learner enabling personalized tutoring; context-knowledge comprises domain- and task-relevant information. The framework holds that because GSR behavior is non-deterministic, engineering what the robot knows can make desired behaviors more reliable.
requirements: The robot's knowledge base must be deliberately curated and aligned with user and expert perspectives, since configuration left solely to developers may misalign with privacy and educational norms.
constraints: The framework addresses informational prerequisites, not the robot's appearance, system reliability, or the integration process, which the authors state were not explored.
target_learners: university students in higher education
target_learning_goals: responsible and effective tutoring support for learning lecture content
examples: The interview guideline asked participants what role and personality the robot should have (self-knowledge), what student information would help it interact effectively (user-knowledge), and what course and environment knowledge it would require (context-knowledge).
key_sources: S. Vonschallen, D. Oberle, T. Schmiedel, and F. Eyssel. (2026). Knowledge-Based Design Requirements for Generative Social Robots in Higher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12873

article_title: Knowledge-Based Design Requirements for Generative Social Robots in Higher Education
citation: S. Vonschallen, D. Oberle, T. Schmiedel, and F. Eyssel. (2026). Knowledge-Based Design Requirements for Generative Social Robots in Higher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12873
title: Make privacy-sensitive GSR features optional and student-controlled to guarantee user autonomy
description: Because user-knowledge personalization depends on processing sensitive student data, the article holds that ethical considerations of privacy, consent, and data security are fundamental. User autonomy "should always be guaranteed by making privacy-sensitive features optional and student-controlled", including emotion detection and physical-environment perception, with informed consent required before processing student-related data.
requirements: Students must give informed consent for personal information to be processed, and technical privacy and security standards must be upheld.
constraints: The article notes some participants did not find certain information (e.g., hobbies) useful, and physical-environment perception may infringe on data protection.
target_learners: university students in higher education
target_learning_goals: responsible and ethically appropriate tutoring interactions
examples: Participants stated students need informed consent and the option to deny access to private information; the authors recommend locally deployable models to increase control over sensitive information.
key_sources: S. Vonschallen, D. Oberle, T. Schmiedel, and F. Eyssel. (2026). Knowledge-Based Design Requirements for Generative Social Robots in Higher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12873

article_title: A Multi-Agent Approach to Validate and Refine LLM-Generated Personalized Math Problems
citation: Fareya Ikram, Nischal Ashok Kumar, Junyang Lu, Hunter McNichols, Candace Walkington, Neil Heffernan, and Andrew S. Lan. (2026). A Multi-Agent Approach to Validate and Refine LLM-Generated Personalized Math Problems. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05160
title: Multi-agent generate–validate–revise framework with four specialized validator agents for math problem personalization
description: The framework formalizes context personalization of math problems as an iterative generate–validate–revise loop. A conversion agent generates an initial topic-aligned candidate problem, and "four independentvalidator agentsthat return a binary decision (pass/fail) and brief diagnostic feedback" check the candidate against solvability, realism, readability, and authenticity criteria; one or more refinement agents then revise the candidate using validator feedback until all validators pass or a maximum iteration count is reached. The framework is evaluated on 600 ASSISTments problems personalized to 20 student interest topics.
requirements: A target topic reflecting a learner's interest, a target grade reading level computed with the Flesch–Kincaid metric, and validator feedback to drive refinement
constraints: Refinement iterates for at most k iterations (set to k=3 in the evaluation) and stops early only if the candidate passes all validator agent checks
target_learners: middle school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: math word problem solving with personally interesting contexts
examples: The article's Table 1 example converts a pizza-slice circle problem to a basketball court context, where the realism validator fails a 7-inch center circle and the refinement agent revises it to 7 ft
key_sources: Fareya Ikram, Nischal Ashok Kumar, Junyang Lu, Hunter McNichols, Candace Walkington, Neil Heffernan, and Andrew S. Lan. (2026). A Multi-Agent Approach to Validate and Refine LLM-Generated Personalized Math Problems. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05160

article_title: LaTA: A Drop-in, FERPA-Compliant Local-LLM Autograder for Upper-Division STEM Coursework
citation: Jesse A. Rodríguez. (2026). LaTA: A Drop-In, FERPA-Compliant Local-LLM Autograder for Upper-Division STEM Coursework. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05410
title: LaTA: an open-source, on-premises four-stage LLM autograder for LaTeX-native STEM coursework
description: LaTA is a drop-in, open-source (AGPLv3) autograder that runs entirely on commodity on-premises hardware. As the article states, it "implements a four-stage pipeline (ingest, segment, grade, report) using a locally hosted open-weight chain-of-thought LLM grader (gpt-oss:120b)" that compares student work to an instructor reference solution and applies a YAML rubric with binary per-item scoring. It adds Pydantic-validated typed data objects, hybrid regex-first segmentation with an LLM fallback, dual-channel feedback (TA audit reasoning plus Socratic student hints), five-layer prompt-injection defence, self-healing LaTeX compilation, and a Gradescope-integrated corrections/regrade workflow.
requirements: Students submit LaTeX source (.tex plus compiled PDF) via Gradescope, which the article calls the precondition that makes the OCR-free design viable
A single on-premises inference host (here a Mac Studio with 256 GB unified memory) running Ollama with the segmenter and grader models
An instructor-authored reference solution and YAML rubric per assignment
constraints: LaTA v1 does not grade hand-drawn or Python-generated plots; these were graded by visual inspection and declared via points_awarded_elsewhere
Occasional leakage of reference-solution information into student feedback documents occurred at a low rate (~5% of feedback documents)
target_learners: upper-division undergraduate engineering students (~200-student numerical methods course)
target_learning_goals: formulating and solving initial value, boundary value, and partial differential equations
selecting an appropriate numerical method for a mechanical-engineering problem
examples: Deployed as the grader of record in ME 373, Winter 2026, grading every weekly assignment for approximately 200 students on a single Mac Studio at $0 marginal cost per assignment
A corrections mode regraded resubmissions while preserving originally awarded extra credit, and a no-downgrade policy kept previously correct items awarded
key_sources: Jesse A. Rodríguez. (2026). LaTA: A Drop-In, FERPA-Compliant Local-LLM Autograder for Upper-Division STEM Coursework. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05410

article_title: Improving Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring by Differentiating Human Tutor Roles Based on Student Needs
citation: Ashish Gurung, Ge Gao, Jordan Gutterman, Danielle R. Thomas, Shivang Gupta, Lee Branstetter, Emma Brunskill, Vincent Aleven, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2026). Improving Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring by Differentiating Human Tutor Roles Based on Student Needs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11155
title: Differentiate human tutor roles by student need: tutors proactively initiate support for lower-performing students while higher-performing students receive reactive, on-demand support
description: This policy matches the intensity of human support to student needs in hybrid human-AI tutoring. Students below the within-grade median on prior performance receive tutor-initiated motivational and conceptual support, while higher-performing students work independently with on-demand access. The article proposes "a proactive-reactive tutoring policy that matches the intensity of human support to student needs," maximizing human support for students who need it most while maintaining the autonomy of students who benefit from working independently.
requirements: A prior performance measure (within-grade median of prior-year state test scores) to classify students as lower- or higher-performing
Remote human tutors trained to provide motivational and conceptual support during AI-tutor practice sessions
constraints: The dichotomous median split may oversimplify the relationship between student need and optimal tutoring intensity; students far below the median may need more intensive support than the 1:4 proactive ratio provided
Allocation relied on a single baseline performance measure, producing static rather than dynamic grouping
target_learners: Middle school students in grades 5-8 practicing mathematics with an AI tutor
target_learning_goals: Academic growth on standardized math tests
Engagement (time on task) and skill proficiency in AI-tutor practice
examples: 635 students in grades 5-8 were assigned by within-grade median prior state test scores to proactive (below median) or reactive (at or above median) tutoring during twice-weekly IXL math sessions with remote tutors on Zoom
key_sources: Ashish Gurung, Ge Gao, Jordan Gutterman, Danielle R. Thomas, Shivang Gupta, Lee Branstetter, Emma Brunskill, Vincent Aleven, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2026). Improving Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring by Differentiating Human Tutor Roles Based on Student Needs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11155

article_title: Understanding How International Students in the U.S. Are Using Conversational AI to Support Cross-Cultural Adaptation
citation: Nourian, L.; Callis, A.; Patterson, S.; Miao, J.; Heard, J.; Tigwell, G. W. (2026). Understanding How International Students in the U.S. Are Using Conversational AI to Support Cross-Cultural Adaptation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15127
title: Kim's stress-adaptation-growth framework of cross-cultural adaptation
description: The article frames its survey instrument using Kim's Cross-Cultural Adaptation framework, in which adaptation is "a dynamic process of 'stress-adaptation-growth'" where the challenges of cultural shock act as a catalyst for personal transformation. Stress is treated as a prerequisite for adapting and growing, forcing individuals to constantly learn new skills to operate in unfamiliar environments, making adaptation an iterative process of resolving tensions between cultural perspectives. The survey's parts map onto the framework's phases: challenges (stress), AI usage actions (adaptation), and growth.
requirements: The framework presupposes exposure to stressors in the host environment as the driver of adaptation and growth
constraints: The article applies it to first-time international students in the US who had not studied in another country before
target_learners: international students in the US
target_learning_goals: cross-cultural adaptation skills
learning new skills to operate in unfamiliar environments
examples: The survey's four parts were designed around the framework's phases: stress and challenges, adaptation actions with AI, and growth and improvement ratings
key_sources: Nourian, L.; Callis, A.; Patterson, S.; Miao, J.; Heard, J.; Tigwell, G. W. (2026). Understanding How International Students in the U.S. Are Using Conversational AI to Support Cross-Cultural Adaptation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15127

article_title: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human-AI Complementarities in Education
citation: Bharat Anand, Lihi Idan. (2026). Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work (Working Paper). https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18143
title: AI Interaction Competence (AIC) as a new dimension of human capital governing who captures value from GenAI access
description: The article introduces AI Interaction Competence (AIC) as "the ability to elicit, evaluate, and apply model outputs effectively", a form of human capital that determines how individuals translate AI access into performance. It is operationalized as three component skills: formulating precise goal-oriented prompts, filtering and verifying outputs for accuracy and bias rather than accepting them at face value, and iterating interactively by combining human judgment with machine suggestions. In the experiment AIC was inferred from behavioral performance rather than self-assessment, and it emerged as the decisive moderator of learning gains.
requirements: Requires users to engage in iterative problem solving: formulating prompts, interpreting probabilistic outputs, and verifying content quality
Measured behaviorally rather than by self-report in the study
constraints: A skill not formally taught, not evenly distributed, and not easily signaled by existing academic markers
target_learners: Early-career knowledge workers
University engineering students
target_learning_goals: Effective use of generative AI systems in knowledge work
Self-directed learning of technical material
examples: In the randomized experiment, AIC was inferred from behavioral performance and tested as a moderator via Treatment × AIC and three-way interaction analyses
key_sources: Bharat Anand, Lihi Idan. (2026). Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work (Working Paper). https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18143

article_title: Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human-AI Complementarities in Education
citation: Bharat Anand, Lihi Idan. (2026). Generative AI and the Productivity Divide: Human–AI Complementarities in Education and Knowledge Work (Working Paper). https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18143
title: Pair GenAI access with short AIC micro-training and light process scaffolds to capture value consistently and reduce performance variance
description: The article recommends that organizations treat AI access as the beginning, not the endpoint, of adoption: value realization depends on complementary routines. It advises that "Firms can address this gap through targeted micro-training that focuses on prompting logic, verification heuristics, and synthesis structure", coupled with light scaffolds such as standardized prompt templates or review checklists, analogous to standard operating procedures. The goal is to raise the performance floor and reduce variance without lowering mean performance.
requirements: Diagnose AI Interaction Competence gaps among employees
Embed micro-trainings into onboarding and workflow cycles
constraints: The scaffolding evidence comes from novice participants in a controlled learning experiment with weakly significant effects
target_learners: Early-career knowledge workers
New or transitioning employees in knowledge-intensive firms
target_learning_goals: Consistent, high-quality use of AI outputs in knowledge work
Reduced dispersion in AI-mediated performance
examples: The experiment's scaffolding arm gave novice participants a high-level conceptual roadmap of essential LLM topics with recommended sequencing, lowering score variance (SD=.14 vs SD=.22) without lowering the mean

article_title: KT4EQG: Personalized Exercise Question Generation via Knowledge Tracing
citation: Xinyi Gao, Qiucheng Wu, Lu Ding, Q. Vera Liao, Kaizhi Qian, Ying Xu, Shiyu Chang, Yang Zhang. (2026). KT4EQG: Personalized Exercise Question Generation via Knowledge Tracing. Preprint. Under review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23933
title: KT4EQG framework: knowledge-tracing-guided personalized question generation decomposed into education value and question-concept alignment
description: KT4EQG is a two-component framework for personalized educational question generation. A knowledge tracing model (KT2, a hidden Markov tree over a hierarchy of knowledge concepts) estimates each student's concept-level mastery and selects the KC with the highest education value, defined as "the potential improvement in the student's overall knowledge mastery after practicing". An LLM-based generator, trained via supervised fine-tuning then reinforcement learning with a learned alignment reward, produces a question grounded in the selected concept. The authors state that "KT4EQG decomposes the question evaluation into concept-level educational value and question-concept alignment value".
requirements: A knowledge tracing model providing posterior mastery probabilities per knowledge concept
KC annotations or a constructed KC tree for the target domain
A trained alignment verifier to supply the reinforcement learning reward
constraints: KT2 assumes each question is associated with one KC and correctness depends only on mastery of that KC
Experiments fix question difficulty to medium for KT-based evaluations
Evaluation is simulation-based, with student state updates assuming successful practice
target_learners: third grade mathematics students (per the generation prompt)
MOOC learners in wine knowledge, circuit design, and education theory modules
target_learning_goals: improving overall knowledge mastery across a domain's knowledge concepts
practicing the knowledge concept offering the greatest individual learning benefit
examples: On XES3G5M the framework generated a chicken-rabbit problem requiring reasoning over two entity types for the concept Multiple Quantities Chicken-Rabbit Problem
key_sources: Xinyi Gao, Qiucheng Wu, Lu Ding, Q. Vera Liao, Kaizhi Qian, Ying Xu, Shiyu Chang, Yang Zhang. (2026). KT4EQG: Personalized Exercise Question Generation via Knowledge Tracing. Preprint. Under review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23933

article_title: KT4EQG: Personalized Exercise Question Generation via Knowledge Tracing
citation: Xinyi Gao, Qiucheng Wu, Lu Ding, Q. Vera Liao, Kaizhi Qian, Ying Xu, Shiyu Chang, Yang Zhang. (2026). KT4EQG: Personalized Exercise Question Generation via Knowledge Tracing. Preprint. Under review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23933
title: KT4EQG system with released code
description: KT4EQG is an implemented personalized question generation system combining the KT2 knowledge tracer, a QWEN3-8B-based question generator trained with SFT and GRPO reinforcement learning, and an alignment verifier built on ALL-MINILM-L6-V2. The paper notes "Code available at https://github.com/UCSB-NLP-Chang/KT4EQG". The system was evaluated on XES3G5M and MOOCRADAR across six knowledge modules, with training on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs and the verifier trained on a single RTX 3090 Ti.
requirements: Hierarchical KC annotations (expert-annotated for XES3G5M; LLM-constructed trees for MOOCRADAR)
A base LLM for generation and an embedding model backbone for the verifier
constraints: Experiments extend to 300 students per module for the three largest XES3G5M modules; smaller MOOCRADAR modules have 130-260 students
target_learners: third grade mathematics students
MOOC learners
target_learning_goals: generating practice questions targeting each student's most beneficial knowledge concept
examples: The alignment verifier was trained for 70 epochs with batch size 64 and temperature 0.07, using sibling concepts from the KC tree as hard negatives
