article_title: 'It Felt a Bit Eerie": Exploring Humanlike Interactions During Collaborative Writing with an Artificial Agent'
citation: Michael Yin, Angela Chiang, Samuel Rhys Cox, and Robert Xiao. (2026). "It Felt a Bit Eerie": Exploring Humanlike Interactions During Collaborative Writing with an Artificial Agent. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24729
title: Three-variant AI-assisted collaborative writing text editor
description: A custom web-based text editor in which an LLM-backed artificial agent acts as a peer editor offering replacement suggestions and comments in an Editing Pane. The authors "built three variants of an AI-assisted text editor along a spectrum of simulated humanlike interaction (synchronous and with a cursor) to machinelike interaction (asynchronous and without a cursor)". The suggestion suite was constant across variants; variants differed only in temporal and visual humanlikeness. It was built with React and ProseMirror on the front end and a Python Flask back end calling the OpenAI gpt-4o API.
requirements: An LLM backend (OpenAI gpt-4o API calls) generating replacement and comment suggestions from the chunked text and previous suggestions
constraints: Humanlike behaviour heuristics (suggestion timing, cursor motion, typing speed) were tweaked subjectively and based on averages; the authors note "there is no 'average' human"
target_learners: adult writers in a lab study (18+, fluent in English)
target_learning_goals: collaborative writing and revision with AI support
examples: Heuristics for humanlike behaviour were derived from a formative study with 8 HCI researchers acting as peer editors, plus literature-based typing-speed parameters
key_sources: Michael Yin, Angela Chiang, Samuel Rhys Cox, and Robert Xiao. (2026). "It Felt a Bit Eerie": Exploring Humanlike Interactions During Collaborative Writing with an Artificial Agent. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24729

article_title: 'It Felt a Bit Eerie": Exploring Humanlike Interactions During Collaborative Writing with an Artificial Agent'
citation: Michael Yin, Angela Chiang, Samuel Rhys Cox, and Robert Xiao. (2026). "It Felt a Bit Eerie": Exploring Humanlike Interactions During Collaborative Writing with an Artificial Agent. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24729
title: Social presence with social costs: humanlike interaction design of artificial agents
description: An account extending CASA theory to interaction-level design cues: shaping when (temporal humanlikeness) and how (visual humanlikeness) an agent interacts elicits social presence, which supports collaboration (efficiency, intent understanding, social connection) but also produces social costs such as feeling watched, judged, distracted, and misaligned. As the authors put it, "while humanlike collaborative systems do elicit social presence, this can potentially lead to social costs as well". The account holds that these costs are exacerbated without the alignment present in human–human collaboration, and can be somewhat alleviated through visible alignment and shared understanding.
requirements: Interaction design cues (synchrony, apparent effort via cursor) that participants read as humanlike
constraints: Studied in a collaborative writing task with an LLM peer editor; costs arise especially without human–human-style alignment
target_learners: adult writers collaborating with AI agents
target_learning_goals: effective and socially comfortable human–AI collaborative writing
examples: The three-variant user study manipulated temporal and visual humanlikeness and traced both benefits (efficiency, understanding) and costs (surveillance, overload) to social presence
key_sources: Michael Yin, Angela Chiang, Samuel Rhys Cox, and Robert Xiao. (2026). "It Felt a Bit Eerie": Exploring Humanlike Interactions During Collaborative Writing with an Artificial Agent. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24729

article_title: The Role of Instructional Guidance in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Empirical Evidence from Construction Engineering
citation: Xiaoyu Hou, Bo Xiao, Hexu Liu and Shane Mueller. (2026). The Role of Instructional Guidance in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Empirical Evidence from Construction Engineering Education.
title: Five-step prompting framework (Clarify, Organize, Integrate, Differentiate, Correct) operationalizing Generative Learning Theory in AI-supported review
description: The article introduces a five-step interaction framework that translates Generative Learning Theory's selecting, organizing, and integrating processes into observable student–AI interaction behaviors during review. "The framework guides students through a structured sequence consisting of Clarify, Organize, Integrate, Differentiate, and Correct." Each step has an instructional purpose and example prompt (e.g., asking for the 2–3 most important key points, a real-world example, a commonly confused concept, and the most important misconception). The sequence structures AI use as guided cognitive activity rather than open-ended querying.
requirements: A course-aligned generative AI platform with which learners can pose the structured prompts for each topic before proceeding to another
constraints: The structured sequence may not accommodate all individual learning preferences, and the study tested only this single prompting strategy without comparison to alternative designs
target_learners: undergraduate construction engineering students without prior construction management coursework
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding, organization, and integration of course content during self-directed review
examples: In the experiment, prompted participants applied the full five-step prompt sequence for each selected topic using the RAG-based course platform
key_sources: Xiaoyu Hou, Bo Xiao, Hexu Liu and Shane Mueller. (2026). The Role of Instructional Guidance in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Empirical Evidence from Construction Engineering Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05509

article_title: The Role of Instructional Guidance in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Empirical Evidence from Construction Engineering
citation: Xiaoyu Hou, Bo Xiao, Hexu Liu and Shane Mueller. (2026). The Role of Instructional Guidance in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Empirical Evidence from Construction Engineering Education.
title: Retrieval-augmented generative AI learning platform for construction education
description: A web-based generative AI–supported learning platform developed for construction education that "enables document-grounded interaction with course materials and generates source-linked responses aligned with curated instructional resources." It uses a retrieval-augmented generation architecture combining semantic retrieval with large language model generation to constrain responses to course-specific content. Prior evaluations included expert review of accuracy and relevance, automated grounding assessment, and a formative classroom usability evaluation; the same configuration and knowledge base served both AI conditions in the experiment.
requirements: A curated course-aligned knowledge base and prior evaluation establishing response reliability and instructional alignment
constraints: Responses are constrained to course-specific content via the RAG architecture
target_learners: undergraduate construction engineering students
target_learning_goals: self-directed review of construction course concepts with source-linked explanations
examples: Both the prompted and unprompted conditions in the controlled experiment interacted with this identical platform and corpus

article_title: The Role of Instructional Guidance in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Empirical Evidence from Construction Engineering
citation: Xiaoyu Hou, Bo Xiao, Hexu Liu and Shane Mueller. (2026). The Role of Instructional Guidance in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Empirical Evidence from Construction Engineering Education.
title: Design AI-supported learning environments with explicit interaction structures, since access to AI alone does not improve higher-order learning
description: The article's design implication is that prompting functions as instructional scaffolding embedded in the interaction process, directing attention, supporting organization, and encouraging reflective evaluation. "Designing AI systems with explicit interaction structures may therefore be essential for supporting higher-order learning outcomes, particularly in contexts that require explanation, reasoning, and conceptual understanding." The unprompted condition's lack of improvement shows simple access to AI does not inherently yield better outcomes.
requirements: An AI-supported learning environment in which the interaction sequence can be prescribed to learners during self-directed review
constraints: Evidence comes from a single instructional context with a moderate, unbalanced sample and a short-term task without retention or transfer measures
target_learners: undergraduate students in domain-specific higher education
target_learning_goals: higher-order outcomes requiring explanation, reasoning, and conceptual understanding
examples: The prompted condition guided learners through clarification, organization, and verification steps, producing more systematic engagement aligned with task demands

article_title: Hybrid E-Assessment in Higher Education: Semi-Automated Grading of Paper-Based Written Examinations
citation: Hartwig Grabowski, Michael Canz. (2026). Hybrid E-Assessment in Higher Education: Semi-Automated Grading of Paper-Based Written Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08855
title: Coding format: a thin letter-capture layer on top of a freely designed paper task
description: The pattern keeps the examination task freely designed on paper while making results machine-readable. Assessment-relevant intermediate results are transferred into predefined answer fields, "Each gap is assigned a fixed set of letter-based answer options, for example A to Z", and students carry out the derivation by hand before entering one letter per gap in an answer table. The large option pool keeps random guessing unlikely without turning the task into a closed question format, and the letter assignment is only a capture layer, so the didactic design stays independent of the scoring mechanism.
requirements: Assessment-relevant intermediate results must be expressible as entries in predefined letter-based answer fields
constraints: Configuration files are needed to map pages to table regions and table columns to assessment criteria and point values, and the initial setup remains a fixed cost for each examination
target_learners: higher education students in large-cohort foundational courses
target_learning_goals: complex reasoning and stepwise problem solving assessed in summative examinations
examples: The free-fall derivation from the physics example recast so students derive by hand and enter one letter per gap (1)-(6); a database query based on a schema diagram; a program-completion task
key_sources: Hartwig Grabowski, Michael Canz. (2026). Hybrid E-Assessment in Higher Education: Semi-Automated Grading of Paper-Based Written Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08855

article_title: Hybrid E-Assessment in Higher Education: Semi-Automated Grading of Paper-Based Written Examinations
citation: Hartwig Grabowski, Michael Canz. (2026). Hybrid E-Assessment in Higher Education: Semi-Automated Grading of Paper-Based Written Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08855
title: In summative e-assessment, technology should support grading and post-processing without constraining the design of complex, stepwise problem-solving tasks
description: The principle holds that paper provides the design freedom for didactically rich examinations, and automation should enter at the standardized capture and evaluation of answers rather than at restriction of the task architecture. As the article states, "technology should support grading and post-processing without constraining the design of complex, stepwise problem-solving tasks". Existing paper examinations can be adapted to a structured answer-field or coding format with manageable effort while maintaining substantive and didactic freedom.
requirements: A structured answer-field or coding format that captures assessment-relevant intermediate results
constraints: Fully automated grading narrows the range of didactically meaningful task formats when closed formats cannot represent derivation, application, and transfer
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: summative assessment that both measures performance and supports reasoning and learning
examples: The article's free-fall physics task, where students derive the impact velocity by hand and the mass parameter cancels within the calculation, showing the examination acting as a learning opportunity
key_sources: Hartwig Grabowski, Michael Canz. (2026). Hybrid E-Assessment in Higher Education: Semi-Automated Grading of Paper-Based Written Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08855

article_title: Detecting Knowledge Gaps from Conversational AI Interactions Using Curriculum Prerequisite Graphs
citation: Youssef Medhat, Junsoo Park, Ploy Thajchayapong and Ashok K. Goel. (2026). Detecting Knowledge Gaps from Conversational AI Interactions Using Curriculum Prerequisite Graphs. CSEDM'26: 10th Workshop on Computer Science Educational Data Mining. https://dilab.gatech.edu
title: GPT-4-extracted curriculum prerequisite knowledge graph (54 topic nodes, 47 directed prerequisite edges)
description: A prerequisite knowledge graph extracted by GPT-4 from 26 lesson PDFs of a graduate-level AI course, following a three-stage protocol of topic extraction, boundary consolidation, and edge extraction. The graph contains "54 topic nodes and 47 directed prerequisite edges" and serves two roles: its topic nodes provide the closed label space for classification and survey alignment, and its directed prerequisite edges encode curriculum structure for future per-student gap propagation. The authors describe it as "a low-cost, instructor-auditable way to obtain a topic–edge artifact".
requirements: A course instructor with domain expertise to run and audit the GPT-4 extraction protocol over lesson PDFs
constraints: The authors do not claim the graph is the unique correct structure; only unambiguous, non-bidirectional GPT-4 prerequisite judgments are retained
target_learners: graduate-level AI course students
target_learning_goals: mapping student questions to curriculum topics
identifying topic-level knowledge gaps
examples: Sample extracted edges include Semantic Networks → Frames, Case-Based Reasoning → Analogical Reasoning, and Logic → Explanation-Based Learning, matching the course textbook's lesson ordering

article_title: What do you mean by human-AI collaboration: Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it
citation: Mutlu Cukurova. (2026). What do you mean by 'human–AI collaboration'? Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it. Submitted to the Handbook of AI and the Future of Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5843-4854
title: Five-level diagnostic taxonomy of human–AI teaming defined by observable affordances
description: The chapter proposes a diagnostic taxonomy of human–AI teaming with five levels: transactional, situational, operational, praxical, and synergistic. Each level 'introduces one additional affordance over the level beneath it', and 'the classification is functional and is intended to be coded from observable behaviour' such as whether the system surfaces state, accepts governance, revises durably from feedback, or co-reasons. Interaction types are querying, monitoring, governing, adapting, and co-reasoning; diagnosis proceeds top-down, classifying a system at the highest threshold it meets.
requirements: Coding from observable behaviour in deployment rather than unverifiable architectural claims
constraints: The levels are not strict supersets but minimum-affordance thresholds; mixed profiles are resolved by recording the highest threshold met
The taxonomy is a map of affordances, not a quality ranking; higher is not uniformly better
target_learners: teachers and learners using AI systems in education
target_learning_goals: distinguishing genuine collaboration from other human–AI interaction types
examples: A general-purpose chatbot used for one-shot lesson-plan drafting sits at the transactional level; real-time classroom dashboards with AI models are situational; configurable intelligent tutoring platforms are operational

article_title: What do you mean by human-AI collaboration: Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it
citation: Mutlu Cukurova. (2026). What do you mean by 'human–AI collaboration'? Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it. Submitted to the Handbook of AI and the Future of Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5843-4854
title: Five requirements that characterise collaboration in a strong sense
description: Drawing on the socio-cognitive, socio-cultural, and shared-knowledge traditions, the chapter argues 'that at least five requirements characterise collaboration in a strong sense': a negotiated and partly symmetric situation, shared and negotiated goals, a low and shifting division of labour, interactivity with synchronicity and negotiability, and mutual modelling, grounding, and socially shared regulation. Collaboration is thereby 'a graded construct, not a binary one', present only when joint activity is sustained at a high level along several dimensions at once.
requirements: Situations in which asymmetry remains dynamic, negotiated, and mutually consequential rather than fixed at design time
constraints: Pure symmetry is rare and not strictly necessary; what matters is that asymmetry is negotiated and mutually consequential
target_learners: researchers, designers, and policymakers evaluating human–AI learning systems
target_learning_goals: defining and assessing collaborative learning conditions
examples: Dillenbourg's lost-keys thought experiment illustrates that coincident outcomes do not amount to shared intentions

article_title: What do you mean by human-AI collaboration: Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it
citation: Mutlu Cukurova. (2026). What do you mean by 'human–AI collaboration'? Prerequisite functions and the affordances needed to achieve it. Submitted to the Handbook of AI and the Future of Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5843-4854
title: Grant AI revision authority only with the human's final authority, full auditability, and clear accountability
description: An AI system with the standing to challenge a user's reasons can also resist a correct user or entrench an error. The chapter therefore argues that 'Revision authority is therefore safe only when paired with the human's final authority, full auditability of the disagreement, and clear lines of accountability', so that dissent comes with a record of how it was resolved before dissent-capable systems are deployed at scale in classrooms.
requirements: Human final authority preserved; a record of how dissent was resolved; full auditability of the disagreement
constraints: Structured deliberation forced indiscriminately fatigues users and breeds rubber-stamping; deliberation should trigger only when it would change the decision
target_learners: teachers and learners in classrooms using dissent-capable AI systems
target_learning_goals: safe and accountable co-reasoning and shared decision-making with AI
examples: The chapter warns that an AI with the standing to resist a user can also resist a correct user, entrench an error, or make consequential moves without transparency

article_title: Knowledge Distillation for Automated AI Tutor Evaluation
citation: Tahmid Al Hannan, Diego Garcia, Alex Njoroge, Suha Al Juboori, Tarek Sakakini. (2026). Knowledge Distillation for Automated AI Tutor Evaluation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10647
title: FATE: a lightweight 8B-parameter LLM evaluator of AI tutors across four pedagogical dimensions
description: FATE (FLC AI Tutor Evaluator) is a specialized evaluator built on Llama 3.1 8B that assesses AI tutor responses across the four BEA 2025 dimensions: Mistake Identification, Mistake Location, Providing Guidance, and Actionability. The authors describe it as "a lightweight evaluator based on Llama 3.1 8B" trained on 1,450 student-tutor conversations using knowledge distillation from Claude Opus 4.7. Four task-specific models were fine-tuned, one per dimension, each using prompts describing the dialogue history and evaluation rubric.
requirements: Requires the BEA 2025 Shared Task annotated dataset of mathematics tutoring dialogues with expert labels on the four pedagogical dimensions
Requires LoRA fine-tuning with 4-bit quantization on A100 and T4 GPUs as described
constraints: Each dimension receives one of three labels (Yes, To Some Extent, or No), so evaluation is categorical rather than open-ended
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students interacting with AI tutors
target_learning_goals: Assessment of pedagogical quality of AI tutor responses in mathematics tutoring dialogues
examples: The authors deployed FATE to benchmark commercial AI tutors including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek on BEA 2025 conversation histories

article_title: Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children
citation: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377
title: Kutti AI: a voice-first, offline-capable learning companion for visually-impaired children
description: Kutti AI is a cross-platform mobile application (React Native/Expo, TypeScript) in which "the entire learning loop—presenting a concept, posing a question, capturing the answer, detecting difficulty, and giving feedback—is conducted through speech". It uses on-device Whisper ASR, platform text-to-speech, and a PostgreSQL (Supabase) backend with row-level security, and is intended to be distributed free of charge. The prototype supports English and Tamil.
requirements: Every function must be reachable and completable through speech and audio feedback alone; visual elements must never be required (R1)
constraints: The prototype has not yet been evaluated with visually-impaired children under controlled conditions; reported results are qualitative and formative
target_learners: visually-impaired children in early education
children in low-connectivity underserved communities
target_learning_goals: curriculum concepts delivered through spoken conversation
early learning foundational skills
examples: Built as a working prototype during the Half Baked hackathon, supporting English and Tamil
key_sources: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377

article_title: Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children
citation: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377
title: Multi-signal struggle detection fusing latency, wrong-attempt, and hesitation-keyword signals
description: Kutti AI's adaptivity rests on a struggle-detection engine that "fuses three independent signals and acts the moment any of them indicates difficulty": response latency beyond a threshold, wrong-attempt counts, and hesitation keywords in the transcript. Any single signal can fire, so the system reacts to silence, error, and verbalized uncertainty using lightweight on-device computation, triggering hints, simplified questions, or encouragement in real time.
requirements: Simplified question variants must be authored in advance as part of lesson content
Thresholds (e.g., a 2.5-second pause threshold) must be set to balance responsiveness against thinking time
constraints: Fixed parameters (2.5-second pause threshold, two-attempt limit, 0.6 similarity threshold) should become adaptive and personalized per the authors
target_learners: young visually-impaired learners
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement and persistence when a child struggles
examples: In the prototype, a pause beyond 2.5 seconds triggers a spoken hint; after two incorrect attempts a pre-authored simplified question is presented; hesitation cues such as "don't know" trigger encouragement
key_sources: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377

article_title: Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children
citation: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377
title: Three-layer cross-language answer-matching pipeline for tolerant evaluation of spoken answers
description: To judge young children's spoken answers fairly, Kutti AI evaluates responses through a three-layer pipeline: language-aware translation/transliteration when the child answers in a different language than the lesson expects, Levenshtein-based fuzzy matching accepting responses above a similarity threshold (0.6 in the prototype), and normalization (lowercasing, stripping filler words and punctuation). The layers "let the system accept a wide range of legitimate answers—cross-language, mispronounced, or disfluent—while still distinguishing genuinely incorrect responses."
requirements: Similarity threshold tuning; the design assumes children's ASR is error-prone, which the authors ground in prior evidence that ASR for children is substantially less accurate than for adults
constraints: Keyword-based hesitation detection could be extended toward richer prosodic or acoustic sentiment analysis while preserving on-device, privacy-respecting operation
target_learners: young children who code-switch between languages
children with pronunciation variation
target_learning_goals: fair spoken-answer evaluation in multilingual early learning
examples: A child answering "one" in English to a Tamil prompt can still match after translation/transliteration; near-miss pronunciations are accepted above the 0.6 similarity threshold
key_sources: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377

article_title: Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children
citation: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377
title: Design children's voice interfaces for being misheard, not just heard
description: The article's first lesson is that for young children, ASR errors and disfluencies are the norm, so tolerant multi-layer answer matching is "a first-class requirement in a children's voice interface". Without it, the authors report, correct answers were frequently rejected and the experience felt punitive. Robust matching should therefore be treated as core design, not an optional refinement.
requirements: A tolerant, multi-layer answer-matching pipeline (translation/transliteration, fuzzy matching, normalization)
target_learners: young children whose speech ASR misrecognizes
target_learning_goals: accurate and fair evaluation of spoken answers
examples: In the Kutti AI prototype, removing the tolerant matching layers caused correct answers to be frequently rejected
key_sources: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377

article_title: Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children
citation: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377
title: Detect learner struggle with multiple fused signals because struggle is multi-modal
description: The article's second lesson: "No single signal reliably captures difficulty." Silence, wrong answers, and verbalized uncertainty each miss cases the others catch, and the authors report that fusing them "produced far more humane behavior than any one alone." Struggle detection in adaptive learning systems should therefore combine temporal, behavioral, and linguistic signals.
requirements: Lightweight on-device computation so the detection loop stays fast and offline-capable
target_learners: young learners using voice-first systems
target_learning_goals: timely supportive intervention when a learner is stuck or discouraged
examples: Kutti AI evaluates pause duration, wrong-attempt count, and hesitation keywords together, with any one able to fire

title: Move speech recognition on-device to make voice learning tools reach low-connectivity communities
description: The article's third lesson is that "Offline capability changes who the system can reach": moving ASR on-device was the decision that made the app relevant to low-connectivity settings, and accessibility and connectivity constraints are intertwined for this population. The core loop (transcription, lesson delivery, struggle detection, answer matching) operates without a network, with progress synchronizing opportunistically.
requirements: Locally cached lesson content and an embedded on-device ASR model
constraints: The design trades some on-device compute and storage for availability
target_learners: children in underserved low-connectivity communities
target_learning_goals: uninterrupted access to spoken lesson delivery and feedback
examples: Kutti AI runs an embedded Whisper model on-device and caches lessons locally, syncing progress when connectivity returns

citation: Kadharmoideen Fadurudeen. (2026). Kutti AI: A Voice-First, Offline-Capable Learning Companion with Real-Time Struggle Detection for Visually-Impaired Children. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22377
title: Five-stage spoken learning loop with supplementary visual affordances
description: Kutti AI's interaction design is "a spoken conversation with five stages": welcome (a single large haptic-enabled control), spoken lesson delivery paced with natural pauses, voice response captured by a large microphone control or hands-free mode, adaptive response (encouragement, hint, or simplified question), and a spoken summary with an engagement score (0–100). Visual affordances—screen-reader compatibility, large touch targets, haptic confirmation, high-contrast scheme—are strictly supplementary for low-vision users and sighted caregivers.
requirements: Visual elements may exist for sighted caregivers but must never be required (R1)
target_learners: visually-impaired children
low-vision users and sighted caregivers

examples: On completion the child hears an engagement score (0–100) and encouraging feedback, and the session is persisted for progress tracking

article_title: IKS-Instruct: A 24,000-Example Multilingual Dataset for Teaching Language Models Indian Knowledge Systems
citation: Shwetha Singaravelu, Gayathri Muruganantham, Lakshmi Rajendran, Santhosh Sivasubramani. (2026). IKS-Instruct: A 24,000-Example Multilingual Dataset for Teaching Language Models Indian Knowledge Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23322
title: IKS-Instruct dataset
description: IKS-Instruct is a released dataset of instruction-response pairs for teaching language models Indian Knowledge Systems pedagogy. The paper presents "a dataset of 24,795 instruction-response pairs for teaching language models to deliver educational content grounded in Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS)" spanning seven languages, 41 pedagogical techniques, and CBSE classes 6-12. Pairs come from six source categories and are stored in JSONL with structured metadata including source provenance, technique classification, language, subject, class level, and quality scores.
requirements: Pairs must pass the five-stage quality filtering pipeline including Teacher Fidelity scoring and multi-judge evaluation
constraints: Language distribution is imbalanced (English 36.1%, Malayalam 6.3%); CBSE alignment covers only classes 6-12; oral and manuscript-only traditions are not represented
target_learners: CBSE students in classes 6 through 12
target_learning_goals: IKS-grounded instruction across mathematics, science, social science, ethics, language, and AI/data science
examples: The released v1.9 dataset contains 24,795 pairs, with classical text corpus pairs the largest category at 27.5%
key_sources: Shwetha Singaravelu, Gayathri Muruganantham, Lakshmi Rajendran, Santhosh Sivasubramani. (2026). IKS-Instruct: A 24,000-Example Multilingual Dataset for Teaching Language Models Indian Knowledge Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23322

article_title: IKS-Instruct: A 24,000-Example Multilingual Dataset for Teaching Language Models Indian Knowledge Systems
citation: Shwetha Singaravelu, Gayathri Muruganantham, Lakshmi Rajendran, Santhosh Sivasubramani. (2026). IKS-Instruct: A 24,000-Example Multilingual Dataset for Teaching Language Models Indian Knowledge Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.23322
title: Multi-judge quality assessment framework
description: A quality-evaluation framework in which independent language-model judges score instruction responses across multiple dimensions, with per-model quality reported as the median of per-judge overall scores. The paper states that "Quality is assessed through a multi-judge evaluation framework in which independent language models score responses on 12 dimensions" grouped into IKS Fidelity, Pedagogy, Content, and Adaptation categories. A stratified sample of 1,201 items is scored by a uniform five-judge external panel, with Nemotron-family judges excluded to avoid self-preference circularity.
requirements: Multiple independent judges applied identically to every model; stratified sampling by language and technique category
constraints: Language-model judges exhibit systematic biases (favoring longer, formal responses); residual Llama-lineage circularity remains; scores are comparative under a fixed panel, not calibrated ratings
target_learners: Researchers and builders of educational AI systems
target_learning_goals: Assessing pedagogical quality, technique fidelity, and cultural depth of AI-generated instructional content
examples: The uniform five-judge panel (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Dracarys-70B, GPT-4o-mini) scored 1,201 stratified items with median aggregation

article_title: Measuring Cognitive Engagement in Collaborative Discourse with an Extended ICAP Framework: Comparing Human Annotation, In-Context Learning, and Reflective LLM Agents
citation: Lan Anh Do, Hanling Jiang, Shuchin Aeron, Ayanna K. Thomas. (2026). Measuring Cognitive Engagement in Collaborative Discourse with an Extended ICAP Framework: Comparing Human Annotation, In-Context Learning, and Reflective LLM Agents. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28651
title: Extended 7-point ICAP framework for cognitive engagement in collaborative discourse
description: The article extends the ICAP framework (Passive, Active, Constructive, Interactive) into a 7-point ordered scale with intermediate levels between adjacent modes, to "capture differences in participation when instances did not align cleanly with a single mode". Level 1 is passive listening, Level 3 active participation such as agreement, Level 5 constructive proposals with reasoning, and Levels 6–7 sustained two- or three-plus-turn interactive exchanges. It was used to code trial-level engagement of individuals in three-person collaborative problem solving.
requirements: Trained annotators and a codebook with criteria for each level; turn boundaries defined as all utterances by one speaker until another begins
constraints: Developed and validated on a single logical inference task (letters-to-numbers) with undergraduate three-person groups; mid-level categories (3–5) showed the greatest ambiguity
target_learners: undergraduate students working in three-person groups
target_learning_goals: characterizing cognitive engagement during collaborative problem-solving discourse
examples: Annotators labeled each trial's expression and guess phases; Criteria Version 2 added detailed rules such as counting simple corrections as Level 3 and random guesses as Level 5
key_sources: Lan Anh Do, Hanling Jiang, Shuchin Aeron, Ayanna K. Thomas. (2026). Measuring Cognitive Engagement in Collaborative Discourse with an Extended ICAP Framework: Comparing Human Annotation, In-Context Learning, and Reflective LLM Agents. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28651

article_title: Measuring Cognitive Engagement in Collaborative Discourse with an Extended ICAP Framework: Comparing Human Annotation, In-Context Learning, and Reflective LLM Agents
citation: Lan Anh Do, Hanling Jiang, Shuchin Aeron, Ayanna K. Thomas. (2026). Measuring Cognitive Engagement in Collaborative Discourse with an Extended ICAP Framework: Comparing Human Annotation, In-Context Learning, and Reflective LLM Agents. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28651
title: Self-reflective LLM annotation agent with iterative criteria refinement and short-term memory
description: An LLM-based agent that labels each discourse sample, then reflects to identify weaknesses in the current coding framework and applies revision actions (modify, add, delete, hold, merge) before labeling the next sample. It "retained short-term memory of the three most recently labeled samples and the three most recent versions of the criteria", enabling progressive self-refinement beyond single-prompt labeling. In experiments the agents consistently chose only to modify existing levels, preserving the seven-level structure. Code is released at https://github.com/HanlingJ/human-icl-llm-agent.
requirements: An initial criteria version, labeled samples, and a foundation LLM (GPT-4o or GPT-5.2); memory buffer of recent samples and criteria versions
constraints: Agent refinement relied solely on each agent's own analysis without discussion; agent-refined frameworks showed greater cross-model variability (QWK 0.655–0.790) than human-refined ones
target_learners: researchers annotating collaborative learning discourse
target_learning_goals: scalable measurement of cognitive engagement in collaborative discourse
examples: The agent's reflection identified gaps such as proposals without justification being implicitly treated as Level 4 and vague turn-taking language for Levels 6–7

article_title: Human-LLM Collaborative Inductive Coding for Conceptualizing K-12 Educator AI Use
citation: Liu, A., Sun, M., Esbenshade, L., Xiao, M., Tian, V., Zhang, Z., & He, K. (2026). Human-LLM Collaborative Inductive Coding for Conceptualizing K-12 Educator AI Use. https://osf.io/ju59q/overview?view_only=96afb71945044b8794e113f9763cc74a
title: Division of interpretive labor: the LLM as a labeling instrument, not an interpretive agent, with humans retaining conceptual authority
description: The article's organizing methodological framework positions the LLM as a component whose contributions are inspected rather than trusted: it generates candidate labels, structured annotations, and suggested unifications, while researchers decide what enters, merges, or is discarded in the codebook. As the authors put it, "the model's role was confined to proposing, and the researchers' role was to dispose." This human-in-the-loop stance is presented as the safeguard that keeps the interpretive chain of custody intact, absorbs model changes between phases, and makes sites of potential model bias inspectable.
requirements: Human researchers must read raw data alongside model outputs, memo decisions including misleading model proposals, and confront the instrument with data no model preprocessed
constraints: Model-proposed candidate labels are not strictly reproducible across commercial model versions; designs in which model output is itself the finding lack this protection
target_learners: Qualitative researchers considering LLM assistance in codebook development
target_learning_goals: Preserving human interpretive authority while scaling qualitative coding of large interaction corpora
examples: The pipeline crossed a model change from Claude 3 Sonnet to Claude 3.5 Haiku between the axial and selective phases without threatening validity because outputs were always subject to human disposition.
key_sources: Liu, A., Sun, M., Esbenshade, L., Xiao, M., Tian, V., Zhang, Z., & He, K. (2026). Human-LLM Collaborative Inductive Coding for Conceptualizing K-12 Educator AI Use. https://osf.io/ju59q/overview?view_only=96afb71945044b8794e113f9763cc74a

article_title: Policy Fragmentation or Institutional Alignment? Institutional Governance of AI in Universities and Business Schools
citation: Lydia Manikonda and Dominique Outlaw. (2026). Policy Fragmentation or Institutional Alignment? Institutional Governance of AI in Universities and Business Schools.
title: Layer AI governance: a university-wide risk-management base with unit-specific contextual policies
description: The article proposes that institutions govern AI in two coordinated layers: a foundational university-wide policy ensuring "consistency, legal compliance, and academic integrity across all disciplines", and unit-specific contextual policies that honor university guidelines while fostering student learning. It further recommends integrating procurement needs with teaching needs, standardizing disclosure across courses, and maintaining a continuous feedback loop between pedagogy and policy with regular review as technology and workforce demands evolve.
requirements: University-wide guardrails addressing transparency, plagiarism definitions, and strict rules prohibiting upload of sensitive information to AI platforms
Collaborative mechanisms such as inter-department policy committees comprising faculty across units and students across disciplines
constraints: The goal is not a one-size-fits-all solution but a framework institutions adapt to their specific contexts
target_learners: higher education students, particularly business and finance students
target_learning_goals: responsible and effective AI use
workforce readiness with AI literacy
critical thinking to evaluate AI-generated outputs
examples: The article recommends starting with the University-wide risk management policy, then adding department-level contextual policies that mitigate confusion while honoring university-wide guidelines.

article_title: Beyond Compliance: A Proposed Framework for Ethical Governance of Student Data in Learning Analytics
citation: S. Varadaraju and B. Vijayakumar. (2026). Beyond Compliance: A Proposed Framework for Ethical Governance of Student Data in Learning Analytics. EDULEARN26 Proceedings, IATED. https://doi.org/10.21125/edulearn.2026.1927
title: The LEAGUE framework: six pillars for ethical governance of student data in learning analytics
description: LEAGUE is a six-pillar institutional review model for ethical governance of student data in learning analytics. The article states that "The LEAGUE framework organizes ethical review around six pillars: Lawfulness, Equity, Agency, Governance, Utility, and Ethics by Design." It was developed through a structured synthesis of learning analytics, educational data mining, data ethics, policy, value-sensitive design, and capability-oriented educational justice literature, and is demonstrated through an illustrative early alert case.
requirements: Institutional structures that allocate responsibility for reviewing, approving, monitoring, and revising analytics systems, with documented review processes, cross-functional oversight, role clarity, and periodic reassessment
constraints: It is a conceptual model rather than an empirically validated instrument, and it is not a substitute for technical fairness testing or legal counsel
International applicability beyond the FERPA and GDPR contexts emphasized here has not been evaluated
target_learners: higher education students whose data are used in learning analytics systems
target_learning_goals: ethical and educationally meaningful institutional use of student data to support learning
examples: The article applies LEAGUE pillar by pillar to an early alert system for first-year gateway courses, asking under Equity whether indicators are fair proxies for risk and under Governance who approved the score and can change thresholds
key_sources: S. Varadaraju and B. Vijayakumar. (2026). Beyond Compliance: A Proposed Framework for Ethical Governance of Student Data in Learning Analytics. EDULEARN26 Proceedings, IATED. https://doi.org/10.21125/edulearn.2026.1927

Students scoring 60 or higher appear on an advisor dashboard, with outreach expected within 48 hours. The case is illustrative, not an empirical evaluation.

constraints: The case is a hypothetical university scenario used for demonstration, not a studied deployment
target_learners: first-year students in gateway courses

title: Governance maturity progression from compliance-only to AI-ready governance of learning analytics
description: The article reads LEAGUE as a maturity progression with five levels: compliance-only review; documented governance with recorded roles and repeatable practices; ethical governance reviewing equity, agency, and utility alongside compliance; continuous monitoring with scheduled reassessment including model performance and drift; and AI-ready governance extending review to LLM, agentic, and generative student-facing systems. The article states "Institutions frequently begin at a compliance-only posture and can advance toward continuous, AI-ready governance."
requirements: Scheduled reassessment that revisits model performance rather than treating initial approval as final
constraints: The maturity levels are presented as a conceptual summary (Table 4), not a validated measurement instrument; the article calls for quantitative assessment rubrics as future work
target_learners: higher education institutions and their governance bodies
target_learning_goals: progressive institutional capability for ethical governance of student data and AI-enabled student services
examples: Table 4 lists the five levels from compliance-only review limited to FERPA and GDPR through AI-ready governance extending the same review to LLM and agentic systems

article_title: INSIDE the Student's Mind: Jointly Modeling Latent Reasoning and Action in LLM Student Simulators
citation: Rose Niousha, Minwoo Kang, Narges Norouzi. (2026). INSIDE the Student's Mind: Jointly Modeling Latent Reasoning and Action in LLM Student Simulators. Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10492
title: INSIDE: internal dialogue as an intermediate cognitive layer preceding student actions in LLM student simulation
description: INSIDE is a student-modeling framework that fine-tunes LLMs to generate a verbalized internal dialogue before producing the student's next code submission. A teacher LLM (GPT-5) performs retrospective inference over the interaction context and the observed next submission, first producing structured cognitive, affective, and action states inspired by Bloom's Taxonomy, then a first-person think trace used as fine-tuning supervision. The article states that "INSIDE introduces internal dialogue as an intermediate cognitive layer that precedes student actions during learning interactions, capturing the intent that leads to each attempt rather than only explaining mistakes after the fact." Unlike reconstructive post-hoc accounts of errors, the framework models reasoning that precedes each attempt, jointly modeling how and why students act.
requirements: Requires student interaction data with sequential code submissions and associated AI tutor feedback, and a teacher LLM to generate retrospective reasoning traces for fine-tuning supervision.
constraints: Internal dialogue is reconstructed rather than observed; the article notes LLMs "may struggle to faithfully reconstruct novice reasoning patterns," so traces may reflect more coherent reasoning than real students exhibit.
target_learners: Novice undergraduate students in an introductory Python programming course
target_learning_goals: Programming problem-solving with iterative code revision in response to AI tutor and autograder feedback
examples: Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, and Qwen3-8B with LoRA (r=16, alpha=32) on paired think traces and actions from Spring 2025 course data, evaluated against prompting baselines including Bloom-inspired structured CoT.
key_sources: Rose Niousha, Minwoo Kang, Narges Norouzi. (2026). INSIDE the Student's Mind: Jointly Modeling Latent Reasoning and Action in LLM Student Simulators. Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10492

title: Multi-attempt student code submission dataset from a Berkeley introductory programming course with AI tutor feedback
description: A dataset of student code submission streams from an introductory programming course at UC Berkeley (~900 students per semester), spanning Spring 2024 and Spring 2025 and covering the first five Python homework assignments. Each attempt records the student's code, autograder results, and natural-language feedback from an LLM-based tutor for consenting students. The article reports partitioning "using Spring 2025 for training (445 students, 2,022 submission streams, 6,911 total submissions) and Spring 2024 for testing (479 students, 1,546 submission streams, 6,316 total submissions)," with test_OP (5,262 submissions) and test_NP (1,054 submissions) generalization subsets. The data received IRB approval and identifiers were anonymized.

article_title: Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity
citation: Jonathan A. Karr Jr., Grigorii Khvatskii, Ting Hua, and Nitesh V. Chawla. (2026). Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity. Proceedings of the ACM AI Leadership Summit (AILS '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11256
title: Treat detector output as weak evidence, never standalone misconduct evidence; pair any flag with drafting history and human judgment
description: The article's central policy recommendation is that AI-detector scores are structurally unreliable as sole evidence of misconduct because compliant light editing triggers flags while humanized synthetic text evades detection. It states that "Detector output must be treated as weak evidence, not default misconduct evidence" and that "Any flag must be paired with drafting history and sanctions shall be reserved for cases where human judgment supports a lack of appropriate student effort." Institutions should also expect higher flag rates in non-STEM prose and follow FERPA/GDPR rules before uploading student work to third-party services.
requirements: Any flag must be paired with drafting history and human judgment before sanctions
constraints: Findings are based on published English abstracts, not student essays; detector behavior on classroom genres may differ
Labels are proxy-based at a fixed τ = 0.50; 2023–2025 positives are flag rates, not confirmed false positives
Results used one rewrite generator, two detectors, and one humanizer and may not generalize to other tools
target_learners: higher education students
multilingual and novice writers
target_learning_goals: academic integrity policy and fair assessment of AI-assisted student writing
examples: The study flagged 64–80% of light Gemini edits of human abstracts while more than 96% of humanized AI rewrites evaded Pangram and GPTZero

article_title: Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity
citation: Jonathan A. Karr Jr., Grigorii Khvatskii, Ting Hua, and Nitesh V. Chawla. (2026). Why AI Detection Fails for Academic Integrity. Proceedings of the ACM AI Leadership Summit (AILS '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11256
title: Proxy-labeled AI-detection error-analysis corpus and released evaluation pipeline (642 OpenAlex abstracts, three rewrite conditions, two detectors, one humanizer)
description: A controlled evaluation corpus and pipeline for quantifying AI-detector error rates under proxy labels. The authors sampled English abstracts from OpenAlex in chemistry, computer science, political science, and theology for 2013–2015 and 2023–2025; "After requiring 25 to 500 words and PDF access (≈20% loss), we retained 642 abstracts." Each abstract contributed an original plus three Gemini 3 Flash rewrites (refine abstract-only, refine abstract+article, new article-only), scored with Pangram 3.2 and GPTZero before and after Undetectable AI v11 humanization. Analysis code is released at the article's GitHub repository.
requirements: PDF access and 25–500 word length filtering; paid API access for detection and humanization
constraints: English-only corpus of published abstracts, not student essays; corpus size constrained by API and humanization cost
target_learners: academic integrity researchers and administrators
target_learning_goals: evaluating false-positive and false-negative behavior of commercial AI-text detectors
examples: The pipeline scored all variants at τ = 0.50 and re-scored outputs after humanization, producing the paper-clustered error-rate estimates in Table 9

article_title: Addressing Trust in AI Systems through Education: A Didactic Perspective
citation: Pierre Haritz, Hendrik Krone, and Thomas Liebig. (2026). Addressing Trust in AI Systems through Education: A Didactic Perspective. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02453
title: ICE-T: a didactic framework integrating intermodal transfer, computational thinking, and explanatory thinking for ML education
description: ICE-T is a multi-faceted didactic framework for teaching machine learning whose name mnemonically captures its components: Intermodal Transfer grounded in Bruner's enactive-iconic-symbolic principle, Computational Thinking operationalized through the Use-Modify-Create progression, and Explanatory Thinking supported by the PETSP-ML process model. The article states the framework "unifies the three didactic facets described above into a coherent, actionable framework for ML education". The three facets are treated as orthogonal dimensions of a single learning unit: EIS modes structure how a concept is represented, UMC structures the degree of student autonomy, and PETSP-ML structures the temporal sequence, with which combinations are realized left as a deliberate educator design decision.
requirements: Educators deliberately decide which combinations of representational mode, UMC stage, and process phase are realized at each point of a learning unit
constraints: The connection between ICE-T and trust calibration is, at this stage, theoretical and has not itself been evaluated; its empirical grounding is limited to the K-12 landscape
target_learners: K-12 students with little or no prior exposure to programming
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of machine learning
computational thinking
explanatory thinking about ML systems
calibrated trust in AI systems
examples: A decision-tree animal classification unit: students physically sort animal cards (enactive), construct a visual decision tree on a whiteboard (iconic), implement classification rules in code (symbolic), progress through Use, Modify, and Create within each modality, and follow the PETSP-ML stages from task understanding to model training and evaluation
key_sources: Pierre Haritz, Hendrik Krone, and Thomas Liebig. (2026). Addressing Trust in AI Systems through Education: A Didactic Perspective. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02453

article_title: Addressing Trust in AI Systems through Education: A Didactic Perspective
citation: Pierre Haritz, Hendrik Krone, and Thomas Liebig. (2026). Addressing Trust in AI Systems through Education: A Didactic Perspective. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02453
title: PETSP-ML: a four-stage classroom process model for explanatory thinking in machine learning, adapted from CRISP-DM
description: PETSP-ML (Promotion of Explanatory Thinking Standard Process for Machine Learning) is a process model the authors developed "to promote explanatory thinking in a structured manner", adapted from the Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining (CRISP-DM). It reorganizes CRISP-DM's six phases into four classroom-aligned stages: Task Understanding, Data Phase (merging data understanding and preparation), Model Understanding, and Model Training and Evaluation, with an iterative structure encouraging students to revisit earlier stages. Its deliberate departure from professional practice is making model understanding a distinct, prerequisite stage before model training and shifting focus away from performance metrics.
requirements: Model Understanding is treated as a distinct, prerequisite stage before model training, reflecting the pedagogical priority of building conceptual foundations before procedural skills
constraints: CRISP-DM's original formulation is not directly suited to educational settings, where objectives, constraints, and prior knowledge differ substantially from industrial projects
target_learners: K-12 students learning machine learning
target_learning_goals: explanatory thinking about how and why ML systems behave as they do
understanding of training data, algorithmic mechanisms, evaluation metrics, and sources of error or bias
examples: In the Data Phase students collect, inspect, and prepare data while engaging critically with data quality, representativeness, labeling accuracy, and potential biases
key_sources: Pierre Haritz, Hendrik Krone, and Thomas Liebig. (2026). Addressing Trust in AI Systems through Education: A Didactic Perspective. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02453

article_title: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework for AI-Assisted Scoring in Large-Scale Writing Assessment
citation: Curi, M. E., Capdehourat, G., Amigo, I., Romano, M., Serra, R., Silveira, A., Peri, A. (2026). A Human-in-the-Loop Framework for AI-Assisted Scoring in Large-Scale Writing Assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05143
title: Human-in-the-Loop AI-assisted evaluation framework for high-stakes writing assessment
description: A decision-oriented operational framework integrating LLM-based scoring of the Writing section into a national exam workflow while keeping humans in charge of outcome-determining decisions. Its central principle is "ensuring that no final decision affecting test outcomes is made without appropriate human oversight." The workflow (Fig. 8) runs a calibration phase (50–100 texts) to validate the AI model and adapt prompts, scores all responses automatically, applies IRT and Bookmark cut scores, reviews candidates whose pass/fail outcome depends on the Writing section, and recalibrates cut scores after review. Other test sections remain scored by current operational procedures.
requirements: A calibration phase (50–100 texts) to validate the AI model and adapt prompts to the current test topic; IRT and Bookmark cut-score procedures to assign proficiency levels before routing decisions.
constraints: The study was conducted under offline experimental conditions, and operational deployment may surface additional challenges related to monitoring, drift, and edge cases; the workload reduction varies across editions depending on candidate performance in other test sections.
target_learners: Over-age adults (21+) seeking lower secondary education certification in Uruguay's national Acredita EB assessment
target_learning_goals: Reliable, fair rubric-based scoring of Spanish argumentative writing for high-stakes pass/fail certification decisions
examples: In the 2024 and 2025 editions, responses the AI classified as passing could be accepted with high confidence, while AI-failing responses were routed to expert human raters before any final certification decision.

article_title: Exploring K-12 Teachers' Perceptions of Students' Relationships with AI Companions: Boundaries, Intervention Strategies, and Design Implications
citation: Qing Xiao, Wenhan Xie, Ziyu Deng, Ruiwei Xiao, Ziyue Feng, Xie He, Shiyu Zhang, John Stamper, Hong Shen, and Xinying Hou. (2026). Exploring K-12 Teachers' Perceptions of Students' Relationships with AI Companions: Boundaries, Intervention Strategies, and Design Implications. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13479
title: AI companion literacy: a relational extension of AI literacy
description: The article introduces AI companion literacy as an extension of AI literacy that shifts the object of instruction from operating and evaluating AI systems to understanding and navigating AI relationships. It argues existing frameworks cover "competencies for evaluating a tool's output" but not recognizing when engagement has become relational, understanding what such a relationship is and is not, and knowing when to step back. Its closest curricular relatives are sex education, social-emotional learning, and social media literacy.
requirements: Requires competencies beyond existing AI literacy frameworks: recognizing when engagement with an AI has become relational, understanding what such a relationship is and is not, and knowing when to step back from it
constraints: The article states its goal is not to endorse AI companions for K-12 students and regards restricting or banning them as a legitimate response
target_learners: K-12 students across elementary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: Navigating relationships with AI companions
Recognizing when AI engagement has become relational
Knowing what is safe to share and what dependence looks like
examples: Teachers converged that a companion is a program rather than a person, what is safe to share, and what dependence looks like should be taught, with Romantic Partner content withheld for younger grades

article_title: Incipit: Axiom-Grounded Scaffolding for Human-AI Literary Creation
citation: Qiang Liu and Chunyi Zhao. (2026). Literary Axioms: A Conceptual Framework for Literary Creation, Interpretation, and Evaluation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25504
title: Literary Axioms framework: configuration, realization, and reader reconstruction as an interpretive cycle
description: The framework treats a literary work as the realization of a selected configuration of provisional organizing premises (literary axioms) rather than of a theme. It distinguishes an open axiom space, a selected working configuration with relations and planned realization means, the completed work, and situated reader reconstructions. As the authors state, "A work's conceptual organization can be investigated through a selected set of premises and the relations that make them jointly significant." Composition develops consequences of selected premises while reading infers organizing commitments from their realization; neither direction is a formal inference calculus.
requirements: An application must state its unit of analysis, its reading context, and the evidence available for its claims
constraints: The framework applies where a writer or reader can articulate organizing commitments and connect them to particular textual or formal choices
Where sonic, bodily, or visual experience resists propositional description, the appropriate output may be a partial configuration with an explicit remainder, or no useful configuration at all
Literary axioms are natural-language interpretations, not premises in a formal deductive system
target_learners: creative-writing students
literature students
literary scholars
target_learning_goals: literary interpretation
literary creation and revision
literary evaluation
examples: A worked conceptual miniature places the premises that care can require personal sacrifice and that care obligations do not extinguish personal autonomy in tension across two alternative realizations of the same scene
key_sources: Qiang Liu and Chunyi Zhao. (2026). Literary Axioms: A Conceptual Framework for Literary Creation, Interpretation, and Evaluation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25504

article_title: Incipit: Axiom-Grounded Scaffolding for Human-AI Literary Creation
citation: Qiang Liu and Chunyi Zhao. (2026). Literary Axioms: A Conceptual Framework for Literary Creation, Interpretation, and Evaluation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25504
title: Five relational, multidimensional dimensions of literary evaluation
description: The framework organizes literary evaluation around five dimensions: interpretive coherence, contextual reach, distinctiveness, realization fidelity, and interpretive richness. The article states that "Coherence, contextual reach, distinctiveness, realization fidelity, and interpretive richness identify different achievements and failures." Each dimension is operationalized as a question (for example, whether competent readers can construct more than one grounded reconstruction), and the framework deliberately does not combine them into a scalar literary-quality measure.
requirements: Evaluation requires a stated comparison corpus and reader context
constraints: Broad contextual scope is not a proxy for quality; situated works may be important precisely because of their specificity
Distinctiveness is relational and time-dependent, and the dataset currently lacks the comparison corpus and attribution needed for a novelty estimate
target_learners: literary critics
creative-writing students
digital-humanities researchers
target_learning_goals: literary evaluation
critique of literary works
examples: The article specifies operational questions for each dimension, such as whether textual choices repeatedly make the selected claims available rather than merely describing the author's topic

title: Literary axiom dataset: 1,455 Chinese-language records with typed mappings and relationships
description: A concrete implementation of the framework consisting of axioms_consolidated.json and relationships.json, with statements, descriptions, and notes primarily in Chinese. The abstract reports that "A concrete implementation contains 1,455 Chinese-language records, 1,464 mappings to 149 works, and 472 typed relationships." Records carry category (content/form), contextual-scope type, abstraction level, domain/sub-domain, era and region context lists, keywords, and literary examples; mappings use primary, secondary, and technique roles, and relationship links use five typed labels.

constraints: Full literary source texts are not part of these artifacts
The snapshot is highly work-local and should not be treated as a balanced ontology of literary concepts
Relationship strength values are curator-supplied confidence-like annotations, not probabilities or empirical scores

digital-humanities researchers
creative-writing researchers
target_learning_goals: literary interpretation
computational creativity research
examples: The stored skeleton for The Great Gatsby contains 12 mappings with primary, secondary, and technique roles, including limited first-person narration as a technique record
