article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Instructional governance: the designed allocation of authority, agency, accountability, context, and evaluation visibility in AI-mediated teaching interactions
description: The article defines instructional governance as "the designed allocation of pedagogical authority, learner agency, human accountability, contextual boundaries, and evaluation visibility within an AI-mediated teaching interaction". It locates governance at the level where educators and students encounter AI: prompts, rubrics, approval gates, interfaces, dashboards, style guides, and course-specific constraints. The construct complements institutional policy by making governance choices visible in concrete instructional artifacts and workflows.
requirements: Governance must be encoded in a teaching tool's interaction model, constraints, and workflow rather than left to policy documents alone
constraints: Framed for computing and first-year engineering education contexts
target_learners: computing and first-year engineering students
target_learning_goals: responsible and pedagogically aligned use of generative AI in programming instruction
examples: The paper applies the construct across a portfolio of seven AI teaching tools, including rubric-anchored GTA simulations, reflection-oriented code companions, and staff-reviewed forum-response systems
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Six-dimension governance profile framework for characterizing AI teaching tools
description: A governance profile is "an explicit account of how an AI-mediated teaching tool distributes pedagogical authority, learner agency, human accountability, contextual boundaries, and evaluation visibility". The framework comprises six dimensions: pedagogical grounding, AI instructional authority, human accountability and control, learner agency and cognitive engagement, context specificity and boundary setting, and evaluation visibility and revision. Each dimension carries a core design question, typical mechanisms, and evidence of fit, avoiding collapse of governance into a single strict-to-permissive continuum.
requirements: Dimensions are analytically separable but interact in practice; profiles must be matched to the tool's instructional function
constraints: Constructed abductively from seven institutional tools and tested on four published systems; not intended as an exhaustive taxonomy of AI tools in computing education
target_learners: computing educators
tool builders
education researchers
target_learning_goals: designing, comparing, and evaluating AI-mediated learning environments
examples: Table 1 maps each dimension to mechanisms such as instructor-authored rubrics, staff approval gates, reflection prompts, and prompt and content versioning
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Match the governance profile to the instructional function (governance fit)
description: The article argues that "responsible scale in genAI-supported computing education depends on governance fit: coherence between the instructional function of a tool and the governance mechanisms in its design". Tools performing different functions — drafting official forum replies, simulating students for GTA rehearsal, prompting reflection, critiquing code style — should not share one interaction pattern, because each assigns different authority to the AI, responsibility to humans, and intellectual work to learners.
requirements: Designers must specify the instructional function of a tool before selecting governance mechanisms such as rubrics, approval gates, or reflection schemas
constraints: The goal is not a universal permission policy for genAI in computing courses
target_learners: computing educators
instructional staff
target_learning_goals: aligning AI tool design with intended learning processes
examples: BoilerTAI's approval gate is described as "the core workflow" for official course communication, while Owlgorithm is governed through learner reflection rather than answer delivery
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Governance carried by instructional artifacts that predate the AI system
description: A recurring cross-case pattern in which "governance is often carried by instructional artifacts that predate the AI system: rubrics, learning objectives, scenario banks, style guides, or content development workflows". These artifacts encode local values into the tool and provide a stable reference for evaluating outputs that would otherwise be judged only by surface plausibility. GLOW (rubric anchoring), Owlgorithm (reflection schema), CodeStylist (course style guide), and GAIDE (reproducible workflow) instantiate this pattern.
requirements: Local artifacts such as rubrics or style guides must exist and be encoded into the tool's constraints
constraints: Artifacts must be maintained as course materials change
target_learners: computing students
graduate teaching assistants
course instructors
target_learning_goals: rubric-aligned practice
self-explanation
course-specific code style
instructor content development
examples: GLOW constrains AI-simulated student personas with an office-hour conversation rubric interpreted through programmatic coaching
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Governance enacted by workflow placement, with human-in-the-loop specified as a concrete workflow relation
description: A second cross-case pattern in which governance is enacted by placing the AI at a specific point in the instructional workflow. BoilerTAI gives the AI authority to draft forum responses while staff approve what becomes visible; BoilerSketch places TA supervision around diagram generation because diagrams "can appear authoritative even when they encode a subtle misconception". The article stresses that "human in the loop" is most useful when specified as a concrete workflow relation, since configuring, vetting, editing, approving, interpreting, and coaching are different forms of control.
requirements: A specific workflow point must exist where human review or approval can be inserted before outputs reach students
constraints: Supervision is described as especially appropriate for routine topics where staff can rapidly inspect generated representations
target_learners: computing students
instructional staff and TAs
target_learning_goals: accountable official course communication
conceptually correct diagrammatic explanation
examples: BoilerTAI addresses forum response scaling while preserving staff accountability for the final instructional message
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Governance through learner role design: preserving student intellectual work via critique, reflection, debugging, and revision
description: A third cross-case pattern in which governance operates through the learner role the tool constructs. AI-Lab, Owlgorithm, and CodeStylist preserve meaningful student work by shaping AI use around critique, reflection, debugging, and revision. The article states that "learner agency is not abstract; it is an interaction pattern that can be designed" — for example, Owlgorithm prompts explanation after accepted submissions and debugging after failed ones, while CodeStylist positions AI feedback as an invitation to revise.
requirements: The interaction must leave the central learning work — reasoning, debugging, revision decisions — with the student
target_learners: early undergraduate computing students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive reflection
judgment about AI output
code revision and style improvement
examples: AI-Lab expects students to interrogate AI output rather than merely consume it, developing judgment about when AI output is useful or misleading
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education
citation: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098
title: Governance strengthened through visibility and revision: each profile points to the evidence that matters for it
description: A fourth cross-case pattern: "governance becomes stronger when it is visible to instructors and revisable". Rubric-domain analytics, edit and approval traces, student ratings, survey and focus-group evidence, and staff review make tool behavior inspectable and allow revision of rubrics, prompts, scenarios, and approval practices. Because each tool performs a different instructional function, a single portfolio cannot be evaluated through one common outcome measure; instead each governance profile links design choices to evaluation choices.
requirements: Logs, dashboards, edit traces, or ratings must be collected and interpreted by course staff
constraints: Evidence of fit differs by profile — e.g., rubric alignment for rubric-governed tools, edit traces and staff workload for approval-gate tools
target_learners: course instructors
program leaders
target_learning_goals: continuous improvement of AI-mediated instruction
examples: For BoilerTAI, relevant evidence includes response timeliness, final answer quality, staff edit effort, and student satisfaction
key_sources: Ethan Dickey. (2026). Instructional Governance by Design: A Framework for AI in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26098

article_title: HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving
citation: Hyoungwook Jin, Weirui Peng, Jieun Han, Q. Vera Liao, and Xu Wang. (2026). HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28918
title: HelpCoach: an in situ chat-interface add-on scaffolding targeted help-seeking
description: HelpCoach is an add-on to chat interfaces that scaffolds students in formulating specific questions during problem solving. It monitors question specificity in real time, assessing whether each question identifies both a knowledge component and a scaffold type, and provides feedback to keep students aware of targeted help-seeking. When a question is not specific, it prompts templated revision with lists of knowledge components and scaffold types, and a scoped-exploration module recommends three relevant knowledge components and three scaffold types from students' code and chat history. Scaffolds fade as students demonstrate targeted help-seeking.
requirements: Requires initial inputs specifying the relevant knowledge components (e.g., via cognitive task analysis, learner-sourcing, or AI generation) and scaffold types for the target task.
constraints: The article expects generalization across domains with well-defined knowledge components, such as mathematics and science, but states it requires initial inputs that specify the relevant knowledge components and scaffold types.
target_learners: college students learning web programming
target_learning_goals: targeted help-seeking during AI-supported problem solving
metacognitive skills of assessing question specificity and selecting scaffolds
examples: In the lab study, HelpCoach participants completed three Vue.js programming tasks with a GPT-5.4-mini chatbot, receiving specificity ratings, templated revision prompts only for non-specific questions, and scoped suggestions marked with a star.
key_sources: Hyoungwook Jin, Weirui Peng, Jieun Han, Q. Vera Liao, and Xu Wang. (2026). HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28918

article_title: HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving
citation: Hyoungwook Jin, Weirui Peng, Jieun Han, Q. Vera Liao, and Xu Wang. (2026). HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28918
title: The pathway to targeted help-seeking: three metacognitive skills
description: Drawing on Nelson-LeGall's help-seeking model, the article defines targeted help-seeking as a student-driven, self-regulated process in which students retain agency by specifying the knowledge and scaffold they want. It hypothesizes that moving from poor to targeted help-seeking requires three metacognitive skills: students need to assess the specificity of their questions, recognize the types of knowledge and scaffolds they can request, and decide which forms of help best fit their needs. HelpCoach's three features are each mapped onto one of these skills.
requirements: Learners must be able to identify relevant knowledge components and available scaffold types to exercise the three skills.
constraints: Students may initially lack these metacognitive skills and struggle to develop them independently, and may overestimate their self-regulation.
target_learners: students using GenAI chatbots for problem-solving
target_learning_goals: self-regulated, targeted help-seeking
metacognitive awareness of knowledge gaps and scaffold options
examples: The article maps HelpCoach's specificity monitoring, templated revision, and scoped exploration onto the three steps of the pathway (Figure 4).
key_sources: Hyoungwook Jin, Weirui Peng, Jieun Han, Q. Vera Liao, and Xu Wang. (2026). HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28918

article_title: HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving
citation: Hyoungwook Jin, Weirui Peng, Jieun Han, Q. Vera Liao, and Xu Wang. (2026). HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28918
title: Open dataset of student-chatbot interaction logs, code snapshots, and knowledge and self-regulation measures
description: The article releases an open dataset collected from its user studies, consisting of student-chatbot interaction logs (5,650 messages), students' problem-solving logs (7,266 code snapshots), and measurements of their knowledge and self-reported self-regulation. Study 1 contributed 1,286, 944, and 1,163 messages across the three tasks plus 3,851 code-edit logs; Study 2 contributed 1,080, 693, and 646 messages plus 2,704 code-edit records. The full dataset, including LLM prompts and time spent per activity, is available in the supplementary materials.
requirements: The dataset is released as supplementary materials accompanying the article.
constraints: Data come from college students learning Vue.js web programming with GPT-5.4-mini chatbots, so scope is limited to that setting.
target_learners: researchers studying AI-supported help-seeking
target_learning_goals: analysis of question specificity and help-seeking behavior in student-chatbot interactions
examples: Study 1's analytic dataset included 1,286 messages from Programming Task 1, 944 from Task 2, and 1,163 from Task 3.
key_sources: Hyoungwook Jin, Weirui Peng, Jieun Han, Q. Vera Liao, and Xu Wang. (2026). HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28918

article_title: HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving
citation: Hyoungwook Jin, Weirui Peng, Jieun Han, Q. Vera Liao, and Xu Wang. (2026). HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28918
title: Scaffold help-seeking in situ during tasks rather than only before or after them
description: The article argues that help-seeking skills develop more effectively when practiced within hands-on cognitive tasks rather than trained apart from them. Its in situ scaffolding intervenes at the individual message level during cognitive learning activities, on the hypothesis that such domain-embedded practice is more effective because self-regulation often begins as a domain-specific metacognitive skill and later develops into a more domain-independent skill. The approach combines specificity monitoring, templated revision, and context-aware recommendations with performance-based fading.
requirements: Requires real-time assessment of question specificity and task-context inputs (code state, chat history) to time and target the scaffold.
constraints: Fixed, every-other-turn scaffold appearance was disruptive when students no longer needed it, motivating adaptive timing to avoid the expertise reversal effect.
target_learners: college students using GenAI chatbots for problem-solving
target_learning_goals: targeted help-seeking and self-regulation during AI-supported learning
examples: HelpCoach intervenes with the revision scaffold only when a question is not specific, and the revision prompt naturally fades as students increasingly formulate specific questions.
key_sources: Hyoungwook Jin, Weirui Peng, Jieun Han, Q. Vera Liao, and Xu Wang. (2026). HelpCoach: Scaffolding Targeted AI Help-Seeking During Problem-Solving. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28918

article_title: Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning
citation: Qusay H. Mahmoud. (2026). Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning. Preprint, September 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29473
title: Comprehension debt: deferred learning and maintenance cost when AI-assisted production outpaces the ability to explain, test, modify, and justify software
description: Comprehension debt, building on Ahmad's socio-cognitive account of GenAI-assisted student projects, is defined in this review as "thedeferred learning, maintenance, and accountability cost incurred when AI-assisted artifact production outpaces the learner's or team's ability to explain, test, modify, and justify the artifact". Individual indicators include inability to explain control or data flow, poor defect localization, and inadequate test-oracle design; team indicators include uneven ownership and undocumented provenance. Conventional activities—delayed change requests, walkthroughs, independent tests, live debugging—can be repurposed as debt probes comparing what was produced with what can later be demonstrated. Frequency of AI use is a poor proxy: heavy use with active verification can carry low debt.
requirements: Assessment must compare what was produced with what can later be explained, tested, modified, and justified, using measures such as explanation quality, tracing accuracy, and independently designed tests
constraints: The construct remains a research agenda rather than a validated scalar metric
It is not identical to technical debt, academic misconduct, ordinary forgetting, or low code quality
target_learners: software engineering students
student project teams
target_learning_goals: retained code comprehension
independent verification and maintenance capability
accountability for AI-assisted artifacts
examples: Ahmad's underlying study drew on 621 reflective diaries from 207 students, identifying black-box acceptance, context mismatch, dependency-induced atrophy, verification bypass, and AI as a comprehension scaffold
key_sources: Qusay H. Mahmoud. (2026). Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning. Preprint, September 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29473

article_title: Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning
citation: Qusay H. Mahmoud. (2026). Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning. Preprint, September 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29473
title: AASEE framework: five non-linear AI integration levels crossed by four evidence-of-learning obligations (explain, verify, modify, account)
description: The AI-Augmented Software Engineering Education (AASEE) framework connects the scope of delegated engineering work and its lifecycle consequence to observable evidence of retained human competence. "Table 2 summarizes the five AASEE integration levels, their educational focus, typical forms of delegation, and the evidence or safeguards associated with each": tool awareness, guardrailed AI-assisted development, AI-collaborative engineering, AI governance, and agentic and AI systems engineering. Across all levels, four obligations—explain, verify, modify, and account—make retained competence visible; "Together, these obligations shift assessment from visible authorship to visible judgment". Levels are selected from the learning objective, not pursued as a maturity ladder.
requirements: Learning objectives are stated without reference to a tool before choosing an integration level
Evidence obligations (explanation, independent verification, modification under changed conditions, provenance and accountability) must accompany any delegation
constraints: Higher levels are not inherently better; a first-year tracing exercise may remain AI-restricted even where agent orchestration is taught elsewhere
Agentic curriculum proposals are not yet validated learning models
target_learners: software engineering students
computing students
engineering faculty designing courses
target_learning_goals: calibrated trust in AI output
disciplined delegation under lifecycle responsibility
supervision of agentic AI systems
retained independent competence
examples: A testing course at Level 3 has students obtain an initial test suite from an LLM, then classify the input space, justify oracles, add cases, and respond to a seeded defect or change request
A capstone combining Levels 4 and 5 defines task boundaries, permissions, sandboxes, acceptance tests, review ownership, and a recovery plan before an agent touches a repository
key_sources: Qusay H. Mahmoud. (2026). Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning. Preprint, September 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29473

article_title: LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning
citation: Nizam Kadir. (2026). LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning. Technical research report. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02699
title: LearnAdapt Praxis five-stage learning workspace (Frame, Learn, Build, Validate, Transfer)
description: Praxis is a web application in the LearnAdapt ecosystem that structures an adult workplace-learning project across five stages: Frame, Learn, Build, Validate and Transfer. Learners "begin with their own starting response, engage with course material, develop a five-field specification, record validation observations and respond to a different scenario." The server stores a locked baseline, versioned specifications, hint records, validation observations and a separate transfer response, and enforces prerequisites such as a saved specification and validation observations before transfer begins.
requirements: A saved specification and validation observations are server prerequisites before transfer begins; a locked baseline is required before later substantive commands
constraints: The specification is a structured learning artefact, not an executable workplace application; the system does not execute external tests or certify deployment readiness
target_learners: adults in workplace learning programmes
target_learning_goals: framing workplace problems, designing AI-supported services, validation reasoning, independent transfer
examples: The report's Table 1 relates each visible stage to its stored evidence and its interpretation limit, such as a saved reflection not establishing understanding
key_sources: Nizam Kadir. (2026). LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning. Technical research report. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02699

article_title: LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning
citation: Nizam Kadir. (2026). LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning. Technical research report. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02699
title: Retain inspectable provenance records of assisted and independent work, while treating them as application evidence rather than learning-gain evidence
description: The report argues that retaining versions, activity events, coaching records and authenticated actors makes future studies more interpretable by preserving the conditions under which an artefact was produced, but that these records support only limited inferences. It states that "an event label such as authenticated learning activity describes an application provenance category, not a psychological finding", and Table 5 distinguishes supported interpretations (e.g. text was saved in a particular sequence) from unsupported ones (e.g. that a change measures a learning gain).
requirements: Study design and collection context determine the evidential status of records; a course protocol must determine when facilitator feedback is delivered if unaided performance is an outcome of interest
constraints: The JSON schema is not a conformant W3C PROV serialisation, does not capture every interaction, and does not store a tamper-evident audit log or full model-request archive
target_learners: adults in workplace learning programmes
target_learning_goals: independent reasoning and transfer in AI-supported design work
examples: The rehearsal's final exports retained the submitted transfer state, server-assigned reviewer identity, source-labelled timestamped events and notices separating activity records from learning-gain inference
key_sources: Nizam Kadir. (2026). LearnAdapt Praxis: Controlled AI Assistance and Evidence Traces for Adult Workplace Learning. Technical research report. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02699

article_title: From Learning Analytics to Educational Interventions: Enhancing Decision-Making and Learning Design
citation: Svetec, B., Divjak, B., & Kadoić, N. (2026). From learning analytics to educational interventions: enhancing decision-making and learning design. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00620-x
title: Seven-enabler framework for trustworthy LA-based educational interventions
description: A framework of seven institutional practices, capabilities or capacities that support, facilitate and enhance the implementation of educational interventions based on trustworthy learning analytics: institutional strategic orientation, pedagogical & other research foundations, available resources, pedagogical support, ethics & data governance, stakeholder engagement, and quality assurance. The article defines enablers as "institutional practices, capabilities or capacities that support, facilitate and enhance the implementation of educational interventions based on trustworthy LA" and positions trustworthiness as the prerequisite without which LA-based interventions are not meaningful. The framework was developed via survey, Delphi, and SNAP prioritization.
requirements: Trustworthy LA as a prerequisite: the article states trustworthiness is the prerequisite without which LA as a tool for informing educational interventions is not meaningful
constraints: The article states the enablers are not to be interpreted as dimensions of trustworthy LA but as conditions enabling LA-based educational interventions
The article states their relative importance may vary depending on institutional context and the maturity of LA systems
target_learners: Higher education institutions and educational leaders
Teachers and learning designers
target_learning_goals: Data-informed educational decision-making
Learning design and educational change based on trustworthy learning analytics
examples: The study identified the enablers through a survey of 34 e-course participants, a two-round Delphi with international experts, and SNAP prioritization with 12 experts
key_sources: Svetec, B., Divjak, B., & Kadoić, N. (2026). From learning analytics to educational interventions: enhancing decision-making and learning design. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00620-x

article_title: AI-based digital cheating at university, and the case for new ethical pedagogies
citation: Sandra Leaton Gray, Dominic Edsall, Dimitris Parapadakis. (2025). AI-Based Digital Cheating At University, and the Case for New Ethical Pedagogies. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09642-y
title: Combined Theory of Planned Behaviour and Self-Efficacy account of AI-era cheating
description: The article combines Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behaviour with Bandura's Self-Efficacy Theory to explain student decisions to cheat with AI. TPB explains how "attitudes towards cheating, peer influence, and perceived ability to avoid detection" contribute to cheating decisions, while Self-Efficacy Theory explains how beliefs about competence shape perceived control. The combined account holds that a key aspect of cheating is "the interaction between technology's ease of misuse and the individual factors that influence students' choices". The article uses it to argue that banning technologies alone does not deal with the problem at source.
requirements: Understanding both motivational factors (attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioural control) and individual confidence in academic ability and AI-tool use
constraints: Self-Efficacy Theory does not factor in variables in the external environment or deal specifically with cheating, as the article states
The article sets aside external-to-the-student factors such as variable quality of tuition for reasons of space
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
ethical decision-making about AI tool use
examples: The article applies the combined account to argue that a student confident in using AI tools might see less risk of getting caught, increasing the likelihood of dishonesty
key_sources: Sandra Leaton Gray, Dominic Edsall, Dimitris Parapadakis. (2025). AI-Based Digital Cheating At University, and the Case for New Ethical Pedagogies. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09642-y

article_title: AI-based digital cheating at university, and the case for new ethical pedagogies
citation: Sandra Leaton Gray, Dominic Edsall, Dimitris Parapadakis. (2025). AI-Based Digital Cheating At University, and the Case for New Ethical Pedagogies. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09642-y
title: Design validity-driven, rehumanised assessments rather than relying on detection and surveillance
description: The article argues that safeguarding academic integrity requires moving beyond detection towards "validity-driven assessment designs that cultivate ethical agency". Its core validity argument is that "an assessment that can be answered by AI in a way that deceives an assessor is an assessment whose answer is intellectually trivial", so the technology exposes assessments that were already failing their fundamental purpose. Rehumanised approaches such as interactive viva-style examinations or peer-mediated assessments are proposed to foster engagement and reduce reliance on AI tools.
requirements: Assessments must genuinely reflect students' understanding and abilities rather than keyword identification, information compilation and paraphrasing
Investment in bespoke, single-use materials tailored to specific learning outcomes
constraints: Bespoke single-use materials take time, which conflicts with contemporary university workload models
Equitable access to resources (digital divides, accommodation quality, caring responsibilities) remains a fundamental barrier to academic integrity
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: deep learning
authentic demonstration of knowledge and ability
ethical formation
examples: Baird and Clare's case used weekly in-class invigilated tests, a red-flag system, random team reassignment, takedown notices, and single-use video case studies to rehumanise and personalise assessment
key_sources: Sandra Leaton Gray, Dominic Edsall, Dimitris Parapadakis. (2025). AI-Based Digital Cheating At University, and the Case for New Ethical Pedagogies. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-025-09642-y

article_title: Analysing AI utilisation in education through learner question types: A constructivist approach
citation: Lee, H., Atif, A., & Kang, K. (2026). Analysing AI utilisation in education through learner question types: A constructivist approach. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 79–96. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10657
title: Constructivist three-role taxonomy of learner-generated questions: knowledge transmitter, facilitator and co-learner
description: The article organises learner-generated questions through a constructivist framework drawing on Piaget and Vygotsky's theories, in which student inquiries are categorised into three roles: "knowledge transmitter, facilitator and co-learner". This taxonomy serves as the class scheme that the NLP models are trained and evaluated against, linking question type to inquiry depth and to personalised learning and adaptive feedback in educational settings.
requirements: Learner-generated questions must be collected and expert labelled into the three roles before models can be trained on the taxonomy.
constraints: The article notes models struggle to distinguish the higher-order facilitator and co-learner categories, limiting automated use of those classes.
target_learners: higher education students in information technology courses
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking through learner questioning
personalised learning and adaptive feedback
examples: Student inquiries from 11 students across 12 information technology courses were categorised into the three roles and used as classification targets.
key_sources: Lee, H., Atif, A., & Kang, K. (2026). Analysing AI utilisation in education through learner question types: A constructivist approach. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 79–96. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10657

article_title: Analysing AI utilisation in education through learner question types: A constructivist approach
citation: Lee, H., Atif, A., & Kang, K. (2026). Analysing AI utilisation in education through learner question types: A constructivist approach. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 79–96. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10657
title: Dataset of 434 expert-labelled authentic learner questions augmented to balance class distributions
description: A corpus of "434 authentic questions" collected from "11 students across 12 information technology courses", which were "expert labelled and augmented to balance class distributions". The dataset instantiates the constructivist three-role question taxonomy and serves as the training and evaluation data for the BERT, DeBERTa and RoBERTa classification models tested in the study.
requirements: Expert labelling of questions into the three role categories, plus augmentation to balance class distributions.
constraints: Data derive from 11 students across 12 information technology courses, a small single-discipline base the article itself flags via its call for cross-disciplinary validation.
target_learners: higher education information technology students
target_learning_goals: classifying learner inquiry depth to support personalised feedback
examples: The corpus fed the evaluation in which DeBERTa reached the highest overall accuracy (86.36%).

article_title: Differential engagement with generative artificial intelligence in higher education: Gender, motivation, and achievement trajectories
citation: Yuan-Hsuan Lee and Jiun-Yu Wu. (2026). Differential engagement with generative artificial intelligence in higher education: Gender, motivation, and achievement trajectories. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00615-8
title: StatBot: a RAG-enhanced GPT-4 chatbot deployed as a voluntary virtual teaching assistant for graduate statistics courses
description: StatBot is a Retrieval-Augmented Generation chatbot built on GPT-4 that served as a virtual teaching assistant in three graduate statistics courses. As the article describes it, "StatBot was developed based on the GPT-4 large language model within a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework to support instructional interactions in the introductory statistics course." It retrieves from a curated corpus of lecture transcriptions, slides, textbooks, assignments, examinations, answer keys, and Q&A archives via vector-based semantic similarity, then applies a post-generation guardrail module that refines tone and pedagogical alignment, outputs "answer not found" when retrieval is insufficient, and appends source-based citations. It was integrated with the LINE messaging platform via Azure services and use was encouraged but not mandatory.
requirements: A curated internal knowledge base of course-specific instructional materials for retrieval
Deployment infrastructure (Azure Bot Service, OpenAI Service, Blob Storage, Key Vault, App Service) for real-time messaging integration
constraints: StatBot use was not permitted during quizzes and examinations
If retrieved source content is deemed insufficient, the system outputs "answer not found" rather than answering
target_learners: graduate students in introductory, advanced, and multivariate statistics courses
target_learning_goals: statistics content mastery
self-directed problem-solving during a semester-long data analytics project
examples: 97 graduate students across three courses generated 2,819 logged interactions over a 16-week semester under a policy encouraging transparent AI-use disclosure on the final project

title: DBagent: an LLM-based educational agent combining RAG over a course knowledge base, external tool calling, memory, and ReAct reasoning
description: DBagent is a domain-specific educational agent built for an undergraduate database course on a university-wide educational AI infrastructure. It integrates a local course knowledge base via RAG, invokes external tools (search engine, image recognition, academic paper search, calculation, visualization), retains chat history in a memory module, and uses the ReAct reasoning pattern, which "enables LLMs to solve complex problems by alternating between logical reasoning and external execution". It uses Deepseek-r1-671b as base model and personalizes replies with the student's nickname.

Specialized training for students on interaction strategies such as Chain-of-thought prompting

article_title: GenAI assessment and language equity: Drawing the line between support and substitution
citation: Grace Li. (2026). GenAI Assessment and Language Equity: Drawing the Line between Support and Substitution. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09760-1
title: Support–substitution framework: a purpose-based policy architecture for GenAI assessment in multilingual cohorts
description: The article's central framework separates legitimate language support (grammar, clarity, translation for comprehension, surface-level editing) from impermissible substitution (generation or material restructuring of reasoning, analysis, evidence, or sources). It is purpose-based rather than tool-based, ties permission to the assessment construct, and uses calibrated disclosure feasible for multilingual cohorts. As the article states, the framework is 'purpose-based rather than tool-based, uses calibrated disclosure that is feasible for multilingual cohorts, and links enforcement to reasons, proportionality, and evidence standards'. It is anchored in indirect discrimination logic, procedural fairness, and Kane's and Messick's validity accounts.
requirements: Permitted use must be expressly authorised in the assessment instructions for the specific task
The construct the task is intended to evidence must be re-specified to reflect the broader permission
Disclosure must be calibrated to make the permitted use visible without imposing disproportionate burden
constraints: The analysis is conceptual and governance-oriented, not empirical; it does not measure student behaviour or policy comprehension
Illustrative reference points are drawn from the Australian sector (TEQSA, Universities Australia)
target_learners: EAL and multilingual students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Fair assessment of disciplinary reasoning independent of English fluency
Academic integrity governance that distinguishes language support from substantive substitution
examples: A policy-analysis assessment where GenAI may generate an initial list of policy options under disclosure, with marks attaching to the student's verification, selection, and defence of the options
key_sources: Grace Li. (2026). GenAI Assessment and Language Equity: Drawing the Line between Support and Substitution. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09760-1

article_title: GenAI assessment and language equity: Drawing the line between support and substitution
citation: Grace Li. (2026). GenAI Assessment and Language Equity: Drawing the Line between Support and Substitution. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09760-1
title: Shift integrity governance from detection to assessment design
description: The article recommends a design-first approach that creates observable learning traces, clarifies what is being assessed, and makes the integrity boundary operational before submission. It argues this 'moves integrity governance away from suspicion and surveillance and toward transparent design and accountable decision-making', creating safe harbours for legitimate language assistance while preserving prohibitions on substitution. Detection-led responses are limited and risk cohort-skewed injustice.
requirements: Assessment designs that make reasoning visible and clarify the construct
Institutional commitment to redesigning assessment rather than relying on tool bans or blanket disclosure
constraints: Detector outputs may have a triage role but rarely constitute proof; over-reliance increases the risk of false positives and cohort-skewed error
target_learners: EAL and multilingual students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Protecting assessment validity and fairness while permitting legitimate language support
examples: Regulators and quality agencies such as TEQSA emphasise that detection-led responses are limited and assessment design must play a central role in learning assurance

article_title: GenAI assessment and language equity: Drawing the line between support and substitution
citation: Grace Li. (2026). GenAI Assessment and Language Equity: Drawing the Line between Support and Substitution. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09760-1
title: Box 1 quick tests for distinguishing support from substitution
description: Box 1 operationalises the support–substitution distinction with working definitions, quick tests, and illustrative edge cases. Permitted language support is defined as surface-level interventions improving readability 'without adding ideas, sources, or analytical structure'; substitution is defined as interventions creating or materially reshaping the substantive content. The quick tests ask whether an interaction would produce a new idea, a new source, or a re-ordering of analysis, functioning as a shared discretion-discipline device for markers.
requirements: Institutions adopting the framework should expand the edge-case list iteratively as practice generates new grey zones
constraints: The tests are deliberately conservative; where uncertainty remains, the focus should shift to learning traces and the student's ability to explain reasoning steps
target_learners: EAL and multilingual students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Ex ante clarity about permitted and prohibited GenAI functions for a specific task
examples: Edge cases include sentence-level clarity edits that preserve meaning (support) versus paragraph-level re-composition that changes emphasis (substitution)
key_sources: Grace Li. (2026). GenAI Assessment and Language Equity: Drawing the Line between Support and Substitution. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09760-1

article_title: GenAI assessment and language equity: Drawing the line between support and substitution
citation: Grace Li. (2026). GenAI Assessment and Language Equity: Drawing the Line between Support and Substitution. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09760-1
title: Box 3 decision rubric for integrity decision-makers
description: Box 3 provides a standardised rubric guiding integrity decisions: acceptable evidence types (staged submissions, drafts, student explanation of process, verifiable source trail, viva-style checks), weak proxies that should not be determinative (polished language, sudden fluency, non-native phrasing, single detection scores), the decision question on the balance of probabilities, proportionality mapping, and reasons and reviewability requirements. It is designed to 'discipline discretion, improve consistency across markers and faculties, and support reviewability in appeals'.
requirements: Decisions must record reasons linked to the construct and the communicated boundary
Students must have a meaningful opportunity to respond
constraints: Detection outputs may be used only as triage prompts, not as determinative evidence
target_learners: EAL and multilingual students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Consistent, reviewable, proportionate integrity decision-making under evidentiary uncertainty
examples: Proportionality mapping: educative response for non-disclosure of permitted support; mark-level penalties where institutional notice was ambiguous; escalation for repeated or deliberate substitution

article_title: From disengaged to self-determined: a latent transition analysis of students' AI learning motivation
citation: Liang, S., Yau, K. W., Meng, H., Chiu, T. K. F., King, I., Yam, Y., & Chai, C. S. (2026). From disengaged to self-determined: A latent transition analysis of students' AI learning motivation. Education and Information Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-026-13998-y
title: SDT-based five-indicator operationalization of AI learning motivation
description: The study extends Self-Determination Theory to AI education by operationalizing need satisfaction through five indicators: competence as confidence in learning AI (AICF) and perceived mastery of basic AI knowledge (AIKG), relatedness as AI for social good (AISG) and ethical use of AI (AIET), and autonomy as behavioral intention to learn AI (AIBI). As the article states, "Students' AICF and AIKG capture the competence dimension, as they reflect students' beliefs about their ability to understand and master AI concepts." All scales showed Cronbach's α ≥ 0.85 and full longitudinal measurement invariance was supported.
requirements: Validated self-report instruments for the five need-satisfaction indicators, rated on a 7-point Likert scale
Longitudinal measurement invariance across time points before comparing profiles
constraints: Relies on self-report measures of motivation, which the authors note may be subject to social desirability bias or limited metacognitive awareness
target_learners: Secondary school students (Grades 7–9) in AI education
target_learning_goals: Sustained motivational engagement in AI learning
AI literacy development
examples: The framework was applied to 2,086 Hong Kong secondary students across a year-long AI curriculum using pre- and post-test surveys

article_title: Beyond a single role: Justifying a role-adaptive framework for AI companions through a comparative study in elementary book talk
citation: Liao, C.-Y. (2026). Beyond a single role: Justifying a role-adaptive framework for ai companions through a comparative study in elementary book talk. Education and Information Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-026-13958-6
title: Role-Adaptive AI Companion Framework: a Modular Adaptive Agent that dynamically switches between Student Peer, Teacher Assistant, and Parent Advisor roles
description: The framework conceptualizes an AI companion as a Modular Adaptive Agent (MAA), inspired by Multi-Agent Systems role-differentiation principles, that "dynamically transitions between three primary roles: the ‘Student Peer’ (facilitating low-stakes dialogue), the ‘Teacher Assistant’ (providing diagnostic analytics), and the ‘Parent Advisor’ (offering actionable home-based guid - ance)." Its core principle is context-aware role adaptability: the agent perceives the user and pedagogical task and modulates its functions, interactional style, and communication register through a modular configuration mechanism, triggered by cues such as user login or task selection. The framework is grounded in scaffolding theory, Learning Companion System principles, and socio-ecological views of family involvement, and its transition logic is justified by the article's empirical competence-gap findings.
requirements: A unified data backbone with Role-Based Access Control and privacy-preserving data protocols so role-appropriate information is shared selectively
Triggers such as user identity or task selection to activate the appropriate role
Access to student interaction data, curriculum data, and student profiles for adaptation
constraints: Conceptualized specifically for elementary reading education and book talk within programs like MSSR
The framework itself was not implemented or evaluated; the empirical study tested only a fixed single-role instantiation
target_learners: Elementary school students in reading programs
Their teachers
Their parents
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and reflective book talk
Factual recall, emotional response, and future-oriented application (4F dimensions)
Teacher instructional decision-making and parental support of reading at home
examples: The formative study instantiated only the Student Peer role using a Whisper-plus-GPT-3.5 conversational system, isolating the single-role baseline the framework is meant to transcend

article_title: Beyond a single role: Justifying a role-adaptive framework for AI companions through a comparative study in elementary book talk
citation: Liao, C.-Y. (2026). Beyond a single role: Justifying a role-adaptive framework for ai companions through a comparative study in elementary book talk. Education and Information Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-026-13958-6
title: Three role-integration design principles: integrated data governance, context-driven role switching, and synergistic human-AI collaboration
description: The article specifies three paramount design principles for orchestrating multiple AI roles into a cohesive whole. "Permissions and Data Sharing form the ethical backbone of the framework," implemented through Role-Based Access Control so the Teacher Assistant role provides detailed analytics while the Parent Advisor role generates aggregated, non-identifiable summaries. Context-driven adaptability operates on two levels: explicit role switching via pre-defined triggers and implicit stylistic adaptation that recalibrates scaffolding in real time. Synergistic human-AI collaboration requires communication protocols so insights from one role, such as the Student Peer mode, inform another, such as the Teacher Assistant interface.
requirements: Robust Role-Based Access Control and privacy-preserving data protocols compliant with regulations such as GDPR and FERPA
Clear, pre-defined triggers for explicit role switching
Interface loops designed to manage the interplay of roles, users, activities, and data flows
constraints: Stated for the proposed framework's orchestration of roles, not empirically tested in the study
target_learners: Elementary school students
Teachers
Parents
target_learning_goals: Coordinated multi-stakeholder support for reading education and book talk
examples: The Teacher Assistant role exposes configurable analysis parameters and reviewable dashboards, while the Parent Advisor role allows parents to customize information focus to prevent overload

article_title: Tool, Tutor, or Crutch?: A Grounded Theory of Cognitive Scaffolding and Offloading in AI-Assisted Programming Education
citation: Liu, D., Fan, G., & Pan, L. (2026). Tool, tutor, or crutch?: A grounded theory of cognitive scaffolding and offloading in AI-assisted programming education. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00592-w
title: Domain Mastery versus Tool Mastery tension model with Scaffolding and Offloading loops
description: A grounded-theory process model explaining how learners navigate between Domain Mastery, described as "conceptualization, explanation, and evaluation", and Tool Mastery, "procedural efficiency with AI". The model posits two recurrent feedback loops: a Scaffolding Loop, in which learners inquire, test, modify, and explain AI output while retaining germane processing, and an Offloading Loop, in which rapid delegation suppresses germane processing. It is interpreted through Cognitive Load Theory and Self-Determination Theory and is offered as an interpretive, non-causal account that reconciles the performance–learning paradox.
requirements: Interpretation through Cognitive Load Theory and Self-Determination Theory as primary lenses, with ZPD and Cognitive Apprenticeship as sensitizing concepts
constraints: The article states it describes associations rather than causal mechanisms; loops can co-exist within one assignment and learners move between them over time
target_learners: undergraduate programming students
target_learning_goals: durable conceptual understanding and evaluative skill in programming
examples: Categories emerged from constant comparison across an AI-enabled section and a human pair-programming contrast section over 16 weeks, using interviews, logs, and concept maps

article_title: Automated Coding of Content and Pedagogical Content Knowledge of Mathematics Using a Multi-Agent Large Language Model
citation: Copur-Gencturk, Y., Moreno, K., Chu, Y., Li, H., & Tang, J. (2026). Automated coding of content and pedagogical content knowledge of mathematics using a multi-agent large language model. ZDM – Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01796-2
title: GradeOpt: a multi-agent LLM coding framework with Grader, Reflector, and Refiner agents
description: GradeOpt is a multi-agent LLM framework for coding open-ended responses against human coding manuals. The article states that "GradeOpt automates the coding instruction process through collaboration among three LLM-powered agents: Grader, Reflector, and Refiner." Grader codes responses using only the rubric and guidelines; Reflector conducts error analysis on disagreements with human codes; Refiner revises Grader's instructions by adding clarification points without altering coding criteria. Refinement runs up to six rounds per item, with a 70/10/20 train/validation/test split and validation used only for early stopping and model selection.
requirements: A coding manual developed for human coders, including rubric, coding guidelines, and sample coded responses with justifications
Training data with agreed-on human codes for the refinement loop
constraints: The article notes results depend on the specificity of the coding manual and that all rubrics in this study used three categories
The dataset was limited to a single mathematics topic, ratios and proportional relationships
target_learners: U.S. middle school mathematics teachers (whose open-ended assessment responses are coded)
target_learning_goals: Measuring teachers' content knowledge and pedagogical content knowledge of ratios and proportional relationships
examples: In the worked illustration, Reflector identified that a response referencing finding the difference indicated additive reasoning, and Refiner added a clarification that statements describing maintaining a constant difference should be coded as 2.

citation: Copur-Gencturk, Y., Moreno, K., Chu, Y., Li, H., & Tang, J. (2026). Automated coding of content and pedagogical content knowledge of mathematics using a multi-agent large language model. ZDM – Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01796-2
title: Two-domain conceptualization of mathematics teacher knowledge: CK and PCK with three PCK subdomains
description: The article's conceptual framework treats content-specific knowledge for teaching mathematics as two domains, CK and PCK. CK is understanding "the mathematical meaning of rules and strategies," connections among ideas, and reasoning and problem solving in the school curriculum, operationalized through proportional-reasoning items. PCK is conceptualized as content-specific pedagogy comprising three subdomains: knowledge of mathematical tasks, knowledge of students' mathematical thinking, and knowledge of teaching mathematics, each encompassing knowing as well as reasoning and application. This framework guided the development of the open-ended items that GradeOpt and the comparison models coded.
requirements: Items situated in teaching contexts, because the contextualized nature of PCK limits what multiple-choice items can capture
Coding manuals with construct descriptions, 3-point rubrics, and sample coded responses with justifications
constraints: The framework as operationalized here covers ratios and proportional relationships in middle school mathematics only
target_learners: U.S. middle school mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: Measuring teachers' content knowledge and pedagogical content knowledge of ratios and proportional relationships
examples: The nine PCK items coded in the study comprised knowledge of mathematical tasks (2), knowledge of students' mathematical thinking (2), and knowledge of teaching mathematics (5), each scored with a 3-point rubric.

article_title: Large language models as grading assistants in public health education: a method-comparison study of essay-style exam assessment
citation: Brevik A, Jerpseth H and Lafontan SR (2026). Large language models as grading assistants in public health education: a method-comparison study of essay-style exam assessment. Front. Educ. 11:1904452. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1904452
title: Use LLMs as supervised grading assistants rather than autonomous graders for essay-style exams
description: The article concludes that LLMs can support essay grading in health sciences education but only under human oversight. It reports that "LLMs may currently be better suited as supervised grading assistants than as autonomous graders," because moderate agreement with humans combined with session-to-session variability makes default-setting autonomous grading unreliable for high-stakes assessment. The principle directs implementation toward assistance, verification, and efficiency support rather than replacement of human judgment.
requirements: Human oversight and transparency when integrating LLMs into educational assessment
Verification of LLM-suggested grades by human examiners before grades are finalized
constraints: Autonomous LLM-based grading using default settings is not currently reliable for high-stakes assessment tasks
Agreement was sensitive to operational conditions including prompt context, file upload volume, and repeated execution
target_learners: master's-level public health and health sciences students
target_learning_goals: reliable grading of long-form, essay-style exam answers
examples: The study compared LLM-assigned A-F grades with published human grades on 32 anonymized master's exam submissions and found only moderate, unstable alignment.

citation: Vangelis Tsiligkiris. (2026). What students ask matters: LLM interaction depth, task quality, and immediate recall in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00617-6
title: Privacy-preserving instrumentation pipeline linking LLM conversational telemetry to learning outcomes
description: A replicable, GDPR-aligned pipeline that records every prompt and response in a custom Streamlit application backed by Gemini 1.5 Flash, generating a random six-character pseudonymous ID that links logs, assessments, and submissions without personally identifiable information. The article states it "demonstrates a replicable, privacy-preserving instrumentation pipeline that links anonymised conversational telemetry with assessment data under GDPR-aligned conditions". Logs carry millisecond timestamps, character counts, and latency metrics, written to an append-only Google Sheet and exported as CSV for scripted preprocessing with validity checks.

Pseudonymous session identifiers and encrypted, access-restricted storage per the article's privacy-by-design description
constraints: Minimal conversation history was supplied to the model to support reproducibility and cost control, which the article notes may limit adaptation to prior turns

target_learning_goals: linking observable LLM interaction behaviour to measurable learning outcomes
examples: The study used the pipeline in a 90-minute session: pre-test, LLM-assisted neuroeconomics case task, post-test, with real-time log capture and linkage integrity verified by staff

citation: Vangelis Tsiligkiris. (2026). What students ask matters: LLM interaction depth, task quality, and immediate recall in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00617-6
title: Dissociation between performance quality and short-term recall in LLM-supported study
description: The article's central explanatory account: the same interaction signal — explanation-seeking depth — relates positively to applied task quality but not to immediate recall, indicating "a dissociation between performance quality and short-term recall in LLM-supported study". It aligns this with cognitive-psychology evidence that elaboration improves comprehension while retrieval practice consolidates retention, and with cognitive off-loading and "illusion of competence" accounts: fluent on-demand explanations may limit effortful retrieval and encoding when the learning sequence lacks explicit retrieval demands.
requirements: Interpretation rests on a lexical depth proxy rather than verified cognitive engagement, as the article itself states
constraints: Single-group design, small sample (n = 22), immediate testing only, and keyword-based depth proxies, as the article lists
target_learners: higher education students using LLMs in study sessions
target_learning_goals: applied task quality
knowledge recall and retention
examples: The study modelled task quality and recall side by side against the same interaction traces, finding depth predicted one but not the other
key_sources: Vangelis Tsiligkiris. (2026). What students ask matters: LLM interaction depth, task quality, and immediate recall in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00617-6

article_title: Exploring the Capacity of Large Language Models to Simulate Students' Scientific Thinking: Insights for Responsive Teaching
citation: Nguyen, H., & Cao, J. (2026). Exploring the Capacity of Large Language Models to Simulate Students' Scientific Thinking: Insights for Responsive Teaching. Journal of Science Education and Technology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-026-10333-5
title: Responsive teaching: attending to, connecting, and pursuing the substance of students' ideas
description: The article's organizing framework defines responsive teaching as practices that "foreground and pursue the substance of students' ideas" — attending to the substance of students' ideas, connecting them to disciplinary ideas, and pursuing students' thinking. It builds on both a cognitive perspective (students' epistemological resources as fine-grained knowledge elements teachers can recognize) and a sociocultural perspective (meaning-making through social interaction). The study operationalizes it by prompting LLMs to simulate varied student ideas, including partial or incorrect reasoning, so teachers can anticipate and respond to student thinking.
requirements: Teachers need opportunities to practice sensemaking about specific student thinking within their instructional contexts
constraints: Teachers may avoid epistemic uncertainty or treat it superficially rather than pushing student thinking
target_learners: K-12 science students
pre-service and in-service science teachers
target_learning_goals: scientific sensemaking
teacher responsiveness to student ideas
examples: The storyline approach anchors instruction in questions connected to students' experiences; instructional materials can include partially complete or incorrect student ideas for teachers to build on

title: OpenSciEd lesson-idea dataset of 49 lesson plans and 8820 LLM-simulated student ideas
description: The study's core artifact is a dataset built from "suggested student ideas in OpenSciEd lesson plans", which were created through pilot data collection and teacher consultation. The authors "selected nine learning units across three domains (life sciences, physics, and chemistry) and three grade levels (elementary, middle, and high school) and extracted 49 lesson plans", each with 28 ideas on average (SD = 10). Six LLMs then generated 30 simulated ideas per lesson (1470 per LLM; 8820 total) using a structured prompt covering learning standards, prior instruction, activity description, task description, and simulation instruction.
requirements: Lesson plans with detailed activity descriptions and suggested student ideas to ground the generation prompts
constraints: The lesson ideas come from pilot data collection and teacher predictions, which the authors note might not fully represent student ideas
target_learners: elementary, middle, and high school science students
target_learning_goals: simulating open-ended student responses to science investigation activities
examples: The prompt instructed LLMs to simulate language and reasoning styles including possible partial or incorrect scientific reasoning

article_title: LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning
citation: LearnLM Team, Google. (2024). LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16429
title: Pedagogical instruction following: conditioning model behavior on system-level pedagogy instructions
description: The report's central framework recasts injecting pedagogy into generative AI not as fixing one definition of good tutoring but as instruction following for pedagogical System Instructions. The authors "cast our work aspedagogical instruction following, meaning that we contextualize training and evaluation examples with system-level instructions that describe desired pedagogical behavior." This lets teachers or developers specify desired behavior, avoids conflicts of persona or style when mixing pedagogical data into Gemini's training mixture, and treats pedagogy as hard constraints (e.g. "do not reveal the answer") plus soft guidelines (e.g. "use a motivating tone").
requirements: Training and evaluation conversations must each begin with a specific System Instruction describing the pedagogical behavior present in that conversation; vague instructions are counterproductive because the model learns to ignore them.
constraints: The authors note pedagogy is "prohibitively difficult to define" across grade levels, subjects, languages, cultures and philosophies, so the framework deliberately avoids committing to any particular definition of pedagogy.
target_learners: learners across grade levels and subjects interacting with AI tutors
independent EdTech users and classroom students
target_learning_goals: tutoring and teaching interactions guided by teacher- or developer-specified pedagogical behavior
examples: LearnLM conversations were seeded with pedagogically focused System Instructions, and human preference raters labeled model samples on adherence to those instructions to train reward models for RLHF.
key_sources: LearnLM Team, Google. (2024). LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16429

article_title: LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning
citation: LearnLM Team, Google. (2024). LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.16429
title: LearnLM: a Gemini 1.5 Pro-based model co-trained for pedagogical instruction following
description: LearnLM is an experimental model available on Google AI Studio, built on Gemini 1.5 Pro (gemini-1.5-pro-002) by co-training: the team mixed pedagogical SFT demonstration data and human preference data (reward model and RLHF) directly into Gemini's post-training stages. The authors state they "co-train with Gemini, meaning we mix our data directly with Gemini's SFT, RM, and RL stages", which lets the model learn new instruction following without forgetting core reasoning, multimodal, factuality, safety, or multi-turn properties, and keeps LearnLM in sync as the Gemini recipe evolves.
requirements: Pedagogical data must be conditioned on specific System Instructions so it can be mixed with general conversational data without conflicts of persona or style.
constraints: A subset of LearnLM improvements is part of the recently released Gemini 2.0 models; the evaluated version is a point-in-time artifact compared against model versions as of 2024-10-01.
target_learners: students and independent learners using AI tutoring products
target_learning_goals: interactive tutor-led exercises specified by teachers or developers through system instructions
examples: The model is offered as an experimental release on Google AI Studio with documentation of example use cases and suggested prompts.

description: CulturAIEd is an LLM-powered system built on streamlit with the gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 model that helps teachers contextualize AI literacy activities through CRP principles. It combines "demographic characteristics of the students, rubric-based feedback, and just-in-time coaching" and offers two tiers of lesson modifications, basic and advanced, based on a CRT checklist, plus an interactive chatbot simulating instructional coaching.

description: The article frames CRP, rooted in Ladson-Billings' foundational work, as "promoting academic success, developing cultural competence, and fostering sociopolitical consciousness." It presents Geneva Gay's Culturally Responsive Teaching (CRT) as a closely aligned concept emphasizing "more explicit strategies for operationalizing cultural responsiveness within daily teaching practices," particularly for modifying course materials. CulturAIEd operationalizes these ideas via a CRT checklist with levels from Contributions to Social Action.

constraints: The article notes existing literature warns against the risk of routinizing CRP

The article states "The strength of RAG lies in its ability to produce contextually accurate content by incorporating the generated output into factual data." Lessons follow a five-section structure (Title Page, Scenario I, Instruction, Scenario II, Conclusion) and can be generated in one to five segments.

article_title: AgenticMath: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Agentic-based Math Data Generation
citation: Xianyang Liu, Yilin Liu, Shuai Wang, Hao Cheng, Andrew Estornell, Yuzhi Zhao, Jun Shu, Jiaheng Wei. (2025). AgenticMath: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Agentic-based Math Data Generation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19361
title: AgenticMathQA: curated 30K/60K/90K math reasoning dataset
description: AgenticMathQA is the released training dataset produced by the AgenticMath pipeline, offered in curated 30K, 60K, and 90K versions. The article states: "We release AgenticMathQA, a curated dataset in 30K, 60K, and 90K versions." Unlike prior scale-focused approaches, it emphasizes "clarity, correctness, and diversity, providing higher-quality supervision for mathematical reasoning." The 30K version combines 15K seed problems with solutions and 15K AgenticMath-synthesized problem-solution pairs; larger sizes duplicate each problem with multiple solutions.
requirements: Built from GSM8K and MATH seed problems filtered at a quality threshold of score 3
Synthesized pairs must pass the Stage 4 ranking-based selection targeting 15K high-quality pairs
constraints: The article notes the study focuses primarily on text-based mathematical problems; extension to multimodal settings remains future work
Large-scale synthesis beyond the explored sample sizes was not conducted due to computational and resource constraints
target_learners: 3B-8B parameter large language models undergoing supervised fine-tuning
target_learning_goals: Mathematical reasoning on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks
examples: The 30K setting consists of 15K seed problems and 15K AgenticMath-synthesized problems; scaling to 60K and 90K is achieved by duplicating each problem with multiple solutions

article_title: AgenticMath: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Agentic-based Math Data Generation
citation: Xianyang Liu, Yilin Liu, Shuai Wang, Hao Cheng, Andrew Estornell, Yuzhi Zhao, Jun Shu, Jiaheng Wei. (2025). AgenticMath: Enhancing LLM Reasoning via Agentic-based Math Data Generation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19361
title: AgenticMath four-stage multi-agent data generation framework
description: AgenticMath is an automated multi-agent framework enforcing quality control at every stage of mathematical data generation. It proceeds in four stages: seed problem filtering (LLM scoring on complexity, information value, and clarity with k-NN score curation), agentic problem generation (rephrase, review, and revise agents with an iterative loop), solution generation (one-shot chain-of-thought prompting), and synthetic-data evaluation with ranking-based selection. The article describes it as "an automated multi-agent framework that enforces quality control at every stage of mathematical data generation," following a "Less Is More" principle to yield a data-efficient, high-quality dataset.
requirements: LLM agents (GPT-4o-mini) for scoring, rephrasing, review, revision, and solution generation
Seed problems sourced from human-authored corpora (GSM8K and MATH)
Quality thresholds: seed filtering score of 3 and review-revise threshold of 4.5 with up to three iterations
constraints: The article notes current study focuses on text-based mathematical problems; multimodal extension remains future work
Scalability under substantially larger data budgets was not evaluated due to computational and resource constraints
target_learners: 3B-8B parameter large language models undergoing supervised fine-tuning
target_learning_goals: Generating high-quality mathematical question-answer pairs to improve LLM mathematical reasoning
examples: Each filtered seed problem is expanded into six rephrased variants; the review-revise loop runs at most three iterations with early stopping once the 4.5 threshold is met
