article_title: Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education
citation: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://www.openstax.org
title: Learning Context Framework for AI Applications: five dimensions of learner context
description: The Learning Context (LC) Framework structures what AI education systems should know about a learner across five organizing questions: Who (learner factors such as prior knowledge, misconceptions, psychosocial traits), With whom (peers and instructors), What (content, task difficulty and domain), When (stable traits versus volatile states and intraindividual change), and Where (digital environment from micro- to meso-system, based on Bronfenbrenner's ecological levels). The article proposes it because "the ﬁeld lacks a computationally tractable theory for representing LC at scale," and pairs the dimensions with AI opportunities such as contextualized instructional design strategies and edtech affordances (feedback, prompts, practice quizzes).
requirements: Representation must be grounded in learning science, computationally amenable, machine-readable, and human-interpretable
constraints: Current AI systems capture only the context visible through direct user interaction, operationalizing a narrow subset of these dimensions
target_learners: K-12 and college learners using AI-based learning tools
target_learning_goals: Deep, robust learning via context-aware personalization rather than shallow mimicry
examples: The framework's dimensions were instantiated in four LLM vignettes and translated into the LC data structure of Theme 2
key_sources: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24362

article_title: Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education
citation: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://www.openstax.org
title: Multi-layered Learning Context graph data structure with modular design principles
description: The LC data structure translates the five framework dimensions into computational components: a learner vector, a dynamic social graph, graph-based content representations aligned to standards such as IEEE LOM and xAPI, a temporal index with recency weighting and spacing intervals, and environmental/platform metadata. "These ﬁve components form a multi-layered LC graph, where nodes correspond to entities (learner, content, peers, activities) and edges encode relationships and interactions." It can be structured as a JSON-LD schema or a knowledge graph compatible with graph databases such as Neo4j, enabling warm-start reasoning from accumulated context.
requirements: Modularity: each LC dimension forms an independently addressable module enabling selective access and updating
Extensibility: new dimensions can be added without schema overhaul
Interpretable embeddings: human-readable context snapshots for instructors and learners
Cross-system consistency: standardized metadata for interoperability across AI tools and platforms
constraints: Certain key components, such as belief-based models, are not yet fully developed
target_learners: Learners using AI-based teaching and learning systems across multiple tools
target_learning_goals: Personalized, context-aware instructional support across sessions and platforms
examples: Figure 6 illustrates four representation approaches with distinct trade-offs; Figure 7 shows an example belief-based model for a Grade-10 learner struggling with quadratic equations

title: Belief-based models (BBMs) capturing what learners actually believe
description: Belief-based models are a proposed LC component intended to capture learners' mental models, assumptions, preferences, and misconceptions—the beliefs that shape how they think, learn, and engage with content. The article positions them as under development: "we are working towards a BBM component that captures what learners actually believe." Their rationale is that beliefs shape learning trajectories in ways factual-knowledge modeling alone cannot capture, so beliefs must be represented as part of the broader Learning Context rather than only as mastered skills.
requirements: Beliefs must be represented as part of the broader LC, alongside factual knowledge models
constraints: The BBM component is not yet (fully) developed
target_learners: Learners whose misconceptions and beliefs shape their learning trajectories, e.g., Grade-10 algebra learners
target_learning_goals: Representing and responding to learner misconceptions and beliefs during instruction
examples: Figure 7 shows an example BBM for Sarah, a Grade-10 learner struggling with quadratic equations, including underlying belief, erroneous example, and triggering feature

article_title: Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education
citation: Naiming Liu, Brittany Bradford, Johaun Hatchett, Gabriel Diaz, Lorenzo Luzi, Zichao Wang, Debshila Basu Mallick, Richard Baraniuk. (2025). Learning Context: A Unified Framework and Roadmap for Context-Aware AI in Education. https://www.openstax.org
title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) as the interoperability layer for warm-starting AI education tools
description: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the open-standards mechanism the article proposes for making Learning Context portable across AI tools, so that learner context accumulated in one system can be consumed by another. "By leveraging the Model Context Protocol (MCP), we will enable a wide range of AI tools to “warm-start” with durable context and achieve continual, long-term personalization." MCP addresses the problem that context is lost whenever a learner switches tools, and is one of the four research questions of the LC technology theme: how modern AI systems can interoperate securely through open standards.
requirements: Standardized metadata ensuring cross-system consistency and interoperability across AI tools and learning platforms
constraints: Realizing cross-tool context portability requires substantial R&D on scalable, privacy-aware data infrastructure
target_learners: Learners who use multiple AI tools and learning platforms across their learning journeys
target_learning_goals: Continual, long-term personalization via durable, portable learner context
examples: The article's implementation strategy embeds the LC in the OpenStax digital learning platform ecosystem with SafeInsights privacy-preserving enclaves

article_title: OpenLearnLM Benchmark: A Unified Framework for Evaluating Knowledge, Skill, and Attitude in Educational Large Language Models
citation: Unggi Lee, Sookbun Lee, Heungsoo Choi, Jinseo Lee, Haeun Park, Younghoon Jeon, Sungmin Cho, Minju Kang, Junbo Koh, Jiyeong Bae, Minwoo Nam, Juyeon Eun, Yeonji Jung, Yeil Jeong. (2026). OpenLearnLM Benchmark: A Unified Framework for Evaluating Knowledge, Skill, and Attitude in Educational Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13882
title: OpenLearnLM Benchmark dataset: 124K+ items spanning Knowledge, Skills, and Attitude axes
description: OpenLearnLM is an open benchmark dataset for evaluating educational LLMs across three axes. The article states: "Our benchmark comprises 124K+ items spanning multiple subjects, educational roles, and difficulty levels based on Bloom's taxonomy." The Knowledge domain contains 2,304 multiple-choice items (918 content, 1,386 pedagogical) sourced from C-Eval, GPQA, KICE, and the Pedagogy Benchmark; the Skills domain comprises 122,425 generated items (99.6% generation success rate, ~116,000 train / 6,100 test); the Attitude domain includes 14 scenario-based items. Quality assurance used an LLM-as-Judge rubric with a 99.9% pass rate (122,365 of 122,439 items).
requirements: Items must pass a five-criterion LLM-as-Judge quality rubric with a passing threshold of 20 points, including critical minimums for answer accuracy (3) and question clarity (2)
constraints: The Attitude domain contains only 14 scenario-based items (12 standard stances, 2 deception)
Skills items were generated by gpt-5-mini rather than authored by humans
target_learners: LLMs deployed as educational tutors, assessors, and instructional assistants
target_learning_goals: Evaluation of educational capability across knowledge, practical skill, and attitude
examples: Knowledge items were sourced from C-Eval and GPQA (918 items) and KICE and Pedagogy Benchmark (1,386 items) rather than solely synthetic generation
key_sources: Unggi Lee, Sookbun Lee, Heungsoo Choi, Jinseo Lee, Haeun Park, Younghoon Jeon, Sungmin Cho, Minju Kang, Junbo Koh, Jiyeong Bae, Minwoo Nam, Juyeon Eun, Yeonji Jung, Yeil Jeong. (2026). article_title: OpenLearnLM Benchmark: A Unified Framework for Evaluating Knowledge, Skill, and Attitude in Educational Large Language Models
citation: Unggi Lee, Sookbun Lee, Heungsoo Choi, Jinseo Lee, Haeun Park, Younghoon Jeon, Sungmin Cho, Minju Kang, Junbo Koh, Jiyeong Bae, Minwoo Nam, Juyeon Eun, Yeonji Jung, Yeil Jeong. (2026). OpenLearnLM Benchmark: A Unified Framework for Evaluating Knowledge, Skill, and Attitude in Educational Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.13882
title: KSA three-axis evaluation framework with a four-level Skills hierarchy (Center→Role→Scenario→Sub-scenario)
description: The framework operationalizes educational LLM capability using the KSA (Knowledge-Skills-Attitude) model from educational assessment. The article states: "The Skills domain comprises 122,425 items across 6 Centers, 11 Roles, 46 Scenarios, and 81 Sub-scenarios." Knowledge covers curriculum-based content and pedagogical knowledge; Skills measures situated capability through tasks emulating real educational decisions, with difficulty tiers from Bloom's and Krathwohl's taxonomies; Attitude examines epistemic, instructional, and normative-ethical stances plus deception resistance via Alignment Faking. The hierarchy contextualizes tasks by institutional function (Center), professional responsibility (Role), task type (Scenario), and task variant (Sub-scenario).
requirements: Evaluation requires domain-matched methods: exact-match accuracy for Knowledge, LLM-as-Judge with scenario-specific 10-point rubrics for Skills, and LLM-as-Judge plus Alignment Faking comparison for Attitude
constraints: The framework is grounded in the KSA model from educational assessment and Bloom's/Krathwohl's taxonomies; the article notes future work is needed for multilingual contexts and real classroom interaction data
target_learners: LLMs acting as educational partners across teaching, learning, assessment, counseling, research, and administration contexts
target_learning_goals: Multidimensional educational competence beyond factual accuracy, including situated skill and pedagogical value alignment
examples: Each of the 81 sub-scenarios has a dedicated 10-point rubric defining quality levels from inadequate (1–2) to exemplary (9–10)

article_title: Can LLMs Model Incorrect Student Reasoning? A Case Study on Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions
citation: Yanick Zengaffinen, Andreas Opedal, Donya Rooein, Kv Aditya Srivatsa, Shashank Sonkar, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). Can LLMs Model Incorrect Student Reasoning? A Case Study on Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15547
title: A ten-strategy taxonomy of distractor-generation strategies grounded in learning-science literature and observed LLM reasoning
description: The article introduces a taxonomy of ten distractor-generation strategies, "grounded in learning-science literature and empirical observations of LLMs’ reasoning traces", spanning task understanding (INTER, CORR), candidate construction (LINK, ERR_DESC, ERR_SIM, INST), quality control and selection (PLAUS, DISCR, CURATE), and cross-cutting reconsideration (RECON). It was built by merging expert-practice strategies from the literature with strategies extracted via manual open coding of LLM traces, and is applied to annotate 885 reasoning traces span by span.
requirements: Requires reasoning traces (CoT or reasoning prompting) that can be annotated with strategy tags; direct prompting produces no intermediate traces to analyze.
constraints: The article notes reasoning traces are not guaranteed to faithfully reflect the underlying decision process, so strategies are descriptions of externalized reasoning rather than mechanistic claims.
target_learners: AI-in-education researchers and assessment designers modeling student misconceptions
target_learning_goals: Generating plausible, misconception-aligned distractors for multiple-choice assessment items
examples: The article annotates a DEEPSEEK-V3.2 trace for the problem "Simplify the following if possible: (6+9m)/3", labeling spans for correct-answer reference, error description, error simulation, outcome instantiation, plausibility assessment, final set curation, and discriminability check.

article_title: AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance
citation: Grace Liu, Brian Christian, Tsvetomira Dumbalska, Michiel A. Bakker, Rachit Dubey. (2026). AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance. Published as a conference paper at COLM 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04721
title: Short-sighted AI collaboration: instant-answer assistance erodes persistence via shifted effort reference points and lost metacognitive calibration
description: The article frames current AI systems as "fundamentallyshort-termcollaborators" that provide instant, complete answers and rarely refuse, in contrast to good human collaborators who balance helping with fostering autonomy. It proposes two mechanisms for the observed persistence decline: hedonic-adaptation-like shifting of the reference point for how long a task should take, making unaided work feel counterfactually more effortful and self-reinforcing further offloading; and removal of the productive struggle through which people develop accurate self-knowledge, undermining the metacognitive calibration that sustains persistence. The theory situates the findings within the cognitive offloading and AI-induced deskilling literature.
requirements: AI systems currently optimized for short-term helpfulness and instant answers; the theory explains effects observed after brief (∼10 minute) AI-assisted problem-solving sessions.
constraints: The mechanisms are the authors' interpretation, not directly tested; experiments captured only brief AI exposure, and whether effects accumulate or attenuate with prolonged use remains an open question.
target_learners: Adult online research participants solving fraction and reading-comprehension tasks
Learners using AI assistants for reasoning-intensive tasks
target_learning_goals: Persistence through difficulty
Independent problem-solving and metacognitive calibration
examples: In the experiments, participants given a GPT-5 sidebar assistant for learning problems were then tested without it and showed lower solve rates and higher skip rates than never-assisted controls.

citation: Jana Gonnermann-Müller, Jennifer Haase, Nicolas Leins, Thomas Kosch, Sebastian Pokutta. (2026). LLM-Based Educational Simulation: Evaluating Temporal Student Persona Stability Across ADHD-Related Persona Specifications. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06307
title: Dual-assessment framework for evaluating LLM human simulations via joint self-report and observer-rated persona measurement
description: A methodology adapted from clinical psychology that jointly measures self-reported characteristics and observer-rated behavioral expressions of an LLM persona. Self-report scores measure how the persona agent characterizes itself when directly prompted with questionnaire items, while observer-report scores measure which persona-relevant behaviors are expressed in generated narratives or conversational segments. The framework's central contribution is exposing self–observer dissociation: "LLMs reliably report the assigned persona when directly asked, yet their spontaneous behavioral expression of that persona degrades in unscripted conversation." It also distinguishes between-conversation from within-conversation stability as complementary temporal dimensions.
requirements: Requires a validated instrument with parallel self-report and observer-report forms (here the CAARS ADHD Index) and independent raters blind to persona instructions
constraints: Neither measure provides direct access to the model's internal state; the framework measures consistency of expression, not representational validity or clinical authenticity

target_learning_goals: Temporal stability of simulated learner personas across and within interactions
examples: Experiment I administered the 26-item CAARS self-report short form to persona agents and had three independent LLM raters complete the 30-item observer short form on each narrative

title: Treat interaction structure as a primary design variable for stable LLM learner simulations, not an afterthought to model selection
description: When building simulation-based tools with sustained, path-dependent learner interactions, designers should engineer the conversational protocol itself: anchoring interactions with recurring task-relevant prompts standardizes opportunities for persona-relevant expression at each checkpoint. Across five models and two scenarios, "structured conversation design produced more temporally consistent observer-rated behavior" without model changes or fine-tuning. title: Curriculum cognition: structured understanding of how knowledge is organized and visually presented
description: The article names curriculum cognition as the construct that existing benchmarks fail to test and current instruction-tuning data fails to teach. It defines it as "the structured understanding of how knowledge is organized and visually presented, including prerequisite chains, concept taxonomies, experiment-concept links, and pedagogical sequencing." A competent teacher knows not only that a topic exists but what it requires as prerequisites, where it sits in the taxonomy, and where in the textbook it first appears. The K12-KGraph resources are designed to measure and teach this construct.

constraints: Operationalized for the Chinese K-12 People's Education Press curriculum across mathematics, physics, chemistry, and biology

article_title: Simulating Students or Sycophantic Problem Solving? On Misconception Faithfulness of LLM Simulators
citation: Heejin Do, Shashank Sonkar, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). Simulating Students or Sycophantic Problem Solving? On Misconception Faithfulness of LLM Simulators. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12748
title: Misconception faithfulness framework: misconception-contrastive feedback protocol and Selective Flip Score
description: The article proposes a diagnostic framework evaluating whether an LLM student simulator "preserves misconception-consistent belief state and selectively updates it only when feedback addresses the underlying misconception." Its core is a misconception-contrastive feedback protocol comparing targeted feedback (addressing the true misconception), misaligned feedback (targeting a different plausible misconception), and generic feedback (only signaling incorrectness), from which the Selective Flip Score SFS = FT − ½(FM + FG) quantifies selective sensitivity. The framework also includes a six-category student response taxonomy distinguishing content-sensitive updates (correct flip, constructive pushback) from content-insensitive ones (sycophantic flip, passive maintain).

Feedback conditions must isolate semantic alignment as the primary source of variation
constraints: The framework focuses on mathematics domains with misconceptions drawn from existing taxonomies; extending to less structured domains remains future work
SFS measures observable behavioral updates rather than latent belief states directly
Teacher feedback and response classifications are generated by LLMs rather than human-authored
target_learners: LLM-based student simulators used to train and evaluate AI tutors and human educators
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing and responding to misconception-driven student reasoning during tutoring interaction
examples: The framework was applied to seven instruction-tuned LLMs (4B–120B) on the Malrule and EEDI datasets under base and reflective prompting, and used as the reward basis for SFT, DPO, and GRPO post-training.

title: QLoRA-based SFT pipeline for phoneme-controlled children's story generation with three 8B LLMs and four experimental designs
description: The article builds a pipeline that fine-tunes Llama 3 8B, Apertus 8B-instruct-2509, and Granite 3.3 8b-instruct using QLoRA (4-bit NF4 quantization with LoRA adapters, rank 32, alpha 64) on input-target pairs pairing curriculum lesson phonemes with 2,580 stories generated zero-shot by GPT-4o and Llama 3.3 70B from the 129-lesson UFLI K-2 curriculum. title: Ellis's model of information-seeking behaviors as an analytical lens for studying GenAI-mediated learning
description: Ellis's model (Ellis, Cox, and Hall 1993) characterizes information seeking as eight observable behaviors: "starting (initiating information seeking), chaining (following connections to pursue a line of inquiry), browsing (casually seeking information in potential areas of interest), differentiating (using known differences to filter information), monitoring (regularly following particular sources), extracting (selectively identifying relevant information), verifying (checking the correctness of information), and ending (wrapping up)." citation: Chenguang Wang, Ming Li, Xinyue Zeng, Zhuochun Li, Hong Jiao, Tianyi Zhou, Dawei Zhou. (2026). Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28186
title: Cognitive episodes: an eight-way taxonomy of functional problem-solving states grounded in Schoenfeld's Episode Theory
description: Cognitive episodes organize LLM reasoning traces into temporally ordered functional problem-solving states. The framework builds on Schoenfeld's Episode Theory, which "models the problem-solving process as a temporally ordered sequence of functional episodes", comprising Read, Analyze, Plan, Implement, Explore, Verify, and Monitor, plus an added Answer episode capturing final answer commitment. In this article the taxonomy supplies a cognitively grounded vocabulary for characterizing how problem-solving burden is distributed across stages of long reasoning traces, enabling interpretable difficulty prediction.

constraints: The article states model-generated reasoning traces are proxy evidence, not direct observations of human cognition

target_learning_goals: Predicting and interpreting human item difficulty in educational assessment

article_title: Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction
citation: Chenguang Wang, Ming Li, Xinyue Zeng, Zhuochun Li, Hong Jiao, Tianyi Zhou, Dawei Zhou. (2026). Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28186
title: Epi2Diff framework: episode-induced process representations combined with semantic embeddings for item difficulty prediction
description: Epi2Diff (Episode to Difficulty) converts model-generated reasoning traces into sentence-level episode sequences and extracts compact features capturing reasoning effort. Its episode-induced process representation "combines three complementary groups of features: length features capturing the overall scale of the reasoning process, episode-distribution features characterizing its composition across episode types, and transition features encoding its local sequential organization". These 83 process features are concatenated with a Sentence-BERT item embedding, averaged across direct, weak, medium, and strong prompting profiles, and fed to a supervised predictor (XGBoost across all datasets). Code is released at the article's GitHub website.
requirements: Access to a reasoning-oriented LLM to generate traces under multiple prompting profiles, and a trained episode-labeling classifier
constraints: The article states the prompting profiles "should not be interpreted as validated simulations of human students or ability levels"

The ethics section states automated predictions must not be the sole basis for test construction, item approval, placement, or licensure decisions, and deployment should include expert review, validation, subgroup fairness analysis, and monitoring for distribution shift
target_learners: Examinees of large-scale assessments (SAT, Cambridge English Qualifications, USMLE) whose items are being calibrated
target_learning_goals: Accurate, interpretable prediction of human item difficulty for test construction and item-quality review
examples: Applied to four benchmarks: USMLE (667 items), Cambridge (793 questions), SAT Reading & Writing (1,338 questions), and SAT Math (1,075 questions)

title: Sentence-level episode-labeling corpus and RoBERTa classifier trained on ThinkARM annotations
description: To support sentence-level episode profiling, the authors build a labeled corpus from ThinkARM reasoning-trace annotations of traces generated by five reasoning models on Omni-MATH. After cleaning, the corpus contains 231,913 labeled sentence–episode pairs for training and validation, with a human-verified gold set of 7,067 sentences reserved for testing. A RoBERTa-based classifier trained on this corpus performs eight-way episode prediction; "On the human-annotated gold test set, the classifier achieves an accuracy of0.799, a macro-F1 of0.761, and a micro-F1 of0.799", and is then used as the automatic episode labeler in Epi2Diff.
requirements: Sentence segmentation of reasoning traces and GPT-5 annotations plus a human-verified gold set for final testing
constraints: The corpus is drawn from Omni-MATH mathematical reasoning traces, and the article calls for testing process signatures across additional assessment domains, reasoning models, and item formats
target_learners: Assessment items across mathematical, verbal, reading-comprehension, and medical domains
target_learning_goals: Automatic labeling of reasoning-trace sentences with problem-solving episode categories for difficulty modeling
examples: Used to label every sentence of QwQ-32B and Qwen3-32B traces in the Epi2Diff pipeline

article_title: Four Types of LLM Reliance and Their Predictors Among Undergraduate Writers: A Mixed-Methods Study at a Minority-Serving R1 University
citation: Shahin Hossain. (2026). Four Types of LLM Reliance and Their Predictors Among Undergraduate Writers: A Mixed-Methods Study at a Minority-Serving R1 University. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28749
title: Two-Tier Predictive Architecture of LLM Reliance: AI Literacy determines type direction, Expectancy-Value beliefs determine intensity, structured by Biggs' 3P Model
description: The article integrates three frameworks into a two-tier predictive architecture for LLM reliance. At the predictive level, the AI Literacy Framework accounts for the type of reliance students adopt, while Expectancy-Value Theory explains the intensity of reliance; at the structural level, Biggs' Presage-Process-Product Model supplies the architecture connecting presage factors, reliance behavior, and writing outcomes. The article states these frameworks form "separate yet interlocking explanatory systems," and that "AI literacy and EVT beliefs function as distinct, non-redundant predictors." The architecture underpins the study's four-type taxonomy and its claim that interventions targeting one dimension will not affect the other.
requirements: Measurement of both AI literacy (knowledge, evaluation, ethics) and Expectancy-Value beliefs as separate predictor systems
Classification of reliance type via subscale means against a defined endorsement threshold
constraints: The article notes non-significant moderation findings should be interpreted as inconclusive because the achieved sample was slightly below the moderation power target
target_learners: Undergraduate writers at minority-serving institutions
target_learning_goals: Academic writing with generative AI
AI literacy and ethical engagement with LLMs

article_title: Four Types of LLM Reliance and Their Predictors Among Undergraduate Writers: A Mixed-Methods Study at a Minority-Serving R1 University
citation: Shahin Hossain. (2026). Four Types of LLM Reliance and Their Predictors Among Undergraduate Writers: A Mixed-Methods Study at a Minority-Serving R1 University. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28749
title: LLM Reliance Scale: 20-item, four-subscale instrument distinguishing reliance type from reliance intensity
description: The LLM Reliance Scale is a 20-item instrument developed in this study across four subscales: Strategic (8 items, with Deliberate Use and Critical Evaluation facets), Instrumental (4 items on bounded mechanical use), Dialogic (4 items on iterative co-construction with AI as a thinking partner), and Dependent (4 items measuring "cognitive abdication; wholesale outsourcing of writing tasks with minimal critical oversight"). All items use 7-point Likert scales. It was developed through construct definition, item generation, expert content review, pilot administration (n=143), and main-study psychometric evaluation, and is designed to measure reliance type rather than frequency of use.
requirements: Items anchored to one dimension of one construct with behavioral and temporal specificity
Future refinement should include a structured expert panel using the I-CVI procedure with a minimum of five raters and a retention threshold of I-CVI ≥ .78
constraints: Instrumental and Dialogic subscales show an HTMT of .891, exceeding the .85 threshold, so discriminant validity for that pair is not supported
The Prior Exposure subscale fell below the conventional reliability threshold (α = .664)
Formal I-CVI computation was not conducted, acknowledged as a validation limitation
target_learners: Undergraduate students using LLMs for academic writing
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing qualitatively different forms of LLM reliance for assessment and support
examples: Main-study reliability: Instrumental α = .877, Dependent α = .879, Dialogic α = .859, Strategic α = .786

article_title: Exploring the Value of Diverse LLM Explanations in Introductory Programming
citation: Seth Bernstein, Paul Denny, Juho Leinonen, Kush Patel, Rayhona Nasimova, Matt Littlefield, and Stephen MacNeil. (2026). Exploring the Value of Diverse LLM Explanations in Introductory Programming. SIGCSE Virtual '26. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28882
title: Three-dimension semantic diversity framework for LLM code explanations (function, concept, goal)
description: The article operationalizes explanation diversity as three distinct semantic dimensions drawn from prior work on code comprehension: function, concept, and goal. In the Diverse condition, "we issued three distinct prompts targeting function, concept, and goal as the three dimensions, generating one explanation per dimension." These dimensions were chosen because prior work identifies them as distinct cognitive registers: "understanding what code does, why the underlying mechanism works, and what the program is trying to accomplish." Generic explanations, by contrast, were produced by issuing the identical prompt three times, covering the snippet in an all-purpose way. The framework is grounded in Variation Theory, which holds that learners grasp a concept when they see systematic variation exposing its critical features.
requirements: GPT-4o (or similar LLM) used to generate one explanation per dimension with distinct prompts targeting function, concept, and goal
constraints: The authors note the sources of variation employed may not have been aligned with the dimensions students needed to discern, and the study did not compare outcomes across the three explanation dimensions individually
target_learners: first-year computing students learning recursion in C
target_learning_goals: code comprehension and understanding of recursion concepts
examples: Students saw three explanations per snippet from one condition only: either three generic plain-text summaries or three dimension-targeted explanations (function, concept, goal)

article_title: Less Deliberate in Teams: Student LLM Use Across Individual and Collaborative Work
citation: Sehrish Basir Nizamani, Zannah Ziew, Saad Nizamani, and Khyati Goyal. (2026). Less Deliberate in Teams: Student LLM Use Across Individual and Collaborative Work. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30860
title: Interleave individual and team assignments to help students maintain AI practices across both contexts
description: The article's course design interleaved individual homework and team milestones in close temporal proximity, and the authors argue this "provides a natural scaffold that purely sequential designs lack." The rapid recovery at TP2 suggests that "returning to individual work between team milestones may help students maintain their AI practices across both contexts," whereas extended team phases without intervening individual work may show more persistent suppression.
requirements: Course schedules must alternate individual and team assignments rather than separating them into distinct phases.
constraints: The authors caution that instructors designing courses with extended team phases and no intervening individual work may observe more persistent suppression than they found.
target_learners: Undergraduate computing students in project-based courses
target_learning_goals: Maintaining deliberate LLM engagement and verification practices across individual and collaborative work
examples: In the studied course, usage recovered from 39.6% at TP1 to 75.0% at TP2 after an intervening individual homework (HW5 followed TP2 in the schedule).

article_title: Learning behavior accounts for background-related advantage in AI-assisted education
citation: Jingwei Yi, Yueqi Xie, Jiyan He, Rui Ye, Junming Huang, Bin Zhu, Sean Rintel, Yu Xie, Xing Xie, and Fangzhao Wu. (2026). Learning behavior accounts for background-related advantage in AI-assisted education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10101v1
title: Five-pattern taxonomy of AI-use learning behavior: limited engagement (abstention, rote-adoption) versus proactive and critical engagement (active-trial, verification, error-correction)
description: The article proposes a framework characterizing how students interact with an AI assistant during assignment work, distinguishing limited engagement from "proactive and critical engagement." Annotators labeled chat events for prior attempt, request purpose, and answer modification, then aggregated to student-level patterns: "Abstention denotes completing the assignment without using the assistant despite having GPT access. Rote-adoption denotes direct use of AI-generated answers with minimal independent reasoning. Active-trial denotes independent attempts before consulting the assistant." Verification and error-correction capture checking and revising AI outputs. The framework organizes the study's behavioral annotation, regression, and mediation-style analyses.
requirements: Platform interaction logs and chat records from the assignment phase, manually annotated per chat event
GPT access during assignment work so behavior patterns can be observed
constraints: The error-correction pattern was absent in Python because GPT-4o answers were near ceiling in accuracy, leaving few observable cases
target_learners: adult university students without prior exposure to the target subject
target_learning_goals: near-term learning of Python programming and game theory as measured by exam score
examples: Chat-log annotation of experimental participants' assignment-phase interactions in the Python and game theory courses

title: Design problems (DPs): concise scenario-based transfer prompts for assessing higher-order thinking in PjBL
description: Design problems are concise, scenario-based exam prompts that ask students to apply project concepts in a new, realistic situation, targeting analysis, evaluation, and creation in Bloom's taxonomy. The article's prompt template requires that "The problem should begin with a short, realistic scenario" and that "The expected answer length is a few sentences to one paragraph." DPs were generated with LLMs, expert-rated on five criteria, and deployed as 30-minute supervised in-class assessments worth 2% of course grades.

The system "was intentionally designed not as a "one-shot" fully automated generation tool but as an interactive and augmentative workflow", positioning educators as retaining final judgment over quality while using AI as an efficient assistant. Educator review occurs after stages 1 and 2; stage 3 is fully automated.

title: Nine design principles for TTS-optimized narration scripts plus a five-stage Expert–Novice dialogue pattern
description: The article presents nine optimization strategies for TTS narration scripts (Table 1), including audience specification, difficulty calibration, sentence length control of approximately 30–40 characters, pacing, audio quality considerations, objective expression, linguistic expression of emotion, reading rhythm, and visual coordination with slides. For dialogue mode it specifies a five-stage basic pattern—"Expert introduces a concept → Novice asks a question→ Expert elaborates→ Novice rephrases→ Expert confirms and extends"—with a speech ratio of Expert 7: Novice 3 and approximately 2–3 sentences per utterance, plus five question strategies (Why, How, What-if, association, confirmation).
requirements: Narration scripts must be optimized for the listenability specific to TTS, since human-written scripts tend to use written-language expressions that cause awkward synthesized speech
constraints: The system does not faithfully implement all elements of cognitive apprenticeship; fading is not realized, and the phrase inspired by is used throughout

engineering undergraduates (named as possible audience specification)
target_learning_goals: comprehensible narrated lesson video content across subjects
examples: Single-speaker mode follows a structured composition of opening→ introduction→ main content→ reinforcement→ confirmation→ summary→ closing with linguistic emphasis markers

title: Expert–Novice dialogue narration design inspired by cognitive apprenticeship theory
description: The article adapts cognitive apprenticeship theory to author fixed Expert–Novice dialogue narration in advance, rather than as live interaction. The Expert "is responsible for providing accurate knowledge, offering explanations through metaphors and concrete examples", while the Novice "acts as a proxy for the learner by asking naive questions", rephrasing in their own words, and confirming understanding. Table 2 maps dialogue elements to cognitive apprenticeship: modeling as verbalization of the Expert's thought process, coaching as Expert responses to the Novice, and scaffolding as stepwise support via the five-stage pattern. The design aims to preemptively resolve learners' latent questions and provide vicarious experience.
requirements: Two distinct TTS voices assigned to the personas (Enceladus for Expert, Autonoe for Novice) with prompt-engineered speaker characteristics
constraints: Fading (gradual reduction of support) is not realized; the system borrows only the inspiration of the Expert–×–Novice dialogue structure
What learners receive is a fixed artifact rather than an interaction, which the authors state is what makes it deliverable at curriculum scale and also what limits it

target_learning_goals: understanding of lesson concepts through vicarious dialogue and self-explanation

article_title: Learning Engagement Assistant (LEA): Cross-Course Scalability and Classroom Evaluation of an Agentic AI Tutoring System
citation: Rumble, T., Zarrin, J., Lovell, P. G., Falconer, R. (2026). Learning Engagement Assistant (LEA): Cross-Course Scalability and Classroom Evaluation of an Agentic AI Tutoring System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13370
title: LEA (Learning Engagement Assistant): a tri-modal agentic AI tutoring system combining course-specific RAG, KC models, and learner-state orchestration
description: LEA is an agentic AI tutoring system delivering adaptive, personalised instruction through three integrated modes — Chat, Tutor, and Quiz — grounded in a course-specific RAG vector database and a hierarchical Knowledge Component model. Its Agent Orchestrator "continuously estimates the learner's CL, ZPD, and motivational state to dynamically adjust scaffolding type, task difficulty, and feedback timing." The system separates orchestration logic from knowledge representation, so new courses require only two interchangeable artifacts: the RAG library and the KC model.
requirements: A course-specific RAG library (ChromaDB vector store) and a KC model (hierarchical JSON of Learning Objectives and Granular Objectives) must be authored per course via the three-stage onboarding pipeline with human-in-the-loop review.
constraints: Auxiliary content-generation logic downstream of the orchestration layer can encode single-course assumptions, as shown by the hardcoded Python question generation; Faithfulness declines with curriculum distance from the original course.
target_learners: higher education students (MSc and undergraduate) in computing and social science courses
target_learning_goals: course-specific conceptual understanding, procedural skill practice, and formative self-assessment aligned with course learning objectives
examples: Deployed across CMP511, CMP202, and PSY555 at Abertay University; source code and illustrative datasets are available at https://github.com/tep00018/LEA.
key_sources: Rumble, T., Zarrin, J., Lovell, P. G., Falconer, R. (2026). Learning Engagement Assistant (LEA): Cross-Course Scalability and Classroom Evaluation of an Agentic AI Tutoring System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13370

article_title: Learning Engagement Assistant (LEA): Cross-Course Scalability and Classroom Evaluation of an Agentic AI Tutoring System
citation: Rumble, T., Zarrin, J., Lovell, P. G., Falconer, R. (2026). Learning Engagement Assistant (LEA): Cross-Course Scalability and Classroom Evaluation of an Agentic AI Tutoring System. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.13370
title: Integrated Psychological Framework: cognitive load, ZPD, engagement, and motivation theories grounding LEA's learner-state modelling
description: LEA's adaptive mechanisms are grounded in four frameworks — Cognitive Load Theory, Zone of Proximal Development and constructivist learning theory, engagement theory (Self-Determination Theory and Situated Expectancy-Value Theory), and motivation and self-efficacy theory (Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory and Zimmerman's self-regulation model). Together these "define the Integrated Psychological Framework that informs LEA's learner-state modelling and scaffolding decisions via the Agent Orchestrator." Cognitive load is computed as a weighted combination of task difficulty, recent accuracy, fatigue, and task type; ZPD is the mean accuracy across the last four responses targeting a 50–80% performance band; motivation state is inferred from persistence, sentiment, and performance trends.
requirements: Non-invasive behavioural and performance indicators (task completion time, accuracy, persistence, sentiment) from which the orchestrator infers learner state.
constraints: The classroom pilot's qualitative reports of scaffolding rigidity and affirmation fatigue are, per the authors, the first evidence of how these models perform against learners whose states they did not generate; CL coefficient calibration remains open to refinement.
target_learners: higher education students using LEA as a voluntary study aid
target_learning_goals: adaptive scaffolding within the learner's zone of proximal development, sustained motivation and engagement, and management of cognitive load during tutoring interactions
examples: Four motivation states (cold start, motivation drop, plateau, maintained high motivation) each trigger a corresponding instructional strategy grounded in Self-Determination Theory, such as autonomy support during cold start and challenge escalation during plateau.

article_title: Distinguishing Artificial from Authentic: Evaluating LLMs for Detecting LLM-Generated Content
citation: Juho Leinonen, Paul Denny. (2026). Distinguishing Artificial from Authentic: Evaluating LLMs for Detecting LLM-Generated Content. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20446
title: Do not treat LLM-based detection as a standalone evidence source for academic integrity decisions
description: The article recommends that LLM-based detection of AI-generated student work should be used only with caution and not as sole evidence in academic integrity decisions. Its experiments showed detection is "stronglytask-dependent", unreliable for short-answer formats, and sensitive to relatively small prompt changes, so a standalone detector risks wrong accusations of misconduct. The recommendation is grounded in the study's own failure modes rather than general policy argument.
requirements: Detection outputs should be interpreted per task type, since detectability does not transfer uniformly across assessment formats.
constraints: Results reflect a single LLM-based detector and a single course context; prompt effects should be interpreted within each exercise type rather than compared across types.
target_learners: university engineering students in an introductory programming course
target_learning_goals: academic integrity assessment of student submissions
examples: The study evaluated GPT-4o detection across programming, reflection, and short-answer exercises from one course and found the short-answer task was the only type where real student responses scored higher on LLM-likelihood than LLM-generated ones.

title: PEA: a three-dimensional analytic lens of Policy, Enforcement, and Authority for assistance governance in LLM-based programming support
description: PEA organizes assistance governance around three design questions: what forms of assistance are allowed or restricted (Policy), how those boundaries are implemented (Enforcement), and who can control them during use (Authority). The authors state: "This What–How–Who structure was initially informed by the 5W1H design heuristic". article_title: The Easy Trap: Why LLMs Underestimate Misconception-Driven Difficulty
citation: La Hadi, A., Alibasa, M. J., Chen, G., & Asyhari, A. T. (2025). The “Easy Trap”: Why LLMs Underestimate Misconception-Driven Difficulty.
title: Curricular versus cognitive difficulty: LLMs encode instructional sequencing expectations rather than misconception-driven difficulty
description: The article distinguishes two forms of difficulty: "curricular difficulty, reflected in LLM-generated estimates based on procedural and textual features" and "cognitive difficulty, reflected in empirical performance shaped by learner misconceptions." It argues LLMs approximate what should be easy based on instructional sequencing rather than what is actually difficult due to persistent misconceptions, producing systematic underestimation of misconception-driven items — the "Easy Trap." This account explains why fraction items introduced early in curricula but conceptually conflicting are rated easy by LLMs yet prove hardest for undergraduates.
requirements: Requires empirical learner performance data (CTT p-values or IRT difficulty parameters) to contrast against model-generated difficulty estimates
constraints: Evidence comes from fraction arithmetic among Indonesian undergraduates; the article states it remains unclear whether the phenomenon appears in other mathematical domains such as algebra, geometry, or calculus
target_learners: undergraduate students in mandatory mathematics courses
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of item difficulty for assessment design and adaptive learning systems

article_title: The Easy Trap: Why LLMs Underestimate Misconception-Driven Difficulty
citation: La Hadi, A., Alibasa, M. J., Chen, G., & Asyhari, A. T. (2025). The “Easy Trap”: Why LLMs Underestimate Misconception-Driven Difficulty.
title: Treat LLM-generated difficulty estimates as provisional heuristics requiring empirical validation, not validated difficulty values
description: Because LLMs systematically misclassify which items will challenge students, the article recommends that "LLM estimates should be treated as provisional heuristics requiring empirical validation, not ground validated difficulty values." Assessment systems should be grounded in empirical learner data rather than relying solely on model-generated difficulty estimates, especially for high-stakes decisions and adaptive sequencing where misconception-driven items are systematically rated as easier than they are.
requirements: Empirical validation against real student response data (e.g., CTT or IRT calibration) before difficulty estimates inform instructional decisions
constraints: The article cautions against depending on single difficulty estimates for high-stakes decisions because repeated queries of identical prompts produce varying interpretations
target_learners: undergraduate students in mathematics courses
target_learning_goals: accurate item sequencing and learner ability calibration in adaptive assessment
examples: The study's repeated query analyses showed LLMs often produce varying interpretations of identical prompts across users and attempts

article_title: Aligning LLM-Simulated and Human Examinees for Psychometric Calibration: A Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling Approach
citation: Wenjie Zhou, Yunting Liu, Renjiao Tang, & Mark Wilson. (2026). Aligning LLM-Simulated and Human Examinees for Psychometric Calibration: A Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling Approach. https://osf.io/p6fam/
title: Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling (CDP): a six-step zero-shot framework for simulating examinees with binary attribute-mastery profiles
description: CDP is a zero-shot framework that draws on cognitive diagnostic models "to represent each simulated examinee as a binary attribute-mastery profile and prompts an LLM to generate item responses consistent with that profile." It proceeds in six steps: construct decomposition into binary attributes, mastery-pattern formation over 2^K patterns, natural-language rendering of mastered and unmastered skills, simulated pool assembly under an uninformative (uniform) or informative (population-prevalence) sampling distribution, response generation, and standard psychometric analysis. It applies the generative logic of assessment design traditions in the opposite direction: it generates examinees rather than items.
requirements: An attribute-level description of the test (attribute decomposition and Q-matrix) produced by content analysis or existing assessment-design artifacts
constraints: The informative variant requires an information source about the target population, such as a prior CDM fit, expert judgment, or published statistics
Alignment achieved is psychometric rather than cognitive: matching parameters does not imply human-like solution processes
target_learners: Simulated examinees representing school populations such as middle-school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Psychometric item calibration and cognitive diagnostic assessment design for constructs decomposable into binary attributes
examples: Applied to the Tatsuoka fraction-subtraction dataset with five attributes and 15 items, evaluating eight LLM configurations under no-profile, uninformative, and informative conditions
key_sources: Wenjie Zhou, Yunting Liu, Renjiao Tang, & Mark Wilson. (2026). Aligning LLM-Simulated and Human Examinees for Psychometric Calibration: A Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling Approach. https://osf.io/p6fam/

article_title: Aligning LLM-Simulated and Human Examinees for Psychometric Calibration: A Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling Approach
citation: Wenjie Zhou, Yunting Liu, Renjiao Tang, & Mark Wilson. (2026). Aligning LLM-Simulated and Human Examinees for Psychometric Calibration: A Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling Approach. https://osf.io/p6fam/
title: Evaluate LLM-simulated examinees at multiple levels — distribution, profile, and item — because no single indicator captures all misalignment
description: The article's three-tier evaluation framework (distribution, profile, item) revealed discrepancies that no single indicator would have captured: a configuration can match the overall distribution while misaligning at the profile level, or rank items correctly while producing parameter values far from the human scale. The authors "suggest that future studies evaluating LLM-based simulation adopt multi-level assessment". Profile-level analysis in particular offers an actionable diagnostic pinpointing which mastery patterns the model handles well and where fidelity breaks down.
requirements: A human-examinee reference dataset and a cognitive model fit (such as a CDM) to define profile-level expectations
constraints: Demonstrated on a single 15-item, five-attribute instrument with 536 examinees; the informative prior was in-sample, marking an upper bound
target_learners: Researchers and testing programs evaluating LLM-based examinee simulation
target_learning_goals: Validating simulated examinee data for psychometric calibration before operational use
examples: The study evaluated alignment via overlapping coefficients at the distribution level, prevalence-weighted profile correlations, and Spearman/Pearson correlations with bias and RMSE at the item level

article_title: Rethinking LLM-Judged Helpfulness as a Pedagogy Signal: A Pre-Registered Audit Across Tutor Models
citation: Shuyi Fan, Boyuan Deng, Mengyu Xu, Jiale Liu, Hongyang Zhang, Qiaoxin Yang, Chongyang Gao. (2026). Rethinking LLM-Judged Helpfulness as a Pedagogy Signal: A Pre-Registered Audit Across Tutor Models. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28128
title: Controlled tutor-audit testbed: ConvTutor, PedTutor, and cold baseline over identical frozen weights with a weak simulated student
description: A within-base testbed in which two tutoring policies are instantiated from identical frozen model weights so that only the policy layer differs. ConvTutor is a minimal one-call helpful tutor whose answer-giving is emergent; PedTutor is a four-node routed policy with a learner-state tracker and three responders (problem decomposer, answer-deferral gate, hint cascade). All conditions face one deliberately weak simulated student, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, with "about11% unaided accuracy", making tutoring load-bearing, plus a no-tutor cold baseline and a frozen 19-problem mixture/weighted-average instrument.
requirements: A weak simulated student so that tutoring is load-bearing and a process contrast is measurable
Frozen judge, rubrics, metric definitions, and outcome-interpretation table fixed before confirmatory data collection
constraints: The serving vendor co-varies with the tutor base and Gemini's provider enforces a minimum reasoning setting, so no base is a pure base-model swap
Results describe one simulated learner on one algebra domain and do not license claims about human learners
target_learners: Simulated weak algebra learners (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct)
target_learning_goals: Translating word problems into mixture or weighted-average balance equations
examples: Ten replicates per condition per base gave 90 confirmatory sessions; each session ran six tutored training problems followed by immediate, interference, delayed, and transfer probes answered unassisted

title: Pair pedagogy-targeted rubrics with deterministic process measures rather than relying on a single general-purpose helpfulness score for tutor evaluation

The only result that held across tutor bases without evaluator dependence came from the deterministic detectors, so the authors recommend that "Tutorevaluationshouldpairpedagogy-targetedrubricswithdeterministicprocess measures". Leakage and independence could be tested as penalties or filters for pedagogical preference pairs.

Deterministic process detectors (answer leakage, next-turn independence) computed over the answer phase

The study uses two LLM judges without human validation, limiting generalization

article_title: To Facilitate or not to Facilitate: Human and LLM Facilitator Tendencies in Online Discussions
citation: Dimitris Tsirmpas, Katerina Korre, John Pavlopoulos. (2026). To Facilitate or not to Facilitate: Human and LLM Facilitator Tendencies in Online Discussions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28643
title: PEFK: a standardized multi-domain facilitation dataset
description: PEFK (Prosocial and Effective Facilitation in Konversations) is a standardized, multi-domain compilation of facilitation-related datasets listed by Korre et al. (2025), covering online forums and oral discussions such as debates and radio. The authors "standardizes metadata, metrics, and labeling schemes according to a simple, unified schema", making it suitable as a benchmark on facilitator interventions. It supports analysis under all three facilitation definitions, including escalation and toxicity fields, though the latter are not used in the study.
requirements: Datasets must be harmonized to the unified PEFK schema (conv_id, message_id, is_moderator, escalated, toxicity, etc.)
constraints: The Fora dataset is not publicly available because it may contain personally identifying information; the corpus is not distributed separately
Datasets are predominantly English-language and drawn from specific online or institutional settings
target_learners: researchers and designers of online discussion facilitation systems
target_learning_goals: predicting and understanding facilitative interventions in online discussions
examples: Nine source datasets including WikiConv (17,806,373 comments), CeRI, WikiTactics, IQ2, WHoW, and Fora are compiled with a Fac. column denoting facilitator information availability
key_sources: Dimitris Tsirmpas, Katerina Korre, John Pavlopoulos. (2026). To Facilitate or not to Facilitate: Human and LLM Facilitator Tendencies in Online Discussions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28643

article_title: To Facilitate or not to Facilitate: Human and LLM Facilitator Tendencies in Online Discussions
citation: Dimitris Tsirmpas, Katerina Korre, John Pavlopoulos. (2026). To Facilitate or not to Facilitate: Human and LLM Facilitator Tendencies in Online Discussions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28643
title: Three definitions of facilitative intervention: escalation, professional facilitation, and human judgment
description: The article isolates a taxonomy of three definitions of what a facilitative intervention is, finding "three common definitions implicitly used in prior work; escalation, professional facilitation, and facilitative comments". Definition 1 (escalation) ties intervention to the point where a discussion would derail, offering an unambiguous ground truth but missing successful interventions and other facilitator duties. Definition 2 (professional facilitation) treats all comments by a facilitator as facilitative, which is simple but requires identifiable professional facilitators. Definition 3 (human judgment) asks whether the majority agree facilitation is necessary, giving fine-grained but subjective labels.
requirements: Def. 2 requires that professional facilitators exist and can be identified; Def. 1 requires an unambiguous platform signal that a discussion has escalated
constraints: Def. 1 is inherently restrictive, excluding duties like summarizing and managing participation; Def. 2 excludes most web-crawled datasets; Def. 3 leaves ambiguous cases
target_learners: NLP researchers and designers of automated facilitation systems
target_learning_goals: defining and labeling facilitative interventions for model training and evaluation
examples: Table 1 shows the same discussion annotated under D1–D3, where Marie's facilitator comments differ in label per definition

article_title: To Facilitate or not to Facilitate: Human and LLM Facilitator Tendencies in Online Discussions
citation: Dimitris Tsirmpas, Katerina Korre, John Pavlopoulos. (2026). To Facilitate or not to Facilitate: Human and LLM Facilitator Tendencies in Online Discussions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28643
title: Prefer trained encoder-only classifiers over out-of-the-box LLMs for facilitation timing prediction
description: The article recommends that, for predicting when a facilitator would intervene, trained encoder-only classifiers such as ModernBert may be "a much more scalable, reliable and viable solution compared to LLMs for the task, even though they have been overlooked in current literature". The recommendation rests on the finding that out-of-the-box LLMs with generic prompting are inconsistent, while ModernBert classifiers are more consistent and score the highest F1p across all datasets. An additional advantage the authors note is that the probability threshold can be tuned to configure how proactive or cautious the classifier is.
requirements: Training data from established facilitation datasets with facilitator information; separate models for oral and written datasets due to substantial differences in text format
constraints: Performance remains bounded by the low ceiling imposed by current datasets; boosting LLM classifier performance was outside the scope of this work
target_learners: developers of automated facilitation and moderation systems for online discussions
target_learning_goals: reliably predicting when facilitative intervention is needed in online discussions
examples: The authors trained ModernBert classifiers on PEFK subsets with a 60–20–20 split and evaluated six open-source LLMs on 2,000 randomly sampled test instances

citation: Germana Bertoli, Ilaria Amelia Caggiano, Francesca Lagioia, Riccardo Rovatti, Giovanni Sartor, Emiliano Troisi. (2025). What out-of-the-box LLMs can(t) do in law? A Turing test in Italian exams for lawyers, judges and notaries. https://github.com/SSIGPRO/LLMs-in-legal-professions
title: Five-category taxonomy of legal failures in LLM notarial drafting
description: A purpose-built classification of recurring LLM errors in notarial drafting, developed as a pilot analysis from expert evaluations. It jointly considers the requirements of notarial assignments and the soundness of the underlying legal reasoning, including consistency between proposed solutions, their justification, and theoretical discussion. "On this basis, we distinguish five main categories": legal-source failure, reasoning failure, pertinence failure, lexical failure, and formal failure. Even the best-performing model exhibited deficiencies across all categories in the inter vivos act.
requirements: Developed from expert evaluations of LLM-generated notarial deeds against the assignment's requirements and the soundness of the underlying legal reasoning
constraints: Presented as a pilot analysis based on a small number of exam papers and three expert evaluators
target_learners: legal professionals
LLM developers and evaluators
target_learning_goals: diagnosing recurring failure patterns in LLM legal drafting
examples: In the inter vivos act, even Gemini 2.5 Pro exhibited deficiencies across all categories, with a predominance of formal and reasoning failures; in the mortis causa assignment, ChatGPT-5 incurred reasoning failures and residual formal defects.

citation: Germana Bertoli, Ilaria Amelia Caggiano, Francesca Lagioia, Riccardo Rovatti, Giovanni Sartor, Emiliano Troisi. (2025). What out-of-the-box LLMs can(t) do in law? A Turing test in Italian exams for lawyers, judges and notaries. https://github.com/SSIGPRO/LLMs-in-legal-professions
title: Blind Turing-test evaluation protocol for LLM legal exam papers
description: An evaluation design in which LLM-generated and human exam papers are formatted identically and anonymously assessed by expert examiners using official criteria. Three domain experts who had served on national board committees each evaluated five uniformly formatted papers with no indication of authorship. "we employed highly skilled professionals with direct experience in national boards as evaluators, through a 'Turing Test' approach, capturing qualitative nuances, often missed by automated metrics." The human benchmark was the highest-scoring candidate's real exam paper, digitised via OCR and manually verified.
requirements: Expert evaluators with direct national-board examination experience
Uniform formatting making LLM and human papers visually indistinguishable
Official assessment grids from the Italian Ministry of Justice
constraints: Limited number of exam papers and a small pool of three expert evaluators, constraining statistical generalisation
LLMs had internet access while human candidates were restricted to limited legal materials
Situated within the Italian legal system
target_learners: legal professional candidates
AI-in-law researchers
target_learning_goals: assessing LLM legal competence under authentic professional examination conditions
examples: Prompts used a simple uniform structure with a persona declaration, task description, verbatim exam question, and instructions; case-law references were removed from all documents to ensure uniformity.

article_title: Using LLMs to Detect Growth in Computational Thinking in Introductory Physics
citation: Sean Savage, Anand Shanker, Grace Michlitsch, and N. Sanjay Rebello. (2026). Using LLMs to Detect Growth in Computational Thinking in Introductory Physics. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06200
title: Three open-ended survey questions assessing CT practices in physics contexts
description: The instrument consists of three open-ended survey questions designed to require simultaneous application of physics concepts and specific CT practices, refined by three experts in physics education and computational science. The article states it was "iteratively refined by a group of three experts in physics education and computational science to ensure construct validity." Q25 asks students to interpret a Python-generated mechanical energy vs. position graph; Q26 asks them to trace algorithmic logic in a Python script modeling an elastic collision; Q27 asks them to propose parameters and boundary conditions for a sled-on-hill simulation. Systems Thinking was integrated into all three prompts.
requirements: Responses are scored on independent 0–2 scales per CT practice plus a Physics Correctness scale based on valid physical criteria met
constraints: The authors state Q27 serves poorly as a pre- versus post-instruction survey instrument owing to a ceiling effect and must be revised
target_learners: introductory calculus-based engineering physics students at a large public university
target_learning_goals: computational thinking practices in physics, including data practices, computational problem-solving, modeling and simulation, and systems thinking
examples: Administered online via Brightspace proctored by Respondus Monitor as a Week 1 pre-test and Week 15 post-test; 936 students completed both surveys

article_title: From Evaluated Models to Evaluation Aids: A Multi-Evidence Study of LLM-Based Difficulty Calibration for Programming Examinations
citation: Hongfei Yan, Jiangkai Xiong, Yiqing Li, and Chong Chen. (2026). From Evaluated Models to Evaluation Aids: A Multi-Evidence Study of LLM-Based Difficulty Calibration for Programming Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07523
title: Two forms of the AI difficulty ruler: solving-based and review-based evidence
description: The article distinguishes two forms of the AI ruler. The solving-based ruler has AI read problems, generate code, and submit to the online judge, producing process data such as pass rate, attempts, running time, and error type. The review-based ruler has AI provide structured scores for concept, implementation, debugging, complexity-risk, reading, and overall difficulty without submitting code. The article states the solving-based evidence "constitutes the empirical basis for choosing a unified reviewer in the subsequent review-based extension," while the review-based form is low-cost and scalable but lacks real judging feedback.
requirements: The review-based ruler must preserve reviewable source metadata such as model version, prompt hash, run date, endpoint, and sampling parameters, and its scores need validation against student performance, teacher judgment, or multi-reviewer agreement.
constraints: The review-based result "can only be interpreted as a preliminary/exploratory ruler and cannot replace a multi-reviewer consistency test," and the single-reviewer batch runs through a third-party endpoint whose model label cannot certify an official upstream model.
target_learners: university students in programming courses
target_learning_goals: valid interpretation of programming-exam difficulty for item setting and parallel-class fairness
examples: Ten models solved an 8-problem exam synchronously with 120 students; a single reviewer scored 79, 26, and 106 problems via auditable API batches with archived prompts, schemas, and raw responses.
key_sources: Hongfei Yan, Jiangkai Xiong, Yiqing Li, and Chong Chen. (2026). From Evaluated Models to Evaluation Aids: A Multi-Evidence Study of LLM-Based Difficulty Calibration for Programming Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07523

article_title: From Evaluated Models to Evaluation Aids: A Multi-Evidence Study of LLM-Based Difficulty Calibration for Programming Examinations
citation: Hongfei Yan, Jiangkai Xiong, Yiqing Li, and Chong Chen. (2026). From Evaluated Models to Evaluation Aids: A Multi-Evidence Study of LLM-Based Difficulty Calibration for Programming Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07523
title: Use AI difficulty evidence as auxiliary discussion material for teachers, never for individual student evaluation or automatic grade adjustment
description: The principle positions AI answering and review results as auxiliary evidence within an evidence chain jointly constituted by student performance, online-judge process data, teacher judgment, and problem context. The article designs the AI difficulty ruler "as discussion material for the teachers' item-setting community, rather than an automatic decision system," emphasizing "AI augmenting teacher judgment" rather than replacing it, and states AI difficulty scales "must not be used for individual student evaluation or automatic grade adjustment."
requirements: AI evidence must be interpreted jointly with student-population performance, problem provenance, the teacher's preset objectives, and the course's training path, and cannot be converted into score-adjustment rules apart from the instructional context.
constraints: The article defines explicit limits of use: the third-party endpoint's model-identity boundary, the single-reviewer design, and review-output instability mean AI difficulty scales must not be used for individual student evaluation or automatic grade adjustment.
target_learners: university programming-course teachers and item-setting communities
target_learning_goals: fair parallel-class examination design and problem validation
examples: The study used AI review to decompose exam structure into discussable dimensions such as item count, high-difficulty ratio, and item-bank exposure, and to flag problem risks for teacher review rather than to adjust scores.

article_title: Rethinking Higher Education: From Fixed Curricula to Learnity Graphs
citation: Smadar Szekely, Judith Gal-Ezer, and David Harel. (2018). Rethinking Higher Education: From Fixed Curricula to Learnity Graphs. J. ACM 37, 4, Article 111. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08543
title: Learnity graphs: representing learning as an evolving network of learning entities
description: The article proposes representing learning as a network of interconnected learning entities rather than fixed curricular sequences. A learnity is "a minimal meaningful unit, which captures a capability, concept, experience, or demonstrated competence", and learnities connected through relationships such as dependencies, integration, composition and specialization form a learnity graph. The framework integrates academic, professional, and personal learning into one developmental structure that can complement or replace conventional CVs.
requirements: Clear criteria for creating, aggregating, and validating learnities within the graph
A shared representational language and standardization for cross-institutional use, including definitions of learnities, relationships, development levels, contexts, and evidence types
constraints: Overly rigid standardization risks reproducing the limitations of traditional curricula; frameworks should guide rather than constrain
Building a full operational system remains a challenge for future interdisciplinary research
target_learners: higher education students
lifelong learners across academic, professional, and personal contexts
target_learning_goals: representing and guiding lifelong developmental learning trajectories integrating knowledge, skills, experience, and artifacts
examples: Figure 1 shows the learnity graph of a second-year computer science student combining academic and industry experience; Figure 3 shows a real estate lawyer's graph reflecting legal education and professional practice
key_sources: Smadar Szekely, Judith Gal-Ezer, and David Harel. (2018). Rethinking Higher Education: From Fixed Curricula to Learnity Graphs. J. ACM 37, 4, Article 111. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08543

article_title: Rethinking Higher Education: From Fixed Curricula to Learnity Graphs
citation: Smadar Szekely, Judith Gal-Ezer, and David Harel. (2018). Rethinking Higher Education: From Fixed Curricula to Learnity Graphs. J. ACM 37, 4, Article 111. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08543
title: Learnity graph design considerations: granularity, relationship types, and orthogonal structural dimensions
description: The article enumerates design considerations for constructing learnity graphs. Nodes vary in granularity, with some learnities emerging "from the integration of multiple learnities into higher-level competencies"; edges capture prerequisite dependencies, interdisciplinary interactions, specialization pathways, and compositional integration; and layers represent depth of development while subgraphs represent context such as academic, professional, or self-directed learning. These dimensions should be orthogonal and provide complementary perspectives on development.
requirements: Clear criteria for creating, aggregating, and validating learnities to avoid graph inflation and preserve interpretability
Structural dimensions designed to be orthogonal and complementary
constraints: Constructing learnity graphs may seem complex, though the authors point to the existing body of work on graph visualization as suggesting the graphs can be effectively structured and interpreted
target_learners: higher education students
lifelong learners
target_learning_goals: modeling learning processes and analyzing development and transfer across domains
examples: A programming learnity may include knowledge (syntax, control structures), skills (implementation, debugging), artifacts (code, projects), and experience (collaboration, industry work), linked by prerequisite, compositional, and interdisciplinary edges

article_title: LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure
citation: Fanfei Li, Jana Zeller, Manuel Prada-Corral, Thaddäus Wiedemer, Prasanna Mayilvahanan, Ryan Cotterell, Wieland Brendel. (2026). LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13545
title: LittleCurriculum: an 88B-token K-5-filtered pretraining corpus derived from FineWeb-Edu
description: LittleCurriculum is a curated 88B-token pretraining corpus built from FineWeb-Edu and filtered to contain only U.S. elementary school (K-5) material. The article describes it as "a curated 88B-token dataset to only contain elementary school (K–5) content", constructed via a multi-stage pipeline of age-of-acquisition pre-filtering, LLM-as-a-judge annotation and classifier training, symbolic filtering, and frequency sampling. It is released with the LittleLearner model as a developmentally restricted sandbox for controlled-exposure experiments.

constraints: The corpus is a precision-first subset: the pipeline preserves only ~35% of ground-truth K-5 passages on CommonCoreText, so it is not an exhaustive sample of elementary school material
target_learners: Researchers studying language-model knowledge acquisition under controlled exposure
target_learning_goals: Studying how models acquire, represent, and use knowledge under a well-defined K-5 training scope
examples: Filtered from FineWeb-Edu to K-5 content and validated on CommonCoreText and the external WeeBit corpus

article_title: LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure
citation: Fanfei Li, Jana Zeller, Manuel Prada-Corral, Thaddäus Wiedemer, Prasanna Mayilvahanan, Ryan Cotterell, Wieland Brendel. (2026). LittleLearner: Language Models Under Pedagogically Controlled Knowledge Exposure. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13545
title: LittleLearner: a 5B-parameter language model trained from scratch on the K-5 corpus
description: LittleLearner is a 5B-parameter language model trained from scratch on LittleCurriculum, following the Qwen3 architecture and pretrained for 100 hours on 8 NVIDIA B200 GPUs. The article positions the model and dataset together as "a sandbox for probing data acquisition, representation, and utilization within a well-defined training scope", enabling clean attribution of capability changes to training exposure rather than unknown prior knowledge.
requirements: Trained on the LittleCurriculum corpus; comparisons use an UNFILTERED control model of the same size and recipe trained on unfiltered FineWeb-Edu
constraints: The article acknowledges that at 5B scale "certain emergent behaviors like in-context learning may be less pronounced than at frontier scales"
target_learners: Researchers studying knowledge acquisition, transfer, calibration, and extension in language models
target_learning_goals: Separating genuine capability acquisition from elicitation of latent pretraining knowledge
examples: Qualitative comparisons show LittleLearner answers in-scope questions like a student while giving inappropriate answers to out-of-scope questions such as Schrödinger's cat
