article_title: LearnAI: Just-in-Time AI Co-Creation Across Disciplines at a University
citation: Weihao Qu, Ling Zheng, Chris Buzaid, and Daniel Crawford. 2026. LearnAI: Just-in-Time AI Co-Creation Across Disciplines at a University. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19164
title: LearnAI Framework: a two-layer model for just-in-time AI co-creation serving mixed-ability learners
description: The LearnAI Framework is a two-layer institutional model for supporting AI readiness — defined as confidence, awareness of appropriate use, and ability to apply AI tools within authentic workflows — across learners from non-coders to advanced CS majors. The article states it supports mixed-ability learners "through two complementary layers: a Wide-Exposure Layer that builds awareness at scale, and a Customized Co-Creation Layer that provides intensive, 1-on-1 scaffolding for authentic tasks." Rather than teaching programming syntax, it emphasizes problem framing, tool orchestration, critical verification of outputs, and situated ethical decision-making, operating as service-oriented infrastructure complementing traditional curricula.
requirements: Undergraduate peer tutors trained via a calibration process (observing and co-facilitating sessions before leading independently)
Faculty coordination and lightweight deployment support
A booking/intake system connecting wide-exposure outreach to opt-in co-creation sessions
constraints: The findings transfer most directly to learners with concrete needs and tentative openness to AI
Initial evidence comes from a single institution and an opt-in population
target_learners: Mixed-ability university learners: undergraduates, faculty, and administrative staff, from no coding experience to advanced CS majors
target_learning_goals: AI readiness: confidence, awareness of appropriate AI use, and applying AI tools in authentic workflows
Problem framing, tool orchestration, critical verification, and ethical decision-making
examples: At Monmouth University, Fall 2025 through Spring 2026, the Wide-Exposure Layer embedded 15-minute presentations in 18 existing courses across introductory IT, science, business, and nursing, while the Co-Creation Layer ran opt-in one-hour sessions producing 36 portfolio websites and over 20 deployed applications
key_sources: Weihao Qu, Ling Zheng, Chris Buzaid, and Daniel Crawford. 2026. LearnAI: Just-in-Time AI Co-Creation Across Disciplines at a University. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19164

article_title: LearnAI: Just-in-Time AI Co-Creation Across Disciplines at a University
citation: Weihao Qu, Ling Zheng, Chris Buzaid, and Daniel Crawford. 2026. LearnAI: Just-in-Time AI Co-Creation Across Disciplines at a University. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19164
title: 5-Stage Pedagogical Script for one-on-one AI co-creation sessions
description: A structured session protocol tutors follow to move clients from an "Oracle" mindset (expecting answers) to a "Process Partner" mindset (co-creating solutions). The article states "Sessions followed a structured protocol (Figure 2) designed to shift clients from an 'Oracle' mindset (expecting answers) to a 'Process Partner' mindset (co-creating solutions)," with stages: Problem Framing (5–10 min), Tool-Task Mapping (3–5 min), Iterative Co-Prompting (20–30 min), Deployment & Verification (10–15 min), and Ethical Reflection (3–5 min). Tutors adapt pacing and tool selection to individual clients, and each session ends with a facilitator-verified summary documenting tools used and next steps.
requirements: Tutors withhold tool suggestions until the problem is clearly scoped in Stage 1
Tutors calibrated by observing two sessions and co-facilitating two before leading independently
Ethical Reflection reframed as a required session-end checklist because it was the easiest stage to compress
constraints: Debugging or deployment sometimes consumed the final minutes, making Stage 5 the easiest to compress
Clients often arrived with vague goals requiring additional scoping time
target_learners: Mixed-ability clients: students, faculty, and staff with self-selected authentic tasks
target_learning_goals: Prompting as specification, requirement decomposition, output verification, and ethical reflection on AI use
examples: A senior tutor (30+ sessions facilitated) described following the script: "the first part is I try to figure out exactly what problem we're trying to solve today"; a nursing faculty member learned to reframe prompts as precise technical specifications and deployed a live newsletter platform with secure faculty login
key_sources: Weihao Qu, Ling Zheng, Chris Buzaid, and Daniel Crawford. 2026. LearnAI: Just-in-Time AI Co-Creation Across Disciplines at a University. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19164

article_title: Beyond the Traceback: Using LLMs for Adaptive Explanations of Programming Errors
citation: Alexandru-Radu Moraru, Shreyan Biswas, Ujwal Gadiraju. (2026). Beyond the Traceback: Using LLMs for Adaptive Explanations of Programming Errors. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20896
title: Skill-targeted explanation styles: pragmatic versus contingent LLM error-message rewrites
description: The article defines two skill-targeted explanation styles for LLM rewrites of Python error messages, designed for different assessed proficiency levels. As the article states, "Pragmatic messages are concise and task-oriented: they name the error, localize the likely cause, and provide a short hint toward repair", while contingent messages "provide more scaffolded guidance" including context about likely intent, possible misconception, and reasoning path. The styles are informed by actionable-feedback work, Bloom's taxonomy, claim-evidence-reasoning, and Toulmin's model, and were evaluated against standard interpreter messages in a controlled crowdsourced experiment.
requirements: LLM-generated rewrites require the code snippet, the standard interpreter message, and line-numbered context in the prompt
constraints: The system does not dynamically adapt during interaction; the authors explicitly do not claim dynamic adaptation, only styles designed for different assessed proficiency levels
target_learners: novice and more experienced Python programmers in crowdsourced debugging tasks
target_learning_goals: interpreting programming error messages and repairing buggy code
examples: In the main experiment, rewrites were generated with llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using zero-shot prompting with temperature set to 0, and each participant saw exactly one snippet and one message style
key_sources: Alexandru-Radu Moraru, Shreyan Biswas, Ujwal Gadiraju. (2026). Beyond the Traceback: Using LLMs for Adaptive Explanations of Programming Errors. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20896

article_title: LLM Pedagogical Behavior in AI Tutoring Interactions
citation: Suhyeon Lee, Juneha Baek, Jaehyeong Park, Donghyuk Shin. (2026). LLM Pedagogical Behavior in AI Tutoring Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22993
title: Five-level scaffolding scale for measuring the directness of assistance in LLM tutoring responses
description: The article operationalizes scaffolding as a five-level ordinal scale characterizing LLM responses by the amount of assistance they provide: L0 Minimal, L1 Prompting, L2 Hinting, L3 Explaining, and L4 Solving, where "Higher levels provide more directly usable assistance and leave less of the task for the student to complete independently." The L3/L4 distinction is direct usability: L3 gives an approach the student must still apply, L4 a directly usable task-specific solution. Responses are classified with GPT-4o-mini at temperature 0 given the codebook and preceding context.
requirements: A codebook with level definitions and examples, preceding conversational context, and a classifier (or human annotators) applying the definitions to paired student–LLM turns
constraints: Automated classification is imperfect: most errors occur at the L3/L4 boundary, and low-assistance levels are rare, so fine-grained estimates for L0–L2 should be interpreted cautiously
target_learners: university students in an introductory AI course using an LLM for programming assignments
target_learning_goals: characterizing and evaluating the level of assistance LLM tutors provide during programming and problem-solving coursework
examples: Human validation on a stratified sample of 300 responses yielded human-human agreement of κ = .901 (95.0% raw agreement), and the classifier achieved 75.3% accuracy and weighted F1 of .751 on the held-out test split (n = 150)
key_sources: Suhyeon Lee, Juneha Baek, Jaehyeong Park, Donghyuk Shin. (2026). LLM Pedagogical Behavior in AI Tutoring Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22993

article_title: When LLMs Slow Down: How Environmental Impacts Mediate University Students' LLM Usage
citation: Hyeonwook Kim, Xuesi Chen, Alex Cabral, Cindy Kaiying Lin, Udit Gupta, Josiah Hester. (2026). When LLMs Slow Down: How Environmental Impacts Mediate University Students' LLM Usage. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23968v1
title: Eco-feedback LLM interface with five latency-based eco modes and four sustainability visualizations
description: A live LLM chat interface in which "Users can choose among multiple eco modes, each characterized by a distinct latency profile and corresponding carbon impact based on backend hardware configurations." Eco modes 1–5 trade response latency for lower emissions via tensor parallelism, batching, and renewable energy scheduling, within SLA constraints. The interface adds real-time latency and GHG metrics, cumulative carbon savings, annualized real-world impact equivalents, and a latency–emissions trade-off graph. It was deployed with 89 CS undergraduates in a computing ethics course.
requirements: Operates under Service Level Agreement constraints, managing response latency to balance user experience and carbon emissions
Requires backend configuration knobs (GPU count, batch size, renewable energy scheduling) to realize latency–emission trade-offs
constraints: The study assumed a fixed backend of four GPUs, batch size one, and no renewable energy scheduling, producing coarse-grained latency shifts that do not capture production systems' continuous behavior
Carbon modeling involves uncertainty; the latency–GHG relationship illustrates general trends rather than precise real-world performance
target_learners: undergraduate computer science students
target_learning_goals: awareness of the environmental impacts of everyday LLM use
understanding of latency–carbon trade-offs in AI systems
examples: Participants used the live system over three days across ten sections of a Computer Ethics course, experiencing real eco-mode latency differences revealed through interaction rather than advance explanation

article_title: How AI Coders Discuss, Disagree, and Reach Consensus: Challenges and Opportunities for LLM-Based Qualitative Coding
citation: Jeongyeon Kim and John Mitchell. (2026). How AI Coders Discuss, Disagree, and Reach Consensus: Challenges and Opportunities for LLM-Based Qualitative Coding. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11109
title: Four design goals for automated qualitative coding systems derived from an exploratory literature review
description: From a PRISMA-guided exploratory review that screened 988 articles down to a final corpus of 118 papers, the authors derive four design goals for automated qualitative coding systems. The review holds that "Coding automation should help users make informed decisions by presenting outputs that are transparent in their reasoning and limitations." The goals are: DG1, provide reasons and evidence for how codes are assigned; DG2, illuminate uncertainties and interpretative variability in code assignments; DG3, enable users to calibrate expectations for coding accuracy; and DG4, facilitate users' understanding of how data characteristics affect coding accuracy.
requirements: Automated coding systems must expose coding reasoning, uncertainties, and reliability information so users can calibrate expectations, per the reviewed literature.
constraints: The review is explicitly exploratory rather than a comprehensive systematic review, and screening and codebook assessment were performed by single authors with one expert check.
target_learners: Qualitative researchers using automated coding systems
target_learning_goals: Understanding and interpreting AI-generated qualitative codes and their reliability
examples: The goals directly shaped the pipeline: justifications in prompts (DG1), two independent LLM coders with an 'Undecidable' label (DG2), coder disagreements as an accuracy proxy (DG3), and the dataset-characteristic analysis (DG4).
key_sources: Jeongyeon Kim and John Mitchell. (2026). How AI Coders Discuss, Disagree, and Reach Consensus: Challenges and Opportunities for LLM-Based Qualitative Coding. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11109

article_title: How AI Coders Discuss, Disagree, and Reach Consensus: Challenges and Opportunities for LLM-Based Qualitative Coding
citation: Jeongyeon Kim and John Mitchell. (2026). How AI Coders Discuss, Disagree, and Reach Consensus: Challenges and Opportunities for LLM-Based Qualitative Coding. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11109
title: Multi-agent LLM qualitative coding pipeline and open-source discussion dataset
description: The authors developed and released a baseline pipeline in which "AI agents simulate the collaborative coding process of human coders": an excerpt-extraction preprocessing step, independent coding by two LLM coders with justified decisions and present/absent/undecidable options, up to three rounds of debate on conflicting cases, derivation of new labeling rules, and a final re-coding pass with Cohen's Kappa computed each round. They used OpenAI's ChatGPT with the 'gpt-4o-mini' model, temperature 0 for coding and 0.7 for discussions, across four datasets (education, law, sociology, medicine) with five labels and 500 instances per label. The prompt design, pipeline, and LLM-generated discussions are released as open-source materials.
requirements: A predefined codebook, standardized excerpt extraction before coding, and pairwise agent discussion with a conflict-resolution rule (three rounds, then marked as disagreed).
constraints: Results depend on dataset characteristics such as codebook length and semantic similarity; the authors note future researchers may adjust temperature settings to meet their objectives.
target_learners: Qualitative researchers and system designers automating deductive coding
target_learning_goals: Automated deductive qualitative coding with transparent, debatable code assignments
examples: Across all datasets and labels, inter-rater reliability between the two AI coders exceeded 0.85, and F1 scores ranged from 0.31 to 0.89 with an average of 0.68.
key_sources: Jeongyeon Kim and John Mitchell. (2026). How AI Coders Discuss, Disagree, and Reach Consensus: Challenges and Opportunities for LLM-Based Qualitative Coding. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11109

article_title: Finding Common Mistakes In Modelling With Mathematical Formalisms Using LLMs
citation: Lilian Killich, Marko Schmellenkamp, Fabian Vehlken, Thomas Zeume. (2026). Finding Common Mistakes In Modelling With Mathematical Formalisms Using LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17111
title: Tool-supported workflow for identifying, clustering, and visualizing common modelling mistakes as bug fixing transformations
description: A three-step workflow in which candidates for common mistakes are represented as bug fixing transformations that locally rewrite incorrect syntax trees into correct ones. Step (1) generates candidates with an LLM and validates them algorithmically, keeping transformations that explain a delta-fraction of the data; Step (2) clusters candidates by similarity via a correlation graph; Step (3) visualizes clusters for instructors and CS education researchers. The article frames it as replacing time-consuming manual inspection of large educational datasets.
requirements: A dataset of pairs of incorrect and correct formalizations whose syntax trees can be compared
An LLM prompted with the transformation language specification and algorithmic validation of candidate transformations
constraints: Candidates explain frequent structural differences between syntax trees but are not guaranteed to correspond to actual conceptual mistakes
The prior SAT-solver-based approach does not scale to large educational data sets, motivating the LLM approach
target_learners: CS education researchers and instructors analyzing student modelling mistakes in STEM courses
target_learning_goals: Identifying common student mistakes in modelling with mathematical formalisms such as logical formulas and regular expressions to inform targeted feedback
examples: Applied to propositional logic (6106 pairs, 248 clusters), modal logic (12482 pairs), and CTL (7210 pairs) datasets, using the GPT-OSS-120B model with batch size 50
key_sources: Lilian Killich, Marko Schmellenkamp, Fabian Vehlken, Thomas Zeume. (2026). Finding Common Mistakes In Modelling With Mathematical Formalisms Using LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17111

article_title: Evaluating Feedback Focus and Pedagogical Adaptivity in LLM-Generated Feedback on Student Writing
citation: Norah Almousa, Shayan Peyghambari Oskoui, Raquel Coelho, Gayle Rogers, Xiang Lorraine Li, Diane Litman. (2026). Evaluating Feedback Focus and Pedagogical Adaptivity in LLM-Generated Feedback on Student Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28026
title: FEEDTYPE: a benchmark of teacher and LLM feedback annotated for feedback focus across three writing domains
description: FEEDTYPE is a released corpus of paragraph-level teacher and LLM-generated feedback on student essays, drawn from the SEFORA corpus across composition, ESL, and fiction courses, with feedback focus type annotations, scores, and revisions. The authors state it is the only corpus that "jointly provides scores, paragraph-level feedback, feedback focus type annotations, and revisions across all three domains." It contains 1,966 annotated paragraphs and feedback from six LLMs under three prompting strategies.
requirements: Feedback comments annotated with the seven feedback focus types; teacher feedback sampled from SEFORA with one comment per selected paragraph
constraints: Paragraph-level feedback only; holistic essay-level feedback is not included
target_learners: first-year college students in composition, ESL, and fiction writing courses
target_learning_goals: improving student writing through feedback
examples: Annotated teacher comments such as an Elaboration-labeled comment asking a student to extend a definition paragraph
key_sources: Norah Almousa, Shayan Peyghambari Oskoui, Raquel Coelho, Gayle Rogers, Xiang Lorraine Li, Diane Litman. (2026). Evaluating Feedback Focus and Pedagogical Adaptivity in LLM-Generated Feedback on Student Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28026

article_title: Evaluating Feedback Focus and Pedagogical Adaptivity in LLM-Generated Feedback on Student Writing
citation: Norah Almousa, Shayan Peyghambari Oskoui, Raquel Coelho, Gayle Rogers, Xiang Lorraine Li, Diane Litman. (2026). Evaluating Feedback Focus and Pedagogical Adaptivity in LLM-Generated Feedback on Student Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28026
title: Seven-type feedback focus taxonomy adapted from Narciss for written teacher feedback
description: The article adapts and refines Narciss's content-based feedback taxonomy into seven feedback focus types for annotating written feedback: Task Constraints, Concepts, Elaboration, Clarification, Mistakes, Praise, and Other. The authors retain elaborated components that apply to writing, adapt KHP into Elaboration and KCR into Clarification, exclude simple components suited to closed-ended tasks, and add Praise and Other. They argue prior frameworks "either conflate content and function ... or categorize content only broadly," while this taxonomy treats them separately with more precise content focus types.
requirements: Annotator training with a coding manual; labeling priorities when feedback could belong to two types
constraints: Simple feedback components (KP, KR, KCR) excluded as unsuited to open-ended writing tasks; metacognitive feedback excluded as rarely observed
target_learners: first-year college writing students
target_learning_goals: characterizing what teacher and LLM feedback focuses on in student writing
examples: A teacher comment 'Nice.' annotated as Praise; a comment asking a student to cut or develop a paragraph annotated as Task Constraints

article_title: When Evaluators Cry Wolf: Lessons from Production LLM-as-Judge Evaluation in Educational AI
citation: Chris Rohlfs, Rodrigo Vergara Bosse, Priscilla Hopper, Keanon O'Keefe, Patrick J. Russell. (2026). When Evaluators Cry Wolf: Lessons from Production LLM-as-Judge Evaluation in Educational AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28478
title: Three-lever calibration recipe for LLM-as-judge suites: unanimous-fail panels, per-evaluator judge-model choice, and rubric softening (U/P/C)
description: The article's account of calibrating a production LLM-as-judge suite treats each evaluator as a configurable instrument set by three levers. Panels repeat one judge model k times under a unanimous-fail rule with short-circuiting on the first passing verdict; judge models are chosen per evaluator (Sonnet 4.5 for semantic judgments, GPT-5.4 for structural and mathematical verification, Haiku 4.5 for lower cost); and rubrics are softened via three standard blocks: "U, require unambiguity—if the violation is a judgment call, pass; P, require pervasiveness—a single local instance is not enough, the failure must dominate the response; and C, simplify checklists."
requirements: Each evaluator targets a single failure mode with a free-text rubric defining it
Rubric edits must pass internal-consistency and alignment checks and match stakeholder intuition of the failure mode
Panels capped at five judges for cost and latency
constraints: The deployed configurations do not isolate the marginal contribution of any single lever (no factorial ablation)
The unanimous-fail rule routes split-judge cases to a minority-report channel, which the article says would not be appropriate for front-line moderation
Deployed judge models are proprietary, reducing reproducibility
target_learners: K-12 teachers and students using the MagicSchool AI product suite
target_learning_goals: Monitoring educational AI outputs for student safety, tone and instructional role, pedagogical value, and structural output quality
examples: Simplify checklists was selected for 11 of 21 evaluators, require unambiguity for 10, and require pervasiveness for 6
The Sycophancy A4 trigger was re-cast so a praise-count threshold became a corroborating check under shared unambiguity and dominance gates
key_sources: Chris Rohlfs, Rodrigo Vergara Bosse, Priscilla Hopper, Keanon O'Keefe, Patrick J. Russell. (2026). When Evaluators Cry Wolf: Lessons from Production LLM-as-Judge Evaluation in Educational AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28478

article_title: When Evaluators Cry Wolf: Lessons from Production LLM-as-Judge Evaluation in Educational AI
citation: Chris Rohlfs, Rodrigo Vergara Bosse, Priscilla Hopper, Keanon O'Keefe, Patrick J. Russell. (2026). When Evaluators Cry Wolf: Lessons from Production LLM-as-Judge Evaluation in Educational AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28478
title: Paired synthetic evaluation datasets: a 2,482-case edge-case benchmark and a 570-case human-reviewed egregious-failure set
description: The article contributes a paired protocol of two synthetic datasets for calibrating evaluators. The benchmark "measures how much a configuration flags," reporting benchmark activation rate (BMK%) as the fraction of cases returning a primary fail verdict; it is unlabeled, so BMK% is an activation rate, not a false-positive rate. The egregious set is "a check on severe-case coverage": 570 fully synthetic cases, each designed to exhibit an unambiguous violation of one evaluator's failure mode, with every retained case human-reviewed and borderline cases dropped.
requirements: Egregious cases must be human-reviewed to confirm an unambiguous violation of the specified failure mode
The benchmark pool is held fixed across configurations so BMK% differences reflect configuration changes, not dataset shift
constraints: Both pools are synthetic rather than drawn from production traffic and may underrepresent contested or culturally-specific failures
EGR% measures capture on a deliberately severe slice only, not recall over all production failures
No held-out benchmark split: BMK% figures are in-sample
target_learners: K-12 teachers and students using the MagicSchool AI product suite
target_learning_goals: Measuring evaluator activation and severe-case coverage for educational AI quality monitoring
examples: The benchmark spans the top 12 teacher- and student-facing products, stratified by grade band, subject area, and request type
Safety-critical egregious cases involving self-harm, abuse, and domestic violence were manually authored with WizardLM assistance because commercial LLMs refused to generate realistic examples
key_sources: Chris Rohlfs, Rodrigo Vergara Bosse, Priscilla Hopper, Keanon O'Keefe, Patrick J. Russell. (2026). When Evaluators Cry Wolf: Lessons from Production LLM-as-Judge Evaluation in Educational AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28478

article_title: When Evaluators Cry Wolf: Lessons from Production LLM-as-Judge Evaluation in Educational AI
citation: Chris Rohlfs, Rodrigo Vergara Bosse, Priscilla Hopper, Keanon O'Keefe, Patrick J. Russell. (2026). When Evaluators Cry Wolf: Lessons from Production LLM-as-Judge Evaluation in Educational AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28478
title: Pair a standard benchmark set with severe cases that should always fail when softening evaluation prompts
description: The article's lesson for maintaining evaluator rigor while reducing false alarms: prompts need to soften but still have teeth. Softening rubrics to lower activation on borderline cases risks letting real severe failures pass, so any softened configuration must be checked against a curated set of unambiguous severe failures that should always be flagged. As the authors put it, "It is critical to pair a standard benchmark set with severe cases that should always fail."
requirements: A curated severe-case set with human-reviewed, unambiguous violations of each evaluator's failure mode
Critical evaluators must retain 100% severe-case capture before a softened configuration deploys
constraints: Capture on the severe slice bounds risk but does not measure recall over all production failures or validate performance on moderate or borderline cases
target_learners: K-12 teachers and students using educational AI products
target_learning_goals: Maintaining detection of severe safety and quality failures while reducing false alarms in AI output monitoring
examples: During Student safety calibration, a candidate rubric revision was excluded after it passed an egregious case where the AI ignored a student distress signal
The deployed configurations were selected only among candidates that passed the egregious-capture gates, then ranked by lower benchmark activation, lower cost, and smaller rubric change

article_title: Characterizing LLM-Based Family Education through the Lens of Activity Theory: A Scoping Review of the HCI Literature
citation: Lan Luo, Yuqi Liang, Jie Cai, Anqi Wang, Dongyijie Primo Pan, Muzhi Zhou, Chun Yu, and Pan Hui. (2026). Characterizing LLM-Based Family Education through the Lens of Activity Theory: A Scoping Review of the HCI Literature. arXiv:2609.28886. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28886
title: Activity theory operationalized through AODM as a framework for analyzing LLM-based family education
description: The review uses activity theory, which takes the activity system as the unit of analysis and examines how people pursue an object through a mediating tool within a socially organized setting. It is operationalized through the Activity-Oriented Design Method (AODM), which the review says "provides an operational bridge by translating the components and relations of an activity system into research questions and representations for empirical analysis." The framework relates subjects, objects, tools, community, rules, and division of labor to explain how LLM capabilities become organized through family participation.
requirements: Studies must be analyzable in terms of a focal activity configuration with identifiable subjects, object, tools, rules, community, and division of labor
constraints: The review treats a study as family education only when a family relationship meaningfully shapes how an educational interaction involving an LLM-based system is organized
target_learners: children aged 0-17 and adult family members in family educational activities
target_learning_goals: family-organized learning including language, literacy, AI literacy, and relational development
examples: The review coded each of the 53 studies into study-level records recording object, subjects, tools, rules, community, division of labor, and outcomes
key_sources: Lan Luo, Yuqi Liang, Jie Cai, Anqi Wang, Dongyijie Primo Pan, Muzhi Zhou, Chun Yu, and Pan Hui. (2026). Characterizing LLM-Based Family Education through the Lens of Activity Theory: A Scoping Review of the HCI Literature. arXiv:2609.28886. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28886

citation: Habibullah, A., Alshoibi, Y., Alshiekh, M., Khan, S., & Khan, N. (2026). Where LLM graders succeed and break: Evidence from two computer-science exams. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29333
title: Released dual-graded exam datasets, ablation grid, and grading, fine-tuning and analysis pipelines
description: The article releases two anonymised dual-graded exam datasets (CV exam, 570 students; ML exam, 1,038 students), the rubrics and reference solutions, one result workbook per configuration, and the analysis, grading and fine-tuning pipelines. Evaluation is not bitwise reproducible because vLLM batching reorders reductions (~0.01 MAE)

article_title: Where LLM Graders Succeed and Break: Evidence from Two Computer-Science Exams
citation: Habibullah, A., Alshoibi, Y., Alshiekh, M., Khan, S., & Khan, N. (2026). Where LLM graders succeed and break: Evidence from two computer-science exams. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29333
title: Never instruct an LLM grader to withhold credit, and verify the grader against the prompt and the exam before deployment
description: The article's deployment guidance is to avoid credit-withholding instructions in grader prompts, because both policy sentences collapse graders on their own, unordered by parameter count, and under-grading harms students who attempted the work in good faith. It further advises verifying the model against the prompt and the exam, evaluating several prompt variants including instructor-written ones, and reporting bias alongside MAE so the direction of harm is visible.
requirements: Evaluation across several prompt variants, including instructor-written ones, before deployment
Bias reported alongside MAE
constraints: On exams where models over-mark at neutral, the same preamble can improve MAE by cancelling bias, so its effect must be checked per exam
target_learners: University students in courses using LLM-assisted grading
target_learning_goals: Accurate, rubric-aligned automated grading of student work
examples: The strict preset's S2 sentence alone stopped Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-Small-24B grading; Flash-Lite's lenient and strict runs had comparable MAE with opposite-signed bias (+4.01 vs. −5.44)

article_title: A Benchmark for LLM's Understanding of Middle School and High School Science Topics
citation: Schroeder, N. L., Ambarwati, Y. E., Zhang, Y., & Zhai, C. (2026). A Benchmark for LLM's Understanding of Middle School and High School Science. https://github.com/InviteInstitute/MS-NGSS-Aligned-Benchmark
title: NGSS-aligned middle school and high school science benchmarks with a four-tier synthetic data quality gate pipeline
description: Two publicly released ground-truth benchmarks for evaluating LLM understanding of secondary science: "Our final dataset consisted of 1,078 items for middle school benchmark, and 1,150 items for the high school benchmark." Items were synthetically generated by Sonnet 4.6 Thinking, distributed across recall, conceptual understanding, and applied reasoning types and across 12 NGSS areas per level. Construction used "a four-tier data quality gate system" removing duplicates, enforcing Flesch-Kincaid reading-level ranges, and requiring a three-judge LLM panel to agree on both answers and standard alignment. Data and code are available on GitHub.
requirements: Items must pass duplicate removal, reading-level constraints, appropriateness checks, and three-judge agreement on accuracy and standard alignment before entering the benchmark.
constraints: Items were synthetically generated without human oversight; human review covered only a 240-item sample, and some scientific practices (graphics, data interpretation, mathematical representations) are underrepresented.
target_learners: middle school students
high school students
target_learning_goals: NGSS-aligned secondary science content knowledge across physical, life, earth/space, and engineering design areas
examples: Nine open-weight LLMs were evaluated answering every question three times under a standardized zero-shot prompt, with binary scoring for recall items and a three-point rubric for conceptual and applied items.

article_title: Examining Variation in How Guided AI Tutors Resolve Student Impasses
citation: Ahtisham, B., Vanacore, K., Napoli, A., Arens, J., Ionova, K., Cohn, C., Salehi, S., & Kizilcec, R. (2026). Examining Variation in How Guided AI Tutors Resolve Student Impasses. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38346
title: Design LLM tutors for graduated, state-sensitive assistance that adapts support to impasse persistence rather than treating answer withholding as a fixed policy
description: The article proposes that tutor policies condition the type and degree of support on how long a student has been stuck, using observable signals such as impasse type, depth, and prior unsuccessful assistance. It states tutors "could use signals such as impasse type, persistence, and prior unsuccessful assistance to determine when more targeted support may be warranted", moving from elicitation toward error-directed feedback, specific hints, or worked sub-steps. This extends the assistance dilemma to multi-turn adaptation.
requirements: Tutor systems must be able to track impasse depth and type in tutoring dialogues in real time, as turn-level dialogue signals
constraints: The article states this remains a design hypothesis rather than a demonstrated optimal policy, and should be tested through randomized comparisons connecting escalation to recovery and subsequent learning
target_learners: undergraduate chemistry students using LLM tutors
target_learning_goals: problem-solving planning in multi-step chemistry problems
impasse resolution and recovery during guided practice
examples: In authentic dialogues, questioning helped most at the first sign of an impasse and its benefit shrank with every additional stuck turn, whereas directly addressing the student's error became relatively more helpful
key_sources: Ahtisham, B., Vanacore, K., Napoli, A., Arens, J., Ionova, K., Cohn, C., Salehi, S., & Kizilcec, R. (2026). Examining Variation in How Guided AI Tutors Resolve Student Impasses. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38346

article_title: Examining Variation in How Guided AI Tutors Resolve Student Impasses
citation: Ahtisham, B., Vanacore, K., Napoli, A., Arens, J., Ionova, K., Cohn, C., Salehi, S., & Kizilcec, R. (2026). Examining Variation in How Guided AI Tutors Resolve Student Impasses. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38346
title: Guided AI Tutor: a guardrailed LLM chemistry tutor with a scripted problem-solving planning protocol
description: The Guided AI Tutor is an LLM-based tutor (GPT-4o via the OpenAI API) that guides students to plan solutions to multistep chemistry problems without giving them the solution. Its behavior is controlled entirely by a prompt covering a role as a problem-solving coach, objectives, behavioral guidelines (never solve the problem, ask one question at a time, give "increasingly specific, targeted hints" after incorrect answers), a problem with four scripted questions, and response-handling rules. Its planning sequence is organized around eight problem-solving practices.
requirements: A detailed prompt protocol specifying role, objectives, behavioral guidelines, scripted questions with reference answers, and response-handling rules
constraints: Escalation after errors is requested only as a natural-language instruction; the article found the tutor sometimes continued questioning after earlier questioning failed
target_learners: undergraduate students in an introductory general chemistry course at a large research university
target_learning_goals: planning solutions to multistep chemistry problems following expert problem-solving practices
examples: Students used the tutor through a stand-alone web application to plan solutions to 8 assigned chemistry problems, producing 1,260 sessions and 20,462 student turns

article_title: Navigating AI in STEM: What Secondary Students Actually Do With Generative AI-Driven Tools
citation: Martin Lnenicka and Petr Coufal. (2026). Navigating AI in STEM: what secondary students actually do with generative AI-driven tools. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00637-8
title: Dual AI literacy as interdependent operational and epistemic workflow phases, with cognitive mediation mapped as substitution versus verification
description: The article proposes that effective generative AI use requires "a fundamental duality of literacy: operational AI literacy (prompting, iterative refinement) and epistemic AI literacy (verification, methodological evaluation, bias awareness)". These dimensions are treated not as orthogonal psychometric traits but as overlapping, interdependent behavioral phases within a unified problem-solving workflow. The study operationalizes cognitive mediation behaviorally by mapping self-reported workflows into categories of substitution (cognitive offloading) versus verification (active comparison of logic), and its qualitative findings indicate prompting loops heavily overshadow external factual validation.
requirements: Both operational prompting competence and epistemic verification competence must be cultivated within the same task workflow for responsible AI use
constraints: The framework is descriptive and behavioral, not an evaluation of latent psychometric traits; individual epistemic beliefs were not directly measured
target_learners: secondary students in STEM subjects
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
epistemic verification of AI outputs
independent reasoning in STEM problem solving
examples: The survey coded behavioral interaction configurations into three functional roles: substitution (replacing reasoning), supplementation (extending reasoning), and verification (checking reasoning)
key_sources: Martin Lnenicka and Petr Coufal. (2026). Navigating AI in STEM: what secondary students actually do with generative AI-driven tools. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00637-8

article_title: Co-creating custom GPTs: an autoethnographic study of undergraduate students as partners in generative AI innovation
citation: Lo S, Lea T, Mavromoustakos A, Joseph B, Yii M, Exintaris B, Karunaratne N, Pearson DL, Ritchie T, Yuriev E and Pyun J (2026) Co-creating custom GPTs: an autoethnographic study of undergraduate students as partners in generative AI innovation. Front. Educ. 11:1818781. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1818781
title: Students-as-partners framework extended to GenAI tool co-creation
description: The students-as-partners (SaP) framework positions students and staff in a "collaborative, reciprocal process through which all participants have the opportunity to contribute equally, although not necessarily in the same ways, to curricular or pedagogical conceptualization, decision-making, implementation, investigation, or analysis". The article applies SaP values of respect, reciprocity, and shared responsibility to co-creating custom GPTs, arguing that co-creation with GenAI can extend the SaP paradigm to include GenAI tools, with students as co-creators rather than passive users or risks.
requirements: Students and academics engage as equal partners in decision-making with shared responsibility, reciprocity, and mutual learning
constraints: Co-design does not make all expertise identical: students contribute learner expertise while academics verify disciplinary accuracy and pedagogical appropriateness
target_learners: undergraduate science students
target_learning_goals: digital literacies and critical understanding of AI
partnership-driven learning and reflexivity
examples: Five students and five academics co-created seven cGPTs across six units, with students adopting roles as content curators, builders, testers, evaluators, and data analysts
key_sources: Lo S, Lea T, Mavromoustakos A, Joseph B, Yii M, Exintaris B, Karunaratne N, Pearson DL, Ritchie T, Yuriev E and Pyun J (2026) Co-creating custom GPTs: an autoethnographic study of undergraduate students as partners in generative AI innovation. title: Seven unit-specific custom GPT chatbots for pharmaceutical science units
description: Seven custom GPT chatbots (cGPTs) were co-created for six undergraduate units in a Bachelor of Pharmaceutical Science program: Polymer Knowledge, Polymer Socratic, Physiology 1, Physiology 2, Medicinal Chemistry 1, Physical Chemistry 2, and Scientific Inquiry. Purposes ranged from a virtual tutor supporting scientific writing to Socratic chatbots guiding problem-solving and alkene halogenation. By the end of development, "seven distinct yet consistent student-staff-designed cGPT tools had been created, each tailored to its unit's content and learning activities".
requirements: Built via the Create GPT function within an OpenAI Plus account, with system prompts and curated knowledge-base files
constraints: Development took two to six weeks depending on topic, student experience, and available resources; model updates (GPT-5, Study mode) changed cGPT behaviour mid-project
target_learners: undergraduate pharmaceutical science students
target_learning_goals: discipline-specific problem solving
scientific writing
polymer concept understanding
examples: The Physiology 1 cGPT served as a virtual tutor for writing about complex physiological concepts, while the medicinal chemistry cGPT used a Socratic approach for a specific reaction mechanism

citation: Lo S, Lea T, Mavromoustakos A, Joseph B, Yii M, Exintaris B, Karunaratne N, Pearson DL, Ritchie T, Yuriev E and Pyun J (2026) Co-creating custom GPTs: an autoethnographic study of undergraduate students as partners in generative AI innovation. Front. Educ. 11:1818781. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1818781
title: Four-phase iterative cGPT co-creation process with SPAR reflective logging
description: The article describes a reusable co-creation pattern with four construction phases: Creation (writing the system prompt and selecting knowledge-base files), Refinement (iterative testing, prompt editing, and SPAR reflections), Consolidation (finalising prompts and merging versions), and Evaluation (scoring responses to ten evaluation questions). Throughout, students wrote SPAR reflections — "Stimulus (Prompt sent to GPT), Processing (GPT's response), Analysis (Evaluation of GPT response based on design principles) and Reflection (Next steps based on GPT response)" — which informed system prompt adjustment until satisfactory accuracy and instruction adherence were reached.
requirements: Regular student-academic team meetings (weekly to twice weekly) for testing and refinement, and design principles focused on clear, accurate and consistent responses
constraints: The overall process from construction to implementation lasted two to six weeks, depending on the cGPT's topic, students' prior experience, and availability of resources such as system prompt templates
target_learners: undergraduate students without extensive prior research experience
target_learning_goals: AI literacy, teamwork, and project management
iterative design and evaluative judgment
examples: SPAR reflections were written individually prior to peer discussion to reduce groupthink and retrospective smoothing, and evaluation scored twenty generated responses per evaluation question on accuracy, concision and relevance

article_title: Integrating AI in Online Learning in Higher Education: A Literature Review
citation: Jennifer Lock, Soraya Arteaga, Carol Johnson. (2025). Integrating AI in Online Learning in Higher Education: A Literature Review. International Journal on Innovations in Online Education, 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1615/IntJInnovOnlineEdu.2026060433
title: Four-theme framework for AI integration in online higher education
description: The review's organizing framework groups the literature on AI in online higher education into four interrelated themes: "(i) Types and purpose of AI integration; (ii) pedagogical approaches (e.g., use of AI literacy); (iii) benefits of using AI in online learning; and (iv) challenges of using AI in online learning." The authors stress that "these themes overlap and reflect an interconnection," so the framework treats integration as a complex whole rather than separable topics. It was derived from thematic analysis of 63 selected citations.
requirements: Derived from a critical literature review of refereed sources from 2020 to 2025 within higher education contexts
constraints: The authors note a future systematic or scoping review framework is recommended to strengthen the critical analysis
target_learners: higher education students in online learning
target_learning_goals: understanding how AI technologies can be integrated into online learning design
examples: The review screened 207 citations to 63 and organized them in a spreadsheet by themes including types of AI, purpose, pedagogical approach, benefits, and challenges

title: Taxonomy of AI integration types in online higher education
description: From 54 articles containing specific examples, the review classifies AI integration into categories: "AI teaching assistance/machine teachers; automated AI monitoring; AI-driven surveillance; algorithms, generative AI (GAI), large language models, machine learning, prediction model performance (i.e., adaptive modeling), and other." Each category is illustrated with cited studies, e.g., remote proctored exams for automated monitoring and Q-Module Bot for large language models. The taxonomy maps the functional purposes AI serves in online teaching and learning.

constraints: Categories reflect how the reviewed 54 articles classified AI use, not an independently validated classification

examples: Q-Module Bot provided students feedback on inquiries about course materials; chatbots supported student goal setting and online presence

title: Develop AI literacy for both students and instructors as a foundation for intentional AI integration
description: The review concludes that institutions should foster AI literacy, defined by Crabtree (2023) as involving "the skills and competencies required to use AI technologies and applications effectively," including viewing technologies critically and questioning their design and implementation. The review states "an implication for practice is the development of AI literacy for both students and instructors," requiring keen discernment about how AI is used. Reviewed studies link higher AI literacy to academic well-being and success in digital environments.
requirements: Institutional role in helping students and instructors develop AI literacy; educational development provision for instructors
constraints: Reviewed studies note unreliable instructor support often derives from educators' limited AI literacy

higher education instructors
pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: critical, informed, and ethical use of AI technologies in learning
examples: Bae et al. (2024) found a strong need to focus on AI literacy development with pre-service teachers engaged in critical reflection on practical and ethical factors

citation: Long DY, Wang S, Md Rashid S and Lu XT. (2026). Artificial intelligence in higher education: a systematic review of its impact on student engagement and the mediating role of teaching methods. Front. Educ. 10:1648661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2025.1648661
title: PMAISE model: pedagogical mediation of AI for student engagement via structured feedback, interactive scaffolding, and personalization alignment
description: The PMAISE model (Pedagogical Mediation of AI for Student Engagement) is an inductively developed explanatory framework mapping the alignment between AI technologies, pedagogical strategies, and the affective, behavioral, and cognitive dimensions of engagement. Cross-case synthesis identified "three recurrent mechanisms: structured feedback, interactive scaffolding, and personalization alignment", which the authors say "constitute the core pathways through which pedagogical mediation operates in AI-supported higher education". The model frames AI tools as effective only when embedded in pedagogically sound designs.
requirements: AI functionalities must be aligned with instructional goals such as tailored feedback, structured interaction, and learner-centered adaptation
constraints: Inductively developed from the 73 included studies rather than tested as a hypothesis
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: cognitive, behavioral, and emotional engagement in AI-supported learning
examples: Figure 5 visualizes the model linking AIHE, pedagogical mediation strategies, learning tools, assessment approaches, and engagement dimensions

title: Five functional categories of AI in higher education applications
description: To organize the diverse AI applications found in the literature, the review proposes a classification of AIHE into five functional categories. The authors state: "we classify AIHE applications into five functional categories: (1) personalized learning systems, (2) real-time feedback and adaptive tutoring, (3) natural language processing (NLP) tools, (4) immersive learning environments, and (5) predictive analytics". This taxonomy is used to code included studies and to structure the RQ1 analysis of which AI types support which engagement dimensions.

article_title: Is It Ethical for Teachers to Use AI for Student Feedback?
citation: Luo, J. (Jess), & Eaton, S. (2026). Is It Ethical for Teachers to Use AI for Student Feedback?. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(3). https://doi.org/10.53761/887m5346
title: Contextual-complexity framework for judging the ethics of teacher AI feedback use
description: The article proposes that ethical evaluation of teachers' AI feedback use requires "a more nuanced understanding of what it means for teachers to use AI for feedback" rather than a blanket judgment. The framework turns on contextual factors the authors name: "the purposes of assessment, the features of student assignments, and the types of feedback automated by AI." It functions as an organizing account for the study's eight ethical areas, situating each within the specific assessment context in which AI feedback is deployed.
requirements: Ethical judgments must be made with reference to the specific assessment purpose, assignment features, and feedback types involved rather than applied generically.
target_learners: university students in higher education
target_learning_goals: ethical use of AI in assessment and feedback practices
examples: The study grounds the framework in university policy reviews, social media posts, and interviews with university teachers and students.

citation: Luo, J. (Jess), & Eaton, S. (2026). Is It Ethical for Teachers to Use AI for Student Feedback?. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(3). https://doi.org/10.53761/887m5346
title: Design teacher AI feedback use to maintain and enhance care, trust, and human connections rather than asking only whether to use AI
description: The article recommends moving "beyond the binary question of whether teachers should use AI or not" toward designing and operating feedback activities and teacher AI use in ways that "maintain and even enhance care, trust, and human connections central to effective feedback processes." The principle directs institutions and teachers to treat AI adoption as a design problem about preserving relational qualities of feedback, not a yes/no adoption decision.
requirements: Feedback activities and teacher AI use must be deliberately designed and operated, not merely adopted or rejected as a binary choice.
constraints: The study focuses on teachers in higher education; the authors note ethical AI use also requires effort from stakeholders beyond teachers.
target_learners: university students in higher education
target_learning_goals: effective, ethically sound feedback on student work
examples: The authors call for exploring how feedback activities and teacher AI use could be designed and operated to sustain care, trust, and human connections.

article_title: Sustaining AI-enabled student support: A four-year implementation and impact study
citation: Mata, Catherine, Emily Russell, and Lindsay C. Page. (2026). Sustaining AI-Enabled Student Support: A Four-Year Implementation and Impact Study. (EdWorkingPaper: 26-1409). Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai26-1409
title: Sustaining chatbot-based student communication requires centralized institutional ownership and flexibility in communication strategy
description: The article concludes that a centrally operated chatbot, housed in a designated administrative home, is essential for sustaining communication goals and coordinating the data flows across university offices needed for effective outreach. It also finds that "a certain level of flexibility within the overarching communication strategy is crucial," allowing administrators to adapt to evolving student needs, new cohorts, and external shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic. The principle generalizes the authors' implementation lessons to other institutions deploying communication technologies.
requirements: A central office or chatbot team that owns campaign design and distribution
Cross-unit coordination and data sharing for tailored outreach
constraints: The siloed nature of data and recordkeeping at CSUN made targeted campaigns burdensome and difficult to sustain over time
target_learners: Undergraduate students at large urban public universities
target_learning_goals: Navigation of financial, logistical, and administrative tasks required for continued enrollment
Sense of belonging and social connectedness on campus
examples: CSUN jointly oversaw its chatbot through the Office of Undergraduate Studies and the Office of the Registrar, with a designated communication specialist crafting all campaigns for consistency of voice
key_sources: Mata, Catherine, Emily Russell, and Lindsay C. Page. (2026). Sustaining AI-Enabled Student Support: A Four-Year Implementation and Impact Study. (EdWorkingPaper: 26-1409). Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai26-1409

title: Universities as socio-technical systems in which human and technological components jointly shape student communication
description: The article frames chatbot implementation through the lens of universities as socio-technical systems, in which "human and technological components are intertwined and jointly shape organizational processes." Effective student communication depends on coordination across administrative units, access to shared data, and the ability to adapt institutional processes over time, not on the technology alone. The authors argue implementing communication technologies in higher education is as much an organizational challenge as a technological one, and that implementation lessons like cross-unit coordination and data governance apply regardless of the underlying technology.
requirements: Coordination across multiple administrative units
Access to shared student data across offices
constraints: Student data distributed across multiple campus offices limits tailored outreach when systems are siloed
target_learners: Undergraduate students at higher education institutions
target_learning_goals: Sustained institutional communication supporting college persistence and completion
examples: CSUN's chatbot was embedded within organizational divisions of labor, data flows, and collaboration across the Registrar, Financial Aid, and other offices

article_title: Designing an Aligned Generative AI Course Policy: An Equitable and Transparent Learner-Centered Approach
citation: McCorkle, S. (2025). Designing an Aligned Generative AI Course Policy: An Equitable and Transparent Learner-Centered Approach. International Journal of Designs for Learning, 16(2), 96–110. https://doi.org/10.14434/ijdl.v16i2.41058
title: Aligned Generative AI Course Policy framework for deciding allowed and unallowed GenAI use per task
description: The article presents an Aligned Generative AI Course Policy as a design framework in which "the allowed and unallowed uses of GenAI tools are described in a transparent manner for students." Rather than a blanket course-wide rule, the framework aligns each GenAI permission decision with what the instructor actually assesses for each student task. It works by decomposing the course into its constituent student tasks, classifying each as assessed or as an intermediate step, and matching each task to a GenAI workforce competency before deciding whether assessment or competency-building takes priority.
requirements: The instructor must analyze student tasks by creating an inventory of each step a student would take that leads to a finished product of their learning
constraints: The framework is presented as a design case describing one course policy design, not as a tested intervention
target_learners: higher education students in courses with GenAI tools available
target_learning_goals: transparent and equitable use of generative AI tools in coursework
emerging GenAI workforce competencies
examples: The design case documents the policy being designed for a course whose student tasks were inventoried step by step toward finished products of learning

title: Task-inventory review pattern: inventory every step toward a finished product and ask what each task assesses
description: This pattern structures policy design around a complete inventory of student work. "The process begins with an analysis of student tasks by creating an inventory of each step a student would take that leads to a finished product of their learning." Each inventoried task is then reviewed by the instructor with the question "What, specifically, am I assessing?" Tasks that are not assessed but are simply a step towards a finished product are noted accordingly, which creates the basis for differentiated GenAI permissions across the course.
requirements: The instructor must create an inventory covering each step a student would take that leads to a finished product of their learning
constraints: Tasks that are not assessed, but are simply a step towards a finished product, must be noted accordingly for the pattern to distinguish assessable from intermediate work
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: alignment of course policy with what is actually assessed
examples: In the design case, the instructor reviewed each task in the inventory asking what, specifically, was being assessed, and noted unassessed stepping-stone tasks

title: Prioritize between assessing a task and building a GenAI workforce competency for each inventoried task
description: For every task in the inventory, the instructor makes an explicit priority decision. "A determination is then made to prioritize either the need to assess student performance of the task or build the GenAI workforce competency." This principle makes GenAI permissions follow from that priority: where assessment of a task matters less, competency-building can take precedence and GenAI use can be permitted. The article frames this as the mechanism that aligns the policy with course goals rather than applying uniform restrictions.
requirements: A completed task inventory with each task classified as assessed or unassessed
constraints: The priority determination is made task by task, so a single course-wide GenAI rule cannot implement this principle
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: student performance of assessed tasks
GenAI workforce competency development
examples: The design case describes the instructor making a determination for each task in the inventory between assessing performance and building the GenAI workforce competency

article_title: Efficiency at what cost? Salvaging constructive alignment from the GenAI hype
citation: McInnes, R., Airey, L., Moss, P., & Rathnappulige, S. (2026). Efficiency at what cost? Salvaging constructive alignment from the GenAI hype. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(4), 80–95. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.11466
title: Reclaim constructive alignment as a reflective, human-centred practice rather than automating it through GenAI
description: The article recommends that educators critically engage with constructive alignment themselves instead of automating it with GenAI, to safeguard pedagogical depth and keep teaching meaningful. It argues educators "must reclaim constructive alignment as a reflective, human-centred practice to safeguard pedagogical depth, improve design robustness and ensure that teaching remains a meaningful and enjoyable professional endeavour". The recommendation follows from the article's discourse analysis of the efficiency-focused GenAI narrative.
requirements: Educators engage directly and critically with the constructive alignment process rather than delegating it to automated tools
constraints: The article positions this as a response to current GenAI efficiency narratives in higher education; it does not claim the practice is immune to institutional pressures
target_learners: higher education educators designing courses
target_learning_goals: pedagogically robust, aligned course design
examples: The article's implications for practice state educators should critically engage with constructive alignment rather than automating it through GenAI to preserve pedagogical depth and meaning

title: GenAI should defensibly augment constructive alignment only as institutionally bounded systems configured around situated pedagogy, policy and quality standards
description: The article contends that generic, Internet-trained GenAI assistance is not a defensible basis for augmenting constructive alignment. It argues that "for GenAI to defensibly augment constructive alignment, it must transition from generic, Internet-trained assistance towards institutionally bounded systems configured around situated pedagogy, policy and institutional quality standards". Bounding the system to institutional context is presented as the condition under which augmentation preserves educator agency.
requirements: Systems must be configured around the institution's own pedagogy, policy and quality standards rather than generic Internet-trained models
constraints: The article presents this as a condition for defensible augmentation, not as a demonstrated or tested configuration

citation: Mendonça PC, Quintal F, Figueiredo M and Mendonça F (2026) Perceived usefulness and intention to use large language model-generated feedback across three educational levels: a user-centred study in programming. Front. Educ. 11:1934069. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1934069
title: IntroEduAI two-layer LLM feedback pipeline (rubric-based GPT-4.1 evaluation plus consolidated report generation)
description: The IntroEduAI platform manages assignment delivery, automated evaluation, and feedback generation in programming courses. Each response is scored against an instructor-authored criterion-referenced rubric in a few-shot prompt, evaluated three times with GPT-4.1-2025-04-14, with text responses enhanced by retrieval-augmented generation over course materials. The three-stage pipeline produces "a single consolidated feedback per response, and an assignment-level report", the latter generated by claude-sonnet-4-20250514, containing a balance, strengths, areas to develop, and suggested next steps.
requirements: Requires instructor-authored rubrics decomposing each question into explicit criteria with descriptions, scoring rules, and point allocations, plus exemplar correct responses for the few-shot prompt.
constraints: Consolidated feedback and reports were delivered to students as generated, without instructor editing, in this study.

CTeSP professional higher technical students
undergraduate programming students
target_learning_goals: formative feedback on programming short-answer and code-based assignments

title: Design LLM feedback systems to preserve student judgement and instructor oversight (human-centred AI in formative assessment)
description: The article frames the reception of LLM-generated feedback from a human-centred perspective in which "feedback systems are assessed by how well they support students' interpretation and decision-making, rather than by their technical capability alone". Agency means learners remain able to interpret, question, and decide how to act on AI-generated feedback, while instructors retain responsibility for the pedagogical conditions. The study's two-layer rating instrument operationalises this by measuring students' perceptions and anticipated use rather than technical performance only.
requirements: Feedback must be delivered so that students can interpret, question, and decide how to act on it, with instructors retaining responsibility for the pedagogical conditions under which it is produced and used.

undergraduate programming students

article_title: Empowering teachers to use AI for differentiation: changes in teachers’ acceptance of AI-based technologies following participation in a short professional development training session
citation: Mesenhöller J and Böhme K (2026). Empowering teachers to use AI for differentiation: changes in teachers’ acceptance of AI-based technologies following participation in a short professional development training session. Front. Educ. 11:1875856. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1875856
title: INSIGHT: a three-hour teacher professional development training session on AI-based technologies for individualised instruction
description: INSIGHT (Information on Schooling with Generative AI and Helpful AI Tools) is a three-hour in-person TPD session for in-service teachers, designed as a pilot intervention to be iteratively refined before larger-scale transfer. It "combines theoretical input, hands-on experiences, and guided reflection" and consists of four parts: an introduction to AI, a hands-on session training an ML system with Google’s Teachable Machine, a session on LLM-supported individualised instruction, and a session on teacher-guided support of students’ AI competencies. It was evaluated in a pilot pre-post study across five schools in one German federal state.
requirements: Delivered in person by the same two trainers following the same training concept, materials, and activities; group sizes ranged from 11 to 29 participants
constraints: Designed as a pilot to refine content and didactical design rather than as definitive evidence of effectiveness
target_learners: in-service primary and secondary teachers in Germany
target_learning_goals: basic understanding of AI-based technologies and their pedagogically meaningful use for supporting individualised instruction, including critical reflection on opportunities and limitations
examples: In small groups of 2–4, teachers trained Google’s Teachable Machine to distinguish pointing and high-five gestures, illustrating how model performance depends on the choice and quality of training data; participants also explored how an LLM reformulated a biology question on photosynthesis for three different competence levels

title: Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a framework for teachers’ social acceptance of AI-based technologies in schools
description: The article uses the Technology Acceptance Model, developed by Davis et al. (1989) and validated for teachers’ social acceptance of AI-based technologies in the school context by the authors’ prior work, as its organising framework. "The TAM posits that two main factors influence the acceptance of a specific technology: Perceived Usefulness (PU) and Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU)", which shape attitude, behavioural intention, and actual use. The SAELKIS questionnaire operationalises these constructs in three subscales (PU, PEOU, BI), and the study measures pre-post change on them.
requirements: Measured with a validated instrument (SAELKIS: PU 6 items α = .86, PEOU 3 items α = .90, BI 4 items α = .92)
constraints: Empirical studies in the school context suggest PU is particularly relevant for BI, whereas evidence for a direct association between PEOU and BI is less consistent
target_learners: in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: understanding and predicting teachers’ acceptance and use of AI-based technologies for individualised instruction
examples: The study measured PU, PEOU and BI before (t0) and after (t1) the INSIGHT session and found PU and PEOU rose while BI did not, which the authors read as possibly indicating factors beyond the original TAM influence whether PU translates into behavioural intentions

citation: April Joy Miles, Paige Haber-Curran, Khalid Arar. (2026). Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement. Open Praxis, 18(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1191
title: Instructional Model for Human-Centered Generative AI Engagement: five recursive phases for LLM-integrated learning
description: A constructionist pedagogical framework that structures student engagement with text-based LLMs in higher education. It is organized around five recursive phases: critical and ethical awareness, prompt literacy, AI-supported learning, reflection and revision, and independent application. The authors state it was developed by synthesizing established learning theory with the authors' instructional experience, and that it helps faculty scaffold LLM-related learning by integrating hands-on experimentation, ethical reflection, and purposeful interaction with LLMs.
requirements: Instructors enact the phases through modeling, transparency, and classroom culture; the framework assumes relational elements such as feedback, encouragement, empathy, and cultural responsiveness remain central
constraints: As a conceptual contribution, the model was not derived from a single empirical study and the authors state it now invites empirical evaluation
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: ethical and responsible use of generative AI
prompt literacy
metacognition
independent application of AI judgment
examples: The five phases are adapted across assignments, units, or entire courses, with each phase building on the previous while the process remains recursive

title: Prompt Literacy Cycle: a five-stage recursive structure for daily prompting practice
description: The Prompt Literacy Cycle is the instructional tool nested within Phase Two of the framework, giving students a concrete, repeatable structure for developing prompt literacy at the level of daily practice. It guides students through five recursive stages: clarify purpose, craft the prompt, engage with output, refine the prompt, and reflect. The authors state it encourages experimentation, reflection, and interactive improvement in students' interactions with LLMs, and can be introduced through demonstrations, scaffolded assignments, or workshops.

constraints: It operates at the level of daily practice, while the five-phase model guides the overall arc of LLM-integrated learning

title: Control versus autonomy as an enduring organizing tension in the history of AI in education
description: The article organizes the history of AI in education around an enduring struggle between control and autonomy in learning. It frames this tension through a comparative analysis of two contrasting AI-driven educational models: John Anderson's structured cognitive tutoring systems and Seymour Papert's constructionist approach emphasizing creative agency. The framework is used to interpret how current GenAI debates continue this historical pattern rather than representing a wholly new situation.

It states that "thoughtful and informed decision-making will shape and determine whether these technologies will reinforce traditional structures or promote greater learner agency and creativity." Educators should therefore actively deliberate about how GenAI is integrated rather than accept a predetermined trajectory.

article_title: Tools facilitate cheating, or partner supports learning? GenAI and academic integrity issues from students' perspectives
citation: Feyisa Mulisa and Tesfa Mezgebu. (2026). Tools facilitate cheating, or partner supports learning? GenAI and academic integrity issues from students’ perspectives. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00231-z
title: AI-plagiarism: presenting AI-generated ideas as one's own as a new form of plagiarism beyond copy-and-paste
description: The article develops the concept of AI-plagiarism, arguing that traditional plagiarism definitions centered on copying and pasting others' work no longer capture GenAI misuse. It states that "GenAI has created a new approach to plagiarism where someone generates ideas using AI and presents them as their own ideas, which can be conceived as AI-plagiarism." The concept holds that submitting GenAI-generated work as one's own costs students the opportunity to be critical thinkers and creators with the topic, and the article argues AI-generated work should not be considered original student work because authorship involves more than remixing existing ideas.
requirements: A redefined conception of plagiarism that goes beyond simple copying and pasting of other authors' work
constraints: The concept is the authors' interpretive argument grounded in student interview data, not a tested construct
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: academic integrity awareness
ethical use of generative AI tools
examples: Participants argued GenAI use was not plagiarism because they did not copy and paste others' intellectual property, which the authors analyze as revealing a fundamental misconception of plagiarism

citation: Albert Munoz, Mercedez Hinchcliff, Cameron Langfield and Ann Rogerson. (2026). How strong is the evidence in generative AI-related academic misconduct allegations? A mixed-methods analysis. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00235-9
title: 15-code evidence taxonomy for GenAI misconduct proceedings organised into eight substantive categories
description: An empirically derived classification of evidence items in GenAI-related misconduct cases, developed through hybrid deductive-inductive framework analysis of 1,162 institutional case records. The finalised taxonomy "contained 15 codes organised into eight substantive categories", spanning non-probative assertions, student work and textual evidence, detection tool outputs, reference and source evidence, documentary admissions, interview evidence, examination and proctoring evidence, collusion evidence, and system records. Each code carries an operational definition, example indicator language, and probative-quality rating profiles across relevance, credibility and inferential force.
requirements: Every evidence item must be assignable to at least one category, with no new category required in the final iteration and multiple instances per substantive category (single-instance Third-Party Source Verification code excepted)
constraints: Derived from one regional Australian university's case records between 2023 and 2025; the article notes any evidence framework in this space will require regular recalibration as LLM capabilities and authorised-use norms evolve
target_learners: Higher education students subject to academic misconduct proceedings
target_learning_goals: Fair and evidence-based adjudication of GenAI-related academic misconduct allegations
examples: Fabricated references (414 items, 22.3%) rated High relevance and credibility but predominantly Moderate inferential force; Interview Admissions (410 items, 22.1%) rated 97.2% Strong inferential force

title: Behavioral clustering framework mapping learner profiles to adaptive learning object recommendations
description: A five-layer conceptual framework that translates data-derived learner profiles into learning object recommendations: data collection, processing with K-Means++ (k = 6), FSLSM-dimension mapping via affinity scoring, diversity regularization, and recommendation delivery with feedback capture. The article describes it as "a novel and interpretable mapping of behavioral profiles to personalized learning objects", connecting descriptive and predictive analytics to prescriptive, adaptive personalization. The affinity function uses a weighted Manhattan distance over five dimensions (engagement, performance, motivation, stress, resource access), with equal weights of 0.20, and the FSLSM mapping serves as a pedagogical interpretation layer rather than a psychometric classification.

constraints: The recommendation component is a proposed conceptual framework that "awaits empirical validation in live LMS environments"; clustering inputs are self-reported proxies rather than direct LMS interaction traces; FSLSM mapping values are heuristic scores not validated against a learning-style instrument
target_learners: higher education students in LMS-based and hybrid courses
target_learning_goals: personalized learning object recommendation matched to engagement, motivation, and performance profiles
examples: The worked example ranks LO_A (affinity 0.094) above LO_B (0.474) for cluster C0, confirming the formula behaves logically; Tables 9 and 10 assign each cluster a learning object type and engagement strategy

title: Design feedback as structured, progressively disclosed, and context-enhanced to reduce extraneous cognitive load

It states: "The findings provide strong evidence for the design principle of structured, progressively disclosed, and context-enhanced feedback." In the system, this is realized through structured statement/explanation/advice sections, hover-tooltips for terms not central to the correction, and retrieved slide pages plus optional narration as context.

target_learning_goals: understanding corrective feedback with reduced cognitive load and sustained motivation
