article_title: Marked Pedagogies: Examining Linguistic Biases in Personalized Automated Writing Feedback
citation: Mei Tan, Lena Phalen, and Dorottya Demszky. 2026. Marked Pedagogies: Examining Linguistic Biases in Personalized Automated Writing Feedback. In LAK 2026: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK 2026). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://doi.org/10.1145/3785022.3785113
title: Marked Pedagogies: systematic shifts in LLM feedback language that reveal pedagogical orientations changing with prompted student characteristics
description: Marked Pedagogies is the article's framework, grounded in the sociolinguistic notion of markedness, in which "dominant groups (e.g., White and male identities in the U.S.) function as institutional norms while nondominant groups are socially and linguistically marked." The framework defines Marked Pedagogies as "systematic shifts in feedback language that reveal how LLMs' underlying pedagogical orientations change in response to prompted student characteristics." It is operationalized through contrastive prompting, Marked Words log-odds lexical analysis, and a concentration metric, and names named pedagogies of disapproval, language inadequacy, lowered expectations, cultural stereotypes, emotional connection, and enthusiasm.
requirements: Contrastive prompt conditions (marked, comparative, baseline) over the same essays to isolate the effect of student attributes
A lexical-difference method (log-odds ratios with Dirichlet prior, |z| > 1.96, minimum frequency 30) to identify distinctive words
constraints: Findings draw on two writing assignments from a single dataset of middle school persuasive essays; generalization to other genres, grade levels, and assignments is untested
Only four LLMs were evaluated; model-level differences were not quantified
Attributes were examined singularly and independently, though intersectional in real-world settings; analyses drew on U.S. stereotypes
target_learners: middle school (eighth-grade) students in English Language Arts
target_learning_goals: writing feedback and revision in persuasive/argumentative writing
examples: The article identifies a Marked Pedagogy of disapproval in which high achievers are positioned as capable writers with expanding potential while lower achievers are positioned as error-prone and in need of correction
The article identifies a Marked Pedagogy of enthusiasm in which unmotivated students are met with enthusiasm whereas motivated students receive direct, higher-level critique

article_title: Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models
citation: Naiming Liu, Xinghe Chen, Richard Baraniuk, Mrinmaya Sachan, and Shashank Sonkar. (2026). Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00818
title: MalAlgoLib: graph-based library generating algebra problems with correct and misconception-specific step-by-step solution traces
description: MalAlgoLib (Mal-Algorithm Library) operationalizes the mal-rule view of misconceptions by representing equation solving as a directed acyclic graph of problem types, where each misconception is an alternative transition yielding an erroneous trace. It "covers 16 linear-equation problem types and 20 misconceptions drawn from established taxonomies", enabling scalable generation of paired correct and misconception-driven traces. Its design principles are extensibility across equation types, modularity in misconception modeling, and faithful representation of cognitive error patterns.
requirements: New problem types are added by implementing a reduce() method linking to an existing type; new misconceptions are added as alternative transitions without modifying existing problem-type implementations.
constraints: The library handles linear equations with one variable, including forms with parentheses and multiple terms.
target_learners: Algebra learners whose misconceptions are being modeled
target_learning_goals: Linear equation solving with correct and erroneous step-by-step reasoning traces
examples: The library generated the controlled training data for the student-model, tutor-model, and no-steps ablation experiments in Section 5.
key_sources: Naiming Liu, Xinghe Chen, Richard Baraniuk, Mrinmaya Sachan, and Shashank Sonkar. (2026). Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00818

article_title: Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models
citation: Naiming Liu, Xinghe Chen, Richard Baraniuk, Mrinmaya Sachan, and Shashank Sonkar. (2026). Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00818
title: Two complementary misconception-acquisition formalizations: the Novice Student Misconception Model and the Expert Tutor Misconception Model
description: The article formalizes misconception acquisition from two perspectives. The Novice Student Misconception Model simulates an individual student holding one specific misconception and must satisfy Misconception Replication on applicable types plus Correct Reasoning Preservation on non-applicable types. The Expert Tutor Misconception Model captures the spectrum of misconceptions a tutor encounters across students, a computational analogue of teachers' Knowledge of Student Misconceptions, and must replicate every training misconception while maintaining Overall Correct Accuracy across all problem types. Both use thresholds where "We setθm =θ c = 90%in all experiments."
requirements: Acquisition is defined by printed thresholds: MA at or above the misconception threshold on applicable types and correct accuracy at or above the correctness threshold on the required problem-type set.
constraints: The tutor model must solve all problem types correctly when prompted, not just non-applicable ones, making its criterion more demanding than the student model's.
target_learners: Individual algebra students (student model) and tutors recognizing error patterns across a student population (tutor model)
target_learning_goals: Faithful simulation of misconception-driven errors and recognition of diverse student error patterns
examples: Experiments instantiated both models by fine-tuning Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Phi-4-4B-Mini, and Qwen-3-4B-Instruct, each first trained on 2000 correct examples per problem type to reach OCA of at least 90%.
key_sources: Naiming Liu, Xinghe Chen, Richard Baraniuk, Mrinmaya Sachan, and Shashank Sonkar. (2026). Misconception Acquisition Dynamics in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00818

article_title: Beyond the AI Tutor: Social Learning with LLM Agents
citation: Harsh Kumar, Zi Kang (Jace) Mu, Jonathan Vincentius, Ashton Anderson. (2026). Human Thinking under Plural LLM Assistance: Mathematical Problem Solving and Open-Ended Writing. Working Paper, July 2026, Toronto, Canada. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02677
title: Plural LLM assistance as a configurable arrangement of support around the user
description: This framework treats LLM assistance as a design space defined by arrangement rather than only by model capability or response quality. As the article puts it, "LLM assistance can vary not only in model capability or response quality, but also in how support is arranged, e.g., one voice or many, one model or several, generalist or specialist roles". The framework holds that roles and personas are interfaces and prompting choices rather than human-like social actors, and that arrangement affects performance, confidence, and diversity of thought. The two experiments instantiate this space with tutor/peer arrangements in math and single-versus-role-specialized-duo arrangements in writing.
requirements: LLM agents instantiated with distinct system prompts defining roles, with learners introduced to each agent's strengths and tendencies so they can calibrate trust
constraints: The explored design space is deliberately narrow: agent count, error types, role specializations, and interaction structure were held largely constant, and the experiments are a first step rather than a definitive map
target_learners: adult crowdworkers solving math problems or writing essays
target_learning_goals: mathematical problem solving and retention
open-ended argumentative and creative writing quality and idea diversity
examples: Experiment-1 compared Control, Peers Only, Tutor Only, and Tutor + Peers support conditions during lesson phases, then measured unassisted test accuracy on isomorphic problems.
Experiment-2 compared no AI, a single generalist assistant, and a pair of role-specialized assistants (Claude and ChatGPT with complementary roles) for argumentative and creative essay writing.

article_title: The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows
citation: Hyunwoo Kim, Harin Yu, Hanau Yi. (2026). The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14807
title: The LLM fallacy: a cognitive attribution error in which LLM-assisted outputs are misattributed as evidence of independent competence
description: The article introduces the LLM fallacy as "a cognitive attribution error in which individuals misinterpret LLM-assisted outputs as evidence of their own independent competence, producing a systematic divergence between perceived and actual capability." It distinguishes the construct from hallucination, automation bias, and cognitive offloading: unlike those, it concerns how outputs are absorbed into self-assessment rather than output correctness or reliance. The paper positions it as an extension of self-assessment error research to hybrid human-AI workflows.
requirements: The task must involve LLM-mediated output generation producing content that would otherwise require domain expertise
The interaction must be seamless enough that the human-input/system-output distinction is not salient
The output must exhibit fluency or coherence typically associated with skilled human performance
constraints: A conceptual construct; the article states empirical validation is still needed
target_learners: LLM users in writing, programming, analysis, and multilingual communication
target_learning_goals: Accurate metacognitive self-assessment of one's own competence when using AI assistance
key_sources: Hyunwoo Kim, Harin Yu, Hanau Yi. (2026). The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14807

article_title: The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows
citation: Hyunwoo Kim, Harin Yu, Hanau Yi. (2026). The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14807
title: Mechanistic framework: opacity, fluency, and immediacy produce capability divergence via attribution ambiguity and cognitive outsourcing
description: The article proposes a mechanism in which LLM interaction properties — opacity (hidden generation process), fluency (surface-level coherence), and interactional immediacy — shape cognitive mediation processes of attribution ambiguity and cognitive outsourcing, which produce misattribution and capability divergence. As Figure 1 summarizes, capability divergence (ΔC) "emerges from the interaction of system-level properties, namely opacity, fluency, and immediacy, mediated by attribution ambiguity and cognitive outsourcing." Pipeline opacity prevents users from tracing how outputs are produced, while fluency acts as a heuristic metacognitive cue.
requirements: Repeated LLM-mediated workflows in which intermediate generative steps are not visible to the user
constraints: Proposed conceptual account; the article frames it as motivating systematic empirical investigation
target_learners: Users of LLM systems in knowledge work
target_learning_goals: Understanding how AI interaction shapes metacognitive monitoring and self-attribution
key_sources: Hyunwoo Kim, Harin Yu, Hanau Yi. (2026). The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14807

article_title: The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows
citation: Hyunwoo Kim, Harin Yu, Hanau Yi. (2026). The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14807
title: Typology of LLM fallacy manifestations across computational, linguistic, analytical, creative, epistemic, and professional domains
description: The article introduces a multi-domain typology in which the same attributional mechanism takes different forms: in the computational domain, execution is misread as technical competence; in the linguistic domain, users conflate fluency with internalized language ability; in the epistemic domain, access to summaries is equated with mastery, "aligns with the illusion of explanatory depth"; and in professional signaling, users report LLM-assisted outputs as independent skill. The article states the common structure is "a dissociation between externally supported performance and internally grounded understanding."
requirements: Tasks in which LLMs perform cognitively demanding work the user could not fully perform unaided
constraints: The article presents no domain-comparative data; it calls for domain-specific studies as future work
target_learners: LLM users across coding, multilingual writing, analysis, creative work, learning, and professional contexts
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing system-assisted performance from independently grounded competence
key_sources: Hyunwoo Kim, Harin Yu, Hanau Yi. (2026). The LLM Fallacy: Misattribution in AI-Assisted Cognitive Workflows. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14807

article_title: Math Education Digital Shadows for facilitating learning with LLMs: Math performance, anxiety and confidence in simulated students and AIs
citation: Esposito, N., Tricarico, A., Porzio, L., Aghazadeh Ardebili, A., & Stella, M. (2026). Math Education Digital Shadows for Investigating Learning with GenAI: Mathematics Performance, Anxiety, and Confidence in LLMs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27618
title: MEDS dataset of 28,000 LLM runs across four mathematics-education tasks
description: MEDS is a multimodal, LLM-generated dataset mapping how large language models reason about mathematics under human-shadow and AI-assistant conditions. Each record includes prompts, psychological and sociodemographic metadata, and four tasks: interviews, three psychometric questionnaires, a cognitive network, and 18 high-school quiz items. The article states that "MEDS comprises 28,000 runs from 14 LLMs (i.e., Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, IBM Granite, Microsoft Phi, and xAI Grok) generated under human-shadow and AI-assistant conditions." Records are publicly available on GitHub as JSON files.
requirements: Runs must be generated under specified constraints: four tasks, prompting mode, and persona profile, with structured JSON outputs
constraints: The article states MEDS is not a proxy for human opinion and is not statistically representative of any specific country
target_learners: learning scientists
developers of AI mathematics tutors
target_learning_goals: mathematics performance
mathematics anxiety and self-efficacy
semantic attitudes toward mathematics
examples: Each run completed four tasks: interviews about mathematics, MSES/AMAS/MSEAQ psychometric ratings, 50-cue-word semantic associations, and 18 multiple-choice problems with reasoning and confidence scores

article_title: Math Education Digital Shadows for facilitating learning with LLMs: Math performance, anxiety and confidence in simulated students and AIs
citation: Esposito, N., Tricarico, A., Porzio, L., Aghazadeh Ardebili, A., & Stella, M. (2026). Math Education Digital Shadows for Investigating Learning with GenAI: Mathematics Performance, Anxiety, and Confidence in LLMs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27618
title: Digital shadowing as a framework for recording LLM behaviour under controlled conditions
description: Digital shadowing is the article's organising methodological framework: unlike digital twins, shadows record system behaviour without feedback loops. The article states that "digital shadows record what a system does across controlled conditions without updating, simulating, or influencing external counterparts." A Math Education Digital Shadow is defined as a structured record of an LLM's mathematics-related psychological profile and problem-solving behaviour under specified constraints. Human shadows simulate synthetic individuals defined by sociodemographic and psychological attributes, while AI assistants respond as themselves.
requirements: A structured record combining persona attributes, prompting mode, and task outputs so latent human variables become experimentally manipulable
constraints: The article notes MEDS is systematically generated using only LLMs with no human input
target_learners: LLM-based synthetic respondents in education research
target_learning_goals: studying prompt-conditioned LLM behaviour in mathematics education
examples: Human shadows were assigned persona dictionaries with age, gender, education, and Big Five traits; AI-assistant mode set the persona field to null

article_title: From Surface Learning to Deep Understanding: A Grounded AI Tutoring System for Moodle
citation: Anna Ostrowska, Michał Kukla, Gabriela Majstrak, Jan Opala, Sebastian Pergała, Jan Skwarek, Anna Wróblewska. (2026). From Surface Learning to Deep Understanding: A Grounded AI Tutoring System for Moodle. https://tinyurl.com/mrytc2dr
title: AI Teaching & Learning Assistant: a modular, open-source Moodle plugin grounding LLM tutoring and content generation in teacher-provided materials via RAG
description: The AI Teaching & Learning Assistant is a modular Moodle plugin that leverages Retrieval-Augmented Generation to deliver grounded tutoring and content generation. It has a dual-centric design: students get an interactive chatbot with three modes, a quiz center, and a learning dashboard, while educators get a Human-in-the-loop workspace where AI-generated materials stay unreviewed until manually approved. The architecture uses a PHP Moodle plugin, a Next.js/React frontend, a FastAPI backend, and hybrid storage (PostgreSQL, ChromaDB, MinIO), containerized with Docker. The article describes it as "a modular Moodle plugin that leverages Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to deliver high-quality, hallucination-free education".
requirements: Teacher-provided course materials must be ingested and indexed so RAG responses and quizzes are grounded in verified sources
Teachers must review and approve AI-generated content before it is released to students
constraints: Grounding depends on the quality and coverage of the teacher-provided materials ingested per course
Data is isolated between different courses by the modular architecture
target_learners: higher education students
university instructors
target_learning_goals: deep conceptual understanding of course material
long-term retention
self-assessment via personalized quizzes
examples: Students interacted with the chatbot, generated and solved quizzes based on real academic materials such as NLP and Machine Learning course notes, and navigated the learning dashboard

article_title: Cognitive Agent Compilation for Explicit Problem Solver Modeling
citation: Hyeongdon Moon, Carolyn Rosé, and John Stamper. (2026). Cognitive Agent Compilation for Explicit Problem Solver Modeling. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07040
title: Cognitive Agent Compilation: a failure-driven loop compiling Teacher LLM knowledge into an explicit Knowledge Base
description: CAC is a pipeline that converts a strong model's problem-solving capability into a target agent operating over an explicit knowledge representation. It separates knowledge representation, problem-solving policy, and verification/update rules through a four-step failure-driven cycle: solve, analyze failure, update the Knowledge Base, and retry. The authors state the goal is 'not merely compression, but explicitness', so behavior is attributable to a declared knowledge state rather than latent weights.
requirements: The Teacher LLM must be able to predict behavioral shifts from adding or removing knowledge elements and correct the agent solely by modifying the Knowledge Base
constraints: The authors treat CAC not as a validated cognitive replica but as a bounded and inspectable problem-solving model; design goals are not validated against student traces
target_learners: students in intelligent tutoring system settings
target_learning_goals: problem-solving knowledge represented as explicit knowledge components and misconceptions
examples: A prototype compiled with an SLM Cognitive Agent and a gemma-3-27b-it Teacher LLM over the OLI_Biology dataset
key_sources: Hyeongdon Moon, Carolyn Rosé, and John Stamper. (2026). Cognitive Agent Compilation for Explicit Problem Solver Modeling. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07040

article_title: Cognitive Agent Compilation for Explicit Problem Solver Modeling
citation: Hyeongdon Moon, Carolyn Rosé, and John Stamper. (2026). Cognitive Agent Compilation for Explicit Problem Solver Modeling. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07040
title: SLM prototype Cognitive Agent with QKV-style retrieval over a natural-language Knowledge Base
description: The prototype Cognitive Agent uses Qwen2.5-2B as its core SLM, embedding-gemma (300M parameters) for similarity-based retrieval, and a locally run 4-bit quantized gemma-3-27b-it Teacher LLM, all under zero-shot prompting. Knowledge is stored in natural language across three fields: a description, the applicable Goal state, and the applicable Working Memory state. At each step the SLM deterministically selects one of three actions: set a subgoal, update working memory, or produce a final answer.
requirements: The SLM must reliably follow the structured output format; the Teacher needs carefully specified prompts and three MCP tools for KB inference, similarity scoring, and DM submission
constraints: The authors note the SLM executor retains 'a residual black-box component whose internal prior knowledge cannot be fully inspected'
target_learners: modeled biology students in the OLI_Biology dataset context
target_learning_goals: declarative knowledge retrieval and multi-step problem solving
examples: Experiment code released at a public GitHub repository and a demo with detailed experiment output samples

article_title: MBP-KT: Learning Global Collaborative Information from Meta-Behavioral Pattern for Enhanced Knowledge Tracing
citation: Yuhao Jia, Duantengchuan Li, Jinsong Chen, Zhongjie Mao, Mingwen Tong, Yue Li, Xiaoguang Wang. (2026). MBP-KT: Learning Global Collaborative Information from Meta-Behavioral Pattern for Enhanced Knowledge Tracing. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08697
title: MBP-KT: a meta-behavioral pattern-aware framework for extracting and injecting global collaborative information in knowledge tracing
description: MBP-KT is a three-component framework for knowledge tracing. It first applies a meta-behavioral operator transformation that maps adjacent interactions into Start, Same and Diff operators, decoupling knowledge states from specific questions. It then extracts frequently occurring behavior patterns via a sliding window into a global collaborative pattern matrix, and finally injects the resulting prior into RNN, memory-network, Transformer and state-based KT models. The article states it 'provides general injection strategies to introduce the extracted global collaborative information into various downstream KT models, ensuring the universality of the collaborative information.'
requirements: Requires raw interaction sequences with question, knowledge-concept set and binary correctness, and a training set from which frequent meta-behavioral patterns can be mined with a sliding window and minimum frequency threshold
constraints: The framework targets sequential-model-based KT approaches; injection is described for RNN, memory network, Transformer and state-based families
Gains depend on dataset characteristics: the article attributes smaller gains on XES3G5M to its larger number of knowledge concepts influencing meta-behavioral sequence construction
target_learners: learners whose interaction logs are modeled in knowledge tracing systems
target_learning_goals: predicting learners' knowledge states and next-question performance
examples: On ASSISTments2009, EdNet-KT1 and XES3G5M, MBP-KT-enhanced versions of DKT, DKVMN, AKT, SAINT, UKT, ReKT and Mamba were compared against the base models under an identical training configuration
key_sources: Yuhao Jia, Duantengchuan Li, Jinsong Chen, Zhongjie Mao, Mingwen Tong, Yue Li, Xiaoguang Wang. (2026). MBP-KT: Learning Global Collaborative Information from Meta-Behavioral Pattern for Enhanced Knowledge Tracing. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08697

article_title: MBP-KT: Learning Global Collaborative Information from Meta-Behavioral Pattern for Enhanced Knowledge Tracing
citation: Yuhao Jia, Duantengchuan Li, Jinsong Chen, Zhongjie Mao, Mingwen Tong, Yue Li, Xiaoguang Wang. (2026). MBP-KT: Learning Global Collaborative Information from Meta-Behavioral Pattern for Enhanced Knowledge Tracing. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08697
title: Three real-world KT benchmark datasets: ASSISTments2009, EdNet-KT1 and XES3G5M
description: The article evaluates MBP-KT on three widely-used educational datasets spanning different scales and sparsity levels: ASSISTments2009 (5,766 learners, 13,441 questions, 412,332 interactions, 99.47% sparsity), EdNet-KT1 (6,609 learners, 12,100 questions, 2,148,355 interactions, 97.31% sparsity), and XES3G5M (18,066 learners, 7,645 questions, 5,168,974 interactions, 96.26% sparsity). Evaluation used a single-point prediction protocol with maximum sequence length L=30, and sequences shorter than 5 interactions were filtered out.
requirements: Interaction sequences partitioned into non-overlapping segments of maximum length 30; sequences with fewer than 5 interactions filtered out prior to training
constraints: The learner-question interaction matrix sparsity remains exceptionally high across all datasets, ranging from 96.26% and peaking at 99.47% on ASSISTments2009
target_learners: learners on online tutoring and exercise platforms represented in the three datasets
target_learning_goals: predicting next-question response correctness from historical interaction logs
examples: Training used an identical fixed configuration for all models: Adam optimizer without weight decay, learning rate 1×10−3, batch size 32, 5 epochs

article_title: An Interpretable Closed-Loop Intelligent Tutoring System for Multimodal Affective Feedback in Asynchronous Presentation Training
citation: Hung-Yue Suen and Kuo-En Hung. (2026). An Interpretable Closed-Loop Intelligent Tutoring System for Multimodal Affective Feedback in Asynchronous Presentation Training. IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1109/TLT.2026.3693864
title: Closed-loop three-layer interpretable ITS architecture linking multimodal scoring, expressive diagnostics, and conversational coaching
description: The article proposes an ITS architecture that treats assessment not as an endpoint but as part of a closed loop of practice, feedback, and behavioral adjustment. It is "structured as a closed-loop feedback system with three distinct layers": a performance layer presenting Overall Rating and six BARS dimension scores, an emotion-aware expressive diagnosis layer treating audience-facing cues as behavioral signals, and a Conversational AI Tutor that resolves learner queries using retrieved analytic evidence. The design aims to move learners from performance awareness to interpretation to actionable change.

A retrieval layer restricting tutor generation to the learner's own multimodal records
constraints: Asynchronous, upload-based design; no real-time feedback during live performance
Multimodal signals are summarized rather than modeled temporally
Adapting to a new rubric or domain requires re-annotation and retraining (cold-start dependency)
target_learners: adult learners and working professionals practicing on-camera oral presentation
target_learning_goals: on-camera oral presentation delivery and content skills
examples: In the 30-day field study, learners reviewed dashboard feedback and interacted with the AI tutor between pretest and posttest submissions, with additional evaluative uploads disabled to encourage distributed practice.

title: Seven-dimensional BARS rubric for on-camera presentation skills with expert-annotated MOOC dataset
description: The system operationalizes a seven-dimensional Behaviorally Anchored Rating Scale (Topic, Content, Clarity, Voice & Talk, Eye Contact, Nonverbal Expressiveness, and Overall Rating), with each dimension anchored at levels 1, 3, and 5 and intermediate ratings permitted. The rubric was adapted from a prior scale through expert workshops to make each dimension observable in single-camera instructor videos. It supervised training of the scoring models on 10,360 two-second MOOC video segments rated holistically by three independent annotators per video.

article_title: An Interpretable Closed-Loop Intelligent Tutoring System for Multimodal Affective Feedback in Asynchronous Presentation Training
citation: Hung-Yue Suen and Kuo-En Hung. (2026). An Interpretable Closed-Loop Intelligent Tutoring System for Multimodal Affective Feedback in Asynchronous Presentation Training. IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1109/TLT.2026.3693864
title: Retrieval-augmented Conversational AI Tutor with modular GROW-aligned coaching routines
description: The Conversational AI Tutor is a retrieval-grounded conversational module built on GPT-4.1 with a RAG layer that anchors each response in the learner's own multimodal records (transcripts, BARS scores, emotion descriptors, feature summaries) and maintains records across submissions for longitudinal reflection. The tutor implements three modular routines—performance summarization, strength and weakness highlighting, and translation of analytic indicators into learner-facing concepts—with phrasing drawn from a curated library of expert coaching aligned to the BARS rubric and the GROW model (Goals, Reality, Options, Will).

constraints: The RAG layer restricts generation to retrieved sources from the learner's own records, minimizing unconstrained free-form output

description: In the system's expressive diagnosis layer, affective signals are explicitly not designed to capture the speaker's internal emotional states; instead they capture "expressive cues that are perceivable by an audience and that shape how the presentation is received," consistent with observer-based affect perception research. Facial expressions support interpretation of Nonverbal Expressiveness, vocal and verbal expressions support Voice & Talk, and lexical expressions contextualize Topic, Content, and Clarity. article_title: MindCopilot: Towards Formalizing and Evaluating Granular Human-LLM Co-Writing
citation: Youqing Fang, Yinhao Tang, Yanan Sun, Jiangning Liu, Ziyi Wang, Xun Zhao, Bin Liu, Weiming Zhang, Kuikun Liu, Wenwei Zhang, Kai Chen. (2026). MindCopilot: Towards Formalizing and Evaluating Granular Human-LLM Co-Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23535
title: Human-in-the-Loop MDP formulation of co-writing
description: The article models interactive co-writing as a sequential decision process in which the assistant proposes context-aware suggestions and the human author responds with accept, reject, or edit actions that update the document state. It states: "We model this iterative process as a Human-in-the-Loop Markov Decision Process (HitL-MDP), which makes explicit the division of roles between proposing and deciding." The formulation defines the process as M=<S,A,U,T> with transitions enacted through human actions, and grounds learning and evaluation in observable human responses to system proposals.
requirements: Suggestions must be non-binding, with all document updates determined by the human author, so that acceptance and editing behavior is observable.
constraints: The framework targets suggestion-based interactive completion, an abstraction of real-world authoring; generalization to other collaborative forms such as outlining assistance or structural critiquing remains an open question.
target_learners: adult writers using LLM writing assistants
target_learning_goals: sustaining writing flow and author intent alignment during human-AI co-writing
examples: The formulation is operationalized by instantiating acceptance decisions as a learnable component for downstream reinforcement-learning optimization.

article_title: MindCopilot: Towards Formalizing and Evaluating Granular Human-LLM Co-Writing
citation: Youqing Fang, Yinhao Tang, Yanan Sun, Jiangning Liu, Ziyi Wang, Xun Zhao, Bin Liu, Weiming Zhang, Kuikun Liu, Wenwei Zhang, Kai Chen. (2026). MindCopilot: Towards Formalizing and Evaluating Granular Human-LLM Co-Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23535
title: Four-level taxonomy of co-writing interaction paradigms (L0-L3)
description: The article organizes co-writing systems into four paradigms that differ in initiative distribution, contextual signals for intent inference, and adaptivity. It states: "We organize co-writing systems into four interaction paradigms, as summarized in Table 3." L0 is user-initiated collaboration reacting to explicit intent; L1 is stateless proactive collaboration predicting intent from local context; L2 is stateful proactive collaboration conditioning on interaction history; L3 is adaptive proactive collaboration with adaptive intent modeling. The taxonomy provides a unified lens for analyzing user acceptance and editing behavior.
requirements: Quantitative comparison requires paradigms where interaction events are well-defined and directly comparable, which the article states holds for L1 and L2.
constraints: L3 is treated as an analysis-driven paradigm whose evaluation is reserved for downstream system design and user studies, not the controlled quantitative comparison.
target_learners: adult writers using LLM writing assistants
target_learning_goals: aligning assistant initiative with user intent during writing
examples: The user study instantiated all four interaction paradigms with a unified LLM backend (GPT-5.1) in an online interactive writing system.

citation: Youqing Fang, Yinhao Tang, Yanan Sun, Jiangning Liu, Ziyi Wang, Xun Zhao, Bin Liu, Weiming Zhang, Kuikun Liu, Wenwei Zhang, Kai Chen. (2026). MindCopilot: Towards Formalizing and Evaluating Granular Human-LLM Co-Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23535
title: Co-Writing Fidelity Suite (HAR and KED metrics)
description: A set of interaction-aware evaluation metrics for human-AI co-writing. The article states: "we introduce the Co-Writing Fidelity Suite, a set of interaction-aware metrics designed to evaluate human-AI collaboration along two complementary dimensions: alignment and interaction friction." Hierarchical Acceptance Rate models acceptance as a structured multi-stage decision, while Knowledge-aware Editing Distance weights edit operations by cognitive cost, so that semantic rewrites and factual corrections cost more than surface edits. The suite is validated against expert annotation, editing-duration logs, simulation, and a user study.
requirements: KED evaluation requires writing logs recording human revisions to AI-generated suggestions together with timestamps, using editing duration as a behavioral proxy for cognitive effort.
constraints: The metrics are designed for suggestion-based proactive completion; the authors state that how HAR and KED generalize to tool-augmented or multi-agent co-writing settings remains a promising future direction.
target_learners: adult writers using LLM writing assistants
target_learning_goals: evaluating user-assistant alignment and cognitive editing effort in co-writing systems
examples: HAR was evaluated on 1.2K expert-annotated instances with a checklist-style protocol; KED was evaluated using writing logs from the CoAuthor dataset.

article_title: A Taxonomy of Metacognitive Learning Scenarios in Professional Contexts: Integrating Systems Theory with Empirical Constraints
citation: Gibson, D. C., Azukas, M. E., & Yilmaz Soylu, M. (2025). A Taxonomy of Metacognitive Learning Scenarios in Professional Contexts: Integrating Systems Theory with Empirical Constraints.
title: Six-node open systems model of metacognition
description: The article proposes a six-node open systems architecture synthesizing Flavell, Nelson and Narens, Koriat, and COPES: "Environment (external context and task demands), Input (information entering the learner's system), Processes (active cognitive/metacognitive operations), Structures (stable knowledge representations, beliefs, standards), Output (generated products and behaviors), and Feedback (information about output quality and environmental response)." Monitoring is modeled as upward Processes→Structures flow and control as downward Structures→Processes flow, with a mandatory external backbone Output→Feedback→Environment→Input. It serves as the common language for enumerating learning scenarios.
requirements: Cross-cluster connections must preserve psychological realism: Input always flows into the internal system and Output always flows from it
constraints: The six-node model necessarily simplifies complex processes; Structures aggregates diverse metacognitive knowledge into a single node
target_learners: professional learners in workplace contexts
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and control
self-regulated professional learning
examples: The model was implemented in the DOT Framework and used to generate 216 combinatorial learning scenarios for an AI-enabled Coach

citation: Gabelmann, J., Jahn, F., Baum, K., van Rossum, S., Wuenscher, E., Gros, T. P., Wolf, V. (2026). Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30187
title: Six design desiderata for responsible LLM-based educational systems
description: The article derives six design desiderata for responsible LLM-based educational systems: differentiated pedagogical control, preservation of epistemic agency, process-level transparency, effective human oversight, explicit handling of value conflicts, and anticipatory robustness and revisability. These are stated as 'a selection of necessary design conditions for responsible AI in this context, rather than as a complete or sufficient specification'. Each desideratum constrains how a system must be built, not merely how it should behave.
requirements: Desiderata must be specific to the educational deployment context and have direct architectural implications
constraints: They are necessary conditions, not a complete or sufficient specification of responsible educational systems
target_learners: students using LLM-based learning assistance
target_learning_goals: responsible AI-supported exercise solving and skill development

citation: Gabelmann, J., Jahn, F., Baum, K., van Rossum, S., Wuenscher, E., Gros, T. P., Wolf, V. (2026). Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30187
title: MALA: a modular agentic AI chatbot architecture for exercise-solving assistance
description: MALA (Modular Artificial Learning Assistance) decomposes tutoring into a two-stage process of intent classification and task-specific execution. A central classifier routes each student message to one of four specialized modules: a hint module that handles requests where students ask for 'a starting point, the next step, or a nudge toward the solution', an explanation module constrained to short structured messages, a feedback module with a reasoning-then-evaluation-then-output workflow, and a fallback/safety module deflecting prompt-injection attempts. It was prototyped with GPT-4o for guiding students through problem-solving exercises and optionally generating new exercises.
requirements: Each module is governed by a dedicated system prompt aligned with its educational goal; a sample solution is provided in the feedback prompt to mitigate hallucinated corrections
constraints: It does not serve as a general-purpose tutor or study planner
target_learners: undergraduate computer science students
target_learning_goals: exercise solving with preserved epistemic agency
examples: In an adversarial test, the hint module consistently refused to give the full solution despite escalating urgency claims, offering guiding questions instead

citation: Gabelmann, J., Jahn, F., Baum, K., van Rossum, S., Wuenscher, E., Gros, T. P., Wolf, V. (2026). Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30187
title: Reasoning-before-response workflow: hidden CoT reasoning followed by brief pedagogical output
description: The hint and feedback modules use a two-stage generation process in which the LLM first produces a hidden reasoning block analyzing student progress or solution correctness, then generates the visible pedagogical output. This resolves the conflict between concise responses that avoid cognitive overload and Chain-of-Thought generation, and 'directly serves D2 (preservation of epistemic agency) by ensuring the student still performs the "heavy lifting" of the cognitive task'. The feedback module adds a correctness classification step before output.
requirements: Internal reasoning must be guided by task-specific prompts; feedback grounding uses a sample solution in the prompt
constraints: Hidden reasoning is not shown to the user
target_learners: students solving exercises with chatbot assistance
target_learning_goals: scaffolding within the zone of proximal development without giving away solutions
examples: The hint module determines a 'minimal effective dose' of information for the current context before producing the visible hint

description: The exercise-generation tool maps its three difficulty levels directly onto Bloom's Taxonomy cognitive levels within the system prompt: easy prompts tasks focused on remembering and understanding, medium on applying and analyzing, and hard on evaluating and creating. The authors state this 'ensures that the task's complexity is grounded in established theory', aligning generated exercises with the pedagogical goal of challenging students across cognitive levels.

title: Learning objective graphs for curriculum-aligned adaptive tutoring
description: The proposed architecture structures tutoring around Learning Objective (LO) graphs that represent the course curriculum as a network of nodes with edges indicating interdependencies and prerequisites between concepts. Mapping student performance on exercises onto the graph tracks progress across the course and enables adaptive learning, such as maintaining the student within their ZPD across a sequence of topics. If the system detects recurring struggle with a specific LO, it can proactively suggest lower-difficulty exercises or targeted explanations from a prerequisite node.

article_title: LearnOpt: Recovering the Latent Cognitive Structure of Standardized Examinations via Knowledge Graphs and Constrained Optimization
citation: Joy Bose, Om Thomas. (2025). LearnOpt: Recovering the Latent Cognitive Structure of Standardized Examinations via Knowledge Graphs and Constrained Optimization. https://github.com/learnopt/learnopt
title: LearnOpt framework: exam preparation as constrained optimization over an LLM-built exam knowledge graph with BKT mastery updates
description: LearnOpt reframes exam preparation as a constrained optimization problem: it ingests historical question papers, LLM-tags each question with chapter, topic, difficulty and skill via a chain-of-evidence prompt, builds a knowledge graph in FalkorDB with prerequisite edges, and "produces a ranked, time-bounded study plan specifying which concept subgroups to study, in what sequence, and with what expected score gain." Mastery is initialized from self-report and updated via standard BKT; the objective is solved with Google OR-Tools CP-SAT and re-run after each study session. Its substantive extension over the Embibe PAJ precedent is a skill-weighted objective coupling the exam's empirical cognitive-operation distribution into the reward signal.
requirements: Historical question papers in PDF format, an official syllabus, and a student mastery vector as inputs; full question text including options for reliable skill tagging
constraints: Validated on MCQ exams; transfer to subjective or coding assessments requires further work
Mastery vectors initialized from self-report introduce subjective bias; optimization evaluation is simulation-based with no measured student outcomes
target_learners: NEET and JEE aspirants preparing for standardized examinations
target_learning_goals: Efficient allocation of limited preparation time across topics and cognitive skills to maximize expected exam score
examples: Applied to 1,496 NEET questions (2016-2024) and the 110-question single-correct MCQ subset of JEEBench; code, knowledge graph, and annotated dataset released publicly
key_sources: Joy Bose, Om Thomas. (2025). LearnOpt: Recovering the Latent Cognitive Structure of Standardized Examinations via Knowledge Graphs and Constrained Optimization. https://github.com/learnopt/learnopt

article_title: LearnOpt: Recovering the Latent Cognitive Structure of Standardized Examinations via Knowledge Graphs and Constrained Optimization
citation: Joy Bose, Om Thomas. (2025). LearnOpt: Recovering the Latent Cognitive Structure of Standardized Examinations via Knowledge Graphs and Constrained Optimization. https://github.com/learnopt/learnopt
title: Five-category latent skill taxonomy for science MCQs (S1-S5), chosen for surface-structural discriminability
description: The taxonomy defines five skill categories calibrated to NEET-type science MCQs: S1 Direct Recall, S2 Conceptual Application, S3 Multi-concept Integration, S4 Quantitative Reasoning, and S5 Elimination and Negation. "Categories are chosen for structural discriminability: each can be identified from the surface form of the question without requiring inference about latent cognitive depth, which maximizes inter-rater reliability." S1-S4 map approximately to revised Bloom levels, while S5 does not appear in standard taxonomies and is introduced to capture format-driven falsification operations; the design follows collapsed Bloom rubrics that achieved higher inter-rater reliability than six-level schemes.
requirements: Full question text including options, since reliable skill tagging with this pipeline requires full question-and-options text
constraints: The S2/S3/S4 boundary is where inter-model agreement is weakest (kappa 0.51 overall); the taxonomy describes exam design, not necessarily where students should focus effort
target_learners: NEET and JEE aspirants; coaching centers analyzing question banks
target_learning_goals: Characterizing the cognitive operations standardized exams demand, to weight study-time allocation by skill category
examples: S5 items include "which of the following is NOT/EXCEPT" formats, Assertion-Reason and twin-statement items; S5 rose to 30.7-35.2% of NEET questions post-2023

article_title: Measuring Whether LLM Tutors Teach or Solve: A Diagnostic for Educational Impact
citation: Junyi Yao, Zihao Zheng, and Baichuan Li. (2026). Beyond Helpfulness: A Teaching-over-Solving Diagnostic for Measuring Educational Impact in LLM Tutors. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16206
title: Teaching-over-solving diagnostic: separating answer-production ability from learning-support behavior via solving and pedagogy composites and their gap
description: The article proposes a lightweight diagnostic that reaggregates public tutoring benchmark scores into two composites: a solving composite (problem solving, solution correctness, mistake location, mistake correction) and a pedagogy composite (socratic questioning, scaffolding win rate, pedagogy instruction-following win rate, hard scaffolding, hard pedagogy instruction-following). For each model it defines "Gap(m) = Teach(m)−Solve(m)", where positive values indicate models relatively stronger on pedagogy than on solving. It is intended for education-oriented NLP work that lacks private classroom data.
requirements: Requires public benchmark artifacts reporting task-level scores that can be grouped into solving-oriented and pedagogy-oriented composites, with no student-private data.
constraints: The article states its grouping is "intended as a transparent diagnostic rather than a definitive taxonomy" and that alternative task groupings could change the reported gaps.
target_learners: learners interacting with LLM tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: learning support and student-agency-preserving tutoring behavior in educational NLP evaluation
examples: Applied to the eight-model MathTutorBench leaderboard, the diagnostic yields gaps ranging from +0.077 for LLaMA3.1-8B-Instruct to −0.452 for Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct.

article_title: MedEasy: Designing AI Standardized Patients for Clinical Consultation Training
citation: Zhiqi Gao, Huarui Luo, Guo Zhu, Bingquan Zhang, Dongyijie Primo Pan, Yizhan Feng, Jiahuan Pei, Jie Li, Benyou Wang. (2026). MedEasy: Designing AI Standardized Patients for Clinical Consultation Training. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17512
title: MedEasy: a multi-agent AI standardized-patient system for structured consultation practice
description: MedEasy is a web-based, multi-agent virtual standardized patient system that treats a virtual consultation as a staged process of patient dialogue, clinical action, decision submission, documentation, and post-session review. Its architecture separates "intent recognition, case-grounded patient response, action-contingent clinical findings, and trajectory-level evaluation." An Auxiliary Agent maps learner utterances to a 31-category clinical intent framework, a Patient Agent generates case-grounded responses, and an Evaluation Agent reviews the completed session against expert criteria. The Patient and Evaluation Agents use Gemini 2.5 Pro and the Auxiliary Agent uses Gemini 2.5 Flash.
requirements: A structured case library with expert-authored case records and a clinical intent framework must be authored offline before runtime consultation.
constraints: The Evaluation Agent's review "applies the scope defined in the authored teaching case" and is used for formative post-session review rather than formal grading.
target_learners: clinical-year medical students
target_learning_goals: clinical consultation skills including history taking, examination selection, diagnosis, treatment planning, patient education, and medical-record writing
examples: The case library contains 20 clinical cases selected by a panel of medical experts, balanced by patient gender and spanning three age groups, seven major organ systems, and 16 diagnoses.

citation: Zhiqi Gao, Huarui Luo, Guo Zhu, Bingquan Zhang, Dongyijie Primo Pan, Yizhan Feng, Jiahuan Pei, Jie Li, Benyou Wang. (2026). MedEasy: Designing AI Standardized Patients for Clinical Consultation Training. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17512
title: Trajectory-based formative feedback against expert-authored case standards
description: MedEasy's post-session evaluation compares the retained consultation trajectory — dialogue history, recognized intents, elicited facts, clinical actions, decisions, and medical-record entries — with an expert-authored reference answer. "The evaluation follows six modules: history taking, physical examination, auxiliary examination, diagnostic reasoning, treatment planning, and overall performance." For each module the agent identifies completed and omitted items and explains the diagnostic relevance of omissions, producing itemized formative feedback rather than a score alone.
requirements: An expert-authored reference answer and case-specific criteria must be supplied for each case; the agent is prohibited from adding requirements outside the expert standard.
constraints: Feedback credibility depends on the content and scope of the supplied standard; criteria designed for one learner stage, specialty context, or teaching objective may not transfer directly to another setting.
target_learners: clinical-year medical students
target_learning_goals: formative review of consultation performance including history taking, examination and test selection, diagnostic reasoning, and treatment planning
examples: The post-session interface presents module-level performance, a scoring basis, competency summary, itemized review of suggested and missed items, and humanistic-care feedback.

article_title: Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human-Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation
citation: Pei-Yu Tseng, Mahir Akgun, and Peng Liu. (2026). Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human–Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23629
title: AI-assisted pretest question generation workflow with generator, evaluator, and controller components
description: The article presents an AI-assisted workflow for pretest question development with three iterative components: automated generation grounded in instructional materials, rubric-based evaluation of question quality, and iterative selection of high-quality questions. The Generator produces candidate questions each round; the Evaluator scores questions on rubric dimensions and removes those below level 3 on relevance or clarity, then runs blind pairwise comparison flagging contradictions; the Controller analyzes gaps in quality and topic coverage and feeds back to the Generator. Both generator and evaluator use GPT-5.1.
requirements: Requires four inputs: course material, a scenario, key concepts, and a rubric defining the quality dimensions of openness, cognitive depth, relevance, and clarity
constraints: The study is situated in an intermediate-level statistics course in the Cybersecurity major, focusing on multiple regression for undergraduate learners
target_learners: undergraduate Cybersecurity students in an intermediate-level statistics course
target_learning_goals: pretest questions aligned with learning objectives on multiple regression, spanning openness and cognitive depth dimensions
examples: In each run the generator produced 12 candidate questions per round across 15 rounds, yielding 180 candidates, with approximately 120 retained per rubric version for diversity across the 3×3 openness–depth space
key_sources: Pei-Yu Tseng, Mahir Akgun, and Peng Liu. (2026). Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human–Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23629

article_title: Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human-Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation
citation: Pei-Yu Tseng, Mahir Akgun, and Peng Liu. (2026). Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human–Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23629
title: Rubric revision pattern: separate construct from surface cues, specify valid evidence, make scoring logic operational, and make adjacent boundaries explicit
description: When machine raters misread rubric constructs, the article distills four revision principles from its mismatch analysis. For openness: (P1) separate the intended construct from misleading surface cues, making clear that openness depends on response-space breadth rather than on whether a question appears to have a single correct answer, and (P2) specify what counts as valid evidence for each score level. For depth: (P3) make the scoring logic operational rather than purely descriptive, with a classification structure, examples, and an explicit decision rule, and (P4) make adjacent score boundaries explicit.
requirements: Requires diagnosing recurring machine scoring heuristics that diverge from the rubric's intended meaning before revising
constraints: Derived from mismatches observed for the openness and depth dimensions in one LLM-based evaluation workflow; relevance and clarity already aligned near-perfectly
target_learners: undergraduate Cybersecurity students in an intermediate-level statistics course
target_learning_goals: accurate machine evaluation of pretest question openness and cognitive depth
examples: The machine treated explanatory wording such as explain or why as evidence of analytical reasoning and treated procedural articulation as evaluative synthesis; the revised rubric addressed these with explicit decision rules
key_sources: Pei-Yu Tseng, Mahir Akgun, and Peng Liu. (2026). Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human–Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23629

article_title: Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human-Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation
citation: Pei-Yu Tseng, Mahir Akgun, and Peng Liu. (2026). Why Machines Misread Pedagogical Quality: Human–Machine Alignment in LLM-Based Pretest Question Evaluation. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23629
title: For LLM-based evaluation, operationalized criteria with explicit decision boundaries matter more than prompting the model to reason more carefully
description: The article concludes that for LLM-based evaluation of pedagogical quality, providing operationalized criteria with explicit decision boundaries plays a more critical role than prompting the model to reason more carefully. Rubric revision produced larger alignment gains than rationale-first evaluation, yet the two interventions are complementary, with the highest human–machine alignment achieved when combining an operationalized rubric with rationale-first evaluation.
requirements: Requires a rubric whose constructs are made explicit for machine use, with classification structures, examples, and explicit decision rules
constraints: The study compares two evaluation modes within a single LLM-based workflow rather than benchmarking a broader set of alternative evaluation methods, and does not claim improved alignment yields better pretest questions, teaching decisions, or student learning outcomes
target_learners: undergraduate Cybersecurity students in an intermediate-level statistics course
target_learning_goals: reliable machine assessment of pretest question quality across openness, depth, relevance, and clarity
examples: Rationale-first evaluation required the evaluator to enumerate distinct plausible answer directions for openness and pass through a decision gate for depth before assigning a final level

article_title: Visualizing Engineering Fundamentals: Design of Mixed Reality and Physical Toolkits for Effective Learning
citation: Rakib, M. A. N., Akter, S., Sridhar, E. P., Biswas, S., Raihan, M. R., & Rahman, M. (2025). Visualizing Engineering Fundamentals: Design of Mixed Reality and Physical Toolkits for Effective Learning. Manuscript under review at Ergonomics in Design: The Quarterly of Human Factors Applications. https://www.uta.edu
title: Three learner types in immersive and tangible mechanics learning: Knowing Through Doing, Tactile-visual, and Goal-oriented
description: The article's thematic analysis identifies a taxonomy of three learner types based on how participants perceived their assigned MR or ET modality, rather than classifying users as novice or expert. "Knowing Through Doing Learners" actively engage with tangible tools and extend knowledge to future applications; "Tactile-visual Learners" value rich visualizations and want more advanced digital toolkits; "Goal-oriented Learners" "prioritized efficiency and outcomes over exploration," needing streamlined workflows. The taxonomy informs the recommendation to provide multiple interaction pathways.
requirements: Design must accommodate learners responding differently to tactile, visual, and goal-oriented approaches
constraints: Derived from 24 participants in a single Engineering Mechanics topic, based on perceptions of assigned modalities
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students who completed a foundational mechanics course
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of beam theory and beam bending behavior
examples: ET 8 described the beam experiment with a scale showing forces at different points; MR 8 asked for applying topics to a real-life scenario; TC 5 reported difficulty visualizing why one loading situation behaves differently than another.

article_title: Mind the Trust Gap: Identifying (Mis)alignments in Teacher-Student Views Toward Control and Agency in K-12 Classroom AI
citation: Tomohiro Nagashima, Lisa Siegrist, Niklas Scholz, Shintaro Sato, Martina Vincoli, and Man Su. 2026. Mind the Trust Gap: Identifying (Mis)alignments in Teacher-Student Views Toward Control and Agency in K-12 Classroom AI. Proc. ACM Hum.-Comput. Interact. 10, 6, Article CSCW124. https://doi.org/10.1145/3816972
title: Four-dimensional framework of student-AI decision-making control in AI-supported classrooms
description: The article organizes its scenarios and analysis around four key areas of decision-making agency and control between students and AI systems, adopted from Vincoli et al.: Content Control (selecting what to learn), Help-Seeking/Giving Control (balance between help students seek and help the system offers), Data Control (how much and what data to share), and Co-Orchestration Control (how much and with whom students collaborate). The article states that "the decision-making space today is more complex than a linear progression from low to high control on one dimension," and structured eight storyboards so each dimension had one full-learner-control and one full-AI-control scenario.
requirements: Scenarios and analysis must address each of the four dimensions rather than a single control dimension
constraints: The framework is adopted from prior work (Vincoli et al.) rather than developed in this article
target_learners: K-12 school students
K-12 school teachers
target_learning_goals: Understanding and negotiating decision-making control when learning with AI-based systems
examples: Eight storyboards were created, two per dimension, showing full learner control versus full AI control with positive and negative endings

citation: Tomohiro Nagashima, Lisa Siegrist, Niklas Scholz, Shintaro Sato, Martina Vincoli, and Man Su. 2026. Mind the Trust Gap: Identifying (Mis)alignments in Teacher-Student Views Toward Control and Agency in K-12 Classroom AI. Proc. ACM Hum.-Comput. Interact. 10, 6, Article CSCW124. https://doi.org/10.1145/3816972
title: Speed-dating storyboard method with pair-matching analysis for eliciting multi-stakeholder views on classroom AI
description: The study used a qualitative speed-dating method in which 16 students and 15 teachers in Germany individually reacted to eight storyboards (five scenes each, with positive and negative endings) about AI use in classrooms, presented in random order with guiding questions. Sessions lasted about 45 to 60 minutes and produced roughly 14.0 hours of student recordings and 17.4 hours of teacher recordings. Open coding yielded 644 student and 637 teacher codes; Affinity Diagramming produced low-level themes, and a pair-matching analysis across 438 individual low-level themes yielded 55 matched pairs, grouped into 11 mid-level and five high-level themes. Storyboards are available on OSF.
requirements: Scenarios should present both extremes (full learner vs. full AI control) and positive/negative endings to avoid biased responses
Student and teacher versions of scenarios should depict identical situations from each stakeholder's point of view
constraints: Conducted in Germany, where few participants had used AI-based learning systems, and the authors note the German school context may differ from other educational contexts
The authors state they did not use inter-rater reliability statistics or predefined coding schemes, following Affinity Diagramming conventions
target_learners: K-12 school students
K-12 school teachers
target_learning_goals: Eliciting stakeholder preferences and (mis)alignments regarding student versus AI decision-making control
examples: A storyboard on AI-based automatic group assignment showed a positive ending (effective collaboration) and a negative ending (teacher unable to change grouping despite a student's request)

article_title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Scientific Visualization Literacy
citation: Patrick Phuoc Do, Chau M. Ta, Chaoli Wang. (2026). Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Scientific Visualization Literacy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15176v2
title: SVLAT: Scientific Visualization Literacy Assessment Test
description: SVLAT is a standardized, psychometrically grounded instrument for measuring how well non-experts read, understand, and interpret scientific visualizations and illustrations. It "consists of 49 items based on 18 scientific visualizations and illustrations, including static images and animations, spanning 8 SciVis techniques and 11 task types." It follows a closed-world design in which each item is intended to be answerable using only the provided visualization and caption. In this article it serves as the benchmark for evaluating MLLM SciVis literacy, with a human baseline established via an online tryout with 485 non-expert participants.
requirements: Items are answered under a closed-world design using only the provided visualization and caption, limiting reliance on external knowledge.
constraints: Some tasks are represented by only one or two items, which limits the reliability of per-task estimates.
target_learners: non-expert adults (human baseline participants ages 18-65)
target_learning_goals: reading, understanding, and interpreting scientific visualizations and illustrations
examples: Used to benchmark three closed-source and three open-source MLLMs against a human baseline of 485 participants.
key_sources: Patrick Phuoc Do, Chau M. Ta, Chaoli Wang. (2026). Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Scientific Visualization Literacy. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15176

article_title: Informal Learning Emerges in Everyday Human-LLM Interaction
citation: Chen, Z., Li, H., Xiao, Z., Qu, H., & Xie, X. (2026). Informal learning emerges in everyday human–LLM interaction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17643
title: Turn-level behavioural signatures of informal learning: ICAP engagement depth and scaffolding translated into role-specific labels for naturalistic human–LLM logs
description: The article translates learning-science constructs into role-specific, turn-level behavioural signatures for naturalistic logs: user turns are coded by engagement depth (passive, active, constructive, drawing on the ICAP framework), and assistant turns by whether they deliver requested content or provide scaffolded support, further characterized by support intent (metacognitive, cognitive, affective) and support form (feedback, hinting, instructing, explaining, modelling, questioning). The framework states that "Labels indicate observable learning-oriented participation, not durable learning outcomes or causal instructional effects." It supports analyses of engagement presence, contextual organization and support–engagement coupling at conversation-level, support-form and adjacent-turn scales.
requirements: Requires theory-grounded codebook development, independent human review, prompt calibration and corpus-scale LLM-assisted labelling of turns, as described in the annotation workflow
constraints: Labels are behavioural indicators rather than direct evidence of retention, transfer or skill development
The ICAP interactive category is not used as a turn-level user label because every record is already a human–assistant exchange
target_learners: Adult everyday users of general-purpose LLM assistants in coding and writing tasks
target_learning_goals: Observable learning-oriented participation during everyday task-focused human–LLM problem solving
examples: Applied to 128,569 conversations from WildChat, LMSYS Chat and ShareChat, yielding 491,685 user turns and 489,785 assistant turns coded at three scales
key_sources: Chen, Z., Li, H., Xiao, Z., Qu, H., & Xie, X. (2026). Informal learning emerges in everyday human–LLM interaction. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17643

article_title: Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning
citation: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047
title: MAI-AI: Metacognitive Awareness Inventory for Artificial Intelligence
description: The MAI-AI is an AI-centered adaptation of the shortened Metacognitive Awareness Inventory and the MSLQ, used to assess students' metacognitive awareness of AI-assisted learning. As the article states, "the MAI-AI questionnaire consists of 29 questions (28 in post), divided into 6 constructs": Attitudes towards AI, AI Engagement, AI Literacy, Metacognitive Knowledge of Cognition, Metacognitive Regulation of Cognition, and Autonomy & Control. All questions use a five-point Likert scale with subscale averages as scores ranging from 1 to 5. It was administered at pre-test, post-test, and five-week follow-up.
requirements: Administered as repeated self-report; the article notes the instrument is still awaiting validation.
constraints: The article notes self-report limitations including social desirability bias and possible familiarity effects from repeated exposure to the same instrument.
target_learners: first-year university engineering students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness of AI-assisted learning (knowledge and regulation of cognition)
examples: Used at three time points (T0, T1, T5) in the quasi-experiment with 126 students.
key_sources: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047

article_title: Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning
citation: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047
title: Structured experiential exercise cycle: GenAI-assisted task, distraction, then unaided transfer task
description: Each experiential exercise in the intervention followed a three-step cycle: "(1) participants perform a task with the help of a GenAI system (approx. 5-10 min), (2) afterwards, participants performs a distraction task, on an unrelated topic (approx. 5 min), (3) finally participant perform a similar task related to the initial one, this time without the help of any GenAI systems (approx. 10 min)." The intervention paired two productive exercises (generation effect, Socratic questioning) with two unproductive ones (solution bypass, passive summary) so students directly experienced consequences of productive and unproductive GenAI use. Each exercise specified the task, the form of GenAI interaction, and a built-in reflection step.
requirements: Students receive condensed direct instruction before each exercise; the exercise specifies the task, the form of GenAI interaction, and a built-in reflection step.
constraints: The article describes this as structured and scaffolded practice providing the guidance novice learners require, not minimally guided discovery.
target_learners: first-year university engineering students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness of productive and unproductive GenAI collaboration patterns
examples: Productive Exercise 1, 'The Generation Effect Activator', had students write a summary unaided, revise it from GenAI feedback, then apply concepts to novel scenarios after a distraction task.
key_sources: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047

article_title: Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning
citation: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047
title: Prioritize hands-on experiential activities over lecture-based instruction when cultivating metacognitive awareness of AI-assisted learning
description: The article advises that "Practitioners are thus advised to primarily rely on experiential and hands-on approaches for cultivating metacognitive awareness in AI-assisted learning." Experiential instruction produced larger immediate gains in knowledge of cognition and engagement, and although instructional approaches eventually reached comparable levels, that convergence took weeks to unfold. The principle holds that hands-on experience of productive and unproductive GenAI use builds strategy knowledge faster than lecture while also supporting slower-developing regulatory behaviour.
requirements: Experiential sessions must be matched on total instruction time with lecture alternatives so differences reflect the mode of learning rather than exposure or time on task.
constraints: Immediate gains in knowledge and engagement were not matched by an immediate rise in regulation of cognition; the authors warn that greater engagement without regulation may itself lead to cognitive offloading.
target_learners: first-year university engineering students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge and regulation of cognition in AI-assisted learning
examples: The study's experiential condition replaced a full lecture with a condensed introduction followed by four structured exercises enacting productive and unproductive GenAI interactions.
key_sources: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047

article_title: Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning
citation: Pau Benazet i Montobbio, Janne Rotter, Davinia Hernández-Leo. (2026). Experiential Versus Instructional Approaches for Eliciting Metacognitive Awareness in AI-Assisted Learning: A Short-Term Longitudinal Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20047
title: Temporal decoupling of metacognitive knowledge and regulation under experiential AI-assisted learning
description: The article proposes that components of metacognitive awareness are not only separable but "can be temporally decoupled under experiential AI-assisted learning": knowledge of cognition rises immediately while regulation of cognition develops later through reflection. Drawing on the experiential learning cycle, it suggests the immediate knowledge gain "may have functioned as the basis that students gradually converted into reflective regulation", making the two gains part of a single developmental process rather than independent outcomes. This account explains why a null immediate result for regulation may mask delayed experiential effects.
requirements: Assessment designs must include delayed follow-up measurements, since relying solely on post-test measurements risks misclassifying regulatory effects that only emerge over time.
constraints: The between-group regulation difference did not reach statistical significance, possibly due to a lack of power, so long-term regulatory advantage warrants future exploration.
target_learners: first-year university engineering students
target_learning_goals: development of metacognitive knowledge and regulation of cognition in AI-assisted learning
examples: In the study, the experiential group's MKC gain appeared at post-test while its MRC gain emerged only at the five-week follow-up.

article_title: MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education
citation: Qian Wu, Xinrong Zhou, Zizhan Ma, Kai Chen, Zheyao Gao, Xun Lin, Hongqiu Wu, Longfei Gou, Yixiao Liu, Ann Sin Nga Lau, Qi Dou. (2026). MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21570
title: MedGame dual-engine framework: Medical Narrative Designer plus Story Director for case-to-game transformation
description: MedGame is a generative framework that transforms static clinical cases into structured, executable storytelling games. It "adopts a dual-engine architecture that decouples clinical narrative ideation from technical orchestration": a Medical Narrative Designer synthesizes raw patient summaries into a hierarchical Clinical Storyline with Acts, Scenes, and Decision Nodes, and a Story Director maps that storyline into a directed acyclic graph of multimodal generation primitives for rendering. The storyline serves as the interface between the two engines.
requirements: Generated storylines must be faithful to the source case, expose meaningful decision checkpoints, remain medically plausible, and stay machine-executable (enforced via a Pydantic schema and medical rubrics).
constraints: The linear storyline formulation is motivated by the deterministic source case format, not by an assumption that clinical reasoning itself is linear; branching story graphs are discussed as an extension.
target_learners: medical students
residents
physicians
target_learning_goals: case-based clinical reasoning
diagnostic and therapeutic decision-making
examples: A 15-year-old boy's ER case was adapted into a storyline with Acts such as 'A Bloody Alarm' and Scenes for laboratory and imaging decisions, with decision nodes asking which diagnostic tests to order.
key_sources: Qian Wu, Xinrong Zhou, Zizhan Ma, Kai Chen, Zheyao Gao, Xun Lin, Hongqiu Wu, Longfei Gou, Yixiao Liu, Ann Sin Nga Lau, Qi Dou. (2026). MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21570
