citation: Qian Wu, Xinrong Zhou, Zizhan Ma, Kai Chen, Zheyao Gao, Xun Lin, Hongqiu Wu, Longfei Gou, Yixiao Liu, Ann Sin Nga Lau, Qi Dou. (2026). MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21570
title: MedGame Bench: 5,000-case benchmark for Medical Narrative Generation and Story Direction
description: MedGame Bench is a case-grounded benchmark and evaluation protocol built from public patient summaries in the PMC-Patients Dataset. The authors "sample 5,000 cases balanced across eight medical specialties" and partition them into a fixed 4,000/1,000 train–test split. It contains two evaluation tracks aligned with the dual-engine design, scored on structural validity, story adaptation, medical accuracy, educational quality, and task reasonability, with structure checked by rule-based validation and content indicators rated by LLM-as-a-Judge on a 1–10 scale.
requirements: Evaluation uses automated rule-based checking for structure validation and GPT-5.2 LLM-as-a-Judge scoring with rubrics for content-oriented indicators.
constraints: The benchmark is built from PMC-Patients case-report-derived summaries; high-similarity patient variants across the train–test split are tracked and analyzed for related-case effects.
target_learners: medical students
residents
physicians
target_learning_goals: case-based clinical reasoning
medical narrative generation
multimodal orchestration planning
examples: The benchmark samples 5,000 cases across cardiology, endocrinology, gastroenterology, hematology/oncology, nephrology, neurology, respiratory and critical care, and rheumatology, with 625 cases per specialty.

article_title: Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition
citation: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096
title: A taxonomy of 17 cognitively-grounded flashcard interaction types across three learning categories
description: Memdora's central design contribution is a taxonomy of 17 interaction types across three learning categories: Language (6 types), By Heart (1 type with 3 retrieval modes), and Exam (10 types). Each type is paired with a primary cognitive-science citation, e.g. Vocabulary is grounded in "retrieval practice [15]" and Concept in "elaborative interrogation [7]". The taxonomy is built on three principles: "retrieval effort produces retention", "format should match learning goal", and "transparency builds metacognition".
requirements: Each interaction type must be grounded in peer-reviewed cognitive science research with per-type citations and design rationale documented
constraints: The efficacy of these types within Memdora, and in combination with FSRS-6 scheduling, has not been empirically evaluated
target_learners: language learners
students preparing for exams
learners memorizing extended passages verbatim
target_learning_goals: vocabulary and phrase acquisition in a target language
verbatim memorization of extended passages
conceptual understanding and exam preparation
examples: The paper documents all 17 types in Table 1 with interaction descriptions and primary citations, e.g. Cloze: supply missing word in target-language sentence, grounded in Bransford & Johnson [4]
key_sources: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096

article_title: Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition
citation: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096
title: Memdora: cross-platform AI spaced repetition system with single-gesture capture and FSRS-6 scheduling
description: Memdora is a cross-platform SRS deployed on iOS, Android, Web, and browser extensions for Chrome, Edge, and Firefox. Its capture layer offers four modalities including "using the browser extension to highlight text on any web page", collapsing card-creation context-switching cost to near zero. All cards are scheduled with FSRS-6, which "maintains per-card estimates of memory stability (S) and retrievability (R)" and runs client-side on mobile for offline scheduling.
requirements: A large language model generation pipeline with structured output prompting and content-type classification routing items to appropriate interaction types
constraints: The AI generation pipeline may produce cards of variable quality in highly specialized domains
target_learners: language learners reviewing during commutes
readers capturing content from web pages
target_learning_goals: long-term retention through spaced retrieval practice
examples: The browser extension supports in-context vocabulary recall: hovering over a word already in the user's deck displays the card with its current FSRS-6 retention percentage without opening the application
key_sources: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096

article_title: Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition
citation: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096
title: Collaborative deck layer with live synchronization and independent per-follower scheduling
description: Memdora's collaborative layer lets users publish decks publicly, to friends, or privately; published decks appear in a Discover feed where users follow them. When the deck owner adds, edits, or removes a card, "all followers' copies update instantly—no re-follow required", while "each follower maintains independent FSRS-6 scheduling state, learning at their own pace". The infrastructure uses a publish-subscribe model with server-side scheduling state.
requirements: A publish-subscribe infrastructure with each follower maintaining independent scheduling state server-side
constraints: The collaborative deck features have not yet been evaluated in a formal educational setting; deployment may reveal unmet needs around teacher workflows and institutional authentication
target_learners: students following a teacher's shared deck
community deck followers
target_learning_goals: shared vocabulary learning with teacher-curated content
examples: The paper describes classroom use: a teacher publishes a shared vocabulary deck, students follow it, and the teacher can push new cards or corrections that propagate to all students automatically
key_sources: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096

article_title: Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition
citation: Ruiyang Zhang. (2027). Memdora: Designing Cognitively-Grounded Flashcard Interactions for AI-Powered Spaced Repetition. Proceedings of ACM International Conference on Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI '27). https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25096
title: Effort-based behavioral reward system incentivizing cognitive engagement rather than app presence
description: Memdora rewards cognitive effort through two mechanisms: a Study Time Reward granting bonus AI generation credits for "completing 5 continuous minutes of active card review", and a Volume Reward for reviewing 100 cards in a day. A Streak System tracks consecutive days of actual card review rather than app opening, providing continuity motivation through loss aversion. This contrasts with presence-based rewards the paper says produce superficial engagement.
requirements: Rewards must be tied to actual card review (5 continuous minutes of study, 100 cards per day) rather than mere app interaction
constraints: The effort-based reward system has not been evaluated; a future study is planned comparing learning depth metrics between effort-rewarded and presence-rewarded conditions
target_learners: daily SRS users needing engagement continuity
target_learning_goals: sustained daily retrieval practice
examples: Users earn AI generation credits for completing 5 continuous minutes of study and for reviewing 100 cards per day

title: By Heart single card type with three self-selectable retrieval modes of varying difficulty
description: For verbatim memorization of extended passages, By Heart presents one card type with three user-selectable retrieval modes: Strip Peek (all lines hidden, tap to reveal for 2 seconds, highest effort), Step Through (past lines dimmed, current line bold), and First Word (opening word only as cue, lowest effort). The modes are "three points on the cue-target continuum identified in retrieval practice research", and self-selection per session operationalizes desirable difficulties within a practical UI.
requirements: Displaying all three options simultaneously so the difficulty spectrum is explicit, supporting learner agency over difficulty selection
constraints: Claimed as the first SRS system to operationalize self-selected difficulty for extended passage memorization, to the authors' knowledge
target_learners: learners memorizing poems, scripts, or extended passages verbatim
target_learning_goals: verbatim memorization of extended passages
examples: The three modes are demonstrated on the same poem (Dylan Thomas, The Force That Through the Green Fuse), with difficulty increasing from First Word to Strip Peek

title: Make algorithmic memory predictions visible to build learner metacognition and trust
description: Memdora displays each card's current FSRS-6 retention percentage during review and per-card retention estimates alongside next review dates in the deck browser, "enabling learners to identify their weakest cards at a glance". The design principle is that "transparency builds metacognition: making algorithmic memory predictions visible promotes learner trust and self-regulation", responding to SmartFlash's finding that transparency in AI educational systems is essential for learner acceptance.
requirements: A scheduling algorithm that computes per-card retention estimates, displayed during review and in the deck browser
target_learners: SRS learners reviewing scheduled cards
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness of one's own memory state
examples: Every card displays the current retention percentage computed by FSRS-6 in the top-right corner during review

article_title: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for Multi-Lecture Educational Reasoning
citation: Sahil Al Farib, Momota Ahsana Meem, Sheikh Redwanul Islam, and Md. Tanvir Raihan. (2026). Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for Multi-Lecture Educational Reasoning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03161
title: Evidence-grounded multimodal lecture-to-KG pipeline
description: An end-to-end pipeline combining "timestamped automatic speech recognition (ASR), high-recall anchor selection, OCR, grounded vision-language extraction, validation, canonicalization, KG construction, and GraphRAG-style retrieval." Its design constraint is that "a concept or relationship is promoted only when tied to lecture evidence." Unlike slide- or transcript-only educational KG pipelines, it treats video frames, OCR output, and transcript segments as three simultaneous evidence sources for the same anchor, capturing diagram- and equation-only content. The output is a NetworkX MultiDiGraph whose edges carry relation type, lecture, timestamp, anchor, evidence quotation, and confidence.
requirements: Every mention must cite transcript, OCR, or visual evidence before entering the graph; extraction is constrained to a fixed education-oriented relation vocabulary of eight permitted types
constraints: Validation improves auditability but does not by itself guarantee factual correctness; the evaluation covers only three lectures from one series
target_learners: instructors and learners using lecture-video question answering in neural-network coursework
target_learning_goals: answering lecture questions about concepts, prerequisites, and cross-lecture relationships in instructional video
examples: On three 3Blue1Brown lectures the pipeline processed 3,118 frames, 756 transcript segments, and 559 anchors, producing 172 canonical concepts and 282 relationships
key_sources: Sahil Al Farib, Momota Ahsana Meem, Sheikh Redwanul Islam, and Md. Tanvir Raihan. (2026). Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for Multi-Lecture Educational Reasoning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03161

article_title: Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for Multi-Lecture Educational Reasoning
citation: Sahil Al Farib, Momota Ahsana Meem, Sheikh Redwanul Islam, and Md. Tanvir Raihan. (2026). Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for Multi-Lecture Educational Reasoning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03161
title: Evidence-grounding extraction schema for auditable educational knowledge graphs
description: The paper's organizing framework is an extraction schema in which every extracted item retains "evidence, confidence, modality, lecture, timestamp, frame, and anchor identifiers." A concept records name, definition, evidence quotation, source modality, and confidence; a relationship records source, target, one of eight permitted types, evidence quotation, modality, and confidence. The authors argue such auditability matters in education because unsupported claims can mislead learners and instructors need to inspect or correct extracted knowledge. Each retained mention records its full provenance, reducing the risk of a structurally plausible but unsupported VLM-generated graph.
requirements: Transcript- and OCR-sourced claims must occur in the evidence pool; visual-only concepts require stronger confidence; confidence below 0.55 is removed
constraints: The authors state validation improves auditability but does not by itself guarantee factual correctness
target_learners: instructors inspecting or correcting automatically extracted course knowledge
target_learning_goals: trustworthy, traceable lecture question answering over multi-lecture course content
examples: Each edge in the constructed graph records endpoints, type, and supporting evidence, so answers can be traced to a specific transcript span, OCR string, or frame
key_sources: Sahil Al Farib, Momota Ahsana Meem, Sheikh Redwanul Islam, and Md. Tanvir Raihan. (2026). Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Knowledge Graph Construction for Multi-Lecture Educational Reasoning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03161

article_title: Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation
citation: Jean-Pierre Briot. (2026). Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05176
title: Two approaches to AI in music: autonomous generators versus interactive composition assistants, with distinct educational significance
description: The article distinguishes two philosophies of AI in music. Autonomous generators such as Suno and Udio produce complete pieces from a text prompt, while composition assistants such as FlowComposer and the Continuator support the human creator interactively. The article argues the distinction matters enormously for education: the former positions students as consumers of AI output, while the latter positions AI as an extension of the student's own creative agency. It also notes a fundamental audio-versus-symbolic divide, with symbolic representations being interpretable, controllable, and educationally meaningful.
requirements: Systems in the assistant lineage must allow the composer to retain full intentionality and control over the compositional refinement process
constraints: Autonomous generators are described as end-to-end, requiring complete regeneration for any structural modification, with no lever for intervention at the compositional level
target_learners: music students in higher education and conservatory settings
target_learning_goals: creative music-making with AI tools
critical evaluation of AI music systems
examples: FlowComposer was validated in the creation of the album Hello World in 2018, subordinated throughout to the artistic vision of professional musicians; the Continuator learned a player's style and continued in that style at performance time
key_sources: Jean-Pierre Briot. (2026). Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05176

article_title: Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation
citation: Jean-Pierre Briot. (2026). Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05176
title: FlowComposer and the Continuator: interactive AI composition assistants
description: Two landmark composition assistants developed by François Pachet and collaborators at Sony CSL-Paris. FlowComposer is a score-centered assistant within the ERC Flow Machines project in which the musician can interactively write and edit a score and solicit melodic or harmonic sketches from a chosen stylistic corpus, with constraints imposed on generation. The Continuator operates at performance time, learning the style of a player from what they have just played and immediately continuing in that style, supporting real-time improvisation. Experiments with professional musicians and with children showed strong engagement, surprise, and a heightened sense of musical agency.
requirements: The composer must retain full intentionality and control over the compositional refinement process and structural and aesthetic decisions
constraints: Both systems are based on Markov models rather than current deep learning models, which the article notes are lighter and easier to integrate with constraints
target_learners: music students
professional musicians
children in creative music-making contexts
target_learning_goals: interactive composition
improvisation
reflective musical creativity
examples: FlowComposer was used in creating the album Hello World in 2018; the Continuator generated strong engagement and heightened musical agency in experiments with professional musicians and children
key_sources: Jean-Pierre Briot. (2026). Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05176

article_title: Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation
citation: Jean-Pierre Briot. (2026). Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05176
title: The paradox of creators: digital diffusion and value dilution in the dematerialized music economy
description: Drawing on François Pachet, the article argues that dematerialization of the musical artifact is really a dematerialization of scarcity: the transition from physical to digital artifacts implies a transition from uniqueness and rarity to ubiquity and value dilution. Digital technologies give creators unprecedented reach while structurally destroying the economic value of the content they distribute — better diffusion and lower value are two sides of a same coin. Generative AI deepens this paradox by flooding distribution channels with machine-produced content at near-zero marginal cost.
requirements: Music education must equip students both to reach audiences widely and to develop artistic distinctiveness and economic literacy to sustain a creative life amid hyperabundance
constraints: The article notes diversification is a survival strategy for individuals, not a fix for industry economics, and works better for musicians with time, digital literacy, and existing audience
target_learners: music students preparing for professional careers
target_learning_goals: economic literacy for creative careers
artistic distinctiveness in a saturated market
examples: The article notes a track can accumulate millions of plays while its creator earns less than the price of a coffee, and that over 100,000 new tracks are added to Spotify each day
key_sources: Jean-Pierre Briot. (2026). Challenges for Musical Education in the Age of AI and Digital Transformation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05176

article_title: A multi-agent AI classroom based on dual-process reasoning hazards: a pilot with prospective physics teachers
citation: Eugenio Tufino. (2026). A multi-agent AI classroom based on dual-process reasoning hazards: a pilot with prospective physics teachers. https://huggingface.co/spaces
title: Five-agent DPT simulated classroom on a static-friction problem
description: A simulated class of five AI students, each embodying a distinct point of failure in the reasoning process: Davide (Hazards A+B), Elena (Hazard C), Tommaso (Hazard D), Chiara (in transition) and Andrea (a near-expert peer). It runs on an LLM via a Gradio application on Hugging Face Spaces, with personas defined entirely in the system prompt, session reset and one-click export of the anonymised conversation log. Named agents respond, with roughly 30% probability a second agent intervenes, and an open question draws two to four responses.
requirements: Requires a valid API key from a supported LLM provider, supplied by the user; no specialised infrastructure or model training is needed.
constraints: The hazards are reified into stable characters — a deliberate pedagogical simplification the framework itself warns against.
Participants noted the environment's limits as a proxy for real classrooms: "real students do not ask all those questions".
target_learners: prospective physics teachers in MSc programs
target_learning_goals: responding in real time to student reasoning with differentiated questioning strategies
examples: In one opening exchange, within three turns the participant elicited Davide's intuitive rule and set up a conflict with the observed situation.
key_sources: Eugenio Tufino. (2026). A multi-agent AI classroom based on dual-process reasoning hazards: a pilot with prospective physics teachers. https://huggingface.co/spaces

article_title: A multi-agent AI classroom based on dual-process reasoning hazards: a pilot with prospective physics teachers
citation: Eugenio Tufino. (2026). A multi-agent AI classroom based on dual-process reasoning hazards: a pilot with prospective physics teachers. https://huggingface.co/spaces
title: Dual-process reasoning hazards framework with hazard-matched questioning strategies
description: Dual-process theories describe reasoning as the interplay of a fast, automatic Process 1 producing a provisional mental model and a slow, effortful Process 2 that evaluates it. Physics education research maps four hazards along the reasoning path: intuition may supply an incorrect first model (A); a confident reasoner may accept it without scrutiny (B); analysis may be biased towards rationalising the initial answer (C); or the mindware may be insufficient to detect the error (D). The course matched each hazard to a questioning strategy from the ISLE framework: guiding questions for A and B, conflict between formula and known result for C, and falling-back questions for D.
requirements: Each hazard was explicitly matched to a strategy in the lesson preceding the simulation.
constraints: Hazards are failure points of a process, not student types; reifying them as stable characters is a simplification.
target_learners: prospective physics teachers
secondary-school physics students whose reasoning the teachers diagnose
target_learning_goals: diagnosing student reasoning hazards
selecting questions matched to the hazard
examples: Lesson 1 used the block-and-magnet sequence so participants encountered the framework as an explanation of their own reasoning: 93% answered the screening question correctly while the class split 50%–50% on the magnet question.
key_sources: Eugenio Tufino. (2026). A multi-agent AI classroom based on dual-process reasoning hazards: a pilot with prospective physics teachers. https://huggingface.co/spaces

article_title: Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilities
citation: Christopher Ormerod and YoungKoung Kim. (2026). Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10154v1
title: Simulated-respondent framework: fine-tuning an LLM to reproduce option-choice patterns across discretized ability levels so item parameters can be read off the resulting curves
description: The framework bins student ability into L labeled intervals (Table 2, from Foundational to Elite mastery), prompts the LLM to answer as a student of a given ability level with the correct answer supplied, and trains it with an MSE loss on next-token option probabilities against interval-averaged MCM/3PL probabilities. As the abstract states, "By learning to reproduce the systematic error patterns of students across a discrete range of abilities, the LLM implicitly captures the underlying response probabilities encoded in the 3PL and MCM curves", allowing difficulty to be approximated from predicted option probabilities.
requirements: A calibrated dataset of responses with independently derived student ability levels, and IRT-fitted 3PL/MCM target curves per item
constraints: Each mapping arrow in the pipeline introduces approximation error, so reported correlations are best read as lower bounds
LoRA was applied only to Gated Attention components, adapting roughly a quarter of the layers a conventional transformer would expose
target_learners: students at discretized ability levels answering multiple-choice mathematics items
target_learning_goals: item difficulty estimation for assessment design and test form assembly
examples: The framework was applied to 4,848 mathematics items generated from 970 item models, with stimuli and options allowed to carry image components combined into a single image
key_sources: Christopher Ormerod and YoungKoung Kim. (2026). Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10154

article_title: Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilities
citation: Christopher Ormerod and YoungKoung Kim. (2026). Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10154v1
title: Multimodal mathematics item-response corpus: 970 item models, 4,848 items, 13.88 million responses
description: The study's dataset consists of multiple-choice mathematics items, each with a stimulus and four options where stimulus and options may include image components combined into one image, generated from item models specifying structure, content and variable features. The article reports "There were a total of 970 item models and a total of 4,848 items" and "There are 13.88 million responses", split into train, development and test sets by item model to avoid conflation, with approximately 2860 responses per item on average.
requirements: Responses tied to independently derived ability levels from a larger calibrated dataset of items
constraints: Items were split by item model rather than at random, to avoid conflation between related generated items
target_learners: students responding to large-scale mathematics assessment items
target_learning_goals: item parameter estimation and difficulty calibration for assessment development
examples: Table 1 splits items into 727 item models / 3633 items for training, 97 / 485 for development, and 146 / 730 for test

article_title: An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria
citation: Nwogo, E. U., Ihianle, I. K., Machado, P., Bird, J. J., Lotfi, A., Shuaib, A. A., Akinwumi, I. I., & Oluranti, J. (2026). An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15738
title: Curated Nigerian Pidgin English corpus of 416,343 text entries scraped from BBC Pidgin and Prime9ja, publicly released for fine-tuning and evaluation
description: A web-scraped corpus of Nigerian Pidgin English built from publicly accessible news platforms including BBC Pidgin and Prime9ja, cleaned through lowercasing, deduplication and normalisation, and formatted into instruction-style conversational pairs. The authors state "the final dataset comprises 416,343 high-quality Nigerian Pidgin English text entries spanning news reporting, commentary, and informal discourse". It was used to fine-tune the platform's Pidgin-aware LLM and released publicly via Zenodo and Hugging Face.
requirements: Responsible scraping practices as described: public content only, exclusion of user-restricted pages, and request rate-limiting
constraints: Sourced from informal news reporting and commentary, encompassing narrative, conversational, and domain-specific expressions rather than curated pedagogical text
target_learners: Nigerian learners in multilingual, low-resource educational contexts
target_learning_goals: Linguistic alignment of AI-generated instructional content in Nigerian Pidgin English
examples: The corpus was tokenised with AutoTokenizer and used to fine-tune a LLaMA-based instruction model via LoRA

article_title: An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria
citation: Nwogo, E. U., Ihianle, I. K., Machado, P., Bird, J. J., Lotfi, A., Shuaib, A. A., Akinwumi, I. I., & Oluranti, J. (2026). An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15738
title: AI-enhanced personalised and adaptive learning platform: layered architecture integrating fine-tuned Pidgin-aware LLM, RAG, bilingual translation engine, and rule-based adaptive assessment
description: A modular, layered educational platform (presentation, application, AI services, data, and integration layers) delivering conversational AI, adaptive assessment, and multilingual content delivery. Its chatbot operates in Translate, Ask, and Ask/Translate modes, with web-based retrieval triggered "when the similarity score falls below a 60% threshold". RAG grounds LLM outputs in a vector database (Qdrant) to address static curricula and hallucination-prone generation, and the full implementation is publicly accessible as STEMHub.
requirements: Persistent learner data infrastructure (PostgreSQL and Qdrant) and backend APIs hosting the transformer-based language model and RAG components
constraints: Designed for resource-constrained deployment; quantisation trade-offs between semantic fidelity and inference latency constrain model choice
target_learners: Learners and educators in Nigerian multilingual, low-resource educational settings
target_learning_goals: Context-aware learning support, adaptive assessment, and personalised feedback in English and Nigerian Pidgin English
examples: Figures 13 and 14 show the integrated instructional environment with external resources and AI-generated assessments; the fine-tuned model is downloadable from Zenodo and Hugging Face

article_title: An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria
citation: Nwogo, E. U., Ihianle, I. K., Machado, P., Bird, J. J., Lotfi, A., Shuaib, A. A., Akinwumi, I. I., & Oluranti, J. (2026). An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15738
title: Use a transparent rule-based performance-scoring formula combining academic scores with non-cognitive attributes to keep adaptive educational decisions interpretable and accountable
description: The platform computes a final performance score from the academic score A and averaged non-cognitive scores (age, health status, motivation, study time, language proficiency, prior experience) using an explicit formula with a maximum non-cognitive weight of 0.1. The authors state that "by explicitly defining the contribution of each factor, the system avoids the opacity often associated with purely data-driven models, making it suitable for educational environments where accountability is essential". The score then drives personalised content delivery and targeted feedback interventions.
requirements: Explicit definition of each factor's contribution; selected non-cognitive attributes must be collected and maintained in learner profiles
constraints: The article states machine learning-based approaches could be applied, but a rule-based method was adopted for clarity, interpretability, and suitability for educational decision-making; the non-cognitive weight is capped at 0.1
target_learners: Learners in under-resourced educational systems where accountability and transparency in assessment are required
target_learning_goals: Holistic learner assessment beyond academic achievement and adaptive personalised feedback
examples: Two student cases computed with Equation (3): Student 1 (academic 83.75, performance 86.15) received a concise explanation, Student 2 (academic 40.00, performance 42.30) received a more scaffolded one

citation: Jahangir Alam SM, Md Khalid Syfullaha, Saad Ahmed, Munira Akter Mou, A K Z Rasel Rahman, A.K.M. Masudur Rahman, Mohammed Sowket Ali. (2026). title: Answer-level JSON record linking a randomized scan to question, model answer, and rubric criteria with performance-level marking rules
description: Each dataset record is one JSON object paired with one randomized PDF filename. The object stores answer_id, pdf_file, Subject, question, model_answer, and total_marks, plus a variable-length rubrics array whose elements store criterion text, gained_marks, and marking_rules. "The four performance keys areExcellent,Good,Average, andPoor." This structure keeps grading context next to the file reference and supports answer-level loading without joining separate tables.

article_title: Mind the Student: Behavioral and Contextual Cues for Automated Engagement Prediction in Online Learning
citation: Alperen Kantarcı, Visvanathan Ramesh, and Gemma Roig. 2026. Mind the Student: Behavioral and Contextual Cues for Automated Engagement Prediction in Online Learning. ICMI '26, Napoli, Italy. https://doi.org/10.1145/3776574.3832485
title: Multimodal engagement-prediction framework with Perceiver IO fusion, hierarchical Bayesian participant context, and uncertainty-aware heads
description: A computational framework that jointly predicts a continuous engagement score in [1,5] and a binary label from tutoring-video clips. It fuses pretrained encoders (V-JEPA 2 for student and instructor video, CLIP for screen content, AudioMAE for audio) with five explicit behavioral streams — "head pose, CWT head dynamics, facial action units, gaze/head angles, and emotion prediction probabilities" — through a Perceiver IO latent bottleneck. Student and instructor personalities are modeled as variational posteriors over learnable embeddings with partial pooling toward a shared prior, and evidential NIG regression and SNGP classification heads output predictions with explicit epistemic uncertainty.
requirements: Pretrained encoders for video, screen, and audio modalities; personality metadata are optional and masked at test time
A student-independent evaluation split so that training and testing sets contain different students
constraints: The authors state the population prior in the Bayesian context layer is too weakly constrained to prevent the model from fitting student appearance rather than engagement dynamics
Perceiver IO mean-pooling over 64 frames suppresses within-clip fluctuations because each clip receives a single label
target_learners: students in online tutoring sessions
target_learning_goals: automated prediction of student engagement level from behavioral and contextual cues
examples: The framework was entered in the CASED challenge, where it achieved competitive regression performance (RMSE 0.68, matching the best methods) while producing calibrated epistemic uncertainty estimates at inference time

citation: Changgen Li, Han Hu, Christy Dunlap, Nathaniel House, and Jonathan Wai. (2025). Giving Mechanical Engineers Intelligent Tools: A Project-Based AI Education Curriculum in Thermal Engineering. https://github.com/hanhuark/machine-learning-for-engineers
title: MLME: an open-access, project-based AI curriculum for thermal engineering totaling 39.1 hours with four core projects and three optional projects
description: The Machine Learning for Mechanical Engineers (MLME) course at UARK integrates AI into thermal engineering for ME students, distinct from computer-science AI courses by focusing on selection and implementation of AI algorithms for thermal problems. The article states the course is "organized into a timeline format ... totaling 39.1 hours, and covers various topics such as linear regression, multilayer perceptron (MLP), convolutional neural networks (CNN), and time series analysis." Four assignment projects cover heat flux prediction (MLP, GPR), pre-/post-CHF image classification (CNN), unsupervised PCA/SVD clustering, and RNN time-series prediction of vapor fraction; three extra projects and student-proposed projects serve as final-exam options. Syllabus, data, and code are released in open-access repositories.

target_learners: mechanical engineering undergraduate and graduate students
target_learning_goals: develop, train, and test ML models using Python (TensorFlow) and MATLAB
apply ML to thermal engineering problems such as boiling monitoring, diagnosis, and prediction
NACE professional competencies including critical thinking, communication, teamwork, technology, leadership, and professionalism
examples: Project 2 requires students to train CNNs to classify pre-CHF and post-CHF boiling images and report confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, ROC, and AUC
Project 4 requires an RNN to forecast vapor fraction of future frames from past frames, varying input and output sequence lengths

The levels are, from the base: curiosity and self-motivation as the foundational attitude; foundational STEM knowledge provided just-in-time within each project; an introduction level teaching core ML theories and techniques; an application level practicing algorithms on publicly available datasets; and an advanced level covering thermal theory topics and the four integrative projects.

title: Math with Matt: an LLM-enhanced algebra ITS with a mindful pedagogical agent
description: Math with Matt is an ITS for linear systems of equations built in CTAT, offering three math units (substitution, elimination, equalization) with three-level hints and immediate feedback, plus mindfulness components: an LLM-based mindful chat (GPT-4o-mini), a 60-second guided breathing exercise, and mindful hint/feedback language. article_title: Mechanics Cognitive Diagnostic: Testing Fine-Grained Learning Objectives in Introductory Physics
citation: Vy Le, Jayson M. Nissen, Jason W. Morphew, Hua Hua Chang, and Ben Van Dusen. (2026). Mechanics Cognitive Diagnostic: Testing Fine-Grained Learning Objectives in Introductory Physics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.09584
title: MCD-v2: a cognitive diagnostic computerized adaptive test reporting mastery of 14 fine-grained learning objectives in introductory mechanics
description: MCD-v2 is "a cognitive diagnostic computerized adaptive test that reports students' mastery of fine-grained learning objectives (LOs) throughout instruction." It was built with evidence-centered design: the authors "defined 14 LOs from introductory mechanics textbooks and AP Physics standards, mapped FCI, FMCE, and EMCS items onto them with a Q-matrix." Unlike fixed-length pretest-posttest RBAs, it is designed to be administered adaptively during a semester, giving instructors and students LO-level mastery feedback during instruction rather than after a course ends. The item bank reuses assessments physics courses already administer, delivered through the LASSO platform.

Response data large enough to stabilize DINA parameter estimates, gathered through the LASSO platform
constraints: The current bank covers only 14 of the 35 planned LOs and lacks items for rotational mechanics and mathematical reasoning
Establishing measurement invariance across administrations is required before interpreting change in LO mastery over time

target_learning_goals: 14 mechanics learning objectives spanning vectors, kinematics, Newton's laws, energy, and momentum

title: Evidence-centered design as the framework linking MCD learning objectives to observable response evidence
description: The article frames MCD development within evidence-centered design (ECD), in which "the student models specify the knowledge an assessment makes claims about, and the evidence models specify the link between observed responses and those claims." ECD comprises five models (student, evidence, task, assembly, and delivery); this paper focuses on the student models (the 14 LOs) and evidence models (the Q-matrix and DINA model). The authors treat DINA fit and classification accuracy as validity evidence for the student models, testing whether the LOs defined a priori are measurable and separable in student responses.

title: Multidimensional evaluation framework separating reference-answer similarity, structured-output stability, and domain-specific correctness
description: The article proposes an evaluation framework for educational question-answering models that combines automatic text metrics with structured-output features and bootstrap confidence intervals. ROUGE-1/2/L measure lexical overlap, BERTScore-F1 measures semantic proximity, and has_solution/has_method/has_teaching_points coverage rates measure conformity to the pedagogical template. The framework's central boundary condition is that "ROUGE and BERTScore primarily capture lexical and semantic proximity, while the structured-output metrics measure template stability" — none can certify formula accuracy, derivational rigor, or instructional usefulness, which require expert assessment or task-specific rubrics.
requirements: A held-out test set of course questions with structured reference answers
Expert assessment or task-specific rubrics for evaluating domain-specific correctness
constraints: Metrics do not directly establish improvements in domain-specific reasoning or mathematical correctness
No bootstrap confidence interval was calculated for BERTScore-F1 because per-sample values were not retained
target_learners: upper-level undergraduate automation and electrical engineering students
target_learning_goals: evaluating course-specific question-answering models for instructional use
examples: The framework used paired bootstrap resampling with B=10,000 iterations to compute 95% confidence intervals for ROUGE and structured-output gains

description: The article frames LLM-assisted VR instruction as a mediation process connecting three layers: expert expression, executable operations, and learner-facing representations. Technical executability alone is insufficient because generated actions must remain inspectable and controllable by the instructor.

title: MUSE: a 12-task benchmark of artistic image understanding for situated education
description: MUSE is a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models on artistic image understanding in image-based language learning and educational interaction. It contains "2,400 questions over 1,174 images" at 1920×1080 resolution, spanning 12 tasks across five capability dimensions: visual perception, semantic understanding, affective interpretation, compositional reasoning, and cultural understanding. article_title: Designing Against Deskilling: Metacognitive Feedback Reduces Cognitive Offloading to LLM Assistants
citation: Sebastian Maier, Kai Schwabe, Manuel Schneider, and Stefan Feuerriegel. (2026). Designing Against Deskilling: Metacognitive Feedback Reduces Cognitive Offloading to LLM Assistants. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20143
title: Cognitive offloading paradigm extended to LLM-assisted learning, distinguishing answer offloading from instrumental help
description: The article extends the cognitive offloading paradigm to LLM-assisted learning by focusing on users' decisions about how much of a task to solve themselves versus hand over to the assistant. It defines cognitive offloading as "using actions or external tools to change a task's processing requirements and reduce cognitive demand" and coins "answer offloading" for requesting the complete solution, which removes the effortful processing on which durable learning depends, in contrast to instrumental help such as asking how to approach a problem, which leaves practice intact. The amount of help requested is treated as an offloading decision shaped by effort, incentives, confidence, and metacognitive monitoring.
requirements: The assistant must leave the offloading decision to the learner; in the study the LLM provided guidance by default and complete answers only on explicit request, so offloading reflected an active, deliberate choice.
constraints: The article notes offloading is not harmful per se; whether reduced cognitive effort helps or harms skill development depends on what is offloaded relative to the skill being developed.
target_learners: Adult online participants practicing fraction arithmetic (aged 18-80)
target_learning_goals: Fraction arithmetic procedure skill; regulating how much cognitive work to delegate to an LLM assistant
examples: In the study, requesting the complete answer reduced the reward to 1 point while any number of guidance requests preserved the full 10 points, operationalizing the distinction between answer offloading and guided help.

article_title: Designing Against Deskilling: Metacognitive Feedback Reduces Cognitive Offloading to LLM Assistants
citation: Sebastian Maier, Kai Schwabe, Manuel Schneider, and Stefan Feuerriegel. (2026). Designing Against Deskilling: Metacognitive Feedback Reduces Cognitive Offloading to LLM Assistants. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20143
title: Custom LLM practice platform with validated offloading classifier for extent-of-support labeling
description: The article built a custom web platform (React frontend, Python backend, PostgreSQL) giving full experimental control and logging of a fraction-arithmetic learning session with an LLM assistant built on GPT-OSS-120B accessed via Amazon Bedrock at temperature 0. A custom LLM-based offloading classifier, combined with a rule-based numerical check, labeled the highest level of support requested per item across four levels: no AI use, guided help, intermediate result, and complete answer. Validation showed that on a held-out set of 198 dialogues "the classifier agreed with the intended labels in every case, yielding no confirmed classification error."
requirements: The system prompt was iteratively validated against a fixed evaluation set of 55 synthetic participant messages until no unrequested solution was given, no requested answer was withheld, and every stated number was correct; the configuration was frozen before data collection.
constraints: The classifier was developed on 198 synthetic tutoring dialogues and frozen before launch; evaluation is reported only on a separate held-out set of 198 dialogues.
target_learners: Adult online participants practicing fraction arithmetic
target_learning_goals: Measuring and incentivizing the extent of LLM assistance requested during practice
examples: The classifier's four-level labels determined reward points in the reward conditions and operationalized the answer-offloading outcome.

article_title: LLMersion: A Local-First AI Agent Framework for Low-Cost Home Language Learning toward Educational Equity
citation: Guo, Q., Tang, J., Huang, X., Lin, H.-Y., Zhong, Y., & Zhuang, X. (2026). LLMersion: A Local-First AI Agent Framework for Low-Cost Home Language Learning toward Educational Equity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29672
title: Four binding constraints on low-cost, personalized, equitable language education (C1-C4)
description: The article distills its evidence review into four constraints that have bound low-cost, personalized, equitable language education: "C1: the human oral provision is intrinsically expensive"; C2, that technological substitutes presuppose connectivity and recurring payment; C3, that substitute content has been fixed and cannot ingest the learner's own documents; and C4, that capable software has never run on cheap hardware. Each row of its Table 1 taxonomy is an instance of one constraint. The scheme of the paper is built on the claimed dissolution of C4, which it argues makes C2 and C3 unnecessary and bypasses rather than solves C1.
requirements: The constraints are derived from the article's evidence review of learner needs and prior technologies; using the taxonomy requires the published evidence base it assembles.
constraints: The article states C1 is a fact about humans and will not change, while C2 and C3 are design choices and C4 was, until recently, a fact about software.
target_learners: self-directed second-language learners in resource-constrained households
target_learning_goals: second-language listening, reading, speaking, and writing as one bound skill
examples: Table 1 maps eight difficulties of second-language acquisition under resource scarcity onto the four constraints, each with a prior technological answer and its documented limit.

article_title: LLMersion: A Local-First AI Agent Framework for Low-Cost Home Language Learning toward Educational Equity
citation: Guo, Q., Tang, J., Huang, X., Lin, H.-Y., Zhong, Y., & Zhuang, X. (2026). LLMersion: A Local-First AI Agent Framework for Low-Cost Home Language Learning toward Educational Equity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29672
title: Four design principles for a local-first AI language-tutor scheme (P1-P4)
description: The article's scheme is organized as four design principles, each answering one identified constraint: "(P1) a web interface backed entirely by local, free, lowest-hardware-cost models"; (P2) the complete listening-reading-speaking-writing loop "played in the teacher's order"; (P3) the learner's own documents and self-built vocabulary as first-class input rather than a fixed curriculum; and (P4) a codebase that is AI-written, AI-understood, and AI-updated so customization does not require professional engineering. The pattern operates at whole-program grain: the four principles together define how a home language-learning agent is composed and maintained.
requirements: Small open-weight models that fit commodity household hardware, since the scheme stands or falls on whether machines low-cost households own can run the stack.
constraints: The article states the scheme establishes feasibility, not efficacy: whether the software teaches is a separate, measurable question.
target_learners: home learners of English lacking access to oral tutoring, including offline households
target_learning_goals: integrated listening-reading-speaking-writing practice over the learner's own materials
examples: The released reference instance LLMersion-1 implements all four principles, and was itself built and is maintained via the AI-maintained-code workflow of P4.

citation: Guo, Q., Tang, J., Huang, X., Lin, H.-Y., Zhong, Y., & Zhuang, X. (2026). LLMersion: A Local-First AI Agent Framework for Low-Cost Home Language Learning toward Educational Equity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29672
title: LLMersion-1: released open-source local four-skill language-learning prototype with companion Narrator tool
description: LLMersion-1 is a released, open-source reference instance implementing all four principles: a browser interface backed by a local service that turns any document into a synchronized listen-read-speak-write session, plus an optional nightly curation agent. Its modules perform the tutor's roles: read-aloud with sentence-synchronized highlighting and inline translation, segmental pronunciation feedback from a phoneme-level CTC aligner, push-to-talk conversation with grammar-coach correction cards, and writing correction with vocabulary checks. A companion program, LLMersion Narrator, produces narrated MP3s and read-along MP4s. The authors state they "claim no learning outcomes" and provide a designed but not yet administered feedback instrument.
requirements: A one-time model download after which no network is required; commodity hardware with 8-16 GB memory for the full resident component set.
constraints: The article states the prototype remains under active development, the feedback instrument is designed but not yet administered, and free-conversation pronunciation feedback cannot catch a word so mispronounced that the recognizer heard a different word.
target_learners: self-directed second-language learners, exemplified by a Chinese-speaking learner of English, on low-cost home hardware
target_learning_goals: integrated listening, reading, speaking, and writing practice over the learner's own documents and self-built vocabulary
examples: The codebase was written, debugged, and extended in AI-assisted sessions, with substitutable components as plug-in registries and pedagogical behavior in editable prompt files.

title: Synergetic coupled-system model of the science classroom with verification norm, requirement, and materiality
description: The article proposes a coupled-system model in which the student, the generative model, and scientific practice interact as coupled subsystems. As the abstract states, "the classroom verification norm is the order parameter, the teacher-set verification requirement the control parameter, and materiality the boundary condition." The requirement is exogenous and adjustable in graded steps, while the norm emerges from mutually observable verification acts and then constrains individual behavior through the slaving principle, outlasting the requirement that seeded it.
requirements: Materiality in the form of laboratory work, observation, and data collection must keep the classroom system open to reality, treated as structurally necessary
constraints: Synergetic is used as a structured analogy with rules of correspondence; no claim is made that classroom dynamics conform to the equations of laser physics
target_learners: secondary science students
undergraduate science students
target_learning_goals: developing a classroom norm of verifying model output against independent sources
examples: The mechanism runs in a loop of four steps: a requirement prompts verification acts, the acts become visible and are taken up by peers, perceived practice shifts, and the perceived practice then regulates individual acts

EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education, 22(10), em2943. https://doi.org/10.29333/ejmste/19481
title: Tripartite distinction of epistemic authority: warranted dependence, perceived authority, and uncritical deference
description: The article distinguishes three situations of epistemic reliance to give the concept of epistemic authority more careful handling than it usually receives. "Warranted epistemic dependence refers to justified reliance on a source whose claims can be traced, whose errors can be estimated, and whose authority can be contested." Perceived authority arises from surface features such as fluency, immediacy, and apparent certainty, while uncritical deference suspends any demand for justification. Only the third is at odds with the aims of science education; the identified risk is the slide from the second to the third.
requirements: Vigilance is framed as calibrated trust rather than generalized distrust, compatible with the trust teachers and scientific institutions legitimately command
constraints: The risk identified concerns the slide from perceived authority to uncritical deference, not reliance on sources as such
target_learners: secondary science students

target_learning_goals: calibrating trust in AI-generated and scientific sources
understanding epistemic authority in science

article_title: Beyond Automation: AI as a Pedagogical Mediator in Collaborative Learning
citation: Niari, M. (2026). Beyond Automation: AI as a Pedagogical Mediator in Collaborative Learning. Umanistica Digitale, 10(24), 121–142. https://doi.org/10.60923/issn.2532-8816/24266
title: AI as a pedagogical mediator framework for collaborative learning
description: The paper's central framework reconceptualizes AI in collaborative learning not as a tutor, peer, or automated orchestrator but as a pedagogical mediator. It states: "This paper advances a conceptual framework that reconceptualizes AI as a pedagogical mediator in collaborative learning environments." The framework positions AI as "an active participant in the orchestration of interaction, epistemic sense-making, and regulatory processes, without displacing learner or teacher agency." It is grounded in socio-cultural theory, distributed cognition, and connectivist perspectives, and treats mediation as the function through which agency, authority, and responsibility are redistributed across human and non-human actors.
requirements: AI systems must participate in orchestrating interaction, epistemic sense-making, and regulatory processes rather than replacing human agents
constraints: The framework explicitly does not displace learner or teacher agency; it is a conceptual contribution, not an empirically tested system
target_learners: learners in collaborative learning environments
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
shared regulation of learning
epistemic sense-making
examples: The paper contrasts its mediator framing with treating AI as a tutor, peer, or automated orchestrator, and applies the framing to interaction, epistemic agency, and shared regulation in collaborative learning design.

title: Three mediating functions of AI: interactional, epistemic, and regulatory
description: Within the mediator framework, the paper articulates a taxonomy of three mediating functions AI can perform in collaborative learning. As the abstract states, "it articulates key mediating functions of AI, interactional, epistemic, and regulatory, and examines their implications for collaborative learning design." The interactional function concerns shaping interaction among learners, the epistemic function concerns epistemic sense-making, and the regulatory function concerns shared regulatory processes. Each function is examined for its design implications without assigning AI a displacing tutorial role.
requirements: Designers must consider all three functions when integrating AI into collaborative learning environments
constraints: The functions are theorized, not empirically validated in this paper

socially shared regulation

title: Revised AI literacy framework: TIECD dimensions specified into ten AI Literacy Elements (AILEs)
description: The review proposes a revised AI literacy framework that preserves the TIECD areas (Technology, Impact, Ethics, Collaboration, Design) while specifying ten operational AI Literacy Elements under them: Fundamental AI Concepts, Computational Thinking, Data Literacy, Social Reasoning, Creative Imagination, Ethical Awareness, Using AI, Creating with AI, Managing AI, and Designing AI. The authors state it advances existing conceptualizations by "establishing data literacy as a distinct and foundational element" and "reconceptualizing collaboration into three operational elements", positioning it as "a theoretically robust and contextually grounded model for embedding AI literacy into K-12 STEAM education".

article_title: The role of generative AI in facilitating children’s creative thinking and cognitive development: a systematic scoping review
citation: Niu T, Liu H, Pang P, Luo YT and Liu T (2026) The role of generative AI in facilitating children's creative thinking and cognitive development: a systematic scoping review. Front. Psychol. 17:1880052. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1880052
title: Four-modality taxonomy of GenAI used with children: text-based, multi-modal, image-based, and audio/music-based
description: The review organizes the GenAI technologies used across the included studies into four modalities: text-based GenAI (12 studies, mainly LLMs such as ChatGPT 3.5/4, Gemini and Claude), multi-modal text-and-image GenAI (seven studies), image-based text-to-image tools such as Midjourney and DALL-E 2 (four studies), and audio/music-based GenAI (one study). The review states that "Text-based and multi-modal GenAI are the dominant modalities used in the included studies, with image-based GenAI as a secondary focus, and audio/music-based GenAI minimally represented", attributing the distribution to the maturity and accessibility of each modality for K-12 creative learning.
requirements: Studies must apply GenAI (LLMs, image synthesis, or multi-modal tools) to children's creative-thinking outcomes to be classified within this taxonomy
constraints: Audio/music-based GenAI is minimally represented, with only one study, reflecting the relative immaturity of child-appropriate audio tools as the review states
target_learners: school-aged children and young adolescents (core target ages 6–15)
target_learning_goals: creative thinking dimensions including originality, fluency, flexibility, and elaboration
examples: Image-based GenAI is described as decoupling creative intent from technical artistic execution, enabling children with limited fine motor skills to visualize their creative ideas

citation: Niu T, Liu H, Pang P, Luo YT and Liu T (2026) The role of generative AI in facilitating children's creative thinking and cognitive development: a systematic scoping review. Front. Psychol. 17:1880052. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1880052
title: Three intervention forms for GenAI in children's creative learning: workshop-based, classroom-integrated, and comparative interaction designs
description: The review classifies GenAI interventions into recurring forms: workshop-based interventions (nine studies), typically 90-min sessions with 4–10 total sessions over 1–4 months and participatory co-creation of prompts; classroom-based integrated interventions (seven studies) embedded in formal curricula from single 60-min sessions to 10-week programs; and comparative interaction interventions (five studies) completing identical creative tasks with GenAI versus human scaffolding or different modalities. The review reports that "Workshop-based interventions (nine studies) are the most common form across both formal and informal settings, typically consisting of 90-min sessions with 4–10 total sessions delivered over 1–4 months."

constraints: No long-term longitudinal interventions appear in the included studies; comparative interaction interventions have short durations of 5–60 min per task
target_learners: primary and lower-secondary students in formal and informal settings
target_learning_goals: creative ideation, storytelling, visual expression, and creative problem-solving
examples: Examples the review prints include AI-enhanced game-based learning for scientific creativity, digital storytelling projects for language arts, and poetry writing with ChatGPT integrated into CTL frameworks

article_title: Beyond Task Completion: A Theoretical Integration and Framework for Guiding Students' ChatGPT Use for Learning
citation: Øby, E. (2026). Beyond Task Completion: A Theoretical Integration and Framework for Guiding Students’ ChatGPT Use for Learning. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. https://doi.org/10.53761/5apqd333
title: An integrative framework explaining students' ChatGPT use through cognitive load, goal orientation, self-efficacy and task relevance
description: The article develops an explanatory framework for students' ChatGPT use grounded in foundational learning theories. As the abstract states, it draws "on cognitive load theory and goal orientation theory and incorporating self-efficacy and task relevance as mediating constructs", undertaking "a theory-driven synthesis of four perspectives relevant to how students engage with complex academic tasks". The framework clarifies how cognitive demands, motivational orientations, perceived competence and perceived task value shape students' decisions about when and how to rely on generative AI during academic work.

citation: Ortiz-Bonnin, S., & Blahopoulou, J. (2025). Chat or cheat? Academic dishonesty, risk perceptions, and ChatGPT usage in higher education students. Social Psychology of Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11218-025-10080-2
title: Rational Choice Theory account of student ChatGPT usage decisions
description: The article applies Rational Choice Theory (Becker, 1968) to explain students' ChatGPT use: "individuals act to maximize personal utility by assessing the potential benefits and costs of different actions." Students weigh benefits such as saving time, reducing effort, or obtaining better grades against costs including likelihood of detection and severity of institutional sanctions. The article pairs RCT with Perceived Academic Dishonesty, arguing RCT captures rational risk-benefit evaluation while PAD captures ethical and normative considerations, and the study's mediation findings are interpreted as consistent with RCT.

constraints: The article notes the low detectability of ChatGPT-based plagiarism may weaken the deterrent effect of academic sanctions
Cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation of the modeled relationships

target_learning_goals: ethical decision-making about AI tool use in academic work
examples: The study tested RCT-derived hypotheses H1a/H1b (negative risk-usage links) and H3a/H3b (risk as mediator) in a 468-student survey

citation: Martinez-Roig, R., Aragonés-González, M., & Cazorla, M. (2026). Exploring the implementation of the Pepper social robot in formal education: a scoping review. Journal of New Approaches in Educational Research, 15, 22. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44322-026-00072-1
title: Pedagogical mediation as the determining factor in social robots' educational implementation
description: The review's central explanatory account: the educational value of a social robot such as Pepper depends less on its physical presence or multimodal interaction than on the pedagogical conditions surrounding its use. The review concludes that "its contribution depends on instructional design, the purpose of the activity, student profile, technical stability and teacher mediation", positioning the robot as a supportive pedagogical resource rather than a teacher substitute. Benefits are interpreted as products of the relationship between pedagogical objectives, student profile, teacher role and technical conditions of use.

constraints: The review warns against technocentric approaches and against attributing excessive agency to the robot; benefits should not be attributed solely to the robot's presence

target_learning_goals: Motivation and engagement

Curriculum learning in mathematics, language and STEM
examples: The review cites Serholt et al. (2020), where 'trouble and repair' situations in child-robot interaction demonstrated the need for adult intervention to sustain mathematics activities

title: Integrated GDCT–SDT–SPT framework for agentic AI-supported online learning
description: The article proposes an integrated theoretical framework in which Holmberg's Guided Didactic Conversation Theory, Self-Determination Theory, and Social Presence Theory are "viewed not as additive, but as interlinked theoretical approaches". GDCT forms the pedagogical and interactional layer explaining dialogue, guidance, feedback, and responsiveness; SDT explains how psychological needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness) relate to learning motivation; SPT explains how interactivity, information sharing, and collaboration form social presence. The two pathways converge at learner engagement, which relates to perceived learner performance.

UTAUT supplies performance expectancy and effort expectancy; TPB supplies attitude and perceived behavioural control; behavioural intention sits closest to behaviour. The authors argue UTAUT alone is "good at predicting a person's intention but weak at explaining the behaviour", motivating the integration.

title: Six-dimension structural model of ethical generative AI use
description: The article proposes and tests a structural framework in which ethical GenAI use is an integrative behavioral outcome predicted by six theoretically differentiated dimensions: ethical and technical AI literacy, academic integrity and transparency, critical thinking and content verification, self-regulation and academic responsibility, data protection/privacy/risk management, and institutional guidance and ethics education. The endogenous construct "captures whether these principles are translated into responsible academic practice across multiple domains." citation: Selen Galiç, Mathias Tejera, Sebastián Parodi, Markus Hohenwarter, Zsolt Lavicza. (2026). Preservice mathematics teachers' noticing in AI-based simulations: transitions among attending, interpreting, and shaping. ZDM – Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-026-01805-4
title: Teacher Noticing of Rationality Framework (TNRF)
description: The TNRF builds on van Es and Sherin's expanded noticing framework of attending, interpreting, and shaping, and "extends van Es and Sherin's (2021) framework by specifying the object of noticing more precisely as students' mathematical thinking". It operationalises students' thinking through Habermas's theory of rationality as observable behaviours: justifying statements, selecting and using appropriate tools, and communicating with appropriate terminology and representations. Attending targets manifestations of rational behaviour rather than surface correctness; interpreting evaluates the quality of participation in mathematical practices; shaping structures conditions under which rational behaviour becomes visible.
requirements: Requires teachers' professional knowledge and an inquiry stance to interpret behaviours through the rationality lens rather than simple correctness judgments
constraints: The article applies the framework specifically to the equal-sign context, with coding adapted to the construct map of the equal sign (Matthews et al., 2012)
target_learners: Preservice mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: Noticing students' mathematical thinking in the context of the equal sign as equivalence
examples: The study used the TNRF to inform a deductive coding scheme with subcodes under each noticing dimension, applied to reflection papers and chat interactions

title: AI-based simulation environment with virtual student and mentor chatbots built on GPT-4o
description: The environment comprises chatbots for three virtual secondary students (aged 11–12) each embodying a specific equal-sign misconception, paired with a targeted task and a video of the student's solution, plus a virtual mentor chatbot giving feedback on strengths, aspects to improve, and suggestions. "The AI-based simulations were built on OpenAI's GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024)", with personas, aims, recipients, themes and chat structure defined through explicit prompt engineering following Park and Choo (2024). Prototypes were tested by researchers, then piloted with preservice teachers in Austria, inservice teachers in Spanish, and expert educators in Turkish before implementation.
requirements: Prompt engineering defining persona, aim, recipients, themes and chat structure with few-shot examples; iterative pilot testing to address overly elaborate student responses and descriptive rather than actionable mentor feedback
constraints: The article acknowledges the tasks used may have influenced noticing transitions, and that AI-generated responses may be overly verbose, mathematically inaccurate, or epistemically misleading, requiring scrutiny by users

target_learning_goals: Practising eliciting, interpreting, and responding to student thinking about the equal sign; rehearsing questioning strategies with feedback

description: The implementation was organised as a repeating weekly structure in which "each week consisting of four phases". description: The chapter adapts the innovation-economics 'knowledge triangle' to education as the volume's organising framework. It argues that education in this model 'encompasses the entire multi-level system of education', including administration and practice, not only university teaching. article_title: Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning
citation: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237
title: Four-layer model of pedagogical safety for educational RL (structural, progress, behavioral, alignment) with the RHSI severity metric
description: The article formalizes pedagogical safety as four constraint classes: "Structural Safety (C1):Prerequisites are architecturally enforced via action masking", progress safety (C2, windowed mastery gain), behavioral safety (C3, minimum cognitive demand), and alignment safety (C4, engagement coupled to mastery). A policy is pedagogically safe if it simultaneously satisfies C1–C4, with an ε-relaxed weighted-norm version for practice. The Reward Hacking Severity Index quantifies the degree to which a policy simultaneously achieves high return and high violation, bounded in [0,1]. The authors argue via informal propositions that no proper subset of the four constraints implies the full set.
requirements: Constraint thresholds must be calibrated to the specific domain (e.g., εprog from a mastery-only baseline's per-window progress distribution; δmin=0.4 set at the ICAP passive/active boundary)
constraints: C1 is enforced architecturally and excluded from the aggregate violation vector (v1≡0 by convention)
The framework's safety guarantees hold with respect to estimated mastery, not necessarily true mastery
Constraint independence arguments are informal sufficiency arguments rather than formal proofs
target_learners: Learners in intelligent tutoring systems, simulated here as struggling, average, and advanced programming-education profiles
target_learning_goals: Genuine mastery of domain concepts (27 Python concepts) rather than proxy engagement maximization
examples: SmartTutor enforces C1 via action masking and C3 via an action selection module online; C2 and C4 are evaluated as offline safety metrics from session logs
key_sources: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237

article_title: Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning
citation: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237
title: SmartTutor simulated Python tutoring testbed for evaluating pedagogical safety in educational RL
description: SmartTutor is a simulated Python tutoring environment comprising "a knowledge graph of 27 Python concepts (DAG, max depth 7", a student model with per-concept mastery tracking, a neural contextual bandit agent with UCB action selection over a 124-dimensional state representation, an action selection module enforcing C1 and C3 online, and a configurable reward system. Eight pedagogical actions span cognitive demand from d=0.0 (Encourage) to d=1.0 (Challenge), with Encourage producing zero mastery gain but the largest engagement boost (+0.8). Three learner profiles (Struggling, Average, Advanced) vary initial knowledge, gain multiplier, and confusion threshold.
requirements: A knowledge graph of prerequisite relationships, a student mastery model, and a configurable reward system with engagement, mastery, and pedagogical-appropriateness components
constraints: Simulated learners use a heuristic mastery update rather than full BKT inference and do not capture motivation, fatigue, or off-task behavior
The single domain (Python programming) limits generalizability to other subjects and curricula
target_learners: Simulated programming learners (struggling, average, advanced profiles)
target_learning_goals: Mastery of Python programming concepts
examples: Each main condition ran 30 sessions (3 profiles × 10 random seeds × 150 interactions per session), yielding 4,500 interactions per condition and 18,000 total across main conditions
key_sources: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237

article_title: Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning
citation: Oluseyi Olukolaa, Nick Rahimia. (2026). Pedagogical Safety in Educational Reinforcement Learning: Formalizing and Detecting Reward Hacking in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04237
title: Reward design alone may be insufficient to ensure pedagogically aligned behavior in educational RL; pair reward shaping with architectural constraints
description: The article's central design recommendation is that weighted reward combinations do not by themselves prevent reward hacking when a zero-learning, high-engagement action exists; architectural constraints (prerequisite masking plus a minimum cognitive-demand floor) are needed. The abstract states that "reward design alone may be insufficient to ensure pedagogically aligned behavior in educational RL, at least in the simulated environment studied here", and the constrained architecture lowered RHSI from 0.317 to 0.102. The authors' future-work section suggests integrating constraints into the optimization itself as Lagrangian terms in a Constrained MDP, with C3 receiving the highest weight.
requirements: An action space in which cognitive demand per action can be quantified, and the ability to mask actions or filter action selection online
constraints: Demonstrated only in simulation with a single weight configuration for the multi-objective condition; human validation with real learners remains essential before deployment
target_learners: Learners using RL-based intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Genuine mastery gains rather than proxy engagement maximization
examples: SmartTutor Full enforces C1 via action masking and C3 via a demand floor (δmin=0.4) during training, while C2 and C4 are monitored as offline metrics
