article_title: Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling
citation: Hooshyar, D.; Šír, G.; Yang, Y.; Kärkkäinen, T.; Hämäläinen, R.; Krivich, E.; Cukurova, M.; Gašević, D.; Azevedo, R. (2026). Neural-Symbolic Knowledge Tracing: Injecting Educational Knowledge into Deep Learning for Responsible Learner Modelling. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08263
title: Responsible-DKT: a neural-symbolic deep knowledge tracing framework injecting symbolic educational knowledge into sequential neural architectures
description: Responsible-DKT is a neural-symbolic variant of DKT that unifies symbolic inputs, learnable embeddings, recurrent dynamics, output prediction, and pedagogical rules in a single differentiable logic program built with Lifted Relational Neural Networks. The article states it "is a neural-symbolic variant of DKT that injects symbolic educational knowledge into sequential neural architectures". Rules such as mastered and not_mastered modulate rather than override neural predictions, and the grounded computation graph supports local and global explanations. RNNs are used as a proof-of-concept, with the approach applicable to other architectures such as Transformers.
requirements: Symbolic educational knowledge (e.g., mastery and non-mastery rules) supplied by educators or domain experts for injection into the model
Interaction logs structured as ordered per-student sequences of skill, quiz, and correctness tuples

title: PyNeuraLogic framework for lifted relational neural-symbolic learning
description: PyNeuraLogic implements the Lifted Relational Neural Networks paradigm, expressing data as logical predicates and model architectures as parameterized weighted logical rule templates that are grounded into differentiable computation graphs. The article states it "elevates neural-symbolic learning to the relational level, utilizing differentiable first-order logic programming". Because temporal sequences are a linear case of relational graphs, it can subsume RNN and graph architectures while enforcing explicit symbolic rules. The framework is released at the printed GitHub URL and is used here to implement Responsible-DKT.
requirements: Data expressed as logical ground facts and a declared rule template; grounding against available facts to unroll the computation graph before backpropagation
constraints: Propositional-level neural-symbolic models it supersedes struggle with structured or dynamically sized data; the framework's scope is relational, differentiable logic programming
target_learners: Researchers and developers of learner-modelling systems
target_learning_goals: Sequential learner knowledge modelling with injected symbolic educational knowledge
examples: Responsible-DKT was implemented as a single neural-symbolic template in PyNeuraLogic, grounded per student against interaction facts

title: Opiq 6th-grade mathematics interaction dataset from Estonia
description: The study uses time-ordered interaction logs of 6th-grade mathematics students collected in September 2021 from Opiq, a nationally adopted K-12 digital learning platform in Estonia. "The dataset contains 21,471 student–item interactions, each originally described by more than 20 raw attributes." Records were binarized using the first-quartile score threshold (37), students with fewer than two interactions were removed, and data were partitioned at the student level into train/validation/test sets at an approximate 7:1:2 ratio (14,057/2,969/4,428 interactions; 105/15/30 students) across 13 skills.

description: The Responsible-DKT approach is organized as a reusable four-stage pipeline: raw logs are pre-processed into chronological per-student sequences, symbolic training samples are generated as sequence-to-sequence ground facts and queries, a neural-symbolic model integrates embeddings, recurrence, and symbolic rules, and evaluation combines predictive metrics with interpretability analyses. title: Inject conservative symbolic mastery and non-mastery rules to stabilize sequential knowledge-tracing predictions
description: The article recommends encoding pedagogically motivated constraints as learnable-weight symbolic rules that modulate neural predictions when simple evidence patterns occur in the interaction history. Specifically, "three incorrect responses on the same skill or quiz activate a not_mastered rule, providing a conservative signal that discourages premature overestimation of mastery", while two consecutive correct responses activate a mastered rule. These constraints help mitigate common DKT instabilities where mastery probabilities move contrary to recent responses, while preserving interpretability through the rule structure.
requirements: Interaction histories sufficient to detect the evidence patterns; rule weights learnable or fixed to enforce stronger pedagogical constraints when desired
constraints: Lower thresholds than prior mastery-learning work (e.g., seven learning opportunities) were adopted to suit the shorter and sparser sequences in this dataset; symbolic components modulate rather than override neural predictions
target_learners: K-12 learners in digital practice environments with sparse interaction sequences
target_learning_goals: Temporally consistent, pedagogically aligned mastery estimation
examples: In Responsible-DKT, triggered rules contribute additional evidence to the correctness predicate alongside the recurrent state and an averaged historical embedding pathway

description: SCRIPT adopts the standard four-models ITS approach: "a Pedagogical Model, a Learner Model, a Domain Model, and a User Interface." The pedagogical model follows VanLehn's inner/outer loop differentiation: "The outer loop is responsible for task selection and the inner loop is responsible for generating feedback to steps inside programming tasks." The domain model holds tasks, a competency model (Q-matrix), and difficulty information; the learner model derives competency states from UI actions via a knowledge tracing algorithm. article_title: The Pedagogy of AI Mistakes: Fostering Higher-Order Thinking
citation: Hosseini, H. (2026). The Pedagogy of AI Mistakes: Fostering Higher-Order Thinking. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05472
title: AI-as-learning-companion: leveraging LLM fallibility through a critique-refinement cycle to develop higher-order thinking
description: The paper's central framework reframes generative AI errors and hallucinations as a pedagogical resource rather than a limitation. By treating AI as a "learning companion" whose imperfect outputs prompt analysis, evaluation, and reflection, instructors structure an "iterative critique-refinement cycle" in which "AI's imperfect outputs serve as catalysts for evaluation, positioning critique as the central mechanism driving higher-order cognition". The cycle of generation, evaluation, and revision is aligned with Bloom's taxonomy, shifting emphasis from knowledge and application toward analysis, evaluation, and creation, and fostering metacognitive engagement.
requirements: Instruction must extend beyond domain knowledge to include the ability to evaluate, contextualize, and revise AI-generated outputs
Structured opportunities for evaluation and revision with imperfect responses
constraints: Over-reliance on AI can impede the development of core cognitive skills, so use must be scaffolded
target_learners: undergraduate computer science students
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking (analysis, evaluation, creation)
metacognitive skills including self-monitoring and error detection
critical evaluation of AI-generated solutions
examples: Weekly AI Modules in a database design course structured prompting strategies, failure-mode analysis, and a recurring Santa's Workshop case study around the critique-refinement cycle

citation: Ran Bi, Shiyao Wei, Yuanyiyi Zhou. (2026). Prober.ai: Gated Inquiry-Based Feedback via LLM-Constrained Personas for Argumentative Writing Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05598
title: Pedagogical friction: reflection-gated feedback architecture in which cognitive effort precedes support
description: The article introduces pedagogical friction as a first-class architectural primitive: revision suggestions are gated behind an intelligent reflection gate that assesses the student's written defense for substance and, if thin, coaches rather than answers. The two-phase API design (/challenge → /unlock) ensures that "genuine cognitive effort—not merely a keystroke—precedes the delivery of revision support." The gate uses a deterministic assessment layer (length floor, reasoning markers, topical relevance) followed by a model-side status check, and after two coached attempts a genuine effort is released to a scaffolded hint.

A deterministic assessment layer checking length, reasoning markers, and question-specific relevance
constraints: The architecture supports only up to two coaching turns per question, not open-ended multi-turn dialogue
If an unlocked suggestion is misaligned, there is no mechanism for iteratively refining the defense–suggestion exchange
target_learners: K–12 students developing argumentative writing skills
students preparing for standardized assessments such as AP English Language and GRE Analytical Writing
target_learning_goals: argumentative writing quality
metacognitive reflection and self-explanation
examples: In the deployed system, a defense failing the deterministic layer receives a targeted coaching nudge such as adding a because-style reasoning link, and only a defense clearing both gate layers reaches the model-side unlock

title: Write–Challenge–Defend–Improve cyclical interaction loop
description: The system's user interaction follows a cyclical four-phase model: the student writes an essay, selects a critical persona and receives structured inquiry-based questions with no evaluative language, writes a reflective defense for each question, and only after the defense clears the reflection gate unlocks a concrete revision suggestion and writing tip built on the student's own reasoning. The student then incorporates these into the draft and may re-enter the loop with revised text. The article states the loop is designed so that "cognitive effort always precedes the delivery of suggestions, ensuring the student remains the primary agent of revision."

title: The AI should never write for the student: preserve cognitive effort in AI-assisted writing tools
description: The article's core design principle is that AI writing support must never reduce the cognitive load required for argumentation: the system functions exclusively as a structured questioner, asking rather than telling, and deliberately withholds solutions until the student has demonstrated reflective engagement. This is motivated by cited evidence that AI-generated text availability suppresses independent reasoning and that facilitative (question-based) feedback is more strongly associated with long-term learning gains than directive feedback. The article argues that "pedagogical friction is a feature, not a bug" in AI-assisted education design.

constraints: Claims about cognitive engagement preservation and learning outcomes remain theoretical, grounded in prior literature rather than empirical validation specific to this system

standardized-assessment preparation students
target_learning_goals: durable argumentative writing skill development
metacognitive reflection
examples: Prober.ai refuses to generate or rewrite text, eliminating the cognitive shortcut that enables outsourcing, per the article's account of cited EEG and behavioral evidence

description: NSMQ Riddles is a benchmark dataset of scientific and mathematical riddles drawn from round 5 of Ghana's National Science and Maths Quiz, an annual live TV competition for senior secondary school students. The article states the dataset "consists of 1,840 riddle questions comprising 11 years of questions from round 5 of the NSMQ, ranging from 2009 to 2021". Each riddle contains a minimum of three clues that start vague and become more specific, with answers that are usually a number, word, or short phrase, allowing automatic evaluation via Exact Match and Fuzzy Match accuracy. citation: Fernandes, D., Buschek, D., Tankelevitch, L., Kosch, T., & Welsch, R. (2026). Explaining Too Much? Understanding How Large Language Model Reasoning Traces Influence Performance and Metacognition. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25856
title: Reasoning traces as user-facing interface artifacts rather than transparent windows into model cognition
description: The article proposes that LLM reasoning traces are best understood as user-facing interface artifacts rather than windows into model cognition: what matters is not whether a trace faithfully reflects the model's computation but how its format shapes users' metacognitive processes. The authors state that "reasoning traces are best understood as user-facing interface artifacts rather than transparent windows into model cognition", positioning the faithfulness problem as a further design risk because users may calibrate reliance on unreliable representations of model thinking.
requirements: The framing applies to trace output treated from a user-facing perspective, regardless of its internal validity, as the article states.
constraints: A model's chain-of-thought output and the internal computations that produce its answer can diverge, so traces may not faithfully represent how the model arrived at its answer.

target_learning_goals: calibrated self-evaluation and reliance on AI assistance during reasoning
examples: In the experiment, summary traces preserved performance while elevating trust and hedonic appeal, and full traces impaired performance and produced the largest overestimation gap.

citation: Fernandes, D., Buschek, D., Tankelevitch, L., Kosch, T., & Welsch, R. (2026). Explaining Too Much? Understanding How Large Language Model Reasoning Traces Influence Performance and Metacognition. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25856
title: Scaffold metacognitive support by eliciting users' own reasoning before exposing the model's reasoning traces or answer
description: Because no trace format supported calibrated self-evaluation, the article argues that calibration is unlikely to emerge from the traces themselves and should instead be scaffolded by interactions that elicit users' own reasoning first. The authors write that "Metacognitive support must instead be scaffolded by interactions that elicit users' own reasoning before exposing the model's reasoning traces or answer." The Full-trace interface's Final Answer button, which required engagement with the trace before revealing the answer, illustrates deliberately sequencing exposure to encourage independent reasoning prior to model influence.
requirements: Interface designs must sequence exposure so that users commit to or articulate their own reasoning before the model's trace or answer is revealed.
constraints: The article presents this as a design direction argued from the finding that no trace format supported calibration; it was not itself manipulated as a condition in the experiment.
target_learners: adults solving reasoning problems with AI assistance
target_learning_goals: metacognitive accuracy and calibrated reliance on AI
examples: The Full-trace condition required participants to engage with the reasoning trace before a Final Answer button revealed the model's answer, encouraging independent reasoning prior to model influence.

article_title: Persistent AI Agents in Academic Research: A Single-Investigator Implementation Case Study
citation: Anas H. Alzahrani, MD, PhD, MPH. (2026). Persistent AI Agents in Academic Research: A Single-Investigator Implementation Case Study. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26870
title: PARE-M v0.1: a measurement framework for persistent agentic research environments
description: PARE-M (Persistent Agentic Research Environment Measurement) v0.1 is a descriptive measurement framework the article introduces for evaluating persistent agentic research environments. It "separates utilization, output, resource, reproducibility, and governance domains and requires that each reported metric include a numerator, denominator, time window, and computation rule." Its named metrics include active-day fraction, de-duplicated record count, capped-gap active-time estimate, cache-dominance ratio, output-proxy rate, governance-event rate, and artifact-surface breadth. The article uses it to organize all reported outcomes of the 115-day case.
requirements: Each reported metric must include a numerator, denominator, time window, and computation rule, as the framework requires.
constraints: The framework is descriptive; the article states governance events are author-coded and require independent validation, and that the case does not estimate causal productivity effects.
target_learners: academic researchers and physician-scientists using persistent AI agents in research workflows
target_learning_goals: describing and evaluating persistent agentic research environments across utilization, output, resource, reproducibility, and governance domains
examples: The article applies PARE-M v0.1 to report ADF = 0.835, DRC = 75,671, OPR = 5.02, GER = 9.26, and ASB = 10 for the 115-day case.

article_title: Learning after COVID-19 and the ICT career aspirations: Are students entering the AI era with weaker skills?
citation: Popa, D. M., Oprea, S.-V., & Bâra, A. (2022). Learning after COVID-19 and the ICT career aspirations: Are students entering the AI era with weaker skills? Department of Economic Informatics and Cybernetics, Bucharest University of Economic Studies. simona.oprea@csie.ase.ro
title: Latent structural readiness space for digital and AI transformation derived from a variational autoencoder over learning environment indicators
description: The framework trains a variational autoencoder on standardized country-level indicators of autonomy, digital skills and teacher support, projecting them into a two-dimensional latent space interpreted as "a structural readiness space for digital and AI-related transformations in education". Geometric proximity reflects similarity in joint learning environment configurations, and a composite AI Readiness Index is formed as a linear aggregation of the two latent coordinates (α = 0.5). Countries with higher latent readiness tend to show stronger ICT aspiration growth, though the gradient is imperfect.
requirements: Standardized country-level indicators of autonomy, digital skills and teacher support from harmonized PISA data as VAE input
constraints: The article states educational readiness alone does not fully determine ICT aspiration growth, with heterogeneous outcomes among structurally similar countries
target_learners: secondary students across national education systems (PISA populations)
target_learning_goals: digital and AI-era educational readiness; ICT career orientation
examples: The latent space colored by ICT aspiration change (Figure 9) shows a clear but imperfect gradient, and the AI Readiness Index ranking places Korea, Finland, the Netherlands and New Zealand in leading positions

article_title: Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning
citation: Lala Yamazaki and Ramchandra Rimal. (2026). Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14960
title: Wearable Exam Stress Dataset (PhysioNet) processed into a balanced 328,655-sample multivariate classification dataset
description: The study uses the open-access "A Wearable Exam Stress Dataset for Predicting Cognitive Performance in Real-World Settings" from PhysioNet, collected from 10 college students wearing the Empatica E4 wristband during Midterm 1, Midterm 2, and a Final exam. After preprocessing (pivoting to wide format, removing rows with missing values, grade normalization and categorization into A–F, and undersampling to balance classes at 65,731 observations per grade category), "The final processed dataset contains 328,655 samples" with five physiological predictors (ACC, BVP, EDA, HR, TEMP), three exam-participation indicators, and the grade category as target.
requirements: Grades normalized to a percentage scale and categorized into letter grades A to F; class imbalance handled by undersampling to 65,731 observations per grade category
constraints: Data collected from 10 college students during three exam sessions; rows with missing values were removed
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: predicting academic exam outcomes from physiological stress indicators
examples: Participants wore the E4 wristband during three exam sessions; each midterm lasted 1.5 hours and the final exam 3 hours

article_title: Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning
citation: Lala Yamazaki and Ramchandra Rimal. (2026). Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14960
title: Encoder-only transformer with classification head adapted for numerical physiological data classification
description: The authors adapt the original transformer architecture for classification of tabular physiological data: the decoder is removed and a classification head (linear transformation followed by softmax over grade categories A–F) is added to the encoder output. Each physiological feature is treated as an individual token in the input sequence, with embedding and positional encoding preserving temporal structure, and multi-head self-attention capturing dependencies among physiological features. The article states, "Specifically, only the encoder component of the transformer was retained, as our task requires generating a single output—predicted performance category—rather than producing a sequential output," and reports this is the first attempt to implement transformer architecture to model academic outcomes using physiological signals.
requirements: Input physiological data embedded as dense vectors with positional encoding added to maintain sequence order; a classification head with softmax converts encoder output into grade-category probabilities
constraints: Tuned configuration used 8 heads, 3 layers, dropout probability 0, d_model 256, 128 hidden-layer neurons, batch size 128, and sequence length 128
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: predicting exam grade categories from multivariate physiological stress signals
examples: The adapted transformer achieved a mean test accuracy of 0.9039 ± 0.0081 over 30 replicates
key_sources: Lala Yamazaki and Ramchandra Rimal. (2026). Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14960

article_title: Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning
citation: Lala Yamazaki and Ramchandra Rimal. (2026). Leveraging Physiological Signals to Predict Exam Outcomes with Machine Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14960
title: Interpret physiological predictions within broader context; never use them as standalone decision-making tools
description: The article's ethics section recommends that predictions of academic performance derived from physiological data be treated as one input among many rather than as autonomous decision tools. It states that such predictions "should be interpreted within the context of other influential factors, such as personal circumstances, environmental conditions, and mental health considerations, to guarantee fairness and mitigate biases." High-stakes decisions such as educational interventions must incorporate these insights within a broader context to avoid imposing undue stress and unintended consequences on students.
requirements: Use of publicly accessible datasets and fully documented computational methodologies, including model parameters and hyperparameters, to promote reproducibility; averaging findings over multiple runs
constraints: Predictions are not intended to stand alone as decision-making tools; high-stakes decisions must incorporate broader context
target_learners: college students in high-stress exam settings
target_learning_goals: supporting student well-being and mental health awareness alongside academic performance monitoring
examples: The article suggests educators, mental health professionals, and stakeholders can leverage the study's framework to build stress-monitoring and performance-prediction tools that uphold ethical standards

article_title: ParaTutor: LLM Mediated Parent Child Tutoring through Role Separated Scaffolding Interface in Real Time
citation: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030
title: Three-phase tutoring structure for math word problems: understanding, calculation, and summarization
description: The article identifies a three-phase structure organizing parent-child math word problem tutoring. The article states that "word problem solving was described as a process that embodies three recurrent phases, namely understanding, calculation, and summarization." Each phase establishes a temporary focus of attention and shared expectations about what counts as progress, regulating when reasoning advances and how instructional authority is distributed. Phase boundaries are actively enforced by parents rather than implicitly assumed, serving as an interactional script that guides instruction and regulates problem-solving behavior.
requirements: Parents must actively enforce phase boundaries and authorize transitions between phases for the structure to regulate tutoring interaction
constraints: Derived from interviews with 11 Chinese parents and 2 teachers in the context of upper-elementary math word problem tutoring
Aligns with classical problem solving models according to the article
target_learners: Upper elementary students in grades 4-6 (ages 10-12)
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem solving including interpretation, calculation, and reflection
examples: Parents asked children to restate problems in their own words before calculation (understanding phase)
Teachers instructed students to return to the question instead of correcting numbers blindly (calculation to understanding transition)
Parents prompted children to articulate underlying principles after solving (summarization phase)
key_sources: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030

article_title: ParaTutor: LLM Mediated Parent Child Tutoring through Role Separated Scaffolding Interface in Real Time
citation: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030
title: Three-dimensional scaffolding design coordinating user roles, tutoring phases, and guidance strategies
description: ParaTutor organizes its support as a design that "coordinates user roles, tutoring phases, and guidance strategies during parent-child math tutoring." The role dimension differentiates support between parents (guidance for conducting tutoring) and children (visual grounding for interpreting problems). The phase dimension structures how support changes across understanding, calculation, and summarization. The strategy dimension translates tutoring goals into concrete parent-facing guidance including suggested actions, example language, and ways of using the child-facing visualization. Together these dimensions define ParaTutor as a scaffold for parent-led tutoring.
requirements: A shared internal state maintained by a Main Agent that stores the current problem, active phase, interaction history, selected mode, child progress, and visualization state
Phase transitions controlled by explicit rule-based conditions rather than LLM decisions
Two synchronized panels separating parent-facing and child-facing interfaces
constraints: Designed for parent-child dyads in home math word problem tutoring, not single-user learning
Visual grounding withholds procedural solution steps reserved for parent-facing scaffolding
target_learners: Parent-child dyads with children aged 10-12 in grades 4-6
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem solving with shared understanding and active reasoning
examples: In the understanding phase, agents prioritize segmentation and grounding prompts while withholding solution procedures
In the calculation phase, agents support error localization and guided questioning
In the summarization phase, agents support reflection, consolidation, and transfer prompts
key_sources: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030

article_title: ParaTutor: LLM Mediated Parent Child Tutoring through Role Separated Scaffolding Interface in Real Time
citation: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030
title: ParaTutor: multi-agent LLM-based scaffolding system for home math word-problem tutoring
description: ParaTutor is "a multi-agent LLM-based scaffolding system for home math word-problem tutoring" that "distributes support across user roles by providing parents with strategy, language, repair, and phase scaffolds, while providing children with visual grounding for problem interpretation." The system consists of a Main Agent, phase-specific scaffolding agents, and a visual grounding module. The Main Agent maintains a shared internal state and invokes only scaffolding agents relevant to the current phase sequentially. A rule-based state-to-diagram generation pipeline renders interactive visualizations from the evolving shared state rather than revealing worked solutions.
requirements: An internet-connected computer for remote use
Parents attend an orientation session covering system use
Phase transitions require joint confirmation from parent and child
constraints: Evaluated with children aged 10-12 in grades 4-6 in Chinese home tutoring contexts
Visual grounding module is rule-based rather than LLM-generated
Positioned as a third party supporting parent-led tutoring rather than replacing parental involvement
target_learners: Parent-child dyads with children aged 10-12 in grades 4-6 in Chinese home tutoring contexts
target_learning_goals: Math word problem solving including perimeter-based counting, two-category constraint problems, and age-related reasoning
examples: The Main Agent prioritizes agents for task simplification and situational guidance in the understanding phase
The visual grounding module maps extracted entities, numerical attributes, and relational constraints to graphical primitives and layout rules
Children dragged age markers and adjusted time sliders to test whether interpretations were consistent with problem relations
key_sources: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030

article_title: ParaTutor: LLM Mediated Parent Child Tutoring through Role Separated Scaffolding Interface in Real Time
citation: LUO Lan, WANG Anqi, ZHOU Muzhi, ZHU Junhua, CAI Jie, YU Ao, and PAN Hui. (2024). ParaTutor: Coordinating Parent-Child Math Tutoring through Role-Separated LLM Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.18030
title: Parent scaffolding strategies across three tutoring phases for math word problems
description: The formative study identified "recurring scaffolding moves that parents use" that "shape turn-taking, pacing, and the distribution of responsibility during problem solving." In the understanding phase, parents used task simplification and situational guidance. In the calculation phase, they used feedback and correction, demonstration and imitation, and independent-thinking strategies. In the summarization phase, they used review and consolidation and practical application. These strategies are organized by the three-phase tutoring structure and represent how parents without formal training distribute instructional responsibility during home math tutoring.
requirements: Parents must maintain distinct instructional roles where they guide the process while children remain responsible for reasoning and solution generation
constraints: Identified from interviews with 11 Chinese parents of children in grades 4-6
Some strategies such as systematic review were noted as too time-consuming by some parents
Demonstration and imitation raised concerns about differing from teachers' approaches
target_learners: Children in grades 4-6 (ages 10-12) receiving home math tutoring from parents
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem solving across understanding, calculation, and summarization phases
examples: A parent used a pen to circle parts of the problem on paper so the child could gradually understand it (task simplification)
A parent drew diagrams to clarify relationships when questions were too long (situational guidance)
A parent asked children to articulate their solution process before offering help (independent-thinking strategy)

article_title: Automated Recommendation of Programming Learning Content Using Pattern-based Knowledge Components
citation: Muntasir Hoq, Griffin Pitts, Zhangqi Duan, Arun Balajiee Lekshmi Narayanan, Mohammad Hassany, Andrew Lan, Peter Brusilovsky and Bita Akram. (2026). Automated Recommendation of Programming Learning Content Using Pattern-based Knowledge Components. CSEDM'26: 10th Educational Data Mining in Computer Science Education Workshop. https://educationaldatamining.org
title: Pattern-based knowledge component framework for representing programming learning activities
description: The framework defines knowledge components as "recurring, semantically meaningful structural patterns based on important subtrees from program Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs)". Discovery proceeds in four steps: SANN-guided subtree extraction trained on topic labels, normalization that anonymizes identifiers and canonicalizes syntactic alternatives, context-aware encoding of normalized subtree sequences with a β-VAE, and K-means clustering of latent vectors into KCs. Activities are then mapped to IDF-weighted knowledge vectors and compared by cosine similarity, yielding finer-grained, implementation-level signals such as guarded loop traversals and accumulator updates.
requirements: Training the extraction pipeline requires coarse-grained topic labels for challenges and examples
Expert-defined bundle information is deliberately withheld from SANN training so patterns reflect topic-level regularities
constraints: The first pipeline step uses topic labels for training, limiting direct application to unlabeled corpora, as the authors state in Limitations
target_learners: introductory programming students
target_learning_goals: mastering foundational programming concepts and patterns
retrieving instructionally aligned worked examples and practice challenges
examples: Applied to the PCEX Python corpus, where each program is mapped to a binary KC-incidence vector, IDF-reweighted, L2-normalized, and ranked by cosine similarity

article_title: The Paternalistic Filter: Epistemic Injustice and Differential Refusal in LLM-Mediated History Education for Marginalized Romanian Students
citation: Alexis Popovici, Andrei Ionascu, Adrian Marius Dumitran. (2026). The Paternalistic Filter: Epistemic Injustice and Differential Refusal in LLM-Mediated History Education for Marginalized Romanian Students. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11292
title: Epistemic paternalism in LLM tutoring as hermeneutical injustice
description: The article's central explanatory framework holds that LLM tutors constitute "epistemic paternalism: withholding civic complexity from marginalized learners while replacing it with victimization-centered narratives." Drawing on Fricker's hermeneutical injustice—a gap in interpretive resources that disadvantages groups in understanding their social experience—the authors argue safety alignment acts as a paternalistic filter transforming conversational AI into "agents of narrative segregation." The framework unifies the audit's four empirical patterns (refusal, gatekeeping, lexical simplification, framing shifts) as one mechanism.
requirements: Requires deployment of LLMs as conversational tutors for politically contested historical content to marginalized learner populations
constraints: Established for a single contested event (the 1989 Romanian Revolution) and single-turn interactions; the authors state future work must verify whether the patterns are universal across other cultural contexts and multi-turn tutoring
target_learners: Marginalized secondary students, including Roma and low socio-economic tier learners
target_learning_goals: Understanding contested national history as political actors with access to interpretive tools and civic agency
examples: The audit operationalized the framework via five metrics: Differential Refusal, Coup Gap, Type-Token Ratio, Agency Theft Ratio, and Mean Justification Scores
key_sources: Alexis Popovici, Andrei Ionascu, Adrian Marius Dumitran. (2026). The Paternalistic Filter: Epistemic Injustice and Differential Refusal in LLM-Mediated History Education for Marginalized Romanian Students. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11292

title: Open audit dataset of 1,800 LLM history-tutor responses across five personas
description: The article releases a reproducible audit corpus: 1,800 independent API calls across four LLMs (GPT_OSS, LLaMA, Deepseek, Kimi K2) with five embedded student personas and three prompt types (general explanation, causes/consequences, justification score), run at temperature 0 with n=30 iterations per condition. The authors state "all exact prompts, persona definitions, and raw API data are available" publicly, enabling replication of differential refusal, coup-gap, TTR, agency-theft, and justification-score analyses.

citation: Steve Woollaston, Brendan Flanagan, Yuko Toyokawa and Hiroaki Ogata. (2026). Penny: Transition Network Analysis of Learner-Chatbot Interactions in Scaffolded EFL Writing. Preprint, accepted at the 1st Workshop on Transition Network Analysis (TNA) at LAK '26.
title: Penny: an LLM-powered EFL writing support chatbot with structured feedback guidelines
description: Penny is a generative AI chatbot powered by GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024–08–06) that scaffolds English writing practice three to four times per week with daily prompts. Learners must write at least 100 characters before requesting feedback, and feedback is given in English or Japanese. Its system prompt directs it to "Adapt to the student's level", review grammar and syntax, enhance vocabulary, encourage and support, limit responses to 50 words, and keep the student on topic.
requirements: Learners must write a minimum of 100 characters before the Check my writing button becomes active
The system prompt supplies the student's name, proficiency level, chat language and the day's writing prompt
constraints: Learners could not engage with future writing prompts past the present day
The writing textbox only accepted English characters
target_learners: Japanese junior high school EFL learners aged 14–16
target_learning_goals: English as a Foreign Language writing accuracy and engagement with written corrective feedback
examples: Used by three EFL classes (n = 119) at a high performing public school in Japan over four months

citation: Steve Woollaston, Brendan Flanagan, Yuko Toyokawa and Hiroaki Ogata. (2026). Penny: Transition Network Analysis of Learner-Chatbot Interactions in Scaffolded EFL Writing. Preprint, accepted at the 1st Workshop on Transition Network Analysis (TNA) at LAK '26.
title: Transition Network Analysis as a framework for modelling temporal learner-chatbot interaction
description: Transition Network Analysis (TNA) models learning processes as networks of discrete behavioural states connected by directed, probabilistic transitions, computed here with a web-based TNA Shiny app. Unlike frequency counts, it "maps the temporal trajectory of learner actions", operationalising the error treatment sequence in interactionist SLA. In this study it revealed the Revision and Chat Loops and enabled network-level metrics (density, reciprocity) and proficiency-group comparisons.
requirements: Events must be coded into discrete states, with classification validated against human raters
Transitions below a chosen probability threshold (here 0.05) may be pruned for visualisation while metrics use the full dataset
constraints: The authors note their chi-squared analysis does not isolate specific edge-level differences and recommend permutation testing for specific transition pathways
target_learners: Researchers and designers analysing learner-chatbot interaction logs
target_learning_goals: Understanding temporal dynamics of feedback uptake and dialogue in AI-scaffolded writing
examples: Applied to 63,328 coded events from Japanese EFL learners using Penny, yielding a 10-node, 26-edge network

article_title: When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041
title: Post-instrumental learning: formation of capacities needed for agency and accountability under extensive AI delegation
description: Post-instrumental learning is the article's central framework: the formation of capacities that remain necessary for agency, responsibility, and meaning when many products of learning can be delegated to AI. It is defined as "the formation of capacities that remain necessary for agency, responsibility, and meaning under extensive AI delegation". The term does not deny learning's instrumental value; it marks a shift in emphasis, from whether people must produce outputs unaided to whether they retain the capacities to set ends, ask for reasons, contest decisions, refuse harmful dependence, revise practices, and participate in the forms of life AI helps mediate.
requirements: Delegated work must remain connected to purposes, reasons, alternatives, and repair through people, intermediaries, and institutions
constraints: The account is a normative conceptual analysis, not an empirical measurement of learning loss or a design proposal for one educational technology
target_learners: students
professionals
citizens affected by AI-mediated institutional practices
target_learning_goals: preserving capacities for agency, responsibility, and accountability under AI delegation

article_title: When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041
title: Capacity dissolution: erosion of the practices that keep delegated work answerable, distinct from deskilling
description: Capacity dissolution is the article's name for the central risk of AI delegation: a breakdown in the relation among an output, the person or institution that claims or relies on it, and the practice that makes that claim answerable. The article defines it as "a breakdown in the relation among an output, the person or institution that claims or relies on it, and the practice that makes that claim answerable". It is distinguished from deskilling, automation complacency, and diminished contestability: its object is the institutional relation that keeps delegated work answerable, and it can arise while specialists retain skill, performance stays high, and a formal appeal route exists. Its warning sign is successful output production alongside erosion of the learning practices that sustain accountability.
requirements: Recurring occasions for use and institutions that make capacity use consequential, since capacity is sustained by practice rather than stored privately
constraints: Distinct from ordinary deskilling: a person may stop a routine calculation without losing meaningful agency; dissolution concerns the practices that make delegated work answerable
target_learners: students
clinicians
caseworkers
managers
public officials
target_learning_goals: maintaining the judgment needed to set ends, use reasons, and make challenge consequential

article_title: When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041
title: Five-capacity framework: end-setting, reason-giving, contestability, refusal/revision, and participation as a minimum functional set
description: The article proposes five capacities as the core of post-instrumental learning: "end-setting, reason-giving, contestability,refusal/revision, and participation. They form a proposed minimum functional set, not a complete theory of education." End-setting keeps purposes open to judgment; reason-giving connects outputs to inspectable considerations; contestability supplies routes to challenge; refusal/revision makes exit and redesign possible; participation sustains the shared practices in which the others are learned. Table 1 translates each capacity into an institutional design question and a failure mode, for example that without contestability "Affected people encounter decisions as settled facts". The capacities are interdependent but not interchangeable and should be distributed across affected people, intermediaries, and communities.
requirements: Distribution across affected people, institutional intermediaries, and public or professional communities, so delegation remains accountable rather than private dependence on expertise
constraints: The claim is normative and functional rather than psychometric; the capacities may overlap and are not an empirically validated scale
target_learners: affected persons
intermediaries such as teachers, clinicians, caseworkers, lawyers, engineers, and public officials
professional and public communities
target_learning_goals: setting ends, giving reasons, contesting decisions, refusing and revising dependence, and participating in shared practices

title: Lightweight capacity impact statement: a five-judgment deliberative record for AI deployment review
description: A capacity impact statement is a governance artifact the article proposes to make deployment review concrete. It records five judgments: the changed practice and responsible roles; the capacity the prior practice formed or evidenced; who needs that capacity or relies on its certification; how the new workflow preserves an opportunity to exercise it and what evidence makes that opportunity credible; and an observable trigger for review or repair. The article describes it as "a deliberative record, not a validated scale or universal score", whose purpose is to make the institution's reasons inspectable and revisable. It can be incorporated into course approval, assessment moderation, procurement, or periodic review, with depth and review interval scaled to stakes and reversibility.
requirements: An observable trigger for review or repair, and credible evidence that the workflow preserves an opportunity to exercise the capacity
constraints: It is a deliberative record, not a validated scale or universal score; depth and review interval should scale with the stakes and reversibility of the workflow
target_learners: institutions deploying AI systems
course approvers
procurement and review bodies
target_learning_goals: maintaining institutional capacity to understand, challenge, and revise AI-mediated practices over time
examples: The article's example: an AI-supported research essay where repeated inability of students to defend source selection or revise arguments meets the review trigger, prompting task revision or restored guided practice

description: A curated dataset of 1,000 captioned nuclear energy images assembled from three sources: 348 images from books and encyclopedias, 119 from journal publications, and 533 from nuclear news websites. It covers seven action classes {fall, punch, jump, kick, throw, run, sit} plus a background meta-class of ordinary classroom actions, and comprises 1296 synthetic samples and 574 real-world samples annotated with poses, action classes, and temporal boundaries. article_title: Robust and Efficient Motion Reasoning for Privacy-Aware Classroom Incident Recognition
citation: Paritosh Parmar, Landy Lan, Hong Yang, Chen Yi, Chiat Pin Tay. (2026). Robust and Efficient Motion Reasoning for Privacy-Aware Classroom Incident Recognition. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05115
title: Hierarchical multi-order kinematic representation with multi-objective knowledge distillation framework
description: A motion-reasoning framework in which human actions are represented as a hierarchy of kinematic orders: "we represent motion using joint positions, velocities, and accelerations, which are later encoded by dedicated order-specific backbones." Order-specific representations are fused by weighted averaging into a multi-order teacher, which is distilled via a multi-objective loss (temperature-scaled KL distillation plus supervised classification) into a substantially smaller student operating only on zeroth-order joint positions. The design compresses along two axes: from multi-order inputs to a single zeroth-order stream, and from a larger teacher network to a smaller student.
requirements: Temporal preprocessing before computing derivatives, since higher-order kinematic features amplify errors present in lower-order pose estimates; missing joints are linearly interpolated and trajectories smoothed with a Savitzky–Golay filter
constraints: In the implementation the fusion weights are set manually
The deployed student operates only on a single zeroth-order joint-position stream at inference
target_learners: preschool students and teachers in monitored classrooms
target_learning_goals: privacy-preserving recognition of classroom safety incidents from pose sequences alone
examples: Instantiated with STGCN++ backbones: 64-base-channel order-specific teachers and a 32-channel student, with distillation temperature 4 and loss weights {λKD, λCls} = {0.3, 1.0}

description: Precision Education is a paradigm in which AI continuously analyzes academic, behavioral, financial, and career data to identify emerging risks, recommend personalized interventions, and align academic decisions with career success. The paper organizes the field's evolution across five stages, from descriptive reporting to what it calls "Stage 5: Autonomous and adaptive student success." It argues the field has invested heavily in Stage 3 predictive analytics while "The value proposition of Precision Education lives in Stages 4 and 5." The framing pairs data science with "warm humanity": technology identifies the signal, human judgment shapes the response.

title: Student Digital Twin: a continuously updated learner model built for counterfactual simulation, not dashboard display
description: A Student Digital Twin is defined as "a continuously evolving model of an individual learner's academic performance, learning behavior, career interests, degree progression, financial circumstances, co-curricular engagement, and workforce preparedness." Its purpose is "to simulate": answering counterfactual questions such as what happens if a gateway course is repeated with tutoring, or if the student changes majors. It cautions the twin "is not the person" and should be a decision aid, not an oracle.

article_title: Principal Trait Analysis: Towards Deriving 'Skills' in Human-AI Collaboration
citation: Hunter McNichols, Kai Du, Andrew Lan. (2026). PRINCIPAL TRAIT ANALYSIS: TOWARDS DERIVING "SKILLS" IN HUMAN-AI COLLABORATION. A preprint - August 13, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11460
title: Principal Trait Analysis (PTA): a four-stage, PCA-inspired pipeline for deriving behavioral traits from human-AI conversation corpora
description: PTA is a data-driven methodology that "produces a representative set of textual descriptions we callprincipal traitsfrom a corpus of human collaborator-AI collaborative conversation sessions." It runs four stages: LLM-prompted behavior-observation extraction (generic or theory-lens), embedding-based top-down and agglomerative clustering into candidate traits, LLM-as-a-judge scoring of each session on a 1-5 Likert scale, and greedy principal-trait selection trading off relevance (item-total correlation plus factor-analysis communality) against redundancy in score and text-embedding space. Trait selection mirrors PCA's variance-maximizing criterion adapted to text, where orthogonality is undefined.

LLM prompting and text-embedding infrastructure for extraction, clustering, scoring, and selection

title: Proof-of-concept Early Warning System flagging high-attrition-risk active students
description: An Early Warning System (EWS) that deploys the survey-trained Random Forest pipeline over currently active students, assigning continuous attrition risk scores (0–100%) and tiering students into High (≥67%), Medium (33–67%), and Low (<33%) risk. Applied to 22 active students, it "identified 4 students as High Risk (18%)". The flagged students all had A or A+ DSA grades, irregular upsolving habits, and no mentor support, matching the Skill-Application Paradox signature. The article treats the flags as indicators for proactive mentoring outreach, not deterministic predictions.

target_learning_goals: Sustained participation and skill development in competitive programming

article_title: The Policy Deficit in AI × Social-Emotional Learning Research
citation: Tran Van Cuong, Liu Yihan, Nguyen Van Tuong. (2026). The Policy Deficit in AI x Social-Emotional Learning Research.
title: WH-question framework for decomposing policy implications into Who, What, Why, When/Where, and How
description: The review adapts a framework from Dello Russo et al. (2023) in which each policy implication is treated as "a short narrative that can be broken down into several parts": who it addresses, what actions it suggests, why they matter, when and where they apply, and how strongly they are framed (modal verbs such as must, should, could). The authors coded 31 implication narratives against these five dimensions, mapped onto their five research questions, using an a priori codebook refined through pilot coding with disagreement resolved in discussion with a third author.
requirements: Each distinct implication statement is treated as a single unit of analysis, allowing multiple codes within a dimension
constraints: Coding implicit policy implications can be subjective, as the authors state
target_learners: education researchers writing AI × SEL studies
target_learning_goals: writing evidence-grounded, actor-oriented policy implications
examples: The review coded 31 implication narratives from 18 papers, finding prescriptive framing in 24 claims and tentative framing in 7

article_title: The Policy Deficit in AI × Social-Emotional Learning Research
citation: Tran Van Cuong, Liu Yihan, Nguyen Van Tuong. (2026). The Policy Deficit in AI x Social-Emotional Learning Research.
title: The techno-solutionist trap: AI × SEL research foregrounds technical potential while leaving institutional conditions under-specified
description: The review characterizes the field as dominated by "techno-solutionism": the belief that AI applications will inherently solve SEL challenges without sufficient engagement with institutional or regulatory hurdles that prevent scaling. Policy, when mentioned, is treated as a "horizon" rather than practice-oriented tools, risking a "pilot-study paradox" where robust results fail to achieve real-world impact for lack of regulatory and resource-allocation frameworks. The authors propose reorienting from "implication-as-afterthought" to "implication-as-methodology", designing research with policy in mind from the start.
requirements: Researchers, reviewers, and editors must foreground policy considerations despite incentives prioritizing technical novelty
constraints: The authors note rapid technology lifecycles and rigid academic publication formats complicate integrating deep policy suggestions into short papers
target_learners: AI × SEL researchers, editors, reviewers, and policymakers
target_learning_goals: translating AI × SEL research findings into educational governance and implementation
examples: The review found some papers promise policy implications in impact statements yet ignore them in the main text

article_title: Privacy-Preserving Heterogeneous Multi-LLM Federated Inference for Cognitive Diagnosis
citation: Yagna Manasa Boyapati, Chong Yu, Tianyu Jiang, Justin Zhan. (2026). Privacy-Preserving Heterogeneous Multi-LLM Federated Inference for Cognitive Diagnosis. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02947
title: Privacy-preserving heterogeneous multi-LLM federated inference framework for cognitive diagnosis
description: A four-stage framework in which heterogeneous commercial LLMs (LLaMA-3.3-70B, GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3-Haiku) independently predict student knowledge states via engineered prompts, add calibrated Laplace noise locally to their prediction outputs, and aggregate with residual correction. The article describes it as "the first privacy-preserving heterogeneous multi-LLM federated inference framework for cognitive diagnosis", operating entirely at the prediction level with models frozen and accessible only via black-box APIs. It integrates Q-matrix theory to constrain prompts to relevant concepts and rests on an honest-but-curious trust paradigm.
requirements: Commercial LLM API access for each federated entity; a Q-matrix (expert-crafted or automatically generated) mapping questions to knowledge concepts; local calibration data per entity for residual correction terms.
constraints: The privacy guarantee follows an honest-but-curious trust paradigm: LDP shields published diagnostic outputs but does not prevent commercial API providers from logging submitted queries.
The framework is evaluated on structured educational domains; extension to open-ended assessment tasks may require adapted prompt engineering.
Residual correction may require periodic recalibration when providers release model updates.
target_learners: K-12 and secondary students in mathematics and academic assessment settings (ASSIST09, GSM8K, UCI Student Performance populations)
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing student mastery of specific knowledge concepts and skills to support intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning
examples: The framework was instantiated with LLaMA-3.3-70B via Groq API, GPT-4o-mini via OpenAI API, and Claude-3-Haiku via Anthropic API, each holding a disjoint local dataset subset for calibration, and evaluated on ASSIST09, GSM8K, and UCI Student Performance.

article_title: PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews
citation: Zabaleta, M. & Lin, B. (2026). PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11559
title: PRISMA-LLM: a three-layer reporting framework for LLM-assisted systematic reviews
description: PRISMA-LLM is an evidence-informed reporting framework for LLM-assisted and AI-enabled systematic-review workflows, organized to complement PRISMA 2020. It has three layers: "a universal checklist specifies the information that should be reported across LLM-assisted review workflows"; five implementation-disclosure levels organize technical detail needed to reconstruct workflows; and consequence-sensitive evaluation expectations determine when validation should exceed the minimum associated with a disclosure level. Its empirical basis is the recurring evaluation and limitation dimensions observed in SciLitBench and the association between workflow type and reporting coverage.
requirements: Every LLM-assisted review should identify the system and task, describe inputs and outputs, report human oversight, disclose evaluation and failures, and provide reproducibility materials where possible
constraints: The levels are disclosure tiers, not risk tiers
It is not presently an official extension endorsed by the PRISMA Executive and has not undergone formal consensus development or prospective user testing
Its purpose is not to certify the quality or safety of an AI workflow
target_learners: researchers conducting AI-assisted systematic reviews
review authors and auditors in evidence synthesis
target_learning_goals: transparent, auditable reporting of AI-assisted review workflows
distinguishing implementation disclosure from consequence-sensitive evaluation
examples: The framework was developed from SciLitBench reporting patterns, workflow choices encountered while building SciLitBench, and comparison with PRISMA 2020, PRISMA-S, and adjacent AI-reporting proposals

article_title: PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews
citation: Zabaleta, M. & Lin, B. (2026). PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11559
title: PRISMA-LLM 16-item universal reporting checklist (Table 1)
description: The PRISMA-LLM checklist is a page-sized, user-facing set of 16 items (LLM-1 through LLM-16) spanning identification, rationale, methods, results, discussion, availability, and disclosure sections. It asks authors to report system identity and version, task and disclosure level, inputs and document processing, prompts and settings, outputs and post-processing, human oversight, evaluation and errors, limitations, reproducibility materials, and support or competing interests. It is "intended to be used alongside PRISMA 2020 rather than as a replacement for it."

article_title: PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews
citation: Zabaleta, M. & Lin, B. (2026). PRISMA-LLM: An Empirical Reporting Framework for AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11559
title: Five cumulative implementation-disclosure levels with a consequence-sensitive evaluation override
description: PRISMA-LLM organizes implementation disclosure into five cumulative levels: off-the-shelf software; prompt-only LLM; structured/engineered workflows; retrieval/adapted/single-agent workflows; and multi-agent/swarm systems, each adding the technical detail needed to reconstruct the workflow. Minimum evaluation breadth increases with implementation complexity, but "implementation level is not a risk score": a consequence override requires stronger validation at any level when outputs can change the evidence base, human verification is limited, the system is proprietary or mutable, or errors are hard to reconstruct or reverse.
requirements: Each level adds the implementation detail of the previous level, from product/version and settings at Level 1 to agent roles, coordination, handoffs, and cross-agent audit logs at Level 5
constraints: The levels summarize implementation complexity rather than methodological risk
Reporting richness remains a descriptive empirical index because no compliance cutoff has undergone prospective validation
target_learners: review teams using LLM or AI-enabled automation
methodologists designing reporting standards
target_learning_goals: graded, reconstructable disclosure of AI workflow implementation
calibrating evaluation expectations to task consequence
examples: Supplementary Figure S6 maps the cumulative minimum reporting dimensions associated with the five implementation levels

article_title: PAUSE: A Privacy-Preserving Self-Reflection Tool for AI-Associated Cognitive Offloading
citation: Mahbub Ul Alam. (2026). PAUSE: A Privacy-Preserving Self-Reflection Tool for AI-Associated Cognitive Offloading. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13155
title: Four-domain mapping of AI-associated cognitive offloading (D1-D4)
description: The article defines AI-associated cognitive offloading as the pattern where "what gets delegated is the thinking itself: reasoning through a problem, generating ideas, learning new material, or communicating with other people". It organises reflection around four domains grounded in the 2023-2026 literature: reasoning and critical thinking, creativity and originality, research and learning, and social and communicative capacity. Each domain is treated as a continuum on which self-reported behavioural patterns indicate offloading depth, not underlying ability. The author states these are "a working vocabulary grounded in the literature, not a tested factor structure".
requirements: Domains are read as indicators of self-reported offloading patterns, not measures of underlying ability
constraints: The four-domain structure is a working organisation, not a confirmed factor structure
Scope is limited to consumer-facing LLM-class tools, excluding recommender systems and embodied AI
The emotional strand (anxiety, AI guilt, emotional dependence) falls outside the current scope
target_learners: Adult LLM users (researchers, creatives, students, knowledge workers, software engineers)
target_learning_goals: Maintaining reasoning, creativity, learning, and social-communicative capacities while using generative AI
examples: Figure 1 maps the four domains D1-D4 onto distinct strands of the 2023-2026 empirical literature feeding into the self-check

citation: Mahbub Ul Alam. (2026). PAUSE: A Privacy-Preserving Self-Reflection Tool for AI-Associated Cognitive Offloading. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13155
title: PAUSE self-reflection web tool
description: PAUSE (Patterns of AI Use: Self-Examination) is a public, no-login web tool that "delivers a short, free, no-login self-check, scores it entirely in the browser, and returns descriptive, domain-aware reflections". It pairs reverse-scored behavioural Likert items with a claim-evaluation reasoning probe, a 90-second Alternative Uses creativity probe, and a retrospective before-and-after block reported separately as a trajectory indicator. Domain readings are scaled 0-100 and mapped to four fixed descriptive bands, with no overall composite. The author frames it as a reflective design probe, not a validated instrument.
requirements: At least three items answered per domain for a reading to display
JavaScript enabled, since rendering and scoring run client-side
Respondents aged 18 or over per the soft age check
constraints: Not a validated psychological instrument; presents no reliability or validity evidence
Cross-sectional, so it describes current patterns rather than accumulated change
Not designed for minors; readings must not drive consequential decisions
target_learners: Adults who regularly use LLM-based AI tools
target_learning_goals: Self-awareness of AI-associated cognitive offloading patterns and more deliberate AI engagement
examples: A worked example scores a fabricated creative professional at D1=71 (Moderate) and demonstrates a six-month comparison via return tokens

citation: Mahbub Ul Alam. (2026). PAUSE: A Privacy-Preserving Self-Reflection Tool for AI-Associated Cognitive Offloading. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13155
title: Citation-grounded behavioural item design with reverse scoring
description: PAUSE's items follow a reusable design pattern: every LLM-era item is anchored to a 2023-2026 paper, items are behavioural rather than dispositional, and roughly one third per domain are reverse-scored, since "Roughly one third of the items per domain (two or three of seven) are reverse-scored to counter acquiescence". Each scored item carries an expandable rationale panel and a reference panel quoting the anchoring study with a resolvable DOI, so respondents can inspect the evidence behind a question. All items include a not-applicable option, and unanswered items are dropped rather than imputed.
requirements: Each item needs an anchoring study with an exact quotable passage and resolvable DOI
Probe non-responses must be scored as not applicable, never as uncritical acceptance
constraints: Anchors are supporting evidence for an item's framing, not validation of it
Several anchoring studies are recent preprints
Some items conflate early consultation with substitution, an imperfect proxy for whether reasoning stayed engaged
target_learners: Adult self-reflecting LLM users
target_learning_goals: Accurate self-assessment of AI-use behaviours across four offloading domains
examples: Item B5 renders the behavioural task, a Why this question panel, and a Reference panel quoting Dergaa et al. (2024) with a DOI

article_title: PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning
citation: Yu Liu, Zeming Liu, Tianle Zhang, Zihao Cheng, Yuhang Guo, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang, Yunhong Wang, Haifeng Wang. (2026). PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18861
title: PersonaPath benchmark for Knowledge-Centric learning path planning
description: PersonaPath is a benchmark that "pairs 2,000 fine-grained learner personas with a hierarchical knowledge graph of 347 textbooks, 1,751 units, and 4,092 concepts across 77 subjects" connected by prerequisite dependencies. Given a learner profile, mastery state, and target unit, a model must generate a prerequisite-respecting path that adapts to prior knowledge and reaches the goal. Personas are stratified into Low-, Average-, and High-performing archetypes in an approximate 1:3:1 ratio, and paths are scored on Validity, Adaptivity, and Efficiency with a joint Final Pass criterion.
requirements: Explicit learner goals, a prerequisite knowledge structure, and learner-specific mastery states are the three inputs the pipeline is designed around
constraints: The benchmark is grounded in Chinese textbooks and curricula; learner states and mastery updates are synthetic
target_learners: learners from primary school to higher education in the Chinese curriculum
target_learning_goals: goal-directed, prerequisite-aware selection and ordering of knowledge toward a target unit
examples: Two educators independently rated 100 sampled personas on a 5-point Likert scale, with mean ratings from 4.11 to 4.68 and ICC(2,2) from 0.74 to 0.85

citation: Yu Liu, Zeming Liu, Tianle Zhang, Zihao Cheng, Yuhang Guo, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang, Yunhong Wang, Haifeng Wang. (2026). PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18861
title: Knowledge-Centric (KC) paradigm for learning path planning
description: The KC paradigm contrasts with the dominant Exercise-Centric (EC) recommendation paradigm: instead of inferring the next exercise from item-level interaction logs, "a Knowledge-Centric (KC) paradigm, which decides what knowledge a learner should study and in what order." A KC planner reads each learner's progress and goal, selects knowledge from a structured knowledge space, and orders it into a path respecting prerequisite relations among concepts. Evaluation requires explicit learner personas, long-term goals, and curriculum-scale prerequisite structures together, since the goal sets the destination, the mastery state the starting point, and the prerequisite graph the routes between them.
requirements: Evaluation requires explicit learner personas, long-term goals, and curriculum-scale prerequisite structures jointly
constraints: Existing benchmarks primarily support exercise recommendation and rarely jointly provide these components, per the article
target_learners: learners with similar exercise records but different goals
target_learning_goals: selecting and ordering knowledge, not exercises, toward an explicit target
examples: Figure 1 contrasts two students with identical correctness records who need different paths because their targets differ

It was evaluated in a within-subjects study against V1.

article_title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
citation: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Hengyi Feng, Mingrui Chen, Sizhe Qiu, Wentao Zhang. (2026). OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23088
title: Four-capability taxonomy for organizing educational foundation-model supervision
description: OmniEdu organizes education-specific supervision around four complementary capability categories defined "according to the behaviors to be learned" rather than by source or subject. Subject competence covers solving K-12 problems and explaining answers across mathematics, science, reading, and writing; curriculum grounding captures grade-level alignment, knowledge points, prerequisite relations, and difficulty; diagnostic reasoning targets identifying errors and misconceptions and inferring missing prerequisites; pedagogical action and scaffolding covers selecting and executing interventions such as hints, questions, prerequisite review, or direct explanation. The taxonomy provides a common language for both data construction and evaluation.
requirements: Each example is assigned to a single primary capability according to its main supervision objective, with other properties retained as secondary metadata.
constraints: The taxonomy is designed for K-12 educational scenarios and is implemented through fine-grained task buckets within each capability.

target_learning_goals: Subject problem solving
Curriculum-structured knowledge
Error diagnosis and misconception repair
Pedagogically appropriate tutoring responses
examples: The final corpus allocates 45.5% of examples to subject competence, 20.3% to pedagogical action and scaffolding, 13.4% to curriculum grounding, and 7.8% to diagnostic reasoning, plus 12.9% general-purpose instruction.

article_title: OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching
citation: Hao Liang, Qihan Lin, Meiyi Qiang, Linzhuang Sun, Hengyi Feng, Mingrui Chen, Sizhe Qiu, Wentao Zhang. (2026). OmniEdu: Open Foundation Models for Learning and Teaching. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23088
title: OmniEdu capability-oriented instruction-tuning corpus and six-stage data pipeline
description: A reproducible data-construction pipeline that curates an education-specific pool of approximately 1.34M examples drawn from more than 100 datasets and educational resources into 60,951 high-quality examples containing about 12.0M supervised response tokens. The six stages combine deterministic cleaning and evaluation decontamination, LLM-assisted semantic auditing and rewriting with 0-100 usability scoring, task-specific quality scoring, k-center greedy diversity selection over BGE-M3 embeddings under token budgets, and pedagogical instruction assignment. Together with 9,048 general-purpose examples, the final corpus contains 69,999 examples and 15.96M supervised response tokens, with provenance and audit metadata retained throughout.

constraints: Examples overlapping the final evaluation set are removed to prevent evaluation contamination; rewritten examples are retained only if re-audited as keep.
