citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community.
title: Framework for institutional change in the AI era: arrival technologies versus adoption technologies across six dimensions
description: The article applies the authors' framework for leading institutional change in the AI era, which distinguishes AI as an "arrival technology" that "disrupt[s] our practices and bypass[es] our evaluation and dissemination processes" from prior adoption technologies with strong evidence bases. Table 1 lays out six dimensions of AI-driven change (evidence base, rate of change, scope and intended use, faculty agency, change agent role, student role) with design implications: humble and local inquiries, approaches over tools, broadening learning goals, mapping disruption and needs, facilitating collective inquiry, and treating students as partners. The workshop series is presented as one instantiation of this framework.
requirements: Change initiatives proceed through local and humble exploration rather than dissemination of unevidenced practices
constraints: The framework addresses arrival technologies that lack a pedagogical evidence base and change rapidly, unlike evidence-based adoption technologies
target_learners: University physics faculty
target_learning_goals: Departmental capacity to respond collectively to AI-driven change in teaching and assessment
examples: The six-session workshop series operationalized the framework by surfacing local data, facilitating small-group inquiry, and building a shared repository
key_sources: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23887

article_title: A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community
citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community.
title: Workshop session structure: local data, small-group testing, collective discussion
description: Each of the six sessions followed a common three-part structure: facilitators presented local data or department-sourced materials, faculty tested and reflected on the materials in small groups, and the whole group discussed them together. The article states: "We started by sharing local data, whether around AI policies and use or activities gathered from different courses, and then had faculty test and reflect on the materials in small groups, followed by collective discussion." This structure embodies the framework's principles of leading with student use and facilitating collective inquiry rather than disseminating best practices.
requirements: Local data and department-sourced materials must be available to anchor each session
constraints: Framed as collective, local inquiry rather than a general faculty training workshop
target_learners: University physics faculty in a departmental learning community
target_learning_goals: Developing shared departmental approaches to AI use in courses
examples: Session 3 opened with survey data on students' correctness-checking, then faculty tested AI chatbots on real anonymized homework in small groups before collective discussion
key_sources: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23887

article_title: A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community
citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A Workshop Series for Effective Use of AI in Uncertain Times: Building a Physics Faculty Learning Community.
title: Shared departmental repository of AI-related teaching resources
description: The series' central product is a shared, evolving departmental repository pairing curated materials with framing for their use. The article reports: "Currently, it holds 5 entries, each pairing curated materials with brief framing for how to use them." Entries cover AI syllabus statements (including four sample policies spanning no use to full use), classroom discussion materials, student surveys with results across courses, homework tasks with AI integration, and assessment structures such as oral exams. Materials were shared with the department at the start of the following semester and continue to be updated.
requirements: Ongoing curation to keep the repository current as tools and practices evolve
constraints: The repository was also intended partly as a response to involving colleagues who did not participate in the series
target_learners: University physics faculty
target_learning_goals: Shaping course AI policies, classroom discussions, homework tasks, and assessment approaches
examples: The AI syllabus statements entry offers four sample policies spanning from no AI use to limited, conditional, and full-use

article_title: From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning
citation: Xinchen Ma, Shuimu Wang, Gaole He, Yanbin Zhang, Chunyang Wang, Yunshi Lan, Weining Qian. (2026). From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24083
title: PIVOT: a three-stage pedagogy-guided instructional video tutoring framework
description: PIVOT is described as "a three-stage pedagogy-guided generative video tutoring framework for STEM education that supports active learning". Stage 1 generates structured instructional storyboards organizing objectives, prerequisite activation, explanations, visual plans, worked examples, and assessment probes. Stage 2 transforms the storyboard into shot-level Manim animations with a multimodal pedagogical verification harness covering layout, factual, and cognitive clarity, plus constrained layout prompting and automated code repair. Stage 3 generates storyboard-grounded quizzes and targeted remediation videos conditioned on learner responses, forming a closed feedback loop.
requirements: A learner-specified topic or learning goal as input
Storyboard generation must precede executable Manim code generation, narration synthesis, assessment construction, and multimodal verification
constraints: The system performs interaction-level adaptation conditioned on immediate learner responses rather than maintaining a fully personalized long-term learner model, with no long-term knowledge tracing or curriculum progression modeling
The multi-stage pipeline introduces substantially higher computational cost than direct multimedia synthesis approaches
target_learners: STEM learners at high-school and university level
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of STEM knowledge points in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and computer science
Correction of misconceptions through targeted remediation
examples: For the topic Bubble Sort, the storyboard specifies learning objectives, prerequisite activation of arrays and loops, a worked example on array [5, 1, 4, 2, 8], and an assessment probe on which element is fixed after the first pass
key_sources: Xinchen Ma, Shuimu Wang, Gaole He, Yanbin Zhang, Chunyang Wang, Yunshi Lan, Weining Qian. (2026). From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24083

article_title: From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning
citation: Xinchen Ma, Shuimu Wang, Gaole He, Yanbin Zhang, Chunyang Wang, Yunshi Lan, Weining Qian. (2026). From Content Generation to Learning Support: Pedagogy-Guided Generative Video Tutors for STEM Learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24083
title: Six-component pedagogically grounded instructional storyboard structure
description: The framework's instructional planning stage produces a storyboard whose components are "grounded in educational the-ory, each serving a clear pedagogical purpose": Learning Objectives, Prerequisite Activation, Concept Explanations, Visual Representation Plans, Worked Examples, and Diagnostic Assessment Probes. Each component is tied to an educational-theory rationale (e.g., Bloom's taxonomy for objectives, cognitive load for prerequisite activation, multimedia learning principles for visual plans, worked-example research for examples, formative assessment for probes). The storyboard serves as the semantic backbone for downstream code generation, narration, assessment, and verification.
requirements: Storyboard must progress from prerequisite knowledge to core concepts, then to examples and assessment
Each shot should focus on one local learning goal
Narration should explain why the concept works, not only describe what appears on screen
target_learners: STEM learners in high-school and university settings
target_learning_goals: Structured conceptual understanding of a specified STEM topic
Early detection of misconceptions via diagnostic probes
examples: The generated Bubble Sort storyboard defines the objective of understanding adjacent comparisons and swaps, activates prior knowledge of arrays and loops, and includes an assessment probe targeting the misconception that the smallest element is fixed first

article_title: From Sentiment Classification to Actionable and Responsible Feedback: A Scoping Review and Evidence Map of NLP in Student Evaluation of Teaching, 2015–2026
citation: Eicher, J., & da Silva, R. (2026). From Sentiment Classification to Actionable and Responsible Feedback: A Scoping Review and Evidence Map of NLP in Student Evaluation of Teaching, 2015–2026. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27939
title: Five-axis evidence map framework: a technical axis (RQ1) read against four value dimensions (analytical depth, methodological validation and reporting, actionability, responsible use)
description: The review's organizing framework separates technical sophistication (RQ1: tasks, methods, technological families, contexts) from four analytically separate value dimensions (RQ2–RQ5). The review states it "distinguishes technical sophistication (RQ1) from four related but analytically separate value dimensions (RQ2–RQ5)" covering depth, validation and reporting, actionability, and responsible use. Its core argument is that "Technical complexity should therefore not be used as a proxy for analytical depth, methodological robustness, educational usefulness, or responsible use." The framework is operationalized through seven extraction domains and versioned coding rules (D1–D5 depth, A0–A5 actionability, M1–M11 reporting indicators) applied to 421 studies.
requirements: Requires verbatim-evidence extraction with adjudication so that composite constructs (D1–D5, A0–A5) are derived by explicit, versioned coding rules rather than assigned directly by LLM judges
constraints: The review states all proportions and cross-tabulations are descriptive of the 421 mapped studies, not causal effects or population estimates, because the corpus was built without probability sampling
target_learners: higher education instructors and institutions using student evaluation of teaching
target_learning_goals: actionable and responsible use of NLP analysis of open-ended teaching-evaluation comments
examples: The review maps 421 studies along the five axes and identifies the A2+ to A3+ actionability cliff as the map's sharpest quantified gap
key_sources: Eicher, J., & da Silva, R. (2026). From Sentiment Classification to Actionable and Responsible Feedback: A Scoping Review and Evidence Map of NLP in Student Evaluation of Teaching, 2015–2026. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27939

article_title: From Sentiment Classification to Actionable and Responsible Feedback: A Scoping Review and Evidence Map of NLP in Student Evaluation of Teaching, 2015–2026
citation: Eicher, J., & da Silva, R. (2026). From Sentiment Classification to Actionable and Responsible Feedback: A Scoping Review and Evidence Map of NLP in Student Evaluation of Teaching, 2015–2026. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27939
title: Versioned reproducibility repository for the SET-NLP evidence map (code, study list, prompts, codebooks, adjudication bases)
description: A public GitHub deposit containing the materials needed to audit and reconstruct the review's analyses. The review states: "The materials needed to audit and reconstruct this review's analyses are available in a versioned code repository" at https://github.com/rafa-rodriguess/LT_NLP_SET_pub. The deposit includes the classification and prevalence code, the canonical list of the 421 included studies, the inventories of the 38 original and 32 supplementary extraction questions, operational prompt texts for discovery, screening, eligibility, and extraction, the frozen M10/M11 denominator policy and codebook, the PRISMA-ScR checklist, and the canonical bases of model responses and human adjudications. Reconstruction from the frozen bases does not require calling the models.
requirements: Audit and reconstruction rely on the frozen bases in the deposit; full texts of the primary studies are not redistributed, with license, persistent identifier, and version label indicated in the repository
constraints: The review notes reconstruction does not claim bit-for-bit re-execution on the same proprietary weights after deprecation
target_learners: researchers conducting or auditing AI-assisted systematic and scoping reviews
target_learning_goals: reproducible, auditable evidence synthesis of NLP in student evaluation of teaching
examples: The deposit preserves the original extraction and the supplementary extension separately, and coverage labels do not recode N=421

article_title: PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation
citation: Rashid Azraf Jahin, Saadman Sajid, Khan Raiyan Ibne Reza, Sumaiya Tabassum Nimi. (2026). PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation. IEEE CSDE 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00664v1
title: PhysicsMate benchmark of 1,834 curriculum-grounded Bengali physics QA pairs
description: PhysicsMate is a benchmark of 1,834 question-answer pairs derived from the official NCTB Grade 9-10 physics textbook (13 chapters, 359 pages), written in formal Bengali. Each pair is "linked to a specific knowledge node and originating semantic unit", giving curricular provenance back to textbook passages. The corpus is partitioned into training (n = 1,374; 74.9%), validation (n = 185; 10.1%) and held-out test (n = 275; 15.0%) sets, stratified by chapter, with programmatic checks that no question ID appears in more than one partition. The benchmark and knowledge graph are released with a Dataset Card.
requirements: Each benchmark item must be grounded in a specific NCTB textbook passage kept as metadata, so answers use the source curriculum's terminology, formulas and unit conventions.
constraints: The benchmark covers a single national curriculum, NCTB Grade 9-10 physics, and generalization to other syllabi or subjects has not been tested.
target_learners: Grade 9-10 secondary physics students in Bengali-medium education
target_learning_goals: Curriculum-aligned secondary physics question answering in Bengali
examples: Chapter 1 (Physical Quantities and Measurement) contributes the most items (302), while Chapter 12 (Magnetic Effects of Current) contributes the fewest (82).
key_sources: Rashid Azraf Jahin, Saadman Sajid, Khan Raiyan Ibne Reza, Sumaiya Tabassum Nimi. (2026). PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation. IEEE CSDE 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00664

article_title: PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation
citation: Rashid Azraf Jahin, Saadman Sajid, Khan Raiyan Ibne Reza, Sumaiya Tabassum Nimi. (2026). PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation. IEEE CSDE 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00664v1
title: Multi-relational knowledge graph of the NCTB physics syllabus with ten ontological node types
description: The knowledge graph formalizes the 13-chapter NCTB syllabus as a multi-relational structure with 1,760 nodes across 10 ontological types (concepts, questions, quantities, figures, examples, entities, definitions, formulas, laws, HSC topics) and 2,600 directed edges spanning 30 relation types. Relations include curricular hierarchy (part_of), applicability (applies_to), visual grounding (illustrates), example relations (example_of), dependency (depends_on) and provenance (derived_from). The graph serves as "a structured curricular index of the source material" used for category-level analysis, with every node traceable to source textbook pages.
requirements: Extraction uses a predefined domain ontology and a fixed structured prompt so equivalent curricular facts receive consistent representation, and each record retains source-page provenance.
constraints: The 10-node ontology maps directly to STEM domains; non-STEM or humanities curricula would require restructuring the declarative and procedural primitives into causal, temporal and narrative relation types.
target_learners: Grade 9-10 secondary physics students in Bengali-medium education
target_learning_goals: Structured curricular knowledge representation enabling category-level evaluation of physics QA
examples: Table I reports node counts per type, e.g. 397 concepts, 224 quantities, 83 formulas and 65 laws.

citation: Rashid Azraf Jahin, Saadman Sajid, Khan Raiyan Ibne Reza, Sumaiya Tabassum Nimi. (2026). PhysicsMate: A Curriculum-Grounded Bengali Benchmark for Secondary Physics QA with Small-Model Adaptation. IEEE CSDE 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00664v1
title: Curriculum-grounded ontology framework for building educational QA benchmarks
description: The article proposes an end-to-end framework in which a national curriculum textbook is ingested via OCR and semantic chunking, formalized against a predefined domain ontology, and used to construct a provenance-traced QA benchmark with category-level evaluation. Unlike prior systems that construct graphs from text, PhysicsMate "utilizes the curriculum-defined ontology to build and partition the benchmark and support the category-level evaluation". The authors argue the framework generalizes to adjacent disciplines (secondary chemistry, biology) and to neighbouring South Asian curricula sharing classical physics and SI units at Grade 9-10.
requirements: A curriculum textbook serving as the source of truth, a predefined ontology matching the domain's knowledge types, and structured extraction prompts that limit representation variability.
constraints: Humanities curricula require restructuring declarative and procedural primitives into causal, temporal and narrative relation types; generalization to other syllabi has not been tested.
target_learners: Secondary students in national-curriculum systems, particularly under-resourced regional education ecosystems in South Asia
target_learning_goals: Curriculum-aligned STEM question answering and controlled category-level model evaluation
examples: The extraction pipeline yielded 811 semantic units from three-page contextual windows with two-page overlaps, each traceable to its originating text.

article_title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware–Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
citation: Sidney Shapiro and Joshua Lindemann. (2026). On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware–Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02510
title: CourseChat: an on-premises multi-course RAG tutor with course-isolated collections, twin serving nodes, and prebuilt quiz banks
description: CourseChat is an on-premises retrieval-augmented generation tutor for undergraduate business courses, deployed behind a campus web gateway and intended for Moodle-embedded use. As the abstract states, "Six isolated course offerings—each keyed by its own course reference number (CRN)—share twin edge AI hosts running a FastAPI service, a local vector database, and a local large language model (LLM) served by Ollama." It offers grounded conversation with citations and module-scoped practice quizzes, keeping textbooks and student dialogue on institutional infrastructure.
requirements: Isolation is enforced by separate course ids, separate on-disk trees, separate Qdrant collections, and ?course= routing
constraints: The authors state the results do not establish learning gains; faculty ratings, peak-load capacity, and complete public-gateway acceptance remain separate evaluation needs
target_learners: undergraduate business education students
target_learning_goals: engaging with assigned course material
independent problem attempts with hints and feedback
checking explanations against course sources
examples: Six offerings (Courses 1–6) share one application binary while remaining isolated at the data and routing layers; production runs llama3.1:8b on both nodes

citation: Sidney Shapiro and Joshua Lindemann. (2026). On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware–Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02510
title: Treat model choice, evidence selection, serving compatibility, and product design as a joint engineering decision when building a campus AI tutor
description: The article argues that a tutoring system's quality cannot be improved by swapping one component in isolation: latency, memory, retrieval, and product surfaces interact. As the abstract concludes, "The results support treating model choice, evidence selection, serving compatibility, and product design as a joint engineering decision." The bake-off held the retrieval stack fixed to make generator comparisons interpretable, and a separate experiment changed model and response contract together so its gains could not be attributed to scale alone.
requirements: Keep the serving retrieval stack fixed during model comparisons so failures are traceable
Promotion requires clearing a classroom speed gate plus a demonstrated quality improvement
constraints: The authors state they do not claim that 8B is universally optimal, and no controlled learning-outcome comparison is reported
target_learners: undergraduate business education students
target_learning_goals: grounded explanations of assigned course material
reliable practice with course-scoped feedback
examples: The project retained the 8B production model despite sufficient memory to trial larger candidates, because no replacement demonstrated the required combination of quality, continuity, integration, and operational readiness

article_title: The psychological mechanisms and behavioral determinants of academic integrity in the age of artificial intelligence
citation: Yilmaz A (2026) The psychological mechanisms and behavioral determinants of academic integrity in the age of artificial intelligence. Front. Psychol. 17:1853790. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1853790
title: Stimulus–Organism–Response framework for AI-assisted academic dishonesty as a moderated mediation process
description: The article organizes AI-assisted academic dishonesty within the Stimulus–Organism–Response (SOR) framework, in which psychological vulnerabilities and socio-contextual conditions act as stimuli, cheating tendency is the organismic mechanism, and dishonesty is the behavioral response, with AI use as a moderating technological condition. The authors state the "SOR framework is well aligned with the proposed moderated mediation model, as it explains how psychological and contextual stimuli may be linked to AI-assisted academic dishonesty through cheating tendency." The model was tested with 1,045 undergraduates using PROCESS Model 14.
requirements: Measurement of psychological antecedents, cheating tendency, AI use, dishonesty, and social-contextual factors as distinct constructs
constraints: AI use is positioned as a behavioral amplifier in a non-causal statistical sense, not a direct cause of unethical behavior
target_learners: undergraduate university students
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
ethical use of AI in academic work
examples: The study tested the model with seven measurement instruments, Pearson correlations, multiple regression, and Hayes' PROCESS Model 14 with 5,000-sample bootstrapping.

article_title: Governing generative AI in higher education: Emerging policy approaches and support ecosystems at innovative U.S. universities
citation: Qian, Y. (2026). Governing generative AI in higher education: emerging policy approaches and support ecosystems at innovative U.S. Universities. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00233-x
title: Four-pillar framework for GenAI-era academic integrity: accountability, transparency, equity, and privacy
description: The article proposes that academic integrity when GenAI is permitted under stated conditions is organized by "a four-pillar framework for GenAI-era integrity: accountability, transparency, equity, and privacy." Accountability frames human agency in collaboration, with users expected to steer, critique, verify, and revise AI outputs rather than defer to them. Transparency operates through disclosure and attribution as a design principle reducing ambiguity before submission. Equity holds that integrity expectations are fair only when students have comparable opportunities to access and understand tools and norms. Privacy is treated as an integrity condition because inappropriate data sharing can undermine fairness and erode trust. Together the pillars define the conditions under which AI-assisted academic work can remain legitimate.
requirements: Integrity expectations must be paired with comparable student access to tools and norms for the equity pillar to hold
constraints: The framework is derived from document analysis of 50 innovation-oriented U.S. universities and is offered as analytically transferable insight, not statistical generalizability
target_learners: higher education students
higher education instructors
target_learning_goals: responsible and ethical use of generative AI in academic work
academic integrity under AI-permitted conditions
examples: Arizona State's syllabus toolkit characterizes AI tools as partners in work while emphasizing that humans must iterate on AI outputs
Yale's guidance instructs community members not to enter confidential, legally restricted, or moderate/high-risk data into AI tools
key_sources: Qian, Y. (2026). Governing generative AI in higher education: emerging policy approaches and support ecosystems at innovative U.S. Universities. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00233-x

title: Shift academic integrity effort from policing to design by pairing integrity policies with assessment innovation and AI literacy
description: The article recommends that institutions move away from detector-based enforcement toward a pedagogy-first integrity model. It advises investing in "process-rich assignments that include drafts, prompt logs, reflections, oral explanations, and revision histories" and mainstreaming AI literacy as a core academic capability rather than a remediation activity. This principle follows from the study's findings that institutions converge on detector skepticism and AI-literacy support while assignment-redesign resources remain scarce, indicating a gap between guidance and implementation supports.

Every syllabus carries a clear AI policy with standardized options
constraints: Assessment-redesign strategies increase instructional workload and do not eliminate ambiguity

It argues the study "challenges traditional cognitive taxonomies and calls for reimagining AI literacy as a multidimensional competence encompassing creativity, ethics, and critical reasoning essential for navigating AI-mediated learning environments." The framework arises from the study's finding that students' GenAI use engaged creativity, ethical reasoning, and epistemic vigilance together rather than separately.

citation: Reed, J. M., Ferdig, R. E., Dodson, T. M., Gunstad, J., & Hughes, J. W. (2026). AI Literacy and Scenario-based Ethical Judgment About Generative AI Among Undergraduate Students. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09757-w
title: Six adapted GenAI ethical scenarios for assessing scenario-based ethical judgment
description: A six-scenario measure adapted with permission from Dodson et al. (2025), presenting dilemmas mirroring common academic situations where AI might be used, with response options of ethical, unethical, or unsure. Three scenarios depict learning-support uses and three depict substitutionary uses. The article notes "Internal consistency for the six-item measure was modest (KR-20 = 0.61)", which the authors attribute to the ceiling effect and limited variability.
requirements: Scenarios are scored dichotomously as correct or incorrect, with unsure coded as incorrect
constraints: Modest internal consistency (KR-20 = 0.61)
Pronounced ceiling effect limited ability to differentiate judgment in ambiguous situations
Fixed presentation order means order or priming effects cannot be excluded
target_learners: undergraduate students across majors
target_learning_goals: ethical judgment about generative AI use in academic contexts
examples: Q1 presents a student using AI to summarize textbook notes and verifying with her professor; Q5 presents a student minimally editing an AI-generated assignment before submitting it

title: Bounded authority model for teacher–AI authority distribution
description: The bounded authority model describes how teachers distribute authority between themselves and AI systems interacting with students. It has two dimensions: authority boundaries, where "teachers retain ultimate control because professional responsibility cannot be delegated", and expertise boundaries, where "AI lacks teachers’ contextual knowledge of students, classrooms, and institutions". The article states this model "operationalizes bounded authority" through protective layers and extends beyond education to other high-stakes professional domains.
requirements: AI systems operate under human supervision rather than autonomously
constraints: Derived from a qualitative study with six secondary teachers in education contexts
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: safe and appropriate use of LLM-powered chatbots in teacher-supervised learning activities

article_title: College students’ metacognitive awareness of generative-AI reliance: an experimental study of decision confidence and attribution bias
citation: Ren S (2026) College students’ metacognitive awareness of generative-AI reliance: an experimental study of decision confidence and attribution bias. Front. Psychol. 17:1926110. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1926110
title: Metacognitive dependence: a descriptive framework for perceived–behavioral reliance mismatch in AI-assisted decisions
description: The article introduces "metacognitive dependence" as an integrative conceptual label for a specific mismatch: students' observable reliance on generative-AI advice may diverge from their awareness of how strongly that advice shaped their judgment. The authors state the term is "not treated here as a validated unitary latent trait"; it organizes four theoretically related but distinct indicators — behavioral reliance, perceived reliance, decision confidence, and attributional responsibility. The framework also distinguishes overreliance (acceptance of incorrect AI advice) from trust calibration and metacognitive monitoring accuracy.
requirements: Behavioral reliance, awareness calibration, confidence, and attribution are analyzed separately rather than as one psychometric construct
constraints: The framework is descriptive; evidence that the measures change together is not psychometric proof of a single latent construct
target_learners: undergraduate students using generative AI for academic decisions
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring of AI influence on judgments and decisions
examples: In the experiment, open ChatGPT support produced a negative mean signed discrepancy (behavioral reliance exceeding perceived reliance), while reflection brought signed discrepancy near zero.

citation: Ren S (2026) College students’ metacognitive awareness of generative-AI reliance: an experimental study of decision confidence and attribution bias. Front. Psychol. 17:1926110. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1926110
title: Insert a brief pre-decision metacognitive reflection prompt after AI consultation to promote discriminative reliance on AI advice
description: Before finalizing an AI-assisted answer, students respond to short prompts evaluating their own understanding, the AI's trustworthiness, and reasons for accepting or rejecting the recommendation. In the experiment the prompts asked, among other things, "Which part of the AI explanation is supported by evidence rather than ﬂuency?" This minimal intervention reduced acceptance of incorrect AI advice and improved perceived–behavioral correspondence without suppressing use of correct advice.
requirements: AI-assisted task setting where students submit an initial answer before consulting AI, allowing the prompt to sit between the AI interaction and the final answer
constraints: Findings concern bounded academic decision tasks rather than long-term learning; the model was queried dynamically so exact response replication is impossible
target_learners: undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: calibrated trust in AI advice; resistance to plausible but incorrect recommendations
examples: Participants in the reflection condition answered three metacognitive prompts after the ChatGPT interaction and before finalizing answers, and spent longer per AI-assisted trial (104.7 vs. 86.4 seconds).

article_title: Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development
citation: Dai (2026). Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1829268
title: FRAC Feedback Literacy Script (Filter–Reason–Act–Check)
description: FRAC is a four-step feedback literacy script that guides students' processing of external AI feedback: "Filter, identifying the type of problem addressed by the feedback; Reason, judging whether the feedback was valid and relevant to the current task", then Act (implementing adopted feedback as a specific revision) and Check (reviewing whether the revision achieved the intended result). Training lasted approximately 15 to 25 minutes before T1 with brief reviews before T1 and T2; students recorded decision sheets at T1 and T2 as process data, with return rates exceeding 90% per round.
requirements: Students must process AI feedback systematically through the script and complete decision sheets recording how they handled each feedback item
constraints: In this study it was implemented with undergraduate English majors using Claude Sonnet 4 feedback during T1 and T2 only
target_learners: undergraduate English majors with basic academic writing skills
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation and effective uptake of AI-generated writing feedback
deep revision of argumentative essays
examples: FRAC group and combined group students completed decision sheets at T1 and T2 recording how they processed AI feedback; implementation was verified through submission rates, completeness checks, and classroom observations

citation: Dai (2026). Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1829268
title: APCA Assessment-Performance Calibration Activity
description: APCA is a self-assessment calibration training organized around "a process of “self-assessment-comparison-adjustment,” requiring students to repeatedly compare their own judgments with external evaluations across multiple task rounds". It has four stages: Anchor (reviewing sample texts at different quality levels), Predict (estimating one's score and confidence), Compare (identifying judgment bias against teacher ratings), and Adjust (modifying evaluation strategies based on recurring over- or underestimation). Each round lasted approximately 10 to 15 minutes with structured calibration logs, implemented continuously from T0 to T3, with log completion exceeding 90% per round.
requirements: Students complete structured calibration logs recording predicted score, confidence judgment, discrepancy from the teacher rating, and reflection on recurring bias, reviewed against a unified feedback protocol
constraints: The APCA group showed lower raw self-assessment error at baseline, so analyses used baseline-adjusted models; self-assessment and comparison stages were retained at T3 even though AI support was withdrawn
target_learners: undergraduate English majors with basic academic writing skills
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of writing quality
reduction of overconfidence in self-judgment
examples: In each round students completed a calibration log and the researcher provided brief written comments for use in the next task

citation: Dai (2026). Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1829268
title: Embed AI writing tools within instructional support structures rather than treating them merely as instant feedback sources
description: The article concludes that when AI writing tools are used in teaching, "they should not be treated merely as sources of instant feedback. Instead, they should be embedded within specific instructional support structures", so students develop independent judgment and self-regulated learning while using feedback. The rationale is that AI feedback does not automatically improve writing; its value depends on whether learners can evaluate, select, and transform feedback into revision decisions, as shown by the differentiated effects of FRAC and APCA.
requirements: Structured metacognitive support (feedback-processing scripts and/or calibration activities) must accompany AI feedback access
constraints: Evidence comes from one study of English majors at a single university; the article calls for testing in more diverse contexts
target_learners: undergraduate L2/EFL writers using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: independent revision judgment
self-regulated writing development with AI support
examples: The study embedded AI feedback within FRAC decision sheets and APCA calibration logs across four writing task points rather than providing AI feedback alone

article_title: ProductiveMath: A Generative-AI-Powered App to Support Productive Failure Teaching
citation: Antonio Laverghetta Jr., Simone Luchini, Averie Linell, Roni Reiter-Palmon and Roger Beaty. (2024). The creative psychometric item generator: a framework for item generation and validation using large language models. CREAI 2024: Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Creativity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00202
title: CPIG: the creative psychometric item generator framework
description: CPIG is an iterative LLM-based framework for generating and validating creativity test items for the creative problem-solving (CPS) task. It uses LLMs as "item generators" to write items, "item response generators" to create human-like solutions under baseline, demographic, or psychometric prompting profiles, and an item scorer (a roberta-base originality model) to select k high-originality items as few-shot exemplars for the next generation round. The article hypothesizes that "items with high quality should enable more creative responses and will tend to elicit better originality scores on average than those that are of lower quality," making originality a proxy for item quality. It extends automated item generation, which has focused on multiple-choice cognitive and non-cognitive items, into the creativity domain.
requirements: Items must describe sufficiently complex yet ambiguous scenarios with no canonically correct solution, and the framework requires an automated originality scoring model validated against human ratings
constraints: The framework optimizes originality only, which the authors note is just one metric for judging creative outputs; item quality depends directly on the automated evaluation, and the authors caution against using CPIG items with human participants until more extensive review
target_learners: human test takers of creativity assessments
LLM test takers used as human simulacra
target_learning_goals: measuring creative problem-solving and originality of ideas
examples: In each trial, word lists generated by gpt-3.5-turbo constrain item generation, and four selected exemplar items are included in the prompt for the next of five iterations
key_sources: Antonio Laverghetta Jr., Simone Luchini, Averie Linell, Roni Reiter-Palmon and Roger Beaty. (2024). The creative psychometric item generator: a framework for item generation and validation using large language models. CREAI 2024: Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Creativity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00202

article_title: ProductiveMath: A Generative-AI-Powered App to Support Productive Failure Teaching
citation: Antonio Laverghetta Jr., Simone Luchini, Averie Linell, Roni Reiter-Palmon and Roger Beaty. (2024). The creative psychometric item generator: a framework for item generation and validation using large language models. CREAI 2024: Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Creativity. https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.00202
title: Multi-stage prompting with rule-based quality filters for LLM item generation
description: CPIG's item generation follows a multi-stage prompting pattern: a first LLM produces word lists (three names, a place, and an action) that item-generator LLMs must incorporate, which the authors say helps "maximize diversity in scenario content by using different word lists to ensure no two item generation prompts are the same." Generated scenarios then pass rule-based validity filters: a Flesch reading-ease floor of 45 with a 140-token minimum, a string blacklist targeting priming (e.g., scenarios containing "on the one hand" or "is torn between"), and a required termination string. The pattern is meant to reduce, not replace, human expert review of items.
requirements: Human experts make the final decision on which items to include in a creativity assessment; the filters only eliminate items unlikely to be valid
constraints: The authors do not claim the priming string list is comprehensive, stating only that it eliminated most priming in generated scenarios
target_learners: human test takers of creativity assessments
target_learning_goals: generating valid, diverse creative problem-solving test items
examples: Scenarios are dropped if they lack the string "I am finished with this scenario." or score below 45 on Flesch reading ease; each word list gets at most 10 generation attempts

article_title: Teacher Involvement in Developing Sustainable Education Materials for AI Integration in Green Energy Education
citation: Riandi Riandi, Ismail Ismail, Ida Kaniawati, Wahyu Sopandi, Diana Ayu Rostikawati, Defrizal Hamka & Suhendar Suhendar. (2026). Teacher involvement in developing sustainable education materials for AI integration in green energy education. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-34422-4
title: Integrated conceptual model of AI integration in green energy education combining Constructivism, TAM, and TPACK
description: The article proposes a conceptual model integrating three theoretical frameworks to explain teachers' ability to integrate AI into green energy education. It states: "Figure 2 presents a revised conceptual model that integrates three main theoretical frameworks: Constructivism, Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK)." Constructivism frames ESD material development as reflective, collaborative practice; TAM contributes AI knowledge and attitudes as cognitive and affective readiness; TPACK is represented by a Perceived TPACK construct capturing self-assessed ability to integrate technology, pedagogy, and content. Five constructs are theorised to influence AI Integration Ability directly.
requirements: Measurement of the five constructs (AI knowledge, attitudes toward AI, use of AI in green education, ESD material development, ability to use AI) via validated questionnaire indicators
constraints: The model was tested as an exploratory baseline assessment in which participants received no specific AI training before the survey

article_title: The impact of risk perception on perceived benefits of generative artificial intelligence users—an empirical study based on university students
citation: Du W, Ning S, Shi Y and Chen Y. (2026). The impact of risk perception on perceived benefits of generative artificial intelligence users—an empirical study based on university students. Front. Psychol. 17:1866428. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1866428
title: Integrated CAT–PMT–TAM/UTAUT2 risk–benefit framework for Gen AI use
description: The article integrates Cognitive Appraisal Theory, Protection Motivation Theory, and TAM/UTAUT2 into a unified framework explaining how risk perception dimensions relate to perceived benefits. Risk dimensions serve as primary appraisals of threat; students then conduct secondary appraisal of controllability and coping resources. Per PMT, high coping appraisal triggers adaptive, problem-focused coping associated with higher perceived benefits, while low coping appraisal triggers maladaptive coping. The framework predicts the risk–benefit relationship is "non-linear and dimension-speciﬁc".
requirements: Risk perception must be measured as multiple distinct dimensions rather than a unitary construct
The framework assumes students' coping self-efficacy and perceived controllability vary across risk types
constraints: The article states the relationship between risk perception and perceived benefit is non-linear and dimension-specific, so linear uniform-risk assumptions do not apply

target_learning_goals: understanding and managing AI-related risks
responsible and effective Gen AI use in academic and daily contexts
examples: The study operationalized five risk dimensions (information, security, technical, ethical, legal) and five benefit dimensions and tested the framework via hierarchical and threshold regression on 814 valid questionnaires

(2026). AIED unplugged, teacher workload, and numeracy learning: a clustered quasi-experimental mixed-methods study. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00465-x
title: AIED Unplugged (AIED-U): a paradigm for AI in education in resource-constrained settings, with the teacher as proxy
description: AIED-U is a paradigm for designing AIED for settings with limited technological infrastructure and digital skills, guided by five principles. The article states that "Conformity requires solutions to fit the infrastructure schools already have rather than demanding new hardware", Disconnect requires usability under intermittent or absent internet, Unskillfulness requires no advanced digital skills, Multi-user recognizes shared devices, and Proxy means "the teacher operates the system on behalf of students who continue to work with paper and pen". In this study the paradigm is instantiated by a numeracy app evaluated against usual practice.
requirements: Solutions must fit existing school infrastructure, remain usable without internet, and not demand advanced digital skills from users
constraints: The paradigm assumes no dedicated device per student, so students benefit through indirect interaction mediated by the teacher rather than direct student-system interaction

target_learning_goals: numeracy and arithmetic skills aligned with the BNCC curriculum
examples: In the evaluated system, the teacher photographs students' paper solution sheets with a smartphone; the app recognizes and evaluates the equations and generates error-specific feedback the teacher presents to students

article_title: Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI
citation: Jasper Roe, Mike Perkins, Louie Giray. (2026). Assessment twins: An approach for strengthening assessment validity in the age of generative AI. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.3
title: Assessment twins: two deliberately linked assessment components addressing the same outcomes through different modes of evidence
description: The article names and substantively describes assessment twins as a redesign approach for the GenAI era. Twins are conceptualised as "two deliberately linked components that address the same learning outcomes through different modes of evidence, scheduled closely together to allow for cross-verification". The pairing lets instructors triangulate evidence across formats so that validity can be checked even when one format is vulnerable to generative AI misuse.
requirements: The two components must address the same learning outcomes and be scheduled closely together to allow cross-verification.
constraints: The authors acknowledge challenges including resource intensity, equity concerns, and the need for empirical validation.
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: course learning outcomes assessed through GenAI-vulnerable formats
examples: The article proposes pairing pedagogically valuable yet GenAI-vulnerable assessment formats so evidence can be triangulated across the twin tasks.

description: The article applies Messick's unified validity framework as its organizing analytic axis, systematically mapping GenAI threats across six validity facets. As the abstract states, the authors "use Messick's unified validity framework to systematically map the ways in which GenAI threatens content, structural, consequential, generalisability, substantive, and external validity". This gives assessment designers a structured taxonomy for diagnosing which facets of validity a GenAI-vulnerable task loses.

title: Three-area student-identified taxonomy of GenAI curriculum development priorities
description: This taxonomy organises student-identified priorities for GenAI curriculum development into three areas: understanding and optimising GenAI functionality, exploring GenAI applications across contexts, and navigating ethical and legal dimensions of GenAI. It emerged from thematic analysis of qualitative responses from 166 undergraduate business students in a capstone unit, who expressed "strong support for integrating GenAI knowledge and application into higher education curricula". The taxonomy functions as a framework for universities designing GenAI-integrated curricula and for structuring student consultation on digital capability and employability.

citation: Afef Saihi and Vian Ahmed. (2026). Uncovering adoption personas for generative AI in higher education: a clustering-based segmentation approach. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00583-z
title: Persona-based, person-centered framework for understanding GenAI chatbot adoption in higher education
description: The article introduces a persona-based framework that moves beyond aggregate, variable-centered adoption models such as TAM and UTAUT by identifying latent user segments. It argues that variable-centered models "rely on the assumption of user homogeneity, estimating average structural relationships across entire populations", which obscures meaningful variation. Using unsupervised clustering on validated adoption constructs, the framework yields personas grounded in "psychographic and behavioral clustering" rather than demographic segmentation, and is positioned as complementing, not replacing, the prior SEM model.
requirements: Requires validated, psychometrically sound multi-item constructs as clustering input, as established in prior SEM validation
constraints: The approach does not model causal relationships; it examines how perceptual constructs naturally combine into user configurations
target_learners: higher education students
higher education educators
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting adoption of GenAI chatbots for academic support and learning-related activities
examples: The study applied hierarchical agglomerative clustering with Ward's linkage followed by k-means on 13 composite variables from 192 respondents to construct the personas.

title: Two-stage clustering pattern: hierarchical clustering to determine k, then k-means for final segmentation
description: A reusable analytical pattern for constructing user personas from survey data. In the first stage, "hierarchical agglomerative clustering, using Ward's linkage method and Euclidean distance" is applied, with dendrograms and silhouette coefficients informing the choice of cluster count. In the second stage, that optimal k is used as input for k-means clustering, a centroid-based algorithm valued for scalability and interpretability. Cluster quality is then assessed with internal validation indices such as the Silhouette Score, Calinski-Harabasz Index, and Davies-Bouldin Index.

article_title: Knowing Its Name, Not Its Nature: Word Association Mapping of Student AI Cognition and Evidence-Based Micro-Credential Design in Turkish Higher Education
citation: İsmail Şan and Hanife Gülhan Orhan Karsak. (2026). Knowing its name, not its nature: word association mapping of student AI cognition and evidence-based micro-credential design in Turkish higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00621-w
title: Word Association Test as a cognitive-structure diagnostic instrument for needs-assessment-driven curriculum design
description: The Word Association Test (WAT) is a psycholinguistic instrument grounded in spreading-activation and associationist models of semantic memory, used here to map the organisational structure of students' AI cognition. The article explains that the test "measures cognitive structure not as the presence or absence of individual concepts but as the pattern of associative connections among them". Early, frequent responses indicate highly integrated concepts; late or rare responses indicate peripheral or fragmented understanding. The study operationalises this through a seven-stage protocol — normalisation to 65 canonical codes, frequency and Z-score banding, Kendall's τ with FDR correction, PROXSCAL multidimensional scaling, and hierarchical threshold network analysis — and links the resulting map directly to micro-credential design decisions.
requirements: Administration with a time limit and no prompting to promote spontaneous activation, as the study implemented with a three-minute limit
constraints: The article notes semantic distance reveals the existence of a relationship rather than its specific nature

The sample excludes Turkey's most research-intensive and technologically advanced universities, so the authors advise against generalising to institutions of that profile without independent empirical verification
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: mapping learners' existing cognitive structures around AI to inform AI literacy curriculum sequencing
examples: The study administered an online written WAT with the stimulus word 'artificial intelligence' to 436 students at four Turkish public universities, yielding 1376 raw tokens analysed through the seven-stage protocol

title: Ethical AI and Workforce Readiness (EAWR) micro-credential framework
description: The Ethical AI and Workforce Readiness micro-credential framework is the study's proposed credential architecture, derived directly from the WAT diagnostic findings. The abstract states "the study proposes an Ethical AI and Workforce Readiness micro-credential framework that bridges the gap between functional use and conceptual mastery". Unlike approaches that treat AI ethics as a separate add-on to technical curricula, the framework embeds ethical considerations throughout the competency structure. Each analytical layer of the WAT protocol generates a specific design implication for the framework, targeting the diagnosed absences: algorithmic transparency, ethical governance, and technical mechanisms that remain conceptually absent from students' associative networks.

citation: Xiyu Wang, Fatemeh Dadashipour, Basori, Yukiko Maeda, & Jennifer C. Richardson. (2026). Scaffolding systematic reviews in learning design and technology through mentoring and AI integration. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10629-8
title: Systematic reviews as intentional learning experiences scaffolded by mentoring that combines methodological guidance with emotional scaffolding
description: The article frames systematic reviews "as intentional learning experiences that unfold across stages of the review and require mentoring and technological support." Mentoring is described as "an integrated support system that combined methodological guidance with emotional scaffolding" rather than solely procedural knowledge transmission. Mentoring was embedded across stages: guiding search refinement, joint discussion of borderline screening decisions, and collaborative coding, reducing the cognitive and emotional burden of evaluative judgments and supporting both technical competence and confidence.
requirements: Mentoring support embedded across multiple stages of the review process, or peer-based discussion groups when individual mentoring is not feasible
constraints: The account draws on one team's experience conducting an SR in the interdisciplinary LDT field; the authors position it as a practical guide for similarly complex fields
target_learners: graduate students and novice researchers conducting systematic reviews
target_learning_goals: systematic review methodology
critical appraisal skills
confidence in handling ambiguity and evaluative judgment
examples: Experienced researchers guided novices in refining search scopes and selecting databases; mentoring at screening involved joint discussion of inclusion and exclusion decisions for borderline cases
key_sources: Xiyu Wang, Fatemeh Dadashipour, Basori, Yukiko Maeda, & Jennifer C. Richardson. (2026). Scaffolding systematic reviews in learning design and technology through mentoring and AI integration. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10629-8

article_title: Scaffolding Systematic Reviews in Learning Design and Technology Through Mentoring and AI Integration
citation: Xiyu Wang, Fatemeh Dadashipour, Basori, Yukiko Maeda, & Jennifer C. Richardson. (2026). Scaffolding systematic reviews in learning design and technology through mentoring and AI integration. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10629-8
title: Treat automation in systematic reviews as a complement rather than a substitute, with careful documentation and human oversight
description: The article concludes that "the automation is best treated as a complement rather than a substitute" in systematic reviews. While automation reduced procedural burdens such as screening, "interpretive decisions still required substantial human oversight." The team tested LLM-based extraction tools (MetaMate) but chose not to integrate them because "currently available tools cannot ensure that the extracted content is verifiably grounded in the original text." Selective use can enhance efficiency while human verification safeguards interpretive rigor and credibility.
requirements: Careful documentation and human oversight to preserve interpretive rigor and credibility; researchers need both technical skills and methodological understanding to leverage emerging tools
constraints: Automation development and effectiveness are uneven across review stages; tasks requiring contextual interpretation, reconciliation of ambiguous reporting, or integrative synthesis remain difficult to automate
target_learners: SR teams in interdisciplinary fields such as LDT
target_learning_goals: balancing efficiency and credibility in technology-supported systematic reviews
examples: The team used Covidence's ML-based prioritization to reorder studies by previous screening decisions, but declined to substitute machine extraction for human coding

article_title: Designing a mobile chatbot-based learning journaling system for intrinsic motivation and engagement
citation: Sven Scheu, Simone N. Loeffler and Alexander Maedche. (2026). Designing a mobile chatbot-based learning journaling system for intrinsic motivation and engagement. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00589-7
title: Mobile chatbot-based learning journaling system with example-based course and LLM journaling assistant
description: A fully functional mobile chatbot-based learning journaling system that guides students through structured reflective journal entries. It instantiates two design principles: an example-based built-in course with a seven-day structure providing modeled responses, and an LLM-based journaling assistant that scaffolds entries by summarizing the user's preliminary response, asking a clarifying question, and generating up to three alternative first-person formulations using OpenAI's gpt−3.5-turbo-1106 model. The system also includes seven topic-based journal templates, a general template, optional daily summaries of the last five entries, and 9 P.M. reminders. It was evaluated in a 2×2 randomized field experiment over 22 days.
requirements: Students need a personal smartphone to install the application and native or near-native German-speaking proficiency
Journaling needs to be supported by instructions, as unguided learners do not engage sufficiently in germane processes
constraints: The chatbot was rule-based with a primarily linear conversation flow following templates
The assistant was used by only 55.91% of participants after the onboarding session
External support risks encouraging cognitive offloading if it formulates reflection on behalf of the student
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
reflective journaling
intrinsic motivation for journaling
examples: In the field experiment, participants created 1904 journal entries, on average 10.64 entries per participant (SD = 6.46), and the course was completed by 75.58% of users with the course

article_title: Multidimensional perceived school support and AI learning anxiety among university students: the mediating roles of control-value appraisals
citation: Jiang H, Chen B and Chen Q (2026). Multidimensional perceived school support and AI learning anxiety among university students: the mediating roles of control-value appraisals. Front. Psychol. 17:1951992. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1951992
title: Control-value theory integrated with social support theory and TAM as an account of AI learning anxiety
description: The article proposes an integrated framework in which control-value theory is the principal account of AI learning anxiety: "achievement emotions reﬂect learners' judgments of how much control they have over activities and outcomes and how much value they place on them". AI learning self-efficacy operationalizes perceived control, and AI perceived usefulness (from TAM) operationalizes value. Social support theory supplies the three dimensions of perceived school support (emotional, informational, instrumental), specified as a distal contextual correlate of students' immediate appraisals. The model was tested with SEM in a sample of Chinese undergraduates.
requirements: Requires measurement of perceived school support, AI learning self-efficacy, AI perceived usefulness, and AI learning anxiety as distinct constructs
constraints: The article states the sequential ordering reflects the proposed structural model rather than an empirically established temporal process, and the design cannot establish causal mediation
target_learners: university undergraduates using AI tools in their learning
target_learning_goals: emotional adjustment to AI-supported learning, including reduced AI learning anxiety and informed judgments of AI's educational value
examples: The structural model specified PSS as a second-order construct with paths to ASE, APU, and ALA, and sequential mediation through self-efficacy then perceived usefulness.
key_sources: Jiang H, Chen B and Chen Q (2026). Multidimensional perceived school support and AI learning anxiety among university students: the mediating roles of control-value appraisals. Front. Psychol. 17:1951992. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1951992

title: Integrated framework embedding SEC within AI literacy for education
description: The review proposes a conceptual model that embeds social-emotional competencies within AI literacy, built by juxtaposing AI literacy frameworks (Long & Magerko; Ng et al.) with the SEC/CASEL framework. It states: 'By embedding SEC within AI literacy, this study contributes to understanding how AI technologies can foster emotional and relational skills while addressing ethical challenges in education.' The framework aims at a technologically adept and emotionally intelligent educational ecosystem, with AI literacy as the foundational concept and SEC/CASEL as complementary. It was derived through thematic analysis of a curated 19-source corpus.
requirements: A curated interdisciplinary knowledge base spanning AI literacy and SEC, as assembled by the SETCOM project
constraints: The review acknowledges potential selection bias and subjective interpretation of findings in narrative reviews
Synthesising concepts as of 2017 may not capture the most recent progressions in the rapidly evolving AI domain

social-emotional competencies

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Postplagiarism as an educational integrity framework reframing integrity around responsibility rather than control
description: The paper adopts Eaton's postplagiarism as a lens for rethinking educational integrity in GenAI-augmented contexts, recognizing hybrid human-GenAI writing as a contemporary condition of academic work. It states that postplagiarism "does not abandon integrity standards; it reframes them around responsibility rather than control", so integrity is defined not by whether GenAI was used but by how decisions were justified and disclosed. The paper extends this ethical orientation into structural assessment design.
requirements: Assessment design and institutional policy must support integrity as an enacted ethical practice rather than enforce it technologically
constraints: The framework addresses GenAI-augmented academic work in which responsibility for academic decisions remains with the human author
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: ethical academic practice and responsible GenAI use
examples: The paper operationalizes postplagiarism through four illustrative assessment practices that foreground transparency, justification, and accountability
key_sources: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Design assessment so that integrity is enacted through transparent, justified decision-making rather than inferred from technological absence
description: The paper's central design principle: assessment should be reconceptualized as the primary site where educational integrity is enacted, shifting attention "from whether GenAI was used to how academic choices were made and responsibility exercised". Assessment structures that foreground decision-making, transparency, and justification render integrity visible within hybrid human-GenAI work and scaffold accountability instead of relying on surveillance.
requirements: Assessment tasks must explicitly require justification, verification, and articulation of decision-making
Educators need shared criteria and professional calibration to interpret articulated judgement consistently
constraints: The paper notes these designs may become performative, with learners aligning discourse to expectations without internalizing commitments
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: accountable ethical reasoning and evaluative judgement in GenAI-augmented work
examples: The paper distinguishes integrity-oriented assessment from authentic assessment: authenticity asks whether a task mirrors real-world practice, whereas integrity-oriented design asks whether learners can justify decisions
key_sources: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Annotated decision trails as integrity artefacts documenting evaluative decisions about GenAI contributions
description: Annotated decision trails invite learners to document how GenAI contributed to their work and why particular outputs were retained, modified, or rejected in relation to disciplinary criteria. The paper describes them as "integrity artefacts, documenting how learners navigate responsibility within hybrid human-GenAI systems", rendering ethical decision-making observable without surveillance technologies. They also address equity by holding all learners accountable for articulating judgement regardless of language proficiency.
requirements: Scalability in larger enrolment contexts is supported by focused annotation of selected decision points and rubric criteria attending to quality of reasoning rather than volume of reflection
constraints: The paper offers these as illustrative rather than evidentiary mechanisms, not comprehensive pedagogical frameworks
target_learners: higher education students using GenAI tools
target_learning_goals: transparent disclosure of evaluative reasoning and accountability for academic decisions
examples: Appendix A models the practice reflexively, documenting the author's decisions to accept or reject ChatGPT5 revision suggestions during manuscript preparation

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Verification and accountability practices requiring learners to demonstrate how GenAI-sourced claims were checked
description: Verification practices require learners to demonstrate how claims were checked, what sources were consulted, and how discrepancies or uncertainty were addressed. The paper positions verification as "an ethical responsibility inherent to academic work", operationalizing accountability: learners remain responsible for accuracy regardless of whether claims originated from GenAI. This makes integrity enacted through epistemic vigilance rather than presumed through trust in technological outputs.
requirements: Assessment must make verification an explicit component rather than treating GenAI inaccuracies as evidence of misconduct
constraints: Responds to the probabilistic nature of GenAI outputs, which may include fabricated citations or misleading summaries
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: critical information literacy and disciplinary accountability
examples: The paper connects such practices to emerging paired-component designs that verify learning outcomes in AI-vulnerable contexts

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Oral defence and dialogic accountability as integrity artefacts evaluating understanding rather than artefacts
description: Oral defence practices provide a dialogic mechanism through which learners articulate and justify academic decision-making in GenAI-augmented work, with prompts about where and how GenAI supported the work and which outputs were rejected or revised and why. The paper argues that "responsiveness to probing questions, conceptual grasp of disciplinary ideas, and the ability to articulate boundaries of appropriateness provide more robust indicators of learning and responsibility than similarity metrics or probabilistic detection tools."
requirements: Clear criteria, shared calibration among instructors, and flexibility in modality are essential; evaluative criteria must prioritize conceptual understanding rather than rhetorical fluency alone
constraints: In larger classes, formats may need adaptation through brief structured conferences, small-group dialogic checks, or selective sampling
target_learners: higher education students, including those with diverse language backgrounds
target_learning_goals: ownership of meaning, limitations, and disciplinary implications of GenAI-augmented work
examples: Typical prompts ask where and how GenAI supported the work, or how the final product might be adapted for a specific learner, context, or disciplinary constraint

citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Draft differences and version history practices foregrounding developmental accountability across drafts
description: Draft comparison practices invite learners to compare selected versions of their work to explain what changed, what role GenAI played at different stages, and how revisions improved clarity, accuracy, or alignment with disciplinary criteria. The paper frames this as "developmental accountability": learners demonstrate responsibility not by producing a single untainted artefact but by showing how evaluative decisions evolved across drafts. Version history functions as an integrity artefact capturing learning trajectories.
requirements: Expectations for specificity, justification, and alignment with disciplinary criteria help mitigate the risk of selective self-presentation
constraints: The emphasis is on purposeful reflection on moments of learning and judgement, not exhaustive tracking; grading attends to progression and coherence rather than quantity of revisions
target_learners: higher education students using GenAI across drafting stages
target_learning_goals: articulating how evaluative judgement evolved across revisions
examples: Early drafts may reflect substantial technological scaffolding during ideation, while later revisions increasingly reflect learner agency and disciplinary understanding

article_title: Towards sustainable AI knowledge-base assistants in computer science education: on-premise deployment and optimization with open educational resources
citation: Shen X, Feng L, Hua S, Liu D, Xie Z and Liu B (2026) Towards sustainable AI knowledge-base assistants in computer science education: on-premise deployment and optimization with open educational resources. Front. Psychol. 17:1843444. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1843444
title: On-premise OER-based AI knowledge-base assistant system for computer science education
description: A three-subsystem architecture comprising an LMS Layer, a Knowledge Base Layer with structured extraction and a FAISS vector index, and an AI Inference Layer with curriculum alignment and model optimization modules. The article states that "all components operate entirely on-premise on a consumer-grade GPU (RTX 3060, 12 GB VRAM), with no external API calls". It ingests 82 open-licensed Markdown documents (~347,000 tokens) from MIT OpenCourseWare, OpenStax, CS50 and WikiCS, and serves student queries via retrieval-augmented generation with quantized Qwen-7B or DeepSeek-MoE models.
requirements: Openly licensed OER documents (Creative Commons or OSI-compatible) as the knowledge corpus
A consumer-grade GPU with at least 12 GB VRAM for deployment
constraints: The article characterizes it as a knowledge-base assistant rather than a validated intelligent tutor; no controlled learner study was conducted
Evaluation dataset drawn from English-medium OER platforms; multilingual extension is future work
target_learners: introductory undergraduate computer science students
target_learning_goals: factual recall, concept explanation, and multi-hop reasoning about introductory computer science topics
examples: Deployed on an NVIDIA RTX 3060 (12 GB GDDR6) with Qwen-7B and DeepSeek-MoE variants, evaluated on 300 OER-derived queries

citation: Qianrun Mao. (2024). Fostering Self-Directed Growth with Generative AI: Toward a New Learning Analytics Framework. https://www.google.com/search?q=Fostering+Self-Directed+Growth+with+Generative+AI+Toward+a+New+Learning+Analytics+Framework
title: Self-Directed Growth: a competency of independently driving iterative, sustainable SDL cycles fueled by Capacity to Aspire
description: Self-Directed Growth is defined as "a competency reflects by the increased progression to drive an ongoing, iterative, and sustainable SDL process independently, fueled by an enhanced Capacity to Aspire". It positions the learner as initiator, executor, assessor, and primary agent of their own SDL journey, extending SDL beyond achieving predefined outcomes in pre-assigned tasks toward independently constructing and assessing one's own SDL process guided by an internal compass. The article presents it as an advanced extension of the broader SDL framework and the central construct of the A2PL model.
