constraints: The article states its foundations remain largely conceptual and that variability in learners' intrinsic motivation, metacognitive maturity, and socio-cultural positioning is not fully accounted for in the model

title: A2PL framework: three foundational pillars (Capacity to Aspire, Complex Thinking, Self-Assessment) reconfigured around Self-Directed Growth
description: The Aspire to Potentials for Learners framework reconfigures the three foundational pillars of SDL summarized by Morris (2019): "The Capacity to Aspire represents the core essence of humanistic philosophy; Complex Thinking serves as the foundation of constructivist epistemology; and Self-Assessment embodies the principles of pragmatic philosophy". At the center is Self-Directed Growth, and together the pillars represent a learning process that is individual, purposeful, and developmental. The framework aligns summative self-assessment with the two layers of Capacity to Aspire within and across learning cycles.

title: A2PL three-level intervention design: Person, Task, and Person x Task levels
description: The A2PL intervention operates at three levels. At the Person level, learners reflect on aspirations and long-term vision of societal achievement and professional growth. At the Task level, "Learners and GAI co-create complex thinking tasks within real world scenarios that align with learners' aspirations". At the Person x Task level, learners construct a summative self-assessment framework by aligning identified ability, skill, and strategy gaps with task-aligned personal aims, fostering a more clearly defined strategic learning pathway. Starting from the second round, reflective practices adjust alignment and initiate a new SDL cycle.
requirements: GAI must refrain from disclosing that the assessment pertains directly to SDL, so learners' frameworks indicate internalized skills rather than prompted responses
constraints: The article states success is contingent on whether learners' summative self-assessment frameworks reflect analytical cognition of SDL into the depth of its procedures and components

target_learning_goals: self-monitoring, self-regulation, self-reflection, and self-evaluation

description: A browser-based system with three modules: a teacher-facing web interface for preparing storytelling activities, a web application connecting the interface to LLM modules, and a locally runnable fine-tuned LLM so data stays local. article_title: From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education
citation: Iizalaarab Elhaimeur and Nikos Chrisochoides. (2026). From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24807
title: Spoke-and-Wheel teaching architecture: three quantum-specialist agents in parallel coordinated by a Synthesizer
description: ITAS's teaching architecture decomposes tutoring by task: three specialist agents (Video, Guidance, Code) analyze each student question in parallel, each reasoning only within its designated scope, and a Synthesizer Agent integrates their outputs using a priority hierarchy with code errors first, then conceptual gaps, then video references. The design responds to the prototype's task-boundary hallucinations, which the authors attribute to cognitive overload of a single overloaded agent. Specialization is said to reduce hallucination via cognitive load reduction, task interference elimination, and synthesis filtering. The three-agent count "emerged empirically; two agents conflated code and concepts, while four added coordination overhead without reliability improvement."
requirements: Each agent must carry quantum-specific domain knowledge, e.g. a timestamp-indexed concept map for the Video Agent and a hand-curated Qiskit error catalog for the Code Agent
constraints: A controlled, blinded comparison against the prototype on the same input set remains future work
target_learners: graduate quantum information science students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of quantum information science
Qiskit implementation skills
video lecture comprehension
examples: A student question about a QiskitError applying Pauli-Z was handled by parallel Video, Code, and Guidance agent analyses synthesized into one response addressing video context, code diagnosis, and conceptual confirmation

title: ITAS conversational instructor analytics agent
description: A single-agent conversational analytics system that lets instructors interrogate deployment data through natural language while preserving student privacy. The agent "queries pre-aggregated BigQuery summaries, assembles results with lesson metadata, and produces a natural language response", narrating pre-queried data without writing SQL or performing calculations. It cross-references video seek data, code execution logs, and checkpoint submissions to surface aggregate pedagogical patterns, never returning individual transcripts or identifiable interaction logs. The narrow-scope design applies the same reliability principle as the teaching architecture.

title: Exercise coverage must match content coverage in self-paced quantum courses
description: Drawn from the dead zone finding, this principle holds that students treat exercises as the operational definition of required material in a self-paced course. The article states that "Any quantum concept without a corresponding implementation exercise risks being skipped regardless of its importance". In the pilot, students stopped watching the Module 2 lecture where exercise coverage ended, and the instructor closed the gap by adding multi-qubit checkpoints. Designers should map every lecture concept to at least one implementation exercise.
requirements: A checkpoint or exercise should exist for each lecture concept instructors expect students to engage with
constraints: Evidence comes from a single pilot deployment with five graduate students and no control group
target_learners: graduate students in self-paced quantum computing courses
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement with full curriculum content, including multi-qubit and entanglement topics
examples: The instructor revised the Module 2 exercise set to include multi-qubit checkpoints after the analytics agent identified the coverage gap

citation: Iizalaarab Elhaimeur and Nikos Chrisochoides. (2026). From Prototype to Classroom: An Intelligent Tutoring System for Quantum Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24807
title: Checkpoints should enforce implementation approach alongside output correctness
description: In quantum computing, multiple implementations can produce identical measurement statistics while reflecting different levels of understanding, so autograding should verify both the output and the construction approach. The article reports that "Submissions were rejected not only for incorrect results but for correct results reached through implementations that did not satisfy the approach criteria, a distinction that would be invisible to a system checking outputs alone". ITAS implements this through per-checkpoint autograding instructions that reject hardcoded outputs while accepting any solution demonstrating genuine understanding.
requirements: Per-checkpoint instructions must specify both the expected output and the criteria for acceptable implementations
constraints: Unlike platforms enforcing a single predetermined solution path, checkpoints must accept any valid implementation satisfying both criteria simultaneously
target_learners: graduate quantum computing students completing programming checkpoints
target_learning_goals: genuine conceptual understanding of quantum formalism rather than hardcoded correct outputs
examples: The Autograding Agent returned a structured JSON response with a boolean pass flag and reasoning separating the two criteria

It develops a scoring rubric mapping four criteria (visibility and reach, persona, trust and authority artifacts, mystification) onto front-stage performance, each scored 1-5, and an MCDA rubric extending this to text, image, and layout. The authors offer this as a methodological template extending beyond humanizers specifically.

citation: Stefano Bannò, Kate Knill, Mark Gales. (2026). Towards Self-Referential Analytic Assessment: A Profile-Based Approach to L2 Writing Evaluation with LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04298
title: Self-referential analytic assessment framework
description: An evaluation paradigm for analytic essay scoring that shifts from normative (inter-learner ranking) to within-learner interpretation of analytic profiles. "Self-referential analytic assessment focuses on intra-learner variability, identifying aspects where a student performs significantly better or worse than their average proficiency." Standardised analytic scores are averaged within a learner, and deviations of each aspect from that average define a dual binary classification task for positive and negative feedback, using a one-standard-deviation threshold. The article positions this as a stricter, more pedagogically relevant test of analytic assessment capability and the first such framework for L2 AES.
requirements: A reference signal that is internally consistent and psychometrically calibrated, obtained here via two-facet Rasch modelling and infit-based rater selection
Standardised scores across all analytic aspects so deviations are comparable
constraints: The one-standard-deviation threshold is described as a heuristic choice, albeit one aligned with psychometric methodology

target_learning_goals: Diagnostic identification of relative strengths and weaknesses across analytic writing proficiency aspects
examples: The framework was implemented on ICNALE GRA essays with reference fair average scores from 12 Rasch-selected raters, comparing GPT-4.1, Qwen 2.5 72B, Llama 3.1 70B, and operational raters

article_title: Evaluating Prompt Injection Defenses for Educational LLM Tutors: Security-Usability-Latency Trade-offs
citation: Alexandre Cristovão Maiorano. (2026). Evaluating Prompt Injection Defenses for Educational LLM Tutors: Security-Usability-Latency Trade-offs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06669
title: Four-layer defense-in-depth architecture for educational LLM guardrails
description: The article describes a "defense-in-depth mechanism comprising four distinct layers": deterministic lexical pattern filters (Layer 1), structural output validation (Layer 2), contextual sandboxing with explicit delimiters (Layer 3), and session-level behavioral heuristics (Layer 4). It is "designed as a progressive filter", starting with high-speed deterministic checks and escalating to structural, contextual, and session-level behavioral analysis, with each layer targeting a specific class of attack vectors while minimizing false positives on benign educational queries.
requirements: Layer 1 requires curated language-specific regex patterns; Layer 4 requires temporal metadata and repeated variations from real session traces to function
constraints: Layer 4 blocks zero attacks in the offline single-turn benchmark and is relevant only for online multi-turn enforcement; indirect injection is explicitly out of scope
target_learners: students in programming education tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: preventing answer extraction while permitting legitimate clarification, hint-seeking, and debugging help
examples: Layer 1 uses 30 curated regular expression patterns grouped into English jailbreak, Portuguese, and educational extraction families; Layer 2 enforces JSON-structure constraints and scans for HTML/XSS-like patterns

The article provides "a reproducible controlled protocol (480 queries) with confusion matrix reporting, latency decomposition, statistical uncertainty quantification" and releases a complete reproducibility package (Docker, dataset, scripts) in a public GitHub repository for independent verification.

article_title: Evaluating Prompt Injection Defenses for Educational LLM Tutors: Security-Usability-Latency Trade-offs
citation: Alexandre Cristovão Maiorano. (2026). Evaluating Prompt Injection Defenses for Educational LLM Tutors: Security-Usability-Latency Trade-offs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06669
title: Select educational AI guardrails as explicit trade-offs among bypass resistance, false-positive behavior, and latency
description: The article argues that "guardrail choices in educational AI should be made as explicit trade-offs among bypass resistance, false-positive behavior, and latency, rather than from isolated metrics." Because false positives carry direct pedagogical cost in tutoring systems, the optimal operating point depends on institutional risk and usability requirements: NeMo's balanced rail blocks all attacks but frustrates roughly 1 in 6 students, while the multi-layer pipeline preserves usability at higher residual bypass.
requirements: Institutional tolerance for false positives and latency must be specified before selecting a guardrail configuration
constraints: The article does not claim absolute security; a 46.34% input-gate bypass indicates significant residual risk, and latency figures are hardware-dependent
target_learners: students in educational AI tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: preserving pedagogical integrity and productive struggle while maintaining access to legitimate help
examples: The sensitivity sweep (Table 9) shows three configurations reaching 0% FPR that differ by orders of magnitude in latency and monetary cost rather than usability

article_title: Reinforcement Learning Measurement Model
citation: Wenqian Xu, Feng Ji. (2026). Reinforcement Learning Measurement Model. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09305
title: Reinforcement Learning Measurement Model (RLMM)
description: The RLMM is a psychometric measurement framework for sequential process data that treats a person's inverse-temperature parameter βj as an ability to choose higher-valued actions under a Boltzmann policy. It replaces the MDP-MM's person-specific tabular value functions with "a shared parametric action-value function Qθ(s,a)", using centered and globally normalized advantages, a soft Bellman-consistency penalty encoding known task dynamics, and a block-coordinate MAP estimation procedure. It also yields step-level influence diagnostics that identify behaviorally critical decisions.
requirements: Known task dynamics (transition and reward structure) used in the soft Bellman-consistency penalty
Identification constraints: state-wise centering and global normalization of the advantage function to remove softmax translation and co-scaling freedom
constraints: Uses a single positive ability parameter, which the authors note cannot fully capture strategy selection, task persistence, and exploration patterns
In open-ended environments, estimates depend on how researchers define states, actions, and rewards
target_learners: learners in interactive technology-based assessments
students playing open-ended educational games
target_learning_goals: measuring latent decision-making ability from action-sequence process data
examples: Applied to peg-solitaire simulations with known true abilities and to AQUALAB gameplay logs from the Open Game Data export
key_sources: Wenqian Xu, Feng Ji. (2026). Reinforcement Learning Measurement Model. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09305

title: KITE: an intent-aware RAG tutoring architecture combining multi-stage retrieval with pedagogical response strategies
description: KITE (Knowledge-Informed Tutoring Engine) is a RAG-based intelligent tutoring system for course-grounded dialogue on algorithmic reasoning and problem-solving. As the article states, "the system includes five components: document preprocessing, embedding generation, multi-stage retrieval, intent-aware response generation, and session management." Each query is classified by pedagogical intent, and the classified intent determines the response strategy: grounded explanations for direct and conceptual questions, Socratic assessment for validation, diagnostic hint progressions for debugging, and step-by-step state-tracing for algorithm tracing. Retrieval combines dense bi-encoder search, hybrid scoring (70% dense, 30% BM25), MMR with λ = 0.7, cross-encoder reranking, and source-based boosting, passing the top eight chunks to GPT-5.
requirements: Requires course materials for document ingestion and a keyword and pattern-matching intent classifier to route queries to response strategies
constraints: The article notes strong retrieval alone does not ensure effective tutoring; responses may still be too direct or mismatched to the student's need
target_learners: university students in an Introduction to AI course
target_learning_goals: algorithmic reasoning
algorithm tracing
debugging
problem-solving
examples: For algorithm tracing queries, KITE retrieves procedural steps from course materials and applies them step by step, maintaining state variables such as OPEN lists and CLOSED sets

article_title: REC-CBM: Rubric-Aware Error-Correction Concept Bottleneck Models for Trustworthy Open-Ended Grading
citation: Chengshuai Zhao, Fan Zhang, Kumar Satvik Chaudhary, Yiwen Li, Lo Pang-Yun Ting, Ying-Chih Chen, Huan Liu. (2025). REC-CBM: Rubric-Aware Error-Correction Concept Bottleneck Models for Trustworthy Open-Ended Grading. https://github.com/scott-f-zhang/REC-CBM
title: REC-CBM framework: rubric-aware error-correction concept bottleneck model for trustworthy open-ended grading
description: REC-CBM is a concept bottleneck model for open-ended grading that integrates three components: a rubric-aware concept encoder that learns concept-specific representations over responses using a concept query bank, an ordinal pairwise calibration objective that preserves ranking structure among rubric dimensions, and a latent concept error-correction module that denoises concept predictions before final grade prediction while preserving interpretability. The framework uses two-stage training: Stage I learns rubric-aligned concept predictors, and Stage II fits latent-correction parameters on frozen concept outputs. The article states this design "preserves the interpretable bottleneck while cor-recting concept-level noise before grade prediction."
requirements: Requires human-annotated rubric-aligned concept labels for training, produced here through a human-in-the-loop annotation pipeline with three domain experts and LLM-assisted initial annotation
constraints: Applied to open-ended grading of short answers, essays, and reading-comprehension answers; the article notes future work will extend to multilingual and domain-specific assessment
target_learners: students whose written open-ended responses are graded
target_learning_goals: accurate and interpretable automated grading of open-ended responses
examples: Evaluated on Mohler short-answer grading, ASAP 2.0 essay scoring, and MOCHA reading-comprehension answer grading benchmarks

description: The authors curate and annotate three public open-ended grading benchmarks with rubric-aligned concept labels: Mohler short-answer grading (2,273 samples, 8 concepts, 3 concept levels, 6 grade levels), ASAP 2.0 essay scoring (17,292 samples, 8 concepts, 5 concept levels, 6 grade levels), and MOCHA reading-comprehension answer grading (31,069 samples, 7 concepts, 3 concept levels, 5 grade levels). None of the three benchmarks originally included concept-level annotations, so the authors create them using a human-in-the-loop pipeline. Code and data are released at https://github.com/scott-f-zhang/REC-CBM and https://huggingface.co/datasets/scott-f-zhang/REC-CBM.

citation: Chengshuai Zhao, Fan Zhang, Kumar Satvik Chaudhary, Yiwen Li, Lo Pang-Yun Ting, Ying-Chih Chen, Huan Liu. (2025). REC-CBM: Rubric-Aware Error-Correction Concept Bottleneck Models for Trustworthy Open-Ended Grading. https://github.com/scott-f-zhang/REC-CBM
title: Route automated grading predictions through human-interpretable rubric-level concepts so educators can inspect, verify, and intervene
description: In high-stakes educational assessment, raw accuracy alone is insufficient; instructors need to understand why a score was produced and how to intervene on questionable judgments. Routing grading predictions through human-interpretable rubric-level concepts provides a mechanistic guarantee of transparency, decomposing the final grade into rubric-level concept predictions that educators can examine or modify. The article states this enables educators to "inspect, verify, and intervene on reasoning," supporting intervention and auditing and promoting pedagogical usefulness through concept-level outputs aligned with feedback categories.
requirements: Rubric-aligned concept annotations must cover the dominant rubric axes that determine the holistic grade, be non-redundant, and have ordinally interpretable anchored descriptors
constraints: Standard CBMs assume shared latent space and evenly spaced categories, requiring rubric-aware encoding and ordinal calibration to work well for fine-grained grading
target_learners: educators and instructors using automated grading systems
target_learning_goals: trustworthy and transparent automated grading of open-ended student responses
examples: REC-CBM implements this by decomposing grading into per-concept ordinal predictions with token-level attention evidence, corrected posteriors, and additive per-concept contributions to the grade logit

article_title: From Scoring to Explanations: Evaluating SHAP and LLM Rationales for Rubric-based Teaching Quality Assessment
citation: Ivo Bueno, Babette Bühler, Philipp Stark, Tim Fütterer, Ulrich Trautwein, Dorottya Demszky, Heather Hill, Enkelejda Kasneci. (2026). From Scoring to Explanations: Evaluating SHAP and LLM Rationales for Rubric-based Teaching Quality Assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05180
title: A general framework for sentence-level interpretability of rubric-based scoring combining SHAP attributions with LLM rationales
description: The article proposes "a general framework for sentence-level interpretability of rubric-based scoring that combines model-agnostic Shapley value attributions with LLM-generated rationales". It casts rubric-based teaching quality assessment as text scoring with model-agnostic sentence-level explanations, where an explanation method maps an input and model to a ranked list of sentences claimed most influential. Faithfulness is evaluated via a deletion-based protocol that progressively removes top-k units and measures prediction change, extended to cross-model settings where explanations from one architecture perturb another. It was instantiated on the CLASS Quality of Feedback dimension using the NCTE corpus with fine-tuned PLMs and instruction-tuned LLMs.
requirements: Identical sentence segmentation, deletion rules, and deterministic LLM decoding across compared models, as the article states all experiments use
constraints: The deletion-based protocol perturbs natural discourse structure and may alter pragmatic meaning, limiting its ability to reflect true causal influence
The article does not evaluate whether identified sentences align with underlying rubric constructs (construct relevance)
target_learners: teachers receiving automated feedback on classroom transcripts
target_learning_goals: understanding which parts of classroom dialogue drive automated teaching quality assessments
examples: Applied to 6,005 NCTE transcript segments annotated on the CLASS Quality of Feedback 1–7 scale, comparing eight fine-tuned PLMs with nine instruction-tuned LLMs

title: Position automated rubric-based scoring systems as decision-support tools that augment rather than replace human raters in high-stakes settings
description: The article argues that in high-stakes educational contexts, automated scoring systems "should not replace human raters in high-stakes settings", because models trained on human annotations may inherit subjective judgments or structural biases and propagate them at scale. Instead, such systems "should be positioned as self-assessment or decision-support tools that augment, rather than replace, professional judgment". The article further stresses that scores and explanations are probabilistic and imperfect, and that interpretability methods are intended to support teacher reflection and informed decision-making rather than serve as authoritative assessments.
requirements: Educators and stakeholders must be able to understand how and why a model arrives at a given score, requiring transparency of scores and explanations
constraints: Unchecked deployment in high-stakes settings may create self-reinforcing feedback loops of biased predictions
Model predictions and explanations risk being interpreted as objective ground truth

target_learning_goals: supporting teacher reflection and informed decision-making about automated teaching quality assessments

In the faculty workshop's usage, "verification" in this context encompasses a spectrum of rigor: from informal code review and testing, through static analysis and type-system-guided development, to full formal verification using proof assistants. Humans act as a senior software engineer verifying AI-generated code, and the whitepaper argues this spectrum aligns with a three-level framework from the formal methods education literature that can be embedded in existing courses without additional curricular expansion.

citation: Rania Abdelghani, Peter Kaiser, and Kou Murayama. (2026). Regulating the AI Tutor: Intentions, Help-Seeking, and Self-Regulated Learning in Adolescent GenAI Use. Accepted at the NextGen Learning Interfaces Workshop, AIED 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08568
title: Turn-level coding framework combining SRL, help-seeking, and mathematical modeling codes with LLM-specific constructs of epistemic vigilance and agency over the AI
description: The article proposes a hybrid turn-level coding framework applied to each task-relevant student turn in AI-tutor conversations. Deductive codes follow Zimmerman's cyclical SRL model (PLAN, MONITOR, REQUEST, EVALUATE), with REQUEST turns further coded as instrumental or executive and by content type, plus a Blum-based modeling-process code. Two inductive LLM-specific constructs were derived via an exploratory pass with Gemini 2.5 Pro: "Epistemic vigilance is a three-valued code (not_applicable, caught, missed) capturing whether a student reacts to an inaccurate or mismatched AI turn", and a binary "Agency over the AI" marker capturing attempts to shape the AI's role, format, or scaffolding.
requirements: Task-relevant student turns from AI-tutor chat logs; a stratified human-validation pass by domain experts to establish per-construct reliability
constraints: Behavioral analyses currently rely on AI coding alone; human validation is ongoing
Derived from an exploratory pass on a randomly selected 30% of conversations

target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning and help-seeking during AI-supported mathematics learning

title: Functionalist perspective of shame and guilt as social signals regulating behavior
description: The article adopts a functionalist perspective of social emotions, which "conceptualizes emotions as adaptive regulators of behavior in social contexts." Within this framing, guilt is oriented toward a specific behavior and motivates reparative action, whereas shame is oriented toward the self and elicits withdrawal, concealment, or identity threat. The framework guided the interview protocol and inductive coding, focusing on how students evaluated their behaviors and identities in relation to AI use, while remaining open to unanticipated patterns.

citation: Neagu, A., Wong, J. T. H., Messer, M., Nelson, R., & Johnson, P. B. (2026). Rethinking Scaffolding in LLM Tutors: The Interactional Mismatch Between Benchmarks and Real-World Deployments. Pluralistic Alignment Workshop @ ICML 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15766
title: Learning-context mismatch account of scaffolding uptake in student-chatbot interaction
description: The article proposes that student uptake of chatbot scaffolding is governed by a mismatch between the chatbot's pedagogical framing and the student's learning context, including immediate goals, prior knowledge, invested effort, and task stakes. It argues that "bypassing scaffolding is not necessarily detrimental; rather, it frequently highlights a mismatch between a chatbot's pedagogical framing and the student's learning goals". The account draws on help-seeking theory, distinguishing instrumental from executive help-seeking, and explains why uptake varies within single chats and across deployments.
requirements: Evaluation of scaffolding must be grounded in the student's learning context, since uptake depends on situational factors such as the student's immediate goal and task stakes.
constraints: The account is offered as the authors' interpretation of observed uptake patterns, not as a tested causal model.
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students using LLM chatbots for self-study and learning tasks
target_learning_goals: Effective use of scaffolded AI tutoring support; self-regulated help-seeking
examples: The paper cites Yang et al. (2025) documenting that mastery-oriented students asked conceptual questions while work-avoidance-oriented students asked implementation-oriented questions.

title: Two-metric turn-level evaluation pipeline: Chatbot Scaffolding and Student Uptake
description: An evaluation pipeline that scores both sides of student-chatbot interactions at the turn level. As the article defines them, "We define two turn-levels metrics:Chatbot Scaffoldingas how much scaffolding the chatbot provides andStudent Uptakeas how much the student takes up the scaffolding". GPT-5-mini acts as an ordinal classifier on a 1-5 scale per turn, with turn-level scores aggregated to per-chat means; uptake is mapped onto a signed -1 to +1 scale showing who drives the chat flow. It was applied across nine datasets totalling 9,490 valid chats.
requirements: Chats must contain at least one turn of informative student-chatbot messages; uninformative or structurally predefined exchanges and single-turn chats are filtered out before scoring.
constraints: The Student Uptake metric captures whether the student takes up the chatbot's framing, but not whether that uptake is productive for learning.

title: Reusable structured prompt template built up across lesson sections
description: The lesson taught students a reusable template for constructing prompts, built up throughout the lesson sections, to help them remember to address each learning objective. The template prompts learners to "Write me a Python function that takes as input [describe the input, including its type] and it should output [describe the output, including its type], that [explain how the function transforms the input into the output]" plus an example input and expected output. It operationalizes the Gulf of Envisioning dimensions of describing the problem, phrasing prompts, and assessing output.
requirements: Instruction across the five learning objectives so students can fill each template slot (input, output, transformation, example)
constraints: Taught in the context of Promptly-style tasks requiring natural-language specification of computational intent rather than code writing
target_learners: end-user programmers
novice LLM users
target_learning_goals: articulating inputs, outputs, and transformations to an LLM
reducing vague or underspecified prompts
examples: The template was built up throughout the lesson's five sections and used in guided Promptly practice

title: Gulf of Envisioning framework as a design lens for prompting instruction
description: The article adopts the Gulf of Envisioning framework (Subramonyam et al.) to explain why learners may fail even when using powerful AI tools, and uses it to organize its intervention. "By scaffolding learners' ability to describe the problem (capability), phrase prompts effectively (instruction), and assess output quality (intentionality), we aim to reduce the cognitive gap between intent and implementation." The lesson's five learning objectives are aligned with the framework's three gaps, framing prompt-based programming as a learnable CS-specific skill.
requirements: Instruction and practice addressing each of the three dimensions: capability, instruction, and intentionality
constraints: Applied in this article to prompt-based programming tasks where learners specify computational intent in natural language
target_learners: end-user programmers
novices using LLMs for programming
target_learning_goals: expressing computational intent clearly to LLMs
evaluating LLM-generated code
examples: The lesson mapped specifying function structure to the instructional gap, describing data transformation to the capability gap, and debugging failed prompts to the intentionality gap

title: Q-Learning Lab: a single-file bilingual browser tool for teaching tabular Q-learning
description: Q-Learning Lab is a 'single-file, browser-based, bilingual (Thai/English) tool for teaching tabular Q-learning that requires no installation and no network connection.' It renders a 5×5 gridworld with color-coded Q-values and policy arrows, exposes a live Bellman-substitution panel showing the numeric update at every step, logs every transition with the full pre-action Q-row, and exports the trace as CSV for learner-side analysis.

citation: Jueng, Ekkachai. (2026). Q-Learning Lab: Teaching Reinforcement Learning Through Learner-Generated Trace Analysis. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10802
title: Learn–export–analyze loop: learners analyze a trace their own agent generated
description: The tool's central design pattern is a learn–export–analyze loop: learners run their own agent, export the complete decision trace as CSV, and analyze it themselves, producing learning curves, value heatmaps, and visitation maps. Learners 'do not analyze a canned dataset' but data 'their own agent generated minutes earlier', making the analysis an act of reflection on their own experiment rather than an exercise on foreign data.

constraints: The on-screen log keeps only the latest 500 steps and the fast-training mode skips logging, so long training runs are only partially traced.
target_learners: undergraduate students meeting Q-learning for the first time
target_learning_goals: interpreting learning curves and value heatmaps
connecting the Bellman update to observed learning dynamics
examples: students train an agent, export the trace, and answer analysis questions in a spreadsheet or notebook: plot return per episode; compute the exploration ratio per episode; build a visitation heatmap and compare it with the value heatmap

title: Learner-as-analyst: mechanistic transparency reframes the learner from spectator to analyst of a recorded process
description: The article's organizing stance holds that every quantity in the Bellman update should be inspectable at every step, with the record of those steps belonging to the learner. article_title: Representation Robustness under Executable Reasoning Constraints in Large Language Models for Mathematical Problem Solving
citation: Sagnik Nath, Edith Aurora Graf, Liang Zhang and Diego Zapata-Rivera. (2026). Representation Robustness under Executable Reasoning Constraints in Large Language Models for Mathematical Problem Solving. https://github.com/sagniknath91/HCI-2026-dataset/blob/main/datasheet.csv
title: Benchmark designers should use controlled families of representational variants rather than single-form problem instances
description: The article recommends that math benchmarks stop treating representationally equivalent formulations as interchangeable. Because performance varies substantially across representations of the same mathematical structure even under deterministic decoding, high benchmark scores may reflect "sensitivity to favored surface forms rather than stable representation-invariant ability". Controlled families of representational variants make it possible to distinguish robustness from overfitting to presentation style, and the article extends this to any domain admitting multiple surface realizations of the same structure.
requirements: Problems must admit multiple mathematically equivalent surface realizations (e.g., story, symbolic, word-equation, isomorphic paraphrase forms) so variants can be compared.
constraints: The article's evidence comes from middle-school through early high-school algebra problems solvable with one or two variable algebraic reasoning; it flags other domains only as facing similar potential risks.
target_learners: developers and evaluators of AI-assisted math problem solving systems
benchmark and dataset designers
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of LLM math reasoning evaluation results
distinguishing representation-invariant reasoning from surface-form sensitivity
examples: The study instantiated each of 85 source story problems in story, symbolic-equation, word-equation, and isomorphic paraphrase variants and evaluated 5 LLMs across them under two interaction conditions.

title: Human-in-the-loop human–AI–human collaboration workflow for critical prompt engineering
description: A six-step structured workflow introduced in Week 3 to scaffold critical human–AI–human collaboration: cognitive activation before prompting, prompt formulation, AI output generation, critical evaluation with fact and bias checking as gatekeeping, iterative refinement via new prompts, and group consensus on final internalization. The article states that "Drawing on the principle of cognitive activation, students were instructed to generate their own initial ideas before querying the AI", a step explicitly intended to mitigate offloading and reduce anchoring effects. Groups applied the workflow in a TikTok script co-creation task using DeepSeek.

Students generate their own initial ideas before querying the AI

prompt engineering skill

Students did not experience this merely as technical training but as a deliberate challenge to their initial blind trust in algorithmic outputs.

title: For under-resourced learners, design targeted pedagogical interventions around human–AI collaboration rather than relying on technical training alone
description: The article argues that providing GenAI access and technical training is insufficient for ethnic minority and other under-resourced students, because without pedagogical guidance they may use GenAI as a shortcut that fosters cognitive complacency. The authors conclude that "technical training alone is insufficient; educators should design targeted pedagogical interventions around human–AI collaboration to avoid cognitive complacency and cultivate epistemic agency." The recommendation rests on the study's discourse, reflection, and self-efficacy findings showing scaffolding shifted students from passive consumption to critical co-creation.

article_title: SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis
citation: Shixian Zhou, Minghuan Shen, Xiaolin Wen, Zijun Qiu, Yongliang Jiang, Xiangyang Wu, Fei Wu, Yong Wang, and Zhiguang Zhou. (2026). SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29413
title: EEG-fNIRS bimodal complementarity framework for attention quantification
description: The article's attention modeling framework rests on the complementary strengths of EEG and fNIRS. EEG offers millisecond-level temporal resolution sensitive to rapid stimulus changes but is susceptible to motion artifacts, while fNIRS suffers hemodynamic latency yet provides region-level spatial specificity and greater tolerance to movement. As the authors state, "EEG primarily contributes high-temporal-resolution neural dynamics, whereas fNIRS provides complementary region-level spatial information over the targeted cortical regions." These complementary properties motivate the bimodal input, with fused features feeding a DDQN that outputs high, medium, or low attention levels.
requirements: Simultaneous EEG and fNIRS acquisition over prefrontal and temporal regions subserving attention and audiovisual cognitive processing
constraints: The channel layout can only bias measured data toward top-down control and multimodal integration and cannot completely separate them
target_learners: pilot-cohort students watching instructional videos in video-based learning
target_learning_goals: stable, accurate, temporally fine-grained quantification of student attention during instructional video viewing
examples: Channels were placed over prefrontal and temporal regions, deliberately avoiding the occipital lobe to prevent early visual responses from contaminating recordings
key_sources: Shixian Zhou, Minghuan Shen, Xiaolin Wen, Zijun Qiu, Yongliang Jiang, Xiangyang Wu, Fei Wu, Yong Wang, and Zhiguang Zhou. (2026). SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29413

article_title: SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis
citation: Shixian Zhou, Minghuan Shen, Xiaolin Wen, Zijun Qiu, Yongliang Jiang, Xiangyang Wu, Fei Wu, Yong Wang, and Zhiguang Zhou. (2026). SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29413
title: SAVVY interactive visual analytics system with Concept, Group, and Individual modules
description: SAVVY is an interactive visual analytics system that integrates visual and auditory attention to support top-down exploration of student attention variations in video-based learning. It comprises three coordinated visualization modules linked by a shared timeline: a Concept Module presenting course content structure and concept-level attention distribution, a Group Module visualizing group attention trends alongside audiovisual information density, and an Individual Module providing multi-temporal-resolution attention trajectories. The modules incorporate "course content structure, audiovisual information density, and attentional resource allocation," enabling teachers to analyze causes of attention fluctuations and inform instructional video improvement through a top-down workflow from course overview to individual verification.
requirements: A preprocessed multimodal brain dataset with quantified attention levels and processed instructional videos supplying course structure and information density
constraints: The system addresses video-side factors an instructor can control and does not model learner-side factors such as fatigue, mind-wandering, sleep, or prior familiarity
target_learners: teachers and course instructors revising instructional videos for video-based learning
target_learning_goals: locating when and why student attention declines and determining which instructional video content needs revision
examples: In Case 1, E1 used the Concept Module to screen concepts, the Group Module to discover anomalous information density and attention contributions, and the Individual Module to verify causes of attention decline in a convolutional neural networks course

article_title: SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis
citation: Shixian Zhou, Minghuan Shen, Xiaolin Wen, Zijun Qiu, Yongliang Jiang, Xiangyang Wu, Fei Wu, Yong Wang, and Zhiguang Zhou. (2026). SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29413
title: Six design requirements organized by concept, group, and individual analysis objects for attention visualization
description: From a preliminary study with four education experts, the authors derived six design requirements (R1-R6) categorized by three analysis objects: the course concept, the student group, and the individual student. The Concept category analyzes attention from the course structure for rapid screening and preliminary attribution; the Group category focuses on temporal attention trends and audiovisual instructional design; and the Individual category centers on "each student's detailed attention trajectory and audiovisual attention allocation." The decomposition matches the experts' agreed top-down workflow from overall course structure to specific causes of attention fluctuations.
requirements: Accurate extraction of concepts and their relationships as a prerequisite for helping teachers review the overall course structure
constraints: Group aggregated results may mask individual differences, as attention patterns observed at the group level may not hold consistently across individual students
target_learners: teachers and course instructors analyzing pilot-cohort attention data
target_learning_goals: locating low-engagement segments and diagnosing audiovisual instructional design deficiencies in instructional videos
examples: R2 aggregates attention distribution by concept with concept importance shown via occurrence frequency and duration; R5 supports switching between multiple temporal resolutions for individual trajectories

article_title: SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis
citation: Shixian Zhou, Minghuan Shen, Xiaolin Wen, Zijun Qiu, Yongliang Jiang, Xiangyang Wu, Fei Wu, Yong Wang, and Zhiguang Zhou. (2026). SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29413
title: Content-derived visual and auditory information density metrics grounded in LC4MP
description: Grounded in the Limited Capacity Model of Motivated Mediated Message Processing (LC4MP), SAVVY quantifies information density of both visual and auditory channels per slide-transition-induced event segment. Visual density combines edge density of image regions (detected with Mask R-CNN), average normalized IDF surprisal of slide text (detected with DBNet), weighted by region area ratios; auditory density uses the entropy of the narration's word distribution divided by narration duration, plus semantic similarity between slide text and transcript to capture cross-channel redundancy. The authors caution these are "content-derived proxy indicators" describing the presented content itself, not learners' internal cognitive states.
requirements: Instructional videos with slides and narration transcripts for region detection, transcription, and per-segment computation
constraints: The metrics describe the presented content itself, not learners' internal cognitive states, nor the amount of information each learner actually and selectively takes in
target_learners: teachers assessing the appropriateness of audiovisual design in instructional videos
target_learning_goals: diagnosing whether visual or auditory information density contributes to low student attention
examples: Edge density was chosen for image regions because instructional graphics are mostly structured diagrams composed of lines, boundaries, arrows, grids, and contours

citation: Shahin Hossain, Sima Ahmadi, Leqi Li, Idowu David Awoyemi, Wei Huang, Chenxi Zhou, Jujia Li, Samaa Haniya, Shapla Khanam, Tasbirun Mashreka Subaha. (2026). Rethinking Generative AI Literacy: An Integrative, Developmental, and Dialectical Framework for K–12 Teacher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01705
title: RAIL-Ed framework: responsible GenAI literacy for K–12 teachers as six interdependent pillars
description: RAIL-Ed is a justice-centered architecture for GenAI literacy in K–12 teacher education, spanning pre-service and in-service teachers. It defines GenAI literacy for teachers as "the integrated capacity of teachers to understand how generative systems produce outputs, to evaluate those outputs critically, to collaborate with them in pedagogically and ethically responsible ways, and to exercise principled agency, including restraint, over their role in learning." Six pillars operationalize this definition, grounded in Freirean critical pedagogy, Deweyan inquiry, Vygotskian sociocultural theory, and Shneiderman's human-centered AI. Equity is built in as a constitutive commitment rather than a separate pillar.
requirements: Each pillar must name a capacity whose absence produces a distinct, documented pedagogical failure; each must admit a distinct developmental trajectory; and each must be groundable in the four theoretical traditions
constraints: The framework is conceptual and awaiting empirical validation; the authors state it does not provide empirical validation or present a finalized product
target_learners: K–12 pre-service teachers
K–12 in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: GenAI literacy: understanding generative systems, critical evaluation of outputs, responsible human–AI collaboration, ethical reasoning, and principled agency
examples: Derived through a hybrid systematic review (PRISMA-style search and screening) and qualitative framework analysis of 67 studies from 934 initial records (2023–2025), coded against five concept-analysis dimensions

title: Dialectical commitment: the same GenAI affordance can deepen or displace learning depending on teacher literacy
description: RAIL-Ed's dialectical commitment holds that generative AI affordances simultaneously enable and constrain learning. As the paper states, "It is also dialectical, acknowledging that generative AI affordances simultaneously enable and constrain learning: the same capabilities that support source discovery can produce fabricated information (the source discovery–fabrication paradox), and the efficiency gained through AI use can undermine the development of underlying skills." Outcomes therefore depend on the literacies users bring, making cultivation of that literacy, not tool adoption, the object of design. This commitment follows, in the authors' account, from combining Vygotskian mediation with Freirean attention to structures of power.
requirements: Treats risks and benefits as conditional outcomes of educator and learner capacity, which the framework specifies through its six pillars
constraints: Conceptual, drawn from affordance theory (Gibson, 1979) and the four theoretical traditions; not empirically validated in this paper
target_learners: K–12 pre-service teachers
K–12 in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: Judging when a generative affordance deepens versus displaces learning; cultivating literacies that determine outcomes of AI engagement
examples: The paper names the source discovery–fabrication paradox: the same capability that supports source discovery can produce fabricated information

article_title: ProPRL: Property-Aware Prerequisite Relation Learning in Educational Knowledge Graphs
citation: Xinghe Cheng, Jiapu Wang, Chaobo He, Ruihai Dong, Quanlong Guan. (2026). ProPRL: Property-Aware Prerequisite Relation Learning in Educational Knowledge Graphs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03006
title: ProPRL: a property-aware framework for prerequisite relation learning with multi-view representation, pair-conditioned gating, and an irreversibility constraint
description: ProPRL is a framework that learns prerequisite relations over ordered concept pairs in educational knowledge graphs. It learns complementary concept embeddings from a concept-resource hypergraph and a directed learning-behavior graph, using "direction-preserving personalized multi-hop propagation to aggregate multi-hop behavioral evidence". A Pair-conditioned Gate constructs view-specific representations for each candidate ordered pair and adaptively weights the two views, and an Irreversibility Constraint applies "an anti-symmetry regularizer that penalizes simultaneously highpredictionsfor(ci,cj)and(cj,ci)". Training jointly optimizes resource-aware, behavior-aware, and fused branches with a teacher-detached consistency loss.
requirements: Requires an educational dataset with a concept set, resources, learner interaction sequences, and observed prerequisite labels for training
constraints: Hyperparameters such as α and λ are dataset-dependent and selected on a validation set
Requires an appropriately small learning rate for reliable optimization
target_learners: learners in MOOC, university course, and lecture-bank educational settings
target_learning_goals: accurate prerequisite relation prediction to support curriculum planning, learning path recommendation, and adaptive instruction
examples: Evaluated on MOOC, LectureBank, and UCD benchmarks against general-purpose and task-specific baselines, with ablation, case study, hyperparameter, and efficiency studies

citation: Alessia Ciacco, Luigi Di Puglia Pugliese, Francesca Guerriero. (2026). School network reorganization under educational and spatial constraints using classical and quantum optimization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05427
title: An ILP optimization framework for school network aggregation under institutional, territorial, and accessibility constraints
description: The article proposes an Integer Linear Programming model for regional school network reorganization in the Italian context. As the authors state, it "jointly incorporates institutional compatibility, administrative regulations, school aggregation decisions, road-network travel-time accessibility, territorial fragility, and school capacity constraints." The model decides which autonomous school institutions retain administrative autonomy as hubs and which are aggregated into them, without closing physical facilities. It is framed as addressing the aggregation component of reorganization, not end-to-end planning including closure or transport.
requirements: Institutional, territorial, and demographic data on schools, including enrollments, road-network travel times, and territorial criticality levels
A policy parameter defining the minimum proportion of schools that must remain active
constraints: The article states the model "does not constitute a complete end-to-end school network reorganization model including all possible planning decisions, such as school opening or closure, facility relocation, capacity expansion, transport planning, multi-period demographic evolution, or budget allocation"
target_learners: school-age students in regional school networks
target_learning_goals: maintaining adequate educational service provision and accessibility across territories during school network reorganization

title: Synthetic benchmark instance generator for school aggregation problems
description: Because no public benchmark existed, the article developed a structured random instance generator producing synthetic yet realistic regional school networks. It reproduces hierarchical settlement geography (provincial capitals, large, medium, and small municipalities), heterogeneous school types and educational tracks, and differentiated territorial criticality levels. Four instance sizes were considered with n in {250,500,750,1000}, spanning medium-scale to large-scale regional planning scenarios, with schools clustered around municipality centers via bivariate Gaussian sampling.

constraints: Instances are synthetic and abstract; the article notes limitations of the tested benchmark instances for quantum evaluation

title: ResidencyRL simulated clinical training environment with documentation API, LLM patient simulator, and structured autorater
description: ResidencyRL is an online multi-turn reinforcement learning training environment in which a clinical AI agent conducts complete simulated patient encounters. The environment exposes "an LLM-driven patient simulator and a structured API allowing the agent to document the encounter (e.g., diagnosis, management plan)", with rollouts scaling to 60 dialogue turns and 8 tool calls. An LLM autorater processes the encounter transcript and tool calls to yield a structured reward heavily weighted by clinical accuracy rubrics and critical safety flags. The patient simulator adapts health literacy, information disclosure, and pacing to each scenario's demographic and clinical profile.

target_learning_goals: Sequential clinical decision-making including history-taking, differential diagnosis, management planning, clinical documentation, and patient-centered communication
examples: The article shows a 22-turn training rollout in which the agent elicits a hidden Kratom tea consumption history by specifically asking about herbal supplements and correctly identifies Kratom-induced constipation as the primary diagnosis

title: Four-stage scenario generation pipeline with demographic sampling, quality verification, and adversarial extension packs
description: The scenario generation pipeline synthesizes and curates diverse clinical scenarios through four stages: demographic and behavioral attribute sampling from US population distributions including Big Five personality traits, condition-targeted LLM generation grounded in the DDXPlus evidence corpus, LLM-as-judge quality verification across five dimensions, and character-trigram TF-IDF deduplication. As the article states, "A generative proposer-judge pipeline synthesizes and curates diverse clinical scenarios based on targeted demographic and behavioral patient profiles." Two extension packs supplement the base scenarios: targeted history-taking scenarios across a four-domain taxonomy where critical information is withheld unless specifically prompted, and adversarial safety scenarios across a 9-category clinical safety taxonomy.

constraints: Sampling only common presentations may leave the model unprepared for unconventional case presentations where diagnostic error carries the highest clinical cost

title: Practice-based clinical mastery through progressively challenging simulated encounters
description: The article's organizing premise is that clinical competence, for AI as for physicians, is developed through practice rather than acquired through static knowledge testing alone. As the authors state, "ResidencyRL is built on a simple premise: clinical mastery, for AI as for physicians, is developed through practice." The framework draws a direct analogy to medical residency, where trainees convert academic knowledge into clinical expertise through years of supervised encounters with diverse feedback and progressively greater autonomy. It holds that a trainee who scores perfectly on examinations may still fail when presentations are atypical, and that the gap is a failure of clinical process rather than medical knowledge — a process that can be optimized through multi-turn RL in simulation.
requirements: Requires simulated environments with sufficient fidelity that competencies trained in simulation transfer to real clinical settings
Requires a curriculum spanning routine, targeted history-taking, and adversarial scenario types to develop distinct clinical competencies
constraints: Prospective validation with real-world workflows remains necessary to establish clinical utility
The competence ceiling of simulation-based training is bounded by environment fidelity

article_title: Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access
citation: Lier Jin, Lan Hu, Binqi Shen, Hanyu Cai, and Yuting Xin. (2026). Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08942
title: Prompt privilege and prompt equity: framing prompt-formulation sensitivity as an AI accessibility problem
description: The article names prompt privilege as an accessibility challenge in which users with greater prompting expertise systematically obtain better model performance despite expressing the same underlying intent, and prompt equity as the counterpart property of consistent performance across users expressing semantically equivalent requests in different communication styles. It reframes prompt-formulation sensitivity as an accessibility problem in addition to a security or optimization one, and operationalizes equity with the Prompt Equity Score, where higher PES values indicate smaller performance disparities across user cohorts and therefore greater prompt equity, whereas lower values indicate stronger prompt privilege.
requirements: Measurement requires systematically varying user communication styles while holding the underlying task and language model fixed, so observed differences are attributable to prompt formulation rather than task difficulty or information content.
constraints: Existing prompt-robustness research the article builds on addresses adversarial settings; the framework concerns non-adversarial, naturally occurring communication-style differences.
target_learners: users with limited health and digital literacy
everyday users without formal medical training or prompt-engineering expertise
target_learning_goals: obtaining comparable AI assistance for the same underlying information need
equitable access to medical information and decision support through LLMs
examples: The framework is instantiated on MedQA with cohorts from Low Literacy to Prompt Engineer, quantified by a baseline Prompt Equity Score of 0.9959
key_sources: Lier Jin, Lan Hu, Binqi Shen, Hanyu Cai, and Yuting Xin. (2026). Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08942

article_title: Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access
citation: Lier Jin, Lan Hu, Binqi Shen, Hanyu Cai, and Yuting Xin. (2026). Same Question, Different Answer? Measuring and Mitigating Prompt Privilege for Equitable AI Access. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08942
title: Prompt Equity Transformer (PET), an accessibility-oriented prompt normalization agent
description: PET is an LLM-based agent that automatically transforms heterogeneous user inputs into semantically equivalent prompts with standardized reasoning guidance while preserving the user's original intent. It optimizes expected downstream task performance subject to a predefined semantic-preservation threshold, and does not introduce new information or modify the user's underlying request. Positioned as middleware, it functions as an intelligent accessibility layer between users and foundation models, shifting prompt-optimization responsibility from user to system without modifying the underlying foundation model.
requirements: Semantic similarity between the original and transformed prompts must meet a predefined semantic-preservation threshold, and rewriting must preserve the user's original intent.
constraints: Experiments are limited to the healthcare domain (MedQA) and to GPT-5.4-mini; PET currently operates as a static normalization agent, leaving adaptive capabilities such as clarification questions or personalized rewriting strategies for future versions.
target_learners: users with limited health literacy and limited digital literacy
users lacking specialized prompt-engineering knowledge
target_learning_goals: receiving comparable model performance regardless of communication style
obtaining high-quality AI assistance without specialized prompting skills
examples: Applied as a preprocessing step to normalize prompts from the Low Literacy, Everyday User, and Educated User cohorts, while the Prompt Engineer cohort serves as an upper-bound reference

title: MedQA semantically equivalent user-cohort benchmark for measuring prompt privilege
description: A benchmark construction methodology that instantiates prompt privilege on the MedQA benchmark: for each original MedQA question, four additional semantically equivalent prompt variants are generated representing distinct user cohorts — Low Literacy, Everyday User, Educated User, and Prompt Engineer. Variants are produced with GPT-5.5 under rewriting instructions that preserve all clinically relevant information, answer choices, and the original ground-truth label, so observed performance differences can be attributed to prompt formulation rather than task difficulty or information content.
requirements: Clinical facts, symptoms, diagnoses, treatments, and reasoning cues may not be added, removed, or altered — only linguistic characteristics such as vocabulary complexity, terminology, sentence structure, and communication style are modified to match the target user cohort.
constraints: The Prompt Engineer cohort does not represent a linguistic population; it augments the original question with explicit reasoning instructions as an upper-bound performance reference.

typical adults without formal medical training
college-educated individuals without professional medical training
expert prompt engineers
target_learning_goals: answering clinical reasoning questions
comparing model performance across users who share identical information needs but communicate differently

title: Treat prompt quality as an accessibility variable: shift prompt-optimization responsibility from the user to the AI system
description: The article argues accessibility-oriented AI design should move from user-centered prompt engineering toward system-centered accessibility: rather than expecting users to learn increasingly sophisticated prompting strategies, PET shifts the responsibility for prompt optimization from the user to the AI system, functioning as an intelligent accessibility layer between users and foundation models. The conclusion states prompt quality should be treated as an accessibility variable rather than solely a user responsibility, so systems accommodate diverse communication styles, literacy levels, and technical backgrounds.
requirements: A normalization layer must rewrite user requests into semantically equivalent prompts while preserving original intent, so assistance stays comparable across user populations.
constraints: Demonstrated with a static normalization agent on healthcare question answering; the article calls for testing generality across domains and model families.

users without prompt-engineering expertise across healthcare, education, and public services
target_learning_goals: receiving high-quality AI assistance without specialized prompt-engineering expertise
equitable access to advanced language model capabilities
examples: PET was deployed as preprocessing before inference and eliminated the statistically significant Low Literacy versus Prompt Engineer disparity while preserving semantic fidelity

article_title: From Student Risk Prediction to SC2R: Semantics-Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Educational Decision Support
citation: Ngoc Luyen Le, Marie-Hélène Abel, Bertrand Laforge. (2026). From Student Risk Prediction to SC2R: Semantics-Constrained Counterfactual Recourse for Educational Decision Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17618
title: SC2R: a semantics-constrained counterfactual recourse framework for educational decision support
description: SC2R is a three-component pipeline for educational decision support: a predictive component estimating next-assessment success, an integer-programming recourse component generating candidate intervention plans over a discrete action space, and a semantic validation layer using SHACL. Plans are represented as RDF graphs and are "retained only if it satisfies the semantic feasibility condition" S(Gπ) = 1. The framework treats recourse as a constrained decision-support problem rather than geometric perturbation in feature space, turning counterfactual recourse into a machine-checkable process.
requirements: A calibrated predictive model operating on predicted probabilities rather than hard class labels
Candidate plans encoded as RDF graphs using the intervention vocabulary so SHACL validation can check them
constraints: The evaluation is offline, model-based, and observational; the authors state it does not establish that following a generated plan would improve student outcomes
target_learners: students in digital learning environments at risk of failing an upcoming assessment
target_learning_goals: next-assessment pass/fail outcomes and actionable intervention planning
examples: On OULAD, snapshots at d-14 and d-7 feed a calibrated logistic regression, an IP solver generates plans, and SHACL validation filters them before evaluation

title: RDF/OWL/SKOS intervention-plan vocabulary with SHACL constraint layer
description: A lightweight RDF vocabulary, using the prefix cbe: within a competency-based education ontology extended for recourse representation, centered on the classes cbe:ActionPlan and cbe:Action. A plan is linked to actions via cbe:hasAction and to student and assessment via cbe:forStudent and cbe:forAssessment; SKOS provides "a controlled and extensible classification of activity types" such as quiz practice, forum participation, or resource review. SHACL shapes enforce timing (snapshotDay <= from <= to <= dueDay), budget (sum of action costs <= budget), and optional availability constraints, making plans machine-readable and checkable.

Activity types need known availability windows for the optional availability constraint
constraints: The current action vocabulary is described as necessarily simplified and derived from structured learner activity signals rather than richer pedagogical interaction data

description: The evaluation protocol constructs two snapshots per eligible student per assessment, at t = d-14 and t = d-7 before the due day, using only information available up to snapshot time; post-t interactions and assessments are excluded. description: The article recommends that educational recourse outputs be treated as machine-checkable intervention plans subject to explicit semantic constraints rather than accepted on model validity alone. title: Ecological Co-Agency Framework: relational, regulatory, and pedagogical co-agency bounded by human epistemic accountability

article_title: A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant
citation: Saptarshi Basu, Sandeep Kakar, Ashok Goel. (2026). A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03402
title: Hybrid micro-level personalization framework combining learner-driven preferences with system-driven Bloom's Taxonomy cognitive assessment
description: A framework for personalizing LLM/RAG teaching assistants at the level of individual student questions. It represents learner characteristics through self-assessed metacognitive knowledge and question-level cognitive complexity via Bloom's Taxonomy, plus five Felder-Silverman-derived preferences (abstraction, verbosity, perception, processing, understanding). The article states "The combination of learner characteristics and preferences produces 96 distinct learner profiles" and that "This creates a hybrid framework combining learner-driven adaptability with system-driven adaptivity." It contrasts with prior adaptive systems that adapt content selection or sequencing by instead adapting response form.

An engineered prompt encoding all learner attributes must condition the LLM within the existing RAG pipeline and course-specific knowledge base
constraints: Personalization modifies the form and presentation of responses while preserving grounding in retrieved instructional content
Treated as user-selected preferences rather than fixed psychometric classifications

target_learning_goals: tailoring instructional explanations to learner preferences and question cognitive complexity

title: Pulla: a Parsons problem tool with client-side behavioral tracing, an instructor dashboard, and on-demand AI difficulty analysis
description: Pulla extends CodeCheck, an open-source web-based programming assessment platform, with "a behavioral instrumentation layer designed to capture students' problem-solving processes while working on Parsons problems". It records six interaction event types (e.g., parsons_tile_click, parsons_erase, check_submit, parsons_guess) plus submission snapshots with per-block green/yellow/red feedback, persisted to PostgreSQL. An instructor dashboard shows per-student attempt histories and activity logs, and an on-demand GPT-4.1-mini pipeline produces labeled per-student difficulty reports and class-level PowerPoint summary slides. article_title: Faithful Where It Can Be Checked: Auditing a Reflection Agent Against Its System Prompt in a Randomized Trial
citation: Subigya K. Nepal, Serena Soh, Noah Vinoya, SoHyun Park, Mahnaz Roshanaei, and Gabriella Harari. 2027. Faithful Where It Can Be Checked: Auditing a Reflection Agent Against Its System Prompt in a Randomized Trial. In Proceedings of CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '27). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19635
title: Countable versus dispositional prompt rules, audited from deployment transcripts
description: The paper's organizing framework splits system-prompt instructions into two kinds. Countable rules "set targets that anyone can check from the output, such as the two-sentence cap on replies", while dispositional rules "describe how the agent should behave or its manner, such as not being overly agreeable". Instruction-following benchmarks only test the first kind, leaving manner rules unmeasured; the paper supplies the missing scoring mechanism through human coders and validated LLM annotators applied to a deployment's own transcripts, treating an unaudited agent as an unverified treatment in the health-intervention sense.
requirements: Complete conversation logs from the deployment, a randomized comparison so outcomes can be interpreted, and ideally the same model running more than one prompt so failures can be traced to the model or the wording
constraints: Differences in agent behavior between the two studies are descriptive only, because the sample and the prompt changed together between studies
target_learners: emerging adults in career reflection programs
target_learning_goals: career exploration and commitment-making
reflective self-insight
examples: The audit coded all 17,930 trial turns for nine agent moves and participant commitment language, validated annotators field by field against two human coders, and compared behavior rates against each prompt's own written rules

title: Write prompt rules you can verify from transcripts and then verify them; budget decision demands and accept a declined decision
description: The paper distills its audit into two design rules for reflection agents. First, "write prompt rules you can verify from transcripts, and then verify them", because manner rules can fail in nearly every conversation without anyone noticing. Second, it yields "a concrete design rule for reflection agents: budget decision demands and accept it when a participant declines to decide", since repeated demands to decide were the behavior tied to greater career doubt while flattery showed no link to any outcome.

article_title: A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support
citation: Abhishek Jaiswal, Zoe Falomir. (2026). A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20349
title: Hybrid qualitative-plus-center-of-mass model for reasoning about path and support in Camelot Jr.
description: The article presents a hybrid qualitative solver for Camelot Jr. that formalizes the game state symbolically and integrates physics. The agent 'leverages a symbolic paradigm to investigate the game state using common-sense logic, formalizing environmental interactions through qualitative structural affordances', while 'we integrate this symbolic layer with a numerical center-of-mass (COM) stability logic' because the game mechanics involve complex physical equilibria. Qualitative modules describe the grid, blocks, orientations and walkable affordances; the numerical COM logic verifies that block assemblies remain stable under gravitational torque; a graph traversal module checks path connectivity.
requirements: Game states must be translatable into the qualitative grid representation with blocks, towers, Knight and Princess positions
Every placed structure must satisfy the global stability rule under gravitational torque before a path is evaluated
constraints: The model is designed for the Camelot Jr. block-puzzle domain and its specific rules (fixed towers, mandatory use of all inventory blocks, ramp cells that cannot support other blocks)
target_learners: children developing spatial reasoning skills
players of spatial block-puzzle games
target_learning_goals: structural stability reasoning
spatial path planning and visualization
examples: The solver places inventory blocks one by one, verifies COM stability of the full assembly, then extracts a walkable path from Knight to Princess via cell affordances
key_sources: Abhishek Jaiswal, Zoe Falomir. (2026). A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20349

citation: Abhishek Jaiswal, Zoe Falomir. (2026). A Qualitative Model for Reasoning about Path and Support. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20349
title: Camelot Jr. recursive backtracking solver agent
description: A game-playing agent for Camelot Jr. implemented as 'a recursive backtracking protocol' that searches the permutation space of the block inventory for arrangements satisfying two independent criteria: Static Stability and Path Connectivity. Mirroring a human player, it places blocks one after another, evaluates structural validity once the inventory is fully deployed, and then evaluates path connectivity. It also 'implements geometric pruning strategies to cut off impractical search branches that cannot connect the start and the end points with the remaining inventory'.
requirements: A limited block inventory and grid layout defining the challenge
Support-footprint validation before committing to each placement
Backtracking with state reversion when stability or path criteria fail
constraints: Stability is checked only after all blocks are placed, since counterweights can stabilize an initially unstable arrangement

children training spatial skills
target_learning_goals: block placement under stability constraints
pathfinding from start to goal
examples: Algorithm 1 recursively selects unused blocks, tests orientations and positions, prunes placements without valid support, and reverts state on failure

The solver uses this matrix to explore valid placements during backtracking.
