article_title: A Risk-Adaptive and Evidence-Constrained Framework for Generative AI Feedback in Programming Education
citation: Shihao Wang. (2026). A Risk-Adaptive and Evidence-Constrained Framework for Generative AI Feedback in Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29874
title: Risk-adaptive, evidence-constrained framework linking prediction, capacity-aware decision, and grounded feedback generation
description: The article introduces a five-stage framework connecting observation, prediction, decision, generation, and evaluation for personalized programming feedback. Calibrated risk guides intervention timing under fixed feedback capacity, bounded task and code evidence grounds diagnostic statements, and an "Evidence-Gated Progressive Assistance" policy orders support from self-checks through concept reminders to localized hints and focused review. The framework keeps predictive validity, policy value, and feedback quality as distinct evaluation endpoints while using the same temporally ordered evidence.
requirements: Time-valid learner representations with predictors restricted to information available at the intervention point
Student-disjoint evaluation partitions and validation-fitted probability calibration before threshold deployment
constraints: Evaluated retrospectively on recorded trajectories from one introductory programming course; prospective learner outcomes such as knowledge mastery and retention are named as future evaluation targets, not measured here
target_learners: introductory programming students in higher education
target_learning_goals: knowledge mastery in programming
self-regulated learning
task transfer
delayed retention
examples: The study instantiated the framework with 2993 failed-submission states from 215 students, four matched feedback conditions for 136 cases, and fixed-capacity and sequential threshold policies replayed over recorded trajectories.

citation: Shihao Wang. (2026). A Risk-Adaptive and Evidence-Constrained Framework for Generative AI Feedback in Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29874
title: Gate AI feedback generation on recorded evidence and escalate assistance progressively with calibrated risk
description: The article recommends that feedback systems let calibrated risk guide intervention timing, constrain feedback content to recorded evidence, and progress assistance from self-checks to localized hints when warranted. Each generated message contains an evidence-based observation, a feasible next action, a learner self-check, and an optional exact code excerpt, and the instruction "prohibited complete solutions and claims not supported by the supplied evidence." Unverifiable references are removed rather than retained.

Calibrated risk estimates with validation-fitted thresholds
Automated structural and source-verification checks with a repair pass and human review routing
constraints: The article notes that unrestricted generative assistance can improve supported practice while reducing later unassisted performance, motivating guardrails; the progressive-assistance mapping was evaluated on structural and provenance checks, not on learning outcomes

target_learning_goals: independent debugging and revision behavior
self-regulated monitoring and verification

article_title: Helpful or harmful? Generative AI dependence, self-reported critical thinking disposition, and self-perceived employability among business students
citation: Shojaei SA, Armosh F, Lihe R, Hamacha R and Labib J (2026) Helpful or harmful? generative AI dependence, self-reported critical thinking disposition, and self-perceived employability among business students. Front. Educ. 11:1885990. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1885990
title: Augmentation–automation distinction with cognitive offloading and habit formation as a boundary-condition account of GenAI's educational effects
description: The article integrates four complementary perspectives to explain why GenAI use can help or harm learning. It states that "Cognitive load theory explains why bounded GenAI use may free cognitive resources for higher-order activities; cognitive offloading explains why excessive reliance may reduce opportunities for independent cognitive practice" and that habit-formation theory explains increasingly automatic reliance. The augmentation–automation distinction supplies the boundary-condition logic: at lower dependence, use functions as augmentation (comparing, verifying, evaluating), while at higher dependence it becomes substitutive, bypassing independent attempts and accepting outputs with limited scrutiny.
requirements: GenAI dependence must be modelled both as an endogenous construct and as a moderator, with direct paths from dependence to the outcomes retained as constituent main effects of a properly specified interaction model.
constraints: The article states the cross-sectional evidence should not be interpreted as demonstrating a temporal transition from augmentation to dependence; longitudinal or repeated-measures research is needed.

GenAI dependence encompasses several related experiences (habitual reliance, limited verification, access-related discomfort, reduced confidence), so results should not be interpreted as proving one single psychological mechanism causes the outcomes.
target_learners: undergraduate business students
target_learning_goals: critical-thinking disposition
self-perceived employability
responsible and reflective GenAI use
examples: The study operationalised dependence as a moderator of the GenAI use–outcome associations in a PLS-SEM model of 412 Omani business students, with simple-slopes analysis showing attenuation at high dependence.

citation: Sidorkin, A. M. (2026). From One-Size Texts to Tailored Readings: Student Experiences with AI-Generated Course Materials. Open Praxis, 18(3), 506–522. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1141
title: Dual tailoring: simultaneous individualization of readings along interest and comprehension-level dimensions within an AI-mediated workflow
description: Dual tailoring is the article's descriptive design label (explicitly "not a new theory") for an instructional configuration combining two individualization dimensions in one AI-mediated workflow. Interest tailoring adapts readings to professional context, sector, and role through examples and cases; comprehension-level tailoring adjusts "pacing, scaffolding, explanatory depth" via definitions, stepwise structures, and check-for-understanding prompts. Both are supported by iterative prompting, in which students request follow-ups to reframe, deepen, simplify, localize, or apply a first-pass reading.
requirements: Requires iterative prompting: students must request follow-up questions rather than accept a single generated text, with instructor-controlled constraints through the reading prompt template.
constraints: The term is a descriptive design label, not a new theory; the study does not test tutoring-level learning gains and includes no comparison condition.

target_learning_goals: coverage of core educational leadership concepts
calibrating reading depth to professional work context
examples: Weekly readings in LEAD 503 were generated via a Class Companion bot, with students asking at least three follow-up questions before submitting reading logs as PDFs.

citation: Martin Sposato. (2025). Artificial intelligence in educational leadership: a comprehensive taxonomy and future directions. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00517-1
title: Ten-domain taxonomy of AI applications in educational leadership
description: The article develops a taxonomy that synthesizes AI applications in higher education leadership into ten distinct domains: Administrative Efficiency, Personalized Learning, Enhancing Teaching Practices, Decision-Making and Policy Formulation, Student Support Services, Organizational Leadership and Strategic Planning, Governance and Compliance, Community Engagement and Communication, Ethical AI Leadership, and DEI Initiatives. title: Future-trends framework: five core trends shaping AI in educational leadership
description: Table 2 of the article maps five core future trends and their implications: AI-augmented decision making, advanced personalized learning, evolution of work roles, privacy and data ethics, and equity considerations. Each trend is paired with a primary impact, key challenges, and opportunities—for instance, AI-augmented decision making promises enhanced data-driven leadership but requires "Balancing AI insights with human judgment." The article frames these as developments leaders must prepare for, including possible new roles such as AI Ethics Officers or Educational Data Scientists.
requirements: Educational leaders will need to manage transitions so that AI complements rather than replaces human expertise
constraints: The article frames these as potential future directions, not established findings; it notes open questions about balancing AI-driven insights with human judgment and about AI widening existing gaps
target_learners: educational leaders
policymakers
target_learning_goals: anticipating and governing AI-driven change in educational institutions
examples: Table 2 pairs the equity trend with the challenge of ensuring AI does not widen existing gaps and the opportunity of more inclusive educational experiences

title: Three-cluster thematic map of AI-in-medical-education scholarship: predictive modeling, generative AI in education, and ethics/healthcare integration
description: The article organizes the field's keyword landscape into three distinct clusters: "Traditional AI and predictive modeling" (machine learning, deep learning, classification, prediction, explainable AI, performance, quality, risk); "Medical education and generative AI" (medical education, ChatGPT, large language models, generative AI, medical students); and "Ethics, knowledge and healthcare integration" (ethics, bias, healthcare, education, knowledge). article_title: Standardized Assessment of LLM English Proficiency
citation: Shangchao Min, Shaonan Wang, Xinyu Gao, Hui Wang, Zhiling Jin, and 2 more. (2026). Standardized Assessment of LLM English Proficiency. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-8820245/v1
title: CSEBench: a CSE-aligned benchmark of 624 expert-annotated multiple-choice items with human response data
description: CSEBench is a publicly released benchmark for assessing LLM English proficiency against China's Standards of English Language Ability. It comprises "624 expert-annotated multiple-choice questions spanning CSE Levels 2–7", each annotated with CSE difficulty level, one of four target subskills (vocabulary, syntax, phonology, cohesion/discourse), student level, sublabels, average accuracy, and discrimination. Items come from two diagnostic forms (junior-high, 39 items; college, 35 items) linked by 13 anchor items, with responses from 2,050 Chinese EFL learners. The dataset is publicly available on OSF.
requirements: Items require expert annotation of CSE difficulty level and subskill, plus IRT-estimated difficulty from human response data for calibration
constraints: Spans only CSE Levels 2–7, producing ceiling effects for frontier closed-source models
Does not capture productive skills such as speaking and writing, nor interactional competence or pragmatic appropriateness
target_learners: Chinese EFL learners in Grade 8 and college sophomore cohorts
target_learning_goals: English proficiency assessment across vocabulary, syntax, phonology, and cohesion/discourse subskills
examples: Two large-scale diagnostic forms were assembled from an existing item bank: a junior-high form with 39 items and a college form with 35 items, sharing 13 anchor items for linking
key_sources: Shangchao Min, Shaonan Wang, Xinyu Gao, Hui Wang, Zhiling Jin, and 2 more. (2026). Standardized Assessment of LLM English Proficiency. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-8820245/v1

article_title: Standardized Assessment of LLM English Proficiency
citation: Shangchao Min, Shaonan Wang, Xinyu Gao, Hui Wang, Zhiling Jin, and 2 more. (2026). Standardized Assessment of LLM English Proficiency. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-8820245/v1
title: Psychometric pipeline for mapping LLM performance onto interpretable proficiency levels and subskill mastery
description: The article's organizing framework integrates educational measurement methods into LLM evaluation: "we estimate item difficulty using a two-parameter logistic (2PL) item response theory (IRT) model fitted to responses from 2,050 Chinese EFL learners", then conduct a Bookmark standard-setting study with trained experts to establish cut scores for CSE Levels 3–6, and finally perform cognitive diagnosis using an expert-defined Q-matrix with higher-order cognitive diagnosis models selected by fit (HO-GDINA won). This yields scale-referenced proficiency levels and subskill mastery probabilities rather than raw accuracy, enabling educationally meaningful interpretation of model ability.
requirements: Human response data for item calibration
Expert standard-setting panel familiar with CSE descriptors
Expert-defined Q-matrix mapping items to attributes
constraints: The item bank contains few CSE-7 items, limiting reliable claims about proficiency above CSE-6
Proficiency estimates may vary with prompt design, exemplar selection, or formatting
target_learners: LLMs evaluated as simulated language users, calibrated against Chinese EFL learners
target_learning_goals: Proficiency-level reporting and subskill diagnosis for English language ability
examples: The Bookmark standard-setting session involved panelist training, then two rounds of judgments, with Round 2 placements used as final cut scores for CSE Levels 3–6

article_title: Still Emerging: Understanding Generative AI Use in Higher Education
citation: Kahn P, Carrigan M, Wyman I, Liu R, Smith P, Andonegui AR, Murtagh L and Song F (2026) Still emerging: understanding Generative AI use in Higher Education. Front. Educ. 11:1885253. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1885253
title: Address GAI challenges through staff-student relationships and imagined affordances, not only AI literacy training
description: The article argues that framing the challenges of GAI in Higher Education as a technical problem of learning design or student AI literacy is insufficient. Because affordances are imagined relationally, staff must imagine both the tools and how students imagine them: "The affordances of GAI need to be imagined effectively by both students and staff if the technology is to serve educational purposes effectively." The authors recommend reconstructing the challenges in terms of teacher/student and peer relationships within which reflexivity is exercised.
requirements: Staff need sustained engagement and practical experimentation with GAI tools to appreciate educationally appropriate uses
constraints: The article cautions that experimentation relies on staff having the time and autonomy required, which an imperative to automate threatens to undercut
target_learners: Higher Education staff and students
target_learning_goals: Educationally appropriate use of generative AI tools in academic study, teaching and assessment
examples: The study found staff possessed limited knowledge of student GAI use and that variation in staff use and expertise made it difficult for many staff to appreciate educationally appropriate uses or the extent to which students manifested them

article_title: Advancing diagram-based reasoning in AI tutoring systems: a structural approach for STEM education
citation: Sun Y., Liao Y. & Ma X. (2026). Advancing diagram-based reasoning in AI tutoring systems: a structural approach for STEM education. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00459-9
title: StructRAG: a pattern-aware framework combining visual parsing with pattern-level structural reasoning for diagram interpretation
description: StructRAG is a four-component framework for interpreting engineering diagrams in AI tutoring systems. It converts a student-uploaded diagram image into a graph representation, retrieves structurally similar templates from a curated library, constructs pattern-aware prompts, and uses GPT-4 to reason about structural completeness. As printed, "StructRAG is composed of four main components: (1) Diagram-to-Graph Conversion, (2) Structural Pattern Retrieval, (3) Pattern-Aware Prompt Construction, and (4) LLM-Guided Structural Reasoning and Correction." The core idea is shifting "from surface-level recognition to pattern-level validation", so missing connections can be inferred from structural logic rather than pixel-perfect recognition.
requirements: Requires a curated library of abstract graph templates built independently of the evaluation questions
Requires OCR-based visual recognition plus classical computer vision line and contour extraction to produce an initial graph and an uncertain-edge set
constraints: When both the connection trace and one of its endpoints are absent, the visual module may still produce an incomplete graph
Dense mesh diagrams may contain crossings that cannot be reliably distinguished from actual junctions
target_learners: STEM students in electrical engineering, computer science, and systems engineering
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of structural engineering diagrams such as circuit schematics and network topologies
Structure-aware feedback and automated grading of diagram-based assessment
examples: The framework was evaluated on 1,650 STEM questions, achieving 89.3% question-level accuracy and 93.0% edge-level F1

article_title: Advancing diagram-based reasoning in AI tutoring systems: a structural approach for STEM education
citation: Sun Y., Liao Y. & Ma X. (2026). Advancing diagram-based reasoning in AI tutoring systems: a structural approach for STEM education. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00459-9
title: 1,650-question STEM diagram dataset collected via campus-wide submission campaign
description: The evaluation dataset was built from a campus-wide question submission campaign launched in April 2024, spanning four months, which received 2,047 unique submissions from STEM faculty and students. Twelve experienced STEM educators independently reviewed the submissions, removing duplicates and trivial or invalid entries such as diagrams with fewer than 8 nodes and edges. "After applying these ﬁlters, a total of 1,650 valid and structurally meaningful questions were retained for further experimentation." The questions span electrical engineering, computer science, and systems analysis, with star, ring, chain/bus, bridge/mesh, tree, hybrid, and layered topologies. A data-separation audit confirmed no overlap with the template library.
requirements: Submissions were required to include at least one diagram image with a minimum combined count of 8 nodes and edges
constraints: The full dataset cannot be publicly released because it contains university teaching and assessment materials; it may be provided upon reasonable request subject to institutional approval
target_learners: STEM faculty and students contributing assessment questions
target_learning_goals: Evaluating AI interpretation of topological reasoning tasks across STEM disciplines
examples: Distribution includes 347 star, 288 ring, 373 chain/bus, and 462 bridge/mesh topology questions

article_title: Advancing diagram-based reasoning in AI tutoring systems: a structural approach for STEM education
citation: Sun Y., Liao Y. & Ma X. (2026). Advancing diagram-based reasoning in AI tutoring systems: a structural approach for STEM education. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00459-9
title: Curated library of 375 abstract graph templates built with 12 STEM educators
description: The template library is a collection of abstract, unlabeled graph templates representing canonical engineering structures such as star networks, cascaded filters, ring topologies, bridge circuits, and bus-based interconnections. To build it, the authors "collaborated with 12 STEM educators from the departments of Electrical Engineering, Computer Science, and Systems Engineering", who identified representative diagrams from printed undergraduate teaching materials; "This process resulted in a collection of 375 canonical diagrams." Educators abstracted each diagram into an unlabeled graph template retaining only connectivity information, with labels, values, component types, and layout removed. The library was finalized before evaluation and kept fixed throughout all experiments.
requirements: Templates must be abstracted to unlabeled graphs with question text, node labels, numerical values, component types, annotations, and visual layout removed
The library must remain independent of the evaluation questions; a provenance and image-level audit confirmed no shared source
constraints: The library contains neither original diagram images nor corresponding question answers
Broad topology categories and structurally similar variants were retained because the framework is designed to retrieve canonical structural patterns
target_learners: Undergraduate STEM students whose teaching materials supplied the source diagrams
target_learning_goals: Retrieving canonical structural patterns to validate and correct student-submitted diagram graphs
examples: Template distribution: 92 star, 65 ring, 88 chain/bus, 109 bridge/mesh, and 21 other topology templates

article_title: From answer machine to collaborative partner: impact of structured generative AI training on scientific problem solving in STEM education
citation: Huang, B., Xie, L., Liu, Y., Liu, X., Tang, H., Feng, X., Qiao, C., Guo, Q., Wu, C., & Bao, L. (2026). From answer machine to collaborative partner: impact of structured generative AI training on scientific problem solving in STEM education. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00652-9
title: Effective GenAI integration requires pedagogical scaffolding rather than mere access to the tool
description: The article concludes that giving students access to GenAI is not sufficient for productive human-AI collaboration; instruction must explicitly scaffold strategic use. As the authors state, "Effective GenAI integration requires pedagogical scaffolding rather than mere access to the tool itself." The 45-minute training operationalized this via SRL-aligned prompting strategies and remediation strategies for GenAI limitations, yielding higher revision performance and more strategic engagement.
requirements: Training must explicitly teach students how to use GenAI as a cognitive partner, including its strengths, limitations, SRL-aligned prompting strategies, and remediation strategies for deficiencies
constraints: The observed benefits concern short-term engagement: training fostered more strategic engagement with GenAI in the short term, within a single-session design
target_learners: sophomore STEM students in calculus-based introductory physics
target_learning_goals: AI-assisted scientific problem solving and revision
AI literacy
self-regulated use of GenAI
examples: The RCT compared a 45-minute structured GenAI training session against advanced problem-solving strategies training without AI guidance, assessing revision of CSEM answers with Doubao

article_title: Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices
citation: Strydom, S. (2026). Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.11
title: Seven dynamic human-GAI paradigms grounded in personal epistemological beliefs
description: The article introduces a framework of seven human-generative AI paradigms: "guarded, possibility-focused, augmented, pioneering, symbiotic, values-based and equity". Each paradigm is outlined and examined against five epistemological dimensions, so that a person's or group's beliefs about knowledge shape how they engage with generative AI. The paradigms are presented as dynamic rather than fixed, offering a lens for interpreting human-GAI interaction in higher education.
requirements: Grounding in personal epistemological beliefs: the framework interprets engagement through beliefs about the source, certainty, organisation, control and speed of knowledge acquisition
constraints: The author notes "the framework remains an exploratory heuristic requiring empirical validation"
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: understanding and shaping human-GAI engagement in learning contexts
examples: The article outlines each of the seven paradigms and examines them against the five epistemological dimensions

citation: Strydom, S. (2026). Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.11
title: Five epistemological dimensions as a lens on human-GAI engagement
description: Drawing on Schommer (1994) and Schommer-Aikins and Easter (2008)'s multidimensional model, the article differentiates five dimensions of personal epistemological beliefs: "the source of knowledge, certainty of knowledge, organisation of knowledge, control of knowledge acquisition and speed of knowledge acquisition". The author contends these dimensions "offer an understanding of human-GAI engagement", serving as the analytical axes against which the seven paradigms are examined.
requirements: Adopts the multidimensional model of Schommer (1994) and Schommer-Aikins and Easter (2008) as its theoretical basis

target_learning_goals: interpreting learners' and educators' beliefs about knowledge in AI-mediated learning
examples: Each of the seven paradigms is examined against the five epistemological dimensions

article_title: Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices
citation: Strydom, S. (2026). Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.11
title: Human-GAI engagement patterns vary across disciplinary, socio-technical and institutional contexts
description: The article conceptualises human-GAI paradigms as "enacted patterns of engagement that emerge across different disciplinary, socio-technical and institutional contexts". This means engagement with generative AI is not a stable individual attribute but a pattern that takes shape within a specific discipline's knowledge practices, an institution's socio-technical arrangements, and its governance environment. Designers of learning and policy should therefore expect and plan for context-dependent variation in how staff and students engage with GAI.
requirements: Analysis of engagement must attend to the disciplinary, socio-technical and institutional context in which it occurs
constraints: The framework is offered as an exploratory heuristic requiring empirical validation
target_learners: higher education students and educators
target_learning_goals: context-sensitive design of AI-supported learning activities and policies
examples: The article examines each of the seven paradigms against the five epistemological dimensions as patterns emerging across contexts

article_title: Student-AI Interaction in Computer-Assisted Consecutive Interpreting: Patterns and Performance
citation: Kuang H, Li J and Weng Y (2026) Student-AI interaction in computer-assisted consecutive interpreting: patterns and performance. Front. Psychol. 17:1890808. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1890808
title: Structure AI-training to foster stable, balanced student-AI interaction rather than prescribing workflows
description: The article's training course emphasized "exploratory engagement and critical reflections rather than prescribing specific interpreting workflows," and trained students showed higher cross-stage pattern consistency (66.7% vs 50.0%) and more AI-oriented profiles. The authors present this as evidence that formal training shapes predictable AI interaction strategies, informing interpreter education where effective AI integration hinges on rapid, selective, accountable AI use.

constraints: The article's instruction emphasized exploratory engagement rather than prescribed workflows; findings come from a quasi-experimental group comparison of 22 trainees

target_learning_goals: effective and stable interaction with AI support (ASR/MT) during complex bilingual tasks

article_title: Literacy demands placed on students in student–GenAI entanglements in higher education
citation: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7
title: Extended Strobel taxonomy of five student–GenAI entanglement types organized by degree of creativity and degree of modification
description: The paper extends Strobel et al.'s (2024) taxonomy of GenAI applications — originally derived from 100 commercial and professional applications — into a classification lens for educational settings. The five types are Generator, Reimaginator, Synthesizer, Assistant, and Enabler, differing along two dimensions: "the degree of creativity — the extent to which GenAI output aims to innovate rather than improve, and 2) the degree of modification — the extent to which the GenAI output departs from the input." Each type is operationalized for higher education (e.g., Enabler reinterpreted as a competence-scaffolding role targeting higher-order competences), enabling classification of how epistemic work is distributed between student and GenAI in a learning activity.
requirements: Each study is assigned one primary category, since the analytical question of which entanglement type a study foregrounds is single-valued
constraints: The taxonomy was originally designed to describe commercial GenAI applications, and the Enabler category required substantial reinterpretation for educational settings
target_learners: higher education students (undergraduate and postgraduate)
target_learning_goals: literacy in student–GenAI entangled academic practices
examples: A nursing student prompting GenAI to draft a patient care plan from a brief case description exemplifies Generator; a structured argumentation exercise with GenAI to strengthen critical thinking exemplifies Enabler
key_sources: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7

article_title: Literacy demands placed on students in student–GenAI entanglements in higher education
citation: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7
title: Dohn's three-level framework of competence demands applied to literacy demands: domain-internal, activity-internal, and activity-framing levels
description: The paper uses Dohn's (2009a, b) context-level framework to analyze literacy demands as context-sensitive expectations placed on students at three interacting levels. The "domain-internal level" concerns domain-specific traits, facts, and perspectives; the "activity-internal level" concerns how the activity is performed, such as integrating GenAI inputs into coherent writing; and the "activity-framing level" concerns how the setting norms the activity, such as institutional expectations about individually authored work. The levels are analytical rather than isolated: demands interact with, frame, concretize, interfere with, and contradict each other, producing a unity of demands negotiated in every concrete situation that may be incoherent.
requirements: The levels are analytical and must be treated as interacting and mutually framing, not as exerting influence in isolation
constraints: The unity of demands cannot be predicted in advance but emerges in the dynamic interplay of humans, technologies, institutional structures, and norms
target_learners: higher education students working with GenAI
target_learning_goals: participating in academic practices with GenAI in ways valued within those practices
examples: Domain-internal demand example: that GenAI can be biased due to bias in the training data; activity-framing example: not handing in a report as one's own that was written by someone else
key_sources: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7

article_title: Literacy demands placed on students in student–GenAI entanglements in higher education
citation: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7
title: Tension between individualistic person-focused competence and person-plus tool-mediated competence as the explanation for which GenAI entanglements higher education accommodates
description: The paper's central explanatory framework holds that educational settings dominantly understand competence as an individually possessed object located in and evaluated for the individual, while professional GenAI practice operates on a sociocultural 'person-plus' premise where competence is situated doing distributed between persons and tools. Introducing GenAI activities can introduce the person-plus-competence logic at the activity-internal level while the activity-framing level remains governed by individualistic expectations, predictably generating tensions — illustrated by extensive debates over GenAI as cheating versus legitimate learning support. Because the five entanglement types distribute epistemic work differently, this conflict emerges to different degrees across types.
requirements: Analysis requires distinguishing the activity-internal level, where GenAI use may embody distributed competence, from the activity-framing level governed by institutional expectations
constraints: The tension does not arise uniformly across all forms of student–GenAI entanglement; it emerges to different degrees and in different forms across the five types
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: recognizing and negotiating conflicting competence expectations in GenAI-supported academic work
examples: Historical parallel: the pocket calculator and the flexible pole were once seen as cheating because they did not allow true expression of individually possessed competence, yet both are now widely accepted
key_sources: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7

article_title: Literacy demands placed on students in student–GenAI entanglements in higher education
citation: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7
title: Make the literacy demands of each entanglement type explicit to students (transparency)
description: The first design principle the review derives is transparency: "teachers could make the literacy demands of each type of entanglement explicit to students." For Assistant and Enabler activities, where demands largely cohere across levels, this means clarifying what individual competence means in GenAI-supported work, including where the boundary lies between legitimate use and overreliance. For Generator, Reimaginator, and Synthesizer activities, where demands are more fractured, it means naming the tension directly — for example, that Reimaginator students take epistemic responsibility for outputs they did not conventionally produce while being evaluated as if individually authored.
requirements: Teachers must clarify how epistemic work may be distributed between students and GenAI, what counts as legitimate participation, and how the activity relates to institutional expectations
constraints: The appropriate form of transparency differs by entanglement type: clarifying boundaries for coherent types versus naming tensions directly for fractured types
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: identifying tensions embedded in GenAI activities and responding to them productively rather than experiencing them as confusion
examples: In Reimaginator entanglement, teachers clarify that students are asked to take epistemic responsibility for outputs they did not produce in a conventional sense while still being evaluated as if the work were individually authored
key_sources: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7

article_title: Literacy demands placed on students in student–GenAI entanglements in higher education
citation: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7
title: Sequence GenAI activities across the entanglement spectrum, starting from coherent types and moving toward more distributed forms (progression)
description: The second design principle is progression: "teachers could consider designing activities that span multiple entanglement types." Because Assistant and Enabler entanglements dominate, many students encounter mainly institutionally coherent distributions of epistemic work and may graduate into professional contexts where Generator, Reimaginator, and Synthesizer entanglements are common without the literacy to navigate them. A workable starting point is Assistant or Enabler activities, from which teachers can then introduce Synthesizer, Generator, and Reimaginator activities to develop confidence, critical awareness, and capacity to manage more distributed epistemic work.
requirements: Activity sequences must move gradually across the entanglement spectrum, beginning with types whose literacy demands are relatively coherent
constraints: The progression is not simply about exposure to different GenAI tools; its purpose is developing competence to recognize, evaluate, and take responsibility for epistemic work distribution
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: navigating a broader range of epistemic distributions and exercising a broader range of literacy forms
examples: Starting with Assistant or Enabler activities where students can focus on calibrating GenAI's role in relation to their own work, then introducing Synthesizer, Generator, and Reimaginator activities
key_sources: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7

article_title: Literacy demands placed on students in student–GenAI entanglements in higher education
citation: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7
title: Build explicit reflection into GenAI activities to develop meta-level literacy in recognizing and negotiating conflicting demands (reflection and negotiation)
description: The third design principle is reflection and negotiation, not just compliance. Because different entanglement types distribute epistemic work in structurally distinct ways and generate sometimes conflicting literacy demands across the three levels, the key competence students need is "not mastery of any single entanglement type, but the capacity to recognize the implicit expectations of a given context and negotiate tensions when those expectations conflict." Teachers can design for this by building explicit reflection into GenAI activities, asking students to articulate what the activity demanded, where they experienced tension or uncertainty, and how they navigated it.
requirements: Reflection must be built explicitly into GenAI activities, prompting students to articulate demands, tensions, and navigation strategies rather than only completing the task
constraints: Over time is required: the reflective practice develops competence to recognize literacy demands of novel entanglement types gradually
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: meta-level literacy: understanding what an activity requires, how epistemic responsibility is distributed, and how to act appropriately within the entanglement
examples: Asking students not only to complete a task with GenAI but to articulate what the activity demanded of them, where they experienced tension or uncertainty, and how they navigated it
key_sources: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7

title: Unplugged explainable machine-learning activities using feature matrices to classify geometric shapes
description: This pattern has learners create explainable feature matrices to classify geometric shapes, making machine-learning algorithms visible without complex software. The article states participants "created explainable feature matrices to classify geometric shapes, making machine-learning algorithms visible and accessible without requiring complex software or technological tools". It was delivered online within K–12 teacher professional development.
requirements: No complex software or technological tools are required, per the article's description of the activities
constraints: Studied with ten K–12 educators in an online PD context
target_learners: K–12 educators
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
understanding of machine-learning classification processes
examples: Ten K–12 educators in the online PD program created explainable feature matrices to classify geometric shapes

article_title: Between perceived competence and artificial intelligence: academic self-efficacy profiles in university students with motor disabilities
citation: Suriá-Martínez R, García-Castillo F, López-Sánchez C and García del Castillo JA (2026). Between perceived competence and artificial intelligence: academic self-efficacy profiles in university students with motor disabilities. Front. Educ. 11:1956192. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1956192
title: Multidimensional model of academic self-efficacy comprising Attention, Communication, and Excellence
description: The article adopts a multidimensional account of academic self-efficacy in which "Blanco et al. (2016) proposed a model comprising three dimensions: Attention, Communication, and Excellence." Attention concerns concentrating on academic tasks and processing information; Communication concerns interaction and information exchange in collaborative learning contexts; Excellence is linked to planning, goal setting, and an academic achievement orientation. The study operationalizes the model with the EACA scale and uses its three dimensions as LPA indicators and SEM predictors.
requirements: Measurement via the EACA scale, whose three dimensions together explain 58.44% of the total variance, with subscale alphas between 0.78 and 0.83 as printed
constraints: The article analyzes only the current perceived self-efficacy condition of the EACA, not ideal-scenario or greater-effort responses
target_learners: higher education students with motor disabilities
target_learning_goals: academic self-efficacy beliefs about organizing and executing actions to achieve academic goals
examples: The study used the EACA's three dimensions as LPA indicators, yielding low, moderate, and high self-efficacy profiles, and as SEM predictors of AI use

title: Perception of AI Utility Questionnaire (12 items; educational, informational, and emotional support)
description: A 12-item questionnaire designed for this study measuring students' perceived utility of AI in academic contexts across three dimensions: educational support, informational support, and emotional support, each with four items rated on a 5-point Likert scale. An EFA found "The three factors jointly accounted for 70% of the total variance," with loadings from 0.45 to 0.82, and a CFA on an independent sample of 85 students provided preliminary support for the three-factor structure. Reliabilities were α = 0.85, 0.82, 0.80, and 0.87 overall.
requirements: Administration via an accessible platform compatible with screen readers and assistive technology, or in-person sessions in architecturally adapted spaces
constraints: The CFA sample of 85 was relatively limited, so the factorial structure was interpreted as preliminary evidence rather than definitive psychometric validity
target_learners: higher education students with motor disabilities
target_learning_goals: perceived utility of AI for educational, informational, and emotional academic support
examples: Used as the dependent measure in one-way ANOVAs comparing the three self-efficacy profiles and as the endogenous outcome in the SEM

article_title: Aligning ChatGPT with E-Portfolio Assessment as EFL Learning Model: Its Effect on Students' Speaking Performance and Feedback Literacy
citation: I Putu Yoga Laksana, Ni Made Ratminingsih, Made Hery Santosa & I Putu Indra Kusuma. (2026). Aligning ChatGPT with E-Portfolio Assessment as EFL Learning Model: Its Effect on Student's Speaking Performance and Feedback Literacy. Technology in Language Teaching & Learning, 8, 103616. https://doi.org/10.29140/tltl.2026.103616
title: The CEA model: ChatGPT aligned with e-portfolio assessment as an integrated EFL learning framework
description: The CEA model integrates ChatGPT with e-portfolio assessment so that AI-generated individualized feedback and portfolio-based documentation, peer feedback, and reflection operate as one learning ecosystem. In the study, "Padlet as the primary e-portfolio environment and ChatGPT as the individualized feedback system represented the entire practical framework of the CEA model." Students practiced speaking with ChatGPT voice-mode interaction, recorded video performances, uploaded them to Padlet, exchanged peer comments, and wrote self-reflections via Google Form. The model is grounded in social cognitive, constructivist, and connectivist theories and was designed to cultivate critical assessment of AI feedback, since AI feedback cannot be assumed universally reliable.
requirements: Structured pedagogical integration: students must be taught how to interact with ChatGPT (e.g., voice-mode interaction) and to use the e-portfolio for feedback, reflection, and archiving, rather than having unrestricted access
constraints: The control condition in the study was traditional e-portfolio practice without structured AI integration, not a completely AI-free group; the researchers could not rule out independent out-of-class AI access
The authors identify the differing affordances of Padlet versus Google Drive as a possible confounding variable
target_learners: first-semester vocational college EFL students (ages 18-20)
target_learning_goals: EFL speaking performance (fluency, accuracy, complexity)
feedback literacy
examples: Over 8 weeks, experimental-group students drafted ideas and practiced with friends and ChatGPT, recorded 3 to 5-minute video performances, uploaded them to Padlet, received lecturer and peer comments, and wrote self-reflections on a Google Form

title: Padlet-plus-ChatGPT digital workspace configuration for e-portfolio speaking tasks
description: In the CEA implementation, students used two linked platforms: Padlet as the primary e-portfolio environment for uploading recorded speaking videos, receiving peer comments, and exchanging collaborative feedback, and ChatGPT as a secondary workspace. The article states that "students used ChatGPT as a secondary digital workspace to help them organize the feedback generated by AI, capture their self-reflections using a Google Form, and archive practice transcripts to refer back to when they were working alone." Speaking performances were 3 to 5-minute recorded videos evaluated with rubrics covering complexity, accuracy, and fluency.

constraints: Padlet was chosen for its multimodal, collaborative, socially visible interface; the control group's Google Drive lacked these features, which the authors flag as a possible confound

giving and using feedback

citation: I Putu Yoga Laksana, Ni Made Ratminingsih, Made Hery Santosa & I Putu Indra Kusuma. (2026). Technology in Language Teaching & Learning, 8, 103616. https://doi.org/10.29140/tltl.2026.103616
title: Integrate AI tools into language learning through pedagogically structured use rather than unrestricted access
description: The article argues that ChatGPT's educational benefits are conditional on how teachers structure and supervise its use, citing evidence that benefits are maximal under teacher structuring and that unsupervised use carries risks of dependence and "high-tech plagiarism." It concludes that "using artificial intelligence effectively necessitates that it be designed for specific pedagogical purposes rather than just having unrestricted access to it by students." The CEA model operationalizes this by embedding ChatGPT within structured e-portfolio tasks with defined feedback, reflection, and archiving roles.
requirements: Teacher-designed tasks that assign AI a specific pedagogical role (e.g., targeted feedback, idea development, pronunciation practice) within a structured learning framework
constraints: The article notes dangers of unsupervised ChatGPT use, including dependence on the tool and high-tech plagiarism
AI feedback reliability is limited: ChatGPT detects surface errors better than deeper structural or argument errors
target_learners: EFL learners in higher and vocational education
target_learning_goals: language skill development through AI-assisted feedback
critical evaluation of AI feedback
examples: In the CEA condition, ChatGPT use was structured within e-portfolio cycles of drafting, practicing, recording, uploading, peer commenting, and self-reflection, while the control group received no structured instruction to use generative AI

citation: Sutedjo A, Chowdhury M and Liu SP (2026) Assessing faculty self-perceived knowledge in using generative AI to teach 21st-century skills. Front. Educ. 11:1913310. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1913310
title: Adapted TPACK-21 questionnaire for GenAI-infused higher education instruction
description: A seven-subscale self-report instrument adapted from the Valtonen et al. (2017) TPACK-21 survey to measure faculty self-perceived knowledge for GenAI integration. The adaptation "retained the same seven constructs and underlying theoretical structure as the original instrument"; modifications were limited to clarifying the definition of ICT and rewording scale language. Items use a six-point scale from needing a lot of additional knowledge to having extensive knowledge.
requirements: Respondents self-rate knowledge on the six-point scale; the article notes self-report is considered appropriate in the TPACK literature
constraints: No formal expert panel review was conducted
the adaptation has not yet undergone independent psychometric validation specific to this population
target_learners: higher education instructional faculty (tenured/tenure-track and Academic Professional Track)
target_learning_goals: self-perceived knowledge for GenAI integration supporting 21st-century skills
examples: Administered to 127 faculty over an 87-day period (April 5 to June 30, 2024), with Cronbach's α of .87–.98 across subscales

citation: Sutedjo A, Chowdhury M and Liu SP (2026) Assessing faculty self-perceived knowledge in using generative AI to teach 21st-century skills. Front. Educ. 11:1913310. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1913310
title: Sequence GenAI faculty development from foundational GenAI literacy toward discipline-specific integration activities
description: The article recommends that professional development first build a shared baseline of GenAI literacy through hands-on experimentation with GenAI tools in teaching and assessment contexts, before introducing complex integration tasks, and that programs be structured around discipline-specific use cases connecting GenAI affordances to faculty subject matter. Investment should be distributed broadly across the full faculty population since low technology-integrated knowledge held across every demographic subgroup.
requirements: Programs must directly engage with disciplinary content rather than remain generic
institutional support including faculty time, recognition, communities of practice, and alignment with promotion and tenure criteria
constraints: The gateway role of TK is an interpretive hypothesis the cross-sectional design cannot test

target_learning_goals: GenAI integration into teaching to foster 21st-century skills
examples: The survey found low TPK, TCK, and TPACK scores across all subgroups, supporting broad distribution of professional development investment

article_title: The synthetic position: generative artificial intelligence and the suspension of self-authorship in emerging adulthood
citation: Du P, Zhou Y, Zhou Z, Wang H and Cao Q (2026). The synthetic position: generative artificial intelligence and the suspension of self-authorship in emerging adulthood. Front. Psychol. 17:1922087. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1922087
title: The synthetic position: a new type within Dialogical Self Theory's society of mind
description: The synthetic position is the article's proposed category for a large language model engaged in self-formative dialogue within Dialogical Self Theory. The theory conceives the self as "a dynamic multiplicity of relatively autonomous I-positions, each able to be voiced and enter into dialogue with the others"; the synthetic position enters that society with four joint properties: protean, frictionless, simulated counter-positioning, and authored elsewhere. The article argues this combination is "jointly and reliably present to an extent that is only ever partial in a human other", so the existing typology neither contains nor anticipates it.
requirements: The article treats the synthetic position as present when the system is engaged in self-formative dialogue — exchanges directed at who one is to become — as distinct from information-seeking
constraints: The load-bearing property (irreducibility) is a matter of degree: personalization that remains fully revisable at the user's discretion supplies no irreducibility, and future systems holding commitments against revision would begin to leave the category
target_learners: Emerging adults (late teens to late twenties) using generative AI for self-formative dialogue
target_learning_goals: Self-authorship, identity formation, deliberation over values, commitments and possible selves
examples: The article distinguishes the synthetic position from internalized human others, ordinary tools, and extended mind (e.g., a notebook) in Table 1
key_sources: Du P, Zhou Y, Zhou Z, Wang H and Cao Q (2026). The synthetic position: generative artificial intelligence and the suspension of self-authorship in emerging adulthood. Front. Psychol. 17:1922087. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1922087

article_title: The synthetic position: generative artificial intelligence and the suspension of self-authorship in emerging adulthood
citation: Du P, Zhou Y, Zhou Z, Wang H and Cao Q (2026). The synthetic position: generative artificial intelligence and the suspension of self-authorship in emerging adulthood. Front. Psychol. 17:1922087. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1922087
title: Authorial suspension: a self densely voiced yet un-authored
description: Authorial suspension is the article's name for the outcome condition: a self whose many voices are articulated and in incessant conversation, but whose integrative act is performed elsewhere, so the person lacks "the felt sense of being the author of the conversation". Suspension carries two senses: held aloft, and deferred, left open. It is identified behaviorally by three markers: a fluency-ownership gap, deferral of commitment despite exhausted deliberation, and an overview unavailable when the system is withdrawn.
requirements: Identification requires behavioral markers: the withdrawal probe, in which a person must convene the inner conversation without the system, is reserved for the third marker
constraints: It is a disturbance in the locus of authorship, not in its presence, development, or coherence; the article states the condition is reversible in principle and that its premise — that authorship ought to be located in the individual — is not culturally universal
target_learners: Emerging adults habitually enlisting generative AI for self-formative dialogue
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing delegated from exercised self-authorship; recognizing un-authored self-narratives
examples: Table 2 distinguishes authorial suspension from the in-between feeling of emerging adulthood, moratorium, diffusion, multiphrenia, and unattained self-authorship, each with candidate operational markers
key_sources: Du P, Zhou Y, Zhou Z, Wang H and Cao Q (2026). The synthetic position: generative artificial intelligence and the suspension of self-authorship in emerging adulthood. Front. Psychol. 17:1922087. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1922087

article_title: The Competence Paradox: Negotiating Ease, Risk, and Creative Identity in Text-to-Image Generative AI Use Among Art and Design Students
citation: Liu Y, Meng M and Zhang Y (2026) The competence paradox: negotiating ease, risk, and creative identity in text-to-image generative AI use among art and design students. Front. Psychol. 17:1858187. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1858187
title: Extended UTAUT framework with creative competence for T2I GenAI adoption in studio-based creative education
description: The article builds a contextualized extension of UTAUT for text-to-image generative AI in art and design education. It retains the four canonical constructs and adds novelty value, perceived risk, and a new domain-specific construct: "we conceptualize Creative Competence (CC) as a domain-speciﬁc self-eﬃcacy construct" capturing the ability to translate ideas into prompts, steer outputs via advanced controls, iteratively revise generations, and critically evaluate alignment with creative vision. The framework treats adoption as shaped by risk interpretation and creative identity, not solely utilitarian predictors.
requirements: Requires instructor-informed, context-specific model building: Study 1 focus groups identified the extension constructs before the survey
constraints: The article states the SEM showed acceptable but not optimal fit (CFI = 0.873, TLI = 0.849) and explained limited variance in use behavior and perceived risk
Sample drawn from a single national context and relatively well-resourced institutions, interpreted as context-sensitive rather than universally generalizable
target_learners: Higher education art and design students (undergraduate and graduate)
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting students' adoption and selective use of text-to-image generative AI in studio coursework
examples: Study 2 tested the model with a questionnaire of 417 students (400 retained) across three Chinese universities using two-step SEM with bootstrapped indirect effects

article_title: Purpose Before Policy: Academic Integrity, Generative AI, and Rhetorical Stance
citation: Tristan B. Taylor & Travis LaCroix. (2026). Purpose before policy: academic integrity, generative AI, and rhetorical stance. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-026-01706-1
title: Rhetorical framework for institutional identity: Burke's terministic screen, Bitzer's rhetorical situation, and Booth's rhetorical stance and its three corruptions
description: The article assembles three rhetorical frameworks to analyse how universities construct institutional identity through mission statements. Burke supplies a philosophical account of meaning-making as symbolic action, centred on the terministic screen, where every linguistic choice simultaneously "reflects, selects, and deflects reality". Bitzer delineates the conditions under which rhetorical action is intelligible and effective, defining the rhetorical situation as exigence plus constraints. Booth identifies the characteristic modes of rhetorical failure: the Entertainer's stance (ethos over substance), the Advertiser's stance (pathos at the cost of accuracy), and the Pedant's stance. The article applies these to mission statements from the U15, Russell Group, and Ivy League as a diagnostic lens on aspirational institutional discourse.
requirements: Application requires publicly available mission statements as the genre of institutional discourse analysed, articulating official self-understanding to heterogeneous audiences
constraints: The authors state the analysis is illustrative rather than exhaustive and not representative in a statistical sense; it is a diagnostic lens on aspirational discourse, not evidence of day-to-day institutional practice
target_learners: higher education students
university administrators and faculty
target_learning_goals: understanding institutional academic integrity environments
interpreting institutional policy discourse around emerging technologies
examples: The article reads the University of Waterloo's motto-based mission as the Entertainer's stance and Dartmouth's 'most promising students ... responsible leadership' as the Advertiser's stance.
key_sources: Tristan B. Taylor & Travis LaCroix. (2026). Purpose before policy: academic integrity, generative AI, and rhetorical stance. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-026-01706-1

article_title: Purpose Before Policy: Academic Integrity, Generative AI, and Rhetorical Stance
citation: Tristan B. Taylor & Travis LaCroix. (2026). Purpose before policy: academic integrity, generative AI, and rhetorical stance. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-026-01706-1
title: Ensure coherence between stated missions, pedagogical practices, and technology approaches before enforcing academic integrity standards on students
description: The article's central design recommendation for institutions: universities "cannot credibly enforce integrity standards in the age of AI without first ensuring coherence between their stated missions, pedagogical practices, and approaches to emerging technologies". Because integrity functions as a social contract, institutions must first uphold their own obligations to clarity, coherence, and educational purpose; misaligned curricula and policies that individualise responsibility undermine institutional credibility. The principle addresses systemic conditions rather than student character.
requirements: Institutions must clearly articulate their educational goals and communicate the function and purpose of higher education to stakeholders before holding students accountable
constraints: The authors note universities operate through fragmented, localised practices varying across faculties, departments, and classrooms, and that GenAI exposes misalignments rather than creating them
target_learners: higher education undergraduates
university administrators
instructors
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
coherent institutional policy and pedagogy around emerging technologies
examples: The article contrasts institutions with contradictory stances (endorsing AI tools while policing their use) with the argument that policy contradictions produce moral double binds that incentivise misconduct.
key_sources: Tristan B. Taylor & Travis LaCroix. (2026). Purpose before policy: academic integrity, generative AI, and rhetorical stance. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-026-01706-1

article_title: The StudyChat Dataset: Analyzing Student Dialogues With ChatGPT in an Artificial Intelligence Course
citation: Hunter McNichols, Fareya Ikram, and Andrew Lan. 2026. The StudyChat Dataset: Analyzing Student Dialogues With ChatGPT in an Artificial Intelligence Course. In LAK26: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference (LAK 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3785022.3785029
title: StudyChat: a public dataset of annotated student–LLM tutoring dialogues from a university AI course
description: StudyChat is a publicly available dataset capturing real-world student interactions with an LLM-powered tutoring chatbot deployed in a semester-long, university-level artificial intelligence course. The authors deployed a web application replicating ChatGPT's core functionalities and logged interactions while students worked on Python programming assignments. It contains 2,214 conversations from 203 students totaling 16,851 utterances, plus 924 graded assignment submissions, all annotated with dialogue act labels and filtered for PII.
requirements: Student consent for data collection and sharing of assignment submissions
constraints: Drawn from a single upper-division AI course, which the authors state limits generalizability
Participants knew conversations were recorded, so behaviors may have been altered by the Hawthorne Effect
target_learners: upper-division university undergraduate CS students
target_learning_goals: understanding student LLM usage behavior in programming assignments
examples: Students used the gpt-4o-mini-backed tool without restrictions on 7 graded assignments across Fall 2024 and Spring 2025

title: Two-level dialogue act labeling schema for student–LLM interactions, applied at scale via LLM prompting
description: The authors developed a two-leveled dialogue act schema with 8 broad labels and 31 specific labels (Writing, Editing, Contextual Questions, Conceptual Questions, Verification, Context, Off Topic, Misc), built on prior co-programming work and their own systematic review of the conversations. Annotation at scale used a GPT4.1 prompting approach; human validation reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.910 for broad labels and 0.788 for specific labels, and human–LLM agreement on a held-out set was on par with human inter-annotator agreement.

Iterative annotator agreement checks to refine the schema

citation: Tao Wu, Jingyuan Chen, Wang Lin, Mengze Li, Yumeng Zhu, Ang Li, Kun Kuang, Fei Wu. (2025). Embracing Imperfection: Simulating Students with Diverse Cognitive Levels Using LLM-based Agents. https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19997
title: Student_100 dataset for student simulation
description: Student_100 is a dataset the authors built from the online programming platform PTA for evaluating student simulation. It contains 100 students, each with 50 well-annotated task-solving records: 40 past learning records and 10 simulation records, each including a Python programming task, the student's solving behavior with error analysis, and the student-written code. Records were restricted to those completed within a week to keep cognitive states stable, and 10 trained annotators added task descriptions and behavior evaluations. The article reports it forms "a reliable foundation for student simulation tasks."
requirements: Datasets for this task need a stable cognitive state per student, sequential task-solving records, and detailed annotations including task statements, solving behavior, and solutions, as the article states.
constraints: Validation in the article is constrained to programming domains, primarily due to the accessibility of relevant data.
target_learners: Python programming students on the PTA online platform
target_learning_goals: Python programming task-solving behavior and error patterns
examples: Each student sequence uses 40 records as past learning records and 10 as simulation records; 10 well-trained annotators provided detailed task descriptions and behavior evaluations.

article_title: Learning by Teaching: Engaging Students as Instructors of Large Language Models in Computer Science Education
citation: Xinming Yang, Haasil Pujara, Jun Li. (2025). Learning by Teaching: Engaging Students as Instructors of Large Language Models in Computer Science Education. Published as a conference paper at COLM 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05979
title: Socrates: a playground-and-grader system for deploying learning-by-teaching LLM assignments
description: Socrates is a system that "incorporates LLMs as virtual students to enhance learning in CS courses." Instructors write assignment questions in a JSON text file; the playground converts this into a Jupyter notebook served through a Voilà session as a web UI where students answer and interact with the LLM, and the grader re-sends each student's prompt to the LLM, verifies outputs against sample correct outputs with an LLM Yes/No judgment, and applies a self-consistency threshold. It is designed for ease of use by instructors with limited programming knowledge.
requirements: A controlled, uniform, non-modifiable interaction environment to ensure assessment fairness and uphold academic integrity
Instructors define questions, test cases, sample correct outputs, and self-consistency thresholds in the JSON assignment file
constraints: A graphical user interface for question design is left as future work
Full reproducibility is limited by inability to share raw student data and dependency on third-party, potentially evolving, commercial LLM APIs
target_learners: undergraduate computer science students
target_learning_goals: computer organization and assembly language competencies, including data representation, digital logic, and assembly programming
examples: In the deployment, four assignments built with Socrates were completed prior to the regular module assignments in the course

article_title: Learning by Teaching: Engaging Students as Instructors of Large Language Models in Computer Science Education
citation: Xinming Yang, Haasil Pujara, Jun Li. (2025). Learning by Teaching: Engaging Students as Instructors of Large Language Models in Computer Science Education. Published as a conference paper at COLM 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05979
title: Role-reversal pedagogy: positioning the student as instructor of an LLM to convert passive consumption into active knowledge construction
description: The article's organizing framework inverts the dominant LLM-as-tutor paradigm: "we propose to use LLMs in a reversed role, i.e., let a student teach an LLM to solve a question," so that "a student will be pushed to understand the materials behind the given question." It is grounded in the protégé effect, where the act of teaching deepens the instructor's own understanding, and in constructivist learning theory, with novel underspecified scenarios requiring students to define the rules of a new system. The framework targets over-reliance risks the authors identify in tutor-mode LLM use.
requirements: Questions must be designed so the LLM cannot solve them independently, creating a knowledge gap only the student can bridge
constraints: The authors state the study does not isolate the specific cognitive effects of re-encoding versus other factors
Designing questions robust against all forms of sophisticated gaming, such as remapping the novel problem onto a known equivalent, remains an open challenge
target_learners: undergraduate computer science students
target_learning_goals: active knowledge construction and mastery of core course competencies instead of passive information consumption
examples: The framework was instantiated in the Socrates system with four assignments in a Computer Organization and Assembly Language course

article_title: Student Development Agent: Risk-free Simulation for Evaluating AIED Innovations
citation: Jianxiao Jiang, Yu Zhang. (2025). Student Development Agent: Risk-free Simulation for Evaluating AIED Innovations. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09183
title: Student development agent framework: learning environment, endowment dimensions, developmental dimensions, actions, behaviors, and history
description: The article defines a design framework whose input includes "the learning environment, the endowment dimensions of students, the developmental dimensions of students, the actions defining how student agents can interact with the given learning environment," and whose output is simulated learning behaviors and changes in developmental dimensions. Developmental dimensions serve as "both outcomes for one period and inputs for the next period," enabling iterative simulation, while history records past trajectories. This framework targets prospective evaluation of AIED innovations without exposing real students.
requirements: An LLM simulation approach with categorization and value assignment, empirical findings acquisition, prompt construction, and iterative simulation, as the article specifies
constraints: The learning environment and endowment dimensions are considered stable along the simulation process in this design
target_learners: students with diverse characteristics in AI-powered educational settings
target_learning_goals: simulating long-term developmental trajectories of cognitive and non-cognitive outcomes
examples: The framework was applied in a case study simulating 42 students' non-cognitive development on the MAIC platform

citation: Jianxiao Jiang, Yu Zhang. (2025). Student Development Agent: Risk-free Simulation for Evaluating AIED Innovations. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09183
title: General education categorization: a two-level taxonomy of 3 categories and 33 subcategories built from Web of Science literature
description: The article constructed a general education categorization from 343,238 Web of Science papers via a pipeline of "literature screening, term extraction, embedding generation, coarse categorization and semantic clustering," refined by two domain experts. The result comprises three main categories—learning environment (14 subcategories), endowment dimensions (13 subcategories), and developmental dimensions (8 subcategories)—used to assign values to student development agents and support empirical findings retrieval.
requirements: Expert review and refinement of the clusters, as the article's pipeline includes expert card-sorting evaluation

target_learning_goals: standardizing representation of learning environments, learner endowments, and developmental outcomes for simulation

article_title: Student Development Agent: Risk-free Simulation for Evaluating AIED Innovations
citation: Jianxiao Jiang, Yu Zhang. (2025). Student Development Agent: Risk-free Simulation for Evaluating AIED Innovations. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.09183
title: Use LLM-based student development simulation as a risk-free pre-deployment evaluation of AIED innovations to avoid exposing real students to uncertain effects
description: The article argues that because educational interventions may carry irreversible effects, novel AIED designs should be prospectively evaluated before exposure to students. Its framework enables "a risk-free simulation process" that "directly avoids exposing actual students to uncertain effects of new teaching approaches, assessment methods, or adaptive feedback mechanisms," so that initial prototyping and experimentation occur without risking learners' academic or psychological well-being.
requirements: A validated student development agent whose predictions align with real outcomes sufficiently to inform decisions
constraints: The framework is presented as an initial, preliminary evaluation safeguarding students while supporting innovation pace, not a replacement for empirical studies
target_learners: students who would otherwise be exposed to untested AIED interventions
target_learning_goals: anticipating benefits and harms of educational designs on cognitive and non-cognitive development before deployment
examples: The MAIC case study evaluated simulated students' non-cognitive development without administering the course to new real students
