article_title: Simulating Students with Large Language Models: A Review of Architecture, Mechanisms, and Role Modelling in Education with Generative AI
citation: Luis Marquez-Carpintero, Alberto Lopez-Sellers, Miguel Cazorla. (2025). Simulating Students with Large Language Models: A Review of Architecture, Mechanisms, and Role Modelling in Education with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06078
title: Three-strategy taxonomy for modelling student knowledge in Simulated Students: direct prompts, knowledge tracing, and knowledge graphs with heuristics
description: The review organises knowledge modelling for LLM-based Simulated Students into three strategies. In direct prompt-based simulation, "Knowledge levels, common mistakes, or learning styles are directly defined within the LLM prompt", which is easy and customisable but risks overly idealised behaviour. Knowledge tracing tracks mastery of knowledge components over time with models such as DKT, DKVMN, AKT, or LLM-KT, offering strong prediction and real-time adaptation at the cost of technical complexity and data needs. Knowledge graphs and heuristics define the knowledge state with structured representations and explicit rules, giving high interpretability but requiring extensive manual curation. The review uses this taxonomy to structure its analysis of how simulated agents acquire, forget, and apply knowledge.
requirements: Direct prompt simulation relies heavily on prompt quality; knowledge tracing requires large datasets; knowledge graphs require extensive manual curation
constraints: Knowledge tracing interpretation can be challenging; knowledge graphs struggle with dynamic learning processes
target_learners: virtual simulated students in educational research
target_learning_goals: representing learner knowledge states, mastery, and misconceptions in simulation
examples: The review summarises the three strategies with advantages and limitations in Table 1, and describes Generative Students sampling mastered, confused and unknown knowledge components to craft learner personas
key_sources: Luis Marquez-Carpintero, Alberto Lopez-Sellers, Miguel Cazorla. (2025). Simulating Students with Large Language Models: A Review of Architecture, Mechanisms, and Role Modelling in Education with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06078

article_title: Simulating Students with Large Language Models: A Review of Architecture, Mechanisms, and Role Modelling in Education with Generative AI
citation: Luis Marquez-Carpintero, Alberto Lopez-Sellers, Miguel Cazorla. (2025). Simulating Students with Large Language Models: A Review of Architecture, Mechanisms, and Role Modelling in Education with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06078
title: Agent4Edu: a personalized learning simulator with LLM-based generative agents and a three-operation memory module
description: Agent4Edu is a personalized learning simulator in which "LLM-based generative agents simulate student response data and detailed problem-solving behaviour". Agents carry predefined student profiles, memory modules, and action modules for personalized learning scenarios, selecting, understanding, analyzing, and responding to exercises in a human-like manner. Its memory management system includes three operations: memory retrieval from short- and long-term stores, memory writing that promotes reinforced observations into short- or long-term memory, and memory reflection (summary and corrective forms) occurring exclusively in long-term memory. The review presents it as an example of integrating cognitive and affective elements such as dynamic cognitive states into simulated learner architectures.
requirements: Agents require predefined student profiles, memory modules, and action modules designed for personalized learning scenarios
constraints: The review notes traditional simulators are often limited to short-term memory, which this architecture addresses by combining factual response records with learning memory summaries
target_learners: virtual simulated students in personalized learning scenarios
target_learning_goals: simulating student responses and problem-solving behaviour for prediction and personalized learning research
examples: The review describes agents capable of selecting, understanding, analyzing, and responding to exercises in a human-like manner, allowing more accurate prediction of student responses

article_title: TeachBench - Evaluating LLM Teaching Ability
citation: Zheng Li, Siyao Song, Jingyuan Ma, Rui Li, Ying Zeng, Minghao Li, Zhifang Sui. (2026). TeachBench: A Syllabus-Grounded Framework for Evaluating Teaching Ability in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21375
title: TeachBench: a syllabus-grounded framework measuring LLM teaching capability via post-instruction student performance improvement
description: TeachBench evaluates LLMs as teacher agents by having them conduct multi-turn instruction over structured knowledge points derived from an exam syllabus, with a fixed-capability student agent as a learner proxy. Teaching effectiveness is "assessed by the student's performance improvement after instruction", enabling controlled comparison across teacher agents. Restricting teachers to knowledge points and example problems "avoids information leakage and enables reuse of existing benchmarks". The workflow has three stages: knowledge structuring, a teaching loop, and evaluation.
requirements: A structured knowledge tree extracted from an exam syllabus, questions annotated with knowledge paths, and a fixed student agent with room for improvement
constraints: The student agent is an LLM proxy, which the authors state "may not fully reflect the diversity and complexity of human learning behaviors"; no human-teacher baseline is included
target_learners: LLM student agents proxying learners preparing for the Chinese National College Entrance Examination (Gaokao)
target_learning_goals: Mastery of syllabus-defined knowledge points across mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, history, geography, and politics
examples: Instantiated on Gaokao syllabi and C-Eval questions, with 1,089 tagged evaluation questions across seven subjects
key_sources: Zheng Li, Siyao Song, Jingyuan Ma, Rui Li, Ying Zeng, Minghao Li, Zhifang Sui. (2026). TeachBench: A Syllabus-Grounded Framework for Evaluating Teaching Ability in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21375

article_title: TeachBench - Evaluating LLM Teaching Ability
citation: Zheng Li, Siyao Song, Jingyuan Ma, Rui Li, Ying Zeng, Minghao Li, Zhifang Sui. (2026). TeachBench: A Syllabus-Grounded Framework for Evaluating Teaching Ability in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21375
title: TeachBench knowledge-structured benchmark: Gaokao knowledge tree, LLM tagger, and difficulty-graded question generator
description: The benchmark converts Gaokao syllabi into a knowledge structure tree (semi-automatically built with Gemini-3 and GPT-5, then manually inspected), tags each question with root-to-leaf knowledge paths via an LLM tagger using depth-first traversal, and generates example problems at three difficulty levels per knowledge point. The final dataset "contains 1,089 questions in total" across seven subjects, with Mathematics (166), Physics (143), Chemistry (140), Biology (165), History (125), Geography (175), and Politics (175). Generated items undergo second-pass verification for alignment, answer correctness, and difficulty appropriateness.
requirements: Manual inspection of the knowledge tree and verifier acceptance of generated items under knowledge-point alignment, answer correctness, and difficulty criteria
constraints: Level 3 items must not directly reuse official Gaokao items; questions failing tagging after up to six attempts are dropped
target_learners: LLM teacher and student agents evaluated on Gaokao-domain knowledge
target_learning_goals: Syllabus-defined knowledge points across seven Gaokao subjects
examples: The generator produces three problems per knowledge point: easy in-class exercises, medium unit-quiz-style practice, and hard Gaokao-level reasoning items

article_title: Simulating Novice Students Using Machine Unlearning and Relearning in Large Language Models
citation: Jiajia Song, Zhihan Guo, and Jionghao Lin. (2026). Simulating Novice Students Using Machine Unlearning and Relearning in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26142
title: Knowledge-level student simulation pipeline: machine unlearning to initialize a stable novice state, then supervised and coach-guided relearning to model growth under tutoring
description: This framework replaces prompt-only role assignment with model-level knowledge degradation for LLM teachable agents. It argues that "prompt-based role assignment does not alter the model's underlying pre-trained knowledge, often leading to expert knowledge leakage and unstable role fidelity". The pipeline runs in three stages: machine unlearning of targeted knowledge components via LoRA, controlled relearning via supervised fine-tuning on forgotten QA pairs, and instructional relearning in a three-agent teachable-agent environment where a coach agent gives corrective feedback used as training signals.
requirements: A curated dataset with concept labels so unlearning targets can be drawn at knowledge-component and question levels
A capable full-knowledge coach LLM to deliver corrective feedback during instructional relearning
constraints: Experiments used only Python MCQs and a single base language model, which the authors state may limit generalisability to other subjects, task formats, or model architectures
The method operates at the level of knowledge representations and may not capture complex cognitive and social factors in human learning, such as affective processes
target_learners: Human students acting as tutors in learning-by-teaching settings
Teachers and tutors in practice-based professional development
target_learning_goals: Learning by teaching: explaining, diagnosing misconceptions, and giving feedback to a novice tutee
Conceptual understanding of Python programming knowledge components
examples: Unlearning Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 on Python MCQ knowledge components, then relearning via supervised fine-tuning or a DeepSeek-V3.2 coach agent in a three-agent dialogue environment
key_sources: Jiajia Song, Zhihan Guo, and Jionghao Lin. (2026). Simulating Novice Students Using Machine Unlearning and Relearning in Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.26142

article_title: Application-Driven Pedagogical Knowledge Optimization of Open-Source LLMs via Reinforcement Learning and Supervised
citation: Singh, N. P., Wang, X., Garikipati, A., Ciobanu, M., Mao, Q., & Das, R. (2026). Application-Driven Pedagogical Knowledge Optimization of Open-Source LLMs via Reinforcement Learning and Supervised Fine-Tuning. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06385
title: RL-SFT-RL: a multi-stage pipeline combining pedagogically aligned RL, difficulty-weighted SFT on RL-generated synthetic data, and an optional second RL round
description: The article proposes a three-phase training framework formalized in Algorithm 1: an initial RL stage (DAPO with asymmetric clipping) that identifies and trains on the base model's hard negatives; an SFT phase that uses the RL-trained model to synthesize training data, filtered and weighted by difficulty; and an optional second RL round reusing the Phase 1 hard dataset. The authors describe "a virtuous cycle of improvement" in which each stage builds on the previous one, and state the pipeline "comprising the initial RL stage for hard-negative identification, the difficulty-weighted SFT phase for knowledge distillation, and the optional final RL refinement" is formalized in Algorithm 1.
requirements: A base model with a benchmark (here CDPK) usable to identify failure modes via repeated attempts, plus a reward model trained to prioritize pedagogically sound responses that guide learners rather than simply providing answers
constraints: The third RL stage is optional; the article reports primary results only on teacher-exam-style multiple-choice questions from CDPK
target_learners: developers of educational AI tutors for classroom and platform integration
target_learning_goals: cross-domain pedagogical knowledge (strategic teaching capacity distinct from content knowledge)
examples: The pipeline transformed Qwen3-32B into EduQwen 32B-RL1 (94.13%), EduQwen 32B-SFT (96.20%), and EduQwen 32B-SFT-RL2 (96.52%) on the CDPK Benchmark

The models are positioned as high-precision pedagogical tutors suitable for classroom and platform integration, offering transparency, customizability, and cost-efficiency relative to proprietary APIs.

article_title: Application-Driven Pedagogical Knowledge Optimization of Open-Source LLMs via Reinforcement Learning and Supervised
citation: Singh, N. P., Wang, X., Garikipati, A., Ciobanu, M., Mao, Q., & Das, R. (2026). Application-Driven Pedagogical Knowledge Optimization of Open-Source LLMs via Reinforcement Learning and Supervised Fine-Tuning. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.06385
title: Target LLM training on the model's own failure modes with progressive difficulty and difficulty-weighted sampling
description: The article's training strategy identifies the base model's weaknesses empirically and concentrates learning capacity there. The base model was tested with 30 attempts per question; questions answered correctly in all attempts were excluded, and the remainder were sorted by error frequency into a difficulty-ordered curriculum. In SFT, questions with high baseline accuracy contributed a single representative example while difficult questions retained all high-quality examples, with increased training weights on high-difficulty items. The authors report this "difficulty-aware training strategy helped address the typical performance degradation that models experience on complex edge cases."
requirements: A labeled question bank with a ground truth answer key and the compute to run repeated attempts (30 per question) per item to estimate error frequency
constraints: Demonstrated on teacher-exam-style multiple-choice questions; the article notes future work should examine free-form tutoring dialogs
target_learners: developers fine-tuning LLMs for pedagogical domains
target_learning_goals: pedagogical knowledge, particularly performance on challenging pedagogical scenarios
examples: The first RL stage used a difficulty-ordered curriculum of 440 training data points; the SFT phase yielded 1,050 difficulty-ordered points from 40,000 generated responses

As the article states, it "defines institutional support as a facilitating condition, confidence as self-efficacy, concerns as inhibitors, and attitudes as behavioral intention." The analysis extends UTAUT by exploring how institutional and psychological factors jointly shape AI adoption in teaching, using moderated regression and mediation to test the mapped relationships.

article_title: Multimodal Dialogue in STEM Education
citation: Akshay Syal, Lawrence Swaminathan Xavier Prince, Evin Gultepe, Nik Bear Brown, Srinivas Sridhar. (2026). A Dialogue-Based Framework for Correcting Multimodal Errors in AI-Assisted STEM Education.
title: Structured multimodal dialogue functions as a scaffolding strategy that decomposes visually integrated tasks into sequenced steps before problem-solving
description: The article frames its intervention as an instructional design principle: "the structured multimodal dialogue developed in this study functions as a scaffolding strategy that decomposes a complex, visually integrated task into discrete, sequenced steps." Drawing on cognitive load management, the dialogue first elicits an explicit visual description, corrects misidentified elements, and only then prompts problem-solving, mirroring pedagogical scaffolding used in human tutoring. The authors position it as "a replicable instructional pattern" adoptable without model changes.
requirements: Corrections in the intermediate step must be restricted to observable visual properties of the source image, without hints regarding underlying physics principles or formulas.
constraints: The intervention was tested on each strategy independently rather than in combination, and problems requiring graphical outputs were excluded.
target_learners: undergraduate physics students using AI tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: reliable AI-assisted problem-solving on image-rich STEM content
examples: The three-step dialogue asked models to describe the figure, received researcher correction of misidentified visual elements such as a force vector direction or a graph intercept value, and then prompted problem-solving.
key_sources: Akshay Syal, Lawrence Swaminathan Xavier Prince, Evin Gultepe, Nik Bear Brown, Srinivas Sridhar. (2026). A Dialogue-Based Framework for Correcting Multimodal Errors in AI-Assisted STEM Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04131

article_title: Multimodal Dialogue in STEM Education
citation: Akshay Syal, Lawrence Swaminathan Xavier Prince, Evin Gultepe, Nik Bear Brown, Srinivas Sridhar. (2026). A Dialogue-Based Framework for Correcting Multimodal Errors in AI-Assisted STEM Education.
title: Three-step structured multimodal dialogue intervention protocol (describe, correct, solve)
description: A prompting protocol for correcting LLM multimodal errors, described as follows: "The intervention followed a three-step dialogue: (i) 'Describe what you observe in the figure/graph,' (ii) researcher correction of any misidentified visual elements, and (iii) 'Solve the problem'." Step (ii) corrections were limited to observable visual properties, such as clarifying a force vector direction or a graph intercept value, without physics hints. It was applied to all incorrect baseline responses and corrected 82% of errors without model retraining.
requirements: Access to the model via web interface or programmatic API workflow with chat history maintained per question.
constraints: No inter-rater verification was performed to confirm researcher corrections stayed free of domain-relevant information; the article recommends blind auditing of correction content.
target_learners: undergraduate physics students
educators integrating AI tutoring
target_learning_goals: correcting LLM errors on image-dependent physics problems
examples: For GPT-5 and Gemini-3-pro the intervention was executed programmatically with full chat history; for Sonnet-4.5 it was conducted manually via the web interface with no carry-over between questions.

article_title: Characterizing Students' LLM Usage Behaviors and Their Association with Learning in Critical Thinking Tasks
citation: Minju Park, Ivan Orozco Vasquez, and Cristina Conati. (2026). Characterizing Students' LLM Usage Behaviors and Their Association with Learning in Critical Thinking Tasks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04534
title: A bottom-up taxonomy of seven student LLM usage categories organized into three support types (student-driven, LLM-driven, comprehension)
description: The article presents a refined bottom-up coding scheme of students' LLM use, derived iteratively from LLM-use reports in a research-oriented course and cross-labeled by student initiative. The final scheme has seven categories (Improving Language, Confirming Ideas, Generating Ideas, Summarizing, Generating Answers, Information Extraction, Clarifying Concepts), which the article says are "organized into three higher-level types of support types based on the role the LLM played in the student's work": student-driven support, LLM-driven support, and comprehension support.
requirements: Students must report their LLM use (model, prompts, output) so submissions can be coded against the scheme; coding requires qualitative analysis of reported prompts and outputs.
constraints: The scheme was developed for reading, reasoning, and critiquing academic papers in one research-methods course context; the article notes coding schemes reflect the demands of their learning domains.
target_learners: undergraduate students in a research-methods course
target_learning_goals: critical reading of research papers
critical summary writing
discussion-point generation
examples: The refinement merged Paragraph from Bullet Points into Improving Language and split Information Extraction out of Clarifying Concepts based on observed student reports.

citation: Minju Park, Ivan Orozco Vasquez, and Cristina Conati. (2026). Characterizing Students' LLM Usage Behaviors and Their Association with Learning in Critical Thinking Tasks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04534
title: Provide guidance on effective LLM usage early in the course, when usage differences most affect performance
description: The article recommends that instructors offer guidance on effective LLM use at the start of a course, because differences in how and how much students used LLMs were associated with performance gaps mainly on early assessments, with gaps narrowing as students gained experience. The authors state that "providing guidance on effective LLM usage early in the course may help accelerate appropriate and productive adoption."
requirements: Assessments must give students opportunities to experience the impact of their LLM usage on their own performance, or additional scaffolding, feedback, or explicit guidance may be necessary.
constraints: In settings where the connection between assignments and exams is less explicit and consequences of LLM use are less observable, the authors state additional instructional scaffolding, feedback, or explicit guidance may be necessary.
target_learners: undergraduate students using LLMs in coursework
target_learning_goals: effective and learning-oriented LLM use
critical thinking and unaided exam performance
examples: In the studied course, students could directly experience the impact of LLM usage on midterm performance because exams mirrored the assignment tasks; gaps narrowed over the term without explicit guidance.

article_title: Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments
citation: Zaki Kurdya, Mohammed Zuqlam, Salem Amassi, Shady Telbany, Motaz Saad. (2026). Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05842
title: Taklif.AI: an LLM-powered platform generating interest-based personalized college assignments
description: Taklif.AI is "a platform that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically generate personalized assignments tailored to individual student interests", distinguishing itself from platforms that personalize only on academic performance metrics by incorporating extracurricular interests and cultural context. It runs on a four-layer serverless AWS architecture (Next.js web layer, Lambda API layer, DynamoDB/S3 storage, and an AI layer using LangChain, LiteLLM and LangSmith) with Llama 3.3 70B as the primary model. The platform personalizes or simplifies assignments but does not evaluate submissions or alter core learning objectives.
requirements: Students self-report extracurricular interests that pass interest guardrails; input assignments must be recognized as valid academic assignments
constraints: The platform does not evaluate or assess student submissions, nor alter the fundamental structure or core learning objectives of assignments
Primarily tested on programming and mathematics assignments
Evaluation of actual learning outcomes is beyond the scope of the paper and planned as future work
target_learners: undergraduate college students
higher education educators
target_learning_goals: engagement with course assignments across domains such as programming and mathematics
examples: A Two Sum programming assignment was personalized with an astronomy context (telescope alignment), and a set theory assignment was personalized with a basketball coaching context, preserving constraints and mathematical content verbatim
key_sources: Zaki Kurdya, Mohammed Zuqlam, Salem Amassi, Shady Telbany, Motaz Saad. (2026). Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05842

title: Interest-contextualized assignment rewriting that preserves original learning objectives verbatim
description: This pattern rewrites a general assignment so that its surface context comes from the student's interest domain while the task itself is unchanged. The article's examples show that "the personalization layer contextualizes the assignment within the student’s interest domain (telescope alignment for astronomy, basketball coaching for sports enthusiasts) while preserving all original learning objectives, constraints, and mathematical content verbatim". The approach generalized across domains (programming to discrete mathematics) and interest types (STEM to sports) in the printed examples.
requirements: A validated student interest and a valid source assignment, processed through the personalize-assignment prompt with constraints such as no explicit hints or solutions and content length not exceeding a 50% increment over the original
constraints: Highly abstract mathematical content such as real-analysis proofs may resist contextual framing without trivializing the material
Overly elaborate interest-based narratives could distract students from core learning objectives

target_learning_goals: maintaining learning objectives while increasing personal relevance and engagement of assignments
examples: A Two Sum programming task reframed as telescope alignment for an astronomy interest, and a set theory task reframed through basketball coaching, both keeping constraints and mathematical content verbatim

citation: Zaki Kurdya, Mohammed Zuqlam, Salem Amassi, Shady Telbany, Motaz Saad. (2026). Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05842
title: Interest-based personalization grounded in Self-Determination Theory and the Four-Phase Model of Interest Development
description: The article grounds its interest-based approach in two frameworks it names: Self-Determination Theory, "which emphasizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as key drivers of intrinsic motivation", and the Four-Phase Model of Interest Development, "which suggests that situational interest can mature into sustained individual interest through repeated exposure to meaningful content". Taklif.AI operationalizes this rationale by aligning assignment contexts with students' self-reported out-of-school interests, extending prior work that confined personalization to subject-specific or classroom interests.
requirements: Access to students' self-reported interests; the article notes self-reports may not reflect genuine engagement drivers
constraints: Prior studies cited confined personalization to subject-specific or classroom interests, neglecting broader out-of-school interests
Whether interest framing genuinely aids comprehension or merely adds stylistic embellishment requires empirical investigation
target_learners: higher education students with diverse cultural backgrounds and interests
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation and engagement through personally relevant assignment contexts
examples: Taklif.AI incorporates extracurricular interests and cultural contexts into assignment generation, unlike platforms personalizing on academic performance metrics alone

title: Six specialized role-assigned prompts sharing a four-part structure for assignment generation and guardrails
description: Taklif.AI's prompt engineering pipeline assigns distinct LLM roles and tasks across six prompts (personalize-assignment, simplify-assignment, assignment-guardrails, interest-guardrails, output-guardrails, pdf-ocr). Zero-shot prompting is adopted to maximize generalizability, with prompts iteratively refined using LangSmith evaluation tools.

constraints: Zero-shot prompting (no in-context examples) is used rather than few-shot exemplars

educators generating assignments at scale
target_learning_goals: personalized and simplified assignment generation with safety and relevance validation
examples: The personalize-assignment prompt assigns a Learning Experience Designer role with customization, creativity, cultural sensitivity, and fairness skills, and outputs JSON with a title and Markdown content

article_title: Quality-Conditioned Agreement in Automated Short Answer Scoring: Mid-Range Degradation and the Impact of Task-Specific Adaptation
citation: Abigail Victoria Gurin Schleifer, Moriah Ariely, Beata Beigman Klebanov, Asaf Salman, Giora Alexandron. (2026). Quality-Conditioned Agreement in Automated Short Answer Scoring: Mid-Range Degradation and the Impact of Task-Specific Adaptation. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07647v2
title: Quality-conditioned fairness: automated scoring must maintain consistent accuracy across the full spectrum of response quality
description: Quality-conditioned fairness is the standard the article proposes for evaluating automated scoring: "the requirement that automated scoring systems maintain consistent accuracy across the full spectrum of response quality". The article grounds it empirically: scoring errors concentrate on mid-range responses "typically produced by students whose knowledge is still developing", who may benefit most from formative feedback, making mid-range inaccuracy a fairness concern rather than mere noise.
requirements: states of knowledge must be detected accurately and equitably so that learners at different current states receive appropriate learning support rather than inappropriate help
constraints: the article shows current few-shot LLM scoring violates this standard in the mid-range; generalizability beyond the two biology items remains to be established
target_learners: high-school biology students (grades 10-12)
students with developing (partial) understanding
target_learning_goals: accurate and equitable scoring of open-ended scientific explanations
formative feedback targeting partially correct understanding
examples: the article turns mid-range degradation from an unknown bias into a known bias, a step it describes as necessary toward improving fairness in educational AI

As human-scored data accumulates and fine-tuning becomes feasible, the scoring can be automated more fully.

article_title: Sycophantic AI makes human interaction feel more effortful and less satisfying over time
citation: Lujain Ibrahim, Franziska Sofia Hafner, Myra Cheng, Cinoo Lee, Rebecca Anselmetti, Robb Willer, Luc Rocher, Diyi Yang. (2026). Sycophantic AI makes human interaction feel more effortful and less satisfying over time. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07912
title: Relational account of AI sycophancy
description: The article's organizing framework: the central long-term risk of sycophantic AI lies not in distorted judgments from single conversations but in how repeated effortless affirmation reshapes users' close relationships. As the authors put it, "by providing effortless understanding, sycophantic AI can raise the bar against which human relationships are judged." Sycophantic AI supplies the emotional and esteem support people associate with close others, so human relationships that still require effort may come to feel insufficient, shifting patterns of social support at scale.
requirements: Repeated exposure over weeks, not single conversations, for the relational effects to emerge
constraints: Effects observed after three weeks; whether they intensify or plateau over months or years remains an open question
Sample reflects a particular cultural context; effects could differ in direction or magnitude in populations with different norms around social support
target_learners: Adult AI chatbot users seeking personal advice and support
target_learning_goals: Understanding how AI interaction styles shape users' expectations of and satisfaction with human relationships
examples: In the three-week longitudinal study, participants conversing with a sycophantic AI became nearly as likely to seek personal advice from it as from close friends and family

title: Agentic AI ecosystems: coordinated networks of autonomous, goal-directed agents characterized by autonomy, coordination, adaptability, and context-awareness
description: The article defines agentic AI ecosystems as interconnected configurations of numerous autonomous specialized agents that communicate, coordinate tasks, and optimise workflows across domains and functions, enabling system-level intelligence with emergent capabilities surpassing individual components. It states that "Agentic ecosystems are defined by several key characteristics such as, autonomy (agents operate independently while aligning with system -level goals), coordination (agents communicate and collaborate effectively), adaptability (systems respond dynamically to changing contexts), and context -awareness". Unlike traditional agents limited to predefined tasks, agentic systems continuously plan, learn, and adjust behavior based on evolving contexts.

citation: Cassandra Lucas, Anshul Bihani, Rohini Kukka, Chun-Hua Tsai, Jaydeb Sarker, and Mia Mohammad Imran. 2026. TowardsSocratiCode: Designing a Generative AI-Based Programming Tutor for K-12 Students through a 4-Week Participatory Design Study. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17857
title: SocratiCode: a Socratic, adaptive generative-AI tutoring framework for beginner programming
description: SocratiCode is a prompt-based generative-AI tutoring framework that operationalizes Socratic tutoring principles—guided questioning, reflection, incremental hints, and learner-paced progression—for K-12 beginner programming. It embeds structural elements such as introductions, examples, practice, summaries, and follow-up tasks that "maintain coherence and create natural stopping points," and elicits minimal background information to adjust pacing, analogies, and explanations. The framework draws on adaptive learning theory, generative-AI education research, prompt engineering, and Socratic tutoring principles, and was refined through participatory design with two K-12 learners.

Findings are preliminary; other generative AI models may behave differently under similar conditions

target_learning_goals: Introductory Python programming concepts and problem-solving skills
examples: The final prompt template specified role and audience, learner adaptation, lesson flow, reinforcement, tutorial closure with a hard-stop, interaction rules pausing after exercises, and scope constraints teaching only requested concepts

article_title: Simulating Learners' Task-Selection Strategies and System Constraints in Mastery Learning
citation: Haley Noh, Aarna Chowdhary, Jeroen Ooge, Vincent Aleven, Conrad Borchers. (2026). Simulating Learners' Task-Selection Strategies and System Constraints in Mastery Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21613
title: Simulation-based framework for evaluating learner task-selection strategies and system constraints in mastery-based ITS
description: A simulation framework that models mastery learning as a repeated problem-level decision cycle in which simulated learners select skills via predefined strategies, the system selects problems, performance is generated via AFM, and mastery is updated via BKT with a 95% mastery threshold. It is grounded in real student interaction data from two math ITS datasets and enables "controlled comparison of learner strategies and system constraints under standardized conditions" prior to classroom deployment. The framework supports close-the-loop experimentation by identifying which learner behaviors warrant targeted system constraints.
requirements: Real student interaction data to fit AFM and BKT parameters and derive typical solution paths
A mastery threshold (95% posterior mastery probability) and predefined task-selection decision rules
constraints: Models a limited set of strategies and constraints and does not capture motivational, metacognitive, or affective factors
Focuses on a task-selection-first setup and does not model direct problem-selection, multi-task-selection, or fully system-driven sequencing
Learner strategies are modeled as static rather than adapting over time
target_learners: middle school and high school mathematics students in ITS environments
target_learning_goals: efficient skill mastery in multi-step mathematical problem solving
examples: Simulations of 1,000 learners per condition using PSLC DataShop datasets for equation solving (58 problems, 10 skills) and graph interpretation (31 problems, 13 skills), with open-source simulation and analysis code
key_sources: Haley Noh, Aarna Chowdhary, Jeroen Ooge, Vincent Aleven, Conrad Borchers. (2026). Simulating Learners' Task-Selection Strategies and System Constraints in Mastery Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21613

article_title: Simulating Learners' Task-Selection Strategies and System Constraints in Mastery Learning
citation: Haley Noh, Aarna Chowdhary, Jeroen Ooge, Vincent Aleven, Conrad Borchers. (2026). Simulating Learners' Task-Selection Strategies and System Constraints in Mastery Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21613
title: Apply system constraints selectively to inefficient learner task-selection strategies rather than uniformly
description: In shared-control mastery-based ITS, constraints on task and problem selection should target the learner strategies that produce inefficiencies rather than being applied to everyone. The simulations show constraints sharply reduce overpractice for the risk-averse strategy while having little effect on efficient strategies, so "applying the same constraints to all learner types is unnecessary". This preserves learner autonomy and motivational benefits for students whose strategies already align with mastery objectives.
requirements: Estimates of individual learners' task-selection strategies or learner state to decide when constraints apply
Constraints that bound rather than remove learner choice to preserve autonomy
constraints: Overly prominent system constraints may undermine student autonomy perceptions and lower motivation
target_learners: middle school and high school mathematics students using shared-control ITS
target_learning_goals: efficient mastery of mathematical skills with preserved learner autonomy
examples: The simulation applied closer-to-mastery, further-from-mastery, prefer-easier, and prefer-harder constraints across eight task-selection strategies to identify which learner behaviors warrant targeted constraints

article_title: StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
citation: Siddhartha Pradhan, Yanping Pei, Morgan Lee, Puyuan Zhang, Erin Ottmar, and Adam C. Sales. (2026). StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23048
title: StanBKT: an open-source Python package for Bayesian estimation of BKT models in Stan
description: StanBKT is an open-source Python package for estimating classical BKT models and several extensions using Bayesian inference in Stan. It provides a unified interface for model specification, parameter estimation, and posterior analysis, including filtered and smoothed latent-state estimation, posterior predictive prediction, visualization utilities, and diagnostics such as ESS, MCSE, and R-hat. Source code is public on GitHub, installable via pip, with online documentation and worked examples.
requirements: A compatible C++ toolchain is required because Stan models are transpiled to C++ and compiled before execution
target_learners: students working in intelligent tutoring systems whose response sequences are modeled
target_learning_goals: estimating mastery, learning, forgetting, guessing, and slipping parameters from student interaction data
examples: The package fits models through a three-stage workflow of model specification, parameter estimation, and analysis, demonstrated in a worked example with simulated data for 100 students and 30 problems
key_sources: Siddhartha Pradhan, Yanping Pei, Morgan Lee, Puyuan Zhang, Erin Ottmar, and Adam C. Sales. (2026). StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23048

article_title: StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
citation: Siddhartha Pradhan, Yanping Pei, Morgan Lee, Puyuan Zhang, Erin Ottmar, and Adam C. Sales. (2026). StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23048
title: Bayesian formulation of BKT: priors, posterior inference, and hierarchical partial pooling
description: The article frames BKT estimation as Bayesian inference: parameters are treated as random variables with prior distributions, and inference targets the posterior P(theta | Y), which "explicitly captures parameter uncertainty" and propagates it to downstream analyses such as mastery trajectories and group comparisons. The framework motivates Bayesian estimation on four grounds: principled uncertainty quantification, incorporation of prior knowledge for regularization, mitigation of BKT identifiability issues via informative priors, and natural extension to hierarchical models with partial pooling across students, skills, or items, which is "particularly beneficial in sparse-data settings common in educational experiments."
requirements: Approximate inference (MCMC or variational) is required because exact inference is intractable due to exponentially many latent state sequences
constraints: Approximate methods such as VI and Pathfinder produce biased approximations that often underestimate posterior uncertainty and simplify dependencies among parameters
target_learners: students in intelligent tutoring systems and educational experiments modeled via knowledge tracing
target_learning_goals: quantifying uncertainty in learning, forgetting, guessing, and slipping parameters for adaptive instruction and intervention comparison
examples: StanBKT implements this formulation with logit-scale priors, half-scaled-logit bounds on guess and slip, and hierarchical priors with learned between-group variance
key_sources: Siddhartha Pradhan, Yanping Pei, Morgan Lee, Puyuan Zhang, Erin Ottmar, and Adam C. Sales. (2026). StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23048

article_title: StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
citation: Siddhartha Pradhan, Yanping Pei, Morgan Lee, Puyuan Zhang, Erin Ottmar, and Adam C. Sales. (2026). StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23048
title: Three pooling formulations for BKT: standard, multi (group-specific), and hierarchical (partial pooling)
description: StanBKT organizes BKT formulations into three pooling types. Standard BKT shares a single parameter set across all students (full pooling, assuming homogeneous learning and response behavior). Multi BKT estimates a separate parameter set for each predefined group such as classrooms, treatment conditions, or individual students, enabling direct comparison across groups. Hierarchical BKT introduces partial pooling through hierarchical priors, decomposing each parameter into a global component and group-level deviations with a learned variance controlling shrinkage. The article states this formulation "stabilizes and regularizes estimates in sparse data contexts while preserving systematic differences across groups."
requirements: Grouped and hierarchical variants require a group identifier column in the interaction data
constraints: Standard BKT assumes homogeneous learning and response behavior across students and items
target_learners: students grouped by classroom, treatment condition, cohort, or individual
target_learning_goals: comparing learning dynamics across experimental conditions and stabilizing estimates in sparse-data settings
examples: The perceptual cue reanalysis used Multi BKT with condition-specific parameters across the nine spacing-by-color conditions, fit via MCMC
key_sources: Siddhartha Pradhan, Yanping Pei, Morgan Lee, Puyuan Zhang, Erin Ottmar, and Adam C. Sales. (2026). StanBKT: Rethinking Parameter Estimation in Bayesian Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23048

article_title: Socially fluent AI decouples conversational signals from source identity in online interaction
citation: Lixiang Yan, Yueqiao Jin, Xibin Han, Dragan Gasevic. (2026). Socially fluent AI decouples conversational signals from source identity in online interaction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23426
title: Truth-default theory extended to presumed human identity in computer-mediated interaction
description: The article applies truth-default theory — the account that in ordinary interaction people default to presuming honesty and benign intent unless contextual triggers raise suspicion — to presumed human identity in synchronous text-based interaction. It argues that socially fluent AI "effectively decoupled social signaling from source identity, rendering established computer-mediated communication heuristics non-diagnostic". The theory explains why participants exhibited a slight bias toward human attribution and why suspicion cues such as perceived scriptedness or rapid response can be shared by both AI and human targets.
requirements: Undisclosed interaction under truth-default conditions, where suspicion is not externally prompted
constraints: Findings bounded to undisclosed, synchronous, text-based group interaction; identity inference may differ with richer modalities or explicit warnings that AI may be present
target_learners: adult online collaborators
target_learning_goals: inferring interlocutor identity and intent from conversational cues in online interaction
examples: Participants exhibited a slight bias toward human attribution (β = 1.065) and expressed uncertainty frequently, yet neither improved discrimination sensitivity

article_title: Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation
citation: Salsman, J. (2026). Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26428
title: slidesqaqa: a Flask-based system for generating pedagogical questions from PDF slide decks
description: slidesqaqa is a single-server Python Flask application that takes a PDF presentation as input, renders each slide into a visual thumbnail, extracts native text with PyMuPDF, and coordinates a four-phase LLM workflow. The system outputs "a comprehensive, hierarchical JSON structure that details the deck's topics, categorizes slide roles, defines specific learning goals, and provides bounded, context-aware comprehension questions." A frontend UI serves as a real-time log viewer and data visualizer.
requirements: Requires PyMuPDF for document extraction and integration with the Google GenAI SDK for multimodal inference
constraints: Reliance on a specific proprietary LLM (Gemini) poses reproducibility and long-term stability risks if API models are updated or deprecated
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in technical lecture courses
target_learning_goals: comprehension of slide-based lecture content in technical subjects such as NLP and deep learning
examples: Evaluated on the "Self-Attention and Transformers" (cs224n-2024-lecture08-transformers) and "Neural Constituency Parsing" (cs288-sp23-neural-parsing) lecture decks

article_title: Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation
citation: Salsman, J. (2026). Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26428
title: Four-stage windowed pipeline architecture for deck-level question generation
description: The article's organizing architecture is a multi-pass generative pipeline: a Window Planner that "Analyzes overlapping windows of slides, creating a contact sheet image to infer titles, summaries, modalities, roles, and a provisional question budget"; a Deck Synthesis phase merging window analyses into one coherent deck plan; a Slide Annotator generating questions per slide using deck context; and a Reconciliation phase evaluating the full-deck annotation for redundancies and unbalanced coverage. The windowed design is intended to mitigate LLM context limits while preserving the presentation's narrative flow.
requirements: All outputs must conform to strongly typed JSON schemas (Pydantic models SlidePlan, SlideAnnotationModel, ReconciliationModel) to ensure data integrity
constraints: The multi-pass architecture incurs substantial LLM inference latency and API costs on large decks
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in technical lecture courses
target_learning_goals: deck-level pedagogical scaffolding of comprehension questions across a full presentation
examples: The reconciliation phase re-runs annotation with adjusted budgets when actions such as rewrite, expand, or reduce are needed

citation: Salsman, J. (2026). Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26428
title: Modality-based question budget allocation favoring mechanism slides over structural slides
description: The system allocates a bounded question budget per slide based on detected modality and pedagogical role. The window planner prompt instructs: "Favor low budgets for title , agenda , transition , administrative , appendix , and r epe at ed recap slides ." and "Favor higher budgets for rich mechanism , comparison , result , diagram , chart , table , or s y n t h e s i s slides ." Budgets range from 0 to 5, and zero questions are explicitly acceptable, so generation effort concentrates on core pedagogical material.
requirements: Slide modality types and deck roles must be drawn from the fixed label vocabularies defined in the window planner prompt
constraints: Budgets are capped between 0 and 5 per slide, though the deck synthesis prompt notes some slides may deserve more than three questions
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in technical lecture courses
target_learning_goals: balanced question coverage aligned with instructional importance across heterogeneous slide types
examples: The reconciliation phase uses an action vocabulary of keep, reduce, expand, zero_out, and rewrite with a new question budget between 0 and 5 per slide

article_title: How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops -- A Taxonomy
citation: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966v1
title: A hierarchical taxonomy of novice difficulties with selection and iteration in code reading
description: The article introduces a fine-grained taxonomy categorizing novice programmers' difficulties with reading control flow constructs. Its top dimension is the control structure involved (selection or iteration), with lower levels grouping difficulties by what students do not understand and then by how they struggle. The authors state it categorizes "difficulties specifically related to reading and understanding the control flow constructs selection and iteration". It is intended to harmonize research results, classify errors unambiguously, and hint at undiscovered difficulties.
requirements: It is scoped to conceptual-knowledge difficulties in reading code, excluding syntactic, lexical, and writing-only difficulties
constraints: It covers imperative languages such as C, C++, Python and Java and block-based languages like Scratch; the authors note they do not claim to have incorporated every paper on control-structure difficulties yet
target_learners: novice programmers in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: understanding of control flow, conditional statements, and loops
examples: Categories with literature references retain the source's wording; categories without references are newly created or newly found difficulties from the authors' own research
key_sources: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966

article_title: How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops -- A Taxonomy
citation: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966v1
title: Extended Taxonomy Design Process (ETDP) as an iterative method for building taxonomies
description: The ETDP, described by Kundisch et al. and adopted as this article's method, is an iterative, user-centered taxonomy design methodology with six phases: problem specification, objective definition (including a meta-characteristic and ending conditions), development, demonstration and analysis, evaluation, and communication. The article emphasizes that "the ETDP is inherently iterative, allowing taxonomy designers to continuously update, extend, and refine existing taxonomies without restarting the entire design procedure". It supports both empirical-to-conceptual and conceptual-to-empirical building approaches.
requirements: Designers must determine the meta-characteristic, objective and subjective ending conditions, and evaluation goals upfront
constraints: Taxonomies should be judged by suitability for their intended purpose, not as right or wrong
target_learners: taxonomy designers and computing education researchers
target_learning_goals: structuring and classifying phenomena such as student difficulties
examples: This article applies the ETDP with a conceptual-to-empirical start, justified by the existing substantial body of research on student difficulties
key_sources: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966

article_title: How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops -- A Taxonomy
citation: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966v1
title: Distinctions among error, difficulty, and misconception, with misconceptions as potentially fragile knowledge
description: The article defines a terminology framework for classifying student problems: an error is a concrete incidence of a mistake, a difficulty is the underlying misunderstanding or erroneous cognitive behavior that causes errors, and a misconception is a difficulty grounded in an incorrect mental model. The authors define a misconception as "a specific kind of difficulty that is based in a concrete mental model about a specific programming concept that does not align with reality". They also argue misconceptions need not be stable, challenging prior definitions.
requirements: The terms must be used distinctly to avoid confusion, since they are sometimes used interchangeably in the literature
constraints: The authors challenge the definition that misconceptions are necessarily stable and systematically repeated, noting novice programming misconceptions can be fragile knowledge
target_learners: novice programmers
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of programming constructs
examples: The framework treats misconceptions as non-binary, allowing students to hold semi-correct or multiple notions of a concept at the same time
key_sources: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966

citation: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966v1
title: Selection branch of the taxonomy: five categories of conditional-statement difficulties
description: The selection branch classifies difficulties with conditional statements into five categories: the selective nature of selection statements, boundaries of the selection body, the else-branch, timing of condition check, and nesting. Example categories include thinking all branches execute independent of their condition and confusion between "if(C) A; else B;" and "if (C) A; B;". Many categories carry literature references, while others are newly created from the authors' own research.
requirements: Applies to difficulties in reading code containing selection statements, within the paper's conceptual-knowledge scope
constraints: Syntactic and lexical errors are excluded as fundamentally different in nature
target_learners: novice programmers in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: understanding conditional statements and their execution
examples: The nesting category includes confusion between sequencing versus nesting of if-statements and ignoring an if-condition inside a loop

article_title: How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops -- A Taxonomy
citation: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966v1
title: Iteration branch of the taxonomy: seven categories of loop difficulties
description: The iteration branch classifies difficulties with loops into seven categories: the repeating nature of iteration statements, interaction with code outside the loop, order of execution of loop parts, state (including control-variable difficulties), difficulties with the loop condition, nesting, and break and continue. Examples include the "loop is if" belief and thinking nested loops execute simultaneously. The branch draws on both cited literature and the authors' own interview and test data.
requirements: Applies to conceptual difficulties in reading iteration statements; the loop is described as consisting of four parts: initialization, condition check, body, and update of control variable
constraints: Some entries, such as struggling to identify ranges from relational operators, are noted by the authors as possibly lexical difficulties but kept for their conceptual component
target_learners: novice programmers in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: understanding loops, loop conditions, control variables, and nested iteration
examples: The break and continue category records beliefs such as "break is continue" and thinking break terminates the whole program

article_title: 'It''s OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing'
citation: Kim, Jiyoon; Toyama, Kentaro; Kim, Sangmi; Carroll, John. (2026). "It's OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29090
title: Five-sites framework of AI-use expectations in a course
description: The article proposes that for any given course, concepts of appropriate AI use for academic writing are housed in five distinct sites: faculty intention, formal policy, student interpretation, student self-policy, and student practice. These sites, whether explicit or implicit, formal or informal, often differ from one another, and the divergences create openings for re-interpretation of ethically questionable AI use. The framework explains how instructor expectations are translated, interpreted, personalized, and enacted, with the boundary of acceptable use softening at each site.
requirements: Analysis of a course requires access to both syllabi or formal policy documents and student accounts of their interpretation and practice, as the article obtained through interviews, syllabi, chat logs, and submissions.
constraints: Faculty intention was not measured directly; the article states it was inferred from syllabi and participant interviews because faculty were not interviewed.
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding and negotiating course AI policies in academic writing
examples: The article illustrates site mismatches with a student who copied AI text believing idea-generation permission covered it, students who misremembered or mixed up policies across courses, and students who violated their own stated norms in practice.
key_sources: Kim, Jiyoon; Toyama, Kentaro; Kim, Sangmi; Carroll, John. (2026). "It's OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29090

article_title: 'It''s OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing'
citation: Kim, Jiyoon; Toyama, Kentaro; Kim, Sangmi; Carroll, John. (2026). "It's OK Because...": The Wild West of Student Rationalization of AI Use in Academic Writing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29090
title: Taxonomy of 23 student rationalizations for AI use in six classes
description: The article presents a taxonomy of 23 distinct moral justifications, termed Rationalizations (R1–R23), that students use to justify AI use in writing assignments, grouped into six Rationalization Classes: victimless behavior, minimal AI contribution, ex ante contribution, post hoc contribution, responsibility denial, and perceived benefit. Definitions were developed inductively from participant accounts through thematic analysis of interviews, chat logs, and course documents, with representative participant quotes for each rationalization. The taxonomy classifies the justifications rather than the AI-use practices themselves, so the same practice can be justified through different rationalizations.
requirements: The taxonomy was built from semi-structured interview excerpts in which participants described or justified their AI use, consolidated from 46 subcodes through team consensus.
constraints: The article notes space limits prevented in-depth description of every rationalization, and the sample comprised students who self-reported at least sometimes using AI for writing.
target_learners: undergraduate students using generative AI for academic writing
target_learning_goals: moral sense-making about acceptable AI assistance in academic writing
examples: Class examples include R3 Busywork (AI acceptable for low-value assignments), R6 My Ideas (core ideas originated with the student), R12 My Style (output sounding like the student makes it theirs), R13 Normalization, and R19 Time Economy.

citation: Junsoo Park, Youssef Medhat, Htet Phyo Wai, Ploy Thajchayapong and Ashok K. Goel. (2026). title: Interpretable decision layer for outcome-independent coordination of teacher and student feedback
description: A transparent mechanism that combines teacher and student feedback to rank course topics needing attention without grades or outcome labels. It integrates three signals — gap prevalence, survey disagreement, and teacher friction — into a topic priority score with a per-topic decision record explaining each ranking. The article states it "organizes teacher, student, and researcher roles around this shared decision process," positioning the layer as supporting human–AI co-agency rather than replacing instructor judgment.

constraints: Weights are specified rather than learned in the current implementation; the study reflects one graduate-level course offering and findings are preliminary and exploratory
target_learners: graduate CS students in an AI-augmented classroom
target_learning_goals: timely identification of course topics requiring instructional attention before graded outcomes are available
examples: In the study offering, the highest-ranked topics were analogical reasoning, frames, planning, case-based reasoning, and knowledge-based AI, each accompanied by a per-topic decision record

article_title: Special-R1: Reinforcement Learning for Special Education — Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training
citation: Unggi Lee, Jihoi Na, Yeil Jeong, Haeun Park, Yeonju Jang. (2026). Reinforcement Learning for Special Education: Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30670
title: Special-R1: disability-aware pedagogical RL coupling a two-dimensional adaptive prompt with a persona-aware Thinking Reward
description: Special-R1 is a framework extending pedagogical multi-turn RL to special education. It factors pedagogical support into two orthogonal dimensions: a support level (amount) mapped from the learner's baseline accuracy to Maximum, Moderate, or Minimum support following the I-Do / We-Do / You-Do progression, and a support style (manner) drawn from the learner's disability profile, so that "thewhatcomes from the support level, thehowcomes from the disability profile." Its second component is a persona-aware Thinking Reward whose judge is prompted with the learner's disability profile and scores whether the thinking trace reflects disability-appropriate reasoning, which the authors describe as "the first reward we are aware of that explicitly scoresdisability-appropriatereasoning."
requirements: Requires a pre-measured baseline accuracy of the student simulator on the given problem type to select the support level, and a structured disability rubric with learning characteristics, communication patterns, and recommended tutor strategies.
constraints: Every student in the framework is a disability-conditioned LLM simulator; improvements on judge-based metrics have not been validated with real learners with disabilities.
Experiments use 7-8B tutors; behavior at larger scales remains to be studied.
target_learners: Learners with disabilities across five profiles: intellectual disability, specific learning disability, autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and emotional/behavioral disorder
target_learning_goals: Multi-domain tutoring covering mathematics, reading comprehension, social reasoning, and life skills
examples: The adaptive prompt maps baseline accuracy in [0.01, 0.20) to Maximum support (micro-steps, concrete examples), [0.20, 0.40) to Moderate support, and [0.40, 0.60) to Minimum support with open-ended questions.
key_sources: Unggi Lee, Jihoi Na, Yeil Jeong, Haeun Park, Yeonju Jang. (2026). Reinforcement Learning for Special Education: Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30670

title: Released Special-R1 artifacts: multi-domain ZPD-filtered corpus, SPED-Tutor-Mix evaluation set, seven checkpoints, and disability-aware evaluation pipeline
description: The article releases the training and evaluation artifacts behind Special-R1. The training corpus contains approximately 54k problems across four domains (mathematics, reading comprehension, social reasoning, life skills), filtered to a ZPD window of 1-60% solve rate by the Llama-3.1-8B student simulator and annotated with baseline accuracy. The evaluation set is the persona-augmented SPED-Tutor-Mix test split in which "every item carries a disability profile so that persona-aware metrics can be computed." The disability rubric is released as disability_types.yaml alongside the code, together with all seven model checkpoints and the evaluation pipeline.
requirements: The corpus is ZPD-filtered to problems with 1-60% solve rate by the frozen student simulator before training.
constraints: The corpus contains a comparatively small number of LD-appropriate mathematics items, which the authors link to the sld_math weakness.
target_learners: LLM tutors being aligned for learners with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Multi-domain tutoring: mathematics, reading comprehension, social reasoning, and life skills

article_title: Special-R1: Reinforcement Learning for Special Education — Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training
citation: Unggi Lee, Jihoi Na, Yeil Jeong, Haeun Park, Yeonju Jang. (2026). Reinforcement Learning for Special Education: Aligning LLM Tutors to Diverse Learners through Disability-Adaptive Training. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30670
title: Calibrate both the amount and the style of tutor support to the learner: support level from baseline accuracy, style from disability-specific access needs
description: The article argues effective special-education tutoring demands two simultaneous adjustments: the amount of support, calibrated to the learner's zone of proximal development, and the style of support, calibrated to disability-specific access needs through Explicit Instruction, the Prompting Hierarchy, High-Leverage Practices, and Universal Design for Learning. Special-R1 operationalizes both axes inside the tutor's system prompt and the judge of its thinking trace, and its ablations show the prompt-style axis is the single largest driver of persona-aware Fit gains. The framework treats these as orthogonal dimensions rather than a single generic pedagogical prompt.
requirements: A pre-measured baseline accuracy per problem type to select the support level, and a structured disability profile specifying recommended tutor strategies, communication patterns, and learning characteristics.
constraints: The Thinking Reward component of the framework only becomes effective when combined with adaptive prompting; under static prompts the accept/reject judge saturates.
target_learners: Learners with disabilities in one-on-one LLM tutoring
target_learning_goals: Scaffolded problem-solving support tailored to disability-specific access needs
examples: The tutor prompt variants SPED-static and SPED-adaptive draw style verbatim from the disability profile's tutor_strategies, communication_patterns, and learning_characteristics fields, with SPED-adaptive selecting the support level dynamically from baseline accuracy.

article_title: Simulating Students' Java Programming Errors with Large Language Models
citation: Ali Keramati, Jie Cao, Iman Mohammadi, Mark Warschauer, Yang Shi. (2026). Simulating Students' Java Programming Errors with Large Language Models. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14113
title: Diversity-alignment trade-off framework for LLM student-error simulation
description: The article proposes two dimensions, diversity and alignment, as central to the usefulness of LLMs as proxies for authentic student errors. Models strong in diversity (e.g., Gemini) often exhibit weaker alignment, and vice versa, with Claude Sonnet 4 described as "the most balanced option". The framework holds that model choice should be guided by analytic goals: diversity-oriented models explore the breadth of potential misconceptions, while alignment-oriented models approximate authentic error distributions. Struggling level acts as a moderator within this framework, raising diversity while lowering fidelity.
requirements: Evaluation must assess both diversity (e.g., pairwise AST edit distances) and alignment (nearest distance to authentic submissions) simultaneously
constraints: Even the most balanced model varied across tasks and prompts, so no single LLM is universally optimal
target_learners: introductory Java programming students
target_learning_goals: realistic simulation of novice logical errors for feedback design and misconception analysis
examples: Figure 5 plots the trade-off between alignment (fidelity) and diversity across the five evaluated models
key_sources: Ali Keramati, Jie Cao, Iman Mohammadi, Mark Warschauer, Yang Shi. (2026). Simulating Students' Java Programming Errors with Large Language Models. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14113

article_title: What Robots Do Matters More Than What They Look Like: Task Context Shapes Trust in Educational HRI
citation: Anna-Maria Velentza, Konstantina Nikou, Anne-Gwenn Bosser, Nikolaos Fachantidis. (2026). What Robots Do Matters More Than What They Look Like: Task Context Shapes Trust in Educational HRI. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22What+Robots+Do+Matters+More+Than+What+They+Look+Like%22
title: Align robot behavior and interaction capabilities with task requirements rather than prioritizing anthropomorphic appearance when deploying educational robots
description: The article recommends that educational robot design and deployment focus on matching what robots do to interaction goals instead of relying on looks. It states that "designers of educational robots should prioritize aligning robot behavior and interaction capabilities with task requirements rather than focusing primarily on anthropomorphic appearance". Robots may be accepted as instructional guides regardless of embodiment, while emotionally sensitive tasks need extra design work such as transparency, privacy assurances, or enhanced socio-emotional behaviors.
requirements: Robots must be positioned within educational workflows according to task demands, with behavioral or relational mechanisms added before use in emotionally sensitive interactions
constraints: Findings come from video-based, script-controlled short-term evaluations with a homogeneous sample of Greek undergraduate future educators; the article notes video-mediation can mitigate appearance effects and calls for testing real-time, longitudinal, and broader-population interactions
target_learners: undergraduate future educators (pre-service teachers)
target_learning_goals: trust in socially assistive robots across educational tasks (teaching, procedural instruction, personal-information discussion)
examples: In the experiment, all three robots delivered identical scripts across teaching, instruction, and personal-information tasks, and trust followed task type (T2 > T1 > T3) while robot type showed no meaningful effect

title: Ten-item Greek-language trust questionnaire assembled from established HRI trust scales with Lawshe content validation
description: A 10-item questionnaire rated on a five-point Likert scale after each video, developed by a multidisciplinary group of psychologists, engineers, and teachers by combining items from established trust and perception questionnaires (including trust perception, Jian et al., Kohn et al., and Godspeed items). Items cover willingness, competence, explicit trust, relative performance, reliability, and communication clarity. Content validity was assessed with Lawshe's CVR by five experts: "The resulting CVR met the critical threshold for five experts (CVR = .883, two-tailed p = .05)". Internal consistency across robot–task conditions ranged from α = .853 to .948.
requirements: Items were adapted to Greek following the bilingual-speakers technique and reviewed by five subject-matter experts
constraints: Validated with a five-expert panel and used with Greek-speaking undergraduate education students
target_learners: undergraduate future educators
target_learning_goals: measuring trust in robots across educational interaction tasks
examples: The same 10 items followed each of the nine videos, with mandatory responses and Cronbach's α between .85 and .95 across conditions

citation: Anna-Maria Velentza, Konstantina Nikou, Anne-Gwenn Bosser, Nikolaos Fachantidis. (2026). What Robots Do Matters More Than What They Look Like: Task Context Shapes Trust in Educational HRI. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22What+Robots+Do+Matters+More+Than+What+They+Look+Like%22
title: Trust calibration account: users adjust reliance on robots according to perceived task risk, uncertainty, and expected competence rather than appearance
description: The article explains its findings through trust calibration theories from automation research. On this account, users calibrate trust to contextual demands: "users adjust their reliance on artificial agents according to perceived task risk, uncertainty, and expected system competence rather than agent appearance alone". Instructional tasks are structured, goal-oriented, and objectively verifiable, reducing uncertainty and promoting confidence, whereas personal conversations involving emotional disclosure introduce higher social and privacy sensitivity, leading users to apply stricter trust criteria.
requirements: Applies to interactions where users can perceive task risk and expected agent competence, such as structured instruction versus personal disclosure
constraints: Offered as the authors' interpretation of this study's video-based results, consistent with cited contextual-factor findings; not directly tested as a mechanism in the experiment
target_learners: undergraduate future educators
target_learning_goals: calibration of trust in socially assistive robots across educational task contexts
examples: The article links the T2 > T1 > T3 trust ordering to lower perceived risk in verifiable instructional tasks and higher privacy sensitivity in personal-information discussions

article_title: Co-Creating Buildable and Open Social Robot Study Companions with University Students
citation: Farnaz Baksh, Matevž B. Zorec, Feiazie Baksh, and Karl Kruusamäe. (2026). Co-Creating Buildable and Open Social Robot Study Companions with University Students. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15239v1
title: Buildability and serviceability as social affordances of the human-robot relationship
description: The article proposes that hands-on assembly is an interaction-shaping variable rather than a hardware prerequisite: assembly establishes the user's stance toward the robot as a co-created artefact rather than a delivered product. It argues that treating buildability and serviceability as constituent elements of the human-robot relationship "reframes assembly as the opening move of social interaction", linking material co-creation to attachment, ownership, and sustained engagement. The framework draws on a lifecycle perspective that treats maintenance and repair as core components of the user experience, extending Design for Assembly and Design for Disassembly principles into the initial build phase.
requirements: The robot must be an open-source hardware platform whose build, repair, and maintenance are accessible to end users rather than pre-assembled or black-box.
constraints: Single-session study designs cannot capture long-term attachment or perceived agency, as the article states in its limitations.
target_learners: university students building open-source social robots
target_learning_goals: technical agency and self-efficacy through hands-on hardware building
psychological ownership of a co-created artefact
examples: Study 2 participants treated the partially-built robot as something worth protecting before any social interaction had taken place, and used affective vocabulary such as fun, engaging, and cool about the build.
