title: Robot Study Companion (RSC) v4.1 open-source social robot chassis
description: The RSC is an affordable, compact, 3D-printed desktop social robot built around a Raspberry Pi with peripherals enabling multimodal interaction, including a touchscreen, servo-driven flippers, an LED ring, microphones, and speakers. The v4.1 chassis redesign applies DfA and DfD interventions: a twist-lock chassis replacing internal screws, snap-fit speaker base and front panel, one-way component fits with fiducial markers, print-in-place latches giving tool-free SD/USB access, a bespoke expansion PCB consolidating wiring breakouts, and a rewritten step-by-step guide with synchronised video and text. All open-source artefacts are released at the project site for community contribution.
requirements: Assembly relies on 3D-printed reinforced parts and off-the-shelf electronics; the rewritten documentation guide at the project site supports the build.
constraints: The v4.1 documentation was deliberately kept in an alpha state during evaluation, and the designations v4 and v4.1 refer specifically to the chassis mechanical design, not electronics or software tracks.

first-time robot builders in Guyana and Estonia

technical agency and emotional support via a physical companion
examples: Two replication cases (Guyana capstone students, an Estonia one-day workshop) informed the v4 to v4.1 transition, and Studies 1 and 2 evaluated the redesigned chassis.

article_title: PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback
citation: Wei Xia, Jin Wu, Haoran Shi, Xiangyu Wang, Chanjin Zheng. (2026). PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20287
title: PsyScore: a psychometrically-aware framework unifying diagnostic scoring and ZPD-scaffolded feedback through a shared latent ability representation
description: PsyScore couples three modules: a Trait-Adaptive Neural GPCM Scorer that embeds the Graded Partial Credit Model in a BERT-based architecture to estimate latent ability θ; a ZPD-Conditional Feedback Generator that maps θ to instructional strategies via multi-agent fusion; and a Multi-Perspective Evaluation Strategy. The framework's premise is that "modeling student ability within a shared psychometric latent space can unify interpretable scoring and ZPD-aligned feedback", turning AES from summative scoring into formative diagnosis.
requirements: Requires fine-grained analytic trait labels (e.g., Voice, Organization) for trait-adaptive scorer training
Requires heterogeneous LLM agents plus a fusion model for feedback generation
constraints: Multi-agent consensus trades off inference latency, limiting real-time classroom deployment
Simulated revision cannot model motivational dynamics, epistemic trust, or cognitive fatigue
target_learners: K-12 and secondary essay writers across argumentative, source-based, and narrative genres
target_learning_goals: Writing proficiency across multiple traits (content, organization, conventions, voice, etc.)
examples: On ASAP++, the framework's scorer reached QWK 0.747 and its feedback module was evaluated via LLM-judge preference, simulated revision, and a three-expert blind study

citation: Wei Xia, Jin Wu, Haoran Shi, Xiangyu Wang, Chanjin Zheng. (2026). PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20287
title: ZPD-aligned strategy mapping: deterministic mapping of latent ability θ to explicit instruction, targeted scaffolding, or intellectual challenge
description: PsyScore defines a deterministic mapping from estimated ability to a pedagogical control token: explicit directive instruction for struggling learners (θ < −1.0), targeted scaffolding for developing learners (−1.0 ≤ θ ≤ 1.0), and intellectual challenge via Socratic questioning for advanced learners (θ > 1.0). The article states the "ZPD boundary values are designed to operationalize scaffolding theory within a computational framework", and traits with discrimination above 1.2 receive higher prompt attention.
requirements: A validated latent ability estimate (θ) from the IRT scorer is required to select the strategy
constraints: Strategy thresholds (−1.0, 1.0) are design values grounded in the authors' operationalization of scaffolding theory, not empirically derived optima
target_learners: Essay writers across proficiency levels, from struggling to advanced
target_learning_goals: Proficiency-appropriate writing feedback: error correction, guided improvement, or rhetorical refinement
examples: Table 10 maps θ < −1.0 to explicit directive instruction on grammar and mechanics, −1.0 ≤ θ ≤ 1.0 to targeted scaffolding balancing praise with 1-2 improvement areas, and θ > 1.0 to intellectual challenge via open-ended questions

article_title: Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information
citation: Ryosuke Nagai, Kyohei Atarashi, Koh Takeuchi, Jill-Jênn Vie, and Hisashi Kashima. (2026). Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20611
title: Pseudo-temporal ordering: inclusion relations among snapshot skill sets as a proxy for learning progression
description: The article proposes a framework in which, absent temporal logs, set-inclusion relations among learners' mastered-skill sets induce a pseudo-temporal axis: a learner whose mastered-skill set is a superset of another's can be viewed as a plausible later state. Learning is modeled as accumulation of expected one-skill increments, so that "a learner's mastered-skill set expands monotonically over time" under a non-forgetting assumption. This supports next-skill prediction from CDM-derived snapshot mastery patterns.
requirements: A predefined mapping between items and skills from cognitive diagnostic models to produce binary mastery patterns
The non-forgetting assumption that once a skill is mastered it remains mastered
constraints: Relies on a non-forgetting assumption; forgetting mechanisms are not incorporated
Evaluated on a restricted real-world subset of learners who attempted all skills
target_learners: Learners in large-scale periodic assessment settings with only snapshot data
target_learning_goals: Predicting the next skill to be acquired to support adaptive instruction
examples: Applied to PISA-style cross-sectional assessment settings where learner data are snapshots rather than temporal traces
key_sources: Ryosuke Nagai, Kyohei Atarashi, Koh Takeuchi, Jill-Jênn Vie, and Hisashi Kashima. (2026). Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20611

article_title: Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information
citation: Ryosuke Nagai, Kyohei Atarashi, Koh Takeuchi, Jill-Jênn Vie, and Hisashi Kashima. (2026). Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20611
title: Neural expected-increment model with Upper Bounded Softmax for next-skill prediction
description: The article introduces a feed-forward neural model that maps a continuous mastery state to a distribution over the next skill using the Upper Bounded Softmax function, which assigns probability mass only to currently unmastered skills. Parameters are trained by minimizing squared reconstruction error of observed mastery patterns with L1 regularization that "promotes sparse and interpretable dependencies among skills." Repeatedly accumulating expected increments approximates intermediate acquisition states.
requirements: Continuous intermediate state representations relaxed from binary mastery patterns
Output constrained to the simplex intersected with unmastered skills
constraints: Direct path enumeration is infeasible as the number of possible acquisition paths grows exponentially, so complete paths are not modeled
target_learners: Learners assessed via cognitive diagnostic models in snapshot settings
target_learning_goals: Predicting the conditional distribution of the next acquired skill
examples: The model reconstructs each observed mastery pattern by applying the state update as many times as skills mastered

article_title: Students' Perception Accuracy of Partners' AI Use and its Relation to Collaboration Performance
citation: Laura Graf, Ramona Beinstingel, Stephan Krusche, Oleksandra Poquet. (2026). Students' Perception Accuracy of Partners' AI Use and its Relation to Collaboration Performance. Preprint, Technical University of Munich. https://tum.de
title: Heuristic-inference account of partner AI-use beliefs under observability constraints
description: The article proposes that when a coordination-relevant behaviour such as AI use is not directly observable, collaborators form beliefs about partners through heuristic inference rather than partner-specific knowledge. Two heuristics are named: social projection, where "individuals assume partners to be similar to them and use their own behaviour as a reference point for judging others", and normative expectation, assumptions about what behaviour is typical or appropriate in a context. The study's partial-correlation results support the dominance of assumed similarity, reframing AI-use transparency as a coordination resource rather than only an integrity concern.
requirements: Requires a collaboration context where partners' AI use is private and observable work traces no longer distinguish own work from AI generation
constraints: Assumed-similarity effects may be pronounced when partners are already acquainted, as in this sample
The account is supported by observational, self-report data and should not be interpreted causally
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: accurate perception of collaborators' AI use during collaborative programming
effective team coordination in AI-supported collaborative work
examples: In the study, students' estimates of partners' task-level AI use correlated strongly with their own usage profiles (median r = .73), and partner-specific residual accuracy was low
key_sources: Laura Graf, Ramona Beinstingel, Stephan Krusche, Oleksandra Poquet. (2026). Students' Perception Accuracy of Partners' AI Use and its Relation to Collaboration Performance. Preprint, Technical University of Munich. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23237

article_title: SupplyNet: Supporting Visual Exploratory Learning in Supply Chain via Contextual Multi-Agent Simulation
citation: Yanjia Li, Kelcy Kexin Han, Tianrui Hu, Yi-Fan Cao, Huamin Qu, Sicheng Song. (2026). SupplyNet: Supporting Visual Exploratory Learning in Supply Chain via Contextual Multi-Agent Simulation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24694
title: SupplyNet: a gamified visual simulation system with graph-structured LLM multi-agent simulation, branching timeline, and analysis console
description: SupplyNet is a gamified visual simulation system for university SCM students, built on "a contextual graph-based LLM multi-agent framework that models interdependent supply chain dynamics and provides responsive feedback through tiered challenges." It integrates an interactive Graph Structure View, a Timeline Tree Map for branching what-if exploration, and a task-oriented Analysis Console with financial, operations, and logistics dashboards. Agents are powered by OpenAI's gpt-4o model, with agent-specific subgraph retrieval and heuristic Golden Rules as input.
requirements: Requires an LLM-backed multi-agent simulation core maintaining supply chain state as a directed graph, a database of temporal snapshots, and a front-end visual interface connected by a bidirectional data flow.
constraints: Designed and evaluated in the context of supply chain management, with the learning objective centered on inventory management.
target_learners: university students studying supply chain management
target_learning_goals: understanding dynamic supply chain interdependencies
inventory management decision making
counterfactual and causal reasoning about operational outcomes
examples: Users select a company role and challenge level in onboarding, manage the simulation in the Graph Structure View, branch parallel trajectories in the Timeline Tree Map, and inspect KPI dashboards in the Analysis Console.

citation: Yanjia Li, Kelcy Kexin Han, Tianrui Hu, Yi-Fan Cao, Huamin Qu, Sicheng Song. (2026). SupplyNet: Supporting Visual Exploratory Learning in Supply Chain via Contextual Multi-Agent Simulation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24694
title: Reusable simulation architecture for dynamic relational learning environments
description: The article abstracts SupplyNet's pipeline into "a reusable simulation architecture for dynamic relational learning environments." A graph represents domain entities, dependencies, and time-varying states; agents and learners observe relevant subgraphs, take domain-specific actions, and trigger state transitions; a database stores temporal snapshots supporting replay, branching, and comparison. The reusable layer separates from a domain-specific layer so other subjects can reuse the architecture by replacing the domain schema, transition rules, agent heuristics, event types, and learning metrics.
requirements: Subjects must be modelable as dynamic relational systems involving multiple connected entities, local decisions or disturbances, delayed propagation of effects, and trade-offs that learners need to diagnose over time.
constraints: The architecture was designed and evaluated only in the supply chain management context; cross-subject instantiations are discussed as future work.
target_learners: university students in domains modelable as dynamic relational systems
target_learning_goals: diagnosing delayed propagation of effects and trade-offs in interconnected systems

Touching and Feeling the Data: A Reusable Software Pipeline for Tactile Statistical Graphs in Accessible Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01214
title: Three-layer reusable pipeline for generating 3D-printed tactile statistical graphs
description: An open-source software pipeline of about 1,500 lines of JavaScript across 15 files that turns plate dimensions, chart type, and numeric data into print-ready binary STL files. Layer 1 derives tactile parameters from plate dimensions, Layer 2 provides shared chart scaffolding with five modular builders (scatter, bar, histogram, line, box plots), and an optional Layer 3 uses a multimodal LLM to extract chart specifications from uploaded images. The article states it is "the first open-source pipeline that automatically generates 3D-printed tactile statistical graphs from either typed data or chart images". Geometry runs locally via JSCAD with a Three.js browser preview; the Anthropic API key is needed only for image extraction.
requirements: Node.js (v18+) with Express for the server; an Anthropic API key only if the optional image-extraction layer is used
constraints: Plate dimensions are clamped to [80,250] mm; review of LLM-extracted specifications is mandatory before STL generation
target_learners: blind and low-vision students in statistics courses
target_learning_goals: exploring statistical distributions, trends, and relationships through haptic interaction with tactile graphs
examples: The pipeline produced a 150×150 mm tactile histogram plate with raised bars, axis rails, and dual-format labels, previewed in Three.js

title: Derive tactile graph parameters from tactile perception research rather than ad hoc choices
description: The pipeline's parameter derivation layer computes feature heights and spacings automatically from plate dimensions using established tactile perception findings, so every generated chart is readable by touch without per-chart manual tuning. Data features are set at 1.5 mm, three times the "0.5 mm height discriminability floor" from Lederman and Klatzky, and scatter-point separation is 3.5 mm, exceeding the 2–3 mm two-point discrimination threshold. Axis rails are taller than data features so a sweeping finger distinguishes structural boundaries from encoded data.
requirements: Plate dimensions in millimeters as input; adherence to BANA guidelines and Library of Congress Braille dot geometry for labels
constraints: Parameters are derived for FDM-printed plates within the clamped [80,250] mm dimension range
target_learners: blind and low-vision students reading tactile graphs by fingertip
target_learning_goals: haptic discrimination of chart structure, data features, and labels
examples: The derivation layer sets baseplate thickness via a clamp formula, reserves an 18 mm margin for dual-format labels, and sets Braille dots at 0.6 mm per Library of Congress standard

citation: Amrita Ganguly, Sai Sharanya Garika, Aditya Johri. (2026). Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Uncovering+Students%27+Mental+Models+of+Generative+Artificial+Intelligence%22
title: Five-category taxonomy of undergraduate mental models of generative AI
description: The article proposes a taxonomy of students' mental models of GenAI derived from hierarchical clustering of concept maps. The five categories are technical-process based, educational tool based, transitional, consequence aware, and integrated; the authors state the clustering "revealed five distinct characteristics of student's mental model answering RQ1." Each category describes how students organize GenAI knowledge, from underlying technologies to collective responsibility. The taxonomy is positioned as preliminary and intended as a diagnostic lens for instruction and guideline design.
requirements: Concept map elicitation plus hierarchical clustering of map components to derive the categories
constraints: Preliminary WIP results; the authors state future qualitative analysis and validation via interviews or think-aloud studies is needed
target_learners: undergraduate students in information technology programs
target_learning_goals: AI literacy and responsible, ethical use of generative AI
examples: Cluster 5 grouped ethics, privacy, human oversight, and academic stakeholders, which the authors label an integrated and risk-aware mental model

The authors write that faculty can use "the cluster structure as a diagnostic framework such as identifying where students' mental models lie and designing learning activities that stretch their thinking across cluster boundaries." The goal is an integrated mental model holding technical, educational, ethical, and governance dimensions as interdependent.

title: Concept map elicitation with holistic scoring and hierarchical clustering for studying GenAI mental models
description: The article's methodology combines concept map collection, holistic scoring, and hierarchical clustering to externalize mental models. Maps from a technology ethics course assignment were scored by two researchers on comprehensiveness, organization, and correctness on a 1-to-3 scale with pluses and minuses, mapped to a nine-point scale and four levels; 64 of 86 enrolled students' maps were retained after exclusions. Components were coded with a 16-code inductive codebook and clustered, with merge height indicating dissimilarity. The authors offer this as an initial elicitation step to be validated with interviews or think-aloud studies.

target_learning_goals: eliciting and diagnosing students' conceptual understanding of generative AI

article_title: Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing
citation: Andres Karjus, Janika Leoste, Tiia Õun. (2026). Student Evaluation of Repeated AI Feedback Across a Semester of Writing. arXiv:2607.16115 [cs.CY]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.16115
title: Design AI-feedback coursework so the intended learning work does not depend on the final text alone
description: The article argues that integrating AI feedback changes what a writing task becomes, and that AI feedback should not be evaluated only by whether students like it. Its educational value depends on the surrounding task: "whether students still have to write, and are motivated to interpret, question,andintegratefeedbackaspartoftheirownwritingprocess." The authors recommend requirements such as revision following feedback, comparison with reflection criteria, and follow-up rationales.

constraints: No single design feature completely prevents AI delegation of the parts meant to exercise student judgment; prohibition can be ignored and prescribed rationales, revisions, and self-reports can also be generated

target_learning_goals: reflective writing
feedback literacy
critical and selective use of AI feedback
examples: The course tied writing and feedback use to earlier in-class contexts and the authors suggest version histories or brief peer- or teacher-facing explanations to shift the task toward showing situated decisions

It is a smartphone-based coding curriculum covering basic programming concepts such as variables, conditionals, loops, functions, classes, objects, and arrays, taught in the Processing language (an open-source, Java-based language), with students writing and running programs in the APDE Android app. The course was the setting for the motivation survey analyzed in this poster.

citation: Helen Weixu Chen, Victoria Sakhnini, and Lesley Istead. (2026). Make or Take: How Students Navigate Self-Created and Instructor-Provided Cheat Sheets. ACM Trans. Comput. Educ. https://doi.org/10.1145/3834566
title: Three recurring tensions shaping student cheat sheet decisions
description: The article organizes its qualitative findings around three tensions that recur in students' cheat sheet decisions: "1) trust in instructor judgment versus trust in their own knowledge needs, 2) coverage versus clarity, and 3) effort versus payoff." These tensions structure the themes of choice rationales (trust, cognitive efficiency, personalization), shifting attitudes over the term, and practical constraints such as legibility and information density. The framework also treats the tensions as evolving, with early convenience- or deference-based decisions giving way to more deliberate preparation strategies.

target_learning_goals: exam preparation strategies
self-regulated learning
student agency in assessment
examples: Table 1 maps themes to the three categories, e.g. P1's trust in instructor relevance, P23's anxiety reduction through control, and P15's realization of misalignment.

title: Encourage students to create their own exam cheat sheets within fair and inclusive structural constraints
description: The article recommends that "instructors may consider encouraging students to create their own cheat sheets, rather than relying on instructor-provided versions," arguing that creation functions as a form of self-regulated learning requiring students to prioritize, organize, and synthesize information. Fairness and integrity concerns are addressed by structural constraints such as limiting sheets to a double-sided page, and policies must remain inclusive by allowing pedagogically equivalent alternatives. The article reports no statistically significant performance difference between formats, so the recommendation rests on engagement and preparation behaviour rather than measured achievement.

self-regulated learning
exam preparation

description: The article argues that when overall ability is the leading factor in prediction, simpler explainable models should be preferred over less explainable ones. The authors state: "If ability is the leading factor, less explainable models may be highly undesirable as they could introduce biases into the predictions and reduce accountability to the students impacted." Their explainable models reached competitive accuracy of around 78%, offering a benchmark showing explainability need not sacrifice performance.

article_title: Is Solving Better Than Evaluating GenAI Solutions?
citation: Ethan Dickey, Marios Mertzanidis, Alexandros Psomas. (2026). Is Solving Better Than Evaluating GenAI Solutions? https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27586v1
title: Incorporate structured GenAI-evaluation activities into algorithms coursework without expecting automatic learning gains; scaffold evaluation beyond simple error diagnosis
description: The article's design recommendation is that GenAI-evaluation tasks can be incorporated into algorithms coursework safely, since "GenAI-evaluation activities can be incorporated into algorithms coursework without broad performance losses". However, meaningful gains require deliberate scaffolding: the authors recommend future assignments "push students beyond simple diagnosis" by asking students to identify the first invalid step, construct counterexamples, propose corrected algorithms or invariants, and explain why the corrected solution works. Pedagogical value depends more on scaffolding than on exposure to AI output itself.
requirements: Deliberate scaffolding that pushes students beyond simple error diagnosis, such as identifying the first invalid step, constructing counterexamples, and proposing corrected solutions
constraints: In this implementation, evaluation tasks produced no measurable summative or transfer gains over direct solving
target_learners: undergraduate students in junior-level algorithms courses
target_learning_goals: algorithm design, proof of correctness, runtime analysis, and transfer of abstract algorithmic reasoning
examples: The study asked evaluating students to grade a ChatGPT-4o solution, distinguishing minor bugs (e.g., calculation errors) from major bugs (wrong algorithm, invalid recurrence, missing invariant, flawed proof step), and found most students did not change study habits
key_sources: Ethan Dickey, Marios Mertzanidis, Alexandros Psomas. (2026). Is Solving Better Than Evaluating GenAI Solutions? https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27586

article_title: The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations
citation: Ilya Mikhelson. (2026). The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29624
title: The Socratic Test framework: decoupled Bloom's prompting and SOLO evaluation to map the Zone of Proximal Development
description: The Socratic Test is an adaptive, typed conversational assessment that standardizes the method of measurement without standardizing prompts. It decouples two taxonomies: "Bloom's Taxonomy dictates the cognitive difficulty of theprompt, the AI utilizes the SOLO Taxonomy... to measure the structural quality of theresponse." Rooted in Dynamic Assessment, it quantifies the ZPD by differentiating Independent from Assisted Performance via a scaffolding discount factor. SOLO's structural criteria are presented as observable and defensible, shifting grading from semantic interpretation to structural complexity.
requirements: An AI proctor capable of real-time Bloom-level prompting and provisional SOLO classification, with instructor calibration of the SOLO baseline before mass grading
constraints: Real-time SOLO assessment is strictly provisional and conservative; inaccuracies are absorbed by the oversampled evidence buffer and corrected in the post-exam pipeline
The author notes controlled comparisons against traditional oral and written exams are still required

article_title: The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations
citation: Ilya Mikhelson. (2026). The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29624
title: Non-compensatory capped-bucket grading across topic-by-tier matrix cells
description: The grading architecture rejects compensatory scoring in favor of "Non-Compensatory Grading": instructors configure capped buckets per topic and cognitive tier, and the total score aggregates min(cap, earned points) per cell. Points per interaction follow P(b,s,k) = γk·V(b,s), where V(b,s) is monotonically increasing with the Bloom level and γk discounts assisted performance. Once a bucket is full, further low-level answers yield zero additional points, preventing grinding of foundational questions from compensating for missing higher-order evidence.
requirements: Instructor-defined 2D grading matrix (or 1D topic-level caps in Organic Mode) with point capacities per tier and deterministic logging of Bloom level and hint count per interaction
constraints: Students cannot manually pivot between cognitive tiers within a topic, as foundational tiers must be completed to scaffold advanced topics
target_learners: higher education students in instructor-configured courses
target_learning_goals: demonstrating mastery at each required cognitive tier rather than accumulating low-level points
examples: Table 2 shows a conceptual matrix for an introductory Economics course with tier caps of 10-15 points and a 100-point total; Appendix A walks through a 40-point Price Controls topic at 120% oversampling

citation: Ilya Mikhelson. (2026). The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29624
title: socratictest.com: a summative conversational assessment platform with evidence buffers, shadow ledger, and human-AI grading pipeline
description: The author developed socratictest.com, "a custom software platform explicitly engineered to administer the Socratic Test modality," architected as a summative assessment engine with a decoupled design separating the real-time proctoring engine from the final deterministic gradebook. Core mechanics include an oversampled Evidence Buffer (e.g., 120%), a hidden Shadow Ledger logging baseline point values for skipped or exhausted prompts, user-directed pivoting with state resurrection, an Out-of-Scope audit protocol, and a 7-step grading pipeline with instructor calibration, validation, override, and an appeals queue.
requirements: Instructor configuration of grading matrices, oversample rates, and participation in the calibration and audit steps of the grading pipeline
constraints: Real-time SOLO evaluation is provisional and cannot gate progression directly, to avoid trapping students behind AI hallucinations; out-of-scope flags are initially treated as skips pending post-exam audit
target_learners: higher education students and instructors in pilot university courses
target_learning_goals: reliable summative assessment of conceptual mastery through adaptive conversation
examples: In the Appendix A case study, a verified hallucination (a Phillips Curve prompt) was converted from a 12-point shadow penalty into earned Synthesis points, and a Global Exclusion Rule protected other students who encountered the same flawed premise

article_title: Navigating the skill diversity frontier: How skill complexity explains worker resilience
citation: Carpanelli, M., Duszynski, J. & Stephany, F. (2026). Navigating the skill diversity frontier: How skill complexity explains worker resilience. Working paper, Oxford Internet Institute. https://oii.ox.ac.uk
title: Skill complexity framework: productive capital, adaptive capital, and the diversity frontier
description: The framework models human capital as a structured skill system rather than a list of attributes. It decomposes portfolios into productive capital, defined as "the market value associated with specialised expertise", and adaptive capital, "the flexibility generated by spanning multiple skill domains". It further postulates that specialisation constrains attainable diversity, yielding the diversity frontier: an inverse U-shaped upper envelope of diversity given specialisation. Workers on the frontier combine domain-specific expertise with cross-domain capabilities and are expected to be best positioned to learn, move, and adapt to technological change.
requirements: A directed skill network reconstructed from observed skill co-occurrence, with hierarchy inferred from asymmetric conditional probabilities and domains identified via community detection
constraints: The analysis remains associational rather than causal, despite the use of lagged explanatory variables and extensive controls
LinkedIn profiles over-represent digitally engaged and highly skilled occupations, and listed skills are self-reported
target_learners: Adult workers in knowledge-intensive labour markets facing technological change
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of new and AI-relevant skills
Occupational mobility and reskilling pathway identification
examples: The study operationalises the framework with specialisation as average inverse normalised local reaching centrality, diversity as Hill diversity across 12 Louvain skill domains, and a frontier score ranging from 0 to 1 within 100 specialisation groups

article_title: TACT: Taxonomy-Aligned Post-Training for Pedagogically Adaptive English Tutoring
citation: Dongjie Yang, Siyan Lin, Leixian Shen, Rui Sheng, Huamin Qu, and Zixin Chen. (2026). TACT: Taxonomy-Aligned Post-Training for Pedagogically Adaptive English Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03952
title: TACT dual-taxonomy framework: a 13-strategy tutor-strategy taxonomy linked to a two-axis student-move taxonomy operationalizing conditional feedback decisions
description: TACT organizes ESL tutoring as a pedagogical decision space connecting learner-state annotation, tutor-strategy selection, and next-turn response generation. The student-move taxonomy records the learner's latest turn along two dimensions, move type and move status, where only Answer/Attempt moves can be Adequate or Problematic and other types are Non-evaluable. The tutor-strategy taxonomy "contains 13 strategies representing the intended pedagogical function of the next tutor turn", spanning prompting, backchanneling, affective feedback, verification, error flagging, hinting, guided revision, and direct correction. The mapping from student moves to strategies is conditional rather than deterministic, depending on proficiency, task difficulty, dialogue history, and prior support. Annotation reliability reached kappa of 0.708 for tutor strategy, 0.722 for move type, and 1.000 for move status.
requirements: Annotated authentic tutoring dialogue with codebooks and inter-annotator reliability checks to instantiate the two taxonomies
constraints: The article notes label abstraction is a limitation: real teachers blend instruction, affect, pacing, and rapport in ways a compact taxonomy does not always separate
target_learners: English-as-a-second-language learners across CEFR levels B1-C2
target_learning_goals: Conversational ESL proficiency through adaptive tutor feedback and scaffolding
examples: Expert annotators developed the coding scheme iteratively from 50 dialogue contexts, then independently double-coded 20 held-out contexts for inter-annotator reliability before corpus-scale annotation.
key_sources: Dongjie Yang, Siyan Lin, Leixian Shen, Rui Sheng, Huamin Qu, and Zixin Chen. (2026). TACT: Taxonomy-Aligned Post-Training for Pedagogically Adaptive English Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03952

title: TACTCorpus and TACTBench: released annotated ESL tutoring corpus and strategy-balanced diagnostic benchmark
description: TACTCorpus is a model-assisted, human-audited resource derived from 260 authentic one-to-one English tutoring sessions from TSCC v2, containing 32,379 annotation records including tutor-strategy labels, student-move labels, and augmentation metadata, with a training split of 2,702 next-teacher-turn response-generation examples. TACTBench is a "strategy-balanced, optimization-aligned diagnostic benchmark" of 78 manually verified tutoring contexts scored on five rubric dimensions (Move, Agency, ESL, Tone, Conc.) plus accept, leak, and off-task judge flags. The article states it releases the data, benchmark, and model weights to support reproducible research.
requirements: Authentic anonymized tutoring dialogue as source data and quality-controlled annotation with codebook adjudication
constraints: TACTBench is designed around the specified TACT construct, so the article says improvements should be interpreted alongside disaggregated rubric dimensions, judge flags, and external transfer checks rather than as universal proof of better teaching

citation: Dongjie Yang, Siyan Lin, Leixian Shen, Rui Sheng, Huamin Qu, and Zixin Chen. (2026). TACT: Taxonomy-Aligned Post-Training for Pedagogically Adaptive English Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03952
title: TACTutor: open 4B model post-trained with SFT and taxonomy-grounded GRPO for adaptive ESL tutoring
description: TACTutor is an open 4B model produced by post-training Qwen3.5-4B through parameter-efficient supervised fine-tuning with LoRA followed by taxonomy-grounded Group Relative Policy Optimization. The GRPO reward combines a mean normalized task score with grounding, format, and strategy terms plus judge-level penalties for unacceptability, answer leakage or over-helping, and off-task errors, with a KL constraint against the frozen SFT reference policy. The article says the reward is "transparent and auditable rather than an opaque optimization of a single benchmark score", and model weights are released.
requirements: A frozen pedagogical judge with hidden reference responses, gold taxonomy labels, and an evaluation rubric to produce reward scores and failure flags
constraints: The article states the main limitation is that next-turn response quality is not the same as long-term learning, since a locally well-scaffolded response's effect depends on learner motivation, prior knowledge, repeated interaction, and classroom context
target_learners: English-as-a-second-language learners, including local deployment on personal devices for privacy and latency
target_learning_goals: Learner-contingent pedagogical decision-making: selecting appropriate tutor strategies and levels of support in ESL dialogue

article_title: A Bottom-Up Taxonomy of Student Discourse with a Socratic AI Physics Tutor
citation: Syed Furqan Abbas Hashmi and N. Sanjay Rebello. (2026). A bottom-up taxonomy of student discourse with a Socratic AI physics tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07373
title: Socratic AI physics tutor with retrieval-augmented generation deployed as an optional recitation study aid
description: The article studies a custom Socratic AI tutor deployed in five of 34 recitation sections of an introductory calculus-based mechanics course (enrollment 1,508) as an optional extra-credit study aid. It is described as "a custom Socratic AI tutor built as a Django web application with a PostgreSQL backend and a retrieval-audmented generation pipeline over course materials", meaning LLM responses are conditioned on relevant course-material excerpts. Its system prompt instructed the model to use Socratic prompting and to scaffold conceptual setup before symbolic execution, and logging captured all turns at the message level.
requirements: Students use the tutor to work through assigned recitation problems; logging must capture all turns at the message level for analysis.
constraints: The system prompt withholds direct answers and direction in favor of Socratic questioning; the studied corpus is from one week's recitation problem context.
target_learners: introductory calculus-based mechanics students, primarily future engineers
target_learning_goals: multi-step mechanics problem solving involving energy conservation and centripetal acceleration
examples: The corpus analyzed consists of 5,513 total messages from 240 individual students across 221 completed student sessions, of which 2,874 are student turns.

article_title: A Bottom-Up Taxonomy of Student Discourse with a Socratic AI Physics Tutor
citation: Syed Furqan Abbas Hashmi and N. Sanjay Rebello. (2026). A bottom-up taxonomy of student discourse with a Socratic AI physics tutor. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07373
title: Emergent LLM coding plus embedding-based consolidation pipeline for large-scale student-discourse taxonomies
description: A two-step methodological framework, framed as the LLM analog of open coding in grounded theory, for converting large student-tutor transcript corpora into interpretable discourse categories. Step 1 asks an LLM coder to assign each turn an emergent free-text label using the previous four conversational turns as context, yielding 833 unique raw labels. Step 2 consolidates near-paraphrase labels via text embeddings, cosine distance, and agglomerative clustering with average linkage at a distance threshold of 0.40, followed by LLM-generated canonical category names, producing 357 consolidated categories. The approach follows computational grounded theory, letting categories be discovered rather than projected from a fixed codebook.
requirements: A context window of prior conversational turns (four turns was the smallest window recovering consistent labels for context-dependent moves); a distance-threshold sweep with human coherence inspection to select the clustering threshold; validation against expert coding.
constraints: Single-rater coherence judgments establish only face validity; rerunning consolidation with a different embedding model could shift category boundaries; specific category labels reflect the single mechanics problem context and will not transfer to tutors covering other content.
target_learners: introductory physics students interacting with AI tutors
target_learning_goals: characterizing student discourse and engagement with AI-tutor scaffolding
examples: The threshold 0.40 was selected as the largest setting at which ≥90% of inspected groups were judged coherent (47 of 50).

citation: Ching-Jung Cheng, Yu-Chan Chung, Bing-Chen Chiu, Yu-Hsuan Lin, and Jia-Wei Liao. 2026. Exploring AI-Supported Disciplinary Mediation in Student Project Teams' Text-Based Communication: A Probe-Grounded Co-Design Study. OzCHI '26. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07503
title: Spritz: a Discord-based LLM technology probe for AI-mediated interdisciplinary team communication
description: Spritz is a Discord-based AI conversational agent designed as a technology probe for interdisciplinary team communication, "enabling participants to reflect on the role, value, and boundaries of AI mediation rather than evaluating a mature system". It monitors shared-channel messages for semantic and pragmatic tensions, pauses the discussion, elicits individual perspectives in private channels, and returns anonymized syntheses to the group. In the study, four three-person groups completed a 15-minute resource-allocation discussion, with an average of two detected tension episodes per session.
requirements: Its design was guided by three goals: detecting potential collaboration tensions, supporting members in articulating implicit reasoning through private reflection, and helping the group compare alternative perspectives through anonymized synthesis
constraints: Detection used a fixed 0.7 confidence threshold and a ten-message trigger that were design choices for the exploratory probe and were not empirically calibrated; the authors state they do not know how accurately Spritz detected boundaries under this configuration
target_learners: university students in interdisciplinary project teams
target_learning_goals: negotiating disciplinary differences in text-based collaborative problem-solving
examples: Four groups of three students role-played technical, business, and UX members allocating 10 resource points across fixing defects, refining the business narrative, and user research while Spritz mediated

title: Semantic and pragmatic disciplinary boundaries as the two recurring forms of boundary in interdisciplinary team communication
description: Drawing on boundary-crossing literature, the article frames interdisciplinary collaboration differences as two recurring boundary forms: "semantic boundaries, where the same term carries different meaning across fields, and pragmatic boundaries, where members’ goals and values conflict even when they understand one another". This taxonomy organizes what the Spritz probe was designed to detect and underpins the study's account of why text-based, facilitator-less student teams leave differences implicit until they surface as friction. It also connects to the perspective-making and perspective-taking framing the authors use to describe the probe's support functions.

constraints: The article focuses on text-based, unstructured channels such as Slack or Discord in temporary teams lacking a dedicated facilitator
target_learners: university students in interdisciplinary project-based learning teams
target_learning_goals: cross-disciplinary communication and coordination in collaborative problem-solving

article_title: Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages
citation: Avijit Roy, Proma Roy. (2026). Structural Silence: When AI Infrastructure Fails Speakers of Underrepresented Languages — A Case Study in Bengali, the Digital Divide, and the Hidden Cost of English-Centric Design. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.12278
title: Structural Silence: four interlocking infrastructure failures that systematically exclude a language from AI
description: Structural silence is the article's explanatory framework: "the systematic exclusion of a language from AI infrastructure not through explicit policy but through the accumulated weight of design decisions that were never made with that language in mind." It organizes four interlocking failures—web presence gap, training token deficit, tokenization penalty, and connectivity exclusion—that intensify one another over time. Bengali, with roughly 285 million speakers, classical recognition, and an active NLP research community, serves as the case demonstrating that uneven performance reflects infrastructure-level resource distribution rather than model quality alone.
requirements: Each failure compounds the others, so the framework requires analysis at corpus, tokenizer, benchmark, and deployment layers together
constraints: The article's contribution is explicitly explanatory and diagnostic rather than a new benchmark or empirical dataset
Evidence is drawn from published benchmarks, public indicators, and educational theory rather than newly collected learner data
target_learners: Bengali-speaking learners in low-connectivity environments
Speakers of underrepresented languages
target_learning_goals: Access to AI-assisted educational support (debugging help, concept explanation, feedback) in one's native language
examples: The paper consolidates Sangraha/Common Corpus token counts, BenLLM-Eval results, BBS ICT survey figures, and Cognitive Load Theory findings into one account of why Bengali AI support is uneven

description: The article argues dataset scarcity for underrepresented languages is a structural barrier shaped by funding and publication incentives, not a natural scarcity or individual researcher limitation. Researchers who treat such infrastructure as preliminary work reproduce the asymmetry that later appears in model performance.

Quantization and parameter-efficient fine-tuning make local inference on consumer hardware feasible, with sustainability co-benefits.

article_title: From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond)
citation: Lucile Favero, Juan Antonio Pérez-Ortiz, Tanja Käser, Nuria Oliver. (2026). From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond). arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17451
title: Self-reinforcing harm cycle linking cognition, agency, emotion, and ethics
description: An integrative conceptual framework organizing the risks of substitution-style AI in education into four interrelated dimensions — cognition, agency, emotional well-being, and ethics — connected by a reinforcing cycle. As the paper states, "These four dimensions are not independent; they interact through a reinforcing cycle." Cognitive offloading reduces effortful reasoning, diminished effort feeds illusory learning and overtrust, overtrust weakens agency, and reduced agency intensifies emotional harms such as anxiety, lower self-efficacy, and dependency, with ethical and structural factors amplifying individual-level effects. The framework is grounded in learning theory and in students' own reflections, with the clearest student-evidenced link being reliance on AI and diminished thinking.
requirements: Applies to AI systems that substitute for human cognitive effort rather than to every AI system or learner; the authors explicitly disclaim universal claims
constraints: The closing connection of the cycle is described as weakly evidenced in the students' exploratory data (dashed link in Figure 1); the essay cohort is illustrative, not representative
target_learners: school and higher-education learners using AI tools
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
learner agency
emotional resilience
academic integrity
examples: Figure 1 depicts the cycle: substitution erodes capacities while scaffolding builds critical thinking, agency, resilience, and trust

article_title: From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond)
citation: Lucile Favero, Juan Antonio Pérez-Ortiz, Tanja Käser, Nuria Oliver. (2026). From Substitution to Scaffolding: Breaking the Self-Reinforcing Harm Cycle of AI in Education (and Beyond). arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17451
title: Scaffold, do not substitute: AI should support effort rather than replace it
description: The paper's unifying design principle: AI systems that mediate human thinking should preserve and manage cognitive friction — withholding immediate answers, prompting recall, asking questions, surfacing uncertainty — instead of delivering pre-digested solutions that bypass effort. As the authors put it, "The principle that emerges,scaffold, do not substitute, defines a challenge for the AI ecosystem as a whole." It extends beyond education to any system that mediates human cognition, which can either weaken human capabilities through substitution or strengthen them through scaffolding.
requirements: Systems must be able to decide when to withhold an answer, ask a question, surface uncertainty, or present alternative perspectives; builders must treat scaffolding as a first-class capability
constraints: The principle is derived from a small, homogeneous exploratory essay cohort and from argument rather than controlled testing; the authors make no claims of statistical generalizability
target_learners: learners across educational settings
AI system builders
educators and policymakers
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
independent reasoning
learner agency
durable understanding
examples: Students requested an AI that does not provide solutions so they must find the correct answer themselves, and valued one that asks fundamental questions students must explain and answer

citation: Iyiola E. Olatunji, Alberick Euraste Djire, Jacques Klein, and Tegawendé F. Bissyandé. 2026. Do Not Copy/Paste: Soft Barriers for Copying in AI-Assisted Programming. Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3834554
title: AI code handoff problem and handoff-aware AI-assisted programming as a design perspective
description: The paper identifies the AI code handoff problem: "the unmanaged transition from AI-generated text to executable or persistent software artifacts". It proposes handoff-aware AI-assisted programming, in which coding assistants explicitly shape how generated code is transferred, inspected, tested, or attributed, treating the handoff boundary as a software engineering design surface where transfer policies vary by context (education favors reconstruction; professional codebases require provenance, review, testing, or security checks).

constraints: Transfer policies should vary by context; educational and professional settings favor different defaults
target_learners: programming students
professional software developers
target_learning_goals: code comprehension and reconstruction
responsible and reviewed use of AI-generated code
examples: The paper instantiates one point in this design space—soft-barrier handoff—using Unicode perturbations as a minimal technical probe

citation: Iyiola E. Olatunji, Alberick Euraste Djire, Jacques Klein, and Tegawendé F. Bissyandé. 2026. Do Not Copy/Paste: Soft Barriers for Copying in AI-Assisted Programming. Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3834554
title: Unicode perturbation families implemented as system-prompt soft barriers
description: The paper implements soft barriers as a system prompt instructing the model to inject specific Unicode characters into user-defined identifiers during generation, leaving keywords, operators, literals, and built-in names unchanged. Four families are evaluated: "Invisible chars" (zero-width characters inside identifiers), "Homoglyphs" (ASCII letters replaced by visually identical Unicode equivalents), "BIDI reordering" (directionality overrides altering internal byte order), and "Deletions" (backspace/delete controls erasing adjacent rendered characters). The mechanism requires no model retraining or environment changes.
requirements: Only a system prompt; no model retraining, decoder change, or execution-environment modification
constraints: Any real deployment should be institutionally approved, disclosed at the policy level, and accessibility-tested; motivated users can bypass via clean-output requests, text normalizers, or retyping
target_learners: programming students using AI coding assistants
target_learning_goals: discouraging unexamined transfer of AI-generated code
promoting reading, editing, and reconstruction of generated code
examples: Full prompt templates for all families are released in the paper's repository; Figure 1 shows a homoglyph example where pasting triggers an execution error

description: Table 1 enumerates the handoff design space the paper proposes for AI coding assistants: Direct (code transfers immediately with no intervention), Explanation-first (assistant provides reasoning before code, promoting inspection), Soft-barrier (code is readable but naive copy-paste execution fails), Review-gated (transfer requires a summary, test, or confirmation step), Test-gated (insertion is blocked until the learner runs or writes tests), and Provenance-marked (generated code carries metadata for attribution or auditing). These types could form a policy layer between an LLM and an IDE, LMS, or repository.

title: Spec-Driven Development (SDD): a development methodology in which AI agents generate code from structured specification documents that developers must verify
description: SDD is a software development methodology proposed for use with AI agents, positioned as an alternative to Vibe Coding. "This approach involves deﬁning detailed speciﬁcations cl early at the early stages of development and having AI agents gener ate code based on those speciﬁcations." Its distinguishing feature is that agents proceed from structured specification documents rather than ambiguous natural-language instructions, with specifications describing architectural patterns, coding conventions, security requirements, and testing strategies that agents treat as constraints. Because developers must understand and verify the generated documents and code, the authors judge SDD more suitable than Vibe Coding for project-based courses where students take responsibility for AI outputs.

constraints: SDD demands greater expertise compared to Vibe Coding, per the authors

target_learning_goals: application development skills
understanding and verifying AI-generated specifications and code
examples: In the SDPBL course, the existing SDD requirements-analysis and design phases were redefined as an investigation phase, and a review phase was added after implementation, yielding a four-phase workflow

article_title: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators
citation: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591
title: The F/R decomposition: student simulators as jointly faithful and guidance-responsive proxies for tutor optimization
description: The article formalizes per-student student simulation as a measurable target with two properties. First, "behavioral fidelity: how well the simulator reproduces a student's own response to a problem, including that student's characteristic mistakes and strengths". Second, "guidance responsiveness", how readily the simulator updates its response in the direction tutor guidance steers. The framework is motivated by educational measurement's two targets — independent production and progress with support, the zone of proximal development that dynamic assessment operationalizes — and turns student simulation into an optimizable objective for AI tutor training.
requirements: A useful simulator must satisfy both properties together; the high-F, high-R corner is the target, since F and R measure separable capabilities.
constraints: The authors note F and R capture a student's state and its one-step update under guidance, not fuller learning dynamics such as acquisition, retention, and forgetting across many interactions.
target_learners: individual real learners in chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics
target_learning_goals: reproducing individual student responses and their revision under tutor guidance
examples: The framework scores every method on the same held-out per-student records, e.g. chess fidelity as move-prediction accuracy and responsiveness as corrected-move rate.
key_sources: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591

article_title: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators
citation: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591
title: StudentSimEval: a standardized per-student simulator benchmark over 60 students in chess, L2 writing, and math with released code
description: StudentSimEval is a standardized evaluation protocol spanning 60 students across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. It "turns public learner corpora into a fixed per-student record schema with per-student train/held-out splits, and scores every method on two metrics, behavioral fidelity (F) and guidance responsiveness (R)". Because every method is fit on the same per-student records and scored on the same held-out records, simulators from any family are directly comparable; the authors release the construction pipeline, per-student splits, and evaluation code so others can score new methods and extend the benchmark.
requirements: Evaluation uses frozen per-student held-out sets scored identically for every method, with per-student evaluation records disjoint from training data.
constraints: The multi-turn corpora are real-teacher-annotated for L2 but LLM-tutor-generated under fixed style templates for chess and math, where the LLM determines only the wording of guidance.
target_learners: real human students: 30 chess players, 15 L2 English learners, 15 math students
target_learning_goals: measuring behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness of student simulators
examples: Chess records come from the Lichess May 2025 database, L2 essays from the EFCAMDAT corpus, and math from a foundational-assistance corpus of annotated open-ended problems.
key_sources: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591

article_title: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators
citation: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591
title: Two-stage pooled-then-specialized training: pretrain a domain base simulator on pooled student data, then specialize one adapter per student
description: StudentSim overcomes sparse per-student data with a two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 trains one domain-specific base simulator on records pooled across all students, learning "common mistake patterns, the response format expected in the domain, and the pathway from natural-language tutor guidance to a changed response". Stage 2 initializes from that base and adapts it to one specific student using only that student's own recorded responses and tutor-guidance interactions, producing one LoRA adapter per student on a shared Qwen3-4B-Instruct backbone.
requirements: Stage 1 must supply what is shared across students and cannot be learned reliably from one student's sparse data alone; Stage 2 then supplies what is specific to each individual.
constraints: Per-student data is sparse: a learner in the L2 corpus writes three essays at the median, and more than two thirds write five or fewer; training one simulator end-to-end per student from such records would overfit.
target_learners: individual learners with sparse recorded interaction data in chess, L2 writing, or math
target_learning_goals: simulating an individual student's baseline responses and their revision after tutor guidance
examples: In chess, the article reports that performance drops when pooled records are replaced with repeated records from one student, supporting the pooled stage.

article_title: Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation
citation: Christoforos Fragkiadakis, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag. (2026). Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02232
title: DIPSER multimodal classroom dataset for in-person student engagement and attention recognition
description: DIPSER (Dataset for In-Person Student Engagement Recognition in the Wild) synchronizes camera recordings with smartwatch sensor data to capture student attention and emotional states during scheduled educational activities without experimental staging. It provides RGB facial images at 640× 480 pixels at approximately 10 frames per second, wearable sensors (heart rate, linear acceleration, gyroscope, rotation vector, ambient light) at up to 100 Hz, per-second attention labels on a scale from 1 to 5, emotion annotations across 9 categories, and automatically inferred demographic metadata. "The dataset contains recordings from 57 subjects, organized into three groups of 16–21 students, and comprises 9 distinct educational scenarios, ranging from passive learning settings (lectures) to highly interactive activities (robotics experimentation)."
requirements: Synchronized multimodal recordings with per-second attention labels and demographic metadata for subgroup-aware modeling
constraints: Approximately 95% of subjects were classified as white (Caucasian), leading to the exclusion of race as a fairness axis due to this imbalance
Demographic attributes are automatically inferred rather than self-reported
The authors note its real-world setting, demographic imbalance, and the subjectivity of human annotations introduce realistic sources of bias
target_learners: classroom students across secondary and higher education age groups (13–44)
target_learning_goals: continuous estimation of student attention during passive and interactive learning activities
examples: Used in this study with subject-level splits (39 train, 9 validation, 9 test subjects), 10-second rolling windows, and inverse-frequency weighting for imbalanced attention labels
key_sources: Christoforos Fragkiadakis, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag. (2026). Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02232

article_title: Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation
citation: Christoforos Fragkiadakis, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag. (2026). Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02232
title: Subject-level demographic MAE-gap fairness regularization for multimodal attention models
description: An in-processing fairness framework that adds a demographic disparity penalty to the training objective of a multimodal attention model. Per-subject MAEs are averaged within each demographic group, and "The fairness penalty was defined as the gap between the highest and lowest group-level subject MAE", weighted by a trade-off parameter λ added to the weighted MSE task loss. Regularization is introduced after a two-epoch warm-up, with subject- and group-balanced batch sampling so every represented subject contributes equally to the penalty. λ is selected on validation data subject to a constraint that mean validation MAE increases by no more than 0.02 relative to the unregularized baseline.
requirements: Subject- and group-balanced batch sampling so all protected groups are represented in the penalty
A warm-up period optimizing only prediction MSE before adding the fairness term
Validation-based λ selection with an accuracy-degradation cap
constraints: In this study the validation-level fairness improvements did not consistently generalize to held-out subjects or repeated subject-level splits
Fairness constraints can modify the predictive optimum and create accuracy–fairness trade-offs
target_learners: classroom students in demographic subgroups defined by inferred gender and age
target_learning_goals: reducing demographic error disparities in continuous student attention estimation while preserving predictive performance
examples: Applied to the Residual Fusion Transformer with λ=0.7 for gender and λ=0.8 for age objectives, each evaluated across 10 training seeds
key_sources: Christoforos Fragkiadakis, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag. (2026). Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02232

article_title: Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation
citation: Christoforos Fragkiadakis, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag. (2026). Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02232
title: Evaluate fairness-aware learning models with subgroup-aware metrics, repeated subject-level validation, and joint interpretation of disparity and accuracy
description: Because aggregate predictive metrics can conceal demographic disparities and single-split validation can overstate fairness gains, this principle holds that fairness claims require subgroup-level evaluation alongside overall and worst-group error, tested across repeated subject-level splits. The article concludes that "stable fairness improvements require stronger evidence than a single validation split or a reduction in one disparity metric." Disparity metrics should be interpreted jointly with predictive accuracy, since lower disparities do not necessarily correspond to better outcomes for all demographic groups.
requirements: Subgroup and worst-group error metrics computed per demographic axis
Repeated subject-level train-validation-test splits with paired comparisons
Sufficient numbers of independent subjects per subgroup
constraints: With very few subjects per subgroup, subgroup and worst-group metrics can be strongly influenced by individual participant behavior
Automatically inferred rather than self-reported demographic attributes add uncertainty
target_learners: students in demographic subgroups of educational AI deployments
target_learning_goals: reliable, fairness-aware evaluation of automated student attention and engagement estimation
examples: The study evaluated overall MAE, worst-group MAE, and best-to-worst subgroup MAE gaps for each fairness axis, and ran repeated subject-level split experiments with paired baseline and fairness-model comparisons

article_title: SWIM: Student Writing Simulation via Proficiency-Conditioned Generation
citation: Heejin Do, Jakub Kontak, Mrinmaya Sachan. (2026). SWIM: Student Writing Simulation via Proficiency-Conditioned Generation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2609.03215. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03215
title: SWIM: proficiency-conditioned essay generation task with AES-based profile-alignment evaluation and the Proficiency Alignment Reward
description: SWIM formalizes student writing simulation as proficiency-conditioned essay generation: given a writing prompt and a target trait-score profile, a generator produces an essay exhibiting the specified writing behavior, and "an AES-based evaluation framework for" measuring profile alignment scores the output with a frozen multi-trait AES verifier using QWK. The authors train generators via SFT on real (essay, profile) pairs and then refine them with GRPO using the Proficiency Alignment Reward, a dense per-sample reward based on trait-normalized accuracy against the target profile.
requirements: A trait-score-annotated essay corpus with prompt-specific rubrics and score ranges, and a frozen multi-trait AES verifier as external evaluator
constraints: Evaluation relies on AES as a proxy for fidelity and cannot fully replace human judgment of authenticity
Experiments cover a limited set of writing prompts and proficiency distributions on ASAP/ASAP++
Static proficiency profiles do not model evolving learner states such as knowledge, motivation, or writing strategies over time
target_learners: simulated K-12 and secondary student writers across grade levels in the ASAP/ASAP++ corpus
target_learning_goals: reproducing multidimensional writing proficiency (content, organization, lexical choice, sentence fluency, conventions) at specified levels
examples: GRPO-trained Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct generated qualitatively distinct essays for ASAP Prompt 5 at target Overall scores 1/4, 2/4, and 4/4, with length and structural sophistication scaling with the requested level

article_title: Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education
citation: Rayed AlGhamdi. (2026). Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6277-2124
title: Feedback utility versus evaluative authority: a conceptual distinction between accepting AI as feedback mechanism and accepting AI as grader
description: The paper contributes a conceptual distinction "that has not been clearly named in the existing literature: between students' acceptance of AI as a feedback mechanism (feedback utility) and their acceptance of AI as an evaluator with grading authority (evaluative authority)." The two are analytically separate judgements rather than opposite ends of a single approval scale. The authors argue this distinction helps reconcile competing findings in the algorithm-trust literature, since students may appreciate AI for some functions and resist it for others within the same evaluation event.
requirements: Analysis must attend to how students separate functions of AI within the same evaluation event rather than asking whether students accept or reject AI evaluation as a whole
constraints: Derived from a small, purposive sample of 13 students in one Saudi computing course; the authors state the patterns should not be generalized without further research
target_learners: undergraduate computing students in higher education
target_learning_goals: reasoning about trust, fairness, and legitimacy of AI-mediated writing assessment
examples: Participants endorsed AI for initial feedback while questioning its use for final grading, and even enthusiastic participants framed endorsement as relating to learning support rather than grading authority

citation: Rayed AlGhamdi. (2026). Who Should Grade My Work? Student Perspectives on Transparent AI-Assisted Writing Assessment in Higher Education. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6277-2124
title: Three-principle framework for ethical GenAI integration in writing assessment: transparency, human mediation, reflective practice
description: The paper proposes "a three-principle framework (transparency, human mediation, reflective practice) for ethical GenAI integration in writing assessment." Transparency functions not merely as disclosure but as a pedagogical strategy that surfaces learners' assumptions, concerns, and values regarding GenAI. Human mediation reflects participants' positioning of the instructor as the appropriate authority over grading decisions and a safeguard against AI error. Reflective practice reflects the post-assessment reflective design in which students examined the evaluation itself.
requirements: GenAI evaluation must be aligned with a rubric-based prompt tied to task objectives; students must be explicitly informed that an AI generated the feedback and score
constraints: Proposed within the bounded context and sample of this study; the authors acknowledge other tools may offer enhanced data-protection guarantees and institutional policies on AI tool selection are evolving rapidly
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education writing courses
target_learning_goals: critical engagement with AI-mediated feedback and assessment
examples: The study's design explicitly informed students that ChatGPT evaluated their handwritten work before a reflective task on agreement, learning, and opinions about AI as evaluator

article_title: Flawed but Memorable: Student Critical Reception of Interest-Personalized GenAI Analogies in Computing Education
citation: Seth Bernstein and Naaz Sibia. 2026. Flawed but Memorable: Student Critical Reception of Interest-Personalized GenAI Analogies in Computing Education. Koli Calling '26. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06095
title: Two-sided analogy auditing: target-domain and source-domain knowledge jointly support evaluation of an analogical mapping
description: The article's conceptual account of how learners evaluate analogies. Target-concept knowledge identifies the relations an analogy must preserve, while source-domain knowledge determines whether those relations hold there; the article states "neither side is sufficient alone." A familiar source may make an analogy both more engaging and more inspectable, giving interest personalization a possible epistemic role in addition to its motivational role. The account reframes expertise as source-domain or target-domain expertise rather than a single construct.
requirements: Evaluating an analogy requires knowledge of both the computing concept and the analogy's source domain
constraints: Because explanation format and personalization varied together in the design, the study cannot isolate personalization as the cause of the observed scrutiny
target_learners: undergraduate computing students who have completed CS2
target_learning_goals: critically evaluating AI-generated analogical explanations of computing concepts such as linked lists and recursion
examples: Participants who knew an analogy's source domain well, such as P6 with One Piece, audited the source side of the mapping directly and located the point of structural divergence.

article_title: Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment
citation: Masum Hasan, Ron Epstein, Thomas Carroll, Ehsan Hoque. (2026). Scalable AI-based clinical communication training and automated assessment. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22517
title: SOPHIE 2.0: a browser-based self-service platform for AI-patient communication practice with automated feedback and assessment
description: SOPHIE 2.0 is a browser-based platform combining an audiovisual virtual avatar patient, real-time LLM-generated dialogue, and automated personalized feedback. Its library spans "24 clinical scenarios" across cardiology, primary care, oncology, critical care, pediatrics, neonatology, surgery, dental, and oral health, with virtual patients of diverse ages, genders, ethnicities, and appearances. Learners select a scenario, complete an encounter, receive immediate transcript-based feedback on the 3E skills, and repeat practice without a live facilitator, standardized patient, or human rater. Conversational backends are GPT-4o-mini and HAL, a Qwen2.5 14B model optimized with Direct Preference Optimization on approximately 7,500 medical conversation pairs.
requirements: An internet-connected device; the study required participants to have medical education or certification and English communication
constraints: The Tavus video avatar platform limits the maximum number of concurrent users depending on the payment plan
target_learners: physicians and other clinicians
resident physicians
nursing professionals
medical or pre-medical students

article_title: What Fidelity Metrics Miss: A Structural Check on Synthetic Educational Data
citation: Inoue, H., & Yasutake, K. (2026). What Fidelity Metrics Miss: A Structural Check on Synthetic Educational Data. Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Computers in Education. Asia-Pacific Society for Computers in Education. https://library.apsce.net
title: Weekly β0 structural check: connected components of a weekly proximity graph over learners tracked across a term
description: A structural summary of how a cohort divides in each week: learners are represented as points in a feature space, connected when Euclidean distance falls below a threshold ε, and β0 counts the connected components of the graph, read as "the number of distinct behavioural groups the cohort forms that week". Tracked across weeks it describes reorganisation rather than level. It requires no optimisation or random seed, is defined for disconnected graphs, and is computed identically on real and synthetic cohorts.

A complete learner-by-week feature grid with features standardised on a common scale across weeks
constraints: The platform's disclosure rules do not permit component-wise maxima
The authors do not argue β0 is a good measure of learning nor interpret its level educationally
Which structural descriptor serves non-stationarity description best is left open

target_learning_goals: describing week-to-week reorganisation of cohort behavioural structure in learning-process data
examples: Applied to four annual cohorts of lower-secondary study-habit logs with weekly study time in six time-of-day bands, and to four OULAD presentations with weekly click counts on six activity types
