title: Skill-sustaining reliance: reflective AI engagement assessed for long-term sustainability of human agency and expertise
description: The paper introduces the concern of "skill-sustaining reliance": designing and evaluating reflective AI-engagement mechanisms not only for immediate decision quality but for whether professionals "still develop their own expertise or slowly lose the capacity for independent judgement". It organises the problem around four challenges: varying user effects, efficiency-driven workflows, habituation of scaffolding, and the short-term evidence gap. Its contribution is a set of open questions (Q1–Q4) for the research community about the conditions under which reflective AI engagement can be sustained in practice.

It runs randomized pre/post learning-gain studies comparing AI tutors, human tutors, and control, and produces five leaderboards covering lesson planning, practice-problem creation, conversational pedagogy, cost, and engagement. The article states three conditions: the technology improves human capabilities; an improved human is better at using the technology; and better use leads to consistent further gains. article_title: SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging
citation: Zhiwei Yang, Jiahua Yang, Huiru Lin, Xing Chen, and Quanlong Guan. (2026). SRJudge: Empowering Large Language Models with Selective Reasoning for Fine-Grained Knowledge Concept Tagging. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36982
title: SRJudge: a three-stage Select-Reason-Judge framework for fine-grained knowledge concept tagging
description: SRJudge decomposes knowledge concept tagging into three stages. A fine-tuned BERT-based Selector first narrows the candidate space: "the Selector first picks K(≪ |Φ|)candidates ... reducing the decision space". A lightweight LLM Reasoner, trained with a pruned GRPO reinforcement-learning strategy and a task-specific reward combining format, accuracy and dynamic position rewards, recommends a concept with reasons over the shortlist. A frozen larger LLM Judger then evaluates the rationality of the reasoning and issues the final verdict from a global perspective. The framework addresses the problem that LLMs "struggle to select the correct concept from a large-scale candidate set due to the high dimensionality of the decision space".
requirements: A labeled dataset for supervised fine-tuning of the Selector, plus unlabeled instances for continued pre-training, as the article states the Selector is fine-tuned on a labeled dataset
constraints: The Reasoner operates only on the top-K shortlist produced by the Selector, so concepts outside the shortlist cannot be selected
target_learners: educational platforms and MOOCs tagging exercises for grade 7-12 mathematics, biology and physics
target_learning_goals: accurate assignment of fine-grained knowledge concept labels to exercises and solutions
examples: On S Math, S Bio and S Phy, the Selector shortlists K=5 candidates, the Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct Reasoner reasons over them under GRPO, and Qwen3-32B acts as Judger

title: S Bio and S Phy: two new knowledge concept tagging datasets for cross-discipline validation

title: Hybrid query-resolution platform routing queries across AI assistant, peer layer, curated FAQ corpus and administrator escalation
description: A deployed support platform for a large online internship programme that routes each raised query across four paths: an AI chatbot answering only from a curated FAQ corpus, a peer layer where any participant may answer, administrator handling, and a scripted facility. The article states that "The platform routes a raised query first to the AI chatbot, which answers only from a curated corpus of verified FAQ entries, a deliberate restriction that prevents unverified procedural guidance". Peer answers pass through administrator acceptance and senior-administrator final approval before release, and the corpus was revised daily so rule or schedule changes were reflected the same day.

citation: Nizamani, S. B., Lee, Y., Donekal Chandrashekar, N., Ellis, M., & Ramakrishnan, N. (2026). Understanding Student Use of Large Language Models Across Computer Science Subfields. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01158
title: Demystify, use, and reflect: a structured LLM-intervention course design positioning LLMs as tools for supported learning
description: The course design centers on a structured intervention that works by "demystifying LLMs, how they work, their capabilities, and their probabilistic nature and limitations, alongside guided use through prompting strategies and iterative interaction". Rather than mandating or banning LLM use, the course leaves the decision to each student, requires students to understand, explain, and acknowledge AI-generated contributions, and adds a post-assignment reflection survey capturing prompt counts, role conceptualization, and verification strategies. This study extends the intervention by examining how its effects vary at the subfield level rather than only in aggregate.

Findings are tied to the specific assignments and instructional practices of a single course context

target_learning_goals: Informed and responsible LLM use
Effective prompting and iterative interaction
Assessing the reliability of LLM-generated responses

citation: Hansol Lee. (2026). Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00461-1
title: Teacher intervention in AI-based instruction operates as a cyclical four-phase process of monitoring, judgment, intervention, and orchestration
description: The review conceptualizes teacher intervention as an integrated framework connecting AI-generated information with classroom practice. Analysis of the 29 included studies showed that "teacher intervention operates as a cyclical process comprising monitoring, judgment, intervention, and orchestration." AI outputs do not constitute pedagogical intervention by themselves; they gain instructional meaning only when teachers interpret, judge, and translate them into situated classroom support, and each link in the cycle is not automatic.
requirements: Teachers must interpret and judge AI-generated information before it becomes pedagogical action; the framework presupposes teacher presence in AI-based instruction
constraints: Derived from a synthesis of 29 K-12 studies published 2016-2025, relatively concentrated in middle and high school mathematics and science contexts

target_learning_goals: Transforming AI-generated information into pedagogical action and classroom adjustment
examples: The review presents the framework in Fig. 2, organizing the synthesis of processes, strategies, and effects across the 29 studies

citation: Hansol Lee. (2026). Teacher intervention in K-12 AI-based instruction: a systematic review of processes, strategies, and effects. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-026-00461-1
title: Three teacher intervention strategies in AI-based instruction: pedagogical translation of AI outputs, design of learning support, and reconstruction of interaction structures
description: The review identifies three strategies teachers use to intervene in AI-based instruction. "First, the pedagogical translation of AI outputs refers to the strategy by which teachers transform AI-generated information according to students' levels and classroom contexts, select what should be addressed, and turn it into actionable pedagogical practice." The second strategy organizes cognitive, affective-motivational, and procedural/self-regulatory support; the third coordinates peer interaction and student-AI interaction structures. The strategies are not mutually exclusive and can operate together within a single intervention scene.
requirements: Teachers need time and authority to interpret and select AI information, and the information itself must be interpretable, for translation to occur smoothly
constraints: Pedagogical translation can become a burden and increase teachers' cognitive load when information is excessive, hard to interpret, or there is insufficient time to review it

target_learning_goals: Supporting student learning through transformed AI information, designed support, and structured interactions
examples: In Yao et al. (2025), teachers selected, revised, supplemented, summarized, or deleted AI chatbot feedback according to students' writing levels and task purposes

citation: Tang J, Li P, Luo R (2026) Teacher feedback VS AI-assisted peer feedback in L2 writing: A quasi-experimental study in a Chinese University. PLoS One 21(6): e0345976. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0345976
title: Sociocultural account of feedback as scaffolding aligned to the Zone of Proximal Development
description: The article applies Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory, specifically scaffolding and the Zone of Proximal Development, to L2 writing feedback: feedback is "an external scaffold whose value depends on its precise alignment with the learner's cognitive potential within the ZPD and its gradual withdrawal at appropriate moments". Within this account, teacher feedback acts as expert-provided dynamic scaffolding with authority and context sensitivity, while AI-assisted peer feedback acts as technology-mediated collaborative scaffolding offering real-time, standardized support. citation: Wong, S. S. H., & Qiu, S. X. (2026). Think First, ChatGPT Later: Guiding Human–AI Collaboration for Learning Gains in Independent Human Creativity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10118-7
title: ISAR model: four types of AI effects on learning
description: The ISAR model proposed by Bauer et al. (2025) distinguishes four types of effects AI can exert on learning: inversion (AI leads to reduced cognitive processing and learning), substitution (AI provides instructional equivalence without changing cognitive processing), augmentation (AI enhances instruction with additional support without necessarily deepening processing), and redefinition (AI fosters deep constructive or interactive processes to enhance learning). The present study's findings align with the distinction between shallow appropriation (inversion-like) and deep collaborative engagement (redefinition-like) effects of AI.

title: Seven sample prompts scaffolding collaborative ChatGPT interaction in creative problem-solving
description: A set of seven sample prompts presented to the regulated-AI group to scaffold collaborative interaction with ChatGPT during the creative product improvement task. The prompts covered processes such as seeking refinements and feedback, elaborating on promising ideas, comparing and evaluating ideas, connecting and combining ideas, identifying weaknesses, and refining selected ideas based on feedback. Participants were told the prompts were illustrative and could use their own prompts following the same principles.
requirements: Learners must have their own initial ideas to bring into the interaction
Access to ChatGPT during the collaboration phase
constraints: Designed for a creative product improvement task; participants could adapt wording freely
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: collaborative idea improvement with generative AI
metacognitive evaluation of ideas
examples: Sample prompt: asking ChatGPT what can be changed or added to make one's own initial bunny-improvement ideas better

article_title: Decoding symmetric and asymmetric pathways in generative AI learning adoption: a multi-method study
citation: Xin Tian, Musa Adekunle Ayanwale, Rethabile Rosemary Molefi, Preeti Manchanda, Nurgün Gençel and Barakat Olabisi Ogunjoun. (2026). Decoding symmetric and asymmetric pathways in generative AI learning adoption: a multi-method study. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00613-w
title: Integrated UTAUT3–ARCS hybrid-logic framework of Gen-AI adoption
description: The article integrates the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT3) with Keller's ARCS Motivation Model into a dual-layer account of Gen-AI adoption. UTAUT3 answers "Can I use this technology effectively?", whereas ARCS answers "Will I continue to engage with it for learning?". The framework posits a hybrid logic in which cognitive beliefs enable acceptance, motivational experiences sustain engagement, and habitual interaction normalizes use; ARCS is positioned as a motivational layer that reinforces or undermines cognitive evaluations and the pathway from intention to use.
requirements: Measurement of both acceptance beliefs (PE, EE, SI, FC, HM, HB, PI) and the four ARCS dimensions as distinct constructs, with satisfaction treated as an outcome-based evaluation distinct from hedonic motivation and habit
constraints: Tested in a low-resource higher education context (Lesotho) with cross-sectional data, so structural paths are interpreted as theory-consistent associations rather than definitive causal effects

target_learning_goals: Sustained adoption and use of generative AI tools for academic learning tasks
examples: The study operationalized the framework with ten constructs on a six-point Likert scale, validated via expert review (S-CVI/Ave = 0.94) and MGRM-IRT, and tested it with PLS-SEM, NCA, fsQCA, and machine learning on data from 842 Lesotho students

article_title: Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem
citation: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527
title: Trust in chatbots defined as willingness to act on outputs without independent verification, calibrated when it matches actual accuracy and verifiability
description: The article grounds a conceptual framework connecting trust, credibility, and calibration across psychology, communication, and human factors research. It defines trust in a chatbot as "a user’s willingness to accept and act on its outputs without independent verification," treating trust as an attitude and reliance as its behavioral expression. Calibration may fail in two directions: misuse (overtrust) and disuse (distrust). The framework separates trust from trustworthiness, a property of the trusted party, and from reliance behavior.
requirements: Applies to settings where the user cannot inspect how an answer was produced and a wrong answer carries consequences
constraints: The article sets aside computing research that treats trust as a quantity one system computes about another, because its trustor is a person
target_learners: Chatbot users in education, healthcare, and everyday information seeking
target_learning_goals: Calibrated evaluation of AI-generated information
key_sources: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527

article_title: Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem
citation: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527
title: Two-dimensional user typology: ability to verify and motivation to verify yield four profiles with distinct calibration risks
description: The article collapses Hoff and Bashir's three layers of trust in automation into two functional dimensions: "The ability to verify rests on domain expertise and AI literacy," while motivation draws on need for cognition and epistemological beliefs. Crossing the dimensions yields four profiles: high-both users near calibrated trust, high-ability/low-motivation users at risk of complacent overtrust, low-ability/high-motivation users whose checks misfire, and low-both users most exposed to overtrust. Profiles are positions, not identities, and shift across tasks.
requirements: Design interventions must be matched to profiles, since the question is not simply whether an intervention works but for whom
constraints: The typology is deliberately simple and the boundaries between profiles are soft
target_learners: Chatbot users varying in domain expertise, AI literacy, and motivation
target_learning_goals: Matching trust-calibration interventions to user profiles
examples: Figure 1 maps each calibration risk to the intervention families most likely to address it
key_sources: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527

article_title: Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem
citation: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527
title: Five interpretability affordance strategies: source transparency, rationale generation, uncertainty expression, interactive scrutiny, and progressive disclosure
description: The article proposes that "interpretability can be built into the interaction through five strategies," each serving three goals: protecting the user's ability to judge, making the system contestable, and preserving usability. The strategies are source transparency (inline citations, RAG, confidence-calibrated hyperlinks), rationale generation paired with source attribution, uncertainty expression, interactive scrutiny tools, and progressive disclosure with layered explanations. Each has a boundary located by the user typology.
requirements: Rationales must be paired with source attribution and presented as a useful account, not a faithful report of internal processing
constraints: Every strategy waits for the user to act, so these affordances serve motivated profiles well and barely touch unmotivated ones
target_learners: Motivated chatbot users across ability levels
target_learning_goals: Making evaluation of chatbot outputs possible
examples: Cai et al. (2019) found clinicians worked more effectively with layered explanations than with either full technical detail or no explanation
key_sources: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527

article_title: Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem
citation: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527
title: Engagement friction must be proportional, adaptive, transparent, non-paternalistic, and treated as an empirical hypothesis
description: The article states five principles governing engagement mechanisms in use: "Friction must be proportional, so that low-stakes queries stay frictionless while high-stakes queries carry more." Mechanisms must be adaptive to the user profile, transparent about why they slow the user down, non-paternalistic so users can always override them, and treated as empirical hypotheses with testable effects on calibration, accuracy, and satisfaction. An operating rule adds that interpretability stays on for everyone while friction is off by default.
requirements: Friction triggers only when the query is high stakes and recent behavior suggests uncritical acceptance, escalating in small steps and stopping at the first step that produces verification
constraints: A rising skip rate is the signal that the dose has gone too far
target_learners: All chatbot users, with friction dosed by observed behavior
target_learning_goals: Calibrating trust without rationing information
examples: Figure 2 translates the operating rule into a candidate adaptive design sequence responding to query stakes and observable interaction behavior
key_sources: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527

article_title: Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem
citation: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527
title: Swiss cheese model of trust calibration: layered interpretability affordances, engagement mechanisms, and literacy cover one another's gaps
description: The article borrows Reason's Swiss cheese model as its integrating frame: "every safety barrier has holes, yet stacked barriers rarely let a hazard through all of them at once." Interpretability affordances miss unmotivated users; engagement mechanisms catch them but may miss users whose checks are ineffective; literacy building closes gaps slowly but durably. A user who cannot evaluate citations may still be reached by a dialogue scaffold or a social signal, so layered combinations can make uncritical acceptance rare.
requirements: No single intervention can fully recalibrate user trust, so layers must be combined
constraints: Each layer's holes are located by the user typology, and literacy building works slowly
target_learners: All chatbot users across the four typology profiles
target_learning_goals: Reducing uncritical acceptance of chatbot outputs
examples: The COVID-19 pandemic publicized the model, where masks, ventilation, and vaccines were each imperfect and jointly effective
key_sources: Jaidka K and Cai M. (2026). Why we believe chatbots: trust calibration as a design problem. Front. Psychol. 17:1935527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1935527

article_title: Trust calibration and perceived developmental gains in university students' collaboration with generative AI: an exploratory sequential mixed methods study
citation: Fan Bu and Wei Li (2026). Trust calibration and perceived developmental gains in university students' collaboration with generative AI: an exploratory sequential mixed methods study. Front. Psychol. 17:1861072. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1861072
title: A four-construct process model of GenAI-supported learning: contextual support, trust calibration, collaborative regulation, and perceived transfer gains
description: The article proposes a layered process model in which contextual support (teacher guidance, assessment design, peer norms, institutional policy) is a context-level antecedent; trust calibration is a judgment-level hinge; collaborative regulation is a process-level mechanism of prompting, checking, comparing, rewriting, and integrating; and perceived transfer gains is an outcome-level, author-developed construct. Trust calibration is defined as the degree to which trust is "appropriately matched to task demands, output quality, and system limitations rather than being indiscriminately high or low". The model is grounded in social cognitive theory, self-regulated learning theory, cognitive load theory, and human-automation trust research.
requirements: Constructs are differentiated by analytic level (context, judgment, process, outcome) to reduce overlap among psychologically adjacent variables
constraints: The outcome is perceived transfer gains, not objective competence improvement; the model tests a focal analytic direction and does not claim a permanently one-way sequence, and cognitive load is not measured
target_learners: university undergraduates using GenAI for academic tasks
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
appropriate reliance on AI output
evaluative judgment and cross-task strategy transfer
examples: Study 1 interviews elicited task-sensitive reliance, e.g. a student who would use AI for ideas or wording but would not trust a citation or technical claim until verifying it

citation: Fan Bu and Wei Li (2026). Trust calibration and perceived developmental gains in university students' collaboration with generative AI: an exploratory sequential mixed methods study. Front. Psychol. 17:1861072. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1861072
title: A 22-item self-report instrument measuring contextual support, trust calibration, collaborative regulation, and perceived transfer gains
description: A five-point Likert-scale self-report instrument developed from the qualitative phase rather than assembled solely from pre-existing scales. "The ﬁnal instrument contained 22 items: six measuring contextual support, ﬁve measuring trust calibration, six measuring collaborative regulation, and ﬁve measuring perceived transfer gains." Items were reviewed by educational psychology researchers and higher education instructors, pilot tested with 94 undergraduates, and administered to a formal sample of 642 valid responses for CFA and SEM.
requirements: Items were drafted to represent one construct and one primary idea, avoiding double-barreled statements, technical terminology, and overly general evaluations of GenAI
constraints: Perceived-transfer-gain items capture subjective perceptions of developmental change across tasks rather than objectively demonstrated competence
target_learners: university undergraduates
target_learning_goals: measuring contextual conditions, trust judgments, regulatory behavior, and perceived developmental outcomes in GenAI-supported learning

citation: Fan Bu and Wei Li (2026). Trust calibration and perceived developmental gains in university students' collaboration with generative AI: an exploratory sequential mixed methods study. Front. Psychol. 17:1861072. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1861072
title: Design GenAI-supported learning around contextual guidance, calibrated trust, and active regulation rather than expecting benefits from use frequency alone
description: The article's findings indicate that developmental benefits of student-GenAI collaboration depend on an instructional environment that frames appropriate use and on students' active management of the interaction. The authors conclude that benefits "are better understood as theory consistent structural relationships shaped by contextual guidance, calibrated trust, and active regulation rather than as automatic consequences of frequent AI use". Educational design should therefore provide boundary cues, process-oriented assessment, and norms that support task-sensitive trust judgments and enacted regulation.
requirements: An instructional environment providing teacher guidance, assessment design, peer modeling, and institutional norms surrounding GenAI use
constraints: Findings are cross-sectional self-report; the outcome is perceived transfer gains rather than objectively demonstrated competence, so the principle rests on subjective outcome measures
target_learners: university undergraduates using GenAI in coursework
target_learning_goals: calibrated trust in AI output
active regulation of human-AI collaboration
perceived transfer of evaluative judgment and strategies across tasks

article_title: How trust prospectively predicts perceived fairness and learning motivation toward AI teaching assistants: a three-wave within-person longitudinal study
citation: Fu L, Ouyang Z and Wu Q (2026). How trust prospectively predicts perceived fairness and learning motivation toward AI teaching assistants: a three-wave within-person longitudinal study. Front. Psychol. 17:1900061. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1900061
title: Temporally ordered trust→fairness→motivation model for AI teaching assistants with three within-person mechanisms
description: The article proposes a temporally ordered model in which trust functions as an antecedent cognitive-affective orientation associated with subsequent within-person change in fairness evaluations, which in turn influence motivational outcomes. It rests on three mechanisms: an attributional schema mechanism, a cognitive load mechanism, and a justice-emotion mechanism. As the article states, "trust creates attributional schemas that filter fairness evaluations: high-trust individuals interpret ambiguous system behaviors charitably, attributing apparent inconsistencies to benign causes, whereas low-trust individuals engage in vigilant monitoring for injustice evidence". The model integrates trust theory, organizational justice theory, and self-determination theory, and was tested with RI-CLPM longitudinal mediation.
requirements: Three-wave (or longer) longitudinal measurement with intervals matched to the theorized timescale of trust–fairness recalibration
Random-intercept decomposition to separate stable between-person trait variance from within-person fluctuation
constraints: The article notes cross-sectional designs cannot separate stable between-person differences from genuine within-person change, motivating the longitudinal specification
Benevolence trust may function differently for non-sentient AI than in interpersonal trust contexts, as the article acknowledges
target_learners: undergraduate students using AI teaching assistants in higher education
target_learning_goals: sustained learning motivation toward AI-mediated instruction
examples: The study tested the model with a three-wave RI-CLPM (N = 450, 4-week intervals) including longitudinal mediation via bias-corrected bootstrapping

article_title: How trust prospectively predicts perceived fairness and learning motivation toward AI teaching assistants: a three-wave within-person longitudinal study
citation: Fu L, Ouyang Z and Wu Q (2026). How trust prospectively predicts perceived fairness and learning motivation toward AI teaching assistants: a three-wave within-person longitudinal study. Front. Psychol. 17:1900061. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1900061
title: Cultivate ability trust early and ensure procedural transparency when deploying AI teaching assistants
description: The article's findings point to design levers for human-centered AI teaching assistants: because within-person trust increases prospectively predict fairness perceptions (with ability trust the strongest antecedent) and procedural justice preferentially relates to intrinsic motivation, the authors recommend "early ability-trust cultivation and procedural transparency as candidate targets for psychologically grounded, human-centered AITA design". Procedural fairness in this context emphasizes transparency of algorithmic decision rules, consistency of application, and availability of corrective mechanisms.
requirements: AITA deployment contexts where students accumulate sustained interaction experience over weeks
Measurement or monitoring of students' trust and fairness perceptions to target the ability and procedural dimensions
constraints: The article explicitly cautions that "an observational design cannot establish that intervening on them would produce the corresponding changes"
The procedural-justice advantage for intrinsic motivation was suggestive rather than definitive, as the direct coefficient-difference test did not reach conventional significance
target_learners: undergraduate students in courses using AI teaching assistants
target_learning_goals: learning motivation and sustained engagement with AI-mediated instruction
examples: In the study, ability trust showed the strongest within-person effects on subsequent fairness (β = 0.11–0.14), and procedural justice at Time 2 predicted intrinsic motivation at Time 3 (β = 0.16)

title: Feedback literacy as a set of capabilities including dispositions for meaningful partnership with teachers in feedback processes
description: The paper treats feedback literacy as a set of student capabilities that can be deliberately developed, extending beyond receiving feedback to the dispositions needed for engagement with teachers about feedback. It states these capabilities include "the dispositions required for a meaningful partnership with their teachers in relation to feedback". The AI automated feedback tool is positioned as one means of promoting and further developing these capabilities in higher education students.

title: Reframe AI feedback tools as developing students' feedback literacy rather than only providing more immediate feedback
description: The paper proposes shifting the design rationale for AI in teaching: rather than using AI mainly to give students immediate and more feedback while reducing teacher workload, AI tools should be chosen and configured to promote students' feedback literacy capabilities. article_title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence Anxiety and Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence in University Students' Job Finding Anxiety
citation: Üstün, A. G., & Danacıoğlu, N. (2026). The Role of Artificial Intelligence Anxiety and Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence in University Students’ Job Finding Anxiety. Participatory Educational Research, 13(2), 143-164. https://doi.org/10.17275/per.26.23.13.2
title: Social Cognitive Career Theory and Technology Acceptance Model as framework for AI-related career anxiety
description: The study interprets its findings within two frameworks. Social Cognitive Career Theory (Lent et al., 1994) is described as explaining career development through self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and goal setting, so that concerns and negative attitudes toward AI can shape students' perceptions of their future careers. The Technology Acceptance Model (Davis, 1989) explains technology acceptance through "perceived usefulness and ease of use", linking attitudes and intentions toward technology to anxiety. Together they frame AI-related emotional responses as influences on career planning and sectoral expectations.
requirements: The framework assumes career expectations are shaped by environmental factors, self-efficacy, personal experiences, and cognitive-emotional processes, as the article states within SCCT.
target_learners: university students approaching graduation
target_learning_goals: career planning and preparedness for labor market entry under technological transformation
examples: The authors interpret the moderate AI anxiety–job finding anxiety correlation as SCCT-consistent and the negative-attitudes link as TAM-consistent.

article_title: Who wrote this? Evaluating the reliability of AI detection tools in higher education
citation: Marijke Van Vlasselaer, Filip Van Droogenbroeck and Bram Spruyt. (2026). Who wrote this? Evaluating the reliability of AI detection tools in higher education. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00226-w
title: Use AI detection scores only as initial flags that trigger further review, never as sole evidence in high-stakes academic integrity decisions
description: The article recommends that institutions treat AI detection tool output as one component of a broader evaluation strategy rather than as decisive proof of misconduct. It argues that "tools like Pangram could be considered as an initial flag for further investigation" and that "A flagged result should trigger a more thorough review of the student’s paper content, rather than relying on an AI detection tool to draw a final conclusion." This follows from the study's finding that tools vary strongly in accuracy and can severely underestimate AI content.
requirements: Institutions establish clear and explicit policies outlining when and how the use of generative AI constitutes a breach of academic integrity
constraints: The article notes some tools may use conservative thresholds to avoid falsely labelling human-written text as AI-generated, which may increase the number of false negatives
target_learners: higher education students, particularly master's thesis writers
target_learning_goals: academic integrity in written academic work
examples: The study applied Pangram to 1,163 master's theses and recommends flagged results trigger a more thorough review of the student's paper content rather than a final conclusion

article_title: The AI guilt complex: Moral emotions and ethical dilemmas in academic technology adoption
citation: Diane Vassallo. (2026). The AI Guilt Complex: Moral Emotions and Ethical Dilemmas in Academic Technology Adoption. Journal of Academic Ethics (2026) 24:53. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09726-3
title: AI Guilt Index: a preliminary four-item measure of AI-related guilt in academic contexts
description: The AI Guilt Index is a four-item Likert-scale instrument developed for this study to measure AI-related moral distress among academics, covering credibility worry, feeling like cheating, feeling bad about task automation, and remorse after AI use. Exploratory factor analysis of ten moral-emotion items revealed a unidimensional structure accounting for 63.5% of variance (KMO = 0.93), and the four retained items showed "excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.88)" with item-total correlations from 0.68 to 0.80. Items were adapted from the GASP and State Shame and Guilt Scale. The mean score in the sample was 2.39 (SD = 1.01).
requirements: Requires validation in larger samples; the authors state it was not intended as a definitive measure of AI-related guilt but as an initial exploratory instrument
constraints: Developed and tested only in a single-institution exploratory sample of 109 academics; the item on teaching students about academic integrity was excluded on conceptual grounds
target_learners: University academic staff (lecturers to professors, postdoctoral researchers)
target_learning_goals: Measuring moral emotions (guilt) surrounding AI tool adoption in academic practice
examples: In the survey, 22.9% of participants (n = 25) exceeded the scale midpoint, indicating substantial guilt in about one quarter of the sample

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence in university chemistry education: a critical review using Johnstone’s chemistry triplet and Biggs’ 3P model
citation: Vega-Baudrit JR and Rivera Álvarez A (2026) Generative artificial intelligence in university chemistry education: a critical review using Johnstone’s chemistry triplet and Biggs’ 3P model. Front. Educ. 11:1918707. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1918707
title: Verification-centered Johnstone-3P architecture for GenAI in university chemistry education
description: The review proposes an explanatory architecture in which Johnstone's chemistry triplet (macroscopic, submicroscopic, symbolic domains, with representational translation as a cross-domain process rather than a fourth level) supplies a chemistry-specific epistemic test, and Biggs' Presage-Process-Product model supplies the pedagogical conditions. As the review states, "Johnstone’s triplet identifies the disciplinary location of this risk, while Biggs’ 3P model shows that outcomes depend on readiness, task design, policy, and assessment." Presage conditions shape learners' capacity to verify; process-level prompting, critique, and revision operate across the three domains; product outcomes must be demonstrated rather than assumed.
requirements: Learners must possess sufficient prior chemistry knowledge and representational competence to verify outputs, since students cannot verify what they do not understand
constraints: The review treats representational translation as a cross-domain reasoning process, not a fourth level of the triplet
The framework is developed for university chemistry, biochemistry, chemical engineering, and chemistry teacher education contexts
target_learners: University chemistry students
Preservice and in-service chemistry teachers
Chemical engineering students
target_learning_goals: Coordinating macroscopic, submicroscopic, and symbolic reasoning
Chemical accuracy and representational fluency
Professional judgment and laboratory responsibility

citation: Vega-Baudrit JR and Rivera Álvarez A (2026) Generative artificial intelligence in university chemistry education: a critical review using Johnstone’s chemistry triplet and Biggs’ 3P model. Front. Educ. 11:1918707. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1918707
title: Make verification an assessed activity, not merely a recommendation
description: This principle holds that verification of GenAI outputs should be built into assessment so that chemical judgment, not fluent production, is the assessed construct. The review states that "Verification should be assessed, not merely recommended" and that student reasoning should remain visible through prompt logs, annotated outputs, drafts, calculations, oral defense, and revision histories. Verification must be operationalized through chemistry-specific checks such as conservation, units, valence, electron flow, stereochemistry, spectral consistency, data provenance, experimental feasibility, and safety.
requirements: Assessment tasks must require students to identify AI errors, defend corrections, or explain why a generated answer should be rejected
Evidence of thinking such as prompt logs, intermediate calculations, and revision histories must be preserved
constraints: A generic recommendation to verify AI output is insufficient without chemistry-specific checks
target_learners: University chemistry students
target_learning_goals: Chemical judgment and verification skills
Independent reasoning in AI-supported tasks
examples: The review describes verification-centered assessment in which students identify an AI error, defend a correction, compare alternative representations, reproduce reasoning without AI, or explain why a generated answer should be rejected

title: Use GenAI for comparison and critique rather than as an authority
description: The review recommends positioning GenAI as a fallible object of disciplinary inquiry rather than an autonomous source of chemical truth. As it states, "GenAI should be used for comparison and critique rather than as an authority", with students asking for alternatives and counterexamples and comparing outputs with textbooks, primary literature, and experimental data. Classroom implementations cited used generated responses as objects of critique rather than final answers, turning model failures into assessable evidence of chemical reasoning.
requirements: Tasks must make uncertainty and error visible, for example by asking students to formulate questions that expose model limitations
constraints: The review notes that a design rewarding only the final product makes outsourcing rational
target_learners: University chemistry students
Preservice chemistry teachers
target_learning_goals: Critical evaluation of AI-generated chemical explanations
Metacognition and critical thinking
examples: Exintaris et al. (2023) and Guo and Lee (2023) used generated responses as objects of critique; Lopez-Perez et al. (2026) asked students to formulate questions exposing ChatGPT's limitations

title: Require qualified human review before GenAI is used for laboratory procedures and process decisions
description: In laboratory and chemical-engineering contexts, the review sets a higher threshold for acceptable error: "GenAI should not authorize procedures, hazard controls, equipment settings, or process decisions without qualified human review." Even when outputs are useful for ideation, responsibility remains with the human operator and institution. The review reports that AI-supported laboratory manuals became educationally useful only when implemented under professional validation and supervision, so the learning system, not the chatbot alone, produced the value.
requirements: Professional validation and supervision of AI-generated laboratory materials
Dimensional checks and validation against process constraints in chemical engineering uses
constraints: GenAI outputs in these contexts may omit quantities, propose unsafe conditions, confuse analytical logic, or require substantial expert correction
target_learners: University chemistry laboratory students
Chemical engineering students
target_learning_goals: Laboratory safety and procedural judgment
Physical interpretability of process models
examples: Yim and Lui (2026) implemented AI-supported laboratory manuals under professional validation and supervision

article_title: Beyond checking: verification quality, reliance calibration, and learning in generative AI-assisted higher education
citation: Wei J and Shang Y (2026). Beyond checking: verification quality, reliance calibration, and learning in generative AI-assisted higher education. Front. Psychol. 17:1965371. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1965371
title: Seven analytically ordered measurement targets for critical engagement with GenAI outputs
description: The review proposes a construct-validity framework separating seven measurement targets: epistemic evaluation, verification initiation, process quality, success, reliance decisions, immediate task performance, and independent learning. It argues that broad labels such as "critical" or "responsible" AI use "can obscure distinct outcomes" — a learner may check without a strong process, and a correct final answer does not establish retention or unaided performance. The ordering is analytic, not a validated causal sequence.
requirements: Measures must support distinct interpretations within a nomological network rather than being treated as interchangeable indicators
constraints: The map is an analytic ordering rather than a validated causal model
Searches were targeted rather than systematic
target_learners: higher education students using generative AI
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of AI-generated information
verification of AI claims
calibrated reliance on AI outputs
examples: Table 1 contrasts how representative studies operationalize verification, reliance calibration, and learning outcomes

article_title: Beyond checking: verification quality, reliance calibration, and learning in generative AI-assisted higher education
citation: Wei J and Shang Y (2026). Beyond checking: verification quality, reliance calibration, and learning in generative AI-assisted higher education. Front. Psychol. 17:1965371. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1965371
title: Reliance calibration as an output-contingent classification of reliance decisions
description: The review defines reliance calibration as "an item-level, output-contingent classification of whether a reliance decision was appropriate given AI-output quality", distinguishing it from trust (a psychological attitude) and reliance (an observable decision). For mixed-quality outputs, calibration may be judged at claim level or on a graded appropriateness scale, because one response can contain accurate, incomplete, and misleading elements simultaneously. Accepting faulty content constitutes over-reliance; rejecting useful content constitutes under-reliance.
requirements: A reference standard for AI-output quality is required before a reliance decision can be classified as calibrated
constraints: A trust scale cannot substitute for an observed reliance decision
HCI reviews note heterogeneous definitions of appropriate reliance
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: appropriate reliance on AI assistance
examples: Zheng et al. combined AI competence/relevance, follow/not-follow behavior, and final correctness in 315 student-ChatGPT quiz conversations to distinguish appropriate and inappropriate reliance

citation: Vogt P, Wolf N, Jordan S, Volz-Willems S, Jäger J, Dupont F. (2026). Can students identify AI? – A cross-sectional quantitative study about AI recognition in tablet-based MCQ assessment among fifth-year undergraduate medical students at Saarland University, Germany. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10410-8
title: Expert-panel human-review workflow for AI-generated MCQ drafting in a high-stakes exam
description: A structured workflow in which LLMs (ChatGPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro) received the full blended-learning curriculum and generated MCQs via sequential prompting, followed by expert-panel review. The panel "accepted 82% of the questions", applied "limited expert refinement" to retained items, and excluded items needing substantial revision; 30 AI questions (18 ChatGPT, 12 Gemini) entered the exam. The authors position it so "AI-generated MCQs serve as template, while humans remain responsible for quality control".

Provision of the full curriculum and learning materials to the LLMs for generation

target_learning_goals: Family Medicine clinical decision-making and clinical reasoning assessment
examples: In the 2024 FM examination, 44 LLM-generated MCQs were reviewed, 36 (81.8%) accepted, and 30 used alongside 30 NLE questions under a 90-minute time limit

title: Maintain structured human expert oversight when integrating AI-generated MCQs into assessment
description: The article recommends that AI-generated MCQs enter assessment only within a structured review process in which "humans remain responsible for quality control". Because AI output can be indistinguishable from human-written items, undetected errors or biases could pass uncritically into exams; the authors state the findings "suggest maintaining human oversight to minimize AI mistakes and avoid a possible specialty bias". Reviewing, rather than drafting, is where educator effort shifts.

Items requiring substantial content or structural revision are excluded rather than rewritten
constraints: Non-recognition of AI content "could lead to uncritical use on both sides"
AI output can carry structural biases from training data, such as the observed bias underestimating Family Medicine competency

target_learning_goals: valid and curriculum-aligned summative assessment of clinical decision-making
examples: In the study's exam, the expert panel eliminated 18.2% of initially generated MCQs and refined retained items to the German primary care and guideline context before use

citation: Voicu, C.-G. (2026). AI-Mediated Learning and the Restructuring of Interpretive Cognition: A Developmental-Critical Model for Social Sciences and Humanities Education. Journal of Digital Pedagogy, 5(1) 37-51. https://doi.org/10.61071/JDP .2665
title: Developmental-Critical Model for AI-Mediated SSH Pedagogy with Six Checkpoints
description: A three-stage pedagogical framework guiding learners from AI-dependent toward AI-critical interpretation, grounded in cognitive-developmental theory, hermeneutics, and critical pedagogy. It is "operationalized through six pedagogical checkpoints that scaffold interpretive autonomy": interpretive grounding prior to AI use, contextual anchoring of AI outputs, critical examination of algorithmic structures, hybrid authorship transparency, reflexive epistemic positioning, and dialogic engagement under human control. Each checkpoint addresses an observed risk including interpretive shortcutting, epistemic outsourcing, and loss of authorial voice, and is derived from the observed interactional patterns.
requirements: Learners engage directly with primary materials before using AI tools (interpretive grounding)
Pedagogical mediation that keeps AI functioning as scaffold rather than substitute for reasoning
constraints: The article states the model is "a flexible framework whose application may vary across disciplines, learner profiles, and levels of AI integration"
Based on qualitative, context-specific observations from a single classroom; does not aim for statistical generalization
target_learners: Lower secondary students (aged 13-15) in SSH education
target_learning_goals: Critical AI literacy
Epistemic responsibility
Interpretive autonomy
examples: The six checkpoints were derived directly from observed interactional patterns in 42 coded episodes and correspond to transitions between the three developmental stages

article_title: The impact of career adapt-abilities on AI anxiety among English majors: a dual perspective analysis based on core self-evaluations at the person- and variable-centered
citation: Wang X (2026) The impact of career adapt-abilities on AI anxiety among English majors: a dual perspective analysis based on core self-evaluations at the person- and variable-centered. Front. Psychol. 17:1767791. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1767791
title: Integrated resource–internalization–anxiety pathway linking Career Construction Theory and Conservation of Resources Theory
description: The article proposes an integrative framework in which career adapt-abilities, as Career Construction Theory-defined psychosocial resources, reduce AI anxiety partly through core self-evaluations, the cognitive internalization mechanism emphasized in Conservation of Resources Theory. The article states that "adapt-abilities are not merely 'resources' in a general sense; they are theorized to generate mastery experiences and proactive coping, which are then consolidated into more positive core self-evaluations". Higher core self-evaluations then lower AI anxiety by weakening threat appraisal and enhancing perceived controllability. The framework predicts the protective effect is partially indirect and partially direct.
requirements: Career adapt-abilities must undergo cognitive appraisal and internalization into core self-evaluations to exert their protective function
constraints: Tested in a cross-sectional design among English majors facing AI-driven substitution pressures in language-related occupations
target_learners: English major undergraduates and graduate students in Chinese universities
target_learning_goals: Career adapt-abilities development
management of AI-related occupational anxiety
examples: The dual-analytic strategy tested the pathway via variable-centered mediation and person-centered latent profile analysis, with both strategies converging on the protective role of career adapt-abilities

description: A large longitudinal dataset of one-on-one, project-based tutoring sessions between PhD-level tutors and students across more than 150 subjects, collected through the Polygence platform. The article states it "comprises more than 100,000 hours of one-on-one, longitudinal student–tutor interactions in multiple modalities," including meeting transcripts, shared documents, and chat. It was anonymized on internal servers and used for post-training and benchmarking LLMs for education.

title: Multi-turn evaluation protocol combining a fine-tuned student model with single-shot LLM judging
description: A novel evaluation protocol in which a fine-tuned student model and a candidate tutor model generate synthetic multi-turn dialogues that are scored by conversational statistics and a reasoning LLM judge, with results aggregated. The article introduces "a novel multi-turn evaluation protocol that combines a fine-tuned student model and a fine-tuned tutor model to generate a large number of synthetic dialogues." Each evaluation point corresponds to 100 simulated conversations (10 repetitions across 10 student models) to limit variability and ensure reproducibility.

A dedicated LLM judge (Gemini 2.5 Flash) to detect conversation end and a turn limit to prevent indefinite conversations
constraints: The article notes the six benchmarks are intentionally simple proxies; optimizing solely for them does not guarantee high-quality teaching

target_learning_goals: Measuring conversational and pedagogical quality of AI tutors across multi-turn dialogue
examples: The protocol was used to benchmark models from OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and XAI against human tutors on six metrics

title: Pipeline for transcribing, diarizing, and cleaning single-track tutoring audio into post-training dialogue data
description: A multi-step data pipeline that converts dual-track Zoom recordings of tutoring sessions into polished tutor-student transcripts suitable for text-based fine-tuning. Audio is merged and trimmed, transcribed with ElevenLabs' API, diarized using per-speaker activity masks, and cleaned with a reasoning model (Gemini 2.5 Pro) through punctuation normalization, backchannel removal, anonymization, and coherence smoothing with enforced turn-taking, followed by human spot checks.

Human spot checks to ensure transcripts meet the quality bar for post-training
constraints: The article notes prior work shows quality outweighs quantity during fine-tuning, motivating the multi-step cleaning

article_title: Towards Synergistic Teacher-AI Interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Mutlu Cukurova, Wannapon Suraworachet, Qi Zhou, and Sahan Bulathwela. (2025). Towards Synergistic Teacher-AI Interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19580
title: Five levels of teacher-AI teaming: transactional, situational, operational, praxical and synergistic
description: The chapter proposes an orthogonal conceptual framework of teacher-AI teaming focused on information flows, decisions and actions shared between teacher and AI, grounded in distributed cognition. The authors state: "we propose (1) transactional, (2) situational, (3) operational, (4) praxical and (5) synergistic levels of teaming, as shown in Fig. 8.1." Levels run from minimal request-response interactions to mutual co-adaptation, and the framework is validated against a systematic review of teacher-facing AI studies. The authors caution the levels "need not always follow a progressive ordered hierarchy" and that improving teaming level does not guarantee improving teaching performance.
requirements: Systems must be positioned within the framework by analysing current interaction affordances before improvement directions can be identified
constraints: The levels need not follow a progressive ordered hierarchy; higher teaming levels do not guarantee better teaching performance; educational contexts are fuzzy and require context-sensitive teaming rather than aiming for synergy in every interaction
target_learners: teachers using AI tools in educational contexts
target_learning_goals: teacher competence development through AI interaction
design of pedagogically aligned GenAI systems
examples: The chapter illustrates each level with a teacher support application example, such as a teacher requesting AI to translate text (transactional) and iterative PCA co-design with simulated students (praxical)
key_sources: Mutlu Cukurova, Wannapon Suraworachet, Qi Zhou, and Sahan Bulathwela. (2025). Towards Synergistic Teacher-AI Interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19580

article_title: Towards Synergistic Teacher-AI Interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Mutlu Cukurova, Wannapon Suraworachet, Qi Zhou, and Sahan Bulathwela. (2025). Towards Synergistic Teacher-AI Interactions with Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19580
title: Replacement, complementarity and augmentation as three levels of AI integration and their competence impacts
description: The chapter draws on Cukurova's three levels of AI integration along the automation-control spectrum. It states: "Replacement refers to a situation where AI systems independently operate teaching tasks without, or with minimal, teacher oversight (high AI automation with low teacher control)." Complementarity involves AI enhancing teacher capabilities with active teacher control, aiming to maintain or improve human competence, while augmentation seeks superior performance through interwoven interactions improving both agents. The chapter notes this conceptualisation does not clarify how interactions unfold at a granular level.
requirements: Understanding which integration level applies requires analysing the degree of AI automation versus teacher control in a given system
constraints: The framework does not clarify how interactions unfold at a granular level, offering limited guidance on how teacher-AI interactions should be productively designed
target_learners: teachers
educational system designers
target_learning_goals: protecting and developing teacher competence under AI integration
examples: The chapter uses this spectrum to frame concerns that replacement can lead human competence to flatten or decline even when task performance improves

article_title: Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models
citation: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473
title: Goal-by-Environment framework for classifying simulated student systems
description: The article proposes organizing the simulated-student design space along two dimensions: behavioral goals (performance, learning, human aspects) and environment (subject domain, learner population, interaction modality). Its purpose is comparability: "two systems can both be called “simulated students” yet be incommensurate", so making the dimensions explicit prevents overclaiming and aligns evaluation with the fidelity notion actually claimed for a given setting.
requirements: A system must declare which behavioral goal it targets and in which environment it is deployed for its evaluation to be interpretable
constraints: Simulators built for different goals and environments are not directly comparable to one another
target_learners: Researchers and developers of LLM-based educational simulation systems
target_learning_goals: Educational validity and comparability of simulated-learner evaluations
examples: Table 1 maps the four applied contexts (teacher training, social learning, data generation, content evaluation) onto behavioral goals and environmental considerations

article_title: Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models
citation: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473
title: Epistemic State Specification (ESS) with five levels E0–E4
description: ESS is a required system declaration stating what the simulated learner can access at a given moment, how errors are generated, and whether and how the state changes over time. The article operationalizes it as "a lightweight reporting label with five levels", from E0 (unspecified) through E1 static bounded, E2 curriculum-indexed, and E3 misconception-structured, to E4 calibrated or learned against human interaction data. It is intended to prevent overclaiming and enable cross-system comparison.
requirements: Each simulated-student system must explicitly declare its epistemic state specification as a cross-cutting reporting artifact
constraints: The authors note real-world model behaviors often exhibit fluctuating or indeterminate knowledge boundaries, which the E0–E4 taxonomy idealizes for analytical clarity
target_learners: Researchers building and evaluating LLM-based student simulators
target_learning_goals: Falsifiable, auditable claims about simulated learner competence and learning dynamics
examples: Appendix B provides illustrative examples of several ESS levels applied to named systems
key_sources: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473

article_title: Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models
citation: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473
title: Evaluate simulated students on goal-aligned fidelity rather than surface realism
description: The article recommends that evaluation prioritize whether simulated behavior matches the simulator's declared behavioral goal and environment, not fluency or generic humanness. "Evaluation should prioritize goal-aligned fidelity rather than surface realism", because fluent dialogue can mask implausible learning dynamics, and simulators built for different purposes require fundamentally different success criteria. Metrics should be derived from the goal: error distributions for performance settings, trajectory metrics for learning settings, interactional metrics for human-aspects settings.
requirements: Metrics must be derived from the simulator's behavioral goal and deployment environment; learning-oriented settings require trajectory metrics such as gradual improvement and sensitivity to feedback
constraints: The fidelity-evaluation gap arises when fluent dialogue and generic humanness scores are taken as evidence of educational validity
target_learners: Researchers and evaluators of simulated student systems
target_learning_goals: Valid, non-overclaimed evaluation of simulated learner fidelity
examples: The article specifies that performance and data-generation settings call for controlled error distributions and resistance to drifting into expert reasoning
key_sources: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473

article_title: Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models
citation: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473
title: Pair LLMs with explicit learner-state representations and transition rules for longitudinal simulation
description: For modeling learning trajectories, the article recommends hybrid architectures that pair an LLM with an explicit learner-state representation and a defined transition rule, such as knowledge tracing, proficiency variables, misconception graphs, or cognitive models. It argues that "Longitudinal simulation benefits from explicit learning mechanisms rather than context-window prompting alone", because prompt-only approaches yield abrupt novice-to-expert jumps and unstable competence across turns. This makes trajectories interpretable and calibratable and failures diagnosable.
requirements: An explicit learner-state representation and a defined transition rule paired with the LLM, so that learning trajectories are interpretable and calibratable
constraints: Prompt-only approaches often yield unrealistic dynamics, including abrupt novice-to-expert jumps, unstable competence across turns, and brittle dependence on phrasing
target_learners: Developers of LLM-based simulated students for longitudinal learning simulation
target_learning_goals: Valid modeling of learning trajectories and sensitivity to instructional interventions
examples: The article names knowledge tracing, proficiency variables, misconception graphs, and cognitive models as candidate explicit learner-state representations with defined transition rules
key_sources: Zhihao Yuan, Yunze Xiao, Ming Li, Weihao Xuan, Richard Tong, Mona Diab, Tom Mitchell. (2026). Towards Valid Student Simulation with Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05473

article_title: Computer Science Achievement and Writing Skills Predict Vibe Coding Proficiency
citation: Sverrir Thorgeirsson, Theo B. Weidmann, and Zhendong Su. 2026. Computer Science Achievement and Writing Skills Predict Vibe Coding Proficiency. Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791666
title: Expert-vetted assessment suite of GUI-oriented vibe-coding tasks with scoring criteria
description: A curated set of natural-language programming tasks for measuring GUI-oriented vibe-coding proficiency, produced via a two-stage Delphi-style consensus process with eight subject-matter experts from four countries. The article states it offers "an expert-designed set of natural-language programming tasks produced via a structured consensus process with eight subject-matter experts", accompanied by clear scoring criteria and predefined rubrics, intended to support replication, cross-cohort comparison, and possibly instructional use. Tasks were rated on interdisciplinarity, authenticity, challenge, purpose clarity, and culture fairness, with selected tasks reaching median ratings of at least 4.
requirements: Tasks must meet the panel's seven criteria, including that the topic "should resonate beyond computer science, engaging at least one other domain" and be implementable end-to-end in roughly 10–15 minutes of iterative prompting.
constraints: The suite targets "pure" or no-code vibe coding and captures only a limited subset of more algorithmic-centric vibe coding.
target_learners: tertiary-level students who have completed an introductory computer-science course
target_learning_goals: vibe-coding proficiency: iteratively specifying, refining, and debugging program behavior through text prompts and observed behavior alone
examples: Selected tasks included an exam scheduler, a meal planner, and a course registration platform; a third, deliberately decontextualized toy application was added to stress expressive specification without LLM-helpful task labels.
key_sources: Sverrir Thorgeirsson, Theo B. Weidmann, and Zhendong Su. 2026. Computer Science Achievement and Writing Skills Predict Vibe Coding Proficiency. Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791666

title: Purpose-built no-code vibe-coding research platform for controlled experimentation
description: A custom web platform built for controlled study of LLM-native software creation. Unlike commercial tools, "our own platform deliberately conceals the code entirely, consistent with the original definition of vibe coding", retaining a chat window on the left and app preview on the right, with rollback, a blurred live stream of model output, task descriptions, and a timer. It was informed by a survey of Replit, Cursor, Lovable, and Bolt, runs on Claude Sonnet 4 with a diff-based update mechanism, and logs feature exploration of sample applications to support reproducible, privacy-compliant evaluation.
requirements: The integrated AI model must not retain participant inputs or train on participants' prompts, per the ethics committee's data-protection requirements.
constraints: Exposing source code is intentionally avoided, as it would introduce an additional interaction mode and risk confounding the pure vibe-coding construct.
target_learners: tertiary-level students in controlled laboratory studies
target_learning_goals: measuring proficiency in iterative, behavior-guided natural-language programming
examples: The authors built the sample applications with the platform itself and instrumented them to track and display whether participants had tried all features before submission.

description: Because both written communication and CS achievement independently predict vibe-coding performance, the article argues its results can guide when educators and tool builders should emphasize prompt-writing versus CS fundamentals. The authors state that "The results have implications for both tool design and curriculum design (e.g., where to emphasize writing versus CS fundamentals)", for example in designing systems that teach users to write better prompts. The principle treats the two predictors as complementary levers rather than substitutes, with CS achievement carrying more unique variance in a joint model.

article_title: TeachingCoach: A Fine-Tuned Scaffolding Chatbot for Instructional Guidance to Instructors
citation: Isabel Molnar, Peiyu Li, Si Chen, Sugana Chawla, James Lang, Ronald Metoyer, Ting Hua, Nitesh V. Chawla. (2026). TeachingCoach: A Fine-Tuned Scaffolding Chatbot for Instructional Guidance to Instructors. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18189
title: TeachingCoach data-centric pipeline: rule extraction, synthetic dialogue generation, expert filtering, and fine-tuning
description: TeachingCoach is built through a pipeline in which experts extract pedagogical rules from authoritative education resources, GPT-4o generates teacher profiles, teaching challenges, and multi-turn synthetic dialogues, human experts filter the dialogues, and the curated data fine-tune a LLaMA-2-13B-Chat model. The article states that "experts extract 36 core instructional rules and encode them as structured system prompts," anchoring conversations in evidence-based practices. Dialogues progress through clarifying the challenge, exploring strategies, planning next steps, and reflecting.
requirements: Access to authoritative education resources from which experts extract and encode instructional rules as structured system prompts
Human expert review to remove conversations that are inconsistent, repetitive, or pedagogically unsound
constraints: The evaluation focused on instructors' perceptions and did not directly assess student learning outcomes
target_learners: Higher education instructors
Teaching assistants and instructional staff
target_learning_goals: Instructional problem identification, diagnosis, and strategy development
Reflective teaching practice
examples: Each conversation starts from a validated teaching dilemma violating one of the 36 practices, paired with a synthetic instructor profile, and unfolds over 20-30 turns mirroring teaching-center consultations

Each dialogue includes a system message with phase-keyed teaching rules, a user message with profile and challenge, and assistant messages that first predict a step descriptor and then generate the response.

Expert filtering for quality before fine-tuning

article_title: Trust and Reliance on AI in Education: AI Literacy and Need for Cognition as Moderators
citation: Griffin Pitts, Neha Rani, and Weedguet Mildort. (2026). Trust and Reliance on AI in Education: AI Literacy and Need for Cognition as Moderators. Preprint, accepted to AIED 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01114
title: Human–AI reliance framework distinguishing appropriate reliance, overreliance, and underreliance
description: The article adopts a human–AI reliance framework, following prior conceptualizations, that distinguishes three modes of reliance on AI output. In its words, "Appropriate reliance occurs when students accept correct AI recommendations and reject incorrect ones, demonstrating calibrated trust and critical evaluation." Overreliance occurs when students accept flawed AI-generated guidance without sufficient verification, while underreliance occurs when students dismiss accurate and potentially helpful AI support. The framework structures the study's behavioral measures and its interpretation of the trust–reliance findings.
requirements: A task context in which AI recommendations can be classified as correct or incorrect so that accept/reject decisions can be scored against recommendation correctness
constraints: The article notes its operationalization collapses different response strategies, such as careful checking, prior knowledge, or superficial cues, into a single score
target_learners: undergraduate students in computing-related courses
target_learning_goals: calibrated reliance on AI assistance during problem-solving
critical evaluation of AI-generated recommendations
examples: The study coded each problem-level decision as accepted or rejected relative to recommendation correctness and aggregated these into appropriate reliance, overreliance, and underreliance proportions
