article_title: MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator
citation: Rares-Alexandru Roșcan, Gabriel Petre, Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Angela-Liliana Dumitran. (2026). MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08947
title: MuTSE: an interactive human-in-the-loop web application for evaluating LLM-generated text simplifications
description: MuTSE is a web application that supports concurrent execution of P×M prompt-model permutations for text simplification, generating a comparison matrix in real time. It integrates a tiered semantic alignment engine with a linearity bias heuristic (λ), readability metrics (e.g., Flesch-Kincaid), and a customizable manual annotation system. The article states it is "designed to streamline the evaluation of LLM-generated text simplifications across arbitrary CEFR proficiency targets," serving educators selecting texts and NLP researchers building annotated datasets.
requirements: Cloud-based serverless LLM access (e.g., Together AI) or local models, plus a Python/FastAPI backend and Vue.js 3 frontend
constraints: Relies on a local JSON-based persistence layer that does not scale for concurrent multi-user deployments in large laboratory settings
Users face initial deployment friction regarding environment configuration (e.g., Python, Node.js dependencies)
target_learners: Language learners at CEFR proficiency targets such as A2 and B1
target_learning_goals: Matching text complexity to learner proficiency through text simplification
examples: The platform is pre-loaded with a curated set of 5 pre-defined prompts for standard language proficiency objectives (e.g., A2, B1)
Users can dynamically add new models by inputting the model's official string identifier without altering the codebase
key_sources: Rares-Alexandru Roșcan, Gabriel Petre, Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Angela-Liliana Dumitran. (2026). MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08947

article_title: MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator
citation: Rares-Alexandru Roșcan, Gabriel Petre, Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Angela-Liliana Dumitran. (2026). MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08947
title: Tiered semantic alignment engine with hierarchical embedding fallback and linearity bias heuristic
description: MuTSE's Semantic Alignment Engine visually maps original sentences to their simplified counterparts using a three-tier cascade: a 384-dimensional multilingual transformer embedding (paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2), a hybrid TF-IDF fallback with word- and character-level n-grams, and a tertiary positional fallback. A linearity factor λ penalizes positionally distant alignments via Score(i,j) = CosineSim − |Pos_rel(i) − Pos_rel(j)| × λ, adjustable in real time between 0 and 2 with a default of 0.5. The article describes the linearity bias as "a structural regularizer, effectively offsetting the reduced discriminative capacity inherent to heavily compressed embedding models."
requirements: Sentence embeddings from the multilingual model, with TF-IDF and positional fallbacks for resilience and hardware agnosticism
constraints: The λ default of 0.5 is user-adjustable between 0 and 2; the article notes MT evaluation would require recalibrating λ because cross-lingual syntactic restructuring may not adhere to monotonic sentence order
target_learners: Educators and applied linguists evaluating simplified texts
target_learning_goals: Qualitative evaluation of text simplification for educational purposes
examples: Fig. 2 contrasts pure semantic matching (λ = 0.00) showing scattered, positionally distant alignments with strict positional penalty (λ = 2.00) resolving false positives and enforcing monotonic alignment
key_sources: Rares-Alexandru Roșcan, Gabriel Petre, Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Angela-Liliana Dumitran. (2026). MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08947

article_title: MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator
citation: Rares-Alexandru Roșcan, Gabriel Petre, Adrian-Marius Dumitran, Angela-Liliana Dumitran. (2026). MuTSE: A Human-in-the-Loop Multi-use Text Simplification Evaluator. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.08947
title: Evaluation-agnostic annotation framework with user-defined dimensions, arbitrary rating scales, and weighted aggregation
description: MuTSE operates as an evaluation-agnostic framework with zero predefined metrics: evaluators build custom assessment criteria from scratch in the Settings module, define arbitrary numerical rating scales from binary (1-to-2) up to continuous 100-point sliders, and assign relative impact weights from 0.1 to 10.0. The system normalizes and aggregates manual inputs to compute a weighted overall performance percentage for each generated column. The article motivates this by noting "a pervasive lack of standardization and extreme diversity in evaluation methodologies and terminology across the field."
requirements: Evaluators must define their own dimensions, scales, and weights through the Settings module before annotation
constraints: The article cites debate over rating scales, noting discrete Likert scales' application frequently deviates from best practices and researchers advocate continuous scales
target_learners: Educators and applied linguists assessing simplified texts
target_learning_goals: Qualitative scoring of simplification quality on dimensions such as fluency and meaning preservation
examples: The interface embeds the exact cosine-similarity alignment score inline with each generated sentence to accelerate detection of unwanted LLM conversational artifacts or unprompted semantic hallucinations

article_title: Mathematics Teachers’ Interactions with a Multi-Agent System for Personalized Problem Generation
citation: Walkington, C., Beauchamp, T., Ikram, F., Koçyiğit Gürbüz, M., Xia, F., Lee, M., Lan, A. (2025). Mathematics Teachers’ Interactions with a Multi-Agent System for Personalized Problem Generation.
title: Multi-agent teacher-in-the-loop architecture for context personalization
description: The article introduces a multi-agent, teacher-in-the-loop architecture for context personalization in which a teacher enters a base problem and desired topic, an LLM generates the problem, and then four AI agents evaluate it using criteria each specializes in: mathematical accuracy, authenticity, readability, and realism. Each agent has a specified role and prompt and returns a binary pass/fail decision. Failed cases trigger a refinement agent that revises the problem, iterating until all evaluations pass or a maximum of five refinement steps is reached. After refinement, teachers can further author the problem before submitting it.
requirements: A teacher provides a base problem and a topic, and can choose whether to retain or modify the original numerical values
constraints: The process iterates until all agent evaluations pass or a maximum number of refinement steps is reached (five in this study)
target_learners: Middle school mathematics students (7th grade)
target_learning_goals: Personalized mathematics word problems aligned to student interests
examples: Eight middle school mathematics teachers created 212 problems in ASSISTments using the system and assigned these problems to their students

It is hosted on an EC2 instance and designed to integrate with ASSISTments, an online homework system. citation: Walkington, C., Beauchamp, T., Ikram, F., Koçyiğit Gürbüz, M., Xia, F., Lee, M., Lan, A. (2025). Mathematics Teachers’ Interactions with a Multi-Agent System for Personalized Problem Generation.
title: Four specialized evaluation agents for LLM-generated problems
description: The system employs four agents that each evaluate a different dimension of generated problems: an Authenticity agent evaluating whether the context is age-appropriate and likely to be relatable for middle school learners; a Realism agent evaluating whether quantities, units, and contextual details are plausible for the chosen topic; a Reading-level agent evaluating whether vocabulary and sentence complexity match the intended reading level; and a Hallucination agent evaluating whether the problem is mathematically consistent with the original. Each agent returns a binary pass/fail decision, and failed cases return identified issues that are combined and provided to a refinement agent.

article_title: Teacher-Authored Prompts for Configuring Student-AI Dialogue: K-12 Classroom Implementation
citation: Alex Liu, Min Sun, Lief Esbenshade, Victor Tian, Zachary Zhang, and Kevin He. (2026). Teacher-Authored Prompts for Configuring StudentAI Dialogue: K12 Classroom Implementation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16738
title: TASD: teacher-authored prompt layers as orchestration levers for configuring student-AI dialogue
description: TASD (Colleague AI Classroom Teaching Aide) frames student-AI interaction as a configurable classroom routine rather than an autonomous tutor. It uses a three-layer structure: a foundational LLM, a researcher-designed system-level prompt, and a top layer of teacher-authored prompts encoding local goals, plus a student-facing opening instruction. The article treats teacher prompts as "interaction design artifacts" that specify what students work on, how the AI structures participation, and what boundaries preserve responsible use, positioning teacher-authored prompt layers as levers translating pedagogical intent into structured dialogue.
requirements: Teachers must author both an AI-facing shared prompting layer and a student-facing opening instruction to launch the activity
constraints: The article notes the need for additional supports to reliably sustain higher-order reasoning during enactment, given the persistent DOK under-targeting gap
target_learners: K-12 middle school (grades 6–8) and high school (grades 9–12) students across mathematics, science, ELA, social studies, world languages, and CTE
target_learning_goals: Task-aligned classroom discussion
higher-order thinking and cognitive demand realization
responsible AI use
examples: In the Spring 2025 pilot, 16 teachers implemented 77 TASD activities generating 1,479 student-AI conversations with 878 unique students

citation: Alex Liu, Min Sun, Lief Esbenshade, Victor Tian, Zachary Zhang, and Kevin He. (2026). Teacher-Authored Prompts for Configuring StudentAI Dialogue: K12 Classroom Implementation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16738
title: Recurring teacher authoring schema for encoding instructional intent in AI prompts (role, discourse moves, constraints, evidence demands, finish line)
description: Across pilot configurations the authors observed a recurring schema of five schema elements for encoding instructional intent in teacher prompting layers: AI role, discourse moves, constraints, evidence and rigor demands, and finish line. Each element functions as a pre-specification that makes progress legible and intervention points predictable across many simultaneous conversations. The article reports that "we observed a recurring schema for encoding instructional intent that maps directly onto our prompt-coding dimensions and subsequent conversation outcomes," illustrated in Table 1 with paraphrased examples such as "Act as a coach; do not give final answers."

constraints: The article notes most teachers used scaffolding sparingly, which may indicate unfamiliarity with AI-powered tools leading to underutilization of available scaffolding mechanisms

managing concurrent AI conversations
scaffolding responsible use

article_title: Temporal Smoothness Doubly Robust Learning for Debiased Knowledge Tracing
citation: Peilin Zhan, Wei Chen, Weilin Chen, Shuyi Pan, Ruichu Cai. (2026). Temporal Smoothness Doubly Robust Learning for Debiased Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05958
title: Temporal Smoothness Doubly Robust (TSDR) framework for debiased knowledge tracing
description: TSDR is a model-agnostic debiasing framework for knowledge tracing that integrates a doubly robust estimator — combining Inverse Propensity Weighting with error imputation — with a temporal smoothness regularizer on the imputation model's latent trajectory. The article states that "TSDR jointly optimizes the KT predictor and the imputation model with a smoothness regularizer, effectively reducing variance while preserving the unbiasedness guarantee of DR." It treats each time step's knowledge state as a temporal "user" and co-optimizes propensity, imputation, and KT models via an alternating strategy. The smoothness constraint is motivated by the Power Law of Practice, characterizing skill acquisition as a smooth power-function trajectory.
requirements: A propensity model and an error imputation model trained jointly with the KT backbone via the alternating procedure of Algorithm 1
A smoothness coefficient lambda controlling the strength of the temporal smoothness regularization
constraints: The joint optimization of auxiliary modules incurs additional training overhead, though the article states this cost is confined to the offline phase and does not compromise online inference efficiency
target_learners: students interacting with intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning systems
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of students' dynamic knowledge states for predicting future question mastery
examples: Applied as a plug-and-play module to six KT backbones (DKT, AKT, simpleKT, FoLiBiKT, SparseKT, DisKT) on nine real-world benchmark datasets
key_sources: Peilin Zhan, Wei Chen, Weilin Chen, Shuyi Pan, Ruichu Cai. (2026). Temporal Smoothness Doubly Robust Learning for Debiased Knowledge Tracing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05958

article_title: The University AI Didn''t Replace: Rethinking Universities in the AI Era
citation: Binkowski, K. P., & Hopkins, A. (2026). The University AI Didn't Replace: Rethinking Universities in the AI Era. Macquarie University. https://www.mq.edu.au/
title: Four-level framework of institutional AI adoption in universities, from defensive containment to AI-embedded transformation
description: The article names and substantively describes a four-level framework of institutional response to generative AI: "ranging from defensive restriction to full integration of AI into educational systems, with many institutions presently operating around Level 0 or Level 1". Level 0 treats AI as an integrity threat and restricts it; Level 1 is informal, individual-educator experimentation without institutional recognition; Level 2 is strategic integration into policy and curriculum; Level 3 embeds AI in core infrastructure with learning reorganised around AI-supported reasoning. A 2x2 matrix (Figure 1) maps levels by degree of AI integration and institutional recognition.
requirements: Institutional recognition and structural alignment, including policies, workload models, and promotion frameworks, to move beyond Level 1
constraints: The framework is a descriptive summary of institutional response stages, not a tested model; the authors note it is not completely clear whether exemplar institutions are genuinely at the strategic adoption stage
target_learners: university students in AI-rich higher education environments
target_learning_goals: AI-supported reasoning, judgment, and responsible AI use
examples: The paper positions Macquarie University's case studies as illustrating movement from Level 1 informal innovation toward Level 2 strategic integration
key_sources: Binkowski, K. P., & Hopkins, A. (2026). The University AI Didn't Replace: Rethinking Universities in the AI Era. Macquarie University. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07056

article_title: The University AI Didn''t Replace: Rethinking Universities in the AI Era
citation: Binkowski, K. P., & Hopkins, A. (2026). The University AI Didn't Replace: Rethinking Universities in the AI Era. Macquarie University. https://www.mq.edu.au/
title: Three emerging assessment-redesign approaches for AI-rich environments: AI-supported independent work, process-oriented reflective assessment, and observed authentic performance
description: Across its case studies the article identifies "three emerging approaches: AI-supported independent work, process-oriented and reflective assessment, and observed or authentic performance-based tasks". In the first, AI use is explicitly permitted but bounded by student accountability for interpretation and synthesis; in the second, learning is demonstrated through development over time with portfolios, reflection, and viva voce; in the third, understanding is evaluated through live performance and questioning. The pattern is reusable at unit level for assessment design where AI is available to students.
requirements: Assessment designs that foreground reasoning, justification, and process over product
constraints: The article states such redesign is significantly more complex and time-intensive than traditional assessment
target_learners: undergraduate university students across disciplines
target_learning_goals: disciplinary reasoning, metacognition, justification of thinking in real time
examples: The Protein Portfolio in BMOL2201/6201 with AI supporting feedback and referencing; weekly seminar tasks with reflection in APPL8241; Shark Tank pitches with questioning in MKTG1001

article_title: Understanding Student Effort Using Response-Time Propensities During Problem Solving
citation: Conrad Borchers, Lijin Zhang, Kexin Yang, Tomohiro Nagashima, and Benjamin W. Domingue. 2026. Understanding Student Effort Using Response-Time Propensities During Problem Solving. Proceedings of the Thirteenth ACM Conference on Learning @ Scale (L@S '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3774398.3811624
title: Response-time propensities: a difficulty-adjusted, trait-like measure of typical step-level pacing
description: Response-time propensities are a log-derived measure of students' typical step-to-step response timing in intelligent tutoring systems, estimated as student-level random intercepts from a hierarchical model of log-transformed step latencies with random effects for students and skills. The article defines them as "difficulty- and context-adjusted, trait-like differences in students' typical response timing during tutoring", where trait-like captures typical pacing while within-person speed can still vary across steps. They are intended as a process construct complementing correctness-based knowledge estimates, capturing how students distribute time across steps.
requirements: Step-level log data with timestamps, problem and step identifiers, knowledge components, and outcome codes, as logged by the tutoring systems
constraints: The article states response time remains an inherently ambiguous behavioral trace; longer delays may reflect classroom interruptions, off-task behavior, or reading time not distinguishable in log data alone
Results are bounded by step-based mathematics tutors in U.S. classrooms with short interaction cycles and limited text per step
target_learners: middle- and high-school mathematics students using step-based intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: effort regulation and persistence during multi-step algebra problem solving
examples: Student and skill random intercepts were estimated from log-transformed step-to-step response times across eight DataShop datasets collected between 2020 and 2023

article_title: When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals?
citation: Zhengxu Li, Junling Wang, and April Yi Wang. (2026). When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals? arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10672
title: Control timing as a design dimension for AI-assisted visual authoring: pre-, mid-, and post-generation control
description: The article introduces "control timing" as a key design dimension in AI-assisted visual authoring, operationalized through three interaction paradigms that differ in when teachers intervene relative to AI output. Pre-generation control means users "specify intent solely through natural language prompts before generation"; mid-generation control means users "inspect and confirm an explicit layout structure before the system completes generation"; post-generation control means users "directly modify AI-generated visuals after generation through object-level edits". The framework holds task content constant and varies only the timing of human control.
requirements: The paradigms require a multi-stage generation pipeline with distinct points (intent specification, intermediate planning, localized refinement) at which control can be exercised.
constraints: The article instantiates and evaluates the three paradigms only for primary mathematics word problems in a single-session study.
target_learners: primary mathematics teachers (Grades 1–6)
target_learning_goals: creating pedagogically correct instructional visuals for arithmetic word problems
examples: A web-based prototype implemented all three paradigms for the same math word problems, using GPT-5 for text understanding and GPT-image-1.5 for image generation, with Math2Visual powering the post-gen pipeline.
key_sources: Zhengxu Li, Junling Wang, and April Yi Wang. (2026). When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals? arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10672

article_title: When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals?
citation: Zhengxu Li, Junling Wang, and April Yi Wang. (2026). When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals? arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10672
title: In correctness-sensitive educational domains, make correctness auditable: support verifiable, localized correction rather than relying on output quality alone
description: The article argues that in correctness-sensitive domains such as mathematics education, "output quality alone is an insufficient success criterion" and that "Auditability emerges as a foundational design requirement". Teachers evaluated visuals by representational fidelity — whether structure preserved intended mathematical relationships and quantities — and valued post-generation control because it let them inspect, verify, and enforce correctness without inferring hidden system behavior. Systems should make correctness visible and support bounded, local correction that does not cause unintended changes elsewhere.
requirements: Teachers must be able to directly inspect and verify correctness-critical details of generated visuals without needing to infer hidden system behavior.
constraints: The article notes verification in the study relied largely on manual inspection, placing sustained cognitive demands on teachers, and recommends future constraint-aware generation and automatic consistency checks.
target_learners: primary mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: ensuring instructional visuals faithfully represent quantities, relations, and groupings
examples: In the study, post-gen visuals were editable SVG objects whose local edits were deterministic and immediately visible, letting teachers correct single objects without global side effects.
key_sources: Zhengxu Li, Junling Wang, and April Yi Wang. (2026). When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals? arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10672

Pre-gen uses a conversational interface routing classified intents; mid-gen generates an editable JSON layout of bounding boxes before rendering; post-gen uses Math2Visual to render problems as editable SVG elements on a canvas. The prototype is released at https://github.com/ViktorLee426/Visual4Math with supplementary materials on OSF.

article_title: What Makes Words Hard? Sakura at BEA 2026 Shared Task on Vocabulary Difficulty Prediction
citation: Adam Nohejl, Xuanxin Wu, Yusuke Ide, Maria Angelica Riera Machin, Yi-Ning Chang, Hitomi Yanaka. (2026). Sakura at BEA 2026 Shared Task 1: What Makes Vocabulary Difficult? https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14257
title: Soft-target cross-entropy fine-tuning with probability-weighted inference for continuous value prediction
description: A fine-tuning technique for LLMs and MLMs to predict continuous values. The model is prompted to predict values on a discrete integer scale, and the continuous target is expressed as a probability-weighted sum of its two nearest scale points, used as the soft target in cross-entropy loss. At inference, the output is a token probability-weighted mean. The article states the method "sidesteps this apparent misalignment between text generation and the prediction of continuous values." It requires a single token to be predicted, so it works for both LLMs and MLMs via masked token prediction.
requirements: A pre-trained LLM or MLM with a token vocabulary and a discrete integer scale whose points bracket the continuous targets
A single-token prediction setup, with prompts for LLMs or masked token prediction for MLMs
constraints: Tested only on this shared task's KVL data; the article states its suitability for other tasks and settings is yet to be investigated, and on smaller or noisier data its impact may be less pronounced
target_learners: L1 Chinese, German, and Spanish learners of English
target_learning_goals: Predicting the production difficulty of English vocabulary test items
examples: Used to fine-tune GLM-4, Qwen2.5, and Ministral-3 LLMs and mmBERT and XLM-RoBERTa MLMs for the BEA 2026 shared task, achieving the top open-track result
key_sources: Adam Nohejl, Xuanxin Wu, Yusuke Ide, Maria Angelica Riera Machin, Yi-Ning Chang, Hitomi Yanaka. (2026). Sakura at BEA 2026 Shared Task 1: What Makes Vocabulary Difficult? https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14257

title: British Council Knowledge-based Vocabulary Lists (KVL) difficulty dataset
description: A large dataset of vocabulary difficulty scores for L1 Chinese, German, and Spanish learners of English, spanning thousands of vocabulary test items from the British Council's Knowledge-based Vocabulary Lists. Each test item consists of an equivalent L1 word, an L1 context, and a clue giving the first letter of the English word and its length in letters, targeting productive knowledge. Difficulty scores are intercept values of a generalized linear mixed model, i.e., the log-odds of a learner responding correctly, typically ranging from -5 to +5 with higher values easier.
requirements: Test items pairing an L1 word and context with a first-letter and length clue for the English word
Learner response data used to fit GLMM intercepts as difficulty scores
constraints: The article reports that difficulty scores are often affected by spelling difficulty and the construction of the test items in addition to genuine production difficulty, which could affect the utility of the dataset for other uses such as creating reading materials matched to the learner's level
target_learners: L1 Chinese, German, and Spanish learners of English
target_learning_goals: Written production of English vocabulary

title: Design hybrid-control orchestration tools by starting with structured teacher guidance and progressively increasing student autonomy as activities unfold.
description: The article recommends hybrid-control designs for analytic-based orchestration tools in pairing contexts: "We recommend ensuring structured teacher guidance in the beginning, while progressively increasing student autonomy over time as activities unfold." This follows from findings that neither teachers nor students favored full student control, and that preferences varied across the pairing stages. The principle guides designers to scaffold authority early and open more student decision space as collaboration becomes established.

article_title: The Tutoring Effectiveness Index: Predicting LLM Math Tutor Quality from Four Conversation Signals
citation: Shim Jaechang and Unggi Lee. 2026. The Tutoring Effectiveness Index: Predicting LLM Math Tutor Quality from Four Conversation Signals. In Proceedings of The 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM '26). https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30666
title: Tutoring Effectiveness Index (TEI): a training-free, judge-free four-signal index for scoring candidate tutor responses
description: TEI is a fixed-weight linear index over four signals computed without any external model at selection time: "a Schoenfeld-Verify keyword ratio, a math-step density, an ends-question rate, and a deep-reasoning gate from the Deep-Thinking Ratio (DTR) probe". Verification and explicit math content are rewarded, ending tutor turns with questions is penalised, and the DTR gate adds a small bonus. Weights (α, β, γ, δ) = (1.0, 0.75, 1.0, 0.5) are fixed a priori from theory to preserve the training-free, judge-free property.
requirements: Runs on a frozen reasoning LLM that exposes explicit thinking traces, enabling per-token DTR computation via forward hooks
constraints: The four weights are fixed a priori from theory; domain calibration could improve performance at the cost of re-introducing a labelled-outcome requirement
The Schoenfeld V signal is regex-derived and surface-level; a GPT-4o-mini paragraph classifier disagrees with it on more than half of paragraphs
All experiments are in mathematics, so TEI weights and signals may need re-derivation for other subjects
target_learners: students tutored by LLM math tutors (simulated GPT-4o-mini student in the evaluation)
target_learning_goals: improving math problem-solving success in multi-turn LLM tutoring dialogues
examples: TEI@8 uses 4.1× the tokens of greedy decoding (16,334 vs. 3,984) and roughly half the cost of Cons@8 (31,868)

article_title: TurtleAI: Benchmarking Multimodal Models for Visual Programming in Turtle Graphics
citation: Chao Wen, Jacqueline Staub, and Adish Singla. (2026). TURTLEAI: Benchmarking Multimodal Models for Visual Programming in Turtle Graphics. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03626
title: TURTLEAI benchmark: 823 Turtle Graphics visual programming tasks with datasets, evaluation framework, and data generation technique
description: TURTLEAI is a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on education-oriented visual programming in Turtle Graphics, comprising "(i) TURTLEAI-DS, a collection of evaluation datasets; (ii) TURTLEAI- Eval, an evaluation framework for assessing the correctness of synthesized code; and (iii) TURTLEAI-Datagen, a data generation technique". It contains 823 tasks curated from XLogoOnline tasks used by students in grades 3-6, organized into DSReal (102 real-world tasks), DSCraft (102 hand-drawn renderings), and DSSyn (619 synthetic tasks), across six task categories and three difficulty levels. TURTLEAI-Eval canonicalizes drawings to achieve invariance to translation, scale, and line width before symbolic or embedding-based comparison, with 99.1% and 98.1% agreement with human judgments respectively. The benchmark is publicly released for further research.
requirements: Tasks require generating Python code as a function draw(t) that replicates a target image and satisfies the text-based instruction
constraints: The evaluation framework's normalization step makes comparison invariant to size, translation, and line width, which the authors note may discard meaningful geometric variations essential in inverse graphics tasks

researchers evaluating vision-language models on educational visual programming

programming concepts such as loops, conditionals, and geometric transformations

article_title: Securing the Sandbox: A Rootless Containerized Framework for Process-Oriented Monitoring in Computer Graphics Education
citation: Germán Arroyo, Luis López, and Juan Carlos Torres. (2026). Securing the Sandbox: A Rootless Containerized Framework for Process-Oriented Monitoring in Computer Graphics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05929
title: VISMATIC: a secured, low-cost JupyterHub sandbox for process-oriented monitoring in Computer Graphics education
description: VISMATIC is a defense-in-depth framework pairing a JupyterHub execution environment with rootless Podman containerization, loop-device ext4 storage quotas, an Apache2 SSL reverse proxy, and Raspberry Pi hardware. It intercepts explicit HTTP API requests—file modifications, kernel executions, and terminal operations—rather than passive heartbeats, so instructors can "analyze macro-level interaction rhythms and immediately flag the sudden 'copy-paste' injections characteristic of off-platform generative AI usage." Student accounts are provisioned via CSV-based initialization with randomized credentials and animal-themed pseudonyms, keeping behavioral logs cryptographically separated from academic records.
requirements: A closed-source, server-side-only Computer Graphics library so students must remain connected to the platform to complete activities
Centralized JupyterHub orchestration with PAM-based isolated system accounts and an Apache2 reverse proxy with mandatory SSL encryption
constraints: The authors state that no system can achieve absolute security; the contribution is a defense-in-depth mitigation, not a guarantee
The approach cannot extract sub-second keystroke patterns, only macro-level interactions
target_learners: undergraduate and master's Computer Graphics students
target_learning_goals: authentic iterative programming practice
mathematical foundations of computer graphics such as geometric transformations, lighting models, and rendering pipelines
examples: Deployed on a Raspberry Pi 5 with each student session capped at 1.5 CPU cores and 0.5 GB RAM, evaluated with a pilot cohort of 19 active students

citation: Germán Arroyo, Luis López, and Juan Carlos Torres. (2026). Securing the Sandbox: A Rootless Containerized Framework for Process-Oriented Monitoring in Computer Graphics Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05929
title: Four-metric behavioral taxonomy for distinguishing authentic iterative coding from automated workflows
description: The article defines four analytical metrics derived from explicit API event logs to "differentiate authentic learning behaviors from automated or externally synthesized workflows": (a) a class rhythm heatmap of temporal interaction density, (b) cumulative platform engagement showing staircase-like growth, (c) session intensity defined as the ratio of recorded explicit actions to session duration, and (d) daily work volume aggregating events over 24-hour periods. Triangulated, these metrics anchor a behavioral profile distinguishing iterative human development—variable intensity, plateaus, diurnal rhythms—from rigid, unbroken automated patterns.

Explicit human-driven API interception instead of passive keep-alive telemetry, which fires approximately every 300 seconds regardless of human interaction
constraints: API-level event logs capture interaction patterns but not intent; the metrics cannot independently prove academic misconduct
target_learners: undergraduate and master's students in computer programming courses
target_learning_goals: monitoring authentic iterative development processes
detecting automated or AI-assisted code synthesis
examples: Applied to a pilot cohort of 19 students producing 1,880 discrete API events over approximately 57 active student-hours

article_title: TibetCPR: A Multimodal Tactile Feedback System to Enhance Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Training in High-Altitude
citation: Yibo Meng, Ruiqi Chen, Zhiming Liu, and Xiaolan Ding. (2026). TibetCPR: A Multimodal Tactile Feedback System to Enhance Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Training in High-Altitude Regions of Tibet. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07765
title: TibetCPR: a low-cost, self-guided multimodal CPR training system with electrotactile depth feedback, visual rhythm cues, and a Tibetan-language snow-lotus narrative game
description: TibetCPR is "a low-cost, self-guided CPR training system that pairs depth-driven electrotactile feedback with rhythm-driven visual cues within a Tibetan-language narrative." It comprises a wrist-worn electrotactile unit with hydrogel electrodes, a mannequin with an embedded piezoelectric pressure sensor, and a game-UI screen. A deterministic per-compression loop maps peak force to TENS/none/EMS depth signals and running rate to blue/green/red visual states, while correct compressions advance a four-stage snow-lotus blooming sequence that sustains motivation without an instructor.
requirements: Physical chest compression on the mannequin as the sole and primary control input, with all system responses driven directly by real-time compression performance
constraints: Feedback is kept salient but intermittent and boundary-locked, firing only when a compression falls outside the recommended depth range, to avoid overwhelming users during physically demanding compressions
target_learners: CPR-naive lay community members in high-altitude, resource-limited regions, spanning heterogeneous ages, occupations, and educational backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Stable regulation of chest compression depth and rhythm for bystander CPR readiness
examples: Evaluated in a randomised study with 40 lay community members aged 19–56 in the Tibet Autonomous Region, none with prior CPR training

article_title: Test-Driven, AI-Assisted Learning: Replacing Lectures with Weekly Closed-Book Tests
citation: Jin-Guo Liu, Shang-Qi Lu, Xin-Ran Shi, Long-Li Zheng, Wei Wang. (2026). Test-Driven, AI-Assisted Learning: Replacing Lectures with Weekly Closed-Book Tests. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23315
title: TDAA: high-frequency closed-book tests paired with a human-reviewed AI production harness
description: TDAA is a course-level design pattern coupling two cycles: students prepare with aligned materials and face a weekly closed-book gate, while an instructor-side AI harness drafts, reviews, and grades the materials under human approval. The paper states the pairing directly: "high-frequency tests preserve individual accountability, while AI agents make material production and marking scalable." Without the agent layer weekly testing is infeasible for one instructor; without the test gate AI-assisted preparation offers no reliable check on unaided performance.
requirements: A visible preparation path of learning sheets and aligned validation practice so the closed-book tests feel fair rather than arbitrary
A version-controlled agent workspace with human review before any AI draft reaches students
constraints: Evidence is limited to one small, proof-heavy course without a control group; transfer to large or non-proof courses is a hypothesis for future offerings, not a result
target_learners: upper-level undergraduate data-science students in a proof-heavy course
target_learning_goals: unaided problem-solving and proof-writing in theory of computation
examples: DSAA 3071 ran 13 weeks with a 30-minute closed-book test, 120-minute self-paced study block, and 20-minute discussion each week, with 30% weekly tests and 70% final exam
key_sources: Jin-Guo Liu, Shang-Qi Lu, Xin-Ran Shi, Long-Li Zheng, Wei Wang. (2026). Test-Driven, AI-Assisted Learning: Replacing Lectures with Weekly Closed-Book Tests. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.23315

article_title: A Durability and Cross-Language Transfer Benchmark for a Validated Teaching-Feedback Classification Protocol
citation: Esteban U. Vega Barajas. (2026). A Durability and Cross-Language Transfer Benchmark for a Validated Teaching-Feedback Classification Protocol. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11873
title: Reproducible balanced 45,000-comment English sentiment corpus and released build recipe
description: A released community artifact: a balanced English sentiment corpus sampled from the public RateMyProfessor research release, holding "45,000 comments across three sentiment classes with fixed splits and a fixed seed" (15,000 per class; train 31,500, development 6,750, test 6,750; mean length 231 characters). Labels derive deterministically from star ratings (positive at least 4, negative at most 2, neutral otherwise). The authors release "the build recipe, namely the script, the seed, and the split indices, so the sample is exactly reproducible, with its provenance and license stated"; raw review text is not redistributed under the source CC BY-NC-SA license.
requirements: The underlying review text remains governed by the source CC BY-NC-SA license; reconstruction via the released indices inherits its non-commercial terms
constraints: Star-derived labels are a convenience signal validated only at kappa 0.66 against human labels; corrupted structural metadata in the source means no per-institution or per-region claims
target_learners: higher-education teaching-evaluation feedback (institutional NLP use case)
target_learning_goals: classifying open-ended teaching-evaluation comments by sentiment for institutional triage and improvement
examples: Uniform per-class reservoir sampling over the full 9.54M-review file at seed 20260616, with escaped-byte decoding, dropping comments under 15 characters, and exact-duplicate removal

article_title: A Durability and Cross-Language Transfer Benchmark for a Validated Teaching-Feedback Classification Protocol
citation: Esteban U. Vega Barajas. (2026). A Durability and Cross-Language Transfer Benchmark for a Validated Teaching-Feedback Classification Protocol. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11873
title: Carry forward the documented protocol, not the model: annotation guide, reliability measurement, validation design, and auditability survive model and language change
description: The article's central design principle for institutional NLP adoption: what an institution carries forward is the documented procedure rather than any particular model. The authors argue that if a modern LLM wins on raw accuracy, "that is an expected finding, and it reinforces the claim that what an institution carries forward is the documented procedure: the annotation guide, the reliability measurement, the validation design, and the interpretability analysis." The benchmark operationalizes this by holding the protocol fixed while varying model generation and language, showing the protocol holds across all arms with "no single arm is load-bearing".
requirements: A written annotation guide, an explicit reliability measurement, stratified cross-validation for model selection, and a held-out test set untouched until final reporting
constraints: The article reports paired comparisons as descriptive only and claims no statistical significance; the Spanish ordering rests on a single stratified split with a 233-comment held-out set
target_learners: institutional staff and researchers processing open-ended teaching-evaluation feedback in higher education
target_learning_goals: building durable, auditable, reliability-checked classification procedures for teaching-feedback analysis that survive changes of model and language
examples: The benchmark slotted every newer model, from TF-IDF through frozen BETO and e5 encoders to prompted LLMs, into the same annotation guide, splits, and held-out evaluation, and none forced the auditability or cost story to collapse

article_title: A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI
citation: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518
title: Five-pillar tool-invariant framework for competent use of any computational method
description: The article organizes what a learner must know to use any computational method—pencil, calculator, library, or agentic AI—into five pillars: inputs and outputs, conceptual understanding of the method, terminology, sensemaking, and operating the tool. The author states that "competent use of any computational method, at any scale, with any tool, requires five things," and argues the pillars' content changes little across tool eras while their curricular weight shifts; under agentic AI, sensemaking becomes load-bearing. Table I maps the pillars to antecedent constructs in the computational-thinking literature, with the re-weighting offered as the new element.
requirements: The framework is offered as a structure for practitioner adaptation, not an empirically tested conclusion; the article notes the field lacks controlled studies of students learning computational physics through agentic AI.
constraints: The five pillars largely repackage constructs already in the computational-thinking literature; what the article claims as new is the re-weighting under agentic mediation, validation authority, and the assessment consequence.
target_learners: undergraduate physics students, from introductory through senior-level computational courses
target_learning_goals: competent, verifiable use of computational methods including agent-orchestrated simulation
examples: The article illustrates the pillars at two rungs: a child adding 2 + 3 and a senior directing an AI agent to build a molecular dynamics simulation.
key_sources: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518

article_title: A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI
citation: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518
title: Principle of validation authority: delegation is safe exactly where the delegator can validate outputs
description: The article introduces the principle of validation authority, grounded in a bespoke-versus-socially-validated distinction: a library routine is opaque but socially validated through published algorithms, testing, and millions of users, while an AI-generated simulation is opaque and bespoke, "an artifact with a population of one, produced by a stochastic process whose competence boundary is jagged and invisible." The author's generalization is that "delegation is safe exactly where the delegator retains the ability to validate the outputs," which redefines a computational physics course as training validation authority over physical simulations.
requirements: Courses adopting this framing must train disciplinary verification checks the user knows to demand, since a physics simulation's correctness is not observable in use.
constraints: The principle marks a boundary: anyone can delegate in domains like personal productivity apps where correctness is observable in use, but not where correctness must be established by disciplinary checks.
target_learners: undergraduate physics students directing AI agents
target_learning_goals: judgment about when delegation to computational tools is safe and how to validate outputs
examples: The article applies the principle to distinguish a trusted library FFT from a bespoke agent-generated trajectory, noting a wrong trajectory renders as beautifully as a right one.
key_sources: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518

article_title: A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI
citation: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518
title: Specify-Predict-Delegate-Verify-Interpret workflow for AI-era computational work
description: The article organizes its five pillars into a repeating workflow: "Specify → Predict → Delegate → Verify → Interpret; Iterate." Students specify the problem, inputs, outputs, and physical model; predict the result before any execution as a Fermi estimate; delegate execution to the tool; verify output against the prediction; interpret physically and iterate. The author argues a student who has committed to an expectation is testing a hypothesis when the plot appears, while one who has not is merely looking at a picture. Calibrated reliance—knowing how much verification is owed for this tool on this task—threads through the loop.
requirements: Prediction must be made before execution, without the tool, so the later verification has a committed expectation to test against.
constraints: The required verification depth scales with the tool: a calculator needs a glance, a community-validated library routine interface-level checks, a bespoke agent-generated simulation the full battery every time.
target_learners: undergraduate physics students
target_learning_goals: orchestrating AI-assisted computational work with verification and physical interpretation
examples: The article's supplementary progression walks tasks from single-digit addition to agent-orchestrated molecular dynamics, recording at each rung what the era's tool absorbs and what remains human.
key_sources: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518

article_title: A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI
citation: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518
title: Nine-check verification-and-validation repertoire (V1–V9) for classroom sensemaking
description: The article operationalizes the sensemaking pillar as a cumulative repertoire of nine checks scaled from professional verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification: units and dimensions, order of magnitude, known-answer checks, self-consistency, convergence, conservation, independence, limiting cases, and comparison with experiment. Each check enters at a particular rung of the task progression and remains required thereafter. The author emphasizes that "every check in this repertoire is physics or mathematics content, not programming content," that the checks are cumulative and cheap, and that they bound rather than close the space of undetected errors.
requirements: Checks must be enforced as course culture; the article argues their low cost is what makes them enforceable rather than aspirational policy.
constraints: The checks bound, but do not close, the space of undetected errors; stronger code verification by manufactured solutions requires contributory code expertise the course deliberately does not build, and when the agent executes the checks, each check inherits the trust problem of the system under test.
target_learners: undergraduate physics students across the computational progression
target_learning_goals: sensemaking and verification of computational outputs in physics
examples: V3 known-answer check: integrate x^2 before e^-x^2; simulate the drag-free projectile before adding drag. V7 independence distinguishes a genuinely different method (gold standard) from re-querying the agent (weakest, correlated samples).
key_sources: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518

article_title: Evaluating a Visual Query Tracer and Builder for Learning Declarative Logic Programming
citation: Julián Méndez, Lukas Gerlach, Tobias Wieland, Alex Ivliev, Markus Krötzsch, Raimund Dachselt. (2026). Evaluating a Visual Query Tracer and Builder for Learning Declarative Logic Programming. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18864
title: Nemo Explain Visualizer (nev): an interactive visual query tracer and builder for Datalog reasoning
description: Nemo Explain Visualizer (nev) is a free, open-source web-based visual explanation tool for the Nemo Datalog reasoner, described as "an interactive visual query tracer and builder for Nemo". Its interface combines a main visual trace editor, an indented tree explorer view, and a fact-tables view. It supports type 1 queries (proof traces for individual facts) and type 2 queries that take a proof-tree shape and populate it with facts, letting users add or remove rules, restrict queries, focus on a rule, and undo/redo modifications.
requirements: Runs on top of the Nemo reasoner and the Nemo Web frontend, which compute explorable explanation data (traces) on demand
constraints: The article states the tool is without specific learning features; it was designed with and for expert users for debugging and development
target_learners: university students learning declarative logic programming
expert Datalog developers
target_learning_goals: understanding rule-based reasoning and proof traces in Datalog
debugging and inspecting Datalog programs
examples: In the study, participants used nev to inspect traces, find minimal-cost paths, and modify queries to find paths of specific length on weighted graphs

article_title: Teachy Mini: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Knowledge-Based Generative Social Robot for Higher Education
citation: Stephan Vonschallen, Karim Kaufmann, Dominique Oberle, Friederike Eyssel, Theresa Schmiedel. (2026). Teachy Mini: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Knowledge-Based Generative Social Robot for Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22345
title: Knowledge-Based Design (KBD): responsible tutoring behavior in generative social robots depends on the robot's self-, user-, and context-knowledge
description: KBD is a design framework holding that responsible robot tutoring behavior depends on what knowledge the robot possesses, organized into three types. The article states the underlying assumption that "responsible robot behavior depends on the availability ofself-,user-, andcontext-knowledge". Self-knowledge covers the robot's role (default study buddy), friendliness, conscientiousness, and assertiveness; user-knowledge covers learner-specific information such as goals, motivation type, emotional state, and background, with privacy and informed consent; context-knowledge covers official learning materials, course information, educational strategies, and optionally the physical environment. The framework was derived from a qualitative interview study with university students and lecturers and operationalized in Teachy Mini.
requirements: The robot must possess the specified self-, user-, and context-knowledge for responsible behavior to manifest; the framework specifies informational prerequisites rather than abstract ethical principles.
constraints: The 'course information' requirement applies to interactions over longer periods and was not integrated in the single-session prototype; 'physical learning environment' received only mixed support due to privacy concerns.
target_learners: university students in higher education learning lecture content
target_learning_goals: responsible and effective tutoring of lecture content, including factual accuracy, transparency, personalization, and pedagogically appropriate support
examples: Teachy Mini operationalized selected KBD requirements via dynamic system prompting, retrieval-augmented generation over uploaded lecture slides, and stateful prompt orchestration with regex-detected dialogue states.
key_sources: Stephan Vonschallen, Karim Kaufmann, Dominique Oberle, Friederike Eyssel, Theresa Schmiedel. (2026). Teachy Mini: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Knowledge-Based Generative Social Robot for Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22345

article_title: Teachy Mini: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Knowledge-Based Generative Social Robot for Higher Education
citation: Stephan Vonschallen, Karim Kaufmann, Dominique Oberle, Friederike Eyssel, Theresa Schmiedel. (2026). Teachy Mini: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Knowledge-Based Generative Social Robot for Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22345
title: Teachy Mini: a knowledge-based generative social robot tutoring prototype on the Reachy Mini platform
description: Teachy Mini is a generative social robot tutoring prototype built on the open-source Reachy Mini desktop platform, supporting spoken dialogue and head/antenna social cues via the OpenAI Realtime API. The authors "usedthreemainmethodstoprovidetherobotwiththerequiredknowledge:Dynamic system prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, andstateful prompt orchestration". It personalizes through a seven-question onboarding profile, retrieves uploaded PDF lecture slides for grounded explanations, detects conversational states (frustration, confusion, requests for depth) via regex, and injects state-specific instructions such as rephrasing explanations with a concrete analogy. Implementation code is on GitHub and materials on researchbox.org (ID: #8129).
requirements: Requires an external knowledge source for RAG grounding, an onboarding conversation to build the learner profile, and predefined verbal patterns for state detection.
constraints: Designed as an experimental single-session implementation, not a fully deployable educational system; learning progress was only partly accounted for and only the study-buddy role profile was evaluated.
target_learners: university students and recent graduates in single-session tutoring interactions
target_learning_goals: learning lecture content (research methodologies) through slide-grounded explanation, Socratic questioning, and personalized scaffolding
examples: In the evaluation, KBD and control versions shared the same Reachy Mini hardware and language model, differing only in the structured KBD configuration.

article_title: Beyond Perspectives: A Trio-Ethnography of Interpretation Evolution in LLM-Supported Programming Education
citation: Jennie Ren, Jordan H. McDowell, and Kyrie Zhixuan Zhou. (2026). Beyond Perspectives: A Trio-Ethnography of Interpretation Evolution in LLM-Supported Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22463
title: Trio-ethnography as a mechanism for evolving educators' interpretations of student learning through dialogue
description: Trio-ethnography brings three participants (here two computing educators with contrasting instructional philosophies and one undergraduate student) into reflective conversation as co-inquirers. The article uses it not to compare perspectives but as a process in which "student dialogue as evidence" progressively refines educators' interpretations across three stages: initial educator dialogue, student dialogue, and educator reflective reconstruction. It positions the method as narrowing the gap between observable programming products and actual AI-supported learning processes.

Structured dialogue stages in which student narratives are treated as evidence for interpretive reconstruction
constraints: The article states reconstructed interpretations are contextually situated rather than universally representative, based on a single trio in one setting

undergraduate computer science students

instructional adaptation in the LLM era

citation: Jennie Ren, Jordan H. McDowell, and Kyrie Zhixuan Zhou. (2026). Beyond Perspectives: A Trio-Ethnography of Interpretation Evolution in LLM-Supported Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22463
title: Reposition AI in programming education from a classroom-policy issue to a teachable component of pedagogy
description: The article argues programming education should shift from regulating AI use to designing learning environments where students learn with AI. article_title: 'From Idea to Classroom in Days: Using "Vibe Coding" to Create a Programming Process Visualizer from IDE Activity Logs'
citation: Heidi Taveter and Marina Lepp. (2026). From Idea to Classroom in Days: Using “Vibe Coding” to Create a Programming Process Visualizer from IDE Activity Logs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24757
title: Thonny Log Visualizer: a teacher-facing web application that turns Thonny IDE logs into interpretable programming-process views
description: Thonny Log Visualizer is a web application that analyzes log files generated by Thonny, an IDE for Python, and produces interpretable views of students' programming processes. Per-student dashboards include an interactive activity timeline, a compact session summary, a code-size graph, a programming-process replay with an event feed, a paste-events view, and integrity-related indicators; cohort-level views include a sortable 'All people' table and comparison views for pair typing patterns and first-run progress. Teachers can upload a single log, a ZIP archive, or a folder, and the system parses all logs, groups them by student, and supports student-by-student navigation.
requirements: Students must complete mandatory tasks in Thonny and submit the corresponding log files, since the visualizer depends on the course requirement that students complete the mandatory tasks in Thonny and submit the corresponding log files
constraints: The interpretable views are intended to support follow-up discussion and manual review, rather than to serve as automated judgments
target_learners: introductory programming course students
target_learning_goals: programming process awareness for teacher decision-making
formative feedback
academic-integrity clarification
examples: Used in a February 2026 pilot in an introductory programming course with 160 participants, where five teachers reviewed logs using both single-student and cohort workflows

article_title: 'From Idea to Classroom in Days: Using "Vibe Coding" to Create a Programming Process Visualizer from IDE Activity Logs'
citation: Heidi Taveter and Marina Lepp. (2026). From Idea to Classroom in Days: Using “Vibe Coding” to Create a Programming Process Visualizer from IDE Activity Logs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24757
title: Four design goals for teacher-facing programming-process visualization: visibility, workflow support, formative feedback, and non-automated integrity clarification
description: The article organizes the tool's design around four stated goals: DG1 making students' programming processes visible to teachers through interpretable views; DG2 supporting teacher decision-making through workflows for both quick individual inspection and efficient review of larger log sets; DG3 supporting process-informed formative feedback; and DG4 supporting clarification of academic-integrity concerns without automating judgment. For DG3, the tool should help teachers "identify situations in which students may need support, such as repeated run-error cycles with limited progress, a late start of the program execution, or unusually long periods of inactivity." The framework translates prior programming-process research into teacher-facing views.
requirements: Underlying IDE activity logs must be available, since the views summarize signals such as runs, errors, debugs, pauses, and copy-paste behavior captured in Thonny logs
constraints: Integrity-related indicators are intended as warning signals rather than automated determinations, with interpretation left to teachers
target_learners: teachers of large introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: teacher triage and case prioritization
timely formative feedback
academic-integrity case clarification
examples: The implemented dashboard operationalizes the goals with an activity timeline, session summary, code-size graph, replay, paste-events view, and cohort-level comparison views

title: Surface process-based integrity signals as warning signals for teacher review rather than automated plagiarism judgments

title: INJECT Exercise Platform (IXP): open-source web environment for delivering and evaluating digital tabletop exercises
description: IXP is a "lightweight, open-source web-based learning environment designed to deliver and evaluate TTXs" that transitions the pen-and-paper format into a digital one. It delivers injects based on time or milestone completion, defines scenarios in YAML files, simulates tools such as email, a browser, and a firewall, logs trainee actions, and provides dashboards and JSONL export. Versions v1–v5 added on-demand exercises, multi-tenancy, an exercise editor, a Visual Studio Code extension, and support for up to 100 parallel teams.
requirements: Exercise scenarios must be defined in human- and machine-readable YAML files or via the built-in editor
constraints: Fully automated on-demand exercises are restricted to elements that can be automatically evaluated, such as multiple-choice questionnaires
target_learners: undergraduate cybersecurity students
vocational school students
high school students in extracurricular activities
target_learning_goals: incident response collaboration
security awareness
team-based problem solving
examples: Used to deliver 25 exercises from October 2024 to March 2026, including discussion and simulation exercises on phishing, insider threat, and personal-data breach response

Each phase has a defined purpose, from establishing whether the exercise is worth building to post-exercise analysis and improvement of future runs.

article_title: Teaching Intro AI When the Tools Can Do the Homework: A Course Redesign and a Student Bill of Rights
citation: Yusuf Pisan. (2026). Teaching Intro AI When the Tools Can Do the Homework: A Course Redesign and a Student Bill of Rights. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05175
title: Assessment without examinations: weight moved to in-class exercises, reflective writing, and a defended team project that resist unattributed automation
description: This pattern rebuilds grading around tasks a language model cannot quietly ghost-write, on the bet that "an assessment a model can silently complete is a weak assessment." The Spring 2026 grade comprised in-class exercises done in the room in a fixed hour (20 percent), weekly projects that may be reflection, programming, or a mix (40 percent), and a team project (40 percent), with no midterm or final. Reflective writing carries a first-person account of the student's own process, and in-class exercises were graded complete-or-incomplete on submission with AI scores advisory only.
requirements: In-class exercises require a fixed scheduled hour in the room and produce an artifact on the spot
Reflective writing must be required to be in the student's own voice
constraints: The author's own students, asked to design fair grading for such a course, mostly reinvented proctored or handwritten assessment, the strongest internal challenge to this structure
The author makes no causal or learning-outcome claims for the structure
target_learners: upper-division undergraduate computer science students
target_learning_goals: artificial intelligence fundamentals
engineering judgment and supervision of AI tools
reflective practice
examples: The Spring 2026 CSS 382 grade was in-class exercises 20 percent, weekly projects 40 percent, and team project 40 percent, with the syllabus stating there was no final exam

article_title: Vibe Compiler: A Research-Logic Synthesis Tool That Runs without Prompt Engineering -Toward Enhancing Metacognition for Sustaining Agency in the Age of Generative AI-
citation: Riichiro Mizoguchi, Tomoki Aburatani, Kento Koike, Machi Shimmei. (2026). Vibe Compiler: A Research-Logic Synthesis Tool That Runs without Prompt Engineering —Toward Enhancing Metacognition for Sustaining Agency in the Age of Generative AI—. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05545
title: Synthesis–Analysis Reciprocity Model: intellectual construction as a mutual-constraint loop between Synthesis and Analysis
description: The model decomposes intellectual construction into Synthesis, which selects and combines known logical components according to a purpose, and Analysis, which critically evaluates the artifact against objective criteria. Its defining feature is mutual constraint: "the output of Analysis is not consumed as an evaluation result; it flows back immediately as a constraint on the next Synthesis." The model is developed as a dual-layer structure — a learner layer (arithmetic problem posing, reading comprehension) and a researcher layer (research-logic type checking) — sharing one reciprocity mechanism with only the Analysis mapping swapped out. The authors position it against introspective models such as reflection and self-regulated learning, which lack an external objective indicator.
requirements: A reference solution must be presentable for a given artifact (AI as an Oracle), whose errors are woven into the design as occasions for reverse Analysis
The user must possess a minimum of domain knowledge and be able to respond to the AI's remarks with grounds
constraints: Application to complete novices falls outside the present scope
The loop structure is acknowledged as isomorphic to existing reciprocity models (Geneplore, co-evolution, DBR); the claimed novelty is the mechanism that stimulates the reciprocity from outside
target_learners: Researchers building research logic
Learners in arithmetic problem posing and Japanese reading comprehension
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive honing and evaluative judgment
Construction of coherent research logic
examples: The Vibe Compiler prototype implements the researcher layer by type-checking drafts against a paper ontology
The paper itself was produced as an output of the second layer, which the authors call a relation of self-application

Vibe Compiler: A Research-Logic Synthesis Tool That Runs without Prompt Engineering —Toward Enhancing Metacognition for Sustaining Agency in the Age of Generative AI—. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05545

title: Four quadrants and four types of structural-gap origin: a vocabulary decomposing who synthesized and who analyzed
description: The framework superimposes the distinction between executing agents (human, AI) on the distinction between cognitive functions (Synthesis, Analysis), yielding quadrants Q1 (human Synthesis), Q2 (AI Synthesis), Q3 (human Analysis), and Q4 (AI Analysis). From these, four types of structural-gap origin are derived, with Type (IV) — Vibe Compiling — placing the gap "between the AI's output and the human's judgment." The authors argue the quadrants make describable what the single word "done" conflates: what the AI evaluated versus what the user could evaluate, and what the AI made versus what the user constructed.
requirements: Both the function distinction and the agent distinction must be drawn together for the design demand (reserve Q3 and purpose-setting Q1 to the human) to be statable
constraints: Agent columns name the side that principally carries each mapping, not an exclusive right to execute it
The internal thought process after a probe does not appear in the classificatory variables
target_learners: Researchers and designers of AI-supported learning and research systems
target_learning_goals: Protecting and driving human metacognition and epistemic agency under AI assistance
examples: Draft V1 of the paper is cited as an instance of Type (II), where the type was almost fully satisfied while human content stayed empty
The vocabulary is proposed as a design question to put to any support system: against whose Synthesis or Analysis does it elicit a gap

title: Vibe Compiler: a research-logic compiler that turns Vibes into research logic via a 16-parameter paper ontology
description: Vibe Compiler is a prototype research-logic compiler, built on NotebookLM and Gemini, that helps researchers turn vague intuitions (Vibes) into coherent research logic. It "treats compilation failures as signs that logical components are missing" and, rather than filling gaps autonomously, "returns reflective questions that prompt researchers to develop the missing reasoning themselves." It puts the 16 parameters of a paper ontology to work as a type system, with a dialogue design and user interface equipped with Null checks, consistency checks, probing triggers, and an acceptance path for reverse Analysis.
requirements: Seven kinds of content-oriented materials must be fed in; the ontology runs as unformalized prose documents written for human readers
Objective structural indicators must be computed with accuracy acceptable in practice
constraints: The Oracle premise can break down as difficulty rises, which the design treats as an occasion for evaluation
Quantitative effects on evaluative judgment (RQ2, RQ3, RQ5) are formulated but not yet verified
target_learners: Researchers writing scholarly papers
target_learning_goals: Articulating missing logical components in research plans
Maintaining epistemic agency when using generative AI
examples: The prototype executed the type check against the paper ontology and built the logical structure of the position paper itself, with execution logs as support

title: Structural-gap-driven metacognitive support: treat the gap between subjective intention and objective structure as the engine of metacognition
description: This principle holds that the dissonance between a user's subjective intention toward an artifact and its structural reality, computed from objective indicators, should be treated "not as a defect to be removed but the occasion that makes the user ask anew what they had misjudged." The support system externalizes quantitative structural parameters, forces them into confrontation with subjective self-assessment, and recirculates the resulting gap as a constraint on the next act of construction. The authors contrast this with standard methods whose criteria are given from outside and whose evaluation results never flow back as constraints.
requirements: Objective structural indicators computable by the AI with practically acceptable accuracy
Domain-specific structural-complexity parameters definable by hand for each target domain
constraints: The approach presupposes users with minimum domain knowledge; complete novices are out of scope
Whether presenting the structural gap significantly improves evaluative judgment awaits quantitative evaluation
target_learners: Researchers
Learners engaged in problem posing and reading comprehension
target_learning_goals: Evaluative judgment
Metacognitive monitoring of one's own constructions
examples: Vibe Compiler detects unfilled slots via type checks and returns probing questions rather than corrections
The learner-layer example contrasts a problem poser rating a one-step problem as fairly difficult with the problem's actual structure

citation: Lin, Yi-Cheng; Guo, Yu-Kai; Chen, Szu-Chi; Feng, Bo-Han; Hsu, Yun-Man; Hsieh, Hsiang; Lin, Yu-Jung; Wu, Yue-Ling; Dong, Jia-Kai; Cheng, An-Yu; Huang, Yu-Han; Ieong, Lok-Lam; Chen, Kuan-Yu; Tchouang, Ming-Douo; Sun, Shao-Hua; Lin, Che; Ding, Jian-Jiun; Lee, Hung-yi. title: Teaching Monster Challenge benchmark: single-shot instructional video generation conditioned on a learner persona, with a three-layer evaluation protocol
description: A benchmark in which each item gives a system a course_requirement and a learner_persona and requires one complete instructional video generated end-to-end with no human in the loop. Items span four AP-aligned secondary STEM subjects; matched pairs hold the requirement fixed and vary the persona so that "Differencing within a pair removes item-level confounds." Evaluation proceeds through an LLM-judge screen, crowdsourced pairwise comparison aggregated into Elo ratings, and an expert panel ranking. The items, rubric, scoring traces, and human judgments are released as a testbed.
requirements: Systems must return a complete video within a 30-minute generation budget per API request, with no human in the loop.
constraints: Limited to AP-aligned secondary STEM subjects in English; evaluates single-shot generation rather than interactive tutoring.
target_learners: secondary-school STEM learners described by persona (grade level, prior knowledge, attention span)
target_learning_goals: persona-adapted explanation of AP-level STEM topics
examples: The first edition ran a Warm-up phase (46 teams, 1,696 videos), a Preliminary phase (77 teams, 1,612 videos), and a Final phase with 48 videos from three finalists judged by a ten-member expert panel.

title: Four-dimension evaluation framework operationalizing Shulman's teacher-knowledge taxonomy for instructional video
description: The benchmark scores videos on four dimensions, the first three of which "correspondtoShulman'sthreekindsofteacher knowledge": Content Accuracy measures factual correctness and freedom from hallucination; Pedagogical Logic measures scaffolding, coherence, and clarity of exposition; Learner Adaptability measures whether content matches the learner's grade level, attention span, and prior knowledge, operationalizing "thetransformationthatisthe core of PCK"; and Engagement and Multimodal Presentation measures pacing, visual–speech alignment, and strategies such as analogies, drawing on Mayer's Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning.

constraints: Measures teaching quality as a proxy for learning, since measuring learning gains directly from each video is infeasible at benchmark scale.

target_learning_goals: factual accuracy, coherent instructional sequencing, learner adaptation, and engaging multimodal presentation
examples: Layer 1 scores selected the top systems for Layer 2; the four dimension means for all submissions were 4.31, 4.19, 3.77, and 3.86.

title: Six-stage cascade architecture for end-to-end instructional video generation
description: Nearly all submissions instantiate a six-stage cascade: "persona parsing and routing, lesson planning, slide and script composition, visual rendering, narration synthesis, and assembly." Recurring design choices include structuring the persona as JSON conditioning for every stage, difficulty-based model routing, web-search grounding of lesson plans, Bloom's-taxonomy constraints enforced by closed-loop LLM review, HTML/CSS slide templates with reviewer–fixer loops, split handling of conceptual versus mathematical figures, two-step planning for Manim animation, and word-level forced alignment of narration to animation.
