article_title: VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding
citation: Ruqi Sun, Jiaping Li, Wenhui Tao, Ximing Zheng, Yuefeng Tan, Jiahao Wei, and Yuxin Ma. (2026). VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09698
title: VeriForge mixed-initiative writing system with proactive highlighting, dual-stream querying, Knowledge Canvas, and graph-based RAG
description: VeriForge is a mixed-initiative writing environment that divides cognitive labor so "the system assumes initiative over domain discovery while the author retains full initiative over narrative synthesis". Its front-end couples flow-aware proactive inline highlighting (fading in after a 5-second keystroke pause), a dual-stream query panel pairing conversational text with color-coded source-anchored Knowledge Cards, and a spatial Knowledge Canvas with gold nodes from highlights and silver nodes from queries connected by AI Auto-Reasoned edges. A graph-based RAG back-end in Neo4j binds provenance to every node at ingestion time, so "every retrieved fact remains traceable to its exact source passage".
requirements: Authors upload curated domain source texts, which the system ingests into a domain knowledge graph, typically requiring 5 to 10 minutes per book
constraints: Evaluated in 30-minute cold-start sessions on historical martial-arts writing domains; the authors state this bounds where VeriForge has been shown to work, not where the problem exists
target_learners: Fiction writers venturing into unfamiliar domains, including hobbyists and online novelists
target_learning_goals: Discovering and integrating unfamiliar domain knowledge into narrative prose with verisimilitude
examples: In the system walkthrough, novelist Marie drafts a medieval duel; the system highlights longsword after a 5-second keystroke pause, and a Knowledge Card separates an AI-generated description from a quoted source passage
key_sources: Ruqi Sun, Jiaping Li, Wenhui Tao, Ximing Zheng, Yuefeng Tan, Jiahao Wei, and Yuxin Ma. (2026). VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09698

article_title: VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding
citation: Ruqi Sun, Jiaping Li, Wenhui Tao, Ximing Zheng, Yuefeng Tan, Jiahao Wei, and Yuxin Ma. (2026). VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09698
title: Discovery-synthesis split: system initiative over domain discovery, author initiative over narrative synthesis
description: The article's organizing design framework divides cognitive labor in AI-assisted writing: the system takes initiative only over domain discovery, where the Illusion of Explanatory Depth renders authors unable to act for themselves, while the author retains full initiative over narrative synthesis. The authors argue the cognitive work of transforming knowledge into one's own prose is itself the mechanism through which deeper understanding forms, grounding the framework in the knowledge-transforming model of written composition. They propose it generalizes to journalism and documentary filmmaking, with parameters such as cue aggressiveness and source traceability calibrated to each domain's epistemic conditions.
requirements: A domain where practitioners face blind spots they cannot self-diagnose and where voice, interpretation, and judgment constitute the output's core value
constraints: The authors state generalizing the split is not plug-and-play: a journalist on deadline has a narrower discovery window, and an academic in their own specialty faces a shallower IOED
target_learners: Creative writers and knowledge workers producing domain-specific work in unfamiliar domains
target_learning_goals: Knowledge-transforming: synthesizing unfamiliar specialized domain facts into authentic prose
examples: VeriForge implements the split by having the system monitor drafts and surface highlights while authors alone write and integrate narrative prose

citation: Ruqi Sun, Jiaping Li, Wenhui Tao, Ximing Zheng, Yuefeng Tan, Jiahao Wei, and Yuxin Ma. (2026). VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09698
title: Present retrieved domain knowledge as structured, source-traceable raw material rather than finished prose to preserve authorial ownership
description: The article recommends that AI writing support deliver discovered domain facts as structured raw material linked to its exact source passage, rather than near-final generated prose. Participants distrusted AI-generated prose partly because it threatened their voice — one described generic AI vocabulary as carrying a "plastic texture" — while facts traced to a specific primary source felt trustworthy enough to adopt directly. Presenting knowledge as raw ingredients for active synthesis is positioned as the lever that restores trust while preserving authorial agency over narrative voice.
requirements: Retrieved knowledge must be linked to its exact source passage, preserving verifiability
constraints: The authors note this interpretation draws on participants' retrospective comparisons with prior tools rather than a controlled manipulation within their study
target_learners: Fiction writers using AI assistance for domain-specific drafting
target_learning_goals: Integrating domain knowledge into prose while retaining authorial voice and ownership
examples: VeriForge's Knowledge Cards separate an AI-generated description from a quoted source passage, and participants like P05 used the system exclusively for technique names and historical facts but refused to let it touch his combat scenes

article_title: Jointly Predicting Courses and Grades Using a Transformer-Based Model (TRACE)
citation: Paul Savala. (2026). Jointly Predicting Courses and Grades Using a Transformer-Based Model. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13409
title: TRACE: a Transformer architecture with semester-level concurrency encoding and joint course-set/grade prediction
description: TRACE (a TRansformer for Academic Course-grade Estimation) encodes a student's major, course and grade history with separate embedding layers and positional encodings based on relative semester, so all courses in the same semester share a temporal vector, enforcing a permutation-invariant representation within each term while preserving order across terms. Its decoder jointly predicts the next semester's course set and grades, trained with a novel loss combining KL divergence over the course distribution and MSE for grade regression. The author states this "enforces a permutation-invariant representation within each semester, which we argue more accurately reflects the unordered nature of concurrent enrollments."
requirements: Requires historical enrollment, grade and major data from which course and major embeddings are learned without hand-encoded features
A weighting factor ω balancing the two loss terms should be optimized via cross-validation; the author found a value near one was optimal
constraints: New courses outside the training vocabulary map to an <OTHER> token, limiting prediction for novel curricula
A cold-start problem exists for new students with no academic history
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: predicting next-semester course enrollment and grade performance for early alert and advising
examples: Trained on 5326 students, 360 courses, 48 majors and 18 semesters (Fall 2014 through Fall 2023) from a single American university, with 90/10 train-test split
key_sources: Paul Savala. (2026). Jointly Predicting Courses and Grades Using a Transformer-Based Model. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13409

title: Aptitude-Treatment Interaction as the framework for matching dialogue format to learner characteristics
description: The article applies the Aptitude-Treatment Interaction (ATI) framework, in which "learning outcomes are jointly determined by the combination of learner characteristics (aptitude) and instructional method (treatment)". Learner characteristics — the CE and RCE factors of experiential learning style and critical thinking disposition — serve as aptitudes, while the three LLM+TTS dialogue formats (TS, SS, TT) serve as treatments. The framework motivates examining which format is more effective for learners with which style, and grounds the study's recommendation to personalize format selection.

constraints: The article notes detecting interaction effects generally requires a larger sample size than detecting main effects

target_learning_goals: data science literacy and data-driven career education content

article_title: TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education
citation: David Barron, Xiaohang Tang, Rezky Dwisantika, Minsun Kim, David H. Smith IV, Jiaming Cui, and Yan Chen. 2026. TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26184
title: TutorTrace dataset of IDE telemetry, behavioral segments, and observable metrics from 480 learners across four introductory Python deployments
description: TutorTrace is a publicly available dataset from a task-based IDE platform with LLM support, capturing "approximately 180K telemetry events, 13,633 behavioral segments, and 27 continuously computed metrics" surrounding 1,386 AI interactions across four deployments in two introductory Python courses (N=480). It uniquely combines raw IDE telemetry, AI query and response logs, task outcome data, and expert-validated behavioral classification (Table 1). The dataset, taxonomy, classifier, and code are released via a GitHub repository.

constraints: Data were collected during short introductory programming tasks at a single institution, limiting generalizability across courses, tasks, populations, and learning environments
target_learners: introductory Python programming students in higher education
target_learning_goals: programming problem-solving behavior around AI-assisted help-seeking
examples: Deployments 1–2 used a list-indexing task with a 15-minute limit; Deployments 3–4 used a nested-lists task with a 10-minute limit

article_title: TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education
citation: David Barron, Xiaohang Tang, Rezky Dwisantika, Minsun Kim, David H. Smith IV, Jiaming Cui, and Yan Chen. 2026. TutorTrace: A Dataset and Taxonomy for Classifying Learner Behavioral States during AI-Assisted Programming Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26184
title: TutorTrace three-window behavioral taxonomy of ten learner profiles around AI help-seeking
description: The taxonomy organizes learner activity surrounding AI help-seeking into three temporal windows: before the first AI query (Cold Start, Oriented, Struggling), between consecutive queries (Passive, Iterating, Debugging, Spinning), and session-wide re-querying patterns (Passive Re-querying, Active Testing, Untested Editing) — ten profiles in total. Profiles were derived via outcome-guided K-means clustering over window-specific metric pools, with rule-defined profiles for zero-effort observations. Each profile carries an expert-informed intervention strategy supplied to the AI tutor's prompt, e.g. Cold Start: "Scaffold task entry. Offer pseudocode with blanks."
requirements: Behavioral abstraction pipeline computing observable metrics and behavioral sequences in real time from IDE telemetry
constraints: Window 1 and 2 profiles were selected through an exploratory procedure partly informed by task-completion differences; completion rates are descriptive, not independent validation
target_learners: introductory Python programming students using AI tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: productive, guided help-seeking and independent effort between AI queries
examples: Window 3 clustering at K=3 (silhouette 0.399) produced assignments identical across 20 random seeds (ARI=1.000)

title: TutorTrace automated behavioral classifier transforming raw IDE telemetry into labeled behavioral sequences in real time
description: The TutorTrace classifier is an automated pipeline that transforms raw IDE telemetry into labeled behavioral sequences in real time. Its rules are grounded in the judgment of four domain-expert annotators who coded session replays with a codebook of behaviors such as Implementing, Debugging, Thinking, and Seeking Help, refined over 10 pilot sessions. Validation triangulated learner self-reports, expert annotations, and the automated classifier: "overall Cohen's𝜅 ranged from 0.73 to 0.83, and overall raw agreement ranged from 78% to 87%" (Table 4).

constraints: The rule-based auto-segmentation pipeline lacks semantic understanding of learner code and intent; for example it may classify edits as Debugging while an unresolved error remains even when the learner is implementing an unrelated feature
target_learners: introductory Python programming students whose sessions are classified
target_learning_goals: real-time detection of learner behavioral states to support adaptive AI tutoring
examples: A user study with 13 participants who completed two Python tasks and self-labeled their behavior provided the self-report side of the three-way agreement analysis

article_title: With a Thermomix You Lose the Ability to Cook: A Kitchen Machine Analogy for Applications of Generative AI in Education
citation: Rummel, N., Nachtigall, V., & Panadero, E. (2026). “With a Thermomix You Lose the Ability to Cook”: A Kitchen Machine Analogy for Applications of Generative AI in Education.
title: ICAP framework: four modes of cognitive engagement from passive to interactive
description: The ICAP framework, as deployed in this article, distinguishes four modes of cognitive engagement — Passive, Active, Constructive, and Interactive — that differ in the cognitive effort learners invest in modifying existing and creating new learning products. The authors map each of their four Thermomix/generative-AI use cases onto one mode, from passively following guided instructions to co-constructing knowledge in dialogue. They use it to argue that "higher modes of engagement leading to superior learning outcomes" anchors the analogy between cooking and learning with AI.
requirements: Distinguishing use cases by the degree of cognitive effort learners invest, from receiving outputs to collaboratively co-constructing knowledge
constraints: The article treats the mode-outcome ordering as a hypothesized assumption of the framework, not as a result tested in this paper
target_learners: students using generative AI tools in educational settings
target_learning_goals: meaningful cognitive engagement with learning tasks
examples: The article assigns its four scenarios to Passive/Substitution, Active/Augmentation, Constructive/Modification, and Interactive/Redefinition in Table 1

title: SAMR model: four levels of technology use from substitution to redefinition
description: The SAMR model, as presented in this article, distinguishes four levels of educational technology use: Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, and Redefinition, differing in how far technology enhances and transforms learning compared to learning without it. Lower levels replace traditional activities with or without functional improvement; higher levels redesign tasks or create entirely new ones. The authors use SAMR alongside ICAP to classify both Thermomix cooking practices and generative AI learning uses, arguing the analogy extends to learning with technology generally.
requirements: Classifying technology use by whether it replaces, functionally enhances, redesigns, or fundamentally creates new tasks
constraints: The article applies SAMR analytically to illustrative scenarios; it reports no empirical test of the model's levels
target_learners: educators integrating generative AI into instruction
target_learning_goals: appropriate selection of technology-supported learning activities
examples: Guided cooking and full AI assignment outsourcing are classed as Substitution; community recipe sharing and real-time adaptive AI feedback as Redefinition

title: The Thermomix analogy as a conceptual lens for generative AI in education
description: The article's central contribution is an analogy between the Thermomix smart kitchen appliance and generative AI in education. Both tools integrate previously distributed functions into one interface, provoke enthusiasm and skill-loss critiques, and can be used in ways ranging from passive substitution to interactive redefinition. The authors offer this as "a conceptual lens that makes visible the spectrum of possible uses of generative AI", aiming to move debate beyond whether AI supports learning toward how use shapes learning processes, identity, agency, and evaluation.

constraints: The authors note media-comparison designs risk confounding numerous factors and yield limited insight; future research must disentangle the conditions under which generative AI fosters or hinders productive learning

target_learning_goals: critical reflection on how AI use shapes learning processes and learner identity

title: Redesign assignments so learners critically engage with AI outputs rather than merely consume them
description: This principle holds that teachers should restructure tasks so that generative AI outputs become material for brainstorming, evaluation, and reflection rather than ready-made answers. In the article's terms, "the modification stage is evident when teachers redesign their assignments so that learners are not merely tasked with searching for information and synthesizing it, but are instead prompted to engage in new forms of interaction" such as critically evaluating AI-provided information and drawing their own conclusions. This positions AI as a catalyst for meaning-making and self-reflection.

constraints: The article notes reliance on AI for basic functions risks diminishing acquisition of foundational skills such as composing grammatically correct texts from scratch

article_title: Three Pathways of Student-AI Interaction: Constraint-First Design for Higher-Order Thinking
citation: Zahra, F. T. (2025). Three Pathways of Student-AI Interaction: Constraint-First Design for Higher-Order Thinking. Manuscript under blind review; framework first presented at EAAI-25, Philadelphia, PA.
title: Three Paths of Student-AI Interaction typology
description: A typological framework identifying three qualitatively distinct modes of student-AI engagement: Passive Review (student accepts AI output with minimal scrutiny, unidirectional, limited higher-order opportunity), Direct Question (transactional gap-filling with surface evaluation, moderate opportunity), and Strategic Dialogue (dialogic, recursive, critical, metacognitive engagement with AI as a thinking partner, substantial opportunity). The article states "The typology distinguishes three paths—Passive Review, Direct Question, and Strategic Dialogue" and links them to degrees of cognitive and epistemic agency, mapping onto a developmental trajectory of AI literacy from treating AI as authoritative to maintaining epistemic agency. Its core claim is that learning outcomes depend on which path students are on, not whether they use AI.
requirements: A codebook with labels mapped to paths, trained coders, and interaction logs of student-AI exchanges to classify
constraints: The article notes the Path 1/2 boundary is the most contested site of the coding scheme and the framework needs testing across larger samples, disciplines, and settings
target_learners: undergraduate students in AI-integrated coursework
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking
critical thinking
AI literacy
examples: Composite personas ground each path: Aisha and Malik (Path 1), Kofi and Amara (Path 2), Carmen and Jamal (Path 3); Table 1 compares the paths across behavior, engagement mode, and opportunity for higher-order thinking.

title: Next Level Teaching Blueprint (NLTB): three-stage constraint-first design for Strategic Dialogue
description: A replicable instructional design system with three sequenced stages and explicit interaction protocols, described by the article as having "a theoretical logic linking each element to Path 3 engagement." Stage 1 has students engage the problem fully without AI and document reasoning, securing epistemic agency and structurally preventing Paths 1 and 2. Stage 2 operationalizes Path 3 under explicit constraints: students share their Stage 1 reasoning, ask AI to challenge it, and probe responses; answers, summaries, and drafts are not permitted. Stage 3 requires metacognitive comparison of original versus AI-augmented thinking and construction of an integrated, evaluated position.

constraints: The article states formal evaluation of the campus-wide initiative is beyond the scope of the paper, and a controlled comparison of scaffolded and unscaffolded conditions remains to be run

target_learning_goals: Strategic Dialogue engagement

citation: Dang, C. T., & Nguyen, A. (2026). Verified, not generated: expert-verified AI study materials and the distribution of learning gains in a university course.
title: Judgement burden: the expertise and effort a learner must supply to screen AI output before learning from it
description: Judgement burden is a learner-level construct explaining when generative AI narrows versus widens attainment gaps. The article defines it: "the expertise and effort a learner must supply to distinguish usable from unusable AI output before learning from it". It has two components — variability of output quality and the location of responsibility for checking. Where learners must check variable output, gains accrue to those with the knowledge to check it; where checking is done before release, gains accrue to those who lacked that knowledge. It is related to, but distinct from, cognitive load: checking AI output is extraneous load whose source and bearer the construct names.
requirements: AI-generated material whose quality varies, so that someone must check it before it can be trusted for learning
constraints: The article states the design cannot separate verification from the material it accompanied, so the account's screening prediction (unverified release should produce smaller lower-tail gains) is untested in its data
target_learners: first-year university students in a compulsory economics course
target_learning_goals: examination performance in undergraduate economics, particularly for lower-attaining students
examples: The study's deployment moved the burden upstream: a named graduate teaching assistant checked every NotebookLM output against source materials before release under the label "AI-generated and academically verified".

citation: Dang, C. T., & Nguyen, A. (2026). Verified, not generated: expert-verified AI study materials and the distribution of learning gains in a university course.
title: Issue AI-generated study materials only after checking by a named expert who is disclosed to students
description: The article defines expert-verified AI study materials by "three jointly necessary features": generation "by a source-grounded model from the course’s own documents", checking "by a named expert before release", and a label disclosing "both their AI origin and their verification". Verification screens errors, signals a low-cost reason to engage, and relocates rather than removes labour. The article recommends assigning verification to staff with subject expertise and a teaching relationship with students, counting it in workload allocations, and keeping a log of verification time and changes per item.
requirements: A named verifier with subject expertise and a relationship with the students, since trust attached to a verifier students knew from tutorials
constraints: Source-grounding reduces but does not eliminate hallucination, which is why named verification is required; a label naming an unknown or anonymous checker may not carry the same weight, and a label can keep signalling after checking becomes cursory
target_learners: undergraduate students in large introductory courses where prior preparation varies most
target_learning_goals: examination performance on core course content, particularly for lower-attaining students
examples: In 2024/25 the Part 2 lecturer generated podcasts, FAQs and study guides in Google NotebookLM from course documents; the GTA checked definitions, terminology, examples and quiz answers against sources, revising prompts or regenerating sections rather than accepting first drafts; producing and verifying each weekly set took about 30 minutes.

article_title: Explaining learning engagement in AI-assisted learning through teacher support and achievement goals: insights from goal-setting theory
citation: Yongliang Wang & Yaobo Wang. (2026). Explaining learning engagement in AI-assisted learning through teacher support and achievement goals: insights from goal-setting theory. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications 13:1215. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-07636-8
title: Goal-setting Theory extended to AI-assisted learning: approach-oriented goals as the primary motivational pathways from external support to engagement
description: Goal-setting Theory, articulated by Locke and refined by Locke and Latham, holds that consciously set goals regulate action, with specific, challenging, attainable goals directing attention, energizing effort, sustaining persistence, and fostering strategy development. The study integrates teacher support, the 2×2 achievement goal framework, and engagement into a single structural model and argues that in AI-assisted environments, where "immediate feedback and visible progress indicators" make goal pursuit more salient and self-regulated, approach-oriented goals become the primary pathways translating external support into engagement, while avoidance goals do not function as effective conduits.
requirements: Learners must be operating in AI-assisted learning environments characterized by immediate feedback and visible progress indicators for the context-sensitive extension to apply
constraints: The extension is grounded in cross-sectional self-report data, which the authors state prevents causal inferences
target_learners: Chinese university EFL students with prior AI-assisted learning experience
target_learning_goals: English language learning engagement and motivation in AI-assisted contexts
examples: The study tested a hypothesized model (Fig. 1) linking teacher support, four achievement goal orientations, and engagement with SEM in a sample of 758 learners

article_title: Reflective AI use and student engagement in AI-supported programming: technology acceptance, programming self-efficacy, and behavioral trace evidence
citation: Wang S and Zhao J (2026) Reflective AI use and student engagement in AI-supported programming: technology acceptance, programming self-efficacy, and behavioral trace evidence. Front. Psychol. 17:1929887. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1929887
title: Reflective AI Acceptance Integration Framework (RAIAF)
description: RAIAF is an evidence-integration design that organizes three complementary data branches for studying reflective AI use in AI-supported programming: a survey SEM linking technology acceptance, reflective use, programming self-efficacy, and engagement; exploratory coding of Copilot Critical Engagement texts into a four-level RUItext index; and early-window behavioral trace prediction from DTA logs. The article states "RAIAF is an evidence-integration design rather than a new machine-learning architecture or a claim that the three datasets measure the same process," and that "The datasets contain diﬀerent participants and contexts and are not pooled." It is explicitly conservative, reporting where hypothesized paths are not supported.
requirements: Separate datasets with different participants and contexts that are not pooled; the DTA module contains programming behavior without a direct measure of AI use
constraints: The DTA module cannot confirm the survey and text modules; behavioral feature names are theory-informed descriptions of log patterns, not measurements of latent reflective AI use or self-efficacy
target_learners: novice programming students in AI-supported programming environments
target_learning_goals: reflective evaluation and revision of AI-generated feedback
programming self-efficacy
student engagement in AI-supported programming
examples: The survey branch used a parcel-based latent SEM (CFI = 0.951); the text branch double-coded 66 nonblank responses; the log branch extracted baseline, recovery, and persistence feature groups from a 40% course-calendar window
key_sources: Wang S and Zhao J (2026) Reflective AI use and student engagement in AI-supported programming: technology acceptance, programming self-efficacy, and behavioral trace evidence. Front. Psychol. 17:1929887. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1929887

article_title: Reflective AI use and student engagement in AI-supported programming: technology acceptance, programming self-efficacy, and behavioral trace evidence
citation: Wang S and Zhao J (2026) Reflective AI use and student engagement in AI-supported programming: technology acceptance, programming self-efficacy, and behavioral trace evidence. Front. Psychol. 17:1929887. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1929887
title: Use behavioral trace evidence as a cautious complement to psychological measurement, not as its replacement or validation
description: The article recommends treating log-derived behavioral indicators (recovery, persistence, activity features) as complementary evidence about programming behavior rather than as direct measures of reflective AI use or self-efficacy. It states: "Thepresentworkdiﬀersfromthisliteraturebyusingbehavioral trace evidence as a cautious complement to psychological analysis rather than as a replacement or validation of psychological measurement." Feature names are theory-informed descriptions of log patterns, and incremental predictive value should be tested through controlled ablation against activity-only baselines.
requirements: Explicit acknowledgment that behavioral approximations are not direct psychological measurements; ablation testing against theoretically simpler activity-only baselines
constraints: DTA does not measure AI use, reflection, or self-efficacy directly; the activity-defined engagement label overlaps with baseline predictors and provides no independent psychological criterion; no practical intervention benefit has been demonstrated
target_learners: novice programming students in AI-supported and log-instrumented programming courses
target_learning_goals: reflective engagement with AI-generated feedback
final task completion and engagement prediction from early behavior
examples: The DTA ablation compared Baseline, Baseline + Reflective, Baseline + SE-related, and Full configurations, finding only a small, unstable held-out Macro-F1 gain for final success and no material improvement for activity-defined engagement

article_title: The Safety Gap: Restoring Productive Struggle Through Pedagogically Aligned Generative AI
citation: Wang H and Shan W (2026). The safety gap: restoring productive struggle through pedagogically aligned generative AI. Front. Educ. 11:1757622. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1757622
title: The Safety Gap: divergence between AI-assisted performance and unassisted capability to verify output
description: The Safety Gap is the article's central concept: the divergence between the polished output a learner produces with generative AI and their ability to independently reproduce or verify that output. The authors define it as 'the widening chasm between the surface-level competence a student displays when supported by helpful AI tools and their actual, unassisted cognitive capability', later reframing it as an Epistemic Discrepancy between user capability and tool output. Figure 1 presents this as a conjectural conceptual model rather than an empirical plot.
requirements: Unassisted capability must be observable independently of AI-assisted performance, which the article argues requires preserved AI-free spaces where baseline capability can be observed, practiced, and assessed.
constraints: The article presents the Safety Gap via a figure intended as a conjectural conceptual model rather than an empirical plot; no empirical measurement of the gap is reported.
target_learners: novice learners in medical education
target_learning_goals: independent judgment
metacognitive awareness
capacity to verify AI-assisted outputs

article_title: The Safety Gap: Restoring Productive Struggle Through Pedagogically Aligned Generative AI
citation: Wang H and Shan W (2026). The safety gap: restoring productive struggle through pedagogically aligned generative AI. Front. Educ. 11:1757622. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1757622
title: A three-architecture taxonomy of educational generative AI: Oracle, Socratic tutor, and adversarial agent
description: The article organizes the educational AI landscape into three interaction-design architectures. The Oracle category comprises generic chatbots optimized for immediacy, which the authors call the primary drivers of the Safety Gap; the Socratic tutor withholds direct answers and offers hints to support schema construction; the adversarial agent critiques student work or plants plausible errors to build epistemic vigilance. As the article states, it contrasts 'generic Oracle models that prioritize immediacy with education-speciﬁc architectures (Socratic and Adversarial) designed to induce productive struggle and mitigate the Safety Gap'.
requirements: Socratic and adversarial behavior requires deliberate configuration via system prompts or educational wrappers, since general-purpose models are trained to satisfy user requests immediately.
constraints: The taxonomy is the authors' own analytic categorization; the label Oracle is their own analytic term for answer-delivery systems, not terminology taken from any cited source.
target_learners: novice learners in medical education
students using generative AI tools in educational settings
target_learning_goals: productive struggle and schema construction
epistemic vigilance

article_title: Reimagining teacher-AI co-design in learning task design: trends and perspectives
citation: Zongran Wang, Liu Mingzhuo & A.Y.M. Atiquil Islam. (2026). Reimagining teacher-AI co-design in learning task design: trends and perspectives. HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES COMMUNICATIONS. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06981-y
title: Functional-affordance framework of teacher-AI co-design: efficiency, responsiveness, creativity, and equity as interdependent dimensions
description: The review proposes a framework in which AI tools are selected for four pedagogical affordances: efficiency, responsiveness, creativity, and equity. The review states "this study identified four recurrent affordance types as efficiency, responsiveness, creativity, and equity, which reflect how AI functionality intervenes in core aspects of design." The affordances are conceptualized as interacting levers: "the four identified affordances do not function as isolated features but as interdependent dimensions of teacher–AI co-design." The framework reframes AI as a co-agent that reorganizes the temporal, cognitive, and relational structures of teaching, and can serve as a diagnostic tool for identifying overreliance on narrow AI functions.
requirements: Requires analysis of how specific AI features afford solutions to teachers' design problems such as reducing workload, responding to student variability, enriching content, or promoting inclusivity
constraints: The synthesis reveals a concentration of use around specific GenAI functions, especially prompt generation and scenario simulation, risking narrowing the scope of AI-supported instructional design
target_learners: K-12 and higher education teachers acting as instructional designers
target_learning_goals: Design of effective, equitable, and adaptive learning tasks with AI support
examples: Figure 5 presents a function-affordance matrix showing which of the 28 reviewed studies reported each function-affordance pairing, with creativity and equity tied to a broader range of AI features than efficiency and responsiveness.
key_sources: Zongran Wang, Liu Mingzhuo & A.Y.M. Atiquil Islam. (2026). Reimagining teacher-AI co-design in learning task design: trends and perspectives. HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES COMMUNICATIONS. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-026-06981-y

article_title: Pedagogical partnerships with generative AI in higher education: how dual cognitive pathways paradoxically enable transformative learning
citation: Wang, S. and Zhang, H. (2026). Pedagogical partnerships with generative AI in higher education: how dual cognitive pathways paradoxically enable transformative learning. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00585-x
title: Dual cognitive pathway model of Human-GenAI pedagogical partnerships: vigilance and offloading as simultaneous, synergistic routes to transformative learning
description: The article proposes a theoretical model in which Human-GenAI pedagogical partnerships simultaneously activate two cognitive pathways — cognitive vigilance (critical evaluation of AI outputs) and cognitive offloading (strategic delegation of tasks) — both of which feed transformative learning experience, with efficiency orientation moderating both pathways. The model "reconceptualizes student-AI dynamics from a zero-sum resource competition to a synergistic collaboration", extending transformative learning theory to AI-mediated contexts. It was tested via PLS-SEM, IPMA, fsQCA, and interviews across three cultural contexts.
requirements: Students must have direct experience using commercially available, general-purpose generative AI tools in their academic workflows
Partnership orientation toward AI as a collaborative intellectual partner
constraints: Studied among higher-education business students in China, Europe, and the United States using self-report survey measures
Benefits of offloading are non-monotonic and may only manifest after a certain threshold of engagement is reached
target_learners: Higher education business students (undergraduate, master's, doctoral)
target_learning_goals: Transformative learning: critical reflection on assumptions and perspective reconstruction in AI-mediated academic work
examples: The model was operationalized as a PLS-SEM mediation-moderation architecture tested on a three-wave survey of 912 students, with R2 = 0.475 for transformative learning experience
key_sources: Wang, S. and Zhang, H. (2026). Pedagogical partnerships with generative AI in higher education: how dual cognitive pathways paradoxically enable transformative learning. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00585-x

article_title: Generative AI and Student Collaboration: A Scoping Review of Group Work Processes, Outcomes, and Risks
citation: Wei, Y., and Perkins, M. (2026). Generative AI and student collaboration: a scoping review of group work processes, outcomes, and risks. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00217-x
title: Eight-theme analytical framework for GenAI in higher-education group work
description: The review constructs eight recurring themes via reflexive thematic analysis of 18 studies: GenAI reconfigures knowledge development, reshapes higher-order thinking, mediates communication, transforms team interaction, improves administrative efficiency, provides personalised feedback, and raises data privacy/security/transparency and bias/fairness/accuracy concerns. The authors state the themes "can be used as an analytical framework to examine or design collaborative learning (CL) activities involving GenAI" and as predefined categories for future studies. Themes are conceptually integrated and often in tension rather than siloed.
requirements: Studies of GenAI in group work can be coded against the eight themes as predefined categories
constraints: Evidence across themes is uneven; privacy, bias and accuracy concerns are often discussed conceptually rather than examined empirically
target_learners: higher education students working in groups
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning processes and outcomes in AI-mediated group work
examples: Themes were built through six-stage Braun and Clarke thematic analysis, with codes such as "GenAI facilitates asynchronous interactions" grouped into broader themes

article_title: Cultivating Agency and Responsible AI Use Through the AI-ARC Framework
citation: Wood, D., & Moss, S. (2026). Cultivating Agency and Responsible AI Use Through the AI-ARC Framework. Journal of Instructional Design and Technology, 1(1), 8–17. https://doi.org/10.65201/CJHS2205
title: AI-ARC framework: Ask, Reflect, Create as a student-facing scaffold for responsible AI use
description: AI-ARC is a three-stage, student-facing framework for ethical and reflective collaboration with generative AI, adapted from the AI-ICE evaluative model. The paper describes it as "a practical, student-facing model for cultivating ethical and reflective collaboration with AI" in which Ask emphasizes inquiry, Reflect emphasizes critical evaluation, and Create emphasizes originality and ethical authorship. It functions both as a roadmap students follow and as a design heuristic for instructional designers.
requirements: Students progress through the three stages of asking purposeful questions, reflecting critically on AI outputs, and creating original work, with student agency central at each stage
constraints: The paper presents AI-ARC as a conceptual framework with stated potential rather than an empirically tested intervention
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students using generative AI
target_learning_goals: responsible AI use
student agency
critical thinking
ethical reasoning
creative synthesis
examples: Table 1 outlines each stage with its focus, the role of student agency, and example questions students might use to guide engagement

article_title: Transcription is not generation: Distinguishing non-generative AI tool use from academic misconduct in higher education assessment
citation: Craig Wright. (2026). Transcription is not generation: distinguishing non-generative AI tool use from academic misconduct in higher education assessment. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00234-w
title: Three-category typology of AI output functions: novel content production, error-correcting reconstruction, and format conversion
description: The paper proposes a typology distinguishing three functionally distinct categories of AI output that policy discussion frequently conflates. Category A is novel content production, where the machine creates content the student did not author; Category B is error-correcting reconstruction, where the system 'resolves ambiguity in the existing content' during recognition; Category C is format conversion, a clerical operation producing no intellectual content. The typology grounds the paper's argument that Category C falls outside the purpose of generative-AI prohibitions, while Category B is a grey zone requiring case-by-case assessment.
requirements: A precise definition of generation is necessary to draw the policy boundary clearly, per the paper's stated purpose for the typology
constraints: The paper does not claim that the Category B/C boundary can be identified bright-line in every case
The typology is a proposal that has not been empirically validated
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: academic integrity policy interpretation
assessment validity
examples: Scenario contrasts: prompting a platform to solve a system of ODEs is Category A; instructing it to transcribe handwriting into LaTeX exactly as written is Category C
key_sources: Craig Wright. (2026). Transcription is not generation: distinguishing non-generative AI tool use from academic misconduct in higher education assessment. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00234-w

article_title: Transcription is not generation: Distinguishing non-generative AI tool use from academic misconduct in higher education assessment
citation: Craig Wright. (2026). Transcription is not generation: distinguishing non-generative AI tool use from academic misconduct in higher education assessment. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00234-w
title: Assess AI use by the function performed, not the platform used
description: The paper argues that academic integrity judgements should turn on which AI function was performed rather than which platform was used: 'The question for academic integrity purposes, on the view defended here, is not 'which platform was used?' but 'which function was performed?'' Multi-functional platforms possess both generative and non-generative capabilities, so platform identity cannot determine whether a prohibition is engaged. The principle is argued to be implicit in existing institutional practice with grammar checkers and dictation software.
requirements: If an institution's position is that any interaction with any platform possessing generative capabilities constitutes prohibited use, the paper argues that such a position must be stated explicitly
constraints: The paper acknowledges some institutions do restrict tools like Grammarly and makes no claim about universal practice
The paper does not claim to have systematically surveyed every institutional policy
target_learners: higher education students
faculty and misconduct panel members
target_learning_goals: fair application of academic integrity policy
assessment validity
examples: The paper argues a student using a platform solely for OCR transcription of handwritten work into LaTeX has not used the generative function, so a 'generative AI' prohibition is not engaged
key_sources: Craig Wright. (2026). Transcription is not generation: distinguishing non-generative AI tool use from academic misconduct in higher education assessment. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00234-w

article_title: Evaluation Indicator System for AI Certificate Programs
citation: Zijing Wu and Qiang Li. (2026). Evaluation indicator system for AI certificate programs. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00604-x
title: TPACK-extended five-dimension evaluation framework for AI certificate programs
description: The article extends the TPACK framework (Mishra & Koehler, 2006) into program-level credential evaluation by mapping five criteria dimensions onto TPACK components: curriculum design as CK, instructional implementation as PK, technical support as TK, faculty competence as the integrative TPACK core, and a newly added Cross-Cultural Adaptability dimension as TPACK-Extended. The framework comprises three hierarchical layers—Goal (A), Criteria (B1–B5), and Indicators (S1–S20)—operationalized through 20 indicators refined via Delphi consultation. It is used to structure AHP-FAHP weighting of pedagogical transformation potential. The article states the framework "extended TPACK by adding the Cross-Cultural Adaptability dimension (B5)".
requirements: Expert panel input (the article used a stratified purposive sample of 18 experts within the 15–20 range recommended by Saaty for AHP studies) and Delphi refinement of indicators
constraints: The study captures expert perceptions of pedagogical transformation potential, not empirical observations of actual teaching practices; AHP weights represent normative priorities rather than descriptive evidence
target_learners: higher education students in AI certificate programs
target_learning_goals: AI competency development, pedagogical transformation of AI credential programs
examples: The framework was instantiated as Table 1, an indicator system with 9-level Saaty scale anchors for 20 sub-indicators coded S1–S20 across criteria layers B1–B5.

article_title: Evaluation Indicator System for AI Certificate Programs
citation: Zijing Wu and Qiang Li. (2026). Evaluation indicator system for AI certificate programs. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00604-x
title: AI Certificate Pedagogical Transformation Effectiveness Evaluation Indicator System (20 indicators, S1–S20)
description: A structured indicator system (Table 1) operationalizing the five TPACK-mapped criteria dimensions through 20 sub-indicators coded S1–S20, each with 9-level Saaty scale anchors (e.g., S1 curriculum-AI frontier alignment: 1 = highly aligned, 9 = severely disconnected; S6 AI core competency achievement rate; S15 student data privacy protection technical compliance). Indicators were derived from the literature and refined through Delphi expert consultation. Pre-testing confirmed content validity: "88.89% (16 of 18) of experts judged the Saaty scale anchor settings to be consistent with educational realities".
requirements: Delphi expert consultation and pre-testing with the full expert panel for content validity
constraints: All indicators are expert-perceived proxies; the Impact (Effect) metric was not measured in this study and requires longitudinal or experimental data
target_learners: higher education students in AI certificate programs
target_learning_goals: evaluation of AI certificate program quality and pedagogical transformation potential
examples: The system was applied with 18 Chinese experts via two structured questionnaires: an AHP pairwise comparison survey on the 1–9 Saaty scale and a FAHP fuzzy assessment survey on a 5-point Likert scale, with three Delphi rounds at 10-day intervals.

article_title: Profiles and Transitions of Psychological Adaptation in AI-Assisted Japanese Language Learning
citation: Wu Y (2026) Proﬁles and transitions of psychological adaptation in AI-assisted Japanese language learning. Front. Psychol. 17:1837484. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1837484
title: Job Demands–Resources-based demand–resource configuration account of psychological adaptation to AI-assisted language learning
description: The article draws on Job Demands–Resources theory to give its three latent profiles substantive meaning: technostress is treated as a context-specific demand and resilience as a personal resource, so adaptation is "a person-speciﬁc demand–resource conﬁguration." A demand-dominant configuration (high technostress, low resilience) reflects vulnerability to maladaptation, a resource-advantaged configuration (low technostress, high resilience) reflects positive adaptation, and intermediate configurations reflect a tentative balance. The framework also links the profiles to a health-impairment pathway (burnout) and a resource-supported motivational pathway (self-efficacy).
requirements: Both a demand indicator (technostress) and a resource indicator (resilience) must be measured jointly, since adaptation is defined by their configuration rather than either construct alone
constraints: The article states the number and configuration of profiles were not specified in advance, so outcome differences were examined through research questions rather than directional hypotheses
target_learners: tertiary-level learners of Japanese using AI-based tools
target_learning_goals: sustaining psychological adaptation, self-efficacy, and wellbeing in AI-assisted language learning
examples: Latent profile analyses across three waves identified maladaptive, moderate, and positive adaptation profiles whose proportions shifted toward more adaptive configurations over the semester

article_title: Integrating LLM with consortium blockchain for personalized and verifiable online education in higher education
citation: Fuan Xiao, Jiahui Huang, Jia-Xin Huang, Huali Ren and Lang Li. (2026). Integrating LLM with consortium blockchain for personalized and verifiable online education in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00618-5
title: Integrated LLM-plus-consortium-blockchain architecture for accountable online education
description: The article proposes a framework in which "LLM based services provide the intelligent educational interface, while a permissioned consortium blockchain serves as a secure and tamper proof ledger". The LLM layer delivers conversational tutoring, content generation, and automated grading; the blockchain layer records enrollments, grades, certificates, and AI-mediated actions as tamper-evident transactions governed by smart contracts, so AI errors are immutably logged and traceable for accountability. The integration is bidirectional: the AI personalizes instruction using the learner's verifiable on-chain history, while every AI output is anchored on-chain.
requirements: A consortium of authorized institutions (e.g., universities and education authorities) must collectively operate the blockchain nodes and share governance
constraints: Low-risk tutoring interactions are not recorded on-chain to protect privacy; recording learner consultation logs is optional and configurable
target_learners: higher education students in online courses
working professionals in continuous education
target_learning_goals: personalized tutoring and feedback
verifiable academic credentials and assessment
examples: The prototype couples a lightweight LMS front-end with an automated tutoring and grading engine, committing every critical event to a Hyperledger Fabric consortium ledger with off-chain feedback anchored by cryptographic hashes

International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00618-5

title: Hyperledger Fabric prototype with four educational smart contracts

citation: Yan D (2026). A critical narrative synthesis of psychological correlates, measurement, and reported findings on conversational AI engagement and dependence-related constructs. Front. Psychol. 17:1827795. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1827795
title: Provisional framework separating use orientation (instrumental-cognitive vs. relational-emotional) from regulation
description: An interpretive, hypothesis-generating framework organizing conversational-AI engagement along two questions: what users seek (use orientation: mainly instrumental-cognitive or relational-emotional) and how regulated their engagement remains (calibrated vs. increasingly difficult to control). The article states: "At the level of use orientation, engagement may be mainly instrumental-cognitive or relational-emotional." Either orientation may be useful, compensatory, or dysregulated. It was developed during synthesis, not preregistered, and is not a validated factor structure, causal pathway, or developmental sequence.
requirements: Requires independent testing of its temporal ordering, cultural stability, and platform specificity before use as a measurement or causal model
constraints: Not a validated factor structure, causal pathway, or clinical model; developed from the same corpus it organizes and not tested against an independent evidence set

target_learning_goals: Distinguishing instrumental-cognitive from relational-emotional AI use and calibrated from dysregulated engagement
examples: The synthesis coded 22 first-order empirical records into relational-emotional engagement (13), dysregulated dependence (5), and instrumental-cognitive reliance (4) domains

citation: Yan D (2026). A critical narrative synthesis of psychological correlates, measurement, and reported findings on conversational AI engagement and dependence-related constructs. Front. Psychol. 17:1827795. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1827795
title: Construct-boundary taxonomy distinguishing trust, reliance, over-reliance, attachment/companionship, and dysregulated dependence
description: The review argues the literature treats trust, reliance, over-reliance, attachment, companionship, problematic use, and dependence as one continuum when they are non-equivalent constructs. Trust concerns expectations about system competence; reliance is the behavioral decision to delegate; over-reliance is delegation without adequate scrutiny; attachment and companionship concern emotional closeness; and "Dysregulated dependence and problematic use require stronger evidence of impaired control, compulsive return, withdrawal-like discomfort, or negative impact." Conversational-AI engagement serves as the broad, non-pathologizing umbrella term.
requirements: Dependence labeling requires evidence of impaired control or functional harm, not merely frequent use, reliance, or attachment
constraints: The taxonomy is an interpretive organization of the corpus, not a validated latent structure
target_learners: Researchers, instrument developers, and educators interpreting AI-use measures
target_learning_goals: Construct separation and design-matched claims about AI engagement and dependence
examples: Table 2 maps each construct to core meaning, typical indicators, and main interpretive risk, e.g. confusing positive expectations with behavioral delegation for trust

title: Monitor conversational-AI use for well-being rather than diagnosing dependence from frequency, attachment, or platform use alone
description: For mental health and digital well-being, the review recommends monitoring rather than clinical thresholds: conversational AI may provide disclosure, perceived support, or temporary loneliness relief when human support is scarce. It states the current literature "does not justify diagnosing dependence from frequency, attachment, or platform use alone." Frequent use, reliance, or attachment should not be labeled dependence without impaired control or harm, while supportive experiences do not rule out dysregulation or substitution risk.
requirements: Assessment must separately evidence impaired control or functional harm before dependence labeling
constraints: Evidence for short-term benefits is limited and context dependent; no single platform feature has been shown to cause dependence
target_learners: Conversational-AI users, including students, companion-app users, and clinically vulnerable groups flagged for future study
target_learning_goals: Healthy calibration of AI engagement and preservation of human ties and independent judgment
examples: The review identifies anthropomorphic language, exclusivity, emotional reinforcement, continuity, and frictionless return as design features raising testable questions about deepening engagement

citation: Ye, P.-G., Mo, K., Long, Y., Liu, M., Sang, H., & Zheng, J. (2026). ARPG+: a simulation-based study of real-time coaching for educational LLM prompting. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00606-9
title: Six-dimensional prompt quality vector as a diagnostic, comparable, and policy-relevant representation
description: ARPG+ models prompt quality as a six-dimensional vector covering "structural completeness, semantic clarity, contextual grounding, task specificity, constraint explicitness, and output conventions." The representation is described as diagnostic (each dimension maps to concrete coaching actions), comparable across time (enabling progress tracking), and policy-relevant (feeding safety and benefit terms). The authors state the dimension choice is "an informed design commitment rather than the output of an empirical dimensionality search," anchored in prior prompt-engineering and AI-literacy work.
requirements: Each dimension maps to concrete coaching actions (e.g., low structural completeness suggests adding a skeleton; low semantic clarity triggers a disambiguating question).
constraints: The authors state the six dimensions are an informed design commitment, not the output of an empirical dimensionality search; empirical refinement including confirmatory factor analysis on real-learner corpora is identified as a priority.
target_learners: Novice LLM users learning to prompt
target_learning_goals: Prompt engineering skill
AI literacy
examples: Each dimension maps to a micro-action: low structural completeness yields a skeleton hint; weak contextual grounding suggests a citation or data reference; missing output conventions offers a format example.

citation: Ye, P.-G., Mo, K., Long, Y., Liu, M., Sang, H., & Zheng, J. (2026). ARPG+: a simulation-based study of real-time coaching for educational LLM prompting. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00606-9
title: Operationalizing cognitive load theory and ZPD into real-time coaching signals
description: The article transforms cognitive load theory and zone of proximal development into "calibratable, real-time signals": an overload-risk estimator grounded in intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load proxies; a normalized Struggle Index quantifying interactional friction from editing and pausing behaviors; and an uncertainty-aware ability tracker maintaining dynamic ZPD boundaries. Overload risk is computed via a capacity-normalized sigmoid mapping that discounts germane effort as beneficial. ZPD is represented as a time-varying band [µt − κσt, µt + κσt] compared against estimated task demand.
requirements: Lightweight telemetry (dwell time, edits, revokes, hint clicks) and prompt text features must be available each turn to populate load proxies and capability beliefs.
constraints: All computations are validated only on LLM-based simulated learners; the authors state this does not constitute empirical validation with real students.
target_learners: Novice LLM users across cognitive profiles
target_learning_goals: Prompting skill development
Metacognitive regulation of effort
examples: The coach increases help when task demand exceeds the ZPD upper boundary, reduces help when demand falls well below, and treats overload risk exceeding tolerance as above-ZPD regardless of demand.

title: ARPG+ dual-process real-time coaching system
description: ARPG+ is a hierarchical real-time coaching system coupling "a lightweight fast path with selectively triggered deep analysis under explicit latency budgets." A unified trigger variable combines abrupt quality shifts, sustained struggle, safety concerns, and scheduled probes into one decision. The system senses prompt drafts, conversation history, and telemetry; interprets them through cognitive load, ZPD, and metacognitive lenses; decides between fast-path and deep-path interventions; and acts with adaptive type, granularity, and intensity. Latency budgets are 50 ms for the fast path and 300 ms for the deep path.
requirements: A dual-model architecture separating behavior generation from independent evaluation; calibrated hyperparameters including overload tolerance ρ = 0.7 and ZPD multiplier κ = 1.5.
constraints: Evaluated only with LLM-based simulated learners; the authors state this is evidence of system feasibility and simulation-based performance, not educational effectiveness.
target_learners: Novice to advanced LLM users in educational settings
target_learning_goals: Prompt quality improvement
Independence from coaching support
Cognitive load management
examples: Most turns finish on the fast path within budget; the deep path is reserved for moments that are difficult, risky, or diagnostically valuable.

title: Four-dimension feedback perception framework (objectivity, usefulness, genuineness, credibility)
description: The study adopts, from Nazaretsky et al., a framework in which student perceptions of feedback comprise "four key dimensions: objectivity, usefulness, genuineness, and the credibility of the feedback provider." Objectivity concerns fair, factual alignment between feedback content and actual performance; usefulness measures how meaningful and pertinent the feedback is for improvement; genuineness indicates authenticity and personal significance; and credibility concerns whether the provider is seen as trustworthy and well-intentioned. article_title: Designing for Authentic Assessment: A Scoping Review
citation: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Zilu Du. (2025). Designing for authentic assessment: a scoping review. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-025-01588-9
title: Six-dimensional framework of authentic assessment characteristics in and beyond workplaces
description: The review proposes a six-dimensional framework for authentic assessment (AA) characteristics consisting of authenticity in assessment, cognitive challenges, assessment criteria, feedback, student agency and social collaboration. It extends prior frameworks (Gulikers et al. 2004; Ashford-Rowe et al. 2014; Villarroel et al. 2018) by distinguishing multiple meanings of authenticity — assessment, professional, digital, self and social authenticity — and by adding student agency and social collaboration as design elements. The review states it 'underscores the design of student agency, which enables students to integrate their knowledge, actions and identity across various practices'. The framework was used to code the 37 included studies.
requirements: Assessment designs must be coded against all six dimensions to determine whether and how design elements are incorporated
constraints: The framework's novelty rests on few studies addressing the broader (student and societal) perspectives of authenticity
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: authentic assessment design that supports meaningful engagement, employability and societal contribution
examples: The authors used the framework to systematically code how 37 empirical studies designed authentic assessment, calculating the number of studies mentioning each design element.

citation: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Zilu Du. (2025). Designing for authentic assessment: a scoping review. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-025-01588-9
title: Learning-oriented and collaborative four-step design framework for authentic assessment
description: To address the design challenges of professional-authenticity dominance, passive student roles and lack of care and connection, the review proposes a learning-oriented and collaborative design framework for AA. It is 'a cyclical and recursive process which involves four steps': (1) deciding assessment goals and focus through collaborative negotiation between educators and students; (2) creating assessment context and task mirroring real-world scenarios; (3) designing assessment criteria and student engagement, including co-designed criteria and judgement activities such as peer assessment; and (4) planning feedback and students' self-reflection that is learning- and future-oriented and transformative.
requirements: Critical conversations between students and important others (institutions, educators, industry professionals, wider society) to align tasks with real-world expectations and students' needs
constraints: Designers must manage a trade-off between authenticity and feasibility, balancing real-world task complexity with practical constraints of the learning environment
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: meaningful engagement, evaluative judgement, ownership of assessment, preparation for post-graduation work and social development
examples: The framework responds to the review's findings that only three studies considered social authenticity, only eight gave students choices, and only five connected students with industry or community partners.

The framework positions educators as guides who balance GenAI's automation and personalization affordances against integrity, bias, and transparency risks in computer science education.

description: The CTAT student model specifies four CT constructs — Data, Conditionals, Loops, and Testing and Debugging — as the focal knowledge, skills, and abilities measured in an AI training context. It combines Brennan and Resnick's CT concepts-and-practices framework with Tedre et al.'s CT 2.0 framework, which "brings in data-driven and AI-related practices". The article states: "As a result, four CT constructs were selected: Data, Conditionals, Loops, and Testing and Debugging, which align with the AI training process". Items use a notebook-style Python interface with schematic diagrams and visual symbols to reduce literacy and code-comprehension barriers, and combine AI model training tasks with text-based programming.

citation: Zhenxin Zhang, Ziyu Ding, Mengyun Liu and Haiwei Sang. (2026). RACES: reward-aligned consistent essay scoring with large language models. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00607-8
title: RACES: a reward-aligned, consistency-regularized framework for LLM-based automated essay scoring
description: RACES (Reward-Aligned Consistent Essay Scoring) is a unified AES framework that "integrates LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning, reward modeling, and PPO with KL regularization". It runs an offline inference–feedback–optimization loop: LoRA SFT establishes basic score-label mapping with standardized prompts; a reward model learns ranking preferences between preferred proxy responses and harder negative samples; PPO with KL divergence and critic constraints optimizes the policy while limiting distribution drift. Alignment is proxy-based, using LLM-generated feedback rather than human-written comments.
requirements: Human-assigned score labels (ASAP 2.0 scores) as ground truth, plus auxiliary LLM-generated feedback comments for reward modeling
A frozen reference model for the KL penalty and a frozen reward model initializing the critic
constraints: Evaluated offline on a single public dataset with synthetic proxy feedback; alignment is proxy-based rather than fully human-grounded
No full component-level ablation or matched comparison with other alignment methods yet
target_learners: higher-education students whose essays undergo large-scale writing assessment
target_learning_goals: reliable preliminary scoring of argumentative essays to support writing evaluation and identification of borderline cases for human review
examples: The framework was instantiated with LLaMA2-7B and Qwen2.5-Instruct-7B policy models and GPT2-XL or Mistral-7B reward models, trained on the ASAP 2.0 dataset

description: Appraisal Theory extends the interpersonal metafunction within Systemic Functional Linguistics and, as the article states, "provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing evaluative meaning in discourse". It comprises three subsystems — Attitude (Affect, Judgement, Appreciation), Engagement (Monoglossic vs. Heteroglossic, with Contract and Expand), and Graduation (Force and Focus). The study applies it, with particular focus on Engagement, to code 16,234 appraisal instances across 168 essays and compare dialogic positioning across draft types.

constraints: Justify is a later extension to the Proclaim system introduced by White (2012), not part of the original framework
