title: Closed-loop adaptive teaching assistance model integrating perception, evaluation, generation and feedback for music education
description: The article proposes an adaptive teaching assistance model for music education organized as a closed-loop path of "perception evaluation generation feedback". Student performance audio and multidimensional behavioral data build a big data repository; a multimodal contrastive learning transformer aligns audio features with symbolic music knowledge via cosine similarity loss; analysis results are mapped into a reward space; and the PPO algorithm fine-tunes generation parameters in real time so that output scores and accompaniments adapt to learner progress. The design forms "a reverse drive from evaluation to generation", establishing "an automated closed loop from monitoring to generation to intervention".
requirements: Performance audio capture and standard digital score input must be available so the CMT can align heterogeneous modalities in a shared high-dimensional space
The big data analysis module must quantify performance into reward signals and capability defect matrices to constrain the PPO generation policy
constraints: The article states educational statements should be interpreted within the scope of testing conditions and technical proxy indicators reported
The system was validated as a technical framework with the educational comparison serving as an auxiliary demonstration
target_learners: undergraduate music majors
target_learning_goals: instrumental performance skills in pitch, rhythm and dynamic control
personalized practice content matched to learner skill level
examples: In the 12-week quasi-experiment the experimental group used the adaptive system for real-time feedback and generated exercise tracks while the control group received traditional teacher-led verbal feedback
key_sources: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703

article_title: Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics
citation: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703
title: Cross-modal transformer (CMT) module aligning performance audio with symbolic score features
description: The Cross-Modal Transformer is the feature-alignment core of the model, chosen over simple concatenation or additive attention because it "dynamically captures cross-modal correlations via the cross-attention mechanism". Audio is represented with MFCC features at a 44,100 Hz sampling rate and the score modality uses 512-dimensional word embeddings; both are fused in a 1,024-dimensional CMT architecture (6 layers, 8 attention heads, ~48M parameters) trained with a contrastive loss using cosine similarity, batch size N and temperature τ = 0.07. The module outputs aligned feature vectors that feed both the big data analysis module and the generative AI module.
requirements: Synchronous PCM audio input and digitized score text in Event Encoding Sequence Format
Pre-training of the CMT feature extraction layers (on MAESTRO v3.0.0) before the layers are frozen for deployment
constraints: CQT was computed only for auxiliary visualization and was not provided to the model; all reported performance metrics reflect MFCC-based processing only
Piano and guitar practice excerpts were restricted to monophonic melodic lines to maintain compatibility with the audio processing pipeline
target_learners: undergraduate music majors learning piano, violin, flute or guitar
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis of pitch, rhythm and expressive deviations in student performance
examples: The architecture configuration fixed 6 layers, 8 attention heads, hidden dimension 1,024, dropout 0.1, and sinusoidal positional encoding across all experiments
key_sources: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703

article_title: Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics
citation: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703
title: Multidimensional performance evaluation and reward-mapping module using DTW, GMM and weighted Euclidean distance
description: The big data analysis module quantifies learner performance along three dimensions: rhythm stability via Dynamic Time Warping (±15 ms threshold, weight 0.35), pitch accuracy via Gaussian Mixture Model fitting (±10 cents, weight 0.40), and dynamic control via velocity mapping (±8 levels, weight 0.25). Dimensions are min-max normalized and aggregated with a weighted Euclidean distance into a comprehensive evaluation score D, which is mapped into real-time reward signals Rt and capability defect matrices Mt used as constraints for the PPO framework. Thresholds were derived from expert consensus among three senior instructors rating 50 pilot recordings, with weights assigned via the Analytic Hierarchy Process.
requirements: Expert-derived error thresholds and AHP-assigned weights fixed across experiments to maintain a consistent evaluation standard
Relaxed thresholds (±20 ms, ±15 cents) for absolute beginners during the first 2 weeks of intervention to prevent over-correction
constraints: Thresholds were held constant across instruments and proficiency levels on the stated rationale that perceptual criteria for rhythmic stability and pitch accuracy are instrument-independent
target_learners: undergraduate music majors
target_learning_goals: objective diagnosis of skill gaps in rhythm, pitch and dynamics
examples: Inter-annotator agreement for expert annotation of the 4,320 recordings was κ = 0.87 for pitch accuracy, rhythmic stability and dynamic control
key_sources: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703

article_title: Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics
citation: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703
title: PPO reinforcement learning generative policy converting evaluation signals into adaptive exercise tracks
description: The generative module uses Proximal Policy Optimization with a clipped-surrogate objective to convert teaching evaluation indicators into reward functions and adjust generation parameters in real time. The state is the learner's performance feature vector plus current exercise difficulty; actions are a three-dimensional continuous vector controlling tempo multiplier (0.7–1.3), dynamic range compression (0.5–1.5) and note density factor (0.6–1.4). The per-step reward Rt = −Dt + αΔDt balances current accuracy against progress with α = 0.3, each step corresponding to 30 s of practice; PPO used clipping coefficient 0.2, γ = 0.99, GAE λ = 0.95, and training stopped when validation reward did not improve for 30 consecutive episodes.
requirements: The skill deficiency probability matrix output by the big data analysis module as input to the generative network
A decoder with temporal memory (recursive neural network with attention-based mask decoding) to synthesize MIDI sequences and waveform parameters
constraints: PPO was selected partly because clipping prevents destructive policy changes that could collapse the artistic logic of generated songs during excessive parameter updates
target_learners: undergraduate music majors
target_learning_goals: generated practice exercises matched to the learner's real-time skill progression
examples: Each 60-min session constituted one episode of 120 time steps, with episodic return the sum of per-step rewards over the 120 steps
key_sources: Zhu Z, Luo C and Li L (2026) Adaptive teaching assistance model combining generative AI and big data analytics. Front. Psychol. 17:1844703. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1844703

title: MAESTRO v3.0.0 pretraining corpus and custom 4,320-recording student dataset
description: The study used two data sources. For initial pretraining of the CMT's feature extraction layers it used the MAESTRO v3.0.0 dataset (https://magenta.tensorflow.org/datasets/maestro, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), containing "approximately 200 h of solo piano performances (1,276 MIDI-aligned audio recordings)"; the authors argue solo-piano pretraining transfers to other tonal instruments because the CMT learns cross-modal alignment at the score-feature level. For the educational study it built a custom repository of approximately 4,320 audio recordings (120 participants × 12 weeks × 3 excerpts) totaling 2,160 minutes, annotated by two expert instructors with inter-annotator agreement κ = 0.87.
requirements: Participant-level split into training (70%, N = 84), validation (15%, N = 18) and test (15%, N = 18) partitions with no within-participant cross-partition leakage
Feature normalization using only training-set statistics to prevent information leakage
constraints: No participant, session, or musical excerpt overlap between the pretraining corpus and the student dataset; MAESTRO samples were used solely to initialize foundational layers
All model components were finalized before the 12-week intervention; the system operated solely in fixed-policy inference mode with no online learning
target_learners: undergraduate music majors with ≥ 3 years of formal training on piano, violin, flute or guitar
target_learning_goals: model pretraining for cross-modal audio-score alignment
evaluation of adaptive feedback in instrumental practice
examples: Repertoire covered Baroque (30%), Classical (35%), Romantic (20%), and Contemporary (15%) styles, with instruments distributed piano n = 48, violin n = 32, flute n = 24, guitar n = 16

article_title: Against frictionless AI
citation: Emily Zohar, Paul Bloom & Michael Inzlicht. (2026). Against frictionless AI. Communications Psychology 4:39. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-026-00402-1
title: Friction as a construct: difficulty during goal pursuit that enhances learning, meaning, and motivation
description: The article defines friction as "the experience of difficulty during goal pursuit, often accompanied by negative feelings like frustration and corrective feedback" and argues it "enhances learning, generates meaning and pleasure, and makes us better people." It organizes the comment around applying this construct to intellectual work and social relationships, warning that frictionless AI strips away beneficial friction along with excess friction.
requirements: Friction must be moderate rather than excessive to produce benefits
constraints: The authors state friction's benefits are not unlimited; excessive friction overwhelms
target_learners: AI users in academic and everyday settings
learners at earlier developmental stages
target_learning_goals: deeper comprehension and retention
meaningful engagement with work
examples: The article contrasts a hiker reaching a summit through sustained effort with someone taking a chairlift to the same destination

article_title: Against frictionless AI
citation: Emily Zohar, Paul Bloom & Michael Inzlicht. (2026). Against frictionless AI. Communications Psychology 4:39. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-026-00402-1
title: Harness AI's benefits while preserving the friction that drives learning, connection, and meaning
description: The article recommends preserving beneficial friction when adopting AI: "The goal should be to harness AI'sb e n eﬁts while preserving the friction that makes us human— the struggle that teaches us, the loneliness that connects us, and the effort that gives our achievements meaning." It applies this by timing AI use to developmental stage and reserving frictionless AI for cases where friction offers little benefit.
requirements: Distinguish excess friction, which offers little benefit, from beneficial friction worth preserving
Match AI use to the user's developmental stage and existing skills
constraints: The authors concede AI's benefits are often overwhelming in intellectual work and it would be perverse to abandon it in some cases, even if valuable friction is sacrificed
target_learners: younger learners in earlier developmental stages
professionals in later career stages using AI as a supplement
target_learning_goals: deeper comprehension and retention
perseverance and willingness to strive
meaningful engagement
examples: The article recommends that younger learners, like students asked to show their work even when calculators exist, need to struggle, reason, and revise through the full process before benefiting from shortcuts

article_title: \"Is this a trap?\": Student teachers' perceptions and adoption of GenAI in assessments in three teacher education courses
citation: Zou, T. X. P., Hounsell, D., Huijser, H., & Tse, R. T. L. (2026). “Is this a trap?”: Student teachers’ perceptions and adoption of GenAI in assessments in three teacher education courses. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 1–17. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10549
title: Maintain consistent GenAI assessment policies and communicate them clearly to students
description: The study concludes that GenAI assessment policy should be consistent and communicated effectively. It states that "This study shows the importance of consistent assessment policies and effective communication", and that "Effective communication with students about what GenAI usage is or is not allowed in assessment is critical to avoid misunderstanding." The principle directs instructors to state explicitly what GenAI use is permitted in each assessment so students are not left guessing.
requirements: Instructors must specify what GenAI usage is or is not allowed in each assessment and convey this clearly to students.
target_learners: teacher education students in higher education
target_learning_goals: authentic demonstration of learning in non-exam assessments without unwanted GenAI reliance
examples: The three teacher education courses embedded GenAI use in assessment with declarations of GenAI use in submitted assignments, and the study derived the communication recommendation from students' reported misunderstandings and concerns.

title: Personalise or contextualise assessments to reduce students' reliance on GenAI
description: Among the article's implications for practice or policy, it states that "Personalising and/or contextualising assessments helps reduce students' reliance on GenAI." The principle holds that assessment tasks tied to students' own contexts give them less reason or opportunity to offload work to GenAI, addressing the assessment-design reasons students gave for their adoption decisions.

target_learning_goals: independent completion of assessments with reduced GenAI reliance

Its implications add that "Course leaders should consider the overall policy and context for using GenAI in assessment beyond their own courses." This addresses inconsistency students encounter when policies differ across a programme.

title: Socio-technical view of student GenAI adoption in assessment
description: The study adopts "a socio-technical view that recognises the sociocultural and technological factors influencing students’ behaviours" toward GenAI in assessment. Rather than treating GenAI use as an individual choice alone, this framing explains adoption decisions as shaped jointly by assessment design, perceived value, self-confidence, plagiarism concerns, and course policies, which is why the authors recommend policy and communication interventions at course and programme level.

target_learning_goals: understanding and regulating students' use of GenAI in completing assessments

citation: Yanhong Zuo, Xiatinghan Xu, Leigh Ann Dunning. (2026). “Will AI steal my glory?”: Power relations perceived by college instructors when grappling with Generative AI. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(1), 31-50. https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.1.8
title: Four power centers shape college instructors' perceptions of Generative AI in writing instruction
description: The study proposes a polycentric account of instructor sense-making around Generative AI: instructors' perceptions are shaped not by a single authority but by four interacting centers. As the abstract states, inductive analysis identifies centers "including the global impact of AI, the university and department, colleagues, and students." This framework organizes how writing instructors weigh external, institutional, peer, and learner pressures when deciding how to respond to GenAI in their courses.

constraints: Derived from an instrumental case study of college instructors in writing instruction
target_learners: College instructors teaching writing
target_learning_goals: Understanding and responding to Generative AI in writing instruction
examples: The study's inductive analysis of college instructors grappling with Generative AI identified the four centers as the forces shaping their perceptions.

article_title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
citation: Rose E. Wang, Ana T. Ribeiro, Carly D. Robinson, Susanna Loeb, and Dora Demszky. (2025). Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise. arXiv:2410.03017v2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03017v2
title: Tutor CoPilot: an in-platform Human-AI tool giving tutors real-time, customizable expert-like guidance
description: Tutor CoPilot is a Human-AI system embedded in a virtual tutoring platform (problem display, shared whiteboard, chat window) as "a new Tutor CoPilot button" tutors activate during sessions. It pulls the conversation context, lesson topic, and chosen strategy, de-identifies names via placeholders, limits shared context to the 10 most recent messages, and generates expert-like suggestions using the Bridge method. Tutors can edit, regenerate, or switch strategies (e.g., provide a hint, worked example, similar problem). It recorded 2,000+ uses at an estimated cost of $20 per tutor annually.
requirements: Integration into a live tutoring platform with chat-based conversation context, lesson topic, and a strategy selection mechanism
De-identification of student and tutor names before sending context to external LM services
constraints: Currently chat-based; adapting to in-person tutoring would require processing speech or visual inputs
Privacy safeguard limits shared conversation context to the 10 most recent messages, and pilots found tutors preferred interaction quality with more context included
Tutors reported suggestions occasionally lacked alignment with students' grade levels
target_learners: K-12 students in grades 3-8 from Title I, historically under-served communities (80% Hispanic, 67% economically disadvantaged)
target_learning_goals: Mastery of grade-level mathematics lesson topics, assessed by exit-ticket passage
examples: Pilot studies with 10-20 tutors surfaced a response-time bottleneck — the tool took longer than 30 seconds to respond — which was fixed before deployment; the second pilot showed significant response time improvements and strong tutor satisfaction
key_sources: Rose E. Wang, Ana T. Ribeiro, Carly D. Robinson, Susanna Loeb, and Dora Demszky. (2025). Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise. arXiv:2410.03017v2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03017

article_title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
citation: Rose E. Wang, Ana T. Ribeiro, Carly D. Robinson, Susanna Loeb, and Dora Demszky. (2025). Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise. arXiv:2410.03017v2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03017v2
title: Taxonomy of high-quality strategies that foster understanding versus low-quality strategies that lead students to the solution
description: The article defines a two-category taxonomy of tutor moves in mathematics tutoring, drawing on prior work. High-quality strategies "foster students' understanding": prompting the student to explain, asking questions to guide thinking, and affirming the student's correct attempt. Low-quality strategies "lead students directly to the solution or passively engage students": asking the student to retry, giving away the answer/explanation, giving away the solution strategy, and encouraging the student in a generic way. Binary RoBERTa classifiers identified these strategies at scale with F1-scores between 0.65 and 0.90.
requirements: Labeled message data to train classifiers (3,000 sampled tutor messages, GPT-4 first-pass labeling, manual verification, fine-tuning with class-balancing loss)
constraints: Developed for K-12 mathematics tutoring chat interactions
target_learners: K-12 mathematics students in grades 3-8
target_learning_goals: Deeper conceptual understanding of mathematics rather than task completion
examples: Table 1 lists each strategy with definitions, examples (e.g., 'What number can we multiply the number 10 to get an equal value of 100?'), frequency over the labeled dataset, and test F1 score
key_sources: Rose E. Wang, Ana T. Ribeiro, Carly D. Robinson, Susanna Loeb, and Dora Demszky. (2025). Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise. arXiv:2410.03017v2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03017

article_title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
citation: Rose E. Wang, Ana T. Ribeiro, Carly D. Robinson, Susanna Loeb, and Dora Demszky. (2025). Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise. arXiv:2410.03017v2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03017v2
title: Human-AI real-time expertise scaling: models of expert thinking embedded in human workflows complement human contextual knowledge
description: The article's theory of change holds that many tutors lack the experience to respond effectively in the moment, producing low-quality responses like generic feedback or giving away the answer. "By offering real-time guidance tailored to the conversation and following high-quality strategies, Tutor CoPilot empowers tutors with the right language to develop the student's understanding." The approach combines complementary strengths: AI lacks educators' grounded, context-specific knowledge of curricula, assessment standards, and individual students, but can provide real-time guidance during instructional moments, while the human selects expert-curated strategies — without which LMs tend to default to repetitive strategies.
requirements: Extraction of latent expert reasoning (via think-aloud protocols, as in the Bridge method) to adapt LMs to generate expert-like suggestions
A human in the loop selecting expert-curated strategies to instruct the LM
constraints: Out-of-the-box LMs trained on Web data often fail in real-world learning settings; fine-tuning and prompt engineering focus on surface-level language patterns and overlook latent reasoning processes
Transferability to other domains depends on specific tasks, workflows, and levels of domain complexity
target_learners: Novice educators (tutors) serving K-12 students from under-served communities
target_learning_goals: Improved quality of live instructional interactions and student mathematics mastery
examples: Tutor CoPilot operationalizes the model by generating suggestions from the de-identified conversation, lesson topic, and chosen strategy, lightening tutors' cognitive load by eliminating the need to prompt the model themselves

article_title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
citation: Nataliya Kosmyna, Eugene Hauptmann, Ye Tong Yuan, Jessica Situ, Xian-Hao Liao, Ashly Vivian Beresnitzky, Iris Braunstein, Pattie Maes. (2009). Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task. Preprint, under review. https://www.brainonllm.com/
title: Cognitive debt: accumulated cognitive cost of relying on an AI assistant for essay writing
description: The article's organizing account is that using an LLM for essay writing accrues a "Cognitive Debt" — a cumulative cost carried across sessions, visible as reduced neural connectivity, impaired quoting and memory, and low ownership even after the tool is removed. It frames this via cognitive offloading concerns, arguing that reduced immediate cognitive load may come at the price of diminished engagement in deep analytical processes during learning tasks.
requirements: The account is grounded in a four-session longitudinal design with EEG, NLP, and interview measures, including the session-4 crossover reassignment of participants.
constraints: The authors present the study as a preliminary guide to understanding cognitive and practical impacts of AI on learning environments, not a definitive account.
target_learners: adult essay writers (participants writing SAT-style essays)
target_learning_goals: essay writing
memory and recall of one's own writing
critical engagement with produced text
examples: Session 4 crossover: LLM-to-Brain participants wrote without tools and showed weaker connectivity; Brain-to-LLM participants showed a connectivity spike across bands.
key_sources: Nataliya Kosmyna, Eugene Hauptmann, Ye Tong Yuan, Jessica Situ, Xian-Hao Liao, Ashly Vivian Beresnitzky, Iris Braunstein, Pattie Maes. (2009). Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task. Preprint, under review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08872

article_title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
citation: Nataliya Kosmyna, Eugene Hauptmann, Ye Tong Yuan, Jessica Situ, Xian-Hao Liao, Ashly Vivian Beresnitzky, Iris Braunstein, Pattie Maes. (2009). Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task. Preprint, under review. https://www.brainonllm.com/
title: Treat LLM assistance in essay-writing instruction cautiously, since sustained reliance was associated with reduced neural engagement, ownership, and recall
description: The article recommends that educators treat LLM use in writing tasks as carrying measurable cognitive costs: over four sessions, LLM users showed the weakest neural coupling, low essay ownership, and reduced ability to quote their own essays, and the authors argue this demonstrates "a likely decrease in learning skills". The principle is to preserve AI-free writing experiences so learners retain strong engagement, rather than defaulting to LLM assistance.
requirements: Learners need opportunities for tool-free essay writing to maintain strong neural engagement, ownership, and quoting ability as observed in the Brain-only group.
constraints: The authors offer the study as a preliminary guide; the Search Engine group had no session 4, and only 18 of 54 participants completed session 4.
target_learners: students writing essays in educational contexts

memory encoding of one's own text
sense of ownership over produced work

article_title: LearnLens: LLM-Enabled Personalised, Curriculum-Grounded Feedback with Educators in the Loop
citation: Runcong Zhao, Artem Bobrov, Jiazheng Li, Cesare Aloisi, Yulan He. (2025). LearnLens: LLM-Enabled Personalised, Curriculum-Grounded Feedback with Educators in the Loop. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04295
title: LearnLens: a dual-interface LLM feedback system with error-aware assessment, curriculum-grounded generation, and educator oversight
description: LearnLens is a modular LLM-based system for personalised, curriculum-aligned feedback in science education. It comprises an error-aware assessment module that captures nuanced reasoning errors, a curriculum-grounded generation module using a structured topic-linked memory chain, and an educator-in-the-loop interface for customisation and oversight. Teacher tools include student grouping, quiz creation, curriculum-aligned rubric generation, performance visualisation, and interactive feedback modification; a separate student interface delivers timely, tailored feedback.
requirements: Requires local LLM deployment to address student data privacy concerns
Requires a curated bank of pre-authored questions and curriculum-aligned mark schemes
constraints: The demo focuses on GCSE science, though the authors state it can be tailored to students across all educational levels
No student evaluation has been conducted; the authors acknowledge this and plan to address it in future work
target_learners: GCSE science students
target_learning_goals: Science conceptual understanding and reasoning
Timely, actionable feedback on short-essay science answers
examples: Teachers create quizzes tied to national curriculum topics, generate mark schemes with extended reasoning time, and refine flagged feedback through a conversational interface, with edits applicable to a single question or propagated across the entire quiz

article_title: LearnLens: LLM-Enabled Personalised, Curriculum-Grounded Feedback with Educators in the Loop
citation: Runcong Zhao, Artem Bobrov, Jiazheng Li, Cesare Aloisi, Yulan He. (2025). LearnLens: LLM-Enabled Personalised, Curriculum-Grounded Feedback with Educators in the Loop. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04295
title: Chain-of-Concept: topic-graph organisation of past assessments replacing similarity-based retrieval
description: Chain-of-Concept is the article's framework for curriculum-grounded retrieval. Rather than storing past assessment records sequentially and relying on surface-level embedding similarity, it organises records as a topic graph in which questions are decomposed into sub-question nodes labelled with curriculum topics, and retrieval is confined to the topic subgraph matching the query's topics. The authors state that topic filtering removes cross-topic noise, yielding more coherent evidence, and that the module then analyses pupil errors and prior knowledge to choose the most effective feedback strategy.
requirements: Questions must be decomposed into sub-question nodes and labelled with one or more curriculum topics
A FAISS-based ranker is used for scoring within the filtered topic subgraph
constraints: Retrieval is confined to the topic subgraph matching the query's tagged topics, so records sharing no topic with the query are excluded
target_learners: GCSE science students
target_learning_goals: Personalised, curriculum-aligned feedback generation
examples: Figure 3 contrasts traditional RAG, where records are stored sequentially without explicit logical structure, with the proposed approach organising past assessments by topic-level relationships

article_title: Comprehensive Review of Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Meriem Zerkouk, Miloud Mihoubi and Belkacem Chikhaoui. (2025). A Comprehensive Review of AI-based Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Applications and Challenges. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18882
title: Four-component architecture of Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Domain Model, Student Model, Tutor Model, and User Interface
description: The review describes the four-component architecture as "a widely accepted framework for defining ITS". The Domain Model encapsulates concepts, rules, and problem-solving strategies as an expert knowledge base for assessing performance and identifying errors. The Student Model continuously monitors learners' progress, adapting to cognitive and affective states, often refined with Bayesian networks, ML algorithms, and data mining. The Tutor Model determines instructional strategies and when and how to intervene, while the User Interface facilitates student-system communication using human-computer interaction principles.
requirements: Requires a Domain Model representing the subject matter so student input can be compared against expert knowledge for accurate feedback
Requires a Student Model continuously updated from learner interactions to predict student needs and learning paths
target_learners: Learners in traditional classrooms and online learning platforms
Distance learners and students in large classrooms
target_learning_goals: Individualized instruction and personalized feedback across subject domains
Real-time feedback and adaptation to varied learning paces
examples: The review illustrates the architecture with Figure 1, citing [62], and notes methods such as Bayesian networks and ML algorithms are employed to refine the Student Model's accuracy

article_title: Comprehensive Review of Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Meriem Zerkouk, Miloud Mihoubi and Belkacem Chikhaoui. (2025). A Comprehensive Review of AI-based Intelligent Tutoring Systems: Applications and Challenges. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18882
title: Taxonomy of pedagogical strategies in ITS: rule-based/expert systems, case-based reasoning, and cognitive tutors, grounded in established learning theories
description: The review organizes ITS pedagogical strategies into rule-based and expert systems using if-then rules and knowledge bases, case-based reasoning systems matching current learner situations to stored past cases, and cognitive tutors providing step-by-step guidance based on cognitive models of knowledge acquisition. It states these strategies "are often implemented using rule-based systems, expert systems, case-based reasoning, and cognitive tutors". The review also links designs to learning theories: constructivist theory supports exploratory and problem-based scenarios, Self-Regulated Learning theory is reflected in learner modeling and formative feedback, and Cognitive Load Theory guides task complexity adjustment and stepwise hints.
requirements: CBR success depends on the quality and relevance of stored cases
Accurate cognitive models for cognitive tutors require extensive domain expertise and iterative refinement
constraints: Rule-based and expert systems can be complex to develop and maintain for domains with many rules
Cognitive tutors can be resource-intensive and their effectiveness varies by implementation and context
CBR systems can become computationally intensive when retrieving cases from large datasets
target_learners: Students in domains such as mathematics, programming, physics, and medical diagnosis
target_learning_goals: Individualized problem-solving support
Personalized instruction and feedback adapted to learner responses
examples: Named systems include GUIDON and the LISP Tutor for medical diagnosis, AutoTutor, CBR-Tutor, CBR-Works, Carnegie Learning's Cognitive Tutor, ACT-R Tutors, SQL-Tutor, Andes Physics Tutor, and Electronix Tutor

title: Systematic review corpus of 127 included ITS studies selected via PRISMA from 37,617 initial records
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus assembled through a Kitchenham-style systematic literature search across Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Springer. The selection process states that "37,617 articles were initially identified, 9,485 were eliminated after deduplication, 2,112 were excluded after screening titles and abstracts, and finally, 127 articles were included for full review, supplemented by 26 reports from specialized web sources". Inclusion criteria required evaluation of educational effectiveness in real learning environments, empirical data, validation of 6 weeks or more, samples of 100 or more participants, and peer-reviewed English-language papers.

constraints: Studies outside real learning environments, prototypes without evaluation results, validations under 6 weeks, and samples under 100 participants were excluded

target_learning_goals: Understanding how ITS operate in real educational settings and their pedagogical effectiveness

citation: Jiayi Wang, Ruiwei Xiao, Xinying Hou, John Stamper. (2025). Enabling Multi-Agent Systems as Learning Designers: Applying Learning Sciences to AI Instructional Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16659
title: Knowledge–Learning–Instruction (KLI) framework as an organizing theory for AI instructional design
description: The KLI framework connects knowledge components, learning processes, and instructional principles to support robust learning. The article states that "effective instruction requires careful alignment among three core elements": Knowledge Components as the goals of learning, Learning Processes describing how learning occurs, and Instructional Principles as the methods facilitating those processes. The authors use KLI to guide the reasoning of their multi-agent systems, grounding AI instructional design in an evidence-based instructional theory rather than leaving pedagogy to user prompts.

constraints: The study was limited to a single pedagogical framework (KLI) and a specific set of MAS architectures

target_learning_goals: Curriculum-aligned STEM learning objectives from authentic lesson plan libraries
examples: The MAS-Roles system operationalizes KLI through a five-stage pipeline of KC, Learning Process, Instructional Principle, Design, and Feedback agents; MAS-CMD gives all three persona agents the same KLI guidance

citation: Jiayi Wang, Ruiwei Xiao, Xinying Hou, John Stamper. (2025). Enabling Multi-Agent Systems as Learning Designers: Applying Learning Sciences to AI Instructional Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16659
title: Embed learning science principles directly into AI system architectures rather than relying on teacher prompting
description: The article argues that pedagogical expertise should shift "from the user's prompt to the LLM's internal architecture", because most teachers lack the time or expertise to encode pedagogical nuance into prompts. Its key contribution is "showing that embedding learning science principles directly into AI architectures is an effective way to produce pedagogically sound materials", bridging the prompting gap and moving AI from a content generator to a pedagogical partner.
requirements: Access to an LLM-based generation system whose architecture encodes a pedagogical framework, so teachers need not supply expert prompts themselves
constraints: The most effective architecture (MAS-CMD) carried substantially greater latency and token usage; the study evaluated designed activities, not classroom implementation, so there is no direct evidence of impact on student learning outcomes
target_learners: K-12 educators designing instruction with generative AI
target_learning_goals: Production of pedagogically sound, classroom-ready learning activities
examples: The study instantiated this principle by embedding the KLI framework into MAS-Roles and MAS-CMD and comparing them against a single-agent baseline simulating typical teacher prompts

description: The article designs and implements three systems for generating K-12 learning activities. The Single-Agent System (SAS) is a baseline representing naive teacher prompting, appending context to the phrase "Generate learning activity". MAS-Roles is a sequential five-stage pipeline of KC, Learning Process, Instructional Principle, Design, and Feedback agents guided by KLI. article_title: Confirming Correct, Missing the Rest: LLM Tutoring Agents Struggle Where Feedback Matters Most
citation: Tahreem Yasir, Wenbo Li, Sam Gilson, Sutapa Dey Tithi, Xiaoyi Tian, Tiffany Barnes. (2026). Confirming Correct, Missing the Rest: LLM Tutoring Agents Struggle Where Feedback Matters Most. arXiv:2605.16207. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16207
title: Three-way KG-grounded diagnosis of student proof steps (optimal, valid-alternative, incorrect)
description: The article's organizing evaluation framework classifies each student next step into three pedagogically distinct categories using a knowledge graph encoding all valid inference paths for each problem. The article states that "Unlike prior benchmarks relying on binary correctness, our KG encodes all valid inference paths, enabling three-way diagnosis." A step is Optimal if it follows an expert-authored path and strictly reduces distance to the conclusion, Valid-alternative if it is a valid inference that does not reduce distance, and Incorrect if it is not derivable under any valid rule. Edge-level annotation of rules and parent statements enables verification of both what was derived and how the derivation is justified.
requirements: A knowledge graph exhaustively enumerating all reachable proof states via forward chaining under a closed rule set, which the article notes is feasible in propositional logic
Edge-level annotation of inference rule and parent statements so that symbolically valid but inferentially unjustified steps can be flagged
constraints: The article limits the framework to propositional logic, where exhaustive solution-space enumeration is tractable; findings may not generalize to domains where enumeration is not tractable or symbolic constraints are weaker
target_learners: undergraduate Discrete Mathematics students using a propositional logic tutoring system
target_learning_goals: step-level propositional logic proof reasoning and inference rule application
examples: The benchmark encodes 32 proof problems from a logic tutor's interaction logs as knowledge graphs and classifies 10,836 LLM-simulated next-step solutions against them

article_title: How YouTube Frames ChatGPT Use in Education: An Epistemic Network Analysis with Supporting Multimodal Metadata
citation: Shayla Sharmin, Mohammad Al-Ratrout, Mohammad Fahim Abrar, and Roghayeh Leila Barmaki. (2025). How YouTube Frames ChatGPT Use in Education: An Epistemic Network Analysis with Supporting Multimodal Metadata. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08698
title: Three-orientation epistemic framework for ChatGPT framing in informal learning discourse
description: The article proposes that public AI education content is structured not as a learning-to-output binary but as three coherent epistemic constellations: ChatGPT as "a conceptual scaffold for thinking" (G1), as retrieval practice and skill-building (G2), and as "a tool for output generation" (G3). The framework is operationalized through nine binary codes across framing (pedagogical, instrumental, conditional, critical) and strategy (scaffolding, metacognition, active recall, task completion, evaluating response) dimensions, and validated with ENA co-occurrence structure plus multimodal metadata. It links G1 to Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development and G2 to the testing effect.
requirements: Requires transcript chunking into 3–5 sentence analytical units and binary coding with the nine-code scheme (inter-rater κ > 0.70) before ENA with a moving stanza window of size 4
constraints: The authors caution that ENA results describe internal co-occurrence patterns within predefined groups rather than independently confirming group separation, and the coding scheme reflects the researchers' theoretical perspective
target_learners: self-directed adult learners on informal platforms such as YouTube
target_learning_goals: understanding how to use LLMs such as ChatGPT for learning versus productivity
examples: G1's mean network was anchored by a Scaffolding–Pedagogical edge (mean weight 0.43); G3's dominant edge was Instrumental–Task_Completion (0.40) with Pedagogical and Active_Recall near-absent

citation: Adnan Labib, Yixuan Huang, Jiahui Wu, John Maurice Gayed, Zheng Yuan, Qiao Wang. (2026). WrAFT: a Modularized Automated Writing Evaluation System for Argumentative Essays. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14524
title: WrAFT: deployable modular AWE system with interactive UI for in-line corrective edits and anchored comments
description: WrAFT (Writing Assessment and Feedback Tool) is a modular LLM-powered automated writing evaluation system for argumentative essays, combining a fine-tuned GPT-4o scoring module, a GPT-4o surface-level feedback module, and Claude 3.7 macro and micro deep-level feedback pipelines. Its interactive UI shows a predicted score, a surface-level tab with three display modes including track-changes, and a deep-level tab modeled after Microsoft Word's Comment feature with color-coded highlights. The article states "An interactive user interface has been developed for the system, publicly available and free to use", with a deployable code package on GitHub and a web application at wraft.net.

students engaged in argumentative writing

grammar and mechanics accuracy
higher-order writing skills such as coherence and argumentation

title: Modular decomposition of AWE into scoring, surface-level feedback, and deep-level feedback

The abstract states that "WrAFT adopts a modular design by dividing the automated writing evaluation (AWE) tasks into scoring, surface-level feedback and deep-level feedback." constraints: The article notes specialized models handling different aspects can produce better assessments than unified approaches, but the system was developed and tested only on argumentative essays with writing prompts

surface-level error correction
higher-order writing qualities including organization, coherence and argumentation

title: SocraticEdu: a 797-trajectory Socratic tutoring corpus reconstructed from a live Chinese children's science Q&A platform
description: SocraticEdu is a training corpus of 797 multi-turn Socratic tutoring trajectories in conversational Chinese, reconstructed from logs of the Dr. Curious platform serving primary-school students ages 8–12 across 14 schools. It combines 395 real trajectories from dialogue replay of logged follow-ups with 402 synthetic trajectories generated in three tutoring styles, spanning seven elementary-science domains. The article states it "provides the supervised warm-up data before GRPO" after intent filtering retained 8,911 science-oriented queries and 134 high-value seeds were selected.

Scientific-intent filtering (character-level TF-IDF logistic regression, macro-F1=0.9805±0.0022) to remove off-topic queries
constraints: No personally identifiable information is released with SocraticEdu
Synthetic trajectories were needed to cover seeds without long real chains

article_title: Beyond Direct Answering: Aligning Educational LLMs as Socratic Guides via Heuristic Reinforcement Learning
citation: Xiaokun Wang, Siyu Song, Wentao Liu, Xiaodong Zou. (2026). Beyond Direct Answering: Aligning Educational LLMs as Socratic Guides via Heuristic Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22996
title: HeuristicEdu: an SFT-then-GRPO alignment pipeline with a three-component heuristic reward for Socratic tutoring
description: HeuristicEdu is a two-phase alignment pipeline that redirects an instruction-tuned LLM from direct answer delivery toward Socratic guided inquiry. Phase 1 is supervised fine-tuning on the SocraticEdu corpus; Phase 2 applies GRPO with the composite reward Rtotal = αRcog + βReng − γRdir, where Rcog measures normalized Bloom's-taxonomy cognitive lift between turns via an LLM judge, Reng scores engagement cues via an Engagement Proxy Model, and Rdir penalizes novel keyword leakage with a Kquery correction for student-introduced terms. The article states "Section 7 shows that γ= 0is optimal in practice", and the pipeline includes inference-time spell correction and intent filtering before evaluation with SE and CD metrics.
requirements: A supervised warm-up corpus of Socratic trajectories (SocraticEdu, 797 trajectories)
An LLM judge for Bloom's levels and an Engagement Proxy Model for reward scoring
Curated keyword sets Ki per seed question for the directness term and leakage evaluation
constraints: The directness penalty Rdir is harmful as a GRPO reward (γ=0 optimal in practice), though explicit term constraints can reduce inference-time leakage
Results are demonstrated on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with a 30-question held-out test set; margins below 0.10 are treated as indicative
target_learners: Chinese primary-school students ages 8-12 in K-12 science platforms
target_learning_goals: Guided discovery of core science concepts through progressive Socratic questioning rather than direct answer delivery
examples: GRPO-aligned model responses open with analogies and exploratory questions (e.g., asking what color the sky is at sunset) rather than direct disclosure of Rayleigh scattering

title: SE and CD: outcome-oriented evaluation metrics for closed-loop Socratic tutoring assessment
description: The article introduces two evaluation metrics for Socratic tutoring beyond surface fluency. Scaffolding Effectiveness (SE) measures the proportion of test questions where the tutor guides a simulated student to self-express the core concept without uttering any keyword in Ki, over up to four dialogue rounds. Conversation Depth (CD) measures the fraction of consecutive guide–student turn pairs whose Sentence-BERT embeddings have cosine similarity below 0.70, indicating semantic progression. The article notes "novelty alone does not guarantee successful scaffolding", so CD is reported with SE and leakage. The student simulator was validated against held-out real follow-ups with mean SBERT similarity 0.449±0.220.
requirements: A fixed gold concept and keyword set Ki per test question
An LLM student simulator and concept judge (Qwen-plus / Qwen-turbo) held fixed across systems
SBERT encoder with threshold θ=0.70 for CD
constraints: SE and CD are simulation-based metrics; simulator validity was checked against 30 questions with recorded follow-ups, yielding on-topic but non-duplicate behavior
target_learners: Simulated and real primary-school science students ages 8-12
target_learning_goals: Assessing whether tutoring dialogues move students to self-express target concepts through progressive inquiry

article_title: A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Workforce Readiness for Smart Manufacturing in the AI Era
citation: Smith, Dalton Ross; Whittington, Wilburn; Martinez, Alejandro; Duncan, Aidan; Li, Gang. (2026). A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Workforce Readiness for Smart Manufacturing in the AI Era. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11540
title: Workforce Readiness Level (WRL): a nine-stage, TRL-like scale of individual manufacturing competency
description: The WRL is a ranked measure of an individual's demonstrated competency to perform, supervise, or improve manufacturing tasks, reported as an integer from 1 to 9. It adapts NASA's Technology Readiness Level structure to people: "structurally similar to NASA's Technology Readiness Level scale, that lays out progressive competency milestones for AI-era manufacturing". Stages group into awareness (1-3), applied practice (4-6), and autonomous leadership (7-9) bands, with stackable-credential articulation points at WRL 3, 5, and 7, and descriptors written as observable behaviors so two raters can score them.
requirements: Competency must be demonstrated through observable performance on artifacts, not coursework completion or self-report
Progression is stage-gated and monotonic, so downstream stakeholders can rely on the construct without re-arguing evidence
constraints: The nine-level count is inherited from TRL/MRL as a design choice, not derived from data; whether a coarser or finer partition fits competency growth is left open
The mechanism is domain-general; the AI-specific content lies in the pillar choice, and adaptation to low-AI settings is outside the paper's scope
target_learners: pre-service engineering students
incumbent manufacturing workers
target_learning_goals: AI-era smart-manufacturing competency from awareness through autonomous innovation leadership
examples: Programs publish example artifacts for each stage, such as a reference cobot-teaching pendant program for WRL 4, so raters and learners share a concrete target

title: Four-pillar competency rubric: digital/AI literacy, CPS fluency, human-machine collaboration, data-driven decision making
description: Each WRL stage is evaluated along four conceptually distinct pillars: "digital and AI literacy, cyber-physical systems fluency, human-machine collaboration, and data-driven decision making". Pillars were synthesized from Industry 4.0 competency literature and refined to foreground AI-specific competencies; each pillar carries anchored stage examples so the same construct is evidenced differently at WRL 2 versus WRL 7. Scoring pillars separately lets the no-thin-pillar rule detect lopsided profiles such as a strong coder who cannot read an SPC chart.
requirements: Exactly four pillars are retained to keep the rubric manageable for two raters and a single-page transcript while keeping the domains non-overlapping
constraints: The four-pillar partition is a design assumption, not a validated factor structure; establishing the number and statistical independence of the dimensions would require a construct-validity study such as confirmatory factor analysis
target_learners: pre-service engineering students
incumbent manufacturing workers
target_learning_goals: information-side, machine-side, human-side, and decision-side manufacturing competencies

citation: Brian Wright. (2026). Potential for Enhanced Learning in Machine Learning Classes by Using Wiki LLM Indexing. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25303
title: LLM-compiled wiki knowledge representation over an authentic course corpus
description: An ingest-time knowledge representation in which a course corpus is compiled into a linked wiki: "concept pages synthesized by an LLM, cross links between related pages, and citations from every page back to the raw sourcematerials." At query time the LLM navigates and reads relevant pages rather than receiving similarity-ranked chunks. In this study it covered 12 pages (7 course concept pages such as K-Nearest Neighbors, Decision Trees, and ML Bias & Fairness, plus 5 navigational/meta pages) built from a frozen DS3001/DS3021 corpus snapshot, and served as Arm B in the head-to-head comparison against vector RAG.

constraints: Generalization is untested beyond a single course corpus (DS3001) and its topic mix; the evaluated wiki covered only the subset of DS 3021 compiled into 12 pages.
target_learners: undergraduate machine learning students (DS3001/DS3021)
target_learning_goals: answering course questions grounded in vetted course materials
linking concepts across course units
tracing claims back to source lectures and readings
examples: Arm B compiled the same DS3001/DS3021 corpus used by the vector RAG control into a raw/+wiki/ structure, and the LLM navigated wiki pages at query time while Arm A retrieved top-k chunks from a 21-vector index.

title: Five-part question taxonomy with multi-endpoint metrics for evaluating course-grounded AI tutors
description: The article extends a prior 30-question generic/specific set into a five-part taxonomy of classroom question types: "(a) single fact lookup, (b) multi hop concept linking, (c) thematic explanation and synthesis, (d) contradictionandambiguityhandling(Houetal.2024),and (e) curriculum update questions probing sensitivity to revisedmaterials." Questions were human-generated with reference answers and word limits and balanced across course topics, yielding 59 retained questions (45 topic-page, 14 cross-page). title: Treat citation-traceability as a deployment requirement for classroom AI tools in machine learning courses
description: The article argues that what matters pedagogically is not just answer correctness but whether "a claim can be traced back to the lecture, slide, or reading that introduced it." A fluent, plausible, ungrounded answer is the more dangerous classroom failure mode because it short-circuits the student's check against source material, whereas a wrong-but-checkable answer keeps the student positioned as the one doing the checking. The author suggests this could argue for treating citation-traceability as a deployment requirement rather than an optional feature, and notes it could help develop trust in the emerging Teacher-Student-LLM dynamic in machine learning classrooms.
requirements: The knowledge representation must preserve where content originated and let a student follow any claim back to its source, as the compiled wiki's citations do.
constraints: The article states further testing is needed before generalizing; the groundedness evidence comes from a single-run evaluation on one course corpus, not from classroom deployments with students.

instructors teaching machine learning courses
target_learning_goals: students verifying AI tutor claims against course source materials
keeping students positioned as the ones doing the checking rather than outsourcing judgment to the tool
examples: In the evaluation, the compiled wiki's citations let a student and instructor trace any claim back to the lecture that introduced it, and the wiki arm was grounded in 98% of answers versus 81% for vector RAG.

title: Cross-semester concept cross-linking in a course AI tutor surfaces concept recurrence under conditions associated with durable learning
description: The article argues that explicit cross-linking benefits concepts that recur across a semester, using squared-error loss as its example: met first as the objective linear regression minimizes, then as the variance-reduction criterion a regression tree uses to choose a split. Retrieval over raw materials has no reason to connect these occurrences, while "A compiled wiki page, by contrast, can carry an explicit link back to where the concept was first introduced." The author links this to distributed practice, retrieval practice, and interleaving literature, noting that revisiting a concept at a delay in an unfamiliar context is close to the textbook definition of conditions under which retrieval converts fragile encoding into durable learning.
requirements: The representation must carry explicit links from later occurrences of a concept back to where it was first introduced, exposing connections students would otherwise have to notice unaided.
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretation supported by cited external literature (Cepeda et al. 2006; Karpicke and Roediger 2008; Rohrer and Taylor 2007), not as a learning outcome measured in this study.
target_learners: undergraduate machine learning students in courses that build throughout the semester
target_learning_goals: durable understanding of concepts that recur across course units in different forms
transfer across topics sharing deep structure
examples: The article reports this exact scenario occurred during testing: a loss-function citation trail exposing the regression-to-trees transition for squared-error loss.

article_title: Learning with pedagogical agents in extended reality: A conceptual research-based framework of agent-centered learning in immersive media environments (ACLIME)
citation: Ross, M., & Kaspar, K. (2025). Learning with pedagogical agents in extended reality: A conceptual research-based framework of agent-centered learning in immersive media environments (ACLIME). https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5092-6798
title: ACLIME framework: technical foundation, psychological clusters, and instructional design principles as moderators of agent-centered learning in immersive media
description: ACLIME is a conceptual framework structuring human-agent interaction in immersive learning media. The immersive medium (AR, AV, or VR), the pedagogical agent, and the learner's virtual representation form the technical foundation; from these emerge psychological clusters covering social interaction with the agent, the learner's experience of the agent, the learner's virtual self-experience, and immediate learning factors. The article states that instructional design principles are "conceptualized as moderators of the relationship between technical foundation and psychological dimensions," and that realizing potentials facilitates long-term learning outcomes while risks impede them. It covers the full XR spectrum including AR and restricts scope to one learner interacting with one agent.
requirements: Requires immersive media with high immersion and multimodal, body-based interactivity as the technical foundation
constraints: Restricted to the prototypical interaction of one learner with one pedagogical agent; multiple-agent and mixed-group scenarios remain unconsidered

Instructional design principles are addressed only at a conceptual level
target_learners: learners in schools, companies, and institutions of higher education using immersive media
target_learning_goals: factual, conceptual, procedural, and transfer knowledge facilitated by pedagogical agents

title: Uncanny Valley Theory as a boundary condition on agent realism in immersive learning environments
description: The review invokes Uncanny Valley Theory (Mori et al., 2012) as a risk qualifier for the otherwise positive effects of heightened agent realism. According to the review, "agents with increasing realism are perceived positively at first and enjoy greater trust, but if the similarity to real people exceeds a certain threshold and reaches the 'uncanny valley' this leads to a sudden rejection." Only when the valley is overcome does perception become positive again. The review states many studies over the last decade have shown this effect and its neurophysiological correlates, and concludes that designers must ensure realism quality does not fall into the uncanny valley when building sound human-agent spaces in immersive environments.
requirements: Agent realism quality must be managed so that similarity to real people does not fall into the uncanny valley
constraints: The effect is described as occurring only when similarity to real people exceeds a certain threshold

target_learning_goals: social interaction and relationship building with pedagogical agents supporting learning

title: Body avatarization continuum: levels of learner representation from real body to full avatar
description: The review adopts Genay et al. (2022)'s body avatarization continuum to describe learner representation in immersive media. Virtualization ranges "from representation through the real body to a completely virtual representation through an avatar," with two interim levels: body accessorization (adding virtual elements such as virtual clothing or digital eyeglasses to a real body) and partial avatarization (partially modifying the body, e.g., changing skin color or adding a third hand). Full avatarization is possible in all immersive formats (VR, AV, and AR), whereas real body representation, body accessorization, and partial avatarization require see-through head-mounted displays and can be implemented only in AV and AR.
requirements: Real body representation, body accessorization, and partial avatarization require head-mounted displays with see-through function
constraints: Full avatarization is possible in all immersive formats; the other forms only in AV and AR

target_learning_goals: virtual self-experience, self-presence, and embodiment during immersive learning

title: Ground immersive agent-centered learning design in learning theory via theory-driven design principles that harness potentials and mitigate risks
description: The review recommends that the specific design of immersive agent-centered learning environments be firmly grounded in learning theory, using theory-driven design principles to translate technical possibilities into pedagogically meaningful learning. Design principles capture meta-level design knowledge addressing a class of design problems, are derived from core theories and empirical research abstracted into meta-requirements, and are instantiated through concrete implementable design features. The review states these principles "moderate the extent to which the psychological potentials of pedagogical agents in immersive media environments can be realized and associated risks mitigated."

constraints: The principles are highly context-dependent (target group, learning goals, content) and are addressed only at a conceptual level in the article

target_learning_goals: translating XR technical capabilities into learning experiences and outcomes with pedagogical agents

article_title: Turn to chatbots for sharing feelings or seeking solutions? Differential associations of preferences for chatbot-mediated self-disclosure and instrumental help-seeking with adolescent interpersonal behaviors in the United States and Hong Kong
citation: Huinan Hu, Mojtaba Habibi Asgarabad, Enyi Jen, H. N. Cheung. (2026). Turn to chatbots for sharing feelings or seeking solutions? Differential associations of preferences for chatbot-mediated self-disclosure and instrumental help-seeking with adolescent interpersonal behaviors in the United States and Hong Kong. https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/qm6bg_v1
title: Culturally situated extension of the CASA paradigm: anthropomorphism and cultural foundations of human-computer relationships condition the outcomes of chatbot-mediated self-disclosure
description: The article builds on the computers-are-social-actors (CASA) paradigm, in which "individuals may mindlessly apply social heuristics (e.g., reciprocity, politeness, loyalty) to computers that exhibit social presence cues", and argues it must incorporate cultural context. East Asian animistic traditions and Confucian self-reflection norms foster anthropomorphizing chatbots, making self-disclosure adaptive, while Western human exceptionalism may leave US adolescents feeling emotionally disregarded. The authors state that "cultural foundations (e.g., differences in anthropomorphizing technology) should be integrated into the CASA diagram".
requirements: The account presupposes that conversation preferences translate into actual chatbot interactions, which the study did not measure
constraints: The authors label the proposed mechanisms tentative explanations to be verified in future interaction-based research
Direct evidence for CASA processes in adolescents remains limited, as the paradigm and its supporting evidence derive from general (mostly adult) populations
target_learners: adolescents in the US and Hong Kong
target_learning_goals: social and emotional development through human-AI interaction
adaptive coping and interpersonal behavior
examples: HK adolescents' self-disclosure preference related to adaptive coping and positive behaviors, whereas US adolescents' related to maladaptive coping and more bullying

article_title: Identifying the ethical values and norms for artificial intelligence in education: A systematic literature review
citation: Agarwal, B., Urlings, C., van Lankveld, G., & Klemke, R. (2022). Identifying the Ethical Values and Norms of Artificial Intelligence in Education: a Systematic Literature Review. Open University of the Netherlands. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7347-8465
title: Thematic grouping of AIED ethical value definitions into common-term themes
description: The review organises ethical value definitions collected from the literature into themes based on recurring key terms: "Data stewardship: definitions with the terms 'data' or 'information'", non-discrimination (bias, discrimination, diversity), explicability (explain, understand, justify), human oversight (people, someone, third party, self), and goodwill (well-being, consequences, harm, control). Second-level theme names were coined by the review's authors, except explicability, adopted from Floridi et al. (2018) as an umbrella term. Pedagogical appropriateness, fitting no theme, was placed in a theme on its own, later named educational aptness.
requirements: Articles must provide consolidated definitions of ethical values, identified via definitional phrases such as 'defined as', 'means', or 'refers to'
constraints: Based on literature published after 2010 and available in English; only 16 of 25 included articles provided value definitions
target_learners: students and teachers affected by AIED systems across K-12 and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: ethical design and use of AI in education
examples: Definitions such as privacy ('Individual's right to access and control the disclosure of their personal information') were collected per term and grouped into the mind-map themes

citation: Agarwal, B., Urlings, C., van Lankveld, G., & Klemke, R. (2022). Identifying the Ethical Values and Norms of Artificial Intelligence in Education: a Systematic Literature Review. Open University of the Netherlands. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7347-8465
title: Four stakeholder sets for AIED ethical norms: developers, educational institutes, end users, and regulators
description: The review classifies the addressees of AIED ethical norms into four stakeholder sets, adopting Smuha's (2022) classification with one renaming. Developers comprise "companies and AIED researchers who are involved in the implementation and development of AIED applications"; educational institutes (replacing 'deployers') are institutions ensuring applications meet requirements; end users are students, teachers and parents directly affected; regulators are government and policymakers ensuring compliance. Norms from 13 of 15 norm-providing articles were mapped to these sets, with two articles classified as unspecified users.
requirements: Norms must state or imply the stakeholders they address; articles not specifying stakeholders are grouped separately as unspecified users
constraints: Public entities were not considered in the analysis, motivating the renaming of deployers to educational institutes
target_learners: students, teachers, and parents as end users of AIED applications
target_learning_goals: assigning ethical responsibility for AIED implementation across stakeholder groups
examples: The stakeholder set referenced most regarding norms was developers (six articles), followed by deployers (five), regulators (four) and end users (two)

article_title: The agency gap in AI-supported writing: how reactive and proactive agent designs shape multimodal reasoning
citation: Yueqiao Jin, Kaixun Yang, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Dragan Gašević and Lixiang Yan. (2025). The Agency Gap in AI-Supported Writing: How Reactive and Proactive Agent Designs Shape Multimodal Reasoning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04398
title: The agency gap: a relational construct describing mismatch between AI agent initiative and learner GenAI literacy
description: The agency gap is the article's primary theoretical contribution: a relational conceptualisation of a mismatch between the initiative an AI agent demands (reactive or proactive) and the learner's capacity to initiate, monitor, evaluate, and internalise AI-supported reasoning. It concerns alignment of learner capability and interaction design rather than an individual deficit. Under-support arises when lower-literacy learners meet strongly reactive environments; over-direction arises when capable learners meet rigidly proactive environments. It is examined through converging evidence from discourse networks, writing outcomes, and reflections, not measured as a latent construct.
requirements: Requires characterising both the agent's initiative structure and the learner's GenAI literacy to diagnose alignment
constraints: The article states it is not a new general theory of agency and not an established or directly measured latent construct; neither agent design is assumed universally superior
target_learners: higher education students using generative AI for academic writing
target_learning_goals: independent multimodal analytical writing
learner agency in human–AI interaction

title: Reactive and proactive AI writing agents on a minimalist multimodal writing platform
description: The study developed two AI agents that manipulated conversational initiative while holding other features constant: both used the same interface, visual inputs, VizChat architecture, Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline, visualisation knowledge base, and multimodal GPT-4o model. The reactive agent generated only when the learner messaged; the proactive agent followed an expert-authored conversational state sequence, initiating orientation and ordered guiding questions per visual and giving confirmatory, clarifying, or corrective feedback grounded in visual evidence. The platform comprised a display area, a writing space, and a condition-specific chat or instructions component.
requirements: Requires the same underlying model, retrieval pipeline, and task materials across conditions so the contrast isolates who initiates and sequences support
constraints: The proactive sequence's triggering events, question order, target knowledge, and completion rules were fixed across participants; the prompt prohibited asking about non-displayed visuals and repeating questions
target_learners: medical and nursing students interpreting healthcare simulation visualisations
target_learning_goals: multimodal analytical writing from data visualisations
examples: In the proactive condition the sequence contained one question for the bar chart, two for the communication network, and three for the ward map, ending with a synthesis prompt

title: Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test (GLAT), a 20-item performance-based instrument
description: The GLAT is a performance-based 20-item multiple-choice instrument measuring generative AI literacy across four dimensions: understanding, applying, creating with, and making ethical judgements about GenAI. Each item has four response options, and a corrected total score (with correction for guessing) served as a standardised continuous predictor in the study's regression and mediation models. It was chosen over self-report confidence scales because it assesses demonstrated knowledge relevant to prompting, evaluating, and using generative systems.
requirements: Requires the published correction-for-guessing formula for four-option items; the study relied on the instrument's published validation evidence rather than new factor validation
constraints: Published validation includes expert review and a 204-participant item-relevance study; the article notes its own modest sample precluded new factor validation
target_learners: higher education students using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: measuring demonstrated generative AI literacy including prompting and evaluative judgement
examples: Published validation evidence reports Cronbach's α = 0.76 and a stable two-parameter logistic model (RMSEA = 0.007)

citation: Han Xue, Cao Jing, Wang Zi, Luo Heng. (2026). The Effects of Agent Type and Feedback Style on Self-Directed Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071069
title: Multidimensional framework for examining AI-generated feedback in self-directed learning
description: The article proposes a structured analytical framework of "four interrelated dimensions: feedback quality, self-regulatory behaviors, learning experiences, and learning outcomes" for examining AI-supported feedback use in self-directed learning. Feedback quality covers accuracy, specificity, and task alignment; self-regulatory behaviors cover monitoring, evaluation, and revision; learning experiences cover technology acceptance, engagement, critical thinking disposition, and cognitive load; outcomes are operationalized as short-term task-specific improvement via gain scores. The framework connects feedback design features to learners' interpretive and regulatory processes.
requirements: Multiple data sources: coded interaction logs, experience questionnaires, and gain-scored drafts
Operational definitions and coding anchors for each dimension
constraints: The authors state the dimensions "should not be understood as an exhaustive model of self-directed learning itself"
Outcomes reflect immediate task performance improvement rather than long-term learning, transfer, or general SDL development
target_learners: Postgraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Self-directed learning skills
Instructional design quality
Self-regulated feedback use
examples: The 2×2 mixed factorial study measured all four dimensions for each of 51 participants across two instructional design tasks

title: Customized vs. general-purpose LLM-based educational agents on the Coze platform
description: The study built four AI agents on the Coze platform, all on the same LLM (Kimi-32K) with identical interfaces and dialogue parameters. "Customized agents used two specialized knowledge bases alongside prompts: the “Instructional Design Textbook,” covering key design principles, and the “Instructional Design Evaluation Rubric,” with a seven-dimensional evaluation framework." Customized agents followed a predefined workflow ordering the seven dimensions with entry and termination conditions, while general-purpose agents relied only on prompts, with progression determined by the model's context. Feedback style (Socratic questioning vs. directive correction) was operationalized within each agent type.
requirements: Domain-specific knowledge bases and a structured evaluation rubric for the customized configuration
Anchoring of feedback to the student's submission to avoid generalized advice
constraints: All agents shared one underlying model and platform, so differences reflect configuration rather than base-model architecture

examples: Socratic prompts such as “Have you considered …?” versus directive feedback that directly pointed out deficiencies and gave improvement directions

title: Align agent knowledge configuration with feedback delivery style when designing AI feedback scaffolding
description: The article argues from a scaffolding perspective that agent type and feedback style jointly constitute AI feedback scaffolding: "the effect of AI feedback depends not only on agent type or feedback style alone, but on how a specific agent type and feedback style jointly constitute scaffolding that matches learners' current needs." citation: V.G. Kremen, O.M. Spirin, O.I. Liashenko, S.H. Lytvynova, Y.I. Malovanyi, O.P. Pinchuk, O.M. Sokolyuk, S.O. Semerikov. (2026). title: Integrative three-layer framework for AI adoption readiness among education managers
description: The article proposes an integrative framework synthesizing UTAUT, organizational readiness theory, and configurational theory to explain AI adoption readiness among education managers. UTAUT explains personal readiness through perceived usefulness, ease of use, and social influence; organizational readiness theory explains "psychological readiness (change commitment and change efficacy) and structural readiness (resource availability, policy clarity, and institutional support)"; and configurational theory explains how barriers combine. The framework treats the personal–institutional readiness gap as the tension between individual motivation and organizational capacity, with LCA typology as a classification layer.
requirements: Each theory addresses a distinct analytical layer — individual readiness, institutional readiness, and barrier configurations — without duplicating mechanisms
constraints: The manager typology layer is a classification (segmentation) layer, not tested as a statistical mediator

target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting institutional AI adoption readiness
examples: The framework guided hypotheses H1–H4 tested with the 395-manager survey, combining descriptive, person-centered (LCA), and set-theoretic (fsQCA) analyses
