description: The Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework, introduced by Garrison et al. and adopted by AI-ALOE as a core design framework, holds that "a meaningful educational experience occurs through the interaction of teaching presence, social presence, and cognitive presence". Cognitive presence is the learner's internal engagement; social presence is group collaboration and authentic self-projection; teaching presence is the organizational structure, design, and facilitation of the environment. The article uses CoI to label each of its 19 design guidelines by the presence(s) they support, noting the presences are interconnected and that G1 (data practices) sits outside the framework.

constraints: Guideline G1 (data practices) was not assigned a Community of Inquiry component because aligning with it would not increase student cognitive, social, or teaching presence

citation: Song Hongfeng, Hu Anqi, Li Xueyan. (2026). Beyond Positive or Negative: Latent Profiles of University Students’ AI Attitude and Their Career-Development Correlates. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16091460
title: Configurational, bivalent framework of AI attitudes as within-person combinations of capability appraisal, threat, and AI creative self-efficacy
description: The study adapts Park et al.'s (2024) AAAW multidimensional framework to university students, treating AI attitudes as configurations rather than a single favorable-unfavorable continuum. Six indicators capture "evaluations of AI capability, perceived use-related and career-related threat, and AI creative self-efficacy." Building on the evaluative-space model and cognitive appraisal theory, favorable and unfavorable reactions can coexist within individuals, so a person-centered latent profile approach reveals evaluative complexity that an overall attitude score would obscure.
requirements: Person-centered analysis (latent profile analysis) over multiple object-anchored attitude indicators rather than a single composite score
constraints: Framework was developed for workplace settings and adapted to university students; AI creative self-efficacy replaces personal utility as a contextually adapted, non-equivalent indicator
target_learners: first-year university students preparing for AI-affected careers
target_learning_goals: career preparation and adaptive readiness in response to AI-driven change
examples: Four empirically derived profiles: Positive Empowerment, Anxious Acceptance, Low-Perception Detached, and High-Perception High-Vigilance

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health
citation: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393
title: Ethics-of-care redefinition of connectedness as a demand-driven, two-way, responsive process
description: The article redefines connectedness as 'A relational experience of demand satisfaction formed by subjects engaging in caring interactions with other beings based on genuine needs, via two-way investment and reciprocal responsive confirmation.' It claims three advances over prior definitions: the logical starting point shifts from emotion to demand identification, one-sided perception becomes two-way mutual investment, and the value of connectedness becomes demand satisfaction and self-confirmation rather than mere anxiety reduction. The construct is grounded in Noddings' care practice of engrossment, motivational displacement, and reciprocal response confirmation, and explicitly incorporates ethical questions about who defines needs and bears responsibility for response.
requirements: Connectedness must be understood as generated through a cyclic mechanism of need identification, behavioral investment, and responsive confirmation rather than as a static relational state.
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: social-emotional development
identity formation
examples: The article contrasts its definition with Hagerty et al.'s human relatedness theory, which explains associative states through four relatedness capacity elements without deconstructing the generative mechanism of connectedness.
key_sources: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health
citation: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393
title: Continuum hypothesis of caring relationships ordering entities by descending responsiveness
description: The paper proposes that 'All entities that trigger a sense of connectedness in individuals form a spectrum ordered by descending responsiveness.' Humans with full moral subjectivity occupy one end, animals with limited subjectivity and nonverbal responses the middle, and nature and artifacts without subjective consciousness the other end. AI occupies an exclusive zone: it can simulate empathy, attention, and acceptance with response intensity approximating human interaction, yet its feedback stems from algorithmic optimization rather than genuine subjective care. Differences across the spectrum lie in the authenticity, symmetry, and subjectivity of mutual feedback, not in whether connection exists.
requirements: The spectrum is defined by each entity's responsiveness and co-constructive capacity rather than by whether the entity is human.
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: understanding human-AI relational bonds
examples: The article cites human-pet bond research showing individuals form stable caring connections with animals even without symmetric linguistic communication.
key_sources: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health
citation: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393
title: Neo-ecological restructuring of connectedness: virtual microsystems and AI as a quasi-people actor
description: Drawing on Navarro and Tudge's neo-ecological theory, the article describes how microsystems split into parallel physical and virtual categories, with technology treated as 'an actor capable of generating proximal developmental processes' rather than a mere tool. The updated theory formally recognizes anthropomorphic AI as a quasi-people actor within virtual microsystems. Because AI is neither a real human nor a passive tool but can sustain long-term personalized two-way interaction, its entry into adolescents' daily ecologies creates the theoretical necessity of defining artificial intelligence connectedness as an independent subtype of connectedness.
requirements: The framework maintains continuity with Bronfenbrenner's PPCT model, extending only the microsystem structure.
constraints: The article notes competing frameworks such as Ecological Techno-Microsystem Theory treat technology only as an influencing factor within the microsystem, not an independent ecological level.
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: developmental analysis of digital-era social ecologies
examples: Virtual microsystem interactions are shaped by platform structures and affordances such as synchronicity, anonymity, information retention, and algorithmic recommendation.
key_sources: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health
citation: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393
title: Artificial intelligence connectedness: definition and three-dimensional structure
description: The article defines artificial intelligence connectedness as 'A novel relational experience formed through sustained interactions with anthropomorphic AI, wherein individuals construct algorithms as responsive "quasi-subjects" and attain need satisfaction through asymmetric responsive confirmation.' Its three dimensions are demand identification, two-way behavioral engagement, and responsive confirmation, each with proposed self-report sample items for Likert-scale measurement. The construct is characterized as psychologically real yet ethically asymmetric, positioned as a digital subtype of connectedness coexisting with traditional interpersonal and self-connectedness in adolescents' relational ecosystems.
requirements: Measurement is proposed via self-report scales using Likert 5-point or 7-point scoring across the three dimensions.
constraints: The article states the construct is currently theoretical; its scientific validity and applicability remain to be verified through standardized measurement tools and systematic empirical research.
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: measuring and understanding adolescent human-AI relational bonds
examples: Sample items include 'I feel this AI truly understands my inner thoughts and feelings' for demand identification and 'I am willing to invest time to maintain the interactional relationship with this AI' for two-way behavioral engagement.
key_sources: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health
citation: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393
title: Dual connectedness framework: mental health impacts depend on AI connectedness paired with traditional connectedness
description: The article's core interpretive model holds that 'the mental health impacts of artificial intelligence connectedness depend on its relative level paired with traditional offline connectedness rather than its absolute intensity alone.' When traditional bonds satisfy adolescents' identity confirmation demands, AI connectedness acts as a supplementary protective factor; when human caregivers fail to recognize real inner demands, it produces compensatory substitution effects. The framework integrates competing viewpoints such as displacement versus stimulation hypotheses into a single system and is claimed to explain conditional shifts that single constructs like AI attachment cannot.
requirements: Testing the framework requires simultaneously measuring both traditional and artificial intelligence connectedness.
constraints: The framework's propositions are theoretically deduced hypotheses whose validity awaits verification by subsequent empirical research.
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: understanding mental health mechanisms of digital-era adolescents
examples: The article proposes that under high traditional connectedness AI connectedness shows no significant correlation with social withdrawal, while under low traditional connectedness it shows a significant positive correlation.

(2024) and grounded in Self-Determination Theory and Uses and Gratifications Theory. The article states that "Huang et al. (2024) classified motivations for AI use into four categories: escape motivation, social motivation, instrumental motivation, and entertainment motivation." Each category is defined by function: avoidance of stress, interpersonal connection, goal-oriented information seeking, and enjoyment or relaxation. The taxonomy structures the parallel mediation model tested in the study.

article_title: Contextualizing AI-Supported Emotion Regulation Through Sport and Exercise in Higher Education: A Conceptual Reframing
citation: Zhang Yuze, Hadier Syed Ghufran, Liu Yinghai, Guo Yanlan. (2026). Contextualizing AI-Supported Emotion Regulation Through Sport and Exercise in Higher Education: A Conceptual Reframing. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071173
title: Human–technology–environment framework for AI-supported emotion regulation in higher education
description: The article's central conceptual contribution repositions AI from autonomous interpreter of students' inner states to contextual support tool within sport and exercise settings. "We propose a human–technology–environment framework comprising multimodal contextual profiling, autonomy-supportive task adaptation, feedback–reflection–practice loops, peer and campus support integration, and human-in-the-loop governance." Students, teachers, coaches, counselors, and sport psychologists remain primary agents of interpretation and ethical judgment; AI supplies pattern recognition, visualization, documentation, and prompts; the environment supplies task structures, peer relations, spaces, routines, and governance. The five pathways are offered as design principles requiring empirical testing, not established causal mechanisms.
requirements: AI outputs should support, not replace, professional and pedagogical judgment
Data collection should be limited to what is necessary and consented
constraints: The study does not test intervention effects; the pathways are conceptual and require empirical testing
The framework was derived from a narrow AI-discourse corpus plus theory-informed synthesis

target_learning_goals: emotion regulation through sport and exercise
sustained, autonomy-supportive engagement in physical activity

citation: Zhang Yuze, Hadier Syed Ghufran, Liu Yinghai, Guo Yanlan. (2026). Contextualizing AI-Supported Emotion Regulation Through Sport and Exercise in Higher Education: A Conceptual Reframing. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071173
title: Implement AI-supported emotion regulation with human-in-the-loop governance to prevent support becoming surveillance
description: The article argues ethical governance must precede technical optimization when emotional data, student populations, and educational authority combine. It lists seven issues — privacy, consent, data minimization, transparency, bias, autonomy, and human oversight — noting that "AI outputs should support, not replace, professional and pedagogical judgment". A stated failure mode is "the transformation of support into surveillance", for example monitoring tied to attendance, grading, or disciplinary decisions.
requirements: Students should know what is collected, why, and how it will be used
Bias testing and explainability, since models may misread emotion across gender, culture, disability, language, and neurodiversity
constraints: Monitoring can easily become coercive if emotional analytics are tied to attendance, performance grading, disciplinary decisions, or institutional risk management

target_learning_goals: safe, ethically responsible engagement with AI-supported emotion regulation tools

title: Refined five-criterion plan quality rubric for children's if-then plans
description: The study adapted the Schaaf et al. (2025) plan quality rubric into a five-category binary checklist assessing the situational cue of children's implementation intentions: specificity, externality, salience, appropriateness, and temporal precision, yielding total scores from 0 to 5. The refinement separated characteristics that the original category-based rubric had treated jointly, which had "thereby limiting diagnostic precision". Inter-rater reliability ranged from κ = .63 to κ = .95 across dimensions.

constraints: Remains primarily suited for assessing action initiation plans in children's everyday activities, not adults or other plan types

citation: Sukjaitham, S., Schaaf, M., Brod, G., & Breitwieser, J. (2026). Adaptivity Makes Feedback Effective: Evidence From AI-Generated Feedback on Children's Plans. Preprint. https://osf.io/4w6rz/overview?view_only=dd3ec8d2878243579a463ccd0d77d723
title: Quality-matched feedback design: LLM adaptive feedback versus expert generic guidance materials
description: The study released a web-based feedback provider system, six scenario-based planning tasks, five expert-written generic guidance versions, a Chain-of-Thought prompt for GPT-4-generated adaptive feedback, and a five-dimension feedback quality rubric (specificity, suggestions, explanation, remarks, formulation). Both conditions were "equivalent in instructional purpose, structure, tone, length, and complexity", differing only in response-contingent adaptation. All materials are publicly available on the OSF.
requirements: Feedback quality must be verified with the rubric as a manipulation check so conditions differ only in adaptivity
constraints: Adaptive feedback was generated with ChatGPT-4 via the OpenAI API; model comparison was beyond the scope of the study

target_learning_goals: improving the quality of if-then plans as a self-regulated learning strategy

citation: Sukjaitham, S., Schaaf, M., Brod, G., & Breitwieser, J. (2026). Adaptivity Makes Feedback Effective: Evidence From AI-Generated Feedback on Children's Plans. Preprint. https://osf.io/4w6rz/overview?view_only=dd3ec8d2878243579a463ccd0d77d723
title: Response-contingent adaptivity as a core mechanism of feedback effectiveness
description: The article proposes that contingent adaptation of feedback to learners' momentary responses is a functionally relevant mechanism of feedback effectiveness, distinct from feedback quality, motivational tone, or structural clarity. In a preregistered experiment, feedback that addressed each child's specific plan produced larger plan-quality gains and higher perceived usefulness than structurally equivalent generic guidance. The authors conclude that "response-contingent adaptation constitutes a meaningful and functionally relevant dimension of instructional feedback", strengthening the interaction between feedback and the learner's evolving task performance rather than representing superficial customization.
requirements: A comparison condition matched on quality, structure, tone, and length is needed to isolate adaptivity as the active ingredient
constraints: Evidence comes from short-term effects in a highly structured setting with constrained tasks (children wrote only the if-component); generalization to complex, ill-defined tasks, other age groups, and less structured environments remains untested
target_learners: children aged 10-13 in fifth and sixth grade
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use, specifically planning with implementation intentions
examples: LLM feedback referenced the child's own plan (e.g., suggesting a concrete cue like finishing homework before starting), while generic guidance stated the same five quality criteria without referencing the response

citation: Kaşarcı İsmail, Yurt Eyüp. (2026). Effectiveness of AI-Supported Game-Based Learning: A Systematic Review of Outcomes, Challenges, and Future Directions. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071050
title: Three-pathway model of AI-GBL effectiveness: cognitive load optimization, motivational scaffolding, and epistemic scaffolding
description: The review proposes that AI-GBL operates through three distinct theoretical pathways grounded in cognitive load theory, self-determination theory, and Vygotsky's zone of proximal development. As the review states, "AI-GBL operates through three distinct pathways: cognitive load optimization (calibrating task difficulty to individual capacity), motivational scaffolding (maintaining optimal challenge and timely feedback), and epistemic scaffolding (AI characters supporting contextually appropriate knowledge construction)". The model explains why AI-GBL achieves outcomes that neither AI tutoring nor conventional GBL achieves alone, and is supported in the review by adaptive difficulty research, LLM scaffolding studies, and AI NPC evidence.
requirements: AI mechanisms must be aligned with learning theory rather than chosen for algorithmic sophistication
constraints: The review notes the model is supported by thematic synthesis of heterogeneous studies, not quantitative meta-analysis

target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition
motivation
higher-order thinking
examples: The review cites adaptive difficulty research (Panjaburee et al., 2025), LLM scaffolding studies (Huang & Chen, 2025; Ngu et al., 2025), and AI NPC evidence (Chernbumroong et al., 2026) as supporting the three pathways

article_title: Artificial intelligence and feedback in university education: effectiveness and student perceptions
citation: Grion, Valentina; Doria, Beatrice; Agostini, Daniele; Slaviero, Giorgia. (2026). Artificial intelligence and feedback in university education: effectiveness and student perceptions. Assessment and Evaluation in Higher Education. https://dx.doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2697962
title: Embed AI-generated feedback in a strong pedagogical architecture with assessment literacy and explicit criteria, so its source matters less than its context
description: This principle holds that the effectiveness of formative feedback depends on the surrounding design rather than on whether it comes from a human teacher or a large language model. The article concludes that feedback effectiveness "depends less on its source than on the pedagogical architecture in which it is embedded." When embedded in a course with strong assessment literacy and explicit criteria, AI-generated feedback "can function as a credible component of formative assessment in higher education." The study operationalised this by giving all three feedback conditions the same project-based setting and criteria.

Explicit assessment criteria shared across feedback conditions
constraints: Evidence comes from one project-based university course; comparability was established within that embedded architecture, not for AI feedback in general

target_learning_goals: improving project performance through formative feedback
examples: 47 student groups were randomly assigned to GPT-o4-mini, DeepSeek R1, or expert teacher feedback within one project-based course, with equivalence and non-inferiority analyses comparing sources

article_title: From AI Intuition to AI Literacy: A Dual Framework for K-12 Education
citation: Beau, M., & Lazar, M. (2025). From AI Intuition to AI Literacy: A Dual Framework for K-12 Education. International School of Boston. https://resources.finalsite.net/images/v1760105856/isboston/njqucrdzeyxvmtjr4cla/WhitePaper_AI_October2025.pdf
title: Dual framework of AI literacy and AI intuition for K-12 education
description: The article proposes a dual framework in which AI literacy and AI intuition are complementary dimensions of learning with AI. AI literacy is "a structured, largely static set of competencies" while AI intuition is "a dynamic learning process". The framework holds that the two are "not sequential stages but interdependent dimensions of learning": literacy supplies conceptual clarity and ethical guardrails, intuition supplies practical wisdom for uncertain contexts, and together they move students from passive users to critical, reflective users of AI.
requirements: Instructional designs must intentionally cultivate both dimensions rather than focusing solely on final outputs or technical correctness
constraints: Position paper grounded in philosophy, AI-education literature, and classroom implementation at one school; the authors state the goal is to strengthen, not replace, existing AI literacy frameworks
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
responsible and critical use of generative AI
context-sensitive judgment about AI behavior

article_title: From AI Intuition to AI Literacy: A Dual Framework for K-12 Education
citation: Beau, M., & Lazar, M. (2025). From AI Intuition to AI Literacy: A Dual Framework for K-12 Education. International School of Boston. https://resources.finalsite.net/images/v1760105856/isboston/njqucrdzeyxvmtjr4cla/WhitePaper_AI_October2025.pdf
title: AI intuition as experiential, inductive understanding developed through an iterative learning cycle
description: AI intuition is defined as "an experiential, inductive understanding of AI systems developed through exploration, trial-and-error, and reflective engagement, enabling learners to anticipate AI behavior, adapt strategies, and make context-dependent decisions". It is a structured form of tacit understanding, not guesswork, that emerges through repeated interaction, use, comparison, and failure. In classrooms it develops through an iterative cycle of exploration, observation, reflection, and adaptation, through which learners build heuristics about how prompts, constraints, and task contexts influence AI outputs.
requirements: Instructional designs that explicitly support the experiential learning cycle and make each phase visible and assessable
constraints: The concept is extended from Flechtner and colleagues' university-level design education work to K-12; the authors note it has not previously been extended to K-12 education
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: anticipating AI behavior and failure modes
developing rules of thumb for when to trust, verify, or disengage from AI
examples: In AI-assisted research activities using platforms such as NotebookLM, students explore through prompt variation, challenge systems with atypical or contradictory queries, and reflect on emerging patterns and limitations

citation: Beau, M., & Lazar, M. (2025). From AI Intuition to AI Literacy: A Dual Framework for K-12 Education. International School of Boston. https://resources.finalsite.net/images/v1760105856/isboston/njqucrdzeyxvmtjr4cla/WhitePaper_AI_October2025.pdf
title: Four core AI literacy competencies: conceptual understanding, practical application, critical evaluation, ethical judgment
description: The article adopts the widely accepted definition of AI literacy as "a set of knowledge, skills, and dispositions that enable learners to understand how AI systems work, use them appropriately, evaluate their outputs critically, and engage with them ethically and responsibly". It structures this into four competencies: conceptual understanding of data, models, learning, bias and limitations; practical application in authentic tasks; critical evaluation using verification strategies and cross-checking; and ethical and responsible judgment about academic integrity, privacy, authorship, fairness and societal impact.
requirements: Structured and guided classroom activities such as source verification, bias analysis, and discussions of academic integrity
constraints: The article characterizes AI literacy as largely static and structured, and argues it alone cannot account for the experiential dimension of learning with AI
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: understanding how AI systems work
critical evaluation of AI outputs
ethical and responsible AI use
examples: The competency structure is presented in Figure 1 as the static component of the dual framework
key_sources: Beau, M., & Lazar, M. (2025). From AI Intuition to AI Literacy: A Dual Framework for K-12 Education. International School of Boston. https://resources.finalsite.net/images/v1760105856/isboston/njqucrdzeyxvmtjr4cla/WhitePaper_AI_October2025.pdf

article_title: A Multidimensional Analysis of AI Literacy Determinants: External Resources, Digital Skills, and Psychological Profile Among University Students
citation: Chow Tak Sang, To Ken, Lam Bess Yin Hung, Lau Kung Wong. (2026). A Multidimensional Analysis of AI Literacy Determinants: External Resources, Digital Skills, and Psychological Profile Among University Students. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081448
title: Social cognitive theory as an integrative framework mapping external, experiential, and psychological determinants of AI literacy
description: The article grounds its three-block predictor model in Bandura's social cognitive theory, whose "central proposition ... is triadic reciprocal determinism", holding that functioning arises from continuous interaction of environmental, personal, and behavioural determinants. Perceived resources and teacher support map to environmental determinants (instructional scaffolding), prior digital competence to enactive mastery experience, and innovativeness, anxiety, and growth mindset to the dispositional, affective, and cognitive facets of personal determinants. The framework is additionally read through the multi-level digital divide perspective, connecting findings to equity in AI education.
requirements: All three determinant domains must be measured concurrently for incremental contributions to be interpretable, since incremental value is relational rather than intrinsic to a predictor
constraints: The article notes the framework's equity implication — that equalising access alone will not equalise outcomes if learner-level determinants carry weight — rests on cross-sectional correlational evidence
target_learners: undergraduate university students
target_learning_goals: AI literacy development
responsible and effective engagement with generative AI
examples: The study's hierarchical regression entered covariates, external resources, digital competence, and psychological variables in four steps mirroring the framework's blocks
key_sources: Chow Tak Sang, To Ken, Lam Bess Yin Hung, Lau Kung Wong. (2026). A Multidimensional Analysis of AI Literacy Determinants: External Resources, Digital Skills, and Psychological Profile Among University Students. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081448

article_title: The AI Literacy Heptagon: A Structured Approach to AI Literacy in Higher Education
citation: Veronika Hackl, Alexandra Elena Müller, Maximilian Sailer. (2025). The AI Literacy Heptagon: A Structured Approach to AI Literacy in Higher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.18900
title: The AI Literacy Heptagon: a seven-dimensional framework with four Bloom-based proficiency levels for AIL in higher education
description: The AI Literacy Heptagon is a framework structuring AIL in higher education around seven dimensions: Technical Knowledge and Skills, Application Proficiency, Critical Thinking Ability, Integration Skills, Legal and Regulatory Knowledge, Ethical Awareness and Reasoning, and Social Impact Understanding. It adds four competency levels (Unaware, Beginner, Intermediate, Expert) derived from Bloom's taxonomy, and distinguishes generic AIL (Beginner in all dimensions) from domain-specific extensions. The heptagonal shape represents the dimensions as equal, aiming to reduce cognitive load while not oversimplifying the construct.
requirements: Dimensions must be treated as interconnected and equal to foster perspectives beyond the dominant technical focus
constraints: Expert-level visualization lacks sufficient granularity, per expert validation feedback
The knowledge-skills-attitudes three-dimensional nature is not explicitly represented in the visual model
target_learners: higher education students across disciplines
target_learning_goals: AI literacy: critically engaging with AI technologies, understanding their societal and ethical implications, and applying them responsibly
examples: Expert-led curriculum mapping of an AI Engineering Bachelor's program and a Media Pedagogy curriculum produced heptagon profiles of intended curricular focus
key_sources: Veronika Hackl, Alexandra Elena Müller, Maximilian Sailer. (2025). The AI Literacy Heptagon: A Structured Approach to AI Literacy in Higher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.18900

citation: Veronika Hackl, Alexandra Elena Müller, Maximilian Sailer. (2025). The AI Literacy Heptagon: A Structured Approach to AI Literacy in Higher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.18900
title: Anchor AIL curriculum design in a synthesized working definition that explicitly enumerates competency dimensions and varies emphasis by discipline
description: The article proposes a working definition of AIL in higher education as the ability to "critically engage with AI technologies, understand their societal and ethical implications, and apply them responsibly", operationalized across technical, applicational, critical thinking, ethical, social, integrational, and legal dimensions. The final clause acknowledges variations in emphasis depending on the disciplinary context, connecting the definition to the adaptable Heptagon framework and addressing dimensions underrepresented in prior conceptualizations.
requirements: An education-specific definition that differentiates AIL from related literacies such as Digital, Media, and Information Literacy
constraints: The working definition is expected to undergo further refinement as AI technologies evolve
target_learners: higher education students and curriculum developers
target_learning_goals: AI literacy as a multifaceted competency construct
examples: The definition's second sentence explicitly lists the seven core dimensions that form the basis of the Heptagon model

article_title: Artificial Intelligence as a Personal Coach: A Narrative Review of Benefits and Risks in Educational and Health Contexts
citation: Potel, J. T., & Kumashiro, M. (2026). Artificial Intelligence as a Personal Coach: A Narrative Review of Benefits and Risks in Educational and Health Contexts. Behavioral Sciences, 16(8), 1431. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081431
title: Working classification of chatbot and language-model technologies for AI coaching
description: The review proposes a working taxonomy of coaching technologies, from rule-based programming (fixed rules and scripted responses) through task-oriented and ML-enhanced NLP/NLU chatbots to early LLMs and mass-market general-purpose LLMs. It distinguishes how systems are programmed (purpose-built versus general-purpose) and used (alone versus with human coaches), noting an AI system performs a coaching function when interaction supports goal clarification, self-reflection, feedback, action planning, motivation, or behavior change. This classification organizes the evidence review and risk analysis.
requirements: Research must distinguish whether users interacted with a purpose-built coaching chatbot or a general-purpose LLM, since findings may not transfer between categories
constraints: The categories are illustrative rather than mutually exclusive because a single system may combine scripted rules, NLP, NLU, machine-learning, and LLM-based components
target_learners: adults and students seeking personal development guidance in educational and health contexts
target_learning_goals: goal clarification, self-reflection, feedback, action planning, motivation, behavior change
key_sources: Potel, J. T., & Kumashiro, M. (2026). Artificial Intelligence as a Personal Coach: A Narrative Review of Benefits and Risks in Educational and Health Contexts. Behavioral Sciences, 16(8), 1431. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081431

article_title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence-Supported Instruction on Student Learning in STEM: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Doğan Yunus, Kılıç Zeynep, Kalınkara Yusuf, Talan Tarık. (2026). The Impact of Artificial Intelligence-Supported Instruction on Student Learning in STEM: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence14060109
title: Treat AI as a pedagogical partner that extends, rather than replaces, the teacher
description: The article recommends conceptualizing AI-supported instruction as a complement to teaching rather than an autonomous instructional agent. It states: "AI should be conceptualized as a pedagogical partner rather than an autonomous instructional agent." The meta-analytic evidence of a moderate, heterogeneous effect underpins this: AI extends instructional capacity while teachers remain essential for guiding interpretation, facilitating deeper understanding, and supporting higher-order thinking.
requirements: Teacher involvement for guiding interpretation, facilitating deeper understanding, and supporting higher-order thinking processes
constraints: The article cautions that AI is not inherently effective but becomes effective under specific pedagogical and contextual conditions, and that its effectiveness depends on instructional design quality
target_learners: primary, secondary, high school, and university students in STEM education
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in STEM subjects
examples: The meta-analysis of 35 experimental and quasi-experimental studies found a pooled g = 0.670 with high heterogeneity, which the authors read as evidence that AI amplifies effective pedagogy rather than substituting for it

article_title: Assessing AI-TPACK readiness in mathematics teacher education: The role of self-efficacy and teaching beliefs
citation: Meijuan Xie, Liling Luo. (2025). The Status Quo and Future of AI-TPACK for Mathematics Teacher Education Students: A Case Study in Chinese Universities. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13533
title: AI-TPACK framework: integrating artificial intelligence into TPACK
description: The AI-TPACK framework adapts the TPACK framework by adding artificial-intelligence elements to the technology dimension. As the article puts it, "It incorporates elements of artificial intelligence on top of TPACK in order to facilitate the integration of these technologies in education". Integrating AI into TK and intertwining it with PK and CK forms AI-TPK and AI-TCK, which combine with PCK to develop AI-TPACK. The framework demands deep integration of human instructors with AI technology, fostering tripartite co-creation of technological, content, and pedagogical elements through human and machine cognition, and obliges educators to master AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems and robot teachers.
requirements: Teachers must possess proficiency in AI technology and integrate it with conventional pedagogical approaches and subject knowledge
target_learners: mathematics teacher education students (MTES)
target_learning_goals: integrating AI technology with mathematical content and pedagogy (AI-TK, AI-TCK, AI-TPK, AI-TPACK)
examples: The article operationalised the framework as a 24-item scale measuring AI-TK, AI-TCK, AI-TPK and AI-TPACK administered to 412 MTES in seven Chinese universities
key_sources: Meijuan Xie, Liling Luo. (2025). The Status Quo and Future of AI-TPACK for Mathematics Teacher Education Students: A Case Study in Chinese Universities. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13533

article_title: Assessing AI-TPACK readiness in mathematics teacher education: The role of self-efficacy and teaching beliefs
citation: Meijuan Xie, Liling Luo. (2025). The Status Quo and Future of AI-TPACK for Mathematics Teacher Education Students: A Case Study in Chinese Universities. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13533
title: Validated AI-TPACK scale for mathematics teacher education students
description: A questionnaire scale the authors designed and validated to measure MTES competence on six variables: AI-TK, AI-TCK, AI-TPK, AI-TPACK, self-efficacy, and teaching beliefs. The revised instrument "contained six variables and 24 items and each variable hold four items", with "the options of each item is a 7-point Likert type ranged from “1: strongly disagree” to “7: strongly agree”". It was refined via a pre-test with 128 senior MTES using EFA and CFA (KMO = 0.937; Cronbach's alphas 0.899–0.934 across factors) before post-testing on 412 students.
requirements: Administration via EFA/CFA-validated items after removing items not loading on predetermined factors
target_learners: mathematics teacher education students in universities
target_learning_goals: assessing AI-TPACK competence, self-efficacy and teaching beliefs
examples: Pre-test with 128 valid questionnaires from senior MTES in one university; factor loadings ranged from 0.466 to 0.879 with total variance of 83.87%

article_title: Artificial intelligence in vocational education and training: A systematic review of educational purposes, theoretical conceptualizations, and empirical effectiveness
citation: Deutscher, V., Thomann, H., Zlatkin-Troitschanskaia, O., Weyland, U., Abele, S., Danek, A. H., Greiff, S., Rausch, A., Seeber, S., Seifried, J., & Winther, E. (2026). Artificial intelligence in vocational education and training: A systematic review of educational purposes, theoretical conceptualizations, and empirical effectiveness. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 11 (2026) 100628. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100628
title: Three paradigms of AI integration in education: AI-directed learner-as-receiver, AI-supported learner-as-collaborator, AI-empowered learner-as-leader
description: The review adopts Ouyang and Jiao's (2021) framework, which "frames the educational role of AI along three paradigms that reflect increasing levels of learner agency": AI-directed (learner-as-receiver, rooted in behaviorism, with AI structuring content and giving prescriptive feedback), AI-supported (learner-as-collaborator, grounded in cognitive and social constructivist theories, with dialogic tutoring and exploratory environments), and AI-empowered (learner-as-leader, aligned with connectivism and complex adaptive systems theory, where learners co-design learning trajectories). The review uses this framework as the coding scheme for RQ3 on theoretical conceptualization of human–AI interaction.
requirements: The framework is used to code each study's theoretical grounding and AI's role in learner interaction, requiring classification of pedagogical foundations, technological manifestations, and the human–AI interface.
constraints: The review notes that in the AI-supported paradigm the learning space and learning goals are mostly predefined, and that the reviewed VET studies concentrate in the AI-directed paradigm.
target_learners: vocational education and training learners
target_learning_goals: characterizing the pedagogical role of AI in learning environments
examples: The review coded all 26 included studies against this framework, finding most applications in the AI-directed paradigm with traditional intelligent tutoring systems as prototypes.

article_title: Artificial intelligence in vocational education and training: A systematic review of educational purposes, theoretical conceptualizations, and empirical effectiveness
citation: Deutscher, V., Thomann, H., Zlatkin-Troitschanskaia, O., Weyland, U., Abele, S., Danek, A. H., Greiff, S., Rausch, A., Seeber, S., Seifried, J., & Winther, E. (2026). Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 11 (2026) 100628. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100628
title: Curriculum-Instruction-Assessment triad taxonomy of AI educational purposes in VET
description: Building on Wang et al. (2024) and Dai et al. (2025), the review organizes AI applications in VET "into the main categories of the Curriculum-Instruction-Assessment-Triad (Pellegrino, 2012)", plus holistic system-level functions. The curriculum domain covers curriculum creation and analysis; the instruction domain distinguishes seven pedagogical functions (instructional planning, adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring, conversational agents, content curation, instructional creation, authentic simulation); the assessment domain covers intelligent assessment and profiling/prediction; holistic functions include administration and guidance. Table 1 maps each purpose to AI types (ML, NLP, rule-based, computer vision) and example applications.
requirements: The taxonomy requires classifying each AI application by educational purpose, AI type, and example application, as operationalized in the review's coding scheme and Appendix 1.
constraints: The review found instructional applications dominate the evidence base while curriculum- and assessment-oriented uses remain marginal, and it excluded AI as a learning object (AI literacy) from scope.
target_learners: vocational education and training learners
target_learning_goals: mapping AI applications to educational purposes in vocational contexts
examples: Conversational agents were the most prevalent instructional subcategory (ten studies); iXR accounted for eight studies; profiling and prediction appeared in two dropout-risk studies.

article_title: Transforming Nursing Education with Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review (2010–2025)
citation: Alrazeeni, D. M., Alharrasi, M., Khan, R. M. K., Biswas, R. K., Tama, I. J., Halder, C. R., Deb, B., Bashar, F., & Akter, F. (2026). Transforming Nursing Education with Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review (2010–2025). SAGE Open Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1177/23779608261424597
title: Four-area taxonomy of AI integration in nursing education: personalized learning, simulation-based training, automated assessment, and institutional analytics
description: The review organizes its synthesis of 28 empirical studies into four thematic application areas of AI in nursing education. As the abstract states, "AI-enhanced nursing education in four main areas: (a) personalized learning systems tailored content to individual needs, (b) simulation-based training improved decision-making in high-acuity scenarios, (c) automated assessment tools provided immediate, unbiased feedback, and (d) at the institutional level, AI supported curriculum management and predictive analytics." The taxonomy structures the narrative synthesis, with studies grouped thematically under these focus areas.
requirements: Empirical studies of AI applications in academic, clinical, or hybrid nursing education contexts with measurable outcomes
constraints: Derived from 28 studies, most from middle- and high-income countries, which the review notes may limit generalizability

target_learning_goals: clinical competencies
diagnostic reasoning
knowledge acquisition

article_title: How Online Learners Engage in Self-Directed Modeling: A Behavioral Analysis
citation: Sungeun An, Jennifer Hammock, Ashok Goel. (2025). How Online Learners Engage in Self-Directed Modeling: A Behavioral Analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00506-5
title: Three-pattern framework of self-directed modeling behavior (Observation, Construction, Exploration)
description: The article proposes a framework for understanding how online learners engage in self-directed modeling outside traditional classrooms, built from learning analytics on VERA logs. It identifies "three distinct behavioral patterns—Observation, Construction, and Exploration—that reflect varying levels of engagement and interaction", links them to learning theories such as constructivism and situated cognition, and maps detailed Markov transition clusters onto the three types. Observation involves parameter experimentation on existing models, Construction short building sessions, and Exploration full construction-parameterization-simulation cycles.
requirements: Behavioral log data capturing modeling actions (construction, parameterization, simulation) so activity sequences can be extracted and clustered
constraints: Developed from log data of unspecified online learners without demographic or contextual information, which the authors state limits generalizability
target_learners: self-directed online learners using ecological modeling tools
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning through modeling
ecological systems understanding
examples: Clustering 822 activity sequences from 315 VERA learners into the three types, then mapping nine Markov clusters onto them (Table 1)

title: VERA (Virtual Experimentation Research Assistant) ecological modeling tool
description: VERA is a publicly available online tool for ecological modeling, accessible via the Smithsonian's Encyclopedia of Life site, that "supports conceptual modeling, agent-based simulations, and hypothesis-driven experiments". It uses the Component-Mechanism-Phenomenon (CMP) language grounded in biodiversity knowledge bases, scaffolds parameter setting with Encyclopedia of Life trait data, and automatically generates NetLogo agent-based simulations from conceptual models via an AI compiler, supporting model-simulate-refine loops. Its detailed interaction logging (17 distinct actions, clickstream data, XML models) enables fine-grained learning analytics research.
requirements: Access to the Encyclopedia of Life biodiversity knowledge base for parameter scaffolding
interaction logging infrastructure to capture modeling actions
constraints: The article states demographic data such as grade level or scores are not collected, as with other open online platforms
target_learners: novice learners
self-directed online learners
target_learning_goals: ecological conceptual modeling
hypothesis-driven experimentation
examples: A study on college students demonstrated that use of VERA improves content knowledge of ecological systems (An et al., 2018), as cited by the article

article_title: Leveraging AI for Rapid Generation of Physics Simulations in Education: Building Your Own Virtual Lab
citation: Yossi Ben-Zion, Roi Einhorn Zarzecki, Joshua Glazer, Noah D. Finkelstein. (2024). Leveraging AI for Rapid Generation of Physics Simulations in Education: Building Your Own Virtual Lab. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07482
title: Prompt-based LLM workflow for generating interactive physics simulations without programming expertise
description: The article describes a workflow in which educators or students give a predefined prompt to an LLM (ChatGPT or Claude), receive HTML and JavaScript code, and run it in a browser. The authors state the process "requires no advanced programming knowledge" and that iterative dialogue with the model yields simulations "customized for different educational contexts". It is offered as a complement to professionally developed simulations.
requirements: Access to an LLM such as ChatGPT or Claude and a modern web browser to open the generated .html file
constraints: The authors state it is not intended to replace robust simulations like PhET, and some corrections through human supervision typically remain necessary
target_learners: physics educators
undergraduate and school physics students
target_learning_goals: exploring physical systems through interactive simulations
hands-on experience with large language models
examples: Simulations generated for the simple pendulum, the 2D Ising model, and the 2D and 3D random walker using OpenAI's O1 and Claude 3.5 Sonnet
key_sources: Yossi Ben-Zion, Roi Einhorn Zarzecki, Joshua Glazer, Noah D. Finkelstein. (2024). Leveraging AI for Rapid Generation of Physics Simulations in Education: Building Your Own Virtual Lab. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.07482

title: Two-type validation framework: technical validation and physical validation of AI-generated simulations
description: The article names and describes two complementary validation types for LLM-generated simulations. "Technical validation tests the simulation's behavior under various conditions and assess its response to parameter changes", while "Physical validation compares simulation results to known analytical solutions and verify consistency with established physical laws". The framework is applied to each of the three demonstrated simulations and can be conducted through natural-language dialogue with the model.
requirements: Validation against known analytical solutions or established physical laws requires the target system to have expected behaviors the user can check
constraints: LLM variability means even identical prompts can produce different outputs, necessitating comprehensive validation strategies

physics educators
target_learning_goals: evaluating reliability of AI-generated tools
strengthening physics understanding by checking results against established laws
examples: Pendulum physical tests checked period accuracy against T = 2π√(L/g); Ising tests checked the critical temperature Tc = 2.269 for J = 1, H = 0

title: Multimodal fusion framework combining transformer text classification with computational-linguistic feature analysis for readability assessment
description: The article proposes a framework in which fine-tuned transformer encoders (frozen, output layer removed) are fused with a neural network trained on numerical linguistic features (lexical diversity, readability formulae, part-of-speech counts, sentiment, named entities) through a unified output layer. The authors state the aim "to increase classification performance while maintaining model complexity, selecting pareto-optimal models in the trade-off between capability and real-world accessibility", motivated by traditional readability formulae lacking semantic depth and large language models being too computationally complex for school hardware.

constraints: Validated only on UK Key Stage 2–5 classification of public-domain English texts; the authors note internationalisation as future work

citation: Breideband, T., Bush, J. B., Reitman, J. G., Rose, S., Weatherley, J., Penuel, W. R., & D'Mello, S. (2025). title: CoBi: an AI-based classroom-wide collaboration support system with privacy-preserving visualizations
description: CoBi is a classroom-wide AI system that "uses speech recognition and language understanding to create non-evaluative and privacy-preserving visualizations of uplifting small group student discourse." Audio is captured with omnidirectional table-top microphones, streamed in 10-s chunks, transcribed with Whisper ASR, and classified by discourse classifiers to detect when students enact community agreements. Feedback is always aggregated at the classroom level; student- or group-level feedback is not available, a design constraint to protect privacy and build trust.
requirements: Commodity equipment including omnidirectional microphones and Chromebooks; a scalable cloud-based speech processing pipeline; embedding in the Sensor Immersion curriculum unit
constraints: Visualizations are aggregated at classroom level only; only three CA categories were currently representable in noticings; system operates under low-bandwidth conditions
target_learners: middle school students in K-12 classrooms
target_learning_goals: collaboration skills and community agreement enactment
examples: Deployed in two classroom studies with 61 students across six middle school classrooms in the Western US

description: The article organizes CoBi around a routine in which "students establish, enact, and revisit CAs, occurring before, during, and after collaborative learning activities, respectively." article_title: AI-interaction literacy: reflections on how generative AI might be used to support self-regulated learning in higher education
citation: Linus Brunnström & Lisa Palmqvist. (2026). AI-interaction literacy: reflections on how generative AI might be used to support self-regulated learning in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2731261
title: AI-interaction literacy: the capacity to steer, evaluate, and learn from iterative GenAI interaction
description: AI-interaction literacy is the article's name for a specific capacity within broader AI literacy: "the ability to steer, evaluate, and learn from iterative interaction with GenAI". It concerns how self-regulatory processes are enacted with a system that responds fluently but not necessarily reliably or pedagogically, and includes formulating prompts, identifying when answers are too broad or complex, requesting clarification, comparing explanations, questioning claims, and deciding how to use or reject feedback. The authors position it as a specific enactment of broader AI literacy, particularly applying, evaluating, and integrating AI-generated output within a learning process.
requirements: The learner must possess self-regulatory skills in advance to tune the GenAI into a genuinely helpful partner, since the article found productive use demanded these skills.
constraints: The article notes it remains untested whether students could achieve the qualitative-phase progression using general, uninformed prompts alone, and that the emphasis on prompt quality may shift as GenAI systems develop.
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning with generative AI
evaluating and using AI-generated feedback
examples: In the demonstration, enacting this literacy meant telling the system its answers were overwhelming, asking explicitly for simplification, and requesting the learning process be structured in smaller steps.
key_sources: Linus Brunnström & Lisa Palmqvist. (2026). AI-interaction literacy: reflections on how generative AI might be used to support self-regulated learning in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2731261

title: Teachers should explicitly teach AI-interaction literacy, with particular attention to students with lower academic self-efficacy or less developed study skills
description: The article proposes that higher education teachers develop an explicit strategy for teaching students how to use GenAI in self-regulated learning, treating productive GenAI use as a learned competence rather than an intuitive one. This means teaching "how to formulate productive prompts, how to recognise when a response is too abstract or too broad, and how to structure a learning session around small, manageable goals". The responsibility for cultivating this competence, the authors argue, cannot rest with the student alone.
requirements: Teachers need an explicit strategy for teaching GenAI-supported self-regulated learning, not only disciplinary content.
constraints: Without such instruction, the article states GenAI risks becoming a tool that widens rather than narrows the performance gap between students.
target_learners: higher education students, particularly those with lower academic self-efficacy or less developed study skills
target_learning_goals: AI-interaction literacy
self-regulated learning with generative AI
examples: The demonstration's own calibration work — requesting simplification, narrowing scope, and condensing an overwhelming plan into a three-step loop — illustrates the competence the principle says should be taught.

title: Take-home assessments should emphasise evaluating knowledge at the qualitative phase of the SOLO taxonomy, with recall-based knowledge assessed in-class
description: Because GenAI is, in the authors' words, "a powerful tool for producing quantitative, factoid-type content", they propose that take-home assessments place strong emphasis on evaluating knowledge corresponding to the qualitative phase of the SOLO taxonomy. The rationale is assessment validity: a submitted artefact may no longer provide sufficient evidence of the student's own understanding when chatbots can produce plausible responses. Quantitative, recall-based knowledge is instead proposed for in-class formats where GenAI is not available as an aid.
requirements: Assessment formats such as take-home exams that explicitly promote critical thinking and independent problem-solving.
constraints: The proposal responds to the demonstrated risk that polished, multistructural AI output can be submitted as ready-to-submit text without indicating learning.
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of qualitative, relational understanding
examples: The demonstration's initial prompt produced a polished, essay-ready answer that would most likely receive a pass yet remained a collection of factoids without explanation.

article_title: Building AI Companions that Prioritize Learning over Performance
citation: Khosravi, H., Gašević, D., Sadiq, S., Yan, L., Lodge, J. M., Tangen, J. M., Denny, P., DiCerbo, K., Buckingham Shum, S., & Baker, R. S. (2026). Building AI Companions that Prioritise Learning over Performance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04816
title: AI learning companions framework: pedagogical, adaptive, and responsible design foundations
description: The paper introduces AI learning companions as "adaptive, pedagogically informed, LLM-powered agents designed for integration into learning environments" and proposes a design framework on three interrelated foundations. The pedagogical foundation addresses how students learn with AI; the adaptive foundation addresses how AI learns about students through modelling cognitive, affective, and behavioural data; and the responsible design foundation keeps systems "transparent, accountable, inclusive, and secure". The framework is illustrated through five case studies across educational contexts.
requirements: Companions must be deliberately engineered to prioritise durable learning over short-term performance rather than relying on prompt-level tutor roles
constraints: The paper states current tools' limitations are revealed by the case studies, and prompt-based approaches cannot match the adaptivity of ITSs
target_learners: students across diverse educational contexts and levels
target_learning_goals: durable understanding
metacognitive growth
learner agency

title: Nine-dimension contrast between AI for work and AI for learning
description: Figure 1 formalises the contrast between AI designed for professional productivity and AI designed for learning across nine dimensions, including purpose, what AI does, nature of interaction, relationship to cognitive effort, relationship to error, measures of success, key failure mode, design principle, and theoretical grounding. In work contexts "AI performs or co-performs the cognitive task on behalf of the user, each interaction is transactional and stateless"; in learning contexts AI must scaffold and challenge the learner, with success measured by retention, transfer, and metacognitive growth.
requirements: Learning-oriented AI must preserve productive struggle and withhold direct answers as a deliberate design feature
constraints: The paper states the reorientation demands a fundamental reconceptualisation, not a minor adjustment to prompting strategy or interface design
target_learners: designers and educators building AI tools for education
target_learning_goals: retention
transfer
metacognitive growth

title: Four pedagogical principles for AI companion design derived from the HELF
description: Building on the Higher Education Learning Framework, the paper derives four principles for AI companion design: "deep and interactive learning, which prompts learners to actively process and connect new knowledge through varied cognitive tasks; guided scaffolding, which delivers adaptive guidance calibrated to the learner's Zone of Proximal Development"; learning to learn and higher-order learning, fostering metacognition and autonomy; and contextual learning, situating learning in authentic contexts for transfer and disciplinary identity. Each principle carries concrete companion strategies such as prompting generation and retrieval rather than provision.
requirements: Companions must make the student do the thinking rather than present information passively
constraints: The paper notes current prompting approaches casting the model as a Socratic tutor often remain limited in scope and provide only surface-level support

title: Four-stage adaptive cycle: Capture, Model, Adapt, Evolve
description: The adaptive foundation organises adaptivity into "a four-stage adaptive cycle, Capture, Model, Adapt, and Evolve, that enables AI companions to transform raw learner interactions into personalised and pedagogically grounded support". Capture records digital footprints including LLM dialogue traces; Model builds multi-dimensional learner models combining LLM interpretation with knowledge tracing and memory algorithms; Adapt harmonises personalised guidance with socially shared regulation via outer and inner loops; Evolve treats instructional decisions as hypotheses tested through controlled experiments, bandit algorithms, and simulated learners.
requirements: Sustained adaptation requires overcoming the statelessness of most current LLM applications, where each interaction begins without memory of the last
constraints: The paper warns that fully automated adaptivity can make students passive recipients who offload metacognitive control, motivating shared regulation designs
target_learners: learners in digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: personalised feedback

continuous system improvement

title: Responsible design foundation: security, transparency, accountability, and inclusion commitments
description: The responsible design foundation organises trustworthy practice around "four interwoven commitments: security, transparency, accountability, and inclusion". Security protects privacy, data, and digital wellbeing through lawful data practices and psychological safety; transparency makes AI processes visible and explainable, building on XAI-ED and Open Learner Models; accountability retains human oversight with human-in-the-loop checkpoints for high-stakes inferences and dispute channels; inclusion ensures companions are fair, accessible, and responsive to diverse learners, abilities, languages, and contexts.
requirements: High-stakes inferences such as mastery promotion, at-risk flags, and achievement predictions should incorporate human-in-the-loop checkpoints
constraints: The paper states accountability must be learning-aligned: companions should be evaluated on impact on retention, transfer, metacognition, and durable learning, not only output accuracy

target_learning_goals: calibrated trust
learner agency
equitable access to AI-supported learning

title: Ecological three-level lens (micro, macro, chrono) for analyzing how AI reshapes digital literacy frameworks
description: The review organizes its analysis with Bronfenbrenner's ecological perspective, treating digital literacy as the developmental outcome of interplay between individuals and nested environmental systems across time. It distinguishes three levels: "the micro-level ecologies focus on digital literacy practices situated in school contexts; the macro-level ecologies foreground structural drivers, such as cultural and economic factors, of the digital divide across countries and regions in the AI era; and the chrono-level ecologies trace the conceptual evolution of digital literacy in response to advances in AI." Each level anchors one research question of the review.

constraints: The review applies the lens to school-context digital literacy frameworks published January 2014 to February 2025

educators including teachers and school leaders

title: Human-AI collaborative thematic analysis process guided by the IAVES framework
description: The study adapted Braun and Clarke's six-phase reflexive thematic analysis to incorporate systematic human-AI collaboration guided by the IAVES framework for Human-Centered AI Interaction. Multiple GenAI models were used strategically: "AI functioned instrumentally during systematic coding activities, as well as worked as an intellectual partner during interpretive theme development". Nine AI-proposed candidate themes were refined into twelve final themes through human disaggregation, with human researchers retaining full interpretive authority at all decision gates and cross-validation across models functioning as triangulation.
requirements: Human researchers retain interpretive authority and subject AI contributions to the same validation standards expected of human analytical work
constraints: The authors acknowledge that the internal reasoning processes of large language models are not transparent and the basis on which patterns are identified or weighted cannot be fully audited
target_learners: education researchers
qualitative researchers
target_learning_goals: conducting rigorous human-AI collaborative qualitative analysis
examples: ChatGPT-5.1 was used for coding and initial theme generation and Claude 4.5 Sonnet for theme interrogation and argumentation analysis via an auto-interview technique.

citation: Mireia Vendrell, Samantha-Kaye Johnston. (2026). Scaffolding critical thinking with generative AI: Design principles for integrating large language models in higher education. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100572
title: A design-oriented pedagogical framework for integrating LLMs to scaffold critical thinking in higher education
description: The article proposes a normative, design-oriented framework grounded in Design-Based Research, instructional-design theory, AI ethics and Freirean critical pedagogy. It links three risks of unstructured LLM use to six intellectual processes and eight design principles, arguing that 'the value of generative AI in education is not technical but fundamentally pedagogical'. It positions LLMs as objects of inquiry learners must interrogate rather than as tutors or efficiency supports.
requirements: Requires deliberate instructional sequencing and alignment of principles with the cognitive, metacognitive and epistemic processes they support
constraints: The authors state the framework 'is not intended as a definitive or universal solution, but as provisional pedagogical orientation that must remain open to critique, adaptation, and contextual interpretation'
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
epistemic agency
metacognitive regulation
examples: Two illustrative classroom scenarios (prompt design and AI-mediated argument construction) operationalise the framework's principles

title: Six essential intellectual processes underpinning critical thinking in AI-mediated learning
description: Drawing on Bloom's revised taxonomy, Halpern's model of critical thinking and the APA Delphi Report, the article articulates 'six essential and interrelated processes: conceptual interpretation, inferential reasoning, evaluative judgement, metacognitive regulation, intellectual curiosity, and epistemic integrity'. Each is defined and mapped in Table 1 to the risks of unstructured LLM use and to ethical foundations such as human agency and epistemic responsibility. The processes are both cognitive and dispositional.
requirements: Processes must be 'intentionally scaffolded through pedagogy' rather than assumed to emerge spontaneously
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
epistemic integrity
intellectual curiosity
examples: Table 1 maps each process to a risk (e.g., cognitive offloading threatens conceptual interpretation) and to theoretical foundations

title: Eight design principles for integrating LLMs while preserving critical thinking
description: The article enumerates eight actionable principles aligned with the six intellectual processes: preserve cognitive friction, scaffold LLMs as thinking partners, embed evaluation as standard practice, activate metacognitive self-regulation, encourage intellectual humility and curiosity, foster epistemic integrity, align assessment with intended cognition, and balance AI-mediated and AI-free phases. Table 2 maps each principle to the processes it supports, e.g., P8 'Develops independent reasoning before using AI, strengthening agency and self-regulation'.
requirements: Principles require deliberate orchestration of pre-AI, during-AI and post-AI learning activities rather than blanket policies
constraints: Scenarios are offered 'not as fixed templates or best practices, but as situated examples intended to provoke adaptation, critique, and redesign'

evaluative judgement
epistemic agency

article_title: Teacher or Artificial Intelligence? The Effect of Decision-Making Agent on Junior High School Students’ Decision Acceptance: A Moderated Mediation Model
citation: Zhang Zhen; Fan Siyu; Qi Chunhui. (2026). Teacher or Artificial Intelligence? The Effect of Decision-Making Agent on Junior High School Students’ Decision Acceptance: A Moderated Mediation Model. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071227
title: Moderated mediation model of educational decision acceptance integrating authority acceptance theory and organizational justice theory
description: The article proposes and empirically validates a moderated mediation model in which the decision-making agent (teacher vs. AI) predicts students' decision acceptance both directly and indirectly through perceived fairness, with explanatory feedback moderating the first-stage path. Grounded in "authority acceptance theory and organizational justice theory", it treats perceived fairness as "a core mediator linking decision-maker characteristics and final decision acceptance". The model was tested with PROCESS Model 8 and "empirically validated (see Figure 4)" in a 2×2 experiment with 250 seventh-graders.
requirements: Measurement of perceived fairness and decision acceptance as distinct self-report constructs, with the decision-making agent manipulated as the independent variable
constraints: Conclusions are bounded by unfavorable evaluation outcomes (a score of 6/10); outcome favorability is proposed as an additional boundary condition for future models
target_learners: junior high school students (seventh grade)
target_learning_goals: students' acceptance of educational evaluation decisions and perceptions of fairness in human–AI educational decision-making
examples: The article tested the model with a 2 (teacher vs. AI) × 2 (explanation vs. without explanation) vignette experiment on mathematics homework grading among seventh-graders
key_sources: Zhang Zhen; Fan Siyu; Qi Chunhui. (2026). Teacher or Artificial Intelligence? The Effect of Decision-Making Agent on Junior High School Students’ Decision Acceptance: A Moderated Mediation Model. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071227

article_title: Enhancing enthusiasm for STEM education with AI: Domain-specific chatbot as personalized learning assistant
citation: Cilia Ricarda Rücker, Sebastian Becker-Genschow. (2025). Enhancing enthusiasm for STEM education with AI: Domain-specific chatbot as personalized learning assistant. Computers and Education Open. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2025.100315
title: ADA: a domain-specific AI chatbot for secondary mathematics using Socratic dialogue, RAG, and a Wolfram Alpha plugin
description: ADA is a Custom Generative Pre-Trained Transformer built on GPT-4 via a GDPR-compliant API, designed as a learning assistant for secondary STEM education. Rather than giving answers, "ADA utilized questioning techniques to assist students in discovering mathematical relationships independently", providing individualized scaffolding. It combines prompt engineering with retrieval-augmented generation over a curated knowledge base, uses the Wolfram Alpha plugin to verify calculations, and integrates motivational design informed by Self-Determination Theory with gender-inclusive phrasing.
requirements: A curated knowledge base of curriculum content and intervention materials to reduce hallucinations
Privacy-compliant API access and a chat interface requiring no prior technical knowledge
constraints: Hallucinations persist as an inherent limitation of language models even with safeguards; the risk of plausible but incorrect outputs cannot be eliminated
target_learners: ninth-grade secondary mathematics students
target_learning_goals: estimating square roots with the Heron method
conceptual understanding of mathematical procedures
examples: In the study, EG students accessed ADA via school laptops during a double lesson on the Heron method while CG students used static help cards
