article_title: The Scaffolded AI literacy (SAIL) framework: Results of a Delphi study for equitable AI literacy framework design in education
citation: MacCallum K., Parsons D. & Mohaghegh M. (2026). The Scaffolded AI Literacy (SAIL) Framework: Results of a Delphi Study for Equitable AI Literacy Framework Design in Education. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100584
title: The Scaffolded AI Literacy (SAIL) framework: four age-agnostic levels of scaffolded AI competency development
description: SAIL is an AI literacy framework developed from a Delphi study that structures learning as a scaffolded pathway through competency levels applicable across ages and educational stages. It defines "the four (three plus one) levels of the framework", where the final stage (AI++) represents movement beyond AI literacy into expert practice. The framework is explicitly age agnostic: higher levels suit older learners, but "Level 1 concepts were appropriate (indeed, essential) to all age groups", with educators adapting delivery to context. Its scaffolding rationale draws on Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and activity theory, guiding learners from supported stages toward autonomy.
requirements: Educators integrate activities and opportunities within the framework's pedagogical structure, since the article states a scaffolded framework cannot on its own provide scaffolded learning.
constraints: The framework cannot directly solve first-level digital divide infrastructural issues such as connectivity and devices.
Higher levels (3 and above) are more suited to older learners, with delivery adapted to age and context.
target_learners: All learners across early years, primary, secondary, and higher education
Educators developing their own AI literacy
target_learning_goals: AI literacy: understanding AI concepts, applying and evaluating AI, and critical, ethical, and culturally informed engagement with AI
examples: A scaffolded competency example: Level 1 asks learners to "Define and recognise common AI terms and features", progressing to evaluating architectures at Level 3 and mastery of advanced AI concepts at AI++.
key_sources: MacCallum K., Parsons D. & Mohaghegh M. (2026). The Scaffolded AI Literacy (SAIL) Framework: Results of a Delphi Study for Equitable AI Literacy Framework Design in Education. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100584

article_title: The Scaffolded AI literacy (SAIL) framework: Results of a Delphi study for equitable AI literacy framework design in education
citation: MacCallum K., Parsons D. & Mohaghegh M. (2026). The Scaffolded AI Literacy (SAIL) Framework: Results of a Delphi Study for Equitable AI Literacy Framework Design in Education. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100584
title: Three domains and six categories with key ideas mapping competencies across all levels
description: SAIL organises its content as a matrix: three domains (AI Concepts; Application of AI and Technical Skills; AI Digital Citizenship) each containing two categories, giving six categories in total. The article states that "The six categories together ensure that there is an appropriate mix of knowledge, skills, and critical thinking." Each category is represented at every level, and each competency is mapped across the four levels using a set of key ideas, so a given competency can be followed and developed in stages as the learner progresses. This structure makes progression between levels visible and supports cross-referencing of content between categories.
requirements: Competencies must be worded and placed so that progression between levels is evident, which the researchers achieved through iterative refinement and panel feedback.
target_learners: Learners at all levels of education
Educators planning AI literacy curricula
target_learning_goals: Balanced development of AI knowledge, technical and cognitive skills, and critical thinking about AI
examples: The six categories include The Impacts of AI, What AI Is and How It Works, Cognitive Skills, Applied Skills, Social Cultural and Ethical Issues, and Risks and Mitigations.
key_sources: MacCallum K., Parsons D. & Mohaghegh M. (2026). The Scaffolded AI Literacy (SAIL) Framework: Results of a Delphi Study for Equitable AI Literacy Framework Design in Education. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100584

article_title: “AI is reducing options I had used”: exploring faculty perceptions of accessible course design in a ChatGPT world
citation: Gurher Sidhu, Fatima Atif, Franz Newland. (2025). "AI is reducing options I had used": exploring faculty perceptions of accessible course design in a ChatGPT world. York University. https://www.yorku.ca
title: Universal Design for Learning: three pillars of multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression
description: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is an inclusive pedagogy, inspired by universal design in architecture, that seeks to design learning environments accessible to as many learners as possible. Following its three pillars, "teachers should aim to provide: multiple means of engagement, or motivation, with course material; multiple means of representation... and, multiple means of action and expression, or diverse assessment methods". The study uses UDL as the framework against which faculty awareness and implementation of twenty techniques is assessed.
requirements: Sufficient uptake by professors for UDL to reduce the burden on accessibility services and students
constraints: UDL will not meet all students' needs and does not replace individual accommodations entirely
Applied in a post-secondary context where individual accommodations follow a medical model while UDL aligns with the social model of disability
target_learners: Post-secondary students, including those with and without formal accessibility needs
target_learning_goals: Accessible learning environments through multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression
examples: The survey rated faculty familiarity and implementation of twenty UDL techniques such as closed captioning, flexible deadlines, and OCR-readable PDFs
key_sources: Gurher Sidhu, Fatima Atif, Franz Newland. (2025). "AI is reducing options I had used": exploring faculty perceptions of accessible course design in a ChatGPT world. York University. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/e4hmv_v1

article_title: Exploring University Faculty's AI Well-Being: A Structural Equation Model of Social Supports, AI Literacy, and Technological Self-Efficacy
citation: Liu, W.; Li, Y.; Yan, Y.; Wang, J.; Wang, J.; Zhang, H. (2026). Exploring University Faculty’s AI Well-Being: A Structural Equation Model of Social Supports, AI Literacy, and Technological Self-Efficacy. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071168
title: Support–literacy–well-being pathway integrating social support theory and self-determination theory
description: The article proposes an explanatory framework in which external supports (social and organizational) strengthen internal capacities (AI literacy and technological self-efficacy), which in turn foster faculty AI-related well-being. The authors state: "we propose a sequential psychological model: External Support → Internal Capacities (AI literacy/self-efficacy) → AI Well-being". It combines social support theory's external resource buffering with self-determination theory's satisfaction of autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs, positioning AI literacy as the mechanism through which contextual supports are internalized as professional competence.
requirements: Supportive environments that provide collegial collaboration, institutional resources, and skill-development opportunities through which psychological needs for relatedness and competence can be fulfilled
constraints: Tested in a cross-sectional survey at a single research-intensive university in China, so causal inference and generalization are limited as the authors state
target_learners: University faculty in AI-integrated higher education
target_learning_goals: Faculty psychological adaptation and well-being during AI integration; AI literacy development
examples: The authors empirically tested the framework with SEM on survey data from 502 faculty, finding the hypothesized H1–H6 paths supported

title: Localized faculty AI literacy scale based on UNESCO's 2024 AI Competency Framework for Teachers
description: A 15-item, five-point Likert survey instrument developed by the authors to measure faculty AI literacy. It is grounded in UNESCO's 2024 AI Competency Framework for Teachers: "The scale encompassed five core aspects: Human-Centered Mindset, Ethics of AI, AI Foundations and Applications, AI Pedagogy, and AI for Professional Development", each assessed at three developmental levels (Acquire, Deepen, Create). In this study it showed strong internal consistency (KMO = 0.948; Cronbach's α = 0.953) and served as the key mediating variable.
requirements: Expert review and pilot testing for content validity and contextual appropriateness, as the authors describe for their instruments
target_learners: University faculty
target_learning_goals: Assessing faculty AI literacy across cognitive, technical, ethical, and pedagogical capabilities
examples: Sample items include "Recognizing that AI tools are human-driven" and "Effectively applying AI in instructional design and implementation"

title: PERMA-based AI well-being scale for faculty in AI-integrated teaching
description: A five-item Likert-scale instrument the authors developed to measure faculty AI well-being, defined as positive psychological functioning in AI-supported teaching and academic work. It is built on Seligman's PERMA model: "It included five items, each corresponding to one dimension of the PERMA framework", covering positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment in relation to AI use. It showed the highest AVE (0.851) and C.R. (0.966) among the study's constructs.
requirements: Deliberately multidimensional framing that captures positive functioning rather than merely the absence of technostress, as the authors state motivated the PERMA choice
constraints: The authors note the very high Cronbach's α (0.966) may indicate item redundancy and that the brief operationalization may not fully capture the multidimensional nature of digital well-being
target_learners: University faculty
target_learning_goals: Measuring positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, and accomplishment in AI-supported work
examples: Sample items include "Using AI makes me feel happy and satisfied in my work" and "AI assists my work, giving me a strong sense of achievement"

article_title: Fostering collaborative futures: Multidisciplinary approaches to AI integration in educational ecosystems
citation: Rwitajit Majumdar, Dirk Ifenthaler, Clara Schumacher, Enda Donlon, Hsiao-Ping Hsu, Jason Zagami, Maaike Heitink, Wolfgang Mueller. (2026). Fostering collaborative futures: Multidisciplinary approaches to AI integration in educational ecosystems. Computers and Education Open 11 (2026) 100405. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100405
title: Educational ecosystem perspective on AI integration
description: The article defines an education ecosystem as "a dynamic, sustainable, and interconnected network of individuals, institutions, data, technologies, policies, and processes, as well as cultures that collectively influence and impact the teaching and learning" in formal, non-formal, and informal contexts. It uses this framework to position AI not as an isolated technological intervention but as embedded within interdependent ecosystem components, arguing the five Delphi trends map onto human actors, data flows, institutional infrastructures, cultural norms, and governance structures, and that sustainable adoption requires coordinated action across policy, practice, and research.
requirements: Requires attention to interdependencies among pedagogy, infrastructure, policy, and ethics rather than isolated interventions
constraints: The article notes educational institutions are sociotechnical systems shaped by historical practices, professional cultures, power relations, and competing stakeholder interests, so integration is not a straightforward insertion of technology
target_learners: Learners and educators across formal, non-formal, and informal educational contexts
target_learning_goals: Effective, ethical, and equitable integration of AI in teaching and learning
examples: The authors interpret the five Delphi trends as nodes within a larger sociotechnical network, e.g. competence development depending on institutional professional learning systems and policy support
key_sources: Rwitajit Majumdar, Dirk Ifenthaler, Clara Schumacher, Enda Donlon, Hsiao-Ping Hsu, Jason Zagami, Maaike Heitink, Wolfgang Mueller. (2026). title: Four stakeholder personas for AI-enhanced educational ecosystems
description: The article reports that the working group "synthesised four personas that represented key stakeholders in AI-enhanced educational ecosystems": the Teacher (Educator), the Ed-tech Developer, the Researcher, and the Policymaker. Built from model-card style notes and field observations from cross-visits to other EDUsummIT working groups, each persona captures stakeholder-specific concerns such as workload and safe AI use, access to learner data and interoperability, ethics and evidence-informed evaluation, and funding and regulatory frameworks. Workshop participants adopted one persona in small groups to identify needs, challenges, and recommendations tied to the ranked AI trends.
requirements: Grounding in real evidence about stakeholder attitudes and needs, compiled from field notes and cross-visit observations
constraints: The personas represent institutional-level stakeholders; students and parents were not represented at this stage
target_learners: Educators, ed-tech developers, researchers, and policymakers in AI-enhanced educational ecosystems
target_learning_goals: Contextualising AI integration challenges and generating stakeholder-specific recommendations
examples: Groups adopting the Teacher persona discussed classroom implementation, workload, and implications of AI for assessment and professional identity

article_title: Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, and Learner Agency in Higher Education: A Scoping Review
citation: Wang Guanhua, Wang Wenna, Yang Daozhou, Ren Jifan. (2026). Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, and Learner Agency in Higher Education: A Scoping Review. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071150
title: Dual-pattern framework: GenAI use in higher education splits into agency-supportive and agency-eroding patterns
description: The review's organizing framework interprets GenAI's educational significance through two recurring patterns rather than a single effect. Agency-supportive patterns involve self-regulated learning, self-efficacy, feedback literacy, and reflective engagement, while agency-eroding patterns involve cognitive offloading, overreliance, dependence, and uncritical uptake. The review states these are "best interpreted through an interpretive dual-pattern account" and stresses they are a configurative synthesis of heterogeneous evidence, not causal effect estimates.
requirements: Evidence must be charted as substantively addressing agency or offloading mechanisms, not merely keyword presence
constraints: The framework is an interpretive synthesis of heterogeneous, mostly non-causal evidence, not a causal model or ranking of mechanisms
target_learners: higher education students (undergraduate and postgraduate)
target_learning_goals: maintaining learner agency in AI-supported learning
self-regulated learning
critical evaluation of AI output
examples: The review charted 123 studies, with 118 contributing to the agency-supportive theme family and 108 to the agency-eroding/offloading theme family
key_sources: Wang Guanhua, Wang Wenna, Yang Daozhou, Ren Jifan. (2026). Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, and Learner Agency in Higher Education: A Scoping Review. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071150

citation: Wang Guanhua, Wang Wenna, Yang Daozhou, Ren Jifan. (2026). Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, and Learner Agency in Higher Education: A Scoping Review. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071150
title: Learner agency in GenAI contexts as a multidimensional, context-sensitive construct
description: The review treats learner agency as learners' capacity to purposefully direct, monitor, evaluate, and take responsibility for their learning while interacting with GenAI, not as a synonym for autonomy or participation. It synthesizes operationalizations including L. Xia et al.'s three-dimensional scale (key abilities, active actions, essential mental characteristics) and Yang et al.'s distinction among receptive, resistive, resourceful, and reflective engagement. The review concludes "learner agency in GenAI-supported higher education should be understood as a multidimensional and context-sensitive construct."
requirements: Agency must be examined through how learners interpret, control, and act upon AI support, not inferred from tool use or attitudes alone
constraints: The construct is context-sensitive: the same technology may support agentic engagement in one context and passive dependence in another
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: directing and evaluating one's own AI-supported learning
exercising evaluative judgement over AI output
examples: L. Xia et al. (2025) developed a student learning agency scale for GenAI-supported contexts with three interrelated dimensions

article_title: Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, and Learner Agency in Higher Education: A Scoping Review
citation: Wang Guanhua, Wang Wenna, Yang Daozhou, Ren Jifan. (2026). Generative AI, Cognitive Offloading, and Learner Agency in Higher Education: A Scoping Review. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071150
title: Embed GenAI pedagogically as scaffolded, augmentation-oriented support rather than replacement-oriented direct-answer use
description: The review's central pedagogical principle is that GenAI's educational value depends less on the technology than on how it is embedded. Scaffolded designs that provide hints, prompts, feedback, and intermediate guidance keep learners as active interpreters who inspect, revise, and justify reasoning, whereas direct-answer designs invite passive acceptance of output. The review reports that "scaffolded use is more beneficial than direct-answer use in the studies that directly compared or discussed these designs."
requirements: Learning designs must preserve reflection, evaluation, and responsibility; learners need guidance on how to use GenAI
constraints: The review notes benefits are rarely automatic and depend on learners remaining cognitively and metacognitively involved
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: maintaining learner agency during AI-supported tasks
reflective and evaluative engagement with AI support
examples: Studies of guidance-based, Socratic, and scaffolded GenAI designs reviewed in Section 4.5, in which learners remained active interpreters when AI provided hints and intermediate guidance rather than final answers

article_title: Designing for Reach: Seven Levers and the Student Alone with AI
citation: Halani, A. (2026). Designing for Reach: Seven Levers and the Student Alone with AI. Tang Institute at Phillips Academy. https://www.tanginstitute.andover.edu
title: Seven-lever course-design framework for shaping student AI use
description: The framework defines a lever as "a recurring feature of the course environment that students experience, that can be configured differently by someone within the institution, and that may influence what students do with or without direct supervision." The seven levers are Structure (what pays), Material (what they work on and when), Practice (how the room runs), Response (what gets said back), Norms (what is normal), Frame (what they understand about why), and Relationship (what is safe). Every classroom has a setting on all seven, whether chosen or defaulted, and none of the levers is specific to AI.
requirements: Each lever must be a recurring, experienceable feature of the course environment configurable by someone within the institution
constraints: The framework is offered as a heuristic taxonomy, not a validated or necessarily exhaustive model, and does not establish causal effects for particular configurations
Class size, contact hours, and tracking are conditions of the cultural surround, not levers
target_learners: secondary and university mathematics students
target_learning_goals: protecting independent thinking when AI use is unobserved
deepening rather than shortcutting reasoning
examples: The paper describes three full lever-setting tables for a think-first classroom, a direct-instruction classroom, and a Harkness classroom

As the paper puts it, "Two teachers may have clearly identifiable settings on all seven levers and still create substantially different learning experiences because they are pursuing different outcomes."

article_title: Applying psychometric methods to distinguish between human and generative AI responses to multiple-choice assessments
citation: Alona Strugatski and Giora Alexandron. (2025). Applying Item Response Theory to Distinguish Between Human and Generative AI Responses to Multiple-Choice Assessments. LAK'25 pre-print. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.02713
title: IRT-based person-fit statistics as a conceptual framework for distinguishing GenAI from human response patterns in MCQ assessment
description: The paper proposes applying Item Response Theory and, within it, Person-Fit Statistics to educational assessment as a lens for detecting GenAI cheating. PFS is "a collection of statistical methods designed to assess the alignment between an individual's test performance and an expected response pattern". Because AI and human intelligence differ architecturally, AI cheating manifests as deviations from expected human response patterns, quantified by non-parametric statistics (G, G*, U3, ZU3) computed per examinee. The framework grounds a learning-analytics approach in established educational measurement theory rather than ad-hoc detection heuristics.
requirements: Tests of at least 20 items, since short tests may not provide enough data to reliably detect aberrant patterns
Cheating must remain non-normative for aberrancy-based detection to work
constraints: Sensitive to the level of pollution
Applied retrospectively and less appropriate for real-time detection
High PFS misfit can also arise from legitimate conditions such as learning disabilities
target_learners: high-school students taking formative chemistry assessments
prospective students taking high-stakes entrance exams
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of learner ability on multiple-choice instruments
academic integrity of MCQ-based summative assessment
examples: The framework was instantiated on a 22-item chemistry diagnostic (931 respondents) and a 20-item psychometric quantitative chapter (over 4,800 respondents), with 20 runs each of ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
key_sources: Alona Strugatski and Giora Alexandron. (2025). Applying Item Response Theory to Distinguish Between Human and Generative AI Responses to Multiple-Choice Assessments. LAK'25 pre-print. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.02713

citation: Jiang Hongzhan, Wang Ziyan, Shen Wanting, Meng Meiqi, Yang Dan, Li Xuejing, Hao Yufang. (2026). AI-Powered Simulation for Nursing Education: Mixed Methods Systematic Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/95167
title: Four-category taxonomy of AI-powered simulation modalities in nursing education
description: The review organizes AI-powered nursing simulations into four categories "distinguished by their technical architectures and pedagogical mechanisms": generative AI/large language models, AI-driven virtual patients/mannequins, AI-enhanced VR/mixed reality, and AI chatbots/tutors. citation: Yueqiao Jin, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Dragan Gašević and Lixiang Yan. (2024). GLAT: The Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00283
title: Prefer performance-based GenAI literacy assessment over self-report instruments when measuring actual competencies
description: The article argues that self-reported AI literacy instruments capture perceived abilities but "may introduce biases that obscure a more reliable measure of literacy levels", and that performance-based assessments evaluate actual competencies through direct engagement. It developed GLAT as a performance-based alternative and showed its scores predicted GenAI-supported task performance better than a validated self-report scale. The principle directs educators and researchers toward performance measures when the goal is assessing real capability to use generative tools.

citation: Salim Nabhan, Anita Habók. (2026). Language teachers' AI literacy: A psychometric study based on the ED-AI framework. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 10 (2026) 100583. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100583
title: ED-AI literacy framework: six dimensions of AI literacy for education
description: The ED-AI literacy framework (Allen & Kendeou, 2024), as adopted and operationalized in this study, conceptualizes educational AI literacy across six dimensions: knowledge, evaluation, collaboration, contextualization, autonomy, and ethics. The article defines knowledge as "Teachers' understanding of fundamental AI concepts, tools, and their applications within educational contexts" and evaluation as the ability to "critically analyze and compare various AI tools for educational purposes." The framework was selected using the IMPACT criteria (Interestingness, Matching, Parsimony, Applicability, Conceptual rigor, Testability) and grounds the TAILS item-to-construct mapping.
requirements: Dimensions must be operationalizable as distinct yet interrelated constructs measurable through established psychometric procedures
constraints: The article bounds validation claims to preservice English language teacher populations and comparable contexts
target_learners: preservice English language teachers
target_learning_goals: AI literacy for AI-integrated language teaching, including pedagogical judgment, contextual adaptation, and ethical decision-making
examples: TAILS items were generated per dimension and mapped one-to-one to constructs, e.g., an ethics item: "I actively consider students' privacy when using AI tools."

citation: Jerin George Mathew, Sumayya Taher, Anindita Kundu, Denilson Barbosa. (2026). LLMs Do Not Grade Essays Like Humans. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23714
title: Framework combining LLM scoring, generated feedback, and essay-feature analysis
description: The article proposes an analysis framework in which "Essays are first evaluated by LLMs to produce both predicted scores and textual feedback." Essay-level features (length, Flesch Reading Ease readability, and LanguageTool error counts) and feedback-derived signals (trait-specific praise and criticism via aspect-based sentiment analysis with a DeBERTa-v3 ABSA model, confidence above 0.9) are then extracted and related to the scores. The framework was applied to GPT-3.5, GPT-4.1, GPT-5-mini, and Llama 2, 3, and 4 models on the ASAP and DREsS datasets to compare LLM scores with human ratings and examine how feedback sentiment and essay characteristics relate to assigned scores.

citation: Nicola Brocca, Davide Garassino. (2026). LLMs in text linguistics teaching: an exploratory study with genAI novices in higher education. Computers and Education Open 11 (2026) 100414. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100414
title: Human-in-the-loop LLM workflow as a metacognitive framework for AI-assisted learning
description: The article conceptualizes LLM integration in learning through a Human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflow in which learners alternate between manual analysis, prompting, evaluating model outputs, and refining prompts. The authors state that "This interaction between human and machine reflects a metacognitive process, in which users continuously monitor the adequacy of the LLM's output and adjust their strategies accordingly". In the study, this framework grounded the deductive coding of student prompts and underpins the conclusion that prompting and output evaluation are metacognitive practices. It draws on distributed cognition, delegating to the LLM the operations it performs more efficiently than humans while keeping interpretation human-driven.
requirements: Learners must alternate between manual analysis, prompting, and evaluating model outputs, with each cycle requiring reflection and adjustment
constraints: The study applies the framework in a text linguistics class; the authors note cross-disciplinary relevance but the empirical grounding here is one small classroom case
target_learners: genAI novices in higher education
target_learning_goals: metacognitive competence in AI-assisted tasks
subject-specific text analysis skills
examples: The intervention required students to first analyze a newspaper text manually, then prompt an LLM, compare outputs, and refine prompts

title: Pair-based, discovery-oriented LLM analysis activity following an eight-week disciplinary module
description: The intervention's design combined two pedagogical principles: Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development, realized through paired work, and Dewey's learning through experience, realized as an authentic discovery-oriented task without explicit prompt-engineering instruction. Students first completed an eight-week instructional module on text linguistics concepts, then manually analyzed a newspaper article, and finally used an LLM to verify their analysis, creating their own prompts and comparing AI-generated analysis with their own. The activity was part of the course exam program and completed at home over two weeks.

title: LLMs Unplugged open resource suite: lessons, instructor notes, and n-gram booklet software tools at www.llmsunplugged.org
description: LLMs Unplugged is a freely available (CC BY-NC-SA) collection of unplugged activities for teaching language-model fundamentals, hosted at www.llmsunplugged.org. article_title: LUDIA: A Design and Evidence Statement
citation: Stark, B., & Rostan, J. (2026). LUDIA: A design and evidence statement (Version 1.0). Ask LUDIA. https://askludia.com/en
title: LUDIA: a no-cost, private, multilingual AI thought partner grounding educators in UDL
description: LUDIA is a browser-based AI tool for educators, instructional designers, and learning leaders, described as "a no-cost, private, multilingual AI thought partner that connects educators with the Universal Design for Learning framework". Unlike general-purpose chatbots used as solution engines, it is engineered to ground every response in the UDL Guidelines, connect the educator's situation to relevant Guidelines so the reasoning is visible, and offer options to weigh rather than instructions to follow. It relaunches in August 2026 on a purpose-built platform with no accounts, no cookies, and no server-side chat storage.
requirements: Requires a browser and an internet connection; the user must confirm they are 18 or older
constraints: The authors state they hold no evidence that LUDIA improves learning; the relaunched tool has no outcome data, no efficacy trial, and no monitoring because it has not yet been used
Machine-translated languages other than English have not been validated by professional translators and may contain errors
Cost-free is not always-available: the self-funded architecture caps how many educators it can serve at one moment
target_learners: Educators, instructional designers, and learning leaders in schools and learning organisations
target_learning_goals: Identifying and reducing barriers in the design of instruction and learning environments using the UDL Guidelines
examples: Beta tested ahead of relaunch by a global community of volunteer educators in their own planning and design work across languages, education systems, and cultural contexts

article_title: LUDIA: A Design and Evidence Statement
citation: Stark, B., & Rostan, J. (2026). LUDIA: A design and evidence statement (Version 1.0). Ask LUDIA. https://askludia.com/en
title: Universal Design for Learning as a design lens grounded in learner variability
description: The statement grounds LUDIA in CAST's Universal Design for Learning framework, which supports educators in designing learning experiences and environments for the full range of learners, "anticipating and embracing variability from the start, rather than focusing on perceived deficits in learners". CAST states the premise as "there is no average brain. Variability is the dominant feature of the nervous system" and describes three principles — Engagement, Representation, and Action and Expression — as aligning to affective, recognition, and strategic networks, a framing CAST itself calls a simplified model useful for thinking about design rather than a claim about how the brain works. The Guidelines are a lens for finding barriers in existing designs, not a prescription or checklist, and Guidelines 3.0 positions UDL alongside asset-based approaches such as Funds of Knowledge and Disability Studies.
requirements: Educators or instructional designers must make the teaching-method decisions; the framework does not say which method to teach by
constraints: The authors note the evidence base of the framework LUDIA rests on is under active and legitimate challenge
UDL originated in the United States and its uptake in national policy is uneven
target_learners: Educators, instructional designers, and learning leaders designing for the full range of learners
target_learning_goals: Reducing barriers to learning while honouring learners' multiple identities and specific learning goals

article_title: LUDIA: A Design and Evidence Statement
citation: Stark, B., & Rostan, J. (2026). LUDIA: A design and evidence statement (Version 1.0). Ask LUDIA. https://askludia.com/en
title: Design AI planning tools to redirect attention from fixing the learner to reducing barriers in the design
description: The principle holds that the barrier lives in the design, not in the learner, and that an AI thought partner for inclusive design should embody this by default. LUDIA is described as "redirecting educators away from fixing the learner and towards reducing barriers in the design of instruction and learning environments", doing so in every exchange without being asked, and supporting educators in working through engagement, representation, and action and expression before a learner meets the barrier. The authors tie this to an asset-based mindset in which focusing on strengths and embracing learner variability creates space to identify and reduce barriers within the designer's circle of influence.

title: Privacy and accessibility as architecture, not settings, in an educator AI tool
description: The relaunched LUDIA embodies a design pattern in which privacy and accessibility are treated as "the architecture" rather than settings: no cookies, no accounts, no server-side chat content, no data collected for model training, and exchanges that are downloadable and re-uploadable. target_learning_goals: Universal access to inclusive design support regardless of institutional backing, connectivity, or language

article_title: Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols
citation: Li Shijin & Liu Junjian. (2026). Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081365
title: Reciprocal monitoring–control architecture with planning as prospective control and regulation as adaptive control
description: The study organizes observable metacognitive processes through the reciprocal monitoring–control architecture, in which "monitoring provides information about the current state of cognition, whereas control selects, initiates, modifies, or terminates subsequent cognitive activity." Within it, planning is treated as prospective control and regulation as adaptive changes made after evaluation or feedback. The metacognitive agent is the learner, with GenAI treated as an external cognitive resource whose outputs become objects of monitoring and control; a prompt can externalize planning, a criterion judgment can externalize monitoring, and a targeted revision can externalize regulation.
requirements: Coding requires separating prospective organization (planning), evaluative checking without enacted change (monitoring), and observable modification after feedback or evaluation (regulation) as mutually exclusive primary labels
constraints: The study does not assess metacognitive knowledge, motivation, affect, monitoring accuracy, or learning outcomes; a fluent model response is not itself evidence of learner metacognition
target_learners: undergraduate students using generative AI for instructional-design tasks
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and control during GenAI-assisted learning tasks
examples: In the 90-minute DeepSeek task, prompts specifying goals or constraints were coded as planning, judgments comparing model responses with task criteria as monitoring, and revisions after such judgments as regulation
key_sources: Li Shijin & Liu Junjian. (2026). Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081365

article_title: Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols
citation: Li Shijin & Liu Junjian. (2026). Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081365
title: Two-dimensional rubric coding operational process category and depth of explicit metacognitive evidence
description: The article introduces a shared coding rubric applied identically to interaction logs and think-aloud speech. "Dimension 1, operational process category, answered what metacognitive function was observable and assigned planning, monitoring, or regulation. Dimension 2, depth of explicit metacognitive evidence, answered how explicitly and integratively the unit articulated a goal, criterion, procedure, evaluation, or transfer and assigned implicit, awareness, strategic, or reflective." Depth is an ordinal property of the evidence in a semantic unit, not a taxonomy of processes or a measure of learner proficiency, and boundary rules govern ambiguous cases such as criterion-free versus criterion-tied judgments.
requirements: Trained double coding with consensus resolution; the reported agreement was process category κ = 0.90 (logs) and 0.87 (think-aloud), evidence depth κ = 0.86 and 0.85
constraints: The rubric classifies evidence in units rather than learners; its construct validity as a general scale has not been established, and separate unitization reliability was not reported
target_learners: undergraduate students in teacher-education and related majors
target_learning_goals: describing observable planning, monitoring, and regulation evidence in GenAI-assisted work
examples: A monitoring unit stating a concern without a criterion was coded awareness depth, while one invoking an observable-performance criterion was coded strategic depth

article_title: Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols
citation: Li Shijin & Liu Junjian. (2026). Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081365
title: Design GenAI learning activities with reciprocal monitoring–control checkpoints that link criteria, judgments, and revisions
description: The article proposes, as a design hypothesis rather than an established recommendation, scaffolds that make the informational relation between monitoring and control explicit: "Such a scaffold could prompt learners to externalize a goal or evaluative criterion as prospective control, compare the current AI response or developing artifact with that criterion, select and justify an adaptation when a discrepancy is identified, and monitor the resulting state." In a ZPD-informed variant, prompt frequency and specificity could be adjusted or faded as learners demonstrate they can articulate and apply their own criteria.
requirements: Controlled studies comparing alternative scaffolds with independently assessed outcomes are needed before efficacy can be claimed
constraints: The authors state these features should be regarded as design propositions rather than evidence-based prescriptions, because the task explicitly encouraged planning and revision
target_learners: undergraduate learners working with generative AI on structured design tasks
target_learning_goals: coordinating monitoring with control when evaluating and revising AI-generated content
examples: The proposed cycle has learners state a criterion before generation, record a judgment after inspecting output, and connect any revision to that judgment, with new information returning the learner to any function
key_sources: Li Shijin & Liu Junjian. (2026). Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081365

article_title: Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols
citation: Li Shijin & Liu Junjian. (2026). Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081365
title: Combine interaction traces with brief learner-authored checkpoints for formative visibility, treating channels as complementary
description: Because verbalized monitoring and enacted control leave different observable traces, the article recommends that, where feasible and ethically appropriate, "educators could combine low-burden interaction traces with brief learner-authored checkpoints to improve formative visibility, not to enable surveillance, automated proficiency scoring, or validation of one source against the other." The absence of evidence in one channel should not be taken as evidence the process did not occur: logs can preserve revisions without rationales, while speech can preserve evaluations never enacted.
requirements: Formative interpretation should rely on temporally linked participant-level sequences rather than pooled label prevalence, using a coding scheme validated for the task, population, and GenAI system
constraints: The authors warn against surveillance use, automated proficiency scoring, and treating either channel as a criterion measure
target_learners: undergraduate learners in GenAI-supported courses
target_learning_goals: making monitoring–control coordination visible for formative feedback
examples: When a revision appears in the log without an articulated rationale, an instructor might invite the learner to explain the basis for the change; when a discrepancy is verbalized without action, the learner might be prompted to decide whether adaptation is warranted

article_title: Exploring Middle School Students' Interactions and Perceptions of Using Generative AI in STEAM Learning Environments
citation: Zhao Qianhui and Li Shuhui. (2026). Exploring Middle School Students' Interactions and Perceptions of Using Generative AI in STEAM Learning Environments. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16091626
title: Two-dimensional conceptual framework for student–GenAI interaction and perception in STEAM learning
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework with two dimensions: student–GenAI interaction and students' perceptions of GenAI use. The interaction dimension examines interaction "from three perspectives: the 'Student–GenAI' perspective, the 'Student' perspective, and the 'GenAI' perspective", comprising four sub-dimensions: interaction content, student standpoint, prompt type, and prompt purpose. The perception dimension covers satisfaction, trust level, and GenAI utility. The framework maintains interpretation at the behavioral level because the same interaction behavior may reflect different cognitive processes across contexts.
requirements: Interaction content coding requires joint analysis of both prompts and GenAI responses; other sub-dimensions are coded from prompts alone
constraints: Interpretation is maintained at the behavioral level, not the cognitive level
Interaction logs represent group-level rather than individual-level interactions because students shared one device
target_learners: middle school (eighth-grade) students
target_learning_goals: characterizing student–GenAI interaction behaviors and perceptions in interdisciplinary STEAM learning
examples: Applied to code 310 interaction entries across two STEAM modules, with Cohen's κ values of 0.964, 0.975, 0.943, and 1.000 for the four interaction sub-dimensions

article_title: Observer Perceptions of GenAI Use and Interpersonal Trust: The Roles of Warmth, Competence, and AI Literacy
citation: Zhang Zhen, Geng Jiaying, Qi Chunhui. (2026). Observer Perceptions of GenAI Use and Interpersonal Trust: The Roles of Warmth, Competence, and AI Literacy. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071221
title: Stereotype Content Model account of observers' evaluations of GenAI users along warmth and competence dimensions
description: The article applies the Stereotype Content Model (Fiske et al., 2002) to the human–AI–human triad, in which observers judge a GenAI user along two fundamental dimensions before adjusting trust. As the article states, "SCM posits that individuals judge others along two fundamental dimensions of social perception: warmth (e.g., friendliness, sincerity, morality) and competence (e.g., intelligence, ambition, efficiency)". In this study the framework explains why GenAI use reduces trust: use lowers perceived warmth and competence, which in turn lower interpersonal trust. It is combined with social cognitive theory to motivate perceived AI literacy as a contextual moderator.
requirements: Observers must form person perceptions of a specific target user, operationalized here via a recall method and peer-rating scales
constraints: The article tests the framework in a cross-sectional, recall-based peer-evaluation context among Chinese university students; causal inferences are precluded by the design
target_learners: university students evaluating peers
target_learning_goals: understanding social evaluation of AI users in academic collaboration
examples: Participants recalled a specific classmate who had used AI and rated the target's warmth, competence, AI literacy, and trustworthiness on adapted scales

article_title: Community-Based AI Learning: Redistributing Artificial Intelligence's Epistemic Authority in Education
citation: Santiago Ojeda-Ramirez, Symone Gyles and Kylie Peppler. 2026. Community-Based AI Learning: Redistributing Artificial Intelligence's Epistemic Authority in Education. In Proceedings of 2026 Conference for Research on Equitable and Sustained Participation in Engineering, Computing, and Technology (RESPECT 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3796496.3811760
title: Community-based AI learning: a framework anchoring AI education in community epistemologies
description: The paper defines community-based AI learning as "an approach to learning with and about AI that anchors epistemic activity in locally meaningful concerns, redistributes authority across heterogeneous forms of expertise, and orients AI engagement toward collective sense-making and action in relation to lived conditions." Drawing on community-based science education and constructionism, it positions learners and communities as legitimate knowers alongside AI systems, treating local experience as the evaluative standard for AI outputs rather than a cultural enrichment resource.
requirements: Learning must be anchored in locally meaningful community concerns rather than abstract or universally transferable AI knowledge
constraints: The paper is a perspective piece; the framework is theorized, not empirically tested in this article
target_learners: K-12 and higher education learners engaging with generative AI
target_learning_goals: Critical AI literacy
Epistemic judgment about when to trust, interrogate, or reject AI
examples: The paper sketches a unit in which students design something real for their community—a restaurant concept, a neighborhood tool, a local cultural archive—using AI as a design resource while community practitioners serve as co-evaluative judges.

title: Three commitments of community-based AI learning: epistemic fine tuning, redistribution of authority, and situated discernment
description: The framework rests on "three interrelated commitments": situated epistemic negotiation, redistribution of epistemic authority, and collective discernment and action. Together these processes "localize critical AI literacy by calibrating trust, foregrounding community knowledge, and supporting collective judgment about when to design with, interrogate, or reject AI." The commitments integrate constructionist making, community-based epistemologies, and critical AI literacy into a situated theory of learning.
requirements: AI outputs must be engaged as materials for interpretation and deliberation, not definitive conclusions
constraints: Criticality is not uniform across settings; it is shaped by geography, infrastructure, exposure to harm, and local histories of technological entanglement
target_learners: Learners in communities encountering AI-mediated knowledge systems
target_learning_goals: Calibrating trust in AI
Collective judgment about designing with, interrogating, or rejecting AI

title: Epistemic fine tuning: learner-centered recalibration of trust in AI outputs
description: The paper redefines fine tuning from a technical ML operation into a learner-centered process: "We use the term to describe a learner-centered calibration of how AI outputs are interpreted, trusted, and used when learning is anchored in community concerns." Learners treat AI claims as partial and decontextualized, adjusting confidence by comparing outputs against lived experience, local histories, and community expertise, making trust of AI outputs conditional and context dependent.
requirements: Learners must have access to community-grounded knowledge as an interpretive resource for comparing against AI outputs
constraints: Epistemic fine tuning is not a model adaptation; it adjusts the learner's stance, not the model's parameters
target_learners: Students learning with and about AI in community-anchored settings
target_learning_goals: Conditional, context-dependent trust calibration of AI outputs
examples: A student who knows their neighborhood's economic conditions, food culture, or family history can notice when an AI output describes a place that does not match the place they actually live in, and explain why.

title: Redistribute epistemic authority by positioning AI as one voice among many in a community of inquiry
description: Community-based AI learning "refuses the configuration of AI as ultimate authority and, instead, positions learners as legitimate knowers of their communities." Authority becomes relational and conditional as learners evaluate when AI assistance is appropriate and when it should be resisted, supplemented, or rejected. In practice, AI outputs are evaluated through dialogue with people holding situated local knowledge, reorienting AI education from student-machine toward human-community epistemic relationships.
requirements: Learning spaces must include community members whose lived experience and local knowledge can shape what students accept or question in AI outputs
constraints: The redistribution does not dismiss AI; it reframes it as one interpretive input among others
target_learners: Students and educators in AI-integrated classrooms
target_learning_goals: Judging when AI assistance is appropriate, should be supplemented, or rejected
examples: Jadallah and Ballard are cited as finding that community members brought knowledge of specific watersheds, land histories, and local ecological conditions that professional scientists did not hold.

title: Cultivate technoskepticism: continuously examine what relationships communities want with technology
description: The paper adopts Pleasants and colleagues' construct of technoskepticism as a disposition cultivated by community-based AI learning: "a disposition toward continuously examining the relationships communities want to have with technology, asking whose needs AI serves, and whether its presence produces more wellbeing or more harm." This evaluation may lead to conditional use shaped by community criteria, or to refusal when AI misrepresents or harms the people it claims to serve.

article_title: You've Got AI Friend in Me: LLMs as Collaborative Learning Partners
citation: Daniel M. Oppenheimer, Trent N. Cash, Allison E. Connell Pensky. (2025). You've Got AI Friend in Me: LLMs as Collaborative Learning Partners. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00521-6
title: LLMs as collaborative learning partners: elaboration and argumentation mechanisms applied to student-LLM interaction
description: The article extends collaborative learning theory to human-LLM collaboration. It defines collaborative learning via three components: "The learner must be working with an external entity", a shared goal, and an educational outcome. It identifies elaboration (students sharing knowledge, reinforced by LLMs' conversational prompts and responses) and argumentation (LLMs critiquing and challenging student beliefs) as the mechanisms LLMs can support, while avoiding human-team problems like social loafing. It positions LLMs as peers or sounding boards rather than expert tutors.
requirements: Students must maintain skepticism toward LLM output and engage in bi-directional elaboration and argumentation rather than offloading work or treating the LLM as an authoritative expert
constraints: Human-human collaboration is typically reciprocal whereas human-LLM interaction is not inherently beneficial to the LLM; LLMs may hallucinate or be unwilling to contradict student misunderstandings
target_learners: college students in introductory courses
target_learning_goals: argumentative reasoning
argumentative writing
prompt engineering
examples: The course assignments operationalized the framework: students elaborated via 300-word argumentative essays, then prompted an LLM to critique the argument as thoroughly as possible, then rebutted or updated their argument

citation: François PARLANT. (2025). Can You Feel It? A Practical Guide to Emotional Micro-Interventions for Higher Education Teachers (and Others). https://osf.io/tuw2a/overview
title: Affective Pedagogical Content Knowledge (APCK): an extension of PCK integrating content, student difficulties, and affective-strategic knowledge
description: The article proposes APCK as a specialized extension of Shulman's Pedagogical Content Knowledge for affectively charged domains. It "integrates three knowledge bases": content mastery, knowledge of common conceptual and emotional bottlenecks, and "Affective-Strategic Knowledge: A repertoire of verbal and non-verbal strategies (micro-interventions) designed to navigate those emotional bottlenecks while advancing content learning." The guide metaphor (content expert, group dynamist, logistical scout) embodies APCK in action.
requirements: Requires the instructor to synthesize knowledge of the terrain (content), the travelers (students), and the journey (learning process) for moment-by-moment decisions
constraints: The article states the evidence for the framework is anecdotal and qualitative, drawn from reflective practice

target_learning_goals: Student resilience, self-efficacy, and engagement in high-stakes learning
examples: The expert guide is not just a historian (content expert) but also a Group Dynamist who reads morale and a Logistical Scout who anticipates pitfalls and prepares remedies

article_title: 'Advancing Problem-Based Learning in Biomedical Engineering in the Era of Generative AI'
citation: Micky C. Nnamdi, J. Ben Tamo, Benoit Marteau, Wenqi Shi, May D. Wang. (2026). Advancing Problem-Based Learning in Biomedical Engineering in the Era of Generative AI. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.16558
title: Modularized PBL+AI framework for biomedical engineering education
description: A four-module instructional architecture that embeds generative AI inside problem-based learning for biomedical AI courses. The article states that "The design positions GenAI as a knowledge summarization module that accelerates baseline learning and supports code optimization, while preserving the role of PBL in fostering innovation and synthesis." The modules are Problem Formation (authentic biomedical briefs with curated deidentified datasets), Knowledge Inquiry Supported by AI, Problem-Solving (prototyping with team-instrumented debugging), and Presentation (reports, demos, peer review). AI is framed as a scaffold and baseline assembler of existing knowledge rather than a shortcut to solutions.
requirements: Biomedical problem briefs anchored in real-world clinical or research scenarios with curated, deidentified datasets
Institutionally approved AI tools that have undergone security and privacy review
Instructor and TA facilitation with formative feedback at milestone stages
constraints: The article notes traditional PBL constraints historically limited activities to theoretical planning or preliminary prototypes; the framework addresses this with institutional compute infrastructure (PACE, industry partners) and standardized access policies
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate biomedical engineering students
interdisciplinary teams balancing ML/AI experience, biomedical knowledge, and programming proficiency
target_learning_goals: biomedical AI concepts and technical depth
critical thinking and literature critique
teamwork and scientific communication
ethical, regulatory, and clinical awareness
examples: Implemented 2021–2023 at Georgia Tech in BHI, MIP, and Biostatistics courses with milestones M1–M4 (knowledge inquiry, proposal, prototype and model card, final report and demo)

title: AI guardrails policy set for PBL courses
description: A five-part guardrail package governing student GenAI use in PBL courses: tool restrictions, data protection, disclosure and validation, code provenance, and equity of access. Approved tools (e.g., Copilot, Zoom AI Companion, Teams Premium) were provided to ensure equitable access, AI-assisted code segments were marked with comments, and no PII or protected health information could be submitted to any AI tool.

citation: Michael Rowe. (2026). Problem-based learning and the structural conditions for productive AI integration. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/haet3_v1
title: Structural alignment of PBL's core features with the conditions for productive AI integration
description: The essay's central framework: problem-based learning's four defining structural features — problem-driven inquiry, collaborative knowledge construction, facilitation over instruction, and metacognitive reflection — are the same conditions under which AI integration becomes educationally productive rather than substitutive. The alignment is claimed to be structural, not retrospective, since PBL was designed around these conditions before AI existed. The essay states: "PBL's structural features are the conditions for productive AI integration." The argument extends beyond PBL to any pedagogy sharing these features.
requirements: A pedagogy must share the structural features: problem-driven inquiry, collaborative knowledge construction, facilitation over instruction, and metacognitive reflection
constraints: The argument concerns what PBL was designed to create, not what every programme empirically delivers; it produces theoretical warrant, not empirical proof; the author declares a prior commitment to PBL-compatible pedagogy

target_learning_goals: professional judgement and adaptive expertise
critical evaluation of AI outputs
metacognitive reflection
examples: The essay traces the alignment to PBL's origins at McMaster University as a response to transmission-based curricula, citing Barrows (1986) and Norman & Schmidt (1992)

article_title: 'Problem-Based Learning and the Structural Conditions for Productive AI Integration'
citation: Michael Rowe. (2026). Problem-based learning and the structural conditions for productive AI integration. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/haet3_v1
title: Load-bearing versus offloadable cognitive demand determines whether AI offloading is formative
description: The essay reframes the cognitive offloading concern: the question is not whether AI removes cognitive demand but whether the removed demand was building a capability the learner needs. Load-bearing demand (judgement, reasoning, professional identity) cannot be offloaded without developmental loss; offloadable demand (retrieval, formatting, production mechanics) can be. The essay states: "Not all cognitive demand is equally formative." It grounds the distinction in Rowe and Lynch's (2025) information context / personal context framework around context sovereignty.
requirements: A diagnostic account of which layer of difficulty each cognitive task builds, distinguishing writing-as-thinking from writing-as-production

title: Taste versus technique: judgement is the scarce capability when execution becomes cheap
description: Drawing on Rowe and Olivier (forthcoming), the essay distinguishes technique — the execution layer of knowledge work (searching, drafting, coding, formatting) that AI absorbs — from taste, the judgement layer: "the capacity to determine what is worth doing, to recognise quality, to distinguish the substantive from the merely competent." article_title: Evidence and Theory for why the Best Example-Problem Ratio To Optimize Learning Gain Depends on Knowledge Content
citation: Rachatasumrit, N., Koedinger, K. R., & Carvalho, P. F. (2023). Evidence and theory for why the best example-problem ratio to optimize learning gain depends on knowledge content. https://osf.io/29wpe
title: Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) framework: knowledge-component taxonomy linking content type to learning processes and instructional principles
description: The KLI framework is a taxonomic and conceptual framework relating instructional events, learning events, and knowledge components (KCs). It classifies KCs by whether conditions and responses are constant or variable: verbatim facts are constant-condition, constant-response KCs, while skills such as computing a shape's area are variable-condition, variable-response KCs. The article uses KLI to predict that memory and fluency processes suit facts whereas induction and refinement processes suit skills, explaining why retrieval practice benefits facts and example study benefits skills.
requirements: A clear classification of knowledge content, as the article states testing the hypothesis requires
constraints: Learning events and knowledge components cannot be directly observed and must be inferred from assessment events
target_learners: K-12 and adult learners acquiring facts and skills
target_learning_goals: Verbatim fact retention
General skill acquisition and application
examples: The article classifies 'Sudan has the most pyramids of any country in the world' as a constant-condition, constant-response KC and triangle-area calculation as a variable-condition, variable-response KC

article_title: Evidence and Theory for why the Best Example-Problem Ratio To Optimize Learning Gain Depends on Knowledge Content
citation: Rachatasumrit, N., Koedinger, K. R., & Carvalho, P. F. (2023). Evidence and theory for why the best example-problem ratio to optimize learning gain depends on knowledge content. https://osf.io/29wpe
title: Apprentice Learner (AL) computational framework with an added memory mechanism as an executable theory of example-versus-practice learning
description: The AL framework is a computational architecture in which simulated learners acquire and refine if-then production rules through induction: when no rule fits a problem state, the agent requests a demonstration and translates the example into a new rule, and performance feedback prompts refinement of rule conditions. This work added a memory mechanism based on Pavlik and Anderson's ACT-R memory model, giving rules an activation strength with trial ages and decay rates so that recall is stochastic and rules can be forgotten. The article uses AL agents trained on the same four conditions as human participants as an executable theory that reproduces the cross-over interaction.
requirements: Some minimal feedback is required: without any signal the model cannot update memory traces or refine over-general rules
constraints: The simulation simplified problem encoding to parsed input states (e.g., shape type, line lengths), assuming diagram parsing is prior knowledge humans bring
target_learners: Simulated K-12 learners of math and geometry content
target_learning_goals: Fact memorization
Skill acquisition via induction from worked examples
examples: Agents pretrained to match human pretest performance (M = 0.59 and 0.60 for facts and skills) completed 16 pretest questions, 4 study sessions, and 16 posttest questions after a waiting period

article_title: Evidence and Theory for why the Best Example-Problem Ratio To Optimize Learning Gain Depends on Knowledge Content
citation: Rachatasumrit, N., Koedinger, K. R., & Carvalho, P. F. (2023). Evidence and theory for why the best example-problem ratio to optimize learning gain depends on knowledge content. https://osf.io/29wpe
title: Match the example-problem ratio to the knowledge content: favor practice testing for verbatim facts and example-integrated practice for general skills
description: This principle holds that the best mixture of worked examples and practice problems depends on the type of knowledge being learned. Because retrieval practice strengthens memory processes suited to constant-condition, constant-response content, while example study supports the inductive processes needed for variable-condition, variable-response skills, instruction should allocate more retrieval practice when teaching verbatim facts and more example study when teaching generalizable skills. The article demonstrates this cross-over empirically and computationally.
requirements: A classification of the target content as verbatim fact versus general skill, per the KLI taxonomy
constraints: The evidence comes from a short geometry-area task with a brief retention interval; the article notes testing gains may not extend to novel tasks per prior work it cites
target_learners: Adult learners (Mechanical Turk participants) learning geometry facts and skills
target_learning_goals: Verbatim fact retention
General skill acquisition and application
examples: Experiment 1 assigned participants to EPPP (one example then three practice trials) or EPEP (alternating example and practice trials) for facts or skills and measured pre-post gains

description: The article assembles Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory with Cultural-Historical Activity Theory into a five-level model (self, classroom/group, state/geopolitical, cultural norms, global) for analysing AI ethics in education. article_title: RAISE the Standard: A Framework for Transparent Reporting of Artificial Intelligence Studies in Education
citation: Allison, J. (2026). RAISE the Standard: A Framework for Transparent Reporting of Artificial Intelligence Studies in Education. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 64(1), 3-15. https://doi.org/10.1177/07356331251377430
title: RAISE framework: a 30-item reporting checklist across ten thematic domains for AI studies in education
description: RAISE (Reporting AI Studies in Education) is a structured reporting standard for empirical studies involving AI as part of the educational experience. The article states it "is a structured reporting checklist comprising 30 core items" and that "the 30 items are grouped into ten thematic domains, where each domain contains specific items that ask authors to clarify what was done, why, how, and with what implications." The ten domains span educational justification, AI system specification, AI role and interaction, accessibility and cultural fit, setting and participants, human involvement, study design, ethics, transparency and reproducibility, and limitations. The framework "does not mandate any particular method, model, or ideology; rather, it insists that whatever choices are made, they are made visible."
requirements: Authors submitting work which includes AI as a key contributing factor to the pedagogical intervention or approach complete the checklist items
constraints: The framework does not mandate any particular method, model, or ideology; it requires visibility of choices rather than specific choices
target_learners: Researchers reporting AI studies across K-12, higher education, and informal learning
target_learning_goals: Transparent, replicable reporting of AI-enabled educational interventions
examples: The editorial walks through the inclusion rationale for each of the ten domain areas, citing recent literature motivating each
key_sources: Allison, J. (2026). RAISE the Standard: A Framework for Transparent Reporting of Artificial Intelligence Studies in Education. Journal of Educational Computing Research, 64(1), 3-15. https://doi.org/10.1177/07356331251377430

The checklist operationalises the ten thematic domains as 30 items asking authors to clarify what was done, why, how, and with what implications, and is intended for use by authors preparing manuscripts, reviewers questioning AI-enabled research, and editors assessing submissions.

description: The RAISE 2025 Ethics and Risk Matrix (Figure 2) is a supplementary fillable table complementing the core checklist. Authors identify relevant risks by thematic category and describe potential impacts and mitigation strategies. description: Because prompt outcomes and learner effects vary with model versions and settings, the article argues that reporting model identity, version, provider, access conditions, and key configuration choices is essential for interpreting results and enabling replication. It states: "Prompt outcomes and learner effects can change substantially with different model versions or settings, so transparent details regarding specifications is not optional but core methodological information." article_title: Generating In-Context, Personalized Feedback for Intelligent Tutors with Large Language Models
citation: Reddig, J. M., Arora, A., & MacLellan, C. J. (2025). Generating In-Context, Personalized Feedback for Intelligent Tutors with Large Language Models. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00505-6
title: Ground LLM feedback generation in ITS structure by including expected answers, solution steps, interface, and skill estimates in the prompt
description: The article proposes embedding LLMs within intelligent tutoring systems so that structured ITS data grounds generation and reduces factual inaccuracy. As the authors state, "Intelligent Tutoring Systems can provide a grounding mechanism to help LLMs overcome these limitations by including structured information in the prompt." When ITS data such as the expected answer and solution steps is in the prompt, the model does not need to predict mathematical answers, and the LLM can offer partial guidance between steps aligned with the tutor's pedagogical framework. The article's prompt-engineering results support this: accuracy rose as interface and skill-estimate context were added.
requirements: The ITS must supply structured context in the prompt, including the student's input, the correct answer, the tutor interface, and the skill mastery estimate, as the article's final prompt did.
constraints: Even with the extended context given, GPT-4 still underperformed when identifying errors in complex, multi-step problems that require greater contextual awareness.
target_learners: adult math learners in College Algebra
target_learning_goals: corrective feedback for algebra errors
error diagnosis and targeted hint generation
examples: The authors incorporated most of the relevant information available in the Apprentice Tutors platform into the prompt, including the student's input, the correct answer, the tutor interface, and the skill mastery estimate, and performed three rounds of prompt engineering on the factoring tutors.

article_title: Reinforcement Learning in Education: A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Anna Riedmann, Philipp Schaper, Birgit Lugrin. (2025). Reinforcement Learning in Education: A Systematic Literature Review. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00494-6
title: Two-axis taxonomy of RL-based adaptation in education: content-related versus guidance-related
description: The review organizes RL-based educational applications by the kind of action the RL agent takes, distinguishing two main categories. The content-related category covers instructional sequencing (also called reinforcement scheduling) of learning activities to create personalized learning plans, including selecting content and adjusting pace or difficulty. The guidance-related category covers pedagogical strategies: "selecting the type of activity or hint to provide in response to a given learning task or problem", including hint generation, personalized feedback, and tutorial planning. This extends Doroudi et al.'s instructional-sequencing focus to a more holistic scope.
requirements: Studies must implement a single-agent RL algorithm whose actions are either instructional activities or problem-solving steps to be classifiable in this taxonomy
constraints: Student modeling, learning-content generation, bandit-based A/B testing, and multi-agent systems are explicitly excluded from the taxonomy's scope
target_learners: learners across preschool, school, higher education, and adult education contexts as covered by the reviewed studies
target_learning_goals: adaptive and personalized learning through content sequencing and pedagogical guidance
examples: The review classified 53 included papers as content-based and 36 as guidance-related using this taxonomy

article_title: The Evolution of Research on AI and Education Across Four Decades: Insights from the AIxEd Framework
citation: Sina Rismanchian & Shayan Doroudi. (2025). The Evolution of Research on AI and Education Across Four Decades: Insights from the AIxEd Framework. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35:2797–2820. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00483-9
title: AI×Ed framework: two axes (role of AI, end user) yielding four quadrants for categorizing AI-in-education research
description: AI×Ed is a categorization framework for research at the intersection of AI and education. Its vertical axis distinguishes "AI as an applied tool vs. AI as an analogy to HI" (human intelligence), and its horizontal axis distinguishes whether the primary end user is a researcher or a learner, with teachers, practitioners, policymakers, and parents in between. The two axes give rise to four quadrants, each highlighting a particular role AI can play in education, such as learner-facing intelligent tutoring systems (upper right), educational data mining (upper left), computational models of learning (lower left), and children writing AI programs to reflect on their own thinking (lower right). The authors use it to code and compare AIED and IJAIED papers across four decades.
requirements: Each paper is given a single point based on the main focus of the work as identified by the authors; multi-faceted works receive a holistic judgment positioning them between locations
constraints: The authors state the framework "may not be rich enough to capture all work in AIED or some work may be very difficult to situate in either or both axes"
The exact position of papers in relation to neighboring points is arbitrary; points within a small cluster are generally interchangeable
target_learners: AIED researchers and scholars categorizing AI-in-education research
target_learning_goals: Understanding and categorizing the diverse roles AI can play in education and learning research
examples: The authors located each paper in AIED proceedings (1985, 1993, 2021, 2024) and IJAIED volumes (2004, 2014, 2021) within the framework's quadrants, e.g., classifying VanLehn's Cascade as AI as an analogy for HI and OLAE as AI as an applied tool

title: Five institutional supports recur as readiness enablers for AI-supported teaching
description: Across the evidence sources the synthesis identifies a recurring set of institutional conditions that enable faculty readiness for AI-supported teaching. These are: "(1) access to appropriate AI tools and resources; (2) AI literacy and skills training; (3) curated best practices and use cases; (4) clear guidelines for AI in teaching; and (5) an environment that encourages innovation and tolerates failure". The pattern is used to organize capacity-building priorities, with the inverse signal that 80% of faculty do not find institutional AI guidelines comprehensive marking policy ambiguity as a readiness inhibitor.
requirements: Institutional investment in guidelines, training, curated best practices, tool access, and an innovation-tolerant environment
constraints: Sector surveys are not uniformly comparable across countries and roles, per the article's methodological limitations
target_learners: Higher education faculty
target_learning_goals: Effective and epistemically sound integration of GenAI into teaching and assessment
examples: The Digital Education Council survey's top enablers: access to tools (65%), AI literacy training (64%), best-practice collections (60%), and clear guidelines (50%)
