title: EPIQ-AI Readiness Framework: readiness as alignment across epistemic, pedagogical, institutional, and quality-and-compliance domains
description: The EPIQ-AI Readiness Framework is the article's principal contribution: a higher-education-specific readiness theory integrating technology acceptance, teacher knowledge (TPACK), and organizational readiness for change traditions. It posits that "credible AI-supported teaching and scalable online delivery require alignment across micro-level faculty capacities and macro-level institutional systems, mediated by pedagogical and assessment design capacity". Readiness is reframed as a sociotechnical and epistemic condition rather than an individual skills deficit, organized into four domains: epistemic, pedagogical, institutional, and quality-and-compliance readiness, operationalized through a dashboard of threshold indicators.

title: AI-aware assessment patterns shift evaluation toward process evidence and demonstration of judgment
description: Because GenAI can produce plausible text at scale, the article argues that presented fluency no longer plausibly indicates individual mastery, so assessment validity must depend on task design, process evidence, and demonstration of judgment rather than product-only evaluation. citation: Nikolai Maurer, Mathea Brückner, Christoph Thyssen, Sebastian Becker-Genschow, Johannes Huwer. (2026). Science educators' AI literacy and AI usage in teaching: Implications for post-qualification programs. Computers and Education Open 10. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100376
title: TPACK adapted for AI (TPACKAI) with two development pathways for in-service science educators
description: The article adapts the TPACK model for AI, using the terms TKAI, TCKAI, TPKAI, and TPACKAI, and proposes two pathways for in-service teachers to develop TPACKAI. Path A enriches existing pedagogical content knowledge with AI-related technological knowledge (TKAI), so that teachers "can thus enable teachers to use AI efficiently as a tool for the preparation and follow-up of lessons". Path B builds knowledge of AI's role in the science subjects (TCKAI) and combines it with PCK so teachers can use AI as subject matter. The article classifies the measured general AI literacy as TKAI and TPKAI.

constraints: The TPACK model's limitations regarding generative AI must be considered; the article notes it needs extension to socio-cultural and ethical aspects as in the DPACK model
Further research is needed to test the two pathways and define the competencies of subject-specific AI literacy
target_learners: in-service secondary science educators
target_learning_goals: using AI as a tool for lesson preparation, follow-up, and individualized support
using AI as subject matter in science lessons
examples: The study assessed teachers' general AI literacy with the Hornberger et al. test and interpreted the scores as indicating the presence of TPKAI and TKAI
Fig. 6 depicts the TPACK model adapted for AI with the two possible pathways to support TPACKAI development among in-service teachers

title: Six-facet model of AI literacy: affective experiences, usage skills, cognitive evaluation, ethical norms, responsible use, and self-development
description: The article proposes a six-facet model of AI literacy building on the ABCE and KSAVE models by adding two new factors. The authors define AI literacy as "the responsible use of AI within ethical standards, characterized by the experience of positive emotions, proficiency in employing AI tools, clear and rational cognitive frameworks, and a commitment to continually enhancing one's theoretical understanding and practical proficiency in AI for the purpose of fostering self-development." Responsible use combines prudent engagement and self-accountability; self-development captures dynamic future potential alongside static competencies.
requirements: Scale items must be designed from the outset to suit adolescents, young adults, and midlife adults to achieve cross-age equivalence
constraints: The authors note the model's dimensions map onto DigCompEdu only partially, since DigCompEdu focuses on educators and broader digital technologies

title: SFAILQ: 32-item Six-Facet Artificial Intelligence Literacy Questionnaire
description: The SFAILQ is a 32-item self-report questionnaire assessing six AI literacy dimensions: affective experiences (5 items), usage skills (5 items), cognitive evaluation (6 items), ethical norms (6 items), responsible use (4 items), and self-development (6 items). It was developed with 2443 Chinese participants aged 12 to 60 using a random split-half design: item reduction on Sample 1 (N = 1217) and reliability/validity testing on Sample 2 (N = 1226). The article reports it "demonstrated high internal consistency, construct validity, convergent validity, discriminant validity, and criterion-related validity."

description: The review conceptualizes GenAI-specific TPK as knowledge of teaching and learning through GenAI, extending the TPACK framework because conventional TPACK "does not fully account for the adaptive, autonomous, reflective and ethical dimensions unique to GenAI." citation: Ó Ceallaigh, T. J. & Murphy, S. (2026). Teaching the teachers: A systematic review of genAI-specific technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK) in teacher education. Computers and Education Open, 10, 100367. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100367
title: Intelligent-TPACK: extending TPACK with ethical reasoning, inclusiveness, and fairness for AI integration
description: Intelligent-TPACK is a framework the review describes as extending the TPACK model "by integrating dimensions of ethical reasoning, inclusiveness, and fairness, emphasizing teachers' capacity to align AI tools with pedagogical intent and ethical responsibility." The review reports, citing Celik (2023), that the framework was developed through scale development and structural modeling with in-service teachers, and that ethical fairness and inclusiveness strongly predict teachers' readiness to use AI responsibly. It serves in the review as an empirical model of AI-specific teacher knowledge in which ethics is integral to intelligent tool use.
requirements: Integration of fairness, inclusiveness, and ethics into teacher training and AI integration frameworks
constraints: The review notes the complexity of such models often exceeds the capacity of existing institutional systems to provide targeted support
target_learners: In-service and pre-service teachers
Teacher educators
target_learning_goals: Responsible AI tool use aligned with pedagogical intent
Ethical evaluation of AI outputs
examples: Celik (2023) developed the framework with a Finnish national sample of in-service teachers using scale development and structural modeling, as reported in the review
key_sources: Ó Ceallaigh, T. J. & Murphy, S. (2026). Teaching the teachers: A systematic review of genAI-specific technological pedagogical knowledge (TPK) in teacher education. Computers and Education Open, 10, 100367. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100367

article_title: Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education
citation: Matt Bower, Jodie Torrington, Jennifer W. M. Lai. (2026). 2026 Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education. https://bit.ly/2026GenAITypologyData
title: Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education: nine categories of educator-used generative AI tools
description: A taxonomy arranging generative AI tools used in educational contexts into nine categories: General-Purpose Large Language Models, Image Creation Tools, Audio and Music Generation Tools, Video Generation Tools, Presentation Generation Tools, Research and Study Tools, AI Tutoring and Chatbots, Custom Education Tools, and Other Miscellaneous Tools. It continues the authors' earlier Web 2.0 and free web-based learning technology typologies, and each tool receives a brief description and link so educators can judge fit for their teaching and learning contexts.
requirements: Tools included must have been reported by two or more educators and be publicly available with a free version
constraints: Not an exhaustive list; represents a snapshot of educator-reported usage in 2025-2026
Some tools offer functionality across multiple categories
target_learners: educators across early childhood, elementary, high school and higher education
target_learning_goals: informed selection of generative AI tools aligned with pedagogical goals and values
examples: ChatGPT appears in the General-Purpose Large Language Models, Image Creation Tools, and Presentation Generation Tools categories, reflecting educators' use of this tool for multiple purposes
key_sources: Matt Bower, Jodie Torrington, Jennifer W. M. Lai. (2026). 2026 Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education. https://bit.ly/2026GenAITypologyData

article_title: Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education
citation: Matt Bower, Jodie Torrington, Jennifer W. M. Lai. (2026). 2026 Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education. https://bit.ly/2026GenAITypologyData
title: 2026 GenAI Typology survey dataset of educator tool usage
description: The dataset underlying the typology comes from a Generative AI Pedagogies and Technologies Questionnaire distributed internationally, predominantly via professional education networks on LinkedIn and Facebook. Educators nominated specific tools they used within each of the nine categories, with an Other Miscellaneous category capturing tools that did not fit. The article states: "The dataset can be found at https://bit.ly/2026GenAITypologyData" and reports 211 completed responses from educators in 9 countries across elementary school, high school and higher education.
requirements: Publicly available at the printed link
constraints: Responses collected in late 2025; represents a single point-in-time snapshot
target_learners: educators from nine countries spanning early childhood through higher education
target_learning_goals: identifying frequently used generative AI tools in educational practice
examples: Only tools with a frequency greater than 1, meaning used by two or more educators, were included in the final typology

article_title: Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education
citation: Matt Bower, Jodie Torrington, Jennifer W. M. Lai. (2026). 2026 Typology of Generative AI Tools for Education. https://bit.ly/2026GenAITypologyData
title: Select generative AI tools through educator agency and informed decision-making aligned with pedagogical goals, rather than adopting uncritically or avoiding out of fear
description: The article argues that realizing generative AI's educational opportunities requires educator agency and informed decision making: rather than adopting generative AI uncritically, educators need frameworks and resources to make thoughtful choices about which tools align with their pedagogical goals and values. The typology is offered as a practical reference point for this selection, while stressing that finding the right tool is only the beginning and thoughtful integration requires critical evaluation.
requirements: Educators need frameworks and resources supporting thoughtful tool choice
constraints: The article states the typology is a snapshot of a rapidly evolving landscape, so the list will change over time
target_learners: educators across school and higher education sectors
target_learning_goals: aligning generative AI tool selection with pedagogical goals, student needs, and educational values
examples: The typology provides brief descriptions and links for each of the 50 tools to support educators in making informed decisions about which tools might suit their teaching and learning contexts

article_title: Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education
citation: Tzirides, Anastasia Olga (Olnancy), Galla, Michele, Cope, Bill, & Kalantzis, Mary. (2025). Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education.
title: Thinking Through AI framework: three dimensions for studying and co-designing AI-mediated learning
description: The Thinking Through AI framework is a methodological approach integrating cyber-social research with cognitive labs and think-aloud protocols to create continuous feedback loops in AI tool development. It is structured around three core dimensions: students' cognitive engagement with AI, educators' instructional strategies embedding rubrics and knowledge repositories, and the collaborative design of AI tools and learning experiences via Learning Experience Research (LXR). The article states it is 'a methodological approach that integrates principles of cyber-social research with cognitive labs and think-aloud protocols to facilitate continuous feedback loops in the development and implementation of AI-driven educational tools.'
requirements: Sustained engagement of students, educators, and developers in iterative design cycles, with think-aloud sessions and post-course surveys providing user input
constraints: Its iterative nature demands significant time and resources, requiring sustained engagement from all stakeholders
target_learners: middle school students
educators
AI tool developers
target_learning_goals: writing instruction
cognitive engagement with AI systems
AI tool co-design
examples: The framework guided a case study of the CGScholar AI Helper at a rural Alaska middle school, where think-aloud sessions with a structured moderator guide captured student interactions with the AI writing tool.
key_sources: Tzirides, Anastasia Olga (Olnancy), Galla, Michele, Cope, Bill, & Kalantzis, Mary. (2025). Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/s8hqe_v1

article_title: Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education
citation: Tzirides, Anastasia Olga (Olnancy), Galla, Michele, Cope, Bill, & Kalantzis, Mary. (2025). Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education.
title: CGScholar AI Helper: cloud-based AI writing feedback tool with rubric-guided, teacher-steerable feedback
description: The CGScholar AI Helper is a cloud-based web application supporting student writing through AI-driven feedback and iterative revision. It uses a split-screen interface with a multimodal text editor and a feedback area, a workflow of drafting, AI feedback, revision, optional peer review, reflection, and publication, and prompt engineering with multi-agent and chain-of-thought approaches. Retrieval-Augmented Generation 'prioritizes teacher-approved materials from the knowledge base over the foundation language models (LLMs) to ensure factually accurate feedback.' Teachers supply rubrics and knowledge bases; AI feedback appears one criterion at a time, and students can request clarifications.
requirements: Teachers provide an assessment rubric with criteria, rating levels, and descriptions, plus a knowledge base of relevant instructional materials
constraints: The study notes technical issues such as delays in feedback generation and occasional system errors, and that the tool's feedback vocabulary was challenging for some students
target_learners: middle school students
K-12 writing classrooms
target_learning_goals: writing development
revision based on formative feedback
examples: In the Alaska case study, the tool was integrated into a journal writing activity on belonging, with a teacher-created rubric assessing topic clarity, supporting evidence, explanation, conclusion, formal tone, organization, and mechanics on a four-point scale.
key_sources: Tzirides, Anastasia Olga (Olnancy), Galla, Michele, Cope, Bill, & Kalantzis, Mary. (2025). Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/s8hqe_v1

article_title: Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education
citation: Tzirides, Anastasia Olga (Olnancy), Galla, Michele, Cope, Bill, & Kalantzis, Mary. (2025). Thinking Through AI: Advancing Cognitive and Collaborative Research for AI in Education.
title: Embed educators' pedagogical elements (rubrics and knowledge bases) within AI tools so feedback aligns with instructional goals
description: The principle holds that educators should embed pedagogical elements such as rubrics and knowledge repositories within AI systems, enabling personalized and adaptive learning experiences aligned with students' needs and pedagogical objectives. In the AI Helper, teachers set up projects by providing an assessment rubric and a knowledge base, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation prioritizes teacher-approved materials over foundation LLMs to keep feedback factually accurate. The article states this integration 'ensures that AI tools align with students' individual needs while also supporting pedagogical objectives.'
requirements: Teachers must supply rubric criteria, rating levels, descriptions, and a knowledge base of instructional materials, customizable or selected from the CGScholar library
constraints: The article notes variability in students' interpretations of AI-generated feedback and that some students struggled with the language complexity of the AI's suggestions
target_learners: middle school students
educators designing AI-supported writing instruction
target_learning_goals: writing instruction
formative assessment aligned with rubric criteria
examples: The participating teacher provided a structured writing rubric assessing topic clarity, supporting evidence, explanation, conclusion, formal tone, organization, and mechanics, each rated on a four-point scale.

article_title: AI Literacy in Secondary Education: Framework, Assessment, and Professional Development in the Ukrainian Context
citation: Marienko, M. V., Markova, O. M., & Semerikov, S. O. (2026). AI literacy in secondary education: framework, assessment, and professional development in the Ukrainian context. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 10, 100605. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100605
title: Five-level AI literacy competency framework integrated with three paradigms of AI in education
description: The article proposes a conceptual five-level AI literacy competency model for secondary educators — Awareness, Application, Evaluation, Creation, Ethics — visualized as a developmental pyramid. The framework is "a conceptual five-level AI literacy competency model integrated with the three paradigms of AI in education" (AI-directed, AI-supported, AI-empowered), mapping competency levels to each paradigm's demands. Levels 1-4 align with Ng et al.'s categories while ethics is separated as a distinct highest level reflecting ethical reasoning as a sophisticated capability requiring deliberate development.
requirements: Future research should subject the framework to psychometric validation through confirmatory factor analysis, as the article states
constraints: The article presents it as a conceptual framework synthesizing existing literature and empirical observations, not yet psychometrically validated
target_learners: secondary education teachers
teacher educators
target_learning_goals: AI literacy competency development across awareness, application, evaluation, creation, and ethical reasoning
examples: The article maps digital storytelling with AI as addressing all five levels simultaneously, from awareness of AI capabilities to ethical considerations of authorship and authenticity
key_sources: Marienko, M. V., Markova, O. M., & Semerikov, S. O. (2026). AI literacy in secondary education: framework, assessment, and professional development in the Ukrainian context. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 10, 100605. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100605

title: Curated catalog of 22 EOSC AI services mapped to secondary school subjects
description: Study 4 systematically searched the EOSC Marketplace using AI- and ML-related keywords, filtering candidates against predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria with independent dual assessment and consensus, producing a curated catalog for educator reference. The analysis found that "Systematic analysis identified 22 EOSC AI services applicable to secondary education." Services were mapped to six subject areas, with biology (7 services) and geography (6) accounting for the largest share, reflecting the European research infrastructure's emphasis on environmental and earth sciences.

constraints: Services that were purely research-oriented without educational potential or inaccessible without institutional affiliation were excluded

target_learning_goals: subject-specific AI integration in biology, geography, chemistry, physics, and mathematics instruction
examples: Mapped services include AI-GeoSpecies and GBIF hosted portals for species identification in biology, and Copernicus Data Space and WEkEO for spatial data analysis in geography

article_title: The Impact of Unscaffolded GenAI Use on Pre-Service Teachers' AI Readiness, Self-Regulated Learning, Critical Thinking, and Instructional Design Performance: A Quasi-Experimental Study
citation: Zhang Jun, Peng Yuting, Deng Xinyue, Zeng Qin, Wang Kai. (2026). The Impact of Unscaffolded GenAI Use on Pre-Service Teachers’ AI Readiness, Self-Regulated Learning, Critical Thinking, and Instructional Design Performance: A Quasi-Experimental Study. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071114
title: Unscaffolded GenAI use as self-initiated engagement without GenAI-specific guidance, framed by cognitive load theory and the zone of proximal development
description: The article defines unscaffolded GenAI use as "learners’ self-initiated and self-regulated engagement with GenAI in the absence of GenAI-specific instructional guidance or pre-designed prompting frameworks", drawing on self-regulated learning perspectives. It frames the problem with scaffolding theory and the zone of proximal development, which emphasize structured guidance for novices, and with cognitive load theory, which holds that effective support should reduce extraneous load. The framework motivates examining outcomes when GenAI is permitted but not scaffolded in authentic course contexts.
requirements: Requires examining outcomes in authentic course contexts before designing GenAI scaffolds, so that scaffolds are neither superficial nor overly restrictive
constraints: The article treats the construct as defined for pre-service teachers in formal course contexts where GenAI-specific scaffolding is absent
target_learners: pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: instructional design competence
self-regulated learning
critical thinking
AI readiness
examples: In the study, the experimental class used GenAI for reflection questions, design ideas, and lesson plans with no prompting frameworks or guidance, while the control class worked only from instructor materials

article_title: The Impact of Unscaffolded GenAI Use on Pre-Service Teachers' AI Readiness, Self-Regulated Learning, Critical Thinking, and Instructional Design Performance: A Quasi-Experimental Study
citation: Zhang Jun, Peng Yuting, Deng Xinyue, Zeng Qin, Wang Kai. (2026). The Impact of Unscaffolded GenAI Use on Pre-Service Teachers’ AI Readiness, Self-Regulated Learning, Critical Thinking, and Instructional Design Performance: A Quasi-Experimental Study. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071114
title: Provide tailored scaffolds that guide pre-service teachers' GenAI use styles and strategies rather than permitting unscaffolded access alone
description: The article concludes that unscaffolded GenAI access alone was insufficient to support pre-service teachers' professional learning and was less favorable for instructional design performance. It states that "This further highlights the need for tailored scaffolds to guide students’ GenAI use styles and strategies", and that pre-service teachers may need support not only in how to operate GenAI but in clarifying why and when to use it during instructional design. The principle directs scaffold design toward goal alignment, evaluation of outputs, and reflection.
requirements: Scaffolds should address how, why, and when to use GenAI, including support for clarifying task purposes and evaluating AI-generated outputs against disciplinary pedagogical requirements
constraints: Evidence comes from one 11-week quasi-experiment in a chemistry instructional design course with 52 pre-service teachers; the authors state the lower design scores should not be interpreted as evidence that GenAI necessarily weakens competence
target_learners: pre-service teachers
novice instructional designers
target_learning_goals: instructional design competence
critical evaluation of AI-generated content
self-regulated use of GenAI
examples: The experimental group was permitted GenAI use with no training, prompting frameworks, or systematic guidance, and scored lower on instructional design performance than the control group

article_title: Ask Me Anything: Exploring Children's Attitudes Toward an Age-tailored AI-powered Chatbot
citation: Saniya Vahedian Movahed and Fred Martin. (2025). Ask Me Anything: Exploring children's attitudes toward an age-tailored AI-powered chatbot. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14217
title: Ask Me Anything (AMA): a topic-specific, age-tailored child-friendly chatbot
description: Ask Me Anything is a Python chatbot built with CustomTkinter and the ChatGPT API that "answers only topic-specific questions" in three areas: astronomy, sneakers and shoes, and dinosaurs. Its interface has a sidebar for name, grade, age range, and topic selection, and a main area for questions and answers. Prompts include topic and age variables (7-9, 9-11, 12-14) so responses are age-appropriate and on-topic. It was tested with 63 K-8 students; source code is publicly available.
requirements: Uses the OpenAI API with a prompt template carrying topic and age variables to constrain responses to the selected topic and age band
constraints: Answers only its three selected topics; off-topic queries are declined by design
target_learners: K-8 students aged 7-14
target_learning_goals: Fostering balanced and informed engagement with AI technology in educational settings
examples: Used by 63 students over two days at a partner K-8 school, with 3-10 minutes of interaction each and post-surveys
key_sources: Saniya Vahedian Movahed and Fred Martin. (2025). Ask Me Anything: Exploring children's attitudes toward an age-tailored AI-powered chatbot. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14217

article_title: Ask Me Anything: Exploring Children's Attitudes Toward an Age-tailored AI-powered Chatbot
citation: Saniya Vahedian Movahed and Fred Martin. (2025). Ask Me Anything: Exploring children's attitudes toward an age-tailored AI-powered chatbot. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14217
title: Three design considerations for a child-friendly educational chatbot: topic focus, age-appropriate context management, and a simple fun interface
description: The authors enumerate three design considerations for AMA: "(1) to encourage engagement by focusing conversation on specific topics; (2) to respond to children in an age-appropriate and on-topic manner (context management); and (3) to provide a simple and fun user interface." Topic focus drives targeted questioning and engagement; context management uses age and topic variables in the API prompt; the single-screen interface uses playful images, clear font, and simple layout.
requirements: A prompt template carrying topic and age variables
Selection of a language model that reliably stays on-topic
constraints: Prompt instructions alone did not keep gpt-3.5-turbo on-topic; engine choice mattered
target_learners: Elementary and middle school students
target_learning_goals: Safe, engaging, age-appropriate interaction with conversational AI
examples: AMA's deployed text-davinci-002 system declined an off-topic question with 'I can only answer questions about sneakers and shoes' and then answered the student's on-topic follow-up

article_title: VARIA: Benchmarking Frontier LLMs on Construct-Equivalent Assessment Variant Generation
citation: Ernesto Lee. (2026). VARIA: Benchmarking Frontier LLMs on Construct-Equivalent Assessment Variant Generation. https://openrouter.ai
title: VARIA four-property formalisation of the AIAA integrity-via-variation hypothesis
description: VARIA formalises the claim that an LLM can generate assessment variant sets that are simultaneously surface-distinct, construct-equivalent, rubric-applicable and difficulty-matched. It "defines a blueprint as a triple of competency, analytic rubric, and canonical solution" and operationalises four properties P1-P4 with metrics (TF-IDF cosine and 4-gram overlap for diversity, an LLM judge for construct equivalence, Flesch reading-ease dispersion for difficulty parity) combined into a joint integrity score J. The framework makes the AIAA claim falsifiable: a generator fails if no prompting setting satisfies all four constraints jointly.
requirements: A blueprint specifying competency, analytic rubric and canonical solution; application-specific thresholds for the four properties; an LLM judge for the construct-equivalence score.
constraints: The pilot's joint score contains no rubric-stability (P3) term and gives surface diversity two of four components; both diversity metrics are lexical, so deep paraphrases of the same scenario could evade them.
target_learners: higher-education students in applied AI and data analytics courses
target_learning_goals: integrity-bearing parallel-forms generation of open-response performance assessment tasks
examples: The pilot instantiates the framework on three blueprints: an audit-style performance task, a data-pipeline bias investigation, and a stakeholder communication task for a model failure.
key_sources: Ernesto Lee. (2026). VARIA: Benchmarking Frontier LLMs on Construct-Equivalent Assessment Variant Generation. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/u6xef_v2

article_title: VARIA: Benchmarking Frontier LLMs on Construct-Equivalent Assessment Variant Generation
citation: Ernesto Lee. (2026). VARIA: Benchmarking Frontier LLMs on Construct-Equivalent Assessment Variant Generation. https://openrouter.ai
title: Released VARIA benchmark package with follow-up harness
description: The authors release the VARIA benchmark as a code package containing the three pilot blueprints with rubrics and canonical solutions (blueprints.json), a held-out distant-discipline fourth blueprint (Constructing a Historical Argument from Primary Sources) pre-registered as a generalisation probe, four prompting strategies, five complementary metrics, and an evaluation harness. They "release VARIA together with a ready-to-run follow-up harness" implementing per-variant cross-family judging, the full rubric-stability protocol, and multi-run and larger-N regimes (run_followup.py), plus gap_analysis.py for the paired permutation tests.
requirements: API access to frontier generators and judges; local compute for the GPT-2 reference and metric computation; execution of the pre-registered follow-up protocols.
constraints: The pilot covers only the N = 10 regime of the pre-registered N in {10, 35, 100}; the held-out blueprint B4 is not part of the pilot's 60 cells.
target_learners: higher-education institutions deploying AI-generated assessment variants
target_learning_goals: benchmarking LLM capability to generate construct-equivalent, surface-distinct assessment variants
examples: The pilot executed 57 API-driven generation conditions in approximately 50 minutes plus 3 local GPT-2 conditions in roughly two minutes, at a total cost of approximately ten US dollars.
key_sources: Ernesto Lee. (2026). VARIA: Benchmarking Frontier LLMs on Construct-Equivalent Assessment Variant Generation. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/u6xef_v2

article_title: \"If You Can't Dance Your Program, You Can't Write It\": Challenges and Implications for AI in Education
citation: Ronnie Videla, Simon Penny, Wendy Ross. (2025). 'If you can't dance your program, you can't write it': Challenges and Implications for AI in Education.
title: Embodied AI: a post-cognitivist framework grounding intelligent behavior and learning in physical interaction with the environment
description: The article advances Embodied AI as an epistemological and pedagogical framework contrasting with symbolic, disembodied AI. It states that "Embodied AI, which posits that intelligent behavior emerges from physical interactions with the environment, offers a compelling framework for understanding learning as an embodied process." It draws on post-cognitivist research "including frameworks such as 4E (embodied, enactive, embedded, extended) and SEEED (situated, embodied, enactive, embedded, distributed)", treating the body as the constitutive core of thought and knowledge as arising from organism–environment coupling rather than symbolic representation.
requirements: Educational design must integrate body, environment, and culture, recognizing that meaning emerges through interaction rather than isolated linguistic representation
constraints: The article notes its effective implementation requires material, institutional, and formative conditions that are often lacking in many educational settings
target_learners: learners across elementary through tertiary education
target_learning_goals: situated, creative, and critical understanding through embodied, sensorimotor engagement
examples: The article cites Brooks' subsumption architecture, in which layers of activity directly connect perception with action without centralized internal representations, as a precursor of this paradigm.
key_sources: Ronnie Videla, Simon Penny, Wendy Ross. (2025). 'If you can't dance your program, you can't write it': Challenges and Implications for AI in Education. https://doi.org/10.1145/3759257

article_title: \"If You Can't Dance Your Program, You Can't Write It\": Challenges and Implications for AI in Education
citation: Ronnie Videla, Simon Penny, Wendy Ross. (2025). 'If you can't dance your program, you can't write it': Challenges and Implications for AI in Education.
title: Sensorimotor debilities: the loss of multimodal agency, proprioception, and tactile engagement in digital and GenAI-mediated interaction
description: The article adopts Penny's concept of sensorimotor debilities to name the embodied costs of interaction with digital technologies, particularly GenAI. It states: "These debilities manifest as a loss of multimodal agency, weakening the sense of proprioception, kinesthetic awareness, and tactile engagement that emerge from being alive, moving, and sensorially interacting with the world." The devaluation of craftsmanship and DIY making practices further erodes aesthetic and experiential dimensions tied to acting, feeling, and meaning-making through movement, which the authors link to impoverished educational experiences as AI spreads in education.
requirements: Design must shift AI's reliance on vision and text toward interaction that is lived, embodied, and negotiated in real time
constraints: The article warns that lack of impetus to build an embodied research programme in AI will lead to impoverished educational experiences
target_learners: all learners in AI-mediated educational settings
target_learning_goals: preservation of multimodal agency, proprioceptive awareness, and tacit embodied knowing
examples: The article cites the 'Organs without Bodies' exhibition generating physical objects with AI as provoking reflection on creation without the bodies of artisans.
key_sources: Lb

article_title: \"If You Can't Dance Your Program, You Can't Write It\": Challenges and Implications for AI in Education
citation: Ronnie Videla, Simon Penny, Wendy Ross. (2025). 'If you can't dance your program, you can't write it': Challenges and Implications for AI in Education.
title: Seven design principles for critical and transformative integration of Embodied AI in education
description: The article proposes "a set of pedagogical principles aimed at the critical and transformative integration of Embodied AI in contemporary educational contexts", methodologically grounded in Design-Based Research. The seven principles are: (i) overcoming natural language models as epistemic centers; (ii) situationality to generate meaningful connections; (iii) distributed creativity and co-agency; (iv) embracing uncertainty, failure, and improvisation; (v) critical awareness of bias and algorithmic performativity; (vi) embodied sensorimotor multimodality; and (vii) ecological design for open pedagogical innovation.
requirements: Pedagogical redesign situated in experience, the body, creativity, and emergence, moving away from mere instrumentalization of teaching through technology
constraints: The article notes implementation requires material, institutional, and formative conditions often lacking in educational settings
target_learners: elementary through tertiary learners in AI-integrated curricula
target_learning_goals: creative, critical, collaborative, and situated learning with AI
examples: Principle (vi) calls for educational experiences where vision, gesture, speech, movement, and touch are recognized as legitimate modalities of knowing and expressing.
key_sources: Ronnie Videla, Simon Penny, Wendy Ross. (2025). 'If you can't dance your program, you can't write it': Challenges and Implications for AI in Education. https://doi.org/10.1145/3759257

article_title: \"If You Can't Dance Your Program, You Can't Write It\": Challenges and Implications for AI in Education
citation: Ronnie Videla, Simon Penny, Wendy Ross. (2025). 'If you can't dance your program, you can't write it': Challenges and Implications for AI in Education.
title: NAO humanoid robot with Choregraphe programming environment for embodied educational support
description: The article cites the humanoid robot NAO, used to support students with autism spectrum disorders, as a notable advancement transferring Embodied AI principles into education. Its programming environment Choregraphe "relies on visual blocks and Python code, facilitates the creation of integrated multimodal behaviors (voice, vision, touch, movement)", yet the article reports it "still lacks flexibility in unpredictable scenarios", with improvisational and adaptive operation remaining in early stages.
requirements: Open environments sensitive to situational emergence, which the article says remain underdeveloped
constraints: The system's ability to operate improvisationally or adaptively remains in its early stages, reflecting a structural gap in development
target_learners: students with autism spectrum disorders
target_learning_goals: embodied, multimodal learning support integrating voice, vision, touch, and movement
examples: The article describes Choregraphe as enabling creation of integrated multimodal behaviors combining voice, vision, touch, and movement.

article_title: When Do Undergraduate Students Prefer AI? Insights into AI Scoring and Feedback
citation: Yildirim-Erbasli, S. N., Ilgun Dibek, M., Thomas, M. L., & Lesoway, N. (2026). When Do Undergraduate Students Prefer AI? Insights into AI Scoring and Feedback. Behavioral Sciences, 16(7), 1196. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071196
title: Perceptions versus preferences as distinct constructs in student evaluation of AI assessment
description: The article distinguishes two constructs in how students respond to AI-based assessment. Perceptions are evaluative beliefs about the systems themselves: "Student perceptions refer to learners' evaluative beliefs and judgments regarding the characteristics of AI technologies, such as their usefulness, credibility, effectiveness, or fairness". Preferences, by contrast, capture "students' choices among alternative assessment arrangements, such as AI-generated scoring, human evaluation, or hybrid models". The framework draws on technology acceptance research and is used throughout the study to explain why positive perceptions of AI usefulness do not translate into preferences for AI authority in grading.
requirements: Both constructs must be measured separately; positive perceptions alone do not indicate preferred assessment arrangements.
constraints: The distinction is drawn for AI-based scoring and feedback in higher education assessment contexts.
target_learners: undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: understanding student acceptance of AI-based assessment and feedback
examples: The survey measured AI scoring perceptions, AI feedback perceptions, AI preferences, and AI-versus-human preferences as separate subscales with Cronbach's alpha values of 0.73 to 0.78.

article_title: Where Artificial Intelligence Enters Teacher Work
citation: Holster, J. (2026). Where Artificial Intelligence Enters Teacher Work. https://www.oecd.org/en/data/datasets/talis-2024-database.html
title: Design AI implementation and governance at the task level, attending to responsibility, data, oversight, and the checking work AI introduces
description: The article argues that because AI allocation differs sharply across professional tasks, adoption rates should not be treated as evidence that AI changes all parts of teacher work the same way. It recommends that "AI implementation and governance should be designed at the task level, with explicit attention to professional responsibility, student data, oversight, and the checking work introduced by AI use." It also warns against treating greater AI use as a normative endpoint for teacher development, since teachers retain responsibility for evaluating AI-supported work.
requirements: Teachers need meaningful autonomy over adoption, allocation, and continued use, including discretion over whether AI involvement is worthwhile
constraints: The large special-education association concerns reported use, not quality or benefit
TALIS records whether AI is used for a task, not how it participates with human use, and provides no direct evidence about output quality, verification burden, or student outcomes
target_learners: lower-secondary teachers
teacher candidates in preparation programs
target_learning_goals: professional judgment about where AI belongs in teaching work
verification and oversight of AI-supported tasks
examples: The study's Practitioner Notes state adoption rates should not be treated as evidence that AI is changing all parts of teacher work in the same way, and that teacher candidates can practice identifying why they would involve AI and what conditions would lead them to pause, revise, reallocate, or refuse a use case.

article_title: The Impact of Explainable AI on Teachers' Trust and Acceptance of AI EdTech Recommendations: The Power of Domain-specific Explanations
citation: Yael Feldman-Maggor, Mutlu Cukurova, Carmel Kent, Giora Alexandron. (2025). The Impact of Explainable AI on Teachers' Trust and Acceptance of AI EdTech Recommendations: The Power of Domain-specific Explanations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00486-6
title: Adapted Hoff and Bashir trust-in-automation model integrating XAI and understandability for AI-EdTech
description: The article adapts Hoff and Bashir's (2013, 2015) 'trust in automation' model to AI-EdTech by treating XAI features as system design features and placing understandability as the factor connecting XAI and trust. As the authors state, "XAI increases the system's understandability by enabling the user to interpret its output and validate it against the expected outcome", and this validation of system performance establishes trust, which in turn increases acceptance. The model explains why different XAI schemes differ in their impact on trust: through their differing understandability. Qualitative findings later added validation of recommendations by experience and situational acceptance factors to the framework.
requirements: Effective XAI interfaces that enable users to interpret and validate system output against expected outcomes
constraints: The article notes the relation between understandability and trust is not straightforward; some teachers require real classroom experience before trusting the system
target_learners: in-service high-school teachers using AI recommendation tools
target_learning_goals: teachers' informed evaluation and adoption of AI-EdTech recommendations for personalized instruction
examples: The model was validated in a within-subject staged experiment where 41 chemistry teachers received data-driven then domain-driven explanations of GrouPer's cluster recommendations

article_title: The Impact of Explainable AI on Teachers' Trust and Acceptance of AI EdTech Recommendations: The Power of Domain-specific Explanations
citation: Yael Feldman-Maggor, Mutlu Cukurova, Carmel Kent, Giora Alexandron. (2025). The Impact of Explainable AI on Teachers' Trust and Acceptance of AI EdTech Recommendations: The Power of Domain-specific Explanations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00486-6
title: GrouPer AI-based student-grouping recommendation tool
description: GrouPer is an AI-for-Teacher technology supporting personalized instruction in science education. Its analysis engine "uses an unsupervised machine learning algorithm (cluster analysis) to perform a multidimensional analysis of student responses to interactive assessment items", dividing students into clusters with similar knowledge profiles. The clusters are presented in an interactive dashboard that enables teachers to examine each cluster's performance and assign learning activities adapted to student groups' strengths and weaknesses. In this study it served as the research vehicle for studying trust and explainability, with both XAI explanation types presented textually alongside the dashboard.
requirements: Teachers receive background information about how the tool operates before evaluating its recommendations
constraints: Clustering generates bottom-up grouping based on similarity rather than predetermined categories, so "the criteria for similarity can often be difficult to comprehend and explain"; validating its interface was not part of the current research
target_learners: in-service high-school science (chemistry) teachers
target_learning_goals: formative assessment: analyzing student performance data and assigning follow-up activities adapted to student-group needs
examples: Teachers performed an authentic data analysis task with the dashboard, receiving feature-importance (data-driven) then semantic curricular (domain-driven) explanations of the cluster recommendations

article_title: Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence
citation: Lixiang Yan and Dragan Gašević. (2026). Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07813
title: Agentivism: a mid-range learning theory of durable human capability through selective delegation, verification, reconstruction, and transfer under reduced support
description: Agentivism is a mid-range conceptual learning theory for human-AI interaction. It defines learning as "durable growth in human capability that occurs when learners delegate selectively to generative or agentic AI, monitor and verify AI contributions, and reconstruct AI-assisted performance into knowledge and skill that remain available beyond the immediate interaction". Its explanatory core lies in "four linked mechanisms (Fig. 1): delegated agency, epistemic monitoring and verification, reconstructive internalization, and transfer under reduced support". The theory treats allocation of agency during interaction as a central explanatory variable and distinguishes assisted performance from learning, arguing that learning can no longer be inferred from performance alone when AI contributes directly to task completion.
requirements: Learning must be judged by what the learner can later explain, adapt, and transfer with reduced dependence on the same AI support, not by immediate task success.
constraints: The article states it "does not claim that all forms of learning through human-AI interaction follow one fixed sequence or can be reduced to a single explanatory principle".
It is not yet a formal computational model of learning and will require refinement as forms of AI support and institutional uses evolve.
target_learners: Learners using generative or agentic AI in writing, inquiry, problem solving, tutoring, and professional learning
target_learning_goals: Durable, transferable human capability developed through human-AI interaction
examples: The article maps six empirically testable propositions (P1–P6) onto the four core mechanisms, illustrating how predictions about learning outcomes arise from specific process components.
key_sources: Lixiang Yan and Dragan Gašević. (2026). Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07813

article_title: Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence
citation: Lixiang Yan and Dragan Gašević. (2026). Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07813
title: Design AI-supported learning so the learner remains responsible for framing, criteria, evidence comparison, and justification
description: This pedagogical principle holds that productive use of AI depends less on whether AI is present than on whether the learning design preserves the learner's responsibility for judgment. The article recommends that "Instructors should therefore prefer tasks and supports that require learners to frame the problem, articulate criteria, compare AI suggestions with evidence, and explain why accepted outputs are appropriate". For assessment, it argues that final products are increasingly insufficient indicators of learning and that "valid assessment requires evidence of the process through which the learner engaged that support, including revision patterns, justification, source checking, and what can later be reproduced or adapted with less assistance".
requirements: Tasks must require learners to frame the problem, articulate criteria, compare AI suggestions with evidence, and explain why accepted outputs are appropriate.
constraints: The article states the educational aim should not be to eliminate assistance but to ensure that assistance does not replace the learner's role as author, evaluator, and explainer.
target_learners: Instructors and assessment designers in writing, inquiry, and problem solving with AI
target_learning_goals: Reconstructive internalization of AI-assisted outputs into independently usable knowledge and skill
examples: The article cites well-designed AI tutoring that scaffolds reasoning sequentially, AI-enhanced simulations that require problem decomposition, and AI-supported writing that requires source comparison as showing learning gains when the learner remains responsible for judgment and integration.
key_sources: Lixiang Yan and Dragan Gašević. (2026). Agentivism: a learning theory for the age of artificial intelligence. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07813

article_title: A Case Study of Integrating AI Literacy Education in a Biology Class
citation: Shenghua Zha, Marcy Maulucci Bragdon, Na Gong, Jinhui Wang, Silas Leavesley, Rachel Eaton, Erin Bosarge. (2025). A Case Study of Integrating AI Literacy Education in a Biology Class. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00476-8
title: Adapted IRC framework for novice students' interdisciplinary reasoning in integrated AI education
description: The study adapts Shen et al.'s (2015) interdisciplinary reasoning and communication (IRC) framework for novice high-school students rather than experts. The original framework's skills of "integration, translation, transfer, and transformation" were modified: the codes of integration and transformation were eliminated for lack of occurrence, translation was renamed explanation, and codes were added to distinguish correct from vague or incorrect answers and to pinpoint missing interdisciplinary reasoning. The adapted coding book distinguishes correct explanation, vague or incorrect explanation, no explanation, transfer, and no transfer.
requirements: Two raters coding independently with inter-rater reliability checks; the study reports Cohen's Kappa of 0.88 before consensus discussion
constraints: Integration and transformation codes were eliminated because they did not occur in students' written answers in Lessons 1, 3, and 4; the framework was adapted for novices, not experts
target_learners: high-school honors biology students
target_learning_goals: interdisciplinary reasoning connecting AI and biology knowledge
examples: Matrix coding queries on students' answers to the last open-ended questions of Lessons 1, 3, and 4 extracted patterns of explaining and transferring biology and AI knowledge

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework
citation: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513
title: Ecological framework for student engagement with GenAI feedback
description: The paper proposes a tentative framework (Figure 1) theorising how opportunities and constraints in the GenAI feedback environment influence student feedback engagement from eliciting through processing to enacting. It is underpinned by an ecological perspective in which 'the positive alignment between individuals and their environments plays a crucial role in determining how students engage with feedback'. The framework also foregrounds student feedback literacy specific to the GenAI context and its synergy with the environment.
requirements: Students must possess the skills and dispositions (feedback literacy) to perceive and act on feedback opportunities afforded by the environment
constraints: Existing ecological frameworks focus on traditional learning environments and do not account for GenAI's transformative impact, so the framework was adapted for the GenAI context
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: engaging with feedback to improve work and learning strategies
examples: The framework was developed through a four-step process of literature search, analysis, adaptation and refinement, then refined through peer feedback from the co-authors
key_sources: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework
citation: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513
title: Process view of feedback engagement across eliciting, processing and enacting stages
description: Adopting Malecka et al.'s three stages of feedback (eliciting, processing, enacting), the paper offers a process view of feedback engagement that differs from holistic models. 'The process view identifies opportunities and constraints of GenAI at each feedback stage, enabling educators and researchers to tailor scaffolds for stage-specific feedback engagement.' Active engagement may take different forms at each stage, from overt question-asking in eliciting to invisible critical judgement in processing.
requirements: Educators and researchers must analyse each feedback stage separately to design stage-specific scaffolds
constraints: The paper notes student feedback engagement had previously 'not been specified regarding different stages of the feedback process' in the literature
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: seeking, making sense of, and acting on feedback
examples: The paper scrutinises GenAI's influence separately at the eliciting, processing and enacting stages
key_sources: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework
citation: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513
title: Cyclical self-regulation feedback model for feedback engagement in a GenAI context
description: Adapting Zimmerman's cyclical self-regulated learning model, the paper proposes a cyclical self-regulation feedback model (Figure 2) with three phases: feedback forethought (setting feedback goals and planning based on understanding of GenAI's capabilities and limitations), feedback control (self-observation and self-monitoring of prompts and GenAI responses, refining interactions), and feedback retrospect (reflecting on feedback effectiveness and developing ethical awareness). 'This cyclical process ensures that feedback generated from GenAI is iterative and progressive, fostering continuous engagement and development.' The phases are interwoven with the eliciting, processing and enacting stages.
requirements: Students exercise agency to adapt to the new feedback environment; teachers assist with goal definition and model metacognitive strategies
constraints: The paper states that because GenAI application in feedback practices is still at an early stage, 'any current conceptualisations should remain provisional as GenAI evolves'
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: self-regulating feedback processes and enhancing feedback literacy
examples: Educators and researchers can use the model to identify primary challenges at each stage and design interventions facilitating adaptation to the GenAI feedback environment
key_sources: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework
citation: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Phillip Dawson & Zi Yan (2025) Generative artificial intelligence as an enabler of student feedback engagement: a framework, Higher Education Research & Development, 44:5, 1289-1304, https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2025.2476513
title: Orchestrate GenAI feedback with student feedback literacy for positive alignment
description: The paper's central design principle is that GenAI becomes an enabler of feedback engagement only when orchestrated with what students bring, especially their feedback literacy. A mismatch between an individual's feedback literacy and the GenAI environment's affordances 'could lessen the enabling role of GenAI in feedback engagement', so the challenge is 'constructing synergies between individual students' feedback literacy and the GenAI feedback environment'.
requirements: Students must develop feedback literacy capacities suited to the GenAI context, including prompt writing, evaluative judgement and ethical awareness
constraints: GenAI's affordances do not necessarily lead to in-depth student feedback engagement without this alignment
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: deep engagement with feedback for learning improvement
examples: Student B's high feedback literacy enabled deep engagement with ChatGPT feedback, while Student A's low literacy led to superficial copying of revisions

article_title: What Platform Scores Miss: Multidimensional Evaluation of AI Teaching Agents in Medical Education
citation: Zhang Hui, Qu Lihui, Zheng Jianmin, Xiong Yi, Bai Hongbo, Ji Ruiying, Liu Guohui, Chen Wanling, Cheng Zirui, Chen Youbang, Yang Chun-tao. (2026). What Platform Scores Miss: Multidimensional Evaluation of AI Teaching Agents in Medical Education. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/96819
title: Eight-dimension pedagogical evaluation rubric for AI teaching agents
description: The article introduces a transparent, standardized 8-dimension rubric (100 points) designed to assess agent teaching quality rather than student response quality, covering "knowledge accuracy, pedagogical guidance, knowledge coverage, role-play quality, difficulty calibration, medical safety, student engagement, and feedback quality." Weights were assigned on conceptual grounds, with the two core teaching functions at 20 points each and the two supportive dimensions at 5 points each. It was operationalized through LLM scoring under standardized instructions and validated against cross-model agreement and a blinded human expert.
requirements: Scoring by LLM evaluators under standardized instructions with repeated runs, plus human expert calibration on a stratified subset
constraints: Dimension weights were set without formal student or educator input; empirically derived weights are future work
Expert calibration rested on a single expert, precluding expert-to-expert reliability

target_learning_goals: endocrinology curriculum knowledge
clinical communication and role-play skills
pedagogical quality of AI tutors
examples: Applied to 167 student-agent dialogues from 8 agents on the Chaoxing platform, scored 4 times each by 3 LLM evaluators and rescored on 40 dialogues by a medical-education expert

citation: Zhao Yan, Yue Yuhe, Sun Zhonghua, Jiang Qiang, Li Gangsheng. (2025). Does Generative Artificial Intelligence Improve Students’ Higher-Order Thinking? A Meta-Analysis Based on 29 Experiments and Quasi-Experiments. Journal of Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence13120160
title: Higher-order thinking as an integrated three-component capacity: critical thinking, creative thinking, and problem-solving ability
description: The article adopts a conceptualization of higher-order thinking rooted in Bloom's taxonomy and its revision, in which HOT is "an integrated cognitive capacity, highly dependent on metacognitive awareness". Its core components are held to be critical thinking, creative thinking, and problem-solving ability, which the authors describe as activated synergistically in complex problem situations: critical thinking analyzes and evaluates information, creative thinking generates diverse solutions, and problem-solving ability constructs and implements strategies. The meta-analysis operationalizes HOT through these three dimensions.

constraints: The article notes that specific classifications of HOT vary across disciplinary contexts, with discipline-specific dimensional lists differing from the cross-disciplinary consensus

article_title: Academic Erasure: The Disappearance of Complexity Under AI-Supported Writing
citation: Chinomso Nwagboso & Sunday Atuba. (2026). Academic erasure: the disappearance of complexity under AI-supported writing. Teaching in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/13562517.2026.2707601
title: Academic erasure: loss of depth, voice, and engagement in AI-shaped student writing operating through compliance
description: Academic erasure is the study's central concept: "the disappearance of depth, voice, and engagement in student writing shaped by AI-driven norms". Unlike marginalisation, which excludes students who fail to meet standards, erasure operates through compliance — the student may meet all standards yet produce epistemically vacuous work. The article characterises it by three features: superficial structure without depth, fluency without complexity, and generic tone with weak positioning, and frames it as structurally enabled by institutions that reward fluency and output.
requirements: Assessment cultures that reward fluency, presentation, and output over argumentation and intellectual risk, which the article says create conditions in which AI use is rational
constraints: The concept is theorised from educator discourse only; the article states the findings are not statistically generalisable and that empirical validation through comparative textual analysis remains future work
target_learners: higher education students
secondary students
target_learning_goals: academic writing
critical thinking
epistemic agency
examples: Educators describe writing that 'sounds too perfect' yet lacks substance, and AI-generated essays that are polished but textually uninhabited
key_sources: Chinomso Nwagboso & Sunday Atuba. (2026). Academic erasure: the disappearance of complexity under AI-supported writing. Teaching in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/13562517.2026.2707601

article_title: Academic Erasure: The Disappearance of Complexity Under AI-Supported Writing
citation: Chinomso Nwagboso & Sunday Atuba. (2026). Academic erasure: the disappearance of complexity under AI-supported writing. Teaching in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/13562517.2026.2707601
title: Epistemic delegation and epistemic singularity as the two mechanisms producing academic erasure
description: The article frames academic erasure as the joint effect of two mechanisms. Epistemic delegation is "the displacement of that labour onto generative AI, the act of handing over the work of thinking to machines optimised for fluency"; the article argues it is structured by design, since AI systems interpolate rather than reason. Epistemic singularity names the homogenisation effect at scale, in which disciplinary, cultural, and individual variation collapses into a dominant AI-optimised register. Together they displace the slow, situated cognitive work writing is meant to support.
requirements: Student access to generative AI tools in high-stakes, time-pressured, or confidence-poor contexts, which the article says makes delegation a rational shortcut
constraints: The article presents this as theoretical framing grounded in educator discourse, not a tested causal model; it notes planned comparative analysis of AI-generated outputs versus pre-AI writing was not undertaken in this study
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction through writing
authorial voice
disciplinary positioning
examples: Students prompting an AI to write an essay bypass the iterative work of formulating arguments, working through tensions, and synthesising sources

article_title: Effectiveness of adaptive versus non-adaptive intelligent tutoring systems in early primary mathematics
citation: Sibley, L., Berner, T., & Schmalfeldt, T. (2026). Effectiveness of adaptive versus non-adaptive intelligent tutoring systems in early primary mathematics. Computers and Education Open 11. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100420
title: Intelligent tutoring systems as three-model architectures operationalizing formative assessment
description: The article describes ITS as autonomous technologies that continuously assess learners' progress through formative assessment and deliver tailored instructional support. It states that "ITS typically consist of three core components: a domain model (representing the knowledge to be learned), a student model (tracking individual learning progress and misconceptions), and a tutoring model (or pedagogical module) that determines what instructional support to provide". Based on these models, ITS provide individualized support such as hints and error-specific feedback and adapt task sequencing to ensure mastery before progression. In this study the architecture was implemented in a CTAT+TutorShop tutor with Bayesian Knowledge Tracing driving task selection.
requirements: A diagnostic engine enabling real-time adaptations based on students' responses, integrating learner modeling, adaptive task sequencing, and dynamic feedback mechanisms
constraints: The article notes ITS cannot fully replace the pedagogical sensitivity of human teachers
target_learners: second-grade primary school students
target_learning_goals: second-grade mathematics: addition and subtraction with and without carrying or borrowing
examples: The study's tutor covered 13 arithmetic skills with increasing complexity, used graduated spoken-audio hints, and selected tasks via the Sequential Mastery Learning – Easier First algorithm based on BKT mastery estimates
key_sources: Sibley, L., Berner, T., & Schmalfeldt, T. (2026). Effectiveness of adaptive versus non-adaptive intelligent tutoring systems in early primary mathematics. Computers and Education Open 11. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100420

article_title: A scoping review of generative AI-powered agentic AI in education: Research landscape, agentic capabilities
citation: Wang, N., Zou, D., Xie, H., & Qin, S. J. (2026). A scoping review of generative AI-powered agentic AI in education: Research landscape, agentic capabilities, and insights from the frontier agent paradigm, exemplified by OpenClaw. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 11. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100653
title: Six-dimensional agentic capability framework rated on a 1–5 ordinal scale, grounded in activity theory and scaffolding theory
description: The review develops a coding rubric rating six agentic capability dimensions — autonomy and proactivity; planning and reasoning depth; memory and context management; tool and environment interaction; multi-agent collaboration; and robustness, explainability and governance — each on "A 1–5 ordinal scale" capturing thresholds from non-agentic to fully agentic behaviour. Activity theory anchors the dimensions educationally (e.g., autonomy maps to the subject, governance to rules), and scaffolding theory supplements interpretation of planning, memory, and governance dimensions.
requirements: Dimensions must be ratable from reported agent architecture, interaction design, and evaluation setup without fine-grained interaction logs or proprietary benchmarks.
constraints: The article states the framework "is not a psychometric measurement tool" and that formal external expert validation was not conducted, so capability scores should be interpreted with this in mind.
target_learners: Researchers and coders of educational agentic AI literature
target_learning_goals: Mapping and evaluating the agentic capabilities of educational AI systems
examples: The rubric was pilot-tested on 20 randomly selected studies with two independent coders, and level descriptors were refined with LLM assistance before full corpus coding.

Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 11. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100653
title: Definition of generative AI-powered agentic AI via three core characteristics: task autonomy, goal-directed reasoning, and memory- and context-aware interaction
description: The review defines agentic AI as systems "powered by generative AI, that exhibit goal-directed autonomy": perceiving the environment, reasoning about goals, formulating and executing multi-step plans, adapting behaviour, and coordinating with tools, other agents, or human stakeholders. Three core characteristics distinguish educational agentic systems from general-purpose text generators: task autonomy, goal-directed reasoning and adaptive decision-making, and memory- and context-aware interaction; multi-step planning and multi-agent collaboration may be present but are not required for inclusion.
requirements: A study qualifies when the system is designed for an educational purpose and demonstrates at least one core agentic characteristic; fully autonomous operation is not required, as capability is treated as a matter of degree.
constraints: Studies where generative AI is used only as a general-purpose text-generation or prompt-response tool without a designed educational agent workflow are excluded.
target_learners: Educational AI researchers and system designers
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing agentic educational systems from general-purpose generative AI tools
examples: Concrete examples given include an adaptive tutor diagnosing misconceptions through dialogue, a role-playing simulator adopting a patient or historical persona, a curriculum curator, and multi-agent orchestration under human oversight.

article_title: AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought
citation: Dalsgaard, C., & Prilop, C. N. (2026). AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought. Journal of Research on Technology in Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/15391523.2026.2695013
title: Framework for reflective thought: examination, construction, and empirical versus theoretical reflection as mediating processes
description: The article applies a framework for reflective thought (Dalsgaard, 2018, 2020), drawing on Dewey's inquiry and Schön's reflection-in-action, to analyze whether students' AI practices are epistemic. Reflective thought is goal-directed and performed through iterative processes of examination (goal-directed study of materials), construction (developing hypotheses, methods, solutions), and reflection. It operates with two kinds of reflection: "Empirical reflection is an evaluation of the result of an action (solution) in relation to the goal of the action", while theoretical reflection evaluates the solution in relation to concepts or theories. The framework is used to code interview data and to map how AI supports each process (Figures 1 and 3).
requirements: Tools define how goals can be achieved, so the framework presupposes identifying the mediating instruments in students' goal-directed activity
constraints: Developed from Dewey's and Davydov's distinctions; applied here to upper secondary students' schoolwork with generative AI chatbots
target_learners: upper secondary school students
target_learning_goals: reflective thought and knowledge construction in subject-area schoolwork
examples: Students writing a political speech engage in empirical reflection by assessing whether it resembles an actual speech, and theoretical reflection by relating it to rhetorical devices such as logos and pathos
key_sources: Dalsgaard, C., & Prilop, C. N. (2026). AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought. Journal of Research on Technology in Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/15391523.2026.2695013

citation: Dalsgaard, C., & Prilop, C. N. (2026). AI as a cognitive partner in learning: Emerging epistemic practices of reflective thought. Journal of Research on Technology in Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/15391523.2026.2695013
title: Expanded versus novel epistemic practices when students form hybrid minds with AI as an external memory system
description: The article's organizing taxonomy distinguishes expanded (or transformed) epistemic practices, where AI substitutes or augments existing tools and sequences of steps, from genuinely novel epistemic practices, where AI enables processes previously impossible without external human input — particularly theoretical and empirical reflection. It builds on Säljö's hybrid minds account, in which "Hybrid minds operate in environments of external symbolic storages where human reasoning is located at the intersection of the human mind and external, technological resources", and on Salomon et al.'s cognitive partnership concept. Figure 3 summarizes expanded and novel practices of reflective thought using AI.
requirements: Students must engage with AI as a cognitive partner within learning processes rather than merely outsourcing tasks
constraints: Novel practices of examination or construction may only emerge under certain conditions, whereas theoretical and empirical reflection reveal distinct novel components
target_learners: upper secondary school students
target_learning_goals: epistemic practices of learning and knowledge construction with generative AI
examples: Customized overviews of a subject area and co-generated idea catalogues are given as cases where novel examination or construction practices may emerge

title: Cultivate, do not ban: teach students to use AI as a mediating tool for reflective thought within process-oriented assignments
description: The article's central implication for teaching practice is "not to ban AI use, but to cultivate students' abilities to engage with AI tools as mediating tools for reflective thought". Teachers should redirect focus from products toward processes, frame AI use within examination, construction, and reflection, and show how AI supports each process differently — explanations for examination, methods when stuck in construction, and improvement suggestions for reflection. Teachers should make the processes visible, for instance through assignments where students demonstrate and reflect on cognitive partnership processes.
requirements: Teachers make the reflective thought processes visible in class, e.g. assignments where students demonstrate cognitive partnership processes
constraints: Risk remains that students use AI to outsource cognitive processes; the recommendation targets partnership use, not product-level outsourcing
target_learners: upper secondary school students
target_learning_goals: reflective thought, examination, construction, and reflection in subject-area work
examples: In the project, 59 teachers from eight schools developed exploratory action plans with AI-based student assignments across two five-month intervention cycles

title: One-year action and design-based research project on AI use across eight Danish upper secondary schools
description: The empirical basis of the study is a one-year action and design-based research project in which "59 teachers from eight upper secondary schools developed action plans for interventions in the form of teaching activities using AI". Teachers attended an initiating workshop introducing cognitive partnership and epistemic practices, completed five-month interventions, then revised plans in a second workshop cycle. Data consist of eight student group interviews with 48 students (28 male, 20 female), most aged 16–19, analyzed via reflexive thematic analysis. Outcomes were the research findings and teacher-designed teaching plans.

description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 27 studies selected with the PRISMA 2020 methodology from a Scopus search conducted on July 16, 2024. The search query targeted "artificial intelligence" AND collaborative AND learning AND higher AND education, yielding 163 articles, of which 27 studies were included after screening. Studies were coded by focus area, methodology, application, key findings, and AI methods.
requirements: Studies published 2014–2024 in English, focused on AI-based collaborative learning in higher education, with empirical, case-study, or meta-analytic designs
constraints: Single-database (Scopus) search; findings are described by the author as status-quo in nature, reflecting the present state of research
