title: Four-category functional taxonomy of AI tools shaping collaborative learning in higher education
description: The review organizes AI tools by underlying functionality into four categories: predictive analytics (machine learning models, early warning systems) that predict student success and identify at-risk students; language-based systems (chatbots, large language models, natural language processors) enabling close-in-time interaction and automatic feedback; recommender algorithms personalizing learning through resource proposals and peer matching; and intelligent tutoring and monitoring applications recording emotional states and performance for context-adaptive feedback. This taxonomy structures the review's synthesis of how AI enriches collaborative learning processes and outcomes.
requirements: Categorizing AI methods based on underlying functionalities to enable an analytic perspective on how AI enriches collaborative learning
constraints: The literature reviewed is mostly centred on subsymbolic AI, largely disregarding symbolic reasoning systems and hybrid models

enhanced student engagement

article_title: 'Architecting an AI-Driven Decision Support System for Enhanced Online Learning and Assessment'
citation: Mahamad, S.; Chin, Y.H.; Zulmuksah, N.I.N.; Haque, M.M.; Shaheen, M.; Nisar, K. (2025). Technical Review: Architecting an AI-Driven Decision Support System for Enhanced Online Learning and Assessment. Future Internet 2025, 17, 383. https://doi.org/10.3390/fi17090383
title: Modular four-module AI-DSS architecture for online learning and assessment
description: The review proposes a flexible, modular AI-driven decision support system architecture built around four main elements: data collection, AI processing, a decision-making core, and a user interface, integrated with existing LMSs via standards like Learning Tools Interoperability. As the article states, "this review puts forward a flexible, modular AI-DSS design built around four main elements: gathering data, processing with AI, a decision-making core, and an intuitive user interface". The data collection module aggregates performance, behavioral, demographic, and course metadata with preprocessing for GDPR/FERPA compliance; the AI processing module runs ML, NLP, knowledge-based, and deep learning streams; the decision engine generates personalized learning paths, automated grades, and feedback with explainability mechanisms; and a feedback loop channels user interactions back for continuous refinement.
requirements: Diverse, high-quality learner data (performance, behavioral, demographic, course metadata) sourced from LMS platforms
Integration with LMSs via standard APIs such as Learning Tools Interoperability
constraints: Deep learning components are computationally intensive, posing challenges for resource-constrained environments
Compliance with GDPR and FERPA requires anonymization and encryption in the data pipeline
target_learners: online learners in MOOCs, institutional LMSs, and adaptive learning environments
target_learning_goals: personalized learning pathways
automated and formative/summative assessment
timely actionable feedback
examples: The article contrasts the proposed architecture with Coursera's centralized ML recommendations and edX's LMS-integrated NLP grading, claiming federated learning and a hybrid RL-ML decision engine as innovations

article_title: 'Architecting an AI-Driven Decision Support System for Enhanced Online Learning and Assessment'
citation: Mahamad, S.; Chin, Y.H.; Zulmuksah, N.I.N.; Haque, M.M.; Shaheen, M.; Nisar, K. (2025). Technical Review: Architecting an AI-Driven Decision Support System for Enhanced Online Learning and Assessment. Future Internet 2025, 17, 383. https://doi.org/10.3390/fi17090383
title: Combined quantitative–qualitative evaluation framework and metric set for AI-DSSs
description: The review defines a balanced evaluation approach for AI-driven decision support systems combining technical metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, scalability, response time) with user-focused outcomes (user satisfaction via validated surveys drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, and engagement measured through interaction frequency, task completion rates, or time-on-task). Quantitative methods include k-fold cross-validation and statistical comparisons via t-tests or ANOVA; qualitative methods include surveys, interviews, and case studies. The article concludes that "By combining these complementary approaches, evaluations achieve a balance of technical precision and practical relevance, ensuring AI-DSSs meet both performance and user needs."
requirements: Both quantitative performance metrics and qualitative user-perspective data must be collected
Statistical methods such as t-tests or ANOVA for comparison against traditional systems
constraints: Trade-offs are inherent: high deep-learning accuracy (92%) increases latency (30–60%), and real-time response (<1 s) trades accuracy in complex tasks
target_learners: online learners in MOOCs, institutional LMSs, and adaptive learning environments
target_learning_goals: reliable evaluation of AI-supported learning and assessment systems
examples: Table 11 of the article defines each metric, e.g., accuracy as the proportion of correct predictions made by the AI model over total predictions

article_title: Mapping the Scaffolding of Metacognition and Learning by AI Tools in STEM Classrooms: A Bibliometric-Systematic Review
citation: Tsakeni, Maria, Stephen C. Nwafor, Moeketsi Mosia, and Felix O. Egara. 2025. Mapping the Scaffolding of Metacognition and Learning by AI Tools in STEM Classrooms: A Bibliometric–Systematic Review Approach (2005–2025). Journal of Intelligence 13: 148. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence13110148
title: Scaffolding versus sharing metacognition: a distinction between AI-supported and AI-distributed metacognitive regulation
description: The review distinguishes two ways AI can be involved in learners' metacognition. Scaffolding "treats metacognition as a human capacity that can be supported and extended through prompts, feedback, or adaptive interventions, thereby allowing learners to retain agency and responsibility." Sharing, by contrast, "distributes metacognitive functions between human and AI agents, where AI may compensate for weak regulation." The review positions AI primarily as a scaffolding tool while noting sharing must be critically evaluated because it risks substitution of learner strategy development.
requirements: AI involvement must be designed so learners retain agency and responsibility for their regulation
constraints: Sharing risks limiting learners' opportunities to develop independent strategies if applied uncritically
target_learners: STEM students in secondary and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: metacognitive planning, monitoring, and evaluation of learning
examples: The review's 24-study synthesis coded 23 studies as human-centred scaffolding orientations and one (Walker et al. 2025) as posthumanist sharing of regulation

article_title: Mapping the Scaffolding of Metacognition and Learning by AI Tools in STEM Classrooms: A Bibliometric-Systematic Review
citation: Tsakeni, Maria, Stephen C. Nwafor, Moeketsi Mosia, and Felix O. Egara. 2025. Mapping the Scaffolding of Metacognition and Learning by AI Tools in STEM Classrooms: A Bibliometric–Systematic Review Approach (2005–2025). Journal of Intelligence 13: 148. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence13110148
title: Three-framework lens: Flavell's metacognition theory, General Systems Theory, and human-centred versus posthumanist AI paradigms
description: The review interprets how AI tools scaffold metacognition through "three complementary frameworks: Flavell's Theory of Metacognition (1979), General Systems Theory (GST), and Human-Centred vs. Posthumanist AI paradigms." Flavell's model, with Nelson and Narens' object-level/meta-level distinction, interprets AI support for both task performance and strategic monitoring. GST conceptualises STEM classrooms as interconnected adaptive systems where students, teachers, technologies, and pedagogies interact dynamically. The human-centred paradigm regards AI as supporting human agency under ethical oversight, while the posthumanist paradigm conceptualises learning as co-regulated between humans and AI systems.
requirements: Application of the frameworks requires distinguishing whether AI is framed as a supportive tool or a co-agent in reflective processes
constraints: The review clarifies that what is shared is not metacognition itself but the regulation of learning experiences scaffolded by AI alongside human agency
target_learners: STEM learners across primary, secondary, and tertiary levels
target_learning_goals: metacognitive development and self-regulated learning in STEM
examples: The review applies the lens to interpret keyword shifts from reflection and teacher scaffolding toward system-level reflection and machine awareness

article_title: AI Mindset – An Empirically Tested Theoretical Framework on the Psychological Factors Shaping AI Competence and AI Use
citation: Feng, S., Koch, M. J., & Carolus, A. (2026). AI Mindset – An empirically tested theoretical framework on the psychological factors shaping AI competence and AI use. Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100402
title: AI Mindset framework: a triadic structure of dispositional factors, contextual and social facilitation, and technology-related appraisals explaining teachers' AI use
description: The AI Mindset framework integrates constructs from social-cognitive, socio-technical and motivation theories into three domains: dispositional factors (personality, basic psychological needs, self-efficacy, self-regulation), contextual and social facilitation (social influence, habit), and technology-related appraisals (attitudes, performance and effort expectancy, hedonic motivation). The article states it is "a cohesive triadic structure comprising dispositional factors, contextual and social facilitations, and technology-related appraisals" shaping tendencies to adopt AI. It extends technology-acceptance models by organising these domains jointly in relation to pedagogical AI competence and AI use.
requirements: Intended to supplement and integrate with, rather than replace, established models such as the Technology Acceptance Model, UTAUT2 and the Theory of Planned Behaviour
constraints: The article notes the incremental explanatory value of the framework requires further investigation because competing theoretical models were not directly compared
target_learners: K-12 schoolteachers
target_learning_goals: Understanding psychological factors associated with teachers' AI competence development and AI use in teaching practice
examples: The framework was operationalised as a mediation structural equation model tested with survey data from 224 teachers, with pedagogical AI competence specified as mediator between AI Mindset factors and AI use

title: Professional development for teachers' AI engagement should extend beyond attitudes to develop pedagogical and ethical AI competence
description: Because pedagogical AI competence showed a strong positive association with AI use and carried several indirect associations from AI Mindset factors, the authors recommend that professional development address competence directly. The article states that "Professional development programmes should therefore extend beyond attitudes towards AI to include the development of AI competence, particularly pedagogical and ethical competences." article_title: 'Artificial Intelligence in Online Education: A Systematic Review of Its Impact on Learner Engagement and Satisfaction'
citation: Ana Katalinic, Vanja Slavuj, Danijela Jaksic. (2026). Artificial Intelligence in Online Education: A Systematic Review of Its Impact on Learner Engagement and Satisfaction. Educ. Sci. 2026, 16, 389. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16030389
title: Self-Determination Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model as explanatory frameworks for AI-supported engagement and satisfaction
description: The review frames learner engagement and satisfaction in digital environments through two named theories. Self-Determination Theory holds that "individuals are more motivated and actively engaged when their basic psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness are supported". The Technology Acceptance Model explains adoption through perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use; the review reports that when SDT needs are satisfied, learners perceive technologies as more useful and easier to use, increasing satisfaction and continued-use intention.
requirements: Application presupposes AI tools that support learners' needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness, and that learners perceive as useful and easy to use.
target_learners: higher education students in online courses
target_learning_goals: learner motivation
engagement
satisfaction
technology acceptance
examples: The review cites empirical work reporting that satisfying autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs increases perceived usefulness, ease of use, satisfaction, and intention to continue using digital platforms.

article_title: 'AI-Supported Problem-Based Learning for Enhancing Computational Thinking'
citation: Ayanwale, M. A., & Omeh, C. B. (2026). AI-supported problem-based learning for enhancing computational thinking skills in STEM education. Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans 7 (2026) 100263. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100263
title: AI-PBL as Social Constructivist scaffolding: AI tools act as more capable peers within learners' Zone of Proximal Development
description: The study's theoretical framework grounds AI-supported PBL in Vygotsky's Social Constructivism, positioning intelligent systems as digital "more capable peers" within the learner's Zone of Proximal Development. AI supports learning through three functions the article names: "Problem formulation", "Exploration", and "Reflection" — AI agents help define problem parameters, intelligent tutoring systems and reinforcement learning agents simulate robotic behaviors and offer real-time debugging support, and chatbots and analytics tools prompt metacognitive dialogue. In resource-constrained Nigerian university settings, the framework is offered as a scalable, context-aware solution that promotes equity and bridges the digital divide.
requirements: AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Teachable Machine) embedded in inquiry-driven PBL instruction to provide adaptive scaffolding and feedback
constraints: Traditional PBL models rely heavily on instructor facilitation and may be constrained by limited resources, especially in developing contexts
target_learners: First-year undergraduate students in computer robotics programming courses
target_learning_goals: Computational thinking skills (abstraction, decomposition, algorithm design, debugging, metacognitive reflection)
Academic achievement in computer robotics programming
examples: In a search-and-rescue robot task, AI tools guided students in selecting sensors, simulated decision-making algorithms, and provided feedback on classifier accuracy.

title: 14-week localized, adaptive AI-PBL intervention for computer robotics programming
description: The intervention integrated AI tools into problem-based learning over 14 weeks (42 instructional hours) for first-year computer education students. "Localized" emphasizes grounding projects in authentic, context-specific challenges such as maze navigation, assistive robotics, recycling, and search-and-rescue tasks. "Adaptive" highlights the dynamic role of AI tools—ChatGPT for idea generation, debugging, and decision logic, and Teachable Machine for training classifiers—that provided iterative feedback and cognitive scaffolding. Students designed a line-following robot, a service robot for visually impaired individuals, a recycling-sorting robot, and a search-and-rescue robot, with Arduino kits providing tactile programming experience.

constraints: The control group received traditional lecture-based teaching on the same content without AI integration

examples: Week 8: students used Teachable Machine to build classifiers distinguishing recyclables by shape and color, integrated into robotic arms for automated classification.

article_title: AI refusal in higher education: the right to refuse, the duty to understand and the diagnostic value of non-use
citation: Zagami, J. (2026). AI refusal in higher education: the right to refuse, the duty to understand and the diagnostic value of non-use. Higher Education Research & Development, 45(7), 2287-2294. https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2026.2694409
title: AI refusal as a role-structured spectrum of non-use, opt-out, restriction, bounded use and institutional delay
description: The article develops AI refusal as a conceptual and diagnostic category rather than a single measurable behaviour. It argues that 'refusal in higher education should be understood as a spectrum of non- use, opt-out, restriction, bounded use and institutional delay', whose meaning changes across roles because universities are role-structured and publicly accountable. Different AI systems (chatbots, analytics, proctoring, plagiarism detection) differ in visibility, risk and user control, so refusing one is not the same as refusing another. The theory draws on technology non-use scholarship that treats non-use as socially meaningful rather than a deficit.
requirements: Interpret refusal in relation to the specific AI system, the actor's role, and the conditions of agency, rather than as one behaviour
constraints: The article does not measure refusal prevalence or offer a systematic review; it is a conceptual and diagnostic category
target_learners: higher education students
academics
professional staff
institutional leaders
target_learning_goals: defensible decision-making about when AI serves, compromises, or must be refused in learning and academic work
examples: A student choosing not to use a chatbot (personal); a course team prohibiting generative AI for a task evidencing unaided reasoning (pedagogical); a university delaying procurement pending privacy and accountability clarity (institutional)

citation: Zagami, J. (2026). AI refusal in higher education: the right to refuse, the duty to understand and the diagnostic value of non-use. Higher Education Research & Development, 45(7), 2287-2294. https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2026.2694409
title: Protect the right to private refusal while holding role-based non-use accountable through a duty to understand
description: The article distinguishes private refusal — a protected right not to use AI in personal intellectual, creative or everyday life — from role-based refusal, which requires justification where AI materially shapes educational, scholarly, administrative or governance activity. The duty to understand 'should not be converted into a managerial requirement to use commercial systems'; it includes the capacity to reject, restrict, audit and critique AI. Refusal is thus one of the most important forms of AI literacy.
requirements: Universities must provide trustworthy guidance, explainable assessment rules, accessible development and explicit boundaries around acceptable use so the duty to understand does not become a hidden workload
constraints: Where AI is embedded in infrastructure individuals do not choose, refusal shifts from individual use to procurement, policy, audit and contestability
target_learners: higher education students
academics and teacher educators
professional staff
institutional leaders
target_learning_goals: AI literacy including the capacity to decide when a system should not be used and to justify one's relation to AI
examples: A researcher using AI-enabled search must understand enough to assess reliability, bias and attribution; a teacher educator preparing graduates for AI-mediated schools cannot simply refuse to understand AI

citation: Zagami, J. (2026). AI refusal in higher education: the right to refuse, the duty to understand and the diagnostic value of non-use. Higher Education Research & Development, 45(7), 2287-2294. https://doi.org/10.1080/07294360.2026.2694409
title: Set critical AI practice as the preferred institutional norm: capacity to use, refuse, critique, audit and govern AI by purpose
description: The article proposes a deliberative language distinguishing private refusal, principled role-based non-use, bounded professional use, critical AI practice, uninformed non-engagement and compulsory adoption. 'Critical AI practice is the preferred institutional norm because it involves the capacity to use, refuse, critique, audit and govern AI depending on purpose.' Both extremes — uninformed non-engagement and compulsory adoption — are treated as risks, and institutional strategy should define what AI should not do, not merely how it can be scaled.
requirements: Institutional deliberation capable of distinguishing which decisions require human review, which systems require audit, which uses require disclosure and which procurement choices require public justification
constraints: Administrative AI systems should preserve human review, contestability and escalation because individual refusal is not always possible for embedded infrastructure
target_learners: higher education students and staff
university governance and leadership
target_learning_goals: governing AI so technological capacity is subordinated to educational purpose
examples: The article lists embedded systems — spam filtering, learning analytics, plagiarism detection, accessibility tools — where refusal is displaced to procurement, audit and contestability levels

article_title: AI and student motivation: A scoping review
citation: Jiajing Li, Ronnel B. King, Ching Sing Chai, Vivian WY Lee & Ruyi Li. (2026). AI and student motivation: A scoping review. Journal of Research on Technology in Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/15391523.2026.2672515
title: Eight-type taxonomy of AI education tools in motivation research, with generative AI dominant
description: The review derives an exploratory classification of the AI tools used in the 156 reviewed studies, which "can be broadly classified into eight distinct types based on their core technical features and instructional contexts." The types include generative AI tools, intelligent adaptive educational platforms, subject-specific feedback tools, voice assistants and speech-based AI systems, AI-driven educational games and gamification tools, multimodal AI analytics and recognition tools, learning management systems, and embodied educational robots. Generative AI dominates (n = 76, 48.1%), with chatbots built on large language models the most popular within that category.
requirements: The classification was derived exploratorily from the tools' core technical features and instructional contexts as described in the reviewed studies
constraints: The review states there is no one-size-fits-all taxonomy for educational AI tools
target_learners: elementary through graduate students in AI-supported learning
target_learning_goals: student motivation in AI-supported learning environments
examples: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT accounted for 48.1% of reviewed studies; intelligent adaptive educational platforms appeared 26 times (16.5%)

title: Integrate AI-supported experimental design with professional validation to make authentic inquiry manageable in undergraduate laboratories
description: The article presents an approach where students use AI to design lab manuals for real-world sample analysis, then implement them experimentally. AI's "rapid response and capacity to produce extensive information from user prompts" helps students narrow broad topics and develop manuals, making Level 3 authentic inquiry more accessible. Independent professional validation ensures safety and feasibility before implementation.

critical thinking
problem-solving
troubleshooting
scientific communication

title: Almeida Bauer Zytkuewisz rubric for characterizing levels of inquiry in undergraduate laboratories
description: A rubric that differentiates laboratory activities into six levels (originally five, recently updated) based on six characteristics: problem/question, theory/background, procedure/design, result/analysis, results communication, and conclusions. The level of inquiry is determined by the amount of information provided to students. Level 3 authentic inquiry provides no information for any characteristic and is considered impractical in undergraduate courses due to difficulty, complexity, safety risks, and students' limited technical expertise. This article's activity was designed to align with Level 3.
requirements: Characterization of laboratory activities across six information-provision dimensions
constraints: Level 3 authentic inquiry is often considered impractical in undergraduate laboratory courses due to inherent difficulty, complexity, safety risks, and students' lack of technical expertise
target_learners: undergraduate laboratory students
target_learning_goals: characterizing inquiry levels in laboratory course design
examples: The article's lab manual design project aligned with Level 3 by providing six broad topics without predefined problems or theoretical backgrounds

article_title: Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach
citation: Adeeb Obaid Alsuhaymi and Fouad Ahmed Atallah. (2026). Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach. Sustainability 2026, 18, 1257. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18031257
title: Conditional model of AI and sustainable education: AI supports sustainable education only under five governance conditions
description: The article synthesizes its four analytical results into a conditional explanatory model stating that AI supports sustainable education only when five conditions hold: sustainability is not substituted by efficiency metrics, datafication is governed by public-oriented and ethical accountability, normative friction constrains instrumental adoption, equity is treated as a governance responsibility, and epistemic integrity is actively protected. The article states: "AI supports sustainable education only when (i) sustainability is not substituted by efficiency metrics, (ii) datafication is governed by public-oriented and ethical accountability, (iii) normative friction constrains instrumental adoption, (iv) equity is treated as a governance responsibility, (v) epistemic integrity is actively protected". It positions the model as moving beyond the generic claim that AI has benefits and risks by specifying mechanisms, boundary conditions, and governance pathways.
requirements: Explicit educational purposes, ethical constraints, equity-oriented governance, and protection of epistemic integrity must subordinate AI adoption
constraints: The model is derived from qualitative value-critical analysis of literature, not from empirical evaluation of specific AI applications
target_learners: learners in AI-mediated educational systems across higher education and value-based educational contexts
target_learning_goals: long-term intellectual, ethical, and social flourishing; educational purpose, equity, epistemic integrity, and governance of AI-mediated learning
examples: Table 2 summarizes each analytical result with its core mechanism, risk under weak governance, and boundary condition for sustainable education
key_sources: Adeeb Obaid Alsuhaymi and Fouad Ahmed Atallah. (2026). Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach. Sustainability 2026, 18, 1257. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18031257

article_title: Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach
citation: Adeeb Obaid Alsuhaymi and Fouad Ahmed Atallah. (2026). Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach. Sustainability 2026, 18, 1257. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18031257
title: Three-way distinction between sustainable education, sustainability in education, and education for sustainable development
description: The article adopts, as a heuristic entry point, the analytical distinction between three concepts. Sustainability in education emphasizes institutional durability, efficiency, and system continuity; education for sustainable development focuses on curricular and pedagogical alignment with sustainability-related goals; and sustainable education is "a value-based and human-centered educational orientation concerned with long-term intellectual, ethical, and social flourishing". The article argues that failing to maintain these distinctions has generated conceptual ambiguity, allowing technologization to be treated as a proxy for sustainability rather than as a means that must itself be critically evaluated. It uses sustainable education as its primary analytical lens while situating it in dialogue with human-centered educational theory, critical educational technology scholarship, and AI governance frameworks.
requirements: The distinctions must be maintained analytically to avoid conflating technological efficiency, institutional resilience, and policy compliance with educational sustainability
constraints: The article employs the distinctions as a heuristic and comparative reference, rather than as a self-validating or exhaustive framework
target_learners: learners across educational systems affected by AI-driven digitalization
target_learning_goals: clarifying what sustainability should mean in educational contexts; protecting formative, ethical, and democratic purposes of education
examples: The article's discussion distinguishes system sustainability from sustainable education, noting AI-enabled outcomes like administrative automation enhance operational sustainability without necessarily advancing sustainable education as a normative project
key_sources: Adeeb Obaid Alsuhaymi and Fouad Ahmed Atallah. (2026). Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach. Sustainability 2026, 18, 1257. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18031257

article_title: Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach
citation: Adeeb Obaid Alsuhaymi and Fouad Ahmed Atallah. (2026). Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach. Sustainability 2026, 18, 1257. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18031257
title: Subordinate AI and digitalization to coherent normative, ethical, and governance frameworks that prioritize educational purpose, social justice, and human dignity
description: The article's central design recommendation is that achieving sustainable education in the digital age depends not on AI adoption per se but on governance. It concludes that sustainable education depends "on subordinating AI and digitalization to coherent normative, ethical, and governance frameworks that prioritize educational purpose, social justice, and human dignity". In practice this means embedding equity-oriented design principles, transparent data governance, accountability mechanisms for algorithmic decision-making, and explicit norms of academic integrity in educational policy, so that platform logic is subordinated to educational ethics rather than the reverse.
requirements: Institutions must adopt public-oriented governance frameworks, including transparent data governance, limits on extractive data practices, and accountability mechanisms for algorithmic decision-making
constraints: Positive AI outcomes are contingent upon adequate infrastructure, institutional capacity, teacher training, and pedagogical integration; AI may exacerbate inequality unless equity-oriented governance is deliberately embedded
target_learners: all learners in AI-mediated educational systems, particularly those from low-income, rural, or marginalized backgrounds
target_learning_goals: protecting educational purpose, social justice, human dignity, epistemic integrity, and academic integrity in AI-mediated education
examples: The article's integrated result specifies five conditions for sustainable AI adoption, including public-oriented data governance, deliberative oversight, equity-oriented design, and clear norms of academic integrity and human-centered assessment

article_title: Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership
citation: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957
title: Integrated framework linking cognitive ownership, mutual evaluation, and outcome-aligned verification for assessing AI-assisted work
description: The article develops a conceptual framework connecting cognitive ownership, mutual evaluation, and selected verification performances so that institutions can make bounded claims about learner capability. It distinguishes product quality, capability demonstrated during assessment, and learning established through change and retention. The framework's contribution is integrative: it specifies relationships among existing ideas within an assessment design and explains how competing evidence should affect decisions. As the author states, these components "support bounded claims about learner capability while preserving legitimate opportunities for AI-assisted work."
requirements: The assessor must explicitly state the claim to be supported and the assistance conditions under which performance is interpreted
constraints: The framework is proposed rather than empirically validated; no validated instrument, established threshold, or demonstrated treatment effect is presented
It concerns capability demonstrated within specified tasks and conditions, and is not a psychological ownership scale, a test of legal authorship, or an instrument for identifying misconduct
target_learners: higher education students in tasks involving analysis, interpretation, design, or professional judgment
target_learning_goals: individual analytical capability under specified assistance conditions
effective collaboration with AI while remaining accountable for consequential decisions
examples: A worked hypothetical graduate leadership-development course illustrates task design, scoring weights, verification with live generative assistance excluded, a transfer variation, and responses to conflicting evidence
key_sources: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957

article_title: Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership
citation: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957
title: Cognitive ownership defined as demonstrated capacity to understand, evaluate, adapt, and accept responsibility for consequential reasoning under stated assistance conditions
description: Cognitive ownership is defined as a task-specific, conditional construct: the learner's demonstrated capacity to understand, evaluate, adapt, and accept responsibility for consequential reasoning represented in assessed work. It is an inference supported by performances, not a directly observed mental state. The article distinguishes product quality, provenance, demonstrated capability, and learning, noting that an AI-use declaration addresses provenance only. The author writes that ownership "names an inference supported by performances" and that the interpretation "should be no broader than the sampled performances justify."
requirements: Assessment must explicitly state the conditions of assistance under which ownership performances are elicited
constraints: The construct is task-specific: competence in judging one task does not establish ownership of different reasoning in another
Competent performance with permitted resources should not be reported as unaided competence unless the assessment supports that interpretation
target_learners: higher education students, particularly adults in applied professional programs
target_learning_goals: accountability for consequential reasoning in assessed work
examples: A student who can explain a choice, identify an error, and adapt the reasoning to a new case provides stronger support for the ownership inference than a student who merely states the work is understood

citation: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957
title: Eight ownership indicators organized into four assessment domains (understanding, epistemic judgment, adaptive performance, reflective accountability)
description: The framework retains eight indicators — explanation, verification, reconstruction, challenge, judgment, transfer, defense, and reflection — organized into four domains: understanding, epistemic judgment, adaptive performance, and reflective accountability. Table 1 pairs each domain with observable evidence and a stated limit of the inference. The author cautions that "the domains and examples are proposed design categories, not a validated scale" and that the grouping is a design proposal, not an empirically established factor structure.
requirements: Evidence and assistance conditions should be aligned with the course outcome and the consequences of the assessment decision
The four domains should not be treated as interchangeable measures that can always compensate for one another
constraints: A short assignment may sample only two domains, whereas a capstone may require broader coverage
Repetition of a familiar account may not establish adaptable understanding; one task does not establish broad competence or long-term retention
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: demonstrating understanding, epistemic judgment, adaptive performance, and reflective accountability in assessed work
examples: For a policy analysis, the student might reconstruct the connection between an intervention, its assumptions, and the expected outcome; for a programming task, trace how a central function handles a problematic input

article_title: Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership
citation: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957
title: Mutual evaluation: independent learner and instructor judgments compared with evidence-based, documented responses to disagreement
description: Mutual evaluation is a structured process in which learner and instructor independently evaluate the same work against shared criteria, compare their reasons, examine discrepancies, and document a warranted response. The instructor retains responsibility for standards and the final decision; reconciliation means accounting for differences, not forcing consensus or averaging ratings. The author stresses that "agreement is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence of ownership; reasoned judgment and corroborated performance provide the relevant support."
requirements: Criteria, permitted assistance, and evidence types are disclosed before submission; students practice applying criteria before evaluative performance carries substantial grading consequences
The learner records an evaluation before receiving the instructor's comments, and the instructor evaluates independently before seeing the student's ratings whenever feasible
constraints: Students may imitate rubric language, generate an insightful self-critique with AI, or agree to avoid conflict; instructors may misread disagreement as resistance, so assessors should score the disciplinary adequacy of reasons
target_learners: higher education students and their instructors
target_learning_goals: evaluative judgment about quality of work
evidence-based reasoning about discrepancies between self- and instructor evaluation
examples: In the worked example, a student rates a readiness matrix highly; the instructor questions whether the case supports the readiness judgments, and the student must identify which entries derive from case evidence and which are provisional assumptions

citation: Solomon Sunday Oyelere. (2026). title: ASTRA Synthetic Benchmark Dataset: an open synthetic trace dataset for collaborative programming evaluation
description: An openly archived synthetic dataset mirroring the ASTRA logging schema, encoding a prespecified between-subjects design across three conditions (alone_tutor, pair_tutor, pair_multiagent) and a bank of 20 short Python tasks. It provides turn-level dialogue traces with speaker roles, task-level artefacts (submitted code, correctness, retries, time-to-correct, verification indicators), and a derived-metrics table with precomputed summaries. The article states it is "best interpreted as simulated evidence that supports benchmarking and method development".

constraints: Synthetic, not observational data about real learners; results support benchmarking and method development, not causal estimates of learning effects
target_learners: Researchers and developers of trace-based evaluation methods for AI-supported collaborative programming
target_learning_goals: Measurement of interaction dynamics, participation balance, reciprocal engagement, and verification behaviours in introductory programming
examples: The dataset encodes 540 participants across three conditions, 360 sessions, and 1440 task episodes over 20 Python tasks

title: ASTRA social–cognitive framework for multi-agent tutoring
description: A framework formalising how social, cognitive, and regulatory information guides multi-agent tutoring in collaborative programming. It models a session as a partially observable multi-agent process in which "ASTRA instantiates the latent state z_t using a structured Cognitive–Affective–Social Model (CASM)" with cognitive, metacognitive, socio-emotional, and group-regulation components. Role-differentiated agents (Tutor, Facilitator, optional Coordinator) condition policies on a belief state over this latent state, and support is framed as optimising a multi-objective reward over task progress, metacognitive quality, and participation-oriented equity proxies.

constraints: The current prototype does not learn policies by optimising the reward; it approximates desirable behaviour via role-specific prompting and scheduling

target_learning_goals: Coordinated cognitive support, metacognitive regulation, and participation-oriented facilitation during collaborative programming

title: Operationalise equity in AI-mediated collaboration as participation balance and reciprocal engagement measurable from traces
description: In collaborative programming with AI support, define equity narrowly as trace-measurable properties of dyadic interaction rather than demographic outcomes. The article states "equity is operationalised specifically as participation balance and reciprocal engagement within dyads, rather than as demographic equity outcomes", captured through turn-share and word-share asymmetries, imbalance indices, peer-referencing, and reciprocal engagement rates. Analyses treat dyads as the substantive unit for participation-balance measures because such constructs are meaningfully defined at the group level.

article_title: A systematic review of the roles of agentic AI in higher education
citation: Simon Baradziej. (2026). A systematic review of the roles of agentic AI in higher education. Social Sciences & Humanities Open. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssaho.2026.103418
title: Six-role taxonomy of agentic AI in higher education
description: The review organises the agentic-AI-in-higher-education literature into a role-based taxonomy derived from thematic synthesis of 48 included studies. As the review states, "six discrete thematic roles for agentic AI in higher education were identified: personalised learning and adaptive tutoring; automated assessment and feedback; teaching assistance and augmentation; administrative and student support; curriculum design and workforce alignment; and research support and academic operations." Roles are not mutually exclusive; Table 5 reports their frequencies (18, 12, 11, 8, 5, and 4 studies respectively).

constraints: Roles are not mutually exclusive in practice; several studies reported systems serving more than one function

target_learning_goals: understanding the roles agentic AI assumes across university functions including teaching, assessment, administration, curriculum, and research

article_title: A systematic review of the roles of agentic AI in higher education
citation: Simon Baradziej. (2026). A systematic review of the roles of agentic AI in higher education. Social Sciences & Humanities Open. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssaho.2026.103418
title: Defining features of agentic AI: autonomy, planning, tool use, and persistent memory
description: The review defines agentic AI as an architectural class distinguished from generative and rule-based AI by intersecting properties. "Agentic AI denotes a class of system architectures rather than a single technology characterised by several intersecting properties. Autonomy is the foundational attribute: the agent executes tasks and makes decisions without requiring human instruction at each step." Additional properties include reactivity, proactivity, learning ability, tool use, memory, and planning. The review operationalised this definition in screening: a study was classified as agentic when its system met at least three of four criteria (autonomy, planning, tool use, persistent memory).
requirements: Classification as agentic requires meeting at least three of the four defining criteria: autonomy, planning, tool use, and persistent memory
constraints: Generative AI lacks goal-directed planning, tool invocation, and persistent memory as first-class features; traditional autonomous systems execute fixed algorithms without adaptive reasoning
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: distinguishing agentic AI from generative and rule-based AI in educational deployments

article_title: Beyond Detection: Redesigning Authentic Assessment in an AI-Mediated World
citation: Kickbusch, S., Ashford-Rowe, K., Kemp, A., Boreland, J., & Huijser, H. (2025). Beyond Detection: Redesigning Authentic Assessment in an AI-Mediated World. Education Sciences, 15(11), 1537. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci15111537
title: Authenticity reconceptualised as a four-dimensional continuum for AI-present assessment
description: The paper reconceptualises authenticity as "a multidimensional continuum rather than a binary", locating it across four intersecting dimensions: task–context alignment with contemporary professional practice, foregrounding of professional judgement and ethics, visibility of process (iteration, critique, rationale), and appropriate use of tools including AI within human decision-making. Different design strategies emphasise different dimensions, and combining strategies strengthens authenticity only when it deepens performance on these dimensions. The appropriate level of authenticity is stage-appropriate across a program of study.
requirements: Assessment tasks must make student judgement and process evident and assessable for a design to count as authentic under this framework
constraints: The framework is conceptual; the authors state the pattern set "invites future empirical evaluation"

target_learning_goals: professional judgement and ethics
critical and ethical use of AI tools
process transparency and justification of decisions
examples: The paper applies the framework to discipline exemplars in engineering and design, education, creative industries, healthcare, business and finance

description: The paper offers discipline-agnostic learning design patterns that position AI as a collaborator rather than a cheating application. Patterns include "tasks that require students to critique, adapt and verify AI outputs", explicit process transparency (prompts, iterations, rationale), and assessable demonstrations of digital discernment and ethical judgement. Patterns are treated as design propositions—named solutions to recurrent problems under AI-present conditions—and are intended to scaffold local adaptation across disciplines.

description: The paper proposes that authenticity should build across a program via a progressive release of complexity. Early-stage units emphasise transparency artefacts such as process logs, prompt records and short oral defences; mid-stage units add collaboration, negotiated briefs and peer review; capstones introduce external stakeholders, open-ended briefs, and negotiated criteria with explicit ethical framing and critical use of digital tools. title: Sharples' embedded system approach for GenAI in distance learning organisations
description: An ecological, systems-level framework, built on Bronfenbrenner's Ecological Systems Theory, for how distance learning organisations should approach GenAI. It treats learners' engagement with AI as influenced by layers of interactions with peers, family, learning materials, tutors, student services, IT support, quality assurance, government regulators and tech companies. The article applies it to organise the six AIDA studies, mapping stakeholders and institutional layers, and lists its elements: "build awareness and leadership support, fostering collaborative cultures, using data for decision-making, and a commitment to continuous learning."

title: AIDA: the Open University's AI Digital Assistant with GraphRAG grounding and a pedagogical knowledge graph
description: AIDA is a human-centred GenAI digital assistant co-developed by the OU's Knowledge Media Institute, Institute of Educational Technology and Digital Services. Unlike generic LLM deployments, "AIDA was explicitly architected to prioritise provenance, transparency, and pedagogical intent": it uses a staged retrieval-augmented generation strategy extended to a GraphRAG architecture grounding all responses in curated OU content, with direct links back to originating resources so students can verify sources. A dedicated Knowledge Graph encodes the learning task, pedagogical approach, AIDA's role, domain, course level and interaction language, enabling scaffolding, reflection prompts, formative feedback and activity generation. It runs on the OU's Azure Enterprise platform, primarily using GPT-4o.

title: Cognitive apprenticeship as a design and analytic framework for AI-delivered scaffolding
description: The article uses cognitive apprenticeship (Collins et al., 1991) both to configure the Aspen chatbot's pedagogical support and to code its responses for analysis. The framework treats six strategies as coordinated rather than isolated moves: "modeling makes expert reasoning visible, coaching provides tailored feedback and guidance as students attempt the task, and scaffolding supplies temporary structured support," while articulation, reflection, and exploration move students toward cognitive and metacognitive control. The pedagogical meaning of any single move depends on how it connects to others in interaction, which motivated Epistemic Network Analysis of AI-student exchanges.
requirements: Support strategies must operate as coordinated forms of connected support rather than isolated moves
constraints: Applying the framework to AI-delivered scaffolding is a relatively new context, allowing examination of where its strategies succeed or break down when enacted by an LLM agent

target_learning_goals: formulating and revising scientific research questions and hypotheses
examples: Aspen was configured to model expert-like reasoning, coach with targeted feedback, scaffold tasks into steps, prompt articulation, support reflection, and encourage exploration across the inquiry cycle

title: Three collaborative engagement patterns explaining group revision trajectories with AI support
description: The article conceptualizes collaborative engagement as how students jointly work with chatbot support in peer discussion as they interpret, evaluate, adapt, and attempt to use it. It distinguishes three patterns: "Model uptake occurs when students treat chatbot input as a resource for joint reasoning"; cognitive offloading occurs when students shift intellectual work to the chatbot by accepting revisions without evaluation; and collaborative impasse occurs when group work stalls because students cannot establish a shared interpretation of the chatbot's input. Together these show whether AI support became a resource for collective reasoning, a substitute for it, or a point of breakdown.

constraints: The same AI response may lead to different revision trajectories depending on how groups make sense of or work around it

citation: Winstone, N. E., Gravett, K., Bearman, M., Noble, C., Jensen, L. X., Jones, A., & Nicola-Richmond, K. (2026). The care-full craft of feedback in an age of generative AI. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 51(5), 911-927. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2643333
title: Feedback as emergent encounters within a process-oriented (rather than information-transmission) view of feedback
description: The paper frames feedback through a process-oriented view that foregrounds learning: feedback is what happens when students make sense of information about performance and use it for improvement, not the transmission of comments. The 'feedback encounter' construct positions feedback as emergent from educator comments, digital technologies, peers, or self-evaluation. The authors argue GenAI tools functioning as automated comment generators risk replicating outdated transmission views, producing 'dangling data' that students do not use meaningfully.
requirements: Institutional integration of GenAI into feedback must start from the understanding that feedback is a situated, iterative, affective, relational process, not comment delivery
constraints: The authors warn that as long as GenAI tools function primarily as automated comment generators, they risk replicating information-centric feedback practices
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: student sense-making and uptake of feedback information for future improvement
examples: Students regularly engaging in feedback encounters with chatbots, which appeal because of ease of access, understandability, and being perceived as less daunting than seeking feedback from educators

title: Nelson's tripartite framework of evaluative judgement (hard, soft, dynamic) adapted to statistical data analysis
description: The study adopts Nelson's (2018) tripartite framework, in which "Nelson distinguishes between three interrelated dimensions of evaluative judgement: hard, soft, and dynamic." Hard judgement is the "critical, accuracy-oriented appraisal of statistical outputs"; soft judgement assesses the value, relevance and significance of findings; dynamic judgement monitors the whole analytical process as iterative. The article redefines all three dimensions for statistical contexts and uses them as the deductive coding template for its thematic analysis.
requirements: Domain-specific adaptation: the article states evaluative judgement is not universally transferable but shaped by disciplinary standards, so the framework requires contextual redefinition per domain.
constraints: The article notes the framework's applicability to statistical data analysis was previously insufficiently explored and treats it as a flexible heuristic rather than a validated instrument for this domain.

title: 10-item self-report questionnaire for critical use of genAI
description: The authors developed a 10-item theory-guided questionnaire mapping critical validation behaviors such as cross-checking outputs and verifying factual accuracy, rated on a 5-point Likert scale. Example items include “I verify whether AI-generated calculations or statistical results are correct” and “I compare genAI responses with other sources or literature.” Internal consistency was acceptable (Cronbach’s α = 0.78), and its positive correlation with need for cognition was taken as preliminary validity evidence.

examples: Administered in a fixed online questionnaire sequence with behavioral measures placed before dispositional measures to minimize priming effects

article_title: A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI
citation: Inie, N., Kristensen, A. M., Misfeldt, M., & Dalsgaard, P. (2026). A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522
title: Three theoretical traditions for studying critical thinking: cognitive-psychological, philosophical, and educational
description: The review organizes critical thinking research into three traditions that differ in focus and methods: the cognitive-psychological tradition, the philosophical tradition, and the educational tradition. The authors describe "the theoretical backgrounds of critical thinking as it is viewed and studied in the cognitive-psychological tradition, the philosophical tradition, and the educational tradition", and use this tripartite framework both to code the 80 reviewed studies and to structure their proposed research agenda for future HCI work.
requirements: Researchers situating a study in a tradition must choose methods and evaluations appropriate to that tradition, as the review's agenda outlines
constraints: The traditions disagree on the role of dispositions, domain specificity, transferability, and the role of criteria, so no single definition spans them
target_learners: HCI researchers studying critical thinking with or about AI
target_learning_goals: Theory-grounded definition, measurement, and study design for critical thinking research
examples: The review's data extraction coded each included study by which theoretical tradition it situates itself in, based on cited theoretical sources or evaluation methods
key_sources: Inie, N., Kristensen, A. M., Misfeldt, M., & Dalsgaard, P. (2026). A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522

article_title: A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI
citation: Inie, N., Kristensen, A. M., Misfeldt, M., & Dalsgaard, P. (2026). A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522
title: Cognitive-psychological account: critical thinking as goal-directed skill involving cognitive skills and strategies, related to fluid intelligence and executive functioning
description: In the cognitive-psychological tradition, "critical thinking is a type of thinking that is goal-directed and involves using cognitive skills and strategies that increase the likelihood of a desirable outcome (Halpern, 2013)". The review links the construct conceptually to fluid intelligence and executive functions, particularly cognitive flexibility, and stresses that it is a trainable skill requiring time and practice. Assessment in this tradition typically uses psychometric multiple-choice tests of skills and dispositions, plus newer performance-based assessments.
requirements: Assessment typically uses validated instruments or controlled laboratory-based studies with a limited number of factors
constraints: Quantitative tests rarely encourage elaborate reflections and multiple solutions to a problem otherwise associated with critical thinking
target_learners: Adults and students whose critical thinking skills and dispositions are assessed or trained
target_learning_goals: Purposeful, reflective judgment; argument analysis; reasoning; problem solving
examples: Standardized tests named in the review include the California Critical Thinking Skills Test with 34 multiple-choice items and the Halpern Critical Thinking Assessment with 25 everyday scenarios

article_title: A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI
citation: Inie, N., Kristensen, A. M., Misfeldt, M., & Dalsgaard, P. (2026). A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522
title: Philosophical tradition: critical thinking as reflective judgment, dialogue, lived experience, and critique of power, inspiring critical and speculative design in HCI
description: The review presents critical thinking as a broader philosophical orientation concerned with cultivating reflective judgment, questioning taken-for-granted assumptions, and articulating values, informed by pragmatism, dialogic perspectives, phenomenology, and critical theory. It notes that "In HCI, this has inspired critical and speculative design, feminist HCI, and value-sensitive design", approaches that make visible the values systems embody and create openings for users to question technologies.
requirements: Communicating context-specific criteria (laws, regulations, norms, or ideals) used for judgment is essential in this tradition
constraints: This tradition treats critical thinking as partly political, oriented toward transforming the conditions in which technologies are designed and used, not only analysis
target_learners: HCI researchers and designers; users of computational systems
target_learning_goals: Reflective judgment; questioning assumptions; articulating values; critique of technological mediation
examples: The review traces pragmatist inquiry from Peirce, James, and Dewey through Schön's reflective practitioner into research-through-design in HCI
key_sources: Inie, N., Kristensen, A. M., Misfeldt, M., & Dalsgaard, P. (2026). A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522

title: Educational tradition: critical thinking as reflection and inquiry, higher-order taxonomic competence, and socially engaged critique
description: The review characterizes the educational tradition by reflection and inquiry traced to Dewey, a taxonomic view of critical thinking as higher-order thinking, and social engagement grounded in critical social theory. It notes that "In Bloom's taxonomy (Bloom, 1956), critical thinking is placed high in the hierarchy of cognitive skills, marking the progression from rote learning and comprehension toward analysis, synthesis, and ultimately evaluation", and describes the related SOLO taxonomy and dispositions that develop over time.
requirements: Mainstream educational assessment ties critical thinking to examinations and grading aligned with specified learning objectives
constraints: Dispositions such as openness and courage to think differently are not simply taught in one or two lessons; they develop over time
target_learners: Students in higher education and cross-national assessments (e.g., 15-year-old PISA participants)
target_learning_goals: Higher-order competence integrating knowledge and skills in sound judgment; learner independence; reflection on justice and social alternatives
examples: The review names international assessments that operationalize critical thinking: PISA creative problem solving, ICILS critical reading, and ICCS democratic knowledge

article_title: Promoting Critical Thinking in Biological Sciences in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: The Role of Higher Education
citation: Papaneophytou, C.; Nicolaou, S.A. (2025). Promoting Critical Thinking in Biological Sciences in the Era of Artificial Intelligence: The Role of Higher Education. Trends High. Educ. 2025, 4, 24. https://doi.org/10.3390/higheredu4020024
title: Critical thinking as purposeful, self-regulatory judgment with cognitive skills and dispositions (Facione Delphi framework and Ennis definition)
description: The review organizes critical thinking around two established definitions. Facione's Delphi Report defines CT as "purposeful, self-regulatory judgment" involving interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, and explanation, plus dispositions such as open-mindedness, inquisitiveness, and truth-seeking. Ennis defines CT as "reasonable reflective thinking focused on deciding what to believe or do" and emphasizes its teachability through direct instruction, practice, and feedback. The review applies these frameworks to AI-mediated learning in biology, arguing students need reflective tendencies to question and ethically evaluate AI-generated information.
requirements: Instruction must embed CT across disciplines through direct instruction, practice, and feedback, as Ennis advocates
constraints: The review notes CT is cultivated through experiential learning rather than direct instruction alone, embodying a lifestyle of active engagement with information
target_learners: undergraduate biological sciences students in higher education
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills and dispositions for scientific inquiry and evaluation of AI-generated information
examples: The review lists Delphi cognitive skills: analysis, inference, evaluation, plus interpretation, explanation, and self-regulation

title: Intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) for STEM and biological sciences education
description: An ITS is "a computer-based learning platform that employs AI algorithms to guide students toward deeper understanding", adjusting content delivery, questions, and feedback to each learner's mastery level and learning style. The review describes AutoTutor's conversational dialogues with animated avatars, newer systems (iTalk2Learn, GIFT, DeepTutor, ASSISTments, deep knowledge tracing systems), and biology-specific tools such as ALEKS, BioTutor, VIPER, and COMET. It reports ITSs have been shown to be effective in STEM subjects and are used in biology, bioinformatics, and other STEM courses.

constraints: The review notes AIEd is an emerging field with lagging applications compared to sectors like applied science and finance
target_learners: university students in biology, bioinformatics, and STEM courses, from STEM fundamentals to advanced computational biology
target_learning_goals: deeper conceptual understanding, reasoning skills, and identification of knowledge gaps through adaptive personalized tutoring
examples: AutoTutor engages physics students in conversational dialogues; BioTutor offers adaptive questioning and scaffolding for cellular biology and genetics topics

title: Interactive science laboratories (ISLs) developing critical thinking through nine mechanisms
description: The review enumerates the ways virtual labs and computer simulation-based labs develop CT among biological science students: problem solving and hypothesis testing, application of theoretical knowledge, decision-making under constraints, development of inquiry-based skills via 'what if' features, enhanced observing and analyzing ability, feedback and reflection, collaboration and communication, integration of cross-disciplinary knowledge, and promoting creativity. Examples include VHEalthlab, Froguts, BioInteractive, SimUText Ecology, CellCraft, and Learn.Genetics. All ISLs provide immediate feedback, which the review calls "a crucial aspect in reflective learning".

constraints: ISLs are positioned as solutions where physical alternatives are unavailable, too costly, or excessively hazardous

citation: Demir, R., & Akar, C. (2025). Transforming Clicks into Critical Thinking: An AI-Based Media Literacy Program for Children. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-6786882/v1
title: AI-integrated 5E learning cycle for critical media literacy in elementary grades
description: An 18-hour instructional pattern that maps each phase of the 5E learning cycle (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate) onto specific AI and digital tools, activities, and national curriculum outcomes. The article states it involved "an 18-hour instructional intervention designed using the 5E learning cycle model—Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate—integrated with AI-based tools to foster critical media literacy among elementary school students." Tools such as ChatGPT, Perplexity AI, Canva AI, and Grammarly were embedded within pedagogical tasks rather than used as standalone applications, and the sequence was aligned with the Turkish Language and Social Studies curricula.
requirements: Alignment with national curriculum outcomes (Turkish Language and Social Studies programs)
Digital tools selected for pedagogical potency and technological accessibility in low-resource settings
constraints: The participating school had a socioeconomically disadvantaged profile, shaping tool choices toward accessible options

target_learning_goals: critical media literacy (reading and writing)
digital citizenship
ethical and reflective media use
examples: Engagement used curated YouTube videos with real-time ChatGPT questioning and Mentimeter word clouds; Elaboration had students create digital posters and slogans with Canva AI and Grammarly and receive peer feedback via Padlet.

title: Hobbs's five-part media literacy model operationalized through participatory culture theory
description: The study's theoretical foundation combines Hobbs's five-domain media literacy framework with Jenkins's participatory culture theory. The article states: "The theoretical foundation of this study draws from Hobbs's (2011) ve-part media literacy model—access, analysis, evaluation, creation, and re ection—stressing learner agency in meaning-making and content creation." This model is operationalized through Jenkins's (2009) Participatory Culture Theory, which sees learners as active contributors in digital spaces rather than mere consumers. In the discussion, the authors report that students demonstrated gains across all five dimensions and that the integration proved "pedagogically coherent and practically viable."
requirements: Instruction that engages learners as active contributors and creators of media content, not only consumers
constraints: The framework was implemented and evaluated in a single fourth-grade setting in Turkey; the authors note the sample size and geographic scope may limit generalizability

title: Joughin's six-dimension taxonomy characterizes oral assessments
description: The article presents a taxonomy of oral assessments along six dimensions: primary content type, interaction, authenticity, structure, examiners, and orality. It also distinguishes two qualities oral assessments can measure: "the student's oral skills in communication, and the second is the command of the content as demonstrated through the oral medium." The article uses this taxonomy to show oral assessments vary widely in form, from presentation to dialogue, and that educators' design choices along these dimensions determine what the assessment measures.

oral communication skills

title: Implement oral assessments with clear guidelines, rubrics, question banks, and student-facing support to reduce anxiety and protect fairness
description: The article's practical recommendations hold that oral assessments work well only when carefully prepared: students "should be given information about the schedule and assessment criteria beforehand and have some experience of the format," assessments should use a clear mastery-level rubric with a bank of questions linked to learning objectives, and educators should provide student-facing support such as recorded mock assessments and no-stakes practice to reduce anxiety, particularly for high school and undergraduate students.

reduced test anxiety
academic integrity

article_title: Game-Based and Gamified Robotics Education: A Comparative Systematic Review and Design Guidelines
citation: Syed Tanzim Mubarrat, Byung-Cheol Min, Tianyu Shao, E. Cho Smith, Bedrich Benes, Alejandra J. Magana, Christos Mousas, and Dominic Kao. (2026). Game-Based and Gamified Robotics Education: A Comparative Systematic Review and Design Guidelines. Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791338
title: Approach–context–pedagogy coupling framework for game-based and gamified robotics education
description: The review's organizing framework holds that instructional approach (GBL vs. gamification), learning context (formal vs. informal), and pedagogical model are coupled in robotics education: "GBL more prevalent in informal settings, while gamification dominated formal classrooms" and gamification "favored project-based learning". The framework maps three dominant pedagogies — experiential learning, project-based learning, and constructivist learning — onto approaches and contexts, with formal classrooms leaning toward PBL-driven designs and informal settings favoring experiential approaches with higher proportions of constructivist elements.
requirements: Coding of studies requires classifying approach (using Deterding et al. and Sailer and Homner definitions), learning context (based on the intervention rather than the evaluation design), and pedagogical model for each study.
constraints: The association is descriptive of the 2014–2025 corpus of 95 studies; the review reports it as an observed pattern with χ² tests, not as a causal account.
target_learners: K-12 through graduate learners in formal and informal robotics settings
target_learning_goals: robotics-related skills including programming, software development, and understanding of robotic systems
examples: The review's 2×2 contingency analyses showed approach × context was significant (χ²(1)=14.16, p<0.001, Cramer's V = 0.37) and PBL was more frequent in gamified studies (χ²(1)=6.76, p=.009).

article_title: GenAI Use and GenAI-Assisted Learning Procrastination in University Students: The Roles of Planned Behavior Constructs and Learning GenAI Anxiety
citation: Li Zilin, Huang Jiali, Cui Zhaodi. (2026). GenAI Use and GenAI-Assisted Learning Procrastination in University Students: The Roles of Planned Behavior Constructs and Learning GenAI Anxiety. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071256
title: GenAI-assisted learning procrastination as a TPB-based intention–behavior gap construct distinct from deliberate non-use
description: The article extends the Theory of Planned Behavior to GenAI-assisted learning by defining GenAI-assisted learning procrastination (GALP) as "the unnecessary delay in initiating or completing the use of GenAI to support learning tasks, despite holding a genuine intention to use the technology". Within this framework, attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control shape intention, which relates to procrastination, while learning GenAI anxiety acts as a boundary condition on the intention–procrastination link. The authors explicitly position this as "a contextual extension of TPB rather than a fundamental theoretical breakthrough".
requirements: The focal behavior must be clearly specified so that attitude, norm, control, intention, and outcome refer to the same target behavior, as the article states.
constraints: The framework is offered as initial empirical evidence from a cross-sectional design; findings are conditional associations rather than causal evidence, and generalizability requires further investigation.
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: timely completion of GenAI-assisted learning tasks such as daily assignments, final-term assignments, and examination preparation
examples: The study operationalized all TPB constructs with self-developed scales referencing the focal behavior of GenAI-assisted learning task completion and tested the model with path analysis among 1243 Chinese university students.
key_sources: Li Zilin, Huang Jiali, Cui Zhaodi. (2026). GenAI Use and GenAI-Assisted Learning Procrastination in University Students: The Roles of Planned Behavior Constructs and Learning GenAI Anxiety. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071256

article_title: GenAI Use and GenAI-Assisted Learning Procrastination in University Students: The Roles of Planned Behavior Constructs and Learning GenAI Anxiety
citation: Li Zilin, Huang Jiali, Cui Zhaodi. (2026). GenAI Use and GenAI-Assisted Learning Procrastination in University Students: The Roles of Planned Behavior Constructs and Learning GenAI Anxiety. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071256
title: Treat timely GenAI use as distinct from responsible use, and distinguish deliberate non-use from procrastination
description: The article cautions educators and researchers against equating low GenAI-assisted learning procrastination with good learning. It states that "Lower GALP—that is, more timely use of GenAI—should not be equated with responsible or effective GenAI use", because timely use may reflect habitual or superficial engagement. It also distinguishes procrastination from reasoned avoidance: "Such intentional non-use is qualitatively distinct from procrastination (i.e., delay despite intention)". Designs and measures should therefore capture the intention–behavior gap rather than mere frequency of use.
requirements: Measures of GenAI-related procrastination must capture unnecessary delay despite genuine intention, not general non-use or deliberate avoidance.
constraints: The article's GALP measure did not capture intentional non-use, so the negative use–procrastination association applies only to delay despite intention, not to pedagogically motivated avoidance.
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: responsible and timely use of generative AI in learning tasks
examples: The authors note students may deliberately limit or avoid GenAI to cultivate independent problem-solving skills or comply with academic integrity policies, decisions the GALP measure did not capture.
