article_title: A Hybrid Reasoning Framework for Artificial Intelligence Assessment Rubric Generation in Human and Automated Contexts: Evidence from an Undergraduate Programming Course
citation: Pedro C. Mendonça, Filipe Quintal, Mário Figueiredo, Karolina Baras, Fábio Mendonça. (2026). A hybrid reasoning framework for artificial intelligence assessment rubric generation in human and automated contexts: Evidence from an undergraduate programming course. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence 11 (2026) 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100663
title: HARMOGEN-R: a two-stage hybrid framework for AI rubric generation with reasoning-enhanced generation and low-temperature synthesis
description: HARMOGEN-R (Hybrid Assessment Rubric Model Generation with Reasoning) is a two-stage rubric generation pipeline. In stage one, reasoning-capable LLMs generate several candidate rubrics under a high temperature setting "to promote variation in criterion formulation and scoring structure"; in stage two, a synthesis model from the same provider family consolidates the candidates into a single rubric at low temperature (T = 1.0 for generation, T = 0.1 for synthesis). It supports a structured mode, in which predefined criteria and point allocations from the human baseline are supplied, and a free-form mode, in which the model defines criteria autonomously. Implemented with OpenAI (o3-mini, GPT-4o) and DeepSeek (deepseek-r1-distill-llama-70b, deepseek-chat) families, it produced four AI rubric variants per assessment for comparison against a human-created baseline.
requirements: Access to hosted API endpoints for both generation and evaluation stages; each initial generation prompt includes the assessment question, an exemplar correct response, two generic rubric examples, and explicit score-distribution instructions
constraints: The study states its benchmark human rubric's role should be interpreted in operational rather than absolute terms, since no external formal validation of rubric quality was performed
All models were accessed through hosted API endpoints; no model was deployed on institutional infrastructure
target_learners: Undergraduate computer engineering students in first-year programming courses
target_learning_goals: Formative assessment of open-ended programming and short-answer responses in data structures and algorithms
examples: For each rubric condition the initial model generated three independent candidate rubrics, merged during synthesis into a single final version, across three formative programming assignments

title: IntroEduAI platform for assessment collection and parallel human/LLM evaluation
description: IntroEduAI is a web-based platform, originally developed for prior research on automated formative assessment, that served as the technical infrastructure for assessment collection and automated evaluation in this study. It implements a Model-View-Controller architecture using Flask with REST API endpoints for LLM integration, and supports rubric upload and configuration, student response collection, parallel human and LLM-based evaluation, and data aggregation for export. Automated evaluation uses few-shot prompting with rubric integration; for text questions it adds Retrieval-Augmented Generation via LangChain and ChromaDB over course materials (1000-character chunks with 200-character overlap, top-5 retrieval), while code questions are evaluated without external retrieval.

constraints: Across the five rubric conditions the question text, exemplar responses, and retrieval configuration were identical, so the rubric was the only prompt component that varied

article_title: A Hybrid Collaborative Filtering and Knowledge Graph-Based Cross-Domain Recommendation Method for Multimodal Teaching Resources
citation: Bin Liu, Xiaoli Sun, Jia Song. (2026). A hybrid collaborative filtering and knowledge graph-based cross-domain recommendation method for multimodal teaching resources. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100678
title: Pedagogically structured knowledge graph with four instructional dimensions and ability/progress-aware CF fusion
description: The framework organizes teaching resources, concepts, and learner attributes in a knowledge graph whose relations fall into three categories (content/domain, skill/goal, and pedagogical-alignment relations). Each resource entity is decomposed into four instructional dimensions — teaching context, cognitive level, technological feature, and cultural adaptability — whose embeddings yield dimension-specific cosine similarities combined into user-dependent semantic similarity via attention weights. An adaptive fusion coefficient λu, computed from learner ability (LAE), progress (LPT), and interest (IPI) indices, balances semantic and behavioral scores so that "A learner with higher ability, more stable progress and stronger overall interest receives a larger λu". The recommendation process runs from explicit instructional requirements through KG semantic expansion, CF refinement, and score fusion.
requirements: Resource metadata normalized into a unified schema and mapped into the knowledge graph
Learner interaction logs with view duration, completion ratio, and click signals to construct IPI, LAE, and LPT indices
Explicit instructional requirements (domain, skills, difficulty, modality, cultural preferences) encoded as a query vector
constraints: The schema is kept fixed across all experiments and can be extended when additional pedagogical metadata become available
All evaluations are on historical interaction logs; reported improvements reflect recommendation quality rather than educational or learning effectiveness
target_learners: English language learners in classroom, blended, and self-directed study scenarios
target_learning_goals: Matching multimodal English teaching resources to learner ability, progress, and instructional requirements across domains
examples: Resources carry metadata such as the example 'Past Tense in Narratives' mapped to triples like 'aligned with cognitive level Apply' and 'suitable for context Self-study'

article_title: Positioning Generative AI in EFL Peer Feedback: Training Feedback Literacy and Enabling Uptake in Speaking Classes
citation: Bradley Irwin and Theron Muller. (2026). Positioning Generative AI in EFL Peer Feedback: Training Feedback Literacy and Enabling Uptake in Speaking Classes. Educ. Sci. 2026, 16, 544. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16040544
title: GenAI as Trainer and Synthesizer: two complementary roles in EFL speaking peer feedback
description: The article proposes a theory-informed design framework positioning generative AI in two constrained roles within L2 speaking peer feedback. The Trainer supports feedback givers through "calibration with exemplars, rubric-guided practice, and feedback-on-feedback", while the Synthesizer supports recipients by aggregating peer input into concise, actionable guidance linked to criteria and learning goals. The roles are design patterns, not validated systems, targeting the twin bottlenecks of feedback production and uptake.
requirements: Teachers remain in the loop to approve prompts, audit outputs, and integrate GenAI-generated, teacher-curated artifacts into instruction
constraints: The design patterns' scope "excludes automated grading, unsupervised private tutoring, and high-stakes decisions"
The account is conceptual and "does not present new empirical data"; the expectations "remain provisional and require empirical testing"

target_learning_goals: Peer feedback quality and uptake in L2 speaking
Feedback literacy development
examples: The Trainer revises global comments like "Nice voice" into criterion-referenced diagnoses with time-coded evidence; the Synthesizer drafts uptake reports grouping comments by criterion with prioritized themes

article_title: Can ChatGPT Replace the Teacher in Assessment? A Review of Research on the Use of Large Language Models in Grading and Providing Feedback
citation: Marcin Jukiewicz and Michał Wyrwa. (2026). Can ChatGPT Replace the Teacher in Assessment? A Review of Research on the Use of Large Language Models in Grading and Providing Feedback. Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 680. https://doi.org/10.3390/app16020680
title: Three-role taxonomy of GenAI operationalization in grading workflows: automatic grader, grader-plus-feedback-generator, and co-grader
description: The review organizes how GenAI is operationalized in assessment workflows by the role the model plays. In most studies AI acted as "an automatic grader, independently assigning points or grades to student responses with minimal human involvement"; in others it both assigned a score and generated feedback on strengths and weaknesses; and in co-grading it suggested a grade the educator could verify. The taxonomy is paired with a task-type distribution (essays in 16 studies, short written answers in 11) and a prompting characterization: GenAI was typically guided using rubric- or exemplar-based prompts, with 32 studies including a scoring rubric or sample correct answer.
requirements: Deployment requires deciding the model's role (automatic grader, grader plus feedback generator, or co-grader) and supplying rubric- or exemplar-based prompts.
constraints: The taxonomy derives from the 42 studies reviewed, published 2023–2025, most in higher education.
target_learners: students across educational levels, from primary school through higher education
target_learning_goals: accurate grading and feedback on student written work, short answers, code, and calculation tasks
examples: The review counts 20 studies using API integration and 16 entering data manually into the ChatGPT interface.

title: Deploy GenAI grading as an assistive tool within a hybrid, human-in-the-loop framework rather than as an autonomous teacher replacement
description: The review concludes that LLMs can support teachers by automating routine grading and generating rapid feedback at scale, but "they cannot fully replace human judgment, especially in high-stakes or subjective assessments." GenAI-based scoring systems should be integrated within a hybrid, human-in-the-loop framework that maintains transparency, oversight, fairness, and adaptability, with human educators validating grades and AI-produced feedback. Oversight is described as especially critical for high-stakes grading contexts and wherever subjective interpretation is required.
requirements: Human oversight to catch errors, address bias and transparency concerns, and provide contextual and empathetic judgment; institutional safeguards.
constraints: The review states current LLMs struggle with errors, algorithmic biases, loss of coherence, and lack full contextual understanding.

citation: Kostopoulos, G., Gkamas, V., Rigou, M., & Kotsiantis, S. (2025). Agentic AI in Education: State of the Art and Future Directions. IEEE Access. https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2025.3620473

description: The review proposes an organizing taxonomy for educational agentic AI built on three axes. The first axis covers pedagogical roles (tutor, coach/mentor, companion, instructor's assistant, curriculum planner); the second orders systems from reactive to adaptive, proactive and collaborative agents by autonomy; the third distinguishes text-based, graphical/avatar, embodied and multimodal agents. As the authors state, "we propose a taxonomy based on three axes: pedagogical role, autonomy level and embodiment", summarized in their Figure 2.
requirements: Systems are classified by stated purpose, decision-making flexibility and interface modality, so classification requires documented system behavior on each axis
constraints: The taxonomy classifies existing and developing systems as described by the survey; it is a descriptive scheme, not an empirically validated instrument

target_learning_goals: personalized instruction, self-regulated learning, collaborative problem-solving

title: Six-criterion operational checklist for classifying a system as agentic
description: The review operationalizes agentic AI with a checklist of six verifiable criteria covering autonomy, reasoning, memory, planning, goal-directed interaction and related capabilities. A system counts as agentic if it meets at least four criteria: "In this survey, a system is considered agentic if it satisfies at least four of these criteria." The threshold is intended to exclude reactive chatbots while accommodating diverse architectures; the authors give the example of a tutoring system that plans multi-turn lessons, remembers learner progress, triggers prompts autonomously and provides formative feedback.

title: Explainable-by-design framework coupling dual-lens hierarchical attention, trust-gated inference, and on-the-spot explanation generation
description: The framework is an LLM-based teacher assessment architecture in which trustworthiness and explainability are built into inference rather than appended afterward. It couples "a global lens aligned to curriculum standards and a local lens aligned to subject-specific rubrics" with a Trust-Gated Inference module combining Monte-Carlo-dropout calibration and adversarial debiasing, and an On-the-Spot Explanation generator that shares the same fused representation and predicted score used for decision making, so explanations are decision-consistent and curriculum-anchored. Trust gating exposes uncertainty and bias alerts and can output Reject with reason.

constraints: Experiments primarily evaluate text and ASR transcripts due to dataset availability, not full multimodal input

It conceptualizes AI literacy as "a holistic construct comprising cognitive, technical, ethical, and affective dimensions", entailing both the capacity to use and build AI systems and the critical disposition to question their design, purpose, and societal impact. title: AI-SEE: a pedagogical framework integrating AI across the engineering curriculum as a cognitive scaffold and system-optimization resource
description: AI-SEE (Artificial Intelligence-Integrated Sustainable Engineering Education) is a pedagogical framework structured around an input-process-output logic, in which institutional conditions, learner characteristics, and external contexts feed a pedagogical process of four pillars whose intended outputs are sustainability-related knowledge, attitudes, and behavioral orientations. citation: Mengjia Liu, Harwati Hashim, Nur Ainil Sulaiman. (2026). A systematic review of emerging technology applications for teaching English as a foreign language across different educational levels. Educational Research Review 52 (2026) 100795. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100795
title: Five effective pedagogical practices for integrating emerging technologies into EFL curricula: personalization, authentic contexts, collaborative learning, multimodal integration, and cultural responsiveness
description: The review's thematic synthesis, using a hybrid deductive–inductive coding procedure in NVivo 14, identified "five key areas of effective practice for integrating emerging technologies into EFL curricula." The five parent themes were derived deductively from SLA-grounded affordances literature, while fifteen sub-themes (e.g., "self-regulated pacing," "anxiety-reducing low-stakes practice," "cultural identity preservation") were refined or generated inductively from the 33 studies (inter-coder reliability κ = 0.81). The review presents this as "an empirically grounded framework for technology implementation decisions" and stresses that effective integration is fundamentally pedagogical rather than technological.

constraints: Cultural responsiveness was less frequently documented in the corpus, representing a gap the review notes warrants further investigation

target_learning_goals: English language proficiency across speaking, writing, reading, listening, vocabulary, and grammar
engagement and motivation in technology-mediated language learning
examples: Personalization spanned AI speech recognition for primary phonics (Hu, 2021), self-regulated mobile grammar systems (Wang et al., 2021), and AWE feedback at tertiary level (Yildiz & Kuru Gonen, 2024)

citation: Mengjia Liu, Harwati Hashim, Nur Ainil Sulaiman. (2026). A systematic review of emerging technology applications for teaching English as a foreign language across different educational levels. Educational Research Review 52 (2026) 100795. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100795
title: Five categories of implementation challenges for emerging technologies in TEFL: technical infrastructure, teacher preparation, time constraints, student adaptation, and resource limitations
description: The review's hybrid deductive–inductive analysis of RQ4 data yielded "Five categories of implementation challenges emerged from the analysis, each with level-specific manifestations and proposed solutions." Technical infrastructure problems (connectivity, device compatibility) were acute in primary and secondary settings in developing countries; teacher preparation gaps included technical operation, pedagogical strategies, assessment design, and troubleshooting; time constraints were sharpest in settings with rigid curricula and high-stakes examinations; student adaptation difficulties affected younger learners and those with limited prior technology exposure; and hardware/software costs constrained resource-limited contexts. The review concludes that "practical implementation barriers evolve more slowly and require sustained, systemic institutional and policy attention rather than one-time investments."
requirements: Sustained, systemic institutional and policy attention rather than one-time investments
constraints: Infrastructure challenges persisted across the review period (2015–2024), suggesting technological advancement alone does not resolve access inequities
target_learners: EFL learners and teachers at primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, particularly in developing-country contexts

article_title: A Systematic Review of Emerging Technology Applications for Teaching English as a Foreign Language Across Different Educational Levels
citation: Mengjia Liu, Harwati Hashim, Nur Ainil Sulaiman. (2026). A systematic review of emerging technology applications for teaching English as a foreign language across different educational levels. Educational Research Review 52 (2026) 100795. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100795
title: Operational definition of emerging technologies in TEFL: novel, rapidly adopted tools and pedagogical approaches aligned with SLA theory, with context-dependent and temporally dynamic emerging status
description: The review synthesizes prior definitions (Veletsianos, 2010; Rotolo et al., 2015; the New Media Consortium's one-to-five-year horizon) into an operational definition: "Emerging technologies in TEFL are innovative tools, platforms, or pedagogical approaches that have the potential to significantly transform language teaching and learning practices." The definition characterizes these technologies by novelty within specific educational contexts, rapid adoption rates, alignment with second language acquisition theories, potential for enhancing authentic communication and cultural understanding, and the co-presence of promising impact and implementation uncertainties. It treats 'emerging' status as dynamic, context-dependent, and typically spanning a one-to-five-year period of initial integration and evaluation. This definition serves as the conceptual foundation for the review's inclusion criteria and technology categorization.
requirements: Alignment with second language acquisition theories
potential for enhancing authentic communication and cultural understanding
constraints: The 'emerging' status of technologies is dynamic and context-dependent, varying across regions and institutional settings
target_learners: EFL learners across primary, secondary, and tertiary education globally
target_learning_goals: Principled categorization and evaluation of technologies for English language teaching
examples: The definition enabled a principled yet inclusive approach to technology categorization across diverse global TEFL contexts in the review's eligibility criteria

title: Four-question framework positioning LLMs as a systemic lever for reforming higher education teaching, curriculum alignment, feedback and assessment
description: The review organizes its synthesis around four research questions: how LLMs can "foster critical thinking, collaborative skills, and problem-solving", reduce the gap between theoretical curricula and real-world skills, deliver personalized feedback in large courses, and support assessment development. It frames LLM effects as "transversal, influencing multiple dimensions of higher education systems", positioning the technology as addressing persistent problems: memorization-focused teaching, misaligned curricula, delayed feedback and limited skill development in large classes. article_title: A Framework for Evaluation of Large Language Models in Essay Assessment: Reliability, Alignment, and Causal Reasoning
citation: Tongxi Liu, Luyao Ye, Wei Yan. (2026). A framework for evaluation of large language models in essay assessment: Reliability, alignment, and causal reasoning. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100565
title: Three-layered assessment framework for evaluating LLMs in essay assessment
description: A framework the article operationalizes to evaluate LLM essay scoring along three layers: consistency and reliability evaluation, human-LLM alignment analysis, and causal discovery analysis. Consistency assesses whether a model "maintains stable relative rankings of essay quality across repeated runs using identical prompts", while reliability captures absolute agreement of numeric outputs across runs; alignment serves as a measure of external validity against expert judgments; and causal discovery identifies "causal relationships between linguistic features and predicted scores". The article applies it to five LLMs scoring 60 higher-education essays.
requirements: Repeated independent scoring runs under identical prompts to separate stochastic variation from systematic behavior
Expert human ratings on standardized rubrics as an external validity benchmark
Linguistic feature extraction with theoretically grounded domain classification for the causal layer
constraints: Developed and applied to long English essays by non-native speakers in higher education, scored on the IELTS Task 2 rubric
target_learners: Higher education students, specifically non-native English speakers whose long essays are assessed
target_learning_goals: Reliable, valid, and interpretable automated assessment of extended academic writing
examples: Applied to GPT-4.1, Llama 4 Maverick, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4, and DeepSeek R1 scoring 60 essays three times each against three calibrated expert raters

title: Validate LLM scoring systems for reliability before classroom deployment and adopt predefined reliability thresholds for high-stakes use
description: The article argues that just as human raters undergo calibration and moderation, LLMs should be empirically validated for reliability before classroom deployment. It recommends technical safeguards — "multi-run averaging, deterministic inference (via fixed random seeds or low-temperature decoding), and ensemble-based calibration" — as algorithmic counterparts to inter-rater moderation, and institutional adoption of predefined reliability thresholds (e.g., ICC ≥ 0.90) as operational standards for high-stakes assessments.

Technical safeguards such as multi-run averaging or deterministic inference
Institutionally adopted reliability thresholds for high-stakes contexts

target_learning_goals: Fair, trustworthy, and reproducible automated writing assessment
examples: The article proposes ICC ≥ 0.90 as an operational standard for high-stakes AI scoring, mirroring the human benchmark established in its own data

article_title: Fostering self-regulated learning through adaptive learning technology: A differentiated perspective on the role of feedback
citation: Mathias Mejeh, Yvonne M. Fromm (2026). Fostering self-regulated learning through adaptive learning technology: A differentiated perspective on the role of feedback. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102394
title: Feedback as a phase-sensitive mechanism within SRL cycles
description: The article theorizes adaptive feedback not as a uniform external input but as a mechanism whose function depends on where in the SRL cycle it is taken up. Building on the self-regulation process model (Schmitz & Wiese, 2006), it links directive feedback to translating forethought into regulatory behavior, informative feedback to monitoring and calibration during reflection, and transformative feedback to connecting post-actional reflection to subsequent forethought, while stressing these alignments are not exclusive to one phase. The study "provides a basis for theorizing feedback as a phase-sensitive mechanism within SRL cycles, rather than as a uniform external input."
requirements: Feedback uptake must be linked to phase-specific SRL appraisals to determine when different feedback functions apply
constraints: The article's own results showed moderating effects were limited and inconsistent, so the mechanism's benefits are conditional rather than uniform
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning across pre-actional, actional, and post-actional phases
examples: In studybuddy, strategy videos operationalized directive feedback, the dashboard informative feedback, and combined use transformative feedback, with uptake recorded weekly from log files

title: studybuddy adaptive learning technology with personalized SRL strategies and dashboard
description: studybuddy is the adaptive learning technology implemented over eight weeks in a university stochastics course, through which 194 students accessed weekly homework and SRL-support features. It "comprises four components aiming to assist students' SRL: an automated feedback system, a digital dashboard, personalized SRL strategies, and a planning tool." When a pre- or post-task self-report fell below a threshold, the system recommended an SRL strategy video; the dashboard visualized weekly responses as individualized progress curves and functioned as an indirect informational feedback source encouraging autonomous adjustment.
requirements: Adaptation was rule-based, triggered by self-report thresholds; engagement with the prompted videos and dashboard was voluntary
constraints: The dashboard did not provide prescriptive feedback; rule-based thresholds were limited in capturing fine-grained temporal dynamics of SRL over cycles

title: Embed ALT feedback into instructional design and adapt feedback type to learners' cognitive, motivational, and emotional resources
description: The article recommends that adaptive learning technology not stand apart from teaching but be woven into course design with explicit expectations for feedback engagement, and that the type of feedback offered be matched to learners' current (meta-)cognitive, motivational, and emotional resources. Because comprehensive feedback did not necessarily improve SRL and some interactions were negative, timing and uptake are treated as key boundary conditions. The authors state that "ALTs should not be deployed as stand-alone feedback add-ons but should be embedded into instructional design through clear guidance on when and how students are expected to engage with feedback."

constraints: Findings should be interpreted with caution due to the marginal significance of several effects; feedback effectiveness is context-dependent

citation: Tatyana Ivanova. (2026). Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning. Mathematics 2026, 14, 808. https://doi.org/10.3390/math14050808
title: Hybrid layered knowledge base architecture for personalized e-learning built on systems of mapped ontologies, rules, and data-driven techniques
description: The article proposes a conceptual model of a layered, hybrid knowledge base architecture grounded in mathematical logic for intelligent educational systems. It extends the classical four-model ITS architecture by replacing each single ontology with systems of mapped ontologies and adding storage for procedural knowledge as rules, non-crisp knowledge via fuzzy or probabilistic DL extensions, and implicit knowledge via learning analytics and machine learning. The article states it "differs from most other research in this field by proposing systems of mapped ontologies in the place of every single ontology."
requirements: Requires mapped ontologies, rules, and statistics-based technologies to be integrated so that DL-based and transparent rule-based reasoning can support tutoring decisions and learning path generation
constraints: The number of layers and ontologies in every layer cannot be strictly specified; it depends on every specific implementation
target_learners: learners in intelligent educational systems and intelligent tutoring systems across formal education and professional training
target_learning_goals: personalized and adaptive tutoring, learning path generation and recommendation, knowledge tracing
examples: The architecture incorporates the four main models of the typical ontology-based ITS (domain, student, tutoring, user interface) with mapped ontology systems in each

title: Classification of educational knowledge for personalization: declarative/procedural, explicit/implicit, and crisp/fuzzy/probabilistic
description: The article classifies the knowledge needed to organize personalized intelligent tutoring along several axes: by semantics into declarative and procedural knowledge; by how it is learned and expressed into explicit and implicit knowledge; and by certainty into crisp, fuzzy, and probabilistic knowledge. It argues that probabilistic and fuzzy knowledge are frequent in education because learning is uncertain and variable, and that implicit knowledge is typically acquired informally and extracted through statistical and machine learning approaches. The article states that "Tutoring domains involving real-world data, human behavior, or inference almost always contain not only crisp but also fuzzy or probabilistic knowledge."
requirements: Knowledge models supporting personalization must enable representation of both declarative and procedural knowledge, both implicit and explicit knowledge, and crisp, vague, and probabilistic knowledge
constraints: Technologies for modeling non-crisp knowledge are not mature, per the article
target_learners: learners in intelligent educational systems
target_learning_goals: effective support of personalization through appropriate knowledge representation
examples: Fuzzy learner knowledge includes partial mastery or overlapping skill levels; motivation, engagement, and confidence are represented as fuzzy concepts

description: The article organizes tutoring domain knowledge as a layered system of ontologies: an upper-level domain ontology for very general concepts and alignment, cross-domain ontologies for interoperability across related subjects, core domain ontologies for generic subject concepts, educational domain ontologies for single tutoring subjects (coarse-grained for curriculum planning and fine-grained for performance-based personalized learning), and task-oriented sub-domain ontologies such as assessment-linked, competency-based, prerequisite, and problem-solving ontologies. The article states that layered systems let "complex knowledge can be represented in a well-structured, modular, and evolvable way, separating general from specific entities."

title: Combine ontologies with sequencing rules, learning analytics, and machine learning for effective personalized learning
description: The article argues that ontologies alone are insufficient for personalized learning because they are mostly static or slowly evolving and have limited handling of uncertainty, while personalization needs dynamic adaptation based on real-time learner behavior. It therefore recommends combining ontologies with teaching strategies expressed as sequencing rules, learning analytics to infer and predict learner needs, and machine learning techniques for extracting and storing implicit knowledge. The article states: "For effective personalized learning, ontologies should be combined with: teaching strategies, expressed effectively by sequencing rules; learning analytics (to infer and predict learner needs); machine learning techniques for extracting and storing implicit knowledge."

constraints: Ontologies are mostly static or slowly evolving and have limited handling of uncertainty, per the article

The article states that "Balancing expressiveness and computational complexity is one of the core design decisions in DL ontologies."

article_title: Peer and AI Review + Reflection (PAIRR): A Human-Centered Approach to Formative Assessment
citation: Sperber, Lisa; MacArthur, Marit; Minnillo, Sophia; Stillman, Nicholas; Whithaus, Carl. (2025). Peer and AI Review + Reflection (PAIRR): A human-centered approach to formative assessment. Computers and Composition 76. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compcom.2025.102921
title: PAIRR: peer review followed by rubric-driven AI feedback plus structured critical reflection
description: PAIRR is a formative-assessment sequence in which students draft, give and receive peer review, then prompt ChatGPT for feedback using an adapted prompt plus the instructor's rubric, and finally critically assess both kinds of feedback and reflect on revisions. Students are tasked with assessing AI feedback on their drafts, rather than taking it at face value, and determining if and how that feedback aligns with their writing goals. AI feedback comes after a complete draft to avoid interfering with drafting cognition and to discourage overreliance.

Scaffolded peer review prior to AI feedback
Guided practice and readings on ethical AI use and acknowledgment
constraints: Implemented and studied with ChatGPT 3.5 one-shot feedback, though the authors state the approach can be used with any AI tool
AI may reflect linguistic and cultural biases present in LLM training data

target_learning_goals: Improving drafts through formative feedback
Developing AI literacy and critical evaluation of AI outputs
Exercising writerly agency and metacognitive revision planning
examples: In the study, students in 10 writing and three large WI courses completed readings on AI and ethics, drafted, exchanged peer review, prompted ChatGPT with the rubric, assessed both feedback types, and revised with reflections on each source's role

article_title: A Posthumanist Approach to AI Literacy
citation: Zhaozhe Wang, Chaoran Wang. (2025). A posthumanist approach to AI literacy. Computers and Composition 76 (2025) 102933. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compcom.2025.102933
title: A posthumanist approach to AI literacy: meaning emerges through human-AI intra-actions
description: This framework reframes AI literacy away from anthropocentric models in which humans use AI tools toward meaning-making. Drawing on Barad, Latour, Bennett, and Deleuze and Guattari, it holds that agency is distributed and enacted through intra-actions of human agents and non-human actants. As the authors put it, it "frames AI literacy as an understanding of how meaning emerges through human-AI intra-actions." Literacy with AI is thus relational work rather than transactional work, extending the New Literacy Studies' situated-practices view to include AI actancy.
requirements: Educators and students must develop meta-awareness of AI-mediated ways of meaning-making across AI-charged, AI-free, and in-between contexts
constraints: The authors caution against corporate anthropomorphism, e.g. discourse that AI boosts productivity, which shapes a transactional view of human-AI relations
target_learners: language and literacy students
multilingual postsecondary writers
target_learning_goals: critical AI literacy
understanding distributed agency in AI-mediated meaning-making
examples: The authors analyzed two students' AI-assisted writing through the lenses of conceptualization, positionality, intra-actions, and evaluation of AI affordances

article_title: A Posthumanist Approach to AI Literacy
citation: Zhaozhe Wang, Chaoran Wang. (2025). A posthumanist approach to AI literacy. Computers and Composition 76 (2025) 102933. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compcom.2025.102933
title: Assemblage and rhizomaticity as posthumanist concepts for AI-mediated literacy
description: The article deploys Deleuze and Guattari's assemblage and rhizomaticity, elaborated by Bennett, Leander and Burriss, and Sherman et al., to explain how posthumanist relationality plays out in AI-mediated literacy. An assemblage is "always temporarily formed as diverse human agents, nonhuman actants, discourses, and signs come into contact and relate to one another," and assemblages operate rhizomatically, shifting and reconfiguring in any direction. Literacy practices are conceived as forming assemblages in which AI may partake, co-producing meaning with human writers.
requirements: Analysis must attend to language as part of the assemblage, since language mediates human-AI relational dynamics and may reinforce linguistic hierarchies in multilingual contexts
target_learners: literacy researchers and educators
postsecondary writers
target_learning_goals: understanding co-produced meaning in human-AI composing
examples: The authors describe a student's ongoing dialogues with an AI chatbot in which ideas build on AI-generated texts while AI adapts to the student's inputs

article_title: Preservice Early Childhood Educators' Engagement with Generative AI in Science Activity Design: The Case of Magnetism
citation: George Efthimiou, Katerina Plakitsi. (2026). Preservice Early Childhood Educators' Engagement with Generative AI in Science Activity Design: The Case of Magnetism. https://www.mdpi.com/journal/educationsciences
title: CHAT-based account of generative AI as a cognitive mediating tool in didactic transformation
description: The article frames lesson planning as a Cultural-Historical Activity Theory system in which the preservice teacher is the subject and the didactic transformation of a magnetism activity is the object, with the LLM entering as a mediating artifact. From this view, "Generative AI is not just a content -producing machine, but actually a cognitive mediator" that can introduce novel approaches or overly advanced concepts while lacking awareness of the physical classroom setting. The framework predicts friction between algorithmic generation and situated preschool pedagogy, which the study's findings illustrate.
requirements: The activity system requires a human educator who performs scientific and pedagogical gatekeeping of AI proposals
constraints: The tool "lacks the contextual awareness of the physical setting of the classroom"
target_learners: preservice early childhood educators
target_learning_goals: designing developmentally appropriate preschool science activities on magnetism
examples: Participants first designed activities unmediated for 15 minutes, then interacted with a twelve-prompt Prompt Pack for 20 minutes, then redesigned for 25 minutes.

article_title: Preservice Early Childhood Educators' Engagement with Generative AI in Science Activity Design: The Case of Magnetism
citation: George Efthimiou, Katerina Plakitsi. (2026). Preservice Early Childhood Educators' Engagement with Generative AI in Science Activity Design: The Case of Magnetism. https://www.mdpi.com/journal/educationsciences
title: Teacher education should shift from teaching prompt-writing technical skills to developing critical pedagogical filtering of AI outputs
description: Because novice teachers already use AI effectively for brainstorming but cannot rely on its pedagogical judgments, the article argues teacher preparation should train educators to evaluate, prune and rebuild machine-generated lesson plans. As the authors state, "teacher education should shift from technical skills to developing critical pedagogical filtering", so that future educators learn to "dismantle AI outputs" and reconstruct activities according to their didactic training. This keeps responsibility for didactic transformation with the human teacher.
requirements: University courses must give practice taking an AI-created lesson plan, removing developmentally inappropriate elements, and rebuilding the activity
constraints: Without building critical resistance, early childhood lessons risk becoming uniform and failing to engage real children, per the authors
target_learners: preservice early childhood educators
novice teachers in university training
target_learning_goals: evaluating AI-generated content for developmental appropriateness
didactic transformation of scientific concepts for young learners
examples: In the workshop, participants used a specially designed checklist to rate AI suggestions for developmental appropriateness, fabricated data and physical safety risks.

article_title: Estimating Item Difficulty Using Large Language Models and Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms
citation: Pooya Razavi, Sonya Powers. (2025). Estimating Item Difficulty Using Large Language Models and Tree-Based Machine Learning Algorithms. Edmentum. https://www.edmentum.com
title: SME-elicited feature set for LLM item evaluation, combining domain-general and domain-specific cognitive and linguistic features
description: A catalog of item features developed through focus groups with four subject matter experts from the assessment design team and cross-referenced with prior literature, then rated by GPT-4o for each item. The process yielded "both domain-general features, which SMEs considered relevant to both subjects (e.g., Cognitive Load, Depth of Knowledge), and domain-specific features (e.g., Symbolic Reasoning for math; Figurative Language for reading)". Math items were rated on 20 targeted questions and reading items on 13, using numeric (e.g., 1-10), binary (Y/N), and DOK (1-4) scales, plus a holistic 1-100 overall difficulty rating. These ratings served as predictors in the tree-based models.
requirements: SME focus groups grounded in the specific item pool to identify difficulty-relevant features
LLM prompts specifying response options or ranges for each feature
constraints: One math feature (evaluating someone else's calculations) was excluded for near-zero variance
Features already available as item metadata (grade level, domain, word count, item type) were excluded from the LLM rating task
target_learners: K-5 students taking mathematics and reading assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of item difficulty for adaptive assessment and item development
examples: Four SMEs with at least five years of K-12 assessment design experience participated in two one-hour video-conference focus groups (a math dyad and a reading triad), costing approximately two hours each.

article_title: RoboBlockly Studio: Conversational Block Programming With Embodied Robot Feedback for Computational Thinking
citation: Leyi Li, Chenyu Du, Jiafei Sun, Erick Purwanto, and Qing Zhang. (2026). RoboBlockly Studio: Conversational Block Programming with Embodied Robot Feedback for Computational Thinking. Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3800645.3813071
title: RoboBlockly Studio: integrated block-based programming, conversational AI teaching agent, and embodied robot execution
description: RoboBlockly Studio is a web-based framework integrating "block-based visual programming, conversational AI, and robot embodiment to enhance the development of computational thinking skills". The backend converts visual code to Python and transmits it via WebSocket to a Mecanum-wheeled robot with a multi-joint arm running ROS 2 on a Jetson Orin Nano. The AI agent (GPT-4o via OpenAI API, temperature 0, not fine-tuned) checks tasks, produces block-grounded feedback, and provides hints, with prompts encoding task rules and a rolling 20-message interaction history including the workspace XML.
requirements: Task-specific prompts that explicitly encode the relevant rules, constraints, and success criteria for each task to reduce unconstrained model judgment
constraints: During program execution, the robot cannot be interrupted or controlled; learners observe, consult the AI, and revise through subsequent runs
target_learners: high school students with no prior programming experience
target_learning_goals: computational thinking: decomposition, abstraction, algorithms, debugging
examples: Students author programs in a dual-panel interface, submit them via a chat bubble with a Run the Robot button, and observe execution on a 5×5 grid mat with obstacles and manipulable cubes
key_sources: Leyi Li, Chenyu Du, Jiafei Sun, Erick Purwanto, and Qing Zhang. (2026). RoboBlockly Studio: Conversational Block Programming with Embodied Robot Feedback for Computational Thinking. Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3800645.3813071

article_title: RoboBlockly Studio: Conversational Block Programming With Embodied Robot Feedback for Computational Thinking
citation: Leyi Li, Chenyu Du, Jiafei Sun, Erick Purwanto, and Qing Zhang. (2026). RoboBlockly Studio: Conversational Block Programming with Embodied Robot Feedback for Computational Thinking. Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3800645.3813071
title: Three-tier progressive CT task structure: complete missing blocks, fix incorrect blocks, translate natural-language problems
description: RoboBlockly Studio organizes tasks into "three progressive levels of difficulty" aligned to design goal DG2. Introductory tasks require students to complete partially provided programs by inserting missing blocks; intermediate tasks require analyzing programs with deliberate flaws and correcting them; advanced tasks present text-based problems that students translate into executable block programs. The tiered structure implements progressive reduction of instructional support so novices build skills stepwise, and the study found students experienced it as a structured learning trajectory supporting warm-up, engagement, and increasingly reflective problem solving.
requirements: Progressive reduction of instructional support through tiered scaffolding so novice learners build skills within a controlled and stepwise learning environment
constraints: Tasks are designed for short classroom sessions and must fit teachers' time constraints and lesson structures
target_learners: high school novices without prior programming experience
target_learning_goals: abstraction, decomposition, debugging, and algorithmic design
examples: Introductory tasks have students add missing blocks so a robot traverses a grid; intermediate tasks include Minefield Exploration on a 5×5 grid; advanced tasks include the Wolf, Sheep, and Cabbage river-crossing puzzle and the Knight's Chessboard Challenge

article_title: A systematic review of student engagement research in adaptive learning platforms
citation: Patricia D. Simon, Lily Min Zeng, Luke K. Fryer. (2026). A systematic review of student engagement research in adaptive learning platforms. Computers and Education Open. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100360
title: Extended four-component student engagement framework (behavioral, affective, cognitive, agentic) applied to adaptive learning platforms
description: The review adopts an integrated framework combining Fredricks et al.'s three common engagement dimensions with Reeve and Tseng's extension. As the review states, "Reeve and Tseng [16] extended this framework and proposed a fourth component called agentic engagement." Behavioral engagement covers observable participation such as time and effort; affective engagement covers attitudes, motivation, confidence and persistence; cognitive engagement covers self-regulation and deep processing; agentic engagement covers students' constructive contribution into the flow of instruction, such as help-seeking. The framework guided deductive coding of the 44 included studies.
requirements: Operationalized definitions of each engagement component to code indicators consistently across studies
constraints: The review notes contentions in how the dimensions are conceptualized, with challenges regarding measurement and statistical methodology, and only moderate interrater reliability in categorizing engagement types
target_learners: Students across educational levels using adaptive learning platforms
target_learning_goals: Understanding and promoting student engagement in technology-mediated, adaptive learning environments
examples: The review coded presence or absence of engagement indicators in 44 articles using these operationalized definitions, with two rounds of interrater reliability checking
key_sources: Patricia D. Simon, Lily Min Zeng, Luke K. Fryer. (2026). A systematic review of student engagement research in adaptive learning platforms. Computers and Education Open. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100360

article_title: Understanding Student Dependency on AI: The Role of AI Literacy, Academic Self-Efficacy, and Resource Management Strategies
citation: Hilit Maizel, Maya Kalman Halevi, Miri Sarid, and Rony Tutian. (2026). Understanding Student Dependency on AI: The Role of AI Literacy, Academic Self-Efficacy, and Resource Management Strategies. Educ. Sci. 2026, 16, 1123. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16071123
title: Integrative three-mechanism model of AI dependency: enabling capacity, compensatory motivation, and self-regulatory function
description: The article proposes that AI dependency "emerges from the interplay of three theoretically distinct mechanisms: an enabling capacity, a compensatory motivation, and a self-regulatory function". Skill-based AI literacy enables offloading by lowering the effort of delegating tasks; self-efficacy beliefs (academic and AI-specific) operate as a unified compensatory mechanism reducing motivational pressure to over-rely; and resource management strategies translate motivational tendencies into action, with effort regulation buffering and help seeking potentially channeling dependency. The model generates directional hypotheses tested via regression and motivates a person-centered cluster analysis.
requirements: Measures distinguishing skill-based from belief-based dimensions of AI literacy (e.g., the MAILS subscales used here)
constraints: Developed and tested with cross-sectional self-report data; the regression coefficients do not establish causal effects
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: balanced and intentional AI engagement in academic work
examples: The model's hypotheses were tested with a multiple regression on 478 Israeli higher education students and complemented by a K-means cluster analysis of literacy-dependency profiles
key_sources: Hilit Maizel, Maya Kalman Halevi, Miri Sarid, and Rony Tutian. (2026). Understanding Student Dependency on AI: The Role of AI Literacy, Academic Self-Efficacy, and Resource Management Strategies. Educ. Sci. 2026, 16, 1123. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci16071123

article_title: Exploring Teachers' Instrumental Orchestration and Roles in High School Mathematics Classes Using AI-Based Digital Tools
citation: Yun Hwa Noh & Hee-jeong Kim. (2026). Exploring teachers' instrumental orchestration and roles in high school mathematics classes using AI-based digital tools. The Mathematical Education 65(2), 309-335. https://doi.org/10.63311/mathedu.26.6525
title: Instrumental orchestration framework extended to AI-based digital learning contexts with agentic AI
description: The study extends the instrumental orchestration framework (didactical configuration, exploitation mode, didactical performance) to classrooms where AI tools act as agentic artifacts. It defines agentic AI as AI that "학습자의 반응을 실시간으로 분석하고 교사의 개입없이 자율적으로 피드백을 생성하고 제공하는" — distinct from tools operating only on explicit user manipulation. Three new orchestration types (dashboard-monitoring, AI-correcting, AI-mediating) are added to the Drijvers et al. type system, and teacher roles are analyzed with an AI-TPACK-based role framework plus an inductively derived knowledge-transmitter category.
requirements: An AI-based digital tool that analyzes student solution processes in real time and autonomously generates individualized feedback and dashboard data for the teacher
constraints: Derived from a single experienced, highly AI-proficient teacher; other tools or teachers may yield different orchestration patterns, as the authors state in their limitations
target_learners: High school mathematics students (grade 10) in one-to-one device classrooms
target_learning_goals: Mathematics concepts and problem solving (rational and irrational functions unit) supported by AI-based personalized feedback
examples: Six lessons on rational and irrational functions using AI digital educational materials, Snorkl, and OneNote, with episodes segmented at tool transitions

article_title: Theoretical Perspectives on Teaching with Robots: From Interdisciplinary Prerequisites and Necessities in Today’s Classrooms to Five Different Types of Robots
citation: Christ, O., Riedl, R., Schmid, J., Zürcher, P., & Thilo, F. (2026). Theoretical Perspectives on Teaching with Robots: From Interdisciplinary Prerequisites and Necessities in Today's Classrooms to Five Different Types of Robots. AI Educ. 2, 28. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030028
title: 4E cognition framework as a heuristic for designing embodied learning technology
description: The article presents 4E cognition as a framework in which cognition is 'not solely a brain-based process, but is also influenced by the body, the environment, and interactions'. Its four dimensions—embodied, embedded, enacted, and extended—are used to explain how learning is distributed across bodies, tools, and social environments, and to map design features of social robots onto learning processes. The authors position MindMatters as an applied instantiation of 4E principles.
requirements: Learning environments must incorporate interactive elements and real-world engagement for the framework to apply to technology-enhanced learning
constraints: Critics argue the approach sometimes blurs the boundaries of cognition, making it difficult to delineate what constitutes cognitive processes
target_learners: school students in primary and secondary education
target_learning_goals: social development
well-being and resilience
cognitive development
examples: The article maps each 4E dimension onto general design features of social robots, e.g. embodied cognition reflected in robots enabling physical interaction and sensorimotor engagement

citation: Christ, O., Riedl, R., Schmid, J., Zürcher, P., & Thilo, F. (2026). Theoretical Perspectives on Teaching with Robots: From Interdisciplinary Prerequisites and Necessities in Today's Classrooms to Five Different Types of Robots. AI Educ. 2, 28. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030028
title: Five-type typology of pedagogical social robots for classroom support
description: Developed through five two-hour design-thinking workshops with a team of seven experts, the typology distinguishes five functionally distinct pedagogical roles: 'non-interactive demonstration, haptic interaction, one-on-one empathic dialogue, externally guided performative agents, and situated behavioural reflection'. Earlier iterations produced seven categories, merged during a consensus process. The types are defined by key characteristics, relevant situations, added value, and weaknesses, and are illustrated in Figure 1a–e.
requirements: An impactful use of robots in classrooms requires both a concrete pedagogical setting and a situated design of the robots
constraints: The typology is not intended as an empirically validated classification, but as a heuristic design framework; it is not exhaustive
target_learners: pupils between the ages of eight and fifteen
target_learning_goals: emotional learning
social competence
conflict mediation skills
examples: Robot type a enacts a generic conflict scenario to illustrate generalisable dynamics, whereas type e re-enacts a specific, previously observed classroom situation for situated reflection

title: Mapping robot types onto 4E cognition dimensions and competence domains
description: The article systematically links each robot type to 4E cognition dimensions and to three competence domains. 'Embodied cognition is most strongly reflected in robot type b, which enables physical interaction and sensorimotor engagement', while embedded cognition appears in group-based types a, d, and e, enacted cognition in types b, c, and d, and extended cognition in types c and e. The three competence domains—socio-emotional, digital/media, and metacognitive—are 'differentially supported by the distinct interactional configurations of each robot type'.
requirements: Competence domains must be explicitly integrated into the design of robot-supported interventions
constraints: The mapping is conceptual and awaits empirical validation through the planned teacher focus groups

target_learning_goals: socio-emotional competence
digital and media competence
metacognitive and reflective competence
examples: Robot type c enables development of socio-emotional competence in a protected one-on-one setting, particularly regarding self-disclosure and trust

title: MindMatters school-based mental health promotion programme
description: MindMatters is 'a school-based, comprehensive framework for promoting mental health and resilience that was originally developed in Australia' and implemented in Swiss primary and secondary schools since 2003 by Radix. It follows a holistic, ecological whole-school approach with modules such as 'How are you?', 'Dealing with stress—staying balanced', and 'Bullying? Not in our school!'. The article selects it as the concrete programme for which the five robot types were designed.

title: AI technology stack enabling adaptive and socially responsive educational robots
description: The article specifies the AI foundations underpinning the proposed robot types: 'natural-language processing (NLP) for dialogic interaction, affective computing for emotion recognition and expression, reinforcement learning for adaptive behaviour modulation, and behaviour-prediction models that support personalised engagement'. Integrated into multimodal sensor architectures, these components let robots interpret speech, gestures, facial expressions, and proxemics in real time. The article frames this as hybrid intelligence in which human and machine capabilities co-evolve.

article_title: A Tripartite Feedback Framework for AI-Assisted Assessment of Complex Reports in Higher Education
citation: Venetsanos, D. T. (2026). A Tripartite Feedback Framework for AI-Assisted Assessment of Complex Reports in Higher Education. AI Educ. 2026, 2, 26. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030026
title: Tripartite feedback framework: three feedback levels distinguished by epistemic status for human-AI task allocation
description: The framework distinguishes three analytically distinct feedback levels: low-level structural and presentational feedback, intermediate-level factual content validation, and high-level critical evaluation and synthesis. It categorizes feedback by epistemic status — "rule-based/factual verification/interpretive evaluation" — to provide "a basis for human–technology decisions". The levels are "distinct dimensions, not a hierarchy", and the framework complements rather than replaces Hattie and Timperley's learning-level model.
requirements: Feedback tasks must be mapped to their cognitive demands and epistemic status before allocation decisions between AI systems and human assessors are made
constraints: The framework "does not claim that its three levels map neatly onto all disciplines or all report genres"; empirical work is needed to test whether the distinctions hold in practice
target_learners: higher education students submitting complex written reports
target_learning_goals: professional communication standards
factual and procedural correctness
critical evaluation and disciplinary reasoning
examples: A chemistry laboratory report receives low-level feedback on a missing figure caption, intermediate-level checking of a calculated yield against reference values, and high-level feedback on whether the method chosen was appropriate and justified
key_sources: Venetsanos, D. T. (2026). A Tripartite Feedback Framework for AI-Assisted Assessment of Complex Reports in Higher Education. AI Educ. 2026, 2, 26. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030026

article_title: A Tripartite Feedback Framework for AI-Assisted Assessment of Complex Reports in Higher Education
citation: Venetsanos, D. T. (2026). A Tripartite Feedback Framework for AI-Assisted Assessment of Complex Reports in Higher Education. AI Educ. 2026, 2, 26. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030026
title: Frame AI as flagging issues for human review rather than as authoritative verification
description: This principle holds that AI systems in assessment should be positioned as surfacing potential issues for expert human review, with interfaces that "surface AI reasoning for review, not verdicts". It responds to the risk that LLMs perform statistical pattern-matching rather than logical verification, and it preserves human final authority over all feedback reaching students.
requirements: Hybrid architectures combining rule-based checks with language models, humans retained as final authorities, and interfaces surfacing AI reasoning for review
constraints: LLMs may accept incorrect work resembling correct patterns, reject unusual correct approaches, or miss uncommon errors
target_learners: higher education students submitting complex written reports
target_learning_goals: factual accuracy and procedural correctness in reports
examples: The article proposes AI-supported intermediate-level checking explicitly framed as flagging potential issues for expert human review rather than generating autonomous feedback
key_sources: Venetsanos, D. T. (2026). A Tripartite Feedback Framework for AI-Assisted Assessment of Complex Reports in Higher Education. AI Educ. 2026, 2, 26. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030026

article_title: A Tripartite Feedback Framework for AI-Assisted Assessment of Complex Reports in Higher Education
citation: Venetsanos, D. T. (2026). A Tripartite Feedback Framework for AI-Assisted Assessment of Complex Reports in Higher Education. AI Educ. 2026, 2, 26. https://doi.org/10.3390/aieduc2030026
title: Report Assessment & Feedback (RAF) procedure with human-in-the-loop approval of all feedback reports
description: The RAF procedure is a flowchart (Figure 1) for AI-assisted report assessment. The system generates a low-level feedback (LLF) report and an intermediate-level feedback (ILF) report; the human assessor evaluates and can modify both, then provides high-level feedback (HLF); the system ranks comments and generates a student-facing Final Feedback Report (FFR), which the assessor can modify and approve for release. "In all cases, the human assessor is included in the loop, deciding whether to accept, reject, or modify the low- and intermediate-level feedback generated."
requirements: Pre-definition of the list of factual check points with relative importance, a rubric for human high-level feedback, and human assessor review at each stage
constraints: The article notes both the frequency and the type of action the human-in-the-loop takes are of importance; high-frequency oversight may reduce efficiency gains and create workflow bottlenecks
target_learners: higher education students submitting complex reports
target_learning_goals: multi-level assessment feedback with clear attribution of sources
examples: For multiple reports, the flowchart can be applied per report in sequence or reports processed in batches in parallel

article_title: Retrieval Practice Consistently Benefits Student Learning: a Systematic Review of Applied Research in Schools and Classrooms
citation: I. Elaine Allen and Jeff Seaman with Russell Poulin and Terri Taylor Straut. (2016). Online Report Card - Tracking Online Education in the United States. Babson Survey Research Group. https://onlinelearningconsortium.org
title: Course-mode taxonomy by proportion of content delivered online (traditional, web-facilitated, blended/hybrid, online)
description: The report defines a four-category classification of higher education courses by the proportion of content delivered online, used consistently across its thirteen annual surveys and presented to respondents at the start of the survey. An "online course is defined as one in which at least 80% of the course content is delivered online," face-to-face covers 0-29% (traditional and web-facilitated), and blended/hybrid covers 30-80% with typically reduced face-to-face meetings. It contrasts these with IPEDS's separate distance education definition.
requirements: Respondents must be presented these definitions at the beginning of the survey and in individual questions, as the report states it does
constraints: IPEDS uses a different definition for distance education than the survey's course-mode categories
target_learners: U.S. higher education students
target_learning_goals: Characterizing online, blended, and face-to-face course delivery modes for institutional reporting and policy analysis
examples: The report's prototypical classification table assigns 1-29% of content online to web-facilitated courses and 30-79% to blended/hybrid courses
