article_title: Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
citation: Alfieri, L., Brooks, P. J., Aldrich, N. J., & Tenenbaum, H. R. (2011). Does Discovery-Based Instruction Enhance Learning? Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(1), 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021017
title: Definition and taxonomy of discovery-learning conditions (unassisted vs. enhanced)
description: The article defines discovery learning as occurring "whenever the learner is not provided with the target information or conceptual understanding and must find it independently and with only the provided materials." It organizes the heterogeneous literature into unassisted types (unassisted, invention, matched probes, simulation, work with a naive peer) and enhanced types (generation, elicited explanation, guided discovery), each coded as moderators in the two meta-analyses. This taxonomy underpins the central finding that guidance, not discovery per se, determines effectiveness.
requirements: Studies must provide useable statistical information and comparable conditions differing in type of instruction
constraints: The field lacks a precise definition; at times the discovery condition is defined more by the comparison method than by the learning methods themselves
target_learners: children
adolescents
adults
target_learning_goals: domain learning across math, computer skills, science, problem solving, physical/motor, and verbal/social skills
examples: The meta-analyses coded 580 unassisted comparisons and 360 enhanced comparisons using this taxonomy, with inter-coder kappa of .87
key_sources: Alfieri, L., Brooks, P. J., Aldrich, N. J., & Tenenbaum, H. R. (2011). Does Discovery-Based Instruction Enhance Learning? Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(1), 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021017

article_title: Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
citation: Alfieri, L., Brooks, P. J., Aldrich, N. J., & Tenenbaum, H. R. (2011). Does Discovery-Based Instruction Enhance Learning? Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(1), 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021017
title: Provide feedback, worked examples, scaffolding, and elicited explanations rather than unassisted discovery
description: The article concludes that "unassisted discovery does not benefit learners, whereas feedback, worked examples, scaffolding, and elicited explanations do." Designers of discovery-based instruction should embed guidance — regular feedback, provided solutions, scaffolded support, or prompts to self-explain — because enhanced discovery outperformed other instruction (d = 0.30) while unassisted discovery underperformed explicit teaching (d = -0.38).
requirements: Discovery tasks must include a guidance mechanism (feedback, worked examples, scaffolding, or elicited explanation) to produce the enhanced-discovery advantage
constraints: Pure, unassisted discovery-learning practices lack evidence of improving learning outcomes and should be abandoned, per the article's reading of Mayer (2004)
target_learners: children
adolescents
adults
target_learning_goals: acquisition of concepts, strategies, and problem-solving skills across academic domains
examples: The enhanced-discovery meta-analysis coded generation, elicited explanation, and guided discovery conditions, which together yielded d = 0.30 over comparison instruction
key_sources: Alfieri, L., Brooks, P. J., Aldrich, N. J., & Tenenbaum, H. R. (2011). Does Discovery-Based Instruction Enhance Learning? Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(1), 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021017

article_title: Synthesizing Results From Empirical Research on Computer-Based Scaffolding in STEM Education: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Belland, B. R., Walker, A. E., Kim, N. J., & Lefler, M. (2017). Synthesizing Results From Empirical Research on Computer-Based Scaffolding in STEM Education: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 87(2), 309-344. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654316670999
title: Framework of computer-based scaffolding design characteristics and moderators
description: The article organizes computer-based scaffolding research along several coded dimensions: context of use (problem-based, case-based, design-based, project-based, inquiry-based, modeling/visualization, problem solving), scaffolding change (none, fading, adding, fading/adding), scaffolding logic (none, performance adapted, self-selected, fixed), scaffolding scope (generic or context-specific), and scaffolding intervention type, where "conceptual scaffolding suggests things to consider when addressing the problem" while strategic, metacognitive, and motivation scaffolding boot strategies, self-evaluation, and motivational variables respectively. This framework guided coding of all 333 outcomes and the meta-analysis's moderator questions.
requirements: Studies must employ scaffolding as defined by Wood et al. (1976) while learners engage ill-structured STEM problems, with a control condition and sufficient information to calculate effect sizes
constraints: The synthesis covers studies published between January 1, 1993, and December 31, 2014, measuring cognitive outcomes only; motivational and metacognitive outcomes were excluded by scope
target_learners: primary through adult learners in STEM education
target_learning_goals: cognitive outcomes including deep content knowledge, problem-solving and argumentation ability
examples: The SE-Coach adjusted both frequency and nature of scaffolding via a probabilistic model of student understanding; Chang et al. (2001) let students self-select hints through feedback and hint buttons
key_sources: Belland, B. R., Walker, A. E., Kim, N. J., & Lefler, M. (2017). Synthesizing Results From Empirical Research on Computer-Based Scaffolding in STEM Education: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 87(2), 309-344. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654316670999

article_title: Inducing Self-Explanation: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Bisra, K., Liu, Q., Nesbit, J. C., Salimi, F., & Winne, P. H. (2018). Inducing Self-Explanation: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 703–725. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9434-x
title: Self-explanation as a generative learning process
description: The article defines self-explanation as "a process by which learners generate inferences about causal connections or conceptual relationships". It treats self-explanation as something that can be induced in learners through prompts delivered while they are studying material or solving problems, and the meta-analysis evaluates learning outcomes for participants who received such prompts. This framing positions self-explanation as a constructive, inference-generating activity rather than mere restatement.
requirements: Learners must receive self-explanation prompts while studying or solving problems for the induced process to occur as studied in the meta-analysis.
target_learners: learners across education levels studied in the included self-explanation research
target_learning_goals: generating inferences about causal connections and conceptual relationships
examples: The meta-analysis located studies in which participants received self-explanation prompts while studying text, studying worked problems, or solving problems.
key_sources: Bisra, K., Liu, Q., Nesbit, J. C., Salimi, F., & Winne, P. H. (2018). Inducing Self-Explanation: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 703–725. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9434-x

article_title: Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators.
citation: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209
title: Attentional bias framework (sequential attention theory) of interleaved learning
description: The attentional bias framework, also called sequential attention theory, explains positional-relations effects in inductive learning by what presentation format highlights: "an interleaved presentation highlights differences between items, whereas a blocked presentation highlights similarities." Interleaving is therefore predicted to be better when between-category differences are crucial (low-discriminability, highly similar exemplars), and blocking better when within-category similarities are crucial (high-discriminability exemplars). The meta-analysis used this framework to motivate its similarity and complexity moderators.
requirements: Applies to inductive category learning where success depends on discriminating exemplars from different categories
constraints: The framework predicts a blocking advantage in high-discriminability conditions where within-category similarities are crucial
target_learners: college students
school students
adult learners
target_learning_goals: inductive category learning and category discrimination
examples: The meta-analysis coded rater-based within- and between-category similarity ratings of 71 material sets and tested them as moderators of the interleaving effect.
key_sources: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209

article_title: Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators.
citation: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209
title: Discriminative contrast hypothesis of the interleaving effect
description: The discriminative contrast hypothesis (Kang & Pashler, 2012) holds that interleaving benefits inductive learning because juxtaposing items of different categories close together in time promotes "discriminative contrasts of subsequent items, which might benefit inductive learning." It is based on the observation that temporal spacing between items hinders inductive learning in interleaved conditions and has no advantage in blocked conditions. The meta-analysis coded temporal spacing between successive items to test this assumption.
requirements: Items of different categories must be juxtaposed closely in time for discriminative contrasts to arise
constraints: The hypothesis addresses temporal spacing, which the meta-analysis analyzed separately because only four studies fell in the spaced categories
target_learners: college students
adult learners
target_learning_goals: inductive category learning and discrimination between categories
examples: The meta-analysis coded the time elapsed between presentations of successive items into three categories, with immediate succession as the reference category.
key_sources: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209

article_title: Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators.
citation: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209
title: Massing-aids-induction hypothesis (blocking advantage account)
description: The massing-aids-induction hypothesis, coined by Kornell and Bjork (2008) who do not advocate it, holds that "blocking enhances inductive learning by facilitating the recognition of similarities among nonidentical items within a category." It cannot explain positive interleaving effects but addresses the advantage of blocked over interleaved presentation, and may help interpret studies in which interleaving failed, such as word-material studies showing a blocking effect. The meta-analysis's negative effect for words is consistent with this account.
requirements: Applies when successful inductive learning depends on identifying features shared by exemplars within a category
constraints: Cannot explain positive interleaving effects; addresses only blocking advantages
target_learners: college students
adult learners
target_learning_goals: inductive learning of concepts defined by shared features
examples: Sorensen and Woltz (2016) found interleaving led to poorer outcomes than blocking when items of different conceptual categories were words, a condition the article cites as consistent with this hypothesis.
key_sources: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209

article_title: Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators.
citation: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209
title: Evaluate setting and learning material before applying interleaving in educational settings
description: Because the interleaving effect's magnitude and even direction depend on the type and characteristics of the learning material, the article concludes that "interleaving can effectively foster inductive learning but that the setting and the type of learning material must be considered." Educators should verify that material resembles the conditions where interleaving works (e.g., visually similar categories) before adopting it, and should "use with caution in certain conditions, especially for expository texts and words."
requirements: Learning material and setting should be evaluated for similarity structure before adopting interleaved sequencing
constraints: Interleaving showed a blocking advantage for word materials and no significant effect for expository texts and tastes
target_learners: college students
school students
adult learners
target_learning_goals: inductive category learning and classification
examples: The meta-analysis quantified material-type differences, with paintings at g = 0.67 and words at g = -0.39, as the empirical basis for this recommendation.
key_sources: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209

article_title: The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice
citation: Carpenter, S.K., Pan, S.C. & Butler, A.C. (2022). The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice. Nature Reviews Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-022-00089-1
title: Learner metacognition as awareness and regulation of one's own learning
description: The review organizes its third strand of findings around metacognition, defined in terms of "learners' awareness and regulation of their own learning". It argues that findings in this area show the need to improve learners' subjective mental models of effective learning, because faulty mental models lead learners away from strategies like spacing and retrieval practice. The framework connects strategy underuse to monitoring and regulation failures in self-directed study.
requirements: Learners must be in situations where they monitor and regulate their own learning for the framework's implications to apply
target_learners: lifelong learners across educational levels
target_learning_goals: effective selection and use of learning strategies such as spacing and retrieval practice
examples: The review uses this framework to interpret why learners underuse spacing and retrieval practice and to motivate improving learners' subjective mental models of how to learn effectively
key_sources: Carpenter, S.K., Pan, S.C. & Butler, A.C. (2022). The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice. Nature Reviews Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-022-00089-1

article_title: The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice
citation: Carpenter, S.K., Pan, S.C. & Butler, A.C. (2022). The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice. Nature Reviews Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-022-00089-1
title: Successive relearning: a technique combining spacing and retrieval practice
description: Successive relearning is a learning technique that combines spacing and retrieval practice, presented in the review as a potent method for obtaining and maintaining knowledge. The review devotes figures to the "Successive relearning paradigm" and "Successive relearning results", and cites work describing it as "an effective learning technique that combines spacing and retrieval". It is illustrated with classic evidence of spaced retrieval practice benefiting foreign language vocabulary retention in adults over years.
requirements: Requires repeated retrieval practice episodes distributed over time (spaced) rather than massed
target_learners: adult learners
students in courses with durable retention goals
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of knowledge such as foreign language vocabulary
examples: The review cites a classic study demonstrating benefits of spaced retrieval practice (successive relearning) on foreign language vocabulary in adults over a period of 5 years
key_sources: Carpenter, S.K., Pan, S.C. & Butler, A.C. (2022). The science of effective learning with spacing and retrieval practice. Nature Reviews Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44159-022-00089-1

article_title: Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis.
citation: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks: A Review and Quantitative Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354
title: Distributed practice framework distinguishing spacing effects from lag effects
description: The article organizes the distributed practice literature around temporal variables it defines explicitly: interstudy interval (ISI), the interval separating study episodes of the same material, and retention interval, the interval between the last study episode and the final test. It distinguishes the spacing effect, "enhanced learning during spaced as compared with massed study episodes for a given item," from the lag effect, comparisons of different levels of spacing, and treats distributed practice as the generic term encompassing both. This distinction proved, in the authors' words, helpful in quantifying how retention depends jointly on ISI and retention interval.
requirements: Studies must include at least two learning episodes per item, or one massed presentation with lag under 1 s, and a recall final test
constraints: The review is restricted to verbal memory tasks using recall as the performance measure, excluding recognition and frequency-judgment measures and clinical populations
target_learners: learners of verbal information across ages, including children and older adults
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of verbal material
key_sources: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks: A Review and Quantitative Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354

article_title: Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis.
citation: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks: A Review and Quantitative Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354
title: Choose the interstudy interval in relation to the intended retention interval
description: Because the ISI producing maximal retention increases as the retention interval increases, instruction should not fix one universally optimal spacing gap. The article states the practical stakes directly: "One can hardly select an ISI that optimizes instruction unless one knows how learning depends upon ISI; if that function varies with retention interval, this too must be considered in designing the most efficient procedures for pedagogy or training." Designers should therefore estimate how long learners will need to retain material and set spacing accordingly, keeping in mind that very long lags can produce smaller effects.
requirements: Knowledge of the target retention interval before selecting the ISI
constraints: The literature poorly represents combinations of long ISIs with long retention intervals, so precise optimal values for long delays remain uncertain
target_learners: learners of verbal information in instructional or training settings
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied verbal material
examples: The review's lag analyses found the optimal ISI bin increased as retention interval increased, and within-study studies (e.g., Cepeda et al., 2005; Gordon, 1925) showed subday ISIs optimal at subday retention intervals and supraday ISIs optimal at supraday retention intervals
key_sources: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed Practice in Verbal Recall Tasks: A Review and Quantitative Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354

article_title: Eight Ways to Promote Generative Learning
citation: Fiorella, L., & Mayer, R. E. (2016). Eight Ways to Promote Generative Learning. Educational Psychology Review, 28, 717–741. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9348-9
title: Generative learning theory grounded in Wittrock's generative model of comprehension and reflected in Mayer's select-organize-integrate (SOI) framework
description: The article organizes its review around generative learning theory, which it describes as "grounded in Wittrock's (1974) generative model of comprehension and reflected in more recent frameworks of active learning, such as Mayer's (2014) select-organize-integrate (SOI) framework." The theory holds that learning occurs when learners actively make sense of material by reorganizing and integrating it with prior knowledge, rather than passively receiving it. The eight strategies the review covers are presented as instructional implementations of this generative account of comprehension and active learning.
requirements: Learners must actively engage in sense-making processes that connect new information to prior knowledge for the theory's predicted benefits to occur
target_learners: Learners across educational settings studying to-be-learned informational material
target_learning_goals: Meaningful comprehension and transfer of learned material to new situations
examples: The review uses the theory to structure its treatment of eight strategies, providing for each "a description, review exemplary research studies, discuss potential boundary conditions, and provide practical recommendations for implementation."
key_sources: Fiorella, L., & Mayer, R. E. (2016). Eight Ways to Promote Generative Learning. Educational Psychology Review, 28, 717–741. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9348-9

article_title: Eight Ways to Promote Generative Learning
citation: Fiorella, L., & Mayer, R. E. (2016). Eight Ways to Promote Generative Learning. Educational Psychology Review, 28, 717–741. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9348-9
title: Eight generative learning strategies: summarizing, mapping, drawing, imagining, self-testing, self-explaining, teaching, and enacting
description: The article's central organizing taxonomy is a set of eight learning strategies "intended to promote generative learning." The set spans verbal-summative strategies (summarizing), visual-structural strategies (mapping, drawing), imagery strategies (imagining), verification strategies (self-testing), elaboration strategies (self-explaining), social strategies (teaching), and embodied strategies (enacting). Each strategy is treated in the review with a description, exemplary research, boundary conditions, and implementation recommendations.
requirements: Each strategy must be implemented so that learners generate cognitive products that reorganize and integrate material with prior knowledge
target_learners: Students learning expository or instructional material across age levels
target_learning_goals: Generative processing leading to understanding and transfer
examples: The abstract enumerates the eight strategies: "summarizing, mapping, drawing, imagining, self-testing, self-explaining, teaching, and enacting."

article_title: Concreteness Fading in Mathematics and Science Instruction: a Systematic Review
citation: Fyfe, E. R., McNeil, N. M., Son, J. Y., & Goldstone, R. L. (2014). Concreteness Fading in Mathematics and Science Instruction: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9249-3
title: Concreteness fading: a framework combining concrete and abstract instructional materials
description: Concreteness fading is an instructional framework in which learners begin with concrete materials and then move explicitly and gradually to more abstract representations. The article positions it as an approach that moves beyond the dichotomy of treating concrete and abstract materials independently, arguing that "concreteness fading provides advantages that go beyond the sum of the benefits of concrete and abstract materials." It is proposed for mathematics and science instruction.
requirements: Instruction must begin with concrete materials and then explicitly and gradually fade to the more abstract, per the article's recommendation
constraints: The framework is proposed for domains such as mathematics and science instruction
target_learners: Learners of mathematics and science
target_learning_goals: Interpreting abstract symbols
Grounding abstract thinking in perceptual and physical experience
Transfer of generalizable properties
key_sources: Fyfe, E. R., McNeil, N. M., Son, J. Y., & Goldstone, R. L. (2014). Concreteness Fading in Mathematics and Science Instruction: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9249-3

article_title: Concreteness Fading in Mathematics and Science Instruction: a Systematic Review
citation: Fyfe, E. R., McNeil, N. M., Son, J. Y., & Goldstone, R. L. (2014). Concreteness Fading in Mathematics and Science Instruction: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9249-3
title: Begin with concrete materials and explicitly and gradually fade to abstract ones
description: This principle holds that mathematics and science instruction should start with concrete materials and then transition deliberately to abstract representations, rather than choosing one or the other. The article states: "we recommend beginning with concrete materials and then explicitly and gradually fading to the more abstract." The fading must be explicit and gradual so learners can connect concrete understanding to abstract symbols.
requirements: The transition from concrete to abstract must be explicit and gradual rather than abrupt
constraints: Recommended particularly for domains such as mathematics and science
target_learners: Mathematics and science learners
target_learning_goals: Understanding abstract symbols and concepts
examples: The review recommends this sequence as a way to combine the advantages of concrete and abstract materials in mathematics and science instruction

article_title: The Power of Feedback
citation: Martínez Carrillo, E. (2018). Una aproximación a los estilos de retroalimentación en tutoría de trabajo de grado en educación superior. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://repository.upn.edu.co
title: Modelo de estilos de retroalimentación de trabajo de grado en educación superior
description: La tesis propone un modelo (Figura 15) que organiza la retroalimentación del tutor de trabajo de grado en 4 estilos definidos por dos dimensiones: el énfasis de la retroalimentación (en la tarea o en el proceso) y la cercanía psicológica (cálida o formal). La autora indica que los estilos cumplen "una noción diferenciadora de las conductas de los tutores" y "tiene un carácter neutral, donde no se presenta una jerarquía de un estilo sobre otro". El modelo se construyó a partir del análisis de enunciados de tutorías grabadas y se proyecta validarlo en otros contextos y niveles de formación.
requirements: Validación del modelo en otros contextos de tutoría y otros niveles de formación, según las proyecciones del estudio
Construcción futura de un instrumento que permita medir estilos en este contexto de tutoría
constraints: El estudio fue de carácter transversal, por lo que no se verificó la permanencia en el tiempo del comportamiento de los individuos
target_learners: Estudiantes de pregrado que desarrollan trabajos de grado
target_learning_goals: Retroalimentación formativa en el desarrollo del trabajo de grado
Comprensión del rol docente en tutoría
examples: Las tutorías de 6 docentes de pregrado de una universidad privada de Bogotá fueron grabadas en audio y sus enunciados codificados según las 5 categorías
key_sources: Martínez Carrillo, E. (2018). Una aproximación a los estilos de retroalimentación en tutoría de trabajo de grado en educación superior. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://repository.upn.edu.co

article_title: The Power of Feedback
citation: Martínez Carrillo, E. (2018). Una aproximación a los estilos de retroalimentación en tutoría de trabajo de grado en educación superior. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://repository.upn.edu.co
title: Modelo de retroalimentación de Hattie y Timperley (2007) con cuatro niveles: tarea, proceso, autorregulación y yo
description: La tesis adopta el modelo de Hattie y Timperley (2007) como marco para comprender la retroalimentación en tutoría. El modelo "propone 4 niveles de retroalimentación" descritos como "nivel de tarea; nivel de proceso o procedimientos necesarios para completar la tarea; nivel meta-cognitivo o de estrategias de autorregulación puestas en juego para avanzar en la consecución de la tarea; nivel personal, del yo". Cada nivel cumple funciones distintas: el de tarea es correctivo, el de proceso ofrece información paso a paso, el de autorregulación facilita la autoevaluación y el del yo contiene poca información de tarea.
requirements: Ubicar la retroalimentación en una perspectiva constructivista donde el estudiante asume un rol activo
constraints: Los comentarios del nivel del yo contienen poca información relacionada con la tarea y rara vez se convierten en mayor compromiso con el aprendizaje
target_learners: Estudiantes de educación superior en tutoría de trabajo de grado
target_learning_goals: Retroalimentación efectiva orientada a la tarea, el proceso y la autorregulación
examples: La tesis usa este modelo (Tabla 5) para definir las categorías de análisis de los enunciados de tutoría, distinguiendo énfasis en la tarea, en el proceso y en la autorregulación
key_sources: Martínez Carrillo, E. (2018). Una aproximación a los estilos de retroalimentación en tutoría de trabajo de grado en educación superior. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://repository.upn.edu.co

article_title: The Power of Feedback
citation: Martínez Carrillo, E. (2018). Una aproximación a los estilos de retroalimentación en tutoría de trabajo de grado en educación superior. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://repository.upn.edu.co
title: Diseño mixto con grabación en audio de tutorías de 6 docentes tutores de trabajo de grado
description: Elemento metodológico central de la tesis: un estudio con diseño mixto en el que el análisis cualitativo de los enunciados se categoriza y transforma en datos cuantitativos. La muestra, por conveniencia y no probabilística, correspondió a 6 docentes de una universidad privada de Bogotá; "el muestreo se realizó por conveniencia y es de carácter no probabilístico, la muestra de participantes correspondió a 6 docentes". La técnica de recolección fue "el registro del desarrollo de la tutoría mediante la grabación del audio durante el desarrollo de la tutoría".
requirements: Docentes con mínimo tres años de experiencia en tutoría, asignación de tutoría de trabajos de grado en el semestre, máximo dos estudiantes por trabajo, formación de maestría y presencia de ambos sexos
constraints: Muestreo por conveniencia no probabilístico en una sola facultad (Psicología) de una universidad privada de Bogotá

target_learning_goals: Caracterización de la retroalimentación docente en tutoría

article_title: Expertise Reversal Effect and Its Implications for Learner-Tailored Instruction
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2007). Expertise Reversal Effect and Its Implications for Learner-Tailored Instruction. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 509–539. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9054-3
title: Cognitive load theory provides the prediction and explanation of the expertise reversal effect
description: The review organizes the expertise reversal effect within cognitive load theory, the framework in which interactions between prior knowledge and instructional effectiveness have been investigated. The article states the findings have "cognitive load theory-based prediction and explanation", meaning the theory predicts which techniques suit which expertise levels and explains reversals in terms of changing load as knowledge develops. It serves here as the explanatory account the review uses to interpret the reviewed empirical patterns.
requirements: Instructional techniques whose effectiveness varies with learner expertise, so that prior knowledge level can be treated as a moderating variable
target_learners: Learners across levels of prior knowledge or expertise in a domain
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of domain knowledge and skills under techniques matched to expertise level
examples: The review interprets recent empirical findings on the expertise reversal effect through this cognitive load account.

article_title: Expertise Reversal Effect and Its Implications for Learner-Tailored Instruction
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2007). Expertise Reversal Effect and Its Implications for Learner-Tailored Instruction. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 509–539. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9054-3
title: Instruction should be tailored to the learner's level of prior knowledge or expertise
description: Because instructional effectiveness reverses with expertise, the review draws implications for "the design of learner-tailored instructional systems": instruction should be adapted to the learner's current knowledge level rather than fixed for all. The review presents this tailoring as the design consequence of the expertise reversal findings, with recent experimental attempts implementing the findings in adaptive environments. It applies wherever learner expertise varies within the target population.
requirements: Means of determining or tracking learners' current knowledge or expertise level so instruction can be matched to it
target_learners: Learners at differing levels of prior knowledge in a domain
target_learning_goals: Efficient acquisition of domain knowledge and skills
examples: The review discusses recent experimental attempts of implementing these findings into realistic adaptive learning environments.

title: Adaptive learning environments implementing expertise reversal findings
description: The review covers "some recent experimental attempts of implementing these findings into realistic adaptive learning environments": instructional systems that adjust techniques or support to learner expertise based on the expertise reversal literature. The review reports on these attempts as recent experimental work rather than settled deployments.

article_title: Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work: An Analysis of the Failure of Constructivist, Discovery, Problem-Based, Experiential, and Inquiry-Based Teaching
citation: Kirschner, P; Sweller, John; Clark, Robert. (2006). Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work: An analysis of the failure of constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential, and inquiry-based teaching. Journal Article. http://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/50516
title: Human cognitive architecture, expert-novice differences, and cognitive load as the explanatory framework for the superiority of guided instruction
description: The article explains the superiority of guided instruction in terms of human cognitive architecture, expert-novice differences, and cognitive load. It argues that unguided or minimally guided approaches "ignore both the structures that constitute human cognitive architecture" and the accumulated empirical evidence. The framework treats the learner's cognitive architecture as the reason external guidance is needed during skill acquisition, with prior knowledge eventually supplying internal guidance.
requirements: Instructional approaches must take account of the structures that constitute human cognitive architecture, which the article says minimally guided approaches ignore.
constraints: The advantage of guidance recedes when learners have sufficiently high prior knowledge to provide internal guidance.
target_learners: Novice learners in constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential, and inquiry-based instructional settings
target_learning_goals: Effective and efficient acquisition of knowledge and skills through guided instruction
key_sources: Kirschner, P; Sweller, John; Clark, Robert. (2006). Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work: An analysis of the failure of constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential, and inquiry-based teaching. Journal Article. http://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/50516

article_title: Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work: An Analysis of the Failure of Constructivist, Discovery, Problem-Based, Experiential, and Inquiry-Based Teaching
citation: Kirschner, P; Sweller, John; Clark, Robert. (2006). Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work: An analysis of the failure of constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential, and inquiry-based teaching. Journal Article. http://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/50516
title: Design instruction with a strong emphasis on guidance of the student learning process, especially for novices
description: The article recommends that instruction place "a strong emphasis on guidance of the student learning process," because minimally guided approaches are less effective and less efficient given human cognitive architecture. Guidance is most critical for learners without high prior knowledge, since sufficiently knowledgeable learners can supply their own internal guidance. This principle follows from the article's synthesis of half-century empirical evidence and cognitive load reasoning.
requirements: Guidance must be designed in accordance with the structures that constitute human cognitive architecture, which the article says minimally guided approaches ignore.
constraints: The advantage of guidance begins to recede when learners have sufficiently high prior knowledge to provide internal guidance.
target_learners: Novice learners lacking the prior knowledge needed for internal guidance
target_learning_goals: Effective and efficient learning of knowledge and skills
examples: The article contrasts guided instruction with constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential, and inquiry-based teaching approaches that minimize guidance.

article_title: The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory.
citation: Kluger, A. N., & DeNisi, A. (1996). The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory. Psychological Bulletin, 119(2), 254-284. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.119.2.254
title: Feedback Intervention Theory (FIT): feedback shifts attention among hierarchically organized task-learning, task-motivation, and meta-task (self-related) levels
description: FIT is a hybrid theory integrating control theory, goal setting theory, action theory, action identification theory, and learned helplessness research to explain variable feedback-intervention effects. Its five arguments hold that behavior is regulated by feedback-standard comparisons, standards are hierarchical, attention is limited, attention normally rests at a moderate level, and feedback interventions redirect attention. The authors "divided the hierarchy into three levels of linked processes involved in the regulation of task performance: meta-task processes involving the self, task-motivation processes involving the focal task, and task-learning processes involving the task details of the focal task."
requirements: Feedback interventions command considerable attention because any FI has potentially serious implications for the self, which is what allows them to alter the locus of attention
constraints: The three-level hierarchy is only an abstraction; the authors state the hierarchy is probably more complex and contains more sublevels
target_learners: students
employees
any task performers receiving externally provided feedback
target_learning_goals: task performance improvement through feedback
examples: The authors tested FIT by subjecting putative moderators identified by FIT to moderator analyses of the meta-analytic effects

article_title: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Benefit of Spacing out Retrieval Practice Episodes on Retention
citation: Latimier, A., Peyre, H., & Ramus, F. (2021). A Meta-Analytic Review of the Benefit of Spacing out Retrieval Practice Episodes on Retention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09572-8
title: Spaced retrieval practice as the combination of two desirable difficulties
description: The article defines spaced retrieval practice as a learning strategy in which "repetitions of the same retrieval event [are] distributed through time". It frames this strategy as combining two desirable difficulties: retrieval practice and the spacing effect. The framework organises the meta-analysis into two questions — spaced versus massed retrieval practice, and expanding versus uniform spacing schedules — and positions spacing of retrieval episodes as the mechanism by which final retention is enhanced.
requirements: Learning episodes must involve actual retrieval events on the same content, distributed through time, for the strategy to apply as defined
constraints: The benefit concerns final retention of the same content; the article finds no support for progressively increasing inter-retrieval intervals until the retention test
target_learners: learners across the 29 included studies, spanning classroom and laboratory settings
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied content
examples: The meta-analysis operationalised the framework by dividing 29 studies into subset 1 (spaced vs massed retrieval) and subset 2 (expanding vs uniform schedules)
key_sources: Latimier, A., Peyre, H., & Ramus, F. (2021). A Meta-Analytic Review of the Benefit of Spacing out Retrieval Practice Episodes on Retention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09572-8

article_title: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Benefit of Spacing out Retrieval Practice Episodes on Retention
citation: Latimier, A., Peyre, H., & Ramus, F. (2021). A Meta-Analytic Review of the Benefit of Spacing out Retrieval Practice Episodes on Retention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09572-8
title: Space out retrieval practice episodes on the same content, but do not assume intervals must progressively expand
description: The article's overall conclusion is that "these results support the advantage of spacing out the retrieval practice episodes on the same content, but do not support the widely held belief that inter-retrieval intervals should be progressively increased until a retention test". Designers should therefore distribute retrieval practice over time, while uniform spacing schedules perform as well as expanding ones overall. The expanding schedule's advantage appears only when items are tested many times.
requirements: Retrieval practice episodes must target the same content and be distributed through time rather than massed
constraints: Progressively increasing inter-retrieval intervals is not supported overall; the expanding schedule only becomes more beneficial than the uniform one as the number of exposures increases
target_learners: students in classroom and laboratory learning settings
target_learning_goals: final retention of learned content
examples: The review aggregated 39 effect sizes for the spaced-versus-massed contrast and 54 for the expanding-versus-uniform contrast to reach this recommendation
key_sources: Latimier, A., Peyre, H., & Ramus, F. (2021). A Meta-Analytic Review of the Benefit of Spacing out Retrieval Practice Episodes on Retention. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09572-8

article_title: Applying the science of learning: Evidence-based principles for the design of multimedia instruction.
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2008). Applying the Science of Learning: Evidence-Based Principles for the Design of Multimedia Instruction. American Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0012841
title: Cognitive theory of multimedia learning: dual channels, limited capacity, and active processing
description: The article presents the cognitive theory of multimedia learning as a framework explaining how people learn from words and pictures. It rests on three assumptions: dual channels, limited capacity, and active processing, with selecting, organizing, and integrating as core processes moving information from sensory memory through working memory to long-term memory. The article states that "The most relevant elements in a science of learning are (a) dual channels—the idea that humans possess separate channels for processing visual and verbal material; (b) limited capacity—the idea that each channel can process only a small amount of material at any one time." The 10 design principles are described as theoretically grounded in this theory.
requirements: Instructional design decisions should be judged against research-based theories of how people learn
constraints: The theory assumes each channel can process only a small amount of material at any one time
target_learners: learners in multimedia instructional settings, from school students to employees in training
target_learning_goals: deep learning and transfer of multimedia lesson content
examples: Figure 2 depicts the theory: words and pictures enter sensory memory, are selected into verbal and pictorial channels of working memory, organized into models, and integrated with prior knowledge in long-term memory
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2008). Applying the Science of Learning: Evidence-Based Principles for the Design of Multimedia Instruction. American Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066x.63.8.760

article_title: Applying the science of learning: Evidence-based principles for the design of multimedia instruction.
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2008). Applying the Science of Learning: Evidence-Based Principles for the Design of Multimedia Instruction. American Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0012841
title: Two-way street approach: reciprocal relation between science of learning and science of instruction
description: The article proposes that learning theory and educational practice stand in a reciprocal relation, contrasting this with a one-way street approach (theory applied to lessons) and a dead end street approach (theory divorced from authentic challenges). The article states that "in the two-way street approach, there is a reciprocal relation between learning theory and educational practice in which the science of learning must be expanded to be able to explain how learning works in authentic learning situations." It frames this as basic research on applied problems, inspired by Stokes's use-inspired basic research, and illustrates it with the 10 multimedia principles.
requirements: Research must address authentic learning situations while still testing learning theory
constraints: The article notes the one-way street approach yields theories of limited applicability beyond contrived lab settings
target_learners: educational researchers and instructional designers
target_learning_goals: understanding how to design instruction that fosters learning
examples: The article's 10 multimedia principles are offered as an exemplar of merging theoretical and practical goals
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2008). Applying the Science of Learning: Evidence-Based Principles for the Design of Multimedia Instruction. American Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066x.63.8.760

article_title: Transfer of test-enhanced learning: Meta-analytic review and synthesis.
citation: Steven C. Pan and Timothy C. Rickard. (2018). Transfer of Test-Enhanced Learning: Meta-Analytic Review and Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/bul0000151
title: Three-factor framework for transfer of test-enhanced learning
description: The review's synthesis motivates a three-factor framework for transfer of test-enhanced learning, organized around the factors the meta-analysis identified as governing positive transfer: response congruency between initial and final tests, elaborated retrieval practice, and initial test performance. The authors state that "our results motivate a three-factor framework for transfer of test-enhanced learning and have practical implications for the effective use of practice testing in educational and other training contexts." The framework integrates the category-level findings with the moderator analyses and the publication-bias results.
requirements: Positive transfer depends on the presence of the identified moderators; the intercept analyses often indicated no positive transfer when none of the moderators are present
constraints: Developed from studies using the three-phase test-enhanced learning paradigm with a nontesting reexposure control, mostly with young adult university samples
target_learners: Learners in educational and other training contexts, primarily university students in the underlying studies
target_learning_goals: Flexible, transferable learning rather than retention of identical test items
examples: The framework is motivated by the meta-analysis of 192 transfer effect sizes spanning six major transfer categories from near to far transfer
key_sources: Steven C. Pan and Timothy C. Rickard. (2018). Transfer of Test-Enhanced Learning: Meta-Analytic Review and Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/bul0000151

article_title: Transfer of test-enhanced learning: Meta-analytic review and synthesis.
citation: Steven C. Pan and Timothy C. Rickard. (2018). Transfer of Test-Enhanced Learning: Meta-Analytic Review and Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/bul0000151
title: Process accounts of transfer of test-enhanced learning: elaborative retrieval, mediator effectiveness, and dual memory theories
description: The review summarizes three process-based theoretical accounts that incorporate transfer. The elaborative retrieval hypothesis "posits that a process of spreading activation occurs during the search for correct answers on tests," creating multiple retrieval routes that can aid recall of semantically related information on transfer tests. The mediator effectiveness hypothesis "posits that mediators (i.e., a word, phrase, or concept that links a cue with a target) activated during testing support improved final test performance," including when mediators or linked information must be recalled on a transfer test. Dual memory theory holds that "two routes to retrieval are accessible for a tested response," but predicts only study memory is accessible when different responses are required, yielding no positive transfer.
requirements: Each account addresses specific transfer categories: mediator and related word cues for the first two, rearranged responses for dual memory theory
constraints: The review notes many theoretical accounts of test-enhanced learning do not directly address transfer; dual memory theory predicts no positive transfer when different responses are required on a transfer test
target_learners: Learners in laboratory and educational studies of retrieval practice
target_learning_goals: Recall of tested and semantically related, untested information
examples: The review cites Carpenter (2011) and Chan (2009) for spreading-activation accounts of transfer to semantically related cues, and Rickard and Pan (2017) for dual memory theory
key_sources: Steven C. Pan and Timothy C. Rickard. (2018). Transfer of Test-Enhanced Learning: Meta-Analytic Review and Synthesis. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/bul0000151

article_title: Prequestioning and Pretesting Effects: a Review of Empirical Research, Theoretical Perspectives, and Implications for Educational Practice
citation: Steven C. Pan, Shana K. Carpenter. (2023). Prequestioning and Pretesting Effects: a Review of Empirical Research, Theoretical Perspectives, and Implications for Educational Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09814-5
title: Three-stage framework of prequestioning and pretesting effects
description: The review proposes that the cognitive mechanisms underlying prequestioning and pretesting effects "can be represented by a three-stage framework" in which test-induced changes in subsequent learning behaviors, and possibly other processes, explain the benefits. It organizes how pre-instruction testing alters learners' engagement with subsequent study of correct answers, offering a structure for interpreting effects across materials and settings. The framework is presented as a synthesis of current theoretical perspectives rather than a tested model.
requirements: An opportunity to study the correct answers after the initial test, as the review states benefits occur "if there is an opportunity to study the correct answers afterwards"
constraints: The review states the underlying cognitive mechanisms only "appear to involve" test-induced changes and possibly other processes, and that further research is needed to clarify theoretical issues
target_learners: Undergraduate students and similar-aged learners, as in most reviewed studies
K-12 and medical students in the classroom and clinical studies reviewed
target_learning_goals: Retention of directly tested content
Transfer to untested materials, inferences, and classification of new exemplars
examples: The review uses the framework to interpret findings across text, video, word-pair, and trivia-fact studies, and to motivate future research on moderating factors

article_title: How Fading Worked Solution Steps Works – A Cognitive Load Perspective
citation: Renkl, A., Atkinson, R.K. & Große, C.S. (2004). How Fading Worked Solution Steps Works – A Cognitive Load Perspective. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:TRUC.0000021815.74806.f6
title: Fade out worked solution steps successively to support the transition from example study to problem solving
description: This principle holds that, to move learners from studying worked examples in early skill acquisition to independent problem solving, instruction should "successivelyfade out worked solution steps" rather than using traditional example-problem pairs. The article examines this from a cognitive load perspective across two computer-based experiments. The mechanism the authors ultimately identify is reduced unproductive learning events rather than increased self-explanations.
requirements: A computer-based or otherwise structured learning environment in which worked solution steps can be successively faded across the progression from examples to problems
constraints: The position of the faded steps did not influence learning outcomes, so the principle does not specify a particular fading position; the hypothesized self-explanation trigger mechanism was not confirmed in the think-aloud analysis
target_learners: Learners in earlier stages of skill acquisition transitioning to problem solving
target_learning_goals: Cognitive skill acquisition and problem solving
examples: Two experiments used a computer-based learning environment containing faded worked solution steps; Experiment 2 collected thinking-aloud protocols during learner interaction with the environment.

article_title: A Meta-analysis of the Segmenting Effect
citation: Rey, G.D., Beege, M., Nebel, S., Wirzberger, M., Schmitt, T.H., & Schneider, S. (2019). A Meta-analysis of the Segmenting Effect. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 389–419. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9456-4
title: Explanatory accounts of the segmenting effect: designer-imposed chunking and structuring, more processing time, and individual pace adaptation
description: The meta-analysis frames the segmenting effect within the cognitive theory of multimedia learning and tests three candidate explanations: that segmenting by the instructional designer facilitates chunking and structuring of the material, that it provides more time for processing the instruction, and that it allows learners to adapt the presentation pace to their individual needs. The article states: "The meta-analysis tests different explanations for the segmenting effect that concern facilitating chunking and structuring due to segmenting the multimedia instruction by the instructional designer, providing more time for processing the instruction and allowing the learners to adapt the presentation pace to their individual needs."
requirements: Explanations are tested against the meta-analytic evidence from 56 investigations of segmented versus continuous multimedia instruction.
target_learners: learners studying multimedia instructional materials
target_learning_goals: retention and transfer of multimedia instruction content
examples: The meta-analysis evaluates these explanations using moderation analyses, including the prior-knowledge moderation of retention performance.

article_title: The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect.
citation: Rowland, C. A. (2014, August 25). The Effect of Testing Versus Restudy on Retention: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Testing Effect. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0037559
title: The bifurcation model of the testing effect
description: The bifurcation model (Kornell, Bjork, & Garcia, 2011) explains testing effects in terms of final test difficulty rather than initial test conditions. In the article's words, "study (and restudy) provides a modest increase to memory strength, whereas testing provides a more substantial increase, but only to those items successfully retrieved." Because testing strengthens only retrieved items, the model predicts testing effects are more likely, and larger, when the final test is more difficult. The article treats it as a viable framework for characterizing patterns across the literature.
requirements: Applies to designs comparing testing with restudy where item-level retrieval success at the intervening phase can bifurcate the tested items
constraints: The framework makes no assumptions about the impact of initial test conditions in dictating the degree of strength increment
target_learners: Adult laboratory participants learning verbal materials
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of studied information
examples: The article cites the frequently observed finding that testing effects increase with longer retention intervals as base support for the role of final test difficulty.
key_sources: Rowland, C. A. (2014, August 25). The Effect of Testing Versus Restudy on Retention: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Testing Effect. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0037559

article_title: The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect.
citation: Rowland, C. A. (2014, August 25). The Effect of Testing Versus Restudy on Retention: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Testing Effect. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0037559
title: Transfer appropriate processing (TAP) theory of the testing effect
description: TAP theory, drawing from Morris, Bransford, and Franks (1977), explains the testing effect via overlap in processing between initial and final tests. The article states that "TAP theory states that an initial test during learning, compared with restudy (or no test), induces a greater similarity with the type of processing that occurs at the final test." Its clear prediction is that the larger the overlap in processing required for initial and final testing, the larger the benefit of the initial test. The article notes it remains influential despite mixed empirical support.
requirements: Prediction requires variation or classification of initial and final test formats to assess processing overlap
constraints: The article reports results problematic for the theory, including studies where matching initial and final test characteristics yielded no benefit or suboptimal performance
target_learners: Adult laboratory participants learning verbal or multimedia materials
target_learning_goals: Retention and transfer of studied material
examples: Johnson and Mayer (2009) found a crossover interaction between practice test type and final test type, with performance highest when initial and final test types matched.
key_sources: Rowland, C. A. (2014, August 25). The Effect of Testing Versus Restudy on Retention: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Testing Effect. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0037559

article_title: The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect.
citation: Rowland, C. A. (2014, August 25). The Effect of Testing Versus Restudy on Retention: A Meta-Analytic Review of the Testing Effect. Psychological Bulletin. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/a0037559
title: The elaborative retrieval hypothesis of the testing effect
description: The elaborative retrieval hypothesis (Carpenter, 2009; Carpenter & DeLosh, 2006) holds that testing benefits retention because retrieval elaborates the memory trace. Carpenter (2009) "proposed a mechanism for such elaboration, whereby engaging in a retrieval attempt produces an elaboration of the target of the memory search through the activation of semantic associates of the target." Generated erroneous candidates may later serve as retrieval cues for the target. The hypothesis predicts larger testing effects for weakly associated cue-target pairs and for more difficult initial tests.
requirements: Cue-target materials with semantic content that affords activation of semantic associates during retrieval
constraints: The meta-analysis found only limited support for semantic elaboration accounts of the testing effect
target_learners: Adult laboratory participants learning paired associates
target_learning_goals: Retention of cue-target pairs
examples: Carpenter (2009) demonstrated that weakly associated cue-target pairs generate larger testing effects than strongly associated pairs, attributed to greater elaboration potential.

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
citation: Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09465-5
title: Cognitive load theory's cognitive architecture: working memory limits for novel information disappear for information retrieved from long-term memory
description: The review's foundational framework holds that novel information is processed by a capacity- and duration-limited working memory and then stored in an unlimited long-term memory. The article states that "Working memory was limited in capacity and duration when dealing with novel information but these limitations effectively disappeared when working memory dealt with information transferred from long-term memory." Instruction's major function is therefore to accumulate organised information in long-term memory, drawing on Ericsson and Kintsch's long-term working memory account.
requirements: Instruction presenting novel information must be organised to respect working memory limits
constraints: The limits apply to novel information; familiar information retrieved from long-term memory is not subject to them
target_learners: all learners acquiring novel, biologically secondary information
target_learning_goals: construction of knowledge in long-term memory
examples: The 1998 article's architecture, revisited here, grounded seven original cognitive load effects including the worked example and split-attention effects
key_sources: Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09465-5

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
citation: Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09465-5
title: Biologically primary versus biologically secondary knowledge distinction grounds cognitive load theory in evolutionary educational psychology
description: Post-1998 CLT categorises knowledge using Geary's distinction: biologically primary knowledge is evolved, acquired effortlessly and automatically without explicit teaching, and is modular; biologically secondary knowledge is culturally determined, domain-specific, and requires conscious effort and explicit instruction. The article states that "All secondary knowledge tends to require conscious effort on the part of the learner and explicit instruction on the part of an instructor." Educational institutions exist because of the need to acquire secondary knowledge.
requirements: Biologically secondary skills must be explicitly taught and actively learned
constraints: Attempts to teach purely generic-cognitive (primary) skills lead to dead-ends, per Sala and Gobet as cited; primary skills can only assist, not substitute for, secondary learning
target_learners: students in education and training contexts
target_learning_goals: acquisition of domain-specific biologically secondary knowledge
examples: The SBAR communication method for medical emergency teams: speaking is primary, but the specific SBAR reporting procedure is secondary and teachable
key_sources: Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09465-5

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
citation: Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09465-5
title: Five biologically primary principles of natural information processing systems underlie cognitive load theory
description: The review describes human cognition as a natural information processing system mimicking biological evolution, characterised by five principles: information store, borrowing and reorganising, randomness as genesis, narrow limits of change, and environmental organising and linking. The article states these "can be described by five basic, biologically primary principles. These principles provide the cognitive architecture that underlies the instructional procedures of cognitive load theory." They explain why explicit instruction reduces working memory load compared with random generate-and-test discovery.
requirements: Instruction should accord with the architecture: explicit, organised to reduce working memory load
constraints: The narrow limits of change principle's fixed-capacity assumption must be modified to allow working memory depletion after effort and recovery after rest, per Chen et al. as cited
target_learners: all learners
target_learning_goals: constructing and storing knowledge in long-term memory to govern appropriate action
examples: Borrowing information from others reduces working memory load compared with generating it via random generate and test during problem solving

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later
citation: Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09465-5
title: 4C/ID model extends cognitive load theory to course and curriculum design through four components
description: The four-component instructional design (4C/ID) model, developed in parallel with CLT on the same cognitive architecture, designs whole courses for complex learning with high element interactivity. The article states that "The 4C/ID model provides an important extension to cognitive load theory because it focuses on the design of educational programs of longer duration (e.g. courses or whole curricula)." Its four components are learning tasks, supportive information, procedural information, and part-task practice, managing intrinsic, extraneous and germane load respectively.
requirements: Learning tasks organised in increasing complexity levels with fading support; supportive information presented apart from task performance; procedural information presented just-in-time
constraints: The model exclusively deals with complex learning; over-reliance on part-task practice is not helpful for complex learning
target_learners: learners in longer educational programs developing complex skills or professional competencies
target_learning_goals: coordination of recurrent and non-recurrent constituent skills; knowledge automation
examples: Learning tasks are sequenced as a spiral curriculum with diminishing guidance, using the completion strategy from worked examples via completion tasks to conventional tasks

article_title: Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math
citation: Theobald Elli J. et al. (2020). Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1916903117
title: Heads-and-hearts hypothesis: gap reduction requires combining deliberate practice with inclusive teaching
description: The heads-and-hearts hypothesis is the authors' proposed explanation for the extensive variation in active learning's efficacy across studies. It holds that "meaningful reductions in achievement gaps only occur when course designs combine deliberate practice with inclusive teaching". Deliberate practice comprises extensive focused effort on relevant tasks, scaffolded exercises addressing specific deficits, immediate feedback, and repetition; inclusive teaching emphasizes treating students with dignity and respect, communicating confidence in students' ability to meet high standards, and genuine interest in their growth. The authors claim these elements act synergistically for underrepresented students facing stereotype threat, microaggressions, and underpreparation.
requirements: Course designs must combine deliberate practice elements with a classroom culture supporting inclusion
constraints: Explicit and rigorous testing of the heads-and-hearts hypothesis has yet to be done, per the authors
target_learners: Underrepresented minority and low-income undergraduate STEM students
target_learning_goals: Reducing achievement gaps in STEM course performance and retention
examples: The authors note the intensity data are consistent with the deliberate practice element, and cite a chemistry companion course combining belonging interventions with peer-led group problem-solving that narrowed gaps while controlling for self-selection bias
key_sources: Theobald Elli J. et al. (2020). Active learning narrows achievement gaps for underrepresented students in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and math. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1916903117

title: Individual-participant-data meta-analysis datasets of examination scores and passing rates disaggregated by minoritized-group status
description: Two compiled datasets underpin the analysis: 9,238 individual student examination records from 15 studies and 51 course sections, and 44,606 student records on passing rates from 26 studies and 174 course sections, disaggregated by race/ethnicity/URM status or socioeconomic status (e.g., Pell Grant eligibility). The authors obtained raw by-student data by contacting authors of 297 eligible studies. All data are openly available: "All data used in the analyses are available at https://github.com/ejtheobald/Gaps_Metaanalysis".
requirements: Datasets must disaggregate student information by URM status or socioeconomic status to identify students from MGS
constraints: Only 41 of 297 coded studies provided disaggregated data usable for the MGS analysis

target_learning_goals: Quantifying achievement gaps and instructional-treatment effects for underrepresented student subgroups

article_title: The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research
citation: Wisniewski B, Zierer K and Hattie J (2020) The Power of Feedback Revisited: A Meta-Analysis of Educational Feedback Research. Front. Psychol. 10:3087. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.03087
title: Treat different forms of feedback as independent measures and provide information-rich feedback rather than praise, rewards, or punishment
description: The article concludes that "Feedback must be recognized as a complex and diﬀerentiated construct that includes many diﬀerent forms with, at times, quite diﬀerent eﬀects on student learning." Because high-information feedback (task, process, and self-regulation content) shows a very large effect while reinforcement and punishment show low effects, designers should specify and deliver feedback rich in information about mistakes, their causes, and how to avoid them, and should not aggregate feedback into a single average treatment.
requirements: Feedback must convey information on task level and, ideally, process and self-regulation levels, not merely pleasant or aversive consequences
constraints: The authors note "a danger lies in over-simpliﬁcations, simply using average eﬀect sizes, and ignoring the variability across many studies, inﬂuences, contexts, and moderators"
target_learners: kindergarten through university students
target_learning_goals: cognitive achievement and motor skill outcomes
examples: The meta-analysis coded feedback as reinforcement/punishment, corrective, or high-information and found d = 0.99 for high-information versus d = 0.24 for reinforcement/punishment

article_title: Testing (quizzing) boosts classroom learning: A systematic and meta-analytic review.
citation: Yang, C., Luo, L., Vadillo, M. A., Yu, R., & Shanks, D. R. (2020). Testing (Quizzing) Boosts Classroom Learning: A Systematic and Meta-Analytic Review. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000309
title: Additional exposure, transfer-appropriate processing, and motivation theories account for the classroom testing effect; retrieval effort theory is not supported
description: The review evaluates four theoretical accounts of test-enhanced learning and concludes that "the research findings support the additional exposure, transfer-appropriate processing, and motivation theories to account for the classroom testing effect, but not the retrieval effort theory". Additional exposure attributes gains to reexposure of recalled material; transfer-appropriate processing to shared mental processes between quizzes and exams; motivation to enhanced effort, engagement, and test expectancy. The review stresses these accounts are "not necessarily mutually exclusive".
requirements: Moderator analyses linking effect sizes to control-condition reexposure, format consistency, and motivational indicators to adjudicate among the accounts
constraints: The review notes the retrieval effort prediction (recall tests beating recognition tests) was contradicted in classroom data, and that mechanisms proposed from laboratory research may have limited applicability to the classroom
target_learners: Elementary, middle school, high school, and university/college students across 18 subject categories
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention of studied knowledge, concept comprehension, and knowledge application in problem solving
examples: The review cites Schrank (2016) finding daily-exam class attendance stayed near 90% across a semester while control attendance fell to about 66%, as motivational support
key_sources: Yang, C., Luo, L., Vadillo, M. A., Yu, R., & Shanks, D. R. (2020). Testing (Quizzing) Boosts Classroom Learning: A Systematic and Meta-Analytic Review. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000309

article_title: A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
citation: Yeager, D. S., Hanselman, P., Walton, G. M., Murray, J. S., Crosnoe, R., Muller, C., Tipton, E., Schneider, B., Hulleman, C. S., Hinojosa, C. P., Paunesku, D., Romero, C., Flint, K., Roberts, A., Trott, J., Iachan, R., Buontempo, J., Yang, S. M., Carvalho, C. M., Hahn, P. R., Gopalan, M., Mhatre, P., Ferguson, R., Duckworth, A. title: Seed-and-soil account: sustained intervention effects require both an adaptive belief change and a congruent school context
description: The article's explanatory framework for its moderation findings: a psychological intervention supplies a high-quality seed (an adaptive belief system), but the effect is sustained only in conductive soil, a school context congruent with the proffered belief system. The authors write that "Sustained change may therefore require both a high-quality seed (an adaptive belief system conveyed by a compelling intervention) and conductive soil in which that seed can grow (a context congruent with the proffered belief system)". It explains why GPA effects were larger where peer norms supported challenge-seeking.
requirements: An intervention that conveys a compelling adaptive belief system
A school context, such as supportive peer norms, congruent with the proffered belief system
constraints: The article notes it cannot draw causal conclusions about school norms because norms were measured, not manipulated
target_learners: Ninth-grade students in secondary school, especially lower-achieving students
target_learning_goals: Sustained academic improvement in grades and rigorous course-taking
examples: In the National Study of Learning Mindsets, GPA effects among lower-achieving students were larger in low- and medium-achieving schools with supportive behavioural challenge-seeking norms
