title: Short online growth mindset intervention module (two self-administered sessions)
description: A scalable, low-cost online module of two self-administered sessions of roughly 25 minutes each, delivered about 20 days apart during school hours, that teaches that intellectual abilities can be developed. It uses the metaphor that the brain is like a muscle, stories from older students and admired adults, and a self-persuasion exercise teaching the idea to a struggling future ninth-grader. The article states "The intervention consisted of two self-administered online sessions that lasted approximately 25 min each and occurred roughly 20 days apart during regular school hours". The module will be available at no cost to secondary schools in the United States or Canada via PERTS.
requirements: Delivery early in the school year to set in motion a positive self-reinforcing cycle
High implementation fidelity, achieved in the median school with 97% of screens viewed
constraints: The article emphasizes that not all forms of growth mindset interventions can be expected to increase grades or advanced course-taking, even in targeted subgroups

article_title: Verbal redundancy in multimedia learning environments: A meta-analysis.
citation: Adesope, O. O., & Nesbit, J. C. (2012). Verbal Redundancy in Multimedia Learning Environments: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0026147
title: Dual Processing Theory of Multimedia Learning as an account of verbal redundancy effects
description: The article reviews the dual processing theory of multimedia learning (DPTML), which rests on three assumptions: working memory has partially independent auditory and visual systems, each limited in capacity, and learning occurs when information in each mode is selected, organized, and integrated. DPTML predicts that learners concurrently reading and hearing a message hold verbal and visual representations in functionally distinct working memories, so "Information that is misperceived in one modality is available through the other modality." The article uses DPTML as the theoretical prediction that spoken–written presentations should exceed spoken-only and written-only ones, a prediction the meta-analysis partly disconfirms.
requirements: Concurrent presentation of verbal information in both spoken and written modes during multimedia learning
constraints: The meta-analysis found no advantage of spoken–written over written-only presentation, contradicting DPTML's prediction of greater learning from spoken–written than either unimodal format
target_learners: postsecondary students
K-12 students
second-language learners
target_learning_goals: retention and transfer of multimedia instructional content
examples: The meta-analysis tested DPTML's prediction across 57 independent effect sizes comparing spoken–written, spoken-only, and written-only presentations
key_sources: Adesope, O. O., & Nesbit, J. C. (2012). Verbal Redundancy in Multimedia Learning Environments: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0026147

article_title: Verbal redundancy in multimedia learning environments: A meta-analysis.
citation: Adesope, O. O., & Nesbit, J. C. (2012). Verbal Redundancy in Multimedia Learning Environments: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0026147
title: Add spoken–written redundancy for system-paced, picture-free multimedia aimed at low-knowledge or less fluent readers, using written key terms rather than verbatim text
description: The article's design implication is that verbal redundancy should be applied selectively: adding text to audio narration benefits learning when learners cannot control pacing and materials lack pictorial components, and written text should display key terms extracted from the narration rather than reproduce it verbatim. The article reports that "presentations that use written key terms from spoken narrations are associated with greater learning than are fully redundant spoken–written presentations." Benefits concentrate among low prior knowledge, second-language, and nonfluent readers.
requirements: System-paced presentation without learner control over pacing
Learning materials free of concurrent diagrams, images, or animation
Written text drawn from key terms or abridgements of the narration
constraints: Not beneficial when learners can pause, rewind, or slow materials themselves (learner-paced studies showed no detectable effect)
Not beneficial when images or animation are concurrently presented (g = 0.06)
High prior knowledge learners showed no advantage (g = –0.05)
target_learners: low prior knowledge learners
second-language learners
early or nonfluent readers
target_learning_goals: retention of narrated multimedia content
examples: Mayer and Johnson (2008) studies cited in the article used key phrases of two or three words appearing at appropriate diagram locations as the phrases were spoken

article_title: Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning.
citation: Rohrer, D., Dedrick, R. F., & Stershic, S. (2015). Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(3), 900-908. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000001
title: Strategy-choice account: solving a mathematics problem requires discriminating problem kinds and associating each kind with a strategy, and interleaved practice trains this choice
description: The article proposes that a mathematics problem's solution has two steps: choosing a strategy and executing it. In its formal terms, "the choice of an appropriate strategy requires students to both discriminate between different kinds of problems ... and associate each kind of problem with an appropriate strategy". Blocked practice removes the need for choice because students know the strategy before reading the problem, whereas interleaved practice forces strategy choice on the basis of the problem itself, as tests do. The authors argue this, plus the inherent spacing interleaving guarantees, explains its benefits.
requirements: Assignments must juxtapose different kinds of problems so that students must select a strategy from the problem features rather than from lesson context
constraints: Blocked practice is not to be avoided entirely; a small block immediately after introducing a skill may help students focus on execution of the strategy
target_learners: seventh-grade mathematics students
mathematics students at elementary, middle school, and college levels
target_learning_goals: choosing an appropriate solution strategy for mathematics problems
retention of mathematics skills
key_sources: Rohrer, D., Dedrick, R. F., & Stershic, S. (2015). Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(3), 900-908. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000001

article_title: Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning.
citation: Rohrer, D., Dedrick, R. F., & Stershic, S. (2015). Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(3), 900-908. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000001
title: Rearrange mathematics practice so a portion of each assignment mixes different kinds of problems (interleaved practice)
description: The article recommends rearranging, rather than rewriting, existing practice material: with interleaved practice, "a portion of each assignment includes a set of different kinds of problems presented in an intermixed order". This forces students to choose a strategy based on the problem itself and distributes problems of the same kind across assignments, producing spacing. The authors state creators of textbooks or software "need only rearrange practice problems before releasing the next edition, without altering the problems or lessons".
requirements: Assignments must include a small block of new-skill problems plus one problem on each of several previously learned skills
Teachers must present solutions and students correct errors; teacher buy-in benefits from understanding the logic of strategy choice
constraints: Benefits might have been smaller if test problems required greater transfer
A more intensive review might have benefited the blocked condition more
Generalization to a wider variety of material and more teachers and students remains unknown
target_learners: middle school mathematics students
mathematics students across elementary, middle school, and college levels
target_learning_goals: strategy selection for mathematics problems
delayed retention of mathematics skills
examples: In the experiment, each assignment included four problems on the skill learned that day plus one problem on each of eight different skills learned previously; teachers reported they would use and recommend the intervention
key_sources: Rohrer, D., Dedrick, R. F., & Stershic, S. (2015). Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning. Journal of Educational Psychology, 107(3), 900-908. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000001

article_title: Multimedia Design for Learning: An Overview of Reviews With Meta-Meta-Analysis
citation: Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Harris, N. R., Sanders, T., Parker, P., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C. (2022). Multimedia design for learning: An overview of reviews with meta-meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211052329
title: Cognitive Load Theory: learning is constrained by working memory limits and load type
description: Cognitive Load Theory describes how learning is affected by the natural limits of working memory, distinguishing intrinsic load (complexity inherent in the task, operationalised as element interactivity) from extrinsic load (complexity a teacher adds that detracts from learning). The article uses it as one of two organising theories whose hypothesised design principles are tested against meta-analytic evidence. Newer models treat germane load as "a type of intrinsic load for more complex schema construction" rather than a third load type.
requirements: Designs must reduce extraneous load so freed working memory can be directed to processes that facilitate learning
constraints: The theory applies beyond multimedia learning (e.g., goal-free effect, worked examples), per the article
target_learners: all learners of multimedia instructional materials
target_learning_goals: managing cognitive load during knowledge acquisition
key_sources: Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Harris, N. R., Sanders, T., Parker, P., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C. (2022). Multimedia design for learning: An overview of reviews with meta-meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211052329

article_title: Multimedia Design for Learning: An Overview of Reviews With Meta-Meta-Analysis
citation: Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Harris, N. R., Sanders, T., Parker, P., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C. (2022). Multimedia design for learning: An overview of reviews with meta-meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211052329
title: Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning: dual-channel, limited-capacity, active processing
description: The Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning applies Cognitive Load Theory to multimedia, assuming "two parallel systems, one for what we see and one for what we hear" (the dual-channel assumption), limited attention capacity per channel, and active processing whereby mere passive exposure is insufficient. The article tests its hypothesised design principles (modality, contiguity, signaling, etc.) against pooled meta-analytic effects and concludes the results supported many tenets of both theories.
requirements: Good multimedia should use each channel in its natural format: seeing images and hearing sounds
constraints: The theory specifically addresses multimedia combining words and pictures, not single-channel media
target_learners: learners of multimedia instructional materials across education levels
target_learning_goals: leveraging visual and auditory channels to manage cognitive load
key_sources: Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Harris, N. R., Sanders, T., Parker, P., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C. (2022). Multimedia design for learning: An overview of reviews with meta-meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211052329

article_title: When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure
citation: Tanmay Sinha and Manu Kapur. (2021). When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211019105
title: Productive Failure as a high-fidelity subset of PS-I designs within preparation for future learning
description: Productive Failure (PF) is a design paradigm in which an initial generation-and-exploration phase has students activate prior knowledge and generate multiple, typically failing, representations and solution methods for problems on not-yet-taught concepts, followed by a consolidation phase in which instruction builds on student-generated solutions. The article situates PF as "a subset of PS-I designs that fall under the broader design paradigm of preparation for future learning", and defines PF design fidelity as "the extent to which these criteria are implemented within a PS-I design". The rationale is "to design for failure in the initial learning to minimize failure in the longer term".
requirements: Seven coded fidelity criteria: problems affording multiple RSMs, evidence of multiple RSM generation, affective draw of the problem, group work as participation structure, instruction building on student solutions, and social surround facilitation in both the problem-solving and instruction phases
constraints: Not all PS-I designs are PF; only those following the PF design principles of Kapur and Bielaczyc (2012) count, and the article notes the least represented criteria are social surround facilitation, instruction building on student solutions, and group work
target_learners: Students from 2nd grade through undergraduates and professionals learning new concepts in math, science, medicine, and other domains
target_learning_goals: Conceptual knowledge and transfer of newly taught concepts
key_sources: Tanmay Sinha and Manu Kapur. (2021). When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211019105

article_title: The Expertise Reversal Effect
citation: Kalyuga, S., Ayres, P., Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (2003). The Expertise Reversal Effect. Educational Psychologist, 38(1), 23-31. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3801_4
title: The expertise reversal effect: the reversal of cognitive load effects with increasing learner expertise, explained by schema-based guidance replacing instruction-based guidance
description: The article names and substantively describes the expertise reversal effect as "the reversal of cognitive load ef- fects with expertise": instructional techniques highly effective for inexperienced learners lose effectiveness or become negative for experienced learners. Its cognitive-load explanation is that novices lack schemas, so instructional guidance acts as a substitute, while experts' activated schemas provide full guidance, and redundancy between the two causes cross-referencing that "will require addi- tional working memory resources and might cause a cognitive overload." The review traces the effect's interaction with split-attention, redundancy, modality, worked-example, isolated-interacting elements, and imagination effects.
requirements: Instructional designs must be tailored to the level of experience of intended learners, without which "the effectiveness of instructional designs is likely to be random."
constraints: In the isolated-interacting elements studies the review reports no full reversal, only elimination of the effect with increased expertise.
target_learners: learners at all levels of domain-specific expertise, from novices to experienced learners
target_learning_goals: schema construction and automation
examples: The review cites experiments on electrical circuit diagrams, industrial machinery instruction, mechanical trade apprenticeship, spreadsheet learning, and database use in which effects reversed or disappeared with increased expertise.
key_sources: Kalyuga, S., Ayres, P., Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (2003). The Expertise Reversal Effect. Educational Psychologist, 38(1), 23-31. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3801_4

article_title: The Expertise Reversal Effect
citation: Kalyuga, S., Ayres, P., Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (2003). The Expertise Reversal Effect. Educational Psychologist, 38(1), 23-31. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3801_4
title: Tailor instructional design, including gradually fading guidance, to the level of learner experience
description: The article's central instructional implication is that "instructional design should be tailored to the level of experience of intended learners"; otherwise, effectiveness "is likely to be random" and design recommendations "can be potentially quite counterproductive." As supporting practice, it reports that Renkl and colleagues consistently showed detailed worked examples suit novices but "should be gradually faded out with increased levels of learner knowledge and be replaced by problems," with fading superior to an abrupt switch.
requirements: Ongoing assessment of learner expertise in the specific domain so guidance can be matched or faded as knowledge grows.
constraints: Recommendations based on a particular design can reverse as expertise increases, so a fixed design recommendation is limited to its learner-expertise range.
target_learners: novice and more experienced learners in a domain
target_learning_goals: efficient schema construction and automation
examples: Renkl, Atkinson, Maier, and Staley (2002) found that a fading-out procedure from worked examples to problems was superior to an abrupt switch.
key_sources: Kalyuga, S., Ayres, P., Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (2003). The Expertise Reversal Effect. Educational Psychologist, 38(1), 23-31. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3801_4

article_title: Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning
citation: Manu Kapur (2016). Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning. Educational Psychologist, 51(2), 289-299. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1155457
title: Four design possibilities arising from the incommensurability of performance and learning
description: The article proposes a 2x2 framework crossing short-term performance and longer-term learning outcomes, yielding four design possibilities. It states that "Exploiting the incommensurability between learning and performance results in four possibilities for design: productive success, productive failure, unproductive success, and unproductive failure." Productive success maximizes both; productive failure sacrifices initial performance for longer-term learning; unproductive success shows an "illusion of learning in initial high performance"; unproductive failure maximizes neither. The framework is used to reposition direct instruction and discovery learning as extremes of a larger design space.
requirements: The framework presupposes that conditions maximizing initial performance can be distinguished empirically from conditions maximizing longer-term learning
constraints: The categorization is explicitly relative: what seems productive success against one comparison can seem unproductive success against another
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students learning novel concepts
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding
transfer
long-term retention
examples: Direct instruction is analyzed as a productive success relative to pure discovery learning but potentially an unproductive success relative to productive failure and productive success designs
key_sources: Manu Kapur (2016). Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning. Educational Psychologist, 51(2), 289-299. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1155457

article_title: Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning
citation: Manu Kapur (2016). Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning. Educational Psychologist, 51(2), 289-299. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1155457
title: Four design features for realizing the benefits of productive failure
description: A synthesis across productive failure studies yields four interdependent design features for the initial problem-solving phase and subsequent consolidation. The article states the task "should be challenging enough to engage the learner in the exploration, but not so challenging that the learner gives up," must "admit multiple solutions, strategies, and representations," should "activate learner's prior knowledge—formal as well as intuitive," and requires a teacher or expert to build on student-generated solutions by comparing and contrasting them with the correct solution. In classrooms, disciplinary norms and expectations for problem solving should also be set and reinforced.
requirements: A consolidation phase in which a teacher or expert compares and contrasts student-generated solutions with the correct solution, directing attention to critical features of the targeted concept
constraints: Benefits depend on the problem activating prior knowledge even when learners have not formally learned the concept; in classroom ecologies, disciplinary norms and expectations must be set and reinforced
target_learners: school students learning novel concepts in domains such as mathematics
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding
transfer
encoding of critical features
examples: The pattern derives from a synthesis of quasi-experimental classroom studies and controlled experiments on productive failure and preparation for future learning cited in the article
key_sources: Manu Kapur (2016). Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning. Educational Psychologist, 51(2), 289-299. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1155457

article_title: Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning
citation: Manu Kapur (2016). Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning. Educational Psychologist, 51(2), 289-299. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1155457
title: Rethinking cognitive load theory's assumptions in light of productive failure findings
description: The article argues cognitive load theory needs a rethink of two basic assumptions: that cognitive load is the main mechanism of learning, and that higher cognitive load is monotonically bad for learning. It states "It may also not always be true that the higher the cognitive load, the worse the learning," since higher load can drive attention and activate prior knowledge that helps students learn from instruction. Evidence from productive failure research shows the initial problem-solving phase engenders higher cognitive load yet leads to better learning from subsequent instruction. The article also argues CLT's definition of learning as schema acquisition is too narrow and its proponents have theoretically underdetermined CLT by assuming learners have no prior knowledge.
requirements: Consideration of cognitive, social, and cultural mechanisms alongside cognitive load, with the choice of mechanisms depending on learning goals
constraints: Kalyuga and Singh (2015) are cited as arguing CLT's recommendations may be limited to contexts where the instructional goal is schema acquisition of basic knowledge, not complex problem-based learning environments
target_learners: novice learners encountering novel concepts
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding
transfer
prior knowledge activation
examples: The article cites Kalyuga et al. (2001) showing worked-example benefits disappeared as domain knowledge increased, and argues CLT allows but underresearches using unguided problem solving to activate learners' prior knowledge
key_sources: Manu Kapur (2016). Examining Productive Failure, Productive Success, Unproductive Failure, and Unproductive Success in Learning. Educational Psychologist, 51(2), 289-299. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1155457

article_title: The Effect of Teacher Coaching on Instruction and Achievement: A Meta-Analysis of the Causal Evidence
citation: Kraft, M.A., Blazar, D., Hogan, D. (2018). The effect of teaching coaching on instruction and achievement: A meta-analysis of the causal evidence. Review of Educational Research, 88(4), 547-588. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318759268
title: Theory of action for teacher coaching: individualized observation-and-feedback cycles translate teacher knowledge into classroom practice and student achievement
description: The article situates coaching within a PD theory of action (Figure 1) in which student achievement rises only through changes in teacher knowledge and classroom practice, with coaching as the key lever for translating knowledge into practice. Coaching is characterized by "an observation and feedback cycle in an ongoing instructional or clinical situation" and is defined as individualized, intensive, sustained, context-specific, and focused on deliberate practice of specific skills. The authors use this framework to define their working definition of coaching interventions and to motivate the instruction and achievement outcomes they meta-analyze.
requirements: Coaches are instructional experts who work one-on-one with teachers, interacting at least every couple of weeks over an extended period, within the teachers' own classrooms
constraints: The article excludes teacher preparation and induction programs and programs where coaches also provided direct services to students, since effects on achievement could not be attributed to improved instruction
target_learners: in-service early childhood through 12th grade teachers in the U.S. and other developed nations
target_learning_goals: improving teachers' classroom instructional practice
raising student achievement on standardized assessments
examples: The meta-analysis codes 60 causal studies against this framework, including complementary elements such as group trainings, instructional content, and video libraries
key_sources: Kraft, M.A., Blazar, D., Hogan, D. (2018). The effect of teaching coaching on instruction and achievement: A meta-analysis of the causal evidence. Review of Educational Research, 88(4), 547-588. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318759268

article_title: The Effect of Teacher Coaching on Instruction and Achievement: A Meta-Analysis of the Causal Evidence
citation: Kraft, M.A., Blazar, D., Hogan, D. (2018). The effect of teaching coaching on instruction and achievement: A meta-analysis of the causal evidence. Review of Educational Research, 88(4), 547-588. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318759268
title: Pair coaching with group trainings and instructional materials rather than relying on coaching alone
description: The article's exploratory meta-analytic regressions indicate that coaching programs are more strongly associated with improved instruction and achievement when coaching is embedded in a broader PD package. Pairing coaching with group trainings was associated with larger effects on both outcomes, and pairing it with instructional resources such as curriculum was associated with "greater gains (0.21 SD larger)" on instruction. The authors interpret this as consistent with teachers building baseline skills before engaging directly with a coach.
requirements: Coaching must be combined with at least one complementary PD element such as group trainings, instructional content materials, or video libraries
constraints: These meta-analytic regressions are descriptive and do not capture the causal effect of a given program feature; limited statistical power prevents ruling out smaller relationships
target_learners: in-service pre-kindergarten through 12th grade teachers
target_learning_goals: improving instructional practice
raising student achievement
examples: In the reviewed sample, 48 of 60 studies combined coaching with group trainings, 22 provided instructional content materials, and 14 supplemented coaching with video exemplars

article_title: Meta-Analysis of Inquiry-Based Learning: Effects of Guidance
citation: Lazonder, A. W., & Harmsen, R. (2016). Meta-analysis of inquiry-based learning: Effects of guidance. Review of Educational Research, 86(3), 681-718. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315627366
title: Six-type typology of inquiry learning guidance ordered by specificity
description: The meta-analysis adopts T. De Jong and Lazonder's (2014) framework, which "organized their framework according to the specificity of the guidance learners need to successfully perform an inquiry." It orders six types from least to most specific: process constraints, status overviews, prompts, heuristics, scaffolds, and explanations. Process constraints "give no overt directions at all but instead organize the inquiry into a series of manageable subtasks"; prompts "remind the learner to perform a particular action"; scaffolds assist "by explaining what to do and how to do it"; explanations "offer the most specific type of guidance." Each type is matched to an intended audience in Table 1, from learners with matured inquiry skills to learners largely incognizant of the action.
requirements: Guidance must be classified by its specificity (extensiveness/explicitness) rather than by the inquiry phase or skill it supports, so that differential effects across age groups can be tested
constraints: Category labels reflect the meta-analysis's terminology and "do not necessarily match the designation used in the original study"; scaffolding fading is often absent in short-term inquiries because inquiry skills develop slowly
target_learners: Learners aged 5 to 22 in math and science education, from children to adolescents
target_learning_goals: Scientific reasoning skills: generating hypotheses, designing experiments, evaluating evidence, and acquiring domain knowledge through inquiry
examples: The Go-Lab environment incorporates scaffolds assisting elementary, middle school, and high school learners in formulating research questions, generating hypotheses, and designing experiments
key_sources: Lazonder, A. W., & Harmsen, R. (2016). Meta-analysis of inquiry-based learning: Effects of guidance. Review of Educational Research, 86(3), 681-718. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315627366

article_title: Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Meta-Analytic Review
citation: Kulik, J. A., & Fletcher, J. D. (2016). Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Meta-Analytic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315581420
title: Defining features of intelligent tutoring systems: knowledge structures plus inner- and outer-loop tutoring behaviors
description: The review distinguishes intelligent tutoring systems (ITSs) from earlier CAI tutors structurally and behaviorally. Structurally, ITSs combine an explicit domain-knowledge model, a dynamic student model, a pedagogical module, and a user interface, drawing hints and feedback from "organized knowledge databases, or information structures". Behaviorally, following VanLehn, "ITSs display both inner- and outer-loop behaviors, whereas CAI tutors display outer-loop behaviors only": inner-loop support (prompting, hinting) occurs while the student works on a problem, outer-loop support (feedback, new problems) at end of problem. The meta-analysis used expert classification plus the during-problem-help criterion to identify ITSs.
requirements: The article treats helping learners while they work on a problem, not just after solutions are recorded, as a practical criterion for classifying a tutor as an ITS.
target_learners: learners in K-12, postsecondary, and military training settings evaluated in ITS studies
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge and problem-solving skills taught by intelligent tutoring systems
examples: The 50 evaluated systems ranged from Cognitive Tutor and the DARPA Digital Tutor to Sherlock 2, AutoTutor, and KERMIT, all classified as step-based or substep-based ITSs.
key_sources: Kulik, J. A., & Fletcher, J. D. (2016). Effectiveness of Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Meta-Analytic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315581420

article_title: Learning from Examples: Instructional Principles from the Worked Examples Research
citation: Atkinson, R. K., Derry, S. J., Renkl, A., & Wortham, D. (2000). Learning from Examples: Instructional Principles from the Worked Examples Research. Review of Educational Research, 70(2), 181-214. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543070002181
title: A three-factor causal framework organizes the factors that influence learning from worked examples
description: The review proposes a framework representing a causal model of the major factors shown to influence learning from worked examples, which it defines as 'instructional devices that provide an expert's problem solution for a learner to study'. The framework groups moderators into 'intra-example features, in other words, how the example is designed', inter-example features concerning relationships among examples and practice problems within a lesson, and individual differences in how students self-explain examples.
requirements: Effective examples must have highly integrated components, employing multiple modalities in presentation and emphasizing conceptual structure by labeling or segmenting
Examples should be presented in close proximity to matched practice problems
constraints: Studying worked examples is not the preferred method when the instructional goal is the third stage of skill acquisition, automatic performance, where problem-solving practice is of critical importance
target_learners: novices in domains such as mathematics, physics, and computer programming
target_learning_goals: acquisition of problem-solving schemas
transfer to novel problems
examples: The review derives the framework from laboratory experiments and classroom investigations across mathematics, physics, and computer programming, deliberately drawing on multiple research groups and theoretical viewpoints rather than one research program

article_title: Improving Students’ Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology
citation: Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58. https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100612453266
title: Replace rereading and highlighting with more effective techniques such as practice testing
description: The monograph recommends that students abandon the popular but inconsistently effective techniques of rereading and highlighting in favor of better-supported alternatives. It states that "Most students report rereading and highlighting, yet these techniques do not consistently boost students' performance, so other techniques should be used in their place (e.g., practice testing instead of rereading)." The recommendation follows directly from the low utility assessments of those techniques.
requirements: Students must be able to implement the replacement technique without assistance, per the monograph's selection criteria
target_learners: students from elementary grades through college regulating their own learning
target_learning_goals: improving retention and achievement across content domains
examples: The monograph explicitly names practice testing as the substitute for rereading

article_title: Improving Students’ Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology
citation: Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58. https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100612453266
title: Four-category framework for evaluating the generalizability of learning techniques
description: The monograph organizes each technique review around four categories of variables, inspired by Jenkins' (1979) model: "materials, learning conditions, student characteristics, and criterion tasks." Materials pertain to the content to be learned; learning conditions concern how and where the technique is implemented (e.g., dosage, group vs. individual); student characteristics include age, ability, prior knowledge, and motivation; criterion tasks range from cued recall to problem solving and essay writing. Each of the 10 technique reviews assesses generalizability across these categories before assigning a utility rating.
requirements: Sufficient empirical evidence must be available for each technique to permit a preliminary assessment of efficacy across the categories
constraints: The framework excludes techniques requiring advanced technologies or extensive teacher-prepared materials, per the monograph's selection criteria
target_learners: students and teachers selecting techniques for self-regulated learning across content domains
target_learning_goals: evaluating which learning techniques support retention, comprehension, and transfer
examples: Each of the 10 technique reviews is structured with sections on learning conditions, student characteristics, materials, criterion tasks, educational contexts, implementation, and overall assessment

article_title: A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy
citation: Jonathan Firth, Ian Rivers and James Boyle. (2021). A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy. Review of Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/rev3.3266
title: Discriminative-contrast hypothesis of the interleaving effect
description: Proposed by Kang and Pashler (2012), this account explains the interleaving benefit through "increased opportunities to compare and contrast exemplars if they are seen side by side or adjacent in a series". It explains why spacing items out can be harmful to interleaving — the review notes the two phenomena are not additive — and why interleaving unrelated items (e.g. science terms with vocabulary) is not beneficial. The review treats it as the leading candidate explanation alongside attentional accounts.
requirements: Materials must be related category exemplars such that juxtaposition creates meaningful contrast between categories
constraints: Spacing and interleaving are not additive; spacing items out can reduce or eliminate the interleaving benefit
target_learners: secondary school students and above
university undergraduates
target_learning_goals: inductive concept learning and categorisation
transfer to novel exemplars
examples: Zulkiply and Burt (2013a) went as far as to call interleaving 'the compare and contrast effect'
key_sources: Jonathan Firth, Ian Rivers and James Boyle. (2021). A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy. Review of Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/rev3.3266

article_title: A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy
citation: Jonathan Firth, Ian Rivers and James Boyle. (2021). A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy. Review of Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/rev3.3266
title: Attentional accounts of the interleaving effect: attention attenuation and attentional bias
description: The review describes two related attentional explanations. The attention-attenuation hypothesis (Wahlheim, Dunlosky, and Jacoby, 2011) holds that "blocking is inferior because attention dwindles when learners see repeated examples of the same type", supported by Metcalfe and Xu's (2016) mind-wandering probes showing more mind wandering in blocked conditions. The attentional-bias hypothesis (Carvalho and Goldstone) holds that interleaving directs attention to between-category differences while blocking directs attention to within-category similarities, implying the similarity of examples may matter as much as order.
requirements: Learners must attend to contrasts between adjacent examples for the interleaving benefit to arise
constraints: Attentional-bias account implies classroom application is highly context specific, drawing on teachers' professional knowledge of the material
target_learners: secondary school students and above
university undergraduates
target_learning_goals: inductive concept learning
sustained attention during example study
examples: Metcalfe and Xu (2016) presented paintings with a mind-wandering probe and found mind wandering at a higher level during the blocked condition
key_sources: Jonathan Firth, Ian Rivers and James Boyle. (2021). A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy. Review of Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/rev3.3266

article_title: The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes
citation: Michelene T. H. Chi & Ruth Wylie. (2014). The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychologist, 49(4), 219-243. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2014.965823
title: The ICAP Framework: A Taxonomy of Four Modes of Cognitive Engagement Based on Overt Behaviors
description: The ICAP framework is a taxonomy that differentiates students' cognitive engagement into four modes based on the overt behaviors they display while learning: Interactive, Constructive, Active, and Passive. The framework proposes that "engagement behaviors can be categorized and differentiated into one of four modes" and that each mode corresponds to different underlying knowledge-change processes. It provides "specific domain-general guidelines for creating more engaging lessons as well as modifying existing activities to increase engagement, using simple overt measures of behavior to assess the level to which students are engaged." The framework is intended to help teachers and educational designers classify and design learning activities.
requirements: Overt behaviors must be content relevant to be classified into a mode
A content analysis of learners' responses is necessary to confirm the actual mode of an activity
constraints: Overt behaviors are a proxy, not a perfect measure — students may be covertly processing deeply while appearing passive
Boundaries between modes are not totally rigid; some activities fall on the boundary between two categories
target_learners: K-12 students
higher education students
target_learning_goals: improved learning outcomes across subject matters through differentiated cognitive engagement
examples: While reading a text, students can be reading silently (passive), underlining (active), taking notes in one's own words (constructive), or asking a friend questions about the materials (interactive)
key_sources: Michelene T. H. Chi & Ruth Wylie. (2014). The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychologist, 49(4), 219-243. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2014.965823

article_title: The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes
citation: Michelene T. H. Chi & Ruth Wylie. (2014). The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychologist, 49(4), 219-243. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2014.965823
title: Knowledge-Change Processes Underlying Each ICAP Mode: Storing, Integrating, Inferring, and Co-Inferring
description: The article postulates four broad types of knowledge-change processes, each associated with one mode of engagement. Passive engagement involves isolated "storing" of information in an encapsulated manner without integration with prior knowledge. Active engagement involves "integrating" processes in which manipulated information activates relevant prior knowledge and new information is assimilated into the activated schema. Constructive engagement involves "inferring" processes including inducing, deducing, revising, repairing, reorganizing, and reflecting. Interactive engagement involves "co-inferring" processes where "each learner infers new knowledge from activated and integrated knowledge and iteratively infers knowledge with new inputs from conversational partner(s)."
requirements: Knowledge-change processes are assumed to be relatively distinct from task-specific learning processes
The same set of knowledge-change processes is assumed for all activities within a given mode
constraints: The authors state their main assumption is not whether they have postulated the processes accurately but rather that they are relatively different for each mode
target_learners: K-12 students
higher education students
target_learning_goals: understanding how different engagement modes produce different changes in knowledge structures
examples: A student who read about blood clots could recite the textbook explanation but gave a contradictory answer when asked to use her own theory, suggesting the new ideas were stored in an isolated or encapsulated way
key_sources: Michelene T. H. Chi & Ruth Wylie. (2014). The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychologist, 49(4), 219-243. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2014.965823

article_title: Active learning increases student performance in science, engineering, and mathematics
citation: Freeman S, Eddy SL, McDonough M, Smith MK, Okoroafor N, Jordt H, Wenderoth MP. (2014). Active learning increases student performance in science, engineering, and mathematics. PNAS 111(23):8410-8415. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1319030111
title: Consensus working definition of active learning versus traditional lecturing
description: The article establishes an operational definition of active learning built from written definitions collected from 338 audience members at biology departmental seminars, then coded into a consensus statement: "Active learning engages students in the process of learning through activities and/or discussion in class, as opposed to passively listening to an expert." It emphasizes higher-order thinking and often involves group work. Traditional lecturing is defined, following Bligh, as continuous exposition by the teacher, with student activity limited to note-taking and occasional unprompted questions. This definition governed which studies were admitted to the meta-analysis.
requirements: Studies admitted to the comparison had total class time devoted to each approach not differing by more than 30 min/wk
constraints: The definition spans a wide array of activities and intensities, from 10% to 100% of class time, so the meta-analysis evaluates the average effect of any active learning type
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students
target_learning_goals: course examination performance
concept-inventory performance
course failure rates
examples: Interventions coded under the definition included occasional group problem-solving, in-class worksheets or tutorials, personal response systems with or without peer instruction, problem-based learning, and studio or workshop course designs.

article_title: Meta-analysis of the modality effect
citation: Ginns, P. (2005). Meta-analysis of the modality effect. Learning and Instruction, 15(4), 313-331. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2005.07.001
title: Cognitive load theory account of the modality effect via dual working-memory channels
description: Cognitive load theory explains the modality effect through Baddeley's working-memory model: presenting graphics visually for processing in the visual cache while presenting associated text auditorily for processing in the phonological loop effectively expands working memory capacity for learning. If all information is presented visually, the learner must process everything in the visual cache, increasing the likelihood working memory is overloaded and learning impeded. The article contrasts this capacity-expansion account with Tabbers' temporal-contiguity explanation and Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning, which emphasises richer referential connections between dual-mode representations.
requirements: Applies when textual and graphical information are related and must be mentally integrated
Learners are novices for whom the material imposes high element interactivity
constraints: Tabbers' experiments found the effect disappeared or reversed under self-paced conditions, questioning the simple capacity-expansion explanation
Kalyuga et al. (2000) found the modality effect disappeared and reversed as learner expertise increased
target_learners: novice learners across primary, secondary and adult education
target_learning_goals: comprehension and schema construction from multimedia instructional materials combining graphics and text
examples: The meta-analysis tested the theory's predictions that element interactivity and pacing moderate the effect
key_sources: Ginns, P. (2005). Meta-analysis of the modality effect. Learning and Instruction, 15(4), 313-331. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2005.07.001

article_title: Integrating information: A meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects
citation: Ginns, P. (2006). Integrating information: A meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects. Learning and Instruction, 16(6), 511-525. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.10.001
title: Cognitive Load Theory account of split-attention costs
description: Cognitive load theory is an instructional design theory foregrounding human cognitive architecture: a limited working memory that can be circumvented by schemas in long-term memory. It "identifies several sources of mental effort (i.e., cognitive load) which, when acting in concert, may overload available working memory resources and retard learning" — intrinsic load from element interactivity, extraneous load from unsuitable design, and germane load from suitable design. The meta-analysis uses this account to explain why separating related elements in space or time forces extraneous search-and-match or rehearsal activity that retards schema construction.
requirements: Instructional materials must take account of the limits of students' working memory and their interaction with long-term memory schemas
constraints: Element interactivity cannot be objectively counted; it depends on learners' prior knowledge, so researchers match materials to knowledge levels
target_learners: novice learners
target_learning_goals: schema construction and automation from complex instructional materials
examples: The meta-analysis tests the theory's prediction that reducing split attention aids learning, especially for high element interactivity materials
key_sources: Ginns, P. (2006). Integrating information: A meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects. Learning and Instruction, 16(6), 511-525. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.10.001

article_title: Integrating information: A meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects
citation: Ginns, P. (2006). Integrating information: A meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects. Learning and Instruction, 16(6), 511-525. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.10.001
title: For novices learning complex materials, increase spatial or temporal contiguity of related elements of information
description: When related elements of to-be-learned information (e.g. a diagram and its formulae, words and pictures) are separated in space or time, designers should physically integrate them or present them concurrently. The meta-analysis shows "increasing integration supports learning across a wide variety of educational domains, media, and levels", with gains "consistently higher than the mean effect derived by Hattie (1987)" for novices studying complex materials. Integration reduces extraneous search-and-match or rehearsal load, freeing capacity for schema construction.
requirements: Related elements must be mutually referring and unintelligible in isolation; learners should be novices relative to the material
constraints: Effects established only for novices; for more experienced learners integrated formats can become redundant and counter-productive (expertise reversal)
target_learners: novice learners across senior primary school, secondary school, technical college, and adult education
target_learning_goals: learning from complex, high element interactivity instructional materials in mathematics, science, and engineering/technical domains
examples: Studies integrated diagrams with related instructions in worked examples, presented narration concurrently with animation, and colour-coded associated referents to reduce search
key_sources: Ginns, P. (2006). Integrating information: A meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects. Learning and Instruction, 16(6), 511-525. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.10.001

article_title: What Schools Need to Know About Fostering School Belonging: a Meta-analysis
citation: Allen, K., Kern, M.L., Vella-Brodrick, D., Hattie, J., & Waters, L. (2018). What Schools Need to Know About Fostering School Belonging: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 1–34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9389-8
title: Ten student-level themes influence school belonging during adolescence
description: The article organizes the fragmented school belonging literature into a taxonomy of ten student-level themes identified through systematic review: "academic motivation, emotional stability, personal characteristics, parent support, peer support, teacher support, gender, race and ethnicity, extracurricular activities and environmental/school safety". This taxonomy resolves inconsistency in terminology and structures the subsequent meta-analysis of each theme's association with belonging.
requirements: Themes were derived from a systematic review of research on school belonging at the student level during adolescence in educational settings
constraints: The taxonomy addresses the student level during adolescence; the article notes research on school belonging has been "fragmented and diluted by inconsistency in the use of terminology"
target_learners: school-aged children
secondary students
target_learning_goals: school belonging
psychological functioning
examples: The systematic review identified the ten themes, which were then each meta-analytically examined across 51 studies

article_title: How deliberation makes better citizens: The Danish Deliberative Poll on the euro
citation: Vibeke Normann Andersen and Kasper M. Hansen. (2007). How deliberation makes better citizens: The Danish Deliberative Poll on the euro. European Journal of Political Research, Volume 46, Issue 4, pp. 531-556. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1475-6765.2007.00699.x
title: The Deliberative Poll as a quasi-experimental model of deliberative democracy
description: The Deliberative Poll is a deliberative-democracy instrument in which a representative sample of citizens assembles to deliberate on a policy question, and its effects are studied quasi-experimentally. The article states: "As a quasi-experiment, the Deliberative Poll is an example of deliberative democracy." In this Danish application, "a representative sample of 364 Danish citizens assembled to deliberate on Denmark's participation in the single currency," and the resulting opinion change, knowledge gains and improved reasoned opinion formation are treated as evidence about what deliberation does to citizens.
requirements: A representative sample of citizens assembled for deliberation on a defined policy subject
Pre/post measurement of opinions and knowledge to support quasi-experimental analysis
constraints: Findings are tied to a single national Poll on the euro in Denmark; the article treats the Poll as one example of deliberative democracy rather than a general test
target_learners: Adult citizens in a national representative sample
target_learning_goals: Forming reasoned political opinions
Increasing knowledge of the deliberated policy issue
examples: The Danish national Deliberative Poll on the euro, in which 364 citizens deliberated on Denmark's participation in the single currency

article_title: How deliberation makes better citizens: The Danish Deliberative Poll on the euro
citation: Vibeke Normann Andersen and Kasper M. Hansen. (2007). How deliberation makes better citizens: The Danish Deliberative Poll on the euro. European Journal of Political Research, Volume 46, Issue 4, pp. 531-556. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1475-6765.2007.00699.x
title: Four-dimension framework for analyzing deliberative processes
description: The article organizes its analysis of the Deliberative Poll around four research questions that together form an evaluative framework for deliberative processes. As printed: "Four research questions regarding these deliberative processes are analyzed: openness and access, the quality of deliberation, efficiency and effectiveness, and publicity and accountability." Each dimension captures a distinct requirement a deliberative forum must meet — who may take part, how well the deliberation proceeds, whether it produces results, and whether it is publicly accountable — and the Danish euro Poll is assessed along all four.
requirements: A concrete deliberative forum (such as a Deliberative Poll) to which the four questions can be applied
constraints: The framework is applied here to one national Deliberative Poll on the single European currency
target_learners: Adult citizens participating in national deliberative forums
target_learning_goals: Evaluating the quality and democratic legitimacy of deliberative processes
examples: Analysis of the Danish Deliberative Poll on the euro along openness and access, quality of deliberation, efficiency and effectiveness, and publicity and accountability

article_title: Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications
citation: Harold J. Kushner and G. George Yin. (2003). Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications, Second Edition. Springer-Verlag, New York. https://www.springer-ny.com
title: Stochastic approximation paradigm: recursive stochastic difference equations with small step sizes
description: The book's organizing framework is the stochastic approximation paradigm, in which "a stochastic diﬀerence equation such asθn+1 = θn +ϵnYn" is iterated, where θn is a parameter estimate, Yn is a random variable derived from noise-corrupted observations, and the step size is small and may go to zero. One "recursively adjusts the parameter so that some goal is met asymptotically." The book concerns the qualitative and asymptotic properties of such recursive algorithms across their diverse application forms, including constrained variants where iterates are projected back to a set if they leave it.
requirements: A goal to be met asymptotically through recursive parameter adjustment based on noisy observations
constraints: In applications where the optimal value changes with time, step size is kept strictly away from zero rather than sent to zero
target_learners: Graduate students and researchers in applied probability, optimization, and adaptive systems
target_learning_goals: Understanding and applying recursive stochastic algorithms for root finding, function minimization, and on-line optimization under noise
examples: Root finding for an unknown function via noisy measurements, recursive Monte Carlo minimization, and parameter adjustment for drug dosage level estimation
key_sources: Harold J. Kushner and G. George Yin. (2003). Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications, Second Edition. Springer-Verlag, New York. https://doi.org/10.1007/b97441

article_title: Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications
citation: Harold J. Kushner and G. George Yin. (2003). Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications, Second Edition. Springer-Verlag, New York. https://www.springer-ny.com
title: ODE method for analyzing stochastic approximation convergence
description: The ODE (ordinary differential equation) method, introduced by Ljung and extensively developed by Kushner and coworkers, is the book's central analytical technique. "The main idea is to show that, asymptotically, the noise eﬀects average out so that the asymptotic behavior is determined eﬀectively by that of a 'mean' ODE." The ODE is obtained by local analysis, averaging the observations as though the parameter were fixed. The authors state that "the ODE method has become a fundamental technique in the current toolbox" and note that constraints, state dependent noise, discontinuities, and other difficulties can be handled, with the ODE replaced by a constrained ODE or differential inclusion as needed.
requirements: Averaging/weak ergodic conditions on the noise processes
Interpolation of the discrete iterates into a continuous time process
constraints: Depending on the application, the ODE might be replaced by a constrained (projected) ODE or a differential inclusion
target_learners: Graduate students and researchers in stochastic optimization and recursive algorithm analysis
target_learning_goals: Proving convergence and rate of convergence of recursive stochastic algorithms under general noise processes and constraints
examples: Convergence proofs for an animal learning example with random step sizes and a pattern classification problem (Chapter 5)
key_sources: Harold J. Kushner and G. George Yin. (2003). Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications, Second Edition. Springer-Verlag, New York. https://doi.org/10.1007/b97441

article_title: Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications
citation: Harold J. Kushner and G. George Yin. (2003). Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications, Second Edition. Springer-Verlag, New York. https://www.springer-ny.com
title: Constrain or truncate stochastic approximation iterates rather than allowing unbounded iterates
description: The book advocates constrained algorithms in which iterates that leave a prescribed set are projected back into it. When a parameter takes excessive values, "one would normally alter the unconstrained algorithm if the parameter θ took on excessive values. The simplest alteration is truncation." The authors argue that "allowing unbounded iterates seems to be of greater mathematical than practical interest," because model physics at large parameter values are often poorly known. Practical algorithms should also include other safeguards against bad noise or inappropriate step sizes.
requirements: A constraint set H to which iterates are projected when they leave it
Other safeguards ensuring robustness against bad noise or inappropriate step sizes
constraints: Constraints are needed because the physics of models at large parameter values are often poorly known or inconvenient to model, so convenient mathematical assumptions may be meaningless there
target_learners: Practitioners implementing stochastic approximation algorithms in signal processing, communications, and adaptive control
target_learning_goals: Designing robust recursive stochastic algorithms that converge reliably in practical systems
examples: In the queue optimization problem of Chapter 2, the parameter controls the service rate, and excessive service-rate values would trigger truncation
key_sources: Harold J. Kushner and G. George Yin. (2003). Stochastic Approximation and Recursive Algorithms and Applications, Second Edition. Springer-Verlag, New York. https://doi.org/10.1007/b97441

article_title: Annual Age-Grouping and Athlete Development
citation: Cobley, S., Baker, J., Wattie, N., McKenna, J. (2009). Annual Age-Grouping and Athlete Development. Sports Med 39, 235–256. https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200939030-00005
title: Relative age effects (RAEs) as participation and attainment constraints arising from annual age-grouping
description: The article defines RAEs as constraints on sport participation and long-term attainment that arise when athletes are organized into annual age-group cohorts. It states that RAEs occur "as a result of chronological age and associated physical (e.g. height) differences as well as selection practices in annual age-grouped cohorts." The framework links organizational strategy (annual age-grouping), physical maturation differences within cohorts, and selection practices as jointly producing the effect.
requirements: Annual age-grouped cohorts with selection practices that differentiate athletes within the cohort
constraints: The effect is framed for sport contexts organized by annual age-grouping
target_learners: youth and adolescent sport participants
target_learning_goals: sport participation and long-term athlete attainment

title: Meta-analytic dataset of 38 RAE studies across 14 sports and 16 countries
description: The article assembles and re-examines a corpus for the first meta-analysis of RAEs: "A total of 38 studies, spanning 1984–2007, containing 253 independent samples across 14 sports and 16 countries" were combined "using odds ratios and random effects procedures for combining study estimates." article_title: A Unilateral Grading Contract to Improve Learning and Teaching
citation: Danielewicz, Jane and Peter Elbow. (2009). A Unilateral Grading Contract to Improve Learning and Teaching. College Composition and Communication 61(2). https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.14394/23309
title: Guarantee a grade for completing specified activities so teacher and student attention shifts from grading to learning
description: The article's core design recommendation: specify in writing the activities that reliably produce good writing, and promise the base grade for completing them regardless of judged quality. The stated aim is that "teachers and students give as much attention as possible to writing and as little as possible to grades." Evaluation continues throughout the semester, but it is decoupled from the base grade, so feedback stops functioning as a grade signal and students keep control over concrete activities they can fulfill.
requirements: The contract must list activities the teacher has found reliable in producing the target quality of work over the term
All decisions about what is acceptable for the base grade must be made without regard to judgments of work quality
constraints: Institutional settings that require final grades force hybridity; the authors would not use grades at all outside such institutions
Students desperate for grades higher than the base grade remain in hock to teacher evaluation
target_learners: first-year college writing students
honors students
basic writers
students alienated from writing
target_learning_goals: improved writing quality
sustained effort, revision, and participation in writing processes
examples: Jane and Peter use essentially the same ten-provision contract in their first-year writing courses, guaranteeing a B for attendance, meeting due dates, participation, informal writing, peer feedback, substantive revision, copyediting, conferences, and portfolio submission
key_sources: Danielewicz, Jane and Peter Elbow. (2009). A Unilateral Grading Contract to Improve Learning and Teaching. College Composition and Communication 61(2). https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.14394/23309

article_title: A Unilateral Grading Contract to Improve Learning and Teaching
citation: Danielewicz, Jane and Peter Elbow. (2009). A Unilateral Grading Contract to Improve Learning and Teaching. College Composition and Communication 61(2). https://hdl.handle.net/20.500.14394/23309
title: Hybrid grading: behavior-based grades up to a threshold, quality-based grades above it
description: The article's organizing framework splits the grading scale by what earns the grade: below the threshold (B), the grade rests wholly on observable behaviors and completion; above it, the grade rests wholly on judged quality of writing. As the authors put it, "about behaviors, we take the gloves off; about quality of writing, we give students the power to decide (again, up to the grade of B)." The framework lets teachers maintain high standards of quality while rewarding behaviors that improve writing, and it underlies their claims about feedback, motivation, and grade inflation.
requirements: A base grade available to every student, not dependent on skill or prior training
Base-grade decisions made without regard to judgments of work quality
constraints: Extending the contract to a contract for an A would require dropping those constraints and specifying quality criteria not every student could attain
The authors developed the framework at strong public universities, though they report Shor and colleagues used contracts with working-class students at urban, commuter colleges
target_learners: first-year college writing students
honors students
basic writers
students alienated from writing
target_learning_goals: writing quality
processes such as revision and peer review
examples: Throughout the semester the authors use only three possible grades—not satisfactory for B, satisfactory for B, and better than B—deferring distinctions among higher grades until final portfolios are read

article_title: A General Method of Empirical Q-matrix Validation

title: Discrimination-index rationale for Q-matrix validation grounded in mathematical proofs of lemmas and a theorem

The abstract states: "The rationale for using the index as the basis for a proposed validation method is provided in the form of mathematical proofs to several relevant lemmas and a theorem." The index is defined for CDMs subsumed by the generalized DINA model, so the framework is general rather than tied to one specific CDM.

article_title: Algorithm Aversion: People Erroneously Avoid Algorithms after Seeing Them Err
citation: Berkeley J. Dietvorst, Joseph P. Simmons, and Cade Massey. (2014). Algorithm Aversion: People Erroneously Avoid Algorithms After Seeing Them Err. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000033
title: Algorithm aversion: greater intolerance for error from algorithms than from humans
description: The article names and substantively describes algorithm aversion, the tendency to avoid algorithmic forecasters in favor of inferior human forecasters. It proposes a mechanism: people "more quickly lose confidence in algorithmic than human forecasters after seeing them make the same mistake," so seeing an algorithm perform and err increases aversion even when the algorithm outperforms. The construct frames the five studies, in which experience with the forecaster is manipulated before participants bet on forecasts.
requirements: Algorithms must occasionally err visibly for the aversion to arise; without experience with the algorithm, participants often choose it
constraints: The article notes its studies cannot say whether the effect would persist if algorithms were many times more accurate than humans than the advantage tested here
target_learners: adult forecasters and decision makers choosing between human and algorithmic judgment
target_learning_goals: choosing between human and statistical forecasting methods when making predictions
examples: In five studies, participants forecast MBA applicants' success or U.S. states' airline-passenger ranks and chose whether to tie incentives to the model's or a human's forecasts

article_title: ‘Models of’ versus ‘Models for’
citation: Gouvea, J., Passmore, C. (2017). 'Models of' versus 'Models for'. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-017-9884-4
title: The models of versus models for heuristic distinguishes representational from purpose-driven conceptions of models
description: The article presents a heuristic contrasting two ways of understanding models in science. Models can be understood in terms of how they represent phenomena in the world (models of), or with respect to the aims and intentions of a cognitive agent (models for). The authors present this contrast as a tool educators can use to notice and interpret how models are positioned in standards, curriculum, and classrooms.
requirements: Educators must examine standards, curriculum materials, and classroom practice through the lens of the aims and intentions of model users, not only representational accuracy.
constraints: The authors present the contrast as a heuristic, not a tested instructional intervention.
target_learners: K-12 science students
target_learning_goals: Understanding the role of models and modeling in science
examples: The authors use the heuristic to examine how the practice of developing and using models is positioned in the Framework for K-12 Science Education and the Next Generation Science Standards.
key_sources: Gouvea, J., Passmore, C. (2017). 'Models of' versus 'Models for'. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-017-9884-4

article_title: ‘Models of’ versus ‘Models for’
citation: Gouvea, J., Passmore, C. (2017). 'Models of' versus 'Models for'. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-017-9884-4
title: Use the models of versus models for heuristic to notice and interpret how models are positioned in standards, curriculum, and classrooms
description: The article recommends that educators apply the models of versus models for contrast as an interpretive lens. Rather than treating models only as representations of phenomena, educators should attend to the aims and intentions models serve when enacting the modeling practice in science classrooms. The authors frame this as a way to examine the role the practice of developing and using models plays in science and how it can be leveraged in a science classroom.
requirements: Educators must have access to standards, curriculum, and classroom instances of modeling to which the heuristic can be applied.
constraints: The article presents the heuristic as a lens for noticing and interpreting, not as a validated instructional procedure.
target_learners: K-12 science students
target_learning_goals: Meaningful engagement in the scientific practice of developing and using models
examples: The authors present the heuristic in response to the inclusion of developing and using models in the Framework for K-12 Science Education and the Next Generation Science Standards.

citation: Gouvea, J., Passmore, C. (2017). 'Models of' versus 'Models for'. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-017-9884-4
title: An agent-based account of models grounds the enactment of modeling in science classrooms
description: The article advances an agent-based account of models drawn from philosophy of science, in which models are understood relative to a cognitive agent's aims and intentions rather than solely as representations of phenomena in the world. The authors use this account to derive implications for enacting modeling in science classrooms, contrasting it with purely representational (semantic) views of models.

constraints: The account is presented as a philosophical position with implications for classrooms, not as an empirically tested model of learning.

examples: The authors discuss implications of this view for enacting modeling in science classrooms under the NGSS.

article_title: Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government
citation: DAN M. KAHAN, ELLEN PETERS, ERICA CANTRELL DAWSON and PAUL SLOVIC. (2017). Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government. Behavioural Public Policy, Volume 1, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/bpp.2016.2
title: Identity-protective cognition thesis (ICT)
description: ICT is the article's explanatory framework for persistent public conflict over societal risks. It "treats cultural conflict as disabling the faculties that members of the public use to make sense of decision-relevant science". On this account, people with greater reasoning skill are not more accurate on identity-charged data; instead they "use their quantitative-reasoning capacity selectively to conform their interpretation of the data to the result most consistent with their political outlooks". The experiment's finding that polarization increased with numeracy was read as supporting this thesis over the science comprehension thesis.
requirements: A dataset whose correct interpretation bears on positions tied to the perceiver's cultural or political identity, so that motivated interpretation can operate.
constraints: The article's supporting evidence comes from an experiment using a gun control ban framing; the thesis is offered as an account of culturally charged decision-relevant science, not of all quantitative reasoning, where numerate subjects did substantially better.
target_learners: general public members interpreting decision-relevant science
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of empirical data bearing on politically contested societal risks
examples: The article's experiment reframed one dataset as a gun control ban study, inducing polarization that grew with numeracy.

article_title: Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government
citation: DAN M. KAHAN, ELLEN PETERS, ERICA CANTRELL DAWSON and PAUL SLOVIC. (2017). Motivated numeracy and enlightened self-government. Behavioural Public Policy, Volume 1, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/bpp.2016.2
title: Science comprehension thesis (SCT)
description: SCT is the rival account the article tested. It "identifies defects in the public's knowledge and reasoning capacities as the source of such controversies" over societal risks. The thesis predicts that individuals with greater science comprehension — here operationalized as numeracy, "a measure of the ability and disposition to make use of quantitative information" — should interpret contested data more accurately and thus be less polarized. The experiment disconfirmed this prediction: polarization was greatest among the most numerate subjects.
requirements: A population measurable on knowledge and reasoning capacities (here numeracy) so that comprehension deficits can be related to risk controversy.
constraints: The article reports that this thesis was not supported in its experiment: polarization increased rather than abated among the highest-numeracy subjects.
target_learners: general public members interpreting decision-relevant science
target_learning_goals: accurate causal inference from empirical data
examples: The article used the skin rash framing to show numeracy helps when data are uncharged, isolating what SCT cannot explain about charged data.
