article_title: Gender Inequality in Deliberative Participation
citation: Christopher F. Karpowitz, Tali Mendelberg, and Lee Shaker. (2012). Gender Inequality in Deliberative Participation. American Political Science Review, Volume 106, Issue 3, pp. 533-547. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055412000329
title: Gender composition interacts with decision rule to shape inequality in deliberation
description: The article proposes that inequality in deliberation is not fixed but depends on an interaction between two institutional and social features of the deliberating group. It moves "beyond the debate by hypothesizing that the group's gender composition interacts with its decision rule to exacerbate or erase the inequalities". The framework explains when deliberation equalizes women's voice and authority and when it does not, and it is tested experimentally with many groups.
requirements: Groups must vary in gender composition and operate under specified decision rules for the interaction to be observed
constraints: Tested in experimental deliberation settings with many groups, as described in the article
target_learners: adult participants in deliberative forums
target_learning_goals: equal voice and authority in group deliberation
examples: The article tests the hypothesis and alternatives using experimental data with many groups and links between individuals' attitudes and speech.
key_sources: Christopher F. Karpowitz, Tali Mendelberg, and Lee Shaker. (2012). Gender Inequality in Deliberative Participation. American Political Science Review, Volume 106, Issue 3, pp. 533-547. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055412000329

article_title: Gender Inequality in Deliberative Participation
citation: Christopher F. Karpowitz, Tali Mendelberg, and Lee Shaker. (2012). Gender Inequality in Deliberative Participation. American Political Science Review, Volume 106, Issue 3, pp. 533-547. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055412000329
title: Fit deliberative procedure to the social context to avoid gender inequality
description: The article's design recommendation is that deliberative settings can be arranged to avoid gender inequality by matching institutional procedure to the situation's social context. As the authors state, "Deliberative design can avoid inequality by fitting institutional procedure to the social context of the situation." In practice this means choosing decision rules in light of the group's gender composition, per the interaction finding.
requirements: Designers must know or control the group's gender composition and choose a decision rule deliberately
constraints: The article's supporting evidence comes from experimental deliberation groups; the available text reports the finding at the level of rule-by-composition combinations
target_learners: adult citizens in deliberative forums
target_learning_goals: equal voice and authority in deliberation
examples: The article reports the gap disappears under unanimous rule and few women, or under majority rule and many women.

citation: Korpershoek, H., Harms, T., de Boer, H., van Kuijk, M., & Doolaard, S. (2016). A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Classroom Management Strategies and Classroom Management Programs on Students' Academic, Behavioral, Emotional, and Motivational Outcomes. title: Four-category taxonomy of classroom management strategy foci: teacher, student behavior, social-emotional development, and teacher–student relationships
description: The meta-analysis organizes classroom management programs by coding each included intervention for the presence or absence of four categories of strategies. As the article states, "Programs were coded for the presence/absence of four categories of strategies: focusing on the teacher, on student behavior, on students’ social-emotional development, and on teacher–student relationships." This taxonomy serves as the organizing framework for the moderator analyses of which strategy foci drive intervention effectiveness in primary education.

constraints: Applied to primary education intervention studies published 2003–2013

description: The evidence base of the meta-analysis is a corpus of controlled intervention studies of classroom management strategies and programs in primary education. The article states that "The analysis included 54 random and nonrandom controlled intervention studies published in the past decade (2003–2013)." Studies were coded for four strategy categories and outcomes spanning academic, behavioral, social-emotional, and motivational domains, yielding an average effect of g = 0.22 across outcomes.

constraints: Limited to studies published 2003–2013

article_title: Do Experiences With Nature Promote Learning? Converging Evidence of a Cause-and-Effect Relationship
citation: Kuo M, Barnes M and Jordan C (2019) Do Experiences With Nature Promote Learning? Converging Evidence of a Cause-and-Effect Relationship. Front. Psychol. 10:305. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.00305
title: Eight-pathway framework linking nature experiences to learning and development
description: The review proposes a framework (Figure 1) in which experiences with nature promote academic learning, personal development, and environmental stewardship via at least eight distinct pathways: five centered in the learner (rejuvenated attention, stress relief, self-discipline, motivation and enjoyment, physical activity and fitness) and three in the learning context (calmer, quieter, safer settings; warmer, more cooperative relations; loose parts plus autonomy fostering beneficial play). The review states that "at least eight distinct pathways plausibly contribute to these outcomes" and that the multiplicity of mechanisms may explain the consistency of the nature-learning relationship. Relationships with experimental support are marked with an asterisk in the figure; qualified causal language is used elsewhere.
requirements: Evidence for each pathway must be distinguished between experimental cause-and-effect evidence and merely converging associational evidence, as the review does
constraints: The review uses qualified causal language (e.g., "seems to increase") where converging but non-experimental evidence points to a likely causal relationship; loose-parts play effects on child development have yet to be quantitatively demonstrated
target_learners: children and students in formal and informal educational settings
target_learning_goals: academic learning
personal development
environmental stewardship
examples: The review maps exposures (e.g., classroom views of trees, school gardens, field trips), mechanisms, and outcomes in Figure 1, marking experimentally supported links such as nature boosting concentration and retention of subject matter

article_title: Towards a Theory of When and How Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Supports Learning
citation: Loibl, K., Roll, I. & Rummel, N. (2017). Towards a Theory of When and How Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Supports Learning. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 693–715. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9379-x
title: Initial theory of PS-I: a set of interconnected cognitive mechanisms accounting for when and how problem solving followed by instruction supports learning
description: The article proposes an initial theory of PS-I built on a set of interconnected cognitive mechanisms. The authors state that "The second goal is to identify a set of interconnected cognitive mechanisms that may account for these outcomes" and that "Empirical evidence from PS-I literature is associated with these mechanisms and supports an initial theory of PS-I." The theory explains both positive and negative effects of PS-I implementations: "positive and negative effects of PS-I are explained using the suggested mechanisms." It organizes the review's empirical findings into a mechanism-based explanatory account of the two-phase instructional scheme.
requirements: The theory links mechanisms to empirical evidence from PS-I literature, as the article associates "Empirical evidence from PS-I literature" with the mechanisms
constraints: The article labels it an "initial theory of PS-I"
target_learners: learners in PS-I implementations (e.g., mathematics and statistics students in the reviewed studies)
target_learning_goals: conceptual and procedural learning outcomes addressed by PS-I approaches
examples: The review associates empirical evidence from PS-I studies with the mechanisms and uses them to explain positive and negative effects.
key_sources: Loibl, K., Roll, I. & Rummel, N. (2017). Towards a Theory of When and How Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Supports Learning. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 693–715. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9379-x

citation: Loibl, K., Roll, I. & Rummel, N. (2017). Towards a Theory of When and How Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Supports Learning. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 693–715. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9379-x
title: Taxonomy of PS-I implementations: mapping designs by commonalities and differences, with Productive Failure and Invention as prominent examples
description: The article organizes the landscape of PS-I approaches by mapping implementations and identifying shared and differing design features. It states the first goal is "to map the landscape of different PS-I implementations, to identify commonalities and differences in designs, and to associate the identified design features with patterns in the learning outcomes." Productive Failure and Invention are named as often cited examples: "Two often cited examples of instructional approaches following the PS-I scheme include Productive Failure and Invention." The taxonomy serves as the organizing framework for the review's outcome analysis.
requirements: Design features must be identifiable across implementations so they can be associated with learning outcome patterns
constraints: Wording differences across conditions that are natural (e.g., invent a formula versus solve using a formula) are not counted as design confounds, per the article's notes
target_learners: designers and researchers of PS-I instruction; learners in problem-solving-first settings
target_learning_goals: preparing learners for learning from subsequent instruction
examples: Productive Failure and Invention are the two often cited PS-I examples the review uses to illustrate the scheme.

article_title: Towards a Theory of When and How Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Supports Learning
citation: Loibl, K., Roll, I. & Rummel, N. (2017). Towards a Theory of When and How Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Supports Learning. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 693–715. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9379-x
title: PS-I lesson structure: an initial problem-solving phase followed by an instruction phase
description: The article defines PS-I as a class of learning approaches combining two phases: "an initial problem-solving phase followed by an instruction phase (PS-I)." This two-phase structure is the reusable lesson-level pattern that Productive Failure and Invention instantiate. The pattern's effectiveness depends on how the phases are designed, with the review showing the instruction phase must feature contrasting cases or build on student solutions. The pattern orients learners before canonical instruction is provided.
requirements: A genuine initial problem-solving phase must precede the instruction phase
The instruction phase must implement contrasting cases or build on student solutions to foster learning
constraints: PS-I without the identified design features is not associated with learning gains in the review
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students in domains such as mathematics and statistics
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding and preparation for future learning from instruction
examples: Productive Failure and Invention are named by the article as often cited instructional approaches following the PS-I scheme.

article_title: INPUT, INTERACTION, AND SECOND LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT
citation: Alison Mackey. (1999). INPUT, INTERACTION, AND SECOND LANGUAGE DEVELOPMENT: An Empirical Study of Question Formation in ESL. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 21(4). https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263199004027
title: Long's (1996) updated interactionist hypothesis: implicit negative feedback obtained through negotiated interaction facilitates SLA
description: The study is framed by Long's (1996) updated version of the interactionist hypothesis, which "claims thatimplicit negative feedback, which can be obtained through negotiated interaction, facilitatesSLA." Similar claims are attributed to Pica (1994) and Gass (1997). The article tests this framework empirically by manipulating learners' participation in task-based conversational interaction and measuring grammatical development. It positions the hypothesis against prior partial support from studies of production, lexical acquisition, pushed output, and recasts.
requirements: Conversational interaction must provide opportunities for negotiated interaction through which implicit negative feedback can be obtained
constraints: Prior studies cited in the article, such as Loschky (1994), did not find effects for interaction on grammatical development
target_learners: adult ESL learners of varying L1 backgrounds
target_learning_goals: second language grammatical development, specifically question formation
examples: The study assigned 34 adult ESL learners to four experimental groups and one control group for task-based interaction in a pretest-posttest design

title: Task-based interaction treatment for ESL question formation development
description: The instructional element evaluated in this study was task-based conversational interaction delivered to adult ESL learners working on question formation. Learners (N = 34, varying L1 backgrounds) were divided into four experimental groups and one control group and "took part in task-based interaction." Development was measured with a pretest-posttest design, with research questions targeting the developmental outcomes of taking part in various types of interaction. The element operationalizes the interactionist hypothesis in a classroom-relevant L2 grammar context.
requirements: Learners must actively participate in the interaction for developmental benefits, per the study's findings
target_learners: adult ESL learners of varying L1 backgrounds

grammatical development

article_title: Purposely Teaching for the Promotion of Higher-order Thinking Skills: A Case of Critical Thinking
citation: Miri, B., David, BC. & Uri, Z. (2007). Purposely Teaching for the Promotion of Higher-order Thinking Skills: A Case of Critical Thinking. Res Sci Educ 37, 353–369. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11165-006-9029-2
title: Teach higher order thinking purposely and persistently to develop students' critical thinking capabilities
description: The article's central design recommendation is that teachers should "purposely and persistently practice higher order thinking strategies" rather than relying on traditional instruction, because the study found significant critical thinking gains only in the group so taught. It presents this as giving "a good chance for a consequent development of critical thinking capabilities". The principle applies within science education classrooms where teachers deliberately plan for thinking skills.
requirements: Teachers must deliberately plan and persistently enact higher order thinking strategies over time, not teach traditionally
constraints: Evidence base is a longitudinal case study within science education; the article states a good chance of development, not a guaranteed outcome
target_learners: high school students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
disposition towards critical thinking
examples: An experimental group of 57 science students exposed to higher order thinking teaching strategies showed significant critical thinking improvement while traditionally taught controls did not

article_title: Modeling Individualization in a Bayesian Networks Implementation of Knowledge Tracing
citation: Pardos, Z.A., Heffernan, N.T. (2010). Modeling Individualization in a Bayesian Networks Implementation of Knowledge Tracing. UMAP 2010, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 6075. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-13470-8_24
title: Individualized Bayesian knowledge tracing framework
description: The article introduces a reformulation of the knowledge tracing model within a Bayesian networks framework so that individual student parameters can be estimated. It formulates "the individualization problem entirely within a Bayesian networks framework that fits individualized as well as skill specific parameters simultaneously, in a single step." This extends the Corbett and Anderson knowledge tracing approach, which the field had used for over a decade without allowing individual learning rates or individualized initial knowledge estimates.
requirements: A Bayesian networks implementation of knowledge tracing that can fit individual student parameters alongside skill-specific parameters in a single step
target_learners: Students using intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of student knowledge and skill mastery
examples: The authors applied the framework to real-world data from 42 problem sets in an intelligent tutoring system

article_title: Bayesian knowledge tracing, logistic models, and beyond: an overview of learner modeling techniques
citation: Chris Piech, Jonathan Bassen, Jonathan Huang, Surya Ganguli, Mehran Sahami, Leonidas Guibas, Jascha Sohl-Dickstein. (2015). Deep Knowledge Tracing. https://github.com/chrispiech/DeepKnowledgeTracing
title: Deep Knowledge Tracing: modeling latent student knowledge with recurrent neural networks
description: Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT) applies recurrent neural networks that are deep in time to model a student's latent knowledge state and its temporal dynamics as large vectors of artificial neurons. The latent representation is learned from interaction data rather than hard-coded from expert concept labels. Inputs are one-hot encodings (or random compressed vectors for large feature spaces) of the exercise-answered/correctness tuple, and outputs are predicted probabilities of correctness for each exercise. The article evaluates the LSTM and vanilla RNN variants on simulated, Khan Academy, and Assistments data.
requirements: Requires large amounts of student interaction training data, which the authors say makes RNNs well suited to online education environments
constraints: One disadvantage of RNNs over simple hidden Markov methods is that they require large amounts of training data, making them ill-suited to a small classroom environment, per the article
target_learners: Students interacting with online educational platforms and intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Prediction of student performance on future exercises; modeling knowledge growth over time
examples: The article trains an LSTM with hidden dimensionality of 200 and mini-batch size 100 using stochastic gradient descent with dropout and truncated gradients.
key_sources: Chris Piech, Jonathan Bassen, Jonathan Huang, Surya Ganguli, Mehran Sahami, Leonidas Guibas, Jascha Sohl-Dickstein. (2015). Deep Knowledge Tracing. https://github.com/chrispiech/DeepKnowledgeTracing

This release supports replication of the LSTM/RNN knowledge tracing results and reuse of the training pipeline in follow-up work.

article_title: Learner Control in Hypermedia Environments
citation: Scheiter, K., & Gerjets, P. (2007). Learner Control in Hypermedia Environments. Educational Psychology Review 19, 285–307. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9046-3
title: Learner control as the defining feature distinguishing hypermedia learning environments from system-controlled multimedia
description: The article frames hypermedia systems as characterized by a high level of interactivity, which "is referred to as learner control in the respective literature." Learner control is treated as a major advantage of hypermedia for learning and instruction because it might increase interest and motivation, facilitate adaptive instruction, and provide affordances for active and constructive information processing. The review uses this framing to organize its analysis of why effectiveness findings are ambiguous.
requirements: Learners must actually exercise control over navigation and information processing within the hypermedia environment for the proposed motivational and adaptive benefits to apply
constraints: The article states the advantages are potential: learner control "might" increase interest and motivation, and the review argues effectiveness is difficult to demonstrate
target_learners: Students learning with hypermedia systems
target_learning_goals: Knowledge acquisition from hypermedia learning environments
examples: The review analyzes instructional potentials of learner-controlled hypermedia environments against the ambiguous results of effectiveness studies
key_sources: Scheiter, K., & Gerjets, P. (2007). Learner Control in Hypermedia Environments. Educational Psychology Review 19, 285–307. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9046-3

article_title: Learner Control in Hypermedia Environments
citation: Scheiter, K., & Gerjets, P. (2007). Learner Control in Hypermedia Environments. Educational Psychology Review 19, 285–307. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9046-3
title: Use hypermedia for learning in a sensible way, since effectiveness depends on how it is used
description: The review advances the claim "that hypermedia may be effective only if used in a sensible way," positioning sensible use — rather than hypermedia per se — as the condition for effectiveness. This principle follows from the review's analysis of usability problems, moderating learner characteristics, and conceptual and methodological weaknesses in the research base. It is used to derive guidelines for further research on hypermedia learning.
requirements: Design and use of hypermedia must take into account usability problems, learner characteristics, and conceptual foundations identified in the review
constraints: The article states effectiveness "may" occur only under sensible use; it does not specify operational thresholds in the available text
target_learners: Students learning with hypermedia environments
target_learning_goals: Effective learning from learner-controlled hypermedia instruction
examples: The review derives "a couple of guidelines for further research on hypermedia learning" from this claim and its supporting findings

article_title: Cooperative Learning and Academic Achievement: Why Does Groupwork Work?. [Aprendizaje cooperativo y rendimiento académico: ¿por qué funciona el trabajo en grupo?]

title: Four theoretical perspectives on achievement effects of cooperative learning
description: The chapter organizes explanations for cooperative learning's achievement effects into four named perspectives: "Motivational, social cohesion, developmental, and cognitive elaboration." Each perspective offers a different account of why students working in small groups to help each other learn produces achievement gains, and the chapter reviews evidence for each before reconciling them.

constraints: The perspectives concern achievement effects of cooperative learning specifically, not other outcomes

title: Design cooperative learning with group goals and individual accountability for group success
description: Because classroom evidence primarily supports the motivational perspective, effective cooperative learning should emphasize "the use of group goals and individual accountability for group success." Students work in small groups toward shared goals, and each member's individual performance must count toward the group's success, creating incentive structures that motivate helping.
requirements: Group goals must be used and individual accountability for group success must be established for the motivational mechanism to operate
constraints: This principle reflects the perspective that classroom evidence primarily supports; the review notes methods from other perspectives also contribute under certain conditions
target_learners: students in classroom cooperative learning groups
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
examples: The review identifies group goals and individual accountability as the design features emphasized by the motivational perspective that classroom research primarily supports

citation: Slavin, R. E. (2014). Cooperative Learning and Academic Achievement: Why Does Groupwork Work?. Anales De Psicología, 30(3), 785–791. https://doi.org/10.6018/analesps.30.3.201201
title: Unified theory reconciling the four perspectives on cooperative learning effects
description: The chapter's culminating contribution is a unified theory that reconciles the motivational, social cohesion, developmental, and cognitive elaboration perspectives into a single account of why groupwork works. Rather than treating the four perspectives as competing, the unified theory integrates them so that each perspective's methods can be understood as contributing to achievement under the conditions the chapter identifies.
requirements: Must accommodate the evidence that classroom research primarily supports the motivational perspective while allowing all four perspectives to contribute under certain conditions
constraints: The theory concerns achievement effects of cooperative learning methods
target_learners: students in cooperative learning groups
target_learning_goals: academic achievement

article_title: Professional Learning Communities: A Review of the Literature
citation: Stoll, L., Bolam, R., McMahon, A., Wallace, M., & Thomas, S. (2006). Professional Learning Communities: A Review of the Literature. Journal of Educational Change. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10833-006-0001-8
title: Capacity as a blend of motivation, skill, positive learning, organisational conditions and culture, and infrastructure of support
description: The review defines capacity as a composite construct: "Capacity is a complex blend of motivation, skill, positive learning, organisational conditions and culture, and infrastructure of support." Together these components give individuals, groups, whole school communities and school systems "the power to get involved in and sustain learning over time." The framework spans individual and collective levels, from single teachers to whole school systems, and underpins the review's argument that building capacity is critical for sustainable improvement.
requirements: Building capacity requires attention to all components of the blend, not only individual teacher skill

school staff
whole school communities
target_learning_goals: sustaining learning and improvement over time
promoting pupils' learning

title: Professional learning communities as a vehicle for capacity building and sustainable school improvement
description: The review positions professional learning communities (PLCs) as an organisational approach to school improvement: "Developing professional learning communities appears to hold considerable promise for capacity building for sustainable improvement." It notes that PLCs have "become a 'hot topic' in many countries," indicating wide international policy and practice interest. The framework connects teacher learning communities to the capacity blend of motivation, skill, organisational conditions and support infrastructure described elsewhere in the review.

constraints: The promise is stated with hedging ('appears to hold considerable promise'), not as a demonstrated effect

article_title: Effectiveness of Critical Thinking Instruction in Higher Education: A Systematic Review of Intervention Studies
citation: Dawit T. Tiruneh, An Verburgh & Jan Elen. (2014). Effectiveness of Critical Thinking Instruction in Higher Education: A Systematic Review of Intervention Studies. Higher Education Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/hes.v4n1p1
title: Ennis's four-approach taxonomy of critical thinking instruction: general, infusion, immersion, and mixed
description: The review adopts Ennis's (1989) taxonomy organizing CT instruction into four approaches. In the general approach, CT is taught separately from subject matter; the infusion approach integrates CT instruction in subject matter while making general CT principles explicit; the immersion approach embeds CT in subjects without making principles explicit; and the mixed approach combines the general approach with infusion or immersion, with a separate thread teaching general CT principles alongside subject-specific CT instruction. The review uses this taxonomy to categorize all 33 included studies.
requirements: CT skills must be identifiable and definable as domain-independent skills that can be taught and transferred
constraints: The review notes the associated assumption that domain-independent thinking skills can be taught and transferred to daily-life situations
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills and dispositions
examples: All 33 studies were categorized: general approach 5 studies (15%), infusion 9 (27%), immersion 16 (49%), mixed 3 (9%)

article_title: The role of biomedical knowledge in diagnosis of difficult clinical cases
citation: Woods, N.N., Brooks, L.R. & Norman, G.R. (2007). The role of biomedical knowledge in diagnosis of difficult clinical cases. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 12, 417–426. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-006-9054-y
title: Teach causal mechanisms alongside clinical features to prepare novices for difficult diagnoses
description: The article's results support teaching underlying causal mechanisms, not just clinical feature lists, when preparing novices for difficult diagnostic challenges. Causal training improved performance on cases with irrelevant findings and unfamiliar terminology, and the unfamiliar-terminology advantage persisted one week after training. The authors conclude the studies "provide additional support for the critical role of biomedical knowledge in diagnosis of difficult clinical cases."
requirements: Learners must be taught the underlying causal mechanisms of the diseases, not only a list of clinical features.
constraints: Evidence comes from artificial diseases learned by novice diagnosticians in two experiments, not from routine clinical cases.
target_learners: novice diagnosticians
medical students
target_learning_goals: diagnostic accuracy on difficult clinical cases
examples: In Experiment 1, participants were taught artificial diseases using either knowledge of causal mechanisms or a list of clinical features, then tested on cases with irrelevant findings and unfamiliar terminology.

article_title: Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language
citation: Junko Yamashita. (2013). Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language. Reading in a Foreign Language, 25(2). http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Day and Bamford's (1998) two models of L2 reading attitude formation and motivation to read
description: This article adopts two models proposed by Day and Bamford (1998), described as "the only ones currently depicting the relationship between reading attitudes and ER in the context of L2 reading." The acquisition model hypothesizes four sources of L2 reading attitudes: L1 reading attitudes, previous L2 reading experiences, attitudes to the L2 and its culture and people, and L2 classroom environment. The motivation model, based in spirit on Expectancy + Value models, holds that materials and L2 reading attitudes have primary importance in determining motivation to read, and the article uses the models to explain how ER may create a virtuous circle of reading.
requirements: The article states the models remain untested: "no study has ever attempted to test them," so sounder L2-specific theoretical frameworks are needed
constraints: The article notes the virtuous circle may not always arise because factors not affected by L2 ER, such as L1 reading attitudes, can also influence motivation
target_learners: L2/EFL readers, e.g., Japanese university EFL learners
target_learning_goals: Formation of positive L2 reading attitudes and motivation to read extensively
examples: The article interprets its finding that comfort increased more than practical value as consistent with the model's claim that positive attitudes enhance the decision to read
key_sources: Junko Yamashita. (2013). Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language. Reading in a Foreign Language, 25(2). http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl

article_title: Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language
citation: Junko Yamashita. (2013). Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language. Reading in a Foreign Language, 25(2). http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: 15-week university extensive reading course with free choice of graded readers and book reports
description: A 15-week compulsory EFL course at a Japanese university met weekly for 90 minutes; "During class, students were able to access approximately 500 graded English readers (a series of Oxford, Cambridge, Heinemann, and Penguin), and were encouraged to choose whichever books they wanted to read." The class split between administration/activities and free voluntary silent reading; students submitted a B5-size book report per book as the credit requirement and were graded on participation and amount read. Students read 649 pages (SD = 201), about 13 readers or 120,634 words, on average.
requirements: A library of graded readers at varied levels must be accessible, and book reports were required for credit
constraints: The author states results are an outcome of this study's context and generalizability to other educational and socio-cultural circumstances may be limited
target_learners: Second-year Japanese university undergraduates learning EFL
target_learning_goals: Improved L2 reading attitudes (comfort, anxiety, intellectual value) through sustained extensive reading
examples: All students chose to write their book reports in Japanese, and five students additionally read their own paperbacks outside the graded-reader stock
key_sources: Junko Yamashita. (2013). Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language. Reading in a Foreign Language, 25(2). http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl

article_title: Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language
citation: Junko Yamashita. (2013). Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language. Reading in a Foreign Language, 25(2). http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl
title: Best-practice circumstances for implementing extensive reading in reading classes
description: The article enumerates the circumstances under which classes that incorporate ER best operate, following Day and Bamford (2002): "a variety of reading materials are available on a wide range of topics at different levels of linguistic difficulty; students choose what they want to read, read unassisted, and view reading as its own reward." It adds that students often read faster because they select materials of interest at an appropriate difficulty level, and teachers act as model readers who guide rather than explicitly teach. The study's own course instantiated these circumstances.
requirements: A variety of reading materials across topics and difficulty levels must be available; students must be able to choose their own books and read unassisted
constraints: The article notes there are different ways of implementing ER (e.g., exclusively outside class or using only a small portion of class time), so the pattern is one implementation among several
target_learners: L2/EFL learners in classroom reading programs
target_learning_goals: Developing good reading habits, liking for reading, and L2 reading attitude
examples: In the study's course, the latter half of each 90-minute class was devoted to free, voluntary silent reading at students' own pace, with the teacher answering questions individually and advising
key_sources: Junko Yamashita. (2013). Effects of extensive reading on reading attitudes in a foreign language. Reading in a Foreign Language, 25(2). http://nflrc.hawaii.edu/rfl

article_title: Altering School Climate through School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports
citation: Bradshaw, C. P., Koth, C. W., Thornton, L. A., & Leaf, P. J. (2009). Altering School Climate through School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports: Findings from a Group-Randomized Effectiveness Trial. Prevention Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-008-0114-9
title: School-wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS)
description: PBIS is a universal, school-wide prevention strategy aimed at reducing disruptive behavior problems, described in the article as "a universal, school-wide prevention strategy that is currently implemented in over 7,500 schools". It operates as a whole-school prevention model whose implementation was tested in a group-randomized effectiveness trial in 37 elementary schools, where trained schools varied in how quickly they adopted the model. The article treats PBIS as an organizational as well as behavioral intervention, linking it to staff-reported school climate.
requirements: School-wide adoption across the whole school rather than a classroom-level program
Implementation fidelity monitoring, which the article found necessary to detect effects on some organizational dimensions
constraints: Effects on collegial leadership and institutional integrity were significant only when implementation fidelity was included in the model
target_learners: elementary school students
elementary school staff
target_learning_goals: reduce disruptive behavior problems
improve school organizational health and climate
examples: A group-randomized controlled effectiveness trial assigned 37 elementary schools to trained versus comparison conditions over 5 years

citation: Bradshaw, C. P., Koth, C. W., Thornton, L. A., & Leaf, P. J. (2009). Altering School Climate through School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports: Findings from a Group-Randomized Effectiveness Trial. Prevention Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-008-0114-9
title: School organizational health as a multidimensional climate construct shaped by whole-school prevention models
description: The article treats school organizational health as a staff-reported, multidimensional property of schools, naming overall organizational health plus the dimensions resource influence, staff affiliation, academic emphasis, collegial leadership, and institutional integrity. It positions this construct as responsive to school-wide prevention models: the trial showed PBIS altered these staff-reported dimensions over 5 years. The construct is further framed as a contextual characteristic that may mediate intervention effects on student performance, making organizational climate a target and mechanism for school-wide intervention design.
requirements: Measurement via staff reports analyzed with longitudinal multilevel models to separate individual and school levels
constraints: The article's evidence comes from elementary schools in a 5-year trial; generalization to other levels is not tested here
target_learners: elementary school staff
school administrators
target_learning_goals: improve school climate and organizational functioning
support implementation of school-wide behavior interventions
examples: Longitudinal multilevel analyses of 2,596 staff across 37 elementary schools over the 5-year trial

article_title: Getting a Read on the App Stores: A Market Scan and Analysis of Children's Literacy Apps
citation: Vaala, S., Ly, A., & Levine, M.H. (2015). Getting a read on the app stores: A market scan and analysis of children's literacy apps. New York, NY: The Joan Ganz Cooney Center at Sesame Workshop. https://www.joanganzcooneycenter.org
title: Design educational apps for intergenerational joint media engagement with explicit multi-user features
description: The report recommends that developers of children's educational apps build in features that engage multiple users, because "Young children learn best when another caring individual joins in the process." Suggested design moves include designing with the child's interests in mind, adding content or mechanics challenging enough to hold an older co-user's interest, and enabling co-users to create content together. This recommendation responds to the scan's finding that almost no popular literacy apps currently include such features.
requirements: Developers must add explicit design features that engage multiple users, such as collaborative or competitive co-use mechanics
constraints: The scan found only two apps in the sample had explicit co-use functions, so current-market exemplars are scarce
target_learners: children ages 0-8 learning language and literacy
target_learning_goals: language and literacy development through adult-child co-use of digital media
examples: The report suggests "incorporating content or mechanics that are more challenging to maintain an older user's interest, and enabling co-users to create content together"

article_title: Effects of School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Child Behavior Problems
citation: Catherine P. Bradshaw, Tracy E. Waasdorp, Philip J. Leaf. (2012). Effects of School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Child Behavior Problems. Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2012-0243
title: SWPBIS as a 3-tiered universal prevention framework altering the school's organizational context
description: SWPBIS is a noncurricular universal prevention strategy that "aims to alter the school 's organizational context to implement enhanced procedures and systems to guide data-based decisions related to student behavior problems and academics." It applies behavioral, social learning, and organizational principles school-wide, establishes positively stated expectations taught to all students and staff, and implements "a 3-tiered prevention framework" in which selective and indicated programs complement universal components. In this trial it was delivered via team training, booster sessions, and monthly behavior-support coaching.
requirements: Schools form SWPBIS teams of 5 to 6 members who attend an initial 2-day summer training co-led by a developer and annual 2-day booster training events
At least monthly on-site support and technical assistance from a trained behavior support coach
constraints: Most of the more than 16,000 implementing schools have focused on the universal components rather than the full 3-tiered model
Some children do not respond adequately to the universal model
target_learners: Elementary school children (kindergarten through grade 2 cohorts in the trial)
target_learning_goals: Reducing aggressive and disruptive behavior
Improving prosocial behavior and emotion regulation
Reducing office discipline referrals
examples: In the 4-year group RCT, 21 schools received SWPBIS training and coaching led by the PBIS Maryland State Leadership Team while 16 comparison schools refrained from implementing SWPBIS for 4 years

article_title: Examining variation in the impact of school-wide positive behavioral interventions and supports
citation: Bradshaw, C. P., Waasdorp, T. E., & Leaf, P. J. (2015). Examining Variation in the Impact of School-Wide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports: Findings From a Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0037630
title: SWPBIS is a multitiered whole-school prevention framework aimed at altering the school environment
description: The article describes Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports as "a multitiered system o f supports framework aimed at altering the school environment through improved systems, data-based decision making, and implemention of evidence-based practices." It applies behavioral, social learning, and organizational principles across all school contexts to prevent disruptive behavior and enhance school climate. The model follows a three-tiered prevention model in which selective (Tier 2) and indicated (Tier 3) programs complement universal (Tier 1) school-wide components. Most of the more than 20,000 implementing schools focus on the universal elements due to resource needs.
requirements: Implementation of all three tiers as the model calls for, though most schools implement only universal school-wide elements
constraints: The trial trained schools only in the universal (Tier 1) school-wide supports, so causal inferences are limited to those elements
target_learners: Elementary school children in kindergarten through grade 2
target_learning_goals: Preventing disruptive and aggressive behavior
Enhancing school climate and social-emotional functioning
examples: 37 Maryland elementary schools were randomized to SWPBIS (21) or comparison (16), with SWPBIS schools receiving two-day summer training, annual boosters, and monthly on-site coaching

article_title: Using adaptive learning technologies to personalize instruction to student interests
citation: Walkington, C. A. (2013). Using adaptive learning technologies to personalize instruction to student interests: The impact of relevant contexts on performance and learning outcomes. Journal of Educational Data Mining, 5(1). https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM
title: Interest-based framework for context personalization: individual, situational, and topic interest in adaptive learning
description: The article frames context personalization within Hidi and Renninger's interest framework, defining interest as "the psychological state of engaging or the predisposition to re-engage with particular classes of objects, events, or ideas over time." It distinguishes individual interest (stable preferences with stored value and knowledge), situational interest (attention-focusing reaction to environmental stimuli), and topic interest (interest triggered by a specific topic). Personalization is positioned as both an environmental modification to trigger and maintain situational interest and a way of leveraging individual interests in out-of-school topics. The framework connects interest activation to improved situation-model construction in mathematical word problem solving.
requirements: Instructional contexts must be matched to learners' actual interests via an assessment such as an interests survey
Interest-based triggers must be tied explicitly to the content to be learned rather than being decorative or incidental
constraints: Personalization effects are moderated by learner ability level, with strongest effects for struggling students
Effects are moderated by task difficulty, with the largest impacts on hard knowledge components
target_learners: secondary mathematics students
ninth-grade Algebra I students
target_learning_goals: writing symbolic equations from story scenarios
algebraic expression-writing and linear functions
examples: Students rated interest in 9 topic areas on a 4-point survey, and the tutor selected the highest-rated interest variation of each story problem
key_sources: Walkington, C. A. (2013). Using adaptive learning technologies to personalize instruction to student interests: The impact of relevant contexts on performance and learning outcomes. Journal of Educational Data Mining, 5(1). https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM

citation: Catherine P. Bradshaw, Mary M. Mitchell, & Philip J. Leaf. (2010). title: SWPBIS three-tiered prevention model
description: SWPBIS is a universal, schoolwide prevention strategy that "aims to alter school environments by creating improved systems and procedures that promote positive change in student behavior by targeting staff behaviors." It draws on behavioral, social learning, and organizational behavioral principles, and sits at the universal level of a three-tiered public health prevention model that also includes secondary (targeted/selective) and tertiary (individual/indicated) systems of support. The universal model is implemented through seven steps covering team formation, coaching, defined and taught expectations, reward systems, response to violations, and data-based decision making.
requirements: A SWPBIS team of 6 to 10 staff members and an administrator, an external behavioral support coach, and a formal data system for discipline data
constraints: This study examined only the universal SWPBIS model; targeted and indicated supports were not systematically implemented across trial schools
target_learners: all elementary school students (universal, schoolwide)
target_learning_goals: positive student behavior, reduced disruptive behavior, improved school climate

title: Seven-step schoolwide implementation of universal SWPBIS
description: The article describes the universal SWPBIS model as "implemented by following these seven steps, which map onto the model's critical features": forming a SWPBIS team of 6 to 10 staff with an administrator; an external behavioral support coach providing on-site consultation; defining three to five positively stated schoolwide expectations; teaching those expectations to all students; a schoolwide reinforcement system; an agreed-upon system for responding to behavioral violations; and a formal system to collect, analyze, and use disciplinary data for data-based decision making. These steps were measured by the 29-item School-Wide Evaluation Tool.

target_learning_goals: positive behavioral expectations, consistent discipline, reduced problem behavior
examples: Schools established expectations such as "Be respectful, responsible, and ready to learn" posted in all classrooms and nonclassroom settings, with tangible reinforcers like "gotcha" tickets

title: School-Wide Information System (SWIS)
description: SWIS is "an Internet-based data entry and reporting system" used to collect and manage student discipline referral data by school staff. article_title: Continued Progress: Promising Evidence on Personalized Learning
citation: John F. Pane, Elizabeth D. Steiner, Matthew D. Baird, Laura S. Hamilton. (2015). Continued Progress: Promising Evidence on Personalized Learning. RAND Corporation. https://www.rand.org/t/RR1365z2
title: Five-strategy framework of personalized learning: learner profiles, personal learning paths, competency-based progression, flexible learning environments, and college and career readiness
description: The report organizes school design features around five strategies identified by funders and leaders in the personalized learning space. Each "strategy encompasses a set of tools and features of the personalized learning environment"; some, like flexible pathways, are "central to a personalized approach," while others such as technology are enablers. The framework structures the report's implementation analysis of the 32 NGLC schools.
requirements: Schools adopting the framework implement learner profiles, personal learning paths, competency-based progression, flexible learning environments, and an emphasis on college and career readiness
constraints: There is not yet one shared definition of personalized learning; schools showed considerable diversity in instructional model details
target_learners: K-12 students in charter and district schools implementing personalized learning
target_learning_goals: Tailoring instruction to individual needs, skills, and interests; college and career readiness; student ownership of learning
examples: The 32 NGLC schools' implementation of each of the five strategies was assessed via administrator interviews, teacher and student surveys, teacher logs, and site visits
key_sources: John F. Pane, Elizabeth D. Steiner, Matthew D. Baird, Laura S. Hamilton. (2015). Continued Progress: Promising Evidence on Personalized Learning. RAND Corporation. https://www.rand.org/t/RR1365z2

article_title: The Impact of Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Bullying and Peer Rejection
citation: Waasdorp TE, Bradshaw CP, Leaf PJ. (2012). The Impact of Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Bullying and Peer Rejection: A Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial. Arch Pediatr Adolesc Med. 2012;166(2):149-156. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/archpediatrics/fullarticle/
title: SWPBIS: a noncurricular, universal, three-tiered schoolwide behavior support model
description: SWPBIS is described as "a noncurricular, universal prevention model that draws on behavioral, social learning, and organizational principles." A SWPBIS team establishes 3 to 5 positively stated schoolwide expectations that are posted, taught to all students and staff, and reinforced through praise and tangible rewards, with data on problem behaviors used to guide supervision and more intensive supports. It follows a 3-tiered public health prevention approach, layering targeted and indicated programs onto the universal model. In this trial, 21 elementary schools received training and coaching and reached high-fidelity implementation.
requirements: Internal SWPBIS teams attend initial training and annual booster training
On-site support from a trained behavior support coach
Data collection on student behaviors to monitor the universal program
constraints: In this trial intervention schools received training on the universal SWPBIS model only; more intensive selective and indicated tiers were not layered on
target_learners: Elementary school students (kindergarten through grade 5)
target_learning_goals: Positive social and classroom behavior
Reduced bullying and peer rejection
Improved school climate
examples: School teams established expectations such as "be respectful, responsible, and ready to learn," posted across settings and reinforced with tickets
key_sources: Waasdorp TE, Bradshaw CP, Leaf PJ. (2012). The Impact of Schoolwide Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports on Bullying and Peer Rejection: A Randomized Controlled Effectiveness Trial. Arch Pediatr Adolesc Med. 2012;166(2):149-156. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/archpediatrics/fullarticle/

Arch Pediatr Adolesc Med. 2012;166(2):149-156. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/archpediatrics/fullarticle/
title: Implement universal, positively oriented schoolwide prevention as an alternative to zero-tolerance bullying policies
description: The article argues that because zero-tolerance approaches "have not been shown to be effective," schools should adopt "positive schoolwide prevention efforts that involve all school staff and are implemented across all school settings." SWPBIS operationalizes this by establishing common behavioral expectations across all contexts and involving all staff in prevention activities, improving school climate as a lever for reducing bullying.
requirements: All school staff involvement in prevention activities
A common set of behavioral expectations across all school contexts
constraints: The article notes effects were small and the trial schools volunteered, limiting generalizability
target_learners: All students in elementary schools
target_learning_goals: Prevention of bullying and peer rejection
Improved school climate and culture
examples: In the trial, 21 schools implemented SWPBIS with schoolwide expectations, reinforcement, data-based supervision of hot spots, and staff training, and showed attenuated growth in bullying and rejection relative to 16 comparison schools

article_title: Interaction in Distance Education and Online Learning: Using Evidence and Theory to Improve Practice
citation: Abrami, P.C., Bernard, R.M., Bures, E.M., Borokhovski, E., Tamim, R.M. (2012). Interaction in Distance Education and Online Learning: Using Evidence and Theory to Improve Practice. In: Moller, L., Huett, J. (eds) The Next Generation of Distance Education. Springer, Boston, MA. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-1785-9_4
title: Three-type interaction taxonomy for distance and online learning
description: The chapter organizes interaction in distance and online learning into three types: "among students, between the instructor and students, and between students and course content". This taxonomy, drawn from the interaction literature in distance education, serves as the organizing axis for the chapter's review of evidence and its recommendations for instructional improvement in the next generation of distance and online learning.
requirements: Instruction in distance and online learning settings should provide for all three interaction types when designing courses

target_learning_goals: achievement and engagement in distance and online learning

article_title: Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus
citation: Nameera Akhtar, Frances Dunham and Philip J. Dunham. (1991). Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus. Journal of Child Language, Volume 18, Issue 1, pp. 41-49. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000900013283
title: Attentional regulation account: joint attentional focus explains the relationship between maternal directives and vocabulary development
description: The article proposes an explanatory account in which the effect of maternal directives on vocabulary depends on whether the directive respects the child's current focus of attention. Because prescriptives "are most often used to redirect a child's attention to a different object or activity", the authors hypothesize that "attentional regulation underlies this negative relationship" between directiveness and vocabulary growth. Directives delivered within a joint focus of attention are predicted to be beneficial, while attention-changing directives are not.
requirements: Coding of maternal directives by their relation to the child's focus of attention (LEADING vs FOLLOWING), as the study operationalized the account
constraints: The account is tested with a small correlational sample of twelve mother-child dyads, so causal direction is not established in the available text
target_learners: 13-month-old children (aged 1;1 at observation)
target_learning_goals: Early productive vocabulary development
examples: The study videotaped twelve mothers interacting with children aged 1;1 and coded 100 maternal utterances each for pragmatic intent, distinguishing LEADING from FOLLOWING prescriptives
key_sources: Nameera Akhtar, Frances Dunham and Philip J. Dunham. (1991). Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus. Journal of Child Language, Volume 18, Issue 1, pp. 41-49. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000900013283

article_title: Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus
citation: Nameera Akhtar, Frances Dunham and Philip J. Dunham. (1991). Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus. Journal of Child Language, Volume 18, Issue 1, pp. 41-49. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000900013283
title: Direct a young child's behaviour only within a joint focus of attention to support vocabulary learning
description: The article concludes that adult directives can aid early word learning when they follow, rather than redirect, the child's current attention. As the abstract states, "given joint focus, directing a 13-month-old's behaviour can have beneficial effects on subsequent vocabulary development". Caregivers and educators should therefore embed behavioural directives in activities the child is already attending to, rather than pulling attention to new objects or activities.
requirements: The adult must establish or share the child's current focus of attention before issuing the directive
constraints: Evidence comes from a correlational study of twelve mother-child dyads observed at 1;1 with vocabulary measured at 1;10; the article does not establish causation
target_learners: Toddlers around 13 months of age
target_learning_goals: Productive early vocabulary
examples: The study distinguished FOLLOW-prescriptives, which followed the child's focus of attention, from LEADING-prescriptives, which changed it, and found only the FOLLOW type correlated with later vocabulary
key_sources: Nameera Akhtar, Frances Dunham and Philip J. Dunham. (1991). Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus. Journal of Child Language, Volume 18, Issue 1, pp. 41-49. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000900013283

title: LEADING/FOLLOWING prescriptive coding scheme for maternal directives
description: A coding scheme introduced in this study for classifying maternal prescriptives by their relation to the child's attention. As printed: "Prescriptives were coded as either changing (LEADING) or FOLLOWING the child's focus of attention." It was applied to 100 maternal utterances per mother, drawn from videotaped interactions with twelve children aged 1;1, coded for pragmatic intent. The scheme operationalizes the joint-attention account of directive effectiveness.
requirements: Videotaped mother-child interaction samples and coding of maternal utterances for pragmatic intent
constraints: Applied in this study to a sample of twelve mothers with 100 utterances each at child age 1;1
target_learners: 13-month-old children
target_learning_goals: Understanding caregiver input that supports early vocabulary development
examples: The scheme split prescriptives into LEADING and FOLLOWING categories, enabling the finding that only FOLLOW-prescriptives correlated with vocabulary at 1;10

article_title: Constructivism in Science Education
citation: Michael R. Matthews (ed.). (1998). Constructivism in Science Education: A Philosophical Examination. Kluwer Academic Publishers. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-011-5032-3
title: Educational constructivism spans three distinct kinds of theory: theories of learning, theories of teaching, and constructivist epistemologies
description: The volume's organizing taxonomy distinguishes three constructivist strands that are frequently conflated. As the preface states, "there are constructivist theories of learning - originally the personal constructivism of Piaget and the social constructivism of Vygotsky; there are constructivist theories of teaching" echoing Socratic and progressivist pedagogy, "and there are constructivist theories of knowledge, or constructivist epistemologies." The book's project is to untangle and evaluate these varied positions through philosophical analysis.
requirements: Philosophical analysis to disentangle the varieties before evaluation
constraints: The preface notes the varieties are frequently confused in educational literature
target_learners: science teachers
teacher educators
target_learning_goals: understanding the nature of science
epistemological foundations of science teaching
examples: Chapters by von Glasersfeld (radical constructivist epistemology), Nola and Suchting (critiques), Bickhard (taxonomy of constructivisms), and Grandy (cognitive vs metaphysical constructivism) each treat one strand
key_sources: Michael R. Matthews (ed.). (1998). Constructivism in Science Education: A Philosophical Examination. Kluwer Academic Publishers. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-011-5032-3

article_title: Does animation enhance learning? A meta-analysis
citation: BERNEY, Sandra, BETRANCOURT, Mireille. (2016). Does animation enhance learning? A meta-analysis. Computers and education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.06.005
title: Meta-analytic corpus of 61 primary studies comparing animated and static graphics
description: The evidence base of this meta-analysis is a systematically searched corpus of experimental studies comparing animated versus static graphic displays for knowledge acquisition. The authors state that "A total of 50 papers were considered, and consecutively 61 primary studies (N = 7036), yielding 140 pair-wise comparisons" of the two visualization types in multimedia instructional material, analyzed with a random-effects model. The corpus serves as the dataset underlying the overall effect and all moderator analyses.
requirements: Studies must be experimental comparisons of animated vs. static graphics in the context of knowledge acquisition, as the systematic search specified
constraints: Limited to multimedia instructional material; findings characterize that body of studies rather than all animation use
target_learners: learners in experimental studies of multimedia instruction
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition from animated versus static graphic visualizations

article_title: Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval
citation: Monica S. Birnbaum, Nate Kornell, Elizabeth Ligon Bjork, & Robert A. Bjork. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0272-7
title: Discriminative-contrast hypothesis of the interleaving benefit
description: The article's central explanatory account: interleaving benefits inductive learning because it juxtaposes exemplars of different categories, which highlights the differences that separate categories and supports discrimination learning. The authors define it as the idea "that we refer to as the discriminative-contrast hypothesis", building on Kang and Pashler (2012) and Goldstone's observation that frequent alternation highlights features distinguishing categories. The three experiments test its strong predictions within interleaved conditions.
requirements: Applies to inductive category learning where the goal is classifying new exemplars into appropriate categories, so knowing what distinguishes categories is crucial
constraints: The authors note simultaneous presentation results may not extend to single presentations because simultaneous presentation places greater demands on working memory
target_learners: adult learners studying naturalistic visual categories
target_learning_goals: inductive concept and category learning
discrimination between similar categories
examples: Experiment 1 held total spacing constant and showed that only the condition interrupting between-category juxtaposition impaired performance
key_sources: Monica S. Birnbaum, Nate Kornell, Elizabeth Ligon Bjork, & Robert A. Bjork. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0272-7

article_title: Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval
citation: Monica S. Birnbaum, Nate Kornell, Elizabeth Ligon Bjork, & Robert A. Bjork. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0272-7
title: Dual-process framework: blocking supports within-category similarity processing, interleaving supports between-category difference processing
description: The authors adopt a conceptual framework in which "blocking facilitates processing of similarities within a category, whereas interleaving facilitates processing of differences between categories". Because categories are defined by both similarities and differences, both processes matter, and the optimal schedule depends on which is harder for the given materials. The framework is offered to reconcile apparently divergent prior findings that blocking sometimes helped.
requirements: Learners must process both within-category similarities and between-category differences for complete category learning
constraints: The authors speculate tentatively that prior blocking benefits arose when materials made identifying similarities difficult, noting the prior studies used artificial categories, more practice trials, and fewer categories
target_learners: learners acquiring naturalistic categories
target_learning_goals: category learning balancing similarity and difference processing
examples: Zulkiply and Burt found blocking more effective for highly discriminable categories and interleaving critical for low-discriminability categories, which the authors cite as supporting the framework
key_sources: Monica S. Birnbaum, Nate Kornell, Elizabeth Ligon Bjork, & Robert A. Bjork. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0272-7

article_title: Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval
citation: Monica S. Birnbaum, Nate Kornell, Elizabeth Ligon Bjork, & Robert A. Bjork. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0272-7
title: Interleave exemplars of different categories for inductive learning, and achieve spacing by increasing lag rather than inserting gaps
description: The article's foremost practical implication is "that successful inductive learning entails the juxtaposing of exemplars from different categories so as to promote discriminative contrast". Because inserted filler tasks can interrupt discrimination processing, the authors advise that "Increasing the lag between interleaved items may be wiser than inserting gaps between inductive-learning trials". Spacing remains valuable when it does not interfere with discriminative contrast.
requirements: Learning goal must be inductive category learning in which learners must classify new exemplars
constraints: Spacing that interrupts juxtaposition of interleaved categories impaired learning in Experiment 1; the authors acknowledge a possible untested upper limit to how much spacing can occur before performance suffers
target_learners: classroom learners studying naturalistic categories, including mathematics problem types
target_learning_goals: inductive category learning
discriminating between confusable categories of problems or exemplars
examples: Taylor and Rohrer's mathematics study found interleaving enhanced delayed-test problem solving even with spacing held constant, which the authors cite as extending the implication beyond visual categories

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of Adventure Therapy Outcomes and Moderators
citation: Daniel J. Bowen and James T. Neill. (2013). A Meta-Analysis of Adventure Therapy Outcomes and Moderators. The Open Psychology Journal, 2013, 6, 28-53. http://www.daniel-bowen.com.au/meta-analysis
title: Adventure therapy outcome meta-analytic dataset and coding manual (197 studies, 2,908 effect sizes, 206 samples)
description: A systematically assembled corpus of adventure therapy outcome studies published between 1967 and 2012, identified via electronic databases, specific journals, websites and listservs, related meta-analyses, expert emails and bibliographies. It comprises "2,908 effect sizes from 206 unique samples within 197 studies", covering 17,728 unique participants, coded with a manual "available from http://www.daniel-bowen.com.au/meta-analysis" along with detailed breakdowns by 67 specific outcomes. The dataset underpins all effect size, publication bias and moderator analyses in the study.
requirements: Studies must report pre- and post-program outcomes with sufficient statistical information (M, SD, n) to calculate standardised mean effect sizes, and be reported in English from 1960 onward
constraints: Only standardised mean change effect sizes were used, so studies reporting only post-test treatment-versus-control results (N = 50) were excluded; only English-language studies were included
target_learners: adventure therapy program participants including at-risk youth, clinical and adjudicated populations, adults and families
target_learning_goals: psychological and behavioural functioning outcomes across eight outcome categories
examples: Detailed breakdown of effect sizes by each of the 67 specific outcomes is available from the authors' website

article_title: Effective Educational Videos: Principles and Guidelines for Maximizing Student Learning from Video Content
citation: Brame Cynthia J. (2016). Effective Educational Videos: Principles and Guidelines for Maximizing Student Learning from Video Content. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-03-0125
title: Cognitive load theory and the cognitive theory of multimedia learning as the framework for educational video design
description: The essay organizes video design around cognitive load theory (Sweller) and the cognitive theory of multimedia learning (Mayer). It describes sensory, working, and long-term memory, and states that "any learning experience has three components": intrinsic load, germane load, and extraneous load. Multimedia learning adds two limited-capacity channels, visual/pictorial and auditory/verbal, whose combined use maximizes working memory capacity. Instructors should minimize extraneous load, manage intrinsic load, and optimize germane load.
requirements: Designers must consider the intrinsic load of the subject and structure high-load material carefully
Working memory must be prompted to process only the most crucial information for encoding into long-term memory
constraints: Either channel can be overwhelmed by high cognitive load
What counts as extraneous information changes as learners move from novice toward expert status
target_learners: higher education students
biology students
target_learning_goals: effective learning from educational video content
examples: The essay illustrates intrinsic load with word pairs versus grammar, and naming mitosis stages versus understanding cell cycle control
key_sources: Brame Cynthia J. (2016). Effective Educational Videos: Principles and Guidelines for Maximizing Student Learning from Video Content. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-03-0125

article_title: Lateral reading: College students learn to critically evaluate internet sources in an online course
citation: Breakstone, J., Smith, M., Connors, P., Ortega, T., Kerr, D., & Wineburg, S. (2021). Lateral reading: College students learn to critically evaluate internet sources in an online course. Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) Misinformation Review. https://doi.org/10.37016/mr-2020-56
title: Four one-hour course-embedded modules teaching fact checkers' evaluation strategies in an asynchronous nutrition course
description: The intervention consisted of four required, roughly hour-long weekly modules embedded in an asynchronous online nutrition course at a large state university. Each module combined three activity types: "videos provided direct instruction about evaluating the credibility of Internet sources" (Crash Course videos), guided evaluations of online sources tied to course content, and screencasts of a researcher modeling lateral reading, described as "cognitive modeling, an instructional approach that makes expert strategies visible to novice learners." Modules also addressed misconceptions such as trusting dot-org domains.
requirements: Modules were required course components with points awarded for completion, though module quality did not affect course grades
Examples tied to the course's subject matter (nutrition sources)
constraints: Instruction was delivered asynchronously via a learning management system; module quality did not affect course grades
target_learners: Undergraduate students in a required nutrition course, including majors and students fulfilling a general education requirement
target_learning_goals: Evaluating the credibility of online sources using fact checkers' strategies, especially lateral reading
examples: Module 2 introduced lateral reading with a Crash Course video, then students evaluated an American Council on Science and Health article and watched a screencast of a researcher applying lateral reading to it
key_sources: Breakstone, J., Smith, M., Connors, P., Ortega, T., Kerr, D., & Wineburg, S. (2021). Lateral reading: College students learn to critically evaluate internet sources in an online course. Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) Misinformation Review. https://doi.org/10.37016/mr-2020-56

article_title: Lateral reading: College students learn to critically evaluate internet sources in an online course
citation: Breakstone, J., Smith, M., Connors, P., Ortega, T., Kerr, D., & Wineburg, S. (2021). Lateral reading: College students learn to critically evaluate internet sources in an online course. Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) Misinformation Review. https://doi.org/10.37016/mr-2020-56
title: Lateral reading: the professional fact checkers' strategy of leaving an unfamiliar site to consult the broader Web
description: Lateral reading is "the act of leaving an unknown website to consult other sources to evaluate the original site," derived from observations of professional fact checkers whose approaches were compared with those of undergraduates and history professors. While academics and students read vertically, staying on the target site, fact checkers "left it almost immediately and opened new tabs across the horizontal axis of their browser," answering who is behind the information, what the evidence is, and what other sources say. The article frames these as "fast and frugal" heuristics and builds its curriculum on them.
requirements: Consulting trusted sources from the broader Web rather than judging a site by its own surface features
constraints: Prior research showed students tend to evaluate a website by remaining on it without turning to the open Web, which motivated the emphasis on lateral reading
target_learners: College students
Middle school and high school students (per prior interventions the article cites)
target_learning_goals: Judging the credibility of unfamiliar online sources quickly and accurately
examples: Fact checkers in the underlying observational study evaluated unfamiliar websites with screens recorded, leaving sites to consult the broader Web
