article_title: Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing
citation: Andrew C. Butler and Henry L. Roediger III. (2008). Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing. Memory & Cognition, 36(3), 604-616. https://doi.org/10.3758/MC.36.3.604
title: Provide feedback on multiple-choice tests to boost retention and prevent acquisition of misinformation
description: The article recommends that educators give feedback after multiple-choice tests because feedback lets students correct errors and maintain correct responses. In the experiment, "both immediate and delayed feedback increased the proportion of correct responses and reduced the proportion of intrusions" on a delayed cued recall test, and delayed feedback produced the best retention. Feedback also improved students' calibration of what they actually knew.
requirements: Feedback must include the correct response, not merely correct–incorrect indication, for students to encode the right answer
constraints: Without prior study and without feedback, multiple-choice testing was net harmful (intrusions exceeded correct responses)
Delayed feedback outperformed immediate feedback for correct responses, though both equally reduced intrusions
target_learners: higher education students studying prose passages
target_learning_goals: retention of factual material from texts
avoiding acquisition of false knowledge from lure items
examples: Subjects received feedback consisting of accuracy indication, re-presentation of the question, the response selected, and the correct response, either immediately or at the end of the test
key_sources: Andrew C. Butler and Henry L. Roediger III. (2008). Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing. Memory & Cognition, 36(3), 604-616. https://doi.org/10.3758/MC.36.3.604

article_title: Preventing social isolation and loneliness among older people: a systematic review of health promotion interventions
citation: MIMA CATTAN, MARTIN WHITE, JOHN BOND and ALISON LEARMOUTH. (2005). Preventing social isolation and loneliness among older people: a systematic review of health promotion interventions. Ageing & Society, Volume 25, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0144686X04002594
title: Four-category typology of health promotion interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness among older people
description: The review organises interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness among older people into four categories: "'group' (n=17); 'one-to-one' (n=10); 'service provision' (n=3); and 'community development' (n=1)". The typology sorts thirty quantitative outcome studies published between 1970 and 2002 by delivery format, enabling the review's comparison of effectiveness across intervention types. It underpins the review's finding that group activities with educational or support input predominated among effective interventions.
requirements: Quantitative outcome studies of health promotion interventions targeting social isolation and loneliness among older people, identified via electronic databases, journals, abstracts and key informants
constraints: Based on studies published between 1970 and 2002, most conducted in the USA and Canada
target_learners: older people
target_learning_goals: preventing and alleviating social isolation and loneliness
examples: The review categorised thirty identified studies: group (n=17), one-to-one (n=10), service provision (n=3) and community development (n=1).

article_title: Digital Games, Design, and Learning
citation: Clark, D. B., Tanner-Smith, E. E., & Killingsworth, S. S. (2016). Digital Games, Design, and Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 86(1). https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315582065
title: Attend to game design features, not just the medium, when designing games for learning
description: The meta-analysis argues that the learning value of digital games depends on specific design features rather than on the medium as such. It introduced value-added comparisons — "the efficacy of a standard version of a game relative to an enhanced version augmented to test a theoretical design proposition" — precisely to isolate design contributions, and found augmented designs outperformed standard versions. Moderators such as session count, player configuration, visual realism, and story relevance further show design characteristics shape effects.
requirements: Studies or designs must allow comparison of an enhanced game variant against an equivalent standard version of the same game to isolate the design feature's contribution.
constraints: Only one enhancement category (enhanced scaffolding) had substantial representation; other categories' effects were not significantly different from zero, likely due to small numbers of effect sizes.
target_learners: K–16 students, ages 6 to 25
target_learning_goals: Cognitive, intrapersonal, and interpersonal learning outcomes aligned with the NRC Education for Life and Work framework
examples: The review synthesized 40 value-added effect sizes from 20 studies comparing enhanced versus standard game versions, finding g = 0.34 overall and g = 0.41 for enhanced scaffolding designs.
key_sources: Clark, D. B., Tanner-Smith, E. E., & Killingsworth, S. S. (2016). Digital Games, Design, and Learning: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 86(1). https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315582065

article_title: The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature
citation: Benjamin Cleveland & Kenn Fisher. (2014). The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature. Learning Environ Res 17, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10984-013-9149-3
title: Building performance evaluation as the broader evaluative framework into which post-occupancy evaluation has recently evolved
description: The review presents building performance evaluation as a broader evaluative framework that grew out of post-occupancy evaluation. As the authors state, "We then discuss the recent evolution of POE into the broader evaluative framework of building performance evaluation." The framework is positioned as the current state of practice for evaluating buildings in use, providing the context within which learning-space evaluation approaches are later compared. The review uses this evolution to frame its critical analysis of how physical learning environments have been assessed.
requirements: Evaluation of buildings in use, extending beyond occupancy-focused POE to a broader performance framing as the article describes
constraints: The article presents this as a framework evolution for non-domestic buildings generally, not as a validated instrument for learning environments
target_learners: Students in higher education and school learning environments
target_learning_goals: Understanding how physical learning environments support teaching and learning
key_sources: Benjamin Cleveland & Kenn Fisher. (2014). The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature. Learning Environ Res 17, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10984-013-9149-3

article_title: The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature
citation: Benjamin Cleveland & Kenn Fisher. (2014). The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature. Learning Environ Res 17, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10984-013-9149-3
title: Post-occupancy evaluation as a developed methodology for evaluating non-domestic buildings
description: Post-occupancy evaluation (POE) is presented as an established methodology for evaluating non-domestic buildings, which the review charts historically to contextualize learning-space evaluation. The authors write that "we initially chart the development of post-occupancy evaluation (POE) for non-domestic buildings." POE serves as the foundational evaluative tradition from which the later, broader building performance evaluation framework emerged, and the review treats its development as the starting point for understanding how learning environments have been evaluated.
requirements: Buildings that are occupied and in use, so that performance after occupancy can be evaluated
constraints: Originally developed for non-domestic buildings rather than specifically for learning environments
target_learners: Students in school and higher education physical learning environments
target_learning_goals: Evaluating whether physical learning environments support intended educational activities
key_sources: Benjamin Cleveland & Kenn Fisher. (2014). The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature. Learning Environ Res 17, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10984-013-9149-3

article_title: The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature
citation: Benjamin Cleveland & Kenn Fisher. (2014). The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature. Learning Environ Res 17, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10984-013-9149-3
title: Evaluate physical learning environments from a rigorous pedagogical perspective
description: The review's central recommendation is that evaluation of physical learning environments should be grounded more rigorously in pedagogy rather than relying on building-focused methods alone. As the authors put it, "an argument is put forward for the evaluation of physical learning environments from a more rigorous pedagogical perspective." This principle directs evaluators to judge learning spaces against contemporary teaching and learning approaches, not only against building performance criteria. It follows directly from the gaps the review identifies in existing evaluative approaches.
requirements: Evaluation frameworks must incorporate contemporary approaches to teaching and learning, not only building performance measures
constraints: Existing approaches, including POE-derived methods, are positioned as insufficient on their own for pedagogically rigorous evaluation
target_learners: Students in higher education and school learning environments
target_learning_goals: Aligning physical learning environment evaluation with pedagogical goals and contemporary teaching practices
examples: The review compares and critically analyzes selected higher education and school evaluation approaches in view of contemporary approaches to teaching and learning before advancing this argument
key_sources: Benjamin Cleveland & Kenn Fisher. (2014). The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature. Learning Environ Res 17, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10984-013-9149-3

citation: Ruíz Montero, P. J., & Bru Serrano, M. (2021). La educación física y el deporte como servicio hacia los más vulnerables: beneficios del aprendizaje-servicio. Red Euroamericana de Investigación y Docencia en Educación Física. https://www.riadis.es
title: La metodología Aprendizaje-Servicio (ApS) como marco para desarrollar competencias prácticas y valores en estudiantes universitarios
description: El catálogo presenta el Aprendizaje-Servicio (ApS) como metodología socioeducativa aplicada desde la educación física y el deporte. Según el prólogo, "Dicha metodología permite, desde la práctica socioeducativa, y en este caso vinculada también a la educación física y el deporte, fomentar en los estudiantes competencias prácticas relacionadas con un mayor compromiso con la sociedad así como valores de igualdad, respecto, tolerancia y justicia social". Los proyectos descritos la aplican con estudiantes del Doble Grado en Educación Primaria y Ciencias de la Actividad Física y del Deporte que intervienen con colectivos vulnerables.

constraints: Se documenta en el contexto específico de la Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla y sus centros colaboradores (CETI, Centro Asistencial Gota de Leche)

aplicación práctica de contenido curricular

article_title: Peer Instruction: Engaging Students One-on-One, All At Once
citation: Crouch, C. H., Watkins, J., Fagen, A. P., & Mazur, E. (2003). Peer Instruction: Engaging Students One-on-One, All At Once. Research-Based Reform of University Physics. https://scholar.google.com
title: Align every course element with active engagement, since gains are greatest when the questioning strategy is accompanied by other engagement strategies
description: The article reports that gains in student understanding are greatest when the PI questioning strategy is accompanied by other strategies that increase engagement, "so that every element of the course serves to involve students actively." This includes exams with both conceptual and quantitative questions, cooperative discussion sections, pre-class reading assignments, grading that rewards participation rather than correctness on ConcepTests, and an absolute grading scale to remove competition.
requirements: examinations should include both conceptual short essay and quantitative problem-solving questions because exams drive how students study
a cooperative classroom atmosphere, with students not graded on the correctness of ConcepTest answers
constraints: assigning pre-class reading, although helpful, is not required for using Peer Instruction
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory physics courses, including non-majors and physics majors
target_learning_goals: conceptual reasoning alongside quantitative problem solving, and sustained student engagement across all course components
examples: At Harvard the authors introduced free-response reading assignments and cooperative learning into discussion sections in 1996, and the normalized gain continued to rise as more course components were modified to engage students actively
key_sources: Crouch, C. H., Watkins, J., Fagen, A. P., & Mazur, E. (2003). Peer Instruction: Engaging Students One-on-One, All At Once. Research-Based Reform of University Physics. https://scholar.google.com

article_title: BEYOND EXPLICIT RULE LEARNING
citation: Robert M. DeKeyser. (1997). Beyond Explicit Rule Learning: Automatizing Second Language Morphosyntax. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 19, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263197002040
title: Skill acquisition theory accounts for L2 morphosyntactic automatization
description: The article interprets its findings within current skill acquisition theory, the framework holding that cognitive skills — including second language morphosyntactic skills — are acquired through practice and become automatized gradually. The study's results are presented as support: skill-specific learning and power-function improvement over 8 weeks of practice match the theory's predictions for other cognitive skills. The author states the results "are consistent with current skill acquisition theory."
requirements: Learners must first reach criterion on metalinguistic tests of the rules before systematic practice toward automatization
constraints: Evidence comes from taught rules in an artificial language practiced under computer-controlled conditions
target_learners: adult second language learners in a controlled experimental setting
target_learning_goals: automatization of explicitly learned L2 morphosyntactic rules in comprehension and production
examples: 61 subjects were taught four morphosyntactic rules and 32 vocabulary items in an artificial language, then practiced them for 8 weeks in computer-controlled comprehension and production tasks
key_sources: Robert M. DeKeyser. (1997). Beyond Explicit Rule Learning: Automatizing Second Language Morphosyntax. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 19, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263197002040

citation: Robert M. DeKeyser. (1997). Beyond Explicit Rule Learning: Automatizing Second Language Morphosyntax. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 19, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263197002040
title: Modality-varied practice design: equal comprehension and production practice with rule-to-modality assignment varied between groups
description: This design pattern holds total practice constant while varying which rules are practiced in which modality. All subjects were taught the same rules and received the same amount of comprehension and production practice, but "which ruleswere practiced in comprehension and which in production varied between groups." Comprehension practice consisted of choosing between pictures to match a sentence; production practice consisted of typing the correct sentence corresponding to a picture. This allows skill-specificity of practice to be assessed.
requirements: A set of distinct rules that can be assigned differentially to comprehension and production practice
Learners at criterion on metalinguistic tests before practice begins
constraints: As implemented, the pattern was used with an artificial language and computer-controlled practice over 8 weeks
target_learners: adult second language learners
target_learning_goals: developing comprehension and production skill for specific morphosyntactic rules
examples: Comprehension practice consisted of choosing between pictures displayed on the computer screen to match a sentence; production practice consisted of typing the correct sentence corresponding to a picture

article_title:
THE ROBUSTNESS OF CRITICAL PERIOD EFFECTS IN SECOND LANGUAGE
ACQUISITION
citation: Robert M. DeKeyser. (2000). THE ROBUSTNESS OF CRITICAL PERIOD EFFECTS IN SECOND LANGUAGE ACQUISITION. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 22, Issue 4. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100004022
title: Fundamental Difference Hypothesis: adults lose implicit domain-specific language learning mechanisms and rely on problem-solving capacities
description: The Fundamental Difference Hypothesis (Bley-Vroman, 1988) holds that children learn language almost completely through implicit domain-specific mechanisms, whereas adults have largely lost the ability to learn a language without reflecting on its structure. Adults must instead use alternative mechanisms, "drawing especially on their problem-solving capacities, to learn a second language." The article tests this hypothesis empirically with adult immigrants.
requirements: The hypothesis implies that only adults with a high level of verbal analytical ability will reach near-native competence in their second language.
target_learners: adult second language learners
target_learning_goals: second language grammatical competence
examples: The study tested the hypothesis with 57 adult Hungarian-speaking immigrants using a grammaticality judgment test.

article_title:
THE ROBUSTNESS OF CRITICAL PERIOD EFFECTS IN SECOND LANGUAGE
ACQUISITION
citation: Robert M. DeKeyser. (2000). THE ROBUSTNESS OF CRITICAL PERIOD EFFECTS IN SECOND LANGUAGE ACQUISITION. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 22, Issue 4. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100004022
title: Reconceptualized Critical Period Hypothesis limited to implicit learning mechanisms, with no exceptions to age effects
description: The article proposes reconceptualizing the Critical Period Hypothesis by limiting its scope to implicit learning mechanisms. Under this scope limitation, the apparent exceptions to age effects are explained as adults succeeding through explicit, analytically mediated learning rather than implicit acquisition. The article concludes that "there may be no exceptions to the age effects that the hypothesis seeks to explain."
requirements: The hypothesis must be scoped to implicit learning mechanisms for the no-exceptions conclusion to follow.
target_learners: child and adult second language learners
target_learning_goals: implicit second language acquisition
examples: The few adult immigrants who scored within the child-arrival range had high verbal analytical ability, consistent with explicit rather than implicit learning.

The authors state they synthesized "the results of empirical studies (n = 21) on this topic since 1995" and that "We extracted 78 effect sizes from the included studies." Outcomes covered are language and math performance in primary education.

article_title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
citation: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser. (2023). Generative artificial intelligence enhances creativity but reduces the diversity of novel content. https://aspredicted.org/136723
title: Dual-pathway account: GenAI ideas as springboard versus anchor for human creativity
description: The article proposes two non-exclusive causal pathways by which access to GenAI ideas can affect human creative output. In the enhancing pathway, generated ideas serve as a "springboard" for the human mind, offering starting points that branch into a "tree structure" of storylines and helping writers overcome "writer's block" and the fear of a blank page. In the hampering pathway, GenAI anchors the writer to a specific starting idea, restricting the variability of the writer's own ideas and yielding derivative output. The study's findings — creativity gains alongside increased story similarity — are interpreted through both pathways operating at once.
requirements: Access to GenAI-generated starting ideas during a creative production task, with the writer free to use or ignore them
constraints: The two pathways "may not be mutually exclusive": enhancement on some dimensions (e.g. novelty) need not accompany enhancement on others (e.g. usefulness)
target_learners: adult writers on open-ended creative production tasks
target_learning_goals: produce creative written content (novel and useful stories)
examples: The experiment operationalized the pathways by offering writers one or up to five three-sentence GPT-4 story ideas versus no access, then measuring both evaluated creativity and embedding-based story similarity.
key_sources: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser. (2023). Generative artificial intelligence enhances creativity but reduces the diversity of novel content. https://aspredicted.org/136723

article_title: Shared Picture Book Reading Interventions for Child Language Development: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Dowdall, N., Melendez-Torres, G. J., Murray, L., Gardiner, F., Harrtford, L. & Cooper, P.J. (2020). Shared picture book reading interventions for child language development: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Child Development, 91(2). https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13225
title: Deliver book-sharing interventions with sufficient dosage (multiple sessions, over 60 minutes of contact time)
description: The review concludes that brief interventions are unlikely to improve children's language, while multi-session programmes with extended instructor-caregiver contact time are highly likely to do so. It states that "brief interventions being unlikely to result in improvements in children's language abilities" whereas "Interventions involving multiple sessions, on the other hand, with extended contact time between the instructor and caregiver, are highly likely to result in improvements to child language." The principle is to design caregiver training with enough sessions and contact time to change caregiver book-sharing behaviour.
requirements: Training must exceed roughly 60 minutes of collective contact time, delivered across multiple sessions with an instructor
constraints: The dose categorization was crude (a near median split at 60 minutes); the dose contrast for expressive language showed only weak evidence (p=0.07) and for receptive language was non-significant (p=0.11)
target_learners: Caregivers of children aged 1-6 years
target_learning_goals: Child expressive and receptive language development through interactive shared picture book reading
examples: In the included studies, dose varied from a nurse spending approximately five minutes during well-child visits discussing shared reading to an 18-session home programme; 10 of the 19 studies involved training time in excess of 60 minutes with caregivers

article_title: Kindergarten Entrance Age and Children’s Achievement
citation: Todd E. Elder and Darren H. Lubotsky. (2009). Kindergarten Entrance Age and Children’s Achievement: Impacts of State Policies, Family Background, and Peers. Journal of Human Resources. https://doi.org/10.3368/jhr.44.3.641
title: Interpret kindergarten entrance-age achievement gaps as evidence of prior skill accumulation, not of older children learning more in school
description: The article’s evidence supports reading entrance-age achievement differences as reflecting skills children bring to school rather than differences in capacity to learn once there. The authors “present evidence that the positive relationship between kindergarten entrance age and school achievement primarily reflects skill accumulation prior to kindergarten.” The timing pattern — the gap “appears during the first months of kindergarten” and “declines sharply in subsequent years” — is the basis for this interpretation, along with its concentration among upper-income children.
requirements: Achievement data spanning the first months of kindergarten and subsequent years are needed to distinguish pre-entry skill accumulation from in-school learning differences.
constraints: The interpretation rests on the article’s stated pattern that the association declines sharply after the first months of kindergarten; the full supporting analyses were not available in the supplied text.
target_learners: kindergarten-age children
target_learning_goals: achievement test performance in early elementary school
examples: The article contrasts the interpretation that older entrants learn more in school with its finding that the gap appears immediately at kindergarten entry and fades in later years.
key_sources: Todd E. Elder and Darren H. Lubotsky. (2009). Kindergarten Entrance Age and Children’s Achievement: Impacts of State Policies, Family Background, and Peers. Journal of Human Resources. https://doi.org/10.3368/jhr.44.3.641

article_title: Interlanguage Variability in Narrative Discourse: Style Shifting in the Use of the Past Tense
citation: Rod Ellis. (1987). Interlanguage Variability in Narrative Discourse: Style Shifting in the Use of the Past Tense. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 9, Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100006483
title: Style shifting in interlanguage varies by linguistic feature within a single discourse mode
description: The study frames interlanguage variability as style shifting that can be observed within one discourse mode by manipulating planning time, rather than by comparing different tasks or discourse types as previous studies did. It examines three past tense morphemes—regular past, irregular past, and past copula—among 17 intermediate L2 learners, and finds that "Different patterns of style shifting were observed for three morphemes, suggesting that the nature of the linguistic feature under investigation is a determining factor."
requirements: Data collection under at least two conditions differing in planning time within the same discourse mode
constraints: Findings concern intermediate L2 learners of English and the three past tense morphemes studied
target_learners: intermediate L2 learners of English
target_learning_goals: accurate use of past tense morphemes in narrative discourse
examples: Data were collected under planned writing, planned speech, and unplanned speech conditions in narrative discourse

article_title: DOES FORM-FOCUSED INSTRUCTION AFFECT THE ACQUISITION OF IMPLICIT KNOWLEDGE?
citation: Rod Ellis. (2002). Does Form-Focused Instruction Affect the Acquisition of Implicit Knowledge? A Review of the Research. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 24, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263102002073
title: The role of form-focused instruction in implicit L2 knowledge is a contested theoretical question between peripheral and facilitative/necessary positions
description: The article organizes its review around a theoretical controversy over whether form-focused instruction contributes to second language implicit knowledge. On one side, "Krashen (1993) has argued that the effects of FFI on acquisition are peripheral"; on the other, "N. Ellis (this issue) sees FFI as facilitative and even necessary for developing implicit L2 knowledge." The review of 11 studies of free production is positioned as evidence bearing on this dispute, and its synthesis comes down on the facilitative side.
requirements: Resolving the question requires studies that measure implicit knowledge through learners' free production rather than only controlled or monitored performance
constraints: The review's evidence base is 11 studies of FFI effects on free production, and its conclusions are hedged as what the review "suggests"
target_learners: second language learners
target_learning_goals: development of implicit L2 knowledge, particularly grammatical form
examples: The article reviews 11 studies that examined the effect of FFI on learners' free production as the empirical test of the two theoretical positions.
key_sources: Rod Ellis. (2002). Does Form-Focused Instruction Affect the Acquisition of Implicit Knowledge? A Review of the Research. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 24, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263102002073

article_title: FREQUENCY EFFECTS IN LANGUAGE PROCESSING
citation: Nick C. Ellis. (2002). Frequency Effects in Language Processing: A Review with Implications for Theories of Implicit and Explicit Language Acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 24, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263102002024
title: Usage-based exemplar theory of language acquisition
description: The review endorses usage-based theories in which "the acquisition of language is exemplar based". Acquisition proceeds as "the piecemeal learning of many thousands of constructions and the frequency-biased abstraction of regularities within them", so that "The regularities of language emerge from experience as categories and prototypical patterns". The article uses this framework to interpret the frequency effects it documents and to explain the developmental sequence of second language acquisition.
requirements: Learners must be exposed to substantial input, since regularities are abstracted in a frequency-biased way from experienced exemplars.
target_learners: second language learners
target_learning_goals: acquisition of constructions, categories, and prototypical patterns of the target language
key_sources: Nick C. Ellis. (2002). Frequency Effects in Language Processing: A Review with Implications for Theories of Implicit and Explicit Language Acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 24, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263102002024

article_title: FREQUENCY EFFECTS IN LANGUAGE PROCESSING
citation: Nick C. Ellis. (2002). Frequency Effects in Language Processing: A Review with Implications for Theories of Implicit and Explicit Language Acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 24, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263102002024
title: Determinants of pattern productivity in construction learning
description: The review identifies a set of learning mechanisms that determine how productive linguistic patterns become. As printed, "Determinants of pattern productivity include the power law of practice, cue competition and constraint satisfaction, connectionist learning, and effects of type and token frequency". This framework explains why some constructions generalize while others remain item-bound, and it connects second language acquisition to general principles of learning drawn from cognitive psychology and connectionism.
requirements: Pattern productivity depends on the interplay of practice history, cue competition, and the type versus token frequency of exemplars.
target_learners: second language learners
target_learning_goals: developing productive command of grammatical constructions
key_sources: Nick C. Ellis. (2002). Frequency Effects in Language Processing: A Review with Implications for Theories of Implicit and Explicit Language Acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 24, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263102002024

article_title: Learning Loss Due to School Closures During the COVID-19 Pandemic
citation: Engzell P., Frey A., Verhagen M. D. (2021). Learning loss due to school closures during the COVID-19 pandemic. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2022376118
title: Anonymized Dutch student-monitoring test-score dataset covering 15% of primary schools, 2017 to 2020
description: The study uses a fully anonymized dataset of national standardized test scores obtained through a partnership with the Mirror Foundation, covering "15% of all primary schools" and broadly representative of the national student body. It includes biannual test scores in math, spelling, and reading for students aged 8 to 11, plus demographics and school characteristics, with composite reliability correlating above 0.80 across 2 study years. Analysis scripts are available online at the authors' GitHub repository.
requirements: Access requires a partnership arrangement comparable to the one the authors used, since the data are confidential due to ethical and legal constraints.
constraints: The data underlying the study are confidential and cannot be shared directly; equivalent data are being added to existing datasets such as the Nationaal Cohortonderzoek Onderwijs.
target_learners: Dutch primary school students aged 8 to 11 (grades 4 to 7)
target_learning_goals: Mathematics, spelling, and reading achievement measured by national standardized tests
examples: The authors partnered with the Mirror Foundation, an independent research foundation associated with a third-party data service provider, to obtain the anonymized test-score data.

citation: Fielding, M. (2001). Students as Radical Agents of Change. Journal of Educational Change, 2, 123–141. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1017949213447
title: Students as Researchers: a radical approach positioning students as agents of change rather than data sources
description: Students as Researchers is presented as a radical alternative to conventional student consultation, in which students undertake research on their own schooling and act as agents of change. The abstract contrasts it with consultation that embeds "unwitting manipulation" and reaffirms "the compelling nature of the ``Students as Researchers'' approach". The approach is grounded in the author's joint work with a UK high school running since 1996.

constraints: The article's full text was not available; the account here rests on the abstract's own framing

democratic agency in education
examples: The still-current joint work in a UK high school developed since 1996, described with practical examples

article_title: Examining the Effectiveness of School-Bullying Intervention Programs Globally: a Meta-analysis
citation: Hannah Gaffney, David P. Farrington, & Maria M. Ttofi. (2019). Examining the Effectiveness of School-Bullying Intervention Programs Globally: a Meta-analysis. International Journal of Bullying Prevention. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42380-019-0007-4
title: The whole-school approach to bullying prevention
description: The whole-school approach, first introduced by Dan Olweus in Norway, is an organizing framework for anti-bullying programs that "incorporates individuals involved in every aspect of students' lives," including peers, parents, teachers, and the wider community, not only the students involved in bullying. Programs such as KiVa and ViSC apply it with a socio-ecological theoretical framework. The meta-analysis found it "was not always the most effective": OBPP was highly effective, KiVa only marginally so, ViSC undesirable, while the non-whole-school NoTrap! was most effective for victimization.
requirements: Requires engagement of the whole school community: students, peers, parents, teachers, and the wider community
constraints: The article concludes the whole-school approach "might not be effective for every individual student," citing high-trajectory victimization participants who showed lesser decreases
target_learners: School children and adolescents aged 4 to 18
target_learning_goals: Reducing bullying perpetration and victimization in schools
examples: OBPP, KiVa, and ViSC all adopted the whole-school approach; NoTrap! instead used a peer-led online forum with trained student moderators.

article_title: Examining the Effectiveness of School-Bullying Intervention Programs Globally: a Meta-analysis
citation: Hannah Gaffney, David P. Farrington, & Maria M. Ttofi. (2019). Examining the Effectiveness of School-Bullying Intervention Programs Globally: a Meta-analysis. International Journal of Bullying Prevention. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42380-019-0007-4
title: Four repeatedly evaluated anti-bullying programs: KiVa, OBPP, NoTrap!, and ViSC
description: Of 65 different school-based bullying programs in the meta-analysis, only four were evaluated more than twice across locations: KiVa, OBPP, NoTrap!, and ViSC. KiVa targets bystanders to reduce social rewards for bullies and includes a virtual-learning element; OBPP is a whole-school program operating at school, classroom, individual, and community levels; NoTrap! is a web-based program engaging students as peer-educators moderating an anti-bullying forum; ViSC is a 1-year train-the-trainer program with 13 student lessons. Table 1 compares their components.
requirements: Programs in the meta-analysis required an operational definition of school bullying, quantitative perpetration/victimization measures, and an experimental or quasi-experimental design with a control group
constraints: The article notes the four programs "incorporated quite similar intervention components," with NoTrap! the most different, yet their effectiveness varied greatly
target_learners: School children and adolescents, primarily primary and secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Reducing school-bullying perpetration and victimization, and building empathy, self-efficacy, and anti-bullying attitudes
examples: KiVa includes classroom lesson plans with group discussion, role-play, anti-bullying videos, and an anti-bullying computer game; ViSC students complete 13 lessons and a class project.

article_title: Review of the effects of citizenship education
citation: E. Geboers, F. Geijsel, W. Admiraal, G. ten Dam. (2013). Review of the effects of citizenship education. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2012.02.001
title: Two-domain organization of citizenship: political and social domains
description: The review organizes students' citizenship into at least two domains, the political and the social, and uses this distinction to characterize the empirical literature it surveys. It reports that "the political domain of citizenship to be emphasized more than the social domain," indicating that research on citizenship education has concentrated on political aspects of citizenship while giving comparatively less attention to social aspects. The framework serves as the review's organizing axis for describing what citizenship education effects concern.
requirements: Empirical studies of citizenship education must specify which domain of citizenship their outcomes concern for the domain distinction to be applied.
constraints: The review's corpus of 2003-2009 studies emphasized the political domain more than the social domain, so evidence on social-domain outcomes is comparatively limited.
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: citizenship development in political and social domains
key_sources: E. Geboers, F. Geijsel, W. Admiraal, G. ten Dam. (2013). Review of the effects of citizenship education. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2012.02.001

article_title: Review of the effects of citizenship education
citation: E. Geboers, F. Geijsel, W. Admiraal, G. ten Dam. (2013). Review of the effects of citizenship education. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2012.02.001
title: Schools should provide citizenship education because they can play a significant role in students' citizenship development
description: The review proceeds from the premise that "schools can play a significant role in the citizenship development of students," and notes that in most contemporary modern societies schools are obligated to provide citizenship education. The review's findings on effective forms — an open democratic classroom climate and a formal curriculum with citizenship projects and courses — indicate which implementations of this obligation appear promising for secondary schools.
requirements: Schools must be positioned to offer either an open democratic classroom climate or a formal curriculum including citizenship projects and courses.
constraints: The effectiveness of different forms of citizenship education is still unclear according to the review.
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: citizenship development
examples: The review identifies classroom-climate approaches and formal curricula with citizenship projects and courses as the forms appearing effective in the 2003-2009 literature.

article_title: Implementation Intentions and Goal Achievement: A Meta‐analysis of Effects and Processes
citation: Gollwitzer, Peter M., Sheeran, Paschal. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: a meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69-119. https://nbn-resolving.de/urn:nbn:de:bsz:352-opus-56534
title: Implementation intentions as if-then plans that specify the when, where, and how of goal striving in advance
description: The article defines an implementation intention as a plan that "spells out the when, where, and how of goal striving in advance" in the format "If situation Y is encountered, then I will initiate goal-directed behavior X!". The framework holds that strong goal intentions alone do not guarantee achievement because people may fail to deal effectively with self-regulatory problems during goal striving; implementation intentions address this by pre-linking a critical situation to a goal-directed response, which the meta-analysis links to enhanced cue accessibility and automated responding.
requirements: A specified critical situation (when/where) and a specified goal-directed response (how) must be linked in an if-then format formed in advance of goal striving.
target_learners: individuals pursuing personal or task goals
target_learning_goals: goal attainment and self-regulation of goal striving

It covered "systematic reviews of professional behavior change interventions published between 1966 and 1998" and identified "Forty-one reviews... covering a wide range of interventions and behaviors." This review-of-reviews structure maps which intervention families (passive dissemination, educational outreach, reminders, multifaceted approaches) have what kind of evidence, making the literature accessible to decision makers.

article_title: Sense of Belonging as a Predictor of Intentions to Persist Among African American and White First-Year College Students
citation: Hausmann, L.R.M., Schofield, J.W. & Woods, R.L. (2007). Sense of Belonging as a Predictor of Intentions to Persist Among African American and White First-Year College Students. Research in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11162-007-9052-9
title: College retention programs should address students' sense of belonging, since belonging predicts persistence intentions and can be bolstered by intervention
description: The article argues that retention programming should incorporate students' sense of belonging to their university. Belonging predicted persistence intentions controlling for other predictors, and a randomized intervention to enhance belonging slowed the typical first-year decline. The authors state that "implications for the development of college retention programs and for existing models of student persistence are discussed," grounding the recommendation in both the predictive and the intervention findings.
requirements: Programs must be able to reach first-year students during the academic year, when belonging and persistence intentions decline.
constraints: The intervention evidence concerns slowing the decline in sense of belonging, not directly demonstrating improved retention.
target_learners: African American and white first-year college students
target_learning_goals: Persistence intentions and retention in higher education
examples: First-year students were randomly assigned to a belonging-enhancing intervention or one of two control groups and surveyed three times across the academic year.

article_title: Problem-Based Learning: What and How Do Students Learn?
citation: Hmelo-Silver, C.E. (2004). Problem-Based Learning: What and How Do Students Learn?. Educational Psychology Review, 16, 235–266. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:EDPR.0000034022.16470.f3
title: Problem-based learning as an instructional method of learning through facilitated problem solving
description: The article defines problem-based learning (PBL) as an instructional method in which "students learn through facilitated problem solving." Learning centers on "a complex problem that does not have a single correct answer." Students work in collaborative groups to identify what they need to learn, engage in self-directed learning, apply new knowledge to the problem, and reflect on what they learned and on the effectiveness of the strategies employed. The teacher acts to facilitate the learning process rather than to provide knowledge. The article presents this as a constructivist, experience-based approach with a long history in problem-based approaches to learning.
requirements: A complex problem without a single correct answer around which student learning is organized
A teacher who facilitates the learning process rather than providing knowledge directly
target_learners: students in medical education
gifted education students
K-12 and higher education students
target_learning_goals: flexible knowledge
problem-solving skills
self-directed learning skills
examples: The article describes the PBL cycle: students identify learning needs in collaborative groups, engage in self-directed learning, apply new knowledge to the problem, and reflect on learning and strategy effectiveness.
key_sources: Hmelo-Silver, C.E. (2004). Problem-Based Learning: What and How Do Students Learn?. Educational Psychology Review, 16, 235–266. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:EDPR.0000034022.16470.f3

description: The article enumerates five goals of PBL: "1) flexible knowledge, 2) effective problem-solving skills, 3) SDL skills, 4) effective collaboration skills, and 5) intrinsic motivation." This goal framework organizes the article's examination of the nature of learning in PBL and its review of empirical evidence. The framework distinguishes content knowledge goals (flexible knowledge) from strategy goals (problem solving, self-directed learning), social goals (collaboration), and affective goals (intrinsic motivation).

constraints: The article notes considerable research exists on the first three goals but little on the last two

self-directed learning skills
effective collaboration skills
intrinsic motivation

title: In PBL the teacher facilitates learning rather than providing knowledge
description: The article states that in PBL "the teacher acts to facilitate the learning process rather than to provide knowledge." This facilitation role supports students as they work through complex problems in collaborative groups, identify their learning needs, engage in self-directed learning, and reflect on their learning and strategies. The principle positions the instructor as a guide to the problem-solving and self-directed learning process rather than as a primary source of content transmission.

article_title: Problem-Based Learning: What and How Do Students Learn?
citation: Hmelo-Silver, C.E. (2004). Problem-Based Learning: What and How Do Students Learn?. Educational Psychology Review, 16, 235–266. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:EDPR.0000034022.16470.f3
title: PBL learning cycle: problem solving, self-directed learning, application, and reflection
description: The article describes a recurring instructional sequence in PBL: "Students work in collaborative groups to identify what they need to learn in order to solve a problem. They engage in self-directed learning (SDL) and then apply their new knowledge to the problem and reflect on what they learned and the effectiveness of the strategies employed." This cycle organizes learning around a complex problem, alternates collaborative identification of learning needs with individual self-directed study, and closes with reflection on both content and strategy effectiveness.
requirements: A complex problem without a single correct answer
Collaborative groups
Opportunities for self-directed learning between group sessions
target_learners: students in PBL courses
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning skills
problem-solving skills
flexible knowledge
examples: The article presents this cycle as the defining structure of how students learn in PBL.
key_sources: Hmelo-Silver, C.E. (2004). Problem-Based Learning: What and How Do Students Learn?. Educational Psychology Review, 16, 235–266. https://doi.org/10.1023/B:EDPR.0000034022.16470.f3

article_title: Audience Perspective in Young Writers’ Composing and Revising
citation: Holliway, D.R., McCutchen, D. (2004). Audience Perspective in Young Writers' Composing and Revising. In: Allal, L., Chanquoy, L., Largy, P. (eds) Revision Cognitive and Instructional Processes. Studies in Writing, vol 13. Springer, Dordrecht. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-007-1048-1_6
title: Give young writers tasks that duplicate their readers' experiences to improve audience-aware revision
description: This principle holds that writing instruction should let students experience what their readers experience, rather than only receiving feedback about their text. The article's findings indicate that "when young writers engage in a task that duplicates their readers' experiences, they could more accurately revise their descriptive writing to meet their readers' informational needs." It works by building reader insight directly into the composing and revising task.
requirements: A writing task in which students take on or re-experience the reader's perspective, such as the reading-as-the-reader condition
constraints: Evidence reported is for descriptive essays by 5th and 9th grade US students
target_learners: 5th grade students
9th grade students
target_learning_goals: Audience awareness in writing
Revising descriptive writing to meet readers' informational needs
examples: Students revised descriptive essays and drafted new ones under a reading-as-the-reader condition, showing consistent significant improvement in both grades
key_sources: Holliway, D.R., McCutchen, D. (2004). Audience Perspective in Young Writers' Composing and Revising. In: Allal, L., Chanquoy, L., Largy, P. citation: Holliway, D.R., McCutchen, D. (2004). Audience Perspective in Young Writers' Composing and Revising. In: Allal, L., Chanquoy, L., Largy, P. (eds) Revision Cognitive and Instructional Processes. Studies in Writing, vol 13. Springer, Dordrecht. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-007-1048-1_6
title: Three-condition revision design varying reader insight (feedback only, rating-as-the-reader, reading-as-the-reader)
description: An instructional comparison design for studying audience perspective in writing: three revision conditions that "varied in the amount of reader insight they offered." The feedback-only condition gives writer-directed feedback; rating-as-the-reader and reading-as-the-reader progressively increase the writer's experience of the reader's perspective. The design was used with 5th and 9th graders composing and revising descriptive essays.
requirements: Descriptive writing tasks and a way to operationalize differing levels of reader insight across conditions
constraints: Studied in the context of descriptive essay revision and drafting by 5th and 9th grade US students
target_learners: 5th grade students
9th grade students
target_learning_goals: Audience-aware revision of descriptive writing
examples: The study's conditions were a feedback only condition, a rating-as-the-reader condition, and a reading-as-the-reader condition

article_title: Foreign and second language anxiety
citation: Elaine K. Horwitz. (2010). Foreign and second language anxiety. Language Teaching, Volume 43, Issue 2, April 2010, pp. 154-167. https://doi.org/10.1017/S026144480999036X
title: Foreign language anxiety (FLA) as a situation-specific anxiety construct
description: The article identifies foreign language anxiety (FLA) as a unique form of anxiety, identified in the mid-1980s, that some people experience in response to learning or using a second language. It is 'categorized as a situation-specific anxiety', comparable in kind to other familiar anxiety manifestations such as stage fright or test anxiety. This situation-specific conceptualization is what allowed language anxiety to be studied as a distinct construct rather than as generic anxiety.
requirements: Must be treated as distinct from trait, state, and achievement anxiety rather than as a generic anxiety measure
constraints: Applies specifically to anxiety experienced in response to learning and/or using an L2, not to anxiety in general
target_learners: second and foreign language learners
target_learning_goals: second language learning and production
examples: The article situates FLA's identification in the mid-1980s as a turning point after earlier mixed findings on anxiety and achievement

article_title: A further study of productive failure in mathematical problem solving: unpacking the design components
citation: Kapur, M. (2011). A further study of productive failure in mathematical problem solving: unpacking the design components. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9144-3
title: Productive failure: complex problem solving in small groups without instructional facilitation until teacher-led consolidation
description: Productive failure is a learning design in which students first solve complex problems in small groups without instructional facilitation, and instruction follows only afterwards. As the article defines it, PF is a design "where they solved complex problems in small groups without any instructional facilitation up until a teacher-led consolidation." The design deliberately allows seemingly failing exploration before consolidation, and this study unpacks its design components by comparing it against fully facilitated and lecture-practice variants.
requirements: Complex problems solved in small groups before any instructional facilitation
A teacher-led consolidation phase following the unguided problem-solving phase
target_learners: Seventh-grade mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Mathematical problem solving, including well-structured and higher-order application problems and flexible use of representations
examples: In this study, seventh-grade students in the PF condition solved complex problems in small groups without facilitation until a teacher-led consolidation, and were then post-tested on well-structured, higher-order application, and representational flexibility items.
key_sources: Kapur, M. (2011). A further study of productive failure in mathematical problem solving: unpacking the design components. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9144-3

article_title: A further study of productive failure in mathematical problem solving: unpacking the design components
citation: Kapur, M. (2011). A further study of productive failure in mathematical problem solving: unpacking the design components. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9144-3
title: Facilitated complex problem solving (FCPS) condition
description: FCPS is the comparison condition in this study: it is "the same as the PF condition except that students received instructional facilitation throughout their lessons." It serves as the design component that isolates the role of unguided exploration in productive failure, since it holds the complex group problem solving constant while removing the initial period without facilitation.
requirements: Complex problems solved in small groups
Instructional facilitation provided throughout the lessons
target_learners: Seventh-grade mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Mathematical problem solving
examples: Students in this condition worked on the same complex problems as PF students but received instructional facilitation throughout their lessons.
key_sources: Kapur, M. (2011). A further study of productive failure in mathematical problem solving: unpacking the design components. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9144-3

article_title: A further study of productive failure in mathematical problem solving: unpacking the design components
citation: Kapur, M. (2011). A further study of productive failure in mathematical problem solving: unpacking the design components. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9144-3
title: Traditional lecture and practice (LP) condition
description: The lecture and practice condition is the traditional baseline against which productive failure and facilitated problem solving were compared in this three-condition study. Students taught by the same teacher experienced traditional lecture and practice instruction, and their post-test performance on well-structured and higher-order application problems, plus representation flexibility, was compared with the other two designs.
requirements: Traditional lecture followed by practice as the instructional format
target_learners: Seventh-grade mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Mathematical problem solving
examples: One of the three learning designs experienced by the 109 students was traditional lecture and practice taught by the same Singapore school teacher.

article_title: Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1)
citation: Kearney CA, Gonzálvez C, Graczyk PA and Fornander MJ (2019) Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1). Front. Psychol. 10:2222. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02222
title: Taxonomy of categorical terms for school attendance problems
description: The review organizes the field's historical categorical vocabulary: school attendance as "a student's complete in-class physical presence during an academic day" and absenteeism as its absence, sometimes excused or unexcused. It defines truancy (illegal, unexcused absenteeism used to trigger legal consequences), school refusal (absence due to emotional difficulties), school withdrawal (parent-initiated absence), and school exclusion (school-initiated absence), noting these terms vary across disciplines and jurisdictions.
requirements: Terms must be defined within a jurisdiction or discipline because definitions vary across contexts
constraints: Considerable controversy and heterogeneity remain even with respect to these characterizations
target_learners: children and adolescents in primary and secondary school
target_learning_goals: promoting school attendance and reducing absenteeism
examples: School districts use truancy thresholds such as 10 unexcused absences in a semester to trigger legal or administrative consequences
key_sources: Kearney CA, Gonzálvez C, Graczyk PA and Fornander MJ (2019) Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1). Front. Psychol. 10:2222. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02222

article_title: Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1)
citation: Kearney CA, Gonzálvez C, Graczyk PA and Fornander MJ (2019) Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1). Front. Psychol. 10:2222. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02222
title: Definitional spectrum of school attendance and its problems from full presence to complete absence
description: The review presents a dimensional approach placing school attendance and its problems on a spectrum "ranging from full presence to complete absence" (Figure 1). The left side includes attendance with little difficulty and early warning signs such as frequent requests to leave the classroom; the middle covers mixed attendance such as tardiness and periodic absences; the right side covers complete absenteeism, stayout, and dropout. The spectrum captures fluid peri-attendance phenomena and treats dropout as a process rather than an event.
requirements: Specific, operational definitions for each panel of the spectrum remain needed
constraints: Lacks current utility in school districts and research studies, provides no etiological or functional information, and is not linked to prevention or intervention protocols
target_learners: children and adolescents in primary and secondary school
target_learning_goals: rapid, real-time assessment of type of school attendance problem
examples: Pflug and Schneider (2016) found among students with absenteeism in the past 7 days that 35.0% missed a single class or part of a school day, 31.3% missed an entire day, and 33.7% missed 2+ days
key_sources: Kearney CA, Gonzálvez C, Graczyk PA and Fornander MJ (2019) Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1). article_title: Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1)
citation: Kearney CA, Gonzálvez C, Graczyk PA and Fornander MJ (2019) Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1). Front. Psychol. 10:2222. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02222
title: Multi-tiered system of supports (MTSS) model for school attendance and absenteeism
description: The review describes an MTSS model arranging SA/A prevention and intervention into three tiers: Tier 1 universal approaches promoting school-wide attendance and preventing absenteeism for all students; Tier 2 approaches for emerging, acute, or mild to moderate absenteeism; and Tier 3 approaches for chronic and severe absenteeism. The model's dimensions include severity of absenteeism, degree of risk or contextual factors, target of intervention, and intervention intensity, designed to eschew a "wait to fail" mentality in favor of active monitoring and immediate intervention.
requirements: Implementation fidelity; attendance measures included in district MTSS models
constraints: Remains in development; absenteeism rates in some schools are so overwhelming that entry into Tiers 2 and 3 is strained; how it fits with academic, behavioral, and social MTSS approaches remains to be seen
target_learners: all students in a school, with targeted subgroups at Tiers 2 and 3
target_learning_goals: promoting school attendance, preventing and remediating absenteeism and dropout
examples: Cook et al. (2017) evaluated a program with Tier 1 home visits and mobile telephone contact, Tier 2 attendance data monitoring, and Tier 3 referrals to specialists for chronic absenteeism
key_sources: Kearney CA, Gonzálvez C, Graczyk PA and Fornander MJ (2019) Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1). citation: Kearney CA, Gonzálvez C, Graczyk PA and Fornander MJ (2019) Reconciling Contemporary Approaches to School Attendance and School Absenteeism: Toward Promotion and Nimble Response, Global Policy Review and Implementation, and Future Adaptability (Part 1). Front. Psychol. 10:2222. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02222
title: Functional model of school attendance problems with four maintaining functions
description: Kearney and colleagues' functional model focuses on variables that maintain or reinforce school attendance problems, designed primarily for Tier 2-type, child-initiated problems. The postulated functions are refusal to attend school to (1) avoid school-based stimuli provoking negative affectivity, (2) escape aversive social and/or evaluative situations, (3) seek attention from significant others, and/or (4) pursue tangible rewards outside of school. The first two reflect negative reinforcement and the latter two positive reinforcement.
requirements: A profile of the relative strength of each functional condition is recommended during case analysis
constraints: Designed primarily as a clinical approach for Tier 2-type school attendance problems, particularly child-initiated attendance problems
target_learners: children and adolescents with child-initiated school attendance problems
target_learning_goals: matching prescriptive treatment packages to the function of a student's attendance problem
examples: The model links to prescriptive treatment packages adapted across educational, mental health, and medical settings

article_title: Does noise affect learning? A short review on noise effects on cognitive performance in children
citation: Klatte M, Bergström K and Lachmann T (2013) Does noise affect learning? A short review on noise effects on cognitive performance in children. Front. Psychol. 4:578. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00578
title: Design classrooms and school siting for favorable listening conditions, because effective listening is a linchpin of school learning
description: The review argues that children need more favorable listening conditions than adults for decoding and processing oral information, and that this has practical implications for the acoustical design of classrooms, "since effective listening is a linchpin of school learning". It extends this to school placement near airports and noise-abatement policy. Despite existing standards for ambient noise and reverberation, many classrooms still do not fit young listeners' needs.
requirements: Classroom ambient noise levels and reverberation meeting international and national standards developed in past decades
constraints: The review reports many classrooms still do not fit the needs of young listeners despite the standards
Chronic noise effects are usually small in magnitude and confounding variables were not always sufficiently controlled
target_learners: elementary school children
young children including second-language learners and children with language or attention disorders
target_learning_goals: speech perception and listening comprehension
reading and prereading skills
examples: Studies simulating classroom-like conditions of noise and reverberation reported severe impairments in children's listening performance
key_sources: Klatte M, Bergström K and Lachmann T (2013) Does noise affect learning? A short review on noise effects on cognitive performance in children. Front. Psychol. 4:578. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00578

article_title: Peer and Self Assessment in Massive Online Classes
citation: Kulkarni, C., Koh Pang Wei, Le, H., Chia, D., Papadopoulos, K., Cheng, J., Koller, D., Klemmer, S. R. (2015). Peer and Self Assessment in Massive Online Classes. In: Design Thinking Research, Understanding Innovation. Springer, Cham. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-06823-7_9
title: Short, customizable feedback snippets for qualitative peer feedback
description: The article introduces short, reusable feedback snippets that peer graders can customize when reviewing assignments. They are designed to "cover common issues with assignments", so that students receive "more qualitative peer feedback" than numeric grades alone would provide. The snippets were introduced as one of the paper's interventions alongside bias feedback and a data-driven rubric-improvement approach.
requirements: Peer graders need a shared vocabulary of common assignment issues so snippets can be customized to each submission
target_learners: students in massive online classes
target_learning_goals: providing and receiving qualitative peer feedback on design assignments
examples: Used in the HCI online class's peer assessment system so reviewers could attach structured qualitative comments to grades
key_sources: Kulkarni, C., Koh Pang Wei, Le, H., Chia, D., Papadopoulos, K., Cheng, J., Koller, D., Klemmer, S. R. (2015). Peer and Self Assessment in Massive Online Classes. In: Design Thinking Research, Understanding Innovation. Springer, Cham. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-06823-7_9

article_title: Peer and Self Assessment in Massive Online Classes
citation: Kulkarni, C., Koh Pang Wei, Le, H., Chia, D., Papadopoulos, K., Cheng, J., Koller, D., Klemmer, S. R. (2015). Peer and Self Assessment in Massive Online Classes. In: Design Thinking Research, Understanding Innovation. Springer, Cham. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-06823-7_9
title: Data-driven approach highlighting high-variance grading items for rubric improvement
description: The article introduces "a data-driven approach that highlights high-variance items for improvement": grading data are analyzed to find rubric items on which peer graders disagree strongly, flagging them for revision. This let instructors target rubric changes where grading was least consistent, and it complemented the finding that well-worded rubrics have lower variance.
requirements: Requires peer grading data across graders so item-level variance can be computed
target_learners: instructors of large online classes
target_learning_goals: improving reliability of peer assessment rubrics
examples: Applied to the class's rubrics; after revising rubrics, median grading error decreased from 12.4 to 9.9%

article_title: Computerized Cognitive Training in Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Effect Modifiers
citation: Lampit A, Hallock H, Valenzuela M (2014) Computerized Cognitive Training in Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Effect Modifiers. PLoS Med 11(11): e1001756. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1001756
title: Design CCT for older adults as supervised group-based training at 1–3 sessions per week with sessions of at least 30 minutes
description: The review's moderator analyses ground a design principle: efficacy in healthy older adults "is to a large extent determined by design choices." Group-based delivery (g = 0.29) and 1–3 weekly sessions were effective, while home-based delivery and more than three sessions per week were ineffective, and sessions shorter than 30 min showed only weak evidence of efficacy. The authors conclude that "Consistently ineffective design choices should therefore be avoided."
requirements: Group-based delivery with a trainer present to support adherence, fidelity, and motivation, as the article describes group-based practice variables
constraints: Evidence limited to healthy older adults without dementia or MCI; durability of gains not addressed
Sessions shorter than 30 min show only weak evidence of efficacy
target_learners: cognitively healthy older adults (mean age 60+)
target_learning_goals: improving cognitive performance, particularly processing speed, nonverbal memory, working memory, and visuospatial skills
examples: Future studies incorporating supervised group-based delivery and a session frequency of 2–3 sessions per week can anticipate an approximate effect size of g = 0.29, per the authors' power calculation
key_sources: Lampit A, Hallock H, Valenzuela M (2014) Computerized Cognitive Training in Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Effect Modifiers. PLoS Med 11(11): e1001756. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1001756

article_title: Computerized Cognitive Training in Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Effect Modifiers
citation: Lampit A, Hallock H, Valenzuela M (2014) Computerized Cognitive Training in Cognitively Healthy Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Effect Modifiers. PLoS Med 11(11): e1001756. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1001756
title: CCT program content taxonomy: speed of processing, working memory, attention, multidomain, and video games
description: The review classifies CCT interventions into five content types: "speed of processing (SOP) training, WM training, attention training, multidomain training, and video games." Video games are defined as computer programs distributed for entertainment purposes before being tried as cognitive interventions. Across the 52 included datasets, 24 studies used multidomain training, nine SOP, nine WM, six attention, and four video games, with delivery split between group-based (61.5%) and home-based (36.5%) settings.
requirements: Programs must involve at least 4 h of practice on standardized computerized tasks or video games with clear cognitive rationale
constraints: Lab-specific interventions not involving computer interaction were excluded from the review's scope
target_learners: cognitively healthy older adults
target_learning_goals: enhancing cognitive performance across multiple domains
examples: Included programs ranged from commercial packages (CogniFit, Lumosity, Brain Fitness) to in-house programs and entertainment video games such as Rise of Nations and Tetris

article_title: Focus-on-Form and Corrective Feedback in Communicative Language Teaching
citation: Patsy M. Lightbown and Nina Spada. (1990). Focus-on-Form and Corrective Feedback in Communicative Language Teaching: Effects on Second Language Learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 12, Issue 4. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100009517
title: Competing views of the role of form-focused instruction in second language learning as an interpretive framework
description: The article frames its findings within what it calls "current competing views of the role of form-focused instruction in second language learning". This framework contrasts positions on whether explicit attention to linguistic form is needed within communicative language teaching, and the study's between-class accuracy differences are used as evidence brought to bear on that debate. The article positions its observational findings as informing this theoretical controversy rather than testing a single model.
requirements: Classroom observation data capable of characterizing teachers' form-focused instruction and learner accuracy outcomes
constraints: The framework is applied to communicative language teaching contexts with young learners in intensive ESL programs
target_learners: Elementary school students aged 10–12 in intensive ESL programs
target_learning_goals: Second language (English) oral accuracy and comprehension
examples: The study discusses its between-class accuracy findings in terms of the competing views rather than endorsing one position outright

article_title: Professional communities and student achievement – a meta-analysis
citation: Lomos, C., Hofman, R. H., & Bosker, R. J. (2011). Professional communities and student achievement - a meta-analysis. School Effectiveness and School Improvement, 22(2), 121-148. https://doi.org/10.1080/09243453.2010.550467
title: Professional community as a school-level construct whose conceptualization and operationalization vary across empirical studies
description: Professional community is a school-environment construct studied over three decades; the article notes it "has gained considerable momentum in the theoretical and empirical studies in this field". The article presents a comprehensive synthesis of available theories and their implications for how the concept should be conceptualized and operationalized, and then tests its relationship to student achievement meta-analytically. The construct lacks a universal definition, so its measurement differs across studies.
requirements: Conceptual and empirical validation of the concept's key dimensions, as the article discusses
constraints: No universal definition has been formulated
Operationalization differs across the various empirical studies conducted on the subject
target_learners: Students in elementary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Student achievement
examples: The article synthesizes theories of professional community and meta-analyzes studies of its effect on student achievement
key_sources: Lomos, C., Hofman, R. H., & Bosker, R. J. (2011). Professional communities and student achievement - a meta-analysis. School Effectiveness and School Improvement, 22(2), 121-148. https://doi.org/10.1080/09243453.2010.550467

article_title: Professional communities and student achievement – a meta-analysis
citation: Lomos, C., Hofman, R. H., & Bosker, R. J. (2011). Professional communities and student achievement - a meta-analysis. School Effectiveness and School Improvement, 22(2), 121-148. https://doi.org/10.1080/09243453.2010.550467
title: Validate the key dimensions of professional community conceptually and empirically before relying on the construct in school-improvement work
description: Because professional community lacks a universal definition and is operationalized inconsistently across studies, the article argues that the concept's key dimensions need conceptual and empirical validation. The article states that "the need for the conceptual and empirical validation of the concept's key dimension was discussed". This principle directs researchers and school designers to establish definitional and measurement validity before drawing on the construct.
requirements: A validated set of the concept's key dimensions, established both conceptually and empirically
constraints: Current operationalization differs across empirical studies, limiting comparability of findings
target_learners: Students in elementary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Student achievement
examples: The meta-analysis pooled heterogeneous studies whose operationalizations of professional community differ, motivating the authors' call for validation of key dimensions
