article_title: Comprehensible Input and Second Language Acquisition
citation: Lester Loschky. (1994). Comprehensible Input and Second Language Acquisition: What is the Relationship? Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 16, Issue 3, pp. 303-323. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100013103
title: Input hypothesis and its interactionist modification as competing accounts of the comprehension-acquisition relationship
description: The study is framed as an empirical test of Krashen's input hypothesis and Long's modification of it, which hold that second language acquisition is driven by comprehensible input, with negotiated interaction serving as a route to comprehension. The article experimentally operationalizes this by contrasting "unmodified input with no interaction," "premodified input with no interaction," and "unmodified input with the chance for negotiated interaction," and by measuring both comprehension and subsequent acquisition. Its findings complicate the hypothesis: interaction aided moment-to-moment comprehension but comprehension differences did not predict acquisition gains.
requirements: Testing the hypothesis requires experimentally differentiating input and interaction conditions and measuring both moment-to-moment comprehension and subsequent acquisition outcomes
constraints: The study used Japanese as the target language and two Japanese locative structures plus vocabulary as acquisition measures
target_learners: Second language learners of Japanese
target_learning_goals: L2 listening comprehension
vocabulary recognition
acquisition of Japanese locative grammatical structures
examples: The article states: "This study attempts to test aspects of the input hypothesis (Krashen, 1980, 1983, 1985) and Long's modification of it (Long, 1980, 1983a, 1985)."

article_title: Effects of captioning on video comprehension and incidental vocabulary learning
citation: Montero Perez, M., Peters, E., Clarebout, G., & Desmet, P. (2014). Effects of Captioning on Video Comprehension and Incidental Vocabulary Learning. Language Learning & Technology 18(1), 118–141. http://llt.msu.edu/issues/february2014/monteroperezetal.pdf
title: Vanderplank's speculative model of language learning through captioned video: 'taking out' language via attention and adaptation
description: Vanderplank's (1990) model explains how learners extract language from captioned video. The article summarizes it: "the 'taking out' of language from captioned video consists of both attention and adaptation." Attention is a conscious selection process based on "noting and gathering" information plus a reflective component in which learners notice a gap between their L2 knowledge and the captioned input; adaptation is the selection of linguistic elements learners attend to "for [their] own purposes." The study invokes this model to interpret why captioning supported form recognition and clip association.
requirements: Learners must attend to and process the captioned input while watching video for meaning
constraints: The article presents the model as speculative and invokes it as an interpretive frame, not as a tested prediction of this study
target_learners: (high-)intermediate L2 learners of French
target_learning_goals: Incidental vocabulary learning from captioned L2 video
examples: The authors state their form recognition and clip association results "are consistent with Vanderplank's model (1990), in which the role of subtitles was considered crucial to taking out words from captioned input."

article_title: Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks
citation: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0
title: Taxonomy of five categories of theoretical approaches in implementation science organized by three overarching aims
description: The article proposes a taxonomy that distinguishes five categories of theoretical approaches used in implementation science: process models, determinant frameworks, classic theories, implementation theories and evaluation frameworks. These map onto three overarching aims: "describing and/or guiding the process of translating research into practice", "understanding and/or explaining what influences implementation outcomes", and "evaluating implementation". The second aim is further broken down into determinant frameworks, classic theories and implementation theories based on origins, development, knowledge sources, stated aims and applications.
requirements: Users must recognize that the categories differ in assumptions, aims and characteristics, which have implications for their use
constraints: The categories are not always recognized as separate types of approaches in the literature, and there is considerable overlap between some of the categories
target_learners: implementation researchers
implementation practitioners in health care
target_learning_goals: selecting appropriate theoretical approaches for implementation research and practice
examples: Table 1 lists the five categories with descriptions and examples such as the Knowledge-to-Action Model, PARIHS, CFIR, COM-B and RE-AIM

article_title: Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks
citation: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0
title: Process models: theoretical approaches that describe and/or guide the process of translating research into practice
description: Process models are the first category in the taxonomy. They "specify steps (stages, phases) in the process of translating research into practice", aiming to describe and/or guide that process. A subtype, action (or planned action) models, "provides practical guidance in the planning and execution of implementation endeavours". Examples include the Stetler Model, the ACE Star Model, the Knowledge-to-Action Framework, the Iowa Model, the Ottawa Model, the Quality Implementation Framework and models by Grol and Wensing and by Pronovost et al. Early models depicted rational, linear transfer from producers to users, while later models emphasize facilitation and context.
requirements: Careful, deliberate planning, especially in the early stages of implementation endeavours
constraints: The actual process is not necessarily sequential, even though the models present an ideal step-wise, orderly, linear view
target_learners: implementation practitioners
health care teams planning implementation
target_learning_goals: planning and managing the translation of research into practice
examples: Many action models originate from the nursing-led field of research use, e.g. the Stetler Model and the Iowa Model
key_sources: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0

article_title: Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks
citation: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0
title: Determinant frameworks: descriptive structures specifying classes of determinants influencing implementation outcomes
description: Determinant frameworks form the second category. They "specify types (also known as classes or domains) of determinants and individual determinants, which act as barriers and enablers (independent variables) that influence implementation outcomes (dependent variables)". Their overarching aim is to understand and/or explain influences on implementation outcomes, e.g. predicting or retrospectively interpreting outcomes. Examples include PARIHS, CFIR, the Ecological Framework by Durlak and DuPre, and the Theoretical Domains Framework. They are multilevel and imply a systems approach, but "do not address how change takes place or any causal mechanisms, underscoring that they should not be considered theories".
requirements: Information about what influences implementation outcomes is potentially useful for designing and executing implementation strategies that aim to change relevant determinants
constraints: Most determinant frameworks provide limited how-to support since the determinants usually are too generic to provide sufficient detail for guiding an implementation process; they do not explicitly take a process perspective
target_learners: implementation researchers
health care quality improvement practitioners
target_learning_goals: understanding and explaining influences on implementation outcomes
examples: PARIHS emerged from the observation that successful implementation might be premised on three key determinants: characteristics of the evidence, context and facilitation
key_sources: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0

article_title: Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks
citation: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0
title: Classic theories: theories from external fields applied to explain aspects of implementation
description: Classic (or classic change) theories constitute the third category: theories originating from fields external to implementation science, such as psychology, sociology and organizational theory, applied to provide understanding and/or explanation of aspects of implementation. They are considered passive relative to action models because they "describe change mechanisms and explain how change occurs without ambitions to actually bring about change". Examples include the Theory of Planned Behaviour, Social Cognitive Theory, social network theories, communities of practice, organizational theories and the Theory of Diffusion.
requirements: Relevance to the determinant type being analysed, e.g. psychological theories for user/adopter characteristics and organizational theories for context
constraints: Organizational theories' actual use in empirical implementation studies is relatively limited despite increased interest
target_learners: implementation researchers
target_learning_goals: explaining determinants of implementation outcomes at individual, collective and organizational levels
examples: The Theory of Diffusion's innovation attributes (relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, observability) are widely applied in individual studies and determinant frameworks
key_sources: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0

article_title: Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks
citation: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0
title: Implementation theories: theories developed or adapted by implementation researchers to explain implementation
description: The fourth category comprises theories developed by implementation researchers, from scratch or by adapting existing theories and concepts, to provide understanding and/or explanation of aspects of implementation. Examples include Implementation Climate, Absorptive Capacity, Organizational Readiness, COM-B and Normalization Process Theory. Adaptation "allows researchers to prioritize aspects considered to be most critical", improving relevance to particular circumstances. COM-B posits that capability, opportunity and motivation generate behaviour, which in turn influences the three components; Normalization Process Theory identifies four determinants of embedding complex interventions in practice.
requirements: Adaptation of existing theories should prioritize aspects most critical to analysing the how and why of implementation
target_learners: implementation researchers
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms of implementation and embedding of interventions in practice
examples: Normalization Process Theory began as a model based on empirical studies of implementing new technologies and was later developed into a theory
key_sources: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0

article_title: Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks
citation: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0
title: Evaluation frameworks: structures specifying aspects of implementation that could be evaluated
description: The fifth category, evaluation frameworks, provides "a structure for evaluating implementation endeavours" by specifying aspects of implementation that could be evaluated to determine implementation success. Examples are RE-AIM (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance), PRECEDE-PROCEED, and Proctor et al.'s framework of eight implementation outcomes: acceptability, adoption, appropriateness, costs, feasibility, fidelity, penetration and sustainability. Approaches from the other four categories can also serve evaluation purposes because they specify concepts that may be operationalized and measured.
requirements: Specification of concepts and constructs that may be operationalized and measured
target_learners: implementation researchers
program evaluators in health services
target_learning_goals: evaluating implementation success
examples: Proctor et al.'s framework was developed on the basis of a narrative literature review proposing eight conceptually distinct outcomes

article_title: Video improves learning in higher education: A systematic review
citation: Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Sanders, T., Parker, P., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C. (2021). Video Improves Learning in Higher Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research, 91(2), 204–236. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654321990713
title: Maintain or increase interactivity when moving teaching content to video
description: The review's discussion recommends that shifting didactic content onto video should not reduce the interactive opportunities students receive. It reports that "moving content to video is more effective when teachers maintain, or even increase, the level of active learning offered to students", and suggests online discussions and embedded questions (e.g., using H5p or EdPuzzle) can raise interactivity in multimedia. This frees face-to-face time for discussion and other dynamic interactions.
requirements: Video-based instruction must offer interactivity at least equivalent to the teaching it replaces, e.g., embedded questions or online discussion.

target_learning_goals: knowledge and skill acquisition in higher education courses
examples: The review found videos were effective when both conditions had equivalent interactivity (g = 0.33) and particularly effective when video conditions added interactivity such as co-viewing with a peer (g = 0.62), but showed no benefit when the control condition was more interactive.

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Zimmerman's Cyclical Phases model of SRL: forethought, performance, self-reflection
description: Zimmerman's Cyclical Phases model organizes self-regulated learning into three recursive phases. Per the review, in the forethought phase "the students analyze the task, set goals, plan how to reach them" energized by motivational beliefs; in the performance phase they execute the task while monitoring progress and using self-control strategies; in the self-reflection phase they assess performance and make attributions whose self-reactions influence later task engagement. The review treats it as the individual-level process model comparable to the other five SRL models analyzed.
requirements: Describes SRL at the individual level, parallel to the other reviewed models
target_learners: students across educational levels
target_learning_goals: strategic self-regulated learning
examples: Cleary et al. trained 50 college students in basketball free throws across conditions training different numbers of SRL phases

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Boekaerts' Dual Processing self-regulation model: mastery/growth versus well-being pathways
description: Boekaerts' Dual Processing self-regulation model describes how student appraisals determine which goal pathway activates during learning. The review states the model "described two parallel processing modes: (a) a mastery or learning mode and (b) a coping or well-being mode." When students perceive a task as threatening, negative cognitions and emotions trigger well-being protection; when the task fits their goals, positive cognitions trigger the mastery/growth pathway. The model assigns three purposes to self-regulation: expanding knowledge and skills, preventing threat to the self, and protecting commitments by re-routing attention from the well-being to the mastery pathway.
requirements: Student appraisals of the task determine which pathway is activated
constraints: Students who start in the mastery/growth pathway may switch to the well-being pathway if they detect cues they might not be successful
target_learners: students in secondary and vocational education
students across educational levels
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
emotion regulation during learning
examples: Boekaerts developed the On-line Motivation Questionnaire to measure task-specific feelings, thoughts and effort before and after tasks

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Winne and Hadwin's metacognitive SRL model: four recursive phases and the COPES architecture
description: Winne and Hadwin's model takes a strongly metacognitive, information-processing view of SRL. The review states that "studying is powered by SRL across four linked phases that are open and recursive and are comprehended in a feedback loop": task definition, goal setting and planning, enacting study tactics and strategies, and metacognitively adapting studying. SRL deploys five task facets identified by "the COPES acronym" — Conditions, Operations, Products, Evaluations, Standards — with operations described as SMART (Searching, Monitoring, Assembling, Rehearsing, Translating). Students constantly monitor activities against standards, aligning the model with self-assessment research.
requirements: Scaffolding tools that record trace and log data are used to measure SRL under this model, since no classical questionnaires exist
constraints: The model figure contains no reference to emotions and only an allusion to motivation
target_learners: students in computer-supported learning settings
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring against standards
strategic study tactics
examples: Winne's team developed nStudy and gStudy, computer-supported learning environments that scaffold SRL while recording trace data

title: Pintrich's SRL model: four phases crossed with four areas for regulation
description: Pintrich's model, presented in the first SRL handbook, structures SRL as four phases — forethought/planning/activation, monitoring, control, and reaction and reflection — each crossed with four areas for regulation: cognition, motivation/affect, behavior and context. The review notes this combination "offers a comprehensive picture that includes a significant number of SRL processes." The behavior-regulation area, covering "individual's attempts to control their own overt behavior," is unique among the six reviewed models, and the context area covers students' attempts to monitor, control and regulate the learning context.

constraints: The review states there is no empirical evidence directly addressing validation of Pintrich's model itself, only MSLQ validation data

high school students

title: Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ)
description: The MSLQ is Pintrich's widely used self-report instrument for measuring SRL and motivation. The review reports it "is composed of 15 scales, divided into a motivation section with 31 items, and a learning strategies (SRL) section with 50 items" subdivided into cognitive, metacognitive and resource management scales. Its strength is combining SRL and motivation measures, offering detailed information about students' learning strategy use. Versions exist for college and high school students, and two recent reviews found it the most used instrument in SRL and in self-efficacy measurement.

high school students

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Efklides' MASRL model: Person level and Task×Person level interaction of metacognition, motivation and affect
description: Efklides' Metacognitive and Affective Model of Self-Regulated Learning (MASRL) distinguishes two interacting levels. The Person level (macrolevel) is top-down and goal-driven, comprising cognition, motivation, self-concept, affect, volition, metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive skills. The Task×Person level (microlevel) is bottom-up and data-driven, where metacognitive activity takes control and attention moves to task-specific mechanisms. The review calls this distinction "probably the most salient feature of the MARSL model," and states the model clarifies how metacognition, motivation and affect interact via the macro and micro levels, with four basic functions at the microlevel: cognition, metacognition, affect, and regulation of affect and effort.
requirements: Empirical support rests on studies showing interactions among metacognition, motivation and affect at the two levels
constraints: Offers a different conceptualization of top-down/bottom-up processing than Boekaerts and Corno's account
target_learners: students across educational levels
target_learning_goals: metacognitive experiences during task execution
regulation of affect and effort
examples: Efklides created the Metacognitive Experiences Questionnaire exploring judgments and feelings about cognitive processing

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Front. Psychol. 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: SSRL model: three modes of regulation in collaborative learning (SRL, CoRL, SSRL)
description: The Hadwin, Järvelä and Miller model addresses regulation in collaborative and computer-supported learning. It proposes three modes: individual self-regulation adapting to interaction with group members; co-regulation, which "refers broadly to affordances and constraints stimulating the (student's) appropriation of strategic planning, enactment, reflection, and adaptation"; and socially shared regulation, where "deliberate, strategic and transactive planning, task enactment, reflection and adaptation" emerge through transactive exchanges among group members. SSRL unfolds in four loosely sequenced, recursively linked feedback loops adapted from Winne and Hadwin, extending regulation from the "I" or "you" level to collective activity.
requirements: Group members must commit to group work, establish shared common ground, and negotiate and share task perceptions, strategies and goals
constraints: The CoRL mode's use has not been consistent in the field and it has been the most disputed regulatory level; CoRL and SSRL can both occur as groups progress through different collaboration phases
target_learners: students in collaborative and computer-supported collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: shared regulation of group learning
collaborative planning and evaluation
examples: A review by Panadero and Järvelä found empirical evidence of SSRL occurrence in cognitive, metacognitive, motivational and emotional shared areas

article_title: Assimilating complex information
citation: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813
title: The isolated-interacting elements two-phase instructional approach
description: The thesis develops a two-phase instructional approach for complex material. In the first phase the material's element interactivity is artificially reduced by presenting information as isolated elements that can be processed serially rather than simultaneously in working memory; in the second phase all the information for understanding is presented. The control instruction presented all information for understanding in both phases. The approach aims to promote schema construction in order to foster understanding while avoiding early working-memory overload.
requirements: Complex material whose element interactivity can be analysed and artificially reduced in a first instructional phase
A second phase in which all the information required for understanding is presented
constraints: A possible consequence of artificially reducing element interactivity may be an initial decrease in a student's capacity for understanding, per the thesis's own hypothesis statement
target_learners: Novice students learning complex information (e.g. apprentices at the Email training centre and BHP Ltd.)
target_learning_goals: Understanding of complex, high element-interactivity content and schema construction
examples: Experiments 1 and 2 used isolated and interacting elements instructional materials; Experiments 3 and 4 used oven baking and oven electrical circuit materials; Experiment 5 used fault finding tests

title: Schema construction as the mechanism underlying the isolated-interacting elements effect
description: The thesis proposes that schema construction is the mechanism underlying the success of the isolated-interacting elements instructional method. The first, isolated-elements phase is designed to allow learners to build component schemas without overwhelming working memory, and the second, interacting-elements phase then integrates them. The thesis states that evidence was provided in support of this proposal, linking the instructional sequence to the cognitive architecture in which schemas reduce working-memory load by storing organised knowledge in long term memory.
requirements: Instruction sequenced so that component schemas can be constructed before interacting elements are presented
constraints: The mechanism claim is supported within the five experiments of this thesis on complex technical material; the supplied text reports no test beyond these domains
target_learners: Novice and more experienced learners of complex technical information
target_learning_goals: Schema construction and understanding of complex, element-interactive material
examples: The thesis's experiments measured whether the isolated-then-interacting sequence produced better understanding, interpreted via schema construction

title: Cognitive load theory as the generative framework of the thesis
description: The thesis is grounded in cognitive load theory, which is based on the assumption that features of human cognitive architecture have important implications for how we learn and understand. The theory distinguishes sources of cognitive load, including intrinsic load tied to element interactivity and extraneous load imposed by instructional design, and generates instructional techniques such as goal-free problems, worked examples, and split-attention, redundancy and modality effects. The five experiments reported in the thesis were generated by this theory.
requirements: Assumptions about human cognitive architecture, particularly limited working memory and long-term memory schema storage
constraints: The supplied text presents the theory as background framework; its detailed treatment of load sources lies in Chapter 2, not fully included in the supplied excerpt
target_learners: Learners of complex information across educational and training settings
target_learning_goals: Effective learning and understanding of complex material under working memory constraints
examples: The thesis's Chapter 2 lists instructional techniques generated by the theory, including goal free problems, worked examples, and the split attention, redundancy and modality effects

article_title: Assimilating complex information
citation: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813
title: Schemas reduce working memory load by incorporating interacting elements as single units
description: Within the thesis's account of cognitive architecture, human cognition circumvents the severely limited capacity of working memory by constructing schemas that organise elements of information categorically and store them in long term memory. Schemas shift the burden of storage to long term memory, and interacting elements that would otherwise overwhelm working memory can be incorporated in a schema that acts as a single element and imposes a minimal working memory load. This account underpins the thesis's rationale for reducing element interactivity during early instruction.
requirements: Prior knowledge organised into schemas stored in long term memory
constraints: The account is presented as the thesis's theoretical framing of memory and schema research, not as a new empirical result of the five experiments
target_learners: All learners processing complex, element-interactive information
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and learning of complex material within working memory limits
examples: The thesis illustrates the account with algebraic schemas: a/b = c can be transformed into a = cb and both equations processed easily in working memory by anyone competent at elementary algebra

article_title: A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning
citation: Spanjers, I. A. E., van Gog, T., & van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2010). A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9135-6
title: Cognitive load / transience account: segmentation reduces extraneous load from information transience by dividing content into smaller units and providing processing pauses
description: This account, grounded in cognitive load theory and the time-based resource-sharing model of working memory, explains why transient dynamic visualizations can hinder learning: information is continuously replaced, so learners must maintain earlier information in working memory while processing new incoming information. Segmentation addresses this because "pauses between segments provide students with sufficient time to attend to necessary cognitive activities on the bit of information presented in the previous segment, without having to simultaneously attend to new incoming information." The review attributes the effectiveness of segmentation partly to this reduction of the co-occurrence of processing activities.
requirements: Applies to complex dynamic visualizations that are high in intrinsic load, where extraneous load must be decreased so learning is not hampered
constraints: Providing pauses increases total available learning time, but the review argues the effect is not simply due to learning time, citing Hasler et al. (2007) where learning time was equal across conditions
target_learners: Students learning from complex dynamic visualizations, especially novices
target_learning_goals: Understanding of processes and procedures depicted in animations and videos
examples: The review interprets the segmented-condition advantages in the Mayer and Chandler (2001), Moreno (2007), and Hasler et al. (2007) studies through this load-reduction mechanism

article_title: A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning
citation: Spanjers, I. A. E., van Gog, T., & van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2010). A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9135-6
title: Event segmentation theory: people mentally segment dynamic visualizations during perception, and instructional segmentation can cue relevant event boundaries
description: Event segmentation theory (Zacks et al. 2007) "describes the processes underlying mental segmentation": people form event models in working memory, predict what happens next, and distinguish an event boundary when predictions and incoming sensory information differ too much. Physical and structural changes decrease predictability and mark boundaries; more extensive processing occurs at boundaries, so more information about them is stored in long-term memory. The review proposes that instructional segmentation works partly by cueing these boundaries — "rather than relying on students' ability to mentally segment the dynamic visualisations, this is done for them" — aiding perception of the underlying structure and chunking.
requirements: Event boundaries in the material should correspond to meaningful subevents or substeps of the depicted process or procedure
constraints: Students with higher levels of prior knowledge might not need these temporal cues or might even be hampered by them, because guidance must be reconciled with their available schemas
target_learners: Students learning from dynamic visualizations of processes and procedures, particularly novices
target_learning_goals: Perceiving the structure underlying a depicted process or procedure; remembering subevents and their temporal order
examples: The review links segmentation to Catrambone's work on labeled, visually isolated calculation substeps, which raised learning outcomes and prompted students to mention substeps in their procedure descriptions
key_sources: Spanjers, I. A. E., van Gog, T., & van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2010). A Theoretical Analysis of How Segmentation of Dynamic Visualizations Optimizes Students' Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9135-6

article_title: Mad City Mystery: Developing Scientific Argumentation Skills with a Place-based Augmented Reality Game on Handheld Computers
citation: Squire, K.D., Jan, M. (2007). Mad City Mystery: Developing Scientific Argumentation Skills with a Place-based Augmented Reality Game on Handheld Computers. J Sci Educ Technol 16, 5–29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-006-9037-z
title: Post-progressive pedagogy through narrative game play: developing narrative accounts of scientific phenomena as a mechanism for scientific argumentation
description: The article proposes that location-based augmented reality games can create a "post-progressive" pedagogy in which students are immersed in authentic scientific inquiry and required to perform in adult scientific discourses. Its core mechanism is that "Through game play, players are required to develop narrative accounts of scientific phenomena, a process that requires them to develop and argue scientific explanations." Game features then scaffold this thinking, providing supports the authors say are "non-existent in most inquiry-based learning environments."
requirements: Handheld augmented reality game structures that position players as investigators developing and defending explanations
constraints: The authors note that time constraints alone might disqualify the game from being considered authentic in any meaningful respect
target_learners: middle school and similar-aged students in environmental science
target_learning_goals: scientific argumentation
developing and arguing scientific explanations
examples: In Mad City Mystery, players investigated an environmental science mystery, developing narrative accounts of phenomena such as mercury contamination
key_sources: Squire, K.D., Jan, M. (2007). Mad City Mystery: Developing Scientific Argumentation Skills with a Place-based Augmented Reality Game on Handheld Computers. J Sci Educ Technol 16, 5–29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-006-9037-z

article_title: Mad City Mystery: Developing Scientific Argumentation Skills with a Place-based Augmented Reality Game on Handheld Computers
citation: Squire, K.D., Jan, M. (2007). Mad City Mystery: Developing Scientific Argumentation Skills with a Place-based Augmented Reality Game on Handheld Computers. J Sci Educ Technol 16, 5–29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-006-9037-z
title: Mad City Mystery: a place-based augmented reality curriculum on handheld computers for environmental science
description: Mad City Mystery is an Augmented Reality curriculum used on handheld computers to support learning in environmental science, investigated across three cases in a design-based research study. The game places students in an environmental mystery (involving possible contamination, e.g. mercury and PCBs) where they interpret readings and build arguments. The authors investigate "whether augmented reality games on handhelds can be used to engage students in scientific thinking (particularly argumentation), how game structures affect students' thinking, the impact of role playing on learning, and the role of the physical environment in shaping learning."
requirements: Handheld computers running the augmented reality platform and a physical location to play in
constraints: The authors acknowledge that time constraints alone might disqualify the game from being considered authentic in any meaningful respect
target_learners: students in environmental science (roughly 28 students across three cases)
target_learning_goals: scientific argumentation
environmental science reasoning
examples: Students interpreted a marginally high mercury reading as evidence in the environment; the authors note the group was probably justified in that interpretation but not in throwing out their hypothesis altogether

article_title: When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms
citation: Strobel, J., & van Barneveld, A. (2009). When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-Based Learning, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1046
title: Qualitative meta-synthesis as a method for reconciling divergent meta-analyses of PBL effectiveness
description: The article's organizing approach is a qualitative meta-synthesis: rather than computing a new pooled estimate, it compares and contrasts the assumptions and findings of existing meta-analyses of PBL. The method treats divergent meta-analytic conclusions as data, explaining apparent contradictions (e.g., retention outcomes) by the type of outcome measured. As the article states, "This study used a qualitative meta-synthesis approach to compare and contrast the assumptions and findings of the meta-analytical research on the effectiveness of PBL."
requirements: Requires a body of existing meta-analyses on the topic whose assumptions and findings can be compared and contrasted
constraints: Conclusions are qualitative syntheses of prior meta-analyses rather than new pooled effect estimates
target_learners: students in PBL and conventional classrooms across disciplines
target_learning_goals: long-term retention, skill development, short-term retention on standardized exams
examples: The synthesis reconciled meta-analytic disagreement by showing PBL advantages on long-term retention, skill development, and satisfaction, and traditional-instruction advantages on short-term board-exam retention.
key_sources: Strobel, J., & van Barneveld, A. (2009). When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-Based Learning, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1046

article_title: When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms
citation: Strobel, J., & van Barneveld, A. (2009). When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-Based Learning, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1046
title: Match the choice between PBL and conventional instruction to the targeted retention horizon and outcome
description: Because the meta-analytic evidence shows divergent advantages by outcome type, instructional designers should choose PBL when the goal is long-term retention, skill development, or learner and teacher satisfaction, and conventional instruction when the goal is short-term retention on standardized board exams. The synthesis found "PBL was superior when it comes to long-term retention, skill development and satisfaction of students and teachers, while traditional approaches were more effective for short-term retention as measured by standardized board exams."
requirements: Clarity about which outcome matters for the program: long-term retention and skills versus short-term standardized exam performance
constraints: The short-term retention evidence is specific to standardized board exams as the outcome measure
target_learners: students in higher education and professional programs using PBL
target_learning_goals: long-term retention, skill development, satisfaction, standardized exam performance
examples: The meta-synthesis compared PBL with traditional instruction across meta-analyses and found the advantage flips depending on whether the outcome is long-term retention and skills or short-term board-exam performance.
key_sources: Strobel, J., & van Barneveld, A. (2009). When is PBL More Effective? A Meta-synthesis of Meta-analyses Comparing PBL to Conventional Classrooms. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-Based Learning, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1046

article_title: A Meta-analysis of the Effectiveness of Intervention Programs Designed to Support Autonomy
citation: Su, Y.-L., & Reeve, J. (2011). A Meta-analysis of the Effectiveness of Intervention Programs Designed to Support Autonomy. Educational Psychology Review, 23, 159–188. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9142-7
title: Design autonomy-support training programs that train multiple elements of autonomy support in brief, skill-based, multimedia sessions
description: The article's moderator results are presented as design guidance for future programs: relatively more effective programs "trained multiple elements of autonomy support" and were "presented in relatively brief (1–3 h) sessions in a laboratory training setting that focused on skill-based activities and utilized multiple types of media." The authors state the results "identified the conditions under which future programs can be designed to be highly effective."
requirements: Programs must target people who support others' autonomy, such as teachers
constraints: The small number of included studies warrants caution, as the authors state
target_learners: teachers
other professionals who support others' autonomy
target_learning_goals: adopting an autonomy-supportive motivating or teaching style
examples: The meta-analysis compared program subcategories on delivery format, session length, setting, activity type, and media use

article_title: A Meta-analysis of the Effectiveness of Intervention Programs Designed to Support Autonomy
citation: Su, Y.-L., & Reeve, J. (2011). A Meta-analysis of the Effectiveness of Intervention Programs Designed to Support Autonomy. Educational Psychology Review, 23, 159–188. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9142-7
title: Autonomy-supportive training programs as a class of interventions grounded in self-determination theory
description: The article treats autonomy-supportive training programs as an identifiable class of interventions designed to help people (teachers, parents, managers, health-care providers) support the autonomy of others, grounded in self-determination theory. Its purpose was "to determine whether training intervention programs designed to help people support the autonomy of others are effective and, second, to identify the set of conditions that allowed these interventions to be most effective." The framework organizes programs by trained elements, delivery format, and recipient characteristics.
requirements: Trainees must interact with others whose autonomy they can support (e.g., students, patients, employees)
constraints: Effectiveness conclusions rest on 19 studies, a small number the authors say warrants caution
target_learners: teachers
trainees and experienced professionals
health-care providers
target_learning_goals: supporting others' autonomy
adopting autonomy-supportive behaviors
examples: Included studies ranged from classroom teacher training (e.g., deCharms, Reeve) to medical-student and smoking-cessation interventions (e.g., Williams and colleagues)

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design
citation: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205
title: Cognitive load theory's model of human cognitive architecture: limited working memory with modality-based subcomponents and unlimited long-term memory holding schemas
description: The article's organizing framework is a model of human cognitive architecture underpinning cognitive load theory. It assumes "a limited capacity working memory that includes partially independent subcomponents to deal with auditory/verbal material and visual/2- or 3-dimensional information" alongside "an effectively unlimited long-term memory, holding schemas that vary in their degree of automation." These structures and functions are the basis from which the theory derives its instructional guidelines.
requirements: Instructional applications must respect the limited capacity of working memory when presenting information
constraints: The architecture is stated as the theory's assumption, not as a directly tested finding in the text available
target_learners: All learners processing new instructional material
target_learning_goals: Schema construction and automation in domain learning
key_sources: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design
citation: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205
title: Design instruction to reduce working memory load and encourage schema construction
description: The article's central design principle is that instruction should be built on "the assumption that working memory load should be reduced and schema construction encouraged." Because working memory is limited while schema construction drives learning, presentation of information should be arranged to lower unnecessary load and support schema building. The article reports that a variety of novel instructional procedures were designed on this basis.
requirements: Instructional designers must know which activities impose working memory load and which support schema construction
target_learners: All learners of instructional materials designed under cognitive load theory
target_learning_goals: Optimizing intellectual performance through schema construction
examples: The article states that cognitive architecture structures "have been used to design a variety of novel instructional procedures" based on the load-reduction and schema-construction assumption
key_sources: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205

article_title: Benefits and Pitfalls of Multimedia and Interactive Features in Technology-Enhanced Storybooks
citation: Takacs, Z. K., Swart, E. K., & Bus, A. G. (2015). Benefits and Pitfalls of Multimedia and Interactive Features in Technology-Enhanced Storybooks: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 85(4), 698-739. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654314566989
title: Cognitive processing account: dual-channel multimedia integration helps, extraneous interactivity overloads young children's working memory
description: The article interprets its findings through the cognitive theory of multimedia learning and cognitive load theory. Dual coding theory holds that "verbal and nonverbal information are processed in two separate but interconnected channels," so congruent animation, music, and sound support comprehension rather than overload. Conversely, the coherence effect predicts deeper learning when extraneous materials are excluded; interactive features such as games and hotspots may act as seductive extraneous material, forcing task switching between story comprehension and play that places excessive load on young children's limited working memory.
requirements: Multimedia additions must be congruent with the narration to support rather than distract from comprehension
constraints: Even story-relevant interactive features may disturb comprehension because comprehending and playing are fundamentally different tasks requiring switching
target_learners: preschool and elementary-school children (ages 3-10)
target_learning_goals: story comprehension
vocabulary learning
code-related literacy skills
examples: The meta-analysis tested these predictions by contrasting multimedia-only, interactive-only, and multimedia-interactive stories across 43 studies
key_sources: Takacs, Z. K., Swart, E. K., & Bus, A. G. (2015). Benefits and Pitfalls of Multimedia and Interactive Features in Technology-Enhanced Storybooks: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 85(4), 698-739. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654314566989

article_title: SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT
citation: Yasser Teimouri, Julia Goetze, and Luke Plonsky. (2019). SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYSIS. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 41, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263118000311
title: Meta-analytic corpus of 97 reports, 105 independent samples, and 216 effect sizes on L2 anxiety and achievement
description: The study assembled a meta-analytic dataset on L2 anxiety and achievement. Following a comprehensive search, "a sample of 97 reports were identified, contributing a total of 105 independent samples (N = 19,933) from 23 countries," yielding 216 effect sizes (correlations). The corpus underpins the aggregate estimate and moderator analyses. The study earned an Open Data badge, with materials available at the IRIS database.
requirements: Comprehensive search to identify eligible reports of the anxiety–achievement relationship
target_learners: second language learners across 23 countries and multiple educational levels
target_learning_goals: second language achievement
examples: 97 reports contributing 105 independent samples (N = 19,933) from 23 countries

citation: Yasser Teimouri, Julia Goetze, and Luke Plonsky. (2019). SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYSIS. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 41, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263118000311
title: L2 anxiety as a negatively acting affective variable in L2 learning with (non)linguistic moderators
description: The article frames L2 anxiety as an affective variable with a demonstrably negative role in L2 learning, moderated by linguistic and nonlinguistic variables. It states the study "provides firm evidence for both the negative role of L2 anxiety in L2 learning and the moderating effects of a number of (non)linguistic variables." The framework builds on decades of empirical and theoretical attention to L2 anxiety and its relationship with achievement.
requirements: Measurement of both anxiety (various types) and language achievement to estimate the relationship
constraints: Effect sizes vary across achievement measure types, educational levels, target languages, and anxiety types, so the negative association is not uniform
target_learners: second language learners
target_learning_goals: second language achievement
examples: Meta-analysis of 216 correlations yielding a mean r = −.36

article_title: The effectiveness of peer tutoring in further and higher education: A typology and review of the literature
citation: Topping, K.J. (1996). The effectiveness of peer tutoring in further and higher education: A typology and review of the literature. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00138870
title: A typology of peer tutoring in further and higher education
description: The article provides a clear definition and typology of peer tutoring as an organizing framework for the field. It argues that "The increasing use of peer tutoring in this context necessitates a clear definition and typology, which are outlined", and the review is organized around "the many different types and formats of peer tutoring within colleges and universities". The typology serves to structure the review of effectiveness research across these varied formats.
requirements: A clear definition and typology of peer tutoring is needed to make sense of the increasing use of peer tutoring in further and higher education.
target_learners: students in further and higher education (colleges and universities)
target_learning_goals: academic learning outcomes supported through peer tutoring arrangements
examples: The review uses the typology to organize the substantial existing research on the effectiveness of the many different types and formats of peer tutoring within colleges and universities.

article_title: Effectiveness of school-based programs to reduce bullying: a systematic and meta-analytic review
citation: Maria M. Ttofi, David P. Farrington. (2011). Effectiveness of school-based programs to reduce bullying: a systematic and meta-analytic review. J Exp Criminol. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11292-010-9109-1
title: Systematic review corpus of 622 reports yielding 53 program evaluations and 44 meta-analyzable effect sizes
description: The review assembled an evidence corpus by hand-searching all volumes of 35 journals from 1983 to the end of May 2009 and 18 electronic databases, including non-English reports and unpublished work. Of "622 reports concerned with bullying prevention", 89 reports describing 53 different program evaluations were included, and 44 provided calculable effect sizes for bullying or victimization. Evaluations spanned four design types: randomized experiments, before-and-after intervention-control comparisons, other intervention-control comparisons, and age-cohort designs.
requirements: Studies must compare an intervention group receiving an anti-bullying program with a control group that did not receive it
constraints: Nine evaluations (in 12 reports) were excluded from the meta-analysis due to missing values, lack of data, or implausible effect sizes
target_learners: school students in primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: reduction of bullying behavior
reduction of peer victimization
examples: Included programs range from the Olweus Bullying Prevention Program evaluations in Norway to the KiVa program, Steps to Respect, and the Sheffield project

article_title: Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives
citation: Tzuriel, D. (2000). Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009032414088
title: Dynamic/interactive assessment grounded in Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and Feuerstein's mediated learning experience
description: Dynamic/interactive assessment (DA) is an assessment approach motivated by the inadequacy of conventional static tests, which fail "to provide accurate information about the individual's learning ability, specific deficient functions, change processes, and mediational strategies that are responsible for cognitive modifiability." The review states that "the theoretical foundations of the presented research derive from Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, specifically the zone of proximal development concept, and Feuerstein's mediated learning experience theory." DA is used with young children in educational and intervention contexts to assess learning potential rather than static performance.
requirements: An examiner mediates during assessment so that change processes and mediational strategies responsible for cognitive modifiability can be observed, rather than only static performance.
constraints: The review notes that crucial issues of cost-effectiveness, training, reliability and validity, and generalization remain to be addressed.
target_learners: young children
minority children
learning disabled children
target_learning_goals: assessing learning potential and cognitive modifiability
learning how to learn skills
key_sources: Tzuriel, D. (2000). Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009032414088

citation: Tzuriel, D. (2000). Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009032414088
title: Cognitive Modifiability Battery (CMB): a dynamic assessment and intervention instrument
description: The Cognitive Modifiability Battery (CMB) is a dynamic instrument named in the review's reference list as "The Cognitive Modifiability Battery (CMB): Assessment and Intervention-Instruction Manual" (Tzuriel, 1995a). It is cited both as a dynamic assessment instrument and, in conference papers listed by the review, as an intervention tool used in clinical and educational work with children with complex learning difficulties and in speech language therapy.
requirements: Use requires the instrument's instruction manual and training in dynamic assessment procedures.

children with complex learning difficulties

article_title: Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives
citation: Tzuriel, D. (2000). Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009032414088
title: Use dynamic assessment with young children because treatment decisions should be made as early as possible
description: The review recommends dynamic assessment for young children because early identification matters: "a growing need for DA with young children has emerged recently because decisions about treatment should be made as early as possible." Static testing alone does not yield the information about learning ability and change processes needed for such early decisions, so DA is positioned as the assessment approach suited to early educational and intervention decision-making.
requirements: Examiners trained in dynamic assessment and mediational strategies are needed to administer DA with young children.
constraints: The review flags cost-effectiveness, training, reliability and validity, and generalization as crucial open issues for DA practice.
target_learners: young children
preschool children

informing early treatment decisions

article_title: Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model
citation: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Clark, R.E. & de Croock, M.B.M. (2002). Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model. ETR&D. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504993
title: The 4C/ID-model: a four-component instructional design system for training complex skills
description: The article describes the four-component instructional design system (4C/ID-model), developed originally by van Merriënboer and others in the early 1990s for the design of training programs for complex skills. The model structures training blueprints for complex learning around four interrelated components and specifies instructional methods for each component coupled to the basic learning processes involved in complex learning. The article presents the model's blueprint structure and illustrates it with a worked-out example.
requirements: Designers must produce training blueprints for complex learning that include all four interrelated components
constraints: The model was developed for the design of training programs for complex skills
target_learners: learners acquiring complex skills
target_learning_goals: complex skill acquisition and transfer
examples: A fully worked-out example of a training blueprint for searching for literature is provided in the article
key_sources: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Clark, R.E. & de Croock, M.B.M. (2002). Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model. ETR&D. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504993

article_title: Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model
citation: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Clark, R.E. & de Croock, M.B.M. (2002). Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model. ETR&D. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504993
title: Couple instructional methods for each component to the basic learning processes involved in complex learning
description: In the 4C/ID approach, instructional methods are not chosen arbitrarily for each blueprint component; the article states that "Instructional methods for each component are coupled to the basic learning processes involved in complex learning". This principle directs designers to select methods for learning tasks, supportive information, just-in-time information, and part-task practice by reference to the learning processes those methods must support.
requirements: Designers must identify the basic learning processes involved in complex learning before selecting instructional methods for each component

target_learning_goals: complex skill acquisition
examples: The article's worked-out training blueprint for searching for literature applies this coupling of methods to learning processes
