title: Training blueprint structure for complex learning with associated instructional methods
description: The article discusses "the structure of training blueprints for complex learning and associated instructional methods". A blueprint in this pattern is a design document that lays out the four interrelated components — learning tasks, supportive information, just-in-time information, and part-task practice — together with the instructional methods attached to each, providing the overall architecture for a training program for complex skills.
requirements: Blueprints must include the four interrelated components and associated instructional methods
constraints: Applies to complex learning rather than simple task training
target_learners: learners in training programs for complex skills
target_learning_goals: complex learning
key_sources: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Clark, R.E. & de Croock, M.B.M. (2002). Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model. ETR&D. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504993

article_title: The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning
citation: Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer and Liesbeth Kester. (2005). The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning. The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, pp. 71-94. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511816819.006
title: The 4C-ID model claims four components are necessary to realize complex learning
description: The chapter presents the Four-Component Instructional Design (4C-ID) model as a framework for designing environments for complex learning. As the abstract states, "The Four-Component Instructional Design (4C-ID) model claims that four components are necessary to realize complex learning: (1) learning tasks, (2) supportive information, (3) procedural information, and (4) part-task practice." The chapter uses this framework to organize multimedia design guidance, relating multimedia principles to each of the four components.
requirements: Instruction for complex learning must include learning tasks, supportive information, procedural information, and part-task practice as distinct components
target_learners: Learners acquiring complex cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: Complex learning integrating multiple knowledge and skill components
key_sources: Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer and Liesbeth Kester. (2005). The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning. The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, pp. 71-94. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511816819.006

article_title: The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning
citation: Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer and Liesbeth Kester. (2005). The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning. The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, pp. 71-94. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511816819.006
title: Four learning processes are each facilitated by multimedia principles tied to one 4C-ID component
description: The chapter organizes 14 multimedia principles by mapping each of the four 4C-ID components to a distinct learning process and a matching multimedia environment. The abstract states the chapter "relates 14 multimedia principles to each of the four components," with inductive learning for learning tasks, elaboration and mindful abstraction for supportive information, knowledge compilation for procedural information, and psychological strengthening for part-task practice.
requirements: Multimedia principles must be selected to match the learning process each component is intended to facilitate
constraints: The framework is presented for design of multimedia learning environments; research implications and limitations are discussed in the chapter
target_learners: Learners acquiring complex cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: Complex skill acquisition through coordinated multimedia environments
key_sources: Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer and Liesbeth Kester. (2005). The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning. The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, pp. 71-94. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511816819.006

article_title: The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning
citation: Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer and Liesbeth Kester. (2005). The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning. The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, pp. 71-94. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511816819.006
title: Electronic Performance Support Systems (EPSSs) as the environment for consulting procedural information
description: The chapter assigns Electronic Performance Support Systems (EPSSs) to the procedural-information component of 4C-ID. The abstract states: "They may consult procedural information in Electronic Performance Support Systems (EPSSs), where principles facilitate a process of knowledge compilation." In this arrangement, EPSSs serve as just-in-time repositories of procedural information that learners consult while working on tasks, with multimedia principles chosen to support knowledge compilation.
requirements: An EPSS in which procedural information can be consulted during task performance
target_learners: Learners acquiring complex cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: Knowledge compilation of procedural information
key_sources: Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer and Liesbeth Kester. (2005). The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning. The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, pp. 71-94. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511816819.006

article_title: The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning
citation: Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer and Liesbeth Kester. (2005). The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning. The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, pp. 71-94. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511816819.006
title: Drill and practice Computer-Based Training (CBT) programs for part-task practice
description: The chapter assigns drill and practice Computer-Based Training (CBT) programs to the part-task-practice component of 4C-ID. The abstract states: "Finally, they may be involved in part-task practice with drill and practice Computer-Based Training (CBT) programs, where principles facilitate a process of psychological strengthening." CBT programs thus serve as the multimedia environment in which constituent skills are practiced to automaticity, with multimedia principles selected to support strengthening.
requirements: Drill and practice CBT programs targeting part-tasks that benefit from repetition
target_learners: Learners acquiring complex cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: Automatization of recurring skill aspects through psychological strengthening
key_sources: Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer and Liesbeth Kester. (2005). The Four-Component Instructional Design Model : Multimedia Principles in Environments for Complex Learning. The Cambridge Handbook of Multimedia Learning, pp. 71-94. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511816819.006

article_title: The Promise and Practice of Learner-Generated Drawing: Literature Review and Synthesis
citation: Van Meter, P., Garner, J. (2005). The Promise and Practice of Learner-Generated Drawing: Literature Review and Synthesis. Educ Psychol Rev 17, 285–325. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-005-8136-3
title: A theoretical framework for learner-generated drawing built by extending Mayer's processes of selection, organization, and integration
description: The article proposes a theoretical framework for understanding the drawing strategy by extending R. E. Mayer's (1993) theoretical processes of selection, organization, and integration. The framework is intended to guide and organize future research efforts, and earlier proposed hypotheses are incorporated into its explanatory constructs. It serves as the review's organizing account of how learner-generated drawing supports learning.
requirements: The framework is grounded in current understandings of cognitive and strategic processing, as the review states it organizes hypotheses around such understandings.
target_learners: learners using drawing as a learning strategy across content areas
target_learning_goals: learning from text through construction of representative illustrations
examples: The review incorporates its earlier proposed hypotheses into the explanatory constructs of the theoretical perspective.
key_sources: Van Meter, P., Garner, J. (2005). The Promise and Practice of Learner-Generated Drawing: Literature Review and Synthesis. Educ Psychol Rev 17, 285–325. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-005-8136-3

article_title: The Promise and Practice of Learner-Generated Drawing: Literature Review and Synthesis
citation: Van Meter, P., Garner, J. (2005). The Promise and Practice of Learner-Generated Drawing: Literature Review and Synthesis. Educ Psychol Rev 17, 285–325. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-005-8136-3
title: Learner-generated drawing as a learning strategy in which learners construct representative illustrations
description: Learner-generated drawing is a strategy in which learners construct representative illustrations in support of learning goals. The article reviews both applied and empirical literature on this strategy with the purpose of stimulating research on it. It treats the strategy as a comprehension strategy whose effectiveness depends on cognitive and strategic processing, as reflected in its key words: drawing, learning strategy, comprehension strategy, and cognitive processes.
requirements: Learners must construct representative illustrations in support of learning goals.
target_learners: learners from primary grades through adults, as represented in the reviewed literature
target_learning_goals: comprehension and learning from text
examples: The review covers applied readings and empirical studies of learners constructing illustrations to support learning goals.
key_sources: Van Meter, P., Garner, J. (2005). The Promise and Practice of Learner-Generated Drawing: Literature Review and Synthesis. Educ Psychol Rev 17, 285–325. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-005-8136-3

article_title: Explicit Instruction and Input Processing
citation: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979
title: Input processing: learner strategies in processing input as the basis for determining explicit instruction
description: Input processing is the framework the article uses to link second language acquisition to how learners process input data. It holds that "learner strategies in input processing" should serve as "the starting point for determining what explicit instruction should look like." Processing instruction operationalizes this by having learners practice processing input rather than producing output after grammar explanation.
requirements: Instruction must be designed around identified learner strategies in input processing.
target_learners: second language learners in classroom instruction
target_learning_goals: grammatical interpretation and production of the targeted linguistic form
examples: The experiment's processing instruction treatment involved "explanation and practice/experience processing input data."
key_sources: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979

article_title: Explicit Instruction and Input Processing
citation: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979
title: Design explicit grammar instruction around input processing rather than output practice
description: The article recommends structuring explicit grammar instruction so that, after explanation, learners practice processing input data instead of practicing output. This processing instruction approach "involves explanation and practice/experience processing input data, taking learner strategies in input processing as the starting point," in contrast to traditional instruction's explanation plus output practice.
requirements: A grammatical point to target and knowledge of the learner strategies in input processing for that point.
target_learners: second language learners
target_learning_goals: accurate comprehension and production of targeted grammatical forms
examples: The study's processing instruction condition paired grammatical explanation with input-processing practice activities.
key_sources: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979

article_title: Explicit Instruction and Input Processing
citation: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979
title: Sentence-level interpretation and production tasks as pretest-posttest measures of grammar instruction effects
description: This element is the assessment battery used in the experiment: pretest and posttest measures "involving both a sentence-level interpretation (comprehension) task and a sentence-level production task," with scores "submitted to an analysis of variance." It operationalizes comprehension and production outcomes for comparing explicit instruction treatments.
requirements: Target grammatical material expressible at the sentence level for both interpretation and production testing.
target_learners: second language learners in instructed settings
target_learning_goals: measuring sentence-level comprehension and production of a grammatical form
examples: The experiment administered these tasks as pretests and posttests across the processing instruction and traditional instruction conditions.
key_sources: Bill VanPatten and Teresa Cadierno. (1993). Explicit Instruction and Input Processing. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100011979

article_title: Sex Differences in Performance on the Mathematics Section of the Scholastic Aptitude Test: A Bidirectional Validity Study
citation: Howard Wainer, Linda Steinberg. (1992). Sex Differences in Performance on the Mathematics Section of the Scholastic Aptitude Test: A Bidirectional Validity Study. Harvard Educational Review. https://doi.org/10.17763/haer.62.3.1p1555011301r133
title: Bidirectional validity study: evaluating a test by matching examinees on the criterion the test predicts
description: The bidirectional validity approach examines a test's fairness by working backward from the criterion: examinees are matched on the outcome the test is supposed to predict (here, type of math course taken and grade received in first-year college math), and their test scores are compared. Wainer and Steinberg apply it to the SAT-M with "almost 47,000 men and women" and complement it with a prospective regression analysis of the same data. Differences in test scores among equally performing examinees indicate differences in the test's predictive validity across groups.
requirements: Requires a large dataset linking test scores to the criterion performance (course taken and grade received) so examinees can be matched on outcome.
constraints: The article states the data do not allow conclusions about the cause of the observed score differences.
target_learners: college students taking first-year mathematics courses
target_learning_goals: accurate and equitable prediction of college mathematics performance from admissions test scores
examples: Matching almost 47,000 men and women on type of math course taken and grade received, then comparing SAT-M scores; a prospective regression analysis of the same data.
key_sources: Howard Wainer, Linda Steinberg. (1992). Sex Differences in Performance on the Mathematics Section of the Scholastic Aptitude Test: A Bidirectional Validity Study. Harvard Educational Review. https://doi.org/10.17763/haer.62.3.1p1555011301r133

article_title: Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments
citation: Wang, F., & Hannafin, M. J. (2005). Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments. ETR&D, 53, 5–23. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504682
title: The article defines design-based research and identifies its characteristics
description: The article undertakes to define design-based research and identify its characteristics as a methodology for technology-enhanced learning environments. According to the abstract, the authors "define and identify characteristics of design-based research", establishing what counts as DBR and how it differs from other educational research approaches. This definitional work organizes the paper's subsequent treatment of DBR's importance, implementation principles, and challenges for TELE development.
requirements: The methodology must be defined and its characteristics identified before it can be applied to TELE research and design, as the article's stated purpose requires.
target_learners: Educational researchers and instructional designers working with technology-enhanced learning environments
target_learning_goals: Understanding and applying design-based research methodology in TELE research and design
key_sources: Wang, F., & Hannafin, M. J. (2005). Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments. ETR&D, 53, 5–23. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504682

article_title: Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments
citation: Wang, F., & Hannafin, M. J. (2005). Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments. ETR&D, 53, 5–23. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504682
title: Implement design-based research with TELEs according to proposed principles
description: The article proposes principles for implementing design-based research in work on technology-enhanced learning environments. The abstract states that the authors "propose principles for implementing design-based research with TELEs", offering guidance for researchers who conduct DBR studies of TELEs. These principles are intended to make DBR implementation with TELEs systematic and disciplined.
requirements: Researchers implementing DBR with TELEs should follow the article's proposed principles for that implementation.
target_learners: Educational researchers and instructional designers conducting DBR studies of TELEs
target_learning_goals: Conducting design-based research on technology-enhanced learning environments
key_sources: Wang, F., & Hannafin, M. J. (2005). Design-based research and technology-enhanced learning environments. ETR&D, 53, 5–23. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504682

article_title: Mindfulness-based interventions in schoolsâ€”a systematic review and meta-analysis
citation: Charlotte Zenner, Solveig Herrnleben-Kurz and Harald Walach. (2014). Mindfulness-based interventions in schools—a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00603
title: Common components of school-based mindfulness intervention programs
description: The review catalogued the components of the 24 school-based mindfulness programs. All programs used breath awareness, described as "the traditional essential exercise," and most combined multiple components including working with thoughts and emotions, psycho-education, awareness of senses and daily-life practices, and group discussion. Programs drew on mindfulness theory (100%), often linked to MBSR, MBCT, DBT, and ACT, and two thirds used manualized programs such as MindfulSchools or Learning to BREATHE.
requirements: Programs need well defined goals, explicit guidelines, training, and quality control described for evaluation, per Weare and Nind as cited by the review
constraints: Many manualized programs lacked sufficient guidance material for implementation, and only two had an enduring presence of more than five years
target_learners: pupils and students from grade 1 to 12
target_learning_goals: cultivating mindfulness, attentional and emotional self-regulation, and stress resilience
examples: Interventions varied from 4 to 24 weeks (median 8), typically 45 min once a week, totaling 160 to 3700 min of practice with a median of 420 min
key_sources: Charlotte Zenner, Solveig Herrnleben-Kurz and Harald Walach. (2014). Mindfulness-based interventions in schools—a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00603

article_title: Mindfulness-based interventions in schoolsâ€”a systematic review and meta-analysis
citation: Charlotte Zenner, Solveig Herrnleben-Kurz and Harald Walach. (2014). Mindfulness-based interventions in schools—a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00603
title: Five-domain outcome taxonomy for evaluating school-based mindfulness interventions
description: The review organizes outcome measures into five domains: perceived stress and coping (S) and emotional problems (E) measured via self-report scales, factors of resilience (R) via self-report, cognitive performance (C) measured by performance tests, and third person ratings (T) from parent and teacher questionnaires. This taxonomy structures both the review's domain-specific effect size analysis and its overview of the measures used across studies, addressing the diversity of outcome measures in the field.
requirements: Outcome measures must be quantitative data referring to psychological aspects, per the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: Reliability of measures could not be used to adjust effect sizes because authors did not consistently report reliability and reported measures were not compatible
target_learners: pupils and students from grade 1 to 12
target_learning_goals: psychological outcomes of mindfulness training: stress, resilience, emotional problems, cognitive performance
examples: Cognitive performance was mostly quantified by attention tests; one study used a creativity test and another a mind wandering paradigm
key_sources: Charlotte Zenner, Solveig Herrnleben-Kurz and Harald Walach. (2014). Mindfulness-based interventions in schools—a systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00603

article_title: SYNCHRONOUS COMPUTER-MEDIATED COMMUNICATION AND INTERACTION
citation: Nicole Ziegler. (2016). SYNCHRONOUS COMPUTER-MEDIATED COMMUNICATION AND INTERACTION: A Meta-Analysis. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 38(3). https://doi.org/10.1017/S027226311500025X
title: Use interaction in either SCMC or FTF contexts to support L2 development, choosing mode by target outcome
description: This principle holds that conversational interaction supports second language development in both synchronous computer-mediated and face-to-face modes, so practitioners need not reserve interaction for physical classrooms. Because the meta-analysis found "no significant differences between SCMC and FTF" overall, mode selection can follow practical constraints. However, outcome type matters: SCMC showed advantages for "productive and written measures" while FTF favored "receptive and oral learning outcomes."
requirements: Interaction must occur in either synchronous computer-mediated or face-to-face communication contexts, as both were associated with significant L2 development
constraints: Mode-specific advantages are small; overall SCMC–FTF differences were not statistically significant
target_learners: second language learners in the studies meta-analyzed (1990–2012)
target_learning_goals: second language development across productive, written, receptive, and oral outcomes
examples: The meta-analysis synthesized 14 primary studies (journal articles and dissertations, 1990–2012) comparing interaction effectiveness across SCMC and FTF contexts
key_sources: Nicole Ziegler. (2016). SYNCHRONOUS COMPUTER-MEDIATED COMMUNICATION AND INTERACTION: A Meta-Analysis. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 38(3). https://doi.org/10.1017/S027226311500025X

article_title: Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality
citation: Abry, T., Rimm-Kaufman, S.E. & Curby, T.W. (2017). Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality. Prevention Science, 18, 193–203. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-016-0743-3
title: Responsive Classroom core component indices: Morning Meeting, Rule Creation, Interactive Modeling, and Academic Choice
description: The Responsive Classroom approach is a school-based social and emotional learning program whose implementation was indexed through four core components. The article states that "Indices of teachers' implementation of Morning Meeting, Rule Creation, Interactive Modeling, and Academic Choice were derived from a combination of teacher-reported surveys and classroom observations." These component indices served as predictors of teacher–student classroom interaction quality among 143 treatment teachers in third, fourth, and fifth grade classrooms within a randomized controlled trial.
requirements: Implementation measured via a combination of teacher-reported surveys and classroom observations
target_learners: Elementary school students in third, fourth, and fifth grade
target_learning_goals: Social and emotional learning
Quality of teacher–student classroom interactions
examples: Ratings of teacher–student classroom interactions were aggregated across five observations conducted throughout the school year.
key_sources: Abry, T., Rimm-Kaufman, S.E. & Curby, T.W. (2017). Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality. Prevention Science, 18, 193–203. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-016-0743-3

article_title: Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality
citation: Abry, T., Rimm-Kaufman, S.E. & Curby, T.W. (2017). Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality. Prevention Science, 18, 193–203. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-016-0743-3
title: Examine individual program components to identify active ingredients for intervention optimization and teacher professional development
description: Rather than treating a social and emotional learning program as an undifferentiated package, the article recommends analyzing variation in teachers' implementation of individual program components to find which carry the greatest leverage. As the authors state, "Results highlight the value of examining individual program components toward the identification of program active ingredients that can inform intervention optimization and teacher professional development." This component-level lens showed the four Responsive Classroom components were not equally related to interaction quality.
requirements: Implementation data on individual program components, derived from teacher-reported surveys and classroom observations
constraints: Findings come from variation in implementation among treatment teachers within one randomized controlled trial, not from manipulating components experimentally
target_learners: Elementary school students in grade 3–5 classrooms
target_learning_goals: Improving emotional, organizational, and instructional quality of teacher–student interactions
examples: The study indexed four Responsive Classroom components and found Morning Meeting, Rule Creation, Interactive Modeling, and Academic Choice differed in their relations to interaction quality.
key_sources: Abry, T., Rimm-Kaufman, S.E. & Curby, T.W. (2017). Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality. Prevention Science, 18, 193–203. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-016-0743-3

article_title: The impact of educational chatbot on student learning experience
citation: Ait Baha, T., El Hajji, M., Es-Saady, Y., & Fadili, H. (2024). The impact of educational chatbot on student learning experience. Education and Information Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-023-12166-w
title: NLP- and deep-learning-based educational chatbot for teaching Logo to secondary school learners
description: The article presents an experimental educational chatbot built on recent Natural Language Processing and deep learning techniques, intended to instruct secondary school learners Logo, an educational programming language. It was "implemented and evaluated in Moroccan public schools" with support from teachers of the Regional Center for Education and Training Professions of Souss Massa. Its intended function is providing replies suited to each learner's specific needs within an e-learning setting.
requirements: Integration into an e-learning system so the chatbot can provide replies suited to each learner's specific needs
constraints: Evaluated only with secondary school learners in Moroccan public schools learning Logo
target_learners: secondary school learners
target_learning_goals: learning the Logo educational programming language
examples: The chatbot was implemented and evaluated in Moroccan public schools with the support of teachers from the Regional Center for Education and Training Professions of Souss Massa.
key_sources: Ait Baha, T., El Hajji, M., Es-Saady, Y., & Fadili, H. (2024). The impact of educational chatbot on student learning experience. Education and Information Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-023-12166-w

article_title: The impact of educational chatbot on student learning experience
citation: Ait Baha, T., El Hajji, M., Es-Saady, Y., & Fadili, H. (2024). The impact of educational chatbot on student learning experience. Education and Information Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10639-023-12166-w
title: Integrate conversational agents into smart classrooms to create a supportive environment that encourages student interaction, engagement, and academic achievement
description: The authors recommend integrating AI conversational systems into smart classrooms as a way to build a supportive learning environment. They state that such integration "will not only create a supportive environment by encouraging good interactions with students" but also increase learner engagement and help learners "achieve better academic objectives". The recommendation extends the chatbot's role from a standalone tutor to a component of the classroom environment.
requirements: An AI chatbot integrated into a smart classroom setting alongside student interaction opportunities
constraints: Stated by the authors as an expectation about future integration, not a tested result in the reported experiments
target_learners: secondary school learners
target_learning_goals: engagement and academic achievement in technology-supported classrooms
examples: The reported experiments evaluated the chatbot with 109 students in three classes in Moroccan public schools.

article_title: ChatGPT: Revolutionizing student achievement in the electronic magnetism unit for eleventh-grade students in Emirates schools
citation: Alneyadi, S., & Wardat, Y. (2023). ChatGPT: Revolutionizing student achievement in the electronic magnetism unit for eleventh-grade students in Emirates schools. Contemporary Educational Technology, 15(4), ep448. https://doi.org/10.30935/cedtech/13417
title: Use language models like ChatGPT as supplementary resources rather than replacements for traditional teaching
description: The article recommends that language models support, not substitute for, conventional instruction. It states that because such models "may occasionally provide inaccurate or incomplete information," they "should be used as supplementary resources rather than replacements for traditional teaching and learning methods." The study's experimental group used ChatGPT alongside regular instruction whenever students needed help with course content.
requirements: Teachers must remain involved, since model outputs may be inaccurate or incomplete and require verification from credible sources.
constraints: The article notes ethical considerations related to data privacy and bias must be addressed when using language models in education.
target_learners: Eleventh-grade physics students in UAE secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Understanding electronic magnetism concepts and improving physics achievement
examples: The experimental group was instructed to utilize ChatGPT whenever they required assistance with the course content during the study period, while the control group received traditional teaching.
key_sources: Alneyadi, S., & Wardat, Y. (2023). ChatGPT: Revolutionizing student achievement in the electronic magnetism unit for eleventh-grade students in Emirates schools. Contemporary Educational Technology, 15(4), ep448. https://doi.org/10.30935/cedtech/13417

article_title: ChatGPT: Revolutionizing student achievement in the electronic magnetism unit for eleventh-grade students in Emirates schools
citation: Alneyadi, S., & Wardat, Y. (2023). ChatGPT: Revolutionizing student achievement in the electronic magnetism unit for eleventh-grade students in Emirates schools. Contemporary Educational Technology, 15(4), ep448. https://doi.org/10.30935/cedtech/13417
title: 25-item electronic magnetism cognitive achievement test
description: The study's achievement instrument is a test of 25 multiple-choice items categorized by Bloom's taxonomy levels (remember, understand, apply, analyze), scored one mark per correct answer for a maximum of 25. Expert review established validity, and test-retest reliability was 0.92, which the authors say "indicates that the cognitive achievement test possesses satisfactory reliability for use in this study."
requirements: Administered as a pre-test at the beginning of the study and a post-test at the conclusion, with a mean completion time of 60 minutes.
target_learners: Eleventh-grade students in Emirates schools
target_learning_goals: Measuring achievement in electronic magnetism across knowing, applying, and reasoning cognitive levels
examples: Difficulty coefficients ranged from 0.50 to 0.77 and discrimination coefficients from 0.35 to 0.72, calculated from an exploratory sample administration.

article_title: ONE SIZE FITS ALL?: Recasts, Prompts, and L2 Learning
citation: Ahlem Ammar and Nina Spada. (2006). ONE SIZE FITS ALL?: Recasts, Prompts, and L2 Learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 28, Issue 4. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060268
title: Four-week form-focused intervention on third-person possessive determiners his and her
description: An instructional intervention delivered to grade 6 intensive ESL classes over 4 weeks, targeting the English third-person possessive determiners his and her, described in the article as "a difficult aspect of English grammar for these Francophone learners of English." Two experimental conditions embedded corrective feedback (recasts for one group, prompts for the other) while a control group received no such feedback. Learner knowledge was measured with written and oral tasks at three time points.
requirements: Delivered within intact grade 6 intensive ESL classes in the Montreal area
constraints: Targeted a single grammatical structure (his and her) rather than grammar broadly

citation: Yunjo An, Ji Hyun Yu and Shadarra James. (2025). International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-025-00507-3
title: Faculty GenAI guidance pattern: syllabus statements, course policy communication, and redesigned authentic/process-oriented assessments
description: The article identifies a recurring pattern in faculty-targeted GenAI guidelines: providing template syllabus statements (e.g., Stanford's three categories from "AI tools permitted freely" to "AI tools not permitted"), advising faculty to set and communicate course policies (54%), and redesigning assignments and assessments (48%). Specifically, "authentic assessments (e.g., real-world tasks, projects), process-oriented assessments (e.g., low-stakes writing, drafts, presentations, oral exams, portfolios), and assignments requiring higher-order thinking were commonly recommended". This pattern operationalizes institutional guidance for teaching in the GenAI era.

constraints: The article notes guidance for faculty can become burdensome since continuous revisions are recommended in the policies (citing McDonald et al., 2024)

article_title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: A framework that supplies a rationale for formative assessment within theories of pedagogy and unifies the diverse set of practices described as formative.
description: The article proposes a framework whose purpose is twofold: to give formative assessment a rationale located within broader theories of pedagogy, and to unify the heterogeneous practices that have been called formative. The authors state that "This paper aims to offer such a rationale, within a framework which can also unify the diverse set of practices which have been described as formative." The framework is then used analytically to connect formative assessment with other pedagogic initiatives and with literatures on self-regulated learning and classroom discourse, and to guide teacher implementation work.
requirements: Serves as an organizing rationale for practices already described as formative; it presupposes the existing body of formative assessment practice it seeks to unify.
constraints: The article presents it as a rationale and unifying framework, not as an empirically tested model; the full text beyond the abstract was not accessible here.
target_learners: Classroom learners across school subjects
target_learning_goals: Improving learning through formative assessment practices embedded in pedagogy
examples: The article states the framework is used to relate formative assessment to cognitive acceleration, dynamic assessment, self-regulated learning models, and classroom discourse.

citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5

description: A second organizing contribution of the article is a set of theoretical linkages: the framework connects formative assessment to neighbouring pedagogic initiatives and research literatures. The abstract states: "The analysis is used to relate formative assessment both to other pedagogic initiatives, notably cognitive acceleration and dynamic assessment, and to some of the existing literature on models of self-regulated learning and on classroom discourse." This positions formative assessment not as an isolated assessment technique but as continuous with pedagogies that regulate and accelerate learning, with dynamic assessment traditions, with self-regulation models, and with classroom dialogue research.
requirements: The linkages depend on the article's unifying framework for formative assessment within pedagogy.
constraints: The article presents these as relations established by theoretical analysis, not as empirically demonstrated equivalences.

target_learning_goals: Regulating and developing learning through assessment, dialogue, and cognitive acceleration
examples: The article's keywords list the linked constructs: formative assessment, assessment for learning, dynamic assessment, self-regulation, cognitive acceleration, and dialogue.

The abstract states the framework "should indicate potentially fruitful lines for further enquiry, whilst at the same time opening up new ways of helping teachers to implement formative practices more effectively." The principle is that theoretical clarification of formative assessment is a route to more effective professional support for teachers, not merely an academic exercise.

constraints: The article states this as an intended payoff of the framework; it does not report tested implementation outcomes in the accessible text.

title: Success criteria and learning intentions as components of formative practice.
description: In a note, the article identifies explicitly communicated goals for learning as an important component of formative classroom practice: "The importance of “success criteria” and “learning intentions” was emphasised by Clarke (2001)." Success criteria and learning intentions function as elements that make the intended learning visible to students, supporting the regulation of learning that the article's framework treats as central to formative assessment. The article cites this emphasis rather than developing it at length in the accessible text.
requirements: Teachers must articulate learning intentions and success criteria so that students know what valued learning looks like.
constraints: The article attributes the emphasis to Clarke (2001) and does not elaborate implementation detail in the accessible text.

target_learning_goals: Clarifying intended learning and criteria for success to support self-regulation

citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: A working definition of learning as an experience-driven increase in capacities to respond in valued ways.
description: To anchor its framework, the article offers an explicit definition of learning in a note: "we would define learning as an increase, brought about by experience, in the capacities of an organism to react in valued ways in response to stimuli." The definition is offered defensively — the authors supply it for those who think defining formative assessment merely shifts the definitional burden onto the word learning. It makes valued response capacities, experience, and change over time the constituents of learning, which in turn delimits what counts as formative evidence of learning.
requirements: Any account of formative assessment needs a working definition of learning; this one ties learning to experience and to valued ways of responding.
constraints: The authors present it as a stipulated definition for a specific objection, not as an established empirical result.
target_learners: All learners in instructional settings addressed by the framework
target_learning_goals: Increasing learners' capacities to respond in valued ways
examples: The note supplies the definition in response to the objection that defining formative assessment merely moves the burden of definition onto the word learning.

title: Growth rather than mastery as the preferred term for a focus on learning achievement in formative assessment.
description: In discussing self-regulation literature, the article makes a deliberate terminological choice. The note records that "Boekearts and Corno use two terms, growth and mastery, with both, apparently interchangeable, to stand for a focus on learning achievement; we have preferred the first of these here because mastery denotes a sense of completion whereas growth does not." The choice reflects a theoretical stance: formative assessment concerns ongoing development of learning rather than terminal attainment, so growth is the more apt term within the article's framework.
requirements: Writers on formative assessment and self-regulation should choose achievement-focus terminology consciously, since connotations differ.
constraints: The choice is argued on the connotations of the two words, not on empirical evidence.

target_learning_goals: Conceptualising learning achievement as ongoing growth rather than completed mastery
examples: The article adopts Boekaerts and Corno's growth term while explaining why mastery was set aside.

citation: Borge, M., Smith, B.K. & Aldemir, T. (2024). Using generative ai as a simulation to support higher-order thinking. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 19, 479–532. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09437-0
title: GenAI as a social interaction and cultural simulation tool for practicing collective sensemaking skills
description: The article frames chat-based generative AI as a learning environment in which learners can engage in collaborative sense-making with an AI partner. Its initial findings "indicate the promise of GenAI as a valuable social interaction and cultural simulation tool for learners to practice collective sensemaking skills". The framework positions GenAI technology as capable of creating "stimulating new learning environments that support complex sense-making activities", with the AI serving as a partner rather than an answer source.
requirements: Requires a chat-based generative AI tool with which learners can interact collaboratively
constraints: Chat-based GenAI technologies have "a tendency to provide definitive answers unsupported by evidence"
target_learners: Students in larger courses or broader audiences
target_learning_goals: Collective sensemaking skills
Metacognition and sociometacognition
examples: The case study examined expert use of a chat-based generative AI tool (ChatGPT 3.5) in human–computer collaborative interactions

article_title: Using generative ai as a simulation to support higher-order thinking
citation: Borge, M., Smith, B.K. & Aldemir, T. (2024). Using generative ai as a simulation to support higher-order thinking. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 19, 479–532. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09437-0
title: Sociometacognition: knowledge about, awareness of, and ability to regulate individual and collective cognition
description: The article defines metacognition and sociometacognition as "knowledge about, awareness of, and ability to regulate individual (meta) and collective (sociometa) cognition". This two-level construct distinguishes regulation of one's own cognition from regulation of a group's collective cognition, and the study asks whether human–GenAI collaborative interactions can support both levels. It grounds the paper's inquiry into how AI partners might participate in regulating collective thinking during sense-making.
requirements: Learners must engage in collaborative interactions in which both individual and collective cognition can be monitored and regulated
target_learners: Students engaged in collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: Regulation of individual cognition
Regulation of collective cognition

The article notes that "ChatGPT 3.5 was used in this paper. This is the version that anyone can use for free, versus paid versions that use the GPT-4 large language model." It is positioned as a social interaction and cultural simulation tool for practicing collective sensemaking, with the caveat that it tends to provide definitive answers unsupported by evidence.

article_title: Unpacking the Term “Self-Management”: Understanding Intervention Applications Within the School-Based Literature
citation: Briesch, A.M., Daniels, B. & Beneville, M. (2019). Unpacking the Term “Self-Management”: Understanding Intervention Applications Within the School-Based Literature. J Behav Educ 28, 54–77. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10864-018-9303-1
title: Taxonomy of eight primary self-management intervention configurations used in school-based single-case research
description: The review organizes the school-based self-management literature by the specific intervention configuration employed, distinguishing approaches such as prompted self-monitoring, self-monitoring plus reinforcement based on both accuracy and performance, and prompted self-monitoring plus graphing. The authors state that "eight primary approaches to self-management were utilized across more than one study" within the 56 studies reviewed. This taxonomy provides the organizing framework for evaluating component-level effectiveness.
requirements: Interventions must be describable by their specific component configuration (e.g., prompting, reinforcement, graphing) to be classified within the taxonomy.
constraints: Derived from single-case design studies in school-based literature only.
target_learners: K-12 students with behavioral needs, including students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Improved classroom behavior such as on-task behavior and reduced disruptive or off-task behavior
examples: The review classified 56 single-case studies and found prompted self-monitoring in 23 of them, self-monitoring plus reinforcement in 6, and prompted self-monitoring plus graphing in 5.
key_sources: Briesch, A.M., Daniels, B. & Beneville, M. (2019). Unpacking the Term “Self-Management”: Understanding Intervention Applications Within the School-Based Literature. J Behav Educ 28, 54–77. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10864-018-9303-1

article_title: Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components
citation: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6
title: Mobile-app based learning diaries for daily SRL self-monitoring
description: A novel mobile-app based diary used in the study as a daily self-monitoring tool administered before and after study sessions. The diary asks about affect (e.g. "How do you feel at moment?" with rated items such as Active and Determined), motivation (e.g. "Today, I am studying because I find the topic very interesting"), and learning strategies (e.g. "Today, I have made a time schedule"), using Likert-type response scales. It replaces paper-and-pencil diaries, which the authors note are limited in reach.
requirements: Administered as daily diary entries before and after study sessions via a mobile app
target_learners: University students from mixed disciplines and study modes
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning strategy use and motivation
examples: Appendix 2 prints example diary questions on affect, motivation, and learning strategies asked before and after study sessions
key_sources: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6

article_title: Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components
citation: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6
title: Three-session discipline-independent online SRL training program
description: An online SRL training program delivered in three sessions designed as mini-chapters containing "micro-learnings in the form of written and video content, activities, reflective tasks and quizzes". Session 1 covers SRL overview, components, the three phases of SRL, goal setting (SMART goals), barriers, and time management. Session 2 covers distractions and procrastination, learning strategies (critical thinking, organisation, elaboration, mnemonics, paraphrasing, note making, self-questioning), resource management, and metacognitive strategies. Session 3 covers dealing with failure, attribution theory, motivation, self-efficacy, and self-reflection.
requirements: Delivered online so it can reach large numbers of participants independent of discipline
target_learners: University students from mixed disciplines and study modes
target_learning_goals: SRL knowledge, metacognitive and cognitive strategies, resource management strategies
examples: Appendix 3 lists the session topics and content, including a time management planner and a time management style self-assessment quiz
key_sources: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6

citation: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6
title: Use discipline-independent online SRL training coupled with mobile-app diaries to reach more students than face-to-face or discipline-dependent formats
description: The article recommends overcoming the reach limits of existing SRL training formats: "Face-to-face training, discipline-dependent training, and paper-and-pencil diaries are limited in the number of students they can reach." The study implemented discipline-independent online training together with novel mobile-app based diaries, and the combined condition improved more than other conditions, supporting this scalable delivery approach for improving SRL.
requirements: Online delivery of training plus a mobile-app based daily diary
target_learners: University students from mixed disciplines and study modes
target_learning_goals: Improved self-regulated learning
examples: The randomised control study implemented the discipline-independent online training and mobile-app diaries with 73 university students
key_sources: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6

article_title: Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components
citation: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6
title: Self-regulated learning as a multi-component construct with metacognitive, cognitive, and resource management strategies
description: The article treats self-regulated learning as a multi-component construct whose trainable components include SRL knowledge, metacognitive strategies, cognitive strategies, and resource management strategies. It reports that participants "improved on SRL knowledge, metacognitive strategies, cognitive strategies (elaboration, organisation and critical thinking), and resources management strategies (time-management and effort regulation)". The training program's structure mirrors this taxonomy, with dedicated content on learning strategies, resource management, and metacognitive strategies, and the three phases of SRL.
requirements: Measurement of distinct SRL components (e.g. via SRL knowledge test and strategy measures) to detect component-specific improvement
target_learners: University students
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning knowledge and strategy use
examples: The training program's three sessions map onto the taxonomy: learning strategies, resource management, and metacognitive strategies in session 2

article_title: The development of student feedback literacy: enabling uptake of feedback
citation: David Carless & David Boud. (2018). The development of student feedback literacy: enabling uptake of feedback. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 43(8), 1315-1325. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2018.1463354
title: Student feedback literacy framework: appreciating feedback, making judgments, managing affect, taking action
description: The article defines student feedback literacy as "the understandings, capacities and dispositions needed to make sense of information and use it to enhance work or learning strategies". It proposes four inter-related features — appreciating feedback, making judgments, managing affect, and taking action — represented in Figure 1 with bi-directional arrows linking the first three, whose combination is proposed to maximise potential for student action. Each feature is elaborated with three numbered characteristics of feedback literate students.
requirements: Students need opportunities to use feedback within the curriculum and appreciation of how feedback can operate effectively
constraints: The framework is proposed for undergraduates in higher education; the authors note postgraduate and workplace levels remain to be investigated
target_learners: undergraduate higher education students
target_learning_goals: making sense of feedback information and using it to enhance work or learning strategies
examples: Figure 1 lists three numbered capacities under each of the four features, e.g. feedback literate students "maintain emotional equilibrium and avoid defensiveness when receiving critical feedback"

article_title: Using Spacing to Enhance Diverse Forms of Learning: Review of Recent Research and Implications for Instruction
citation: Carpenter, S.K., Cepeda, N.J., Rohrer, D., Kang, S.H.K., & Pashler, H. (2012). Using Spacing to Enhance Diverse Forms of Learning: Review of Recent Research and Implications for Instruction. Educational Psychology Review, 24, 369–378. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9205-z
title: Incorporate spacing into everyday instruction by separating study sessions over time rather than massing them
description: The article closes by offering guidance on applying spacing research to teaching: it "conclude[s] with a list of recommendations on how spacing might be incorporated into everyday instruction". The principle is that instructors should schedule multiple study or review opportunities separated in time rather than in immediate succession, because spaced sessions improve final-test performance. The specific recommendations are listed in the article body, which is not available in the preview text.
requirements: Instruction must include multiple study opportunities that can be distributed across time rather than delivered in one massed session.
target_learners: students in everyday instructional settings
target_learning_goals: durable memory retention of studied material
examples: The authors state the article concludes with a list of recommendations on how spacing might be incorporated into everyday instruction.

article_title: The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations
citation: Susanne Carroll, Merrill Swain, and Yves Roberge. (1992). The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations. Applied Psycholinguistics, Volume 13, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400005555
title: Experimental French suffixation feedback-training task with feedback and guessing sessions
description: The study's instrument was an individual training task on two rules of French suffixation administered to 79 adult native speakers of English with intermediate (39) and advanced (40) proficiency in French. In the article's words, "Experimental subjects received correction if they gave erroneous responses to stimuli in a “feedback” session." Afterward all subjects guessed responses to novel stimuli and were retested twice on the feedback items, while comparison subjects "dealt with the same stimuli but were never corrected."
requirements: Subjects must be individually trained on the two suffixation rules before the feedback session
constraints: The task was administered in an experimental setting with adult intermediate and advanced French learners, not in ordinary classroom instruction
target_learners: adult intermediate and advanced learners of French
target_learning_goals: learning morphological generalizations of French suffixation, including absolute exceptions
examples: Experimental subjects were corrected for erroneous responses during the feedback session; comparison subjects handled the same stimuli without correction
key_sources: Susanne Carroll, Merrill Swain, and Yves Roberge. (1992). The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations. Applied Psycholinguistics, Volume 13, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400005555

article_title: The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations
citation: Susanne Carroll, Merrill Swain, and Yves Roberge. (1992). The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations. Applied Psycholinguistics, Volume 13, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400005555
title: Expect explicit correction to improve performance on corrected items, not to guarantee generalized rule learning
description: This principle captures the study's central dissociation: correction improved responses on the corrected items themselves, yet "comparisons of guessing responses between experimental and comparison groups showed no evidence of learned generalizations." Designers of feedback activities should therefore treat explicit correction as supporting item-level accuracy, and should not assume that corrected practice alone produces learners' generalization of a morphological rule to new items.
requirements: Learners must encounter the corrected items in a feedback session and then be probed with novel stimuli to check whether generalization occurred
constraints: Demonstrated only for adult English speakers learning two rules of French suffixation in an experimental setting; generalization was not observed even with correction
target_learners: adult second language learners
target_learning_goals: morphological generalizations in a second language
examples: In the experiment, corrected learners outperformed comparison learners on feedback items while guessing responses to novel stimuli showed no learned generalizations in either group
key_sources: Susanne Carroll, Merrill Swain, and Yves Roberge. (1992). The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations. Applied Psycholinguistics, Volume 13, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400005555

article_title: Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback
citation: Susanne Carroll and Merrill Swain. (1993). Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback: An Empirical Study of the Learning of Linguistic Generalizations. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100012158
title: Four-type negative feedback manipulation contrasted with a no-feedback comparison group
description: The study operationalizes negative feedback as four distinct types assigned between groups. Upon an error, "Group A subjects were given explicit metalinguistic information about the generalization we hoped they would learn"; "Group B subjects were told that their response was wrong"; "Group C subjects were corrected when they erred, giving them a model of the response desired along with implicit negative evidence that their response was incorrect"; and "Group D subjects, having made an error, were asked if they were sure about their response." A comparison group received no feedback. This taxonomy separates explicit metalinguistic, explicit rejection, model-plus-implicit-negative-evidence, and elicit-confirmation feedback types.
requirements: Learners must first be trained on the target structure so that errors can be elicited and feedback delivered upon error
constraints: Feedback was delivered in response to errors on a single trained structure, the English dative alternation, with adult Spanish-speaking ESL learners
target_learners: Adult Spanish-speaking learners of English as a second language
target_learning_goals: Learning abstract constraints on the English dative alternation
examples: Subjects were divided into groups according to the type of feedback they received when they made an error, with a no-feedback comparison group
key_sources: Susanne Carroll and Merrill Swain. (1993). Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback: An Empirical Study of the Learning of Linguistic Generalizations. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100012158

article_title: Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback
citation: Susanne Carroll and Merrill Swain. (1993). Explicit and Implicit Negative Feedback: An Empirical Study of the Learning of Linguistic Generalizations. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 15, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100012158
title: Dative alternation training task presented as a simple structural change
description: The learning target and task of the experiment: the English dative alternation, an abstract generalization that learners tend to overgeneralize. All subjects received training on the alternation before the feedback manipulation; the abstract states that "All subjects were trained on the alternation, which was presented in terms of a simple structural change." The task served to elicit errors on which the different feedback types were then delivered.
requirements: Training on the alternation precedes the feedback manipulation for all subjects
constraints: The structure was presented as a simple structural change rather than in full abstract complexity
target_learners: Adult Spanish-speaking learners of English as a second language
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of the English dative alternation and its abstract constraints
examples: All subjects were trained on the alternation before being divided into feedback groups

article_title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
citation: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7
title: Taxonomy of K-12 AI literacy approaches: learning experiences versus theoretical/implementation perspectives
description: The review organizes the K-12 AI literacy field into two broad thematic categories: learning experiences and theoretical perspectives on implementation. Learning experiences cover understanding AI concepts, how AI works, tools for AI, and living with AI; the implementation category covers curriculum design, AI as a subject, student perspective, teacher training, support resources, and gender diversity. The review states: "the papers were classified into two broad thematic categories according to the type of educational approach, namely, learning experience and theoretical perspective." Each main category was further subdivided to structure the field (Fig. 6).
requirements: Documents must concern AI literacy or AI education at the K-12 level, excluding computer-based learning and intelligent tutoring systems
constraints: Based on Scopus-indexed documents only; search conducted between 21 October 2021 and 9 March 2023
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Understanding AI concepts and techniques
Critically evaluating AI technology
examples: Figure 6 shows the full taxonomy of identified categories and subcategories
key_sources: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7

article_title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
citation: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7
title: K-12 AI literacy requires a competency framework to guide didactic proposals and define a sequenced, modular, personalized curriculum
description: The review concludes that a competency framework is needed to guide didactic proposals for AI literacy in K-12 and to define a curriculum reflecting sequence and academic continuity. It states: "These studies highlight the need for a competency framework to guide the design of didactic proposals for AI literacy in K-12 in educational institutions." Such a curriculum "should be modular and personalized" and adjusted to the conditions of the schools, and learning experiences should be based on clearly defined competencies within an AI literacy framework.
requirements: Clearly defined competencies in a particular AI literacy framework
Curriculum adjusted to the conditions of the schools
constraints: The review notes AI teaching at K-12 is not yet prevalent in formal settings and is considered challenging
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: AI literacy competencies across AI concepts, applications, and ethics and security
examples: Van Brummelen et al. (2021a) designed a five-day online workshop based on the AI competencies proposed by Long and Magerko (2020)
key_sources: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7

article_title: AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review
citation: Casal-Otero, L., Catala, A., Fernández-Morante, C., Taboada, M., Cebreiro, B., & Barro, S. (2023). AI literacy in K-12: a systematic literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-023-00418-7
title: Teachers should be prioritized and involved in the co-design of AI literacy didactic proposals, supported by TPACK-based training
description: The review identifies teachers as key players for integrating AI literacy in K-12 and concludes didactic proposals must be co-designed and implemented by the teachers at the schools involved. It reports a shortage of teachers with AI training and proposes working with teachers in training or in schools as an effective solution. It highlights TPACK as the model for the knowledge teachers need: "teachers imparting AI to K-12 students require TPACK to build an environment and facilitate project-based classes that solve problems using AI technologies."

Identification of teachers' perceptions and knowledge about AI
constraints: Teachers can swing between total resistance and overconfidence; resistance could arise from inadequate, inappropriate, irrelevant, or outdated professional development
target_learners: K-12 students
Pre-service and practicing teachers
target_learning_goals: Teacher professional development in AI
Integration of AI into teaching-learning processes
examples: The review reports co-design of ML curricula between AI researchers and K-12 teachers as an important current issue

article_title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
citation: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8
title: Five perceived benefit categories of GenAI in student learning: personalized support, writing and brainstorming, research and analysis, multimedia, and administrative support
description: Thematic analysis of open-ended survey responses (n = 387 coded by two coders with a consensus codebook) yielded five benefit categories students gave for willingness to use GenAI: "1. Personalized and immediate learning support", "2. Writing and brainstorming support", "3. Research and analysis support", "4. Visual and audio multi-media support", and "5. Administrative support" (Table 5). Students described GenAI as a virtual tutor giving immediate answers, a writing assistant for idea generation and polishing, a research aid for literature searching and hypothesis generation, and a handler of repetitive tasks.
requirements: Applies where students have access to GenAI tools and tasks suited to learning support, writing, research, multimedia creation, or administrative work
constraints: Perceptions from a convenience sample of Hong Kong university students; GenAI was not yet fully used in formal academic settings at the time of the study
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate university students
target_learning_goals: learning support, writing skills, research and analysis skills, multimedia creation
examples: A student described ChatGPT as "a top student" offering help when no one else could; an English major proposed generating short texts to memorize vocabulary; science and engineering students used DALL-E and Stable Diffusion to create artwork.
key_sources: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8

article_title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
citation: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8
title: Six perceived challenge categories of GenAI: accuracy and transparency, privacy and ethics, holistic competencies, career prospects, human values, and uncertain policies
description: Thematic analysis of open-ended responses yielded six challenge categories: "1. Accuracy and transparency", "2. Privacy and ethical issues", "3. Holistic competencies", "4. Career prospects", "5. Human values", and "6. Uncertain policies" (Table 5). Students worried they "cannot predict or accurately verify the accuracy or validity of AI generated information", about data privacy, plagiarism detection, over-reliance harming critical thinking and creativity, job replacement, value misalignment and inequality, and the absence of institutional guidance.
requirements: Relevant where institutions are integrating GenAI into coursework and need to anticipate student concerns
constraints: Perceptions from a convenience sample of Hong Kong university students; more than half of participants expressed concerns while some were optimistic
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate university students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking, creativity, academic integrity awareness, career preparation
examples: A computer science student feared losing his job "due to the advent of ChatGPT"; a social science student worried AI "can obtain our private information easily"; one student noted "It is always dangerous to use things you cannot understand".
key_sources: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8

article_title: Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education
citation: Chan, C. K. Y., & Hu, W. (2023). Students’ voices on generative AI: perceptions, benefits, and challenges in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:43. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00411-8
title: Biggs' 3P (Presage–Process–Product) model as the framework linking student perceptions of GenAI to learning approaches and outcomes
description: The article adopts John Biggs' 3P (Presage–Process–Product) model as its explanatory framework: "students’ perceptions of their learning environment, their abilities, and the teaching strategies used have a significant impact on their approach to learning", which in turn influences outcomes. Positive perceptions foster a deep approach seeking understanding and connections; negative perceptions foster a surface approach focused on memorizing minimum requirements. The authors use this to argue that understanding students' GenAI perceptions lets educators tailor integration so students adopt a deep approach.
requirements: Requires attention to how students perceive the learning environment, including technologies such as GenAI, when designing teaching and assessment
constraints: The model is applied interpretively; the study did not test the model's predictions about GenAI use empirically
target_learners: university students in higher education
target_learning_goals: deep approaches to learning, effective integration of GenAI into teaching and learning
examples: The authors argue that when students perceive GenAI as a valuable and supportive resource they are more likely to adopt a deep approach to learning, and that perception insights can inform institutional GenAI guidelines.

article_title: The Expertise Reversal Effect is a Variant of the More General Element Interactivity Effect
citation: Chen, O., Kalyuga, S. & Sweller, J. (2017). The Expertise Reversal Effect is a Variant of the More General Element Interactivity Effect. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9359-1
title: Unified cognitive load account: the expertise reversal effect as a variant of the element interactivity effect
description: The article proposes, within cognitive load theory, a unifying account in which the expertise reversal effect is subsumed under the element interactivity effect. It argues that "the two effects may be intertwined with the expertise reversal effect constituting a particular example of the element interactivity effect." On this account, both effects reflect the same underlying mechanism — changes in the number of interacting elements that must be processed in working memory — triggered by different factors. The article supports the contention with empirical evidence from prior studies.
requirements: Both effects must be interpreted within the framework of cognitive load theory, where element interactivity determines working memory load
constraints: The article presents this as an argued contention supported by empirical evidence, not as a directly tested new hypothesis
target_learners: Learners across levels of expertise in cognitive load theory instructional contexts
target_learning_goals: Managing cognitive load when learning novel or complex material
