citation: Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans, Ilya Sutskever. (2018). Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training. Preprint. Work in progress. https://cdn.openai.com/research-covers/language-unsupervised/language_understanding_paper.pdf
title: Generative pre-training followed by discriminative fine-tuning as a semi-supervised framework for language understanding
description: The article introduces a two-stage semi-supervised framework: a high-capacity language model is first trained on a large unlabeled corpus with a language modeling objective, then adapted to supervised target tasks. As the article states, "Our training procedure consists of two stages. The ﬁrst stage is learning a high-capacity language model on a large corpus of text." The goal is a universal representation that transfers with little adaptation across diverse tasks.
requirements: Access to a large corpus of unlabeled text and several datasets with manually annotated training examples for the target tasks
constraints: The target tasks are not required to be in the same domain as the unlabeled corpus, per the article's setup
target_learners: natural language processing researchers and practitioners
target_learning_goals: natural language understanding across inference, question answering, similarity, and classification tasks
examples: A 12-layer decoder-only transformer pre-trained on BooksCorpus and fine-tuned on twelve NLU benchmark datasets

title: Task-aware input transformations for fine-tuning a pre-trained transformer on structured inputs
description: A set of task-specific input transformations that convert structured inputs (sentence pairs, document-question-answer triplets) into ordered token sequences the pre-trained model can process, using delimiter tokens and traversal-style processing. The article states: "we use a traversal-style approach [52], where we convert structured inputs into an ordered sequence that our pre-trained model can process." This enables effective transfer with minimal architectural change per task.
requirements: Randomly initialized start and end tokens added to every transformation, plus delimiter tokens between concatenated segments
constraints: The article notes the auxiliary LM objective during fine-tuning helps larger datasets but smaller datasets do not benefit

examples: For similarity tasks both sentence orderings are processed independently and the representations are added element-wise; for question answering, document, question, and each answer are concatenated with a delimiter and scored via softmax

article_title: The Opportunity Atlas: Mapping the Childhood Roots of Social Mobility
citation: Raj Chetty, John N. Friedman, Nathaniel Hendren, Maggie R. Jones, and Sonya R. Porter. (2018). The Opportunity Atlas: Mapping the Childhood Roots of Social Mobility. NBER Working Paper No. 25147. http://www.nber.org/papers/w25147
title: The Opportunity Atlas: public tract-level dataset and interactive mapping tool of children's adult outcomes
description: The Opportunity Atlas is a publicly available dataset providing "the ﬁrst comprehensive estimates of children’s long-term outcomes across neigh­borhoods in the U.S." at the Census tract level, constructed from Census, tax, and ACS microdata covering 20.5 million children in the 1978-83 birth cohorts. It releases estimates of household income, incarceration, teenage birth, and other outcomes by parental income percentile, race, and gender, through "an interactive mapping tool and in downloadable ﬂat ﬁles" with a codebook, plus county and commuting-zone estimates.

article_title: Dual coding theory and education
citation: Clark, J.M., Paivio, A. Dual coding theory and education. Educ Psychol Rev 3, 149–210 (1991). https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01320076
title: Dual coding theory explains behavior and experience via associative processes on modality-specific verbal and nonverbal representations
description: Dual coding theory (DCT) is an explanatory framework in which human behavior and experience arise from dynamic associative processes operating over two classes of representation. As the article states, DCT "explains human behavior and experience in terms of dynamic associative processes that operate on a rich network of modality-specific verbal and nonverbal (or imagery) representations." The theory serves as the organizing framework the authors then apply to educational phenomena such as comprehension, memory, instruction, and motivation.
requirements: The theory presupposes a rich network of modality-specific verbal and nonverbal (imagery) representations on which associative processes operate

target_learning_goals: representation and comprehension of knowledge
learning and memory of school material

description: The article recommends grounding pedagogical practice in the concrete models that dual coding theory offers for the behavior and experience of educational participants. It argues that "the concrete models that DCT offers for the behavior and experience of students, teachers, and educational psychologists further our understanding of educational phenomena and strengthen related pedagogical practices." The principle treats DCT-based modeling as a route to improved educational design and understanding.

article_title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
citation: Crompton, H., & Burke, D. (2023). Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00392-8
title: Five usage codes for AI in higher education: Assessment/Evaluation, Predicting, AI Assistant, Intelligent Tutoring System, and Managing Student Learning
description: This systematic review used grounded coding of 138 articles to let uses of AI in higher education emerge from the data rather than fitting them to pre-existing frameworks. The review reports that "Five usage codes emerged from the data: (1) Assessment/Evaluation, (2) Predicting, (3) AI Assistant, (4) Intelligent Tutoring System (ITS), and (5) Managing Student Learning." Each code has axial codes as subcategories, e.g. automatic assessment, prediction of dropouts, chatbots, adaptive tutoring, and learning analytics.
requirements: Grounded coding of primary studies' descriptions of AI use, with in vivo codes and constant comparison until codes are theoretically saturated
constraints: Derived from peer-reviewed journal articles published 2016–2022 in English; conference proceedings and gray literature excluded
target_learners: higher education students
higher education instructors
higher education managers
target_learning_goals: understanding how artificial intelligence is used across higher education contexts
examples: The review delineated each code with a figure of codes and axial codes, e.g. six axial codes under Assessment/Evaluation and ten axial codes under Predicting

title: Hattie and Timperley's feedback model: three dimensions (feeding up, feeding back, feeding forward) and four levels (task, process, self-regulation, self)
description: The article adopts this theoretical framework to analyse the effectiveness of textual feedback. It "categorized effective feedback into three dimensions (i.e., feeding up, feeding back and feeding forward) and four-level focuses (i.e., task, process, self-regulatory, and self )". Feeding up tells students where they are going; feeding back answers how they are going; feeding forward addresses where to go next. The authors chose it because it "has been adopted widely in previous research to analyse textual feedback", unlike Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick's principles judged too general.
requirements: Annotators trained in the framework's three dimensions and four levels to label feedback content
constraints: The article notes effectiveness of feedback goes beyond the content coverage of feedback, so this single framework does not capture relational or feedback-literacy dimensions
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: assessment feedback quality on writing tasks
examples: Two experts annotated 309 feedback pieces using the framework's dimensions and levels, with a third expert resolving inconsistencies

citation: Rick de Graaff. (1997). The Experanto Experiment: Effects of Explicit Instruction on Second Language Acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 19(2). https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263197002064
title: Computer-controlled self-study course in the artificial language Experanto
description: The article's instructional element is a "computer-controlled self-study course in an artificial language" (Experanto), used to deliver L2 input and explicit instruction to university students under controlled conditions. Two groups of 27 students differing in exposure to explicit instruction worked through the course, and "computer-controlledposttests" measured acquisition of four L2 structures. The computer control of both instruction and testing is what allowed the presence or absence of explicit instruction to be manipulated experimentally.
requirements: Learners work through the course in self-study mode under computer control, with exposure to explicit instruction varied between groups.

article_title: A Meta‐Analysis and Meta‐Regression of Incidental Second Language Word Learning from Spoken Input
citation: de Vos, J. F., Schriefers, H., Nivard, M. G., & Lemhöfer, K. (2018). A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression of Incidental Second Language Word Learning from Spoken Input. Language Learning. https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12296
title: Involvement Load Hypothesis as a mechanism account of incidental word learning
description: The article presents the Involvement Load Hypothesis (Laufer & Hulstijn, 2001) as one mechanism explaining why incidental exposure can produce learning. It holds that "Involvement is seen as consisting of three dimensions: need, search, and evaluation", and that "activities that require a higher involvement from the learner are expected to lead to more learning". The article cites a prior meta-analysis finding support for it, and uses such mechanism accounts to motivate why meaning-focused activities differ in effectiveness.
requirements: Learning activities must differ in the motivational (need) and cognitive (search, evaluation) demands they place on learners for the hypothesis to predict differential learning.
constraints: The article reports the hypothesis as tested on output-versus-reading comparisons in prior work, not directly tested in its own meta-regression.
target_learners: second language learners
target_learning_goals: incidental L2 vocabulary learning from meaning-focused activities
examples: The article cites Huang, Willson, and Eslami (2012) finding that participants who completed an output task acquired more vocabulary than those who only read a text.

In the trial, "Teachers in the 10 intervention classrooms implemented weekly lessons and extension activities across a 9-month period." article_title: Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades
citation: Droop, M.; van Elsäcker, W.; Voeten, M. J. M.; Verhoeven, L. (2016). Long-Term Effects of Strategic Reading Instruction in the Intermediate Elementary Grades. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1065528
title: SRI program: sustained multiple-strategy instruction grounded in self-regulated learning and cognitive apprenticeship
description: The SRI program aims "to create independent self-regulated readers who are capable of applying appropriate reading strategies in various contexts." It draws on self-regulated learning theory and cognitive apprenticeship, teaching a limited set of nine strategies (predicting, relating to background knowledge, monitoring, deriving word meaning from context, visualizing, questioning, generating main idea, summarizing, evaluating) before, during, and after reading. Teacher modeling occurs in the meaningful context of reading aloud award-nominated children's literature three times weekly, followed by independent reading of self-chosen books with a strategy checklist on which students note problems and solutions, and weekly transfer lessons in content areas such as science. Regulation gradually shifts from teacher to students across the two years.
requirements: Teachers receive training (two three-hour meetings, a mid-year meeting, and an evaluation meeting) with video clips demonstrating strategy modeling, plus observation and coaching in November of each year
A collection of narrative and informative books at varied levels must be available for independent reading
constraints: Experimental schools were not allowed to use their own reading comprehension curriculum for the duration of the study
target_learners: Third and fourth grade elementary students of varying reading levels
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Knowledge and self-regulated use of reading strategies
examples: In Grade 3 strategies were introduced one by one over nine weeks; in Grade 4 three strategies were modeled at a time and students increasingly assisted in modeling

title: Read-aloud lesson structure integrating modeling, independent reading, and reflection
description: Each SRI lesson follows a fixed 40-minute structure: "(a) introduction of 5 minutes, (b) 15 minutes reading aloud including 5 minutes modeling of one or two strategies to the whole class, (c) 15 minutes individual independent reading with application of strategies and making notes, and (d) 5 minutes whole-class evaluation." The pattern embeds strategy modeling in authentic, motivating read-alouds of children's literature, then has students immediately apply the modeled strategies during independent reading of self-chosen books, recording problems and solutions on a strategy checklist, and closes with whole-class reflection on whether the strategy helped comprehension.
requirements: Well-written, interesting children's literature with manuals highlighting two or three moments to model a strategy
A strategy checklist and folder for each student
constraints: Teachers initially reported difficulty fitting the lessons in forty minutes, though they became accustomed to the structure during the year
target_learners: Intermediate elementary students (Grades 3–4)
target_learning_goals: Application of reading strategies during authentic reading
Self-regulated strategy use
examples: Books included works by Tosca Menten, Mirjam Oldenhave, and Lydia Rood; students chose books from classroom or school libraries at their own reading level

description: The article recommends that strategy instruction be embedded in meaningful contexts: "reading aloud children's books may offer a rich and meaningful context to model the strategies," and "Strategies modeled during read-aloud sessions may be applied during independent reading and transferred to content area reading." Teachers not only modeled the strategy but explicitly explained why they used it, following the cognitive apprenticeship principle of teacher-as-model. This contrasts with control curricula where students read identical short texts and answered written questions without a meaningful context.

title: Consolidating AI risk management frameworks with utilitarian ethics for responsible generative AI use
description: This account proposes that organisations manage generative AI risks by combining the NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework with utilitarian ethical reasoning. The NIST framework "can guide the organisations developing, adopting, and implementing AI solutions to systematically assess, understand, and manage risks", with risks mapped to the context of use. Utilitarianism then supplies "a flexible result-oriented lens for formulating and testing policies at each stage of the risk management cycle", prioritising impacts on each stakeholder. The article argues the two should be consolidated so decisions about ChatGPT design, adoption and evolution provide the most good or least harm for society.

Responsible AI toolkits and frameworks embedding ethical perspectives

target_learning_goals: Ethical decision-making and responsible use of generative AI tools

article_title: IMPLICIT AND EXPLICIT CORRECTIVE FEEDBACK AND THE ACQUISITION OF L2 GRAMMAR
citation: Rod Ellis, Shawn Loewen and Rosemary Erlam. (2006). Implicit and Explicit Corrective Feedback and the Acquisition of L2 Grammar. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 28, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060141
title: Synergy account: explicit corrective feedback in communicative activity can foster implicit as well as explicit knowledge
description: The article frames corrective feedback via the implicit/explicit learning and knowledge distinction, drawing on connectionist models in which "conscious and unconscious processes are dynamically involved together in every cognitive task and in every learning episode." Metalinguistic time-outs from communicating are proposed as a context for melding conscious and unconscious processes, so explicit feedback caters to implicit as well as explicit learning. The study's delayed-posttest gains in oral imitation are presented as consistent with this account.
requirements: Feedback must be recognized by the learner as corrective and the error located, per Carroll's autonomous induction theory as cited in the article
constraints: The article notes no single exchange can guarantee that the targeted form will enter implicit memory; repeated exchanges directed at the same form might be expected to do so
target_learners: low-intermediate second language English learners
target_learning_goals: acquisition of L2 grammar (regular past tense -ed), implicit and explicit L2 knowledge
examples: The study operationalized explicit feedback as metalinguistic explanation and implicit feedback as partial recasts during communicative tasks

title: AI should not be the sole source of feedback; human expertise remains crucial
description: The article's practitioner implication is that AI-generated feedback should not replace instructor feedback. Its experiment showed students receiving AI feedback had significantly lower score improvements, and the authors conclude that "AI should not be the sole source of feedback, as human expertise is crucial." They attribute this to instructors' contextual awareness and AI's risk of hallucination and generic feedback.

constraints: Based on one Java programming course with 35 students; the authors note the finding may not generalise to other assignments, languages or larger samples

target_learning_goals: improving programming work based on feedback

citation: Escalante, J., Pack, A., & Barrett, A. (2023). AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:57. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00425-2
title: Use a blended approach combining AI-generated and human feedback for ENL writing instruction
description: The article recommends a mixed approach to writing feedback that capitalizes on each modality's strengths: the clarity and specificity of AI-generated feedback and the engagement and speaking-practice benefits of human interaction. Since Study 1 found no outcome difference and Study 2 found a near-even preference split with "clear advantages to both forms of feedback apparent from the data", the authors conclude AI feedback "can likely be incorporated into ENL essay evaluation without affecting learning outcomes" alongside human tutoring.
requirements: Access to a GPT-4-based feedback pipeline with a carefully engineered prompt, and human tutors available to discuss AI-generated feedback with students
constraints: In this study students emailed AI feedback had no opportunity to ask follow-up questions to the AI, which the authors suggest limited AI preference

target_learning_goals: Academic writing improvement in content, coherence, language use, and use of sources and evidence

article_title: Parental Involvement and Students' Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Fan, X., Chen, M. (2001). Parental Involvement and Students' Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009048817385
title: Parental involvement as a multidimensional construct whose components relate differently to achievement
description: The article treats parental involvement not as a unitary construct but as a set of distinguishable components — including parental aspiration/expectation for children's education achievement and parental home supervision — whose relationships with academic achievement differ in strength. Its moderator analysis organizes the quantitative literature around these components, finding that "parental aspiration/expectation for children's education achievement has the strongest relationship, whereas parental home supervision has the weakest relationship." It further distinguishes achievement measurement as global versus subject-specific, making indicator type a second organizing axis.
requirements: Empirical studies must operationalize parental involvement in distinguishable components and report quantitative relationships with achievement measures for the moderator synthesis to apply.
constraints: Component-level and indicator-type effect magnitudes are not printed in the available text; the framework is supported by the article's moderator analysis of the quantitative literature it synthesized.
target_learners: K-12 school students
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement as measured by global indicators (e.g., GPA) and subject-specific indicators (e.g., math grades)
examples: The meta-analysis's moderator analysis ranked involvement components by relationship strength with achievement and compared global versus subject-specific achievement indicators.

article_title: Beware of metacognitive laziness: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on learning motivation, processes, and performance
citation: Fan, Y., Tang, L., Le, H., Shen, K., Tan, S., Zhao, Y., Shen, Y., Li, X., & Gasevic, D. (2025). Beware of Metacognitive Laziness: Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Learning Motivation, Processes, and Performance. British Journal of Educational Technology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjet.13544
title: Metacognitive laziness: dependence on AI assistance that offloads metacognitive load and weakens association of metacognitive processes with learning tasks
description: The article defines metacognitive laziness as "learners' dependence on AI assistance, oﬄoading metacognitive load, and less eﬀectively associating responsible metacognitive processes with learning tasks". It extends cognitive offloading (Risko and Gilbert) and disfluency accounts (Alter et al.): reliance on AI-generated outputs removes the cognitive difficulty that triggers deeper analytical processing. The authors ground the construct empirically in the AI group's process maps, which centred on consulting ChatGPT with relatively fewer metacognitive processes such as evaluation and orientation.
requirements: Learners must have access to an AI agent that can take over monitoring and evaluation during learning tasks
constraints: Observed in a single lab-based English writing-revising task with university students; the authors call for multi-task and cross-context studies to test generalisability
target_learners: university students learning with generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning and metacognitive engagement in writing tasks
examples: AI-group learners predominantly relied on consulting ChatGPT during revision, forming a loop between revising, evaluating and interacting with the agent

citation: Fan, Y., Tang, L., Le, H., Shen, K., Tan, S., Zhao, Y., Shen, Y., Li, X., & Gasevic, D. (2025). title: When learning with AI, learners should actively engage metacognitive processes such as evaluation, monitoring and orientation rather than blindly following ChatGPT feedback to complete tasks efficiently
description: The article's practitioner guidance states that "When using AI in learning, learners should focus on deepening their understanding of knowledge and actively engage in metacognitive processes such as evaluation, monitoring, and orientation, rather than blindly following ChatGPT's feedback solely to complete tasks eﬃciently". This principle follows from the study's findings that ChatGPT support reduced metacognitive engagement while boosting short-term essay scores without improving knowledge gain or transfer. Teachers are advised to consider which tasks suit AI assistance, stimulate intrinsic motivation, and develop scaffolding for active learning.

target_learning_goals: deep understanding of knowledge and active metacognitive engagement during AI-assisted learning
examples: In the study, checklist tools that guided rubric-based self-evaluation increased Evaluation processes, while the ChatGPT group's process maps centred on consulting the AI with fewer metacognitive processes

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence in secondary STEM education in the light of Human Flourishing: a scoping literature review
citation: Alissa Fock and Hans-Stefan Siller. (2025). Generative artificial intelligence in secondary STEM education in the light of Human Flourishing: a scoping literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00589-5
title: Three OECD themes framing AI and Human Flourishing: broadening human capabilities, restoring meaning to individual lives, and developing new models for the future
description: The review adopts the OECD (2024b) framework of three themes for examining how AI shapes Human Flourishing: "AI and broadening human capabilities", "AI and restoring meaning to individual lives", and "AI and developing new models for the future". These themes structure both the theoretical specification of STEM Education for Human Flourishing and the three research questions of the review, and are used to evaluate to what extent current literature addresses the resulting research desiderata.
requirements: Applied to education considering both students and teachers as central players in educational processes
constraints: The authors state the elaborations are not exhaustive and serve as a preliminary specification for the field
target_learners: secondary school students in STEM disciplines
STEM teachers
target_learning_goals: non-cognitive capabilities such as ethical decision-making, empathy, and perspective-taking alongside STEM disciplinary learning
examples: The review operationalizes the themes as three research questions on non-cognitive aspects and ethics, application and perception of generative AI, and development of new models
key_sources: Alissa Fock and Hans-Stefan Siller. (2025). Generative artificial intelligence in secondary STEM education in the light of Human Flourishing: a scoping literature review. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00589-5

article_title: Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology
citation: Freeman Scott, Haak David, Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2011). Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.10-08-0105
title: Highly structured course design: daily and weekly active-learning exercises with frequent low-stakes formative assessment
description: The highly structured course design assigns "daily and weekly active-learning exercises with the goal of providing constant practice with the analytical skills required to do well on exams," in contrast to low-structure courses based on lecturing and two or three midterms plus a comprehensive final. Its components, added in implementation order, were clicker questions in peer-instruction format, weekly online peer-graded practice exams, open-book reading quizzes on basic vocabulary and concepts, class notes summaries aimed at metacognition, and in-class group exercises with random-call participation replacing Socratic lecturing. Moderate structure added clickers and practice exams; high structure added reading quizzes and group exercises.
requirements: Requires frequent low-stakes assessment points (clicker questions, practice exams, reading quizzes) that together represent a minority of total course points, with exams remaining the primary determinant of grade
constraints: The study population was sophomores who had completed a chemistry prerequisite, so failure rates were lower than at many other institutions before any intervention
target_learners: Undergraduate biology majors in large introductory gateway courses
target_learning_goals: Higher-order cognitive skills at the application and analysis levels of Bloom's taxonomy, and reduced course failure
examples: In Autumn 2007 and Autumn 2009 quarters, class sessions consisted of a series of 3- to 5-min mini-lectures around clicker questions or group exercises, with five or six group exercises per session and 12–15 students called on each day
key_sources: Freeman Scott, Haak David, Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2011). Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.10-08-0105

article_title: Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology
citation: Freeman Scott, Haak David, Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2011). Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.10-08-0105
title: Weighted Bloom's Index and Predicted Exam Score: two new tools for assessing exam equivalence across quarters or courses
description: The study introduces two methods for controlling for exam difficulty in longitudinal course comparisons. The Weighted Bloom's Index "summarizes the average Bloom's level of exam questions weighted by the points possible," computed from independent Bloom's ratings by three trained TAs blind to quarter and hypothesis. The Predicted Exam Score uses three experienced peer-TA graders to predict the average points students would receive on each exam question part. The two metrics were strongly and negatively associated (r = −0.72 for the 18 exams), and both indicated that exams in the highly structured quarters were harder.
requirements: Requires trained raters blind to the study's intent, with norming sessions and decision rules (consensus, majority rule, middle value for sequential ratings, arithmetic average for nonsequential) to assign levels or predicted points to every question part
constraints: Because both indices were computed from data on all exam questions, there is no sample variance and no statistical significance testing is possible when comparing exams
target_learners: STEM education researchers and instructors comparing exams across quarters, courses, or institutions
target_learning_goals: Ensuring that observed changes in student performance reflect course design rather than changes in exam difficulty
examples: Three Bloom's raters each assessed 295 exam questions and assigned 724 Bloom's levels; at least two of three agreed on the identical Bloom's level for 85% of questions rated
key_sources: Freeman Scott, Haak David, Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2011). Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.10-08-0105

article_title: Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology
citation: Freeman Scott, Haak David, Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2011). Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.10-08-0105
title: Use pre-class reading quizzes on lower-order content to free class time for higher-order active learning
description: The article argues that reading quizzes focused on Levels 1 and 2 of Bloom's taxonomy shift the burden of learning basic vocabulary and concepts to the student, "free[ing] time in class for active learning exercises that challenge students to apply concepts, analyze data, propose experimental designs, or evaluate conflicting pieces of evidence." This answers the standard objection that active learning requires drastically reducing content coverage. Because Bloom's taxonomy is hierarchical, students cannot work at the application or analysis level without knowing the basic vocabulary and concepts, so the authors see reading quizzes as an essential component of successful highly structured course designs.
requirements: Reading quizzes must be paired with in-class activities that operate at higher Bloom's levels; without them, informal group activities or peer instruction with clickers are unlikely to be maximally effective
target_learners: Undergraduates in large introductory STEM gateway courses
target_learning_goals: Acquiring basic vocabulary and concepts independently, and developing application- and analysis-level skills in class
examples: Reading quizzes in the study consisted of 5–10 open-book, open-note multiple-choice questions delivered online, opening after class and closing the morning of the next class, summing to about 8% of total course points
key_sources: Freeman Scott, Haak David, Wenderoth Mary Pat. (2011). Increased Course Structure Improves Performance in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.10-08-0105

article_title: Financial Incentives and Student Achievement: Evidence from Randomized Trials *
citation: Roland G. Fryer, Jr. (2010). Financial Incentives and Student Achievement: Evidence from Randomized Trials. NBER Working Paper No. 15898. http://www.nber.org/papers/w15898
title: Students lack knowledge of the educational production function, explaining why input incentives outperform output incentives
description: This theory holds that students do not understand how inputs map to achievement outputs, so they cannot translate excitement about rewards into improved performance. Students paid for inputs (reading books, attending class) did not need to know the production function — they simply needed to perform the incentivized behavior. The article calls this the "leading theory" because it is the only one confirmed by significant qualitative observations. Three alternative theories — lack of self-control, noisy output with risk aversion, and complementary inputs — are also consistent with the data.
requirements: Students must be incentivized for specific, actionable inputs rather than for distal outputs like test scores
constraints: The article states the theory is supported by qualitative observations but acknowledges three competing theories also fit the experimental data
target_learners: urban public school students in elementary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: reading achievement
mathematics achievement
attendance and behavior
examples: A qualitative team of seven researchers observed twelve students and their families and ten classrooms in NYC, finding students were elated by incentives but did not know how to convert excitement into achievement
key_sources: Roland G. Fryer, Jr. (2010). Financial Incentives and Student Achievement: Evidence from Randomized Trials. NBER Working Paper No. 15898. http://www.nber.org/papers/w15898

article_title: Analysing the Impact of Artificial Intelligence and Computational Sciences on Student Performance: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
citation: García-Martínez, I., Fernández-Batanero, J. M., Fernández-Cerero, J., & León, S. P. (2023). Analysing the Impact of Artificial Intelligence and Computational Sciences on Student Performance: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Journal of New Approaches in Educational Research, 12(1), 171-197. https://doi.org/10.7821/naer.2023.1.1240
title: Taxonomy of EAI modalities in education: applications, simulations, virtual reality and augmented reality
description: The review organizes the educational AI literature by intervention type, finding that studies "address the potential of EAI on student performance through applications (n = 8), simulations (n = 8), VR (n = 4) and AR (n = 2)". Applications are described as contextualised to subject matter and educational level, including intelligent tutoring and games; simulations provide scenarios for discovery learning with easy access, individualisation potential and low cost; VR and AR offer immersive and manipulative learning situations. The taxonomy underpins the moderator analysis of effect sizes by AI type.
requirements: Interventions must be classifiable into one of the four modalities the review codes: applications, simulations, VR or AR.
constraints: The review notes apps tend to be used more frequently by teachers due to greater accessibility, while modalities such as Big Data require a higher level of literacy and involve ethical issues.
target_learners: primary education students
secondary education students
vocational education students
university students
target_learning_goals: student academic performance across STEM and other subject areas
examples: The 25 included studies were coded by modality, e.g. Supercharged! as an application, virtual chemistry laboratories as simulations, and AR-based problem-based learning with FenAR software.

article_title: Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise
citation: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1
title: Negative knowledge: experientially acquired knowledge about what is wrong and to be avoided
description: The article defines negative knowledge as "experientially acquired knowledge about what is wrong and what is to be avoided during performance in a given work situation". Grounded in constructivist theorization, knowledge is a "map of what reality allows us to do", and negative knowledge is "non-viable knowledge that is heuristically valuable" — knowing what is wrong helps identify viable paths. The concept is positioned as augmenting theories of professional knowledge and expertise.
requirements: Knowledge must be understood in constructivist terms as viable or non-viable relative to individual goals
constraints: The article works from an individual, cognitive perspective before expanding to a socio-cultural level
target_learners: professionals in workplace settings
target_learning_goals: professional learning
learning from errors
expertise development
examples: A New York taxi driver's negative knowledge "Do not drive via Broadway!" enables avoiding a congested route
key_sources: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1

article_title: Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise
citation: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1
title: Two complementary facets of negative knowledge: procedural and declarative
description: The article distinguishes two complementary facets. The procedural aspect is "to know what not to do" — part of professionals' practical know-how about workplace tasks, drawing on Minsky's negative expertise and Oser and Spychiger's contrastive definition. The declarative aspect is "to know what not to know" — awareness of deficient aspects of one's own knowledge, including informed versus uninformed not-knowing and trivial versus non-trivial incompetence (Heid 1996). Both facets are advanced together for research on professional learning.
requirements: Both facets should be considered together, as the article treats them as complementary
constraints: The declarative aspect is not focused on actions or strategies
target_learners: professionals
novices entering a professional domain
target_learning_goals: awareness of one's own knowledge deficits
avoiding ineffective actions
examples: The Nepalese hospital example of "Seven easy ways to kill a newborn infant" illustrates procedural negative knowledge arising from practical experience
key_sources: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1

article_title: Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise
citation: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1
title: Error-related learning as experiential learning producing negative knowledge through analysis, reflection, regret and correction
description: The article conceptualizes learning from errors at work as a special form of experiential learning in which errors challenge individual mental models and provide starting points for modification — through differentiation, replacement of parts, or indexing weak areas. Analysis and reflection are crucial mediating activities, and Oser and Spychiger propose that "regret and correction are required for building negative knowledge from an error". Bauer and Mulder's framework involves cause analysis, developing new avoidance strategies, and experimentation with implementation.
requirements: Reflection and analysis of the error episode; regret and correction per Oser and Spychiger
constraints: What constitutes an error involves norm-based judgments that may differ substantially between workplaces and individuals
target_learners: professionals learning at the workplace
target_learning_goals: learning from errors
building negative knowledge
professional development
examples: Flight simulator training lets pilots learn from almost authentic critical experience without fatal consequences, building procedural negative knowledge
key_sources: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1

article_title: Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise
citation: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1
title: Prompting task technique (PTT) for eliciting workplace negative knowledge
description: The PTT is an experimental elicitation technique in which individuals are presented keywords or small phrases that activate related cognitive content. In an ongoing aged care nursing study, subjects are confronted with 20 diagnoses of varying typicality, each accompanied by the questions "What should be avoided?" and what one should pay special attention to. The pairing with a more general question was adopted because the avoidance question alone was experienced as difficult to answer.
requirements: Prompts paired with a general reflection question, since the direct avoidance question was experienced as quite difficult to answer
constraints: The PTT does not permit any directive intervention during data collection, and its broad focus may make it hard for subjects to dig up their negative knowledge
target_learners: professionals in aged care nursing
target_learning_goals: eliciting and studying the structure and function of negative knowledge
examples: A quasi-longitudinal PTT study compares bank employees: novices with less than two years of experience, semi-experts up to ten years, and experts with more than ten years
key_sources: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1

article_title: Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise
citation: M. Gartmeier, J. Bauer, H. Gruber, H. Heid. (2008). Negative Knowledge: Understanding Professional Learning and Expertise. Vocations and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12186-008-9006-1
title: Critical incident technique (CIT) for tracing the episodic origins of negative knowledge
description: The CIT elicits episodes of negative knowledge, traces their origins in past individual experience, and explores the complexity of present conditions. It rests on the assumption that critical incidents are events holding significant potential for gaining insight into error-prone aspects of a work context. A two-phase design is proposed: first identifying critical incidents, possibly with ambulatory assessment methods such as photo elicitation, then semi-structured interviews about the personal theories and knowledge that guided action.
requirements: A two phase design: identification of critical incidents followed by semi-structured interviews
constraints: The CIT offers a general framework rather than concrete methodological guidelines
target_learners: professionals reflecting on workplace error episodes
target_learning_goals: understanding how negative knowledge develops from critical experience
examples: Research questions include which episodes negative knowledge relates to and whether it is shared with colleagues

article_title: Outsourcing Memory to External Tools: A Review of ‘Intention Offloading’
citation: Gilbert, S. J., Boldt, A., Sachdeva, C., Scarampi, C., & Tsai, P.-C. (2023). Outsourcing Memory to External Tools: A Review of 'Intention Offloading'. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-022-02139-4
title: Intention offloading framework: storing intentions in extended environments alongside brain-based memory
description: Intention offloading is defined as 'the process of creating a cue in the external environment to trigger a delayed intention', a specific case of cognitive offloading. The review argues intentions are stored in 'our extended physical and social environments, not just in our brains', and that the phenomenon provides a testbed for interrelations between memory, planning, metacognitive monitoring and control, and decision making. It organises research on measurement, triggers (metacognition, effort avoidance, strategy perseveration), lifespan change, and neural mechanisms.
requirements: Individuals must have a free choice between internal memory and external reminder-setting for the paradigm to measure offloading strategy
constraints: Laboratory tasks reviewed use short retention intervals of seconds to minutes, and the authors note most studies used 'rather artificial experimental tasks'
target_learners: adults
children
older adults
target_learning_goals: remembering and fulfilling delayed intentions
examples: The Gilbert (2015a) web-based paradigm where participants drag numbered circles and can set reminders by placing target circles next to their instructed location

article_title: Component-levels theory of the effects of spacing of repetitions on recall and recognition
citation: Glenberg, A. M. (1979). Component-level theory of the effects of spacing of repetitions on recall and recognition. Memory & Cognition, 7(2), 95-112. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03197564
title: Component-levels theory of spacing effects: three informational components plus encoding and retrieval principles
description: The theory proposes that episodic traces contain three types of components: contextual, structural, and descriptive. The name derives from the fact that "The theory specifies three types of components that represent three types of information assumed to be important in most verbal learning and memory tasks." Two abstract principles govern spacing effects: "arepetition is potentially effective to the degree that the second presentation allows for the storage of information distinct from that stored at the first presentation," and realization of this potential "is controlled by the conditions at the time of the memory test, the retrieval environment." Contextual components are encoded automatically; structural and descriptive encoding depends on control processes. Cue-trace component matching, following the encoding specificity principle, determines retrieval.
requirements: Requires verbal learning and memory tasks in which repeated stimuli are encoded into multicomponent episodic traces
Requires a retrieval environment whose cues can be characterized by their component content and bias
constraints: The theory is designed for distributed practice and spacing effects with verbal stimuli in verbal learning and memory paradigms
The article notes that most reviewed experiments were not specifically designed to test the theory, so some analyses are post hoc
target_learners: Adult learners in verbal memory experiments (introductory psychology students)
target_learning_goals: Recall and recognition of repeated verbal material as a function of spacing of repetitions
examples: The theory integrates encoding variability approaches and predicts monotonically increasing, inverted U-shaped, or decreasing lag functions depending on cue bias, as illustrated in Figure 1

article_title: Incidental vocabulary learning in a natural reading context: an eye-tracking study
citation: Aline Godfroid, Jieun Ahn, Ina Choi, Laura Ballard, Yaqiong Cui, Suzanne Johnston, Shinhye Lee, Abdhi Sarkar and Hyung-Jo Yoon (2017). Incidental vocabulary learning in a natural reading context: an eye-tracking study. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition, Volume 21, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1366728917000219
title: Quantity and quality of lexical processing jointly drive incremental vocabulary development
description: The article advances an account in which two aspects of lexical processing during reading support incidental vocabulary growth: quantity, indexed by number of exposures, and quality, indexed by total reading time. The authors conclude that "both quantity and quality of lexical processing aid incremental vocabulary development" and that the two "may reveal themselves differently in readers’ eye movement records", so different eye-movement measures capture different aspects of processing.
requirements: Eye-movement records from natural reading of connected text
Vocabulary learning measured for both word form and word meaning
constraints: The account is drawn from a single eye-tracking study in which participants read one authentic novel in two sessions.
target_learners: native and non-native English speakers reading authentic texts
target_learning_goals: incidental vocabulary learning of word form and meaning
examples: Growth curve modeling of eye-tracking data during novel reading linked exposure count to form and meaning learning and total reading time to meaning learning

article_title: A meta-analysis of morphological interventions: effects on literacy achievement of children with literacy difficulties
citation: U.S. Department of Education, National Center for Education Statistics. (2007). Reading 2007: National Assessment of Educational Progress at Grades 4 and 8. NCES 2007–496. https://nationsreportcard.gov
title: NAEP reading framework: reading performance measured in two dimensions — three contexts for reading and four aspects of reading
description: The NAEP reading framework is the blueprint specifying what the reading assessment measures. It defines reading broadly as developing a general understanding of texts, interpreting texts, and using texts for different purposes, and views reading as "an interactive and dynamic process involving the reader, the text, and the context of the reading experience." It specifies two dimensions: three contexts for reading (literary experience, information, performing a task) guiding text selection, and four aspects of reading guiding question types. The framework has guided the assessment since 1992 with updates that did not change content, permitting trend comparisons.
requirements: Assessment time is distributed across the aspects of reading per framework targets (e.g., 60% at grade 4 for general understanding/developing interpretation combined)
constraints: All three contexts are assessed at grade 8 but only two at grade 4
Scales are set separately for each context, so direct comparisons cannot be made from one context to another
target_learners: fourth-grade students
eighth-grade students
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension across literary experience, information, and task-performance contexts
examples: The 2007 fourth-grade assessment included 10 reading passages and 100 questions divided between reading for literary experience and reading for information

citation: U.S. Department of Education, National Center for Education Statistics. (2007). Reading 2007: National Assessment of Educational Progress at Grades 4 and 8. NCES 2007–496. https://nationsreportcard.gov
title: NAEP reading assessment design: matrix sampling of passages, achievement levels, and item maps for interpreting scale scores
description: The 2007 NAEP reading assessment is a nationally representative measure in which "each student took just a portion of the test, consisting of two 25-minute sections or one 50-minute section," with multiple-choice and constructed-response questions. Results are reported on a 0–500 scale, as percentages at or above Basic, Proficient, and Advanced achievement levels, and via item maps showing what students at different scale points can do. In 2007 more than 350,000 students at grades 4 and 8 participated, including 191,000 fourth-graders in 7,830 schools.
requirements: Testing accommodations for students with disabilities and English language learners, introduced in 1998, to allow fair participation
constraints: A portion of students remains excluded even with accommodations; variation in exclusion and accommodation rates should be considered when comparing performance over time and across states
Achievement levels are used on a trial basis and should be interpreted with caution

eighth-grade students

examples: An item map shows fourth-graders near the middle of the Basic range (average score 220) were likely to recognize the meaning of specialized vocabulary from context

article_title: Preparatory effects of problem solving versus studying examples prior to instruction
citation: Christian Hartmann, Tamara van Gog, Nikol Rummel. (2021). Preparatory effects of problem solving versus studying examples prior to instruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09528-z
title: Preparatory mechanisms account for problem solving prior to instruction (prior knowledge activation, awareness of knowledge gaps, deep feature recognition)
description: The article works within the PF account that attempting (or observing) failed problem solving before instruction prepares learners through three mechanisms: "prior knowledge activation, awareness of knowledge gaps, and deep feature recognition". Activated incomplete schemas help learners integrate new conceptual knowledge during subsequent instruction, and awareness of gaps should make instruction more effective. The study tested these mechanisms against a vicarious-failure alternative and found the mechanism evidence mixed.
requirements: Learners must attempt or observe solution attempts on a complex but not ill-defined problem before receiving instruction on the canonical solution
constraints: The article states it had no direct measure of prior knowledge activation in all conditions, so the activation explanation remains speculative
The knowledge gap awareness items are described as rather unspecific, not assessing explicit knowledge about why a solution attempt failed
target_learners: secondary school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of statistical variance concepts
examples: Students generated or observed failed solution attempts on a soccer cover-story task about variance before receiving instruction on mean absolute deviation
key_sources: Christian Hartmann, Tamara van Gog, Nikol Rummel. (2021). Preparatory effects of problem solving versus studying examples prior to instruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09528-z

article_title: A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling
citation: Henseler, J., Ringle, C. M., & Sarstedt, M. (2015). A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling. J. of the Acad. Mark. Sci. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8
title: Heterotrait-monotrait ratio (HTMT) of correlations as a discriminant validity criterion
description: The HTMT is a ratio derived from the multitrait-multimethod matrix: "the average of the heterotrait-heteromethod correlations" (correlations of indicators across constructs) "relative to the average of the monotrait-heteromethod correlations" (correlations of indicators within the same construct), with the geometric mean taken of the two within-construct averages. It estimates the correlation between two constructs without requiring factor analysis or construct scores, so it can be computed from a correlation matrix alone. It can be applied as a criterion against a threshold (0.85 or 0.90) or as a bootstrap-based statistical test (HTMT inference) with Bonferroni adjustment.
requirements: At least two reflectively measured constructs measured with multiple indicators from the same respondents
For HTMT inference, bootstrapping to construct confidence intervals and Bonferroni adjustment for multiple construct pairs
constraints: The HTMT-based criteria assume reflectively measured constructs; applying them to formatively measured constructs is problematic because neither monotrait-heteromethod nor heterotrait-heteromethod correlations of formative indicators are indicative of discriminant validity
target_learners: Researchers and practitioners using variance-based SEM in marketing and other social sciences disciplines
target_learning_goals: Correct assessment of discriminant validity as part of measurement model evaluation in variance-based SEM
examples: In the ACSI empirical example (N = 10,417), HTMT values ranged from 0.53 to 0.95, with HTMT.85 flagging two construct pairs and HTMT.90 one
key_sources: Henseler, J., Ringle, C. M., & Sarstedt, M. (2015). A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling. J. of the Acad. Mark. Sci. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8

article_title: A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling
citation: Henseler, J., Ringle, C. M., & Sarstedt, M. (2015). A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling. J. of the Acad. Mark. Sci. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8
title: Use HTMT criteria rather than the Fornell-Larcker criterion or cross-loadings for discriminant validity assessment in variance-based SEM
description: The article recommends replacing the traditional Fornell-Larcker and cross-loadings checks with HTMT-based assessment: "we strongly recommend drawing on the HTMT criteria for discriminant validity assessment in variance-based SEM." The choice among HTMT.85, HTMT.90, and HTMT inference depends on the model set-up and how conservative the researcher wishes to be: HTMT.85 is the strictest standard, while HTMT.90 or HTMT inference suit settings where constructs are conceptually different but empirically hard to distinguish.
requirements: Access to item-level correlations or raw data to compute HTMT
A decision on the threshold or test variant appropriate to the constructs' conceptual similarity
constraints: HTMT.85 can point to problems where HTMT.90 and HTMT inference indicate validity is established; HTMT inference is unlikely to flag problems even at correlations close to 1.0 when loadings are homogeneous and high or the sample is large
target_learners: Researchers and practitioners applying variance-based SEM in marketing and other social sciences
target_learning_goals: Reliable evaluation of measurement models before interpreting structural relationships
examples: The authors suggest HTMT.90 or HTMT inference for technology acceptance models where intention to use and actual use are conceptually different but empirically difficult to distinguish, and HTMT.85 where the strictest standards are followed
key_sources: Henseler, J., Ringle, C. M., & Sarstedt, M. (2015). A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling. J. of the Acad. Mark. Sci. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8

citation: Hew, K. F., Huang, W., Du, J., & Jia, C. (2023). Using chatbots to support student goal setting and social presence in fully online activities: learner engagement and perceptions. Journal of Computing in Higher Education, 35, 40–68. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12528-022-09338-x
title: Goal-setting chatbot using five SMART-framework questions before online class
description: A chatbot used in Study 1 to support student goal setting in a fully online course. Prior to attending class, participants completed a goal-setting activity with the chatbot, which “engaged participants with five questions developed based on the SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, and timely) goal setting framework”. The chatbot served as a pre-class self-regulation prompt for online learners.

article_title: Leveraging the Potential of Large Language Models in Education Through Playful and Game-Based Learning
citation: Huber, S. E., Kiili, K., Nebel, S., Ryan, R. M., Sailer, M., & Ninaus, M. (2024). Leveraging the Potential of Large Language Models in Education Through Playful and Game-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09868-z
title: Three learning processes of expertise development through practice
description: The article describes a framework, drawing on Elvira et al. and Tynjälä, in which novices advancing from easier to more difficult problems engage in three learning processes: transforming conceptual into experiential knowledge, explicating experiential into conceptual knowledge, and reflecting on both to improve problem-solving strategies and metacognitive and self-regulatory skills. Continuous practice integrating these knowledge forms "utilizes already existing expertise and contributes to its further development." The article uses this framework to argue why outsourcing practice to LLMs threatens expertise.
requirements: Development and preservation of expertise require practicing domain-specific problem-solving capabilities.
constraints: Modern theories acknowledge that many factors besides practice contribute to expertise development.
target_learners: novices developing domain expertise in formal education
target_learning_goals: domain-specific problem-solving expertise
metacognitive and self-regulatory skills
examples: The article applies the framework to Papert's Logo approach, showing how playful experimentation nurtured all three learning processes.

article_title: Leveraging the Potential of Large Language Models in Education Through Playful and Game-Based Learning
citation: Huber, S. E., Kiili, K., Nebel, S., Ryan, R. M., Sailer, M., & Ninaus, M. (2024). Leveraging the Potential of Large Language Models in Education Through Playful and Game-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09868-z
title: Treat LLMs as tools for meaningful playful activity rather than as means to outsource task accomplishment
description: Following Papert's constructionist use of computers, the article recommends that instead of seeing LLMs as possibilities to outsource task accomplishment, they be "understood as tools that can be utilized to engage in a meaningful activity." The interface (e.g., ChatGPT prompting) plays the role Logo played for Papert's students, and proficiency in it entails practicing the very domain expertise it presupposes, providing some protection from over-reliance.
requirements: Users need sufficient domain expertise so that prompt engineering results in reliable and useful output.
constraints: Risks may be more severe for learners who are not yet domain experts, whose goals may be mere task accomplishment.
target_learners: learners and domain experts using LLMs in education
target_learning_goals: domain expertise development
prompt engineering competence
examples: Prompt engineering as playful interaction: exploring various aspects of a topic by varying prompt patterns and techniques.

citation: Huber, S. E., Kiili, K., Nebel, S., Ryan, R. M., Sailer, M., & Ninaus, M. (2024). Leveraging the Potential of Large Language Models in Education Through Playful and Game-Based Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09868-z
title: Problem-based gaming model emphasizing experiential learning and reflection
description: The article presents the problem-based gaming model (Kiili, 2007), which "emphasizes the meaning of experiential learning and reflection in educational games." In the model, the level of reflection concerns whether the player considers consequences of actions and changes in the game world to create better playing strategies (double-loop learning) or merely applies a previously formed strategy (single-loop learning). Games triggering double-loop learning persuade players to test hypotheses and consider learning content deeply from several perspectives.
requirements: Educational game design must create game mechanics that trigger meaningful reflection practices.
constraints: Reflection is especially important for games that require problem-solving, such as simulation games.
target_learners: players of educational games in formal and informal learning
target_learning_goals: problem-solving strategies
reflection on learning content
examples: The article argues the ability to reflect may be the main factor determining who learns effectively from experience.

description: An instructional approach in which students develop educational computer games and assess one another's work, proposed "for improving students' learning achievements, motivations and problem-solving skills." It was implemented in a science course at an elementary school, where the experimental group learned with it while a control group learned with the conventional game development approach. learning motivation

article_title: DECONSTRUCTING COMPREHENSIBILITY
citation: Talia Isaacs and Pavel Trofimovich. (2012). DECONSTRUCTING COMPREHENSIBILITY: Identifying the Linguistic Influences on Listeners' L2 Comprehensibility Ratings. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 34, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263112000150
title: Comprehensibility as listeners' perceptions of how easily they understand L2 speech
description: The article treats comprehensibility as "a major concept in second language (L2) pronunciation research that denotes listeners' perceptions of how easily they understand L2 speech." It is presented as "central to interlocutors' communicative success in real-world contexts" and as a construct modeled in oral proficiency scales such as TOEFL and IELTS. The study operationalizes it through native listeners' scalar judgments of L2 speakers' speech, which are then related to linguistic measures of the speech itself.
requirements: Listeners provide scalar judgments of L2 speech samples that can be correlated with quantitative linguistic measures of those samples.
target_learners: adult L2 learners of English
target_learning_goals: L2 speaking and pronunciation proficiency as perceived by listeners
examples: The study elicited scalar comprehensibility judgments from 60 native English listeners on speech samples of 40 native French learners of English.

title: Mixed-methods design combining 19 speech measures, listener ratings, and teacher introspective reports
description: The study's methodology combined quantitative and qualitative strands: "a mixed-methods approach was used" in which "speech samples of 40 native French learners of English were analyzed using 19 quantitative speech measures, including segmental, suprasegmental, fluency, lexical, grammatical, and discourse-level variables." These measures were correlated with 60 native English listeners' scalar judgments, and three ESL teachers provided introspective reports on the linguistic aspects they attended to, with findings integrated through data triangulation.

citation: Jansen, R. S., van Leeuwen, A., Janssen, J., Jak, S., & Kester, L. (2019). Self-regulated learning partially mediates the effect of self-regulated learning interventions on achievement in higher education: A meta-analysis. Educational Research Review, 28, 100292. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2019.100292
title: SRL as a three-phase process comprising metacognitive and resource management activities
description: The article adopts an SRL framework in which self-regulating learners are "metacognitively, behaviorally, and motivationally active" and proceed through a preparatory, performance, and appraisal phase. Metacognitive activities include goal setting, strategic planning, comprehension monitoring, strategy regulation, and reflection; behavioral and motivational regulation (time management, environmental structuring, help seeking, effort regulation) are grouped as resource management activities. The framework structures how interventions and measures are coded in the meta-analyses.
requirements: Learners must possess an adequate repertoire of cognitive strategies to be able to successfully self-regulate, per the article's rationale for the cognitive-strategies moderator.
constraints: Task motivation (task value, goal orientation, self-efficacy) is treated as a precursor outside SRL, following the models the article adheres to.
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills
academic achievement
examples: The coding scheme classified SRL measures and intervention targets into metacognitive and resource management activity categories clustered for the moderator analyses.

Educational Research Review, 28, 100292. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2019.100292
title: Three-relations mediation framework linking SRL interventions, SRL activity, and achievement
description: The article organizes the field around three relations: the effect of SRL interventions on achievement (relation 1), the effect of interventions on SRL activity (relation 2), and the relation between SRL activity and achievement (relation 3), with SRL activity hypothesized as the mediator. Prior reviews each covered only part of this framework; this study is presented as the first comprehensive meta-analysis including all three relations at once, enabling a formal mediation test via MASEM.
requirements: Estimating the mediation requires data on all three relations; the article notes only three primary studies included statistical information on all three.
constraints: MASEM could not yet apply three-level models for nested effect sizes or evaluate continuous moderators, per the article's stated shortcomings.
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: understanding how SRL interventions produce achievement effects
examples: The framework (Fig. 1) guided the literature searches, coding scheme, and the three research questions about factors influencing each relation.

description: Drawing on prior reviews showing that secondary students benefited more from metacognitive reflection than from metacognitive instruction, the article reasons that higher education students have internalized more SRL knowledge and should therefore be stimulated to reflect on and activate what they already know, for example through scaffolding with prompts to self-explain steps to mastery. article_title: Expertise reversal effect and its instructional implications: introduction to the special issue
citation: Slava Kalyuga, Alexander Renkl. (2010). Expertise reversal effect and its instructional implications: introduction to the special issue. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9102-0
title: Cognitive load imbalance account of the expertise reversal effect
description: Within cognitive load theory, the expertise reversal effect is explained by imbalances between the learner's organized knowledge base and provided instructional guidance. For novices, knowledge gaps not compensated by guidance cause unsupported search and excessive extraneous load; for advanced learners, overlaps between available knowledge and guidance mean redundant explanations must be integrated and cross-referenced, consuming additional resources. The article states that "instructional guidance that is essential for novices may inhibit learning for more experienced learners by interfering with retrieval and application of their available knowledge structures."
requirements: Instructional support must be matched to the learner's current level of domain expertise to optimize cognitive load
constraints: The account rests on a cognitive architecture of limited working memory and unlimited long-term memory, and was supported by subjective mental-load rating measures
target_learners: learners at varying levels of prior domain knowledge, from novices to experts
target_learning_goals: efficient acquisition of domain knowledge and skills under manageable cognitive load
key_sources: Slava Kalyuga, Alexander Renkl. (2010). Expertise reversal effect and its instructional implications: introduction to the special issue. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9102-0

article_title: Expertise reversal effect and its instructional implications: introduction to the special issue
citation: Slava Kalyuga, Alexander Renkl. (2010). Expertise reversal effect and its instructional implications: introduction to the special issue. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9102-0
title: Adjust instructional methods and guidance as learners acquire more experience in a specific domain
description: The major instructional design implication of expertise reversal research is the need to adjust instructional methods and procedures as learners acquire more experience in a specific domain. Appropriate support should be provided to novices, while unnecessary guidance is removed as proficiency grows: "appropriate instructional support should be provided to novice learners, while unnecessary guidance removed as the learners acquire higher levels of proficiency in a specific domain."
requirements: Ongoing assessment of learners' changing levels of domain expertise
constraints: Guidance beneficial for novices may inhibit learning for experienced learners, especially if they cannot ignore or avoid processing redundant explanations
target_learners: learners progressing from novice to higher levels of proficiency in a domain
target_learning_goals: optimizing cognitive load across stages of skill acquisition

article_title: Knowledge elaboration: A cognitive load perspective
citation: Ramírez Ruiz, J. J. (2018). Efecto de un andamiaje de autoeficacia en el estilo cognitivo, el logro de aprendizaje y la carga cognitiva. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://bibliotecadigital.upn.edu.co
title: Ambiente computacional "sólidos geométricos" con andamiaje de autoeficacia (metas, autoevaluación y mensajes motivacionales)
description: Ambiente de aprendizaje computacional para geometría en educación básica primaria, compuesto por tres módulos de aprendizaje con información textual y gráfica, actividades y evaluación final de diez preguntas. La versión con andamiaje incluye una estrategia para "promover las experiencias de éxito" y hacer consciente al estudiante de sus capacidades: "El andamiaje permitió a los estudiantes elegir metas, autoevaluarse y encontrar mensajes motivacionales". La versión sin andamiaje conserva la misma estructura conceptual, interfaz, actividades y evaluación, pero carece de la estrategia motivacional.

Instrumentos de medición previos y posteriores: EFT para estilo cognitivo, subescala de autoeficacia del MSLQ, cuestionario de carga cognitiva de Leppink et al. (2014) por módulo y prueba de conocimientos final

target_learning_goals: Aprendizaje de contenidos matemáticos de geometría
Percepción de autoeficacia académica

article_title: Knowledge elaboration: A cognitive load perspective
citation: Ramírez Ruiz, J. J. (2018). Efecto de un andamiaje de autoeficacia en el estilo cognitivo, el logro de aprendizaje y la carga cognitiva. Tesis de maestría, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional, Bogotá. https://bibliotecadigital.upn.edu.co
title: Teoría social cognitiva de la autoeficacia y la agencia humana (Bandura) como marco del andamiaje motivacional
description: La tesis adopta el marco de Bandura: la autoeficacia se define como "las creencias en las propias capacidades para organizar y ejecutar los cursos de acción requeridos para manejar situaciones futuras". En el marco de la teoría social cognitiva se plantean "cuatro características distintivas de la agencia humana: la intención, previsión, auto-reactividad y auto- reflexión". La autoeficacia actúa sobre procesos cognitivos, motivacionales, emocionales y de selección, y es el mecanismo de reflexión más importante; una mayor percepción de autoeficacia mejora el esfuerzo y la recuperación al fracaso, influyendo sobre el logro.

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: How Many Types of Load Does It Really Need?
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2011). Cognitive Load Theory: How Many Types of Load Does It Really Need?. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9150-7
title: Redefined germane load as actual working memory resources devoted to dealing with intrinsic rather than extraneous load
description: The article proposes a possible redefinition under which germane load could keep an independent role within the cognitive load framework. Following a recent suggestion the article attributes to John Sweller, germane load would refer to "the actual working memory resources devoted to dealing with intrinsic rather than extraneous load". This reframing ties germane load to the processing of intrinsic load rather than treating it as a separate additive load type. It is offered as a conditional alternative to dropping the concept entirely.
requirements: The redefinition presupposes retaining the intrinsic/extraneous distinction within the cognitive load framework
constraints: The article presents this redefinition as conditional: germane load might have an independent role only if redefined in this way
target_learners: All learners addressed by cognitive load theory
target_learning_goals: Managing working memory load during learning and instruction
examples: The article cites John Sweller's recent suggestion as the source of this redefinition of germane load
