article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: How Many Types of Load Does It Really Need?
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2011). Cognitive Load Theory: How Many Types of Load Does It Really Need?. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9150-7
title: Traditional description of cognitive load theory as three separate and additive load types
description: The article characterizes the traditional formulation of cognitive load theory as one in which the theory "has been traditionally described as involving three separate and additive types of load". In this traditional account, germane load is "considered as a learning-relevant load complementing extraneous and intrinsic load". This three-component additive structure is the target of the article's critique and the baseline against which its dual-framework proposal is argued.
requirements: The framework distinguishes intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load as separate additive components
constraints: The article argues this traditional treatment makes germane load indistinguishable from intrinsic load
target_learners: All learners addressed by cognitive load theory
target_learning_goals: Explaining and managing working memory load in instructional design
examples: The article's abstract states the traditional description and the role of germane load as a learning-relevant load complementing the other two types

title: Integrating LLMs into education requires developing teacher and learner competencies and literacies about the technology, its limitations, and its unexpected brittleness
description: The paper argues that using LLMs in education demands that teachers and learners develop competencies and literacies to understand both the technology and its limits. It states that LLMs in education "require teachers and learners to develop sets of competencies and literacies necessary to both understand the technology as well as their limitations and unexpected brittleness of such systems." This positions AI literacy as a precondition for responsible classroom integration rather than an optional add-on.

constraints: The paper notes limitations such as lack of interpretability, potential for bias, and unexpected brittleness in relatively simple tasks.

article_title: AI literacy and its implications for prompt engineering strategies
citation: Knoth, N., Tolzin, A., Janson, A., & Leimeister, J. M. (2024). AI literacy and its implications for prompt engineering strategies. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2024.100225
title: Skill-based approach to prompt engineering for non-expert users of LLM-based AI systems
description: The article introduces a skill-based approach to prompt engineering, treating the formulation of instructions to LLMs as a learnable skill rather than an ad hoc activity. Prompt engineering is defined as "a skill of formulating precise and well-structured instructions to elicit desired responses or information from the LLM, optimizing the effectiveness of the interaction". The approach is applied to non-expert users, specifically students in higher education, and is linked empirically to output quality and AI literacy.

constraints: Research on non-expert perspectives and on how AI literacy affects prompting behavior is described as lacking

non-expert users of LLM-based AI systems
target_learning_goals: formulating precise and well-structured instructions to LLMs
effective goal-directed use of generative AI tools
examples: The study examined students' intuitive behaviors towards LLM-based AI systems and linked prompt engineering skill quality to LLM output quality

article_title: Exploring the Assistance Dilemma in Experiments with Cognitive Tutors
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Vincent Aleven. (2007). Exploring the Assistance Dilemma in Experiments with Cognitive Tutors. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9049-0
title: The assistance dilemma: balancing information giving and withholding in learning environments
description: The article names and frames the "assistance dilemma" as a fundamental open problem in instructional science: "How should learning environments balance information or assistance giving and withholding to achieve optimal student learning?" It treats results from Cognitive Tutor experiments comparing forms of interactivity as partial answers to this general question, and argues the field needs "specific conditions and parameters that indicate when and to what extent to use information giving versus information withholding forms of interaction."
requirements: Further experimental science to yield specific conditions and parameters indicating when and to what extent to use information giving versus information withholding interactions
constraints: The article states how best to achieve the balance "remains a fundamental open problem in instructional science"
target_learners: Students using intelligent tutoring systems across subject-matter areas
target_learning_goals: Optimal student learning from interactive problem-solving environments

title: Cognitive Tutors: interactive problem-solving environments with step-by-step feedback, error messages, hints, and problem selection
description: Cognitive Tutors are intelligent tutors "based on cognitive psychology theory of problem solving and learning." They "provide a rich problem-solving environment with tutorial guidance in the form of step-by-step feedback, specific messages in response to common errors, and on-demand instructional hints" and "also select problems based on individual student performance." As they matured and spread to new subject-matter areas, they have been used as a research platform, particularly to explore interactive methods supporting metacognition.

article_title: Role of AI chatbots in education: systematic literature review
citation: Lasha Labadze, Maya Grigolia and Lela Machaidze. (2023). Role of AI chatbots in education: systematic literature review. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00426-1
title: Four research gaps framework for chatbot-in-education research: long-term effects, student characteristics, pedagogical strategies, and user experience
description: The review identifies four aspects missing from existing literature reviews: (a) the enduring, long-term impacts of chatbot integration rather than immediate effects; (b) how different student groups such as age, prior knowledge, and learning styles interact with chatbot technology; (c) the specific pedagogical strategies chatbots employ to achieve learning gains; and (d) deeper exploration of user experience, including usability, perceived usefulness, satisfaction, and preferences. The review states these gaps "would significantly benefit the field of education" and frames them as directions for future research.
requirements: Future studies addressing these gaps require rigorous designs covering long-term effects, student characteristics, pedagogical strategies, and user experience
constraints: The review notes existing studies focus on immediate impact and on learning outcomes as a whole, without variation by student characteristics

educators

article_title: A meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools
citation: Li, S., Zeng, C., Liu, H., Jia, J., Liang, M., Cha, Y., Lim, C. P., & Wu, X. (2025). A meta-analysis of AI-enabled personalized STEM education in schools. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00566-y
title: Adapted Personalized Learning Continuum Framework (PLCF) for categorizing AI-enabled personalized learning models
description: The article adapts the Personalized Learning Continuum Framework of Lokey-Vega and Stephens (2019) as an analytical lens for classifying AI-enabled personalized learning models along the proportion of Academic Learning Time spent on automated versus student-centered pedagogies and the distribution of power and agency. Model A is "fully automated, with 100% of ALT delivered through an adaptive platform and minimal teacher or peer involvement"; Model B is a balanced hybrid; Model C is learner-driven with 80% collaborative, project-based learning. target_learning_goals: Personalized STEM learning across knowledge, skills, engagement, and attitudes

article_title: Errors During Exploration and Consolidation—The Effectiveness of Productive Failure as Sequentially Guided Discovery Learning
citation: Julie McNamara and Meghan M. Shaughnessy. (2011). Student errors: What can they tell us about what students DO understand? Math Solutions. https://www.mathsolutions.com
title: Errors as partial understandings: incorrect responses as normal parts of developing understanding
description: The article advances the view, drawing on Saxe et al. (2010) and Wells & Coffey (2005), that student errors are often "partial understandings" or "correct answers to slightly different questions" rather than carelessness or global misunderstanding. Exposing and discussing these responses is presented as productive for deepening and refining students' thinking. Teachers are urged to acknowledge what students do know and build on it.

constraints: The article frames this as a practitioner perspective drawing on cited research rather than reporting new empirical data of its own

rational number concepts

article_title: DIFFERENTIAL EFFECTS OF PROMPTS AND RECASTS IN FORM-FOCUSED INSTRUCTION
citation: Roy Lyster. (2004). DIFFERENTIAL EFFECTS OF PROMPTS AND RECASTS IN FORM-FOCUSED INSTRUCTION. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 26, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263104263021
title: Noun-ending form-focused instruction embedded in subject-matter teaching
description: An instructional treatment that draws learners' attention to selected French noun endings that reliably predict grammatical gender and provides practice associating endings with gender attribution. It was "implemented in the context of regular subject-matter instruction by three of the four teachers, each with two classes, for approximately 9 hours during a 5-week period," while a comparison teacher taught the same subject matter without FFI. The treatment targets written and oral gender-attribution accuracy in immersion students.

Selected noun endings that reliably predict grammatical gender
Opportunities for practice in associating endings with gender attribution

target_learning_goals: Accurately assigning grammatical gender to French nouns

title: Rule-based representation and proceduralization account of form-focused instruction effects
description: The article interprets its findings through a skill-acquisition account in which form-focused instruction helps L2 learners build explicit, rule-based representations of grammatical forms and then proceduralize that knowledge through practice and feedback. Prompts are positioned as especially suited to this account because they push learners to produce and self-repair target forms, supporting the move from declarative rule knowledge toward proceduralized use, whereas recasts provide only models of the correct form.

Opportunities for practice associating forms with their targets

article_title: INTERACTIONAL FEEDBACK AND INSTRUCTIONAL COUNTERBALANCE
citation: Roy Lyster and Hirohide Mori. (2006). Interactional feedback and instructional counterbalance. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 28(2), 269-300. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060128
title: The counterbalance hypothesis
description: The counterbalance hypothesis holds that "instructional activities and interactional feedback that act as a counterbalance to a classroom's predominant communicative orientation are likely to prove more effective than instructional activities and interactional feedback that are congruent with its predominant communicative orientation." It was introduced by Lyster and Mori based on their finding of distinctively varied uptake and repair patterns across French and Japanese immersion, supported by an analysis of each setting's overall communicative orientation. It functions as an explanatory account of why the same feedback types produced different repair outcomes in different instructional settings.
requirements: Knowledge of the classroom's predominant communicative orientation, established through analysis of the instructional setting
constraints: Effectiveness claims are framed as likelihood ("are likely to prove more effective"), grounded in the two immersion settings analyzed
target_learners: Elementary-school immersion students learning a second language
target_learning_goals: Second language accuracy and repair of learner errors during communicative interaction
examples: The authors derived the hypothesis from contrasting French immersion, where prompts produced the most repair, with Japanese immersion, where recasts did
key_sources: Roy Lyster and Hirohide Mori. (2006). Interactional feedback and instructional counterbalance. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 28(2), 269-300. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060128

article_title: INTERACTIONAL FEEDBACK AND INSTRUCTIONAL COUNTERBALANCE
citation: Roy Lyster and Hirohide Mori. (2006). Interactional feedback and instructional counterbalance. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 28(2), 269-300. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060128
title: Select instructional activities and interactional feedback that counterbalance, rather than match, a classroom's predominant communicative orientation
description: This principle translates the counterbalance hypothesis into design guidance: because feedback congruent with a classroom's dominant communicative orientation is predicted to be less effective, teachers should choose "instructional activities and interactional feedback that act as a counterbalance to a classroom's predominant communicative orientation." The article grounds this in its comparative finding that repair patterns differed by setting, and in its analysis of each setting's overall communicative orientation. It implies first diagnosing the orientation, then selecting the feedback type that offsets it.
requirements: An analysis of the instructional setting's overall communicative orientation before selecting feedback types
constraints: The article states the hypothesis as a likelihood of greater effectiveness, not a demonstrated optimum
target_learners: Elementary-school second language learners in immersion settings
target_learning_goals: Learner uptake and repair following corrective feedback
examples: In French immersion, where recasts predominated but prompts produced the largest proportion of repair, prompts act as the counterbalancing feedback type

High guidance combined direct instruction with inquiry questions, while low guidance used only inquiry questions. The design allowed timing of guidance to be isolated as the manipulated factor.

long-term transfer of experimentation skills

article_title: A generative theory of textbook design: Using annotated illustrations to foster meaningful learning of science text
citation: Mayer, R.E., Steinhoff, K., Bower, G., & Mars, R. (1995). A generative theory of textbook design: Using annotated illustrations to foster meaningful learning of science text. ETR&D, 43, 31-41. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02300480
title: Generative theory of multimedia learning
description: The article interprets its results in light of a generative theory of multimedia learning, which "posits that meaningful learning requires constructing connections between visual and verbal representations of a system." The theory explains why annotated illustrations integrated with text fostered transfer: they support building cross-representational links during learning. It draws on generative views of learning as an active constructive process.
requirements: Learning materials must present visual and verbal representations that learners can connect during learning
constraints: The theory is applied here to learning of explanatory science text with illustrations by college students
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning of explanatory science text and problem-solving transfer
examples: In three experiments, annotated lightning-formation illustrations placed adjacent to corresponding text paragraphs produced more creative transfer solutions than the same illustrations shown separately without annotations.

The article found the transfer benefit of integrated illustrations "depended on incorporating annotations (i.e., captions and labels) into the illustrations rather than placing illustrations close to corresponding paragraphs."

title: Pienemann and Johnston's developmental sequence for ESL question formation as an operationalization of L2 development
description: The study operationalizes ESL question development as "stage advancement in Pienemann and Johnston's developmental sequence for ESL question formation" (Pienemann & Johnston, 1987; Pienemann, Johnston, & Brindley, 1988). Learners' stage assignment on this sequence was measured across four oral production tests to determine whether it changed over time, providing a developmental outcome measure for the feedback and modified-output analyses.

Sixty Thai EFL learners completed these tasks and four oral production tests over an 8-week period, allowing the study to separate the contribution of feedback provision from learners' production of modified output.

article_title: A Review of Self-Management Interventions Targeting Academic Outcomes for Students with Emotional and Behavioral Disorders
citation: Mooney, P., Ryan, J. B., Uhing, B. M., Reid, R., & Epstein, M. H. (2005). A Review of Self-Management Interventions Targeting Academic Outcomes for Students with Emotional and Behavioral Disorders. Journal of Behavioral Education, 14, 203–221. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10864-005-6298-1
title: Self-management intervention taxonomy for academic outcomes: self-evaluation, self-monitoring, strategy instruction, self-instruction, and multiple-component interventions
description: The review organizes academic self-management interventions for students with emotional and behavioral disorders into five technique types, reporting that "Self-monitoring interventions were the predominant type of self-management technique used by researchers." The taxonomy distinguishes self-evaluation, self-monitoring, strategy instruction techniques, self-instruction techniques, and multiple-component interventions, each with its own mean effect size in the synthesis. It serves as the organizing axis for the review's analysis of intervention effectiveness.
requirements: Studies must be classifiable into one of the five intervention types for the taxonomy's effect-size comparisons
constraints: Derived from 22 single-subject studies of children and adolescents with emotional and behavioral disorders published in 20 articles
target_learners: children and adolescents with emotional and behavioral disorders
target_learning_goals: academic outcomes including math calculation, writing, reading, and social studies skills
examples: The review classified each of the 22 included studies by intervention type and computed mean ES per type, from self-evaluation (1.13) to self-instruction techniques (2.71)

article_title: The Self-Regulation-View in Writing-to-Learn: Using Journal Writing to Optimize Cognitive Load in Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Nückles, M., Roelle, J., Glogger-Frey, I., Waldeyer, J., & Renkl, A. (2020). The Self-Regulation-View in Writing-to-Learn: Using Journal Writing to Optimize Cognitive Load in Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09541-1
title: The self-regulation view in writing-to-learn: combining genre-free expressive journal writing with systematic prompting of self-regulatory processes
description: The self-regulation view holds that journal writing scaffolds self-regulated learning through cognitive offloading: written text serves as an external representation and memory aid that frees working-memory capacity for metacognitive reflection, and the genre-free principle further offloads writers from rhetorical demands. The authors term this idea of combining free and expressive writing with systematic prompting of self-regulatory processes the self-regulation view of writing-to-learn, positioning it between the romantic view (spontaneous expressive writing suffices) and the classic view (rhetorical genre instantiation produces learning). It draws on models of self-regulated learning theory and cognitive load theory.
requirements: Instructional support via prompts eliciting cognitive (elaboration, organization) and metacognitive (monitoring, regulation) learning strategies, because learners spontaneously keep invested mental effort at a minimum
constraints: Learners need sufficient mastery of transcription skills (spelling, handwriting/typing); the approach was developed for university students and extended to secondary school students
target_learners: university students
secondary school students
target_learning_goals: deep comprehension of subject matter
self-regulated learning
long-term retention
examples: Learning journal entries after lectures or seminar sessions in which students identify main points, elaborate with examples, monitor comprehension gaps, and plan remedial strategies

article_title: The Self-Regulation-View in Writing-to-Learn: Using Journal Writing to Optimize Cognitive Load in Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Nückles, M., Roelle, J., Glogger-Frey, I., Waldeyer, J., & Renkl, A. (2020). The Self-Regulation-View in Writing-to-Learn: Using Journal Writing to Optimize Cognitive Load in Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09541-1
title: The genre-free principle: journal writing without prescribed rhetorical structure as a variant of the goal-free effect in cognitive load theory
description: The genre-free principle holds that learning journals, unlike genres such as argumentative essays or scientific reports, have no conventionalized rhetorical structure, so a high-quality learning journal entry is not expected to be a rhetorically well-shaped text. The authors suggest this principle can be considered, at least on a more general level, as a particular variant of the goal-free effect in cognitive load theory: taking away the goal to stick to a rhetorical format allows learners to devote more cognitive capacity to germane processing of subject matter rather than to extraneous genre-conforming strategies.
requirements: The writing task must genuinely lack a prescribed rhetorical format so writers are offloaded from instantiating rhetorical schemata
constraints: Stated as a theoretical assumption grounded in cognitive load theory rather than as a separately tested manipulation in the studies summarized
target_learners: novice writers in secondary and higher education
target_learning_goals: germane processing of subject matter
deep comprehension

article_title: Meta-analysis in Second Language Research: Choices and Challenges
citation: Frederick L. Oswald and Luke Plonsky. (2010). Meta-analysis in Second Language Research: Choices and Challenges. Annual Review of Applied Linguistics, Volume 30. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0267190510000115
title: Four-stage model of conducting a meta-analysis in SLA research
description: The review organizes the conduct of a meta-analysis in second language acquisition research into four typical stages: "defining the research domain," "developing a reliable coding scheme," "analyzing data," and "interpreting results." The model frames meta-analysis as a staged process in which each stage requires choices, and the article uses it to structure its discussion of the benefits and challenges that inform those decisions in SLA meta-analyses.
requirements: Each stage requires deliberate decisions by the researcher; the coding scheme must be developed to be reliable for the results to be meaningful
constraints: The model is presented as describing typical stages of meta-analysis in SLA research specifically
target_learners: second language acquisition researchers conducting syntheses
target_learning_goals: systematic quantitative synthesis of L2 research findings
examples: The review describes typical stages of a meta-analysis in second language acquisition (SLA) research across four numbered steps

article_title: Meta-analysis in Second Language Research: Choices and Challenges
citation: Frederick L. Oswald and Luke Plonsky. (2010). Meta-analysis in Second Language Research: Choices and Challenges. Annual Review of Applied Linguistics, Volume 30. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0267190510000115
title: Plan meta-analyses carefully, use sound statistical methods, and ground them in relevant theory so they can inform theory, research, practice, and policy
description: This principle holds that a meta-analysis in applied linguistics delivers critical information only under three conditions: it must be "well planned," "employs sound statistical methods," and be "based on a thorough understanding of relevant theory." When these hold, the review states the meta-analysis "can provide critical information that informs theory as well as future research, practice, and policy." The article presents this as the general condition for meta-analysis to benefit SLA.
requirements: Careful planning of the meta-analysis
Sound statistical methods
Thorough understanding of relevant theory
constraints: The informative value is conditional; the article does not claim all meta-analyses provide critical information

research consumers in language education
target_learning_goals: producing and interpreting trustworthy quantitative research syntheses in language learning research
examples: The review's concluding general statement ties well-planned, statistically sound, theory-based meta-analysis to informing theory, research, practice, and policy

article_title: The effects of educational robotics in STEM education: a multilevel meta-analysis
citation: Fan Ouyang and Weiqi Xu. (2024). The effects of educational robotics in STEM education: a multilevel meta-analysis. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-024-00469-4
title: Robot-assisted STEM education as a complex system of interacting elements
description: The article frames robot-assisted STEM education as a complex system arising from interactions among multiple elements beyond the technology itself. It states that robot-assisted STEM education "can be viewed as a complex system that arises from the interactions between technologies (i.e., educational robotics), human subjects (e.g., instructors, students), information (e.g., discipline knowledge), mediums (e.g., interactive types), and external environment (e.g., intervention durations)". This holistic framing motivates the coding of eight moderator variables (discipline, educational level, instructor support, instructional strategy, interactive type, intervention duration, robotic type, control group condition) in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Analysis of robotics effects must consider technological, human, informational, medium, and environmental elements together rather than the technology alone
constraints: The framework is theoretical; the meta-analysis found only discipline significantly moderated effects empirically
target_learners: K-16 students in STEM courses
target_learning_goals: Understanding conditions under which educational robotics improves STEM learning
examples: The authors coded eight moderator variables spanning technology, human, information, medium, and environment elements across the 21 included studies

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Zimmerman's Cyclical Phases model of SRL: forethought, performance, and self-reflection
description: Zimmerman's Cyclical Phases model organizes self-regulated learning into three recurring phases. As the review states, "Zimmerman's (2000) SRL model is organized in three phases: forethought, performance and self-reflection". In forethought students analyze the task, set goals and plan; in performance they execute the task while monitoring progress and using self-control strategies; in self-reflection they assess performance and make attributions whose self-reactions influence later task approaches. The review analyzes this model as Zimmerman's contribution comparable in level to the other five SRL models.
requirements: Students must engage in task analysis, goal setting and planning before performance for the cycle to operate as described
constraints: The review analyzes the Cyclical Phases model rather than Zimmerman's Triadic or Multi-Level models, to keep comparison at the same level as the other models
target_learners: school and college students learning academic and athletic skills
target_learning_goals: strategic, self-regulated approach to learning tasks
examples: The review reports Cleary et al. (2006) trained 50 college students in basketball free throws across conditions training one, two, or three SRL phases
key_sources: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Boekaerts' Dual Processing self-regulation model: mastery/growth and well-being pathways
description: Boekaerts' Dual Processing model describes two parallel processing modes in SRL: a mastery or learning mode and a coping or well-being mode. The review explains that "the appraisals made by the students are crucial to determine which goal pathway the students will activate": threatening appraisals trigger negative cognitions and emotions and a well-being pathway, while congruent appraisals trigger positive cognitions and a mastery/growth pathway. The model names three purposes of self-regulation (expanding knowledge and skills, preventing threat to the self, protecting commitments) and gives emotions a key role, with volitional and emotion regulation strategies as bottom-up strategies.
requirements: Student appraisals of the task determine which pathway is activated, so appraisal-sensitive situations are needed to observe the model's dynamics
constraints: Students who start in the mastery/growth pathway may switch to the well-being pathway if they detect cues they might not be successful
target_learners: students in primary, secondary and vocational education
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement in learning tasks and emotion regulation during learning
examples: Boekaerts developed the On-line Motivation Questionnaire to measure task-specific feelings, thoughts and effort before and after tasks
key_sources: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Winne and Hadwin's four-phase metacognitive SRL model with the COPES architecture
description: Winne and Hadwin's model takes a strongly metacognitive, information-processing perspective on SRL. The review notes that "studying is powered by SRL across four linked phases that are open and recursive and are comprehended in a feedback loop": task definition, goal setting and planning, enacting study tactics and strategies, and metacognitively adapting studying. SRL deploys five task facets captured by the COPES acronym (Conditions, Operations, Products, Evaluations, Standards), with operations described as SMART (Searching, Monitoring, Assembling, Rehearsing and Translating). The model figure contains no reference to emotions and only an allusion to motivation.
requirements: Monitoring against standards and criteria is central, so tasks must provide standards against which products can be evaluated
constraints: The model figure does not explicitly include emotions, which the review notes as a salient feature
target_learners: students in computer-supported and self-directed learning settings
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and adaptation of study tactics and strategies
examples: Winne's team developed nStudy and gStudy, computer-supported learning environments that scaffold SRL while recording trace and log data
key_sources: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Pintrich's SRL model: four phases across cognition, motivation/affect, behavior, and context
description: Pintrich's model structures SRL as four phases, each with four areas for regulation. The review states that "SRL is compounded by four phases: (1) Forethought, planning and activation; (2) Monitoring; (3) Control; and (4) Reaction and reflection", each with regulation of cognition, motivation/affect, behavior, and context. The review highlights that Pintrich's is the only model analyzed that includes regulation of overt behavior, and that his questionnaire, the MSLQ, remains widely used in SRL research.
requirements: The model assumes students can attempt to monitor, control and regulate their own learning context as well as their cognition and motivation
constraints: The review reports there is no empirical evidence directly addressing validation of Pintrich's model itself; empirical data exist on the MSLQ questionnaire
target_learners: college and high school students
target_learning_goals: integration of motivation and strategy use in learning
examples: The MSLQ comprises 15 scales: a motivation section with 31 items and a learning strategies section with 50 items subdivided into cognitive, metacognitive, and resource management scales
key_sources: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Efklides' MASRL model: Person (macrolevel) and Task×Person (microlevel) interactions of metacognition, motivation, and affect
description: Efklides' Metacognitive and Affective Model of Self-Regulated Learning (MASRL) distinguishes two levels. The review describes that "there is the Person level-also called macrolevel-which is the most 'traditional' view of SRL and comprehends the personal characteristics of the student", operating top-down around students' goals, and a Task×Person (microlevel) that is bottom-up and data-driven, where metacognitive monitoring takes control during task execution. The model clarifies relationships among metacognition, motivation, and affect via the interaction of the two levels and offers a different top-down/bottom-up conceptualization from Boekaerts and Corno.
requirements: Empirical support requires research showing interactions among metacognition, motivation, and affect at both levels and the effects of task demands on both
constraints: The microlevel operates during task execution, the phase the review describes as having the highest cognitive load
target_learners: students performing academic tasks across domains
target_learning_goals: integration of metacognitive experiences with motivation and affect during task performance
examples: Efklides (2002) created the Metacognitive Experiences Questionnaire exploring judgments and feelings about cognitive processing
key_sources: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research
citation: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422
title: Hadwin, Järvelä, and Miller's SSRL model: three modes of regulation in collaborative learning
description: The socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) model addresses regulation in collaborative settings. The review states the model "proposed the existence of three modes of regulation in collaborative settings: self-regulation (SRL), co-regulation (CoRL), and shared regulation (SSRL)". SSRL occurs when deliberate, strategic and transactive planning, task enactment, reflection and adaptation are taken within a group, extending regulation from the 'I' or 'you' level to collective activity. SSRL unfolds in four recursively linked feedback loops adapted from Winne and Hadwin, and the forthcoming version introduces Winne's COPES architecture.
requirements: Group members must commit to group work, establish shared common ground, and negotiate and share task perceptions, strategies, and goals
constraints: The CoRL mode has been in dispute in the field due to inconsistent use, and CoRL and SSRL may both occur as groups progress through collaboration phases
target_learners: students in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) settings
target_learning_goals: shared regulation of group learning tasks
examples: Current instruments combine scaffolding and measures in context, such as computer-supported environments promoting group awareness, planning, and evaluation, plus multimodal data including eye tracking and physiological responses
key_sources: Panadero, E. (2017). A Review of Self-regulated Learning: Six Models and Four Directions for Research. Frontiers in Psychology, 8:422. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00422

article_title: Phases of inquiry-based learning: Definitions and the inquiry cycle
citation: Constantinos C. Manoli, Margus Pedaste, Mario Mäeots, Leo Siiman, Ton de Jong, Siswa A. N. van Riesen, Ellen T. Kamp, Zacharias C. Zacharia, Eleftheria Tsourlidaki. (2015). Phases of inquiry-based learning: definitions and the inquiry cycle. Educational Research Review. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-01206700
title: Synthesized inquiry cycle framework combining Orientation, Conceptualization, Investigation, Conclusion, and Discussion
description: The article develops a synthesized framework describing an inquiry cycle in which all identified phases and sub-phases are present. As the authors state, "inquiry-based learning begins with Orientation and flows through Conceptualization to Investigation, where several cycles are possible," and inquiry "usually ends with the Conclusion phase." The Discussion phase connects to all other phases because it can occur at any time during or after inquiry. No prior framework in the reviewed literature brought all of these phases and sub-phases together.
requirements: All five general phases and their sub-phases must be represented in the cycle
constraints: The Discussion phase is potentially present at every point rather than fixed in sequence
target_learners: science learners in curricula using inquiry-based learning
target_learning_goals: conducting scientific inquiry through orientation, conceptualization, investigation, conclusion, and discussion
examples: The review synthesized 32 articles describing inquiry phases or whole inquiry cycles into one framework
key_sources: Constantinos C. Manoli, Margus Pedaste, Mario Mäeots, Leo Siiman, Ton de Jong, Siswa A. N. van Riesen, Ellen T. Kamp, Zacharias C. Zacharia, Eleftheria Tsourlidaki. (2015). Phases of inquiry-based learning: definitions and the inquiry cycle. Educational Research Review. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-01206700

article_title: Beyond the Turk: Alternative platforms for crowdsourcing behavioral research
citation: Eyal Peer, Laura Brandimarte, Sonam Samat, & Alessandro Acquisti. (2016). Beyond the Turk: Alternative platforms for crowdsourcing behavioral research. https://osf.io/murdt
title: A five-measure framework for evaluating crowdsourcing research platforms over time
description: The article proposes a reusable evaluation framework for comparing online participant-recruitment platforms along multiple dimensions of data quality and population characteristics. In its own words, "This framework, which includes measures of attention, reliability, reproducibility, naivety and dishonesty, could also be used to evaluate new platforms that may arise in the future". Each measure is operationalized with a concrete task: attention-check questions, internal reliability (Cronbach's alpha), replication of known effects, self-reported familiarity with common research materials, and an incentive-compatible die-roll cheating task. The authors apply it to MTurk, CrowdFlower, Prolific Academic, and a university participant pool, and show it can track platforms over time after events such as pricing changes.
requirements: Access to run identical tasks across the platforms being compared, including an incentive-compatible bonus mechanism for the dishonesty measure
constraints: The article notes the roots and causes of the differences found between the platforms remain unclear, since participants could only be sampled and not allocated across platforms
target_learners: behavioral researchers recruiting human subjects online
target_learning_goals: selecting and evaluating online participant-recruitment platforms for experimental and survey research
examples: In Study 1, 831 participants across CF, ProA, CBDR, and MTurk completed scales, four JDM tasks, attention checks, naivety probes, and a die-roll task under a common one-week recruitment window
key_sources: Eyal Peer, Laura Brandimarte, Sonam Samat, & Alessandro Acquisti. (2016). Beyond the Turk: Alternative platforms for crowdsourcing behavioral research. https://osf.io/murdt

article_title: INCIDENTAL L2 VOCABULARY ACQUISITION FROM AND WHILE READING
citation: Pellicer-Sánchez, Ana. (2016). Incidental L2 Vocabulary Acquisition From and While Reading: An Eye-Tracking Study. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 38(1), 97-130. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263115000224
title: Design extensive reading materials so that unknown vocabulary items recur about eight times for substantial incidental learning
description: The study's findings support building repeated encounters of unknown vocabulary into extensive reading materials. L2 readers needed about "three to four encounters" before reading times on unknown items dropped significantly, and by eight encounters previously unknown words were read like known words while form and meaning recognition reached high levels. Materials should therefore embed target items at least eight times within a limited time span.
requirements: Target items must recur multiple times within a single coherent text; the study embedded six nonwords, each repeated eight times, in a 2,300-word story with about 98% coverage of known vocabulary.
constraints: Gains were measured on an immediate posttest with advanced L2 readers; the delayed-test analysis included only 14 of the initial 23 participants, which the article notes makes generalizability less robust.
target_learners: Advanced L2 readers of English
target_learning_goals: Incidental acquisition of word form and meaning from reading
examples: Participants read a 2,300-word story in which six nonwords and six control words each appeared eight times, with eye movements recorded and three vocabulary tests administered afterward.

article_title: Effects of a formative assessment script on how vocational students generate formative feedback to a peer’s or their own performance
citation: Peters, O., Körndle, H. & Narciss, S. (2018). Effects of a formative assessment script on how vocational students generate formative feedback to a peer's or their own performance. Eur J Psychol Educ, 33, 117–143. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10212-017-0344-y
title: Formative Assessment Script (FAS) for generating formative peer and internal feedback
description: The FAS is a collaboration-script instructional support designed to scaffold vocational students in generating formative feedback, in separate versions for feedback to a peer's performance and to one's own performance. The study investigated "effects of a formative assessment script (FAS) that was designed to support vocational students in generating feedback to (1) a peer's and (2) their own performance." It was applied during a technical planning task in which students first produced individual drafts and then gave feedback on a fictitious erroneous peer draft and on their own drafts.
requirements: Students work on a performance product (a draft) that can be evaluated against criteria, so that feedback comments, detected errors, and improvement suggestions can be generated.
constraints: Benefits for internal feedback are partial: no gains in detecting missing information or generating improvement suggestions for one's own draft.
target_learners: vocational students
target_learning_goals: generating formative feedback to a peer's performance
generating internal feedback to one's own performance
examples: Students produced individual drafts for a technical planning task, then gave peer feedback on a fictitious erroneous peer draft and subsequently on their own drafts, with or without FAS support.

article_title: INCIDENTAL VOCABULARY ACQUISITION THROUGH VIEWING L2 TELEVISION AND FACTORS THAT AFFECT LEARNING
citation: Elke Peters and Stuart Webb. (2018). INCIDENTAL VOCABULARY ACQUISITION THROUGH VIEWING L2 TELEVISION AND FACTORS THAT AFFECT LEARNING. Studies in Second Language Acquisition. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263117000407
title: Two-experiment viewing design measuring form recognition, meaning recall, and meaning recognition
description: The article's empirical apparatus consists of two experiments with Dutch-speaking EFL learners who viewed TV material, with vocabulary learning assessed through three measures. As printed: "Two experiments were conducted with Dutch-speaking EFL learners to measure the effects of viewing TV on form recognition and meaning recall (Experiment 1) and meaning recognition (Experiment 2)." The design pairs viewing of audio-visual input with distinct receptive vocabulary knowledge measures, allowing learning to be detected at different levels of word knowledge.
requirements: Dutch-speaking EFL learners as participants viewing TV material, with vocabulary knowledge measured through form recognition, meaning recall, and meaning recognition tests
target_learners: Dutch-speaking EFL learners
target_learning_goals: incidental L2 vocabulary learning from audio-visual input (form recognition, meaning recall, meaning recognition)
examples: Experiment 1 measured form recognition and meaning recall; Experiment 2 measured meaning recognition, both after viewing TV

article_title: A Conceptual Framework for Assessing Motivation and Self-Regulated Learning in College Students
citation: Pintrich, P.R. (2004). A Conceptual Framework for Assessing Motivation and Self-Regulated Learning in College Students. Educational Psychology Review, 16, 385–407. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-004-0006-x
title: A self-regulatory (SRL) conceptual framework for assessing student motivation and self-regulated learning in the college classroom
description: The article presents a conceptual framework for assessing student motivation and self-regulated learning in the college classroom. It is explicitly grounded in a self-regulatory perspective: "The framework is based on a self-regulatory (SRL) perspective on student motivation and learning in contrast to a student approaches to learning (SAL) perspective." The framework is intended to guide assessment of motivation and learning among college students and to inform future research in this area.
requirements: Assessment of college student motivation and learning should be designed from a self-regulatory (SRL) perspective rather than a student approaches to learning (SAL) perspective
constraints: The framework is scoped to the college classroom context
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: student motivation
self-regulated learning

title: Instruments for assessing college student motivation and learning should be developed from the SRL conceptual framework
description: The article states that the SRL conceptual framework carries implications for measurement design: it discusses "the implications of the SRL conceptual framework for developing instruments to assess college student motivation and learning." The principle is that assessment instruments for college motivation and learning should be built on the self-regulatory perspective rather than alternative framings such as SAL.
requirements: Instrument developers should adopt the SRL conceptual framework as the basis for assessing college student motivation and learning

article_title: Four Ways of Considering Emotion in Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Plass, J. L., & Kalyuga, S. (2019). Four Ways of Considering Emotion in Cognitive Load Theory. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 339–359. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09473-5
title: Four-perspective taxonomy of emotion–cognitive load relationships understood through an interval view of cognitive load
description: The article organizes the relationship between emotion and cognitive load theory into four perspectives: emotion as extraneous load, emotion's direct effects on encoding, storage, and retrieval, emotion as part of intrinsic load, and emotion's effect on motivation and mental effort. The authors state that "These four ways of considering emotion as part of CLT are best understood when taking an interval view of cognitive load." The taxonomy serves as a framework for integrating emotion into cognitive load theory rather than treating emotion as a single undifferentiated factor.
requirements: Cognitive load theory must be interpreted through an interval view of cognitive load for the four perspectives to be coherent
constraints: The framework is theoretical; the article presents it as a discussion of perspectives rather than an empirically tested model
target_learners: learners in cognitive-load-relevant instructional settings
target_learning_goals: understanding how emotion interacts with cognitive load during learning

article_title: Exploring the impact of artificial intelligence on teaching and learning in higher education
citation: Popenici, S. A. D., & Kerr, S. (2017). Exploring the impact of artificial intelligence on teaching and learning in higher education. Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning, 12:22. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41039-017-0062-8
title: Teacherbots: AI-based virtual teaching assistants for content delivery, feedback and supervision
description: Teacherbots are defined by the article as "any machine-based software or hardware that assumes the role traditionally performed by a teacher assistant in organizing information and providing fast answers to a wide set of predictable questions". They can facilitate, monitor, assess and manage student learning in online spaces, providing bespoke content, supervision and guidance. The article presents them as a disruptive alternative to traditional teaching assistants, exemplified by Jill Watson on IBM's Watson platform.
requirements: A platform such as IBM Watson capable of providing an automated teacher presence for the duration of a course
constraints: The article notes that in 2017 there is little exploration of what a teacherbot is and what its capabilities are now and in a predictable future
target_learners: Higher education students in blended or fully online courses, including massive enrolments
target_learning_goals: Content delivery, basic and administrative feedback, supervision, and personalized learning support at scale
examples: Professor Ashok Goel's knowledge-based artificial intelligence course in Georgia Tech's online Master in Computer Sciences program used the Jill Watson teaching assistant

title: Use AI in higher education to extend human capabilities rather than replace sound pedagogy
description: The article's central design recommendation is that "The real potential of technology in higher education is — when properly used — to extend human capabilities and possibilities of teaching, learning, and research". Institutions should stay alert to tendencies to treat technological progress as a replacement for good teaching, and maintain education as a human-centric endeavor in which humans identify problems, critique risks and nurture creativity.

constraints: The article warns the AI hype can become an unquestioned panacea and that control over hidden algorithms must not be monopolized by a few technology companies

target_learning_goals: Building educated minds and responsible citizens, including creativity, flexibility and capacity to act under uncertainty
examples: The paper recommends retaining contact time and personal guidance by faculty while using intelligent machines to meet the learning and support needs of massive numbers of students

article_title: Improving comprehension online: effects of deep vocabulary instruction with bilingual and monolingual fifth graders
citation: Proctor, C.P., Dalton, B., Uccelli, P., Biancarosa, G., Mo, E., Snow, C., & Neugebauer, S. (2011). Improving comprehension online: effects of deep vocabulary instruction with bilingual and monolingual fifth graders. Read Writ 24, 517–544. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9218-2
title: Internet-delivered universally designed multimedia vocabulary intervention with bilingual text access
description: An Internet-delivered intervention in which students read multimedia texts with embedded vocabulary instruction and reading strategy support, designed to be universally accessible to English-speaking and Spanish–English-speaking students. The article describes that "Intervention students read eight multimedia texts with embedded instruction on 40 words and reading strategy support" and that "Students could access all texts and activities in Spanish and English." It was evaluated against a control group over 16 weeks with 240 fifth graders.

constraints: Evaluated in a quasi-experimental design with fifth graders, about half Spanish–English bilinguals

English-speaking students

Reading comprehension

article_title: Studying Visual Displays: How to Instructionally Support Learning
citation: Renkl, A., & Scheiter, K. (2017). Studying Visual Displays: How to Instructionally Support Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9340-4
title: Taxonomy of instructional support for visual displays: material-oriented versus learner-oriented interventions
description: The review organizes empirically tested support procedures for learning from visual displays along one axis: whether the intervention changes the learning material or the learner. Material-oriented interventions modify the displays themselves, "for example, reducing the visual displays' complexity, cueing/signaling, or physically integrating text and pictures." Learner-oriented interventions instead target the person, referring to "the training of learning prerequisites, pre-training, and prompting." This two-branch taxonomy structures the review's overview of effectiveness evidence.
requirements: Applies to learning from visual displays in learning materials, where support procedures have been empirically tested
target_learners: Learners working with visual displays in learning materials
target_learning_goals: Learning from pictures and multimedia materials
Comprehension of multiple representations
examples: The review's overview of effectiveness evidence is structured by this distinction, with material-oriented examples such as cueing/signaling and learner-oriented examples such as pre-training and prompting.
key_sources: Renkl, A., & Scheiter, K. (2017). Studying Visual Displays: How to Instructionally Support Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9340-4

article_title: Studying Visual Displays: How to Instructionally Support Learning
citation: Renkl, A., & Scheiter, K. (2017). Studying Visual Displays: How to Instructionally Support Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9340-4
title: Choose support procedures for visual displays based on knowledge of the difficulties learners have with them
description: The review recommends that support for learning from visual displays be selected on a diagnostic basis: because displays "pose substantial demands on learners," knowledge of "the main difficulties that learners have when learning from visual displays" is "an important basis for selecting appropriate support procedures." The review then maps such procedures onto the material-oriented versus learner-oriented taxonomy, so that the chosen intervention addresses the diagnosed difficulty rather than being applied indiscriminately.
requirements: A prior analysis of which difficulties learners actually have with the displays in question
target_learners: Learners using visual displays in learning materials
target_learning_goals: Learning from pictures and multimedia materials
examples: The review structures its overview of empirically tested support procedures by first identifying learner difficulties and then presenting material-oriented and learner-oriented interventions matched to them.

article_title: Depressive effects of underlining and adjunct questions on children's recall of text
citation: Rickards, J.P., Denner, P.R. (1979). Depressive effects of underlining and adjunct questions on children's recall of text. Instructional Science, 8, 81–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00054983
title: Exercise caution when adding underlining and adjunct postquestions to text for young readers, since they may depress rather than support recall
description: This principle captures the article's cautionary conclusion for instructional design: the study's results suggested that "underlining and adjunct questions may hinder rather than help recall performance in young readers". It applies to designers of text materials for children who would otherwise assume these common study aids are beneficial. The evidence base is a single experiment with ten-year-olds, so the caution is scoped to young readers rather than learners generally.
requirements: Applies when designing text-based materials for young (around ten-year-old) readers who are expected to study and recall passage content.
constraints: Based on one experiment with ten-year-old children; the article frames the effect with hedging ("may hinder rather than help"), so it is a caution, not a demonstrated optimum or prohibition.
target_learners: Ten-year-old school children (elementary-age readers)
target_learning_goals: Recall of prose passage content, including superordinate conceptual material and subordinate passage details
examples: In the experiment, children given both underlining and conceptual postquestions after every paragraph showed the most depressed recall of passage details.
key_sources: Rickards, J.P., Denner, P.R. (1979). Depressive effects of underlining and adjunct questions on children's recall of text. Instructional Science, 8, 81–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00054983

article_title: Depressive effects of underlining and adjunct questions on children's recall of text
citation: Rickards, J.P., Denner, P.R. (1979). Depressive effects of underlining and adjunct questions on children's recall of text. Instructional Science, 8, 81–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00054983
title: Underlining and conceptual postquestion manipulation for children's text study (Rickards & Denner 1979 experiment)
description: An experimental instructional manipulation in which ten-year-old children (N=69) studied text under crossed conditions: "conceptual postquestions after every paragraph of text" versus none, and either children "generated their own underlining of one sentence per paragraph", received text with topic sentences underlined for them, or received text with no underlining. The design was used to test how these study aids affect children's recall of superordinate and subordinate passage content.
requirements: Requires prose passages structured with identifiable topic sentences per paragraph so that underlining conditions and conceptual postquestions can target superordinate material.
constraints: Studied with ten-year-old children reading paragraphed text; the reported outcome is recall of passage material, not transfer or later comprehension measures.
target_learners: Ten-year-old school children
target_learning_goals: Recall of conceptual (superordinate) and detail (subordinate) content from prose text
examples: Half the sample received conceptual postquestions after every paragraph; the other half received none, crossed with self-generated underlining, experimenter-underlined topic sentences, or no underlining.
key_sources: Rickards, J.P., Denner, P.R. (1979). Depressive effects of underlining and adjunct questions on children's recall of text. Instructional Science, 8, 81–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00054983

article_title: Eliciting explanations: Constraints on when self-explanation aids learning
citation: Bethany Rittle-Johnson & Abbey M. Loehr. (2017). Eliciting explanations: Constraints on when self-explanation aids learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 24, 1501–1510. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-016-1079-5
title: Four-constraint framework for when prompted self-explanation aids learning
description: The article proposes that self-explanation's effectiveness is bounded by four constraints: the target outcomes and domain, what is being explained, the design of explanation prompts, and effectiveness relative to alternative instructional techniques. As the authors state, the constraints "will facilitate a priori predictions of whether prompted self-explanation will improve learning in a particular context." The framework is grounded in the processes of knowledge integration and knowledge generalization that self-explanation is thought to support.
requirements: Learners must generate explanations that are inferences going beyond the given information, generated by and for the learner
constraints: The constraints address prompted self-explanation, defined by condition, not spontaneous self-explanation, because control-condition learners may self-explain spontaneously
target_learners: learners across a range of age groups, from preschool children to adults
target_learning_goals: comprehension
transfer
retention of new information
examples: The authors synthesized experimentally manipulated self-explanation studies identified via PsychInfo and ERIC searches and citation checking
key_sources: Bethany Rittle-Johnson & Abbey M. Loehr. (2017). Eliciting explanations: Constraints on when self-explanation aids learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 24, 1501–1510. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-016-1079-5

article_title: Eliciting explanations: Constraints on when self-explanation aids learning
citation: Bethany Rittle-Johnson & Abbey M. Loehr. (2017). Eliciting explanations: Constraints on when self-explanation aids learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 24, 1501–1510. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-016-1079-5
title: Dual-process account: self-explanation promotes learning via knowledge integration and knowledge generalization
description: The article's explanatory account holds that self-explanation aids comprehension "by promoting knowledge integration" — linking new information together or with prior knowledge — and aids comprehension and transfer "by guiding attention to structural features over surface features," increasing generalization. These two cognitive processes jointly explain why self-explanation helps transfer in principle-governed domains yet can impair detail recall and the learning of exceptions.
requirements: Learners must generate inferences that go beyond the given information, whether about expert-presented content or their own problem solving
constraints: The account presupposes domains where generalization of principles or heuristics is appropriate; generalizing can overlook exceptions and reduce attention to details
target_learners: learners across a range of prior knowledge levels, particularly those with limited prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: comprehension
generalization
transfer
examples: Learners' explanations of worked examples often linked solution steps to prior knowledge or information in the text
key_sources: Bethany Rittle-Johnson & Abbey M. Loehr. (2017). Eliciting explanations: Constraints on when self-explanation aids learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 24, 1501–1510. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-016-1079-5

article_title: Exploring the Factors Influencing Artificial Intelligence Adoption among Gen Z University Students: the Role of Self-Efficacy and Perceived Trust
citation: Mohd Shafie Rosli, Nor Shela Saleh, Azlah Md. Ali, Suaibah Abu Bakar. (2026). Exploring the Factors Influencing Artificial Intelligence Adoption among Gen Z University Students: the Role of Self-Efficacy and Perceived Trust. Journal for STEM Education Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41979-025-00171-2
title: Extended UTAUT framework for Gen Z AI adoption integrating self-efficacy and perceived trust
description: The article proposes an extended UTAUT conceptual framework in which behavioural intention to adopt AI among Gen Z university students is modelled from performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, self-efficacy and perceived trust, with behavioural intention predicting usage behaviour. The authors state the study "has provided an improved and tested theoretical framework to enhance understanding of AI adoption in the field, with an R² value of 0.751". Facilitating conditions were deliberately excluded from the framework on demographic and theoretical grounds.
requirements: Requires survey measurement of PE, EE, SI, SE, PT, BI and UB constructs with validated Likert-scale items adapted from prior UTAUT research
constraints: Facilitating conditions excluded: the article states "it is not suitable to include FC when studying specific demographics, such as Gen Z"
Findings may reflect Gen Z's intention to adopt technology beyond the academic sphere, as the authors note
target_learners: Gen Z university students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Adoption and continued use of AI technologies for academic learning
examples: The framework was tested with covariance-based SEM on 349 Malaysian university students sampled in two cohorts, using SmartPLS 4 and IBM Amos 24
key_sources: Mohd Shafie Rosli, Nor Shela Saleh, Azlah Md. Ali, Suaibah Abu Bakar. (2026). article_title: Student Diversity Representation and Reporting in Universal School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Programs: Implications for Generalizability
citation: Rowe, H. L., & Trickett, E. J. (2018). Student Diversity Representation and Reporting in Universal School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Programs: Implications for Generalizability. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9425-3
title: Five-characteristic framework of student diversity for evaluating universal SEL interventions
description: The review operationalizes student diversity for evaluating universal SEL interventions in terms of five demographic characteristics: "gender, race/ethnicity, SES, disability status, and sexual orientation/gender identity." It uses this framework to assess how and when demographic characteristics were reported, whether they were analyzed as moderators of program outcomes, and how differential effects entered generalizability discussions. The framework organizes the review's content analysis of published evaluations.
requirements: Demographic information must be reported at the same level as the level of analysis; the review excluded district-level SES when the intervention was administered at grade level
constraints: The review excluded moderation tests of three-way interactions because each moderator's unique effects could not be teased apart
target_learners: children and adolescents in universal school-based SEL programs
target_learning_goals: social and emotional learning outcomes
examples: The review coded published SEL evaluations against these five diversity characteristics to assess reporting, moderation testing, and generalizability discussion
key_sources: Rowe, H. L., & Trickett, E. J. (2018). Student Diversity Representation and Reporting in Universal School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Programs: Implications for Generalizability. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9425-3

article_title: Student Diversity Representation and Reporting in Universal School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Programs: Implications for Generalizability
citation: Rowe, H. L., & Trickett, E. J. (2018). Student Diversity Representation and Reporting in Universal School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Programs: Implications for Generalizability. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9425-3
title: Exercise caution when generalizing universal SEL program effects across diverse student groups
description: Because the reviewed evaluations reported diversity characteristics inconsistently and rarely tested moderation with adequate justification, the review "suggests caution about the generalizability of the reviewed SEL programs across diverse groups of children and adolescents." Evaluators and program adopters should not assume universal SEL effects hold uniformly across gender, race/ethnicity, SES, disability status, and sexual orientation/gender identity without subgroup-relevant evidence.
requirements: Evaluations should report demographic characteristics and test or justify moderation analyses before generalizability claims are made
constraints: The caution applies to the reviewed universal school-based SEL programs, not to targeted or indicated interventions
target_learners: children and adolescents in universal school-based SEL programs
target_learning_goals: social and emotional learning outcomes
examples: The review's analysis of published SEL evaluations found inconsistent demographic reporting and few, weakly justified moderation tests, grounding the generalizability caution
