article_title: Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems
citation: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714
title: Sadler's theory of formative assessment applies wherever multiple criteria are used to judge the quality of student responses
description: The article presents a theory of formative assessment framed around judgments of response quality rather than simple correctness. It states that the theory "is relevant to a broad spectrum of learning outcomes in a wide variety of subjects" and "applies wherever multiple criteria are used in making judgments about the quality of student responses". Its central premise is that improvement requires students to monitor the quality of their own work during production.
requirements: Learning outcomes must be of a kind where student responses are judged against multiple quality criteria rather than scored simply as correct or incorrect
constraints: The theory "has less relevance for outcomes in which student responses may be assessed simply as correct or incorrect"
target_learners: students across a wide variety of subjects
target_learning_goals: improving the quality of student responses judged against multiple criteria
key_sources: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714

article_title: Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems
citation: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714
title: Feedback is defined by its function in formative assessment, differing from the traditional educational-research definition
description: The article adopts a particular definition of feedback chosen "to highlight its function in formative assessment". It notes that "This definition differs in several significant respects from that traditionally found in educational research", positioning feedback in terms of the information learners need to close the gap between current and intended quality rather than as any information following a response.
requirements: Feedback must be understood and used in terms of its function in formative assessment rather than as any post-response information
target_learners: students receiving feedback on qualitative work
target_learning_goals: using feedback to improve the quality of their own work
key_sources: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714

article_title: Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems
citation: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714
title: Develop students' evaluative expertise by providing direct authentic evaluative experience
description: The article argues that the evaluative capacities underlying self-monitoring — appreciating high quality, comparing one's work objectively with that standard, and holding tactics for modifying work — are learnable. It states: "It is argued that these skills can be developed by providing direct authentic evaluative experience for students." Instructional design should therefore build in opportunities for students to make and refine quality judgments themselves.
requirements: Instructional systems must make explicit provision for the acquisition of evaluative expertise
target_learners: students producing work judged against quality criteria
target_learning_goals: developing evaluative skill, appreciation of quality standards, and modification tactics
key_sources: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714

article_title: Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems
citation: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714
title: Effective feedback requires three conditions that enable students to act on information about the gap between their work and the standard
description: The article identifies "Three conditions for effective feedback" and discusses their implications. Grounded in its functional definition of feedback, the principle holds that feedback is effective only when students can appreciate what high quality is, evaluate their own work against it, and act to modify it — otherwise information about the quality gap cannot be used by the learner.
requirements: Feedback must be accompanied by conditions enabling students to recognize the quality standard, evaluate their own work against it, and modify their work accordingly
constraints: Less relevant for outcomes where responses are simply correct or incorrect
target_learners: students in subjects where response quality is judged on multiple criteria
target_learning_goals: closing the gap between current and intended quality of student work
key_sources: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714

article_title: A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Schnotz, W., Kürschner, C. (2007). A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory. Educational Psychology Review 19, 469–508. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9053-4
title: Reconsidered cognitive load theory distinguishing intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load and their conceptual problems
description: The article re-examines cognitive load theory by analyzing the conceptual distinctions between different kinds of cognitive load. It argues that "the theory allows different and contradicting possibilities to explain some empirical results", so that "various generalizations of empirical results become questionable". The theory is reconsidered from the perspective of Vygotski's zone of proximal development and from research on implicit learning.
requirements: The framework requires distinguishing task performance from learning as related but fundamentally different processes
constraints: The article states the conceptual distinctions between different kinds of cognitive load are not fully equivalent, making some generalizations questionable
target_learners: learners in instructional settings generally
target_learning_goals: knowledge and skill acquisition
key_sources: Schnotz, W., Kürschner, C. (2007). A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory. Educational Psychology Review 19, 469–508. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9053-4

article_title: A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Schnotz, W., Kürschner, C. (2007). A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory. Educational Psychology Review 19, 469–508. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9053-4
title: Zone of proximal development perspective on cognitive load theory
description: The article reconsiders cognitive load theory "from the perspective of Vygotski's concept of the zone of proximal development". On this reading, learning happens within a zone in which tasks are neither too easy nor too difficult, so the relation between load and learning is not simply monotonic: load that is within the learner's zone supports learning, while minimal load may fall outside it.
requirements: Instructional tasks must be matched to the learner's zone of proximal development rather than simply minimizing load
target_learners: learners working at the edge of their current capabilities
target_learning_goals: skill and knowledge acquisition within the zone of proximal development
key_sources: Schnotz, W., Kürschner, C. (2007). A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory. Educational Psychology Review 19, 469–508. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9053-4

article_title: A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Schnotz, W., Kürschner, C. (2007). A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory. Educational Psychology Review 19, 469–508. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9053-4
title: Implicit learning perspective on cognitive load theory
description: The article also reconsiders cognitive load theory "from the perspective of research on implicit learning". Because implicit learning can proceed without deliberate, load-bearing processing, high deliberate load does not necessarily prevent learning, which further undermines the assumption that reducing load always benefits learning.
requirements: A theory of instructional load must account for implicit as well as explicit learning mechanisms
target_learners: learners acquiring skills implicitly, including complex skill domains
target_learning_goals: implicit acquisition of patterns and skills
key_sources: Schnotz, W., Kürschner, C. (2007). A Reconsideration of Cognitive Load Theory. Educational Psychology Review 19, 469–508. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9053-4

article_title: Better P-curves: Making P-curve analysis more robust to errors, fraud, and ambitious P-hacking, a Reply to Ulrich and Miller (2015).
citation: Simonsohn, U., Simmons, J. P., & Nelson, L. D. (2015). Better P-Curves: Making P-Curve Analysis More Robust To Errors, Fraud, and Ambitious P-Hacking, A Reply To Ulrich and Miller (2015). Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 144(6), 1146–1152. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000104
title: P-curve analysis: the distribution of significant p values diagnoses evidential value, null results, and p-hacking
description: P-curve analysis is a tool for assessing whether a set of statistically significant findings contains evidential value. It examines the distribution of significant p values: "True effects, those that differ from zero, lead to right-skewed p-curves (e.g., more .01s than .04s). Nonexistent effects lead to flat p-curves". Many forms of p-hacking lead to left-skewed p-curves, so a right-skewed observed p-curve rules out selective reporting of significant results as the sole explanation.
requirements: Included p values must test the hypothesis of interest, have a uniform distribution under the null, and be statistically independent of other p values
constraints: The framework assumes that among significant results, the magnitude of the p value does not affect whether it gets reported
target_learners: researchers conducting or evaluating p-curve analyses
target_learning_goals: assessing whether a set of published studies contains evidential value
examples: The authors applied p-curve to a set of JPSP experiments reported only with a covariate, observing a significantly left-skewed p-curve

article_title: Differential benefits of explicit failure-driven and success-driven scaffolding in problem-solving prior to instruction.
citation: Sinha, T., Kapur, M., West, R., Catasta, M., Hauswirth, M., & Trninic, D. (2021). Differential Benefits of Explicit Failure-Driven and Success-Driven Scaffolding in Problem-Solving Prior to Instruction. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(3), 530–555. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000483
title: Explicit failure-driven scaffolding via problematizing to facilitate problem-space exploration
description: The article describes a scaffolding design that explicitly pushes student problem-solving toward failure by nudging students to generate suboptimal solutions. The stated rationale is that such scaffolding facilitates problem-space exploration, giving students opportunities to entertain exploratory hypotheses and experience initial failures before instruction. This operationalizes failure in preparatory problem-solving as a designed, scaffolded experience rather than an incidental one.
requirements: Problem-solving must occur before instruction so that exploratory hypotheses and initial failures can prepare students to learn from follow-up instruction.
constraints: The article's rationale for explicit failure scaffolding is rooted in facilitating problem-space exploration; its measured benefits were higher constructive reasoning quality, not higher posttest conceptual understanding.
target_learners: Classroom students in the intervention (N = 221)
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of the target learning concepts
Quality of constructive reasoning during problem-solving
examples: The intervention designed scaffolds to explicitly push student problem-solving toward failure via problematizing, nudging students to generate suboptimal solutions.
key_sources: Sinha, T., Kapur, M., West, R., Catasta, M., Hauswirth, M., & Trninic, D. (2021). Differential Benefits of Explicit Failure-Driven and Success-Driven Scaffolding in Problem-Solving Prior to Instruction. article_title: Differential benefits of explicit failure-driven and success-driven scaffolding in problem-solving prior to instruction.
citation: Sinha, T., Kapur, M., West, R., Catasta, M., Hauswirth, M., & Trninic, D. (2021). Differential Benefits of Explicit Failure-Driven and Success-Driven Scaffolding in Problem-Solving Prior to Instruction. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(3), 530–555. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000483
title: Explicit success-driven scaffolding via structuring with low-specificity heuristics
description: The article describes a contrasting scaffolding design that explicitly pushes student problem-solving toward success by nudging students to generate optimal solutions through heuristics with low specificity. Structuring supports successful initial problem-solving attempts before instruction, providing a comparison point for the failure-driven approach. The low specificity of the heuristics is the design feature that keeps the support from fully solving the problem for students.
requirements: Heuristics provided must have low specificity so that students still generate the optimal solutions themselves rather than being given them outright.
constraints: Success-driven scaffolding matched failure-driven scaffolding on posttest conceptual understanding but did not produce the higher constructive reasoning quality seen under failure-driven scaffolding.
target_learners: Classroom students in the intervention (N = 221)
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of the target learning concepts
Generating optimal solutions during preparatory problem-solving
examples: The intervention designed scaffolds to explicitly push student problem-solving toward success via structuring, giving students heuristics with low specificity.

article_title: Differential benefits of explicit failure-driven and success-driven scaffolding in problem-solving prior to instruction.
citation: Sinha, T., Kapur, M., West, R., Catasta, M., Hauswirth, M., & Trninic, D. (2021). Differential Benefits of Explicit Failure-Driven and Success-Driven Scaffolding in Problem-Solving Prior to Instruction. Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(3), 530–555. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000483
title: Design preparatory problem-solving scaffolds that explicitly engineer either success or failure before instruction
description: The article recommends designing scaffolds that explicitly push student problem-solving toward success via structuring or toward failure via problematizing, rather than leaving preparatory problem-solving unscaffolded. Both routes prepared students to learn from follow-up instruction with similar posttest conceptual understanding, while failure-driven scaffolding additionally raised constructive reasoning quality. Choice of scaffold can therefore be tuned to the targeted outcome.
requirements: Problem-solving must precede instruction, and scaffolds must explicitly push students toward either suboptimal (failure) or optimal (success) solutions.
constraints: The pedagogical value of success versus failure in initial problem-solving was still unclear in prior work; the differential benefits were more salient for the more difficult learning concept.
target_learners: Classroom students learning concepts through problem-solving prior to instruction
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding from follow-up instruction
Constructive reasoning quality
examples: In the classroom intervention (N = 221), scaffolds were designed to explicitly push problem-solving toward success via structuring and toward failure via problematizing, followed by instruction and posttests.

article_title: Enhancing academic writing skills and motivation: assessing the efficacy of ChatGPT in AI-assisted language learning for EFL students
citation: Song, C., and Song, Y. (2023). Enhancing academic writing skills and motivation: assessing the efficacy of ChatGPT in AI-assisted language learning for EFL students. Frontiers in Psychology. https://www.frontiersin.org
title: ChatGPT as an AI chatbot writing-assistance tool in EFL academic writing instruction
description: ChatGPT is the AI tool integrated into the experimental writing condition. The article presents it as an AI-powered chatbot that supports learners' academic writing by providing on-demand assistance on written texts, and positions it as a resource for addressing the time and practice constraints EFL learners face in developing academic writing skills and sustaining writing motivation.
requirements: Learners need access to the ChatGPT platform during writing tasks
Instructors must guide students in how to request and evaluate the assistance the tool provides
constraints: The article notes that over-reliance on AI-generated feedback may hinder learners' development of independent writing skills, so the tool's role requires careful framing
target_learners: EFL university students developing academic writing
target_learning_goals: Academic writing quality
Writing motivation
examples: The experimental group's writing instruction incorporated ChatGPT access across the intervention period, and its post-test writing motivation exceeded the control group's

article_title: Enhancing academic writing skills and motivation: assessing the efficacy of ChatGPT in AI-assisted language learning for EFL students
citation: Song, C., and Song, Y. (2023). Enhancing academic writing skills and motivation: assessing the efficacy of ChatGPT in AI-assisted language learning for EFL students. Frontiers in Psychology. https://www.frontiersin.org
title: Integrate AI chatbots into writing courses to supplement instruction while safeguarding learners' independent writing development
description: This principle holds that automated AI feedback should complement, not replace, instruction in L2 writing courses. The article's evidence that ChatGPT-integrated instruction produced significantly higher writing motivation than conventional instruction supports integration, while its caution that over-reliance on AI-generated feedback may hinder independent writing skills requires instructors to frame the tool's role and teach critical evaluation of its output.

constraints: Over-reliance on AI-generated feedback may hinder the development of learners' independent writing skills, per the article's stated concern

Learner engagement

article_title: Cognitive ease at a cost: LLMs reduce mental effort but compromise depth in student scientific inquiry
citation: Matthias Stadler, Maria Bannert, Michael Sailer. (2024). Cognitive ease at a cost: LLMs reduce mental effort but compromise depth in student scientific inquiry. Computers in Human Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2024.108386
title: Cognitive load–self-regulation tradeoff account of information-search tool effects on learning quality
description: The article frames its findings with cognitive load theory (Sweller) and self-regulated learning (Zimmerman), synthesised via Seufert et al.'s tradeoff between cognitive load and cognitive resources: "learnersengageinself-regulatedlearningtothefullestextentwhenconfrontedwithtasks ofmediumdifficulty". Tasks that are too simple (like LLM research, in the authors' interpretation) evoke little strategic processing, while moderately demanding search fosters germane load and deeper processing. The study uses this account to explain why reduced load with LLMs co-occurred with lower-quality justifications.
requirements: The account presupposes that the task is within learners' capability range — the article notes it is unlikely an information search task is too difficult for educated adults, but it may be experienced as too simple to require much self-regulation.
constraints: The mediation test of this account was explicitly exploratory and dependent on the H2 result.
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: quality of argumentation and justification in socio-scientific reasoning

title: Five-component framework of quality formative feedback on writing
description: The study operationalizes quality formative feedback on writing using five deductively coded components: the degree to which feedback "was criteria-based, provided clear directions for improvement, was accurate, prioritized essential features, and used a supportive tone." Each component is scored 1-5 with anchored rubric descriptors (e.g., criteria-based ranges from all feedback generic to consistently explicit genre criteria; supportive tone ranges from directive, unaffirming language to suggestive, affirming language). The framework, derived from a literature review and expert consultation, grounds the Writer(s)-Within-Community model's reconceptualization process, where quality feedback helps students compare their writing to genre ideals and identify specific improvement steps.

constraints: Timeliness was deliberately excluded as an evaluation criterion in this study

target_learning_goals: improving source-based argumentative writing through formative feedback and revision
examples: Raters double-coded 15% of the sample (n = 60), achieving exact agreement of 68-87% and Cohen's Kappa of .71 to .84 across the five components

title: ChatGPT v.3.5 prompting protocol for generating formative writing feedback
description: A four-part prompting protocol the researchers developed through multiple cycles of prompting and feedback analysis to elicit formative feedback from ChatGPT (v.3.5) on student essays. The protocol instructs ChatGPT to "roleplay as a secondary school teacher," use "a friendly and encouraging tone," provide 2-3 pieces of specific and actionable feedback matching human-scorer instructions, and includes both the essay prompt and the source texts students used. A low temperature setting of .1 was used to reduce randomness. Unlike prior automated writing evaluation systems, ChatGPT required no training on a human-scored corpus.

description: A web-based homework platform developed by the authors through which students submitted homework responses and peer assessments. In treatment weeks, students "provided scores and comments on the homework responses of three peers" and received feedback from three peers; all responses and reviews were anonymized before distribution. Control students submitted online and were graded by instructors, with feedback delivered simultaneously to both groups and the same solution key provided.

title: Matched randomized crossover design for within-student comparison of an instructional treatment
description: A course-level experimental pattern in which each student serves as their own control across units of a course. Students are assigned to treatment and control in different orders over the units (e.g., TCTC, CTCT, TCCT, CTTC), which, as the authors note, "eliminates what is arguably the largest source of variability in educational studies: variation between students." Matching students on covariates before assigning complementary treatments further guards against baseline differences.
requirements: A course with multiple parallel units so each student can experience both treatment and control; covariate information (e.g., class year, previous statistics experience) for matched-pairs randomization; blinded grading of assessments.
constraints: Excluding non-compliers estimates the effect on the subpopulation of students who would be affected by the intervention, as the authors state.

target_learning_goals: estimating the causal effect of an instructional treatment on achievement

title: Cognitive load theory's model of human cognitive architecture: limited working memory with modality-based subcomponents and an effectively unlimited long-term memory holding schemas
description: The article presents cognitive load theory as resting on a specific cognitive architecture. It assumes "a limited capacity working memory that includes partially independent subcomponents to deal with auditory/verbal material and visual/2- or 3-dimensional information" alongside "an effectively unlimited long-term memory, holding schemas that vary in their degree of automation." These structures are the basis from which the theory derives its instructional guidelines.
requirements: Instructional guidelines derived from the theory depend on the assumed architecture of limited working memory and schema-based long-term memory.

description: The article states that cognitive load theory's cognitive architecture has been used to design novel instructional procedures "based on the assumption that working memory load should be reduced and schema construction encouraged." The principle directs designers to present information in ways that lower unnecessary working memory demands while supporting the building and automation of schemas in long-term memory.

citation: Sweller, J. (2010). Element Interactivity and Intrinsic, Extraneous, and Germane Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 123–138. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9128-5
title: Element interactivity as the single underlying mechanism of all three cognitive load types
description: The article proposes a unified theoretical account in which element interactivity serves as the basic defining mechanism not only of intrinsic cognitive load, as in prior cognitive load theory, but of extraneous and germane load as well. The article states that "element interactivity has been used as the basic, defining mechanism of intrinsic cognitive load for many years" and extends this to the other load types, linking all three to a single construct.
requirements: Cognitive load types must be interpretable in terms of the number of interacting elements that must be processed in working memory
constraints: The account is a theoretical proposal analyzed conceptually rather than tested with new empirical data in the available text

title: Judge instructional procedures by whether the element interactivity they impose is essential to the task
description: Because the article grounds both intrinsic and extraneous load in element interactivity, instructional design should ask whether the interactivity a task imposes is "essential to the task at hand" or merely "a function of instructional procedures". Interactivity essential to the task reflects intrinsic load, while interactivity introduced by the way material is presented reflects extraneous load and is a target for design reduction.

citation: Tai, J., Ajjawi, R., Boud, D., Dawson, P., & Panadero, E. (2018). Developing evaluative judgement: enabling students to make decisions about the quality of work. Higher Education, 76, 467–481. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-017-0220-3
title: Evaluative judgement: the capability to make decisions about the quality of work of self and others
description: The paper defines evaluative judgement as "the capability to make decisions about the quality of work of self and others", simplifying an earlier definition by Tai et al. (2016). It has two complementary components: understanding what constitutes quality, and applying that understanding through appraisal of one's own or others' work. The paper positions it as an integrating concept underpinning self-assessment, peer assessment, exemplars and feedback, aimed at preparing students for future learning and practice beyond graduation.
requirements: Development of evaluative judgement must be deliberate and deliberated upon, through repeated engagement with standards and appraisal of work
constraints: Evaluative judgement is contextual and domain specific: what constitutes quality depends on the setting and disciplinary area, though the capability of identifying criteria may cross domains

title: Quality-script development: evaluative judgement grows through staged expertise from analytical to pattern-based judgement
description: The paper hypothesises, drawing on the staged theory of expertise of decision-making (Schmidt and Rikers 2007), that students develop "quality scripts" analogous to illness scripts in medical training. Through repeated exposure to work, consideration of standards, and justification of decisions, knowledge about quality becomes linked and chunked into patterns, so judgement becomes less analytical and more intuitive, with analytical reasoning retained as a safety mechanism for non-fitting problems.

constraints: The account is a hypothesis the authors propose by analogy to medical decision-making expertise, not an empirically tested result

description: Across the five practices, the paper identifies shared design features: "active and iterative engagement with criteria, the enactment of judgements on diverse samples of work, dialogic feedback with peers and tutors oriented towards understanding quality", and articulation and justification of judgements with a focus on both immediate and future tasks. Evaluative judgement refocuses these activities as pedagogies producing students who can judge effectively within and beyond the course.

article_title: Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI?
citation: Touretzky, D.; Gardner-McCune, C.; Martin, F.; and Seehorn, D. (2019). Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI? The Thirty-Third AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-19). https://www.aaai.org
title: Five thematic strands ('big ideas') organizing K-12 AI guidelines
description: The AI for K-12 working group frames its guidelines around five big ideas in AI: computers perceive the world using sensors; agents maintain models/representations of the world and use them for reasoning; computers can learn from data; making agents interact comfortably with humans is a substantial challenge; and AI applications can impact society in both positive and negative ways. The authors state the guidelines "will unpack AI's 'Big Ideas' along five thematic strands, and organize them by four grade bands". They chose this formulation over a traditional division into application areas because it "better meets the needs of K-12 students and teachers".
requirements: Guidelines are developed via a collaboration between AI experts and K-12 teachers
constraints: The authors note others might frame the field differently and welcome community feedback
target_learners: K-12 students in grade bands K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-12
target_learning_goals: Understanding core AI concepts: perception, representation and reasoning, machine learning, human-AI interaction, and societal/ethical impacts of AI
examples: The current draft lists each big idea with grade-band expectations, e.g., K-2 students interact with voice-based agents while grades 9-12 students train perceptual classifiers
key_sources: Touretzky, D.; Gardner-McCune, C.; Martin, F.; and Seehorn, D. (2019). Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI? The Thirty-Third AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-19). https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v33i01.33019795

article_title: Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI?
citation: Touretzky, D.; Gardner-McCune, C.; Martin, F.; and Seehorn, D. (2019). Envisioning AI for K-12: What Should Every Child Know about AI? The Thirty-Third AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI-19). https://www.aaai.org
title: Grade-band progression of AI competencies from K-2 through 9-12
description: For each big idea, the draft guidelines specify what students should know and be able to do in four grade bands: K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-12. The progression moves from experiencing and examining AI (e.g., interacting with voice agents, examining "the world map created by Calypso for Cozmo") toward modifying applications, then creating complex applications, and finally demonstrating limitations and training systems, e.g., grades 9-12 students "should be able identify and demonstrate the limitations of machine perception systems and use machine learning tools".
requirements: Age-appropriate AI tools and programming frameworks with AI primitives at each band
target_learners: K-2, 3-5, 6-8, and 9-12 students
target_learning_goals: Progressively deeper understanding of machine perception, representation, machine learning, natural language interaction, and AI ethics
examples: Grades 6-8 students measure how well a trained system generalizes to novel inputs and understand how training-data biases affect performance

The initiative "will not be developing a curriculum of its own"; instead it "will establish guidelines that future curricula should meet, and curate an online resources directory" to help educators locate tools and curricula.

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Complex Learning: Recent Developments and Future Directions
citation: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Sweller, J. (2005). Cognitive Load Theory and Complex Learning: Recent Developments and Future Directions. Educ Psychol Rev 17, 147–177 (2005). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-005-3951-0
title: Cognitive Load Theory grounded in an analogy between human cognitive architecture and biological evolution
description: The article frames Cognitive Load Theory by connecting the cognitive processes assumed by CLT to the processes used by biological evolution, strengthening the theory's cognitive base. As the abstract states, the article "strengthens the cognitive base of CLT by linking cognitive processes to the processes used by biological evolution." This evolutionary analogy serves as the theoretical foundation for the instructional-design developments the review then discusses.
requirements: The framework presupposes the CLT account of cognitive architecture relating working memory limits to long-term memory schemas
target_learners: Learners acquiring complex cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: Complex learning and schema construction

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Complex Learning: Recent Developments and Future Directions
citation: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Sweller, J. (2005). Cognitive Load Theory and Complex Learning: Recent Developments and Future Directions. Educ Psychol Rev 17, 147–177 (2005). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-005-3951-0
title: Use real-life tasks as the driving force for complex learning
description: The article endorses the current instructional-design view that whole, real-life tasks should organize complex learning rather than decontextualized part practice. It states that recent CLT developments relate to "the current view in instructional design that real-life tasks should be the driving force for complex learning." Because such tasks impose high intrinsic load, this principle must be paired with load-management methods such as scaffolding and fading.
requirements: New methods to manage the high intrinsic cognitive load of real-life tasks
constraints: Intrinsic cognitive load of real-life tasks is often high, so the principle cannot be applied without load management
target_learners: Learners acquiring complex cognitive skills
target_learning_goals: Transferable performance of complex, real-life tasks

description: An extensive reading program in which 60 EFL learners read 10 Level 1 and 10 Level 2 graded readers over 37 weeks during two terms. Two sets of 100 target words were chosen from each set of graded readers and tested on three occasions (pretest, immediate posttest, delayed posttest). Learners were divided into high-, intermediate-, and low-level groups based on "their scores on pretests of target vocabulary and Vocabulary Levels Test scores," allowing gains to be compared across prior-knowledge levels.

description: The article's results indicate that "prior vocabulary knowledge may have a large impact on the amount of vocabulary learning made through extensive reading": learners with higher prior knowledge gained more (63.18%) than lower-knowledge learners (28.12%). This supports matching graded reader difficulty and vocabulary demands to learners' existing vocabulary size so that extensive reading yields vocabulary growth for all proficiency levels.

citation: Wei, X., Wang, L., Lee, L.-K., & Liu, R. (2025). title: Four-dimension team creative performance framework for DST evaluation (novelty, relevance, user experience, sustainability)
description: The study adopted Liu et al.'s (2023) TCP assessment framework comprising four dimensions: "novelty, relevance, user experience, and sustainability." Novelty assesses originality and innovation; relevance focuses on practical applicability; user experience evaluates engagement through authenticity, cultural immersion, and audience connection; sustainability considers long-term viability across environmental, cultural, and economic factors. The framework was operationalized with two to three criteria per dimension on a ten-point scale, weighted 30% each for sustainability and user experience and 20% each for novelty and relevance.
requirements: Evaluation requires multiple expert raters with high inter-rater consistency (ICC > 0.8)
constraints: Designed specifically for evaluating TCP in complex, collaborative DST contexts
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: team creativity performance in collaborative digital story creation
examples: Three experts (two in educational technology, one in DST research) rated six DST products per group using this framework, achieving ICC = 0.89

title: GAI-assisted DST creation pattern integrating problem-based learning across four DST stages and six projects

article_title: Picture this! Effects of photographs, diagrams, animations, and sketching on learning and beliefs about learning from a geoscience text
citation: Wiley, J. (2019). Picture this! Effects of photographs, diagrams, animations, and sketching on learning and beliefs about learning from a geoscience text. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 33, 9-19. https://doi.org/10.1002/acp.3495
title: Deception account of seduction effects on comprehension monitoring
description: The deception account holds that the presence of even instructionally-relevant images can deceive readers about their own level of understanding, producing illusions of comprehension. The article states that "the presence of even instructionally-relevant images can impact readers' ability to monitor their understanding", so poor learning may follow from investing too little effort in building a mental model. It extends traditional seduction-effect research beyond irrelevant decorative images to relevant animations and diagrams.
requirements: Readers must make predictive judgments of understanding that can be compared against actual learning outcomes to detect illusions
constraints: The article notes not every image type undermined monitoring; the presence of any type of image was not sufficient to harm monitoring accuracy compared to no-image conditions
target_learners: undergraduate students reading expository science texts
target_learning_goals: accurate comprehension monitoring and causal understanding of scientific processes from expository text
examples: Readers exposed to animated diagrams experienced illusions of understanding, while readers instructed to sketch a model of the earth's climate system did not

article_title: Learning against the machine: the double edged sword of (Gen)AI in STEM education
citation: Peter Wulff and Marcus Kubsch. (2025). Learning against the machine: the double edged sword of (Gen)AI in STEM education. International Journal of STEM Education 12:66. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00588-6
title: Active knowledge integration account of STEM learning: conceptual learning as effortful, embodied integration against ingrained preconceptions
description: The article frames STEM learning as an active process of integrating abstract knowledge against intuitive preconceptions, requiring struggle, metacognitive processing, embodiment, and social support. It states that "Conceptual learning requires active knowledge integration, oftentimes against our ingrained intuitive understandings and preconceptions of how the world works." It further stresses that "Active learning should entail experiences of struggle and encountering difficulties that are essential for in-depth reasoning and metacognitive processing." The account draws on social learning theories and on Fiorella's three sense-making modes of explaining, visualizing, and enacting, and is used as the benchmark against which GenAI tools are judged.
requirements: Educational institutions must cultivate conceptual learning and critical thinking from early childhood to graduation, especially via STEM disciplines
constraints: Conceptual learning and critical thinking are described as not coming naturally to humans, whose evolutionary endowment makes them intuitive and unreflected thinkers
target_learners: STEM learners from early childhood to graduation
target_learning_goals: Conceptual learning
Critical thinking
Problem-solving skills
examples: The article cites Fiorella (2023) on explaining, visualizing, and enacting as sense-making modes essential for active learning, and empirical work by Deslauriers et al. (2011) and Freeman et al. (2014) showing active-learning affordances can enhance outcomes.

article_title: Learning against the machine: the double edged sword of (Gen)AI in STEM education
citation: Peter Wulff and Marcus Kubsch. (2025). Learning against the machine: the double edged sword of (Gen)AI in STEM education. International Journal of STEM Education 12:66. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00588-6
title: Systemic three-level perspective on GenAI in STEM education: macro, meso, and micro levels with bidirectional feedback
description: The article organizes GenAI's permeation of STEM education across three systemic levels: "macro (education system), meso (institutions, classrooms, and teachers), and micro (individual learners)". Figure 1 depicts bidirectional feedback among these levels and co-evolving GenAI systems whose data and design influence, and are influenced by, educational practice. The perspective is used to trace how barriers such as metacognitive laziness, de-skilling, automation bias, and misplaced trust propagate across levels, e.g., auto-escalating hints nudging teachers to reshape tasks and reduce opportunities to explain, visualize, and enact.
requirements: Research methodologies capable of examining system-level effects, such as population-based and epidemiological approaches, are needed to study these dynamics
constraints: The article notes these dynamics are nuanced and difficult to observe, and that constraining GenAI use in one context may be counterbalanced by use at home or via other platforms
target_learners: Individual STEM learners
Teachers
Educational institutions and policy actors
target_learning_goals: Active and reflective engagement with STEM subject matter
examples: The article describes a possible vicious cycle in which GenAI-generated data fed back into training data poisons the well, citing Qiu et al. (2025) and Shumailov et al. (2024).
key_sources: Peter Wulff and Marcus Kubsch. (2025). Learning against the machine: the double edged sword of (Gen)AI in STEM education. International Journal of STEM Education 12:66. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00588-6

article_title: Learning against the machine: the double edged sword of (Gen)AI in STEM education
citation: Peter Wulff and Marcus Kubsch. (2025). Learning against the machine: the double edged sword of (Gen)AI in STEM education. International Journal of STEM Education 12:66. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00588-6
title: Treat GenAI adoption in STEM education with a default assumption that it might hamper active learning, placing the burden of proof on adopters
description: The article recommends that responsible actors adopt GenAI only with substantive pedagogical, ethical, and economic rationales, stating "The default assumption should be that GenAI might hamper active learning in STEM disciplines". It argues the onus lies on institutions and providers to prove their systems worthy of adoption for learning, "just as new drugs have to be rigorously approved in the medical sector", and that performing well on exams does not count as evidence of usefulness for STEM learning.
requirements: A robust, empirically grounded argument for why to use GenAI instead of other tools or reforms, supported by replicable discipline-based research
constraints: The article acknowledges adoption is arguably not a question of if but of when, and that no conclusive evidence on when, how, and why has yet been gathered
target_learners: STEM learners at all educational levels
target_learning_goals: Active, critical, and in-depth engagement with STEM subject matter
examples: The authors report that ChatGPT's study mode did not convince them in multiple trials given lack of pedagogically grounded guidance and repeated factual errors, and that they would not recommend a GenAI-generated textbook's basketball example for Newton's third law.
key_sources: Peter Wulff and Marcus Kubsch. (2025). Learning against the machine: the double edged sword of (Gen)AI in STEM education. International Journal of STEM Education 12:66. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00588-6

citation: National Science and Technology Council, Committee on Technology. (2016). Preparing for the Future of Artificial Intelligence. Executive Office of the President. https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp
title: Provide ethical training to every student learning AI, computer science, or data science, augmented with technical tools and methods for preventing unacceptable outcomes
description: The report recommends that ethical training for AI practitioners and students is a necessary part of the solution to AI's fairness and safety challenges. It states that "Ideally, every student learning AI, computer science, or data science would be exposed to curriculum and discussion on related ethics and security topics." It adds that ethics alone is not sufficient and "ethical training should be augmented with technical tools and methods for putting good intentions into practice."
requirements: Curriculum and discussion on ethics and security topics must be available to students learning AI, computer science, or data science, per the report's recommendation
constraints: The report states ethics alone is not sufficient: ethical training should be augmented with technical tools and methods
target_learners: students learning AI, computer science, or data science
target_learning_goals: understanding ethical and security responsibilities of AI practitioners
putting good intentions into practice through technical work
examples: The report's Fairness, Safety, and Governance section recommends exposing every AI, computer science, or data science student to ethics and security curriculum and discussion

article_title: A Systematic Review Mapping of AI Literacy Progression in K–12
citation: National Science and Technology Council, Committee on Technology. (2016). Preparing for the Future of Artificial Intelligence. Executive Office of the President. https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp
title: Human-machine teaming and intelligence augmentation: machines complementing rather than substituting for human work
description: The report distinguishes teaming from automation: "in some cases a machine will complement human work," and "Systems that aim to complement human cognitive capabilities are sometimes referred to as intelligence augmentation." It holds that "a human-machine team can be more effective than either one alone, using the strengths of one to compensate for the weaknesses of the other," illustrated by chess and radiology examples. This framework contrasts with automation, where a machine substitutes for human work.
requirements: Systems must be designed with the goal of complementing human cognitive capabilities rather than replacing them
constraints: The report notes top computers are much stronger players than any human in chess, yet a weaker computer with a human teammate can often beat a stronger computer player
target_learners: human workers collaborating with AI systems
students learning about AI
target_learning_goals: understanding when machines should complement rather than substitute for human work
examples: Chess: a weaker computer with a human teammate can often beat a stronger computer player
Radiology: combined AI and human input lowered lymph-node cancer detection error to 0.5 percent
key_sources: National Science and Technology Council, Committee on Technology. (2016). Preparing for the Future of Artificial Intelligence. Executive Office of the President. https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp

article_title: A Systematic Review Mapping of AI Literacy Progression in K–12
citation: National Science and Technology Council, Committee on Technology. (2016). Preparing for the Future of Artificial Intelligence. Executive Office of the President. https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp
title: Taxonomies of artificial intelligence: thinking/acting like humans versus rationally, and five methodological tribes
description: The report notes there is no single universally accepted definition of AI and surveys expert taxonomies. A popular AI textbook's taxonomy distinguishes "systems that think like humans," "systems that act like humans," systems that think rationally, and systems that act rationally. It also reports Pedro Domingos's five tribes of AI researchers — symbolists, connectionists, evolutionaries, Bayesians, and analogizers — and Frank Chen's five problem categories, illustrating the field's diversity of problems and solutions.
requirements: Users of the taxonomy should recognize that AI boundaries are uncertain and have tended to shift over time, as the report states
constraints: The report states the diversity of AI problems and solutions makes it difficult to define a bright-line distinction between what constitutes AI and what does not
target_learners: students learning AI
policymakers seeking to understand AI
target_learning_goals: understanding the scope and variety of AI problems, methods, and definitions
examples: The report quotes the Russell and Norvig four-category taxonomy and Domingos's five tribes as differing expert taxonomies
key_sources: National Science and Technology Council, Committee on Technology. (2016). Preparing for the Future of Artificial Intelligence. Executive Office of the President. https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp

article_title: A Systematic Review Mapping of AI Literacy Progression in K–12
citation: National Science and Technology Council, Committee on Technology. (2016). Preparing for the Future of Artificial Intelligence. Executive Office of the President. https://www.whitehouse.gov/ostp
title: Machine learning as statistical learning from data, contrasted with expert systems
description: The report defines modern machine learning as "a statistical process that starts with a body of data and tries to derive a rule or procedure that explains the data or can predict future data." This learning-from-data approach contrasts with the older expert-system approach, in which programmers translate human experts' rules into code. The report describes training (adjusting model parameters to maximize an objective function), test-set evaluation, and generalization to unseen cases as the core workflow.
requirements: Applying machine learning requires a historical data set divided into training and test sets, a chosen model with adjustable parameters, and a defined objective function
constraints: The report states it is typically not possible to extract a straightforward explanation for why a trained model is effective, and even the best models can fail in unpredictable ways, such as on adversarial images
target_learners: students learning AI or data science
practitioners applying machine learning
target_learning_goals: understanding how machine learning differs from rule-based expert systems
understanding training, evaluation, and generalization
examples: The report's fraud-detection example: a company uses a labeled data set of past login attempts to derive a rule predicting which future attempts are likely fraudulent

title: Biology learning chatbot system providing instant out-of-class interaction and learning support
description: The article develops an educational chatbot system for biology learning that lets students "interact with a chatbot out of class anytime and anywhere and further obtain instant learning supports." It was designed to support students learning and reviewing biology knowledge outside class, and was evaluated in a grade 7 quasi-experiment against traditional biology learning.

article_title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
citation: Zawacki-Richter, O., Bond, M., & Gouverneur, F. (2019). Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators? International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-019-0171-0
title: Four areas of AIEd applications in higher education
description: This systematic review of 146 articles on AI in higher education organizes the literature into four application areas derived through iterative coding: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. The framework maps AI-based services onto the student life-cycle, spanning institutional and administrative services as well as academic support for teaching and learning. It provides a shared vocabulary for educators navigating a fragmented field where terminology varies widely across studies.
requirements: Articles must report on AI applications within higher education contexts
constraints: The taxonomy emerged from literature published between 2007 and 2018 and may not capture newer AIEd developments
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: understanding the landscape of AI applications in higher education

article_title: The effects of over-reliance on AI dialogue systems on students' cognitive abilities: a systematic review
citation: Chunpeng Zhai, Santoso Wibowo and Lily D. Li. (2024). The effects of over-reliance on AI dialogue systems on students' cognitive abilities: a systematic review. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-024-00316-7
title: Cognitive-shortcut (heuristic) account of AI over-reliance
description: The review's explanatory account of why over-reliance arising from ethical issues of AI affects cognitive abilities: users favor efficient cognitive shortcuts, or heuristics, even when AI presents ethical problems. The review states that "individuals increasingly favor fast and optimal solutions over slow ones constrained by practicality", and links this to cognitive biases in which judgments deviate from rationality, producing uncritical acceptance of AI-generated information. It serves as the review's central perspective for organizing how ethical issues translate into dependency and diminished judgment.
requirements: Users must face AI-generated recommendations whose reliability they struggle to assess for the shortcut tendency to operate as described
constraints: The review draws its data from higher education contexts and does not consider cognitive developmental differences across age groups such as teenagers and primary or secondary school students
target_learners: students in higher education and academic research contexts
target_learning_goals: decision-making
critical thinking
analytical thinking

citation: Saif Alneyadi and Yousef Wardat. (2024). Integrating ChatGPT in Grade 12 Quantum Theory Education: An Exploratory Study at Emirate School (UAE). International Journal of Information and Education Technology, Vol. 14, No. 3. https://doi.org/10.18178/ijiet.2024.14.3.2061
title: Quantum Theory Test: a 30-item achievement test organized into Knowing, Applying, and Reasoning sections built on Bloom's taxonomy
description: The study's achievement instrument is "a single form of the test" of 30 questions organized into three sections of ten questions each (Knowing, Applying, Reasoning), crafted using Bloom's taxonomy levels from remembering to creating. Validity was checked by a panel of UAE expert arbitrators, and a pilot found discrimination coefficients of 0.35–0.72 and difficulty coefficients of 0.50–0.77. It measured pre- and post-test achievement in both study groups.

article_title: Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education
citation: Agran, M., Blanchard, C., Wehmeyer, M., & Hughes, C. (2002). Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education. Remedial and Special Education, 23(5), 279-288. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Self-Determined Learning Model of Instruction
description: The self-determined learning model of instruction is "designed to enable teachers to teach students a self -regulated problem -solving process in which students set their own goals and select and use one or more student -directed learning strate gies (e.g., self -monitoring, self -instruction) to achieve them." It comprises three instructional phases — set a goal, take action, and adjust goal or plan — each presenting a problem the student solves through a means-ends sequence connecting the student's actual state to a goal state. In this study, students used the model to select target behaviors and self-evaluate progress in general education classes.
requirements: Students must be able to identify a desired goal and the actions or learning needed to achieve it, with teacher facilitation; one student in the study required a higher level of teacher assistance
target_learners: middle school students with intellectual or developmental disabilities in general education classes
target_learning_goals: self-regulated problem solving
goal setting and attainment
self-determination skills
examples: Each student completed two worksheets leading through the first two phases, responding to questions such as "What do you have to do or change to reach your goal?"
key_sources: Agran, M., Blanchard, C., Wehmeyer, M., & Hughes, C. (2002). Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education. Remedial and Special Education, 23(5), 279-288. https://doi.org/10.1177/07419325020230050301

article_title: Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education
citation: Agran, M., Blanchard, C., Wehmeyer, M., & Hughes, C. (2002). Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education. Remedial and Special Education, 23(5), 279-288. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Embed problem-solving instruction into existing general education instructional programming
description: The study used an approach in which "problem solving was embedded or integrated into the existing instructional programming con ducted at that time," so the strategy fit the natural context of the classroom rather than requiring a separate intervention setting. This allowed instruction for students with developmental disabilities to occur entirely in general education content classes (science, life skills, and English) with class sizes of 22 to 35 students. All instruction was provided within those existing classes rather than in pull-out settings.
requirements: General education teachers must create and arrange opportunities within existing class activities for students to perform target behaviors and practice the strategy
constraints: The findings are specific to the target behaviors investigated; the authors state future research on other behaviors is needed
target_learners: students with developmental disabilities participating in general education
target_learning_goals: applying problem solving to classroom behaviors within the general curriculum
examples: Teachers created from three to five opportunities each day for the students to perform their target behaviors within their regular classes, with no peer support

title: Problem-solving cue cards
description: Cue cards were a support element of the training: "Cue cards were developed to teach students the steps and their sequence in the process, and students were instructed to refer to the cards if they forgot the steps in the strategy." They served as a memory scaffold so students did not need to ask the questions aloud in the general education classroom; students used the steps and, when necessary, a cue card to work through each daily challenge.
requirements: Students first rehearse the problem-solving questions out loud until they can recall the steps and their sequence
target_learners: students with intellectual or developmental disabilities
target_learning_goals: recalling and sequencing problem-solving steps independently in class

article_title: Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education
citation: Agran, M., Blanchard, C., Wehmeyer, M., & Hughes, C. (2002). Increasing the Problem-Solving Skills of Students with Developmental Disabilities Participating in General Education. Remedial and Special Education, 23(5), 279-288. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Use curricular augmentation — teaching self-directed learning strategies — to help students with disabilities succeed in the general curriculum
description: The article endorses curricular augmentation, one of three levels of curricular modification, because "it changes neither the curri culum nor the way it is pre sented but instead provides the student with one or more learning strategies that will allow him or her to become 'active learners' and learn to regulate his or her own behav ior." Goal-setting and problem-solving skills are named as important augmentative skills. The present study's problem-solving approach is offered as a validated, student-friendly way to exercise this level of modification in inclusive settings.
requirements: Students must be taught strategies that fit the existing curriculum rather than altering content or its presentation
target_learners: students with mental retardation or developmental disabilities in inclusive settings
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
problem solving as a cross-curricular skill
examples: The authors cite a survey in which problem solving was the highest ranked skills area (4.6 on a scale of 1 to 5) for students with mild to severe disabilities in inclusive settings

article_title: Promoting Learning and Achievement Through Self-Assessment
citation: Arciniegas Trejos, C. M. (2008). Using Journals for Learners' Reflection and Self-Assessment. The Internet TESL Journal, Vol. XIV, No. 10. http://iteslj.org/Techniques/Arciniegas-LearnersJournals.html
title: Learning journals as a recurring record of communicative tasks paired with structured reflection and self-assessment
description: The article describes learning journals as more than collections of assignments: they are tools learners use regularly to reflect on and assess their own progress over time. In the reported class, after each communicative task (e.g., preparing recommendations for a walking tour in Bogotá), learners wrote reflections and self-assessments in their journals following teacher-provided guidelines. The pattern combines authentic language-use tasks with structured written self-evaluation entries across a course cycle.
requirements: Learners need tasks that involve active use of recently learned language so journal entries describe real communicative performance.
Teachers must provide reflection and self-assessment guidelines so learners know what elements to address in each entry.
constraints: The article reports implementation in one high-beginner adult EFL class over a three-month cycle at a single language institute; it does not claim generalizability beyond this setting.
target_learners: high-beginner adult EFL learners
target_learning_goals: communicative ability in English
self-regulated learning and reflection on language performance
examples: After a group task preparing walking-tour recommendations using 'should', learners answered guideline questions such as 'Did I contribute to my group's work by participating actively in my group's discussions?' and recorded answers in their journals.
key_sources: Arciniegas Trejos, C. M. (2008). Using Journals for Learners' Reflection and Self-Assessment. The Internet TESL Journal, Vol. XIV, No. 10. http://iteslj.org/Techniques/Arciniegas-LearnersJournals.html

article_title: Promoting Learning and Achievement Through Self-Assessment
citation: Arciniegas Trejos, C. M. (2008). Using Journals for Learners' Reflection and Self-Assessment. The Internet TESL Journal, Vol. XIV, No. 10. http://iteslj.org/Techniques/Arciniegas-LearnersJournals.html
title: Provide explicit guidelines for reflection and self-assessment so learners know what to evaluate
description: The article recommends that teachers provide the guidelines learners will follow for reflection and self-assessment, stating it is 'of primary importance' so learners have a clear idea of what elements are involved in developing and assessing tasks. In the reported class, guidelines asked learners whether they contributed actively, integrated new language orally and in writing, activated target expressions, and identified similarities and differences across groups.
requirements: Teachers must define tasks in advance and explain how learners are expected to work through them gradually.
Guidelines should be explained from the beginning along with the journal's purpose and role in the course.
constraints: The article notes some learners still did not know how to reflect despite guidelines, so guidelines alone may not suffice without teacher help.
target_learners: adult EFL learners
high-beginner language learners
target_learning_goals: self-assessment of communicative performance
reflection on learning process
examples: The walking-tour task used five guideline questions, including 'Did I integrate the new language I learned in the unit orally and in writing? Give examples.'

citation: Arciniegas Trejos, C. M. (2008). Using Journals for Learners' Reflection and Self-Assessment. The Internet TESL Journal, Vol. XIV, No. 10. http://iteslj.org/Techniques/Arciniegas-LearnersJournals.html
title: Self-regulated learning as the rationale for journal-based self-assessment
description: The article grounds journal use in self-regulated learning, citing O'Malley and Valdez Pierce: 'Student self-assessment is a key element in authentic assessment and in self-regulated learning.' Self-regulated learners collaborate, see the connection between effort and success, monitor their own performance, and evaluate their progress and accomplishments. Journals operationalize these behaviors by prompting regular reflection and self-assessment.
requirements: Learners must be given regular opportunities to reflect on and assess their own progress for self-regulation to develop.
constraints: The framework is attributed to O'Malley and Valdez Pierce's book on authentic assessment for English language learners; the article applies it rather than testing it.
target_learners: English language learners
adult learners
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
monitoring and evaluating one's own progress
examples: The article quotes the source's claim that self-regulated learners 'monitor their own performance and evaluate their progress and accomplishments' as the goal journals serve.

article_title: A Framework for Designing Scaffolds That Improve Motivation and Cognition
citation: Belland Brian R., Kim ChanMin, Hannafin Michael J. (2013). A Framework for Designing Scaffolds That Improve Motivation and Cognition. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2013.838920
title: Motivational scaffolding framework: six motivationally grounded goals for scaffold design in PBL
description: The article's central framework holds that scaffolds in problem-based learning environments should be designed around six motivational goals. As the authors state, "our framework posits that motivation-enhancing scaffolds in PBL should promote these six goals that are broadly supported by motivation theories: establish task value, promote mastery goals, promote belonging, promote emotion regulation, promote expectancy for success, and promote autonomy." Achieving these goals is expected to raise behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement, since "motivation is a basis for subsequent engagement." The framework is elaborated into seventeen numbered scaffolding strategies in Table 1.
requirements: Scaffolds must be designed intentionally to encourage motivation rather than assuming authentic problems automatically engage students
Sustained situational interest requires content knowledge and a belief in task value
constraints: Framework addresses computer-based scaffolds in PBL; teacher scaffolds are acknowledged but beyond the article's scope
The article synthesizes motivation theories, adopting single terms where constructs differ in nuance, to keep focus on design implications
target_learners: K-12 and university students working on authentic, ill-structured problems in PBL environments
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement and motivation during extended problem-based learning
Deep conceptual learning and problem-solving in authentic inquiry
examples: Table 1 enumerates strategies per goal, e.g., prompting students to choose a problem aspect connecting to their interests, and using noncontrolling language in scaffolding messages

article_title: The Role of Repeated Exposure to Multimodal Input in Incidental Acquisition of Foreign Language Vocabulary
citation: Marie-Josée Bisson, Walter J. B. van Heuven, Kathy Conklin, and Richard J. Tunney. (2014). The Role of Repeated Exposure to Multimodal Input in Incidental Acquisition of Foreign Language Vocabulary. Language Learning 64:4. https://doi.org/10.1111/lang.12085
title: Variation of the Ebbinghaus savings paradigm for detecting early incidental vocabulary gains
description: This methodology exposes learners to novel words incidentally, then asks them to learn the words explicitly, with half of the explicit-phase words previously encountered and half completely new. The article states it was "sensitive enough to detect vocabulary acquisition from two exposures to FL words", detecting "traces of word knowledge that had not necessarily reached the threshold for explicit recognition". It is offered as a more sensitive alternative to traditional recognition and recall tests in incidental vocabulary research.
requirements: Requires a prior incidental learning phase using one set of words and a matched control set withheld from that phase, counterbalanced across participants
constraints: The article notes it "is not possible to determine whether the knowledge acquired during the incidental learning phase was purely below the recognition threshold or at the level of recognition" and, because feedback was given, the type of knowledge acquired incidentally cannot be concluded
target_learners: Adult beginner foreign language learners
target_learning_goals: Early form-meaning knowledge of foreign language vocabulary
examples: Participants completed 200 letter-search trials with Welsh words, pictures, and audio, then blocks of translation-recognition trials with feedback until reaching an 80% block accuracy criterion

article_title: Testing beyond words: Using tests to enhance visuospatial map learning
citation: Shana K. Carpenter and Harold Pashler. (2007). Testing beyond words: Using tests to enhance visuospatial map learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 14 (3), 474-478. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03194009
title: Covert retrieval with self-scoring as a method for extending the testing effect to nonverbal, visuospatial materials
description: The article introduces a method in which a learner views a map with one feature deleted, forms a mental image of the missing feature and its location, then presses a key to view the complete map and self-scores as correct or incorrect, as with flash cards. The authors note that "the testing effect may not always require overt retrieval" and that "when a person is motivated to learn, he or she can score his or her own responses". The method allows tests to be applied where verbal responses cannot easily be collected and scored.
requirements: A computer or display that can present the complete material and versions with individual features deleted
Learners motivated to honestly self-score whether they retrieved the missing feature and its location
constraints: The direct benefit of retrieval versus the indirect benefit of diagnosing unlearned items was not separated in the study
Subjects could probably base covert retrievals partly on working memory to some degree
target_learners: undergraduate students learning map-based material
target_learning_goals: visuospatial map knowledge such as locations of roads, rivers, and buildings
examples: Subjects studied a map for 20 sec, then repeatedly saw it with one of 12 features missing for 100 sec of test trials, forming a mental image before the complete map reappeared

article_title: The influence of retrieval on retention
citation: Carrier, M., & Pashler, H. (1992). The influence of retrieval on retention. Memory & Cognition, 20(6), 633-642. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03204076
title: Error-correction learning models account for the retrieval advantage; Hebbian-type models do not
description: The article proposes that network models with error-correction learning (e.g., McClelland & Rumelhart, 1986) naturally explain why retrieval beats study: an attempted retrieval generates an estimate of the response, and connections are modified to reduce the error between that estimate and the canonical representation. Presenting the response itself may "contaminate" the estimate, reducing learning in the pure ST condition, an account the authors compare to associative blocking in Pavlovian conditioning. By contrast, the authors argue it is "not clear why memory storage would be more effective when the subject was deprived of one of the patterns to be associated" under Hebbian and other distributed models.
requirements: Learners must generate a response estimate during the trial so that error correction against the canonical representation can occur
constraints: The authors state the present results and analyses do not provide sufficient information to distinguish between direct retrieval contributions to learning and the error-correction account, and that the concept of a retrieval route is inherently vague
target_learners: adult learners of paired-associate material
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of paired associations
examples: The article maps the account onto the Rescorla/Wagner model of blocking, where conditioning to CS1 is reduced when the US is already expected from CS2
key_sources: Carrier, M., & Pashler, H. (1992). The influence of retrieval on retention. Memory & Cognition, 20(6), 633-642. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03202713

article_title: The influence of retrieval on retention
citation: Carrier, M., & Pashler, H. (1992). The influence of retrieval on retention. Memory & Cognition, 20(6), 633-642. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03204076
title: After some learning is achieved, learners should be given forced retrievals without the target material present
description: The article draws a direct practical implication from its findings: "the optimal method of paired-associate learning should include a large number of test trials" and, after some degree of learning, the learner should face forced retrievals without the target material present. This follows from the four experiments showing that retrieval produced better retention than equivalent-time study. The authors note flashcards embody an implicit belief in test trials, but say the phenomenon is hardly mentioned in the educational literature and call for analysis of where test trials help.
requirements: Some degree of learning must already have been achieved before the forced-retrieval trials
constraints: The evidence comes from paired-associate rote learning with undergraduate subjects in controlled laboratory experiments
target_learners: learners of paired-associate or vocabulary material
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of learned pairs
examples: In the TTST condition, subjects attempted to say the response term aloud during a 5-sec period in which only the stimulus term was present, before the response term appeared

article_title: Young Children Can Learn Scientific Reasoning with Teachable Agents
citation: Doris B. Chin, Ilsa M. Dohmen, and Daniel L. Schwartz. (2013). Young Children Can Learn Scientific Reasoning with Teachable Agents. IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1109/TLT.2013.24
title: Three design principles for teachable agents: visible thinking, independent performance with recursive feedback, and student responsibility for the agent
description: The article organizes teachable agent (TA) design around three principles drawn from the learning sciences: the TA "makes its thought processes visible"; it "exhibits independent performance to produce recursive feedback," grounded in Premack's recursive thought and the prote´ge´ effect; and it engenders social responsibility toward the agent (naming, customization, game rewards). The authors stress the main value is that the principles "bring these positive learning mechanisms together into a single learning technology," instantiated in Betty's Brain.
requirements: The teacher, curriculum specialist, or researcher must produce hidden expert maps so the system can generate questions and feedback
constraints: The principles are not intended to exclude other approaches to TA design; they reflect features that asserted themselves over 15 years of work
target_learners: elementary-school students (studied with 9-10-year-old fourth-graders)
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning schemas such as hierarchical class-inclusion reasoning
science content understanding
examples: Taxonomy Betty traces its reasoning by progressively highlighting links and nodes; the Triple-A-Challenge game show uses a hidden expert map to evaluate the agent's answers
