article_title: Young Children Can Learn Scientific Reasoning with Teachable Agents
citation: Doris B. Chin, Ilsa M. Dohmen, and Daniel L. Schwartz. (2013). Young Children Can Learn Scientific Reasoning with Teachable Agents. IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1109/TLT.2013.24
title: Taxonomy Betty (Betty's Brain variant): a teachable agent for hierarchical scientific reasoning
description: Taxonomy Betty is a variant of Betty's Brain in which students teach a computer agent by building concept maps with "type-of" and "has-property" links, then quiz the agent or enter it in the Triple-A-Challenge game. The TA chains through the taught map using artificial intelligence and "tracing its reasoning by progressively highlighting the links and nodes it traverses," and also unfolds its reasoning in text. It was used by fourth-graders alongside the FOSS Environments kit.
requirements: Students receive the nodes unconnected and connect them to teach the agent; four hierarchical expert maps were produced for the FOSS kit
constraints: The TAs always reason correctly, so wrong answers reflect incorrect links and nodes taught by the student

target_learning_goals: hierarchical reasoning about organisms, taxonomies, and ecosystems
examples: Over the unit, TA students logged in an average of 9.6 times, made 167.4 map edits, had agents take 34.1 quizzes, and played 21.7 games

article_title: The influence of concept mapping on achievement, self-regulation, and self-efficacy in students of English as a second language
citation: Pasana Chularut. (2001). The Influence of Concept Mapping on Achievement, Self-Regulation, and Self-Efficacy in Students of English as a Second Language. Doctoral dissertation, University of Oklahoma. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED3004889
title: Concept mapping as a metacognitive learning strategy grounded in Ausubel's assimilation theory of meaningful learning
description: The article frames concept mapping as a technique rooted in Ausubel's assimilation theory: "meaningful learning occurs when new knowledge is related to existing concepts in the learner's cognitive structure." A concept map is "a graphic arrangement of the key concepts in a body of subject matter with connecting lines labelled to show valid and meaningful relationships," and concept mapping is treated as a metacognitive strategy assisting learners in understanding concepts, relationships, and the hierarchical nature of knowledge. The study applies this framework to ESL students learning from English text.
requirements: Learners must choose to relate new knowledge to relevant concepts and propositions they already know, rather than incorporating it arbitrarily (rote learning).
constraints: The article notes rotely learned material is more easily forgotten since it lacks linkages to existing concepts.
target_learners: ESL students in university intensive English programs
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and meaningful learning from English text
examples: Participants constructed concept maps from reading passages during strategy training and practice phases.

article_title: The influence of concept mapping on achievement, self-regulation, and self-efficacy in students of English as a second language
citation: Pasana Chularut. (2001). The Influence of Concept Mapping on Achievement, Self-Regulation, and Self-Efficacy in Students of English as a Second Language. Doctoral dissertation, University of Oklahoma. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED3004889
title: Social cognitive theory of self-regulation linking concept mapping to self-observation, self-judgment, self-reaction, and self-efficacy
description: The article's theoretical framework is social cognitive theory, in which "self-regulation as entailing at least four components: goal setting, self-observation, self-judgment, and self-reaction." During concept mapping, students act as observers of their own learning, notice whether their map is developing toward their goals, judge and evaluate their maps against standards, and react with satisfaction or revision. The article argues that beliefs about progress enhance self-efficacy, so "self-regulation may be an inherent part of the use of concept mapping," and that self-efficacy is further influenced by the self-regulation process.
requirements: Students need a proximal and challenging goal, such as illustrating interrelationships among concepts, to organize their efforts during mapping.
constraints: The four components other than goal setting interact with one another rather than operating exclusively.
target_learners: ESL students learning from text
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning, self-monitoring, knowledge acquisition strategies, and self-efficacy for learning from text
examples: Students examined maps they constructed so that misconceptions and holes in understanding became apparent, revising maps as needed.

title: Provide explicit learning-strategy training and sustained practice when introducing concept mapping to language learners
description: The article's treatment phases show that concept mapping was introduced through structured instruction followed by practice rather than mere exposure: the procedure included pre-testing, learning strategy training, learning strategy practice, and post-testing. Related reviewed studies gave experimental groups "two one-hour lessons and two one-hour practice sessions on concept mapping" before requiring maps every lesson. The principle is that ESL students, who may have little experience using learning strategies in English, benefit from explicit training and repeated practice in the strategy before it supports learning from text.

article_title: Chatting and cheating: Ensuring academic integrity in the era of ChatGPT
citation: Debby R. E. Cotton, Peter A. Cotton & J. Reuben Shipway (2024) Chatting and cheating: Ensuring academic integrity in the era of ChatGPT, Innovations in Education and Teaching International, 61:2, 228-239. https://doi.org/10.1080/14703297.2023.2190148
title: ChatGPT as a dual opportunity-and-threat for higher education assessment
description: The article organises ChatGPT's role in higher education along two axes: opportunities (asynchronous communication, collaboration and student groups, remote learning, personalised and game-based assessments, immediate feedback, real-time grading freeing instructors for higher-level tasks) and challenges (plagiarism, unfair advantage for students with access, and responses that "may not accurately reflect the student's true level of understanding"). Its conclusion is that universities can address the threats through a proactive, ethical approach combining policy, training and detection.

university staff and academic integrity policymakers

responsible and ethical use of AI tools

article_title: Scientific Discovery Learning with Computer Simulations of Conceptual Domains
citation: Ton de Jong, Wouter R. van Joolingen. (1998). Scientific Discovery Learning with Computer Simulations of Conceptual Domains. Review of Educational Research. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190680v1
title: Provide domain information concurrently with the simulation, not before it
description: Learners in discovery learning with simulations benefit from direct access to domain knowledge (concepts, facts, rules, principles) while interacting with the simulation, e.g., via hypertext dictionaries. The review concludes such access "seems effective as long as the information is presented concurrently with the simulation so that the information is available at the appropriate moment". Pre-simulation information delivery was not effective in the studies reviewed.
requirements: Information must be available at the moment the learner needs it during interaction with the simulation
constraints: Information provided before interaction with the simulation was not effective in Leutner's and Elshout and Veenman's studies
target_learners: Learners with insufficient prior knowledge working with simulations
target_learning_goals: Domain knowledge of concepts, rules, and principles
Functional knowledge of the simulated system
examples: Shute's ITS on electricity let learners request definitions via hypertext links, with positive effects on a composite post-test
Leutner's agricultural simulation study found permanently available information helped domain knowledge acquisition

The review finds this measure "seems to have a clear effect on the learning outcome", and reports frequent voluntary use of assignments with positive effects on intuitive knowledge in several studies.

Planning and goal setting in discovery learning

article_title: The impact of patient, intervention, comparison, outcome (PICO) as a search strategy tool on literature search quality: a systematic review
citation: Mette Brandt Eriksen, PhD; Tove Faber Frandsen, PhD. (2018). The impact of patient, intervention, comparison, outcome (PICO) as a search strategy tool on literature search quality: a systematic review. Journal of the Medical Library Association 106 (4). https://doi.org/10.5195/jmla.2018.345
title: Three-criterion risk-of-bias framework for studies evaluating search strategy tools
description: Because no validated risk-of-bias tool existed for studies evaluating search strategy tools, the review authors developed, by consensus, a self-developed set of three criteria: "searcher skills", "match between model and question", and "quality of searches". Each criterion comprises individual considerations (e.g., searcher training and prior familiarity with tools, fit of model to topic, number of search blocks, relevance assessment against a gold standard, and consistent adaptation of searches across databases) judged as low, high, or unclear risk of bias. The framework is used to assess the three included studies and proposed as guidance for future research on this topic.
requirements: Studies must report searcher skills, the fit between the conceptualizing model and the research question, and how searches were performed and adapted per database for the criteria to be assessable.
constraints: The review states the tool "was not validated", and applying a model not fit for the research area, unequal search blocks, or relevance assessment without a gold standard or expert group is treated as high risk of bias.
target_learners: information specialists
systematic reviewers
librarians
target_learning_goals: designing and evaluating literature search strategies for evidence synthesis
examples: Applied to the three included studies, the criteria yielded high or unclear risk of bias for all three: searcher skills high for Hoogendam et al., model-question fit high for Agoritsas et al. and Methley et al., and quality of searches low only for Methley et al.

article_title: The Long-Term Distributional and Welfare Effects of Covid-19 School Closures
citation: Nicola Fuchs-Schündeln, Dirk Krueger, Alexander Ludwig, and Irina Popova. (2020). The Long-Term Distributional and Welfare Effects of Covid-19 School Closures. NBER Working Paper 27773. http://www.nber.org/papers/w27773
title: A quantitative life-cycle model of child human capital production combining public schooling investment with parental time and money investments
description: The article builds a heterogeneous-agent partial-equilibrium life-cycle model in which "public investment through schooling is combined with parental time and resource investments in the production of child human capital at different stages." The multi-layer CES human capital production function features self-productivity (higher human capital in one period raises it in the next) and dynamic complementarity (investment pays out more the higher existing human capital). Parents choose time and monetary investments, inter-vivos transfers, and children make education choices among no high school completion, high school, and college. The model is calibrated to PSID, PSID-CDS, and NLSY79 moments and used as a "quantitative laboratory" for school-closure thought experiments.
requirements: Calibrated parameters of the human capital production function, taken from the literature or matched to U.S. household micro data moments on parental investments
constraints: The model excludes innate ability complementarities: it "does not feature innate ability, only innate human capital"
The age-16 human capital process "ignores parental inputs entirely" and children's own investments, which the authors call a crude approximation
target_learners: Children aged 4 to 14 at the time of the school-closure shock
target_learning_goals: Human capital accumulation, high school completion, college attendance, and long-run earnings
examples: School and child care closures are modeled as a temporary six-month reduction in public investment ig into child human capital production

description: The article calibrates children's innate ability (initial human capital) distribution from test scores in the PSID Child Development Supplement surveys I-III, merged with the PSID. article_title: Spacing repetitions over 1 week
citation: Glenberg, A. M., & Lehmann, T. S. (1980). Spacing repetitions over 1 week. Memory & Cognition, 8(6), 528-538. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03213734
title: Component-levels theory: spacing effects arise from differential storage of contextual components and their match with the retrieval context
description: Component-levels theory (Glenberg, 1979) proposes that study encodes three component types—descriptive, structural (interitem associations), and contextual—and that "the variability in the encoding of all components increases as a function of repetition spacing", termed differential storage. Contextual components are aligned on a rate-of-change continuum from local (quickly changing) to global (slowly changing). Retrieval constructs a cue from the test context; traces activate in proportion to shared components, with cue overload making global components weaker cues. The theory explains the proportionality rule by applying the same storage-retrieval processes at different points on the context-change continuum.
requirements: Retrieval depends on the match between stored contextual components and the context available at the test; the account presumes free-recall testing without experimenter-provided cues
constraints: Differential storage of descriptive components was shown to have little effect on free-recall spacing effects
Within-list lag effects persist when structural (interitem) components are stored, since associative cues are independent of test context
target_learners: adult students in introductory psychology
target_learning_goals: free recall of repeated verbal material over retention intervals up to 2 weeks
examples: The theory predicted a four-way interaction in Experiment 1's within-list data that was significant, and predicted no same-different task interaction in Experiment 3, which was observed (F < 1).
key_sources: Glenberg, A. M., & Lehmann, T. S. (1980). Spacing repetitions over 1 week. Memory & Cognition, 8(6), 528-538. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03213772

article_title: Isolated and interrelated concepts
citation: Goldstone, R. L. (1996). Isolated and interrelated concepts. Memory & Cognition, 24 (5), 608-628. http://cognitrn.PSYCH-indiana.edu
title: Continuum of conceptual interrelatedness with converging manipulations and diagnostics
description: A framework placing concepts on a continuum from purely isolated (independent detectors or templates/prototypes) to purely interrelated (characterizations defined relative to competitor concepts). A concept "is interrelated with respect to another concept to the extent that its char­acterization is influenced by the other concept." The article operationalizes the continuum via three manipulations (instructions, category alternation frequency, labels) and two indicators (nondiagnostic-feature use; prototype vs. caricature categorization), using converging operations, and proposes a connectionist model in which interrelation depends on connection strength.
requirements: Converging operations: confidence in the construct increases only because manipulations and indicators provide mutually consistent results
constraints: The methods diagnose only interrelatedness arising from competition between mutually exclusive, simultaneously acquired artificial categories; semantic-association and theory-cohabitation interrelations were not evaluated
target_learners: adult laboratory learners of artificial categories
target_learning_goals: concept representation and category learning
examples: Experiment 1 used imagery versus discriminating-feature instructions; Experiment 2 varied alternation frequency; Experiment 3 used symmetric versus negation labels; a connectionist simulation was presented to model intermediate degrees of interrelation
key_sources: Goldstone, R. L. (1996). Isolated and interrelated concepts. Memory & Cognition, 24 (5), 608-628. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03201087

article_title: Individual differences, rereading, and self-explanation: Concurrent processing and cue validity as constraints on metacomprehension accuracy
citation: Griffin, T. D., Wiley, J., & Thiede, K. W. (2008). Individual differences, rereading, and self-explanation: Concurrent processing and cue validity as constraints on metacomprehension accuracy. Memory & Cognition, 36(1), 93-103. https://doi.org/10.3758/MC.36.1.93
title: Concurrent-processing and cue-validity account of metacomprehension accuracy
description: The article proposes that metacomprehension accuracy is constrained by two factors: the concurrent-processing demand of monitoring while comprehending, and the validity and accessibility of cues. Its core assumptions are "that metacognitive monitoring is a distinct process secondary to the processes being monitored," and that some comprehension-predicting cues are less accessible after reading than during reading. Rereading reduces low-level text-processing demands, letting lower-ability and lower-WMC readers attend to metalevel cues; self-explanation increases access to inference-level cues valid for situation-model-level tests, improving accuracy for all readers.
requirements: Accurate concurrent monitoring requires available attentional resources, which vary with reading ability and working memory capacity
constraints: The article states the results may be particular to situations with relatively long texts explaining complex causal or logical relations, with inference- and situation-model-level tests
The article states it did not directly observe when readers were monitoring, and the evidence that accuracy was impacted by the ability to attend to the metalevel while reading is indirect
target_learners: College students reading explanatory texts
target_learning_goals: Accurate monitoring of one's own text comprehension
examples: Experiments 1 and 2 with explanatory natural/social-science texts and inference verification tests
Comparison to prejudgment generation tasks (summary/keyword listing) that also push readers toward situation-model cues

The study describes it as enabling students to communicate "like talking to peers, get help and explanation on learning materials, and get instant feedback". article_title: The costs and benefits of providing feedback during learning
citation: Matthew Jensen Hays, Nate Kornell, and Robert A. Bjork. (2010). The costs and benefits of providing feedback during learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review. https://doi.org/10.3758/PBR.17.6.797
title: When study time is fixed, skip feedback after successful retrieval in favor of additional retrieval attempts
description: This principle holds that under a constrained time budget, presenting feedback after an already-successful retrieval wastes time that could fund further retrieval practice, which benefits memory more. The article's experiment showed that "skipping a feedback trial allowed time for an additional trial," and that final recall was higher when skipping was permitted. The authors state that "providing feedback is not universally beneficial" and can have "a negative net effect on learning."
requirements: Learners or the system must be able to judge or guess response correctness so feedback is skipped mainly after successful retrievals
Total learning time must be constrained, so time saved converts into additional retrieval trials
constraints: Feedback remains beneficial after incorrect responses and after correct responses made with low confidence or when feedback is delayed
Learners are typically unaware that retrieval outperforms restudy, so unguided skipping may be nonoptimal in other paradigms
target_learners: adult learners studying paired-associate material such as vocabulary flash cards
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of verbal, vocabulary, or factual material
examples: In the experiment, the computer skipped feedback after correct responses to make room for more test trials, and participants who skipped feedback themselves recalled more on the 24–48-hour delayed final test
key_sources: Matthew Jensen Hays, Nate Kornell, and Robert A. Bjork. (2010). The costs and benefits of providing feedback during learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review. https://doi.org/10.3758/PBR.17.6.797

article_title: The costs and benefits of providing feedback during learning
citation: Matthew Jensen Hays, Nate Kornell, and Robert A. Bjork. (2010). The costs and benefits of providing feedback during learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review. https://doi.org/10.3758/PBR.17.6.797
title: New theory of disuse: learning increments are inversely proportional to the accessibility of the to-be-learned information
description: The article invokes the new theory of disuse (Bjork & Bjork, 1992) as its explanatory framework for why feedback after successful retrieval adds little. In this framework, "the magnitude of a learning increment is inversely proportional to the accessibility of the to-be-learned information." It predicts that feedback following a successful retrieval should have virtually no effect on learning, a prediction borne out by prior studies and consistent with the present results. The framework also explains the two cases where feedback after a correct response helps: when information is not fully accessible (low-confidence correct answers, delayed feedback).
requirements: Applies to learning situations where the to-be-learned information's accessibility can vary across retrievals
constraints: The article cites the framework as background theory from Bjork and Bjork (1992), not as a model tested directly in this experiment
target_learners: all learners of verbal or factual material
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and transfer
examples: The authors apply the framework to explain why immediate feedback after correct responses yields no retention benefit in Pashler et al. (2005) and in the present experiment

article_title: Teacher Turnover and Teacher Shortages: An Organizational Analysis
citation: Ingersoll, R. M. (2001). Teacher Turnover and Teacher Shortages: An Organizational Analysis. American Educational Research Journal, 38(3), 499-534. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Teacher+Turnover+and+Teacher+Shortages+Ingersoll
title: Organizational perspective on teacher turnover and school staffing problems
description: Drawn from the sociology of organizations, occupations, and work, this framework holds that teacher turnover and staffing problems cannot be fully understood without examining employing organizations. It rests on three premises: "understanding employee turnover is important because of its link to the performance and effectiveness of organizations"; turnover must be examined "at the level of the organization"; and turnover requires examining "the character and conditions of the organizations within which employees work." From this view, migration matters as much as attrition, and high turnover is both outcome and cause of school dysfunction.
requirements: Analysis must examine turnover at the organizational level, treating both migration and attrition as relevant departures
constraints: The article states it does not attempt a comprehensive analysis of all aspects of school organization that may affect turnover, focusing on four policy-amenable conditions
target_learners: School administrators and policymakers concerned with teacher retention
target_learning_goals: Understanding and reducing school staffing problems through improved teacher retention
examples: The study applied the framework to SASS/TFS data, testing four organizational conditions—compensation, administrative support, conflict, and faculty influence—across a range of schools and turnover subsets.
key_sources: Ingersoll, R. M. (2001). Teacher Turnover and Teacher Shortages: An Organizational Analysis. American Educational Research Journal, 38(3), 499-534. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Teacher+Turnover+and+Teacher+Shortages+Ingersoll

article_title: Teacher Turnover and Teacher Shortages: An Organizational Analysis
citation: Ingersoll, R. M. (2001). Teacher Turnover and Teacher Shortages: An Organizational Analysis. American Educational Research Journal, 38(3), 499-534. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Teacher+Turnover+and+Teacher+Shortages+Ingersoll
title: Address organizational sources of low retention, not just recruitment, to solve school staffing problems
description: Because staffing problems stem primarily from excess demand created by departing teachers rather than insufficient supply, the article argues the solution lies in decreasing demand rather than increasing supply. As it concludes, "teacher recruitment programs alone will not solve the staffing problems of schools if they do not also address the organizational sources of low retention." Recruitment initiatives should therefore be paired with improvements to workplace conditions such as administrative support, student discipline, and faculty influence.
requirements: Policymakers must diagnose whether local staffing problems arise from turnover-driven excess demand rather than supply deficits before choosing interventions
constraints: The article's evidence base is the SASS/TFS surveys of the late 1980s through mid-1990s; self-reported departure reasons are retrospective attributions subject to bias
target_learners: Education policymakers, district administrators, and school leaders
target_learning_goals: Reducing school staffing problems and improving teacher retention
examples: The article contrasts the dominant supply-side policy response—troops-to-teachers, Teach for America, alternative licensing, and financial incentives—with its demand-side findings from the SASS/TFS analysis.

article_title: Modelling the long-run learning impact of the Covid-19 learning shock: Actions to (more than) mitigate loss
citation: Kaffenberger, Michelle. (2021). Modelling the long-run learning impact of the Covid-19 learning shock: Actions to (more than) mitigate loss. International Journal of Educational Development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijedudev.2020.102326
title: Trapezoidal pedagogical production function model of learning
description: A calibrated model (from Kaffenberger and Pritchett, 2020) in which learning in a grade is a trapezoidal function of a student's initial skill level, defined by width, height, slope and centre parameters. The article explains that "the PPF assumes there is a range of initial skill levels within which children learn and above and below which they do not", and a pace parameter shifts the PPF from one grade to the next. Calibrated to PISA-D countries, it is used here to simulate Covid-19 shock and mitigation scenarios through grade 10.
requirements: Calibration to a learning assessment (here PISA-D) plus grade attainment data to model dropout after each grade
constraints: The model does not currently allow differentiation across countries; it is calibrated to the PISA-D average
Assumes dropout stays constant at pre-pandemic levels and builds in no macro shocks to spending or household income
target_learners: Grade 3 cohorts in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: Foundational mathematics and literacy learning sustained through grade 10
examples: Parameters calibrated so the top 43 percent of the grade 10 distribution replicates observed PISA-D results (pace 45, slope 0.15, width 153)

title: Plan remediation on reopening and build it into lasting reorientation of instruction to children's learning levels
description: The article recommends that systems begin planning remedial programmes immediately, and that while doing so they "build programmes and train teachers in ways that can continue to produce benefits beyond the period immediately following reopening". Remediation requires formative assessment of children's levels and teacher empowerment to adapt instruction; maintaining these practices — ongoing formative assessment, curriculum adjustment, and coaching or structured pedagogy support — is what turns a recovery programme into a 'build back better' scenario that surpasses pre-shock learning.
requirements: Formative assessments to identify children's learning levels on return
Teacher training and professional development, with teachers allowed and empowered to adapt the curriculum
constraints: The exact form must take each system's context, existing capabilities and constraints into account
target_learners: Children returning to school after Covid-19 closures, especially primary-grade cohorts in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: Catch-up on foundational skills and sustained learning gains through later grades
examples: The modelled remediation scenario covered the missed third of the grade 3 curriculum during grade 4 before resuming the normal pace; the reorientation scenario used an optimised pace of 35, a 22 percent reduction from 45

article_title: Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations
citation: Klaus Krippendorff. (2004). Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations. Human Communication Research 30, 3: 411-433. https://astro.temple.edu/~lombard/carman.htm
title: Three conditions for an agreement coefficient to serve as an index of data reliability
description: The article proposes that agreement, which is what is measured, becomes an index of reliability, which is what is inferred, only when three conditions hold. The coefficient must (1) be applied to proper reliability data produced by duplicating the coding process with independent coders; (2) it must treat units as separately categorizable and coders as interchangeable, since it "treats units of analysis as separately describable or categorizable, without, however, presuming any knowledge about the correctness of their descriptions"; and (3) its values must correlate with the conditions under which one relies on imperfect data, with anchor values for perfect reliability and chance. The framework organizes the article's evaluation of seven coefficients.
requirements: Reliability data must be generated by widely available coders following the same explicit instructions, working independently on identical units
constraints: No single coefficient can determine that coders are available, instructed, independent, and coding identical units; researchers must ensure these preconditions themselves
target_learners: content analysis researchers
communication researchers
target_learning_goals: inferring data reliability from intercoder agreement
examples: The article applies the three conditions to seven dichotomous two-coder coefficients, including %-agreement, Scott's pi, Cohen's kappa, Benini's beta, and Bennett et al.'s S
key_sources: Klaus Krippendorff. (2004). Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations. Human Communication Research 30, 3: 411-433. https://astro.temple.edu/~lombard/carman.htm

article_title: Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations
citation: Klaus Krippendorff. (2004). Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations. Human Communication Research 30, 3: 411-433. https://astro.temple.edu/~lombard/carman.htm
title: Use only chance-corrected agreement coefficients satisfying interchangeability and population-reference conditions; reject %-agreement, correlation, and association measures as reliability indices
description: The article recommends inferring reliability only from chance-corrected agreement coefficients that treat coders as interchangeable and refer to the population of data. It states: "The use of %-agreement should be actively discouraged, especially as a fallback criterion." Association, correlation, and consistency coefficients, Cohen's kappa, Benini's beta, Cronbach's alpha, and %-agreement should be rejected as incompatible with reliability concerns. Alpha, applicable to multiple coders and many metrics including missing data and small samples, is offered as the general choice, reducing to Scott's pi for two coders, large samples, and nominal data.
requirements: A decisive coefficient must measure agreements within multiple descriptions regardless of numbers and kinds of coders
constraints: Kappa should be restricted to reliability studies in which one pair of coders judges all units and unequal coder preferences are not problematic, per Fleiss
target_learners: content analysts
researchers generating coded data
target_learning_goals: testing the reproducibility of data-making processes
examples: Figure 2 derives the dichotomous forms of seven coefficients, and the recommendations section names which to reject and which to prefer

article_title: Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations
citation: Klaus Krippendorff. (2004). Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations. Human Communication Research 30, 3: 411-433. https://astro.temple.edu/~lombard/carman.htm
title: Set acceptable agreement levels according to the costs of drawing invalid conclusions, with suggested alpha thresholds of .800 and .667 for scholarly work
description: The article argues that the minimum acceptable agreement must depend on the stakes of the analysis: "An acceptable level of agreement below which data are to be rejected as too unreliable must be chosen depending on the costs of drawing invalid conclusions from these data." For scholarship, the author suggests requiring alpha >= .800, or alpha >= .667 where tentative conclusions suffice, while insisting there are no magical numbers except perfect agreement and that standards should be verified by experiments. Confidence intervals should be consulted; null-hypothesis tests against chance have no bearing on reliability.
requirements: Thresholds must be chosen by weighing the consequences of invalid conclusions, with higher stakes such as legal or policy decisions requiring far higher criteria
constraints: The suggested .800 and .667 standards were proposed for alpha only; other coefficients may require different standards
target_learners: content analysis researchers
scholars using coded data
target_learning_goals: choosing defensible reliability decision criteria
examples: The article contrasts content analyses informing legal decisions or war-and-peace questions with those merely supporting scholarly arguments

article_title: The Effectiveness of "Teach for America" and Other Under-certified Teachers
citation: Laczko-Kerr, I., & Berliner, D. C. (2002, September 6). The Effectiveness of "Teach for America" and Other Under-certified Teachers on Student Academic Achievement: A Case of Harmful Public Policy. Education Policy Analysis Archives, 10(37). http://epaa.asu.edu/epaa/v10n37/
title: Professional control versus popular control of entry into teaching
description: The article describes, citing Wise (1994a), two methods of controlling entry into the teaching profession. "Professional control allows the teaching profession to monitor who becomes a teacher" through specified certification standards, while "popular control allows public demand to control who is placed in classrooms, with much less concern for their qualifications" — emergency certificates being an example of the latter. The article uses this framework to argue that demand-based policies allowing uncertified teachers downgrade certification and prevent teaching from meeting a criterion of a profession.
requirements: Certification standards and political mechanisms through which the profession monitors who becomes a teacher
constraints: The article frames the framework as contested: interpretations of this literature are intertwined with the ideology of the researchers
target_learners: K-12 public school students, particularly those in low-income urban and rural districts
target_learning_goals: Access to qualified teachers of record supporting academic achievement in reading, mathematics, and language arts
examples: The article treats Arizona's issuance of emergency certificates during teacher shortages as an instance of popular control

article_title: Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs
citation: Lakens, D. (2013). Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00863
title: Two viewpoints on effect sizes: the generalizable effect size estimate viewpoint versus the statistical significance viewpoint
description: The article distinguishes two perspectives on which effect size is the "true" effect size for the same data. The generalizable effect size estimate viewpoint seeks metrics that can be interpreted across studies regardless of design, regarding within-subjects effect sizes like η²p as overestimations. The statistical significance viewpoint treats individual differences as irrelevant to the tested hypothesis and prefers effect sizes and confidence intervals that reflect the statistical test, so design-dependent values are a benefit of a more powerful design. The article notes the viewpoints are not mutually exclusive but determine practical reporting choices.
requirements: Researchers must decide which viewpoint their reported effect size serves, since the choice determines the practical reporting decisions they make
constraints: The article applies the distinction to standardized mean differences in between- and within-subjects designs for t-tests and ANOVAs
target_learners: experimental researchers in psychology and education
target_learning_goals: calculating and reporting effect sizes for t-tests and ANOVAs
planning sample sizes via a-priori power analysis
examples: The article illustrates the divergence with the same two observations yielding η²p of 0.26 or 0.71 depending on design
key_sources: Lakens, D. (2013). Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00863

article_title: Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs
citation: Lakens, D. (2013). Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00863
title: Always report effect sizes, specify the standardizer used, report generalized eta squared for ANOVAs, and interpret effect sizes rather than relying on Cohen's benchmarks
description: The article's discussion sets four reporting practices for cumulative science: effect sizes should always be reported; for Cohen's d the standardizer must be specified, for example with subscripts (ds, dz, drm, dav); for ANOVAs, generalized eta squared should be reported instead of or in addition to partial eta squared; and effect sizes should be interpreted by comparison with other effects in the literature or via the common language effect size rather than the benchmarks provided by Cohen (1988).
requirements: Reporting effect sizes based on Cohen's d requires specifying which standardizer is used
constraints: The article limits its scope to effect sizes for standardized mean differences in t-tests and ANOVAs, not all research designs
target_learners: researchers planning and reporting experimental studies
target_learning_goals: transparent reporting of effect magnitudes
facilitating meta-analyses and power analyses
examples: The article's worked example reports Hedges's gs = 1.08 with means, SDs, t-value, and 95% CI, and adds a common language effect size interpretation that the preference for Movie 1 is 79%

citation: Lakens, D. (2013). Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00863
title: Supplementary spreadsheet for effect size calculations
description: A supplementary spreadsheet accompanies the article "to make it as easy as possible for researchers to incorporate effect size calculations into their workflow." article_title: Self-explanation in the domain of statistics: an expertise reversal effect
citation: Leppink, J., Broers, N. J., Imbos, T., van der Vleuten, C. P. M., & Berger, M. P. F. (2012). Self-explanation in the domain of statistics: an expertise reversal effect. Higher Education, 63, 771-785. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-011-9476-1
title: Fading instructional guidance as prior knowledge develops: guided, semi-guided, then unguided problem-solving
description: The article proposes that, for a given subject matter and complexity level, educational practice could "strive for decreasing guidance as the course proceeds", moving through three phases: guided problem-solving with worked-out examples, semi-guided or self-guided problem-solving in which students integrate an indicated set of propositions into arguments, and unguided problem-solving in which learners select relevant premises themselves, closer to real statistical practice. The experiment grounds the first two phases: novices profited from worked-out examples while more knowledgeable students profited from formulating arguments.
requirements: Guidance level must be matched to students' current prior knowledge, increasing guidance for novices and reducing it as knowledge develops
constraints: Grounded in a single experiment on a small body of statistics subject matter (about one page of text) with a 50-minute exam; the unguided phase is proposed for future study rather than tested here

target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of statistics
Argumentation integrating statistical propositions

citation: Leppink, J., Broers, N. J., Imbos, T., van der Vleuten, C. P. M., & Berger, M. P. F. (2012). Self-explanation in the domain of statistics: an expertise reversal effect. Higher Education, 63, 771-785. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-011-9476-1

Matching the instructional method to the learner's current prior knowledge avoids the expertise reversal effect the experiment demonstrated.

article_title: The memorial consequences of multiple-choice testing
citation: Marsh, E. J., Roediger, H. L., III, Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2007). The memorial consequences of multiple-choice testing. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 14(2), 194-199. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03192794
title: Design multiple-choice testing to include immediate feedback, a don't-know option with penalties, and varied question formats to reduce the learning of false facts
description: The review offers educators concrete ways to keep the memorial benefits of multiple-choice testing while limiting its negative side effects. Its recommendations are to "give immediate feedback," to follow the SAT II's example of "offering a 'don't know' option, with a penalty for selecting a wrong answer," and to change how concepts are tested across exams. Tools such as the IFAT (Immediate Feedback Test) implement the feedback recommendation by letting students scratch until they reach the starred correct answer.

constraints: Switching from a definitional multiple-choice question to an application cued recall question reduced but did not eliminate negative testing effects

citation: Bruce M. McLaren & Deanne M. Adams & Richard E. Mayer. (2015). Delayed Learning Effects with Erroneous Examples: a Study of Learning Decimals with a Web-Based Tutor. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society 2015. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0064-x
title: Erroneous examples as a desirable difficulty that promotes generative processing and durable learning
description: The article proposes that prompting students to identify, explain, and fix errors in someone else's solution primes deeper cognitive processing than solving problems alone. Erroneous example study "involves elements of both example studyand problem solving" and may strengthen "don't do X" knowledge alongside procedural knowledge, developing multiple cognitive paths. Learning from erroneous examples "can be seen as similar to a desirable difficulty," explained via cognitive load theory's generative/germane processing, producing delayed but not immediate learning benefits.
requirements: Students must be prompted to actively identify, explain, and fix errors rather than passively view erroneous solutions
Correctness feedback is needed so students do not learn the incorrect way to solve problems
constraints: Evidence so far shows the benefit on delayed tests given a week later, not on immediate tests
Demonstrated for a single middle-school decimals topic with mostly single-step problems

target_learning_goals: decimal number concepts and procedures
overcoming common decimal misconceptions
examples: Students reviewed a fictional student's error, identified the misconception from options, fixed the solution, and explained the correct procedure, with correctness feedback at every step.

Erroneous example items walked students through reviewing, identifying, fixing, and explaining a fictional student's error, with green/red and text feedback. Erroneous examples necessitated extensions to CTAT software for the identify-explain-fix interface steps.

article_title: Promoting Access to the General Curriculum by Teaching Self-Determination Skills
citation: Palmer, Susan B.; Wehmeyer, Michael L.; Gipson, Krista; Agran, Martin. (2004). Promoting access to the general curriculum by teaching self-determination skills. Exceptional Children, 70(4), 427-439. https://hdl.handle.net/1808/10978
title: Promote self-determination linked to standards as an entry point for access to the general curriculum for all students, including those with severe disabilities
description: The article argues that access models often overlook students with more severe disabilities, and that promoting self-determination tied to academic standards is a practical entry point for including them in the general curriculum. It states that "Promoting self-determination linked to standards is an entry point to ensuring access to the general curriculum for all students, including students with severe disabilities." The principle works by giving students strategies, such as problem-solving and study planning, that they apply to standards-aligned academic content. The article's intervention demonstrated this approach with middle school students with intellectual disabilities.
requirements: Self-determination instruction must be linked to academic standards (language arts, science, social studies) rather than taught in isolation
constraints: The article notes that existing models to achieve access often neglect students with more severe disabilities
target_learners: middle school students with intellectual disabilities, including students with severe disabilities
target_learning_goals: access to and participation in the general curriculum
self-determination skills such as problem-solving and study planning
examples: Middle school students with intellectual disabilities alternately learned problem-solving and study planning skills linked to language arts, science, and social studies standards.

description: The article frames self-determination not merely as a personal competency but as a functional mechanism of curricular access: teaching these skills supplies students with additional means of engaging the general curriculum. As the authors put it, "Promoting self-determination provides students with disabilities with additional strategies to access the general curriculum." In this account, problem-solving and study planning operate as strategies students deploy to participate in standards-based academic work. The framework was substantiated in an intervention with middle school students with intellectual disabilities in which both skill groups outperformed an alternating control condition.

constraints: The account addresses students with disabilities, including severe disabilities, for whom standard access models are described as often neglectful

article_title: Examining the efficiency of schedules of distributed retrieval practice
citation: Pyc, M. A., & Rawson, K. A. (2007). Examining the efficiency of schedules of distributed retrieval practice. Memory & Cognition, 35(8), 1917-1927. https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/BF03193420
title: Discontinue practice with items once they are correctly recalled, but only after a sufficiently long initial interval between study and first practice test
description: This principle implements a dropout (variable) test-restudy schedule: items correctly recalled during a practice test are removed from the practice stack so remaining trials go to unlearned items. The article shows this yields "levels of memory similar to those obtained with conventional schedules of learning" while using significantly fewer trials — but only when the initial interstimulus interval was long (23 items); a 5-item initial interval dropout schedule produced lower final recall. The authors mirror the flashcard strategy students already report using spontaneously.
requirements: Practice must combine retrieval (test) with restudy of the answer on each trial.
The interval between initial study and the first test-restudy trial must be long enough that items are no longer readily available in working memory.
constraints: Evidence comes from Swahili-English paired associates with a 40-min retention interval; the authors state that "the efficiency of dropout schedules with more complex materials and longer test delays should be established before strong, general recommendations can be made."
Dropping recalled items incurred a measurable cost relative to a long-ISI conventional schedule (23-23-23) in Experiment 2, offset by gains on initially incorrect items.
target_learners: undergraduate students learning course material
students studying vocabulary with flashcards
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of paired-associate material
efficient allocation of limited study time
examples: In Experiment 1 and 2, items correctly recalled on a test-restudy trial were removed from the to-be-learned list, and freed trials were allocated to initially incorrect items, which received up to six trials.

article_title: Evolution and Revolution in Artificial Intelligence in Education
citation: Ido Roll & Ruth Wylie. (2016). Evolution and Revolution in Artificial Intelligence in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 582-599. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0110-3
title: Three shifts in education — goals, practices, and environment — challenge AIED's present focus
description: The article clusters recent developments in education into three groups: goals, practices, and environment. Goals move toward adaptive expertise, knowledge application, collaboration, and self-regulated learning, with assessment shifting to ongoing formative measures; practices incorporate authentic problems, group work, and increased complexity, with personalization a major challenge; environment extends learning beyond the classroom to informal and workplace settings, exemplified by MOOCs. The authors argue these changes "offer significant challenges to the present focus of AIED" and are sometimes in conflict, e.g., MOOCs' talking-head format versus the guide-on-the-side trend.
requirements: The analysis focuses on changes that affect AIED specifically; the cluster reflects the article's own grouping of recent educational developments.
constraints: The article notes the trends are often at conflict with one another, as in MOOCs versus the guide-on-the-side classroom trend.

workplace learners
target_learning_goals: adaptive expertise
collaboration
self-regulated learning

description: The article argues that instead of stand-alone plug-and-play environments, ILEs should be designed as one component of an ecosystem of classroom activities, instruction, and out-of-classroom activities, mindful of the intended environment from early design. Teachers should become active collaborators and participants, and ILEs should be embedded in cultural norms and broadened to informal and workplace contexts, since education is a socio-cultural phenomenon.

title: The mentor metaphor: a new vision for ILEs beyond the two-sigma human-tutor benchmark
description: The article proposes replacing the human-tutor metaphor — which frames ILEs as one-on-one, time-limited, and space-constrained — with a mentor metaphor. ILEs have unique affordances: they can be "collaborative, omnipresent, and portable", supporting learning anytime, anywhere, by anyone. An appropriate metaphor offers a vision and concrete evaluation goals; the authors do not argue the two-sigma problem is solved or irrelevant, but want that level of improvement across tasks, contexts, and goals, including life-long skills, peers, and learners' life problems.

article_title: An examination of the seductive details effect in terms of working memory capacity
citation: Sanchez, C. A., & Wiley, J. (2006). An examination of the seductive details effect in terms of working memory capacity. Memory & Cognition, 34(2), 344-355. https://link.springer.com/journal/13421
title: Controlled attention perspective of working memory capacity
description: The article contrasts the controlled attention view with the traditional limited-capacity view of working memory. From this perspective, "WMC from the controlled attention perspective is the ability to control attention and deal with irrelevant information, and not simply the amount of information that can reside in working memory." Individual differences arise from the ability to ignore irrelevant information on the basis of a specific relevant goal, not from a limited amount of activation. Both experiments support this view: the seduction deficit appeared only for low-WMC readers and only when irrelevant illustrations were present, and eye-tracking showed high-WMC readers selectively ignored the seductive images.
requirements: Requires tasks containing irrelevant or interfering information, since differences between WMC groups emerge only when irrelevant information must be ignored
constraints: The article notes this account was tested with seductive images; the diversion hypothesis had already been ruled out for seductive images by prior work cited in the article
target_learners: undergraduate readers of expository scientific text
target_learning_goals: comprehension and situation-model construction from illustrated expository text
examples: Experiment 1 compared low- and high-WMC readers (prescreened with OSPAN and RSPAN) across nonillustrated, conceptually illustrated, and seductively illustrated conditions; Experiment 2 tracked their eye movements while reading the seductively illustrated text.

article_title: Knowledge as a formative construct: A good alpha is not always better
citation: Stadler, Matthias, Michael Sailer, and Frank Fischer. 2021. “Knowledge as a formative construct: a good alpha is not always better.” New Ideas in Psychology 60: 100832. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.newideapsych.2020.100832.
title: Formative versus reflective measurement models as a framework for relating constructs to their indicators
description: The article distinguishes two measurement models. In reflective models, "manifest indicators can be the effects" of latent variables, as with general intelligence; in formative models, indicators "form a latent construct or cause the changes that occur in it", as with socioeconomic status. The article uses this framework, adapted from Bollen and Lennox, to argue that domain knowledge assessment usually misfits reflective assumptions.
requirements: Researchers must provide persuasive theoretical arguments for the merit of each formative indicator, since inclusion or exclusion of an indicator changes the construct.
constraints: The article frames this as an argument about construct conceptualization in structural equation modeling, not a tested empirical result.
target_learners: students whose domain knowledge is assessed in educational research
target_learning_goals: valid assessment and modeling of domain knowledge
examples: The article contrasts general intelligence as a reflective example with socioeconomic status, where income, education and occupational prestige form the construct.

title: Match a knowledge assessment's measurement model to the construct's theoretical conceptualization before applying scale-quality criteria
description: The article argues researchers should check whether their theoretical conceptualization of a construct is represented in its empirical operationalization before applying reflective scale-development criteria. It concludes with the hope that researchers "review their assessments of domain knowledge" and consider whether conceptualization matches operationalization, since a mismatch "can lead to critical misrepresentation and misinterpretation".
requirements: A clear theoretical construct definition, including arguments for and against each indicator, is pivotal for formative models.
constraints: The article notes other, more general issues with Cronbach's alpha exist that it could not discuss, referring readers to Trizano-Hermosilla and Alvarado (2016).

citation: Steinert, S., Avila, K. E., Ruzika, S., Kuhn, J., & Küchemann, S. (2024). Harnessing large language models to develop research-based learning assistants for formative feedback. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-024-00354-1
title: LEAP: a web platform where teachers pre-prompt LLMs to assign tasks with formative feedback
description: LEAP (Learning with AI about Physics) is a web-based application that lets teachers create physics tasks and set instructions for the LLM without programming skills. Teachers complete four fields (task name, question, instructions for the LLM, correct answer) and share a link with students, who submit answers and receive LLM-generated formative feedback. The article states LEAP "empowers educators to create content and formulate prompts for the LLM" so that feedback types can be tailored without technical expertise. The platform uses Flask, SQLAlchemy, MariaDB, Gunicorn and Nginx, and currently offers OpenAI models, with GPT-4o mini free.

title: Six research-based scaffold types for LLM formative feedback
description: The article enumerates six types of scaffolds that systematic prompting can elicit from an LLM, rooted in educational research: cognitive sense-making, cognitive elaboration, cognitive self-explanation, cognitive partial task solution, metacognitive scaffolds, and motivational scaffolds. title: Self-regulated learning as interplay of cognition, metacognition, and motivation, supported by formative feedback
description: The article's theoretical background frames self-regulated learning as a mental activity in which individuals control thoughts, actions, and feelings to steer their learning, built on three key processes: cognition (acquiring knowledge and understanding), metacognition ("thinking about thinking", i.e., planning, monitoring, and adjusting strategies), and motivation (the readiness to exert effort toward goals). Formative feedback delivered during learning is presented as a crucial component for supporting these SRL strategies by stimulating metacognitive processes such as self-monitoring. LEAP is designed to address all three dimensions through different prompt types.

citation: Steinert, S., Avila, K. E., Ruzika, S., Kuhn, J., & Küchemann, S. (2024). Harnessing large language models to develop research-based learning assistants for formative feedback. Smart Learning Environments. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40561-024-00354-1
title: Synchronize educational technology advances with empirical research and theoretical frameworks
description: The article argues that deploying LLMs in education should be guided by empirically validated theories from pedagogy, didactics, and educational psychology rather than by technology alone, since simply providing information via an interface is insufficient for learning. The authors emphasize "the critical importance of synchronizing educational technological advances with empirical research and theoretical frameworks" so that LLM applications in education are positive and effective. LEAP's prompt design operationalizes this by grounding each feedback type in cited prior research.

constraints: The authors note that empirical research is indispensable to verify the learning gains and the effectiveness of feedback provided by LLMs

article_title: Guidance during mathematical problem solving.
citation: Ahmad Tarmizi, Rohani. (1991). Guidance During Mathematical Problem Solving. Doctoral thesis, University of New South Wales. http://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/69310
title: Split-attention cognitive load account of guidance effects
description: The thesis explains its experimental results through cognitive load and attention: guidance such as worked examples normally reduces load and directs attention appropriately, helping schema acquisition. However, domains like geometry require learners to "mentally integrate multiple sources of information, resulting in splitting of attention", which raises load and eliminates the guidance benefit. Presenting information in a unitary format removes the split, restoring the worked-example advantage.
requirements: Guidance material must avoid requiring learners to mentally integrate multiple, physically separated sources of information for the benefit to appear
constraints: The benefit of worked examples and similar guidance is eliminated in areas such as geometry where multiple sources must be integrated and attention is split
target_learners: school mathematics students
novice problem solvers
target_learning_goals: acquisition of problem-solving schemas in mathematics and science
examples: Circle geometry problems in which text and diagram were first separated (splitting attention) and then presented in a unitary, integrated format across Experiments 1-5

article_title: Guidance during mathematical problem solving.
citation: Ahmad Tarmizi, Rohani. (1991). Guidance During Mathematical Problem Solving. Doctoral thesis, University of New South Wales. http://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/69310
title: Means-ends analysis as a problem-solving strategy that inhibits learning
description: Means-ends analysis is a general problem-solving strategy in which the solver reduces the difference between the current state and the goal state by applying appropriate operators, creating subgoals when operators cannot be applied. The thesis reviews evidence that most novice problem solvers use it, hypothesizes that it imposes heavy cognitive load and misdirects attention compared to studying worked examples, and therefore treats it as a mechanism that can inhibit schema acquisition during learning.
requirements: A problem with a defined goal state and operators that reduce differences between current and goal states
constraints: Applied mainly by solvers not highly familiar with the subject matter; the thesis argues its search for operators consumes working-memory resources that could otherwise go to schema acquisition
target_learners: novice problem solvers in mathematics and science
target_learning_goals: schema acquisition and rule automation rather than mere solution of a given problem
examples: GPS, the General Problem Solver, solving Tower of Hanoi and other transformation problems via means-ends analysis; water-jug experiments showing move selection governed by the means-ends heuristic

article_title: Self-regulated learning training programs enhance university students’ academic performance, self-regulated learning strategies, and motivation: A meta-analysis
citation: Theobald, M. (2021). Self-Regulated Learning Training Programs Enhance University Students' Academic Performance, Self-Regulated Learning Strategies, and Motivation: A Meta-Analysis. Contemporary Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cedpsych.2021.101976
title: SRL strategy taxonomy: cognitive, metacognitive, and resource management strategies within a three-phase cyclical process
description: The article organizes self-regulated learning as a dynamic, cyclical process in which "learning sessions can be divided into three phases: a preparatory phase, a performance phase, and an appraisal phase." Learners' strategies are classified into three families: cognitive strategies (rehearsal, elaboration, organization) that acquire and integrate knowledge; metacognitive strategies (goal setting and planning, monitoring, reflection) that monitor and control cognition across all phases; and resource management strategies regulating internal resources (attention, effort, motivation) and external resources (learning environment, time management). The article uses this taxonomy to categorize training outcomes in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Training programs must address the specific SRL strategy families (cognitive, metacognitive, resource management) that the taxonomy distinguishes for their effects to be classified and compared.
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategies
academic performance
motivation

article_title: The spacing effect in free recall emerges with development
citation: Thomas C. Toppino and William DiGeorge. (1984). The spacing effect in free recall emerges with development. Memory & Cognition, 12(2), 118-122. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+spacing+effect+in+free+recall+emerges+with+development+Memory+%26+Cognition+1984
title: Deficient-processing and encoding-variability theories of the spacing effect
description: The article organizes spacing-effect explanations into two major categories. Deficient-processing theories explain "poor memory for massed repetitions" by assuming one presentation is not fully processed, with processing increasing as spacing grows; encoding-variability theories hold that "repetition facilitates mem­ory to the extent that each presentation is encoded differently, thereby establishing more ways to access the information at retrieval." The authors evaluate both categories against their developmental findings.
requirements: An adequate general account must incorporate processes that become active later in childhood rather than relying solely on automatic encoding processes operative from early infancy
constraints: The authors state that encoding variability theories are often vague about whether variable encoding is involuntary or the result of voluntary strategies
target_learners: preschool children
first-grade children
adult learners
target_learning_goals: memory for repeated information in free recall
examples: The authors judge the voluntary-attention deficient-processing theory most compatible with their results, assuming the strategy of not fully processing the second occurrence of a massed repetition develops between roughly ages 4 and 6
key_sources: Thomas C. Toppino and William DiGeorge. (1984). The spacing effect in free recall emerges with development. Memory & Cognition, 12(2), 118-122. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+spacing+effect+in+free+recall+emerges+with+development+Memory+%26+Cognition+1984

article_title: The spacing effect in free recall emerges with development
citation: Thomas C. Toppino and William DiGeorge. (1984). The spacing effect in free recall emerges with development. Memory & Cognition, 12(2), 118-122. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+spacing+effect+in+free+recall+emerges+with+development+Memory+%26+Cognition+1984
title: Accounts of the spacing effect must include processes acquired or developed during childhood, not only hard-wired mechanisms
description: The article argues that because the spacing effect in free recall is absent in preschoolers but present in first-graders, explanations "cannot rely solely on automatic encoding processes that are operative from early infancy, but must incorpo­rate processes that become active later in childhood." Any hard-wired mechanism suggested by infant recognition data may be limited to recognition memory, with free recall depending on developed or acquired processes.
requirements: An adequate account must explain why the spacing effect emerges between approximately ages 4 and 6
constraints: If a primitive mechanism underlies the spacing effect in free recall, it is apparently not sufficient to produce the phenomenon until augmented by other developing processes
target_learners: preschool children
first-grade children
target_learning_goals: memory for repeated information
examples: The authors propose that a voluntary strategy of diverting attention from the second occurrence of massed repetitions may be acquired between ages 4 and 6, consistent with the developmental trend for attention to become increasingly active and directed

article_title: ChatGPT improves creative problem-solving performance in university students: An experimental study
citation: Urban, M., Děchtěrenko, F., Lukavský, J., Hrabalová, V., Svacha, F., Brom, C., & Urban, K. (2024). ChatGPT Improves Creative Problem-Solving Performance in University Students: An Experimental Study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105031
title: Hybrid human-AI regulation (HHAIR) theory as applied to metacognitive demands of ChatGPT-assisted problem-solving
description: Hybrid human-AI regulation theory (attributed to Molenaar) holds that working with generative AI demands strong metacognitive skills because learners combine their own ideas with AI output: they must "select relevant information, reiterating and clarifying ideas, debugging errors, and adjusting their approach to ensure coherence and meaningfulness." The study uses the theory to motivate hypotheses about self-efficacy, monitoring accuracy, metacognitive experiences, and mental effort when solving ill-defined tasks with ChatGPT, and concludes that effective regulation requires students to attend to valid metacognitive cues rather than perceived ease.
requirements: Learners must possess or develop metacognitive monitoring and self-evaluation skills to assess AI-generated and self-generated ideas
Students must perform accurate self-evaluation of final outcomes containing both student- and ChatGPT-generated ideas
constraints: The study reports that perceived ease and usefulness act as invalid cues, so regulation based on metacognitive experiences alone may be inaccurate
target_learners: university students using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: creative problem-solving on ill-defined tasks
metacognitive monitoring and self-evaluation of AI-assisted work
examples: The preregistered experiment measured self-efficacy, self-evaluation bias, task interest, difficulty, and mental effort with and without ChatGPT during a Product Improvement Task

article_title: ChatGPT improves creative problem-solving performance in university students: An experimental study
citation: Urban, M., Děchtěrenko, F., Lukavský, J., Hrabalová, V., Svacha, F., Brom, C., & Urban, K. (2024). ChatGPT Improves Creative Problem-Solving Performance in University Students: An Experimental Study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105031
title: Students using generative AI should ground self-evaluations in valid metacognitive cues rather than perceived ease of AI-assisted problem-solving
description: The article recommends that "To regulate effectively, students using AI tools should focus on valid metacognitive cues instead of the perceived ease of ChatGPT-assisted problem-solving." This follows from its findings that ChatGPT lowered perceived difficulty and effort, yet lower perceived difficulty and higher perceived usefulness of ChatGPT were each associated with overestimating one's performance. Instruction that makes these invalid cues explicit may help learners calibrate self-evaluations of AI-assisted outcomes.
requirements: Learners need awareness that perceived ease and perceived usefulness of AI are unreliable indicators of solution quality and originality
constraints: Supporting evidence is exploratory correlation; the article states these results require further investigation and come from a single laboratory task with limited ecological validity
target_learners: university students
students using generative AI in higher education
target_learning_goals: accurate self-evaluation and metacognitive calibration of AI-assisted problem-solving
examples: The experiment measured self-evaluation bias indices and found higher perceived usefulness of ChatGPT associated with greater overestimation despite no correlation with actual performance

article_title: Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives
citation: Tamara van Gog & Nikol Rummel. (2010). Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9134-7
title: Social-cognitive account of observational learning: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation as subfunctions
description: The review presents Bandura's account of how modeling examples work: observers acquire a cognitive (symbolic) representation of the model's behavior that outlasts the modeling situation, so "observational learning can occur without imitation taking place". Effective observational learning requires attention to the relevant aspects of modeled behavior, retention via constructive encoding and rehearsal, ability to reproduce depending on representation quality and component skills, and motivation determining whether the behavior is exhibited. The review uses this to explain why model characteristics and attentional processes matter in modeling example design.
requirements: The learner must pay attention to the relevant aspects of the modeled behavior
constraints: Modeled behavior that is too complex for the learner may result in fragmentary learning; novices may have difficulty detecting errors and may rehearse faulty behavior
target_learners: novices
children
adults in training settings
target_learning_goals: acquisition of cognitive and motor skills through observation
key_sources: Tamara van Gog & Nikol Rummel. (2010). Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9134-7

article_title: Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives
citation: Tamara van Gog & Nikol Rummel. (2010). Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9134-7
title: Cognitive load explanation of why worked examples outperform unsupported problem solving for novices
description: The review explains the worked example effect via cognitive load theory: conventional problems force novices into weak strategies like means-ends analysis, which "imposes a high load on working memory but is not effective for learning", contributing little to schema construction. Worked examples prevent these weak strategies, allowing learners to devote cognitive capacity to studying the worked-out solution procedure and constructing a cognitive schema. The same theory underpins design guidelines (split-attention, redundancy) and delivery strategies such as fading and random sequencing.
requirements: Examples designed to avoid split-attention and redundancy so capacity goes to schema construction
constraints: Effect applies to novices; guidance reverses for knowledgeable learners
target_learners: novice learners
target_learning_goals: building cognitive schemas for problem solving
key_sources: Tamara van Gog & Nikol Rummel. (2010). Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9134-7

article_title: Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives
citation: Tamara van Gog & Nikol Rummel. (2010). Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9134-7
title: Design worked examples to avoid split-attention and redundancy
description: The review reports that early worked-example research showed example study is not always more effective than problem solving and that design plays a crucial role. This yielded guidelines to "avoid split-attention by integrating mutually referring information sources such as text and picture/diagram" and to avoid redundancy, presenting multiple information sources only when both are necessary for comprehension, since an easily-understood-in-isolation source should be left out. Spoken rather than written text can also integrate pictorial information.
requirements: Mutually referring information sources (text and picture/diagram) must be physically or temporally integrated
constraints: Redundant sources should be omitted only when they can be easily understood in isolation
target_learners: novice learners
target_learning_goals: learning problem-solving procedures from worked examples
examples: Tarmizi and Sweller's work on split-attention in geometry examples; Mousavi et al. providing spoken rather than written text with pictorial information
