article_title: Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion
citation: Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2011). Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9080-x
title: On-line versus off-line methods for assessing strategy use
description: The article distinguishes two families of strategy-use assessment. On-line methods, such as thinking aloud, observation, eye-movement registration, and logfile registration, take "measurements taken concurrent to task performance" and code actual behavior against externally defined criteria. Off-line methods, such as questionnaires (e.g., MSLQ) and interviews, ask learners about strategy use before or after performance, so answers rest on reconstruction from memory of past experiences. The article uses this framework to evaluate the five special-issue instruments.
requirements: On-line methods need to be individually administered and coded according to a coding scheme; logfile coding systems must be validated with other on-line methods for each new task and learner group
constraints: Thinking aloud may be incomplete (tip-of-the-iceberg) and intrusive for poor readers; observations and logfiles capture only overt behavior; off-line methods risk memory failure and distortion
target_learners: learners during reading and text studying
target_learning_goals: assessment of cognitive and metacognitive strategy use
examples: Schellings' task-specific questionnaire and Bräten and Strømsø's MTSI are classified as retrospective off-line questionnaires; Magliano et al.'s RSAT indirect questioning is also off-line, with questions posed after each sentence disappears
key_sources: Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2011). Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9080-x

article_title: Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion
citation: Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2011). Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9080-x
title: Three levels of strategy use: availability deficiency, prompted use, and spontaneous production
description: The article distinguishes three levels of strategy use relevant to interpreting prompted assessments: "(1) inadequate strategy use due to an availability deficiency, (2) prompted use of available strategies that may otherwise suffer from a production deficiency, and (3) spontaneously produced strategies." Prompted assessment methods such as MC-question enactment can detect availability deficiencies but cannot separate prompted use from spontaneous use.
requirements: Distinguishing all three levels requires assessments conducted first without prompting and only then with prompting (Veenman et al. 2000, 2005)
constraints: Prompting strategy use prior or concurrent to task performance restricts the scope of assessments to availability deficiencies; confidence ratings may assess inadequate calibration but not spontaneous use of calibration strategies
target_learners: learners being assessed for reading strategy use
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of spontaneous versus prompted strategy use
examples: Cromley and Azevedo's prompted enactment method provides valuable information about level 1 but cannot distinguish levels 2 and 3
key_sources: Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2011). Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9080-x

article_title: Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion
citation: Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2011). Alternative assessment of strategy use with self-report instruments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9080-x
title: Treat off-line self-report assessments of strategy use as prone to memory-reconstruction and prompting threats, and pursue more validation work
description: The article's concluding recommendation: designers and users of strategy-use assessments should remain aware that "off-line methods might suffer from memory-reconstruction and prompting problems that produce flawed answers to retrospective questions." Prompting prior or concurrent to task performance restricts assessment scope to availability deficiencies. Despite inventive new instruments, more validation work is needed against the three validity criteria.
requirements: New assessment methods require thorough examination to gain understanding of what these methods precisely are measuring
constraints: Memory-reconstruction and prompting problems cannot be entirely resolved by minimizing delay or task-specific wording; they only mitigate the problem
target_learners: learners whose strategy use is assessed with self-report instruments
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of reading strategy use
examples: The discussion reviews the five special-issue instruments under the three validity criteria and concludes not all of them passed the test

article_title: Self-Determination and Positive Adult Outcomes: A Follow-up Study of Youth with Mental Retardation or Learning Disabilities
citation: Michael Wehmeyer, Michelle Schwartz. (1997). Self-Determination and Positive Adult Outcomes: A Follow-Up Study of Youth with Mental Retardation or Learning Disabilities. Exceptional Children, 63(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Self-Determination+and+Positive+Adult+Outcomes+Wehmeyer+Schwartz
title: Wehmeyer's definitional framework of self-determination as acting as the primary causal agent in one's life, with four essential characteristics
description: The article defines self-determination as "acting as the primary causal agent in one's life and making choices and decisions regarding one's quality of life free from undue external influence or interference". An act is self-determined if it reflects four essential characteristics: the individual acts autonomously, the behaviors are self-regulated, the person acts in a psychologically empowered manner, and the person acts in a self-realizing manner. The framework was empirically validated with more than 400 adults with mental retardation and operationalized in The Arc's Self-Determination Scale.
requirements: Measurement requires a validated instrument capturing each essential characteristic, as operationalized in The Arc's Self-Determination Scale
constraints: The framework was developed and validated with people with cognitive disabilities; the article measures it via self-report for adolescents with cognitive disabilities

students with mental retardation or learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: self-determination as an educational and transition outcome
autonomy, self-regulation, psychological empowerment, and self-realization
examples: The Arc's Self-Determination Scale was used to measure students with mental retardation and learning disabilities during their final year of high school

It was normed with 500 students with and without cognitive disabilities in rural, urban, and suburban districts in five states.

article_title: Artificial intelligence in language instruction: impact on English learning achievement, L2 motivation, and self-regulated learning
citation: Wei L (2023) Artificial intelligence in language instruction: impact on English learning achievement, L2 motivation, and self-regulated learning. Front. Psychol. 14:1261955. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1261955
title: Vygotskian social constructivism and the ZPD as a framework for AI as a collaborative partner in language learning
description: The study grounds its design in Vygotsky's social constructivism, in which "These interactions serve as cognitive scaffolding, supporting less proficient learners in the acquisition and development of their knowledge". The Zone of Proximal Development has two levels: an actual level of independent ability and a potential level realized through interaction with more capable peers or tools. In this framing, the AI tool acts as the more proficient partner: experimental-group learners "engage with an AI-assisted language learning tool, which serves as a collaborative partner in the language learning process", advancing toward their ZPD, while control learners scaffold one another through peer interaction. The framework links AI interaction to the transition from other-regulation to self-regulation.
requirements: Learners must engage in interactive, collaborative language learning activities with the AI tool or proficient peers for scaffolding to occur
constraints: The article presents the ZPD framing as an interpretive lens; it does not test scaffolding mechanisms directly
target_learners: university EFL learners with intermediate English proficiency
target_learning_goals: English grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing skills; L2 motivation; self-regulated learning
examples: Experimental learners used Duolingo as a collaborative partner while control learners worked with peers in teacher-led classes over the same 10 weeks

title: Duolingo AI-mediated language learning platform used to deliver personalized EFL instruction
description: Duolingo served as the AI-mediated instructional platform for the experimental group over a 10-week intervention. Learners had access to "interactive exercises, online quizzes, language games, and real-time feedback tailored to their individual performance on the platform", with at least 2 hours per week of supplementary out-of-class use. The control group received traditional instruction with textbooks, lectures, grammar drills, and writing exercises for the same duration. Interview participants described the platform as engaging, adaptive to their pace, and convenient for practice anywhere.

constraints: Studied with intermediate-proficiency Chinese university EFL learners with no prior AI-mediated instruction experience

article_title: The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021
citation: Weiqi Xu and Fan Ouyang. (2022). The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-022-00377-5
title: General system theory frames AI-STEM as an organic system of five interdependent elements
description: The review adopts general system theory (GST) as its organizing framework, arguing that a system is greater than the sum of its parts. From this perspective, AI-STEM is viewed as an organic system containing five basic elements: subject (instructor, learner), information (learning content), medium (carrier of information), environment (educational context), and technology (AI techniques as an external element). The framework was operationalized as a coding scheme applied to 63 empirical articles, with Krippendorff's alpha reliability of 0.91 among two raters, to examine how AI integrates with and influences the other elements and their mutual relationships.
requirements: The framework requires identifying the internal elements of the educational system and the functional relationships between them, per the article's holistic principle
constraints: Technology (e.g., AI techniques) is treated as an external element impacting the functions of the educational system, as the article states
target_learners: Instructors and learners in STEM education across kindergarten to higher education
target_learning_goals: Holistic understanding of how AI technologies integrate with STEM educational systems
examples: The authors coded 63 AI-STEM articles on dimensions including instructor involvement, instructional strategy, educational level, sample size, learning outcome, learning content, medium, context, and AI technique

article_title: The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021
citation: Weiqi Xu and Fan Ouyang. (2022). The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-022-00377-5
title: Six categories of AI applications in STEM education with sub-categories
description: The review's central taxonomy classifies AI applications in STEM education into six categories: learning prediction, intelligent tutoring system, student behavior detection, automation, educational robots, and others. Each category is further divided into sub-categories, e.g., learning prediction splits into learning performance prediction (N = 14) and at-risk student prediction (N = 4); intelligent tutoring systems split into instructional content delivery, recommendation of personalized learning path, and resource recommendation. The taxonomy emerged from content analysis of 63 empirical studies published 2011–2021 and serves as the review's answer to its first research question.
requirements: Classification was based on a GST-derived coding scheme applied by two raters with consensus on conflicting codes
constraints: Only AI-supported robots were included, since robots contain various techniques and the review considered the research topic
target_learners: STEM learners from kindergarten through higher education
target_learning_goals: Selecting and applying AI techniques to support STEM instruction and learning
examples: Learning prediction was the largest category (N = 18, 29%), followed by intelligent tutoring systems (N = 16, 25%) and student behavior detection (N = 13, 21%)

article_title: The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021
citation: Weiqi Xu and Fan Ouyang. (2022). The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-022-00377-5
title: Integrate AI into STEM education by considering the whole educational system, not merely applying AI technologies
description: The review's guiding principle is that high-quality STEM education with AI requires holistic integration rather than technology deployment alone. As the article states, achieving a high quality of STEM education requires careful consideration of complex social, pedagogical, environmental factors rather than merely applying AI technologies. Grounded in general system theory, applying AI as an external technology element influences the other system elements (subject, information, medium, environment) and the relationships between them, so selection of AI techniques should adapt to these multiple elements.
requirements: AI technique selection must adapt to the multiple elements (e.g., subject, information, environment) in STEM education with the goal of high-quality instruction and learning
constraints: The article notes the field is confronted with the challenge of integrating diverse AI techniques in the complex STEM educational system
target_learners: STEM learners and instructors across educational levels
target_learning_goals: High-quality STEM instruction and learning supported by AI technologies
examples: The review mapped how each AI category distributed across learning contents, instructional strategies, educational levels, media, and contexts to inform integration decisions

article_title: The effects of hypertext glosses on L2 vocabulary acquisition: a meta-analysis
citation: Yun, J. H. (2008). The Effects of Hypertext Glosses on L2 Vocabulary Acquisition: A Meta-Analysis. Doctoral dissertation, University of Kansas. https://kuscholarworks.ku.edu
title: Mayer's Generative Theory of Multimedia Learning as the theoretical basis for hypertext gloss effects on L2 vocabulary
description: The dissertation adopts Mayer's Generative Theory of Multimedia Learning, built on Paivio's dual coding theory, as its organizing framework. It holds that the brain has separate visual and verbal coding systems, and that "both pictorial and written input collaboratively enhance L2 readers' reading comprehension and vocabulary learning" when learners integrate the two representations. Learners must select relevant verbal and visual information, build coherent verbal and visual mental representations, and connect them. The framework motivates the text + visual versus text-only comparison tested in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Learners must be cognitively capable of dealing with both written and pictorial information at the same time, as the article states better vocabulary learning with multimedia input is more likely under that condition.
constraints: The article notes low-proficiency learners are less likely to take advantage of multimedia learning environments due to high cognitive load when given two types of annotations, so multimedia input does not always enhance all learners' vocabulary performance.
target_learners: L2 learners (ESL/EFL, SFL, JFL, GFL) at university or college level reading computerized texts
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary acquisition during computerized reading
Reading comprehension of authentic L2 texts
examples: The dissertation's meta-analysis of text-only versus text + visual gloss conditions was framed as a test of this theory's prediction that combined verbal and pictorial input benefits vocabulary learning.

Data were collected via game learning analytics for 15 months, with 4124 users playing more than 28187 games.

article_title: When you know that you know and when you think that you know but you don’t
citation: Zechmeister, E. B., & Shaughnessy, J. J. (1980). When you know that you know and when you think that you know but you don't. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 15(1), 41-44. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03334497
title: Attenuation of attention hypothesis with an overconfidence basis: learners underprocess massed repetitions because they believe massed items are already known
description: The attenuation of attention hypothesis explains the spacing effect by asserting that "learners pay less atten­tion to massed repetitions than to distributed repetit ions" because massed repetitions occur near the item's initial presentation. This article supplies the missing reason for that inattention: retrieved ease at a massed repetition gives undue confidence of memory strength, so learners judge MP items as already learned and skip further processing. The MP-over-DP rating overconfidence found in the experiment supports this account.
requirements: The learner must make (implicit or explicit) judgments about an item's encoding status at the time of a massed repetition
constraints: The article notes results are equally consistent with underestimation of recall likelihood for DP items rather than overestimation for MP items
Further study is needed, per the authors, to determine factors that facilitate or retard accuracy of judging what is known
target_learners: college students studying verbal material
target_learning_goals: free recall of verbal items
calibration of self-assessment of learning during study
examples: Subjects rated MP items as more recallable than DP items in every study block while recalling them less well, supporting the assumption that the inattention to massed presentations stems from overestimating memory for them
key_sources: Zechmeister, E. B., & Shaughnessy, J. J. (1980). When you know that you know and when you think that you know but you don't. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 15(1), 41-44. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03329756

article_title: When you know that you know and when you think that you know but you don’t
citation: Zechmeister, E. B., & Shaughnessy, J. J. (1980). When you know that you know and when you think that you know but you don't. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 15(1), 41-44. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03334497
title: Do not rely on learners' sense of knowing for massed-repetition study: ease of re-encountering an item breeds unwarranted confidence
description: Because learners "think that they know" massed-presented items when they do not, self-assessments made immediately after massed repetition are unreliable guides for study decisions. The principle warns students and instructors that fluency at re-encountering material can produce undue confidence, so judgments of knowing should not be trusted for closely repeated material when deciding whether further study is needed.
requirements: A study situation in which learners monitor their own learning and allocate further effort accordingly
constraints: The article's evidence concerns within-list massed vs. distributed repetition of common nouns in free recall; the basis of the monitoring inaccuracy was not specified by the results
target_learners: college students
students preparing for examinations
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of learning
effective allocation of study time
examples: Students who claim after a poor exam, "I thought I really knew the material" may have equated time spent studying with amount learned while processing was inadequate for permanent memory registration

article_title: Student differences in self-regulated learning: Relating grade, sex, and giftedness to self-efficacy and strategy use.
citation: Martínez Bernal, J. A. (2017). Efecto del automonitoreo en el logro de aprendizaje, su relación con el estilo de aprendizaje y estilo cognitivo en un ambiente web de aprendizaje. Tesis doctoral, Universidad Pedagógica Nacional. https://biblioteca.upn.edu.co
title: Modelo de integración entre metacognición y autorregulación con el monitoreo metacognitivo como eje
description: La tesis construye un marco teórico que recoge la metacognición vista como proceso de monitoreo y control y la integra con el ciclo del aprendizaje autorregulado. Según el texto, se analiza el ciclo del aprendizaje autorregulado y "se presenta un modelo de integración que toma como eje el monitoreo metacognitivo". El modelo articula las fases de previsión, implementación y autorreflexión, y reconoce tres momentos clave para promover el automonitoreo: la autoevaluación, el monitoreo de las estrategias y de su implementación, y el monitoreo de los esfuerzos de adaptación. Este modelo fundamenta el diseño de los mensajes metacognitivos del andamiaje computacional.
requirements: Comprender el ciclo de la metacognición a partir de la interacción entre el nivel objeto y el nivel meta, activada por el flujo de información generado por las estrategias de monitoreo y control
constraints: El texto señala que la mejor estrategia para promover el automonitoreo en ambientes virtuales parece todavía no estar clara, e incluso que esta acción podría competir con el propio proceso de aprendizaje
target_learners: Estudiantes universitarios, en particular estudiantes de medicina en ambientes web
target_learning_goals: Desarrollo de habilidades metacognitivas de automonitoreo y autorregulación del aprendizaje

title: Andamiaje metacognitivo computacional con mensajes genéricos y específicos en un curso web de Monitoreo Hemodinámico del Paciente Adulto
description: Elemento instruccional desarrollado para entregar mensajes metacognitivos en los módulos del 1 al 6 de un curso web. Los mensajes "se envían antes y después de cada evaluación", con características diferentes según el grupo: los del grupo AABW-1 son genéricos y promueven el automonitoreo de las categorías gruesas de las fases del ciclo de aprendizaje autorregulado, mientras que los del grupo AABW-2 son específicos y promueven de forma puntual el monitoreo de cada subcategoría del ciclo. El ambiente incluyó el test de estilo cognitivo (EFT), el test de Grasha y el cuestionario MSLQ, y culminó con una prueba estandarizada de conocimiento.
requirements: Un ambiente web de aprendizaje con módulos de contenido y evaluaciones periódicas en torno a las cuales se entregan los mensajes metacognitivos
constraints: El grupo de control no recibió ningún tipo de mensaje metacognitivo, lo que define el contraste evaluado en el estudio
target_learners: Estudiantes de medicina de educación superior
target_learning_goals: Logro de aprendizaje en contenido del curso y desarrollo de habilidades de automonitoreo metacognitivo
examples: Los grupos experimentales recibieron mensajes metacognitivos genéricos y específicos, respectivamente, y el grupo de control no recibió ningún tipo de mensaje metacognitivo

article_title: From Gatekeeping to Engagement: A Multicontextual, Mixed Method Study of Student Academic Engagement in Introductory STEM Courses
citation: Gasiewski, J. A., Eagan, M. K., Garcia, G. A., Hurtado, S., & Chang, M. J. (2012). From Gatekeeping to Engagement: A Multicontextual, Mixed Method Study of Student Academic Engagement in Introductory STEM Courses. Research in Higher Education, 53, 229–261. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11162-011-9247-y
title: Behavioral academic engagement in introductory STEM, measured as an eight-item student-behavior construct
description: The study operationalizes engagement as mainly behavioral, drawing on Fredricks et al.'s multifaceted construct that includes behavioral, emotional, and cognitive dimensions but focusing on observable academic task involvement. Eight items compose the factor: "frequency with which students asked questions in class, discussed course grades or assignments with the instructor, attended professor's office hours, participated in class discussions, tutored other students in their introductory STEM course, reviewed class material before it was covered, attended review or help sessions to enhance understanding of course content, and studied with students from their introductory STEM course." Principal axis factoring yielded a single factor (Cronbach's α = 0.75), with emotional-engagement items loading separately.
requirements: Survey items capturing the eight behavioral indicators must be administered to students currently enrolled in the course
constraints: The construct intentionally excludes emotional and cognitive engagement, which the factor analysis showed load separately
Engagement is self-reported and behavioral; grades and persistence outcomes are not measured directly
target_learners: Undergraduate students in introductory STEM courses
target_learning_goals: Academic engagement behaviors supporting persistence in STEM majors
examples: Used as the dependent variable in a three-level HLM across 2,873 students, 73 courses, and 15 institutions

citation: Gasiewski, J. A., Eagan, M. K., Garcia, G. A., Hurtado, S., & Chang, M. J. (2012). From Gatekeeping to Engagement: A Multicontextual, Mixed Method Study of Student Academic Engagement in Introductory STEM Courses. Research in Higher Education, 53, 229–261. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11162-011-9247-y
title: In introductory STEM courses, signal openness to student questions and take responsibility for student success to support engagement
description: Because behavioral engagement depends on the classroom context instructors create, instructors should consistently signal accessibility cues: welcoming even elementary questions, acknowledging their role in helping students succeed, and making time for individualized attention. The HLM showed "Faculty agreement: In my classroom, there is no such thing as a question that is too elementary" positively predicted engagement, while agreeing that success is primarily up to students or that there is not enough time for individualized attention negatively predicted it. Reducing lecture time in favor of discussion and group work complements this climate work.
requirements: Faculty must convey genuine accessibility cues rather than simply stating policies; students' felt comfort asking questions is the proximate predictor
constraints: Course-level climate variables account for a marginal share of engagement variance (3.1% across classrooms), so instructor climate alone will not transform student engagement
target_learners: Undergraduates in large introductory STEM gatekeeper courses
target_learning_goals: Behavioral academic engagement, including question-asking, help-seeking, and collaboration
examples: Faculty survey items measured instructor agreement with statements about classroom climate, and the authors discuss instructional implications of signaling openness to questions and a role in student success

article_title: Face-to-Face Interaction with Pedagogical Agents, Twenty Years Later
citation: W. Lewis Johnson & James C. Lester. (2015). Face-to-Face Interaction with Pedagogical Agents, Twenty Years Later. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0065-9
title: Pedagogical agents as autonomous characters cohabiting learning environments
description: The pedagogical agent concept, as formulated in the authors' 2000 article, conceptualizes agents as autonomous characters that cohabit learning environments with students to create rich, face-to-face learning interactions. The framework emphasizes the multimodal, visually embodied nature of agents and enumerates capabilities including interactive demonstrations, navigational guidance, gaze and gesture as attentional guides, nonverbal feedback, conversational signals, conveying and eliciting emotion, virtual teammates, and adaptive pedagogical interaction. The article traces how the concept evolved, with researchers dropping animated and extending the concept to static images, and how roles diversified into teachable agents, learning companions, and virtual role-players.
requirements: The choice of agent realization (animated, static image, or disembodied voice) depends on the educational context and the agent's role in that context
constraints: Relatively little work since 2000 on interactive demonstrations and navigational guidance, because most agents do not cohabit virtual worlds with learners
target_learners: K-12 students
university students
training audiences in business, defense, intelligence, and healthcare
target_learning_goals: domain learning supported by interactive learning environments
cultural and language training
team training
examples: STEVE demonstrating interactive demonstrations and navigational guidance in virtual environments; Herman the Bug giving nonverbal feedback including cartwheels across the screen

article_title: Face-to-Face Interaction with Pedagogical Agents, Twenty Years Later
citation: W. Lewis Johnson & James C. Lester. (2015). Face-to-Face Interaction with Pedagogical Agents, Twenty Years Later. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0065-9
title: Alelo VCAT Virtual Cultural Awareness Trainers with multi-role Virtual Coach
description: VCATs are training systems in which learners acquire knowledge about other cultures and apply it in simulated encounters with virtual role-players, with advice and feedback from a Virtual Coach. The Virtual Coach shifts realization across the course: animated character at the start, fading to a less obtrusive presence, narrator as a disembodied voice, off-screen coach during role-plays popping up as a static image, and fading away entirely at the end so learners demonstrate the task unassisted. VCATs have been developed for over 80 countries and over 50,000 trainees have taken VCAT courses, providing evidence about which agent realizations fit which roles.
requirements: The agent's role must be clear to learners; the authors found that an unclear role can have a negative effect on learning effectiveness, as when one agent played both teammate and coach in Tactical Iraqi
constraints: For virtual role-players there are very few instances in which it makes sense for them to be disembodied voices
target_learners: adult trainees in cultural awareness courses
target_learning_goals: cross-cultural knowledge and intercultural interaction skills
examples: Separating role-player and coach functions in VCATs allowed the coach to fade away while role-playing functions continued

title: RALL-E robot-assisted language learning prototype
description: RALL-E (Robot-Assisted Language Learning in Education) is an Alelo project that migrates agent technology to the Robokind R25 robot, producing a prototype that can engage in conversation in Chinese. The concept is being tested in collaboration with the Virginia Department of Education and the Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology in Alexandria, Virginia. Embedding agent technology into the robot lets learners engage naturally in mixed-initiative conversation more than with a screen-displayed agent; the approach descends from the STEVE work in that agent and learners cohabit a shared world, but the robot enters the learners' real world rather than learners entering the agent's virtual world.
requirements: Robot hardware enabling the pedagogical agent to enter the real world of the learners
target_learners: high school language learners
target_learning_goals: Chinese language conversation practice
examples: The prototype robot can engage in conversation in Chinese

article_title: Coaching effectiveness: the coach–athlete relationship at its heart
citation: Jowett, S. (2017). Coaching Effectiveness: The Coach-Athlete Relationship at its Heart. Current Opinion in Psychology, 16, 154-158. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2017.05.006
title: The 4Cs operational model of coach-athlete relationship quality
description: The article describes the 4Cs model, which gives operational meaning to the quality of the coach-athlete relationship. It comprises closeness, reflecting an affective bond through mutual respect, trust, appreciation and liking; commitment, reflecting thoughts of maintaining a close relationship over time; complementarity, reflecting interpersonal behaviours of leadership and co-operation; and co-orientation, reflecting interdependence in views of the relationship. The review positions this quality as a medium allowing coaches and athletes to express wishes and fulfil ambitions, and as a barometer of coaching effectiveness.
requirements: Measurement of the quality dimensions requires validated instruments; the review notes that development and validation of Coach-Athlete Relationship Questionnaires facilitated the measurement of closeness, commitment and complementarity
target_learners: athletes in sport coaching contexts
target_learning_goals: coaching effectiveness
performance and wellbeing of athletes and coaches
examples: The review cites a series of qualitative studies exploring content and functions of successful and less successful relationships, operationalised through the 4Cs
key_sources: Jowett, S. (2017). Coaching Effectiveness: The Coach-Athlete Relationship at its Heart. Current Opinion in Psychology, 16, 154-158. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2017.05.006

article_title: Coaching effectiveness: the coach–athlete relationship at its heart
citation: Jowett, S. (2017). Coaching Effectiveness: The Coach-Athlete Relationship at its Heart. Current Opinion in Psychology, 16, 154-158. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2017.05.006
title: System model of coaching effectiveness placing the dyadic relationship at its heart
description: The article proposes a system model, depicted in Figure 1, where the coach and the athlete are placed at the heart of coaching effectiveness, with coaches' and athletes' knowledge and outcomes as important interconnected factors, all embedded in the sport and personal context alongside leadership, communication and conflict. It argues that coaches and athletes are locked into a two-person (dyadic) relationship whose quality can offer a measure of coaching and its effectiveness, and that over time it is the working relationship that is likely to determine what knowledge is required to bring about important outcomes.
requirements: Conceptual and operational clarity in defining coaching effectiveness; the review states that conceptualisations not accompanied by clear operationalisations are difficult to quantify and reliably measure
target_learners: coaches
athletes
target_learning_goals: understanding coaching effectiveness
coaching practice and education
examples: Figure 1 depicts coach and athlete knowledge, relationship and outcomes interconnected within the sport and personal context, with leadership, communication and conflict as additional factors

article_title: Coaching effectiveness: the coach–athlete relationship at its heart
citation: Jowett, S. (2017). Coaching Effectiveness: The Coach-Athlete Relationship at its Heart. Current Opinion in Psychology, 16, 154-158. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2017.05.006
title: Adopt a coach-athlete-centred rather than solely athlete-centred or coach-centred view of coaching
description: The article recommends viewing coaching as coach-athlete-centred rather than athlete-centred or coach-centred. It argues that when coaching is viewed as either athlete-centred or coach-centred, its scope, quality and functions become restricted, whereas the coach-athlete-centred view is inclusive and mutually empowering, and that neither the coach nor the athlete can do it alone. The relationship becomes the medium that motivates, assures, satisfies, comforts and supports both parties to enhance sport experience, performance and well-being.
requirements: Coaches and athletes must develop and maintain a relationship in which both engage with one another, since effective coaching is understood through the quality of the connections they develop
constraints: The article frames this as a conceptual proposal supported by anecdotal and empirical evidence rather than a tested intervention
target_learners: coaches
athletes
target_learning_goals: coaching effectiveness
long-term development, personal growth and transformation
examples: The review cites Nash and colleagues' finding that expert coaches plan and execute training sessions with individual athletes' needs in mind, which it argues is achievable only when coaches and athletes connect in ways that allow trust, commitment, and mutual understanding

article_title: Race and gender differences in how sense of belonging influences decisions to major in STEM
citation: Katherine Rainey, Melissa Dancy, Roslyn Mickelson, Elizabeth Stearns and Stephanie Moller. (2018). Race and gender differences in how sense of belonging influences decisions to major in STEM. International Journal of STEM Education 5:10. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-018-0115-6
title: An intersectional account of STEM sense of belonging structured by four contributing factors
description: The article organizes students' belonging reports through an intersectional lens: identity axes of race and gender "are not unitary and mutually exclusive, but instead interact to construct one's identity." Within this framework, belonging is explained by four coded factors—interpersonal relationships, science identity, personal interest, and competence—defined for both having and lacking each reason (Table 1). The framework also links belonging to representation: demographic similarity to others in a field is described as positively impacting belonging. It is used descriptively to interpret who persists in and leaves STEM majors.
requirements: Data must capture students' self-reported belonging and permit disaggregation by race and gender intersections, which the article's interview protocol and coding scheme were designed to do
constraints: The study recorded only two axes of identity, race and gender, a limitation the authors acknowledge
Findings come from a self-selected purposive sample of North Carolina college seniors, which the authors say restricts generalizability beyond the sample
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students
women and students of color in STEM
target_learning_goals: persistence and retention in STEM majors
sense of belonging in STEM fields
examples: Interview codes applied to responses about belonging, e.g., a white female biology major coded as having interpersonal relationships said, 'Most of my friends are biology majors. I feel like it's where I belong.'

article_title: Gap Analysis: An Innovative Look at Gateway Courses and Student Retention
citation: Bloemer, W., Day, S., & Swan, K. (2017). Gap analysis: An innovative look at gateway courses and student retention. Online Learning, 21(3), 5-14. https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v21i3.1233
title: Judge course effectiveness relative to predicted DFW rates for the enrolled population rather than by raw DFW rankings alone
description: The article argues institutional attention should go to courses whose observed outcomes deviate from expectations. It predicts DFW probability per student using student type, life-cycle stage, prior GPA and prior DFW fraction, then computes the "difference (Gap) between them" to rank courses. This avoids misplaced or harmful fixes on courses simply serving a difficult population.
requirements: Predictive model of DFW probability per student using student type, academic-life-cycle stage, prior cumulative GPA, and fraction of previous courses with DFW grades
Institutional records linking end-of-term grades to courses over multiple years
constraints: Expected-rate approaches may need to differ across institutions based on local factors impacting student success
Very low observed DFW rates against substantial predicted rates may indicate grade inflation or concern rather than effectiveness
target_learners: undergraduate degree-seeking students
gateway-course students
target_learning_goals: course completion
retention and degree completion
examples: Courses with alarmingly high raw DFW rates receded out of the alarm range when gaps were considered, and a mid-ranked course rose into the top 5 by gap
key_sources: Bloemer, W., Day, S., & Swan, K. (2017). Gap analysis: An innovative look at gateway courses and student retention. Online Learning, 21(3), 5-14. https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v21i3.1233

article_title: Gap Analysis: An Innovative Look at Gateway Courses and Student Retention
citation: Bloemer, W., Day, S., & Swan, K. (2017). Gap analysis: An innovative look at gateway courses and student retention. Online Learning, 21(3), 5-14. https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v21i3.1233
title: Gateway-course effects are mediated by student type and academic stage rather than uniform across students
description: The article's organizing account is that course effectiveness must be judged in context: students enter "with widely different backgrounds and learning goals" and "change significantly over the course of their studies." It operationalizes this by classifying students into four Student Types (Native Freshmen, Honors Freshmen, On-ground Transfers, Online Transfers) and five life-cycle stages (First Term, Second Term, Second Year, Third Year, Later), and predicting outcomes from these plus prior GPA and DFW fraction. The authors state the results "plainly suggest that the effects of gateway courses are mediated by student types and academic stages."
requirements: Classification of students by entry type (freshman vs transfer, honors, online vs on-ground) and academic life-cycle stage
Course-level grade and persistence records tied to short-term enrollment measures
constraints: Results are clearly limited to the undergraduate population at the university studied
target_learners: undergraduate degree-seeking students
first-time freshmen
transfer students
target_learning_goals: predicting course success
retention and degree completion
examples: The four-year institutional dataset at a small Midwestern public university was analyzed with binary logistic regression predicting DFW probability per course
key_sources: Bloemer, W., Day, S., & Swan, K. (2017). Gap analysis: An innovative look at gateway courses and student retention. Online Learning, 21(3), 5-14. https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v21i3.1233

article_title: Gap Analysis: An Innovative Look at Gateway Courses and Student Retention
citation: Bloemer, W., Day, S., & Swan, K. (2017). Gap analysis: An innovative look at gateway courses and student retention. Online Learning, 21(3), 5-14. https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v21i3.1233
title: Gap-analysis method for identifying gateway courses via predicted versus observed DFW rates and persistence gaps
description: A learning-analytics method using institutional student records. A binary logistic regression predicts the probability a student posts a D, F, or W grade using Student Type, life-cycle stage, prior cumulative GPA, and prior DFW fraction; predicted and observed rates are recorded per course and "the difference (Gap) between them calculated." A second gap compares persistence of students in a course to students in all courses of the same type at the same degree-path point, by student type and stage.
requirements: Multi-year institutional records of end-of-term grades and next-term enrollment or graduation
Student classification into types and life-cycle stages
Predictive model including prior GPA and prior fraction of DFW grades, which "is known to add predictive power over prior GPA alone"
constraints: DFW rates use end-of-term grades rather than final transcript grades
Persistence is measured as enrollment in the next regularly scheduled term or graduation
target_learners: undergraduate degree-seeking students
target_learning_goals: identifying courses needing intervention
improving retention
examples: Applied to 34 general education courses at a small Midwestern public university over four years
key_sources: Bloemer, W., Day, S., & Swan, K. (2017). Gap analysis: An innovative look at gateway courses and student retention. Online Learning, 21(3), 5-14. https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v21i3.1233

article_title: Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process
citation: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244
title: Participatory research as an umbrella research-to-action approach
description: The article defines participatory research (PR) as an "umbrella term for research designs, methods, and frameworks" that "use systematic inquiry in direct collaboration with those affected by the issue being studied for the purpose of action or change". PR replaces the "subjects" of traditional research with collaborators — stakeholders, community members, and end-users with insider knowledge and lived expertise — who share leadership in the research process. The article presents PR as valued across disciplines for solving complex problems and for producing research relevant to real-world contexts.
requirements: Direct engagement of local priorities and perspectives through partnerships between researchers and those with lived expertise of the issue
constraints: The specific PR approach and its nomenclature vary widely across disciplines
target_learners: Researchers new to participatory research
Community partners and stakeholders in collaborative inquiry
target_learning_goals: Conducting collaborative, democratic systematic inquiry
Translating research into real-world action
examples: The article describes an academic-community partnership using a citizen science approach to collect and interpret soil samples for environmental justice work
key_sources: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244

article_title: Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process
citation: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244
title: The choice-points model mapping participation decisions onto the research process
description: The article's central organizing model depicts "choice points" — "the intersection between participation and steps in the research cycle". At each and all phases of research, partners decide which tools and methods will produce the desired level of participation: stakeholders identify their needs and goals, researchers identify the fundamental needs of research, and academic-community partnerships work together to make choices meeting both. Choices may yield highly participatory strategies at some steps and more researcher-driven strategies at others; the article stresses "there is no prescription for the "right" way to do PR".
requirements: Stakeholders must identify their needs and goals of the research process
Researchers must identify the fundamental needs of research to provide the desired evidence, outcome, or impact
Academic-community partnerships must collaborate on the choices
constraints: Choices might lead to highly participatory strategies for some steps and more researcher-driven strategies at others; no single right way is prescribed
target_learners: Academic-community partnerships
Researchers designing participatory studies
target_learning_goals: Choosing research tools and methods that achieve the desired level of stakeholder participation at each research stage
examples: Figure 1 depicts participation choice points across the research process, and Figure 2 gives example participatory methods for each step
key_sources: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244

article_title: Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process
citation: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244
title: Engagement as a continuum from outreach to shared leadership
description: The article conceptualizes stakeholder engagement not as a dichotomy but as "a continuum ranging from academic-driven research to equitable shared decision making". It aligns three frameworks: an NIH continuum from outreach (researchers provide information) to shared leadership (final decision making at the community level); Key and colleagues' range from community informed to community driven; and the IAP2 Spectrum of Public Participation from inform to empower. The article draws one implication: "the choice of participation level is closely tied to the impact research will have in real world settings".
requirements: Deliberate choices about the desired level of participation at each stage
constraints: Terms and definitions differ across the three frameworks, though the implications are the same
target_learners: Community-engaged researchers
Community partners
target_learning_goals: Assessing and selecting appropriate levels of community engagement in research
examples: Community Advisory Boards tend to operate on the involve level; training neighborhood residents as co-researchers exemplifies the collaborate level
key_sources: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244

article_title: Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process
citation: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244
title: Table 1 taxonomy of participatory research frameworks, orientations, and approaches
description: Table 1 compiles the article's taxonomy of PR frameworks across disciplines, including action research, action learning, appreciative inquiry, asset-based community development, citizen science, community-based participatory research, decolonizing methodologies, participatory action research, participatory evaluation, popular education, practitioner inquiry, and user-centered design research. Each entry carries a definition, variations, and key sources. The article notes "the breadth of terms describing the PR orientation is vast", but the frameworks "share in common a value in doing research with those who are typically the subjects of research, rather than on them".
requirements: Used as a demonstration that researchers within almost every discipline view research as collaborative inquiry with goals beyond knowledge generation
constraints: The article states the table is not intended to be an exhaustive list of PR frameworks
target_learners: Researchers new to participatory research seeking an entry point into PR traditions
target_learning_goals: Recognizing PR orientations across disciplines and locating source literature
examples: Educational action research is listed as action research conducted in educational and school settings, with teacher action research as a variation
key_sources: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244

article_title: Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process
citation: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244
title: Any research method or tool can be made participatory through collaborative choice and use
description: The article argues that conventional methods like surveys and focus groups "are not off the table" in participatory research; they "can be adapted and re-thought so they are approached in a participatory way". Because "the distinguishing feature of participatory research is stakeholder power in decision making and implementation", the article concludes that "any research method or tool can be participatory if chosen and/or utilized collaboratively between academic and community partners".
requirements: Stakeholder power in decision making and implementation
Collaborative choice and/or use of the method by academic and community partners
constraints: Methods are participatory only when approached collaboratively; used conventionally, the same tools function at lower participation levels
target_learners: Academic-community partnerships
Researchers adapting conventional methods
target_learning_goals: Designing shared decision-making into data collection, analysis, and dissemination
examples: Focus groups co-designed, co-facilitated, and collaboratively analyzed by community co-investigators; collaboratively developed and administered community needs-assessment surveys
key_sources: Vaughn, L. M., & Jacquez, F. (2020). Participatory Research Methods – Choice Points in the Research Process. Journal of Participatory Research Methods, 1(1). https://doi.org/10.35844/001c.13244

article_title: A hierarchical model of cognitive flexibility in children: Extending the relationship between flexibility, creativity and academic achievement
citation: Arán Filippetti, Vanessa; Krumm, Gabriela Liliana (2020). A hierarchical model of cognitive flexibility in children: Extending the relationship between flexibility, creativity and academic achievement. Child Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2019.1711034
title: Hierarchical model of cognitive flexibility: spontaneous flexibility as a higher-level form distinct from lower-level shifting
description: The article proposes a hierarchical account in which cognitive flexibility comprises two related components: reactive flexibility and spontaneous flexibility. Spontaneous flexibility is characterized as "the ability to generate diverse responses driven by internal stimuli," and the authors raise "the question whether considering SF as a higher-level form of cognitive flexibility (different from a lower-level shifting skill) could be an interesting approach for the study of cognitive flexibility in children." The model is grounded in the two-factor CFA solution and the differential executive and academic-creativity correlates reported in the two studies.
requirements: Performance-based tasks capable of indexing reactive flexibility and spontaneous flexibility as separable factors in children
constraints: The hierarchical framing is raised as an open question for future study rather than asserted as an established finding
target_learners: children aged 8 to 13
target_learning_goals: cognitive flexibility
creative divergent response generation
reading comprehension
writing
examples: Study 1 (n = 112) fit a two-factor CFA solution; Study 2 (n = 177) linked spontaneous flexibility to creativity via hierarchical regressions and SEM models.
key_sources: Arán Filippetti, Vanessa; Krumm, Gabriela Liliana (2020). A hierarchical model of cognitive flexibility in children: Extending the relationship between flexibility, creativity and academic achievement. Child Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2019.1711034

article_title: “Visual” Cortex Responds to Spoken Language in Blind Children
citation: Bedny, M., H. Richardson, and R. Saxe. (2015). "Visual" Cortex Responds to Spoken Language in Blind Children. Journal of Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1523/jneurosci.0634-15.2015
title: In the absence of visual input, spoken language colonizes the visual system during brain development
description: The article proposes that early in life, human cortex has a remarkably broad computational capacity, such that "the same cortical tissue can take on visual perception and language functions." In blindness, "spoken language colonizes the visual system during brain development," with language responses appearing early and remaining stable while sound responses grow with age. The account explains why occipital cortex in blind individuals responds to sound and spoken language.
requirements: Requires the absence of visual input from early in development for spoken language to colonize occipital cortex.
constraints: The account is drawn from a cross-sectional developmental sample of blind and sighted children aged 4–17.
target_learners: blind children and adolescents
target_learning_goals: cortical specialization for language in the absence of visual input
examples: Blind and sighted children aged 4–17 listened to stories and two auditory control conditions (unfamiliar foreign speech, and music) while occipital responses were measured.
key_sources: Bedny, M., H. Richardson, and R. Saxe. (2015). "Visual" Cortex Responds to Spoken Language in Blind Children. Journal of Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1523/jneurosci.0634-15.2015

article_title: Adverse childhood experiences and trajectories of internalizing, externalizing, and prosocial behaviors from childhood to adolescence
citation: Leonardo Bevilacqua, Yvonne Kelly, Anja Heilmann, Naomi Priest, Rebecca E. Lacey. (2021). Adverse childhood experiences and trajectories of internalizing, externalizing, and prosocial behaviors from childhood to adolescence. Child Abuse & Neglect 112 (2021) 104890. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2020.104890
title: Consider both the number and the specific type of early stressors when predicting and intervening on children's mental health development
description: The article's conclusions state that accounting for both the count of stressors and their specific type helps predict mental health development and guide intervention. It reports that "taking into account not only the number of stressors that individuals are exposed to from very early age, but also the specific type of stressors, is helpful in predicting an individual's mental health development, and thus implement appropriate intervention programmes". This rests on the study's finding that ACE scores and individual ACEs each added information, with different ACEs showing different outcome-specific associations.
requirements: ACE information collected prospectively from early childhood, ideally from multiple informants
constraints: The study measured ACEs only at 9 months and 3 years and lacked data on sexual abuse, racial discrimination, and family antisocial behavior
target_learners: children from early childhood through adolescence
target_learning_goals: social-emotional development, including internalizing, externalizing, and prosocial behavior
examples: The study compared ACE score, individual ACE, and LCA cluster operationalisations against SDQ trajectories at ages 3, 5, 7, 11, and 14 in the Millennium Cohort Study
key_sources: Leonardo Bevilacqua, Yvonne Kelly, Anja Heilmann, Naomi Priest, Rebecca E. Lacey. (2021). Adverse childhood experiences and trajectories of internalizing, externalizing, and prosocial behaviors from childhood to adolescence. Child Abuse & Neglect 112 (2021) 104890. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2020.104890

article_title: Early Adverse Experiences and the Developing Brain
citation: Bick, J., Nelson, C. (2016). Early Adverse Experiences and the Developing Brain. Neuropsychopharmacol. https://doi.org/10.1038/npp.2015.252
title: Two distinct forms of early adversity: childhood maltreatment in family environments and extreme psychosocial deprivation in institutional rearing
description: The review organizes its account of early adversity around two distinct forms. The first is exposure to "childhood maltreatment in family environments", and the second is exposure to "extreme psychosocial deprivation in contexts of institutional rearing". The article treats these as separate experiences of adverse rearing, each imposing distinct challenges to the developing brain, and reviews evidence on each form's neurodevelopmental consequences and on intervention for each.
requirements: The framework applies to children exposed to these two adverse rearing conditions early in life.
constraints: The review's scope is limited to these two forms of adversity rather than all adverse experiences.
target_learners: children exposed to early-life adversity
target_learning_goals: understanding how adverse caregiving environments shape neurodevelopmental risk
examples: The review devotes parallel treatment to maltreatment in family settings and to institutional rearing as its two focal adversity types.
key_sources: Bick, J., Nelson, C. (2016). Early Adverse Experiences and the Developing Brain. Neuropsychopharmacol. https://doi.org/10.1038/npp.2015.252

article_title: Early Adverse Experiences and the Developing Brain
citation: Bick, J., Nelson, C. (2016). Early Adverse Experiences and the Developing Brain. Neuropsychopharmacol. https://doi.org/10.1038/npp.2015.252
title: Early adversity as violation of species-expected caregiving conditions that challenges the developing brain
description: The review proposes a mechanistic framing in which adverse early experiences are understood as departures from the caregiving conditions the species expects. It states that maltreatment and institutional rearing each "represent violations of species-expected caregiving conditions, thereby imposing challenges to the developing brain". On this account, neurodevelopmental risk arises because the developing brain is confronted with caregiving input outside the expected range, and the review uses this framing to organize its discussion of brain consequences and remediation.
requirements: Understanding the effects requires considering the caregiving environment children experience relative to species-expected conditions.
constraints: The account is presented as a framing discussion of the reviewed evidence, not as a directly tested model in the supplied text.
target_learners: children exposed to early-life adversity
target_learning_goals: explaining why atypical caregiving disrupts neurodevelopment
examples: The review applies this framing to both of its focal adversity forms, maltreatment and institutional rearing.
key_sources: Bick, J., Nelson, C. (2016). Early Adverse Experiences and the Developing Brain. Neuropsychopharmacol. https://doi.org/10.1038/npp.2015.252

article_title: Physical Activity and Cognitive Functioning of Children: A Systematic Review
citation: Bidzan-Bluma Ilona, Lipowska Małgorzata. (2018). Physical Activity and Cognitive Functioning of Children: A Systematic Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph15040800
title: Model of the influence of sport on children's physical, mental, and social resources
description: The authors developed a model, presented in Figure 2, outlining how sport influences three resource domains in children in late childhood: physical resources (e.g., physical fitness, motor skills), mental resources (cognitive functioning, executive functions, motivation, ability to set goals, self-control, and emotional functioning), and social resources (e.g., social support, fostering positive values, and etiquette). The model holds that these results are relevant "independent of whether the physical activity is unorganized free play or organized activity, such as for a sports club and school activities". It synthesizes the review's findings across attention, thinking, language, learning, and memory.
requirements: Based on the review's included studies of physical activity and cognition in children; the authors built it on prior models (McMorris et al.; Diehl et al.)
constraints: Developed from a review whose included studies were limited in number, cultural balance, and methodological quality, per the authors' own limitations section
target_learners: children in late childhood (pre-adolescence)
target_learning_goals: cognitive functioning, executive functions, emotional functioning, social values
examples: The review's Figure 2 depicts the model of sport's influence on physical, mental, and social resources, developed by the authors.
key_sources: Bidzan-Bluma Ilona, Lipowska Małgorzata. (2018). Physical Activity and Cognitive Functioning of Children: A Systematic Review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph15040800

article_title: Orthographic learning during reading: the role of whole‐word visual processing
citation: Marie-Line Bosse, Nathalie Chaves, Pierre Largy, Sylviane Valdois. (2015). Orthographic learning during reading: the role of whole-word visual processing. Journal of Research in Reading, 38, pp.141-158. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01551.x
title: Self-teaching hypothesis: orthographic knowledge is acquired incidentally during reading through phonological recoding
description: The self-teaching hypothesis holds that knowledge of words' orthographic structure is acquired incidentally as children read, driven by phonological recoding of the printed string. In this article it frames the research question: the study tested whether visual processing of the whole letter string additionally contributes to orthographic learning beyond recoding. The authors conclude that "the ability to process the entire orthographic letter string at once during reading contributes to efficient orthographic learning", extending the account.
requirements: Reading experience with decodable letter strings, since acquisition occurs incidentally during reading through phonological recoding.
target_learners: French children in third to fifth grade learning to read
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of word-specific orthographic knowledge (spelling) during reading
examples: The study asked French children to read pseudowords and then assessed memorisation of the targets' orthographic form.
key_sources: Marie-Line Bosse, Nathalie Chaves, Pierre Largy, Sylviane Valdois. (2015). Orthographic learning during reading: the role of whole-word visual processing. Journal of Research in Reading, 38, pp.141-158. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01551.x

article_title: Inhibitory control and counterintuitive science and maths reasoning in adolescence
citation: Brookman-Byrne A, Mareschal D, Tolmie AK, Dumontheil I (2018) Inhibitory control and counterintuitive science and maths reasoning in adolescence. PLoS ONE 13(6): e0198973. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0198973
title: Inhibitory control account of counterintuitive reasoning: naïve theories and misleading cues persist and must be suppressed
description: The article endorses the account that learning counterintuitive science and maths concepts does not replace prior concepts: "prior beliefs remain in the face of new evidence" and misconceptions persist into adulthood. Inhibitory control, "the ability to suppress a prepotent response or irrelevant information", is thought to allow suppression of naïve theories, incorrect strategies, or misleading perceptual cues during counterintuitive reasoning. The study's findings that semantic inhibition related to accuracy and response inhibition to reaction times are offered as further support for this hypothesis in adolescence.
requirements: Reasoning about concepts where a misconception may be held, so that an intuitive response competes with the correct counterintuitive answer
constraints: The article states the association between inhibitory control and counterintuitive reasoning is correlational; intervention studies would be needed to establish causality, which the current paper could not address directly
target_learners: Adolescents aged 11–15 years in secondary school science and maths
target_learning_goals: Counterintuitive science and maths reasoning aligned with the Key Stage 3 curriculum
examples: The study measured response inhibition with simple and complex Go/No-Go tasks and semantic inhibition with a numerical Stroop task, alongside a novel 48-problem-set science and maths misconceptions task
key_sources: Brookman-Byrne A, Mareschal D, Tolmie AK, Dumontheil I (2018) Inhibitory control and counterintuitive science and maths reasoning in adolescence. PLoS ONE 13(6): e0198973. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0198973

article_title: A meta-analytic investigation of the role of reward on inhibitory control
citation: Burton, S., Knibb, G., & Jones, A. (2021). A meta-analytic investigation of the role of reward on inhibitory control. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1177/17470218211008895
title: Inhibitory control as a transient, motivation-sensitive state rather than a stable trait
description: The article frames inhibitory control not as a fixed trait but as a state that fluctuates with motivational context, drawing on value-based models in which "IC is a value-based process and represents a trade-off between short- and long-term rewards". Reward prospect raises the momentary value (gain) of inhibition relative to its costs, so expression of IC depends on internal and external factors. The meta-analytic reward effect is presented as support for this account.
requirements: Requires tasks in which reward for successful inhibition is manipulated against a no-reward control condition
constraints: The article could not examine reactive versus proactive control due to lack of data, so conclusions cannot be drawn about which mechanism reward affects
target_learners: Adults
Children and adolescents
Clinical populations including ADHD and substance use disorder
target_learning_goals: Improving inhibitory control and self-regulation through motivational context
examples: The meta-analysis pooled rewarded versus non-rewarded inhibition trials across stop signal, go/no-go, Flanker, Simon, Stroop, and Anti-saccade tasks
key_sources: Burton, S., Knibb, G., & Jones, A. (2021). A meta-analytic investigation of the role of reward on inhibitory control. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1177/17470218211008895

article_title: Development and Plasticity of Cognitive Flexibility in Early and Middle Childhood
citation: Buttelmann F and Karbach J (2017). Development and Plasticity of Cognitive Flexibility in Early and Middle Childhood. Front. Psychol. 8:1040. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01040
title: Metacognitive EF training: qualitatively changing how children engage executive functions to support flexible adaptation and transfer
description: The review proposes metacognitive training as a promising new approach to promoting cognitive flexibility in childhood. Unlike training that enhances the quantity of EF children can engage, it would "change qualitatively how they engage EF as a function of task diﬃculty", training children to reflect on how to approach new tasks by weighing the costs (e.g., mental effort) and benefits (e.g., rewards) of available control strategies. Because this approach is relatively task-unspecific, the authors argue it may support transfer of flexibility training to untrained tasks and abilities.
requirements: Training should encourage performance evaluation, including error detection and feedback processing, which are still gradually developing in young children.
constraints: The approach is proposed on the basis of a few recent studies; the review states metacognitive instructions have rarely been applied in cognitive-training research and mechanisms of training and transfer effects are not fully understood.
target_learners: typically developing children from preschool to elementary school age
target_learning_goals: cognitive flexibility and executive function development
transfer of training to untrained tasks
examples: Espinet et al. trained 2- to 4-year-olds with corrective feedback and reflection instructions; Moriguchi et al. had preschoolers explain task rules to a puppet.
key_sources: Buttelmann F and Karbach J (2017). Development and Plasticity of Cognitive Flexibility in Early and Middle Childhood. Front. Psychol. 8:1040. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01040

article_title: Fitness, physical activity and academic achievement in overweight/obese children
citation: Cadenas-Sanchez, C., Migueles, J. H., Esteban-Cornejo, I., Mora-Gonzalez, J., Henriksson, P., Rodriguez-Ayllon, M., Molina-García, P., Löf, M., Labayen, I., Hillman, C. H., Catena, A., & Ortega, F. B. (2020). Fitness, physical activity, and academic achievement in overweight/obese children. Journal of Sports Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2020.1729516
title: Public health strategies should improve multiple aspects of fitness, not only cardiorespiratory fitness, to support academic achievement in children with overweight/obesity
description: The article recommends that interventions and public health strategies target the full set of health-related fitness components rather than cardiorespiratory fitness alone. The authors state that "public health strategies should focus on improving multiple aspects of fitness as an effective approach to enhance academic achievement in children", grounded in their finding that muscular strength and speed-agility, alongside cardiorespiratory fitness, were positively associated with academic outcomes in children with overweight/obesity. The recommendation is framed as requiring verification by future randomized controlled trials.
requirements: Future randomized controlled trials are needed to verify the cross-sectional associations before causal claims can be made
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional and cannot draw causality
Most fitness associations attenuated or disappeared after adjustment for BMI and cardiorespiratory fitness
The limited sample size, especially in the 1-RM or school grade outcomes, reduces the power of the analyses
target_learners: Children aged 8-11 years with overweight/obesity
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement including language, mathematics, and science skills
examples: The ActiveBrains project, a randomized controlled trial of a 20-week physical activity intervention in children with overweight/obesity, within which this baseline analysis was conducted
key_sources: Cadenas-Sanchez, C., Migueles, J. H., Esteban-Cornejo, I., Mora-Gonzalez, J., Henriksson, P., Rodriguez-Ayllon, M., Molina-García, P., Löf, M., Labayen, I., Hillman, C. H., Catena, A., & Ortega, F. B. (2020). Fitness, physical activity, and academic achievement in overweight/obese children. Journal of Sports Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2020.1729516

article_title: The longitudinal association between children’s growth mindset in senior primary school and their parents’ growth mindset
citation: Jiao Chen and Chunhui Liu. (2023). The longitudinal association between children’s growth mindset in senior primary school and their parents’ growth mindset. Front. Psychol. 14:1110944. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1110944
title: Identity control and intergenerational transmission accounts of how parental beliefs shape children's mindsets
description: The article frames parental influence on children's growth mindset through intergenerational transmission theory, in which parental characteristics pass to offspring via genes and environment, and identity control theory, under which children perceive others' attitudes, compare them with their own standards, and adjust. The article states that when children find that parents believe ability can change through effort, they internalize this belief, so "children’s perceived parental beliefs and behaviors can predict their mindset." This framework motivates testing mothers' and fathers' trajectories separately.
requirements: Parents and children must interact regularly so that children can perceive parental beliefs and behaviors during parenting
constraints: The article notes previous studies have not found a direct correlation between parents' mindset and children's mindset, so the framework's empirical support in this study is limited to the maternal paths found
target_learners: senior primary school children (grades 4–6)
target_learning_goals: children's beliefs about the malleability of ability (growth mindset)
examples: The study tested the framework with five-wave parallel process latent growth models separating fathers and mothers, finding support only for maternal paths
key_sources: Jiao Chen and Chunhui Liu. (2023). The longitudinal association between children’s growth mindset in senior primary school and their parents’ growth mindset. Front. Psychol. 14:1110944. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1110944

article_title: Students’ Sense of Belonging at School in 41 Countries
citation: M.M. Chiu, B.W.Y. Chow, C. McBride, S.T. Mol. (2016). Students’ sense of belonging at school in 41 countries: cross-cultural variability. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022022115617031
title: An ecological model of students' sense of belonging at school spanning country, family, school, teacher, and student levels
description: The article proposes an ecological model in which students' sense of belonging at school (SOBAS) is related to attributes at multiple nested levels: countries (egalitarianism, collectivism), families (immigrant status, language, SES, books, wealth, communication), schoolmates (SES, social communication), teachers (teacher-student relationship, support, disciplinary climate), and students (reading achievement, self-efficacy, self-concept). As the abstract states, "This ecological model shows how attributes at multiple levels are related to SOBAS." The model organizes the study's multilevel analyses of 193,073 students in 41 countries.
requirements: Multilevel analyses linking attributes at country, family, school, teacher, and student levels to SOBAS, as in the study's survey and test data from 41 countries
target_learners: 15-year-old students in secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Students' sense of belonging at school
examples: The study examined whether SOBAS differed across attributes of countries, families, schools, teachers, or students using multilevel analyses of survey and test data.
