article_title: Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind
citation: I.K. Christoffels, L. Steenbergen, W.P.M. van den Wildenberg, L.S. Colzato. (2015). Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind. Psychological Research, 79(3), 371-379. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-014-0575-3
title: Global–local switching paradigm as a measure of cognitive flexibility and attentional processing style
description: The global–local switching paradigm is the behavioral task used in this study to assess cognitive control in high-school students. The article describes it as a task that "provides well-established measures of cognitive flexibility and attentional processing style". Students in both the bilingual-education and regular-education groups performed the paradigm, and its switching costs and global precedence effect served as the outcome measures contrasting the two groups.
requirements: Administered to both comparison groups so switching costs and the global precedence effect can be contrasted between educational programs
target_learners: Dutch high-school students
target_learning_goals: Assessment of cognitive flexibility and attentional processing style
examples: Two groups of Dutch high-school students, one taught in English and Dutch and one in regular Dutch classes, performed the paradigm in this study
key_sources: I.K. Christoffels, L. Steenbergen, W.P.M. van den Wildenberg, L.S. Colzato. (2015). Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind. Psychological Research, 79(3), 371-379. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-014-0575-3

article_title: Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind
citation: I.K. Christoffels, L. Steenbergen, W.P.M. van den Wildenberg, L.S. Colzato. (2015). Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind. Psychological Research, 79(3), 371-379. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-014-0575-3
title: Bilingual language use requires and trains a flexible mindset for rapid switching between languages
description: The article's explanatory account holds that managing two languages places demands on cognitive control: "Speaking two languages (or more) requires people to develop a flexible mindset to rapidly switch back and forth between languages". On this view, the daily practice of moving between languages exercises domain-general cognitive flexibility, which is why the authors predicted and found smaller switching costs and a reduced global precedence effect in bilingually educated students. The study is offered as support for the idea that bilingual education promotes cognitive flexibility.
requirements: Sustained use of and switching between two languages, as in bilingual education programs, to exercise the flexible mindset
target_learners: High-school students in bilingual education programs
target_learning_goals: Development of cognitive flexibility and attentional control through bilingual language use
examples: The authors predicted that bilingually educated students would show smaller switching costs and a decreased global precedence effect, and reported both results
key_sources: I.K. Christoffels, L. Steenbergen, W.P.M. van den Wildenberg, L.S. Colzato. (2015). Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind. Psychological Research, 79(3), 371-379. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-014-0575-3

article_title: Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind
citation: I.K. Christoffels, L. Steenbergen, W.P.M. van den Wildenberg, L.S. Colzato. (2015). Two is better than one: bilingual education promotes the flexible mind. Psychological Research, 79(3), 371-379. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-014-0575-3
title: Offer bilingual education to promote students' cognitive flexibility and a focused scope of attention
description: The article recommends bilingual education as a route to cognitive benefits: "Our findings support the idea that bilingual education promotes cognitive flexibility and a bias towards a more focused 'scope' of attention". Teaching students in both English and Dutch, rather than only in Dutch, was associated with smaller switching costs and a decreased global precedence effect on a well-established switching paradigm. The principle treats the bilingual curriculum itself as the design lever for these executive advantages.
requirements: Instruction delivered in two languages (English and Dutch in this study) rather than a single-language regular curriculum
constraints: Evidence comes from a comparison of two groups of Dutch high-school students on one paradigm; the abstract reports no effect sizes
target_learners: High-school students
target_learning_goals: Cognitive flexibility
Focused attentional scope
examples: Dutch high-school students followed either regular classes in Dutch or were taught in both English and Dutch, and completed a global–local switching paradigm

article_title: Where science starts: Spontaneous experiments in preschoolers’ exploratory play
citation: Cook, Claire, Noah D. Goodman, and Laura E. Schulz. (2011). Where Science Starts: Spontaneous Experiments in Preschoolers' Exploratory Play. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2011.03.003
title: Expected-information-gain framework: integrating prior knowledge about causal hypotheses with knowledge about possible actions
description: The article frames exploratory play with probabilistic models of expected information gain. On this account, learners integrate "prior knowledge about causal hypotheses" with "knowledge about possible actions that might generate data relevant to those hypotheses"; the action side is captured by affordances, or "action possibilities", in the environment. The article uses this framework to predict when preschoolers' play will be selective versus indiscriminate, testing it by manipulating stimulus properties and cause base rates.
requirements: The framework requires integrating prior knowledge about causal hypotheses with knowledge about possible actions that might generate relevant data
target_learners: preschool children (mean age 54 months)
target_learning_goals: causal learning through exploratory play
scientific inquiry skills such as variable isolation
examples: The article manipulated the physical properties of stimuli and the base rate of candidate causes and observed children's exploratory play under ambiguous and unambiguous evidence.
key_sources: Cook, Claire, Noah D. Goodman, and Laura E. Schulz. (2011). Where Science Starts: Spontaneous Experiments in Preschoolers' Exploratory Play. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2011.03.003

article_title: Cognitive and environmental predictors of early literacy skills
citation: Davidse, N. J., de Jong, M. T., Bus, A. G., Huijbregts, S. C. J., & Swaab, H. (2010). Cognitive and environmental predictors of early literacy skills. Read Writ 24, 395–412. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-010-9233-3
title: Book-cover recognition test as a proximal measure of children's book exposure
description: A child-completed test in which children are shown covers of 41 familiar Dutch picture storybooks and asked who the characters are, what the story is called, and what it is about; coders judge whether the child is acquainted with the book, excluding mere knowledge of merchandised characters. The article presents it as "a new instrument—the book-cover recognition test—as a proximal measure of children's book exposure in research and individual assessments of children's literacy environment". In this study it mediated the HLE–literacy relationship and outperformed questionnaire-based HLE measures.
requirements: Picture books selected from top sales and library lending lists so items vary in familiarity
Coding that distinguishes genuine story knowledge from merchandising-based character recognition
constraints: Alpha reliability was .67 in this study
Stainthorp (1997) warned title-recognition scores can be inflated when books are serialized on television
target_learners: Preschool and junior kindergarten children (ages 4–5)
target_learning_goals: Assessing children's book exposure as a predictor of vocabulary and letter knowledge
examples: Children recognized on average 2.68 (SD = 2.34) of 41 book covers; intercoder reliability for the test was .78
key_sources: Davidse, N. J., de Jong, M. T., Bus, A. G., Huijbregts, S. C. J., & Swaab, H. (2010). Cognitive and environmental predictors of early literacy skills. Read Writ 24, 395–412. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-010-9233-3

article_title: Cognitive and environmental predictors of early literacy skills
citation: Davidse, N. J., de Jong, M. T., Bus, A. G., Huijbregts, S. C. J., & Swaab, H. (2010). Cognitive and environmental predictors of early literacy skills. Read Writ 24, 395–412. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-010-9233-3
title: Share books with all preschool children regardless of their cognitive control skills
description: The study's implication is that book sharing benefits young children across the cognitive control spectrum: "The results also support the hypothesis that book sharing is beneﬁcial for all children. So far, there is no evidence for the hypothesis that effects of book exposure depend on child characteristics such as cognitive control skills." Educators and parents therefore need not gate shared-reading opportunities on children's short-term memory, inhibition, or sustained attention in the preschool years.
requirements: Book exposure opportunities in the preschool period (home, daycare, preschool, or library settings)
constraints: Evidence is correlational; causality cannot be concluded
Tested only in a homogeneous low-to-middle SES native Dutch sample; moderation may emerge in less homogeneous groups or when children practice independently (e.g., from Grade 1)
target_learners: Preschool and junior kindergarten children
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary growth and early code-related (letter) knowledge
examples: In the study, children below and above the median on cognitive control measures benefited equally from book exposure as indicated by the book-cover recognition test

article_title: The unique role of verbal memory, vocabulary, concentration and self-efficacy in children’s listening comprehension in upper elementary grades
citation: E. de Bree, M. Zee. (2021). The unique role of verbal memory, vocabulary, concentration and self-efficacy in children's listening comprehension in upper elementary grades. First Language. https://doi.org/10.1177/0142723720941680
title: Models of listening comprehension assigning a dominant role to vocabulary, extendable to broader student-related resources
description: The article engages with models of listening comprehension that give vocabulary a dominant role across the elementary years. The authors state the findings "relate to models of listening comprehension that state a dominant role for vocabulary, also in the upper elementary years," and that the results "imply that the models could extend to evaluating broader student-related resources, such as academic self-efficacy." The study's SEM results on 442 children support the vocabulary pathway and motivate extending such models beyond linguistic skills.
requirements: Applicable to modeling listening comprehension contributors across elementary grades, including upper elementary years
constraints: The authors note findings on general cognitive resources fit a pattern of mixed findings in previous research, motivating further research into contributors throughout the elementary years
target_learners: Upper elementary school children aged 9-12
target_learning_goals: Listening comprehension of oral texts
examples: Structural equation models of 442 children's oral text comprehension, vocabulary, verbal memory, self-efficacy and concentration

article_title: Effects of physical activity on executive functions, attention and academic performance in preadolescent children: a meta-analysis
citation: de Greeff, J. W., Bosker, R. J., Oosterlaan, J., Visscher, C., & Hartman, E. (2018). Effects of physical activity on executive functions, attention and academic performance in preadolescent children: a meta-analysis. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport, 21(5), 501-507. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsams.2017.09.595
title: Subdomain taxonomy for physical activity effects: four executive function, three attention and three academic performance subdomains
description: The meta-analysis organises its outcome measures into a taxonomy of cognitive and academic subdomains: "Four subdomains of executive functions (inhibition, working memory, cognitive flexibility and planning), three subdomains of attention (selective, divided and sustained) and three subdomains of academic performance (mathematics, spelling and reading) were distinguished." This structure lets intervention effects be quantified separately per subdomain and by study design, activity type and intervention duration. It frames how the reviewed intervention studies' outcomes were classified and pooled.
requirements: Intervention studies must measure outcomes in terms of the distinguished subdomains for effects to be pooled within them
constraints: Applied to preadolescent children aged 6-12 and to intervention studies published between 2000 and April 2017
target_learners: preadolescent children aged 6-12
target_learning_goals: executive functions
attention
academic performance
examples: The review pooled 31 intervention studies and estimated effects separately for acute versus longitudinal designs and for aerobic versus cognitively engaging activity.

article_title: A review of control processes and their locus in language switching
citation: Mathieu Declerck & Andrea M. Philipp. (2015). A review of control processes and their locus in language switching. Psychon Bull Rev. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-015-0836-1
title: Language switching paradigms: cued, alternating, voluntary, and sequence-based variants for studying language control
description: The review organizes language switching research around four paradigms that differ in how languages and concepts are cued: cued switching with visual language cues, alternating switching with predictable sequences, voluntary switching based on endogenous choices, and sequence-based language switching (SBLS) with memorized sequences and no visual cues or stimuli. The authors state that "a large variety of language switching paradigms with individual strengths and weaknesses can be used to study language control in language switching." Each paradigm affords different manipulations, such as time-based intervals in cued switching and switch-rate measures in voluntary switching.
requirements: Bilingual participants and a task in which languages must be produced or comprehended on separate trials, with switch and repetition trials distinguishable
constraints: Comprehension studies generally do not implement explicit visual language cues, so cued switching research is mainly production-based
target_learners: Bilinguals across proficiency levels, including second language learners and highly proficient bilinguals
target_learning_goals: Understanding mechanisms and loci of bilingual language control during speech production and comprehension
examples: Meuter and Allport's cued paradigm used digits as concepts and colored rectangles as language cues; SBLS used overlearned sequences such as weekdays or numbers with an auditory response signal
key_sources: Mathieu Declerck & Andrea M. Philipp. (2015). A review of control processes and their locus in language switching. Psychon Bull Rev. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-015-0836-1

article_title: A review of control processes and their locus in language switching
citation: Mathieu Declerck & Andrea M. Philipp. (2015). A review of control processes and their locus in language switching. Psychon Bull Rev. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-015-0836-1
title: Models of language control propose divergent loci: concept level, lemma level, and processing outside language processing
description: The review contrasts control models by their proposed functional locus. The inhibitory control model (Green, 1998) explains switch costs via reactive, persisting inhibition; the BIA family accounts for comprehension-based control via language nodes inhibiting competing words; and non-inhibitory models propose language-cue activation instead. The authors note "several loci of language control have been proposed, ranging from the concept level, lemma level, and a processing stage outside of language processing," and that several models propose more than one locus, both within and outside language processing.
requirements: A processing-stage architecture of language production or comprehension in which candidate loci (concept, lemma, phonology, orthography) can be distinguished empirically
constraints: The review's main focus is on behavioral results; nonbehavioral evidence is treated only in other reviews
target_learners: Bilinguals across proficiency levels
target_learning_goals: Understanding where in the language processing system control mechanisms operate during bilingual language switching
examples: In the modified ICM, language schemas activate language nodes whose inhibition targets lemmas of the non-target language; the BIA+ distinguishes a word identification system from a task/decision system outside language processing
key_sources: Mathieu Declerck & Andrea M. Philipp. (2015). A review of control processes and their locus in language switching. Psychon Bull Rev. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-015-0836-1

article_title: Sweat it out? The effects of physical exercise on cognition and behavior in children and adults with ADHD: a systematic literature review
citation: Den Heijer, A. E., Groen, Y., Tucha, L., Fuermaier, A. B. M., Koerts, J., Lange, K. W., Thome, J., & Tucha, O. (2017). Sweat it out? The effects of physical exercise on cognition and behavior in children and adults with ADHD: a systematic literature review. J Neural Transm 124(Suppl 1):S3–S26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00702-016-1593-7
title: Three-axis categorization framework for exercise effects in ADHD: exercise type, effect duration, and outcome measure
description: The review organizes the exercise-in-ADHD literature along three axes: "exercise type (cardio versus non-cardio), duration of effects (acute versus chronic), and outcome measures (cognitive, behav- ioral/socio-emotional, and physical/(neuro) physiological)". Cardio exercise raises heart rate and oxygen use over relatively long durations (running, cycling, swimming); non-cardio exercise is performed at lower energy levels (yoga, walking, playground activity). Acute effects are those measurable up to 24 h after exercise; chronic effects persist beyond 24 h after interventions of one to ten weeks. All 29 tabulated studies are classified within this framework.
requirements: Studies must describe some form of exercise, include an ADHD group, and be written in English, with outcomes classifiable into the three outcome-measure categories.
constraints: The review deemed it unjustified to reliably compare effect sizes across studies because of profound variation in samples, medication use, tests, and designs.
target_learners: children with ADHD
adults with ADHD
target_learning_goals: executive functions
attention
behavioral and socio-emotional functioning
physical and (neuro)physiological outcomes
examples: The review tabulated 29 studies (25 in children, 4 in adults) within this framework, calculating Cohen's d effect sizes where possible.

article_title: Sweat it out? The effects of physical exercise on cognition and behavior in children and adults with ADHD: a systematic literature review
citation: Den Heijer, A. E., Groen, Y., Tucha, L., Fuermaier, A. B. M., Koerts, J., Lange, K. W., Thome, J., & Tucha, O. (2017). Sweat it out? The effects of physical exercise on cognition and behavior in children and adults with ADHD: a systematic literature review. J Neural Transm 124(Suppl 1):S3–S26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00702-016-1593-7
title: Offer physical exercise as a promising alternative or additional treatment option for patients with ADHD, especially cardio exercise
description: The review concludes that "physical exercise represents a promising alternative or additional treatment option for patients with ADHD", with acute and chronic beneficial effects of especially cardio exercise on cognitive, behavioral, and socio-emotional functions. It suggests exercise "could be combined with other treatment approaches of ADHD" rather than replacing them. The recommendation is explicitly provisional: the authors call for "more well-controlled studies on this topic, in both children and adults".
requirements: Exercise programs should be deliverable alongside existing ADHD treatment approaches; effects are best supported for cardio exercise.
constraints: Non-cardio exercise effects remain more questionable; the evidence base needs more well-controlled studies in both children and adults before firm implementation conclusions.
target_learners: children with ADHD
adults with ADHD
target_learning_goals: executive functioning
attention
behavioral and socio-emotional functioning
examples: Reviewed interventions included treadmill running, cycling, aerobic and motor-skills programs of 30–90 minutes several times weekly over 5–12 weeks.

article_title: Cognitive and emotional math problems largely dissociate: Prevalence of developmental dyscalculia and mathematics anxiety.
citation: Devine, A., Hill, F., Carey, E., & Szűcs, D. (2017). Cognitive and Emotional Math Problems Largely Dissociate: Prevalence of Developmental Dyscalculia and Mathematics Anxiety.
title: Competing accounts of the MA–performance relationship: the Deficit Theory, the Debilitating Anxiety Model, and the Reciprocal Theory
description: The article reviews three explanatory accounts of the negative MA–performance association. The Deficit Theory "claims that anxiety emerges a result of an awareness of poor mathematics performance in the past". The Debilitating Anxiety Model posits that high anxiety interferes with performance via disruption of pre-processing, processing and retrieval, and via avoidance of mathematics-related situations. The Reciprocal Theory holds the relationship functions bidirectionally as a vicious circle. The article argues the two models may operate simultaneously and that its comorbidity findings qualify the Deficit Theory.
requirements: Distinguishing the models requires study designs sensitive to their different time courses: longitudinal studies for the Deficit Theory, experimental studies for the Debilitating Anxiety Model.
constraints: The article states the evidence supporting the two models is in conflict and that its own cross-sectional design could not determine the direction of the association.
target_learners: primary and secondary school children (8- to 13-year-olds)
target_learning_goals: mathematics performance
mathematics anxiety
examples: The article cites longitudinal data (Luo et al., 2014; Cargnelutti et al., 2016) suggesting the MA–performance relationship functions reciprocally.
key_sources: Devine, A., Hill, F., Carey, E., & Szűcs, D. (2017). Cognitive and Emotional Math Problems Largely Dissociate: Prevalence of Developmental Dyscalculia and Mathematics Anxiety. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000222

article_title: Cognitive and emotional math problems largely dissociate: Prevalence of developmental dyscalculia and mathematics anxiety.
citation: Devine, A., Hill, F., Carey, E., & Szűcs, D. (2017). Cognitive and Emotional Math Problems Largely Dissociate: Prevalence of Developmental Dyscalculia and Mathematics Anxiety.
title: Treat cognitive and emotional mathematics problems with different interventions: anxiety-focused support for high MA, skills and working-memory-focused support for DD
description: Because cognitive and emotional mathematics problems largely dissociate, the article recommends that interventions be matched to the problem type. It states that "Different intervention methods need to be developed to prevent and treat emotional and cognitive blocks of mathematical development." Children with MA are likely to benefit from anxiety-focused interventions such as systematic desensitisation, cognitive restructuring, or expressive writing, whereas children with DD without high MA are likely to benefit from interventions targeting mathematical skills, working memory and visuo-spatial processing.
requirements: Identifying MA in the classroom is essential so that children can be equipped with appropriate coping strategies for dealing with anxious reactions towards mathematics, particularly around assessment.
constraints: The article's cross-sectional design could not determine the direction of the MA–performance association; the recommendation rests on the observed dissociation of prevalence rather than a tested intervention in this study.
target_learners: primary and secondary school children with mathematics anxiety or developmental dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: mathematics performance
mathematics anxiety reduction
numerical skills and working memory development
examples: The article cites Hembree (1990): interventions focusing on systematic desensitisation or cognitive restructuring resulted in improvements in mathematics performance.
The article cites Ramirez and Beilock (2011): writing about one's anxieties before an examination produced performance benefits, theorised to free up working memory resources.

article_title: The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying
citation: Peadar Donohoe and Carmel O’Sullivan. (2015). The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying. Scenario, Volume 2015 · Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.33178/scenario.9.1.6
title: The Bullying Prevention Pack (BPP)
description: The BPP is a systematic bullying prevention intervention that fosters learner vocabulary and knowledge about bullying through role-play and discussions, aiming to create "a heightened awareness of the effects of bullying on peers" and a defending culture. It was enacted over a five-week period in each of two school years: Week 1 covered bullying in the school and definitions; Week 2 introduced participant players with improvised role-plays and discussion questions; Week 3 addressed the onlooker role; Week 4 coached confident defending behaviours; Week 5 involved signing an anti-bullying contract. Monthly teacher-led check-ups followed the initial intervention.
requirements: Teacher-led classroom discussions with open questions before introducing literature-based definitions
Teachers coached on BPP implementation
Monthly follow-up check-ups by the class teacher after the five-week programme
constraints: Role-plays were reported as problematic for some junior-strand teachers, with some role-plays described as over young learners' heads or too complicated
Overly long instructions were a common complaint; handouts were amended to concise, jargon-free bullet points
Junior teachers reduced the amount of bullying types and Bullying Circle players introduced to young learners
target_learners: Primary school pupils, ages 5-12, in designated disadvantaged schools
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of bullying definitions, types and participant roles
Empathy for targets of bullying
Confident defending and reporting behaviour
examples: Over two school years the BPP was trialled with 231 male pupils and 13 teachers at an inner-city Cork school, and was extended to a whole-school basis in year two at the principal's request
key_sources: Peadar Donohoe and Carmel O’Sullivan. (2015). The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying. Scenario, Volume 2015 · Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.33178/scenario.9.1.6

article_title: The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying
citation: Peadar Donohoe and Carmel O’Sullivan. (2015). The Bullying Prevention Pack: Fostering Vocabulary and Knowledge on the Topic of Bullying and Prevention using Role-Play and Discussion to Reduce Primary School Bullying. Scenario, Volume 2015 · Issue 1. https://doi.org/10.33178/scenario.9.1.6
title: The Bullying Circle of participant player roles
description: The BPP teaches that "Bullying is often a group process which can involve various participant players": children are not just bullies or victims but can act as assistants who encourage bullying, lookouts who watch for intervening teachers, or defenders who try to stop it. Roles are fluid, with students playing multiple positions across incidents. The pack uses an adapted Bullying Circle (Donohoe and Dummigan 2015, adapted from Olweus 1993) and asks learners to relate these roles to their own experiences, naming the types of players involved in school incidents without naming or blaming any peer.
requirements: Learners are introduced to the roles and asked to relate them to their own experiences before role-playing
constraints: Roles are fluid; a learner may bully in one incident, be targeted in another, or intervene
target_learners: Primary school pupils
target_learning_goals: Understanding participant roles in bullying incidents
Metacognitive reflection on one's own possible roles
examples: Learners voluntarily described bullying incidents that happened in the school and were asked to name the type of Bullying Circle players involved

The stated aim was "to keep the contract ﬂuid and responsive to learner needs" and to reinforce long-term institutional support, because the literature suggests schools with high bullying prevalence often lack a culture that supports interventions over time.

A learner-signed contract aligned with the school's anti-bullying policy

title: No name, no blame discussion of bullying incidents
description: The BPP adopts the 'no name, no blame' approach (Maines and Robinson 1997) when learners discuss real bullying incidents: peers describe what happened and the player roles involved without identifying or blaming any child. Teachers in both strands and all learner focus groups reported this approach was a significant aid to the discussions, as one fourth-class participant put it: "we could just tell out what happened without feeling bad about it". Empathy for those targeted

article_title: Inhibition and Updating, but Not Switching, Predict Developmental Dyslexia and Individual Variation in Reading Ability
citation: Doyle C, Smeaton AF, Roche RAP and Boran L (2018) Inhibition and Updating, but Not Switching, Predict Developmental Dyslexia and Individual Variation in Reading Ability. Front. Psychol. 9:795. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.00795
title: Miyake and Friedman's 3-factor model of core executive functions (inhibition, updating, switching)
description: The article organizes its profiling study around the 3-factor model of executive function, in which executive function comprises three core related but separable abilities. It states that "Inhibition is deﬁned as the ability to override inappropriate responses, regulate appropriate behaviour and control attenti on by focusing on relevant information and ﬁltering out distracting information; updating is the ability to hold and continuousl y update information in working memory from moment to moment; and switching is the ability to rapidly adapt to changing task demands." The model holds that the three are related through a common executive function (inhibition) while updating and switching are specific, and that complex tasks lack the specificity to detect fine-grained core processes. The study applies this framework to dyslexia using multiple measures per construct.
requirements: Sensitive measurement requires multiple tasks per construct with significant loadings onto core executive function constructs in prior latent variable analyses and frontal brain activation
constraints: Latent variable analysis, considered the most sensitive approach, could not be conducted in this study due to sample size constraints
target_learners: children aged 10-12 with and without developmental dyslexia
target_learning_goals: reading ability and executive function profiling
key_sources: Doyle C, Smeaton AF, Roche RAP and Boran L (2018) Inhibition and Updating, but Not Switching, Predict Developmental Dyslexia and Individual Variation in Reading Ability. Front. Psychol. 9:795. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.00795

article_title: The Association Between Cognitive Performance and Speech-in-Noise Perception for Adult Listeners: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Dryden Adam, Allen Harriet A., Henshaw Helen, Heinrich Antje. (2017). The Association Between Cognitive Performance and Speech-in-Noise Perception for Adult Listeners: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis. Trends in Hearing. https://doi.org/10.1177/2331216517744675
title: Dual classification framework: cognitive domains/subdomains and a speech-target-by-masker matrix for systematizing cognition–SiN studies
description: The review organizes the heterogeneous literature with two categorization systems. Cognitive measures are abstracted from individual tests into "five cognitive domains (attention, executive processes, memory, intelligence, and processing speed) and nine cognitive subdomains" based on established theories. SiN tests are classified by target lexical complexity (phonemes/syllables, words, sentences) and by masker type ordered on a continuum of decreasing energetic and increasing informational masking (unmodulated noise, modulated noise, >2-talker babble, ≤2-talker babble). This matrix enables fine-grained meta-analysis of specific cognition-by-listening-situation combinations.
requirements: Cognitive tests must be assignable to a single main subdomain; tests loading on multiple domains or not readily definable (e.g., the Text reception threshold) were excluded
constraints: Intelligibility levels, adaptive versus nonadaptive paradigms, and signal presentation are not distinguished within categories, a simplification the authors state was necessary given test heterogeneity
target_learners: Adult listeners (18+) with hearing from normal sensitivity to moderate hearing loss, unaided
target_learning_goals: Understanding the role of cognitive abilities in speech-in-noise perception
examples: The 25 included studies' 59 cognitive measures and eight target–masker combinations were mapped onto this framework before meta-analysis
key_sources: Dryden Adam, Allen Harriet A., Henshaw Helen, Heinrich Antje. (2017). The Association Between Cognitive Performance and Speech-in-Noise Perception for Adult Listeners: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis. Trends in Hearing. https://doi.org/10.1177/2331216517744675

article_title: Institutional Racism and Campus Racial Climate: Struggles for Sense of Belonging and Academic Success Among Black Students in the K-12 Public Schools
citation: Evelyn Ezikwelu. (2020). Institutional Racism and Campus Racial Climate: Struggles for Sense of Belonging Among Black Students in K-12 Public Schools. Journal of Critical Thought and Praxis, 10(1). https://www.iastatedigitalpress.com/jctp/
title: Critical race theory as an analytical framework for institutional racism in schools
description: The review uses critical race theory (CRT), defined as "a theoretical framework that examines race and racism represented by the dominant group's ways of cultural expression and practices," emerged from law in the 1970s. CRT comprises five tenets: "the permanence of racism, interest convergence, the critique of liberalism, counter-storytelling, and Whiteness as property." The review applies the tenet that race is a social construct and systemic phenomenon to analyze how Whiteness is preserved over minoritized groups in schools.
requirements: Analysis through CRT requires acknowledging the existence of race and racism as the issue causing institutional racism in schools
constraints: The review utilizes only one CRT tenet's logical frame (race as social construct and systemic phenomenon), not all five tenets
target_learners: Black students in K-12 public schools
target_learning_goals: Sense of belonging
Academic success
examples: The review analyzed 64 manuscripts through CRT and racial battle fatigue lenses, with one common theme emerging: campus racial climate versus institutional racism
key_sources: Evelyn Ezikwelu. (2020). Institutional Racism and Campus Racial Climate: Struggles for Sense of Belonging Among Black Students in K-12 Public Schools. Journal of Critical Thought and Praxis, 10(1). https://www.iastatedigitalpress.com/jctp/

article_title: Institutional Racism and Campus Racial Climate: Struggles for Sense of Belonging and Academic Success Among Black Students in the K-12 Public Schools
citation: Evelyn Ezikwelu. (2020). Institutional Racism and Campus Racial Climate: Struggles for Sense of Belonging Among Black Students in K-12 Public Schools. Journal of Critical Thought and Praxis, 10(1). https://www.iastatedigitalpress.com/jctp/
title: Racial battle fatigue as a framework for race-based discriminatory stress
description: Racial battle fatigue is the framework the review uses to explain the psychosocial costs of institutional racism. Its definition "includes the emotional, physiological, psychological, and behavioral strains that are imposed on Black students as they struggle to cope with institutional racism (Smith, 2003)." The review uses this lens to show that subtle race-based discriminatory stresses, including microaggressions and unconscious degradations, carry psychological implications that undermine Black students' belonging and academic success.
requirements: Analysis requires recognizing that much racial discrimination in White-dominated school environments is subtle and unconscious rather than overt
constraints: The framework is applied to Black students' experiences in White-dominated K-12 and higher education settings as reviewed
target_learners: Black students in K-12 public schools
target_learning_goals: Sense of belonging
Self-identity
Academic success
examples: Smith (2008) used racial battle fatigue theory to demonstrate that the psychological impacts of racism are draining and counter-productive for Black students pursuing academic goals
key_sources: Evelyn Ezikwelu. (2020). Institutional Racism and Campus Racial Climate: Struggles for Sense of Belonging Among Black Students in K-12 Public Schools. Journal of Critical Thought and Praxis, 10(1). https://www.iastatedigitalpress.com/jctp/

article_title: States of curiosity and interest enhance memory differently in adolescents and in children
citation: Fandakova Yana, Gruber Matthias J. (2021). States of curiosity and interest enhance memory differently in adolescents and in children. Developmental Science, 24(1), e13005. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.13005
title: Information prediction errors (IPEs) as a driver of memory, in line with reward prediction errors and the information gap theory
description: The article frames IPEs as "the discrepancy between post-information interest and pre-information curiosity", proposed as an important driver of memory (Marvin & Shohamy, 2016). IPEs are presented as a critical aspect of information gap theory, which postulates that predicting whether expected information will resolve uncertainty is critical for curiosity, and as parallel to reward prediction errors, which are "a key driver of learning in various contexts". The study computes an IPE score per trial as the difference between initial curiosity rating and post-answer interest rating and uses it to predict recall.
requirements: Requires participants to rate pre-information curiosity and post-information interest so the discrepancy can be computed per trial
constraints: The article notes the neural mechanisms of IPEs in a trivia paradigm have not been directly investigated, and how IPEs map onto reward prediction errors neurally is not known
target_learners: children and adolescents aged 10–14 years
target_learning_goals: episodic memory for newly learned factual information (trivia answers)
examples: In the study, an IPE score was computed for each trial as the difference between the initial curiosity rating and the post-answer interest rating, following Marvin & Shohamy (2016)
key_sources: Fandakova Yana, Gruber Matthias J. (2021). States of curiosity and interest enhance memory differently in adolescents and in children. Developmental Science, 24(1), e13005. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.13005

article_title: The association between poor reading and internalising problems: A systematic review and meta-analysis
citation: Francis, D. A.; Caruana, N.; Hudson, J. L.; McArthur, G. M. (2019). The association between poor reading and internalising problems: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2018.09.002
title: Eight-moderator framework for explaining inconsistent findings on poor reading and internalising problems
description: The article proposes eight potential moderators that may explain inconsistent findings across studies of poor reading and internalising problems: "anxiety disorder subtype", poor reading subtype, attention, sex, age, ethnicity, type of informant, and type of internalising measure (clinical interview versus questionnaire). The framework treats mixed results across studies as a red flag for heterogeneity, suggesting only a subgroup of poor readers may have internalising problems. It organises the review's second aim of evaluating theoretical and methodological moderators of the association.
requirements: Subgroup analyses require 10 or more studies per moderator to yield reliable comparisons of effect sizes, as the article states for its planned analyses.
constraints: The review could not test any of the eight moderators meta-analytically because there were fewer than 10 studies per subgroup; moderator evidence was only narratively synthesised.
target_learners: poor readers aged 6 to 12 years, adolescents aged 13 to 18 years, and adults aged 18+ years
target_learning_goals: understanding emotional risk (anxiety and depression) associated with poor reading
examples: The review coded studies into subgroups such as five anxiety disorder subtypes, four poor reading subtypes, and four informant types before finding the subgroups underpowered.
key_sources: Francis, D. A.; Caruana, N.; Hudson, J. L.; McArthur, G. M. (2019). The association between poor reading and internalising problems: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpr.2018.09.002

article_title: Deaf Individuals’ Bilingual Abilities: American Sign Language Proficiency, Reading Skills, and Family Characteristics
citation: Freel, B. L., Clark, M. D., Anderson, M. L., Gilbert, G. L., Musyoka, M. M., & Hauser, P. C. (2011). Deaf Individuals’ Bilingual Abilities: American Sign Language Proficiency, Reading Skills, and Family Characteristics. Psychology, 2(1), 18-23. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2011.21003
title: Linguistic Interdependence Theory applied to deaf bilingual education
description: Cummins' Linguistic Interdependence Theory holds that competence in a second language is a function of proficiency in one's first language. Applied to deaf learners, the article states that "individuals who have full comma nd of ASL as a first language are better disposed to learn English as a second language". The study uses this framework to interpret its finding that ASL proficiency and reading skill correlate positively, supporting ASL as a bridge to English print.
requirements: A well-developed first language (ASL) must be established before or alongside second-language (English) instruction
constraints: The article notes the equality of ASL is not always upheld in practice, as ASL grammar courses are often not offered and no national formal ASL curriculum exists
target_learners: deaf children and adults acquiring English literacy through ASL
target_learning_goals: English reading comprehension
first-language ASL development
examples: The study measured ASL proficiency with the ASL-SRT and English reading with the WJ III Passage Comprehension subtest in 55 deaf adults
key_sources: Freel, B. L., Clark, M. D., Anderson, M. L., Gilbert, G. L., Musyoka, M. M., & Hauser, P. C. (2011). Deaf Individuals’ Bilingual Abilities: American Sign Language Proficiency, Reading Skills, and Family Characteristics. Psychology, 2(1), 18-23. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2011.21003

article_title: Deaf Individuals’ Bilingual Abilities: American Sign Language Proficiency, Reading Skills, and Family Characteristics
citation: Freel, B. L., Clark, M. D., Anderson, M. L., Gilbert, G. L., Musyoka, M. M., & Hauser, P. C. (2011). Deaf Individuals’ Bilingual Abilities: American Sign Language Proficiency, Reading Skills, and Family Characteristics. Psychology, 2(1), 18-23. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2011.21003
title: Use well-developed ASL as a bridge when teaching English literacy to deaf learners
description: The article argues that instruction for deaf children should build on a fully developed first language rather than apply strategies designed for hearing children. It reports that "fluent ASL-English bilinguals possess grammatically-structured ASL that serves as a bridge to the acquisition of written English", and that teachers often fail to map ASL grammar onto English grammar for students. Bilingual education programs using ASL for general communication and for teaching English, reading, and writing are the recommended approach.
requirements: Teachers must clearly distinguish grammatical differences between ASL and English and teach students how to map one grammar onto the other
Comprehensive development of ASL as a first language should be a priority
constraints: The article notes deaf children often arrive at school without a developed first language, and no national research-based ASL curriculum exists
target_learners: deaf children in bilingual education programs
target_learning_goals: English literacy
reading comprehension
examples: The study's finding that native signers exhibited more proficient bilingual abilities than non-native signers supports the bridge role of early full ASL exposure

article_title: Metacognitive monitoring of working memory performance and its relationship to academic achievement in Grade 4 children
citation: Freeman, Emily E.; Karayanidis, Frini; Chalmers, Kerry A. (2017). Metacognitive monitoring of working memory performance and its relationship to academic achievement in Grade 4 children. Learning and Individual Differences, Vol. 57. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2017.06.003
title: Working Memory Power Test for Children (WMPT)
description: The WMPT is a computer-administered test of children's working memory with five levels of increasing difficulty, from a Memorise condition to a 4-Swap condition requiring four position swaps. It is "unique in that it captures both accuracy and confidence information and thus provides an opportunity to measure metacognitive monitoring ability in children". After each item the child rates confidence on a 4-point scale from guessed to definitely right. The article reports the test has good reliability (.85).
requirements: Requires children to give a confidence rating on a 4-point scale after each item, enabling calculation of calibration measures
constraints: Developed by ebilities, a publisher and supplier of online cognitive ability tests; validity evidence cited as under review at the time
target_learners: Grade 4 primary school children (aged approximately 9-11 years)
target_learning_goals: Working memory assessment
metacognitive monitoring calibration
examples: In the study, children completed 25 problems across five levels (Memorise, 1-Swap, 2-Swap, 3-Swap, 4-Swap) on a laptop computer during the school day
key_sources: Freeman, Emily E.; Karayanidis, Frini; Chalmers, Kerry A. (2017). Metacognitive monitoring of working memory performance and its relationship to academic achievement in Grade 4 children. Learning and Individual Differences, Vol. 57. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2017.06.003

article_title: Examining the relationship of empathy, social support, and prosocial behavior of adolescents in China: a structural equation modeling approach
citation: Fu W, Wang C, Chai H, Xue R. (2022). Examining the relationship of empathy, social support, and prosocial behavior of adolescents in China: a structural equation modeling approach. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-022-01296-0
title: Interpersonal-emotion account of prosocial behavior: internal empathy and external social support jointly shape prosociality
description: The article frames prosocial behavior development as depending on internal factors (empathy) and external factors (social support), explored "from the perspective of interpersonal emotion" based on the biological emotion theory of prosocial behavior. High-empathy individuals more actively perceive care and support from others, building relationships that yield more support, which in turn fosters prosocial behavior; the buffer effect hypothesis is invoked for how perceived support underpins prosociality.
requirements: Measurement of both internal (empathy) and external (social support) factors to capture the mechanism
constraints: Tested in a Chinese adolescent sample; the authors note prosocial behavior is affected by the social and cultural environment
target_learners: Adolescents
target_learning_goals: Prosocial behavior and social competence
examples: The structural equation model tested empathy, social support, and prosocial behavior as three linked variables with social support as mediator
key_sources: Fu W, Wang C, Chai H, Xue R. (2022). Examining the relationship of empathy, social support, and prosocial behavior of adolescents in China: a structural equation modeling approach. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-022-01296-0

article_title: Social exclusion affects working memory performance in young adolescent girls
citation: Fuhrmann D., Casey C.S., Speekenbrink M., Blakemore S.-J. (2019). Social exclusion affects working memory performance in young adolescent girls. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2019.100718
title: Design and time school social-exclusion interventions with age differences in cognitive vulnerability in mind
description: The article's stated practical implication is that responses to exclusion differ by age, so anti-bullying and social-exclusion work in schools should be designed and timed with those differences in mind. The authors write that their findings "underlin[e] the need to consider age differences in response to exclusion in the design and timing of social exclusion interventions in schools", because young adolescent girls' verbal working memory was affected by even a brief virtual exclusion while older groups' was not.
requirements: Interventions should be matched to the developmental stage of the students, since only young adolescents showed cognitive performance effects in this study
constraints: Evidence comes from a short virtual exclusion simulation with female participants only; the authors note real-life exclusion is repeated and more personal, and effects on males are unknown
target_learners: young adolescent girls (aged 10.1-14.0) in secondary schools
mid-adolescents and adults as comparison groups
target_learning_goals: protecting working-memory-dependent academic performance from the effects of peer exclusion
examples: In the experiment, young adolescents (N=36) showed reduced n-back accuracy after exclusion while mid-adolescents and adults did not, and all groups completed the tasks individually in schools or the lab
key_sources: Fuhrmann D., Casey C.S., Speekenbrink M., Blakemore S.-J. (2019). Social exclusion affects working memory performance in young adolescent girls. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2019.100718

article_title: Social exclusion affects working memory performance in young adolescent girls
citation: Fuhrmann D., Casey C.S., Speekenbrink M., Blakemore S.-J. (2019). Social exclusion affects working memory performance in young adolescent girls. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2019.100718
title: Adolescence as a sensitive period of social development
description: The article frames adolescence as a developmental window in which the social environment has a heightened effect on brain and behaviour. It states that "Adolescence has been proposed to be a sensitive period of social development, during which the social environment has a heightened effect on brain and behaviour", citing rodent work showing a window for social-isolation effects in late juvenile/early adolescent stages. The study's age-dependent working-memory result is presented as consistent with this framing, while mood effects were age-independent.
requirements: Interpretation of age-dependent effects as sensitive-period evidence requires comparing age groups within the same paradigm, as this study did with three age groups
constraints: The authors note the interaction should be interpreted with caution (p = 0.058 with age continuous) and that whether sensitivity peaks in late childhood/early adolescence or simply declines over development remains an open question
target_learners: adolescents aged roughly 10-18
target_learning_goals: understanding how the social environment affects cognitive performance and learning during adolescence
examples: Rodent studies cited show social isolation reduced exploratory behaviour only if it occurred between postnatal day 25 and 45, more than before or after
key_sources: Fuhrmann D., Casey C.S., Speekenbrink M., Blakemore S.-J. (2019). Social exclusion affects working memory performance in young adolescent girls. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2019.100718

article_title: Sensory Processing Problems in Children with ADHD, a Systematic Review
citation: Ghanizadeh A. (2011). Sensory Processing Problems in Children with ADHD, a Systematic Review. Psychiatry Investig 2011;8:89-94. https://doi.org/10.4306/pi.2011.8.2.89
title: Taxonomy of sensory processing problem types: over-responsivity, under-responsivity, sensory-seeking, and sensory discrimination problems
description: The review organizes sensory processing problems as impairments in detection, modulation, or interpretation of stimuli, and distinguishes named types: sensory over-responsivity, where individuals "respond to sensory stimuli in the way that is faster, longer, or more intense than what is expected"; under-responsivity, where individuals are unaware or slow to respond; sensory-seeking, where individuals crave sensory experiences; and sensory discrimination problems, characterized by difficulty interpreting specific characteristics of stimuli. Modalities are not separate and interact with each other.
requirements: Assessment of sensory profiles of children with behavioral problems in clinical practice, as the review recommends
constraints: The etiology of sensory processing is unknown according to the review
target_learners: children with ADHD
target_learning_goals: recognizing and managing sensory processing problems that affect daily responses and classroom behavior
examples: The review gives examples such as defensiveness to hair-brushing for tactile sensitivity, and being puzzled about a sound's origin for auditory hyposensitivity
key_sources: Ghanizadeh A. (2011). Sensory Processing Problems in Children with ADHD, a Systematic Review. Psychiatry Investig 2011;8:89-94. https://doi.org/10.4306/pi.2011.8.2.89

article_title: Sensory Processing Problems in Children with ADHD, a Systematic Review
citation: Ghanizadeh A. (2011). Sensory Processing Problems in Children with ADHD, a Systematic Review. Psychiatry Investig 2011;8:89-94. https://doi.org/10.4306/pi.2011.8.2.89
title: Sensory Profile parent-reported questionnaire and related checklists for assessing sensory processing in children with ADHD
description: The review describes the Sensory Profile as "a widely used parent reported standardized questionnaire" in which children's responses to sensory events in daily life are rated by their parents. It assesses auditory, visual, taste/smell, body position, movement, and touch processing, plus activity level and social/emotional responses. Related instruments include a parent-reported auditory processing problem checklist (hypersensitivity and hyposensitivity to sounds) and a tactile sensory dysfunction checklist covering hypersensitivity, hyposensitivity, and poor tactile perception and discrimination.
requirements: More developed, valid, and reliable measurements are required, per the review's conclusion
constraints: Most published studies rely on parent reports, and parents of these children often suffer from psychiatric disorders such as depression and anxiety, which may impact their reports
target_learners: children with ADHD
target_learning_goals: identifying sensory processing problems to guide management and educational support
examples: The 11 reviewed studies all used questionnaire or parent-reported measures, including the Short Sensory Profile and the Sensory Over-Responsivity Inventory
key_sources: Ghanizadeh A. (2011). Sensory Processing Problems in Children with ADHD, a Systematic Review. Psychiatry Investig 2011;8:89-94. https://doi.org/10.4306/pi.2011.8.2.89

article_title: Individual Differences in Inhibitory Control, Not Non-Verbal Number Acuity, Correlate with Mathematics Achievement
citation: Gilmore C, Attridge N, Clayton S, Cragg L, Johnson S, Marlow N, Simms V, Inglis M. (2013). Individual Differences in Inhibitory Control, Not Non-Verbal Number Acuity, Correlate with Mathematics Achievement. PLoS ONE 8(6): e67374. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0067374
title: Inhibition-based account of dot comparison task performance
description: The article proposes that a dot comparison trial can be solved in two ways: by responding to salient visual characteristics such as dot size or area, or by inhibiting that response and answering on the basis of approximate number representations. Because congruent trials reward the visual-cue route while incongruent trials punish it, "an individuals' score on a dot comparison task will reflect not only the precision of their nonsymbolic representations, but also their inhibition skills". The account explains why dot comparison performance correlates with mathematics achievement: the inhibition component, not representational precision, drives the correlation.
requirements: Task formats must include incongruent trials in which visual characteristics conflict with number for the inhibition component to be engaged
constraints: The authors state it remains to be established whether and how the ANS is involved in early symbolic number learning
target_learners: children aged 4-11 years
school-aged children from diverse socio-economic backgrounds
target_learning_goals: understanding the cognitive underpinnings of mathematics achievement
examples: Experiment 1 used Pica-style congruent and incongruent dot arrays; Experiment 2 used Gebuis and Reynvoet stimuli with a NEPSY-II inhibition subtest separating inhibition from naming speed.
key_sources: Gilmore C, Attridge N, Clayton S, Cragg L, Johnson S, Marlow N, Simms V, Inglis M. (2013). Individual Differences in Inhibitory Control, Not Non-Verbal Number Acuity, Correlate with Mathematics Achievement. PLoS ONE 8(6): e67374. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0067374

article_title: The Impact of Bilingualism on Executive Functions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review Based on the PRISMA Method
citation: Giovannoli J, Martella D, Federico F, Pirchio S and Casagrande M (2020) The Impact of Bilingualism on Executive Functions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review Based on the PRISMA Method. Front. Psychol. 11:574789. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.574789
title: Bilingual advantage theory: constant control of two co-active languages trains executive functions
description: The bilingual advantage theory holds that because both of a bilingual's languages remain active, constantly controlling them to select the context-appropriate one acts as continuous training for executive functions. The review presents this as the theory whose empirical support it evaluates, tracing it to Green's Joint Activation Model, in which a general suppression mechanism inhibits the non-target language. The review frames it as the most controversial topic in bilingualism research.
requirements: Studies must compare bilingual and monolingual groups on executive function measures to test the theory's predictions
constraints: The review reports that results are controversial and that the term bilingual advantage has been questioned in favor of the more neutral term bilingual effect
target_learners: children and adolescents aged 5-17
target_learning_goals: executive function development: inhibition, cognitive flexibility, working memory

article_title: The Impact of Bilingualism on Executive Functions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review Based on the PRISMA Method
citation: Giovannoli J, Martella D, Federico F, Pirchio S and Casagrande M (2020) The Impact of Bilingualism on Executive Functions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review Based on the PRISMA Method. Front. Psychol. 11:574789. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.574789
title: Adaptive control hypothesis: three interaction contexts shape which control processes bilinguals use
description: Green and Abutalebi's Adaptive control hypothesis, as presented in the review, holds that the communicative context in which bilinguals interact determines whether their languages cooperate or compete, and thus which control processes support communication. The review quotes the hypothesis identifying three possible contexts of interaction: single-language, dual-language, and dense code-switching contexts. It is offered as an explanatory framework for why bilingual effects may vary across studies and settings.
requirements: The communicative context of language use must be characterized, since each context is characterized by a different use of control processes
constraints: The review notes most included studies did not indicate the language context in which the children were immersed
target_learners: children and adolescents aged 5-17
target_learning_goals: understanding how language-use context shapes executive control development

article_title: Influence of race/ethnicity and income on the link between adverse childhood experiences and child flourishing
citation: Goldstein, E., Topitzes, J., Miller-Cribbs, J. & Brown, R. L. (2021). Influence of race/ethnicity and income on the link between adverse childhood experiences and child flourishing. Pediatric Research. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41390-020-01188-6
title: Resilience-science framework: family resilience as a protective, partially mediating mechanism between childhood adversity and child flourishing
description: The article is informed by resilience science, which holds that identifying protective factors and processes is central to promoting child flourishing amid adversity. Family resilience is defined as "the ability of a family to withstand and rebound from disruptive life events" and is measured in the NSCH as a four-item composite (talking together, working together to solve problems, knowing strengths to draw on, staying hopeful). In the study's moderated-mediation model, this family-level construct operates as the mediator through which cumulative ACEs are partly transmitted to reduced flourishing in learning, task persistence, and self-regulation.
requirements: Requires measurement of family-level protective processes, operationalized here as the four-item NSCH family resilience composite requiring most-of-the-time or all-of-the-time responses on each indicator
constraints: The article states family resilience is only a partial mediator, so additional mediating influences are needed to explain the ACEs-flourishing association
Family resilience was found harder to muster for Black and Hispanic children facing adversity
target_learners: children ages 6-17 in the United States
target_learning_goals: interest and curiosity in learning new things
persistence in finishing tasks
emotional and behavioral self-regulation under challenge
examples: The study estimated family resilience as a latent mediator in a stacked-group probit moderated-mediation model using Mplus on 2016-17 NSCH data

article_title: Activating Culturally Empathic Motivation in Diverse Students
citation: Donald E Grant Jr. & Jerell B. Hill. (2020). Activating Culturally Empathic Motivation in Diverse Students. Journal of Education and Learning, 9(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v9n5p45
title: Motivational Framework for Culturally Responsive Teaching (MFCRT) with four motivational conditions
description: The article presents the Motivational Framework for Culturally Responsive Teaching (MFCRT), developed by Wlodkowski and Ginsberg (1995), as a way to ensure relevance in education and promote intrinsic motivation. It is activated through four motivational conditions that work collectively and individually: inclusion (respect and connectedness), attitude (relevance and volition), meaning (engagement and challenge), and competence (effectiveness and authenticity). Each condition pairs criteria with an explanation of how learners experience increased intrinsic motivation, such as feeling safe and able to exhibit authenticity under inclusion.
requirements: Educators must operationalize the four conditions dynamically, both collectively and individually, to enhance intrinsic motivation to learn.
constraints: The framework is presented as adapted from Wlodkowski & Ginsberg (1995); the article reports no direct empirical test of it.
target_learners: diverse K-12 students
learners from marginalized or intersectional groups
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation for learning
culturally responsive engagement
examples: The article's Table 2 lists the four conditions with criteria and explanations, adapted from Wlodkowski & Ginsberg (1995).

article_title: Activating Culturally Empathic Motivation in Diverse Students
citation: Donald E Grant Jr. & Jerell B. Hill. (2020). Activating Culturally Empathic Motivation in Diverse Students. Journal of Education and Learning, 9(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v9n5p45
title: Self-determination theory: goal-driven behavior resting on competence, autonomy, and relatedness
description: The article describes self-determination theory as aimed at explaining an individual's goal-driven behaviors, incorporating four motivational valences (intrinsic, introjected, extrinsic, and identified). The theory rests on a foundation of three psychological needs thought to be universal and instinctive: competence, the belief that one has the skills and tools to perform well; autonomy, the belief that one acts out of one's own volition; and relatedness, the belief that shared experience can support meaningful relationships. The article also cites its model in which school engagement mediates the influence of autonomy and belongingness on academic and psychological outcomes.
requirements: School-based autonomy and belongingness are emphasized as important to academic achievement and psychological adjustment.
constraints: The article notes the mediation model had only been evaluated on academic outcomes to date (Van Ryzin, Gravely, & Roseth, 2009).
target_learners: school-aged students
diverse learners
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation
academic achievement
psychological adjustment
examples: The article uses the four motivational types (intrinsic, introjected, extrinsic, identified) in Table 1 to frame its discussion.

article_title: A Systematic Review of the Consequences of Stigma and Stereotype Threat for Individuals With Specific Learning Disabilities
citation: Haft Stephanie L., Greiner de Magalhães Caroline, Hoeft Fumiko. (2023). A Systematic Review of the Consequences of Stigma and Stereotype Threat for Individuals With Specific Learning Disabilities. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/00222194221087383
title: Framework distinguishing SLD stigma (including stigma consciousness and self-stigma) from stereotype threat as two contributors to poorer outcomes in SLDs
description: The review organizes the literature around two related constructs: stigma, "the devaluation of an attribute based on negative attitudes, stereotypes, or beliefs," and stereotype threat, "a more specific situation in which an individual fears confirming those negative beliefs." Within stigma it distinguishes stigma consciousness (perception of societal views, e.g., worry over judgment and expected differential treatment) from self-stigma (internalization of those views). The SLD label can function as a stigmatizing marker, and the framework maps proximal mechanisms (e.g., anxiety, self-efficacy) onto downstream consequences (Figure 3).
requirements: Studies must measure SLD-specific stigma (stigma consciousness or internalized stigma) or experimentally induce stereotype threat in samples of individuals with SLDs
constraints: The review notes stereotype threat effects vary by sample, setting, outcome measure, and the type of threat-activating cue (blatant vs. indirect and subtle)
target_learners: children, adolescents, and adults with specific learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: psychological adjustment (self-esteem, anxiety, depression)
academic performance and motivation
examples: The review's Figure 3 summarizes connections between SLD-related stigma/stereotype threat, proximal mechanisms, downstream consequences, and moderating environmental and individual variables

article_title: Testing the Difference between School Level and Academic Mindset in the Classroom: Implications for Developing Student Psycho-Social Skills in Secondary School Classrooms
citation: Hanson, J. (2017). Testing the Difference between School Level and Academic Mindset in the Classroom: Implications for Developing Student Psycho-Social Skills in Secondary School Classrooms. Journal of Educational Issues, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.5296/jei.v3i1.10479
title: Academic mindset as a four-component psycho-social classroom construct
description: The article describes academic mindset as "the beliefs, attitudes, or ways of perceiving oneself in relation to learning and intellectual work that support academic performance" (Farrington et al., 2012). It comprises four distinct mindsets: beliefs of belonging, the ability to grow through effort, that one can succeed on classroom tasks (self-efficacy), and that the work has value. The study operationalizes these on the PERTS instrument at the classroom level, extending individual mindset theory to group/classroom data. Mindset differs from self-efficacy in that mindset is a belief about the malleability of one's traits, whereas self-efficacy is a belief in one's ability to perform a task.
requirements: A reliable Likert-style instrument (PERTS) with subscales for individual mindset, belonging, task relevance, and self-efficacy
constraints: The article notes individual mindset has little correlation with group-level mindset culture in schools
target_learners: students in grades 3-8 classrooms
target_learning_goals: student autonomous choice to engage academic behaviors such as attendance, homework completion, and studying
examples: The PERTS 15-item survey was administered district-wide in April 2016 to measure the four constructs
key_sources: Hanson, J. (2017). Testing the Difference between School Level and Academic Mindset in the Classroom: Implications for Developing Student Psycho-Social Skills in Secondary School Classrooms. Journal of Educational Issues, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.5296/jei.v3i1.10479

article_title: Testing the Difference between School Level and Academic Mindset in the Classroom: Implications for Developing Student Psycho-Social Skills in Secondary School Classrooms
citation: Hanson, J. (2017). Testing the Difference between School Level and Academic Mindset in the Classroom: Implications for Developing Student Psycho-Social Skills in Secondary School Classrooms. Journal of Educational Issues, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.5296/jei.v3i1.10479
title: PERTS 15-item academic mindset survey with four subscales
description: The Project for Educational Research That Scales (PERTS) instrument is a Likert-style self-report scale (1 = Strongly Disagree to 6 = Strongly Agree) with 15 items in four subscales: individual mindset (3 items, reverse scored), sense of belonging in the classroom (4 items), task relevance (4 items), and self-efficacy on classroom tasks (4 items). Reliabilities printed in the article were .820 (belonging), .830 (self-efficacy), .820 (task relevance), and .772 (individual mindset). The scale is widely used in testing academic mindset interventions at the classroom level and has strong face validity in large-scale studies.
requirements: Internal reliability above Chronbach's alpha > .80 is the article's cited acceptable level (Nunnally, 1978); individual mindset at .772 falls below it
constraints: Individual mindset subscale reliability (.772) is below the .80 criterion the article cites
target_learners: students in grades 3-8
target_learning_goals: measuring classroom academic mindset psycho-social constructs
examples: Used with 2,908 students in a rural district for LCAP data collection

article_title: Testing the Difference between School Level and Academic Mindset in the Classroom: Implications for Developing Student Psycho-Social Skills in Secondary School Classrooms
citation: Hanson, J. (2017). Testing the Difference between School Level and Academic Mindset in the Classroom: Implications for Developing Student Psycho-Social Skills in Secondary School Classrooms. Journal of Educational Issues, 3(1). https://doi.org/10.5296/jei.v3i1.10479
title: Three-level model of mindset survey variables: individual, group/classroom, and school
description: Figure 1 of the article presents a model comparing and contrasting variables on three levels of mindset scales: individual, group/classroom, and school. The individual mindset survey, the PERTS survey, and the What's My School Mindset Survey (WMSM) quantify participant self-reports of psycho-social variables found in the literature and reported to improve student engagement in learning. The group-level models are consistent with Bandura's social cognitive theory, explaining reciprocal influences of the group on individuals' beliefs, choices, and behaviors. Research cited suggests interventions at the individual level show less potential for improving outcomes than those at group and organizational levels.
requirements: Likert-style surveys to quantify self-reports of psycho-social variables at each level
constraints: The article notes research suggests the individual's mindset has little correlation with the group level mindset culture in schools
target_learners: students
classroom teachers
school faculty
target_learning_goals: understanding psycho-social influences on student engagement
examples: Hanson, Ruff, and Bangert (2016) used the What's My School Mindset? instrument to quantify a school's growth mindset culture

article_title: The Timing of Learning before Night-Time Sleep Differentially Affects Declarative and Procedural Long-Term Memory Consolidation in Adolescents
citation: Holz J, Piosczyk H, Landmann N, Feige B, Spiegelhalder K, Riemann D, Nissen C, Voderholzer U. (2012). The Timing of Learning before Night-Time Sleep Differentially Affects Declarative and Procedural Long-Term Memory Consolidation in Adolescents. PLoS ONE 7(7): e40963. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0040963
title: Time- and sleep-dependent consolidation: procedural memory consolidates especially effectively when training occurs directly before night-time sleep
description: The article interprets its procedural findings within current models of a time- and sleep-dependent process of motor skill consolidation, in which initially unstable procedural memory representations are especially susceptible to interference in the first hours after training and are strengthened by sleep-specific brain activity. The authors write: "Our observation that motor learning directly before night-time sleep was especially effective fits to current models of a time- and sleep-dependent process of motor skill consolidation." They add that sleep spindles or EEG slow wave activity might foster this consolidation in the procedural memory system.
requirements: A period of night-time sleep occurring within the critical post-learning time window when memory traces are fragile
constraints: The authors note effects might partly reflect circadian phase differences between 3 PM and 9 PM sessions rather than sleep-dependent factors; disentangling would require total-sleep-deprivation control groups
target_learners: Adolescents learning motor skills
target_learning_goals: Procedural (motor skill) memory consolidation
examples: Evening-trained adolescents showed greater finger-tapping speed and accuracy gains than afternoon-trained adolescents at both 24-hour and 7-day retention intervals

article_title: Training Inhibition and Social Cognition in the Classrooms
citation: Honoré N, Houssa M, Volckaert A, Noël M-P and Nader-Grosbois N (2020) Training Inhibition and Social Cognition in the Classrooms. Front. Psychol. 11:1974. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01974
title: Combined inhibition and social cognition classroom training program (18 weekly sessions with metacognitive characters)
description: A manualized classroom program of "eighteen 45-min sessions implemented in the classroom in the presence of the teacher", delivered once a week over 6 months by a trained psychologist. It trains four inhibition components (predominant response, interruption of an ongoing response, external distractors, impulsivity control) through three metacognitive characters — Mr. Stop, the Detective and the Statue — plus ToM and SIP activities of increasing difficulty, with weekly teacher follow-up activities and record books.
requirements: Sessions delivered in the classroom by a trained psychologist in the presence of the teacher
Teachers asked to use the concepts and materials during the rest of the week and keep a weekly record book
constraints: Designed for typically developing 5- and 6-year-olds; children with language disorders or intellectual disabilities were excluded
Activities presented in order of increasing difficulty according to the zone of proximal development
target_learners: Children in the last year of kindergarten (K3) and first year of primary school (P1)
target_learning_goals: Inhibition and executive functions
Theory of Mind
Social information processing
examples: 85% of experimental-group participants attended 16 or more of the 18 sessions; mean teacher involvement was 3.31 ± 1.40 on the 5-point scale
