article_title: Training Inhibition and Social Cognition in the Classrooms
citation: Honoré N, Houssa M, Volckaert A, Noël M-P and Nader-Grosbois N (2020) Training Inhibition and Social Cognition in the Classrooms. Front. Psychol. 11:1974. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01974
title: Combine inhibition and social cognition content in a single classroom-delivered EF training for young children
description: The article argues that because inhibition and social cognition are interdependent — perspective taking requires inhibitory control and both recruit the frontal lobe — a training program should address both together. It states that "it seems important to address social and emotional issues in an EF training program", and implemented this by pairing inhibition games with ToM and SIP activities in each of the 18 classroom sessions.
requirements: Sessions delivered weekly over a sustained period (6 months, 18 sessions), since longer programs yield better EF outcomes per the authors' review of Diamond and Ling
Group format in the classroom to allow socio-cognitive conflicts to emerge
constraints: Effects demonstrated for typically developing 5- and 6-year-olds in conventional-teaching schools in French-speaking Belgium
target_learners: Kindergarten and early primary school children
target_learning_goals: Inhibitory control
Theory of Mind
Social information processing
examples: Each session trained both inhibition and social cognition, with characters reminding children to activate inhibition strategies before each activity

article_title: Visual attention, behavioral inhibition and speech/language outcomes in deaf children with cochlear implants
citation: Horn, D. L., Davis, R. A. O., Pisoni, D. B., & Miyamoto, R. T. (2004). Visual attention, behavioral inhibition and speech/language outcomes in deaf children with cochlear implants. Int Congr Ser. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ics.2004.07.048
title: Subvocal rehearsal and executive function account for the dCPT–outcome relation in deaf children with cochlear implants
description: The article proposes that the dCPT delay task taps cognitive skills tied to speech and language outcomes, offering two candidate mechanisms. It states that "Performance on the dCPT might be more influenced by subvocal rehearsal strategies which are related to speech perception, production, and language measures in deaf children with CIs," citing prior working-memory work, or alternatively that the dCPT loads more heavily on executive functions including behavioral analysis and synthesis. The framework explains why the dCPT, but not the vCPT, correlated with outcomes.
requirements: Further research is needed, as the article states more research is needed to understand how these functions play a role in deaf children acquiring speech-language skills with a CI
constraints: The account is offered as interpretation, not tested within this study
target_learners: prelingually deaf children with cochlear implants
target_learning_goals: spoken language development
speech perception and production
executive function and behavioral inhibition
examples: The dCPT required children to figure out a delay rule of at least 4 s between button presses from visual score-counter feedback in 6 min, which the authors suggest loads on rehearsal or executive control

article_title: Relationship between auditory processing skills and academic achievement of elementary school children
citation: Iva I. Hrastinski, Ana M. Bonetti, Mladen A. Hedjever. (2023). Relationship between auditory processing skills and academic achievement of elementary school children. Specijalna edukacija i rehabilitacija, 22(2), 95-116. https://doi.org/10.5937/specedreh22-37415
title: PSP-1 test battery for screening auditory processing disorder in Croatian children
description: The PSP-1 is a standardized behavioral test battery for screening auditory processing disorder in Croatian children. The article states it "contains four subtests – filtered words, speech in noise, competing (dichotic) words, and competing (dichotic) sentences" and is "the only standardized behavioral assessment of auditory processing skills for children aged 5.5 – 11.5 years in Croatia." Subtests use recorded Croatian speech stimuli presented at 65 dB SPL in a 35–45 minute individual session.
requirements: Administration by a trained examiner in a quiet room using a computer with headphones and calibrated CD-recorded stimuli
constraints: The battery contains no subtests using non-speech sounds, so the ASHA recommendation to use a non-verbal test was not followed
target_learners: Elementary school children aged 5.5–11.5 years in Croatia
target_learning_goals: Screening auditory processing skills relevant to literacy, language and academic achievement

article_title: Adult age differences in the effects of processing on storage in working memory: A meta-analysis.
citation: Jaroslawska, A. J., & Rhodes, S. (2019). Adult Age Diﬀerences in the Eﬀects of Processing on Storage in Working Memory: A Meta-Analysis. Psychology & Aging. https://doi.org/10.1037/pag0000358
title: Task-related moderator framework for age differences in storage-plus-processing working memory costs
description: The article organizes the contradictory literature on aging and dual task costs around five candidate task-related moderators: "1) the impact of equating (i.e., titrating) single task performance across age groups before concurrent tasks are combined, 2) whether the stimulus material used in the tasks is verbal or nonverbal in nature (and whether there is an overlap between domains of storage and processing components), 3) the processing requirements of the secondary task, 4) whether the input/output modality for the storage task matches the input/output modality for the processing task, and 5) whether the processing task imposes a response deadline." The framework explains why prior studies reached conflicting conclusions about disproportionate age-related dual task costs, and the meta-analysis tests each moderator against the pooled effect sizes.
requirements: Studies comparing healthy younger adults (mean age 30 or under) with healthy older adults (mean age 60 or over) on a storage task performed alone and with a concurrent processing task
constraints: The article reports clear evidence of moderation only for titration and task domain; for the remaining moderators "there is no clear evidence of moderation by the other factors"
Studies comparing different levels of memory updating (e.g., n-back) were excluded from the synthesis
target_learners: Healthy younger and older adults in working memory studies
target_learning_goals: Short-term storage and concurrent processing of information in working memory
examples: The meta-analysis coded each included study for titration, stimulus domain, processing task type (cognitive, sensorimotor, or another storage load), modality overlap, and response deadline, then entered these as moderators in meta-regressions

article_title: Fitting in or Feeling Excluded: The Experiences of High School Students with Visual Impairments
citation: Jessup, G; Bundy, AC; Broom, A; Hancock, N. (2018). Fitting in or feeling excluded: The experiences of high school students with visual impairments. https://doi.org/10.1177/0145482X1811200305
title: School staff should ensure adolescents with visual impairments can participate in lessons and facilitate opportunities to reciprocate with peers
description: The article recommends that school staff act on the social dimensions of students' everyday school experience: "The social impact of doing nothing at school provides an imperative for staff members to ensure that adolescents with visual impairments can participate in lessons." Because few school interactions involved giving help, staff may also need to facilitate opportunities for these students to reciprocate with peers. The principle rests on the study's findings about fitting in, acceptance, and interaction patterns at school.
requirements: Staff awareness of students' in-the-moment social experience at school, including participation in lessons and help exchange with peers
constraints: The authors note adolescents may need to lean on their families for assistance with valued out-of-home activities until they can participate independently
target_learners: High school students with visual impairments (blind or low vision)
target_learning_goals: Social participation and inclusion at school; reciprocal peer interaction
examples: Twelve visually impaired high school students completed the same in-the-moment survey seven times daily for seven consecutive days, comparing experiences across home, school, and other contexts

citation: Könen, T., Dirk, J., & Schmiedek, F. (2015). Cognitive benefits of last night's sleep: daily variations in children's sleep behavior are related to working memory fluctuations. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 56(2), 171–182. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.12296
title: FLUX smartphone ambulatory assessment application for children's daily sleep and working memory measurement
description: A dedicated smartphone application developed by the Technology Based Assessment Group at the DIPF for the FLUX project ('Assessment of Cognitive Performance FLUctuations in the School ConteXt'). It was the only available function of the distributed Dell Streak 5 phones, with internet, calls, games, and the regular system menu blocked, and delivered numerical and spatial working memory updating tasks plus sleep and tiredness items at three fixed daily occasions in school and at home for 31 consecutive days.
requirements: Fixed timing in school so teachers could schedule instruction, supervised sessions by teachers and trained research assistants, and individually adapted timing windows out of school
constraints: The application was pretested with 12 third-graders on 15 occasions and the tasks and items were pretested with 75 elementary school children before the main study

target_learning_goals: measuring daily working memory updating performance and self-reported sleep behavior in children's everyday lives
