article_title: Distinguishing short-term memory from working memory
citation: Robert Kail and Lynda K. Hall. (2001). Distinguishing short-term memory from working memory. Memory & Cognition, 29(1), 1-9. https://link.springer.com/journal/13421/29/1
title: Embedded-processes account in which STM is activated long-term memory and WM adds controlled attention
description: The article frames its predictions with theories (Cowan 1988, 1995; Engle, Kane, & Tuholski 1999) in which STM is information in long-term memory activated above threshold, and WM includes STM plus attentional processes. As the article puts it, "WM includesSTM as well as the at-tentionalprocesses used to keep some STM contentsin an activatedstate." Engle and colleagues' version defines WM as a system of active long-term memory traces, activation-maintaining processes, and controlled attention. This framework yields the two predictions the studies test: STM tasks should correlate with but load separately from WM tasks, and WM should predict higher-order cognition better.
requirements: Tasks must tap the hypothesized elements: simple span tasks for active memory traces and complex span tasks for traces plus controlled processing
constraints: No tasks are pure measures of STM or WM; tasks often share other processes such as encoding perceptual information, which inflates cross-construct correlations
target_learners: elementary school children aged 7 to 13
target_learning_goals: understanding the relation between memory storage and controlled attention in cognition and reading
examples: The studies administered digit, letter, and word span as STM tasks and reading, listening, and least number span as WM tasks to test the framework's predictions
key_sources: Robert Kail and Lynda K. Hall. (2001). Distinguishing short-term memory from working memory. Memory & Cognition, 29(1), 1-9. https://link.springer.com/journal/13421/29/1

article_title: Distinguishing short-term memory from working memory
citation: Robert Kail and Lynda K. Hall. (2001). Distinguishing short-term memory from working memory. Memory & Cognition, 29(1), 1-9. https://link.springer.com/journal/13421/29/1
title: Span-task battery distinguishing STM (simple span) from WM (complex span) in children
description: A set of memory tasks administered to 7- to 13-year-olds: digit, letter, and word span as traditional simple span STM measures, and reading span, listening span, and least number span as complex span WM measures requiring concurrent processing. As the article states, "WM was assessed with three tasks in which children remem-bered information while concurrently performing other cognitivetasks." Each span was defined as the largest set recalled perfectly from both sets. The battery also included PIAT-R Reading Recognition for decoding and Woodcock-Johnson Visual Matching and Cross-Out for processing speed.
requirements: Administration in a single session in a constant task order, with order not counterbalanced so individual differences would not be confounded with task order
constraints: Letter span was administered only in Study 1; digit span and least number span only in Study 2
target_learners: children aged 7 to 13
target_learning_goals: measuring distinct memory constructs and their links to word decoding and processing speed
examples: Reading span required children to read sentences aloud, judge truth, and recall final words; least number span required reading three numbers, naming the smallest, then recalling the smallest numbers in order
key_sources: Robert Kail and Lynda K. Hall. (2001). Distinguishing short-term memory from working memory. Memory & Cognition, 29(1), 1-9. https://link.springer.com/journal/13421/29/1

article_title: Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors and Their Association with Self-Regulation in Chilean Children
citation: López-Gil, J.F., Oriol-Granado, X., Izquierdo, M., Ramírez-Vélez, R., Fernández-Vergara, O., Olloquequi, J., & García-Hermoso, A. (2020). Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors and Their Association with Self-Regulation in Chilean Children. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17165676
title: Promote regular physical activity, limited screen time and healthy nutrition together, not in isolation, to support children's self-regulation
description: The article proposes that fostering multiple healthy lifestyle behaviors during childhood may be one potential strategy to promote child social-emotional development, since a greater number of healthy habits was associated with higher self-regulation. It states that "healthy lifestyles, such as regular PA, limited ST, and healthy nutrition promotion, should not be pursued in isolation, but rather as a part of a larger promotion". Regular physical activity emerges as the main habit to emphasize.
requirements: Interventions should integrate multiple components of SR development, which the authors note seems more successful in decreasing health risk behaviors.
constraints: Evidence is cross-sectional; the authors state results need to be confirmed in longitudinal and interventional research.
target_learners: Children aged 8–12 years in low-SES public schools
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation and social-emotional development
examples: The study compared self-regulation across children meeting different numbers and combinations of healthy habits (PA, screen time, Mediterranean Diet) in 1561 Chilean schoolchildren.
key_sources: López-Gil, J.F., Oriol-Granado, X., Izquierdo, M., Ramírez-Vélez, R., Fernández-Vergara, O., Olloquequi, J., & García-Hermoso, A. (2020). Healthy Lifestyle Behaviors and Their Association with Self-Regulation in Chilean Children. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17165676

article_title: Serial-order short-term memory predicts vocabulary development: Evidence from a longitudinal study.
citation: Leclercq, A.-L., & Majerus, S. (2010). Serial Order Short-Term Memory Predicts Vocabulary Development: Evidence from a Longitudinal Study. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018540
title: Item-order distinction in verbal STM and the serial-order account of vocabulary acquisition
description: The article organizes verbal short-term memory into two dissociable components: order information, "the sequential order in which the items are presented", and item information, the phonological, lexical and semantic characteristics of an item. Recent STM models store these in separate but interconnected systems, with a specialized system encoding sequential order and item information represented via temporary activation in the language network. Following Gupta, the authors propose that lexical acquisition and verbal STM capacity are driven by the same serial-order system, which replays activated language representations in correct order, reinforcing newly created lexical representations. The study's longitudinal dissociation — serial order STM, not item STM, predicting vocabulary — is offered as support for this account.
requirements: Tasks must independently maximize serial order versus item retention demands, as the animal race and single nonword delayed repetition tasks were designed to do
constraints: The account is tested here for children aged 4 to 5; the authors note item STM could be a stronger determinant at earlier developmental stages where phonological representation accuracy constrains vocabulary growth
A third, non-controlled ability such as selective attention to serial order or sequential rehearsal might mediate the observed longitudinal relationship
target_learners: typically developing kindergarten children aged 4-5 years
target_learning_goals: vocabulary acquisition
new phonological word-form learning
examples: The serial order reconstruction task presented sequences of seven highly familiar monosyllabic animal names and had children rearrange cards on a staircase, minimizing item demands
The castle task required delayed repetition of single monosyllabic nonwords with low-familiarity diphones while repeating 'bla' during retention to prevent rehearsal
key_sources: Leclercq, A.-L., & Majerus, S. (2010). Serial Order Short-Term Memory Predicts Vocabulary Development: Evidence from a Longitudinal Study. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018540

article_title: Effects of Acute and Chronic Exercises on Executive Function in Children and Adolescents: A Systemic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Liu S, Yu Q, Li Z, Cunha PM, Zhang Y, Kong Z, Lin W, Chen S and Cai Y (2020) Effects of Acute and Chronic Exercises on Executive Function in Children and Adolescents: A Systemic Review and Meta-Analysis. Front. Psychol. 11:554915. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.554915
title: Diamond's three-factor model of executive functions (inhibitory control, working memory, cognitive flexibility)
description: The article adopts Diamond's three-factor model of executive functions as its organizing framework, under which "inhibitory control, working memo ry, and cognitive ﬂexibility are the three core executive funct ions (EF)". These three cognitive abilities are said to work together to influence higher-order executive functions such as reasoning, planning, and problem solving. The review restricts its analysis to these three components because longitudinal evidence linking physical activity to higher-level executive functions in children is scarce. Inhibitory control is defined as the ability to suppress irrelevant reactions, working memory as registering information and performing cognitive operations on it, and cognitive flexibility as the ability to move flexibly to a new situation.
requirements: Outcome measures must target at least one of the three core components: inhibitory control, working memory, or cognitive flexibility
constraints: The review excludes higher-order executive functions such as decision-making and reasoning due to limited longitudinal evidence in children and adolescents
target_learners: children and adolescents aged 5–18 years
target_learning_goals: inhibitory control
working memory
cognitive flexibility
examples: The meta-analysis pooled effects separately for each of the three EF components across 36 RCTs
key_sources: Liu S, Yu Q, Li Z, Cunha PM, Zhang Y, Kong Z, Lin W, Chen S and Cai Y (2020) Effects of Acute and Chronic Exercises on Executive Function in Children and Adolescents: A Systemic Review and Meta-Analysis. Front. Psychol. 11:554915. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.554915

article_title: Executive functions predict literacy and mathematics achievements: The unique contribution of cognitive flexibility in grades 2, 4, and 6
citation: Sofia Magalhães, Luísa Carneiro, Teresa Limpo & Marisa Filipe (2020). Executive functions predict literacy and mathematics achievements: The unique contribution of cognitive flexibility in grades 2, 4, and 6. Child Neuropsychology, 26(7), 934-952. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2020.1740188
title: Three-core-component model of executive functions with higher-order components built on top
description: The article adopts the widely used framework in which executive functions are "a set of cognitive skills involved in goal-directed activities, which are crucial for the regulation of thoughts and actions". It defines "at least three separate but related core components": working memory (storing, manipulating, and processing information during a task), inhibitory control (inhibiting an automatic tendency), and cognitive flexibility (shifting between tasks or goals). Higher-order EF such as planning and fluid intelligence are built from these cores, which share a common executive attention foundation. The study uses this structure to isolate flexibility's unique contribution by controlling for the other components.
requirements: Measures must separate the core components so each can be controlled statistically when testing one component's unique contribution
constraints: The article notes some studies failed to find flexibility as a distinct component, and that flexibility may be less differentiated from working memory and inhibition in young children
target_learners: students in Grades 2, 4, and 6 (ages approximately 7–12)
target_learning_goals: literacy achievement
mathematics achievement
key_sources: Sofia Magalhães, Luísa Carneiro, Teresa Limpo & Marisa Filipe (2020). Executive functions predict literacy and mathematics achievements: The unique contribution of cognitive flexibility in grades 2, 4, and 6. Child Neuropsychology, 26(7), 934-952. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2020.1740188

article_title: The Developing Brain in the Digital Era: A Scoping Review of Structural and Functional Correlates of Screen Time in Adolescence
citation: Marciano Laura, Camerini Anne-Linda, Morese Rosalba. (2021). The Developing Brain in the Digital Era: A Scoping Review of Structural and Functional Correlates of Screen Time in Adolescence. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.671817
title: Dual-systems model of adolescent brain development
description: The review adopts the dual-systems model (Steinberg, 2010) as its developmental framework: the affective-motivational system matures in early adolescent years while the cognitive control system reaches maturity only in young adulthood. According to the review, "the temporal gap between the maturation of the two systems creates a period of greater vulnerability and propensity to risk-taking as well as reward- and novelty-seeking behaviors during middle adolescence." This imbalance frames why screen-based rewarding activities are particularly influential in adolescence.
requirements: Adolescent developmental period in which affective-motivational and cognitive-control systems mature at different rates
constraints: The review presents it as a developmental account of vulnerability, not as a tested explanation of screen-time effects
target_learners: adolescents (pre-adolescence to late adolescence, ages 10-18)
target_learning_goals: understanding self-regulation and reward sensitivity in adolescence
examples: The review uses the model to interpret adolescents' heightened neural responses to rewarding social stimuli and their propensity to seek short-term gratifications
key_sources: Marciano Laura, Camerini Anne-Linda, Morese Rosalba. (2021). The Developing Brain in the Digital Era: A Scoping Review of Structural and Functional Correlates of Screen Time in Adolescence. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.671817

article_title: The Developing Brain in the Digital Era: A Scoping Review of Structural and Functional Correlates of Screen Time in Adolescence
citation: Marciano Laura, Camerini Anne-Linda, Morese Rosalba. (2021). The Developing Brain in the Digital Era: A Scoping Review of Structural and Functional Correlates of Screen Time in Adolescence. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.671817
title: I-PACE model of addictive online behaviors
description: The review summarizes the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model (Brand et al., 2016, 2019), in which "cognition, personality, existing psychopathology, and motivations determine how people use the Internet in a specific way." Early online behaviors provide gratifications and relief from negative moods, creating reward expectancies; repetitive checking and obtained gratifications act as reinforcement, and conditioning processes lead to compulsive use. The imbalance between growing gratifying-oriented urges and diminishing inhibitory control is pivotal for developing online behavioral addictions.
requirements: Cognitive and affective response to Internet use together with obtained gratifications fostering subsequent use
constraints: The review notes the type of environment (online versus offline) may be of secondary importance, although the environment contributes significantly to the manifestation of addictive behaviors
target_learners: adolescents with problematic Internet, smartphone, or social media use
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms behind development and maintenance of addictive online behaviors
examples: The review cites two meta-analyses on Internet Gaming Disorder reporting frontostriatal and fronto-cingulate abnormalities as in line with I-PACE assumptions
key_sources: Marciano Laura, Camerini Anne-Linda, Morese Rosalba. (2021). The Developing Brain in the Digital Era: A Scoping Review of Structural and Functional Correlates of Screen Time in Adolescence. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.671817

article_title: Deaf children's non-verbal working memory is impacted by their language experience
citation: Marshall C, Jones A, Denmark T, Mason K, Atkinson J, Botting N and Morgan G (2015) Deaf children's non-verbal working memory is impacted by their language experience. Front. Psychol. 6:527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00527
title: Language experience, not deafness per se, shapes non-verbal working memory development
description: The article proposes that the quality and timing of language exposure—regardless of modality—drives the development of non-verbal, executive-loaded working memory. As the authors state, "rich language experience from birth, and the good language skills that result from this early age of acquisition, play a critical role in the development of NVWM and in performance on NVWM tasks." The three-group design (hearing, native signers, non-native signers) teases apart auditory experience from language experience, since native signers have full language access without auditory input.
requirements: Comparison groups that differ in language experience but are matched on age and non-verbal reasoning, using non-verbal tasks requiring minimal verbal instruction
constraints: The authors note other developmental differences between native and non-native signers (parental attachment, attention-getting strategies, social-cognitive development) might work alongside language exposure; causal direction over developmental time remains unresolved
target_learners: deaf children aged 6–11 years
children acquiring language in suboptimal early environments
target_learning_goals: development of non-verbal executive-loaded working memory
examples: Native deaf signers (n = 8) exposed to BSL from birth did not differ from hearing children on executive-loaded NVWM tasks, while non-native signers did
key_sources: Marshall C, Jones A, Denmark T, Mason K, Atkinson J, Botting N and Morgan G (2015) Deaf children's non-verbal working memory is impacted by their language experience. Front. Psychol. 6:527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00527

article_title: Deaf children's non-verbal working memory is impacted by their language experience
citation: Marshall C, Jones A, Denmark T, Mason K, Atkinson J, Botting N and Morgan G (2015) Deaf children's non-verbal working memory is impacted by their language experience. Front. Psychol. 6:527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00527
title: Provide deaf children of hearing parents with early accessible language exposure to support working memory development
description: The article argues that because suboptimal early language environments—rather than deafness itself—undermine working memory development, intervention should ensure deaf children of hearing parents receive accessible language early. The authors state: "An obvious implication for interventions with deaf children of hearing parents is for accessible language exposure to be provided early enough and in contexts where it can enhance or interact with working memory skills." This follows from their finding that native signers matched hearing peers on NVWM.
requirements: Language input that is fully accessible to the deaf child (e.g., a sign language) provided from an early age
constraints: The authors note they still lack sufficient information about the timing, amount and quality of sign language exposure necessary to support age-appropriate cognitive development
target_learners: deaf children of hearing non-signing parents
target_learning_goals: supporting working memory and broader cognitive development through early language access
examples: Deaf children with deaf signing parents who received BSL from birth performed comparably to hearing peers on executive-loaded NVWM tasks
key_sources: Marshall C, Jones A, Denmark T, Mason K, Atkinson J, Botting N and Morgan G (2015) Deaf children's non-verbal working memory is impacted by their language experience. Front. Psychol. 6:527. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00527

article_title: Executive Functions in Children Who Experience Bullying Situations
citation: Medeiros W, Torro-Alves N, Malloy-Diniz LF and Minervino CM (2016) Executive Functions in Children Who Experience Bullying Situations. Front. Psychol. 7:1197. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.01197
title: Hot and cold executive functions dichotomy applied to bullying roles
description: The article organizes its findings using the Kerr and Zelazo (2004) distinction between executive function types: "hot (more closely related to motivation and emotional control) and cold (more closely related to logical-rational aspects of cognition) executive functions." Cold functions cover inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility following Diamond's three-core model, while hot functions cover affective decision-making assessed with the Iowa Gambling Task. The authors use this dichotomy to interpret their pattern of results: victims showed greater difficulty on cold tasks whereas bullies showed impairment on the hot task.
requirements: Assessment must separately measure hot components (affective decision-making) and cold components (inhibitory control, working memory, cognitive flexibility) to distinguish role profiles.
constraints: The article states its methodology was transversal, so causal inferences about the investigated aspects cannot be made.
target_learners: children aged 10–11 in elementary school
target_learning_goals: executive functioning and affective decision-making in social behavior regulation
examples: Bullies were impaired on the hot executive function task (IGT Deck A choices) while victims performed worse on cold tasks (TMT-B), supporting the dichotomy's application to bullying roles.
key_sources: Medeiros W, Torro-Alves N, Malloy-Diniz LF and Minervino CM (2016) Executive Functions in Children Who Experience Bullying Situations. Front. Psychol. 7:1197. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.01197

article_title: Longitudinal alterations in brain morphometry mediated the effects of bullying victimization on cognitive development in preadolescents.
citation: Menken Miriam S., Rodriguez Rivera Pedro J., Isaiah Amal, Ernst Thomas, Cloak Christine C., Chang Linda. (2023). Longitudinal alterations in brain morphometry mediated the effects of bullying victimization on cognitive development in preadolescents. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2023.101247
title: Brain morphometry as a partial mediator/suppressor of the effect of bullying victimization on cognitive development
description: The article proposes that structural brain changes in bullying-impacted regions statistically mediate or suppress part of the effect of bullying victimization on cognition. Using LMM-derived bullying-impacted regions, mediation models estimated the indirect effect of bullying on cognitive scores through subcortical volume, cortical volume, surface area, and thickness. The authors report that "Changes in brain morphometry mediate or suppress 7–16% of the effect of bullying on cognition", with fusiform surface area acting as a suppressor and precentral thickness as a partial mediator. The framework follows the AGReMA reporting guideline and a suppression-effect interpretation per MacKinnon et al.
requirements: Longitudinal MRI morphometry and cognitive testing in bullied and matched non-bullied children
Bullying-impacted regions identified first via LMMs before mediation testing
constraints: The mediation model did not allow nesting by scanner, so scanner type was included as a covariate instead
Temporal precedence of bullying before cognitive effects is argued, not experimentally established
target_learners: preadolescent children in the ABCD Study cohort
target_learning_goals: understanding neural mechanisms linking bullying victimization to cognitive outcomes
examples: Mediation analyses showed larger right fusiform surface area suppressed 11.8-15.6% of the bullying effect on crystallized composite and picture vocabulary scores, and thinner precentral cortex mediated 7.0% of the effect on inhibitory control and attention
key_sources: Menken Miriam S., Rodriguez Rivera Pedro J., Isaiah Amal, Ernst Thomas, Cloak Christine C., Chang Linda. (2023). Longitudinal alterations in brain morphometry mediated the effects of bullying victimization on cognitive development in preadolescents. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2023.101247

article_title: Contributions of Motivation, Early Numeracy Skills, and Executive Functioning to Mathematical Performance. A Longitudinal Study
citation: Mercader J, Miranda A, Presentación MJ, Siegenthaler R and Rosel JF (2018) Contributions of Motivation, Early Numeracy Skills, and Executive Functioning to Mathematical Performance. A Longitudinal Study. Front. Psychol. 8:2375. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.02375
title: Multifactorial longitudinal model of mathematical performance with motivation as distal and executive functioning and early numeracy as proximal predictors
description: The article proposes and tests a structural equation model in which mathematical performance in second grade is a function of three kindergarten latent variables: motivation (competence-motivation, attention-persistence, positive internality), executive functioning (inhibition and working memory), and early numeracy skills (procedural counting, conceptual counting, logical operations, symbolic comparison). The model hypothesizes a cascade in which "The latent variable Executive Functioning is inﬂuenced by the latent variable Motivation" and early numeracy skills depend on both, with performance assessed at T2. It is framed by the Opportunity-Propensity model, in which propensity factors such as motivational disposition and prior cognitive skills condition benefit from learning opportunities.
requirements: Assessment of motivational, executive functioning, and early numeracy indicators in early childhood education prior to the mathematical outcome measure
Structural equation modeling to reduce error variance relative to single observable variables
constraints: The model excludes planning/monitoring EF components, linguistic precursors such as phonological awareness, family variables such as socio-economic status, and instructional factors such as type and amount of teaching
target_learners: children in kindergarten (5–6 years) transitioning to early primary education
target_learning_goals: early mathematical performance and identification of its cognitive and motivational precursors
examples: The model was tested with 180 children assessed at two time points using TEDI-MATH, Stroop and tapping inhibition tasks, working memory tasks, the PLBS, and the CASI, with TEMA-3 at T2
key_sources: Mercader J, Miranda A, Presentación MJ, Siegenthaler R and Rosel JF (2018) Contributions of Motivation, Early Numeracy Skills, and Executive Functioning to Mathematical Performance. A Longitudinal Study. Front. Psychol. 8:2375. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.02375

article_title: The Importance of Social Contextual Factors in Peer Relationships of Children with ADHD
citation: Mikami, A. Y., & Normand, S. (2015). The Importance of Social Contextual Factors in Peer Relationships of Children with ADHD. Curr Dev Disord Rep. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40474-014-0036-0
title: Social contextual model of peer problems in ADHD: peer group factors (social devaluation, exclusionary behavior, reputational bias) contribute to peer impairment above and beyond child behavior deficits
description: The review proposes that the traditional conceptualization—explaining ADHD peer problems solely via the child's inappropriate behaviors—is incomplete. It identifies three peer group influences: social devaluation (stigmatizing attitudes toward dissimilar classmates), exclusionary behavior (peers' rejecting acts that broadcast low status), and reputational bias (difficulty revising negative impressions). The model holds that "behavior change in the child with ADHD may be a necessary, but not sufficient, condition to result in peers' acceptance". It is depicted in Fig. 1 as behavior deficits and peer group influences jointly contributing to social problems.
requirements: Interventions must address peer group factors in addition to child behavior deficits to improve peer regard
constraints: The review notes these peer group factors may pertain to children disliked for reasons other than ADHD
target_learners: children with ADHD in general education classrooms
target_learning_goals: improved peer acceptance, friendships, and social functioning
examples: The review's Fig. 1 diagrams children's behavior deficits and peer group influences as parallel contributors to social problems
key_sources: Mikami, A. Y., & Normand, S. (2015). The Importance of Social Contextual Factors in Peer Relationships of Children with ADHD. Curr Dev Disord Rep. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40474-014-0036-0

article_title: A Meta-Analysis Investigating the Association Between Metacognition and Math Performance in Adolescence
citation: Gemma Muncer, Philip A. Higham, Corentin J. Gosling, Samuele Cortese, Henry Wood-Downie, & Julie A. Hadwin. (2021). A Meta-Analysis Investigating the Association Between Metacognition and Math Performance in Adolescence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09620-x
title: Online versus offline measurement as an organising distinction for metacognition assessment
description: The article organises metacognition measures by whether they capture metacognition during task performance or via retrospective self-report. "Offline measures are questionnaires that aim to capture an individual's self-reported perception of their own MC ability based on previous learning experiences", such as the MSLQ, MAI and Jr. MAI, whereas "online measures capture an individual's MC via ongoing behaviour and performance as they complete a task", including think-aloud protocols and behaviour observations. The article notes contested boundary cases (confidence judgements, calibration accuracy, JOLs) classified differently by Saraç and Karakelle, Veenman and van Cleef, and Craig et al., and reports poor correspondence between the two measure types in prior studies.
requirements: A measure must be classifiable as online or offline; the article applies the Veenman and van Cleef (2019) distinction, with think-aloud protocols and behaviour observations classed as online and self-report questionnaires as offline
constraints: The article states that online and offline measures may be measuring different facets of metacognition, given their poor correspondence across studies; classification of JOLs, confidence judgements and calibration scores is contested
target_learners: adolescents aged 11–16 in secondary school mathematics
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness, monitoring and regulation applied to mathematical problem-solving
examples: The review classified each included study's metacognition measure as online or offline (e.g. think-aloud protocols in van der Stel et al. as online; Jr. MAI questionnaires as offline) and used this categorisation in its moderation analysis
key_sources: Gemma Muncer, Philip A. Higham, Corentin J. Gosling, Samuele Cortese, Henry Wood-Downie, & Julie A. Hadwin. (2021). A Meta-Analysis Investigating the Association Between Metacognition and Math Performance in Adolescence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09620-x

article_title: Working Memory and Attention – A Conceptual Analysis and Review
citation: Oberauer, K. (2019). Working Memory and Attention – A Conceptual Analysis and Review. Journal of Cognition, 2(1): 36. https://doi.org/10.5334/joc.58
title: A three-dimensional taxonomy organizing concepts of attention by definition, objects, and mode of control
description: The review proposes a coordinate system for organizing concepts of attention along three dimensions. The first distinguishes attention as a limited resource from attention as "a process of (or mechanism for) selection of information to be processed with priority". The second distinguishes objects of attention along two sub-dimensions (perceptual vs. non-perceptual; things/events vs. goals/actions). The third distinguishes controlled from automatic deployment. Table 1 displays the resulting cells, each describing a distinct form of attention.
requirements: The taxonomy requires distinguishing how attention is defined from what attention is directed at and from what determines its orientation
constraints: The review notes the term executive attention is ambiguously used across two of these dimensions and proposes replacing it with attention to cognitive action and controlled attention
target_learners: cognitive psychology researchers
students of cognitive science
target_learning_goals: understanding the conceptual structure of attention theories
understanding how attention concepts relate to working memory theory
examples: Table 1 in the article displays cells such as selective attention to locations, visual objects, events, features and capture of attention by salient stimuli
key_sources: Oberauer, K. (2019). Working Memory and Attention – A Conceptual Analysis and Review. Journal of Cognition, 2(1): 36. https://doi.org/10.5334/joc.58

article_title: Working Memory and Attention – A Conceptual Analysis and Review
citation: Oberauer, K. (2019). Working Memory and Attention – A Conceptual Analysis and Review. Journal of Cognition, 2(1): 36. https://doi.org/10.5334/joc.58
title: A three-level framework of selection in working memory: activated part of LTM, region of direct access, and focus of attention
description: The review proposes that selection in WM operates at three nested levels: selecting information into WM (the activated part of long-term memory), selecting a subset of the memory set (the region of direct access), and selecting a single item (the focus of attention). Behavioral evidence shows retro-cues can select subsets and then items within subsets, supporting "three levels of selection in WM". The framework has been computationally implemented (Oberauer et al., 2013).
requirements: The framework requires that selection at each level serves a functional purpose, such that selecting multiple items simultaneously is feasible only when doing so does not undercut the purpose of selection
constraints: The review notes it is currently not clear whether more than one WM representation is neurally active at the same time, so the neural characterization of the second versus third level remains open
target_learners: cognitive psychology researchers
students of working memory
target_learning_goals: understanding the architecture of selection within working memory
understanding how retro-cues and item-switch costs reveal levels of selection
examples: Retro-cue paradigms demonstrate that a cue presented one to several seconds into retention can guide attention to one item or a subset, improving memory for cued content at the expense of uncued content
key_sources: Oberauer, K. (2019). Working Memory and Attention – A Conceptual Analysis and Review. Journal of Cognition, 2(1): 36. https://doi.org/10.5334/joc.58

article_title: Neurocognitive mechanisms underlying working memory encoding and retrieval in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
citation: Ortega, R., López, V., Carrasco, X., Escobar, M. J., García, A. M., Parra, M. A. & Aboitiz, F. (2020). Neurocognitive mechanisms underlying working memory encoding and retrieval in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Scientific Reports 10:7771. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-64678-x
title: Attention-guided prioritization and updating account of WM impairment in ADHD: binding intact, encoding and retrieval compromised
description: The article proposes that WM impairment in ADHD arises not from deficient binding or early visual filtering but from compromised attention-dependent encoding and retrieval. It draws on the context updating theory of P3, in which "P3 amplitude reflects the effort to continuously update new relevant information to the representation held in WM", and on resource-allocation accounts. Reduced encoding P3, retrieval P3 that fails to discriminate change, and absent encoding-retrieval P3 correlations in ADHD are read as "a failure in the prioritization of relevant information". The account informs theories of binding in visual WM by showing bound features are held intact despite attentional impairment.
requirements: ERP measurement separating encoding and retrieval stages, as behavioral responses alone cannot discriminate WM stages
constraints: Inferences limited by sample size, possible implicit verbal rehearsal, ADHD heterogeneity, and medication effects, per the authors' limitations section
target_learners: adolescents with ADHD (Combined subtype) aged 12–14
target_learning_goals: understanding working memory encoding, binding and retrieval processes in attentional disorders
examples: A visual short-term memory binding task with no nameable polygons and non-primary colors, spatial locations interchanged between study and test displays, used with 18 ADHD and 18 matched non-ADHD adolescents
key_sources: Ortega, R., López, V., Carrasco, X., Escobar, M. J., García, A. M., Parra, M. A. & Aboitiz, F. (2020). Neurocognitive mechanisms underlying working memory encoding and retrieval in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Scientific Reports 10:7771. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-64678-x

article_title: How bilingualism modulates selective attention in children
citation: Jacqueline Phelps, Adam Attaheri & Mirjana Bozic. (2022). How bilingualism modulates selective attention in children. Scientific Reports 12:6381. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-09989-x
title: Resource-economisation account of bilingual neurocognitive adaptation
description: The article proposes that language selection and inhibition in bilinguals themselves draw on a finite selective attention capacity, so remaining resources must be economised to support optimal task performance. It predicts "no increase—or possibly even a slight reduction" in neural indices of attentional processing combined with a different distribution across task conditions, rather than the enhancement predicted by the bilingual-advantage view. The study's findings of equivalent behaviour with a flatter, overall weaker encoding pattern in bilinguals are read as supporting this redistribution account, extending the adaptive control hypothesis.
requirements: Bilingual language use must impose constant management of competing languages, creating processing demands that draw on attentional resources
constraints: The interpretation of reduced encoding in weak-interference conditions as economisation is described by the authors as tentative
target_learners: typically-developing children aged 7–12
bilingual and monolingual children
target_learning_goals: selective attention as a foundational skill for academic success
examples: Children attended to English narratives while ignoring English, Latin, or Musical Rain interference; bilinguals showed weaker encoding only where interference was weakest
key_sources: Jacqueline Phelps, Adam Attaheri & Mirjana Bozic. (2022). How bilingualism modulates selective attention in children. Scientific Reports 12:6381. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-09989-x

article_title: How bilingualism modulates selective attention in children
citation: Jacqueline Phelps, Adam Attaheri & Mirjana Bozic. (2022). How bilingualism modulates selective attention in children. Scientific Reports 12:6381. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-09989-x
title: Four-condition dichotic listening paradigm with mTRF speech-envelope reconstruction
description: A child-appropriate EEG paradigm in which participants attend to an English narrative in one ear while ignoring interference in the other across four conditions: Single talker (no interference), English–English, English–Latin, and English–Musical Rain. Backward mTRF decoding models reconstruct attended and unattended speech envelopes from 60-channel EEG, with reconstruction accuracy (Pearson's r) as the index of attentional encoding. The article notes the method "maps all available neural data simultaneously" and is suited to multi-channel EEG and natural speech.
requirements: A minimum threshold of five minutes of data per condition for input to the mTRF toolbox
Children old enough to perform selective attention tasks reliably; a minimum age of 6 is recommended in the literature the article cites
constraints: Epoch rejection removed 16.33% of data overall, varying by condition from 12.77% to 19.68%
target_learners: children aged 7–12
target_learning_goals: measuring neural encoding of attended versus unattended speech
examples: Each target story was split into two 3.3-minute blocks with 10 comprehension questions per block; Musical Rain was generated from the target sentences' temporal envelopes filled with synthesized vowel fragments
key_sources: Jacqueline Phelps, Adam Attaheri & Mirjana Bozic. (2022). How bilingualism modulates selective attention in children. Scientific Reports 12:6381. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-09989-x

article_title: Number processing and arithmetic skills in children with cochlear implants
citation: Pixner, S., Leyrer, M., and Moeller, K. (2014). Number processing and arithmetic skills in children with cochlear implants. Frontiers in Psychology 5:1479. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01479
title: Language-dependent place-value processing account of specific arithmetic difficulties in children with cochlear implants
description: The article adopts the view, following LeFevre et al.'s developmental model and the Triple Code model, that mastery of the base-10 place-value structure of the Arabic number system is language dependent. It uses this account to explain why children with CI, despite atypical language development, show qualitatively similar arithmetic performance but specific impairments exactly "when demands on place-value understanding" increase — in borrow subtraction and wider number-line ranges. The account holds that general verbal representations support arithmetic fact retrieval, while quantity and symbol representations are less language dependent.
requirements: The account presupposes atypical or delayed language development as the source of impaired place-value understanding, as in children with CI
constraints: The article did not measure language performance directly, comparing groups instead, and calls for future studies with a combined correlational approach to cross-validate the findings
target_learners: children with cochlear implants
typically developing elementary school children (grades 3–5)
target_learning_goals: place-value understanding of the Arabic base-10 number system
arithmetic fact retrieval
mental arithmetic
examples: Borrow subtraction problems and 0–1000 number line estimation were the two task conditions in which CI children's performance declined disproportionately relative to hearing peers
key_sources: Pixner, S., Leyrer, M., and Moeller, K. (2014). Number processing and arithmetic skills in children with cochlear implants. Frontiers in Psychology 5:1479. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01479

article_title: Number processing and arithmetic skills in children with cochlear implants
citation: Pixner, S., Leyrer, M., and Moeller, K. (2014). Number processing and arithmetic skills in children with cochlear implants. Frontiers in Psychology 5:1479. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01479
title: Give children with cochlear implants extra time on arithmetic and provide focused teaching of the base-10 place-value system
description: Based on the finding that children with CI are generally slower yet qualitatively similar in arithmetic, and specifically weaker when place-value demands rise, the authors draw two educational implications: "children with CI may perform equally well than their hearing peers provided they are given some extra time to solve arithmetic problems" and they "may require more focused teaching of the Arabic base-10 place-value system". This targets the general slowing and the circumscribed place-value difficulty respectively.
requirements: Extra time addresses the observed general response slowing; focused place-value instruction addresses the borrow-subtraction and wide-range number-line difficulties
constraints: Recommendations rest on a single matched-group study of third- to fifth-graders in Austria; the dyscalculia indications may partly reflect the speeded HRT format
target_learners: children with cochlear implants in elementary school
target_learning_goals: arithmetic fluency
place-value understanding of the Arabic base-10 number system
examples: In the study, CI children's latencies were longer across multiplication and subtraction tasks, and their error increase was specific to borrow problems and the 0–1000 number line range
key_sources: Pixner, S., Leyrer, M., and Moeller, K. (2014). Number processing and arithmetic skills in children with cochlear implants. Frontiers in Psychology 5:1479. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01479

article_title: Selective attention within the foveola
citation: Poletti Martina, Rucci Michele, Carrasco Marisa. (2017). Selective attention within the foveola. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.4622
title: Covert attention as a global selection mechanism operating across the entire visual field, including the foveola
description: The article proposes that covert attention is not a process that operates only away from the center of gaze but "the manifestation of a more general mechanism evolved for selectively improving and accelerating processing throughout the visual field, including the region of highest acuity." Selective enhancement can be restricted to very narrow regions and shifted across locations separated by minutes of arc, with allocation varying with task demands and stimulus characteristics. The authors infer the underlying neural processes need high-resolution saliency maps of the central field, continual updating during fixational instability, and spatial updating mechanisms with much higher resolution than those studied in the periphery.
requirements: High-resolution representations of the central visual field and mechanisms for continually updating them during fixational instability, as the article states the controlling processes must include
constraints: The account is grounded in psychophysical experiments with small observer samples (N=5 per experiment) using gaze-contingent retinal stabilization
target_learners: adult observers in visual perception tasks
target_learning_goals: selective spatial attention and fine spatial vision
examples: Experiments 2–4 showed valid-cue benefits and invalid-cue costs within the foveola at 20′ separations, under both stabilized and normal fixation
key_sources: Poletti Martina, Rucci Michele, Carrasco Marisa. (2017). Selective attention within the foveola. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.4622

article_title: Selective attention within the foveola
citation: Poletti Martina, Rucci Michele, Carrasco Marisa. (2017). Selective attention within the foveola. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.4622
title: EyeRIS gaze-contingent display control system with Dual Purkinje Image eyetracking for retinal stabilization
description: EyeRIS is "a custom-developed system based on dedicated hardware, which allows flexible gaze-contingent display control." It acquires eye movement signals from a Dual Purkinje Image eyetracker (spatial resolution 1′, sampled at 1 kHz), processes them in real time, and updates the display to compensate for eye movements, keeping stimuli at fixed foveal eccentricities. Combined with a two-step gaze-contingent calibration procedure, it enabled the first tests of selective attention within the foveola, with a stabilization error of approximately 1′ and a 10 ms system delay.
requirements: High spatial and temporal resolution eye tracking and a two-step gaze-contingent calibration procedure to map eyetracker output into visual angles
constraints: Trials with delay exceeding 14 ms were discarded, and analyses were restricted to trials with good stabilization quality (blinks, saccades, and late microsaccades excluded)
target_learners: adult observers in vision-science experiments
target_learning_goals: precise control of retinal stimulation for studying spatial attention
examples: Stimuli were moved in real time under EyeRIS control to compensate for observer eye movements during Experiments 2 and 3
key_sources: Poletti Martina, Rucci Michele, Carrasco Marisa. (2017). Selective attention within the foveola. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.4622

article_title: Hot and Cool Executive Functions in Adolescence: Development and Contributions to Important Developmental Outcomes
citation: Poon K (2018) Hot and Cool Executive Functions in Adolescence: Development and Contributions to Important Developmental Outcomes. Front. Psychol. 8:2311. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.02311
title: Hot/cool distinction in executive function: cool EF as logic-driven and hot EF as emotion-driven processes underlying goal-directed behavior
description: Executive function is an umbrella term for skills essential for conscious, goal-directed thought and behavior. The framework separates cool EF — psychological processes involving pure logic and critical analysis, elicited under abstract, decontextualized, non-affective conditions (working memory, inhibition, cognitive flexibility, attentional control, planning) — from hot EF, which "involves goal-directed, future-oriented cognitive processes elicited in contexts that generate emotion, motivation, and a tension between instant gratiﬁcation and long-term rewards," including delay gratification and affective decision making. The study uses this distinction to test differential adolescent development and outcome contributions.
requirements: Measurement batteries must separately capture affectively loaded decision contexts (e.g., gambling tasks) and abstract non-affective tasks to operationalize the two facets
constraints: The article notes current research does not make a convincing case for the distinction of the hot and cool forms, though EF is generally agreed to specialize into distinct functions with development
target_learners: typically developing adolescents aged 12–17
target_learning_goals: goal-directed behavior and self-regulation underlying academic performance and psychological adjustment
examples: The study operationalized cool EF with backward digit span, CNT, Stockings of Cambridge, and Stroop, and hot EF with the Cambridge Gambling Task's risk adjustment and delay aversion measures
key_sources: Poon K (2018) Hot and Cool Executive Functions in Adolescence: Development and Contributions to Important Developmental Outcomes. Front. Psychol. 8:2311. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.02311

article_title: Hot and Cool Executive Functions in Adolescence: Development and Contributions to Important Developmental Outcomes
citation: Poon K (2018) Hot and Cool Executive Functions in Adolescence: Development and Contributions to Important Developmental Outcomes. Front. Psychol. 8:2311. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.02311
title: Assess and support executive function during adolescence, a period of EF plasticity with implications for identification and training
description: Because executive function remains malleable well beyond early childhood, adolescence is a strategic window for identifying EF weaknesses and delivering EF-targeted support. The article states: "Given the plastic nature of EF , especia lly over adolescence, the current ﬁndings may have practical implications for future EF identiﬁcation and training." The study's differentiated hot/cool developmental trajectories imply that identification and training efforts should be timed to the facet-specific trajectories the study documents.
requirements: Assessment batteries should distinguish hot and cool EF facets so that identification and training can target the appropriate facet at the appropriate developmental stage
target_learners: typically developing adolescents aged 12–17
target_learning_goals: executive function development supporting academic performance and psychological adjustment
examples: The study measured five EF tasks across six age groups of adolescents and linked facet-specific developmental patterns to grades and parent-rated adjustment, motivating facet-specific identification and training
key_sources: Poon K (2018) Hot and Cool Executive Functions in Adolescence: Development and Contributions to Important Developmental Outcomes. Front. Psychol. 8:2311. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.02311

article_title: Communication, Psychosocial, and Educational Outcomes of Children with Cochlear Implants and Challenges Remaining for Professionals and Parents
citation: Punch, R., & Hyde, M. B. (2011). Communication, Psychosocial, and Educational Outcomes of Children with Cochlear Implants and Challenges Remaining for Professionals and Parents. International Journal of Otolaryngology. https://doi.org/10.1155/2011/573280
title: Mirenda's four-aspect framework for classroom participation
description: The teacher survey used a framework devised by Mirenda to assess the level of participation of children in their school and classroom activities. As the paper describes it, "The framework covers four aspects of participation in regular classrooms: integration, described as physical presence in the regular classroom; academic participation; independence, which is concerned with the level of supports the child needs in order to participate in the classroom; social participation." The authors note it had been used effectively in another Australian study with deaf and hard of hearing students.
requirements: Teachers report on each of the four participation aspects for a specific child in their classroom setting.
constraints: The wellbeing and happiness subscale of the parent survey was excluded from the teacher survey because its items were specific to parents' knowledge of their children.
target_learners: deaf children in regular classrooms
target_learning_goals: assessing classroom participation including integration, academic participation, independence, and social participation
examples: Each teacher in the study completed a survey based on one randomly selected child whom they supported, rated on this framework.
key_sources: Punch, R., & Hyde, M. B. (2011). Communication, Psychosocial, and Educational Outcomes of Children with Cochlear Implants and Challenges Remaining for Professionals and Parents. International Journal of Otolaryngology. https://doi.org/10.1155/2011/573280

article_title: Neural bases of orthographic long-term memory and working memory in dysgraphia
citation: Rapp, Brenda; Purcell, Jeremy; Hillis, Argye; Capasso, Rita; Miceli, Gabriele. (2016). Neural bases of orthographic long-term memory and working memory in dysgraphia. BRAIN. https://doi.org/10.1093/brain/awv348
title: Two-component architecture of spelling: orthographic long-term memory retrieval plus working-memory maintenance before serial motor production
description: The article frames spelling as a multi-component process: information about a word's letters and their order is retrieved from long-term memory, then maintained and processed by working memory in preparation for serial production by the motor system. The article states that "Spelling a word involves the retrieval of information about the word's letters and their order from long-term memory as well as the maintenance and processing of this information by working memory in preparation for serial production by the motor system." This architecture motivates distinguishing dysgraphia forms that selectively affect each component.
requirements: Spelling performance must be interpretable as depending on separable orthographic long-term memory and working memory processes
constraints: The framework is stated for written word production (spelling), not other language tasks
target_learners: individuals with dysgraphia
adults learning or relearning written spelling
target_learning_goals: spelling
retrieval of letter identities and order
written word production
examples: The study classified 27 individuals with deficits affecting only one of the two processes and 6 with deficits affecting both
key_sources: Rapp, Brenda; Purcell, Jeremy; Hillis, Argye; Capasso, Rita; Miceli, Gabriele. (2016). Neural bases of orthographic long-term memory and working memory in dysgraphia. BRAIN. https://doi.org/10.1093/brain/awv348

article_title: Neural correlates of theory of mind reasoning in congenitally blind children
citation: Richardson H., Saxe R., Bedny M. (2023). Neural correlates of theory of mind reasoning in congenitally blind children. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2023.101285
title: Non-visual story-based behavioral ToM task for blind and sighted children
description: A validated, non-visual story-based task measuring ToM reasoning in children aged four to twelve, publicly available at https://osf.io/pavdg/. Children listen to an experimenter read twenty short stories and answer 51 questions, including 22 two-alternative forced choice and 29 open-ended explanation questions targeting "desires, expectations, beliefs, intentions, perceptual access, and knowledge of the characters." Items vary the source modality of mental states (visual, aural, amodal) to test whether blind children show differential comprehension of visual experiences, and 19 control questions verify attention and comprehension.
requirements: Requires children to be fluent English speakers, as stories are read aloud in English and answered verbally
constraints: Designed for use with four- to twelve-year-old children
target_learners: children aged 4-12, including congenitally blind children
target_learning_goals: theory of mind reasoning about beliefs, desires, emotions, and perceptual access
examples: Validated against a previously used ToM task in 21 sighted children: the two tasks correlated even controlling for age and verbal and non-verbal IQ (b=0.46, t=2.6, p=.02)
key_sources: Richardson H., Saxe R., Bedny M. (2023). Neural correlates of theory of mind reasoning in congenitally blind children. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2023.101285

article_title: Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education
citation: Rivas SF, Saiz C and Ossa C (2022) Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education. Front. Psychol. 13:913219. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.913219
title: Components-of-critical-thinking model: cognitive skills, non-cognitive dispositions, and metacognition as a bridging process
description: The article presents a model (Figure 1, Saiz 2020) in which critical thinking comprises cognitive components (perception, learning, memory, and the core skills of reasoning, decision-making, and problem-solving) and non-cognitive components (motivation and interests), with metacognition sharing aspects of both because it "incorporates aspects of both judgment (evaluation) and disposition (control/efficiency) about thoughts." Motivation activates skills while metacognition makes them more effective; the authors argue neither cognitive skills nor dispositions alone suffice to train critical thinking, and relations among components are bidirectional.
requirements: Instruction must address both cognitive and non-cognitive components, since one component is incomplete without the other
constraints: Figure 1 shows only unidirectional relations for didactic reasons, although the authors state relations are in general bidirectional
target_learners: higher education students
secondary school students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
metacognitive awareness and self-regulation
examples: The ARDESOS-DIAPROVE program operationalizes this model by directly teaching reasoning, decision-making, and problem-solving skills while incorporating motivational and metacognitive variables.
key_sources: Rivas SF, Saiz C and Ossa C (2022) Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education. Front. Psychol. 13:913219. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.913219

article_title: Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education
citation: Rivas SF, Saiz C and Ossa C (2022) Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education. Front. Psychol. 13:913219. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.913219
title: Gradual learning control transference in four phases: explicit instruction, guided practice, cooperative practice, individual practice
description: The article's teaching procedure is based on "the philosophy of gradual learning control transference" (Mateos, 2001), in which the teacher models and guides students' cognitive and metacognitive activity, then slowly withdraws support. It develops in four phases: (1) explicit instruction, where the teacher directly explains the skills; (2) guided practice, where the teacher acts as collaborator for self-regulation; (3) cooperative practice, where group work with explaining, elaborating, and justifying promotes consciousness, reflection, and control; and (4) individual practice in evaluation tasks.
requirements: Teacher acts as model and guide, gradually withdrawing support to attain control over the students' learning process
target_learners: first-year university students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
self-regulated learning
examples: In ARDESOS-DIAPROVE, students work in cooperative groups of four in class, then review, correct, and clarify together, receiving rubrics and feedback in every session.
key_sources: Rivas SF, Saiz C and Ossa C (2022) Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education. Front. Psychol. 13:913219. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.913219

article_title: Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education
citation: Rivas SF, Saiz C and Ossa C (2022) Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education. Front. Psychol. 13:913219. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.913219
title: ARDESOS-DIAPROVE program: a 16-week critical thinking intervention integrating PBL and cooperative learning
description: ARDESOS-DIAPROVE (third version) is a classroom program that directly teaches critical thinking skills via Problem-Based Learning and cooperative learning. "The intervention took place over 16 weeks and is designed to be applied in classrooms over a timeframe of 55–60 h" in classes of around 30–35 students divided into groups of four, organized into six activity blocks (nature of critical thinking; problem-solving and effectiveness; explanation and causality; deduction and explanation; argumentation and deduction; problem-solving and decision-making). Tasks use common situations and professional/personal problems, with rubrics for every task and feedback in all sessions.
requirements: Instructors with training and good experience in the program
Tasks contextualized within everyday problems so students perceive skills as useful
constraints: DIAPROVE methodology adds observation development, combined use of facts and deduction, and management of de-confirmation procedures as its foundation
target_learners: first-year psychology university students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
metacognition
problem-solving and decision-making
examples: Evaluation used the PENCRISAL test administered over the Internet via the SelectSurvey.NET V5 platform and the 52-item MAI, with measurements one week before and one week after the intervention.
key_sources: Rivas SF, Saiz C and Ossa C (2022) Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education. Front. Psychol. 13:913219. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.913219

article_title: Validity of the Dynamic Indicators for Basic Early Literacy Skills as an Indicator of Early Literacy for Urban Kindergarten Children
citation: Rouse, H. L., & Fantuzzo, J. W. (2006). Validity of the Dynamic Indicators for Basic Early Literacy Skills as an Indicator of Early Literacy for Urban Kindergarten Children. School Psychology Review, 35(3), 341-355. http://dibels.uoregon.edu
title: Use brief fluency-based early literacy screeners such as the end-of-kindergarten DIBELS subtests to identify at-risk urban kindergartners and guide classroom intervention
description: The article recommends using the three end-of-kindergarten DIBELS subtests as a screening and progress-monitoring tool in urban districts, because the subtests demonstrated concurrent, convergent, discriminant, and predictive validity for a low-income, predominantly minority sample. The authors state the subtests "could be used to guide classroom-based instmction and intervention" and that the short, fluency-based format supports frequent administration and measurement of response to intervention.
requirements: Administration by trained school personnel, as the article notes administration does not require intensive training and can be done by regular school personnel
constraints: Findings are qualified to urban public school kindergarten children; the study sample did not allow exploration of validity for English language learners
target_learners: Kindergarten children in large urban public school districts, primarily low-income and minority students
target_learning_goals: Early literacy skills: alphabet knowledge, phonological awareness, and alphabetic principle (decoding)
examples: The district administered DIBELS districtwide three times per year (October, February, May) by trained early childhood staff; the study validated the three end-of-kindergarten subtests against teacher report, individual assessments, and nationally standardized tests.
key_sources: Rouse, H. L., & Fantuzzo, J. W. (2006). Validity of the Dynamic Indicators for Basic Early Literacy Skills as an Indicator of Early Literacy for Urban Kindergarten Children. School Psychology Review, 35(3), 341-355. https://doi.org/10.1080/02796015.2006.12087971

article_title: Mathematics anxiety in children with developmental dyscalculia
citation: Rubinsten O, Tannock R. (2010). Mathematics anxiety in children with developmental dyscalculia. Behavioral and Brain Functions 6:46. http://www.behavioralandbrainfunctions.com/content/6/1/46
title: Failure-fear-failure cycle: low math achievement from developmental dyscalculia gives rise to math anxiety, which further impedes achievement
description: The article proposes that developmental dyscalculia, an innate, heritable deficit in processing numerical information centered on intraparietal sulcus deficiencies, produces low math achievement from an early age, and that this low achievement leads to math anxiety rather than the reverse. The authors state that "low math achievement due to DD will lead to math anxiety", citing evidence that initial low achievement predicts later math anxiety, and frame the resulting dynamic as a cycle of "failure-fear-failure" that interventions could turn into "success-confidence-success".
requirements: The account presumes DD is a heritable, genetically-based condition with low numerical abilities present from a very early age
constraints: The authors state the causal direction is only a suggested hypothesis, since the current analysis cannot point directly to a causal connection between math anxiety and math achievement
target_learners: children with developmental dyscalculia aged 7 to 13
target_learning_goals: basic arithmetic fact retrieval and numerical processing
examples: The priming experiment showed DD children's arithmetic targets facilitated by negative and math primes, consistent with arithmetic facts being associated with negative emotions
key_sources: Rubinsten O, Tannock R. (2010). Mathematics anxiety in children with developmental dyscalculia. Behavioral and Brain Functions 6:46. http://www.behavioralandbrainfunctions.com/content/6/1/46

article_title: Mathematics anxiety in children with developmental dyscalculia
citation: Rubinsten O, Tannock R. (2010). Mathematics anxiety in children with developmental dyscalculia. Behavioral and Brain Functions 6:46. http://www.behavioralandbrainfunctions.com/content/6/1/46
title: Arithmetic-affective priming task as an indirect measure of math anxiety
description: A novel computerized priming task in which single-digit arithmetic equations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) are preceded by one of four prime word types (positive, neutral, negative, mathematics-related) at a 250 ms stimulus onset asynchrony; participants judge as quickly as possible whether each equation is true or false. The article reports that "our arithmetic-affective priming may be used as an indirect measure of math anxiety", and suggests it is "a useful tool in establishing the affective value of various arithmetic procedures in different types of math-achieving participants".
requirements: Short stimulus onset asynchrony (250 ms) chosen to influence both retrieval from verbal memory and response selection levels
Participants instructed to ignore the prime word while judging the equation
constraints: The affective value of the target arithmetic problems was initially unknown, so relatedness could not be established as in standard affective priming studies
target_learners: children aged 7 to 13 with and without developmental dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: measuring affective responses to simple arithmetic and math anxiety indirectly
examples: Each participant underwent 160 trials using 40 primes four times each, twice with a true equation and twice with a false equation as target
key_sources: Rubinsten O, Tannock R. (2010). Mathematics anxiety in children with developmental dyscalculia. Behavioral and Brain Functions 6:46. http://www.behavioralandbrainfunctions.com/content/6/1/46

article_title: Effect of classroom-based physical activity interventions on attention and on-task behavior in schoolchildren: A systematic review
citation: Ruhland Stefanie, Lange Klaus W. (2021). Effect of classroom-based physical activity interventions on attention and on-task behavior in schoolchildren: A systematic review. Sports Medicine and Health Science. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smhs.2021.08.003
title: Classroom-based physical activity (CB-PA) as physical activity during regular class time, inside or outside the classroom, excluding recess and lunch
description: The review defines CB-PA, following Watson and colleagues, as "PA during regular class time, which can occur either inside or outside the classroom, and which does not include time during school recess or lunch breaks." The construct covers two forms: short units of PA during breaks from lessons, and movement-enriched tuition in which PA mediates curriculum content (e.g., learning multiplication tables via invisible jump rope in TAKE 10!). Interventions may be performed with or without additional equipment, and intensity is mostly moderate to vigorous physical activity.
requirements: PA occurs during regular class time, not during recess or lunch breaks
constraints: Excludes time during school recess or lunch breaks; the review excluded studies of children with behavioral disorders such as ADHD or obesity
target_learners: school-aged children and adolescents aged 4–18 years
target_learning_goals: attention (selective, sustained, divided) and on-task behavior in the classroom
examples: TAKE 10! students learn multiplication tables by performing invisible jump rope; FUNtervals use 20 s high-intensity activity separated by 10 s rest repeated 8 times per day
key_sources: Ruhland Stefanie, Lange Klaus W. (2021). Effect of classroom-based physical activity interventions on attention and on-task behavior in schoolchildren: A systematic review. Sports Medicine and Health Science. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smhs.2021.08.003

article_title: How Can Bullying Victimisation Lead to Lower Academic Achievement? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Mediating Role of Cognitive-Motivational Factors
citation: Muthanna, Samara; Da Silva Nascimento, Bruna; El-Asam, Aiman; Hammuda, Sara; Khattab, Nabil. (2021). How Can Bullying Victimisation Lead to Lower Academic Achievement? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Mediating Role of Cognitive-Motivational Factors. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18052209
title: Self-Determination Theory as the framework explaining how bullying victimisation undermines motivation and achievement
description: The article uses Self-Determination Theory (SDT) as its explanatory framework for why victimisation lowers achievement. SDT "postulates that relatedness, autonomy, and competence are three important factors to maintain positive well-being", and holds that all three needs must be supported for students to feel motivated and reach their academic potential. Negative school conditions such as peer rejection, social exclusion, and bullying may undermine these needs, offering a mechanism account for the mediation findings. The article also draws on expectancy-value theory and achievement goal theory as supporting accounts.
requirements: All three needs (relatedness, autonomy, competence) must be supported in students for motivation and achievement
constraints: The article notes the mechanism is supported by only a limited set of empirical mediation studies to date
target_learners: children and adolescents in school settings (ages 5-17)
target_learning_goals: academic motivation and aspirations
academic engagement
academic achievement
examples: The meta-analysis tests the SDT-consistent prediction that victimisation reduces motivation and engagement, which in turn reduces achievement
key_sources: Muthanna, Samara; Da Silva Nascimento, Bruna; El-Asam, Aiman; Hammuda, Sara; Khattab, Nabil. (2021). How Can Bullying Victimisation Lead to Lower Academic Achievement? article_title: Child maltreatment and ADHD symptoms in a sample of young adults
citation: Sanderud K., Murphy S., Elklit A. (2016). Child maltreatment and ADHD symptoms in a sample of young adults. European Journal of Psychotraumatology. https://doi.org/10.3402/ejpt.v7.32061
title: Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS v1.1) six-item screening measure for probable adult ADHD
description: The ASRS v1.1 is a six-item self-report screening instrument measuring the frequency of core ADHD symptoms — concentration problems, hyperactivity, and memory problems — on a 5-point Likert scale from "never" to "all the time". Items were recoded so a symptom was present at ≥3 on the first three questions and ≥4 on the remaining three, and a binary probable-ADHD variable used a threshold of ≥4. In this study it produced a Cronbach alpha of 0.66 and classified 431 (14.5%) participants above cutoff.
requirements: Respondents answer six frequency items on a 5-point Likert scale; a probable ADHD classification requires the ≥4 threshold on the recoded binary variable
constraints: The article reports a Cronbach alpha of 0.66 in the current sample and notes the measure is a screening tool based on self-report, not a clinical diagnosis
target_learners: young adults (24-year-old cohort)
target_learning_goals: screening for attention, hyperactivity, and memory problems consistent with probable adult ADHD
examples: Used with 2,980 young Danish adults; 431 (14.5%) scored above the cutoff for probable ADHD

article_title: Intelligence and Verbal Short-Term Memory/Working Memory: Their Interrelationships from Childhood to Young Adulthood and Their Impact on Academic Achievement
citation: Schneider Wolfgang, Niklas Frank. (2017). Intelligence and Verbal Short-Term Memory/Working Memory: Their Interrelationships from Childhood to Young Adulthood and Their Impact on Academic Achievement. Journal of Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence5020026
title: Studies of cognitive predictors of achievement should include domain-knowledge indicators at every measurement point
description: The article concludes that IQ and WM may matter mainly in early schooling when domain knowledge is not yet developed, and that their impact fades once prior domain knowledge is estimated. It therefore recommends that "future research on the topic should be based on longitudinal designs" that "include relevant indicators of domain knowledge at each time point in order to estimate the size of specific IQ and WM effects and their changes over time." This is a methodological design principle for research on cognitive predictors of learning.
requirements: Longitudinal designs with several representative measures of IQ and WM during early and later assessment periods, plus relevant indicators of domain knowledge at each time point
constraints: The article notes its own memory measures seem to tap STM more than WM, and different measures had to be used across time points, limiting comparability
target_learners: children and adolescents in school, ages 6 to 23
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension, spelling, and mathematics achievement
examples: The LOGIC reanalysis entered preceding academic achievement as precursors before IQ and WMC in regression and SEM models, which eliminated most cognitive-predictor effects at later waves
