article_title: Neural evidence for enhanced attention to mistakes among school-aged children with a growth mindset
citation: Schroder Hans S., Fisher Megan E., Lin Yanli, Lo Sharon L., Danovitch Judith H., Moser Jason S. (2017). Neural evidence for enhanced attention to mistakes among school-aged children with a growth mindset. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2017.01.004
title: Pe as an index of attention allocation to errors within the mindset nomological network
description: The article treats the error positivity (Pe), an ERP peaking 200–500 ms after errors, as indexing "conscious error awareness and attention allocation to errors". It interprets enlarged Pe among growth-minded children as neural evidence for two mindset-theory predictions: that growth-minded children view errors as more motivationally relevant events and expend more cognitive resources processing and adjusting after mistakes. The Pe is distinguished from the earlier, automatic ERN and likened to the P3b, an ERP component reflecting mobilization of attentional resources to motivationally relevant task events.
requirements: ERP measurement during an error-monitoring task with sufficient error trials for reliable Pe estimation
constraints: The authors note the alternative emotional-responsivity interpretation of the Pe has not been well supported, and the attention-allocation reading in children is their interpretation, with engagement vs. disengagement across development left as an open question
target_learners: school-aged children (ages 6–8) beginning formal schooling
target_learning_goals: resilient response to mistakes and errors during learning
examples: The study recorded ERPs while 123 children completed a zoo-animal go/no-go task, finding larger Pe difference waves among growth-minded children

citation: Silva, H., Lopes, J., Dominguez, C., & Morais, E. (2022). Think-Pair-Share and Roundtable: Two Cooperative Learning Structures to Enhance Critical Thinking Skills of 4th Graders. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 15(1), 11-21. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2022.274
title: Cooperative learning rests on five basic elements that together promote critical thinking
description: The article describes cooperative learning as small heterogeneous groups cooperating toward common goals, structured by five elements: "positive interdependence, individual and group accountability, promotive interaction, social skills, and group processing". When these are present, students share and synthesize ideas, argue about viewpoints, and establish agreements, which the authors hold promotes critical thinking skills. The study's activities were structured so these characteristics were always present.
requirements: Students organized in small heterogeneous groups by achievement and gender
Social skills such as turn-taking, attentive listening, conflict management
Evaluation procedures for group processing
constraints: A lack of social skills is described as probably the main inhibiting factor to success of cooperative groups
target_learners: 4th grade primary students (1st cycle of basic education)
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking skills: observation, interpretation, analysis (inferences), argumentation
examples: The experimental teacher organized heterogeneous groups of four, assigned rotating roles, and ran 21 cooperative activities across Language Arts, Environment Study and Mathematics

International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 15(1), 11-21. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2022.274
title: Think-Pair-Share three-phase discussion structure
description: Think-Pair-Share (TPS) is a cooperative learning technique that unfolds in three phases: Thinking, where students get "time to think individually" about a topic or problem; Pairing, where pairs within groups discuss to reach a common answer; and Share, where pairs share answers and one member reports the group's answer to the class. The article states TPS enables oral and written argumentation and increases response quality by increasing waiting time. It was used with similar frequency to RoundTable across 21 activities.
requirements: Heterogeneous groups of four students
A topic or problem stated by the teacher
Time allocated for individual thinking
target_learners: 4th grade primary students
target_learning_goals: Oral and written argumentation
Critical thinking through discussion of different perspectives
examples: Used in the experimental class across Language Arts, Environment Study and Mathematics on topics such as pollution, children's rights, and community life of bees and ants

International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 15(1), 11-21. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2022.274
title: RoundTable written turn-taking structure
description: RoundTable (Kagan, 1994) is a cooperative method in which the teacher organizes heterogeneous groups of three or four, gives each group a pen and sheet of paper, and presents a task requiring more than one answer. Each member writes an answer or idea within a stipulated time, then passes the paper and pen to the next person; the activity ends when time elapses and each group shares its final product with the class. The article says it helps students solve complex conceptual problems, developing analysis, synthesis, and evaluation skills.
requirements: Heterogeneous groups of three or four students
A task requiring more than one answer
Stipulated time for completion and per-member writing
target_learners: 4th grade primary students
target_learning_goals: Analysis, synthesis, and evaluation skills
Reviewing peers' written work and considering other points of view
examples: Students reviewed work written by peers, which the article says develops conceptual understanding and the ability to evaluate information

title: CTTBE: Critical Thinking Test for Basic Education (48-item researcher-built instrument)
description: Because no Portuguese test assessed critical thinking for basic school students, the authors built the CTTBE from the national Profile of Students at the End of Compulsory Schooling, with items reviewed by two experts for relevance and clarity. It comprises "48 items with visual stimuli printed in color" and verbal stimuli (short authentic texts), assessing Observation (15 restricted-response items), Interpretation (14 multiple-choice), Analysis (18 multiple-choice), and Argumentation (one long-answer item). Reliability is acceptable (α = 0.72).
requirements: Expert review of item relevance and clarity
Pilot testing with a comparable student group
constraints: No critical thinking test validated for this education level existed; the authors state validation would be needed for generalization

article_title: Reward improves cancellation and restraint inhibition across childhood and adolescence.
citation: Sinopoli, K.J., Schachar, R., & Dennis, M. (2011). Reward Improves Cancellation and Restraint Inhibition Across Childhood and Adolescence. Developmental Psychology, 47(5), 1479-89. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0024440
title: Incentive salience account of reward effects on inhibitory control
description: The article offers an incentive salience account (drawing on Berridge) for why reward speeds inhibition: rewards "tag" conditioned stimuli that predict reward value, increasing the incentive salience ("wanting") of the stop signal. Because the stop signal is linked to points leading to a prize while the go response is not rewarded, the net effect is facilitation of SSRT but not response execution. The authors hypothesize the mesocorticolimbic dopamine system adds incentive salience to the stop signal, possibly via IFG-mediated salience-detection pathways or striatal gating.
requirements: Rewards must be contingent on successful inhibitory control trials, so the stop signal becomes linked to a positive outcome
constraints: The authors state it is not possible to elucidate how rewards affected IC in the current study; the account is offered as hypotheses
Participants did not anecdotally report increased pleasure during reward trials, which the authors note weighs against a hedonia account
target_learners: typically developing children aged 7-12
adolescents aged 13-17
target_learning_goals: regulation of thought and action (inhibitory control)
examples: Rewards were earned only for successful inhibition trials, with points displayed on a visual analog scale and a $10 gift certificate prize for reaching 400 points

article_title: Social Class is Dead. Long Live Social Class! Stereotype Threat among Low Socioeconomic Status Individuals
citation: Spencer, B; Castano, E (2007). Social class is dead, long live social class! Stereotype threat among low-socioeconomic individuals. Social Justice Research. https://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s11211-007-0047-7
title: Stereotype threat: stigmatized-group members underperform for fear of confirming a negative ingroup stereotype
description: Stereotype threat is the mechanism by which "members of a stigmatized group perform poorly on a task because they fear confirming a negative stereotype that is associated with their ingroup." The article applies this mechanism to socioeconomic status, treating low-SES students as a stigmatized group whose test performance can be depressed when SES-related threat is made salient or when a test is framed as diagnostic of intelligence. It uses the construct to interpret the performance and self-confidence differences observed across its four experimental threat conditions.
requirements: A negative stereotype associated with the individual's ingroup must be relevant to the task being performed
constraints: The article applies the mechanism to socioeconomic status among American students in standardized testing contexts
target_learners: low-socioeconomic status American students
target_learning_goals: standardized test performance
academic self-confidence
examples: Participants were placed in one of four conditions that varied in level of ''threat'' related to socioeconomic status.
key_sources: Spencer, B; Castano, E (2007). Social class is dead, long live social class! Stereotype threat among low-socioeconomic individuals. Social Justice Research. https://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s11211-007-0047-7

article_title: Balanced Cultural Identities Promote Cognitive Flexibility among Immigrant Children
citation: Spiegler O and Leyendecker B (2017) Balanced Cultural Identities Promote Cognitive Flexibility among Immigrant Children. Front. Psychol. 8:1579. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01579
title: Acculturation complexity model
description: The acculturation complexity model (Tadmor and Tetlock, 2006) links varying levels of engagement with two cultures to cognitive skill development. It proposes that "biculturals with a relatively equal preference for two distinct cultures experience cultural conflicts and a need to resolve these conflicts," and that repeated attempts to resolve cultural discrepancies gradually promote integrative complexity. The present study applies the model to executive functioning, predicting the strongest EF advantage for balanced biculturals, especially on cognitive flexibility tasks.
requirements: Immersion into two distinct or dissonant cultures, which the model argues is most likely to promote cognitive skills
constraints: The model predicts advantages primarily for individuals who endorse both cultures with relatively equal strength, not for those who clearly prefer one culture
target_learners: immigrant-origin children
bicultural individuals
target_learning_goals: cognitive flexibility
integrative complexity
executive functioning
examples: The study tested the model's prediction in Turkish-German children immersed in two markedly distant cultures differing in interdependence–independence, family obligations, religious values, and gender role expectations
key_sources: Spiegler O and Leyendecker B (2017) Balanced Cultural Identities Promote Cognitive Flexibility among Immigrant Children. Front. Psychol. 8:1579. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01579

article_title: The role of selective attention on academic foundations: A cognitive neuroscience perspective
citation: Stevens, Courtney; Bavelier, Daphné. (2012). The role of selective attention on academic foundations: A cognitive neuroscience perspective. Developmental cognitive neuroscience, vol. 2S, p. S30–S48. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2011.11.001
title: Neurobiological framework of selective attention: neural effects of attention, systems for deploying it, and systems for managing response conflict
description: The review organizes the neurobiology of selective attention around two components: the effects of selective attention on neural processing, and the neural systems needed to deploy selective attention and manage response conflict. The abstract states the authors "provide a brief review of the neural bases of selective attention, emphasizing the effects of selective attention on neural processing, as well as the neural systems important to deploying selective attention and managing response conflict." This framework underpins the article's developmental and educational arguments.
requirements: Grounding in research on the neurobiology of attention, as the review draws on that literature
constraints: Presented as a brief review of hypothesized links rather than a tested model
target_learners: children in early education
target_learning_goals: selective attention skills supporting academic foundations
examples: The review's first section reviews the neural bases of selective attention as the foundation for later sections on development and academic domains
key_sources: Stevens, Courtney; Bavelier, Daphné. (2012). The role of selective attention on academic foundations: A cognitive neuroscience perspective. Developmental cognitive neuroscience, vol. 2S, p. S30–S48. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2011.11.001

article_title: The role of selective attention on academic foundations: A cognitive neuroscience perspective
citation: Stevens, Courtney; Bavelier, Daphné. (2012). The role of selective attention on academic foundations: A cognitive neuroscience perspective. Developmental cognitive neuroscience, vol. 2S, p. S30–S48. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2011.11.001
title: Target selective attention skills in education because they are relevant to academic foundations and amenable to training
description: The article proposes that selective attention deserves an important place in education because it both matters for early academic skills and can plausibly be improved. The abstract states: "To the extent that selective attention skills are relevant for academic foundations and amenable to training, they represent an important focus for the field of education." The review develops this principle through its sections on neural bases, development, academic domains, and training.
requirements: Evidence that selective attention is relevant to academic foundations and that it is amenable to training
constraints: The principle is conditional: it holds to the extent that both relevance and trainability are established
target_learners: children in early education
target_learning_goals: selective attention skills supporting language, literacy, and mathematics foundations
examples: The review's final section examines applying these principles to educationally-focused attention-training programs for children

article_title: Developmental dyscalculia is related to visuo-spatial memory and inhibition impairment
citation: Szucs Denes, Devine Amy, Soltesz Fruzsina, Nobes Alison, Gabriel Florence. (2013). Developmental dyscalculia is related to visuo-spatial memory and inhibition impairment. Cortex, 49(10). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cortex.2013.06.007
title: Inhibition impairment as disruption of central executive visuo-spatial working memory in developmental dyscalculia
description: The article proposes an explanatory account in which the WM and inhibition impairments detected in DD are related: "the inhibition impairment may have led to impaired visuo-spatial WM performance". On this view, DD reflects specific impairment of visuo-spatial STM and of the inhibitory processes crucial to visuo-spatial central executive WM function, and IPS differences in DD may relate to interference resolution rather than magnitude representation function.
requirements: Requires measuring STM and WM capacity separately in the verbal and visual modalities, as the article argues modality-specific WM systems dissociate
constraints: The account is offered as a hypothesis; the article states the inhibition impairment may have led to impaired visuo-spatial WM performance rather than demonstrating this causally
target_learners: primary school children with developmental dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement and numerical skills
examples: The study measured inhibition via congruency effects in four Stroop-type experiments and a Stop-signal task, and visuo-spatial WM via the AWMA Odd One Out subtest

article_title: Finding and using students’ funds of knowledge and identity in superdiverse primary schools: a collaborative action research project
citation: J. 't Gilde, M. Volman. (2021). Finding and using students’ funds of knowledge and identity in superdiverse primary schools: a collaborative action research project. Cambridge Journal of Education, 51(6), 673-692. https://doi.org/10.1080/0305764X.2021.1906845
title: Funds of knowledge/identity theory: building on skills and knowledge students acquire in families, communities and peer groups
description: Funds of knowledge/identity (FoK/I) theory is an explanatory framework holding that students acquire skills and knowledge in their families, communities and peer groups that teachers may fail to recognise, particularly across sociocultural difference. The article states that the theory "makes a plea for building on the skills and knowledge that students acquire in their families, communities and peer groups". It is used as the theoretical basis for a collaborative action research project on teaching in superdiverse primary classrooms.
requirements: Teachers must be able to recognise skills and knowledge students acquire outside school that may otherwise go unrecognised.
constraints: The article frames the theory as relevant where teachers and students are from different sociocultural backgrounds in superdiverse classrooms.
target_learners: primary school students in superdiverse classrooms
target_learning_goals: building instruction on students' family, community and peer-group knowledge and skills
examples: The authors used FoK/I theory to frame a collaborative action research project investigating how primary school teachers can use students' FoK/I in their classrooms.
key_sources: J. 't Gilde, M. Volman. (2021). Finding and using students’ funds of knowledge and identity in superdiverse primary schools: a collaborative action research project. Cambridge Journal of Education, 51(6), 673-692. https://doi.org/10.1080/0305764X.2021.1906845

title: Framework for finding students' funds of knowledge and categorising FoK/I-related teaching practices
description: A framework produced by the project's analyses that serves two functions: it "suggests ways to find students’ FoK" and it categorises FoK/I-related teaching practices along two dimensions — (1) individual students' resources vs. collective resources and (2) scope of the teaching activities. It is the article's central artifact for supporting teachers in superdiverse primary classrooms.
requirements: Teachers need ways to find students' funds of knowledge before FoK/I-related teaching practices can be categorised and used.
constraints: Developed within a collaborative action research project in superdiverse primary schools.
target_learners: primary school students in superdiverse classrooms
target_learning_goals: identifying and building on students' funds of knowledge/identity in teaching
examples: The framework emerged from analysis of pre-structured logbooks, teacher interviews and focus groups collected in the project.

article_title: Lower Attentional Skills predict increased exploratory foraging patterns
citation: Van den Driessche, C., Chevrier, F., Cleeremans, A. & Sackur, J. (2019). Lower Attentional Skills predict increased exploratory foraging patterns. Scientific Reports 9:10948. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-46761-0
title: ADHD traits as an exploration-biased tuning of the exploration/exploitation trade-off rather than a pure attention deficit
description: The article proposes that lower attentional skills reflect a search strategy biased toward exploration: children with higher ADHD-rs scores "inserted more often jumps to distant positions in the search space" while sharing the same base local search strategy as other children. The bias is framed as a latent cognitive trait diversely expressed across task contexts, potentially beneficial in sparse environments such as semantic search, and linked to dopaminergic mechanisms and an evolutionary adaptation account of ADHD.
requirements: Applies to non-clinical variation in attention traits, as the study used the ADHD-rs "only as a means to evaluate the cognitive dimension that is at the core of the disorder" with no clinical intent
constraints: Participants were all healthy children, not clinical ADHD; the authors state that in clinical populations dimensions such as motivation or vigilance disorder "might come into play and mitigate the benefits of the exploratory strategy"
The benefit appeared in semantic search but not visual search, where targets were uniformly distributed
target_learners: neurotypical children aged 8 to 11 in mainstream classrooms
target_learning_goals: attention regulation during search and memory retrieval tasks
examples: 87 fourth-grade children performed the Bells Test and an animal fluency task, with search paths analyzed as foraging in visual and word2vec semantic spaces

citation: Femke van der Wilt, Chiel van der Veen, Claudia van Kruistum, Bert van Oers (2019). Why Do Children Become Rejected by Their Peers? A Review of Studies into the Relationship Between Oral Communicative Competence and Sociometric Status in Childhood. Educational Psychology Review (2019) 31:699–724. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09479-z
title: Oral communicative competence as a context-dependent, multifaceted construct
description: The review defines oral communicative competence, following Hymes, as the ability to convey and interpret messages and negotiate meanings interpersonally within specific social contexts. It is "a context-dependent and multifaceted construct that consists of many sub-abilities that need to be integrated to communicate effectively", encompassing socio-linguistic competence alongside structural knowledge of language. The review uses this construct to organize its search terms, its inclusion criteria, and its analysis of how studies operationalize children's communication.
requirements: Assessment should take the interactional context into account, since appropriateness of language use depends on settings, topics, and relationships among people
constraints: The construct is broad and multifaceted, which makes it difficult to define and operationalize; standardized tests may not capture its full complexity
target_learners: children aged 1 to 12 years in mainstream community samples
target_learning_goals: oral communicative competence: using language acceptably and efficiently in particular social contexts

citation: Femke van der Wilt, Chiel van der Veen, Claudia van Kruistum, Bert van Oers (2019). Why Do Children Become Rejected by Their Peers? Educational Psychology Review (2019) 31:699–724. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09479-z
title: Peer nomination procedure for assessing children's sociometric status
description: The peer nomination procedure, developed by Moreno and adapted by Coie et al. (1982), asks children to nominate up to three peers they like and three they dislike. Nominations are used to compute acceptance, rejection, social impact, and social preference, which in turn create the sociometric groups (popular, rejected, neglected, controversial, average). The review reports it is "a reliable and valid method for measuring children 's social position", used in 16 of the 25 reviewed studies, and recommends it remain part of future studies.
requirements: Peer nominations are easy to administer and not time-consuming; they rely on the judgements of peers, who provide unique information on children's behavior
constraints: Reporting on friendships requires verbal skills that younger preschool children often lack, which motivated Nærland's observation-based alternative
target_learners: children aged 1 to 12 years, including young children aged 2 to 5
target_learning_goals: measurement of children's sociometric status within the peer group
examples: Burleson et al. (1992) asked first- and third graders to nominate classmates for four roles and computed standardized social preference and social impact indices

article_title: The Influence of Situational Cues on Children’s Creativity in an Alternative Uses Task and the Moderating Effect of Selective Attention
citation: van Dijk, M., Blom, E., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Leseman, P. P. M. (2020). The Influence of Situational Cues on Children’s Creativity in an Alternative Uses Task and the Moderating Effect of Selective Attention. Journal of Intelligence, 8(4), 37. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence8040037
title: Perception–action affordance account of situated creativity
description: The article proposes that creativity is situated: creative behaviour emerges from detecting alternative action affordances within the common affordance structures of everyday objects, building on Gibson's ecological approach. An "affordance is defined as the match between what a person currently is able to and interested in, on the one hand, and the relevant properties of the physical environment that trigger and enable particular actions of the person, on the other hand". Detecting uncommon uses requires isolating, foregrounding, and recombining nested subordinate affordances, a process in which selective attention plays a central role.
requirements: Individuals must be able to perceptually or imaginatively isolate nested subordinate affordances and object properties from the fixed structure of common affordances
constraints: The study's own findings ran counter to the hypothesis that a high stimulus environment supports creativity, and the authors state the results "do not support the perception–action view on creativity we proposed" in its strong form
target_learners: children aged 9–12 in primary education
target_learning_goals: divergent thinking and creative idea generation
examples: The study operationalised the account with a real-object Alternative Uses Task in low and high stimulus conditions, with selective attention measured by the TEA-Ch Sky Search task
key_sources: van Dijk, M., Blom, E., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Leseman, P. P. M. (2020). The Influence of Situational Cues on Children’s Creativity in an Alternative Uses Task and the Moderating Effect of Selective Attention. Journal of Intelligence, 8(4), 37. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence8040037

article_title: The Influence of Situational Cues on Children’s Creativity in an Alternative Uses Task and the Moderating Effect of Selective Attention
citation: van Dijk, M., Blom, E., Kroesbergen, E. H., & Leseman, P. P. M. (2020). The Influence of Situational Cues on Children’s Creativity in an Alternative Uses Task and the Moderating Effect of Selective Attention. Journal of Intelligence, 8(4), 37. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence8040037
title: Score originality with methods not based on relative response frequency within the sample
description: Because sample-relative originality coding can bias scores when conditions differ in the stimulus array children see, the authors recommend alternative scoring. They state: "we recommend considering alternative ways of coding in future research which are not based on the relative response frequency within the sample, such as using a jury to assess the responses". They also note frequency estimates are more accurate with larger samples and suggest intersubjective rating or automated scoring.
requirements: A scoring method that does not depend on response frequency within the study sample, such as jury rating or automated scoring
constraints: Sample-relative coding may favour conditions in which children's answers draw on idiosyncratic memories rather than a shared stimulus array
target_learners: children aged 9–12 in primary education
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of creative originality
examples: In the study, uses mentioned by less than 10% of the sample were coded as original, and the authors argue this coding may have favoured the low stimulus condition

article_title: Development of Affective Theory of Mind Across Adolescence: Disentangling the Role of Executive Functions
citation: Vetter, Nora C.; Altgassen, Mareike; Phillips, Louise; Mahy, Caitlin; Kliegel, Matthias. (2013). Development of Affective Theory of Mind Across Adolescence: Disentangling the Role of Executive Functions. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2012.733786
title: Theory of mind comprises cognitive and affective components distinguished by mental-state type
description: The article frames theory of mind, "the ability to understand mental states", as involving two kinds of inference: inferences about others' cognitive mental states (cognitive theory of mind) and inferences about others' emotional mental states (affective theory of mind). The study focuses on the affective component and its development across adolescence.
requirements: Measures must distinguish affective from cognitive theory-of-mind inference when assessing development.
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: understanding others' emotional mental states
understanding others' cognitive mental states
examples: The study measured affective theory of mind alongside three executive-function subcomponents in an adolescent sample.

article_title: On the relationship between cultural diversity and creativity in education: The moderating role of communal versus divisional mindset
citation: Vezzali, L., Goclowska, M., Crisp, R. J., & Stathi, S. (2016). On the Relationship between Cultural Diversity and Creativity in Education: The Moderating Role of Communal versus Divisional Mindset. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/
title: Communal versus divisional mindset account of the diversity–creativity link
description: The article proposes that diversity benefits creativity because it disrupts stereotype use and prompts generative thinking, but a salient "divisional mindset" focused on group distinctions activates intergroup differentiation processes at odds with this way of thinking. A "communal mindset" that does not mention group differences leaves the beneficial cognitive effects of diversity intact. In the study, the two mindsets were manipulated orthogonally to group composition via fictional story framings.
requirements: The mindset manipulation must be orthogonal to the actual diversity of the group so its moderating role can be isolated.
constraints: The account was tested only for originality of ideas in children; the specific cognitive process (e.g., flexibility) underlying the effect was not measured.
target_learners: elementary schoolchildren
target_learning_goals: creative thinking (originality of ideas)
examples: Children in the divisional condition imagined two opposing fictional groups (Sun and Moon) with different skin colors; those in the communal condition imagined one cooperative group on planet Astra.
key_sources: Vezzali, L., Goclowska, M., Crisp, R. J., & Stathi, S. (2016). On the Relationship between Cultural Diversity and Creativity in Education: The Moderating Role of Communal versus Divisional Mindset. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/

article_title: The Effects of Physical Exercise on Functional Outcomes in the Treatment of ADHD: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Vysniauske, R., Verburgh, L., Oosterlaan, J., & Molendijk, M. L. (2020). The Effects of Physical Exercise on Functional Outcomes in the Treatment of ADHD: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of attention disorders, 24(5), 644-654. https://doi.org/10.1177/1087054715627489
title: Use physical exercise interventions of longer duration to support functional outcomes in children with ADHD
description: The meta-analysis supports incorporating physical exercise into the treatment of children with ADHD to improve functional outcomes such as executive functions and motor skills. The authors conclude that "exercise has a modest positive impact on ADHD functional outcomes" and that interventions should be designed with sufficient duration, since "longer interventions yielding better results" was the consistent moderator pattern.
requirements: Interventions must target functional outcomes (executive functions, motor skills) in children with ADHD, the population the meta-analysis covers.
constraints: The evidence base is ten publications analyzed with a random-effects model; the overall impact is characterized as modest.
target_learners: children with ADHD
target_learning_goals: executive functions
motor skills
examples: The meta-analysis pooled ten publications reporting effects of physical exercise on motor skills and executive functions in children with ADHD.

motor skills

article_title: Best Practice Framework for Online Safety Education: Results from a Rapid Review of the International Literature, Expert Review, and Stakeholder Consultation
citation: Walsh, K., Pink, E., Ayling, N., Sondergeld, A., Dallaston, E., Tournas, P., Serry, E., Trotter, S., Spanos, T., & Rogic, N. (2022). Best Practice Framework for Online Safety Education: Results from a rapid review of the international literature, expert review, and stakeholder consultation. International Journal of Child-Computer Interaction, 33, Article number: 100474. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijcci.2022.100474
title: Best Practice Framework for Online Safety Education: five elements with 22 effective practices
description: A multi-component national framework for online safety education in Australian schools (Foundation to Year 12), developed via rapid evidence review plus expert and stakeholder validation. The final Framework comprises 5 elements and 22 effective practices. Its elements are: students' rights and responsibilities; resilience and risk; effective whole school approaches; integrated and specific curriculum; and continuous improvement through review and evaluation. It is intended to support schools in teaching online safety, assessing program quality, and guiding best practice.
requirements: High-level framework intended to be universally applied to all school year levels, accompanied by implementation guides and support resources
constraints: Does not address what online safety might look like for children of different ages; developing a year-level curriculum was out of scope
target_learners: School students Foundation to Year 12 in Australian schools
target_learning_goals: Online safety knowledge and skills
digital citizenship
resilience and risk awareness
help-seeking and student agency
examples: The Framework was launched by eSafety on 19 July 2021 with downloadable resources including a 2-page handout, a 23-page Implementation Guide, a Toolkit for Schools, and a Question and Answer series

title: Common characteristics of effective school-based prevention initiatives collated from prevention reviews
description: From hand-searched papers on effective school-based prevention (including Nation et al. 2003, a Cochrane review of the WHO Health Promoting Schools Framework, an implementation scoping review, and WHO INSPIRE), the authors collated a set of themes conceptualised as common characteristics of effective prevention initiatives. These include a whole school approach, knowledgeable and well-trained teachers, leadership support, parent and community engagement, clear goals, effective monitoring and evaluation, developmentally and socio-culturally appropriate learning, varied and highly engaging teaching styles, positive teacher role modelling, avoiding scare tactics and confrontational strategies, and adequate duration, frequency, and intensity.

constraints: Collated from general school-based prevention literature; the authors note a paucity of literature on comprehensive school-based online safety education specifically

health and wellbeing promotion

article_title: The development of metacognitive ability in adolescence
citation: Weil L.G., Fleming S.M., Dumontheil I., Kilford E.J., Weil R.S., Rees G., Dolan R.J., Blakemore S.-J. (2013). The development of metacognitive ability in adolescence. Consciousness and Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.concog.2013.01.004
title: Metacognitive ability as a dissociable monitoring component measured by type II signal detection theory
description: The article treats metacognitive ability as "how accurately participants' confidence in their performance tracks their actual performance", operationalised via type II signal detection theory as the area under the type II ROC curve (Aroc). A psychophysical staircase clamps first-order performance so that confidence judgments can be studied independently of objective accuracy. This dissociation is presented as critical for developmental studies, where performance and awareness are otherwise confounded.
requirements: A task in which objective performance can be dissociated from metacognitive judgments, e.g. by staircase-clamping accuracy
constraints: The measure concerns the confidence–performance relationship on a perceptual task; the authors note they do not test how this corresponds to other forms of metacognition or mentalising
target_learners: adolescents
adults
target_learning_goals: awareness of one's own cognitive processes and performance monitoring
examples: Participants performed a Gabor pop-out interval judgment, then rated confidence 1–6; Aroc was computed from the type II ROC after excluding the first 100 staircase-stabilisation trials.
key_sources: Weil L.G., Fleming S.M., Dumontheil I., Kilford E.J., Weil R.S., Rees G., Dolan R.J., Blakemore S.-J. (2013). The development of metacognitive ability in adolescence. Consciousness and Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.concog.2013.01.004

article_title: The audience effect in adolescence depends on who's looking over your shoulder
citation: Wolf L.K., Bazargani N., Kilford E.J., Dumontheil I., Blakemore S.-J. (2015). The audience effect in adolescence depends on who's looking over your shoulder. Journal of Adolescence, 43, 5–14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2015.05.003
title: Three proposed mechanisms for adolescent peer audience effects: arousal, fear of social evaluation, and self-awareness
description: The article proposes three putative mechanisms underlying performance differences under evaluative observation: "changes in arousal in the presence of others"; increased "fear of social evaluation" leading adolescents to spend time mentalising about how peers judge their abilities, distracting them from the task; and increased self-awareness of discrepancies between current and ideal performance, which in complex tasks may cause excessive self-monitoring. These are offered as hypotheses for future study, not tested results.
requirements: Future studies are needed to test these mechanisms, as the article states the mechanisms are putative and untested.
constraints: The mechanisms are the authors' interpretation, not findings of the experiment; the article did not measure fear of social evaluation.
target_learners: adolescents aged 10–17
target_learning_goals: cognitive task performance (relational reasoning) under social observation
key_sources: Wolf L.K., Bazargani N., Kilford E.J., Dumontheil I., Blakemore S.-J. (2015). The audience effect in adolescence depends on who's looking over your shoulder. Journal of Adolescence, 43, 5–14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2015.05.003

article_title: The audience effect in adolescence depends on who's looking over your shoulder
citation: Wolf L.K., Bazargani N., Kilford E.J., Dumontheil I., Blakemore S.-J. (2015). The audience effect in adolescence depends on who's looking over your shoulder. Journal of Adolescence, 43, 5–14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2015.05.003
title: Consider who is observing when adolescents perform evaluated classwork, since peer observation can impair performance
description: The article's data suggest that adolescent performance on evaluated cognitive work is sensitive to the identity of the observer: "performance on a relational reasoning task in adolescence is sensitive to the identity of the person observing and evaluating their performance". Since lessons, exams and homework are often carried out in the presence of others who implicitly or explicitly evaluate performance, educators should be aware that observation by a peer may impair adolescent performance relative to observation by a non-peer.
requirements: Assessment or classwork situations in which adolescent performance is observed and evaluated by others.
constraints: The article did not test audience effects in an educational setting; effects were shown for a relational reasoning task in female participants from high-achieving academic backgrounds, and further work is needed on collaborative or competitive classroom contexts.
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: relational reasoning performance during evaluated classwork, homework and exams
examples: In the experiment, adolescents solved Raven's-matrix-style problems alone, with a friend watching, or with a female experimenter watching, with the observer silently counting wrong responses.

article_title: The effectiveness of collaborative problem solving in promoting students’ critical thinking: A meta-analysis based on empirical literature
citation: Xu, E., Wang, W., & Wang, Q. (2023). The effectiveness of collaborative problem solving in promoting students' critical thinking: A meta-analysis based on empirical literature. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-023-01508-1
title: Design collaborative problem-solving for critical thinking around real problems, mixed courses, small groups, and teacher-supported scaffolds
description: The article distills its meta-analytic findings into instructional recommendations for teaching critical thinking through collaborative problem-solving. Teachers should "put a special emphasis on the two core elements, which are collaboration and problem-solving, to design real problems based on collaborative situations", implement mixed course teaching in parallel with subject teaching, favor small groups of 2–3 members, and provide teacher-supported learning scaffolds, which showed the largest effect (ES = 0.92).
requirements: Teachers must be able to design real problems grounded in collaborative situations and support discussion, negotiation, and argument among group members.
Mixed course implementation requires combining explicit critical thinking method training with the knowledge content of specific disciplines.
constraints: The recommendations rest on the 36 included studies published 2000–2021 in English and Chinese; the authors note the search may have overlooked studies in other languages and that data on teacher training and learner demographics were partially missing.
The independent-course and 1–4-week subgroups had very few effect quantities, so the teaching-type and duration comparisons are limited.
target_learners: K-12 students and college students
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking, including its attitudinal tendency and cognitive skill dimensions
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 79 effect quantities from 36 experimental or quasi-experimental studies to show mixed courses (ES = 1.34) and 2–3-person groups (ES = 0.99) yielded the largest subgroup effects.

article_title: How getting noticed helps getting on: successful attention capture doubles children's cooperative play
citation: Yuill N, Hinske S, Williams SE and Leith G (2014) How getting noticed helps getting on: successful attention capture doubles children's cooperative play. Front. Psychol. 5:418. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00418
title: Augmented Knights' Castle (AKC): an RFID-augmented Playmobil playset producing context-relevant sounds
description: The Augmented Knights' Castle is "an audio-enhanced Playmobil® medieval castle playset designed to let play ﬁgures 'come alive.'" Play figures carry RFID tags identifying their location, so placing a figure in a specific location produces a previously-programmed context-relevant sound, such as a knight saying "Shall we watch the jousting?" in the courtyard or "Defend the castle!" on the drawbridge. The Study 2 version had around 20 characters with 9 speaking roles at 12 positions, making 55 location-character combinations of sounds, including factual information, sound effects, conversational turns and suggestions. The article uses the AKC both as a play environment and as an experimental instrument for manipulating attention capture.
requirements: Play figures fitted with RFID tags and RFID readers at set locations to detect figure placement and trigger the programmed sounds
constraints: Not every location or figure was tagged for sound, so sound production was only a potential rather than deterministic effect
target_learners: children aged 6 to 11 years in elementary school
target_learning_goals: cooperative social play
joint attention
collaborative narrative construction
examples: In Study 1, 16 triads played for 20 min with either the AKC or the non-augmented KC; in Study 2, 11 triads played two sessions and then performed a joint story.
key_sources: Yuill N, Hinske S, Williams SE and Leith G (2014) How getting noticed helps getting on: successful attention capture doubles children's cooperative play. Front. Psychol. 5:418. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00418

article_title: How getting noticed helps getting on: successful attention capture doubles children's cooperative play
citation: Yuill N, Hinske S, Williams SE and Leith G (2014) How getting noticed helps getting on: successful attention capture doubles children's cooperative play. Front. Psychol. 5:418. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00418
title: Design shared play environments to boost successful attention capture, because getting noticed supports getting on
description: The article argues that cooperative interaction depends on "micromoments of successful attention bids": "The more attention bids succeed, the more likely is cooperation." Environments can therefore be designed with shareable, salient attention-getters — such as context-relevant audio that is simultaneously shared and hard to ignore — to raise the success rate of attention bids and thereby sustain cooperative play and shared understanding. The authors frame this as a method of "experimental technology" for testing how psychological mechanisms support interaction.
requirements: Attention-getting cues that are shareable across the group simultaneously, such as audio, rather than cues specific to one individual
constraints: For groups with atypical patterns of attention to other people, as in autism, the authors suggest environmental support may require less novelty and more time for habituation
target_learners: children in early and middle childhood playing or working in small groups
target_learning_goals: cooperative play and collaboration
shared attention and shared understanding
joint narrative production
examples: The AKC produced context-relevant sounds when tagged figures were placed at tagged locations, and children in the AKC condition sometimes captured attention themselves with visual cues or self-made sound effects when no sound was triggered.

article_title: Improving Stealth Assessment in Game-based Learning with LSTM-based Analytics
citation: Akram, B., Mott, B., Min, W., Boyer, K. E., Wiebe, E., & Lester, J. (2017). Improving Stealth Assessment in Game-based Learning with LSTM-based Analytics. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Improving+Stealth+Assessment+in+Game-based+Learning+with+LSTM-based+Analytics
title: Strategy-based temporal analytics framework for stealth assessment using LSTM evidence models
description: A stealth assessment framework that derives temporal evidence from students' dynamic in-game strategy use rather than only from ECD evidence modeling. Student flip sequences are encoded as n-grams, clustered per task with EM clustering to yield strategy labels, and sequences of strategy cluster memberships across consecutive tasks are fed to an LSTM evidence model that predicts post-test performance. The article states the approach "does not require a labor -intensive process of labeling data" because strategies are discovered unsupervised from log data.
requirements: Learning environments in which students solve problems by performing sequences of actions from a limited pool of available actions, so that behavior traces can be encoded as n-gram flip sequences and clustered
constraints: The article states the approach "is not appropriate for analyzing ill -defined problems where players are not bound to certain actions"
target_learners: middle school students (ages 11-13) learning computational thinking
target_learning_goals: computational thinking, including binary representation, abstraction, and algorithmic thinking
examples: Applied to 11 binary representation tasks in the ENGAGE game's Digital World level, using data from 168 middle school students in four public middle school classrooms
key_sources: Akram, B., Mott, B., Min, W., Boyer, K. E., Wiebe, E., & Lester, J. (2017). Improving Stealth Assessment in Game-based Learning with LSTM-based Analytics. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Improving+Stealth+Assessment+in+Game-based+Learning+with+LSTM-based+Analytics

article_title: Improving Stealth Assessment in Game-based Learning with LSTM-based Analytics
citation: Akram, B., Mott, B., Min, W., Boyer, K. E., Wiebe, E., & Lester, J. (2017). Improving Stealth Assessment in Game-based Learning with LSTM-based Analytics. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Improving+Stealth+Assessment+in+Game-based+Learning+with+LSTM-based+Analytics
title: ENGAGE game-based learning environment for middle school computational thinking
description: ENGAGE is a game-based learning environment built with the Unity engine that introduces computational thinking to middle school students (ages 11-13) through an immersive 3D underwater storyworld. Students program devices with a visual block-based language to solve computational challenges across three levels (Introductory, Digital World, Big Data). The Digital World level's binary lock and lift tasks, in which students flip binary tiles to generate target base-ten values, supplied the behavior trace data for this study.
requirements: Students take turns serving as navigator and driver in pairs, and complete pre- and post-test content knowledge assessments individually
constraints: The analyses reported use behavior trace data from the 11 binary tasks of the Digital World level only
target_learners: middle school students (ages 11-13)
target_learning_goals: computational thinking skills including abstraction and algorithmic thinking, and positive attitudes toward computer science
examples: Over 300 middle school students participated in focus group activities, pilot tests, and classroom studies; 47% of students providing demographics were female

article_title: Training English language student teachers to become reflective teachers
citation: Ali Al-Issa & Ali Al-Bulushi. (2010). Training English Language Student Teachers to Become Reflective Teachers. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 35, 4. https://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajtec/vol35/iss4/4/
title: Three levels of reflection-on-action: descriptive, dialogic/deliberate, and critical
description: The article organises reflective teaching around three forms or levels of reflection-on-action drawn from the literature (van Manen, Hall, Hatton & Smith, Schon). The first is "'random' and 'descriptive'", the lowest level, involving describing and reporting events and returning to experience; the second is "'deliberate' (Hall, 1997) or 'dialogic'", re-evaluating experience and critically analysing situations to generate alternative solutions; the third is "of a more 'critical' nature", locating ELT within wider social, political and cultural contexts and judging the value of the existing context. The levels complement and build on one another, and trainees moved gradually between them can analyse their whole context.
requirements: Student teachers should be trained to move gradually from one level to another
constraints: The article notes the descriptive level does not serve deep learning and students at that level most likely cannot apply understanding to different contexts
target_learners: pre-service ELT student teachers
target_learning_goals: developing reflective teaching practice and critical evaluation of teaching contexts
examples: The article uses the three levels to frame why SQU trainees need training in reflective skills suited to the Omani ELT context
key_sources: Ali Al-Issa & Ali Al-Bulushi. (2010). Training English Language Student Teachers to Become Reflective Teachers. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 35, 4. https://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajtec/vol35/iss4/4/

article_title: Training English language student teachers to become reflective teachers
citation: Ali Al-Issa & Ali Al-Bulushi. (2010). Training English Language Student Teachers to Become Reflective Teachers. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, Vol 35, 4. https://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajtec/vol35/iss4/4/
title: 25-item six-theme reflective-training questionnaire (Cronbach's Alpha = 0.868)
description: A five-point Likert questionnaire of 25 items was created to obtain student teachers' and trainers' attitudes about reflection approaches and strategies, validated by a panel of six specialist judges and piloted with ten randomly-selected student teachers, being "found to be highly reliable (Cronbach’s Alpha = 0.868)". Items were re-categorised under six themes: reflection through self-evaluation, formal instruction, observation, talking, practical experience, and research. It was administered on-line via Google Docs to 90 student teachers (a 39 per cent response rate) and to seven of eight e-mailed trainers (87.5 per cent).
requirements: Items achieving consensus among at least four judges were accepted
constraints: Only 90 of 230 final-year student teachers participated, a 39 per cent response rate
target_learners: final-year ELT student teachers

article_title: Video game training enhances cognitive control in older adults
citation: J. A. Anguera, J. Boccanfuso, J. L. Rintoul, O. Al-Hashimi, F. Faraji, J. Janowich, E. Kong, Y. Larraburo, C. Rolle, E. Johnston & A. Gazzaley. (2013). Video game training enhances cognitive control in older adults. Nature 501. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12486
title: NeuroRacer: a custom-designed three-dimensional video game for assessing and training multitasking-based cognitive control
description: NeuroRacer is a custom-designed three-dimensional video game combining a perceptual discrimination 'sign task' with a concurrent visuomotor 'driving task', used both diagnostically (measuring d' multitasking cost) and as a training platform. The article describes it as a tool that "can be used to assess cognitive abilities across the lifespan, evaluate underlying neural mechanisms, and serve as a powerful tool for cognitive enhancement". Training used an adaptive staircase algorithm adjusting each component task after each 3-min run, with rewards given only when both tasks improved beyond 80%.

Home training on a laptop with compliance monitoring (scheduled sessions, wireless data transfer, weekly contact)

Training benefits on untrained tasks were specific to working memory and sustained attention, with no group × session interactions on processing speed tasks

adults across the lifespan aged 20–79 (assessment)
target_learning_goals: multitasking and interference resolution
sustained attention
working memory

A diagnostic version was played by 174 participants spanning six decades to measure multitasking cost

article_title: Instructional technologies in developing countries: A contextual analysis approach
citation: Arias, S., & Clark, K. A. (2004). Instructional Technologies in Developing Countries: A Contextual Analysis Approach. TechTrends, 48(4), 52-55. https://link.springer.com/journal/11528
title: Adapted context-based analysis model for instructional design in developing countries
description: The article presents an adaptation of Tessmer and Richey's (1997) context-based analysis model, which defines context as a "multilevel body of factors in which learning and performance are embedded." The model investigates context across three temporal aspects—orienting, instructional and transfer—at three levels: learner, immediate environment and organization. The adaptation adds new immediate-environment and organizational factors to the orienting context that are specific to developing-country conditions, so that front-end analysis goes beyond traditional needs assessment.
requirements: Front-end analysis must include analysis of socio-cultural, environmental and institutional factors surrounding the instructional problem
constraints: The adapted factors were proposed for developing-country contexts, though the authors state the factors also exist in developed-country settings
target_learners: learners and trainees in developing countries
target_learning_goals: successful design and implementation of technology-based learning initiatives
examples: Table 2 shows the adapted model with new factors such as motivation, release time, compensation, participation culture, availability of electricity, appropriate facilities, centralized decision making, budget planning capacity and human capacity building

article_title: Instructional technologies in developing countries: A contextual analysis approach
citation: Arias, S., & Clark, K. A. (2004). Instructional Technologies in Developing Countries: A Contextual Analysis Approach. TechTrends, 48(4), 52-55. https://link.springer.com/journal/11528
title: Challenges of instructional technology initiatives in developing countries span socio-cultural, human capacity and infrastructure categories
description: The article enumerates an illustrative list of challenges that "span the social, cultural, environmental and institutional contexts." Socio-cultural and human capacity factors include an incipient culture of participation, centralized decision-making, resources for learning and support, lack of budget planning and scarcity of qualified personnel. Infrastructure factors include unreliable power and telecommunications grids, hardware/software/maintenance/support needs, and adequate facilities such as cooling, ventilation and dust control.
requirements: Designers must account for these factors during the analysis phase rather than assuming the traditional analysis phase covers them
constraints: The list is presented as illustrative, not exhaustive
target_learners: learners in developing countries at primary, secondary, tertiary and adult training levels
target_learning_goals: implementing sustainable instructional technology initiatives
examples: The article notes users in developing countries may only have internet access through low bandwidth connections, and that hot and humid climates require cooling, ventilation and dust control

title: Design for available human capacity by planning maintenance or incorporating a simple maintenance structure
description: Because qualified staff to maintain new instructional technology may not be available, the article states that "the design process for developing country contexts needs to consider the amount of human capacity available for maintenance, or ensure that the design incorporates a very simple maintenance structure." Designers should match system complexity to local maintenance capacity.
requirements: Analysis of local human capacity for maintenance during the design phase
constraints: Arises from the scarcity of qualified personnel challenge in developing countries

citation: Arias, S., & Clark, K. A. (2004). Instructional Technologies in Developing Countries: A Contextual Analysis Approach. TechTrends, 48(4), 52-55. https://link.springer.com/journal/11528
title: Address motivation, release time and compensation during design when technology requires a learning curve
description: The article states that if the instructional technology "requires users to undergo a learning curve, then motivation, release time and compensation must be addressed during the design phase." title: Deployed instructional technology programs in developing countries (interactive radio instruction, Telesecundaria, Enlaces)
description: The article surveys instructional technologies deployed in developing countries across delivery formats including radio, television, computers, the internet, print, audio cassettes and CD-ROMs. Examples include interactive radio instruction launched in Nicaragua in the 1970s to teach mathematics to isolated rural children, Mexico's Telesecundaria providing televised instruction to seventh through ninth graders in remote areas for over thirty years, and Chile's Enlaces Network launched in 1993 to provide teachers and students with new instructional content, information resources and communications for collaboration.

constraints: Examples are historical deployments described to motivate the need for context-based analysis

article_title: Effects of games in STEM education: a meta-analysis on the moderating role of student background characteristics
citation: Michaela Arztmann, Lisette Hornstra, Johan Jeuring & Liesbeth Kester (2023). Effects of games in STEM education: a meta-analysis on the moderating role of student background characteristics. Studies in Science Education, 59:1, 109-145. https://doi.org/10.1080/03057267.2022.2057732
title: Three-category outcome framework for game-based learning research: cognitive, motivational, and behavioural outcomes
description: The article organises game-based learning outcomes into three categories, adapting Hainey et al.'s four categories by merging knowledge acquisition with perceptual and cognitive outcomes. Cognitive outcomes include "assessed learning outcomes, knowledge retention ... or conceptual knowledge"; motivational outcomes combine affect and motivation (intrinsic motivation, interest, self-efficacy, enjoyment); behavioural outcomes include "self-reported strategy use, behavioural engagement, or effort". The framework structures the three separate meta-analyses and the moderator analyses.
requirements: Studies must investigate at least one of the three defined outcome variables to fit the framework
constraints: The sociocultural perspective, focusing on game features such as individual versus collaborative play, is explicitly beyond the scope of this framework's application
target_learners: K1-8 students in STEM subjects
target_learning_goals: STEM knowledge acquisition
STEM motivation
learning-related behaviour
examples: The meta-analysis coded each study's outcome measures into cognition, motivation, or behaviour and ran one random-effects meta-analysis per category.

article_title: Video games can develop graduate skills in higher education students: A randomised trial
citation: Matthew Barr. (2017). Video games can develop graduate skills in higher education students: A randomised trial. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.05.016
title: Suite of eight selected commercial video games played in supervised drop-in game labs
description: The intervention material was a suite of commercial entertainment titles (Borderlands 2, Minecraft, Portal 2, Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light, Warcraft III, Team Fortress 2, Gone Home, Papers, Please) played on twelve Windows PCs in university game labs. Selection required that "no game with a Metacritic score of less than 80 out of 100 was considered", and all but Gone Home and Papers, Please included a substantial multiplayer component. Participants logged about 120 minutes per game (60 minutes each for Gone Home and Papers, Please).
requirements: Games must run on modestly-specified Windows PCs and be relatively inexpensive
A local network setup supporting multiplayer play without an internet connection
constraints: MMORPG titles were excluded because network ports could not be opened and their learning curve exceeded the 2 h allocated per game

adaptability
resourcefulness

title: Drop-in game lab structure preserving flexible play sessions for ecological validity
description: The study's delivery pattern was a supervised lab open on a drop-in basis (9am-5pm Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Fridays) where students managed their own play time within a prescribed per-game log target. The author argues this "partially addresses a common criticism of laboratory-based video game studies", because an arbitrarily defined time limit on play does not mirror normal play circumstances, and that "the lab was arranged to provide better ecological validity" than a rigid temporal structure.

constraints: Even this relaxed drop-in structure is not an accurate reflection of how games are played at home

article_title: Effects of action video game play on cognitive skills: A meta-analysis
citation: Benoit Bediou, Melissa A. Rodgers, Elizabeth Tipton, Richard E. Mayer, C. Shawn Green, and Daphne Bavelier. (2023). Effects of Action Video Game Play on Cognitive Skills: A Meta-Analysis. Technology, Mind, and Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1037/tmb0000102
title: Learning-to-learn account: action game mechanics train attentional control and enable transfer to nongame contexts
description: The article proposes that the game mechanics inherent in action video games—enemies appearing anywhere in a large field of view, cluttered scenes, and many quickly and independently moving targets—place heavy load on perceptual and attentional skills. The authors "proposed that the game mechanics inherent in action video games may be ideally suited to train core cognitive functions, such as attentional control, and in turn facilitate transfer to nongame contexts (learning to learn)". This framework motivates why intervention studies test transfer to untrained cognitive tasks rather than only in-game improvement.
requirements: Intervention designs must contrast action game training with an active control game and measure untrained cognitive tasks at posttest at least 24 hr after training
constraints: The article defines action video games narrowly as first- and third-person shooters, excluding action-like genres such as action RPGs and MOBAs
target_learners: healthy young adults (18–45)
target_learning_goals: perception
top-down attentional control
spatial cognition
transfer of cognitive skill to untrained tasks
examples: The intervention meta-analysis tested this account by contrasting commercially available action games with nonaction control games in pre/post designs with a minimum of 8 hr of training over at least 8 sessions

article_title: Active learning: Effects of core training design elements on self-regulatory processes, learning, and adaptability.
citation: Bell, B. S., & Kozlowski, S. W. J. (2008). Active learning: Effects of core training design elements on self-regulatory processes, learning, and adaptability. Journal of Applied Psychology, 93(2), 296-316. http://digitalcommons.ilr.cornell.edu/articles/410/
title: Integrated active learning framework: three core design elements aligned with cognitive, motivational, and emotional self-regulatory pathways
description: The article derives an integrated theoretical framework for active learning by disentangling multifaceted interventions (error management training, mastery training, guided exploration) into three core design elements. As printed, "these three core training design elements are exploration, training frame, and emotion-control," aligned respectively with trainees' cognitive (metacognitive), motivational (goal orientation, self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation), and emotional (anxiety) self-regulatory processes, which in turn drive knowledge and adaptive transfer.
requirements: Active learning design must go beyond learning by doing and use formal design elements to systematically influence self-regulatory activity during learning
constraints: The model emphasizes distinctiveness of the three pathways for parsimony; the authors acknowledge potential cross-over effects among processes and planned to test alternative models

target_learning_goals: adaptive transfer of complex task skills
self-regulated learning

article_title: Can Online Peer Assessment be Trusted?
citation: Bouzidi, L., & Jaillet, A. (2009). Can Online Peer Assessment be Trusted?. Educational Technology & Society, 12(4), 257-268. https://www.ifets.info/
title: Five-hypothesis validation process for online peer assessment
description: The article proposes a validation procedure in which peer assessment may only be judged valid after five prior conditions are confirmed: teacher reliability, correct test items, internal consistency of the test, reliability of the observation and marking tools, and clear, coherent marking instructions and scale schemes. The authors state that "a method which requires that five hypotheses must be confirmed before checking the validity of peer assessment" was used, operationalised through expert comparison, item analysis (difficulty and discrimination indexes), Cronbach's alpha, tool checks, and marking-scheme coherence checks before a final teacher-peer agreement analysis.
requirements: A teacher deemed a reliable expert assessor, correctly set test items, internally consistent items, reliable computer-assisted marking tools, and clear coherent marking instructions and scale schemes
constraints: The GEE-2007 exam failed the internal-consistency hypothesis and had to be excluded, showing the process can block validity verification for unreliable tests
target_learners: second- and third-year engineering students in exact science courses
target_learning_goals: valid summative and formative assessment of calculations, mathematical reasoning, short algorithms and short texts
examples: The process was applied to three classroom exams (CA-2006, CA-2007, GEE-2007), screening out Q7 of CA-2007 and the whole GEE-2007 exam before the final t-test and correlation analysis

title: Moodle workshop module as the online peer assessment platform

The article reports that "This module is stable and presents a user-friendly environment", but identifies a weakness in its marking tool: the scale scheme was implemented as option buttons from "excellent" to "very poor", a method the authors say can lead to errors.

constraints: The module's option-button marking tool had a weakness that could introduce marking errors

target_learning_goals: online assessment of classroom exam papers with anonymity and multiple assessors

description: The article recommends accepting peer assessment as valid when exams contain exact-science questions (calculations, mathematical reasoning, short algorithms, short texts) and each paper is marked by at least four peers, supported by safeguards. article_title: Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context
citation: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216
title: Cognitive Task Analysis: a three-phase approach to eliciting expert cognition in context
description: CTA is a collection of interview-based qualitative methods for identifying the cognitive processes and skills required to perform complex tasks in demanding, contextually dependent work domains. The article organizes it around three phases: "(i) knowledge elicitation; (ii) data analysis; (iii) knowledge representation" — interviewing or observing experts to break down task steps, eliciting the cognitive processes used during task completion, and mapping knowledge requirements, cues, strategies, and skills into a digestible format that enhances workplace knowledge transfer. It is presented as complementary to existing managerial cognition methods, with a specific focus on the role of context.
requirements: Access to expert participants whose knowledge is the elicitation target
Interviewers familiar with the specifics of the research domain, striving for quasi-expert status
constraints: Unlikely to be suited to studies aiming to elicit generalizable knowledge or quantitatively compare two distinct groups
Lends itself to initial phases of theory development rather than theory testing and confirmation
target_learners: Experts and experienced practitioners in complex work domains
target_learning_goals: Understanding expert cognitive processes, cues, strategies, and knowledge requirements in complex tasks
examples: Applied to emergency command decision-making via the Critical Decision Method and to global leadership via Applied Cognitive Task Analysis
key_sources: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216

article_title: Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context
citation: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216
title: Critical Decision Method (CDM): four-sweep retrospective interview technique
description: CDM is a narrative-based, retrospective interview technique in which experts reflect on a challenging incident in a complex work domain, seeking to identify knowledge requirements, expertise, and goal structures. It proceeds through four sweeps: incident identification with an uninterrupted narrative walkthrough, timeline verification via incident retelling, deepening probes using prepared cognitive probes about cues, goals, options, and uncertainties, and "What if?" probes that generate hypothetical and practical recommendations. Findings can be presented as visual models of core themes or detailed process pathways over time.
requirements: The expert was the decision-maker during the incident (first-person narrative) and their actions directly impacted the outcome
Interviewers familiar with the domain's terminology and work processes
constraints: Pairing with observations and document analysis is not always possible if the decision-making environment is particularly sensitive
target_learners: Experts in high-stakes or complex decision-making domains
target_learning_goals: Unpacking the cognitive processes supporting critical decision-making
examples: Power and Alison (2017) used CDM with emergency responders; Power et al. (2018) used it with ICU referral decisions
key_sources: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216

article_title: Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context
citation: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216
title: Applied Cognitive Task Analysis (ACTA): task diagram, knowledge audit, and cognitive demands table
description: ACTA is an interview technique designed to identify the key cognitive elements required to perform expert tasks, typically in three phases: developing a task diagram, a knowledge audit interview, and data analysis with knowledge representation. Task Diagrams contain three to seven steps aligned with short-term memory; the Knowledge Audit probes aspects of expertise such as big picture, noticing, job smarts, improvising, self-monitoring, and anomalies. Findings are represented in a Cognitive Demands Table highlighting common challenges, errors, and solutions, which can inform future training and job design. ACTA is streamlined and suited to instances in which time is limited.
requirements: A minimum of three to five experts are needed to identify expert cognitive processes
The researcher and participant must identify an incident too complex for a novice to complete
constraints: Participants often find the task diagram phase challenging and offer too much detail, requiring the interviewer to keep the conversation on track
target_learners: High-performing experts completing domain-specific tasks
target_learning_goals: Documenting expert cues and strategies for complex workplace tasks
examples: Osland et al. used ACTA with ten global leadership experts plus ten confirmatory experts, obtaining over 30 hours of Knowledge Audit interview data
