citation: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216
title: Five key questions for determining whether CTA methods fit a research study
description: The article provides an enumerated set of five considerations for judging whether CTA is appropriate: whether the study concerns a complex workplace environment characterized by uncertainty, whether the research focuses on cognition that is hard to articulate, whether relevant experts can be accessed, whether onto-epistemological assumptions have been considered, and whether findings have potential to impact practice. These are printed as question prompts in Table 1, guiding researchers on when CTA fits versus when alternatives such as the Critical Incident Technique are more appropriate.
requirements: Research questions targeting complex cognition rather than task attributes alone
Access to genuine expert participants
constraints: If the research question focuses primarily on identifying task characteristics, the Critical Incident Technique is likely more appropriate
target_learners: Management and organization researchers designing cognition studies
target_learning_goals: Selecting appropriate knowledge-elicitation methods for studying expert cognition
examples: Table 1 pairs each question with prompts, e.g. asking whether the context can be characterized by uncertainty
key_sources: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216

article_title: Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context
citation: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216
title: Translate CTA findings into training, protocols, and knowledge transfer for practitioners
description: The article recommends that researchers applying CTA consider how findings can provide evidence-based insights into how experts carry out workplace activities and be translated into recommendations for improving decision-making and performance. Findings can "be used to translate expert knowledge into training and protocols", offering detailed documentation of complex cognitive processes used by skilled practitioners in situ — an approach described as especially fruitful in medical training, aviation, and the military. Having individuals reflect on their decision-making during critical tasks can improve future performance and facilitate knowledge transfer.
requirements: Findings must yield insights into cognitive challenges and the role of expertise, not merely a compelling story of workplace activities
Working directly with end-users to build collaborative relationships
constraints: Some authors describe a crisis in organizational science where statistically sophisticated methods fail to offer meaningful utility to practitioners — CTA is positioned as a response to this
target_learners: Practitioners, technical specialists, HR practitioners, and trainees in complex work domains
target_learning_goals: Knowledge transfer of expert cognition; improved decision-making and performance
examples: Cognitive Demands Tables represent challenges, errors, and solutions to inform future training and job design
key_sources: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216

article_title: A cross-cultural study of teacher perspectives on teacher roles and adoption of online collaborative learning in higher education
citation: Chang Zhu, Martin Valcke and Tammy Schellens. (2010). A cross-cultural study of teacher perspectives on teacher roles and adoption of online collaborative learning in higher education. European Journal of Teacher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02619761003631849
title: Grasha's five teacher roles framework (expert, formal authority, personal model, facilitator, delegator)
description: The article adopts Grasha's framework of five teaching styles reflecting five teacher roles: the "expert (transmitter of information)", "formal authority (sets standards and defines acceptable ways of doing things)", "personal model (teaches by illustration and direct example)", "facilitator (guides and directs by asking questions, exploring options, suggesting alternatives)", and "delegator (develops students' ability to function autonomously)". The study uses the Teaching Style Survey built on these five scales to measure how teachers in two cultural settings perceive their roles, and expects social-constructivist adopters to favour facilitator and delegator roles over expert, authority and model roles.
requirements: Teachers respond to the 40-item Teaching Style Survey reflecting on a particular undergraduate course they teach
constraints: Almost every teacher adopts different roles to varying degrees rather than a single role
target_learners: university teachers in higher education
target_learning_goals: teacher role perception and adoption of instructional innovations
examples: The study administered all 40 items of the Grasha and Riechmann-Hruska Teaching Style Survey, translated into Chinese and Flemish, with reliability alphas of .70 to .80 across the five role scales.
key_sources: Chang Zhu, Martin Valcke and Tammy Schellens. (2010). A cross-cultural study of teacher perspectives on teacher roles and adoption of online collaborative learning in higher education. European Journal of Teacher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02619761003631849

article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Game telemetry as systematic behavioral observation linking player events to inferences about learning
description: The chapter conceives game telemetry as "the data associated with specific game events, the state of a game, or other parameters of interest," captured to a permanent external store using a predefined record format rather than ad hoc logging. It flows from the behavioral observation tradition, where the two most important properties are "the precise deﬁnition of the behavior to observe" and "the connection between the behavior and a theoretical framework within which the behavior is interpreted." Telemetry is the first element in the chain of reasoning from behavior to inferences about learning.
requirements: The set of behavioral acts of interest must be well defined prior to observation
A clear definition, specified a priori, of what to observe and how to code it, a structured sampling method, a reliable recording method, and reliability and validity evidence of the coding scheme
constraints: The approach focuses solely on supporting measurement of performance of play-learners in serious games, not entertainment or monetization
target_learners: play-learners in serious games, e.g., underprepared students learning fractions
target_learning_goals: inferences about players' learning and performance during gameplay
examples: The telemetry system in Save Patch was based on these guidelines, with behavior defined in terms of the cognitive demands of successful gameplay
key_sources: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3

article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Three types of measures derivable from gameplay telemetry: overall game performance, in-game performance, and in-game strategies
description: The chapter proposes that "three types of measures can be derived from gameplay: (a) overall game performance, (b) in-game performance, and (c) in-game strategies," each with certain uses and selected according to the question being asked. In the case study, overall performance was the last level reached, in-game performance included addition errors, level resets, and player deaths, and in-game strategies were derived from sets or sequences of behaviors analyzed with methods such as cluster analysis.
requirements: Telemetry designed per the chapter's guidelines so events and context are uniquely identifiable
constraints: Measures based on discovery of interesting patterns are more tenuous, since identified patterns must be interpreted in light of the task and the player's presumed domain knowledge
target_learners: players of serious games, e.g., students learning rational-number concepts
target_learning_goals: measuring overall achievement, in-game use of cognitive demands, and player strategies
examples: In Save Patch, overall performance was the last level reached; in-game performance used incorrect rope placements; strategies were identified via cluster analysis
key_sources: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3

article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Design game telemetry to target player behaviors that reflect the cognitive demands of interest
description: Because cognitive processes cannot be observed directly, inferences about their use rest on in-game behaviors and game states. The chapter states that "The game telemetry speciﬁcation should target player behaviors that reﬂect the cognitive demands of interest," where cognitive demands are the intellectual skills required to succeed in the game. A cognitive task analysis informs which mental operations to log, and game mechanics should be designed so that only players with knowledge of X can apply mechanic x, making mechanic x a potential measure of X.
requirements: A cognitive task analysis that provides insight about the mental operations players invoke during play
Precise definition of the behavior to observe and its connection to a theoretical framework
constraints: A specific behavioral act can manifest numerous underlying processes; judicious structuring of the interaction and capture of contextual information are needed to minimize ambiguity
target_learners: players of serious games in education and training settings
target_learning_goals: measuring latent constructs such as adaptive problem-solving, decision-making, and content learning
examples: In a fractions game, the game should allow and log players' attempts to add fractions with unlike denominators rather than disallow the behavior, providing insight into misconceptions
key_sources: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3

article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Record game telemetry at the finest usable grain size with sufficient context to reconstruct events
description: The chapter defines "ﬁnest usable grain size" as "a data element that has a clear deﬁnition associated with it"; a bare click is unusable, whereas a qualified datum such as clicking the reset button is usable. It recommends that "game telemetry should contain sufﬁcient information to describe the context in which the event occurred" in enough detail to link data to a specific school, teacher, period, player, game level, and game state, illustrated by an index-card reconstruction test.
requirements: Each logged data element must have a clear definition, e.g., an attempted addition logged with information about the denominators
Unique player ID, game level, time, and game state information sufficient to reconstruct the record sequence
constraints: Logging at too coarse a grain (e.g., a generic attempted addition) merges events with different explanations, such as same- versus different-denominator additions
target_learners: researchers and analysts using game log data from school-based studies
target_learning_goals: interpreting in-game actions as evidence of domain understanding
examples: In the fractions game, telemetry included the player ID, level, time, the fraction being added, the fraction it was added to, and other game state information
key_sources: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3

article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Represent telemetry data in a format requiring minimal preprocessing, such as a flat file, for non-programmer end users
description: Assuming a typical research environment where programmers may be unavailable, the chapter recommends ease of use over computational efficiency: "We recommend a ﬂat ﬁle representation of the data as this format is simple, easy to explain, easily understood, and portable." More expressive formats like JSON or SQL require a database connection and programming skill, whereas the data's destination is a statistical analysis tool used mostly by non-programmers. A sample flat-file format with fields such as time stamp, user_id, data_code, and game_state is provided.
requirements: A predefined record format so data flow directly into statistical analysis tools
An assumption of multiple data analysts and researchers touching the data over its life span
constraints: The guideline may not apply in high volume environments with dedicated programmers and storage constraints
target_learners: researchers and data analysts without programming experience
target_learning_goals: analyzing game telemetry to derive measures of learning and performance
examples: Table 3.1 shows a flat-file telemetry format with a serial number, time stamp, game_time, user_id, stage, level, data_code, data_description, value fields, and game_state
key_sources: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3

article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Record descriptions of behavior, not inferences, that are unambiguous and contextualized
description: The chapter holds that telemetry "should have the following properties: (a) is a description of behavior and not an inference about why behavior occurs, (b) is unambiguous," and (c) contains sufficient context to link the element to a specific player at a specific point. Logging an inference such as does not understand adding fractions may be inaccurate without validity evidence, restricts later analyses, and can subsume multiple events into uninterpretable aggregates; ambiguity should be avoided so single events remain distinguishable.
requirements: Validity evidence on any interpretation before logging it as an inference
A 1:1 correspondence between the data element and an event, e.g., uniquely identifying which of ten buttons was clicked
Two classes of context: student information (schooling, prior knowledge, demographics, motivation) and game experience information (game state variables, feedback)
constraints: Contextualization is bounded by what is feasible to encode about the conditions under which data were generated
target_learners: players of serious games whose logs are later analyzed by researchers
target_learning_goals: distinguishing actual gameplay behavior from interpretations of competency
examples: Adding two fraction objects incorrectly is logged descriptively as incorrect addition rather than inferentially as the player does not understand how to add fractions
key_sources: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3

article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Save Patch telemetry system with 23 telemetry points grounded in fraction learning goals
description: Save Patch is a researcher-developed game designed to teach the concept of a unit in rational numbers, where players add rope segments at sign posts so Patch travels the correct distance; adding ropes maps to adding fractions with common denominators. "The telemetry system in Save Patch was based on the guidelines described earlier," with "23 telemetry points" covering general conditions, help usage, in-game assessment usage, navigation, object manipulation, game states, and in-game decisions, recording context such as the rope value and sign-post location.
requirements: Telemetry points focused on behaviors presumed to reflect players' math knowledge, with context recorded per Guidelines 1 and 4
Abstraction at the finest usable grain size to support both fine-grained behavioral tokens and aggregate measures
constraints: The game mechanics only provide sensitive measures insofar as they directly require interaction with the to-be-learned content
target_learners: underprepared students in the area of fractions
target_learning_goals: understanding that rational numbers are defined relative to a unit quantity and can be summed only when units are identical
examples: Cluster analysis of Save Patch telemetry identified patterns reflecting the ideal solution, fraction misconceptions, and non-mathematical gaming strategies
key_sources: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3

article_title: Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens
citation: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522
title: Conceptual models as interactive visual learning objects for conceptual learning
description: A conceptual model is defined as a particular kind of learning object: an interactive and visual multimedia representation designed to depict a concept or connected concepts and support conceptual learning. The article describes it as a representation that lets learners manipulate and interrogate represented properties and relationships, drawing on Norman's and Mayer's notions of a conceptual model as a representation designed for teaching and understanding. The author positions it as reusable across purposes, student groups, and delivery devices.
requirements: Should be used in the context of a learning task that triggers conceptually demanding cognitive processing
constraints: The article notes readers should not expect detailed descriptions of data collection and analysis in this paper
target_learners: school students
higher education students
target_learning_goals: conceptual learning of curriculum concepts and their properties and relationships
examples: The Explore Triangle conceptual model lets students drag sliders for base and height, redrawing the triangle and updating values such as the hypotenuse, and can be reused from lower-grade exploration of right-angled triangles to senior work on Pythagorean theorem and trigonometric functions
key_sources: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522

article_title: Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens
citation: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522
title: Design for presentation: visual, interactive, single-screen conceptual models
description: This pattern is the article's first set of recommendations for the content, screen and interface design of a conceptual model. It specifies presenting information predominantly visually, designing for interaction so users manipulate parameters and observe outcomes, arranging elements into a holistic scenario, presenting on a single screen within a small space (most models within 640 by 480 pixels per the author's experience), using audio and video only when necessary, moderating color, avoiding decorative elements, using a single font, and framing functional screen areas.
requirements: Design elements should integrate into a holistic presentational scenario depicting the represented concept
All display elements should serve the purpose of representing a concept
constraints: These recommendations alone do not address instructional uses and are, as the article states, of little use to teachers without the learning-uses set
target_learners: school students
higher education students
target_learning_goals: multimedia representation and manipulation of conceptual knowledge
examples: Reviewers described features of reviewed conceptual models against criteria drawn from the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, and the River model was later designed with a single screen, Arial font only, limited colors, and no decorative elements
key_sources: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522

article_title: Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens
citation: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522
title: Design for small screens: full-screen, landscape, one-step interaction with zooming and floating panels
description: This pattern is the article's second recommendation set, addressing the limited screen area of handheld devices (about 3.5 inches, 320 by 240 pixels at the time). It recommends full-screen and landscape presentation, minimizing scrolling, task-centered design for short contacts, one-step interaction with immediately noticeable updates, a zooming facility to reach display areas beyond the physical screen, and movable, collapsible, overlapping, semi-transparent interactive panels to maximize presented information.
requirements: Single interactions such as changing a slider position should result in immediate, perceptually noticeable screen updates
constraints: Screen size continues to present design challenges; text legibility and the nature of interactions limit design possibilities, as the article reports from prior work
target_learners: school students using handheld devices
target_learning_goals: access to conceptual model content and interaction on small-screen devices
examples: The River conceptual model was displayed full-screen in landscape mode on the HP iPAQ rw6828 with content designed so scrolling was not required, though zooming was not yet utilized and was planned for a redesigned version
key_sources: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522

article_title: Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens
citation: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522
title: Design for learning uses: observation, analysis, experimentation, thinking, and reuse
description: This pattern is the article's third recommendation set, derived from classroom and fieldwork observations, interviews, and review of student work with teachers and students. It classifies learning uses of conceptual models into emerging categories and maps each to a design recommendation: design for observation (linking real world and represented properties), analytical use (inputting real-environment data for processing), experimentation (manipulating parameters and testing generalizations), thinking (triggers and cues supporting mental-model linking), and reuse across environments, devices, and collaborating users.
requirements: Reuse requires that interactivity be supported by a variety of devices and that large-screen presentation not cause split attention problems
constraints: The article states these recommendations present possibilities for learning-task-related uses and must complement the presentation and small-screen sets
target_learners: school students
teachers planning instruction
target_learning_goals: linking theory to the world outside the classroom
inquiry
analysis
experimentation
reflection and collaboration
examples: Table 1 of the article lists each recommendation against identified learning uses such as aid to observations, analytical tool, experimentation environment, external cognitive supplement, preparation tool, collaboration tool, and reflective tool
key_sources: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522

article_title: Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens
citation: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522
title: The River conceptual model learning object
description: The River conceptual model is a Flash-based learning object designed for handheld use in geography fieldwork. It contains information about river parameters, enables calculation of river discharge, presents the impact of riverbed shape on flow rates, and allows identification of common bedrocks along the river. Students manipulate parameters such as position on the river via sliders, with outcomes displayed visually and numerically, and it can be rescaled for computers, projectors, and embedding in PowerPoint or blogs.
requirements: Designed for effective presentation in a 320x240 pixel screen area
Interaction via sliders and clickable spots supported across different devices
constraints: Zooming has not been utilized; a redesigned version should contain this facility, and semi-transparent panels are planned
target_learners: secondary school geography students
target_learning_goals: understanding river parameters, discharge calculation, and downstream changes
examples: The screen was divided into functional areas: the top part presented the river cross-section and its changes, the bottom part presented related content and interactive elements
key_sources: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522

article_title: Game Jams as Valuable Tools for the Development of 21st-Century Skills
citation: Contreras-Espinosa, R.S.; Eguia-Gomez, J.L. (2022). Game Jams as Valuable Tools for the Development of 21st-Century Skills. Sustainability 2022, 14, 2246. https://doi.org/10.3390/su14042246
title: Run game jams as voluntary extracurricular additions to courses rather than core formal-course components
description: The article recommends organizing game jams outside mandatory formal coursework, because voluntariness and novelty sustain motivation. The authors state the idea of introducing game jams in formal school contexts "should be seen as an addition, instead of a core component", warning that mandatory use and repetitive per-subject jams could lose positive learning outcomes.
requirements: Participation should be voluntary to protect motivation
Teachers or tutors need the necessary competencies for game-jam pedagogy
constraints: In public schools in Mexico each subject is taught by a different teacher, so per-subject jams would become repetitive
Formal-course integration depends on the characteristics of each course
target_learners: high school students aged 12–16
target_learning_goals: 21st-century skills: critical thinking, creativity, communication, collaboration
examples: The three studied jams were voluntary events for students of a Mexico City family-development program, organized as additional activities rather than within formal courses
key_sources: Contreras-Espinosa, R.S.; Eguia-Gomez, J.L. (2022). Game Jams as Valuable Tools for the Development of 21st-Century Skills. Sustainability 2022, 14, 2246. https://doi.org/10.3390/su14042246

article_title: Game Jams as Valuable Tools for the Development of 21st-Century Skills
citation: Contreras-Espinosa, R.S.; Eguia-Gomez, J.L. (2022). Game Jams as Valuable Tools for the Development of 21st-Century Skills. Sustainability 2022, 14, 2246. https://doi.org/10.3390/su14042246
title: Game jams as pedagogical spaces combining co-creation, co-production and co-design with four learning types
description: The article frames game jams as constructivist learning environments that emulate industrial processes (co-creation, co-production, co-design) and host four learning types: "The type of learning that takes place during game jams is not very different from that from typical educational environments and includes (1) cooperative, (2) project-based, (3) problem-based, and (4) collaborative learning." Through these processes the events are said to contribute to 4C skill development.
requirements: A tutor able to promote beneficial interaction, which is crucial for collaborative learning to succeed
constraints: In such a short collaborative event it is unrealistic to expect participants to acquire all skills or learn to program
target_learners: adolescent students (12–16) in informal and extracurricular settings
target_learning_goals: critical thinking, creativity, communication, collaboration
examples: The studied jams combined cooperative task division, tutor-supported project work, problem-solving during testing, and collaborative creation of a shared game
key_sources: Contreras-Espinosa, R.S.; Eguia-Gomez, J.L. (2022). Game Jams as Valuable Tools for the Development of 21st-Century Skills. Sustainability 2022, 14, 2246. https://doi.org/10.3390/su14042246

article_title: Game Jams as Valuable Tools for the Development of 21st-Century Skills
citation: Contreras-Espinosa, R.S.; Eguia-Gomez, J.L. (2022). Game Jams as Valuable Tools for the Development of 21st-Century Skills. Sustainability 2022, 14, 2246. https://doi.org/10.3390/su14042246
title: Game jam resource kit: non-digital and digital materials, software, venue and devices for 4C-focused jams
description: A concrete set of materials, tools and venue conditions the article identifies as necessary to organize a game jam aimed at 4C skill development. It includes non-digital brainstorming materials ("pencils, sticky notes, colored paper, dice, cards, cardboard, scissors, and glue"), laptops with software such as Scratch, GameMaker Studio, Adobe Photoshop, Google Drive tools and Unity, plus a venue with electricity, Internet connection, tables, an eating area and quiet resting areas.
requirements: A venue with electricity, Internet connection and working tables
Laptops with event software installed, plus extra devices in case participants' laptops fail
Tutors and voluntary workers to support idea generation, materials and technical problems
constraints: Even paper-based teams should have computer and Internet access to check game mechanics and the event theme
target_learners: adolescent students (12–16) participating in game jams
target_learning_goals: collaborative video-game concept development and 4C skill practice
examples: In the studied events, one workgroup developed concepts and dynamics through paper models, while most games were created with GameMaker Studio, Adobe Photoshop, and Scratch

article_title: Emote aloud during learning with AutoTutor: Applying the Facial Action Coding System to cognitive–affective states during learning
citation: Scotty D. Craig, Sidney D'Mello, Amy Witherspoon, and Art Graesser. (2008). Emote aloud during learning with AutoTutor: Applying the Facial Action Coding System to cognitive/affective states during learning. Cognition and Emotion, 22(5), 777-788. https://doi.org/10.1080/02699930701516759
title: Emote-aloud procedure for on-line identification of affective states during learning
description: The emote-aloud procedure is a modification of the cognitive-science think-aloud method in which participants state aloud the affective state they are feeling while working on a learning task. Participants were given functional definitions of eight affective states drawn from Merriam-Webster OnLine and were video recorded while interacting with AutoTutor, verbalising states "without external prompts from the system or pressure from an experimenter in the room". The method "allows for on-line identification of affective states while working on a task, with minimal task interference" and proved useful for identifying points during learning where affective events occurred.
requirements: Participants must be given functional definitions of the target affective states prior to the session so that utterances are unambiguous
Video recording and labour-intensive coding (transcription, segmenting, interjudge reliability scoring) are needed, so samples are small
constraints: Not all participants are amenable to the procedure: 2 of 7 participants did not express affective states verbally
Unpredictable time samples prevent searching for stable sequential patterns of affective states
target_learners: college undergraduates
target_learning_goals: identification of affective states (anger, boredom, confusion, contempt, curiosity, disgust, eureka, frustration) during complex learning with an intelligent tutoring system
examples: Participants interacted with AutoTutor on computer literacy topics for 90 minutes, saying aloud any of the eight defined affective states whenever they experienced one; 10-second clips ending in an emote-aloud utterance were extracted for FACS coding.
key_sources: Scotty D. Craig, Sidney D'Mello, Amy Witherspoon, and Art Graesser. (2008). Emote aloud during learning with AutoTutor: Applying the Facial Action Coding System to cognitive/affective states during learning. article_title: Comparing frameworks for 21st century skills
citation: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Perennial versus contextual skills distinction for 21st century capabilities
description: The chapter distinguishes "perennial" skills, valuable throughout history such as collaboration, from "contextual" skills unique to the new millennium, such as rapidly filtering huge amounts of incoming data. Perennial skills rise in importance and sophistication in the 21st century, while contextual skills are "novel in history as a valuable capability" and thus new in type. Contextual skills are typically absent from the legacy 20th century curriculum, making the distinction important for deciding what schooling must newly add.
requirements: Requires articulating what to deemphasize in an already crowded curriculum to make room for core 21st century understandings
constraints: Contextual skills are typically not part of the legacy curriculum inherited from 20th century educational systems
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students
target_learning_goals: 21st century work and citizenship capabilities
examples: Collaboration is presented as perennial but growing in importance; filtering signal from noise in data floods is presented as contextual and new in type
key_sources: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: Comparing frameworks for 21st century skills
citation: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Levy and Murnane's expert thinking and complex communication account of 21st century work demands
description: The chapter attributes to economists Levy and Murnane (2004) the claim that declining portions of the labor force do routine cognitive or manual work that computers can be programmed to do, while growing proportions do expert thinking and complex communication that computers cannot. Expert thinking involves "effective pattern matching based on detailed knowledge" plus metacognition about when to switch strategies; complex communication involves constantly adjusted exchange of verbal and nonverbal information as communication evolves unpredictably.
requirements: Grounds the rationale for 21st century skills in changing labor force demands
target_learners: All students preparing for work and citizenship
target_learning_goals: Expert decision making and complex communication
examples: A skilled physician inventing new heuristics when standard protocols fail illustrates expert thinking; a teacher improvising in unpredictable classroom discussion illustrates complex communication
key_sources: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: Comparing frameworks for 21st century skills
citation: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Partnership for 21st Century Skills (P21) framework
description: The P21 framework (2006) serves as the chapter's baseline because it is "more detailed and more widely adopted than any of the alternatives". It comprises core subjects, 21st century content (global awareness, financial and civic literacy, health awareness), learning and thinking skills (critical thinking, communication, creativity, collaboration, contextual learning, information and media literacy), ICT literacy, and life skills such as leadership, ethics, and adaptability. P21 also advocates authentic assessments integrated with core subject assessments.
requirements: Assessments must measure all five results that matter, with 21st century skills assessment integrated with core subjects
constraints: Standardized tests alone can measure only a few of the important skills and knowledge students should learn
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Core subjects plus 21st century content, thinking skills, ICT literacy, and life skills
examples: The chapter outlines P21's five result areas and its position that separate assessments of 21st century skills would defeat infusion into core subjects
key_sources: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: Comparing frameworks for 21st century skills
citation: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Dede's neomillennial learning styles framework
description: Dede (2005) presented a framework of "neomillennial learning styles" based on new digital literacies, describing the learning strengths and preferences technology-using people bring to educational settings. The framework includes fluency in multiple media, active learning based on "collectively seeking, sieving, and synthesizing experiences", expression through non-linear associational webs of representations, and co-design by teachers and students of personalized learning experiences. The chapter notes Web 2.0's shift toward co-construction of resources reinforces these styles.
requirements: Requires educational settings that support mediated, collective, and co-designed learning experiences
target_learners: Technology-using students in educational settings
target_learning_goals: Learning aligned with digital-era strengths and preferences
examples: Authoring a simulation and a webpage to express understanding, in contrast to writing a paper, illustrates non-linear expression
key_sources: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: Comparing frameworks for 21st century skills
citation: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Dede's category system for Web 2.0 tools
description: Dede (2009b) delineated a category system for current Web 2.0 tools with three categories: Sharing (communal bookmarking, photo/video sharing, social networking, writers' workshops/fanfiction), Thinking (blogs, podcasts, online discussion forums), and Co-Creating (wikis/collaborative file creation, mashups/collective media creation, collaborative social change communities). The chapter describes "a loose progression from top to bottom", with sharing leading to thinking together and then collective action by sophisticated groups seeking change.
requirements: Tools support communities of contributors rather than one-way presentation of material
target_learners: Internet-using learners and communities of contributors
target_learning_goals: Collaboration, knowledge co-creation, and collective action
examples: The nine media listed span sharing tools like social networking through co-creating tools like collaborative social change communities
key_sources: Dede, C. (2009). Comparing Frameworks for "21st Century Skills". Harvard Graduate School of Education. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: Intervention Provided to Linguistically Diverse Middle School Students with Severe Reading Difficulties
citation: Denton, C. A., Wexler, J., Vaughn, S., & Bryan, D. (2008). Intervention Provided to Linguistically Diverse Middle School Students with Severe Reading Difficulties. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 79–89. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.00264.x
title: Remediation for middle school minimal responders, especially ELLs with low oral vocabulary, requires considerably greater intensity and longer duration than one semester of daily 40-minute small-group instruction
description: The article proposes that students who are minimal responders to previous intervention need remediation of much greater intensity — longer sessions, reduced group size, increased active engagement — and much longer duration than the 13-week, 40-minute daily intervention tested. The authors state "it may be that considerably more intensive interventions (e.g., 2 hours per day) over considerably longer amounts of time (e.g., 2 years rather than 13 weeks) are required to improve outcomes," citing clinic-based studies with about 2 hours daily that produced large gains.
requirements: Scheduling structures that can accommodate substantially more daily intervention time than a single 40-minute class period
constraints: The authors note this level of intervention intensity "does not ﬁt easily into existing school routines"
target_learners: Middle school students with severe, persistent reading difficulties
English language learners with reading disabilities
Minimal responders to previous remedial or special education intervention
target_learning_goals: Word-level reading and decoding
Reading fluency
Reading comprehension
English oral vocabulary
examples: The study's own intervention (daily 40-minute sessions, groups of 2–4, 13 weeks, average 43 sessions attended) failed to accelerate growth, while cited clinic studies providing nearly 2 hours daily over 8 weeks reported large significant gains
key_sources: Denton, C. A., Wexler, J., Vaughn, S., & Bryan, D. (2008). Intervention Provided to Linguistically Diverse Middle School Students with Severe Reading Difficulties. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 79–89. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.00266.x

article_title: Intervention Provided to Linguistically Diverse Middle School Students with Severe Reading Difficulties
citation: Denton, C. A., Wexler, J., Vaughn, S., & Bryan, D. (2008). Intervention Provided to Linguistically Diverse Middle School Students with Severe Reading Difficulties. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 79–89. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.00264.x
title: Multicomponent middle school reading intervention: modified phonics program with ESL practices, vocabulary, fluency, and comprehension strategy instruction on a 2-day decoding/encoding cycle
description: A research intervention delivered in small groups of two to four students in daily 40-minute sessions over about 13 weeks. It was "a signiﬁcantly modiﬁed version of a phonics-based remedial program" (adapted from the Wilson reading system) augmented with ESL practices, vocabulary instruction, fluency practice, and comprehension strategies. Lessons alternated on a 2-day cycle between decoding days (letter-sound review, decoding rules, word and sentence reading, text reading) and encoding days (dictation, spelling practice, text reading), with heavy emphasis on phonics, word recognition, spelling, and fluency and integrated vocabulary and comprehension strategy instruction.
requirements: Teachers trained at least 10 hours with ongoing coaching and supervision
Small instructional groups of two to four students
Decodable text for applying decoding skills and motivating novels plus expository text for fluency and comprehension practice
constraints: Minimal emphasis on phonological awareness instruction
The majority of lesson time was spent on word-level instruction rather than vocabulary and comprehension, which the authors later hypothesized may have been a mismatch for these students' needs
target_learners: Middle school students (grades 6–8) with severe deficits in word reading, fluency, and comprehension
Spanish-speaking English language learners with identified disabilities
target_learning_goals: Decoding and encoding (spelling)
Word recognition and fluency
Vocabulary development
Comprehension strategy use
examples: Treatment students attended an average of 43 sessions (SD = 9), receiving an average of 29 hours of instruction (SD = 6; range 15–35), with fidelity ratings between 91% and 98% for both interventionists
key_sources: Denton, C. A., Wexler, J., Vaughn, S., & Bryan, D. (2008). Intervention Provided to Linguistically Diverse Middle School Students with Severe Reading Difficulties. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 79–89. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.00266.x

article_title: Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools
citation: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791
title: Stealth assessment: embedding skill measurement invisibly in game play so that player choices supply the assessment data
description: Stealth assessment is an approach in which measurement of a skill is woven into gameplay so that students' ordinary choices generate the assessment data without them knowing they are being assessed. The article describes it as assessments "woven directly and invisibly into the fabric" of the game, with "players' choices during gameplay provide the data needed for assessment." Zoo U applies this by logging dialogue choices, clicks, and time on and off task to compute social skills performance indices, reducing observer reactivity compared with naturalistic observation.
requirements: Extensive logging of player actions (clicks, dialogue choices, timing) so behaviors relevant to the target skill can be scored automatically
constraints: The article notes a key challenge was determining the appropriate level of difficulty to garner enough student variability in responses to develop useful performance indices
target_learners: third- and fourth-grade elementary school students
target_learning_goals: social skills competencies: emotion regulation, impulse control, communication, empathy, cooperation, and initiation
examples: Zoo U scenes present social problems (e.g., feeding the elephant before recess) where impulsive clicks on distractor crates lower the impulse control score
key_sources: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791

article_title: Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools
citation: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791
title: Zoo U: a single-player point-and-click game assessing six social skills in school-like scenes
description: Zoo U is a single-player point-and-click problem-solving game set in a school-like setting with teacher and student NPCs and zoo animals. Subject matter experts used educational and developmental psychology theories to develop six independent social scenes assessing "emotion regulation, impulse control, communication, empathy, cooperation, and initiation." Each scene scores a composite performance index computed from parsed log files, combining dialogue-choice quality, time spent on appropriate versus off-task problem solving, and the ratio of on-task to off-task behaviors.
requirements: Scene content developed by subject matter experts to elicit measurable player behaviors and dialogue choices integral to the assessed social skill
Computer logs tracking the location and time of each mouse click
constraints: Students' scores decline if they diverge too far from on-task behavior; each scene varies in emphasis on NPC interaction versus environment interaction
target_learners: third- and fourth-grade students in regular classrooms
target_learning_goals: assessment of children's social skills aptitude across six social competencies
examples: In the impulse control scene, players must ignore red-herring food crates and read the clipboard feeding instructions to score highly
key_sources: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791

article_title: Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools
citation: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791
title: Iterative data-driven validation pattern: create, test, revise from performance and feedback, and retest until gameplay statistically matches external criteria
description: This design pattern structures assessment-game development as repeated cycles in which the game is created, tested with students, revised based on logged performance and user feedback, and retested until gameplay is statistically matched to independent ratings of the target skill. The article states it "utilized an iterative data-driven validation process in which the game was created, tested, revised based on student performance and feedback, and retested." Two iterative evaluations with third- and fourth-graders refined dialogue choices, verified challenge difficulty, and produced the scoring algorithms.
requirements: Student testing sessions with observers recording attention, areas of difficulty, and reactions
Game logs tracking the location and time of each mouse click
An independent external measure of the target skill for validation
constraints: The article notes the appropriate level of difficulty to obtain useful response variability was not evident a priori and had to be established from captured gameplay
target_learners: elementary school students (third and fourth grade)
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of social skills within an engaging game
examples: A first test with one third-grade (n = 16) and one fourth-grade (n = 23) classroom informed revisions; a revised version was tested with 187 students from 14 classrooms
key_sources: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791

article_title: Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools
citation: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791
title: Combine detailed game logs of socially relevant behavior with external skill measures to incrementally improve embedded assessment accuracy
description: When building an embedded (stealth) assessment, developers should log socially relevant player behavior in detail and analyze it against independent external measures of the same skill, using mismatches to revise items and scoring. The article reports that "detailed game logs of socially relevant player behavior combined with external measures of player social skills provided an eﬃcient vector to incrementally improve the accuracy of the embedded assessments." In Zoo U this meant refining dialogue choices that did not relate in expected directions with teacher ratings.
requirements: Minute annotated logging of the times and locations of every player click event
External measures of the target skill (e.g., teacher ratings) collected for the same students
constraints: The optimal thresholds for behavioral indicators were not evident at initial design and had to be established empirically from gameplay logs
target_learners: elementary school students
target_learning_goals: accurate embedded assessment of social skills
examples: Log data from the first iterative test were used to refine dialogue choices that did not relate in the expected directions with teacher ratings of students' social skills
key_sources: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791

article_title: Processing strategies and the generation effect: Implications for making a better reader
citation: deWinstanley, P. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2004). Processing strategies and the generation effect: Implications for making a better reader. Memory & Cognition, 32(6), 945-955. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03194854
title: Encoding-retrieval match accounts of the generation effect (procedural and transfer-appropriate multifactor accounts)
description: The article describes two accounts of when generation advantages occur, both centered on the relationship between encoding and retrieval. In the procedural account, "participants generating information at study, as opposed to reading it, are more likely to engage in procedures during study that can be reinstated during the retention test." In the transfer-appropriate multifactor account, generation effects occur when the generation task focuses processing on the type of information a later test is sensitive to. The authors use these accounts to interpret both prior findings and their own first-paragraph generation advantage.
requirements: A generation advantage requires a match between the information or procedures strengthened during generation and those demanded by the retention test
constraints: Both accounts predict the advantage disappears when encoding and retrieval processes are mismatched
target_learners: adult learners in laboratory memory experiments
students studying textbook material
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied verbal material
examples: The authors propose that participants used contextual information to generate and then recall items, and that noticing this use led them to attend to contextual information when reading later paragraphs
key_sources: deWinstanley, P. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2004). Processing strategies and the generation effect: Implications for making a better reader. Memory & Cognition, 32(6), 945-955. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03196872

article_title: Processing strategies and the generation effect: Implications for making a better reader
citation: deWinstanley, P. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2004). Processing strategies and the generation effect: Implications for making a better reader. Memory & Cognition, 32(6), 945-955. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03194854
title: Metacognitive knowledge-updating account: learners change encoding strategies only after experiencing differential performance consequences
description: The article interprets its results via Dunlosky and Hertzog's knowledge-updating framework and the metacognitive literature on illusions of competence, in which "learners are not very accurate in taking such readings and often suffer from what has been called illusions of comprehension or competence." Individuals are assumed not to update beliefs about encoding-strategy effectiveness "unless they become aware of the consequential performance differences for information processed with different strategies." Only participants who experienced both generating and reading on the same test upgraded their processing of read items.
requirements: Learners must directly experience the performance consequences of different encoding strategies within the same test context
constraints: Learners are typically unable to judge a strategy's efficacy during its execution and do not switch strategies without experiencing relative effectiveness
target_learners: adult learners studying textbook material
students in self-regulated study contexts
target_learning_goals: adopting more effective encoding strategies for reading
examples: Experiment 2 participants who generated first but never saw both item types on one test failed to appreciate the mnemonic benefit of generating and did not change their processing of read items
key_sources: deWinstanley, P. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2004). Processing strategies and the generation effect: Implications for making a better reader. Memory & Cognition, 32(6), 945-955. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03196872

article_title: Does Instructional Approach Matter? How Elaboration Plays a Crucial Role in Multimedia Learning
citation: Tessa H. S. Eysink & Ton de Jong (2012). Does Instructional Approach Matter? How Elaboration Plays a Crucial Role in Multimedia Learning. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2011.611776
title: Elaboration as the key process explaining learning differences across multimedia instructional approaches
description: The article proposes that differences in learning outcomes between multimedia instructional approaches are explained by the learning processes they elicit, with elaboration as the decisive category. Elaborative processes are defined as those "by which information in the learning environment is processed at a deeper level, in such a way that the information is related and connected to prior knowledge and new information is deduced". The framework distinguishes superficial, elaborative, and regulative processes, and holds that approaches requiring learners to generate (parts of) the subject matter — self-explanation-based and inquiry learning — foster more elaboration than approaches that present material directly.
requirements: Learners must work in an environment whose design elicits generative, elaborative activities such as self-explaining, hypothesizing, or relating and integrating
constraints: The account was developed for multimedia learning environments in a problem-solving domain (probability theory) with learners who had prior knowledge of the topic
target_learners: secondary school students in higher-level pre-university education
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning of mathematics (probability theory), including conceptual understanding and transfer
examples: Think-aloud protocols coded with the generic scheme showed self-explanation-based and inquiry learners engaged in more elaborative processes than hypermedia and observational learners
key_sources: Tessa H. S. Eysink & Ton de Jong (2012). Does Instructional Approach Matter? How Elaboration Plays a Crucial Role in Multimedia Learning. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2011.611776

article_title: Does Instructional Approach Matter? How Elaboration Plays a Crucial Role in Multimedia Learning
citation: Tessa H. S. Eysink & Ton de Jong (2012). Does Instructional Approach Matter? How Elaboration Plays a Crucial Role in Multimedia Learning. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2011.611776
title: Generic learning processes coding scheme for think-aloud protocols
description: A coding scheme used to classify think-aloud utterances into mutually exclusive categories of superficial processes (e.g., reading/watching and filtering, checking solution steps), elaborative processes (developing and testing hypotheses, relating and integrating, giving (self-)explanations), and regulative processes (orienting, planning, monitoring, reflecting). It was piloted and adjusted, and "was constructed to have a generic character allowing the representation of all instructional approaches and applicability to problem-solving domains other than probability theory". Interrater reliability reached .85 (Cohen's kappa) for the three main categories and .74 for subcategories.
requirements: Protocols segmented into utterances, each defined as a statement expressing one distinct learner activity, coded by trained coders
constraints: Reflection was restricted to purely regulative activities, with deeper reflective processes placed in the elaborative category
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: characterizing the learning processes elicited by different instructional approaches
examples: Applied to think-aloud protocols of 40 students working through one of the four probability-theory learning environments
key_sources: Tessa H. S. Eysink & Ton de Jong (2012). Does Instructional Approach Matter? How Elaboration Plays a Crucial Role in Multimedia Learning. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2011.611776

article_title: Quiet or questioning? Students' discussion behaviors in student-centered education across cultures
citation: Janneke M. Frambach, Erik W. Driessen, Philip Beh and Cees P.M. van der Vleuten. (2014). Quiet or questioning? Students' discussion behaviors in student-centered education across cultures. Studies in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/03075079.2012.754865
title: Conceptual model of cultural and contextual factors shaping students' discussion behaviors in student-centered education
description: The study built a conceptual model (Figure 2) linking cultural and contextual factors to students' discussion behaviors and skills in PBL. It holds that students externalize cultural backgrounds and internalize the discussion aspect of PBL, so that 'students' discussion behaviors and skills and their development from the first to the third year were shaped by complex interactions between contextual factors, cultural factors, and the PBL discussion sessions.' The model organizes four cultural factors and six mediating contextual factors.
requirements: Data from interviews, observations, documents and contextual information across multiple institutions to populate the model
constraints: Derived from a qualitative comparative case study in three medical schools; findings do not lend themselves to generalization
target_learners: undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: discussion and communication skills in small-group student-centered learning
key_sources: Janneke M. Frambach, Erik W. Driessen, Philip Beh and Cees P.M. van der Vleuten. (2014). Quiet or questioning? Students' discussion behaviors in student-centered education across cultures. Studies in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/03075079.2012.754865

article_title: Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition?
citation: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0
title: Complex problems are defined by complexity, connectivity, dynamics, intransparency and polytely
description: The article defines a complex problem as one whose solution demands operations on systems with five characteristics drawn from Dörner et al. (1983): "Elements relevant to the solution process are large ( complexity), highly interconnected ( connectivity), and dynamically changing over time ( dynamics). Neither structure nor dynamics are disclosed ( intransparency)" and the goal structure is polytelic, requiring the weighting and coordination of multiple goal facets. This definition distinguishes CPS from simple problem solving and organizes the review.
requirements: Assessment scenarios must realize these characteristics, e.g. computer-simulated microworlds
constraints: The definition is presented as the European research tradition's characterization, not a formally measured taxonomy
target_learners: adult problem solvers in laboratory and real-world decision settings
target_learning_goals: problem solving in complex dynamic systems
examples: Tailorshop and Lohhausen microworlds were built to realize these characteristics under lab conditions
key_sources: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0

article_title: Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition?
citation: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0
title: Complex cognition as goal-directed derivation of new information, contrasted with simple cognition on a hierarchy of explanation levels
description: Following Knauff and Wolf, the article states that "complex cognition deals with all mental processes that are used by an individual for deriving new information out of given information, with the intention to make decisions, solve problems, and plan actions." Simple cognition studies elementary processes like perception, memory or learning in isolation; complex cognition is a shift in hierarchy level of explanation (signal, sign, broader regulation concept), and the whole follows the Gestalt principle of being more than the sum of its parts. Mental processes here include motivational and emotional processes.
requirements: A definition of complexity going beyond difficulty, which the article notes remains open
constraints: The border between simple and complex cognition is explicitly not a clear-cut one with a sharp border
target_learners: adult learners and decision makers
target_learning_goals: deriving new information, decision making, action planning
examples: A ship's captain overseeing a red warning light illustrates complex cognition embedding perception into action regulation
key_sources: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0

article_title: Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition?
citation: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0
title: Macrocognition: cognition in naturalistic, ill-defined decision settings, complementary to microcognition
description: The article presents macrocognition, introduced by Cacciabue and Hollnagel and elaborated by Klein et al., as a descriptor for cognitive activities in natural decision-making settings. Klein et al. "mention phenomena like the following: planning and problem detection using leverage points to construct options, attention management, and uncertainty management." The author argues the key difference from microcognition is "the ill-defined conditions of the tasks and problems under consideration", and that the two approaches are complementary; he contends lab research is not necessarily restricted to microcognition.
requirements: Study settings with ill-defined tasks, whether in the field or in high-external-validity labs and simulators
constraints: The article argues against the belief that macrocognition can only be analyzed outside the lab
target_learners: experienced professionals making decisions in dynamic environments
target_learning_goals: situation assessment, decision making, attention and uncertainty management
examples: Naturalistic Decision Making studies experienced people in dynamic, uncertain, fast-paced environments
key_sources: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0

article_title: Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition?
citation: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0
title: Operative intelligence: process indicators of strategic thinking in complex dynamic systems
description: The article describes Dörner's concept of operative intelligence as "a collection of those factors that determine strategic processes like flexibility, foresight, circumspection, or systematic behavior", concentrating on thinking processes rather than their results. Dörner postulates four process components for managing a complex system: information retrieval and integration, goal elaboration and goal balancing, planning measures and making decisions, and self-management under frustration, time pressure and stress. Process indicators include the breadth and type of questions participants ask and the place, dosage and sequence of decisions.
requirements: Thinking-aloud data collection for question-type indicators; computer-simulated scenarios producing large datasets not reduced to a single score
constraints: The article states the theory offers neither a fully elaborated theory nor a measuring device and still requires refinement
target_learners: adult problem solvers working with simulated dynamic systems
target_learning_goals: strategic information search, goal elaboration, decision making, self-regulation
examples: Dörner differentiated questions for states, dependencies, effects, components, subordination and superordination
key_sources: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0

article_title: Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition?
citation: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0
title: Tailorshop microworld for assessing complex problem solving
description: Tailorshop is a semantically rich computer-simulated microworld first published in 1981: "Tailorshop is a microworld, which realizes the production conditions of a small factory. The participant takes on the role of a manager of a small shirt factory." Participants manipulate ten exogenous input variables (workers, machines, raw material, salaries, social security contributions, maintenance, advertising, shop location, utility van, sales price) across a 24-variable connection diagram, with monthly reports and delayed effects. It stands for the broad interpretation of CPS but has weak psychometric properties.
requirements: Monthly report feedback structure; interventions take effect in the next cycle (demand after two cycles)
constraints: The article states Tailorshop has weak points from a psychometric point of view and suffers one-item-testing
target_learners: adult participants acting as factory managers in CPS studies
target_learning_goals: system exploration, intervention planning, managing production and sales subsystems
examples: Used in numerous studies since 1981, including Barth and Funke's affective-environment experiment

article_title: Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition?
citation: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0
title: MicroDYN: linear structural equation items for psychometrically sound CPS assessment
description: MicroDYN models dynamic problem solving within "the formal framework of linear structural equation systems (LSE-systems)", presenting multiple independent items with exogenous and endogenous variables, main effects, multiple effects, multiple dependencies, side effects and autoregressive processes. Each item runs three stages: free exploration, externalization of the mental model by drawing connections, and a control phase reaching target values. The article credits it with theoretical foundation, scalability, unlimited item generation and ecological validity, and notes "MicroDYN has become the first choice for the PISA 2012 consortium for the world-wide assessment of problem solving."
requirements: Items of minimal but sufficient complexity; participants see between 8 and 12 items of about 6 min each, roughly 1 h total testing time
constraints: Represents selected but important CPS aspects rather than the broad interpretation of CPS
target_learners: large-scale assessment participants, e.g. PISA 2012 test takers
target_learning_goals: identifying unknown causal structures of dynamic systems and controlling them to reach goals
examples: Each item is processed in exploration, model-drawing, and control stages
