article_title: Teaching metacognitive strategies that address executive function processes within a schoolwide curriculum
citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: Executive function as an umbrella term for goal-directed cognitive processes
description: The volume's framing chapter defines executive function as an umbrella construct covering the cognitive processes serving goal-directed behavior. It states that "most of the definitions of executive function include many, but not all, of the following elements": goal setting and planning, organization of behaviors over time, flexibility, attention and memory systems such as working memory, and self-regulatory processes like self-monitoring. The editors note that fuzzy definitions still abound and different theories compete to explain EF development.
requirements: A definition must accommodate partial overlap across proposed element lists, since no unitary definition exists in the field
constraints: The field still lacks a unitary definition; the listed elements are shared by many but not all definitions
target_learners: students with executive function difficulties
learners across K-12 and higher education
target_learning_goals: goal setting
planning
organization
self-monitoring
flexible shifting between approaches
examples: The volume organizes its three parts (theoretical frameworks, diagnostic groups, interventions) around this umbrella definition of EF processes
key_sources: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com

article_title: Teaching metacognitive strategies that address executive function processes within a schoolwide curriculum
citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: Hill, skill, and will: executive function as integration of goal, abilities, and volition
description: Moran and Gardner conceptualize executive function from a multiple-intelligences perspective as emerging from intrapersonal intelligence. They "construe executive function as the integration of three parameters: hill—the establishment of a clear goal; skill—the requisite abilities and techniques for attaining that goal; and will—the volition to begin and persevere until the goal has been reached." These parameters become more complexly integrated with age, and the authors distinguish an apprentice stage of culture-driven control over identity from a master stage of personally defined control over productivity.
requirements: Executive function is analyzed through intrapersonal intelligence, the computational capacity to discern and use information about oneself
constraints: The authors label the two-stage apprentice/master distinction an admitted simplification
target_learners: learners across the lifespan, from toddlers to adults
target_learning_goals: goal establishment
strategy use
perseverance toward goals
self-regulation
examples: The chapter opens with vignettes spanning a toddler forming a sentence to an entrepreneur strategizing an IPO, all framed as executive function events
key_sources: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com

article_title: Teaching metacognitive strategies that address executive function processes within a schoolwide curriculum
citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: EF as how-and-when functions on equal footing with other cognitive domains, not a higher-order pinnacle
description: Denckla argues against hierarchical models that place executive function above other cognition. She concludes the EF domain "is not above other cognitive domains, not some reified and exalted higher-order pinnacle of cognition, not meta- but intra- and intercognitive," and proposes speaking of EF as encompassing how-and-when functions, colloquially getting your act together. She warns the meta- prefix disguises EF's developmental dynamics and ignores subcortical contributions, since EF develops from about 9 months of age into the fourth decade in looping interaction with other domains.
requirements: EF should be understood through systems-and-circuits brain analysis rather than hierarchical meta-levels
constraints: The account is a neuropsychological argument grounded in clinical observation and developmental literature, not a tested model
target_learners: children and adolescents with executive function difficulties
students with ADHD and learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: understanding executive function as action control (initiate, sustain, shift, inhibit)
recognizing EF's reciprocal interaction with language and other domains
examples: Denckla uses a cooking analogy: a meal requires both ingredients and recipes, since the how and when of EF is meaningless without reciprocal interaction with other cognitive and motor domains
key_sources: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com

article_title: Teaching metacognitive strategies that address executive function processes within a schoolwide curriculum
citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive function in education: From theory to practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: Translate executive function terminology into familiar educational language for cross-professional communication
description: Denckla recommends bridging the medical and educational perspectives by translating EF/EDF terminology into words familiar in special education. Professionals comfortable with EF terminology can communicate with education by "translating or analyzing EF into more familiar words like planning, organization, study skills, and self-monitoring/checking skills," terms that have existed in learning disabilities literature for decades. This translation lets brain-based and school-based professionals apply EF concepts without the formidable resonance of the clinical label.
requirements: Professionals must recognize which aspects of attention and memory (executive/selective attention, working memory) fall under the executive domain
constraints: The domains of attention and memory straddle brain-based and school-based understandings, making some splits hard to communicate across professions
target_learners: students with ADHD and learning disabilities served in schools
target_learning_goals: planning
organization
study skills
self-monitoring and checking
examples: Denckla notes organizational planning and working memory have long been recognized in special education under the names sequencing and short-term memory within IEPs

article_title: Game-based learning: A design-based theory of teaching–learning–assessment systems
citation: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/
title: Gordon's transactional troika: assessment, teaching, and learning as inseparable, mutually reinforcing processes
description: Gordon proposes that assessment, teaching, and learning form a dynamic, dialectical system rather than separate stages of education. He writes that he describes them "as a kind of troika or three-legged stool: each element supports and strengthens the others, and none should function independently of the whole." In this transactional view, an assessment is a two-way exchange in which the student is an active agent who interprets tasks, uses feedback, and brings identity and feeling into the interaction. The handbook series is organized around this reconceptualization, treating assessment as embedded in pedagogy rather than as an external verdict passed on learning after the fact.
requirements: Assessment must be implemented in a supportive, trustful environment so it feels like an extension of teaching rather than a judgment from on high
constraints: The authors frame this as a vision requiring institutional change; conventional high-stakes testing regimes currently operate outside this paradigm
target_learners: All learners across preK-12, higher education, workplace, and informal settings
target_learning_goals: Intellective competence and human development
examples: Gordon cites Feuerstein's instrumental enrichment tasks, which functioned as assessments and interventions at once
key_sources: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/

article_title: Game-based learning: A design-based theory of teaching–learning–assessment systems
citation: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/
title: Design assessments as learning opportunities that challenge and teach at the same time
description: The principle holds that assessments should be crafted as rich problems, projects, or simulations that both elicit evidence of learning and produce it. Gordon writes that "assessments can be designed as learning opportunities: rich problems, projects, or simulations that both challenge students to apply their knowledge and teach them something in the process." When students receive scaffolded support such as hints, feedback, and opportunities to try again, the assessment itself contributes to development, shifting it from a static checkpoint to a dynamic, educative experience.
requirements: Scaffolded support (hints, feedback, opportunities to try again) so the assessment contributes to development
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students
target_learning_goals: Problem solving, inquiry skills, deeper learning
examples: A challenging science investigation that doubles as an assessment of inquiry skills and a chance for students to refine experimental reasoning
key_sources: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/

article_title: Game-based learning: A design-based theory of teaching–learning–assessment systems
citation: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/
title: Intellective competence as the holistic aim of assessment in the service of learning
description: Intellective competence is Gordon's term for the broader goal that reconceived assessment should foster and capture. He defines it: "Intellective competence, a term I coined, denotes the ability and disposition to use one's knowledge, strategies, and values to solve problems and to continue learning." It is a holistic notion going beyond memorization of facts or routine skills, encompassing critical thinking, adaptability, creativity, and the capacity to learn how to learn. Assessing for it means posing authentic, complex challenges and analyzing how students approach them, including ingenuity, learning from failure, and trying alternative strategies.
requirements: Assessments that pose authentic, complex challenges and gather evidence of process, not only correctness
target_learners: All learners
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking, adaptability, creativity, learning how to learn
examples: Gordon proposes analyzing whether students showed ingenuity in finding a solution and learned from initial failures
key_sources: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/

article_title: Game-based learning: A design-based theory of teaching–learning–assessment systems
citation: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/
title: Make assessments adaptive and culturally sustaining so human variance is leveraged rather than treated as noise
description: This principle treats learner variance in development, culture, language, and interests as an asset to be understood and leveraged rather than noise to be minimized. Gordon argues assessments "should be able to accommodate different ways of demonstrating learning and provide entry points for learners of varying skill levels (the idea of 'low floor, high ceiling' tasks)" and should be sensitive to the languages, values, prior knowledge, and identities students bring. He links this to equity, noting that when assessment is used purely as a high-stakes gatekeeper it has often exacerbated social inequalities, and that recognizing growth and multiple abilities supports positive learner identity.
requirements: Tasks with low floor and high ceiling; sensitivity to students' cultural contexts and languages; a supportive, trustful environment
constraints: The article states high-stakes gatekeeping uses of assessment have often exacerbated social inequalities, a condition this principle is meant to counter
target_learners: Culturally and linguistically diverse learners, including bilingual students
target_learning_goals: Equitable demonstration of learning, positive learner identity, growth
examples: An assessment that allows a bilingual student to draw on both languages may better capture and cultivate full communicative ability
key_sources: Sireci, S. G., Tucker, E. M., & Gordon, E. W. (Eds.). (2025). Handbook for Assessment in the Service of Learning, Volume II: Reconceptualizing Assessment to Improve Learning. University of Massachusetts Amherst Libraries. https://openpublishing.library.umass.edu/

article_title: An inventory of peer assessment diversity
citation: Gielen, S., Dochy, F., & Onghena, P. (2011). An inventory of peer assessment diversity. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 36(2), 137–155. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221444
title: Inventory of peer assessment diversity: 20 variables grouped into five clusters
description: The article develops a classification framework for describing peer assessment practices, replacing Topping's discrete-variable typology because 'the range of variation appeared to no longer be a list of separate values but rather a continuum, or sometimes even a multi-dimensional space'. Eight new variables were added and another eight extended with extra sub-dimensions, five original variables were absorbed into larger entities, and the 20 resulting variables were grouped into five clusters: decisions concerning use, links to the learning environment, interaction between peers, composition of assessment groups, and management of the assessment procedure.
requirements: Each peer assessment design should be described on all 20 variables for studies to be comparable and synthesizable
constraints: The authors note 'a list of distinguishing features will never be exhaustive'
target_learners: learners in formal and non-formal education participating in peer assessment
target_learning_goals: designing, describing and comparing peer assessment practices
examples: Table 4 of the article prints the full summary of the 20 variables and their dimensions, from Setting and Object through Format, Requirement, Reward, Training/guidance and Quality control
key_sources: Gielen, S., Dochy, F., & Onghena, P. (2011). An inventory of peer assessment diversity. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 36(2), 137–155. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221444

article_title: An inventory of peer assessment diversity
citation: Gielen, S., Dochy, F., & Onghena, P. (2011). An inventory of peer assessment diversity. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 36(2), 137–155. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221444
title: Align peer assessment with curriculum, learning goals and teaching rather than treating it as an add-on
description: The inventory's 'Alignment' variable concerns 'if and how a peer assessment application truly fits into its learning environment, instead of being an artificial add-on'. The article recommends aligning the object of peer assessment with learning goals, integrating the output within teaching, treating summative peer assessment with the care required of summative assessment, and fitting practical arrangements such as output, privacy and contact into the current setting.
requirements: Designers must examine the degree of alignment with the curriculum, learning goals and teaching already present in the course
constraints: The dimensions to consider are numerous and diverse, depending on other components of the learning environment and choices on other inventory variables; the authors call it 'certainly not the easiest variable to discuss'
target_learners: students in courses using peer assessment
target_learning_goals: formative learning from peer feedback and valid summative peer grading
examples: Prins et al. (2005) suggest that 'the ratio between time available for the course and time needed for the assessment has to be guarded' when several time-consuming assignments coexist; van den Berg, Admiraal, and Pilot (2006a) discuss whether peer feedback is followed by a teacher-led plenary discussion

article_title: An inventory of peer assessment diversity
citation: Gielen, S., Dochy, F., & Onghena, P. (2011). An inventory of peer assessment diversity. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 36(2), 137–155. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221444
title: Avoid the term 'co-assessment'; specify how peer and staff assessment relate instead
description: The article advises against the label 'co-assessment' because 'the use of this label, however, masks all details about how teachers' and peers' assessments actually relate to each other'. Instead, the inventory's 'Relationship to other assessments' variable requires specifying whether peer assessment is (partially) substitutional or supplementary, whether re-marking is possible, and, if supplementary, its timing relative to staff assessment and whether parties know each other's judgements.
requirements: Designers must describe the concrete relationship between peer and staff assessment rather than using an umbrella term
constraints: The recommendation applies to designs where students collaborate with staff in assessment; the term is also rejected for designs where students do not take full responsibility
target_learners: students in higher education courses combining peer and staff assessment
target_learning_goals: transparent and comparable description of combined peer–staff assessment arrangements
examples: The article distinguishes substitutional designs where students become 'surrogate' teachers, partially substitutional designs where students act as 'assistant' teachers taking over only part of the assessment, and supplementary designs where peers and staff assess the same performance

article_title: Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research
citation: Graham LA, Gray C, Wagner TH, Illarmo S, Hawn MT, Wren SM, Iannuzzi J, Harris AHS. (2023). Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research. Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-6773.14106
title: A four-step adapted cognitive task analysis framework for clinical environments
description: The article develops a health care setting-adapted version of cognitive task analysis, a suite of methods for studying cognitive processes such as reasoning, problem-solving, and decision-making. The framework guides users through four steps: "(1) Planning, (2) Environmental Analysis, (3) Knowledge Elicitation, and (4) Analyses and Results." It is iterative, drawing on multiple sources of information to moderate the biases of single sources, and is grounded mainly in Crandall et al.'s Working Minds guide. It aims to identify the knowledge, expertise, thought processes, procedures, actors, goals, and mental strategies underlying task completion.
requirements: A clear, focused key study question identifying the task, population, time, and place, from which all other steps evolve
At least two data collection methods, with an environmental analysis preceding knowledge elicitation
A draft of final deliverables and a data analysis plan developed during planning
constraints: Experimental knowledge elicitation methods are often hard to implement in clinical environments without interrupting patient care
target_learners: health services researchers
quality improvement practitioners
implementation scientists
target_learning_goals: characterizing cognitive processes and decision-making underlying clinical tasks
examples: The framework was piloted in an ongoing study of discharging surgical patients, with the key question "Who is involved and what information is needed to discharge a patient after surgery?"
key_sources: Graham LA, Gray C, Wagner TH, Illarmo S, Hawn MT, Wren SM, Iannuzzi J, Harris AHS. (2023). Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research. Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-6773.14106

article_title: Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research
citation: Graham LA, Gray C, Wagner TH, Illarmo S, Hawn MT, Wren SM, Iannuzzi J, Harris AHS. (2023). Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research. Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-6773.14106
title: Critical Decision Method interview protocol with four phases
description: The Critical Decision Method (CDM) is a structured semi-structured interview technique the article uses for knowledge elicitation in Step 3 of its CTA framework. "A traditional CDM interview involves an iterative process of four phases": Identification (recalling real-life task examples), Timeline Verification, Knowledge Deepening (identifying problem-solving strategies along the timeline), and "What if" Queries. In the pilot, interviews probed factors making discharges more complex, such as team disagreement or missing information.
requirements: Audio-recording to allow transcription, coding, and re-review
Purposive sampling of disciplines identified during the environmental analysis
target_learners: health care providers such as nurses, residents, and case managers
target_learning_goals: eliciting expert decision-making strategies and cognitive steps of a clinical task
examples: In the pilot, interviews began by identifying steps, key actors, and roles in recent patient discharges, then constructed a discharge timeline and probed complexity factors
key_sources: Graham LA, Gray C, Wagner TH, Illarmo S, Hawn MT, Wren SM, Iannuzzi J, Harris AHS. (2023). Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research. Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-6773.14106

title: Pair a low-intrusion environmental analysis with knowledge elicitation when studying cognition in busy clinical settings
description: The article recommends sequencing a minimally intrusive environmental scan before more intrusive knowledge elicitation. "Including at least two data collection methods is unique to our health care-setting adapted CTA framework. We developed this progression to minimize intrusion into the clinical environment." The environmental analysis identifies actors, barriers, facilitators, and policies, and refines interview guides and sampling for the subsequent knowledge elicitation step.
requirements: A priori identification of data collection methods and materials during planning
Iterative refinement of knowledge elicitation materials based on environmental scan findings
constraints: Designed for busy clinical environments where intrusion must be minimized
target_learners: health services researchers
quality improvement teams
target_learning_goals: understanding cognitive processes underlying clinical tasks
examples: The pilot used structured observations of morning teaching rounds before beginning CDM interviews after 12 site observations

article_title: Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research
citation: Graham LA, Gray C, Wagner TH, Illarmo S, Hawn MT, Wren SM, Iannuzzi J, Harris AHS. (2023). Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research. Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-6773.14106
title: Cognitive Demands Tables and process flow diagrams as CTA deliverables
description: The article identifies tables, diagrams, and lists of cognitive functions, cues, and subprocesses as common CTA deliverables. Process flow diagrams document cognitive steps to complete a task, while tables breaking out required cognitive tasks by event type are "frequently referred to as “Cognitive Demands Tables” when used in the context of CTA." These tables can include task types, actors, cues, and barriers and facilitators. Fishbone, flowchart, and network diagrams can detail task sequences and potential error points.
requirements: Decisions about which deliverables are most appropriate should be made based on the research audience
Systematic qualitative coding to increase validity, transparency, and reproducibility
target_learners: health services researchers
decision support tool designers
target_learning_goals: documenting and communicating the cognitive demands of a task
examples: The pilot drafted a task flow diagram of the discharge process, a table of key actors, and a table of frequently occurring cues that a patient is ready for discharge

article_title: Improved probabilistic inference as a general learning mechanism with action video games
citation: Green, C.S., Pouget, A., & Bavelier, D. (2010). Improved probabilistic inference as a general learning mechanism with action video games. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2010.07.040
title: Improved probabilistic inference as a general mechanism explaining broad transfer from action video-game play
description: The article proposes that action video-game play improves the nervous system's use of noisy sensory evidence: players learn the statistics of the task's stimuli and accumulate evidence more efficiently, yielding "a more accurate posterior distribution" over choices. Because evidence-accumulation circuits are argued to be shared or multimodal across modalities, this single mechanism explains why game training transfers to widely different tasks. The authors suggest the mechanism "may serve as a signature of training regimens that are likely to produce transfer of learning."
requirements: Training must involve situations that are rarely repeated, so learners must extract stimulus statistics on the fly rather than a task-specific solution
constraints: The authors state they can only speculate about the neural mechanisms of the transfer, listing shared accumulation circuits, fronto-parietal networks, and neuromodulator release as open possibilities for future work
target_learners: young adults with and without action video-game experience
target_learning_goals: probabilistic inference and efficient accumulation of noisy sensory evidence across visual and auditory tasks
key_sources: Green, C.S., Pouget, A., & Bavelier, D. (2010). Improved probabilistic inference as a general learning mechanism with action video games. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2010.07.040

article_title: A Game Design Methodology for Generating a Psychological Profile of Players
citation: Guardiola, E., & Natkin, S. (2015). A Game Design Methodology for Generating a Psychological Profile of Players. In Serious Games Analytics, Methodologies for Performance Measurement, Assessment, and Improvement. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4
title: Nine-step game design methodology for generating a psychological profile of players
description: The article proposes a game design process dedicated to psychological profiling, stating: "Following our framework, we propose a game design process in 9 steps". The steps cover selecting a validated psychological model, setting audience constraints, building an expert validation pipeline, confronting the player model with the psychological model, defining psychometric items inside the gameplay loop, rationalizing content-dimension links, documenting the results interface, running a test-and-analysis protocol, and iterating. Its originality lies in the coexistence of the player model and the psychological model throughout design.
requirements: A scientifically validated psychological model with a referential test for comparison
A pipeline for content validation by domain experts
A documented interface explaining how gameplay elements become items and how the profile is calculated
A test and analysis protocol comparing game results with a classical questionnaire
constraints: The article reports the method applied in one serious game production with timing and budget constraints; validation of psychometric use was not the goal of the first test session
target_learners: vocational guidance audiences from middle school students to adults in career change
target_learning_goals: assessment of vocational interests, motivation and decision style through gameplay
examples: The method was applied step by step during the development of JEU SERAI, a serious game using 18 mini games mapped to Holland RIASEC types
key_sources: Guardiola, E., & Natkin, S. (2015). A Game Design Methodology for Generating a Psychological Profile of Players. In Serious Games Analytics, Methodologies for Performance Measurement, Assessment, and Improvement. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_16

title: JEU SERAI vocational guidance profiling game
description: JEU SERAI is a serious game whose ambition is "to help the vocational guidance of students and adults at an individual level", using game mechanisms to evaluate professional interest, motivation and decision taking. Built by a consortium of two companies, two universities and an adult training association, it contains 18 mini games, three for each Holland RIASEC type, distributed in an open world over three chapters, plus narrative questionnaires, recurrent activities and avatar clothing choices linked to RIASEC types. It produces a RIASEC profile for the player and a data file of item values for analysis.
requirements: Expert review pipeline for content validation
A documented interface linking in-game item values to RIASEC dimension scores
constraints: The goal is not to substitute for a career adviser but to offer an engaging way to make self-assessment psychometric tests
target_learners: middle school students to adults in career change
target_learning_goals: vocational interest self-assessment via RIASEC profile
examples: Mini games include Nice Apple (Realistic, apple harvesting), Omelet (Enterprising, directing a team) and Classified (Conventional, classifying stamps)

citation: Guardiola, E., & Natkin, S. (2015). A Game Design Methodology for Generating a Psychological Profile of Players. In Serious Games Analytics, Methodologies for Performance Measurement, Assessment, and Improvement. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4
title: A profiling game's psychological model must be scientifically validated and must match the profiling intention
description: The article's framework requires that "The psychological model must have been scientifically validated" and that "The chosen psychological model must match the profiling intention", drawing the latter lesson from Silent Hill Shattered Memories, where the psychological model had no strong connection with the intended result. Data must be collected during gameplay and game results must be comparable to those from reliable means such as traditional questionnaires.
requirements: A scientifically validated psychological model with a referential test
Data collected during the gameplay session
Comparability of game results with reliable traditional measures
constraints: Entertainment games using psychological models may not provide results or may lack a strong model-intention connection, as the article reports for Silent Hill
target_learners: players of serious games for assessment and guidance
target_learning_goals: psychological or vocational profiling from gameplay data
examples: The authors selected Holland's RIASEC model for JEU SERAI because it had been scientifically tested since the 1960s and used in vocational guidance tests for decades
key_sources: Guardiola, E., & Natkin, S. (2015). A Game Design Methodology for Generating a Psychological Profile of Players. In Serious Games Analytics, Methodologies for Performance Measurement, Assessment, and Improvement. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_16

article_title: A Game Design Methodology for Generating a Psychological Profile of Players
citation: Guardiola, E., & Natkin, S. (2015). A Game Design Methodology for Generating a Psychological Profile of Players. In Serious Games Analytics, Methodologies for Performance Measurement, Assessment, and Improvement. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4
title: Mini-game structure to prevent gameplay optimization from masking psychological preferences
description: When the first JEU SERAI concept measured strategic preferences through recurrent gameplay tools, the authors found it "might lead us to measure the gameplay optimization process of the player" rather than preference. They therefore "chose to use mini games to avoid the player optimizing gameplay", with each mini game related to one Holland RIASEC type and measuring both player activity and appreciation of the mini game, modeled on life simulation games for a broad audience.
requirements: Each mini game mapped to a dimension of the psychological model
Measurement of both activity and appreciation of the mini game
constraints: The approach was designed for a heterogeneous audience from middle school students to adults, some unfamiliar with computers or games
target_learners: heterogeneous audience from middle school students to adults in career change
target_learning_goals: measurement of vocational interest preferences uncontaminated by gameplay mastery
examples: 18 mini games, 3 for each RIASEC type, were dispatched in an open world over three chapters, such as apple harvesting for Realistic and stamp classifying for Conventional

article_title: A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology.:
citation: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108
title: PARI methodology: a structured dyadic problem-solving interview for cognitive task analysis
description: The PARI (Precursor, Action, Result, Interpretation) methodology is a structured, thinking-aloud interview technique for cognitive task analysis of diagnostic problem solving, developed under the Basic Job Skills program. Per the report, "PARI: Precursor, (or reason for Action), Action, Result, and Interpretation (of result) are problem-solving components of interest in diagnostic tasks." Experts work in dyads: one poses a problem to a naive expert who generates a solution step by step while the first supplies results, followed by rehash sessions probing the reasons for decisions. The approach is grounded in studies of over 200 Air Force technicians in aircraft maintenance specialties whose primary task is troubleshooting.
requirements: A task analyst uses standardized interview questions and structured rehash sessions so data take a standard form comparable across specialties and skill levels
constraints: Developed for aircraft maintenance troubleshooting domains; the report states a future goal is examining generality to nonmaintenance problem-solving domains
target_learners: Air Force aircraft maintenance technicians learning troubleshooting
target_learning_goals: Adaptive troubleshooting and complex problem-solving skill in technical equipment maintenance
examples: Expert dyads solved representative samples of domain problems under realistic task performance conditions, with solutions elaborated in rehash sessions
key_sources: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108. https://doi.org/10.21236/ada303654

article_title: A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology.:
citation: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108
title: BJS cognitive architecture: procedural, declarative (system), and strategic knowledge
description: The report's organizing framework decomposes complex problem-solving performance into three coordinated knowledge components. As quoted from Gott (1989): "The knowledge and processes that constitute that performance are (a) procedural (or how- to-do-it) knowledge, (b) declarative (domain) knowledge of the object (often called system or device knowledge), and (c) strategic (or how- to-decide-what-to-do-and-when) knowledge." Strategic knowledge serves an executive control function, deploying procedural and device knowledge via goals, plans, and decision rules to enable dynamic, opportunistic reasoning. The PARI methodology is designed to capture all three components and their coordinated deployment.
requirements: Analysis must situate knowledge elicitation in authentic problem-solving contexts, since strategic knowledge is overlooked when domain knowledge is analyzed outside its intended use
constraints: The framework targets ill-structured problem-solving domains such as fault diagnosis, where no well-defined algorithm for solution exists
target_learners: Technical trainees acquiring complex troubleshooting expertise
target_learning_goals: Integration of procedural, system, and strategic knowledge for adaptive problem solving
examples: Figure 1 of the report depicts the BJS Cognitive Architecture showing interactions among strategic, system, and procedural knowledge
key_sources: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108. https://doi.org/10.21236/ada303654

article_title: A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology.:
citation: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108
title: ISD task analysis approach
description: Instructional Systems Design is a general-purpose task decomposition methodology widely used by the Air Force since 1972, in which duties are broken into tasks, subtasks, and supporting skills and knowledge via expert observation and documentation review. The report states "The output from an ISD analysis closely parallels the condition-action rules discussed earlier as 'how-to-do-it' or procedural knowledge." Its documentation form and flowchart (Table 1, Figure 2) list steps, decisions, and supporting skills and knowledges for tasks such as isolating defective parts in power supply circuits.
requirements: A subject-matter expert performing the task under simulated or actual job conditions, plus task documentation, for identifying subtasks and supporting knowledge
constraints: The report states ISD is most useful for stable, algorithmic task environments; because the performer knows the problem source in advance, strategic decision processes and alternative device models remain unactivated and undocumented
target_learners: Air Force technical trainees in equipment maintenance specialties
target_learning_goals: Procedural skill for executing prespecified task steps
examples: The report's example ISD form decomposes isolating defective power-supply parts into steps such as checking the fuse for continuity with a multimeter
key_sources: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108. https://doi.org/10.21236/ada303654

article_title: A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology.:
citation: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108
title: GOMS analysis approach
description: GOMS (Goals, Operators, Methods, Selection rules) analysis, developed by Card, Moran, and Newell (1983), models human-computer interaction as an executable model built from goal hierarchies, operator sequences (methods), and selection rules for choosing among methods. The report states "a GOMS analysis models human-computer interaction as relatively domain-independent procedural skills." Data come from videotaped behavior and time-stamped keystroke files coded into operator-sequence protocols, yielding timing information for component goals.
requirements: Empirically derived estimates of user processing speed, short-term memory capacity and duration, and other cognitive parameters, plus protocol data from users performing the task
constraints: System knowledge of how the computer works and domain knowledge are assumed irrelevant and not modeled; the approach was developed for computer tasks rather than knowledge-rich problem solving
target_learners: Computer users performing text-editing and similar interface tasks
target_learning_goals: Efficient execution of procedural human-computer interaction methods
examples: The report reproduces a GOMS model of a text-editing task with goals such as Insert and Delete, operators such as Scroll-to and Type, and selection rules such as the Top 2/3 rule
key_sources: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108. https://doi.org/10.21236/ada303654

article_title: A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology.:
citation: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108
title: Make the reasons for task performance (conceptual support knowledge) explicit for teaching
description: Instruction for complex problem solving should go beyond teaching observable procedure steps and explicitly teach the conceptual support knowledge — why procedures work, when they apply, and what results mean — that underlies adaptive performance. The report states "Making the reasons for task performance explicit (i.e., specifying this conceptual support knowledge) is therefore a central goal of the PARI approach." Such knowledge gives meaning to procedure steps, enables invention of new procedures, and supports reconstruction of forgotten ones in novel situations.
requirements: Task analysis must capture declarative and strategic knowledge, not only procedural knowledge, which requires situated rather than decontextualized elicitation
constraints: The report notes routinized-procedure training remains appropriate for some stable tasks; the principle targets dynamic, unstable task environments where novel situations are frequently encountered
target_learners: Technical trainees preparing for adaptive troubleshooting in complex systems
target_learning_goals: Adaptive application of procedures to novel problem situations
examples: PARI interviews probe experts for the reasons behind actions and interpretations of results during situated problem-solving sessions, and the resulting models guide instruction targeting all three knowledge components
key_sources: Ellen P. Hall, Sherrie P. Gott, Robert A. Pokorny. (1995). A Procedural Guide to Cognitive Task Analysis: The PARI Methodology. Armstrong Laboratory, Human Resources Directorate, Brooks AFB, Texas. AL/HR-TR-1995-0108. https://doi.org/10.21236/ada303654

article_title: Game-based assessment: an integrated model for capturing evidence of learning in play
citation: Richard Halverson, Elizabeth Owen, Nathan Wills, R. Benjamin Shapiro. (2012). Game-Based Assessment: An integrated model for capturing evidence of learning in play. ERIA Working Paper. http://www.eriainteractive.com/index.php
title: Game-Based Assessment (GBA) model: a four-layer design strategy embedding assessment in game design
description: The GBA model is a design strategy developed by the Games, Learning and Society group to capture evidence of player learning during game play rather than treating the game as a black box. It integrates four layers: "the content-model; the game flow design; and the GBA components of the semantic template and learning telemetry." The content model outlines learning goals, game-flow design builds interaction opportunities around them, the semantic template selects which click-stream data may indicate learning, and the learning telemetry layer collects and organizes that data into player profiles for analysis against pre-post measures. It draws on evidence-centered design, stealth assessment, and education data mining.
requirements: Requires designing the game around specific learning goals and a content model agreed with content experts
Requires a semantic template built in coordination with the game-flow design specifying key moments hypothesized to yield learning evidence
Requires a telemetry layer tagging player moves so the data stream can be mapped onto the semantic template
constraints: The authors state they are not yet in a position to deliver results confirming the viability or quality of the GBA model across game spaces
The semantic template's bet-hedging role may narrow the data too severely and leave out information necessary to understanding player interaction and learning
The presentation deliberately focuses on little-g game outcomes and omits Big G social and narrative contexts of game-based learning
target_learners: middle and high school students playing learning games
general lay audiences for public science understanding
target_learning_goals: domain content learning (e.g., stem-cell science processes) embedded in game play
examples: GBA was built into Progenitor X: designers identified 15 key moments in game play and tagged each player move with button, time-stamp, flashing status, tool name, and tag type
key_sources: Richard Halverson, Elizabeth Owen, Nathan Wills, R. Benjamin Shapiro. (2012). Game-Based Assessment: An integrated model for capturing evidence of learning in play. ERIA Working Paper. http://www.eriainteractive.com/index.php

article_title: Game-based assessment: an integrated model for capturing evidence of learning in play
citation: Richard Halverson, Elizabeth Owen, Nathan Wills, R. Benjamin Shapiro. (2012). Game-Based Assessment: An integrated model for capturing evidence of learning in play. ERIA Working Paper. http://www.eriainteractive.com/index.php
title: Progenitor X: a narrative-based, turn-based puzzle game teaching stem-cell science practices
description: Progenitor X is a GLS game "developed in partnership with the Regenerative Medicine research team to present core ideas of cutting edge sciences in context of a game." Players are challenged to cultivate and differentiate stem cells, assemble tissues, and replace organs contaminated with a zombie virus. Completing game play requires solving 10-12 cell, tissue, and organ puzzle cycles, with the final organ cycle functioning as a boss-level requiring a cell-cell-tissue-cell-tissue cycle sequence using all skills learned earlier. Its content model invites players to dissect, collect, cultivate, differentiate and treat diseased tissues with stem cells.
requirements: Requires players to repeat cell-tissue and cell-cell-tissue-cell cycles to complete the game
target_learners: middle and high school students
younger players considering stem-cell research careers
target_learning_goals: lab processes by which scientists manipulate stem cells and use them in treatment
examples: The cell cycle requires populating a grid with ips cells that can be transformed into the target population, and manipulating the cells toward the appropriate transformation

article_title: Enhancing Student Competency Models for Game-Based Learning with a Hybrid Stealth Assessment Framework
citation: Henderson, N., Kumaran, V., Min, W., Mott, B., Wu, Z., Boulden, D., Lord, T., Reichsman, F., Dorsey, C., Wiebe, E., & Lester, J. (2020). Enhancing Student Competency Models for Game-Based Learning with a Hybrid Stealth Assessment Framework. Proceedings of The 13th International Conference on Educational Data Mining (EDM 2020), 92-103. https://educationaldatamining.org/EDM2020/proceedings/
title: Evidence-Centered Design (ECD) as the methodological foundation for stealth assessment in game-based learning environments
description: Evidence-centered design is a systematic approach for designing knowledge assessments in terms of evidentiary arguments, featuring three core models: a task model defining the activities students undertake, an evidence model that processes low-level action sequences into machine-interpretable evidence, and a competency model that dynamically estimates student mastery. In this article, ECD grounds the stealth assessment framework in Geniventure, where the task model consists of "60 challenges across six game levels," the evidence model links gameplay behaviors to targeted genetics concepts, and the competency model estimates mastery of 16 concepts aligned to post-test scores. Stealth assessment conducts real-time processing of data from these three models to inform adaptive scaffolding without disrupting gameplay.
requirements: Validated post-test assessment aligned to the ECD competency model to provide ground-truth competency labels for model training
constraints: Open-ended post-test items must be omitted from competency score calculations due to scoring ambiguity
Concepts with zero-variance post-test responses provide no training signal
target_learners: middle school and high school students (ages 11-18)
target_learning_goals: introductory genetics concepts including heredity, dominance and recessive traits, protein-to-trait relationship, breeding, test cross, and complex inheritance patterns
examples: In Geniventure, the task model defines 60 challenges across 6 levels, the evidence model processes timestamped gameplay actions (allele changes, hint requests, answer submissions), and the competency model estimates mastery of 16 genetics concepts from post-test item correctness
key_sources: Henderson, N., Kumaran, V., Min, W., Mott, B., Wu, Z., Boulden, D., Lord, T., Reichsman, F., Dorsey, C., Wiebe, E., & Lester, J. (2020). Enhancing Student Competency Models for Game-Based Learning with a Hybrid Stealth Assessment Framework. Proceedings of The 13th International Conference on Educational Data Mining (EDM 2020), 92-103. https://educationaldatamining.org/EDM2020/proceedings/

article_title: Enhancing Student Competency Models for Game-Based Learning with a Hybrid Stealth Assessment Framework
citation: Henderson, N., Kumaran, V., Min, W., Mott, B., Wu, Z., Boulden, D., Lord, T., Reichsman, F., Dorsey, C., Wiebe, E., & Lester, J. (2020). Proceedings of The 13th International Conference on Educational Data Mining (EDM 2020), 92-103. https://educationaldatamining.org/EDM2020/proceedings/
title: Geniventure: a game-based learning environment for introductory genetics
description: Geniventure is a game-based learning environment for introductory genetics targeting middle and high school students ages 11-18. Students breed and study drakes, "a model species for dragons," to explore heredity, dominant and recessive traits, and the protein-to-trait relationship. The game consists of "60 increasingly difficult puzzle-like challenges across 6 levels," with scaffolded hints and progressive complexity covering concepts aligned with the Next Generation Science Standards. Students can validate their work at any time and receive system-generated hints based on their perceived understanding. The game records fine-grained trace data including navigated challenges, allele changes, submitted answers, and received hints.
requirements: Timestamped trace data logging of student gameplay interactions for stealth assessment model training
Pre- and post-test assessments aligned to the game's ECD competency model
target_learners: middle school and high school students (ages 11-18)
target_learning_goals: introductory genetics including heredity, dominance and recessive traits, protein-to-trait relationship, breeding and inheritance, test cross, X-linked and polyallelic traits
examples: Students played Geniventure during teacher-led classroom implementations over several days, attempting between 5 and 248 challenges, with gameplay recorded as JSON-format trace data logs

article_title: Motivational engagement and video gaming: a mixed methods study
citation: Bobby Hoffman, Louis Nadelson. (2010). Motivational engagement and video gaming: a mixed methods study. Education Tech Research Dev 58:245-270. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-009-9134-9
title: Social-cognitive coding framework for gaming motivation across planning, monitoring, and reflection phases
description: The article organizes interview data with a social-cognitive framework crossing three phases (antecedent/planning, monitoring/during, reflection/after) with cognitive, affective, and social qualifiers, mirroring phases of self-regulatory behavior. The authors coded this way because "participants revealed video game play was motivated by specific goals which were task directed", because "a social orientation was often communicated by participants as their motivation for playing games", and because specific strategies served game-directed goals. It yielded a Phase I matrix (Table 1) and a Phase II taxonomy of 133 codes from 421 pages of transcripts, grouped into reasons for gaming, experience during gaming, and outcomes of gaming.
requirements: Interview transcripts coded by at least two researchers with exchanged codes and inter-rater reliability for cluster coding reported at .96
constraints: Developed from a subset of 25 highly engaged players (five or more hours per week) playing strategy or problem-solving games, an arbitrary cut-off the authors describe as representing relatively regular and frequent game play
target_learners: undergraduate and master's-level education students who play video games
target_learning_goals: understanding motivational engagement, persistence, and reengagement in discretionary game-based activity
examples: Phase II coding clustered participant statements such as feeling positive after finally learning a game into a self-efficacy category within the affective, reflective cell of the framework

article_title: Evaluating the Evidence Base of Shared Story Reading to Promote Literacy for Students With Extensive Support Needs
citation: Melissa E. Hudson and David W. Test. (2011). Evaluating the Evidence Base of Shared Story Reading to Promote Literacy for Students With Extensive Support Needs. Research & Practice for Persons with Severe Disabilities, 36(1-2), 34-45. http://www.education.uncc.edu/access/
title: Shared story reading: reader-listener interaction around read-aloud age-appropriate literature with supported student interaction
description: Shared story reading (also called read alouds, repeated storybook reading, story-based lesson, and literacy-based lesson) is defined as "a practice used to access age-appropriate literature through reader-listener interaction in which a story is read aloud and student interaction with the reader and the story is supported." Common features include repeated story lines, attention getters, picture symbols paired with words, summarized text with controlled vocabulary, and repeated readings. With older children, lesson content and style reflect age-appropriate literature such as chapters.
requirements: A story is read aloud with supports for the student to interact with the reader about the story
constraints: When used with older children as story-based or literature-based lessons, content and style differ to reflect age-appropriate literature
target_learners: students with extensive support needs (intellectual disability, autism, or multiple disabilities)
target_learning_goals: literacy skills including listening comprehension, vocabulary, comprehension, and emergent literacy
examples: The reviewed studies used adapted, age-appropriate books, with features such as velcroed actual objects on pages and system of least prompts during reading

article_title: Evaluating the Evidence Base of Shared Story Reading to Promote Literacy for Students With Extensive Support Needs
citation: Melissa E. Hudson and David W. Test. (2011). Evaluating the Evidence Base of Shared Story Reading to Promote Literacy for Students With Extensive Support Needs. Research & Practice for Persons with Severe Disabilities, 36(1-2), 34-45. http://www.education.uncc.edu/access/
title: Define literacy broadly for students with extensive support needs to include both access to age-appropriate literature and reading independence
description: The review defines literacy as "skills that increased access to age appropriate literature (e.g., listening comprehension) and reading independence (e.g., vocabulary and comprehension), including emergent literary skills." A broad definition matters because students' skills may fall far below peers; a narrow reading-independence definition could leave students stuck "getting ready to read" or deemed unable to benefit. It also emphasizes shifting materials and instruction as students grow older.
requirements: Literacy instruction should include measures of both access skills (e.g., listening comprehension) and reading-independence skills
constraints: If literacy were defined solely as a bridge to reading independence, students with extensive support needs could be deemed unable to benefit from literacy instruction
target_learners: students with extensive support needs
target_learning_goals: access to age-appropriate literature and reading independence
examples: The review applied this broad definition as an inclusion criterion, requiring at least one literacy dependent variable in reviewed studies
