article_title: Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education
citation: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485
title: Eight interrelated systemic factors determine the effectiveness of graduate attribute achievement, with assessment one among them
description: The paper proposes that graduate attribute achievement depends on eight systemic factors identified by the National Graduate Attributes Project: 'Conceptualisation, Stakeholders, Implementation strategy, Curriculum approach, Assessment, Staff development, Quality assurance, Student-centredness'. The factors were found to interact with and influence each other, so the other seven factors shape assessment practice and add systemic complexity. The paper argues assessment of graduate attributes is 'unlikely to be resolved unless these factors are addressed at a systemic level'.
requirements: Institutional change must address all eight factors together rather than assessment in isolation
constraints: Factors were identified from a study of Australian universities; influence of specific stakeholder groups varies between university types and award programmes
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: graduate attributes such as critical thinking, communication and lifelong learning
examples: The National GAP study investigated Australian universities' efforts to achieve graduate attributes and confirmed assessment as a key determinant of implementation effectiveness
key_sources: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485

article_title: Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education
citation: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485
title: Four orientations of academics' conceptions of graduate attributes: precursory, complementary, translation and enabling
description: The paper presents Barrie's (2006) phenomenographic analysis identifying four distinct orientations academics hold toward graduate attributes: 'precursory, complementary, translation and enabling'. Precursory attributes are fundamental skills for learning; complementary skills sit alongside disciplinary knowledge; translation attributes apply disciplinary knowledge in real-world contexts; enabling attributes 'infuse and enable all scholarly learning' and transcend disciplinary boundaries. Each orientation implies a distinctly different focus for teaching, learning and assessment, and multiple conceptualisations may underpin one institution's practice.
requirements: Assessment design must be matched to the conception of the attribute being assessed
constraints: Students may encounter inconsistent or contradictory evidence requirements for similarly labelled attributes across courses in a single programme
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: graduate attributes including critical thinking and disciplinary application skills
examples: From a complementary perspective a standardised test such as the California Critical Thinking Skills Test may suffice, while an enabling perspective would require students to make and justify a claim to the attribute based on collected evidence
key_sources: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485

article_title: Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education
citation: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485
title: Plan graduate attribute assessment at whole-of-programme level with tasks extending beyond individual course boundaries
description: Because graduate attribute development occurs incrementally as students integrate learnings across a programme, the paper argues assessment must be planned programme-wide rather than course by course. It states that 'the development of graduate attributes requires a whole-of-programme approach to the planning of curriculum, teaching and assessment'. Where modular curricula dominate, assessors need openness to alternative and authentic forms such as capstone tasks that extend across traditional course boundaries.
requirements: Curriculum approach must permit programme-level planning; modular structures alone cannot capture attribute progression
constraints: Much graduate attribute progress is unlikely to be assessable within the time spans of courses or shorter modules
target_learners: university students in degree programmes
target_learning_goals: graduate attribute development and progression across a programme of study
examples: The paper points to 'high impact' and 'integrative' tasks used with paper-based or electronic portfolios as alternatives suited to programme-level attribute assessment
key_sources: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485

article_title: Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education
citation: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485
title: Staff development for attribute assessment must address underlying conceptions and traditions, not just provide technique toolkits
description: The paper argues that 'toolkits' of practical techniques for teaching and assessing graduate attributes are of limited benefit unless related to underlying assumptions about the purpose and focus of assessment. Staff development must also engage long-standing disciplinary traditions and 'signature' pedagogies and assessments, which can produce inertia or resistance to the assessment innovation needed. Assessment design should be justified through understanding of task dimensions such as authenticity and clarity of criteria-attribute relationships.
requirements: Staff development must address conceptions of teaching and learning as well as techniques
constraints: Traditional methods do not always have the capacity for adaptation to the assessment of graduate attributes
target_learners: university academics and teachers
target_learning_goals: valid assessment design for graduate attributes
examples: The paper lists task dimensions including authenticity to practices of a discourse community, authenticity of task conditions, clarity of criteria-attribute relationships, and student involvement fostering metacognitive abilities
key_sources: Clair Hughes and Simon Barrie. (2010). Influences on the assessment of graduate attributes in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930903221485

article_title: Seductive details hamper learning even when they do not disrupt
citation: Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Eitel, A. (2023). Seductive details hamper learning even when they do not disrupt. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09632-w
title: Prompt learners that seductive details are irrelevant to the learning objective to protect recall of pertinent content
description: Before learning, tell learners explicitly that interesting but irrelevant material will not be tested and is not relevant to the learning objective. In this study, such a prompt "reduced students’ perceived relevance and relative processing time for seductive details, which in turn fostered recall performance", and "prompting students about the irrelevance of seductive details made the seductive details effect disappear for recall". The article frames this as reducing the details' diverting potential.
requirements: The prompt must identify which material is irrelevant and which is relevant (e.g., relevant content marked in a red frame) before the learning phase.
constraints: The benefit was demonstrated for recall, not transfer, in an online setting with adult undergraduates.
target_learners: undergraduate students in self-directed online learning
target_learning_goals: recall of pertinent instructional content (lightning formation)
examples: Participants in the irrelevance-prompt condition read that the photographs of lightning-strike consequences were "not relevant to the learning objective and will not be tested later" before a 6.5-minute learning phase.
key_sources: Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Eitel, A. (2023). Seductive details hamper learning even when they do not disrupt. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09632-w

article_title: Seductive details hamper learning even when they do not disrupt
citation: Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Eitel, A. (2023). Seductive details hamper learning even when they do not disrupt. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09632-w
title: Diversion explanation of the seductive details effect
description: Within the cognitive theory of multimedia learning, the diversion explanation holds that seductive details harm learning when learners "build mental models around irrelevant contents (included in seductive details) rather than around the pertinent content". Diversion is stronger when learners erroneously consider the irrelevant content relevant, activating and integrating inadequate prior knowledge. This study designed an irrelevance prompt to make diversion unlikely and found supporting evidence, concluding diversion rather than disruption mainly drives the effect.
requirements: Learners must allocate attention to the seductive information (distraction) before diversion can occur, per the article's framing of distraction as a necessary pre-condition.
constraints: The article notes diversion is hard to sharply distinguish from disruption empirically; the irrelevance prompt may in principle have affected both processes.
target_learners: students learning with multimedia instruction containing interesting but irrelevant details
target_learning_goals: recall and comprehension of pertinent instructional content
examples: Learners who thought the details were relevant reported longer processing times on them and had worse recall outcomes.
key_sources: Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Eitel, A. (2023). Seductive details hamper learning even when they do not disrupt. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09632-w

article_title: A Social-Cognitive Framework for Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions.
citation: Yanghee Kim and Amy L. Baylor. (2006). A Social-Cognitive Framework for Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions. ETR&D, Vol. 54, No. 6, pp. 569–596. https://www.create.usu.edu
title: Social-cognitive framework for designing pedagogical agents as learning companions
description: The article grounds PAL design in three social-cognitive theories: distributed cognition, social interaction (Piaget and Vygotsky), and Bandura's social-cognitive theory. It maps concepts from each theory to PAL functions: distributed cognition supports intellectual partnership, social interaction concepts emphasize intellectual and empathetic transactions, and social-cognitive theory suggests constructs such as gender, ethnicity, and multiplicity. As the authors state, "distributed cognition may support intellectual partnership between a learner and a PAL," and the framework is intended "to provide a theoretical framework for designing the optimal functionalities of PALs."
requirements: Application of the framework depends on advancement of agent technology and accumulation of empirical evidence of instructional impacts, as the authors state.
constraints: The framework is explicitly offered as suggestive, not definitive: the seven constituents are "intended not as definitive but as suggestive for subsequent research."
PALs are not equivalent to human peers; no claim of peer equivalence is made.
target_learners: Learners in computer-based learning environments, from elementary students to college students, as represented in the reviewed studies
target_learning_goals: Cognitive outcomes such as recall, application, and reasoning
Motivational outcomes such as self-efficacy, interest, and engagement
key_sources: Yanghee Kim and Amy L. Baylor. (2006). A Social-Cognitive Framework for Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions. ETR&D, Vol. 54, No. 6, pp. 569–596. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-0637-3

article_title: A Social-Cognitive Framework for Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions.
citation: Yanghee Kim and Amy L. Baylor. (2006). A Social-Cognitive Framework for Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions. ETR&D, Vol. 54, No. 6, pp. 569–596. https://www.create.usu.edu
title: Seven design constituents for pedagogical agents as learning companions
description: The article proposes seven design constituents for instructional PALs drawn from the social-cognitive framework: "(a) competency, (b) interaction type, (c) gender, (d) affect, (e) ethnicity, (f) multiplicity, and (g) feedback." Each constituent is traced to supporting theoretical concepts—for example, distributed cognition suggests competency, interaction type, multiplicity, and feedback, while Bandura's theory suggests gender, ethnicity, and multiplicity. The pattern serves as a design checklist for specifying PAL characteristics in computer-based learning environments.
requirements: Designers should consider learner characteristics such as "competency, age, learning styles" when determining optimal PAL-learner interaction.
Effective PAL feedback should consider feedback type, scope, timing, learner characteristics, and learning goals and contexts simultaneously.
constraints: The constituents are explicitly "not comprehensive" and the literature review is described as modest.
Research on some constituents (ethnicity, feedback) is lacking, and suggestions for optimal design are sometimes contradictory.
target_learners: Learners using computer-based learning environments with simulated peer agents
target_learning_goals: Designing PAL characteristics to support learning, motivation, and social interaction
examples: Table 4 of the article maps each constituent to research variables and outcomes, e.g., low-competent PALs enhancing self-efficacy and proactive PALs enhancing recall.
key_sources: Yanghee Kim and Amy L. Baylor. (2006). A Social-Cognitive Framework for Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions. ETR&D, Vol. 54, No. 6, pp. 569–596. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-0637-3

article_title: Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions: The Role of Agent Competency and Type of Interaction.
citation: Kim, Y., Baylor, A. L., & PALS Group. (2006). Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions: The Role of Agent Competency and Type of Interaction. Educational Technology Research and Development, 54(3), 223-243. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-6499-1
title: PAL design framework: competency and interaction type as crucial design variables for pedagogical agents as learning companions
description: Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions (PALs) are defined as "animated peer-like characters that simulate peer interaction in computer-based learning," grounded in social cognitive theory and peer modeling research. The framework identifies two crucial design variables: the PAL's competency (low vs. high domain knowledge, scripted as novice-like vs. advanced-peer comments) and interaction type (proactive initiation vs. responsive delivery only on request). The experiment showed these variables have different effects on learning, self-efficacy, and attitudes, so the framework treats PAL-learner relations as consistent with human peer relations.
requirements: The PAL must be perceived as peer-like and believable; equipping it with instructor-like advanced competency might undermine peer-likeness
constraints: The findings concern a single skill (instructional planning) over a limited time, and the PALs were prescripted rather than intelligent agents
target_learners: undergraduate novices in a task domain
target_learning_goals: recall and application of domain information; self-efficacy in the task; attitudes toward the agent
examples: The agent Mike, a casual-dressed peer in his early 20s, delivered either novice-like or advanced-peer scripts in a MIMIC-based instructional planning module within a 2x2 experiment
key_sources: Kim, Y., Baylor, A. L., & PALS Group. (2006). Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions: The Role of Agent Competency and Type of Interaction. Educational Technology Research and Development, 54(3), 223-243. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-8805-z

article_title: Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions: The Role of Agent Competency and Type of Interaction.
citation: Kim, Y., Baylor, A. L., & PALS Group. (2006). Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions: The Role of Agent Competency and Type of Interaction. Educational Technology Research and Development, 54(3), 223-243. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-6499-1
title: Design a learning companion agent's competency and interaction type according to the desired learning and motivational goals
description: The article concludes that "the competency and interaction type of a PAL should be designed according to the desired learning and motivational goals." High-competency PALs suit goals focused on knowledge and skill acquisition; low-competency PALs suit contexts where learner self-efficacy or confidence in an unfamiliar domain is a major concern; a proactive role is recommended to supply novices with necessary information they would not request. This flexibility is framed as a strength of PAL environments over human peer-mediated and traditional computer-based learning.
requirements: Designers must choose competency level and interaction control deliberately, since each variable affects different outcome measures
constraints: The desirable interaction type may interact strongly with learner characteristics such as prior knowledge, personality, cognitive styles, and age, so permutations are beneficial only when considering the learner and task at hand
target_learners: novice learners in computer-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: knowledge and skill acquisition; learner self-efficacy and confidence; engagement with agent-provided information
examples: In the experiment, PAL scripts were authored as either novice-like suggestions (8 idea units) or advanced-peer accurate comments (12 idea units), and proactive PALs delivered information on phase entry while responsive PALs spoke only when clicked
key_sources: Kim, Y., Baylor, A. L., & PALS Group. (2006). Pedagogical Agents as Learning Companions: The Role of Agent Competency and Type of Interaction. Educational Technology Research and Development, 54(3), 223-243. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-006-8805-z

article_title: Self-regulated learning strategies predict learner behavior and goal attainment in Massive Open Online Courses
citation: Kizilcec, R. F., Pérez-Sanagustín, M., & Maldonado, J. J. (2017). Self-regulated learning strategies predict learner behavior and goal attainment in Massive Open Online Courses. Computers & Education, 104, 18–33. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.10.001
title: Pintrich's model of self-regulated learning as three categories of trainable strategies
description: The article adopts Pintrich's (2000) model, which defines SRL as "an active, constructive process whereby learners set goals for their learning and then attempt to monitor, regulate and control their cognition, intentions and behavior". The model identifies three categories of strategies learners apply to regulate learning: cognitive strategies (rehearsal, critical thinking, organization, elaboration), metacognitive strategies (goal setting and strategic planning, self-monitoring, self-evaluation), and resource management strategies (time management, help seeking, effort regulation). The authors chose this model over Zimmerman's phase model because its focus on particular strategies suits large-scale quantitative investigation that can inform targeted interventions.
requirements: SRL is treated as a trainable skill, not a fixed trait, developed through experience and practice applying SRL strategies
constraints: The model's strategy focus was chosen for quantitative tractability rather than as a claim about phase-based accounts being wrong
target_learners: adult online learners in self-paced MOOCs
target_learning_goals: attainment of personal course goals such as certification, assessment completion, and lecture completion
examples: The study operationalized six strategy subscales (goal setting, strategic planning, self-evaluation, task strategies, elaboration, help seeking) in a 23-item survey with Cronbach's alpha of at least 0.75
key_sources: Kizilcec, R. F., Pérez-Sanagustín, M., & Maldonado, J. J. (2017). Self-regulated learning strategies predict learner behavior and goal attainment in Massive Open Online Courses. Computers & Education, 104, 18–33. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.10.001

article_title: Collaborative learning through augmented reality role playing
citation: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://education.mit.edu
title: Five criteria for designing collaborative learning challenges
description: The article adopts, from Johnson et al. (1994), a framework of five criteria that collaborative learning challenges should require: positive interdependence, promotive interaction, individual accountability, interpersonal and small group skills, and group processing. Positive interdependence means "one cannot succeed unless everyone succeeds"; promotive interaction means students promote each other's success; individual accountability means each student's performance is assessed and fed back. The authors use these criteria as design lenses in tables mapping game components to collaborative mechanisms in both game generations.
requirements: Game challenges must be designed so that each of the five criteria — positive interdependence, promotive interaction, individual accountability, interpersonal and small group skills, and group processing — is supported
target_learners: high school students
university students
middle school students
target_learning_goals: collaboration
scientific investigation practices
examples: Tables in the article map Environmental Detectives components and the redesigned engine's role-based components onto each of the five criteria
key_sources: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://doi.org/10.3115/1149293.1149333

article_title: Collaborative learning through augmented reality role playing
citation: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://education.mit.edu
title: Environmental Detectives handheld AR environmental consulting simulation
description: Environmental Detectives (ED) is a handheld AR simulation engaging high school and university students in an environmental consulting scenario in which they role play as environmental scientists investigating health concerns linked to toxins in the water supply. Working in teams of two or three with one Pocket PC, one walkie-talkie, a printed map and a notepad, players identify the contaminant, chart its path, and devise remediation plans, collecting simulated field data, interviewing virtual characters, and synthesizing findings into case reports. By design, "no one player can obtain all of the requisite information in the allotted time."
requirements: Each team needs one Pocket PC, one walkie-talkie, a printed map and a notepad; the problem space must be large enough to be geographically subdivided
constraints: In ED there is no role differentiation among players, and since all players use the same software they can potentially access the same information at the same time
target_learners: high school students
university students
target_learning_goals: environmental science investigation
planning investigations balancing quantitative and qualitative data
collaboration
examples: Nearly a dozen classes ran through ED, including a suburban high school environmental science class and a private all-girls high school chemistry class
key_sources: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://doi.org/10.3115/1149293.1149333

article_title: Collaborative learning through augmented reality role playing
citation: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://education.mit.edu
title: Redesigned AR engine with time dependence, cascading events, and distinct player roles (Charles River City and Mad City Murder)
description: To promote greater collaboration between teams, the authors redesigned their core AR game engine, from which two games were created: Charles River City (CRC), combining environmental science and epidemiology, and Mad City Murder (MCM), a mystery investigation. The engine adds "time dependence, cascading events and distinct player roles." Roles receive different information from virtual characters, have different data collection capabilities, and can exchange information via infrared beaming — for example, a detective must beam information about an ill student to a nurse so she can interview and examine symptoms.
requirements: Roles must have distinct information access and data collection capabilities, and devices must support infrared beaming of information between players
constraints: Role overlap must be balanced: too much overlap removes positive interdependence and individual accountability, while too little overlap does not give students enough common ground to discuss the problem space
target_learners: middle school students
high school students
target_learning_goals: collaboration across teams
environmental science and epidemiology investigation
information sharing
examples: In one CRC version, three roles — doctor, environmental scientist, and department of public health expert — each had unique data access, and students beamed and radioed information across teams
key_sources: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://doi.org/10.3115/1149293.1149333

article_title: Collaborative learning through augmented reality role playing
citation: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://education.mit.edu
title: Calibrate role overlap in collaborative AR games: enough common ground to discuss, enough asymmetry to preserve interdependence
description: The article identifies role overlap as a key design consideration for collaborative AR games. Too much overlap between roles "will remove the positive interdependence and individual accountability that encourage collaboration," while too little overlap "does not give the students enough common ground to discuss the problem space." Shared information serves as promotive interaction, reinforcing students and giving them a starting point for discussion around common pieces before working toward unique contributions.
requirements: Roles must be designed with partial overlap: shared information for common ground, unique information for interdependence and accountability
constraints: The article states the effect of varying overlap on learning outcomes has not yet been studied; the authors plan to study how increasing and decreasing overlap affects learning outcomes in future phases
target_learners: middle school students
high school students
university students
target_learning_goals: collaboration
collaborative problem solving
examples: In CRC, all students learned that West Nile Virus was a serious mosquito-borne disease, but only certain roles were privy to the seasonality, the current levels, or the symptoms
key_sources: Klopfer, E., Perry, J., Squire, K., & Jan, M.-F. (2004). Collaborative Learning through Augmented Reality Role Playing. https://doi.org/10.3115/1149293.1149333

article_title: Behavioral economics of education
citation: Alexander Koch, Julia Nafziger, Helena Skyt Nielsen. (2015). Behavioral economics of education. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 115 (2015) 3–17. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2014.09.005
title: Behavioral economics framework for opening the soft-skills black box in education
description: The review proposes that concepts from behavioral and experimental economics—self-control (time-inconsistent preferences), willingness to compete, intrinsic motivation, and self-confidence—substantively describe what soft skills are and how they shape educational investments. It argues that economics of education often treats soft skills as a black box summarized by a parameter, and that 'applying models from behavioral economics and insights from laboratory and field experiments help us to better understand what is going on inside this black box'. The framework links these concepts to the education production function's family, school, and peer inputs.
requirements: Models must integrate behavioral concepts with standard economic theory and be validated empirically, as the article notes these assumptions 'also have to be validated empirically'
constraints: Experimental evidence mostly sheds light on short-run effects; lab and field experiments often use convenience samples, low stakes, and artificial tasks
target_learners: students making educational investment decisions
target_learning_goals: understanding educational investment decisions and achievement through soft skills
key_sources: Alexander Koch, Julia Nafziger, Helena Skyt Nielsen. (2015). Behavioral economics of education. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 115 (2015) 3–17. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2014.09.005

article_title: Behavioral economics of education
citation: Alexander Koch, Julia Nafziger, Helena Skyt Nielsen. (2015). Behavioral economics of education. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 115 (2015) 3–17. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2014.09.005
title: Motivational crowding out: extrinsic rewards can undermine long-term intrinsic motivation via self-confidence inference
description: The review presents Benabou and Tirole's (2003) principal-agent account of motivational crowding out, in which a child with imperfect knowledge of her own ability infers from an offered reward that the principal (parent or teacher) believes her ability is low: 'a higher reward reduces the self-conﬁdence of the child and thereby its intrinsic motivation'. The reward works in the short run by raising the direct payoff from success, but once withdrawn, effort falls because intrinsic motivation was eroded. The review frames this as a key pitfall of incentive provision in education, complementing psychology evidence on crowding out.
requirements: The mechanism requires that the child has imperfect knowledge of her ability and infers the principal's private information from the size of the reward
constraints: The account is a theoretical model interpretation discussed by the review, not a tested experiment; the review notes psychology meta-analyses reach conflicting conclusions about crowding out
target_learners: school students whose motivation is managed by parents or teachers
target_learning_goals: sustaining intrinsic motivation and effort for educational tasks
examples: The review discusses a parent or teacher rewarding a child for studying rather than watching TV, where the reward signals low perceived ability and lowers self-confidence
key_sources: Alexander Koch, Julia Nafziger, Helena Skyt Nielsen. (2015). Behavioral economics of education. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 115 (2015) 3–17. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jebo.2014.09.005

article_title: In vivo experiments on whether supporting metacognition in intelligent tutoring systems yields robust learning
citation: Koedinger, K., Aleven, V., Roll, I., & Baker, R. (2008). In vivo experiments on whether supporting metacognition in intelligent tutoring systems yields robust learning. https://learnlab.org/
title: Four-level framework of goals for metacognitive tutoring toward robust learning
description: The chapter organizes metacognitive tutoring research around four cumulative goals, depicted in Figure 1, in which "less ambitious and more proximal goals... support the more ambitious, ultimate goals above." As printed, "The first goal is for students to improve their metacognitive behavior within the learning environment while they receive metacognitive support," followed by better domain learning, internalization of the practices in subsequent instruction, and accelerated future domain learning. The authors state an ideal experiment measures all four levels, but their work has mainly addressed the first two, with the third addressed only in the help-seeking experiments and the fourth left for future work.
requirements: Experiments evaluating metacognitive support should measure behavior in the supported environment, domain learning, internalized metacognitive behavior, and future domain learning to test the full framework
constraints: So far the research program has focused mainly on the first two goals; the fourth goal remains for future work
target_learners: high-school and middle-school mathematics students using intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: metacognitive strategies such as self-explanation, error self-correction, help seeking, and avoiding gaming the system
examples: The self-explanation and error self-correction lines assessed domain learning only; the help-seeking experiments additionally assessed whether help-seeking behavior improved after the intervention
key_sources: Koedinger, K., Aleven, V., Roll, I., & Baker, R. (2008). In vivo experiments on whether supporting metacognition in intelligent tutoring systems yields robust learning. https://learnlab.org/

article_title: The knowledge-learning-instruction (KLI) framework: Toward bridging the science-practice chasm to enhance robust student learning
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki
title: The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: an intermediate-grain-size framework linking knowledge components, learning events and instructional events
description: The KLI Framework is a theoretical framework (not a falsifiable theory) with three components: a taxonomy of knowledge components, learning processes, and instructional principles. It targets an intermediate 'learning event' grain size between neural theories and macro-level educational theories, so that propositions are 'empirical claims, so they are testable by experiments' and translate both downward to mechanisms and upward to instruction. Its scope is conditions yielding robust learning: long-term retention, transfer, and accelerated future learning.
requirements: Propositions must be elaborated with added assumptions to become theories that generate falsifiable predictions
constraints: The framework itself does not generate precise, falsifiable predictions at the level of theory
Generalizations carry grade- or experience-level boundary conditions from middle school, high school, and early college settings
target_learners: middle school, high school, and early college students in academic courses
target_learning_goals: robust student learning: long-term retention, transfer, and accelerated future learning across academic domains
examples: The framework is grounded in PSLC LearnLab courses spanning Physics, Chemistry, Algebra, Geometry, French, Chinese, and English as a second language
key_sources: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki

article_title: The knowledge-learning-instruction (KLI) framework: Toward bridging the science-practice chasm to enhance robust student learning
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki
title: Taxonomy of knowledge components classified by task features, response, relationship, and rationale
description: The article defines a knowledge component as 'an acquired unit of cognitive function or structure that can be inferred from performance on a set of related tasks' and classifies KCs along four dimensions: whether task features and response are constant or variable, whether the feature-response relationship is implicit or explicit, and whether a rationale is known. This yields categories such as facts (constant-constant, explicit), categories and concepts (variable-constant), productions, skills, rules and plans (variable-variable), and principles with rationales. KCs are chosen at the level where novice students actually make errors.
requirements: KC analysis should stop unpacking when smaller components are performed with sufficiently high accuracy and fluency
KCs must be empirically derived from performance on assessment events rather than pre-determined by designers
constraints: Labels are rough mappings and not necessarily one-to-one with taxonomy cells; the authors note it is an open question whether all 16 cells of the 4-dimensional space exist
target_learners: students in second language, mathematics, and science courses
target_learning_goals: analyzing learning goals into knowledge components to guide instructional design and predict learning difficulty
examples: Table 2 gives examples such as the Chinese radical 日 mapping to 'sun' (a fact), English article selection (a category), and forming plurals (a rule)
key_sources: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki

article_title: The knowledge-learning-instruction (KLI) framework: Toward bridging the science-practice chasm to enhance robust student learning
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki
title: DataShop: an open repository of classroom experimental data for testing learning hypotheses
description: DataShop is a computer repository established by the Pittsburgh Science of Learning Center for experimental data obtained by classroom research, 'open to researchers worldwide'. It supports testing hypotheses about student learning using existing logged data instead of running new experiments, and computes measures such as assistance scores (incorrect entries plus hint requests per step) and step completion times. As of June 2007 it held over 160 data sets, a number the authors note continues to increase.
requirements: Researchers need logged student interaction data from experiments or LearnLab courses deposited in the repository
constraints: The printed data set count (over 160) is dated June 2007 and the authors note it continues to increase
target_learners: researchers studying student learning in K12 and university courses
target_learning_goals: testing causal hypotheses about student learning and providing data for testing simulations of learning models
examples: The article describes computing an assistance score by adding incorrect entries and hint requests, e.g., 2 incorrect entries and 1 hint yields an assistance score of 3
key_sources: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki

article_title: The knowledge-learning-instruction (KLI) framework: Toward bridging the science-practice chasm to enhance robust student learning
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki
title: State instructional principles in terms of knowledge component types rather than subject-matter domains
description: A fundamental KLI assumption is that many learning processes and instructional design decisions 'are not intrinsically domain-based, but are determined by the type of KCs being learned'. The article argues a hypothetical principle like 'drill and practice is not effective for mathematics' is at the wrong level of analysis because it does not say what it is about mathematics that makes the method unsuitable. Instead, design decisions should be associated with KC types and their associated learning processes, such as study-practice trials for fact encoding and prompted self-explanations for explicit concepts and integrative knowledge.
requirements: Instructional design decisions must be tied to an analysis of the target course's knowledge components and their types
constraints: The article leaves open whether domain specificity constrains KC form qualitatively or only quantitatively
target_learners: instructional designers and researchers across academic domains
target_learning_goals: selecting instructional methods matched to the kind of knowledge being taught
examples: The article maps study-practice trials to constant-constant fact encoding, worked examples and tutored practice to implicit category and production learning, and self-explanation prompts to explicit and integrative knowledge
key_sources: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Albert T. Corbett, Charles Perfetti. (2010). The Knowledge-Learning-Instruction (KLI) Framework: Toward Bridging the Science-Practice Chasm to Enhance Robust Student Learning. Carnegie Mellon University Technical Report. http://learnlab.org/research/wiki

article_title: New Potentials for Data-Driven Intelligent Tutoring System Development and Optimization.
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Emma Brunskill, Ryan S.J.d. Baker, Elizabeth A. McLaughlin, and John Stamper. (2012). New Potentials for Data-Driven Intelligent Tutoring System Development and Optimization. http://learnlab.org/datashop
title: DataShop open educational data repository
description: DataShop is an open data repository at the Pittsburgh Science of Learning Center that stores learner interaction data from intelligent tutoring systems and other educational technologies. The article reports it "currently stores more than 350 datasets that include over 200,000 student hours of data from thousands of students at an average of 10 seconds per action, yielding more than 90 million stored student actions." It also enabled a form of "scientist crowdsourcing" in the LFA work, where expert-created alternative Q matrices for shared datasets were unioned into P matrices for automated model search.
requirements: Requires instrumented educational technologies that log student actions at fine grain (average of 10 seconds per action in the stored data).
target_learners: K12 and college students using intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Domain learning in mathematics, science, and other tutored subjects
examples: LFA model-discovery runs across eleven DataShop datasets seeded with expert-created Q matrices.

article_title: New Potentials for Data-Driven Intelligent Tutoring System Development and Optimization.
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Emma Brunskill, Ryan S.J.d. Baker, Elizabeth A. McLaughlin, and John Stamper. (2012). New Potentials for Data-Driven Intelligent Tutoring System Development and Optimization. http://learnlab.org/datashop
title: Four-function framework of intelligent tutoring systems (select, evaluate, suggest, update)
description: The article organizes intelligent tutoring system functionality around four functions supported by a cognitive model and an individual student model, operating inside an across-activity outer loop and a within-activity inner loop. As the article puts it, "Key functions of Intelligent Tutoring Systems, Select, Evaluate, Suggest, and Update (in rectangles) are supported by cognitive model and individual student model components." The outer loop selects and presents activities and updates skill estimates (e.g., via Knowledge Tracing over Knowledge Components); the inner loop evaluates each student action against the cognitive model and suggests next steps or hints. The article uses this framework to map which data-driven techniques develop or optimize which tutor functions.
requirements: A cognitive model of student reasoning and a student model for updating skill estimates, traditionally built through knowledge engineering.
constraints: Traditionally developed through extensive knowledge engineering; the article presents data-driven methods as alternatives for building these components.
target_learners: K12 and college students using intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: Step-by-step problem-solving skill development in domains such as algebra and logic
examples: Model tracing and knowledge tracing in the Algebra Cognitive Tutor implement the inner and outer loops of this framework.

article_title: The Risks of Rewards. ERIC Digest.
citation: Kohn, Alfie. (1994). The Risks of Rewards. ERIC Digest. ERIC Clearinghouse on Elementary and Early Childhood Education Urbana IL. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED376990
title: Avoid classroom management programs that rely on rewards and consequences; build a caring community that solves problems collaboratively
description: This principle holds that educators who want students to take responsibility for their own behavior and to internalize positive values should not use reward- and consequence-based management programs. The recommended alternative is "creating a caring community whose members solve problems collaboratively and decide together how they want their classroom to be." The digest grounds this in its analysis that rewards and punishments are two sides of the same manipulative coin.
requirements: Educators must prioritize internalization of positive values and student self-responsibility over mindless obedience for the alternative to be worth adopting.
constraints: The digest addresses typical practices in classrooms in the United States; ways rewards are used and values considered important differ among and within cultures.

target_learning_goals: Prosocial values and responsibility
Self-directed learning

article_title: Illusions of competence during study can be remedied by manipulations that enhance learners’ sensitivity to retrieval conditions at test
citation: Koriat, A., & Bjork, R. A. (2006). Illusions of competence during study can be remedied by manipulations that enhance learners' sensitivity to retrieval conditions at test. Memory & Cognition, 34(5), 959-972. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03193694
title: The foresight bias account: overconfidence arises from the mismatch between study conditions, where the answer is present, and test conditions, where it is absent
description: The article proposes that judgments of learning made during study are inflated because the answer is present at study but absent, but solicited, at test. It distinguishes a priori association (the probability the cue alone brings the target to mind) from a posteriori association (the perceived association when both words are present), arguing that "a priori associations are the more critical for performance during cued recall" while a posteriori associations dominate predictions. When a posteriori associations are strong relative to a priori ones, learners fall prey to an illusion of competence; remediation requires conditions at study that sensitize learners to retrieval conditions at test.
requirements: Remediation requires creating conditions at study that sensitize learners to retrieval conditions at test, such as test experience or delayed, cue-alone JOLs.
constraints: Delayed JOLs reduced but did not eliminate the foresight bias in Experiment 4.
The account is developed for paired-associate learning with asymmetrically associated word pairs.
target_learners: adult learners studying paired associates
students preparing for exams
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring of future recall
effective allocation of study time
examples: Backward-associated pairs such as cheese–cheddar, whose target-to-cue association is strong but cue-to-target association weak, induced inflated JOLs in Koriat and Bjork's (2005) experiments.
key_sources: Koriat, A., & Bjork, R. A. (2006). Illusions of competence during study can be remedied by manipulations that enhance learners' sensitivity to retrieval conditions at test. Memory & Cognition, 34(5), 959-972. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03193244

article_title: Personalizing e-Learning. The Social Effects of Pedagogical Agents.
citation: Nicole C. Krämer & Gary Bente. (2010). Personalizing e-Learning. The Social Effects of Pedagogical Agents. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9123-x
title: Taxonomy of embodiment aspects and functions of nonverbal behavior for pedagogical agents
description: The article organizes embodiment into static aspects (the visual appearance of the virtual character) and dynamic aspects (nonverbal behavior such as movement, gesture, and facial displays), and proposes that nonverbal behavior serves distinct functions in instructional settings: a modeling function for demonstrating motor tasks, illustrative functions such as pointing gestures, a dialogue management function regulating turn-taking via gaze and backchanneling, and socio-emotional functions via immediacy cues like smiling and proximity. It further characterizes nonverbal communication by procedural character, context dependency, and production outside of awareness, arguing these attributes must shape agent implementation.
requirements: Implementing nonverbal behavior requires taking into account its procedural character, context dependency, and automaticity, as the article states all attributes must be considered
constraints: Current technical implementations remain far from matching the complexity and subtlety of real-life nonverbal behavior, per the article's conclusion
target_learners: e-learning students interacting with pedagogical agents
target_learning_goals: socio-emotional and relational outcomes as moderators or outcomes of learning
examples: The article suggests motion capture or time-series coded videotaped human behavior as routes to more natural agent movements

article_title: Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive #x0022;Quantified Self #x0022;
citation: Kai Kunze, Masakazu Iwamura, Koichi Kise, Seiichi Uchida, and Shinichiro Omachi. (2013). Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive “Quantified Self.” Computer, IEEE Computer Society, October 2013. http://kaikunze.de/papers/2013Kunze-1.pdf
title: Wordometer app for the SMI iView X eye tracker
description: The Wordometer is a prototype application created for the SMI iView X eye tracker that "estimates the number of words a person reads, much like a pedometer counts steps". It works by detecting line breaks from long saccades against the reading direction and feeding them, with eye-gaze features, into a support vector regression algorithm. The article presents it as a reading-habits quantification tool analogous to fitness trackers.
requirements: Requires a mobile eye tracker (the SMI iView X) recording eye gaze while the user reads
constraints: Evaluated only with users reading English documents
target_learners: adult readers
target_learning_goals: quantifying reading volume as a measure of mental fitness
examples: The authors recorded eye movements of numerous users reading English documents and applied a line-break detector before training the word-count estimator

article_title: Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive #x0022;Quantified Self #x0022;
citation: Kai Kunze, Masakazu Iwamura, Koichi Kise, Seiichi Uchida, and Shinichiro Omachi. (2013). Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive “Quantified Self.” Computer, IEEE Computer Society, October 2013. http://kaikunze.de/papers/2013Kunze-1.pdf
title: Cognitive quantified self: mobile sensing applied to cognitive tasks such as reading
description: The article proposes extending activity tracking from physical movement to cognitive tasks, using mobile eye tracking because eye movements are "strongly correlated with cognitive tasks". Just as fitness apps record physical activity, a reading-habits app could record "the number of words read, types of documents read, and periods of concentrated reading to help users become better thinkers". The long-term goal is tracking mental processes to enable self-reflection and optimize mental fitness and well-being.
requirements: Mobile eye-tracking hardware (EOG electrodes or infrared stereo cameras) that can record gaze in real-life settings
constraints: Eye movements also encode attentiveness, fatigue, and emotional state, making it difficult to isolate the object of interest
The authors note the research "raises numerous ethical questions—for example, who should know what we read or how much we understand?"
target_learners: lifelong learners
students in classrooms
target_learning_goals: self-reflection on reading habits
learning-progress awareness
examples: Figure 1 shows a mockup interface for a hypothetical Readit service that records and analyzes reading habits, much like a fitness service such as Fitbit

article_title: Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive #x0022;Quantified Self #x0022;
citation: Kai Kunze, Masakazu Iwamura, Koichi Kise, Seiichi Uchida, and Shinichiro Omachi. (2013). Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive “Quantified Self.” Computer, IEEE Computer Society, October 2013. http://kaikunze.de/papers/2013Kunze-1.pdf
title: Two mobile eye-gaze recording methods: electrooculography and infrared stereo eye tracking
description: The article describes two promising methods for recording eye gaze in real-life mobile settings. Electrooculography (EOG) measures potential changes as the eye moves as a cornea-retina dipole; with this technique "it's possible to recognize reading and other eye movements in realistic everyday scenarios". The alternative tracks gaze with infrared light and stereo cameras, "provides potentially higher accuracy but requires more processing power", inferring motion from iris shape and local face features.
requirements: EOG requires electrodes touching the skin near the eye; infrared tracking requires cameras, infrared LEDs, and more processing power
constraints: EOG electrodes can be uncomfortable even when embedded in eyeglass frames; commercial mobile eye trackers are still quite expensive
target_learners: adult readers
lifelong learners
target_learning_goals: mobile monitoring of reading and cognitive activity
examples: A cheap 3D-printed open source mobile gaze tracker (OMG!) was shown at the MobileHCI conference, and researchers have experimented with front cameras on tablets and phones for low-fidelity gaze detection

article_title: Behavioral Economics of Education: Progress and Possibilities
citation: Adam M. Lavecchia, Heidi Liu, and Philip Oreopoulos. (2014). Behavioral Economics of Education: Progress and Possibilities. NBER Working Paper No. 20609. http://www.nber.org/papers/w20609
title: Dual-system framework of four behavioral barriers to treating education as an investment
description: The review organizes the behavioral economics of education around a dual-system model of intertemporal choice, in which a forward-looking system and an automatic system weigh current costs against distant benefits. It states that "it will be helpful to keep in mind four key implications from this model: (1) some students focus too much on the present ; (2) some rely too much on routine; (3) some students focus too much on negative identities ; and (4) mistakes are more likely to occur with many options or with little information". Each barrier is then treated as a distinct section explaining suboptimal education decisions.
requirements: The framework requires only that the systems implementing the intertemporal tradeoff are not fully developed prior to adulthood, not that two separate neural value systems compete
constraints: The authors note recent neuroscientific evidence rejects an overly dichotomous notion of separate competing neural systems for immediate versus delayed rewards, and state the distinction is not important for their policy discussion
target_learners: youth and adolescents making education decisions
parents making education decisions for children
target_learning_goals: long-run education investment decisions such as attainment, attendance, and homework completion
examples: The review uses the framework to explain procrastination on homework, avoidance of advanced math courses, and failure to complete college applications
key_sources: Adam M. Lavecchia, Heidi Liu, and Philip Oreopoulos. (2014). Behavioral Economics of Education: Progress and Possibilities. NBER Working Paper No. 20609. http://www.nber.org/papers/w20609

article_title: Behavioral Economics of Education: Progress and Possibilities
citation: Adam M. Lavecchia, Heidi Liu, and Philip Oreopoulos. (2014). Behavioral Economics of Education: Progress and Possibilities. NBER Working Paper No. 20609. http://www.nber.org/papers/w20609
title: Design education policies around behavioral barriers: ease learning opportunities, remind students of long-term goals, build self-control, and encourage pride in skill development
description: The review argues that because behavioral barriers, not just returns and costs, shape education decisions, effective policy should reduce the effort of acting on learning opportunities and keep long-term goals salient. It states that "policies that make learning opportunities easier, continually remind students of long-term goals, teach strategies to develop self-control, and encourage youth to take pride in their own skill development are promising approaches for helping foster academic achievement". The principle treats small presentation changes as potentially powerful because they can produce large behavior changes at low cost.
requirements: Interventions must target the correct behavioral barrier; the review notes an ineffective nudge may simply have targeted the wrong barrier
constraints: A nudge that changes behavior does not necessarily prove the underlying intervention improves welfare, and researchers cannot at face value distinguish suboptimal choices from rational long-term weighing of costs and benefits
target_learners: youth and adolescents
students from low-income backgrounds
parents of school-age children
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
high school and postsecondary attainment
long-run education investment behavior
examples: The review cites automatic enrollment defaults in pension plans increasing savings significantly, and text-message homework alerts to parents, as behavioral policies with large effects from small changes

article_title: The Effects of Generative Learning Strategy Prompts and Metacognitive Feedback on Learners' Self-Regulation, Generation Process, and Achievement
citation: Lee, Hyeon Woo. (2008). The effects of generative learning strategy prompts and metacognitive feedback on learners' self-regulation, generation process, and achievement. Dissertation in Instructional Systems, The Pennsylvania State University. https://etda.libraries.psu.edu
title: Generative learning theory: meaningful learning arises from learners actively generating relations between new information and prior knowledge
description: Generative learning theory, attributed to Wittrock, holds that comprehension results from learners' active generation of meaning rather than transfer of presented information into memory. At its essence are processes people use "actively and dynamically to (a) selectively attend to events and (b) generate meaning for events by constructing relations between new or incoming information and previously acquired information, conceptions, and background knowledge". The dissertation uses this theory as the framework for its path model, in which self-regulation controls generative activities and generative strategy use produces knowledge generation. Strategies range from simple coding (underlining, note taking, adjunct questions) to complex coding (summarizing, concept mapping) and elaborative integration (imaging, analogies).
requirements: Learners must be mentally active in creating relationships between new content and what they already know, with motivation and metacognitive control supporting the meaning-making process
constraints: The article notes the effects of generative learning strategies are not always consistent in every learning environment
target_learners: undergraduate students in computer-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: recall and comprehension of complex instructional material through meaningful knowledge generation
examples: The study operationalized generative strategies as highlighting important sentences, note taking, and interacting with adjunct questions within static visualized instruction
key_sources: Lee, Hyeon Woo. (2008). The effects of generative learning strategy prompts and metacognitive feedback on learners' self-regulation, generation process, and achievement. Dissertation in Instructional Systems, The Pennsylvania State University. https://etda.libraries.psu.edu

article_title: The Effects of Generative Learning Strategy Prompts and Metacognitive Feedback on Learners' Self-Regulation, Generation Process, and Achievement
citation: Lee, Hyeon Woo. (2008). The effects of generative learning strategy prompts and metacognitive feedback on learners' self-regulation, generation process, and achievement. Dissertation in Instructional Systems, The Pennsylvania State University. https://etda.libraries.psu.edu
title: Provide cognitive and metacognitive prompts while learners study in computer-based learning environments
description: Because providing generative strategy tools alone may not lead learners to monitor or adjust their learning, designers should pair strategy tools with prompts to use the strategies and with metacognitive feedback on strategy decisions. The study concludes that its positive effects from metacognitive feedback suggest "instructional designers or teachers should provide cognitive and metacognitive prompts while learners study". Prompts direct learners to underline, summarize, and answer adjunct questions; metacognitive feedback reminds learners to evaluate the adequacy of their strategy use.
requirements: Learners must be working with generative learning strategy tools in a computer-based environment so that prompts and feedback can direct and refine strategy use
constraints: Simple prompting alone may not be enough to help learners monitor, be aware of, or adjust their learning processes according to how well they are learning
target_learners: undergraduate students learning from computer-based static visualized instruction
target_learning_goals: self-regulation, quality of generative strategy use, recall and comprehension
examples: Treatment 3 combined strategy tools, written prompts directing underlining, summarizing and adjunct questions, and feedback on students' adjunct-question responses reminding them to evaluate and correct strategy execution

title: Rubric-based assessment of learners' overt generative strategy products (highlighting and notes) with generalizability-theory reliability checks
description: A performance-based assessment approach that measures the quality of learners' overt use of generative learning strategies from their actual products rather than from log files. The study "gathered and analyzed overt evidence of generative learning from learners' highlighting and note-taking products instead of log files" and "developed a rubric for assessing the quality of learner's overt use of generative learning strategies and applied generalizability theory in order to verify the reliability of performance-based assessment". Quality is defined as how well learners highlight sentences carrying the main idea and take notes in their own words to create relationships and meaning.

article_title: Does Curricular Complexity in Computer Science Influence the Representation of Women CS Graduates?
citation: Albert Lionelle, McKenna Quam, Carla Brodley, and Catherine Gill. 2024. Does Curricular Complexity in Computer Science Influence the Representation of Women CS Graduates?. In Proceedings of the 55th ACM Technical Symposium on Computer Science Education V. 1 (SIGCSE 2024). https://doi.org/10.1145/3626252.3630835
title: Curricular analytics: graph-based measures of degree-program complexity (blocking, delay, centrality, structural complexity)
description: Curricular analytics is the study of academic program design and layout, in which a degree plan is translated into a directed acyclic graph of courses and prerequisites. From the graph, four measures are computed: blocking factor (the number of courses reachable from a course node), delay factor (the maximum number of courses that must be completed in sequential order), centrality (the sum of the delay of all paths containing that course), and structural complexity (an unweighted linear combination of delay and blocking, with overall program complexity the sum of individual course complexities). The article uses these measures to compare 60 CS degrees against representation of women graduates.
requirements: A degree map built from a plan of study and each course's pre- and/or co-requisites, translated into a directed acyclic graph
constraints: Delay factor does not account for course availability, terms, enrollment caps, and other real-world factors, so it should not be read as semesters to graduate; structural complexity does not evaluate course content
target_learners: Undergraduate computer science majors
target_learning_goals: On-time progression and graduation through a computing degree program
examples: For the example degree map in Figure 1, Data Structures had blocking factor 11, delay factor 6, centrality 39, and complexity 17, with overall program complexity 175

article_title: A systematic review of tools that support peer assessment
citation: Luxton-Reilly, A. (2009). A systematic review of tools that support peer assessment. Computer Science Education, 19(4), 209-232. https://doi.org/10.1080/08993400903384844
title: Three-category taxonomy of peer assessment tools: generic, domain-specific, and context-specific systems
description: The review classifies online peer assessment tools into three categories based on their design scope. Generic systems are "designed to be highly configurable and support peer review activities in a wide range of disciplines and contexts." Domain-specific systems target a particular artefact type such as essays or programming code. Context-specific systems were "written for use in a specific course and must be rewritten if they are to accommodate other contexts." This taxonomy organises the review's analysis of features across tools.
requirements: Tools must have been designed specifically for supporting peer assessment activities and used in at least one course
constraints: Excludes tools for reviewing individual contributions to teams, standard communication software repurposed for peer review, unimplemented proposals, and conference management tools
target_learners: higher education students
computer science students
target_learning_goals: peer assessment skills
formative feedback literacy
critical evaluation of peers' work
examples: PeerGrader, Web-SPA, OPAS, CeLS, PRAISE and Aropa are classified as generic; CPR, C.A.P., SWoRD and PeerWise as domain-specific; Peers, NetPeas, OASYS, Wolfe and PEARS as context-specific

article_title: A systematic review of tools that support peer assessment

title: Design peer assessment marking criteria to separate objective grading criteria from students' subjective opinions
description: The review reports that making an explicit split between objective grading criteria and personal opinion improves review quality. Kali and Ronen (2005) introduced a fourth, non-graded criterion for students' own opinions, and the review states that "an explicit distinction between objective and subjective criteria improves the quality of the review." Students like expressing a subjective view that does not affect grading, and the distinction improves correlation between student and instructor marks.
requirements: The tool must support a rubric with both graded criteria and a separate non-graded opinion field
constraints: Evidence comes from one undergraduate educational philosophy course using the CeLS system
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: fair and accurate peer assessment
distinguishing objective evaluation from personal opinion
examples: In CeLS, a fourth criterion was introduced to allow students to write their own opinion, which was not considered to be a grading criterion

It states that "the use of exemplars can help students to identify what is good or bad in a given assignment" and that these exemplars "can act as a 'yard-stick' by which students can measure their own performance and that of others." Several tools operationalise this: OASYS distributes scripts across good, intermediate and poor categories; Web-SPA uses multiple review cycles exposing best and worst cases; SWoRD publishes all drafts and ratings; OPAS displays top-ranked assignments.

article_title: Effects of Peer Tutoring With Audio Prompting on Vocabulary Acquisition for Struggling Readers
citation: Mackiewicz, S. M., Wood, C. L., Cooke, N. L., & Mazzotti, V. L. (2011). Effects of Peer Tutoring With Audio Prompting on Vocabulary Acquisition for Struggling Readers. Remedial and Special Education, 32(4), 345–354. https://doi.org/10.1177/0741932510362507
title: VoicePod audio prompting device for naïve peer tutors
description: The VoicePod (Attainment Company Inc., 2006) is "a portable digital recording and playback system that includes multiple, reusable cards." Each card holds a printed text prompt behind a plastic sleeve and an activation strip that plays a recording of up to 10 s when inserted into the pod. In this study eight cards per target word carried the word, definition, example sentences, and fill-in-the-blank items, giving naïve tutors audio models so they could provide correct modeling and feedback. The device was chosen because it was transportable, easily adapted, and cost efficient (about $60 each).
requirements: Tutors must activate the card's recording after each tutee response so feedback can be checked against the recorded model
constraints: Recordings are limited to up to 10 s per card activation
target_learners: fourth-grade struggling readers, including students with high-incidence disabilities
target_learning_goals: vocabulary word meanings and use of words in sentence context
examples: Each tutoring pair received one VoicePod and six sets of eight cards; tutors used the recordings to verify tutee answers during four sessions per week

title: Eight-card audio-prompted tutoring sequence with model-lead-test feedback
description: The study's tutoring routine pairs a scripted card sequence with a feedback strategy: "Tutors used a model-lead-test, feedback strategy (i.e., demonstration, pair practice, independent tutee practice, feedback) to present the words and definitions to the tutees." Eight cards per word move from the word and its definition, through example sentences with the definition substituted, to sentence-choice items, with correct answers praised and errors prompting "listen again" and repetition. Roles then switch so each student serves as tutor and tutee.
requirements: Students must be trained to mastery (100% on a treatment fidelity checklist) on both tutor and tutee roles before independent tutoring
Pairs remain static and are matched on academic and behavioral characteristics
constraints: Sessions were not directly monitored unless researchers were collecting procedural fidelity data

target_learning_goals: acquiring definitions of novel vocabulary words and placing them correctly in context

article_title: Tenacious Assessments: Using In-Game Behaviors to Measure Student Persistence and Challenge Navigation
citation: Malkiewich, L. J., Lee, A., Slater, S., & Chase, C. C. (2016). Tenacious Assessments: Using In-Game Behaviors to Measure Student Persistence and Challenge Navigation. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Tenacious+Assessments+Using+In-Game+Behaviors
title: Three-construct framework for measuring challenge navigation in games: challenge approach, challenge response, and general persistence
description: The article organizes in-game motivational behavior into three constructs: "challenge approach, challenge response, and general persistence". Challenge approach covers how players choose challenging situations and code; challenge response covers what players do after failure, such as reflecting on hints or downgrading code; general persistence is "simply the willingness to continue playing the game", without distinguishing easier from harder levels. The framework guided creation of eleven log-based measures validated against a classic persistence task and learning outcomes.
requirements: Requires fine-grained log or screen-recording data from a game that logs level choices, code complexity, attempts, and timing around failures
constraints: The authors note their measures "were confined by the structure and mechanics of this particular game", e.g. gating makes post-failure level choice a challenge-approach rather than challenge-response behavior
target_learners: fifth-grade students learning computer programming in an after-school program
target_learning_goals: block-based coding knowledge (writing, interpreting, debugging code)
motivational behaviors around challenge
examples: Eleven measures in Table 1 were assigned to the three constructs, e.g. Hards Solved Complex (approach), Careful Hint Reads (response), Coding Time Day 2 (general persistence)
key_sources: Malkiewich, L. J., Lee, A., Slater, S., & Chase, C. C. (2016). Tenacious Assessments: Using In-Game Behaviors to Measure Student Persistence and Challenge Navigation. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Tenacious+Assessments+Using+In-Game+Behaviors

title: Eleven log-derived measures of challenge navigation (Table 1) recorded as percent occurrence or time spent
description: From over 150 candidate measures created from screen recordings and embedded log capture, the authors selected eleven measures of challenge navigation, recorded as "percent occurrence or time spent on a behavior" rather than counts, to avoid confounding with game condition speed. Measures include Hards Solved Complex, Relative-Hards Solved Complex, Careful Hint Reads, Relative-Hard Code Downgrades, and Coding Time Day 2, each labeled as positive or negative indicators of challenge engagement.
requirements: Measures must not be confounded with student skill or with condition-specific pacing; rarely occurring behaviors (less than 5% occurrence) were excluded
constraints: Due to lost video and log data, the measures cover only a portion of the sample (N=18)
target_learners: fifth-grade students learning computer programming
target_learning_goals: measuring persistence and challenge-seeking during gameplay
examples: Levels were labeled relative-hard if a student needed an above-average number of attempts to solve them

title: Measure motivation in games with fine-grained behavioral indicators of willingness to attempt difficult strategies, not just total persistence times
description: The article recommends that game researchers "be more varied in the ways they define, operationalize, and measure student motivation", using log data to capture whether students attempt effortful strategies on hard problems rather than only total persistence times. These fine-grained measures "provide more fine-grained data than traditional assessments of motivation" and related to both a classic persistence measure and learning in this study.

constraints: The authors were "limited in this study by our small sample size and the fact that students only played one game"; measures may need adaptation for games with different structures, e.g. without gating

target_learning_goals: measuring student persistence and challenge navigation as motivational behaviors during learning

title: Seven critical domains synthesize higher education student learning outcome frameworks
description: The report reviews seven higher education outcome frameworks and synthesizes them into seven common domains: creativity, critical thinking, teamwork, communication, digital and information literacy, citizenship, and life skills. Domains were retained only when included in a majority of frameworks: "determining those factors that were included in a majority (at least four of seven) of the frameworks reviewed". Each domain is defined by operational outcomes drawn from the source frameworks.

title: USDOL-ETA General Competency Model Framework
description: The U.S. Department of Labor's Employment and Training Administration developed a competency model to determine worker requirements based on employer and business needs. "The competencies included in this framework are represented by nine tiers, organized in a hierarchical, or stackable fashion, with general competencies at the bottom and job-specific competencies at the top". Lower tiers are broad foundation competencies applicable across industries; upper tiers cover occupation-specific knowledge and management competencies.

title: Distinguish terminal higher education outcomes from underlying workforce skills when designing frameworks and assessments
description: The report argues that frameworks defining what a student should have achieved in college differ from those certifying workforce competencies.
