citation: Marrs, K.A., and Novak, G. (2004). Just-in-Time Teaching in Biology: Creating an Active Learner Classroom Using the Internet. Cell Biology Education 3, 49–61. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.03-11-0022
title: JiTT: a feedback loop between Web-based pre-class assignments and classroom instruction
description: JiTT is a teaching and learning approach that combines traditional in-class instruction with Web communication. Its essence is a feedback loop: faculty post Warm Up assignments before class, students respond, and faculty use those responses to tailor the class session. As the authors state, "The essence of JiTT is the feedback loop between the Web and the classroom," emphasizing active learning, constructivism, and prompt feedback while decreasing traditional lecture.
requirements: Weekly Web-based Warm Up assignments due before class time
Faculty time before class to read and select student responses
A mechanism (CGI-bin or course management software) to collect and display student responses
constraints: JiTT is particularly useful in large enrollment courses and for commuting or part-time students, per the authors
target_learners: undergraduate nonscience majors in large-enrollment biology
advanced undergraduate biology majors and graduate students
target_learning_goals: addressing misconceptions and activating prior knowledge
active learning and cooperative problem solving
formative assessment and prompt feedback
examples: Contemporary Biology N100 (>200 students) and Biotechnology 540 (max 45 students) at IUPUI have used JiTT since 1999, teaching more than 1,000 biology students

title: JiTT lesson cycle: pre-class Warm Up, response-informed interactive lecture, cooperative learning, and post-class relevance essays
description: The article describes four common features structuring each week of a JiTT biology course: an online Dynamic Syllabus updated weekly, Web-based Warm Up assignments due 3 hours before class, an interactive classroom session combining lecture-discussion with cooperative learning exercises, and optional Good For relevance essays. The class session itself is split so that "a modified lecture-discussion is done for the first 3rd of the class, incorporating student Warm Up responses," followed by group work and a second lecture-discussion.

Cooperative learning exercises chosen to give hands-on experience with the concepts discussed

advanced undergraduate and graduate biology students

active practice of course concepts during class
relevance and motivation

article_title: Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466
title: Four-part framework for conceptualizing the tradeoffs of learning analytics methods: sampling, capturing, reduction, and pattern finding
description: The article proposes a framework for thinking about what LA methods add to the learning sciences method space. It states: "We suggest here a simple four-part framework to help us conceptualize this new space of tradeoffs: (a) sampling, (b) capturing, (c) reduction, and (d) pattern ﬁnding." Each part is a stage at which any method trades breadth against depth: sampling concerns which learning phenomena are studied, capturing which aspects are recorded, reduction how captured data are transformed, and pattern finding how patterns are discovered and confirmed. LA reshapes each tradeoff rather than eliminating it.
requirements: Researchers must articulate the learning sciences' fundamental assumptions about learning when selecting among methods, since "Any method that we might use has strengths and weaknesses."
constraints: The article notes that when applying LA, researchers "are more likely to restrict our study to learning activities that are conducted using computers (though, as we will see, this is not an absolute requirement)."
target_learners: Learning sciences researchers and educational researchers selecting research methods
target_learning_goals: Understanding methodological tradeoffs in studying learning processes with computational methods
examples: The framework is used to compare student written responses, video recordings, and computer log files as capture types, and to position LA between traditional quantitative and qualitative methods in reduction labor.
key_sources: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466

article_title: Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466
title: Three fundamental assumptions of the learning sciences perspective on learning: ubiquitous, heterogeneous, and complex
description: The article articulates three assumptions it calls "critical for the selection of research methods": "1. Learning events are not rare events. 2. Learning is a heterogeneous phenomenon. 3. Learning is a complex process." Learning happens in all places and times, takes dramatically different forms from aha moments to incremental change, and involves wandering a complex space of possibilities rather than climbing a unidimensional stairway. These assumptions imply that methods must capture learning across contexts, in diverse forms, and as an unfolding process rather than only start and end points.
requirements: Methods must be "widely deployed to capture learning phenomena of many sorts, across multiple contexts and in diverse forms," and must yield process data, not just outcome data.
target_learners: Learning sciences researchers
target_learning_goals: Framing research questions about learning in ways consistent with the field's core assumptions
examples: The article derives methodological implications directly from the assumptions: complexity of learning motivates collecting data on the process, not just its start and end points.
key_sources: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466

article_title: Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466
title: Three core tool classes of learning analytics: data capture and archiving, data analysis, and data representation and use
description: The article describes a core set of tools that LA contributes to learning research. "Tools for data capture and archiving" extract attributes of student behavior for later analysis, from stored text to real-time speech transcription, facial expression recognition, and eye-gaze tracking. "Tools for data analysis" apply specialized algorithms for search, retrieval, and pattern discovery to very large datasets. "Tools for data representation and use" make discovered patterns useful to researchers, teachers, and learners through new representations and responsive learning technologies.
requirements: Patterns discovered in the data must be made useful not only for researchers but also for teachers and learners, which requires new representations and technologies for each group.
target_learners: Researchers, teachers, and learners using analytics-informed learning environments
target_learning_goals: Capturing, analyzing, representing, and acting on patterns in learning process data
examples: A hypothetical online mathematics game project illustrates the tools: instrumenting the game, running machine learning over the logs, then displaying results to the teacher or students or driving real-time guidance.
key_sources: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466

article_title: Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466
title: Supervised versus unsupervised machine learning methods for automating analysis of learning data
description: The article introduces the machine learning distinction it uses to organize the special issue. "In supervised methods, we begin with a set of instances of data that have already been labeled (i.e., coded), usually by a human coder," producing a classifier that labels uncoded items, with data divided into training, testing, and optionally held-out corpora. "In contrast, unsupervised methods seek to discover structure in data that have not previously been labeled," typically via clustering that requires defining a similarity measure. Unsupervised methods add the burden of interpreting whether clusters are meaningful.
requirements: Supervised classification requires the analyst to determine which features of items are most helpful for predicting labels; unsupervised clustering requires defining a measure of similarity between pairs of data items.
constraints: The article warns that unsupervised clusters "might not turn out to be particularly meaningful" and, if meaningful, may not match categories useful for the research.
target_learners: Learning sciences researchers applying computational methods to learning data
target_learning_goals: Understanding when to use labeled-classification versus structure-discovery approaches for learning data
examples: Two special issue articles (Gobert et al.; Baker et al.) use supervised classification; three (Berland et al.; Sherin; Blikstein et al.) use unsupervised methods.
key_sources: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466

article_title: Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466
title: Do not let ease of data collection or fit with analytics tools restrict what learning phenomena are studied or what questions are asked
description: The article closes with cautions for learning scientists adopting LA. It warns: "we must not restrict ourselves to collecting only the data that are easy to collect," because mouse clicks and key presses "provide only a limited picture of a learning activity" even at the computer, and many learning activities involve no computer at all. It further warns against letting LA shape the research agenda: "it is essential that we do not compromise, that we use LA where it helps us to answer our core questions rather than as the sole guide of what questions to ask."
requirements: Researchers must continue studying learning across contexts—at home and in school, indoors and outdoors—and keep theory primary when framing research questions.
constraints: The principle is stated as a caution for the learning sciences community adopting LA; the article notes LA can also be applied to traditional data such as interview transcripts, as in Sherin's article.
target_learners: Learning sciences researchers and educational designers adopting learning analytics
target_learning_goals: Preserving theoretical integrity and ecological breadth in learning research that uses analytics
examples: The article points to Sherin's contribution as evidence that LA can be applied to traditional interview transcript data rather than only clickstream logs.

citation: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466
title: Five special issue articles demonstrating supervised, unsupervised, and process-characterizing learning analytics across science inquiry, programming, interview, and tutoring data
description: The article summarizes the special issue's contributions as demonstrations of LA method classes. Gobert et al. use supervised classification of log files labeled via text replay tagging to detect students designing controlled experiments in Inq-ITS. Berland et al. use unsupervised methods on program snapshots from the IPRO environment to propose "a framework of three phases of learning to program: explore, tinker, and reﬁne." Sherin automates discovery of student conceptions in interview transcripts; Baker et al. study learning curves in the Genetics Cognitive Tutor; Blikstein et al. associate patterns of program changes with course performance.
requirements: Each article's method requires feature selection or similarity decisions by the analyst, as described for supervised and unsupervised approaches.
constraints: The fifth article, by Blikstein et al., could not be included in the issue due to page limitations and appears in a future issue of JLS.
target_learners: Middle school, high school, and college learners studied in the contributing articles
target_learning_goals: Detecting inquiry skills, programming pathways, student conceptions, and learning-curve patterns from process data
examples: Four of the five articles attempt to characterize unfolding learning processes in a substantial way, using methods such as hidden Markov models.

article_title: Investigating Epistemic Stances in Game Play with Data Mining
citation: Martinez-Garza, M. M., & Clark, D. B. (2017). Investigating Epistemic Stances in Game Play with Data Mining. International Journal of Gaming and Computer-Mediated Simulations, 9(3). https://doi.org/10.4018/IJGCMS.2017070101
title: Two-System Framework (2SM) of game-based learning: player and learner stances organized around fast and slow cognition
description: The 2SM is a cognitive framework applying the two-system model of cognition to educational gaming. It holds that students build a second-order model of a game's encased simulation rather than an accurate mental analogue, and that play alternates between a fast, heuristic-driven player stance (System 1) and a slow, inquiry-oriented learner stance (System 2). The article states: "The premise of the 2SM framework is that students of educational games do not necessarily form accurate mental analogues of the software models that drive the phenomena they experience in-game". Through play students gather conditions, heuristics, and a second-order mental model.
requirements: Play data must be interpretable in terms of fast and slow processing strategies for the framework's stances to be operationalized
constraints: The framework was proposed as part of a general-use explanatory framework and its basic claims were still under investigation in this study

high school students

epistemic stances during game play

title: EPIGAME (The Fuzzy Chronicles): a conceptually-integrated puzzle game for Newtonian kinematics with full action logging
description: EPIGAME, titled The Fuzzy Chronicles, is the third iteration of the SURGE line of digital games for Newtonian kinematics, presented as a series of science-fiction puzzles across 32 levels of generally increasing complexity. Students plan a trajectory, place Boost actions at waypoints, and run the attempt; a planning phase plus its action phase form an attempt. The article states it is "intended to help students advance their understanding of Newtonian kinematics" and that the game "stores all student actions and collects them in a central database", enabling log-file analysis.

force and motion concepts

description: Because the full ECD framework cannot be applied retrospectively to existing game logs, the article recommends emulating its useful features: a student model operationalizing the hypothesized cognitive dynamics (here, the 2SM stances) and an evidence model mapping those dynamics onto observable log variables. The article states "the goal would be to emulate some useful features of ECD, such as the student model and the evidence model". This constrains latent variables, boosts interpretability, and pre-selects likely-significant observed variables.

article_title: Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507
title: Three-genre taxonomy of research on games for learning: value-added, cognitive consequences, and media comparison
description: The book organizes all research on games for learning into three research paradigms. The value-added approach compares a base game against the base game plus one added feature; the cognitive consequences approach compares pretest-to-posttest change for extended off-the-shelf game play versus no play; the media comparison approach compares learning from a game versus conventional media on the same material. The book states it "distinguishes among three genres of game research: the value-added approach, the cognitive consequences approach, and the media comparison approach" and systematizes the field by sorting experiments into these categories.
requirements: Each genre requires methodologically sound experimental comparisons: random assignment, matched treatment and control groups, and appropriate measures of learning outcome
constraints: The taxonomy applies to experimental comparisons meeting basic requirements of experimental methodology, not to speculative essays or methodologically flawed studies
target_learners: K-12 students
college students
workplace trainees
target_learning_goals: academic learning outcomes and cognitive skills from computer games
examples: The book's meta-analysis chapters each address one genre: chapter 5 value-added, chapter 6 cognitive consequences, chapter 7 media comparison
key_sources: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507

article_title: Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507
title: Five defining characteristics of games mapped to game elements
description: The book defines games by five characteristics: "games are interactive, simulated systems that are rule based, responsive, challenging, cumulative, and inviting." Rule-based means events occur within a causal system based on knowable rules; responsive means the environment responds promptly and saliently to player actions; challenging means opportunities to succeed on difficult tasks; cumulative means the current state reflects previous actions; inviting means the environment is interesting and fun. Each characteristic maps to game elements such as feedback, replay, goals, levels, time, reward structure, aesthetics, and storytelling.
requirements: To be called a game, a learning environment must possess all five defining characteristics
constraints: The book treats the line between simulation game and computer game as fuzzy and includes simulations and games in the same category
target_learners: instructional designers
game designers for learning
target_learning_goals: designing educational activities that qualify as games for learning
examples: Table 1.1 maps the responsive characteristic to the game elements of feedback and replay, and the inviting characteristic to aesthetics, curve of interest, and storytelling
key_sources: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507

article_title: Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507
title: Three kinds of cognitive processing during game learning: extraneous, essential, and generative
description: The book applies cognitive load theory to game learning by distinguishing three types of cognitive processing: "extraneous processing, which wastes precious cognitive capacity; essential processing, aimed at attending to and mentally representing the academic content; and generative processing, which involves deeper reflection on the academic content." Extraneous processing is caused by poor game design, essential processing by the inherent difficulty of the material, and generative processing by the player's motivation to engage in learning. The stated goal of effective game design is to reduce extraneous processing, manage essential processing, and foster generative processing.
requirements: Effective game design must manage limited cognitive capacity across the three processing types
target_learners: players of games for learning across K-12, college, and workplace settings
target_learning_goals: academic knowledge and skill acquisition from games
examples: Table 1.3 attributes extraneous processing to poor game design and generative processing to the player's motivation to engage in learning
key_sources: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507

article_title: Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507
title: Balance game features for motivation against instructional features for learning
description: The book recommends that designers manage a fundamental design tension: "Designing effective educational games always involves a tension between including game features for entertainment and instructional features for learning." Game features can promote motivation and generative processing but can also distract the learner and increase extraneous processing; instructional features can guide attention and prime deeper processing but can destroy the fun of game playing and reduce willingness to engage. The challenge is to balance the positive and negative aspects to suit the needs of each learner.
requirements: Designers must include both game features, intended to motivate engagement, and instructional features, intended to foster appropriate cognitive processing
constraints: Instructional features can diminish motivation to learn by reducing the fun of game playing; game features can diminish learning by increasing extraneous processing
target_learners: learners playing educational games in schools and training programs
target_learning_goals: deep learning outcomes through motivated, generative cognitive processing
examples: Table 1.4 summarizes the potential and pitfalls of game features and instructional features in computer games for learning
key_sources: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507

article_title: Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach
citation: Mayer, Richard E. (2014). Computer Games for Learning: An Evidence-Based Approach. The MIT Press. http://direct.mit.edu/books/monograph/4028/bookpreview-pdf/2362507
title: Evaluate games for learning through an evidence-based approach using testable questions, appropriate methods, and learning theory
description: The book advocates that claims about the educational effectiveness of games be evaluated scientifically rather than through unsupported claims, popularity, or anecdotes. "An evidence-based approach to the study of games for learning involves using appropriate research methods, grounded in learning theory, to yield data needed for answering testable questions." The approach is self-correcting: as evidence accumulates, unhelpful accounts of learning with games can be rejected and more useful ones constructed. Reports based primarily on selected anecdotes or testimonials do not qualify as evidence-based.
requirements: Research must pose testable questions, use appropriate research methods, and be grounded in theories of learning relevant to games
constraints: Evidence must come from methodologically sound studies; anecdote, popularity, and unsupported assertion do not qualify
target_learners: instructional designers
educational leaders selecting games
students and researchers of educational games
target_learning_goals: determining the educational effectiveness of computer games for learning
examples: The book reviews only studies that randomly assign participants, match treatment and control groups, and use appropriate measures of learning outcome

article_title: Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment
citation: Mayer, I. (2018). Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment. Simulation & Gaming, 49(6), 602-619. https://doi.org/10.1177/1046878118770831
title: TEAMUP multiplayer 3D team training and assessment game
description: TEAMUP (© The Barn) is a commercial, multiplayer three-dimensional serious game built in the Unreal Development Kit engine in which "Four players need to self-organise, communicate, collaborate and arrange team communication, coordination and leadership in order to solve five levels of puzzles/team challenges". Players stranded on a deserted island must reach the other side to be rescued, with five puzzle levels (door, tile, maze, bridge, pillar) requiring alternating leadership. The game logs any kind of game data, communicates with a scoring, assessment and visualisation tool, and supports distributed play and video recording.
requirements: Four-player teams seated so each player sees only their own screen, communicating only by speech
constraints: Available for team training under a commercial license
target_learners: professionals such as police officers, auditors and consultants
undergraduate and postgraduate students in engineering, management and entrepreneurship
target_learning_goals: team communication, coordination and leadership
team self-organisation and collaboration
examples: Played in 3-4 hour workshop mode with 3-6 teams in parallel, followed by a 1-hour facilitated plenary discussion showing team scores on a central screen

article_title: Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment
citation: Mayer, I. (2018). Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment. Simulation & Gaming, 49(6), 602-619. https://doi.org/10.1177/1046878118770831
title: Internal validity as precondition for game-based team assessment
description: The article frames validation research as preceding intervention research: before asking whether games train teams effectively, one must establish whether in-game measures relate to in-game team quality. "Internal validity implies that teams with better in-game performance also have better team quality, and vice versa. In-game team performance scores by themselves have very little external value." In-game performance serves as a proxy for team quality demonstrated during play, and unobtrusively logged game analytics (stealth assessment) are the key advantage of digital serious games for training and assessment.
requirements: Triangulation of self-reporting, personal observation and digital observation data
In-game team quality factors that are relatively stable and transferrable to the outside world
constraints: Internal validity is a precondition but not a guarantee for external validity
External validity of TEAMUP was not an objective of this study and remains undetermined
target_learners: professional and student teams in organisational training contexts
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of team quality and team performance through game play
examples: The study tested internal validity by correlating logged in-game indicators with psychometric team quality constructs from pre- and post-game questionnaires

article_title: Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment
citation: Mayer, I. (2018). Assessment of Teams in a Digital Game Environment. Simulation & Gaming, 49(6), 602-619. https://doi.org/10.1177/1046878118770831
title: In game-based team assessment, weight avoidable mistakes over team speed
description: Because in-game time and distance are largely driven by team structure such as age and game experience, while avoidable mistakes reflect team cohesiveness and task quality, assessors should focus feedback and judgement on errors rather than speed. The author states: "we should put less emphasis on how fast a team is, and more on how many avoidable mistakes a team makes, for example how many times a known mistake is repeated." Partial validation of the game gives guidance to trainers and assessors on which indicators to trust.
requirements: A game that logs avoidable mistakes unobtrusively, where repeating a known ineffective action is detectable
constraints: Validated for TEAMUP only; results have not been compared with other digital team games and cannot be generalised
target_learners: professional teams in training and assessment programmes
trainers and assessors using serious games
target_learning_goals: valid team assessment and debriefing feedback
examples: In TEAMUP sessions, individual and team scores for time, distance and avoidable mistakes were shown on a central screen to trigger and deepen the plenary debriefing discussion

article_title: A Breakthrough for Josh: How Use of an iPad Facilitated Reading Improvement
citation: McClanahan, B., Williams, K., Kennedy, E., & Tate, S. (2012). A Breakthrough for Josh: How Use of an iPad Facilitated Reading Improvement. TechTrends, 56(3). https://link.springer.com/journal/11528
title: iPad with reading apps and downloadable activities as the medium for individualized reading intervention
description: The iPad served as the presentation medium for a research-based tutoring plan for a struggling reader with ADHD. The tutor used applications such as FlashCards+, the Compound Boogie game, Stories2Go, Vocabulary Builder, Miss Spell's Class, ABC Alphabet Phonics, and an eBook with self-recording, plus downloaded graphic organizers and prediction guides. She reported that "the availability of applications and the ability to download Internet 'finds' directly to the iPad facilitated her planning and the implementation of the lessons." The device's touch screen, stylus notation, and audio recording enabled multimodal engagement with texts.

constraints: Some books the pair read were not available on the iPad, requiring a tape recorder for a similar recording effect; the tutor could not later recall the precise procedure used for on-screen INSERT marking

Reading comprehension strategies
Metacognitive awareness of reading

article_title: A Breakthrough for Josh: How Use of an iPad Facilitated Reading Improvement
citation: McClanahan, B., Williams, K., Kennedy, E., & Tate, S. (2012). A Breakthrough for Josh: How Use of an iPad Facilitated Reading Improvement. TechTrends, 56(3). https://link.springer.com/journal/11528
title: Computer-aided instruction for students with ADHD should present tasks in multiple modalities, chunked, with repeated trials and immediate feedback
description: Drawing on the Raggi and Chronis review, the article identifies characteristics of computer-aided instruction that may promote sustained attention and improved work performance for students with ADHD: "presentation of learning tasks in multiple modalities, the capability of chunking tasks into more manageable pieces, and repeated trials with immediate feedback." CAI also offers one-on-one, self-paced, individualized instruction, often with the novelty of game formatting that promotes engagement and attention. The article states these characteristics directly address the core symptoms of ADHD.
requirements: One-on-one tailored, self-paced delivery
game-like formatting or novelty to promote engagement
constraints: The article notes the research on CAI is often flawed or conflicting; the review found most studies had significant design flaws or small samples

target_learning_goals: Sustained attention during academic tasks
Improved academic work performance
examples: The iPad tutoring sessions embodied these characteristics: game-formatted apps such as Compound Boogie gave repeated trials with immediate feedback, and the touch screen engaged visual and tactile/kinesthetic modalities.

article_title: Evaluation of Evidence-Based Practices in Online Learning: A Meta-Analysis and Review of Online Learning Studies.
citation: Means, Toyama, Murphy, Bakia, & Jones. (2009). Evaluation of Evidence-Based Practices in Online Learning: A Meta-Analysis and Review of Online Learning Studies. U.S. Department of Education. https://www.ed.gov/about/offices/list/opepd/ppss/reports.html
title: Conceptual framework for online learning along three dimensions: replacement vs. enhancement, learning-experience type, and synchronicity
description: The report develops a conceptual framework to guide its literature search and review, "identifying three key components describing online learning": (a) whether the activity serves as a replacement for or an enhancement to conventional face-to-face instruction, (b) the type of learning experience (expository, active, or interactive), and (c) whether communication is primarily synchronous or asynchronous. Exhibit 1 illustrates uses of online learning for each combination of these dimensions. The dimensions were derived from prior distance-learning meta-analyses.
requirements: Online learning applications must be classifiable on each of the three dimensions (objective, learning-experience type, synchronicity) for the framework to differentiate them.
constraints: The report notes the framework was derived from prior meta-analyses of distance learning and captures some of the most important kinds of variation, not all features; many other features such as setting, content type, and technology also apply.

higher education students

article_title: Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice
citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: Executive function as an umbrella term for goal-directed cognitive processes with five recurring elements
description: The volume's Part I introduction defines executive function as "an umbrella term for the complex cognitive processes that serve ongoing, goal-directed behaviors." Most definitions include many, but not all, of five elements: goal setting and planning, organization of behaviors over time, flexibility, attention and memory systems such as working memory, and self-regulatory processes such as self-monitoring. The editors note that fuzzy definitions still abound and different theories compete to explain EF development.
requirements: Definitions must specify which of the five elements they include, since no definition includes all of them
constraints: The field had not achieved a unitary definition of executive function at the time of publication

students with learning disabilities and ADHD

planning
organization
self-monitoring

citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: Denckla's three-level description linking ADHD, executive function dysfunction, and brain localization
description: Denckla's chapter argues that three levels of description must be connected: ADHD at the surface syndromic level, executive function dysfunction (EDF) at the intermediate cognitive analysis level, and frontal, striatal, and cerebellar localizations at the neurological level. She reports that heterogeneity characterized each level, most clearly at the neurological level, and that neuroimaging of disorders such as neurofibromatosis 1 showed ADHD-syndromic characteristics with subcortical abnormalities.
requirements: Assessment and diagnosis must specify which of the three levels is being described
constraints: Heterogeneity within ADHD, within the brains of those with ADHD, and within the EF domain complicates research replication
target_learners: children with ADHD
children with learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: understanding neurodevelopmental bases of academic performance

citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: Hill, skill, and will: executive function as integration of goal, abilities, and volition from a multiple-intelligences perspective
description: Moran and Gardner construe executive function as the integration of three parameters: "hill—the establishment of a clear goal; skill—the requisite abilities and techniques for attaining that goal; and will—the volition to begin and persevere until the goal has been reached." They propose that executive function emerges from intrapersonal intelligence, the capacity to discern and use information about oneself, and that these parameters become more complexly integrated with age and experience across two broad stages, apprentice and master.
requirements: Executive function is understood as operating within temporal, social, and psychological contexts that shape how the three parameters interact
constraints: The authors describe their two-stage apprentice/master account as an admitted simplification
target_learners: learners across the lifespan, from toddlers to adults
target_learning_goals: goal setting
perseverance toward goals
self-relevant orchestration of abilities

article_title: Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice
citation: Meltzer, L. (Ed.). (2007). Executive Function in Education: From Theory to Practice. The Guilford Press. https://www.guilford.com
title: Executive function as 'how and when' functions on equal footing with other cognitive domains, not a higher-order pinnacle
description: Denckla argues against hierarchical models that place executive function above other cognitive domains, calling EF "not meta- but intra- and intercognitive." She proposes speaking of EF as encompassing "how and when" functions, analogous to 'where' and 'when' characterizations of perception, and criticizes the 'meta-' prefix of metacognition as disguising the developmental dynamics of EF and leading to neglect of subcortical contributions. EF develops in interactive, looping fashion with other cognitive domains from about 9 months of age into the fourth decade of life.
requirements: Descriptions of EF must account for its reciprocal interaction with language, memory, and motor domains rather than treating it as an overseer
constraints: The account is grounded in a systems-and-circuits analysis of the brain rather than theory-driven distinctions

students with ADHD and learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: planning and organizing academic work
self-monitoring and checking

article_title: Eye-tracking to model and adapt to user meta-cognition in intelligent learning environments
citation: Christina Merten and Cristina Conati. (2005). Eye-Tracking to Model and Adapt to User Meta-cognition in Intelligent Learning Environments. https://www.cs.ubc.ca
title: ACE's Dynamic Bayesian Network student model with gaze-shift and time nodes as independent predictors of implicit self-explanation
description: ACE's student model is a Dynamic Bayesian Network that assesses exploratory behavior at multiple levels of granularity (exploration cases, exercises, units, and categories) together with knowledge nodes. The revised model separates the causes of implicit self-explanation from its effects, encoding gaze shifts and time on action "as independent predictors as in a naïve Bayesian classifier". This structure is highly modular, allowing the gaze shift and time nodes to be used or ignored as needed, and facilitates learning the conditional probability tables from data.
requirements: Conditional probability tables for the time and gaze shift nodes derived from user-study data frequencies
A threshold over implicitSE node probabilities, set via ROC analysis over training data
constraints: The structure assumes independence between time and the presence of gaze shifts, which the data suggests is not strictly true (a small positive correlation)
The model does not currently include the coach's hint-to-self-explain nodes because no hint data was available from the user study
target_learners: University students learning mathematical functions through exploration
target_learning_goals: Effective exploratory learning of mathematical functions
Self-explanation of instructional material
examples: The model was evaluated against a time-only version and a no-self-explanation version using log files and coded self-explanation data from 36 university students

title: ACE: an adaptive learning environment for exploration-based learning of mathematical functions
description: ACE is "an adaptive learning environment for the dom ain of mathematical functions designed to support student learning through exploration." Its activities are divided into units and exercises; in the Plot Unit, learners explore the relationship between a function's graph and equation by moving the graph and changing equation parameters. A coaching component provides tailored hints when the student model predicts that students have difficulty exploring effectively.

article_title: Culture and Mathematics in School: Boundaries between "Cultural" and "Domain" Knowledge in the Mathematics Classroom and Beyond
citation: Na'ilah Suad Nasir, Victoria Hand and Edd V. Taylor. (2008). Culture and Mathematics in School: Boundaries between "Cultural" and "Domain" Knowledge in the Mathematics Classroom and Beyond. Review of Research in Education, Vol. 32. https://doi.org/10.3102/0091732X07308962
title: Reform mathematics classrooms share four design features: problematizing subject matter, distributed authority, student agency, and accountability to others' thinking
description: A line of research on mathematics classroom cultures identified key features of reform classrooms that foster productive, domain-based inquiry. The article enumerates them: "giving students the opportunity to problematize the subject matter in a way that is meaningful to them, distributing authority to them to develop and evaluate their mathematical methods, supporting students in exercising agency," and holding students accountable to each other's mathematical thinking and questioning. The pattern operates at lesson and classroom-community level, instantiated in studies by Boaler, Chazan, Engle & Conant, Hiebert et al., Lampert, and Yackel & Cobb.
requirements: Classroom norms and practices must be organized so students can problematize meaningful subject matter, exercise agency, and hold each other accountable
constraints: The review notes researchers have questioned how what counts as an argument or mathematical activity relates to participation forms students bring from home communities
target_learners: students in K-12 mathematics classrooms, particularly nondominant and marginalized students
target_learning_goals: productive domain-based mathematical inquiry
constructing and responding to mathematical arguments
examples: Lampert's fifth-grade classroom, where a sociomathematical norm emerged concerning how one engages in a mathematical argument
Railside detracked classrooms using Complex Instruction with groupworthy mathematical tasks

article_title: Culture and Mathematics in School: Boundaries between "Cultural" and "Domain" Knowledge in the Mathematics Classroom and Beyond
citation: Na'ilah Suad Nasir, Victoria Hand and Edd V. Taylor. (2008). Culture and Mathematics in School: Boundaries between "Cultural" and "Domain" Knowledge in the Mathematics Classroom and Beyond. Review of Research in Education, Vol. 32. https://doi.org/10.3102/0091732X07308962
title: Tripartite analytic framework of culture in mathematics learning: knowing, learning, and the educational system as cultural
description: The chapter proposes an analytic framework locating the boundary between cultural and domain mathematics knowledge at three levels of social activity: mathematics knowing as a cultural activity (everyday vs. school math structures and discourse), mathematics learning as a cultural enterprise (classroom vs. home and local community), and mathematics education as a cultural system (access to and positioning in the field). The authors state the levels are "analytically distinct" yet "reflexively related," and they shift gaze between levels to capture how researchers perceive culture-math relations. The framework organizes the chapter's literature synthesis.
requirements: Research questions must specify which level of social activity — knowing, learning, or the system — is being analyzed
constraints: The authors treat the three levels as analytically distinct for the chapter's purposes while recognizing they constitute each other
target_learners: nondominant and marginalized students in American schools, particularly students from groups underperforming in mathematics
target_learning_goals: mathematical knowing and reasoning
equitable access to opportunities to learn rich mathematics
examples: The basketball players' study illustrates the first level: practice-linked knowing inaccessible in the math classroom
NCLB policy debates illustrate the third level, the cultural system of mathematics education

article_title: Expert blind spot: When content knowledge eclipses pedagogical content knowledge
citation: Nathan, M. J., Koedinger, K. R., & Alibali, M. W. (2001). Expert Blind Spot: When Content Knowledge Eclipses Pedagogical Content Knowledge. Proceeding of the Third International Conference on Cognitive Science. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Expert+Blind+Spot%22+Nathan+Koedinger+Alibali
title: Expert Blind Spot hypothesis: advanced content knowledge leads experts to assume learners will find formal representations most accessible
description: The Expert Blind Spot (EBS) hypothesis holds that people with greater content expertise "tend to make assumptions about student learning that turn out to be in conflict with students' actual performance and developmental propensities." Experts believe learners, like themselves, find symbolic formalisms most accessible because of their parsimony, while novices actually acquire knowledge through informal and concrete representations. The article develops EBS through mathematics education examples (New Math, teacher difficulty rankings) and language arts case studies.
requirements: Advanced content knowledge in a domain, unaccompanied by well-developed pedagogical content knowledge
constraints: The article frames EBS for mathematics and language arts education settings
target_learners: middle school, high school and college students
target_learning_goals: mathematical reasoning and algebra problem solving
literary comprehension and English instruction
examples: The New Math movement of the 1950s, which the authors attribute to mathematicians designing curricula around set theory and number theory with little regard to how the domain was to be learned or taught
key_sources: Nathan, M. J., Koedinger, K. R., & Alibali, M. W. (2001). Expert Blind Spot: When Content Knowledge Eclipses Pedagogical Content Knowledge. Proceeding of the Third International Conference on Cognitive Science. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Expert+Blind+Spot%22+Nathan+Koedinger+Alibali

article_title: Expert blind spot: When content knowledge eclipses pedagogical content knowledge
citation: Nathan, M. J., Koedinger, K. R., & Alibali, M. W. (2001). Expert Blind Spot: When Content Knowledge Eclipses Pedagogical Content Knowledge. Proceeding of the Third International Conference on Cognitive Science. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Expert+Blind+Spot%22+Nathan+Koedinger+Alibali
title: Teachers should integrate assessment practices that challenge their assumptions about students' mathematical development
description: Because advanced content knowledge can produce expert-based views of curricula at odds with the learning process, the article argues teachers should "integrate assessment practices in their classroom curricula that have the potential to challenge their assumptions about mathematical development in their students." This grounds instruction in students' actual performance rather than in the teacher's own expert intuitions, and underscores the need for empirically based theories of instruction.
requirements: Assessment practices embedded in classroom curricula that reveal students' actual performance and developmental propensities
constraints: The article develops this recommendation specifically for mathematics and language arts instruction
target_learners: middle school, high school and college students
target_learning_goals: aligning instruction with students' actual developmental processes in mathematics and language arts
examples: Nathan & Koedinger (2000b) compared teachers' difficulty rankings against ninth graders' actual problem-solving performance, revealing high school teachers' rankings were unrelated to student performance

article_title: Snapshot Report – First-Year Persistence and Retention
citation: First-Year Persistence and Retention. (2017). National Student Clearinghouse Snapshot Report. https://nscresearchcenter.org/wp-content/uploads/NSC_SnapshotReport28_PersistenceRetention_Data_Tables.xlsx
title: National Student Clearinghouse first-year persistence and retention snapshot report and downloadable data tables
description: A National Student Clearinghouse snapshot report series tracking first-year persistence (continued enrollment at any institution) and retention (continued enrollment at the starting institution) for fall entering cohorts, with data current through fall 2016. The report defines its measures and cohort-selection rules and states that "Data tables for this snapshot may be downloaded from the NSC Research Center website" as an Excel file. It is sponsored in part by the Lumina Foundation.
requirements: Requires Clearinghouse enrollment and degree records covering participating institutions, with first-time status confirmed from historical records showing no prior college enrollment in the four years prior to the cohort year
constraints: Race and ethnicity data coverage is incomplete (79 percent of the fall 2015 cohort overall; 46 percent in the four-year for-profit sector, for which disaggregated results were omitted)

Beginning with fall 2015, non-degree-seeking students are reported separately, which the report says caused the 2015 spike in part-time retention rate; international students are now included and prior years restated
target_learners: first-time college students in U.S. higher education
target_learning_goals: institutional measurement of first-year student persistence and retention
examples: The report disaggregates fall 2015 rates by enrollment intensity, race and ethnicity, age at entry, and institutional sector, with trend figures covering 2009-2015 cohorts

article_title: Alternate reality gaming and convergence culture
citation: Henrik Örnebring. (2007). Alternate reality gaming and convergence culture: The case of Alias. International Journal of Cultural Studies 10(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/1367877907083079
title: Hierarchy-of-meaning critique of convergence culture: an identifiable ur-text marketed through secondary texts
description: The article proposes a corrective to Jenkins' convergence culture concept. Rather than convergence dissolving text boundaries into decentralized trans-media narratives, it argues convergence creates new opportunities to market a specific text through other texts, with a 'hierarchy of meaning' among texts and a clearly identifiable ur-text (the Alias TV series) marketed through books, comics and ARGs. Reverse flows, where the TV series takes up threads from other media texts, are described as much rarer.
requirements: A commercially produced flagship text (the ur-text) whose fictional universe can be extended across other media platforms.
constraints: The account is developed from analysis of ARGs tied to one TV franchise; the article notes industry ARGs based on existing properties are often more circumscribed and redundant than Jenkins would care to admit.
target_learners: fans and audiences participating in trans-media fictional worlds
target_learning_goals: understanding how participatory media engagement is shaped by commercial production logic
examples: The article reads the Season 1 and Season 2 Alias ARGs as 'add-ons' subordinate to the main text, using a licensing logic it describes as more 'old Hollywood' than new.
key_sources: Henrik Örnebring. (2007). Alternate reality gaming and convergence culture: The case of Alias. International Journal of Cultural Studies 10(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/1367877907083079

article_title: Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia
citation: Innwoo Park and Michael J. Hannafin. (1993). Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia. Educational Technology Research and Development, Vol. 41, No. 3, pp. 63-85. http://www.jstor.org/stable/30218388
title: A three-foundations by three-sources framework for organizing research and theory on interactive multimedia
description: The article proposes a matrix framework for organizing research and theory relevant to interactive multimedia design. As printed, "The matrix shown in Table 1 organizes existing research and theory according to foundations--psychological, pedagogical, technological--and basic sources-general, component, primary." Foundations represent fundamental influences on learning-system design, while sources represent how generalizable the principles are, from media-independent psychological theory to capabilities of specific interactive multimedia technologies. The framework is used throughout the article to root each design principle in identifiable empirical and theoretical referents.
requirements: Design decisions must draw on multiple foundations together, since in practice the foundations and sources interact rather than being applied in isolation
constraints: The principles and implications derived are explicitly not all-inclusive, but represent the range of empirically referenced guidelines extractable from the framework
target_learners: designers and developers of interactive multimedia learning systems
target_learning_goals: grounding interactive multimedia design decisions in empirical research and theory
examples: Table 2 maps specific concepts and authors, such as schema theory, dual coding, anchored instruction, and disorientation, into the framework's cells
key_sources: Innwoo Park and Michael J. Hannafin. (1993). Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia. Educational Technology Research and Development, Vol. 41, No. 3, pp. 63-85. http://www.jstor.org/stable/30218388

article_title: Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia
citation: Innwoo Park and Michael J. Hannafin. (1993). Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia. Educational Technology Research and Development, Vol. 41, No. 3, pp. 63-85. http://www.jstor.org/stable/30218388
title: Embed structural aids and generative activities so learners construct their own meaning
description: This principle holds that multimedia should support learners in selecting, organizing, and integrating content while prompting them to generate personal meaning. The article states that "Meaning is generated by the learner, not imposed on the learner through activities and examples," drawing on Wittrock's generative learning account. Structural organizers such as headings, lesson-structure introductions, summaries, and elaboration strategies should be embedded so learners integrate organized information into existing knowledge structures.
requirements: Structural aids must help learners identify and interpret relevant knowledge, processes guided more explicitly in traditional approaches
constraints: Learners' generated meaning may or may not parallel the designer's intended meaning
target_learners: learners using interactive multimedia systems
target_learning_goals: comprehension and integration of new knowledge with existing knowledge
examples: The article recommends introducing lesson structure, using headings to discriminate essential from supporting concepts, and summarizing key relationships among content
key_sources: Innwoo Park and Michael J. Hannafin. (1993). Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia. Educational Technology Research and Development, Vol. 41, No. 3, pp. 63-85. http://www.jstor.org/stable/30218388

article_title: Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia
citation: Innwoo Park and Michael J. Hannafin. (1993). Empirically-Based Guidelines for the Design of Interactive Multimedia. Educational Technology Research and Development, Vol. 41, No. 3, pp. 63-85. http://www.jstor.org/stable/30218388
title: Support multiple perspectives and cross-referencing to build cognitive flexibility with ill-structured knowledge
description: For ill-structured knowledge, instruction that oversimplifies complex concepts produces rigid cognitive structures that interfere with transfer. The article notes that "Spiro and Feltovich (1991) applied cognitive flexibility theory to the design of hypertext," enabling learners to represent knowledge from different perspectives and understand when and how knowledge applies. Interactive multimedia should provide design overlays that allow the same resources to be used differently according to pedagogical and psychological requirements.
requirements: Design overlays must supply a coherent learning system despite resources that differ in form and reflect different psychological and pedagogical perspectives
constraints: The issue is not technological connectivity but the human rationale for making connections
target_learners: learners studying ill-structured, complex domains
target_learning_goals: cognitive flexibility and transfer of complex knowledge
examples: Overlays might create chronological sequences of events, support student-centered research toward solving a problem, or link conceptual or temporal associations

article_title: An Examination of the Effects of ADHD Coaching on University Students' Executive Functioning
citation: Parker, D. R., Field Hoffman, S., Sawilowsky, S., & Rolands, L. (2010). An Examination of the Effects of ADHD Coaching on University Students' Executive Functioning. Journal of Postsecondary Education and Disability, 24(2), 115-132. https://www.edgefoundation.org
title: Inquiry model of ADHD coaching
description: The article describes ADHD coaching as an "inquiry" model that contrasts with didactic academic services such as tutoring or strategy instruction. Rather than telling students what to do, "coaches use speciﬁc types of questions to model effective executive functioning and to elicit students' own ideas as they increase their capacity to clarify, plan, and take action on goals." Coaches' questions promote reflection and more accurate self-awareness, after which coaches hold clients accountable for acting on their plans, so students learn what supports or restricts their goal attainment.
requirements: Coaches with specialized training and experience coaching students with ADHD
Regular accountability check-ins between sessions
constraints: Developed as a private practice model; distinct from therapy, tutoring, and strategy instruction
target_learners: college students with ADHD
target_learning_goals: executive functioning and self-regulation
academic goal attainment
examples: Coaches asked questions such as "What's important for you to remember as you go through your week?" instead of telling students how to organize a calendar system
key_sources: Parker, D. R., Field Hoffman, S., Sawilowsky, S., & Rolands, L. (2010). An Examination of the Effects of ADHD Coaching on University Students' Executive Functioning. Journal of Postsecondary Education and Disability, 24(2), 115-132. https://www.edgefoundation.org

article_title: An Examination of the Effects of ADHD Coaching on University Students' Executive Functioning
citation: Parker, D. R., Field Hoffman, S., Sawilowsky, S., & Rolands, L. (2010). An Examination of the Effects of ADHD Coaching on University Students' Executive Functioning. Journal of Postsecondary Education and Disability, 24(2), 115-132. https://www.edgefoundation.org
title: Edge Foundation coaching model
description: The Edge Foundation coaching model is the intervention evaluated in this pilot study. Implementation "begins with a two-hour intake session between the coach and student over the phone," followed by weekly pre-scheduled phone calls of approximately 30 minutes plus brief e-mail, text, or follow-up calls as needed. "Edge coaches in particular work with students in seven major areas: scheduling, goal setting, conﬁdence building, organizing, focusing, prioritizing, and persisting at tasks." Coaches help students assess environments, set goals, set structures, and monitor progress through regular check-ins.
requirements: Coaches must complete a specialized training program focused on high school and college students with ADHD
At least 60 hours of prior coaching training for accreditation
A minimum of two years of coaching experience with at least 10 clients
constraints: Delivered remotely by phone and electronic messages rather than in person
target_learners: college students with ADHD
target_learning_goals: scheduling, goal setting, organizing, focusing, prioritizing, and persisting at tasks
examples: Seven undergraduates received weekly half-hour phone coaching sessions across one semester in the pilot study

article_title: Learning styles concepts and evidence
citation: Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D., & Bjork, R. (2009). Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, Volume 9 Number 3. https://journals.sagepub.com/
title: Crossover-interaction criteria framework for validating learning-styles interventions
description: The review defines a four-part experimental design that any credible validation of learning-styles-based instruction must satisfy: learners are classified by learning style, randomly assigned to at least two instructional methods, all take the same achievement test, and results must show a crossover interaction such that "the learning method that optimizes test performance of one learning-style group is different than the learning method that optimizes the test performance of a second learning-style group." The framework distinguishes acceptable evidence (Figs. 1A–1C) from interactions that look like crossovers only when method is plotted on the horizontal axis. It also separates the broad learning-styles hypothesis from the specific meshing hypothesis.
requirements: Studies must classify learners by style measure, randomly assign within style groups to multiple methods, and give all subjects the same achievement test
constraints: A crossover with instructional method on the horizontal axis does not validate the hypothesis; the style variable must be on the horizontal axis
The framework requires only the crossover interaction, not that the optimal method match each group's style (the meshing hypothesis)
target_learners: K-12 through graduate school students
target_learning_goals: Matching instructional presentation format to learners' assessed learning style
examples: Figures 1A–1C illustrate acceptable crossover patterns; Figures 1D–1I and Figure 2 show statistically significant interactions that still provide no support because one method optimizes performance for all learners
key_sources: Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D., & Bjork, R. (2009). Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, Volume 9 Number 3. https://journals.sagepub.com/

article_title: Learning styles concepts and evidence
citation: Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D., & Bjork, R. (2009). Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, Volume 9 Number 3. https://journals.sagepub.com/
title: Do not adopt learning-styles assessments in general educational practice; devote resources to practices with strong evidence bases
description: The review recommends that, given the absence of adequate evidence for learning-styles-based instruction, educators should not incorporate learning-styles assessments into general practice. It states that "limited education resources would better be devoted to adopting other educational practices that have a strong evidence base, of which there are an increasing number." Any further research on learning-styles assessment should use designs capable of detecting the required crossover interaction.
requirements: Any future validation research must classify learners by style, randomly assign methods within style groups, use a common outcome test, and test for a style-by-method crossover interaction
constraints: The review does not claim all versions of learning styles have been refuted; many remain untested, so this is a recommendation against current adoption, not a conclusive refutation
target_learners: Students at all educational levels, kindergarten through graduate school
target_learning_goals: Allocating instructional resources to evidence-based practices rather than style-matched instruction
examples: The review's search found at most one arguable positive study and several methodologically strong studies with negative results, leading to the conclusion that classroom application of learning styles is unwarranted at present
key_sources: Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D., & Bjork, R. (2009). Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, Volume 9 Number 3. https://journals.sagepub.com/

article_title: Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning
citation: Pásztor, Attila, Andrea Magyar, Anita Pásztor-Kovács, and Attila Rausch. 2022. Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning. Journal of Intelligence 10: 59. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10030059
title: Online figurative assessment tool measuring six inductive reasoning processes
description: A domain-general computer-based test of 54 figurative items, nine for each of Klauer's six inductive reasoning processes, administered through the eDia system. Item formats include class formation, odd-one-out, 4-fold cross classification, figural analogies, disturbed series, and matrices. The article reports that "The reliability of the whole test was high, Cronbach's alpha = .91" and that subtest reliabilities were acceptable.
requirements: Administration in school computer labs via the eDia platform within a 45-min lesson
constraints: Subtest reliabilities for Discrimination (.61) and Differentiating relationships (.63) were below .70
target_learners: fifth-grade students
target_learning_goals: inductive reasoning processes (generalization, discrimination, cross classification, recognizing relationships, differentiating relationships, system construction)
examples: The test was administered in schools' computer labs; average testing time was 26.6 min (SD = 7.0 min)
key_sources: Pásztor, Attila, Andrea Magyar, Anita Pásztor-Kovács, and Attila Rausch. 2022. Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning. Journal of Intelligence 10: 59. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10030059

article_title: Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning
citation: Pásztor, Attila, Andrea Magyar, Anita Pásztor-Kovács, and Attila Rausch. 2022. Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning. Journal of Intelligence 10: 59. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10030059
title: Klauer's model of inductive reasoning as six comparison-based processes
description: Klauer's theory defines inductive reasoning as detecting regularities and irregularities through comparison, crossed by two facets: whether similarity, difference, or both must be detected (facet A) and whether attributes or relations are involved (facet B), yielding six processes: Generalization, Discrimination, Cross classification, Recognizing relationships, Differentiating relationships, and System construction. The article states "the core process of inductive reasoning is comparison" and distinguishes inductive reasoning from inductive inference, which goes beyond the situation to unobserved cases. The study operationalized each process with specific item formats such as class formation, analogies, and matrices.
requirements: Assessment and training tasks must be designed per process, with item formats matched to the cognitive operation required (e.g., matrices for System construction)
constraints: The article notes a prior study (de Koning et al. 2003) found the construct unidimensional, and the 1-dimensional model's fit was also acceptable in this study
target_learners: fifth-grade students (model tested across ages in prior programs)
target_learning_goals: inductive reasoning: detecting regularities and irregularities in attributes and relations
examples: The online figurative test operationalized each process: class formation for Generalization, odd-one-out for Discrimination, 4-fold schemes for Cross classification, analogies for Recognizing relationships, disturbed series for Differentiating relationships, matrices for System construction
key_sources: Pásztor, Attila, Andrea Magyar, Anita Pásztor-Kovács, and Attila Rausch. 2022. Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning. Journal of Intelligence 10: 59. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10030059

article_title: Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning
citation: Pásztor, Attila, Andrea Magyar, Anita Pásztor-Kovács, and Attila Rausch. 2022. Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning. Journal of Intelligence 10: 59. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10030059
title: Save the Tree of Life: online game-based training program for inductive reasoning in mathematical content
description: An online training program of 120 learning tasks (20 per inductive reasoning process) embedded in third- and fourth-grade mathematical content, framed by a backstory in which a hero collects potions of water of life to save the Tree of Life. Each task has a feedback loop: immediate feedback, then "constructive feedback which was always formulated to encourage the application of the inductive reasoning process", a Help button with content guidance, and after a third unsuccessful trial the solution with an explanation. Correct answers receive reinforcing feedback naming the applied thinking process to strengthen metacognitive awareness.
requirements: Delivery through the eLea platform in school computer labs; teachers supervise but give no additional instructional support; five weekly sessions of 24 tasks each
constraints: The intervention lasted five weeks among fifth graders; the corrected effect size of .38 accounts for the control group's significant improvement
target_learners: fifth-grade students
target_learning_goals: inductive reasoning processes and mathematical content knowledge (operations, relational symbols, sequences, measurement, geometry)
examples: Students collected on average 19, 19, 17, 16, and 16 potions of water of life out of a maximum of 24 per session, which the authors read as engagement with the game
key_sources: Pásztor, Attila, Andrea Magyar, Anita Pásztor-Kovács, and Attila Rausch. 2022. Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning. Journal of Intelligence 10: 59. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10030059

article_title: Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning
citation: Pásztor, Attila, Andrea Magyar, Anita Pásztor-Kovács, and Attila Rausch. 2022. Online Assessment and Game-Based Development of Inductive Reasoning. Journal of Intelligence 10: 59. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10030059
title: Design game-based cognitive training with graduated feedback loops that name the target thinking process
description: In the Save the Tree of Life program, every learning task was equipped with a graduated feedback loop: an initial unsolved attempt, then process-oriented constructive feedback, then content-specific help via a Help button, then a rephrased prompt, and finally the full solution with explanation after a third failure. The article states this design was intended "to reduce the frustration of the students and to facilitate the learning process and understanding", and that reinforcing feedback on correct solutions gave "an indication of the applied thinking process with the aim of strengthening the learners' metacognitive awareness".
requirements: Feedback messages must be formulated to encourage the specific inductive reasoning process required by the task; a Help button provides mathematical-content guidance; the solution with explanation appears only after repeated failure
constraints: The article reports the design's intent and the program's overall effectiveness; it does not isolate the feedback mechanism's separate contribution
target_learners: fifth-grade students working through mathematical learning tasks
target_learning_goals: inductive reasoning processes and metacognitive awareness of the thinking process applied
examples: For an analogy task the system prompted: 'Think again! What is the relationship between the colored shapes and the numbers on the tags?'; for a disturbed-series task the Help button explained unit conversions such as 1 dg = 10 g
