article_title: Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs
citation: Chris Piech, Jonathan Huang, Zhenghao Chen, Chuong Do, Andrew Ng, Daphne Koller. (2013). Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.2579
title: Probabilistic peer grading models (PG1, PG2, PG3) representing grader bias, reliability, temporal coherence, and coupled score-reliability
description: The article introduces a family of Bayesian models in which each submission has a latent true score, each grader a bias (tendency to "inﬂate or deﬂate her assessment") and a reliability (precision of assessments after bias correction). PG1 places priors over these latents; PG2 adds temporal coherence of bias across assignments (consecutive-assignment bias correlation of 0.33); PG3 couples a grader's reliability to her own grade. Inference uses Gibbs sampling or EM, producing posterior belief distributions over grades rather than single scores.
requirements: Multiple peer grades per submission (the studied courses used four peer grades per student)
Grades normalized to a consistent scale across assignments for the temporal-coherence model (z-scores)
constraints: The article focuses only on the dynamics of bias, not true scores or reliabilities, across assignments

PG3's dependence of a submission's score on graders' scores is weak by design; the authors exclude variables like race, ethnicity, gender, and student-grade temporal coherence (0.46 Pearson) on fairness grounds
target_learners: MOOC students grading peers in large open online courses
target_learning_goals: Accurate and fair assessment of complex, open-ended assignments such as design tasks, essays, and proofs
examples: The models were evaluated on two Coursera HCI offerings with 63,199 peer grades, using supergraded ground-truth submissions averaging 160 assessments each
key_sources: Chris Piech, Jonathan Huang, Zhenghao Chen, Chuong Do, Andrew Ng, Daphne Koller. (2013). Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.2579

article_title: Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs
citation: Chris Piech, Jonathan Huang, Zhenghao Chen, Chuong Do, Andrew Ng, Daphne Koller. (2013). Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.2579
title: Coursera HCI peer grading dataset: 63,199 peer grades from 7,240 students across two course offerings
description: Two consecutive Coursera offerings of the Human Computer Interaction course taught by Scott Klemmer, using a calibrated peer grading system. Per assignment, each student evaluated five randomly selected submissions (one a ground-truth submission) on a rubric and was evaluated by four classmates; the final score was the median of peer grades. The dataset comprises 3,607 students (HCI1) and 3,633 students (HCI2), 13,972 submissions, and 63,199 peer grades — described as "the largest peer grading networks analysed to date".
constraints: HCI2 was used as a hold-out set; models were formulated only on HCI1
A small number (3-5) of submissions per assignment were marked as ground truth and supergraded with on average 160 assessments
target_learners: MOOC students in the HCI course offerings
target_learning_goals: Peer assessment of creative web-site design assignments
examples: Ground-truth submissions were graded by course staff and students were not told which submissions belonged to the ground truth set
key_sources: Chris Piech, Jonathan Huang, Zhenghao Chen, Chuong Do, Andrew Ng, Daphne Koller. (2013). Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.2579

article_title: The Role of Goal Orientation in Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Paul R. Pintrich. (2000). The Role of Goal Orientation in Self-Regulated Learning. Handbook of Self-Regulation, Academic Press. https://www.elsevier.com
title: Pintrich's four-phase, four-area framework for self-regulated learning
description: The chapter proposes a general SRL framework displayed as a table crossing four phases of regulation with four areas for regulation. The phases are described as follows: "Phase 1 involves planning and goal setting as well as activation of perceptions and knowledge of the task and context and the self in relationship to the task," followed by monitoring, control and regulation, and reactions and reflections. The columns cover cognition, motivation/affect, behavior, and context, with the context column included because the personal self actively attempts to monitor and change the environment.
requirements: Learners must be assumed able to monitor, control, and regulate aspects of their own cognition, motivation, behavior, and environment
constraints: The phases are a heuristic; the chapter states there is no strong assumption that the phases are hierarchically or linearly structured such that earlier phases always must occur before later phases
target_learners: students in school and classroom contexts
target_learning_goals: academic learning across domains
self-regulation of cognition, motivation, behavior, and context

article_title: Effect of screen presentation on text reading and revising
citation: Annie Piolat, Jean-Yves Roussey and Olivier Thunin. (1997). Effects of screen presentation on text reading and revising. International Journal of Human-Computer Studies. https://doi.org/10.1006/ijhc.1997.0145
title: Page and Scroll screen-presentation prototypes
description: Two HyperTalk word-processing prototypes compared in both experiments. The Page prototype displayed the text page-by-page with numbered page icons, so "the position of the visible page relative to whole text was always available to participants". The Scroll prototype reproduced conventional scrolling with arrows but, in Experiment 1, deliberately omitted the scroll box, leaving users without an indication of their location in the text. Both showed the same window size and amount of text.
requirements: In Experiment 2 the Page prototype required a module that reformatted text after each correction to keep the page-based layout stable
constraints: The display window was purposely made small (18 lines of about 50 characters) so a short 574-word document could be used with low processing load
target_learners: undergraduate psychology students unfamiliar with word processing
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension and spatial encoding of text
revising and error correction in written texts
examples: Experiment 1 used the Page prototype with four page icons for reading; Experiment 2 used five icons with editing functions for revising

article_title: Effects of a 6-week, co-taught literacy unit on preservice special educators' literacy-education knowledge
citation: Pufpaff, L. A., & Yssel, N. (2010). Effects of a 6-Week, Co-Taught Literacy Unit on Preservice Special Educators' Literacy-Education Knowledge. Psychology in the Schools, 47(5). https://doi.org/10.1002/pits.20485
title: Six-week co-taught literacy unit embedded in special education methods courses
description: An intensive 6-week literacy unit embedded within two existing special education methods courses (mild interventions and intense interventions licensure programs) at a midsize Midwest university. "The 6-week curriculum was developed based on the NRP's (2000) Þve key areas essential for learning to read (i.e., phonemic awareness, phonics, ßuency, vocabulary, and comprehension)" plus emergent literacy and writing/spelling. The unit aimed to give candidates knowledge and skills to implement research-based practices suited to individualized student needs, not a curriculum to teach from directly.
requirements: Candidates must be enrolled in both special education methods courses, which are restricted to students accepted into the Teaching Curriculum for either licensure program.
constraints: The unit is taught during the second half of the semester, which "leaves little time for participants to plan and implement literacy assessment and intervention activities at the conclusion of the unit."
target_learners: Preservice special education teacher candidates in mild and intense interventions licensure programs
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of literacy assessment and instruction across the five critical components of reading, emergent literacy, and writing/spelling for diverse learners with disabilities
examples: Each week addressed one critical component of reading, with the sixth week focused on handwriting, composition, and spelling; an emergent literacy presentation was added in the first week.
key_sources: Pufpaff, L. A., & Yssel, N. (2010). Effects of a 6-Week, Co-Taught Literacy Unit on Preservice Special Educators' Literacy-Education Knowledge. Psychology in the Schools, 47(5). https://doi.org/10.1002/pits.20485

article_title: Effects of a 6-week, co-taught literacy unit on preservice special educators' literacy-education knowledge
citation: Pufpaff, L. A., & Yssel, N. (2010). Effects of a 6-Week, Co-Taught Literacy Unit on Preservice Special Educators' Literacy-Education Knowledge. Psychology in the Schools, 47(5). https://doi.org/10.1002/pits.20485
title: Two-presentation weekly structure pairing typically developing learners' perspective with exceptional learning needs perspective
description: Within each week of the literacy unit, the targeted topic was addressed in two presentations. "During the Þrst presentation each week, the targeted topic was addressed using a chapter from Bursuck and Damer (2007) as the anchor" from the perspective of typically developing learners; "during the second presentation each week, the same topic was addressed from the perspective of students with exceptional learning needs, again using research evidence to guide the content." Assessment and intervention addressed a continuum of strategies for students with disabilities ranging from mild to severe.
requirements: Faculty expertise divided by topic strength, with one faculty member presenting in the first weekly session and topics divided based on perceived strength.
constraints: The curriculum had to address emergent literacy across K-12 grade levels because both licensure programs are K-12.
target_learners: Preservice special education teacher candidates preparing to teach across K-12 grade levels and disability populations
target_learning_goals: Applying research-based literacy assessment and instruction to both typically developing learners and students with exceptional learning needs
examples: Faculty shared personal experiences with literacy assessment and instruction of students with exceptional learning needs to illustrate practical application across disability populations.

article_title: The Effects of Game and Student Characteristics on Persistence in Educational Games: A Hierarchical Linear Modeling Approach
citation: Rahimi, S., Shute, V., & Zhang, Q. (2021). The effects of game and student characteristics on persistence in educational games: A hierarchical linear modeling approach. International Journal of Technology in Education and Science (IJTES), 5(2), 141-165. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijtes.118
title: Stealth assessment of persistence via in-game time-on-task measures
description: Stealth assessment embeds evidence-centered-design models into digital games, collecting log-file performance data as learners play and using statistical methods such as Bayes nets to make real-time inferences about hard-to-measure competencies. In this study, persistence was operationalized as time spent on ultimately unsolved problems plus time above the per-problem average on solved problems, yielding 3,803 data points from 137 students. The authors state that "stealth assessment (Shute, 2011) uses technology-rich environments (e.g., digital games) as vehicles for assessment." Prior work validated such in-game measures against external performance-based measures.
requirements: Log files capturing timestamps of gameplay events per problem
A defined operationalization of persistence (time on unsolved problems and above-average time on solved problems)
constraints: The authors caution that persistence is different from the difficulty of game problems, since harder problems can simply take more time; their measure included unsolved and above-average-time solved problems to partially separate the two
target_learners: Eighth and ninth grade students (grades 7-10 are the game's target population)
target_learning_goals: Persistence as a 21st-century skill
examples: The study parsed Physics Playground log files, coding trophy = none for unsolved problems and selecting solved problems whose solution time exceeded the per-problem average

title: Physics Playground (PP): a 2D physics game with stealth assessment
description: Physics Playground is a problem-based, 2-dimensional game in which each problem's goal is hitting a red balloon with a green ball by drawing simple machines (ramp, lever, springboard, pendulum). The version used had seven playgrounds with 74 problems arrayed easy to difficult, nonlinear free choice of problems, and gold trophies for efficient solutions and silver trophies for other solutions. The authors note that "Across various studies (e.g., Kim & Shute, 2015; Shute et al., 2015; Shute & Ventura, 2013; Wang, 2017), the game has been shown to support students' acquisition of physics concepts via gameplay."
requirements: Players draw simple-machine objects to solve problems; log files record events such as trophies and timestamps
constraints: Only GM difficulty was used to determine the order of problems in this version; problems are presented linearly even though play is nonlinear
target_learners: Students in grades 7-10 learning Newtonian physics
target_learning_goals: Physics concept understanding (force and motion, momentum and energy, torque) and persistence
examples: 137 eighth and ninth graders played the game across four days in a computer lab for about 2.5-3 hours of testing

article_title: Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education
citation: Ritter, S., Anderson, J. R., Koedinger, K. R., & Corbett, A. (2007). Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2007, 14 (2), 249-255. https://www.carnegielearning.com
title: ACT-R theory of cognition as the theoretical basis of Cognitive Tutors
description: ACT-R is a unified theory of cognition implemented as a computer program, which the authors use as the primary theoretical basis of Cognitive Tutors. It holds that there are two basic types of knowledge, procedural and declarative, and that "both declarative and procedural knowledge become strengthened with use (and weakened with disuse)." Learning is a gradual process of encoding, strengthening, and proceduralizing knowledge, and education is most efficient when it focuses students on individual knowledge components of relatively low strength. In the tutor, an active cognitive model traces student actions and tracks skill performance over time.
requirements: A precise, implemented cognitive model of the knowledge components of the target task, since the theory does not itself specify the particular skills for a domain
constraints: A full explanation of ACT-R is beyond the scope of the article; the theory does not specify the particular skills that comprise domain tasks, which must be identified through applied research
target_learners: middle and high school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: mathematical cognition and procedural skill in algebra and geometry
examples: The Cognitive Tutor software includes an active cognitive model that performs model tracing of student actions and tracks individual skill performance in a skillometer, used for problem selection and mastery learning
key_sources: Ritter, S., Anderson, J. R., Koedinger, K. R., & Corbett, A. (2007). Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2007, 14 (2), 249-255. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03194060

article_title: Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education
citation: Ritter, S., Anderson, J. R., Koedinger, K. R., & Corbett, A. (2007). Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2007, 14 (2), 249-255. https://www.carnegielearning.com
title: Carnegie Learning Cognitive Tutor curricula (text plus software plus teacher training)
description: A complete middle- and high-school mathematics course combining text, Cognitive Tutor software, ancillary materials, and teacher training. The inclusion of text supports activities such as "collaboration, diagramming, and writing about mathematics" that are easier on paper, and positions the software as part of primary instruction rather than a bonus or review activity. Pilot implementations led to a model in which students used the software 2 days per week, with classroom activities structured by the text on the other 3 days each week.
requirements: Teacher training and integration into broader classroom goals, since earlier tutors' success appeared highly dependent on the teacher's ability to integrate the software
target_learners: middle and high school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: algebra and geometry skills, problem solving, and multiple representations
examples: Students used the software 2 days per week with text-structured classroom activities on the other 3 days each week

article_title: Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education
citation: Ritter, S., Anderson, J. R., Koedinger, K. R., & Corbett, A. (2007). Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2007, 14 (2), 249-255. https://www.carnegielearning.com
title: Large-scale Cognitive Tutor log dataset from over 7,000 pre-algebra students
description: The article reports a collected dataset from over 7,000 students using Cognitive Tutor in a pre-algebra class, comprising over 35 million observations, amounting to observing an action for each student about every 9.5 sec. The authors expect this database will let them detect subtler factors affecting learning, including the effectiveness of individual tasks, hints, and feedback patterns, and they are starting to apply microgenetic methods to identify key learning experiences.
requirements: Aggregation of student data over the Internet and an expanded customer base to enable deep and broad analysis of student cognition
target_learners: pre-algebra students
target_learning_goals: understanding students' mathematical cognition and improving instruction
examples: The authors are applying microgenetic methods to identify key learning experiences that could contribute to better cognitive models of individual differences

article_title: Evidence-Based Strategies for Reading Instruction of Older Students with Learning Disabilities
citation: Roberts, G., Torgesen, J. K., Boardman, A., & Scammacca, N. (2008). Evidence-Based Strategies for Reading Instruction of Older Students with Learning Disabilities. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 63–69. http://www.centeroninstruction.org/
title: Five adjusted essential areas of reading instruction for older struggling readers
description: The article adapts the National Reading Panel's five essential areas of early reading instruction for older struggling readers, replacing phonemic awareness and phonics with word study and adding motivation. As printed: "for older readers, we would adjust the ﬁve essential areas in the NRP' s report to include these ﬁve areas: (1) word study, (2) ﬂuency, (3) vocabulary, (4) comprehension, and (5) motivation." Each area is then described with features of effective instruction for students in late elementary, middle, and high school.
requirements: Diagnostic testing and analysis to differentiate whether students need advanced word study or continued phonics-level instruction
constraints: Intended for students who continue to struggle with reading in late elementary, middle, and high school, many identified as having LD
target_learners: Older struggling readers with learning disabilities in upper elementary, middle, and high school
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Word reading
Reading motivation
examples: The article organizes its instructional recommendations section by section under these five headings, summarizing meta-analytic evidence for each
key_sources: Roberts, G., Torgesen, J. K., Boardman, A., & Scammacca, N. (2008). Evidence-Based Strategies for Reading Instruction of Older Students with Learning Disabilities. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 63–69. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.00264.x

article_title: Evidence-Based Strategies for Reading Instruction of Older Students with Learning Disabilities
citation: Roberts, G., Torgesen, J. K., Boardman, A., & Scammacca, N. (2008). Evidence-Based Strategies for Reading Instruction of Older Students with Learning Disabilities. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 23(2), 63–69. http://www.centeroninstruction.org/
title: Never substitute wide or repeated reading alone for explicit word study and comprehension strategy instruction
description: The article states plainly that for students with LD, reading practice by itself should not replace explicit instruction: "wide reading or repeated reading by itself should never substitute for systematic, explicit instruction in word study and comprehension strategy use." Fluency instruction may be most effective when combined with word-level and comprehension instruction, since improved fluency frees cognitive resources that strategy instruction helps students use.
requirements: Coordination of fluency practice with focused word-learning instruction tied to the passages used
constraints: Repeated reading gains generalize only to passages sharing many of the same words; effects of differing fluency approaches for older students need additional research
target_learners: Older students with learning disabilities who struggle with reading
target_learning_goals: Reading fluency
Word recognition
Reading comprehension
examples: The article recommends repeated reading of passages with instructional target words embedded in otherwise readable text, and teacher-supported wide reading of texts with a preponderance of known words

article_title: Western science and Islamic learners When disciplines and culture intersect
citation: Ian Robottom and Sharifah Norhaidah. (2008). Western science and Islamic learners: When disciplines and culture intersect. Journal of Research in International Education 7(2). https://doi.org/10.1177/1475240908091302
title: Expanded constructivism: faith- and culture-based dissonances exceed alternative conceptions and should not be treated as misconceptions to be taught out
description: The article proposes that constructivist theory in science education must expand to embrace dissonances rooted in epistemology, ontology and religious commitment. It argues that some constructivist research treats personally constructed meanings that differ from taught science as "misconceptions" to be eliminated, overlooking that for many learners these constructions rest on "much deeper cultural and faith-related beliefs, convictions and commitments." The data from Islamic learners show dissonances "exceed the kind of factors usually referred to in constructivist explanations of the formation of alternative conceptions."
requirements: Recognition that learners' personal biographies continuously shape knowledge acquisition, and that some dissonances are not amenable to change by a well-intentioned teacher
constraints: The article frames this as an interpretation grounded in its Islamic-context studies, not a tested model of conceptual change
target_learners: Islamic-background learners of western science in secondary schools
target_learning_goals: Meaning-making in science education
Reconciling faith-based and scientific knowledge claims
examples: The article reports Malaysian and Australian studies of discord among Muslim science students as the empirical basis for expanding the constructivist concept

article_title: Electronic Versus Print Textbooks: The Influence of Textbook Format on University Students’ Self-Regulated Learning Strategies, Motivation, and Text Anxiety
citation: Amanda J. Rockinson-Szapkiw, Jillian Wendt, and Rebecca Lunde. (2013). Electronic Versus Print Textbooks: The Influence of Textbook Format on University Students' Self-Regulated Learning Strategies, Motivation, and Text Anxiety. American Journal of Distance Education, 27(3), 179-188. https://doi.org/10.1080/08923647.2013.796230
title: Adopt e-textbooks in collegiate classrooms to support students' self-regulated learning strategy use
description: The article recommends offering e-textbooks in collegiate courses because its findings indicate e-textbook users were more likely to employ self-regulated learning strategies while reading. E-textbooks provide "flexible, interactive, manipulative, constructive, active, and searchable elements" that let students make notes, highlight, and explore material nonlinearly. The recommendation rests on a self-selection study with small effect sizes.
requirements: Courses must offer the primary textbook in both e-textbook and print format so students can choose, as the studied bookstore did
constraints: The article reports the effect sizes for the strategy differences were low, indicating little practical significance
Students self-selected format rather than being randomly assigned
Prior studies of e-textbook influence on learning and motivation reported mixed results
target_learners: university undergraduate, masters, and doctoral students in online and face-to-face education courses
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use while reading course textbooks
examples: In the study, 59 face-to-face and online courses offered the primary textbook in both formats during spring 2012, and 106 students chose e-textbooks while 432 chose print

citation: Amanda J. Rockinson-Szapkiw, Jillian Wendt, and Rebecca Lunde. (2013). Electronic Versus Print Textbooks: The Influence of Textbook Format on University Students' Self-Regulated Learning Strategies, Motivation, and Text Anxiety. American Journal of Distance Education, 27(3), 179-188. https://doi.org/10.1080/08923647.2013.796230
title: Self-regulated learning theory as a framework for textbook reading at the university level
description: The article frames textbook reading as a highly autonomous, cognitive and effortful activity governed by self-regulated learning theory. Self-regulated learning is defined as "an active, constructive process whereby learners set goals for their learning and then attempt to monitor, regulate, and control their cognition, motivation, and behavior". The framework comprises two strategies (self-regulation and cognitive strategy use) and two motivational factors (self-efficacy and intrinsic value), which the study measured with the MSLQ and used to test whether textbook format influences strategy use.
requirements: Motivation to read and employment of cognitive strategies while reading are treated as highly autonomous aspects of university-level learning, so learners must self-direct their textbook reading
constraints: The article notes research on e-textbook influence on the academic process is in its infancy and needed prior to widespread adoption
target_learners: university students reading course textbooks in face-to-face or online courses
target_learning_goals: self-regulation of learning
cognitive strategy use during reading
motivation to read
examples: The study operationalized the framework with five MSLQ subscales (text anxiety, cognitive strategy use, self-regulation, self-efficacy, intrinsic value), each with Cronbach's alpha above .70

article_title: Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally
citation: Rogers, P. C., Graham, C. R., & Mayes, C. T. (2007). Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9033-x
title: Four categories of cultural differences affecting cross-cultural online instructional design
description: The study organizes the cultural differences designers encountered into four categories: "general cultural and social expectations, teaching and learning expectations, differences in the use of language and symbols, and technological infrastructure and familiarity." These categories emerged from interviews rather than being imposed from prior frameworks such as Hofstede's, reflecting the study's grounded-theory approach. They serve as a map of where designers should probe learner contexts.
requirements: Designers must investigate each category for the specific learner population rather than assume group-level generalizations apply to individuals
constraints: Categories emerged from 12 practitioners' lived experience in an exploration study; the authors call for research on how each category can be expanded and better measured
target_learners: International and cross-cultural online learners
target_learning_goals: Culturally responsive design of online instruction
examples: Mike described Tongan social protocols around rank affecting reception of distance learning; Ian described Australian indigenous oral traditions complicating literacy assumptions; Joey described unreliable internet access becoming "a barrier and an exclusion instead of an inclusion."
key_sources: Rogers, P. C., Graham, C. R., & Mayes, C. T. (2007). Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9033-x

article_title: Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally
citation: Rogers, P. C., Graham, C. R., & Mayes, C. T. (2007). Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9033-x
title: Bridge-building metaphor for adapting instruction across cultures
description: The article proposes bridge-building as a metaphor for how increased cultural sensitivity changes design practice: designers identify gaps between an instructional experience as designed and learners' expectations and capabilities, then bridge those gaps with additional support. Building bridges stimulates "separating deeper principles from particular application," identifying gaps through immersion, learner feedback in up-front analysis, and formative evaluation, allowing design flexibility, and educating other stakeholders. Shawn emphasized attending to "danger points" where learners may unintentionally misunderstand.
requirements: Designers must discover learners' frames of reference and prerequisite knowledge to locate where bridges are needed
constraints: Derived from practitioner interviews in an exploration study; the authors call for research on how to bridge gaps more effectively
target_learners: International and cross-cultural online learners
target_learning_goals: Making instruction accessible and meaningful across cultural contexts
examples: Rose, developing instruction in Egypt, immersed herself in local environments and used Egyptians' social nature as a bridge toward interaction and team problem solving, also teaching meta-cognitive strategies like brainstorming.
key_sources: Rogers, P. C., Graham, C. R., & Mayes, C. T. (2007). Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9033-x

article_title: Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally
citation: Rogers, P. C., Graham, C. R., & Mayes, C. T. (2007). Cultural competence and instructional design: Exploration research into the delivery of online instruction cross-culturally. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9033-x
title: Design for local context rather than implementing one-size-fits-all content or best practices
description: The article argues that implicit in many online instructional design models is the idea that lesson content determines a one-size-fits-all delivery method, which ignores the differential needs of learners in various contexts. Designers should instead determine priorities that "meet local needs/desires," gain support of influential local people, openly discuss concerns with local staff, and leave social norms and traditions untouched where possible.
requirements: Instructional designers need contact with learners and feedback loops; organizations must allow designer involvement in audience analysis
constraints: The article states changing to a more culturally sensitive design paradigm is difficult given IDT's history of overemphasizing content development
target_learners: International and cross-cultural online learners
target_learning_goals: Relevance and usability of online instruction across cultures
examples: Mike recommended not simply implementing best practices and making the hierarchy a group of facilitators; Carrie described Australian designers demoted to technologist roles producing quick-fix courses without ever meeting students.

article_title: Obtaining more out of less text in CBI: effects of varied text density levels as a function of learner characteristics and control strategy
citation: Ross, S. M., Morrison, G. R., & O'Dell, J. K. (1988). Obtaining More out of Less Text in CBI: Effects of Varied Text Density Levels as a Function of Learner Characteristics and Control Strategy. Educational Communication and Technology, 36(3), 131-142. http://www.jstor.org/stable/30218252
title: Offer low-density text as a standard feature or learner-control option in expository CBI lessons
description: This principle holds that CBI lessons presenting expository material should limit on-screen text to essential words and phrases, since low-density presentations reduced lesson length and reading time without harming learning of facts and concepts. The article recommends that "The availability of low-density text as a standard feature or learner-control option in expository lessons deserves further consideration as a design alternative." It may also make difficult material appear less threatening and easier to read.
requirements: Content must remain unchanged when density is reduced; only modifiers, articles, and non-essential sentences are deleted, keeping the basic information and support material the same.
constraints: The article notes elaborated text should not be discouraged generally, since it is advantageous for learning complex procedural skills and for developing reading and writing skills; low-density use is suggested where displaying long text segments is difficult or costly, as in CBI.
target_learners: undergraduate teacher education majors learning expository statistics content
target_learning_goals: recall of facts and conceptual information, such as central tendency measures
examples: The study developed low-density versions of a five-lesson statistics unit by rules such as reducing sentences to main ideas, using outline form, and deleting non-informative sentences, yielding a 56% word savings with equal achievement.

article_title: A Review of Research in Revising Instructional Text
citation: Mary H. Sawyer. (1991). A Review of Research in Revising Instructional Text. Journal of Reading Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1080/10862969109547744
title: The scenario principle: revising text around human agents, actions, and instantiated contexts based on readers' verbal protocols
description: The scenario principle is a revision framework from the Document Design Project in which text information is "reorganized the information around human agents and their actions" and instantiated with concrete contexts and examples that fill slots in abstract frameworks. It was derived from readers' think-aloud protocols showing that experienced readers radically restructure difficult text into scenarios, and it yielded revision guidelines such as itemizing, turning labels into questions, and scenario-like translations.
requirements: Access to readers' verbal protocols or think-alouds to identify how the target audience actually makes sense of the text
constraints: Developed and validated for functional documents such as regulations, contracts, and insurance policies; the review notes Flower et al. did not test how the scenario principles might best be applied to revising instructional writing
target_learners: Adult readers of public and functional documents, including Medicaid recipients who were typically poor, old, and not well educated
target_learning_goals: Comprehending and correctly using difficult procedural and regulatory text, such as Medicaid forms and insurance policies
examples: Revised headings such as "Who is an eligible student borrower?" replacing "Personal Liability; Occurrence; Social Disadvantage", and the poodle-loss illustration instantiating the insurance concept of Broader Coverage

article_title: Self-efficacy, motivation, and performance
citation: Schunk, D. H. (1995). Self-efficacy, motivation, and performance. Journal of Applied Sport Psychology, 7(2), 112-137. http://www.taylorandfrancis.com/
title: Self-efficacy theory: beliefs about capability shape choice, effort, persistence, and achievement
description: The article presents Bandura's self-efficacy framework, defining self-efficacy as "People's judgments of their capabilities to organize and execute courses of action required to attain designated types of performances." People appraise efficacy from performances, vicarious experiences, persuasion, and physiological reactions. A model (Figure 1) depicts initial efficacy deriving from prior experience, personal qualities, and social support, with task-derived cues feeding back to sustain efficacy and motivation.
requirements: Efficacy information acquired vicariously or persuasively requires validation by actual performance to remain credible
constraints: High self-efficacy will not produce a competent performance when requisite knowledge and skill are lacking
Self-efficacy and outcome expectancies are related but distinct constructs with no automatic relation
target_learners: children in cognitive skill learning
athletes and sport participants
adults in training settings
target_learning_goals: skill acquisition
motivation and persistence
performance improvement
examples: The article reviews interventions using models, goal setting, and feedback as levers for raising self-efficacy across cognitive and sport tasks

article_title: Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age
citation: Daniel L. Schwartz and Dylan Arena. (2013). Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age. The MIT Press. http://www.macfound.org
title: Choice as the interpretative framework for learning assessment
description: This framework holds that "Choice, rather than knowledge, should be the interpretative frame within which learning assessments are organized." The authors argue education's fundamental goal is preparing students to act independently and make good choices, so assessments should evaluate learning-relevant choices about whether, what, how, and when to learn. They contend current assessments primarily measure accrued knowledge and skills, which sends the wrong message about what counts as useful learning, and that digital technologies finally make choice-centered assessment possible.
requirements: Assessments must focus on learning-relevant choices such as how and what to learn, not all choices, and must not enforce beliefs outside publicly sponsored education such as political or religious matters
constraints: The authors restrict the framework to learning-relevant choices, explicitly excluding choices outside the purview of education
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students assessed in formal and informal settings
target_learning_goals: Preparing students to make good learning choices and act independently
examples: The Ohno! Has Talent choicelet assesses the choice to engage in critical thinking by tracking which color-mixing charts students choose to believe
key_sources: Daniel L. Schwartz and Dylan Arena. (2013). Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age. The MIT Press. http://www.macfound.org

article_title: Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age
citation: Daniel L. Schwartz and Dylan Arena. (2013). Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age. The MIT Press. http://www.macfound.org
title: The isolation of knowledge as a critique of knowledge-based assessment
description: The report argues the construct of knowledge is a mismatch for the practical aims of assessment because of what the authors call the isolation of knowledge: "it is isolated from the bulk of social science research; as a description of a mental state, it is isolated from context; and perhaps worst of all, as an organization of information, it is isolated from the rest of the person." Most social sciences focus on choice rather than knowledge, so knowledge-based assessment cannot connect to social processes or to outcomes such as motivation and responses to feedback. The authors present this as a one-sided argument to dethrone knowledge as the central assessed outcome.
requirements: An alternative assessment frame must capture outcomes knowledge tests miss, such as motivations to learn, responses to feedback and change, and abilities to learn when no longer being told what to do
constraints: The authors acknowledge measuring what a student knows helps decide what to do next during instruction and remains essential for repetitive tasks such as licensing drivers
target_learners: Students in formal schooling assessed by current knowledge-based tests
target_learning_goals: Aligning assessment with preparation for life beyond specific trained tasks
examples: The report traces the history of assessment purposes from Binet's intelligence testing through behaviorist performance measures to cognitive knowledge assessment
key_sources: Daniel L. Schwartz and Dylan Arena. (2013). Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age. The MIT Press. http://www.macfound.org

article_title: Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age
citation: Daniel L. Schwartz and Dylan Arena. (2013). Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age. The MIT Press. http://www.macfound.org
title: Ohno! Has Talent choicelet assessment for critical thinking
description: Ohno! Has Talent is a choicelet, defined as a short and engaging game that students want to complete and that requires some learning while logging students' choices relevant to that learning. In the game, students mix primary light colors to make contestants' preferred color beams across three rounds of increasing challenge, using an experiment room for safe trial and a faux shopping catalog of subtractive and additive color charts. Students must use critical thinking to decide which charts to believe, and the game logs their choices. Children play it in ten to twenty minutes.
requirements: A digital environment that logs students' choices in log files generated by the game
constraints: The authors describe the choicelet example as only promissory pending further research
target_learners: Sixth-grade children
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking as the process of deciding what to believe, and learning additive color mixing
examples: A student correctly mixed orange for contestant Otter by choosing two red lights and one green light in the final round
key_sources: Daniel L. Schwartz and Dylan Arena. (2013). Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age. The MIT Press. http://www.macfound.org

article_title: Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age
citation: Daniel L. Schwartz and Dylan Arena. (2013). Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age. The MIT Press. http://www.macfound.org
title: Design nimble choice-based assessments that stand independently of specific instructional packages
description: The report argues for smaller, more nimble choice-based assessments rather than bulky environments like cognitive tutors or full video games. Nimble assessments "do not depend on students completing many hours of a complex game or instructional sequence before it is possible to make any useful assessments." They can target specific choices by design, be built by many people to democratize assessment design, allow the same constellation of choices to be assessed with several measures, and stand independently of a specific instructional package so different learning experiences can be compared.
requirements: Assessment design must target specific choices rather than search for diagnostic patterns among millions of choice combinations in open environments
constraints: The authors note the results from a single, monolithic assessment are questionable because they may reflect unknown peculiarities of the environment
target_learners: Learners in formal and informal settings, including museum visitors
target_learning_goals: Assessing choices critical to learning that most tests miss
examples: The Ohno! Has Talent choicelet is offered as a modest illustration of a nimble, choice-based assessment of critical thinking
key_sources: Daniel L. Schwartz and Dylan Arena. (2013). Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age. The MIT Press. http://www.macfound.org

article_title: Formative and stealth assessment
citation: Shute, V. J., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Formative and stealth assessment. In J.M. Spector et al. (eds.), Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_25
title: Stealth assessment: formative assessment seamlessly woven into immersive learning environments
description: Stealth assessment is "an evidence-based approach to assessment where the tasks that students are engaged with are highly interactive and immersive, such as within video games." Performance data is "continuously gathered during the course of playing/learning" and inferences about competency states are stored in a dynamic learner model. The approach aims to support learning, maintain flow, reduce test anxiety without sacrificing validity and reliability, and "blur the distinction between assessment and learning." It relies on automated scoring and machine-based reasoning to infer competencies across a network of skills.
requirements: Evidence-centered assessment design to structure claims and evidence
Formative assessment and feedback mechanisms to support learning
Automated scoring and machine-based reasoning to infer competency values
constraints: Developing the evidence model is difficult when students collaborate on quests, since individual actions and thinking are hard to trace in a combined effort
Scoring qualitative products such as essays and discussions retains high subjectivity even with comprehensive rubrics
target_learners: K-12 students in game-based or computer-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: Content and key competencies such as creative problem solving
examples: The chapter illustrates stealth assessment in the commercial game Oblivion, inferring creative problem solving from quest actions via Bayesian networks
key_sources: Shute, V. J., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Formative and stealth assessment. In J.M. Spector et al. (eds.), Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_25

article_title: Formative and stealth assessment
citation: Shute, V. J., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Formative and stealth assessment. In J.M. Spector et al. (eds.), Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_25
title: Evidence-centered assessment design (ECD): competency, evidence, task/action, and assembly models
description: ECD is "a conceptual design framework to help in the creation of coherent assessments" supporting "a broad range of assessment types, from classroom quizzes to simulation-based assessments." The competency model defines knowledge, skills, abilities and other attributes as probability distributions per variable; the evidence model specifies what student actions count as evidence and how it statistically links to competency variables; task/action models express situations that evoke required evidence; and the assembly model specifies how the models work together to form a valid assessment. Statistical machinery such as IRT or Bayesian networks links observable data to unobservable competencies.
requirements: Competency models must be developed at an appropriate level of granularity—too large a grain size yields less specific evidence, too fine a grain size increases complexity and resources
constraints: The framework must answer what attributes are to be measured and how they are scored, per the chapter's framing
target_learners: Learners in any assessment context from classroom quizzes to simulations
target_learning_goals: Valid, reliable inference of learner competency states to support diagnosis and instruction
examples: The chapter's Oblivion example instantiates ECD with a creative problem solving competency model, novelty/efficiency indicators, and a Bayes net
key_sources: Shute, V. J., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Formative and stealth assessment. In J.M. Spector et al. (eds.), Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_25

article_title: Formative and stealth assessment
citation: Shute, V. J., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Formative and stealth assessment. In J.M. Spector et al. (eds.), Handbook of Research on Educational Communications and Technology. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-3185-5_25
title: Oblivion stealth assessment example: inferring creative problem solving from quest actions
description: The chapter illustrates stealth assessment in the commercial game Oblivion, a first-person 3D role-playing game where players complete quests. Creative problem solving—"the process of coming up with novel but efﬁcient solutions to a given problem"—is the target competency. Actions such as swimming, levitating, or freezing the river carry novelty and efficiency indicator values (e.g., freezing the river: n = 0.76, e = 0.80) elicited from two Oblivion experts, ranging from 0 to 1. Actions captured in real time feed a Bayesian network that updates competency estimates, which can drive formative feedback or re-sequencing of quests.
requirements: Indicator values learned from real data or elicited from experts
Bayesian network software to link observed actions to competency variables
constraints: In the illustrated case, problem solving (based on efficiency) was valued more than creativity given how the conditional probability distributions were set up
target_learners: Players of immersive games (illustrated with a commercial role-playing game)
target_learning_goals: Creative problem solving
examples: A player levitating over the river produced observed novelty 0.375 ± 0.072 and efficiency 0.875 ± 0.072, and the parent node inferred she was somewhat high on creative problem solving

article_title: Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game
citation: Shute, V. J., Wang, L., Greiff, S., Zhao, W., & Moore, G. (2016). Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game. Computers in Human Behavior, 63, 106-117. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2016.05.047
title: Four-facet problem solving competency model grounded in rule acquisition and rule application
description: The article's competency model divides problem solving skill into four facets: "analyzing givens and constraints", "planning a solution pathway", "using tools and resources effectively and efficiently", and "monitoring and evaluating progress". The first facet maps to rule acquisition and the remaining three to rule application, following recent research distinguishing knowledge acquisition from knowledge application. The model was developed from a literature review and implemented in Bayesian networks, one per game level, to produce overall and facet-level estimates.
requirements: In-game indicators must be identified for each facet to supply evidence to the Bayes nets
constraints: The model was developed and calibrated for middle-school students playing Use Your Brainz; the article notes the need to verify results with a larger sample
target_learners: middle school students (7th grade)
target_learning_goals: problem solving skill, overall and on four facets
examples: The model was implemented in Use Your Brainz with 32 indicators distributed across the four facets and a unique Bayes net for each of 42 game levels

article_title: Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game
citation: Shute, V. J., Wang, L., Greiff, S., Zhao, W., & Moore, G. (2016). Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game. Computers in Human Behavior, 63, 106-117. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2016.05.047
title: Use Your Brainz stealth assessment with 32 indicators and per-level Bayesian networks
description: Use Your Brainz is a slightly modified version of Plants vs. Zombies 2 in which stealth assessment was embedded via Glasslab's access to the source code. The assessment uses 32 in-game indicators (7 for analyzing givens and constraints, 7 for planning, 14 for tool use, 4 for monitoring and evaluating progress), scored into discrete states and linked to competency variables through conditional probability tables configured using Samejima's graded response model. A unique Bayes net was built for each of 42 levels across two worlds, updating estimates in real time from log-file evidence.
requirements: Log-file telemetry capturing the indicator events, and CPT parameters initially set by experts and calibrated with pilot data
constraints: Discrimination estimates were set low (e.g., 0.3 for indicator #37) because game-based assessment involves many confounds such as prior gameplay experience
target_learners: middle school students
target_learning_goals: problem solving skill measurement across four facets
examples: Indicator #37 scores planting Iceberg Lettuce within a Snapdragon's attack range as an inversely coded ratio binned into very good/good/ok/poor states

article_title: Stealth assessment of creativity in a physics video game
citation: Shute, V. J., & Rahimi, S. (2020). Stealth Assessment of Creativity in a Physics Video Game. Computers in Human Behavior. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563220303940
title: Evidence-centered design (ECD) framework for stealth assessment
description: ECD is a framework for designing assessments as evidentiary arguments, consisting of three main models: a Competency Model defining claims about student competencies, an Evidence Model specifying what behaviors constitute evidence, and a Task Model defining tasks that elicit that evidence. In stealth assessment, ECD formalizes claims about the learner and the evidence supporting them, allowing continuous performance data from complex interactive environments like video games. The article uses ECD to build the creativity assessment in Physics Playground, with game levels serving as tasks.
requirements: Assessment must elicit behavior bearing evidence about key competencies and provide principled interpretations of that evidence
target_learners: K-12 students playing educational video games
target_learning_goals: creativity (fluency, flexibility, originality)
conceptual physics understanding
examples: In Physics Playground, the competency model has creativity as parent node of fluency, flexibility, and originality; evidence model variables include number of agents drawn and trajectory deviation from expected solutions
key_sources: Shute, V. J., & Rahimi, S. (2020). Stealth Assessment of Creativity in a Physics Video Game. Computers in Human Behavior. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563220303940

article_title: Stealth assessment of creativity in a physics video game
citation: Shute, V. J., & Rahimi, S. (2020). Stealth Assessment of Creativity in a Physics Video Game. Computers in Human Behavior. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563220303940
title: Stealth assessment: invisible assessment woven into gameplay
description: Stealth assessment involves designing, developing, and weaving assessments directly and invisibly into the fabric of complex learning environments, particularly video games. Evidence for targeted skills comes from players' interactions with the game itself (the processes of play), with inferences about competency states stored in a dynamic learner model in real time. This contrasts with singular outcome measures typical of educational environments. Real-time estimates can drive adaptivity (e.g., adjusting task difficulty) and timely individualized feedback while maintaining flow.
requirements: A well-designed game environment producing rich sequences of player actions that serve as evidence sources
A psychometric model (e.g., Bayesian network) to accumulate evidence into competency estimates
constraints: Requires identifying level-specific in-game behaviors and scoring rules, which the authors note can be tricky depending on the nature of a given level
target_learners: students in game-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: 21st-century competencies such as creativity, problem solving, and physics understanding
examples: Prior stealth assessments have measured problem solving, mathematics, computational thinking, physics, social skills, and conscientiousness in various games
key_sources: Shute, V. J., & Rahimi, S. (2020). Stealth Assessment of Creativity in a Physics Video Game. Computers in Human Behavior. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563220303940

citation: Shute, V. J., & Rahimi, S. (2020). Stealth Assessment of Creativity in a Physics Video Game. Computers in Human Behavior. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563220303940
title: Physics Playground game with creativity stealth assessment
description: Physics Playground is a computer-based game designed to assess and support conceptual understanding of physics principles. Players draw objects (ramps, levers, pendulums, springboards) that become active and interact to move a ball to a balloon, operationalizing Newton's laws. The game includes hundreds of levels solvable in multiple ways, encouraging creative solutions. A Bayesian-network-based stealth assessment estimates fluency, flexibility, and originality from gameplay indicators such as number of agents drawn, variety of agents attempted, and deviation of ball trajectory from expected solutions.
requirements: Level-specific evidence model variables and scoring rules must be established for each level
Bayesian networks built per level using Netica software
constraints: Elaboration facet was excluded from the model because it overlaps with other facets and unique indicators could not be ascertained
target_learners: 8th and 9th grade students
target_learning_goals: conceptual physics understanding
creativity
examples: In the Big Watermill level, directing the ball above the watermill using a lever as fulcrum provides positive evidence for originality

citation: Shute, V. J., & Rahimi, S. (2020). Stealth Assessment of Creativity in a Physics Video Game. Computers in Human Behavior. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563220303940
title: Bayesian network evidence accumulation for real-time competency estimation in games
description: The article implements stealth assessment using Bayesian networks (BNs), one per level, with creativity as a parent node of fluency, flexibility, and originality child nodes. At the end of each level, log files are parsed, observables identified (Evidence Identification) and scored, then absorbed by the level-specific BN (Evidence Accumulation), updating probabilistic competency estimates in real time. BNs offer graphical representation, learning from data, immediate updating, and fast scoring with discrete variables, making them suited for embedded scoring engines.
requirements: Discrete variables for fast scoring
Expert judgments for prior probability distributions
Expected maximization and gradient descent algorithms to update conditional probability tables
constraints: Prior probabilities depend on expert judgments about indicator distributions
target_learners: students in game-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: real-time estimation of competency levels during gameplay
examples: The BN computes P(Creativity = high | evidence) = .75, P(medium) = .23, P(low) = .02 for an example level, converted to an EAP value of .73

title: Score creativity from both novel solutions and creative products, distinguishing creativity from game exploitation
description: When assessing creativity in games, in-game behaviors that violate the rules and mechanics of the game should not count as evidence for creativity, because creativity requires both novelty and relevance/appropriateness. The article illustrates this with the Need Fulcrum level, where drawing lines under the ball solved the level without using any agents of force and motion; this hack was tried by many students and thus was neither original nor rule-abiding. Stealth assessment must differentiate creative solutions from solutions that exploit game features.
requirements: Scoring rules must encode both novelty and appropriateness relative to the rules and mechanics of the game
constraints: Differentiating creative solutions from exploitative ones is level-specific; the authors note establishing indicators and scoring rules can be tricky depending on the nature of a given level
target_learners: 8th and 9th grade students playing educational games
target_learning_goals: creativity (originality, fluency, flexibility)
examples: In the Need Fulcrum level, a solution drawing lines under the ball without any agent of force and motion was scored as providing no evidence for originality because it violated the game's rules
