article_title: Critical Ethical Reasoning and Role-Play
citation: Simkins, D. W., & Steinkuehler, C. (2008). Critical ethical reasoning and role-play. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412008317313
title: Descriptive, critical ethics as a two-axis framework for locating ethical theories and as the chosen framework for ethical reasoning education
description: The article defines a two-axis space for locating ethical theories: normative versus descriptive, and dogmatic versus critical. Normative theories judge instances from a priori premised norms, while descriptive ethics derive norms a posteriori from how people actually act; dogmatic approaches assume all good people agree, while critical ethics requires learning another's norms and evaluating behavior on their own criteria. The authors select descriptive critical ethics as the framework for analysis, arguing it is the most appropriate framework for ethical reasoning education in a diverse democratic society.
requirements: Education in ethical reasoning in a democracy must honor principled disagreement as legitimate rather than impose one ethical system dogmatically
constraints: The article locates most historical moral education movements in the descriptive and dogmatic quadrant, with recent work renewing the critical focus
target_learners: students in democratic civic and moral education
target_learning_goals: critical ethical reasoning
empathy and understanding of others' moral contexts
examples: The study applies this framework to analyze how role-players talk about ethical decisions in games, building categories guided by the principles expressed in the descriptive, critical ethics literature
key_sources: Simkins, D. W., & Steinkuehler, C. (2008). Critical ethical reasoning and role-play. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412008317313

article_title: Critical Ethical Reasoning and Role-Play
citation: Simkins, D. W., & Steinkuehler, C. (2008). Critical ethical reasoning and role-play. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412008317313
title: Four grounded categories of player preference and game features: effecting change, mirroring, social context, and significant decisions
description: From grounded-theory-informed analysis of the interview themes, the article proposes four categories encompassing both preference and fact themes: effecting change (desire for character actions to change the game world), mirroring (desire for emotional bond and for the game world to reflect the valence of the player's actions), social context (desire for a consistent, rich social environment), and significant decisions (desire to control the character's behavior through legitimate, experienced-as-important choices). When applied to the factual themes, the four categories explained them as well, which the authors take as partial validation of the scheme.
requirements: The categories were built up from preference themes and then applied to factual themes to partially check their validity
constraints: The authors caution that the sample is small when positing the validity of the categorization scheme
target_learners: game designers and researchers of role-play learning environments
target_learning_goals: fostering critical ethical reasoning through role-play
examples: The categories are used to derive four criteria for fostering ethical decision making in games, each illustrated with an interview excerpt such as Eileen's Oblivion account of suffering consequences like being bitten by a vampire
key_sources: Simkins, D. W., & Steinkuehler, C. (2008). Critical ethical reasoning and role-play. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412008317313

article_title: Critical Ethical Reasoning and Role-Play
citation: Simkins, D. W., & Steinkuehler, C. (2008). Critical ethical reasoning and role-play. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412008317313
title: Design games for ethical decision making by providing consequential choices, mirrored emotional valence, rich social context, and significant decisions
description: The article derives four design criteria for fostering ethical decision making within games from its four emergent categories. Player choices must have the potential to effect change in the game world; players must have the emotional valence of their choices mirrored back to them, typically through responses of other in-game characters; games must provide a sufficiently rich in-game social context to render actions significant beyond the individual level; and players must be given the opportunity to make significant decisions that let them inhabit their characters with their own game-related intentions, desires, and goals.
requirements: Choices must be legitimate rather than predetermined, since apparent choices where outcomes are identical undermine significance
constraints: The four categories are tightly intertwined and regularly overlap in practice; games vary greatly in how successfully they manage this effect
target_learners: players of role-playing games
learners in role-play-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: critical ethical decision making
empathy and perspective taking
examples: Eileen's Elder Scrolls: Oblivion account illustrates effecting change (no do-over, suffering consequences such as becoming a vampire); Robert's Final Fantasy VI account of Shadow's daughter illustrates mirroring; Fergus's Knights of the Old Republic 2 account of the Jedi's warning illustrates social context; Eileen's assassins guild choice illustrates significant decisions
key_sources: Simkins, D. W., & Steinkuehler, C. (2008). Critical ethical reasoning and role-play. Games and Culture. https://doi.org/10.1177/1555412008317313

article_title: A meta-analytic examination of the instructional effectiveness of computer-based simulation games
citation: Traci Sitzmann. (2011). A Meta-Analytic Examination of the Instructional Effectiveness of Computer-Based Simulation Games. Personnel Psychology, 64, 489-528. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/journal/17446570
title: Interactive cognitive complexity theory: simulation games engage affective and cognitive processes simultaneously
description: Interactive cognitive complexity is an integrative information processing model the article uses as its central theoretical framework for simulation game effectiveness. It "proposes learning is the result of an interaction between variables internal and external to the cognitive systems of trainees": trainees' affective structures (motivation, attitudes) and cognitive structures (memory, knowledge base, executive control) interact with each other and with sensory information from the simulation game in an iterative process that stores new information. Because both affective and cognitive structures are essential, the theory predicts simulation games should outperform other methods because they target both structures. The meta-analytic results are interpreted against this framework.
requirements: Learning must be the primary goal of the simulation game for it to fall under this framework
constraints: The theory applies to instruction delivered via personal computer immersing trainees in a decision-making exercise in an artificial environment
target_learners: adult trainees in work-related training programs
target_learning_goals: work-related knowledge and skills, including declarative knowledge, procedural knowledge, and retention
examples: The meta-analysis tested the theory's prediction that simulation games engage both affective and cognitive processes, finding higher self-efficacy and learning relative to comparison groups.
key_sources: Traci Sitzmann. (2011). A Meta-Analytic Examination of the Instructional Effectiveness of Computer-Based Simulation Games. Personnel Psychology, 64, 489-528. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/journal/17446570

article_title: A meta-analytic examination of the instructional effectiveness of computer-based simulation games
citation: Traci Sitzmann. (2011). A Meta-Analytic Examination of the Instructional Effectiveness of Computer-Based Simulation Games. Personnel Psychology, 64, 489-528. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/journal/17446570
title: Embed simulation games as a supplement within a broader program of instruction rather than using them as standalone instruction
description: This principle holds that simulation games should be embedded in a program of instruction that includes other methods, because games alone rarely suffice for learning a topic. The meta-analysis found that "when simulation games were used as a supplement to other instructional methods, the simulation game group had higher knowledge levels than the comparison group (d = .51)", whereas standalone games yielded d = −.12 favoring the comparison group. The article reasons that when training utilizes a breadth of instructional methods, trainees having difficulty can review material through multiple methods to increase mastery, and debriefing sessions help transfer game learning to the job.
requirements: Other instructional methods must supplement the simulation game so trainees can review material through multiple channels
constraints: Standalone simulation games were counterproductive relative to comparison instruction (d = −.12)
target_learners: adult trainees in work-related and higher-education training programs
target_learning_goals: declarative and procedural knowledge and retention of trained material
examples: The meta-analysis classified studies by whether the simulation game was the sole instructional method or a supplement, and compared each category's effect size against comparison groups.
key_sources: Traci Sitzmann. (2011). A Meta-Analytic Examination of the Instructional Effectiveness of Computer-Based Simulation Games. Personnel Psychology, 64, 489-528. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/journal/17446570

article_title: Taking Control: Stealth Assessment of Deterministic Behaviors Within a Game-Based System
citation: Erica L. Snow, Aaron D. Likens, Laura K. Allen, & Danielle S. McNamara. (2016). Taking Control: Stealth Assessment of Deterministic Behaviors Within a Game-Based System. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0085-5
title: Dynamic analyses of log data (random walks and Hurst exponents) as stealth assessment of behavioral control
description: This framework holds that log data from adaptive learning environments, combined with dynamic systems analyses, can unobtrusively classify students' behavior patterns as deterministic or random while they learn. Random walks visualize each student's trajectory across categorical choices over time, while Hurst exponents quantify persistence: "0.5 < H ≤ 1 indicates persistent (deterministic or controlled) behavior, H = 0.5 signifies random behavior, and 0 ≤ H < 0.5 denotes antipersistent behavior." The article presents this as a stealth alternative to obtrusive self-report measures, which it argues fail to capture dynamic, fine-grained behavior change.
requirements: Log data collection must be intentionally programmed into the system; it is not built into all computerized systems
Numerous data points are needed to reliably calculate Hurst exponents
constraints: The methods must be applied to temporal data
Replication of an in-depth dataset of over 11,000 interactions is difficult; the authors suggest entropy calculations as a lower-data alternative
target_learners: high school students using game-based intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: self-explanation and reading comprehension strategy use
examples: Random walks traced each of 40 students' sequences of choices among four feature categories on orthogonal vectors, yielding a unique walk per student
key_sources: Erica L. Snow, Aaron D. Likens, Laura K. Allen, & Danielle S. McNamara. (2016). Taking Control: Stealth Assessment of Deterministic Behaviors Within a Game-Based System. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0085-5

article_title: Taking Control: Stealth Assessment of Deterministic Behaviors Within a Game-Based System
citation: Erica L. Snow, Aaron D. Likens, Laura K. Allen, & Danielle S. McNamara. (2016). Taking Control: Stealth Assessment of Deterministic Behaviors Within a Game-Based System. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0085-5
title: iSTART-ME game-based intelligent tutoring system with four logged interaction categories
description: iSTART-ME (Interactive Strategy Training for Active Reading and Thinking - Motivationally Enhanced) is a game-based ITS that teaches self-explanation and comprehension strategies for complex science texts through introduction, demonstration, and extended practice modules. In extended practice, students choose among generative practice environments (Coached Practice, Map Conquest, Showdown), six identification mini-games, personalizable features (avatar, background theme, pedagogical buddy), and achievement screens, earning points and iBucks to advance through levels 0 to 25. The study logged "a total of 11,120 game-based interactions, with an average of 278 (SD = 33) choices per student."
requirements: Log data must be intentionally programmed into the system to capture interaction choices
constraints: Only completed actions were retained for the analysis; opened-but-abandoned interactions were not counted
target_learners: high school students learning reading comprehension strategies
target_learning_goals: self-explanation strategy use for complex science texts
examples: In the study, students interacted freely with the full game-based menu across 8 training sessions, choosing among generative practice games, identification mini-games, personalizable features, and achievement screens
key_sources: Erica L. Snow, Aaron D. Likens, Laura K. Allen, & Danielle S. McNamara. (2016). Taking Control: Stealth Assessment of Deterministic Behaviors Within a Game-Based System. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0085-5

article_title: Casual Games, Cognition, and Play across the Lifespan: A Critical Synthesis
citation: Kurt Squire, Garrison Wells, Maria J. Anderson-Coto, and Constance Steinkuehler. 2023. Casual Games, Cognition, and Play across the Lifespan: A Critical Synthesis. ACM Games: Research and Practice, Volume 1, Issue 2, Article 14. https://doi.org/10.1145/3594534
title: Play as an emergent phenomenon of person, intention, game, and context — the unit of analysis for game-based learning research
description: This framework holds that the effects of casual games arise not from the media artifact itself but from play as an emergent phenomenon at the intersection of people, their intentions, the game, and context. The review argues researchers "should take seriously the context of game play, perhaps treating the emergent phenomena of play as the unit of analysis, rather than the media artifact." It draws on the mindset literature, noting that intention and expectation shape outcomes, so the same game can benefit or harm the same players in different contexts.
requirements: Research designs must account for players' motivations, intentions, and the social context of play when evaluating game impact.
constraints: The review treats casual games as a media type rather than a frame of mind for consistency with the existing research literature, while noting future studies may benefit from examining the activity instead.
target_learners: players across the lifespan, including older adults and youth
target_learning_goals: cognitive health
social well-being
emotional well-being
examples: The review's Pokémon Go synthesis shows users who play for social reasons report positive well-being while those playing for escapism or nostalgia report less positive well-being.
key_sources: Kurt Squire, Garrison Wells, Maria J. Anderson-Coto, and Constance Steinkuehler. 2023. Casual Games, Cognition, and Play across the Lifespan: A Critical Synthesis. ACM Games: Research and Practice, Volume 1, Issue 2, Article 14. https://doi.org/10.1145/3594534

article_title: Scientific Habits of Mind in Virtual Worlds
citation: Constance Steinkuehler, Sean Duncan. (2008). Scientific Habits of Mind in Virtual Worlds. J Sci Educ Technol. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-008-9120-8
title: Three-group coding framework for scientific habits of mind in informal game forums
description: The article develops a set of 18 codes (following Chi 1997) based on AAAS benchmarks for scientific literacy, Chinn and Malhotra's framework for evaluating inquiry tasks, and Kuhn's epistemological framework. The codes address "Scientific discursive practices (including social knowledge construction), systems- and model-based reasoning, and tacit epistemologies", applied by four raters with 92% four-way interrater reliability on roughly 10% of the corpus. It deliberately omits content-specific science understanding because the investigated world "makes no claims of correspondence with the natural one".
requirements: Raters with substantial participant-observer experience in the game context; a second WoW-specific content code set coded by two raters with 93% two-way reliability
constraints: Omits content-knowledge aspects of scientific understanding, justified by the study's focus on scientific practices rather than content in a simulated world
target_learners: Informal learners in online game communities
Adolescent and adult game forum participants
target_learning_goals: Scientific habits of mind: argumentation, systems and model-based reasoning, evaluative epistemology
examples: Applied to a random sample of 1,984 posts across 85 threads of the official WoW priest forum, yielding the reported proportions of social knowledge construction, systems-based reasoning, and evaluative epistemology
key_sources: Constance Steinkuehler, Sean Duncan. (2008). Scientific Habits of Mind in Virtual Worlds. J Sci Educ Technol. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-008-9120-8

article_title: A systematic review of game-based assessment in education in the past decade
citation: Su, F., & Zou, D. (2024). A systematic review of game-based assessment in education in the past decade. Knowledge Management & E-Learning, 16(3), 451–476. https://doi.org/10.34105/j.kmel.2024.16.021
title: Evidence-centered design (ECD) as a conceptual framework for integrating assessments into educational games
description: ECD is a conceptual design framework for crafting educational assessment tests, "emphasizing consistency between the evidence gathered and interpreted and the underlying knowledge addressed by assessments". In game-based environments it guides researchers to collect evidence making valid claims about students' competency levels during gameplay. Researchers employing ECD specify the competences to be assessed, outline corresponding assessment tasks, and collect evidence such as interactions and behaviors during gameplay to infer students' mastery levels. The review reports ECD was the most-cited framework (N = 6) and recommends integrating it when crafting GBAs.
requirements: Researchers identify the competences to be assessed and predicted, decide on the evidence required, and design in-game tasks to collect that evidence
constraints: The review notes only two studies used multiple theories, indicating theory use in GBA is largely unitary
target_learners: K-16 and higher-education learners assessed within educational games
target_learning_goals: Valid inference of learners' in-game competencies from gameplay evidence
examples: Shute et al. (2021) used ECD in Physics Playground, analyzing learners' in-game actions to deduce understanding of qualitative physics; Song and Sparks applied ECD in Seaball, evaluating students' arguments to assess reasoning skills
key_sources: Su, F., & Zou, D. (2024). A systematic review of game-based assessment in education in the past decade. Knowledge Management & E-Learning, 16(3), 451–476. https://doi.org/10.34105/j.kmel.2024.16.021

article_title: A systematic review of game-based assessment in education in the past decade
citation: Su, F., & Zou, D. (2024). A systematic review of game-based assessment in education in the past decade. Knowledge Management & E-Learning, 16(3), 451–476. https://doi.org/10.34105/j.kmel.2024.16.021
title: In-game assessment designs are associated with game features, differing systematically across simulation, immersive, video, gamification, puzzle, and board game types
description: The review details how in-game assessment is implemented differently per game genre. Simulation GBA "progressively assessed learners' curriculum knowledge" with performance reflecting real-life actions; immersive GBA "yields rich data on learners' learning experiences" as students complete tasks at different paces; video GBA involves "students using dynamic game elements to address problems, offering open-ended solutions without fixed answers"; gamification-based assessment awards points for predetermined questions; puzzle and board games assess spatial reasoning and quiz performance respectively.
requirements: Games must provide explicit game features and embedded assessment details for in-game assessment to be designed and analyzed
constraints: Assessment approaches differ even for the same game across studies, e.g., Scientopolis used multiple-choice questions in one study and interaction-frequency data in another
target_learners: School and university students across disciplines
target_learning_goals: Assessing subject knowledge, reasoning, inquiry, and problem-solving skills during gameplay
examples: Physics Playground recorded correct/incorrect attempts, time spent, restarts, and objects used in log files to deduce qualitative-physics understanding; Semideus awarded 100-500 coins based on estimation correctness and reduced energy by 15% for inaccurate estimation
key_sources: Su, F., & Zou, D. (2024). A systematic review of game-based assessment in education in the past decade. Knowledge Management & E-Learning, 16(3), 451–476. https://doi.org/10.34105/j.kmel.2024.16.021

article_title: The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization
citation: Huatong Sun. (2006). The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization. Technical Communication Quarterly, 15(4), 457-481. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15427625tcq1504_5
title: Cultural usability framework: usability as a diffusing feature situated at the intersection of immediate and sociocultural contexts
description: The framework of cultural usability integrates key concepts and methods from activity theory, genre theory, and British cultural studies to study local use in context. It "regards usability as a diffusing feature across the activity system" and incorporates cultural factors from both the immediate context and the sociocultural context. It situates culture in the dynamic interactions of instrumental affordances (operation and action levels) and social affordances (activity level, informed by genre theory and British cultural studies), treating usability as both a material interaction with the artifact and an interpretation process.
requirements: Investigation of local use in a context where the collective and the individual meet and where implementation and interpretation interact
constraints: Activity theory alone is good at interpreting tool-mediated production but weak at sign-mediated communication, which the framework supplements with genre theory and British cultural studies
target_learners: usability researchers
technical communication researchers
localization practitioners
target_learning_goals: understanding how cultural and contextual factors shape technology use in local contexts
examples: The framework guided fieldwork in the two-site comparative case study, shaping the 5W analysis of use patterns, genre-based message coding, and circuit-of-culture analysis of interviews
key_sources: Huatong Sun. (2006). The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization. Technical Communication Quarterly, 15(4), 457-481. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15427625tcq1504_3

article_title: The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization
citation: Huatong Sun. (2006). The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization. Technical Communication Quarterly, 15(4), 457-481. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15427625tcq1504_5
title: Circuit of culture: five interlocking processes (representation, identity, production, consumption, regulation) for examining a cultural artifact
description: Borrowed from British cultural studies (du Gay et al., 1997), the circuit of culture examines "five key processes in a development cycle of an artifact": how the artifact is represented, what social identities are associated with it, how it is produced, how it is consumed, and what mechanisms regulate its distribution and use. In the real world these five elements continually overlap and intertwine in complex and contingent ways. Applied to usability, it shows how representation, identity, production, and regulation interact with and contribute to consumption, providing a timeline and developmental perspective missing from activity theory and genre theory.
requirements: A study of the whole circuit of culture is needed to examine a cultural artifact completely
constraints: The five elements overlap and intertwine in complex and contingent ways rather than forming a linear sequence
target_learners: usability researchers
IT product designers
localization specialists
target_learning_goals: analyzing how meanings are mediated by an artifact across its full life cycle
examples: The author maps mobile text messaging onto the circuit, locating developer localization in production and user localization across consumption, regulation, representation, and identity
key_sources: Huatong Sun. (2006). The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization. Technical Communication Quarterly, 15(4), 457-481. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15427625tcq1504_3

article_title: The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization
citation: Huatong Sun. (2006). The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization. Technical Communication Quarterly, 15(4), 457-481. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15427625tcq1504_5
title: Expand the design process to users' sites: treat localization as an open-ended process linking user localization back to design
description: The article argues that localization is an open-ended process reaching beyond the design stage to use and consumption, including both developer localization and user localization. Designers should not "seek to design fully localized interfaces or products (because that is never possible)" or regard shipment as the end of design. Instead they should initiate communication channels, build support networks to enhance user localization, watch use trends emerging from users' sites, and design better instrumental affordances to respond to those trends, connecting use and design on the cultural circuit.
requirements: A deep understanding of concrete use activities in local contexts while considering cultural and structuring factors
An open-system information design with built-in instrumental affordances that invite users to localize the artifact and realize its social affordances
constraints: If the dialogic interaction between developer and user localization is problematic or does not exist, the current use success might eventually dissolve or disappear
target_learners: IT product designers
localization specialists
technical communicators
target_learning_goals: designing IT products that support user localization and postadoption use experience
examples: The author suggests designers of mobile messaging applications examine fun communication and relationship communication practices in the two cultural contexts and ask what design features could support these two types of communication work
key_sources: Huatong Sun. (2006). The Triumph of Users: Achieving Cultural Usability Goals With User Localization. Technical Communication Quarterly, 15(4), 457-481. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15427625tcq1504_3

article_title: An observation study of reading instruction provided to elementary students with learning disabilities in the resource room
citation: Swanson, E. A., & Vaughn, S. (2010). An Observation Study of Reading Instruction Provided to Elementary Students With Learning Disabilities in the Resource Room. Psychology in the Schools, 47(5). https://doi.org/10.1002/pits.20484
title: Instructional Content Emphasis Instrument–Revised (ICE-R) for observing reading instruction
description: The ICE-R is a multidimensional, taxonomically designed observation instrument for coding teachers' reading instruction. It yields "multidimensional descriptions of reading instruction," time allocated to instructional components, student grouping patterns, level of student engagement, and instructional quality. Dimension A codes the main instructional category (e.g., word study, comprehension, fluency), Dimension B the subcategory, and Dimension C grouping practices. Engagement is coded on a 3-point Likert scale and quality on a 4-point scale based on indicators such as explicit instruction and teacher modeling. In this study observers received 6 hours of training and reached 100% agreement on all ICE-R sections before data collection.
requirements: Trained observers; the study required coders to reach at least 90% agreement on a training video and 100% agreement on all ICE-R sections prior to data collection.
constraints: Quality and engagement ratings depend on observer coding of instructional events, with the article noting observer effects such as conspicuous observation as a threat.
target_learners: Elementary students with learning disabilities in resource-room settings
target_learning_goals: Describing and evaluating the quality of reading instruction across phonological awareness, word study, fluency, comprehension, and vocabulary
examples: Observers coded 2,178 minutes of reading instruction across 10 resource-room teachers over three consecutive observation days per classroom.
key_sources: Swanson, E. A., & Vaughn, S. (2010). An Observation Study of Reading Instruction Provided to Elementary Students With Learning Disabilities in the Resource Room. Psychology in the Schools, 47(5). https://doi.org/10.1002/pits.20484

article_title: Students Learn Equally Well From Digital as From Paperbound Texts
citation: Annette Kujawski Taylor. (2011). Students Learn Equally Well From Digital as From Paperbound Texts. Teaching of Psychology, 38(4), 278-281. https://doi.org/10.1177/0098628311421330
title: Choose text delivery medium on cost and convenience grounds, since comprehension is equivalent when students actually read
description: The article concludes that when students actually sit and read the text, the delivery method does not matter, so instructors may adopt digital texts for their practical advantages. As the author puts it, "there is no pedagogical reason to avoid using digital texts. The convenience, in addition to the cost savings, may be important factors in considering the adoption of digital texts." The real instructional challenge is getting students to read in the first place.
requirements: Students must actually read the assigned text; the equivalence finding applies to students who completed the reading under supervised conditions.
constraints: Findings come from a single laboratory study with unfamiliar microeconomics material and marginally passing quiz scores; reading time was not assessed, so effects of reading time on comprehension remain undetermined.
target_learners: college students
introductory psychology students
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of textbook material
long-term retention of course readings
examples: In the study, 74 students were randomly assigned to read a supply-and-demand chapter from either a paperbound or digital text and were quizzed immediately and 1 week later, with no medium differences emerging.
key_sources: Annette Kujawski Taylor. (2011). Students Learn Equally Well From Digital as From Paperbound Texts. Teaching of Psychology, 38(4), 278-281. https://doi.org/10.1177/0098628311421330

article_title: Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities
citation: Keith Topping. (1998). Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543068003249
title: Topping's definition and 17-parameter typology of peer assessment in higher education
description: The article defines peer assessment as "an arrangement in which individuals consider the amount, level, value, worth, quality, or success of the products or outcomes of learning of peers of similar status", restricted to students of similar degree status in higher education. It then develops a typology of 17 parameters of variation (Table 1), including curriculum area, objectives, formative/summative focus, product, relation to staff assessment, directionality, privacy, contact, year, ability, constellations, place, time, requirement and reward. The typology was developed "from immersion in this literature" and warns that sweeping general conclusions are unlikely to be meaningful.
requirements: Projects must be situated on the typology's parameters, since activities vary widely and general conclusions require specifying the configuration
constraints: Excludes paid postgraduates grading undergraduates as surrogate staff members; concerns peers of similar status in higher education
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: formative and summative assessment of peer products and outcomes
examples: The Falchikov (1995a) case study is characterized as a same-year, bilaterally quantitative and qualitative, in-class, compulsory, supplementary, mutual group peer assessment system in oral presentation skills
key_sources: Keith Topping. (1998). Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543068003249

article_title: Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities
citation: Keith Topping. (1998). Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543068003249
title: Computer-assisted peer assessment systems and studies
description: The review identifies computer-assisted peer assessment as "an emerging growth area", enabled by wider availability of word processing and electronic mail. Described implementations include the MUCH (Many Using and Creating Hypermedia) system used in nursing and computer science education, which showed good correspondence with staff assessment though many computer science students were skeptical; Brock's comparison of computerized text analysis with peer feedback for 48 ESL writers; peer assessment of class presentations with computer tools; and University of Portsmouth software that randomly allocated peer assessors, integrated peer and staff marks, calculated weighted final marks, and generated feedback. Few outcome data were yet available.
requirements: Access to word processing, electronic mail or dedicated software; organizational and record-keeping functions for allocation and mark integration
constraints: Few outcome data yet available; student skepticism about computer-mediated peer assessment reported in some settings
target_learners: higher education students
ESL student writers
target_learning_goals: formative feedback on writing and hypermedia products
examples: Brock (1993) found both computerized-feedback and peer-supported ESL groups showed significant writing growth, with peer interaction rated higher for helpfulness in improving content
key_sources: Keith Topping. (1998). Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543068003249

article_title: Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities
citation: Keith Topping. (1998). Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543068003249
title: Theoretical mechanisms of peer assessment: reflexive cognition, feedback quality, and social constructivist accounts
description: The review proposes that peer assessment is reflexive — "learning by assessing" — engaging assessors in reviewing, summarizing, clarifying, diagnosing misconceived knowledge and identifying missing knowledge, which are cognitively demanding and could consolidate understanding. For assessees, negotiated criteria clarify what constitutes high-quality work, and peer feedback offers greater immediacy, frequency and volume that compensate for lower quality. Theoretically it draws on social constructivism, Vygotskian scaffolded learning and purposeful communication, and Piagetian cognitive conflict for reciprocal same-ability assessment. The review cautions that direct tests of these hypothesized mechanisms are still scarce.
requirements: Assessors should be trained to question, prompt, and scaffold rather than merely supply a notionally right answer
constraints: Establishing a single overarching theory is difficult given the multiplicity of subject specialties; direct tests of mechanism hypotheses are scarce; feedback is useful only when recipients act upon it
target_learners: higher education students acting as assessors and assessees
target_learning_goals: cognitive and metacognitive gains, affective benefits, social and transferable skills
examples: The review reports that simple summative, correctional, or didactic feedback is associated with much lower effect sizes than open-ended, suggestive, and formative feedback
key_sources: Keith Topping. (1998). Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543068003249

article_title: Rethinking Education in a Changing World
citation: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/
title: The Faure-Delors heritage: an integrated humanistic vision framed by lifelong learning and four pillars of learning
description: The report identifies the two landmark UNESCO publications as key sources for policy makers, promoting 'an integrated and humanistic vision of education framed by the paradigm of lifelong learning and by the four pillars of learning to be, to know, to do, and to live together'. It treats this vision as a viable foundation for rethinking education, while noting it needs reappraisal under contemporary conditions. The four pillars are described as learning to live together, to know, to do, and to be.
requirements: The report states the vision requires 'a fresh reappraisal of this vision ... that takes into account contemporary conditions' to remain relevant
constraints: Translation of the lifelong learning paradigm into policy 'has remained more problematic in societies both in the North and South' because of the resource mobilisation it implies
target_learners: all children, youth and adults learning throughout life
target_learning_goals: holistic human development across knowing, doing, being and living together
examples: The report cites the 1996 Delors report's four pillars and the 1972 Faure report's introduction of lifelong learning as the forerunners of the current initiative
key_sources: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/

article_title: Rethinking Education in a Changing World
citation: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/
title: Education must serve both adaptation to change and emancipation for social transformation
description: The experts hold that education has a dual role in a rapidly changing world: it must help people cope with change, and it must also empower them to change society. As the report states, 'While education must help people adapt to change, education is also about emancipation and the development of capabilities to effect social transformation.' The initiative therefore rejects a purely technocratic, adaptive view of education and insists on an aspirational, humanistic orientation.
requirements: Identifying the most relevant societal changes and examining whether their consequences are positive or negative before deciding how education should accommodate them
constraints: The report agrees that 'the diverse crises generated by globalization cannot be resolved by education alone'
target_learners: learners in societies undergoing rapid social, economic and technological transformation
target_learning_goals: capacity to adapt to change and to effect social transformation
examples: The Senior Experts' Group agreed the forthcoming report should be 'both inspirational and aspirational' and create a genuine debate on education
key_sources: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/

article_title: Rethinking Education in a Changing World
citation: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/
title: Recognize and integrate alternative knowledge systems and epistemologies of the South in international education debates
description: The report argues that dominant knowledge is a locus of power and that the Delors report spoke from a Northern epistemic location. It recommends that 'voices from the Global South be heard in current international education debates' and that alternative traditional knowledge systems be recognized rather than relegated to an inferior status. Integration of Southern knowledge, paradigms and visions is presented as a starting point for a paradigm shift regarding knowledge for development.
requirements: Recognition of the relationship of power between knowledge systems in the North and South; avoidance of generalizations about lived realities
constraints: The report notes the Delors report 'neglected the epistemology of the South and spoke in one voice from a single perspective'
target_learners: learners and communities in the Global South and multicultural societies
target_learning_goals: respect for cultural diversity and plural knowledge systems in education
examples: The report cites 'sumak kawsay', the Quechua notion of 'buen vivir' or good living, as an alternative conception of development incorporated into some Andean constitutions
key_sources: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/

article_title: Rethinking Education in a Changing World
citation: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/
title: Three time-frames of education: short-term response, mid-term policy, and long-term transformation of mental structures
description: Drawing on Fernand Braudel's three time-frames of history, the report proposes thinking about education's role at three scales. As printed: 'the short-term that attempts to respond to more immediate and urgent concerns; the mid-term perspective that refers to policy, educational structures, pedagogical approaches; and the longer-term perspective that has do to with mentalities and a transformation of mental structures'. The report judges the longer-term transformation of worldviews the most challenging.
requirements: Education policy must be articulated across all three time horizons rather than only the short term
constraints: The report states the longer-term perspective, the transformation of worldviews, is the most challenging
target_learners: societies and education systems at local, national and global levels
target_learning_goals: global responsibility, human dignity and transformation of mental structures
examples: The report frames its guiding questions for education in the 21st century within these three time-frames
key_sources: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/

article_title: Rethinking Education in a Changing World
citation: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/
title: Reaffirm education as a public good and the right to effective and relevant learning for all, throughout life
description: Against trends of privatization of knowledge and blurring public-private boundaries, the report reaffirms that 'The knowledge commons are an integral part of world heritage, and education is a public good that should be made available to all.' It further affirms education as a basic human right — the right of all children, youth and adults to learn throughout life through formal, non-formal and informal experiences — and calls for rethinking the social contract on education as a collective responsibility.
requirements: A broad vision of education that is lifelong and life-wide, articulating formal and non-formal learning with diverse informal learning spaces; State custodial role plus involvement of families, communities, civil society and business
constraints: The report notes great pressure on the State to reduce public expenditure creates a dilemma for the principle of education as a public good
target_learners: all children, youth and adults
target_learning_goals: equitable access to effective and relevant learning throughout life
examples: The report asks whether to adapt the principle of education as a public good to new realities or protect it, and proposes stronger partnerships with associations and non-profit organizations
key_sources: UNESCO Secretariat. (2013). Rethinking Education in a Changing World. UNESCO Education Research and Foresight. https://unesdoc.unesco.org/

article_title: Conversing with pedagogical agents: A phenomenological exploration of interacting with digital entities.
citation: Veletsianos, G. & Miller, C. (2008). Conversing with pedagogical agents: A phenomenological exploration of interacting with digital entities. British Journal of Educational Technology, 39, 6, 969-986. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2007.00797.x
title: Hermeneutic phenomenological inquiry via the four lifeworld existentials for studying human-agent interaction
description: The article applies phenomenological inquiry, which "seeks to examine, understand and interpret observable, yet special events in our everyday life," to human-agent interaction. The experience of any phenomenon is explained through four lifeworld existentials: body, time, space and relations with others. Researchers bracket their preconceptions, treat informant descriptions as true accounts, and derive the essence of the experience through imaginative variation, testing whether each theme is essential. The authors use this lens because interpretive examinations of pedagogical agents have been meager.
requirements: Informants must have experienced the phenomenon in ecologically valid, natural settings rather than artificial experimental conditions
constraints: No one theme is monolithic; the set of derived themes together describe the lived experience
target_learners: learners interacting with conversational agents in electronic learning environments
target_learning_goals: understanding the user experience of conversing with pedagogical agents
examples: The authors analysed two 50-minute phenomenological interviews and 11 written reflections, grouping lived experience descriptions into five theme statements and removing themes one by one to test essentiality.
key_sources: Veletsianos, G. & Miller, C. (2008). Conversing with pedagogical agents: A phenomenological exploration of interacting with digital entities. British Journal of Educational Technology, 39, 6, 969-986. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2007.00797.x

article_title: Conversing with pedagogical agents: A phenomenological exploration of interacting with digital entities.
citation: Veletsianos, G. & Miller, C. (2008). Conversing with pedagogical agents: A phenomenological exploration of interacting with digital entities. British Journal of Educational Technology, 39, 6, 969-986. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2007.00797.x
title: Conversational pedagogical agent with AI-driven dialogue, lip-synchronised audio and conversation memory
description: The agents studied were "animated characters represented in human form" that converse with learners via an artificial intelligence engine matching student comments to agent responses. Responses are delivered in both textual form and computer-generated lip-synchronised audio to accommodate learner preferences, and the agents can reuse prior information exchanged so as to appear to remember previous conversations. Students in the course used the agent voluntarily for assistance or support.
requirements: An artificial intelligence engine that matches student comments to agent responses
target_learners: university students in a 7-week course at a large Midwestern university
target_learning_goals: providing assistance and support for course learning
examples: Log data indicated all students in the course interacted with the pedagogical agents on multiple occasions, with use being the student's choice.

article_title: Conversing with pedagogical agents: A phenomenological exploration of interacting with digital entities.
citation: Veletsianos, G. & Miller, C. (2008). Conversing with pedagogical agents: A phenomenological exploration of interacting with digital entities. British Journal of Educational Technology, 39, 6, 969-986. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2007.00797.x
title: Design pedagogical agents with an equilibrium of utility and usability before investing in aesthetic elements
description: Drawing on interaction design, the article argues that for a pedagogical agent to be perceived as useful, "the design of the agent must embrace an equilibrium of utility and usability." Utility is the array of functionalities satisfying pedagogical requirements, and usability is the effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction with which learners accomplish tasks. Only once this balance is achieved can designers focus on aesthetic elements of the character to potentially enhance the learning experience.
requirements: Functionalities that satisfy the outlined pedagogical requirements and enable learners to accomplish their learning goals
constraints: A usable agent without needed learning support is worthless; a support-rich agent that is difficult to use leads to dissatisfied learners
target_learners: learners interacting with pedagogical agents in digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: accomplishing learning goals through agent-supported tasks
examples: The article cites Mahmood and Ferneley's finding that quality of interaction was perceived as more important than visual design, and calls for further research on these properties with respect to the actual user experience.

article_title: CHAPTER 8 ‒ Assessing Persistence in Educational Games
citation: Ventura, M., Shute, V., & Small, M. (2013). Assessing Persistence in Educational Games. Design Recommendations for Intelligent Tutoring Systems - Volume 2: Adaptive Instructional Management. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+Persistence+in+Educational+Games
title: Newton's Playground: a 2D drawing-based game for qualitative physics
description: Newton's Playground (NP) is a 2D video game aimed at helping middle school students understand qualitative physics, a nonverbal understanding of Newton's three laws, balance, mass, gravity, and energy. It is "a nonlinear video game (i.e. , a game design feature that allows many possible solution paths) where players are challenged to guide a green ball to a red balloon in a 2D environment." Players draw simple machines (ramps, levers, pendulums, springboards) that come to life and obey gravity and Newton's laws. The game contains 74 puzzles across 7 progressively more difficult playgrounds, with silver and gold trophies marking progress.
requirements: Players must draw simple machines on screen and can attach objects with pins; problems are designed to elicit particular sets of agents
target_learners: middle school students
target_learning_goals: qualitative physics understanding (Newton's laws, balance, mass, gravity, momentum, energy)
examples: The chapter describes a puzzle in which the player draws a pendulum on a pin to swing down and hit the ball, manipulating mass distribution and drop angle
key_sources: Ventura, M., Shute, V., & Small, M. (2013). Assessing Persistence in Educational Games. Design Recommendations for Intelligent Tutoring Systems - Volume 2: Adaptive Instructional Management. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+Persistence+in+Educational+Games

article_title: CHAPTER 8 ‒ Assessing Persistence in Educational Games
citation: Ventura, M., Shute, V., & Small, M. (2013). Assessing Persistence in Educational Games. Design Recommendations for Intelligent Tutoring Systems - Volume 2: Adaptive Instructional Management. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+Persistence+in+Educational+Games
title: NP session event logs as embedded assessment data
description: Newton's Playground automatically records detailed gameplay telemetry for assessment purposes. "NP automatically uploads log files to a server for each gaming session (i.e., log activity between login and logout)." Each event log for a puzzle visit records features such as game_time, pause_time, restart_count, object_count, nudge_count, erase_count, pin_count, agent vectors, ball trajectory, silver and gold trophy status, and whether the problem was solved. These logs supplied the raw data from which the game-based assessment of persistence was derived.
requirements: Log files must be uploaded to a server for each gaming session between login and logout
target_learners: middle school students
target_learning_goals: stealth assessment of persistence during gameplay
examples: The chapter prints a sample event log showing game_time of 130.526001 seconds, restart_count of 7, and solved: true
key_sources: Ventura, M., Shute, V., & Small, M. (2013). Assessing Persistence in Educational Games. Design Recommendations for Intelligent Tutoring Systems - Volume 2: Adaptive Instructional Management. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+Persistence+in+Educational+Games

article_title: CHAPTER 8 ‒ Assessing Persistence in Educational Games
citation: Ventura, M., Shute, V., & Small, M. (2013). Assessing Persistence in Educational Games. Design Recommendations for Intelligent Tutoring Systems - Volume 2: Adaptive Instructional Management. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+Persistence+in+Educational+Games
title: Game-based assessment of persistence (GAP): time spent on unsolved problems
description: The GAP is a log-derived, performance-based measure of persistence. As the authors define it, "we developed a game -based assessment of persistence (GAP), which is derived from time spent on unsolved problems over all events in the player's log file over the five sessions." Time on unsolved problems is summed across all repeated attempts and averaged across unsolved problems out of a possible 74; time on solved problems is excluded because solution times primarily reflect skill. Longer times on difficult problems are taken to indicate greater persistence.
requirements: Requires log files recording time spent per problem visit across sessions; longer times spent on difficult problems should indicate greater persistence
constraints: Time on solved problems is not an indicator of persistence because solution times are primarily based on skill
target_learners: middle school students
target_learning_goals: measuring persistence (industriousness) during gameplay
examples: Validation used impossible anagrams and picture comparison tasks where the score is time spent on impossible trials
key_sources: Ventura, M., Shute, V., & Small, M. (2013). Assessing Persistence in Educational Games. Design Recommendations for Intelligent Tutoring Systems - Volume 2: Adaptive Instructional Management. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+Persistence+in+Educational+Games

article_title: CHAPTER 8 ‒ Assessing Persistence in Educational Games
citation: Ventura, M., Shute, V., & Small, M. (2013). Assessing Persistence in Educational Games. Design Recommendations for Intelligent Tutoring Systems - Volume 2: Adaptive Instructional Management. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Assessing+Persistence+in+Educational+Games
title: GIFT Gateway Module for real-time persistence assessment across game-based learning environments
description: The Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT) supports open and dynamic game-based learning environments with distinct messaging protocols. To detect persistence regardless of the educational game used, "a 'Gateway Module ' is incorporated that associates an external educational/training system 's state data with a domain or competency model built within GIFT." This linkage lets disparate systems communicate, enabling real-time assessment of persistence in players, with progress communicated to the learner model for determining transitions in performance or competency and to the pedagogical model for selecting feedback and remediation tactics.
requirements: GIFT requires rules and models built around game interaction that must be explicitly linked to concepts defined inside of the GIFT architecture
target_learners: learners in game-based training and educational environments
target_learning_goals: real-time stealth assessment of persistence and performance transitions in game-based learning
examples: The chapter describes embedding persistence detection within GIFT's domain module so it applies regardless of the educational game being utilized

article_title: Learning in a global society
citation: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org
title: Complex cognition: cognition as individually owned and socially shared, evolving according to the laws of complex adaptive systems
description: Complex cognition is a concept proposed by the author at a Santa Fe Institute seminar (J. Visser, 2000, November). It holds that cognition is a complex phenomenon evolving according to the laws governing complex adaptive systems, whose conditions the author says are well known, citing Gell-Mann (1995) and Holland (1995). The concept integrates the spectrum of views on distributed cognitions described by Salomon (1993), resolving their juxtaposition: "Cognition is individually owned and socially shared at the same time." It underpins the chapter's argument that learning must be understood broadly to remain relevant to adaptive human behavior regarding global issues.
requirements: Account must be taken of the entire developing transdisciplinary knowledge base rooted in disciplines from cognitive science and neuroscience to anthropology and research on effective teaching
constraints: The author presents it as a conceptual proposal rather than an empirically tested model
target_learners: learners at all levels of complex organization, individual and social
target_learning_goals: constructive interaction with change through intelligent behavior
key_sources: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org

article_title: Learning in a global society
citation: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org
title: Learning landscape: an ecological conception of the totality of interrelated learning sub-landscapes, including the instructional landscape
description: The learning landscape is the author's metaphor for the ecological whole composed of multiple sub-landscapes, such as the instructional landscape, the media landscape, and the socio-cultural organization landscape. It results both from the natural interplay of learning entities and from consciously planned action to reshape what nature tends to produce. A truly ecologically functioning learning landscape is "characterized by the smooth integration among all the various sub-landscapes" that compose it. The metaphor extends evaluation of learning environments beyond effectiveness and efficiency to their aesthetic and ethical qualities, with beauty and harmony as indicators of the quality of the ecology of cognition.
requirements: Planners and leaders whose actions impact the learning landscape must be environmentally aware of what else happens in it
constraints: The author judges that governmental planning agencies and much of the distance education effort leave considerable room for improvement in this environmental awareness
target_learners: learners across society at large, in formal and informal settings
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning responsive to global issues and concerns
examples: UNESCO's UNITWIN/UNESCO Chairs program is cited as an example of networking that supports interinstitutional collaboration in the learning landscape
key_sources: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org

article_title: Learning in a global society
citation: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org
title: Redefinition of learning as the disposition to engage in continuous dialogue with the human, social, biological and physical environment
description: The chapter argues learning must be 'undefined' and recast as a disposition to dialogue, expressed at different levels of complex organization, for constructive interaction with change. The proposed redefinition sees human learning as "the disposition of human beings, and of the social entities to which they pertain, to engage in continuous dialogue with the human, social, biological and physical environment, so as to generate intelligent behavior to interact constructively with change" (J. Visser, 2001). This goes beyond learning as particular desired changes in human performance capability and draws on Gell-Mann's view of learning as complex adaptive systems making sense of regularities among randomness.
requirements: A vision of learning that is ubiquitous, unrelated to conditions such as age, time, space and circumstance, manifesting at diverse levels of complex organization
constraints: The author presents this as a possible redefinition grounded in theoretical argument rather than empirical validation
target_learners: human beings and the social entities to which they pertain
target_learning_goals: generating intelligent behavior to interact constructively with change
key_sources: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org

article_title: Learning in a global society
citation: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org
title: Distance education should be judged by whether it contributes to a better world, not merely by improved access, participation and cost
description: The chapter argues that insofar as distance education strives to overcome the shortcomings of school systems, it should be judged by the standards of Article 26 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which links education to "the full development of the human personality" and to strengthening respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. The primary question is therefore not how distance education has improved access and participation and at what cost, but whether it contributes to a better world. This aligns with the UNESCO-convened expert group's recommendation that distance education take a critical look at itself in light of current knowledge about how people learn.
requirements: Willingness to critique established practice against the purposes of education rather than only measures of access and cost-effectiveness
constraints: The author notes the prevailing rhetoric of cost-effectiveness, economies of scale, and parity of esteem has kept thinking about distance education locked in the dominant classroom model
target_learners: distance education practitioners, planners, and educational policymakers
target_learning_goals: education directed toward the full development of the human personality and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms
examples: The UNESCO-convened group of 23 experts meeting in Karlsruhe recommended that distance education take a critical look at itself, asking how existing experience fits present-day society and current knowledge about how people learn
key_sources: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org

article_title: Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles
citation: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x
title: Mayer's multimedia message design principles as a framework for mLearning message design
description: The article presents Mayer and Moreno's theory of multimedia learning as the most widely cited approach to message design, drawing on dual-coding theory, working memory, cognitive load theory and the SOI model. It states that the theory "generates principles for overcoming common types of cognitive overload by building coherence, providing learning cues, creating spatial and temporal contiguity, and reducing redundancy". The article argues these principles are applicable to mLearning, citing the Multiple Modality principle as a guideline for mobile content.
requirements: Designers need a deep understanding of how people learn and how cognition works in realistic settings to organize learning messages appropriately
constraints: Mayer's principles were developed for online and computer-based learning and had not been tested for mobile learning at the time of writing
target_learners: mobile learners in formal and informal settings
target_learning_goals: effective design of instructional messages for mobile devices
examples: The article applies the Multiple Modality principle, advocating explanations in pictures with annotated graphics and related audio, as a guideline for designing mobile content
key_sources: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x

article_title: Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles
citation: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x
title: Typology of mobile devices by information delivery type
description: The article classifies mobile devices into four general categories of information exchange: stand-alone devices, network-centered devices, mobile computers and web portals. Table 1 defines each type by its core mode of information delivery and transmission, gives example devices (iPods, iPhones, laptops, ChromeOS, iPad), and lists the learning activities each supports, such as podcasts on take-away devices or collaborative learning via ad hoc networks. Instructional designers are urged to consider which devices they plan to leverage, as "not all devices provide the same services".
requirements: Designers need a basic understanding of the information delivery capabilities of each device type and the appropriateness of each type for different environments and content
target_learners: mobile learners using varied devices in formal and informal settings
target_learning_goals: matching mLearning content and activities to device capabilities
examples: Table 1 maps stand-alone devices to podcasts and instructional guides, network-centered devices to collaborative learning, mobile computers to portable interactive multimedia, and web portals to thin-client access to online services
key_sources: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x

article_title: Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles
citation: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x
title: Design mLearning content for the least common denominator of mobile devices
description: The article recommends chunking and packing learning content into multimedia messaging services or SMS so it works on a variety of mobile phones, since simple phones have more limited functions than smart phones. Supporting evidence includes the Shanghai Jiaotong survey showing students prefer short video-based materials. The principle holds that content should be usable across the range of devices learners actually carry.
requirements: Learning content needs to be chunked and packed into multimedia messaging services or SMS
target_learners: learners using simple mobile phones as well as smart phones
target_learning_goals: delivering instructional content usable across varied mobile devices
examples: The article cites the survey of 3000 Online College of Shanghai Jiaotong University participants showing preference for video-based materials under 5 minutes per video
key_sources: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x

article_title: Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles
citation: Wang, M. & Shen, R. (2012). Message design for mobile learning: Learning theories, human cognition and design principles. British Journal of Educational Technology, 43(4), 561-575. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2011.01214.x
title: Match design components to learner locations and mobility contexts
description: The article proposes extending the formal/informal categorization of learning environments with the descriptors noisy and quiet, and presents Table 2 mapping four typical learner locations to learning preferences and information delivery styles: subway and bus (visual numerical, short articles with strong pictures), home (auditory-visual-kinesthetic combination), office (written expressive, PPT and e-books), and cafe (auditory, visual and linguistic). The typology draws on visual, auditory and tactile/kinesthetic learning-style theories and directs designers to consider both environmental factors and learner preferences.
requirements: Designers should give thought not only to environmental factors but also to learners' preferences and use different design components to meet the needs of distinctive learners in diverse situations
constraints: It will be hard to predict where learners will be using the mLearning content
target_learners: mobile learners moving across home, transit, office and cafe settings
target_learning_goals: adapting message design to learner mobility and context
examples: Table 2 pairs the subway and bus environment with visual numerical design such as short articles and strong pictures, and the home environment with music, oral content and instructional videos

article_title: The effects of text segmentation on children's reading comprehension∗
citation: David S. Weiss. (1983). The effects of text segmentation on children's reading comprehension. Discourse Processes, 6:1, 77-89. https://doi.org/10.1080/01638538309544555
title: Segment new social studies textbook text along phrase boundaries to improve children's comprehension
description: The article recommends that written text for elementary social studies be typographically segmented at phrase boundaries — either pausal phrase boundaries (where readers pause reading aloud) or syntactic phrase boundaries (noun phrases, verb phrases, and pattern completers on separate lines) — without changing words or punctuation. The author states: "there is support to recommend that new social studies textbooks that are being written should make some use of the syntactic and pausal phrase formats in presenting the content material." The benefit appears without any prior training for students.
requirements: Passages at or above students' grade level; the study tested passages at or above grade level
constraints: Findings apply only to grades 4 and 7 and to normal students, not special education students; effects on very easy passages and with teacher assistance were not tested
target_learners: elementary school students in grades 4 and 7 of good, average, and poor reading levels
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of social studies textbook content
examples: In the study, 648 grade 4 and 7 students read passages in pausal phrase format (mean line length 5.8 words), syntactic phrase format (mean line length three words), or standard prose format, with comprehension measured by a modified cloze test
key_sources: David S. Weiss. (1983). The effects of text segmentation on children's reading comprehension. Discourse Processes, 6:1, 77-89. https://doi.org/10.1080/01638538309544555

article_title: The effects of text segmentation on children's reading comprehension∗
citation: David S. Weiss. (1983). The effects of text segmentation on children's reading comprehension. Discourse Processes, 6:1, 77-89. https://doi.org/10.1080/01638538309544555
title: Visual marking of oral phrase boundaries facilitates children's reading comprehension
description: The article proposes that children comprehend oral discourse better than written discourse because speech supplies "the added underlying structural cues available when the English language is spoken". Written punctuation marks major clauses but not finer boundaries, so the two segmentation formats were designed to present "a visual analogue of the underlying grammatical and structural constituents found in oral discourse". The results lend support to this theory, though the author notes it was not conclusively supported because oral discourse was never directly compared with the segmented written formats.
requirements: The segmentation must mark phrase boundaries without changing the words or punctuation of the text
constraints: The study did not directly compare oral discourse with the segmented written formats, so the theory has not been conclusively supported
target_learners: elementary school children in grades 4 and 7
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of written discourse at or above grade level
examples: The pausal phrase format placed phrases on individual lines (mean 5.8 words) at points where 50% of an adult sample would pause reading aloud; the syntactic phrase format separated noun phrases, verb phrases, and pattern completers (mean three words per line)
key_sources: David S. Weiss. (1983). The effects of text segmentation on children's reading comprehension. Discourse Processes, 6:1, 77-89. https://doi.org/10.1080/01638538309544555

article_title: Examining the Use of Game-Based Assessments for Hiring Autistic Job Seekers
citation: Willis, Colin, Tracy Powell-Rudy, Kelsie Colley, and Joshua Prasad. 2021. Examining the Use of Game-Based Assessments for Hiring Autistic Job Seekers. Journal of Intelligence 9: 53. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence9040053
title: Game-based assessment packages (Disconumbers, Shapedance, Digitspan) measuring non-social cognitive ability
description: The study used two packages of serious games measuring cognitive ability: Disconumbers, a "memory and math-based game"; Shapedance, a "visuospatial ability task similar to the Mental Rotation task"; and Digitspan, a memorization game similar to the digit span task on the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale. Scores range from zero to five, are true interval scores, and games progress through timed levels with increasing challenge. Each game is a serious game intended not to entertain but to make a functional task more engaging.
requirements: Games are combined into packages of two games taken in sequence as part of a longer hiring assessment
constraints: The games measured cognitive traits selected because they are least likely to differentiate autistic and neurotypical individuals; findings do not generalize to other cognitive abilities or content such as emotional intelligence or personality
target_learners: college-graduate job seekers, including autistic job seekers
target_learning_goals: assessment of non-social cognitive ability (working memory, visuospatial ability, math-based memory) for hiring selection
examples: 263 autistic and 323 general-population candidates completed one of the two packages as part of a real-world hiring assessment
key_sources: Willis, Colin, Tracy Powell-Rudy, Kelsie Colley, and Joshua Prasad. 2021. Examining the Use of Game-Based Assessments for Hiring Autistic Job Seekers. Journal of Intelligence 9: 53. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence9040053

article_title: Examining the Use of Game-Based Assessments for Hiring Autistic Job Seekers
citation: Willis, Colin, Tracy Powell-Rudy, Kelsie Colley, and Joshua Prasad. 2021. Examining the Use of Game-Based Assessments for Hiring Autistic Job Seekers. Journal of Intelligence 9: 53. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence9040053
title: Assess non-social cognitive traits in a non-social manner to fairly evaluate autistic and neurotypical candidates
description: The article argues that assessing non-social cognitive traits in a non-social manner may provide a fair way to assess both autistic and neurotypical candidates' readiness for the same job. Removing socially laden demands avoids cognitive disruption that social situations cause autistic individuals, and each game used measured non-social traits found to have the smallest group differences in prior meta-analytic work. The study's results support this for a narrow set of cognitive abilities.
requirements: Assessment content must align with non-social cognitive traits shown to have minimal group differences in traditional formats
constraints: The pattern is not expected to hold for content autistic individuals typically struggle with, such as social or emotional assessments
target_learners: autistic job seekers
neurotypical job seekers
target_learning_goals: fair assessment of job-relevant cognitive ability in selection
examples: The study administered game-based packages measuring working memory, visuospatial ability, and math-based memory, finding no or small group differences
