article_title: Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues.
citation: Woo, H.L. (2009). Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 25, 203-218. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2729.2008.00299.x
title: The APL framework for organizing APA research
description: The APL framework organizes research on animated pedagogical agents around three areas analogous to classroom elements: 'A represents APA characteristics', 'P represents Presentation by the APA', and 'L represents Learners' characteristics'. It is derived from the four fundamental classroom elements (teacher, teaching, students, physical environment), dropping the invariant physical environment. The paper uses it to structure its review of controversial findings and factors in APA-based learning environments.
requirements: An APA must be situated in a learning system that provides support for its instructional rendering, since unlike a real teacher it cannot exist alone
constraints: The APA physical environment is quite invariant and confined to working with a computer and its peripherals, so it is excluded from the framework
target_learners: online and multimedia learners
target_learning_goals: understanding factors affecting APA-based learning environments
examples: The paper reviews anthropomorphism, appearance, modality, agent multiplicity, speech-gesture cooperation, and sensory preference under the three framework areas

article_title: Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues.
citation: Woo, H.L. (2009). Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 25, 203-218. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2729.2008.00299.x
title: Design APA instruction by analysing affordances and matching what agents offer to what users need
description: The paper recommends that APA technology be viewed under the lens of affordance, meaning 'opportunity for action', rather than as a holistic human substitute. Design should begin by analysing the affordances of APAs, then establish a proper match between what the APAs can offer and what the users need, taking learners' background characteristics into account. Under this view, agents with less humanlikeness for specific learning types such as storytelling, short demonstration, or enactment of a scene are seen as tools, so learners impose fewer social expectations and are more amenable to learning with them.
requirements: Design must begin with analysing the affordances of APAs, followed by establishing a proper match between what the APAs can offer and what the users need
constraints: Whether users use the technology's features depends on their prior experience, age level, past domain knowledge, culture, and intention; the technology only offers the opportunity but will not necessarily result in an action
target_learners: online learners using agent-based multimedia environments
target_learning_goals: effective design of agent-based instruction matched to learner needs
examples: The paper suggests using agents with less adaptivity or less humanlikeness for very specific types of learning, such as storytelling, short demonstration, or enactment of a scene

article_title: Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues.
citation: Woo, H.L. (2009). Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 25, 203-218. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2729.2008.00299.x
title: Consider learners' sensory preference together with presentation modality when designing APA lessons
description: The paper proposes that sensory preference be considered an important student characteristic taken into account together with other instructional factors when designing an APA-based lesson. Because most people are brought up using sight more than hearing, and training produces proficiency in one modality, effective APA learning cannot rely on good presentation principles alone; the presentational modality must match coherently with the learner's characteristics. The review cites reports that about 60% of people are visual learners and that about 70% of learners learn well in any given modality.
requirements: The presentational modality must match coherently with the learner's characteristics, like a classroom teacher adopting a style that appeals to students' background
constraints: The review notes research did not discern whether sensory channels are trainable to handle one modality better than the other
target_learners: learners with differing visual and auditory proficiencies
target_learning_goals: balanced visual-auditory interaction in multimedia learning
examples: The review cites the typist shadowing experiment (via Low & Sweller 2005) showing attention for a task depends on familiarization and experience with that task

article_title: Cultural differences in online learning: International student perceptions
citation: Liu, X., Liu, S., Lee, S.-h., & Magjuka, R. J. (2010). Cultural Differences in Online Learning: International Student Perceptions. Educational Technology & Society, 13(3), 177-188. https://www.jstor.org/stable/jeductechsoci.13.3
title: Hofstede's four-dimensional model of cultural differences as a framework for interpreting cross-cultural online learning
description: Hofstede's model characterizes cultural behaviors along four dimensions: power distance, individualism-collectivism, uncertainty avoidance, and masculinity-femininity. The article states that "Hofstede developed a four-dimensional model of cultural differences, which can be used to characterize cultural behaviors that originate from different societies." The authors used this framework to interpret their interview findings, linking students' collectivism, high power distance and uncertainty avoidance to their preferences for structured instruction, group work and reliance on instructors and textbooks. The article notes the model has been criticized as essentialist but considers it a valid framework for analyzing cultural differences in teaching and learning.
requirements: The framework is used to interpret findings about culturally different pedagogical objectives and expectations between teachers and students from different societies
constraints: The article notes the model has been challenged on external validity and labeled an essentialist model of culture emphasizing fixity of identity
target_learners: international students in transnational online programs
target_learning_goals: understanding cultural differences affecting participation and design of online courses
examples: The authors interpreted Eastern students' modest, face-saving personalities and preference for group work as reflecting collectivism and femininity, and U.S. students' independence and competitiveness as individualism and masculinity
key_sources: Liu, X., Liu, S., Lee, S.-h., & Magjuka, R. J. (2010). Cultural Differences in Online Learning: International Student Perceptions. Educational Technology & Society, 13(3), 177-188. https://www.jstor.org/stable/jeductechsoci.13.3

article_title: Cultural differences in online learning: International student perceptions
citation: Liu, X., Liu, S., Lee, S.-h., & Magjuka, R. J. (2010). Cultural Differences in Online Learning: International Student Perceptions. Educational Technology & Society, 13(3), 177-188. https://www.jstor.org/stable/jeductechsoci.13.3
title: Design culturally inclusive online learning environments by building diversity into course design
description: The principle holds that online courses serving international students should incorporate diversity in assessment strategies, technology use and case materials so that all students can participate fully. As the article states, "a culturally inclusive learning environment needs to consider diversity in course design in order to ensure full participation by international students." The authors argue diversity is the best solution for respecting culturally different ways of learning and ensuring equity, while noting a tension between localizing instruction for particular cultures and serving a group with multiple nationalities.
requirements: Instructors need awareness of students' expectations and cultural backgrounds, e.g. through a quick learner analysis, to adjust the diversity of the course
constraints: Localization for one culture may be difficult to implement in a group with multiple nationalities without compromising the interests of students from other nations
target_learners: international students in transnational online courses
target_learning_goals: equal participation and engagement of culturally diverse learners
examples: Students preferred multiple assessment strategies combining memorization and application, and commended a course that balanced local and global cases

article_title: Comparison of children's social problem-solving skills who play videogames and traditional games: A cross-cultural study
citation: Yılmaz, E., Yel, S., & Griffiths, M. D. (2022). Comparison of children's social problem-solving skills who play videogames and traditional games: A cross-cultural study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104548
title: Use educational and serious videogames and active traditional games to support children's social problem-solving development
description: Based on their regression findings, the authors recommend that games primarily produced for educational or serious purposes, which positively predicted SPSIC scores, be used "not only for education and knowledge acquisition but also in the development of social problem -solving skills in school settings". They also advise encouraging children to play such games in out-of-school time and to engage in traditional games keeping them physically and mentally active.
requirements: Games must match children's daily-life play rather than researcher-developed single games, per the study's rationale
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional and non-experimental, so a direct effect cannot be determined as the article states
target_learners: children aged 9-11 in primary school
target_learning_goals: social problem-solving skills
examples: The regression analyses found serious and educational videogames and action, strategy-intelligent, role-playing and sports traditional games positively predicted SPSIC scores

article_title: Comparison of children's social problem-solving skills who play videogames and traditional games: A cross-cultural study
citation: Yılmaz, E., Yel, S., & Griffiths, M. D. (2022). Comparison of children's social problem-solving skills who play videogames and traditional games: A cross-cultural study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104548
title: Social Problem Situations Inventory for Children (SPSIC)
description: The SPSIC (Yılmaz et al., 2021) measures children's social problem-solving skills across "six dimensions (impulse control, communication, cooperation, social initiation, empathy, and emotion regulation)", each with a social problem situation. Children follow four solution steps (defining the problem, producing solutions, identifying the most effective solution and explaining the reason), each scored 0-4 by two coders, for a maximum of 16 points per scenario and 96 overall.
requirements: Responses coded by two trained coders with an experienced third researcher consulted on disagreements
constraints: The best solution chosen could not be tested in the school setting, so children explained why their chosen solution was best
target_learners: children aged 9-11
target_learning_goals: social problem-solving skills
examples: Inter-coder Krippendorff's alpha ranged .963-.984 for the Turkish sample and .954-.988 for the British sample

article_title: University students’ self-regulated learning using digital technologies
citation: Carmen Yot-Domínguez and Carlos Marcelo. (2017). University students' self-regulated learning using digital technologies. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education 14:38. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-017-0076-8
title: University teachers should incorporate digital technologies and create environments that favour independent, self-regulated learning
description: The article recommends that university teachers incorporate digital technologies into learning activities and design environments offering opportunities to seek challenges, reflect on progress, and take responsibility for accomplishments. It argues students' non-use of technologies for learning stems partly from teachers who "neither require nor encourage their use", and that failing to incorporate technologies perpetuates the gap between the university world and the labour and social world.
requirements: Teachers must require or encourage the use of digital technologies in learning activities, since students currently do not adopt them for SRL on their own.
constraints: The recommendation is grounded in a survey of Andalusian university students; the authors note the sample's size and diversity should be expanded and teachers should also be studied.

target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
independent learning with digital technologies
examples: The authors analysed learning activities designed by Andalusian university instructors and found teachers neither require nor encourage technology use for self-regulation; they cite emerging intervention programs and pedagogical frameworks using Web 2.0 and social software to promote SRL.

article_title: Instructional design frameworks and intercultural models
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2009). Instructional Design Frameworks and Intercultural Models. Information Science Reference, IGI Global. http://www.igi-global.com/reference
title: Culture-Based Model (CBM): an intercultural instructional design framework for culture-based ICTs
description: CBM is an intercultural instructional design framework that assists designers, researchers, and practitioners in building culture-based ICTs. The book states that "CBM is an intercultural, instructional design framework that guides designers through the management, design, development, and assessment process while taking into account explicit culture-based considerations." CBM operates inside, outside, and across cultures, and is adaptive: it "can be used in conjunction with traditional instructional design models or on its own." It focuses broadly on the management and design processes and what the content should be, bringing the human element into design disciplines.
requirements: Designers prescribe methods on the basis of preproduction analysis and research, ongoing production, and postproduction
constraints: The book does not claim to incorporate all factors consistent with culture-based designs; it provides a comprehensive set of design factors that, when implemented, can best serve to authenticate a culture-based design
Taking full advantage of the culture-based model is dependent upon including either design experts or culture experts on the project team, per the foreword
target_learners: Instructional designers and e-learning designers
graduate and undergraduate students designing ICTs
researchers
target_learning_goals: Designing culturally responsive instructional products and online environments
analyzing cultures and defining target audiences
examples: Case studies apply CBM to building an educational product from scratch, adding on to an existing video game, re-engineering an e-learning environment, and using the ID-TABLET as a diagnostic evaluation tool

article_title: Instructional design frameworks and intercultural models
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2009). Instructional Design Frameworks and Intercultural Models. Information Science Reference, IGI Global. http://www.igi-global.com/reference
title: CBM ID-TABLET: a management and design system of eight component areas
description: The ID-TABLET is CBM's management and design system, organizing the model into component areas covered across Chapters IV-XIV. These include CBM Inquiry (a monitoring system for the design process), Development (problem solving), Team (decision making), Assessments (forms of evaluation), Brainstorming (primary planning), Learners (instructional goals), Elements (content development across eight chapters), and Training (education about the product). The preface states that "the areas are ordered according to CBM's management and design system—the ID-TABLET," and Section II is designed to be used as a workbook with guiding questions for generic and specialized products.
requirements: Used as a handbook or reference resource; designers selectively attend to only those elements pertinent to a given project
constraints: Given the comprehensiveness of CBM's ID-TABLET, its areas are covered over several chapters; the problem for students may be limiting the number of design factors, given the amount of options offered in CBM
target_learners: Instructional designers
game designers
e-learning designers
students working alone or in small groups
target_learning_goals: Managing and designing culture-based ICT projects from inquiry through training
examples: Chapter XVI presents CBM Guide—Video Game Entries: Preproduction, illustrating an Add-on to an existing video game

article_title: Instructional design frameworks and intercultural models
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2009). Instructional Design Frameworks and Intercultural Models. Information Science Reference, IGI Global. http://www.igi-global.com/reference
title: Twenty-five elements of culture as design factors, treated from anthropological, psychological, and scientific perspectives
description: CBM's Elements component is a taxonomy of culture for design, explicated "from an anthropological point of view, a psychological point of view, and a scientific point of view." The foreword states that "Twenty-five elements of culture are described and explained with examples from throughout the world," and notes these "are not elements that designers typically address." Examples include conceptions of what is beautiful, class and status, non-verbal communication traditions, behavior norms, emotional patterns, orientations toward time, and conceptions of intimate, personal, social and public space. Each element carries guiding questions for gathering culture data.
requirements: Designers use the range of questions provided to gather data related to each culture element
constraints: The taxonomy is selective: designers are advised to attend only to elements pertinent to a given project
target_learners: Instructional designers
researchers analyzing societies, cultures, and groups/individuals
target_learning_goals: Gathering culture data, assessing cultures, and defining target audiences for design
examples: Chapters VII-XIV divide the elements across the anthropology of culture (aesthetics, artifacts, capital, classification), communications, demographics, environment, history, knowledge, language, physiology, relations, resources, the psychology of culture (beliefs and values, experiences, ideas, identity, interests, misconceptions, ways), and the science of culture (anomalies, cultures, futures, infinities, nature)

article_title: Instructional design frameworks and intercultural models
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2009). Instructional Design Frameworks and Intercultural Models. Information Science Reference, IGI Global. http://www.igi-global.com/reference
title: Treat culture as a core construct of all design decisions and make integrating culture an explicit act
description: The book positions culture as a design construct that has been neglected in instructional design. It argues that "Culture is a core construct of all design decisions; however, its potential to improve the design process has been mostly ignored in the field of instructional design," citing reasons such as designers not knowing how to represent culture and the absence of a framework aligning culture with ADDIE. Because designs and designers are not equitable, "Integrating culture in design must be an explicit act"—designing for people means designing with culture in mind.
requirements: Designers must acknowledge their own culture, language, ideologies, and standards, and examine situations from the point of view of the target audience
constraints: The assumption that if one thinks culture, one does culture is not true, per Scheel and Branch as cited
target_learners: Instructional designers
corporate designers working with global markets
educators serving ethnically diverse students
target_learning_goals: Making instruction accessible for diverse groups of people
avoiding imposition of designer ideologies on target audiences
examples: The preface lists situations when culture should be considered, including when learners fail to learn, when users fail to understand user interfaces, and when the design of a product fails learners or users

description: Section III of the book demonstrates CBM's ID-TABLET through four case studies. The preface states that "Section III provides 4 realistic case studies using CBM and the concluding chapter," aligned with CBM's framework. Chapter XV demonstrates custom development of an educational product from scratch; Chapter XVI illustrates an Add-on to an existing video game; Chapter XVII demonstrates re-engineering an e-learning environment; and Chapter XVIII presents the ID-TABLET used as a diagnostic evaluation tool, including a research design specification and an ethnographic instrument.

designers of educational products, games, and e-learning

article_title: Integrating Culture in the Design of ICTs
citation: Patricia A. Young. (2008). Integrating Culture in the Design of ICTs. British Journal of Educational Technology, Vol 39 No 1, 6-17. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8535.2007.00699.x
title: Culture based circumference: design specifications range from generic/culture-neutral to specialised/culture-specific
description: The article proposes a 'culture based circumference' (Figure 1) as an organizing framework for integrating culture in ICT design. Both ends of the continuum are culture based: 'Generic features can be generalised across cultures but they are still culture based', while specialised features 'focus on meeting the needs of the target audience'. Internationalisation produces generic, culture-neutral designs; localisation produces specialised, culture-specific designs. The framework widens the palette designers can draw on beyond either pole alone.
requirements: Designers must understand the needs and inclinations of the target audience, including language, ways of life, religious affiliations, symbols, graphics, values and learning styles
constraints: The article notes this is a sampling of literature, not a complete review, and game design was excluded for space
target_learners: Designers of ICTs for diverse international and local audiences
target_learning_goals: Integrating culture deliberately in the design of information and communication technologies
examples: The article maps internationalisation to the generic pole and localisation to the specialised pole of the circumference

title: Fleer's design principles for culturally specific educational software
description: The article reports a set of design principles derived from cultural research on Australian Aborigines and used to guide software development specific to that audience. The principles focused on 'making the content familiar; including familiar graphics and text; replicating family life and ideologies; supporting academic strengths; incorporating learning strategies; engaging learner-controlled learning; and a ﬂexible design'. The example is described as more specialised than generic, grounding software in the target audience's cultural experiences and ideologies.
requirements: Cultural research describing the target audience's learning strategies and contexts for learning should ground the principles
constraints: The article characterises this example as more specialised than generic on the culture based circumference

target_learning_goals: Software that accurately represents Aboriginal abilities, knowledge and ideologies and prepares learners for the dominant culture

article_title: Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs
citation: Diego Zapata-Rivera, Carol Forsyth, Edith Aurora Graf and Yang Jiang. (2024). Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs. Leveraging Large Language Models for Next Generation Educational Technologies, CEUR Workshop Proceedings. https://ceur-ws.org
title: ECD-based LLM conversation design process with a five-module prompt structure
description: A design framework for building conversation-based assessments with LLMs via prompt engineering, applying Evidence-Centered Design so conversations stay on the domain topic and elicit construct evidence. The prompt comprises five modules: (1) introduction and domain using the persona and audience patterns, e.g. "Your name is John. You are humorous and reliable study partner"; (2) a conversational schema with Socratic questioning, misconception handling, and turn-length limits; (3) persona behavior modeling via negations and response-type handling instructions; (4) restating of the four-step process; and (5) evidence instructions triggering a terminate command and an XML Toulmin evidence diagram aligned to constructs and standards.
requirements: A clear definition of the construct and the behaviors/interactions needed to make claims about student mastery before prompt design
Iterative refinement of prompts, including negations for specific response types, which can result in long prompts that may be difficult to manage
constraints: The mastery score the LLM produces is not yet validated
The approach was developed and illustrated for formative assessment of skills such as science inquiry in a volcano-eruption context
target_learners: middle-school students
target_learning_goals: science inquiry skills
argumentation
communication skills
examples: A prompt assessing science inquiry in the context of volcano eruptions instructed the LLM to keep turns to 100 words or less and to end the conversation and produce evidence when the student types terminate

article_title: Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs
citation: Diego Zapata-Rivera, Carol Forsyth, Edith Aurora Graf and Yang Jiang. (2024). Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs. Leveraging Large Language Models for Next Generation Educational Technologies, CEUR Workshop Proceedings. https://ceur-ws.org
title: Expectation-Misconception Tailored Dialogue framework adapted for assessment rather than tutoring
description: The AutoTutor-based Expectation-Misconception Tailored Dialogue framework structures agent responses around a main question with a pre-programmed complete expected answer. When the student cannot fulfill the answer, the agent provides a pump such as "can you tell me more", then hints (open-ended clues), then prompts (single-word clues), followed by an assertion; stated misconceptions are corrected and correct answers receive an assertion. CBAs adapt this framework but provide less scaffolding information, because the goal is to probe what the student already knows rather than give away the answer, so assertions are often withheld. The framework also defines response categories the agent must recognize: correct, incomplete, irrelevant, meta-communicative, meta-cognitive, and no response.
requirements: Identification of student speech acts, which is integral in determining an appropriate agent response
Expert definition of correctness for the main question in the domain at hand
constraints: CBAs deliberately provide less information in follow-up scaffolding moves than tutorial dialogues, since eliciting evidence rather than teaching is the goal
target_learners: middle-school students
students in formative assessment contexts
target_learning_goals: science inquiry skills
mathematical argumentation
English language skills
examples: In the RegExp/LSA CBA, an irrelevant response prompted the agent to say the remark was not relevant to the conversation and continue with a closing statement and the next scaffolding move

Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs. Leveraging Large Language Models for Next Generation Educational Technologies, CEUR Workshop Proceedings. https://ceur-ws.org

article_title: Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs
citation: Diego Zapata-Rivera, Carol Forsyth, Edith Aurora Graf and Yang Jiang. (2024). Designing and Evaluating Evidence-Centered Design based Conversations for Assessment with LLMs. Leveraging Large Language Models for Next Generation Educational Technologies, CEUR Workshop Proceedings. https://ceur-ws.org
title: ASATA authoring pipeline for RegExp/LSA conversation-based assessments
description: The AutoTutor Script Authoring Tool for Assessment (ASATA) implemented earlier CBAs by converting conversation diagrams into XML scripts, using LSA and RegExp to parse student responses and determine agent reactions. Conversations included one or two virtual agents interacting with the student and lasted between 2-5 turns. The authors describe this as an expensive methodology requiring time and various expertise: "This process took weeks for conversations to go from the initial descriptions to conversation diagrams to actual script conversations implemented into ASATA and tested with user data." Automated script-based testing of regular expressions with sample responses reduced iterations and testing time but remained limited by the time needed to develop and change regular expressions.
requirements: Conversation diagrams documenting construct information, conversation paths, closing statements, and partial scoring rules
Sample responses gathered from experts, small-scale pilot studies, and crowdsourcing efforts for automated testing
constraints: Development and testing were time-consuming, requiring manual entry of possible student responses and weeks of effort per conversation
target_learners: middle-school students
target_learning_goals: science inquiry skills
examples: The 2014 scientific inquiry volcano scenario CBA with two agents, a main question, 2-5 turns, and partial score assignments was built through this pipeline

article_title: The effectiveness of self-regulated learning scaffolds on academic performance in computer-based learning environments: a meta-analysis
citation: Lanqin Zheng. (2016). The effectiveness of self-regulated learning scaffolds on academic performance in computer-based learning environments: a meta-analysis. Asia Pacific Education Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12564-016-9426-9
title: Design SRL scaffolds to support the whole self-regulation process using integrated, multiple, and combined domain-general and domain-specific scaffolds
description: The article recommends that scaffolds in computer-based environments support the entire SRL cycle rather than a single phase, and that designers combine scaffold types. It states scaffolds "should support the whole process of SRL, ranging from setting goals, making plans, and enacting strategies, to adapting metacognition", and that "integrated SRL tools with multiple functions and multiple kinds of scaffolds should be considered as the optimal way to promote academic performance". Scaffold design should also consider contextual factors of learners, environment, and their interactions.
requirements: Scaffolds must address the full SRL cycle: goal setting, planning, strategy enactment, monitoring, self-evaluation, and metacognitive adaptation
constraints: The article notes few adaptive scaffolds were used in the reviewed studies, and suggests adaptive scaffolding may be more beneficial since it adjusts to students' learning needs
target_learners: K-12 students
higher education students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills
academic performance across learning domains
examples: The meta-analysis found integrated SRL tools with multiple functions had the highest effect size among scaffold mechanisms (ES = 0.947), and studies using both scaffold modes had the highest effect (ES = 1.699)

article_title: Working memory development from early childhood to adolescence using two nationally representative samples.
citation: Ahmed, S. F., Ellis, A., Ward, K. P., Chaku, N., & Davis-Kean, P. E. (2022). Working memory development from early childhood to adolescence using two nationally representative samples. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0001396
title: Use national developmental trends of working memory as a reference for interpreting individual studies and timing interventions
description: The article argues that population-level WM growth charts serve as a normative reference, "akin to national height or weight standards in medical settings", allowing researchers to interpret intervention effects independent of age-related change and helping clinicians and educators identify periods of rapid WM growth. The study supplies such trends from ages 3–19 using two nationally representative samples.
requirements: Nationally representative longitudinal data with repeated WM measures across a wide age range
constraints: Findings are verbal WM only and generalizable to the U.S. population, which the authors note is only a small fraction of the human population
target_learners: children and adolescents ages 3–19
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting the development of working memory relevant to learning, reasoning, and problem solving
examples: The authors charted forward and backward digit span from ages 3–19 in the PSID-CDS and numbers reversed across nine waves in the ECLS-K:2011, publishing predicted means by age and wave.

article_title: Working memory development from early childhood to adolescence using two nationally representative samples.
citation: Ahmed, S. F., Ellis, A., Ward, K. P., Chaku, N., & Davis-Kean, P. E. (2022). Working memory development from early childhood to adolescence using two nationally representative samples. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0001396
title: Childhood is a key window of opportunity—and vulnerability—for working memory development, suggesting early timing of WM-supporting efforts
description: Because WM grows most rapidly during childhood, the authors argue this period "may provide a window of opportunity during which the effects of interventions might be the most effective", while also being a time when WM development "might be particularly vulnerable to the effects of negative environmental settings". This supports prioritizing WM-supporting practices and environments in early childhood and elementary education.
requirements: Identification of contextual predictors of WM growth to target supports effectively
constraints: The intervention-timing implication is the authors' interpretation; the study measured normative growth, not intervention effects
target_learners: young children and elementary-school students
target_learning_goals: supporting working memory growth underlying learning and academic skill development
examples: The study's fitted trajectories showed the steepest digit span growth across ages 3–10, leveling off in late childhood before a brief early-adolescent uptick.

article_title: Early predictors of middle school fraction knowledge
citation: Bailey Drew H., Siegler Robert S., Geary David C. (2014). Early Predictors of Middle School Fraction Knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12155
title: Integrated theory of numerical development
description: The article invokes Siegler, Thompson, and Schneider's (2011) integrated theory of numerical development, which "proposes that fractions play a key role in learning the properties that are and are not invariant for real numbers, and thus that learning fractions plays a crucial role in acquiring a mature concept of number". It assumes understanding of fractions is continuous with understanding of whole numbers, so individual differences in the two should be related independent of domain-general abilities. The study's longitudinal findings are presented as consistent with this assumption.
requirements: Understanding that the one property uniting whole numbers and fractions is that they represent magnitudes orderable on a number line
constraints: The theory provided no obvious reason to expect early whole number knowledge to predict later reading achievement, and the reading null was consistent with this
target_learners: children in elementary and middle school learning whole numbers and fractions
target_learning_goals: acquiring a mature concept of number
understanding fraction magnitudes
distinguishing properties invariant for whole numbers versus all real numbers
examples: The study tested the theory's assumption by predicting middle school fraction knowledge from first-grade whole number knowledge while controlling for IQ, executive functioning, and demographics

article_title: Early predictors of middle school fraction knowledge
citation: Bailey Drew H., Siegler Robert S., Geary David C. (2014). Early Predictors of Middle School Fraction Knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12155
title: Focus elementary and middle school mathematics instruction on whole numbers and fractions
description: The article argues that longitudinal evidence lends support to the National Mathematics Advisory Panel's central recommendation that "mathematics instruction in elementary and middle school focus on promoting knowledge of whole numbers and fractions". First graders' whole number magnitude and arithmetic knowledge were uniquely predictive of middle school fraction knowledge, and fifth graders' fraction knowledge predicted tenth graders' mathematics achievement. The authors tie this to the trend toward focusing on fewer mathematical goals pursued in more depth.
requirements: Longitudinal evidence identifying which early strands uniquely contribute to later achievement
constraints: No data are yet available on whether early proficiency in geometry and data analysis/statistics uniquely contributes to later mathematics achievement
target_learners: elementary and middle school students
target_learning_goals: whole number magnitude knowledge
whole number arithmetic proficiency
fraction magnitude and arithmetic knowledge
examples: The authors note the Common Core State Standards Initiative embodies the trend toward focusing on fewer mathematical goals and pursuing them in more depth

article_title: Let me be your guide: physical guidance improves spatial learning for older adults with simulated low vision
citation: Barhorst-Cates Erica M., Rand Kristina M., Creem-Regehr Sarah H. (2017). Let Me be Your Guide: Physical Guidance Improves Spatial Learning for Older Adults with Simulated Low Vision. Experimental Brain Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00221-017-5063-8
title: Reduce mobility monitoring demands (e.g., via physical guidance) to support spatial learning during low-vision navigation
description: The principle holds that safety- and stability-related mobility monitoring consumes attentional resources that would otherwise support spatial learning of an environment, so physically supporting the learner's mobility frees resources for encoding. In the study, "the experimenter instructed the participant to hold onto the experimenter's arm throughout the path" in the guided condition while verbal route guidance was held constant. This improved pointing accuracy and the benefit grew with age.
requirements: The aid must reduce mobility demands without adding navigational guidance that divides attention; the article contrasts physical guidance with GPS-style aids that impair spatial learning
constraints: The cognitive-load (RT) and anxiety measures did not differ between conditions, so the mechanism is not confirmed
Tested only with simulated degraded acuity and contrast sensitivity in a real-world indoor building-scale environment; the article calls for testing in clinical low-vision populations
target_learners: older adults with low vision
adults navigating under degraded viewing conditions
target_learning_goals: survey knowledge / spatial memory of landmarks along a route
examples: Participants walked four unique real-world paths (109–121 m) wearing degraded-vision goggles, two guided and two unguided, with verbal instructions identical across conditions
key_sources: Barhorst-Cates Erica M., Rand Kristina M., Creem-Regehr Sarah H. (2017). Let Me be Your Guide: Physical Guidance Improves Spatial Learning for Older Adults with Simulated Low Vision. Experimental Brain Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00221-017-5063-8

article_title: Let me be your guide: physical guidance improves spatial learning for older adults with simulated low vision
citation: Barhorst-Cates Erica M., Rand Kristina M., Creem-Regehr Sarah H. (2017). Let Me be Your Guide: Physical Guidance Improves Spatial Learning for Older Adults with Simulated Low Vision. Experimental Brain Research. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00221-017-5063-8
title: Mobility-monitoring account: attentional demands of safe mobility compete with spatial learning during low-vision navigation
description: The account holds that navigating with severely degraded vision requires detecting and avoiding obstacles, and that "the attention needed to maintain safe mobility detracts from the pool of attentional resources available for spatial learning of the environment." Physical guidance operates at the level of guiding mobility rather than navigational choices, proposing to free attentional resources at encoding, which distinguishes it from GPS-style aids that divide attention and impair learning. The study's pointing-error results support the account, though the RT cognitive-load measure did not vary between conditions.
requirements: A task in which mobility monitoring (obstacle avoidance, stability) imposes attentional demands separate from route-choice guidance
constraints: The expected RT difference between guidance conditions was not observed in older adults, and the article states further consideration of these lack of differences is needed
target_learners: older adults
low-vision navigators
younger adults under degraded viewing
target_learning_goals: spatial learning of environments during active navigation
examples: Rand et al. (2015) showed younger adults' low-vision spatial learning improved with a physical guide, partially explained by attentional demands measured via auditory reaction time

article_title: Are Individual Differences in Arithmetic Fact Retrieval in Children Related to Inhibition?
citation: Bellon E, Fias W and De Smedt B (2016) Are Individual Differences in Arithmetic Fact Retrieval in Children Related to Inhibition? Front. Psychol. 7:825. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00825
title: Associative-network interference account of arithmetic fact retrieval
description: The article works within the theoretical account that arithmetic facts are stored in an associative network in semantic memory, so that retrieving one fact activates competing facts that must be inhibited. It states that "arithmetic facts are particularly prone to interference" because of shared features, and that poor inhibition could yield specific errors such as answering 6 × 3 = 24. This framework motivated the study's hypothesis that cognitive inhibition would relate to fact retrieval, a hypothesis the data did not support in typically developing children.
requirements: The account presupposes that competing problem-answer associations are formed and stored in long-term memory during fact learning
constraints: The present study's data did not support the predicted inhibition–fact-retrieval association in typically developing third graders
target_learners: typically developing third-grade children learning single-digit arithmetic
target_learning_goals: automatized retrieval of single-digit arithmetic facts
examples: The study used multiplication verification items with table-related false solutions (e.g., 6 × 3 = 24) to probe competing associations

article_title: Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: The common and differential involvement of executive functions in intelligence and creativity
citation: Benedek Mathias, Jauk Emanuel, Sommer Markus, Arendasy Martin, Neubauer Aljoscha C. (2014). Intelligence, creativity, and cognitive control: The common and differential involvement of executive functions in intelligence and creativity. Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.intell.2014.05.007
title: Executive nature of creativity: controlled top-down processes (updating and inhibition) support creative thought
description: The article advances an executive account of creativity, arguing that creative idea generation "does not solely depend on spontaneous thought processes, but strongly relies on controlled top-down activity". Inhibition is thought to suppress dominant, obvious responses so that remote concepts can be retrieved, while working memory supports controlled search of memory and active maintenance of task goals and strategies during idea generation. The study's latent variable findings (updating and inhibition predicting creativity; shifting not) are presented as direct support for this account.
requirements: Measurement of both executive abilities and divergent thinking ability within the same individuals
constraints: Interpretation limited by latent EF factors each defined by task blocks of a single task, and by the possibility of task-specific method variance
target_learners: adults
target_learning_goals: creative idea generation (divergent thinking)
examples: The alternate uses task analysis in the discussion describes how working memory maintains goals such as generating creative uses while searching memory for remote applications

Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.intell.2014.05.007
title: Assess creativity via rated quality of top ideas rather than ideational fluency to avoid confounding with response count
description: The article scored divergent thinking tasks by the top-scoring method, in which creativity scores reflect the average creativity rating of the three highest-rated ideas per task. The authors state this method "was shown to avoid a confounding with the number of responses", allowing latent creativity to reflect the creative quality of ideas rather than sheer output volume. Four raters scored responses holistically on a four-point scale considering originality and appropriateness.
requirements: Multiple experienced raters with acceptable interrater reliability (ICC values reported between .57 and .79)
constraints: Requires holistic rating judgments; the article notes high creativity ratings should only be assigned to ideas that only few people could presumably come up with
target_learners: adults
target_learning_goals: assessment of creative potential (divergent thinking ability)
examples: Four DT tasks (two alternate uses, two instances) were administered with 2 min per task, and creativity scores reflected the average rating of the three top-rated ideas per task

article_title: <p>Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation</p>
citation: Biotteau M, Danna J, Baudou É, Puyjarinet F, Velay J-L, Albaret J-M, Chaix Y. (2019). Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. https://doi.org/10.2147/NDT.S120514
title: Two-category framework of DCD interventions: bottom-up process-oriented versus top-down task-oriented approaches
description: The review organizes DCD intervention methods into two main categories. The bottom-up category contains process-oriented (deficit-oriented) approaches such as kinesthetic training and sensory integration, which assume "a deficit in a specific body function or part ... is responsible for the impaired motor skills" and aim to remediate that underlying deficit. The top-down category contains task-oriented (functional skill) approaches such as neuromotor task training and CO-OP, which teach children the ADLs they need, with children as actors encouraged to think about difficulties and find solutions while adults help explore and validate strategies.
requirements: Interventions supporting participation and activity are key to remediating motor impairments and associated problems in DCD
constraints: Process-oriented approaches were not included in European Academy of Childhood Disabilities recommendations or the 2012 American Academy of Pediatrics policy statement due to weak effects
target_learners: Children with developmental coordination disorder
target_learning_goals: Improving coordinated motor skills and activities of daily living
examples: Neuromotor task training and cognitive orientation to daily occupational performance (CO-OP) as named task-oriented approaches
key_sources: Biotteau M, Danna J, Baudou É, Puyjarinet F, Velay J-L, Albaret J-M, Chaix Y. (2019). Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. https://doi.org/10.2147/NDT.S120514

article_title: <p>Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation</p>
citation: Biotteau M, Danna J, Baudou É, Puyjarinet F, Velay J-L, Albaret J-M, Chaix Y. (2019). Developmental coordination disorder and dysgraphia: signs and symptoms, diagnosis, and rehabilitation. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment. https://doi.org/10.2147/NDT.S120514
title: Standardized assessment tools for DCD and dysgraphia diagnosis (MABC-2, TGMD-2, DCDQ, BHK, Minnesota Handwriting Assessment, ETCH)
description: The review catalogs the standardized instruments used to diagnose DCD and dysgraphia. The MABC-2, the most widely used DCD tool, consists of 8 items across three age ranges (3–6, 7–10, 11–16 years), lasts 40–50 mins, and covers manual dexterity, ball skills, and balance. The TGMD-2 is a norm-referenced measure of gross motor skills with 2 subtests probing 12 skills for children aged 3–10–11 years, lasting 15–20 mins. The DCDQ is a brief parental screening questionnaire for children aged 5–15 years. For dysgraphia, the BHK (standardized on 837 children aged 6–11) yields legibility and speed scores, alongside the Minnesota Handwriting Assessment and the ETCH.
requirements: Guidelines for administration must be followed to ensure reliability of standardized psychomotor batteries and scales
constraints: Unlike DCD, there is no gold standard for diagnosing dysgraphia, probably because writing systems differ substantially between countries and languages
target_learners: Children aged 3–16 suspected of DCD
Children with suspected dysgraphia in Grades 1–6
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing motor coordination and handwriting difficulties and establishing baselines for intervention
examples: The BHK requires participants to copy a text for 5 mins on an unlined sheet, scored on 13 legibility criteria plus writing speed

article_title: Learning from others at work: communities of practice and informal learning
citation: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202.
title: Communities of practice are a useful but insufficient framework for informal workplace learning; loosely and tightly coupled variants and additional conceptualisations are needed
description: The article evaluates Lave and Wenger's and Wenger's communities of practice framework against qualitative data from four workgroups. It finds the framework "provides useful ways of accounting for the phenomenon we are considering", but is "not sufficient for our purposes of dealing with informal learning at work", because some learning networks are more loosely coupled groupings that do not build identity and meaning. The authors propose degrees of coupling, Bernstein's framing, and Engeström's expansive learning as complementary lenses.
requirements: The framework presupposes sustained relationships, shared ways of engaging, and mutual familiarity among members, as in the tightly coupled tiling teachers and HR group.
constraints: Communities of practice form naturally, are often strongly bounded, and may not be easily cultivated; an exclusive focus on them may limit accounts of workplace learning and the kinds of intervention possible.
target_learners: Adult workers in organisational workgroups
target_learning_goals: Informal workplace learning, including mastering organisational processes, negotiating the political, and dealing with the atypical
examples: The tiling teachers and HR group were described as tightly coupled communities of practice; the educational planners, with more frequent reformation and changing membership, were looser and possibly more representative of contemporary organisations.
key_sources: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202. https://doi.org/10.1108/13665620310483895

article_title: Learning from others at work: communities of practice and informal learning
citation: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202.
title: Bernstein's construct of framing applied to communities of practice: strong framing means sharp boundaries on what is transmitted between members, weak framing blurred ones
description: The article imports Bernstein's (1990) construct of framing from studies of curriculum and schooling into the analysis of workplace learning networks. Framing of knowledge is strong "when there is a sharp boundary between what may be transmitted and what may not be transmitted in a learning relationship", and weak where the boundary is blurred. The authors identify strong framing with the tilers and weaker framing with the educational planners, and suggest loosely coupled communities of practice may be regarded as communities in which framing of knowledge is weak.
requirements: Applying framing requires identifying the boundary between what may and may not be transmitted within a learning relationship among network members.
constraints: The construct was developed from studies of curriculum and schooling; the article presents its application to workplace communities of practice as a proposal ('might also be applied').
target_learners: Adult workers in organisational workgroups
target_learning_goals: Understanding the scope and consistency of knowledge transmission within workplace learning networks
examples: Strong framing was identified with the tiling teachers and weaker framing with the educational planners.

article_title: Learning from others at work: communities of practice and informal learning
citation: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202.
title: Engeström's expansive learning: horizontal or sideways learning among peers without a conventional knowledge hierarchy, useful for conceptualising dealing with the atypical
description: The article draws on Engeström's (2001) activity-theoretical notion of expansive learning, articulated in the context of workplace learning. Engeström "draws attention to what he calls horizontal or sideways learning and development in which problem solving occurs essentially through interactions among peers without resort to a conventional knowledge hierarchy". The authors find this a potentially useful way of conceptualising their category of dealing with the atypical, where no set procedure exists and learning must address a problem or contradiction, often crossing workgroup boundaries.
requirements: The construct presupposes a focus on the social and organisational context rather than on individual learning, with contradictions or atypical events as sources of change.
constraints: The article presents expansive learning as a potentially useful conceptualisation for dealing with the atypical, not as a framework validated against the study data.
target_learners: Adult workers in organisational workgroups
target_learning_goals: Dealing with atypical problems for which no set procedure or process exists
examples: The authors link dealing with the atypical to expansive learning because such problem solving can require crossing boundaries of workgroups and practices, which the well-bounded notion of communities of practice cannot adequately capture.

citation: Burin, D. I., Irrazabal, N., Injoque Ricle, I., Saux, G., & Barreyro, J. P. (2018). Self-reported internet skills, previous knowledge and working memory in text comprehension in E-learning. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 15:18. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-018-0099-9
title: Four-domain model of Internet skills (operational, formal, information, strategic)
description: The article adopts van Deursen and van Dijk's taxonomy of Internet skills, in which "Operational skills consist of the actions that allow a person to use digital tools", "Formal skills refer to navigation and orientation in structures specific to digital media", information skills concern searching, comparing, assessing and integrating information, and strategic skills involve using the Internet to achieve personal, professional, or social goals. constraints: The validated version covers only operational, formal/navigation, and informational/evaluation domains; strategic skills were not studied

They recommend that teachers and instructional designers consider this before implementing the common practice of closed-question comprehension checks after lessons.

article_title: “When I Think of Black Girls, I Think of Opportunities”: Black Girls' Identity Development and the Protective Role of Parental Socialization in Educational Settings
citation: Burnett Marketa, McBride Margarett, Green McKenzie N., Cooper Shauna M. (2022). “When I Think of Black Girls, I Think of Opportunities”: Black Girls' Identity Development and the Protective Role of Parental Socialization in Educational Settings. title: Phenomenological Variant of Ecological Systems Theory (PVEST)
description: PVEST is Spencer's model of how Black children process and make meaning of lived experiences. It begins with self-other appraisals—perceptions of how others view one, with attention to biases and stereotypes—and "PVEST posits that how someone makes meaning of these self-other appraisals also impacts their stress engagement which leads to their reactive coping strategies." Stable identities emerge through adaptive or maladaptive coping, leading to adverse or productive outcomes. The study used PVEST as its guiding framework for a theoretical thematic analysis of girls' meaning-making.
requirements: Codes and analysis aligned with PVEST and the research questions, emphasizing youths' own meaning-making as interpreters of their experiences

target_learning_goals: identity development
coping with gendered racism in educational settings
examples: The study's codebook of seven overarching identity and socialization codes was developed to closely align with PVEST and the research questions

article_title: Comprehension skill, inference-making ability, and their relation to knowledge
citation: Kate Cain, Jane V. Oakhill, Marcia A. Barnes, and Peter E. Bryant. (2001). Comprehension skill, inference-making ability, and their relation to knowledge. Memory & Cognition, 29(6), 850-859. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03196476
title: Mental models account of children's text comprehension difficulties: poor comprehenders construct incomplete, poorly integrated representations of text
description: The article interprets children's comprehension difficulties within the mental models framework, in which skilled comprehension requires building a coherent, integrated model of a text as a whole rather than only local links. The authors state that "poor comprehenders construct incomplete representations of text: They are often able to integrate information at a local level but are unable to produce a coherent integrated model of the text as a whole." In this study the framework motivated the distinction between coherence inferences, needed for cohesion, and elaborative inferences, which enrich the representation, and the finding that inference failures leave a poorly integrated text model.
requirements: Assessment of inference making must separate inferences essential for textual coherence from merely elaborative ones
Relevant background knowledge must be available to the learner for knowledge-based inferences to be possible
constraints: The account is applied to children with age-appropriate word-reading and vocabulary skills whose difficulties arise at the text level
The study tested 7- to 8-year-olds listening to a multiepisode story, so scope is limited to that age band and auditory presentation
target_learners: 7- to 8-year-old children with specific reading comprehension deficits despite adequate word-reading skills
target_learning_goals: Text comprehension
Inference making during narrative listening and reading
examples: Children heard a six-episode story about an imaginary planet after learning a 12-fact knowledge base, and answered coherence, elaborative, literal, and simile questions after each episode

article_title: Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood
citation: Checa, P., & Rueda, M. R. (2011). Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2011.591857
title: Promote executive attention and effortful control to help children succeed at school
description: The article recommends that educators and intervention designers attend to children's executive attention and effortful control as foundations for school competence. It states: "Our data point out the importance of promoting executive attention and effortful control in order to help children to be successful at school." The authors argue this evidence "has the potential to guide the design of intervention programs aiming at enhancing school readiness."
requirements: Interventions should target the executive attention network and temperamental effortful control, which the study links to grades and schooling skills.
constraints: The authors note future research is needed to test whether attention training actually results in better academic performance and schooling competence.
target_learners: children in late childhood and early adolescence (around age 12)
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in mathematics and literacy
schooling skills such as rule following and student-role understanding
examples: The study measured executive attention with a combined Flanker-Go/No-Go task and linked interference suppression efficiency to math grades and schooling skills.

article_title: Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood
citation: Checa, P., & Rueda, M. R. (2011). Behavioral and Brain Measures of Executive Attention and School Competence in Late Childhood. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2011.591857
title: Executive attention network as the neural system underlying effortful control and self-regulation
description: Within Posner's neurocognitive model, executive attention is related to a neural network involving the anterior cingulate cortex and prefrontal regions. The article states that "the executive attention network in Posner's model constitutes the neural system underlying EC" (Rueda, Posner, & Rothbart, 2005a). Executive attention is required in situations involving "overcoming well-learned or dominant responses, facing novel and/or dangerous situations, detecting and correcting errors and planning actions." The study uses this framework to interpret correlations between temperament, brain, and school measures.
requirements: The framework assumes measures of executive attention through conflict tasks correlate with parent and/or self-reported measures of effortful control.
constraints: The article notes the influence of effortful control on school competence is not the same at different ages.
target_learners: children and adolescents in school settings
target_learning_goals: self-regulation of cognition and action
school competence and academic achievement
examples: The study used a combined Flanker and Go/No-Go task with EEG to index the efficiency of the executive attention network in twelve-year-olds.

article_title: Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children
citation: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000
title: Chinese version of the Sleep Self-Report (SSR) with validated psychometrics
description: The Sleep Self-Report is a 23-item, 3-point self-report questionnaire assessing children's sleep habits and disturbance, with higher summed scores indicating more disturbed sleep. The authors developed a Chinese version by translation and back-translation and validated it in a separate sample: "Another 433 Chinese children (7–12  y ears old) were recruited to test the psychometric properties of the Chinese version, revealing that the Cronbach's α was 0.82 and retest-reliability (ICC) was 0.87." In the main study it served as the sleep disturbance measure for 204 children.
requirements: Requires children old enough for valid self-report; the article notes the youngest age adapted for SSR is 7 or 8 years old
constraints: Measures subjective multiple aspects of sleep (bedtime resistance, sleep anxiety, daytime sleepiness), not objective sleep duration
target_learners: early primary school children aged 7–12
target_learning_goals: measurement of habitual sleep disturbance as a factor in children's cognitive development
examples: Administered collectively in groups of 20–40 children, with instructions read aloud and about 10 s per item

article_title: Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children
citation: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000
title: Extended 36-trial Red-Blue Test of inhibitory control with reported reliability
description: The Red-Blue Test is a Stroop/Day-Night-adapted computer task in which children name colors according to a reversed rule on an alien planet, scoring correct answers given within 2 s. The authors extended the original 16-trial preschool version to 36 trials for early primary school children, reasoning that children make more errors in later trials and that reliability increases with trial number. They report that "With the increase of trial number, the current test has gained sufficient reliability (split-half r = 0.82, Cronbach α = 0.71)."
requirements: One-to-one administration with two checking trials to ensure the child understands the rule
constraints: Scored by accuracy only, not reaction time; the authors note RT or speed may be more reliable in certain cognitive tests
target_learners: early primary school children aged 7–9
target_learning_goals: assessment of inhibitory control as an executive function component
examples: Used as the inhibitory control measure in the 204-child study, with 36 trials total

article_title: Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children
citation: Chen Y, Wang Y, Wang S, Zhang M and Wu N. (2021). Self-Reported Sleep and Executive Function in Early Primary School Children. Front. Psychol. 12:793000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.793000
title: Three-component model of executive function (inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, working memory)
description: The article adopts the multidimensional conceptualization of executive function in which "It is often postulated in the literature that EF has three elementary components: inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility." Each component is measured by a separate task (Red-Blue Test, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, Backward Digit Span), and the components are moderately associated but separable. The study's design treats each component's link with sleep separately, which the authors say previous research neglecting the multidimensionality tended to miss.
requirements: Separate tasks for each component; the article notes few studies have systematically investigated sleep against all components
constraints: The structure of EF develops with age; the article notes shifting was found mixed with inhibition in young children, so correlation patterns may differ across age groups
target_learners: typically developing children in early primary school
target_learning_goals: understanding how sleep relates to distinct executive function components underlying school performance
examples: Applied in the current study with one classic task per component, administered counterbalanced in about 20 min per child

article_title: Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability
citation: Chiappe, P., Hasher, L., & Siegel, L. S. (2000). Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability. Memory & Cognition, 28(1), 8-17. https://www.psychonomic.org
title: Inhibitory control hypothesis: three functions (access, deletion, restraint) govern working memory contents
description: The article tests the Hasher and colleagues account in which inhibition controls the contents of working memory through three functions. As the article states, "These functions are access, deletion, and restraint": access prevents goal-irrelevant information from entering working memory, deletion suppresses information that has become irrelevant (whose failure yields proactive interference), and restraint prevents strong responses from seizing control so other responses can be considered. The study uses intrusion error types and a mixed span format to index these functions in relation to age and reading skill.
requirements: Assessment requires error analysis of span-task recall, classifying intrusions as current nonfinal, previous, or extraneous
constraints: The article reports the error analyses provided only mixed support for the hypothesis as applied to aging, with no age effects for previous or extraneous intrusions
target_learners: individuals aged 6-49, including those with reading disabilities
target_learning_goals: working memory capacity for storage during processing
word recognition and reading comprehension
examples: Experiment 1 used the blocked listening span format and Experiment 2 a mixed format to test whether reducing proactive interference would diminish age and reading-skill differences
key_sources: Chiappe, P., Hasher, L., & Siegel, L. S. (2000). Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability. Memory & Cognition, 28(1), 8-17. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03211570

article_title: Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability
citation: Chiappe, P., Hasher, L., & Siegel, L. S. (2000). Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability. Memory & Cognition, 28(1), 8-17. https://www.psychonomic.org
title: Minimize proactive interference when measuring or supporting working memory across the lifespan
description: Because age-related declines in working memory span appear when trials are blocked and hence mutually interfering, task procedures that make trials distinctive reduce or eliminate those declines. The article shows that presenting the listening span task in a mixed format, in which each set contains two-, three-, and four-item trials, removed the adult decline seen with the blocked format. This supports designing assessment and instructional tasks so that earlier trials do not proactively interfere with later recall.
requirements: Trial formats must be arranged so that items from earlier trials are distinct from later targets, as in the mixed design
constraints: The mixed format did not eliminate differences between skilled and disabled readers, so reducing proactive interference does not remove reading-skill-related deficits
target_learners: learners across the lifespan, including middle-aged and older adults
target_learning_goals: accurate recall of target information during concurrent processing
examples: Experiment 2 administered three sets each containing a two-item trial followed by a three-item trial and ending with a four-item trial, rather than blocking trials by set size
key_sources: Chiappe, P., Hasher, L., & Siegel, L. S. (2000). Working memory, inhibitory control, and reading disability. Memory & Cognition, 28(1), 8-17. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03211570

article_title: Language development and everyday functioning of children with hearing loss assessed at 3 years of age
citation: Ching Teresa Y. C., Crowe Kathryn, Martin Vivienne, Day Julia, Mahler Nicole, Youn Samantha, Street Laura, Cook Cassandra, Orsini Julia (2010). International journal of speech-language pathology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3094718/
title: Parents’ Evaluation of Aural/oral performance of Children (PEACH) questionnaire
description: The PEACH is an interview-administered parent questionnaire for assessing children’s functional performance in everyday life based on parents’ observations. The article describes it as "applicable for assessing children with hearing loss ranging from mild to profound degrees whose age ranges from 4 weeks to 18 years" and reports it was reliable for evaluating amplification effectiveness in real life. In this study, children’s performance was expressed as deviation from age-appropriate means, and PEACH scores correlated significantly with standardized language measures.
requirements: Administered as an interview with parents; uses normative data and critical differences (Ching & Hill, 2007) to relate performance to normal-hearing peers.
constraints: Performance expressed relative to normative data; applicable across mild to profound hearing loss.
target_learners: children with hearing loss aged 4 weeks to 18 years
target_learning_goals: evaluating aural/oral communicative functioning in everyday life
examples: Used with 61 parents of 3-year-old children in the LOCHI study; mean age-corrected score was −23.5.

description: The article recommends systematic use of parental observations to evaluate communicative functioning of children in real life, because structured tests may not reflect everyday ability. It reports that "the significant correlation with the PEACH provides evidence on convergent validity" of language skills measured in structured and unstructured settings. Parent report also extends assessment to children of non-English speaking background or whose primary mode of communication is not spoken English.

article_title: Gaining control: changing relations between executive control and processing speed and their relevance for mathematics achievement over course of the preschool period
citation: Clark, C. A. C., Nelson, J. M., Garza, J., Sheffield, T. D., Wiebe, S. A., & Espy, K. A. (2014). Gaining control: changing relations between executive control and processing speed and their relevance for mathematics achievement over course of the preschool period. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00107
title: Developmental cascade model: processing speed as a driving mechanism for higher-order cognition including EC
description: The developmental cascade model holds that growth in domain-general processing speed drives gains in higher-order cognition such as working memory and inhibitory control. The article states that "processing speed is conceptualized as a central mental capacity that drives changes in higher-order cognition", with age-related speed gains freeing cognitive resources for executive operations. This study tested the cascade account in early childhood by modeling EC and processing speed as overlapping latents across preschool age points, finding both support (speed contributes substantially to executive performance) and qualitative shifts in their interface over time.
requirements: Latent modeling that simultaneously loads executive tasks on EC and processing speed factors to parse their relative contributions
constraints: The article notes mediation analyses cannot reveal changes in the interplay of processing speed and EC over development, motivating its age-point approach
target_learners: preschool children aged 3 to 5.25 years
target_learning_goals: executive control development supporting mathematics achievement
examples: The study loaded each executive task simultaneously onto EC and processing speed factors at ages 3, 3.75, 4.5, and 5.25, covarying language proficiency
key_sources: Clark, C. A. C., Nelson, J. M., Garza, J., Sheffield, T. D., Wiebe, S. A., & Espy, K. A. (2014).
