article_title: First graders' literacy and self-regulation gains: The effect of individualizing student instruction
citation: Connor Carol McDonald, Ponitz Claire Cameron, Phillips Beth M., Travis Q. Monét, Glasney Stephanie, Morrison Frederick J. (2010). First graders' literacy and self-regulation gains: The effect of individualizing student instruction. Journal of School Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2010.06.003
title: Working model of self-regulation supporting academic growth through teacher practices
description: The article proposes a working model in which self-regulation, defined as "the deliberate modulation of one's responses to stimuli", enables students to focus cognitive resources on learning tasks, ignore distractions, and maximize learning time, thereby producing more efficient literacy learning. Key to the model is the assumption that teacher practices — planning, classroom management, use of routines, and opportunities to work independently and with peers — support the development of stronger self-regulation and hence stronger academic skills. The ISI intervention was designed to test this model (Fig. 1).
requirements: Teachers must be trained in planning, organizing, and classroom management strategies, and provide opportunities for students to practice managing their own behavior
constraints: The evidence for teacher practices contributing to self-regulation was largely correlational prior to this study; the self-regulation effect was evident only for students with initially weak self-regulation
target_learners: First-grade students in elementary classrooms
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation (attention, working memory, inhibitory control)
Early literacy skills including reading comprehension and vocabulary
examples: The ISI intervention operationalized the model through professional development on organizing, minimizing non-instructional time, and planning, delivered via the A2i software
key_sources: Connor Carol McDonald, Ponitz Claire Cameron, Phillips Beth M., Travis Q. Monét, Glasney Stephanie, Morrison Frederick J. (2010). title: Assessment-to-instruction (A2i) web-based planning software
description: The Assessment-to-instruction (A2i) software "translates assessment results into specific recommendations for amounts and types of instruction for each student in the classroom". It automatically records teachers' use, including total minutes of active use, which the study used as a metric of planning and a proxy for intervention fidelity. An integral part of the ISI intervention, A2i includes planning-specific components such as the Literacy Minutes Manager and the Group Activity Planner, and is available at http://isi.fcrr.org.
requirements: Teachers must be trained to use the software to plan individualized instruction, and assessment results must be available to generate recommendations
constraints: A2i use minutes are a proxy for fidelity, not a direct measure of instructional quality; treatment teachers' use ranged widely, from 15 to 370 minutes

target_learning_goals: Individualized literacy instruction matched to students' vocabulary and reading skills

article_title: Neurocognitive development of relational reasoning
citation: Crone Eveline A., Wendelken Carter, van Leijenhorst Linda, Honomichl Ryan D., Christoff Kalina, Bunge Silvia A. (2009). Neurocognitive development of relational reasoning. Developmental Science, 12(1), 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2008.00743.x
title: Relational integration account of rostrolateral prefrontal cortex function
description: The article endorses the account that RLPFC is specifically engaged when multiple relations must be jointly considered, whereas DLPFC is sensitive to task difficulty factors such as working memory and response selection rather than relational complexity per se. In adults, "RLPFC did not differentiate between REL-0 and REL-1 trials (REL-2 > REL-0, REL-1), whereas DLPFC exhibited an increase from REL-0 to REL-1 and from REL-1 to REL-2." The developmental findings extend this account: children recruit RLPFC for both 1st- and 2nd-order relational processing, and the adult specialization for integration is still undergoing change between ages 8 and 12.
requirements: Performance of problems that require joint consideration of multiple relations to detect RLPFC's selective engagement
constraints: The article notes alternative theoretical accounts of RLPFC involvement exist and are not adjudicated here
The account rests on cross-sectional age-group comparison rather than longitudinal within-person change
target_learners: children aged 8-12
adults aged 18-25
target_learning_goals: relational reasoning
relational integration
fluid intelligence
examples: Adults in the RPM-like task showed RLPFC activation selectively for REL-2 problems, replicating Christoff et al. (2001), while children engaged RLPFC for REL-1 as well as REL-2 problems

article_title: Mothers, Intrinsic Math Motivation, Arithmetic Skills, and Math Anxiety in Elementary School
citation: Daches Cohen L and Rubinsten O (2017) Mothers, Intrinsic Math Motivation, Arithmetic Skills, and Math Anxiety in Elementary School. Front. Psychol. 8:1939. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01939
title: Dual-measure framework of math anxiety: accessible self-representations versus inaccessible cognitive structures
description: The article organizes math anxiety assessment around two kinds of representation: accessible self-representations measured by explicit self-report questionnaires such as the AMAS, and inaccessible cognitive structures activated automatically, measured implicitly through attentional bias in the numerical dot-probe task. Its central organizing finding is that "diﬀerent factors predict accessible self-representations as compared to inaccessible cognitive structures of children's math anxiety" — cognitive factors predicted the explicit measure while environmental factors predicted the implicit one. The framework motivates using both kinds of tools when assessing math anxiety in children.
requirements: Assessment must include both an explicit self-report questionnaire and an implicit task such as the numerical dot-probe task, since the two measure distinct facets
constraints: The article notes the explicit and implicit measures were non-significantly correlated in this sample and that the relatively small sample size warrants caution
target_learners: elementary school students (sixth graders)
target_learning_goals: mathematics learning and math anxiety
arithmetic skills
intrinsic math motivation
examples: Sixth graders completed the AMAS self-report questionnaire and the numerical dot-probe task, whose congruency effect served as the implicit measure of attentional bias toward math-related stimuli

article_title: Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience
citation: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003
title: Cognitive flexibility as an emergent property of efficient executive function, measured by set shifting and task switching
description: The review defines cognitive flexibility as "the ability to appropriately adjust one's behavior according to a changing environment" and as "an emergent property of efficient executive function" typically measured with set shifting or task switching paradigms. It adopts Bunge and Zelazo's hierarchy in which set shifting is a lower-level form and task switching the most complex form. Both produce switch costs, reflecting inhibition of the previous response set and reconfiguration to the new task.
requirements: Tasks must produce a switch cost to be valid measures of cognitive flexibility
Consistent operationalization across studies is required
constraints: The construct is difficult to examine due to the multitude of ways it has been described in the literature
target_learners: children and adolescents
adults
clinical populations with neurodevelopmental disorders
target_learning_goals: flexible adjustment of behavior to changing environments
set shifting and task switching

article_title: Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience
citation: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003
title: Cognitive flexibility arises from interplay of nodes within the executive control network rather than a distinct substrate
description: The authors propose that "Cognitive flexibility likely emerges from the interplay of specific nodes in the frontal and parietal cortices" which are not flexibility-specific but are activated across executive functions. Within the domain-general executive control network, "the specific computations among nodes and their anatomical specificity within the broader frontoparietal networks determine which EF is behaviorally observed." Temporal dynamics of inter-node connectivity may distinguish executive functions; salience, dorsal and ventral attention networks, vlPFC and IFJ are proposed to act in sequence during a switch.
requirements: Working memory load must be controlled in task designs to avoid confounds
Causal modeling studies are needed for validation
constraints: The model is speculative at this time and remains to be validated with future causal modeling studies
target_learners: neurotypical adults and children
target_learning_goals: understanding neural mechanisms of flexible cognition

article_title: Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience
citation: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003
title: Dynamic functional connectivity as an analytic approach for relating brain dynamics to cognitive flexibility
description: Dynamic functional connectivity is described as "a new analytic approach" that "attempts to account for variations in brain network topology as a function of time". The review presents it as a tool for quantifying time-varying functional connectivity, commonly implemented with a sliding window approach in fMRI data. It proposes this approach will enable insights into the levels of neural flexibility required for optimal cognitive flexibility in typical and atypical development.
requirements: Quantifies changes in functional connectivity metrics over time
Sliding window approach uses a fixed-length time window shifted by a fixed number of data points
constraints: The functional significance of dynamic functional connectivity in the brain is still under investigation

individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders
target_learning_goals: characterizing neural flexibility underlying cognitive flexibility

article_title: Cognitive flexibility supports the development of cumulative cultural learning in children
citation: Davis, S., Rawlings, B., Clegg, J. M., Ikejimba, D., Watson-Jones, R. E., Whiten, A. & Legare, C. H. (2022). Cognitive flexibility supports the development of cumulative cultural learning in children. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-18231-7
title: Cumulative cultural evolution requires behavioral switching and maintenance of adopted improvements
description: The article frames cumulative cultural evolution (CCE) as "the process of accumulating knowledge and skills that increases the complexity and/or efficiency of technology and other forms of culture over time". It decomposes CCE into switching (relinquishing a current behavior for an improved version) and maintenance (resisting reversion to earlier versions and omitting redundant actions), arguing cognitive flexibility underpins these processes and their ontogeny in childhood.
requirements: Successful CCE requires both behavioral switching to improved versions and maintenance of what has been adopted
constraints: The framework is developed and tested with U.S. children aged 3–5 in a puzzlebox task
target_learners: children aged 3–5 years
target_learning_goals: flexibly switching to more efficient solutions
maintaining adopted solutions and omitting redundant actions
examples: Children learned an inefficient Serialbox method by demonstration, witnessed a more efficient method, and were given multiple further interaction opportunities

article_title: Working Memory Model and Language Learning
citation: Demir, Bora. (2021). Working Memory Model and Language Learning. Shanlax International Journal of Education. https://doi.org/10.34293/education.v9iS2-Sep.4366
title: Baddeley's multi-component Working Memory model as a framework for language learning
description: The article takes Baddeley's (2012) Working Memory model as its theoretical framework for understanding language learning. WM is described as "a complex and limited cognitive system" that enables input "to be temporarily stored, monitored and manipulated". The model comprises a central executive and three slave systems — the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad, and the episodic buffer — each handling different information types. The article uses this structure to map specific WM components onto specific language-learning processes.
requirements: The model is used as a theoretical framework for interpreting language-learning phenomena, requiring researchers to specify which WM component underlies a given language task
constraints: The article notes the model is "not perfectly specified" and "the components of the model and their interrelationships are underspecified" (Andrade, 2001, as cited)
The model's simplicity "fails in reflecting the nature of real cognition" and is "hard to apply to phenomena outside the domain of laboratory short-term memory tasks"
The central executive "remains the least understood component of the model"

article_title: Metacognition and motivation as predictors for mathematics performance of Belgian elementary school children
citation: Desoete, A., Baten, E., Vercaemst, V., De Busschere, A., Baudonck, M., & Vanhaeke, J. (2019). Metacognition and motivation as predictors for mathematics performance of Belgian elementary school children. ZDM Mathematics Education, 51, 667–677. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-018-01020-w
title: Teachers should attend to both mathematical accuracy and fluency, and to metacognitive and motivational aspects, especially for poor performers
description: The article's practical recommendation, drawn from its longitudinal finding that accuracy and fluency have "overlapping yet different predictors", is that teachers pay attention to both aspects of mathematics. Because poor performers were found to be less intrinsically motivated, less metacognitively accurate, and to overestimate their performances more often than well-performing peers in all grades, the authors stress the importance of attending to these metacognitive and motivational aspects in mathematics education.
requirements: Instruction should address both accuracy and fluency as partly distinct outcome aspects of mathematics learning.
constraints: The recommendation rests on the study's Belgian elementary sample tested in January and June; the motivation–accuracy relation was reported for Grade 3.

target_learning_goals: Mathematical accuracy
Mathematical fluency
Metacognitive accuracy of performance evaluation
Intrinsic motivation for mathematics

title: Opportunity–propensity (O–P) model of learning applied to mathematics achievement
description: The opportunity–propensity (O–P) model of learning is the organizing framework of the study, in which factors such as metacognitive postdiction skills, intrinsic motivation and prior proficiency in mathematics function as Propensity factors predicting mathematics performance. The article applies this model longitudinally to Belgian elementary children to test which propensity factors predict mathematical accuracy and fluency over a school semester, finding prior mathematical accuracy to be the especially important propensity factor.

article_title: ADHD Subtype Differences in Reinforcement Sensitivity and Visuospatial Working Memory
citation: Dovis, S., Van der Oord, S., Wiers, R.W., & Prins, P.J.M. (2015). ADHD subtype differences in reinforcement sensitivity and visuospatial working memory. Journal of Clinical Child and Adolescent Psychology, 44(5), 859-874. https://doi.org/10.1080/15374416.2014.895940
title: Dual-component model of visuospatial working memory: short-term memory and central executive
description: The article adopts a model in which visuospatial working memory "is composed of short-term memory (STM) and a central executive (CE)". It uses this decomposition to locate subtype-specific deficits: in ADHD-C both components seem impaired, whereas in ADHD-I only the CE appears impaired while STM is intact. The model also allows motivational impairments to be traced to their effects on the separate WM components. This componential framing organizes the study's experimental comparisons of STM, CE and WM performance across subtypes and reinforcement conditions.
requirements: Tasks must separately index STM and CE components of visuospatial working memory for the decomposition to be tested.
constraints: The article notes that in children with ADHD-C the components only "seem impaired", and no prior studies had investigated these WM components in children with ADHD-I.
target_learners: children aged 9-12
target_learning_goals: visuospatial working memory performance
examples: The study examined effects of standard and high reinforcement on visuospatial WM-, STM-, and CE performance across the two ADHD subtypes and controls.

article_title: ADHD Subtype Differences in Reinforcement Sensitivity and Visuospatial Working Memory
citation: Dovis, S., Van der Oord, S., Wiers, R.W., & Prins, P.J.M. (2015). ADHD subtype differences in reinforcement sensitivity and visuospatial working memory. Journal of Clinical Child and Adolescent Psychology, 44(5), 859-874. https://doi.org/10.1080/15374416.2014.895940
title: Use high reinforcement to improve visuospatial STM and WM performance in children with ADHD
description: The article shows that raising reinforcement above a standard feedback-only level improves visuospatial STM and WM performance in children with ADHD. In the experiment, a high level of reinforcement was operationalized as "feedback + 10 euros" on top of standard feedback. The improvement occurred in both the ADHD-C and ADHD-I subtypes and was "equally pronounced in both subtypes", supporting reinforcement as a motivational lever for these children. The principle applies specifically to STM and WM tasks, not to CE-related performance.
requirements: Reinforcement must be substantially higher than standard feedback alone; the study used feedback plus a monetary reward of 10 euros.
constraints: High reinforcement did not improve CE-related performance, so the benefit is limited to STM and WM components.
The improvement was observed in children with ADHD but not in typically developing controls.
target_learners: children with ADHD aged 9-12
target_learning_goals: visuospatial working memory
visuospatial short-term memory
examples: The experiment compared a standard feedback-only condition with a high-reinforcement condition of feedback + 10 euros in children aged 9-12 with ADHD-I, ADHD-C, and controls.

article_title: The contribution of executive functions to narrative writing in fourth grade children
citation: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2015). The contribution of executive functions to narrative writing in fourth grade children. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-015-9558-z
title: Microstructure/macrostructure framework mapping composition levels to word-, sentence-, and text-level language
description: The article organizes written composition assessment into microstructure (word-level productivity, sentence-level complexity) and macrostructure (text-level content and structure). As printed: "these micro- and macrostructural levels correspond very closely to the levels of language at which text is generated". This framework allowed the study to test whether different EF regulate different composition levels.
requirements: Measures of productivity, complexity, and story content derived from transcribed narratives
constraints: Only three measures (productivity, complexity, story content) were included; other components might tap different abilities

target_learning_goals: written narrative composition skills
examples: Text length indexed productivity, MLTUw indexed complexity, ERRNI story content scoring indexed macrostructure

title: Assess a variety of low- and high-level executive functions with standard neuropsychological measures when studying developing writers
description: The authors argue that conceptualizing EF only as self-regulation strategies misses low-level EF contributions. They state "it is necessary to assess a variety of EF, including low-level EF with standard neuropsychological measures, in order to acquire more insight into the contribution of EF to writing outcome in developing writers". Their broad battery revealed direct and indirect EF contributions.

article_title: How executive functions predict development in syntactic complexity of narrative writing in the upper elementary grades
citation: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2017). How executive functions predict development in syntactic complexity of narrative writing in the upper elementary grades. Reading and Writing, 30, 209–231. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-016-9670-8
title: Developmental model of writing: transcription skills, oral language skills, and executive functions as interacting component skills within working memory
description: The article frames writing development with a developmental model (Berninger & Winn, 2006) in which "three interrelated component skills underlie written text production, as they interact functionally during the writing process in an environment of working memory (WM): transcription skills, oral language skills, and executive functions (EF)." The model specifies constraints influencing the writing process and postulates that the relative influence of each component changes over time: transcription is critical early, and its automatization frees WM resources for language skills and EF, which constrain later composition. The present study tests the model's longitudinal predictions in the upper elementary grades.
requirements: The model assumes a working-memory environment in which component skills interact functionally during text production
constraints: The relative influence of components is hypothesized to shift with development, so predictor importance is age-dependent
target_learners: elementary school children, particularly upper elementary grades (fourth to sixth grade)
target_learning_goals: written composition, especially narrative writing and syntactic complexity of sentences
examples: The study assessed all three components in fourth grade with a broad neuropsychological battery and tested their longitudinal prediction of sixth-grade narrative writing

citation: Drijbooms, E., Groen, M. A., & Verhoeven, L. (2017). How executive functions predict development in syntactic complexity of narrative writing in the upper elementary grades. Reading and Writing, 30, 209–231. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-016-9670-8
title: To improve children's sentence production in written composition in the upper elementary grades, instruction should attend to enhancing executive functions, particularly planning and inhibition
description: The article draws an instructional implication from its longitudinal findings: "in order to improve children's sentence production in written composition in the upper elementary grades, attention needs to be paid to enhancing children's EF, and particularly planning and inhibition skills." This aligns with the idea that children need more extensive training in self-regulation skills to manage written composition. The authors add that such training may be crucial because enhancing syntactic complexity positively impacts overall compositional quality.
requirements: Instruction targeting planning and inhibition should accompany writing instruction in the upper elementary grades
constraints: The recommendation rests on longitudinal correlational prediction, not on a manipulated intervention in this study
target_learners: typically developing children in upper elementary grades (fourth to sixth)
target_learning_goals: sentence production and syntactic complexity in written composition
examples: The study found fourth-grade planning and inhibition predicted improvement in narrative syntactic complexity by sixth grade

article_title: Life Stress Impairs Self-Control in Early Adolescence
citation: Duckworth, A. L., Kim, B., and Tsukayama, E. (2013). Life stress impairs self-control in early adolescence. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00608
title: Hot/cool dual-process account: stress shifts processing toward the hot, impulsive system
description: The article interprets its findings through the hot/cool model (Metcalfe and Mischel, 1999), which "contrasts two opponent systems": a cool system that is "affectively-neutral, flexible, slow, and strategic" and a hot system that is "impulsive and reflexive, responding quickly to salient trigger features." Perceived stress is postulated to modulate the balance, so that as stress increases the cool system becomes dysfunctional and the hot system dominates. The authors present their longitudinal findings as direct, real-world evidence consistent with this account, which previously rested on animal and laboratory studies.
requirements: The account presupposes that perceived stress modulates the relative activity of the two systems
constraints: The article offers this as indirect interpretive support, not a direct test of the model
target_learners: early adolescents
target_learning_goals: self-control over attentional, behavioral, and emotional impulses
examples: The three longitudinal studies are presented as direct evidence that children are more impulsive when negotiating stressful life circumstances

article_title: Exploring variation in measurement as a foundation for statistical thinking in the elementary school
citation: Lyn D English and Jane M Watson. (2015). Exploring variation in measurement as a foundation for statistical thinking in the elementary school. International Journal of STEM Education (2015) 2:3. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-015-0016-x
title: Build early statistical thinking on measurement activities that let students observe, represent and contrast variation in both hand-drawn and software formats
description: The article recommends an early instructional focus on variation and distribution through meaningful measurement activities. Students measure, observe the spread of values, create representations of their own choosing by hand and in software, and contrast two scenarios that embody different sources of variation. The authors conclude that findings "highlight the importance of an early focus on variation and distribution, with meaningful activities that motivate students to conduct and observe measurements, together with creating both hand-drawn and software representations to relate their experiences."
requirements: Activities must be aligned with the school curriculum so they form a core component rather than add-on learning experiences, as the authors state for their design
constraints: The article's evidence comes from year 4 classes in one middle socio-economic school within a 3-year design study; teachers needed preparatory meetings providing professional development on the core statistical ideas
target_learners: elementary school students, specifically year 4 (fourth grade)
target_learning_goals: appreciation of variation in data and measurement
representing and describing variability
using variability to make comparisons
informal inference and prediction
examples: Students measured one student's arm span repeatedly, then each class member once, created hand-drawn and TinkerPlots representations, and completed a delayed assessment 1 to 3 months later

article_title: Exploring variation in measurement as a foundation for statistical thinking in the elementary school
citation: Lyn D English and Jane M Watson. (2015). Exploring variation in measurement as a foundation for statistical thinking in the elementary school. International Journal of STEM Education (2015) 2:3. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-015-0016-x
title: Four-level developmental hierarchy of appreciation of variation (prerequisites, partial recognition, applications, critical aspects)
description: The article adopts, from Watson et al. (2003), a four-level hierarchy of increasing appreciation of variation used to frame its research questions and interpret student responses. Level 1 covers prerequisites such as interpreting context and simple graph reading; level 2, partial recognition, involves "putting ideas in context but focusing on single aspects and neglecting others"; level 3, applications, consolidates ideas in context with inconsistency on the most salient features; level 4, critical aspects, employs complex justification or critical reasoning. The study maps its three research questions to levels 2, 3 and 4 respectively.
requirements: Assessment of responses requires coding criteria that can distinguish descriptions, single-aspect focus, consolidation in context, and complex justification
constraints: The article states its assessment was more general than the Watson et al. survey and could only consider descriptively whether responses exhibited the type of thinking typical of the four levels
target_learners: elementary school students, with the hierarchy spanning grade levels 3 to 9 in its original development
target_learning_goals: understanding of variation in statistical investigations
statistical thinking and informal inference
examples: The study assumed all students had reached level 1, Prerequisites for Variation, and linked research question 1 to level 2, question 2 to level 3, and question 3 to level 4

article_title: Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task
citation: Eriksen, B. A., & Eriksen, C. W. (1974). Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task. Perception & Psychophysics, 16(1), 143-149. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03203257
title: Limited-capacity visual attentional channel with response-selection locus of noise interference
description: The article proposes that visual attention has "a minimal channel size in terms of capacity for simultaneous processing with a capacity exceeding that required for identifying a single letter." Because this unutilized capacity cannot be shut off, letters within about 1 deg of the target are processed simultaneously with it and begin to evoke responses. A selection-and-inhibition process, keyed to the target's location, must then operate; it is slower at closer spacings and when noise indicates the opposite response. The data locate the noise effect at the response-selection stage rather than at input processing.
requirements: A target whose location is known and fixed, so that selection can be made by spatial position verification
constraints: The authors acknowledge a limited-energy parallel processing model could add an input-side decrement at the closest spacing, and that feature-detector submechanisms are not precluded
target_learners: adult laboratory subjects in visual information-processing experiments
target_learning_goals: understanding selective attention and visual information processing
examples: The nonsearch task eliminated visual search by presenting the target always Yz deg above the fixation point, isolating noise effects from search demands
key_sources: Eriksen, B. A., & Eriksen, C. W. (1974). Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task. Perception & Psychophysics, 16(1), 143-149. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03203267

article_title: Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task
citation: Eriksen, B. A., & Eriksen, C. W. (1974). Effects of noise letters upon the identification of a target letter in a nonsearch task. Perception & Psychophysics, 16(1), 143-149. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03203257
title: Eriksen and Eriksen nonsearch flanker paradigm (six-condition tachistoscopic letter task)
description: A tachistoscopic task in which the subject responds with a right or left leverpress to a single target letter (H or K vs S or C) that always appears at a fixed location above fixation during a 1-sec exposure. The target is flanked by three noise letters on each side under five noise conditions (identical, response-compatible, response-incompatible, heterogeneous-similar, heterogeneous-dissimilar) at three between-letter spacings (.06, Yz, and 1 deg of visual angle), plus mixed and blocked target-alone controls. It was designed to provide "an anchor or baseline condition" for noise effects when no visual search is required.
requirements: Subjects thoroughly instructed to respond only to the letter in the target location and ignore all other letters
constraints: Eliminating search removes the confounding of noise effects with assumptions about how display search is carried out, so findings are specific to the nonsearch case
target_learners: adult volunteers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision
target_learning_goals: studying the effects of noise stimuli on target identification independent of visual search
examples: Six experimental sessions of three 32-trial blocks plus one 12-trial single-letter block yielded 24 trials per subject per condition-by-spacing combination

article_title: Top-down modulation: bridging selective attention and working memory
citation: Gazzaley A, Nobre AC. (2012). Top-down modulation: Bridging selective attention and working memory. Trends in Cognitive Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2011.11.014
title: Top-down modulation as a common neural mechanism bridging selective attention and working memory
description: The review proposes that top-down modulation — modulation of neural activity in lower-order sensory areas based on an individual's goals — serves as a common framework for selective attention and working memory. Its core features are "activity modulation in stimulus-selective sensory cortices with concurrent engagement of prefrontal and parietal control regions that function as sources of top-down signals". The mechanism operates across all working memory stages, both when stimuli are present and absent.
requirements: Evidence from human neurophysiological methods (fMRI, EEG/ERP, TMS) indexing sensory-cortex modulation and prefrontal-parietal control engagement
constraints: The review focuses on human neurophysiological studies of visual working memory and delayed-response paradigms
target_learners: adult learners
target_learning_goals: understanding the neural mechanisms supporting attention and working memory
key_sources: Gazzaley A, Nobre AC. (2012). Top-down modulation: Bridging selective attention and working memory. Trends in Cognitive Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2011.11.014

article_title: Individual differences in algebraic cognition: Relation to the approximate number and semantic memory systems
citation: Geary David C., Hoard Mary K., Nugent Lara, Rouder Jeffrey N. (2015). Individual Differences in Algebraic Cognition: Relation to the Approximate Number and Sematic Memory Systems. Journal of experimental child psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2015.07.010
title: Differential cognitive systems account of algebraic competence
description: The article proposes that different brain and cognitive systems support different components of algebraic competence: the approximate number system is engaged in spatial-numerical (coordinate plane) and numerical-only (expression evaluation) quantity judgments, while the hippocampal-dependent semantic memory system supports committing arithmetic facts to long-term memory and forming schema memories for algebra equations. As the authors state, "difficulties in committing addition facts to long-term memory may presage slow formation of memories for the basic structure of algebra equations." The account is grounded in the study's differential regression results and motivates targeted interventions and brain imaging work.
requirements: Assessment of component algebraic skills separately rather than only overall algebra achievement
Control of demographic and domain-general covariates including intelligence, working memory, and symbolic number processing fluency
constraints: The correlational, largely concurrent design means causal relations cannot be inferred
The tasks do not cover all components of algebraic competence, such as factoring and systems of equations
target_learners: 9th-grade algebra students
target_learning_goals: Algebraic competence including coordinate plane knowledge, expression evaluation fluency, and equation schema memory
examples: The study developed a new coordinate plane placement task and adapted expression evaluation and equation memory tasks to measure three component algebra skills in 171 ninth graders

citation: Geboers B, Uiters E, Reijneveld SA, Jansen CJM, Almansa J, Nooyens ACJ, Verschuren WMM, de Winter AF, Picavet HSJ. (2018). Health literacy among older adults is associated with their 10-years' cognitive functioning and decline - the Doetinchem Cohort Study. BMC Geriatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12877-018-0766-7
title: Interventions to mitigate negative impacts of low health literacy should focus on lowering the cognitive demands of health information
description: The article recommends that interventions addressing low health literacy in older adults should reduce the cognitive burden of health materials. Strategies include "the use of plain language in health documents, but also the use of spoken animations and teach-back methods." This principle follows from the finding that poorer cognitive functioning is associated with low health literacy.

health promotion

article_title: Reading, Writing, and Phonological Processing Skills of Adolescents With 10 or More Years of Cochlear Implant Experience
citation: Geers Ann E.; Hayes Heather. (2011). Reading, Writing, and Phonological Processing Skills of Adolescents with 10 or More Years of Cochlear Implant Experience. Ear and Hearing. https://doi.org/10.1097/AUD.0b013e3181fa41fa
title: Picture Spelling Test with phonological plausibility scoring
description: A researcher-designed spelling assessment created because traditional dictation spelling tasks are problematic for deaf children, since "it is difficult to know whether the word was accurately perceived". One hundred familiar, picturable words of varied orthographic length and complexity were presented as photographs, line drawings, or cartoons, and students spelled the named item. A companion phonological plausibility score quantified whether misspellings used plausible letters for each phoneme, referenced to an aligned corpus of word frequencies and pronunciations.
requirements: Items must be picturable and familiar to adolescent vocabulary

constraints: Designed for and used with adolescents with prelingual deafness; accuracy scores cannot disentangle perception from spelling in dictation formats, which motivated the picture format
target_learners: adolescents with prelingual deafness and cochlear implants
target_learning_goals: spelling accuracy
phonological encoding of spoken words in writing
examples: Administered to 112 CI-HS students and 46 hearing controls; CI students spelled 67% of items correctly versus 80% for controls, and 62% of their errors were phonologically plausible versus 89% for controls

article_title: Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy
citation: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf
title: Computer anxiety as a concept-specific anxiety type within a trait–state–concept-specific taxonomy
description: The article organizes anxiety into three types: trait anxiety (pervasive across life experience), state anxiety (fluctuating, responsive to situations), and concept-specific anxiety (associated with a specific situation). Computer anxiety is classified as concept-specific because it "is a feeling that is associated with a person's interaction with computers". The authors later suggest adapting the anxiety construct into these three sub-dimensions for future e-learning research.
requirements: Measuring computer anxiety requires recognizing it as situation-specific rather than a general personality trait
constraints: The study measured anxiety with only four general items; only two (ANX3, ANX4) loaded cleanly on the construct
target_learners: university students using e-learning systems
target_learning_goals: understanding and mitigating computer anxiety in e-learning contexts

article_title: Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy
citation: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf
title: Self-efficacy theory: three dimensions (magnitude, strength, generality) grounded in social learning and outcome expectation
description: Drawing on Bandura, the article describes self-efficacy as a person's belief in their capability to perform specific tasks, consisting of three dimensions: Magnitude (level of task difficulty believed attainable), Strength (confidence in attaining that level), and Generality (degree of generalization across situations). Self-efficacy is context-specific and researchers should capture both magnitude and strength when measuring it. The article applies this to computer self-efficacy in LMS use.
requirements: Measurement should capture both the magnitude and strength dimensions of self-efficacy
constraints: Self-efficacy is context specific, so measures must be tied to the specific technology or task domain
target_learners: university students using e-learning systems
target_learning_goals: understanding how self-efficacy beliefs shape technology-based learning behavior

article_title: Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy
citation: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf
title: Assess and address computer anxiety before introducing students to an LMS
description: Because computer self-efficacy mediates anxiety's negative effect on perceived ease of use, the authors recommend that "prior to introducing prospective students to the LMS they should be tested for any computer anxieties they may have". Addressing anxiety as part of the e-learning experience enhances it, and reducing anxiety increases the return on e-training investment in corporate settings.
requirements: Instructors or administrators need a way to identify students' computer anxiety levels before LMS deployment
constraints: Findings map to the specific LMS and learning tools studied; caution is needed generalizing across other LMS technologies
target_learners: prospective LMS users in higher education
employees in corporate e-training
target_learning_goals: reducing computer anxiety to enhance e-learning experience and performance
examples: The study surveyed 649 students at semester end after a year of LMS use in undergraduate MIS and FIT courses
key_sources: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf

article_title: Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy
citation: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf
title: Design LMSs with simple, interactive, familiar features to reduce anxiety and leverage self-efficacy mediation
description: The authors recommend that designers "integrate simple, interactive, and familiar features in the design of LMSs" and provide incentives to motivate usage, because positive learning experiences are more likely with LMSs that are easy to use and introduce the least anxieties. This assists diffusion via the mediating effect of computer self-efficacy. They also note a trade-off: easier interfaces may reduce effective task manipulation capabilities.
requirements: Designers must balance ease of navigation against effective task manipulation (the cognitive-cost/effective-usage ratio)
constraints: The more 'easy to use' the interface is designed, the less effective the features become, reducing LMS capabilities
target_learners: higher education students
corporate e-training participants
target_learning_goals: supporting positive attitudes and ease of use perceptions in LMS-based learning
examples: The authors suggest it is feasible to build multiple LMS interfaces for students with different levels of computer self-efficacy
key_sources: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf

citation: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf
title: EISEL: web-based learning tool with question pools, immediate feedback, and repetition
description: EISEL is a learning tool within the in-house LMS used in the study. It presents sets of five questions at a time from chapter-based pools (e.g., 38 questions for chapter 1, 112 for chapter 2), shows correct/wrong answers with green/red buttons, and allows students to request new random sets. Students do a minimum of 20 questions, can practice in groups, and develop their own strategies; the objective is engagement with domain content rather than assessment.
requirements: Students are asked to do a minimum of 20 questions but encouraged to do as many as they feel necessary
constraints: Question pools are limited per chapter, varying by chapter
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory MIS and information technology courses
target_learning_goals: engaging students in processing domain content through repeated practice with immediate feedback

article_title: Ethnic Stigma, Academic Anxiety, and Intrinsic Motivation in Middle Childhood
citation: Gillen-O’Neel, C., Ruble, D. N., & Fuligni, A. J. (2011). Ethnic Stigma, Academic Anxiety, and Intrinsic Motivation in Middle Childhood. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2011.01621.x
title: Foster supportive school environments and close interpersonal connections to support intrinsic motivation among ethnic-minority students facing stigma
description: The article suggests that supportive school environments may be important sources of intrinsic motivation among some ethnic-minority children in the face of stigma. School belonging—students' emotional connection with their school and the people at their school—was associated with higher intrinsic motivation and mediated the higher intrinsic motivation of Dominican children. The authors state that interventions aimed at helping students from Latin-American backgrounds maintain academic motivation may benefit from fostering close interpersonal connections at school.
requirements: School belonging must be measured or cultivated as students' emotional connection with their school and the people at their school
constraints: The mediational findings do not imply causality
The Dominican finding may have been due to school-specific factors, as almost all Dominican participants were drawn from two schools
target_learners: elementary-age children from ethnic-minority and immigrant backgrounds
target_learning_goals: maintaining intrinsic motivation for school in the face of stigmatization
examples: For Dominican students, school belonging partially compensated for stigma by contributing directly to higher intrinsic motivation, despite lower public regard
key_sources: Gillen-O’Neel, C., Ruble, D. N., & Fuligni, A. J. (2011). Ethnic Stigma, Academic Anxiety, and Intrinsic Motivation in Middle Childhood. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2011.01621.x

article_title: Ethnic Stigma, Academic Anxiety, and Intrinsic Motivation in Middle Childhood
citation: Gillen-O’Neel, C., Ruble, D. N., & Fuligni, A. J. (2011). Ethnic Stigma, Academic Anxiety, and Intrinsic Motivation in Middle Childhood. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2011.01621.x
title: Consider interventions aimed at increasing perception of group status as a promising area for future academic anxiety research
description: The article reports that perception of status was associated with 31–51% of the higher levels of academic anxiety reported by African-American, Chinese, and Dominican children as compared to their European-American peers. Although the findings are not causal, the authors state that interventions aimed at increasing perception of group status (e.g., community role models) could be a promising area for future academic anxiety research.
requirements: Future research should employ longitudinal or experimental designs to determine whether perceived group status directly affects academic anxiety
constraints: The data were measured concurrently, so the causality in the relationship between perception of group status and academic anxiety has yet to be determined
target_learners: elementary-age children from ethnic-minority backgrounds
target_learning_goals: reducing academic anxiety associated with stigma awareness
examples: The study found group status mediated the ethnic differences in academic anxiety for African-American, Chinese, and Dominican children but not Russians
key_sources: Gillen-O’Neel, C., Ruble, D. N., & Fuligni, A. J. (2011). Ethnic Stigma, Academic Anxiety, and Intrinsic Motivation in Middle Childhood. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2011.01621.x

article_title: Do children with dyslexia present a handwriting deficit? Impact of word orthographic and graphic complexity on handwriting and spelling performance
citation: Gosse, C., & Van Reybroeck, M. (2020). Do children with dyslexia present a handwriting deficit? Impact of word orthographic and graphic complexity on handwriting and spelling performance. Research in Developmental Disabilities, 97(1), 14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ridd.2019.103553
title: Tablet-based single-word dictation task of 40 words varying orthographic and graphic complexity
description: A digital-tablet single-word dictation task used to dissociate spelling from graphomotor performance. Children wrote 40 words whose "target words varied in orthographic complexity and in graphic complexity (simple vs. difficult)", and the task "was scored on spelling accuracy, handwriting quality and handwriting speed", allowing group comparisons across both complexity dimensions simultaneously.
requirements: Administered on a digital tablet so handwriting quality and speed can be scored
Word set must vary in both orthographic complexity and graphic complexity
target_learners: monolingual French-speaking children with and without dyslexia
target_learning_goals: assessing spelling accuracy, handwriting quality and handwriting speed
examples: Twenty-three children with dyslexia, 23 chronological-age matched and 23 spelling-age matched children completed the task
key_sources: Gosse, C., & Van Reybroeck, M. (2020). Do children with dyslexia present a handwriting deficit? Impact of word orthographic and graphic complexity on handwriting and spelling performance. Research in Developmental Disabilities, 97(1), 14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ridd.2019.103553

article_title: Do children with dyslexia present a handwriting deficit? Impact of word orthographic and graphic complexity on handwriting and spelling performance
citation: Gosse, C., & Van Reybroeck, M. (2020). Do children with dyslexia present a handwriting deficit? Impact of word orthographic and graphic complexity on handwriting and spelling performance. Research in Developmental Disabilities, 97(1), 14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ridd.2019.103553
title: Educational and clinical supports for dyslexia should address the graphomotor aspects of writing, not only spelling
description: Because children with dyslexia were more disrupted by the graphic complexity of words than both matched control groups, the authors conclude that "children with dyslexia struggle with the graphomotor aspects of writing". Supports for dyslexia should therefore target handwriting and graphomotor skills in addition to spelling. The article states these findings "have potential implications for educational and clinical supports".
requirements: Supports should be informed by assessment of handwriting under varying graphic complexity, as in the tablet dictation task
constraints: The article reports potential implications; it did not itself evaluate an intervention
target_learners: children with dyslexia
target_learning_goals: handwriting quality and speed alongside spelling
examples: The study manipulated graphic complexity (simple vs. difficult words) on a digital tablet to isolate graphomotor difficulty
key_sources: Gosse, C., & Van Reybroeck, M. (2020). Do children with dyslexia present a handwriting deficit? Impact of word orthographic and graphic complexity on handwriting and spelling performance. Research in Developmental Disabilities, 97(1), 14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ridd.2019.103553

article_title: Perspective-taking ability in bilingual children: Extending advantages in executive control to spatial reasoning
citation: Greenberg Anastasia, Bellana Buddhika, Bialystok Ellen. (2013). Perspective-Taking Ability in Bilingual Children: Extending Advantages in Executive Control to Spatial Reasoning. Cognitive Development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2012.10.002
title: Bilingual executive-control advantage arises from managing jointly activated languages via domain-general inhibitory control
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that for bilinguals "both languages are jointly activated for bilinguals, even in strongly monolingual contexts", creating a need for attentional control of the target language. In Green's (1998) model, this selective attention recruits a domain-general inhibitory control system, and the authors argue this trained control generalizes to nonverbal tasks such as perspective taking. The article also cites Costa and colleagues' monitoring account as a broader alternative.
requirements: Bilingual experience with two actively managed languages, producing joint activation that requires a control mechanism
constraints: Some inhibition types show no bilingual advantage, and advantages appear in infants where active inhibition of a competing language is not relevant, so the article treats inhibition alone as insufficient
target_learners: 8-year-old children
bilingual children
target_learning_goals: executive control
spatial perspective taking
academic problem solving
examples: The study tested the account's prediction that bilinguals would outperform monolinguals on a perspective-taking task relying on executive control but not verbal proficiency.
key_sources: Greenberg Anastasia, Bellana Buddhika, Bialystok Ellen. (2013). Perspective-Taking Ability in Bilingual Children: Extending Advantages in Executive Control to Spatial Reasoning. Cognitive Development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2012.10.002

article_title: Anxiety and Reading Difficulties in Early Elementary School: Evidence for Unidirectional- or Bi-Directional Relations?
citation: Grills-Taquechel, Amie E.; Fletcher, Jack M.; Vaughn, Sharon R.; Stuebing, Karla K. (2012). Anxiety and Reading Difficulties in Early Elementary School: Evidence for Unidirectional- or Bi-Directional Relations? Child Psychiatry and Human Development, 43(1), 35-47. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10578-011-0246-1
title: Competing-models framework of anxiety-reading achievement relations
description: The article organizes the anxiety-achievement association into two competing causal models plus a bidirectional variant: Model 1 holds that increased anxiety interferes with concentration, memory, and information processing, lowering achievement; Model 2 holds that children develop anxiety symptoms in response to repeated classroom failure. The authors note a cycle may develop in which anxiety and learning difficulties continue to influence each other and worsen over time. The study tests these models longitudinally with multidimensional anxiety and two reading domains (decoding and fluency).
requirements: Longitudinal data with anxiety and achievement measured at two or more time points to test predictive direction
constraints: The article states longitudinal data is required to more clearly examine these potential relations; the pilot design cannot establish causal direction
target_learners: Early elementary school children (first grade) in general education classes
target_learning_goals: Reading achievement (decoding and oral reading fluency)
Understanding and reducing anxiety symptoms that co-occur with reading difficulties
examples: The study evaluated 153 first-graders in winter and spring using the MASC anxiety scale, WJBR decoding composite, and CMERS fluency passages, testing each model via hierarchical linear regression
key_sources: Grills-Taquechel, Amie E.; Fletcher, Jack M.; Vaughn, Sharon R.; Stuebing, Karla K. (2012). article_title: Parent praise to toddlers predicts fourth grade academic achievement via children’s incremental mindsets.
citation: Gunderson, E. A., Sorhagen, N. S., Gripshover, S. J., Dweck, C. S., Goldin-Meadow, S., & Levine, S. C. (2018). Parent Praise to Toddlers Predicts Fourth Grade Academic Achievement via Children's Incremental Mindsets. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000444
title: Incremental versus fixed motivational frameworks as a developmental pathway from praise to achievement
description: The article organizes its findings around motivational frameworks: coherent systems of beliefs, attributions, and attitudes toward challenge that follow from children's mindsets about intelligence. Children with an incremental mindset "tend to focus on learning, believe in the efficacy of effort" and show resilience, whereas a fixed mindset leads children to avoid challenges that might reveal low ability. The framework serves as the hypothesized mediator between early process praise and later achievement, and is measured as a composite of trait beliefs, learning goals, and attributions.
requirements: Assessment requires children old enough to report beliefs about trait stability, learning goals, and attributions (here ages 7–8)
constraints: Framework effects are expected mainly when students face challenge or failure; less impact under low challenge
target_learners: elementary school children (2nd–4th grade)
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in mathematics and reading comprehension
adaptive beliefs about intelligence and effort
examples: The study measured frameworks at ages 7–8 with a composite (α = .70) spanning intelligence and sociomoral trait beliefs, learning goals, and attributions
key_sources: Gunderson, E. A., Sorhagen, N. S., Gripshover, S. J., Dweck, C. S., Goldin-Meadow, S., & Levine, S. C. (2018). Parent Praise to Toddlers Predicts Fourth Grade Academic Achievement via Children's Incremental Mindsets. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000444

article_title: Parent praise to toddlers predicts fourth grade academic achievement via children’s incremental mindsets.
citation: Gunderson, E. A., Sorhagen, N. S., Gripshover, S. J., Dweck, C. S., Goldin-Meadow, S., & Levine, S. C. (2018). Parent Praise to Toddlers Predicts Fourth Grade Academic Achievement via Children's Incremental Mindsets. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000444
title: Praise young children's effort and strategies (process) rather than fixed personal qualities to foster incremental mindsets and long-term achievement
description: The article's central design implication for caregivers and teachers is that praise emphasizing children's effort, strategies, and specific actions predicts incremental motivational frameworks, which in turn predict achievement growth years later. Person praise (e.g., "you're so smart") was not related to children's motivational frameworks or achievement in this sample. Interventions "constructed to increase the proportion of praise children hear that emphasizes how their effort and strategies lead to learning may be a fruitful way to foster incremental mindsets and long-term academic achievement."
requirements: Praise should connect effort and strategies to learning outcomes rather than merely noting effort
constraints: Hyperbolic or excessive praise can discourage challenge-seeking, especially for children with low self-esteem; consoling effort without learning outcomes may deflate self-efficacy
target_learners: toddlers and young children (ages 1–3 in the study)
elementary school students
target_learning_goals: fostering incremental mindsets about intelligence
long-term academic achievement in math and reading
examples: Parents' process praise was observed naturalistically at ages 14, 26, and 38 months and coded as a proportion of total praise (18.0% on average)

article_title: Probing the Unique Contributions of Self-Concept, Task Values, and Their Interactions Using Multiple Value Facets and Multiple Academic Outcomes
citation: Guo, J., Nagengast, B., Marsh, H. W., Kelava, A., Gaspard, H., Brandt, H., Cambria, J., Flunger, B., Dicke, A.-L., Häfner, I., Brisson, B., & Trautwein, U. (2016). Probing the Unique Contributions of Self-Concept, Task Values, and Their Interactions Using Multiple Value Facets and Multiple Academic Outcomes. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858415626884
title: Modern expectancy-value theory: multidimensional task value with four components
description: Modern EVT posits that achievement-related performance and choices are most directly influenced by expectancies of success and the subjective value of academic tasks. Task value is multidimensional: "Intrinsic value refers to the extent to which the person gains enjoyment from performing an activity", alongside attainment value (importance and identity relevance), utility value (usefulness), and cost (effort demands, lost alternatives, negative experiences). The study operationalizes these four components via ten facets and tests their unique and interactive prediction of outcomes.
requirements: Value components are measured as latent constructs with multiple facets per component, requiring sufficiently reliable multi-item scales
constraints: Cost is described as the least-studied component of task value
Expectancies of success and academic self-concept are not empirically separable, so self-concept is used as the expectancy measure
target_learners: secondary school students (German ninth-grade academic-track students)
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement, effort, and behavioral engagement as outcomes of motivation
examples: The study measured the four components with 37 items covering 10 facets in 1,868 ninth-graders
key_sources: Guo, J., Nagengast, B., Marsh, H. W., Kelava, A., Gaspard, H., Brandt, H., Cambria, J., Flunger, B., Dicke, A.-L., Häfner, I., Brisson, B., & Trautwein, U. (2016). Probing the Unique Contributions of Self-Concept, Task Values, and Their Interactions Using Multiple Value Facets and Multiple Academic Outcomes. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858415626884

article_title: Probing the Unique Contributions of Self-Concept, Task Values, and Their Interactions Using Multiple Value Facets and Multiple Academic Outcomes
citation: Guo, J., Nagengast, B., Marsh, H. W., Kelava, A., Gaspard, H., Brandt, H., Cambria, J., Flunger, B., Dicke, A.-L., Häfner, I., Brisson, B., & Trautwein, U. (2016). Probing the Unique Contributions of Self-Concept, Task Values, and Their Interactions Using Multiple Value Facets and Multiple Academic Outcomes. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858415626884
title: Second-order bi-factor model with LMS latent interactions for parsing unique value-component effects
description: A latent variable modeling approach integrating a second-order model with a bi-factor model, applied via Mplus with the LMS approach (Klein & Moosbrugger, 2000). The model partitions value-item covariance into "a global (general) value factor representing the common variation shared by all 37 value items", ten orthogonal facet factors, and four second-order value components, allowing each component's unique contribution to be tested over and above global value. The LMS approach "corrects for measurement error of latent constructs and provides unbiased estimates of latent interaction effects".
requirements: Multi-item facet measures per value component and latent variable software (Mplus) supporting the LMS approach
constraints: Fit statistics such as CFI and RMSEA are not available for SEM models including latent interactions, so AIC and BIC were used for model comparison
target_learners: secondary school students (German ninth-grade academic-track students)
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement, effort, and behavioral engagement as outcomes of motivation
examples: Model SO-B-4V fit the data better (CFI = .955; TLI = .949; RMSEA = .039) than the second-order CFA model (Model SO-4V)

article_title: Development of brain systems for nonsymbolic numerosity and the relationship to formal math academic achievement
citation: Haist Frank, Wazny Jarnet H., Toomarian Elizabeth, Adamo Maha. (2015). Development of brain systems for nonsymbolic numerosity and the relationship to formal math academic achievement. Human brain mapping. https://doi.org/10.1002/hbm.22666
title: Two-brain-systems developmental account of nonsymbolic numerosity contributions to math achievement
description: The article proposes that "two different brain systems for nonsymbolic numerosity acuity may contribute to individual differences in math achievement and that the contribution of these systems differs across development." One system is the lateral parietal/IPS approximate number system, whose achievement link is restricted to children; the other is a ventral occipital-temporal visual discrimination system, active in children and adults with shifting regional foci. The account explains why behavioral measures fail while neural measures detect achievement relationships.
requirements: fMRI measurement of a voxelwise neural ratio effect across parametrically varied dot ratios
standardized math achievement and IQ measures to control for general cognitive ability
constraints: the parietal achievement link is restricted to children in this sample
the sample comprised typical through high-achieving individuals, so extension to low-achieving samples is untested
target_learners: school-age children (6-12 years)
adolescents (13-17 years)
adults (18-34 years)
target_learning_goals: formal symbolic mathematics achievement
examples: Whole-brain regressions across 44 participants aged 6-34 controlling for age, FSIQ, and reading achievement
key_sources: Haist Frank, Wazny Jarnet H., Toomarian Elizabeth, Adamo Maha. (2015). Development of brain systems for nonsymbolic numerosity and the relationship to formal math academic achievement. Human brain mapping. https://doi.org/10.1002/hbm.22666

article_title: Development of brain systems for nonsymbolic numerosity and the relationship to formal math academic achievement
citation: Haist Frank, Wazny Jarnet H., Toomarian Elizabeth, Adamo Maha. (2015). Development of brain systems for nonsymbolic numerosity and the relationship to formal math academic achievement. Human brain mapping. https://doi.org/10.1002/hbm.22666
title: The neural ratio effect captures visuospatial attention and cognitive control processes beyond approximate number system acuity
description: The authors argue the NRE is not a pure measure of ANS precision: "the NRE measure of nonsymbolic numerosity is a complex measure capturing aspects of magnitude estimation acuity in addition to visuospatial and cognitive control processes that together show extended developmental trajectories." They point to age effects in superior parietal and precuneus regions tied to attentional processing, and frontal regions tied to cognitive control and inhibitory processes. This account qualifies interpretations of NRE-achievement correlations as reflecting more than numerosity acuity alone.
requirements: interpretation of NRE findings should account for visuospatial attention and cognitive control contributions, not ANS acuity alone
constraints: the account is the authors' interpretation of regional activation patterns, not a directly tested decomposition
target_learners: school-age children (6-12 years)
adolescents (13-17 years)
adults (18-34 years)
target_learning_goals: formal symbolic mathematics achievement
examples: Age-related NRE effects in right inferior and middle frontal gyri, regions the authors link to cognitive control and speed-accuracy tradeoff during difficult magnitude decisions

article_title: Instrumental learning and cognitive flexibility processes are impaired in children exposed to early life stress
citation: Harms Madeline B., Shannon-Bowen Katherine E., Hanson Jamie L., Pollak Seth D. (2018). Instrumental Learning and Cognitive Flexibility Processes are Impaired in Children Exposed to Early Life Stress. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12596
title: General learning mechanism account of early-stress social problems
description: The article proposes that broad social and cognitive deficits in stress-exposed children arise not from domain-specific socio-emotional impairments but from disrupted "general learning mechanisms". Chronic caregiver inconsistency, poor emotional signaling, and reduced exploration create a challenging learning environment that impairs associative learning and flexible updating, which in turn undermines social adaptation. The fMRI task results are presented as converging behavioral and neural support.
requirements: Exposure to severe early life stress such as documented physical abuse
constraints: The account is tested in adolescents with documented childhood physical abuse; SES and abuse co-occur, though findings held when controlling for SES
target_learners: adolescents exposed to early life stress
target_learning_goals: associative learning of stimulus-response contingencies
cognitive flexibility in updating learned associations
examples: The instrumental learning task required responding to images for reward or avoiding response for punishment, then reversing half the associations

article_title: Domain-general mediators of the relation between kindergarten number sense and first-grade mathematics achievement
citation: Hassinger-Das, B., Jordan, N. C., Glutting, J., Irwin, C., & Dyson, N. (2013). Domain General Mediators of the Relation between Kindergarten Number Sense and First-Grade Mathematics Achievement. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2013.09.008
title: Interventions for kindergartners with low number sense should target executive functioning and attention problems in addition to number skills instruction
description: The article recommends that early mathematics interventions for children with low number sense address domain-general skills alongside number competencies. It states: "we provide empirical support for the development of interventions that target these skills, either through specific executive functioning interventions (e.g., Diamond & Lee, 2011) or interventions incorporated into components of mathematics instruction". The recommendation rests on the study's regression and mediation findings.
requirements: Children identified as having low number sense in kindergarten (e.g., screening with a number sense measure such as the NSB)
constraints: The evidence base is limited to high-risk children showing low number sense performance in kindergarten; causal relationships among executive functioning, attention problems, and mathematics outcomes remain to be tested
target_learners: kindergartners with low initial number sense at risk for mathematics difficulties
target_learning_goals: early number sense and first-grade mathematics achievement (calculation and applied problems)
examples: The authors cite their earlier randomized small-group number sense intervention for kindergartners not progressing in mathematics, which produced lasting improvements with moderate to large effect sizes, as context for extending intervention targets to executive functioning and attention.
key_sources: Hassinger-Das, B., Jordan, N. C., Glutting, J., Irwin, C., & Dyson, N. (2013). Domain General Mediators of the Relation between Kindergarten Number Sense and First-Grade Mathematics Achievement. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2013.09.008

article_title: Goal orientation and self-efficacy in relation to memory in adulthood
citation: Hastings, E. C., & West, R. L. (2011). Goal orientation and self-efficacy in relation to memory in adulthood. Neuropsychology, Development, and Cognition. Section B, Aging, Neuropsychology and Cognition, 18(4), 471-493. https://doi.org/10.1080/13825585.2011.575926
title: Achievement goal framework applied to memory in adulthood
description: The article applies Dweck's achievement goal framework, which "proposes that learners approach tasks with one of two goal orientations: learning goals or performance goals". Learning goals concern mastery and improvement, treating failure as part of learning; performance goals focus on test results, treating failure as evidence of low ability. The study is presented as the first empirical validation of this framework with an older adult sample, linking goal orientation to memory self-efficacy and memory performance across adulthood.
requirements: Measurement of dispositional goal orientation (here the Goal Orientation Questionnaire) and domain-specific self-efficacy (here the MSEQ-4) alongside performance
constraints: The framework had not previously been examined with adults and memory; the GOQ used does not distinguish approach and avoidant performance-goal styles
target_learners: younger adults aged 18-22
older adults aged 60-84
target_learning_goals: memory performance
memory self-efficacy
examples: A telephone incidental word game with 40 scored trials followed by surprise free and cued recall, scored out of 30

article_title: Goal orientation and self-efficacy in relation to memory in adulthood
citation: Hastings, E. C., & West, R. L. (2011). Goal orientation and self-efficacy in relation to memory in adulthood. Neuropsychology, Development, and Cognition. Section B, Aging, Neuropsychology and Cognition, 18(4), 471-493. https://doi.org/10.1080/13825585.2011.575926
title: Foster learning goals and avoid performance-goal emphasis when supporting adult memory learners
description: Because dispositional learning goals were adaptive and performance goals maladaptive for memory self-efficacy in adulthood, instruction for adult memory learners should emphasize skill mastery and improvement over outcome evaluation. The article reports that "learning goals had a significant positive effect on memory self-efficacy, and that performance goals had a significant negative effect on self-efficacy", with effects on memory operating indirectly through self-efficacy. Framing memory tasks as opportunities to build mastery rather than as tests of fixed ability aligns with these findings.
requirements: Goal orientation must be measured or addressed alongside domain-specific self-efficacy, since the goals' impact on memory occurred via memory self-efficacy
constraints: The study was cross-sectional; the memory task was an incidental word game that may not have engaged goal orientations, and the authors note a more challenging task might yield different results
target_learners: younger adults aged 18-22
older adults aged 60-84
target_learning_goals: memory performance
memory self-efficacy
examples: The study measured dispositional goal orientation with the GOQ and memory self-efficacy with the MSEQ-4, then assessed free and cued recall in a telephone word game
