article_title: Brief non-symbolic, approximate number practice enhances subsequent exact symbolic arithmetic in children
citation: Hyde, D. C., Khanum, S., & Spelke, E. S. (2014). Brief non-symbolic, approximate number practice enhances subsequent exact symbolic arithmetic in children. Cognition, 131(1), 92-107. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2013.12.007
title: Specialized ANS-to-symbolic-arithmetic link: symbolic arithmetic draws on overlapping structures with the approximate number system, not a generalized magnitude system or common operations
description: The article evaluates three families of accounts for the ANS-mathematics link: ANS-specific dependence, a generalized magnitude system spanning dimensions, and mediation by general cognitive operations such as comparison, ordering, or inhibitory control. Its experimental pattern supports the first: "our data provide evidence that symbolic arithmetic draws on at least some overlapping cognitive and/or neural structures used to represent approximate number." Non-numerical magnitude training with the same operations did not produce the enhancement, and effects were mathematics-specific.
requirements: The account is supported for children still acquiring symbolic mathematics under brief practice and immediate testing conditions
constraints: The article states the scope of the observed practice effect remains unclear and that further research should investigate the role of EF and working memory more directly
target_learners: first-grade children (6-7 years old) learning symbolic arithmetic
target_learning_goals: symbolic arithmetic performance
understanding the cognitive basis of early mathematics learning
examples: Experiment 1 contrasted numerical addition and comparison training against line-length addition and brightness comparison training with matched timing and difficulty
key_sources: Hyde, D. C., Khanum, S., & Spelke, E. S. (2014). Brief non-symbolic, approximate number practice enhances subsequent exact symbolic arithmetic in children. Cognition, 131(1), 92-107. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2013.12.007

article_title: The Relation of Obesity to Performance in Verbal Abilities, Processing Speed, and Cognitive Flexibility in Old Age: The Role of Cognitive Reserve
citation: Ihle, Andreas; Mons, Ute; Perna, Laura; Oris, Michel; Fagot, Delphine; Gabriel, Rainer; Kliegel, Matthias (2016). The Relation of Obesity to Performance in Verbal Abilities, Processing Speed, and Cognitive Flexibility in Old Age: The Role of Cognitive Reserve. Dementia and Geriatric Cognitive Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1159/000448916
title: Cognitive reserve accumulated across the life course buffers detrimental influences of obesity on cognitive functioning in old age
description: The study applies the cognitive reserve framework to explain how accumulated life-course resources (educational attainment, occupation, engagement in activities throughout adulthood) may offset the detrimental influence of obesity on cognitive functioning in old age. The authors conclude that "cognitive reserve accumulated during the life course may reduce the detrimental influences of obesity on cognitive functioning in old age." In this study, cognitive reserve is operationalized through proxies measured across early life and midlife, and its buffering role is tested via moderation and hierarchical regression analyses.
requirements: Cognitive reserve proxies (educational attainment, occupation, engagement in activities throughout adulthood) must be measured to operationalize reserve accumulated in early and midlife.
constraints: The study is cross-sectional; the conclusion that reserve "may reduce" detrimental influences is stated as a suggestion rather than a demonstrated causal mechanism.
target_learners: older adults
target_learning_goals: maintaining cognitive functioning (verbal abilities, processing speed, cognitive flexibility) in old age
examples: The study tested whether obesity's relation to processing speed and cognitive flexibility was moderated by engagement in activities and education, and whether the association disappeared when reserve proxies were added to regression models.

article_title: Working memory influences processing speed and reading fluency in ADHD
citation: Jacobson, L. A., Ryan, M., Martin, R. B., Ewen, J., Mostofsky, S. H., Denckla, M. B., & Mahone, E. M. (2011). Working Memory Influences Processing Speed and Reading Fluency in ADHD. Child Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2010.532204
title: Processing speed as a deconstructable chain: sensory registration, response selection/preparation, and motor output components
description: The article proposes that processing speed, defined as "the time between stimulus onset and response completion", can be decomposed into separable components: sensory registration and perception, response selection and preparation, and response execution (Figure 1). Using the WISC-IV-I Coding and Coding Copy subtests, the study dissociates graphomotor output speed from executive response-selection components, arguing that ADHD-related slowing arises "between sensation/perception and action" in frontally-mediated circuits rather than in posterior perceptual systems.
requirements: Measures permitting dissociation of response components, such as the WISC-IV-I process analysis subtests pairing Coding with Coding Copy
constraints: The authors note the Coding task presents greater vertical scanning demand than Coding Copy, so perceptual demand differences may contribute to group differences on these tasks
target_learners: children ages 9-14 with ADHD
typically developing children
target_learning_goals: reading fluency development
processing speed and executive control
examples: The study regressed sex and Coding Copy performance on Coding to create a residualized CodingR score reflecting response selection and preparation separable from graphomotor output speed
key_sources: Jacobson, L. A., Ryan, M., Martin, R. B., Ewen, J., Mostofsky, S. H., Denckla, M. B., & Mahone, E. M. (2011). Working Memory Influences Processing Speed and Reading Fluency in ADHD. Child Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2010.532204

article_title: Effects of acute bouts of physical activity on children's attention: a systematic review of the literature
citation: Janssen M, Toussaint HM, van Mechelen W, Verhagen EALM. (2014). Effects of acute bouts of physical activity on children's attention: a systematic review of the literature. SpringerPlus. https://doi.org/10.1186/2193-1801-3-410
title: Attention as a gate into working memory mediating PA effects on cognition
description: The review organizes its inquiry around attention defined as "the ability to resist distraction", acting as a gate regulating the flow of sensory information into working memory and conscious awareness. It frames attention as required both for encoding new information and for recalling memories, and as a mediator between physical activity and academic achievement, since deficits in attention are associated with poorer academic performance. This framing justifies focusing the review solely on attention as the outcome measure.
requirements: Attention must be measurable; the review notes attention is always involved in other cognitive processes, making its measurement difficult
constraints: The definition of attention is not unambiguous; selective, divided and sustained attention are distinguished theoretically
target_learners: children aged 4-18
target_learning_goals: attention and cognitive control supporting learning and memory
examples: The review used this framework to justify excluding studies of other cognitive outcomes such as memory or successive processing
key_sources: Janssen M, Toussaint HM, van Mechelen W, Verhagen EALM. (2014). Effects of acute bouts of physical activity on children's attention: a systematic review of the literature. SpringerPlus. https://doi.org/10.1186/2193-1801-3-410

article_title: Attentional Control Buffers the Effect of Public-Speaking Anxiety on Performance
citation: Jones Christopher R., Fazio Russell H., Vasey Michael W. (2012). Attentional Control Buffers the Effect of Public Speaking Anxiety on Performance. Social Psychological and Personality Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/1948550611430166
title: Attentional control theory: anxiety impairs performance by hampering goal-directed attentional processes
description: Attentional control theory, cited from Eysenck, Derakshan, Santos, and Calvo (2007), distinguishes between two relevant attentional systems. As the article states, it "posits that anxiety impairs cognitive performance by hampering goal-directed attentional processes while leaving stimulus-driven processes that respond to environmental cues relatively intact." This disruption leads to increased attention capture by salient stimuli, especially threatening ones. The article uses this framework to motivate the prediction that individuals with greater attentional control capacity should be better equipped to deal with anxiety produced by public speaking.
requirements: The framework presupposes that effective performance on demanding tasks depends on goal-directed attentional processes that must be maintained against stimulus-driven capture.
target_learners: adult learners performing anxiety-inducing public speaking or other demanding cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: maintaining task performance under anxiety by regulating attention toward goal-directed processes
examples: The study measured attentional control with the 20-item Attentional Control Scale and tested the theory's moderating prediction in a public speaking task.
key_sources: Jones Christopher R., Fazio Russell H., Vasey Michael W. (2012). Attentional Control Buffers the Effect of Public Speaking Anxiety on Performance. Social Psychological and Personality Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/1948550611430166

article_title: Math Mindsets and Academic Grit: How Are They Related to Primary Math Achievement?
citation: Kaya, S., & Karakoc, D. (2022). Math Mindsets and Academic Grit: How Are They Related to Primary Math Achievement?. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 10(3), 298-309. https://doi.org/10.30935/scimath/11881
title: Domain-specific math mindset framework (fixed vs growth math mindsets)
description: The article applies Dweck's self-theories to mathematics: students hold either a "fixed math mindset", believing math capability "is innate and fixed", or a "growth math mindset", believing capability "can be developed with practice or instruction". Mindsets are treated as domain-specific, so a person can hold a growth mindset in one field and a fixed one in another. The study measures both with an adapted 6-item scale and models their direct and grit-mediated effects on achievement.
requirements: Domain-specific measurement, since general mindset instruments are argued to explain school achievement less well
constraints: Mindsets tend to be domain-specific and exist independently across domains
target_learners: primary school students (4th grade)
target_learning_goals: math achievement
motivational beliefs about math intelligence
examples: Adapted Dweck items such as: you can change your math intelligence a lot (growth) versus you have a certain amount of math intelligence you cannot change (fixed)
key_sources: Kaya, S., & Karakoc, D. (2022). Math Mindsets and Academic Grit: How Are They Related to Primary Math Achievement?. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 10(3), 298-309. https://doi.org/10.30935/scimath/11881

article_title: Math Mindsets and Academic Grit: How Are They Related to Primary Math Achievement?
citation: Kaya, S., & Karakoc, D. (2022). Math Mindsets and Academic Grit: How Are They Related to Primary Math Achievement?. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, 10(3), 298-309. https://doi.org/10.30935/scimath/11881
title: Academic grit scale (Clark & Malecki 10-item, Turkish adaptation)
description: A 10-item, single-factor, 5-point Likert academic grit scale developed by Clark and Malecki (2019), translated to Turkish and back-translated, pilot-tested with 33 4th graders. In this study CFA showed good fit (CFI=0.99, TLI=0.97, RMSEA=0.08, SRMR=0.04) and Cronbach's alpha was α=0.96. Items include "I push myself to do my personal best in school". It was used to measure school-related grit as mediator.
requirements: Back-translation and piloting for child samples; the original short grit scale yields low reliability for school outcomes
constraints: Not yet compared against general grit in child samples in this study
target_learners: primary school students
target_learning_goals: academic perseverance and effort in schoolwork
examples: Administered with the math mindset scale in a separate class session, taking about 10 minutes

article_title: The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective
citation: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001
title: Self-determination theory as a framework for designing adult training programs
description: Self-determination theory is a general theory of motivation standing in the humanistic tradition, in which the self interacts dialectically with its social environment. It postulates fundamental psychological needs for autonomy, competence and social integration whose satisfaction influences integration of experiences. The article applies it to the design of adult training programs, noting intrinsic motivation can be encouraged by freedom of choice but reduced by threats, deadlines, surveillance or rewards.
requirements: Learning environments must support the fundamental needs of autonomy, competence and social integration for motivation to be internalized
constraints: Intrinsic motivation can be reduced by circumstances such as threats, deadlines, self-observation, observation or assessment, and forms of rewards or feedback
target_learners: adult learners
target_learning_goals: learning motivation
competency development in lifelong learning
examples: The article applies self-determination theory into the design of adult training programs with the goal of integration with self-regulation and reflective learning
key_sources: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001

article_title: The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective
citation: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001
title: Self-regulated learning as a cyclical process model with cognitive, motivational, affective and metacognitive components
description: Self-regulated learning is a central construct of pedagogical psychology in which a learning session is conceptualized as a cycle: objectives and planning, implementation and monitoring, and final evaluation of results. Existing models share cognitive, motivational, affective and metacognitive components. The article cites Zimmerman's triadic interaction, Winne and Hadwin's four phases, and Boekaerts' three areas, and notes these models are being applied to online and mobile learning environments.
requirements: Metacognitive control of the learning process is described as an essential prerequisite for self-regulated learning
target_learners: adult learners
target_learning_goals: self-management of learning
metacognitive monitoring of learning progress
examples: The article describes models applied to new educational contexts including online and mobile learning environments using digital technologies
key_sources: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001

article_title: The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective
citation: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001
title: Reflective learning as problem-initiated critical consideration aimed at implementing and evaluating solutions
description: Reflective learning is defined as more than thinking: a process usually initiated in problem situations and aimed at solving the relevant problem through critical consideration with increased consciousness. Following Stangl, reflection must continue past finding a solution into implementing and critically evaluating concrete new behavior, so reflective learning must itself be learned. The article traces the concept from Dewey through Schön to Kolb's four-phase cyclic reflection model, the most frequently used in adult education.
requirements: Reflection must engage with implementation of the intended solution, so a concrete new behavior must be performed and then critically evaluated
constraints: The article states this type of learning is hardly taught in traditional forms of schooling, which do not encourage implementation of knowledge in concrete problem situations
target_learners: adult learners
reflective practitioners
target_learning_goals: problem-solving competence
professional skills and attitudes
examples: Kolb's four-phase model moves from concrete experience through deepened perception and reflection to a new and more differentiated understanding and a newly planned experience
key_sources: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001

article_title: The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective
citation: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001
title: Integrated triadic model of self-determination, self-regulation and reflection as influencing factors of adult learning
description: The article's core contribution is an integrated dynamic model combining the three learning concepts, illustrated as a triadic framework of the factors influencing adult learning. Its stated advantage is that it reflects all levels of the learning process: preparation, performance and reflection. The model provides the basis for a checklist of guiding questions used as orientation for designing effective adult learning programs.
requirements: Each of the three concepts should be transformed into core points generating sample questions for designing and reflecting on adult learning programs
constraints: The model is presented as a basis for further discussion and research; the article reports no empirical test of it
target_learners: adult learners
adult educators
target_learning_goals: design of effective adult learning programs
integration of motivation, self-management and reflection
examples: The authors developed a triadic framework illustrating the factors influencing adult learning in an integrated model (Figure 1)
key_sources: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001

article_title: The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective
citation: Frank Kellenberg, Joel Schmidt, Christian Werner. (2017). The Adult Learner: Self-Determined, Self-Regulated, and Reflective. Signum Temporis 9(1). https://doi.org/10.1515/sigtem-2017-0001
title: Reflection question tool: sample questions across self-determination, self-regulation and reflection from educator and learner perspectives
description: The reflection question tool is a checklist of sample questions organized by the three areas of self-determination, self-regulation and (self-)reflection, with self-regulation subdivided into plan, monitor and evaluate. It is divided into an Adult Educator Perspective section focusing on preparation of the learning task, and an Adult Learner Perspective section supporting the educator's own self-reflection. The authors state it is by no means comprehensive but provides ideas and direction for educators, trainers and teachers.
requirements: Should be used as orientation to design adult learning programs and reflect on the process, covering preparation, performance and reflection
constraints: The authors state it can be regarded as a basis for further developments through trial and examination in practice, i.e. it is not yet empirically validated
target_learners: adult educators
trainers
teachers
target_learning_goals: designing demand-oriented learning activities
educator self-reflection
examples: Table 1 lists questions such as what choice in terms of topics can be offered, whether strategies offered are effective for the task, and how well the approach worked

article_title: The effects of prior knowledge and text structure on comprehension processes during reading of scientific texts
citation: Kendeou, P., & van den Broek, P. (2007). The effects of prior knowledge and text structure on comprehension processes during reading of scientific texts. Memory & Cognition, 35(7), 1567-1577. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03193591
title: Refutation texts support conceptual change by eliciting coactivation of prior knowledge and text information, enabling inconsistency detection
description: The article proposes a mechanism account of why refutation texts foster conceptual change: during online reading of refutation text, readers coactivate and integrate prior knowledge with text information, which allows them to detect the inconsistency between their knowledge and the text, triggering additional processing to establish coherence. The authors state that "refutation texts help readers engage in conceptual change learning by eliciting coactivation, thereby facilitating inconsistency detection and the establishment of coherence." The account is grounded in the convergent online findings of the two experiments.
requirements: The reader must hold prior knowledge (potentially misconceptions) related to the text topic so that coactivation and inconsistency detection can occur
The text must explicitly identify and refute the misconception rather than merely present correct information
constraints: Conceptual change processes elicited by refutation texts do not inevitably result in successful revision of incorrect ideas, as readers with misconceptions recalled less regardless of structure
The explanation-sentence reading time comparison should be interpreted with caution because explanations differed in content across texts
target_learners: readers of scientific texts with misconceptions about the text topic, such as undergraduates in introductory physics
target_learning_goals: conceptual change in science
comprehension of scientific texts
examples: In Experiment 1, readers with misconceptions generated conceptual change strategies such as experiencing cognitive conflict, responding to conflict, and contrasting information while reading refutation texts
In Experiment 2, readers with misconceptions spent more time reading Newton's law sentences than readers without misconceptions, but only in refutation texts
key_sources: Kendeou, P., & van den Broek, P. (2007). The effects of prior knowledge and text structure on comprehension processes during reading of scientific texts. Memory & Cognition, 35(7), 1567-1577. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03193491

article_title: Writing fluency and quality in kindergarten and first grade: the role of attention, reading, transcription, and oral language
citation: Kent, S., Wanzek, J., Petscher, Y., Al Otaiba, S. S., & Kim, Y.-S. (2014). Writing fluency and quality in kindergarten and first grade: The role of attention, reading, transcription, and oral language. Reading and Writing, 27(7), 1163-1188. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-013-9480-1
title: Not-So-Simple View of Writing with attention as a component factor in early writing development
description: Berninger and Winn's Not-So-Simple View of Writing proposes three primary components: transcription; executive functions regulating focused attention, inhibitory control, and mental shifting during planning, reviewing, and revising; and text generation, the transformation of ideas to language representations. This study's SEM results, in the authors' words, "lend support to their theory at the stage of beginning writing," because a model including attention fit better and attention uniquely predicted fluency and quality concurrently and longitudinally.
requirements: Assessment of attention/self-regulation alongside literacy, transcription, and oral language component skills
constraints: The study assessed only teacher ratings of attention; executive functions such as working memory and self-regulation strategies were not assessed, so support at this age covers supervisory attention only
target_learners: Kindergarten and first-grade students
target_learning_goals: Writing fluency and writing quality (compositional production, ideation, organization, word choice)
examples: A SEM of 265 kindergarten and first-grade students in which the attention factor was included alongside literacy, letter-writing fluency, and oral language factors predicting compositional fluency and quality
key_sources: Kent, S., Wanzek, J., Petscher, Y., Al Otaiba, S. S., & Kim, Y.-S. (2014). Writing fluency and quality in kindergarten and first grade: The role of attention, reading, transcription, and oral language. Reading and Writing, 27(7), 1163-1188. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-013-9480-1

article_title: Mutualistic Coupling Between Vocabulary and Reasoning Supports Cognitive Development During Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood
citation: Kievit, R. A., Lindenberger, U., Goodyer, I. M., Jones, P. B., Fonagy, P., Bullmore, E. T., the Neuroscience in Psychiatry Network, & Dolan, R. J. (2017). Mutualistic Coupling Between Vocabulary and Reasoning Supports Cognitive Development During Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617710785
title: Mutualism model of cognitive development
description: The mutualism model, associated with van der Maas et al. (2006), proposes that "causal interactions between multiple basic cognitive abilities across developmental time" exist, "such that cognitive abilities mutually facilitate longitudinal growth." Under this assumption, developmental change yields a positive manifold even from initially uncorrelated abilities. In this article it was instantiated as a bivariate latent change score model with bidirectional coupling parameters between vocabulary and matrix reasoning, which outperformed g-factor and investment alternatives.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measurement of multiple cognitive domains to estimate coupling parameters
constraints: Evidence here comes from adolescents and young adults (14–25) measured on two occasions with two subtests; the authors note generalizability is limited to this developmental period
target_learners: adolescents and young adults aged 14–25
target_learning_goals: development of fluid reasoning and vocabulary (crystallized knowledge)
examples: Fitted as a bivariate LCS model with coupling parameters conceptually similar to the M matrix in van der Maas et al.'s mutualism model
key_sources: Kievit, R. A., Lindenberger, U., Goodyer, I. M., Jones, P. B., Fonagy, P., Bullmore, E. T., the Neuroscience in Psychiatry Network, & Dolan, R. J. (2017). Mutualistic Coupling Between Vocabulary and Reasoning Supports Cognitive Development During Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617710785

article_title: Mutualistic Coupling Between Vocabulary and Reasoning Supports Cognitive Development During Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood
citation: Kievit, R. A., Lindenberger, U., Goodyer, I. M., Jones, P. B., Fonagy, P., Bullmore, E. T., the Neuroscience in Psychiatry Network, & Dolan, R. J. (2017). Mutualistic Coupling Between Vocabulary and Reasoning Supports Cognitive Development During Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617710785
title: Latent change score modeling framework for comparing developmental theories
description: The article uses bivariate latent change score (LCS) models, which "conceptualize differences between successive measurements as latent change factors," allowing within-subject change to be modeled via self-feedback (β) and coupling (γ) parameters. This framework let the authors translate g-factor, investment, and mutualism accounts into competing psychometric models and compare them directly on the same longitudinal data — something prior studies had not done. The coupling parameter indexes whether change in one domain is affected by the prior level of the other domain.
requirements: At least two measurement occasions per participant; structural equation modeling software (lavaan was used)
constraints: With only two waves, lead-lag relations cannot be modeled; the authors note three or more waves would allow change scores to predict subsequent change scores
target_learners: adolescents and young adults in longitudinal cohort studies
target_learning_goals: quantifying cross-domain developmental dynamics in cognitive abilities
examples: Applied to WASI-II Matrix Reasoning and Vocabulary subtests from the NSPN cohort, with Time 2 scores rescaled for varying intertest intervals
key_sources: Kievit, R. A., Lindenberger, U., Goodyer, I. M., Jones, P. B., Fonagy, P., Bullmore, E. T., the Neuroscience in Psychiatry Network, & Dolan, R. J. (2017). Mutualistic Coupling Between Vocabulary and Reasoning Supports Cognitive Development During Late Adolescence and Early Adulthood. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617710785

article_title: Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders
citation: Kim, Y.-S., Al Otaiba, S., Sidler Folsom, J., & Gruelich, L. (2013). Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 28(3), 461–469. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2013.01.001
title: Attend to multiple component skills — oral language, literacy, and attentiveness — alongside transcription when supporting beginning writing development
description: This principle holds that written composition in early grades draws on multiple component skills beyond transcription: oral language (especially grammatical knowledge), reading comprehension, letter writing automaticity, spelling, and attentiveness. The article states that 'attention needs to be paid to multiple components beyond transcription skills such as children's oral language (e.g., sentence level grammatical knowledge) and attentiveness.' Different component skills relate differentially to substantive quality versus writing conventions dimensions of writing.
requirements: Assessment and instruction should address grammatical knowledge, reading comprehension, letter writing automaticity, spelling, and attentiveness rather than transcription alone
constraints: Findings are correlational from first-grade classrooms in a northern Florida community; causal directionality is not established
target_learners: First-grade students in early elementary classrooms
target_learning_goals: Written composition — substantive quality and writing conventions
examples: The study assessed 527 first graders on expressive vocabulary, grammatical knowledge, reading comprehension, spelling, letter writing automaticity, and teacher-rated attentiveness, then modeled their unique relations to two written composition dimensions
key_sources: Kim, Y.-S., Al Otaiba, S., Sidler Folsom, J., & Gruelich, L. (2013). Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders. article_title: Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders
citation: Kim, Y.-S., Al Otaiba, S., Sidler Folsom, J., & Gruelich, L. (2013). Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 28(3), 461–469. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2013.01.001
title: Promote teacher responsiveness to students' inquiries and responses as a lever for improving beginning writing quality
description: The article concludes that 'teachers' interaction with students, and teachers' responsiveness in particular, may be an important factor to consider and promote in facilitating children's writing development.' Responsiveness was defined as the extent to which teachers selected and incorporated students' responses and experiences in their instruction, rated from classroom observation. This general instructional quality dimension predicted substantive quality of writing even after accounting for child-level skills and content-specific instructional quality.
requirements: Classroom observation or professional development focused on teachers' incorporation of student responses and experiences during literacy instruction
constraints: Instructional quality was based on a single winter observation; the authors caution that 'caution needs to be exercised for interpretation and future replication would be informative'
target_learners: First-grade students
target_learning_goals: Substantive quality of written composition
examples: Teachers rated highly responsive (score of 3) were those effective at selecting and incorporating students' responses and experiences; those punitive toward children's inquiries received low scores

Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders. article_title: Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders
citation: Kim, Y.-S., Al Otaiba, S., Sidler Folsom, J., & Gruelich, L. (2013). Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 28(3), 461–469. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2013.01.001
title: Two-dimension structure of written composition: substantive quality and writing conventions as related but dissociable latent variables
description: The article adopts a trait-based evaluation of written composition in which seven rated aspects (ideas, organization, word choice, sentence flow, spelling, mechanics, handwriting) load onto 'two related (r = .65) but dissociable latent variables': a substantive quality dimension (ideas, organization, word choice, sentence flow) and a writing conventions dimension (spelling, mechanics, handwriting). This structure, established via confirmatory factor analysis in prior work by the authors, served as the outcome framework for the study's multilevel models.
requirements: Writing samples evaluated with an analytic rubric rating the seven aspects on a 1–5 developmental scale
constraints: The voice aspect was excluded due to a floor effect for first-grade children in preliminary work
target_learners: First-grade students (framework derived from and applied to early elementary writers)
target_learning_goals: Written composition assessment and instruction
examples: The study used sum scores of the four substantive-quality aspects and three conventions aspects as outcomes in multilevel models

Language, literacy, attentional behaviors, and instructional quality predictors of written composition for first graders. article_title: Kindergarten predictors of third grade writing
citation: Kim Young-Suk, Al Otaiba Stephanie, Wanzek Jeanne. (2015). Kindergarten Predictors of Third Grade Writing. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.009
title: Simple view and not-so-simple view of writing as frameworks of component skills for developing writers
description: The article organizes its predictor selection around named theoretical models of writing. The simple view of writing holds that "writing is a function of two necessary component skills, ideation and transcription," while the not-so-simple view clusters skills into transcription, text generation, and executive functions/self-regulation, with working memory coordinating them. The knowledge-telling model adds that young children's writing transcribes what they know about topic and genre. The study operationalized these as transcription, oral language, attention, and word-reading predictors.
requirements: The framework assumes writing outcomes can be decomposed into measurable component skills assessed separately from writing quality itself
constraints: The article notes most prior supporting studies were concurrent predictions, and longitudinal predictive studies were lacking before this work
target_learners: children in kindergarten through elementary grades
target_learning_goals: written composition quality in narrative and expository genres
examples: The study selected kindergarten predictors (letter writing automaticity, spelling, oral language, word reading, attention) based on the simple view and not-so-simple view of writing and tested them longitudinally against third-grade writing quality.
key_sources: Kim Young-Suk, Al Otaiba Stephanie, Wanzek Jeanne. (2015). Kindergarten Predictors of Third Grade Writing. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.009

article_title: Adolescents With Chronic Medical Conditions and High School Completion: The Importance of Perceived School Belonging
citation: Kirkpatrick, Kathryn M. (2020). Adolescents With Chronic Medical Conditions and High School Completion: The Importance of Perceived School Belonging. Continuity in Education, 1(1), 50–63. https://doi.org/10.5334/cie.5
title: School belonging as a basic need with identifiable school-level promotive components
description: The article frames belonging as "a basic human need, important for optimal functioning", with school as the primary community outside the family for adolescents. It identifies school environments promoting connectedness as those with "high academic standards, high levels of teacher support, a community where relationships between students and adults are caring and respectful, and safety". It further reports three critical school-level components identified in prior work: high academic expectations coupled with support for learning, positive and respectful student-adult relationships, and physical and emotional safety.
requirements: School environments must offer supportive relationships, structure, and safety for belonging to develop as described
constraints: The three-component list is attributed to prior sources (Blum, 2005; Klem & Connell, 2004; Wingspread, 2004), not tested in this study
target_learners: adolescents in grades 7–12
students with chronic medical conditions
target_learning_goals: academic attainment and high school completion
social and behavioral success at school
examples: The study measured belonging with a five-item Wave I scale covering closeness, part of school, happiness at school, fair teachers, and feeling safe (α = .76)

article_title: Role of linguistic skills in fifth-grade mathematics
citation: Kleemans, T., Segers, E., & Verhoeven, L. (2018). Role of linguistic skills in fifth-grade mathematics. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 167, 404-413. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2017.11.012
title: Extension of the verbal system of the triple code model to include phonological skills and grammatical ability as key variables of exact arithmetic
description: The article positions its findings within the triple code model (Dehaene et al., 2003), whose verbal system holds that arithmetic solution relies on verbal codes stored in a phonological format in long-term memory. The authors propose that the results "hint at an extension of the verbal system of the triple code model" by including both phonological skills and grammatical ability as key variables of exact arithmetic calculations, and note that grammatical ability and arithmetic share underlying rules and recursive principles.
requirements: Basic linguistic skills (phonological skills and grammatical ability) must be measured as distinct constructs rather than composite language measures
constraints: The supporting evidence is correlational and gathered at a single time point, so the direction of the relation between linguistic skills and mathematics cannot be established from this study
target_learners: Fifth-grade students in upper primary education
target_learning_goals: Arithmetic fluency
Geometry
Fractions
examples: The mediation models tested phonological skills and grammatical ability as separate predictors of arithmetic, which served as mediator for geometry and fractions

article_title: Lexical Processing of Nouns and Verbs at 36 Months of Age Predicts Concurrent and Later Vocabulary and School Readiness
citation: Koenig Ashley, Arunachalam Sudha, Saudino Kimberly J. (2020). Lexical processing of nouns and verbs at 36 months of age predicts concurrent and later vocabulary and school readiness. Journal of cognition and development : official journal of the Cognitive Development Society. https://doi.org/10.1080/15248372.2020.1802277
title: Fixation-star lexical processing task with noun and verb trials
description: A variant of Fernald et al.'s (1998) lexical processing task in which, during the Response phase, 'the two images or videos disappeared, and a centrally positioned yellow star appeared, during which children heard the test query'. The two scenes then reappeared with a 'ding' sound to facilitate coding. The task included 13 trials with 7 nouns and 6 verbs, with noun referents shown as static images and verb referents as dynamic videos of people performing everyday actions. Latency was coded manually from video at 30 frames per second as the time from the onset of the 'ding' to the first look to the target scene. Because children look at the center at word onset, latency can be measured on all trials.
requirements: Children must be able to view the two scenes side-by-side and hear the auditory test query; the design requires that children are looking at the center of the screen at word onset so latency of the first saccade toward the target can be measured on all trials.
constraints: Latencies are measured from the onset of when the scenes reappear after word onset rather than from word onset, so they are 'not directly comparable to those in other studies'.
target_learners: typically developing 36-month-old children
target_learning_goals: receptive vocabulary and lexical processing speed for nouns and verbs
examples: In this study the task used 13 trials with target words such as airplane, corn, crab, goldfish, hamburger, rocketship, and squirrel (nouns) and lift, march, rip, roll, shake, and stretch (verbs), with target side counterbalanced across trials.
key_sources: Koenig Ashley, Arunachalam Sudha, Saudino Kimberly J. (2020). Lexical processing of nouns and verbs at 36 months of age predicts concurrent and later vocabulary and school readiness. article_title: The contribution of executive functions to creativity in children: What is the role of crystallized and fluid intelligence?
citation: Krumm, Gabriela Liliana; Arán Filippetti, Vanessa; Gutierrez Saez, Marisel Luisa. (2018). The contribution of executive functions to creativity in children: What is the role of crystallized and fluid intelligence?. Thinking Skills and Creativity. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2018.07.006
title: Executive functions support creativity differentially in children, with shifting central to the intelligence-creativity link
description: The article proposes a model in which creativity in children is supported differentially by distinct executive functions rather than uniformly, and in which crystallized intelligence affects creativity indirectly through shifting. The authors state that "EFs differently support creativity in children" and that SEM showed the Gc effect on creativity "was mediated by shifting". The model was tested with SEM on measures of working memory, inhibition and shifting alongside Gc, Gf and creativity in 209 children aged 8 to 13.
requirements: Requires measures of creativity, crystallized and fluid intelligence, and the three EF components (working memory, inhibition, shifting) to test the differential contributions
constraints: Findings concern children aged 8 to 13; the abstract notes most prior research focused on adult populations
target_learners: children aged 8 to 13
target_learning_goals: creative thinking
examples: SEM analysis of 209 children's creativity, intelligence and EF measures testing mediation of the Gc-creativity relation by shifting

The measures were analyzed with correlational analyses and a Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) approach to examine relations among the three constructs.

article_title: Effects of Mathematics Anxiety and Mathematical Metacognition on Word Problem Solving in Children with and without Mathematical Learning Difficulties
citation: Lai Y, Zhu X, Chen Y, Li Y (2015) Effects of Mathematics Anxiety and Mathematical Metacognition on Word Problem Solving in Children with and without Mathematical Learning Difficulties. PLoS ONE 10(6): e0130570. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0130570
title: Interventions for mathematical learning difficulty should address anxiety during the mathematics learning process and build metacognitive self-image
description: The article recommends that support for children with MLD target learning-process anxiety and metacognition rather than only cognitive deficits: "helping MLD children reduce anxiety during the mathematics learning process should be incorporated into future interventions." It also suggests one benefit of mathematical metacognition may be promoting beliefs about, and self-efficacy for, MLD children's mathematical abilities. The study's mediation and group-difference findings provide the empirical basis for this recommendation.
requirements: Interventions should be informed by assessment of learning mathematics anxiety (LMA) and self-image, since these distinguished MLD children from LA, TA, and HA peers in the study.
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional; the authors state SEM does not warrant causal claims, and the small number of MLD students calls for caution in interpreting mediating effects in MLD children.
target_learners: Children with mathematical learning difficulty (MLD) in elementary school
target_learning_goals: Word problem solving
Mathematics achievement
Reducing anxiety during mathematics learning
examples: The study compared four mathematics achievement groups (MLD, LA, TA, HA) on metacognition and anxiety with IQ partialled out, and found MLD children's LMA higher and self-image lower than TA and HA peers.

article_title: Cognitive Flexibility and Theory of Mind Outcomes Among Foster Children: Preschool Follow-Up Results of a Randomized Clinical Trial
citation: Lewis-Morrarty, E., Dozier, M., Bernard, K., Terracciano, S., & Moore, S. (2012). Cognitive Flexibility and Theory of Mind Outcomes Among Foster Children: Preschool Follow-up Results of a Randomized Clinical Trial. Journal of Adolescent Health. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jadohealth.2012.05.005
title: Attachment and Biobehavioral Catch-up (ABC) intervention
description: The ABC intervention is a "10-session, manualized parenting program aimed at enhancing young children’s self-regulatory capacities by helping caregivers provide nurturing and synchronous care." Interventionists explain the developmental research basis, videotape parent-child interactions so caregivers can practice "following the child’s lead," give video feedback highlighting nurturing versus intrusive or disengaged moments, and help caregivers reflect on how their own early experiences may hinder nurturing care. In this study it was delivered to foster parents of infants and toddlers and evaluated against a control intervention.
requirements: Trained interventionists who deliver the 10 manualized sessions, including video feedback of parent-child interactions
constraints: In this trial it was delivered to parents of foster children placed before age three, prior to 20 months of age
target_learners: Foster parents and other caregivers of infants and toddlers who have experienced early adversity
target_learning_goals: Providing nurturing care in response to child distress
Engaging in synchronous parent-child interactions that support children's self-regulatory development
examples: Foster children randomly assigned to ABC before age 20 months were assessed at ages 4–6 on the Dimensional Change Card Sort and the penny-hiding game

article_title: Developmental Gains in Visuospatial Memory Predict Gains in Mathematics Achievement
citation: Li Y, Geary DC (2013) Developmental Gains in Visuospatial Memory Predict Gains in Mathematics Achievement. PLoS ONE 8(7): e70160. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0070160
title: Differential developmental gains across working memory components change their relative contributions to mathematics learning
description: The article proposes that the three Baddeley-Hitch working memory components—central executive, phonological memory, and visuospatial memory—mature at different rates, so their relative contributions to mathematics achievement shift across development. The authors argue that "differential gains in the central executive, phonological memory, and visuospatial memory could result in across-grade changes in the relative contribution of these components of working memory to mathematics performance." This explains why visuospatial memory relates inconsistently to mathematics in children but consistently in adulthood.
requirements: Longitudinal assessment of working memory components across multiple grades to detect differential gains
constraints: The study's non-experimental method does not allow for strong inferences about mechanisms, per the authors
target_learners: children in kindergarten through fifth grade
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
working memory development
examples: The study assessed 177 children's working memory in first and fifth grade and modeled achievement growth from kindergarten to fifth grade

article_title: The association between children's numerical magnitude processing and mental multi-digit subtraction
citation: Linsen, S., Verschaffel, L., Reynvoet, B., De Smedt, B. (2014). The Association between Children's Numerical Magnitude Processing and Mental Multi-digit Subtraction. Acta Psychologica. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actpsy.2013.10.008
title: Strategy categorization of mental multi-digit subtraction by underlying operation: direct subtraction versus indirect addition
description: The article categorizes children's mental multi-digit subtraction strategies by the operation underlying the solution process: direct subtraction strategies, in which the subtrahend is directly subtracted from the minuend, and indirect addition strategies, in which one determines how much needs to be added to the subtrahend to get to the minuend. A rational task analysis indicates indirect addition is particularly efficient when minuend and subtrahend are close, as in "81 - 79 = ?". The study used this taxonomy to construct items eliciting each strategy type.
requirements: Items must be constructed so that subtrahend size relative to the difference and minuend-subtrahend distance elicit the intended strategy
constraints: The article notes a third class, the indirect subtraction strategy, is excluded from this two-type categorization
target_learners: third-grade children in the number domain 20-100
target_learning_goals: mental multi-digit subtraction calculation
examples: The study constructed 32 subtraction items, half designed to elicit indirect addition (small distance, e.g. 72-67) and half direct subtraction (large distance, e.g. 83-27)
key_sources: Linsen, S., Verschaffel, L., Reynvoet, B., De Smedt, B. (2014). The Association between Children's Numerical Magnitude Processing and Mental Multi-digit Subtraction. Acta Psychologica. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actpsy.2013.10.008

article_title: Association of childhood trauma with cognitive function in healthy adults: a pilot study
citation: Majer M, Nater UM, Lin J-MS, Capuron L, Reeves WC. (2010). Association of childhood trauma with cognitive function in healthy adults: a pilot study. BMC Neurology. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2377-10-61
title: Cognitive deficits should be addressed in the treatment of victims of childhood trauma, independent of psychiatric diagnosis
description: The authors recommend that cognitive impairment observed in adults with childhood trauma exposure should be addressed clinically even when no psychiatric condition is concurrently diagnosed. They found memory deficits in healthy adults with trauma exposure and argue that "Cognitive deficits should be addressed in the treatment of victims of childhood trauma, independent of their being concurrently diagnosed with a psychiatric condition." This principle follows from their observation that trauma-associated memory deficits occur in otherwise healthy individuals.
requirements: Assessment of cognitive function in individuals with childhood trauma exposure, using instruments sensitive to working and long-term memory
constraints: Based on a small pilot study; the authors state results should be considered preliminary
target_learners: Adults with childhood trauma exposure
target_learning_goals: Working memory
Long-term memory
Academic achievement
examples: The pilot study assessed 47 healthy adults using the CANTAB battery and found memory deficits associated with emotional abuse and physical neglect exposure

title: Neuropsychological training should be implemented in comprehensive intervention strategies for individuals with childhood trauma
description: The authors recommend that neuropsychological training be included as a component of comprehensive intervention strategies for individuals with childhood trauma. They argue that "Neuropsychological training should be implemented in a comprehensive intervention strategy for individuals with childhood trauma" and that early intervention may prevent long-term deficits in memory function and academic performance in maltreated children.
requirements: Comprehensive intervention strategy that includes neuropsychological training as a component
constraints: Based on a small pilot study; the authors state results should be considered preliminary

Maltreated children
target_learning_goals: Memory function
Academic performance
examples: The pilot study found that emotional abuse and physical neglect were associated with spatial working memory and pattern recognition memory deficits in healthy adults

article_title: The role of domain-general cognitive abilities and decimal labels in at-risk fourth-grade students' decimal magnitude understanding
citation: Malone Amelia S., Loehr Abbey M., Fuchs Lynn S. (2017). The Role of Domain-General Cognitive Abilities and Decimal Labels in At-Risk Fourth-Grade Students' Decimal Magnitude Understanding. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2017.05.007
title: Use magnitude language (place value labels) when defining decimals to reduce whole-number misconceptions
description: The article recommends that decimal instruction always use place value labels (e.g., reading 0.12 as "twelve hundredths") because such magnitude language supports students' decimal magnitude understanding and reduces misconceptions that decimals behave like whole numbers. The recommendation draws on the study's label correlations and prior label research. The authors caution that "more work is needed to assess the tenability of these recommendations."

constraints: Very little research exists on improving at-risk students' decimal magnitude understanding; tenability not yet assessed

rational number reasoning

article_title: Digital Inclusion in Older Adults: A Comparison Between Face-to-Face and Blended Digital Literacy Workshops
citation: Martínez-Alcalá CI, Rosales-Lagarde A, Alonso-Lavernia MÁ, Ramírez-Salvador JÁ, Jiménez-Rodríguez B, Cepeda-Rebollar RM, López-Noguerola JS, Bautista-Díaz ML and Agis-Juárez RA (2018) Digital Inclusion in Older Adults: A Comparison Between Face-to-Face and Blended Digital Literacy Workshops. Front. ICT 5:21. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2018.00021
title: ASSURE instructional design model for face-to-face and blended older-adult instruction
description: The ASSURE model is the instructional design framework the authors used to structure both workshop modalities. It presents "6 phases: Analyze learners, State objectives, Select instructional methods and materials, Utilize materials, Require learner response, and Evaluation and revision." The authors chose it because it "has the necessary characteristics to implement face-to-face and blended instruction" and can adapt course or lesson design systematically. They credit it with producing adequate structure, attractive text colors and images, quality materials, and clear instructions attentive to older adults' visual, cognitive and emotional characteristics.
requirements: Instructors must analyze learner characteristics, including visual deficiencies, cognitive and emotional abilities, before designing materials
target_learners: older adults aged 60 and above with little or no ICT knowledge
target_learning_goals: digital literacy skills: use and knowledge of computers, the Internet, and daily life devices
examples: The blended workshop was developed under ASSURE guidelines, yielding a space with adequate structure and design, attractive text colors and images, quality teaching materials and clear instructions

title: Senior Digital Literacy Evaluation (SDLE) instrument
description: The SDLE is a 110-item test designed to measure older adults' digital literacy level, divided into three sections: "Use and knowledge of the computer, Use and knowledge of the Internet and Knowledge of domestic and daily life devices." It was content-validated by a panel of 7 doctoral-level experts using Lawshe and Tristan's model, with items below the 0.58 cut-off eliminated (35 items removed from an initial 145). Scores map to competence levels from A+ (Total competence) to B (Low competence); the authors caution these are indicative, not absolute values.

constraints: The authors state the scores are only indicative and it is not possible to assert that the scale provides absolute digital literacy values
target_learners: older adults aged 60 and above
target_learning_goals: measuring digital literacy and technological competencies
examples: Applied pre and post in all six workshops delivered since 2014 to groups of 15–25 older adults

citation: Martínez-Alcalá CI, Rosales-Lagarde A, Alonso-Lavernia MÁ, Ramírez-Salvador JÁ, Jiménez-Rodríguez B, Cepeda-Rebollar RM, López-Noguerola JS, Bautista-Díaz ML and Agis-Juárez RA (2018) Digital Inclusion in Older Adults: A Comparison Between Face-to-Face and Blended Digital Literacy Workshops. title: Four-point educational model for older adults' digital literacy
description: The article proposes that the educational model toward digital literacy of the elderly should be based on 4 important points: "Usefulness of Learning", "Cooperativeness and collaboration", "Fostering social inclusion", and "Promoting autonomy". Learning should be personalized, cooperative, collaborative and meaningful, grounded in andragogy and the biological, psychological and social characteristics of older age. The workshops in this study instantiate this pattern, with tutors trained in andragogy and gerontology support staff providing personalized attention.
requirements: Content must be designed considering the learning styles, interests and expectations of the older individual; motivation should be the main factor in any educational program for this population
target_learners: older adults aged 60 and above with little or no ICT knowledge
target_learning_goals: digital competencies that respond to personal and social needs, social inclusion through the web, and learner autonomy

article_title: Nonverbal Reasoning as a Contributor to Sentence Recognition Outcomes in Adults With Cochlear Implants
citation: Mattingly Jameson K MD, Castellanos Irina PhD, Moberly Aaron C MD. (2018). Nonverbal Reasoning as a Contributor to Sentence Recognition Outcomes in Adults with Cochlear Implants. Otology & Neurotology. https://doi.org/10.1097/MAO.0000000000001998
title: Abbreviated 12-item Raven's Progressive Matrices assessment for clinical prediction of sentence recognition
description: A shortened computerized version of the Raven's Progressive Matrices consisting of the 12 test items that significantly differentiated low- versus high-performing CI users on PRESTO sentence recognition. The article states this "abridged version of the RPM, consisting of only twelve test items instead of the standard 48 items, should be able to be completed in only three to four minutes and may have clinical utility in predicting post-operative performance." It was validated by correlations with sentence recognition in both CI users and normal-hearing controls listening to noise-vocoded speech.
requirements: Administered visually on a touch screen monitor with 3×3 matrices of geometric designs and eight response boxes; requires near vision better than 20/40
constraints: The article states additional studies are needed to determine the test's prognostic utility in CI users, and that correlations are moderate rather than deterministic
target_learners: Post-lingually deafened adults considering or using cochlear implants
target_learning_goals: Predicting degraded speech recognition outcomes from nonverbal reasoning to guide counseling and rehabilitation planning
examples: CI users were categorized as low vs. high performers via a median split on PRESTO whole sentences (cut point 21.67%), and Fisher's Exact Tests on individual RPM items identified the 12-item subset

article_title: Limited knowledge of fraction representations differentiates middle school students with mathematics learning disability (dyscalculia) versus low mathematics achievement
citation: Mazzocco, M. M. M., Myers, G. F., Lewis, K. E., Hanich, L. B., & Murphy, M. M. (2013). Limited knowledge of fraction representations differentiates middle school students with mathematics learning disability (dyscalculia) vs. low mathematics achievement. Journal of experimental child psychology, 115(2), 371-387. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2013.01.005
title: Use visual fraction models to support students with mathematics learning disability, but treat the transition from visual models to Arabic notation as a persistent obstacle
description: The article finds that visual fraction models lead to more accurate magnitude comparisons than Arabic numeral fractions for all ability groups, and that for children with MLD this visual model advantage persists through Grade 8. The authors state that "children in the MLD group may benefit from continued use of visual models as one of several a strategies to support learning about fractions and solving problems involving fractions". However, they caution that if children with MLD rely on models as concrete rather than abstract representations, visual models may not promote thorough conceptual understanding, especially when models are spatially misleading or when transitioning to Arabic notation.
requirements: Visual models should be used alongside other strategies, not as the sole representation
constraints: The article states visual models may not promote the intended conceptual understanding when they are spatially misleading or when transitioning from visual models to Arabic notation; for MLD children the visual model advantage persisted through Grade 8 rather than fading as it did for TA peers
target_learners: Middle school students with mathematics learning disability (dyscalculia)
target_learning_goals: Accurate magnitude comparison of fractions and conceptual understanding of fraction quantities
examples: In the study, accuracy was greatest when visual models involved matching parts and lowest with Arabic numbers, and the spatially misleading format continued to misguide students with MLD through middle school

article_title: Integrating performance assessments across a PK-20 continuum: A locally developed collaboration
citation: McCurdy, K., Reagan, E. M., Schram, T., & Rogers, A. (2018). Integrating performance assessments across a PK-20 continuum: A locally developed collaboration. Education Policy Analysis Archives, 26(14). http://dx.doi.org/10.14507/epaa.26.3437
title: New Hampshire Teacher Candidate Assessment of Performance (NH TCAP)
description: The NH TCAP is a teacher candidate performance assessment adopted in 2013 by a consortium of teacher educators across all New Hampshire institutions of higher education "to support teacher candidate learning and assess readiness to teach." It was adapted from the Performance Assessment for California Teachers for the state context, with agreed implementation issues including scorer training, instructor involvement, and consequentiality. It is housed at the institutional level, is one of multiple measures determining readiness to teach, and is intended to keep evolving as data are collected and analyzed.
requirements: Consortium agreement around key implementation issues such as facilitation with teacher candidates, scorer training, instructor involvement and assistance, and the consequential nature of the assessment
constraints: It is housed at the institutional level and determined by the institutions, in contrast to other teacher candidate performance assessments across the country
target_learners: preservice teacher candidates in New Hampshire institutions of higher education
target_learning_goals: teacher candidate learning and readiness to teach
examples: In 2013 a consortium of teacher educators across all New Hampshire institutions of higher education adopted the NH TCAP, adapting the Performance Assessment for California Teachers (Pecheone & Chung, 2006) for the state context

title: Design performance assessments to balance assessment of learning with assessment for learning
description: The article holds that performance assessment tools should be designed to serve both summative and formative functions: it directs attention to "the challenging aim of designing tools that act as assessments of learning as well as assessments for learning." The NH TCAP is presented as aspiring to strike this balance, providing opportunities for deep and meaningful learning within higher education while also assessing readiness to teach. Because it can evolve as data are analyzed, it serves as a tool for learning at multiple levels.
requirements: Institutional capacity to collect and analyze data about the efficacies and challenges faced by teacher candidates, cooperating teachers, and university faculty so the assessment can continue evolving
constraints: The article calls this a challenging aim, and notes factors such as educator capacity and financial resources potentially limiting full realization of performance assessments

preservice teacher candidates
target_learning_goals: deep and meaningful learning
readiness to teach
examples: The NH TCAP aspires to strike a balance between assessment of and assessment for learning, and serves as a practical example for preservice teacher candidates to explore performance assessments by responding to prompts and unpacking rubrics

title: Multilayered system of assessment practices influenced by actors at all levels
description: The commentary adopts Stosich et al.'s (2018) framing of a "multilayered system of assessment practices" that is "influenced by actors at all levels of the educational system," including decision-makers at the school, district or network, state, and federal level. The article uses this framework to argue that a higher education voice should be added to the ecosystem, operating through a PK-20 rather than PK-12 lens. It also notes the framework's claim that creating such a multilayered system can provide more coherent or fragmented support for performance assessments.
requirements: Multiple stakeholders operating with a shared and co-created vision, characterized by open dialogue that enhances trust across all stakeholders
constraints: The framework is attributed to Stosich et al. (2018) and is developed from their review of PK-12 state-level policies; the commentary extends it to teacher preparation
target_learners: PK-12 students
preservice teacher candidates
target_learning_goals: meaningful student learning supported by coherent assessment systems
examples: The commentary applies the framework to New Hampshire, where PACE and the NH TCAP are locally developed performance assessments reflecting a state culture valuing local influence

citation: McRae, K., Gross, J. J., Weber, J., Robertson, E. R., Sokol-Hessner, P., Ray, R. D., Gabrieli, J. D. E., & Ochsner, K. N. (2012). The development of emotion regulation: an fMRI study of cognitive reappraisal in children, adolescents and young adults. Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience 7(1), 11–22. https://doi.org/10.1093/scan/nsr093
title: Developmental account of cognitive reappraisal: linearly developing cognitive control with nonlinear adolescent social-cognitive recruitment
description: This framework explains reappraisal development as comprising two dissociable components: cognitive control supported by prefrontal regions that develop linearly, and social-cognitive/mental-state-attribution processes showing nonlinear adolescent patterns. The study used "a task that distinguishes negative emotional reactivity from reappraisal ability" across three age groups to test linear versus nonlinear predictions of socio-emotional development.
requirements: Neuroimaging or behavioral measures that separate emotional reactivity from reappraisal ability
Age-span samples covering childhood through young adulthood
constraints: Findings based on cross-sectional comparison of three age groups (10–13, 14–17, 18–22) on one reappraisal task

adolescents (14–17)
young adults (18–22)
target_learning_goals: emotion regulation via cognitive reappraisal
examples: Comparing older children, adolescents, and young adults on a reappraisal task during fMRI scanning

citation: Menken, M. S., Isaiah, A., Liang, H., Rivera, P. R., Cloak, C. C., Reeves, G., Lever, N. A., & Chang, L. (2022). Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 925727. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.925727
title: Bullying intervention strategies should account for sex-specific effects in preadolescent children
description: The article's findings indicate that bullying affects preadolescent boys and girls differently: boys show greater behavioral problems while girls show greater cognitive impacts. The authors state that "Approaches to prevent bullying and mitigate its negative impact must keep in mind the sex of the youth." This principle calls for differentiated intervention design that addresses the distinct profiles of impact by sex.
requirements: Interventions must be designed for preadolescent children in school settings with awareness of sex-specific vulnerability profiles

Bullying was measured solely by caregiver report

cognitive and academic performance

article_title: Reporting and Interpreting Working Memory Performance in n-back Tasks
citation: Meule A (2017). Reporting and Interpreting Working Memory Performance in n-back Tasks. Front. Psychol. 8:352. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00352
title: Report and interpret reaction times and accuracy separately, choosing the measure with more meaningful variability
description: The article argues that reaction times and accuracy in n-back tasks "should not be interpreted interchangeably," because studies reaching similar conclusions from different dependent variables may not be comparable. Researchers should interpret the measure showing meaningful variation for the task at hand, as Hur et al. did by focusing on reaction times in a perception task and accuracy in a working memory task.
requirements: Researchers must report which dependent variable conclusions rest on and consider ceiling effects and variability in each measure.
constraints: The recommendation concerns n-back task performance indices specifically.
target_learners: researchers using n-back tasks to assess working memory
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement and interpretation of working memory performance
examples: Hur et al. focused on reaction times in a 0-back perception task where accuracy showed a ceiling effect, and on accuracy in a 2-back working memory task.
key_sources: Meule A (2017). Reporting and Interpreting Working Memory Performance in n-back Tasks. Front. Psychol. 8:352. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00352

article_title: Reporting and Interpreting Working Memory Performance in n-back Tasks
citation: Meule A (2017). Reporting and Interpreting Working Memory Performance in n-back Tasks. Front. Psychol. 8:352. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00352
title: Differentiate omission and commission errors and report signal-detection indices such as d' and C
description: The article recommends that researchers "not only report accuracy but also diﬀerentiate between omission and commission errors," since the two error types have different correlates. It further suggests reporting indices calculated from hits and false alarms, "such as discrimination index d′ and response bias C," as suggested by researchers using modified n-back versions.
requirements: Researchers must record hits, commission errors, and omission errors separately rather than a single accuracy figure.
constraints: Fine-grained analyses are framed as a way to clarify the n-back task's validity, which has been criticized for lacking clear associations with other working memory tasks.
target_learners: researchers assessing working memory with n-back tasks
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of working memory performance
examples: Kane et al. (2007) and Haatveit et al. (2010) used modified n-back versions with d' and C indices.

article_title: Visual short-term memory through the lifespan: Preserved benefits of context and metacognition.
citation: Daniel J. Mitchell, Cam-CAN (Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience), Rhodri Cusack. (2018). Visual Short-Term Memory Through the Lifespan: Preserved Benefits of Context and Metacognition. Psychology and Aging. https://doi.org/10.1037/pag0000265
title: Mixture-model decomposition of VSTM performance into quantity, quality, and misbinding components
description: The article frames VSTM performance using a continuous color-report paradigm in which a mixture model separates distinct components of performance. As the article states, it fitted a mixture model to the error distribution to give measures of VSTM quantity (K, the expected number of items stored), quality (the precision of items held in memory) and misbinding (the probability of reporting a correct color from a wrong location). The model combines a uniform guessing component with von Mises distributions centered on target and nontarget colors, allowing age-related change to be localized to specific memory components rather than a single aggregate score.
requirements: A continuous report task with response errors measured in color-wheel degrees, fitted with maximum-likelihood mixture model estimation using multiple starting points to avoid local minima.
constraints: K is interpreted empirically as the expected number of items stored without taking a theoretical position on whether storage involves discrete slots or an infinitely divisible resource.
target_learners: healthy adults aged 18 to 89
target_learning_goals: measuring the quantity, quality, and binding accuracy of visual short-term memory representations
examples: The model was fit per participant and memory load, separately for trials with and without probe context, and also to a no-memory control block to estimate sensorimotor ability.
key_sources: Daniel J. Mitchell, Cam-CAN (Cambridge Centre for Ageing and Neuroscience), Rhodri Cusack. (2018). Visual Short-Term Memory Through the Lifespan: Preserved Benefits of Context and Metacognition. Psychology and Aging. https://doi.org/10.1037/pag0000265

article_title: Young Children's Interpretation of Multidigit Number Names: From Emerging Competence to Mastery
citation: Mix, Kelly S., Prather, Richard W., Smith, Linda B., & Stockton, Jerri DaSha. (2014). Young Children's Interpretation of Multidigit Number Names: From Emerging Competence to Mastery. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12197
title: Statistical learning account of emerging place value knowledge
description: The article proposes that children acquire partial understanding of multidigit numerals through statistical learning, "the idea that learners actively make sense of the perceptual stream by tabulating the statistical patterns in it." Because multidigit numerals are ubiquitous in children's environments (room numbers, calendars, price tags), children detect regularities such as two-digit names containing /ee/ and use them, together with single-digit number meanings, to make educated guesses about numeral identity and magnitude. This bootstrapping occurs before formal schooling and parallels statistical learning in language acquisition.
requirements: Exposure to written and spoken multidigit numbers in everyday environments
Prior knowledge of single-digit number meanings
constraints: The correlation between number names and digit strings is imperfect and breaks down for longer number names
The study does not identify the origins of this knowledge or the experiences it depends on
target_learners: Preschool children aged 3 to 7 years
target_learning_goals: Interpreting written multidigit numerals and spoken number names
examples: Children hearing numbers named while seeing them in print on calendars, elevators, and room numbers could detect that thirty-four maps onto XX rather than X
key_sources: Mix, Kelly S., Prather, Richard W., Smith, Linda B., & Stockton, Jerri DaSha. (2014). Young Children's Interpretation of Multidigit Number Names: From Emerging Competence to Mastery. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12197
