title: Begin place value instruction with written symbols and use manipulatives to augment, not introduce, understanding
description: The article recommends that explicit place value instruction start from written symbols, which children already partially understand, rather than from concrete models. It states "Manipulatives thus might not be the entry point for instruction, but better used to augment early understanding, perhaps as a way of making the knowledge latent in the writing system explicit." Experiment 3 supported this: symbols-only training produced significant gains on difficult items while base-10 blocks training did not.
requirements: Knowledge of what children already know about numerals before instruction begins
constraints: Concrete models were not transparent to young children, who performed relatively poorly in blocks conditions
target_learners: Kindergarten and early elementary children
target_learning_goals: Place value understanding and multidigit numeral interpretation
examples: In Experiment 3, symbols-only training led to significant improvement on the 27 items children originally performed at chance, while blocks training did not

article_title: When do socioeconomic resources matter most in early childhood?
citation: Mollborn, S., Lawrence, E., James-Hawkins, L., & Fomby, P. (2014). When Do Socioeconomic Resources Matter Most in Early Childhood? Advances in Life Course Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.alcr.2014.03.001
title: Researchers studying the school transition should expand the concept to include the prekindergarten year.
description: The authors argue that because prekindergarten center-based education is now nearly universal and functions like school in shaping SES-related disparities, the "transition to school" concept should be broadened. They state: "we suggest that future research include the prekindergarten year when studying the transition to school." This reframing locates the peak SES–development relationship within the school transition period.
requirements: Longitudinal data covering the prekindergarten year is needed to study the expanded transition period.
constraints: The authors' evidence is indirect regarding mechanisms; they could not test explanations within the growth curve framework.
target_learners: Children in early childhood (ages 0–5/6)
target_learning_goals: Understanding socioeconomic disparities in cognitive and behavioral school readiness
examples: The study's growth curve models showed the SES–development relationship peaking at the start of prekindergarten rather than at kindergarten entry.
key_sources: Mollborn, S., Lawrence, E., James-Hawkins, L., & Fomby, P. (2014). When Do Socioeconomic Resources Matter Most in Early Childhood? Advances in Life Course Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.alcr.2014.03.001

article_title: When do socioeconomic resources matter most in early childhood?
citation: Mollborn, S., Lawrence, E., James-Hawkins, L., & Fomby, P. (2014). When Do Socioeconomic Resources Matter Most in Early Childhood? Advances in Life Course Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.alcr.2014.03.001
title: Policymakers seeking to reduce inequality should increase attention on the early childhood years around age 4–4½, when socioeconomic resources matter most.
description: The authors' finding that SES–development relationships peak around age 4–4½ implies interventions targeting socioeconomic disadvantage should focus on this period. They write: "our results, which clearly point to a peak in the importance of resources around age 4 or 4½, suggest that policymakers interested in reducing inequality should increase attention on the early childhood years."
requirements: Programs must reach children before and during the prekindergarten year to coincide with the peak SES–development relationship.
constraints: The authors caution that more can be done beyond preschool: "new programs and research should also look beyond preschool for ways to reduce socioeconomic disparities."
target_learners: Disadvantaged children in early childhood
target_learning_goals: Reducing socioeconomic disparities in cognitive and behavioral development
examples: The study found maternal education had the largest peak association (~0.4 SD) with cognitive scores, suggesting family resource interventions during this window may be especially consequential.

article_title: When do socioeconomic resources matter most in early childhood?
citation: Mollborn, S., Lawrence, E., James-Hawkins, L., & Fomby, P. (2014). When Do Socioeconomic Resources Matter Most in Early Childhood? Advances in Life Course Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.alcr.2014.03.001
title: Three competing hypotheses about change in the SES–development relationship across early childhood: constant, decreasing, and increasing.
description: The article articulates three hypotheses drawn from prior literature about how the SES–child development relationship changes across early childhood: (1) a constant relationship, (2) a decreasing relationship (stronger in infancy, per cumulative advantage/path-dependency and fetal-origins logic), and (3) an increasing relationship (stronger at school entry, per school-transition theory). The authors state: "we articulated three competing hypotheses about change in the relationship between SES and cognitive and behavioral development across early childhood."
requirements: Testing requires longitudinal within-child data spanning infancy through kindergarten entry.
constraints: The findings did not neatly support any single hypothesis; the curvilinear peak pattern required a modified version of Hypothesis 3.
target_learners: Children from infancy through kindergarten entry
target_learning_goals: Understanding when socioeconomic resources most influence developmental trajectories
examples: Figure 1 of the article illustrates the three hypothesized forms of the SES–outcome relationship across early childhood.

article_title: The Words Children Hear
citation: Montag Jessica L., Jones Michael N., Smith Linda B. (2015). The words children hear: Picture books and the statistics for language learning. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797615594361

The article states: "Our corpus consists of the text of 100 children’s picture books (68,103 words) that a caregiver might read to infants and very young language learners." Titles were selected from librarian-recommended lists, amazon.com bestsellers, and circulation statistics from the Infant and Preschool sections of a public library, targeting books for children 0 to 60 months. The full book list is printed in Table 1.

article_title: The Words Children Hear
citation: Montag Jessica L., Jones Michael N., Smith Linda B. (2015). The words children hear: Picture books and the statistics for language learning. Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797615594361
title: Lexical and contextual diversity of input as a driver of early language learnability
description: The article's organizing explanatory account: early language learning depends on child-directed input, and learnability is enhanced by diversity of words and contexts. The article states that "learnability is enhanced when individual words or devices are encountered in diverse contexts and when there is more variety in general in the input data," citing computational analyses of aggregated child-directed corpora and individual-differences studies linking type-token ratios to vocabulary development. Picture-book text is presented as a previously unstudied source of such diversity.
requirements: Analyses of the statistical properties of large corpora of child-directed language aggregated over many conversations.
constraints: Type-token ratios depend on sample size and cannot be easily interpreted from a single sample or measure, per the article's sampling-procedure section.
target_learners: infants and very young language learners (0 to 60 months)
target_learning_goals: vocabulary acquisition from the statistical properties of linguistic input
examples: The study operationalized diversity as number of unique word types across multiple token sample sizes drawn randomly from the two corpora.

In this study it served as the kindergarten outcome measuring fluent processing of symbolic and nonsymbolic magnitudes.

constraints: Does not capture the full breadth of symbolic number-system knowledge, only fluent processing and manipulation of quantities associated with Arabic numerals

elementary students at risk of mathematical learning disability
target_learning_goals: fluent processing and manipulation of symbolic and nonsymbolic numerical magnitudes

title: Interventions to improve cardinal knowledge in at-risk preschool children will better prepare them for formal schooling
description: Because preschoolers' cardinal knowledge predicted kindergarten number sets fluency independent of other quantitative skills, domain-general abilities, preliteracy, and parental education, the authors conclude that building this knowledge early is a high-leverage target. They state the results "indicate that interventions to improve this knowledge in at risk preschool children will better prepare them for formal schooling." The study itself was correlational, so intervention studies are needed to confirm the causal benefit.
requirements: Interventions should target understanding of the cardinal value of number words and of collections of items before school entry
constraints: The supporting evidence is correlational; the authors state intervention or experimental studies are needed to fully evaluate the conclusions
The sample was relatively small, especially for regression analyses dividing children into five knower levels, and the approach was exploratory
target_learners: at-risk preschool children in Title I programs
target_learning_goals: understanding the cardinal value of number words and collections of items
preparation for formal school mathematics
examples: The longitudinal study assessed give-a-number and point-to-x at the beginning and end of preschool in 112 Title I preschoolers and linked these measures to kindergarten number sets fluency

article_title: Specific Retrieval Deficit from Long-Term Memory in Children with Poor Arithmetic Facts Abilities
citation: Mussolin, C. and Noël, M-P. (2008). Specific Retrieval Deficit from Long-Term Memory in Children with Poor Arithmetic Facts Abilities. The Open Psychology Journal. https://doi.org/10.2174/1874350100801010026
title: Specific numerical retrieval deficit hypothesis: arithmetic fact retrieval difficulties in MD reflect a deficit specific to the numerical semantic system
description: The article proposes that children with mathematical disorders have a deficit specific to the retrieval of arithmetic facts from long-term memory, rather than a general speed-of-processing, semantic memory, or verbal routine deficit. The authors state that "the difficulties in the retrieval of numbers and arithmetic facts encountered by children with MD could not be attributed to a general deficit in speed of access or to a deficit with verbal material in general, but seem to be specific to the semantic system of numbers." This account aligns with Butterworth's defective number module hypothesis and Dehaene's number sense deficit hypothesis.
requirements: Requires contrasting performance across multiple retrieval tasks tapping different cognitive domains to isolate the numerical specificity of the deficit.
constraints: The article notes it remains open whether PoorAF children used retrieval strategies rather than counting, and whether the deficit reflects access or storage.
target_learners: children with mathematical disorders
children with poor arithmetic fact abilities
target_learning_goals: retrieval of basic arithmetic facts from long-term memory
examples: The study compared 18 PoorAF children to 18 matched controls across six computerized selection tasks, finding slowing only in the multiplication task.

article_title: Math Anxiety in Students With and Without Math Learning Difficulties
citation: Yılmaz Mutlu. (2019). Math Anxiety in Students With and Without Math Learning Difficulties. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 11(5), 471-475. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2019553343
title: Reciprocal relationship model among math anxiety, poor math performance, and working memory
description: The article presents a model (Figure 1) depicting reciprocal relationships among math anxiety, poor math performance, and lack of working memory. It is generally accepted that "the math anxiety affects negatively the mathematical performance by distorting sources of working memory," and learning difficulties in mathematics relate to deficiencies in the central executive of working memory. The model draws on studies the article reviews.
requirements: The model presumes tasks whose performance depends on working memory resources
constraints: The article states it is not clear to what extent math anxiety affects mathematical difficulties and how much the experience of difficulties causes anxiety
target_learners: elementary school students, especially third graders
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement and reduction of math anxiety
examples: Figure 1 in the article depicts the reciprocal relationships among math anxiety, poor math performance, and lack of working memory

article_title: Cognitive and behavioural predictors of adolescents' communicative perspective‐taking and social relationships
citation: Nilsen, E. S., & Bacso, S. A. (2017). Cognitive and Behavioural Predictors of Adolescents’ Communicative Perspective-taking and Social Relationships. Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2017.01.004
title: Communicative perspective-taking relies on domain-general executive function support
description: The article supports a model in which successful use of a conversational partner's perspective requires executive function resources in addition to mentalizing skills. Working memory allows an interlocutor to hold a partner's perspective in mind, while inhibitory control may allow suppression of one's own perspective. The authors state their results "supports the notion that reading the intentions of others relies on domain-general attentional and cognitive resources" and align with a model positing that "individuals also require the support of executive functions in order to make use of this information during conversational exchanges."
requirements: Individuals must possess mentalizing skills as well as executive function resources for perspective use in conversation
constraints: Weakness in executive functioning results in difficulty using a conversational partner's perspective
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: interpreting speakers' communicative intentions
successful peer communication
examples: Adolescents with elevated ADHD traits were less successful at detecting communicative intentions using facial expression, tone, and visual perspective cues

article_title: Visual processing speed
citation: Owsley Cynthia. (2012). Visual Processing Speed. Vision Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visres.2012.11.014
title: Useful field of view (UFOV) construct
description: The useful field of view is the spatial area over which useful information can be acquired rapidly within a single fixation, without eye or head movements. The review states Ball and Roenker "defined the useful field of view as the spatial area over which useful information can be acquired rapidly without the use of eye or head movements (within one fixation)". Its size is not fixed but depends on stimulus configuration and task demands, including foveal load, distractor presence and similarity, and age. It underpins both the clinical UFOV assessment and the speed-of-processing training program.
requirements: Assessment requires brief stimulus displays challenging the observer's processing abilities, with central and peripheral tasks under divided-attention and distractor conditions
constraints: The review notes the construct's size "depends on the situation (stimulus configuration and task demands)", so it is not a fixed sensory field measure
target_learners: older adults
target_learning_goals: visual processing speed under divided attention and visual clutter
examples: The original test used three subtests with high-contrast targets, display durations of 16.67 to 250 ms, and peripheral targets at 10°, 20°, or 30° eccentricity along 8 radial directions
key_sources: Owsley Cynthia. (2012). Visual Processing Speed. Vision Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visres.2012.11.014

article_title: Visual processing speed
citation: Owsley Cynthia. (2012). Visual Processing Speed. Vision Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visres.2012.11.014
title: Processing-inefficiency and attentional-disengagement account of UFOV task difficulties
description: This mechanistic account holds that older adults' UFOV task problems arise not from a shrinking attentional field but from inefficient visual search and difficulty disengaging attention, which slow the processing time needed to complete a task. The review states the fundamental problem "is more likely due to inefficiencies in visual search and problems with attentional disengagement, which in turn slow the visual processing time needed to complete the task at hand". This supports the evolution of the UFOV metric from field size to a duration-threshold measure of processing speed. It contrasts with the earlier field-constriction view and with speed-accuracy trade-off explanations.
requirements: Explanation rests on duration-threshold paradigms where response time is not the dependent measure
constraints: The review notes speed-accuracy trade-off differences may still contribute in laboratory paradigms where reaction time is the dependent measure
target_learners: older adults
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms of age-related slowing in visual processing
examples: Cosman and colleagues found older adults with slowed processing in UFOV subtests 2–4 tended to also have problems attentionally disengaging from a cued location
key_sources: Owsley Cynthia. (2012). Visual Processing Speed. Vision Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visres.2012.11.014

article_title: Visual processing speed
citation: Owsley Cynthia. (2012). Visual Processing Speed. Vision Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visres.2012.11.014
title: UFOV test software (Visual Awareness Research Group)
description: A commercially available personal-computer software version of the useful field of view test, usable with a touch-screen or mouse, with four subtests measuring minimum stimulus duration thresholds for correct central task performance. The review states "The UFOV® test is also briefer than the original version, and can be completed in ≤ 15 minutes", with thresholds ranging from 16.67 to 500 ms. It agrees well with the original test version (0.658 to 0.746) and shows test-retest reliability estimated between .735 and .884 depending on response modality.
requirements: A personal computer with a touch-screen or mouse for administration
constraints: Peripheral targets are presented at ~10° eccentricity only, not at the further eccentricities of the original test
target_learners: older adults
target_learning_goals: assessment of visual processing speed, divided attention, and selective attention
examples: The original version took up to 30 minutes to administer; the software version's fourth subtest makes central target discrimination more difficult

article_title: Longitudinal stability of pre‐reading skill profiles of kindergarten children: implications for early screening and theories of reading
citation: Ozernov-Palchik, O., Norton, E. S., Sideridis, G., Beach, S. D., Wolf, M., Gabrieli, J. D. E., & Gaab, N. (2017). Longitudinal stability of pre-reading skill profiles of kindergarten children: Implications for early screening and theories of reading. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12471
title: Multi-deficit data-driven conceptualization of dyslexia risk profiles
description: The article advances a multi-deficit, person-centered framework in which dyslexia risk is characterized by homogeneous profiles of performance on multiple pre-reading constructs rather than a single core deficit or pre-set cutoffs. The authors note that "a multi-deficit conceptualization of dyslexia is becoming increasingly accepted", and operationalize it via latent profile analysis, which is "a person-centered approach that groups individuals by the probability of their response patterns". The framework yields distinct PA, RAN, and double-deficit risk profiles with different longitudinal reading outcomes.
requirements: Requires a battery of pre-reading measures (PA, RAN, letter knowledge, verbal short-term memory) administered before or at the start of reading instruction
Requires large samples for stable latent profile model estimation
constraints: The authors note the theoretical interpretation could be affected by measure selection; other measures could have yielded profiles aligned with other theories of dyslexia
target_learners: kindergarten and pre-kindergarten children
target_learning_goals: early identification of dyslexia risk
differentiated early literacy intervention
examples: The study fit 1–7 profile models to 1,215 children and selected a 6-class solution, then validated the classes longitudinally against 1st-grade reading measures

title: Screen for dyslexia risk before reading failure using multi-measure profiles rather than one-size-fits-all intervention
description: The article recommends early identification of dyslexia risk using data-driven profiles of pre-reading measures, because risk classification is stable from kindergarten to 1st grade. It argues that "one-size-fits-all interventions will likely be less effective in accommodating the specific deficits and strengths of the various risk profiles", so screening should differentiate PA, RAN, and double-deficit risk to enable targeted remediation before reading failure occurs.
requirements: A kindergarten screening battery covering phonological awareness, RAN, letter knowledge, and verbal short-term memory
Longitudinal follow-up capacity to confirm risk status
constraints: The authors caution that kindergarten screening historically produced false positives of 20% to 60% and false negatives of 10% to 50% in prior studies using cutoff methods
target_learners: kindergarten and pre-kindergarten children at risk for dyslexia
target_learning_goals: early literacy
prevention of reading failure
examples: The study administered a 30–45 minute assessment battery individually and tracked a subset (n=95) to end of 1st grade, finding profile membership predicted reading outcomes

article_title: A burden for the boys: Evidence of stereotype threat in boys' reading performance
citation: Pascal Pansu, Isabelle Régner, Sylvain Max, Pascale Colé, John B. Nezlek, Pascal Huguet. (2016). A burden for the boys: Evidence of stereotype threat in boys' reading performance. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 65, pp.26-30. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2016.02.008
title: Stereotype threat account of the gender gap favoring girls in reading
description: The article extends stereotype threat theory to reading, assuming that boys are negatively stereotyped in this domain. It proposes that situational threat — a test framed as diagnostic of reading ability — depresses boys' performance and thereby contributes to the well-known gender gap favoring girls in reading. The experiment supports the account conditionally: the predicted reversal appeared only among highly-identified students, and the authors present the findings as offering another explanation for the gap.
requirements: A domain in which one gender group is negatively stereotyped (here, boys in reading)
A performance situation that can be framed as diagnostic of ability versus low-stakes
constraints: The pattern was obtained only among highly-identified students
Evidence comes from one experiment with eighty third-grade students

target_learning_goals: reading performance on standardized-style tests

article_title: The Structure of Speed of Processing Across Cultures
citation: Papadopoulos, T. C., Georgiou, G. K., Deng, C., & Das, J. P. (2018). The Structure of Speed of Processing Across Cultures. Advances in Cognitive Psychology, 14(3), 112–125. https://doi.org/10.5709/acp-0243-7
title: PASS theory of intelligence: planning, attention, simultaneous, and successive processing as three cognitive systems
description: The PASS theory of intelligence proposes that cognition is organized in three systems: the planning system (executive functions for regulating and programming behavior, located in the frontal cortex), the attention-arousal system (focused, selective, sustained, effortful activity, located in the posterior parietal cortex), and a processing system including simultaneous coding (arranging information into a holistic pattern) and successive coding (coding information in discrete, serial order), located in posterior occipital, parietal, and temporal cortex. The study operationalized these processes with response-time measures adapted from the D-N CAS.
requirements: Operationalization requires tests consistent with the process of interest, such as the D-N CAS subtests used in this study
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: cognitive processing and assessment of intelligence
examples: The study used Matching Numbers and Planned Connections for planning, Expressive Attention and Number Detection for attention, Matrices and Verbal-Spatial Relations for simultaneous, and Word Series and Sentence Questions for successive processing.

article_title: The interplay between math anxiety and working memory on math performance: a longitudinal study
citation: Pellizzoni, S., Cargnelutti, E., Cuder, A., & Passolunghi, M.C. (2021). The interplay between math anxiety and working memory on math performance: a longitudinal study. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1111/nyas.14722
title: Interventions for math difficulties should combine math training with support for managing anxiety
description: The article recommends that support for children with math difficulties address emotional and cognitive factors together. It states that "rehabilitation programs that focus only on improving math skills and their cognitive precursors might be ineffective if children do not learn how to handle their negative emotional states at the same time." Intervention should therefore pair math-specific training with activities that help children contain and cope with anxiety.
requirements: Assessment of children's anxiety (ideally including teacher ratings) alongside math skills to identify who needs emotional support
constraints: Based on a longitudinal correlational path analysis of 146 Italian third graders; intervention effectiveness was not directly tested in this study
target_learners: primary school children (grades 3–4) with math difficulties
target_learning_goals: math achievement
emotional regulation of math anxiety
examples: The study found anxiety impaired math attainment from an early age via WM, with MA's role emerging later, motivating combined early intervention

title: Teachers' ratings are a useful measure of young children's general anxiety when self-report is unreliable
description: The article argues that measuring general anxiety in young children via self-assessment is problematic and that teacher assessments are a better indicator. It notes "Teachers’ ratings can, therefore, be taken as a useful measure of children's anxiety," and in this study only teacher-rated GA related to math performance and WM, while children's self-ratings did not. Teachers' essential role in assessing the emotional complexities of learning is underscored.

constraints: The DAYS_T teacher-rated anxiety subscale showed modest reliability (0.66) in this sample; the authors call for replication with more reliable tools

examples: In the study, teacher-rated GA (DAYS_T) predicted math performance while children's self-rated GA (RCMAS) did not

article_title: Episodic memory contributions to autobiographical memory and open-ended problem-solving specificity in younger and older adults
citation: Peters, S. L., Fan, C. L., & Sheldon, S. (2019). Episodic memory contributions to autobiographical memory and open-ended problem-solving specificity in younger and older adults. Memory & Cognition, 47, 1592–1605. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-019-00953-1
title: Constructive episodic simulation hypothesis: episodic memory processes support both remembering and imagining hypothetical solutions
description: The constructive episodic simulation hypothesis holds that "episodic memory processes – that are affected by aging – are required to construct both past and hypothetical future events by accessing and associating together autobiographical details into a coherent mental representation" (Schacter & Addis). The article uses this framework to interpret age-related declines in both detail elaboration and event generation across memory and problem-solving tasks.
requirements: Episodic memory processes must be intact for constructing detailed representations of past and hypothetical events
constraints: The article notes executive processes also contribute, particularly to generation, and the study did not include executive function measures

target_learning_goals: autobiographical memory retrieval
open-ended problem solving

citation: Peters, S. L., Fan, C. L., & Sheldon, S. (2019). Episodic memory contributions to autobiographical memory and open-ended problem-solving specificity in younger and older adults. Memory & Cognition, 47, 1592–1605. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-019-00953-1
title: Self Memory System: autobiographical knowledge stored hierarchically with spreading activation across levels
description: The Self Memory System (Conway, 2005; Conway & Pleydell-Pearce, 2000) proposes that "autobiographical knowledge is stored in a hierarchy," with information accessible as lifetime periods, general events, and specific event memories. Retrieving information at any level results in "spreading activation to related elements," such that accessing one specific memory activates other related specific memories or details within that memory.
requirements: Episodic memory processes are needed to access specific event information at any level of the hierarchy
constraints: The article notes debate about whether fluency deficits reflect purely episodic decline or also executive decline

accessing specific autobiographical events

The authors state that "the development of interventions targeting the impact of children's ADHD on their peer relationships and academic attainment may have the added benefit of reducing depression risk". Existing psychosocial interventions targeting social and academic skills may have potential but "this needs to be formally tested".

peer relationship skills
academic attainment

description: The article draws on theories suggesting that a child's sense of competency or failure in peer and academic domains is important in conferring later depression risk. The authors note that "young people who struggle in their school and social lives are more likely to experience feelings of failure and rejection, which leave them more vulnerable to depression and emotional problems". citation: Price, Jodi; Hertzog, Christopher; Dunlosky, John. (2010). Self-Regulated Learning in Younger and Older Adults: Does Aging Affect Metacognitive Control? Neuropsychology, development, and cognition. Section B, Aging, neuropsychology and cognition. https://doi.org/10.1080/13825580903287941
title: Agenda-based regulation (ABR) account of older adults' self-regulated study
description: The agenda-based regulation model holds that item selection should be interpreted with respect to the task goals and agendas learners set, rather than item difficulty alone. The article uses it to explain why older adults avoided difficult items even when those items carried high point values: "older adults may also select and allocate study time based more on an agenda (e.g., avoid more difficult items regardless of their point value or experimenter-determined goals) than on item difficulty". It complements the region of proximal learning model, which both age groups' easy-to-difficult selection order otherwise supported.
requirements: Learners must set or be given task goals and agendas that can be compared against item difficulty and value when interpreting selection behavior
constraints: The article presents ABR as an interpretive account of these two experiments' findings, citing Ariel et al. (in press) for the model's original demonstration with younger adults
target_learners: younger and older adult learners studying paired-associate vocabulary
target_learning_goals: metacognitive control of item selection and study time allocation during self-regulated learning
examples: In Experiment 2, older adults' selections tended to favor easier items regardless of point value even when difficult items were worth the most points

article_title: From scribbles to scrabble: preschool children’s developing knowledge of written language
citation: Puranik, Cynthia S., Lonigan, Christopher J. (2011). From Scribbles to Scrabble: Preschool Children's Developing Knowledge of Written Language. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9220-8
title: Five-task emergent writing assessment protocol with feature-based scoring system
description: The study developed an assessment protocol of five writing tasks: Write Letters, Write Name, Write CVC Words, Picture Description, and Sentence Retell. A detailed scoring system quantified features such as linearity, segmentation, and left-to-right orientation, scored present or absent, with CVC spelling scored on a 7-point invented-spelling scale. The authors note "there is no gold standard for scoring emergent writing" and that no previous study had attempted to quantify features in children's writing. Internal consistencies were high (αs = .92-.96).
requirements: Trained scorers; the feature set scored should be tailored to the task, as the features providing highest cohesion varied with the task being scored
constraints: The spontaneous writing task initially included was dropped because most children could not attempt it; some 3-year-olds showed floor effects on complex tasks
target_learners: preschool children aged 3-5 years
target_learning_goals: emergent writing and written language knowledge
examples: The protocol was pilot-tested with 20 children; inter-rater reliability on ~30% of samples (n = 77) ranged from 93 to 100%
key_sources: Puranik, Cynthia S., Lonigan, Christopher J. (2011). From Scribbles to Scrabble: Preschool Children's Developing Knowledge of Written Language. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9220-8

article_title: From scribbles to scrabble: preschool children’s developing knowledge of written language
citation: Puranik, Cynthia S., Lonigan, Christopher J. (2011). From Scribbles to Scrabble: Preschool Children's Developing Knowledge of Written Language. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9220-8
title: Linearity Hypothesis of writing development: universal features precede language-specific features in a sequential continuum
description: The Linearity Hypothesis holds that writing development proceeds in sequential steps: children first master universal features of writing (linearity, segmentation, lack of iconicity) that reflect the symbolic representational nature of writing, and only then acquire language-specific features such as directionality and symbol shapes. The article contrasts it with the Unified Hypothesis, which predicts simultaneous, unordered acquisition. The study's Guttman scaling results provide "clear evidence for sequential acquisition of writing features," supporting the Linearity Hypothesis.
requirements: Assessment across multiple writing tasks, since single-task evidence (e.g., name writing only) can appear to support the Unified Hypothesis
constraints: The article notes children as young as 3 display language-specific knowledge earlier than Tolchinsky reported, and left-to-right orientation emerged in conjunction with universal features
target_learners: preschool children aged 3-5 years
target_learning_goals: understanding the developmental sequence of written language features
examples: Guttman coefficients of reproducibility of .94 (Write Name) and .98-.99 (composing tasks) supported a fixed feature order
key_sources: Puranik, Cynthia S., Lonigan, Christopher J. (2011). From Scribbles to Scrabble: Preschool Children's Developing Knowledge of Written Language. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9220-8

article_title: Emergent Writing in Preschoolers: Preliminary Evidence for a Theoretical Framework
citation: Puranik, C. S., & Lonigan, C. J. (2014). Emergent Writing in Preschoolers: Preliminary Evidence for a Theoretical Framework. Reading Research Quarterly, 49(4). https://doi.org/10.1002/rrq.79
title: Three-domain organizational framework of emergent writing: Conceptual, Procedural, and Generative Knowledge
description: The framework organizes preschool emergent writing skills into three distinct but correlated domains. Conceptual Knowledge covers understanding of the purposes, conventions, and functions of writing; Procedural Knowledge covers code-related mechanics such as alphabet knowledge, letter writing, name writing, and spelling; Generative Knowledge covers composing beyond the word level. The authors hypothesized that "three distinct but correlated dimensions would account for children’s emergent writing skills," deliberately excluding sociocultural factors because the focus was on the skills children demonstrate while writing. The framework parallels the transcription/text-generation distinction in models of older children's writing.
requirements: Assessment tasks designed to index each of the three domains, as in this study's battery of conceptual, procedural, and generative subtests
constraints: The framework did not include sociocultural factors; it concerns the skills young children demonstrate while writing, not the reasons or contexts for writing use
Cross-sectional data cannot address causal relations between the dimensions
target_learners: Preschool children aged 3 to 5 years
target_learning_goals: Emergent writing skills, including print concepts, letter and word transcription, and early composition
examples: CFA of 372 preschoolers' performance on writing tasks indexing the three domains supported the framework over one- and two-factor alternatives
key_sources: Puranik, C. S., & Lonigan, C. J. (2014). Emergent Writing in Preschoolers: Preliminary Evidence for a Theoretical Framework. Reading Research Quarterly, 49(4). https://doi.org/10.1002/rrq.79

article_title: Emergent Writing in Preschoolers: Preliminary Evidence for a Theoretical Framework
citation: Puranik, C. S., & Lonigan, C. J. (2014). Emergent Writing in Preschoolers: Preliminary Evidence for a Theoretical Framework. Reading Research Quarterly, 49(4). https://doi.org/10.1002/rrq.79
title: Emergent writing assessment battery of conceptual, procedural, and generative subtests for preschoolers
description: A battery of individually administered writing tasks designed to index the three hypothesized emergent writing domains. Conceptual knowledge was measured by Universal Principles of Print, Concepts about Writing, and Functions of Print subtests; procedural knowledge by Identify Letters, Write Letters, Write Name, and Write Words subtests; generative knowledge by Picture Description and Sentence Retell tasks scored for features such as "linearity, segmentation, presence of simple units, left-to-right orientation." Inter-rater reliability on a random 30 percent of responses ranged from 93% to 100%. The closed-ended generative tasks were chosen because pilot work showed preschoolers had difficulty with spontaneous writing.
requirements: Trained examiners administering tasks individually; scoring rubrics for name writing (9-point) and word spelling (7-point) based on prior research
constraints: Several younger children were unable to complete the generative knowledge tasks, resulting in floor effects; internal consistencies for the conceptual knowledge tasks were lower than desirable
target_learners: Preschool children aged 3 to 5 years
target_learning_goals: Assessment of early writing skills across print concepts, transcription mechanics, and early composition
examples: Children wrote six common words scored with a modified Tangel and Blachman spelling rubric crediting phonemes represented
key_sources: Puranik, C. S., & Lonigan, C. J. (2014). Emergent Writing in Preschoolers: Preliminary Evidence for a Theoretical Framework. Reading Research Quarterly, 49(4). https://doi.org/10.1002/rrq.79

article_title: Learning to write letters: Examination of student and letter factors
citation: Puranik Cynthia S., Petscher Yaacov, Lonigan Christopher J. (2014). Learning to Write Letters: Examination of Student and Letter Factors. Journal of experimental child psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2014.07.009
title: Introduce the same letters for teaching letter names and for letter writing
description: The article's instructional implication is that because letter-name knowledge contributed substantially to letter-writing skills, "it might be beneficial to introduce the same letters for teaching letter names and for letter writing." This follows from the finding that knowing a letter's name sharply raised the probability of writing it correctly for 4- and 5-year-olds. The authors caution that such decisions require experimental confirmation, including whether teaching writing is more effective when students already know the letter names.
requirements: Experimental studies should first test whether teaching letter writing when students know letter names produces better letter-writing skills than when they do not
constraints: The authors state this recommendation is provisional and can be made only after experimental questions are addressed
target_learners: preschool children aged 3 to 5
target_learning_goals: letter-writing skill
letter-name knowledge
examples: In the study, children who knew a letter's name had a probability of writing it correctly of .82 versus .50 for 5-year-olds who did not
key_sources: Puranik Cynthia S., Petscher Yaacov, Lonigan Christopher J. (2014). Learning to Write Letters: Examination of Student and Letter Factors. Journal of experimental child psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2014.07.009

article_title: Effects of Socioeconomic Status (SES) Information on Cognitive Ability Inferences: When Low-SES Students Make Use of a Self-Threatening Stereotype
citation: Isabelle Regner, Pascal Huguet, Jean-Marc Monteil. (2002). Effects of socioEconomic status (SES) information on cognitive ability inferences: When low-SES students make use of a self-threatening stereotype. Social Psychology of Education, 5(3), 253-269. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016313908667
title: The SES stereotype: the belief that low-SES individuals are intellectually inferior to their high-SES counterparts
description: The article defines the SES stereotype as "the belief that the low-SES individuals are intellectually inferior to their high-SES counterparts." It treats this stereotype as a shared social belief that can be activated by social class information or by memory performance information, shaping inferences in either direction between SES and cognitive ability. The two studies use this construct to interpret why low-SES students generate stereotype-consistent inferences about targets.
requirements: Social class or memory performance information about targets must be available to trigger stereotype-based inferences
constraints: The reported evidence concerns students' inferences about targets, not their own intellectual performance
target_learners: students of low and high socioeconomic status
low versus high academic achievers
target_learning_goals: understanding how socioeconomic stereotypes shape inferences about intellectual ability
examples: Study 1 gave participants social class information about targets and asked for memory-ability inferences; Study 2 gave memory performance information and asked for inferences about possessions and cultural activities as SES indicators.
key_sources: Isabelle Regner, Pascal Huguet, Jean-Marc Monteil. (2002). Effects of socioEconomic status (SES) information on cognitive ability inferences: When low-SES students make use of a self-threatening stereotype. Social Psychology of Education, 5(3), 253-269. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016313908667

article_title: Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students’ Math Achievement
citation: Ramirez Gerardo, Hooper Sophia Yang, Kersting Nicole B., Ferguson Ronald, Yeager David. (2018). Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students' Math Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858418756052
title: Anxiety-to-practice-to-perceived-mindset account of how teacher math anxiety shapes student math achievement
description: The article proposes that math anxious teachers, through their "teaching comments, behaviors, and teaching practices," create classroom environments that devalue sense-making and effort in favor of memorization and innate ability. Students decode these cues and infer the teacher's beliefs, so that "students who perceive more ability-oriented (as opposed to process-oriented) teaching practices may infer how their potential is regarded by the teacher and the environment." This account bridges teacher math anxiety, organizational incremental theory, and teacher expectancy research, positioning student-perceived teacher mindset as the key mediating construct rather than teachers' knowledge.
requirements: Teachers' classroom actions and practices must be observable by students, who infer beliefs from witnessed behaviors
constraints: The article states the supporting evidence is correlational, which prevents inferring causality
target_learners: ninth-grade adolescent students in mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement (course grades)
students' beliefs about mathematical ability
examples: The study measured student-perceived teacher fixed mindset with three items and process-oriented practices with Tripod 7Cs Challenge items, then tested the mediation chain in a SEM framework.
key_sources: Ramirez Gerardo, Hooper Sophia Yang, Kersting Nicole B., Ferguson Ronald, Yeager David. (2018). Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students' Math Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858418756052

article_title: Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students’ Math Achievement
citation: Ramirez Gerardo, Hooper Sophia Yang, Kersting Nicole B., Ferguson Ronald, Yeager David. (2018). Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students' Math Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858418756052
title: Teachers should hold the conviction that math can be learned by everyone and use instructional strategies emphasizing learning over memorization and ability
description: To combat negative expectancy ("Golem") effects, the article recommends that "teachers must have the conviction that math material can be learned by everyone and use instructional strategies that emphasize learning rather than memorization and abilities." Practices communicating high expectations and personal assurance in students' ability may position students to respond more adaptively to struggle experiences in mathematics. This follows from the finding that reduced process-oriented practices, not lacking knowledge, carried the anxiety effect.
requirements: Teachers must communicate high expectations for math and personal assurance in students' ability to meet those expectations
constraints: The article states its evidence is correlational, so the recommendation rests on mediation models rather than causal manipulation
target_learners: adolescent mathematics students, particularly ninth graders
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
adaptive responses to academic struggle
examples: The study's process-oriented practice items included statements such as "My math teacher wants us to use our thinking skills, not just memorize things" and "My math teacher doesn't let people give up when the work gets hard."
key_sources: Ramirez Gerardo, Hooper Sophia Yang, Kersting Nicole B., Ferguson Ronald, Yeager David. (2018). Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students' Math Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858418756052

article_title: Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students’ Math Achievement
citation: Ramirez Gerardo, Hooper Sophia Yang, Kersting Nicole B., Ferguson Ronald, Yeager David. (2018). Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students' Math Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858418756052
title: Classroom Video Analysis (CVA) assessment of teachers' usable mathematical teaching knowledge
description: The CVA is a video-based instrument that "elicits usable teaching knowledge by asking teachers to analyze teaching episodes shown in video clips of authentic mathematics instruction." Teachers' written responses are scored by trained raters and machine learning techniques according to four rubrics: analysis of the mathematics, analysis of student thinking, suggestions for improvement, and overall depth of interpretation, each scored 0–2. The study used a short three-clip version on variables, expressions, and equations, with internal consistency α = .82 for rater-assigned rubric scores.
requirements: Trained raters or machine-scoring procedures to code written responses against the four rubrics
constraints: The study used only three video clips selected for psychometric functioning, a short version of the full scale
target_learners: mathematics teachers (the assessed population)
target_learning_goals: measuring teachers' usable knowledge for teaching mathematics
examples: Teachers wrote analyses of three clips (two on patterns, one on modeling); responses recounting the episode without analysis scored 0, while in-depth coherent analyses scored 2.
key_sources: Ramirez Gerardo, Hooper Sophia Yang, Kersting Nicole B., Ferguson Ronald, Yeager David. (2018). Teacher Math Anxiety Relates to Adolescent Students' Math Achievement. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/2332858418756052

article_title: Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults
citation: Rogge, A.-K., Röder, B., Zech, A., Nagel, V., Hollander, K., Braumann, K.-M. & Hötting, K. (2017). Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults. Scientific Reports 7:5661. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06071-9
title: Vestibular stimulation as a mediator of exercise effects on memory and spatial cognition
description: The article proposes that "an increased stimulation of the vestibular system during self-motion might be an essential mediator between physical exercise and cognitive functioning". Vestibular nuclei connect to the cerebellum, hippocampus and parietal cortices supporting spatial functions and memory; the authors speculate that balance training induces hippocampal and parietal changes via direct vestibular pathways. This account explains why cognitive gains occurred without cardiorespiratory fitness improvement.
requirements: Training must impose high demands on the vestibular system, e.g. reactive postural adjustments on varying surfaces
constraints: The vestibular mechanism is explicitly speculative: the authors write it "might be speculated" and that whether sub-processes or multisensory integration is essential "must be addressed in future studies"
target_learners: healthy adults aged 19–65
target_learning_goals: memory
spatial cognition
examples: The balance circuit training used eight stations with tasks like single-leg stance while pulled by an elastic strap, designed to force permanent re-stabilization
key_sources: Rogge, A.-K., Röder, B., Zech, A., Nagel, V., Hollander, K., Braumann, K.-M. & Hötting, K. (2017). Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults. Scientific Reports 7:5661. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06071-9

article_title: Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults
citation: Rogge, A.-K., Röder, B., Zech, A., Nagel, V., Hollander, K., Braumann, K.-M. & Hötting, K. (2017). Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults. Scientific Reports 7:5661. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06071-9
title: Physical exercise programs can improve cognition without increasing cardiorespiratory fitness
description: The article concludes that "an increase in cardiorespiratory fitness does not seem to be necessary to induce beneficial effects of physical exercise on cognition". Twelve weeks of balance training improved memory and spatial cognition while VO2peak remained unchanged in both groups, implying multiple mechanisms mediate exercise effects on cognition. This supports prescribing non-aerobic exercise forms for cognitive benefits.
requirements: Exercise form must plausibly engage other physiological systems (here the vestibular system) since fitness gains are not the mediating route
constraints: Demonstrated for balance versus relaxation training in healthy adults; executive functions were unaffected, so benefits may be restricted to memory and spatial functioning
target_learners: healthy adults
individuals unable to participate in aerobic training due to health restrictions
target_learning_goals: memory improvement
spatial cognition
examples: The randomized trial compared 12 weeks of balance circuit training against relaxation training, with neither group changing VO2peak
key_sources: Rogge, A.-K., Röder, B., Zech, A., Nagel, V., Hollander, K., Braumann, K.-M. & Hötting, K. (2017). Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults. Scientific Reports 7:5661. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06071-9

article_title: Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults
citation: Rogge, A.-K., Röder, B., Zech, A., Nagel, V., Hollander, K., Braumann, K.-M. & Hötting, K. (2017). Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults. Scientific Reports 7:5661. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06071-9
title: Progressive, varied balance circuit training with reactive postural challenges
description: The intervention was a balance circuit training on varying surfaces with eight stations per session of 5 minutes each, designed to "induce reactive postural adjustments, forcing participants to permanently re-stabilize". Exercises were progressively adjustable by increasing strap tension, partner distance or removing vision, and were replaced with a new set after six weeks to keep training challenging. Sessions ran twice weekly for 12 weeks in groups of 10–12.
requirements: Progressive difficulty adjustment to participant skill level; new exercise sets after six weeks to maintain challenge
constraints: No explicit strategies were taught; effects were demonstrated against an active relaxation control, not a passive control
target_learners: healthy adults without extensive balance-training experience
target_learning_goals: balance performance
memory
spatial cognition
examples: One task was single-leg stance while being pulled sideways with a strong elastic strap; another was throwing a medicine ball on a wobble board in tandems
key_sources: Rogge, A.-K., Röder, B., Zech, A., Nagel, V., Hollander, K., Braumann, K.-M. & Hötting, K. (2017). Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults. Scientific Reports 7:5661. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06071-9

article_title: Brain hyper‐connectivity and operation‐specific deficits during arithmetic problem solving in children with developmental dyscalculia
citation: Rosenberg-Lee, M., Ashkenazi, S., Chen, T., Young, C. B., Geary, D. C., & Menon, V. (2014). Brain hyper-connectivity and operation-specific deficits during arithmetic problem solving in children with developmental dyscalculia. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12216
title: Hyper-connectivity account of developmental dyscalculia: inappropriate task modulation and hyper-connectivity, rather than under-engagement and under-connectivity, underlie arithmetic difficulties
description: This framework proposes that developmental dyscalculia arises not from under-activation of the intraparietal sulcus but from aberrant modulation of parietal circuits and excessive connectivity between the IPS and multiple brain systems. The article states that "inappropriate task modulation and hyper-connectivity, rather than under-engagement and under-connectivity, are the neural mechanisms underlying problem solving difficulties in children with DD". It reframes DD as a fundamental difference in parietal organization rather than developmentally delayed maturation, grounded in the study's activation and gPPI findings across addition and subtraction.
requirements: Requires well-characterized DD and TD groups matched on IQ, reading ability and working memory to distinguish DD-specific effects from general ability differences
constraints: Based on cross-sectional neuroimaging of 7–9-year-old children performing timed arithmetic verification tasks; the authors note performance differences between groups partly influence connectivity findings
target_learners: Children with developmental dyscalculia aged 7–9 years
target_learning_goals: Single-digit addition and subtraction arithmetic problem solving
examples: gPPI analysis revealed IPS hyper-connectivity with fronto-parietal and default mode networks in DD children during both operations, contrary to the predicted immature under-connectivity pattern
key_sources: Rosenberg-Lee, M., Ashkenazi, S., Chen, T., Young, C. B., Geary, D. C., & Menon, V. (2014). Brain hyper-connectivity and operation-specific deficits during arithmetic problem solving in children with developmental dyscalculia. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12216

article_title: Adolescents and adults need inhibitory control to compare fractions
citation: Rossi, S., Vidal, J., Letang, M., Houdé, O., & Borst, G. (2019). Adolescents and Adults Need Inhibitory Control to Compare Fractions. Journal of Numerical Cognition, 5(3), 314-336. https://doi.org/10.5964/jnc.v5i3.197
title: The negative priming paradigm adapted to misleading strategies as a tool for revealing inhibitory control in school learning
description: The negative priming paradigm, originally designed by Tipper (1985), rests on the logic that "if a distractor (or a strategy) is inhibited on a given item (i.e., the prime), then its activation on the following item (i.e., the probe) should be disrupted". The authors adapted this paradigm so that the misleading strategy required on the prime becomes appropriate on the probe, allowing them to test whether inhibiting the 'greater the whole number, the greater the fraction' strategy is needed to compare fractions with common numerators. The paradigm has been applied across school-learning domains including literacy, mathematics and science to reveal the inhibition of overlearned misleading heuristics.
requirements: Participants must succeed above chance level on the control and test primes for priming effects on the probes to be observed
constraints: The paradigm reveals that a misleading heuristic must be inhibited but provides no information on the strategy that is activated once the misleading heuristic has been inhibited
target_learners: adolescents (Grade 9)
educated adults (undergraduates)
target_learning_goals: fraction magnitude comparison
overcoming the natural number bias
examples: In the test trials, participants compared common-numerator fractions on the prime (requiring inhibition of the misleading strategy) and then common-denominator fractions on the probe, where the strategy was appropriate.
key_sources: Rossi, S., Vidal, J., Letang, M., Houdé, O., & Borst, G. (2019). Adolescents and Adults Need Inhibitory Control to Compare Fractions. Journal of Numerical Cognition, 5(3), 314-336. https://doi.org/10.5964/jnc.v5i3.197

article_title: Instability versus quality: Residential mobility, neighborhood poverty, and children’s self-regulation.
citation: Roy, A. L., McCoy, D. C., & Raver, C. C. (2014). Instability Versus Quality: Residential Mobility, Neighborhood Poverty, and Children's Self-Regulation. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0036984
title: Experiential canalization framework: cumulative exposure to harsh, unpredictable environments disrupts stress physiology and executive function, with children's self-regulation trajectories environmentally modifiable in ways reflecting both insult and repair
description: The article draws on the theoretical framework of experiential canalization to explain how residential mobility and neighborhood poverty may affect children's cognitive and behavioral outcomes. Under this framework, "Cumulative exposure to harsh, unpredictable environments (especially where stressors are outside the individual's control) leads to disruptions in parasympathetic function" (e.g., altered diurnal cortisol patterns), which in turn affect prefrontal synaptic activity and executive function. The authors use this framework to interpret their findings as evidence that children's self-regulation trajectories are environmentally modifiable, reflecting both insult (moves to worse neighborhoods) and repair (moves to better neighborhoods).
requirements: The framework presupposes that stressors are outside the individual's control for the physiological disruption pathway to operate as described.
constraints: The article presents this as a theoretical framework supported by prior studies it cites, not as a mechanism directly tested in the present study.
target_learners: low-income children from preschool through fifth grade
target_learning_goals: executive function and self-regulatory skills underlying behavioral adjustment and early learning
examples: The authors interpret moves to worse neighborhoods as illustrating insult and moves to better neighborhoods as offering points of protection and even remedy, citing Blair & Raver (2012).
key_sources: Roy, A. L., McCoy, D. C., & Raver, C. C. (2014). Instability Versus Quality: Residential Mobility, Neighborhood Poverty, and Children's Self-Regulation. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0036984

article_title: Numbers in the Blind's “Eye”
citation: Salillas E, Grana´ A, El-Yagoubi R, Semenza C (2009) Numbers in the Blind's ''Eye''. PLoS ONE 4(7): e6357. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0006357
title: Mental number line account of the SNARC effect (amodal spatial-numerical representation)
description: The article frames its study with the mental number line account of the SNARC effect: an internal representation of magnitude in which "numbers are represented along a left-to-right oriented mental number line", whose automatic activation produces faster responses to small numbers with the left hand and large numbers with the right. The study uses this framework to test whether number semantics are modality-neutral, arguing that a spatial organization of number representation in people deprived of visual world experience indicates a modality-neutral, hardwired core number representation, and extends the account to attention shifts in auditory space.
requirements: Numerical input culture with left-to-right written numbers, per the article's framing of the SNARC effect
constraints: The article treats the representation's left-to-right orientation as shared by blind and sighted groups but attributes differences in its manipulation (working-memory dependence) to the modality of numerical input
target_learners: adult blind and sighted participants
target_learning_goals: numerical magnitude representation and number-space associations
examples: Auditory number cues (1, 2, 8, 9) followed by lateralized dichotic targets in seven blind and seven sighted adults produced congruent-trial detection advantages in both groups
key_sources: Salillas E, Grana´ A, El-Yagoubi R, Semenza C (2009) Numbers in the Blind's ''Eye''. PLoS ONE 4(7): e6357. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0006357

article_title: Effects of regulating emotions on cognitive performance: What is costly for young adults is not so costly for older adults.
citation: Scheibe, S., & Blanchard-Fields, F. (2009). Effects of Regulating Emotions on Cognitive Performance: What Is Costly for Young Adults Is not so Costly for Older Adults. Psychology and Aging, 24(1), 217-223. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0013807
title: Socioemotional selectivity account of age-related reduction in the cognitive costs of emotion regulation
description: The article frames its findings with socioemotional selectivity theory, in which older adults' awareness that lifetime is shrinking motivates a focus on emotionally meaningful goals. It proposes that "emotion regulation goals are assumed to be chronically activated in older adults, whereas they should be activated in young adults only when the context demands it," and that long-term practice renders regulation less effortful. The study's age-difference findings are interpreted as support for the idea that regulation may become less costly with age.
requirements: Applies to negative-emotion regulation in adulthood where regulation goals can be assumed chronically activated in older adults
constraints: The article notes it remains open whether findings apply to all cognitive task types or all negative emotions; induced sadness has disrupted older adults more in prior strategy-formation tasks
target_learners: young adults
older adults
target_learning_goals: understanding age differences in the cognitive costs of emotion regulation
examples: The experiment induced disgust with a film clip and compared N-Back performance under down-regulation, maintenance, no-instruction, and neutral conditions in young and older adults
key_sources: Scheibe, S., & Blanchard-Fields, F. (2009). Effects of Regulating Emotions on Cognitive Performance: What Is Costly for Young Adults Is not so Costly for Older Adults. Psychology and Aging, 24(1), 217-223. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0013807

article_title: A Longitudinal Examination of Racial Identity and Racial Discrimination Among African American Adolescents
citation: Seaton Eleanor K., Yip Tiffany, Sellers Robert M. (2009). A Longitudinal Examination of Racial Identity and Racial Discrimination Among African American Adolescents. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2009.01268.x
title: Multidimensional Model of Racial Identity (MMRI): centrality and regard dimensions applied to adolescent discrimination research
description: The MMRI articulates individual differences in the meaning and significance African Americans ascribe to racial identity. The article states it "is comprised of four related dimensions, but only two are examined in the present study: centrality and regard". Racial centrality is the significance individuals place on race; regard divides into private regard (personal feelings about being African American) and public regard (beliefs about how broader society views African Americans). The study uses these dimensions to disaggregate which identity aspects respond to discrimination.
requirements: Measurement of the specific dimensions requires the Multidimensional Inventory of Black Identity adapted for youth (MIBI-T)
constraints: Only centrality and regard were examined; the other two MMRI dimensions were not tested in this study
target_learners: African American adolescents aged 14–18
target_learning_goals: Understanding how racial identity dimensions relate to experiences of racial discrimination over adolescence
examples: The study measured centrality, private regard and public regard with three items each from the MIBI-T across three annual waves
key_sources: Seaton Eleanor K., Yip Tiffany, Sellers Robert M. (2009). A Longitudinal Examination of Racial Identity and Racial Discrimination Among African American Adolescents. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2009.01268.x

article_title: A Longitudinal Examination of Racial Identity and Racial Discrimination Among African American Adolescents
citation: Seaton Eleanor K., Yip Tiffany, Sellers Robert M. (2009). A Longitudinal Examination of Racial Identity and Racial Discrimination Among African American Adolescents. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2009.01268.x
title: PVEST: racial discrimination as a chronic stressor around which emergent identities are formed through coping
description: The Phenomenological Variant of Ecological Systems Theory incorporates ecological systems with identity development for minority youth. The article states PVEST "argues that racial discrimination is a risk factor, which increases the net vulnerability for youth of color", and that "emergent identities arise out of coping with stressors like racial discrimination". The authors report their public regard findings support a PVEST tenet that it should not be assumed African American youth form negative identities in the context of racial discrimination.
requirements: Identity development is considered central and foundational, providing the foundation for future productive or adverse behavior
constraints: The framework was tested here only for identity content dimensions (centrality, regard), not identity development processes such as exploration
target_learners: Minority youth, specifically African American adolescents
target_learning_goals: Understanding identity development as coping with racial discrimination as a chronic stressor

citation: Seaton Eleanor K., Yip Tiffany, Sellers Robert M. (2009). A Longitudinal Examination of Racial Identity and Racial Discrimination Among African American Adolescents. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2009.01268.x
title: Daily Life Experiences (DLE) scale for adolescent perceived racial discrimination frequency
description: The DLE is a self-report subscale of the Racism and Life Experiences Scale assessing "daily hassles or the frequency of 'microaggressions' because of race in the past year". Participants rated 18 discriminatory experiences (e.g., "Having your ideas ignored", "Not being taken seriously") on a 0–5 frequency scale. In this sample internal consistency was high at all waves (T1 α = .93; T2 α = .92; T3 α = .92), and the mean across items was computed at each time point.

constraints: The authors note daily diary research has found discrimination to be a low frequency event, so measurement warrants further attention

article_title: Ecological contexts associated with early childhood curiosity: Neighborhood safety, home and parenting quality, and socioeconomic status
citation: Shah PE, Hirsh-Pasek K, Spinelli M, Ozor J, Weeks HM, McCaffery H and Kaciroti N (2023). Ecological contexts associated with early childhood curiosity: Neighborhood safety, home and parenting quality, and socioeconomic status. Front. Psychol. 14:986221. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.986221
title: Ecological (Bronfenbrenner) multi-level framework for contexts fostering early childhood curiosity
description: The article organizes its inquiry with Bronfenbrenner's ecological theory, which "identified the multilevel contexts and social experiences which influence early child development." Proximal (microsystem) contexts include parenting quality and the home environment; distal (mesosystem) contexts include neighborhood safety; macro contexts include poverty and SES. The authors theorize that contexts promoting early learning also promote curiosity, and test each level's association with kindergarten curiosity plus moderation by SES.
requirements: Measures of contexts at each ecological level (parenting observation, HOME inventory, parent-reported neighborhood safety, SES composite) and a curiosity outcome measured in the same cohort
constraints: Applied here to curiosity derived from parent-reported PKBS-2 items at kindergarten in the ECLS-B cohort; the article notes parent-report bias and shared method variance

article_title: Acute stress impairs cognitive flexibility in men, not women
citation: Shields Grant S., Trainor Brian C., Lam Jovian C. W., Yonelinas Andrew P. (2016). Acute Stress Impairs Cognitive Flexibility in Men, Not Women. Stress. https://doi.org/10.1080/10253890.2016.1192603
title: Consider sex as a moderating factor when studying or designing for stress effects on cognition
description: The article argues that stress research and application should not presume males and females respond alike: "stress should not be presumed to influence males and females similarly". Its randomized experiment found stress impaired cognitive flexibility in men but not women, supporting routine analysis of sex as a moderator. The authors also suggest women "may be more suited to high-stress environments requiring cognitive flexibility than men", offered as a tentative implication.
requirements: Studies or design decisions about stress and cognition must record and analyze participant sex rather than assuming uniform stress effects.
constraints: The evidence base is a single acute-stress experiment with undergraduate participants; the article states it is unknown whether chronic stress or nonstudent populations would show the same sex-specific pattern.
target_learners: adult learners in high-stress performance settings
target_learning_goals: maintaining cognitive flexibility under acute stress
examples: 113 healthy adults were randomly assigned to the TSST-G stress induction or a reading/counting control task, then completed the Berg Card Sorting Test.
