article_title: The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A Critical Review
citation: Reid Smith, Pamela Snow, Tanya Serry & Lorraine Hammond (2021) The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A Critical Review, Reading Psychology, 42:3, 214-240, https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2021.1888348
title: Construction-Integration model of reading comprehension (textbase and situation model)
description: The review adopts the Construction-Integration model (Kintsch, 1998; Kintsch & Van Dijk, 1978), in which reading comprises interactions between the literal, propositional representation of a text (the textbase) and a schema formed from background knowledge. The textbase is held in working memory and integrated with preexisting schemata in long-term memory to form a situation model, a dynamically constructed representation that is cumulative and changes through growth, reorganization and error correction. The review uses this framework to interpret differential effects of knowledge on skilled vs. low-skilled readers.
requirements: Working memory must not be too heavily burdened for integration to occur
constraints: Low-skilled readers typically construct less detailed situation models due to less coherent textbase and/or less well-formed schemata
target_learners: primary school children ages 6-12
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of extended texts
key_sources: Reid Smith, Pamela Snow, Tanya Serry & Lorraine Hammond (2021) The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A Critical Review, Reading Psychology, 42:3, 214-240, https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2021.1888348

article_title: The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A Critical Review
citation: Reid Smith, Pamela Snow, Tanya Serry & Lorraine Hammond (2021) The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A Critical Review, Reading Psychology, 42:3, 214-240, https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2021.1888348
title: Explicitly teach background knowledge in a specific, sequenced way as foundational to reading comprehension instruction
description: The review recommends that explicitly teaching background knowledge should be considered foundational to increasing competency in reading, rather than an incidental aspect of instruction. Children would benefit from exposure to background knowledge in a specific, explicit and sequenced way — a knowledge-rich curriculum — in addition to teaching comprehension strategies such as summarizing. This contrasts with the prevalent approach of making generic reading comprehension strategies the prime focus of reading instruction.
requirements: Requires sustained, systematic and sequential building of background knowledge over time
constraints: Runs counter to the prevailing view that knowledge building is less relevant than building so-called soft-skills such as critical thinking and collaboration
target_learners: primary school children ages 6-12
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of extended texts
examples: The review cites the Model of Reading Engagement (MORE) and Content-Area Literacy Instruction (CALI) as models that systematically build a knowledge base over a longer period of time and showed positive and significant effects on proximal reading measures.
key_sources: Reid Smith, Pamela Snow, Tanya Serry & Lorraine Hammond (2021) The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A Critical Review, Reading Psychology, 42:3, 214-240, https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2021.1888348

article_title: The Effects of Age, Control Beliefs, and Feedback on Self-Regulation of Reading and Problem Solving
citation: Soederberg Miller, L. M., & West, R. L. (2010). The Effects of Age, Control Beliefs, and Feedback on Self-Regulation of Reading and Problem Solving. Experimental Aging Research, 36(1), 40-63. https://doi.org/10.1080/03610730903418380
title: Self-Regulation of Language Processing (SRLP) model: readers regulate attention based on goals and perceptions of goal progress via internal and external feedback loops
description: The Self-Regulation of Language Processing model holds that as individuals strive to comprehend a text, they regulate their attention based on their goals and perceptions of how well they believe they are meeting those goals. Readers compare actual comprehension to desired comprehension and use this information, through internal feedback loops and external sources of performance information, to adjust attention. The article states that "individuals compare their actual comprehension levels to their desired comprehension levels and use this information to adjust their attention to meet these goals." This study tested the model's prediction that external feedback influences self-regulatory responses during reading.
requirements: Feedback information, whether intrinsic or extrinsic, must be interpretable by the reader as indicating progress toward or away from reading goals
constraints: The article notes that in later life, allocation policy depends on many factors including fluid abilities, knowledge, and beliefs; this study focused only on the role of control beliefs
target_learners: adult learners
younger adults
older adults
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
problem solving from text
self-regulated attention allocation
examples: Participants read whodunit mysteries segment-by-segment while reading times were recorded, and received false performance feedback after every other trial to test how external information modifies attention allocation
key_sources: Soederberg Miller, L. M., & West, R. L. (2010). The Effects of Age, Control Beliefs, and Feedback on Self-Regulation of Reading and Problem Solving. Experimental Aging Research, 36(1), 40-63. https://doi.org/10.1080/03610730903418380

article_title: The Effects of Age, Control Beliefs, and Feedback on Self-Regulation of Reading and Problem Solving
citation: Soederberg Miller, L. M., & West, R. L. (2010). The Effects of Age, Control Beliefs, and Feedback on Self-Regulation of Reading and Problem Solving. Experimental Aging Research, 36(1), 40-63. https://doi.org/10.1080/03610730903418380
title: Use both subjective and objective measures, including online assessments, to capture the complexity of self-regulation
description: The article's differential findings across outcome measures show that age, control beliefs, and feedback type had different effects on task-specific beliefs, attention, and problem solving accuracy. The authors recommend that "a wide range of measures is needed to fully capture the complexity of self-regulation." They suggest combining subjective measures (beliefs and perceptions) with objective measures (strategy use, time spent, attention), and pairing online real-time assessments with offline measures. This principle guides researchers and designers to avoid relying on a single self-report or performance indicator when evaluating self-regulatory processes.
requirements: Studies of self-regulation should include measures sensitive to different components (beliefs, attention, performance) to detect differential patterns
constraints: The article notes that noncentral memory questions had unacceptable internal consistency (alpha = .05) and were excluded, illustrating measurement challenges in multi-measure designs
target_learners: adult learners
researchers of self-regulation
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
reading comprehension
problem solving
examples: In this study, self-efficacy and expectations showed additive feedback effects while attention showed a three-way interaction with age and control beliefs, demonstrating that different measures reveal different self-regulatory responses

article_title: The increasing role of metacognitive skills in math: a cross-sectional study from a developmental perspective
citation: Van der Stel, M., Veenman, M. V. J., Deelen, K., & Haenen, J. (2010). The increasing role of metacognitive skills in math: a cross-sectional study from a developmental perspective. ZDM Mathematics Education, 42, 219–229. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-009-0224-2
title: Three models of the relation between intellectual ability and metacognitive skillfulness as predictors of learning performance
description: The article describes three mutually exclusive models, attributed to Veenman and colleagues, concerning how intellectual ability and metacognitive skillfulness relate as predictors of learning performance. The intelligence model "regards metacognitive skillfulness as an integral part of intellectual ability", so metacognition has no predictive value independent of intelligence; the independency model treats the two as entirely independent predictors; and the mixed model holds that the two are correlated to a certain extent while metacognition keeps its own unique contribution on top of intellectual ability. The study's results support the mixed model for metacognitive quality.
requirements: Assessment of both intellectual ability and metacognitive skillfulness together with learning performance in the same participants
constraints: The article notes many prior studies are hard to compare due to differences in assessment method (thinking-aloud vs. questionnaires), participants, tasks and domains
target_learners: secondary school students aged 13–15
target_learning_goals: mathematical word-problem solving
key_sources: Van der Stel, M., Veenman, M. V. J., Deelen, K., & Haenen, J. (2010). The increasing role of metacognitive skills in math: a cross-sectional study from a developmental perspective. ZDM Mathematics Education, 42, 219–229. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-009-0224-2

article_title: The increasing role of metacognitive skills in math: a cross-sectional study from a developmental perspective
citation: Van der Stel, M., Veenman, M. V. J., Deelen, K., & Haenen, J. (2010). The increasing role of metacognitive skills in math: a cross-sectional study from a developmental perspective. ZDM Mathematics Education, 42, 219–229. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-009-0224-2
title: Thinking-aloud protocol scoring system for math metacognitive skillfulness (four subscales, quantity and quality)
description: An observational coding system in which thinking-aloud protocols are analyzed for spontaneous metacognitive activities during math problem solving. "Metacognitive skillfulness was divided into four subscales: orientation (O), planning and systematical orderliness (P), evaluation (Ev), and elaboration (El)", with math-specific and general example activities for each (e.g., goal setting, making a sketch, checking an answer by recalculating). Scoring is two-step: utterances are coded per subscale for frequency, and each subscale receives a qualitative score on a five-point scale (0–4), with judges avoiding confounding scores with correctness of content. Interrater reliability was 0.95 and 0.98 for qualitative scores.
requirements: Thinking-aloud protocols collected during task performance; trained judges with criteria per subscale
constraints: Judges intentionally avoided confounding metacognition scores with the correctness or incorrectness of the content matter
target_learners: secondary school students aged 13–15
target_learning_goals: metacognitive regulation of math problem solving
examples: Two judges independently rated six protocols of both years to establish interrater reliability

article_title: Cultural variation in young children’s social motivation for peer collaboration and its relation to the ontogeny of Theory of Mind
citation: Stengelin R, Hepach R, Haun DBM (2020) Cultural variation in young children's social motivation for peer collaboration and its relation to the ontogeny of Theory of Mind. PLoS ONE 15(11): e0242071. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0242071
title: Social Motivation Theory of Autism as an ontogenetic framework linking social motivation to social-cognitive development
description: The article applies the Social Motivation Theory of Autism as a framework in which "children's tendency to seek and like social interactions (i.e., their social motivation) functions as an ontogenetic foundation for social-cognitive development." Children who are motivated to engage with others more frequently spend more time in interactions where they learn to understand and predict others' behaviors. Collaborative endeavors are seen as particularly important because social interdependence urges individuals to track the beliefs, thoughts, and actions of their partners. The study tested predictions from this framework across diverse populations.
requirements: The framework presupposes that social motivation drives engagement in social interactions, which in turn provides learning opportunities for social-cognitive skills
constraints: The current study design does not allow definite conclusions about the causality of the link between social motivation and Theory of Mind
target_learners: children aged 3 to 8 years
target_learning_goals: social-cognitive development
Theory of Mind

citation: Stengelin R, Hepach R, Haun DBM (2020) Cultural variation in young children's social motivation for peer collaboration and its relation to the ontogeny of Theory of Mind. PLoS ONE 15(11): e0242071. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0242071
title: Conceptualize social motivation and cognition within both a cross-cultural and a developmental perspective
description: The authors argue that "the developmental trajectories observed in the current study highlight the necessity to conceptualize social motivation and cognition within both a cross-cultural and a developmental perspective." Even developmental continuities, such as German children's stable preference for collaboration, may result from a dynamic process involving developmental shifts interacting with culturally-specific variables. Researchers should therefore not generalize findings from urban Western populations to other societies without testing them cross-culturally.
requirements: Studies of children's social motivation should include participants from diverse populations and cover a developmental age range
constraints: The vast majority of studies in this area have been conducted in urban Western populations, limiting generalizability
target_learners: children aged 3 to 8 years across diverse cultural populations
target_learning_goals: understanding social motivation for peer collaboration
social-cognitive development

article_title: Differences in the neural mechanisms of selective attention in children from different socioeconomic backgrounds: an event‐related brain potential study
citation: Stevens Courtney, Lauinger Brittni, Neville Helen. (2009). Differences in the neural mechanisms of selective attention in children from different socioeconomic backgrounds: An event-related brain potential study. Developmental Science, 12(4), 634-646. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00807.x
title: Foundational-skill hypothesis: atypical development of core neurocognitive systems (e.g., selective attention) has cascading consequences on later learning
description: The article proposes that academic underachievement among children from lower socioeconomic backgrounds "might be related most strongly to the development of certain foundational skills or neural systems," such that "atypical development of a foundational skill could have cascading consequences on later development and learning." The theory motivates identifying specific neurocognitive deficits early in development so that focused interventions can target these systems. The present ERP study instantiates this framework by tracing the SES-linked attention difference to a specific early mechanism, distractor suppression within 100 msec, and by arguing that difficulty filtering distracting sounds could render typical environments, including classrooms, poorly suited for learning.
requirements: Interventions informed by this framework depend on identifying specific neurocognitive deficits "early in development" so they can target the systems most in need
constraints: The article states the present study "was not designed to answer causal questions about the relationship between the neural mechanisms of selective attention and skill in other domains"; poor spatial resolution of ERPs prevents strong conclusions about which neural networks are involved
target_learners: children aged 3–8 years from diverse socioeconomic backgrounds
target_learning_goals: founding academic skills including selective attention, language, and reading
examples: The article links poor suppression to potential reading difficulty: readers must suppress prepotent responses to similar learned words (e.g., encountering cot without reading it as cat), and letter-focus training interventions are associated with improved decoding skill
key_sources: Stevens Courtney, Lauinger Brittni, Neville Helen. (2009). Differences in the neural mechanisms of selective attention in children from different socioeconomic backgrounds: An event-related brain potential study. Developmental Science, 12(4), 634-646. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00807.x

article_title: Differences in the neural mechanisms of selective attention in children from different socioeconomic backgrounds: an event‐related brain potential study
citation: Stevens Courtney, Lauinger Brittni, Neville Helen. (2009). Differences in the neural mechanisms of selective attention in children from different socioeconomic backgrounds: An event-related brain potential study. Developmental Science, 12(4), 634-646. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00807.x
title: Because neural mechanisms underlying similar behavioral performance can differ by group, assessments should examine underlying processing mechanisms rather than relying on behavior alone
description: The article argues that examining the neural systems underlying a cognitive ability can reveal distinct mechanisms behind similar behavioral performance: "examining the neural systems underlying a particular cognitive ability can identify different mechanisms that give rise to similar impairments in behavioral performance." In the study, children with SLI showed a signal-enhancement deficit while children of lower maternal education showed a distractor-suppression deficit, though both involve impaired selective attention behaviorally. The authors also cite the D'Angiulli et al. study, in which lower-SES adolescents used different attentional mechanisms to achieve similar behavioral performance. This supports designing assessments and interventions informed by the specific processing stage at which difficulty arises.
requirements: Access to process-sensitive measures such as ERPs, which the article notes index attention online "without requiring overt behavioral responses"
constraints: ERP spatial resolution is poor, limiting inferences about specific neural networks; findings here concern early auditory selective attention specifically
target_learners: young children with attention or language difficulties, including children from lower socioeconomic backgrounds and children with specific language impairment
target_learning_goals: accurate identification of which attentional mechanism (signal enhancement vs. distractor suppression) underlies a learner's difficulty
examples: The article contrasts the distractor-suppression deficit it documents in children of lower maternal education with the signal-enhancement deficit previously reported in children with SLI using the same paradigm

Differences in the neural mechanisms of selective attention in children from different socioeconomic backgrounds: An event-related brain potential study. article_title: Age-Related Changes in Sentence Production Abilities and Their Relation to Working-Memory Capacity: Evidence from a Verb-Final Language
citation: Sung JE (2015) Age-Related Changes in Sentence Production Abilities and Their Relation to Working-Memory Capacity: Evidence from a Verb-Final Language. PLoS ONE 10(4): e0119424. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0119424
title: Task-demand manipulation framework for assessing sentence production: task type (memory demand) crossed with word-order canonicity (linguistic computational load)
description: The article proposes manipulating task demands along two axes to capture age-related change in sentence production: memory demands, via a memory-demanding syntactic-priming task versus a relatively memory-free sentence-completion task, and linguistic computational load, via canonical versus noncanonical word order in Korean. The tasks use "a very limited vocabulary used to construct a sentence" to minimize semantic-lexical top-down processing and isolate syntactic performance. The framework predicts that the condition combining the greatest demands best captures aging effects, which the regression results supported.
requirements: Speakers must successfully hold the prime sentence in memory until producing the target sentence for priming effects to occur
constraints: Developed and validated for Korean, a verb-final language with case markers and relatively free word order; canonicity effects may differ in languages with rigid word order
target_learners: healthy adults across the lifespan (ages 21–86)
elderly adults at risk for cognitive decline
target_learning_goals: assessing syntactic sentence-production ability
detecting age-related decline in linguistic and cognitive capacity
examples: Examiners primed full passives such as "the Yellow is pushed by the Blue" and asked participants to describe a target picture using a passive with limited color vocabulary
key_sources: Sung JE (2015) Age-Related Changes in Sentence Production Abilities and Their Relation to Working-Memory Capacity: Evidence from a Verb-Final Language. PLoS ONE 10(4): e0119424. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0119424

article_title: Age-Related Changes in Sentence Production Abilities and Their Relation to Working-Memory Capacity: Evidence from a Verb-Final Language
citation: Sung JE (2015) Age-Related Changes in Sentence Production Abilities and Their Relation to Working-Memory Capacity: Evidence from a Verb-Final Language. PLoS ONE 10(4): e0119424. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0119424
title: Constrained sentence-production tasks with limited color vocabulary (syntactic-priming and sentence-completion tasks)
description: Two novel controlled production instruments for eliciting Korean passive sentences. The syntactic-priming task presents a two-part picture; the examiner describes the prime and the participant produces a target sentence after hearing a primed passive. The sentence-completion task provides the nouns and verb on the picture, with the examiner initiating the first noun phrase. Both use humanized color symbols ("the Red," "the Blue," and "the Yellow") as arguments to control lexical-semantic influence, with 40 stimuli total (20 per task, 10 per canonicity condition).
requirements: Responses are coded correct only when participants construct a passive with correct grammatical markers and verb inflection; using an active voice counts as an error
constraints: Designed to focus only on syntactic features by minimizing semantic-lexical top-down processing, so they do not sample spontaneous or semantically rich production
target_learners: adult Korean speakers, including elderly adults
target_learning_goals: measuring passive-sentence production accuracy
isolating syntactic planning from lexical-semantic processing
examples: Each task was administered as a block with canonical and noncanonical sentences randomly presented, and task order counterbalanced across participants

title: Vignette-based booklet measure of children's acceptance of hypothetical peers with ADHD and depression
description: A data-collection instrument in which participants completed a booklet of questions in response to two vignettes describing the behaviour of hypothetical target peers, one with depression and one with ADHD. It was administered to 595 participants drawn from five age groups spanning early childhood to late adolescence, sampled from schools randomly selected in the east of Ireland. The article describes it as "a booklet of questions in response to two vignettes describing the behaviour of hypothetical target peers with depression and ADHD."
requirements: Requires vignettes describing target peer behaviour and age-appropriate question booklets for each age group.
constraints: Measures responses to hypothetical peers rather than actual classmates.

article_title: Cognitive components of a mathematical processing network in 9‐year‐old children
citation: Szűcs Dénes, Devine Amy, Soltesz Fruzsina, Nobes Alison, Gabriel Florence. (2014). Cognitive components of a mathematical processing network in 9-year-old children. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12144
title: Executive memory function centric model of mathematical processing
description: The article proposes a preliminary network model in which working memory function, relying on executive functions (attentional shifting, updating, inhibition), is core to mathematical processing. Visuo-spatial STM/WM is more directly related to mathematics while verbal STM/WM supports both reading and math; phonological processing and verbal IQ rely on verbal STM/WM capacity. The network "serves mathematical symbol processing and symbol manipulation", with symbols initially grounded in magnitudes and count words, a grounding the study suggests has limited relevance after initial acquisition.
requirements: Requires considering the complex predictor space of mathematics rather than single explanatory factors
constraints: Preliminary model based on 9-year-old children with at least normal reading skill
target_learners: 9-year-old primary school children
target_learning_goals: Mathematical (arithmetic) competence
examples: The best regression model (M3) operationalized the network with Dot Matrix, visual WM, Phonological Decoding, Spatial Orientation, Trail-making and WISC Vocabulary predictors

article_title: Examining the Relationships of Component Reading Skills to Reading Comprehension in Struggling Adult Readers
citation: Tighe, Elizabeth L.; Schatschneider, Christopher. (2016). Examining the Relationships of Component Reading Skills to Reading Comprehension in Struggling Adult Readers: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219414555415
title: Assess and instruct component reading skills, not just global reading measures, in adult literacy programs
description: The article argues that ABE programs should move beyond global reading measures when evaluating and instructing adult learners. It states that global assessments "do not assess component skills" and "provide very limited reading skill profiles of adult learners," and that the identified strong and moderate component skills "should be considered during instructional practices and targeted in intervention and assessment research."
requirements: Component skill measures must be available alongside the global assessments currently used for grade-level equivalency placement.
constraints: The evidence base is limited to 16 studies with high heterogeneity, so the authors advise cautious interpretation.
target_learners: struggling adult readers in Adult Basic Education programs
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
examples: The meta-analysis identified six strongly and three moderately related component skills as candidates for instruction and assessment in ABE settings.

article_title: Preschool interpersonal relationships predict kindergarten achievement: Mediated by gains in emotion knowledge
citation: Torres, M. M., Domitrovich, C. E., & Bierman, K. L. (2015). Preschool Interpersonal Relationships Predict Kindergarten Achievement: Mediated by Gains in Emotion Knowledge. Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appdev.2015.04.008
title: Emotion knowledge as the developmental mediator linking early relationships to academic learning
description: The article advances a developmental model in which warm relationships with teachers and peers create opportunities to learn about emotions through explicit labeling and implicit modeling, and resulting emotion knowledge supports academic learning by promoting self-regulation of attention and emotion. The authors describe a related "process of emotion utilization, in which increasing emotion knowledge enables children to more efficiently channel emotional arousal into constructive thought and action". The study's SEM results are consistent with this model, though the authors stress the analyses do not test causal mechanisms.
requirements: Longitudinal designs controlling for cognitive ability and baseline emotion knowledge and achievement to test the mediation robustly
constraints: The article states the analyses are correlational and causal interpretations are unwarranted; unmeasured variables such as language or executive function may explain the associations
target_learners: economically-disadvantaged preschool children attending Head Start
target_learning_goals: emotion knowledge (identifying and recognizing emotions)
school readiness in emergent literacy and numeracy
examples: The study measured student-teacher closeness and positive peer interactions in fall, emotion knowledge at fall and spring, and achievement through kindergarten, testing the mediation with SEM
key_sources: Torres, M. M., Domitrovich, C. E., & Bierman, K. L. (2015). Preschool Interpersonal Relationships Predict Kindergarten Achievement: Mediated by Gains in Emotion Knowledge. Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appdev.2015.04.008

article_title: Family ethnic socialization and ethnic identity: A family-driven, youth-driven, or reciprocal process?
citation: Umaña-Taylor Adriana J., Zeiders Katharine H., Updegraff Kimberly A. (2013). Family Ethnic Socialization and Ethnic Identity: A Family-Driven, Youth-Driven, or Reciprocal Process? Journal of Family Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031105
title: Family ethnic socialization and youth ethnic identity form a context-sensitive developmental process whose direction depends on family nativity status
description: This framework, grounded in ecological theory (Bronfenbrenner, 1989) and Spencer's PVEST, holds that the direction of effects between family ethnic socialization and youth ethnic identity is not fixed but depends on cultural context, specifically the immigrant status of the family. The article states that 'the association between family ethnic socialization and ethnic identity is context sensitive, with family nativity status being a critical factor that must be considered when determining the stages at which youth and parent forces are most pronounced in this process.' This challenges the implied directional bias in prior work that treated the process as exclusively family-driven.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measures of both family ethnic socialization and youth ethnic identity to test directional paths
constraints: Findings are specific to Mexican-origin youth transitioning from late adolescence to emerging adulthood and based on youths' perceptions of family ethnic socialization
target_learners: Mexican-origin and Latino adolescents and emerging adults
target_learning_goals: Understanding how family ethnic socialization and youth ethnic identity inform one another during development
examples: The study tested three competing models (family-driven, youth-driven, reciprocal) using multiple-group cross-lagged panel analyses across nativity groups
key_sources: Umaña-Taylor Adriana J., Zeiders Katharine H., Updegraff Kimberly A. (2013). Family Ethnic Socialization and Ethnic Identity: A Family-Driven, Youth-Driven, or Reciprocal Process? Journal of Family Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031105

article_title: Ethnic and Racial Identity During Adolescence and Into Young Adulthood: An Integrated Conceptualization
citation: Umaña-Taylor, A. J., Lee, R. M., Rivas-Drake, D., Syed, M., Seaton, E., Quintana, S. M., Cross, W. E. Jr., Schwartz, S. J., & Yip, T. (2014). Ethnic and Racial Identity During Adolescence and Into Young Adulthood: An Integrated Conceptualization. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12196
title: Ethnic-racial identity (ERI) as an integrated metaconstruct covering both ethnic background and racialized experiences
description: The Study Group proposes ERI as a single metaconstruct replacing the conventional split between racial identity and ethnic identity, arguing the distinction is largely nominal and the constructs overlap empirically. ERI is defined as "a multidimensional, psychological construct that reflects the beliefs and attitudes that individuals have about their ethnic–racial group memberships, as well as the processes by which these beliefs and attitudes develop over time." The term is proposed "to capture experiences that reflect both individuals’ ethnic background and their racialized experiences as a member of a particular group in the context of the United States." Components reflect content (beliefs, attitudes) and process (exploration, formation, maintenance), which are deeply intertwined.
requirements: Measures and studies must operationalize both content and process components of ERI rather than only self-categorization labels
constraints: Specificity to sociohistorical context is important; the authors note the proposal is grounded in the U.S. context, though similar processes may operate elsewhere
target_learners: ethnic and racial minority adolescents and young adults in the United States
target_learning_goals: understanding identity formation as a normative developmental process
understanding how beliefs and attitudes about one's ethnic-racial group develop over time
examples: The Study Group reviewed existing models (e.g., Phinney's ethnic identity model, Cross's nigrescence theory, Sellers et al.'s Multidimensional Model of Racial Identity) to build the integrated operationalization
key_sources: Umaña-Taylor, A. J., Lee, R. M., Rivas-Drake, D., Syed, M., Seaton, E., Quintana, S. M., Cross, W. E. Jr., Schwartz, S. J., & Yip, T. (2014). Ethnic and Racial Identity During Adolescence and Into Young Adulthood: An Integrated Conceptualization. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12196

article_title: Ethnic and Racial Identity During Adolescence and Into Young Adulthood: An Integrated Conceptualization
citation: Umaña-Taylor, A. J., Lee, R. M., Rivas-Drake, D., Syed, M., Seaton, E., Quintana, S. M., Cross, W. E. Jr., Schwartz, S. J., & Yip, T. (2014). Ethnic and Racial Identity During Adolescence and Into Young Adulthood: An Integrated Conceptualization. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12196
title: Developmental timeline of ERI components: identification in childhood, exploration and internalization in adolescence, integration in adulthood
description: The article organizes ERI development across periods: childhood involves ethnic–racial labeling, knowledge, and constancy; adolescence adds exploration, centrality, affirmation, public regard, and salience as cognitive and perspective-taking capacities mature; young adulthood adds intersection with other identity domains and narrative coherence. The authors state that "the components of ERI that are relevant at specific developmental periods can be organized with attention to whether they primarily reflect the content of one’s ERI or the process of developing an ERI," and that ERI "is an interaction between maturation and context, and thus takes different forms and has different meanings across the life span."
requirements: Research must attend to which ERI components are developmentally salient in a given period rather than applying uniform measures across ages
constraints: Some components have been empirically examined only in relation to either ethnic or racial identity, not both
target_learners: children
adolescents
young adults from ethnic-racial minority groups
target_learning_goals: understanding age-graded milestones in ethnic-racial identity formation
understanding how cognitive and social development enable identity exploration
examples: Table 1 organizes components by developmental period, distinguishing childhood ethnic–racial identification from adolescent ERI formation

Ethnic and Racial Identity During Adolescence and Into Young Adulthood: An Integrated Conceptualization. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12196

article_title: Beyond the phonological deficit: Semantics contributes indirectly to decoding efficiency in children with dyslexia
citation: van Rijthoven R, Kleemans T, Segers E, Verhoeven L. (2018). Beyond the phonological deficit: Semantics contributes indirectly to decoding efficiency in children with dyslexia. Dyslexia. https://doi.org/10.1002/dys.1597
title: Lexical restructuring account of semantics supporting decoding in dyslexia
description: The article explains its findings with the lexical restructuring hypothesis: as children's lexicons grow in size and semantic relations, pressure increases to make finer phonological distinctions, so lexical representations "start out holistic and become more specified during early and middle childhood". Strong semantic abilities thereby foster phonological awareness and lexical retrieval (rapid naming), which in turn support word and pseudoword decoding. The authors apply this to children with dyslexia, whose broad and deep semantic knowledge may compensate for weak phonological representations.
requirements: A developing lexicon with increasing numbers of words and semantic relations, providing pressure toward finer phonological distinctions
constraints: The authors state the effect of semantics was small and indirect, and that children with dyslexia showed no direct profit from semantic knowledge in learning to read
target_learners: children with dyslexia in early stages of reading development
target_learning_goals: word decoding efficiency
pseudoword decoding efficiency
examples: The study's mediation models operationalized semantics as four WISC-III NL subtests (information, similarities, productive vocabulary, comprehension) and found indirect paths via PA and RAN consistent with this account.
key_sources: van Rijthoven R, Kleemans T, Segers E, Verhoeven L. (2018). Beyond the phonological deficit: Semantics contributes indirectly to decoding efficiency in children with dyslexia. Dyslexia. https://doi.org/10.1002/dys.1597

article_title: The relation between language and arithmetic in bilinguals: insights from different stages of language acquisition
citation: Van Rinsveld A, Brunner M, Landerl K, Schiltz C and Ugen S (2015) The relation between language and arithmetic in bilinguals: insights from different stages of language acquisition. Front. Psychol. 6:265. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00265
title: Language-dependent exact arithmetic: verbal coding of arithmetic facts and verbal working memory in computation
description: The article frames exact arithmetic as relying on language at two levels: simple additions are retrieved as verbally coded arithmetic facts from memory, while complex additions require mental computations that rely on verbal working memory resources such as the phonological loop. The study tests this framework in bilinguals, where task language permeates instructions, presentation and answer production. As the authors state, "arithmetic facts are potentially represented or retrieved from memory in a verbal format and complex arithmetic solving processes rely at least partially on verbal working memory components."
requirements: Task language must permeate instructions, problem presentation and answer production to reveal language effects on arithmetic performance.
constraints: The framework was tested in German-French bilinguals who all acquired arithmetic in German within the Luxembourgish school system.
target_learners: Bilingual secondary-school students and young adults solving arithmetic problems in two languages
target_learning_goals: Exact arithmetic problem solving and arithmetic fact retrieval in a second language
examples: Participants solved 28 simple and 56 complex additions orally in separate German and French sessions, in visual and auditory presentation formats.
key_sources: Van Rinsveld A, Brunner M, Landerl K, Schiltz C and Ugen S (2015) The relation between language and arithmetic in bilinguals: insights from different stages of language acquisition. Front. Psychol. 6:265. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.00265

article_title: How preschool executive functioning predicts several aspects of math achievement in Grades 1 and 3: A longitudinal study
citation: Viterbori, P.; Usai, M. C.; Traverso, L.; De Franchis, V. (2015). How preschool executive functioning predicts several aspects of math achievement in Grades 1 and 3: A longitudinal study. https://hdl.handle.net/11567/813133
title: Early childhood mathematics education should include interventions targeting executive function
description: The article concludes that its longitudinal findings "empirically support interventions that target EF as an important component of early childhood mathematics education." Because preschool WM–flexibility predicted later math achievement, EF training is positioned as a worthwhile component of early math programs. The article presents this as an implication of its predictive results.
requirements: EF components such as working memory–flexibility should be measurable in preschool children
constraints: Support is predictive (longitudinal correlational), not a demonstration that EF training improves math achievement
target_learners: preschool children (age 5)
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement in primary school
examples: The study assessed six EF measures in 175 five-year-olds and tracked math achievement through Grades 1 and 3
key_sources: Viterbori, P.; Usai, M. C.; Traverso, L.; De Franchis, V. (2015). How preschool executive functioning predicts several aspects of math achievement in Grades 1 and 3: A longitudinal study. https://hdl.handle.net/11567/813133

article_title: How preschool executive functioning predicts several aspects of math achievement in Grades 1 and 3: A longitudinal study
citation: Viterbori, P.; Usai, M. C.; Traverso, L.; De Franchis, V. (2015). How preschool executive functioning predicts several aspects of math achievement in Grades 1 and 3: A longitudinal study. https://hdl.handle.net/11567/813133
title: Two-factor model of executive function in kindergarten: inhibition and WM–flexibility as separate dimensions
description: A latent-variable account of executive function in kindergarten children in which "inhibition and working memory (WM)–flexibility were separate dimensions." The model was derived from confirmatory factor analysis of six EF measures and served as the structural basis for predicting later math achievement. It treats EF in this age group as two distinguishable components rather than a unitary capacity.
requirements: Multiple EF measures assessed in preschool to index the latent components
constraints: Structure established for kindergarten-age children in this sample
target_learners: preschool/kindergarten children
target_learning_goals: understanding cognitive predictors of mathematics achievement
key_sources: Viterbori, P.; Usai, M. C.; Traverso, L.; De Franchis, V. (2015). How preschool executive functioning predicts several aspects of math achievement in Grades 1 and 3: A longitudinal study. https://hdl.handle.net/11567/813133

article_title: Motivation deficit in ADHD is associated with dysfunction of the dopamine reward pathway
citation: Volkow ND, Wang GJ, Newcorn JH, Kollins SH, Wigal TL, Telang F, Fowler JS, Goldstein RZ, Klein N, Logan J, Wong C, Swanson JM. (2011). Motivation Deficit in ADHD is Associated with Dysfunction of the Dopamine Reward Pathway. Molecular Psychiatry 16(11). https://doi.org/10.1038/mp.2010.97
title: Hypofunctional mesoaccumbens dopamine reward pathway as an account of motivation deficit in ADHD
description: The article proposes that ADHD involves not only attention deficit and hyperactivity/impulsivity but also motivation deficit reflecting "an hypofunctional DA reward pathway". The mesoaccumbens dopamine pathway projects from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens and is "critically involved in reward and motivation". Reduced D2/D3 receptor and DAT availability there, plus correlations between those PET measures and the Achievement scale only in ADHD participants, are offered as evidence that disrupted reward pathway function underlies lowered motivation and may contribute to inattention.
requirements: PET measures of D2/D3 receptor and DAT availability in midbrain and nucleus accumbens
a trait motivation measure such as the MPQ Achievement scale
constraints: The evidence is correlational; the article states correlations do not necessarily connote causality and directionality between inattention and motivation deficit remains untested
target_learners: adults with ADHD
children with ADHD (by the authors' extrapolation)
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement with tasks that are not inherently rewarding or reinforcing
examples: PET scans with [11C]raclopride and [11C]cocaine in 45 drug-naïve ADHD participants and 41 controls, correlated with MPQ Achievement scores
key_sources: Volkow ND, Wang GJ, Newcorn JH, Kollins SH, Wigal TL, Telang F, Fowler JS, Goldstein RZ, Klein N, Logan J, Wong C, Swanson JM. (2011). Motivation Deficit in ADHD is Associated with Dysfunction of the Dopamine Reward Pathway. Molecular Psychiatry 16(11). https://doi.org/10.1038/mp.2010.97

article_title: Distractibility during retrieval of long-term memory: domain-general interference, neural networks and increased susceptibility in normal aging
citation: Wais, P. E., and Gazzaley, A. (2014). Distractibility during retrieval of long-term memory: domain-general interference, neural networks and increased susceptibility in normal aging. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00280
title: Limited cognitive control resources account for susceptibility to distraction during demanding retrieval and categorization
description: The article proposes that distraction harms memory and categorization because limited cognitive control resources must both guide selection of relevant mnemonic or perceptual details and suppress irrelevant external input. The authors state these resources "have the capability to resolve interference from distractors during tasks of moderate effort" but are overwhelmed when episodic retrieval or prototype categorization adds further demands. The fMRI and rTMS findings locate the control source in left VLPFC connectivity with hippocampus and LOC.
requirements: Tasks must place demands on top-down selection of goal-relevant mnemonic or perceptual details for the resource limitation to matter
constraints: The article states the precise locus where bottom-up distraction interferes with LTM representations remains unclear
target_learners: younger and older adults performing episodic retrieval and categorization tasks
target_learning_goals: retrieval of detailed episodic memories
discrimination of goal-relevant perceptual features during categorization learning
examples: fMRI showed the hippocampus-VLPFC-LOC network's connectivity declined with visual distractors and no longer supported episodic retrieval
key_sources: Wais, P. E., and Gazzaley, A. (2014). Distractibility during retrieval of long-term memory: domain-general interference, neural networks and increased susceptibility in normal aging. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00280

article_title: Handwriting Fluency in Children
citation: Wicki, Werner; Hurschler Lichtsteiner, Sibylle; Saxer Geiger, Andrea; Müller, Marianne (2014). Handwriting fluency in children. Swiss Journal of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1024/1421-0185/a000127
title: Cognitive-resource-saving account of handwriting automaticity
description: The article frames its findings with theories holding that when handwriting becomes automatic, fewer cognitive resources are consumed by the mechanics of writing, freeing capacity for higher-level composition processes such as spelling and text generation. The authors state: "The results are discussed with respect to theories that assume that the automaticity of handwriting is associated with saving cognitive resources." The SEM finding that automaticity predicts orthographic skills independently of visual-motor integration is interpreted in this light.
requirements: Handwriting must reach a level of automaticity for resource savings to be available to other writing processes
constraints: Evidence in this article is cross-sectional and correlational, so the direction of the resource-saving mechanism is not tested
target_learners: children in primary/elementary school (fourth graders)
target_learning_goals: written composition, spelling and orthographic skills
examples: The study measured automaticity of handwriting, stroke pressure, and stroke frequency on a digitizing tablet during a copying task.
key_sources: Wicki, Werner; Hurschler Lichtsteiner, Sibylle; Saxer Geiger, Andrea; Müller, Marianne (2014). Handwriting fluency in children. Swiss Journal of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1024/1421-0185/a000127

article_title: Handwriting Fluency in Children
citation: Wicki, Werner; Hurschler Lichtsteiner, Sibylle; Saxer Geiger, Andrea; Müller, Marianne (2014). Handwriting fluency in children. Swiss Journal of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1024/1421-0185/a000127
title: Digitizing-tablet measures of handwriting automaticity (stroke pressure and stroke frequency)
description: This element is the measurement setup used in the study: a digitizing tablet recording stroke pressure and stroke frequency while children perform a copying task, used to index automaticity of handwriting. The abstract states that "automaticity of handwriting, stroke pressure, and stroke frequency were measured on a digitizing tablet, while visual-motor integration and orthographic skills were assessed by means of standardized tests." These process measures entered the SEM model as indicators of automaticity.
requirements: A digitizing tablet and a copying task are needed to capture stroke-level process measures
constraints: Assessed in a cross-sectional design with fourth-grade children copying text
target_learners: fourth-grade children (mean age 10 years, 7 months)
target_learning_goals: assessment of handwriting fluency and its component processes
examples: Handwriting speed and legibility were assessed by means of a copying task.
key_sources: Wicki, Werner; Hurschler Lichtsteiner, Sibylle; Saxer Geiger, Andrea; Müller, Marianne (2014). Handwriting fluency in children. Swiss Journal of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1024/1421-0185/a000127

article_title: Literacy, Cognitive Function, and Health: Results of the LitCog Study
citation: Wolf, M.S., Curtis, L.M., Wilson, E.A.H., et al. (2012). Literacy, Cognitive Function, and Health: Results of the LitCog Study. J GEN INTERN MED. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-012-2079-4
title: Interventions should respond to all cognitive demands patients face in managing health, beyond reading and numeracy
description: The article recommends that future health interventions look beyond reading and numeracy skills and address the full range of cognitive abilities patients rely on to manage their health. It states: "Future interventions should respond to all of the cognitive demands patients face in managing health, beyond reading and numeracy." This follows from the finding that cognitive abilities substantially account for the health literacy–task performance association.
requirements: Interventions must be designed around the fluid and crystallized cognitive demands of self-care tasks, not only literacy and numeracy content.
constraints: Evidence base is cross-sectional and limited to English-speaking older adults ages 55 to 74.
target_learners: older adults (ages 55 to 74) managing their own health
target_learning_goals: capacity to engage in self-care and achieve desirable health outcomes
examples: The LitCog study assessed performance on healthcare tasks including comprehending print information, recalling spoken and multimedia information, dosing and organizing medication, and healthcare problem-solving.
key_sources: Wolf, M.S., Curtis, L.M., Wilson, E.A.H., et al. (2012). Literacy, Cognitive Function, and Health: Results of the LitCog Study. J GEN INTERN MED. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-012-2079-4

article_title: Aging and cortical mechanisms of speech perception in noise
citation: Wong Patrick C. M., Jin James Xumin, Gunasekera Geshri M., Abel Rebekah, Lee Edward R., Dhar Sumitrajit. (2009). Aging and Cortical Mechanisms of Speech Perception in Noise. Neuropsychologia 47(3), 693-703. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2008.11.032
title: Decline-compensation hypothesis applied to the auditory domain
description: The decline-compensation hypothesis holds that cognitive aging involves "a combination of decline in sensory processing (and cortical activation) that is accompanied by an increase in the recruitment of more general cognitive areas (e.g., prefrontal cortex) as a means of compensation." In this study, the hypothesis was tested against the common cause hypothesis (general decline across sensory and cognitive regions) by examining spoken word perception in noise in younger and older adults with fMRI. The findings — reduced auditory cortex activation with increased prefrontal and precuneus activation that correlated positively with behavior — supported generalizing the hypothesis to the auditory domain.
requirements: Compensation is only claimed when increased activation in attention/working-memory areas is linked to behavioral performance, as the article states: "this hypothesis is only true if indeed increased activation in areas that are associated with attention and working memory is associated with performance."
constraints: The article tested adults with normal peripheral hearing and normal-range cognitive screening; generalization to hearing-impaired or cognitively impaired older adults is not established here.
target_learners: older adult listeners
target_learning_goals: spoken word identification in noisy environments
examples: In the fMRI experiment, older subjects showed reduced right superior temporal activation but increased prefrontal and precuneus activation, and frontal/parietal activation correlated positively with accuracy across all listening conditions.
key_sources: Wong Patrick C. M., Jin James Xumin, Gunasekera Geshri M., Abel Rebekah, Lee Edward R., Dhar Sumitrajit. (2009). Aging and Cortical Mechanisms of Speech Perception in Noise. Neuropsychologia 47(3), 693-703. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2008.11.032

article_title: Distinct influences of affective and cognitive factors on children’s non-verbal and verbal mathematical abilities
citation: Wu, S. S., Chen, L., Battista, C., Watts, A. K. S., Willcutt, E. G., & Menon, V. (2017). Distinct influences of affective and cognitive factors on children's non-verbal and verbal mathematical abilities. Cognition, 166, 118-129. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2017.05.016
title: Working-memory-centered mediation account of affective and cognitive influences on distinct math skill components
description: The article proposes that WM is the central hub through which affective (math anxiety) and attentional factors influence children's mathematics: math anxiety and attention problems reduce WM resources, which in turn support computation and problem solving. Its stated summary is that "WM is a domain-general ability pivotal to children's math performance on both non-verbal and verbal problems". The account distinguishes non-verbal NO, where effects are fully WM-mediated, from verbal MR, where math anxiety also acts directly and reading and attention contribute additional pathways.
requirements: Assessment of WM as a latent construct from multiple subtests (Counting Recall, Backward Digit Recall, Digit Recall, Block Recall), alongside math anxiety, attention, reading, and IQ measures
constraints: Cross-sectional data could not establish causal direction
Tested in a nonclinical sample of 2nd-3rd graders (mean age 8.34 years) with IQ above 80
target_learners: children in early elementary school (2nd-3rd grade)
target_learning_goals: non-verbal computational math skills
verbal math word-problem reasoning
examples: Structural equation modeling in 330 children selected the Full Mediation model for NO (44.1% variance) and a Partial Mediation model for MR (60.4% variance)
key_sources: Wu, S. S., Chen, L., Battista, C., Watts, A. K. S., Willcutt, E. G., & Menon, V. (2017). Distinct influences of affective and cognitive factors on children's non-verbal and verbal mathematical abilities. Cognition, 166, 118-129. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2017.05.016

article_title: Working memory and number line representations in single-digit addition: Approximate versus exact, nonsymbolic versus symbolic
citation: Xenidou-Dervou, I., van der Schoot, M., & van Lieshout, E. C. D. M. (2014). Working Memory and Number Line Representations in Single-digit Addition: Approximate versus Exact, Nonsymbolic versus Symbolic. VU University Amsterdam. https://www.vu.nl
title: The mental model for simple arithmetic
description: The mental model holds that "performance variations across different simple arithmetic problem formats occur because different presentation formats place different demands on one's WM". Before age six, children solve nonsymbolic problems more easily by representing quantities in a readily accessible mental model in the VSSP, while symbolic problems require phonological storage or transcoding via the CE. The study extended the model by adding domain-specific coding, i.e. nonsymbolic and symbolic mental number line representations, tested alongside WM components.
requirements: Predictor tasks must differ from the addition tasks only in storage, manipulation and representation, so mechanisms can be distinguished
constraints: The study tested kindergarteners at the end of the school year in the Netherlands; transcoding direction varied with format familiarity and the authors call the alternate-transcoding interpretation tentative
target_learners: kindergarten children (Mage = 5.98)
target_learning_goals: single-digit mental addition (approximate and exact, nonsymbolic and symbolic)
examples: Four computerized addition tasks differing only in stimulus and response type were administered with Corsi Blocks, digit span forwards/backwards and two computerized number line estimation tasks
key_sources: Xenidou-Dervou, I., van der Schoot, M., & van Lieshout, E. C. D. M. (2014). Working Memory and Number Line Representations in Single-digit Addition: Approximate versus Exact, Nonsymbolic versus Symbolic. VU University Amsterdam. https://doi.org/10.1080/17470218.2014.977303

article_title: Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency
citation: Zhou X, Wei W, Zhang Y, Cui J, and Chen C (2015) Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency. Front. Psychol. 6:1364. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01364
title: The visual perception hypothesis of the numerosity–arithmetic relation
description: The article proposes that a non-numerical factor—visual perception—accounts for the close relation between numerosity processing and mathematical performance because both tasks are typically based on rapid visual information processing. The authors state: "Here we propose that a non-numerical factor—visual perception—can account for the relation between numerosity processing and mathematical performance because both tasks are typically based on rapid visual information processing." This contrasts with the magnitude processing hypothesis and the inhibitory control hypothesis.
requirements: Both numerosity processing and arithmetic tasks must rely on rapid visual information processing for the hypothesis to explain their association
constraints: The hypothesis applies specifically to computational fluency rather than general mathematical achievement, and the speed of visual perception is critical
target_learners: third- to fifth-grade children
target_learning_goals: arithmetic computational fluency
key_sources: Zhou X, Wei W, Zhang Y, Cui J, and Chen C (2015) Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency. Front. Psychol. 6:1364. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01364

article_title: Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency
citation: Zhou X, Wei W, Zhang Y, Cui J, and Chen C (2015) Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency. Front. Psychol. 6:1364. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01364
title: Arithmetic intervention should consider targeting visual perceptual processing
description: Based on the finding that visual perceptual ability accounts for the numerosity–fluency relation, the authors recommend that interventions for mathematical learning difficulty consider visual perceptual processing as a target, rather than focusing solely on non-symbolic quantity processing. They state: "Our results suggest that arithmetic intervention should consider targeting visual perceptual processing." They draw a parallel to reading intervention where action video game play improved reading speed, most likely due to enhanced visual attention.
requirements: Interventions should be designed for children whose arithmetic difficulties may stem from visual perceptual processing rather than magnitude processing deficits
constraints: The recommendation is based on correlational and regression evidence, not on a tested intervention
target_learners: children with mathematical learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: arithmetic computational fluency
key_sources: Zhou X, Wei W, Zhang Y, Cui J, and Chen C (2015) Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency. Front. Psychol. 6:1364. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01364

article_title: Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency
citation: Zhou X, Wei W, Zhang Y, Cui J, and Chen C (2015) Visual perception can account for the close relation between numerosity processing and computational fluency. Front. Psychol. 6:1364. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.01364
title: Online Experimental Psychological System (OPES) computerized cognitive test battery
description: The study used a battery of eight computerized cognitive and mathematical tasks administered via Web-based applications in the Online Experimental Psychological System (OPES). The article states: "A total of eight tasks were used and they were computerized using Web-based applications in the 'Online Experimental Psychological System (OPES)' (www.dweipsy.com/lattice)." The battery included numerosity comparison, figure matching, forward verbal working memory, visual tracing, non-verbal matrix reasoning, mental rotation, choice reaction time, and arithmetic tests for computational fluency.
requirements: Tasks are administered in a computer classroom with experimenters monitoring children and a practice session with feedback before each formal test
constraints: Reliability statistics were not available for the mathematical achievement test and the forward digit span test
target_learners: third- to fifth-grade children
target_learning_goals: assessment of cognitive and mathematical abilities

article_title: Creative Thinking in Adolescents with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
citation: Abraham, Anna; Windmann, Sabine; Siefen, Rainer; Daum, Irene; Güntürkün, Onur. (2006). Creative thinking in adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Child Neuropsychology, 12(2), 111-123. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297040500320691
title: Inhibitory control mechanisms and contextual modulation of creative cognition account for ADHD creativity findings
description: The article offers an explanatory account in which creative cognition is shaped by inhibitory control mechanisms and by the contextual modulation of information processing. Within this account, a widened attentional focus associated with ADHD can help overcome the constraining influence of examples, while weaker inhibitory control can impair tasks requiring a functional invention. The authors use it to interpret the selective advantages and disadvantages their ADHD group showed across creativity measures.
requirements: Applicable to interpreting creativity task performance in populations differing in attentional focus and inhibitory control.
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretation of its findings, not as a directly tested mechanism.
target_learners: adolescents with ADHD
adolescents with conduct disorder
healthy control adolescents
target_learning_goals: creative thinking and creative cognition
key_sources: Abraham, Anna; Windmann, Sabine; Siefen, Rainer; Daum, Irene; Güntürkün, Onur. (2006). Creative thinking in adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Child Neuropsychology, 12(2), 111-123. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297040500320691

article_title: Creative Thinking in Adolescents with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
citation: Abraham, Anna; Windmann, Sabine; Siefen, Rainer; Daum, Irene; Güntürkün, Onur. (2006). Creative thinking in adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Child Neuropsychology, 12(2), 111-123. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297040500320691
title: Multi-measure creativity assessment battery spanning example-constraint and imagery invention tasks
description: The study assessed creativity using several measures rather than a single test, including a task measuring the ability to overcome the constraining influence of examples and an imagery task requiring generation of a functional invention. This multi-measure approach is what allowed the ADHD group's profile to appear selective, with advantages on some measures and disadvantages on others, rather than uniformly better or worse than the comparison groups.
requirements: Multiple distinct creativity measures are needed to reveal selective, task-dependent cognitive profiles.
target_learners: adolescents with ADHD
adolescents with conduct disorder
healthy control adolescents
target_learning_goals: assessment of creative thinking
examples: Performance across several creativity measures was compared in adolescents with ADHD, those with conduct disorder, and a healthy control sample.

article_title: Neurocognitive bases of emotion regulation development in adolescence
citation: Ahmed Saz P., Bittencourt-Hewitt Amanda, Sebastian Catherine L. (2015). Neurocognitive bases of emotion regulation development in adolescence. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6989808/
title: Extended process model of emotion regulation: identification, selection and implementation stages
description: The review adopts the extended process model of emotion regulation (Gross, 2014; Sheppes et al., 2015), which organises regulation into three sequential stages beyond the original process model. As the review states, "This posits that emotion regulation occurs in three stages: (1) Identification, in which an emotional state is identified and the decision over whether or not to regulate this is made; (2) Selection, in which an appropriate regulatory strategy is selected and (3) Implementation". Each stage involves a perception-valuation-action cycle, and the review uses this framework to ask where adolescent development may differ from adults.
requirements: Requires the perception-valuation-action cycle to operate at each stage, as the model specifies
constraints: The review notes most adolescent research addresses only the Implementation stage, with Identification and Selection understudied
target_learners: adolescents aged approximately 10-19
target_learning_goals: recognising when emotion regulation is needed
selecting appropriate regulation strategies
implementing regulation strategies effectively
examples: The review applies the model to ask whether adolescents might fail at the Identification stage when peer presence makes a hedonic state not trigger the valuation of a need to regulate
key_sources: Ahmed Saz P., Bittencourt-Hewitt Amanda, Sebastian Catherine L. (2015). Neurocognitive bases of emotion regulation development in adolescence. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6989808/

article_title: Neurocognitive bases of emotion regulation development in adolescence
citation: Ahmed Saz P., Bittencourt-Hewitt Amanda, Sebastian Catherine L. (2015). Neurocognitive bases of emotion regulation development in adolescence. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6989808/
title: Developmental mismatch account of adolescent emotion regulation
description: The review describes the developmental mismatch or imbalance model, in which prefrontal regulatory systems mature more slowly than limbic systems during adolescence. According to the review, "during adolescence the development of prefrontal regions lags behind that of limbic structures such as the amygdala, ventral striatum (VS) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC)", so adolescents are less effective at regulating emotions during the functional maturity lag. The review also presents the Triadic Systems Model as a refinement adding approach and avoidance systems.
requirements: Posits asynchronous maturation between prefrontal and limbic systems as the basis for adolescent regulatory difficulty
constraints: The review notes the model has been criticised because several studies have not consistently found heightened amygdala responses in adolescence, and heightened VS responses are sometimes associated with adaptive functioning
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: understanding why emotion regulation is harder in adolescence
explaining adolescent emotional reactivity and risk-taking
examples: The review cites Hare et al. (2008) finding exaggerated amygdala activity in adolescents relative to children and adults as consistent with mismatch accounts
key_sources: Ahmed Saz P., Bittencourt-Hewitt Amanda, Sebastian Catherine L. (2015). Neurocognitive bases of emotion regulation development in adolescence. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6989808/

article_title: Identifying Group Work Experiences That Increase Students’ Self-Efficacy for Quantitative Biology Tasks
citation: Aikens, M. L., & Kulacki, A. R. (2023). Identifying Group Work Experiences That Increase Students' Self-Efficacy for Quantitative Biology Tasks. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.22-04-0076
title: Taxonomy of five group work experiences that students report increase their self-efficacy for quantitative biology tasks
description: Through inductive process coding of student open responses, the authors identified experiences during collaborative group work that students report as increasing self-efficacy: "Accomplishing It, Discussing/Working Together, Being Taught/Guided, Asking Questions, Confirming Their Answers, Teaching/Guiding Others, and Consulting with a Teacher." Three peer-help codes were consolidated, yielding five experiences: accomplishing the problems, getting help from peers, confirming answers, teaching others, and consulting with a teacher. The authors deliberately coded experiences rather than Bandura's theoretical sources, reserving source interpretations for the Discussion.
requirements: Open-response survey items asking students to describe experiences and interactions during group work that increased confidence
Inductive process coding with established interrater reliability thresholds
constraints: Experiences were reported too infrequently (fewer than 35 of 429 responses) for some codes to be statistically modeled
Coding reflects student self-reports in one introductory biology course at a primarily White institution
target_learners: Undergraduate introductory biology students
target_learning_goals: Self-efficacy for quantitative biology tasks such as Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and population growth calculations
examples: A student coded as Accomplishing It reported, "Actually doing several calculations increased my confidence."

article_title: Effects of a Structured Decoding Curriculum on Adult Literacy Learners’ Reading Development
citation: Alamprese, J. A., MacArthur, C. A., Price, C., & Knight, D. (2011). Effects of a Structured Decoding Curriculum on Adult Literacy Learners' Reading Development. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555294
title: Making Sense of Decoding and Spelling (MSDS): a structured adult decoding curriculum based on Venezky's morphophonological analysis of English orthography
description: MSDS is a study-developed curriculum designed to teach adult learners to decode and spell words more accurately and fluently, beginning with basic alphabetic decoding and teaching the most common and useful patterns of English words. Its "core theoretical framework for the curriculum is Venezky's work (1970; 1999) on orthography", requiring analysis of morphemes and phonemes and their relationships, consistent with stage theories of spelling development. It embeds explicit metalinguistic information, a metacognitive strategy for decoding multisyllabic words, untimed repeated reading of 50-75 word passages, integrated spelling practice, whole-group scripted lessons, and progress-monitoring assessments about every five lessons.
requirements: Delivered as one component of a comprehensive adult reading course combined with vocabulary and comprehension instruction
Instructor training via two 2-day workshops plus technical assistance
constraints: Designed for efficiency given limited instructional time typical in ABE classes; no curriculum can teach all morphophonemic patterns used in skilled reading
target_learners: Adult basic education learners at the Low-Intermediate level (roughly fourth-to-seventh-grade reading comprehension)
target_learning_goals: Accurate and fluent decoding and spelling of English words
examples: Lessons open with informative texts containing the taught patterns and close with paired repeated reading of a brief smooth-reading passage
key_sources: Alamprese, J. A., MacArthur, C. A., Price, C., & Knight, D. (2011). Effects of a Structured Decoding Curriculum on Adult Literacy Learners' Reading Development. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555294

article_title: A preliminary examination of gut microbiota, sleep, and cognitive flexibility in healthy older adults
citation: Anderson Jason R., Carroll Ian, Azcarate-Peril M. Andrea, Rochette Amber D., Heinberg Leslie J., Peat Christine, Steffen Kristine, Manderino Lisa M., Mitchell James, Gunstad John. (2017). A preliminary examination of gut microbiota, sleep, and cognitive flexibility in healthy older adults. Sleep Medicine, 38, 104-107. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7433257/
title: Altered gut microbiome composition as a possible mechanism linking inadequate sleep to poor neurocognitive outcomes in older adults
description: The article proposes that dysbiosis of the gut microbiome may contribute to cognitive dysfunction associated with chronically poor sleep, framing "altered gut microbiome composition as a possible mechanism linking inadequate sleep to poor neurocognitive outcomes." The account draws on animal-model work showing diet-driven microbiome changes can reduce cognitive flexibility and on human work showing partial sleep restriction alters microbiome composition. The authors position this as a hypothesis requiring prospective and experimental confirmation, not a tested mechanism.
requirements: Prospective and experimental studies to confirm the proposed mediational relationship
constraints: The observational nature of the preliminary study precludes causal conclusions
Cross-sectional assessments can distort mediational relationships
Possible mechanisms such as systemic inflammation were not examined
target_learners: healthy older adults ages 50 to 85
target_learning_goals: cognitive flexibility
executive function
examples: The study measured gut microbiome composition via 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of stool samples and correlated phylum proportions with PSQI scores and Stroop subtest performance
