article_title: When did you stop speaking to yourself? Age-related differences in adolescents’ world knowledge-based audience design
citation: Arvidsson C., Pagmar D., Uddén J. (2022). When did you stop speaking to yourself? Age-related differences in adolescents' world knowledge-based audience design. Royal Society Open Science 9(11): 220305. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.220305
title: Novel world knowledge-based audience design task with post-test knowledge attribution survey
description: A modified director task measuring adaptation to addressees' world knowledge rather than visual perspective. In each trial a pictured addressee (a child or an elderly woman) appears while the speaker records a message about a target referent; "the participant knew the name of the target referent but was expected to assume that the addressee either (i) did not know the name of the target (unknown test condition) or (ii) did know the name of the target (known control condition)". A post-test survey controls for assumed knowledge, yielding a knowledge attribution score, and the AD score subtracts redundant describing in the known condition from sufficient describing in the unknown condition.
requirements: Participants must know the names of target referents and hold condition-matching assumptions, verified by the post-test survey; stimuli require no more than one modifier for an unambiguous description
constraints: Conducted with passive confederates, which the authors note have been criticized since interactive contexts increase speakers' informativeness; individual language ability was not included as a model variable
target_learners: adolescents aged 11–16
target_learning_goals: pragmatic development
audience design in referential production
perspective taking in language production
examples: 36 trials (24 unknown, 12 known) implemented in PsychoPy; the practice trial was always a known-condition trial to prevent participants from adopting constant describing
key_sources: Arvidsson C., Pagmar D., Uddén J. (2022). When did you stop speaking to yourself? Age-related differences in adolescents' world knowledge-based audience design. Royal Society Open Science 9(11): 220305. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.220305

article_title: When did you stop speaking to yourself? Age-related differences in adolescents’ world knowledge-based audience design
citation: Arvidsson C., Pagmar D., Uddén J. (2022). When did you stop speaking to yourself? Age-related differences in adolescents' world knowledge-based audience design. Royal Society Open Science 9(11): 220305. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.220305
title: Processing model distinguishing representation of others' knowledge from its online use in production
description: Following Clark's processing perspective, the article distinguishes assumed knowledge — the speaker's assumption about the addressee's knowledge state — from audience design, the process of adapting utterances to those assumptions during online communication. The findings support "an AD model distinguishing between the representation of others' knowledge as such and the usage of these representations online, where the latter develops later": 11–12-year-olds held adult-like assumptions (KAS near maximum) yet failed to deploy them consistently during production. The model treats listener-specific adjustment as relying on knowledge attribution, executive functions and social interaction experience.
requirements: Distinguishing these two components requires tasks that separately measure assumptions (e.g. prompted post-test surveys) and online production behaviour
constraints: The article states the development of audience design cannot be reduced to possessing relevant knowledge and high executive function; social experience is difficult to measure directly
target_learners: children entering adolescence (11–12)
middle adolescents (15–16)
target_learning_goals: pragmatic competence
use of common ground during online communication
examples: The authors argue pragmatic competence should be regarded as a specific capability with its own developmental trajectory and neurophysiological correlates rather than a composition of domain-general skills

article_title: Working memory, math performance, and math anxiety
citation: Mark H. Ashcraft and Jeremy A. Krause. (2007). Working memory, math performance, and math anxiety. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 14(2), 243-248.
title: Math anxiety functions like a resource-demanding secondary task that compromises working memory during math processing
description: The article proposes that "High math anxiety works much like a dual task setting: Preoccupation with one’s math fears and anxieties functions like a resource-demanding secondary task". This account explains why math anxiety harms performance only when the anxiety is actually aroused, why computation-based span tasks reveal compromised working memory while verbal span tasks do not, and why highly anxious participants suffer most when a secondary task occupies working memory during demanding math. It frames math anxiety as a malleable individual difference with measurable cognitive consequences.
requirements: The anxiety must be actually aroused by the task, as in span tasks that involve computations, for working memory resources to be drained
constraints: The article notes this account is being refined, stating they are currently exploring other ways in which this diversion of working memory affects the outcomes of mental processing
target_learners: college undergraduates
high school and college students in math coursework
target_learning_goals: arithmetic and mathematics performance
math achievement on standardized tests
working memory capacity during computation
examples: The dual-task addition experiment in which highly anxious participants, already wasting working memory resources by attending to their own anxiety, suffered the most in the six-letter load condition with carry problems

article_title: Working Memory for Serial Order Is Dysfunctional in Adults With a History of Developmental Dyscalculia: Evidence From Behavioral and Neuroimaging Data
citation: Attout, Lucie; Salmon, Eric; Majerus, Steve. (2015). Working memory for serial order is dysfunctional in adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia: Evidence from behavioral and neuroimaging data. Developmental Neuropsychology, 40. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2015.1036993
title: Serial order working memory as a distinct component underlying numerical cognition and vulnerable in dyscalculia
description: The article advances the view that short-term memory for serial order is a distinct working memory component, separable from item-based verbal short-term memory, that supports numerical and alphabetical ordered processing. The authors argue that "a specific dysfunction of short-term memory for serial order in developmental dyscalculia" links the behavioral deficit to reduced left intraparietal activation, positioning this component as functionally related to number processing networks.
requirements: Assessment of serial order recall must be separated from item recall measures to observe the specific deficit
constraints: Evidence concerns adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia; generalization to other populations is not established in this article
target_learners: adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: numerical cognition
ordered information processing in working memory
examples: Adults with dyscalculia and controls completed short-term memory tasks distinguishing serial order from item recall, with fMRI recorded during serial order processing
key_sources: Attout, Lucie; Salmon, Eric; Majerus, Steve. (2015). Working memory for serial order is dysfunctional in adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia: Evidence from behavioral and neuroimaging data. Developmental Neuropsychology, 40. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2015.1036993

title: Serial order versus item recall short-term memory task battery with fMRI
description: A task battery contrasting short-term memory for serial order with short-term memory for item information, administered behaviorally and inside the fMRI scanner to adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia and matched controls. The design allows the article to report that participants "were impaired for serial order recall but not for item recall", and to localize serial order processing to left intraparietal cortex.
requirements: Tasks must separately probe serial order and item information to yield the dissociation
constraints: Administered to adults with a history of developmental dyscalculia and controls; not validated here for other groups

matched control adults
target_learning_goals: measuring serial order working memory
measuring item short-term memory
examples: Behavioral serial order and item recall tasks paired with fMRI sessions in the same adult participants

article_title: “I did it wrong, but i know it”: Young children's metacognitive knowledge expressions during peer interactions in math activities
citation: Ebru Aydın, Çağlayan Dinçer. (2022). “I did it wrong, but i know it”: Young children’s metacognitive knowledge expressions during peer interactions in math activities. Thinking Skills and Creativity 45 (2022) 101104. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2022.101104
title: Four-category coding framework for young children's metacognitive knowledge: knowledge of self, others, universal properties of cognition, and task-specific strategies
description: The study develops a coding system for analyzing young children's metacognitive knowledge expressions during peer interactions in mathematical measurement activities. Building on Whitebread et al.'s (2009, 2010) framework and prior research with young children, the authors devised four category codes: "(a) knowledge of self, (b) knowledge of others, (c) knowledge of universal properties of cognition, and (d) knowledge of task-specific strategies." These four metacognitive knowledge variables were used as category codes to code the children's interactions in video transcripts and observation forms. The framework treats knowledge of tasks and strategies together in a task-specific way, since activities included certain mathematical tasks/goals so children's cognitive strategies could be considered in a task-specific way.
requirements: Activities must include certain mathematical tasks/goals so children's cognitive strategies can be considered in a task-specific way
Video recordings and observation forms of peer interactions are needed as data sources
constraints: Developed from and applied to two 5-year-old children in one kindergarten class over 16 measurement activities
The framework was mapped according to but not limited by Whitebread et al.'s (2009, 2010) framework for young children's metacognitive knowledge
target_learners: Young children (5-year-olds) in kindergarten
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive knowledge in mathematical measurement activities
examples: Applied to 28 hours of video recording transcripts of 16 activities; inter-coder agreement of %84.2 on a randomly selected activity

article_title: “I did it wrong, but i know it”: Young children's metacognitive knowledge expressions during peer interactions in math activities
citation: Ebru Aydın, Çağlayan Dinçer. (2022). “I did it wrong, but i know it”: Young children’s metacognitive knowledge expressions during peer interactions in math activities. Thinking Skills and Creativity 45 (2022) 101104. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2022.101104
title: Sixteen mathematical measurement activities across length, area, weight, and volume dimensions designed to elicit peer interaction
description: The study designed and implemented sixteen activities based on the dimensions of mathematical measurement skills of length, area, weight, and volume, with four activities per dimension. Activities were prepared from outcomes and indicators in the Turkish Preschool Education Program, organized and finalized as 13 outcomes and 60 indicators after expert consultation with a preschool education specialist and a mathematics education specialist. The activities "allow peer interactions and they are ordered from easy to difficult." Examples include Animal Shelters (selecting objects of appropriate length), How to Cover It? (covering a surface), Bags (comparing weights), and Cylinders (comparing volumes). All activities were video-recorded with three cameras from different angles.
requirements: Outcomes and indicators based on children's measurement skills selected from the Preschool Education Program
Expert consultation with specialists in preschool education, mathematics education, and early childhood education
constraints: Implemented two days a week, one activity per day, over approximately 10 weeks excluding holidays
Designed for a kindergarten class of 18 children aged 60–68 months, with two children as focal participants
target_learners: Kindergarten children aged 60–68 months
target_learning_goals: Mathematical measurement skills (length, area, weight, volume) and metacognitive knowledge expression
examples: Measuring Rods activity: children create measuring rods with cardboard sticks and place unit lines with objects such as paper clips, sticks, straws, or buttons

article_title: Doing Time Wisely: The Social and Personal Benefits of Higher Education in Prison
citation: Jillian Baranger, Danielle Rousseau, Mary Ellen Mastrorilli, James Matesanz. (2018). Doing Time Wisely: The Social and Personal Benefits of Higher Education in Prison. The Prison Journal. https://doi.org/10.1177/0032885518776380
title: Boston University Prison Education Program
description: The Boston University Prison Education Program is a degree-granting liberal arts college program operating in Massachusetts correctional facilities since 1972, including the state's only women's prison. It "provides a Bachelor in Liberal Arts degree and annual enrollment is approximately one hundred and twenty (120) students", funded entirely by BU scholarships rather than Pell Grants. Students take one to three courses per term in three-hour weekly sessions over 13–14-week semesters, taught by faculty holding at least a Master's Degree. More than 400 of over 1,500 participants have obtained degrees.
requirements: Admission via a two-part entrance examination and a subsequent interview, with approximately 20% to 50% of applicants selected depending on the year
Funding through scholarships provided by Boston University's Metropolitan College
target_learners: Incarcerated adults in Massachusetts state facilities, including a women's prison and pre-release facility, serving short-term and life or long-term sentences
target_learning_goals: Bachelor of Liberal Arts degree attainment across literature, philosophy, social sciences, mathematics, natural sciences, computer sciences, and fine arts
examples: During academic years 1991 through 2017, 54 women graduated the program, 189 took courses without graduating, and 4 completed degrees at BU after release; 2012–2017 women graduates averaged 12.44 semesters and a 3.33 GPA

article_title: Chronic Stereotype Threat Is Associated With Mathematical Achievement on Representative Sample of Secondary Schoolgirls: The Role of Gender Identification, Working Memory, and Intellectual Helplessness
citation: Bedyńska S, Krejtz I and Sedek G (2018) Chronic Stereotype Threat Is Associated With Mathematical Achievement on Representative Sample of Secondary Schoolgirls: The Role of Gender Identification, Working Memory, and Intellectual Helplessness. Front. Psychol. 9:428. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.00428
title: Cognitive exhaustion model of learned helplessness applied to chronic stereotype threat
description: The article proposes a new mechanism by which chronic stereotype threat decreases school achievement, namely intellectual helplessness. It assumes that "repeated experience of stereotype threat works as intellectual helplessness training." After the phase of cognitive mobilization, cognitive exhaustion appears because the individual has no gain from intense cognitive effort. This integrates motivational and cognitive processes as two phases: mobilization and cognitive exhaustion.
requirements: Repeated experience of stereotype threat in a domain such as mathematics
constraints: The mechanism was tested in a cross-sectional design with secondary schoolgirls
target_learners: secondary schoolgirls
target_learning_goals: mathematical achievement
examples: The study measured chronic stereotype threat, intellectual helplessness, and working memory functions in a representative sample of secondary schoolgirls

description: The FAWMT is a working memory assessment adapted from the battery of experimental procedures used by Oberauer et al. It measures three functions: simultaneous storage and processing (counting span task), supervision (set switching task 2 × 2), and relational integration (spatial location memory task). The article states it "has been used in educational research and proved to have a high predictive value of early school mathematical achievement."

title: Chronic Stereotype Threat Scale (seven items)
description: A seven-item scale adapted from Steele and Aronson (1995, Experiment 4) and the Stereotype Vulnerability Scale. It includes two items on being judged by other students, two items on risk of being stereotypically judged by teachers, and three items on generalized stereotype threat. The article reports "The reliability of the scale was high (Cronbach's α = 0.89)" and confirmatory factor analysis indicated the scale was unidimensional.
requirements: 6-point Likert type scale administration
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: measuring chronic stereotype threat experiences in academic domains
examples: Sample item: 'I worry that if I fail during mathematical test, it will prove that all girls are poor at maths'

article_title: Attention, Learning, and Arousal of Experimentally Sleep-restricted Adolescents in a Simulated Classroom
citation: Beebe, D. W., Rose, D., & Amin, R. (2010). Attention, Learning, and Arousal of Experimentally Sleep-Restricted Adolescents in a Simulated Classroom. The Journal of Adolescent Health. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jadohealth.2010.03.005
title: Simulated classroom assessment with educational films, quizzes, and video/EEG monitoring
description: A laboratory analogue of a classroom used to measure learning, attention, and arousal objectively. Participants were "seated behind a table" viewing "30-minute educational films presented on a 19-inch television ~6 feet away", then completed 12-item multiple-choice quizzes; a subset was video-recorded and EEG-monitored. Inattentive behavior was coded by a condition-blind rater in 30-second epochs as look-aways of ≥3 consecutive seconds.
requirements: Educational films of developmentally-appropriate content (The Western Tradition series)
Condition-blind behavioral raters and, for arousal, EEG equipment
constraints: The authors state the technique "has not been previously validated and warrants psychometric attention"
target_learners: adolescents aged 13.9–16.9 years
target_learning_goals: learning from educational film content
classroom attention regulation
examples: Used to compare quiz scores, inattentive behaviors, and theta power after sleep-restricted versus healthy-sleep weeks in a counterbalanced design
key_sources: Beebe, D. W., Rose, D., & Amin, R. (2010). Attention, Learning, and Arousal of Experimentally Sleep-Restricted Adolescents in a Simulated Classroom. The Journal of Adolescent Health. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jadohealth.2010.03.005

article_title: Attention, Learning, and Arousal of Experimentally Sleep-restricted Adolescents in a Simulated Classroom
citation: Beebe, D. W., Rose, D., & Amin, R. (2010). Attention, Learning, and Arousal of Experimentally Sleep-Restricted Adolescents in a Simulated Classroom. The Journal of Adolescent Health. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jadohealth.2010.03.005
title: Treat chronic adolescent sleep restriction as harmful to learning and attention, not benign
description: The article argues that because experimentally restricted sleep causally reduced learning, attention, and arousal in a simulated classroom, chronic sleep restriction among adolescents should not be viewed as harmless even though it is statistically typical. The authors state that "while chronic sleep restriction may be statistically typical for adolescents, it is neither healthy nor benign".
requirements: Recognition that adolescent sleep need is around the recommended 9 hours per school night
constraints: The authors note public-policy studies such as later school start times have been quasi-experimental with subjective outcomes and no clear effect on learning
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: protecting classroom learning and attention from sleep-loss effects
examples: The experimental comparison of 6.5-hour versus 10-hour in-bed conditions over five consecutive nights in adolescents' homes, monitored by actigraphy and sleep diary
key_sources: Beebe, D. W., Rose, D., & Amin, R. (2010). Attention, Learning, and Arousal of Experimentally Sleep-Restricted Adolescents in a Simulated Classroom. The Journal of Adolescent Health. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jadohealth.2010.03.005

article_title: The Racial/Ethnic Composition of Elementary Schools and Young Children’s Academic and Socioemotional Functioning
citation: Benner Aprile D.; Crosnoe Robert. (2011). The Racial/Ethnic Composition of Elementary Schools and Young Children's Academic and Socioemotional Functioning. American Educational Research Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4554342/
title: Integrative conceptual model linking diversity and belongingness perspectives to population stratification
description: The article proposes an integrative conceptual model connecting two developmental perspectives on school racial/ethnic composition. The diversity perspective, drawing on Piagetian disequilibrium, holds that "exposure to diverse worldviews and life perspectives provides opportunities for valuable cognitive exercise," predicting academic gains from heterogeneous student bodies. The belongingness perspective, rooted in attachment theory, holds that meaningful social connections are a fundamental need, predicting socioemotional benefits from same-racial/ethnic peer representation. The model integrates these with a population approach treating race/ethnicity as a marker of position in the U.S. stratification system, hypothesizing suppression effects between the two composition dimensions and moderation by group position.
requirements: Testing requires modeling diversity and proportion same-racial/ethnic peers simultaneously to detect suppression effects
Requires outcome domains disaggregated into academic and socioemotional measures
Requires multiple-group analyses to test stratification-based moderation
constraints: Developed for the transition into elementary school; the authors note the role of diversity and matching might change as children grow and navigate more heterogeneous contexts
Associations are correlational; unobserved confounds cannot be fully ruled out
target_learners: Kindergarten and early elementary school children
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in reading and mathematics
Socioemotional adjustment including externalizing behavior and interpersonal skills
examples: The authors illustrate the model with two Latino students in schools of identical diversity (.66) but different same-racial/ethnic peer representation, showing the two dimensions vary independently
key_sources: Benner Aprile D.; Crosnoe Robert. (2011). The Racial/Ethnic Composition of Elementary Schools and Young Children's Academic and Socioemotional Functioning. American Educational Research Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4554342/

article_title: The Racial/Ethnic Composition of Elementary Schools and Young Children’s Academic and Socioemotional Functioning
citation: Benner Aprile D.; Crosnoe Robert. (2011). The Racial/Ethnic Composition of Elementary Schools and Young Children's Academic and Socioemotional Functioning. American Educational Research Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4554342/
title: Design diverse school contexts that also protect a critical mass of same-racial/ethnic peers to support both academic and socioemotional needs
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that school composition policy should pursue both dimensions simultaneously rather than treating diversity and same-racial/ethnic peer representation as competing goals. The authors state: "If school diversity is a compelling state interest, we must not only embrace the benefits of diversity but also acknowledge the advantages of having more same-racial/ethnic peers so that we can better ensure that diverse school contexts support both the academic and socioemotional needs of all U.S. children." This follows from findings that diversity benefits for achievement were strongest when children also had more same-racial/ethnic peers, and that matching independently supported socioemotional adjustment.
requirements: School assignment or composition decisions must attend to both overall student-body diversity and the representation of each child's own racial/ethnic group
Adequate representation of multiple groups is needed so that matching does not come at the cost of diversity
constraints: The National Research Council suggests a minimum racial/ethnic representation threshold of 15% to protect against feelings of isolation, which the authors propose testing in future studies
Benefits for minority children's achievement were not observed in this kindergarten sample, possibly due to limited exposure duration
target_learners: Elementary school children across racial/ethnic groups
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
Socioemotional well-being and school belonging
examples: The authors cite the National Research Council's 15% minimum representation threshold used in higher education affirmative action and K-12 race-conscious school assignment decisions as a candidate critical-mass benchmark
key_sources: Benner Aprile D.; Crosnoe Robert. (2011). The Racial/Ethnic Composition of Elementary Schools and Young Children's Academic and Socioemotional Functioning. American Educational Research Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4554342/

article_title: Correlates of health and financial literacy in older adults without dementia
citation: Bennett JS, Boyle PA, James BD, Bennett DA. (2012). Correlates of health and financial literacy in older adults without dementia. BMC Geriatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2318-12-30
title: Combined health and financial literacy assessment yielding an averaged total literacy score
description: The article describes a literacy assessment composed of nine health literacy questions (e.g., understanding Medicare, medication instructions, interpreting drug risk) and 23 financial literacy questions (numeracy, compound interest, inflation, financial terms such as FDIC, stocks, and mutual funds), all multiple choice or true/false and scored correct/incorrect. Because the tests differed in item count, subscores were "expressed as the percentage correct out of total items (from 0 – 1)" and "The total literacy score was the average of these two percentages." Total literacy had "adequate internal consistency with a Cronbach 's coefficient alpha of 0.77."
requirements: Administered within the Rush Memory and Aging Project annual clinical evaluation beginning in 2008, with items scored correct or incorrect and subscores converted to percentage correct before averaging
constraints: The authors note they did not use common measures such as REALM or TOFHLA, which makes comparison to prior work difficult
target_learners: community-based older adults without dementia
target_learning_goals: ability to understand and process health and financial information, concepts, and numeracy
examples: Used to assess 556 participants in the Rush Memory and Aging Project, with mean total literacy score of 66% (SD = 15%)
key_sources: Bennett JS, Boyle PA, James BD, Bennett DA. (2012). Correlates of health and financial literacy in older adults without dementia. BMC Geriatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2318-12-30

article_title: Emerging Support for a Role of Exercise in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Intervention Planning
citation: Berwid Olga G., Halperin Jeffrey M. (2012). Emerging Support for a Role of Exercise in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Intervention Planning. Current Psychiatry Reports. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11920-012-0297-4
title: Neurodevelopmental compensation account: ADHD symptom remission reflects later-developing cortical circuitry compensating for underlying deficits via top-down regulatory control
description: The review proposes that ADHD arises from delayed cortical development — children with ADHD follow a trajectory of cortical maturation "delayed by 2 – 3 years relative to their typically-developing peers" — and that symptom decline with age reflects the degree to which later-developing higher cortical circuitry compensates through top-down regulatory control. On this account, remitting individuals show relative normalization of executive functioning and underlying circuitry. The authors use this framework to argue for interventions that enhance neural growth in executive-functioning brain regions.
requirements: Interventions on this account must target underlying neural mechanisms of ADHD rather than symptoms alone
constraints: The authors note normalization of the developmental trajectory being linked to improved outcomes is emerging, not established, data
target_learners: children with ADHD
target_learning_goals: executive functioning and cognitive control development
examples: The review cites longitudinal neuroimaging showing delayed cortical maturation in ADHD and relative normalization of executive functioning in remitters versus persisters
key_sources: Berwid Olga G., Halperin Jeffrey M. (2012). Emerging Support for a Role of Exercise in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Intervention Planning. Current Psychiatry Reports. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11920-012-0297-4

article_title: Components of executive control with advantages for bilingual children in two cultures
citation: Bialystok Ellen, Viswanathan Mythili. (2009). Components of Executive Control with Advantages for Bilingual Children in Two Cultures. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2009.06.014
title: Three-component decomposition of executive control: response suppression, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility
description: The article treats executive control as a set of separable components, building on the widely accepted view that "the executive control system consists of three components: inhibition, updating (also called working memory), and shifting (also called cognitive flexibility)". It further distinguishes two processes conflated under the term inhibition: inhibitory control, resolving conflict "by selectively attending to a relevant stimulus cue and ignoring a competing cue", and response suppression, refraining from an automatically cued response. The faces task operationalizes each component as a specific RT cost, allowing the components to be tested separately in the same children.
requirements: A task that yields separable cost measures for each component in the same population, as the faces task does for children
constraints: The components emerge at different developmental times, so bilingualism may have different influences at different ages
target_learners: 8-year-old children
target_learning_goals: Executive control processes: response suppression, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility
examples: The faces task assessed response suppression by the red-minus-green eye RT difference, inhibitory control by the gaze-shift-minus-straight-eye difference in mixed blocks, and switching by the mixed-minus-blocked difference.
key_sources: Bialystok Ellen, Viswanathan Mythili. (2009). Components of Executive Control with Advantages for Bilingual Children in Two Cultures. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2009.06.014

article_title: Components of executive control with advantages for bilingual children in two cultures
citation: Bialystok Ellen, Viswanathan Mythili. (2009). Components of Executive Control with Advantages for Bilingual Children in Two Cultures. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2009.06.014
title: Faces task: a behavioral anti-saccade variant yielding three executive-control cost measures
description: The faces task is "a behavioral version of an anti-saccade task... developed by Bialystok, Craik, & Ryan (2006)" in which children respond to an asterisk appearing in one of two boxes flanking a schematic face, pressing the same side for green eyes and the opposite side for red eyes. Eyes look straight ahead or shift gaze toward a box, and trials appear in single-color or mixed blocks, producing straight-eye and gaze-shift tasks across blocked and mixed presentations. Sixteen blocks of 24 trials were administered, with counterbalanced orders and practice blocks, allowing calculation of suppression, inhibitory-control, and switching costs.
requirements: A computer with a response key on each side of the monitor and practice blocks of 8 trials before each task
constraints: Accuracy was near ceiling (97-98%) in 8-year-olds, so the task discriminates groups by response time rather than errors
target_learners: 8-year-old children
target_learning_goals: Measuring response suppression, inhibitory control, and task-switching components of executive control
examples: Ninety 8-year-olds in three language groups completed the task with all conditions presented in one of eight counterbalanced orders.
key_sources: Bialystok Ellen, Viswanathan Mythili. (2009). Components of Executive Control with Advantages for Bilingual Children in Two Cultures. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2009.06.014

article_title: Coordination of executive functions in monolingual and bilingual children
citation: Bialystok Ellen. (2011). Coordination of Executive Functions in Monolingual and Bilingual Children. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3139691/
title: Coordination of executive control components as a distinct aspect of executive function development shaped by bilingual experience
description: The article proposes that beyond the three core executive components (selective attention and inhibition, shifting, working memory), effective complex performance depends on a higher-order management function that coordinates them. Bilingual language use is framed as a constant "dual task" situation requiring speakers to "construct speech plans according to the current context", "selectively attend to linguistic structures in the target language while ignoring competition from the other language", and monitor progress. This experience is argued to enhance coordination of the components rather than any single component, and the article states that "an important outcome of bilingualism may be in managing executive control components to address complex goals".
requirements: A task that recruits multiple executive control components simultaneously, such as the dual-modality classification task used here
Groups differing in relevant experience, such as bilingual versus monolingual language use
constraints: The article states the components themselves may be at different levels in the two groups, but the assumption is that the need for coordination is above and beyond those individual levels
The bilingual advantage in this task was limited to the visual task, with verbal production possibly limiting auditory performance
target_learners: 8-year-old children
monolingual and bilingual children
target_learning_goals: coordination of executive control components in complex task performance
executive function development in childhood
examples: 63 8-year-olds classified visual and auditory stimuli as animals or musical instruments in single and dual-modality blocks
Bilinguals outperformed monolinguals in the dual-task condition for the visual task but not the auditory task
key_sources: Bialystok Ellen. (2011). Coordination of Executive Functions in Monolingual and Bilingual Children. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3139691/

article_title: Multiple aspects of self-regulation uniquely predict mathematics but not letter–word knowledge in the early elementary grades.
citation: Blair, C., Ursache, A., Greenberg, M., Vernon-Feagans, L., & The Family Life Project Investigators. (2015). Multiple Aspects of Self-Regulation Uniquely Predict Mathematics but Not Letter–Word Knowledge in the Early Elementary Grades. Developmental Psychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5264531/
title: Hierarchical model of self-regulation spanning physiological, attentional-emotional, and cognitive levels
description: The article outlines an integrated theoretical model in which self-regulation is composed of multiple influences hierarchically organized from genetic to sociocultural levels. At the top are executive functions (cognitive and intentional) and effortful control (temperamental and behavioral), dependent on lower-level stress response physiology including cortisol and alpha amylase. The article states self-regulation is "the volitional and nonvolitional management of attention, emotion, and stress response physiology for purposes of goal-directed action, primarily through executive function abilities."
requirements: Measures at multiple levels: physiological (salivary cortisol and alpha amylase), temperamental (effortful control via direct assessment and questionnaire), and cognitive (executive function tasks)
constraints: The article notes the association between stress hormones and self-regulation is generally an inverted U shape curve, so effects depend on level of arousal
target_learners: children in early elementary grades (prekindergarten through second grade)
target_learning_goals: early mathematics ability
early reading ability
examples: The Family Life Project study measured executive function, effortful control, and stress physiology at 48 months, and teacher/parent effortful control report at 60 months, predicting math and reading growth through second grade
key_sources: Blair, C., Ursache, A., Greenberg, M., Vernon-Feagans, L., & The Family Life Project Investigators. (2015). Multiple Aspects of Self-Regulation Uniquely Predict Mathematics but Not Letter–Word Knowledge in the Early Elementary Grades. Developmental Psychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5264531/

article_title: School Readiness and Self-Regulation: A Developmental Psychobiological Approach
citation: Blair, Clancy & Raver, C. Cybele. (2015). School Readiness and Self-Regulation: A Developmental Psychobiological Approach. Annual Review of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-010814-015221
title: School readiness is best understood through the construct of self-regulation, spanning attention, emotion, and stress regulation
description: The article proposes a unifying framework in which school readiness is understood as the development of self-regulation, including attention focusing, emotion and stress-response regulation, reflection, and positive social interaction. It argues these attributes are interrelated with cognitive abilities, primarily executive functions, and provide the proximal mechanisms through which children acquire knowledge in classroom interactions. The framework unites biological and behavioral levels of analysis shaped by developmental context.
requirements: Research and practice must treat social-emotional and cognitive aspects of readiness as interrelated rather than separate influences
constraints: The framework concerns young children approaching school entry, particularly around age 6
target_learners: young children entering kindergarten and early elementary grades
target_learning_goals: school readiness
early academic learning
self-regulation development
examples: A nationally representative sample of kindergarten teachers endorsed readiness as being able to pay attention, follow directions, and regulate emotion rather than strictly academic skills
key_sources: Blair, Clancy & Raver, C. Cybele. (2015). School Readiness and Self-Regulation: A Developmental Psychobiological Approach. Annual Review of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-010814-015221

article_title: Creativity in ADHD: Goal-Directed Motivation and Domain Specificity
citation: Boot Nathalie, Nevicka Barbara, Baas Matthijs. (2017). Creativity in ADHD: Goal-Directed Motivation and Domain Specificity. Journal of Attention Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/1087054717727352
title: Encourage learners with ADHD to engage in creative tasks that match their preferences and abilities, and reward their creative work
description: The article concludes that people with ADHD may excel in specific creative tasks that match their preferences and abilities, and that "Encouraging them to engage in such tasks and rewarding their creative work may help both themselves, as well as the people around them, to benefit from the positive side of ADHD." This principle directs educators and designers to select creative activities fitting the learner's skills and to add goal-directed incentives such as competition or rewards, which the studies show raise idea originality in ADHD.
requirements: Creative tasks should match the learner's preferences and abilities, as the domain-specific findings indicate selective rather than general creativity advantages
constraints: Evidence is based on self-reported domain creativity rather than actual creative performance
Samples consisted of high-functioning, mainly university-educated adults with ADHD, limiting generalizability
The mechanism underlying the competition effect (monetary reward vs. outperforming an opponent) remains unclear
target_learners: adults with ADHD
higher-education students with ADHD
target_learning_goals: creative idea generation and originality
real-world creative achievement
sustained task engagement during open-ended tasks
examples: In Study 2, participants with ADHD generated more original ideas when competing for a €5 bonus than without competition
ADHD participants reported higher self-perceived creativity in the performance and mechanical/scientific domains than controls
key_sources: Boot Nathalie, Nevicka Barbara, Baas Matthijs. (2017). Creativity in ADHD: Goal-Directed Motivation and Domain Specificity. Journal of Attention Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/1087054717727352

article_title: Community violence exposure and adolescents’ school engagement and academic achievement over time.
citation: Borofsky Larissa A., Kellerman Ilana, Baucom Brian, Oliver Pamella H., Margolin Gayla. (2013). Community Violence Exposure and Adolescents' School Engagement and Academic Achievement Over Time. Psychology of Violence. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034121
title: School engagement as a multifaceted construct with emotional, behavioral, and cognitive components
description: The article adopts a conception of school engagement, drawing on Fredricks and colleagues, as a multifaceted construct reflecting adolescents' day-to-day connection to school. It is "typically conceptualized as having emotional (e.g., enjoying being at school), behavioral (e.g., helping out at school), and cognitive (e.g., feeling interested in school) components". The authors operationalized it with a seven-item self-report measure mapping onto these three facets and treat engagement as more amenable to immediate intervention than achievement.
requirements: Measurement capturing emotional, behavioral, and cognitive facets of adolescents' connection to school
constraints: The article notes there is no one definition of school engagement
target_learners: Adolescents
target_learning_goals: Connection and engagement with the school environment
examples: The study's seven-item measure asked, for example, how much students feel happy at school, help keep their school clean, and feel interested in what is going on at school.
key_sources: Borofsky Larissa A., Kellerman Ilana, Baucom Brian, Oliver Pamella H., Margolin Gayla. (2013). Community Violence Exposure and Adolescents' School Engagement and Academic Achievement Over Time. Psychology of Violence. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034121

article_title: Interventions for struggling adolescent and adult readers: instructional, learner, and situational differences
citation: Mary Beth Calhoon, Hollis S. Scarborough, Brett Miller. (2013). Interventions for struggling adolescent and adult readers: instructional, learner, and situational differences. Read Writ 26:489–494. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-013-9442-7
title: Group-plus-individual (person-oriented) analysis of intervention outcomes
description: This framework holds that evaluating remedial interventions solely by group-level improvement can obscure subgroup effects, so outcomes should be examined "at both the group and individual (or ''person-oriented'') level". The special issue's five papers apply this by comparing persisters with dropouts and gainers with non-gainers, using methods such as WIGROT, latent change scores, and multiple change metrics. The editorial argues this reveals which instructional approaches benefit which learners.
requirements: Outcome data must support both group-level and individual-level classification or growth analyses, as in the five studies composing this special issue.
constraints: The editorial calls the answers yielded by the five projects tentative and preliminary.
target_learners: struggling adolescent readers
adult literacy learners
target_learning_goals: word reading and comprehension gains
persistence and retention in literacy programs
examples: Calhoon and Petscher combined latent change score analyses with individual gain classifications (less than one vs. one or more years of normative growth).
Scarborough et al. used within-individual gains replicated over tests (WIGROT) as the method for identifying gainers.
Frijters et al. characterized individual change using four methods, including the Jacobson-Truax index and hierarchical linear modeling growth rates.
key_sources: Mary Beth Calhoon, Hollis S. Scarborough, Brett Miller. (2013). Interventions for struggling adolescent and adult readers: instructional, learner, and situational differences. Read Writ 26:489–494. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-013-9442-7

article_title: Physical fitness and executive functions in adolescents: cross-sectional associations with academic achievement
citation: Cancela J, Burgo H, Sande E. (2019). Physical fitness and executive functions in adolescents: cross-sectional associations with academic achievement. J. Phys. Ther. Sci. 31: 556–562. https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jpts/31/7/31_17-478/_article
title: Executive functions as covert, goal-directed cognitive skills underlying learning
description: The article frames cognitive functions as the mental processes enabling attention, perception, memory, language and calculation, with executive functions as their goal-directed subset. It states that "EFs are covert, internally self-directed cognitive skills at the service of a goal", directing behavior and cognitive and emotional activity. In the study this framework motivates measuring five EF domains (inhibition/interference, working memory, processing speed, cognitive flexibility, social skills) and testing their links to fitness and academic achievement.
requirements: EF domains must be measured with validated instruments (here Stroop, Wechsler Memory Scale, Symbol Digit Modalities, Trail Making, MESSY)
constraints: The article treats EFs as measured by these specific neuropsychological tests in adolescents aged 12–16
target_learners: secondary school adolescents (12–16 years)
target_learning_goals: executive function domains supporting academic achievement
examples: The study operationalized five EF domains with Stroop, Wechsler memory, Symbol Digit, Trail Making and MESSY tests in 713 adolescents
key_sources: Cancela J, Burgo H, Sande E. (2019). Physical fitness and executive functions in adolescents: cross-sectional associations with academic achievement. J. Phys. Ther. Sci. 31: 556–562. https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jpts/31/7/31_17-478/_article

article_title: Physical fitness and executive functions in adolescents: cross-sectional associations with academic achievement
citation: Cancela J, Burgo H, Sande E. (2019). Physical fitness and executive functions in adolescents: cross-sectional associations with academic achievement. J. Phys. Ther. Sci. 31: 556–562. https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jpts/31/7/31_17-478/_article
title: Physical fitness and executive function assessment battery for adolescents
description: A battery of nine physical tests and five cognitive instruments used to assess adolescents' fitness and executive functions: "resistance strength with the 30-second Chair Stand Test", explosive strength (standing broad jump), agility and speed (10 × 5 m shuttle run, quadrant jump), aerobic endurance (20 m shuttle run, 6 min endurance run), balance (BOT-2), flexibility (Sit and Reach, Back Scratch), plus PAQ-A, Stroop Golden Test, Wechsler Memory Scale, Symbol Digit Modalities Test, Trail Making Test and MESSY Scale. Academic achievement came from school records across six subjects scored 0–10.
requirements: Trained professionals administered the tests over a 5-month period in five randomly selected centers
constraints: Administered to Compulsory Secondary Education students in the Galician Autonomous Community
target_learners: secondary school adolescents (12–16 years)
target_learning_goals: physical fitness and executive function assessment
examples: Data were collected with objective measurements and questionnaires by five trained education professionals

article_title: Examining the Differential Role of General and Specific Processing Speed in Predicting Mathematical Achievement in Junior High School
citation: Cheng Dazhi, Shi Kaihui, Wang Naiyi, Miao Xinyang, Zhou Xinlin. (2022). Examining the Differential Role of General and Specific Processing Speed in Predicting Mathematical Achievement in Junior High School. Journal of Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10010001
title: CHC-based division of processing speed into general (perceptual and decision speed) and specific (reading and arithmetic fluency) components
description: Following the Cattell–Horn–Carroll theory of cognitive abilities as presented by Schneider and McGrew (2012), the article organizes processing speed into two components: general processing speed, comprising perceptual speed and decision speed, and specific processing speed, comprising reading fluency and arithmetic fluency, which the authors treat as representing academic fluency. The article states that "Processing speed is divided into general processing speed (perceptual and decision speed) and specific processing speed (number facility/arithmetic and reading fluency [representing the academic fluency])". The study operationalizes general speed with choice reaction time and figure matching, and specific speed with word semantics and three arithmetic tasks, then tests their differential prediction of achievement.
requirements: Tasks must separately measure perceptual/decision speed and domain-specific symbolic fluency (reading and arithmetic)
constraints: The distinction is tested in junior high school students in a Chinese school context using timed computerized tasks
target_learners: junior high school students (Grade 7–9)
target_learning_goals: mathematical achievement and academic achievement in major subjects (mathematics, Chinese, English)
examples: The study administered choice reaction time and figure matching as general speed tasks, and word semantic, simple subtraction, complex subtraction, and complex multiplication as specific speed tasks
key_sources: Cheng Dazhi, Shi Kaihui, Wang Naiyi, Miao Xinyang, Zhou Xinlin. (2022). Examining the Differential Role of General and Specific Processing Speed in Predicting Mathematical Achievement in Junior High School. Journal of Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.3390/jintelligence10010001

article_title: Underpinnings of the Costs of Flexibility in Preschool Children: The Roles of Inhibition and Working Memory
citation: Chevalier N., Sheffield T. D., Nelson J. M., Clark C. A. C., Wiebe S. A., Espy K. A. (2012). Underpinnings of the Costs of Flexibility in Preschool Children: The Roles of Inhibition and Working Memory. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3308575/
title: Goal representation as a common component linking executive functions, with mixing costs indexing it and local costs indexing switch implementation
description: The article adopts the task-switching framework in which flexibility has two components: goal representation (monitoring for the need to switch and selecting the relevant task goal), indexed by mixing costs, and switch implementation (the actual switch to the newly relevant task-set), indexed by local costs. Mixing costs "mainly reflect the additional necessity of generating/abstracting the relevant task goal," whereas local costs are "viewed as primarily sensitive to difficulties in switch implementation." The authors use this decomposition to test whether inhibition and working memory differentially support the two components, and conclude the executive-skill relation to flexibility "seems exclusively driven by goal representation."
requirements: Task batteries must include both baseline and mixed-task blocks, as in the Shape School, to compute mixing and local costs separately
constraints: Costs are meaningful only for participants with rudimentary switching abilities; perseveration must be modeled to avoid artificial distortion of cost magnitudes
target_learners: preschool children ages 3;9 to 5;3
target_learning_goals: understanding the executive-control processes supporting cognitive flexibility in early childhood
examples: The study computed mixing costs as baseline versus no-shift trial contrasts and local costs as no-shift versus shift trial contrasts within the Shape School switch condition

citation: Chevalier N., Sheffield T. D., Nelson J. M., Clark C. A. C., Wiebe S. A., Espy K. A. (2012). Underpinnings of the Costs of Flexibility in Preschool Children: The Roles of Inhibition and Working Memory. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3308575/
title: Developmental shift from unitary executive control toward increasing reliance on common goal-representation skills across the preschool period
description: The article proposes that the late-emerging relation of inhibition and working memory to mixing costs reflects age-related change in the processes children recruit, "with a shift from bottom-up or task-related processes to increasingly efficient top-down executive skills that are common to flexibility, inhibition and working memory." As children grow older, they "may increasingly draw upon developing goal representation skills to complete flexibility tasks as well as working memory and inhibition tasks." This account reconciles evidence for unitary executive function in preschoolers with the separable three-factor structure observed at later ages, positioning goal representation as possibly "a fundamental component of executive skills."
requirements: Longitudinal or cross-sectional designs spanning multiple preschool ages to detect the changing pattern of relations
constraints: The relation emerges only from age 4;6 onward; no association with inhibition or working memory is observed at age 3;9
target_learners: preschool children ages 3;9 to 5;3
target_learning_goals: understanding developmental changes in executive control and flexibility during early childhood
examples: The authors interpret the age-graded interaction pattern as evidence that older preschoolers recruit maturing goal-representation skills across flexibility, inhibition, and working-memory tasks

citation: Chevalier N., Sheffield T. D., Nelson J. M., Clark C. A. C., Wiebe S. A., Espy K. A. (2012). Underpinnings of the Costs of Flexibility in Preschool Children: The Roles of Inhibition and Working Memory. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3308575/
title: Shape School task with baseline and switch conditions for measuring flexibility components in preschoolers
description: The Shape School is a computerized task in which children name cartoon stimuli by color or shape, conveyed through a story about school activities. It includes a color baseline block (12 test trials), a shape baseline block (6 practice and 12 test trials), and a switch condition (6 practice and 15 test trials) where hatted stimuli cue shape naming and hatless stimuli cue color naming, yielding 10 shift and 4 no-shift trials. The article selected it because it "contains both baseline and mixed-task blocks, and has demonstrated psychometric reliability and validity." Accuracy was coded from videorecorded sessions with 93.83% inter-rater agreement.
requirements: Stimuli must dissociate color and shape dimensions to reduce perseveration in 3-year-olds
Examiner-paced trial progression to accommodate young children's response speeds
constraints: The fixed condition order and limited trial count prevented modeling dimension (color vs. shape) effects on switch costs
target_learners: preschool children ages 3 to 5
target_learning_goals: assessing cognitive flexibility, including goal representation and switch implementation components
examples: Children completed the color baseline, shape baseline, and switch conditions in a single videorecorded laboratory session

citation: Chevalier N., Sheffield T. D., Nelson J. M., Clark C. A. C., Wiebe S. A., Espy K. A. (2012). Underpinnings of the Costs of Flexibility in Preschool Children: The Roles of Inhibition and Working Memory. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3308575/
title: Go/No-Go and Nebraska Barnyard tasks measuring inhibition and working memory in preschoolers
description: The Go/No-Go task, adapted from Simpson and Riggs, presents fish (Go, 75% of trials) and sharks (No-Go, 25%) with children pressing a button for fish and withholding for sharks; the percentage of correct No-Go responses indexes "inhibition of the prepotent, more frequent button press response." The Nebraska Barnyard is a computerized complex span task adapted from the Noisy Book in which children remember sequences of animal names and press corresponding colored boxes, with span scored as "the maximum span length (highest span where the subject was correct on two trials)." Both were standardized before entering multilevel models so their effects on costs were directly comparable.
requirements: Standardization of scores prior to modeling to allow direct comparison of inhibition and working-memory effect magnitudes
Discontinuation criteria in the span task to manage young children's fatigue and noncompliance
target_learners: preschool children ages 3 to 5
target_learning_goals: assessing inhibitory control and working-memory maintenance in early childhood
examples: Children completed 40 Go/No-Go test trials (30 Go, 10 No-Go) and span trials beginning at sequences of two animals

article_title: Predicting word reading and comprehension with executive function and speed measures across development: A latent variable analysis.
citation: Christopher, M. E., Miyake, A., Keenan, J. M., Pennington, B., DeFries, J. C., Wadsworth, S. J., Willcutt, E., & Olson, R. K. (2012). Predicting Word Reading and Comprehension with Executive Function and Speed Measures Across Development: A Latent Variable Analysis. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3360115/
title: Latent variable decomposition of shared versus unique cognitive predictors of separable reading constructs
description: The article's framework models word reading, reading comprehension, and listening comprehension as latent factors and asks which cognitive constructs predict their shared and unique variance. Latent variables represent "only what is common amongst the observed variables that define it, creating a more precise and 'pure' measure of the construct." Structural paths estimate how much change in a cognitive factor predicts change in a reading factor after controlling for correlated factors. The framework allowed the authors to test whether each of four cognitive abilities was a unique predictor and whether relations held across two age groups.
requirements: Multiple observed measures per latent construct to define each factor
Adequate sample size for confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling
constraints: The article states SEM modeling is correlational in nature and loadings should not be interpreted as suggesting that a change in the independent variable causes change in the dependent variable
target_learners: Children ages 8 to 16 learning to read and comprehend text
target_learning_goals: Word reading accuracy
Reading comprehension of extended text
examples: The study used CFA to establish reading and cognitive factors, then SEM with structural paths from each cognitive factor to each reading factor, constrained across age groups

title: Cognitive and reading test battery from the Colorado Learning Disabilities Research Center twin study
description: The study drew on a battery of measures administered across four 2.5-hour testing sessions to 483 twins ages 8 to 16. Working memory was measured with digit span, sentence span, and counting span; inhibition with GDS CPT vigilance and distractibility commission errors and stop-signal reaction time; processing speed with Colorado perceptual speed and ETS identical pictures; naming speed with RAN colors and objects. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 145(4), 451-466. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000146
title: Simple view of reading as a genetic etiological model
description: The study tests the simple view of reading (Hoover & Gough, 1990), which posits that "successful reading comprehension is the product of word reading and listening comprehension skills". The nested and hierarchical reading models provide etiological support: all phenotypic variance in reading comprehension was captured by the common reading latent variable, with word reading and listening comprehension showing independent genetic variance.

article_title: Knowledge is power: How conceptual knowledge transforms visual cognition
citation: Collins, Jessica A., & Olson, Ingrid R. (2014). Knowledge is Power: How Conceptual Knowledge Transforms Visual Cognition. Psychonomic bulletin & review. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-013-0564-3
title: Categorical perception: category knowledge warps perceptual representations along category boundaries
description: Categorical perception is the phenomenon whereby continuous perceptual variation is experienced as discrete qualitative changes organized by learned category boundaries. The review presents it as the most robust evidence that conceptual knowledge penetrates visual analysis: category knowledge abstracts over within-class differences and highlights between-class differences, observed for color, faces, and trained novel objects. It functions as an information-compression mechanism that lets perceivers efficiently process features relevant to behavior.
requirements: Category knowledge or labels relevant to the stimulus dimension must be available to the perceiver
constraints: Within-category differences are attenuated relative to between-category differences, not eliminated; the review notes individuals remain sensitive to within-category phonetic differences
target_learners: adult perceivers
children acquiring category labels
target_learning_goals: learning category structures that organize perceptual dimensions
examples: The rainbow is perceived as seven distinct color bands despite a continuous range of light frequencies; color perception remains categorical even in psychophysically balanced color spaces
key_sources: Collins, Jessica A., & Olson, Ingrid R. (2014). Knowledge is Power: How Conceptual Knowledge Transforms Visual Cognition. Psychonomic bulletin & review. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-013-0564-3

article_title: Knowledge is power: How conceptual knowledge transforms visual cognition
citation: Collins, Jessica A., & Olson, Ingrid R. (2014). Knowledge is Power: How Conceptual Knowledge Transforms Visual Cognition. Psychonomic bulletin & review. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-013-0564-3
title: Label-feedback hypothesis: labels act as modulators of a distributed interactive perceptual process
description: The review presents Lupyan's label-feedback hypothesis as a solution to the paradox that categorical perception is both robust (altering early perceptual processing) and fragile (mitigated by verbal working memory load). Language is treated not as a separate verbal module but as a modulator of a distributed interactive process: category-diagnostic perceptual features automatically activate labels, which feed back to amplify those features, enabling quick and transient modulation of perceptual representations.
requirements: Availability of verbal labels, which can be up- or down-regulated by linguistic manipulations such as verbal working memory load
constraints: The review notes an alternative account: left-lateralized categorical perception may reflect left-hemisphere propensity for category-level discriminations rather than language recruitment per se
target_learners: adult perceivers with established label systems
target_learning_goals: understanding how verbal labels shape perceptual discrimination learning
examples: Occupying verbal working memory interferes with categorical perception of color patches; non-linguistic categories also show categorical perception with left-hemisphere lateralization

citation: Collins, Jessica A., & Olson, Ingrid R. (2014). Knowledge is Power: How Conceptual Knowledge Transforms Visual Cognition. Psychonomic bulletin & review. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-013-0564-3
title: Embodied cognition account: concepts are instantiated in the neural regions required for perception and action
description: The embodied account holds that "concepts are instantiated in the same neural regions required for specific types of perception and action." Support comes from neuroimaging showing sensory and motor areas are recruited during modality-specific semantic tasks (e.g., color knowledge activating left fusiform and lingual gyri), TMS studies showing causal roles of motor cortex in processing motion-related words, and behavioral interactions between motion perception and motion-language comprehension whose direction depends on stimulus saliency and integratability.
requirements: Modality-specific semantic processing that recruits the corresponding sensory or motor cortical systems
constraints: The review concludes the literature does not show embodiment is necessary for semantic understanding; behavioral effects may arise at response selection, and imaging activations may reflect spreading activation from amodal areas
target_learners: adult semantic processors
individuals with varying object-related experience
target_learning_goals: understanding how semantic knowledge is neurally represented
examples: Retrieval of tactile information activates somatosensory, motor, and premotor areas; rTMS to hand-area M1 disrupts processing of hand-related words specifically

article_title: Experiences of racism and subjective cognitive function in African American women
citation: Coogan P, Schon K, Li S, Cozier Y, Bethea T, Rosenberg L. (2020). Experiences of racism and subjective cognitive function in African American women. Alzheimer's & Dementia: Diagnosis, Assessment & Disease Monitoring. https://doi.org/10.1002/dad2.12067
title: Six-question subjective cognitive function scale from the STIDA telephone dementia screener
description: The article ascertained subjective cognitive function in 2015 using "six yes/no questions" developed for the short Structured Telephone Interview for Dementia Assessment (STIDA), a telephone screener for dementia. Each positive response was assigned 1 point for a total score ranging from 0 to 6, categorized as good (0), moderate (1-2), or poor (3-6). The article reports that "Scores based on the questions have correlated well with results from more extensive cognitive assessments", and cites evidence that self-awareness of poor memory predicts dementia and AD onset.

target_learning_goals: Subjective assessment of memory and cognitive function in epidemiological research

article_title: How do different aspects of spatial skills relate to early arithmetic and number line estimation?
citation: Véronique Cornu, Caroline Hornung, Christine Schiltz, Romain Martin. (2017). The predictive role of spatial skills for arithmetic and number line estimation in kindergarten children. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2017.09.002
title: Spatial skills are non-unitary: orientation, visualization and visuo-motor integration are distinct aspects relevant to early mathematics
description: The article treats spatial skills as a non-unitary construct whose different aspects must be differentiated when studying numerical development. It operationalizes three aspects — a spatial orientation task, a spatial visualization task and a visuo-motor integration task — administered at kindergarten to predict later arithmetic and number line estimation. The abstract notes that "due to the construct’s non-unitary nature, different aspects of spatial skills need to be differentiated". This differentiation framework organizes the study's predictor set and motivates its finding that spatial orientation is the key spatial predictor.
requirements: Spatial skills must be measured with separate tasks capturing distinct aspects (orientation, visualization, visuo-motor integration) rather than a single composite
constraints: The framework was examined in kindergarten children predicting arithmetic and number line estimation within a four-month window

target_learning_goals: early arithmetic
number line estimation
understanding numerical development
examples: The study administered a spatial orientation task, a spatial visualization task and a visuo-motor integration task at Time 1 to 125 kindergarten children

article_title: Transfer from spatial education to verbal reasoning and prediction of transfer from learning-related neural change
citation: Cortes, R. A., Peterson, E. G., Kraemer, D. J. M., Kolvoord, R. A., Uttal, D. H., Dinh, N., Weinberger, A. B., Daker, R. J., Lyons, I. M., Goldman, D., & Green, A. E. (2022). Transfer from spatial education to verbal reasoning and prediction of transfer from learning-related neural change. Science Advances. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.abo3555
title: Mental model theory: spatial processes covertly underlie verbal reasoning, implying spatial education can improve verbal ability
description: Mental model theory (MMT) posits that ostensibly verbal information is processed by co-opted neural resources that evolved to support visuospatial operations, with the spatial process of "scanning" supporting mental model–based reasoning. It further holds that reasoning depends on developing the effectiveness of spatial resources and their integration with executive resources, e.g., functional connectivity of posterior parietal cortex to dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. The article uses MMT to derive the educational hypothesis that curricula fostering spatial cognition, especially spatial scanning, should transfer to verbal reasoning, and tests its behavioral and neural predictions in real-world classrooms.
requirements: Curricula must develop the effectiveness of spatial resources (e.g., spatial scanning) and their integration with executive resources, not merely engage spatial processing
constraints: MMT-based improvement is predicted to depend on developing spatial resource effectiveness, not just engagement; the article notes a curriculum focused on three-dimensional rotation might be needed for mental rotation gains
target_learners: high school students in STEM courses
target_learning_goals: verbal deductive reasoning
spatial thinking
examples: The Geospatial Semester curriculum was designed around scanning maps to identify key spatial features and determine how features relate across maps, operationalizing the MMT-based educational hypothesis

title: Geospatial Semester: a GIS-based in-school spatial curriculum for high school STEM
description: The Geospatial Semester is a real-world high school course, first adopted by Virginia high schools in 2005 and now implemented over two semesters, in which students construct and evaluate spatial representations (maps) of real-world geographical datasets using GIS technology. A central component is to develop students' ability to scan maps to identify key spatial features and determine how these features are related across maps, and to foster more frequent use of spatial thinking strategies. Students take the course for either 45 min daily or 90 min every other day and receive college credit from James Madison University, whose faculty mentor the high school teachers. In this study it was the intervention, offered by the schools and completely unaltered by the researchers to ensure ecological validity.

article_title: Working Memory Underpins Cognitive Development, Learning, and Education
citation: Cowan Nelson. (2014). Working Memory Underpins Cognitive Development, Learning, and Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4207727/
title: Working memory as the small amount of information held in an especially accessible state for use in cognitive tasks
description: The article defines working memory as "the small amount of information that can be held in an especially accessible state and used in cognitive tasks," contrasting it with the vast store of long-term memory. It traces the concept from Locke, James, and Miller through Broadbent, Baddeley and Hitch, and Cowan's own embedded-processes model, in which a subset of activated long-term memory lies in the focus of attention. The framework underpins the article's claims about development, learning, and education.
requirements: Working memory must be distinguished from long-term memory, with the focus of attention holding only a few integrated items or chunks within activated long-term memory
constraints: The article notes the reason for the capacity limit is unknown, with biological, evolutionary, and teleological accounts still under debate
target_learners: learners from infancy to old age
target_learning_goals: planning
comprehension
reasoning
problem-solving
examples: The article uses the example of holding the notion of a cat and the notion of stripes at the same time to grasp the tiger concept correctly

citation: Cowan Nelson. (2014). Working Memory Underpins Cognitive Development, Learning, and Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4207727/
title: Adjust instructional materials to the learner's working memory capacity rather than relying on training to expand it
description: The article advocates a complementary approach to working memory training: "we must learn how to adjust the materials to facilitate learning and education with the working memory abilities that the learner has." Organizing knowledge reduces memory load because parts need not be held in mind independently, and building coherent frameworks in long-term memory reduces the number of ideas held separately in working memory.
requirements: Instructional materials must be organized so that ideas can be associated to one another in long-term memory rather than held independently in working memory
constraints: The article states the best way to improve education using working memory knowledge is still controversial
target_learners: children and adults in educational settings
target_learning_goals: comprehension
learning of new concepts
following instructions
examples: The article rewrites a taxing sentence about a fall vacation so the unifying theme comes first, keeping working memory load low for the reader

citation: Cowan Nelson. (2014). Working Memory Underpins Cognitive Development, Learning, and Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4207727/
title: Avoid presenting more than a few items or ideas at once unless they can be rapidly integrated
description: From the summary of what working memory research establishes, the article draws a practical rule: "To avoid overtaxing an individual's working-memory capabilities, one should avoid presenting more than a few items or ideas at once, unless the items can be rapidly integrated." It also advises avoiding making people hold unintegrated information for a very long time, as in sentences that delay the unifying theme.
requirements: Presentations must respect the roughly 3 to 4 chunk capacity limit, or provide rapid integration of items into larger chunks
constraints: The rule applies when learners have limited long-term knowledge of the topic, since expertise allows slots to be filled with complex concepts
target_learners: preschool children following instructions
novice learners reading instructional text
target_learning_goals: comprehension of instructions
reading comprehension
concept formation
examples: The article notes teachers must be sensitive to the possibility that part of a two-step instruction to a preschool child may be forgotten before it is carried out
