article_title: Metacognitive emotion regulation: Children's awareness that changing thoughts and goals can alleviate negative emotions.
citation: Davis, E. L., Levine, L. J., Lench, H. C., & Quas, J. A. (2010). Metacognitive Emotion Regulation: Children’s Awareness that Changing Thoughts and Goals Can Alleviate Negative Emotions. Emotion, 10(4), 498–510. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018428
title: Functionalist appraisal account linking discrete emotions to goal-status change and distinct regulation strategies
description: The article adopts a functionalist model in which "people experience emotions when the status of a goal has changed." Anger arises when a goal is obstructed but reinstatement seems possible and motivates action against obstacles; sadness reflects irrevocable goal failure; fear reflects threatened but not yet occurred goal failure. The authors used this account to predict which regulation strategies children would report for each emotion, and the Study 2 pattern was consistent with it.
requirements: Predicting strategy–emotion matches requires knowing the appraisal profile (goal status) of the specific emotion
constraints: The article notes future research must test whether event controllability, which was not manipulated, also shapes children's strategy selection
target_learners: 5- and 6-year-old children
target_learning_goals: emotion regulation and coping with negative emotions
examples: Children reported changing goals most often for sad events such as a pet's death, where the goal cannot be reinstated, and changing thoughts for frightening events such as a monster under the bed.
key_sources: Davis, E. L., Levine, L. J., Lench, H. C., & Quas, J. A. (2010). Metacognitive Emotion Regulation: Children’s Awareness that Changing Thoughts and Goals Can Alleviate Negative Emotions. Emotion, 10(4), 498–510. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018428

article_title: Metacognitive emotion regulation: Children's awareness that changing thoughts and goals can alleviate negative emotions.
citation: Davis, E. L., Levine, L. J., Lench, H. C., & Quas, J. A. (2010). Metacognitive Emotion Regulation: Children’s Awareness that Changing Thoughts and Goals Can Alleviate Negative Emotions. Emotion, 10(4), 498–510. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018428
title: Assess young children's regulatory knowledge with familiar scenarios and multiple probe opportunities
description: The article argues that abstract, unfamiliar, single-probe tasks led prior research to underestimate 5- and 6-year-olds' metacognitive emotion regulation knowledge. When children were given familiar events and repeated opportunities to suggest strategies, the majority described metacognitive strategies. Assessments of young children's knowledge should therefore use familiar contexts and allow multiple responses before concluding a capability is absent.
requirements: Assessment tasks must use scenarios familiar to the child's own experience and provide repeated follow-up prompts
constraints: The article notes hypothetical tasks may not reflect what children would actually do in a real emotional situation
target_learners: 5- and 6-year-old children entering formal education
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of children's emotion regulation knowledge
examples: In Study 1, children heard four familiar narratives and received eight to sixteen prompts across stories; in Study 2, children recalled their own sad, angry, and scary events and described what they did to feel better.

article_title: Associations between preschool language and first grade reading outcomes in bilingual children
citation: Davison, Megan Dunn; Hammer, Carol; Lawrence, Frank R. (2011). Associations between Preschool Language and First Grade Reading Outcomes in Bilingual Children. Journal of Communication Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3138808/
title: Common Underlying Proficiency (CUP) model of bilingual language and literacy development
description: The CUP model, proposed by Cummins, holds that bilingual children's experience with either language promotes a shared proficiency underlying both languages, which in turn supports literacy in each. The article states that "experience with either language can promote development of the proficiency underlying both languages, given adequate motivation and exposure to both either in school or in the wider environment." This study's cross-language findings—English language growth predicting Spanish reading and vice versa—are presented as empirical support for the model. McSwan and Rolstad's refinement holds that both languages access the same store of knowledge, so transfer occurs as a natural consequence of mental architecture rather than as movement between languages.
requirements: Children need adequate motivation and exposure to both languages for experience in either to promote the shared underlying proficiency
constraints: The article notes application of the CUP model to bilingual preschoolers and later reading outcomes had received relatively little attention before this study
target_learners: bilingual preschool children developing two languages simultaneously
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension and word identification in both first and second language
examples: The study's finding that growth in English receptive language predicted Spanish reading outcomes and Spanish growth predicted English reading outcomes is presented as evidence for the CUP model
key_sources: Davison, Megan Dunn; Hammer, Carol; Lawrence, Frank R. (2011). Associations between Preschool Language and First Grade Reading Outcomes in Bilingual Children. Journal of Communication Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3138808/

article_title: Associations between preschool language and first grade reading outcomes in bilingual children
citation: Davison, Megan Dunn; Hammer, Carol; Lawrence, Frank R. (2011). Associations between Preschool Language and First Grade Reading Outcomes in Bilingual Children. Journal of Communication Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3138808/
title: Assess bilingual children's language growth over time in both languages rather than performance at a single point
description: The article recommends that preschool programs target children's progress in acquiring language rather than their performance on a test at one time. It states that "language assessments that focus upon the growth of children's language development may provide a better understanding of the impact of children's language abilities upon reading development." Because bilingual children's proficiencies in each language are still changing, single-point assessments may miss their current underlying proficiencies; periodic assessment in both languages reveals whether growth is occurring and whether instructional modifications are needed.
requirements: Data on children's language abilities in both languages must be collected at entry to an educational setting and then assessed periodically to determine change in each language
constraints: The study's evidence base is limited to children in English-immersion Head Start classrooms; generalization to other instructional contexts is limited
target_learners: bilingual preschool children from low-socioeconomic backgrounds
target_learning_goals: oral language development in both languages supporting later reading
examples: The study used growth curve modeling across four measurement occasions in Head Start rather than single-point scores, using raw scores to capture individual change patterns

citation: Davison, Megan Dunn; Hammer, Carol; Lawrence, Frank R. (2011). Associations between Preschool Language and First Grade Reading Outcomes in Bilingual Children. Journal of Communication Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3138808/
title: Longitudinal bilingual language and literacy dataset from 81 Head Start children with growth curve analysis
description: The study's dataset comprises 81 bilingual Puerto Rican-heritage children from low-income families in Central Pennsylvania, assessed in fall and spring of two Head Start years and at the end of first grade. Language measures included the TELD-3 and PPVT-III for English, the PLS-3 and TVIP for Spanish, and the WLPB-R letter-word identification and passage comprehension subtests for reading. Children were divided into Home English Communicators (n = 48) and School English Communicators (n = 33) based on mothers' reports of English exposure timing. Growth curve models were estimated using R-software 2.5.1 with measurement occasion as the time metric.
requirements: Participants were typically-developing children who passed hearing and developmental screenings and were eligible for two years of Head Start
constraints: Approximately 20% of children could not be located over the four-year period; language tests were standardized on monolingual populations
target_learners: bilingual preschool children from low-income families
target_learning_goals: predicting first-grade reading outcomes from preschool language growth
examples: Raw scores were used instead of standard scores because standard scores based on monolingual norms would reflect little change for typically-developing children

article_title: Development of Metacognition in Adolescence: The Congruency-Based Metacognition Scale
citation: dos Santos Kawata KH, Ueno Y, Hashimoto R, Yoshino S, Ohta K, Nishida A, Ando S, Nakatani H, Kasai K and Koike S (2021) Development of Metacognition in Adolescence: The Congruency-Based Metacognition Scale. Front. Psychol. 11:565231. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.565231
title: The Congruency-based Metacognition Scale (CMS)
description: The CMS is a questionnaire measuring metacognitive ability and self-judgment accuracy in children and adolescents through perspective-taking congruency. The CMS metacognition score is computed as the sum of absolute differences between the child's third-person-perspective self-report (3PP_Self, e.g., "Does your mother/father think you are kind?") and the parent's first-person-perspective report (1PP_Other, e.g., "Do you think your son/daughter is kind?"). The self-judgment accuracy score is the sum of absolute differences between the child's 1PP_Self and 3PP_Self reports. Lower scores indicate greater capacity on both measures. The scale uses 20 trait adjectives (10 positive, 10 negative) rated on a four-point Likert scale.
requirements: Requires paired child-parent responses: the child completes 1PP_Self and 3PP_Self conditions while the parent completes the 1PP_Other condition
Uses 20 familiar personality-trait adjectives counterbalanced between positive and negative words, rated on a four-point Likert-type scale
constraints: The majority of "other/parents" were represented by maternal rather than paternal figures
The questionnaire may be more reliable for measuring for adolescents, as the sample of children over age 22 was small
target_learners: children and adolescents (age range 10.8-29.3 years in the validation sample)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive ability (awareness and understanding of one's own cognitive status)
self-judgment accuracy
examples: Administered to 633 child-parent pairs across three surveys in Tokyo prefecture between September 2013 and January 2020

article_title: Prevalence and diagnostic validity of motivational impairments and deficits in visuospatial short-term memory and working memory in ADHD subtypes
citation: S. Dovis, S. van der Oord, H.M. Huizenga, R.W. Wiers, P.J.M. Prins. (2015). Prevalence and diagnostic validity of motivational impairments and deficits in visuospatial short-term memory and working memory in ADHD subtypes. European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, 24(5), 575-590. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-014-0612-1
title: Dual-condition reinforcement-sensitivity indexing of visuospatial WM and STM in ADHD subtypes
description: The study operationalizes reinforcement sensitivity by administering the same visuospatial WM and STM tasks under two conditions: a standard feedback-only condition and a high-reinforcement condition adding a monetary reward. Reinforcement sensitivity is then indexed as the difference in performance between the reinforcement conditions, allowing motivational impairment to be measured separately from baseline memory capacity. This design also permits subtype comparisons (ADHD-C vs ADHD-I vs controls) while controlling for the interaction between motivational impairments and cognitive performance.
requirements: Administration of identical visuospatial WM and STM tasks under both a standard feedback-only condition and a high-reinforcement condition
constraints: Reinforcement sensitivity is operationalized only as the performance difference between the two conditions, not as a broader motivational construct
target_learners: children aged 8-12 with ADHD-C or ADHD-I
typically developing children aged 8-12
target_learning_goals: measuring visuospatial working memory and short-term memory capacity
indexing sensitivity to reinforcement
examples: Visuospatial WM and STM tasks were administered in a standard (feedback-only) and a high-reinforcement (feedback + 10 euros) condition to 86 children with ADHD-C, 27 children with ADHD-I, and 62 typically developing controls.

article_title: Dose-Related Effects of Alcohol on Cognitive Functioning
citation: Dry MJ, Burns NR, Nettelbeck T, Farquharson AL, White JM (2012) Dose-Related Effects of Alcohol on Cognitive Functioning. PLoS ONE 7(11): e50977. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0050977
title: Six-test repeated-measures cognitive battery (UFOV, SOPT, IT, TSP, SART, TMT)
description: A battery of six widely used psychometric tests administered in a fixed order (UFOV, SOPT, IT, TSP, SART, TMT) at four time-points, chosen because each measures a process previously shown to be alcohol-sensitive, each is well-known and easily accessible, and each is "suitable for repeated measures designs". The battery could be completed in 40-50 minutes, minimizing variability from rising and falling BACs. TMT forms were symmetrically transformed to remove learning effects across presentations.
requirements: Tasks must be free of strategies producing abrupt outcome changes, or alterable to achieve this, for repeated administration
constraints: The battery requires approximately 40-50 minutes per test-run, which the authors note constrains testing within a stable BAC window
target_learners: adults aged 18-45 years
target_learning_goals: measuring dose-related changes across processing speed, working memory, strategic optimization, vigilance, response inhibition, cognitive flexibility and psychomotor function
examples: Participants completed the battery three times on day 1 for practice and once at baseline plus three dosed time-points on day 2

article_title: Parent, Teacher, and Student Perspectives on How Corrective Lenses Improve Child Wellbeing and School Function
citation: Dudovitz, R. N., Izadpanah, N., Chung, P. J., & Slusser, W. (2016). Parent, Teacher, and Student Perspectives on how Corrective Lenses Improve Child Wellbeing and School Function. Maternal and Child Health Journal. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10995-015-1882-z
title: Vision to Learn (VTL) school-based vision program
description: Vision to Learn is a non-profit, established in 2012, that partners with schools to provide free corrective lenses to low-income students. School nurses conduct screenings; a mobile eye clinic visits the school site, pediatric optometrists perform comprehensive exams after parental consent, students choose frames, and glasses are delivered to the school about two weeks later, with free replacement pairs. The program covers frames, lenses, exams, and administration at roughly $100 per child.
requirements: School nurse support to conduct the initial screening exam, which the article states is the only cost to schools
constraints: The article describes the program for low-income elementary school populations in Los Angeles

target_learning_goals: improving access to and use of corrective lenses to support school function
examples: Three Los Angeles elementary schools (two public, one Catholic) serving predominantly Latino students participated in the evaluation

article_title: Audience effects on the neural correlates of relational reasoning in adolescence
citation: Dumontheil Iroise, Wolf Laura K., Blakemore Sarah-Jayne. (2016). Audience effects on the neural correlates of relational reasoning in adolescence. Neuropsychologia. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2016.05.001
title: Fronto-parietal relational-integration network
description: The article describes relational reasoning as engaging "a fronto-parietal network including the inferior parietal cortex, pre-supplementary motor area, dorsolateral and rostrolateral prefrontal cortices", with the rostrolateral prefrontal cortex specifically associated with relational integration. In the study, this network was functionally defined by the Relational>Control contrast and served as the region-of-interest for testing audience and age modulation. It provides the neural framework within which the peer audience effects were interpreted.
requirements: Defined empirically via the Relational>Control contrast at voxel-level p<0.001 uncorrected and cluster-level pFWE<0.05
constraints: The study examined female participants only, aged 14–16 and 23–28 years
target_learners: mid-adolescents (14–16 years)
adults (23–28 years)
target_learning_goals: relational reasoning
fluid reasoning associated with academic achievement
examples: The contrast revealed activations in preSMA, bilateral inferior and superior parietal lobules, bilateral occipital cortex and bilateral frontal clusters extending into the RLPFC

article_title: Mindsets: A View From Two Eras
citation: Dweck, C. S., & Yeager, D. S. (2019). Mindsets: A View From Two Eras. Perspectives on Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691618804166
title: Mindset meaning-system framework: fixed versus growth mindsets organize goals, effort beliefs, attributions, and persistence
description: The meaning-system framework holds that mindsets are not isolated beliefs but organizing structures that link goals, effort beliefs, attributions, and persistence into a coherent system. The article states that "mindsets create meaning systems" and that when people view ability as fixed, validating ability takes on more importance, high effort may signal low ability, and setbacks are attributed to low ability, curtailing persistence; when people view ability as improvable, learning goals, effort as a tool, and setbacks as information sustain persistence. This framework organizes the first era of mindset research and generates the challenge-seeking and resilience predictions tested in later studies.
requirements: Reliable ways to assess and manipulate mindsets, which the authors describe as hard-won: "It took a lot of hard work to hone the idea and to develop ways to reliably assess and manipulate these theories or mindsets".
constraints: The article notes a growth mindset is not always positive: persistence without progress should be questioned, and a growth mindset can be used for negative ends.
target_learners: students from grade school through college
target_learning_goals: challenge seeking
persistence and resilience after setbacks
academic achievement
key_sources: Dweck, C. S., & Yeager, D. S. (2019). Mindsets: A View From Two Eras. Perspectives on Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691618804166

article_title: Mindsets: A View From Two Eras
citation: Dweck, C. S., & Yeager, D. S. (2019). Mindsets: A View From Two Eras. Perspectives on Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/1745691618804166
title: False growth mindset: educator practices that profess but fail to communicate a growth mindset
description: The article names "false growth mindset", a term coined by Susan Mackie, for practices of educators who profess a growth mindset but implement practices that fail to communicate it, sometimes doing the opposite. The core failure mode is that "many educators, it appeared, simply equated a growth mindset with effort", praising effort even when it was ineffective, which could leave students feeling incompetent; other forms include lecturing on mindset without changing classroom practices, and ignoring achievement differences so advanced students go unchallenged. The concept motivates the call for teacher curricula and mindset-supportive environments.
requirements: Educators need far more guidance than the authors initially provided, plus accurate understanding of what a growth mindset is and practices that embody it.
constraints: Focusing on effort alone, without good strategies, mentorship, and access to resources, can lead to blaming the victim when a person is not successful.
target_learners: K-12 and college students taught by educators implementing mindset practices
target_learning_goals: accurate growth-mindset communication
effective effort and strategy use
challenge seeking
examples: Educators put up posters or gave a lecture on growth mindset and then returned to business as usual, expecting students to do the rest.

article_title: Age and Verbal Fluency: The Mediating Effect of Speed of Processing
citation: Safa A. Elgamal, MBBCh, PhD, Eric A. Roy, PhD, Michael T. Sharratt, PhD. (2011). Age and Verbal Fluency: The Mediating Effect of Speed of Processing. Canadian Geriatrics Journal, Volume 14, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.5770/cgj.v14i3.17
title: Control for processing speed when interpreting similarly timed cognitive tasks across age groups
description: The article recommends that researchers and clinicians controlling for processing speed should be considered essential when interpreting results from similarly timed cognitive tasks, especially when the between-group variable suggests a possible effect for speed of performance. The study demonstrates why: apparent age effects on fluency depended on whether processing speed was controlled, with letter fluency differences emerging only after covariate adjustment. The authors argue that tasks measuring the same cognitive construct may employ different brain processes, so task psychological properties must be appreciated to avoid misinterpreting results.
requirements: Tasks that are similarly timed across comparison groups
A between-group variable that suggests a possible effect for speed of performance
constraints: The article frames this for similarly timed cognitive tasks; it does not claim the recommendation extends to untimed measures
target_learners: older adults undergoing cognitive assessment
healthy adults across the adult lifespan
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of age-related differences in verbal fluency and other timed cognitive measures
examples: The study's ANCOVA models revealed significant letter fluency differences between age groups that the initial ANOVA had not shown, after controlling for the processing speed composite and NART-estimated IQ
key_sources: Safa A. Elgamal, MBBCh, PhD, Eric A. Roy, PhD, Michael T. Sharratt, PhD. (2011). Age and Verbal Fluency: The Mediating Effect of Speed of Processing. Canadian Geriatrics Journal, Volume 14, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.5770/cgj.v14i3.17

article_title: Age and Verbal Fluency: The Mediating Effect of Speed of Processing
citation: Safa A. Elgamal, MBBCh, PhD, Eric A. Roy, PhD, Michael T. Sharratt, PhD. (2011). Age and Verbal Fluency: The Mediating Effect of Speed of Processing. Canadian Geriatrics Journal, Volume 14, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.5770/cgj.v14i3.17
title: Differential aging account: processing speed mediates fluency changes asymmetrically across letter and category tasks
description: The article proposes that aging adversely affects some but not all cognitive domains, and that age-related decline in processing speed contributes to age-related changes in fluency in task-specific ways. For category fluency, slowing partially drives the age-related decline, though a significant portion of the decline remains independent of processing speed. For letter fluency, the relationship is reversed: slow processing masks an enhancement that occurs during the transition from young to middle age. In both cases the age-related change is independent of IQ as measured by the NART. The account holds that decline in one domain may contribute to the apparent decline in another domain that may otherwise remain stationary or even improve with aging.
requirements: Assessment of both fluency types alongside a processing speed measure to detect the differential mediation pattern
constraints: Derived from a cross-sectional design, so results may be confounded by a cohort effect across generations
Sample was highly educated and healthy, which may not represent the true population
target_learners: healthy older adults
adults across the lifespan from young adulthood to old age
target_learning_goals: understanding which cognitive domains decline, remain stable, or improve with normal aging
distinguishing normal age-related cognitive change from impairment warranting further evaluation
examples: Older adults would be able to generate more words in the specified time period if they were not slower than younger adults, per the authors' interpretation of the letter fluency ANCOVA result

article_title: High Cognitive Flexibility Learners Perform Better in Probabilistic Rule Learning
citation: Feng X, Perceval GJ, Feng W and Feng C (2020) High Cognitive Flexibility Learners Perform Better in Probabilistic Rule Learning. Front. Psychol. 11:415. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00415
title: Cognitive flexibility as the ability to switch quickly between tasks and stimulus sets, measured by switch cost
description: The article adopts the understanding that cognitive flexibility refers to "the ability of switching between tasks and stimulus sets in a quick and ﬂexible manner". It operationalizes this construct with the number-letter task, in which the latency difference between switching and non-switching trials is the switch cost, and uses switch cost to divide learners into high and low flexibility groups. The article notes there is still no clear common definition of cognitive flexibility, which influences how the construct is operationalized.
requirements: Measurement requires a task-switching paradigm such as the number-letter task from which a switch cost can be computed; the article argues task-switching paradigms give a purer measure than the WCST by reducing demands for working memory, classified learning and rule reasoning.
constraints: The article states there is still no clear common definition of cognitive flexibility, which can influence how the construct is operationalized in research.
target_learners: undergraduate adults
target_learning_goals: probabilistic rule learning and rule-based decision making
examples: Participants were ranked by switch cost on the number-letter task; the lower 27th percentile formed the high flexibility group and the upper 27th percentile the low flexibility group.

article_title: Trajectories of parental engagement in early childhood among dual-earner families: Effects on child self-control.
citation: Tiago Ferreira, Joana Cadima, Marisa Matias, Joana Marina Vieira, and Teresa Leal; Karine Verschueren; Paula Mena Matos. (2018). Trajectories of Parental Engagement in Early Childhood Among Dual-Earner Families: Effects on Child Self-Control. Developmental Psychology, 54(4), 731–743. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000458
title: Ecological and bioecological framing of parental engagement as a proximal process supporting self-regulation
description: The article frames parental engagement within Bronfenbrenner's bioecological theory, where "human development is driven by reciprocal interactive processes between the developing person and its complex environment." Parent-child shared activities in positive engagement (play, outings, joint projects) are described as "unique opportunities for parents to provide their children with adaptive models of behavioral regulation." Parents act as external regulators of children's emotions and behaviors, supporting internalization of self-control. This framework positions the work-family mesosystem as a context that can either support or undermine these proximal processes through parents' perceived work-family conflict.
requirements: Parents must have opportunities for direct, positive, dyadic interaction with the child in activities that pose emotional challenges
constraints: The framework is applied specifically to dual-earner families with children in the preschool-to-first-grade period in this study
target_learners: four-year-old children in dual-earner families transitioning from preschool to first grade
target_learning_goals: behavioral self-control
emotion regulation in social interactions
socioemotional competence
examples: The study measured engagement via parent reports on the PRQ involvement subscale covering planning free time together, outings, outdoor activities, games, and joint projects

article_title: Trajectories of parental engagement in early childhood among dual-earner families: Effects on child self-control.
citation: Tiago Ferreira, Joana Cadima, Marisa Matias, Joana Marina Vieira, and Teresa Leal; Karine Verschueren; Paula Mena Matos. (2018). title: PRQ involvement subscale as a measure of parental engagement in positive activities
description: The study used the eight-item involvement subscale from the Parenting Relationship Questionnaire—Preschool Form to measure parental engagement. Items tap "parents’ active participation in positive engagement activities, along with the parent’s knowledge of the child’s activities," including planning things to do together, teaching new games, working on projects, taking walks, and doing arts and crafts. Parents rated items on a 4-point Likert scale from never to always. Confirmatory factor analysis showed adequate fit at all three waves for both parents, and measurement invariance held across time and between mothers and fathers. Cronbach's alphas ranged from .84 to .90 for mothers and .84 to .87 for fathers.

Measurement invariance across time and between parents must be established before comparing trajectories

target_learning_goals: measuring frequency of parental engagement in developmentally supportive activities
examples: Sample items include "My child and I plan things to do together" and "My child and I work on projects together"

article_title: Inhibitory Control and Information Processing in ADHD: Comparing the Dual Task and Performance Adjustment Hypotheses
citation: Fosco, W. D., Kofler, M. J., Alderson, R. M., Tarle, S. J., Raiker, J. S., & Sarver, D. E. (2019). Inhibitory Control and Information Processing in ADHD: Comparing the Dual Task and Performance Adjustment Hypotheses. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-018-0504-9
title: Drift diffusion model decomposition of stop-signal slowing: performance adjustment versus dual-task hypotheses
description: The article uses the drift diffusion model (DDM), a well-validated stochastic accumulator model, to decompose task performance into parameters with distinct cognitive interpretations: drift rate (processing speed), boundary separation (response caution), and non-decision time (encoding/motor speed). Within this framework, the dual-task hypothesis predicts slower drift rate and non-decision time with no boundary-separation change, while the performance adjustment hypothesis predicts increased boundary separation with stable drift rate and non-decision time. The study's results matched the performance adjustment pattern. As the article states, "Boundary separation (a) refers to the quantity of information considered before a decision is executed and reflects one's degree of response caution".
requirements: Requires both RT and accuracy data integrated by the model, estimated per participant per task (Kolmogorov-Smirnov algorithm via fast-dm software)
constraints: The article notes non-decision time conflates stimulus encoding and motor response speed, which are not separable in the diffusion model
The study could not determine whether performance adjustments are proactive or reactive
target_learners: children ages 8-13 with and without ADHD
target_learning_goals: understanding neurocognitive mechanisms of inhibitory control and response strategy adjustment
examples: The study estimated drift rate, boundary separation, and non-decision time separately for the No-Tone and Stop-Signal tasks for each child, with acceptable model fit for all participants (all ps > .05)

article_title: Inhibitory Control and Information Processing in ADHD: Comparing the Dual Task and Performance Adjustment Hypotheses
citation: Fosco, W. D., Kofler, M. J., Alderson, R. M., Tarle, S. J., Raiker, J. S., & Sarver, D. E. (2019). Inhibitory Control and Information Processing in ADHD: Comparing the Dual Task and Performance Adjustment Hypotheses. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-018-0504-9
title: Use performance metrics with clearer cognitive interpretations (e.g., diffusion parameters) rather than raw mean reaction time
description: Because mean reaction time conflates distinct cognitive processes, the authors recommend that researchers interpret standard metrics cautiously and prefer measures with clearer cognitive interpretations, such as drift diffusion parameters. In this study, MRT alone would have suggested that stop signals slow processing speed, whereas decomposition showed drift rate was unchanged and slowing reflected increased response caution. As the authors write, "We therefore urge researchers to exercise caution when interpreting standard performance metrics, such as RT and error rates, and to utilize metrics that have clearer cognitive interpretations whenever possible".
requirements: Requires tasks yielding sufficient trial-level RT and accuracy data for diffusion modeling (the article notes excellent parameter recovery with as few as 20 trials per participant)
constraints: Group-difference conclusions are not significantly affected by inflated MRT estimates; the concern applies mainly to aggregating or comparing MRT across studies differing in inhibitory demands
target_learners: children ages 8-13 with and without ADHD
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement and interpretation of cognitive processing in research on attention and self-regulation
examples: If MRT had been the primary outcome in this study, the authors state they would likely have concluded that introducing stop signals slows processing speed, yet drift rate was equivalent across tasks

article_title: The role of metacognition in human social interactions
citation: Frith Chris D. (2012). The role of metacognition in human social interactions. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2012.0123
title: Metacognition comprises implicit and explicit forms serving monitoring and control of cognition
description: The article defines metacognition as the processes by which we monitor and control our own cognitive processes, distinguishing an implicit form that is rapid, automatic and without awareness from an explicit, slow and deliberate form that generates reportable knowledge. It applies the same distinction to mentalizing (metacognition applied to others). This framework organizes the review's argument about social interaction.
requirements: Distinguishing monitoring (reflection on memory/perception) from control (regulation based on that knowledge)
constraints: The article notes the question remains open as to whether the implicit form of self-monitoring should even be called metacognition
target_learners: adults
children
target_learning_goals: understanding metacognitive monitoring and control of one's own cognitive processes
examples: Tip-of-the-tongue states illustrate monitoring; alphabet-search strategies illustrate control; skilled typists slowing after corrected errors illustrate implicit monitoring

article_title: The role of metacognition in human social interactions
citation: Frith Chris D. (2012). The role of metacognition in human social interactions. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2012.0123
title: The we-mode: implicit metacognition automatically adjusts saliency to group-average values during joint action
description: The article proposes that implicit metacognition enables adoption of a we-mode, in which a person's saliency/value map is automatically modified so object values approximate the average of the group derived from implicit estimates of others' goals, knowledge and beliefs. For example, an object within another's reach gains value even if outside one's own. The author proposes this we-mode causes biased pooling of unshared information in group discussion.
requirements: Joint action or mere presence of other people
Implicit estimates of other group members' goals, knowledge and beliefs
constraints: The author notes that if this account is correct, it might be argued it should not be called mentalizing, since others' mental states are not represented as such; people behave as if they were mentalizing
target_learners: adults
children
target_learning_goals: understanding how joint attention and shared goals shape perception and action in collaborative tasks
examples: Objects out of one's own reach but within a partner's reach gain saliency; group discussions favour information held in common (Stasser & Titus, as cited)
key_sources: Frith Chris D. (2012). The role of metacognition in human social interactions. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2012.0123

article_title: The role of metacognition in human social interactions
citation: Frith Chris D. (2012). The role of metacognition in human social interactions. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.2012.0123
title: Explicit metacognition is a uniquely human ability evolved to enhance collaborative decision-making
description: The article argues that explicit metacognition's major function is social: it lets people communicate reflections on action and sensation, share experiences, justify behaviour, and thereby make joint decisions better than the best individual, build accurate world models without objective feedback, and improve individual perception. The author proposes this capacity emerged before language, with language arising as a communicative technology on top of it, distinguishing humans from honeybees whose sharing is automatic and limited to predetermined problems.
requirements: Capacity to discuss perceptual experiences and reasons for actions with others
Willingness to make metacognitive reports even when they do not reflect the true state of affairs
constraints: Absolute certainty about a partner's collaboration can never be achieved, though sufficient confidence suffices in practice
The human capacity for counterfactual representation differs from monkeys quantitatively rather than qualitatively
target_learners: adults
target_learning_goals: understanding the evolutionary and social function of explicit metacognition in human collaboration
examples: Pairs developing unique confidence vocabularies in the odd-ball task; collective intentionality in young children but not chimpanzees (Tomasello, as cited); honeybee waggle-dance sharing as a contrast case

article_title: Stroop task performance across the lifespan: High cognitive reserve in older age is associated with enhanced proactive and reactive interference control
citation: Patrick D. Gajewski, Michael Falkenstein, Sven Th€ones, Edmund Wascher. (2020). Stroop task performance across the lifespan: High cognitive reserve in older age is associated with enhanced proactive and reactive interference control. NeuroImage 207 (2020) 116430. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2019.116430
title: Dual-mechanisms of cognitive control (DMC) framework applied to lifespan interference control
description: The dual-mechanisms of cognitive control framework by Braver (2012) distinguishes two modes of cognitive control. According to the article, "proactive control relies upon the anticipation and prevention of interference before it occurs, whereas reactive control relates to the detection and resolution of interference after its occurrence". The framework proposes that situational factors or individual strategy shift the weighting between the two modes, with situational factors inducing intra-individual variability and stable traits producing inter-individual differences. The study uses the CNV as an index of proactive control and the P2/N2 complex as a correlate of reactive control to locate performance differences between old performer groups within this framework.
requirements: Tasks with high control demands in which proactive and reactive control settings can be dissociated, e.g. cue-based Stroop blocks with preparatory intervals
constraints: The article notes cross-sectional studies are less useful to evaluate compensatory or gain processes
target_learners: young, middle-aged and older adults
target_learning_goals: interference control
executive function
cognitive control in task performance
examples: The study mapped CNV amplitudes onto proactive control and target-locked P2/N2 amplitudes onto reactive control across three Stroop blocks of increasing difficulty
key_sources: Patrick D. Gajewski, Michael Falkenstein, Sven Th€ones, Edmund Wascher. (2020). Stroop task performance across the lifespan: High cognitive reserve in older age is associated with enhanced proactive and reactive interference control. article_title: Stroop task performance across the lifespan: High cognitive reserve in older age is associated with enhanced proactive and reactive interference control
citation: Patrick D. Gajewski, Michael Falkenstein, Sven Th€ones, Edmund Wascher. (2020). Stroop task performance across the lifespan: High cognitive reserve in older age is associated with enhanced proactive and reactive interference control. NeuroImage 207 (2020) 116430. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2019.116430
title: Cognitive reserve as inter-individual differences in neural networks underlying task performance
description: The article adopts the notion of cognitive reserve, which "postulates that inter-individual differences in neural networks underlying task performance allow some people to perform better than others". Reserve accrues from interactions between genetics and environmental factors such as education, physical activity, use of foreign languages, playing an instrument or dancing, skills mediated by neuronal plasticity. High reserve allows compensation for cognitive decline and dementia in older age. The study operationalizes reserve proxies as IQ, education level and foreign language usage, and interprets the enhanced CNV and P2/N2 amplitudes of old high performers as the electrophysiological underpinning of reserve in terms of efficiency, capacity or flexibility.
requirements: Environmental or lifestyle factors that stimulate neuronal plasticity, such as education or cognitively stimulating activities
constraints: The article states inter- and intra-individual differences accrue from complex interactions between genetics and environmental factors, representing widely stable individual properties in old age
target_learners: older adults
target_learning_goals: maintaining executive function and interference control in aging
examples: Old participants were subdivided into low, mid and high performers via inverse efficiency scores, validated against drift-diffusion-model drift rates (r = -.846)

article_title: Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control
citation: Gardiner Paul. (2020). Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2020.100749
title: Framework for epistemic control: a four-stage metacognitive scaffold for collaborative thinking
description: The article proposes a metacognitive framework that scaffolds collaborative thinking on complex problems through four sequential stages: epistemic awareness, epistemic humility, epistemic empathy, and epistemic control. As the abstract states, "Moving from epistemic awareness, through epistemic humility and epistemic empathy, students develop epistemic control." The framework aims to develop students' metacognitive understanding and epistemic awareness to enable epistemic shifting, perspective taking and cross-disciplinary communication, and is summarised in Fig. 1.
requirements: Students first actively reflect on their own disciplinary knowledge tradition, its products and processes, before later stages can develop
constraints: The article presents the framework as a proposal and calls for further research into its benefits across learning contexts; no empirical test of the framework is reported
target_learners: upper secondary students
undergraduate and postgraduate students
target_learning_goals: collaborative creative problem solving on complex problems
interdisciplinary perspective taking and knowledge integration
examples: The framework is presented as a scaffold for individuals working on complex real-world problems in diverse collaborative groups, summarised in Fig. 1

article_title: Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control
citation: Gardiner Paul. (2020). Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2020.100749
title: Epistemic games and forms: disciplines as rule-governed knowledge-making cultures
description: Drawing on Collins and Ferguson (1993), the article frames each discipline as an 'epistemic culture' with a set of rules and strategies: "Each discipline culture has a set of rules and strategies, called epistemic games, that constrain inquiry and target structures." Epistemic games are the mental processes that make knowledge; epistemic forms are the means of communicating and representing inquiry findings. Students are asked 'what do you do in your discipline?' and 'What does that action produce?' to surface their discipline's games and forms, developing domain meta-knowledge that supports creativity within the domain.
requirements: Students need strong understanding of their own domain for epistemic awareness to develop from within it
constraints: The article notes the more disciplines evolve, the more complex and constrained the games and forms become
target_learners: secondary and tertiary students working in disciplinary and interdisciplinary contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding the strengths and limits of one's own way of knowing
domain meta-knowledge supporting disciplinary creativity
examples: Mastering these games and forms grants the learner access to the discipline's community of practice, per Markauskaite and Goodyear (2017)
key_sources: Gardiner Paul. (2020). Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2020.100749

article_title: Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control
citation: Gardiner Paul. (2020). Learning to think together: Creativity, interdisciplinary collaboration and epistemic control. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2020.100749
title: Scaffold creative collaboration by developing epistemic awareness, humility and empathy before expecting epistemic control
description: The article recommends that educators scaffold and structure creative and collaborative learning by moving students through the framework's stages: understanding their own way of knowing, recognising its limits ("Epistemic humility is the understanding that what you know and how you know it, your way of knowing, is not the whole story"), and valuing other disciplines' games and forms. Only then do students reach epistemic control, mobilising a range of ways of knowing for complex problems. Without scaffolds, interdisciplinary discussion risks being adversarial at worst and parallel at best.
requirements: Educators must maintain a safe learning environment where discomfort is intellectual rather than personal or social, balancing epistemic agency and epistemic safety
constraints: The article states educators must be prepared to allow students to sit in discomfort and ambiguity, and that epistemic empathy requires knowledge of other ways of knowing, not just goodwill
target_learners: upper secondary, undergraduate and postgraduate students
target_learning_goals: collaborative creativity on complex problems
willingness to work with ambiguity and integrate disciplinary perspectives
examples: The article argues learning that does not encourage working with ambiguity and collaboration will not prepare students for interdisciplinary teams they will graduate into

article_title: The Relationship between Executive Functions, Working Memory, and Intelligence in Kindergarten Children
citation: Ger Ebru, Roebers Claudia M. (2023). The Relationship between Executive Functions, Working Memory, and Intelligence in Kindergarten Children. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10143737/
title: Target inhibition training as a potential shared component influencing EF, WM, and intelligence in young children
description: The article's practical implication is that inhibition, shown to correlate with both intelligence and verbal WM in kindergartners, may be the most efficient training target. The authors state: "it may be promising to target training inhibition as a potential shared component between EF, WM, and intelligence to have an influence on all three constructs." This rests on their finding that inhibition accuracy correlated with intelligence even after partialling out verbal WM, while the reverse did not hold.
requirements: Interventions should target the inhibition component specifically, as the evidence base for inhibition as the shared component comes from correlational findings in kindergarten-age children.
constraints: The recommendation is based on correlational evidence in 5.5- to 7.5-year-olds, not on a training experiment in this study; the authors note EF training transfer appears to be narrow (Diamond and Ling 2016).
target_learners: Kindergarten children (ages 5.5–7.5)
target_learning_goals: Executive function development, particularly inhibitory control
examples: The study measured inhibition via accuracy in the incongruent block of the Hearts and Flowers task, where children had to press the button opposite to the flower's side, inhibiting a prepotent response established in the congruent hearts block.
key_sources: Ger Ebru, Roebers Claudia M. (2023). The Relationship between Executive Functions, Working Memory, and Intelligence in Kindergarten Children. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10143737/

article_title: The Relationship between Executive Functions, Working Memory, and Intelligence in Kindergarten Children
citation: Ger Ebru, Roebers Claudia M. (2023). The Relationship between Executive Functions, Working Memory, and Intelligence in Kindergarten Children. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10143737/
title: Inhibition rather than monitoring and cognitive control underlies EF–WM–intelligence associations at kindergarten age
description: The article proposes that at kindergarten age, the shared variance between executive functions, working memory, and intelligence is carried primarily by inhibition rather than by metacognitive monitoring and cognitive control (indexed by post-error slowing). The authors conclude: "EF, WM, and intelligence might be linked through inhibition rather than monitoring and cognitive control, at least at kindergarten ages." This framework draws on Miyake et al.'s three-component model of EF and the developmental observation that inhibition is the earliest-developing EF component.
requirements: Assessment of EF components with separate tasks (inhibition, shifting, WM) plus a fluid intelligence measure, as the framework depends on distinguishing component-specific contributions.
constraints: The framework applies to kindergarten ages (5.5–7.5 years); monitoring and cognitive control may explain shared variance only once they reach a substantial level of development, potentially at school age.
target_learners: Kindergarten children (ages 5.5–7.5)
target_learning_goals: Understanding cognitive development of executive functions, working memory, and intelligence
examples: The study operationalized monitoring and cognitive control via post-error slowing in the Hearts and Flowers task and found it unrelated to intelligence or WM, while inhibition accuracy showed the expected associations.
key_sources: Ger Ebru, Roebers Claudia M. (2023). The Relationship between Executive Functions, Working Memory, and Intelligence in Kindergarten Children. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10143737/

article_title: Metacognition for strategy selection during arithmetic problem-solving in young and older adults
citation: Marie Geurten & Patrick Lemaire. (2017). Metacognition for Strategy Selection during Arithmetic Problem Solving in Young and Older Adults. https://www.google.com/search?q=Metacognition+for+Strategy+Selection+during+Arithmetic+Problem+Solving+in+Young+and+Older+Adults
title: Resource account of age invariance and decline in metacognition for strategy selection
description: The article proposes that the accuracy of older adults' metacognitive judgments depends on the cognitive resources a task requires: "Spared metacognitive skills with age would be found for less resource-consuming tasks, and age-related changes for more resource-consuming tasks." In this study, older adults matched young adults' retrospective accuracy under high demands (selection-execution) and exceeded it under low demands (selection-only, homogeneous problems), while their accuracy declined as demands increased. The account is offered to reconcile inconsistent aging findings across tasks.
requirements: Task demands must be measurable or manipulable so that metacognitive accuracy can be compared across less and more resource-consuming conditions
constraints: The authors state further investigations should corroborate the hypothesis, and suggest task-demand effects might be alleviated when crucial cues for accurate judgments are made more salient
target_learners: young adults
older adults
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of one's own strategy selection in arithmetic problem solving
effective regulation of subsequent strategy choices
examples: Older adults' RCJ accuracy was comparable to young adults' in the selection-execution task but higher in the selection-only task, particularly on homogeneous problems

article_title: Neural changes underlying the development of episodic memory during middle childhood
citation: Ghetti Simona; Bunge Silvia A. (2012). Neural Changes Underlying the Development of Episodic Memory During Middle Childhood. Developmental cognitive neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2012.05.002
title: Network account of episodic memory development: concerted maturation of hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and parietal cortex plus long-range connectivity
description: The review's central explanatory framework holds that episodic memory development emerges from a distributed brain network rather than a single region. It proposes that "changes in episodic memory emerge from the concerted effort of a network of relevant brain structures," including local maturational changes in the hippocampus, lateral PFC, and posterior parietal cortex, and changes in long-range connectivity via the uncinate fasciculus, cingulum bundle, and fornix. Hippocampal binding is argued to continue developing during middle childhood rather than being age-invariant, alongside PFC-mediated controlled encoding and retrieval processes.
requirements: Structural or functional neuroimaging evidence tracking multiple network regions and their connecting tracts across development
constraints: An assessment of the relationship between the development of the network as a whole and behavioral changes has yet to be undertaken, per the article's conclusion
target_learners: typically developing children in middle childhood (roughly ages 6–11)
target_learning_goals: episodic memory: encoding, storage, and retrieval of events with contextual detail
examples: The review integrates longitudinal MRI, cross-sectional fMRI, and DTI findings across studies to argue for coordinated hippocampal, prefrontal, and parietal development.
key_sources: Ghetti Simona; Bunge Silvia A. (2012). Neural Changes Underlying the Development of Episodic Memory During Middle Childhood. Developmental cognitive neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2012.05.002

article_title: Helping others use social media: age stereotypes when estimating learner’s success
citation: Harvey J. GINSBURG, Rebecca CAMERON, Roque V. MENDEZ & Michael WESTHOFF. (2016). Helping others use social media: age stereotypes when estimating learner's success. Psychology, Society, & Education, 8(1), 1-12. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1123456
title: Age stereotyping among young SNS users when estimating older learners' success
description: The article proposes that young social media users' lower success estimates for older learners reflect age stereotyping rather than actual learner ability. It argues that because older adults "may generally have more difficulty mastering nuances of social media", younger users may become "less likely to offer assistance", and that such stereotyping "would apply to increasing numbers of older SNS users regardless of their experience levels and proficiencies". The study's declining success estimates with learner age are presented as evidence consistent with this account.
requirements: A helper who is a younger, experienced SNS user estimating a new learner's prospects
constraints: The article frames this as possible stereotyping inferred from hypothetical scenarios; participants' attributions about the hypothetical friends or relatives were not identified
target_learners: university undergraduate Facebook users acting as informal helpers
target_learning_goals: informal helping and teaching of social networking skills to older adult learners
examples: Participants rated KW's perceived success at helping a 20, 40, or 60 year-old friend or family member learn social media, with success estimates falling as learner age rose

article_title: The effects of preexposure to a nonattended stimulus on subsequent learning: Latent inhibition in adults
citation: A. Ginton, G. Urca, and R. E. Lubow. (1975). The effects of preexposure to a nonattended stimulus on subsequent learning: Latent inhibition in adults. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 1975, Vol. 5 (1), 5-8.
title: Attentional account of latent inhibition: lack of an attentional response to the CS at the start of the learning phase is the necessary condition for latent inhibition
description: The article proposes that the necessary condition for producing latent inhibition is the lack of an attentional response to the to-be-conditioned stimulus in the formal learning phase. Nonreinforced preexposure is described as sufficient for infrahumans and children but insufficient for adults, because adult subjects' expectation that something will happen with the tone may increase over presentations. The account holds that masking reduces the stimulus' salience and thereby enhances the occurrence of inattention, and that acquired inattention develops through the preexposure phase as the attentional response diminishes with repeated presentations.
requirements: The preexposure phase must be constructed so the to-be-conditioned stimulus is exposed within a masking situation which provides a plausible explanation for the presence of the stimulus
constraints: Nonreinforced preexposure alone is described as insufficient for producing latent inhibition in adults without a masking situation
target_learners: adult humans
target_learning_goals: conditioned responding to a previously nonreinforced stimulus
examples: The experiment embedded the white-noise CS within a dichotic listening task so it could be perceived as part of the background noise
key_sources: A. Ginton, G. Urca, and R. E. Lubow. (1975). The effects of preexposure to a nonattended stimulus on subsequent learning: Latent inhibition in adults. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 1975, Vol. 5 (1), 5-8. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03336682

article_title: The effects of preexposure to a nonattended stimulus on subsequent learning: Latent inhibition in adults
citation: A. Ginton, G. Urca, and R. E. Lubow. (1975). The effects of preexposure to a nonattended stimulus on subsequent learning: Latent inhibition in adults. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 1975, Vol. 5 (1), 5-8.
title: Dichotic listening preexposure paradigm with CS-scoreboard instrumental conditioning task
description: An experimental apparatus and procedure for studying latent inhibition in adult humans. Subjects attended to one ear of a dichotic tape recording, counting repetitions of paired nonsense syllables, while a white-noise CS was superimposed on one track. In the testing phase, subjects watched a scoreboard and pressed a button whenever they expected a point to be raised, aiming to bring their score down to zero. The criterion for learning was the number of CSs to termination of the experiment, and eye movements were monitored via a mirror to verify which ear was attended.
requirements: Subjects must attend to the designated ear during preexposure, verified by monitoring eye movements
constraints: The experiment terminated either after five consecutive correct presses to the CS or after 31 presentations of the CS
target_learners: undergraduate psychology students
target_learning_goals: learning the rule connecting a white-noise CS to scoreboard point changes
examples: Forty undergraduates were randomly divided into four groups, with the restriction that two males and eight females be included in each group

article_title: The structure of working memory in young children and its relation to intelligence
citation: Gray Shelley, Green Samuel, Alt Mary, Hogan Tiffany P., Kuo Trudy, Brinkley Shara, Cowan Nelson. (2016). The Structure of Working Memory in Young Children and Its Relation to Intelligence. Journal of Memory and Language. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5157932/
title: Cowan's embedded processes model of working memory with central executive, focus of attention, and phonological storage-and-rehearsal factors
description: Cowan's embedded processes model treats working memory as including all components used to hold information temporarily, with "the temporarily activated portion of long-term memory" at its core and, within it, a focus of attention holding several highly processed integrated items at once. The model specifies three factors: central executive, focus of attention, and phonological storage-and-rehearsal. Verbal rehearsal can make maintenance somewhat automatic and less reliant on attention, while nonverbal information that cannot easily be rehearsed requires more attention for maintenance. This study operationalized the model with 13 tasks and found it fit young children's data best.
requirements: Requires tasks that distinguish attention-dependent storage from rehearsal-supported phonological storage, such as running span tasks with unpredictable endpoints
constraints: Verbal rehearsal reduces reliance on the focus of attention only in children old enough, older than about 7 years, to begin rehearsing simple verbal stimuli
target_learners: young school-age children aged 7-9 with typical development
target_learning_goals: understanding the structure of working memory as it supports learning and assessment of working memory components
examples: The study specified the model with central executive tasks (n-back auditory and visual, number updating), focus of attention indicators including digit span running and binding tasks, and phonological storage tasks (digit span, nonword repetition)
key_sources: Gray Shelley, Green Samuel, Alt Mary, Hogan Tiffany P., Kuo Trudy, Brinkley Shara, Cowan Nelson. (2016). The Structure of Working Memory in Young Children and Its Relation to Intelligence. Journal of Memory and Language. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5157932/

article_title: The structure of working memory in young children and its relation to intelligence
citation: Gray Shelley, Green Samuel, Alt Mary, Hogan Tiffany P., Kuo Trudy, Brinkley Shara, Cowan Nelson. (2016). The Structure of Working Memory in Young Children and Its Relation to Intelligence. Journal of Memory and Language. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5157932/
title: Baddeley's multi-component working memory models: three-factor (1974) and four-factor with episodic buffer (2000)
description: Baddeley and Hitch's three-factor model includes "central executive, visuospatial sketchpad, and phonological loop factors," with the phonological loop as a temporary store for speech-based information refreshed by rehearsal and the visuospatial sketchpad as a temporary store for visual and spatial information. Baddeley's 2000 four-factor model added "an episodic buffer" described as a back-up store capable of integrating phonological, visual, and other types of information over space and time, forming an interface between the subsystems and long-term memory. The study tested both models in children; the three-factor model fit well but slightly worse than Cowan's, and the four-factor model failed because the episodic buffer was indistinguishable from the visuospatial sketchpad.
requirements: Requires indicators for each factor, including binding tasks to test the episodic buffer's proposed integrative storage functions
constraints: In this child sample the episodic buffer factor could not be empirically differentiated from the visuospatial sketchpad factor, so the four-factor model was not viable
target_learners: young school-age children aged 7-9 with typical development
target_learning_goals: understanding competing structural accounts of working memory components relevant to learning and assessment
examples: The four-factor model was tested with episodic buffer indicators comprising phonological binding, visuospatial binding, and cross-modal binding tasks

article_title: The structure of working memory in young children and its relation to intelligence
citation: Gray Shelley, Green Samuel, Alt Mary, Hogan Tiffany P., Kuo Trudy, Brinkley Shara, Cowan Nelson. (2016). The Structure of Working Memory in Young Children and Its Relation to Intelligence. Journal of Memory and Language. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5157932/
title: Comprehensive Assessment Battery for Children - Working Memory (CABC-WM): 13 computer-based tasks in a pirate-themed game
description: The Comprehensive Assessment Battery for Children - Working Memory is a computer-based battery of 13 experimental working memory tasks presented "in a computer-based, pirate-themed game that took six to seven 2-hour sessions to complete over a period of approximately two weeks." Tasks span central executive (n-back auditory and visual, number updating), short-term phonological (digit span, digit span running, nonword repetition), short-term visuospatial (location span, location span running, visual span, visual span running), and binding (phonological, visuospatial, cross-modal) domains. A guide pirate delivered instructions and demonstrations, and children earned virtual rocks and gold coins for motivation. Most task reliabilities were moderate to high.
requirements: Children must pass training trials to proceed to each game; tasks are administered individually with children seated 52 cm from a touchscreen monitor
constraints: Children did not know whether individual responses were correct or incorrect during the games; feedback was limited to end-of-session virtual rewards
target_learners: second-grade children ages 7;0-9;1 with typical development
target_learning_goals: measuring central executive, phonological storage, visuospatial storage, attention, and binding components of working memory in children
examples: Nonword repetition included 16 nonwords at 2- to 5-syllable lengths with inter-rater transcription reliability of 87%; phonological binding scoring reliability was 94%

article_title: A Randomized Control Study of Instructional Approaches for Struggling Adult Readers
citation: Greenberg Daphne, Wise Justin, Morris Robin, Fredrick Laura, Nanda Alice O., Pae Hye-K. (2011). A randomized control study of instructional approaches for struggling adult readers. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3237050/
title: Explicit skills instruction versus implicit extensive reading as competing approaches to adult literacy instruction
description: The article frames adult literacy instruction as divided between two approaches. The explicit skills instruction approach "directly teaches adults how to decode and comprehend," operationalized through the SRA/McGraw-Hill Direct Instruction Corrective Reading program, which uses "a graduated sequence of steps," massed practice, immediate specific feedback, scripted lessons, and unison responding. The implicit approach "encourages students to read text that is of interest to them without directly teaching them decoding and comprehension skills," operationalized as Extensive Reading with self-selected high-interest/low-vocabulary books, sustained silent reading, teacher read-alouds, and book discussion, aligned with andragogy and self-directed learning. The study tested both approaches alone and in combination.
requirements: Teachers trained in the specific approach; the explicit program requires instructor scripts, placement tests, and decision rules for additional instruction
constraints: The article notes none of the Extensive Reading effectiveness studies employ systematic scientific measures and controls
target_learners: Adults reading single words between the 3.0 and 5.9 grade equivalency levels, including native speakers and ESL speakers
target_learning_goals: Decoding
reading comprehension
reading fluency
reading vocabulary
engagement with print
examples: Participants were randomly assigned to DF, DCF, ER, DCEF, or C/C conditions, each receiving 8 hours of instruction weekly for an opportunity of 100 hours

title: SRA/McGraw-Hill Direct Instruction Corrective Reading program adapted for struggling adult readers
description: The Corrective Reading program is the explicit instructional intervention used in the DF, DCF, and DCEF conditions. In the Decoding component, "students learned skills such as phonemic relationships, new sound combinations, word endings and letter and sound combinations." In the Comprehension component, students learned to organize related facts and use analogies, classifications, deductions, inductions, descriptions, conclusions, contradictions, and written directions. Placement tests assigned students to levels: 94% started in Decoding B2 and 6% in Decoding B1; 85% started in Comprehension B1 and 15% in Comprehension A. The program includes frequent mastery tests and decision rules for providing additional instruction.
requirements: Instructor scripts, placement tests, mastery tests, and decision rules; teachers received one week of training plus coaching observations five times during the year
constraints: The authors state the programs are based on what is known about remediation for children and question whether that knowledge completely applies to struggling adult readers
target_learners: Adults reading single words at 3.0–5.9 grade equivalency
target_learning_goals: Decoding and comprehension skills
examples: Average decoding lessons completed: 35.88 in DCEF, 47.75 in DCF, and 75.37 in DF; comprehension lessons: 30.88 in DCEF and 33.85 in DCF

citation: Greenberg Daphne, Wise Justin, Morris Robin, Fredrick Laura, Nanda Alice O., Pae Hye-K. (2011). A randomized control study of instructional approaches for struggling adult readers. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3237050/
title: Guided repeated oral reading fluency component with 40% words-per-minute improvement target
description: Three conditions (DF, DCF, DCEF) included a fluency component using a guided repeated oral reading approach. Each participant received a passage at his or her instructional level from Timed Readings Plus or Jamestown Fluency Readers, read it aloud to establish a baseline of correct words per minute, and was given a stopwatch to practice independently for 15 minutes. The target was for learners "to independently practice a passage until they improve their correct words read per minute of that passage by 40% over baseline." Upon meeting or exceeding the target rate, participants moved to a new passage with a new baseline.
requirements: Passages at instructional level, a stopwatch, independent practice time of 15 minutes, and teacher verification of the target rate
target_learners: Struggling adult readers in adult literacy programs
target_learning_goals: Reading fluency (correct words per minute)
examples: Time allocations included 15 minutes of fluency practice in the DF, DCF, and DCEF conditions

title: Extensive Reading approach with high-interest/low-vocabulary library for adult learners
description: The Extensive Reading approach, administered to the ER and DCEF groups, provided "an extensive library of high interest/low vocabulary books" from publishers such as New Readers Press and Peppercorn Books. Students engaged in sustained silent reading, a read-aloud activity during which the teacher read while participants followed along, and book discussions. The teacher acts as a role model of a reader and does not present explicit instruction on how to read. ER students had two 40-minute silent reading blocks, 15 minutes of teacher read-aloud, and 10 minutes each of book discussion; in DCEF this was reduced to roughly 18 minutes of silent reading, 10 minutes of read-aloud, and 5 minutes of discussion.
requirements: A library of authentic materials at students' reading levels; student choice of reading materials based on interest
constraints: The article notes that although many studies show the approach's effectiveness, none employ systematic scientific measures and controls
target_learners: Adult literacy students, including university students and clerical workers per prior studies
target_learning_goals: Reading interest, reading vocabulary, reading skill through wide exposure to literature
examples: The ER group showed the lowest posttest word attack scores (M = 11.36) among the five conditions

article_title: Everyday experiences of memory problems and control: the adaptive role of selective optimization with compensation in the context of memory decline
citation: Hahn Elizabeth A. Ph.D., Lachman Margie E. Ph.D. (2014). Everyday Experiences of Memory Problems and Control: The Adaptive Role of Selective Optimization with Compensation in the Context of Memory Decline. Neuropsychology, development, and cognition. Section B, Aging, neuropsychology and cognition. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4156931/
title: Selective Optimization with Compensation (SOC) as a life-management framework for adapting to age-related losses
description: The article describes SOC as an accommodative strategy framework in which "Selection refers to targeting ones' efforts towards specific goals and activities, optimization is described as expending increased efforts and strategies in order to accomplish specific and relevant goals, and compensation consists of adaptive behaviors and the use of alternative strategies." Selection may be elective or loss-based. The components are expected to "operate together to produce favorable outcomes" by selecting important activities, optimizing performance, and finding alternative strategies, helping individuals focus on gains and adjust to losses. In this study SOC is measured with a 12-item composite and tested as a moderator buffering memory decline effects.
requirements: The framework assumes individuals can target efforts toward specific goals and expend increased effort and alternative strategies to accomplish them.
constraints: The article notes SOC behaviors are effortful and may not be beneficial for all individuals with memory decline, such as those with dementia or pre-dementia states.
target_learners: Older and middle-aged adults experiencing age-related declines in working memory
target_learning_goals: Maintaining everyday cognitive functioning and minimizing everyday memory problems in the context of memory decline
examples: Participants rated themselves on 12 SOC items (elective selection, loss-based selection, optimization, compensation) at Time 2, and the composite was tested as a moderator of weekly control and memory decline in multilevel models.

title: 12-week weekly paper-and-pencil diary protocol for everyday memory problems and perceived control
description: The BOLOS Time 2 battery included a 12-week diary study in which participants completed a weekly report of everyday experiences at the end of each week. The diaries included questions related to "everyday memory problems, perceived control, and a range of health and well-being measures." Everyday memory problems were assessed with 11 items reporting how many days (0-7) each problem occurred, summed to a weekly composite ranging from 0 to 77. Weekly perceived control was a single item asking how much participants felt "in control of my life" that week (1-5). Participants completed the paper-and-pencil diary at home and mailed it back within 24 hours.
requirements: Participants must complete at least two weeks of diaries with complete Time 1 and Time 2 data for inclusion.
constraints: There was a significant drop-off in reports of memory problems over the 12 weeks, so time was included as a covariate; participant burden may result in a drop-off in reports.
target_learners: Community-residing midlife and older adults
target_learning_goals: Assessing naturally-occurring everyday memory problems and weekly fluctuations in perceived control
examples: The current study includes the 103 participants who completed at least two weeks of diaries and had complete data for Time 1 and Time 2.
