article_title: A critical period for second language acquisition: Evidence from 2/3 million English speakers
citation: Hartshorne Joshua K., Tenenbaum Joshua B., Pinker Steven. (2018). A critical period for second language acquisition: Evidence from 2/3 million English speakers. Cognition. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6559801/
title: Exponential Learning with Sigmoidal Decay (ELSD) model of syntax acquisition
description: The ELSD model represents syntax acquisition as "a simple exponential learning process" in which grammatical proficiency grows with experience, with an experience discount factor modeled separately for simultaneous bilinguals, immigrants, and non-immersion learners. The learning rate is a piecewise function: constant from birth to age tc, then declining according to a sigmoid whose parameters control steepness and center. The authors state this structure "allows it to capture a very wide range of developmental trajectories", and they fit it simultaneously to monolingual, immersion, and non-immersion performance curves to estimate when underlying learning ability declines.
requirements: Performance curves for monolinguals, immersion learners, and non-immersion learners with sufficient participants per age bin
A sensitive attainment measure without an artificial ceiling
constraints: The model is necessarily simplified, per the authors' interim discussion
Parameters were fit with Differential Evolution and compared using Monte Carlo split-half cross-validated R2
target_learners: native and non-native English speakers aged 7-89
target_learning_goals: estimating how grammar-learning ability changes with age
examples: Fitted with Differential Evolution; best fit R2 = 0.89 with rate change at 17.4 years

title: WhichEnglish internet grammar quiz dataset (669,498 speakers)
description: An internet quiz at www.gameswithwords.org/WhichEnglish that presented 132 items (95 critical) covering phenomena such as "passivization, clefting, agreement, relative clauses, preposition use", plus dialect-distinguishing items used for recruiting. After exclusions, 669,498 participants aged 7-89 were analyzed across 38 languages with at least 1000 native speakers. Reliability for critical items was Chronbach's alpha = 0.86, and the dataset is available at http://osf.io/pyb8s.

Exclusion of inconsistent or implausible demographic responses
constraints: Analyses restricted to the 95 critical items
Written comprehension modality; production and oral modalities not tested

article_title: American Sign Language Syntax and Analogical Reasoning Skills Are Influenced by Early Acquisition and Age of Entry to Signing Schools for the Deaf
citation: Henner J, Caldwell-Harris CL, Novogrodsky R and Hoffmeister R (2016) American Sign Language Syntax and Analogical Reasoning Skills Are Influenced by Early Acquisition and Age of Entry to Signing Schools for the Deaf. Front. Psychol. 7:1982. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.01982
title: Language experience as a continuum sensitive to maturational age
description: The article proposes that sign-language outcomes form a continuum reflecting cumulative language experience rather than a sharply closing critical window. As the authors state, "Our results demonstrate a continuum of outcomes that reﬂect experience with language as a continuous variable that is sensitive to maturational age." The best outcomes follow exposure from birth, then ASL exposure before age 6, then academic ASL exposure before 12, with the worst after age 12. The framework is used to advise parents to avoid all-or-none thinking about timing of sign language exposure.
requirements: Consistent, fully accessible exposure to ASL from peers and adults, as provided in signing school environments
constraints: The authors note considerable plasticity exists, so late exposure is not without benefit; outcomes depend on amount and timing of exposure
target_learners: Deaf children ages 7;6–18;5 in schools for the Deaf
target_learning_goals: ASL syntactic knowledge
language-based analogical reasoning
examples: Ranking of outcomes by exposure timing: birth signing best, then entry before 6, then before 12, then after 12

title: Provide Deaf children with ASL early, as a primary or supplementary means of communication, rather than withholding sign as a back-up option
description: The article recommends that parents avoid all-or-none thinking about sign language timing and provide ASL as early as possible. As the authors advise, "Our advice is that parents should, when possible, choose ASL as either a primary or a supplementary means of communicating with their Deaf children." This follows from their findings that both birth signing and earlier school entry predict better ASL outcomes, and that most students can benefit from fully accessible ASL exposure.
requirements: Access to fluent signing peers and adults, such as signing schools for the Deaf or signing parents
constraints: The authors note the best outcome is signing from birth, but considerable plasticity exists for later consistent exposure

Deaf children in early intervention or signing schools

subsequent ASL syntactic and analogical reasoning ability

title: American Sign Language Assessment Instrument (ASLAI)
description: The ASLAI is a computerized battery of receptive ASL assessments developed by the research team. As the article describes it, "The ASLAI is a comprehensive battery of 11 multiple choice receptive language tasks presented via computer." Stimuli and responses are presented via video; participants can pause or replay videos and select responses by clicking a button above a corresponding video. Two subtests were analyzed here: a 27-item syntactic judgment task tapping nine ASL syntactic structures, and a 24-item analogy task with six analogy types. Schools received detailed reports of students' ASL abilities for IEP planning.
requirements: Video presentation of stimuli in ASL; computer platform capable of displaying pictures and videos
constraints: The analyzed data came from students who scored above chance (25%) on the tasks; schools provided background records but no parental survey data on home signing amount or socio-economic status

article_title: Metacognition in Later Adulthood
citation: Hertzog C, Dunlosky J. (2011). Metacognition in Later Adulthood: Spared Monitoring Can Benefit Older Adults' Self-regulation. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3903298/
title: Metacognition as monitoring plus control in a reciprocal relation, forming the basis of self-regulated learning
description: The article defines metacognition as "thoughts, beliefs, and other cognitive processes devoted to assessing and controlling one's own cognitions." Monitoring evaluates information from an ongoing cognitive process, such as a retrieval search, while control uses that monitoring to decide whether and how to change cognitive processing, such as restudying what one cannot access. Monitoring and control are in a reciprocal relation and are viewed as critical components of self-regulation. The framework organizes the review's evidence on aging, JOLs, FOKs, and intervention design.
requirements: Monitoring must be empirically validated against objective measures of the judged processes, such as comparing JOLs to later paired-associate recall performance
constraints: The review focuses on relative accuracy (resolution), typically computed as within-person Goodman-Kruskal gamma correlations between judgments and criterion performance
target_learners: older adults
adults across the life span ages 18 to 81
target_learning_goals: episodic memory and paired-associate learning
self-regulated study decisions such as selective restudy
examples: Older adults learning diabetes symptoms monitor whether they can retrieve studied facts about nutrition and blood glucose so they can further review inaccessible information
key_sources: Hertzog C, Dunlosky J. (2011). Metacognition in Later Adulthood: Spared Monitoring Can Benefit Older Adults' Self-regulation. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3903298/

article_title: Metacognition in Later Adulthood
citation: Hertzog C, Dunlosky J. (2011). Metacognition in Later Adulthood: Spared Monitoring Can Benefit Older Adults' Self-regulation. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3903298/
title: Use spared metacognitive monitoring as the basis for compensatory self-regulated learning in older adults
description: The article argues that because aging spares monitoring accuracy, "spared monitoring is available as a resource that older adults can use to improve their learning." Older adults who accurately monitor what they have and have not learned can allocate restudy effort selectively to unlearned items, compensating for age-related declines in learning mechanisms. This principle underlies the article's metacognitive intervention program and its recommendation that monitoring-informed self-regulation supports everyday cognitive functioning.
requirements: Individuals must be able to monitor their learning accurately, e.g., via self-testing akin to making highly accurate delayed JOLs
Study must afford differential allocation of time and effort to unlearned items, e.g., self-paced study
constraints: Training metacognitive self-regulation without explicit transfer discussion showed no transfer to a different kind of memory task, free recall of word lists
target_learners: older adults
target_learning_goals: compensating for age-related memory declines
achieving satisfactory levels of final learning through selective restudy
examples: The Dunlosky et al. (2003) intervention trained older individuals to self-test and focus restudy on unlearned items, producing greater improvements than encoding-strategy training under self-paced study
key_sources: Hertzog C, Dunlosky J. (2011). Metacognition in Later Adulthood: Spared Monitoring Can Benefit Older Adults' Self-regulation. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3903298/

article_title: Metacognition in Later Adulthood
citation: Hertzog C, Dunlosky J. (2011). Metacognition in Later Adulthood: Spared Monitoring Can Benefit Older Adults' Self-regulation. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3903298/
title: Memory-quality account of episodic feeling-of-knowing resolution: FOK accuracy derives from the diagnosticity of cues produced by encoding quality
description: The article advances an explanatory account in which FOK judgments are informed by cue familiarity and by partial information accessed during attempted retrieval, and the resolution of FOKs depends on the quality of the underlying memory representation. As the article states, "rich encoding experiences produce cues that are more diagnostic about the availability of a sought-after target in memory; hence, using these cues will produce more accurate FOKs." Apparent age deficits in episodic FOK resolution may therefore reflect poorer memory representations rather than a monitoring deficit. The account explains why equating memory performance across age groups matters.
requirements: Investigations of age differences in retrieval monitoring should attempt to equate older and younger adults on memory performance to rule out this explanation
constraints: The account applies to FOK judgments for episodic memory tasks where underlying memory quality varies
target_learners: older adults
younger adults
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of whether sought-after information is available in memory
retrieval decisions such as whether to continue search or restudy
examples: In the Hertzog, Dunlosky, and Sinclair (2010) experiment, older adults with a 30-minute delay had better memory performance and better FOK resolution, attributed to more diagnostic encoding information rather than superior monitoring

article_title: Efficacy of Learning Strategies Instruction in Adult Education
citation: Hock Michael F., Mellard Daryl F. (2011). Efficacy of learning strategies instruction in adult basic education. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 4(2), 134-153. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555291
title: Four-phase modified SIM explicit instruction model for adult learners
description: The article describes a modified Strategic Instruction Model (SIM) instructional method adapted for adult-to-adult interaction in four phases: Phase 1 addresses learning readiness, goal setting and commitment; Phase 2 reviews and builds fundamental skills needed for the target strategy; Phase 3 is when "students are expected to master the target strategy"; Phase 4 is a generalization process applying strategies to different text types in academic, employment, and other settings. Within Phases 2 and 3, instructors guide learners through a four-step acquisition process of describe, model, scaffolded practice and feedback, and progress or mastery checks, with scaffolding incrementally removed and progress graphed to keep learners motivated.
requirements: Instructors trained in the scripted strategy and instructional method
Audio or video recording of sessions for fidelity review
constraints: The method was designed for explicit, intensive delivery, which the authors found elusive in adult education settings with typical attendance patterns
target_learners: Adult basic education learners with low literacy or limited educational attainment
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and reading-related subskills
Acquisition and generalization of learning strategies
examples: Instructors modeled strategies by vocalizing their own thinking processes, and learner practice moved from verbal to guided, partner, and independent practice
key_sources: Hock Michael F., Mellard Daryl F. (2011). Efficacy of learning strategies instruction in adult basic education. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 4(2), 134-153. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555291

article_title: Efficacy of Learning Strategies Instruction in Adult Education
citation: Hock Michael F., Mellard Daryl F. (2011). Efficacy of learning strategies instruction in adult basic education. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 4(2), 134-153. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555291
title: Four SIM learning strategies taught in the trial: Bridging, Building Fluency, Prediction, and Summarization
description: The study taught four SIM learning strategies using the existing SIM strategy template: "The Bridging Strategy, The Building Fluency Strategy, The Prediction Strategy, and The Summarization Strategy." Bridging is a word-level decoding strategy using the mnemonic PART with a FIND subroutine for syllabication; Fluency uses two cycles of repeated reading, first word-level then passage-level, re-reading lists 3 to 7 times to mastery; Prediction uses the CLUE mnemonic (check for clues, link to prior knowledge, unveil predictions, examine the reading); Summarization uses the READ mnemonic (review, evaluate, answer with paraphrase, determine a summary). Each strategy presents short sequenced steps with a mnemonic to cue cognitive and metacognitive actions.
requirements: Delivery through the explicit four-phase instructional method
Reading materials appropriate for adults
constraints: Validated with adolescents with SLD in secondary settings with up to 36 weeks available for instruction; in this trial planned instruction was shortened to 19 to 34 hours
target_learners: Adult basic education learners at NRS educational functional levels 2 through 6
target_learning_goals: Word decoding
Oral reading fluency
Prediction and prior-knowledge activation before reading
Summarization and main-idea identification
examples: Bridging teaches readers to underline familiar letter groups in an unfamiliar word, blend the sounds, and check whether the word makes sense in the sentence before moving to later steps
key_sources: Hock Michael F., Mellard Daryl F. (2011). Efficacy of learning strategies instruction in adult basic education. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 4(2), 134-153. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555291

article_title: Efficacy of Learning Strategies Instruction in Adult Education
citation: Hock Michael F., Mellard Daryl F. (2011). Efficacy of learning strategies instruction in adult basic education. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 4(2), 134-153. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555291
title: Deliver learning strategies instruction explicitly, intensively, and systematically, with sufficient dosage for mastery
description: The article's design recommendation, drawn from the SIM validation literature and its own null trial, is that strategy instruction must be delivered in an explicit, intensive, and systematic fashion for learners to reach mastery and for large achievement effects to appear. The trial's four-phase method operationalizes this through describe, model, scaffolded practice with feedback, and mastery checks, but the authors conclude that "these principles proved to be elusive in the AE setting with AE learners" because attendance patterns limited delivered dosage to well under planned hours.
requirements: Sufficient instructional dosage for learners to acquire and automatize the strategy
Settings compatible with intensive delivery
Supports for persistence such as goal setting, progress monitoring, and mastery experiences
constraints: The authors call into question whether such instruction can be delivered in traditional adult education settings, given the conflict between the justified need for more dosage and the contextual and cognitive realities of adult literacy education
target_learners: Adults with low literacy or limited educational attainment
Adolescents with learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Strategic approach to reading tasks
examples: The trial planned 8-week courses of 26 to 32 hours and added persistence supports (monetary incentives, phone calls to absent learners, readiness and goal-setting activities), yet completers still received only 68% to 86% of planned hours
key_sources: Hock Michael F., Mellard Daryl F. (2011). Efficacy of learning strategies instruction in adult basic education. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 4(2), 134-153. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555291

article_title: Word learning in deaf children with cochlear implants: effects of early auditory experience
citation: Derek M. Houston, Jessica Stewart, Aaron Moberly, George Hollich, and Richard T. Miyamoto. (2012). Word learning in deaf children with cochlear implants: effects of early auditory experience. Dev Sci. 2012 May ; 15(3): 448–461. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2012.01140.x
title: Modified Intermodal Preferential Looking Paradigm (IPLP) word-learning task with novel word/object pairings
description: The article describes a modified version of the IPLP word-learning task in which children are trained on two arbitrary novel-word/novel-object pairings (blick and modi) via video and then tested for preferential looking to the target. The authors state that the task 'more closely resembles real life word learning in that the words were arbitrarily related to the objects'. Performance is measured as mean longest look differences between target and nontarget during test blocks.
requirements: Requires children to sit and watch video stimuli in a sound booth; children who cried or were excessively fussy could not complete the procedure
constraints: Tested only at 12 or 18 months after initial CI stimulation; the version used may be a block or two longer than necessary, especially for older children
target_learners: 12- to 40-month-old normal-hearing infants
22- to 40-month-old deaf children with cochlear implants
target_learning_goals: Novel word learning (associating spoken nonwords with novel object referents)
examples: Children were presented with training movies where they could learn two novel-object/novel-word associations, then four blocks of test trials with reminder trials between blocks
key_sources: Derek M. Houston, Jessica Stewart, Aaron Moberly, George Hollich, and Richard T. Miyamoto. (2012). Word learning in deaf children with cochlear implants: effects of early auditory experience. Dev Sci. 2012 May ; 15(3): 448–461. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2012.01140.x

article_title: Word learning in deaf children with cochlear implants: effects of early auditory experience
citation: Derek M. Houston, Jessica Stewart, Aaron Moberly, George Hollich, and Richard T. Miyamoto. (2012). Word learning in deaf children with cochlear implants: effects of early auditory experience. Dev Sci. 2012 May ; 15(3): 448–461. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2012.01140.x
title: Sensitive period for auditory access supporting early spoken word learning begins to close during the first 2 years of life
description: The article proposes that a sensitive period for having access to sound in order to develop the ability to associate spoken words to their referents begins to close during the first 2 years of life. The authors state the findings 'are consistent with the possibility that a sensitive period for access to sound in order to develop the ability to associate spoken words to their referents begins to close during the first 2 years of life but that this sensitive period does not finish closing until at least after 5 years of age'. This account explains why very early implantation facilitates word-learning skills while later implantation does not.
requirements: Requires investigation of age at implantation effects on specific language processes rather than general outcome measures alone
constraints: The sensitive period does not finish closing until at least after 5 years of age, so effects are not absolute after age 2
target_learners: Prelingually deaf children receiving cochlear implants before 2 years of age
target_learning_goals: Early spoken word learning (associating word sound patterns to referents)
examples: The study tested whether congenitally deaf children implanted between 6 and 24 months showed an effect of age at implantation on novel word learning
key_sources: Derek M. Houston, Jessica Stewart, Aaron Moberly, George Hollich, and Richard T. Miyamoto. (2012). Word learning in deaf children with cochlear implants: effects of early auditory experience. Dev Sci. 2012 May ; 15(3): 448–461. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2012.01140.x

article_title: Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish‐learning children
citation: Hurtado Nereyda, Marchman Virginia A., Fernald Anne. (2008). Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish-learning children. Developmental Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2898277/
title: Vocabulary knowledge and speech processing efficiency are interdependent within a synergistic, bidirectional language-learning system shaped by caregiver input
description: The article proposes that vocabulary growth and real-time lexical processing efficiency are not independent outcomes but operate "within a synergistic system of language learning". In one model, processing speed mediates input effects on vocabulary because children who hear more talk are more practiced at parsing speech and accessing semantic representations; in the reverse model, vocabulary knowledge mediates input effects on processing speed because a larger lexicon yields richer lexical and morphosyntactic cues and finer discrimination among confusable word forms. Together they suggest input affects both, which are "mutually influential in a bidirectional fashion".
requirements: Both models require longitudinal measurement of caregiver input, child vocabulary, and real-time processing efficiency to distinguish overlapping from independent influences
constraints: Effects were observed in a sample of primarily low-SES Spanish-speaking families; it is not known whether caregiver talk would relate to children's lexical processing efficiency in middle- or higher-SES families
target_learners: Spanish-learning children aged 18 to 24 months from primarily low-SES families
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary growth
Efficiency of real-time spoken word recognition and comprehension
examples: Regression mediation models in which processing speed mediated input-to-vocabulary relations (Figure 3A) and vocabulary mediated input-to-processing-speed relations (Figure 3B), with bootstrapped indirect effects significantly greater than zero
key_sources: Hurtado Nereyda, Marchman Virginia A., Fernald Anne. (2008). Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish-learning children. Developmental Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2898277/

article_title: Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish‐learning children
citation: Hurtado Nereyda, Marchman Virginia A., Fernald Anne. (2008). Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish-learning children. Developmental Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2898277/
title: Looking-while-listening eye-tracking procedure for measuring infants' real-time speech processing efficiency
description: The looking-while-listening procedure assesses efficiency of online spoken language comprehension in infants and toddlers. On each trial children see pictures of two familiar objects and hear speech naming one; gaze patterns are videotaped and coded frame-by-frame, yielding a high-resolution record of eye movements aligned with target noun onset, with inter-observer agreement averaging 97%. In this study it yielded mean reaction times for shifting from distracter to target picture at 18 and 24 months, used as the measure of speech processing efficiency.
requirements: Familiar target nouns known to most children at the testing age
Trials where the child starts on the distracter and shifts to the target within 300–1800 ms of target-word onset
Frame-by-frame coding of gaze patterns by trained observers
constraints: Mean RTs are based on different numbers of trials across participants because children vary in the likelihood they start on the distracter by chance
target_learners: Infants and toddlers aged 18 to 24 months learning Spanish as a first language
target_learning_goals: Measuring efficiency of real-time spoken word recognition and comprehension
examples: Eight target nouns at 18 months (32 test trials) and four more added at 24 months (36 test trials), stimuli controlled for prosodic comparability, target pictures matched for visual salience and grammatical gender
key_sources: Hurtado Nereyda, Marchman Virginia A., Fernald Anne. (2008). Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish-learning children. Developmental Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2898277/

article_title: Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish‐learning children
citation: Hurtado Nereyda, Marchman Virginia A., Fernald Anne. (2008). Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish-learning children. Developmental Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2898277/
title: Four measures of maternal child-directed speech coded from play-session transcripts
description: The study quantified caregiver input using four measures of maternal speech coded from video-recorded 12-minute play sessions transcribed under CHILDES protocols: number of utterances, number of word tokens, number of word types, and mean length of utterance (MLU, in words per utterance for romance languages). The first two estimate amount of talk during a fixed-length session, word types index lexical diversity, and MLU indexes grammatical complexity. Each maternal word was coded for word root, part of speech, tense, number and person using the Spanish-language mor utility in CHILDES.
requirements: Video- and audio-recorded mother–child play sessions with age-appropriate toys
Transcription by trained native Spanish-speakers following CHILDES protocols
Double-checking of transcripts and codings for accuracy
constraints: Transcripts were reduced to 12 minutes based on the shortest play session, beginning 2 minutes after participants were comfortably engaged
target_learners: Mothers of children aged 18 months in Spanish-speaking, primarily low-SES immigrant families
target_learning_goals: Characterizing quantity, diversity, and grammatical complexity of child-directed speech as predictors of children's lexical development
examples: Mean values at 18 months: 210.6 utterances, 609.1 word tokens, 110.5 word types, MLU 2.9 words (Table 2)
key_sources: Hurtado Nereyda, Marchman Virginia A., Fernald Anne. (2008). Does input influence uptake? Links between maternal talk, processing speed and vocabulary size in Spanish-learning children. Developmental Science. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2898277/

article_title: Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents
citation: Ivcevic Zorana; Eggers Catherine. (2021). Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8003666/
title: Emotion regulation ability as a maximal performance attribute distinct from typical performance self-reports
description: The article adopts a definition of emotion regulation as "a maximal performance attribute—an individual's ability to evaluate the effectiveness of different emotion regulation strategies". This contrasts with typical performance conceptualizations measured through self-report instruments asking about strategy frequency. Maximal performance ERA is assessed through ability tests presenting hypothetical emotion-laden scenarios where respondents judge how effective different actions would be toward achieving a specific regulation goal, scored against expert judgments. The article argues self-reports of emotion abilities are poor predictors because people are poor judges of their own emotion abilities.
requirements: Assessment requires ability tests presenting hypothetical emotion-laden situations with multiple response options
Scoring requires expert judgments guided by empirical research on effective emotion regulation strategies
constraints: Measures potential to evaluate strategies in hypothetical scenarios, not enacted regulation in daily situations
Self-report measures of emotion regulation ability are explicitly not employed due to poor predictive validity
target_learners: adolescents in high school
target_learning_goals: evaluating effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies toward specific goals
examples: The MSCEIT-YV ERA subtest presents six emotion-filled hypothetical scenarios relevant to adolescents, each followed by three potential actions respondents judge for effectiveness
key_sources: Ivcevic Zorana; Eggers Catherine. (2021). Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8003666/

article_title: Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents
citation: Ivcevic Zorana; Eggers Catherine. (2021). Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8003666/
title: Observer reports bridge the gap between measured potential and enacted emotion regulation behavior
description: The article proposes that "observer reports of emotion regulation can bridge the gap between potential (measured by ability tests) and enacted behavior". Performance tests measure the capacity to evaluate regulation strategies in hypothetical scenarios but do not capture whether individuals actually generate and use these strategies in daily situations. Observer reports from knowledgeable acquaintances (here, teachers) provide information about enacted emotion regulation in real-world contexts. The article argues behavior indicating successful emotion regulation depends not only on ability but also on non-ability motivational variables such as perceived efficacy and value of regulating emotions.
requirements: Observers must be knowledgeable about the target individual's behavior in relevant contexts
Teachers were asked to base nominations on what they observed in classes rather than general reputation
constraints: The observer measure used here was based on a single nomination question, which the authors identify as a limitation; multi-item measures would be more reliable
target_learners: adolescents in high school
target_learning_goals: enacting effective emotion regulation in real-world academic and social situations
examples: Teachers nominated up to 5 students at the high and low ends of emotion regulation ability from alphabetical class lists, with nominations standardized and summed across teachers
key_sources: Ivcevic Zorana; Eggers Catherine. (2021). Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. citation: Ivcevic Zorana; Eggers Catherine. (2021). Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8003666/
title: Assess emotion regulation through both performance tests and observer reports to capture distinct predictive information
description: The article concludes that understanding emotion regulation requires "both one's ability—the potential to regulate emotions successfully—and observed behavior—indicators of successful emotion regulation". Because performance-tested ERA and observer reports are only modestly correlated and each independently predicts outcomes, using both provides complementary information neither alone supplies. This is especially valuable "when performance-tested assessments are not possible," since observer reports alone still predict academic and interpersonal outcomes.
requirements: Access to both ability-test administration and knowledgeable observers such as teachers
Observers who have directly observed the target's emotion regulation in relevant contexts
constraints: Observer reports based on single questions are less reliable than multi-item measures would be
The two measures capture distinct constructs and cannot substitute for one another
target_learners: adolescents in high school
target_learning_goals: predicting academic achievement and interpersonal relationship quality from emotion regulation assessment
examples: In this study, 220 students completed the MSCEIT-YV ERA subtest while teachers independently nominated students high and low in emotion regulation, and both measures independently predicted outcomes

title: MSCEIT-YV Emotion Regulation Ability subtest
description: The ERA subtest from the Mayer, Salovey, and Caruso Emotional Intelligence Test—Youth Version measures "one's capacity to evaluate how effective different actions would be toward achieving a specific regulation goal". It presents six emotion-filled hypothetical scenarios describing everyday experiences relevant to adolescents, each followed by three potential actions the respondent rates for effectiveness toward a stated goal. Scoring uses expert scoring against judgments of emotion researchers, and scores are standardized to a mean of 100 and standard deviation of 15.
requirements: Respondents must read and evaluate hypothetical scenarios relevant to their developmental level
Scoring requires expert judgments guided by empirical research on effective emotion regulation strategies
constraints: Measures evaluation of strategies in hypothetical scenarios rather than enacted behavior in daily life
target_learners: adolescents
target_learning_goals: evaluating effectiveness of emotion regulation strategies
examples: One scenario describes Li, excited about an upcoming party but needing to study for an exam the next day, with respondents judging actions toward making Li study

citation: Ivcevic Zorana; Eggers Catherine. (2021). Emotion Regulation Ability: Test Performance and Observer Reports in Predicting Relationship, Achievement and Well-Being Outcomes in Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8003666/
title: Teacher nomination procedure for observer-reported emotion regulation
description: Observer reports were collected through teacher nominations in which teachers selected up to 5 students they considered at the high and low ends of emotion regulation ability from alphabetical lists of students they taught. Nominations of difficulty regulating emotions were assigned −1, nominations of being good at regulating emotions were assigned 1, and non-nominated students received 0. To account for unequal numbers of students taught by different teachers, nominations by each teacher were standardized and summed across all teachers. Teachers were instructed to base judgments on classroom observation rather than general reputation.
requirements: Teachers must have directly observed students in instructional contexts
Nomination lists must be standardized to account for unequal class sizes
constraints: Based on a single nomination question rather than multiple items, which the authors identify as a reliability limitation
Captures teacher-perceived regulation in classroom settings specifically
target_learners: adolescents in high school
target_learning_goals: assessing enacted emotion regulation observable in classroom behavior
examples: Teachers were asked to identify students "good at regulating their emotions (e.g., able to get energized when necessary and calm down when needed)" and those with most difficulty regulating emotions

article_title: A review study about creativity in adolescence: Where is the social context?
citation: van der Zanden, P. J. A. C.; Meijer, P. C.; Beghetto, R. A. (2020). A review study about creativity in adolescence: Where is the social context? Thinking Skills and Creativity, 38, article 100702. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2020.100702
title: Four-category classification of factors in adolescent creativity: individual, parental, educational, and social contextual
description: The review organizes findings from 65 studies on adolescent creativity into a four-category framework: individual factors (demographics, personality and affect, motivation, academic achievement), parental factors (parental support, parental involvement), educational factors (freedom and structure, teacher-student relationship, collaborative learning, playful activities, tools), and social contextual factors. The authors state: "We classified supportive and inhibiting factors into four categories: individual factors, parental factors, educational factors, and social contextual factors." They acknowledge the categories may be interrelated rather than discrete, noting that from a sociocultural standpoint it would be problematic to view the factors as clearly distinguishable.
requirements: Studies must report relationships between specific variables and creativity in adolescents aged 12-19 to be classified within the framework
constraints: The authors acknowledge the categories may be conceptualized as interrelated rather than fixed or discrete, and different researchers may conceptualize them differently
target_learners: Adolescents aged 12-19
target_learning_goals: Creativity development in adolescence
examples: The review mapped each of the 65 sampled studies to Tables 1-3 by which factor category prevailed, and Fig. 1 illustrates the factors as interrelated with bi-directional arrows
key_sources: van der Zanden, P. J. A. C.; Meijer, P. C.; Beghetto, R. A. (2020). A review study about creativity in adolescence: Where is the social context? Thinking Skills and Creativity, 38, article 100702. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2020.100702

article_title: Children’s scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept
citation: Jirout, J. & Klahr, D. (2011). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review (in press, draft). https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/developmental-review
title: Loewenstein's information-gap theory of curiosity as a framework for measuring children's exploratory curiosity
description: The information-gap theory holds that curiosity arises from feelings of deprivation that are aversive and motivate information-seeking to reduce them. The review adopts it as the conceptual framework for evaluating procedures for measuring children's exploratory curiosity, defining curiosity as "the threshold of desired uncertainty in the environment that leads to exploratory behavior." The authors extend it to young children as a stable uncertainty preference.
requirements: Curiosity is operationalized through behavioral measures of exploration under varying uncertainty, since the theory concerns deprivation-motivated information seeking
constraints: The theory does not consider non-aversive information-seeking, such as externally rewarded or general-interest seeking, to be curiosity
target_learners: preschool and early elementary children
target_learning_goals: scientific curiosity and information-seeking behavior
examples: The authors adapted a preference-for-the-unknown task into a new measure of children's exploratory preference under different levels of uncertainty
key_sources: Jirout, J. & Klahr, D. (2011). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review (in press, draft). https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/developmental-review

article_title: Children’s scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept
citation: Jirout, J. & Klahr, D. (2011). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review (in press, draft). https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/developmental-review
title: New paradigm measuring exploratory curiosity in preschool children as threshold of desired uncertainty
description: The article proposes a new behavioral paradigm for measuring exploratory curiosity in preschool children, "defining curiosity as the threshold of desired uncertainty in the environment that leads to exploratory behavior." It adapts and extends a preference-for-the-unknown flap-opening procedure to measure children's exploratory preference under different levels of uncertainty. The authors present data on its reliability and validity and initial developmental results.
requirements: Behavioral measurement, since questionnaire-style measures are inappropriate for this age group
constraints: The paper describes only the first step of designing and implementing a measure of scientific curiosity
target_learners: preschool children
target_learning_goals: scientific curiosity, exploratory behavior, information seeking
examples: Children choose between flaps revealing known versus unknown contents, extending Kreitler et al.'s preference-for-the-unknown task
key_sources: Jirout, J. & Klahr, D. (2011). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review (in press, draft). https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/developmental-review

article_title: Children’s scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept
citation: Jirout, J. & Klahr, D. (2011). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review (in press, draft). https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/developmental-review
title: Use behavioral rather than questionnaire measures to assess young children's curiosity
description: The review recommends assessing children's curiosity through observable exploration and information-seeking rather than self- or teacher-report questionnaires. Behavioral measures "do not require the same levels of comprehension skills and they measure actual exploration and information seeking, which is an essential manifestation of curiosity." The authors build their own preschool measure on this principle, grounding it in the information-gap framework.
requirements: Observable exploratory behavior must be measurable in controlled or naturalistic settings
constraints: Behavioral approaches trade off construct and ecological validity depending on how tightly controlled the situation is
target_learners: young children, especially preschoolers
target_learning_goals: measuring scientific curiosity and exploratory information-seeking
examples: The authors' new paradigm measures children's choices and exploration under varying levels of uncertainty
key_sources: Jirout, J. & Klahr, D. (2011). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review (in press, draft). https://www.sciencedirect.com/journal/developmental-review

article_title: Developmental Dyscalculia in Adults
citation: Liane Kaufmann, Michael von Aster, Silke M. Göbel, Josef Marksteiner, and Elise Klein. (2020). Developmental Dyscalculia in Adults: Current Issues and Open Questions for Future Research. Lernen und Lernstörungen, 9(2), 126–137. https://doi.org/10.1024/2235-0977/a000294
title: Triple-Code-Model of number processing and calculation
description: The Triple-Code-Model (TCM) holds that numerical information is processed by three distinct representational codes supported by regionally and functionally distinct neural substrates: an analogue magnitude representation mediating approximate and discrete quantity processing, a visual Arabic number form supporting recognition of Arabic numerals, and an auditory verbal word frame used for verbally mediated operations and direct arithmetic fact retrieval. The review states the TCM "has shaped decades of numerical cognition research" in healthy adults, patients, and developmental studies, though it may not directly apply to developing brain systems.
requirements: Developed from adult data and mature brain systems; the review notes it might not be directly applicable to developmental brain systems
constraints: Based on adult data, so applicability to developmental populations is limited per the review
target_learners: adults with typical numeracy
adults with developmental dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: number processing and calculation
arithmetic fact retrieval
numerical magnitude representation
examples: The review uses the TCM as the framework for interpreting which neural substrates (IPS, perisylvian language regions, fusiform gyri) support each representational code in adults with and without DD
key_sources: Liane Kaufmann, Michael von Aster, Silke M. Göbel, Josef Marksteiner, and Elise Klein. (2020). Developmental Dyscalculia in Adults: Current Issues and Open Questions for Future Research. Lernen und Lernstörungen, 9(2), 126–137. https://doi.org/10.1024/2235-0977/a000294

article_title: Developmental Dyscalculia in Adults
citation: Liane Kaufmann, Michael von Aster, Silke M. Göbel, Josef Marksteiner, and Elise Klein. (2020). Developmental Dyscalculia in Adults: Current Issues and Open Questions for Future Research. Lernen und Lernstörungen, 9(2), 126–137. https://doi.org/10.1024/2235-0977/a000294
title: ATOM: A Theory of Magnitude proposing shared parietal mechanisms for number, time, and space
description: ATOM (A Theory of Magnitude) proposes that numerical quantity, time, and space share common parietal processing mechanisms, with (intra)parietal cortices supporting an overarching concept of magnitude in a generalized manner. The review cites brain imaging studies showing overlapping neurofunctional circuits across magnitude dimensions, including an fMRI study finding responses that "substantially overlap across all three magnitude dimensions" in right-lateralized regions including the IPS and insula. The review uses ATOM to interpret DD adults' deficits in conceptual size, duration, and length processing as non-numerical magnitude deficits.
requirements: Requires the assumption of a generalized magnitude system spanning numerical and non-numerical dimensions
constraints: The review notes some studies challenge the common magnitude system account, citing independent adaptation mechanisms for numerosity and size
target_learners: adults with developmental dyscalculia
adults with typical numeracy
target_learning_goals: numerical magnitude processing
non-numerical magnitude processing (time, space, size)
examples: The review interprets DD adults' preserved length processing alongside deficient duration processing as compatible with a non-symbolic magnitude deficit including numerosity and duration but excluding length

article_title: Developmental Dyscalculia in Adults
citation: Liane Kaufmann, Michael von Aster, Silke M. Göbel, Josef Marksteiner, and Elise Klein. (2020). Developmental Dyscalculia in Adults: Current Issues and Open Questions for Future Research. Lernen und Lernstörungen, 9(2), 126–137. https://doi.org/10.1024/2235-0977/a000294
title: Tentative working model differentiating number-related and number-unspecific deficiencies in adult DD
description: The review proposes a tentative working model (Figure 3) suggesting a differentiation between number-related and number-unspecific (domain-general) deficiencies characterizing DD in adulthood at both cognitive and brain levels. Number-related core deficiencies include automatic activation of number magnitude knowledge, enumeration, arithmetic fact retrieval, and arithmetic conceptual knowledge; number-unspecific dysfunctions include attentional processes, working memory, and response latencies. The model is offered as a building block for future research to formulate hypotheses, develop diagnostic marker tasks, and design interventions.
requirements: Requires validation by clinical and longitudinal developmental evidence per the review
constraints: The review states the current evidence is based on only a handful of studies and findings should be interpreted with caution
target_learners: adults with developmental dyscalculia

arithmetic
attention and working memory in numerical contexts

article_title: Adherence to a Mediterranean diet and cognitive function in the Age‐Related Eye Disease Studies 1 & 2
citation: Keenan Tiarnán D., Agrón Elvira, Mares Julie A., Clemons Traci E., van Asten Freekje, Swaroop Anand, Chew Emily Y.; AREDS and AREDS2 Research Groups. (2020). Adherence to a Mediterranean diet and cognitive function in the Age-Related Eye Disease Studies 1 & 2. Alzheimer's & Dementia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8328271/
title: Recommend Mediterranean-type dietary patterns in evidence-based dietary guidelines to support cognitive health in aging
description: The article concludes that its findings "may help inform evidence-based dietary recommendations, adding strength to evidence that Mediterranean-type diet patterns may maximize cognitive reserve against impairment and dementia." The principle is that population dietary guidance for older adults should feature Mediterranean-type patterns, with emphasis on fish intake given its additional association with slower decline. It rests on observational associations, not trial evidence.

constraints: Associations are observational and post hoc; residual or unmeasured confounding (e.g., physical activity) is a stated limitation
Generalizability to populations with different dietary patterns or without age-related macular degeneration is not certain

target_learning_goals: maintaining cognitive function and reducing risk of cognitive impairment in aging
examples: In AREDS and AREDS2, aMED tertile 3 versus tertile 1 yielded odds ratios for cognitive impairment of 0.36 and 0.56 respectively, and fish intake quartile 4 showed consistently lower impairment odds in both cohorts

citation: Kemper, S., Kynette, D., Rash, S., O'Brien, K., & Sprott, R. (1989). Life-span changes to adults' language: Effects of memory and genre. Applied Psycholinguistics, 10, 49-66. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400008419
title: Trade-off between syntactic complexity and clarity/interest of prose in adult language production
description: The article proposes that producing complex syntactic structures competes with producing clear and interesting prose. Elderly adults lost left-branching clauses and showed reduced complexity, yet judges found their statements "more interesting and clearer than those from the young adults." The authors treat this pattern as evidence that syntactic elaboration and communicative clarity trade off in adult language production.

Ratings or judgments of clarity and interest alongside syntactic complexity measures
constraints: The trade-off is the authors' interpretation of the rating and complexity patterns, not a directly tested mechanism

older adult learners

syntactic complexity in language production

article_title: The Psychology and Neuroscience of Curiosity
citation: Kidd, Celeste and Hayden, Benjamin Y. (2015). The psychology and neuroscience of curiosity. Neuron. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2015.09.010
title: Tinbergen's Four Questions as an organizing framework for studying curiosity
description: The article proposes studying curiosity through Tinbergen's Four Questions, which "provide four complementary scientific perspectives on any particular type of behavior". The framework offers four vantage points—function, evolution, mechanism, and development—that allow description of a behavior even when its boundaries are not fully delineated. The authors structure their entire review of curiosity research through this lens, arguing it permits study of information-seeking without first settling a strict definition of curiosity.
requirements: A behavior class whose boundaries are not yet fully delineated can still be described from the four complementary vantage points
constraints: The authors present it as a framework for organizing inquiry, not as a settled taxonomy of curiosity subtypes
target_learners: humans across the lifespan
non-human animals including monkeys, rats, and roundworms
target_learning_goals: understanding the function, evolution, mechanism, and development of curiosity and information-seeking
examples: The review's sections on function, evolution, mechanism, and development each apply one of the four questions to curiosity research

article_title: The Psychology and Neuroscience of Curiosity
citation: Kidd, Celeste and Hayden, Benjamin Y. (2015). The psychology and neuroscience of curiosity. Neuron. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2015.09.010
title: Berlyne's two-dimensional taxonomy of curiosity: perceptual versus epistemic, specific versus diversive
description: The article describes Daniel Berlyne's classic taxonomy, in which he "distinguished between the types of curiosity most commonly exhibited by human and non-humans along two dimensions: perceptual versus epistemic, and specific versus diversive". Perceptual curiosity motivates seeking novel stimuli and diminishes with exposure, while epistemic curiosity aims at acquiring knowledge and applies predominantly to humans. Specific curiosity is desire for a particular piece of information; diversive curiosity is a general desire for stimulation, as in boredom. The authors note this categorization may be replaced by newer subtypes motivated by neural and developmental data.
requirements: Distinguishing curiosity types along the two dimensions as the article describes them
constraints: The authors anticipate Berlyne's categories will be replaced with differently-formulated subtypes motivated by new neural and developmental data
target_learners: humans
non-human animals
target_learning_goals: classifying forms of curiosity and information-seeking behavior
examples: Monkeys exhibit specific curiosity when solving mechanical puzzles without extrinsic incentive; rats exhibit diversive curiosity by preferring to explore unfamiliar maze sections

article_title: Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry
citation: Kingir, S. (2013). Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 9(2), 101-114. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2013.922a
title: Prain and Hand's five-element framework for learning from writing in science
description: The article presents Prain and Hand's (1996) framework of five elements guiding learning from writing in science: writing type, writing purpose, audience, topic, and method of text production. Writing type covers varied formats such as letters and brochures; purpose spans reviewing, clarifying, and persuading; audience involves writing for a wide range of readers so students clarify understanding; topic demands that students analyze, represent, or manipulate understanding in a new version; and production method concerns individual or group composing by hand or computer. The study operationalizes the audience element by assigning letter audiences.
requirements: Effective combinations of the five elements are needed for an increased science understanding, as the article states these elements can be combined in a writing activity
constraints: The article notes audience and writing type were the elements most frequently manipulated in writing-to-learn studies, so the framework's other elements are less empirically tested here
target_learners: 9th grade chemistry students
science students at all levels of education
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of science content
science literacy
meaning-making through writing
examples: The study assigned 9th graders to write letters to younger students (6th graders), peers (9th graders), or their teacher after a mixture unit, manipulating the audience element while holding writing type (letter) constant

article_title: Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry
citation: Kingir, S. (2013). Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 9(2), 101-114. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2013.922a
title: Knowledge-transforming model of writing as a mode of learning in science
description: The article contrasts traditional writing, compatible with the knowledge-telling model and emphasizing knowledge transmission and rote memorization, with non-traditional writing aligned with the knowledge-transforming model (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987). In knowledge-transforming writing, students consider prior knowledge, think about the meaning of new concepts, and plan how to communicate meaning to an audience. This occurs in an interactive-constructivist environment emphasizing individual and social knowledge construction, and provides a context for translating between everyday, audience, and science languages.
requirements: An interactive-constructivist learning environment emphasizing both individual and social construction of knowledge, plus influence of prior understandings on new learning
constraints: Traditional writing contexts where students copy teacher or textbook content do not engage the knowledge-transforming processes; the article notes much classroom writing does not go beyond copying
target_learners: 9th grade chemistry students
science learners
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of science concepts
translation between everyday and scientific language
negotiation of ideas
examples: Students writing to younger students and peers moved between everyday language and technical language, unpacking science understandings, while students writing to the teacher tended to use more science information to show what they know
key_sources: Kingir, S. (2013). Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 9(2), 101-114. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2013.922a

title: Use authentic, non-expert audiences in science writing tasks to promote conceptual understanding
description: The article recommends that writing tasks in science be addressed to audiences other than the teacher, because writing for younger students or peers requires translating science language into everyday language, which promotes meaningful learning. It states that finding significant differences in conceptual understanding with respect to the audience factor "encourages use of authentic audiences along with diversified types of writing in learning various science concepts at all levels of education."

The audience should be one for whom the writer must adapt language, such as younger students or peers
constraints: Writing to the teacher did not produce the same benefit because students treated it as evaluation and used technical language; the article also cautions that positive attitudes may partly reflect a novelty effect since students wrote to a different audience only once
target_learners: 9th grade chemistry students
science students at all levels of education
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of science concepts
science literacy
translation of technical language into everyday language
examples: After the mixture unit, 121 students wrote to 6th graders, 92 to 9th-grade peers, and 130 to their teacher; the younger-student and peer groups scored higher on understanding than the teacher group

title: Mixture Achievement Test (MAT)
description: The Mixture Achievement Test is a 17-item multiple-choice instrument developed to assess students' understanding of mixture concepts, with 13 items taken from a prior Chemical Change and Mixture Achievement test and 4 items developed by the researchers. Items cover classification of mixtures, solutions, solubility, factors affecting solubility, and separation of mixtures, each with five alternatives. Content validity was checked by three chemistry educators, and Cronbach alpha was 0.75; it was administered as pre- and posttest taking 25 minutes.
requirements: Administration during regular class sessions by teachers
Scoring with 1 point per correct response, maximum 17
constraints: The article notes the multiple-choice format may have limited detected effect sizes, suggesting essay-type questions might yield medium or large effects

target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of mixture concepts
examples: The MAT was administered to all 524 students as pretest and posttest; posttest means ranged from 6.02 (traditional group) to 6.87 (younger-student audience group)

title: Writing Assessment Scale for audience-directed science writing
description: A researcher-developed 17-item scale assessing students' end-of-unit writing tasks, with each item scored on a 3-point scale (unsatisfactory, satisfactory, very satisfactory). Items address letter structure, grammar, clarity, fluency, conceptual content, use of everyday language, examples, visual representations, and appropriateness for the intended audience. Items concerning language and expression, content, and audience were combined into a total writing score; inter-rater agreement was 94% with Cohen's kappa of 0.89.

Random selection of writing samples for inter-rater reliability checking
constraints: The article notes a limitation that groups were compared on writing scores without controlling students' prewriting scores, so prior writing ability was not accounted for

article_title: The neural coding of creative idea generation across adolescence and early adulthood
citation: Kleibeuker, S. W., Koolschijn, P. C. M. P., Jolles, D. D., De Dreu, C. K. W., and Crone, E. A. (2013). The neural coding of creative idea generation across adolescence and early adulthood. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 7:905. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2013.00905
title: Dual Pathway to Creativity Model (DPCM): flexible processing and perseverance as two routes to creative outcomes
description: The article invokes the Dual Pathway to Creativity Model, in which "creative performance including the generation of original ideas and creative insights are related to ﬂexible, divergent thinking on the one hand and persistent, bottom-up processing on the other." The flexibility pathway involves generating novel ideas through extensive cognitive categories, flexible switching, and distant associations, while the persistence pathway involves systematic and effortful exploration within a few categories. The study operationalizes the flexibility pathway via the Alternative Uses Test, leaving the perseverance pathway unexamined in the fMRI design.
requirements: fMRI tasks that capture perseverance are needed to examine both pathways alone and in combination
constraints: The current study examined only the flexible, divergent thinking pathway; the DPCM highlights another pathway, namely perseverance, which was not captured by the AUT task
target_learners: adolescents (15–17 years)
adults (25–30 years)
target_learning_goals: divergent thinking
creative idea generation
examples: The adapted AUT scanner task operationalized flexible divergent thinking by asking participants to generate as many unusual and original uses of common objects as possible

article_title: Use of Audiovisual Information in Speech Perception by Prelingually Deaf Children with Cochlear Implants: A First Report
citation: Lorin Lachs, David B. Pisoni, and Karen Iler Kirk. (2001). Use of Audiovisual Information in Speech Perception by Prelingually Deaf Children with Cochlear Implants. Ear Hear. 2001 June ; 22(3): 236–251. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/
title: Modality-neutral articulatory information account of audiovisual speech perception and its development through perceptual learning
description: The article frames audiovisual integration as the recovery of the talker's underlying articulations: "the sensory and perceptual information relevant for speech perception is said to be modality-neutral, because it can be carried by more than one sensory modality." Because acoustic and optic specifications arise from the same articulatory gestures, they are lawfully related, and perceptual learning exploits these co-occurrences to build multimodal representations of speech. For prelingually deaf children with implants, these learning processes begin only after implantation, and the article interprets individual differences in audiovisual gain as reflecting the degree to which children have internalized the commonalities between auditory and visual information about speech.
requirements: Perception of information about the articulations of the vocal tract in at least one sensory modality
constraints: For prelingually deafened children with cochlear implants, audiovisual learning processes only begin to develop after they receive their implant and begin to experience lawful relationships between vision and sound
target_learners: Prelingually deafened children with cochlear implants
target_learning_goals: Spoken language comprehension and spoken word recognition through combined auditory and visual speech perception

article_title: Differential effects of socioeconomic status on working and procedural memory systems
citation: Leonard JA, Mackey AP, Finn AS and Gabrieli JDE (2015) Differential effects of socioeconomic status on working and procedural memory systems. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 9:554. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2015.00554
title: Dissociated multiple memory systems: hippocampal-prefrontal declarative/working memory vs. striatal procedural memory
description: The article's organizing framework is a fundamental dissociation between two memory systems with separable neural substrates. Complex working memory and declarative memory "appears to depend upon the integrity of a memory system that involves both MTL and DLPFC regions," whereas procedural memory, "measured implicitly by skill learning over time, does not depend upon the MTL structures supporting declarative and complex working memory, but rather depends upon the integrity of the basal ganglia." The probabilistic classification task is the behavioral probe of the striatal system, with amnesic patients showing intact learning and Parkinson's patients impaired learning. The study uses this framework to predict and interpret SES's selective effects.
requirements: The framework rests on convergent lesion and neuroimaging evidence in humans and animals distinguishing MTL/DLPFC-dependent from basal-ganglia-dependent learning
constraints: The article notes the systems interact: the striatum plays a role in working memory, and probabilistic learning engages both MTL and striatal systems in different ways depending on feedback-based versus paired-association learning
target_learners: adolescents from lower- and higher-SES backgrounds
target_learning_goals: working memory capacity
procedural (implicit) skill learning such as probabilistic classification
examples: The study measured count span (working memory) and probabilistic classification (procedural memory) alongside hippocampal, DLPFC, and caudate volumes in the same adolescents.

article_title: How the home learning environment contributes to children’s social–emotional competence: A moderated mediation model
citation: Li S, Tang Y and Zheng Y (2023) How the home learning environment contributes to children's social–emotional competence: A moderated mediation model. Front. Psychol. 14:1065978. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1065978
title: Three-dimension conceptualization of the home learning environment grounded in the bio-ecological model
description: The article conceptualizes the home learning environment within the bio-ecological model of human development, distinguishing distal and proximal processes. It defines three dimensions: "structural family characteristics, parental beliefs and interests, and educational processes", with educational processes at the core as the proximal "engine" of development. Distal factors include family income, occupational status, and parental educational beliefs; proximal processes are parent–child interactions in educational activities such as reading, singing, and play. The framework underpins the study's hypothesized moderated mediation model.
requirements: The framework assumes parents and teachers can report reliably on home learning environment and child competence via questionnaires
constraints: Conceptualized for children aged 3–6 in the Chinese preschool context
The article notes no general or common operational definition of home learning environment exists across studies

target_learning_goals: social–emotional competence development including cognitive control, emotional expressivity, empathy and prosocial behaviors, and emotion regulation
examples: The study operationalized the three dimensions in a revised Home Learning Environment Questionnaire with 30 items and tested them in a latent variable SEM with 443 children

description: The article treats phonological processing as a construct whose cognitive underpinnings are debated, noting that "there is controversy about the cognitive skills underlying this construct." It operationalizes the construct through distinct components — phonological awareness, phonological memory, rapid naming — examined alongside visual processing as predictors of reading and writing. The factor analysis separating these components supports treating them as distinguishable skills rather than a unitary ability.

citation: Miller, M., Hanford, R. B., Fassbender, C., Duke, M., & Schweitzer, J. B. (2011). Affect Recognition in Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Journal of Attention Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3950374/
title: Diagnostic Analysis of Nonverbal Accuracy (DANVA) as a measure of adult facial and vocal affect recognition
description: The DANVA is the standardized instrument this study used to assess nonverbal affect recognition in adults, measuring "nonverbal facial and vocal affect recognition skills" through 24 adult face photos and 24 audio-taped sentence recordings, each depicting happy, sad, angry, or fearful emotions at two intensity levels. Participants view each face for no more than 5 seconds or hear each recording, then identify the emotion. Scores are error counts by channel, emotion, and intensity. The article reports internal consistency of .78 to .90 for adult facial stimuli and .75 for vocal stimuli among middle-aged adults, with test-retest reliability of .84 over two months.

article_title: Affect Recognition in Adults With ADHD
citation: Miller, M., Hanford, R. B., Fassbender, C., Duke, M., & Schweitzer, J. B. (2011). Affect Recognition in Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder. Journal of Attention Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3950374/
title: Inattention-specific account of affect recognition deficits in adult ADHD
description: The article advances an explanatory account in which affect recognition difficulties in adult ADHD are tied specifically to inattentive symptoms rather than to hyperactive-impulsive symptoms or to ADHD diagnosis as a category. The authors state that "the ANOVA and regression results link inattentive symptoms with affect decoding deficits and provide some evidence of linking ADHD with deficits in fearful affect recognition specifically." They propose that adults with more severe inattentive symptoms may fail to attend to social cues, have less social interaction experience, and be more passive in social situations, producing decoding errors. The account also entertains whether deficits reflect an attention problem rather than impaired emotional processing per se.
requirements: Replication in larger, more heterogeneous samples to confirm the inattention-specific pattern
constraints: The authors state the finding is in need of replication and that the study sample was small and highly intelligent, limiting generalizability

article_title: Benefits of a bedtime routine in young children: Sleep, development, and beyond
citation: Mindell Jodi A., Williamson Ariel A. (2018). Benefits of a bedtime routine in young children: Sleep, development, and beyond. Sleep medicine reviews. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.smrv.2017.10.007
title: Conceptual model of bedtime routine benefits for broad child development (ages 0-5)
description: The article proposes a conceptual model (Fig. 1) in which "increased bedtime routine consistency and engagement in positive, healthy bedtime routine activities are critical in conferring improved developmental outcomes." Outcome domains are sleep, child mood/emotional-behavioral regulation, parent and family stress and functioning, and child language development/literacy/cognition, with child self-care/health and parent-child bonding/attachment hypothesized as additional outcomes. The model embeds the routine in a social-ecological framework with child, familial, and contextual factors, and excludes maladaptive activities such as television viewing. Mechanisms of action are deliberately not specified in the model.
requirements: Routine consistency (implementation on most nights) and engagement in positive, healthy bedtime routine activities
constraints: The model does not include specific mechanisms of action
Defined adaptive and maladaptive activities may not apply to all children; activities should be tailored to the individual child and family
The model is likely not exhaustive regarding outcomes

caregivers and families of young children

language development and literacy
emotional and behavioral regulation
parent-child attachment
family functioning

description: The article organizes common adaptive bedtime routine activities into "the broader domains of 1) nutrition, 2) hygiene, 3) communication, and 4) physical contact," each hypothesized to contribute to positive developmental outcomes. The domains were chosen based on cross-cultural commonalities in routine components and available early childhood research, and the authors note the list is not exhaustive and activities vary across cultures and contexts.

Consistent nightly implementation of the routine

Activities should be tailored to the individual child and family

article_title: Relationship between cognitive function and prevalence of decrease in intrinsic academic motivation in adolescents
citation: Mizuno K, Tanaka M, Fukuda S, Imai-Matsumura K, Watanabe Y. (2011). Relationship between cognitive function and prevalence of decrease in intrinsic academic motivation in adolescents. Behavioral and Brain Functions 7:4. https://doi.org/10.1186/1744-9081-7-4
title: Use verbal memory tests (digit span forward and kana pick-out) to objectively evaluate the extent of decreased intrinsic academic motivation in junior high students
description: The article recommends measuring capacity for verbal memory as an objective indicator of decreased intrinsic academic motivation in early adolescence. It states that "measurement of capacity for verbal memory is useful for objectively evaluating the extent of decrease in intrinsic academic motivation", naming the digit span forward test and kana pick-out test as appropriate for this age group. This rests on the cross-sectional associations reported for junior high students.
requirements: Applies to junior high school students (7th-9th grade); the associations were not found in elementary students.
constraints: Cross-sectional findings do not establish cause-and-effect; the study had a limited number of participants and did not measure socioeconomic or psychological status or intelligence quotient.
target_learners: Junior high school students (grades 7-9)
target_learning_goals: Early detection of decline in intrinsic academic motivation
examples: The study administered the digit span forward test and kana pick-out test alongside a 30-item intrinsic academic motivation questionnaire to students in grades 4-9 in Hyogo Prefecture, Japan.
