article_title: Adults with dyslexia exhibit large effects of crowding, increased dependence on cues, and detrimental effects of distractors in visual search tasks
citation: Moores, E., Cassim, R. and Talcott, J.B. (2011). Adults with dyslexia exhibit large effects of crowding, increased dependence on cues, and detrimental effects of distractors in visual search tasks. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2011.00285
title: Visual attention deficits in dyslexia require multi-factor accounts combining crowding, cue dependence and distractor exclusion
description: The article proposes that visual attention in dyslexia must be understood through the combined influences of crowding, attention orientation and focussing of attention/distractor exclusion, rather than any single mechanism. It reports that "AwD do not use cues less, but they do use cues less successfully" and that "It is not clear how any single theory on its own can fully account for the entirety of findings presented here." The account holds that crowding effects operate independently from, and in parallel with, the allocation of visual attention, and that pre-cueing eliminated effects of crowding for AwD.
requirements: Simultaneous investigation of crowding, orientation and distractor exclusion factors rather than isolated paradigms
constraints: The article states further research should aim to confirm that greater set size effects occur independently of task difficulty and in other paradigms
target_learners: adults with dyslexia
target_learning_goals: understanding visual attention contributions to literacy difficulties in dyslexia
examples: Calibrated discrimination accuracy across conditions for each individual, then compared relative performance across display types, cue types and difficulties

article_title: Latinos’ Changing Ethnic Group Representation From Elementary to Middle School: Perceived Belonging and Academic Achievement
citation: Morales-Chicas Jessica, Graham Sandra. (2017). Latinos’ Changing Ethnic Group Representation From Elementary to Middle School: Perceived Belonging and Academic Achievement. Journal of Research on Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1111/jora.12292
title: Stage–environment fit extended to ethnic minority youth: mismatch between same-ethnic representation across the middle school transition and adolescents' developmental needs
description: Stage–environment fit theory holds that "the middle school transition can be especially challenging because of the mismatch between the developmental needs of early adolescents and the school environment to which they are transitioning." The article extends this framework to ethnic minority youth by proposing ethnic incongruence — a decline in same-ethnic peers from elementary to middle school — as a specific mismatch, since same-ethnic group esteem and belonging grow in early adolescence and Latinos tend to be more collectivistic. The framework predicts poorer adjustment when fewer same-ethnic peers accompany the transition, and treats school-level diversity as a dimension that can buffer developmental mismatch.
requirements: Applies during school transitions where ethnic representation changes between departing and receiving schools, at a developmental period when same-ethnic peer preference heightens
constraints: The article notes the theory "has rarely addressed mismatches that might be particularly challenging for ethnic minority youth"; the extension is tested cross-sectionally at one time point only
target_learners: Latino early adolescents transitioning from elementary to middle school
target_learning_goals: School belonging
Academic achievement (GPA)
examples: The study measured representation change by subtracting each student's elementary-school Latino proportion from the middle-school proportion, and Simpson's diversity index at the school level, then tested the cross-level interaction.

article_title: Enhanced verbal abilities in the congenitally blind
citation: Occelli Valeria, Lacey Simon, Stephens Careese, Merabet Lotfi B., Sathian K. (2017). Enhanced Verbal Abilities in The Congenitally Blind. Experimental Brain Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5436932/
title: Congenital blindness confers a specific verbal advantage rather than a general memory enhancement
description: The article proposes that congenital blindness produces superiority specifically in verbal abilities rather than a domain-general enhancement of memory. This account explains why blind participants outperformed sighted controls on verbal memory, verbal fluency, and verbal working memory while performing equally on spatial memory and spatial imagery. The authors suggest "congenital blindness induces stronger reliance on verbal information, and that such reliance leads to better verbal memory, and potentially other verbal skills, through practice."
requirements: Requires congenital blindness from birth, as the account rests on lifelong adaptation to the absence of visual input
constraints: The mechanism by which the superiority of verbal abilities occurs is currently unknown, per the authors
The study tested a limited range of tasks, so whether superiority extends across all language skills remains open
target_learners: Congenitally blind adults
target_learning_goals: Verbal memory and verbal skill development
examples: Blind participants outperformed sighted controls on all verbal tasks but not on spatial tasks in the same participants
key_sources: Occelli Valeria, Lacey Simon, Stephens Careese, Merabet Lotfi B., Sathian K. (2017). Enhanced Verbal Abilities in The Congenitally Blind. Experimental Brain Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5436932/

article_title: Enhanced verbal abilities in the congenitally blind
citation: Occelli Valeria, Lacey Simon, Stephens Careese, Merabet Lotfi B., Sathian K. (2017). Enhanced Verbal Abilities in The Congenitally Blind. Experimental Brain Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5436932/
title: Visual cortex involvement in language processing may underlie the verbal advantage in congenital blindness
description: The article proposes a neural account for the verbal advantage: visual cortical areas in congenitally blind people are recruited for language processing. The authors cite evidence that covert verb generation recruits early visual cortex, that visual cortical activity during word-list recall correlates with verbal memory performance, and that visual cortex shows stronger resting-state connectivity with language areas in the congenitally blind. This framework links cross-modal neuroplasticity to the behavioral verbal superiority observed in this study.
requirements: Requires congenital blindness, as the neural reorganization is attributed to the absence of vision from birth
constraints: The authors state the mechanism by which the superiority of verbal abilities occurs is currently unknown; this neural account is offered as a possibility
target_learners: Congenitally blind adults
target_learning_goals: Understanding neural bases of verbal memory and language processing
examples: Covert verb generation in response to nouns presented via Braille or auditory input recruits activity in early visual cortex

article_title: The Effect of Structured Exercise on Short-Term Memory Subsystems: New Insight on Training Activities
citation: Ottoboni Giovanni, Ceciliani Andrea, Tessari Alessia. (2021). The Effect of Structured Exercise on Short-Term Memory Subsystems: New Insight on Training Activities. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph18147545
title: Baddeley's working-memory model extended with a visuo-motor short-term memory subsystem (gestural buffer)
description: The article frames its study within an implemented version of Baddeley's working-memory model comprising short-term memory subsystems for auditory-verbal, visuo-spatial, and visuo-motor information. As the article states, it "includes the two STM subsystems specific for visuo-spatial information and auditory-verbal information postulated by Baddley and an STM subsystem specific for visuo-motor information, i.e., the gestural buffer". The study uses this structure to predict which subsystems acute open- versus closed-skill exercise should affect.
requirements: STM tasks targeting each subsystem (verbal, spatial, motor) to measure subsystem-specific spans
constraints: The motor task was an ad-hoc span task developed for this study using meaningless upper-limb gestures from the STIMA, reproduced in mirror configuration
target_learners: primary-school children aged 7–10 years
target_learning_goals: short-term memory storage capacity across verbal, visuo-spatial and motor subsystems
examples: The study measured verbal span with the WISC-IV digit span, spatial span with the Corsi task, and motor span with an ad-hoc gesture-reproduction task

article_title: Effects of age on metacognitive efficiency
citation: Palmer E.C., David A.S., Fleming S.M. (2014). Effects of age on metacognitive efficiency. Consciousness and Cognition. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4154452/
title: Meta-d′/d′ as a performance-controlled measure of metacognitive efficiency
description: Meta-d′/d′ is a signal detection theoretic measure that quantifies metacognitive efficiency independently of primary task performance. The article explains that "Meta-d′/d′ is a relative measure: given a certain level of processing capacity (d′), meta-d′/d′ quantifies the extent to which a metacognitively optimal observer is aware of their performance." A value of 1 is metacognitively ideal; values below 1 indicate a failure of metacognitive awareness. The study uses it to dissociate metacognitive efficiency from age-related changes in task performance, which confound measures such as the gamma correlation.
requirements: Requires confidence ratings collected on each trial alongside a primary task, and computation of both d′ and meta-d′ from the same data
constraints: Values greater than 1 may occur when the initial judgment is made under time pressure, as the article notes
target_learners: Adults aged 18–84 in laboratory studies of perception and memory
target_learning_goals: Quantifying the efficiency with which confidence ratings discriminate between correct and incorrect trials
examples: Applied to a staircase-controlled perceptual task and a 2-AFC word recognition memory task in adults aged 18–84
key_sources: Palmer E.C., David A.S., Fleming S.M. (2014). Effects of age on metacognitive efficiency. Consciousness and Cognition. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4154452/

article_title: Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents
citation: Pandey A, Hale D, Das S, Goddings A-L, Blakemore S-J, Viner RM. (2018). Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6059379/
title: Prefer curriculum-based self-regulation interventions in schools because they require no considerable additional time or staff resources and reach children where they already are.
description: The review recommends curriculum-based interventions as the preferred delivery model for self-regulation improvement in schools. This recommendation rests on three factors the article states: curriculum interventions were "delivered in schools by training of teachers without a need for considerable additional resource in terms of time and staff"; children and adolescents "spend a considerable part of their time at school between the ages of 5 and 18 years and thus are easily accessible for interventions"; and curriculum-based approaches were the most common type used (21 of 50 interventions, 42%), with 16 of 21 (76%) reporting consistent SR improvements.
requirements: Teachers receive professional training to implement the predefined curriculum in classrooms
constraints: Fidelity was infrequently measured and reported (11 of 21 curriculum interventions; 52%)
target_learners: Children and adolescents aged 5 to 18 years in school settings
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation skills including emotion control, positive interactions, avoiding inappropriate actions, and self-directed learning
examples: Curriculum-based interventions included a combination of teachers' professional training and classroom-based activities based on a predefined curriculum, embedded within the existing school routine, using strategies such as circle-time games, storytelling, book reading, and self-talk in preschool and kindergarten, and role play, cognitive modeling, and psychoeducational group therapeutic lessons in older children
key_sources: Pandey A, Hale D, Das S, Goddings A-L, Blakemore S-J, Viner RM. (2018). Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6059379/

article_title: Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents
citation: Pandey A, Hale D, Das S, Goddings A-L, Blakemore S-J, Viner RM. (2018). Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6059379/
title: Five-category taxonomy of universal self-regulation interventions: curriculum-based, mindfulness and yoga, family-based, exercise-based, and social and personal skills.
description: The review organizes the 50 included interventions into five categories: "curriculum based, mindfulness and yoga, family based, exercise based, and other social and personal skills–based intervention strategies/delivery methods." These classifications were based on discussion between the review team members. Curriculum-based interventions (21 of 50, 42%) combine teacher professional training with classroom activities; mindfulness and yoga interventions (8 studies) are short-duration school-based programs with qualified instructors; family-based interventions (9 studies) involve parents and/or siblings; exercise-based interventions (6 studies) use physical activity; and social and personal skills interventions (6 studies) use small-group training with frameworks of personal responsibility, model behavior, and conflict resolution.
requirements: Classification was based on discussion between the review team members (A.P., D.H., and S.D.) rather than a pre-specified coding scheme
constraints: The review notes no advantage of 1 type of intervention over another with regards to effect on distal outcomes
target_learners: Children and adolescents aged 0 to 19 years in universal (non-targeted) settings
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation: controlling emotions, positive interactions with others, avoiding inappropriate or aggressive actions, and self-directed learning

article_title: Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents
citation: Pandey A, Hale D, Das S, Goddings A-L, Blakemore S-J, Viner RM. (2018). Effectiveness of Universal Self-regulation–Based Interventions in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6059379/
title: Evidence base of 49 randomized clinical trials evaluating 50 universal self-regulation interventions with 23,098 participants aged 2 to 17 years.
description: The review's evidence base comprises 49 studies reporting 50 interventions meeting all eligibility criteria, including "a total of 23,098 participants, a mean of 462 participants per study." Records were published over a span of 4 decades (1977-2017). On quality assessment using the Effective Public Health Practice Project Quality Assessment Tool, 3 studies were rated as high quality, 38 as moderate, and 8 as poor. The most common reason for downgrading was lack of blinding of participants (46 studies, 93.8%). Participants were predominantly in primary/elementary school (13,403, 58.0%) and preschool (6,566, 28.4%), with 84.8% in the United States and 34.3% low income.
requirements: Studies had to report cluster randomized trials or randomized clinical trials, evaluate universal interventions, include outcomes associated with self-regulation skills, and be published in a peer-reviewed journal with full text available in English
constraints: The review was limited to published literature in the English language and may have missed unpublished work and studies in other languages; generalizability may be affected by the substantial number of studies conducted in the United States
target_learners: Children and adolescents aged 2 to 17 years (median 6.0 years) across preschool, primary, middle, and high school settings
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation outcomes measured via validated tools including the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function, Head Toes Knees Shoulders task, and Flanker tasks

article_title: Interaction of threat and verbal working memory in adolescents
citation: Patel Nilam, Vytal Katherine, Pavletic Nevia, Stoodley Catherine, Pine Daniel S., Grillon Christian, Ernst Monique. (2016). Interaction of Threat and Verbal Working Memory in Adolescents. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.12582
title: Limited cognitive resources account of the threat–working memory interaction
description: The article's central explanatory framework holds that anxiety and cognition compete for a shared pool of cognitive resources whose availability depends on task load. As the authors state, "low-load cognitive tasks leave resources available for threat to be processed and to interfere with cognitive performance, whereas high-load cognitive tasks deplete cognitive resources such that threat cannot be processed and thus does not interfere with performance." The account is used to explain both the accuracy impairment at low/medium load and the abolition of anxiety-potentiated startle at high load, in adolescents and adults alike.
requirements: A cognitive task with manipulable load levels spanning low to high resource demands
A sustained anxiety induction and a physiological anxiety measure to index threat processing
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretation of its findings, not a directly tested mechanism; neural mechanisms were not assessed and would require functional neuroimaging
target_learners: adolescents (10–17 years)
adults
target_learning_goals: maintaining working memory performance under sustained anxiety or threat
examples: In the experiment, accuracy was impaired under threat at 1-back and 2-back but not 3-back, and anxiety-potentiated startle was abolished at 3-back, matching the resource-depletion account

article_title: Promoting a Sense of Belonging in Online Learning Communities of Inquiry
citation: Peacock, S., & Cowan, J. (2019). Promoting a Sense of Belonging in Online Learning Communities of Inquiry. Online Learning, 23(2). https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v23i2.1488
title: Adapted Community of Inquiry Framework organised around three overlapping Influences: Trusting, Meaning-making and Deepening understanding
description: The article adapts the well-known Community of Inquiry Framework, shifting attention from the three Presences to their overlapping intersections, which the authors entitle Influences. As the abstract states, "This revision of the well-known Framework focuses upon the overlapping intersections of the three Presences, entitled Influences: 'Trusting', 'Meaning-making' and 'Deepening understanding'." Each Influence is treated as a locus of tutor facilitative activity through which online learners' sense of belonging can be nurtured, with guidance and examples offered for each.
requirements: Tutors must treat the Influences as overlapping intersections of the three Presences rather than as separate categories
constraints: The framework is framed specifically for online learning communities of inquiry
target_learners: online learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: nurturing online learners' sense of belonging to promote and consolidate learning
examples: For each Influence, guidance illustrated by examples is offered, leading to particular suggestions for the online tutor's facilitative activities

title: Online tutors should deliberately nurture learners' sense of belonging as part of their facilitative activities
description: The article's central design recommendation is that nurturing online learners' sense of belonging is an important aspect of the online tutor's facilitative activities. It states that it "seeks to specify how tutors may nurture online learners' SoB", and that its suggestions "concentrate upon the promotion of a sense of belonging as an important aspect of the online tutor's facilitative activities". article_title: Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers?
citation: Michelle S. Peter, Samantha Durrant, Andrew Jessop, Amy Bidgood, Julian M. Pine, Caroline F. Rowland. (2019). Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers? Cognitive Psychology 115 (2019) 101238. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2019.101238
title: Two competing accounts of the processing speed–vocabulary relationship: facilitation versus lexical entrenchment
description: The article frames two hypotheses about why processing speed relates to vocabulary. On the facilitation account, "faster processing of familiar words frees up resources that can then be dedicated to the learning of new words". On the reverse account, drawn from the adult literature, larger vocabularies yield stronger, more entrenched lexical representations that are accessed faster, so children with large vocabularies are simply better at processing familiar words with no implications for later growth. The study tests these by asking whether processing speed predicts future vocabulary growth over and above concurrent vocabulary size.
requirements: Testing requires showing that processing speed predicts the rate of future vocabulary growth, not just concurrent correlations with vocabulary size
constraints: Most prior work reports only concurrent relationships or does not control for concurrent vocabulary, limiting causal interpretation
target_learners: toddlers in the second and third year of life
target_learning_goals: vocabulary acquisition
lexical processing efficiency
examples: The study tested whether children with faster processing speed grow their vocabularies faster against the alternative that large-vocabulary children are merely faster to process familiar words
key_sources: Michelle S. Peter, Samantha Durrant, Andrew Jessop, Amy Bidgood, Julian M. Pine, Caroline F. Rowland. (2019). Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers? Cognitive Psychology 115 (2019) 101238. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2019.101238

article_title: Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers?
citation: Michelle S. Peter, Samantha Durrant, Andrew Jessop, Amy Bidgood, Julian M. Pine, Caroline F. Rowland. (2019). Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers? Cognitive Psychology 115 (2019) 101238. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2019.101238
title: Direct versus indirect routes from processing speed to syntax acquisition
description: The article outlines two models by which processing speed could affect syntax acquisition. On the indirect route, syntax emerges from lexical knowledge, so processing speed would act on syntax via vocabulary learning and its relationship with syntax "would disappear once we control for vocabulary". On the direct route, more efficient processing of familiar words helps track relations and co-occurrences between words, a skill necessary for syntactic development, so faster processing should predict syntactic growth even after concurrent vocabulary is taken into account. The study's syntax analyses were designed to adjudicate between these accounts.
requirements: Adjudicating the accounts requires growth curve analysis of syntactic growth with concurrent vocabulary controlled
constraints: Only one prior study (Fernald et al., 2006) had reported concurrent relations between processing speed and syntactic measures, not predictive ones
target_learners: toddlers in the second and third year of life
target_learning_goals: syntactic development
productive syntax measured via M3L and syntactic complexity
examples: The article contrasts the lexical-emergence view (Bates & Goodman, 1999; Marchman & Bates, 1994) with the direct-tracking view (Marchman & Fernald, 2008)

article_title: Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers?
citation: Michelle S. Peter, Samantha Durrant, Andrew Jessop, Amy Bidgood, Julian M. Pine, Caroline F. Rowland. (2019). Does speed of processing or vocabulary size predict later language growth in toddlers? Cognitive Psychology 115 (2019) 101238. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogpsych.2019.101238
title: Language 0–5 Project longitudinal cohort with looking-while-listening processing speed measurement
description: The Language 0–5 Project is a large longitudinal cohort in the North West of England from which this study draws its data. A total of 95 families were recruited, with a final sample of 90 contributing data at one or more measurement points. Children were tested in the laboratory at the University of Liverpool at 19, 25, and 31 months using a looking-while-listening paradigm with eye-tracking (EyeLink 1000 Plus), and caregivers completed repeated vocabulary checklists (UK-CDI, Lincoln CDI, CDI-III) between 8 and 37 months. The method is documented on the project's OSF site.
requirements: Caregivers completed vocabulary checklists in the week prior to lab visits or on paper during the session
constraints: Children with fewer than 25% good trials were excluded at each measurement point; RT was calculated only on distractor-initial trials where the child looked at the distracter at target word onset
target_learners: monolingual English-learning toddlers, born full-term and typically developing
target_learning_goals: speed of lexical processing
expressive vocabulary growth
productive syntax growth
examples: At 19 months children saw 64 test trials across two blocks with eight nouns each presented eight times as target; at 25 and 31 months adjective-noun combinations were added to increase challenge

article_title: Measuring the development of inhibitory control: The challenge of heterotypic continuity
citation: Petersen, I. T., Hoyniak, C. P., McQuillan, M. E., Bates, J. E., & Staples, A. D. (2016). Measuring the development of inhibitory control: The challenge of heterotypic continuity. Developmental Review, 40, 25-71. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dr.2016.02.001
title: Four-cluster taxonomy of complex inhibitory control task demands: perceptual, performance, association, and motivational inhibition
description: The review groups complex inhibitory control tasks into four a priori clusters by task demand: "perceptual inhibition, performance inhibition, association inhibition, and motivational inhibition". Perceptual tasks inhibit perceptual information (e.g., Baby Stroop, Spatial Conflict); performance tasks use a cue to signal when to inhibit on a subset of trials (Bear/Dragon, Simon Says); association tasks require inhibition plus a competing response on all trials (Day/Night, Hand Game); motivational or 'hot' tasks add a motivational component (Less is More, Tower). The authors note this distinction between performance and association inhibition is one they believe no other group has made, and call it speculative but possibly useful.
requirements: Tasks must be classifiable by their demand structure; the authors caution the clusters are not mutually exclusive because all measures tap multiple aspects of inhibitory control
constraints: The authors describe the grouping as an oversimplification and the performance/association distinction as speculative
target_learners: typically-developing children under 8 years of age
target_learning_goals: measuring the development of inhibitory control as a component of self-regulation
key_sources: Petersen, I. T., Hoyniak, C. P., McQuillan, M. E., Bates, J. E., & Staples, A. D. (2016). Measuring the development of inhibitory control: The challenge of heterotypic continuity. Developmental Review, 40, 25-71. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dr.2016.02.001

article_title: Measuring the development of inhibitory control: The challenge of heterotypic continuity
citation: Petersen, I. T., Hoyniak, C. P., McQuillan, M. E., Bates, J. E., & Staples, A. D. (2016). Measuring the development of inhibitory control: The challenge of heterotypic continuity. Developmental Review, 40, 25-71. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dr.2016.02.001
title: Heterotypic continuity of inhibitory control: the same underlying construct changes its behavioral manifestation across development, with two implications for measurement
description: The review's organizing framework is heterotypic continuity, defined as "the manifestation of the same underlying process through different behavioral presentations at different developmental periods". Inhibitory control is continuous in function but appears differently in toddlers (e.g., using words rather than physical aggression to get a toy) than in older children (e.g., inhibiting an action despite social pressure). Self-regulation also shifts from reliance on external sources of control to internal, self-initiated control. The framework yields two measurement implications: the same measure may not reflect the same construct at different ages, and describing heterotypic continuity may require using different measures across time.
requirements: Longitudinal measurement must be guided by theory and construct validity, with attention to developmental appropriateness, developmental sensitivity, and construct validity across the study's time frame
constraints: Scores on the same measure across time may reflect changes in the measure's meaning rather than real construct change; the framework applies to domains showing heterotypic continuity
target_learners: children from toddlerhood through adolescence
target_learning_goals: valid longitudinal assessment of inhibitory control and self-regulation development

article_title: The Association between Physical Activity During the Day and Long-Term Memory Stability
citation: Pontifex, M. B., Gwizdala, K. L., Parks, A. C., Pfeiffer, K. A. & Fenn, K. M. (2016). The Association between Physical Activity During the Day and Long-Term Memory Stability. Scientific Reports 6, 38148. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep38148
title: Schedule physical activity opportunities so they avoid the 1–2 hours after encoding and fall before retrieval rather than counting total daily activity
description: The article argues that for long-term memory of newly learned declarative material, when activity occurs matters more than how much occurs across the day. Activity roughly 1–2 hours after encoding was "detrimental to the maintenance of information in long-term memory", while activity in the hour before retrieval was associated with greater maintenance. The authors suggest "superior long-term memory of declarative information occurs when physical activity opportunities are more strategically aligned" to fall before encoding or before retrieval.
requirements: Knowledge of when encoding and retrieval occur relative to the schedule of physical activity opportunities
constraints: Findings are cross-sectional and exploratory; the authors state further research is necessary to validate the existence and relative timings of these critical periods, and mechanisms may differ across the lifespan
target_learners: college-aged young adults
target_learning_goals: retention of declarative, paired-associate information over a 12-hour interval
examples: Participants wore heart rate monitors across a 12-hour interval between learning and testing, and sliding-window regressions identified the two critical periods rather than prescribing activity in advance

article_title: An Integrative View of School Functioning: Transactions Between Self-Regulation, School Engagement, and Teacher–Child Relationship Quality
citation: Portilla Ximena A., Ballard Parissa J., Adler Nancy E., Boyce W. Thomas, Obradović Jelena. (2014). An Integrative View of School Functioning: Transactions between Self-Regulation, School Engagement, and Teacher-Child Relationship Quality. Child development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12259
title: Transactional model of development applied to early schooling: children's behaviors and teacher-child relationship quality shape each other bidirectionally over time
description: Extending Sameroff and MacKenzie's (2003) transactional model to a school context, the article theorizes that children's behaviors and the classroom environment, indexed by teacher-child relationship quality, "interact through bidirectional processes" over time, forming patterns that serve as both inputs and outcomes to development. The study tested this with nested path models across kindergarten and first grade, finding transactions operated across different domains (self-regulation to conflict; conflict and engagement) rather than within the same domain.
requirements: Longitudinal designs that control for longitudinal stability and within-time covariation to detect transactional pathways
constraints: In this study, bidirectional transactions between conflict and self-regulation were not supported; effects ran unidirectionally from self-regulation to conflict
target_learners: Young children transitioning into formal schooling (kindergarten and first grade)
target_learning_goals: School readiness, self-regulation, teacher-child relationship quality, school engagement, and academic competence
examples: Doumen and colleagues (2008) found children's aggressive behavior at kindergarten onset led to greater teacher-child conflict by mid-year, which led to more aggressive behavior by year end

article_title: Metacognitive scaffolding boosts cognitive and neural benefits following executive attention training in children
citation: Pozuelos, J.P., Cómbita, L.M., Abundis-Gutiérrez, A., Paz-Alonso, P.M., Conejero A., Guerra, S., & Rueda, M.R. (2019). Metacognitive scaffolding boosts cognitive and neural benefits following executive attention training in children. Developmental Science, 22: e12756. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12756
title: Metacognitive scaffolding amplifies brain plasticity and cognitive efficiency effects of process-based training
description: The article proposes that adding metacognitive scaffolding to process-based training changes how training affects the brain and cognition. It frames its results as showing that "metacognitive scaffolding boosts the influence of process-based training on cognitive efficiency and brain plasticity related to cognitive control", with the N2 ERP component associated with conflict processing serving as the neural marker of this amplified plasticity. The framework links educational scaffolding and metacognitive strategies to computerized training outcomes.
requirements: A computerized process-based training program whose effects can be indexed at cognitive and neural levels, with scaffolding layered on top
constraints: Proposed on the basis of one training study in typically developing preschoolers; the abstract presents it as an interpretation of the reported results
target_learners: typically developing preschoolers
target_learning_goals: executive attention and cognitive control
cognitive efficiency
examples: Preschoolers in the metacognitive group showed both larger intelligence gains and increased N2 responses, and N2 change predicted intelligence gain within that group

Metacognitive scaffolding boosts cognitive and neural benefits following executive attention training in children. Developmental Science, 22: e12756. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12756

article_title: Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity
citation: Preiss David D. (2022). Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9500634/
title: Framework: managing the interaction between metacognition and mind wandering is the main role of cognitive flexibility in creativity
description: The article advances a general framework in which cognitive flexibility during the creative process involves a strategic use of mind wandering by means of metacognitive regulation. Creators alternate between spontaneous cognition, which feeds originality during idea generation, and controlled cognition, which feeds appropriateness during idea evaluation. The author states that "managing the interaction between metacognition and mind wandering is the main role of cognitive flexibility in creativity" and that balancing metacognition during generation and exploration of pre-inventive structures is a quintessential part of creativity. The framework applies specifically to creative production involving generation and exploration of ideas, not to trial-and-error or serendipity.
requirements: Applies only to creative production involving generation and exploration of ideas
constraints: Does not fit cases involving trial-and-error or serendipity, which the author notes do not fit this conception very well
target_learners: creators across domains
students developing creative skills
target_learning_goals: understanding the role of cognitive flexibility in creative processes
managing attention and metacognition during idea generation and evaluation
examples: Figure 1 summarizes the process of alternating between spontaneous and controlled cognition across idea generation and idea evaluation
key_sources: Preiss David D. (2022). Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9500634/

article_title: Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity
citation: Preiss David D. (2022). Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9500634/
title: Efklides' three-dimensional model of metacognition maps onto the generative and exploratory stages of creativity
description: The article adopts Efklides' distinction between three dimensions of metacognition: metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive experiences, and metacognitive abilities. Metacognitive knowledge is declarative knowledge including information about persons, strategies, tasks, and goals; metacognitive experiences refer to awareness and feelings during task implementation; metacognitive abilities are skills used to control cognition, including planning, regulation, and evaluation. The author argues these dimensions are engaged differently across creative stages: "Metacognitive experiences are, probably, more important in the generative stage than in the exploratory stage", while metacognitive knowledge is more influential in exploratory stages, and abilities are triggered during both stages.
requirements: Distinguishes metacognitive knowledge, experiences, and abilities as separate dimensions
constraints: The mapping of dimensions onto creative stages is the author's theoretical proposal, not a tested result
target_learners: creators across domains
students developing creative skills
target_learning_goals: understanding how different metacognitive dimensions support idea generation versus evaluation
examples: The author proposes metacognitive experiences help identify attentional shifts during idea generation, particularly mind wandering
key_sources: Preiss David D. (2022). Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9500634/

article_title: Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity
citation: Preiss David D. (2022). Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9500634/
title: Four-C developmental model of creativity (mini-C, little-C, Pro-C, Big-C) with evolving metacognition across levels
description: The article reviews Kaufman and Beghetto's (2009) four-level developmental model of creativity. Mini-C involves creative insights during learning, represented by emerging mental constructions; little-C involves products triggering positive assessment from peers or teachers; Pro-C involves professional contributions deemed original and appropriate by gatekeepers of a field; Big-C involves eminent creativity producing an entire body of work that has made a difference in a cultural field. The author complements this model by arguing that spontaneous cognition dominates at mini-C and little-C levels, while controlled cognition and metacognitive assessment become increasingly important at Pro-C and Big-C levels, where "Metacognitive judgments are not self-generated" but incorporate field standards.
requirements: Distinguishes four levels of creativity with different sources of evaluation
constraints: The authors do not think it is necessary to pass through each level to become an eminent creator
target_learners: children and adolescents developing creativity
professional creators
eminent creators
target_learning_goals: understanding developmental trajectories of creativity
understanding how metacognition evolves with creative expertise
examples: Table 1 summarizes how metacognition evolves at the four levels, from exploration and improvisation at mini-C to developing networks of enterprise at Big-C

article_title: Hippocampal-neocortical functional reorganization underlies children's cognitive development
citation: Qin Shaozheng, Cho Soohyun, Chen Tianwen, Rosenberg-Lee Miriam, Geary David C., Menon Vinod. (2014). Hippocampal-neocortical functional reorganization underlies children's cognitive development. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.3788
title: Hippocampal-neocortical consolidation account of the development of memory-based problem solving
description: The article advances an account in which the hippocampus plays a time-limited role in the early phase of academic knowledge acquisition, fostering rapid binding of new information that is gradually consolidated into neocortical representations. The authors write that "the hippocampus plays a critical, but time-limited, role in the early phase of knowledge acquisition, and this hippocampal dependence is reduced following reconfiguration of neocortical connections and stabilization of newly acquired knowledge – a process referred to as consolidation." Their longitudinal and cross-sectional findings — rising then falling hippocampal engagement, connectivity-predicted retrieval gains, and increasing representational stability — are presented as support for this consolidation framework in children's arithmetic learning.
requirements: Longitudinal or cross-sectional assessment spanning the transition from procedure-based to memory-based strategies, with behavioral strategy measurement alongside brain imaging
constraints: Evidence for the consolidation model was primarily based on animal studies, and the authors note how such mechanisms operate in humans during children's early learning was unknown
target_learners: typically developing children ages 7-9
adolescents ages 14-17
adults ages 19-22
target_learning_goals: memory-based arithmetic fact retrieval
transition from procedure-based to memory-based problem solving
examples: The longitudinal fMRI study of 28 children over 1.2 years showed increased hippocampal engagement paralleling the shift from counting to retrieval, and cross-sectional data showed engagement declining to adult-like levels by adolescence.
key_sources: Qin Shaozheng, Cho Soohyun, Chen Tianwen, Rosenberg-Lee Miriam, Geary David C., Menon Vinod. (2014). Hippocampal-neocortical functional reorganization underlies children's cognitive development. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.3788

article_title: Cognitive flexibility-related prefrontal activation in preschoolers: A biological approach to temperamental effortful control
citation: Quiñones-Camacho Laura E., Fishburn Frank A., Camacho M. Catalina, Wakschlag Lauren S., Perlman Susan B. (2019). Cognitive flexibility-related prefrontal activation in preschoolers: A biological approach to temperamental effortful control. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6969345/
title: Integrative model of temperament, behavior, and brain activation for cognitive flexibility
description: The article tests and supports an integrative individual-differences model in which "individual differences in behavioral responses are supported by differential recruitment of key neural regions and networks." Specifically, parent-reported temperamental effortful control (a latent factor of attentional focusing, inhibitory control, perceptual sensitivity, and low intensity pleasure) is linked to both cognitive flexibility task behavior and DLPFC activation measured with fNIRS during a child-friendly Stroop task in preschoolers. The model proposes that children with greater effortful control recruit the DLPFC more efficiently, requiring less activation for similar performance.
requirements: Parent-report measure of temperamental effortful control (CBQ short form)
A cognitive flexibility task appropriate for the age group
Neuroimaging capable of measuring prefrontal activation in young children
constraints: Cross-sectional design; no longitudinal data, limiting interpretation of how associations change across early childhood
Task also likely required inhibitory control and working memory, complicating dimension-specific interpretation
Only one form of cognitive flexibility was measured; other aspects might show different patterns
Focused on PFC only; the model could apply to other neural networks
target_learners: preschool-aged children (4-5 years old)
target_learning_goals: understanding individual differences in cognitive flexibility and effortful control
examples: SEM analysis in 123 preschoolers linked parent-reported effortful control to both Stroop accuracy and DLPFC activation during the Pet Store Stroop task

Cognitive flexibility-related prefrontal activation in preschoolers: A biological approach to temperamental effortful control. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6969345/

article_title: Intelligence quotient, short-term memory and study habits as academic achievement predictors of elementary school: A follow-up study
citation: Alberto Quilez-Robres, Alejandro González-Andrade, Zaira Ortega and Sandra Santiago-Ramajo. (2020). Intelligence Quotient, short-term memory and study habits as academic achievement predictors of elementary school: a follow-up study. https://www.frontiersin.org
title: Psychoeducational evaluation of low-achieving elementary pupils should assess study habits alongside IQ, and study-habit programs should start before age 8
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that evaluation of children with poor achievement must not rest on cognitive variables alone: "it is essential to measure  study habits also". Because study habits significantly predicted achievement in both years and are, per the authors, easy to learn, the article recommends programs "focused on improving the study  habits of children before 8 years". IQ and study habits should be evaluated preferentially, while short-term memory is apparently less important, though the authors call for more research on that point.
requirements: Evaluation of children with low academic performance should include both IQ and study-habit measures rather than cognitive variables alone.
constraints: The authors note more research is needed on the role of short-term memory, and results come from a small medium-high socioeconomic sample.
target_learners: Elementary school pupils aged 8-9 years
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement across curricular subjects
examples: The study measured study habits with the SHTQ questionnaire in 3rd grade and found study habits a significant predictor of grades in both 3rd and 4th grade.

article_title: Cognitive Effects of Social Media Use: A Case of Older Adults
citation: Kelly Quinn. (2018). Cognitive Effects of Social Media Use: A Case of Older Adults. Social Media + Society. https://doi.org/10.1177/2056305118787203
title: Social media as cognitive as well as social technologies: platform use demands inhibitory control and other cognitive processes
description: The article proposes that social media platforms should be understood not only as social technologies but as cognitive ones, because their functions "include important cognitive processes such as recollecting and reminiscing, retrieving information, offering spaces for reflection." It further argues that the dense, competing information flows of platforms (newsfeeds, advertisements, connection recommendations, chat boxes) require users to prioritize relevant information and discard irrelevant flows, so that "users must filter their attention to relevant information flows" to use the platforms effectively. This account explains why social media use may exercise inhibitory control, and it frames the study's finding of inhibitory-control improvement among older adult users.
requirements: Platforms present multiple competing information flows that users must prioritize and filter
constraints: The article notes that how social technologies shape cognitive processing "is only now being investigated and understood"
target_learners: Older adults aged 65 and older learning to use social media platforms
target_learning_goals: Executive-function skills, particularly inhibitory control and attention filtering, developed through navigating social media information flows
examples: The article links newsfeeds, advertisements, connection recommendations, and chat boxes to an increased demand for inhibitory control among platform users

article_title: What you say, and how you say it: Preschoolers' growth in vocabulary and communication skills differentially predict kindergarten academic achievement and self‐regulation
citation: Ramsook K. Ashana, Welsh Janet A., Bierman Karen L. (2020). What you say, and how you say it: Preschoolers' growth in vocabulary and communication skills differentially predict kindergarten academic achievement and self‐regulation. title: Two-dimension account of early language: structural language (vocabulary) versus social communication (pragmatic) skills as distinct contributors to school functioning
description: The article distinguishes structural linguistic competencies such as vocabulary from "competency in using language effectively in social contexts, referred to as social communication or pragmatic language skills". Social communication covers using language to initiate interactions, settle disagreements, express ideas clearly, and understand spoken instructions. The study treats these as moderately correlated yet distinct dimensions that differentially predict academic achievement and self-regulation, with social communication uniquely predicting self-regulation.
requirements: Assessment must capture both dimensions separately; the study used an expressive vocabulary test and an 11-item teacher-rated Social Communication Scale
constraints: The social communication measure relied on teacher ratings relative to age norms, with somewhat low inter-rater reliability; mechanisms linking it to self-regulation are not well understood

school readiness

article_title: Physical Exercise and Fitness Level Are Related to Cognitive and Psychosocial Functioning in Adolescents
citation: Reigal, R. E., Hernández-Mendo, A., Juárez-Ruiz de Mier, R., and Morales-Sánchez, V. (2020). Physical Exercise and Fitness Level Are Related to Cognitive and Psychosocial Functioning in Adolescents. Front. Psychol. 11:1777. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01777
title: Promote regular physical exercise and fitness development among adolescents to support cognitive and psychosocial functioning
description: The article concludes that adolescents who practiced more weekly exercise and had higher fitness scored better on cognitive and psychosocial tests, and recommends promoting exercise: "it is necessary to continue promoting the practice of physical exercise among the young population." It frames active lifestyle habits as bringing "the most direct and indirect beneﬁts to their health and well-being," supporting academic and social functioning.
requirements: Exercise should be sufficient in intensity and frequency to raise physical fitness, since fitness level rather than hours alone was the stronger correlate.

Psychosocial well-being (self-efficacy, self-rated health, life satisfaction)

article_title: The effects of teamwork on critical thinking: A serial mediation analysis of the influence of work skills and educational motivation in secondary school students

article_title: Automaticity of word recognition is a unique predictor of reading fluency in middle-school students.
citation: Roembke Tanja C., Hazeltine Eliot, Reed Deborah K., McMurray Bob. (2019). Automaticity of Word Recognition is a Unique Predictor of Reading Fluency in Middle-School Students. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000279
title: Multi-pathway framework of automatic word recognition (O→S and O→P→S routes)
description: The article describes a connectionist multi-pathway framework in which readers access meaning either directly from spelling (orthography to semantics, O→S) or indirectly via decoding (O→P→S). It states that "Both the O→S and O→P→S pathways are implemented over learnable networks of connections, which transmit activation more or less efficiently depending on how well these connections are organized." Automaticity could reflect pathway dominance or be achievable in both pathways to varying degrees, including for nonwords. The study's tasks were designed to shift reliance toward one pathway or the other.
requirements: Tasks must be designed to change the degree to which OS or OP pathways contribute, since pathways cannot be truly isolated
constraints: The article notes pathways cannot be truly isolated, as readers likely use a combination to solve most tasks

description: The article argues that roughly half of struggling middle-school readers show word-level deficits despite adequate GPC knowledge, suggesting their difficulty lies in deploying knowledge automatically. It states that "an emphasis on automaticity may offer a useful target of intervention for those middle-school readers who still struggle with word-level skills." article_title: Creativity in Collaborative Learning across the Life Span
citation: Margarida Romero, Pirkko Hyvönen, Elena Barberà. (2012). Creativity in Collaborative Learning across the Life Span. Creative Education. https://doi.org/10.4236/ce.2012.34066
title: Creative collaboration as a socio-cognitive, co-constructed process supported by technology
description: The article defines creative collaboration by combining a socio-cognitive view of creativity with a co-construction view of collaboration. Creativity is considered "from a socio-cognitive viewpoint in terms of both an individual and a shared process", and collaboration is defined not as mere cooperation "but rather to the co-construction of shared understanding". In this framing, "creative" denotes the quality of collaboration, where the aim is to act together to find diverse ways to use technologies in order to enhance well-being and active ageing. The article uses this concept to organize its literature review on creativity in collaborative learning across the life span.
requirements: Collaboration must go beyond a sense of belonging or cooperation toward co-construction of shared understanding
constraints: Creative collaboration based on a collaborative tradition "has not yet attracted much research interest", per the article

citation: Margarida Romero, Pirkko Hyvönen, Elena Barberà. (2012). Creativity in Collaborative Learning across the Life Span. Creative Education. https://doi.org/10.4236/ce.2012.34066
title: Three theoretical perspectives on late adulthood: normative crisis, successful aging, and specific or partial theories
description: The article distinguishes three theoretical perspectives on late adulthood. First, theories about normative crisis, which are "basically descriptive and rely on age-related sequences in the human life span structured by developmental phase", including Erikson's "eight ages", Piaget's "genetic epistemology" and Baltes's vital cycles. Second, theories about successful aging, which are "not based on developmental deficits" but "driven by a satisfactory construct of life", describing ways to arrive at high personal satisfaction by adapting to change. Third, specific or partial theories focused precisely on the period of older adulthood, dealing mainly with cognitive achievement and sensory functions, socio-emotional selectivity, and developmental contextualism. All these perspectives agree that late adulthood is a period of adaptation to new personal resources.
requirements: The perspectives are used to frame the specificities of the elderly target group and their creative capabilities
constraints: Older adults "have not been the subject of extensive study to date", per the article
target_learners: older adults in later life
target_learning_goals: understanding creative capabilities in late adulthood
adaptation to new personal resources
examples: The article uses these perspectives to explain the paradox that older adults experience progressive decline in activity yet are better able to adapt, supporting so-called practical intelligence or wisdom in decision-making

citation: Ana Rothes, Marina S. Lemos, and Teresa Gonçalves. (2017). Motivational Profiles of Adult Learners. Adult Education Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1177/0741713616669588
title: Create autonomy-supportive adult learning environments that give choices, validate prior experience, and provide meaningful rationales
description: The article recommends that educators of adults build environments supporting the three basic needs SDT identifies. "Educators should create a learning environment that is autonomy-supportive, that is, one in which learners are given choices (e.g., more alternative educational paths and options), as well as opportunities to participate and share experiences." Adults' prior experiences should be validated, meaningful rationales given for less interesting activities, and tasks set at an optimal challenge level with effective feedback.

The recommendation rests on this study's finding that autonomous motivation predicted better outcomes, while controlled motivation's effects need further investigation

title: Developmental scenario: different aspects of input quality matter at different child ages
description: The article proposes a developmental scenario in which the most beneficial type of caregiver input shifts with child age. As the authors state, "the results are consistent with a developmental scenario in which quantity of input is most important during the second year of life, the diversity or sophistication of the vocabulary in the input is most important during the third year of life, and the use of decontextualized language such as narrative and explanations in the input is most beneficial during the fourth year of life." This framework organizes the study's regression findings by age period and implies that scaffolding should match the child's current language ability.

Control of SES, prior vocabulary skill, and input quantity when testing each input dimension

Not all features of input quality were examined

title: PPVT-III as an independent standardized measure of receptive vocabulary
description: The Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test (PPVT-III; Dunn & Dunn, 1997) served as the vocabulary outcome measure, administered by a researcher at child ages 30, 42, and 54 months. The authors chose it because "the PPVT is a widely used measure of vocabulary skill and, importantly, because it provides data that is independent from the parent-child interaction." This independence allowed the study to test whether caregiver input predicts vocabulary skill measured outside the interaction, avoiding contamination from concurrent caregiver speech. Raw scores were converted to age-appropriate standardized scores based on published norms.

citation: Rowe Anna D.; Fitness Julie. (2018). Understanding the Role of Negative Emotions in Adult Learning and Achievement: A Social Functional Perspective. Behavioral Sciences. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5836010/
title: Social functional and prototype approach to understanding discrete negative emotions in learning
description: The article adopts a social-functionalist perspective conceiving emotions as felt responses to appraisals of events, categorized into discrete emotion families that motivate potentially adaptive behaviors. It pairs this with prototype theory, in which "emotion prototypes are held to be mental representations of emotion concepts and categories" organized around exemplars, shaping how people label, interpret, remember and act on emotions. This framework extends Pekrun's control-value theory by exploring a broader range of negative emotions across social and epistemic as well as achievement contexts.

constraints: The framework does not account for specific functions of discrete emotions or how emotions resolve interpersonal problems, per the authors' critique of assimilation-accommodation accounts

academic faculty
target_learning_goals: understanding the role of emotions in learning and achievement
developing emotion knowledge and regulation
examples: The study coded emotions using participants' own words, then by valence, then into basic emotion categories following Shaver et al.'s hierarchical organization of emotion knowledge

article_title: An Introduction to Ecological Active Learning
citation: Azzurra Ruggeri. (2022). An Introduction to Ecological Active Learning. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/09637214221112114
title: Ecological active-learning framework: learning strategies are adaptive tools matched to environmental structure
description: The article introduces ecological active learning as a developmental framework focusing on children's ability to adapt and tailor active-learning strategies to the structure and characteristics of a learning environment. It builds on bounded and ecological rationality, understanding rationality as a match between a subject's mental abilities and the structure of the environment. Strategies are 'like tools in a toolbox: No strategy is suitable for all problems, just as different tasks call for different tools.' The framework is the first to apply this perspective to the developmental trajectory of information-search strategies across the life span.
requirements: Learners must be able to detect, and potentially actively discover, the structural characteristics of the learning environment in order to adapt their strategies to them
constraints: The framework focuses on adaptiveness rather than effectiveness measured against adults' default performance; effectiveness of strategies cannot be measured in absolute terms but depends on task characteristics, available resources, and the learner's prior knowledge
target_learners: children from infancy through late childhood, with implications across the life span
target_learning_goals: adaptive information search and question asking
exploration and hypothesis testing
examples: The Toma the monster question-asking examples illustrate how constraint seeking suits uniform hypothesis distributions while hypothesis scanning suits skewed distributions

title: Intrinsic reinforcement signals in the ventral striatum during standard cognitive tasks
description: The article proposes that ventral striatum responses to correct responses during ordinary cognitive tasks, without external feedback or rewards, represent "intrinsic reinforcement signals". The account draws on the reward prediction error framework: correct responses are less expected at higher task difficulty, so they provoke larger reinforcement responses, analogous to unexpected rewards. The authors suggest this provides "a plausible neural correlate for the prior observation and common experience that accurate performance is reinforcing in proportion to the difficulty of the task".
requirements: A cognitive task that parametrically varies difficulty, such as the n-back task, so that correct responses vary in how expected they are
constraints: The design does not directly link VS response to subject-level motivation; the authors note future studies should vary reward contingencies and obtain subjective measures of response confidence, reward sensitivity, and intrinsic motivation

adolescents
young adults aged 8-22
target_learning_goals: working memory performance
intrinsic motivation during cognitive task performance
examples: Participants performed 0-back, 1-back, and 2-back conditions with fractal stimuli and received no performance feedback at any point

article_title: Epistemic Curiosity and Situational Interest: Distant Cousins or Identical Twins?
citation: Henk G. Schmidt & Jerome I. Rotgans. (2021). Epistemic Curiosity and Situational Interest: Distant Cousins or Identical Twins?. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09539-9
title: Knowledge-deprivation account: situational interest and epistemic curiosity share one knowledge-gap mechanism
description: The knowledge-deprivation account holds that both situational interest and epistemic curiosity arise when a person confronts a problem they cannot immediately explain, experiences a gap between what they know and need to know, and is motivated to close it; acquiring relevant knowledge satisfies the drive and the motivation subsides. The article summarizes Rotgans and Schmidt's version: "(a) Confronted with a problem not immediately understood, a person engages in an attempt to retrieve knowledge from long-term memory" and "(c) This awareness of a knowledge deficit leads to increased situational interest for information that may help eliminating the deficit". The article argues the same mechanism explains epistemic curiosity, treating the two constructs as "identical twins".
requirements: A problem or triggering event the learner cannot immediately understand
The learner must become aware of a knowledge deficit
Relevant explanatory knowledge must be available to close the gap
constraints: The article notes findings are preliminary and need further confirmation
Situational interest may also be aroused by contexts other than knowledge-gap confrontation, which would broaden the concept beyond the account's boundaries
target_learners: secondary-school students
target_learning_goals: motivating engagement with new subject matter
driving knowledge acquisition in response to problems
examples: Study 2 aroused both measures with the Mpemba effect problem in treatment students and satiated them with an evaporation text

It was used in both studies to measure momentary curiosity about the physics of heat.

article_title: Self-Control Outdoes Fluid Reasoning in Explaining Vocational and Academic Performance—But Does It?
citation: Schmidt FTC, Lindner C, Etzel JM and Retelsdorf J (2020) Self-Control Outdoes Fluid Reasoning in Explaining Vocational and Academic Performance—But Does It? Front. Psychol. 11:757. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00757
title: Resource-oriented response-conflict account of trait self-control
description: The article adopts a recent resource-oriented conceptualization of trait self-control in which highly self-controlled individuals succeed not by investing more effort but by handling response conflicts — competing behavioral tendencies between valued goals and short-term rewards — more effectively. The article states that "Individuals with higher self-control are more sensitive to detecting response conflicts, use more effortless strategies to deal with these conflicts" and downregulate them before they become obstacles. This account is used to predict that self-control matters more in high-stakes situations (grades) than low-stakes ones (research tests), where few response conflicts arise.
requirements: Achievement situations must involve response conflicts between valued long-term goals and more immediately rewarding alternatives for trait self-control to confer an advantage
constraints: The article notes it cannot explain whether response-conflict resolution is merely a preliminary step before higher-effort investment, which may actually explain the results
target_learners: young adults in vocational training
target_learning_goals: scholastic achievement as reflected in grades and standardized domain-specific test performance
examples: The study contrasted high-stakes major GPA with low-stakes curriculum-based mathematics and physics tests to test the account's differential predictions

title: Three-component model of writing proficiency: linguistic knowledge, accessibility/fluency, and metacognitive knowledge
description: The article organizes writing proficiency into three hypothesized components: linguistic knowledge (vocabulary, grammar), the fluency or accessibility of that knowledge (speed of processing), and metacognitive knowledge. Using structural equation modeling, the components' relative contributions to L1 (Dutch) and L2 (English) writing were estimated and compared. The model treats writing as drawing on both knowledge resources and the efficiency with which they can be retrieved, allowing cross-language comparison of component weights.

description: The study administered a battery of measures to 281 grade 8 students covering linguistic knowledge, speed of processing (fluency/accessibility), and metacognitive knowledge in both Dutch (L1) and English (L2), alongside writing performance tasks. These measures served as observed indicators in structural equation models estimating each component's contribution to writing. article_title: Language learning, socioeconomic status, and child‐directed speech
citation: Schwab Jessica F., Lew-Williams Casey. (2016). Language learning, socioeconomic status, and child-directed speech. Wiley interdisciplinary reviews. Cognitive science. https://doi.org/10.1002/wcs.1393
title: Child-directed speech as a multi-feature input register whose prosodic, structural, and social characteristics differentially drive early language learning
description: The review organizes child-directed speech (CDS) as a speech register "characterized by higher pitch, shorter utterances, more repetition, and other features that differentiate it from adult-directed speech." It taxonomizes CDS features into sound-level (pitch contours, clarity), structural (isolated words, sentence frames, repetition), and social (contingency, referential transparency) characteristics, each linked to specific learning outcomes—phoneme discrimination, segmentation, word mapping, and grammar. The framework holds that features act differentially across learning domains and developmental windows, and that infants are active participants in eliciting CDS.
requirements: Caregiver input in naturalistic interaction; the framework concerns children learning language from caregiver speech rather than from screens or recorded media
constraints: The review notes few CDS-feature experiments have directly examined SES, and findings are drawn primarily from US samples
target_learners: infants and toddlers from birth through the third year of life
target_learning_goals: speech perception and phoneme discrimination
word segmentation
vocabulary and word learning
early grammar
examples: Laboratory studies reviewed include segmentation of words from CDS but not ADS, faster noun interpretation in sentence frames, and word learning from repeated exposures across successive sentences

article_title: Ethnic identity: Evidence of protective effects for young, Latino children
citation: Serrano-Villar, M., & Calzada, E. J. (2016). Ethnic identity: Evidence of protective effects for young, Latino children. Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appdev.2015.11.002
title: Bernal et al.'s developmental model of early ethnic identity: self-identification, constancy, knowledge, and preference
description: The study adopts a model of pre-adolescent ethnic identity, drawn from Bernal and colleagues and the social identity developmental literature, in which ethnic identity comprises self-identification, constancy, knowledge, and preferences. The article states the components "reflect a set of self-ideas about one's ethnic group membership" and that once ethnicity is integrated into the self, it guides information-processing toward ethnic-specific knowledge, behaviors, and feelings/preferences. The present study applies this model to MA and DA children aged 4–6 using a newly developed interview.
requirements: Requires children's emerging symbolic thought and social-category awareness, which the article locates in the early childhood years
constraints: The article notes the original model had not been subsequently tested before this study, leaving open replicability and generalizability to other Latino groups and contexts
target_learners: Young Latino children in pre-kindergarten and kindergarten (ages approximately 4–6)
target_learning_goals: Development of ethnic self-identification, constancy, knowledge, and preferences as components of social identity
examples: The study assessed each component with forced-choice and open-ended interview items, scoring self-identification and constancy dichotomously and coding knowledge and preference responses with trained bilingual coders (97% agreement)
key_sources: Serrano-Villar, M., & Calzada, E. J. (2016). Ethnic identity: Evidence of protective effects for young, Latino children. Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appdev.2015.11.002

article_title: Ethnic identity: Evidence of protective effects for young, Latino children
citation: Serrano-Villar, M., & Calzada, E. J. (2016). Ethnic identity: Evidence of protective effects for young, Latino children. Journal of Applied Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.appdev.2015.11.002
title: Early Childhood Ethnic Identity Interview (ECEII)
description: The ECEII is a child interview developed for this study based on Bernal et al.'s ethnic identity research and Ruble and colleagues' gender identity research. It consists of open- and close-ended questions administered bilingually, assessing self-identification, constancy (stability), knowledge, and preference, with scoring based on past gold-standard social identity measures. The article reports the constancy scale was revised from six items to a two-item scale due to low internal consistency.
requirements: Administration by bilingual research assistants in the child's dominant language; verbatim recording and consensus coding of open-ended responses
constraints: The original six-item constancy scale was dropped "because of low internal consistency between items" and replaced with a revised scale based on Bernal et al. (1990)
target_learners: Pre-kindergarten and kindergarten children from Mexican American and Dominican American families
target_learning_goals: Measurement of early ethnic identity components (self-identification, constancy, knowledge, preference)
examples: Children were asked "Are you a Mexican/Dominican boy or a Chinese boy/girl?" for self-identification and a parallel grown-up question for stability; preferences were assessed with four playmate illustrations varying in skin tone and phenotype
