article_title: How does mathematics anxiety impair mathematical abilities? Investigating the link between math anxiety, working memory, and number processing
citation: Skagerlund K, Östergren R, Västfjäll D, Träff U (2019) How does mathematics anxiety impair mathematical abilities? Investigating the link between math anxiety, working memory, and number processing. PLoS ONE 14(1): e0211283. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0211283
title: Tailor math-anxiety interventions to the specific pathway being targeted (WM, number processing, or distal avoidance)
description: Because the study found MA operates through three distinct pathways — WM interference, degraded symbolic number processing, and a direct/distal effect — the authors recommend that interventions be matched to the pathway. They state one "possible way in which one might be able to leverage the current results would be to tailor interventions directed at each specific pathway", citing expressive writing for the WM route, exposure-based desensitization for the number-processing route, and early positive climate work for the distal route.
requirements: Assessment or theory identifying which pathway dominates for the learner and task type, since pathway strength varies with the kind of mathematical problem being solved
constraints: Recommendation is derived from a correlational SEM study of adults; the cited intervention studies (expressive writing, tutoring) are prior work, not tested in this study
target_learners: adults with mathematics anxiety
students in primary school (for early preventive intervention)
target_learning_goals: arithmetic calculation
numeracy and risk literacy
positive attitudes toward mathematics
examples: The authors cite expressive writing before exams as lowering ruminating behavior and mitigating the WM drain, and intensive math tutoring as lowering amygdala activity in children with high MA
key_sources: Skagerlund K, Östergren R, Västfjäll D, Träff U (2019) How does mathematics anxiety impair mathematical abilities? Investigating the link between math anxiety, working memory, and number processing. PLoS ONE 14(1): e0211283. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0211283

article_title: How does mathematics anxiety impair mathematical abilities? Investigating the link between math anxiety, working memory, and number processing
citation: Skagerlund K, Östergren R, Västfjäll D, Träff U (2019) How does mathematics anxiety impair mathematical abilities? Investigating the link between math anxiety, working memory, and number processing. PLoS ONE 14(1): e0211283. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0211283
title: Three-pathway model of how math anxiety impairs mathematical performance
description: The article's organizing framework: MA impedes math performance through (1) an indirect pathway via working memory ability, supporting the 'affective drop' hypothesis in which negative emotions and self-referential worry drain WM resources needed for computation; (2) an indirect pathway via symbolic number processing, corroborating domain-specific mechanisms pertaining to number; and (3) a direct effect of MA on math performance, possibly due to distal avoidance behavior. The model was instantiated as two SEM path models (arithmetic and numeracy) and the pathways' relative strength varied by task type.
requirements: Measures of WM, symbolic number processing, MA, and the math outcome, modeled jointly (e.g., via SEM) to separate direct from indirect effects
constraints: Correlational SEM in adults; the authors state longitudinal and experimental manipulations are needed to make firm claims about directions of causality; BNT reliability (α = .41) limits the numeracy model
target_learners: adults (university students) with varying levels of math anxiety
target_learning_goals: arithmetic calculation ability
numeracy
examples: Two fitted path models: MA→WM→arithmetic (standardized -.15) and MA→WM→numeracy (standardized -.14) were significant, while MA→NP→numeracy was not

article_title: Early life stress and development: potential mechanisms for adverse outcomes
citation: Karen E. Smith and Seth D. Pollak. (2020). Early life stress and development: potential mechanisms for adverse outcomes. Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1186/s11689-020-09337-y
title: General (lumping) models treat early life stress as a heterogeneous cumulative category of adverse events
description: The review describes general or lumping models as one of two predominant approaches to conceptualizing early life stress. In this approach, various types of stressors are treated as a heterogeneous, broad category, and individuals are queried about whether they experienced a pre-defined set of potential adverse events in childhood, with total exposure summed. Examples include Life Stressors Checklists and the Adverse Child Experiences Scale. The approach rests on animal literature suggesting repeated exposure to stress, regardless of type, chronically activates stress response systems and alters neural synaptic plasticity.
requirements: Assessment instruments that query a pre-defined set of potential adverse events in childhood and sum total exposure, such as Life Stressors Checklists and the Adverse Child Experiences Scale
constraints: The review states cumulative models have lacked consistent insight into the neurobiological mechanisms underlying individual differences in children's responses to stress
target_learners: children exposed to chronic or extreme stress in early life
target_learning_goals: understanding how cumulative adversity shapes neurobiological development and long-term cognitive, emotional, and behavioral outcomes
examples: A recent longitudinal study from 18 months to mid-adulthood found that cumulative stress rather than physical abuse alone was predictive of adult depressive symptoms
key_sources: Karen E. Smith and Seth D. Pollak. (2020). Early life stress and development: potential mechanisms for adverse outcomes. Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1186/s11689-020-09337-y

article_title: Early life stress and development: potential mechanisms for adverse outcomes
citation: Karen E. Smith and Seth D. Pollak. (2020). Early life stress and development: potential mechanisms for adverse outcomes. Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1186/s11689-020-09337-y
title: Specific (splitting) models assume different types of adversity confer distinct effects on separable neural systems
description: The review describes specific or splitting models as a reaction to cumulative models, based on the premise that different types of adversity each confer specific effects, and links to neurobiological or cognitive systems may be masked by heterogeneous samples. An increasingly prevalent variant conceptualizes potential stressors as a lack of expected inputs (deprivation, including neglect, food deprivation, and institutionalization) or a presence of direct threat to the child (threat, including physical abuse, sexual abuse, and exposure to violence). These approaches are grounded in animal models demonstrating some specificity in the effects of certain types of stressors on neurobiological systems.
requirements: Assessment approaches that distinguish types or dimensions of adversity, such as deprivation versus threat, rather than summing heterogeneous events
constraints: The review notes different types of stressors often co-occur, creating conceptual issues and making it difficult to determine if one specific type or dimension of stressor is driving an effect
target_learners: children exposed to chronic or extreme stress in early life
target_learning_goals: identifying the distinct neurobiological mechanisms linking specific types of early adversity to development
examples: The review cites work conceptualizing stressors as deprivation (neglect, food deprivation, institutionalization) versus threat (physical abuse, sexual abuse, exposure to violence)
key_sources: Karen E. Smith and Seth D. Pollak. (2020). Early life stress and development: potential mechanisms for adverse outcomes. Journal of Neurodevelopmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1186/s11689-020-09337-y

article_title: Complicating Access: Digital Inequality and Adult Learning in a Public Access Computing Space
citation: Smythe, S., & Breshears, S. (2017). Complicating Access: Digital Inequality And Adult Learning In A Public-Access Computing Space. The Canadian Journal for the Study of Adult Education, 29(1), 67-81. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1139334
title: Digital policies should attend to the learning needs of those on the margins of access through affordable Internet and appropriate, timely, consistent digital learning opportunities
description: The article argues that digital inclusion policy equating access to a connection with inclusion masks persistent inequalities in use and experience. It recommends that policy be designed for those on the margins "who will benefit most from affordable Internet and from appropriate, timely, and consistent opportunities for digital learning," grounded in ethnographic evidence that access is contingent and precarious.
requirements: Policy must be informed by the actual experiences of people at the margins of digital access, not only by model-user imaginaries.
constraints: The article focuses on the Canadian policy context and a single community-based computing site; recommendations are framed for adult educators and policy makers in that setting.
target_learners: Adults on the margins of digital access, including low-income adults, new immigrants, and seniors
target_learning_goals: Digital literacy and meaningful participation in online environments
examples: The Digital Café provided free access, computers, and just-in-time volunteer tutor support for tasks like email, job applications, and government forms.
key_sources: Smythe, S., & Breshears, S. (2017). Complicating Access: Digital Inequality And Adult Learning In A Public-Access Computing Space. The Canadian Journal for the Study of Adult Education, 29(1), 67-81. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1139334

article_title: Complicating Access: Digital Inequality and Adult Learning in a Public Access Computing Space
citation: Smythe, S., & Breshears, S. (2017). Complicating Access: Digital Inequality And Adult Learning In A Public-Access Computing Space. The Canadian Journal for the Study of Adult Education, 29(1), 67-81. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1139334
title: Policy anthropology "studying through" approach tracing digital access from policy texts to the lives of those affected
description: The article adopts a policy anthropology approach (Wedel & Feldman, 2005) employing "studying through," in which policy analysis follows "the source of a policy—its discourses, prescriptions, and programs—through to those affected by the policies." It combines a wide lens of critical policy analysis with a finely grained ethnographic lens into actual use and experiences of digital access and learning, treating policy as an imaginary that imposes ideal types of the "normal" citizen.
requirements: A complementary spatial perspective bringing into focus both local lives and distant policy actors within the same frame.
constraints: The authors note a shorter-term ethnographic study could not trace wavering access over time, and policy analysis alone could not capture disconnections between imaginaries and actualities.
target_learners: Adult educators and policy makers seeking to understand digital inequality
target_learning_goals: Understanding how digital policies materialize in everyday adult learning experiences
examples: The study mapped federal, provincial, and municipal digital policy texts, then followed them into the Digital Café ethnography of Malek's access story.

article_title: Complicating Access: Digital Inequality and Adult Learning in a Public Access Computing Space
citation: Smythe, S., & Breshears, S. (2017). Complicating Access: Digital Inequality And Adult Learning In A Public-Access Computing Space. The Canadian Journal for the Study of Adult Education, 29(1), 67-81. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1139334
title: The Digital Café: a drop-in public-access computing and learning space
description: The Digital Café is a two-hour weekly drop-in program in a suburb of Vancouver, BC, offering free Internet, computers, and just-in-time volunteer tutor support for tasks such as email, job applications, online government forms, and social media. It began in 2008 as a Community Access Program site. The room was often full before the 3 p.m. start time with adults between 35 and 75, mostly new immigrants.
requirements: Volunteer tutors to provide one-to-one just-in-time support; a sociable, informal atmosphere (coffee, tea, snacks).
constraints: The article notes the program operated on a shoestring and that participants' security of access rested precariously on the availability of working computers and volunteer tutors.
target_learners: Adults aged 35-75, mostly new immigrants, referred by employment or social service agencies or the library
target_learning_goals: Everyday computer tasks, email, job applications, government forms, and social media use
examples: Malek attended almost weekly over a year, progressing from being unable to use a computer to emailing family and using Facebook, before his fluency faltered when his laptop and home connection failed.

article_title: Psychosocial Adversity in Early Childhood and Language and Literacy Skills in Adolescence: The Role of Speech-Language Pathology in Prevention, Policy, and Practice
citation: Pamela C. Snow. (2021). Psychosocial Adversity in Early Childhood and Language and Literacy Skills in Adolescence: The Role of Speech-Language Pathology in Prevention, Policy, and Practice. Perspectives of the ASHA Special Interest Groups. https://doi.org/10.1044/2020_PERSP-20-00120
title: The Language House framework linking social-emotional well-being, language, literacy, and academic achievement
description: The Language House (Snow, 2020) is a metaphorical schema, displayed in Figure 1, that "depicts the developmental links between social – emotional well-being, language and literacy development, and academic achievement, culminating in opportunities to participate in the social and economic mainstream." It provides a framework for speech-language pathologists to raise the profile of language and literacy difficulties among vulnerable children, for example when advocating to policy makers for underserved populations. It is also intended for raising clinicians' awareness of undocumented maltreatment histories affecting treatment engagement, and for preservice education to reinforce the developmental interplay across domains that clinical presentations do not map onto service delivery silos.
requirements: Use requires situating a child's language and literacy skills within their social-emotional and developmental history, including possible undocumented maltreatment
constraints: The article presents it as a metaphorical advocacy and education schema, not a tested predictive model
target_learners: Vulnerable children and adolescents with maltreatment histories
Preservice speech-language pathology students
target_learning_goals: Understanding developmental links between social-emotional well-being, language, literacy, and academic achievement
examples: The article proposes its use in advocating to policy makers for speech-language pathology services for underserved populations and in preservice SLP education

article_title: Observing writing processes of struggling adult writers with collaborative writing
citation: Sturm, A. (2016). Observing writing processes of struggling adult writers with collaborative writing. Journal of Writing Research, 8(2), 301-344. https://doi.org/10.17239/jowr-2016.08.02.05
title: Triangulated multi-source assessment of writing processes and writing knowledge
description: A methodological framework combining three elements to examine writing processes of struggling adult writers: observation of collaborative writing tasks, analyses of written texts, and structured individual interviews with retrospective and prospective parts. The article states "This methodical approach provides productive tools to assess writing processes and writing knowledge of struggling adult writers" and visualizes the triangulation in a case study.
requirements: Combining observation of collaborative writing tasks, text analyses, and structured individual interviews
target_learners: struggling adult writers
target_learning_goals: writing processes
writing knowledge
examples: The study triangulates data from the different sources in a case study of struggling adult writers.

article_title: Understanding deficient emotional self-regulation in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a controlled study
citation: Surman Craig B. H., Biederman Joseph, Spencer Thomas, Miller Carolyn A., McDermott Katie M., Faraone Stephen V. (2013). Understanding deficient emotional self-regulation in adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a controlled study. Attention deficit and hyperactivity disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4009378/
title: DESR as an emotional expression of ADHD-related self-regulation difficulty, partially independent of comorbidity
description: The article frames deficient emotional self-regulation as the affective arm of ADHD's self-regulation deficit, following Barkley's proposal that DESR traits be considered a core feature rather than associated symptoms. It operationalizes DESR with eight self-report items covering temper, frustration, and emotional overreaction, and interprets its findings as consistent with "the idea that DESR is an emotional expression of the ADHD patient’s difficulties with self-regulation." The framework holds that DESR is overrepresented in ADHD, partially independent of comorbid disorders, and functionally consequential.
requirements: DESR is measured here via eight self-report Barkley Current Behavior Scale items rated over the prior 6 months
constraints: The article states it cannot identify from its data whether DESR should be considered as co-occurring with ADHD or a result of ADHD
the sample was primarily Caucasian and may not generalize to other ethnic groups
target_learners: adults with ADHD
target_learning_goals: understanding emotional self-regulation difficulties associated with adult ADHD
examples: The study operationalized emotional impulsivity using items from the Barkley Current Behavior Scale and tested the framework in a controlled community sample

article_title: Prospective Study of Insufficient Sleep and Neurobehavioral Functioning Among School-Age Children
citation: Taveras Elsie M. MD, MPH; Rifas-Shiman Sheryl L. MPH; Bub Kristen L. EdD; Gillman Matthew W. MD, SM; Oken Emily MD, MPH. (2017). Prospective Study of Insufficient Sleep and Neurobehavioral Functioning among School-Age Children. Academic Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5545152/
title: Promote optimal age-specific sleep duration in early childhood to support cognitive and behavioral functioning
description: The article concludes that insufficient sleep in the preschool and early school years is associated with poorer mother- and teacher-reported neurobehavioral functioning in mid-childhood, and states that "our results indicate that interventions to promote optimal sleep duration in early childhood could have positive effects on cognitive and behavioral functioning." The principle directs caregivers, educators, and health providers to treat age-appropriate sleep duration (≥11 h/day at 3-4 years; ≥10 h/day at 5-7 years, per National Sleep Foundation recommendations used in the study) as a foundational condition for executive function and social-emotional development.
requirements: Sleep duration must meet age-specific recommendations (e.g., ≥11 hours/day at ages 3-4; ≥10 hours/day at ages 5-7) as categorized from maternal reports in the study
constraints: Evidence is observational; the article notes residual confounding and reverse causation (e.g., anxiety or depression preceding poor sleep) cannot be ruled out
Sleep duration was estimated by maternal questionnaire rather than objective measures such as accelerometers or diaries
The cohort is of relatively high socioeconomic status, potentially limiting generalizability to lower socioeconomic environments
target_learners: children ages 3-7 years in preschool and early school years
target_learning_goals: executive function (attention shifting, working memory, inhibitory control)
behavioral and social-emotional functioning
examples: The study categorized sleep against National Sleep Foundation age-specific recommendations and found children below those thresholds at ages 3-4 and 5-7 had worse BRIEF and SDQ scores at age 7

article_title: Prospective Study of Insufficient Sleep and Neurobehavioral Functioning Among School-Age Children
citation: Taveras Elsie M. MD, MPH; Rifas-Shiman Sheryl L. MPH; Bub Kristen L. EdD; Gillman Matthew W. MD, SM; Oken Emily MD, MPH. (2017). Prospective Study of Insufficient Sleep and Neurobehavioral Functioning among School-Age Children. Academic Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5545152/
title: Sleep duration as an early-life influence on child neurobehavioral processes (executive function, behavior, social-emotional functioning)
description: This framework holds that sleep duration across infancy and early childhood is prospectively associated with neurobehavioral processes in mid-childhood, measured via the BRIEF (executive function, including behavioral regulation and metacognition) and the SDQ (behavioral and social-emotional difficulties). The article frames sleep as "influencing neurobehavioral processes including executive function, behavior, or social-emotional functioning," and hypothesized that "insufficient sleep at multiple time points throughout childhood would be associated with poorer child executive function, behavior, and social-emotional functioning as independently reported by mothers and teachers." Findings support the framework for preschool and early school ages but not consistently for infancy.
requirements: Multi-rater assessment (mothers and teachers independently) across home and school settings to detect situation-specific difficulties
Longitudinal sleep data from infancy onward, with later models adjusted for sleep at earlier ages
Validated instruments: the 86-item BRIEF and 25-item SDQ
constraints: Associations were inconsistent for infancy; no lasting effect of the shortest infant sleep durations was found
Only sleep duration was examined as the exposure; sleep fragmentation, variability, and timing were not measured
Neurobehavioral functioning was measured only at age 7, limiting causal ordering inference
target_learners: children from infancy through age 7
target_learning_goals: executive function development
behavioral self-regulation
emotional regulation and social-emotional functioning
examples: Project Viva categorized sleep at three age periods against National Sleep Foundation recommendations and modeled associations with age-7 BRIEF and SDQ outcomes from mothers and teachers

article_title: The use of automated procedures by older adults with high arithmetic skills during addition problem solving.
citation: Thevenot, C., Dewi, J., Bagnoud, J., Wolfer, P., Fayol, M., & Castel, C. (2018). The use of automated procedures by older adults with high arithmetic skills during addition problem solving. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Automated counting procedure model of simple addition: the '+' sign pre-activates an abstract procedure, likely scrolling a mental number line, rather than triggering retrieval of stored facts
description: The article advances an alternative to dominant fact-retrieval accounts of simple addition. It proposes that presenting the "+" sign pre-activates an abstract procedure — possibly "a mental representation akin to a mental number line along which individuals' attention could make displacements by one" — which is then executed to solve the problem. Within this model, "automated counting procedures could therefore be limited to additions up to 4 elements", matching the subitizing range, and such procedures "are probably run to completion by experts without awareness", which explains why adults report retrieval. The model predicts sign priming for non-tie additions but not for multiplication, ties, or +0 problems, exactly the pattern observed here in both age groups.
requirements: The priming effect is only observable in individuals with high arithmetic proficiency; the authors note priming effects "cannot be observed, whatever the categories of problems, when we consider the whole population".
constraints: The article states the paradigm's characteristics "do not allow the generalization of our interpretations to the whole population of elderly individuals"; whether less efficient individuals use automated procedures or the paradigm fails to reveal them remains unknown.
target_learners: older adults with high arithmetic skills
young adults with high arithmetic skills
target_learning_goals: simple one-digit addition problem solving
arithmetic fluency
key_sources: Thevenot, C., Dewi, J., Bagnoud, J., Wolfer, P., Fayol, M., & Castel, C. (2018). The use of automated procedures by older adults with high arithmetic skills during addition problem solving. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED

article_title: The use of automated procedures by older adults with high arithmetic skills during addition problem solving.
citation: Thevenot, C., Dewi, J., Bagnoud, J., Wolfer, P., Fayol, M., & Castel, C. (2018). The use of automated procedures by older adults with high arithmetic skills during addition problem solving. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Train counting procedures through intensive practice before old age rather than overemphasizing rote memorization of arithmetic facts
description: The article argues that because arithmetic expertise in addition is "most likely to be achieved through procedural automatization than retrieval of the answers from long-term memory", overemphasizing rote memorization during learning "may be misguided". Instead, "repeated use of a procedure as counting might be more efficient than memorization of direct associations between operands and answers". Because intensive practice in old age does not yield the performance levels reached by younger adults, the authors conclude that "training programs take place before the cognitive system departs excessively from its optimum level of efficiency".
requirements: Intensive, repeated practice of counting procedures, administered before the cognitive system departs excessively from its optimum level of efficiency.
constraints: Intensive practice in old age does not bring the same level of performance as that reached by younger adults (citing Maquestiaux et al., 2013; Touron et al., 2001).
target_learners: primary school children
adults of new generations
adults who do not age so successfully
target_learning_goals: arithmetic fluency
automatization of counting procedures
preservation of arithmetic abilities into old age
examples: The article cites Tournaki (2003) showing that an intervention based on repetitive counting-on from the largest addend (3 + 4 = 5, 6, 7) is more efficient to develop arithmetic skills than a drill-and-practice training program.
key_sources: Thevenot, C., Dewi, J., Bagnoud, J., Wolfer, P., Fayol, M., & Castel, C. (2018). The use of automated procedures by older adults with high arithmetic skills during addition problem solving. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED

article_title: Sleep Patterns and School Readiness of Pre-Kindergarteners from Racially and Ethnically Diverse, Low-Income Backgrounds
citation: Turnbull Khara L. P. PhD; Mateus Deiby Mayaris Cubides; LoCasale-Crouch Jennifer PhD; Lewin Daniel S. Ph.D., D.ABSM; CBSM; Williford Amanda P. PhD. (2022). Sleep Patterns and School Readiness of Pre-Kindergarteners from Racially/Ethnically Diverse, Low-Income Backgrounds: A Secondary Data Analysis. The Journal of Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10621568/
title: Consistent sleep routines and more optimal sleep health may serve as a protective mechanism for language, social-emotional-behavioral regulation, and approaches to learning of low-income pre-kindergarteners
description: This principle holds that predictable, consistent morning and bedtime routines and more optimal sleep health support school readiness development in children from low-income backgrounds, regardless of family income level. The article states "Consistent sleep routines and more optimal sleep health may serve as a protective mechanism for the language development, social-emotional-behavioral regulation and approaches to learning of pre-kindergarteners from racially/ethnically diverse, low-income backgrounds." It is grounded in the study's latent class and regression findings linking the earlier, longer, consistent class to stronger expressive vocabulary, emotion regulation, assertiveness, and approaches to learning.
requirements: Requires parent-reported sleep health information covering timing, nighttime sleep duration, and sleep-related behaviors
constraints: The overarching study design does not permit causal inference
Results are not generalizable beyond the study sample
Naps were not measured in a way that would permit calculating total 24-hour sleep duration
target_learners: Pre-kindergarteners from racially/ethnically diverse, low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Language development
Social-emotional-behavioral regulation
Approaches to learning
examples: Latent class analysis identified an earlier, longer, consistent sleep health class comprising 87% of the sample, whose members had earlier bedtimes, longer nighttime sleep, more consistent routines, and less pre-bedtime caffeine
key_sources: Turnbull Khara L. P. PhD; Mateus Deiby Mayaris Cubides; LoCasale-Crouch Jennifer PhD; Lewin Daniel S. Ph.D., D.ABSM; CBSM; Williford Amanda P. PhD. (2022). Sleep Patterns and School Readiness of Pre-Kindergarteners from Racially/Ethnically Diverse, Low-Income Backgrounds: A Secondary Data Analysis. The Journal of Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10621568/

article_title: The effects of readers’ goals on inference generation and memory for texts
citation: P. van den Broek, R. F. Lorch, Jr., T. Linderholm, & M. Gustafson. (2001). The effects of readers' goals on inference generation and memory for texts. Memory & Cognition, 29(8), 1081-1087. https://link.springer.com/journal/13414
title: Standards of coherence as the mechanism by which reading goals shape inference generation and memory
description: The article proposes that as readers proceed through a text they maintain "standards of coherence that act as criteria for comprehension," which "dictate the inferential activities in which the readers engage at each point during reading." A reading goal prompts the reader to select particular standards, operationalizing the goal; a strict standard yields coherence-producing inferences at a cost of greater effort, while a relaxed standard yields less effortful reading but a less coherent representation. The framework integrates bottom-up and top-down accounts of inference generation and connects goal-based reading theories to computational models of text comprehension.
requirements: A reading goal that the reader translates into relevant standards of coherence
constraints: The article states none of the existing reading models provides details on how goals influence the standards readers employ
target_learners: college students reading expository text
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
construction of coherent memory representations of text
examples: Study-goal readers employed stringent standards focused on intratextual relations, generating explanatory and predictive inferences, paraphrases, and repetitions; entertainment-goal readers adopted a relaxed standard, generating associations and evaluations connected to personal experience
key_sources: P. van den Broek, R. F. Lorch, Jr., T. Linderholm, & M. Gustafson. (2001). The effects of readers' goals on inference generation and memory for texts. Memory & Cognition, 29(8), 1081-1087. https://link.springer.com/journal/13414

article_title: Building on Prior Knowledge: Schema-dependent Encoding Processes Relate to Academic Performance
citation: van Kesteren, M. T. R., Rijpkema, M., Ruiter, D. J., Morris, R. G. M., & Fernández, G. (2014). Building on Prior Knowledge: Schema-dependent Encoding Processes Relate to Academic Performance. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 26(10), 2250–2261. https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn_a_00630
title: Schema-dependent MTL–mPFC balance account of conceptual encoding
description: The article proposes that a pre-existing schema shifts the balance of encoding processing between the medial prefrontal cortex and the medial temporal lobe. On this account, "mPFC serves to assimilate new information into a schema by activating (or retrieving) the schema enabling integration of novel information, whereas MTL detects mismatches with a schema and serves to bind directly different parts of the memory trace into a specific episodic memory." Schema-related encoding thus shows enhanced mPFC activity and reduced mPFC–hippocampal coupling, while schema-unrelated encoding shows enhanced MTL activity and coupling. The account extends prior consolidation-shift findings by showing the balance shift is already present at encoding.
requirements: A pre-existing conceptual schema activated by related prior knowledge
constraints: The study tested memory only after 24 hr and cannot dissociate encoding from consolidation effects
Selection and abstraction subprocesses of schema-related learning, presumably in posterior perceptual regions, were not tapped
target_learners: second-year university undergraduates
target_learning_goals: acquisition and retention of new conceptual disciplinary knowledge
examples: Participants encoded curriculum-embedded factual sentences related or unrelated to their first-year discipline knowledge while brain activity and connectivity were measured with fMRI
key_sources: van Kesteren, M. T. R., Rijpkema, M., Ruiter, D. J., Morris, R. G. M., & Fernández, G. (2014). Building on Prior Knowledge: Schema-dependent Encoding Processes Relate to Academic Performance. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 26(10), 2250–2261. https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn_a_00630

article_title: Building on Prior Knowledge: Schema-dependent Encoding Processes Relate to Academic Performance
citation: van Kesteren, M. T. R., Rijpkema, M., Ruiter, D. J., Morris, R. G. M., & Fernández, G. (2014). Building on Prior Knowledge: Schema-dependent Encoding Processes Relate to Academic Performance. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 26(10), 2250–2261. https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn_a_00630
title: Structure curricula so new material connects to students' existing conceptual schemas
description: Because activated prior conceptual schemas facilitate encoding and long-term retention of new related material, the article recommends that learning be built on well-structured prior knowledge: "Optimal construction and usage of a schema is thus recommended to lead to better structured learning." In the study, this was operationalized by constructing sentences that each contained at least one term learned in the first year of study and one new term from later courses, embedding the experiment within the actual university curriculum.
requirements: Knowledge of what conceptual schemas learners already possess, so new material can be matched to it
constraints: Benefits apply to information related to an existing schema; mismatching information relies on MTL-dependent binding instead
target_learners: university undergraduates in discipline-specific curricula
target_learning_goals: long-term acquisition and retention of conceptual disciplinary knowledge
examples: Stimulus sentences paired a first-year concept with a new concept (e.g., a known term 'excitatory neurotransmitter' with the new term 'glutamate'), and participants' grades were obtained for Study Year 1 and Study Year 2
key_sources: van Kesteren, M. T. R., Rijpkema, M., Ruiter, D. J., Morris, R. G. M., & Fernández, G. (2014). Building on Prior Knowledge: Schema-dependent Encoding Processes Relate to Academic Performance. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience, 26(10), 2250–2261. https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn_a_00630

article_title: The influence of self-efficacy beliefs for student parents attending university
citation: Tricia M. van Rhijn & Donna S. Lero. (2014). The influence of self-efficacy beliefs for student parents attending university. International Journal of Lifelong Education. http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/02601370.2014.884178
title: School-family balance as a domain-general efficacy construct adapted from work-family balance
description: School-family balance is defined as an individual's perceived ability to manage both school and family role responsibilities, adapted from the work-family balance literature. The article states it is "grounded in an individual's lived experience of the work-family interface and moves beyond individual experiences of conflict and enrichment between roles," emphasizing "an individual's perceived ability to meet the demands of their multiple roles." The construct was measured with six items adapted from Carlson et al.'s Work-Family Balance Scale, with work-related wording changed to school-related, and demonstrated adequate internal reliability (α = .93) and factorial validity in this population.
requirements: Adaptation of validated work-family balance measure with domain-appropriate wording changes
constraints: Developed and validated specifically with student parents; generalizability to other populations not established in this study
target_learners: student parents attending university
target_learning_goals: managing school and family role responsibilities simultaneously
examples: Measured with six items rated on a 5-point Likert scale; sample item: "I am able to negotiate and accomplish what is expected of me at school and in my family"
key_sources: Tricia M. van Rhijn & Donna S. Lero. (2014). The influence of self-efficacy beliefs for student parents attending university. International Journal of Lifelong Education. http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/02601370.2014.884178

article_title: The influence of self-efficacy beliefs for student parents attending university
citation: Tricia M. van Rhijn & Donna S. Lero. (2014). The influence of self-efficacy beliefs for student parents attending university. International Journal of Lifelong Education. http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/02601370.2014.884178
title: Social Cognitive Theory with reciprocal determinism as the framework for understanding student parent experiences
description: The article applies Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory, which "proposes that a triadic perspective is required to understand human functioning: that behaviour, personal factors (cognitive and other internal psychological factors), and environmental events operate in a dynamic fashion to affect a variety of outcomes." Bandura "referred to this triadic interaction as 'reciprocal determinism'." Self-efficacy beliefs are positioned as "the foundation of human agency" such that "people will make choices, expend energy, and persist in tasks that they believe they can achieve." The framework motivates examining both academic and parental self-efficacy domains for student parents managing multiple roles.
requirements: Consideration of behaviour, personal factors, and environmental events together rather than in isolation
constraints: Applied here cross-sectionally; the reciprocal dynamics among the three triadic components were not longitudinally tested
target_learners: adult learners returning to post-secondary education
student parents
target_learning_goals: understanding how efficacy beliefs shape persistence and satisfaction across academic and family domains
examples: The conceptual model positioned academic self-efficacy and parental self-efficacy as predictors of domain-specific satisfaction via school-family balance
key_sources: Tricia M. van Rhijn & Donna S. Lero. (2014). The influence of self-efficacy beliefs for student parents attending university. International Journal of Lifelong Education. http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/02601370.2014.884178

article_title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Is Associated with Selective Attention in Healthy Male High-School Students
citation: Wengaard E, Kristoffersen M, Harris A and Gundersen H (2017) Cardiorespiratory Fitness Is Associated with Selective Attention in Healthy Male High-School Students. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 11:330. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2017.00330
title: Posner cue paradigm visual cognitive task with three stimuli categories for assessing selective attention and inhibitory control
description: The study used a pc-based visual cognitive task based on the Posner cue paradigm to assess reaction time, accuracy and inhibition. The task presented 336 target stimuli across three categories: "no cue", "valid cue" and "invalid cue", where 56 (17%) appeared without a cue, 224 (67%) in the same rectangle as the cue, and 56 (17%) in the opposite rectangle. Participants fixated on a crosshair and pressed keys to indicate which rectangle the target asterisk appeared in, instructed to ignore the cue stimulus.
requirements: Performed on a 13.3-inch laptop programmed with E-prime 2.0
Carried out in a quiet location without distractions, wearing hearing protectors
Oral instruction and a small practice run before the actual task
constraints: Task duration was 9 min and 20 s
The order of inter-stimuli interval, stimuli and cues was fixed for all participants
target_learners: healthy male high-school students
target_learning_goals: selective attention
inhibitory control
reaction time
response accuracy
examples: Mean RT was 376 ± 31 ms for no cue, 293 ± 28 ms for valid cue and 353 ± 35 ms for invalid cue stimuli; error rates were 3.3%, 5.9% and 10.0% respectively
key_sources: Wengaard E, Kristoffersen M, Harris A and Gundersen H (2017) Cardiorespiratory Fitness Is Associated with Selective Attention in Healthy Male High-School Students. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 11:330. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2017.00330

article_title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Is Associated with Selective Attention in Healthy Male High-School Students
citation: Wengaard E, Kristoffersen M, Harris A and Gundersen H (2017) Cardiorespiratory Fitness Is Associated with Selective Attention in Healthy Male High-School Students. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 11:330. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2017.00330
title: Directly measured maximal oxygen uptake test protocol for assessing cardiorespiratory fitness in adolescents
description: The study assessed cardiorespiratory fitness with an incremental treadmill test to volitional exhaustion, using a metabolic system with a 4.2-L mixing chamber. Oxygen uptake was recorded at 30-s intervals, and VO2max was defined when two of three criteria were satisfied: attaining a VO2-plateau, attaining a HR >90% of age-predicted maximum, and attaining a respiratory exchange ratio >1.1. The average of the two highest consecutive 30-s VO2 values was recorded as individual VO2max.
requirements: 10-min warm-up with gradient of 1.7% on a motorized treadmill
Incremental protocol with treadmill-gradient of 5.3% and start velocity of 8 km/h, speed increased 1 km/h each minute until volitional exhaustion
Full system calibration before testing each group and regular volume calibration with a 3 L syringe
constraints: Participants were excluded if diagnosed with heart disease, asthma or any disease potentially affecting the cardiorespiratory system
Participants were asked not to engage in strenuous physical exercise the day before the physical test
target_learners: healthy male high-school students
target_learning_goals: cardiorespiratory fitness measurement
examples: Participants demonstrated above average cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2max score of 54.2 ± 4.9 mL·kg−1·min−1) compared to the age-relative norm of the population (46–50 mL·kg−1·min−1)
key_sources: Wengaard E, Kristoffersen M, Harris A and Gundersen H (2017) Cardiorespiratory Fitness Is Associated with Selective Attention in Healthy Male High-School Students. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 11:330. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2017.00330

article_title: Development of control of attention from different perspectives
citation: Wetzel N (2014) Development of control of attention from different perspectives. Front. Psychol. 5:1000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01000
title: Selective attention as a key function of human information processing that facilitates goal-relevant and inhibits goal-irrelevant processing
description: The editorial frames attention control within an information-processing account: because "The information processing capacity of our brain is limited and we cannot process all incoming stimuli concurrently—we need to select." Selective attention mechanisms "facilitate processing of goal-relevant events and inhibit the processing of goal-irrelevant events." It is described as essential for other cognitive functions like learning, thinking, or memory, and its development is tied to prefrontal maturation and increasing working memory resources.
requirements: A limited processing capacity requiring selection among concurrent stimuli, as the article states
constraints: The framework is presented as an organizing overview of the Research Topic, not as a newly tested model
target_learners: children from infancy through adolescence
children with ADHD
target_learning_goals: attention control and resistance to distraction
handling task-irrelevant information
examples: The Research Topic organizes studies of involuntary attention and distraction, emotion effects on attention control and response inhibition, and ADHD-related distractibility
key_sources: Wetzel N (2014) Development of control of attention from different perspectives. Front. Psychol. 5:1000. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01000

article_title: Auditory Processing in Noise: A Preschool Biomarker for Literacy
citation: White-Schwoch T, Woodruff Carr K, Thompson EC, Anderson S, Nicol T, Bradlow AR, et al. (2015) Auditory Processing in Noise: A Preschool Biomarker for Literacy. PLoS Biol 13(7): e1002196. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1002196
title: Consonants-in-noise neural coding biomarker framework: timing, stability, and spectral-feature measures of the frequency-following response index literacy-relevant auditory precision
description: The article proposes that the precision of subcortical neural coding of speech in noise, measured with the frequency-following response (FFR, also called cABR), underlies language and reading development. It combines three measures from a single recording — "trial-by-trial stability, neural timing, and representation of spectral features that convey phonemic identity" — into a consonants-in-noise score. The framework holds that background noise taxes neural synchrony, so children with poor processing in noise may lag in language development, and that this brain–behavior link precedes reading instruction.
requirements: A standardized FFR recording paradigm: a 170 ms [da] syllable presented against six-talker babble at +10 SNR, with timing, stability, and spectral measures extracted blind to behavioral performance
constraints: The authors state the mechanistic account of inhibitory function and corticocollicular circuitry is speculative: "we must infer midbrain function from far-field electrophysiological recordings"; replication in a larger sample is stated as necessary
target_learners: preschool children ages 3–5 who have not yet learned to read
school-aged children ages 8–14
target_learning_goals: phonological processing
emergent literacy and reading achievement
examples: The framework was operationalized as a regression model whose predictions were applied unchanged to new cohorts in Experiments 2–4.
key_sources: White-Schwoch T, Woodruff Carr K, Thompson EC, Anderson S, Nicol T, Bradlow AR, et al. (2015) Auditory Processing in Noise: A Preschool Biomarker for Literacy. PLoS Biol 13(7): e1002196. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1002196

article_title: Neighborhood Effects in Temporal Perspective
citation: Wodtke, Geoffrey T.; Harding, David J.; Elwert, Felix. (2011). Neighborhood Effects in Temporal Perspective. American Sociological Review. https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122411420816
title: Four categories of neighborhood-effect mechanisms, all involving a temporal dimension of exposure
description: The article organizes theoretical mechanisms linking disadvantaged neighborhoods to educational attainment into four families: "those based on social isolation, social organization, neighborhood resources, and the physical environment." Social isolation theories emphasize role models and cultural repertoires; social organization theories emphasize collective supervision of youth; resource theories emphasize schools and institutions; environmental theories emphasize pollution and housing hazards. The article argues each requires sustained exposure for effects to accumulate or internalize.
requirements: Estimating duration-dependent effects requires measuring neighborhood context repeatedly over childhood rather than at a single point in time
constraints: The article presents these as theoretical mechanisms whose temporal implications motivate the empirical analysis, not as individually tested pathways
target_learners: children and adolescents growing up in disadvantaged neighborhoods
target_learning_goals: high school graduation and progression through school
key_sources: Wodtke, Geoffrey T.; Harding, David J.; Elwert, Felix. (2011). Neighborhood Effects in Temporal Perspective. American Sociological Review. https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122411420816

article_title: Neighborhood Effects in Temporal Perspective
citation: Wodtke, Geoffrey T.; Harding, David J.; Elwert, Felix. (2011). Neighborhood Effects in Temporal Perspective. American Sociological Review. https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122411420816
title: Marginal structural models with inverse probability of treatment weighting for time-varying neighborhood exposures
description: The article adapts a counterfactual framework for time-varying treatments in which "Inverse probability of treatment (IPT) weighting is an alternative approach specifically developed to adjust for confounding by time-varying covariates." A marginal structural model specifies the logit of graduation as a function of duration-weighted exposure (the average of wave-specific quintile treatments). Weighting builds a pseudo-population in which treatment is unconfounded by measured covariates, allowing an unadjusted outcome model to yield unbiased causal effect estimates.
requirements: Assumptions of no unmeasured confounders, no model misspecification, and positivity (nonzero probability of exposure for every confounder combination)
Baseline covariates must still be conditioned on in the outcome model when using stabilized weights
constraints: Selection bias may remain if unobserved factors affect both residential choices and graduation; the no-unobserved-confounding assumption is not testable with the observed data
target_learners: children followed longitudinally in panel studies of residential context
target_learning_goals: causal estimation of cumulative environmental exposure effects on educational attainment
key_sources: Wodtke, Geoffrey T.; Harding, David J.; Elwert, Felix. (2011). Neighborhood Effects in Temporal Perspective. American Sociological Review. https://doi.org/10.1177/0003122411420816

article_title: Examining reciprocal influences among family climate, school attachment, and academic self-regulation: Implications for school success.
citation: Xia, M., Fosco, G. M., & Feinberg, M. E. (2016). Examining Reciprocal Influences Among Family Climate, School Attachment, and Academic Self-Regulation: Implications for School Success. Journal of Family Psychology, 30(4), 442-452. https://doi.org/10.1037/fam0000141
title: Multi-contextual family-systems and ecological framework of adolescent school success
description: Guided by family systems and ecological theories, the study proposes that adolescent school success emerges from the interplay of three domains: family climate, school attachment, and academic self-regulation. Rather than studying these "in relative isolation", the framework models reciprocal, transactional influences among contexts over time, with family climate and school attachment mutually reinforcing each other and each unidirectionally feeding ASR, which in turn drives achievement and adjustment. Figure 1 depicts the hypothesized model.
requirements: Testing the framework requires longitudinal data with repeated measures across the middle school years
constraints: The study measured family climate, school attachment, and ASR with youth-report mono-informant assessments, a limitation the authors state
target_learners: early adolescents (6th through 9th grade)
target_learning_goals: academic self-regulation
school adjustment
academic achievement
examples: The study applied a four-wave cross-lag structural equation model to longitudinal data from 979 6th grade students followed through 9th grade
key_sources: Xia, M., Fosco, G. M., & Feinberg, M. E. (2016). Examining Reciprocal Influences Among Family Climate, School Attachment, and Academic Self-Regulation: Implications for School Success. Journal of Family Psychology, 30(4), 442-452. https://doi.org/10.1037/fam0000141

article_title: Neural correlates of oral word reading, silent reading comprehension, and cognitive subcomponents
citation: Xia Zhichao, Zhang Linjun, Hoeft Fumiko, Gu Bin, Gong Gaolang, Shu Hua. (2018). Neural Correlates of Oral Word Reading, Silent Reading Comprehension, and Cognitive Subcomponents. International Journal of Behavioral Development. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025417727872
title: Multi-componential view of reading with neuroanatomical subdivisions
description: The article frames reading as "multi-componential in nature, i.e., the entire process consists of many subcomponents", with oral word reading and comprehension drawing on partly different subcomponents. It proposes that this hierarchical structure is mirrored at the neuroanatomical level, such that specific brain regions' cortical thickness maps onto specific subcomponents (e.g., LSMG to phonological awareness, LITG to orthography-phonology mapping, LPHP to morphological awareness). The study's findings are presented as "neuroanatomical evidence in support of the multi-componential view of reading" in typically developing Chinese children.
requirements: Requires measuring reading at multiple levels (word reading efficiency and sentence comprehension) alongside tasks tapping distinct cognitive subcomponents
constraints: Evidence here comes from typically developing Chinese children aged 10-12; the authors note the findings need replication with larger sample sizes and cover a limited number of central subcomponents of reading
target_learners: Typically developing children in upper elementary grades (grades 5-6) learning Chinese
target_learning_goals: Oral word reading fluency and silent sentence reading comprehension, and their underlying phonological, orthographic and morphological subcomponents
examples: The study measured word list reading, sentence reading fluency, tone identification and detection, morphological production, and six Chain Test subtests, then regressed subcomponent scores on cortical thickness of reading-defined ROIs.
key_sources: Xia Zhichao, Zhang Linjun, Hoeft Fumiko, Gu Bin, Gong Gaolang, Shu Hua. (2018). Neural Correlates of Oral Word Reading, Silent Reading Comprehension, and Cognitive Subcomponents. International Journal of Behavioral Development. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025417727872

article_title: Visual Processing Matters in Chinese Reading Acquisition and Early Mathematics
citation: Yang X and Meng X (2020) Visual Processing Matters in Chinese Reading Acquisition and Early Mathematics. Front. Psychol. 11:462. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00462
title: Visual processing as a domain-general precursor of early academic learning
description: The article proposes that visual processing — the ability to attend to and distinguish a figure's features such as shape, orientation, color, and size — is a domain-general cognitive precursor supporting both character reading and early mathematics. It argues children must visually discriminate similar characters and mentally represent quantities and number relations, so the same basic visual skill organizes information across academic domains. The article concludes that "visual processing served as a domain-general indicator that contributed to organizing information to help solve diﬀerent types of academic problems, in spite of nonverbal intelligence, inhibitory control, and attention."
requirements: Visual processing must be measured independently of general cognitive abilities (nonverbal IQ, sustained attention, inhibitory control) to demonstrate its unique contribution
constraints: Evidence in this article is longitudinal-correlational; the authors state intervention studies are needed to investigate causality
The orientation discrimination task covers only one kind of visual discrimination (orientation), not shape, color, or size
target_learners: Mainland Chinese kindergarten children transitioning to grade one
target_learning_goals: Chinese character reading
early mathematics (calculation and word problems)
examples: The study measured visual processing with an orientation discrimination task and followed children from senior kindergarten to grade one
key_sources: Yang X and Meng X (2020) Visual Processing Matters in Chinese Reading Acquisition and Early Mathematics. Front. Psychol. 11:462. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00462

article_title: Visual Processing Matters in Chinese Reading Acquisition and Early Mathematics
citation: Yang X and Meng X (2020) Visual Processing Matters in Chinese Reading Acquisition and Early Mathematics. Front. Psychol. 11:462. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00462
title: Orientation discrimination task as a measure of children's visual processing
description: An adaptive psychophysical task used to assess visual processing in young children. Children judge whether a second bicolor segment turned clockwise or anticlockwise relative to a first segment; a three-down-one-up staircase (step size 1.0715°, starting from 10.239°) converges on the orientation discrimination threshold, computed as the mean angle difference over the middle six of ten reversals per block. The article notes "The lower the threshold, the higher the visual processing ability." Children sat 80 cm from the screen, and bicolor segments replaced pure lines to ease task demands for children.
requirements: Children must understand the representation of the segment and the spatial relations between the two segments
Bicolor segments were introduced after piloting because pure lines and dots were too difficult for children
constraints: The authors note this task "is only one kind of visual discrimination" and call for future studies to include other visual processing components such as shape, color, and size
target_learners: Kindergarten and early primary school children
target_learning_goals: Assessment of visual processing as a precursor skill for reading and mathematics
examples: Used at senior kindergarten in a longitudinal study of 82 mainland Chinese children, with reliability 0.79 (Table 1)
key_sources: Yang X and Meng X (2020) Visual Processing Matters in Chinese Reading Acquisition and Early Mathematics. Front. Psychol. 11:462. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00462

article_title: The Effect of Self-Efficacy on Visual Discrimination Sensitivity
citation: Zacharopoulos G, Binetti N, Walsh V, Kanai R (2014) The Effect of Self-Efficacy on Visual Discrimination Sensitivity. PLoS ONE 9(10): e109392. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0109392
title: Self-efficacy theory as a social-cognitive account of behavioural change
description: The article adopts Bandura's self-efficacy theory, described as "perhaps the most widely used model of behavioural change", providing "a novel social-cognitive account of how change in behavioral performance change occurs". The theory predicts that behavioural change is a direct function of the individual's beliefs in one's ability to exercise control over that particular behaviour. The study tests whether this account generalises to low-level perceptual skills, which are otherwise considered a relatively stable trait requiring prolonged training to change.
requirements: The theory presupposes sources of efficacy information such as success or failure experiences in the actual performance, which the article calls "the pivotal source of information influencing one's SE".
constraints: The article notes perceptual sensitivity is known to be a relatively stable trait within individuals that cannot easily be changed without prolonged training, making perceptual tasks a demanding test case for the theory.
target_learners: adult university students
adults from the general population
target_learning_goals: improving task performance through beliefs about one's own competence
examples: The study operationalised the theory by inducing high and low self-efficacy with fake percentile feedback and fictional research findings about ability malleability, then measuring objective perceptual thresholds.

article_title: Maternal emotional support but not cognitive support during problem-solving predicts increases in cognitive flexibility in early childhood
citation: Zeytinoglu, S., Calkins, S. D., & Leerkes, E. M. (2019). Maternal emotional support but not cognitive support during problem-solving predicts increases in cognitive flexibility in early childhood. International Journal of Behavioral Development, 43(1), 12-23. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025418757706
title: Emotional support supports executive function growth via external regulation of arousal and opportunities to practice self-regulation
description: The article proposes a mechanism account in which emotionally supportive caregivers respond to children's needs warmly and encourage autonomy, thereby regulating children's physiological arousal during problem-solving. The article states that "emotionally supportive caregivers likely externally regulate the intensity of children’s physiological arousal and emotions," sustaining arousal levels conducive to coordinating executive functions. Children then internalize regulation strategies, practice executive skills more often, and develop positive attitudes toward cognitively challenging tasks, promoting growth of cognitive flexibility.
requirements: Caregiving observed in collaborative problem-solving contexts where children face cognitively challenging tasks
constraints: The account is the authors' theoretical interpretation; the study's longitudinal design does not test the proposed neural or arousal mechanisms directly
target_learners: children in early childhood (preschool to first grade, ages approximately 4-7)
target_learning_goals: growth of cognitive flexibility and executive functions during early childhood
examples: The study measured emotional support as observed emotional responsiveness, reversed intrusiveness, and reversed negativity during 7-minute mother-child board-game tasks at each wave

title: Interventions for caregivers of young children should target emotional responsiveness and reduce negative and intrusive behaviors to support cognitive flexibility
description: Based on the finding that emotional but not cognitive support predicted growth in cognitive flexibility, the article recommends that "prevention and intervention work aimed towards improving caregivers’ emotional responsiveness and reducing negative and intrusive behaviors may potentially lead to improvements in children’s cognitive flexibility and executive functioning in early childhood." The recommendation is framed as potential, resting on the longitudinal predictive associations rather than a tested intervention.
requirements: Intervention should focus on the emotional dimension of caregiving (responsiveness, non-intrusiveness, low negativity) rather than instructional or cognitive support alone
constraints: The article states the recommendation only "may potentially" lead to improvements; no intervention was tested in this study

article_title: Creativity and flexibility in young children's use of external cognitive strategies.
citation: Armitage, KL; Suddendorf, T; Bulley, A; Bastos, APM; Taylor, AH; Redshaw, J. (2023). Creativity and Flexibility in Young Children's Use of External Cognitive Strategies. Developmental Psychology, 59 (6), pp. 995-1005. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0001562
title: Hidden-prize marking and transfer task paradigm for assessing children's spontaneous external reminder-setting strategies
description: A preregistered experimental paradigm in which children watch an experimenter demonstrate how to mark the location of a hidden prize, helping them retrieve it later, and are then given opportunities across six test trials to spontaneously adopt an external marking strategy. Children who used the strategy at least once were introduced to a "conceptually similar but structurally distinct transfer task" to assess strategy flexibility. It measures self-initiated external metacognitive strategy use across ages 3–8.
requirements: An experimenter demonstration of marking the hidden prize's location before test trials
A conceptually similar but structurally distinct transfer task for assessing strategy modification
constraints: Studied with 3–8-year-olds (N = 72, mostly White) in Australia; scope limited to that sample and setting
target_learners: children aged 3 to 8 years
target_learning_goals: self-initiated use of external cognitive strategies to offload internal cognitive demand
examples: Children watched as an experimenter demonstrated how to mark the location of a hidden prize, then received six test trials and, for adopters, a transfer task

article_title: Creativity and flexibility in young children's use of external cognitive strategies.
citation: Armitage, KL; Suddendorf, T; Bulley, A; Bastos, APM; Taylor, AH; Redshaw, J. (2023). Creativity and Flexibility in Young Children's Use of External Cognitive Strategies. Developmental Psychology, 59 (6), pp. 995-1005. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0001562
title: External metacognitive offloading: awareness of one's own cognitive struggles used to offload internal demand into the environment
description: The article frames a cardinal feature of adult cognition as "the awareness of our own cognitive struggles and the capacity to draw upon this awareness to offload internal demand into the environment." External metacognitive strategies, such as setting physical reminders by marking a hidden prize's location, reduce internal memory demand. The study examines when children begin to self-initiate such strategies and how flexibly they adapt them across contexts, with development evident from age 4 and effective deployment from age 6.
requirements: Awareness of one's own cognitive struggle
An environment that affords external marking or reminder-setting actions
constraints: Developmental emergence is graded: 3-year-olds copy but do not modify strategies; flexible devising of novel strategies appears from age 4
target_learners: children aged 3 to 8 years
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness and offloading of cognitive demand into the environment
examples: Children adopting demonstrated marking strategies and devising novel reminder-setting strategies across six transfer trials

article_title: The association between preschool children's social functioning and their emergent academic skills
citation: Arnold, D. H., Kupersmidt, J. B., Voegler-Lee, M. E., & Marshall, N. (2012). The Association between Preschool Children's Social Functioning and Their Emergent Academic Skills. Early Childhood Research Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2011.12.009
title: Reciprocal model of social functioning and academic development with attention difficulties as a central early mechanism
description: The article describes a model of "reciprocal associations between social functioning and academic skills in which problems in either area can lead to difficulties in the other." In this model, attention difficulties limit children's ability to engage in learning activities and benefit from instruction; academic difficulties later breed frustration and aggression; and prosocial behavior serves as a protective factor by increasing teachers' investment and fostering persistence. The present cross-sectional study is offered as a step toward evaluating this model in low-SES preschoolers, not a full test of it.
requirements: Empirical evaluation differentiating aggression, attention difficulties, and prosocial skills, and controlling for their interrelations
constraints: The article states the study "does not provide a full test of the above model" and is cross-sectional, so reciprocal pathways are not tested
target_learners: Preschool children from low-SES, economically disadvantaged backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Emergent preliteracy, language, and mathematics development
examples: The study assessed 467 preschoolers with teacher-rated IOWA Conners and SSRS measures and independent Woodcock-Johnson and PPVT-III academic tests, analyzed with HLM

article_title: The Effects of Acute Exercise on Mood, Cognition, Neurophysiology, and Neurochemical Pathways: A Review
citation: Basso Julia C., Suzuki Wendy A. (2017). The Effects of Acute Exercise on Mood, Cognition, Neurophysiology, and Neurochemical Pathways: A Review. Brain Plasticity. https://doi.org/10.3233/BPL-160040
title: Reticular-activating hypofrontality theory of acute exercise
description: Dietrich's reticular-activating hypofrontality theory explains brain resource allocation during exercise. As the review states, "during exercise, the brain's finite supply of energy and resources is shifted from areas involved in cognitive processing like the prefrontal cortex towards areas that are important for motor movement and coordination", causing prefrontal hypoperfusion during exercise, followed by a rebound surge of oxygenated blood that enhances prefrontal function. The review presents fNIRS findings on prefrontal activation after exercise in the context of evaluating this theory.
requirements: Requires measurement of prefrontal and motor-region activity during and after exercise, e.g., via fNIRS or fMRI, to evaluate the hypoperfusion and rebound sequence
constraints: The review notes the theory concerns the period during and immediately following exercise; the fNIRS studies it discusses measured only up to 15 minutes after exercise cessation
target_learners: healthy adults
older adults
target_learning_goals: executive function and inhibitory control
mood regulation
examples: The review evaluates the theory using fNIRS studies showing increased left dorsolateral prefrontal activation during Stroop performance after a 10-minute moderate-intensity exercise bout

article_title: Metaphorically speaking: cognitive abilities and the production of figurative language
citation: Roger E. Beaty & Paul J. Silvia. (2013). Metaphorically speaking: cognitive abilities and the production of figurative language. Memory & Cognition. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0258-5
title: Property attribution model as a framework for metaphor generation
description: The article adopts Glucksberg's property attribution model of metaphor comprehension as a framework for conceptualizing metaphor production. Composing a metaphor involves "making an abstract link between a topic and a vehicle by relating similar characteristics", with a superordinate attributive category (e.g., "something that is healing" for music) maintained while searching semantic memory for a vehicle. The authors map this onto CHC abilities: attributive-category formation parallels broad retrieval ability (Gr), and top-down oversight of the search parallels fluid intelligence (Gf).
requirements: A superordinate attributive category must be formed and maintained while searching semantic memory for an appropriate vehicle
constraints: The model is a comprehension framework adopted by analogy for production; the article states an empirical understanding of figurative language production remains elusive
target_learners: adult learners
undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: creative figurative language production
selective retrieval from semantic memory
examples: Participants forming an attributive category for "things that are gross" and selectively retrieving exemplars satisfying those criteria in the creative metaphor task
key_sources: Roger E. Beaty & Paul J. Silvia. (2013). Metaphorically speaking: cognitive abilities and the production of figurative language. Memory & Cognition. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0258-5

article_title: Metaphorically speaking: cognitive abilities and the production of figurative language
citation: Roger E. Beaty & Paul J. Silvia. (2013). Metaphorically speaking: cognitive abilities and the production of figurative language. Memory & Cognition. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0258-5
title: Cattell–Horn–Carroll (CHC) hierarchical model of intelligence as an organizing framework for creative cognition
description: The article uses modern CHC theory, described as "an emerging consensus on the structure of cognitive abilities based on decades of factor-analytic research", which "conceptualizes intelligence as a hierarchical structure of abilities, from narrow (specific abilities, such as inductive reasoning) to broad (global abilities, such as fluid intelligence) to general (g)". Three broad factors—Gf, Gc, and Gr—were modeled as latent variables to predict two kinds of metaphor production, extending the CHC framework into the study of creative cognition.
requirements: Latent-variable measurement of each broad ability via multiple indicator tasks
raters blind to each other's scores and participants' other data
constraints: The study tested only three broad CHC factors in an undergraduate sample with English as primary language; the biology and literature knowledge indicators loaded poorly on Gc and were excluded
target_learners: undergraduate students
adult learners
target_learning_goals: understanding cognitive ability contributions to creative and conventional language production
examples: Gf indexed by letter sets, Cattell Culture Fair series completion, and paper folding tasks; Gr by three verbal fluency tasks; Gc by two vocabulary tests and a history test

article_title: Observed emotional and behavioral indicators of motivation predict school readiness in Head Start graduates
citation: Berhenke, Amanda; Miller, Alison L.; Brown, Eleanor; Seifer, Ronald; Dickstein, Susan. (2011). Observed Emotional and Behavioral Indicators of Motivation Predict School Readiness in Head Start Graduates. Early childhood research quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2011.04.001
title: Conceptual model of observed motivation indicators: mastery motivation behaviors, strategy use, and emotion expression during challenging tasks
description: The article proposes a conceptual model (Figure 1) in which motivation in young children is assessed observationally through three classes of indicators. As the authors state, "we considered the following as indicators of motivation: mastery motivation behaviors (persistence, pride, and competence), strategy use (help-seeking), and emotion expression (positive affect, interest/arousal, sadness, confusion, anxiety, anger, frustration, hostility, and shame) as observed during a challenging task." The model links these indicators to school readiness outcomes: student-teacher relationship quality, learning-related behaviors, and academic competence. It rests on the definition of motivation as the process whereby goal-directed activity is energized and sustained, and on mastery motivation and expectancy-value theory.
requirements: Requires observation of children during challenging tasks, with videotaped coding of facial, vocal, and behavioral cues
constraints: The authors note they were not able to code other aspects of task-focused problem-solving strategies because videotapes were primarily focused on children's faces
target_learners: young children (preschool and kindergarten age)
children at risk for school failure, e.g., Head Start graduates
target_learning_goals: early motivation and engagement relevant to school readiness
academic competence and learning-related classroom behaviors
examples: The model was instantiated in puzzle and trivia challenge tasks administered to 131 Head Start graduates in kindergarten, with emotions and task behaviors coded from video.
key_sources: Berhenke, Amanda; Miller, Alison L.; Brown, Eleanor; Seifer, Ronald; Dickstein, Susan. (2011). Observed Emotional and Behavioral Indicators of Motivation Predict School Readiness in Head Start Graduates. Early childhood research quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2011.04.001

article_title: Observed emotional and behavioral indicators of motivation predict school readiness in Head Start graduates
citation: Berhenke, Amanda; Miller, Alison L.; Brown, Eleanor; Seifer, Ronald; Dickstein, Susan. (2011). Observed Emotional and Behavioral Indicators of Motivation Predict School Readiness in Head Start Graduates. Early childhood research quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2011.04.001
title: Observational challenge-task assessment of motivation with AFFEX-adapted emotion coding and project-developed task behavior codes
description: This assessment consists of five puzzle tasks and a trivia game adapted from Smiley and Dweck (1994), including impossible puzzles and failure-feedback trivia, videotaped and coded for emotion and task behavior. "Emotion (adapted from the AFFEX coding system; Izard, Dougherty, & Hembree, 1989) and task behavior states (a coding system developed for this project) were coded independently by student coding teams using The Observer XT software system." Children were continuously coded into seven mutually exclusive emotion states and three task behavior states, plus discrete events (pride, shame, frustration, hostility, help-seeking, competence). Reliability was established via intraclass correlations on 10% of tapes.
requirements: Requires videotaped task sessions and trained coding teams with reliability checks (ICCs on fourteen tapes, 10% of sample)
constraints: Rare events such as shame and hostility were coded by group consensus and did not occur with sufficient frequency for reliability analyses
target_learners: kindergarten-age children
Head Start graduates in low-income families
target_learning_goals: assessment of motivation via observed emotion expression and task engagement during academic challenge
examples: Children attempted three impossible puzzles and two difficult solvable puzzles, then a trivia game with failure feedback, ending with successfully answered 'kid questions.'
