article_title: Growing syntactic structure and code-mixing in the weaker language: The Ivy Hypothesis
citation: Bernardini, P., & Schlyter, S. (2004). Growing syntactic structure and code-mixing in the weaker language: The Ivy Hypothesis. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition, 7(1), 49-69. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1366728904001270
title: The Ivy Hypothesis: code-mixing as gap-filling where higher syntactic structure comes from the stronger language
description: The Ivy Hypothesis proposes that in interactions meant to be in the weaker language, bilingual children with uneven development use portions of higher syntactic structure lexically instantiated in the stronger language combined with lower portions in the weaker language. The weaker language grows like ivy on the structural tree of the stronger language. The model is grounded in generative syntax within the Minimalist Program, assuming syntax is projected from the lexicon and that bilinguals have one universal syntax and two lexicons. It predicts that as the weaker language lexicon develops, successively higher portions of structure can be realized in that language, and mixing ceases once no functional gap remains.
requirements: A clear and consistent imbalance in syntactic development between the two languages, with one language clearly weaker throughout the acquisition period
constraints: The hypothesis is not claimed to be valid for all children with uneven development; less imbalance may lead to different mixing patterns, and some children do not code-mix at all
target_learners: young bilingual children aged 2-4 with uneven bilingual first language development
target_learning_goals: syntactic development in two first languages
sentence-internal code-mixing patterns
examples: The model was tested against longitudinal data from five Swedish-French/Italian children, comparing syntactic constituents in monolingual and mixed utterances in each recording
key_sources: Bernardini, P., & Schlyter, S. (2004). Growing syntactic structure and code-mixing in the weaker language: The Ivy Hypothesis. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition, 7(1), 49-69. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1366728904001270

article_title: Neural Correlates of Letter Reversal in Children and Adults
citation: Blackburne LK, Eddy MD, Kalra P, Yee D, Sinha P, Gabrieli JDE. (2014) Neural Correlates of Letter Reversal in Children and Adults. PLoS ONE 9(5): e98386. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0098386
title: Orientation-insensitive object recognition account of letter reversal development
description: The article advances the explanatory account that learning to read adapts general object recognition processes that are insensitive to right-left orientation. As the authors put it, "learning to read reflects a specialized adaptation of more general object recognition processes that are insensitive to right-left orientation", so reading experience is needed to overcome this initial orientation insensitivity and establish orientation-specific letter representations. The study's finding that children up to age 12 show no early ERP or fMRI distinction between typical and reversed letters, while adults do, is interpreted as evidence that this specialized, orientation-specific letter perception develops slowly.
requirements: Reading experience over a prolonged developmental period to establish orientation-specific letter representations
constraints: The article states the developmental process remains immature at least through age 12 even in above-average readers; the account is offered as an interpretation of the observed neural differences, not as a directly tested mechanism
target_learners: Children ages 5–12 learning to read
Beginning readers
target_learning_goals: Orientation-specific letter perception and recognition of letters such as b/d and p/q
examples: Children ages 5–12 viewing typical and reversed letters showed no P1 or N170 ERP differences and little fMRI difference, whereas adults showed large differences in the same tasks
key_sources: Blackburne LK, Eddy MD, Kalra P, Yee D, Sinha P, Gabrieli JDE. (2014) Neural Correlates of Letter Reversal in Children and Adults. PLoS ONE 9(5): e98386. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0098386

article_title: Moderating effects of executive functions and the teacher–child relationship on the development of mathematics ability in kindergarten
citation: Blair, Clancy; McKinnon, Rachel D.; the Family Life Project Investigators. (2016). Moderating effects of executive functions and the teacher–child relationship on the development of mathematics ability in kindergarten. Learning and Instruction, 41, 85–93. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.10.001
title: Promote early school progress for children in poverty through approaches that focus on self-regulation and social competence, since these can compensate for weak academic preparedness
description: The article proposes that strength in one school-readiness domain can offset weakness in another: children entering kindergarten with low measured academic ability made greater-than-expected math gains when they had higher executive function or a more positive teacher relationship. It concludes that "innovative approaches to promoting early school progress that focus on self-regulation and social competence" are warranted, citing experimental programs such as the Chicago School Readiness Project and Tools of the Mind as consistent with this view.
requirements: Assessment of children's early academic ability to identify those with low preschool math preparedness who are most likely to benefit
constraints: The supporting evidence is correlational and cannot be interpreted as causal
Moderation was observed in a predominantly low-income rural sample and at the lower end of the preschool math distribution; generalization across SES remains untested
The moderation appeared on the ECLS-K Math battery but not the Applied Problems subtest

target_learning_goals: Early mathematics ability
School readiness and self-regulated learning
examples: The study followed 1005 children from predominantly low-income rural communities and found that for children with low preschool ECLS-K Math scores, higher executive function or a more positive kindergarten teacher relationship was associated with higher-than-expected kindergarten math ability

article_title: The double-edged sword of pedagogy: Instruction limits spontaneous exploration and discovery
citation: Bonawitz Elizabeth, Shafto Patrick, Gweon Hyowon, Goodman Noah D., Spelke Elizabeth, Schulz Laura. (2011). The Double-edged Sword of Pedagogy: Instruction limits spontaneous exploration and discovery. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2010.10.001
title: Bayesian pedagogical-sampling model of instruction as an inductive bias
description: The article formalizes pedagogical learning as rational inference under reciprocal assumptions: a learner rationally updates beliefs given data, and a helpful teacher chooses demonstrations likely to increase the learner's belief in the correct hypothesis (Equations 1' and 2). Under pedagogical sampling, "the learner will infer, by Equation 1’, that the demonstrated functions are exhaustive—all the functions will be demonstrated by a helpful teacher." Under default (weak) sampling, evidence about tested affordances provides no information about untested ones. The model predicts the exploration trade-off tested in both experiments.
requirements: The inference depends on the learner believing the data were chosen by a knowledgeable, helpful teacher; if evidence is sampled randomly or the teacher is interrupted, the default sampling assumption applies and absence of additional functions is not inferred.
constraints: The article treats interrupted or naive demonstrations as non-pedagogical even with superficial ostensive cues; the qualitative conclusion is stated to hold under further iterations of the equations, with scope limited to the modeled pedagogical situations.
target_learners: preschool-aged children (48–72 months)
target_learning_goals: causal learning about novel objects' latent functions
calibrating exploration versus exploitation in discovery
examples: The model motivated Experiment 1's prediction that pedagogically sampled evidence would yield briefer, narrower play and fewer discovered functions, and Experiment 2's 'similar priors' prediction for overheard instruction.

article_title: Symbolic magnitude processing in elementary school children: A group administered paper-and-pencil measure (SYMP Test)
citation: Brankaer, C., Ghesquière, P., & De Smedt, B. (2017). Symbolic magnitude processing in elementary school children: A group administered paper-and-pencil measure (SYMP Test). Behavior Research Methods, 49, 1361–1373. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-016-0792-3
title: SYMP Test: a group-administered paper-and-pencil symbolic magnitude comparison measure with one-digit and two-digit subtests
description: The SYMP Test is a timed paper-and-pencil test of symbolic numerical magnitude processing consisting of two subtests: a one-digit subtest with digits 1–9 and a two-digit subtest with digits 11–99, each with 60 digit pairs. Children cross out the larger digit; the article states that participants "were given 30 s to solve as many items as possible," a limit chosen through pilot studies to assess fluency and avoid ceiling effects. It was designed for quick classroom group administration in large-scale studies.
requirements: Group administration by a trained administrator with a stopwatch, four practice trials per subtest, and a 30 s time limit per subtest
constraints: The two-digit subtest was not administered in Grade 1 because children in that grade had not yet received enough instruction in that number domain
target_learners: Primary school children in Grades 1–6
target_learning_goals: Symbolic numerical magnitude comparison fluency with one- and two-digit Arabic numbers
examples: Administered collectively in classrooms in 10 Flemish elementary schools to 1,588 children, with a motor speed control task administered alongside
key_sources: Brankaer, C., Ghesquière, P., & De Smedt, B. (2017). Symbolic magnitude processing in elementary school children: A group administered paper-and-pencil measure (SYMP Test). Behavior Research Methods, 49, 1361–1373. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-016-0792-3

article_title: Behavioral and electrophysiological indices of inhibitory control in maltreated adolescents and nonmaltreated adolescents
citation: Bruce, J., & Kim, H. K. (2022). Behavioral and Electrophysiological Indices of Inhibitory Control in Maltreated Adolescents and Nonmaltreated Adolescents. Development and Psychopathology. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0954579420001819
title: Stress-physiology account: early adverse experiences impair development of prefrontal inhibitory-control circuitry via HPA activation
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that early adverse experiences cause "acute and/or chronic activation of the HPA system and other systems involved in the response to stress, which in turn impairs the development and subsequent functioning of critical neural regions." Prefrontal regions underlying inhibitory control are considered especially vulnerable because of their protracted developmental course and high density of glucocorticoid receptors. The study's N2 findings are read against this account.
requirements: Interpretation assumes early adverse experiences activate stress-response systems that affect developing prefrontal neural regions, as the article states
constraints: The article notes it cannot be determined from a single early-adolescent assessment whether observed differences represent a delay or a deficit
target_learners: adolescents (12-13 years old) exposed to early adverse experiences
target_learning_goals: inhibitory control and its underlying neural development
examples: The study tested this account by comparing ERP components and accuracy between maltreated and socioeconomically matched nonmaltreated adolescents

article_title: Multi-method brain imaging reveals impaired representations of number as well as altered connectivity in adults with dyscalculia
citation: Bulthé Jessica, Prinsen Jellina, Vanderauwera Jolijn, Duyck Stefanie, Daniels Nicky, Gillebert Céline R., Mantini Dante, Op de Beeck Hans P., De Smedt Bert. (2019). Multi-method brain imaging reveals impaired representations of number as well as altered connectivity in adults with dyscalculia. Neuroimage, 190, 289-302. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2018.06.012
title: Representation-impairment versus disrupted-access hypotheses of neurodevelopmental learning disorders
description: The article organizes its investigation around two hypotheses about the etiology of neurodevelopmental learning disorders such as dyscalculia: impaired cognitive representations versus disrupted connectivity and impaired access to intact representations. It notes these "hypotheses are not mutually exclusive" and applies a multi-method brain imaging approach combining univariate and multivariate fMRI with functional and structural connectivity to test both in one sample. The study concludes both hold: representations are impaired and access is altered.
requirements: Multi-method imaging combining representation-quality measures (MVPA decoding) with connectivity measures in the same sample and task
constraints: Tested in adults with dyscalculia performing a number comparison task; the authors note dyscalculia is heterogeneous and its neural correlates cannot be reduced to one or a few brain areas
target_learners: adults with dyscalculia (specific learning disorder with impairment in mathematics)
target_learning_goals: numerical magnitude processing and calculation-related number representations
examples: 24 adults with dyscalculia and 24 pairwise-matched controls performed symbolic and non-symbolic number comparison in the scanner while univariate, MVPA, and connectivity data were collected

Neuroimage, 190, 289-302. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2018.06.012

article_title: The Neural Development of an Abstract Concept of Number
citation: Cantlon Jessica F., Libertus Melissa E., Pinel Philippe, Dehaene Stanislas, Brannon Elizabeth M., Pelphrey Kevin A. (2009). The Neural Development of an Abstract Concept of Number. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn.2008.21159
title: A core notation-independent neural system for number with developmental frontal mediation
description: The article proposes that "a core neural system integrates notation-independent numerical representations throughout development but, early in development, higher-order brain mechanisms mediate this process." Drawing on primate single-cell work and computational modeling, it suggests "children recruit inferior frontal cortex at an early stage of development to form associations among numerical values at a notation-independent level of abstraction," with parietal cortex becoming the automatic substrate in adulthood. The IFG's role may be domain-general (cognitive control) or task-specific (forming abstract numerical categories).
requirements: Requires an initial period of associative learning between symbolic and nonsymbolic numerical representations, per the modeling studies the article cites
constraints: The article states the precise role of inferior frontal cortex in notation-independent numerical processing cannot be determined by its data alone
The study did not address the specificity of cortical regions for numerical processing
target_learners: 6- to 7-year-old children
adults
target_learning_goals: abstract, notation-independent understanding of numerical values
symbolic number learning (Arabic numerals)
examples: Children showed a positive IFG response to both notations, a robust numerical ratio effect, and a strong correlation with behavioral performance, whereas adults showed no above-baseline IFG activity
key_sources: Cantlon Jessica F., Libertus Melissa E., Pinel Philippe, Dehaene Stanislas, Brannon Elizabeth M., Pelphrey Kevin A. (2009). The Neural Development of an Abstract Concept of Number. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn.2008.21159

article_title: Relation between Visual Motor Integration and Handwriting in Students of Elementary School
citation: Capellini, S. A., Giaconi, C., & Germano, G. D. (2017). Relation between Visual Motor Integration and Handwriting in Students of Elementary School. Psychology, 8, 258-270. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2017.82015
title: Two-type classification of dysgraphia: perceptual and motor dysgraphia
description: The article presents dysgraphia, described per the American Psychiatric Association (2013) as a neurodevelopmental specific learning disorder of written expression, as classifiable into two types. It states "The dysgraphia can be further classified into two types: the perceptual and motor dysgraphia". Perceptual dysgraphia is a difficulty where the student "cannot make the relationship between the symbolic system and spellings that represent sounds, words and phrases", while in motor dysgraphia students "can speak and read, but find difficulties in fine motor skills to write letters, words and numbers". The study uses this framing to interpret grade-level handwriting deficits.
requirements: Classification presupposes assessment separating perceptual (symbol-sound mapping) from motor (fine-motor letter production) components of written expression.
constraints: The article attributes the DSM-5 framing to the American Psychiatric Association (2013) and the two-type distinction to Martins et al. (2013); it reports no test of the taxonomy itself.
target_learners: elementary school students in literacy instruction
target_learning_goals: handwriting and written expression skills
examples: The study interprets 1st-grade dysgraphia as reflecting deficits in visual-motor integration skills as students begin exposure to print and writing demands.
key_sources: Capellini, S. A., Giaconi, C., & Germano, G. D. (2017). Relation between Visual Motor Integration and Handwriting in Students of Elementary School. Psychology, 8, 258-270. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2017.82015

article_title: Relation between Visual Motor Integration and Handwriting in Students of Elementary School
citation: Capellini, S. A., Giaconi, C., & Germano, G. D. (2017). Relation between Visual Motor Integration and Handwriting in Students of Elementary School. Psychology, 8, 258-270. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2017.82015
title: Teach visual-perception and motor-coordination strategies before and during early alphabetization, since students start writing instruction lacking these essential skills
description: Because most 1st-grade students in this study were classified with dysgraphia, the authors conclude that "the students start the alphabetization process without some essential skills, such as viso -perception and motor coord ination", and state this finding "brings an important impact to educational policy". They further suggest that the absence of clear skill progression across grades "might suggest a lack of teac h-ing of strategies in classroom". The principle is that handwriting instruction should be preceded and accompanied by explicit teaching of visual-perceptual and motor-coordination strategies.
requirements: Classroom instruction must include systematic teaching of visual-perception, motor-coordination and visual-motor integration strategies alongside literacy activities.
constraints: The article notes the Dysgraphia Scale estimates are based on a limited number of subjects and that no national scale or test existed in Brazil for these parameters.
target_learners: 1st- to 5th-grade elementary school students in public schools
target_learning_goals: handwriting quality and legibility
visual-motor integration, visual perception and motor coordination
examples: The study found 80% of 1st graders classified with dysgraphia and no clear grade progression in visual-motor skills, which the authors link to missing classroom strategy teaching.
key_sources: Capellini, S. A., Giaconi, C., & Germano, G. D. (2017). Relation between Visual Motor Integration and Handwriting in Students of Elementary School. Psychology, 8, 258-270. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2017.82015

article_title: Is there a relation between visual motor integration and academic achievement in school-aged children with and without ADHD?
citation: Carames, C. N., Irwin, L. N., & Kofler, M. J. (2022). Is There a Relation Between Visual-Motor Integration and Academic Achievement in School-Aged Children with and without ADHD? Child Neuropsychology, 28(2), 224–243. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2021.1967913
title: Visual-motor integration as the coordination of visual perception and motor coordination subcomponents
description: The article treats the visual-motor system as comprising two subcomponents — visual perception (processing ocularly obtained environmental information) and motor coordination (controlling fine and gross motor components of body movement) — whose fluid coordination is termed visual-motor integration. Deficits may arise in either subcomponent or in the integration of the two, and the article measures each separately with the Beery VMI subtests to determine which components predict which academic domains. The framework organizes the study's regressions and its interpretation that ADHD-related academic difficulty may reflect impaired integration rather than impaired subcomponents.
requirements: Separate measurement of visual perception and motor coordination alongside overall visual-motor integration (e.g., the Beery VMI's three subtests) to distinguish subcomponent deficits from integration deficits
constraints: The article notes deficits may stem from subcomponents, from integration, or from other neurological impairments limiting effective integration; the study was not powered to test mediation and could not examine ADHD diagnostic status as a moderator due to sample size
target_learners: School-aged children ages 8–13 with and without ADHD
target_learning_goals: Reading achievement
Math achievement
Written language achievement
examples: The study administered the Beery VMI's Visual-Motor Integration, Visual Perception, and Motor Coordination subtests and regressed KTEA-3 reading, math, and written language composites on all three components
key_sources: Carames, C. N., Irwin, L. N., & Kofler, M. J. (2022). Is There a Relation Between Visual-Motor Integration and Academic Achievement in School-Aged Children with and without ADHD? Child Neuropsychology, 28(2), 224–243. https://doi.org/10.1080/09297049.2021.1967913

article_title: Play it safe or play to learn: mindsets and behavioral self-regulation in kindergarten
citation: Compagnoni, M., Karlen, Y., & Maag Merki, K. (2019). Play it safe or play to learn: mindsets and behavioral self-regulation in kindergarten. Metacognition and Learning, 14, 291–314. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09190-y
title: Puppet-and-touchscreen mindset scale for kindergarteners
description: A newly developed self-report mindset measure for kindergarteners based on the Berkeley Puppet Interview, with a goal-orientation scale (3 items) and a trait-belief scale (4 items). Two plush elephant puppets deliver standardized recorded answers on a touchscreen, and children indicate identification on a 5-point semantic differential scale with a "double binary response strategy" to counter endpoint pushing. The authors note the tool was "motivating for the children, easy to administer" and offers objectivity advantages.
requirements: Multiple-item scales are necessary with young children to ensure reliability, rather than single items
Children must be able to listen to and comprehend the recorded puppet statements; recorded statements can be replayed at the push of a button in case of comprehension problems
constraints: The trait beliefs scale showed low reliability in young children (α = .51), deemed sufficient for new scales and latent modeling
Mindset item distributions were left-skewed even after log transformation, with more children endorsing growth-oriented responses
target_learners: kindergarteners aged 5 to 7 years
target_learning_goals: assessing young children's motivational beliefs about trait stability and mastery versus performance goal orientations
examples: Administered individually in a roughly 25-minute session to 147 Swiss kindergarteners across two visits in spring 2017, with items based on the composite measure used by Gunderson et al. (2013) for children aged 7–8 years
key_sources: Compagnoni, M., Karlen, Y., & Maag Merki, K. (2019). Play it safe or play to learn: mindsets and behavioral self-regulation in kindergarten. Metacognition and Learning, 14, 291–314. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09190-y

article_title: Neural Substrates of Inhibitory Control Maturation in Adolescence
citation: Constantinidis Christos, Luna Beatriz. (2019). Neural Substrates of Inhibitory Control Maturation in Adolescence. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2019.07.004
title: Preparatory-state model of inhibitory control maturation
description: The review proposes an integrative model in which inhibitory control matures primarily through the emergence of neural activity patterns establishing a ready preparatory state, supported by improved inhibitory circuitry and systems-level integration. As the review states, "a primary way in which inhibitory control matures is the emergence of neural activity patterns that establish a ready preparatory state to inhibit a response." These changes support PFC integration, error processing, and planning of effective responses, while leaving the ability to generate single inhibitory responses intact from early development.
requirements: Mature inhibitory circuitry and systems-level integration of prefrontal with oculomotor and subcortical systems
constraints: Adolescent immaturities do not undermine the ability to generate inhibitory responses but limit sustained, controlled engagement of cognitive control
target_learners: adolescents
young adults
target_learning_goals: development of inhibitory control and executive function
examples: Human longitudinal fMRI growth curves of dlPFC and dACC engagement; monkey single-neuron recordings of preparatory ramping and goal representation across adolescence and adulthood
key_sources: Constantinidis Christos, Luna Beatriz. (2019). Neural Substrates of Inhibitory Control Maturation in Adolescence. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2019.07.004

article_title: Developmental Dyslexia and Dysgraphia: What can We Learn from the One About the Other?
citation: Döhla D and Heim S (2016). Developmental Dyslexia and Dysgraphia: What can We Learn from the One About the Other? Front. Psychol. 6:2045. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.02045
title: Hybrid multiple-deficit model of dyslexia allowing single or multiple cognitive deficits
description: The review presents Pennington et al. (2012)'s hybrid model, which organizes four cognitive models of dyslexia by whether there is a single deficit and whether a PA deficit is necessary (Table 1: single phonological deficit, single deficit subtypes, phonological core multiple deficit, multiple deficit). The authors conclude "a hybrid model that encompasses all four possibilities of cognitive single- and multiple deﬁcit models (Table 1) best depicts the causesofdyslexia", because nearly all tested dyslexics had at least one marginal cognitive deficit. The review speculates this hybrid model might also explain developmental dysgraphia.
requirements: Allows a single underlying deficit as well as multiple impaired skills, since many cases show more than one impaired function
constraints: The review notes studies of individual profiles of dysgraphia are urgently needed to test the transfer to dysgraphia
target_learners: school-aged children with reading and writing disorders
target_learning_goals: diagnosis of underlying cognitive deficits in reading and writing disorders
examples: Pennington et al. (2012) compared cognitive single-, multiple- and hybrid deficit models and found nearly all tested dyslexics had at least one marginal (11–25th percentile) cognitive deficit
key_sources: Döhla D and Heim S (2016). Developmental Dyslexia and Dysgraphia: What can We Learn from the One About the Other? Front. Psychol. 6:2045. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.02045

article_title: Developmental Dyslexia and Dysgraphia: What can We Learn from the One About the Other?
citation: Döhla D and Heim S (2016). Developmental Dyslexia and Dysgraphia: What can We Learn from the One About the Other? Front. Psychol. 6:2045. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.02045
title: Cerebellar deficit hypothesis: impaired cerebellar automatization causes reading, writing and spelling problems via distinct routes
description: The review describes the cerebellar deficit hypothesis (Nicolson et al., 2001; Nicolson and Fawcett, 2011), in which the cerebellum supports automatization of articulatory, auditory and motor skills. "a dysfunctional cerebellum can lead to reading as well as writing disorders": writing problems arise from motor skill difficulties, reading problems from phonology based on deficient articulatory skills, and spelling problems from deficient skill automatization, with different cerebellar regions activated for each route. Nicolson and Fawcett's three-stage automaticity-deficit framework (declarative, intermediate, autonomous) and five stages of learning are included.
requirements: The framework assumes the cerebellum supports automatization of basic articulatory, auditory and motor skills
constraints: The review reports mixed outcomes: some studies found no significantly worse automatization results between dyslexics and controls
target_learners: children with dyslexia and dysgraphia
target_learning_goals: automatization of reading, spelling and writing skills
examples: Nicolson and Fawcett (2000) found in a response-blending study that dyslexic children have problems in the initial stage and take longer for intermediate proceduralization
key_sources: Döhla D and Heim S (2016). Developmental Dyslexia and Dysgraphia: What can We Learn from the One About the Other? Front. Psychol. 6:2045. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2015.02045

article_title: The Social Origins of Human Prosociality
citation: Dahl A., Brownell C. A. (2019). The Social Origins of Human Prosociality. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0963721419830386
title: Bidirectional socialization account: prosocial motives develop through two-way caregiver-infant interactions rather than being inherent
description: This framework holds that human infants are "ultrasocial" and open to learning through social exchange from birth, and that helping emerges amid affectively positive participation in games, chores, and cooperative activities. Interactions are bidirectional: infants actively elicit support and guidance, and caregivers adapt their scaffolding to infants' developing competence. The authors conclude that "infants are not inherently prosocial, but gradually develop prosocial motives through various types of bidirectional interactions in the first two years of life," positioning this against accounts that grant parents limited roles.
requirements: Caregivers who respond to infants' initiatives and support their participation in everyday activities, since without such participation and guidance infant helping would not emerge
constraints: The account focuses on interactions with adult caregivers, which the authors call central early on, though peer and sibling interactions also matter
target_learners: infants and toddlers in the first two years of life
target_learning_goals: emergence of helping, sharing, and comforting behavior and of prosocial motives
examples: Naturalistic research showing helping commonly begins when infants watch adults, whereupon adults encourage and assist them in joining the activity; parents do not insist on participation but support it when infants show interest.
key_sources: Dahl A., Brownell C. A. (2019). The Social Origins of Human Prosociality. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0963721419830386

article_title: Examining the Relations Between Self-Regulation and Achievement in Third-Grade Students
citation: Day, Stephanie L.; Connor, Carol M. (2017). Examining the relations between self-regulation and achievement in third grade students. Assessment for Effective Intervention, 42(2), 97-109. https://doi.org/10.1177/1534508416670367
title: Remembering Rules and Regulation Picture Task (RRRP)
description: The RRRP is a direct, individually administered self-regulation assessment in which children place colored blocks on objects in a park picture in a specified order, waiting for 'go' and, in the second half, switching blue for red blocks. The authors report that "The RRRP can be administered in approximately 7 minutes," that inter-rater reliability was .95 (Kappa), and that overall scale reliability was .97. It was designed for use beyond first grade, where the HTKS reaches ceiling.
requirements: A trained tester reads directions aloud and administers the 10 items one-on-one, taking about 7 minutes per child
constraints: The authors note there was some evidence the RRRP may be too easy for some children, and that it must be administered to a larger and more diverse sample and in other grades
target_learners: third grade students (designed to extend to children beyond first grade)
target_learning_goals: assessment of self-regulation skills (working memory, attentional flexibility, inhibitory control)
examples: In the study, the RRRP was administered to 282 third graders from 34 classrooms in fall and spring, with examiners recording correctness, waiting for 'go', and repetitions
key_sources: Day, Stephanie L.; Connor, Carol M. (2017). Examining the relations between self-regulation and achievement in third grade students. Assessment for Effective Intervention, 42(2), 97-109. https://doi.org/10.1177/1534508416670367

article_title: Examining the Relations Between Self-Regulation and Achievement in Third-Grade Students
citation: Day, Stephanie L.; Connor, Carol M. (2017). Examining the relations between self-regulation and achievement in third grade students. Assessment for Effective Intervention, 42(2), 97-109. https://doi.org/10.1177/1534508416670367
title: Self-regulation as coordinated executive functioning: working memory, attentional flexibility, and inhibitory control
description: The article defines self-regulation as an active process of controlling behavior, cognition, motivation, and emotions, supported by three executive functions. The authors state: "We define self-regulation as being supported by executive functioning, specifically working memory, inhibitory control, and attentional flexibility." The RRRP was designed to rely on the coordinated regulation of all three functions, rather than measuring them independently, on the conjecture that coordination matters most for school success.
requirements: Measures must capture the coordination of the three functions rather than each in isolation
constraints: The article notes prior measures typically assessed the three skills independently of one another
target_learners: elementary school children, particularly middle elementary grades
target_learning_goals: understanding how self-regulation supports academic achievement in reading and mathematics
examples: The RRRP requires children to remember block colors, objects, and order (working memory), wait for 'go' (inhibitory control), and switch colors in Part 2, coordinating all three
key_sources: Day, Stephanie L.; Connor, Carol M. (2017). Examining the relations between self-regulation and achievement in third grade students. Assessment for Effective Intervention, 42(2), 97-109. https://doi.org/10.1177/1534508416670367

article_title: Physical fitness and academic performance in primary school children with and without a social disadvantage
citation: de Greeff, J. W.; Hartman, E.; Mullender-Wijnsma, M. J.; Bosker, R. J.; Doolaard, S.; & Visscher, C. (2014). Physical fitness and academic performance in primary school children with and without a social disadvantage. Health Education Research, 29(5), 853-860. https://doi.org/10.1093/her/cyu043
title: Support cardiovascular fitness development in primary school children as a lever for mathematics and spelling performance
description: The article's findings support attending to children's cardiovascular fitness in primary education, because cardiovascular fitness showed positive associations with mathematics (beta = 0.23) and spelling (beta = 0.16), while muscular fitness showed none. The authors conclude there is "a specific link between cardiovascular fitness and mathematics, regardless of socioeconomic status". This suggests fitness-promoting activity in schools may accompany, though not causally demonstrate, academic benefit.
requirements: Cardiovascular fitness must be measured or developed specifically; muscular fitness alone does not show the association.
constraints: The study is cross-sectional and reports associations, not causal effects of fitness training on achievement.
The fitness-spelling association is moderated by social disadvantage status.
target_learners: primary school children (mean age 8.0), including socially disadvantaged children
target_learning_goals: mathematics performance
spelling performance
examples: The study measured cardiovascular and muscular fitness with fitness tests and related them to mathematics, spelling and reading scores of 544 children via multilevel analysis.
key_sources: de Greeff, J. W.; Hartman, E.; Mullender-Wijnsma, M. J.; Bosker, R. J.; Doolaard, S.; & Visscher, C. (2014). Physical fitness and academic performance in primary school children with and without a social disadvantage. Health Education Research, 29(5), 853-860. https://doi.org/10.1093/her/cyu043

article_title: Defective number module or impaired access? Numerical magnitude processing in first graders with mathematical difficulties
citation: Bert De Smedt, Camilla K. Gilmore. (2011). Defective number module or impaired access? Numerical magnitude processing in first graders with mathematical difficulties. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 108, 278–292. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2010.09.003
title: Access deficit hypothesis: mathematical difficulties arise from impaired access to numerical magnitude from symbols
description: The access deficit hypothesis (attributed to Rousselle & Noël, 2007) states that "mathematical difficulties originate from impairments in accessing numerical meaning, i.e. their quantity, from symbols rather than from difficulties in processing numerosity per se." It contrasts with the defective number module hypothesis, which posits a deficit in representing quantities itself. The article tests the two by comparing performance on symbolic versus non-symbolic tasks, and its first-grade findings — symbolic deficits with intact non-symbolic performance — favour the access deficit account.
requirements: Distinguishing the hypotheses requires comparing performance on numerical tasks with and without a symbolic processing requirement
constraints: Evidence remains behavioural; the authors note neural-level abnormalities in non-symbolic processing are not precluded
General factors such as intellectual ability and working memory were not directly administered
target_learners: first-grade children with mathematical difficulties (MLD and LA)
target_learning_goals: accessing numerical magnitude meaning from symbolic numbers
early number sense and arithmetic development
key_sources: Bert De Smedt, Camilla K. Gilmore. (2011). Defective number module or impaired access? Numerical magnitude processing in first graders with mathematical difficulties. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 108, 278–292. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2010.09.003

article_title: Defective number module or impaired access? Numerical magnitude processing in first graders with mathematical difficulties
citation: Bert De Smedt, Camilla K. Gilmore. (2011). Defective number module or impaired access? Numerical magnitude processing in first graders with mathematical difficulties. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 108, 278–292. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2010.09.003
title: Teaching should provide rich opportunities to connect symbols with the quantities they represent
description: Because children with mathematical difficulties are impaired in accessing numerical meaning from symbols, the authors recommend that teaching and intervention "provide plenty of opportunities where children learn to connect symbols and the quantities they represent in rich and meaningful ways." They cite Number Worlds (Griffin, 2004) as a program developed to teach this, and linear number board games (Ramani & Siegler, 2008) as providing multimodal cues linking symbols to quantities.
requirements: Interventions must target the mapping between symbols and quantities rather than numerosity representation per se
constraints: Generalization of board-game findings to children with mathematical difficulties needs further investigation, as the authors note
target_learners: first graders and kindergarteners, particularly children with mathematical difficulties or from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: connecting Arabic numerals to the quantities they represent
numerical magnitude understanding
early arithmetic development
examples: The article cites Ramani and Siegler (2008) showing linear board games enhanced numerical magnitude understanding in kindergarteners from low-income backgrounds, and Booth and Siegler (2008) showing accurate visual number-line representations improved first graders' math learning.
key_sources: Bert De Smedt, Camilla K. Gilmore. (2011). Defective number module or impaired access? Numerical magnitude processing in first graders with mathematical difficulties. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 108, 278–292. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2010.09.003

article_title: Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades
citation: Denton Carolyn A. (2012). Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades: Some Answers and Lingering Questions. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219412442155
title: Three-tier RTI model for primary-grade reading: Tier 1 core instruction, Tier 2 supplemental intervention, Tier 3 intensive intervention
description: The article describes RTI for early reading as a schoolwide, multitiered prevention framework in which "students are provided with evidence-based classroom reading instruction and supplemental intervention when it is needed, and decisions related to intervention are based on student assessment data." Tier 1 is evidence-based core classroom instruction with universal screening; Tier 2 is supplemental intervention for at-risk students; Tier 3 is more intensive intervention for inadequate responders. Progress is monitored with repeated curriculum-based measures, and teacher professional development supports fidelity.
requirements: Student progress monitoring data, typically repeated curriculum-based measures, to inform tier placement decisions
Teacher professional development to ensure high-quality, faithfully delivered instruction at all tiers
constraints: The article focuses on a three-tiered model, noting some RTI systems use four or more tiers
target_learners: Primary-grade students at risk for reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Early reading skills: phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension
key_sources: Denton Carolyn A. (2012). Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades: Some Answers and Lingering Questions. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219412442155

article_title: Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades
citation: Denton Carolyn A. (2012). Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades: Some Answers and Lingering Questions. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219412442155
title: Design early reading intervention for struggling readers to be explicit, targeted, practice-rich, and actively engaging
description: Drawing on research reviews and meta-analyses, the article states that students with reading difficulties benefit from instruction that is purposeful, targeted at important objectives, and progresses from easier to more challenging skills, with mastery monitored so reteaching can occur. "Students with reading difficulties also benefit from (a) explicit instruction in which skills are clearly modeled and key concepts are directly taught," extended guided and independent practice with feedback including engaged reading of connected text, and formats promoting active student involvement and many opportunities to respond.
requirements: Careful monitoring of mastery of key skills and strategies so reteaching can be provided when needed
target_learners: Primary-grade students with reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Foundational reading skills and comprehension
examples: The article cites Mathes et al. (2005), whose two first-grade small-group interventions, one scripted and one flexible, both embodied these characteristics and outperformed typical practice
key_sources: Denton Carolyn A. (2012). Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades: Some Answers and Lingering Questions. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219412442155

article_title: Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades
citation: Denton Carolyn A. (2012). Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades: Some Answers and Lingering Questions. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219412442155
title: Provide intensive Tier 3 intervention promptly to students with the most severe reading difficulties rather than delaying through less intensive tiers
description: The article argues, citing Vaughn, Denton, and Fletcher (2010), that students in Grade 2 and higher performing substantially below grade level may need immediate Tier 3 intensive intervention rather than progressing through Tiers 1 and 2. It is "supported by research evidence that students with the lowest preintervention performance levels require more intensive interventions to close the gap with typically developing students," and delaying intensive intervention may substantially decrease the likelihood that seriously impaired readers learn to read adequately.
requirements: Well-qualified teachers for Tier 3, as recommended by Gersten et al. (2008), given students' severe deficits in phonological processing, processing speed, and verbal working memory
constraints: The article notes Tier 3 group size (1:1 vs. very small groups) may best be decided individually by RTI problem-solving teams
target_learners: Students with severe, persistent reading difficulties in Grade 2 and higher
target_learning_goals: Word reading, decoding, and reading fluency remediation
examples: Torgesen et al. (2001) delivered 1:1 intervention for about 2 hours per day for 8 weeks to Grade 3–5 students with severe reading problems, producing large standard score gains in word reading and comprehension maintained 2 years later, with weaker fluency outcomes
key_sources: Denton Carolyn A. (2012). Response to Intervention for Reading Difficulties in the Primary Grades: Some Answers and Lingering Questions. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219412442155

article_title: Interventions Shown to Aid Executive Function Development in Children 4 to 12 Years Old
citation: Diamond Adele, Lee Kathleen. (2011). Interventions shown to Aid Executive Function Development in Children 4–12 Years Old. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1204529
title: Improve EFs by continually challenging them within activities that also address emotional, social, and physical development rather than focusing narrowly on EFs alone
description: The review distills cross-program lessons: EFs must be continually challenged to see improvements, since groups assigned the same program without difficulty increasing show no EF gains. It concludes the most effective way to improve EFs and academic achievement is probably not to focus narrowly on EFs alone but to also address emotional, social, and physical development, as the four EF-enhancing curricula do.
requirements: Repeated practice with progressively increasing difficulty; even the best activity done rarely produces little benefit
constraints: Computer training tends to be short-duration as interest wanes and highest game levels are reached; after-school options cost money and are not possible for all families
target_learners: children 4–12 years old
target_learning_goals: executive functions: cognitive flexibility, inhibition, working memory
examples: Control groups playing the same training games without difficulty increasing did not show the same gains; the four curricula-based programs reduce classroom stress, cultivate joy and pride, and foster social bonding
key_sources: Diamond Adele, Lee Kathleen. (2011). Interventions shown to Aid Executive Function Development in Children 4–12 Years Old. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1204529

article_title: Interventions Shown to Aid Executive Function Development in Children 4 to 12 Years Old
citation: Diamond Adele, Lee Kathleen. (2011). Interventions shown to Aid Executive Function Development in Children 4–12 Years Old. Science. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1204529
title: Children with initially poorest EFs gain the most from EF interventions, making early EF training a candidate for reducing achievement gaps
description: The review states that lower-income, lower working-memory span, and ADHD children, and in one study boys, generally show the most EF improvement from any program. Because EFs predict later academic performance, early EF training is an excellent candidate for leveling the playing field and reducing the achievement gap between more- and less-advantaged children.
requirements: Programs must be accessible early enough to get children on a positive trajectory; public school curricula hold the greatest promise for accessibility to all
constraints: Since computer training and after-school activities cost money, they are not possible for all families
target_learners: children 4–12 years old, especially lower-income children and those with initially poor EFs
target_learning_goals: executive functions supporting school readiness and academic achievement
examples: Children with initially poor EFs after mindfulness training improved overall and in shifting and monitoring, bringing their scores up to average

article_title: Activities and Programs That Improve Children’s Executive Functions
citation: Diamond Adele. (2012). Activities and Programs That Improve Children's Executive Functions. Current Directions in Psychological Science. https://doi.org/10.1177/0963721412453722
title: Shared design features of school curricula shown to improve children's executive functions
description: The review identifies ten features shared by the two curricula empirically shown to improve children's EFs, Montessori and Tools of the Mind, and notes many also characterize PATHS and CSRP. The curricula "help children exercise their EFs and constantly challenge them to do so at higher levels" while also reducing classroom stress, rarely embarrassing a child, cultivating joy and self-confidence, using hands-on learning, accommodating different rates of progress, emphasizing character development and oral language, engaging children in teaching one another, and fostering social skills and bonding.
requirements: The curriculum must embed EF practice throughout the day in all activities rather than in a single isolated module, as the review says curricula shown to improve EFs do.
constraints: The review notes both Tools of the Mind and CSRP are meant to be used only with children aged 3 to 6, and no program shown to improve EFs has reported benefits in children older than 9 years.
target_learners: Preschool and early-elementary children (ages 3 to 6 for Tools of the Mind and CSRP)
target_learning_goals: Executive functions: inhibitory control, working memory, cognitive flexibility, and school readiness
examples: Disadvantaged preschool children randomly assigned to a CSRP Head Start class showed better EFs than controls at year end and continued to outperform controls in math and reading for the next 3 years, with academic gains mediated almost entirely through improved EFs (Li-Grining et al., 2011).

article_title: Child and environmental risk factors predicting readiness for learning in children at high risk of dyslexia
citation: Dilnot, J., Hamilton, L., Maughan, B. and Snowling, M. (2017). Child and Environmental Risk Factors Predicting Readiness for Learning in Children at High-Risk of Dyslexia. Development & Psychopathology, 29(1). http://dx.doi.org/10.1017/S0954579416000134
title: Family-risk of dyslexia as gene–environment interplay rather than a proxy for genetic risk
description: The article proposes that family-risk of dyslexia is "best conceptualized, not purely as a proxy for genetic risk, but as reflecting gene–environment interplay". Drawing on passive, evocative and active rGE mechanisms, it argues that parental genotype correlates with both the child's genetic risk and the environment parents provide, so familial effects on readiness operate through environmental channels such as a less rich home literacy environment. The study's finding that family-risk adds no variance once contextual risks are controlled supports this reframing.
requirements: A design that measures environmental and child-level risks alongside family-risk status so their unique contributions can be separated
constraints: The current design does not allow us to differentiate active/evocative from passive effects
It is unclear whether parental literacy should itself be considered an index of genetic risk rather than a measure of environmental variability
target_learners: preschool children at family-risk of dyslexia
children with preschool language difficulties
target_learning_goals: reading readiness at school entry
attention and behaviour at school entry
examples: The study assessed family-risk via parental self-report on the Adult Reading Questionnaire, objective literacy testing, discrepancy criteria, or sibling diagnosis

article_title: “My Brain Can Stop”: An ERP Study of Longitudinal Prediction of Inhibitory Control in Adolescence
citation: Einziger Tzlil, Ben-Shachar Mattan S., Devor Tali, Shmueli Michael, Auerbach Judith G., Berger Andrea. (2021). "My Brain Can Stop": An ERP Study of Longitudinal Prediction of Inhibitory Control in Adolescence. Brain Sciences, 11(1), 100. https://doi.org/10.3390/brainsci11010100
title: Detect children at familial and temperamental risk for inhibitory control deficits early so intervention programs can be implemented before negative outcomes accumulate
description: The article argues that because early familial (paternal inattention) and temperamental (low effortful control, especially attentional focusing) risk factors directly predict later dysfunction in the neural mechanism of inhibitory control, early identification of at-risk children is important. The authors state that "early detection of children at risk for inhibitory control deficits could contribute to early intervention programs designed to mitigate future negative outcomes from such a deficit." The principle rests on the study's longitudinal prediction findings rather than on a tested intervention.
requirements: Longitudinal or early-life assessment of familial ADHD symptoms (e.g., paternal inattention in infancy) and child temperament (effortful control at 36 months) to identify at-risk children before symptoms manifest.
constraints: The study tested prediction, not intervention: the design was not suitable to determine causal direction, and the sample was limited to males with a modest sample size and low rates of clinical-range symptom scores.
target_learners: adolescent boys at varying levels of familial risk for ADHD
target_learning_goals: self-regulation and inhibitory control
examples: The prospective longitudinal study measured paternal inattention at 2-6 months and child effortful control at 36 months, then showed these precursors directly predicted adolescent N2 amplitude at 17 years.
key_sources: Einziger Tzlil, Ben-Shachar Mattan S., Devor Tali, Shmueli Michael, Auerbach Judith G., Berger Andrea. (2021). "My Brain Can Stop": An ERP Study of Longitudinal Prediction of Inhibitory Control in Adolescence. Brain Sciences, 11(1), 100. https://doi.org/10.3390/brainsci11010100

article_title: Supporting Student Self-Regulated Learning in Problem- and Project-Based Learning
citation: Mary C. English, Anastasia Kitsantas. (2013). Supporting Self-Regulated Learning in Problem- and Project-Based Learning. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-based Learning. https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1339
title: A theoretical model of the relationship between PBL and self-regulated learning
description: The article presents a theoretical model linking problem- and project-based learning environments to students' self-regulated learning. The model organizes how PBL contexts and teaching practices relate to the SRL processes students must deploy — "setting goals, monitoring, reflecting, and sustaining their motivation" — across the phases of a PBL project. It serves as the framework from which the paper derives its research-driven guidelines for educators on promoting student responsibility for learning.
requirements: The model presupposes PBL settings in which students carry responsibility for the learning process from project start to end
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students engaged in problem- or project-based learning
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills such as goal setting, monitoring, reflection, and motivation maintenance
examples: The paper uses the model to organize research-driven guidelines on how to promote student responsibility for learning in PBL.
key_sources: Mary C. English, Anastasia Kitsantas. (2013). Supporting Self-Regulated Learning in Problem- and Project-Based Learning. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-based Learning. https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1339

article_title: Supporting Student Self-Regulated Learning in Problem- and Project-Based Learning
citation: Mary C. English, Anastasia Kitsantas. (2013). Supporting Self-Regulated Learning in Problem- and Project-Based Learning. Interdisciplinary Journal of Problem-based Learning. https://doi.org/10.7771/1541-5015.1339
title: Design PBL learning environments and teaching practices with intention to support students' self-regulated learning
description: Because SRL processes do not arise spontaneously for many students, the article argues that PBL environments and teaching practices "must be designed with intention to support students' self-regulated learning (SRL)." The principle directs educators to plan environment features and teaching moves deliberately around SRL, rather than assuming responsibility for learning will emerge on its own from the PBL format.
requirements: Educators must deliberately plan learning environment features and teaching practices rather than relying on the PBL format alone
target_learners: students in problem- or project-based learning settings
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning and student responsibility for learning
examples: The paper describes specific learning environment features and teaching practices shown to foster student responsibility for learning in each phase of PBL.

article_title: Socioeconomic status and the brain: prospects for neuroscience-informed policy
citation: Martha J. Farah. (2017). Socioeconomic status and the brain: prospects for neuroscience-informed policy. https://www.upenn.edu
title: Deprivation and threat as distinct dimensions of early adversity with partly different neural mechanisms
description: The article adopts the distinction, attributed to Sheridan and McLaughlin, that different life adversities affect brain development through at least partly different mechanisms. "Sheridan and McLaughlin have distinguished between the impacts of deprivation and threat, which presumably operate in different proportions in poverty and maltreatment, on different neural correlates." Socioeconomic disadvantage is multifactorial and distinct from abuse and neglect, so findings from broader adversity literatures do not automatically transfer to poverty. This framework bounds the scope of SES-neuroscience findings.
requirements: Researchers must treat poverty as a distinct risk category rather than assuming generalization from cumulative-stress or adverse-childhood-experiences literatures
constraints: The article states that findings on adverse childhood experiences or cumulative stress "should not be assumed to generalize to poverty or low SES"
target_learners: children from low socioeconomic status backgrounds
target_learning_goals: understanding how socioeconomic adversity relates to brain development and cognitive development
examples: The article cites a study finding childhood SES and childhood maltreatment have distinct associations with brain structure
key_sources: Martha J. Farah. (2017). Socioeconomic status and the brain: prospects for neuroscience-informed policy. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41583-018-0023-2

article_title: Socioeconomic status and the brain: prospects for neuroscience-informed policy
citation: Martha J. Farah. (2017). Socioeconomic status and the brain: prospects for neuroscience-informed policy. https://www.upenn.edu
title: Avoid critical-period fatalism: contemporary neuroscience does not support sharply defined critical periods, and adult plasticity remains substantial
description: The article argues that emphasis on early sensitive periods in policy discourse can fuel defeatism about helping older children, teens and adults. It responds that "contemporary neuroscience does not support sharply defined critical periods for psychological development, and has only begun to understand age-related changes in plasticity", and that a key recent insight is the plasticity remaining in the adult brain. Earlier intervention may generally be more effective, but expected effectiveness at different ages should inform, not eliminate, resource allocation to older needy populations.
requirements: Policy framing that pairs early-childhood emphasis with continued recognition of later plasticity
constraints: The article acknowledges that with fixed resources, prioritizing earlier interventions may leave older children and adults with less help, and that economists reach a similar earlier-is-better conclusion
target_learners: older children, teens and adults from low socioeconomic status backgrounds
target_learning_goals: maintaining developmental and educational support across the lifespan
examples: The article quotes a critic warning that alarm about irrevocably damaged young brains "can all too easily fuel defeatism" and weaken the case for subsequent help
key_sources: Martha J. Farah. (2017). Socioeconomic status and the brain: prospects for neuroscience-informed policy. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41583-018-0023-2

article_title: Five-Year-Old Children’s Working Memory Can Be Improved When Children Act On A Transparent Goal Cue
citation: Fitamen, C., Blaye, A. & Camos, V. (2019). Five-year-old children's working memory can be improved when children act on a transparent goal cue. Scientific Reports 9:15342. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-51869-4
title: Goal maintenance account of preschoolers' poor working memory performance
description: The article proposes that preschoolers' poor working memory performance may partly reflect goal neglect: when the representation of the task goal (maintaining items for recall) is not sufficiently active amid competing goals, recall suffers. Working memory tasks involve switching between encoding, concurrent-task, maintenance and recall goals, so "memory performance can, at least in part, depend on the efficiency of goals maintenance". Transparent cues and goal-oriented motor activity are proposed as supports for keeping the goal active during the retention interval.
requirements: The task must involve competing goals between encoding, a concurrent activity, and recall, so that goal maintenance is required
constraints: The authors note the alternative hypothesis that finger tracking is too demanding for younger children must be eliminated before final conclusions about the strategy-based interpretation
target_learners: preschool children (4- and 5-year-olds)
target_learning_goals: maintaining task-relevant information in working memory across a retention interval
examples: The study operationalized goal support as a school-bag cue that carried the memory items to the recall point, tracked visually or with a finger during the retention interval
key_sources: Fitamen, C., Blaye, A. & Camos, V. (2019). Five-year-old children's working memory can be improved when children act on a transparent goal cue. Scientific Reports 9:15342. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-51869-4

article_title: Five-Year-Old Children’s Working Memory Can Be Improved When Children Act On A Transparent Goal Cue
citation: Fitamen, C., Blaye, A. & Camos, V. (2019). Five-year-old children's working memory can be improved when children act on a transparent goal cue. Scientific Reports 9:15342. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-51869-4
title: Embed goal-oriented motor activity on a transparent goal cue to scaffold young children's memory for instructions
description: The article recommends that educational settings integrate motor, goal-oriented activity to scaffold memory in young children. A transparent goal cue improves working memory performance only when children act on it continuously — "proposing a goal-oriented gesture on the cue is crucial to boost recall performance". The cue should make the task goal transparent (e.g., a school bag carrying the to-be-recalled items to the recall point) and remain present during the full retention interval.
requirements: A transparent goal cue that remains present during the full retention interval
A motor activity oriented toward the goal that children perform continuously on the cue
constraints: The benefit was shown in 5-year-olds but not in 4-year-olds, for whom the supplementary instructions and fine motor tracking demands may have overloaded attention
target_learners: preschool children, particularly 5-year-olds
target_learning_goals: remembering instructions or items across a delay
maintaining the task goal during a retention interval
examples: In the experiment, 5-year-olds finger-tracked a school-bag cue that transported the memory items to the recall point during a 7,100 ms retention interval, improving recall relative to the abstract cue
key_sources: Fitamen, C., Blaye, A. & Camos, V. (2019). Five-year-old children's working memory can be improved when children act on a transparent goal cue. Scientific Reports 9:15342. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-51869-4

article_title: Five-Year-Old Children’s Working Memory Can Be Improved When Children Act On A Transparent Goal Cue
citation: Fitamen, C., Blaye, A. & Camos, V. (2019). Five-year-old children's working memory can be improved when children act on a transparent goal cue. Scientific Reports 9:15342. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-51869-4
title: Brown-Peterson working memory task with animated goal cue tracking for preschoolers
description: A computerized Brown-Peterson task in which 4- and 5-year-olds memorized series of one to three colored drawings of animals and objects presented visually with their auditory name, then recalled them after a retention interval during which an animated shape moved across the screen. Children tracked the moving shape — an abstract form, an abstract black rectangle cue, or a transparent school-bag cue — either visually or with a finger. Performance was measured by the number of words correctly recalled, with a control condition as baseline for the between-subjects comparison.
requirements: E-Prime 2.0.10 on laptops in a quiet room; two 15-minute sessions with a pause for 4-year-olds; training trials before each session; item names recorded by a male voice and drawings selected to exceed 80% correct denomination at 4 years of age
constraints: Retention intervals differed between age groups (7,800 ms for 4-year-olds, 7,100 ms for 5-year-olds), so the design does not allow direct age comparisons of working memory capacity
target_learners: 4- and 5-year-old preschoolers
target_learning_goals: verbal working memory for picture-item series under a concurrent tracking task
examples: Each child completed a control condition and one of four experimental conditions, with condition order counterbalanced and two experimenters blind to the aim of the experiment

article_title: The development of inhibitory control in adolescence and prospective relations with delinquency
citation: Fosco, W. D., Hawk, L. W. Jr., Colder, C. R., Meisel, S. N., & Lengua, L. J. (2019). The development of inhibitory control in adolescence and prospective relations with delinquency. Journal of Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2019.08.008
title: Nigg's framework distinguishing inhibitory control from self-regulation and impulsivity
description: The article adopts Nigg's (2017) framework in which self-regulation is "a broad, domain-general ability to flexibly and adaptively modulate one's own behavior and internal states," while inhibitory control (response inhibition) involves preventing or stopping an ongoing response and is a building block for more complex cognitive functions. Impulsivity differs in that it "entails disinhibition in the context of valenced stimuli" and prioritizes immediate over delayed consequences, whereas inhibitory control does not consider motivational context. The study uses this framework to justify measuring inhibitory control with both a task and a questionnaire.
requirements: Assessment tools must be selected to match the construct as defined: tasks capture inhibition in a cold cognitive context, questionnaires capture inhibition across motivated everyday contexts
constraints: Questionnaire measures of inhibitory control overlap somewhat with impulsivity measures because items reflect inhibition in contexts with motivation to respond
target_learners: adolescents ages 11–15
target_learning_goals: self-regulation and inhibitory control development
examples: The study operationalized the framework with the Stop Signal Task for task-based inhibitory control and the EATQ-R inhibitory control subscale for questionnaire-based inhibitory control
key_sources: Fosco, W. D., Hawk, L. W. Jr., Colder, C. R., Meisel, S. N., & Lengua, L. J. (2019). The development of inhibitory control in adolescence and prospective relations with delinquency. Journal of Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2019.08.008

article_title: Contribution of sustained attention abilities to real-world academic skills in children
citation: Gallen, C. L., Schaerlaeken, S., Younger, J. W., Project iLEAD Consortium, Anguera, J. A., & Gazzaley, A. (2023). Contribution of sustained attention abilities to real-world academic skills in children. Scientific Reports 13, 2673. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-29427-w
title: ACE-C: a group-administered digital executive function assessment battery for classrooms
description: The Adaptive Cognitive Evaluation Classroom (ACE-C) is a digital assessment battery of nine tasks measuring executive functions such as attention, working memory, and multitasking, administered on iPads to groups of students in school settings. Tasks were "developed from cognitive assessments commonly used in lab-based settings and modified to include adaptive algorithms, motivational trial-by-trial and end-of-task feedback, and a user-friendly interface." Psychometric staircase adaptive algorithms let students perform the same tasks across time points without floor or ceiling effects. This study used its continuous performance task (CPT), adapted from the TOVA, to derive a sustained attention component score.
requirements: Administered on iPads in group school sessions with trained researcher facilitators present; a basic response time task is included at the start of each session for processing-speed correction
constraints: The authors note tablet-based direct assessments are limited in assessing complex behaviors integrating interpersonal dynamics or social and emotional factors
target_learners: children in middle childhood, grades 4-8
target_learning_goals: measurement of sustained attention and other executive functions in naturalistic school contexts
examples: In this study, 725 students completed the ACE-C CPT in group sessions of 7 to 83 students lasting approximately 50 minutes in classrooms, libraries, cafeterias, and gymnasiums
key_sources: Gallen, C. L., Schaerlaeken, S., Younger, J. W., Project iLEAD Consortium, Anguera, J. A., & Gazzaley, A. (2023). Contribution of sustained attention abilities to real-world academic skills in children. Scientific Reports 13, 2673. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-023-29427-w

article_title: The longitudinal relationship between early inhibitory control skills and emergent literacy in preschool children
citation: Gandolfi, E., Traverso, L., Zanobini, M., Usai, M. C., & Viterbori, P. (2021). The longitudinal relationship between early inhibitory control skills and emergent literacy in preschool children. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-021-10131-y
title: Two-component organization of inhibitory control in early childhood: response inhibition and interference suppression
description: The article adopts a conceptualization of inhibitory control as "a set of sub-functions rather than a unique individual ability, already in early preschool years", distinguishing two components that emerge by approximately three years of age. Response inhibition is "the ability to suppress a dominant but inappropriate response in order to display a weaker but more adequate one", assessed with the Circle Drawing task. Interference suppression "develops later than response inhibition and involves the ability to suppress interfering information and to select the piece of information one has to respond to", assessed with the Fish flanker task. The study uses this distinction to test which component longitudinally supports emergent literacy.
requirements: Tasks must tap the two components distinctly; the authors chose two tasks "to maximize the difference between response inhibition and interference suppression processes, taking the suitability of the task for toddlers into account".
constraints: The authors note "this type of organization is not universally accepted (Joyce et al., 2016)" and that research on the latent organization of inhibitory control in childhood has provided mixed results.
target_learners: typically developing monolingual toddlers aged 28–36 months
preschool children aged 4–6 years
target_learning_goals: emergent literacy precursors: phonological awareness and early orthographic knowledge
examples: Children moved puppets along a circle as slowly as possible (Circle Drawing) and pointed to the direction of a central target fish flanked by interfering fishes (Fish task) in a 20-min day-care session.
key_sources: Gandolfi, E., Traverso, L., Zanobini, M., Usai, M. C., & Viterbori, P. (2021). The longitudinal relationship between early inhibitory control skills and emergent literacy in preschool children. Reading and Writing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-021-10131-y

article_title: Fact Retrieval Deficits in Low Achieving Children and Children With Mathematical Learning Disability
citation: Geary, D. C., Hoard, M. K., & Bailey, D. H. (2012). Fact Retrieval Deficits in Low Achieving Children and Children with Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 45(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219410392046
title: Distinct-deficits account: retrieval, procedural, and number-processing deficits arise from partly separable mechanisms rather than one fundamental magnitude deficit
description: The article frames competing accounts of mathematical learning disability: Butterworth's hypothesis that a fundamental deficit in representing and processing numerical magnitude underlies most deficits, versus the possibility of several distinct deficits or delays. The study tests this by asking whether retrieval, procedural, number sets, and number line deficits co-occur, predicting that "If the mechanisms contributing to the procedural, number processing, and retrieval deficits and delays are distinct, then some children should show one or two of these deficits but not all of them." The longitudinal dissociation findings support the distinct-deficits view.
requirements: Longitudinal assessment of multiple mathematical cognition tasks in the same children to test whether deficits co-occur or dissociate
constraints: Conclusions drawn from children in one school district followed from kindergarten to fourth grade
target_learners: elementary school children with mathematical learning difficulties
children with MLD
low achieving children
target_learning_goals: arithmetic fact retrieval
arithmetic procedural competence
numerical magnitude processing
examples: The study separated LA children into mild and severe fact retrieval subgroups and compared their trajectories on retrieval, procedural, number sets, and number line measures
