article_title: Fact Retrieval Deficits in Low Achieving Children and Children With Mathematical Learning Disability
citation: Geary, D. C., Hoard, M. K., & Bailey, D. H. (2012). Fact Retrieval Deficits in Low Achieving Children and Children with Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 45(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219410392046
title: Number Sets Test d-prime measure of fluent processing of small numerosities and Arabic numerals
description: The Number Sets Test, developed by Geary et al. (2007), assesses the speed and accuracy with which children match combinations of object sets and Arabic numerals to target sums of 5 or 9 within time limits (60 s and 90 s per page). A receiver operating characteristic analysis yields a d-prime sensitivity score controlling for response bias. The article reports that "The d-prime scores, but not response bias scores, are correlated with mathematics but not reading achievement, above and beyond the influence of IQ, working memory, and prior grade mathematics and reading achievement scores," and that first-grade d-prime predicted third-grade MLD status better than first-grade mathematics achievement scores.
requirements: Administration with printed time limits (60 sec per page for target 5; 90 sec for target 9) to avoid ceiling effects and assess fluency
ROC analysis to derive the d-prime sensitivity score controlling for response bias
constraints: Items involve magnitudes within and just beyond the subitizing range (< 10)
target_learners: elementary school children in first through fourth grade
target_learning_goals: fluent processing and manipulation of small exact numerosities and Arabic numerals
examples: In the current study the d-prime intercept was one of four mathematical cognition variables entered into the covariate-adjusted group comparison

article_title: Non-symbolic arithmetic abilities and mathematics achievement in the first year of formal schooling
citation: Gilmore Camilla K., McCarthy Shannon E., Spelke Elizabeth S. (2010). Non-symbolic arithmetic abilities and achievement in the first year of formal schooling in mathematics. Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2010.02.002
title: Two-source account of symbolic mathematics mastery: prior non-symbolic numerical abilities plus acquired symbol mastery
description: The article proposes that mastery of symbolic mathematics has two sources: non-symbolic numerical abilities that are present prior to schooling in arithmetic and exist across a broad economic spectrum, and symbol mastery that is acquired during childhood and is accelerated for advantaged children. The account explains why non-symbolic abilities predict school mathematics while socioeconomic gaps persist in achievement but not in non-symbolic tasks. It rests on the finding that "children in the wealthier community outperformed the less advantaged children on the symbolic arithmetic task" in prior work, while non-symbolic abilities were similar across communities.
requirements: Non-symbolic numerical abilities available to children before formal arithmetic instruction
Acquisition of number words and Arabic symbols during childhood
constraints: The article states there is mixed evidence concerning the relationship between non-symbolic numerical abilities and number word mastery, and further research with younger children is needed to distinguish causal directions
target_learners: Kindergarten children (5-6 years old) from diverse socioeconomic backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Early symbolic number and arithmetic learning
examples: Experiment 1 and 2 compared low/middle-SES and high-SES children on non-symbolic addition and mathematics achievement tests

article_title: The role of cognitive inhibition in different components of arithmetic
citation: Camilla Gilmore, Sarah Keeble, Sophie Richardson, Lucy Cragg. (2015). The role of cognitive inhibition in different components of arithmetic. ZDM Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-014-0659-y
title: Dot comparison congruency-effect measure of numerical inhibition
description: A novel technique for assessing inhibition in a numerical context without Arabic digits: participants compare two dot arrays and select the more numerous set while ignoring dot size and array area. The article states that "incongruent trials, but not congruent trials carry a heavy inhibition load", so the difference in performance between congruent and incongruent trials provides a measure of inhibition skill. The authors showed this measure relates to a standard inhibition task and to mathematics achievement, predicting performance even after accounting for non-numerical inhibition.
requirements: Participants must ignore the visual characteristics (dot size, density, area) of the arrays and respond based on number of dots only
constraints: The measure indexes interference control, not response inhibition; the article notes further research with a variety of inhibition tasks is required
target_learners: 11- to 12-year-olds
13- to 14-year-olds
young adults
target_learning_goals: arithmetic achievement
inhibitory control in numerical contexts
examples: In the study, participants completed 6 practice trials and 80 experimental dot comparison trials, with dot numbers ranging from 5 to 28 and ratios from 0.5 to 0.8

article_title: The role of cognitive inhibition in different components of arithmetic
citation: Camilla Gilmore, Sarah Keeble, Sophie Richardson, Lucy Cragg. (2015). The role of cognitive inhibition in different components of arithmetic. ZDM Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-014-0659-y
title: Three-component taxonomy of arithmetic knowledge: factual, procedural and conceptual
description: The article organizes mathematics into components that cut across domains: "Factual knowledge comprises memorized number facts", procedural skill concerns "the accurate and efficient execution of operations" and can be thought of as 'knowing how', and conceptual understanding is "knowledge of the principles and relationships that underlie mathematics" or 'knowing why'. These components are not hierarchically ordered, individuals differ in their profiles across them, and they rely on differential sets of skills. The study used this taxonomy to pinpoint how inhibition relates to specific components rather than general tests.
requirements: Assessment instruments must separately capture each component rather than relying on general standardized mathematics tests
constraints: The article notes relationships among the components are complex and not hierarchically ordered

adults
target_learning_goals: arithmetic factual knowledge
procedural skill
conceptual understanding
examples: The study administered a factual knowledge task (retrieval within 3 s), a procedural skills task (median RT for correct solutions) and a conceptual knowledge task (identifying relationships between problem pairs)

article_title: Reconstructing constructivism: Causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms, and the theory theory.
citation: Gopnik, A., & Wellman, H. M. (2012). Reconstructing constructivism: Causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory. Psychological Bulletin, 138(6), 1085-1108. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0028044
title: Rational constructivism: the theory theory reconstructed on probabilistic Bayesian learning
description: The article proposes a new version of the 'theory theory' in which children's intuitive theories are structured causal representations and theory change is Bayesian inference over hypotheses. It argues this yields 'a constructivist but rigorous and detailed approach to cognitive development', explaining learning of both specific causal hypotheses and abstract framework theories, and resolving the tension between nativist structure and empiricist learning.
requirements: A formal framework specifying structured hypotheses and their probabilistic relations to evidence, so that both conceptual structure and learning can be represented
constraints: The approach is presented as an ideal rational model of learning; the article notes the drawback of 'the vast space of possible hypotheses and possible evidence', raising search problems for which it offers only promising approaches
target_learners: children from infancy through middle childhood
target_learning_goals: construction and revision of intuitive theories of the physical, psychological, biological and social world
examples: The article interweaves reviews of causal statistical learning, informal experimentation through play, imitation and informal pedagogy, and progressive theory-of-mind change as empirical support for this framework
key_sources: Gopnik, A., & Wellman, H. M. (2012). Reconstructing constructivism: Causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory. Psychological Bulletin, 138(6), 1085-1108. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0028044

article_title: Reconstructing constructivism: Causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms, and the theory theory.
citation: Gopnik, A., & Wellman, H. M. (2012). Reconstructing constructivism: Causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory. Psychological Bulletin, 138(6), 1085-1108. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0028044
title: Causal Bayes nets with an interventionist account of causation as a model of intuitive theories
description: Causal Bayes nets represent causal hypotheses as directed graphs whose variables and edges generate patterns of evidence, supporting prediction, intervention and counterfactual inference. The article pairs them with Woodward's interventionist account: 'if there is a direct causal relation between A and B, then, other things equal, intervening to change the probability of A will change the probability of B'. Interventions alter the graph ('graph surgery'), letting learners infer structure from observations and from the outcomes of experiments.
requirements: Assumptions about the parameterization of the graph (e.g., whether causes independently raise effect probability, whether evidence is a random sample) to constrain inferences
constraints: The article notes many hypotheses may be compatible with any evidence pattern (underdetermination), so Bayesian methods rank hypotheses by probability rather than deciding truth outright
target_learners: children and adults learning causal structure
target_learning_goals: causal inference, prediction, intervention planning and counterfactual reasoning
examples: The wine-insomnia example shows how distinguishing a causal chain from a common-cause graph predicts different consequences of intervening on drinking versus partying
key_sources: Gopnik, A., & Wellman, H. M. (2012). Reconstructing constructivism: Causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory. Psychological Bulletin, 138(6), 1085-1108. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0028044

article_title: Reconstructing constructivism: Causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms, and the theory theory.
citation: Gopnik, A., & Wellman, H. M. (2012). Reconstructing constructivism: Causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory. Psychological Bulletin, 138(6), 1085-1108. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0028044
title: Hierarchical causal models representing both specific theories and framework theories
description: The article argues that recently developed hierarchical causal models can capture the theory theory's claim that specific causal theories are embedded in more abstract framework theories. As it states, 'These hierarchical models can characterize broader framework theories along with more specific causal relationships as well as characterize the relations between theories at different levels of abstraction', allowing learning at both local and abstract levels within one Bayesian formalism.
requirements: Probabilistic model formalism that specifies structure and likelihoods at multiple levels of abstraction simultaneously
constraints: Presented as a recent development with promised future work; the article suggests further collaborative projects between developmental and computational cognitive scientists rather than reporting completed tests of hierarchy learning
target_learners: children from infancy through school age
target_learning_goals: learning both specific causal relations and abstract framework theories governing a domain
examples: The article links hierarchy learning to its three highlighted dynamics of theory change: statistical learning, informal experimentation, and variability across intermediate conceptions
key_sources: Gopnik, A., & Wellman, H. M. (2012). Reconstructing constructivism: Causal models, Bayesian learning mechanisms and the theory theory. Psychological Bulletin, 138(6), 1085-1108. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0028044

article_title: Some types of parent number talk count more than others: relations between parents’ input and children’s cardinal-number knowledge
citation: Gunderson Elizabeth A., Levine Susan C. (2011). Some types of parent number talk count more than others: Relations between parents' input and children's cardinal-number knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2011.01050.x
title: Large-number talk as a trigger for inducing the cardinal principle via representational discrepancy
description: The article proposes that children learn cardinal meanings of 1–3 by mapping number words onto the small-exact-number system, but cannot map large number words (4–10) onto either nonverbal system before learning the cardinal principle. Hearing large-number talk creates a "representational discrepancy" that motivates children to figure out what larger number words mean, and counting-and-labeling the same large set lets children notice that the cardinal label matches the last word of the count list. This explains why large-set present-object talk, though rare, is the strongest predictor of cardinal-number knowledge.
requirements: Exposure to number talk about sets of size 4 or greater, ideally with counting and labeling of the same present set
constraints: The account is stated as a hypothesis; the study is correlational and the authors call for experimental training studies to test it causally
target_learners: children aged roughly 14–46 months, prior to or during acquisition of the cardinal principle
target_learning_goals: learning the exact cardinal meanings of number words and the cardinal principle
examples: The article's example of count-plus-label talk about a large set: parents saying "there are four sticks, one, two, three, four" while the child can see the set
key_sources: Gunderson Elizabeth A., Levine Susan C. (2011). Some types of parent number talk count more than others: Relations between parents' input and children's cardinal-number knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2011.01050.x

article_title: Some types of parent number talk count more than others: relations between parents’ input and children’s cardinal-number knowledge
citation: Gunderson Elizabeth A., Levine Susan C. (2011). Some types of parent number talk count more than others: Relations between parents' input and children's cardinal-number knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2011.01050.x
title: Encourage parents of preschoolers to count and label not only small sets but also larger sets (4–10) of present, visible objects
description: The article's policy discussion recommends that, if experimental studies corroborate its findings, parents be encouraged to engage in counting and labeling "not only very small sets of objects but also somewhat larger sets of objects," because such talk may help children figure out the relationship between counting and the cardinal meanings of number words. It notes parents often overestimate children's numerical knowledge and are unsure how to promote early mathematics, and that unlike literacy there has been no concerted effort to inform parents about supportive numerical interactions.
requirements: Experimental corroboration of the correlational findings before making firm recommendations, as the article itself stipulates
constraints: The current evidence is correlational; the authors state controlled experimental studies are critical before concluding causality
target_learners: preschool-aged children (before formal schooling)
target_learning_goals: early number knowledge, especially the cardinal principle
examples: In the study, large-set present-object talk was rare (8.3 percent of number talk instances) yet accounted for 15.7 percent of variance in cardinal knowledge over and above SES
key_sources: Gunderson Elizabeth A., Levine Susan C. (2011). Some types of parent number talk count more than others: Relations between parents' input and children's cardinal-number knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2011.01050.x

article_title: Parent Praise to 1- to 3-Year-Olds Predicts Children's Motivational Frameworks 5 Years Later
citation: Gunderson Elizabeth A., Gripshover Sarah J., Romero Carissa, Dweck Carol S., Goldin-Meadow Susan, Levine Susan C. (2013). Parent Praise to 1-3 Year-Olds Predicts Children's Motivational Frameworks 5 Years Later. Child development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12064
title: Entity and incremental motivational frameworks: coherent belief systems about trait malleability
description: The article defines motivational frameworks as children's entity or incremental theories "in combination with the beliefs, attributions, attitudes and behaviors that go along with those theories". An entity theory holds attributes are fixed and unchangeable, leading to performance goals, negative views of effort and mistakes, and helpless responses to setbacks; an incremental theory holds attributes are malleable, leading to learning goals, positive views of effort, and mastery-oriented responses. The study measured these frameworks in both intelligence and sociomoral domains via a 24-item composite questionnaire.
requirements: Assessed via questionnaires probing beliefs about trait stability, learning versus performance goals, attributions for success and failure, and strategy generation
constraints: Measured in children aged 7-8 years in the intelligence and sociomoral domains
target_learners: children aged 7-8 years
target_learning_goals: beliefs about the malleability of intelligence and sociomoral goodness
challenge preference and attributions for success and failure
examples: The 24-item questionnaire included items such as "Imagine a kid who thinks that a person is a certain amount smart, and they stay pretty much the same. How much do you agree with this kid?"
key_sources: Gunderson Elizabeth A., Gripshover Sarah J., Romero Carissa, Dweck Carol S., Goldin-Meadow Susan, Levine Susan C. (2013). Parent Praise to 1-3 Year-Olds Predicts Children's Motivational Frameworks 5 Years Later. Child development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12064

article_title: Parent Praise to 1- to 3-Year-Olds Predicts Children's Motivational Frameworks 5 Years Later
citation: Gunderson Elizabeth A., Gripshover Sarah J., Romero Carissa, Dweck Carol S., Goldin-Meadow Susan, Levine Susan C. (2013). Parent Praise to 1-3 Year-Olds Predicts Children's Motivational Frameworks 5 Years Later. Child development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12064
title: 24-item motivational frameworks questionnaire (intelligence and sociomoral domains)
description: A composite instrument administered at ages 7-8 across two visits about three months apart, combining 18 intelligence-domain items adapted from prior work and 6 sociomoral yes-or-no items. It assesses "beliefs about trait stability, their preferences for learning versus performance goals, their attributions for success and failure, and their ability to generate strategies for improvement". Items were z-scored and averaged so higher scores indicate more incremental frameworks; the 24-item composite had α = .70.
requirements: Administered orally to children in 2nd or 3rd grade; open-ended items scored with coder reliability (α's ≥ .75)
constraints: Composite reliability α = .70; intelligence-domain reliability α = .61; sixteen children did not complete all 24 items
target_learners: children aged 7-8 years in 2nd or 3rd grade
target_learning_goals: implicit theories of intelligence and sociomoral goodness
goal orientation, attributions, and strategy generation
examples: Item 9 asked, "How much would you like to do mazes that are very hard so you can learn more about doing mazes?"

article_title: Processing Speed is Impaired in Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder, and Relates to Social Communication Abilities
citation: Haigh Sarah M., Walsh Jennifer A., Mazefsky Carla A., Minshew Nancy J., Eack Shaun M. (2018). Processing Speed is Impaired in Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder, and Relates to Social Communication Abilities. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10803-018-3515-z
title: Use standardized measures of processing speed when assessing processing speed in ASD
description: The article recommends that assessments of processing speed in ASD rely on standardized tests rather than ad hoc or inspection-time tasks, because inspection tasks may produce ceiling effects and fail to detect clinically meaningful deficits. The authors state that their findings "advocate for the use of standardized measures of processing speed to ensure that the test is sensitive enough to detect clinically-related deficits." Standardized MATRICS battery measures revealed large deficits that inspection-time methods had missed in prior studies.
requirements: Assessments must use standardized, validated processing speed tests with adequate sensitivity rather than inspection-time or ad hoc tasks.
constraints: The deficit found may reflect perceptual and/or motor output demands shared by the standardized tests themselves.
target_learners: Adults with autism spectrum disorder without intellectual disability
target_learning_goals: Accurate assessment of information processing speed as a target for cognitive intervention
examples: The study administered three standardized MATRICS subtests (Trail Making Test A, Symbol Coding, Category Fluency) and found significant deficits on all of them, whereas prior inspection-time studies had concluded processing speed was intact.
key_sources: Haigh Sarah M., Walsh Jennifer A., Mazefsky Carla A., Minshew Nancy J., Eack Shaun M. (2018). Processing Speed is Impaired in Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder, and Relates to Social Communication Abilities. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10803-018-3515-z

article_title: The relationship between expressive vocabulary knowledge and reading skills for adult struggling readers
citation: Hall, R., Greenberg, D., Laures-Gore, J., & Pae, H. K. (2012). The Relationship Between Expressive Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Skills for Adult Struggling Readers. Journal of Research in Reading. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01537.x
title: Adult literacy instruction should take a balanced approach incorporating word-reading skills, fluency, vocabulary development, and comprehension strategies
description: The article recommends that adult literacy instructors avoid concentrating on any single reading component. Because expressive vocabulary related to comprehension and exception word reading but not to decoding measures, "Concentrating on phonemic awareness and phonics activities alone, for example, will not ensure successful reading comprehension for adults who have poor language skills." Instructors should instead remain mindful of a balanced approach combining word-reading skills, fluency activities, vocabulary development, and reading comprehension strategies.
requirements: Instruction must address multiple reading components rather than phonics alone, because poor oral language skills limit comprehension gains from decoding-focused teaching.
constraints: The supporting evidence is correlational from a single time point; no causal relationships can be drawn.
target_learners: Adult struggling readers reading at third- to fifth-grade levels
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Word reading
Vocabulary development
examples: The study's regression findings showed expressive vocabulary explained significant variance in comprehension and exception word reading but not general or nonword reading, motivating the balanced-instruction recommendation.
key_sources: Hall, R., Greenberg, D., Laures-Gore, J., & Pae, H. K. (2012). The Relationship Between Expressive Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Skills for Adult Struggling Readers. Journal of Research in Reading. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01537.x

article_title: The relationship between expressive vocabulary knowledge and reading skills for adult struggling readers
citation: Hall, R., Greenberg, D., Laures-Gore, J., & Pae, H. K. (2012). The Relationship Between Expressive Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Skills for Adult Struggling Readers. Journal of Research in Reading. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01537.x
title: Triangle model of reading development linking vocabulary knowledge to word reading knowledge
description: The authors invoke the triangle model of reading development (Harm & Seidenberg, 2004; Plaut et al., 1996) to explain why expressive vocabulary relates to exception word reading. In this model, "vocabulary knowledge is connected to word reading knowledge and, therefore, individual differences in vocabulary knowledge are related to individual variability in word reading knowledge." Simulation studies cited by the authors show words with inconsistent phonological mappings rely more on semantic information than words with consistent mappings, accounting for the vocabulary–exception-word link.
requirements: The account presupposes that exception words with inconsistent phonological mappings draw on semantic representations during reading.
constraints: The article offers the model as an interpretive framework for correlational findings; it did not test the model directly.
target_learners: Adult struggling readers reading at third- to fifth-grade levels
target_learning_goals: Exception word reading
Reading comprehension
examples: The authors use the model to interpret their finding that expressive vocabulary significantly explained exception word reading variance, consistent with children's studies they review.
key_sources: Hall, R., Greenberg, D., Laures-Gore, J., & Pae, H. K. (2012). The Relationship Between Expressive Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Skills for Adult Struggling Readers. Journal of Research in Reading. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01537.x

article_title: The relationship between expressive vocabulary knowledge and reading skills for adult struggling readers
citation: Hall, R., Greenberg, D., Laures-Gore, J., & Pae, H. K. (2012). The Relationship Between Expressive Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Skills for Adult Struggling Readers. Journal of Research in Reading. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01537.x
title: Boston Naming Test (BNT) as a measure of expressive vocabulary for adult struggling readers
description: The Boston Naming Test (Kaplan et al., 2001) is a 60-item confrontation naming test in which participants name line drawings of common objects presented in order of increasing difficulty, with stimulus and phonemic cues given after incorrect answers. It "has been normed on participants ages five through 79" but, as the authors note, "the BNT has not been normed on adult struggling readers and, therefore, may not be an accurate measure of their expressive vocabulary." In this study testing began at item 1 rather than the adult-recommended item 30 because prior research indicated object-naming difficulty in this population.
requirements: Administration decisions must account for the population's known object-naming difficulty; this study began at item 1 instead of the recommended item 30 for adults.
constraints: The BNT has not been normed on adult struggling readers, so results may underestimate relationships with reading skills.
target_learners: Adult struggling readers reading at third- to fifth-grade levels
target_learning_goals: Assessment of expressive vocabulary knowledge
examples: Administered individually to 232 adult literacy students; mean total correct was 36 (SD = 7.29), and performance on items 1–30 was worse than the Tombaugh and Hubley (1997) normative sample.
key_sources: Hall, R., Greenberg, D., Laures-Gore, J., & Pae, H. K. (2012). The Relationship Between Expressive Vocabulary Knowledge and Reading Skills for Adult Struggling Readers. Journal of Research in Reading. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9817.2012.01537.x

article_title: The language and literacy development of young dual language learners: A critical review
citation: Hammer, C. S., Hoff, E., Uchikoshi, Y., Gillanders, C., Castro, D., & Sandilos, L. E. (2014). The Language and Literacy Development of Young Dual Language Learners: A Critical Review. Early childhood research quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2014.05.008
title: Language exposure and use as key influences on young DLLs' development
description: The review's organizing account of DLL development holds that the amount of language exposure to and usage of DLLs' two languages plays key roles in their language and literacy development. The review reports that differences in input amount explained DLL-monolingual accuracy differences in grammatical production, that processing efficiency tracks the language children hear more and know better, and that exposure timing (simultaneous versus sequential learning) shapes vocabulary trajectories. It concludes little is known about factors influencing DLL development, with exposure and usage the best-supported candidates.
requirements: Research designs must document children's amount of exposure to and usage of each language for the influence of input to be assessed
constraints: The review states little is known about factors that influence DLLs' development; the exposure-and-usage account is presented as preliminary given few areas with multiple studies
target_learners: Typically developing dual language learners from birth through age five
target_learning_goals: First- and second-language oral language development
Early literacy development
examples: The review cites Bonnesen & Chilla (2011), Nicholls et al. (2011), and Paradis et al. (2010) attributing DLL-monolingual grammatical accuracy differences to amount of input in each language

The review cites Marchman et al. (2010) finding DLL toddlers faster at processing the language they heard more, with processing speed related to vocabulary size within a language but not across languages

article_title: Cognitive flexibility in adolescence: Neural and behavioral mechanisms of reward prediction error processing in adaptive decision making during development
citation: Hauser, T. U., Iannaccone, R., Walitza, S., Brandeis, D., & Brem, S. (2015). Cognitive flexibility in adolescence: Neural and behavioral mechanisms of reward prediction error processing in adaptive decision making during development. Neuroimage, 104, 347-354. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2014.09.018
title: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning model with anticorrelated valuation (RSAV) for reversal learning
description: The RSAV model is a reinforcement learning model in which chosen and unchosen stimulus values are anticorrelated: feedback about the chosen object also informs the value of the unchosen stimulus, and separate learning rates are kept for positive and negative RPEs (αChosen+/−, αUnchosen+/−). The article states that "in reversal learning tasks, the feedback about the chosen object also informs about the value of the unchosen stimulus", and implements the anticorrelation within a risk-sensitive model following Niv et al. (2012), where individual risk sensitivity is assessed by using different learning rates for positive and negative RPEs. Action probabilities are derived with a softmax selection function, and parameters are estimated by maximum log-likelihood with a genetic search algorithm.
requirements: Feedback-based learning in which reward contingencies reverse unpredictably, so that feedback on the chosen option carries information about the unchosen option
Estimation of separate learning-rate parameters for positive and negative prediction errors via maximum-likelihood fitting
constraints: The article notes it was previously shown that models with anticorrelated valuation fit this task better than a standard Rescorla-Wagner model, i.e., the model is tailored to probabilistic reversal learning rather than all learning tasks
target_learners: healthy adolescents aged 12-16 years
healthy adults aged 20-29 years
target_learning_goals: feedback-guided adaptive learning
cognitive flexibility in detecting changes in reward contingencies
examples: Fitted to trial-by-trial choices of 19 adolescents and 17 adults performing a probabilistic reversal learning task with 80%/20% reward probabilities and reversals after at least 6 correct choices
key_sources: Hauser, T. U., Iannaccone, R., Walitza, S., Brandeis, D., & Brem, S. (2015). Cognitive flexibility in adolescence: Neural and behavioral mechanisms of reward prediction error processing in adaptive decision making during development. Neuroimage, 104, 347-354. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2014.09.018

article_title: Improving Preschoolers’ Arithmetic through Number Magnitude Training: The Impact of Non-Symbolic and Symbolic Training
citation: Honoré N, Noël M-P (2016) Improving Preschoolers' Arithmetic through Number Magnitude Training: The Impact of Non-Symbolic and Symbolic Training. PLoS ONE 11(11): e0166685. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0166685
title: Dual-representation view of numerical development
description: The dual-representation view holds that symbolic and non-symbolic numbers activate distinct magnitude representations: dot sets engage an approximate analogue system (the ANS), while symbolic numbers access "a more precise number representation" built through development rather than through mapping onto the ANS. On this view, mathematical learning relies on the ability to process symbolic numbers' magnitude. The present training study contrasts it with the unique-representation view, and the authors conclude their results are in line with it.
requirements: Symbolic and non-symbolic magnitude processing must be measurable separately to test its differential predictions
constraints: The article notes ANS tasks also measure processing of non-numerical parameters covarying with numerosity and inhibitory control
target_learners: preschool children prior to formal mathematics instruction
target_learning_goals: numerical magnitude processing
exact arithmetic
examples: The study trained one group with dot collections and another with Arabic numbers in otherwise identical comparison and number-line games, and only the symbolic group improved in exact arithmetic.
key_sources: Honoré N, Noël M-P (2016) Improving Preschoolers' Arithmetic through Number Magnitude Training: The Impact of Non-Symbolic and Symbolic Training. PLoS ONE 11(11): e0166685. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0166685

article_title: Small-group collaboration and individual knowledge acquisition: The processes of growth during adolescence and early adulthood
citation: Howe, Christine; Zachariou, Antonia. (2017). Small-group collaboration and individual knowledge acquisition: The processes of growth during adolescence and early adulthood. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.10.007
title: Computer-presented trajectories task on objects falling from stationary or moving carriers
description: The study used a computer-presented science task in which pairs discussed and predicted the trajectories objects follow when falling from stationary or moving carriers. The abstract describes a "computer-presented task that required them to discuss and predict the trajectories objects follow when they fall from stationary or moving carriers". It served as the collaborative activity linking group dialogue to post-test measures of individual understanding.
requirements: Pairs of students must discuss and predict object trajectories together
target_learners: students aged 10 to 22 years
target_learning_goals: predicting the trajectories of falling objects (physical science reasoning)
examples: Forty-six pairs of students aged between 10 and 22 years worked on the task in the reported study
key_sources: Howe, Christine; Zachariou, Antonia. (2017). Small-group collaboration and individual knowledge acquisition: The processes of growth during adolescence and early adulthood. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.10.007

article_title: Small-group collaboration and individual knowledge acquisition: The processes of growth during adolescence and early adulthood
citation: Howe, Christine; Zachariou, Antonia. (2017). Small-group collaboration and individual knowledge acquisition: The processes of growth during adolescence and early adulthood. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.10.007
title: Difference-driven account of small-group collaboration: differing opinions drive individual gains while joint constructions play a tangential role
description: The article's organizing account holds that individual understanding is promoted through exchanging differing opinions, while the joint analyses groups construct play a tangential role. As the abstract states, "individual understanding can be promoted through exchanging differing opinions, the joint analyses that groups construct while collaborating play a tangential role". Acceptance of constructions depends on reflection and reconciliation triggered by difference, sometimes occurring after the group session. The reported study tested whether this account extends to adolescence and early adulthood.
requirements: Group dialogue must involve the exchange of differing opinions for the mechanism to operate
constraints: Evidence base in the available text is research with middle to late childhood plus the reported 10-to-22 sample
target_learners: children and adolescents
students in early adulthood
target_learning_goals: individual conceptual understanding gained through small-group collaboration
examples: The reported study of 46 pairs aged 10 to 22 on the falling-objects task confirmed the key role of differing opinions and the limited relevance of collaborative constructions
key_sources: Howe, Christine; Zachariou, Antonia. (2017). Small-group collaboration and individual knowledge acquisition: The processes of growth during adolescence and early adulthood. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.10.007

article_title: Less Efficient Neural Processing Related to Irregular Sleep and Less Sustained Attention in Toddlers
citation: Hoyniak, C. P., Petersen, I. T., McQuillan, M. E., Staples, A. D., & Bates, J. E. (2015). Less Efficient Neural Processing Related to Irregular Sleep and Less Sustained Attention in Toddlers. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2015.1016162
title: P3 latency as an index of neural efficiency of attentional processing in early childhood
description: This framework holds that the P3 ERP component elicited by target stimuli in Oddball tasks indexes attentional and information processing capacity, with "larger amplitudes and shorter latencies... generally associated with better attentional and information processing capacity." Longer P3 latencies indicate poorer neural efficiency surrounding attentional processes. The article applies this framework to toddlers, using target P3 latency as a neurophysiological index linking irregular sleep to sustained attention capacity.
requirements: ERP recording during an active Oddball task with identifiable target P3 component, typically via parietal electrode clusters identified through spatial PCA
constraints: The article notes the P3 is an index of multiple cognitive processes with multiple neural generators, so few specific interpretations have been consistently supported; in toddlers it is uncertain whether the elicited component reflects the same P3 as in adults
target_learners: toddlers ages 2–3
target_learning_goals: sustained attention capacity
neural efficiency of attentional processing
examples: The study elicited a P3-like component from toddlers during an active auditory Oddball task and found longer latencies associated with poorer sustained attention and more irregular sleep
key_sources: Hoyniak, C. P., Petersen, I. T., McQuillan, M. E., Staples, A. D., & Bates, J. E. (2015). Less Efficient Neural Processing Related to Irregular Sleep and Less Sustained Attention in Toddlers. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2015.1016162

article_title: Effects of problem size, operation, and working-memory span on simple-arithmetic strategies: differences between children and adults?
citation: Ineke Imbo · André Vandierendonck. (2008). Effects of problem size, operation, and working-memory span on simple-arithmetic strategies: differences between children and adults? Psychological Research (2008) 72:331–346. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00426-007-0112-8
title: Adaptive strategy choice model (ASCM) of simple-arithmetic strategy selection and efficiency
description: The adaptive strategy choice model (ASCM) of Siegler and Shipley (1995), as described in this article, holds that people have several strategies available and choose the fastest and most accurate one, governed by a confidence criterion determining how sure they must be to state a retrieved answer and a search length determining how many retrieval attempts are made before switching to a procedural strategy. Retrieval efficiency depends on the peakedness of problem–answer associations, whereas procedural efficiency depends on the difficulty of executing the particular procedure. The study used the model to derive the prediction that retrieval frequency correlates with retrieval efficiency but not with procedural efficiency.
requirements: Learners must have multiple strategies available (retrieval and procedural strategies) for the same problems
A confidence criterion and a search length criterion govern when retrieval is preferred over procedural strategies
constraints: The article tests the model's predictions only for simple addition and multiplication in primary-school children (second, fourth, and sixth grade)
target_learners: primary-school children learning simple arithmetic (second, fourth, and sixth graders)
target_learning_goals: simple-arithmetic fact retrieval and procedural strategy use in addition and multiplication
examples: The study regressed retrieval latencies and procedural latencies on percentage retrieval use per grade to test the model's prediction about which efficiencies correlate with retrieval frequency

article_title: Sensori‐motor experience leads to changes in visual processing in the developing brain
citation: James, K. H. (2010). Sensori-motor experience leads to changes in visual processing in the developing brain. Developmental Science, 13(2), 279-288. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00883.x
title: Sensori-motor (embodied) account of functional specialization for letters
description: The article proposes that functional specialization for letters in the developing visual system emerges from sensori-motor experience: perceptual processes "are not encapsulated modules, but instead receive feedback from sensori-motor networks, the strength of which is based on previous experience with the class of stimulus." Writing letters stores sensori-motor associations that are re-activated during visual perception and strengthen visual association cortex responses. The fMRI results — increased letter activation after printing but not visual-only training — are presented as the first evidence that functional specialization emerges from this perceptual-motor coupling in the developing brain.
requirements: Learning must involve integrated sensory and motor activity with the stimulus class, not mere exposure
constraints: The study did not exhaustively test all possible associations; visual-only practice also involved an oral motor response, so results may reflect manual versus oral motor association differences
An attentional-difference alternative explanation is acknowledged and under investigation
target_learners: pre-school children (pre-literate, ~4-5 years old)
target_learning_goals: letter recognition and the neural specialization supporting early literacy
examples: Adults who learned pseudo-letters by writing developed fusiform specialization for them, while visually trained adults did not (James & Atwood, 2009, as cited in the article)
key_sources: James, K. H. (2010). Sensori-motor experience leads to changes in visual processing in the developing brain. Developmental Science, 13(2), 279-288. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00883.x

article_title: Sensori‐motor experience leads to changes in visual processing in the developing brain
citation: James, K. H. (2010). Sensori-motor experience leads to changes in visual processing in the developing brain. Developmental Science, 13(2), 279-288. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00883.x
title: Teach letter recognition through printing practice that couples visual and motor systems
description: Because printing practice couples visual and motor systems and produced neural specialization for letters where visual-only practice did not, the article supports sensori-motor learning strategies for letter instruction. It notes "Educators have implemented sensori-motor learning strategies when teaching children to recognize shapes, including letters" and that "children recognize letters more efficiently after printing practice than when printing is not involved in learning." The principle is to include handwriting/copied-letter production, not just visual recognition drills, in early literacy instruction.
requirements: Training must involve active letter production (copying/writing) with feedback, with stimulus exposure held comparable to comparison conditions
constraints: Behavioural recognition gains in this study were only a non-significant trend; behavioural benefits rest partly on cited work with larger samples
The visual-only comparison condition also involved oral naming, so the critical contrast is manual versus oral motor association
target_learners: pre-school and early-elementary children learning letters
target_learning_goals: letter recognition
early literacy foundations
examples: Children copied highlighted letters and words from a story across four weekly 30-minute training sessions, with feedback on writing accuracy
key_sources: James, K. H. (2010). Sensori-motor experience leads to changes in visual processing in the developing brain. Developmental Science, 13(2), 279-288. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2009.00883.x

article_title: Auditory attention in childhood and adolescence: An event-related potential study of spatial selective attention to one of two simultaneous stories
citation: Karns Christina M., Isbell Elif, Giuliano Ryan J., Neville Helen J. (2015). Auditory attention in childhood and adolescence: An event-related potential study of spatial selective attention to one of two simultaneous stories. Developmental cognitive neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2015.03.001
title: Gain-control account of auditory selective attention across development, with later endogenous attention processes
description: The article advances the account that spatial selective attention operates by modulating the amplitude of maturing auditory early-latency evoked potentials — a gain-control mechanism — and/or by invoking later, potentially endogenous attention processes. Support is the difference-wave analysis showing "a multiphasic morphology that was similar to the attend and unattend waveforms for each age group", taken as "evidence for gain-control modulation". The authors state the evidence "is mixed and seems to depend on probe type": gain control fits nonlinguistic probes, while linguistic probes show sustained later modulation suggesting additional endogenous processing.
requirements: Interpretation requires tracking maturational changes in the underlying auditory evoked potentials, since attention modulation interacts with developing morphology and latency
constraints: The difference-wave morphology does not rule out other mechanisms operating with coincidentally similar morphology and topography
Evidence for gain control is mixed and depends on probe type; a pure gain-control account would predict N1 modulation that was not observed
target_learners: children ages 3–5, 10, 13, and 16 years
young adults 18–26 years
target_learning_goals: auditory spatial selective attention in acoustically noisy, competing-speech environments
examples: Difference-wave time-bin analyses found significant attention effects corresponding with measured P1-N1-P2 peaks, plus prolonged effects at 300–500 ms for linguistic probes across all age groups
key_sources: Karns Christina M., Isbell Elif, Giuliano Ryan J., Neville Helen J. (2015). Auditory attention in childhood and adolescence: An event-related potential study of spatial selective attention to one of two simultaneous stories. Developmental cognitive neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2015.03.001

article_title: Math Circles: A Tool for Promoting Engagement Among Middle School Minority Males
citation: Eugene Kennedy & Lawrence Smolinsky (2016). Math Circles: A Tool for Promoting Engagement among Middle School Minority Males. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 12(4), 717-732. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2016.1223a
title: Six major design components of an inclusive math circle for low-income minority middle school students
description: The authors concluded the circle's effectiveness rested on a set of design components conceptualized as part of an enculturation process into the culture of mathematics: control of the physical environment (meeting in the mathematics department lounge), the circle leader being a professional mathematician, labels and normative expectations from selection, creation of a safe mathematical community, natural peer groupings, games and competition, and conveying the value of mathematics. They state: "We concluded that there were 6 major components of the design that were most effective." The components were identified interpretively from the case, not experimentally manipulated.
requirements: A professional mathematician as circle leader and access to a university mathematics department space
constraints: The article states only one circle was examined and none of the factors considered impactful were systematically manipulated
target_learners: low-income minority middle school students
target_learning_goals: mathematical engagement
positive mathematical identity
enculturation into the community of mathematics
examples: Students met weekly for 90 minutes over 9 months in the mathematics department lounge, played Atari Go with mini-tournaments, and heard discussions of the value of mathematics and the heroes of mathematics

article_title: Math Circles: A Tool for Promoting Engagement Among Middle School Minority Males
citation: Eugene Kennedy & Lawrence Smolinsky (2016). Math Circles: A Tool for Promoting Engagement among Middle School Minority Males. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 12(4), 717-732. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2016.1223a
title: Math circles as enculturation into the community of professional mathematicians
description: The article frames a math circle as "a social structure where participants engage in the depths and intricacies of mathematical thinking, propagate the culture of doing mathematics, and create knowledge." Rooted in Eastern European practice, a professional mathematician inducts youth into the culture of mathematics—its games, talk, reasoning, heroes, myths and values—often in the mathematicians' own workplace. Participation is theorized as enculturation: appropriating the language, values, and habits of mind of the discipline and developing a personal mathematical identity, drawing on a socio-cultural, constructivist view of mathematical learning.
requirements: A professional mathematician willing to spend time with youth and lead the induction into mathematical culture
constraints: The article notes there is only limited research on math circle dynamics, especially for minorities and under-represented groups
target_learners: middle school students
minority and low-income youth
target_learning_goals: mathematical thinking and reasoning
positive mathematical identity
appreciation of mathematical culture
examples: The circle met in the mathematics department lounge, where students encountered artifacts such as a Rubik's Cube, a chess set, and blackboards with complex equations left by graduate students

article_title: Rational snacking: Young children’s decision-making on the marshmallow task is moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability
citation: Kidd, C., Palmeri, H., & Aslin, R. N. (2013). Rational snacking: Young children's decision-making on the marshmallow task is moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability. Cognition, 126(1), 109-114. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2012.08.004
title: Rational decision-making hypothesis of delay of gratification
description: An explanatory account in which children's decisions to wait are framed as rational utility-maximizing choices that depend on beliefs about whether waiting will pay off. As the article puts it, "Waiting is only the rational choice if you believe that a second marshmallow is likely to actually appear after a reasonably short delay"—and that the current reward is not at risk of being taken away. The article uses this framework to interpret wait-time variance as reflecting acquired beliefs about environmental stability rather than only self-control capacity.
requirements: The account presumes children have acquired beliefs about the reliability of promises and the stability of their environment before entering the task
constraints: The article notes rationality must be inferred relative to the goals and expectations of the agent, so the same behavior may be rational for children with different environmental histories
target_learners: young children (preschool-aged, approximately 3;6 to 5;10 in this study)
target_learning_goals: delay of gratification
decision-making under uncertainty about future rewards
examples: Children watched the experimenter either deliver or fail to deliver promised art supplies across two choices, then decided whether to wait 15 min for a second marshmallow
key_sources: Kidd, C., Palmeri, H., & Aslin, R. N. (2013). Rational snacking: Young children's decision-making on the marshmallow task is moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability. Cognition, 126(1), 109-114. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2012.08.004

article_title: Rational snacking: Young children’s decision-making on the marshmallow task is moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability
citation: Kidd, C., Palmeri, H., & Aslin, R. N. (2013). Rational snacking: Young children's decision-making on the marshmallow task is moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability. Cognition, 126(1), 109-114. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2012.08.004
title: Establish demonstrated reliability before asking young children to delay gratification or wait for a better reward
description: Before asking children to forgo an immediate lesser reward for a later greater one, give them direct evidence that promises in this setting are kept. The article demonstrated that "children's sustained decisions to wait for a greater reward rather than quickly taking a lesser reward are strongly influenced by the reliability of the environment (in this case, the reliability of the researcher's verbal assurances)". In the experiment this was done via a two-part art task in which the experimenter either delivered or failed to deliver promised supplies.
requirements: Learners must actually observe the promised better outcome being delivered (or withheld) at least once before the delay decision
constraints: The evidence comes from a single small randomized study (N = 28) with preschool-aged children; the authors note further work is required to test the relative contributions of different factors
target_learners: young children in instructional or experimental settings
target_learning_goals: waiting for larger delayed rewards
self-regulation in the face of immediate temptation
examples: In the reliable condition the researcher returned from both art-task delays with the promised new art supplies and better stickers before the marshmallow task began
key_sources: Kidd, C., Palmeri, H., & Aslin, R. N. (2013). Rational snacking: Young children's decision-making on the marshmallow task is moderated by beliefs about environmental reliability. Cognition, 126(1), 109-114. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2012.08.004

article_title: Influence of aging on visual perception and visual motor integration in Korean adults
citation: Kim E, Park Y-K, Byun Y-H, Park M-S, Kim H. (2014). Influence of aging on visual perception and visual motor integration in Korean adults. Journal of Exercise Rehabilitation 10(4):245-250. https://doi.org/10.12965/jer.140147
title: Regularly check visual perception and visual-motor integration from an individual's 50s as a critical period for detecting cognitive decline
description: The article recommends that visual perception (VP) and visual-motor integration (VMI) be assessed periodically starting in a person's 50s, because scores on both the K-DTVP-2 and VMI-3R were significantly decreased by then relative to the 20s. It states "it can be suggested that VP and VMI should be regularly checked from an individual's 50s, which is a critical period for detecting cognitive decline by aging." Both instruments could be used for determining the level of cognitive deficit by aging.
requirements: Trained examiners; the article reports all examiners completed educational training and pretests verified inter-examiner reliability before the survey.
constraints: The article notes it could not yet be determined which measurement is the most reliable and sensitive to detect cognitive decline by aging.
target_learners: Adults aged 50 and older
target_learning_goals: Detecting age-related cognitive decline through visual perception and visual-motor integration screening
examples: The cross-sectional survey measured 283 adults aged 20-79 across six 10-yr age groups in Daegu and Gyeongbuk, Korea, from April to August 2011.
key_sources: Kim E, Park Y-K, Byun Y-H, Park M-S, Kim H. (2014). Influence of aging on visual perception and visual motor integration in Korean adults. Journal of Exercise Rehabilitation 10(4):245-250. https://doi.org/10.12965/jer.140147

article_title: Influence of aging on visual perception and visual motor integration in Korean adults
citation: Kim E, Park Y-K, Byun Y-H, Park M-S, Kim H. (2014). Influence of aging on visual perception and visual motor integration in Korean adults. Journal of Exercise Rehabilitation 10(4):245-250. https://doi.org/10.12965/jer.140147
title: K-DTVP-2 and VMI-3R assessment instruments for visual perception and visual-motor integration
description: Two standardized instruments used to measure age-related change in visual perception and visual-motor integration. The K-DTVP-2 is the Korean version of DTVP-2, consisting of 8 sub-tests such as "eye-hand coordination" and "figure-ground", yielding a General Visual Perception Quotient (mean 100, SD 15) in about 30 to 60 min; its Cronbach's alpha was .883. The VMI-3R involves copying 24 shapes arranged from simplest to most complex, scored 0 to 50 points in 10 to 13 min; its Cronbach's alpha was .641.
requirements: Examiners trained to perform, analyze, and score the results exactly; raw sub-item scores converted to standard scores for interpretation.
constraints: K-DTVP-2 was designed to measure 4 to 8 yr old children's visual perceptual ability; VMI-3R internal consistency (alpha .641) was lower than K-DTVP-2's.
target_learners: Adults aged 20-79 in this study; instruments span preschool children to adults
target_learning_goals: Measuring visual perceptual ability and visual-motor integration to identify cognitive deficit levels
examples: Principal component analysis extracted one factor explaining 57.1% of total variance for K-DTVP-2 and 54.5% for VMI-3R.

article_title: Exploring the impact of phonological awareness, visual–spatial working memory, and preschool quantity–number competencies on mathematics achievement in elementary school: Findings from a 3-year longitudinal study
citation: Krajewski, K., & Schneider, W. (2009). Exploring the impact of phonological awareness, visual-spatial working memory, and preschool quantity-number competencies on mathematics achievement in elementary school: Findings from a 3-year longitudinal study. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 103(4), 516-531. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2009.03.009
title: Krajewski's three-level developmental model of quantity-number competencies (QNC)
description: A theoretical model of early arithmetical development describing how mathematical competencies are acquired via three developmental levels of quantity-to-number-word linkage. At Level I children recite number words with the words still isolated from quantities; at Level II (imprecise then precise) children understand that number words are linked to quantities and can arrange numbers by size; at Level III children understand part-whole relations and differences between numbers represented with precise number words. The study used this model to derive differential predictions for phonological awareness and visual-spatial working memory, quoting that it "depicts how this linkage might occur and how early mathematical competencies are acquired via three developmental levels".
requirements: Assessment tasks distinguishing number-word sequence knowledge (Level I) from quantity-to-number-word linkage (Level II) and number relations (Level III)
constraints: The authors note the model's level differentiation was necessary to detect the differential predictor effects; studies not differentiating QNC levels found inconsistent phonological-awareness effects
target_learners: preschool and kindergarten children
elementary school children
target_learning_goals: early numerical development
understanding of the number system and quantity-to-number-word linkage
examples: The study operationalized the levels with tasks such as number-word sequence recitation (Level I), quantity-comparison and number-word comparison tasks (Level II), and difference and word problems with concrete material (Level III)

article_title: Print awareness of adult illiterates: a comparison with young pre-readers and low-educated adult readers
citation: Kurvers, J., Van Hout, R., & Vallen, T. (2009). Print awareness of adult illiterates: a comparison with young pre-readers and low-educated adult readers. Read Writ 22, 863-887. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-008-9129-7
title: Print awareness as a construct separate from language awareness, with three sub-domains
description: The article treats print awareness as a pre-reading construct distinct from language awareness, defining it as follows: "Print awareness refers to knowledge about environmental print, knowledge of written signs and graphemes, and knowledge about relationships between speech and writing". It operationalizes this in three sub-domains — environmental print (inscriptions, logos), the writing system (graphemes, signs), and the written register — each assessed with dedicated instruments whose internal consistencies ranged from Cronbach's alpha 0.75 to 0.99. The construct is used to compare unschooled illiterate adults with young pre-readers and low-educated literate adults.
requirements: Assessments must be administered in the participant's preferred first or second language
constraints: The article distinguishes print awareness from language awareness, the ability to reflect on spoken language forms separately from their meanings
target_learners: unschooled adult illiterates
pre-reading kindergarten children
low-educated adult literacy learners
target_learning_goals: concepts about print and written language
recognition of environmental print
understanding how writing represents speech
examples: Six assessment tasks: inscriptions (18 items), logos (9), graphemes (34), signs (14), writing/speech correspondence (7), and characteristics of written language (12)
key_sources: Kurvers, J., Van Hout, R., & Vallen, T. (2009). Print awareness of adult illiterates: a comparison with young pre-readers and low-educated adult readers. Read Writ 22, 863-887. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-008-9129-7

article_title: Print awareness of adult illiterates: a comparison with young pre-readers and low-educated adult readers
citation: Kurvers, J., Van Hout, R., & Vallen, T. (2009). Print awareness of adult illiterates: a comparison with young pre-readers and low-educated adult readers. Read Writ 22, 863-887. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-008-9129-7
title: Build adult literacy teaching on the print knowledge learners bring into the classroom
description: The article argues that effective instruction for unschooled illiterate adults should start from what they already know about print: "effective teaching should be built on the knowledge the students bring into the classroom, knowing more about what adults entering literacy courses know about letters, print or written language can help literacy teachers to adapt their teaching practices to the knowledge and skills of unschooled illiterate adults". The study shows these learners already know the functions and uses of written language and can distinguish writing signs, but lack grapheme knowledge and out-of-context print reading, so instruction can leverage existing functional knowledge while explicitly teaching the code.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of what adult literacy entrants know about letters, print and written language
constraints: Illiterate adults in this study had lived in print-rich environments for years yet had not built a sight vocabulary of environmental print, so exposure alone was not sufficient
target_learners: unschooled adult illiterates entering literacy courses
target_learning_goals: reading and writing in a second language
decoding and grapheme knowledge
examples: The illiterate adults had attended about 60-80 hours of literacy classes at testing; graphemes they recognized best were the first letters introduced in the adult literacy course

article_title: The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students
citation: Lewallen TC, Hunt H, Potts-Datema W, Zaza S, Giles W. (2015). The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12310
title: The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child (WSCC) model: a unified socioecological framework integrating health and education
description: The WSCC model is a conceptual framework developed jointly by ASCD and CDC that combines the Whole Child approach and the coordinated school health approach. The article states that "The WSCC model is designed to provide a shared framework and approach for decision making and action for both sectors to work together." It places the student at the center, surrounds the child with a ring stressing coordination among policy, process, and practice, and an outer ring of school health components emphasizing the school as part of the community. The authors describe it as a socioecological approach directed at the whole school, drawing resources from the whole community.
requirements: Coordination among policy, process, and practice; administrator support, particularly principals, for integration of learning and health
constraints: The article states the model is a framework and not an intervention; specific interventions, curricula, and classroom practices depend on local context
target_learners: K-12 students (pre-K to grade 12)
target_learning_goals: Educational attainment and healthy development; students healthy, safe, engaged, supported, and challenged
examples: Developed through spring 2013 expert panel meetings convened by ASCD and CDC, with outcomes vetted by a review group of stakeholders
key_sources: Lewallen TC, Hunt H, Potts-Datema W, Zaza S, Giles W. (2015). The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12310

article_title: The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students
citation: Lewallen TC, Hunt H, Potts-Datema W, Zaza S, Giles W. (2015). The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12310
title: WSCC model's expanded and renamed school health components (10-component outer ring)
description: The WSCC model's outer ring incorporates and revises the CSH components. The article reports that "the healthy and safe school environment component is now separated into “social and emotional climate” and “physical environment” giving greater attention to each," that family and community involvement is split into community involvement and family engagement, that health promotion for staff becomes employee wellness, and that nutrition services and physical education are expanded to include the nutrition environment and physical activity. Definitions for each component were developed by subject matter experts and vetted with experts in the field.
requirements: Component definitions vetted with experts in the field; qualified, trained staff for components such as health education and physical education
target_learners: K-12 students
target_learning_goals: Health literacy, health-promoting decision making, and academic success supported by a healthy school environment
examples: The nutrition services component expanded to include the nutrition environment; physical education expanded to include physical activity
key_sources: Lewallen TC, Hunt H, Potts-Datema W, Zaza S, Giles W. (2015). The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12310

article_title: The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students
citation: Lewallen TC, Hunt H, Potts-Datema W, Zaza S, Giles W. (2015). The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12310
title: Coordinate policy, process, and practice—with administrator support—when integrating learning and health in schools
description: The WSCC model makes coordination of policy, process, and practice an explicit ring around the student, because prior approaches did not describe these facilitative factors. The article states that "The key to moving from model to action is collaborative development of local school policies, processes, and practices," and that district and school wellness teams working closely with the school administrator combine both sectors' goals most effectively. It recommends starting from a common understanding of the interrelatedness of learning and health.
requirements: Administrator support, particularly principals; joint collaborative policy development followed by implementation into routine practice
constraints: Without coordination, policies, practices, and processes in place, the model would not be effective in achieving its intended outcomes (consultation team observation)
target_learners: K-12 students in schools and districts implementing the model
target_learning_goals: Integration of learning and health outcomes through coordinated school policies, practices, and processes
examples: The consultation team observed that CSH efforts succeeded when viewed as integral to the school's mission and when wellness teams worked with the school administrator

article_title: Counting in Sign Language
citation: Jacqueline Leybaert and Marie-Noëlle Van Cutsem. (2002). Counting in Sign Language. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1006/jecp.2002.2660
title: Belgian French Sign Language number-sign sequence as a base-5, rule-bound visuomanual counting system
description: The article describes Belgian French Sign Language's cardinal number signs as a single-handed, visuomanual system in which "BFSL number signs follows a consistent base-5 rule": from 1 to 5, 6 to 9, 11 to 15, and so on, one adds a finger for the next number, so number is inherently represented in each sign's finger configuration. Decade numbers are snapped configurations, and numbers within decades from 20 are concatenations of decade and unit signs. The article contrasts this with oral French, where the first 16 numbers are conventional and rule-bound structure begins later.
requirements: Learners must be exposed to the BFSL (or signed French) number-sign system, whose structure the article states is the same in signed French and Signed Coded Completed French
constraints: The base-5 structure holds for Belgian French Sign Language and American Sign Language but not for French Sign Language, and the concatenation rule does not apply to numbers between 11 and 19
target_learners: deaf children learning to count in sign language
hearing children learning oral number words
target_learning_goals: acquisition of the conventional number sequence
mapping linguistic counting onto numerosity representations
examples: The article details sign formation: 6 is the thumb alone moved twice, 7 adds the index finger, and 23 is the 20 sign followed by extension of three fingers
key_sources: Jacqueline Leybaert and Marie-Noëlle Van Cutsem. (2002). Counting in Sign Language. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1006/jecp.2002.2660

article_title: Sleep, School Performance, and a School-Based Intervention among School-Aged Children: A Sleep Series Study in China
citation: Li Shenghui, Arguelles Lester, Jiang Fan, Chen Wenjuan, Jin Xingming, Yan Chonghuai, Tian Ying, Hong Xiumei, Qian Ceng, Zhang Jun, Wang Xiaobin, Shen Xiaoming. (2013). Sleep, School Performance, and a School-Based Intervention among School-Aged Children: A Sleep Series Study in China. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0067928
title: Regulate school schedules (later start times) as a lever for children's sleep health
description: The article argues that school schedule, particularly early school start time, is a modifiable policy target for improving children's sleep: "school schedule could be considered as a target for sleep intervention." In its trial, delaying start time by 30 or 60 minutes in primary schools increased sleep duration (15.6 and 22.8 minutes) and reduced daytime sleepiness relative to control schools. The principle treats schedule regulation as a school-level, system-level intervention rather than an individual behavior-change program.
requirements: Schools must share a common start time that can be shifted, with academic and nonacademic activities correspondingly regulated (finishing time moved in the trial).
Comparison groups with similar sleep duration, sleepiness, schedule, socioeconomic background, and achievement are needed to evaluate the change.
constraints: The article states the intervention trial "is not a rigorous randomized control trial at the individual level, and as such, attribution of improved sleep to the regulation of school schedule alone should be prudent."
Gains were modest: only a minority reached the recommended 10 or more hours and about half still reported daytime sleepiness after the change.
target_learners: School-aged children in primary school (fourth and fifth grades in the trial)
target_learning_goals: Sufficient sleep duration and reduced daytime sleepiness as foundations for attention, learning motivation, and academic achievement
examples: Six Shanghai primary schools were randomly assigned (two schools each) to control, 30-minute delay, or 60-minute delay of the 7:30am start time, with finishing time correspondingly moved, and sleep was surveyed before and two years after.
