article_title: Is approximate number precision a stable predictor of math ability?
citation: Libertus Melissa E., Feigenson Lisa, Halberda Justin. (2013). Is Approximate Number Precision a Stable Predictor of Math Ability? Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2013.02.001
title: Approximate Number System (ANS): a noisy, ratio-dependent system for representing numerical magnitudes
description: The Approximate Number System is described as a system for representing numerical information "using noisy mental magnitudes that are normally distributed around the number to be represented." Its hallmark is that representational noise increases with numerosity, so discrimination success depends on the ratio between two numerosities rather than their absolute difference, yielding Weber's Law behavior. The article measures individual ANS acuity via a psychophysical model estimating each participant's Weber fraction w, and treats acuity as improving across development while varying considerably between individuals of the same age.
requirements: Measurement via a non-symbolic numerical comparison task with trials spanning multiple numerical ratios to estimate the Weber fraction
constraints: The article notes ANS proficiency alone is not sufficient to generate formal math concepts, since infants and non-human animals show ANS representations without formal math skill
target_learners: preschool-aged children (3-5 years)
target_learning_goals: non-symbolic numerical estimation and discrimination
early mathematics ability
examples: The study estimated each child's Weber fraction w from 60 test trials using maximum likelihood estimation over a Gaussian model of numerosity representations
key_sources: Libertus Melissa E., Feigenson Lisa, Halberda Justin. (2013). Is Approximate Number Precision a Stable Predictor of Math Ability? Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2013.02.001

article_title: Is approximate number precision a stable predictor of math ability?
citation: Libertus Melissa E., Feigenson Lisa, Halberda Justin. (2013). Is Approximate Number Precision a Stable Predictor of Math Ability? Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2013.02.001
title: Panamath non-symbolic numerical comparison task for assessing ANS acuity in young children
description: Panamath (the Psychophysical Assessment of Numerical Approximation) is a non-symbolic numerical comparison task administered as a free-download software tool. Children see spatially separated blue and yellow dot arrays on a laptop screen and indicate which color has more dots; arrays are visible for 2000 ms, with accuracy and response time recorded via an experimenter keypress. In this study children completed six practice trials followed by 60 test trials with dot numbers from 4 to 15 across four ratio bins, controlling for dot size and cumulative surface area across trial halves.
requirements: An experimenter blind to the screen who records verbal responses to capture response time
Familiarization trials with auditory feedback so children understand the task
constraints: Split-half reliability in this preschool sample was 0.65 at Time 1 and 0.72 at Time 2; the psychophysical model did not yield a reliable w fit for some participants
target_learners: preschool-aged children
target_learning_goals: measuring approximate number system acuity
examples: Used at both time points of the longitudinal study; dots ranged from 4 to 15 with ratio bins 1:2, 2:3, 3:4, and 6:7

article_title: Tracking Grade 10 learners’ geometric reasoning through folding back
citation: Mabotja, S., Chuene, K., Maoto, S., & Kibirige, I. (2018). Tracking Grade 10 learners' geometric reasoning through folding back. Pythagoras, 39(1), a371. https://doi.org/10.4102/pythagoras.v39i1.371
title: Pirie and Kieren's dynamical theory of the growth of mathematical understanding
description: Pirie and Kieren's (1994) dynamical theory describes the growth of mathematical understanding through eight nested levels: primitive knowing, image making, image having, property noticing, formalising, observing, structuring and inventising. The article states that 'the growth in mathematical understanding is neither linear nor unidirectional' and that each layer contains the preceding layer and is contained in the layer that follows. The study used the first five levels to locate learners' understanding during geometry proof tasks, and folding back is the theory's mechanism for back-and-forth movement across layers.
requirements: Learners bring prior knowledge (primitive knowing) to their learning context, which serves as the innermost layer from which understanding grows.
constraints: The article notes Martin (2008) viewed Pirie and Kieren's definition of folding back as having 'remained essentially undeveloped and unelaborated in their work', so how and why folding back occurs is not deeply explored in the original theory.
target_learners: Grade 10 mathematics learners
target_learning_goals: Geometric reasoning and proof
Growth of mathematical understanding
examples: The article pitched the triangle-similarity proof task at the formalising level and interpreted learners' F-shape mnemonic use as working at the property noticing level.
key_sources: Mabotja, S., Chuene, K., Maoto, S., & Kibirige, I. (2018). Tracking Grade 10 learners' geometric reasoning through folding back. Pythagoras, 39(1), a371. https://doi.org/10.4102/pythagoras.v39i1.371

article_title: Tracking Grade 10 learners’ geometric reasoning through folding back
citation: Mabotja, S., Chuene, K., Maoto, S., & Kibirige, I. (2018). Tracking Grade 10 learners' geometric reasoning through folding back. Pythagoras, 39(1), a371. https://doi.org/10.4102/pythagoras.v39i1.371
title: Martin's elaborated framework for describing folding back: source, form and outcome
description: Martin (2008) expands Pirie and Kieren's notion of folding back with three key elements: 'source of intervention, form of actions that leads to folding back and outcome of folding back'. Sources can be teacher, material, peer or self, and are intentional or unintentional, explicit or unfocused. Forms include working at an inner layer using existing understanding, collecting at an inner layer, moving out of topic and working there, and causing a discontinuity. Outcomes are effective or ineffective depending on whether folding back enables further understanding at an outer layer. The study adopted these elements to guide both data analysis and the tracking of learners' geometric reasoning.
requirements: Analysis requires identifying, in learners' conversations, the source of the intervention, the form of folding back, and the outcome of folding back.
constraints: Forms that cause a discontinuity do not result in thickening or enriched understanding of the existing concept.
target_learners: Grade 10 mathematics learners
target_learning_goals: Geometric reasoning through folding back
examples: In Extract 3 the teacher's intentional, explicit intervention directed learners to collect at an inner layer using co-interior angles, an effective form of folding back.

article_title: A longitudinal assessment of the relation between executive function and theory of mind at 3, 4, and 5 years
citation: Marcovitch S., O'Brien M., Calkins S. D., Leerkes E. M., Weaver J. M., Levine D. W. (2014). A Longitudinal Assessment of the Relation between Executive Function and Theory of Mind at 3, 4, and 5 Years. Cognitive Development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2014.07.001
title: Expression and emergence accounts of the EF–ToM relation
description: The article frames two competing accounts of why EF precedes ToM: expression accounts hold that ToM concepts exist but cannot be expressed without sufficient executive skills, while emergence accounts hold that ToM only develops after sufficient EF maturation. The authors note that "EF skills develop prior to and are involved in the expression and/or the emergence of ToM understanding," and propose distinguishing the accounts using ToM tasks with minimized executive demands. Their longitudinal asymmetry is consistent with both.
requirements: Longitudinal designs comparing EF and ToM tasks, ideally ToM tasks that minimize executive demands, to discriminate between the accounts
constraints: The present data support both accounts jointly and do not distinguish expression from emergence; the authors state their data do not directly address whether the asymmetry persists beyond early childhood
target_learners: preschool children aged 3 to 5 years
target_learning_goals: development of theory-of-mind reasoning and executive control
examples: The authors propose testing expression vs. emergence with deception tasks in which executive demands are reduced, citing Hala and Russell (2001)
key_sources: Marcovitch S., O'Brien M., Calkins S. D., Leerkes E. M., Weaver J. M., Levine D. W. (2014). A Longitudinal Assessment of the Relation between Executive Function and Theory of Mind at 3, 4, and 5 Years. Cognitive Development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2014.07.001

article_title: A longitudinal assessment of the relation between executive function and theory of mind at 3, 4, and 5 years
citation: Marcovitch S., O'Brien M., Calkins S. D., Leerkes E. M., Weaver J. M., Levine D. W. (2014). A Longitudinal Assessment of the Relation between Executive Function and Theory of Mind at 3, 4, and 5 Years. Cognitive Development. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2014.07.001
title: Concentrated early-childhood EF training may foster later theory-of-mind development
description: Based on the finding that earlier EF predicts later ToM but not vice versa, the authors recommend concentrated training of EF skills in early childhood, suggesting "one of the most important outcomes of this training may be the development of a sophisticated theory of mind." The recommendation rests on the longitudinal asymmetry rather than on a training manipulation in this study.
requirements: EF training programs appropriate for early childhood, such as the curriculum the authors cite from Diamond et al. (2007)
constraints: The article did not itself test EF training; the recommendation is an inference from longitudinal prediction, and the authors note results may be specific to the tasks used
target_learners: preschool children aged 3 to 5 years
target_learning_goals: executive function skills and, indirectly, theory-of-mind understanding
examples: The authors cite Diamond, Barnett, Thomas, and Munro (2007) as evidence of advantages of concentrated EF training in early childhood

article_title: Number and counting skills in kindergarten as predictors of grade 1 mathematical skills
citation: Martin Rebecca B., Cirino Paul T., Sharp Carla, Barnes Marcia. (2014). Number and counting skills in kindergarten as predictors of grade 1 mathematical skills. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.05.006
title: For struggling students, provide explicit and systematic focus on core skills most closely related to the desired outcome
description: The article recommends that for students who struggle in academic areas, instruction should explicitly and systematically target the core skills most proximal to the outcome, such as Arabic numerals in math. It states "an explicit and systematic focus on core skills that are most closely related to the desired outcome (i.e., words in reading, Arabic numerals in math) may be even more important" for struggling students. This principle follows from the finding that symbolic number skills strongly predict math outcomes.
requirements: Identification of the core skills most proximal to the target outcome for the domain
constraints: The article notes curricula vary in emphasis between conceptual relationships such as discovery learning versus number recognition, sequencing, and number combinations
target_learners: Students who struggle in academic areas, including kindergarten and grade 1 children
target_learning_goals: Early mathematics skills, including number recognition, sequencing, and number combinations
examples: The article cites studies emphasizing counting strategies for improving number combinations and generalizing to story problems in at-risk kindergarten students and students with math difficulties

article_title: Perceived Neighborhood Safety and Adolescent School Functioning
citation: Martin-Storey, A., & Crosnoe, R. (2014). Perceived Neighborhood Safety and Adolescent School Functioning. Applied Developmental Science, 18(2), 61-75. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888691.2014.876276
title: Sliding-scale conceptual model linking neighborhood safety to school outcomes by formality of schooling processes
description: The article proposes a conceptual model in which the strength of the association between perceived neighborhood safety and a school outcome depends on how tied that outcome is to formal versus informal schooling processes. The authors "posited a 'sliding scale' of predictive power based on how much these school outcomes are tied to formal or informal processes of schooling": school attachment, tied to informal processes, should be most strongly associated with perceived safety; standardized test scores, tied to formal processes, least; and grades, which mix the two, fall in the middle. The study's findings partially supported this ordering.
requirements: Outcomes must be classifiable along a formal-to-informal continuum of schooling processes
constraints: The model was tested with correlational SECCYD data on 15-year-olds and only partially supported; causal directionality could not be ascertained
target_learners: adolescents (15-year-olds)
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
graded performance
school attachment and belonging
examples: The study compared test scores, GPA, and school attachment in one SEM framework and found attachment, the most socioemotional outcome, was the only one associated with perceived safety after controls.
key_sources: Martin-Storey, A., & Crosnoe, R. (2014). Perceived Neighborhood Safety and Adolescent School Functioning. Applied Developmental Science, 18(2), 61-75. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888691.2014.876276

article_title: Timing and Intensity of Early Intervention Service Use and Outcomes Among a Safety-Net Population of Children
citation: McManus BM, Richardson Z, Schenkman M, Murphy N, Morrato EH. (2019). Timing and Intensity of Early Intervention Service Use and Outcomes Among a Safety-Net Population of Children. JAMA Network Open. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2018.7529
title: Link pediatric primary care and early intervention records to track EI-eligible children and improve timeliness, intensity, and outcomes
description: The article proposes integrating clinical and EI program data systems as a quality-improvement framework. By linking pediatric primary care electronic health records with EI program records, systems can follow children through EI care planning and service provision and measure care quality metrics such as timeliness, service intensity, and functional outcomes together. The authors state that clinical and EI record linkages could help integrate data to track EI-eligible children and that this data system integration could serve as a framework for other institutions.
requirements: Overlapping catchment areas between health systems and EI programs so children can be linked across records
constraints: Demonstrated in one health system and one EI program serving low-income families, which the authors state limits generalizability of the results
target_learners: Infants and toddlers with developmental delays and disabilities enrolled or referred to early intervention
target_learning_goals: Timely receipt of EI care plans
Adequate EI service intensity
Improved functional outcomes in social-emotional, cognitive, and adaptive/self-care skills
examples: The study linked Denver Health and Rocky Mountain Human Services EI records using a probabilistic matching algorithm, following 722 children through EI care planning and service provision

article_title: Ecocultural patterns of family engagement among low-income Latino families of preschool children.
citation: McWayne, C. M., Melzi, G., Limlingan, M. C., & Schick, A. (2016). Ecocultural Patterns of Family Engagement among Low-income Latino Families of Preschool Children. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0040343
title: Ecocultural theory and niche profiles as a lens for family engagement
description: Ecocultural theory holds that development is embedded in ecological and cultural environments, examining the interplay between individual processes and socio-contextual conditions. The article states that "ecocultural theory presupposes that families organize daily routines and activities according to cultural values, available economic and social resources, community norms, and specific contextual demands." Families occupy distinct "eco-cultural niche profiles," and everyday routines including family engagement are proposed to mediate children's developmental outcomes. The study uses this lens to identify within-group engagement patterns rather than comparing Latino families to a dominant-group standard.
requirements: Assessment of family behavior must include the family's or culture's own values and goals
constraints: The theory guides comparison away from majority-favoring group contrasts by basing comparisons on specific ecocultural circumstances
target_learners: Low-income Latino preschool children in Head Start programs
target_learning_goals: School readiness: language and social skills foundational to the transition into formal schooling
examples: The study applied the niche-profile concept by running latent profile analyses separately for Spanish- and English-speaking caregivers
key_sources: McWayne, C. M., Melzi, G., Limlingan, M. C., & Schick, A. (2016). Ecocultural Patterns of Family Engagement among Low-income Latino Families of Preschool Children. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0040343

article_title: Ecocultural patterns of family engagement among low-income Latino families of preschool children.
citation: McWayne, C. M., Melzi, G., Limlingan, M. C., & Schick, A. (2016). Ecocultural Patterns of Family Engagement among Low-income Latino Families of Preschool Children. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0040343
title: PEFL parent-report measure of Latino family engagement with four dimensions
description: The Parental Engagement of Families from Latino Backgrounds / Participación Educativa de Familias Latinas is a 65-item parent-report measure developed from qualitative focus-group data with low-income Latino Head Start families. "The first three factors described below represent home-based engagement and are believed to reflect cultural values and socio-economic realities of low-income, Latino families living in the United States": Foundational Education (20 items, α = 0.73), Supplemental Education (12 items, α = 0.77), and Future-oriented Teaching (3 items, α = 0.63), plus School Participation (8 items, α = 0.77). Items are rated on a four-point Likert-type scale from Never to Frequently.
requirements: Parent-report administration in the caregiver's preferred language (Spanish or English versions)
constraints: The Future-Oriented Teaching factor's alpha reliability was lower than the others due to the small number of items, and the article urges caution interpreting that dimension
target_learners: Low-income Latino primary caregivers of Head Start preschool children
target_learning_goals: Measuring culturally-contextualized family engagement across home- and school-based dimensions
examples: Used to derive latent engagement profiles in this study's 650-caregiver Head Start sample

article_title: Curiosity: The effects of feedback and confidence on the desire to know.
citation: Metcalfe, J., Vuorre, M., Towner, E., & Eich, T. S. (2023). Curiosity: The effects of feedback and confidence on the desire to know. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, vol. 152, no. 2, pp. 464-482. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001284
title: Region of proximal learning (RPL) model of curiosity
description: The RPL framework holds that curiosity is minimal when people are certain they know an answer and maximal when they believe they almost know it. The article modifies the model from Metcalfe et al. (2017) with a hard knowledge boundary under definitive yes/no feedback and a soft, noisy boundary when feedback truth is uncertain. The authors state the results are "consistent with the region of proximal learning model which proposes that while curiosity is minimal when people are completely certain that they know the answer, it is maximal when people believe that they almost know."
requirements: Metaknowledge that one almost knows is described as critical and necessary for curiosity to be aroused
constraints: The model's soft-boundary predictions apply when the truth of feedback is uncertain; with definitive yes/no feedback the known/unknown boundary is hard
target_learners: adults answering general information questions
target_learning_goals: epistemic curiosity about specific answers to general information questions
examples: Figure 1 illustrates the model with a hard boundary (left panel) for definitive feedback and a soft boundary (right panel) for uncertain feedback

article_title: Behavioral Attention: A Longitudinal Study of Whether and How It Influences the Development of Word Reading and Reading Comprehension Among At-Risk Readers
citation: Miller Amanda C., Fuchs Douglas, Fuchs Lynn S., Compton Donald L., Kearns Devin, Zhang Wenjuan, Yen Loulee, Patton Samuel, Kirchner Danielle. (2014). Behavioral Attention: A Longitudinal Study of Whether and How It Influences the Development of Word Reading and Reading Comprehension among At-Risk Readers. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 7(3), 232-249. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2014.906691
title: Evaluate at-risk students' behavioral attention and add explicit attention-maintaining procedures when implementing intensive reading intervention
description: The article recommends that because teacher-rated attention uniquely predicts at-risk readers' word reading growth, interventionists should assess behavioral attention and consider embedding procedures to sustain it during instruction. It states that "the behavioral attention of at-risk students should be evaluated, and that interventionists and classroom teachers consider the addition of explicit procedures to maintain student attention." The recommendation is grounded in the study's path-analysis findings and prior evidence that attention is malleable.
requirements: Behavioral attention of at-risk students should be evaluated before or during intensive reading intervention
constraints: Prior evidence cited (Dion et al., 2011) suggests decreasing the adverse effect of inattention may not be easy: inattentive students showed little reading gain even with the Good Behavior Game added to PALS
target_learners: at-risk first-grade readers with low behavioral attention
target_learning_goals: word reading growth
reading comprehension
examples: The study itself did not manipulate attention; the authors call for future studies to develop and empirically test attention-boosting procedures embedded in reading interventions and classroom instruction

citation: Miller Amanda C., Fuchs Douglas, Fuchs Lynn S., Compton Donald L., Kearns Devin, Zhang Wenjuan, Yen Loulee, Patton Samuel, Kirchner Danielle. (2014). title: Decoding/Fluency tutoring program: 20-week adaptive one-on-one intervention with six scripted lesson components
description: A one-on-one decoding and fluency treatment delivered over 20 weeks using 10 books ordered by reading difficulty, with placement and lesson repetition/skipping adaptive to student performance. "Each Decoding/Fluency lesson consisted of six scripted components: (1) Sight Words, (2) Sounds, (3) Decodable Words, (4) Spelling, (5) Text Reading and Fluency, and (6) Sight Word Challenge." A Decoding/Fluency Placement Test of 125 items in five bands determined students' starting book. Year 2 added a seventh component, Sentence Read.

constraints: The study excluded the comprehension-training group and no-treatment control group, so the program was studied combined with classroom instruction, not as a standalone comparison
target_learners: first-grade students at risk for reading difficulties

word reading
fluency
examples: Students progressed through increasingly difficult material; lesson performance determined whether they repeated, proceeded, or skipped the next lesson

article_title: Reading enjoyment amongst non-leisure readers can affect achievement in secondary school
citation: Mol SE and Jolles J (2014) Reading enjoyment amongst non-leisure readers can affect achievement in secondary school. Front. Psychol. 5:1214. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01214
title: Positive spiral of reciprocal causation between leisure reading, skills, enjoyment, and achievement
description: The article organizes its predictions around a reciprocal-causation account in which leisure reading builds academic skills, which in turn sustain enjoyment and voluntary reading. The article states that "A positive spiral of reciprocal causation seems to explain that leisure readers increase skills that are important for their academic success, such as their vocabulary and reading comprehension." Better skilled readers are described as more likely to enjoy reading, continue voluntarily, and raise school performance, while non-leisure readers are placed at highest risk of poor achievement. The study uses this model to motivate examining enjoyment and imagery among non-leisure readers in both educational tracks.
requirements: Applies to voluntary leisure reading of books; the article notes it is unknown whether other text types (newspapers, blogs, informative websites) feed the same spiral.
constraints: The article treats the spiral as an explanatory model, not a tested causal path; its own study is correlational.
target_learners: Secondary school students in early adolescence (12- to 13-year-old seventh graders)
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension, vocabulary, and academic achievement in language-based school subjects
examples: The survey of 1,071 Dutch seventh graders tested the model's prediction that non-leisure readers who enjoy reading achieve more, confirming it in most subgroups.
key_sources: Mol SE and Jolles J (2014) Reading enjoyment amongst non-leisure readers can affect achievement in secondary school. Front. Psychol. 5:1214. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01214

article_title: Early language and executive skills predict variations in number and arithmetic skills in children at family-risk of dyslexia and typically developing controls
citation: Moll K., Snowling M. J., Göbel S. M., Hulme C. (2015). Early language and executive skills predict variations in number and arithmetic skills in children at family-risk of dyslexia and typically developing controls. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.03.004
title: Verbal number skills as the mediating pathway from early language and executive skills to formal arithmetic
description: The article proposes a developmental pathway in which language and executive skills at 3–4 years constrain children's ability to learn to count and to match Arabic numerals to verbal labels one year later, and these exact verbal number skills in turn support formal arithmetic. As the authors conclude, "Language and executive skills at 3–4 years of age constrain the ability to learn to count and to match Arabic numerals to their verbal labels one year later and exert an indirect influence on arithmetic ability via these more proximal domain-specific precursors." This account explains why problems in early language development may explain the comorbidity between reading and mathematics disorder.
requirements: Longitudinal assessment beginning before formal education to trace causal influences
constraints: Non-verbal number skills such as estimation or magnitude comparison were not measured, so the theory concerns verbal number skills specifically
target_learners: preschool children aged 3–5
children at family-risk of dyslexia
target_learning_goals: counting
number knowledge
arithmetic development
examples: The multi-group path model fitting this pathway to 169 children showed complete mediation with excellent fit

article_title: The development of self-regulation across early childhood.
citation: Montroy Janelle J., Bowles Ryan P., Skibbe Lori E., McClelland Megan M., Morrison Frederick J. (2016). The Development of Self-Regulation across Early Childhood. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000159
title: Behavioral self-regulation as coordinated integration of executive function skills into overt classroom behavior
description: The article frames behavioral self-regulation as a multi-component construct in which children coordinate executive function skills with motor and verbal functions to produce regulated overt behavior. It states that "Effective self-regulation in the classroom requires that the child seamlessly coordinate multiple aspects of top down control (i.e., executive function) such as attention, working memory, and inhibitory control along with motor or verbal functions". Development involves these initially separate skills becoming organized and integrated over time, with a qualitative shift between ages three and seven. The framework distinguishes cool executive functions, which the HTKS mostly draws on, from hot ones.
requirements: Assessment and support must address the integration of multiple executive function skills rather than single skills in isolation
constraints: The HTKS generally draws on cool aspects of executive function, though no task is entirely free of emotional context
target_learners: children ages three to seven in preschool through early elementary school
target_learning_goals: behavioral self-regulation for classroom functioning
examples: The study used the HTKS task, in which children must do the opposite of paired rules, to assess this integrated form of self-regulation longitudinally
key_sources: Montroy Janelle J., Bowles Ryan P., Skibbe Lori E., McClelland Megan M., Morrison Frederick J. (2016). The Development of Self-Regulation across Early Childhood. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000159

article_title: The development of self-regulation across early childhood.
citation: Montroy Janelle J., Bowles Ryan P., Skibbe Lori E., McClelland Megan M., Morrison Frederick J. (2016). The Development of Self-Regulation across Early Childhood. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000159
title: Head-Toes-Knees-Shoulders (HTKS) task for assessing early childhood behavioral self-regulation
description: The HTKS is a direct assessment of behavioral self-regulation for children ages three to seven. "The HTKS is a short, game-like task where children are asked to 'do the opposite' in regards to a set of paired rules", tapping attention, working memory, and inhibition. Scores range from 0–40, with two points for correct responses and one for self-corrections. The article reports strong reliability (Cronbach's alpha .85–.94 across samples) and validity evidence, and notes growth in HTKS performance does not appear to be a function of practice effects.
requirements: Administered by trained research assistants in a quiet setting; children responding correctly to four or more of the first ten items receive the ten additional two-rule items
constraints: In the first year of the Michigan longitudinal sample only the first half was administered, requiring Rasch-based extrapolation to the full 40-item score
target_learners: children ages three to seven in preschool through early elementary school
target_learning_goals: behavioral self-regulation
examples: Used across all three samples with up to eight measurement occasions per child between preschool and first grade
key_sources: Montroy Janelle J., Bowles Ryan P., Skibbe Lori E., McClelland Megan M., Morrison Frederick J. (2016). The Development of Self-Regulation across Early Childhood. Developmental Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000159

article_title: An Excel sheet for inferring children’s number-knower levels from give-N data
citation: Negen, J., Sarnecka, B. W., & Lee, M. D. (2011). An Excel sheet for inferring children's number-knower levels from give-N data. Behavior Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-011-0134-4
title: The Lee and Sarnecka Bayesian knower-level model of give-N task behavior
description: A probabilistic generative model in which children's give-N answers are understood as Bayesian reasoning based on prior knowledge of number concepts and trial-by-trial experimenter instructions. It specifies a base rate — a distribution of prior probabilities describing what chance responding looks like — which is updated by an evidence value v when the child is asked for N items: known meanings become more likely, other known meanings less likely, and unknown meanings retain base-rate relative probabilities. The article implements it as a graphical model with a knower-level parameter per child.
requirements: Requires computational sampling methods (Markov chain Monte Carlo) to implement, which the article notes demands considerable expertise and effort from users
constraints: The article states implementing the full model would require most developmental researchers to learn a host of new technical skills
target_learners: young children (preschool-aged) being assessed on number concepts
target_learning_goals: inferring stages of number-word and cardinality concept development (knower levels)
examples: The article applies the model to 423 calibration sessions to obtain point probabilities for the Excel approximation, e.g. the chance that a 1-knower gives 1 when asked for one is 83.33%
key_sources: Negen, J., Sarnecka, B. W., & Lee, M. D. (2011). An Excel sheet for inferring children's number-knower levels from give-N data. Behavior Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-011-0134-4

article_title: An Excel sheet for inferring children’s number-knower levels from give-N data
citation: Negen, J., Sarnecka, B. W., & Lee, M. D. (2011). An Excel sheet for inferring children's number-knower levels from give-N data. Behavior Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-011-0134-4
title: Knower-LevelEstimater.xls — an Excel tool for Bayesian-style knower-level inference
description: A Microsoft Excel sheet, available at www.cogsci.uci.edu/cogdev/Negen/Knower-LevelEstimater.xls, that computes an approximation of the full Bayesian model's knower-level inference. The user enters question and response pairs (each in the range 1 to 15) and optional prior weights for knower levels; the sheet automatically calculates the likelihood of each pair conditional on each knower level and outputs posterior probabilities for the six knower levels, plus log-likelihoods and a graph.
requirements: Data entries must be in the range of 1 to 15; the sheet handles one child's data at a time; the child must have had exactly 15 items available to give
constraints: The article states the sheet is only appropriate for experiments in which the child had exactly 15 items to give, and if the child was asked for more than 15 items some other method of analysis must be used
target_learners: young children completing the give-N task
target_learning_goals: estimating a child's number-knower level from give-N task data
examples: In the worked example, a child asked for one through five and giving 1, 2, 3, 3, and 6 with equal priors yields about 60% posterior confidence that the child is a 2-knower
key_sources: Negen, J., Sarnecka, B. W., & Lee, M. D. (2011). An Excel sheet for inferring children's number-knower levels from give-N data. Behavior Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-011-0134-4

article_title: Number-Concept Acquisition and General Vocabulary Development
citation: Negen, J., & Sarnecka, B. W. (2012). Number-Concept Acquisition and General Vocabulary Development. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2012.01815.x
title: Number-knower-level framework: children learn one, two, three (and sometimes four) one at a time, then make an inductive leap to the cardinality principle.
description: The framework describes stages of number-word knowledge: children first recite a count list that is "largely empty of meaning", then learn meanings of "one," "two," "three" (and sometimes "four") one at a time and in order, being called one-knowers, two-knowers, and so on. Sometime after learning these, children make a "major inductive leap" understanding that the last word counted indicates the cardinality of the set — the cardinality principle — becoming CP-knowers. The article uses Give-N task performance to assign each child a knower-level, which serves as the dependent measure throughout.
requirements: Give-N task data with titration-style adaptive trials to classify each child's knower-level
constraints: Knower-level coding as zero through five, spaced evenly, yields correlations smaller than effect-size measures allowing unequal group distances
target_learners: typically-developing children aged 30–60 months
target_learning_goals: acquisition of exact cardinal number-word meanings
examples: Experiment 1's Give-N yielded 3 pre-number-knowers, 4 one-knowers, 4 two-knowers, 2 three-knowers, 2 four-knowers, and 11 CP-knowers
key_sources: Negen, J., & Sarnecka, B. W. (2012). Number-Concept Acquisition and General Vocabulary Development. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2012.01815.x

article_title: Which preschool mathematics competencies are most predictive of fifth grade achievement?
citation: Nguyen, T., Watts, T. W., Duncan, G. J., Clements, D. H., Sarama, J. S., Wolfe, C., & Spitler, M. E. (2016). Which Preschool Mathematics Competencies Are Most Predictive of Fifth Grade Achievement? Early Childhood Research Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2016.02.003
title: Emphasize advanced counting competencies, not just rote verbal counting, in preschool mathematics instruction
description: The article concludes that early mathematics education should promote numeracy, specifically advanced counting: "our findings suggest that early mathematics education should promote the development of numeracy competencies, specifically advanced counting." Teachers should not restrict instruction to basic counting, since advanced counting skills include basic practice while developing cardinality, counting on, and conceptual subitizing. Recommended classroom activities include counting objects in arrays, comparing block-building quantities, and solving simple addition and subtraction problems in geometry or measurement contexts.
requirements: Teachers need focused time and practice on counting embedded throughout the school day, with discussion and clarification of children's ideas
constraints: The authors caution that successfully teaching advanced counting in preschool may not be sufficient for long-run impacts if kindergarten instruction does not build on it, and the underlying associations are correlational
target_learners: preschool-aged children, particularly those from low-income and minority backgrounds
target_learning_goals: early number sense, counting and cardinality, and long-run mathematics achievement
examples: The study coded REMA items into basic counting (verbal counting, one-to-one correspondence, number recognition) and advanced counting (cardinality, counting forward or back from a given number, conceptual subitizing) and found advanced counting more predictive
key_sources: Nguyen, T., Watts, T. W., Duncan, G. J., Clements, D. H., Sarama, J. S., Wolfe, C., & Spitler, M. E. (2016). Which Preschool Mathematics Competencies Are Most Predictive of Fifth Grade Achievement? Early Childhood Research Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2016.02.003

article_title: Developmental Changes in the Profiles of Dyscalculia: An Explanation Based on a Double Exact-and-Approximate Number Representation Model
citation: Noël M-P and Rousselle L (2011) Developmental changes in the profiles of dyscalculia: an explanation based on a double exact-and-approximate number representation model. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 5:165. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2011.00165
title: Double exact-and-approximate number representation model: an exact representation of numerical value built from symbolic number learning, alongside the approximate number system
description: The article proposes that human number cognition rests on two semantic representations: the approximate number system (ANS), shared with animals and yielding noisy magnitude estimates, and an exact representation of numerical value that emerges only through learning symbolic numbers embedded in a counting sequence. The authors argue that "the learning of symbolic numbers would lead to the emergence of a new numerical representation system in human ontogeny," endowed with semantic content based on the ordinal information in the symbol sequence. They use this model to explain the developmental profile of DD: the first deficit concerns building the exact representation, while reduced ANS acuity is a later, secondary consequence.
requirements: Learning of a number system based on the successor function and embedded in a counting process
constraints: The exact representation of large numbers develops only given a counting system; cultures with very limited number lexicon do not develop it beyond 3 or 4, per the evidence the article cites
target_learners: children in typical and atypical numerical development
children with developmental dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: understanding the cardinal meaning of symbolic numbers
building exact representations of natural numbers
examples: The article contrasts this model with the 'simple story' in which number words take their meaning by mapping directly onto the ANS
key_sources: Noël M-P and Rousselle L (2011) Developmental changes in the profiles of dyscalculia: an explanation based on a double exact-and-approximate number representation model. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 5:165. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2011.00165

article_title: Developmental Changes in the Profiles of Dyscalculia: An Explanation Based on a Double Exact-and-Approximate Number Representation Model
citation: Noël M-P and Rousselle L (2011) Developmental changes in the profiles of dyscalculia: an explanation based on a double exact-and-approximate number representation model. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 5:165. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2011.00165
title: Carey's developmental account: exact number concepts built via parallel individuation and the successor function, then mapped onto the ANS
description: The article describes Carey's (2001, 2004, 2009) model as illustrating the standpoint that symbolic number meaning is not gained by simple mapping onto the ANS. Representations of natural numbers are first built on a "parallel individuation" system that keeps track of items in small sets through mental models, providing an exact though implicit representation of small numerosities. The child then must "discover that the cardinal value of a number word is determined by its order on the list, and that successive numbers are related by the function '+1'" — the successor function, worked out by induction. Only after creating this exact representation does the child start to map it with the ANS.
requirements: Discovery of the successor function by induction on knowledge of the cardinal meaning of one through four
A two-stage process in which children first understand that adding one item leads to a cardinal labeled by a word further along the counting list, then that it is labeled by the word just after
constraints: The parallel individuation system is very limited and only allows the child to track 3 or 4 items in parallel
target_learners: preschool and early primary children learning counting and number words
target_learning_goals: acquiring the cardinal meaning of number words
mastering the successor function
examples: Sarnecka and Carey (2008) showed the conceptual jump to the successor function is at least a two-stage process, as the article reports
key_sources: Noël M-P and Rousselle L (2011) Developmental changes in the profiles of dyscalculia: an explanation based on a double exact-and-approximate number representation model. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 5:165. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2011.00165

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives
citation: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8
title: Cognitive load theory: instructional control of working memory load based on the human cognitive architecture
description: CLT is concerned with learning complex cognitive tasks in which learners are overwhelmed by interactive information elements. It uses knowledge of human cognitive architecture — an effectively unlimited long-term memory interacting with a working memory that is "very limited in both capacity and duration" — to generate instructional techniques. Instructional control of excessively high load imposed by complex tasks provides the theory's focus.
requirements: Instruction must be structured around the characteristics of working memory, since WM processes information before it can be stored in long-term memory
constraints: The theory concerns complex cognitive tasks where learners are often overwhelmed by the number of interactive information elements
target_learners: learners of complex cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: schema acquisition in long-term memory
complex problem-solving skill
examples: The article cites worked-example study, part-whole task simplification, task variability, and self-explanation as CLT-generated instructional techniques
key_sources: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives
citation: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8
title: Three categories of cognitive load: intrinsic, extraneous, and germane, with communicating-vessel dynamics
description: CLT identifies three categories of cognitive load: intrinsic load caused by the complexity of the materials, extraneous load caused by poorly designed instructional procedures that interfere with schema acquisition, and germane load, the working memory resources devoted to dealing with intrinsic load. The article states that "it is important to consider extraneous and germane cognitive load as communicating vessels", because reducing extraneous load frees resources for germane processing.
requirements: Extraneous load must first be eliminated; intrinsic load must be managed so that simultaneous processing of all interactive elements remains possible
constraints: When intrinsic cognitive load is high, decreasing extraneous load becomes especially important, otherwise the combination might exceed maximum cognitive capacity
target_learners: learners of complex cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: schema acquisition
effective use of working memory resources
examples: Studying worked examples instead of solving conventional problems is described as an effective way of reducing extraneous load
key_sources: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives
citation: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8
title: Element interactivity as a uniform foundation for redefining intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load
description: The special issue's first article (Sweller) redefines the load constructs by relating them to element interactivity, originally used only to define intrinsic load. Extraneous load is now assumed to be caused by element interactivity not essential to the task at hand, and germane load consists of the WM resources used to deal with element interactivity that contributes to learning. The article reports that defining both intrinsic and extraneous load in terms of element interactivity may allow researchers to analyze it prior to an experiment and more easily predict experimental outcomes.
requirements: Element interactivity must be analyzable prior to an experiment for the predictive advantage to be realized
constraints: The redefinition responds to recent problems of defining and measuring the load categories (e.g., Schnotz and Kürschner 2007)
target_learners: learners of complex cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: schema acquisition
prediction of cognitive load effects
examples: The article states the new conceptualizations could lead to the generation of new instructional procedures
key_sources: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives
citation: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8
title: Integrating cognitive load and social-cognitive research perspectives on example-based learning (worked examples vs. modeling examples)
description: The special issue's third article (Van Gog & Rummel) reviews and contrasts two example-based learning traditions: worked examples, studied in cognitive load research as didactical worked-out problem solutions in written format, and modeling examples, studied in social-cognitive research where learners observe someone performing a task. The article argues the two forms have "clear and interesting connections and analogs" and that studies drawing on both perspectives may advance the knowledge base on example-based learning.
requirements: Researchers must consider measures from both traditions, e.g., cognitive load in modeling-example studies and self-efficacy in worked-example studies
constraints: Model characteristics such as age, gender, and type of performance are not relevant for written worked examples but may matter in video-based examples or animations
target_learners: learners studying worked or modeled problem solutions
target_learning_goals: schema construction from examples
self-efficacy
examples: Modeling-example research considers model characteristics such as mastery vs. coping type of performance
key_sources: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives
citation: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8
title: Generalized knowledge structures at a medium level of generality as a means to facilitate flexible problem-solving skills
description: The special issue's fourth article (Kalyuga, Renkl & Paas) suggests CLT could be improved by increased emphasis on generalized knowledge structures rather than its current emphasis on domain-specific knowledge. The focus is not on generic universal problem-solving heuristics but on domain-specific knowledge at "a medium level of generality between generic knowledge and the routine low-level knowledge structures". Based on a review of theoretical and empirical evidence, the authors conclude such structures could be important for developing flexible expertise.
requirements: The proposed emphasis concerns domain-specific knowledge of medium generality, not generic universal problem-solving heuristics
constraints: CLT's success derives largely from its emphasis on domain-specific knowledge, and it was devised partly as a reaction to failed theories advocating general knowledge structures
target_learners: learners developing flexible problem-solving expertise
target_learning_goals: flexible problem-solving skills
adaptive instruction
examples: The conclusion rests on a review of theoretical foundations and empirical evidence on CLT, problem solving, and adaptive instruction
key_sources: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8

article_title: Fostering Critical Thinking Skills in Preschool Education: Designing, Implementing and Assessing a Multiliteracies-Oriented Program Based on Intercultural Tales
citation: Papadopoulos, I., & Bisiri, E. (2020). Fostering Critical Thinking Skills in Preschool Education: Designing, Implementing and Assessing a Multiliteracies-Oriented Program Based on Intercultural Tales. Multilingual Academic Journal of Education and Social Sciences, 8(1), 87–105. https://doi.org/10.46886/MAJESS/v8-i1/7263
title: Multiliteracies pedagogy organized around four knowledge processes: experiencing, conceptualizing, analyzing, applying
description: The article applies the pedagogy of multiliteracies, in which literacy is treated as active meaning-making across multiple modes rather than sentence-bound rules of spelling and grammar. It states that "The pedagogy of Multiliteracies suggests transformative ways of knowing, the four ‘knowledge processes’: ‘experiencing, conceptualizing, analyzing and applying’", and these processes serve as an outline for educators' pedagogical actions. Each folk-tale thematic unit in the program was designed around these four processes, with tasks such as experiencing the known/new, conceptualizing by naming and with theory, analysing functionally and critically, and applying appropriately and creatively.
requirements: Implementation depends on the active roles of both teachers and learners as instruments of design in a multimodal environment, with teachers facilitating and creating motivating learning conditions
constraints: The article frames the framework for early-childhood literacy instruction in multicultural preschool settings; assessment of multiliterate skills requires alternative methods such as portfolios rather than discrete-point testing
target_learners: preschool children (5-year-olds) in multicultural classrooms
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
multiliteracies and multimodal meaning-making
multicultural sensitivity
examples: Each of the seven folk-tales formed a thematic unit lasting 2 to 3 weeks, with tasks A–L mapped onto the four knowledge processes

Fostering Critical Thinking Skills in Preschool Education: Designing, Implementing and Assessing a Multiliteracies-Oriented Program Based on Intercultural Tales. article_title: Fostering Critical Thinking Skills in Preschool Education: Designing, Implementing and Assessing a Multiliteracies-Oriented Program Based on Intercultural Tales
citation: Papadopoulos, I., & Bisiri, E. (2020). Fostering Critical Thinking Skills in Preschool Education: Designing, Implementing and Assessing a Multiliteracies-Oriented Program Based on Intercultural Tales. Multilingual Academic Journal of Education and Social Sciences, 8(1), 87–105. https://doi.org/10.46886/MAJESS/v8-i1/7263
title: Intercultural folk-tale multiliteracies program for preschool critical thinking
description: A seven-month pedagogical program implemented in a preschool in Larissa, Central Greece, during the school year 2018-2019 with 25 five-year-old children (48% boys, 52% girls). A mini syllabus was "centered around intercultural folk-tales, incorporating multiple creative activities that fostered a more critical stance and behavior of the children." Seven folk-tales from Greece, Albania, Cyprus, Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, North Macedonia and Croatia each formed a thematic unit lasting 2 to 3 weeks, with expected outcomes in critical thinking, social skills and multicultural sensitivity.
requirements: Folk-tales unfamiliar to the children were deliberately chosen, on the researchers' view that children develop more critical tendencies when coming into contact with something not known to them
constraints: Applied to a single class of 25 Greek-origin preschoolers in one school; evaluation relied on qualitative journal and portfolio data
target_learners: preschool children aged 5
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
collaboration and communication
multicultural awareness

article_title: Self-regulation in the pre-adolescent brain
citation: Pas P., Hulshoff Pol H.E., Raemaekers M., Vink M. (2021). Self-regulation in the pre-adolescent brain. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2021.101012
title: Frontal control over subcortical regions as the developmental basis of proactive inhibitory control
description: The article works within a framework in which self-regulation develops through the integration of low-level executive functions such as reactive inhibition into higher-level proactive control, which "has been theorized to depend upon the establishment of frontal control over the rest of the brain, in particular subcortical regions". On this account, the shift from reactive to proactive inhibition strategies is linked to increased frontal activation and increased functional coupling between frontal and subcortical regions. The study tests this framework in pre-adolescent children by relating questionnaire-based self-regulation to frontal activation and cortico-subcortical coupling during a stop-signal anticipation task.
requirements: Measurement of both reactive and proactive inhibition with concurrent fMRI to index frontal activation and functional coupling
constraints: The article notes its cross-sectional data does not provide a definitive answer to how self-regulation increases relate to neural changes
target_learners: Typically developing children aged 8–11
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation and inhibitory control development
examples: The study related EATQ-R self-regulation scores to right mid frontal cortex activation and striatal-motor coupling in 640 children performing the Stop-Signal Anticipation Task
key_sources: Pas P., Hulshoff Pol H.E., Raemaekers M., Vink M. (2021). Self-regulation in the pre-adolescent brain. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2021.101012

article_title: Race Salience and Essentialist Thinking in Racial Stereotype Development
citation: Pauker, K., Ambady, N., & Apfelbaum, E. P. (2010). Race Salience and Essentialist Thinking in Racial Stereotype Development. Child Development, 81(6), 1799–1813. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2010.01511.x
title: Developmental intergroup theory: psychological salience, categorization, and essentialism as core processes in stereotype formation
description: The article draws on Bigler and Liben's (2007) developmental intergroup theory, which proposes that "three core processes contribute to the formation of social stereotypes and prejudice: (a) establishing the psychological salience of different person attributes, (b) categorizing individuals by salient dimensions, and (c) developing sets of traits, behaviors, and emotions that are associated with particular salient social groups." The theory holds that once a dimension becomes salient, essentialism, in-group bias, and explicit and implicit attributions mold the development of stereotyping about that dimension, with perceptual discriminability, proportional group size, and explicit and implicit use shaping salience. The present study tested two components the theory suggests should affect racial stereotyping: race salience and essentialist thinking.
requirements: Race must become a psychologically salient dimension before categorization and stereotype development proceed along it
constraints: The article tested only the race salience and essentialist thinking components of the theory, not the full model
target_learners: children ages 3–10
target_learning_goals: understanding the development of racial stereotypes and prejudice in childhood
examples: The study measured children's spontaneous sorting by race, racial justification, and racial constancy for self and others as operationalizations of the theory's salience and essentialism components
key_sources: Pauker, K., Ambady, N., & Apfelbaum, E. P. (2010). Race Salience and Essentialist Thinking in Racial Stereotype Development. Child Development, 81(6), 1799–1813. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2010.01511.x

article_title: Gendered Pathways: How Mathematics Ability Beliefs Shape Secondary and Postsecondary Course and Degree Field Choices
citation: Perez-Felkner L, Nix S and Thomas K (2017) Gendered Pathways: How Mathematics Ability Beliefs Shape Secondary and Postsecondary Course and Degree Field Choices. Front. Psychol. 8:386. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00386
title: Enhance girls' beliefs about their mathematics ability under challenge, supported by social support from teachers, mentors, parents, and peers
description: The article recommends enhancing students' — especially girls' — beliefs about their mathematics ability when encountering challenging material, because these beliefs predict advanced science coursework and PEMC major selection at every stage. It states that "social support—from teachers, mentors, parents, peers—could be a valuable tool to scaﬀold students through challenges" and help girls counter lower beliefs about their mathematics ability. Recent interventions aiming to build resilience and malleable conceptions of intelligence are cited as promising approaches.
requirements: Feeling challenged is treated as a normal and necessary part of learning, so support should scaffold students through challenges rather than avoid difficulty
constraints: The recommendation rests on longitudinal observational associations, not on a test of the interventions themselves
target_learners: secondary school students, especially girls in mathematics-intensive course pathways
target_learning_goals: persistence in mathematics and science coursework and pursuit of PEMC degree fields
examples: The article cites science camps like SciGirls, recruiting girls into upper level science courses and extracurricular activities, informal science learning experiences, and increasing visibility of women scientists

article_title: Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence
citation: Emily Grossnickle Peterson, Adam B. Weinberger, David H. Uttal, Bob Kolvoord and Adam E. Green. (2020). Spatial activity participation in childhood and adolescence: consistency and relations to spatial thinking in adolescence. Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41235-020-00239-0
title: Bidirectional developmental model of spatial activities and spatial thinking across childhood and adolescence
description: The article proposes that relations between spatial activity participation and spatial thinking are bidirectional and can be examined at a single time point or across development (Fig. 1a, 1b). As the authors state, "participation in spatial activities may improve spatial thinking skills and strategies, and individuals with a greater capacity for spatial thinking may seek out opportunities to engage in spatial activities." The model distinguishes spatial skills from spatial habits of mind as distinct yet correlated facets of spatial thinking, and maps paths linking childhood activity participation, adolescent activity participation, and each facet. The present study tested the paths across development (Fig. 1b) rather than at a single point in time.
requirements: Measures of spatial activity participation at multiple developmental points (here, retrospective childhood CAQ and adolescent SAQ reports) and measures of both spatial skills and spatial habits of mind
constraints: The study was cross-sectional with retrospective self-report, so directionality of the relations could not be established; the authors call for longitudinal and intervention designs to test causal mechanisms
target_learners: Adolescents in grades 10–12
Children and adolescents in STEM education contexts
target_learning_goals: Spatial thinking skills
Spatial habits of mind (spatial problem-solving strategies)
examples: The study regressed Paper Folding and SHOMI jointly on childhood and adolescent activity measures, testing paths B and C of the developmental model

article_title: Fostering alphabet knowledge development: a comparison of two instructional approaches
citation: Piasta, S. B., Purpura, D. J., & Wagner, R. K. (2010). Fostering Alphabet Knowledge Development: A Comparison of Two Instructional Approaches. Reading and Writing, 23(6), 607-626. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11145-009-9174-x
title: Teach letter names and sounds together rather than letter sounds alone when fostering preschool alphabet knowledge
description: The article's central design recommendation is that for U.S. preschoolers, referring to each letter by its name and linking it to its corresponding sound (e.g., "the letter C that makes the sound/k/") fosters letter sound acquisition better than sound-only labeling. The authors state that "combined letter name and sound instruction may be most beneficial for U.S. preschoolers alphabet learning", while noting the mechanism is not entirely clear and more research is needed.
requirements: Instruction delivered in small groups (3-5 children) through scripted lessons of approximately 10-15 minutes, as in the study's 34-lesson curriculum
constraints: The advantage was specific to alphabet knowledge outcomes and did not generalize to other emergent literacy skills

Based on a small-scale study with observed power substantially lower than the intended 80%

target_learning_goals: letter name knowledge
letter sound knowledge
examples: In the study, LNLS lessons referred to each letter by name and linked it to its sound, while LS lessons designated letters only by sound; both taught 26 uppercase letters plus 8 weekly review lessons over 9 weeks

article_title: Physical activity and creativity of children and youths
citation: Piya-amornphan N, Santiworakul A, Cetthakrikul S, Srirug P. (2020). Physical activity and creativity of children and youths. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-020-2017-2
title: Physical activity during childhood supports development of thinking processes including creativity
description: The article advances the account that childhood is a valuable period for developing creative skills because cognitive abilities attributed to prefrontal cortex function are required for creativity, and the prefrontal cortex does not completely mature until the early 20s. It concludes that "optimal physical activity is required during childhood for developing thinking process", positioning physical activity — especially active play — as supportive of cognitive development alongside previously reported links to intelligence and emotional quotients.
requirements: Physical activity during childhood, with active play as the directly reported indicator of physical activity in children and youths
constraints: The account rests on cross-sectional correlations; the article states many factors related to creativity remain and more information is needed to clarify other factors
target_learners: children and youths aged 6–17
target_learning_goals: creativity
cognitive function development
examples: The article cites cross-sectional studies in which increased physical activity was associated with higher intelligence quotient in 135 Saudi high school students and higher emotional quotient in 599 Taiwanese college students

article_title: Costs of Selective Attention: When Children Notice What Adults Miss
citation: Plebanek, D. J., & Sloutsky, V. M. (2017). Costs of Selective Attention: When Children Notice what Adults Miss. Psychological Science, 28(6), 723-732. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617693005
title: Developmental shift from distributed to selective attention account
description: The article proposes that early attention is distributed across multiple stimulus dimensions because attention-control circuits are immature, so young children process task-irrelevant information well; with maturation, top-down selective attention develops, bringing efficiency for relevant information at the cost of attenuated processing of non-selected information. The article states that "Distributed attention early in development (stemming from the immaturity of attention-control circuits, Posner & Rothbart, 2007) results in greater processing of task-irrelevant information than more mature selective attention." Selection is described as supplementing, not replacing, diffuse attention within an attentional hierarchy.
requirements: Immature attention-control circuits in early development for the distributed-attention prediction; mature circuits for the selective-attention prediction
constraints: Young children are unlikely to exhibit top-down selectivity because supporting neural circuits are not fully developed; adults may distribute attention under high task demand such as high working memory load, and aging may also weaken top-down control
target_learners: 4-to-5-year-old children
adults
target_learning_goals: Processing of task-relevant and task-irrelevant information
development of selective attention
examples: Experiment 1 cued/uncued change detection and Experiment 2 visual search with recognition of relevant and irrelevant features, both showing the predicted reversal

title: MD subtype framework: MD-only versus MDRD differential difficulty
description: The article evaluates Geary's hypothesis that math difficulty subtypes represent distinct cognitive profiles. MDRD students' concurrent math and reading difficulty is attributed to weak phonological processing that hinders acquisition of vocabulary and math facts, whereas MD-only students' poor fact recall is attributed to weak number sense. The randomized trial's differential responsiveness finding is offered as support that MD-only versus MDRD "may represent a viable scheme for subtyping mathematics disability."

article_title: Language in the prediction of arithmetics in kindergarten and grade 1
citation: Praet, M., Titeca, D., Ceulemans, A., & Desoete, A. (2013). Language in the prediction of arithmetic in kindergarten and grade 1. Learning and Individual Differences (manuscript LAEIND-D-12-OO174R1). https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/LAEIND-D-12-OO174R1
title: Assess kindergarten language and number naming to inform targeted instruction and interventions for children at risk of arithmetic difficulties
description: The article argues that knowledge of kindergarten predictors should guide early support: "Such knowledge is necessary in order to inform targeted instruction and interventions that address the needs of children at risk". Because expressive language and number naming explained unique variance in early arithmetic, assessing these skills in kindergarten may identify children who need help before formal schooling compounds difficulties. The authors suggest future work test whether intervention on these skills raises grade 1 arithmetic.

children at risk of mathematical learning disabilities

article_title: Physical Fitness Level Is Related to Attention and Concentration in Adolescents
citation: Reigal RE, Moral-Campillo L, Juárez-Ruiz de Mier R, Morillo-Baro JP, Morales-Sánchez V, Pastrana JL and Hernández-Mendo A (2020) Physical Fitness Level Is Related to Attention and Concentration in Adolescents. Front. Psychol. 11:110. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00110
title: Physical activity for adolescents should be demanding enough to overcome a minimum adaptation threshold to benefit cognition
description: This principle holds that mere physical activity participation is not enough for cognitive benefit; activity must be sufficiently exigent to drive fitness adaptation, which the article links to better brain outcomes. It frames fitness level, not activity per se, as the relevant indicator. The article states "the practice of physical activity alone is not enough for the impact on the brain to be noticeable."
requirements: Physical activity of sufficient intensity/exigency to produce measurable fitness adaptation
constraints: The design does not allow causal relationships to be established; the threshold is an interpretation, not a tested optimum
target_learners: adolescents aged 11–15
target_learning_goals: selective attention and concentration as cognitive functions supporting academic and psychosocial adjustment
examples: The study classified participants into lower- and higher-fitness clusters via horizontal jump, 5×10 m speed and VO2max measures, and the higher-fitness cluster scored better on attention and concentration in both genders.

article_title: Differences between presentation methods in working memory procedures: A matter of working memory consolidation.
citation: Ricker Timothy J., Cowan Nelson. (2014). Differences between Presentation Methods in Working Memory Procedures: A Matter of Working Memory Consolidation. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0034301
title: Working memory consolidation account of time-based forgetting
description: The article proposes that a post-encoding consolidation process, continuing after pattern masking, strengthens working memory traces and determines their vulnerability to time-based forgetting. Consolidation is distinguished from encoding: "consolidation is further processing that can occur even after a mask, and that helps makes the representation of the stimulus more resistant to forgetting". The experiments show that "the total amount of time available to consolidate the stimuli into working memory is what is important", reconciling studies that do and do not find duration-based forgetting. Candidate mechanisms discussed include attentional refreshing, neural desynchronization, and pattern identification or chunking.
requirements: Requires an encoded memory trace and central resources for consolidation to proceed after masking, as suggested by Jolicoeur and Dell'Acqua (1998)
constraints: The finding was obtained always with fairly substantial encoding times of at least 250 ms per item
The article does not try to distinguish short-term consolidation empirically from long-term consolidation, calling this a major and difficult future issue
The study did not manipulate interference, so consolidation's effect on interference-based forgetting is speculative
target_learners: adult college students performing working memory tasks
target_learning_goals: understanding maintenance of information in working memory over short retention intervals
examples: Across the four experiments, sequential conditions with post-mask free time showed 0.19-0.22 items forgotten between 1 and 12 s, while conditions without such free time showed 0.39-0.67 items forgotten.

article_title: Creativity: The role of unconscious processes in idea generation and idea selection
citation: Ritter, S.M.; van Baaren, R.B.; Dijksterhuis, A.J. (2012). Creativity: The role of unconscious processes in idea generation and idea selection. Thinking Skills and Creativity, 7, 21-27. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2011.12.002
title: Unconscious thought theory: unconscious thought actively evaluates, weights, and integrates information
description: The article draws on dual process theories distinguishing a conscious, rule-based, controlled system from an unconscious, associative, automatic system, and on the theory of unconscious thought, under which "unconscious thought" is task-related thought occurring while conscious attention is directed elsewhere. It assumes unconscious thought is good at "evaluating, weighting, and integrating attribute information concerning various alternatives", which is why it predicts selection advantages after distraction. The paper extends this account to creativity, proposing the unconscious plays an active rather than merely passive role during incubation.
requirements: A distraction period during which conscious attention is directed elsewhere, so unconscious thought can operate on the task
constraints: The article notes prior research had yielded no sound empirical support for beneficial effects of unconscious processes on creative performance when only idea generation is measured
target_learners: adult students generating creative ideas
target_learning_goals: creative idea generation and selection of one's most creative idea
examples: In both experiments, participants in the unconscious thought condition clicked as quickly as possible on circles appearing at random screen locations for 2 min before listing ideas.
