article_title: Creativity: The role of unconscious processes in idea generation and idea selection
citation: Ritter, S.M.; van Baaren, R.B.; Dijksterhuis, A.J. (2012). Creativity: The role of unconscious processes in idea generation and idea selection. Thinking Skills and Creativity, 7, 21-27. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2011.12.002
title: Insert a period of distraction before idea selection to improve selection of one's most creative idea
description: When learners have generated multiple ideas and must choose which to pursue, the article recommends a brief period of distraction during which unconscious thought can operate, rather than immediate selection or deliberate conscious deliberation. Participants "who had unconsciously thought about their ideas, however, were able to select their most creative and least creative idea from several self-generated ideas", whereas immediate and conscious-thought participants performed poorly at selection. The article presents this as "a means to enhance individuals' creative performance".
requirements: A set of self-generated ideas to choose among, and a roughly 2-minute unrelated distracting task to prevent task-relevant conscious thought
constraints: The benefit appeared for idea selection, not for the number or average creativity of generated ideas; the proposed evaluative-tagging mechanism is acknowledged as speculative
target_learners: adult students and creative professionals
target_learning_goals: selecting one's most creative idea for further elaboration and implementation
examples: In both experiments, participants first listed ideas for 2 min, then unconscious-thought-condition participants performed a rapid circle-clicking distraction task for 2 min before selecting their most creative idea.

article_title: Consequences of Age-Related Cognitive Declines
citation: Salthouse, T. (2012). Consequences of Age-Related Cognitive Declines. Annual Review of Psychology, 63, 201-226. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-120710-100328
title: Typical versus maximal performance distinction as an explanation for absent real-world consequences of cognitive decline
description: This explanatory account holds that everyday outcomes reflect typical functioning whereas cognitive tests assess maximal functioning, so age-related deficits appear only when demands approach maximal levels. The review states: "what we do in daily life reflects our typical level of functioning, whereas cognitive tests attempt to assess our maximal level of functioning". Because people seldom need to function at their maximum, declines may go undetected in daily-life criteria. The review presents this as the first of four candidate explanations for the lab-life discrepancy.
requirements: Outcome criteria must reflect typical rather than maximal performance for the discrepancy to arise
constraints: The account does not deny real declines; it holds they are not detected because people seldom function at the level where deficits would appear
target_learners: adult workers
older adults
target_learning_goals: explaining why laboratory-measured cognitive declines do not necessarily impair everyday occupational and daily functioning
examples: The review contrasts the age distribution of top-scoring reasoning performers, which peaks before age 30, with the age distribution of Fortune 500 CEOs, which peaks near 60

article_title: Sixth-grade students’ reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis
citation: Maike Schindler, Stephan Hußmann, Per Nilsson, Arthur Bakker. (2017). Sixth-grade students' reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis. Math Ed Res J 29:471–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13394-017-0202-x
title: Inferentialist epistemology for analyzing students' mathematical reasoning
description: The article develops an epistemological framework based on Brandom's inferentialism for studying students' reasoning on the order relation of integers. It treats reasoning as social, situated in the 'game of giving and asking for reasons' (GoGAR), implicitly normative, and holistic, with concepts interconnected in students' claims. It asks for the inferences students draw from out-of-school life, the mathematics classroom, contexts, and external representations such as the number line, prioritizing the reasoning itself over internal mental models.
requirements: Empirical settings must explicitly encourage students to make their reasons, inferences, and the origins of their inferences explicit
constraints: The framework does not aim to isolate individual knowledge or abstract mental models from students' utterances
target_learners: sixth-grade mathematics students
target_learning_goals: reasoning on the order relation of integers
examples: Semi-structured, task-oriented clinical interviews in which the interviewer asked 'Why's that?' and 'Where do you know this from?' before and after a lesson series

Students play a board game in groups of four in which each is an indebted person aiming to redeem debts; the board is a number line ('account bar') with positive and negative numbers, and players draw changing account balances with their pieces. Later problems invite reflection on positions on the account bar and the role of the minus sign, with temperatures and altitudes as further contexts.

article_title: The Contribution of Numerical Magnitude Comparison and Phonological Processing to Individual Differences in Fourth Graders’ Multiplication Fact Ability
citation: Schleepen TMJ, Van Mier HI, De Smedt B (2016) The Contribution of Numerical Magnitude Comparison and Phonological Processing to Individual Differences in Fourth Graders' Multiplication Fact Ability. PLoS ONE 11(6): e0158335. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0158335
title: Semantic-coding account: multiplication facts are stored as phonological/verbal codes in an interrelated semantic network, and symbolic magnitude comparison shares semantic mapping processes with fact retrieval
description: The article proposes that multiplication facts are stored in long-term memory as phonological (verbal) codes within a meaningfully organized, interrelated network of arithmetic facts. It argues that "magnitude" is a candidate dimension along which meaning is assigned to stored facts, so faster magnitude comparators can more easily access number-semantic fact representations. It further hypothesizes that symbolic magnitude comparison and multiplication fact retrieval "share the same semantic mapping processes", supported by cited neuroimaging work showing overlapping left temporo-parietal activation.
requirements: Multiplication facts must have been practiced enough that problem-answer pair associations are stored in long-term memory
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation, supported by cited prior work rather than tested directly in this study
target_learners: elementary school children learning single-digit multiplication tables
target_learning_goals: multiplication fact retrieval fluency
examples: The study tested this account by correlating symbolic and nonsymbolic magnitude comparison speed with multiplication fact speed in 63 fourth graders

title: The MACE pedagogy: five key features for integrating geometry and visual arts
description: The MACE pedagogy is an explanatory framework for integrated geometry and visual arts instruction built on five features the article names: "visual arts perception, open activities, reflection, communication with peers, and a specific role of the teacher". Artworks are discussed whole-class with visual thinking strategies; open activities invite artwork production at the boundary of the two disciplines without predetermined solutions; lessons end with reflection making implicit knowledge explicit; peer communication supports creative thinking and geometrical language; and teachers act as facilitators asking open, activating questions. The framework underpins the MACE lesson series and PD program evaluated in the study.

visual arts perception
examples: In the lesson Playing with perspective, students discussed six artworks on perspective and viewpoints, then made photos creating visual illusions in groups of 3-4 students, followed by whole-class reflection

citation: Eveline M. Schoevers & Paul P. M. Leseman & Evelyn H. Kroesbergen. (2019). International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10763-019-10018-z
title: MACE program: nine integrated geometry-visual-arts lessons plus a five-session teacher professional development program
description: The MACE program is an instructional program consisting of "a lesson series for fourth, fifth, and sixth grade students in which geometry and visual arts education were integrated along with a PD program for teachers". The lesson series comprised nine lessons of 60-90 minutes each (five on the theme space, four on patterns), each with a whole-class introduction discussing artworks, an open activity in which students create an artwork in small groups, and a whole-class reflection. The PD program consisted of five 2.5-hour expert-guided sessions with interactive methods, with teachers teaching one or two MACE lessons after each session. It was evaluated in a quasi-experiment with 2909 students in 121 classes and 57 schools.

citation: Spilt, J. L., Hughes, J. N., Wu, J.-Y., & Kwok, O.-M. (2012). Dynamics of Teacher-Student Relationships: Stability and Change across Elementary School and the Influence on Children's Academic Success. Child Development, 83(4), 1180-1195. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8624.2012.01761.x
title: Bioecological and chronic-stress framing of teacher-student relationships as proximal processes whose cumulative exposure shapes development
description: The article applies the bioecological model (Bronfenbrenner & Morris, 2006), which posits four properties of development: "process, person, contexts, and time." Teacher-student interactions are proximal processes whose power depends on person, context, and time, and processes that recur over broader time intervals have greater impact than episodic ones. Combined with chronic stress models from peer-rejection research, this framing motivates modeling cumulative relationship trajectories rather than single-year snapshots, and interpreting chronic conflict's association with underachievement as an effect of prolonged relational adversity.
requirements: Longitudinal repeated measures of relationship quality across multiple years to capture cumulative exposure rather than single-time-point assessments
constraints: The article notes effects of a given process may differ across developmental periods, with long-term TSRQ effects possibly stronger in early school years than later years

academically at-risk children
target_learning_goals: academic achievement growth
school adjustment

article_title: Violations of Core Knowledge Shape Early Learning
citation: Stahl Aimee E., Feigenson Lisa. (2019). Violations of Core Knowledge Shape Early Learning. Topics in Cognitive Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/tops.12389
title: Bayesian prior-strength account of surprise-driven learning from core versus acquired knowledge
description: The article proposes a Bayesian framework in which learners hold priors of varying strength—innate (core knowledge) or learned—and update them to posteriors upon observing events. The larger the prior-to-posterior discrepancy, the greater the surprise and "perhaps the greater the subsequent learning." On this quantitative view, priors set by core knowledge are stronger than those set by acquired associations, so their violation produces larger updates and greater learning enhancement. The authors offer this as one framework that might capture the potency of core versus acquired knowledge violations, while stressing it remains to be tested.
requirements: Empirical approaches capable of quantifying the degree of surprise learners experience and mapping it to subsequent learning, as the authors state will be needed
constraints: The article states this quantitative characterization of core versus acquired violations remains to be seen and will require extended efforts using multiple empirical approaches
target_learners: preverbal infants
young children
target_learning_goals: acquisition of new object properties and word labels following expectancy violation
examples: The gumball machine experiments tested whether improbable events produce graded learning, as a continuous Bayesian account would predict, and found step-like performance instead

citation: Steacy LM, Fuchs D, Gilbert JK, Kearns DM, Elleman AM, Edwards AA. (2020). title: Lexical-feedback account: poor readers rely on the semantic processor when mapping orthography to phonology
description: The article interprets its findings within connectionist models of word reading (e.g., the triangle model), in which lexical feedback from semantics assists mapping between orthographic and phonological forms. It proposes that when sub-lexical mapping is difficult, "meaning is particularly important," and that "students with RD are relying heavily on the semantic processor in word learning efficiency." This explains why imageability and vocabulary grade mattered most for the poorest readers.
requirements: Applicable to word learning contexts where orthographic-phonological mapping is difficult, such as irregular or less decodable words
constraints: The authors state they do not have the correct data to make causal inferences about this relationship

target_learning_goals: Efficient acquisition of word-specific orthographic representations for high-frequency words

Students read from lists of the 500 most frequent words (Educator's Word Frequency Guide) for one minute, with the tutor correcting errors by pronunciation only; "When a student read a word correctly on three consecutive days, the word was removed from the student's list." Tutors reviewed up to three unmastered words and awarded certificates at benchmarks of 10, 50, or 200 words mastered.

article_title: Development of abstract mathematical reasoning: the case of algebra
citation: Susac A, Bubic A, Vrbanc A and Planinic M (2014) Development of abstract mathematical reasoning: the case of algebra. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 8:679. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2014.00679
title: Teachers should repeatedly encourage formal reasoning rather than assuming equation-rearrangement skill transfers after one exposure
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that mastery of equation rearrangement cannot be presumed from a single exposure, because the concrete-to-abstract transition unfolds over years. As the authors state, "teachers should use every opportunity to encourage students to use formal reasoning – both pattern recognition and effective application of mathematical rules and known procedures." This applies across mathematics and science contexts such as physics problem solving.
requirements: Instruction must recur across grades and subjects, since all participants had been taught rearrangement at least one year prior yet still struggled with all-symbol equations.
constraints: The supporting evidence covers simple three-term equations with multiplication/division only; even 16–17-year-olds struggled with the slightly more complex C equations.

target_learning_goals: Abstract algebraic reasoning
equation rearrangement
transfer of equation-solving skill across contexts
examples: In the study, even students taught rearrangement a year earlier were only 82% accurate on all-symbol equations, and half of participants reported concrete strategies such as inserting numbers.

article_title: Sustained attention and prediction: distinct brain maturation trajectories during adolescence
citation: Thillay A, Roux S, Gissot V, Carteau-Martin I, Knight RT, Bonnet-Brilhault F and Bidet-Caulet A (2015) Sustained attention and prediction: distinct brain maturation trajectories during adolescence. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 9:519. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2015.00519
title: Distinct brain maturation trajectories account: sustained attention matures with frontal cortical development while prediction is mature by age 12
description: The article proposes that sustained attention and prediction, though both frontal-dependent optimization processes, follow distinct developmental trajectories through adolescence. Sustained attention continues to mature after age 12, evidenced by improved detection performance and "a frontal shift in P3 and CNV topographies with increasing age", whereas "predictive processing appeared to be mature at age 12". The account attributes the difference to a larger and longer recruitment of the frontal cortex when attention is sustained than during simple predictive processing, with prediction maintenance possibly achieved at lower hierarchical levels such as visual areas.
requirements: EEG recording with tasks that separately load on sustained attention and on manipulated target predictability, as in the visual target detection paradigm used
constraints: The study's gender distribution was biased towards males in the three subsamples
The authors note the study would have been stronger with larger samples, though effects showed large effect sizes

predictive processing
proactive cognitive control

article_title: Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System
citation: Treiman Rebecca, Kessler Brett. (2013). Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System. Language Learning and Development. https://doi.org/10.1080/15475441.2013.812016
title: Spelling instruction should go beyond rote memorization and explicitly teach sound-to-spelling patterns, including context-conditioned choices
description: The review argues that because implicit statistical learning of spelling patterns is slow and incomplete, explicit teaching has an important role. It recommends that instruction cover the sound-to-spelling direction, not only spellings-to-sounds, and teach how context helps choose among alternative spellings: "more direct instruction about the sound-to-spelling direction could be helpful" and it "could be helpful to draw children's attention to the fact that context can help in making these choices". Generic statements can convey generalizations that would otherwise require many instances.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of phonology and spelling so they can interpret children's errors, e.g. recognizing that ‹CHRAP› for trap reflects careful listening plus a misclassification, not inattention.
constraints: The review notes current phonics approaches often rely on worksheets and drills that are boring for children, and that phoneme-level generic statements are harder for children to understand than everyday generics.
target_learners: children learning to spell in alphabetic writing systems, roughly ages 4 to 13
target_learning_goals: conventional spelling accuracy
understanding of sound-to-spelling correspondences and their context conditioning
examples: The review describes whole-language classrooms where children receive no explicit spelling instruction, and contrasts these with phonics instruction, recommending engaging word-pattern teaching methods (Joshi et al., 2008–2009).

article_title: Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System
citation: Treiman Rebecca, Kessler Brett. (2013). Learning to Use an Alphabetic Writing System. Language Learning and Development. https://doi.org/10.1080/15475441.2013.812016
title: Statistical learning account of spelling development
description: The review's organizing framework is statistical learning, defined as "the process whereby organisms pick up patterns by observing and internalizing the relative frequency with which objects and events occur and co-occur". On this account, children first learn salient graphic characteristics of print implicitly, then apply the same mechanisms to phoneme-spelling links, including context-conditioned and morphological patterns. Learning is shaped by the statistics of the writing children see, including their own names, and spelling learning in turn reshapes children's ideas about language.
requirements: Sufficient exposure to examples of writing in the child's environment, since the account holds that children learn letter and digram frequencies from the print around them.
constraints: The review states people are not ideal statistical learners: context conditioning is learned slowly, adults underuse context relative to its strength in the vocabulary, and the account's role in nonalphabetic systems needs further work.
target_learners: preschool and school-age children learning alphabetic writing systems
target_learning_goals: spelling development
implicit knowledge of orthographic patterns
examples: The review interprets prephonological spellers' language-specific letter and digram use, own-name letter use, and the gradual emergence of context sensitivity as manifestations of statistical learning.

article_title: Learning motivation mediates gene-by-socioeconomic status interaction on mathematics achievement in early childhood
citation: Tucker-Drob, Elliot M., & Harden, K. Paige. (2011). Learning Motivation Mediates Gene-by-Socioeconomic Status Interaction on Mathematics Achievement in Early Childhood. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2011.11.015
title: Transactional gene-environment interaction account: high-opportunity environments let children select, evoke, and attend to learning experiences congruent with genetically influenced motivation
description: The article advances a transactional developmental account (citing Dickens and Flynn, Scarr, and Tucker-Drob & Harden) in which heritable variation in achievement is expressed through child-driven processes. As the authors write, "heritable variation in cognition and achievement comes to be expressed through a process by which children select, evoke, and attend to experiences that are congruent with their genetically influenced traits." In high-opportunity environments children can match learning experiences to their genotypes, so achievement becomes increasingly heritable; in low-opportunity environments this matching is constrained and heritable variation stays low. The study's mediation results are presented as evidence for this mechanism operating via learning motivation in early childhood.
requirements: Adequate environmental opportunity for enriching interactions with the proximal environment, so that motivated children can translate non-cognitive traits into cognitive skills
constraints: The authors note that in low-opportunity environments children are less able to match their learning experiences to their genotypes, suppressing heritable variation in achievement
target_learners: four-year-old children (early childhood, prior to formal schooling)
target_learning_goals: early mathematics achievement and school readiness
examples: The bivariate twin analyses showed only the genetic pathway from motivation to achievement varied with SES, which the authors interpret as support for this transactional process

article_title: Children's Effortful Control and Academic Achievement: Mediation Through Social Functioning
citation: Valiente Carlos, Eisenberg Nancy, Haugen Rg, Spinrad Tracy L., Hofer Claire, Liew Jeffrey, Kupfer Anne. (2011). Children's Effortful Control and Academic Achievement: Mediation Through Social Functioning. Early Education and Development, 22(3), 411-433. https://doi.org/10.1080/10409289.2010.505259
title: Effortful control as temperamentally based self-regulation grounded in the executive attention network
description: The article frames effortful control as "a group of temperamentally based skills viewed as the basis of self-regulation," defined by Rothbart and Bates as "the efficiency of executive attention—including the ability to inhibit a dominant response and/or to activate a subdominant response, to plan, and to detect errors." Drawing on Posner's attention networks, the study locates EC in the executive attention network, which monitors and resolves conflicts among other neural networks and is hypothesized to play a central role in regulatory efforts. EC is measured via adult reports of attentional and inhibitory control and behaviorally via persistence or delay tasks.
requirements: Measured through adult reports of attention shifting, attention focusing, and inhibitory control, or behavioral tasks such as persistence and delay of gratification
constraints: EC develops rapidly in the preschool years and continues improving in early school years; the study's sample was primarily Caucasian
target_learners: children in kindergarten through early elementary school
target_learning_goals: self-regulation supporting classroom attention, task completion, and academic achievement
examples: EC was measured with the Children's Behavior Questionnaire subscales and a puzzle task in which persistence without cheating over 4 minutes indexed EC

Administrators are advised to give teachers clear messages supporting the modest time needed for such activities.

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction
citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: A model of twelve divergent thinking activities organised along two dimensions of remoteness and abstractness
description: The article presents a matrix of twelve divergent thinking activities organised along two dimensions: remoteness (the metaphorical distance from a stimulus, running from free association to bisociation) and abstractness (running from association through combination to abstraction). The authors state they "built a model of twelve divergent thinking activities, along two dimensions—remoteness and abstractness" to serve as a framework for teaching students how to generate more original ideas deliberately in visual arts education. Activities range from A1 (associate freely) to C4 (transform), with remoteness and abstractness treated as vectors along which learners can deliberately move to generate more original ideas.

constraints: The model was developed for and applied in the domain of visual arts education with secondary school students

target_learning_goals: Generate original ideas for visual art products through divergent thinking
examples: The article illustrates cell C1 (construct conceptually) with Mondrian's 'Pier and Ocean' composition, and cell C3 (restructure) with the NeoNurture incubator that used car parts for infant incubator design

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction

The lesson "contained five lesson-phases" covering orientation on metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive strategy instruction, divergent thinking strategy instruction with exercises, and evaluation. It was delivered by the first author with a second teacher assisting, within a 14-week photography project on the theme of 'Time-grasping'.

citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: Nelson and Narens' two-level metacognition model applied to regulation of divergent thinking
description: The article applies Nelson and Narens' (1990) model of metamemory to divergent thinking in creative processes. The model posits two levels—an object-level running executive processes (task performance, learning processes) and a meta-level holding a dynamic representation of the object-level—connected by two types of information flow: monitoring (from object-level to meta-level) and control (from meta-level to object-level). The authors use this framework to explain how "regulation of executive processes is enhanced" through a cyclic flow between levels, grounding their instructional design for metacognitive strategy instruction in divergent thinking.
requirements: Learners must possess metacognitive knowledge about tasks, strategies and self to assess task demands and outcomes
Strategy knowledge about the specific executive process (here, divergent thinking) is needed for accurate control
constraints: Applied in the article specifically to divergent thinking processes in visual arts education
target_learners: Secondary school students in visual arts education
target_learning_goals: Monitor and control divergent thinking processes to generate more original ideas
examples: In the intervention lesson, monitoring was enhanced through clarifying knowledge and misunderstandings about creativity, while control was stimulated through interactive discussion providing examples of strategy selection and implementation

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction
citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: Teach divergent thinking through explicit instruction of metacognitive strategy knowledge rather than relying on brainstorming exercises alone
description: The article argues that regular brainstorming exercises in visual arts lessons may limit learning because students need many experiences before building a rich knowledge base for divergent thinking. Instead, it recommends that "students may develop enhanced divergent thinking skills through explicit instruction of metacognition, because then students may learn to understand why, how and when to use which specific divergent thinking activities and strategies." A previous intervention focusing mainly on association improved fluency and flexibility but not originality, motivating a redesign that added generation through combination and abstraction.
requirements: Instruction must cover declarative, procedural, conditional and contextual knowledge about divergent thinking strategies
Teacher modeling and visual examples are needed to make abstract strategy knowledge concrete
constraints: A prior version of the instruction that focused mainly on generation through association did not improve originality of ideas
target_learners: Secondary school students in visual arts education
target_learning_goals: Enhance divergent thinking skills including fluency, flexibility and originality of generated ideas

article_title: Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction
citation: van de Kamp, M.-T., Admiraal, W., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2016). Becoming original: effects of strategy instruction. Instructional Science, 44, 543–566. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9384-y
title: A five-phase lesson structure for metacognitive strategy instruction on divergent thinking
description: The intervention lesson followed a structured sequence of five phases: (1) orientation on metacognitive knowledge activating prior conceptions of creativity, (2) metacognitive strategy instruction exemplifying divergent thinking with visual examples, (3) divergent thinking strategy instruction explaining and exercising the twelve strategies, (4) application through independent use of strategies, and (5) evaluation through reflection and prediction. The authors state that "the specific order of lesson phases was based on studies about the structuring of instructional-learning episodes," grounding the sequence in instructional design theory.
requirements: Each phase builds on the previous one; explicit instruction and teacher modeling are central to phases 2 and 3
Whole-class discussion and peer feedback are used to integrate and evaluate new knowledge

title: Include silent reading in dyslexia diagnosis and treatment, especially for adolescents, alongside oral reading assessment
description: The article recommends that diagnosis and intervention for dyslexia consider both reading modes, because diagnosis is usually based on oral reading while accommodations target silent reading. It states "It seems important to include silent reading in diagnosing reading disabilities and dyslexia especially for adolescents", and that specific treatment of silent reading, in addition to oral reading, should be considered, with continued monitoring of both modes for individuals with dyslexia.

constraints: For primary school children oral and silent fluency are still interchangeable, so the need is greatest from adolescence onwards; the silent task used included simple task performance, which may have underestimated silent reading ability

reading fluency intervention and accommodations

article_title: Exploring the long-term relationship between academic-media multitasking and adolescents’ academic achievement
citation: W.A. van der Schuur, S.E. Baumgartner, S.R. Sumter, P.M. Valkenburg. (2020). Exploring the long-term relationship between academic-media multitasking and adolescents' academic achievement. New Media and Society. https://doi.org/10.1177/1461444819861956
title: Qualify concerns about the long-term impact of academic-media multitasking on adolescent achievement
description: Educators and policymakers should temper alarms that media use during academic activities durably damages adolescent achievement. The article concludes that "concerns regarding the long-term impact of academic-media multitasking on academic achievement need to be qualified", because a three-wave longitudinal study found no direct or indirect long-term achievement effect. Attention problems did increase, so caution remains warranted.
requirements: Base guidance on longitudinal evidence rather than cross-sectional associations, which the study shows can coexist with no long-term effect.
constraints: Findings apply to adolescents aged 11–15 studied over 3–4 month intervals; the study did not establish long-term equivalence, only absence of support for a long-term relationship.
target_learners: adolescents aged 11–15

academic attention
examples: The article's three-wave study with 1215 adolescents found cross-sectional links but no long-term achievement effect, grounding the recommendation to qualify concerns.

title: The computational efficiency model of multiplication problem difficulty
description: The computational efficiency model is an explanatory account of multiplication problem difficulty that the article evaluates against item data. It was contrasted with alternatives using data from two tasks: one in which children used predominantly computational strategies and one in which they were expected to rely mostly on retrieval. The article reports that "In both tasks we found most support for the computational efficiency model", making it the best-supported account of the models compared for both kinds of task data.

title: Counterstorytelling within critical race theory as a framework for understanding marginalized students' mathematics experiences
description: The article grounds its analysis in critical race theory and counterstorytelling, the practice of People of Color naming their own realities. A counterstory 'serves to illuminate these biases and the processes by which they operate and influence educational acts.' The authors combine counterstory with critical ethnography, weaving individual student stories into a collective voice of Latinas/os' lived experiences in mathematics education to counter deficit-based perspectives.
requirements: Experiential knowledge of non-dominant students must be treated as legitimate and critical data, per the article's key tenet of critical race theory
constraints: The counterstories represent a particular group of students across two urban sites and are presented as a collective reflection of shared systemic exclusion
target_learners: Urban Latina/o elementary and middle-grade students
target_learning_goals: Understanding students' perspectives on mathematics learning and schooling conditions

description: The article argues that educational contexts should actively promote and attend to children's spoken judgments about their metacognitive experiences, particularly feelings of difficulty. title: Test of Spatial Assembly (TOSA): a 2-D and 3-D spatial assembly assessment designed for 3-year-olds
description: The TOSA is a non-verbal spatial assembly task created specifically as an assessment for 3-year-olds, comprising 2-D trials recreating pictured designs with magnetized foam shapes and 3-D trials recreating glued Mega Blocks models. It was built because few appropriate spatial tasks exist for 3-year-olds; the article reports "Cronbach's alpha was .802 for all trials that made up the TOSA." Scores are z-scored per portion and averaged.
requirements: Administered individually with trained coders scoring photographs of constructions, with inter-rater agreement of 96-97% as reported

target_learning_goals: Early geometric and spatial reasoning, including part/whole composition and object relative position

title: Early mathematics instruction should include foundational generalizable skills like EF and spatial skills, not only number knowledge
description: The article argues that because EF and spatial skills together account for most variance in preschool mathematics performance, preschool programs that focus exclusively on number knowledge overlook foundational skills. The authors state that "time spent practicing overlooked skills like EF and spatial skills might pay dividends in preparing children to succeed in mathematics," and that early gaps among lower-SES children motivate preschool training in these areas.
requirements: Research must establish malleability of the skills (up for debate for EF), and teachers must be given training and instructional time
constraints: Adoption depends on stakeholders prioritizing generalizable skills over standardized tests that assess only subject-specific knowledge

target_learning_goals: School readiness in mathematics via executive function and spatial skills

citation: Vigna Giulia, Ghidoni Enrico, Burgio Francesca, Danesin Laura, Angelini Damiano, Benavides-Varela Silvia, Semenza Carlo. (2022). Dyscalculia in Early Adulthood: Implications for Numerical Activities of Daily Living. Brain Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/brainsci12030373
title: NADL (Numerical Activities of Daily Living) standardized battery
description: The NADL is a standardized test created "to identify impairments in numerical functions that may cause problems in day-to-day and ecologically valid tasks". It comprises a Participant Interview assessing awareness of numerical abilities, an Informal Test of everyday numerical activities (time, measure, distance, communication, general knowledge, money), and a Formal Test of school-acquired skills (number comprehension, transcoding, mental and written calculation, rules and principles). Maximum scores are 10, 23, and 77 respectively; the original standardization reports Cronbach's alpha = 0.73. In this study it was administered to adults with DD for the first time, as experimental tasks compared against a control group rather than as a diagnostic tool.

constraints: In this study the NADL subtests were not used as diagnostic tools but as experimental hypothesis-driven tasks compared against a control group rather than normative data

awareness of numerical abilities

citation: Wang, Ming-Te; Chow, Angela; Degol, Jessica Lauren; Eccles, Jacquelynne Sue. (2016). title: Expectancy-value theory as a framework for science motivation development
description: The article uses expectancy-value theory as its conceptual framework, defining ability self-concept as expectations for success and confidence in one's ability in a field, and subjective task values as the value placed on a field, including interest, utility value, and attainment value. The theory posits that "students' educational choices are greatly influenced by their cognitive competencies, their ability self-concepts, and the subjective task values they attach to each subject or field." The study applies it by modeling joint trajectories of both constructs and linking them to outcomes.

article_title: Comorbidity Between Reading Disability and Math Disability
citation: Willcutt, E. G., Petrill, S. A., Wu, S., Boada, R., DeFries, J. C., Olson, R. K., & Pennington, B. F. (2013). Comorbidity between reading disability and math disability: Concurrent psychopathology, functional impairment, and neuropsychological functioning. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 46(6), 500-516. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219413477476
title: Correlated liabilities model of RD and MD comorbidity within a multiple-deficit framework
description: The correlated liabilities model holds that RD and MD co-occur more often than chance due to shared etiological influences, while additional disorder-specific influences distinguish them. The article's results "provide the strongest support for a correlated liabilities model in which shared weaknesses in working memory, verbal comprehension, and processing speed increase risk for both RD and MD," with distinct profiles on phoneme awareness, naming speed, and set shifting. This sits within the broader multiple-deficit framework in which developmental disorders arise from additive and interactive effects of multiple neuropsychological weaknesses rather than a single primary deficit.
requirements: Requires a 2 X 2 (RD X MD) group design with groups defined by each disorder alone, comorbid, and neither, plus measures spanning multiple neuropsychological constructs
constraints: The article notes results derive from word reading and math calculations definitions; results might differ for reading comprehension, word problems, or fluency measures
target_learners: children and adolescents ages 8-15 with reading disability, math disability, or both
target_learning_goals: understanding the neuropsychological and etiological basis of reading and math learning disabilities
examples: The CLDRC twin study compared 241 RD-only, 183 MD-only, 188 RD+MD, and 411 control participants, rejecting alternate forms, phenocopy, and three independent disorders models

title: Scale for Early Mathematics Anxiety (SEMA), a 20-item math anxiety measure for second and third graders
description: The SEMA is a 20-item questionnaire the authors developed to assess math anxiety in second and third graders, modeled on the MARS and MARS-E. Its first 10 items assess anxiety about grade-appropriate math problems (number sense, basic functions, measurement, geometry, mathematical reasoning) and the last 10 assess anxiety in social and testing situations. Children rate each item on a five-point scale using graded anxious and non-anxious faces, administered one-on-one with items read aloud. The authors are making SEMA freely available to researchers.

article_title: Math Anxiety in Second and Third Graders and Its Relation to Mathematics Achievement
citation: Wu SS, Barth M, Amin H, Malcarne V and Menon V (2012) Math anxiety in second and third graders and its relation to mathematics achievement. Front. Psychology 3:162. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00162
title: Two-factor structure of early math anxiety: Numerical Processing Anxiety and Situational and Performance Anxiety
description: Exploratory factor analysis of the SEMA confirmed a two-factor structure replicating the MARS and MARS-E. One factor, Numerical Processing Anxiety, captures anxiety about numerical concepts and loaded seven items (e.g., checking whether 9 + 7 = 18 is right); the other, Situational and Performance Anxiety, captures anxiety about situations involving the execution of math and loaded eight items (e.g., doing a math problem on the board in class). The two factors correlated 0.529 (p < 0.001) and had Cronbach's alphas of 0.802 and 0.770 respectively.
requirements: Items loading at least 0.50 on one factor and no greater than 0.40 on the other, per the authors' extraction criteria
constraints: The authors note future studies should explore including additional items related to test, as opposed to performance, anxiety in third and possibly second graders
target_learners: second and third graders
target_learning_goals: understanding the structure of math anxiety in early elementary learners
examples: Principal components analysis with varimax rotation accounted for 29.73% and 8.56% of variance in the first and second factors respectively

title: Remediate math anxiety early, attending to both its numerical and its situational and social aspects
description: The article argues that because math anxiety's detrimental effects on math achievement can be detected in the earliest stages of formal math learning, educators and researchers should remediate math anxiety and its deleterious effects in young children. The authors conclude that remediation may require attention to both the domain-specific numerical information processing aspect and the domain-general situational and social aspect of math anxiety, since both subscales were independently related to achievement.

constraints: The article states additional research is necessary to clarify the behavioral and neural mechanisms by which math anxiety influences math learning in second and third grades

target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement in early elementary school
examples: The study found both the Numerical Processing Anxiety and Situational and Performance Anxiety subscales significantly correlated with the WIAT-II Math Composite score

article_title: Computational Thinking for All: Pedagogical Approaches to Embedding 21st Century Problem Solving in K-12 Classrooms
citation: Yadav, A., Hong, H., & Stephenson, C. (2016). Computational Thinking for All: Pedagogical Approaches to Embedding 21st Century Problem Solving in K-12 Classrooms. TechTrends. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11528-016-0087-7
title: Computational thinking as three key constructs: algorithms, abstraction, and automation
description: The article organizes computational thinking around what Wing (2006) called the three key constructs. It states that "An algorithm (much like a recipe) is a step-by-step series of instructions," that abstraction "involves generalizing and transferring the problem solving process to similar problems," and that automation "involves using digital and simulation tools to mechanize problem solutions." These constructs are presented as foundational to computer science yet applicable across disciplines, framing the article's argument for embedding CT in K-12 content areas.
requirements: Teachers need examples and support to map the three constructs onto their existing subject-area content
constraints: The article presents the constructs as an argumentative framework rather than a tested model

target_learning_goals: problem decomposition
algorithmic problem solving
abstraction and transfer
automation with computing tools

Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000098
title: Design-thinking methodology for improving and scaling psychological interventions: user-centered qualitative inquiry plus rapid randomized A/B testing
description: The article formalizes a methodology for preparing psychological interventions to be scaled, combining two design traditions. User-centered design privileges the user's subjective perspective via qualitative methods and prototypes, because "users may be excellent reporters on what they dislike or are confused by." A/B testing supplies "low-cost, short-term, large-sample, random-assignment experiments to test revisions to intervention content." The methodology was applied to redesign a growth mindset intervention for students transitioning to high school, then evaluated in two experimental studies.
requirements: Access to members of the target population for qualitative feedback on prototypes
A platform or sample enabling rapid, adequately powered randomized A/B experiments on minor content variations
An existing theoretical process model to guide which proxy measures and revisions matter
constraints: The authors state the re-designed intervention was not viewed as final or ready for universal scaling
A/B experiment conclusions were tempered by qualitative feedback because adult Mechanical Turk participants are not the target adolescent population
target_learners: 9th grade students transitioning to public high schools in the United States
target_learning_goals: Growth mindset of intelligence beliefs, challenge-seeking, persistence, and core-course academic achievement
examples: One-on-one meetings, group sessions of 2–10 students, and pilots with 20–25 9th graders reviewing minimally viable intervention drafts; two A/B studies with 7 fully crossed factors across N=3,004 participants

article_title: Conversations with AutoTutor Help Students Learn
citation: Graesser, A. C. (2016). Conversations with AutoTutor Help Students Learn. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0086-4
title: Expectation & misconception-tailored (EMT) dialogue as the core conversation mechanism of AutoTutor and human tutoring
description: EMT dialogue is a conversation mechanism in which the tutor anticipates particular correct answers (expectations) and particular misunderstandings (misconceptions) when asking challenging questions, then tracks student answers across multiple conversational turns via semantic pattern matching. The tutor gives short positive, neutral, or negative feedback and uses pumps ("What else"), hints, or prompts to elicit expectations, contributing assertions when the student fails. The pump-hint-prompt-assertion cycles are implemented in AutoTutor and are frequent in human tutoring. EMT is computationally feasible because it relies on pattern completion rather than interpreting natural language from scratch.
requirements: Requires anticipating the expectations and misconceptions for each question in advance and a semantic matching mechanism to compare student contributions against them
constraints: Relies on semantic pattern matching because full natural language interpretation is beyond reliable NLP boundaries
target_learners: middle school mathematics students
college students
target_learning_goals: deep conceptual answers to challenging questions and problems in domains such as physics and research methods
examples: The mechanism was documented from near 100 videotaped, transcribed tutoring sessions with middle school children in mathematics and college students in research methods, then implemented in AutoTutor.
key_sources: Graesser, A. C. (2016). Conversations with AutoTutor Help Students Learn. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0086-4

article_title: Conversations with AutoTutor Help Students Learn
citation: Graesser, A. C. (2016). Conversations with AutoTutor Help Students Learn. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0086-4
title: Seven trialogue designs for two-agent conversations with a human learner, adaptively administered by learner knowledge
description: Trialogues involve a human interacting with two agents, typically a tutor agent and a student peer agent. Graesser et al. (2015b) identified seven designs: (1) vicarious learning with human observer; (2) vicarious learning with limited human participation via yes/no or single-word prompts; (3) tutor agent interacting with human and student agent; (4) expert agent staging a competition between human and peer agent; (5) human teaches a student agent with tutor facilitation; (6) human interacts with two peer agents varying in proficiency; and (7) human interacts with two agents expressing contradictions or different views. The two agents can model good questions and answers or stage arguments that create cognitive disequilibrium, productive confusion, and deeper learning. The student agent can also fill in missing words when the human's answer is incomplete, circumventing negative short feedback.
requirements: Two agents that can take on different roles, typically one tutor and one student peer, with conversation mechanisms adaptive and flexible like AutoTutor
constraints: The article states research needs to be conducted to assess empirically the conditions under which different trialogue designs facilitate learning and motivation
target_learners: learners with limited knowledge (vicarious designs)
more capable students attempting deeper knowledge (designs 5 and 7)
target_learning_goals: modeling good answers and reasoning, deeper learning through cognitive disequilibrium and productive confusion, motivation through game competition
examples: Trialogues are routinely incorporated in recent AutoTutor applications such as Operation ARIES/ARA for scientific reasoning, iSTART for reading comprehension, CSAL reading interventions for adults, and ETS assessment using ASAT and ACE.

title: AutoTutor Script Authoring Tool (ASAT) and generic AutoTutor Conversation Engine (ACE) licensed for new content and applications
description: The AutoTutor Script Authoring Tool (ASAT, Cai et al. 2015) lets researchers at other universities, businesses, and organizations develop their own content and integrate it with the generic AutoTutor Conversation Engine (ACE). Educational Testing Service is licensing ASAT for assessment in virtual worlds, and the Army Research Laboratory has incorporated AutoTutor in its open source Generalized Intelligent Framework for Tutoring (GIFT).

title: Virtual patients as experiential learning simulations of clinical scenarios
description: Virtual patients are defined as "interactive computer simulations of real-life clinical scenarios for the purpose of health professions training, education, or assessment". The learner acts as a health care provider making decisions about information acquisition, differential diagnosis, and management. The review grounds their educational use in experiential learning theory, in which simulated clinical experiences provide action and reflection mechanisms for information gathering and decision making in a safe environment.

citation: Kron Frederick W. MD, Fetters Michael D. MD, MPH, MA, Scerbo Mark W. PhD, White Casey B. PhD, Lypson Monica L. MD, MHPE, FACP, Padilla Miguel A. PhD, Gliva-McConvey Gayle A., Belfore Lee A. title: MPathic-VR virtual human conversation simulation for advanced healthcare communication training
description: MPathic-VR is a computer-based system in which healthcare learners "talk with virtual humans" — intelligent conversational agents with human appearance — in intercultural and interprofessional scenarios. Learners choose among three responses per exchange, are recorded for verbal and nonverbal behavior, receive a personalized after-action review with video of their nonverbal behaviors, and repeat each scenario. Analyses of learner data drive assessment, feedback, and real-time variation of virtual human behavior.
requirements: Built on specific communication skill learning objectives drawn from established protocols (SPIKES, CRASH, TeamSTEPPS), with a readiness assessment quiz requiring a score of 80% or higher before scenario participation.
constraints: The authors note MPathic-VR was more interactive by design and included two scenarios while assessment covered only the interprofessional content, so OSCE differences may reflect joint effects of content and delivery format.

Nonverbal communication

examples: In the trial, students played an intern breaking bad news to a virtual mother about her daughter's leukemia, then resolving conflict with a virtual oncology nurse, with an after-action review between run-throughs.

article_title: Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality
citation: Lugrin J-L, Latoschik ME, Habel M, Roth D, Seufert C and Grafe S (2016) Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality. Front. ICT 3:26. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2016.00026
title: 3B (Breaking Bad Behaviors): an immersive VR classroom management training system with teacher HMD immersion and instructor desktop control console
description: 3B is a collaborative VR platform in which a trainee teacher is immersed in a real-time 3D virtual classroom of twenty-four semi-autonomous virtual students via a head-mounted display and headphones, while an instructor controls training tasks and feedback through a 2D graphical desktop console. The system uses a client-server architecture on Unreal Engine 4 with Oculus Rift DK2 and Kinect v2 markerless tracking, and was designed as a companion tool for CRM seminars at the University of Würzburg so lecturers can "link theory with practice using the medium of VR". It is built from low-cost consumer hardware and free software for use by practitioners without technical expertise.
requirements: Usable by practitioners without expert knowledge in computer programming or virtual reality; instructors must be able to create new training scenarios without deep technical knowledge
constraints: The physical self is not artificially augmented with sensors; the teacher wears minimum equipment and the system does not impede natural body movement
target_learners: Trainee primary and secondary school teachers in initial teacher education
target_learning_goals: Classroom management skills, particularly preempting, controlling, and mitigating disruptive student behavior
examples: Used in two seminars at the University of Würzburg: Classroom Management and Videobased Reflection of Education
key_sources: Lugrin J-L, Latoschik ME, Habel M, Roth D, Seufert C and Grafe S (2016) Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality. Front. ICT 3:26. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2016.00026

article_title: Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality
citation: Lugrin J-L, Latoschik ME, Habel M, Roth D, Seufert C and Grafe S (2016) Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality. Front. ICT 3:26. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2016.00026
title: Three elements of effective training: realistic exposure, fine control of stimuli, and fine performance feedback
description: The article proposes that effective training depends on three major elements: exposure to realistic training scenarios and stimuli, fine control over training stimuli and scenarios (including adjusting difficulty to the trainee's current competence and repeating identical stimuli), and fine performance feedback that is fine-grained, unambiguous, and timely. The authors note a compromise between realism and control in real classrooms, where "the unpredictability of a real classroom greatly diminishes any control over the exact nature and difficulty of training stimuli". They designed 3B to combine all three elements in an immersive VR simulation.
requirements: Control of stimuli and provision of feedback would ideally occur in a closed real-time loop between trainer and trainee
constraints: In real classrooms, feedback is largely restricted to deferred reviews decoupled from the actual situational context
target_learners: Trainee teachers learning classroom management
target_learning_goals: Adjusting behavior to achieve better results through realistic practice with controlled stimuli and timely feedback
examples: The 3B system implements the three elements via a simulated classroom, instructor-controlled behavior levels, and synchronous and asynchronous feedback

title: Five-level bad behavior classification for virtual students, adopted and extended from Borich's typology
description: The system classifies virtual student behaviors into five intensity levels of perceived disruption — null, low, mid, high, and extreme — with null corresponding to normal behaviors such as a quiet listening student and extreme including behaviors like fighting and screaming. The classification was "adopted and extended" from Borich's (2011) typology, which provides a single dimension with mild, moderate, and severe levels. It provides "a convenient way to systematically control a large set of virtual students to easily raise or lower the level of stress perceived by a teacher", and each level maps to associated animations of the virtual students.
requirements: New character models or animations require only a reference to their name and associated bad behavior categories to be included in the system
constraints: During the evaluation, some animations were not directly controllable by the instructor
target_learners: Trainee teachers practicing responses to disruptive behavior
target_learning_goals: Managing disruptive student behavior at graded intensity levels
examples: Table 1 lists behaviors per level, e.g., whispering at low, talking-neighbors at mid, receiving-phone-call at high, and screaming at extreme

title: One-to-one teacher/instructor paradigm with synchronous and asynchronous feedback in immersive simulation training
description: The 3B training pattern pairs an immersed trainee teacher with a non-immersed instructor who monitors performance and controls stimuli in real time. The instructor interface consists of five boards: instructions, virtual student control, environment viewport, camera control, and feedback. Synchronous feedback uses "Thumb-up"/"Thumb-down" buttons with positive or negative audio cues to guide the teacher during the lecture without interrupting the session, while asynchronous feedback is a detailed evaluation form summarizing the teacher's performance after the session. Both feedback types are automatically logged as performance indicators to measure teacher progress across sessions.
requirements: Instructors were repeatedly reminded to give feedback via an animated message with sound displayed thirty seconds after each new bad-behavior-activation instruction
constraints: An option permits the instructor to enable or disable the audio feedback cues, thereby muting the feedback
target_learners: Trainee teachers in classroom management seminars
target_learning_goals: Adjusting teaching behavior in response to guided feedback on handling disruptive behavior
examples: In the user study, instructors increased class agitation across five phases while giving synchronous audio feedback in one condition and none in the other

citation: Lugrin J-L, Latoschik ME, Habel M, Roth D, Seufert C and Grafe S (2016) Breaking Bad Behaviors: A New Tool for Learning Classroom Management Using Virtual Reality. Front. ICT 3:26. https://doi.org/10.3389/fict.2016.00026
title: Use immersive VR simulation as a safe complement to in-vivo classroom practice for training classroom management coping strategies
description: The article recommends VR simulation as a complement to traditional CRM teaching when real classroom time is insufficient or when realism conflicts with stimulus control and feedback. The 3B platform "aims to better prepare trainee teachers for future in vivo training by letting them experience and practice their coping strategies in a safe environment". Because real classroom disturbances are unpredictable, systematic CRM training currently relies on theory, video analysis, and role-play; an immersive simulation adds realistic stress exposure with controlled, repeatable stimuli and targeted real-time feedback.
requirements: The simulation must realistically elicit stress similar to a real classroom atmosphere, since stress exposure training rests on eliciting emotional responses
constraints: Consumer hardware cannot provide truly interactive photo-realism, so a balance between realism and overall performance (latency, frame rate) must be found
target_learners: Novice and trainee teachers who do not feel sufficiently prepared with regard to CRM
target_learning_goals: Establishing and maintaining order, engaging students, and developing coping strategies for disruptive behavior
examples: 3B was designed with CRM training experts who created the scenarios and virtual student behaviors, and underwent a one-year iterative user-centered development process

article_title: Socio-Cognitive Scaffolding with Computer-Supported Collaboration Scripts: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Freydis Vogel & Christof Wecker & Ingo Kollar & Frank Fischer. (2016). Socio-Cognitive Scaffolding with Computer-Supported Collaboration Scripts: a Meta-Analysis. Educ Psychol Rev (2017) 29:477–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9361-7
title: Script theory of guidance (SToG): internal scripts with four components and external CSCL scaffolds on three hierarchical levels
description: The meta-analysis builds on the script theory of guidance (Fischer, Kollar, Stegmann, and Wecker 2013), in which "collaboration skills can be regarded as 'internal scripts'" that guide understanding and acting in similar situations. Internal scripts comprise four partially hierarchically ordered components: play, scene, scriptlet, and role. External CSCL scripts support learners who lack appropriate internal scripts by prompting cognitive operations, sequencing activities, and distributing them among roles, with scaffolds on play, scene, and scriptlet levels.
requirements: Learners lacking appropriate internal scripts are supported by external CSCL scripts that prompt, sequence, and distribute collaborative activities
constraints: The article notes learners may gradually acquire internal scripts through repeated scripted participation and possible fading of the script
target_learners: Learners collaborating in computer-supported settings whose collaboration skills are not yet fully developed
target_learning_goals: Domain-specific knowledge acquisition
Collaboration skills such as argumentation and peer feedback
examples: The article cites Stegmann et al. (2007), where a CSCL script structuring online discussions improved domain-specific knowledge application, and Rummel et al. (2009), where scripts improved physicians' and psychotherapists' collaboration skills.

citation: Kononowicz A A, Woodham L A, Edelbring S, Stathakarou N, Davies D, Saxena N, Tudor Car L, Carlstedt-Duke J, Car J, Zary N. (2019). Virtual Patient Simulations in Health Professions Education: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis by the Digital Health Education Collaboration. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/14676
title: Virtual patients as interactive clinical scenario simulations grounded in experiential learning theory
description: Virtual patients are defined as "interactive computer simulations of real-life clinical scenarios for the purpose of health professions training, education, or assessment". The learner is cast as a health care provider making decisions about information acquisition, differential diagnosis, and management. The review explains their educational use through experiential learning theory, in which simulated clinical experiences provide information gathering and clinical decision making in a safe environment. The review hypothesizes virtual patients primarily address learning needs in clinical reasoning.
requirements: Screen-based representations of the patient as a whole, introduced by a case description, potentially with patient answers, clinical data, and descriptions of signs and symptoms
constraints: Excludes 3D virtual learning environments, interventions requiring nonstandard equipment, and human-controlled simulations; should complement rather than replace contact with real patients
target_learners: Pre- and postregistration health professions students (medicine, nursing, pharmacy, dentistry, physiotherapy)
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning
Diagnostic processes
Procedural and team skills
examples: Included trials used linear, branched, and free-access navigation schemes with menu-based or keyboard control mechanisms

article_title: Planning prompts increase and forecast course completion in massive open online courses
citation: Yeomans, Michael and Reich, Justin. 2017. "Planning Prompts Increase and Forecast Course Completion in Massive Open Online Courses." Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). https://doi.org/10.1145/3027385.3027416
title: The intention-action gap in MOOC learning and plan-making as a cheap, effective nudge
description: The article frames MOOC non-completion as an instance of the intention-action gap: "Among all of the learners in Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) who intend to complete a course, the majority fail to do so." Drawing on research in similar goal-pursuit domains, it positions plan-making as "a cheap and effective nudge to encourage follow-through", operationalized as open-ended planning prompts delivered at the beginning of a course. The framework treats prompts as helping learners adopt productive frames of mind at the outset of a learning goal, which both encourages and forecasts success.
requirements: Learners must already intend to complete the course; the gap the framework addresses exists among intenders, since the majority of intending learners fail to complete.
target_learners: MOOC learners who intend to complete a course
target_learning_goals: Course completion and follow-through on learning intentions
examples: In three HarvardX courses, some students received open-ended planning prompts at the beginning of a course, raising completion by 29% and certificate payment by 40%.
key_sources: Yeomans, Michael and Reich, Justin. 2017. "Planning Prompts Increase and Forecast Course Completion in Massive Open Online Courses." Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). https://doi.org/10.1145/3027385.3027416

article_title: Planning prompts increase and forecast course completion in massive open online courses
citation: Yeomans, Michael and Reich, Justin. 2017. "Planning Prompts Increase and Forecast Course Completion in Massive Open Online Courses." Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). https://doi.org/10.1145/3027385.3027416
title: Deliver open-ended planning prompts at the outset of a learning experience to encourage follow-through
description: Because most MOOC learners who intend to complete fail to do so, the article recommends plan-making as a low-cost intervention: "plan-making is a cheap and effective nudge to encourage follow-through." In practice, instructors present open-ended planning prompts at the beginning of a course, asking learners to write plans whose content can also serve as an early signal of risk. The article reports this raised completion by 29% and certificate payment by 40% in three HarvardX courses.
requirements: Prompts are open-ended and delivered at the beginning of the course, before goal pursuit begins.
constraints: The effect was largest for students enrolled in traditional schools, so benefits may vary across learner subgroups.
target_learners: MOOC learners intending to complete a course
target_learning_goals: Course completion and certificate payment
examples: Students in three HarvardX courses received open-ended planning prompts at the beginning of a course in a natural field experiment.
key_sources: Yeomans, Michael and Reich, Justin. 2017. "Planning Prompts Increase and Forecast Course Completion in Massive Open Online Courses." Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). https://doi.org/10.1145/3027385.3027416

article_title: The Development and Evaluation of a Self-Questioning Study Technique
citation: Marli E.D.A. Andre and Thomas H. Anderson. (1978). The Development and Evaluation of a Self-Questioning Study Technique. Center for the Study of Reading Technical Report No. 87. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=The+Development+and+Evaluation+of+a+Self-Questioning+Study+Technique
title: Levels-of-processing plus metacognitive monitoring account for self-questioning effectiveness
description: The article offers two explanations for why self-questioning works. First, the levels-of-processing notion holds that "increasing 'depth' implies a greater degree of semantic or cognitive analysis and hence greater retention"; determining main ideas and transforming them into questions entails deeper semantic analysis than rereading. Second, the technique combines metacognitive and cognitive components: it forces the reader to pause frequently, deal with an understanding question, check whether comprehension occurred, and decide on the next strategic action, promoting active monitoring of the learning activity.
requirements: The student must generate questions based on main points of the text, requiring comprehension of the text to answer correctly
constraints: The article presents these as possible explanations, not tested mechanisms
target_learners: high school juniors and seniors studying prose material
target_learning_goals: comprehension and retention of expository prose
examples: The authors attribute the superior criterion performance of question-constructing groups to deeper semantic analysis of the text than reading and rereading
