article_title: Children’s inference generation: The role of vocabulary and working memory
citation: Currie, N. K., & Cain, K. (2015). Children's inference generation: The role of vocabulary and working memory. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 137, 57–75. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2015.03.005
title: Dual-route account: vocabulary supports inference making through word-meaning knowledge and through boosting maintenance of information in working memory
description: The article proposes that vocabulary knowledge supports children's inference making in two ways. First, "inferences involve word knowledge"; local coherence inferences require mapping between synonyms and category exemplars, and global coherence inferences tap knowledge about interrelations between word meanings. Second, children with richer vocabulary have more accurate and available word representations in long-term memory, which supports accurate maintenance of information in verbal working memory during text integration. The mediation findings are read as evidence for this account.
requirements: Assessment of both breadth and depth of vocabulary, since a single receptive vocabulary measure may not tap deeper knowledge of interrelations between words
constraints: The article notes local and global coherence inferences are not truly categorical distinctions; different inferences draw on text information and background knowledge to differing degrees
target_learners: Children aged 6 to 10 years listening to or reading narrative text
target_learning_goals: Generating local and global coherence inferences during discourse comprehension
key_sources: Currie, N. K., & Cain, K. (2015). Children's inference generation: The role of vocabulary and working memory. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 137, 57–75. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2015.03.005

article_title: Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference
citation: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287
title: Noun Phrase Accessibility Hierarchy (NPAH) as predictor of relative clause acquisition difficulty
description: The NPAH is a typological markedness hierarchy ordering relative clause types by accessibility of the relative pronoun's function. The article reports that "the implicational accessibility ordering continues as follows: DIRECT OBJECT, then INDIRECT OBJECT, then OBJECT OF A PREPOSITION, then POSSESSIVE, and finally OBJECT OF A COMPARISON", with SUBJECT relativization universally easiest. It was used to select the instructional sequence and to interpret acquisitional findings from FLA and SLA studies.
requirements: Descriptive and acquisitional research on the target grammatical subsystem to inform sequencing decisions
constraints: The article notes exactly what constitutes difficulty has not yet been clearly established
target_learners: Intermediate-level ESL learners
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of English relativization
examples: The study selected OBJECT OF A PREPOSITION relative clauses, a marked position on the hierarchy, as the focus of instruction
key_sources: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287

article_title: Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference
citation: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287
title: Projection model of markedness-based acquisition (Zobl)
description: The article presents Zobl's projection model, in which markedness conditions in the input allow learners to acquire properties of the target language not represented in the input data, via "acquisition via markedness implications and ... acquisition via correlations between markedness of different but related parameters". The article draws the instructional implication that sequencing should let learners "profit from markedness conditions" rather than proceed from simplest to most difficult.
requirements: Instructional materials sequenced so learners can project from one linguistic context with available data to another without data
constraints: The model's applicability rests on structures entering into implicational markedness relations
target_learners: Second language learners of English
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of grammatical subsystems such as relativization
examples: Zobl's studies of the acquisition of English possessive determiners generally supported the projection model
key_sources: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287

article_title: Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference
citation: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287
title: Computer-assisted reading lessons for relativization instruction (MOG, ROG, and COG treatments)
description: Ten daily computer-assisted reading lessons delivered the treatments to all three groups in a common format: "a text that appeared on the screen in three sequential reading-skills formats—a skimming format, an in-depth reading format, and a scanning format—followed by the two measures of comprehension". The experimental manipulation occurred during Reading for Understanding: the meaning-oriented group received lexical rephrasings and sentence clarification, the rule-oriented group viewed Animated Grammar decomposition and recombination, and controls viewed only the text sentences. Daily comprehension tests and L1 recall summaries were built in.
requirements: Computer laboratory access and daily one-lesson assignments on individual diskettes
Researcher presence to ensure subjects viewed only assigned lessons
constraints: Instruction was limited to restrictive OBJECT OF A PREPOSITION relative clauses within three created stories
target_learners: Middle-proficiency intensive English institute students
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and acquisition of English relative clauses
examples: The computer format was chosen for convenient, controlled administration of treatments and permanent availability of the instruction for future analysis
key_sources: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287

article_title: Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference
citation: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287
title: Operationalize and describe the instructional treatment in effect-of-instruction research
description: The article argues that effect-of-instruction studies fail when instruction is merely given a methods label. It observes that "existing 'methods' of instruction were merely cited, and never described", so the actual implementation of materials was never documented. The study therefore specified approach, method, and procedure, developed materials from SLA theory, and reported the instructional component in detail so the instruction-effect link could be examined directly.
requirements: Instructional treatments must be described and operationalized in the research design, not just labeled
Materials should be based on theory of or empirical findings on SLA
constraints: Global proficiency measures compound the problem of an unoperationalized instructional variable
target_learners: Second language learners in instructed settings
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of instructional effects on interlanguage development
examples: The study limited instruction to one grammatical subsystem, relativization, to alleviate problems of operationalization and assessment
key_sources: Catherine Doughty. (1991). Second Language Instruction Does Make a Difference: Evidence from an Empirical Study of SL Relativization. SSLA, 13, 431-469. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100010287

article_title: What Classroom Observations Reveal About Reading Comprehension Instruction
citation: Dolores Durkin. (1978). What Classroom Observations Reveal About Reading Comprehension Instruction. Technical Report No. 106, Center for the Study of Reading, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.
title: Durkin's eight-category scheme for classifying teachers' comprehension-related behavior
description: The article develops a coding scheme distinguishing comprehension instruction—"Teacher does/says something to help children understand or work out the meaning of more than a single, isolated word"—from seven related categories: application, assignment, help with assignment, review of instruction, preparation for reading, assessment, and prediction. The definition was built after a literature search found no usable definition, and it deliberately excludes single-word work such as phonics. It was applied identically to reading and social studies periods so time use could be compared.
requirements: Observers trained on descriptions and illustrations of each category; classifications checked by the researcher, with unclear cases resolved by discussion or by adding categories
constraints: The instruction/assessment distinction for questioning is acknowledged by the author as not what everyone would call clearly apparent, though observed questioning proved routine enough to classify
target_learners: elementary school students in grades 3-6
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of connected text larger than single words
examples: Categories were used to time 4469 minutes of fourth-grade reading instruction and 2775 minutes of social studies, revealing that assessment far outweighed instruction
key_sources: Dolores Durkin. (1978). What Classroom Observations Reveal About Reading Comprehension Instruction. Technical Report No. 106, Center for the Study of Reading, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. https://doi.org/10.1598/rrq.14.4.2

article_title: What Classroom Observations Reveal About Reading Comprehension Instruction
citation: Dolores Durkin. (1978). What Classroom Observations Reveal About Reading Comprehension Instruction. Technical Report No. 106, Center for the Study of Reading, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.
title: Improving comprehension instruction requires first observing and timing what classrooms currently do
description: The article argues that reform must begin with descriptive data: "it is impossible to improve instruction until what goes on now, and with what frequency, is known." The study therefore observed middle- and upper-grade classrooms specifically to find, describe, and time comprehension instruction, and published its category definitions and directions so other researchers could replicate the observations.
requirements: A workable definition of comprehension instruction that separates it from assessment and from single-word skills
constraints: Observations were limited to times teachers and administrators permitted; the start and end of the school year and holiday-adjacent weeks were excluded
target_learners: elementary school students in middle and upper grades
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension instruction practices
examples: Three sub-studies observed fourth grades, grades 3-6 across three schools, and individual children, with each classroom visited on three successive days spread across the school year

article_title: A cognitive-ecological approach to preventing aggression in urban settings: Initial outcomes for high-risk children.
citation: Metropolitan Area Child Study Research Group. (2002). A Cognitive–Ecological Approach to Preventing Aggression in Urban Settings: Initial Outcomes for High-Risk Children. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037//0022-006X.70.1.179
title: Cognitive–ecological model of aggression prevention
description: The cognitive–ecological model holds that aggression is learned and maintained across multiple social contexts, so prevention must modify both individual cognition and context. The article states its "preventive intervention is directed at modifying both individual social–cognitive and contextual factors relevant to the learning of aggression. We called this approach a cognitive–ecological model." In the MACS trial this translated into stacked intervention levels adding classroom, peer-group, and family contexts, with effectiveness expected to rise as more targeted contexts are added.
requirements: Interventions must target multiple socialization contexts (classroom, peers, family) rather than a single context or component
constraints: The article notes single-component or single-context interventions have limited effectiveness, motivating the multi-context design
target_learners: Elementary school children in inner-city and urban poor communities, especially those at high risk for aggression
target_learning_goals: Reduce aggressive behavior and increase protective factors such as school achievement and social–cognitive skills
examples: The MACS trial assigned 16 schools to control, classroom-only (Level A), classroom plus small-group peer-skills (Level B), and classroom plus peer-skills plus family (Level C) conditions
key_sources: Metropolitan Area Child Study Research Group. (2002). A Cognitive–Ecological Approach to Preventing Aggression in Urban Settings: Initial Outcomes for High-Risk Children. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-006x.70.1.179

article_title: A cognitive-ecological approach to preventing aggression in urban settings: Initial outcomes for high-risk children.
citation: Metropolitan Area Child Study Research Group. (2002). A Cognitive–Ecological Approach to Preventing Aggression in Urban Settings: Initial Outcomes for High-Risk Children. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037//0022-006X.70.1.179
title: Yes I Can social–cognitive classroom curriculum
description: Yes I Can is a 40-lesson social–cognitive classroom curriculum delivered to all children in the classroom over 2 years as the core of the Level A general enhancement intervention. It "covered five areas of social cognition, each related to risk for aggression: self-understanding/self-efficacy, social perspective taking, normative beliefs about aggression, social problem-solving skills, and behavioral scripts." Lessons were linked to reading and math, and teachers were trained via biweekly seminars with fidelity monitoring.
requirements: Delivery with teacher consultation focused on classroom management, prosocial behavior, and cultural competency; trained teacher collaborators and fidelity monitoring
constraints: In this trial the classroom-only condition showed no significant aggression or detectable effects for high-risk children when delivered early or late
target_learners: All children in elementary classrooms regardless of risk, in low-income urban schools
target_learning_goals: Social cognition skills related to aggression risk: self-efficacy, perspective taking, normative beliefs, problem-solving, and behavioral scripts
examples: Teachers received 2 years of biweekly seminars; 94% demonstrated mastery of content at or above the 80% level, and teachers were observed at least four times per academic year
key_sources: Metropolitan Area Child Study Research Group. (2002). A Cognitive–Ecological Approach to Preventing Aggression in Urban Settings: Initial Outcomes for High-Risk Children. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-006x.70.1.179

article_title: What Connections Can We Draw Between Research on Long‐Term Memory and Student Learning?
citation: Fandakova, Yana; Bunge, Silvia A. (2016). What Connections Can We Draw Between Research on Long-Term Memory and Student Learning? Mind, Brain and Education, 10(3). https://doi.org/10.1111/mbe.12123
title: Taxonomy of long-term memory systems relevant to classroom learning
description: The article presents a taxonomy of long-term memory as a framework for educators: long-term memory refers to "memory traces that last for days, months, or years" and is comprised of different systems associated with distinct biological substrates, including episodic memory for events rich in contextual detail, semantic memory for context-independent facts and concepts, and procedural skills. It explains that episodic memory relies heavily on the hippocampus whereas semantic memory depends on distributed cortical representations, and that these systems interact during learning.
requirements: Distinguishing memory forms by their content (events vs. facts vs. skills) and neural substrates
constraints: The article focuses on the forms of long-term memory most directly relevant to classroom learning, not all forms
target_learners: school-age children and adolescents
target_learning_goals: understanding how memory systems support academic learning such as reading, language comprehension, and arithmetic
examples: The article contrasts remembering seeing a lion at the zoo (episodic) with knowing that male lions have manes (semantic)
key_sources: Fandakova, Yana; Bunge, Silvia A. (2016). What Connections Can We Draw Between Research on Long-Term Memory and Student Learning? Mind, Brain and Education, 10(3). https://doi.org/10.1111/mbe.12123

article_title: Creativity in Children with Attention D&#233;ficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)
citation: Gonzalez-Carpio, G., Serrano, J. P., & Nieto, M. (2017). Creativity in Children with Attention Déficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Psychology, 8, 319-334. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2017.83019
title: Neurological and cognitive overlap hypothesis linking ADHD and creativity
description: The article proposes that ADHD and creativity share forms of cognitive and neurological functioning: delayed cortical maturation in prefrontal control regions, difficulty deactivating the default neural network producing a dispersed unfocused mental state, inefficient inhibition of irrelevant stimuli, and shared dopaminergic genetic markers such as the DRD4-7R gene. The article states this immaturity "favors a flexible way of thinking that is not conditioned by expectations or beliefs", so that "Uncontrolled cognition allows us to approach new solutions or creative ideas without limitations". It uses this hypothesis to motivate the empirical comparison of creativity in ADHD and control children.
requirements: The account presupposes unmedicated participants, since pharmacological treatment can change attentional and cognitive-flexibility profiles
constraints: The article presents this as a hypothesis drawn from prior literature, not as a mechanism tested in its own data
target_learners: children aged 8-13 diagnosed with ADHD
target_learning_goals: divergent thinking and creative potential
key_sources: Gonzalez-Carpio, G., Serrano, J. P., & Nieto, M. (2017). Creativity in Children with Attention Déficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Psychology, 8, 319-334. https://doi.org/10.4236/psych.2017.83019

article_title: Academic Identity Formation and Motivation Among Ethnic Minority Adolescents: The Role of the “Self” Between Internal and External Perceptions of Identity
citation: Jamaal S. Matthews, Meeta Banerjee, Fani Lauermann. (2014). Academic Identity Formation and Motivation Among Ethnic Minority Adolescents: The Role of the “Self” Between Internal and External Perceptions of Identity. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12318
title: Two-dimensional academic identity framework: internal value and external belonging as distinct but cohabitating dimensions
description: The article frames academic identity as having two concurrently assessed dimensions: an internally negotiated value dimension (perceived importance, interest, and enjoyment of academic tasks) and an externally supported belonging dimension (school belonging and social interconnectedness). It argues that "a multidimensional conceptualization of identity that includes not only internal attributes (i.e., value) but also ecological interactions such as social belonging more adequately captures identity-based processes," and presents value and belonging as "distinct but cohabitating dimensions of academic identity" whose effects on mastery are partially mediated through SRL.
requirements: Both dimensions must be assessed concurrently, since narrow single-dimension conceptions have reinforced a deficiency paradigm for marginalized adolescents
constraints: Developed and tested with African American and Latino adolescents in urban Title I schools during early to middle adolescence
target_learners: African American and Latino adolescents in urban middle and high schools
target_learning_goals: Achievement motivation, specifically mastery goal orientation and effortful self-regulated learning
examples: The study measured value with the MSLQ intrinsic value subscale (α = .82) and belonging with the Identification with School Questionnaire (α = .81), modeling both simultaneously in mediation and moderated mediation path analyses
key_sources: Jamaal S. Matthews, Meeta Banerjee, Fani Lauermann. (2014). Academic Identity Formation and Motivation Among Ethnic Minority Adolescents: The Role of the “Self” Between Internal and External Perceptions of Identity. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12318

article_title: Learning Words from Context
citation: Nagy, William E.; Herman, Patricia A.; Anderson, Richard C.; Pearson, P. David. (1984). Learning Words from Context. Center for the Study of Reading, Technical Report No. 319, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED248470
title: Incremental word learning: word meanings are acquired in small partial increments across repeated encounters, requiring measures sensitive to partial knowledge
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that "incidental learning from context proceeds in terms of small increments, so that any one encounter with a word in text will be likely to produce only a partial increase in knowledge of that word." A single encounter can still yield substantial, incomplete knowledge (fast mapping), while full mastery extends over years of repeated encounters. The framework explains why prior studies failed to detect context learning: they tested for full word knowledge, which underestimates incremental gains. The study therefore used interviews and multiple-choice items designed to tap partial knowledge at three levels of difficulty.
requirements: Assessment measures must be sensitive to partial word knowledge rather than requiring full, adult-like knowledge of meanings for a correct answer
constraints: Complete learning of a word's meaning is a gradual process, probably extending over years of repeated encounters
target_learners: middle-grade (junior high) students of average and above-average reading ability
target_learning_goals: vocabulary acquisition — partial and full knowledge of word meanings from reading
examples: The study scored interviews on a four-point scale from no correct knowledge to a totally correct answer, and built multiple-choice items at three levels of distractor similarity, to detect small increments of word knowledge
key_sources: Nagy, William E.; Herman, Patricia A.; Anderson, Richard C.; Pearson, P. David. (1984). Learning Words from Context. Center for the Study of Reading, Technical Report No. 319, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED248470

article_title: Academic Race Stereotypes, Academic Self-Concept, and Racial Centrality in African American Youth
citation: Okeke, N. A., Howard, L. C., Kurtz-Costes, B., & Rowley, S. J. (2009). Academic race stereotypes, academic self-concept, and racial centrality in African American youth. Journal of Black Psychology, 35(3), 366–387. https://doi.org/10.1177/0095798409333615
title: Multidimensional model of African American racial identity with four dimensions
description: The article adopts Sellers et al.'s conceptualization of racial identity in African Americans as "a multidimensional construct including four dimensions". Racial salience is how important race is at a particular time and context; racial ideology is beliefs about how African Americans should act; racial regard is evaluative judgment of one's race, with private and public aspects; and racial centrality is "the extent to which race is a central aspect of an individual's self-definition". The study uses the centrality subscale of the MIBI as its moderator variable.
requirements: Measured with the Multidimensional Inventory of Black Identity centrality subscale (6 items, α = .74 in both studies)
constraints: The article examines centrality only; salience, ideology, and regard are not tested as moderators
target_learners: African American middle school adolescents
target_learning_goals: Academic self-concept and achievement motivation
examples: Both studies measured centrality with six MIBI items rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale, e.g., "Being Black is an important part of my self-image"
key_sources: Okeke, N. A., Howard, L. C., Kurtz-Costes, B., & Rowley, S. J. (2009). Academic race stereotypes, academic self-concept, and racial centrality in African American youth. Journal of Black Psychology, 35(3), 366–387. https://doi.org/10.1177/0095798409333615

article_title: Academic Race Stereotypes, Academic Self-Concept, and Racial Centrality in African American Youth
citation: Okeke, N. A., Howard, L. C., Kurtz-Costes, B., & Rowley, S. J. (2009). Academic race stereotypes, academic self-concept, and racial centrality in African American youth. Journal of Black Psychology, 35(3), 366–387. https://doi.org/10.1177/0095798409333615
title: Expectancy-value account: stereotype endorsement directly influences perceptions of one's own competence
description: Drawing on Eccles et al.'s expectancy-value model of achievement motivation, the article theorizes that "a child's perception of stereotypes directly influences perceptions of his or her own competence", so that endorsement of traditional academic race stereotypes would lead to lower self-perceptions of academic competence for African Americans. The two studies test this hypothesis and find support only among youth high in racial centrality, illustrating the interweaving of group and individual identity with motivational beliefs.
requirements: The individual must perceive the stereotype as personally applicable for it to influence self-perceptions
constraints: Support in this article is correlational and cross-sectional; causal direction was not established
target_learners: African American adolescents in middle school
target_learning_goals: Academic self-concept, competence beliefs, achievement motivation
examples: The authors frame both studies as tests of the expectancy-value hypothesis that stereotype endorsement is negatively related to self-perceptions
key_sources: Okeke, N. A., Howard, L. C., Kurtz-Costes, B., & Rowley, S. J. (2009). Academic race stereotypes, academic self-concept, and racial centrality in African American youth. Journal of Black Psychology, 35(3), 366–387. https://doi.org/10.1177/0095798409333615

article_title: The influence of physical activity on the creativity of 10 and 11-year-old school children
citation: Romance, R., Nielsen-Rodríguez, A., Sousa Mendes, R., Dobado-Castañeda, J. C., & Dias, G. (2023). The influence of physical activity on the creativity of 10 and 11-year-old school children. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2023.101295
title: 4E cognition approach to creativity (embodied, embedded, enactive, extended)
description: The article adopts an embodied account in which "creative development happens as a result of the acting on and within an environment". The 4E cognition approach holds that, beyond idea generation, "the role of creative cognition is to guide action", treating human cognition as a dynamical system encompassing brain/mind, body and world/environment including objects, materials and artifacts. On this view, how we learn and develop expertise is shaped, constrained and enacted through exploration and interaction with the physical environment, which motivates studying physical activity as an environmental factor in children's creative development.
requirements: Adopting this account requires treating body movement and physical environment interaction as active components of creative cognition, not merely background variables.
constraints: The article notes few creativity theories still incorporate the embodied aspect, and that specific pedagogical practices leading to creativity have not been identified.
target_learners: Children in the last cycle of primary education (10–11 years old)
target_learning_goals: Development of creative thinking and divergent-thinking capacities
examples: The study operationalises the embodied account by measuring children's daily physical activity with triaxial accelerometry and relating it to Torrance Test divergent-thinking dimensions.
key_sources: Romance, R., Nielsen-Rodríguez, A., Sousa Mendes, R., Dobado-Castañeda, J. C., & Dias, G. (2023). The influence of physical activity on the creativity of 10 and 11-year-old school children. Thinking Skills and Creativity. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2023.101295

article_title: Multisensory Integration as a Window into Orderly and Disrupted Cognition and Communication
citation: Wallace, M. T., Woynaroski, T. G., & Stevenson, R. A. (2020). Multisensory Integration as a Window into Orderly and Disrupted Cognition and Communication. Annual Review of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-psych-010419-051112
title: Multisensory maturation scaffolds the development of higher-order cognitive and communicative skills
description: The review advances a developmental framework in which sensory and multisensory systems, which mature before higher-level cognitive and communicative processes, provide "a key developmental scaffold upon which higher-order representations are formed and refined". Early multisensory development relies heavily on low-level statistical stimulus features, and disruptions in foundational sensory function early in life are proposed to produce cascading effects across developmental domains. The framework is compatible with embodied cognition, the extended mind thesis, and enactivism.
requirements: Sensory and multisensory systems must develop ahead of, and provide foundational input to, higher-order cognitive and linguistic systems
constraints: The review notes that associations between multisensory function and cognition have largely been concurrent and correlational, so causality cannot yet be concluded
target_learners: infants and children in typical and atypical development
target_learning_goals: language acquisition
cognitive development
perceptual representation formation
examples: Quail embryos prenatally exposed to synchronous multisensory stimulation showed enhanced learning and memory for the mother's call relative to asynchronous or unisensory exposure

article_title: From Design to Implementation to Practice a Learning by Teaching System: Betty’s Brain
citation: Gautam Biswas, James R. Segedy, Kritya Bunchongchit. (2016). From Design to Implementation to Practice: a Learning by Teaching System: Betty's Brain. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0057-9
title: Hierarchical task model of open-ended learning environment tasks
description: The paper presents a hierarchical model characterizing the tasks students must perform to succeed in open-ended learning environments such as Betty's Brain, organized as "three broad classes of OELE tasks related to: (i) information seeking and acquisition, (ii) solution construction and refinement, and (iii) solution assessment." Each category is broken into three levels: general task descriptions common across OELEs, Betty's Brain specific instantiations, and system interface features. Directed links represent dependency relations, e.g., solution assessment depends on interpreting quiz results as actionable information for refining the solution in progress.
requirements: Students must learn to perform a diverse set of tasks across the model's three task classes to succeed in teaching Betty
constraints: The model was developed for OELEs generally and Betty's Brain more specifically
target_learners: middle school science students
target_learning_goals: building and refining causal models of science phenomena
self-directed problem solving in open-ended tasks
examples: Used to explain why some students struggled: some are good readers unfamiliar with the causal modeling language; others fail to use quiz results to find correct and incorrect links.
key_sources: Gautam Biswas, James R. Segedy, Kritya Bunchongchit. (2016). From Design to Implementation to Practice: a Learning by Teaching System: Betty's Brain. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0057-9

article_title: From Design to Implementation to Practice a Learning by Teaching System: Betty’s Brain
citation: Gautam Biswas, James R. Segedy, Kritya Bunchongchit. (2016). From Design to Implementation to Practice: a Learning by Teaching System: Betty's Brain. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0057-9
title: Coherence analysis framework and its six activity-trace measures
description: Coherence analysis (CA) is the paper's approach to analyzing learners' problem-solving processes in OELEs by "combining information gleaned from sequences of student actions to produce measures of action coherence." CA assumes that when students encounter information that could improve their solution, they should act on it; edits not justified by recent views are labeled unsupported edits. Six measures are derived from activity traces: edits/annotations per minute, unsupported edit percentage, information viewing percentage, potential generation percentage, used potential percentage, and disengaged percentage.
requirements: The redesigned interface makes only one of the reading, teaching, and quiz interfaces visible at a time, enabling the system to track shifts between activity types
constraints: View counts count toward potential only if page views lasted at least 10 s and quiz results at least 2 s, to filter out irrelevant actions
target_learners: middle school science students
target_learning_goals: characterizing self-regulated learning behavior in open-ended problem solving
examples: CA-derived metrics predicted students' task performance and learning gains and correlated significantly with prior skill levels in the classroom study.

article_title: Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Castro-Alonso, J. C., Wong, R. M., Adesope, O. O., & Paas, F. (2021). Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09587-1
title: Cognitive load theory (redundancy effect) and cognitive theory of multimedia learning (coherence principle) as the account predicting agent dimensionality effects
description: The article uses cognitive load theory and the cognitive theory of multimedia learning as explanatory frameworks for pedagogical agent design. It states that the observed dimensionality difference came "As predicted by the redundancy effect of cognitive load theory and the coherence principle of cognitive theory of multimedia learning". Under these frameworks, adding a 3D agent introduces redundant or extraneous material that the coherence principle and redundancy effect predict will hinder learning, explaining why simpler 2D agents tended to yield larger effects.
requirements: Applies to multimedia learning environments in which an on-screen agent's visual complexity could act as redundant or extraneous material.
constraints: The article presents this account as a prediction confirmed for the 2D-versus-3D contrast, hedged as a tendency rather than a decisive test.
target_learners: Students learning with multimedia environments
target_learning_goals: Multimedia learning outcomes (retention and understanding of instructional content)
examples: The meta-analysis compared pooled effects for 2D agents (g+ = 0.38) and 3D agents (g+ = 0.11) and interpreted the difference through these two frameworks.
key_sources: Castro-Alonso, J. C., Wong, R. M., Adesope, O. O., & Paas, F. (2021). Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09587-1

article_title: Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Castro-Alonso, J. C., Wong, R. M., Adesope, O. O., & Paas, F. (2021). Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09587-1
title: Computers are social actors hypothesis as the account predicting that most agent characteristics do not moderate effectiveness
description: The article tests the computers are social actors hypothesis, which predicts that learners' responses to on-screen characters do not depend strongly on most surface characteristics of the agent. The meta-analysis is described as showing, "As predicted by the computers are social actors hypothesis, most of the agents' characteristics, including nonverbal communication, motion, and voice, appeared not to moderate their effectiveness." This account explains why students may learn similarly from different types of agents despite variation in social cues such as motion and voice.
requirements: Applies to multimedia environments where agents deliver instruction and their social characteristics could plausibly be varied.
constraints: The article's support is a pattern of null moderator results, hedged with appeared not to; it does not establish that no characteristic ever matters.
target_learners: Students learning with multimedia environments
target_learning_goals: Multimedia learning outcomes across varied agent designs
examples: The meta-analysis tested moderator effects of nonverbal communication, motion, and voice and found they appeared not to moderate effectiveness.
key_sources: Castro-Alonso, J. C., Wong, R. M., Adesope, O. O., & Paas, F. (2021). Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09587-1

article_title: Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Castro-Alonso, J. C., Wong, R. M., Adesope, O. O., & Paas, F. (2021). Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09587-1
title: Agent-characteristic moderator taxonomy: appearance, gender, nonverbal communication, motion, and voice
description: The article organizes its meta-analytic tests around a set of agent characteristics that "may moderate their instructional effectiveness, including appearance, gender, nonverbal communication, motion, and voice." This five-branch taxonomy structures which agent design features were hypothesized (by cognitive load theory, cognitive theory of multimedia learning, computers are social actors, social agency theory, uncanny valley, and the action observation network) to change instructional effectiveness, and it frames the moderator analyses reported for the pooled effect sizes.
requirements: Used when designing or evaluating on-screen pedagogical agents in multimedia environments, where each characteristic can be varied independently.
constraints: The meta-analysis found most of these characteristics, except dimensionality (2D vs. 3D), appeared not to moderate effectiveness.
target_learners: Students learning with multimedia environments
target_learning_goals: Selection of pedagogical agent design features for multimedia instruction
examples: The meta-analysis of 32 effect sizes tested predictions of six theories against these five agent characteristics.

article_title: Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Castro-Alonso, J. C., Wong, R. M., Adesope, O. O., & Paas, F. (2021). Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09587-1
title: Prefer simpler 2D pedagogical agents over 3D agents in multimedia learning environments
description: Because the meta-analysis found that 2D agents (g+ = 0.38) tended to be more effective than 3D agents (g+ = 0.11), consistent with the redundancy effect and the coherence principle, designers of multimedia learning environments should default to simpler 2D on-screen characters rather than more elaborate 3D ones. The article's own conclusion is that "students may be able to learn similarly from different types of agents", so the recommendation is a conservative default, not a claim that 3D agents harm learning.
requirements: A multimedia learning environment in which an on-screen pedagogical agent is used to support learning.
constraints: The supporting difference is hedged as a tendency, and the article notes students may learn similarly from different types of agents; 3D agents are not shown to be harmful.
target_learners: Students learning with multimedia environments
target_learning_goals: Multimedia learning outcomes
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 32 effect sizes and compared 2D versus 3D agent conditions, finding g+ = 0.38 versus g+ = 0.11.

article_title: Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts
citation: Radkowitsch, A., Vogel, F., & Fischer, F. (2020). Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 15, 5–47. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09316-4
title: Script theory of guidance: internal collaboration scripts and the optimal external scripting level principle
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that collaborative learners' failure to engage in high-level collaborative processes indicates a lack of "internal collaboration scripts" — flexible cognitive structures of knowledge about collaborative practices, grounded in dynamic memory theory. External CSCL scripts scaffold collaboration by affording specific activities in a likely sequence and distributing roles, compensating for dysfunctional internal scripts. Fischer et al. identify four hierarchical script components — play, scene, scriptlet, and role — and propose the optimal external scripting level principle: learners benefit most from external scripts addressing the hierarchical level whose subordinate components learners do not yet have available.
requirements: External scripts must fit learners' prior knowledge and skills, i.e., the internal script components they have available
constraints: A CSCL script could lead to overscripting if it addresses internal script components on a level the learners are already able to activate, potentially reducing autonomy and motivation
target_learners: K-12 learners
higher education learners
professional development participants
target_learning_goals: collaboration skills
domain learning
key_sources: Radkowitsch, A., Vogel, F., & Fischer, F. (2020). Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 15, 5–47. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09316-4

article_title: Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts
citation: Radkowitsch, A., Vogel, F., & Fischer, F. (2020). Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 15, 5–47. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09316-4
title: Design CSCL scripts to scaffold specific collaborative activities (negotiation, information sharing, coordination) rather than treating transactivity as a single undifferentiated target
description: The article argues that because transactivity encompasses many specific collaborative activities, effectiveness research should and design can target the three social activities of Liu et al.'s collaborative problem-solving framework: sharing ideas or information, negotiating, and coordinating problem solving. CSCL scripts can prompt each activity specifically, and the meta-analysis codes scripts by which activities they scaffold to explain their effects on domain learning and collaboration skills.
requirements: Scripts must prompt activities that address learning partners, targeting the collaborative process of at least two learners
constraints: Coordination skills effects could not be estimated due to a small number of studies; synergistic or differentiated scaffolding is hard to achieve according to the authors
target_learners: K-12 learners
higher education learners
professional development participants
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem-solving skills
domain learning
examples: The meta-analysis categorized each included CSCL script by whether it prompted negotiation, information sharing, or coordination, and by the number and combination of activities prompted

article_title: Socio-Cognitive Scaffolding with Computer-Supported Collaboration Scripts: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Freydis Vogel, Christof Wecker, Ingo Kollar, Frank Fischer. (2016). Socio-Cognitive Scaffolding with Computer-Supported Collaboration Scripts: a Meta-Analysis. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9361-7
title: Script theory of guidance (SToG): internal scripts with four components scaffolded by external CSCL scripts on three levels
description: The meta-analysis builds on the script theory of guidance (Fischer, Kollar, Stegmann, and Wecker 2013), in which collaboration skills are regarded as internal scripts that, once consolidated, guide understanding and acting in similar situations. Internal scripts consist of four partially hierarchically ordered components: play, scene, scriptlet, and role components. External CSCL scripts support learners who lack appropriate internal scripts by prompting cognitive operations, sequencing activities, and distributing them among roles, with scaffolds addressable at the play, scene, and scriptlet levels. The article uses SToG to derive its moderator hypotheses about transactivity and script level.
requirements: Learners must be able to adapt and reconfigure internal script components in new collaborative situations for the scaffolding to modify the internal script
constraints: The article notes learners often cannot spontaneously engage in beneficial collaborative activities because they lack appropriate internal scripts, which is the condition external scripts address
target_learners: learners in computer-supported collaborative learning settings across domains such as computer science, economics, life sciences, educational science, medicine, and psychology
target_learning_goals: domain-specific knowledge acquisition
collaboration skills such as argumentation and peer feedback skills
examples: The article describes how a learner with an internal script for collaborative reading including asking thought-provoking questions might reconfigure script components for a collaborative problem-solving situation
key_sources: Freydis Vogel, Christof Wecker, Ingo Kollar, Frank Fischer. (2016). Socio-Cognitive Scaffolding with Computer-Supported Collaboration Scripts: a Meta-Analysis. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9361-7

article_title: Socio-Cognitive Scaffolding with Computer-Supported Collaboration Scripts: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Freydis Vogel, Christof Wecker, Ingo Kollar, Frank Fischer. (2016). Socio-Cognitive Scaffolding with Computer-Supported Collaboration Scripts: a Meta-Analysis. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9361-7
title: Combine collaboration scripts with content-related scaffolding so the two scaffolds amplify each other (synergistic scaffolding)
description: The article endorses Tabak's notion of synergistic scaffolding: scaffolding targeted at different aspects, such as a collaboration script supporting learners' activities and content-related scaffolding supporting the application of domain-specific knowledge, should amplify each other's effectiveness. CSCL scripts by definition scaffold content-independent aspects of collaboration, so learners may additionally need scaffolds supporting their processing of domain-specific content. The meta-analysis coded studies on three levels of content-related support, from none, through content-related information only, to content-related scaffolds such as worked examples and content schemes.
requirements: Content-related scaffolds must support how learners strategically work with domain-related material, not merely make content available
constraints: The meta-analytic moderator test found the differences among the three support levels were not statistically significant for domain-specific knowledge (Q(df = 2) = 0.77, p = .68)
target_learners: learners in computer-supported collaborative learning environments
target_learning_goals: domain-specific knowledge acquisition
high-quality collaborative learning activities such as social-discursive argumentation
examples: The article cites studies combining CSCL scripts with content schemes (Ertl, Kopp, and Mandl 2008) or scaffolds for hypothesis generation in simulation-based inquiry learning (Gijlers and de Jong 2009)

article_title: Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education
citation: Annelies Raes, Tammy Schellens, and Bram De Wever. (2013). Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.836656
title: WISE (Web-based Inquiry Science Environment) platform for designing and implementing science inquiry activities
description: WISE is an online platform from the University of California at Berkeley developed along the lines of the knowledge integration approach. It "provides a teacher's portal, including possibilities for classroom management, student assessment, and creating or editing curriculum projects" and a student interface with an inquiry map structuring activities in steps. It supports inquiry steps such as exploring a simulation, brainstorming, constructing an argument, and reflection and self-assessments. Students work in pairs and all teamwork is stored in a database accessible to teachers and researchers for assessment. The authors used the WISE authoring environment to create a new global climate change curriculum project codesigned with science teachers and technology specialists.
requirements: Requires teachers or trained facilitators to support implementation; in this study 46 trained Master's students served as actual teachers during the project
constraints: The curriculum project was designed to be closely tied to the regular Flemish curriculum and integrated with local teaching and learning practices
target_learners: Secondary school students in Grades 9 and 10
target_learning_goals: Science knowledge acquisition about global warming and climate change
Science inquiry skills
Interest in science
examples: A new WISE curriculum project on global warming and climate change was implemented across four 50-min lessons in 19 Flemish secondary classes

article_title: Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education
citation: Annelies Raes, Tammy Schellens, and Bram De Wever. (2013). Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.836656
title: Knowledge integration instructional pattern: Elicit ideas, Add new ideas, Distinguish among ideas, Reflect on and integrate ideas
description: This is the instructional pattern structuring activities in the knowledge integration design framework for science curriculum projects (Slotta & Linn, 2009) as implemented in the WISE global climate change project. "Each activity starts with eliciting the ideas that students already hold. Subsequently, students get the opportunity to add new ideas and distinguish among ideas by searching and critiquing Web-based evidence, exploring provided simulations or interactive graphs, and discussing with peers. Finally, students are asked to reﬂect on these ideas in order to integrate them into their repertoire of ideas." The pattern is crossed with four knowledge integration principles: making science accessible, making thinking visible, helping students learn from others, and promoting autonomy.
requirements: Web-based evidence sources, simulations, or interactive graphs for students to search, critique, and explore
Peer discussion opportunities such as classroom debates
target_learners: Secondary school science students across achievement levels and academic tracks
target_learning_goals: Integrated, coherent understanding of scientific topics
Inquiry skills
Interest in science
examples: Table 1 maps the four principles and four pattern phases to project activities such as calculating students' ecological footprint, analyzing CO2 emissions trends in Gapminder World, and an online classroom debate between believers and nonbelievers

article_title: Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education
citation: Annelies Raes, Tammy Schellens, and Bram De Wever. (2013). Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.836656
title: Knowledge integration approach to science learning
description: Knowledge integration is an approach to science learning conceptualized by the Technology Enhanced Learning in Science community, contrasted with the absorption approach of recalling isolated bits of information. It "can be deﬁned as the process of incorporating new information into a body of existing knowledge by guiding students to engage in inquiry (Linn & Eylon, 2011)." It builds on evidence that every student brings a repertoire of rich, confusing, and intriguing ideas to the science class and needs to link their ideas to new ideas and use evidence to sort through alternative ideas. In this study it served as the design basis for the WISE curriculum project and for outcome measures evaluating whether students could link and connect ideas using evidence.
requirements: Instruction that elicits students' existing ideas and provides evidence for sorting among alternative ideas
target_learners: Secondary school science students
target_learning_goals: Knowledge acquisition as integrated understanding rather than recall of isolated facts
Inquiry skills including diagnosing problems, critiquing experiments, and forming coherent arguments
examples: The WISE global climate change project activities were designed according to the knowledge integration instructional pattern and its four principles

article_title: Knowledge Convergence in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: The Role of External Representation Tools
citation: Frank Fischer, Heinz Mandl. (2005). Knowledge Convergence in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: The Role of External Representation Tools. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 14(3), pp.405-441. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190855
title: Knowledge convergence as a two-dimensional construct: convergence of collaborative process (resource use) versus convergence of individual outcomes
description: The article frames knowledge convergence in computer-supported collaborative learning along two distinguishable dimensions: convergence in what learners do during collaboration (their use of knowledge resources) and convergence in what they know afterwards (individual outcomes, further split into factual and application-oriented knowledge). The study's design, varying "the type of external representation (content-specific vs. content-independent) and the collaboration condition (videoconferencing vs. face-to-face)", is built to measure these dimensions separately, and its central finding is that they diverge: strong process convergence coexists with low outcome convergence.
requirements: Measuring convergence requires assessing both resource use during collaboration and individual knowledge outcomes after collaboration, as the study does.
constraints: Outcome convergence was found to be rather low in this study, and the process-outcome relation was examined only exploratorily.
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: factual knowledge
application-oriented knowledge
examples: The study operationalized convergence by comparing learning partners' use of knowledge resources during collaboration and their individual knowledge outcomes after collaboration under four conditions.
key_sources: Frank Fischer, Heinz Mandl. (2005). Knowledge Convergence in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: The Role of External Representation Tools. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 14(3), pp.405-441. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190855

title: External representation tools (content-specific vs. content-independent graphical representations) as collaboration supports
description: Graphical external representation tools provided to collaborating learners, distinguished by whether they are content-specific or content-independent. The article investigates "how two types of graphical representation tools influence the way in which learners use knowledge resources in two different collaboration conditions." Content-specific tools led learners to use more appropriate knowledge resources, while content-independent tools served as the comparison condition.
requirements: The tools are used within collaborative learning settings where learners draw on shared knowledge resources.
constraints: Content-specific representations increased appropriate resource use but did not increase knowledge sharing after collaboration.

target_learning_goals: use of appropriate knowledge resources
shared knowledge in collaborative learning

article_title: The Social and Technological Dimensions of Scaffolding and Related Theoretical Concepts for Learning, Education, and Human Activity
citation: Roy D. Pea. (2004). The Social and Technological Dimensions of Scaffolding and Related Theoretical Concepts for Learning, Education, and Human Activity. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(3), pp.423-451. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190619
title: Scaffolding is theorized as having both social and technological dimensions relevant to learning, education, and human activity
description: The article's title frames scaffolding as a theoretical concept with two named dimensions — the social and the technological — and situates it among 'Related Theoretical Concepts for Learning, Education, and Human Activity'. The article thus treats scaffolding not as a purely interpersonal instructional move but as a construct whose analysis spans both human social interaction and technological tools, within the learning sciences. The supplied text is a repository metadata record, so this characterization rests on the article's own printed title and keyword metadata.
requirements: The framework addresses scaffolding together with related theoretical concepts, rather than scaffolding in isolation, as stated in the article's title.

article_title: Sharing Solutions: Persistence and Grounding in Multimodal Collaborative Problem Solving
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg, David Traum. (2006). Sharing solutions: persistence and grounding in multi-modal collaborative problem solving. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 15 (1), pp.121-151. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327809jls1501_9
title: Persistence as an interpretive framework for media use in multimodal collaborative problem solving
description: The article interprets its multimodal collaboration findings through the concept of persistence: information of differing persistence is routed to media of matching persistence. In the studied setting, a shared whiteboard and a MOO text chat were examined, and "More persistent information is exchanged through the more persistent medium." The framework explains why "The whiteboard was used as a shared memory rather than a grounding tool," linking media properties to grounding behavior in collaborative problem solving.

article_title: The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics
citation: Ayush Gupta, David Hammer, Edward F. Redish. (2008). The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/hlns20
title: Static Ontologies (SO) framework: ontological categories are distinct, stable, and constraining
description: The SO framework, advanced by Chi, Slotta, and colleagues, holds that entities and science concepts belong to a single hierarchical ontological category (matter, processes, mental states) whose trees do not share attributes. The article summarizes its core: "ontological categories are distinct, stable, and constraining", so novices' difficulties with heat, light, current, and diffusion arise from mis-categorizing processes as matter. Conceptual change is re-assignment across trees, and predicates serve as empirical markers of categorization.
requirements: Empirical evidence for categorization is taken from the verbal predicates participants use to describe concepts
constraints: The article contests this framework, arguing it mischaracterizes everyday, expert, and novice reasoning
target_learners: novice physics students
target_learning_goals: understanding of physics concepts such as heat, light, electric current, and diffusion

article_title: The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics
citation: Ayush Gupta, David Hammer, Edward F. Redish. (2008). The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/hlns20
title: Dynamic ontologies account: ontological reasoning is flexible and context-dependent
description: The authors' alternative account holds that entities may have multiple or ambiguous ontological categorizations and that a person's ontological view of an entity is sensitive to context and can vary moment to moment. They argue "that expert ontologies are dynamic and context-dependent as well", and that resources associated with one ontological category are often marshaled productively for understanding concepts in another. Ontological blending is presented as an essential expert skill for concepts like energy, flow, and quantum particles.
requirements: Models of learner knowledge must allow multiple, context-sensitive categorizations of the same concept
constraints: The account is argued from examples in everyday speech, expert discourse, and classroom reasoning rather than from controlled experiments
target_learners: novice physics students
physics instructors
target_learning_goals: ontological flexibility in reasoning about physics concepts

article_title: The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics
citation: Ayush Gupta, David Hammer, Edward F. Redish. (2008). The Case for Dynamic Models of Learners' Ontologies in Physics. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://www.tandfonline.com/journals/hlns20
title: Instruction should build from, not suppress, matter-based reasoning about physics concepts
description: Because matter-based reasoning provides essential resources for novices and experts alike, instruction should help students refine and build from reasoning grounded in experiences of matter rather than prevent it. The authors warn that "instruction that seeks to prevent students from reasoning in ways based on their experiences of matter or of ‘direct processes,' rather than to help them refine and build from that reasoning, is likely to be detrimental to their learning physics". This counters the SO recommendation to avoid matter-like analogies and language.
requirements: Instructors must attend to learners' ontologies, as the authors agree with Chi and Slotta
constraints: Promoting one ontological description exclusively could undermine novices' access to productive cognitive resources and inhibit their transition to expert ontological flexibility
target_learners: novice physics students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of physics concepts such as heat, electric current, and light
examples: The authors cite Slotta and Chi's recommendation that instruction carefully avoid any language, analogies, or phenomena that might reinforce the substance-based view, and contest it

As the abstract states, the paper proceeds 'After distinguishing several conceptions of communication, and highlighting transformative communications for learning'. This framework frames communication not as mere transmission but as a process that can transform participants' understanding, and it serves as the conceptual foundation for the article's argument about how technology should support collaborative learning.

description: The article proposes that distributed multimedia learning environments, delivered via broadband telepresence, can establish transformative communications for learning. Its central design argument is that such environments succeed only when they 'adequally acknowledg[e] the social and material embeddedness of everyday communication' — that is, when the technical design respects that real communication is situated in social relationships and material settings rather than being context-free information transfer.

The principle directs designers and researchers to settle their theoretical commitments about these three constructs before building or evaluating systems, because implicit conceptions of communication shape what systems are built and how their success is judged.

article_title: Developing Symbolic Interpretation Through Literary Argumentation
citation: Teresa Sosa, Allison H. Hall, and Susan R. Goldman; Carol D. Lee. (2015). Developing Symbolic Interpretation Through Literary Argumentation.
title: Domain analysis of literary interpretation: levels of text representation plus point-driven reading
description: The article's domain analysis identifies components of competent literary analysis, grounding basic comprehension in a cognitive discourse processing approach in which "comprehension results in different “levels” of representation of a text, most commonly described as surface code, textbase, and situation model." Because literary reading is "point-driven," the authors postulate additional levels of representation beyond the situation model, so readers construct mental models of the author's possible intentions. The analysis also specifies that valid interpretations rest on textual evidence plus reasoning connecting evidence to interpretive claims, drawing on worldviews and knowledge of other texts.
requirements: Instruction must address multiple foci: textbase and situation model building, rhetorical strategies, and evidence-plus-reasoning for interpretive claims
constraints: The authors note few instructional efforts integrated multiple foci, with Lee's Cultural Modeling Framework as the exception they cite
target_learners: adolescent secondary students in English Language Arts
target_learning_goals: literary analysis and interpretation
making and warranting interpretive claims about symbolism
examples: The module design derived learning objectives from this analysis, sequencing symbol identification, text-evidence-based claims, and patterns of evidence across extended texts.

Texts increased in complexity in parallel, from everyday images and pop songs to a culturally less familiar lengthier text. Supporting worksheets accompanied each phase.

citation: Nilsen, A. P. (2016). Navigating windows into past human minds: A framework of shifting selves in historical perspective taking. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 25, 372-410. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2016.1160830
title: Framework of four shifting self perspectives in historical perspective taking
description: The article proposes that historical perspective taking involves four self perspectives, each with distinct grammatical features: the now-self (present-day first-person statements), the hypothetical past self (first-person conditionals), the imagined past self (first-person present indicative not referring to the present-day self), and the timeless generalized other (generic you, we, people). The framework links HPT to social science research on perspective taking and the self, and is used to analyze how learners process historical material. As the abstract states, "Four shifting “self perspectives” were identified, whereby participants thought as their present-day selves, constructed hypothetical and imagined past selves, and made timeless generalizations about humans."
requirements: Think-aloud or other discourse data in which grammatical forms (pronouns, verb mood, tense) can be analyzed to identify which self perspective is active

article_title: Defensive and Expansive Cycles of Learning: A Study of Home Care Encounters
citation: Nummijoki, J., Engeström, Y., & Sannino, A. (2018). Defensive and expansive cycles of learning: A study of home care encounters. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 27(2), 224-264. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2017.1412970
title: Expansive learning cycle as a framework for analyzing micro-cycles in recurring work encounters
description: The theory of expansive learning (Engeström, 2015) posits that learning is triggered by contradictions in activity systems and proceeds through seven expansive learning actions: questioning, analysis, modeling, examining, implementing, reflecting, and consolidating. The article applies this ideal-typical model to small-scale cycles within single home care encounters, noting that "a small expansive cycle may take place within a single intensive encounter that requires analysis and redesign of the practice." The authors map substance-specific actions of home care clients and workers onto these seven actions to construct working models for empirical analysis.
requirements: Contradictions in the existing activity must be present to trigger learning efforts
A new challenging set of actions and artifacts must be introduced into recurring cycles of scripted actions
constraints: The occurrence of a full-fledged expansive cycle in temporally compressed encounters is not common and typically requires deliberate efforts and interventions
Pure examples of fully expansive or fully defensive cycles were rarely found in the data
target_learners: Home care clients (elderly adults)
Home care workers (professional practitioners)
target_learning_goals: Constructing a qualitatively new pattern of activity oriented at sustainable mobility
Integrating physical mobility exercises into routine work scripts
examples: The authors mapped home care client and worker actions onto the seven expansive cycle actions (Table 1) and used this as a coding scheme for analyzing 30 videotaped visits
key_sources: Nummijoki, J., Engeström, Y., & Sannino, A. (2018). Defensive and expansive cycles of learning: A study of home care encounters. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 27(2), 224-264. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2017.1412970

article_title: Defensive and Expansive Cycles of Learning: A Study of Home Care Encounters
citation: Nummijoki, J., Engeström, Y., & Sannino, A. (2018). Defensive and expansive cycles of learning: A study of home care encounters. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 27(2), 224-264. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2017.1412970
title: Defensive learning cycle: learning to protect routines and avert adoption of novel actions
description: Defensive learning occurs when actors facing a demanding new practice learn to protect their existing routines and avert or forestall adoption of novel actions. The article states that "In such defensive learning, actors learn to protect their routines and to avert and forestall the adoption of novel actions." When combined and repeated, defensive actions may form complex defensive routines. The authors construct a substance-specific model of defensive learning for home care, projecting the vicious circle of fear-of-falling onto both client and worker, and code defensive actions with minus signs across the seven cycle positions.
requirements: Introduction of a demanding new practice that challenges existing routines
Actors must have invested in or identified with the existing practice script
constraints: Defensive learning has received scant attention within the learning sciences until quite recently
Defensive actions may be manifested as passivity and indifference rather than active rejection
target_learners: Home care workers defending standard scripts
Elderly clients preferring passivity and service reception
target_learning_goals: Protecting existing routines from disruption
Averting adoption of novel actions perceived as threatening workload or safety
examples: In Case A, the worker diverted the client's exercise hints toward substitute topics (armchair color, a flower), extinguishing the client's initiative to use the armchair as an exercise device
key_sources: Nummijoki, J., Engeström, Y., & Sannino, A. (2018). Defensive and expansive cycles of learning: A study of home care encounters. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 27(2), 224-264. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2017.1412970

article_title: Defensive and Expansive Cycles of Learning: A Study of Home Care Encounters
citation: Nummijoki, J., Engeström, Y., & Sannino, A. (2018). Defensive and expansive cycles of learning: A study of home care encounters. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 27(2), 224-264. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2017.1412970
title: Mobility Agreement practice for embedding physical exercises in home care visits
description: The Mobility Agreement is a plan negotiated and prepared jointly by the home care worker and the elderly client, with the objective of promoting daily exercises such as stand-ups from a chair, balancing exercises and taking the stairs. It is "primarily an embodied agreement that is re-enacted within regular encounters, in joint physical actions and accompanying verbal and gestural exchanges." It is supported by an illustrated booklet graphically describing typical exercises, recorded in the client's care plan, and designed to break the vicious cycle of fear-of-falling by integrating mobility work into daily chores at home.
requirements: Joint preparation and negotiation between client and home care worker
Integration into regular recurring home care visits
Support of an illustrated exercise booklet
Recording in the client's care plan
constraints: Its potentials and benefits are only disclosed when the dominant script of home care encounters is qualitatively transformed
Each client's life situation is different and the practice must be creatively adapted
Embedding and anchoring exercise actions into daily routines takes time and needs persistent pursuit
target_learners: Elderly home care clients with reduced physical mobility
Home care workers in municipal services
target_learning_goals: Improving muscle strength, balance and functionality
Rediscovering the potentials of one's body
Breaking the vicious cycle of fear of falling and activity restriction
examples: In Case D, the home care team had continuously assessed the client's resources and changed the Mobility Agreement depending on progress and seasons, such as more indoor exercises during winter

article_title: Teacher–Student Dialogue During Classroom Teaching: Does It Really Impact on Student Outcomes?
citation: Howe, C., Hennessy, S., Mercer, N., Vrikki, M., & Wheatley, L. (2018). Teacher-Student Dialogue during Classroom Teaching: Does it Really Impact upon Student Outcomes? To appear in The Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=ES/M007103/1
title: Theoretically productive classroom dialogue framework: five recurring themes plus the cross-cutting theme of high student contribution
description: The article defines theoretically productive dialogue as classroom verbal interaction complying with five recurring themes: open questions, elaboration of previous contributions, reasoned discussion of competing viewpoints, linkage and coordination across contributions, and meta-cognitive engagement with dialogue, plus high student contribution. It states that amongst proposals about optimizing outcomes, "five themes recur", and uses the framework to code routine lessons and test whether the themes relate to student outcomes in teacher-student dialogue, not just small-group work.
requirements: All participants, teachers and students, should contribute fully to ensuring interaction complies with the themes, implying high levels of student involvement
constraints: Researchers differ over which themes they emphasize and over the labels used, especially the term dialogue
The themes emerged from decades of classroom observation and vary in how they are operationalized
target_learners: Primary school students aged 10-11 years (Year 6) in whole-class teacher-student dialogue
target_learning_goals: Curriculum mastery in mathematics, science and literacy
General reasoning
Educationally relevant attitudes
examples: The authors contrast open questions such as asking why Edinburgh became a major cultural centre with closed questions such as asking for the capital of Scotland
key_sources: Howe, C., Hennessy, S., Mercer, N., Vrikki, M., & Wheatley, L. (2018). Teacher-Student Dialogue during Classroom Teaching: Does it Really Impact upon Student Outcomes? To appear in The Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=ES/M007103/1
