citation: Howe, C., Hennessy, S., Mercer, N., Vrikki, M., & Wheatley, L. (2018). Teacher-Student Dialogue during Classroom Teaching: Does it Really Impact upon Student Outcomes? To appear in The Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=ES/M007103/1
title: Turn-level and lesson-level dialogue coding scheme adapted from Hennessy et al. (2016)
description: An observational scheme coding every speaker turn for codes such as ELI, EL, REI, RE, OI, UC, Q, SC, RC, RB and RW, plus five holistic lesson-level ratings (Aims, Monitoring, Reflection, Talk Rules, Student Participation). The article reports that "Video-recorded dialogue was analyzed using a scheme based on work reported by Hennessy, Rojas-Drummond and colleagues", with reliability checks on 9952 turns yielding Pearson rs from .65 to 1.00 (M=.79).
requirements: Video recordings with teacher and ambient microphones
Independent coding of lessons by two researchers for reliability checking
constraints: CI and RC were seldom detected and coordination codes were dropped from further analysis
Talk Rules ratings were discounted because 89% of lessons were rated 0
target_learners: Primary school classes aged 10-11 years
target_learning_goals: Characterizing the quality of teacher-student classroom dialogue
examples: A teacher turn praising a student and elaborating the one-speaker-at-a-time rule was coded A plus EL

citation: Howe, C., Hennessy, S., Mercer, N., Vrikki, M., & Wheatley, L. (2018). Teacher-Student Dialogue during Classroom Teaching: Does it Really Impact upon Student Outcomes? To appear in The Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=ES/M007103/1
title: Six-component student outcome assessment battery (three SATs, science test, reasoning test, PASS)
description: The study assessed six outcomes: Mathematics, SPAG and Reading SATs supplied by teachers, a specially prepared Year 6 science test on inheritance and evolution and fair testing, a specially designed general reasoning test, and the PASS attitude survey. For the science test, "Pilot data indicated that the items had excellent scale properties (Cronbach's alpha across all items=.95; mean square out-fit scores all below 2.00 on Rasch analysis)"; the reasoning test alpha was .98 and PASS alpha .93.
requirements: Teacher-supplied anonymized SAT scores
Trained markers with a scoring manual for science short-text items
Start-of-year NFER baselines matched to each outcome
constraints: Mathematics SAT analyses were based on 61 classes because classes where a colleague taught mathematics were discounted
The science test was omitted in classrooms that had not covered inheritance and evolution
target_learners: Year 6 students in English primary schools (N up to 1784)
target_learning_goals: Curriculum mastery in mathematics, literacy and science
General reasoning
Attitudes to school, self as learner and relationship with teacher
examples: Science items covered fossilization, heritability including of acquired characteristics, and inter-generational adaptation

article_title: Theories of learning as theories of society: A contrapuntal approach to expanding disciplinary authenticity in computing
citation: Philip, T., & Sengupta, P. (2020). Theories of Learning as Theories of Society: A Contrapuntal Approach to Expanding Disciplinary Authenticity in Computing. Journal of the Learning Sciences. http://www.isls.org/
title: Theories of learning are implicit theories of society
description: The article's central framework holds that theories of learning emerge within researchers' sociopolitical contexts and co-construct the worlds they describe, so learning theory cannot be treated as politically neutral. The authors argue that "theories of learning are implicit theories of society" and that the field must attend to "the lens of imperialism" in analyzing learning. This reframes how designs and theories should be evaluated in the Learning Sciences.
requirements: Researchers must treat the sociopolitical context and consequences of learning theories as part of the theory itself, not as external background
constraints: The authors state the field cannot yet predict what will unfold from new theories and methods developed under this lens
target_learners: Learning Sciences researchers and graduate students
target_learning_goals: Understanding learning as political and situated in sociopolitical contexts
examples: The authors reread behaviorism, cognitivism, and sociocultural theory as theories of society, and read disciplinary authenticity in computing education contrapuntally against sociology of immigrant tech workers
key_sources: Philip, T., & Sengupta, P. (2020). Theories of Learning as Theories of Society: A Contrapuntal Approach to Expanding Disciplinary Authenticity in Computing. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2020.1828089

article_title: Theories of learning as theories of society: A contrapuntal approach to expanding disciplinary authenticity in computing
citation: Philip, T., & Sengupta, P. (2020). Theories of Learning as Theories of Society: A Contrapuntal Approach to Expanding Disciplinary Authenticity in Computing. Journal of the Learning Sciences. http://www.isls.org/
title: Contrapuntal reading: juxtaposing designs and theories with histories of empire
description: Building on Said (1993), the article defines contrapuntal reading as drawing out "the logics of and resistances to empire and imperialism that are silent or marginally present" in designs and theories. It complements, rather than replaces, contextual and consequential readings by adding a sharpened analysis of imperialism, asking "Who is simultaneously integral and invisiblized through imperialism in our conceptualizations of learning?" The article demonstrates the lens by reading disciplinary authenticity in computing education alongside sociology of immigrant tech workers.
requirements: An explicit juxtaposition of designs and theories with histories and contemporary processes of imperialism, as Said (1993) outlined
constraints: The authors state contrapuntality is meant to complement, not replace, contextual and consequential readings
target_learners: Learning Sciences researchers and graduate students
target_learning_goals: Analyzing learning designs and theories for their entanglement with empire and imperialism
examples: The article's Said-inspired reading of Mansfield Park surfacing the labor of endarkened people in Antigua, and its juxtaposition of computing education's authenticity construct with Banerjee and Rincon's (2019) study of immigrant tech workers
key_sources: Philip, T., & Sengupta, P. (2020). Theories of Learning as Theories of Society: A Contrapuntal Approach to Expanding Disciplinary Authenticity in Computing. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2020.1828089

article_title: Material syntonicity: Examining computational performance and its materiality through weaving and sewing crafts
citation: Anna Keune (2022). Material syntonicity: Examining computational performance and its materiality through weaving and sewing crafts. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2022.2100704
title: Material syntonicity: ongoing physical intra-action with materials shapes what can be learned computationally
description: Material syntonicity extends Papert's body syntonicity with posthumanist perspectives, shifting attention to the ongoing physical aspects of domain learning. The article theorizes "this ongoing intra-action as material syntonicity, which shifts attention to the ongoing physical aspects of domain learning," capturing how students and craft materials come together and move apart to produce disciplinary phenomena. It disrupts assumptions about the neutrality of dominant notions of computing such as computing as automation, since what counts as computation was contingent on the material: weaving drove automation while fabric manipulation drove speculative 3D modeling.
requirements: Materials must be manipulable tangible media with which learners bodily intra-act during domain performance, as in the matrix-based fiber crafts studied.
constraints: The theory was developed from two matrix-based fiber crafts (weaving and fabric manipulation) in one middle school design studio setting; the article presents it as a material direction for computing education rather than a tested intervention.
target_learners: middle school students aged 11-14
target_learning_goals: computational concepts (variables, conditionals, functions)
broadening what counts as computing
examples: Devanie's weaving moved from irregular skip patterns to regular hourglass patterns as she and the loom repeated intra-actions; Aki's sewing produced folds that counteracted one another through knot-stitch functions on the fabric matrix.
key_sources: Anna Keune (2022). Material syntonicity: Examining computational performance and its materiality through weaving and sewing crafts. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2022.2100704

article_title: Material syntonicity: Examining computational performance and its materiality through weaving and sewing crafts
citation: Anna Keune (2022). Material syntonicity: Examining computational performance and its materiality through weaving and sewing crafts. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2022.2100704
title: Fiber crafts course with weaving and fabric manipulation units in a school design studio
description: A fiber crafts course facilitated within a weekly design studio at a K-8 public charter school, in which 16 middle school students aged 11-14 self-selected into units on weaving and fabric manipulation. Students wove personal designs on backstrap, rigid heddle, and tabletop looms, and sewed 3D shapes using a laser-cut template of a checkered matrix. Students planned designs on grid paper before implementing them, a tool drawn from the crafting community, and were not introduced to computing concepts in relation to crafts during the study.
requirements: Looms warped before sessions and a checkered matrix template for tracing dots onto fabric, so students could engage the matrix structures of both crafts.
constraints: The course consisted of three units of two sessions apiece (1 h 10 min/session); this article focuses on the first two units, and students knew the research concerned fiber crafts and computing.
target_learners: middle school students aged 11-14 in a K-8 public charter school
target_learning_goals: performing computational concepts through personally meaningful craft projects
examples: Students wove an average of 18 rows of plain weave before their first pattern variation, and all students sewed four twisted square units as their first fabric manipulation project.
key_sources: Anna Keune (2022). Material syntonicity: Examining computational performance and its materiality through weaving and sewing crafts. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2022.2100704

article_title: A framework for infrastructuring sustainable innovations in education
citation: Chen, B. (2024). A framework for infrastructuring sustainable innovations in education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2024.2320159
title: The IMPROV framework: six interconnected action areas for infrastructuring sustainable educational innovations
description: The IMPROV framework organizes infrastructuring in education into six interconnected action areas: identifying key social actors and design areas, making visible existing infrastructures, planning possible points of infrastructuring, rallying for coherence-making and infrastructure remaking, orchestrating meta-design and capacity building, and evaluating infrastructures continually. The article states it "oWers actionable guidance on infrastructuring in the learning sciences and education in six interconnected action areas." Its core claim is that sustaining an innovation requires revealing components of existing infrastructures and nurturing stakeholder coherence-making between the innovation and those infrastructures.
requirements: Work in the six areas may occur in parallel or move back-and-forth; the framework requires flexibly responding to emergent needs of the innovation rather than following a strict sequence
constraints: Strategies developed in other disciplines need revisions or new strategies to address persistent problems in education settings, given education's entrenched beliefs, norms, and structures
target_learners: learning designers and researchers
educators and practitioners across K-12 and higher education
target_learning_goals: sustaining learning innovations in authentic educational settings
building capacity for practitioner-led design
examples: The framework is illustrated with examples from Knowledge Building initiatives, including the IdeaMagnets project in a US public school and KB work in a Toronto laboratory school
key_sources: Chen, B. (2024). A framework for infrastructuring sustainable innovations in education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2024.2320159

article_title: A framework for infrastructuring sustainable innovations in education
citation: Chen, B. (2024). A framework for infrastructuring sustainable innovations in education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2024.2320159
title: Knowledge Building pedagogy and Knowledge Forum as a running case of infrastructuring challenges
description: Knowledge Building (KB) is a long-standing learning theory and pedagogy that supports learning by fostering continual idea improvement in a community, supported by digital technologies such as Knowledge Forum. The article uses KB initiatives worldwide as illustrative cases across all six IMPROV areas, noting that "heavy reliance on researchers creates challenges for sustainability" and that friction with existing education systems arises as KB enters new contexts.
requirements: Sustaining KB involves building infrastructures at multiple levels, including classrooms, schools, and regional and international networks
constraints: Emphasis on ongoing researcher involvement in teacher-researcher teams creates sustainability challenges; tensions arise with prescribed curriculum mandates and assessment systems
target_learners: students
teachers
school leaders
policy makers
target_learning_goals: fostering continual idea improvement in knowledge-creating communities
examples: KB sites in Canada, Brazil, China, Italy, and Singapore have reported coherence-making activities; the Curriculum-Ideas Analytics tool maps student discussions onto curricular objectives
key_sources: Chen, B. (2024). A framework for infrastructuring sustainable innovations in education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2024.2320159

article_title: Apprenticeship as a developmental mechanism in argumentation skill development
citation: Song, Yu. (2023). Apprenticeship As a Developmental Mechanism in Argumentation Skill Development. Ph.D. dissertation, Columbia University. https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/Song_columbia_0054D_18218
title: Apprenticeship model of dialogic argumentation skill development
description: The dissertation proposes an apprenticeship model as a mechanism in the development of skill in dialogic argumentation, in which less skilled adolescents engage in one-on-one dialogs with more skilled partners who model "skilled forms of counterargument and use of evidence to support claims" along with questioning and meta-talk. The skill developed dialogically is treated as "a bridge to individual written argument". The model was tested in a multi-week intervention with more skilled versus similarly skilled anonymous partners.
requirements: Learners must engage in extended one-on-one electronic dialogs on controversial issues with partners who display skilled argumentative moves.
constraints: The abstract presents the model as tested with young adolescents on controversial issues; it does not claim generalization beyond this population or format.
target_learners: young adolescents
target_learning_goals: dialogic argumentation skill
individual written argument
examples: Young adolescents were paired with a series of both more skilled and similarly skilled partners, anonymously, in multi-week one-on-one electronic dialogs on controversial issues.
key_sources: Song, Yu. (2023). Apprenticeship As a Developmental Mechanism in Argumentation Skill Development. Ph.D. dissertation, Columbia University. https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/Song_columbia_0054D_18218

article_title: Apprenticeship as a developmental mechanism in argumentation skill development
citation: Song, Yu. (2023). Apprenticeship As a Developmental Mechanism in Argumentation Skill Development. Ph.D. dissertation, Columbia University. https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/Song_columbia_0054D_18218
title: Dialogical model of argument skill development (social-to-individual passage)
description: The dissertation discusses a dialogical model of argument skill development in which higher-order intellectual skills pass "from a social to individual level": engagement in dialogic argumentation with partners, even similarly skilled ones, fosters individual argument skill. The finding that both experimental and comparison groups advanced in individual dialogic argument skills is presented as support for this model, alongside the apprenticeship account.
requirements: Learners must engage in dialogic argumentation on controversial issues, with assessments of individual skill before and after engagement.
constraints: The abstract notes the theoretical significance of the results was discussed in relation to both an apprenticeship model and a dialogical model; it does not adjudicate between them.
target_learners: young adolescents
target_learning_goals: individual dialogic argument skill
transfer of argument skill to individual performance
examples: Both the apprenticeship group and the same-ability comparison group advanced in individual dialogic argument skills following their engagement in argumentation.

article_title: The Effect of Authority on the Persuasiveness of Mathematical Arguments
citation: Matthew Inglis, Juan Pablo Mejia-Ramos. (2008). The Effect of Authority on the Persuasiveness of Mathematical Arguments.
title: Uncertainty-gated authority model of argument evaluation
description: The article proposes a model (illustrated in its Figure 2) in which "the source of an argument only influences the reader's reported level of persuasion if, having read the argument, the reader is left uncertain about it" — that is, an authority figure can only operate on existing uncertainty. It accounts for the heuristic argument (uncertainty present, authority effect found), the formal proofs (little uncertainty, no effect), and the visual argument (students certain it was unacceptable, researchers uncertain, so only researchers showed the effect). The authors note it also predicts authority effects when an argument is too hard to understand or effort is not invested, though this was not tested.
requirements: The reader must be left with some uncertainty about the argument's mathematical status after reading it for authority to influence persuasion
constraints: The authors state the model's prediction about difficulty and time restrictions creating uncertainty has not been tested
Whether extremely complex formal proofs generate enough uncertainty for an authority effect remains an open question
target_learners: undergraduate mathematics students
research-active mathematicians
target_learning_goals: evaluating the persuasiveness of mathematical arguments
gaining conviction in mathematical statements
examples: The model explains why Gowers's heuristic argument showed an authority effect while the induction and Pólya formal proofs did not
key_sources: Matthew Inglis, Juan Pablo Mejia-Ramos. (2008). The Effect of Authority on the Persuasiveness of Mathematical Arguments. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370000802584513

article_title: The Effect of Authority on the Persuasiveness of Mathematical Arguments
citation: Matthew Inglis, Juan Pablo Mejia-Ramos. (2008). The Effect of Authority on the Persuasiveness of Mathematical Arguments.
title: Empower students by reducing their uncertainty about arguments rather than suppressing appeals to authority
description: Because the studies show that reliance on authority appears mainly when readers are uncertain about an argument's status, the authors argue that "relying upon, or looking for, an authority figure should not be seen as undesirable behavior per se." Instead, instruction should focus on "empowering students by ensuring that they are in a position where they do not need to take into account an authority figure", i.e. where they have little uncertainty about the mathematical status of formal arguments. This reframes existing pedagogy that explicitly discourages appeals to expert opinion.
requirements: Instruction must give students enough mathematical resources that they experience little uncertainty about the arguments they evaluate
constraints: The authors note greater mathematical maturity is not always correlated with less uncertainty, as the visual-argument case shows researchers were more uncertain than students
target_learners: undergraduate mathematics students
school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: evaluating mathematical arguments independently of source cues
developing mathematical reasoning about proofs
examples: The article contrasts this approach with instruction designed by Cobb & Yackel, Harel & Sowder, and Stylianides that explicitly discourages students from taking authority into account
key_sources: Matthew Inglis, Juan Pablo Mejia-Ramos. (2008). The Effect of Authority on the Persuasiveness of Mathematical Arguments. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370000802584513

article_title: Constructing Meaning When Reading Poetry: An Expert-Novice Study
citation: Peskin, J. (1998). Constructing meaning when reading poetry: An expert-novice study. Cognition and Instruction, 16(3), 235-263. https://doi.org/10.1207/s1532690xci1603_3
title: Culler's structuralist model of poetic communication: reading poetry is charged with artifice, governed by shared conventions of significance, thematic unity and metaphorical coherence.
description: The article adopts Jonathan Culler's structuralist model as the framework for its second research question, treating reading poetry as "not a natural activity but is charged with artifice", animated by a special set of expectations or conventions assimilated by readers and shared with the author. The primary expectations are the rule of significance (read the poem as expressing a significant attitude to some problem concerning man and/or his relation to the universe), the convention of thematic unity (all parts relate to create a unified, coherent whole), and the conventions of metaphorical coherence (the basis of poetic expression is the metaphor). The study tests whether novices show evidence of having assimilated these conventions, and finds they have.
requirements: Readers must have considerable experience with the conventions, since the study of one poem facilitates the reading of the next
constraints: The conventions impose severe limitations on the set of acceptable or plausible readings rather than guaranteeing comprehension of any particular poem
target_learners: secondary and undergraduate students reading poetry
target_learning_goals: interpreting poetry and constructing coherent readings of literary texts
examples: The study coded think-aloud protocols of eight novices for evidence of the three conventions while reading two period poems.
key_sources: Peskin, J. (1998). Constructing meaning when reading poetry: An expert-novice study. Cognition and Instruction, 16(3), 235-263. https://doi.org/10.1207/s1532690xci1603_1

article_title: Identifying Representational Competence With Multi-Representational Displays
citation: Mike Stieff, Mary Hegarty, Ghislain Deslongchamps. (2011). Identifying Representational Competence with Multi-Representational Displays. Cognition and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2011.558308
title: Multi-representational molecular mechanics Flash animation with model, general equation, numerical equation, and graph
description: A set of three interactive Flash animations adapted from courseware for teaching computer-based molecular modeling to undergraduate chemistry students. Each animation displayed four synchronized representations of a molecular mechanics energy term: "a ball-and-stick model of the molecular system, the general mathematical model used to model its energy, a specific numerical example of the equation, and a graph of the equation". The representations were linked via a mouse-driven slider so users could change the molecular model and observe the resulting energy change on the graph and numerical example.
requirements: Students needed prior instruction in the chemistry topic; participants had completed at least one year of university general chemistry instruction.
constraints: The animations were converted to 17 static frames per animation for eye tracking, interacted with via keyboard arrow keys.
target_learners: undergraduate organic chemistry students
target_learning_goals: understanding molecular mechanics energy terms and the relationship between molecular spatial conformations and energy
examples: Three animations modeled the stretch, angle bend, and dihedral energy terms of the molecular mechanics equation.
key_sources: Mike Stieff, Mary Hegarty, Ghislain Deslongchamps. (2011). Identifying Representational Competence with Multi-Representational Displays. Cognition and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2010.507318

article_title: Do Master Narratives Change Among High School Students? A Characterization of How National History Is Represented
citation: Mario Carretero & Floor van Alphen. (2014). Do Master Narratives Change Among High School Students? A Characterization of How National History Is Represented. Cognition and Instruction, 32(3), 290-312. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2014.919298
title: Four-characteristic model of national historical master narratives
description: The article presents a model distinguishing four characteristics of national historical master narratives: the historical subject established by inclusion and exclusion, identification processes attaching affect and value judgments, historical events simplified around one common narrative theme, and a romantic and essentialist concept of the nation. The model was developed as a unit of analysis for studying how students consume master narratives, and the study applies it to Argentine students' narratives about May 25, 1810. The authors state it 'could be applied to master narratives in other countries, for example, on the American continent.'
requirements: Narratives about a nation's own history that can be analyzed against the four characteristics and their more historical alternatives
constraints: Developed and illustrated with the Argentine myth of origin; contextualization of the specific national narrative is needed because cultural tools are known to be context-specific
target_learners: secondary school history students
target_learning_goals: historical understanding of the national past
critical historical thinking about master narratives
examples: Applied to 38 Argentine students' semistructured interview narratives about May 25, 1810, coded per characteristic with two independent judges agreeing on over 94.5% of a random 30% sample
key_sources: Mario Carretero & Floor van Alphen. (2014). Do Master Narratives Change Among High School Students? A Characterization of How National History Is Represented. Cognition and Instruction, 32(3), 290-312. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2014.919298

article_title: Do Master Narratives Change Among High School Students? A Characterization of How National History Is Represented
citation: Mario Carretero & Floor van Alphen. (2014). Do Master Narratives Change Among High School Students? A Characterization of How National History Is Represented. Cognition and Instruction, 32(3), 290-312. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2014.919298
title: Teach a constructivist nation concept first, then use it to historicize the national subject and events
description: The article proposes that history education aiming at historical understanding of a national past should first aim at a constructivist concept of nation and then use that concept to reflect on the national historical subject and events in the narrative. This sequencing follows from the finding that the nation concept was the master narrative characteristic showing the greatest change and least resistance, while identification remained constant. The authors state this approach 'might help produce historical understanding of a national past.'
requirements: Instruction that addresses the nation concept explicitly before the historical subject and events
constraints: The authors note whether identity construction and critical historical understanding are complementary 'is a matter in need of further research'
target_learners: secondary school history students
target_learning_goals: historical understanding of the national past
overcoming an essentialist concept of nation
examples: In the study, 75% of 11th graders versus 33% of 8th graders demonstrated a constructivist nation concept, and Table 6 suggested the constructivist nation concept was the historical content most often and perhaps most easily appropriated
key_sources: Mario Carretero & Floor van Alphen. (2014). Do Master Narratives Change Among High School Students? A Characterization of How National History Is Represented. Cognition and Instruction, 32(3), 290-312. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2014.919298

article_title: Point and Click or Grab and Heft: Comparing the Influence of Physical and Virtual Instructional Materials on Elementary School Students' Ability to Design Experiments
citation: Triona, L. M., & Klahr, D. (2003). Point and Click or Grab and Heft: Comparing the Influence of Physical and Virtual Instructional Materials on Elementary School Students' Ability to Design Experiments. Cognition and Instruction, 21(2), 149–173. https://doi.org/10.1207/s1532690xci2102_3
title: Substitute virtual for physical instructional materials without loss of learning when the instructional method is preserved
description: When teaching conceptual and procedural goals such as experimental design, computer-based materials that replicate the physical materials' content and allow learners the same design choices can replace physical manipulatives. The study found that "simply replacing the physical materials with virtual materials does not affect the amount of learning or transfer when other aspects of the instruction are preserved." The comparison held teacher, script, time on task, examples, probes, and learners' experiment choices constant across media.
requirements: The method of instruction — instructor, lesson plan, script, time on task, number and type of examples, teacher probes, and learners' selection of experiments — must be the same across the physical and virtual versions.
The virtual materials must depict the same objects and detail as the physical materials, with learners actively designing and setting up experiments.
constraints: Instructional goals that include mastery of a specific perceptual-motor skill, such as making precise incisions during dissections or careful mixing and pouring of liquids, would likely show an effect of medium.
A human instructor presented instruction in both conditions; whether similar learning would occur if students were trained directly from the computer is unknown.
target_learners: fourth- and fifth-grade elementary school students
target_learning_goals: designing unconfounded experiments (control of variables strategy)
examples: Ninety-two fourth- and fifth-graders were randomly assigned to learn CVS with real springs and weights or with mouse-clicked, video-depicted versions of the same springs and weights; all children then transferred to physical ramps a week later.
key_sources: Triona, L. M., & Klahr, D. (2003). Point and Click or Grab and Heft: Comparing the Influence of Physical and Virtual Instructional Materials on Elementary School Students' Ability to Design Experiments. Cognition and Instruction, 21(2), 149–173. https://doi.org/10.1207/s1532690xci2102_02

article_title: Bridging Research and Practice: A Cognitively Based Classroom Intervention for Teaching Experimentation Skills to Elementary School Children
citation: Eva Erdosne Toth, David Klahr, and Zhe Chen. (2000). Bridging Research and Practice: A Cognitively Based Classroom Intervention for Teaching Experimentation Skills to Elementary School Children. Cognition and Instruction, 18(4), 423–459. https://doi.org/10.1207/S1532690XCI1804_2
title: Benchmark lesson: a classroom CVS unit translating the laboratory training procedure
description: The benchmark lesson is a classroom instructional unit that translates the laboratory CVS training procedure into a fourth-grade science lesson using the ramps materials. It consists of exploratory group experiments, about 20 minutes of whole-class expository instruction following five teacher steps (initiate reflective discussion on a bad comparison, model correct thinking, test understanding, reinforce correct thinking, summarize rationale), and application experiments. The authors "attempted to engineer a classroom learning environment (Brown, 1992) that students could refer to during future hands-on activities calling for the design of informative experiments."
requirements: A regular classroom teacher to deliver the expository instruction; students work in groups of 3 to 5 with their own ramp materials and preformatted worksheets for recording setups and outcomes
constraints: Only the ramps domain was used during classroom work (springs and sinking were used in interviews); the lesson is a one-time event focusing on a procedural skill rather than repeated cycles; the teacher did not provide corrective feedback on CVS during exploration or application phases
target_learners: fourth-grade elementary school students
target_learning_goals: designing unconfounded (controlled) experiments using the control of variables strategy
justifying and evaluating experimental designs
examples: Teachers led a short demonstration of ramp setups, a 5-minute domain knowledge pretest, four exploratory group experiments, roughly 20 minutes of whole-class expository instruction, and four application experiments, with students individually recording setups and certainty on worksheets
key_sources: Eva Erdosne Toth, David Klahr, and Zhe Chen. (2000). Bridging Research and Practice: A Cognitively Based Classroom Intervention for Teaching Experimentation Skills to Elementary School Children. Cognition and Instruction, 18(4), 423–459. https://doi.org/10.1207/s1532690xci1804_1

article_title: Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics
citation: Rachel E. Scherr and David Hammer. (2007). Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics. Submitted to Cognition and Instruction. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Student+Behavior+and+Epistemological+Framing
title: Epistemological framing as a resource-based, dynamic-systems account of student sense of an activity
description: The article develops epistemological framing from anthropology and linguistics: to frame a situation is to interpret it based on previous experience, bringing expectations about what could happen and what action is appropriate. In school settings, students form "a sense of what is taking place with respect to knowledge." Building on a resource model, a frame is "a locally coherent pattern of activations" that may span individuals or a group, linking discourse dynamics with models of individual cognition.
requirements: Analysis requires observable verbal, paraverbal, and nonverbal contextualizing cues in social interaction, since frames emerge in and are constituted by interaction
constraints: Frames are local: the coherence may be particular to the moment or context, so identified framings are local shifts within larger framings of a session
target_learners: introductory university physics students working in small collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: students' understanding of knowledge, reasoning, and learning in physics (epistemological framing of instructional activities)
examples: Jasmin's singsong reading from the worksheet versus her loud, pointing commentary on it, recognized by her peer Sheryl
key_sources: Rachel E. Scherr and David Hammer. (2007). Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics. Submitted to Cognition and Instruction. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Student+Behavior+and+Epistemological+Framing

article_title: Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics
citation: Rachel E. Scherr and David Hammer. (2007). Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics. Submitted to Cognition and Instruction. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Student+Behavior+and+Epistemological+Framing
title: Behavioral coding methodology for identifying epistemological framing in group video
description: A real-time observational coding protocol in which coders watch video of small groups without a transcript and note the exact time of changes in vocal register, affect, grammar, gesture production, and body language. Clusters are labeled with meaning-neutral labels (colors), at least two researchers code independently, and whole groups can be coded reliably because "peers typically share the same behavioral cluster." The method achieved 90% inter-rater reliability before discussion, to five seconds' accuracy.
requirements: At least two researchers code the changes independently; clusters are labeled with meaning-neutral labels before interpretation
constraints: The study's data set was a small, deliberately non-representative best-case sample of four hours from three groups in a well-functioning class with experienced TAs
target_learners: small groups of university students in collaborative active-learning activities
target_learning_goals: researchers' ability to observe students' epistemological framing during instruction
examples: Coding of group A's Newton's third law episodes, where the whole group shifted from blue to green behaviors at a transcript line
key_sources: Rachel E. Scherr and David Hammer. (2007). Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics. Submitted to Cognition and Instruction. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Student+Behavior+and+Epistemological+Framing

article_title: Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics
citation: Rachel E. Scherr and David Hammer. (2007). Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics. Submitted to Cognition and Instruction. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Student+Behavior+and+Epistemological+Framing
title: Physics tutorials: worksheet-based group-learning activities replacing traditional recitation
description: Tutorials are worksheets that guide collaborative active learning in small groups around core conceptual issues identified by research as essential. In the studied course, the traditional TA-led recitation was replaced with tutorials in which students worked in small groups making predictions and comparing lines of reasoning, with TAs serving as facilitators rather than lecturers. The tutorials were constructed to emphasize reconciliation of everyday intuitive thinking with formal scientific thinking and to encourage explicit epistemological discussion.
requirements: Teaching assistants serve as facilitators rather than lecturers, engaging students in discussions of difficult concepts
constraints: The article reports the evidence for conceptual gains is almost exclusively pre- and post-testing, with little direct investigation of what happens during the activities
target_learners: junior and senior health and life science majors in large algebra-based introductory physics lectures of approximately 160 students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of basic physics concepts and epistemological and metacognitive gains
examples: The Newton's third law truck-and-car tutorial, the free-body diagrams tutorial, and the electrostatics tutorial analyzed in this study

article_title: Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures
citation: Morra, S.; Bisagno, E.; Caviola, S.; Delfante, C.; Mammarella, I. C. (2019). Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures. Cognition and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2019.1636797
title: Case's central conceptual structures theory, reconsidered with working memory capacity as the developmental driver of quantitative concepts
description: The article reconsiders Case's theory of central conceptual structures (CCS), which describes qualitative developmental levels in children's quantitative concepts. Its lead hypothesis is that "the development of working memory capacity shapes the development of quantitative concepts (whole and rational numbers)". The two studies operationalize whole-number and rational-number CCS as measurable structures whose acquisition is tied to working memory units. Overall, the authors state that "the results support Case's CCS theory and clarify the role of working memory in the acquisition of numerical concepts."
requirements: Measures of the whole-number and rational-number CCS validated against children's working memory capacity
constraints: Evidence reported here covers children from preschool to grade 5 (whole number) and sixth- and seventh-graders (rational number)
target_learners: children from preschool to grade 5
sixth- and seventh-graders
target_learning_goals: whole number understanding
rational number understanding
key_sources: Morra, S.; Bisagno, E.; Caviola, S.; Delfante, C.; Mammarella, I. C. (2019). Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures. Cognition and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2019.1636797

article_title: Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures
citation: Morra, S.; Bisagno, E.; Caviola, S.; Delfante, C.; Mammarella, I. C. (2019). Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures. Cognition and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2019.1636797
title: Validated measure of the whole-number central conceptual structure
description: A validated instrument measuring children's whole-number central conceptual structure, developed and validated in Study I with 779 children from preschool to grade 5. The article reports that Study I "validated a measure of the whole number CCS", establishing that performance on it tracks working memory capacity in developmental-level units. It serves as the operational measure linking quantitative concept development to working memory in the article's tests of Case's theory.
requirements: Administered together with a working memory capacity measure to score developmental levels
target_learners: children from preschool to grade 5
target_learning_goals: whole number understanding
key_sources: Morra, S.; Bisagno, E.; Caviola, S.; Delfante, C.; Mammarella, I. C. (2019). Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures. Cognition and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2019.1636797

article_title: Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures
citation: Morra, S.; Bisagno, E.; Caviola, S.; Delfante, C.; Mammarella, I. C. (2019). Working Memory Capacity and the Development of Quantitative Central Conceptual Structures. Cognition and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2019.1636797
title: Test of the rational-number central conceptual structure with capacity-graded item subsets
description: A test of the rational-number central conceptual structure administered to 92 sixth- and seventh-graders in Study II. The article reports that "a test of the rational number CCS was predicted by working memory capacity" and that the authors "identified 2 subsets of items that demand a capacity of 4 or 5 units, respectively." The capacity-graded subsets make the test a diagnostic tool for locating rational-number understanding relative to working memory units.
requirements: A working memory measure such as the listening span, whose intrusion errors also predict performance
constraints: Studied with sixth- and seventh-graders; applicability to other ages is not reported here
target_learners: sixth- and seventh-graders
target_learning_goals: rational number understanding

article_title: Geopolitical Configuration of Identities and Learning: Othering through the Institutionalized Categorization of “English Language Learners”
citation: Takeuchi, M.A. (2020). Geopolitical configuration of identities and learning: Othering through the institutionalized categorization of “English language learners. Cognition and Instruction. Advance online publication https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2020.1825438
title: Multi-layered identities framework: figurative, positional, and geopolitical layers interact and thicken through repeated practices
description: The article extends Holland et al.'s distinction between figurative identities (“the stories, acts, and characters that make the world a cultural world”) and positional identities (day-to-day relations of power and entitlement) by adding a layer of geopolitical configuration of identities. This added layer captures how colonial and geopolitical histories shape who becomes the Other, deprived of discursive space to speak and represent. Layers can be “thickened or laminated through repeated practices,” framing how interactions unfold and shaping learners' becoming.
requirements: Analysis attends to interactions across micro, meso, and macro timescales of history, since layers are inextricably woven together
constraints: The article states the macro-level geopolitical configuration and colonial matrix of identity had not been fully considered in prior scholarship on identities and mathematics learning
target_learners: elementary students institutionally classified as English language learners
immigrant and refugee students in linguistically diverse schools
target_learning_goals: understanding how identity layers shape access to agentive learning opportunities in mathematics classrooms
examples: The framework was applied to four focal students in a Grade 4 transforming recess mathematics unit, contrasting cases of Cathy and Iris with Daniel and Karim
key_sources: Takeuchi, M.A. (2020). Geopolitical configuration of identities and learning: Othering through the institutionalized categorization of “English language learners. Cognition and Instruction. Advance online publication https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2020.1825438

article_title: Geopolitical Configuration of Identities and Learning: Othering through the Institutionalized Categorization of “English Language Learners”
citation: Takeuchi, M.A. (2020). Geopolitical configuration of identities and learning: Othering through the institutionalized categorization of “English language learners. Cognition and Instruction. Advance online publication https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2020.1825438
title: Transforming recess unit: a mathematics data-management unit in which students survey, graph, and present findings to change school practice
description: A two-week interdisciplinary mathematics unit (two hours a day, five days a week) in which Grade 4 students designed surveys about playground use, represented results with tally charts, frequency tables, and double bar graphs, and presented findings to peers, teachers, the principal, and the school council. The unit connected local curriculum topics of “frequency, graphs, percentage, and measures of the centre of a distribution of values” to students' own issues, aiming to transform the social terrain of the playground.
requirements: Teacher and researcher collaboration to design the unit around issues students identified
Curriculum connections to data management and mapping
Opportunities for students to present results to audiences with power to act
constraints: The article notes some students' marginalized identities were further reinforced in the unit and quieter voices were not heard
target_learners: Grade 4 elementary students in a linguistically diverse urban school
target_learning_goals: data management (survey design, graph representation, ratio, percentage)
measures of centre
comparing two related sets of data
examples: Students mapped areas of the playground more prone to conflict using a bird's-eye view map; Cathy's and Iris's suggestions appeared in school council action items

article_title: Geopolitical Configuration of Identities and Learning: Othering through the Institutionalized Categorization of “English Language Learners”
citation: Takeuchi, M.A. (2020). Geopolitical configuration of identities and learning: Othering through the institutionalized categorization of “English language learners. Cognition and Instruction. Advance online publication https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2020.1825438
title: Design mathematics units on the principle of participatory action research: those most affected by an issue lead the research on it
description: The article advocates designing mathematics instruction so that students affected by a problem take the lead in researching it. The unit “was designed based on the principle of participatory action research in that it encouraged those who were affected most by the particular issues to take the lead in researching those issues.” This created an otherwise-impossible opportunity for students to mobilize mathematics curriculum to transform their recess experiences and to voice desired changes.
requirements: Teachers listen to students' opinions about what they want to change
Teachers facilitate students' access to codes of power
Audiences (administrators, councils) are available to receive student findings
constraints: The article shows the opportunity was unevenly taken up: some students accepted the invitation to present while others did not, and labelled students' access was constrained
target_learners: elementary students
students in economically under-resourced schools
target_learning_goals: applying data practices to authentic school issues
developing agency to effect change in school practices
examples: Teachers were introduced to the participatory action research principle during professional development seminars and co-designed the transforming recess unit with researchers

article_title: Making Space to Sensemake: Epistemic Distancing in Small Group Physics Discussions
citation: Conlin, L. D., & Scherr, R. E. (2012). Making Space to Sensemake: Epistemic Distancing in Small Group Physics Discussions. Preprint under review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Making+Space+to+Sensemake
title: Epistemic distancing as a discursive resource for managing epistemological and affective dynamics
description: Epistemic distancing is defined as "any discourse move by which a participant in conversation downgrades their epistemic stance, for example by hedging, quoting, or joking." It is "epistemic" because it concerns the speaker's commitment to truth, and "distancing" because it creates distance between speaker and claim, protecting affect if the idea is evaluated negatively. The article uses it to explain how tutorial groups co-construct safe spaces for sensemaking, drawing on research on stance-taking and footing shifts.
requirements: Face-to-face collaborative discussion in which ideas are shared and critiqued, where affective risk of rejection exists
constraints: More distancing is not necessarily better; over-distancing can lead groups to avoid conflict or dismiss the activity
target_learners: undergraduate physics students in inquiry-based tutorials
target_learning_goals: collaborative scientific sensemaking about physical mechanisms
examples: Deirdre phrases disagreement about the normal force's direction as a question; Bree reads her written answer with ironic sing-song prosody
key_sources: Conlin, L. D., & Scherr, R. E. (2012). Making Space to Sensemake: Epistemic Distancing in Small Group Physics Discussions. Preprint under review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Making+Space+to+Sensemake

article_title: Making Space to Sensemake: Epistemic Distancing in Small Group Physics Discussions
citation: Conlin, L. D., & Scherr, R. E. (2012). Making Space to Sensemake: Epistemic Distancing in Small Group Physics Discussions. Preprint under review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Making+Space+to+Sensemake
title: Design collaborative learning environments to support management of affective risk, since epistemology and affect are coupled in sensemaking discussions
description: The article argues that inquiry discussions pose an essential tension between generating ideas and critiquing them, and that both sides carry affective risks such as embarrassment. It concludes that research and instruction should consider "the coupled dynamics of epistemology and affect in collaborative sensemaking discussions," and that implications for instruction include "novel ways of encouraging classroom discussion" such as epistemic distancing.
requirements: Collaborative discussions in which students both contribute ideas and critically evaluate each other's ideas
constraints: Groups that distance too much may align against the goals of inquiry curriculum
target_learners: students in inquiry-based science classrooms
target_learning_goals: collaborative scientific sensemaking and argumentation
examples: Tutorial groups used hedging, ironic reading, and question-form disagreements to ease into saying what they think

article_title: Conceptualizing the intersubjective group
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2015). Conceptualizing the intersubjective group. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 10:209–217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9220-4
title: Intersubjectivity as the defining characteristic of CSCL, built and repaired through interaction
description: The article defines intersubjectivity as shared understanding achieved not by individuals holding similar views but by "participating productively in a joint meaning-making discourse within a communal world." A group has intersubjectivity when members "interact well enough to pursue the group's aims." It must be "built up gradually through interaction and repaired frequently." CSCL pedagogies promote it and CSCL technologies support it through communication media and scaffolds for meaning making.
requirements: Groups must interact over time so shared understanding can be built up and repaired through discourse
target_learners: collaborative learning groups in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: joint meaning making and shared understanding
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2015). Conceptualizing the intersubjective group. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 10:209–217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9220-4

article_title: Conceptualizing the intersubjective group
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2015). Conceptualizing the intersubjective group. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 10:209–217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9220-4
title: The group as unit of analysis: collaborative learning as group-level knowledge building, not summed individual learning
description: The article argues CSCL's concept of collaborative learning refers not to "a sum of individual learning" but to "the increase in intersubjective understanding or knowledge building within the group that results from joint meaning making in a shared context." Group understanding may differ from what any individual would say or think alone. Utterance meaning is constructed sequentially through responses to prior actions and elicitation of future behavior, analyzed at the group unit rather than via purported individual mental thoughts.
requirements: Analysis of interactional sequences within functioning groups that have achieved a degree of intersubjectivity
constraints: The article notes the shift to group-level analysis "has been slow coming and is still difficult to implement consistently"
target_learners: researchers and designers of computer-supported collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: group knowledge building and collaborative learning
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2015). Conceptualizing the intersubjective group. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 10:209–217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9220-4

article_title: Conceptualizing the intersubjective group
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2015). Conceptualizing the intersubjective group. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 10:209–217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9220-4
title: Habermas's ideal speech situation and three-worlds distinction as conditions for intersubjectivity in CSCL
description: Drawing on Hammond's introduction of Habermas, the article presents the ideal speech situation—an underlying assumption that "there is no other force of persuasion at work than that of the better argument and no other motivation than the cooperative search for truth"—as a standard for judging knowledge building in chats, forums, or Wikipedia, even though the ideal is never fully achievable. Habermas also distinguishes objective, social, and subjective worlds, each with different validity criteria, giving analysts leverage to apply appropriate evaluative criteria to each level of a team's collaborative work.
requirements: Discourse participants must assume cooperative truth-seeking rather than force or authority as grounds for persuasion
constraints: The ideal speech situation "is never in fact achievable"; other forces and motivations are always present
target_learners: students collaborating online; researchers analyzing collaborative discourse
target_learning_goals: intersubjective meaning making and collaborative knowledge building
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2015). Conceptualizing the intersubjective group. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 10:209–217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9220-4

article_title: Conceptualizing the intersubjective group
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2015). Conceptualizing the intersubjective group. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 10:209–217. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9220-4
title: Metafora dual-interaction space: construction space plus argumentation space supporting learning-to-learn-together
description: The article describes the Metafora system, designed via design-based research by Schwarz and colleagues to support learning-to-learn-together. It pairs "a construction space and an argumentation space": the construction space offers domain-specific modeling applications forming a mutually visible "joint problem space" for collective reflection, while as one member acts, others assess the action in the argumentation space, "either affirming it or questioning it." A sophisticated planning/reflection tool prompts planning steps (collective agency) and team reflection (collective responsibility), going beyond simple chat-plus-construction dual-interaction systems.
requirements: A culture of collaboration: appropriate motivations/rewards, careful training in collaboration and subtle mentoring
constraints: The article states success "also depends on a culture of collaboration" beyond the software itself
target_learners: small groups of students in mathematics or science inquiry
target_learning_goals: argumentation, collective reflection, peer assessment, meta-learning

article_title: An integrated way of using a tangible user interface in a classroom
citation: Cuendet, S., Dehler Zufferey, J., Ortoleva, G., & Dillenbourg, P. (2015). An integrated way of using a tangible user interface in a classroom. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10(2), 183–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9213-3
title: TapaCarp: a tangible user interface environment for training carpenter apprentices
description: TapaCarp is a CSCL environment based on a tangible user interface, designed from the start for classroom usage to help train carpenter apprentices. The article states the system "is based on a tangible user interface (TUI) and was designed to help train carpenter apprentices." It was deployed within a multi-step classroom activity in dual carpentry apprenticeships, where it was used only for a small part of the activity.
requirements: Designed for the constraints of the classroom environment from the start
Embedded in a broader classroom activity rather than used from beginning to end
constraints: A prior study found the tangible nature helped integrate it in the classroom but did not guarantee a meaningful learning activity
target_learners: carpenter apprentices in dual vocational apprenticeships
target_learning_goals: workplace-relevant carpentry knowledge and skills connected to apprenticeship practice
examples: Used in a classroom study with 3 classes of carpenter apprentices over two days for each class

title: Using the technology for only a small part of a classroom activity
description: This design pattern places a CSCL system inside a multi-step classroom activity in which the technology is used only for a small portion, contrasting with the mainstream CSCL assumption that the system must be used from beginning to end. The article calls this "One innovative aspect of the activity is that TapaCarp is used only for a small part of it." The multi-step activity proved usable and fostered many connections to the workplace.

Design grounded in the particular context, here dual carpentry apprenticeships

target_learning_goals: integrating classroom learning with workplace practice

description: The article argues that computers remain scarcely used in classrooms partly because designers neglect classroom constraints, and proposes designing CSCL environments for classroom usage from the start. It states that "the constraints of the classroom environment are neglected by designers" and presents TapaCarp as "a CSCL environment designed for a classroom usage from the start."

Ground the activity design in the specific educational context, such as dual apprenticeships

article_title: A systemic and cognitive view on collaborative knowledge building with wikis
citation: Ulrike Cress & Joachim Kimmerle. (2008). A systemic and cognitive view on collaborative knowledge building with wikis. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9035-z
title: Cress and Kimmerle's systemic-cognitive model of collaborative knowledge building with wikis
description: The article presents "a theoretical framework for describing how learning and collaborative knowledge building take place" by combining Luhmann's sociological systems theory with Piaget's theory of equilibration. The wiki is modeled as an autopoietic social system structurally coupled with users' cognitive systems via language; irritations from one system can be incorporated into the other, enabling co-evolution. Learning occurs through externalization and internalization processes crossing the border between the social system wiki and individual cognitive systems.
requirements: A wiki as a social system and users with cognitive systems that can irritate each other through text-based communication
constraints: The authors note the model addresses the potential of wikis and that possible shortcomings will not take center stage in the analysis
target_learners: wiki users participating in collaborative knowledge building communities
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building
individual learning through wiki participation
examples: The model is illustrated with history-page analyses of the Wikipedia articles on Computer-supported collaborative learning and AIDS origin
key_sources: Ulrike Cress & Joachim Kimmerle. (2008). A systemic and cognitive view on collaborative knowledge building with wikis. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9035-z

article_title: A systemic and cognitive view on collaborative knowledge building with wikis
citation: Ulrike Cress & Joachim Kimmerle. (2008). A systemic and cognitive view on collaborative knowledge building with wikis. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9035-z
title: Use wikis for collaborative knowledge building because they let many users jointly revise one shared artifact
description: The article argues wikis have special potential for computer-supported collaborative knowledge building because users can not only access but change content online, revising text by "adding, deleting, or changing any parts they want to". In this way large groups jointly create one hypertext, allowing collaborative generation of knowledge, and wikis can be considered to support social constructivist learning in general.
requirements: A wiki accessible to all community members, with revision histories so contributions and restructuring are traceable
constraints: The article focuses on wikis' potential and states possible shortcomings will not take center stage in this analysis
target_learners: members of online communities and learners using wikis for educational purposes
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building
debate-based and design-based learning
co-construction of knowledge
examples: Wikipedia, where users collaboratively develop the world's largest encyclopedia, is applied to make the theoretical analysis concrete

article_title: Comparing the effects of representational tools in collaborative and individual inquiry learning
citation: Kolloffel, B., Eysink, T. H. S., & de Jong, T. (2011). Comparing the effects of representational tools in collaborative and individual inquiry learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 223–251. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9110-3
title: Offer representational tools as optional support, and expect uptake to depend heavily on format accessibility
description: The article integrated an electronic on-screen representational tool into a simulation-based inquiry environment so students could "construct an overview or summary of the domain's main concepts, principles, variables, and their mutual relationships". Because support is voluntary in real classrooms, tool use was not obligatory for ecological validity. Uptake then depended strongly on format: roughly half of students used conceptual or textual tools versus about 20% for the arithmetical tool, so designers should not assume provided tools will be used.
requirements: The tool must be available at all times in the learning environment, with a demonstration, practice time, and help available, as the article reports
constraints: Use of the tool was not obligatory, and the article notes tools are often used inadequately or not at all; likelihood of use depends on prior knowledge, motivation, self-regulation, and interest
target_learners: secondary education students (age ~14) learning combinatorics and probability theory
target_learning_goals: domain understanding of combinatorics and probability theory, including conceptual, intuitive, procedural, and situational knowledge
examples: Probe-XMT offered conceptual (concept map), arithmetical, and textual tools; students were strongly advised to use them and informed this would help post-test preparation

article_title: Classical dialogs in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Classical dialogs in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9071-y
title: Event-centered analysis as an alternative to variable-centered methodologies for CSCL processes unfolding over time
description: Peter Reimann proposes an event-centered approach as an alternative to conventional variable-centered methodologies for analyzing processes in CSCL settings. The editorial reports that "tracking events can be more responsive to changing circumstances than plotting values of presumably fixed variables," and that event-centered analysis can account for richer causality and narrative reporting. It reflects on multiple analytic methods in CSCL at a fundamental conceptual level.
requirements: Analytic methods must handle processes that unfold over extended periods of time in CSCL settings
constraints: The editorial notes the approach does not clearly distinguish conversation analysis, uptake diagrams, and thick descriptions by participants' perspective on semantics, temporality, or interaction
target_learners: CSCL researchers and analysts of collaborative learning data
target_learning_goals: Analyzing collaborative learning processes over time

article_title: Classical dialogs in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Classical dialogs in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9071-y
title: Distinction of knowledge creation (community improvement of ideas) from knowledge sharing (transmission) and knowledge construction (individual constructionist)
description: van Aalst clarifies often-confused terminology of alternative theories of learning. The editorial highlights that he "clearly distinguishes 'knowledge creation' — as the community improvement of ideas — from a naïve realist transmission model of 'knowledge sharing' and a cognitive psychology constructionist model of 'knowledge construction.'" Knowledge creation is a social activity oriented to progressive public refinement of ideas and knowledge artifacts.
requirements: Analysts must operationalize the theoretical distinctions within an explicit coding scheme to apply them to empirical data
constraints: The editorial notes the related literature, including this article, speaks ambiguously about the 'sense of community' highlighted as key to knowledge construction
target_learners: Students in classroom collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: Knowledge building and community improvement of ideas

article_title: Classical dialogs in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Classical dialogs in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9071-y
title: Lonchamp's three-level integration of dialog, knowledge, and action analysis for dual-interaction CSCL environments
description: Jacques Lonchamp proposes a systematic integration of three analytic approaches, describing "three levels of analysis — dialog, knowledge, and action — which he claims fit together like semantics, syntax, and pragmatics to provide an integrated view of communication." He applies this within dual-interaction environments built using his generic and customizable Omega+ model.
requirements: Environments must support dual-interaction spaces; analysis requires coordinating the three levels
constraints: The editorial contrasts Lonchamp's designer perspective with Çakır et al.'s practice perspective on a comparable synchronous dual-interaction system
target_learners: Students collaborating in synchronous dual-interaction systems
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge construction in shared digital workspaces

article_title: Classical dialogs in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Classical dialogs in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9071-y
title: Affordances of artifacts are not fully predefined by the technology but depend on established practices consolidated in body schemas or habitus
description: Drawing on Dohn's Merleau-Pontian analysis, the editorial states that "the 'affordances' of an artifact are not fully predefined by the technology" and that affordances of Web 2.0 technologies "depend on our established practices as consolidated in our body schemas (Merleau-Ponty) or habitus (Bourdieu)." This explains why the same tool is enacted differently across situated practices.
requirements: Analysis of technology affordances must attend to users' established practices and embodied dispositions
constraints: Conventional educational structures — grading, instruction traditions, individual-outcome focus — militate against Web 2.0 goals of collective wisdom and social networking
target_learners: University students using Web 2.0 technologies in courses
target_learning_goals: Participating in collective knowledge practices with social technologies

article_title: The effect of a script and a structured interface in grounding discussions
citation: Judith Schoonenboom. (2008). The effect of a script and a structured interface in grounding discussions. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9042-8
title: Three-phased grounding script for distance student groups
description: A collaboration script that "provides a format for carrying out a grounding discussion among students who have to work together at a distance and who do not know each other". It divides grounding into an input phase, in which participants individually make their knowledge and objectives explicit; a discussion phase focused on differences and inconsistencies between members; and a consensus phase in which the group resolves differences and summarizes shared knowledge. Its theoretical rationale draws on small-group work, brainstorming, and CSCW research, on the idea that students should negotiate common goals and build detailed models of each other's knowledge, skills, and motivation.
requirements: Students who do not know each other and work together at a distance on a joint assignment
A discussion forum or comparable environment in which the scripted discussion can take place
constraints: The script pushes but does not force students to interact in a particular way, so unintended use is possible
Too much control in the dialogue can diminish motivation and endanger learner autonomy
target_learners: international distance-education students in small groups of three to six
target_learning_goals: establishing common ground about group members' knowledge, objectives, and qualities before collaborative work
examples: In the European Virtual Seminar, the script's input phase posed seven questions on participants' knowledge and objectives; the discussion phase asked members to identify differences and inconsistencies; the consensus phase asked the group to resolve them and summarize shared knowledge and remaining points of disagreement.
key_sources: Judith Schoonenboom. (2008). The effect of a script and a structured interface in grounding discussions. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9042-8

article_title: The CSCL field matures
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). The CSCL field matures. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 5:1–3. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9077-5
title: Journal article length should be just enough to clearly express and support the claims, and no longer
description: The editors state that the main consideration for article length is having "something important to say, a significant contribution to the field," and that "the length should be just enough to clearly express and support the claims — and no longer." They note most past articles averaged about twenty formatted journal pages, while remaining open to shorter formats and occasional longer articles when the content requires it.
requirements: The article must have something important to say — a significant contribution to the field — before length is considered
constraints: The editors remain open to shorter articles (book reviews, notes, reports) and to occasional longer articles when a complex framework or thorough review requires lengthy motivation, presentation, and illustration
target_learners: CSCL researchers and authors submitting to ijCSCL
target_learning_goals: Academic writing and publication in the learning sciences
examples: In this issue, one paper presents a complex framework requiring lengthy presentation and another reviews an extensive realm of CSCL research with impressive thoroughness; neither strikes the editors as verbose

article_title: Cognizing mediating: Unpacking the entanglement of artifacts with collective minds
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Cognizing mediating: Unpacking the entanglement of artifacts with collective minds. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:187–191. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9148-x
title: Instrumental genesis as the theory of artifact-agent connection best suited to CSCL's small-group level
description: Instrumental genesis, developed in France by Pierre Rabardel and colleagues, describes how the agent-artifact connection evolves over time through usage and re-design. The editorial argues it can more naturally be applied to the small-group collective level central to CSCL than affordances theory (individual-focused) or structuration (societal-level), introducing it to the CSCL community at methodological, technological, and theoretical levels.
requirements: Analysis of how groups enact features of computer-support systems through use
constraints: The editorial notes the theory's application so far rests on high-level descriptions of data rather than detailed empirical analysis
target_learners: small groups of students in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: enacting and appropriating technological artifacts for collaborative learning
examples: The first article in the issue discusses how triads of students enacted a feature of an argumentation-support software system
