article_title: Learning across levels
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Learning across levels. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 8, 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9169-0
title: Emergent interactional resources bridge individual, small-group and community levels of analysis
description: The article proposes that connections between individual learning, group cognition and community knowledge building are mediated by emergent interactional resources. Drawing on Sawyer's theory of collaborative emergence, it argues that frames emerging from small-group interaction 'can take on institutional or cultural-level powers to influence actions at the individual unit.' These ephemeral and stable emergents form an intermediate level of analysis, and tracking them offers a hypothesis about how levels of learning analysis are connected.
requirements: Empirical analysis in each case of how local interactional resources relate to socio-cultural context and individual learning
constraints: The article states the mechanisms involved are often not apparent to participants and that data-based analysis of how the three levels are connected remains scarce
target_learners: collaborative learning groups in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: meaning making in computer-supported collaborative learning
examples: The five papers of the special issue are read as examples of interactional resources bridging levels of analysis
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Learning across levels. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 8, 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9169-0

article_title: Learning across levels
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Learning across levels. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 8, 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9169-0
title: Lifecycle of interactional resources: reification, sedimentation, institutionalization and personalization
description: The article describes a developmental trajectory for interactional resources. Through repetition in group discussion a term or object becomes a reified resource with ephemeral-emergent existence; continued usage yields a sedimented resource retaining meaning across group interactions; sedimented resources may be institutionalized by a larger community or personalized into individual understanding, corresponding to Vygotskian micro-genesis of internalization. The article notes these seminal processes' 'empirical investigation remains as a major challenge for future CSCL research.'
requirements: Repeated use within group discussion for a resource to take on settled significance
constraints: Vygotsky's personalization processes are described as lengthy, complex, non-transparent and little understood
target_learners: small-group and community learners in CSCL
target_learning_goals: shared meaning making and individual internalization of group practices
examples: Husserl's account of geometers' ideas becoming sedimented in geometry's cultural heritage, and Livingston's contrast of discovering versus presenting a proof
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Learning across levels. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 8, 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9169-0

article_title: Collaborating around the tabletop
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2011). Collaborating around the tabletop. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6:485–490. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9135-7
title: Tabletop environments as focal multimedia settings for small-group collaborative knowledge building
description: Stahl proposes tabletop educational environments as a hybrid of oral, literate, and digital interaction, analogizing them to conversation around a tribal fire. He writes that 'the tabletop can integrate physical and digital artifacts, spoken and written texts, and human and computational support to form a focal point, subject matter, and dynamic resource for collaborative knowledge building.' The framing positions tabletops as small-group rather than personal or whole-class media.
requirements: Apparent technological possibilities require considerable interface design, user evaluation, pedagogical structuring, and collaborative culture in order to achieve desirable educational results
target_learners: small groups of learners in classrooms, workplaces, or social gatherings
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building
examples: The journal issue opens a flash theme of introductory papers on interactive tabletops in education

article_title: Collaborating around the tabletop

title: Dillenbourg and Evans enumerate 33 research issues for tabletop computing clustered into four circles
description: The editorial reports that the overview paper by Pierre Dillenbourg and Michael Evans 'enumerates 33 such issues, clustered into the circles of: interaction with the individual student, support for small-group interaction, classroom orchestration, and institutional context.' The catalog highlights the complexity of tabletop interaction and counters the assumption that tabletops are simply more natural than laptops because of direct physical gestures.
requirements: The catalog is intended as a tentative set of central topics for analyzing tabletops in future articles of the flash theme

target_learning_goals: collaborative learning supported by tabletop computing

citation: MULLER MIRZA, Nathalie et al. (2007). Using graphical tools in a phased activity for enhancing dialogical skills: An example with Digalo. International journal of computer-supported collaborative learning, vol. 2, n° 2-3, p. 247–272. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9021-5

The title names it directly: "An example with Digalo", positioned within "Using graphical tools in a phased activity". The article's keywords list "Argumentation" and "TIC" (ICT), indicating that Digalo serves argumentation activity supported by technology. argumentation

The phased structure sequences learners' engagement with the graphical tool (Digalo) so that talk and graphical representation support each other across the activity, rather than treating the tool as a single one-off event.

Activity organized into distinct phases

description: The article is framed by sociocultural psychology applied to argumentation in education, as printed in its keyword list: "Argumentation Interaction sociale Éducation Psychologie socioculturelle TIC". On this view, dialogical skills such as argumentation are social interactions («Interaction sociale») situated in educational settings and developed through culturally mediated activity — here, activity mediated by a graphical tool. article_title: Analyzing roles of individuals in small-group collaboration processes
citation: Gerry Stahl, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen. (2014). Analyzing roles of individuals in small-group collaboration processes. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 365–370. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9204-9
title: Group agency as a methodological orientation for CSCL analysis
description: The editorial proposes viewing collaborative actions — paying attention, adopting a social role, providing leadership, expressing learning — as components of group agency. It states that "Group agency requires joint attention, coordinated action and intersubjective intentionality (shared meaning making)" and that such actions "consist of inter-actions among individual members" that cannot be attributed to any one individual. The authors suggest this orientation "could lead CSCL beyond traditional theories of individual rational decision making and mental representation."
requirements: Analysis must treat small-group and community cognitive processes on a par with the individual unit of analysis, not as secondary influences
constraints: The editorial presents this as a suggested orientation arising from four preliminary studies, not a tested theory
target_learners: small-group collaborators in CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building
intersubjective meaning making
examples: The four studies in the issue are read as taking concrete preliminary steps toward relating individual, small-group and community units of analysis
key_sources: Gerry Stahl, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen. (2014). Analyzing roles of individuals in small-group collaboration processes. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 365–370. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9204-9

article_title: Analyzing roles of individuals in small-group collaboration processes
citation: Gerry Stahl, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen. (2014). Analyzing roles of individuals in small-group collaboration processes. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 365–370. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9204-9
title: Analyze roles and leadership as distributed group processes, not assigned individual attributes
description: The editorial argues against folk-theory conceptions that label individuals as leader, follower, lurker or lazy, and against simply assigning a leadership role to one student per group. It states that "roles being conceptualized as group processes, addressing multiple distinct facets of collaboration and being naturally distributed across the group." Leadership is emergent from group interaction and distributed among group members, moving analysis away from the idea that leaders are just born that way.
requirements: Analytic methods that capture interactions between group members, such as coding bids and uptake or social-network cluster analysis
constraints: The role set detected depends on the specific technology's interaction structures, such as the types of hyperlinks a blog platform affords
target_learners: students in small-group collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: participation in collaborative learning processes
distributed leadership
examples: Mercier et al. classified leadership moves as relational or content bids taken up by the group; Smith Risser and Bottoms derived five role clusters from blog network structure
key_sources: Gerry Stahl, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen. (2014). Analyzing roles of individuals in small-group collaboration processes. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 365–370. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9204-9

article_title: Appropriation of a representational tool in a second-language classroom
citation: Wen, Y., Looi, C.-K., & Chen, W. (2015). Appropriation of a representational tool in a second-language classroom. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10(1), 77–108. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9208-0
title: Cross-media appropriation of representational tools in the networked classroom
description: This account frames technology-mediated learning as taking place "across multiple media in the networked classroom environment where face-to-face and online interactions are intertwined". Appropriation is understood through micro-analysis of cross-media interactions, which the authors deploy "to unravel how different groups of students evolve alternative approaches to appropriating the technology". The framework situates representational-tool use within collaborative second-language writing rather than treating the tool in isolation.

Small-group collaborative activity, here collaborative second-language writing, within which the tool is appropriated

article_title: Future technology workshop: A collaborative method for the design of new learning technologies and activities
citation: Giasemi N. Vavoula and Mike Sharples. (2007). Future Technology Workshop: A Collaborative Method for the Design of New Learning Technologies and Activities. Pre-print, to appear in International Journal of Computer Supported Collaborative Learning, Volume 2, Issue 4, December 2007. https://www.ftw.org.uk
title: The Future Technology Workshop method for envisioning future technology-activity systems
description: The Future Technology Workshop (FTW) is a structured participatory method in which participants with everyday knowledge of a domain envision and design interactions between current and future technology and activity. It organises this exploration as a four-box grid crossing current/future activity with current/future technology, and runs seven sessions: Imagineering, Modelling, Role-play, Retrofit, Everyday, Futurefit and Requirements. The aim is "to reach an informed understanding of how people might interact with technology in the future (box 4 in Table #2) by exploring the possibilities represented by all four boxes".
requirements: Participants familiar with the domain of interest but not generally technology experts
Two or three facilitators managing and recording the sessions
A large room with cheap and portable low-tech prototyping materials
constraints: Targets primarily the Exploratory Design stage of new-generation product design, i.e. product conception
target_learners: children and adults with everyday domain knowledge participating in technology design workshops
target_learning_goals: envisioning future technology-supported activities and specifying requirements for new learning technologies
examples: Used with children and adults to explore new technology-activity systems including interacting with digital photographs and informal science learning

title: Seven-session FTW sequence circling from far future through present to near future
description: The FTW is delivered as a series of seven sessions — Imagineering, Modelling, Role-play, Retrofit, Everyday, Futurefit and Requirements — each with a defined outcome recorded by facilitators. The sequence "starts in Box 4 in Table #2, examining new activity and technology in the far future", then circles through Boxes 3, 1 and 2 and back to 4, travelling from the far future to the present and near future. It is typically run as a half-day event with six to twenty participants plus two or three facilitators.
requirements: A minimum of six and maximum 20 participants plus two or three facilitators
Approximately two hours for the first four sessions and approximately 90 minutes for the remaining three

article_title: Consistent practices in artifact-mediated collaboration
citation: Nathan Dwyer & Daniel D. Suthers. (2006). Consistent practices in artifact-mediated collaboration. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 1: 481–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-006-9001-1
title: Invariants of artifact-mediated collaboration as a basis for abstract design models connecting representational affordances to communicative functions
description: The article proposes that the observed invariants — consistent communicative functions enacted across different media, participants and topics — can form "the basis for user-interface design principles" for collaborative software. The model would connect representational affordances (reorientability, repositionability, space, attachability) to the communicative functions pairs consistently accomplish (awareness management, relatedness, grouping, functional spaces). The authors present it as "a promising first step towards creating an abstract model for design" and note some invariants "challenge common HCI design wisdom." It derives from qualitative observation of six pairs, not from testing designed interfaces.
requirements: Design must tolerate flexible, context-derived meanings rather than rigid GUI mappings between interface elements and functionality
constraints: Derived from short, synchronous, handwriting-limited sessions on wicked problems with no external data or formal evaluation criteria; the authors note a longer time frame might motivate more organizational mechanisms
target_learners: Pairs of students collaborating synchronously via shared written representations
target_learning_goals: Collaborative discussion, negotiation and joint agreement on open-ended problems
examples: Six pairs used paper office supplies (index cards, Post-It notes, large sheets) under a screen that hid faces, with silence required, while video captured the workspace

article_title: Transactive discourse in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Transactive discourse in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:145–147. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9171-6
title: Transactivity as reasoning of one utterance building on another, analyzable at individual or group unit
description: Stahl defines transactivity as "the reasoning of one utterance building on another utterance's reasoning" and argues it can be analyzed two ways: as mental states of individuals A and B exchanging utterances P and Q, or as a group-level unity where meaning lies in the pair P-Q rather than in individual minds. The group-level approach treats the transaction as linguistic analysis of discourse, not of internal states.
requirements: Analysts must share the cultural background and language of the participants to understand the discourse as participants do
constraints: Group-level analysis assumes nothing about internal states beyond what speakers make explicit aloud
target_learners: students from kindergarten to college collaborating via computer media
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building through building on each other's reasoning
examples: The editorial frames four papers in the issue as each grappling with units of analysis for transactivity

citation: Gerry Stahl. (2013). Transactive discourse in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:145–147. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9171-6
title: Thick description as the analytic basis for understanding transactive discourse
description: Stahl draws on Austin and Geertz's notion of thick description: CSCL researchers understand transaction meanings because they share a community with their subjects. He contrasts "a thin description of someone's eye twitching vs. a thick description of someone winking" — a wink is a meaningful transaction requiring subtle cultural knowledge, unlike objective physiological description. Computers cannot formulate or understand thick descriptions of discourse moves.
requirements: The analyst must be a member of the same broad community as the subjects and possess subtle cultural knowledge
constraints: Computers cannot formulate or understand thick descriptions of discourse moves, so automated approaches must be indirect
target_learners: CSCL researchers and analysts of collaborative learning data
target_learning_goals: analysis and measurement of collaborative discourse
examples: Austin's twitch-versus-wink distinction illustrates why objective movement description cannot capture meaningful interaction

title: Design shared-computer collaboration with different but interdependent roles to foster transactive building
description: The editorial reports that in keeping with transactivity theory, kindergarten triads were given "different but interdependent roles or tasks" on a single computer with three mice and distinct screen areas. Interacting on one computer is argued to increase shared attention and hence the tendency to build transactively, developing social skills while pursuing a common goal.

constraints: Reported for young kindergarten children on a single shared computer; effectiveness attributed to combining individual roles with group interaction
target_learners: kindergarten children working in triads
target_learning_goals: social skills and collaborative achievement of a common goal
examples: Triads worked on one computer with three mice and three distinct screen areas, engaging in group processes toward a common goal

title: Wegner's original transactive memory conception differs from later distributed and group cognition theories
description: Stahl notes the 1980s conception of transactivity by Wegner and others was a psychological theory in which individuals hold different knowledge and transact to assist recall of stored information through meta-knowledge about what each other knows. Thus it analyzed group phenomena at the individual unit, contrasted with theories of intersubjective shared understanding where knowledge is spread across people and artifacts or a group co-experiences a joint problem space.
requirements: Distinguishing the two traditions requires attention to whether the unit of analysis is individual mental states or group-level discourse
constraints: The original conception applies to situations where individuals hold different knowledge and assist each other's recall
target_learners: CSCL researchers analyzing collaborative memory and knowledge building
target_learning_goals: theoretical analysis of group knowledge phenomena

citation: Gerry Stahl. (2010). Guiding group cognition in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9091-7
title: Stahl's framework of major influences on group cognition in CSCL
description: The article presents a visualization of "major categories of these influences" on collaborative learning, placing at the center "the dialogical interaction through which individual participants form into a collective knowledge-building agency." Sequential interaction weaves individual Bakhtinian voices into group meaning making, whose shared meanings are embodied in team knowledge artifacts and produce team outcomes driven by the team's task. Surrounding influences include individual resources and experiences, the culture of the discourse community, interaction context, and technology and media.
requirements: Analysis of group cognition must treat the group level of description rather than only individual preconditions
constraints: Individual background, perspectives and abilities are preconditions of collaboration and are of interest to education and psychology in general, but not specifically CSCL's concerns

group problem solving

title: Browser plug-in infrastructure for portable cross-platform collaboration scripts
description: The article describes an infrastructure for collaboration scripts that can be ported to different collaboration environments, developed by Christof Wecker and colleagues. It works "by means of a browser plug-in, which can recognize inputs from different CSCL systems and provide responses in accordance with a cross-platform script definition." Its application was illustrated in a realistic educational application setting.

title: Trust as an internal precondition of productive collaboration, engendered by the collaboration process
description: In the final paper of the issue, Anne Gerdes addresses relations of trust among people, treating trust both as "required by collaborative undertakings as a spontaneous embodied experience of being-in-the-world-with-others" and as something that "may be engendered by the collaboration process itself." The editorial frames this as showing that group interaction depends upon, and helps to construct, internal preconditions of productive collaboration such as mutual trust.
requirements: Attention to the interpersonal resources of group participants themselves rather than only external control of collaboration

target_learning_goals: productive collaboration
mutual trust among participants
examples: Gerdes's essay is described as a new genre for ijRSCL: a brief, deep reflection piece from a pointed perspective

citation: Gerry Stahl. (2010). Guiding group cognition in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9091-7
title: Avoid guiding collaboration so externally that it undermines the group's autonomy, agency and sociability
description: The article warns that CSCL researchers "can become focused on trying to promote and control collaboration from outside the group itself." Taken too far, this can foster strategic communication and impression management, furthering external goals at the expense of "the group's own autonomy, agency, and sociability," and students can be influenced to pursue high grades rather than knowledge building. The recommended response is to return to the interpersonal resources of the participants themselves.
requirements: Support for collaboration should preserve the group's own autonomy, agency, and sociability
constraints: Taken too far, external promotion and control of collaboration fosters strategic communication and impression management
target_learners: students in collaborative learning groups
target_learning_goals: knowledge building rather than grade-seeking strategies
examples: The editorial closes the issue's reflection by returning to interpersonal resources of group participants, via Gerdes's paper on trust

article_title: The mechanics of CSCL macro scripts
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg, Fabrice Hong. (2008). The mechanics of CSCL macro scripts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://hal.science/hal-00692019
title: Perturbation model of CSCL macro script design
description: The article proposes a pedagogical model for designing collaboration scripts in which the script's core action is perturbation: "a script disturbs the natural convergence of a team and in doing so increases the intensity of interaction required between team members". The nature of the perturbation determines which interaction types (argumentation, explanation, regulation) become necessary, giving designers a lever for targeting interaction quality.

target_learners: students working in collaborative learning teams
target_learning_goals: knowledge-productive interactions such as argumentation, explanations and mutual regulation
examples: The model is illustrated using three scripts described in the article

title: Script mechanics as data-structure transformations between phases

Designing a script thus means specifying how the social grouping, the available resources, and the expected products are reconfigured from one phase to the next.

target_learning_goals: structured collaborative learning interactions across script phases

article_title: The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration
citation: Damşa, C. I. (2014). The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2014) 9:247–281. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9193-8
title: Multi-layer analytic framework linking productive interaction, knowledge objects, and shared epistemic agency over time
description: The article constructs an integrative analytic framework in which learning is analyzed as knowledge co-construction across three interwoven layers: productive interactions, knowledge objects, and shared epistemic agency, unfolding in time via interaction trajectories. Knowledge objects are "an externalization of knowledge, 'freezing' knowledge at certain moments in time", accessible to the whole group and usable to produce new knowledge. The unit of analysis is the joint action directed at co-construction of knowledge objects — mediated interaction — rather than the individual or the group. A temporal perspective captures how moment-to-moment episodes build into continuity and how interaction generates actions that affect developing objects.
requirements: Analysis requires identifying theme-based episodes, coding verbal actions within episodes, and pairing key events in interaction with object versions within a maximum of one week
constraints: Productivity is defined in epistemic terms by each case and context rather than universal criteria
The framework was developed and applied in higher-education collaborative research projects
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge co-construction
conducting and reporting empirical research
examples: The analysis combined discourse-analysis coding of episodes, document analysis of report iterations (11 to 29 per group), and qualification of agentic action sequences

citation: Damşa, C. I. (2014). The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2014) 9:247–281. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9193-8
title: Shared epistemic agency as an emerging, group-level capacity for deliberate joint object-oriented interaction
description: The article defines shared epistemic agency as "the capacity to enable a deliberate, joint, object-oriented interaction." The epistemic aspect refers to the group's active involvement with knowledge and its materialization into knowledge objects; sharedness means agency is expressed in joint efforts at the group level, not in each individual member's pursuits. Agency is treated as an emerging, recursive capacity that manifests and unfolds during interaction, drawing on the view that epistemic agency emerges through participation in collective activities rather than residing in the individual mind.
requirements: Intersubjectivity and interaction between participants
Sustained active participation in collective knowledge work
constraints: The construct was analyzed by qualifying sequences of actions showing deliberate, strategic, and reflective conduct within the studied project setting
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: taking initiative in inquiry and knowledge construction
joint management of collaborative research processes
examples: Groups manifesting shared epistemic agency produced knowledge objects that were more complex and suitable to the problems addressed

title: Object-oriented collaborative research project pattern with phased knowledge-object development
description: The redesigned Bachelor Thesis course organized small groups to set up, conduct, and report an empirical research study for external clients across four phases — project initiation, research preparation, construction, and delivery — each producing intermediate objects (project plan, research plan, instruments, drafts) culminating in a final research article and presentation slides. Shared knowledge objects were requested as part of the envisioned problem solutions, positioning students as producers of knowledge rather than mere course-takers. Groups were formed around client-proposed topics and scaffolded to organize and manage their own projects.

article_title: CSCL in Asia
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). CSCL in Asia. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 6:1–7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9112-1
title: Three-level integration framework for educational reform: micro, meso, and macro levels
description: The Singapore presentation by Looi, So, Toh, and Chen is framed around the need to integrate reform efforts at three scales, building on meso-level infrastructure discussion by Jones et al. (2006). As the editorial states, it "distinguishes the micro level of student learning and interaction, the meso level of teacher professional development in the school, and the macro level of national policy and strategic planning." Change must take place simultaneously on many levels, requiring a carefully coordinated, phased, and iterative approach, illustrated by Group Scribbles introduction into Singapore classrooms over several years.
requirements: Change must take place simultaneously on many levels, requiring a carefully coordinated, phased, and iterative approach
target_learners: K-12 students in national school systems
target_learning_goals: 21st century skills including collaborative knowledge building and creative thinking
examples: Embedded researchers worked closely with early-adopter teachers to tune the socio-technical system of Group Scribbles' classroom role, based on analysis of situated student interaction
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). CSCL in Asia. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 6:1–7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9112-1

article_title: CSCL in Asia
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). CSCL in Asia. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 6:1–7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9112-1
title: Abduction and collaborative hypertext as support for multi-faceted classroom inquiry
description: Glassman and Kang present the logic of inquiry — sometimes called abduction in contrast to deduction and induction — as discussed by Dewey and Peirce. Rather than arguing from initial facts to a single conclusion, "abduction involves exploring multiple possibilities suggested by an observation." They propose that computer-supported collaboration media like wikis and blogs could support such multi-faceted inquiry, with collaborative hypertext providing an alternative to traditional linear deductive thinking and supporting complex networks of knowledge exploration, hearkening back to hypertext notions of Engelbart and Nelson.
requirements: Computer-supported collaboration media such as wikis and blogs further developed to support multi-faceted inquiry
constraints: The editorial questions why blogs and wikis should be singled out rather than extensions of discussion forums like Knowledge Forum or WebGuide
target_learners: School students in student-centered inquiry classrooms
target_learning_goals: Innovative thinking and exploration of multiple possibilities from observations
examples: The authors review student experiences in the Philippines, Japan, Taiwan, and Korea taking first steps in Dewey-style student-centered inquiry

article_title: Scaffolding of small groups’ metacognitive activities with an avatar
citation: Molenaar, I., Chiu, M. M., Sleegers, P., & van Boxtel, C. (2011). Scaffolding of small groups' metacognitive activities with an avatar. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 601-624. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9130-z
title: Structuring versus problematizing as two scaffolding mechanisms
description: The article adopts Reiser's distinction between two mechanisms by which scaffolding affects learning. "Structuring simplifies the learning assignment by reducing its complexity, clarifying the underlying components and supporting performance", for example by showing an exemplary plan, while problematizing increases complexity by posing questions that elicit learners' own strategies and metacognitive activities. The study instantiates these as two avatar scaffold conditions and finds they foster qualitatively different student interactions.
requirements: Scaffolds must be context-suitable and delivered at the point in the learning process where the metacognitive activity is typically executed
constraints: Structuring scaffolds encourage attention to the scaffold's information but do not invite students to construct their own metacognitive activities
target_learners: elementary school students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge and domain knowledge during collaborative inquiry
examples: The avatar David showed an exemplary mind-map plan in the structuring condition and asked "How are you going to make a mind map?" in the problematizing condition.
key_sources: Molenaar, I., Chiu, M. M., Sleegers, P., & van Boxtel, C. (2011). Scaffolding of small groups' metacognitive activities with an avatar. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 601-624. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9130-z

article_title: Scaffolding of small groups’ metacognitive activities with an avatar
citation: Molenaar, I., Chiu, M. M., Sleegers, P., & van Boxtel, C. (2011). Scaffolding of small groups' metacognitive activities with an avatar. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 601-624. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9130-z
title: Avatar-based metacognitive scaffolding system in the Ontdeknet learning environment
description: A computerized scaffolding system integrated into the Ontdeknet virtual learning environment, in which the avatar David delivers metacognitive scaffolds to triads. Scaffold timing was based on Zimmerman's model of self-regulated learning and on students' attention focus, with a minimum of 12 scaffolds per condition during the first two lessons. Problematizing scaffolds required responses: "The triads in the problematizing condition were obliged to answer the avatar 's questions in an answer box on the screen". Control triads saw the same avatar without scaffolds to control for a Hawthorne effect.
requirements: Scaffolds must be dynamically timed to instances when metacognitive activities are typically executed in the learning process
target_learners: elementary school students in grades four to six
target_learning_goals: planning, monitoring, and evaluating learning during a collaborative country-exploration assignment
examples: Triads worked six hours on the assignment 'Would you like to live abroad?' about New Zealand or Iceland, consulting an expert inhabitant via the environment.

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Four paradigms of shared knowledge span individual representations, shared objects, shared situations, and shared communities
description: The editorial organizes CSCL analyses of shared knowledge into four paradigms spanning a range from individual to community levels. It states that "Studies of CSCL each tend to focus on a certain form of knowledge and assume a certain way of sharing this knowledge," with choices depending on the study's theoretical position. The paradigms are offered as a lens for reading the issue's four technology-design articles, and the authors note it "may be possible to select the most appropriate paradigm for any given study."
requirements: Studies must make their assumptions about the form of knowledge and mode of sharing explicit
constraints: The question of how the paradigms might fit together is deferred, as "a topic for another time"
target_learners: CSCL researchers and designers of collaborative learning technologies
target_learning_goals: Understanding and analyzing how knowledge is shared in collaborative learning
examples: The editorial maps each of the issue's four articles (wikis, virtual reality, PowerPoint, group formation software) to a different paradigm of shared knowledge
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Paradigm of sharing individual mental representations: group members possess sufficiently similar mental representations they externalize and compare
description: This commonsensical paradigm holds that shared knowledge in a small group means each member possesses the same knowledge, elaborated as "mental representations that are sufficiently similar to specific mental representations of each of the other members." Sharing is a matter of transferring and comparing ideas in ways that typically do not change the ideas. The editorial links it to Clark and Brennan's classic grounding analysis, in which collaborators externalize propositional expressions of their representations.
requirements: Individuals possess well-formed opinions and can unproblematically express them
constraints: Assumes sharing typically does not change the ideas being shared
target_learners: Small collaborating groups
target_learning_goals: Establishing common ground through externalizing and comparing ideas
examples: The editorial cites the grounding analysis of Clark and Brennan (1991), often cited in CSCL research, as this paradigm's classic elaboration
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Paradigm of sharing an object: shared knowledge arises from a group's joint orientation toward a common object of work
description: This paradigm conceives shared knowledge as "a natural consequence of a group being collaboratively involved with the object of their work together": all members are oriented toward the same artifact, problem, or goal and thereby come to share knowledge of it. Once the object is truly shared, no special coordination is needed. The editorial cites analyses of students defining and sharing multiple realizations of a mathematical object and of affordances of an object being enacted interactively.
requirements: The object must be truly shared among participants
target_learners: Student groups collaborating online or in classrooms
target_learning_goals: Constructing new shared knowledge about a common object of work
examples: A cited ijCSCL article (Çakır et al. 2009) describes an online group whose construction of new shared knowledge, such as formulating an algebraic expression, proceeded quickly once all members could see the same mathematical object
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Paradigm of sharing a situation: engagement in collaborative discourse within a common context automatically generates shared knowledge
description: Broadening the object paradigm, this view holds that a group shares knowledge by being situated in a common context — a joint problem space or indexical ground of reference — including the shared object, affordances of the CSCL environment, and the group's past discourse. The editorial states that according to this paradigm, "the engagement in collaborative discourse can automatically generate shared knowledge as an ongoing process," with situation and discourse standing in a mutually constitutive relationship.
requirements: A common context including past group discourse and environmental affordances
target_learners: Collaborating student groups
target_learning_goals: Generating shared knowledge through collaborative discourse
examples: The editorial cites Duranti and Goodwin's claim that talk and context shape each other, and Roschelle and Teasley's joint problem space construct
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Paradigm of sharing a community: shared knowledge comes from belonging to the same communities, cultures, and societies
description: The broadest paradigm argues that the shared knowledge making life together possible "comes from belonging to the same communities, cultures, and societies" — understanding historically accumulated knowledge, values, perspectives, artifacts, and ways of life, largely encapsulated in language. The editorial cites work relating the institutional macro-level to the mezzo-level of collaboration and the micro-level of interaction analysis when broadening computer support to complex technological infrastructures.
requirements: Membership in shared communities, cultures, or societies
target_learners: Learners participating in communities of practice
target_learning_goals: Communication and collaboration grounded in culturally shared understanding
examples: The editorial cites Jones et al. (2006) on relating institutional macro-levels to mezzo- and micro-levels of CSCL design
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Wiki Design Platform with awareness, navigation, communication, and analysis components for online intersubjective space
description: Presented in the issue's first article (Larusson and Alterman), the Wiki Design Platform builds on the wiki's malleable, easy-to-use interface, which the editorial says "is, however, in need of specific kinds of additional functionality for collaborative learning settings." It "provides a suite of awareness, navigation, communication, and analysis components and scaffolds." Two college case studies — HCI design projects and co-blogging about course readings — show different component selections creating an online intersubjective space for different collaboration forms.
requirements: Additional functionality beyond the base wiki interface for collaborative learning settings
constraints: The editorial notes it is not immediately clear which paradigm of shared knowledge the concept of intersubjectivity falls into
target_learners: College students working in teams
target_learning_goals: Collaboration on design projects and co-blogging about course readings
examples: Case study one: student teams collaborating on HCI design projects; case study two: students co-blogging in the wiki about their course readings
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: SMALLab mixed-reality design pivots on three principles: face-to-face interaction, distributed thought and action, and immediate consolidation
description: The SMALLab mixed-reality classroom design, presented by Birchfield and Megowan-Romanowicz, pivots on three principles: direct face-to-face interaction among co-located participants should be cultivated; thought and action should be distributed across multiple participants through an active, generative process unfolding in real time; and immediate spatial and temporal consolidation of emergent conceptual models should follow the active learning process. The editorial states each principle "supports shared knowledge" by providing preconditions and mechanisms for knowledge sharing through structured interaction.
requirements: Computationally mediated space with projection of virtual reality into the physical classroom interacting with student behaviors
target_learners: Whole classrooms of students, including at-risk students
target_learning_goals: Construction of scientific shared knowledge of abstract earth sciences concepts
examples: The reported study demonstrates that situating groups of students in the mixed-reality setting can be highly motivating even for at-risk students
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7

article_title: Paradigms of shared knowledge
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7
title: Ontology framework of categories for analyzing, specifying, and coordinating student needs, theories, technologies, and best practices for theory-driven group formation
description: In the issue's final article, Isotani, Inaba, Ikeda, and Mizoguchi propose the reverse of designing an interaction space first: they "start from the individual students' educational needs and goals to then form group activities that are responsive to those needs." The paper presents "a framework or ontology of categories for analyzing, specifying, and coordinating student needs, theories, technologies, and best practices." The editorial stresses it is not trying to automate group formation but to support teachers as facilitators of collaboration and orchestrators of knowledge sharing.
requirements: Adequate support is required, since expecting teachers to match student needs to CSCL theories, technologies, and pedagogies without support is not feasible
constraints: Not intended to automate group formation; supports teachers in their facilitator role
target_learners: Individual students with differing educational needs and goals
target_learning_goals: Grouping students who can support one another and selecting personally tuned collaborative-learning activities
examples: Starting from individual needs, the authors hypothesize teachers can group students who support one another and select activities helping members achieve their goals as individuals and as a group
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Paradigms of shared knowledge. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9075-7

article_title: Traversing planes of learning
citation: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7
title: Three planes of learning in CSCL: individual, small-group, and community
description: The article names a tripartite unit-of-analysis framework for CSCL: "analyses of CSCL are often conducted on one of three levels: individual learning, small-group cognition or community knowledge building". The planes are actualized in classroom practice, where individual activities precede small-group work that culminates in whole-class sharing. The framework is grounded in CSCL practice and in Vygotsky's foundational role for intersubjective learning.
requirements: Analyses must select a unit of analysis; current analytic methodologies are designed for only one plane
constraints: The planes are intrinsically intertwined, and there is little theoretical understanding of how they are connected
target_learners: students in CSCL settings working individually, in small groups, and in whole-class community discussion
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building and learning analyzed at multiple units of analysis
examples: Typical CSCL classrooms provide initial time for individual activities such as background reading or homework drill, followed by small-group work, then whole-class sharing of group findings
key_sources: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7

article_title: Traversing planes of learning
citation: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7
title: Artifacts as bridges: affordances that open up connections between planes
description: The article develops an account, drawing on Heidegger's analysis of bridges and Bonderup Dohn's affordances, in which artifacts "afford" connecting levels: "A highway ramp or bridge often creates a possibility that did not otherwise exist for going from one level to another at a given point". The connecting is not accidental but belongs to the artifact's nature and design, which opens up a shared world. This supports a post-cognitive shift away from individual-mind-centered analysis toward how language, tools and resources work.
requirements: Resources must be identifiable units of the physical world, including speech and gesture, involved in meaning-making practices
constraints: The account is framed as a helpful physical analogy for conceptual connections between levels of learning, not a model or explanation
target_learners: participants in collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: meaning-making and knowledge building mediated by artifacts and resources
examples: Heidegger's analysis of the Alte Brücke of Heidelberg, and the I-90 bridge ramps across the Hudson River, serve as the physical illustrations
key_sources: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7

article_title: Traversing planes of learning
citation: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7
title: Model of collaborative knowledge building across interconnected planes
description: Figure 3 presents "A model of collaborative knowledge building", adapted from Stahl 2006 Ch. 9, indicating typical processes on each primary plane and "possible paths of influence or connection, as events unfolding on the different planes interpenetrate each other". The boxes and arrows operationalize an infinitely complex matter for concrete analytic work. The article states the figure sketches constraints and flows of influence without claiming to explain or model them.
requirements: The model is intended for concrete analytic work by CSCL researchers on data collected in CSCL settings
constraints: The figure is not meant to reify different levels or activities and does not claim to explain or model the processes
target_learners: CSCL researchers analyzing collaborative learning data
target_learning_goals: understanding how collaborative knowledge building takes place across individual, small-group and community planes
examples: Sequential small-group interaction brings in resources from all three planes, requires co-attention, and may generate new or modified resources retained at the various planes
key_sources: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7

article_title: Traversing planes of learning
citation: Stahl, G. (2012). Traversing planes of learning. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 467–473. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9159-7
title: Design collaboration technologies to support mediation across all planes of learning
description: Because computer technologies play a central role in mediating multi-level learning processes, the article recommends that "innovative technologies should be designed to support this mediation". Design must consider how to prepare groups, individuals and communities to take advantage of designed functionality and promote learning on all planes. This follows directly from the three-planes framework.
requirements: Design processes must consider preparing groups, individuals and communities to take advantage of the designed functionality
target_learners: individuals, small groups, and classroom communities in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: problem-solving, content acquisition and knowledge building across planes
examples: The article cites provision of resources for teacher professional development, scripted collaboration activities and student curriculum as design provisions

article_title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0
title: Three-type taxonomy of CSCL researchers by their relation to theory
description: The editorial organizes CSCL research practice into three kinds of researchers: those who "simply observe results of interventions" without theory, those who "follow a particular theory or theoretical framework that they accept as is", and those who "conduct CSCL research in order to investigate theoretical issues and refine theoretical perspectives specific to CSCL". The third group starts from a framework or commonsensical understanding but aims at pushing theories further and refining conceptualizations of collaborative learning; the issue's articles exemplify this approach.
requirements: Researchers must reflect on their theoretical footing rather than adopt common-sense assumptions unexamined
constraints: Imported frameworks not developed for CSCL "may fail to identify phenomena that are characteristic of CSCL"
target_learners: CSCL researchers
target_learning_goals: Designing and interpreting research on computer-supported collaborative learning
examples: The editorial presents the four ijCSCL volume 5 case studies as exemplars of the third, theory-refining group.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0

article_title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0
title: CSCL processes operate at individual, small-group, and classroom levels that interpenetrate without being reducible
description: The editorial argues that CSCL settings involve processes — "cognitive, knowledge-building, interactional, or identity-forming" — at the small-group and/or classroom level as well as the individual student level. These "Processes at these different levels interpenetrate with each other intimately, without being reducible to any one level". CSCL additionally mediates learning, interaction, and cognition by technological artifacts and computational media, so researchers need more elaborated theories and methods to capture these processes and mediations.
requirements: Theories and methods elaborated enough to capture multiple levels of description and their technological mediations
constraints: Traditional training sciences focus on the individual learner, with culture conceived only at a broad societal level
target_learners: CSCL researchers and practitioners implementing CSCL in practice
target_learning_goals: Understanding collaborative learning as multi-level, artifact-mediated interaction
examples: The issue's articles each focus on different levels and their special mediations, proposing new ways of viewing what takes place there.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0

article_title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0
title: Shared dynamic dialogic space as focal point of children's collective reasoning around interactive whiteboards
description: Drawing on the Kershner, Mercer, Warwick and Kleine Staarman study of elementary students using interactive whiteboards during small-group collaborative discussions, the editorial describes an extension of distributed cognition with "the metaphor of a shared dynamic dialogic space as the focal point of the children's collective reasoning and co-construction of knowledge". The whiteboard functions as a location for focusing shared attention, a referential center for exploratory talk, an external memory, common ground, indexical source for group cognition, and visual foundation for group identity; teacher-instilled 'talk rules' help structure this space.
requirements: Interactive whiteboard functionality combined with teacher-instilled 'talk rules' to structure the dialogic space
target_learners: Elementary students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: Collaborative reasoning and co-construction of shared knowledge
examples: The editorial also calls the construct the 'joint problem space', a way of thinking about how critical dimensions of CSCL interactions come together.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0

article_title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0
title: Three classroom chronotypes — adagio, andante, allegretto — characterize the co-constructed temporality of CSCL interaction
description: From the Ligorio and Ritella Bakhtinian analysis, the editorial presents temporality experienced by the classroom group as "a co-constructed encounter incorporating significant meaning and expression", not an objective, smooth succession of moments. Borrowing musical terminology, the authors "characterize phases of classroom interaction as proceeding with a tempo of adagio, andante, or allegretto"; the three chronotypes correspond to different modes of collaboration, coordinated with the simultaneously established sense of space, constructed by students' responses to each other under specific classroom and technology conditions.
requirements: Analysis of how interaction gradually unfolds during the period studied, rather than comparing initial to final states
constraints: Chronotypes are tied to the specific conditions of the classroom and its technology
target_learners: Students in classroom-based CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: Understanding how collaborative learning unfolds temporally in sequential interaction
examples: The editorial contrasts this with folk theories of learning that focus only on content changing from an initial to a final state.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0

article_title: Beyond folk theories of CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0
title: Study knowledge, roles, space, and time through detailed analysis of situated interaction rather than assuming their characteristics
description: The editorial's closing design recommendation for CSCL research: computer-supported collaborative learning opens a multi-dimensional shared world in an evolving, co-created context, where "Knowledge, roles, space, and time are not simple givens whose characteristics can be assumed". Each must be studied in each case through detailed analysis of the situated interaction. The editorial adds that many research questions can still be rigorously pursued within established perspectives, and the journal welcomes both kinds of studies.
requirements: Detailed analysis of situated interaction in each specific CSCL case
constraints: Not every paper needs to address these theoretical frontiers; traditional frameworks remain appropriate for many questions
target_learners: CSCL researchers
target_learning_goals: Designing CSCL studies that capture characteristic phenomena of computer-supported collaborative learning
examples: The four ijCSCL case studies each propose intriguing extensions to theories important to CSCL, such as distributed cognition, discourse analysis, tacit knowledge, activity theory, and temporal analysis.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). Beyond folk theories of CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9098-0

article_title: An international research community
citation: Stahl, G., Law, N., & Hesse, F. (2012). An international research community. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 341–345. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9155-y
title: Cognitive Work Analysis as a method for analyzing the socio-technical context of educational research settings
description: The editorial describes Cognitive Work Analysis as a technique drawn from engineering fields that Kim MacKinnon applies to educational research. It is offered as a response to recognized weaknesses of design-based research, including that "there is no specified methodology for analyzing the collaborative student usage of CSCL technologies" and the difficulty of generalizing from single case studies. By characterizing a case study's context, the technique is intended to help judge its broader relevance.
requirements: A case-study research setting whose socio-technical context must be characterized to judge broader relevance
constraints: The editors present it as addressing the problem that design-based research rarely yields direct implications for technology re-design and is hard to generalize from a single case-study context
target_learners: CSCL and learning sciences researchers
target_learning_goals: Analyzing and generalizing from case-study research on collaborative learning technologies
examples: MacKinnon's article in the issue illustrates applying the technique to analyzing the socio-technical context of an educational research setting.
key_sources: Stahl, G., Law, N., & Hesse, F. (2012). An international research community. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 341–345. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9155-y

article_title: An international research community
citation: Stahl, G., Law, N., & Hesse, F. (2012). An international research community. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 341–345. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9155-y
title: Four-factor scripting approach for blended learning: space, pedagogical method, participants, and history
description: The final article in the issue, by Mar Pérez-Sanagustín, Patricia Santos, Davinia Hernández-Leo, and Josep Blat, proposes and illustrates a scripting approach the editors describe as "focused on four factors: the space, the pedagogical method, the participants, and the history." The emphasis on space relates to a blended learning geography course that uses mobile and other technologies to support teams of students exploring the urban environment in Barcelona.
requirements: A blended learning setting in which collaboration can be scripted along the four factors
constraints: Illustrated in a geography course using mobile technologies for urban exploration in Barcelona
target_learners: student teams in blended higher-education courses
target_learning_goals: structuring collaboration in blended learning activities
examples: Teams of students exploring the urban environment in Barcelona with mobile and other technologies.

article_title: What does it mean? Students’ procedural and conceptual problem solving in a CSCL environment designed within the field of science education
citation: Krange, I., & Ludvigsen, S. (2008). What does it mean? Students' procedural and conceptual problem solving in a CSCL environment designed within the field of science education. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 3, 25-51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9030-4
title: Socio-cultural dialogical account of CSCL problem solving mediated by three cultural tools
description: The article follows the dialogical strand of CSCL research, in which "the dialogical approach focuses on how tools and resources are used in interaction". Students' problem solving is made in relation to cultural, historical and institutional settings, and the unit of analysis is mediated action. Three mediating means are analysed: the school as curriculum deliverer, the knowledge domain, and the computer tools, whose interconnection is characterised by tensions or interdependent reinforced tendencies that push interactions in certain directions.
requirements: Analysis of moment-by-moment interaction (video-based interaction analysis) to access how the mediating tools operate
constraints: Access to the mediating factors is only available in interactions; the meaning potential of tools is only partly given in advance and partly realised in situated activity
target_learners: lower secondary school students
target_learning_goals: scientific concepts in gene technology and biology
examples: The article analyses three video extracts from a group of four ninth-grade students solving an insulin-protein problem, tracing how curriculum demands, the codontable knowledge domain, and the 3D model and website structure their talk and actions.
key_sources: Krange, I., & Ludvigsen, S. (2008). What does it mean? Students' procedural and conceptual problem solving in a CSCL environment designed within the field of science education. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 3, 25-51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9030-4

title: Networked 3D insulin-protein CSCL environment with supporting website
description: A CSCL environment for gene technology consisting of computer-based 3D models (a research laboratory and a molecular level of the cells where students pick up amino acids and place them in a chain) plus a website presenting the problems and the codontable. "The 3D model was organised for distributed settings, with the participants connected in a local area network (LAN) and supplied with a telecommunication system that allowed them to communicate orally during the whole session." Students and teacher, each in a separate room, shared the 3D models and website as shared objects and were represented by avatars.

A real-time telecommunication system for oral communication
Basic teacher training using the tools ahead of the educational setting
constraints: The 3D model comes with taxations, including weaknesses concerning the conceptual representations and a storyline that partly steals focus from the disciplinary problem

target_learning_goals: reading DNA sequences with a codontable
relating codons to amino acids
building a model of the insulin-protein

article_title: Practice perspectives in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Practice perspectives in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9065-9
title: Practice perspective in CSCL research
description: The practice perspective holds that CSCL research should attend to how people actually interact in dyads and small groups rather than only to controlled variables. It draws on the 'practice turn' in contemporary theory, where focus shifted to 'practices as embodied, materially mediated arrays of human activity centrally organized around shared practical understanding'. The editorial applies it at individual, group, and community levels of description.
requirements: Powerful theories and analytical approaches are required to study practices reflectively
constraints: Practices are not commonly described in terms of regularity among controlled variables
target_learners: students in CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building
examples: The editorial introduces a special issue of ijCSCL whose articles analyze the role of practices in CSCL at individual, group, and community levels.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Practice perspectives in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9065-9

article_title: Practice perspectives in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Practice perspectives in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9065-9
title: Affordances are enacted by user practices, not objective properties of artifacts
description: Following Dohn's article in the issue, affordances should not be treated as objective properties of artifacts independent of their users; they are relative to the 'interaction potential' of the people who see and use the artifacts, grounded in phenomenological accounts of embodiment. The editorial states: 'The affordances of the technologies are to be found not in the plans of the programmers or instructors, but in the practices of the users.'
requirements: Analysis of affordances must examine how user groups enact designed features and adapt their interaction practices
target_learners: students using CSCL technologies
target_learning_goals: collaborative meaning making
examples: In the VMT environment, affordances 'were determined in terms of the ways in which the user groups enacted the designed features and adapted their interaction practices to the technical environment'.

article_title: Practice perspectives in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Practice perspectives in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9065-9
title: Trialogical framework of the K-P Labs Project
description: The trialogical framework distinguishes the individual, collaborative, and object-oriented aspects of learning, shifting the third focus from agents in any configuration to the knowledge object. In classrooms it calls for students, project groups, and classes to engage in 'systematic improvement of ideas and other knowledge objects', echoing activity theory's orientation toward goals and artifacts to be produced.

project groups
classes

article_title: The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools
citation: Andrea Forte. (2015). The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. 10:35–51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9210-6
title: First- and second-order information assessment strategies
description: The article proposes a shallow taxonomy of information assessment strategies developed via grounded theory coding of student interviews. First-order strategies involve "adopting known heuristics for assessing sources", while second-order strategies involve "reflective construction of standards based on students' understanding of how information is produced" and the tasks at hand. The constructs are linked to Scardamalia and Bereiter's first- and second-order learning environments and used to explain how production experience supports reflection on novel publication models.
requirements: Applied to learners engaging with participatory information sources in a perpetually changing information landscape
constraints: Developed through interpretive grounded theory in two high school settings; products of interpretive research are framed as empirically driven hypotheses, not causal proof
target_learners: High school students (juniors and seniors) in science classes
target_learning_goals: Information literacy: finding, assessing, and using information sources
examples: Coding of 57 interviews yielded categories such as "criteria for citing a source", refined via axial coding into the taxonomy
key_sources: Andrea Forte. (2015). The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. 10:35–51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9210-6

article_title: The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools
citation: Andrea Forte. (2015). The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. 10:35–51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9210-6
title: Four dimensions of responsibility for contributing to new knowledge
description: The article unpacks the responsibility students experience when contributing to knowledge building along two axes: shared versus individual, and local versus global. Shared responsibility means advancing a group's knowledge, as in knowledge-building classrooms and some Wikipedia articles; global context means viewing contributions as a social good potentially used by unknown others. In these studies, "the classroom wiki activities did not engender a shared sense of responsibility in the local context of the classroom, it did engender a sense of individual responsibility at a more global level."
requirements: Public information production tasks that place students in the role of supporting others' information needs
constraints: In these studies the shared/local quadrant was not realized; realizing full potential requires guidance and opportunities to support and challenge one another in justifying and critiquing claims
target_learners: High school students contributing to public online information resources
target_learning_goals: Taking responsibility for the quality of shared information; collective cognitive responsibility
examples: Students wrote disease pages and science articles on a public wiki read by unknown others, reporting responsibility for accuracy even if nobody used the resource
