article_title: Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols
citation: Erkens, G., & Janssen, J. (2008). Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 3, 447-470. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9052-6
title: Dialogue Act Coding (DAC) system: five communicative functions and 29 dialogue acts recognized via discourse markers
description: The DAC system identifies "dialogue acts", the communicative function of each utterance typed during online collaboration, building on the Verbal Observation System and discourse-analysis research. Its core assumption is that language users "signal the intended meaning and interpretation of their utterances to their discourse partners by means of explicit 'discourse markers'". It distinguishes five main communicative functions: "(1) Argumentative..., (2) Responsive..., (3) Elicitative..., (4) Informative..., and (5) Imperative (commands)", specifying "a total of 29 different dialogue acts". The system was used in CSCL studies of history and language arts inquiry tasks.
requirements: A limited set of discourse markers must exist in the language so they can be recognized by a computer system
constraints: The filter was designed for the Dutch language and requires translation work for other languages
The procedure only suits variables indicated by specific marker words, phrases, or actions, not more interpretive variables
The system codes most utterances in isolation, not taking preceding or following utterances into account (replies are an exception)
target_learners: secondary pre-university students collaborating online in CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: communicative functions of collaborative dialogue during inquiry tasks, including argumentation, responsiveness, and coordination of collaboration
examples: Table 1 shows a coded fragment of two girls and a boy collaborating on a historical inquiry task, with utterances coded as Inform, Respond, Command, Argue, and Elicit.
key_sources: Erkens, G., & Janssen, J. (2008). Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 3, 447-470. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9052-6

article_title: Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols
citation: Erkens, G., & Janssen, J. (2008). Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 3, 447-470. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9052-6
title: MEPA production rule system for automatic dialogue act coding
description: The Multiple Episode Protocol Analysis (MEPA) computer program hosts a production rule system that automatically categorizes utterances into dialogue acts. "A set of if-then rules uses pattern matching to look for typical words or phrases, in this case for discourse markers or clue phrases." It comprises "a rule system for automatic segmentation of combined utterances in single messages (300 rules) and a rule system for dialogue act coding (1,250 rules)", and "MEPA is able to code a protocol consisting of 1,000 utterances in less than a second." A segmentation filter splits chat contributions on punctuation, connectives, and starting discourse markers, with exception rules preventing erroneous splits.
requirements: Uncoded InfStm? messages (about 10% of a protocol) must still be checked and coded manually by the researcher
constraints: New discourse markers encountered may need to be added to the DAC filter
Filter rules must be specified when coding needs to take preceding or following utterances into account
target_learners: researchers analyzing CSCL collaboration protocols of secondary students
target_learning_goals: automatic identification of dialogue acts in online collaborative learning protocols
examples: The DAC filter assigns the InfStm? default catch-all code to messages for which no matching discourse marker is found, directing the researcher to check them.
key_sources: Erkens, G., & Janssen, J. (2008). Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 3, 447-470. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9052-6

article_title: A prism of CSCL research
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). A prism of CSCL research. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9087-3
title: Mr. Vetro simulation framework for collaborative exploration of the cardiovascular system
description: Mr. Vetro is a student-facing simulation of the human body's cardiovascular system of lungs and heart, built on a substantial extension of the Agentsheets student-programmable simulation design environment. The editorial states that "the Mr. Vetro simulation framework allows students to explore the effects of different variations of physiological parameters within an interdependent complex system." Students collaboratively control the simulation, each simulating an individual organ or contextual parameter through mobile devices, in an approach the authors call collective simulations.
requirements: Small groups of students, each with a mobile device, simulating individual organs or contextual parameters
constraints: The medium is necessarily simplified, implemented in computer graphics, per the editorial's discussion of representing complex scientific phenomena
target_learners: K-12 science students
target_learning_goals: Principles of human anatomy and physiology
Causality in complex systems
examples: Students interact to collaboratively control the simulation of a complex organism under varying conditions by each simulating the role of individual organs or contextual parameters through mobile devices

article_title: A prism of CSCL research
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). A prism of CSCL research. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9087-3
title: Distributed leadership as a group-level collaborative process extending the theory of group cognition
description: The editorial describes distributed leadership as a reciprocal or interactive definition in which leadership necessarily involves uptake or influence on followers, making it a group-level phenomenon rather than a property assigned to individuals. By combining quantitative and qualitative analyses, Gressick and Derry distinguish different specific forms of leadership with different emergent patterns of distribution. The editorial states the study "extends the theory of group cognition by specifying forms of distributed leadership as a collaborative process at the group unit of analysis."
requirements: Analysis at the group unit of analysis rather than the individual
Groups allowed to interact without assigned leadership roles
constraints: Studied with university students in a regular semester-long course taking place largely online
target_learners: University students in online or blended courses
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning processes
Group leadership and coordination
examples: Gressick and Derry's semester-long online university course study distinguishing specific forms of leadership with different emergent patterns of distribution

title: Knowledge Catalyser discussion forum scaffolding metacognition through voting, annotating, critiquing, and revising postings

article_title: Making rounds: The routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers
citation: Christian Greiffenhagen. (2011). Making Rounds: the routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (forthcoming). https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Taxonomy of teacher intervention types during 'making rounds' in computer-based collaborative learning
description: The paper organizes its analysis into distinct types of teacher intervention during rounds: ratifying pupils' work, reminding pupils of neglected task aspects, making suggestions, maintaining classroom control, and making whole-class announcements. Through "a close analysis of different types of teacher interventions into pupils working in pairs with a storyboarding tool", each type is illustrated with transcribed video fragments. The taxonomy describes what teachers actually do, not what they are supposed to do.
requirements: Video or direct observation of teacher activity during pupil pair work at computers
constraints: Derived from one teacher's lessons with one storyboarding task in secondary English; the paper analyses naturally occurring discourse rather than evaluating effectiveness
target_learners: Year 9 secondary school pupils (13-14 year-olds)
target_learning_goals: Engaging with Shakespeare's Macbeth through visual storyboarding
examples: Fragments show the teacher ratifying work, pointing out missing punctuation and spelling, reminding pupils about the caption box, suggesting breaking a monologue into smaller pieces, and a wordless 'BOO' reproach

citation: Christian Greiffenhagen. (2011). Making Rounds: the routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (forthcoming). https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: kar2ouche storyboarding tool for visualizing Macbeth
description: kar2ouche is "an electronic storyboarding tool, which allows pupils to construct their own visual representations of Macbeth in a series of frames". Pupils insert characters, pictures and backgrounds, adjust size, position and pose, and add speech bubbles (for Shakespeare's dialogue), thought bubbles (for their interpretation), and a caption box (for their reasons). It computerises traditional storyboarding to simplify frame construction and make Shakespeare more enjoyable, while supporting exam preparation.
requirements: Teacher introduction covering frame construction, bubble conventions, and caption-box use
Pair arrangement at the computer, the arrangement both study teachers chose
constraints: Used here as one activity within English lessons preparing for Key Stage 3 SATs on Macbeth

target_learning_goals: Close engagement with Shakespeare's text
Creative visual interpretation of scenes
examples: Pupils produced storyboards across lessons; all storyboards were saved and collected after each computer-suite lesson

article_title: Making rounds: The routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers
citation: Christian Greiffenhagen. (2011). Making Rounds: the routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (forthcoming). https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Teacher rounds as the routine organization of monitoring during pair work at computers
description: Once pupils start working in pairs, the teacher does not sit back but 'makes rounds' through the classroom to monitor, evaluate, and control what pupils are doing. The pattern comprises brief visits in which the teacher looks at screens, ratifies or corrects work, reminds pupils of neglected aspects, and makes suggestions. As Sorensen's description quoted in the paper shows, the teacher "wanders around among children", bending down, looking at screens, and talking to pupils.
requirements: An open classroom layout allowing the teacher to approach and view pupil screens
constraints: Open-ended, less sequentially structured computer tasks make it harder for the teacher to see what pupils have done and anticipate what they will do next, per Sorensen's account quoted in the paper
target_learners: Secondary school pupils working in pairs at computers
target_learning_goals: Completing all aspects of a multi-step production task
Staying on task during self-directed pair work
examples: In the study the teacher checked previous frames for empty caption boxes and reminded both individuals and the whole class to write their reasons

article_title: Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation
citation: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013).
title: Unsupervised Dynamic Bayesian Network model of speech style accommodation motivated by Speech Accommodation Theory
description: The model measures speech style accommodation from raw speech without labeled data or hand-crafted indexical features. It uses latent speaking-style states and binary accommodation states over conversational turns, with acoustic-prosodic observation vectors. As the article states, "Our model embodies two premises. First, a person's speech in any turn is a function of his/her speaking style in that turn, which is influenced by their speech style in their previous turn," and style also depends on accommodation to the partner. Parameters are learned with expectation maximization and inference uses the junction tree algorithm; the accommodation score is the fraction of adjacent turns where both partners' most likely style states match.
requirements: Speech recorded on separate channels per speaker, segmented into turns, with acoustic and prosodic features extracted per turn
constraints: The authors acknowledge that the link between theory and model structure could be further explored, and alternative model structures might perform better
target_learners: undergraduate students in face-to-face dyadic debate discussions
target_learning_goals: assessment of group knowledge integration processes, specifically other-oriented transactive contributions
examples: Trained on one set of 38 multi-segment conversations and tested on the other, using 70-dimensional normalized histogram observation vectors computed with the openSmile toolkit
key_sources: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9172-5

article_title: Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation
citation: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013).
title: Transactivity framework: other-oriented versus self-oriented transacts as operationalized building-on-reasoning moves
description: The article operationalizes transactivity as reasoning made explicit that builds on prior reasoning in a discussion. As printed, "our operationalization of transactivity is defined as the process of building on an idea expressed earlier in a conversation using a reasoning statement." Transacts are self-oriented when they operate on the speaker's own prior reasoning and other-oriented when they operate on a partner's reasoning; other-oriented transacts are treated as particularly central to group knowledge integration. Coding proceeds in steps distinguishing reasoning from non-reasoning statements, externalizations from transactive contributions, and self- from other-oriented transacts.
requirements: Segmentation of conversation at independent clause boundaries so reasoning articulations fit within single segments
constraints: Determining whether a sentence contains a reasoning statement is subjective, especially in informal conversational data
target_learners: undergraduate students in dyadic debate discussions
target_learning_goals: explicit reasoning displays that build on prior reasoning during collaborative discussion
examples: Reasoning displays were identified via compare-and-contrast and cause-and-effect relationships between two or more concepts, illustrated with Ottoman Empire debate excerpts in Tables 1 and 2
key_sources: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9172-5

article_title: Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation
citation: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013).
title: Ottoman Empire face-to-face debate corpus with hand-coded transactivity
description: A corpus of face-to-face dyadic debates on the cause of the decline of the Ottoman Empire, collected in a laboratory setting for research on arousal and learning. Male undergraduates aged 18 to 25 argued assigned sides using four-page background packets; debates lasted eight minutes under blocked or freeform conditions. As printed, "A total of 76 sessions (with 152 participants) were collected and used for further analysis, half of which were in the freeform condition." Speech was transcribed, segmented into 5490 independent-clause segments, and coded for transactivity; prevalence averaged 36 other-oriented transacts per session (minimum 22, maximum 60).
requirements: Directional microphones per speaker for clean separate-channel speech recording
constraints: Participants did not know each other beforehand and shared gender, age range, and student status, controlling for known accommodation moderators
target_learners: male undergraduate students aged 18-25
target_learning_goals: argumentive discussion and knowledge integration in debate
examples: The freeform condition allowed free talking for eight minutes, while the blocked condition gave each speaker two-minute turns

article_title: Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation
citation: Gweon, G., Jain, M., McDonough, J., Raj, B., & Rosé, C. P. (2013). Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2013).
title: Ground the design of automated collaborative-process analysis models in theoretical constructs from social and cognitive psychology
description: The article recommends that computational models for automated collaborative-learning process analysis be structured using theories from social and cognitive psychology, so that models capture deep structure in the data and generalize better. The authors state that "The significance of this finding from a methodological standpoint is that it highlights the importance of considering the theoretical foundation for a construct when setting up a machine learning model to use for automated assessment." Theory informed both the feature representation and the DBN model structure, enabling an unsupervised approach requiring neither hand-labeled data nor hand-crafted features.
requirements: Access to a relevant theoretical construct that predicts observable patterns in the interaction data
constraints: State-of-the-art machine learning applied to conversational interactions tends to learn overly specific models that do not work well in new contexts
target_learners: collaborative learning participants in face-to-face or online group work
target_learning_goals: automatic assessment of group knowledge integration processes such as transactivity
examples: Speech Accommodation Theory motivated the DBN structure whose accommodation measure correlated with other-oriented transact prevalence

article_title: Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 139-145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9118-8
title: CSCL pluralism: the field advances through confrontation and critique of multiple paradigms
description: The editorial's organizing framework holds that CSCL, as a multi-disciplinary field with inherently multifaceted goals, should foster an ecology of competing theoretical, methodological, pedagogical and technological perspectives rather than converge on one approach. The authors write that "Scientific revolutions — like political revolutions — advance through the confrontation of viewpoints and the critique of established paradigms," and argue that dominant positions "restrict innovative thinking and practices." ijCSCL is positioned as a venue for dialog among alternative perspectives.
requirements: A venue that publishes and juxtaposes alternative paradigms so viewpoints can be confronted and critiqued
constraints: The authors frame this as a stance for the research field, not a tested empirical result
target_learners: CSCL researchers and the learning sciences community
target_learning_goals: Advancing theory-building and research practice in computer-supported collaborative learning
examples: The issue pairs counter-poised papers on theory, analysis, and technology so contrasting approaches are presented side by side

article_title: Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 139-145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9118-8
title: Three levels of analysis in CSCL: individual, small group, and community
description: The editorial organizes CSCL theory by the unit at which learning is located: theories foreground the individual, the small group, or the community level of analysis, tracing respectively to cooperative learning research, Vygotsky's view that individual cognition is derivative of intersubjective experience, and Lave's perspective on learning as participation in a community of practice. The authors state that "a full analysis must take into account all three levels and their essential interpenetration," while noting any given analyst is usually well advised to focus on one level in accordance with a specific research interest.
requirements: Analysts choose a focal level aligned with their research interest while acknowledging the other levels
constraints: The editorial presents this as an organizing scheme for existing theories, not an empirically tested model
target_learners: CSCL researchers and learning scientists
target_learning_goals: Selecting an appropriate unit of analysis for collaborative learning research
examples: Pifarre and Kleine Staarman's wiki study is placed in the small-group dialogicality vein; Jorczak's Collaborative Information Processing model is placed in the individual-cognition vein
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 139-145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9118-8

article_title: Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 139-145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9118-8
title: Use mixed methods: statistical analysis to confirm hypotheses, close interaction analysis to reveal mechanisms
description: The editorial recommends combining quantitative and qualitative analysis rather than arguing for the superiority of either, calling the quantitative-versus-qualitative dichotomy increasingly recognized as false. It observes that "a statistical analysis can suggest or even confirm a hypothesis, but then a close inspection of how an individual interaction took place may be needed to indicate underlying mechanisms or processes," while a single case raises questions of typicality that a statistical result can address.
requirements: Data and driving research interests should determine which methods are selected, adapted, or created
constraints: Analysis of a single case raises questions of typicality or generalizability that statistics can motivate
target_learners: CSCL researchers and learning analysts
target_learning_goals: Designing analysis strategies for collaborative learning data
examples: The representation-study authors note the need and promise close inspection in future work; the floor-control experiment only became interpretable through log analysis of each condition

article_title: Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 139-145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9118-8
title: Co-referencing typology and coding scheme for analyzing collaborative interaction around external representations
description: The Evans, Feenstra, Ryon and McNeill article provides analytic tools for collaborative interactions around external representations, honing in on "co-referencing": multiple people referencing the same thing through a deictic word, a pointing gesture, or any verbal, physical, or virtual action referencing something as intended by more than one person. The editorial reports that "a systematic typology of forms and levels of co-reference is sketched and a method of coding co-references in their temporality is proposed and illustrated," enabling both qualitative sense of co-construction and quantitative comparison across cases.
requirements: A coding scheme applied to discourse so co-references can be tracked and compiled into quantitative measures
constraints: Illustrated on dyadic interaction; the editorial does not report validation statistics
target_learners: CSCL researchers analyzing collaborative interaction
target_learning_goals: Analyzing intersubjectivity and distributed cognition in dyadic discourse and gesture
examples: Paying attention to co-referential actions within a dyadic interaction gives an analyst a qualitative sense of the co-construction process and shared meaning making

article_title: Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 139-145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9118-8
title: Hong Kong Knowledge-Building Teachers Network (KBTN): a network connecting policy, teacher peer support, research, theory and technology
description: KBTN is a teacher network in Hong Kong, funded continuously since 2006 by the Hong Kong Ministry of Education in line with reforms going back to 2000, and based on Scardamalia and Bereiter's knowledge-building theory and the Knowledge Forum environment. The editorial describes it as "a meeting place of forward-looking government policy initiatives, teacher peer support, CSCL researcher initiative, well-established CSCL theory, and the use of CSCL technology." Chan analyzes it at macro, meso, and micro levels of transformation from an action researcher's perspective.
requirements: Sustained funding and alignment with government educational reform policy
constraints: Chan refrains from final evaluation or recommendation, recognizing the effort is ongoing and its lessons must be resituated in other settings

target_learning_goals: Connecting CSCL insights to local educational policy and classroom practice
examples: In Hong Kong the impetus was driven more by researchers and teachers and a relatively mature technology was introduced, whereas in Singapore the government led and technology design was still evolving

article_title: The core features of CSCL: Social situation, collaborative knowledge processes and their design
citation: Cress, U., Stahl, G., Ludvigsen, S., & Law, N. (2015). The core features of CSCL: Social situation, collaborative knowledge processes and their design. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10, 109-116. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9214-2
title: Awareness tools as CSCL social enhancements that make otherwise invisible cues visible
description: In contrast to the view that computer mediation filters out social context cues, the editors describe mediational tools as offering "social enhancements to the interaction". Awareness tools "may present information about the social situation or about the group members, which would not be available in normal, non-mediated communication", including peers' knowledge, activities, expertise, status or relations, sometimes aggregated to make conclusions salient, such as activity levels or recommended learning partners.
requirements: The CSCL tool must communicate social cues about the members and the group for awareness information to be conveyed
target_learners: collaborative learners in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: participation in collaborative learning interactions
examples: An awareness tool can provide information about peers' activity levels or recommend suitable learning partners

article_title: The core features of CSCL: Social situation, collaborative knowledge processes and their design
citation: Cress, U., Stahl, G., Ludvigsen, S., & Law, N. (2015). The core features of CSCL: Social situation, collaborative knowledge processes and their design. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10, 109-116. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9214-2
title: Group cognition: emergent meaning-making at the group unit of analysis as CSCL's gold standard
description: The editors present CSCL's vision that collaboration is more than exchanging information: participants "jointly create something new", which they call a kind of gold standard. "CSCL has the vision that being in a group can not only empower individual learning and performance, but can also enable emergent meaning-making processes at the group unit of analysis". CSCL therefore aims to show the group interaction itself has a knowledge-constructing effect, going beyond cooperative learning's efficiency comparisons.
requirements: Analysis of detailed interaction processes is needed to show what kind of learning takes place in the group
constraints: Pivotal moments of shared meaning making remain rare, poorly understood and unpredictable; they can be identified in retrospect but not reliably predicted
target_learners: collaborative learner groups in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: joint meaning making and construction of new knowledge
examples: The editors contrast this vision with cooperative learning research that only compared learning efficiency across collaborative situations

title: TaraCarp tangible tabletop environment for carpenter vocational training
description: TaraCarp is a tangible user interface in the Cuendet, Dehler-Zufferey, Ortoleva and Dillenbourg study of classroom orchestration in vocational training for carpenters. "This top-down camera-projector tabletop system combines real and virtual artifacts." Apprentices cut a virtual object, print and improve plans, then pair up and cut real blocks according to each other's plans; the tabletops also serve as scripting and teacher orchestration tools.
requirements: Design based on detailed studies of how carpenters do their work, to minimize tacit-knowledge and school-to-work transfer problems
constraints: Further studies are needed to clarify how exactly students benefit from the collaboration
target_learners: carpenter apprentices in vocational training
target_learning_goals: practical and tacit knowledge of carpentry plan marking and cutting
examples: Each student cuts an object virtually, prints the plan, exchanges plans with a partner, marks out a real block and cuts it according to the other learner's plan

article_title: Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children’s collaborative learning groups
citation: E. M. Mercier, S. E. Higgins, Laura da Costa. (2014). Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children's collaborative learning groups. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9201-z
title: Two-type taxonomy of emergent leadership: intellectual and organizational leadership moves
description: The article adapts the Li et al. (2007) coding scheme to distinguish two types of emergent leadership in collaborative groups. Intellectual leadership comprises Topic Control and Idea Management and Development, moves that address "the intellectual aspects of the activity, such as idea management and development." Organizational leadership comprises Planning and Organizing, Turn Management and Acknowledgment, moves that support "the group's interaction process, helping monitor and influence turn taking and participation." Leadership is defined as emerging only when leadership bids are accepted by the group; ignored bids are failed bids, and the bid-maker cannot be defined as a leader.
requirements: Leadership moves must be accepted by other group members to count as leadership; a bid ignored by the group is a failed bid and does not make the bidder a leader.
constraints: The taxonomy was developed and applied with children in year six collaborative mystery tasks in England; the article notes the role of group spokesperson appears different from the leadership described and was beyond its scope.
target_learners: primary school students (year six, mean age about 10.6 years)
target_learning_goals: participating effectively in collaborative learning groups
managing group participation and intellectual progress during collaborative tasks
examples: In the opening vignette, Amy organized the group and managed turn-taking while Georgia pushed the ideas forward intellectually, illustrating the two leadership types in one group.
key_sources: E. M. Mercier, S. E. Higgins, Laura da Costa. (2014). Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children's collaborative learning groups. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9201-z

article_title: Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children’s collaborative learning groups
citation: E. M. Mercier, S. E. Higgins, Laura da Costa. (2014). Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children's collaborative learning groups. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9201-z
title: Attend to how students engage in collaborative tasks so all students participate in both the intellectual and organizational demands
description: Because emergent leadership in collaborative groups is systematically distributed, with intellectual and organizational roles often taken by different students, the article argues that "attention should be paid to how students are engaging in collaborative learning tasks to ensure all students participate in the intellectual as well as organizational demands of the task." Teachers monitoring group work should look beyond whether the task is organized smoothly and check that students who organize are also engaging in the intellectual work, and vice versa.
requirements: Teachers or designers must be able to observe or capture students' interactions during collaborative tasks to notice which students are making intellectual versus organizational moves.
constraints: Findings come from year six pupils working on mystery framework tasks in history and mathematics in English primary schools; the article notes outcomes were similar across groups in study one so leadership-outcome relations were not explored there.
target_learners: primary school students working in small collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: equitable participation in collaborative learning
engagement in both idea development and group organization
examples: In study one, Amy in the opening vignette organized participation and turn-taking but did less of the intellectual work and appeared somewhat confused by the final solution.
key_sources: E. M. Mercier, S. E. Higgins, Laura da Costa. (2014). Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children's collaborative learning groups. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9201-z

article_title: Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children’s collaborative learning groups
citation: E. M. Mercier, S. E. Higgins, Laura da Costa. (2014). Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children's collaborative learning groups. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9201-z
title: Specify behaviors carefully if a leader role is assigned to collaborative groups
description: The article's abstract and findings indicate that because leadership naturally splits into intellectual and organizational components taken by different students, "care should be taken to specify behaviors if the roleof leader is assigned to collaborative groups." Assigning a single undifferentiated leader role risks loading one student with behaviors that naturally distribute across members, so any assigned role should spell out which leadership behaviors it covers.
requirements: If a leader role is assigned, the specific behaviors expected of that role must be specified rather than leaving a single generic leader role.
constraints: The recommendation derives from observed emergent patterns in year-six groups on mystery tasks; the article did not experimentally test assigned leader roles.
target_learners: primary school students in collaborative learning groups
target_learning_goals: effective role assignment in collaborative group work
examples: The article contrasts instructor-managed participation via assigned roles or scripts with groups managing their own participation, motivating the examination of emergent leadership.

article_title: The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies
citation: Diana Laurillard. (2009). The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (ijCSCL), 4, pp.5-20. https://hal.science/hal-00592750
title: Start technology-enhanced learning design from the requirements of education — learners' and teachers' needs — rather than from the technology
description: The article argues that exploiting collaborative technologies for learning requires beginning with educational requirements rather than with the affordances of the technology. As the abstract puts it, "To get the best from them for education we need to start with the requirements of education, in terms of both learners and teachers needs." The principle directs designers to derive technology use from what learners and teachers need, instead of adapting teaching to whatever a new tool happens to offer.
requirements: Designers must identify learners' and teachers' needs before selecting or adapting a technology for learning.
constraints: The article notes that technologies themselves are rarely designed with teaching and learning in mind, so educational requirements must be imposed on them rather than assumed of them.
target_learners: learners using collaborative technologies
target_learning_goals: genuinely enhanced learning experiences through technology-supported collaboration
examples: The paper's own approach: building what is known about what it takes to learn into a pedagogical framework used to challenge digital technologies.
key_sources: Diana Laurillard. (2009). The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (ijCSCL), 4, pp.5-20. https://hal.science/hal-00592750

article_title: The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies
citation: Diana Laurillard. (2009). The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (ijCSCL), 4, pp.5-20. https://hal.science/hal-00592750
title: A pedagogical framework built from what it takes to learn, used to challenge digital technologies
description: The article proposes using knowledge of learning to construct a pedagogical framework against which digital technologies can be evaluated and challenged. The abstract states: "The argument put forward in this paper is to use what we know about what it takes to learn, and build this into a pedagogical framework with which to challenge digital technologies to deliver a genuinely enhanced learning experience." The framework functions as an evaluative lens derived from learning theory; the article's keywords include "conversational framework", "learning theory" and "pedagogy", indicating the framework's grounding in the author's conversational framework tradition.
requirements: The framework must be built from established knowledge about what it takes to learn.
constraints: The framework is intended to challenge technologies to enhance learning, not to describe the technologies themselves; technologies are rarely designed with teaching and learning in mind.
target_learners: learners in technology-supported collaborative settings
target_learning_goals: enhanced learning experience through pedagogically challenged technology design
examples: The paper applies the framework to collaborative technologies that enable learners to share and exchange ideas and digital products.

article_title: Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools
citation: Lu, J., Lajoie, S. P., & Wiseman, J. (2010). Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 5, 283–298. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9092-6
title: The Deteriorating Patient (DP) role play as an interactive, contextualized extension of medical PBL addressing its text-based, decontextualized, cognition-only limitations
description: The DP role play is a medical simulation in which students collaboratively manage a deteriorating patient by playing on-call student, junior resident, and senior resident roles, while the teacher plays the duty nurse and the patient. It retains PBL's hypothesize-and-test structure but, per the article, "instead of reading about a case, the students are role-playing a case." It was created to address Hoffmann and Ritchie's three PBL limitations by providing "an interactive, contextualized environment, where both cognitive and affective considerations are met." Student questioning is guided by the ABCDEF emergency algorithm and by nurse feedback on vital signs and labs.
requirements: Students take differentiated roles (on-call student, junior and senior residents) with the teacher simulating the patient and duty nurse
Scenarios simulate emergencies students will encounter in hospital wards and emergency rooms
constraints: Originally only about half the students in a class could participate in each one-hour role play due to time limitations; this case study added small-group collaboration to include all students
target_learners: third-year medical students in internal medicine
target_learning_goals: emergency decision making under deteriorating conditions
collaborative problem solving
managing anxiety and communication with patients
examples: Students ask the nurse about vital signs, breathing, and circulation; when a student runs into difficulty the teacher prompts calling the junior resident, then the senior resident, simulating how real emergencies unfold
key_sources: Lu, J., Lajoie, S. P., & Wiseman, J. (2010). Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 5, 283–298. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9092-6

article_title: Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools
citation: Lu, J., Lajoie, S. P., & Wiseman, J. (2010). Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 5, 283–298. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9092-6
title: Interactive-whiteboard CSCL toolset with shared visualization menus and collaborative argumentation annotations
description: A wireless interactive whiteboard (eBeam) with Bluetooth connects a server and three subgroup laptops on a local network, capturing traditional-whiteboard notes in real time into a meeting application visible on all laptops. Shared visualization tools provide "content specific menus" for patient history, vital signs, prescriptions, and decisions, structured like a hospital chart with vital signs placed centrally to highlight deterioration. Collaborative argumentation tools let observing students annotate, comment on, and suggest alternatives to the role-playing students' decisions, e.g. clinical suggestions like "listen to the lungs" or biomedical interpretations like "relevance of prednisone."
requirements: Networked laptops linked to the interactive whiteboard for each subgroup
Teacher documentation captured electronically in real time
target_learners: third-year medical students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: constructing shared problem spaces
connecting biomedical and clinical knowledge
collaborative decision making
examples: Vital signs are put in the middle of the display to highlight the deteriorating situation, with decisions and prescriptions marked parallel to changing vital signs

article_title: Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools
citation: Lu, J., Lajoie, S. P., & Wiseman, J. (2010). Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 5, 283–298. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9092-6
title: Design CSCL visualization and argumentation tools so externalized group work frees the teacher from task structuring to scaffold by increasing challenge
description: Because the interactive whiteboard records and shares all subgroups' contributions, the teacher gains a broadened basis for informed classroom scaffolding and spends less time providing cognitive assistance and structuring the task. The article concludes that such tools "mediate the teachers scaffolding by freeing up their time to extend student abilities with greater challenges based on the shared problem-solving space of the group rather than scaffold the rules of the activity." Appropriate scaffolding still depends on the teacher's domain knowledge and pedagogy experience.
requirements: Technology that provides a visual record of what students understood and shared across subgroups
A teacher with domain knowledge and pedagogy experience to select among expanded scaffolding choices
constraints: The finding is from a case study of one expert teacher (30 years of clinical and teaching experience) blinded to the research questions, in a medical training context
target_learners: small-group collaborative learners in medical PBL
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving
adaptive problem-solving behavior
examples: In the IW condition the teacher created scaffolding strategies based on what was recorded and shared by all subgroups, and the nurse talked less than in the TW group

article_title: Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge-construction, and knowledge-creation discourses
citation: Jan van Aalst. (2009). Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge-construction, and knowledge-creation discourses. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9069-5
title: Three modes of discourse: knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge creation
description: The article articulates three modes of asynchronous computer-mediated discourse corresponding to three theoretical perspectives: "Knowledge sharing refers to a transmission theory of communication (see Pea 1994), knowledge construction to cognitive psychology (constructivism), and knowledge creation to interactive learning mediated by shared objects (Paavola et al. 2004)." Knowledge creation, in Bereiter and Scardamalia's model, treats a class as a community whose ideas are intellectual artifacts residing in the community's discourse, requiring design-mode work on explanations and belief-mode discourse for goals, mentoring, and evaluation. The framework is used to map four group discourses and to explain between-group differences in collective knowledge advancement.
requirements: Discourse must be examined in balance across modes, since a community may mix modes and individual epistemic beliefs differ
constraints: The article notes evidence of meta-discourse may not be strong in an inquiry of only 8 weeks
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: collaborative inquiry and collective knowledge advancement
examples: The four group discourses were mapped onto the modes: Group A showed threshold knowledge creation, one group knowledge sharing, and two hybrids of all three modes.
key_sources: Jan van Aalst. (2009). Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge-construction, and knowledge-creation discourses. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9069-5

article_title: Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge-construction, and knowledge-creation discourses
citation: Jan van Aalst. (2009). Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge-construction, and knowledge-creation discourses. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9069-5
title: Discourse coding scheme with seven main codes and 33 subcodes
description: A coding scheme developed to analyze asynchronous group discourse in Knowledge Forum and to identify mechanisms explaining between-group differences in summary-note performance. As printed, "It includes seven main codes: Community, Ideas, Questions, Information, Links, Agency, and Meta-Discourse." Each of 33 subcodes was rated low, medium, or high for its relevance to knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge creation. Notes were coded in Atlas-ti QDA software (399 notes, approximately 60,000 words), with inter-rater reliability of .82 (Cohen kappa) on the mode-relevance ratings.
requirements: Coding requires iterative refinement of code definitions on sample data and a consistency check after an absence, as the researcher did with 12% of quotes needing recoding
constraints: Employing a second coder was not possible for the main coding, so consistency was checked by the researcher returning to the data after about 3 months
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: characterizing collaborative online discourse for knowledge creation
examples: The subcode fact (under Ideas) was rated high for knowledge sharing and low for both other modes; Major review was rated low, medium, and high across the three modes respectively.

article_title: The affordance of anchored discussion for the collaborative processing of academic texts
citation: van der Pol, J., Admiraal, W., & Simons, P.R.J. (2006). The affordance of anchored discussion for the collaborative processing of academic texts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 1(3), 339–357. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-006-9657-6
title: Anchored discussion: linked artifact-centered discourse creating a stronger collaborative context
description: Anchored discussion is a design for online discussion in which the article under discussion is displayed adjacent to the threaded discussion and messages can be anchored to specific passages of the text. Unlike shared annotation, which starts from personal notes made visible to peers, anchored discussion "starts from the notion of collaborative discussion that is contextualized or 'anchored' within a specific content," displaying "both artifact and discussion in a linked, yet independent manner." The article argues this document-centeredness defines a stronger collaborative context that focuses participants' collaborative intentions and gives messages a stronger frame of reference, reducing the effort needed for grounding and clarification.
requirements: The discussion environment must physically present the text online adjacent to the threaded discussion and allow anchoring messages to specific passages of the text.
constraints: The article notes technical issues with the studied system (such as the placement of certain buttons) that should be resolved in further development.

The observed advantages concern the early stages of collaborative literature processing by undergraduates; for more personal and critical discussion among participants with sufficient understanding, the authors suggest traditional forum discussion might be better suited.
target_learners: Undergraduate students processing academic literature in higher education
target_learning_goals: Collaborative comprehension and processing of academic texts
examples: In the study, 18 student groups in a first-year pedagogy course discussed two articles over two-week rounds, half in the anchored system and half in a Blackboard forum, producing 1,133 task-related messages.
key_sources: van der Pol, J., Admiraal, W., & Simons, P.R.J. (2006). The affordance of anchored discussion for the collaborative processing of academic texts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 1(3), 339–357. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-006-9657-6

article_title: Reigniting CSCL flash themes
citation: Gerry Stahl, Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse. (2013). Reigniting CSCL flash themes. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:369–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9185-0
title: Joint attention as foundational to collaborative interaction, investigable through eye-tracking support of gaze coordination
description: The editors present joint attention as foundational to collaborative interaction and human sociality: from infancy on, people learn to use different forms and media of joint attention to make intersubjective sense, and communication requires a coordinated orientation to a shared object understood as shared. For two people to solve a problem together, they must take the problem as the same problem and see the object as the same object. The issue's eye-tracking study investigates this by letting students see where their partners' eyes are gazing at a like screen, so that staring in a similar direction can be elaborated into a sense of making shared meaning.
requirements: Objective data on gaze must be tied to intersubjective meaning making if gaze is to be used as an indicator of joint attention

target_learning_goals: joint attention
intersubjectivity
shared understanding
co-construction of meaning

article_title: Reigniting CSCL flash themes
citation: Gerry Stahl, Nancy Law & Friedrich Hesse. (2013). Reigniting CSCL flash themes. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 8:369–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-013-9185-0
title: CSCL research must remain centrally concerned with meaning making in joint activity, however technological the theme or objective the methodology
description: The editors conclude that no matter how technological the theme and no matter how objective the methodology, issues of human group meaning making must still be centrally addressed in CSCL. They invoke Koschmann's formulation that the field must be "centrally concerned with meaning and the practices of meaning making in the context of joint activity, and the ways in which these practices are mediated through designed artifacts." This principle orients evaluation of all four flash themes, from gaze indicators to learning-analytics visualizations.
requirements: Research designs must connect objective interaction data to intersubjective meaning making
target_learners: CSCL researchers and educational designers
target_learning_goals: collaborative meaning making
intersubjectivity
examples: The editors apply this principle critically to each study: gaze data must be tied to meaning making, argument quality is an attribute of group interaction, and abstract analytics representations raise the question of how participants make sense of them.

article_title: Wiki-supported collaborative learning in primary education: How a dialogic space is created for thinking together
citation: Pifarré, M. & Kleine Staarman, J. (2011). Wiki-supported collaborative learning in primary education: How a dialogic space is created for thinking together. International Journal of Computer Supported Collaborative Learning, 6(2), 187-205. https://www.springer.com/journal/11412
title: Dialogic space and intersubjectivity as a framework for analysing wiki-supported collaborative learning
description: The article adopts a dialogic perspective, drawing on Wegerif's notion of a "dialogic space" — the social realm within which people think and act collectively — and on intersubjectivity, the process of developing communality in joint activity through reciprocal perspective setting and taking. It applies Mercer's three-part typology of talk (Disputational, Cumulative, Exploratory) as a heuristic framework to characterise wiki interaction, arguing this dialogic approach is needed to capture the collaborative dimension of computer-supported collaborative learning and to help educators diagnose and scaffold missing aspects of students' collaboration.
requirements: Participants must develop an intersubjective orientation towards each other's perspectives for collaborative knowledge co-construction
constraints: The typology is used as a heuristic frame of reference, not a validated coding scheme in this study
target_learners: primary education students (9-10 years old)
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
reasoning and argumentation in science writing
examples: The study analysed two groups of six students' negotiation-space episodes using the talk typology

article_title: Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application
citation: Overdijk, M. & van Diggelen, W. (2008). Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9038-4
title: Tool appropriation as mutual shaping between learners and technology
description: The paper defines tool appropriation as a process in which learners make sense of a tool's properties and find 'a way of doing' to carry out their task, constructing essential characteristics of the tool while working with it. Mutual shaping is central: "the actions of the learner are shaped through interaction with the tool, while at the same time the effects of the tool are shaped through the learner's actions." Appropriation becomes manifest during critical events, such as when learners lack directions for use or a use has an unexpected effect.
requirements: Groups must coordinate their exploratory effort and arrive at shared conventions of use
constraints: The concept is developed for small-group appropriation of collaborative technology in classroom settings over relatively short periods
target_learners: secondary school students collaborating with CSCL tools
target_learning_goals: collaborative argumentation and discussion
examples: The study examined how seven groups of three students appropriated a graphical shared workspace during a two-lesson role-play discussion about the public image of Spanish Salou

article_title: Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application
citation: Overdijk, M. & van Diggelen, W. (2008). Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-008-9038-4
title: Three basic orientations towards a shared workspace shape organizing principles
description: The paper distinguishes three orientations students may take towards a shared workspace: "(1) an orientation towards establishing and maintaining a direct and ongoing interaction between the members of the group; (2) an orientation towards the construction of a personal line of reasoning without direct interaction with the other members of the group; and (3) an orientation towards submitting contributions without expressing a relation between these contributions." These orientations lead to different principles for organization of contributions in the drawing space.
requirements: Analysis of appropriation requires distinguishing a personal dimension of actions in the tool from a collective dimension of interaction via the tool
constraints: The orientations were identified in one classroom case study of argumentative discussion
target_learners: secondary school students in small-group CSCL activities
target_learning_goals: organizing shared contributions during argumentative discussion
examples: Four focal groups were selected because each arrived at different organizing principles based on one of the three orientations

title: Designers and teachers should treat tool use as emergent from group negotiation rather than fixed by tool properties
description: The paper argues against technological determinism in CSCL: the use and effect of a tool are not predictable from the tool's properties alone but depend on how it is appropriated. Because "a technological artefact has a degree of 'interpretative flexibility'," designers and researchers should expect groups to negotiate conventions of use and should avoid imposing a single intended way of using a tool.
requirements: Instructions about the tool should be limited so researchers or teachers do not impose their intentions of how the tool should be used
constraints: Derived from a case study of one classroom using one graphical shared workspace configuration

target_learning_goals: collaborative argumentation supported by shared workspaces
examples: In the study, the tool was introduced via a slide show of basic properties followed by an exploratory session, with deliberately limited instructions

title: Graphical shared workspace for argumentative discussion
description: A CSCL tool consisting of a shared drawing area and a graphical notation system supporting specific kinds of communicative acts. Students choose contribution cards (labeled 'argument pro', 'argument contra', and 'source'), add textual messages, use comment windows for elaboration, and connect cards with links. The graphical modality is synchronous while the textual modality is quasi-synchronous, meaning "a participant can not be interrupted when he formulates a textual contribution."

constraints: Contributions can be deleted only by the person who contributed them; the drawing area requires scrolling navigation bars when enlarged beyond the default frame

citation: Gerry Stahl, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law & Sten Ludvigsen. (2014). Analyzing the multidimensional construction of knowledge in diverse contexts. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2014) 9:1–6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9189-4

description: The editorial presents Timmis's use of Activity Theory as a framework for "understanding the complex interrelations between discourse, actions, and community, and as a result how new technological innovations and knowledge-creation practices can be appropriated and sustained." It references micro, meso, and macro units of analysis—individuals' actions, small-group discourse, and community practices—and expands the theory toward dialogicality and communicative action, treating small-group interaction as the intermediate level bridging micro and macro.

title: Framing online discussion as a multi-user knowledge-building epistemic game for young students
description: Bielaczyc and Ow introduce about-10-year-old Singapore students to collaborative knowledge building by framing online discussion as a multi-user knowledge-building ("epistemic") game in which players progressively improve tentative ideas proposed in response to a topic. In Knowledge Forum, postings are categorized by knowledge-building roles ("my theory," "I need to know," etc.), other students respond to or build on notes, and progress takes place through interaction among the notes, which serve as interactional resources for the group process.

refining tentative theories of scientific phenomena

citation: Chan, C. K. K. (2011). Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9121-0
title: Three interacting themes for examining CSCL classroom innovation: context and systemic change, capacity and community building, and innovation as inquiry
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework of three interacting themes for examining how CSCL research creates innovation in classrooms: "context and systemic change, capacity and community building, and innovation as a process of inquiry." These themes organize the analysis of knowledge-building innovation in Hong Kong across macro, meso, and micro levels of the educational ecological system. The framework treats innovation as emergent changes at nested system levels rather than a single-site implementation.

constraints: The framework was developed from the Hong Kong knowledge-building case and its specific socio-cultural context

Twenty-first-century skills

title: Knowledge-building pedagogy model with initial acculturation to collaborative culture before introducing Knowledge Forum
description: A design pattern emergent from failed starts in the Hong Kong teacher network: students are first acculturated to a collaborative culture before the Knowledge Forum tool is introduced. This reverses the typical Canadian approach where "Knowledge Forum is usually included at the start of knowledge building." The pattern addresses the tendency of new teachers and students to focus on the tool rather than collaborative knowledge construction.

It uses a secondment scheme (50% release time) and later a university-school partnership scheme with teacher associates. The network connects researchers and teachers to implement and scale up knowledge building across 18-29 schools per year, spanning curriculum areas from science to liberal studies.

article_title: Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building
citation: Eddy Y.C. Lee, Carol K.K. Chan, & Jan van Aalst. (2006). Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-006-6844-4
title: Knowledge-building portfolios as assessment that characterizes and scaffolds collective knowledge advances
description: Knowledge-building portfolios are student-produced records in which learners select exemplary clusters of computer notes and write reflections explaining how the notes evidence knowledge building, guided by principles. Unlike conventional portfolios of individual best work, the article "pioneered the notion of knowledge-building portfolios for which students are asked to identify collective knowledge advances." A portfolio note is a "rise-above" note hyperlinked to referenced notes, and "A portfolio is a group accomplishment with multiple contributions from students—it shows that knowledge is distributed and it emerges through collective inquiry." The portfolio is designed to both measure and foster inquiry, mediating individual and group understanding through principles and reflections.
requirements: Students work in a Knowledge Forum database whose notes they can hyperlink, reference, and organize into clusters
A set of knowledge-building principles is provided as criteria for note selection and explanation
constraints: Developed and examined in a design research program with graduate, Grade 12, and grade-nine Geography classes in Hong Kong using Knowledge Forum
target_learners: secondary school students (grade-nine Geography students in this study)
target_learning_goals: collaborative inquiry and knowledge building
domain conceptual understanding
self- and community-assessment of knowledge advances
examples: Students prepared a portfolio of four clusters of notes with explanations, posted in the Assessment View, codeable on a 6-point rating scheme with inter-rater reliability .88

description: The article's key design principle is that "The key design principle involved turning over epistemic agency to students"; students themselves identify knowledge-building episodes in the computer discourse, guided by knowledge-building principles used as criteria. This makes assessment dual-purpose: it both measures and fosters inquiry, since "Assessment should be designed as a tool that both measures and fosters deeper inquiry and collaboration." The portfolio-plus-principles condition, which most embodied this agency, produced deeper inquiry and understanding than comparison classes.

Assessment tasks must be embedded in the instructional process, with principles provided as selection and writing scaffolds
constraints: Effectiveness was examined against Knowledge Forum-only and portfolio-only conditions in quasi-experimental classroom settings; conditio nal complexity is acknowledged by the authors

conceptual understanding

description: The article grounds its collaboration assessment in a joint theoretical frame: dialogism together with "a cohesion-based model of discourse". It treats collaboration as the intertwining of ideas or points of view among participants, "a central element of dialogue performed in CSCL environments". This frame motivates both computational models the article proposes and validates for collaboration assessment.

article_title: A decade of CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2015). A decade of CSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9222-2
title: Group-level post-cognitive paradigm of CSCL: cognition and knowledge building occur at dialogical, small-group and community levels beyond the individual mind
description: The editorial describes the founding theoretical shift of CSCL: transcending cognitive science by extending the unit of cognition beyond individual mental representations to structures of interaction. The author writes that it was time to extend "the unit of cognition beyond the boundaries of the individual mind" and that post-cognitive theories "began to postulate structures and practices at the group level." This paradigm, drawing on distributed cognition, activity theory and conversation analysis, dominates CSCL theory and frames collaborative learning as meaning negotiation and dialogical interaction rather than individual knowledge transfer.
requirements: Research and technology must treat small-group interaction, not individual cognition, as the primary unit of analysis
constraints: The article notes the paradigm has been less influential in technology design and analysis methodology than in theory
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students engaged in collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge building
Group cognition
Dialogical meaning negotiation
examples: The editorial cites the Virtual Math Teams Project as a concrete model of DBR exploring CSCL technology, pedagogy, curriculum, methodology and theory within an integrated post-cognitive approach

article_title: CSCL towards the future: The second decade of ijCSCL
citation: Sten Ludvigsen. (2016). CSCL towards the future: The second decade of ijCSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9230-x
title: Three interdependent layers of units of analysis in CSCL: individual, small group, and community
description: The editorial proposes a conceptual framing of CSCL research units of analysis as three interdependent layers. As printed: "Conceptually, one could frame the different units of analysis in CSCL as three interdependent layers— individual, small group and community — all of which are needed to understand and explain collaborative learning with computational tools." The framing holds that different theoretical orientations (cognitive, socio-cognitive, socio-cultural) direct analytic attention to different layers, and that a full understanding requires all three, including how individual contributions constitute group collaborative efforts.
requirements: Research designs must allow variation in units of analysis and levels of description across the three layers
constraints: The editorial presents this as a conceptual framing, not an empirically tested model
target_learners: collaborative learners in schools, higher education, and leisure time
target_learning_goals: understanding and explaining collaborative learning with computational tools
examples: The editorial notes it may be easier to design scaffolds for an individual's social and cognitive functions than for the social and content-based scaffolds of small groups and larger social units

article_title: CSCL towards the future: The second decade of ijCSCL
citation: Sten Ludvigsen. (2016). CSCL towards the future: The second decade of ijCSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9230-x
title: Use design-based research in CSCL to test new technological features and representations with clear scope and rigor
description: The editorial endorses design-based research as a methodological approach tightly related to CSCL. As printed: "In the CSCL field, DBR is an approach that makes it possible to test new technological features and representations (e.g., visualizations) with a clear scope and rigor (Jeong et al. 2014)." The editorial notes DBR principles have been altered toward use of both experimental and ethnographic methods, beyond the classical pre-posttest design with control groups in naturalistic settings.

constraints: The editorial notes the classical DBR method was based on pre-posttest design with control groups in naturalistic settings, and principles have since been altered
target_learners: collaborative learners across CSCL research settings
target_learning_goals: testing and improving technology-supported collaborative learning designs

citation: Anniken Furberg. (2016). Teacher support in computer-supported lab work: bridging the gap between lab experiments and students' conceptual understanding. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9229-3
title: SCY-Lab forensic mission digital learning environment with designated support tools
description: SCY-Lab is a digital learning environment from the SCY project containing tools supporting conceptual understanding and inquiry skills. Its forensic mission is "a highly structured environment featuring designated digital support tools" where most tools are text editors with "directive questions or sentence openers". In this study three tools scaffolded annotation of DNA profiles, writing conclusions, and producing an official forensic report, alongside information resources such as a forensics handbook and DNA animations.
requirements: Students work in supported group-based activities with designated tools per task
A teacher available for help-seeking during tool use
constraints: Was used here with one upper secondary class in a genetics/forensics project; the study examines it in a naturalistic intervention setting

Analysing, concluding and reporting lab experiment findings

title: Sociocultural perspective on support and help-seeking in CSCL settings
description: The study frames helping and support from a sociocultural point of view, grounding it in Vygotsky's zone of proximal development: "the difference between what a learner can do with and without help from more experienced individuals," making help-seeking essential to developing skills and conceptual understanding. Digital learning environments embed representations displaying experts' knowledge, and language is the primary tool for mediating thinking, with discourse as a "social mode of thinking". Learning is seen as dialogical meaning-making among participants in specific settings, including help-seeking sessions where students also account for achievements and convey conceptual and work-process challenges.

Interacting participants in specific settings for dialogical sense-making
constraints: Every scientific field encompasses valid terms and ways of talking; students cannot develop just any interpretation
In ordinary classrooms, learning also involves responding to institutional practices, values and expectations expressed by the teacher

target_learning_goals: Development of conceptual understanding of scientific phenomena and inquiry practices
examples: Excerpts analysed as sequential exchanges where meaning is created between utterances rather than in single turns

article_title: The symmetry of partner modelling
citation: Dillenbourg, P., Lemaignan, S., Sangin, M., Nova, N., & Molinari, G. (2016). The symmetry of partner modelling. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9235-5
title: Mutual modelling in collaboration: each partner needs some model of what the other partners know, want and intend
description: The article frames collaborative tasks as requiring "some level of mutual modelling", i.e. a representation each partner holds of what the others know, want and intend at a given time. The deliberate term "some model" stresses that such representations are "not necessarily detailed or complete". The framework is used to pose the article's research question: whether partner-model quality depends on the modeler's representational ability, the modelée's clarity, or the quality of their interactions. It links partner modelling to the psycholinguistic machinery of common ground in collaborative learning.

constraints: The model is explicitly partial: "not necessarily detailed or complete"
target_learners: collaborating peers in dyads or small teams
target_learning_goals: building shared understanding during collaborative problem solving and collaborative learning
examples: The five experiments varied in terms of tasks (how important it is to build an accurate model) and settings (how difficult it is to build an accurate model).

article_title: CSCL: connecting the social, emotional and cognitive dimensions
citation: Ludvigsen, S. (2016). CSCL: connecting the social, emotional and cognitive dimensions. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 11, 115–121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9236-4
title: Three-dimension framework relating social, emotional and cognitive functions in collaborative argumentation
description: The editorial highlights Polo et al.'s model for analyzing how the social, emotional and cognitive dimensions of collaboration interrelate in argumentation, a combination it says is seldom considered in a single empirical analysis. The analysis explores argumentation from a linguistic perspective, with the tonality of discourse objects as a key concept influencing how participants put forward an argumentative claim. The editorial says other CSCL researchers could use this model "as a framework for analyzing how social, emotional, and cognitive functions interrelate", while noting the dimensions are not equally important in an interactional sequence.
requirements: Analyses must consider all three dimensions together rather than in isolation, since the article notes it is seldom that all three are considered in a single empirical analysis.
constraints: The editorial notes the three dimensions are not equally important in an interactional sequence.

knowledge construction
