citation: Yang, Y., van Aalst, J., Chan, C.K.K., & Tian, W. (2016). Reflective assessment in knowledge building by students with low academic achievement. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9239-1
title: Reflective assessment as collaborative, embedded metacognitive assessment for knowledge building
description: Reflective assessment is a framework in which students reflect on criteria or learning goals, generate their own feedback, and improve ongoing learning. The article states it "does not merely evaluate what students have done and point to the next predetermined step, but involves student directing their efforts to improve their ongoing learning." It is collaborative: "not everyone in the community needs to be highly metacognitive for the process to be effective." Students scaffold one another's metacognitive development through social modeling. The study deployed it with KCA to support knowledge building in low-achieving students.

Requires prompt sheets or structured supports to help students make sense of assessment data

knowledge building
collective responsibility for community knowledge

description: The Knowledge Connections Analyzer (KCA) is a Web-based assessment tool that "queries the Knowledge Forum database to collect information on four intuitive questions related to knowledge building." It "displays quantitative data in pie charts and bar graphs and qualitative information in text-based tables." The tool uses social-media analogies such as friends and followers to analyze community collaboration. The study used the first two questions, focusing on community collaboration and synthesis/rise-above, to support reflective assessment among low-achieving students.

article_title: Toward a classification of discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions
citation: Fu, E. L. F., van Aalst, J., & Chan, C. K. K. (2016). Toward a classification of discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 11, 441-478. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9245-3
title: Nine discourse patterns classified into three modes of online discourse: knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge building
description: The study developed a classification of nine discourse patterns that occur in text-based asynchronous discussion forums, organized under van Aalst's (2009) three-mode framework. Knowledge sharing comprises five patterns (fact-oriented, cumulative, repetitive, simple argumentation, disputational); knowledge construction comprises two (explanatory and problem-centered inquiry, complex argumentation); knowledge building comprises two (progressive inquiry, sustained discourse for community advance). The authors state the goal was to Bdevelop a classification for a range of discourse patterns that occur in text-based asynchronous discussionforums, and that can aid in the distinction of three modes of discourse: knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge building.
requirements: Qualitative coding and narrative analysis of inquiry threads in Knowledge Forum databases
constraints: Patterns were identified from three discussion views in one professional development project in Hong Kong; generalizability to other contexts is not established in the text provided
target_learners: Grade 5 and Grade 10 students in Knowledge Building Teacher Network classrooms
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge building in collaborative online discourse

title: Co-investigation of students' online discourse with teachers deepens principle-based understanding of knowledge building and generates feedback for teaching improvement
description: In the Knowledge Building Teacher Network, teachers and researchers met weekly to design and improve teaching practices, and teachers were guided to co-investigate their students' online discourse through the three modes of discourse framework and knowledge-building principles. The authors report that BCo-investigation into the online discourse not only generated feedback for the teachers to improve their teaching practices, but also became a method for them to deepen their principle-based understanding of knowledge building. This addresses the problem of Blethal mutationBwhere learning principles are lost when designs are implemented.

A framework of discourse modes and knowledge-building principles to structure the analysis

description: The GRT is a text-mining tool developed by Erkens, Bodemer, and Hoppe to support both teachers and students in the classroom. The editors write that "This tool makes it possible to transform students' written text into variables, and to use the variables for forming groups and visualizing information from a cognitive perspective." It thus operationalizes heterogeneous-group formation combined with cognitive group-awareness support.

description: Fu, van Aalst, and Chan classify discourse in asynchronous online discussions using a coding scheme with dimensions such as agency, community, idea, information, linking, meta-discourse, and questions. The editors state "The authors identify seven discourse patterns within three modes of discourse. These discourse patterns can be divided into three clusters": knowledge sharing (disputational talk), knowledge construction (explanatory and problem-centered inquiry, complex argumentation), and knowledge building (progressive inquiry, sustained discourse and community advancement). The taxonomy shows not all patterns are equally productive for learning.

constraints: Not all discourse patterns are equally productive for learning

title: Functional system incorporating tools as the unit of analysis for CSCL microanalysis
description: Arnseth and Krange argue, building on Vygotsky and Wertsch, that "the unit of analysis needs to be a functional system incorporating tools." This stance opens up understanding of the multiplicity of activities, in which collaboration between students and computational tools can take multiple paths, and analysts must understand how participants orient themselves through a series of activities and why they choose specific paths. The editors present it as grounding ethnographic description combined with detailed turn-by-turn interaction analysis of upper-secondary students' inquiry into energy phenomena.

description: Across the CSCL studies in this issue, the editors emphasize that "The teacher's role is important in CSCL studies as an interactional partner scaffolding students in their efforts to become more productive in their academic work." article_title: Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings
citation: Elin Johansson, Oskar Lindwall, Hans Rystedt. (2017). Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9252-z
title: The three-phase debriefing model (description, analysis, application) structuring the post-simulation discussions
description: The investigated debriefings were organized around "a specific model for debriefing" with "three main phases: description, analysis, and application". Description begins with a 'blow out' in which each participant names one prominent feeling, followed by factual description of the scenario; the analysis phase, the most extensive part, is devoted to joint discussion and analysis of students' conduct; application involves students summarizing what they learned. Video clips of key events were introduced within the analysis phase.
requirements: A facilitator guides the phases; the analysis phase hosts the displayed key-event video clips
Participating students and observing students who watched via live video
constraints: Discussions focused primarily on what worked well and what could be improved rather than on what had not gone well

target_learning_goals: interprofessional teamwork, communication and non-technical skills such as SBAR, speak up and closed loop communication

description: The editorial foregrounds Stahl's methodological focus on "group practices" in CSCL, positioned between individual mental representations and cultural practices. Drawing on design-based research in collaborative mathematics, it argues "CSCL can be re-conceptualized as the design of technology to foster the adoption of group practices by student teams." The editorial applies this lens to all four full papers, identifying each study's targeted group practices.

title: The venue construct: a virtual collaboration space emerging from negotiated agreement on problems and objectives
description: From Alterman and Harsch's study of wiki- and blog-based collaborative writing, the editorial presents the "conceptual construct of a venue" as "a virtual space for collaboration that emerges as the participants succeed in negotiating an agreement on the problem(s) and objective(s) for joint problem solving." The nature of a venue depends on task design (e.g., role assignment) and the online platform; different venues afford different collaboration practices.
requirements: Participants must succeed in negotiating agreement on problems and objectives for joint problem solving for a venue to emerge
constraints: The venue's nature depends on task design and platform features; issues of ownership, identity and participation differ between wikis and blogs
target_learners: undergraduate students in small groups of five to seven
target_learning_goals: joint problem solving and collaborative writing in asynchronous online settings
examples: 19 teams in an undergraduate Internet and Society course completed four collaborative writing projects alternating between wiki-based and blog-based environments

citation: Nancy Law, Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Carolyn P. Rose. (2017). Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9253-y
title: Divergent Collaborative Learning Mechanisms (DCLM) framework for coding collaboration with divergent goals
description: The editorial describes Tissenbaum, Berland, and Lyons' framework "for recognizing and coding collaboration and divergent learning — Divergent Collaborative Learning Mechanisms (DCLM)", used to analyze museum visitors' interactions with an interactive digital tabletop exhibit. It challenges the assumption that productive collaboration requires shared objectives, showing collaborative learning occurred among visitors "while holding divergent conceptions and pursuing divergent goals."
requirements: A designed tabletop exhibit supporting loosely-coupled interactions so visitors can explore independently while observing and interacting with others
constraints: The framework was applied in a museum setting with naturalistic visitor groups; the editorial notes relatively few tabletop studies had a clear CSCL theoretical stance
target_learners: museum visitors in informal learning settings
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning under divergent goals, e.g., about electric circuits
examples: Interaction analysis was used to analyze joint effort among visitors interacting with a tabletop exhibit supporting loosely-coupled exploration

article_title: Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design
citation: Nancy Law, Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Carolyn P. Rose. (2017). Fostering targeted group practices as a Core focus for CSCL task and technology design. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9253-y
title: Design CSCL learning environments and tasks so that targeted group practices actually emerge
description: The editorial derives from all five papers a shared design focus: necessary group practices for productive collaboration "do not happen automatically" and must be fostered by "the design of the learning environment, including the learning technology and the learning task(s), as well as the instructor facilitation." Analysis of social interaction and group practices should "systematically inform the design, testing, and refinement of CSCL environments and practices."
requirements: Task design, technology design and instructor facilitation must jointly support the emergence of the targeted group practices; analysis of interaction should feed design iterations
constraints: The editorial notes coupling levels, technologies and venues differed greatly across contexts, so targeted practices must be matched to the specific context and domain
target_learners: student teams, museum visitors, children, and interprofessional student groups
target_learning_goals: productive collaborative learning and domain-specific collaboration practices
examples: Role assignment on wikis shaped venues; tabletop exhibits were designed for loosely-coupled interactions; instructors facilitated third-person reflection in debriefings

article_title: Frameworks for mass collaboration, adaptable scripts, complex systems theory, and collaborative writing
citation: Ludvigsen, S., Law, N., Rosé, C. P., & Stahl, G. (2017). Frameworks for mass collaboration, adaptable scripts, complex systems theory, and collaborative writing. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 12, 127–131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9257-7
title: A3C framework: attendance, coordination, cooperation, and collaboration as interaction types for designing mass collaboration activities
description: The editorial describes the A3C framework, presented by Jeong, Cress, Moskaliuk, and Kimmerle, which organizes mass collaboration (such as co-editing a Wikipedia page or working in Scratch) into four interaction types: "attendance, coordination, cooperation, and collaboration, which they refer to as the A3C framework". How participants choose to interact depends on "their goals, tasks, artifacts, and more generally, the environment". The framework implies social interaction can range from "rather loose or highly committed and intense".
requirements: Interaction choices must be understood relative to participants' goals, tasks, artifacts, and the environment in which actions are performed
constraints: The four types of interaction should not be viewed as a monotonic progression from simple to advanced, or seen as strongly interdependent
target_learners: participants in online mass collaboration communities and MOOCs
target_learning_goals: learning through mass collaboration and coordinated social interaction
examples: The editorial cites co-editing a Wikipedia page and working in Scratch as design contexts for the framework
key_sources: Ludvigsen, S., Law, N., Rosé, C. P., & Stahl, G. (2017). Frameworks for mass collaboration, adaptable scripts, complex systems theory, and collaborative writing. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 12, 127–131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9257-7

article_title: Frameworks for mass collaboration, adaptable scripts, complex systems theory, and collaborative writing
citation: Ludvigsen, S., Law, N., Rosé, C. P., & Stahl, G. (2017). Frameworks for mass collaboration, adaptable scripts, complex systems theory, and collaborative writing. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 12, 127–131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9257-7
title: Complex adaptive systems theory as a lens for CSCL: self-organization, emergence, interdependencies, and hierarchical nesting of levels
description: The editorial positions complex adaptive systems theory as a lens for explaining complex phenomena in CSCL, listing its key concepts: "self-organization, emergence, interdependencies, and hierarchical nesting of levels". It notes the approach has been rare in CSCL apart from work inspired by Cress and Kimmerle. Self-organization is described as rare in education because "educational activities are most often heavily influenced by teacher instruction and social norms that regulate actions".
requirements: Analysis must be able to bridge gaps between individuals, groups, and the community, as the Vogler et al. study does by taking the group as a starting point
constraints: Self-organization can be rare in education because educational activities are most often heavily influenced by teacher instruction and social norms
target_learners: students in synchronous online learning environments
target_learning_goals: understanding emerging participation and meaning-making in collaborative online learning
examples: The editors state that the use of complex adaptive systems theory in the Vogler et al. study can be suggestive for the CSCL community
key_sources: Ludvigsen, S., Law, N., Rosé, C. P., & Stahl, G. (2017). Frameworks for mass collaboration, adaptable scripts, complex systems theory, and collaborative writing. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 12, 127–131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9257-7

article_title: Divisive or facilitative: The two faces of technology in CSCL
citation: Carolyn P. Rosé, Sten Ludvigsen, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress & Gerry Stahl. (2017). Divisive or facilitative: The two faces of technology in CSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12:215–220. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9265-7
title: Positioning theory as a lens for power relationships and authority during collaboration
description: Positioning theory, attributed to Davies and Harré, treats the rhetorical choices made by speakers as negotiating a place within a conceptual space relative to one another. The editors describe it as a lens for studying power relationships and authority over knowledge in collaboration, with dimensions including emotional closeness, power, and status. Unlike roles, positioning can change over an extended interaction, which makes status differences achievements in interaction.
requirements: An extended interaction to observe, since shifts in positioning unfold from time to time and are consequential for interaction analysis
constraints: Contrasted with the concept of roles, which are more static; positioning is dynamic rather than fixed
target_learners: secondary school students in collaborative pairs
target_learning_goals: negotiating power and status during peer collaboration around shared technology
examples: The editorial reports that two case-study dyads were examined as positioning was negotiated over time, both individually and in comparison to one another
key_sources: Carolyn P. Rosé, Sten Ludvigsen, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress & Gerry Stahl. (2017). Divisive or facilitative: The two faces of technology in CSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12:215–220. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9265-7

article_title: Divisive or facilitative: The two faces of technology in CSCL
citation: Carolyn P. Rosé, Sten Ludvigsen, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress & Gerry Stahl. (2017). Divisive or facilitative: The two faces of technology in CSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12:215–220. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9265-7
title: Design scaffolding with attention to over-scripting risk and plan for fading scripting support over time
description: The editorial highlights integration of multiple scaffolds as carrying a danger of over-scripting or script interference, and notes that fading of scripts offers promise for reducing scripting over time and thus potentially avoiding over-scripting. Fading remains associated with many open and difficult questions, but the principle is that scaffold intensity should be designed to be reduced rather than fixed.
requirements: Knowledge of student-level variables such as prior knowledge and working-memory capacity that moderate scaffolding effectiveness
constraints: Fading is a topic with few landmark studies so far and many open and difficult questions; the Matthew Effect means scaffolding may benefit high-prior-knowledge students more than the low-prior-knowledge students it targets
target_learners: post-secondary mathematics students
undergraduate psychology students
target_learning_goals: mathematical argumentation skills
collaborative argumentation
examples: The editorial points to potential dynamic fading that responds in real time to differences in argumentation patterns based on automated analysis, and to fading connected to different appropriation trajectories for students

article_title: Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies
citation: Ludvigsen, S., Cress, U., Law, N., Stahl, G., & Rosé, C. P. (2017). Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12, 337–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9268-4
title: Co-Census interactive design capturing visitor identity data to spark dialogue
description: Co-Census is software used as part of an interactive museum design; it "captures data about visitors' identities and some aspects of their lives (family and work), based on a few questions." The design idea is "that the personalized data should spark more interest and increase the quality of the dialogues that are performed during the museum visit." It lets participants control visualizations produced by their bodily movements and interact with other participants.
requirements: Participants contribute personal data about identities and aspects of their lives via a few questions for the design to personalize dialogue.
target_learners: Museum visitors in dyads and groups
target_learning_goals: Increasing dialogue quality and interest during interactive-exhibit experiences
examples: Co-Census was used in Roberts and Lyons' experimental-design study in a museum setting.
key_sources: Ludvigsen, S., Cress, U., Law, N., Stahl, G., & Rosé, C. P. (2017). Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12, 337–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9268-4

article_title: Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies
citation: Ludvigsen, S., Cress, U., Law, N., Stahl, G., & Rosé, C. P. (2017). Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12, 337–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9268-4
title: Interaction geography: an analytical approach connecting physical movement and talk in museum settings
description: Interaction geography is an analytical approach introduced by Shapiro, Hall, and Owens that connects "novel forms of analyses" to constitute "the key elements of the analytical approach." It extends interaction analysis by including physical movements: through movement analysis researchers "can explore how the syntax of space creates an 'interaction geography' from which visitors' gestures and activities can be analyzed."
requirements: Data on participants' movements and talk across forms of representation such as photographs, videos, descriptions, and online conversations.
constraints: The study is "the first step in exploring the use of interaction geography"; further studies "in a variety of settings would be necessary to explore the potential contribution."
target_learners: Museum visitors, including groups with diverse professional backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Meaning-making through movement, gestures, and talk across representations
examples: The study was performed in a cultural heritage museum with data collected from 22 groups, some of whose members were music professionals.
key_sources: Ludvigsen, S., Cress, U., Law, N., Stahl, G., & Rosé, C. P. (2017). Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12, 337–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9268-4

article_title: Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies
citation: Ludvigsen, S., Cress, U., Law, N., Stahl, G., & Rosé, C. P. (2017). Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12, 337–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9268-4
title: Eight controversies framing the future direction of the CSCL field
description: Wise and Schwarz's review distills "eight controversies in the field" from written interviews with CSCL experts, written as debates between a provocateur and a conciliator and viewed as "narrative reviews of the field." The eight provocations range from tool frameworks and learner agency versus collaborative scripting, through collaboration ideology and co-alienation of analytical and interpretive approaches, to computational approaches, learning analytics, evolving or becoming irrelevant, and giving up on educational change.
requirements: The controversies rest on a synthesis of review studies and written interviews with CSCL experts, plus the authors' own work in the field.
constraints: The paper is written in an unconventional argumentative-dialogue genre, and its positions are provocations rather than settled conclusions.
target_learners: CSCL researchers and the learning-sciences community
target_learning_goals: Framing unresolved foundational debates about collaborative learning research and design
examples: Provocations include 'The blossoming of CSCL tools necessitates "one framework to rule them all"' and 'Prioritize learner agency over collaborative scripting.'

article_title: Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1
title: Three interdependent planes of analysis — personal, interpersonal, and institutional — as a socio-cultural stance for CSCL
description: The editorial frames CSCL classroom analysis from a socio-cultural stance in which human development and learning rest on "the interdependencies among microgenesis, ontogenesis, and sociogenesis," which Rogoff labeled personal, interpersonal, and institutional planes of analysis. Each analytic level can be focused on individually, but actions emerge as parts of interrelated planes. Key concepts such as mediation, appropriation and emergence can be used across levels. The editorial uses this framework to discuss White's mathematics classroom-network study of connecting levels of activity.
requirements: Empirical analysis may focus on one plane, but does so with the understanding that actions emerge as parts of interrelated planes.
constraints: Digital infrastructures connecting students and teachers to multiple worlds make the connection between levels more complex than before, making the classroom more complex for both students and teachers.
target_learners: students in institutional classroom settings
target_learning_goals: understanding how individual actions, group processes and collective activities mediate each other in collaborative learning
examples: The editorial connects the three planes to White's study of Terms and Operations and Graphing in Groups digital tools in mathematics classrooms.
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1

article_title: Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1
title: PISA collaborative problem-solving framework as a scaffold for fine-grained CSCL research
description: The editorial describes the PISA framework (OECD 2017) as emphasizing "the relevance of establishing and maintaining shared understanding for collaborative problem solving" and being used as the analytic stance in the Bause et al. multi-touch study. The editors argue it "may be used to scaffold CSCL research, as it provides a clear conceptual framework for the processes that have to be considered.", helping explain under what conditions computational support may be beneficial.
requirements: Provides a clear conceptual framework for the processes that have to be considered in collaborative problem solving.
target_learners: CSCL researchers studying collaborative problem solving
target_learning_goals: establishing and maintaining shared understanding in collaborative problem solving
examples: The Bause et al. multi-touch table study uses the PISA framework as its analytic stance.
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1

article_title: Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1
title: Study regulation at the interpersonal level, focusing on the interdependency between individual action and social context
description: The editorial reports that Su et al. advocate studying regulation "using the inter-personal level as the starting point and focusing on the interdependency between individual action and social context", rather than conceptualizing regulation mainly as self-regulation with the individual as unit of analysis. Analysis across self-regulation, co-regulation, and social regulation levels is recommended for CSCL research.
requirements: Analysis on self-regulation, co-regulation, and social regulation levels, as in the Su et al. study's aim.
target_learners: collaborative learners in small groups, e.g., second-language students
target_learning_goals: social and content regulation during collaborative learning
examples: Su et al.'s 16-week wiki-supported ESL literature-circle study analyzed chat logs with coding for social intentionality, regulation processes, and emotions.
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1

article_title: Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1
title: Common ground (shared understanding) as a necessary condition for collaborative problem solving
description: The editorial states that "fostering mutual understanding, which is variously labeled common knowledge, common ground, inter-subjectivity, and shared understanding" is one of the most important problems with computer support in collaborative settings. If participants do not agree on the framing and direction of problem solving, they cannot communicate effectively. Multiple studies in the issue, including Borge et al.'s, are said to corroborate that establishing and maintaining common ground is necessary for solving a problem collaboratively.
requirements: Participants must agree on the framing and direction of the problem solving to communicate effectively.
constraints: Not all conditions and tools lead to productive and efficient collaboration; characterizing the formal and intentional settings that evoke productive interactional processes is hard.
target_learners: collaborating students in computer-supported small groups
target_learning_goals: shared understanding of task and task-related processes
examples: Multi-touch table external representations support reasoning by making it visible and shared, thereby facilitating joint thinking.
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law, Gerry Stahl, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2018). Multiple forms of regulation and coordination across levels in educational settings. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9274-1

article_title: From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y
title: Natural information processing system: five principles underlying cognitive load theory
description: The article grounds cognitive load theory in an architecture in which biologically secondary knowledge processing is analogous to evolution by natural selection, described by five principles: information store, borrowing and reorganising, randomness as genesis, narrow limits of change, and environmental organising and linking. Long-term memory provides the store; working memory is severely limited for novel information but has no known limits for organised information retrieved from long-term memory. The authors state these systems 'can be described using five principles summarised in Table 1'.
requirements: Novel information must be processed by a working memory limited in capacity and duration, while information retrieved from long-term memory is unconstrained
constraints: The limits of change principle applies only to novel information, not familiar information retrieved from long-term memory
target_learners: learners acquiring biologically secondary (school-taught) knowledge
target_learning_goals: acquisition of domain-specific knowledge and skills in long-term memory
examples: Table 1 lists the five principles and their functions, e.g. the information store principle: 'Store information in long-term memory for indefinite periods'
key_sources: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y

article_title: From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y
title: Biologically primary versus biologically secondary knowledge distinction
description: Drawing on Geary's evolutionary educational psychology, the article distinguishes knowledge we evolved to acquire (primary, modular, acquired 'easily, unconsciously, and without explicit instruction', including generic-cognitive skills like problem solving and communication) from biologically secondary skills such as reading, mathematics, and computer use, which are domain-specific, acquired consciously with effort, and require explicit instruction. Primary knowledge is used to leverage acquisition of secondary knowledge, so collaboration, being biologically primary, may under some circumstances improve acquisition of secondary knowledge.
requirements: Biologically secondary skills require explicit instruction and considerable effort to acquire
constraints: Most generic-cognitive skills such as problem-solving, planning, or generalising are biologically primary and not the appropriate target of formal instruction
target_learners: learners in education and training institutions
target_learning_goals: domain-specific biologically secondary knowledge
examples: The article notes learning the French word-pair for cat does not interact with the word-pair for dog, while writing sentences in French involves interacting elements
key_sources: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y

article_title: From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y
title: Mutual cognitive interdependence principle
description: A sub-principle of the borrowing and reorganising principle added to cognitive load theory to account for collaboration. The article states it 'acts as a subsidiary of the borrowing and re-organising principle by detailing how cognitive systems (i.e., inter-cognitive processes) acquire information between them', presupposing relative openness between cognitive systems and attending to intrinsic transactive processes. It holds that individuals depend on the instructor's guidance, appropriate peer interactions, and appropriate instructional environments of collaboration, without reducing them to the components of an individual system.
requirements: Relative openness between cognitive systems and transactive processes that allow cognitive exchange between them
constraints: The relation between systems and their environment must not be reduced to the cognitive components of an individual system
target_learners: collaborators in face-to-face or computer-supported groups
target_learning_goals: inter-cognitive exchange and shared knowledge construction
examples: The article says incorporating this principle into cognitive load theory's architecture 'provides the basis for the collective working memory effect'
key_sources: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y

article_title: From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y
title: Nine collaborative cognitive load principles relating task, learner and team characteristics to extraneous transactive load
description: The article distills its analysis into a table of nine principles stating when collaboration's transactional activities cause extraneous load: task complexity, task guidance and support, domain expertise, collaboration skills, team size, team roles, team composition, prior task experience, and prior team experience. Each principle states a direction, for example that 'Effective collaboration occurs when a task is complex enough to justify the extra time and effort involved in the necessary transactional activities', and that more guidance, expertise, roles, or prior experience lower the extraneous load caused by transactive activities.
requirements: Collaborative tasks should be selected and teams configured so that transactive activities stay task-related and extraneous load is minimised
constraints: If a task is not complex enough, unnecessary transactional activities cause extraneous cognitive load and are detrimental to learning
target_learners: students learning collaboratively in classrooms or CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: acquisition of biologically secondary, domain-specific knowledge through collaboration
examples: The article derives the principles from team characteristics including 'team size, the roles learners can or must carry out, team composition, and the prior experience of team members working with each other'
key_sources: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y

article_title: Different technologies, methodologies and epistemologies—is CSCL a community or communities?
citation: Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rose, Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen. (2018). Different technologies, methodologies and epistemologies—is CSCL a community or communities? Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9280-3
title: Collaborative cognitive load theory: extending cognitive load theory to collaborative learning with collective working memory and transactional costs
description: Kirschner, Sweller, Kirschner and Zambrano's theoretical treatise extends cognitive load theory to collaborative contexts to "generate principles specific to the design and study of collaborative learning". It takes a strictly information processing model of learning where working memory capacity is a primary factor. Collaborators gain access to a larger collective working memory, but part of working memory is devoted to "transactive activities involved in the collaborative process", so benefits depend on group experience working together. The authors also claim the theory "will be able to explain why CSCL does not always work".
requirements: Teachers are advised to think explicitly about the cognitive properties of the students, task characteristics and group composition when deciding whether to adopt collaborative learning
constraints: The editorial characterizes it as taking a strictly information processing model, which the editors place on the analytical end of the epistemic spectrum, misaligned with the constructivist, socio-cultural and social psychology frameworks popular in CSCL
target_learners: students learning through collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning outcomes in complex subject domains such as mathematics
examples: The editorial positions the treatise against Provocation #4, contrasting its analytical epistemology with the interpretive orientation of the other three papers in the issue
key_sources: Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rose, Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen. (2018). Different technologies, methodologies and epistemologies—is CSCL a community or communities? Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9280-3

article_title: Different technologies, methodologies and epistemologies—is CSCL a community or communities?
citation: Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rose, Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen. (2018). Different technologies, methodologies and epistemologies—is CSCL a community or communities? Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9280-3
title: Support theoretical and methodological diversity in CSCL and use squib-format venues to foster productive multivocality
description: The editors hold that CSCL as a field advances through multivocal conversations and debates rather than a single framework. They write that "theoretical and methodological diversity are essential to advances in CSCL" and that co-habitation of different approaches should stimulate debate. The journal's squib format was created specifically "to serve as a venue for scholarly interactions to achieve productive multivocality and avoid co-alienation".
requirements: Venues that publish quality- and rigor-grounded work regardless of theoretical grounds, plus debate formats such as squibs, to carry disagreements forward
constraints: The editorial cautions against a single comprehensive framework as the assumed goal; Rummel's proposed "kernel" taxonomy is treated as one conversation move rather than a resolution
target_learners: CSCL researchers and the learning sciences community

citation: Cress, U., Stahl, G., Rose, C., Law, N., & Ludvigsen, S. (2018). Forming social systems by coupling minds at different levels of cognition: Design, tools, and research methods. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 13, 235–240. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9284-z
title: Four-stage framework of coupling minds across levels of information processing
description: The authors organize CSCL research on coupling individual minds into social systems around four stages of information processing: attention, core cognition, metacognition, and activities. They write that 'The coupling processes themselves can take place at different stages of information processing' and map one paper in the issue to each level, noting each level requires different tools and analysis methods. The framework links theories of joint attention, knowledge integration, socially shared regulation, and collaborative writing activity.

title: Use scripts and awareness visualizations as coupling mechanisms because they force consideration of partners' actions and perspectives
description: The editorial presents collaboration scripts and visualizations as primary tools for coupling individual minds at different processing levels. It states that 'The high efficacy of scripts as coupling means is not surprising, as they force the individuals to consider the actions and perspectives of their partners', while visualization is a more implicit support that fosters awareness. Across the issue, scripts appear at the cognitive, metacognitive, and activity levels, and visualizations also serve researchers as analysis tools.

collaborative writing quality

article_title: Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments
citation: Peter Holtz & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress. (2018). Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9285-y
title: Productive friction: socio-cognitive conflicts resolved productively drive learning and knowledge construction
description: The article defines productive friction, adapted from organization science, as "the process of overcoming obstacles in a productive way that, in turn, leads to individual learning and collaborative knowledge construction." It uses the term broadly for discrepancies between individuals' thoughts, values, and attitudes, or between an individual's schemas and a group's view, that can be resolved so as to foster epistemic growth. Building on Piaget's socio-cognitive conflict, the article applies the concept to large-scale mass collaboration, arguing that too little friction limits learning while too much risks polarization or community rift.
requirements: Resolution of discrepancies must occur in a way that productively fosters epistemic growth rather than ignoring ideas or splitting the community
constraints: If friction is too low, chances for learning are limited; if too high on the individual level, learners will most likely fail to adapt; too much friction at the social level can lead to ignored ideas or a rift in the community
target_learners: individual contributors in large-scale online collaboration environments such as Wikipedia
target_learning_goals: individual learning and collaborative knowledge construction through resolving socio-cognitive conflicts
examples: The article operationalizes friction in Wikipedia as the difference between an author's and an article's view, betweenness scores of boundary-spanning articles, and editors contributing to articles representing opinions other than their own
key_sources: Peter Holtz & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress. (2018). Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9285-y

article_title: Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments
citation: Peter Holtz & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress. (2018). Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9285-y
title: Co-evolution model of individual learning and collective knowledge construction
description: The co-evolution model (Cress and Kimmerle) "combines the individual and the social levels." It "predicts that conflicts between individual and collective perspectives (as presented in collaboratively created artifacts) may make the two systems involved drift over time: In the case of the cognitive system, the drift can be called learning; in the case of the social system, this drift constitutes knowledge construction." The cognitive and social systems are structurally coupled and co-evolve toward greater capabilities in handling complexity, with persons and digital artifacts as the key entities.
requirements: Interactions between persons and collaboratively created digital artifacts in which conflicts between individual and collective perspectives arise
constraints: The model is presented for online environments where artifact-mediated collaboration makes acts of communication traceable in artifacts
target_learners: individuals participating in mass collaboration and CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: individual learning and collective knowledge construction as coupled, mutually triggering processes
examples: The three illustrative Wikipedia studies were framed by the co-evolution model and aimed "to identify the role of productive friction for learning and knowledge construction"

title: Cognitive-systemic stance: knowledge development at individual and social-system levels triggered by productive friction
description: The cognitive-systemic stance, developed by Cress and colleagues, builds on cognitive psychology and general system theory to investigate conceptual change by connecting "both individual cognitive systems and the individual’s interactions with the larger environment — the social systems." Within this framework, Holtz et al. hypothesize that "knowledge development at the levels of both individual and social system is triggered by productive friction," meaning that resolving sociocognitive conflicts is part of actions and activities. The editorial presents this as the theoretical frame for three big data methods applied to Wikipedia.
requirements: Big data analysis must be framed by a clear and well-developed theoretical framework, per the authors' emphasized stance
constraints: The framework's empirical example in this issue is Wikipedia environments
target_learners: individuals and large online communities engaged in mass collaboration
target_learning_goals: conceptual change
collaborative knowledge development
examples: Holtz, Kimmerle, and Cress present automatic text classification, cluster analysis of knowledge dynamics in Wikipedia articles, and social network analysis as three big data approaches

title: When digital resources replace the textbook as the main resource, designers and teachers must establish additional supports and scaffolds
description: The editorial argues that the sequential organization of textbooks historically provided well-established structures for student actions, but "when other resources become more important, designers, teachers, and students need to establish additional forms of supports and scaffolds for learning." Working with digital resources makes students' and teachers' tasks more complex and in need of more social and cognitive framing. The first two papers of the issue address how to support students working with digital resources.

citation: Solli, A., Mäkitalo, Å., & Hillman, T. (2018). Rendering controversial socioscientific issues legible through digital mapping tools. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9286-x
title: Gephi network visualization tool for controversy mapping in classrooms
description: Gephi is "an interactive visualization and exploration tool for all kinds of networks" used by students to render hyperlinked website corpora as network maps. It displays nodes as websites and edges as hyperlinks, showing "the relative centrality of a website in relation to a particular issue" through size (inbound links), position (edge quantity), and color attributes that update in real time as students rank, filter, and colorize nodes.
requirements: A corpus of hyperlink data exported as a network file, generated by collecting web browsing data with a tool such as Navicrawler
constraints: Operates only on relationships between nodes, not website content; multi-purpose functions irrelevant to students' categorizing task; not developed for pedagogical use or for judging trustworthiness of claims
target_learners: upper secondary science students
target_learning_goals: evaluating information sources and distinguishing scientific from non-scientific claims about socio-scientific controversies
examples: Students working on the HPV vaccine controversy produced maps typically based on visits to approximately 400 websites, coloring nodes by category (public, media, against the vaccine)

title: Six-phase controversy mapping project sequence for science classrooms
description: A project-level design pattern in which students work through six phases: (1) surfing and scraping the internet on a controversial issue with Navicrawler logging visited URLs, (2) selecting and importing data to Gephi, (3) re-presenting data as a map of actors, (4) sharing and discussing maps with peers, (5) participating in a debate enacting an identified actor, and (6) a reflective seminar. The map serves as "an aid in explaining and discussing their controversy."
requirements: Teachers, researchers, and IT pedagogical developers collaborate on project design; the mapping activity is embedded in a multi-week science-in-society project with curriculum-aligned grading criteria
constraints: Tools were originally developed for university research on sociotechnical debates, not schools; students need guidance since studies indicate the need for more support when searching for SSIs online

target_learning_goals: evaluating source types, distinguishing scientific from non-scientific claims, understanding science-society relations, ethical discussion of science's role in society
examples: A three-week November 2015 project in a Swedish upper secondary school with four experienced teachers; student groups targeted electronic waste, HPV vaccine, prenatal diagnosis, or animal testing controversies

title: Sociocultural tool-mediated activity approach to analyzing collaborative digital tool use
description: The study adopts a sociocultural approach in which cultural artifacts are "the means through which we as humans make meaning," resisting the material/ideational distinction. The unit of analysis is "tool-mediated activities"—how participants engage with technologies present in a situation—accounting for human action as socioculturally embedded and contingent on social, institutional, and material conditions.

citation: Schnaubert, L., & Bodemer, D. (2019). Providing different types of group awareness information to guide collaborative learning. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 14, 7–51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9293-y
title: Two types of group awareness information: cognitive (assumptions) and metacognitive (confidence)
description: The article distinguishes two kinds of group awareness information meant to "guide collaborative learning activities by providing knowledge-related information to the learners." Cognitive group awareness information concerns "the learners' assumptions" (factor 1), while metacognitive group awareness information concerns "their confidence" (factor 2), treated as independent factors. The framework combines CSCL research with research on metacognition, and its effects are tested on individual metacognitive and cognitive outcome measures and on regulation of the collaborative process.

constraints: Study confined to dyads of university students discussing blood-sugar regulation and diabetes mellitus
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge about blood-sugar regulation and diabetes mellitus
metacognitive monitoring (confidence)
examples: In the experimental study the two information types were crossed as factor 1 (assumptions) and factor 2 (confidence) with individual and process outcome measures

title: Cognitive group awareness tools providing knowledge-related information in CSCL
description: Cognitive group awareness tools are components of CSCL environments that display knowledge-related information about learning partners: "Cognitive group awareness tools are a means to guide collaborative learning activities by providing knowledge-related information to the learners." In this article such tools were used to visualize dyad members' assumptions and confidence during collaborative discussion, with the aim of guiding regulation of the joint learning process. They are positioned against a backdrop where positive effects are established but the information displayed varies widely.

constraints: In this study, the tools affected joint regulation but did not have the expected impact on learning outcomes

description: When designing CSCL support, visualize knowledge-related awareness information because visualized information strongly impacts learners' joint regulation: "visualizing information strongly impacts joint regulation and that learners seem to integrate the information provided to steer their learning." Designers should therefore expect the tool to steer which topics dyads discuss and how they coordinate, rather than to raise test outcomes by itself. The principle rests on the article's experimental comparison of cognitive and metacognitive awareness information.

title: RIDE rules for effective collaboration
description: The RIDE rules — Respect, Intelligent collaboration, Deciding together, and Encouraging — are communication rules summarizing essential characteristics of effective collaboration, derived by Saab et al. (2007) from a literature review and adapted for this study's vocational target group. The article states they "reflect communicative activities that are seen as essential for effective collaboration" and formed the basis for the definition of effective collaboration, driving both the classroom instruction's content and the reflection tool's assessment items and sub-rules (e.g., share relevant information, check if everyone agrees before acting, encourage others to participate).
requirements: Students need to know the RIDE rules; the instruction explains each rule's relevance with good and poor examples before collaboration begins.
constraints: The rules were originally tested as support for synchronous distance communication by Saab et al. (2007), not face-to-face vocational classrooms.
target_learners: First-year technical secondary vocational (MBO) students
target_learning_goals: Collaboration skills and effective communication during collaborative inquiry learning
examples: Chat excerpts showing good and poor examples of each sub-rule were evaluated during instruction, and sub-rules were displayed in the tool's feed up and feed forward phases.

title: Collaboration reflection tool (feed up, feed back, feed forward)
description: An online tool that prompts and scaffolds joint reflection on collaborative behavior, structured in three phases per Hattie and Timperley's feedback model. In the "feed up" phase students rate their own and each other's collaborative behavior on a ten-point scale for each RIDE rule; in the "feed back" phase they see a graphical representation of team and individual scores; in the "feed forward" phase they discuss what went well and formulate joint improvement goals. Completion takes up to ten minutes and the tool was offered four times at set points in the CSCL environment.
requirements: All team members complete each phase (individually for feed up and feed back, collaboratively for feed forward); content is based on the RIDE rules familiar from instruction.
constraints: The tool required students to have used the CSCL environment before; there was no tool after module one so students could get used to the environment, and completion takes up to ten minutes.
target_learners: First-year technical secondary vocational (MBO) students
target_learning_goals: Awareness of effective collaboration characteristics and improvement of students' own collaborative behavior
examples: Tool sessions at the end of modules two through five showed students their team's average scores per RIDE rule and previously formulated goals to discuss whether they had been reached.

title: Combine collaboration instruction with prompted joint reflection (self- and peer-assessment plus goal setting) rather than offering instruction alone
description: The article's central design recommendation is that teaching collaboration skills requires more than instruction about effective-collaboration characteristics: only a combination of conventional instruction and a tool prompting joint reflection — through self- and peer-assessment and collaborative goal setting — affected both collaborative behavior and knowledge acquisition in this study. The results section and discussion support this: instruction alone "benefits neither their collaborative behavior nor their knowledge acquisition", whereas instruction plus reflection prompting students to connect instructed characteristics to their actual behavior did.

constraints: The authors note it remains unclear which of the tool's working mechanisms (peer assessment vs goal setting) generated the effect; the finding is from technical vocational triads in a CSCL setting.

citation: van Leeuwen, A., Rummel, N., & van Gog, T. (2019). What information should CSCL teacher dashboards provide to help teachers interpret CSCL situations? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 14, 261–289. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09299-x
title: Teacher noticing framework: detection and interpretation of classroom situations
description: The article adopts the teacher noticing framework of Van Es and Sherin to model how teachers make sense of classroom and dashboard situations. It distinguishes two processes: "detection", deciding what deserves attention, and interpretation, reasoning about events and their broader principles. Characteristics include which students and behaviors teachers focus on, the specificity and evidence use of interpretations, and teachers' stance ranging from describing to interpreting. The framework supplies the study's coding scheme and its outcome measures.
requirements: Applied here to the situation where a teacher consults a dashboard rather than directly observing student behavior
constraints: Taking an interpretative stance is not something teachers automatically do or are always capable of, per Van Es and Sherin as cited
target_learners: Primary school teachers
Pre-service primary school teachers
target_learning_goals: Teacher skill in detecting and interpreting student collaboration during CSCL
examples: The experimental study coded teachers' open comments for evidence use, stance (levels 1-4), and specificity based on this framework

title: Three levels of interpretational aid in CSCL teacher dashboards: mirroring, alerting, and advising
description: Building on Soller et al.'s algorithm for collaboration support tools, the article distinguishes dashboards by which agent - tool or teacher - performs detection and interpretation. "Mirroring dashboards" display analyzed data for the teacher to peruse at will; "alerting" dashboards additionally flag groups deviating from a standard; "advising" dashboards "not only display information and alert to certain events, but also assist in the interpretation" by providing advice about what is happening or what action to take. This typology structures the three experimental conditions.
requirements: Alerting and advising require comparing group status to some standard to detect events
Advising requires the system to generate advice referencing the dashboard's indicators
constraints: The article found only one prior example of an advising dashboard in CSCL (Chen 2006), so higher levels of aid are scarcely studied
target_learners: Primary school teachers
Pre-service primary school teachers
target_learning_goals: Teacher monitoring of collaborating students and decisions about support
examples: The experiment instantiated the three levels as three versions of one prototype: information alone, information plus alerts, and information plus alerts plus advisory prompts

description: A teacher dashboard prototype built on MathTutor digital traces for dyads collaborating on fraction assignments, developed through "a teacher co-design methodology" with 10 teachers. It shows a start screen of five dyads and six indicators - attempts needed, chance of trial-and-error behavior, fraction-skill proficiency, activity over time, amount of talk, and solved assignments - with group and class overviews. article_title: Conceptualizing the designs of authentic computer-supported collaborative learning environments in schools
citation: Yotam Hod, Ornit Sagy. (2019). Conceptualizing the Designs of Authentic Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Environments in Schools. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11412-019-09300-7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09300-7
title: A three-cultures framework of authentic learning design distinguishes current, authentic, and intended cultures
description: The article proposes that every design for authenticity involves three distinct but related cultures: the current culture ("a pattern of activities that is developed over time for a community to achieve its valued purposes"), the authentic culture ("the professional or expert culture(s) that the teacher or designer wants the students to enculturate"), and the intended culture, the teacher's or designer's vision or figured world of that authentic culture. This refines Brown et al.'s bicultural classroom-versus-practitioner account by making the intended culture explicit. The review derived it through constant-comparative analysis and found it commensurate with every case examined.
requirements: Designs for authenticity must make the intended culture explicit, since the intended culture is a conceptual bridge between current classroom culture and one or more authentic cultures
constraints: All authentic cultures are current cultures under the article's definitions, but not all current cultures are authentic cultures
target_learners: students in school CSCL environments designed for authenticity
target_learning_goals: enculturation of professional or expert practices in a domain
examples: The review applied the framework to 28 cases from ijCSCL and JLS, validating it with Brown & Campione (1994) and Radinsky et al. (2001) outside the original corpus

title: Pentad-based coding scheme (P, S, T, CS, CL) for classifying authentic CSCL designs
description: The article operationalizes sociocultural design variation with a coding scheme crossing the pentad facets: Participants (P0 teacher, P1 non-authentic practitioners, P2 authentic practitioners), Setting (S0 classroom, S1 non-authentic settings, S2 authentic settings), Time (T0 educational timeframe, T1 authentic timeframe limited by educational timeframe), Computer support (CS0/CS1), and Collaborative learning (CL0-CL2). The scheme "help differentiate between the facets of the pentad in traditional schooling (non-authentic designs), designs for authenticity, and participation in current cultures," giving researchers one shared language across design types.
requirements: Codes for participants and setting are additions to the teacher role; a teacher counts as P2 only if being a practitioner is an intentional part of the design
target_learners: CSCL researchers and designers of authentic learning environments
target_learning_goals: analyzing and classifying designs for authenticity
examples: Case descriptions in Table 5 use codes such as P0S0T0CL1 with CS1 for Knowledge Forum-based knowledge building

title: Visualization tool representing current, authentic, and intended cultures across design categories
description: Figure 1 presents a symbolic system relating the three cultures, showing traditional schooling participation structures, direct participation in authentic cultures outside school, and designs for authenticity filling the gap between them. The authors emphasize it is "not a continuum" but three qualitatively different categories, and that "the visualization serves the purpose of organizing the different patterns of designs into categories with variations," information the coding table alone cannot show.
requirements: Must be read alongside the pentad coding scheme to capture relations between cultures and facets
target_learners: CSCL researchers; new CSCL designers exploring design possibilities
target_learning_goals: mapping and comparing designs for authenticity

citation: Yotam Hod, Ornit Sagy. (2019). Conceptualizing the Designs of Authentic Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Environments in Schools. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11412-019-09300-7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09300-7
title: Baseline simulation design: classroom-based approximation of authentic practice (P0S0T0CL1)
description: The most common design among the reviewed cases is the baseline simulation, coded P0S0T0CL1: students work in the classroom, within the regular timeframe, on classroom tasks that approximate authentic ones, often with computer support. These designs are prevalent because "these designs do not require (a) significant dependency on outside practitioners; (b) going outside of the educational setting; and (c) altering the typical educational timeframe." Enculturation is achieved primarily through boundary objects and activities.
requirements: Boundary objects or activities introduced to the classroom must map to the activity of some professional community
constraints: Students have limited or no direct interaction with practitioners, predominantly not in their setting
target_learners: K-12 and university students in regular classrooms
target_learning_goals: enculturation of domain practices such as scientific discourse, knowledge building, and argumentation
examples: Zhang et al. (2009) used Knowledge Forum and knowledge building activities to adjust participatory structures within the classroom during the normal school schedule; reviewed examples span ChemViz visualizations, wiki-supported ESL writing, and NetLogo ecosystem simulations

citation: Yotam Hod, Ornit Sagy. (2019). Conceptualizing the Designs of Authentic Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Environments in Schools. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11412-019-09300-7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09300-7
title: Baseline hybrid design: direct student-practitioner interaction in authentic settings (P0S0T0 + P2S2T1)
description: The baseline hybrid adds to baseline-simulation characteristics direct interactions with authentic practitioners (P2) within their authentic settings (S2), with timeframes generally authentic but limited by the educational design (T1). In these designs, "the learners have direct interaction with authentic practitioners on activities that serve the practitioners' interests or purposes," unlike simulations where activities serve classroom purposes. All hybrid cases used computer support.
requirements: Activities must serve the practitioners' interests or purposes, not only the classroom's; the design remains within an educational framework, typically regulated by a school instructor
constraints: Participation is not full participation: it may be limited to developmentally appropriate tasks and time restrictions, and continued apprenticeship beyond the design falls outside its framework
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students, and school or camp participants, working with professionals
target_learning_goals: enculturation through apprenticeship-like interactions with practicing professionals
examples: Fisher et al. (2007): University of Siegen information-systems students learned to be by participating in local IT companies (P2S2), balanced with university-based coursework

citation: Yotam Hod, Ornit Sagy. (2019). Conceptualizing the Designs of Authentic Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Environments in Schools. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11412-019-09300-7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09300-7
title: Simulation versus hybrid approaches distinguished by whose goals and purposes the activities serve
description: The article reframes the prevailing participant/setting classification of authentic designs: the crux of the distinction is conceptualized as the extent of students' direct interaction with practitioners and the setting, but the review concludes the decisive criterion is "whose goals and purposes" the activities serve. Simulations aim for classroom culture to "more closely resemble, align with, or approximate the authentic culture" via boundary objects; hybrids place learners in direct interaction with practitioners on activities serving practitioners' purposes, and are therefore preferable termed hybrids rather than full participation.
requirements: Classifying a design requires information about the purpose of activities, not only who participates and where
constraints: Participant and setting information alone does not determine the approach: both approaches can include teachers, non-authentic practitioners, or authentic practitioners
target_learners: designers and researchers of authentic CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: conceptualizing and organizing design variations for authenticity
examples: Radinsky et al.'s (2001) mutual benefit partnership was treated as a simulation-variation C case because the telecommunications company was not an authentic culture and student benefit was a service rather than learning industry practice

title: Designers should make the intended culture explicit, with the teacher acting as a legitimate gatekeeper of values and practices
description: Because authentic designs involve a designer's vision of the authentic culture — a figured world — the review argues the intended culture "must be a vital part of any conceptualization." Without it, people may be misled into thinking authentic designs aim to duplicate professional practice; to the contrary, "in authentic designs there is a legitimate role for a teacher to be a gatekeeper of values and practices, as well as to create developmentally appropriate tasks."
requirements: The intended culture should be defined and communicated as part of any design for authenticity
constraints: The teacher need not be a member of the authentic culture; practitioners are sometimes bad teachers, and the review does not rank the two situations
target_learners: students in classrooms designed for authenticity
target_learning_goals: enculturation of intended (filtered, developmentally appropriate) versions of expert practices
examples: The review's three-culture framework and figured-worlds analysis instantiate this principle across the 28 cases

article_title: Socio-cognitive openness in online knowledge building discourse: does openness keep conversations going?
citation: van Heijst, H., de Jong, F. P. C. M., van Aalst, J., de Hoog, N., & Kirschner, P. A. (2019). Socio-cognitive openness in online knowledge building discourse: does openness keep conversations going? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 14, 165-184. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09303-4
title: Socio-cognitive openness framework: three levels, two dimensions, four discourse acts, and eight components
description: A conceptual framework for analyzing openness in online knowledge building contributions, organized at three levels: dimensions, discourse acts and components (see Fig. 1). The cognitive dimension contains components relating to the mental activities of producing and evaluating knowledge claims, while the social dimension contains components on how the contributor aligns with others and presents him- or herself. Components are grouped in pairs into the discourse acts of building knowledge, expression of uncertainty, community orientation and the expression of self, reflecting the principles of producing knowledge claims and taking intersubjective stance. The framework was operationalized as a binary coding scheme applied in ATLAS.ti to Knowledge Forum notes.
requirements: Coding requires consideration of surrounding contributions in the same conversation, since 'as many contributions build on previous ones, texts of the surrounding contributions in the same conversations were taken into account in the coding decisions'
constraints: The binary coding scheme 'did not capture nuances of openness within each component'; the authors state further development of the coding scheme is warranted
target_learners: Experienced professionals in a part-time Master of Education program
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge building and idea improvement in asynchronous online discourse
examples: Applied to 638 KF notes written by 68 community members from 10 KF views in two cohorts of a Dutch Master's program, with intercoder reliabilities such as K cognitive openness = .94 and K social openness = .89

description: This conceptualization, from Hod and Sagy, categorizes and compares authentic learning scenarios. It builds on a distinction between environments that "match or approximate a learning environment to an authentic culture" and environments where students interact with practitioners in the professional setting itself. The editorial reports it offers a framework for classifying authentic learning environments that can be used to assess existing fieldwork and guide future research.

constraints: Systematic comparison of authenticity in empirical studies is difficult "due to the vast scope of contexts found in studies of classroom practice"

title: Socio-cognitive openness: a CSCL construct with cognitive and social dimensions decomposed into four discourse acts and eight components
description: A new explanatory construct for CSCL developed by van Heijst et al. to explain why actual knowledge-building levels remain low, since "students sometimes do not build upon the prior work of their peers and need scaffolding to do so." It distinguishes two dimensions (cognitive and social) divided into four knowledge-building discourse acts — knowledge-building, expression of uncertainty, community orientation, expression of self — and eight components. The framework was empirically tested by analysis and coding of Knowledge Forum contributions from two mixed cohorts of students and teachers, with its two-factor structure validated.

constraints: Editorially noted that further conceptual and empirical research is needed to combine socio-cognitive openness with related factors such as trust or social capital
