description: The digital environment in which 25 teachers in a professional-development course engaged in conversation on hot and controversial topics is called the "Hot Discussions Platform (HDP)." It "affords both written and oral contributions," with oral contributions taking place in small groups and participants assigned to different group configurations. Its design includes a reflection mode in which a moderator can freeze the discussion or make selected aspects of the discourse available for participants as resources for a new layer of discourse.

title: Micro-ecological approach: a cross-level analytical alternative cutting across individual, group, and community levels in CSCL
description: Borge and Mercier propose this approach as an alternative to the four overarching CSCL learning theories (information-processing, constructivism, socio-constructivist/socio-cultural, group cognition), arguing these lenses are "too narrow to capture the true contextual richness of CSCL in action." It cuts across multiple levels of analysis (individual, group, community) and analyzes how each level influences and is influenced by the others. Events such as different facilitator orchestration moves or a student destroying a Minecraft world would remain unexplained from single-level episode analysis.

constraints: The editorial notes it remains to be seen whether the approach offers a new analytical lens, since the socio-cultural perspective has combined levels of analysis for many years

title: Design CSCL environments from the perspective of participants' emancipatory agency, letting learners select, change, and combine their digital tools
description: From Tchounikine's squib: CSCL settings are often predefined, with participants expected to use specific environment features rather than choosing software tools of their own selection. The principle holds that participants should be "given the opportunity to select, change, and combine the technologies that they think would be most beneficial for their learning trajectories." Design should be envisioned from participants' agency, and learning may become expansive beyond what is given in predefined tasks.

article_title: It is not either or: An initial investigation into combining collaborative and individual learning using an ITS
citation: Olsen, J. K., Rummel, N., & Aleven, V. (2019). It is not either or: An initial investigation into combining collaborative and individual learning using an ITS. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 14, 353-381. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09307-0
title: Combine collaborative and individual learning within ITS-supported activities rather than choosing one or the other
description: The article argues that collaborative and individual learning are often combined in classrooms and that CSCL should investigate "when a combination is beneficial compared to individual or collaborative learning alone." It proposes an initial test of combining both modes within one ITS activity, finding support in higher gains, fewer errors and hints, and higher situational interest. The principle is to treat the two modes as complementary stages of the same activity rather than alternatives.
requirements: An intelligent tutoring system activity is needed that can be run both collaboratively and individually so the two modes can be sequenced within the same learning content.
constraints: The learning-gain advantage was restricted to the 4th grade students in this initial investigation.
target_learners: 4th and 5th grade students learning fractions
target_learning_goals: fraction problem-solving skills
examples: The study compared a combined condition to individual-only and collaborative-only conditions in an ITS for fractions with 382 4th and 5th grade students.

citation: Jonna Malmberg, Eetu Haataja, Tapio Seppänen, Sanna Järvelä. (2019). Are we together or not? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 14:467–490. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09311-4
title: Physiological synchrony as a candidate indicator of meaningful events in CSCL, situated within the socially shared regulation of learning framework
description: The article positions physiological synchrony — an association or interdependence in EDA signals between group members — within the socially shared regulation of learning framework, in which synchrony and monitoring of cognition, behaviour, motivation and emotions are "critical to a group's collaborative progress". It proposes that synchrony may reveal whether individuals are mentally attuned to the same activity even when this is "not verbally expressed". Empirically, synchrony emerged only in groups facing difficulties, suggesting it may "be a new indicator for recognizing meaningful events in CSCL".
requirements: Continuous EDA data captured from each group member with wristband sensors during naturalistic collaborative tasks
constraints: Due to the small size and qualitative nature of these findings, it is not possible to generalize them
Some of these early results are incoherent, and more research is needed to draw a clearer picture of the phenomena in relation to regulation in collaborative learning
target_learners: high school students (aged 15–16) working in small collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving and metacognitive monitoring during collaborative exams
examples: Four groups of three students wore Empatica E4 wristbands while designing a physics experiment during a 90-minute collaborative exam; synchrony was quantified with the physiological concordance index over running 15-s windows.

article_title: Capturing the dynamic and cyclical nature of regulation: Methodological Progress in understanding socially shared regulation in learning
citation: Järvelä, S., Järvenoja, H., & Malmberg, J. (2019). Capturing the dynamic and cyclical nature of regulation: Methodological Progress in understanding socially shared regulation in learning. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09313-2
title: Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) as a group-level regulatory framework alongside self-regulation and co-regulation
description: The article frames regulation in collaborative learning as occurring on an individual–social continuum, where self-regulation (regulating oneself), co-regulation (supporting each other), and socially shared regulation (regulating together) jointly form the relative regulated learning space. It builds on Winne and Hadwin's COPES model of individual SRL cycles, modeling learning as a cyclical process through phases of task perception, goal setting and planning, enacting strategies, and evaluation. SSRL specifically assumes reciprocity: "Socially shared regulation, particularly, assumes reciprocity in regulatory actions between the group members."
requirements: Understanding regulation in social context requires capturing individuals' subjective psychological premises and appraisals simultaneously with interaction processes
constraints: Regulation is not linear but cyclical and temporally fluctuating, making it hard to capture with single-point or retrospective measures
target_learners: students in collaborative learning groups
CSCL participants
target_learning_goals: regulation of cognition, motivation, and emotion during collaborative learning

Capturing the dynamic and cyclical nature of regulation: Methodological Progress in understanding socially shared regulation in learning. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09313-2

title: Learning in Embodied Activity Framework: a sociocultural framework recasting Activity Theory for embodied CSCL
description: The editorial introduces the Learning in Embodied Activity Framework, described as "a Sociocultural Framework for Embodied Cognition" developed by Danish, Eynedy, Saleh and Humburg. It recasts Activity Theory for embodied CSCL experiences, motivated by the difficulty of accounting for both individual and group level phenomena within one framework. The editorial describes its empirical grounding in observations of embodied science learning in mixed reality classroom settings.
requirements: The framework is applied to characterize embodied learning in CSCL experiences, particularly mixed reality settings in naturalistic contexts
constraints: The editors note it is "challenging to account for both individual and group level phenomena within the same framework," which the framework addresses
target_learners: Students in science classrooms engaging in embodied learning activities
target_learning_goals: Embodied science learning through mixed reality collaborative experiences
examples: The article offers a rich exposition of observations from several studies where the framework was used to characterize embodied science learning in classrooms

description: The editorial describes the Augmented Reality Sandbox, a novel environment for embodied CSCL experiences presented by Hod and Twersky. Unlike prior research that "has focused on AR Sandbox activity designs, outcome measures, and user's perceptions of different usability functions", this article probes deeply into the situated processes by which groups engage in CSCL activities, analyzing group interactions spanning material, social, and activity contexts.

constraints: The editorial frames this as a continuation of investigations of authentic learning experiences for science classrooms

article_title: Advocating for group interaction in the age of COVID-19
citation: Sanna Järvelä & Carolyn P. Rosé. (2020). Advocating for group interaction in the age of COVID-19. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09324-4
title: Collaborative learning requires careful design rather than occurring spontaneously
description: The editorial states as field consensus that collaborative learning "is not best conducted in a spontaneous fashion, but careful design of collaborative learning will contribute to effective computer-supported collaborative learning." It notes a decade of work scripting, prompting and structuring collaboration and supporting roles and participation, and identifies evaluating complete designs and their instructional alignment as an open problem. Design-centered research is presented as one emerging methodology addressing it.
requirements: Evaluation must address alignment between the design and its engagement to extract insights for later iterations, as the editorial frames the still-unmet attention.
constraints: The editorial states that how to evaluate the complete designs and their instructional alignment had not yet received attention.
target_learners: students in computer-supported collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: productive collaboration and effective computer-supported collaborative learning
examples: The editorial cites scripting, prompting and structuring the collaboration process and supporting roles and participation as developed approaches over the past decade.

article_title: Advocating for group interaction in the age of COVID-19
citation: Sanna Järvelä & Carolyn P. Rosé. (2020). Advocating for group interaction in the age of COVID-19. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09324-4
title: In remote and post-COVID education, preserve group interaction and connection to counter isolation
description: The editors argue that effective virtual teamwork and computer-supported collaborative learning matter doubly in the pandemic era: for learning impact and because it "offers an amelioration for the isolation that has been felt by some more keenly in recent months". They caution that a return to face-to-face settings driven by safety concerns risks recreating isolation through distancing, and name social-network-analytic methods as one way to maintain awareness of how safety measures affect learning communities socially.
requirements: Educational changes made to preserve health must be paired with methods that maintain awareness of community inner workings from a social perspective.
constraints: The editorial frames this as a danger and a responsibility of the journal community in the emerging Post-COVID world, not a tested intervention.
target_learners: students in online and face-to-face classrooms during and after COVID-19
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning, social connection, and reducing learner isolation
examples: To this end, the editors call for strong empirical research with multidisciplinary methodological and theoretical perspectives addressing post-COVID education.

article_title: Capturing the participation and social dimensions of computer-supported collaborative learning through social network analysis: which method and measures matter?
citation: Mohammed Saqr, et al. (2020). Capturing the participation and social dimensions of computer-supported collaborative learning through social network analysis: which method and measures matter? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 15:227–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09322-6
title: Centrality measures as operationalization of the participatory and social dimensions of CSCL
description: The article organizes SNA-based CSCL measurement around two dimensions. The participatory dimension is captured by degree centralities: outdegree is "frequently calculated as the number of out-posts generated by a learner" and indicates quantity of participation, while indegree counts replies received and indicates prestige or worthiness of contribution. The social dimension is captured by closeness, betweenness and eigenvector centralities; the article states that "Eigenvector centrality captures the social positioning of the students more reliably than the other centrality measures" because it weighs the centrality of a learner's contacts. The study validates which configurations best measure each dimension.
requirements: A network must be constructed from forum interaction data with an explicit tie definition, direction, weight and aggregation choice
Group-size differences require deciding between normalized and raw centrality versions
constraints: Findings derive from problem-based learning courses in medical higher education using Moodle forums
target_learners: university students in problem-based learning courses
target_learning_goals: measuring participatory effort and social positioning in collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The study computed outdegree, indegree, closeness, betweenness and eigenvector centralities for 598 students across 12 PBL courses in multigraph, simplified and weighted configurations

title: Report SNA methodological choices in detail so learning-analytics research can be compared and replicated
description: The article recommends that researchers reporting on social network analysis in learning analytics document their operationalization choices, because measurement robustness underpins reproducibility. It states that "the results emphasize the need for researchers who report on SNA to present in detail their methodological choices so that research is better able to be compared, replicated, and ultimately generalized." The article enumerates nine reportable items, from tie definition and weighting through software versions to community-finding parameters.
requirements: Reports must state tie definition, direction, network mode, weight scheme, node and edge counts, aggregation method and duration, software and versions, visualization software, and community-finding method and parameters
constraints: The guidance is based on evidence from problem-based learning courses in medical higher education
target_learners: learning analytics researchers and educators analyzing CSCL forum data
target_learning_goals: reproducible and valid measurement of participation and social dimensions of collaborative learning
examples: The study itself compared multigraph, simplified and weighted configurations and reported tie definitions, weighting, normalization and software (Igraph in R version 3.52)

citation: Riikonen, S., Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, P., & Hakkarainen, K. (2020). Bringing maker practices to school: tracing discursive and materially mediated aspects of student teams' collaborative making processes. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09330-6
title: Making-Process-Rug video-analysis method
description: The Making-Process-Rug is a visual video-analysis method developed by the authors to trace "social-discursive, materially mediated, individual, and collaborative making processes" across a longitudinal co-invention project. Video is coded in fixed three-minute segments in ELAN using a sociomaterialgetCode template, then converted into layered, color-coded diagrams resembling woven rag rugs that show how verbal and embodied actions intertwine over time. It enables macro-level overview and later zooming to micro-level events such as process organizing, and quantitative comparison of action proportions.
requirements: a systematic coding template adapted to the study's purpose
fixed three-minute segmentation of video data in the ELAN multimedia annotator
constraints: segments with no analyzable action are removed, so rugs reflect adjusted usable video data
target_learners: student teams of adolescents in collaborative making projects
target_learning_goals: characterizing how collaborative invention processes unfold over time
examples: Applied to five seventh-grade teams' roughly 65 h of usable video; rugs revealed model making as the most prominent activity in the four successful teams.
Two teams were independently coded by two investigators to check coding reliability.

title: Epistemic-object account of collaborative making
description: The article frames collaborative making through the construct of epistemic objects: "Epistemic objects are envisioned as well as future-oriented invention ideas, which are characterized by their incompleteness and infinite potential for improvement through sustained iterative efforts." Pursuing such an incompletely specified object keeps a team's discussion, sketching, prototyping and experimentation aligned, and material artifacts such as sketches and prototypes serve as anchors that make vague ideas discussable and force convergence toward shared understanding. The account underpins the authors' explanation of which teams succeeded.
requirements: teams must jointly regulate activity toward the object rather than work on disconnected individual tasks
constraints: the process is emergent and nonlinear, so goals, tools and products cannot be pre-determined, which makes teacher scaffolding challenging
target_learners: adolescent students in teams doing open-ended co-invention challenges
target_learning_goals: co-inventing artifacts
knowledge-creating learning
examples: Bike and MGG shared their epistemic objects and refined them through experimentation and model making across the project, whereas the Plant team generated no such object.

title: Collaborative making project pattern: multi-material, digitally enhanced, holistic, thematically anchored
description: Drawing on craft (sloyd) tradition, the authors characterize school-based collaborative making projects as "1) multi-material, including both soft (e.g., textile) and hard (e.g., metals) materials; 2) digitally enhanced (integrating digital devices and applications); 3) holistic in terms of including all stages of creation from design ideation to experimentation, and from fabrication to evaluation of the final productions." The fourth feature anchors projects on integrative thematic studies orchestrated by teacher teams from multiple subject domains. The pattern was enacted in Finnish craft lessons extended with digital fabrication instruments such as 3D CAD, robotics, e-textiles and GoGo Boards.

title: Interactional Ethnography and dialogic intervisualizing as an analytical lens for multimodal collaborative conversation
description: The editorial describes Bridges et al.'s methodological lens, Interactional Ethnography (IE), as "a logic-of-inquiry that can be used to examine collaborative processes" as undergraduate students and their facilitator work with multimodal text. Its companion conceptualization, dialogic intervisualizing, is designed to capture "the interplay between the conversation, the broader collaborative problem solving processes, and the evolving artifacts produced during the interaction", drawing on Silverstein's concept of indexical order for how conceptual objects are decontextualized and recontextualized across modalities.

citation: Ulrike Cress. (2020). The richness of CSCL environments. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09335-1
title: Knowledge Appropriation Model connecting scaffolded learning and knowledge maturing
description: The Knowledge Appropriation Model, developed by Ley and colleagues and applied by Rodríguez-Triana et al. to the Go-Lab teacher community, "integrates three processes: Knowledge maturing transforms individual knowledge to a collective level." Scaffolding practices support individuals who need help applying shared materials in concrete working situations, and through knowledge appropriation individuals become aware of existing knowledge, interact with others, refine ideas, and adapt existing solutions to new situations. The editorial describes it as a rich theoretical model describing circles of maturation and appropriation that includes processes at the individual level, the social level, and the interaction between the two.
requirements: The model was operationalized with process indicators (created, shared, co-edited, published, used ILSs; help requests; participation in activity events; reuse and refining) applied to shared platform resources.
constraints: The editorial notes the model was tested with quite simple statistics, placing the complexity in the conceptual model rather than the analysis.

target_learning_goals: professional learning about instructional design for inquiry learning
examples: The study defined indicators for each process, such as "Indicators for knowledge maturing are the numbers of created, shared, co-edited, published and used ILSs", and traced implementation of about 40,000 ILSs.

title: Knowledge Appropriation Model (KAM)
description: The Knowledge Appropriation Model describes social practices of learning and knowledge creation in professional settings, based on sociocultural models of knowledge maturation and scaffolding. In this article KAM is the analytical framework used to map 12 practices — such as "Knowledge maturation practices lead to the transformation and maturation of knowledge" through sharing, co-creation, formalization and standardization; scaffolding practices of help-seeking, guidance and fading; and appropriation practices of awareness, adaptation and validation — onto traceable indicators in the Go-Lab community. The model assumes appropriation practices underlie both maturation and scaffolding, connecting collective knowledge with individual application.

constraints: In this study only practices mediated by the Graasp platform could be traced; appropriation was operationalized only as reuse and edition of others' ILSs

target_learning_goals: adoption of inquiry-based learning pedagogy
teacher professional learning and knowledge creation
examples: The study mapped KAM practices onto Graasp log indicators across 40,235 ILSs and found maturation, scaffolding and appropriation traces associated with classroom adoption

title: Graasp ILS authoring platform and the Go-Lab ecosystem for inquiry-based learning
description: Go-Lab is a technological ecosystem supporting inquiry-based learning in STEM built around Inquiry Learning Spaces (ILSs): "pedagogically structured learning environments that can contain online labs, apps, and resources." It comprises Golabz, a repository of apps, labs and ready-to-use ILSs, and Graasp, "a platform for ILS authoring and implementation, as well as for community gathering," plus a help desk and face-to-face training events. From 2009 through December 2019 Graasp reached 37,380 registered teachers and over 100,000 students from 152 countries, with an overall ILS adoption rate of 5.76%.
requirements: Teachers must register and author or copy ILSs; adoption requires implementation with students tracked via student-mode users
constraints: Only practices mediated by Graasp were traceable; the Go-Lab repository does not require logging in, so awareness actions there leave no evidence
target_learners: primary, secondary and higher education STEM teachers
target_learning_goals: designing and implementing inquiry-based learning activities
examples: Teachers create, share, co-create and publish ILSs in Graasp; an ILS was coded as adopted when more than 10 student-mode users were registered to it
key_sources: María Jesús Rodríguez-Triana, Luis P. Prieto, Tobias Ley, Ton de Jong, Denis Gillet. (2020). Social practices in teacher knowledge creation and innovation adoption: a large-scale study in an online instructional design community for inquiry learning. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09331-5

article_title: Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance
citation: Hayashi, Y. (2020). Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09333-3
title: PCA with five types of metacognitive suggestion delivered during dyadic explanation
description: The study used a pedagogical conversational agent (PCA) installed on a server that automatically analyzed learners' word types to determine whether explanations were effective, with a rule-based generator selecting prompts from five types: "Metacognitive suggestion", "facilitation of knowledge integration" (perspective-taking and turn-switching prompts), and "Communication encouragement" including motivational remarks and focus prompts. Suggestions were triggered by keyword detection and delivered verbally in speech lasting an average of three seconds, with a text version presented under the agent image.
requirements: A server-client network platform that transcribes learner speech for keyword detection and delivers prompts at conversation gaps.
Rule-based keyword lists distinguishing efficient explanations (e.g., key task terms) from non-efficient ones (e.g., give-up phrases).
constraints: Suggestions were executed by an experimenter signaling during a momentary gap, capped at a maximum of 10 presentations per task and one per minute.
The technical-coordination process code was excluded because no technical issues arose in this task.
target_learners: Freshman and sophomore psychology students working in same-gender dyads
target_learning_goals: Explaining technical cognitive-science concepts to a partner and integrating two concepts into one topic understanding
examples: Type A example printed: "Please remember that the task is to explain the topic using the two concepts."; Type D motivational remarks such as "Good job! Keep going!"
key_sources: Hayashi, Y. (2020). Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09333-3

article_title: Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance
citation: Hayashi, Y. (2020). Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09333-3
title: Combine gaze-awareness feedback with PCA metacognitive suggestions to improve both coordination and learning gains in computer-mediated collaborative learning
description: The article's design principle is that two complementary facilitation methods — real-time partner gaze feedback supporting joint attention and a PCA providing metacognitive suggestions — should be integrated in collaborative-learning support systems. Gaze feedback improved process coordination but "does not directly scaffold metacognition", while PCA suggestions support self-regulation but lack partner-awareness information; jointly they produced the highest learning gains.
requirements: A system able to show a partner's real-time gaze on shared task materials and to deliver dynamic metacognitive suggestions during collaboration.
A collaborative task where partners hold different knowledge and must explain and integrate perspectives.
constraints: The synergy on learning gains appeared in one 2×2 experiment with psychology freshmen/sophomores in dyads on a jigsaw explanation task; no process-level interaction was found, so the combined advantage concerns gains, not process ratings.
target_learners: University students collaborating remotely or side-by-side without visual contact
target_learning_goals: Knowledge integration and mutual understanding of each partner's distinct concepts in collaborative explanation tasks
examples: In the experiment, learners in the visible-gaze/visible-agent condition achieved higher gain scores and showed the only significant process-performance correlation.
key_sources: Hayashi, Y. (2020). Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09333-3

article_title: Students’ multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment
citation: Anu Kajamaa & Kristiina Kumpulainen. (2020). Students' multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2020) 15:411–444. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09337-z
title: Four intertwined multimodal knowledge practices in makerspace learning: orienting, interpreting, concretizing, and expanding knowledge
description: The article identifies a taxonomy of four multimodal knowledge practices that mediated students' collaborative maker work: "orienting, interpreting, concretizing, and expanding knowledge". Orienting involves selecting challenges, materials and spaces via cumulative talk; interpreting involves verbally reflecting on instructions and ideating; concretizing involves externalizing knowledge into epistemic objects and tangible artifacts; expanding involves critically revising objects and plans when difficulties arise. The practices are realized through discourse, materials, embodied actions and spatial arrangements and guided the creation of shared epistemic objects and artifacts.
requirements: Identification requires analysis of discursive, material, embodied and spatial dimensions of interaction, as coded in the article's three-phase sociocultural discourse and multimodal interaction analysis
constraints: The practices were identified from video data of two student groups in one school's FUSE Studio makerspace, and the authors acknowledge results might have looked different with newly formed groups
target_learners: Elementary students aged 9–12 carrying out STEAM design challenges in small groups
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge creation in STEAM design and making activities
examples: Each practice was illustrated with episodes, such as two boys relocating to the corridor to build a Laser Defender security system, moving through all four practices to a completed artifact.
key_sources: Anu Kajamaa & Kristiina Kumpulainen. (2020). Students' multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2020) 15:411–444. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09337-z

article_title: Students’ multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment
citation: Anu Kajamaa & Kristiina Kumpulainen. (2020). Students' multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2020) 15:411–444. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09337-z
title: FUSE Studio makerspace with 30 self-selected STEAM challenges and leveling difficulty
description: The FUSE Studio is a school-based makerspace concept, originally created at Northwestern University, consisting of "a computer program and hands-on material packages including 30 (pre-given) activities, called challenges". Students freely choose a challenge, partners (or working alone), and pace, via the "My Challenges" web interface with trailer videos. Challenges range from jewelry design to 3D-modelled dream homes, windmills, solar-powered cars, laser mazes and roller coasters, and "level up in difficulty following the basic logic of video game design principles". Assessment is ungraded, using photos, video, digital artifacts and student documentation.
requirements: Digital tools (computers, 3D printers), hands-on material kits, a website providing challenge instructions, and teacher facilitation, with teachers making rounds in the space
constraints: Some challenges are fully digital while others use provided physical kits; teachers do not need advanced digital competence, since FUSE offers low-threshold activity
target_learners: Elementary students (ages 9–12) in elective courses; concept also adopted in other Finnish schools
target_learning_goals: STEAM learning, creative problem solving, collaboration and digital competence through interest-driven design and making
examples: In the study school, students used the computer lab, a neighboring classroom and the corridor for challenges such as building a laser security system for a 'treasure'.
key_sources: Anu Kajamaa & Kristiina Kumpulainen. (2020). Students' multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2020) 15:411–444. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09337-z

article_title: Promoting regulation of equal participation in online collaboration by combining a group awareness tool and adaptive prompts. But does it even matter?
citation: Strauß, S., & Rummel, N. (2021). Promoting regulation of equal participation in online collaboration by combining a group awareness tool and adaptive prompts. But does it even matter? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2021) 16:67–104. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09340-y
title: Group awareness tool with gini-triggered adaptive prompts implemented as Moodle plugins
description: The collaboration support was implemented as Moodle plugins controlled by an automated support system and always visible in the sidebar of the main page, group wiki, and group forum. The GAT visualized participation as bar graphs of words each member contributed to the group's wiki and forum, with a legend identifying members; the adaptive prompt, shown in a box above the GAT, suggested a shared-regulation action plus a motivating statement. Per the article, "If the gini coefficient was equal to 0.5 or greater, a prompt was displayed", drawn from a pool of six synonymous prompts.
requirements: An automated support system that updates counts; the article notes "The support was automatically updated whenever a student had contributed to the group’s wiki or forum".
constraints: Prompts were displayed only when the gini coefficient reached 0.5 or greater; below that threshold the system "informed the group that there are currently no new suggestions available".
The first prompt appeared three days after the task started, to reduce redundant prompts from the first group member opening the conversation.
target_learners: University undergraduate students in an online course working in groups of four
target_learning_goals: Regulating the distribution of participation during online collaboration
Socially shared regulation of collaboration
examples: The bar-graph GAT displayed word counts per member in the group wiki, forum, or total, with toggling checkboxes, online status, and message shortcuts.
key_sources: Strauß, S., & Rummel, N. (2021). Promoting regulation of equal participation in online collaboration by combining a group awareness tool and adaptive prompts. But does it even matter? International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2021) 16:67–104. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09340-y

article_title: Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data
citation: Eberle, J., Stegmann, K., Barrat, A., Fischer, F., & Lund, K. (2021). Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09345-7
title: SocioPatterns RFID badges for measuring face-to-face contact duration
description: SocioPatterns RFID devices were integrated into participants' name badges to measure face-to-face contact during scientific events. The badges perform "bidirectional low-power radio communication": because the body shields the radio frequency and badges are worn on the chest, they exchange packets only when wearers face each other at close range at about 1 to 1.5 m. Data at 20-second temporal resolution were aggregated to one variable, duration of interaction, per dyad across the whole event.
requirements: Base stations must cover the public spaces to be tracked; tracking only occurred within range of base stations located in dining hall, main hall, and workshop rooms.
constraints: Measurement starts only after the first 20 seconds of contact to exclude noise, and brief contacts are thus not captured.
target_learners: Researchers attending scientific events
target_learning_goals: Measuring face-to-face contact as a basis for studying collaboration-network formation
examples: Used at Alpine Rendez-Vous 2011 and 2013 with participants consenting at registration; four participants opted out of wearing the RFID device.
key_sources: Eberle, J., Stegmann, K., Barrat, A., Fischer, F., & Lund, K. (2021). Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09345-7

article_title: Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data
citation: Eberle, J., Stegmann, K., Barrat, A., Fischer, F., & Lund, K. (2021). Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09345-7
title: Paper-based group awareness brochure with participant profiles
description: The group awareness intervention was a paper-based brochure containing profiles of all workshop participants, designed to support cognitive and social group awareness. Each profile included name, picture and contact information plus "information about personal resources (research interests and exemplary publications) and information pointing to their social resources (affiliations and background)". Profiles were compiled from participants' personal websites, and the brochure was given without further instructions at the start of workshops in the experimental condition.
requirements: Information was compiled from participants' websites to spare them providing it; profiles drew on personal websites and registration data.
constraints: The control group received no brochure, and the brochure was given without further instructions.
target_learners: Researchers at interdisciplinary scientific events, including PhD students and experienced researchers
target_learning_goals: Building cognitive and social group awareness of other participants' expertise, interests, and social resources to support selecting collaboration partners
examples: Varied experimentally across workshops in a randomized way at both Alpine Rendez-Vous events; the article notes "we opted for a paper-based brochure as it is easy to use".
key_sources: Eberle, J., Stegmann, K., Barrat, A., Fischer, F., & Lund, K. (2021). Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09345-7

article_title: Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data
citation: Eberle, J., Stegmann, K., Barrat, A., Fischer, F., & Lund, K. (2021). Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09345-7
title: Network-driven and person-driven selection patterns in the initiation of scientific collaborations
description: The article organizes the onset of collaboration around three types of selection of new collaboration partners: face-to-face contact opportunity, network-driven patterns, and person-driven patterns. Network-driven patterns rest on the assumption that "the way in which persons choose relations is strongly influenced by the (local) structure of their social network", making easily accessible network partners more likely, via reciprocity and transitivity. Person-driven patterns are preferences for specific others, studied as homophily (seeking similar others) versus heterophilous selection, with heterophily linked by social capital theory to gaining new resources such as complementary expertise.
requirements: Selecting suitable partners requires cognitive and social group awareness of other community members' personal and social resources.
constraints: Network-driven selection patterns benefit participants with many existing contacts most; newcomers with few previous contacts can benefit much less, and the article notes these mechanisms had only been shown previously in friendship and small-group contexts, not for collaboration onset.
target_learners: Researchers in interdisciplinary scientific communities, especially newcomers
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting how researchers select collaboration partners at scientific events
examples: The framework structured the analysis: effects implemented in RSiena as reciprocity, transitivity, ego/alter/homophily effects for career level and discipline, and contact duration.
key_sources: Eberle, J., Stegmann, K., Barrat, A., Fischer, F., & Lund, K. (2021). Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09345-7

article_title: Forms of collaboration matters: CSCL across the contexts
citation: Sanna Järvelä · Carolyn Rosé. (2021). Forms of collaboration matters: CSCL across the contexts. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:145–149. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09348-4
title: Net.Create network visualization platform for collaborative historical knowledge building
description: Net.Create is a platform presented by Craig et al. that "affords the opportunity for students to co-construct a network representation of pieces of history". Students reason separately and together about what happened and why, layering their own interpretation over network structures that serve as scaffolding for joint reasoning. The editorial describes its use in history instruction on the time of Claudius, Agrippina, and Nero.
requirements: Used so students can "co-construct a network representation of pieces of history" in collaborative history instruction
target_learners: high school history students
target_learning_goals: collaborative historical reasoning
understanding multiple perspectives on why historical events occur and how they are interconnected
examples: Students used Net.Create to develop understanding of the distant past in the time of Claudius, Agrippina, and Nero over two days, analyzed with Activity Theory as a lens.
key_sources: Sanna Järvelä · Carolyn Rosé. (2021). Forms of collaboration matters: CSCL across the contexts. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:145–149. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09348-4

article_title: Forms of collaboration matters: CSCL across the contexts
citation: Sanna Järvelä · Carolyn Rosé. (2021). Forms of collaboration matters: CSCL across the contexts. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:145–149. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09348-4
title: Social sensitivity in CSCL as an individual and collective ability to collaborate constructively, respectfully, and cohesively
description: Isohätälä et al. introduce social sensitivity as "an overarching term to view the complexity of CSCL research". Drawing on the core concepts of CSCL, they broadly define it as "people's individual and collective ability to collaborate constructively, respectfully, and cohesively". It frames calls for crossing theoretical silos, accelerating interdisciplinary multimodal empirical research, and transferring evidence to practice and policy in CSCL.
requirements: A coherent vision requiring CSCL researchers to cross theoretical silos and integrate cognitive and social perspectives
target_learners: students in technology-supported collaborative learning environments
CSCL researchers, learning designers, teachers, and educational technology developers
target_learning_goals: constructively critical, respectful, and cohesive collaboration
examples: The squib's manifesto calls for interdisciplinary partnerships providing evidence about how emerging technologies influence social sensitivity, and for using social sensitivity as a theme in interaction with developers, teachers, and students.
key_sources: Sanna Järvelä · Carolyn Rosé. (2021). Forms of collaboration matters: CSCL across the contexts. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:145–149. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09348-4

article_title: Guidance in computer-supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms
citation: Tarja Pietarinen · Tuire Palonen · Marja Vauras. (2021). Guidance in computer-supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 16, 261–287. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09347-5
title: ViBSE — Virtual Baltic Sea Explorer web-based inquiry learning environment
description: The Virtual Baltic Sea Explorer (ViBSE) is a web-based learning environment used in this study, described as "designed by professionals in education, biology, and chemistry to create a virtual expedition in a research vessel to study environmental changes in the Baltic Sea". It provides a virtual laboratory for experiments, information and material from an authentic research vessel, R/V Aranda, including interviews and an integrated biology–chemistry library, grounded in authentic marine biology data. Its main aim was to scaffold collaborative learning toward deeper understanding through shared problematizing across two disciplines.
requirements: Students worked in small groups with a shared laptop within the structured-inquiry VLE; guidance on VLE use and collaboration was provided before the working period
constraints: The environment was operationalized in English rather than the students' native language
target_learners: 16- to 18-year-old senior high school students in advanced biology or chemistry courses
target_learning_goals: Understanding ocean acidification through interdisciplinary biology-chemistry virtual experimentation and collaborative inquiry
examples: Students completed three 75–95 min sessions covering hypothesis and experiment planning, experimentation and analyses, and conclusions with a joint group presentation
key_sources: Tarja Pietarinen · Tuire Palonen · Marja Vauras. (2021). Guidance in computer-supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 16, 261–287. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09347-5

article_title: Guidance in computer-supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms
citation: Tarja Pietarinen · Tuire Palonen · Marja Vauras. (2021). Guidance in computer-supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 16, 261–287. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09347-5
title: Shared orchestration pattern: whole-class introduction, walking around, group observation and occasional whole-class announcements
description: During technology-enhanced collaborative inquiry without dedicated orchestration tools, all four teachers followed a common classroom orchestration pattern. As the article describes it, they "started with a joint introduction, then walked around the classroom, observing and assessing group performance and occasionally making whole-class announcements, which is in line with the empirical findings of Greiffenhagen (2012)". When walking around, teachers regularly stopped by a group, provided help if needed, and followed the group activity until the target problem was solved before moving on, so groups were not left prematurely without guidance.
requirements: A teacher present in the classroom circulating among autonomous small groups
A technological environment students can largely operate without constant intervention
constraints: Teachers in the study were novices at guiding students in the VLE; time spent observing (over a third of attention) may partly reflect unfamiliarity with the environment
target_learners: High school science students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: Sustaining collaborative scientific inquiry in a virtual laboratory
examples: All four teachers observed their groups and provided task- and technical-related guidance, while socio-emotional support and off-topic discussions occurred only with some groups
key_sources: Tarja Pietarinen · Tuire Palonen · Marja Vauras. (2021). Guidance in computer-supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 16, 261–287. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09347-5

article_title: Guidance in computer-supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms
citation: Tarja Pietarinen · Tuire Palonen · Marja Vauras. (2021). Guidance in computer-supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 16, 261–287. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09347-5
title: Provide stronger socio-emotional support to low-confident collaborative inquiry groups
description: Because the four teachers provided socio-emotional support only minimally (4% of coded guidance), the article argues teachers should deliberately add socio-emotional support during CSCL inquiry. It states that "Stronger socio-emotional support would enhance student engagement and self-efficacy, and consequently, the collective outcome of the less successful groups". This rests on evidence that students with low subject self-efficacy need and benefit from teachers' emotional support, and that selective attention to already-engaged groups can disadvantage low-confidence groups.
requirements: Teachers must attend to and monitor all groups, including those that do not directly ask for help
constraints: The article presents this as a future research and practice concern, not as a manipulated effect tested in this study
target_learners: Secondary science students, especially those with low task-related self-confidence
target_learning_goals: Emotional and social engagement in collaborative science inquiry
examples: In Elisa's classroom the two best outcome groups were left without any socio-emotional support, and one group in each of three classrooms received none
key_sources: Tarja Pietarinen · Tuire Palonen · Marja Vauras. (2021). Guidance in computer-supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. article_title: Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis
citation: Ollesch, L., Heimbuch, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09346-6
title: Group awareness tools framework distinguishing cognitive and behavioral GA information for wiki-based CSCL
description: GATs collect, transform, and present information about group members in collaborative learning environments. The article distinguishes cognitive GATs, which visualize group members' knowledge, interest, or opinions, from behavioral GATs, which visualize activities such as contribution counts. Each type addresses a distinct wiki challenge — selecting meaningful content or stimulating active content production — while providing implicit guidance that supports self-regulated collaboration without explicit instructions. The article argues both types should be understood and designed together rather than in isolation.
requirements: Learners must be in computer-mediated collaborative settings where awareness information is not naturally salient, as the article notes GA information is often not salient enough there.
constraints: The article states that GA tool types are often examined separately or combined without disentangling their specific functions, limiting clarity about their respective roles.
target_learners: University students collaborating in wiki learning environments
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge construction
Collaborative writing quality
examples: The article cites Sangin et al.'s knowledge awareness tool based on pretest scores and Janssen et al.'s participation tool as established examples of each GAT type.
key_sources: Ollesch, L., Heimbuch, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09346-6

article_title: Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis
citation: Ollesch, L., Heimbuch, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09346-6
title: Co-evolution of cognitive and social systems through internalization and externalization in wiki-based learning
description: The article applies a co-evolution account in which individual cognitive systems and collaborative wiki content mutually shape each other. Learners internalize wiki information through internal assimilation or accommodation processes, changing their own knowledge, and externalize it by adding content or restructuring wiki sections. This framework explains why cognitive and behavioral processes are closely intertwined in wiki-based learning.
requirements: Beneficial learning requires encountering information that contrasts with learners' original assumptions.
constraints: Not all types of interaction have the same beneficial effects; simple participation does not guarantee valuable qualitative cognition in wiki collaboration.
target_learners: Wiki users in collaborative learning scenarios
target_learning_goals: Individual knowledge acquisition through wiki interaction
Collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The article connects Piaget's cognitive conflict to wiki collaboration: encountering contrasting viewpoints triggers internal assimilation/accommodation for individual learning and external assimilation/accommodation for wiki restructuring.
key_sources: Ollesch, L., Heimbuch, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09346-6

article_title: Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis
citation: Ollesch, L., Heimbuch, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09346-6
title: Wiki learning environment with knowledge bars and participation bars at individual, group, and subgroup levels
description: A self-designed wiki environment on energy sources in which awareness information appears as horizontal bars in the discussion forum in the header and next to threads. Yellow knowledge bars visualize subgroup knowledge; blue participation bars visualize contribution counts, with low, medium, and high levels presented at individual, whole-group, and subgroup levels across 12 discussion threads on energy types.
requirements: Participants received an explanation of the bar functions without being explicitly told how to deal with such GA information.
constraints: The wiki article itself contained no GA visualizations; bars appeared only in the discussion forum header and beside threads.
target_learners: University students collaborating on wiki articles
target_learning_goals: Collaborative writing
Content selection from discussion forums
examples: Each of the 12 discussion threads on energy types paired two bogus collaborators, one for and one against the energy form, with subgroup knowledge and participation bars displayed beside the thread title.
key_sources: Ollesch, L., Heimbuch, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09346-6

article_title: Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis
citation: Ollesch, L., Heimbuch, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09346-6
title: Develop group awareness tools from a holistic perspective combining cognitive and behavioral information
description: The article concludes that designing GA tools requires a holistic perspective combining both GA information types rather than relying on a single type alone. Because cognitive and behavioral challenges co-occur in wiki learning, and the article argues the two GA information types complement each other, tool developers should present both knowledge-level and participation-level information together in wiki environments.
requirements: Both the cognitive challenge of selecting meaningful content and the behavioral challenge of stimulating active contributions must be addressed simultaneously for GA tools to support wiki learning processes fully.
constraints: Providing one type of GA information might not have been enough to make learners aware of how much and what kind of content is desirable.
target_learners: Wiki-based CSCL participants
Collaborative writing groups in higher education
target_learning_goals: Improving wiki article quality
Supporting collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The study's combination condition presented knowledge bars and participation bars simultaneously in a wiki discussion forum on energy sources, alongside single-type and control conditions for comparison.

article_title: Ethnomethodologically informed
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Ethnomethodologically informed. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9142-3
title: Ethnomethodology as epistemic framing for CSCL research
description: Stahl situates ethnomethodology (EM) as a foundational epistemic orientation for CSCL, defining CSCL as the study of joint meaning and grounding CSCL in EM's explicit study of those methods. This defines CSCL's rational grounding in ethnography, where EM defines attention to methods of intersubjectivity, and links CSCL to conversation analysis as a strand of EM focused on sequential analysis of interaction.
requirements: Sufficient temporal granularity of interaction data (logs, recordings, or transcripts) to support sequential microanalysis of group cognition
constraints: EM case studies use situated, non-generalizable analyses rather than controlled experiments; designed artifacts and collaboration practices must be analyzed from within members' rather than analysts' terminology
target_learners: CSCL researchers
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning methods of intersubjectivity and joint meaning making
examples: Stahl links Koschmann's foundational CSCL framing to Garfinkel's ethnomethodology and conversation analysis as an exemplar EM method
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Ethnomethodologically informed. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9142-3

article_title: Ethnomethodologically informed
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Ethnomethodologically informed. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9142-3
title: Analyze educational technology use from the participants' perspective rather than imposing preconceived codes
description: Stahl argues EM rejects coding schemes, predefined hypotheses, and researcher-imposed frameworks; instead research should use thick description to analyze what learners make mean, what participants can see, and how they display mutual meaning as accountable. In CSCL this means studying learner actions and discourse from the learner's perspective without pre-structuring analysis.
requirements: Data must include naturally occurring interaction (transcripts, logs, recordings) with sufficient detail to display participants' own accountability of meaning
constraints: Limits generalization: single case studies; analysis validity depends on data sessions and consensual reader-check by experienced analysts
target_learners: CSCL researchers
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning: understanding interaction and meaning making from participants' own perspective
examples: Stahl describes how EM researchers use detailed transcripts so readers can validate the analysis via their own cultural understanding
key_sources: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Ethnomethodologically informed. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9142-3

article_title: Ethnomethodologically informed
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Ethnomethodologically informed. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9142-3
title: Base collaborative-technology design on EM findings from interaction analysis
description: Stahl argues the insights obtained from EM interaction analysis can inform CSCL technology and pedagogy design: findings about which moments in interaction cause breakdown, struggle, or confusion can be used to critique a system or lesson and to suggest redesign. This connects EM microanalysis of learner interaction directly to design-based research in CSCL.
requirements: Access to detailed interaction data showing how learners use a specific technology or pedagogy in concrete settings
constraints: Design implications arise from single, situated case studies rather than statistical generalizations
target_learners: CSCL technology and pedagogy designers
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning: designing artifacts and lessons that better mediate collaborative meaning making
examples: Stahl notes EM can contribute to the analysis phase of design-based research (citing the Design-Based Research Collective, 2003)

article_title: Ethnomethodologically informed
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2012). Ethnomethodologically informed. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 7:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9142-3
title: Validate interaction analyses through data sessions and multiple experienced analysts
description: Stahl proposes data sessions—involving multiple analysts reviewing the same data—as a mechanism for guarding against bias and idiosyncrasy in EM case analysis. Because the accountability of discourse makes it intersubjectively understandable, analysts sharing cultural understanding with participants can reach consensus on the meaning displayed. Detailed transcripts are published to allow reader validation.
requirements: Analysts must share the relevant cultural understanding with the discourse participants
constraints: Builds consensus rather than statistical generalization; suited to single or small sets of case studies
target_learners: CSCL researchers
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning: producing intersubjectively valid analyses of group meaning making
examples: EM case-study publications routinely include very detailed transcripts so readers can confirm the analysis from their own cultural understanding

article_title: CSCL artifacts
citation: G. Stahl & S. Ludvigsen & N. Law & U. Cress. (2014). CSCL artifacts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 237–245. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9200-0
title: CSCL defined as a research community concerned with intersubjective meaning making mediated by designed artifacts
description: The editorial modifies Koschmann's paradigm definition of CSCL to foreground artifacts: 'CSCL is a research community that produces papers centrally concerned with intersubjective meaning and the practices of meaning making as joint activity, and how best to design CSCL artifacts to mediate these practices.' An artifact is defined as a physical object created by people and embodying human meaning, whose meaning is projected by designers but must also be enacted by users. The framework treats meaning creation as social and intersubjective, not purely mental.
requirements: Meaning creation must be analyzed as a social process, necessarily intersubjectively defined
constraints: The article notes CSCL research is not defined by fixed attributes, but by the evolving work of an international community
target_learners: student groups collaborating with computer support
target_learning_goals: intersubjective meaning making in joint activity
examples: The editorial presents five pivotal artifact roles in typical CSCL settings, from communication media to co-constructed group products
key_sources: G. Stahl & S. Ludvigsen & N. Law & U. Cress. (2014). CSCL artifacts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 237–245. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9200-0

article_title: CSCL artifacts
citation: G. Stahl & S. Ludvigsen & N. Law & U. Cress. (2014). CSCL artifacts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 237–245. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9200-0
title: Post-cognitive CSCL approach: dialectical, interactional and dynamic analysis of group meaning making
description: The editorial summarizes the CSCL paradigm as a post-cognitive approach 'dialectical (the problem and technological artifacts that mediate the group interaction must be seen to be enacted by that interaction), interactional (group-cognitive phenomena should not be reduced to individual mental structures)'. It is 'dynamic (there should be a concern with developmental processes at multiple levels)'. Learning is treated as essentially intersubjective and interactional, studied at the group unit of analysis rather than through individual pre/post outcomes.
requirements: Analysis must investigate dynamic developmental processes through which individual, small-group and community cognitive practices emerge
constraints: Group-cognitive phenomena are not to be reduced to individual mental structures
target_learners: student dyads and small groups in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: group-level meaning making and collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The two empirical papers in the issue are described as adopting and advancing this dialectical, interactional and dynamic paradigm
key_sources: G. Stahl & S. Ludvigsen & N. Law & U. Cress. (2014). CSCL artifacts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 237–245. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9200-0

article_title: CSCL artifacts
citation: G. Stahl & S. Ludvigsen & N. Law & U. Cress. (2014). CSCL artifacts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 237–245. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9200-0
title: Damşa's three inter-connected layers of small-group learning: productive interaction, knowledge-object development and shared epistemic agency
description: The editorial describes Damşa's analytical framework, in which she 'distinguishes three inter-connected layers of small-group learning: productive interaction, knowledge-object development and shared epistemic agency'. Productive interaction is interaction that potentially contributes to the group production of its target object; the knowledge object is the group's goal, provided from outside but interpreted and refined by the group; agency covers setting goals, pursuing them and concluding when accomplished.
requirements: The objective of producing a report must provide a grounded basis for analyzing interaction
constraints: The knowledge-object objective is largely proposed from outside the group interaction, e.g. by a university course
target_learners: university student teams working on course projects
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction through co-authored artifacts
examples: Interaction is analyzed by how it contributes to evolving the discussion and successive drafts of the team report
key_sources: G. Stahl & S. Ludvigsen & N. Law & U. Cress. (2014). CSCL artifacts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 237–245. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9200-0

article_title: CSCL artifacts
citation: G. Stahl & S. Ludvigsen & N. Law & U. Cress. (2014). CSCL artifacts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 237–245. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9200-0
title: Shared epistemic agency observable in interaction, including referred agency embedded in designed artifacts
description: Building on Emirbayer and Mische, the editorial treats agency as observable in interaction rather than a hypothetical psychological state, and extends it to groups and artifacts: 'Designed artifacts exercise a referred agency, designed into the form of the artifact by the intentions of the designer — and visible in that form.' Interaction can then be viewed as an inter-action among many sources of agency converging in a concrete situation. Group members orient the group subtly toward projected joint goals.
requirements: Agency must be analyzed in excerpts of productive interaction, not inferred as an internal state
constraints: The article notes this does not necessarily involve a rationalist sub-goal hierarchy
target_learners: student groups using designed CSCL software
target_learning_goals: negotiating, reflecting on and carrying out joint action objectives
examples: A software developer embeds goals in software that determine to some extent how it can and cannot be used

article_title: Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding
citation: Ishari Amarasinghe; Davinia Hernández-Leo; H. Ulrich Hoppe (2021). Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09351-9
title: Deconstructed facets of orchestration load
description: The article treats orchestration load not as a black box but as a multifaceted notion encompassing content load (e.g. evaluating multiple student answers), cognitive load (processing new information in short activities), and the effort of diagnosing deviations and using orchestration technology. It models teachers' actionable differences under different support provisions to derive these facets, arguing "all types of load, i.e., content, orchestration and cognitive load, reflect the valuable and attentive cognitive processing teachers are required to engage in real-time". The load a provision adds or removes is read from how it changes teachers' orchestration actions.
requirements: Analysis of orchestration load requires modelling teachers' observable orchestration actions under contrasting support conditions
constraints: Existing definitions of orchestration load remain fuzzy, with different definitions across the literature the article cites; no standard measurements to quantify orchestration load are available
target_learners: teachers orchestrating CSCL activities in co-located classrooms
target_learning_goals: effective real-time regulation of scripted collaborative learning
examples: Six teachers' orchestration actions were modelled with ENA under no-dashboard, mirroring, and guiding conditions to derive load facets
key_sources: Ishari Amarasinghe; Davinia Hernández-Leo; H. Ulrich Hoppe (2021). Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09351-9

article_title: Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding
citation: Ishari Amarasinghe; Davinia Hernández-Leo; H. Ulrich Hoppe (2021). Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09351-9
title: PyramidApp with teacher-facing mirroring and guiding dashboard
description: PyramidApp is a web-based tool implementing a version of the Pyramid collaborative script, providing "an activity authoring space and a teacher-facing LA dashboard for teachers as well as an activity enactment space for students". Teachers configure class size, group size, pyramid levels, durations, and up to 10 expected keywords, and can enable automatic alerts. The dashboard has Responses Related and Participation Related tabs, a timeline with remaining-time countdown, runtime controls (increase time, pause, next level, end), and supporting posting predefined messages to groups. The guiding support adds an alert mechanism flagging critical moments such as missing keywords, skipped submissions, and insufficient remaining submission or voting time.
requirements: Teachers trained beforehand on the dashboard features and functionalities; the article reports around 45 minutes to one hour of training per teacher
constraints: Alert criteria were fixed by the system; one teacher suggested alert thresholds such as the half-of-time rule should be a parameter modifiable by the teacher for activities with longer discussion and rating times
target_learners: higher-education students working in classroom collaborative learning sessions
target_learning_goals: structured consensus-building discussion across individual, small-group, and class-wide social planes
examples: Alerts included no keywords detected within the first 20% of answers, and more-time-for-voting when 50% of groups had not finished voting and 50% of voting time had passed
key_sources: Ishari Amarasinghe; Davinia Hernández-Leo; H. Ulrich Hoppe (2021). Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09351-9

citation: Ishari Amarasinghe; Davinia Hernández-Leo; H. Ulrich Hoppe (2021). Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09351-9
title: Pyramid collaborative learning flow pattern
description: The Pyramid script structures collaborative learning flow so students first solve a problem individually, then join small groups (usually pairs) to share and agree on common solutions via voting and chat, and are progressively merged into increasingly larger groups forming the pyramid structure. It "aims to provide opportunities for all learners to express their solutions and to discuss their ideas with peers" and to support consensus-building across phases one after another. In this study it was enacted with PyramidApp in classrooms with teacher orchestration support.
requirements: Sustained participation from all learners from beginning to end of the consensus-building process; teacher monitoring so groups reaching premature or misleading consensus can be redirected
constraints: Groups advance at different rates, creating idle time for faster groups and potential off-task behaviour, while slower groups need more time; teachers cannot constantly distribute attention across social planes without support
target_learners: classroom learners from individual through pair to large-group phases
target_learning_goals: reaching informed consensus and expressing and discussing ideas with peers
examples: Sessions in the study ranged from 6 to 20 minutes with 7 to 71 students, e.g. a question about sharing knowledge about research writing
