article_title: Socio-technical configurations for productive talk
citation: Peter Reimann. (2021). Socio-technical configurations for productive talk. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:301–306. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09354-6
title: Epistemic Network Analysis reveals temporally ordered patterns in sequentially produced coded data
description: The article describes ENA as an extension of bag-of-words text-mining that adds a sliding time "window" so co-occurrences are counted over meaningful parts of text, called "stanzas". Coded data form the nodes of a transition graph with co-occurrences as edges, allowing graph features and network visualization. The article states that "ENA allows the researcher to reveal temporally ordered patterns in sequentially produced data" and that it enabled nuanced condition differences and a better understanding of Simple questions' roles in talk.
requirements: Input data are coded in some high-level coding framework, such as teacher actions (7 codes) or student dyad interactions (9 categories), as the article describes.
target_learners: collaborative learners in classrooms and pair-programming settings, including students and teachers
target_learning_goals: understanding and explaining patterns of productive collaborative talk and interaction
examples: Amarasinghe and colleagues used ENA to find nuanced differences between mirroring and guidance dashboard conditions; Vandenberg and colleagues used it to understand the different roles Simple questions played.
key_sources: Peter Reimann. (2021). Socio-technical configurations for productive talk. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:301–306. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09354-6

article_title: Socio-technical configurations for productive talk
citation: Peter Reimann. (2021). Socio-technical configurations for productive talk. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:301–306. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09354-6
title: The ICAP framework as a conceptual pillar for collaborative learning benefits in CSCL
description: The article presents ICAP (Chi & Wylie, 2014; Chi et al., 2018) as providing "conceptual and evidential support for the benefits of collaborative learning over and above all other modes of learning". Within its taxonomy, interactive (collaborative) question generation is expected to lead to the highest learning gains, above constructive individual generation and better than active and passive modes. The article argues that, while not specific to computer-supported collaboration, ICAP might well serve as a conceptual pillar for the CSCL field.
requirements: The framework lens implies designing activities that push learners from passive and active modes toward constructive and interactive modes of engagement.
constraints: The article notes ICAP has so far hardly been used in CSCL research, and that closer attention to the role of technology in learning and collaboration would advance it.
target_learners: visitors and learners in CSCL contexts, including museum group visitors
target_learning_goals: maximizing learning gains through interactive modes of cognitive engagement
examples: The museum study used the ICAP taxonomy as its theoretical framework to justify comparing interactive versus constructive question-generation modes.

article_title: Socio-technical configurations for productive talk
citation: Peter Reimann. (2021). Socio-technical configurations for productive talk. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:301–306. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09354-6
title: Task epistemic complexity drives the tension between epistemic and social attention in orchestration
description: Because the study's epistemic artefacts "were not simple yes/no answers, but rather solutions to programming problems", teachers had to invest considerable effort in appraising them, which in the mirroring condition shifted attention toward epistemic rather than social aspects. Designers of collaboration support should therefore anticipate that the effort required to appraise student artefacts consumes orchestration capacity that would otherwise go to social interaction. The article treats this as a genuine tension revealed by the data.
requirements: Teachers need cognitive resources for appraising complex epistemic artefacts; tools should reduce this load (e.g., guidance dashboards) to keep attention balanced.
constraints: The interpretation that the guidance condition balances attention is tentative due to the small sample and absence of learning outcome measures.
target_learners: teachers orchestrating synchronous group work in classrooms
target_learning_goals: balancing attention to epistemic and social aspects of student collaboration
examples: In the six-teacher dashboard study, a variant of the pyramid collaboration script was enacted on individual, group, and class levels with students voting on the quality of programming solutions.

article_title: Many are the ways to learn identifying multi-modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities
citation: Jauwairia Nasir, Aditi Kothiyal, Barbara Bruno, Pierre Dillenbourg. (2021). Many are the ways to learn identifying multi-modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2021) 16:485–523. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09358-2
title: Two-approach multi-modal learning analytics technique linking behavioral clusters to learning outcomes (Approach A backward, Approach B forward)
description: This technique builds behavioral profiles of dyads by clustering teams on multi-modal behaviors (log, video, audio features) and then relating behavioral clusters to learning and performance outcomes. Approach A connects "the learning outcomes back to the behaviors observed during the learning process", while Approach B is "a forward approach as it helps to move from multi-modal behaviors to learning outcomes". Approach B was designed to detect multiple behavioral profiles for the same learning profile, which Approach A's one-cluster-one-profile assumption cannot do; it succeeded where Approach A found no significantly discriminating behavior between its cluster pairs.
requirements: Behavioral clusters from Approach B must show significant differences in learning gains (requirement 1) and a comprehensible one-to-many or many-to-many mapping to learning/performance clusters (requirement 2) before their labels are used as classifier ground truth for the final classifier.
constraints: The dataset treats all behaviors as cross-sectional averages over the entire task duration, not time series data, and behaviors were normalized across teams to values between 0 and 1.
target_learners: Children aged 9 to 12 years working in dyads on open-ended collaborative problems
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of minimum-spanning-tree problems in a problem-based learning activity
examples: The technique applied to the JUSThink dataset produced three behavioral clusters (Expressive Explorers, Calm Tinkerers, Silent Wanderers) with excellent classification results, reported previously in Nasir, Bruno, and Dillenbourg (2020a).

citation: Saqr, M., & López-Pernas, S. (2021). Modelling diffusion in computer-supported collaborative learning: a large scale learning analytics study. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09356-4
title: Diffusion-based centrality framework for measuring uptake in CSCL discourse graphs
description: A framework representing threaded CSCL discussion as a directed post-reply network in which centrality measures operationalize the uptake of ideas and stimulation of further discussion. It combines diffusion-specific measures — "Maximum Neighborhood Component (MNC) is the cardinality of connected neighboring nodes excluding the target node", coreness ("similar to H-index"), cross clique connectivity, and diffusion degree — with traditional degree, closeness, betweenness and eigenvector centralities, positioning uptake capability as a function of position, connectedness and embeddedness in the network.
requirements: A graph representation of post-reply interactions with source, target, and thread structure
target_learners: students in problem-based learning groups
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction and argumentation
examples: In the article's fictional scenario, node G in the network core achieved the highest diffusion centrality while the highest-degree node A ranked only third

title: Dataset of 69 Qassim University PBL course offerings with coded forum interactions
description: An integral Moodle forum dataset of all collaborative-module courses at Qassim University between 2013 and 2019, comprising "69 course offerings (15 different courses)" with "3,277 students" and "97,173 total interactions (of which 8,818 were manually coded)". Posts were coded with an adapted Visschers-Pleijers scheme (Questioning, Information discussion, Argument and debate, Procedural, Off-task), reaching a final Cohen's Kappa of 0.91. Each course grade combined an 80% final exam with forum engagement, continuous assessment and PBL group components.

target_learning_goals: collaborative problem-solving and argumentation in online PBL forums
examples: All 69 offerings were included to avoid selection or publication bias across several academic years

title: A collaborative version of MIT App Inventor for group programming
description: The final full article of the issue presents and evaluates a collaborative extension of MIT App Inventor (MAI), "a popular block-based programming (BBP) learning environment designed to aid new programmers in making quick progress towards producing computer programs by removing the need for as much knowledge of programming language syntax." The study explores interactions afforded by a platform not originally designed to be collaborative, applying analytics to gain visibility into behavior patterns. It contrasts individual vs. collaborative work, heterogeneous vs. homogeneous disciplinary-background teams, and team self-efficacy.

constraints: The platform was not originally designed to be collaborative
target_learners: new programmers, including participants with non-computer-science backgrounds

citation: Carolyn Rosé, Sanna Järvelä. (2021). A theory-driven reflection on context-aware support for collaborative discussions in light of analytics, affordances, and platforms. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09360-8
title: Theory-driven units of analysis for educational dialogue across multiple timescales
description: The Baker, Schwarz, and Ludvigsen Squib argues for deep theoretical understanding of discussion and its unit of analysis to inform methods for analyzing dialogue over different timescales, from episodes to societal-scale argumentative knowledge construction. The editors summarize: its aim is "to argue for the necessity for a deep, theoretical understanding of discussion and its unit of analysis." It proceeds in three parts: collective thinking enacted through dialogue, critical considerations of timescales, and how timescales are accounted for in units of analysis applied to platform data. General theories of dialogue, cognition, and collective activity guide chosen units of analysis and explain their deep meaning.
requirements: A deep, theoretical understanding of discussion and its unit of analysis before building analysis methods
constraints: Applying it requires viewing collaboration at a societal level over long periods of time, where interactions occur everywhere and nowhere, crossing modalities through multivocal interconnectedness
target_learners: CSCL researchers and designers
students engaging in collaborative dialogue in local and global contexts
target_learning_goals: collective thinking and collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The example of worldwide collaborative knowledge construction about COVID: real differences in perspective, identity-based clashes of practices, in an immense group over a very long period within an ill-defined activity

title: Combine diverse datasets across multiple timescales, mixing automatic and human analyses, to make dialogue analytics meaningful
description: The editors close by challenging the field with the question raised by Baker et al.: "how can such diverse data sets, over multiple timescales, involving a combination of automatic and human analyses, be combined in a meaningful way". The principle urges researchers designing CSCL studies and analytics to integrate analyses of discussion data across timescales rather than treating single-scale studies as sufficient, and especially welcomes "dialogue" in between data and theories for the following year's submissions.
requirements: Combining automatic and human analyses over multiple timescales in a meaningful way, guided by general theories of dialogue, cognition and collective activity
constraints: Findings from typical small-scale, traditional study environments must be bridged carefully toward societal-level, long-timescale phenomena

citation: Lenka Schnaubert · Freydis Vogel. (2022). Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09367-9
title: Script theory of guidance: four hierarchical components of internal collaboration scripts
description: The article presents collaboration scripts as learners' activated cognitive schemata guiding behavior in social learning situations. It reports that "The script theory of guidance distinguishes four script components that are related in a sequenced and hierarchical way": scriptlets (single activities), scenes (sets of scriptlets in sequential order), plays (the overarching goal comprising all scenes), and roles (how scriptlets are assigned to individuals). External collaboration scripts scaffold learners toward an ideal internal script.
requirements: Learners activate internal scripts based on their interpretation of a social situation and its perceived goals; to be functional, scripts must integrate activities supportive of knowledge and skill acquisition through collaboration
constraints: Learners may struggle to autonomously activate the most appropriate functional internal script in a given situation
target_learners: collaborative learners in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning skills and knowledge acquisition through collaboration
examples: External collaboration scripts are offered as socio-cognitive scaffolding consisting of a sequence of prompts reflecting play, scene, and scriptlet components

title: Cognitive and social group awareness as distinct facets of social context perception in CSCL
description: The article conceptualizes group awareness as "the perception of relevant social information within the collaborative learning situation." It distinguishes cognitive group awareness (the distribution of knowledge or opinions in the group, affecting content-oriented processes and outcomes) from social group awareness (socio-behavioral and socio-emotional aspects affecting group climate and willingness to participate). Both enable learners to regulate and adapt their collaborative learning to the social configuration.
requirements: Goal-oriented collaboration requires awareness of the social context, especially characteristics of the collaborating group and its members
constraints: Social conditions in CSCL settings are highly dynamic; the technological layer can restrict rather than enrich communication channels, making perception of the social environment harder
target_learners: learners in computer-supported collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: effective collaboration and regulation of collaborative learning processes
examples: Group awareness tools collect, transform, and present social context information to ease or guide collaborative learning

title: Self-regulation as a meta-level mechanism reconfiguring internal collaboration scripts and grounded in group awareness
description: The article proposes an integrative account: metacognitive knowledge about learning processes "is used to reconfigure the currently activated internal script" by activating components from other scripts or integrating newly acquired ones. Group awareness is inherently linked to regulation because self-regulation requires monitoring internal and external conditions, which in collaboration includes social conditions. External scripts can scaffold self-, co-, and shared regulation.
requirements: Learners need self-regulation skills to monitor internal and external conditions, set goals, apply strategies, evaluate success, and adapt strategies against internal standards
constraints: Learners often lack the level of self-regulation skills demanded by social learning scenarios; explicit empirical and theoretical connections among all three concepts remain scarce
target_learners: learners in collaborative learning scenarios
target_learning_goals: metacognitive planning, monitoring, evaluation and adaptation of individual and social learning
examples: Group awareness tools build on self-regulated learning mechanisms by providing information without prescribing activities, relying on learners' skills to use the information

title: Balance script-imposed self-regulation demands by integrating regulation activities into collaboration script scaffolds
description: The editorial draws a design principle from the special-issue studies: "the demands for self-regulation when learning with CSCL scripts can be balanced by integrating self-regulation activities in script scaffolds." Scripts can take over parts of regulatory processes, for example by distributing roles and assigning specific activities to each role, or explicitly scaffold regulation activities such as planning, execution and reflection support. This may then lead to better regulation during learning and eventually improved learning outcomes.
requirements: Careful choices when designing scripts; scripts must either take over parts of the regulatory processes (e.g., via role distribution) or explicitly scaffold regulation activities
constraints: Less structured CSCL scripts leaving learners degrees of freedom and adaptation possibilities demand more self-regulation skills from the learner
target_learners: collaborative learners in CSCL settings, from elementary school to university
target_learning_goals: effective regulation of collaborative learning and improved collaborative learning outcomes
examples: Zimmerman and Land's script distributed roles and assigned activities to each role; Kielstra et al.'s script explicitly scaffolded regulation activities for planning, execution and reflection

article_title: Group awareness and regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Lenka Schnaubert, Daniel Bodemer. (2022). Group awareness and regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09361-1
title: Group awareness defined by six aspects: cognitive, conscious, current, individual, social, perceived as valid
description: The article derives a conceptualization of group awareness (GA) as an individually held, conscious, current cognition about social entities in CSCL, distinguishing it from knowledge, shared mental models and situational awareness. It states that GA can be described through six defining aspects: "(1) GA is cognitive, (2) GA is conscious, (3) GA is current, (4) GA is individual, (5) GA is social, and (6) GA is perceived as valid". Each aspect is argued to carry methodological implications, e.g. individual focus enabling pseudo-collaborative laboratory designs and self-report measurement being possible because GA is conscious.
requirements: GA is conceptualized as valid information on a learner's group that is mentally present within the individual learner, so it must be currently activated rather than merely stored
constraints: GA is not defined as an accurate representation: alignment with reality is a characteristic of specific GA instances, not a defining feature
GA relates to cognitions about social entities, not directly to subject-domain content
target_learners: collaborative learners in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: understanding of learning partners and group characteristics relevant to collaboration
examples: The article illustrates GA formation with two students meeting for a statistics team project, where one infers the other's knowledge and motivation from lecture notes plus prior encounters

title: Group awareness as a working-memory state distinct from group-related knowledge
description: The article positions GA as an acute cognitive state closely connected to working memory: GA is "the instant, salient perception and interpretation of (social) information", not a dormant long-term memory structure. Long-term memory structures such as partner models and social schemata contribute to GA generation, but GA itself is distinguished from group-related knowledge by its currency. Formation draws on both bottom-up information from the current social situation and top-down activated long-term memory structures, which become increasingly integrated over time.
requirements: forms and operates within the limits of working memory capacity
requires at least minimal working memory capacity even when supported by stable memory structures
constraints: under high working memory load, maintaining GA may be hampered, and intensive processing and integration of GA information into long-term memory may be severely restricted
target_learners: individual learners in collaborative learning situations
target_learning_goals: monitoring the current social situation during collaboration

citation: Lenka Schnaubert, Daniel Bodemer. (2022). Group awareness and regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09361-1
title: GA participates in three regulatory cycles: regulating GA, regulating social interaction, and regulating partner schema building
description: The article models GA as an integral part of three regulatory processes during CSCL, illustrated in Fig. 2 as "Three types of regulation: (1) regulating GA, (2) regulating social interaction, (3) regulating partner schema building". In cycle (1) learners metacognitively monitor and control their own partner-related cognitions against task- and situation-appropriate standards. In cycle (2) GA guides how learners act, react, and adapt interaction based on perceived social conditions. In cycle (3) GA serves as the informational basis for refining and correcting partner models stored in long-term memory.
requirements: coherent, relevant GA requires continuous regulation and cannot rely on automatic perception
task demands, technological setup, and availability of social information shape which regulatory processes are possible
constraints: the framework focuses on individual self-regulation of cognition and behavior directed at the social context, explicitly not covering self-, co- and shared regulation of content learning itself
some cited awareness tools are static and not suitable to support the full regulatory cycle
target_learners: learners in CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: social interaction regulation, partner modelling, and self-regulation of group-directed cognition
examples: When learners notice a misalignment in understanding of a key concept, they may discuss it to resolve the conflict, then terminate resolution and move on

title: Use GA tools to provide information that guides learning decisions, but design them as supports for, not replacements of, metacognitive regulation
description: GA tools aim at fostering collaborative learning by providing information necessary to make adequate learning decisions, and they process learner data in ways that may exceed human information-collection capabilities. However, because GA is a psychological construct requiring conscious regulation, the article states that "while GA tools may assist by providing information about learning partners, they do not replace the metacognitive regulation processes involved". Tool-based design should therefore be grounded in a conceptual understanding of GA itself.
requirements: designers need a conceptual understanding of GA before tool-based research can explain collaborative processes or design effective tools
constraints: efforts toward attaining GA are secondary to knowledge construction and may even be harmful to learning under certain circumstances due to collaboration load
static awareness tools not intended to catch the dynamics of collaboration cannot support the full regulatory cycle

description: Group awareness tools, as characterized in this editorial, support collaborative and metacognitive processes through a three-step process: sensing and assessing group processes, transforming that assessment into an understandable representation highlighting important structure, and presenting it back to learners. Their distinctive feature among learning dashboards is that representations are "designed specifically for learners as the target audience," so that what learners perceive aids regulatory processes within groups.

citation: Charles Crook. (2022). CSsCL: the performance of collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09364-y
title: Scripting collaborative learning: external prompts and roles to support regulation of joint activity
description: A collaboration script structures joint learning activity by externally prompting participants with options for action: the article defines scripting as 'structuring a joint activity such that participants are externally prompted with possible options for action', with prompts such as requesting information, checking shared agreement, and summarising progress, often tied to assigned roles. Scripts are conceived both as guides for a specific task and as resources that may cultivate collaboration as a general competence through appropriation of 'internal scripts'. The article discusses how scripting depends on self-regulation and group awareness and is central to CSCL research integrating these three concepts.

Scripts must be interpreted by learners; over-scripting risks mechanical execution
constraints: Consistent definition of a script has proved troublesome in the literature
The term risks being used as just a trendy word for lesson plans unless core scripting is distinguished from the didactic envelope

shared knowledge building across cognitive, motivational, social, and emotional domains

It frames this social intelligence as equipping learners for self-regulation in collaboration and as a competence that may itself be cultivated through experience with collaboration scripts, and discusses social cognition and intersubjectivity as traditions for researching it.

title: Collaboration-as-performance: direction, production, and audience as extensions of the theatre metaphor of scripting
description: The article takes seriously the theatre metaphor implied by 'collaboration script' and elaborates collaboration in performance terms, proposing 'three headings under which this question might be pursued: direction, production, and audience'. Direction places teachers in the director role who help students find meaning in script lines before performing them; production concerns how an intervention is produced as an occasion integrating with classroom routine; audience concerns researchers and report readers as witnesses of the performance. Metaphors risk importing unwanted expectations, such as over-scripting, but can provocatively steer neglected themes.

Research environments such as teacher dashboards may support direction within the flow of joint activity
constraints: The theatre-script imposing force might encourage over-scripting of collaborations
Post-intervention student evaluations may solicit polite, calculated answers
Describing collaboration quality from recorded talk is challenged when reliability comes from local codebooks not adopted by others

cultivating students' confidence and ownership in collaboration

article_title: Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2007). Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9010-8
title: Run a research journal as a mechanism of community-based collaborative learning that pairs publication with detailed anonymous critique and revision.
description: The editorial proposes that a journal serving a research field can function simultaneously as a formal publication channel and as peer-guided learning: virtually all published papers went through "extensive critique and revision," and even rejected papers received detailed reviews. The reviewers and Editorial Board "contributed significantly to guiding the major revisions through which all accepted papers passed," so the community establishes the journal's content and tone. This makes the review process itself a vehicle for mutual assistance and learning within the community.
requirements: An engaged Editorial Board and additional reviewers willing to provide deep, detailed constructive feedback on submissions, including papers that are not ultimately published.
constraints: Journal interaction is anonymous, which the authors say allows critique that is more frank and detailed than at conferences, but it lacks the informality and direct interaction of meetings and conferences.
target_learners: Research authors submitting papers to the CSCL community
target_learning_goals: Improving research writing, argumentation, and understanding of what is needed for future publication
examples: During ijCSCL's first year, virtually all published papers passed through extensive critique and revision, and the many unpublished papers each received several detailed reviews.

article_title: Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2007). Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9010-8
title: Flash-theme special issues on Scripting in CSCL, Methods for Evaluating CSCL, and Graphical Support for CSCL
description: A set of special issues ijCSCL began publishing in its second volume on topics that "flashed" up in the field through spontaneous practitioner concern rather than editorial solicitation. Reviews on these themes are coordinated by Associate Editors—Barbara Wasson for scripting, Claire O'Malley for evaluation methods, and Daniel D. Suthers for graphical support—in a move to broaden editorial responsibilities as the journal becomes more established. The mechanism is intended to let the journal "give voice to the concerns of the field in a timely and flexible way."
requirements: Open responsiveness to workshop-originated topic proposals from practitioners, and Associate Editors to coordinate theme-based reviews.
constraints: The themes were not solicited by the ijCSCL Editorial Board but arose from practitioner workshops and concerns.
target_learners: CSCL researchers and practitioners
target_learning_goals: Advancing CSCL research on scripting, evaluation methods, and graphical support
examples: This year's volume begins with two papers on the flash theme of Learning in Communities, drawn from a 2006 Penn State workshop attended by 29 researchers and sponsored by the NSF.

article_title: Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2007). Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9010-8
title: Community-based CSCL: communities of practice as socio-cultural contexts for collaborative learning
description: An account the editorial frames from the issue's two articles on learning in communities, specifying the collaborative in CSCL as "community based" in the sense that communities of practice, as introduced by Lave and Wenger, provide socio-cultural contexts in which collaborative learning can take place. Fischer, Rohde and Wulf elaborate CoPs with distinctions into networks of practice and communities of interest as variants, and the approach brings CSCW and HCI considerations into the CSCL discussion at what the editorial calls the macro-scale.
requirements: A community context (CoP or variant) within which computer-supported collaboration takes place.
constraints: Illustrated by the issue's articles in relation to universities and to non-profit organizations / NGOs; the editorial notes a reviewer may dispute whether pattern-based theory is strong enough for the field.
target_learners: Members of communities of practice, university students, and volunteers in community-based organizations
target_learning_goals: Learning through participation in communities, including learning how to design and use community-based learning technology
examples: Carroll and Faroque propose frameworks as a middle layer of theoretical constructs mediating between general patterns and individual cases, based on work with non-profit community-based organizations.

title: Assess the quality of computer-supported collaboration processes with theoretically refined, operationalized dimensions of interaction rather than coding alone.
description: The editorial reports that Meier, Spada and Rummel differentiated as many as nine dimensions of interaction for quantitative analysis, derived through bottom-up qualitative content analysis refined by top-down theory-informed considerations. Once operationalized for reliable application, these dimensions supported a rating scheme whose successful application suggested "such a ranking approach has advantages over coding for many research questions, while still allowing a quantitative comparison of alternative conditions."
requirements: Dimensions must be operationalized for reliable application, deriving from a combination of bottom-up qualitative analysis and top-down theory-informed refinement.
constraints: The rating approach is suggested as advantageous for many research questions; it is applied to dyads of college students engaged in videoconferencing, as the editorial reports.
target_learners: College students collaborating via videoconferencing
target_learning_goals: Improving the quality of computer-supported collaboration processes
examples: The rating scheme was developed and successfully applied to assess the quality of computer-supported collaboration processes among dyads of college students engaged in videoconferencing.

article_title: ‘Supporting socially shared regulation during collaborative task-oriented reading’
citation: Kielstra, J., Molenaar, I., van Steensel, R., & Verhoeven, L. (2022). 'Supporting socially shared regulation during collaborative task‑oriented reading'. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 17, 65–105. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09365-x
title: 'Y-read?' digital learning environment with a macro- and micro-level collaboration script for socially shared regulation of task-oriented reading
description: 'Y-read?' is a digital learning environment integrating a collaboration script and the TOR-test, built from four script elements: play, scene, scriptlets and roles. The "macro-level script combines the components 'play', 'scene' and 'roles'" and guides four scenes: pre-task group planning, individual task execution, individual reflection and post-task group reflection. A stated novelty is "a full automation flow of role information and related learning materials to different participants on four different tablets that synchronously drive face-to-face collaboration". Roles were rotated across four lessons.
requirements: Students collaborate face-to-face in groups of four, each with their own device; information distribution follows the Jigsaw distributed-information principle to elicit interdependency.
constraints: Only pre- and post-task regulation was performed collaboratively; task execution and individual reflection were individual phases.
target_learners: prevocational secondary school students (10th grade, average age 15.7)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive regulation of task-oriented reading: task representation, strategy selection, strategy reflection
examples: During pre-task planning, the leader received guiding questions, the writer recorded task-representation ratings on 1–10 scales, the task guard held the task, and the text guard a blurred text showing only title, headers and pictures.
key_sources: Kielstra, J., Molenaar, I., van Steensel, R., & Verhoeven, L. (2022). 'Supporting socially shared regulation during collaborative task‑oriented reading'. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 17, 65–105. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09365-x

article_title: ‘Supporting socially shared regulation during collaborative task-oriented reading’
citation: Kielstra, J., Molenaar, I., van Steensel, R., & Verhoeven, L. (2022). 'Supporting socially shared regulation during collaborative task‑oriented reading'. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 17, 65–105. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09365-x
title: Four types of intra-group social metacognitive interaction (ignored, accepted, shared, co-constructed) as a measure of sharedness in socially shared regulated learning
description: The study's framework for socially shared regulated learning (SSRL) distinguishes levels of sharedness by how group members relate to each other's metacognitive contributions. Metacognitive episodes are coded as one of "four types of intra-group social metacognitive interaction: ignored, accepted, shared and co-constructed". Co-construction, where students build on and elaborate on each other's metacognitive activities, is posited to foster meaningful SSRL and potentially improve individual regulation. Depth of regulation is analysed in parallel as low- versus deep-level orientation, planning and reflection.
requirements: Transcribed group discussion coded at utterance level into metacognitive episodes, with changes in topic marking episode boundaries.
constraints: Interrater reliability was moderate to excellent across the four interaction types (K from 0.71 to 0.93), yet co-constructed episodes were rare in this sample.
target_learners: secondary school students working in collaborative reading groups
target_learning_goals: socially shared metacognitive regulation during collaborative task-oriented reading
examples: Table 2 exemplifies co-construction: one student proposes targeted reading, another confirms, and a third adds the reason 'Because you have to look something up'.

article_title: Collaborative analytics-supported reflective Assessment for Scaffolding Pre-service Teachers’ collaborative Inquiry and Knowledge Building
citation: Yang, Y., Zhu, G., Sun, D., & Chan, C. K. K. (2022). Collaborative analytics-supported reflective Assessment for Scaffolding Pre-service Teachers’ collaborative Inquiry and Knowledge Building. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09372-y
title: A conceptual design framework for PST collaborative inquiry combining knowledge building principles with collaborative-analytics reflective assessment
description: The article proposes a conceptual and design framework in which knowledge building principles emphasise "epistemic agency, idea improvement, community knowledge and transformative assessment" and PSTs take epistemic agency to foster idea improvement using transformative assessment focused on metacognitive reflection. Two key design components follow: sustained idea-driven knowledge building inquiry in Knowledge Forum writing, and collaborative analytics consisting of KBDeX visualizations plus interaction rubrics and prompt questions supporting metacognitive reflection. PSTs use the analytics to reflect on and assess ongoing Knowledge Forum work for deepening inquiry and revision.
requirements: PSTs must engage in sustained idea-driven inquiry for knowledge advancement situated in Knowledge Forum writing, posing questions, co-constructing explanations, building on peers’ ideas, and revising theories
Analytics, rubrics, and prompt questions must be provided so PSTs can reflect and assess their ongoing Knowledge Forum work
constraints: The framework is designed for pre-service teachers developing collaborative inquiry and knowledge building competencies; at the start of the course most PSTs had limited knowledge of and ability in collaborative inquiry and knowledge building
target_learners: pre-service teachers in higher education teacher preparation
target_learning_goals: collaborative inquiry competencies
knowledge building and community knowledge advancement
metacognitive reflection and epistemic agency

title: Transformative assessment should be embedded, concurrent and transparent, and transformative of the inquiry process, with analytics making process and outcome data explicit
description: The article defines reflective and transformative assessment as an extension of formative assessment with three features: "(1) it is embedded, as assessment is an integral part of learning and itself is learning; (2) it entails a concurrent and transparent inquiry process, and the process and outcome data made explicit by analytical tools improve students’ awareness of their current state and understanding of where should they go; and (3) it is transformative". In this study the principle is enacted through KBDeX visualizations, knowledge building interaction rubrics, and scaffold prompt questions that guide collective reflection and adaptation of ongoing inquiry.

Process and outcome data must be made explicit by analytical tools so students can see their current state and where to go next
Assessment must guide students to monitor and reflect on, and transform, their inquiry and learning processes

title: KBDeX (Knowledge Building Discourse Explorer) social network analysis tool used to visualize collaborative ideas and discourse for student reflection
description: KBDeX is "a social network analysis tool designed to visualize and represent collaborative ideas and discourse" (Oshima et al., 2012). Its primary purpose is "to analyze online discourse data to depict community advances", and it is used mostly by researchers; in this study the authors developed KBDeX output as visualization diagrams that students used as feedback on their ongoing Knowledge Forum discussions. Visualizations included growth curves of the cumulative degree centrality of ideas and idea network maps, which PSTs were taught to read and use for reflection and assessment of their discourse.

The editorial writes that Crook pointed to "a concept of multilayered 'relations' as a lens for understanding how increasing knowledge of the synergy between collaboration scripts, self-regulation, and group awareness can help guide us as we design joint activity." Relations are enacted through processes studied via multiple data streams.

article_title: Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach
citation: Shupin Li · Johanna Pöysä-Tarhonen · Päivi Häkkinen (2022). Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:191–223 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09369-7
title: ATC21S framework distinguishing social and cognitive CPS skills enacted in dyadic computer-based assessment
description: The study's organizing framework, from the Assessment and Teaching of 21st Century Skills project (Hesse et al., 2015), divides CPS into two intertwined skill dimensions. In this framework, "social skills refer to the 'collaborative' part of CPS that is often enacted through social interactions with the paired partner, including participation, perspective taking, and social regulation. Cognitive skills, on the other hand, refer to the 'problem-solving' part of CPS, such as task regulation and knowledge building." The study operationalizes these as log-file indicators scored via Rasch modeling with WLE scores across four CPS tasks. It differs from the PISA 2015 framework, which does not separate social from cognitive skills in CPS tasks.
requirements: Log-file action data from computer-based CPS tasks that can be coded into indicators matching the framework's subskills (participation, perspective taking, social regulation, task regulation, knowledge building) for automated Rasch-based scoring.
constraints: Unlike the PISA 2015 CPS framework, this framework separates social skills from cognitive skills in CPS tasks; the authors treat social and cognitive skills as inherently intertwined.
target_learners: school students assessed in pairs in computer-based environments (sixth graders in this study)
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving skills, both social and cognitive
examples: Skill levels 1-6 were identified through weighted likelihood estimate (WLE) scores from four game-like ATC21S tasks: Laughing Clown, Sunflower, Hot Chocolate, and Olive Oil.
key_sources: Shupin Li · Johanna Pöysä-Tarhonen · Päivi Häkkinen (2022). Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:191–223 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09369-7

article_title: Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach
citation: Shupin Li · Johanna Pöysä-Tarhonen · Päivi Häkkinen (2022). Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:191–223 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09369-7
title: Transition networks of action sequences analyzed with five SNA measures (nodes, density, degree centralization, reciprocity, triad census) for dyadic CPS process data
description: A methodological artifact integrating social network analysis with CPS assessment: for each dyad, actions (e.g., drag to move an object, type in a chat window) are nodes and directed weighted links represent transitions where "the first action is followed by the second action in sequence". In the Olive Oil task, analysis relied on "14,448 log file events conducted by 83 pairs". Five measures capture transition patterns: numbers of existing nodes (actions conducted), weighted density (average frequency of transitions among actions), Freeman degree centralization (dispersion of attempts given to different actions), reciprocity (extent to which pairs revisit the previous action immediately), and numbers of the 16 triadic patterns. Self-loops were excluded, and isolated nodes were added so networks had identical node sets for comparison.
requirements: Sequential process data with order-relevant action timestamps from a computer-based CPS environment, with actions categorized (system, transfer, other operational, chat actions) so transitions between different actions can be modeled as weighted directed links.
constraints: The contents of students' chat messages were excluded from the analysis; self-loops (repeating the same action) were excluded because interest was in transitions between different actions; analysis used the Olive Oil task only.
target_learners: paired students in computer-based problem solving assessment
target_learning_goals: analyzing collaborative problem solving processes and productivity via action transition patterns
examples: Fig. 2 visualizes the combined transition network of all 83 pairs, with node size by indegree, edge sizes as weights divided by 150, and colors distinguishing transitions inside, outside, and across the most efficient path.

article_title: Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach
citation: Shupin Li · Johanna Pöysä-Tarhonen · Päivi Häkkinen (2022). Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:191–223 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09369-7
title: When assigning students to pairs for computer-based CPS tasks, attend to both their social and their cognitive CPS skill capacities
description: The article's pedagogical implication: because dyad composition in social and cognitive CPS skills relates to productive CPS, teachers should consider students' social and cognitive capacities when forming pairs for computer-based CPS tasks. The authors state that "our results offer empirical evidence recommending greater awareness of the students' social and cognitive capacities in CPS when assigning them into pairs for computer-based CPS tasks." The principle rests on the finding that pairs with at least one high-social/high-cognitive member conducted more actions and transitions. In authentic classrooms, groups are often formed voluntarily, which the article notes can lead to off-task behavior, so a retrospective look at skill composition matters.
requirements: Awareness of students' individual social and cognitive CPS skill levels (e.g., from assessment reports) before pair assignment; the ATC21S scoring engine produces reports for teacher and student use.
constraints: The pair composition–productivity relationship was examined retrospectively in one asymmetric task (Olive Oil) with randomly assigned pairs of sixth graders; no recommendation follows for optimal pair formations beyond awareness of capacities.
target_learners: sixth-grade students working in dyads in computer-based CPS assessment
target_learning_goals: productive collaboration and collaborative problem solving
examples: The study randomly assigned 166 sixth graders to 83 pairs (female, male, and mixed-gender pairs) and categorized them into five skill-based pair compositions before comparing their transition network measures.

description: The element combines "tangible puppets as mediating manipulates and 3D manipulable animations as perspective-taking manipulatives for role-playing in CSCL". It supports microteaching simulation for pre-service teachers, where the puppets mediate performance and the 3D animations let the teacher take the perspective of imaginary students, including nonverbal representations of characters. The editors call the nonverbal representations a possible key factor in dialogic thinking and performance.

title: Model of the evolution of academically low-achieving students' emotions in Knowledge Building
description: The editors report that the authors "constructed a model of the evolution of emotions of academically low-achieving students in Knowledge Building", based on content and sequential pattern analysis of Knowledge Forum discourse in Visual Arts inquiry. The model traces which emotions occur and how emotions transition across inquiry threads, identifying joy as predominant and frustration and boredom as relatively rare. The editors state it "has implications for designing scaffolding or interventions to facilitate low-achieving students' emotions".
requirements: Built from content analysis and sequential pattern analysis of online Knowledge Forum discourse
constraints: Developed for academically low-achieving secondary students (Grade 9 and 11) in Knowledge Building
target_learners: academically low-achieving secondary school students in Knowledge Building
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting emotional evolution during collaborative knowledge building
examples: 120 students from two Grade 9 and two Grade 11 classes across three secondary schools building knowledge around Visual Arts

title: Enabling expression, recognition and nonverbal display of emotions in digital collaborative spaces can elicit more fruitful reflection
description: The editors' concluding principle is that "Enabling students and teachers to express and recognize participants' emotions in digital discussions and display them in nonverbal ways in virtual spaces has the potential to elicit more fruitful reflection". Technologies, they argue, "offer new representations that afford expression and interpretation of emotions during collaborative interactions". Positive emotions such as curiosity and joy can facilitate learning, while frustration and anxiety can hinder it.

constraints: Stated as potential for eliciting more fruitful reflection

article_title: Evolution of the academic emotions of academically low-achieving students in knowledge building
citation: Yuqin Yang · Gaoxia Zhu · Carol K. K. Chan. (2022). Evolution of the academic emotions of academically low-achieving students in knowledge building. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09380-y
title: Five-path model of the evolution of low-achieving students' emotions in Knowledge Building
description: A model synthesizing significant LSA transitions and mined subsequences across the four classes into five primary paths of emotional evolution: Path 1 joyful engagement with resolvable confusion (joy–curiosity–confusion–joy), Path 2 unresolved confusion leading to boredom (joy–curiosity–confusion–boredom), Path 3 extending to frustration–surprise–anxiety, Path 4 returning from anxiety to joy (joy–curiosity–confusion–boredom–frustration–surprise-anxiety-joy), and Path 5 curiosity-boredom. The article notes "each emotion on the path may go in two directions` and that a thread may manifest one emotion only. The model is intended to inform scaffolding or interventions for low-achieving students.
requirements: Significant sequential transitions (z-score above 1.96) and frequent subsequences identified from emotion-coded Knowledge Forum notes
Emotion coding of notes within inquiry threads using the seven-emotion coding framework
constraints: Constructed from academically low-achieving secondary students in one Band 3 Hong Kong school studying Visual Arts; Paths 2 and 3 confirmed only to a certain extent because surprise and boredom had low frequencies
target_learners: Academically low-achieving secondary students
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge creation and inquiry in Knowledge Building communities
examples: Reading all significant transitions per class and adding links found in most inquiry threads; emotion nodes dragged and some emotions repeated to void crossing arrows in the model figure

title: Three-phase principle-based pedagogical design scaffolding low-achieving students into Knowledge Building
description: A three-phased pedagogical design, refined from a previous four-phased design, that maps sixteen principle-based activities onto Knowledge Building principles (epistemic agency, community knowledge, collective responsibility, improvable ideas, embedded concurrent and transformative assessment). Phase 1 creates a collaborative and reflective culture so students "develop collaboration, inquiry, and reflection skills for productive Knowledge Building inquiry"; Phase 2 engages students in problem-centered collaborative inquiry on Knowledge Forum; Phase 3 deepens inquiry and community knowledge through student-directed portfolio assessment and field trips.

Knowledge Forum with integrated assessment tools such as Social Network Analysis and the Note Contribution applet
constraints: Portfolio activities were not implemented in every class: group portfolio assessment only in Class C, individual portfolio assessments not in Class D, and one activity (designing questions) omitted for Class D, per Table 2

target_learning_goals: Inquiry, collaboration, reflection, and metacognitive skills; critical and creative thinking in Visual Arts
examples: Whole-class and small-group activities such as constructing three-dimensional objects from colorful wires, collaborative concept maps, a Knowledge Building Wall, the Crossing Your Life Point justification game, weekly collective reflection, and museum field trips

title: Tangible puppetry tabletop role-play system with LED mood indicators and recorded bird's-eye animation
description: A tabletop simulation system in which a teacher puppet, student puppets, and props on transparent boxes with location indicators are used for microteaching role-play; a web camera and microphone under a semitransparent tabletop capture voices and puppet movements. Student puppets carry two-colored LEDs representing "distracted, focused, or normal" mental states, and the system "generates an animation based on the recorded locations, rotations, and conditions of each puppet" that is replayed for reflective discussion. In the study's triads, two student teachers played students with multiple puppets while one played teacher.

perspective-taking of imaginary students

title: Dialogic microteaching supported by two complementary manipulatives: mediating puppets and perspective-taking animation
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that achieving dialogic microteaching requires overcoming two challenges: role-playing various imaginary students plausibly, and appropriating their viewpoints in subsequent reflection. Grounded in Bakhtin's dialogism, in which utterances are formed "in anticipation of what the listener will say," the design pairs mediating manipulatives (tangible puppets whose psychological distance reduces anxiety and elicits multivoiced performances) with perspective-taking manipulatives (3D first-person viewpoint switching in reflection). Previous work showed puppetry alone left reflections returning to pre-role-play perspectives, motivating the combined design for immediate transfer of imaginary students' perspectives.
requirements: Student teachers must overcome self-consciousness and evaluation apprehension that makes unaided role-play normative and unrealistic
Reflection must follow the puppetry performance; puppetry alone was "not found to be sufficient" for diverse student perspectives in reflection
constraints: The 3D animation effect was studied as a companion to puppetry role-play in a three-session sequence, not as a stand-alone intervention
target_learners: student teachers in preservice education
target_learning_goals: dialogic pedagogy
perspective-taking of imaginary students
reflection on classroom discourse
examples: The quasi-experimental class design gave all triads puppetry in Session #2 and varied only the reflection medium, then tested persistence in a Session #3 self-performed microteaching without manipulatives

article_title: The temporal dynamics of online problem-based learning: Why and when sequence matters
citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas. (2023). The temporal dynamics of online problem-based learning: Why and when sequence matters. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09385-1
title: Four sequential session types of online PBL interaction: argumentation-triggered, information-triggered, socially-triggered, and facilitated discussions
description: Differential sequence mining with agglomerative hierarchical clustering on the longest common prefix, validated by average silhouette width and R-squared, grouped students' interaction sessions into four types. "The best number of clusters according to ASW and R-squared was four." The Argumentation triggered cluster "contains sessions that always begin with Argue", the Information triggered cluster begins with Share and is short and less argumentative, the Socially triggered cluster begins with social gestures, and Facilitated discussions has a considerable teacher presence. Sessions start most often as Information triggered (39%) and transition freely between types.
requirements: Time-stamped, qualitatively coded interaction data from an online forum so interactions can be ordered and session epochs defined
constraints: Derived from one blended medical PBL course (four offerings) at a single university; session epochs defined by a 20-minute inactivity threshold
target_learners: first-year medical students in blended online PBL
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem-solving and knowledge construction in problem-based learning
examples: Cluster sizes as reported: Argumentation triggered n = 709, Information triggered n = 423, Socially triggered n = 398, Facilitated discussions n = 883
key_sources: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas. (2023). The temporal dynamics of online problem-based learning: Why and when sequence matters. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09385-1

article_title: The temporal dynamics of online problem-based learning: Why and when sequence matters
citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas. (2023). The temporal dynamics of online problem-based learning: Why and when sequence matters. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09385-1
title: Design PBL so that learners initiate interactions, since initiating sequences show the strongest association with performance
description: The article argues that which interactions start matters more than how many occur: "Starting or initiating interactions... showed the highest association with performance, pointing to the importance of initiative and sequencing." In the PBL design, the group's sequence of interaction types predicted grades better than raw counts, with information-triggered and argumentation-triggered patterns showing the strongest positive coefficients. Designers should therefore structure online PBL so students - not bulk facilitation - open discussions and episodes.
requirements: Online PBL interaction data or settings where initiating contributions by learners can be distinguished from responsive ones
constraints: Evidence is correlational from one medical PBL course; the facilitated-discussions pattern itself was not significantly associated with grades
target_learners: medical students in small-group online PBL (groups of 8-10)
target_learning_goals: deep approaches to learning, argumentation, and self-directed problem-solving
examples: In the study, the first-year medical students' weekly problem discussions began online in Moodle forums after a short face-to-face goal-setting session, and information-triggered sessions (beta = 1.72, p = 0.002) showed the largest positive association with grades

Learn (2023) 18:39–66. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09387-z
title: Three-layered AI-driven learning analytics framework for examining CPS from a complex adaptive systems perspective
description: The article proposes a three-layered analytical framework integrating AI algorithms with learning analytics to examine collaborative problem solving as complex adaptive systems: "AI algorithms were incorporated into that framework using multiple learning analytic approaches". Layer 1 codes interactive, cognitive, regulative, behavioural and socio-emotional dimensions; Layer 2 applies multichannel sequence analysis with optimal matching and Ward's clustering to detect pattern types; Layer 3 uses statistical analysis, epistemic network analysis, and hidden Markov modeling to reveal quantitative, structural, and transitional regularities per type.
requirements: Multimodal process data (verbal communication, screen recordings of clickstream behaviour, concept map products) coded into multi-dimensional sequences
constraints: Codes are "proxies for tacit learning processes" with expected overlap between dimensions, which the authors chose to retain in separate channels
Developed and demonstrated on graduate CPS activities in an online synchronous collaboration platform
target_learners: graduate students in educational technology seminar courses
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving skills
knowledge co-construction through concept mapping
examples: Applied to 24 datasets from four graduate-student groups completing ill-structured problems on the Huiyizhuo platform

title: Complex adaptive systems theory account of CPS: multimodal, dynamic and synergistic emergence of a self-organising collaboration system
description: The article interprets CPS through complex adaptive systems theory: group members form "an adaptive, self-organizing system that has a multi-dimensional nature, synergistic relations, and a dynamic evolutionary character". CPS is multimodal (interactive, cognitive, regulative, behavioural, socio-emotional dimensions), dynamic (dsrelations change over time as groups move from communication to behaviour and back), and synergistic (coordination between communication and behaviour, most evident in the high-performing Type 2 groups). This lens breaks with causal, linear models in favour of organic, non-linear, holistic analysis.
requirements: Multimodal multi-dimensional data capturing the interdependent dimensions of collaboration over time
constraints: Studying CPS through this lens "poses significant methodological challenges to traditional statistics" used with homogeneous, unimodal data

Achieving a high-quality synergy between communication and behaviour is described as difficult; external factors such as task difficulty, group configuration, and social learning context limit all groups collaborating synergistically
target_learners: student groups in K-12 and higher education collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: understanding the emergence of adaptive self-organizing group collaboration
examples: HMM state-transition patterns showed groups evolving from communication states, to behaviour states, and back to communication, forming a self-organizing system

article_title: Fostering regulatory processes using computational scaffolding
citation: Leonardo Silva, António Mendes, Anabela Gomes, Gabriel Fortes. (2023). Fostering regulation of learning processes among programming students using computational scaffolding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2023) 18:67–100. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09388-y
title: Social regulation: folding co-regulation and socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) into one socio-cognitive construct
description: The article adopts a socio-cognitive perspective in which regulation of learning occurs individually (SRL) and through social interaction. SSRL "refers to the regulation of learning episodes within a group of people who collectively negotiate and deliberate regulatory strategies to achieve a common shared goal", while co-regulation involves regulatory stimuli arising from interpersonal interactions that temporally guide one person's regulatory processes. Because both emerge from social interactions, the authors fold them "under the term social regulation". This construct guided the design of RESPE's social scaffolds.
requirements: Group interaction contexts (e.g., dyads or triads working on shared programming tasks) in which regulatory stimuli and shared strategy negotiation can occur
constraints: Within the scope of this work the authors did not differentiate co-regulation from SSRL, treating both as social regulation
Understanding how to design social regulation scaffoldings needs further investigation, per the authors
target_learners: novice programming students in introductory higher-education courses
target_learning_goals: regulation of the learning process during individual and collaborative programming (planning, monitoring, self-reflection)
examples: The collaborative software planner externalized students' task-difficulty judgments and shared them among group members to create awareness and generate co-regulation episodes.
key_sources: Leonardo Silva, António Mendes, Anabela Gomes, Gabriel Fortes. (2023). Fostering regulation of learning processes among programming students using computational scaffolding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2023) 18:67–100. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09388-y

article_title: Fostering regulatory processes using computational scaffolding
citation: Leonardo Silva, António Mendes, Anabela Gomes, Gabriel Fortes. (2023). Fostering regulation of learning processes among programming students using computational scaffolding. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2023) 18:67–100. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09388-y
title: Zimmerman's three-phase cyclical SRL model as the design reference for regulatory scaffolding
description: The article uses Zimmerman's model, which "describes SRL as a cyclical process comprising three phases": forethought (understanding and planning the task with motivational beliefs), performance (metacognitive monitoring, cognitive strategies, motivational evaluation during execution), and self-reflection (judgments about performance and reflection on improvement). Knowledge acquired feeds the next cycle. The model "was used as a reference in the design of our proposed regulatory scaffolding", with scaffolds categorized by phase (Fig. 1).
requirements: Scaffolds must be aligned to the three cyclical phases (forethought, performance, self-reflection) so students are supported at planning, execution, and reflection stages
constraints: The authors note the model conceptualizes the student as an individual in isolation from the social environment, which has been subject of critique
target_learners: novice programming students in online introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: planning, monitoring, and self-reflection during programming learning
examples: RESPE scaffolds such as the learning journal and software planner were categorized by Zimmerman's SRL phases (Fig. 1).

title: RESPE: a CSCL platform embedding individual and social regulatory scaffolds for programming learning
description: RESPE is a CSCL environment for introductory programming whose scaffolds foster SRL and social regulation across "cognition, metacognition, behavior, and motivation". Scaffolds include a learning journal, software planner, SRL tips, an intelligent agent, error visualization and analysis, learning dashboard, debug, course progress, exercise solution, and social features such as a collaborative software planner, ranking, dialogue support agent, forum, and help request. Source code is released under CC BY-NC 4.0 at https:// github. com/ lsoar esesi lva/ 32bits, and scaffolds are presented in mandatory or manually activated formats.
requirements: An online introductory programming course with individual and collaborative exercises hosted on the platform; access to the programming editor is gated on answering the software planner questions
constraints: The professor (first author) knew which group his students belonged to, while participants were blind to condition
target_learners: novice programmers with little or no programming background in online university courses
target_learning_goals: learning of programming (variables, conditionals, loops, functions in Python) with regulatory skill support for planning, monitoring, and self-evaluation
examples: In the trial, 70 individual and 8 collaborative exercises were delivered on the platform; students with regulatory support achieved higher grades, and only the social-regulation group excelled at collaborative activities.

article_title: Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments
citation: Wen Huang, Candace Walkington, Mitchell J. Nathan. (2023). Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09397-x
title: Four modalities of embodied collaboration in shared VR environments
description: The article integrates theories of embodied cognition with distributed and extended cognition to focus on four modalities for embodied collaboration in shared VR: actions on virtual objects, gesture, body movement, and speech. These modalities are the semiotic resources learners orchestrate simultaneously or in sequence to build shared geometric understanding. The framework treats the group, not the individual, as the interactional unit of analysis.
requirements: A shared VR environment in which multiple learners can simultaneously manipulate the same virtual object and see each other's avatars and actions in real time
target_learners: in-service mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: collaborative geometric reasoning and embodied mathematical knowledge construction

title: Geometry Simulation Environment (GSE)
description: The GSE is a shared VR simulation installed on Oculus Quest goggles, designed by the research team as part of a design-based research program on mixed reality for geometry learning. Learners log into a single virtual classroom from their homes, see each other's avatars, and collaboratively manipulate shared geometric shapes with real-time measurement displays. Its design supports gestural congruency: virtual objects are manipulated intuitively through hand gestures.
requirements: Oculus Quest VR goggles with hand-tracking capability and a virtual classroom dashboard for joining a shared session
target_learners: secondary mathematics students
in-service mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: geometric conjecture evaluation
3D perspective-taking
volume and scaling reasoning
justification and proof
examples: Participants manipulated cylinders, triangles, cubes, and other solids; critical measurements such as height, volume, and radius were displayed and updated in real time

title: Embodied learning taxonomy distinguishing sensorimotor engagement, gesture congruency, and immersion across four degrees (as reported by Johnson-Glenberg and colleagues)
description: The introduction reports, citing Johnson-Glenberg et al. and its 2017 update, an embodied learning taxonomy that "distinguishes components of embodied learning into three constructs": amount of sensorimotor engagement, congruence of gestures to content, and amount of immersion. Each construct spans four degrees, "the first degree being the lowest level of embodiment and the fourth degree being the highest." These formalized taxonomies and rubrics serve as design tools for XR learning designers and educators.

article_title: Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment
citation: Xintian Tu, Joshua Danish, Megan Humburg, Mengxi Zhou, Nitasha Mathayas, Noel Enyedy, Tessaly Jen. (2023). Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 18:231–258. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09395-z
title: LEAF: the Learning in Embodied Activity Framework connecting CHAT and embodied cognition at individual and collective levels
description: LEAF is the study's organizing framework: it synthesizes cultural-historical activity theory with cognitive theories of embodiment, so that a child running across the room as a gas particle is understood to experience the moment "at both individual and collective levels simultaneously" — feeling speed and proximity while the group negotiates producing a solid or a liquid. Like other CHAT-based theories it treats learning as occurring in activities oriented toward a shared object, with individual actions mediated by artifacts (the projected simulation), community members, rules, and division of labor. The paper uses LEAF to justify analyzing classroom embodied communication and later interview gestures as interrelated levels rather than parallel ones.
requirements: Analysis must attend to embodied cognition and learning at individual and collective levels and the interactions across them, as the framework's stated purpose requires.
constraints: Embodied meanings are activity- and culture-specific: the article notes the same gesture can imply different things in different models (e.g., a pushing gesture as force in one model versus energy transfer in another).
target_learners: elementary school students (first and second grade)
target_learning_goals: science concepts such as particle behavior in states of matter
examples: The framework is applied to the STEP Particles project, where shared goals like producing a state of matter are provided by the teacher and negotiated in interaction.

title: Three embodied communicative acts — showing particle behavior, guiding peers' movement, and responding to suggestions — support collective and individual functions in MR learning
description: Through embodied interaction analysis of the STEP classroom video, the authors grouped students' embodied moves into three communicative acts: using gestures to demonstrate what they knew about particle behavior, giving direction to peers' movement, and following or responding to others' suggestions (including mimicking movements such as the "jellyfish" motion). The iterative analytic sequence shown in the video data determined the acts and their functions, which the authors tabulate with both collective functions (e.g., repair, guiding collective work) and individual functions (e.g., representing one's own ideas, experiencing relative speed and distance). One demonstration episode in which a group came to be recognized as a liquid shows all three acts overlapping.
requirements: A collaborative mixed-reality environment with a shared collective goal in which movement is tracked and displayed, so that communicative acts can be observed and coordinated.
constraints: The acts were identified within the STEP particle curriculum's whole-class embodied activities, debriefings, and interviews with young children; the authors present representative clips rather than claiming exhaustive coverage.
target_learners: elementary school students (first and second grade)
target_learning_goals: communicating and collectively constructing understanding of particle behavior and states of matter
examples: In a day-3 episode, Lily gestured distance, directed peers with 'Stay away back', and the group's coordinated walking and spacing was finally recognized as a liquid by the simulation's state meter.

title: STEP mixed-reality platform: whole-body particle simulation with person tracking and a projected state meter
description: STEP (Science through Technology Enhanced Play) is a mixed-reality environment in which students' tracked movements appear as colored circles representing particles in a projected simulation, with color-coded lines linking nearest neighbors and linked bar graphs displaying the proportion of particles in each state. Technically, "the STEP platform utilizes the Open PTrack person tracking system to monitor student movement via Kinect cameras," feeding a JavaScript web application whose display is projected on a shared classroom screen. Students collectively adjust speed and distance to be recognized as a solid, liquid, or gas, supporting exploration of states of matter and micro–macro connections.
requirements: A networked laptop, Kinect cameras running the Open PTrack tracking system, and a projection screen visible to all students.
constraints: Target content is limited to four particle-behavior characteristics — speed, distance, attraction, and trajectory — within the states-of-matter curriculum.
target_learners: elementary school students (first and second grade)
target_learning_goals: understanding particle behaviors in the three states of matter and connections between microscopic and macroscopic characteristics
examples: Day 1 activity: students add or take away energy from a projected snowman, changing its state among snowman, puddle, or steam.
