title: Assess embodied learning with immersive, embodied assessments that mirror the interactions learners engage in while learning.
description: The article argues that because embodiment is central to environments like STEP, written measures alone may miss what learners know; the authors write that it "may be crucial to develop assessments that are similarly immersive and embodied to mirror the kinds of interactions that learners engage in while learning." Without such assessments, educators "may fail to recognize the richness of children's learning in embodied environments." In this study the principle is instantiated by interview prompts with props (ice cubes, containers, pretend hot plates) that invited body movements and gestures, which revealed understanding the multiple-choice test did not.
requirements: Assessment tasks that allow and encourage gesture and whole-body demonstration, aligned with the embodied activities of the learning design.
constraints: The article frames this as a suggestion for embodied environments, citing prior work; questions remain in the article about reliably drawing out students' embodied understandings.
target_learners: young children in embodied learning environments
target_learning_goals: expressing and evaluating understanding of concepts learned through embodied activity
examples: In the study's interviews, students were shown manipulatives and asked how water on a pretend hot plate would change and how those changes would impact particle behaviors.

title: Deliver even low-effort, general weekly SRL interventions in MOOCs to scaffold participation, retention, and learning
description: The article supports sending weekly email interventions that make the learning analytics dashboard visible and prompt students to interpret visualizations against their goals. Both a generic intervention and a personalized version increased participation, retention, and quiz scores relative to control. The authors conclude that "even the generalized SRL intervention mode, which requires less setup effort on behalf of the teaching staff, can be effective in improving learning outcomes and reducing dropout rates."
requirements: Weekly email interventions sent at the start of each week that direct students to learning analytics visualizations linked to skills needed for the chat activities
constraints: Effects were demonstrated in a 5-week, single-country, Greece-based programming MOOC; the personalized mode significantly outperformed control on SRL scores while the general mode did not; interventions bundled several SRL prompts whose separate effects were not isolated.
target_learners: MOOC learners with heterogeneous self-regulated learning skills
target_learning_goals: Improved participation in collaborative chat activities, course retention, and learning outcomes in an introduction-to-programming MOOC
examples: Three weekly email interventions prompted the general group to consider which learning analytics graphs offered valuable information; the personalized group received named, compliance-tracking messages referencing specific skills and graphs.

citation: Carolyn P. Rosé, Sanna Järvelä. (2023). Enhancing student learning and achievement through orchestration of group processes and group composition. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 18, 323–327. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09408-x
title: Explicit vs implicit scaffolding of collaboration: structured feedback interfaces vs orchestrating group composition
description: The editorial contrasts two scaffolding routes to productive collaborative learning. In the four issue articles, some interventions scaffold processes through "explicit scaffolding", such as a "structured peer feedback interface" or a script prompting deeper discussion, while others work indirectly: "interventions that group students in order to promote productive learning processes can be regarded as implicit scaffolding for collaboration". This framing organizes how the issue's studies─SRL email messages, meta-discourse enrichment, feedback design, and skill-based pairing─support learning. It also introduces the notion of orchestrating group composition and group processes to enhance learning.
requirements: Requires feedback or grouping mechanisms designed with knowledge of student skill levels or self-regulation profiles, as in stratified assignment by latent profiles
constraints: The editorial states past coarse-grained skill pairing failed to demonstrate an impact, so implicit scaffolding via composition depends on sufficiently fine-grained skill assessment

citation: Ulrike Cress · Joachim Kimmerle. (2023). Co-constructing knowledge with generative AI tools: Reflections from a CSCL perspective. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09409-w
title: Co-evolution model: knowledge construction as structural coupling of meaning-based cognitive and social systems
description: The co-evolution model, developed by Cress and Kimmerle, describes knowledge construction as a 'structural coupling of meaning-based cognitive and social systems'. Individual cognitions form an autopoietic cognitive system, while social systems are formed by communication in which utterances lead to further utterances. Both use language as a medium and can mutually irritate each other when expectations are slightly violated, which may lead to individual learning and collective knowledge construction. The article applies this framework to human-AI interaction, asking whether knowledge construction occurs only within human agents or between both agents.
requirements: Both cognitive and social systems use language as a medium through which they can influence each other
constraints: The article leaves open whether knowledge construction happens between human and AI agents, or whether knowledge development happens only within but not between agents
target_learners: learners interacting with generative AI tools
collaborative learning groups
target_learning_goals: individual learning
collective knowledge construction
examples: The authors pose the open question whether human-AI collaboration is 'still a situation where both partners stimulate and irritate each other in such a way that knowledge development happens only within but not between agents'

citation: Natalia Reich-Stiebert, Jan-Bennet Voltmer, Jennifer Raimann, Stefan Stürmer. (2023). The role of first-language heterogeneity in the acquisition of online interaction self-efficacy in CSCL. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 18:513–530. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09411-2
title: SIDE-based account: linguistic cues in computer-mediated collaboration trigger social categorization and stereotype processes
description: The article uses the social identification model of deindividuation effects (SIDE) to explain how first-language heterogeneity harms CSCL interactions. It argues that computer-mediated communication's "relative lack of individualizing cues" increases reliance on "easily available surface-level social categorical information", and that "Linguistic features are generally strong markers of ethnic and cultural category membership", potentially triggering stereotyping, stereotype threat, intergroup bias, and paternalistic communication patterns. The study did not attempt to separate these stereotype-based processes from task-related communication barriers; both are treated as candidate mechanisms behind the heterogeneity effect.
requirements: expressly framed as applying to computer-mediated, written-language CSCL contexts
constraints: the article states it "did not intend to differentiate between task-related and stereotype-based processes as contributors"
target_learners: distance-education university students in CSCL groups
target_learning_goals: online interaction self-efficacy for academic collaboration

article_title: Reflecting on what counts as collaboration: Reaching forward without losing what is behind
citation: Sanna Järvelä, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2023). Reflecting on what counts as collaboration: Reaching forward without losing what is behind. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 18, 457–464. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09415-y
title: Collaboration as active, intentional, shared, effective communication toward a joint goal — the boundary question "what counts as collaboration"
description: The editorial centers on the question "What is the essence of collaboration?" and defines collaboration, following Dillenbourg (1999), as involving "individuals or groups working together to achieve common goals, share ideas, and contribute their efforts toward a collective objective or joint goal." The authors stress it is "active, intentional, shared, and effective communication and participation," and can be scripted and technology-supported. They use boundary cases — talking without a set learning objective, human–agent interaction, intersubjectivity with agents without minds — to push the field to elaborate its concepts as new themes (LA, AR/VR, GenAI) emerge.
requirements: The article presents this as a field-level boundary question that must be kept under active discussion when judging journal scope and integrating new paradigms.
target_learners: CSCL research community and learners in technology-supported collaborative environments
target_learning_goals: Understanding what qualifies an interaction as collaborative learning, including human–agent collaboration
key_sources: Sanna Järvelä, Carolyn P. Rosé. (2023). Reflecting on what counts as collaboration: Reaching forward without losing what is behind. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 18, 457–464. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09415-y

citation: Reet Kasepalu, Pankaj Chejara, Luis P. Prieto, Tobias Ley. (2023). Studying teacher withitness in the wild: comparing a mirroring and an alerting & guiding dashboard for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2023) 18:575–606. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09414-z
title: Teacher withitness: two-dimensional framework of classroom situational awareness plus real-time interventions during collaborative learning
description: Withitness is "the skill of teachers to process and handle classroom situations along two dimensions: classroom awareness (i.e., what is going on in the classroom) and what the teacher is doing to maintain learning (i.e., her interventions)". The article positions it as "the part of orchestration that happens in real-time during the learning activities", narrower than the broad orchestration construct, and draws on Endsley's three levels of situational awareness (perception, comprehension, prediction) measured via adapted SAGAT statements. The study uses this framework to structure its hypotheses H1 and H3.
requirements: Teachers must first achieve situational awareness of classroom events before choosing interventions to sustain learning
constraints: The article focuses less on disciplining students and more on supporting students to learn to work together and coregulate
target_learners: in-service teachers of collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: real-time monitoring and support of collaborative learning

title: CoTrack: MMLA collaboration analytics tool combining mirroring dashboard with an AI alerting & guiding layer
description: CoTrack is a web-based collaboration analytics tool mirroring student behaviour: it "collects audio data along with logs generated by collaborative writing", processing audio in real-time via Voice Activity Detection, Speech-to-Text, Speaking time and Turn taking, plus characters added or deleted in Etherpad. The mirroring dashboard visualises a 'who is talking after whom' network, word-clouds and writing bar graphs; the alerting & guiding layer uses a CNN trained on image-encoded multimodal features to predict ACARS collaboration-quality dimensions, with coregulation suggestions drawn from the Collaboration Intervention Model.

constraints: Model predictions restricted to individual task orientation, cooperative orientation and sustaining mutual understanding; guiding suggestions delivered on paper by a researcher
target_learners: in-service teachers with student groups of 12 to 30
target_learning_goals: monitoring and improving collaboration quality in group work
examples: Twenty lessons with eleven class formations ran with the tool; T17 in the guiding condition followed all groups and received 5 alerts and suggestions for two groups

article_title: Exploring students’ immersive VR experiences as resources for collaborative meaning making and learning
citation: Kenneth Silseth, Rolf Steier, Hans Christian Arnseth. (2024). Exploring students’ immersive VR experiences as resources for collaborative meaning making and learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09413-0
title: Emancipatory immersion as a design goal for VR learning about exclusion and discrimination
description: Emancipatory immersion, developed in the CSCL field by Enyedy and Yoon, is the concept the authors use to interpret how students meaningfully related to the VR stories. Quoting the concept's originators: "we can develop a critical consciousness that promotes epistemological curiosity taking ownership of one's own constructed world." The article stresses it is not about fully identifying with others but about taking part in situations where others' experiences are taken seriously and invited into reflection on one's own lifeworld. The study's four dimensions are presented as manifestations of emancipatory immersion in reflective dialogue.
requirements: A VR environment presenting personal stories about exclusion and discrimination.
Collaborative reflective dialogues after the VR experience in which immersion experiences can be expressed, since one of these reflections occurs only in the dialogues themselves.
constraints: The article explicitly does not interpret emancipatory immersion as becoming someone else or fully understanding the experiences of the people met in the VR environment.
target_learners: upper secondary students
target_learning_goals: developing critical consciousness about exclusion and discrimination
reflecting on how discrimination penetrates students' own lifeworlds
examples: The authors relate students' talk about being morally accountable to people they meet in the film and feeling part of the conversations to emancipatory immersion (Enyedy & Yoon, 2021).

article_title: Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration
citation: Anna Keune. (2024). Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09412-1
title: Baradian posthumanist intra-action and analysis of differences as a framework for studying collaborative learning
description: The paper takes up Barad's (2003) posthumanist approach, which decenters humans without looking past them, to study how knowledge production is bound to material being and doing. Its core distinction is that "the idea of intra-action places a focus on the relationships among parts and the phenomenon that materializes through the jointness of parts," unlike interaction between discrete entities. The framework motivates an analysis of differences between physical states of a phenomenon over time, making humans and materials viewable on an equal plane as co-actants in computational collaborative learning.
requirements: Video data capturing both human and material movements, from multiple angles so material action is not distorted out of frame
constraints: The article limits the analysis to a single researcher's reading cross-checked with a research team and two interdisciplinary scholars
The approach was applied only to the weaving and fabric manipulation units; soft-robotic actuator animation was excluded
target_learners: middle school youth aged 11-14 in maker-centered learning
target_learning_goals: understanding algorithms and computational concepts through tangible crafts
examples: The study applied the analysis of differences to synchronized eye-level and bird's-eye-view videos to identify repetitions and variations of youth-material combinations
key_sources: Anna Keune. (2024). Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09412-1

article_title: Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration
citation: Anna Keune. (2024). Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09412-1
title: Fiber crafts course (weaving and fabric manipulation) as a context for computational learning with middle school youth
description: A 6-session fiber crafts course, facilitated twice at a K-8 charter school, offered weaving with three loom types and fabric manipulation with a laser-cut matrix template as contexts for performing computational concepts. "The participants of the course were 16 middle school students between 11 and 14 years old," self-selected via an interest survey. The crafts were chosen because they are matrix-based, connected historically to computing, and require routine movements that perform algorithms such as loops and conditional pairings.
requirements: Pre-warped looms and prepared materials (laser-cut grid template, threads, needles) so sessions could focus on production
Facilitators familiar with the crafts and with the study's purpose regarding computing-crafting connections
constraints: Facilitators did not ask students to recognize the crafting tools and materials as co-actors
Soft-robotic actuator animation sessions were excluded from this analysis
target_learners: seventh- and eighth-grade students in a maker-centered school program
target_learning_goals: performing computational concepts (loops, variables, conditionals) through physical crafting
examples: Projects included plain weave and gap patterns on backstrap, rigid heddle, and tabletop looms, and twisted-square stitched designs on cotton fabric
key_sources: Anna Keune. (2024). Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09412-1

article_title: Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration
citation: Anna Keune. (2024). Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09412-1
title: Multi-angle video capture disrupting human visual centrality to allow human-material analysis
description: This capture pattern combines eye-level, bird's-eye-view, and close-up turntable videos so that material movements are analytically visible. The study collected approximately 13.5 hours each of eye-level and bird's-eye views plus 435 close-up videos, because data centered predominantly on human actions limits theorizing materially driven phenomena. Viewing angles simultaneously afforded verification of what had been seen from another angle through visual evidence.
requirements: Synchronized timestamps across camera angles, a 360-degree camera rig above the craft table, directional and wireless microphones, and turntable close-ups of projects
constraints: The camera remains "a necessary but distorting component in video-based educational research," so angle and frame choices always include or exclude analytical aspects
target_learners: middle school youth in org small-group making settings
target_learning_goals: capturing collaborative learning processes that involve tangible and computational materials
examples: Eye-level video was the primary source for weaving's z-axis movements; bird's-eye video was primary for fabric manipulation's folded layers; close-ups reverse-engineered production processes
key_sources: Anna Keune. (2024). Learning within fiber-crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human-material collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09412-1

article_title: CSCL has come of age
citation: Michael J. Baker, Peter Reimann. (2024). CSCL has come of age. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2024) 19:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09419-2
title: CSCL's triadic object of study: collaboration, task, and technology
description: The editors characterize CSCL research as organized around an integrated, three-part object of study. As they state, "CSCL research is characterised by the three-fold nature of its integrated object of study: collaboration, with respect to a more or less shared task, involving use of technology." Each of the three terms is theory-laden (e.g. 'task' can be a problem solving goal, a learning object, or the object of activity), a change in one element has repercussions for the others, and the object evolves with society and its technologies. The editorial uses this framework to survey what is currently emerging in CSCL research across all three elements.
requirements: The framework presupposes treating the three elements as interdependent rather than separately studied
constraints: The editorial notes that none of the three key terms is neutral and each is highly theory-laden
target_learners: CSCL researchers and designers of technology-mediated collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: Understanding the structure and evolution of the CSCL field as a basis for research design
examples: The editorial structures its discussion of collaboration (Roschelle & Teasley, Dillenbourg), task domains (STEM vs open-ended domains), and technology change (VR, automated analysis) around the three elements
key_sources: Michael J. Baker, Peter Reimann. (2024). CSCL has come of age. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2024) 19:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09419-2

article_title: CSCL has come of age
citation: Michael J. Baker, Peter Reimann. (2024). CSCL has come of age. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2024) 19:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09419-2
title: Adopt a design science stance so that artefacts and design theories both count as knowledge in CSCL research
description: The editors propose importing Design Science Research from Information Systems into CSCL. DSR holds, quoting the editorial, that "knowledge is possible and valuable not only in abstract form but also in the form of artefacts," with design theories as mid-range theories accounting for why an artefact works, under which circumstances and for whom. Artefacts worth building must be motivated by deep problem understanding and rigorous analysis of existing solutions, and designed iteratively with prototyping and formative evaluation. The editorial invites designs, including via a new Short Paper format.
requirements: Good designs need to be motivated by a deep understanding of the problem, stakeholder needs, and rigorous analysis of existing solutions; designers should follow an established design method and document all steps
constraints: DBR has faced methodological critique as a weak experimental method (Kelly, 2004), raising the question of how such a method can serve as the foundation for advancing learning theories
target_learners: CSCL researchers, learning scientists, and designers of collaborative learning technologies
target_learning_goals: Producing design theories and useful computational and instructional artefacts for collaborative learning
examples: The editorial lists arteacts already developed in CSCL: design documents and models such as wireframes, collaboration scripts, teacher manuals, worksheets, and protocols for reproducible data analysis
key_sources: Michael J. Baker, Peter Reimann. (2024). CSCL has come of age. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2024) 19:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09419-2

article_title: Zooming in: The role of nonverbal behavior in sensing the quality of collaborative group engagement
citation: Paneth, L., Jeitziner, L. T., Rack, O., Opwis, K., & Zahn, C. (2024). Zooming in: The role of nonverbal behavior in sensing the quality of collaborative group engagement. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09422-7
title: Quality of Collaborative Group Engagement (QCGE): a shared, multifaceted, dynamic, contextualized four-dimension group-process construct for CSCL
description: The paper builds on Sinha et al. (2015)'s conceptualization of the quality of collaborative group engagement, which groups 'the quality of collaborative group engagement (QCGE) as shared, multifaceted, dynamic, and contextualized'. Four dimensions are distinguished: behavioral engagement (on-task persistence and effort), social engagement (quality of socio-emotional group interactions), cognitive engagement (collaborative development of understanding via monitoring, planning, evaluating), and conceptual-to-consequential engagement (solving meaningful problems with disciplinary practices and content as conceptual tools). The study treats engagement as fluctuating phases, not a fixed state.
requirements: Requires a QCGE rating scheme applied to video segments of group collaboration, rated low/moderate/high per dimension
constraints: Conceptualizations comprehensive for CSCL contexts emerged only recently and definitions of student engagement lack standard descriptions, per the article
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving
regulation of group learning
domain-specific knowledge building
examples: The study applied the rating scheme to 1-min video segments of 38 triads collaborating on a Sweet Home 3D office design task

article_title: Learning to notice collaboration: examining the impact of professional development on mathematics teachers’ enhanced awareness in CSCL settings
citation: Benzi Slakmon, Rotem Abdu. (2024). Learning to notice collaboration: examining the impact of professional development on mathematics teachers’ enhanced awareness in CSCL settings. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 19:137–155. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09423-6
title: Bakhtinian dialogic framework of four interconnected themes — voices, expanding the dialogue, inter-animation, and relations — as an analytical lens for collaborative dialogue
description: The article operationalizes dialogue through four Bakhtin-inspired themes used both to train teachers and to analyze noticing utterances. A voice is "a perspective about an idea that is communicated to others"; a dialogic gap occurs "when two equally valid and distinct voices interact, driving the dialogue forward"; expansion happens by widening (new voices, alternative solutions) or deepening (critical inquiry of existing voices); inter-animation involves revoicing others, and relations concern mutuality, equal status, and authoritative versus dialogic interaction. These constructs map onto eleven coded dialogic attributes (Table 1) such as persuasive interaction, monologue, and one-leads-another-is-led.
requirements: Teachers or analysts must be introduced to the dialogic concepts and vocabulary (voices, dialogic gap, mutuality), as the participants were in the 80-minute intervention lesson.
constraints: The article warns noticing dialogue cannot be reduced to best-practice behaviors, since attending and responding require balancing the dialogic tension between correctness and additional voices.
target_learners: in-service mathematics teachers working with collaborative problem-solving in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: noticing and supporting productive student dialogue during collaborative learning
examples: The intervention lesson asked teachers to write definitions of dialogue, discussed practices such as allocating individual thinking time before group learning, and asked them to list what they would pay attention to in collaborative learning.
key_sources: Benzi Slakmon, Rotem Abdu. (2024). Learning to notice collaboration: examining the impact of professional development on mathematics teachers’ enhanced awareness in CSCL settings. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 19:137–155. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09423-6

article_title: The perceptions of task cohesion in collaborative learning teams
citation: Zamecnik, A., Kovanović, V., Joksimović, S., Grossmann, G., Ladjal, D., Pardo, A. (2024). The perceptions of task cohesion in collaborative learning teams. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09424-5
title: Four-group taxonomy of team cohesion perception transitions (Aligned, Multifaceted, Regressive, Progressive)
description: The article organises teams by how their shared or divergent cohesion perceptions change between Week 1 and Week 3 into four transition groups: "Aligned (SS) – Week 1: Similar; Week 3: Similar", Multifaceted (DD), Regressive (SD), and Progressive (DS). Of 194 teams, "The number of teams (N) for the Aligned, Multifaceted, Regressive, and Progressive groups were 43, 72, 25, and 54, respectively", all averaging about five members. The taxonomy serves as the grouping variable for performance, engagement and synchrony comparisons.
requirements: Two survey assessment points (Week 1 and Week 3) with team-level agreement scoring (weighted Kappa threshold 0.33) to label perceptions as similar or different
constraints: Derived within a 3-week WIL program; the weighted Kappa 0.33 threshold defines the similar/different boundary, so groups depend on that cutoff
target_learners: Adult learners in team-based work-integrated learning programs
target_learning_goals: Teamwork and collaboration skills
Task cohesion in collaborative learning teams
examples: Teams were randomly grouped into teams of about five members across 15 program sessions, then categorised into one of the four groups based on their Weeks 1 and 3 survey agreement
key_sources: Zamecnik, A., Kovanović, V., Joksimović, S., Grossmann, G., Ladjal, D., Pardo, A. (2024). The perceptions of task cohesion in collaborative learning teams. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09424-5

article_title: Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs
citation: Bo Yang. (2024). Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09426-3
title: Community of Inquiry framework as the analytical lens for cognitive and socio-emotional interaction
description: The study adopts the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework of Garrison et al. (2000) to analyze cognitive and socio-emotional interaction in danmaku and on discussion boards. The article states the framework "delineates three interconnected elements—cognitive presence, social presence, and teaching presence—that collectively contribute to a meaningful educational experience." Cognitive presence is described as having four phases (initiation, exploration, integration, resolution), which the study used to interpret learners' question-asking and knowledge sharing. The original three presences were used rather than later expansions.
requirements: The framework is applied to learner-generated text in asynchronous, video-based online environments; a coding scheme derived from Rourke et al.'s social-presence template operationalizes it
constraints: The study used the original three types of presence and did not adopt later expansions such as additional presence types
Cognitive interaction categories were limited to two categories identified in a pilot analysis
target_learners: MOOC learners, primarily Grade 10 students in an informal Chinese math course
target_learning_goals: Understanding social interaction, collaboration, and cognitive engagement in large-scale online learning
examples: The author coded 2435 danmaku messages and 739 discussion-board posts against the CoI-derived scheme and interpreted initiation/exploration phases as evident but integration/resolution as absent
key_sources: Bo Yang. (2024). Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09426-3

article_title: Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs
citation: Bo Yang. (2024). Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09426-3
title: Combine danmaku with discussion boards so MOOC environments serve both large-community connectedness and small-group exchange
description: The article argues that because the two tools organize mass participation differently—one as a video-synchronized collective space, the other as threaded small-group discussion—pairing them covers complementary learner needs. It states that "learners can simultaneously benefit from both small-group and large-community environments," and that "the combination of danmaku and the discussion board in MOOCs has the potential to address diverse aspects of individual learners' demands." In the studied lecture, different needs such as information retrieval and temporary while-learning connectedness were both satisfied at least to some extent.
requirements: Both tools available on one course webpage, with the discussion board reachable for deeper threads and danmaku switchable in the video player
constraints: Claim rests on one naturalistic lecture in one informal math MOOC; collaboration proper was rare and occurred only in a small portion of knowledge-related discussions
target_learners: Adult and K–12 MOOC learners at large scale, including lurkers
target_learning_goals: Peer support, socio-emotional connectedness, question answering, and knowledge sharing in large-scale online courses
examples: In the studied lecture, two learners wrote detailed calculation explanations on the discussion board in response to questions raised in danmaku, showing synergy between the tools

article_title: Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects
citation: Sini Davies, Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, Kai Hakkarainen. (2024). Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09427-2
title: Epistemic objects as emergent, evolving invention-in-making guiding co-invention
description: Epistemic objects are the emergent envisioned solutions or inventions-in-making that guide and mediate knowledge-creating learning, anchored in science and technology studies. They comprise "the intertwined epistemic and material aspects of design" instantiated in sketches and prototypes, crystallize what participants seek to accomplish and do not yet know, and remain evolving and open to interpretation, actively inviting team members' contributions by raising new questions.
requirements: A shared, deliberately under-refined invention object that team members can interpret and contribute to jointly
constraints: Highly refined digital design artifacts such as CAD models "can be problematic in terms of functioning as epistemic objects and may limit experimentation owing to their high refinement and apparent accuracy"
target_learners: lower-secondary students (13-14 years old) in maker-centered STEAM projects
target_learning_goals: knowledge creation through collaboratively inventing and making materially embodied artifacts
examples: The three analyzed teams each maintained a shared epistemic object (an automated button presser, a smart sleep pillow, a solar power bank), conveying ideas through sketches and prototypes
key_sources: Sini Davies, Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, Kai Hakkarainen. (2024). Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09427-2

article_title: Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects
citation: Sini Davies, Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, Kai Hakkarainen. (2024). Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09427-2
title: Making-Process-Rug video analysis framework for co-invention processes
description: A video analysis framework for tracing situationally interleaving social and material aspects of maker-centered collaborative learning. It provides "a systematic approach to examine situationally interleaving social and material aspects of knowledge-creating learning from video data" through pre-defined coding schemes, 3-min segment coding in ELAN, and graphical timeline charts (co-invention process rugs) that render patterns across design-process, computing, product-design, and science practices and teacher/tutor engagement visible.
requirements: Video data of the collaborative process, a pre-defined coding scheme with analytic themes and coding categories, and coding software (ELAN)
constraints: The 3-min segmentation is described by the authors as relatively coarse but as having provided a good overall insight into the teams' design and making processes
target_learners: researchers and educators analyzing maker-centered and materially mediated collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: portraying temporal trajectories of collaborative learning and epistemic practices in artifact making
examples: Applied to the three teams' co-invention process rugs; inter-rater reliability on the first two SleepSound sessions yielded Cohen's kappa of 0.865 with a standard error of 0.063, 'indicating almost perfect agreement'
key_sources: Sini Davies, Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, Kai Hakkarainen. (2024). Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09427-2

article_title: Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects
citation: Sini Davies, Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen, Kai Hakkarainen. (2024). Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09427-2
title: Balance structuring with flexibility toward emergent ideas rather than scripting maker-centered knowledge creation
description: In maker-centered knowledge-creating learning, teachers should sustain the epistemic practices that help students advance invention ideas instead of following pre-established scripts. The article states teachers must move away from pre-set procedures, "embracing the self-organized, non-linear, and open nature of knowledge-creating, maker-centered learning by carefully balancing sufficient structuring and flexibility toward emergent ideas and practices".
requirements: Teachers who can improvise within studio-like makerspace settings and balance structure with openness to emergent student ideas
constraints: Overly stiff scripting and direct assistance disconnected from the joint activity may disrupt the openness and emergent nature of the process
target_learners: lower-secondary students (13-14 years old) in maker-centered STEAM projects
target_learning_goals: knowledge creation through open-ended collaborative invention
examples: The Sunny team's teacher-introduced redirection simplified the team's epistemic object and was associated with declining product-design application, illustrating the risk of over-directing open-ended work

article_title: Collaborative Problem-Solving in Knowledge-Rich Domains: A Multi-Study Structural Equation Model
citation: Laura Brandl, Matthias Stadler, Constanze Richters, Anika Radkowitsch, Martin R. Fischer, Ralf Schmidmaier, Frank Fischer. (2024). Collaborative Problem-Solving in Knowledge-Rich Domains: A Multi-Study Structural Equation Model. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09425-4
title: Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning (CDR) model relating individual characteristics, collaborative diagnostic activities, and diagnostic outcomes
description: The CDR model describes collaborative diagnostic reasoning in knowledge-rich domains by linking individual characteristics (content knowledge, collaboration knowledge, social skills) via collaborative diagnostic activities to diagnostic outcomes of accuracy, justification, and efficiency. It builds on the dual-search model of scientific discovery, treating evidence and hypothesis spaces as shared cognitive storages, and defines CDR as solving a complex problem collaboratively "by generating and evaluating evidence and hypotheses that can be shared with, elicited from, or negotiated among collaborators". This article tested the model empirically with a structural equation model across three simulation studies and proposed revisions.
requirements: Measurement of individual characteristics, CDAs, and diagnostic outcomes in a controlled simulation setting
constraints: Evidence so far comes from one domain, as the article notes that all studies were in the same medical domain, leaving cross-domain generalizability open
target_learners: intermediate medical students
target_learning_goals: collaborative diagnostic reasoning skill in knowledge-rich problem-solving
examples: The simulation casts the learner as an internist collaborating with an agent-based radiologist to diagnose fictitious fever patient cases
key_sources: Laura Brandl, Matthias Stadler, Constanze Richters, Anika Radkowitsch, Martin R. Fischer, Ralf Schmidmaier, Frank Fischer. (2024). Collaborative Problem-Solving in Knowledge-Rich Domains: A Multi-Study Structural Equation Model. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09425-4

citation: Laura Brandl, Matthias Stadler, Constanze Richters, Anika Radkowitsch, Martin R. Fischer, Ralf Schmidmaier, Frank Fischer. (2024). Collaborative Problem-Solving in Knowledge-Rich Domains: A Multi-Study Structural Equation Model. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09425-4
title: Agent-based CDR simulation for learning and researching collaborative diagnostic reasoning
description: A simulation-based learning environment in which a learner takes the role of an internist collaborating with an agent-based radiologist to diagnose fictitious patient cases with fever. Learners fill out request forms for radiological examinations, and only when they share evidence and hypotheses appropriately for their request do they receive the radiologist's findings. Agents are used because "a standardized and controlled setting" can be created "that would otherwise be hard to establish in collaborations among humans", and log-file process data can be collected without dedicated additional assessments.
requirements: Medical experts per case and examination determine what counts as appropriate sharing for receiving radiological findings
constraints: The agent was not programmed to respond to social nuances, which the authors note may buffer the effect of social skills
target_learners: intermediate medical students (years three to six)
target_learning_goals: collaborative diagnostic activities such as evidence elicitation, evidence sharing, and hypotheses sharing
examples: In the studies the collaboration partner was an agent-based radiologist and each case proceeded from individual record study, to collaboration, to individual final diagnosis and justification

article_title: Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry
citation: Ramy Elmoazen, Mohammed Saqr, Laura Hirsto, Matti Tedre. (2025). Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09431-6
title: Community of inquiry framework as a socio-cognitive foundation for operationalizing online collaborative discourse
description: The article uses the community of inquiry (CoI) framework as the coding lens for role identification, with "three main components, 'social presence, cognitive presence, and teaching presence,' that are necessary for a successful educational experience". Social presence covers affective, interactive and cohesive expression; cognitive presence proceeds through the phases of "triggering event, exploration, integration, and resolution"; teaching presence "organizes, facilitates, and directs" the other presences. The study coded student discourse with ten CoI elements and argues CoI supplies theory that quantitative learning analytics often lacks. Students' teaching presence was included because it can improve role identification.
requirements: Discourse must be codable into the CoI social, cognitive and teaching presence indicators, with trained coders achieving acceptable intercoder agreement
constraints: The framework was developed for asynchronous text-based online discussions; the resolution phase was excluded in this study due to disproportionately few posts (23)
target_learners: higher education students in problem-based learning
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
social interaction and group cohesion
shared teaching and facilitation behaviors
examples: The authors coded 9301 Moodle posts with CoI indicators (kappa rising from 0.76 to 0.88) and used the resulting states as variables for latent class role identification.
key_sources: Ramy Elmoazen, Mohammed Saqr, Laura Hirsto, Matti Tedre. (2025). Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09431-6

article_title: Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry
citation: Ramy Elmoazen, Mohammed Saqr, Laura Hirsto, Matti Tedre. (2025). Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09431-6
title: Multilayered temporal analysis pattern for collaborative learning: roles as states, sequences, and trajectories
description: This analytical pattern combines several learning-analytics methods into layers to capture role dynamics over time: latent class analysis converts CoI-coded discourse into role states, epistemic network analysis maps code co-occurrence within roles, sequence mining orders roles across weeks, and Markov process mining estimates transition probabilities within trajectories. The authors motivate the layering with Reimann et al.'s warning that "relying on a single sequential approach can hide in details due to the ontological flatness of educational data", so that "such a combination yields a much better understanding of the temporal aspects of students' roles".
requirements: Timestamped interaction logs with author identifiers, discourse coded against a theoretical framework in ordered time frames (weekly stanzas), and R tooling (glca, ENA Webkit, TramineR, seqHMM)
constraints: The Markov model was chosen partly because it avoids the data-trimming other process-mining methods require; transitions below 5% probability are thinned for readability
target_learners: students in online discussion-based cross-course collaborative programs
target_learning_goals: understanding and monitoring students' evolving collaboration roles and dispositions
examples: Applied to 13 weeks of PBL discussion across four dental-science courses, the pipeline identified three roles, three trajectories, and their Markov transition structures.
key_sources: Ramy Elmoazen, Mohammed Saqr, Laura Hirsto, Matti Tedre. (2025). Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09431-6
grain_size: course-level analytic pattern spanning multiple consecutive courses

article_title: CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?
citation: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4
title: A3C framework: a broad model of joint participation in large online knowledge communities
description: The editorial cites Jeong et al. (2017)'s "A3C" framework as a broad and useful model for joint interactions in large online knowledge communities. It "integrates different forms of participation, from 'attendance' (being a community member observing the ongoing knowledge building processes), to coordination, cooperation and finally collaboration." The editorial uses it to interpret how mass participation in a MOOC depended on the tools used.
requirements: Applies to large online knowledge communities rather than small synchronous groups
target_learners: members of large online knowledge communities and MOOC participants
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge building in mass online settings
examples: Yang (2024) drew on the A3C framework, combined with socio-emotional analysis, to study mass participation in a MOOC on basic maths, finding participation forms differed between a Danmaku environment and discussion board threads.
key_sources: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4

article_title: CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?
citation: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4
title: Collaboration Sciences: a proposed superclass of CSCL encompassing group dynamics, communication, and organizational learning
description: The authors propose a research domain, a superclass of CSCL, called the Collaboration Sciences, related to but not identical to the Learning Sciences. Blending Learning and Collaboration Sciences would let CSCL "gain a broader perspective on learning under the conditions of technology-mediated collaboration, including forms of group learning that are not designed for in advance", examining groups as learning and interacting entities.
requirements: Shared goals and methods with the Learning Sciences and with constituent fields such as small group research, CSCW, co-design, networked learning, and collaborative creativity
constraints: The authors note the risk that an orientation broader than the LS could lead to a theoretical Tower of Babel
target_learners: CSCL and learning sciences researchers
target_learning_goals: theorising collaboration and group learning in CSCL research
examples: Zamecnik et al. (2024) applying a group-dynamics lens to task cohesion in collaborative learning teams is given as an example of this perspective applied to CSCL.
key_sources: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4

article_title: CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?
citation: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4
title: Formalise theories with computational models (e.g., Bayesian framework) to counter epistemic fragmentation in CSCL
description: The authors recommend striving for a unified language, such as a formalisation strategy, in which different CSCL theories can be expressed, proposing the Bayesian framework as a formal language within reach for CSCL researchers. Formal modelling "makes us think deeply about our theories", highlights gaps and lack of clarity, contributes to open theorising by making assumptions explicit, and yields compact, easily exchanged theories.
requirements: Willingness to specify background knowledge and how it is connected in inferences; Bayesian method basics can be learned in a couple of weeks and are supported by software tools including several R packages
constraints: The authors acknowledge the possibility that CSCL is a research area where formalisation and simulation do not add value (the pitfall of reductionism), comparing it to social psychology's absence of formalized theory
target_learners: CSCL and learning sciences researchers
target_learning_goals: theory building and unification in CSCL; modelling collaborative sense-making and regulation
examples: The authors formalise shared meaning-making as Bayesian inference of P(concept | utterance), and suggest Bayesian modelling of metacognitive regulation as rational choice of learning activities providing a yardstick of optimal performance.
key_sources: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4

article_title: CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?
citation: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4
title: Mentalising in shared meaning-making as Bayesian reasoning under uncertainty
description: The article presents shared meaning-making as requiring 'mind reading' (mental state inference, or mentalizing): hearers infer the concept meant by a peer's word, using contextual, para-verbal and non-verbal signals, world and cultural knowledge, and dialogically established common ground, since a word's conceptual meaning remains hidden beyond its registerable use. The authors propose formalising this as probabilistic inference in a Bayesian framework, computing P(concept | utterance) from the prior P(concept) times the likelihood P(utterance | concept), normalised.
requirements: Listeners must have their own conceptualisations (not necessarily propositional) to compute likelihood of alignment with the speaker's conception; a more knowledgeable listener such as a teacher would know multiple conceptualizations
target_learners: students in collaborative groups; teachers as more knowledgeable listeners
target_learning_goals: shared meaning-making and negotiation of conceptual meaning in dialogue
examples: Applied to a peer saying "force" in a science class: listeners compare the utterance against their own conceptualisations of force to infer the speaker's conception.
key_sources: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4

article_title: CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?
citation: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4
title: Bayesian Networks as a practical, low-threshold formal language for student models, assessment, and collaborative learning theory
description: Bayesian Networks are presented as both a specification language and a computational mechanism with practical value in designing group and learning support systems: they have "been frequently used to build student models (Millán et al., 2010) and for assessment (Almond et al., 2015)". The article argues the technique can also serve to formalise collaborative learning theories, and notes its methodological basics can be learned in a couple of weeks with support from many software tools including several R packages — comparatively low threshold and high ceiling.
requirements: Software tool support, including several R packages; a couple of weeks of method learning, e.g., in a university course
target_learners: CSCL researchers and AIED/educational measurement practitioners
target_learning_goals: student modelling, assessment, and formalising collaborative learning theories
examples: The article also names Agent-based Modelling (Wilensky & Rand, 2015) as another formal approach with potential to counteract epistemic fragmentation in the field.

article_title: Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction
citation: Sebastian Strauß, Isis Tunnigkeit, Julia Eberle, Arlind Avdullahu, Nikol Rummel. (2025). Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09430-7
title: Script theory of guidance: collaboration knowledge resides in internal collaboration scripts that external scripts can reshape
description: The article's explanatory account holds that knowledge about collaboration is encoded in internal collaboration scripts, analogous to cognitive scripts for everyday situations, comprising knowledge and expectations about situation structure, phases, roles, and goal-directed actions. When learners lack effective internal scripts, "external collaboration scripts" provide scaffolds that prescribe beneficial interactions or inhibit undesired patterns. Through repeated guided practice, learners build internal script components; the internalized script "is not a direct replication of the external" but a reconfigured internal representation.
requirements: Learners must actively process the script's action sequences and enact the scripted actions to benefit
constraints: Overscripting: a detailed external script may cause process losses for learners with well-developed internal scripts (expertise-reversal effect); overly vague scripts offer insufficient guidance for learners with low prior knowledge
Concerns that scripts limit learner autonomy and hamper natural interaction are discussed
target_learners: university students collaborating in small groups
target_learning_goals: collaboration skills
examples: The study's script condition embedded a four-phase external script in the video-conference margin with prompts, colored phase bars, progress bars, and audio signals for phase changes

title: External collaboration script with four timed phases and prompt scaffolding displayed during collaboration
description: A text scaffold presented in the margin of the shared video-conference screen during the learning phase, specifying phases and prompts for beneficial interaction. It provided "a sequence of actions (scene-level) and within each phase provided the group with prompts on beneficial actions". The four phases were "coordination (5 min), information pooling (7 min), discussion (10 min), and decision making (7 min)", each with one extra minute to read prompts, color highlighting, a progress bar, and audio signals at phase changes.
requirements: Script adherence was verified by coding video against the prescribed phases (maximum 20 points; weighted κ = 0.94 on a 30% subset)
constraints: Script groups received 34 minutes versus 30 minutes for other conditions due to prompt-reading time
The script directly targeted the interaction, unlike the reflection scaffold
target_learners: university students in three-person groups
target_learning_goals: productive collaborative interaction on information-pooling problems
examples: Groups in the script condition followed phase-structured prompts while solving a kindergarten floor-plan construction problem

title: Reflection scaffold combining a group awareness tool (spider-plot feedback) with guided feed-up, feed-back, and feed-forward phases
description: A post-collaboration autonomy-supportive scaffold modeled on Phielix et al. (2011). Group members individually and anonymously rated their group's interaction quality in a 28-question questionnaire (the GAT, feed-up); averaged ratings were "visualized for the group in the form of spider-plot-diagrams"; the group then viewed the diagrams, reflected on the first collaboration phase (feedback), and discussed and wrote improvement plans in Etherpad (feed-forward) within a 12-minute limit.
requirements: Individual anonymity of ratings before group discussion
A dedicated reflection phase about which groups write concrete plans for the next collaboration
constraints: Applied after the first collaboration phase only, targeting past interaction rather than live interaction
target_learners: university students in three-person groups
target_learning_goals: knowledge about effective collaboration and plans for improving interaction
examples: A group's reflection notes in Fig. 5 included nine suggestions such as 'Share all information' and 'Ask clarification questions'

title: Meier et al. rating schema adopted as the domain-agnostic model of productive collaboration with five aspects and nine dimensions
description: The study's model of productive collaboration is the rating schema by Meier et al. (2007), chosen because it overlaps with PISA 2015 and ACT21S skill frameworks and, unlike the domain-specific FINCA framework, is domain-agnostic and adjustable to specific tasks. It identifies "five aspects of successful computer-supported interdisciplinary collaborative problem-solving processes: communication, coordination, joint information processing, relationship management, and motivation", decomposed into nine dimensions such as sustaining mutual understanding, information pooling, and reaching consensus. It served both to score collaboration knowledge in the tests and to rate interaction quality in the videos.
requirements: Can be adjusted to the specific collaboration task
Supports rating interaction quality at multiple levels
constraints: Originally developed to assess quality of interaction in groups; some dimensions were further differentiated into subcodes for the study's coding manual
target_learners: university students in small groups
target_learning_goals: collaboration skills
examples: Used as codes for the knowledge test scoring (Cohen's κ = 0.74 on 20% of answers) and for two-stage video-based interaction-quality rating (weighted κ = 0.87 on a 20% subset)

title: Determine how to support collaboration by comparing supports along the CSCL support dimensions goal, timing, target, and directivity
description: The article proposes analyzing collaboration supports using Rummel's (2018) twelve-dimension taxonomy, focusing on the most salient dimensions. "Our comparison focuses on the most salient CSCL support dimensions, namely: goal, timing, target, and directivity." External scripts typically act during collaboration, directly target the social interaction, and are directive, whereas reflection scaffolds act before subsequent collaboration, target metacognitive reflection, and leave learners "more autonomy over their interaction". This lens clarifies which learning mechanism each support uses.
requirements: An explicit taxonomy of CSCL support dimensions to structure the comparison
constraints: The remaining dimensions of the framework are contingent on the particular implementation of the support
target_learners: designers of CSCL support tools
target_learning_goals: understanding how support design shapes the acquisition of collaboration skills
examples: The study contrasted its on-line script with its pre-task reflection scaffold on these four dimensions before testing their effects

article_title: Emergent group understanding: Investigating intersubjectivity in sociotechnical interdependencies
citation: Mørch, A. I., Andersen, R., Eie, S., & Mifsud, L. (2024). Emergent group understanding: Investigating intersubjectivity in sociotechnical interdependencies. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09432-5
title: Emergent group understanding conceptual framework (sociotechnical congruence + emergence + intersubjectivity)
description: The article's conceptual framework integrates sociotechnical congruence from software engineering with Mead's emergence and Rommetveit's intersubjectivity, operationalized through proleptic instances (pre-prolepsis/initiation and shared prolepsis/explication). Prior work suggested "initiation–explication in transforming individuals' works into higher-level (recurring) activities", which the authors transfer from CSCW to CSCL. The framework proposes that in small-group conversation, "goal-driven behavior may be triggered by a certain type of unplanned event initiated locally", giving a lens into spontaneous learning toward a shared knowledge object.
requirements: Video-recorded computer-mediated learning activities in small groups for interaction analysis
constraints: The authors state that whether the initiation–explication relationship is one-way or reciprocal are empirical questions to be investigated
target_learners: student teachers
seventh-grade pupils
target_learning_goals: social studies and history understanding
collaborative knowledge building in Minecraft
examples: Applied to reconstructing a nineteenth-century industrial community along the Aker River in Minecraft and video-recorded role-plays

title: Gradient of states of intersubjectivity ordered by density of sociotechnical relations
description: The article reports a preliminary typology of six states of intersubjectivity, ordered by increasing density of sociotechnical interdependencies: vague, technical, fragmented, connected, entangled, and enmeshed intersubjectivity. The authors "adapted a qualitative gradient of intersubjectivity in terms of the density of sociotechnical relations", combining deductive STC-derived coordination needs with inductive themes. Entangled intersubjectivity covers unplanned switching between gaming and academic behavior, and enmeshed intersubjectivity occurs in role-play conversation, both including instances of emergent group understanding.
requirements: Interaction analysis with state descriptives derived by iterative coding among four researchers
constraints: States were derived from data of one profiled group (group 7), with snapshots of a 3-week process
target_learners: student teachers
seventh-grade pupils
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning with Minecraft
shared understanding of social studies topics
examples: Extracts mapped state changes from vague (task interpretation) to enmeshed (video-recorded role-play in Minecraft)

title: Three-phase teaching model for social studies with Minecraft (Introduction, Reconstruction, Transformation)
description: A teaching model resulting from design-based research iterations that organizes social studies teaching with Minecraft Education in three activities: Introduction (teacher lecturing, past orientation, vague intersubjectivity, domain-specific skills), Reconstruction (collaborative design in Minecraft and role-play scriptwriting, present orientation, fragmented intersubjectivity) and Transformation (role-playing and video recording, future orientation, focused intersubjectivity). The current version "suggests how generic and domain-specific skill practices can be combined in three ways", pairing each phase with a temporal orientation, a level of intersubjectivity, and a primary/secondary skill type.
requirements: Minecraft Education environment
teacher facilitation following the model's phases
constraints: Adapted from iteration 2 and further adapted for seventh-grade school teaching, which required additional facilitators

seventh-grade pupils
target_learning_goals: understanding the industrial revolution in Norway
combining generic and domain-specific skills
examples: Group 7 reconstructed the nail factory's administrative buildings and a steel mill on the Aker River and staged a video-recorded role-play

title: Coordinate top-down instructional scaffolding with bottom-up creative, self-determined learning goals to balance creative and instructional learning goals
description: The teaching model coordinates two kinds of learning goals that must be aligned: instructional goals supported top-down by the teaching model, and creative, self-determined bottom-up goals suggested by a learner or group. The article presents this as addressing "the problem of balancing creative and instructional learning goals", transferring the STC insight that top-down and bottom-up coordination should align. In the learning activity, students benefited from both teachers' scaffolding and self-organized group work, letting unplanned creative acts feed into planned instruction.
requirements: A structured teaching model (scaffold) to carry the instructional goals
opportunity for students to set self-determined group goals
constraints: A constructivist dilemma exists between creative and predefined learning goals that the authors aim to untangle, not dissolve
target_learners: student teachers
seventh-grade pupils
target_learning_goals: social studies and history learning
collaborative building and role-play in Minecraft
examples: In the design experiments, teachers scaffolded the three phases while groups self-organized work between weekly sessions

title: Ground the selection of sensors and data for learning analytics in analyses of the learning practices themselves, so the collected data are pedagogically valid
description: The article argues that selecting technologies and sensors for capturing collaboration is a complex task and that data are sometimes not "pedagogically valid." It therefore conducts a design ethnography as one of the first steps in a user-centered, iterative design process, asking which sensors would provide pedagogically valid measures and why, grounding MMLA in educational theory and practice.

title: Embedded assessment: instructors continuously monitor social cues to assess displayed understanding and tailor feedback within ongoing simulator tasks
description: Embedded assessment denotes the close relationship between assessment and instruction during an ongoing task. In simulator-based maritime training, instructors continuously monitor implicit and explicit social cues — student gaze, bodily disposition, and prosodic features of talk such as intonation, volume, pitch, and pace — to make embedded assessments, then use students' displayed understandings in the next turn to correct, clarify, or endorse their work.
requirements: Relies on the instructor's ability to recognize the fit or gap between learning objectives and ongoing activities as they unfold
constraints: Requires professional intersubjectivity that the article says goes beyond even the most advanced MMLA systems developed today

article_title: Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique
citation: Zhou, J., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Ryan, Z., Stiso, C., Murphy, D., Danish, J., Chinn, C. A., & Duncan, R. G. (2025). Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09438-z
title: Direct and soft disagreement taxonomy for coding peer critique talk
description: The study adapts Pomerantz's strong/weak disagreement distinction into a two-category coding scheme for dissenting turns in peer critique. Direct forms — direct negation, challenging rhetorical wh-questions, and sensemaking challenges — were "employed for immediate and overt contradiction with prior statements without delay." Soft forms — hedging, yes-but partial agreement, posing an alternative idea, indirect challenge, and prosody — "were used to imply disagreements rather than overtly contradict others' ideas." The authors preferred the term soft over weak, and expanded the framework with codes emerging from the data; each turn could receive one or more codes.
requirements: Transcribed disagreement instances segmented into episodes, with each dissenting turn coded one or more times using the direct or soft scheme.
constraints: The authors note they "chose to start with a simpler approach" than the richer taxonomies of other CA studies, to establish foundational understanding in CSCL contexts.
target_learners: 5th-grade elementary science students
target_learning_goals: Collaborative argumentation and disagreement management during peer critique
examples: The coding scheme classified a turn like "Yeah, I mean they did write that the entire paragraph, but let's just check it out" as yes, but partial agreement plus hedging.

article_title: Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique
citation: Zhou, J., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Ryan, Z., Stiso, C., Murphy, D., Danish, J., Chinn, C. A., & Duncan, R. G. (2025). Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09438-z
title: MEME: a networked collaborative modeling tool with evidence linking and commenting for peer critique
description: MEME (Modeling and Evidence Mapping Environment) is a CSCL tool supporting students in creating, sharing, evaluating, and revising qualitative models, "organized around entities, processes (mechanisms), and outcomes." Students can access an evidence library of brief reports and simulations, explicitly link evidence to model components with rationales, rate evidence strength, and justify ratings. Its commenting feature lets students comment on specific components of peers' models, select the most relevant evaluation criterion from a menu of class-shared criteria, and reply to comments — creating a shared space for collective, evidence-based modeling with integrated feedback.
requirements: A comment box prompting students to "select the most relevant criterion for their comment from a menu including options aligned with class-shared criteria for model evaluation."
target_learners: 5th-grade elementary science students
target_learning_goals: Building and revising mechanistic models of complex ecosystems using evidence
examples: During the gallery walk, students used MEME to evaluate other groups' models, leave constructive comments, and address received comments synchronously and asynchronously.

article_title: Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique
citation: Zhou, J., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., Ryan, Z., Stiso, C., Murphy, D., Danish, J., Chinn, C. A., & Duncan, R. G. (2025). Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09438-z
title: Design CSCL environments that explicitly cultivate social norms and epistemic goals so students can manage disagreement productively
description: The article argues that productive disagreement in peer critique depends on an environment where students feel safe disagreeing and view disagreement as a path to better knowledge. It states it is "essential to cultivate a CSCL environment where students feel confident and comfortable about managing disagreement," and that "creating such an environment requires intentional development of shared goals and social norms." Norms such as building on ideas, accountability to each other, supporting ideas with reasons, and consensus-building should be established so disagreements become opportunities to construct more accurate scientific knowledge rather than sources of conflict.
requirements: Explicit whole-class instruction outlining expectations, exemplar critiques distinguishing helpful from unhelpful comments, and shared evaluation criteria for models.
constraints: An excessive focus on pursuing group harmony may lead students to avoid overt disagreement, the article warns.
target_learners: 5th-grade elementary science students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: Collaborative argumentation, peer critique, and collective knowledge advancement in scientific modeling
examples: Before the gallery walk, researchers led a whole-class discussion on activity goals, had students identify exemplary critiques, and emphasized use of class-shared criteria and evidence.

article_title: How does collaborative task design shape collaborative knowledge construction and group-level regulation of learning? A study of secondary school students’ interactions in two varied tasks
citation: Zabolotna, K., Nøhr, L., Iwata, M., Spikol, D., Malmberg, J., & Järvenoja, H. (2025). How does collaborative task design shape collaborative knowledge construction and group-level regulation of learning? A study of secondary school students' interactions in two varied tasks. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09442-3
title: Gunawardena et al.'s Interaction Analysis Model (IAM) conceptualizing CKC as five phases from pooling of knowledge to agreement
description: The IAM describes CKC as evolving "from lower mental functions, i.e., 'pooling of knowledge,' to higher mental functions through five distinct CKC phases": (1) sharing and comparing information, (2) discovering and exploring dissonance or disagreement, (3) negotiating shared meaning or co-constructing knowledge, (4) testing the proposed synthesis, and (5) reaching agreement expressed through metacognitive statements indicating cognitive change. The study adopts it because it is grounded in social constructivism, has been empirically validated for video-recorded interactions, and captures CKC through interactions with both peers and artifacts. The authors adapted category descriptions to secondary school interactions and excluded the 'agree' phase due to low frequency.
requirements: Video-recorded collaborative interactions amenable to coding of mutually exclusive CKC phases within utterances
constraints: The 'agree' phase was excluded from modeling due to low frequency in these data
target_learners: Secondary school students (eighth and ninth grade)
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge construction in science and robotics tasks
examples: CKC phases coded in video data from the SimSketch drawing task and the Simua robot-building task, with intercoder reliability κ = 0.82 and κ = 0.73 respectively
