J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09442-3
title: Design CSCL tasks deliberately, because task design—not technology alone—shapes collaborative knowledge construction and group-level regulation
description: The study argues that the nature of a collaborative task determines which collaborative processes students engage in: "the task design, not technology alone, significantly shapes students' learning interactions." Conceptually oriented tasks fostered prolonged cognitive engagement in building shared meaning, while hands-on tasks elicited frequent brief CKC episodes and more emotion–motivation regulation for sustaining positive collaboration. Designers should therefore anticipate the regulatory demands—cognitive or socioemotional—that a task's structure will create.
requirements: Explicit consideration of task structure, content difficulty, and technological setup when designing CSCL activities
constraints: Learners may radically reconfigure how a task is implemented, and actual implementation may differ from the teacher's original plan
target_learners: Secondary school students in technology-enhanced collaborative settings
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge construction and group-level regulation of cognition and emotion–motivation
examples: The study compared a conceptual physics poster task on a shared interactive tabletop with a hands-on robot-hand building task and showed distinct CKC–regulation profiles for each

citation: Pengjin Wang · Fan Chen · Deliang Wang · Gaowei Chen (2025). Enhancing students' dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09443-2
title: Classroom Discourse Analyser (CDA) platform for visualising classroom talk
description: The CDA (Chen et al., 2020) transforms uploaded lesson videos into synchronised transcripts and coloured bubbles sized by turn length, with statistics such as "Total Words" and word-share percentages per speaker, and a ranking function. In this study the research team used CDA to generate visualisations of teachers' lesson recordings that students viewed on iPads alongside clips during forum-based reflection. It had previously been applied in teacher professional learning and, in this study, supported young students' reflection on their own classroom talk.
requirements: Classroom video recordings uploaded to the platform and processed by the research team to generate visual representations
Teachers select clips and devise reflection prompts for students
constraints: The researchers, not the teachers, generated the visualisations from the recordings
target_learners: second-grade (around age 7) primary school students
target_learning_goals: dialogic reflection on classroom participation
ICT/computational thinking subject knowledge
examples: Visualisations of Hazel's and Leo's ICT lessons supported in-class forum reflection in the 3-month intervention

citation: Pengjin Wang · Fan Chen · Deliang Wang · Gaowei Chen (2025). Enhancing students' dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09443-2
title: Four-stage visualisation-supported dialogic reflection (VSDR) implementation cycle
description: VSDR unfolded in four stages across the intervention: teachers record lesson videos; the research team processes videos into visual representations of talk; teachers individually review clips and select segments with relevant visualisations, devising reflection prompts around "'what happened' (facts), 'how to interpret' (reason and evaluation) and 'how to improve' (plan)"; and students use iPads in class to reflect on a discussion forum, reviewing peers' responses and contributing feedback. The pattern mediates students' reflection on classroom talk through context-based group discussion supported by visualised representations.
requirements: Discussion forum with teacher-crafted prompts and technical support for students
Visualised representations integrated with classroom activity videos
constraints: Teachers recorded lessons at different doses (weekly vs bi-weekly), constituting higher- and lower-dose groups rather than a treatment–control contrast
target_learners: primary school students (grade two, around age 7)
target_learning_goals: dialogic reflection on group work and whole-class talk
computational thinking
examples: Hazel's group recorded weekly (14 visualisations) and Leo's bi-weekly (8 visualisations) over three months

title: Dialogic reflection as reflection occurring through discourse with others in a community
description: The article frames dialogic reflection as reflection occurring in a collaborative context, focusing on "the reflection in a community, that is, 'discourse with others'" (Mann & Walsh, 2013), similar to collaborative reflection and reflection through critical friendship, where participants give voice to their thinking while being heard constructively and critically. As an outcome, whether alternative views and others' perspectives are concerned indicates reflection quality, positioning dialogic reflection above routine/technical or descriptive levels and featuring cycles of weighing claims, exploring alternatives and gaining new insights.

constraints: The article focuses on interpersonal reflection in a community rather than intrapersonal reflection

young learners
target_learning_goals: reflective thinking
productive classroom discourse
examples: VSDR operationalises this account by mediating students' discourse about classroom talk with visualisations

article_title: Measuring the quality of collaborative group engagement: Development and validation of the QCGE self-assessment scale (QCGE-SAS)
citation: Loris T. Jeitziner, Lisa Paneth, Oliver Rack, Susanne Bleisch, Carmen Zahn. (2025). Measuring the quality of collaborative group engagement: Development and validation of the QCGE self-assessment scale (QCGE-SAS). Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. title: QCGE-SAS: a standardised self-assessment scale for quality of collaborative group engagement in higher education CSCL
description: The QCGE-SAS is a pragmatic group-level self-assessment instrument operationalising QCGE across behavioural, social, cognitive, and conceptual-to-consequential dimensions with items phrased in first-person plural (e.g. asking about "the subjective experience of the group's collaborative participation during the task"). Items were derived from Sinha et al.'s (2015) QCGE rating scheme, reviewed by an expert panel, and rated on a seven-point Likert scale from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree'. The article positions it as complementing resource-intensive observation-based procedures and multi-method measurement.
requirements: Items take the group as the unit of analysis, worded to make individuals identify with the group as a unit rather than as individuals, and respondents answer about their learning group's collaborative task
constraints: Validated for higher education contexts (undergraduate and postgraduate students in one School of Applied Psychology); the social engagement subscale showed unacceptable reliability
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: quality of collaborative group engagement in CSCL tasks
examples: Administered at the end of courses and at the end of a laboratory CSCL study with groups of three; items were presented in randomised order

citation: Loris T. Jeitziner, Lisa Paneth, Oliver Rack, Susanne Bleisch, Carmen Zahn. (2025). Measuring the quality of collaborative group engagement: Development and validation of the QCGE self-assessment scale (QCGE-SAS). Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09445-8
title: QCGE framework: four dimensions of quality of collaborative group engagement at group level
description: The QCGE construct, from Sinha et al. (2015) and elaborated by Rogat et al. (2022), conceptualises engagement as shared, contextualised and multidimensional at the group level: "behavioural engagement (BE) includes persistence and effort in the task; social engagement (SE) involves the quality of group interactions"; cognitive engagement covers task-centred planning, structuring and monitoring; and conceptual-to-consequential engagement covers using domain-specific methods and connecting ideas to prior knowledge. The article treats QCGE as a key element of shared regulation of learning in CSCL and builds its scale directly on this framework.
requirements: Observable indicators per dimension (on-/off-task behaviour, balanced participation, planning and monitoring, evidence use) ground the rating scheme that the self-assessment items derive from
constraints: Conceptualised for collaborative learning in complex digital learning environments; the dimensions are interrelated rather than independent, and low-quality behavioural sequences can even support cohesion
target_learners: student learning groups in higher education
target_learning_goals: dimension-specific and overall quality of collaborative group engagement
examples: Sinha et al. (2015) tested the framework with ten groups using an observational approach; this article operationalised it as a self-assessment scale for higher education

article_title: Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning
citation: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7
title: ABC-VR: a conceptual framework for collaborative 360VR learning grounded in activity theory
description: ABC-VR is a conceptual framework for designing and researching IVR-mediated collaborative learning, grounded in activity theory and practice theory. It builds on "a dual sense of activity" — the original activity recorded with 360-degree cameras and the collaborative learning activity learners produce in an ABC-VR session. It shifts attention from individual concepts like immersion and presence to group-level meaning-making, where learners "question each other and imagine future actions" and figuratively reason with participants in the original activity.
requirements: Relies on software allowing shared playback of 360-degree video in HMDs, such as CAVA360VR, with tools for pausing, scrubbing and annotating
constraints: Knowledge produced in 360VR remains 'on-action' (Schön, 1983) because recorded activities cannot be manipulated owing to reduced interactivity of 360VR
target_learners: higher education students
professional learners such as teachers and medical students
target_learning_goals: collaborative analysis and reflection on recorded real-world practices
developing shared professional vision
examples: Illustrated via medical knee examination training, mentoring of newly qualified teachers, and a speculative psychiatric multidisciplinary meeting case

article_title: Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning
citation: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7
title: Three hierarchical levels of human activity — operations, actions, activities — as the analytic spine of ABC-VR
description: Adopting activity theory, ABC-VR distinguishes "three hierarchical levels of human activity: operations, actions and activities" (Kaptelinin & Nardi, 2012), which are dynamic and context-dependent. Actions are the starting point of meaning-making; learners can shift down to ask how actions are performed and up to ask why. ABC-VR argues traditional procedural IVR training mostly moves down to isolated operations, while ABC-VR centres on identifying relevant actions and reasoning upward to the motive-level activity.
requirements: Pedagogical designs must create links between the two ends of the activity hierarchy so reflections can be tied to operations and operations to context
constraints: The boundaries between operations, actions and activities depend on the context and the learner's experience
target_learners: learners analysing recorded practices collaboratively
target_learning_goals: understanding both how and why actions are performed in a practice
examples: In the medical case, students identify which knee tests to perform, how they are performed, and why and when they are performed
key_sources: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7

citation: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7
title: Design IVR-supported collaborative learning activities so learners can ask 'What?', 'How?', and 'Why?' about recorded actions
description: Because ABC-VR orients to the activity level, designs should span the hierarchy of operations, actions and activities rather than only training procedure. The article argues traditional IVR designs afford moving from identifying what actions are performed to how, while ABC-VR "also implies asking why actions are performed", and that it is important to design links between the two ends of the activity hierarchy. Shared reflection can be designed through reflection prompts or by including learners with multiple perspectives.
requirements: Design must link procedural knowledge to its situated context and reflections about the broader setting to the operations that drive actions
constraints: Activity-level orientation introduces open-endedness and increases the complexity of designing supportive HCI systems (Kuutti, 1995)
target_learners: medical students
newly qualified teachers
interdisciplinary professional groups
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
classroom interaction analysis
professional communication reflection
examples: Medical students learned both how to decide which knee tests to perform and the steps for performing them; mentoring case participants alternated between identifying actions and reasoning about the overall teaching practice

title: Design virtually mediated environments that are situated in practice, engaging stakeholders to select relevant recorded activities
description: ABC-VR environments should use situated 360-degree recordings of real-world activities rather than computer-generated reproductions, selected collaboratively with learners and practitioners. The article states it is important "to engage with learners/educators/professionals to identify tensions and possibilities in current practices" learners wish to examine, e.g. professors selecting knee-exam sequences or teachers choosing clips to analyse with mentors. Design must also shift from affording social interactivity to social interaction.
requirements: Settings with a tradition for using video (e.g., teacher training) and access to 360-degree capture with appropriate ethical approval
constraints: Recordings are never neutral; they capture a version of a situation as it unfolds
Real knee exams can be difficult to record owing to GDPR concerns
target_learners: students and professionals analysing recorded practices
target_learning_goals: establishing joint attention
perspective taking
collaborative imagining
examples: In the medical case relevant sequences were selected with a professor; in the mentoring case teachers identified relevant clips themselves

citation: Lucas Paulsen, Jacob Davidsen. (2025). Activity-based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09446-7
title: Three collaboration modes for ABC-VR: within-VR, outside VR, and across realities
description: ABC-VR does not limit collaboration to one mode. Within IVR, learners are jointly immersed and can pause, annotate and discuss the recording; outside VR, IVR serves as an individual or shared interactional resource, with learners taking off headsets in a co-located space; across realities, one learner is immersed while others follow on a screen, allowing non-immersed learners to guide the immersed learner in real time. A screen mediates across realities, making the immersed learner's interaction visible to others.
requirements: Software supporting shared playback, pausing, scrubbing and annotation for within-VR mode; a screen-based mediator across realities for the third mode
constraints: Across-realities collaboration limits the immersed learner's access to the bodily conduct of non-immersed learners, risking fractured ecologies
target_learners: immersed learners and their non-immersed peers or mentors
target_learning_goals: collaborative sense-making around recorded activities
examples: Silseth et al. (2024) used individual 360VR experiences as interactional resources for collaboration outside IVR; Paulsen et al. (2022) and Steier (2020) explored across-realities collaboration

title: CAVA360VR — a software platform for within-VR collaborative analysis of 360-degree video
description: CAVA360VR is a software solution that allows learners within IVR to engage and collaborate with 360-degree video recordings (Davidsen & McIlvenny, 2022). Learners have access to tools such as "pause, rewind, annotation and spatialised audio", supporting multi-layered analysis, discussion and debate within the recording. In the mentoring case it additionally allows warping between different camera positions, and using a laser to pinpoint actions and moments in the recorded interaction.
requirements: 360-degree video recordings of relevant activities and HMD hardware; the software layer distinguishing environment content from the interactive layer
constraints: Recordings cannot be manipulated during playback owing to the reduced interactivity of 360VR
target_learners: medical students
teachers and mentors in professional development
target_learning_goals: collaborative video analysis
annotation of key moments in recorded interaction
examples: Used in both empirical cases: medical students immersed in CAVA360VR analysing knee examination footage, and teacher–mentor mentoring sessions

article_title: Understanding the role of I-positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment
citation: Aaron J. Peltoniemi, Joni Lämsä, Sami Lehesvuori, Raija Hämäläinen. (2025). Understanding the role of I-positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09447-6
title: Dialogical self theory (DST) I-positions as a CSCL analytical framework
description: DST holds that, as the article states, "the self is populated by other inner selves that collectively derive from the world and have their own voice, motives, opinions, and knowledge that become present in what are known as I-positions via dialogue in response to the social situation". The article operationalizes four positions — I–it (objectified technological other), I–me (personal knowledge), I–you (encountered other), I–we (collective identity) — grounded at utterance level to visualize knowledge and identity construction in CSCL.
requirements: Discourse must be transcribed and divided into utterances so I-positions can be grounded individually and reviewed through intersubjectivity among researchers
constraints: I-positions in this study are a snapshot of the current state of polyphony at the timing of the learning task, not temporal trajectories
Notions of what constitutes the other within the dialogical self are not always clear, especially with digital technologies
target_learners: undergraduate physics students collaborating in small groups
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction through collaborative inquiry-based problem solving
examples: Four themes from Johnstone's grounding framework were merged onto the four I-positions, one theme per position, with descriptions and example utterances in Appendix Table 2

title: Six discourse functions mapped onto inquiry-based knowledge construction categories
description: The article inductively derived a coding taxonomy: "This resulted in the following six DF: reviewing directions and strategies, sharing and confirming information, brainstorming, empirical evaluation, clarification and elaboration, and submission and reflection." These map onto inquiry-based learning phases — orientation (reviewing directions, sharing information), conceptualization (brainstorming), investigation (empirical evaluation), discussion (clarification and elaboration) and conclusion (submission and reflection) — as a means of segmenting CSCL dialogue by its function for knowledge construction.
requirements: Dialogue chunks whose relevance to a discourse function could not be agreed by all authors are excluded
Coding decisions reviewed by the other three authors through intersubjectivity
constraints: Derived inductively from one thermodynamics task with ten students in one course

examples: Orientation mapped to reviewing directions and strategies plus sharing and confirming information, following Pedaste et al.'s inquiry phases

title: The computer as a dialogical other (technological other) in CSCL
description: The article suggests the computer "can represent a dialogical other that mediates learning and identity in CSCL", intertwining social resources such as interaction with content resources such as technical language and the learning task. Students consulted the technological other (I–it), where the computer's voices included the teacher's, the animator's and other media makers'. From the DST perspective, the computer was thus "not just a knowledge artifact for learning but also a social artifact for promoting or limiting discourse... at personal and group levels".
requirements: The technological other's voices emerge only when acted upon, e.g., by clicking, so the environment must expose task directions and media outputs learners can consult
constraints: Asynchronous technological scaffolding can disrupt the overall cohesiveness of collaboration and dialogue because it can only facilitate, not actively produce learning

target_learning_goals: inquiry-based conceptual understanding and collaborative problem solving
examples: Students could consult the computer's displayed directions and outputs (I–it), which represented a mesh of the teacher's, animator's and media makers' voices

article_title: The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review
citation: Shihui Feng, Ziyi Wei. (2025). The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09450-x
title: CoMPAS framework: six forms modeling the multi-faceted and multi-level nature of individual participation in collaborative learning
description: The CoMPAS framework models individual participation in collaborative learning processes across six components: Cognitive interactions, Coordinative interactions, Metacognitive interactions, Passive participation, solo Active participation, and Socio-emotional interactions. It was induced from a systematic review of 66 empirical studies via reflexive thematic analysis, and the article states it captures "the multi-faceted and multi-level nature of individual participation in collaborative learning processes." The framework distinguishes solitary forms (passive and solo active participation) from interactive forms, with the first two "named as passive participation and solo active participation and the other four forms as cognitive interactions, socioemotional interactions, metacognitive interactions, and coordinative interactions." Passive participation (12 studies) involves receiving information without overt contribution; solo active participation (46 studies) involves manipulating artefacts without interacting; the four interaction forms involve coconstruction with other group members.
requirements: Analysis must use process data rather than outcome-focused approaches, since group deliverables often do not provide direct evidence of individual participation
constraints: Derived from empirical studies meeting inclusion criteria that used process data; studies relying solely on summative individual assessments or group-level artefacts were outside the review's scope
target_learners: students in higher education (38 of 66 studies) and K-12 school contexts (14 of 66 studies) engaged in collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: understanding and assessing individual engagement and contribution within collaborative learning processes
supporting individual-level assessment and personalized feedback during group work
examples: The framework was built inductively from open coding of 66 articles followed by six-phase reflexive thematic analysis, with contributions ranging from solo active participation (45 studies assessed) to cognitive interactions (61 studies) and coordinative interactions (16 studies)
key_sources: Shihui Feng, Ziyi Wei. (2025). The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09450-x

article_title: The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review
citation: Shihui Feng, Ziyi Wei. (2025). The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09450-x
title: Two types of conceptual indicators: direct behavioral indicators versus latent constructs inferred from oral and written inputs
description: The review synthesizes the varied conceptual indicators used to model individual participation into two general types. The first, direct behavioral indicators, are "represented by log data or specific, countable behaviors reflecting individual active or passive participation," such as counts of utterances, submissions, shared-document additions, and forum posts. The second type comprises latent constructs inferred from individuals' conversational, physical, and textual inputs, classified (drawing on the reviewed theories) into individual cognitive participation, metacognitive participation, and socioemotional participation, plus coordinative participation for logistics management. The review notes the direct indicators "demonstrate deliberate and intentional engagement in group work but without necessarily interacting with other group members."
requirements: Distinguishing passive attention indicators (logged-in duration, gazing) from active contributions is stated to be critical for modeling participation
constraints: The latent-construct classification is grounded in the theories the reviewed studies themselves used (regulation of learning, Community of Inquiry)
target_learners: collaborative learning researchers and teachers assessing individual participation
target_learning_goals: gauging individual engagement and contribution from process data in collaborative learning
examples: Direct behavioral indicators included the number of utterances, the number of different types of submissions, additions or revisions in a shared document, and post and reply counts in a forum; latent constructs included negotiating ideas, monitoring task understanding, and expressing social support
key_sources: Shihui Feng, Ziyi Wei. (2025). The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09450-x

article_title: The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review
citation: Shihui Feng, Ziyi Wei. (2025). The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09450-x
title: Four types of collaborative learning process data for analyzing individual participation
description: The review synthesizes the process data used to analyze individual participation into four categories: oral conversational data (N = 28 studies, mostly co-located), textual input data (N = 18, almost all online), log data from CSCL platforms (N = 20, the most common in online settings), and nonverbal physical data (N = 14) including gestures, eye gazing, touch, and electrodermal activity. Fourteen studies employed multimodal data, most combining oral conversation data and nonverbal physical data, which the review says captured "a more comprehensive view of participation." The mapping of data types to participation forms is summarized in the study's Fig. 3.
requirements: Nonverbal physical data were often used together with other process data such as oral communication data to interpret students' physical actions in co-located collaborative learning
constraints: Log data was rarely used to analyze participation forms other than solo active participation and cognitive interactions "owing to its limitations for capturing emotional nuances and the learning processes occurring beyond the collaborative learning platform"
target_learners: students in higher education and K-12 collaborative learning contexts
target_learning_goals: measuring individual participation across cognitive, metacognitive, socioemotional, coordinative, solo active, and passive forms
examples: Törmänen et al. (2022) combined oral conversational data and electrodermal activity data to analyze individual socioemotional participation; Nguyen et al. (2023) used log data frequency and duration of logged behaviors
key_sources: Shihui Feng, Ziyi Wei. (2025). The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09450-x

article_title: Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data
citation: Liang, C., Toyokawa, Y., & Ogata, H. (2025). Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09452-9
title: Mixed genetic algorithm fitness function balancing homogeneous and heterogeneous grouping components
description: The article adapts a mixed genetic algorithm (inspired by Revelo Sanchez et al., 2021) for data-driven group formation. Input characteristics are divided into homogeneous and heterogeneous components, and the group fitness score F′(gk) is "calculated by subtracting the F(gk) score for the homogeneous component from that of the heterogeneous component" (Eq. 2), so desirable groups minimize variance on homogeneous features while maximizing it on heterogeneous ones. The score is interpreted relatively among candidates generated from the same input feature set, and negative values occur when homogeneous-feature variance exceeds heterogeneous-feature variance.
requirements: A student characteristic matrix (e.g., active reading marker clusters vectorized via Jaro–Winkler similarity with a threshold of 0.8) plus explicit decisions on which features are treated as homogeneous versus heterogeneous
constraints: The authors state the fitness value distribution revealed imbalances across groups, "raising important considerations about the trade-off between promoting internal group cohesion and ensuring equity across groups"
The score is interpretable in relative terms, not as an absolute indicator
target_learners: K-12 / senior high school EFL students in classroom collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary learning and text comprehension through collaborative active reading
examples: In the study, difficulty (yellow) markers were set as heterogeneous features and highlight (red) markers as homogeneous features to combine diverse perspectives on difficult content with shared attention on key ideas
key_sources: Liang, C., Toyokawa, Y., & Ogata, H. (2025). Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09452-9

article_title: Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data
citation: Liang, C., Toyokawa, Y., & Ogata, H. (2025). Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09452-9
title: Group formation system with automatic grouping panel, group composition visualization, and Wordcloud group-awareness tool
description: A group formation system embedded in the LEAF infrastructure that automates grouping from learning log data. Teachers configure groups through an automatic grouping panel with pre-configured inputs, view each group's input characteristics via colored bar graphs in a group composition panel, and monitor performance through an evaluation panel for formative feedback. A Wordcloud visualization module acts as a GAT for active reading, displaying key terms highlighted by group members in BookRoll so that, for example, a word "appears prominently among other red markers in the Wordcloud, indicating frequent highlights by multiple group members", supporting discussion initiation and peer learning while preserving privacy by not naming individual proficiency.
requirements: LEAF infrastructure consolidating LMS and BookRoll xAPI interaction logs; marker data collected during an individual active reading phase before grouping
constraints: Logs must be cleaned of duplicated markers in the same area and markers on irrelevant pages, which the authors note calls for context-based data-cleaning methods
Wordcloud comparisons between Used and Non-used students were exploratory post-hoc subgroup analyses
target_learners: Senior high school EFL students and their classroom teacher
target_learning_goals: Vocabulary learning, text comprehension, and group knowledge awareness in collaborative active reading
examples: In the empirical study the system formed 10 four-student groups per condition, presenting Wordclouds derived from each group's marker matrix during the group learning phase

article_title: Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow
citation: Alena Seredko. (2025). Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09451-w
title: Qualitative reconceptualization of scale as a local practical concern of participation fluidity
description: The article reconceptualizes scale from a quantitative property (user numbers, content volume) into a qualitative one: "the defining condition of scale is not simply large numbers of users but rather the open-ended, asynchronous and fluid nature of participation". Even interactions among few participants are shaped by the expectation that future, unknown contributors must understand what is going on, making scale a local concern that shapes how intelligibility is accomplished. This framework motivates the study's sequential analysis of turn design.
requirements: A platform record of durable traces (posts, comments, edits) on which participants and analysts can rely, since "durable traces such as comments and edits maintain joint work as publicly accessible over prolonged periods"
constraints: Developed from ethnomethodological analysis of a small number of Python-tagged threads; the article contrasts it with macro-level quantitative approaches rather than testing it statistically
target_learners: professionals in knowledge-intensive domains
software developers
target_learning_goals: understanding how collaboration is accomplished in large-scale online communities
examples: The study applies the framework by asking how users design turns presupposing any present or future user may read them
key_sources: Alena Seredko. (2025). Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09451-w

article_title: Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow
citation: Alena Seredko. (2025). Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09451-w
title: Intelligibility as practical accomplishment via shared methods in mass collaboration
description: Adopting a practice-based, ethnomethodological perspective, the article treats collaboration as continuously accomplished in participants' 'doings and sayings'. Shared understanding is framed as "intelligibility, i.e., a practical accomplishment through which actions and utterances are produced to be recognized and understood within interaction so that work can go on". The methods sustaining it are "taken-for-granted interactional techniques that produce and sustain intelligibility in joint activities", observed in the sequential organization of platform traces. Shared goals are products of continuous interaction rather than pre-existing.
requirements: Sequential trace data in which each turn's uptake by participants is observable, so repeated patterns across threads can be inferred as collectively relied-upon methods
constraints: The article notes intelligibility remains underexplored on large-scale platforms; group boundaries are difficult or impossible to specify under fluid participation
target_learners: professionals collaborating on online platforms
CSCL researchers
target_learning_goals: sustaining mutual intelligibility in asynchronous joint work
examples: Thread analyses trace request–response sequences, compliance, negotiation, repair and edit reporting as methods of intelligibility
key_sources: Alena Seredko. (2025). Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09451-w

article_title: Talk to the machine: Unleashing the potential of AI to scale dialogic education and reduce polarization
citation: Yifat Ben-David Kolikant, Omri Hadar, Asaf Salman. (2025). Talk to the machine: Unleashing the potential of AI to scale dialogic education and reduce polarization. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09461-8
title: LlamaLo: an LLM chatbot fine-tuned with LoRA on ChangeMyView discussions where a Delta was awarded
description: LlamaLo is a chatbot built by fine-tuning "Llama-2-7b-chat-hf", a pretrained generative model optimized for dialogue use cases, using LoRA on a corpus of 1378 discussions from the ChangeMyView subreddit in which a Delta (an indicator of learning from the other) was granted. Fine-tuning used an instruction-response format with an 80/20 training/validation split, 4-bit quantization, lora_alpha = 16, lora_dropout = 0.1, and r = 64; the authors employed no "under-the-hood" templates, guidelines, or role-based guardrails.
requirements: A training corpus of productive discussions meeting the forum's norms (Delta-awarded CMV threads without deleted posts or users), fine-tuned in an instruction-response format.
constraints: The authors deliberately did not filter content or use guardrail templates, relying on the quality and heavy moderation of the source data.
target_learners: Users discussing contentious topics of their choice
target_learning_goals: Opening and sustaining a personal dialogic space on contentious topics
examples: Developed via LoRA fine-tuning of Llama-2-7b-chat-hf on 1378 Delta-awarded CMV discussions sampled from a dataset used in prior research, then tested in ten discussions on controversial topics.
key_sources: Yifat Ben-David Kolikant, Omri Hadar, Asaf Salman. (2025). Talk to the machine: Unleashing the potential of AI to scale dialogic education and reduce polarization. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09461-8

citation: Yifat Ben-David Kolikant, Omri Hadar, Asaf Salman. (2025). Talk to the machine: Unleashing the potential of AI to scale dialogic education and reduce polarization. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09461-8
title: Responsiveness: the extent and ways one's response takes into account and builds on previous posts, both logically and emotionally
description: The authors introduce responsiveness as a construct for analyzing discussion contributions, defining it as "the extent and ways one's response takes into account and builds on previous posts, both logically and emotionally". They position it against transactivity, which they describe as celebrating the cognitive-epistemic dimension; responsiveness was coined "to allow sensitivity to the social-emotional dimension as well". High responsiveness addresses the essence of the post both logically and emotionally; low responsiveness vaguely refers to the main point or addresses a social-emotional aspect without connection to the core content.
requirements: Analysis of posts in sequence, examining how each builds on previous posts logically and emotionally.
constraints: Applied in this article to analysis of chatbot-generated and human posts in ten discussions on contentious topics.
target_learners: Participants in dialogic discussions on contentious topics
target_learning_goals: Analyzing and supporting constructive discussion that attends to both epistemic and socio-emotional dimensions
examples: The authors coded each LlamaLo post for whether it addressed the essence of the post both logically and emotionally (high) or vaguely referred to the main point (low).

title: Embed chatbot-preceded dialogic practice within macro-scripts as a preparatory phase for peer discussion on contentious topics
description: The article argues the conversation with the machine "should not replace the talk with humans" and should be "embedded in broader macro-scripts" supporting peer discussions on identity-related contentious topics. As a preparatory phase, the chatbot can equip participants with relevant content knowledge, help them identify weaknesses in their arguments, introduce alternative perspectives attuned to their utterances, and let students practice switching roles, arguing for a claim and then against it.
requirements: Careful and thoughtful pedagogical designs (macro-scripts), and further LLM training so that students' sense of safe space is not compromised.
constraints: The chatbot is positioned as a preparatory phase rather than a replacement for human discussion; bias and negative tone issues persist (Fig. 4).
target_learners: Students in schools, described as tomorrow's citizens
target_learning_goals: Engaging with conflicting voices, navigating disagreement productively, and approaching difference with curiosity, openness, and criticality
examples: The authors propose a reflection phase following the interaction with the LLM, including discussion of what happened and an understanding of the LLM itself.

article_title: Age-related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis
citation: Shigen Shimojo, Yugo Hayashi. (2025). Age-related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09456-5
title: ICAP framework as a theory of four hierarchical engagement modes applied to CSCL
description: The article uses the ICAP framework (Chi & Wylie, 2014) as its theoretical model for evaluating cognitive engagement during collaboration. It "classifies learning activities into four modes—passive, active, constructive, and interactive—on the basis of the learner’s level of engagement." In the interactive mode learners coconstruct knowledge through dialogue and coinference; constructive mode involves generating inferences that elaborate understanding. The study operationalizes ICAP through a coding schema of utterance indicators (Table 1) combined with epistemic network analysis to capture engagement temporally.
requirements: Observable discourse data coded against an ICAP-based rubric; at least three codes are needed to build an ENA model
constraints: ICAP coding reliability in this study was Krippendorff's α = 0.68, described as consistent only to some extent
target_learners: older adult learners in lifelong learning settings
university students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding through collaborative elaboration of knowledge
examples: The study coded utterances from paired concept-map explanation tasks into active, constructive, and interactive indicators and ran ENA on the resulting networks

article_title: Age-related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis
citation: Shigen Shimojo, Yugo Hayashi. (2025). Age-related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09456-5
title: Collaborative memory mechanisms of cross-cuing, re-exposure, and error pruning with shared knowledge as an external resource
description: The article reviews an information-processing account of why collaboration aids memory: "Blumen et al. (2013) explain the effects of collaborative learning through three mechanisms: cross-cuing, re-exposure, and error pruning." Cross-cuing treats partners' information as retrieval cues, re-exposure functions as an additional learning session, and error pruning increases correct recall while reducing errors. The study frames older adults' reliance on reactivating memory during interaction in these terms, positioning partners' externalized knowledge as an external cognitive resource integrated with internal cognition.
requirements: Interaction partners who externalize and share knowledge, e.g. via concept maps, so their knowledge can serve as retrieval cues
constraints: The review reports that merely acquiring information about a partner's knowledge is not sufficient to improve group performance
target_learners: older adults
adult learners
target_learning_goals: memory retrieval, encoding, and knowledge elaboration
examples: Older adults' utterance examples include re-reading the study text ('I think it said in the textbook...') to reactivate knowledge before elaborating

article_title: Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games
citation: Taehyun Kim, Mike Tissenbaum. (2025). Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09459-2
title: Tilting in collaborative learning games: anger-driven collapse of group coordination
description: The article adapts the gaming construct of tilt, originally from pinball and esports where it denotes "anger-driven performance collapse," to educational collaborative gameplay. Tilt is defined as a situation where players "experience continuous negative emotions such as anger due to specific events or individuals in the game, leading to impaired decision-making and overall gameplay." In the study, tilt manifested when a student whose ideas were repeatedly rejected disengaged, leaked his team's strategy, and triggered anger spirals that ended productive discourse.
requirements: A collaborative game context where team-level goals and coordination are salient, and anger is typically grounded in teammates' behaviors rather than opponents'.
constraints: The construct is relatively novel in educational research and the authors present it as preliminary insight; once expressions cross impropriety thresholds (e.g., personal attacks) interaction quality can deteriorate rapidly.
target_learners: middle school students (ages 11-14)
target_learning_goals: collaborative discourse and science learning in game-based simulations
examples: Paul, whose alliance proposal was repeatedly rejected, disengaged from his group, told another city 'We will just scam you. Don't trade with us,' and revealed his own group's bidding strategy.
key_sources: Taehyun Kim, Mike Tissenbaum. (2025). Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09459-2

article_title: Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games
citation: Taehyun Kim, Mike Tissenbaum. (2025). Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09459-2
title: City Settlers: a hybrid game-based simulation for whole-class science learning
description: City Settlers is a browser-based, whole-room simulation in which small teams manage and grow cities on a shared planet, engaging both digital and in-person interaction. "In this game-based simulation, there are five key components: resources, trading, buildings, auctions, and city status." Uneven resource distribution drives inter-city trade, random building draws via hidden auctions introduce nondeterminism, and activated buildings produce pollution that spreads to neighboring cities, creating交织 collaboration and competition.
requirements: Shared devices per group (tablets) plus individual devices; a projected shared map; a facilitator/instructor structure with teams at separate tables.
constraints: The game was purpose-built rather than commercial, designed to let students explore the rise and fall of cities belonging to local Indigenous peoples, with no imposed winning conditions.
target_learners: middle school students in STEM summer-camp or classroom settings
target_learning_goals: science learning about city systems, pollution, and resource management through collaborative decision-making
examples: Students played across five city tables with audio recorders and cameras capturing interactions; trading and bidding screens were accessible only from the group's shared tablet.
key_sources: Taehyun Kim, Mike Tissenbaum. (2025). Understanding when anger becomes productive or destructive in collaborative educational games. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09459-2

article_title: Learning to deal with hate speech: An online collective intelligence experiment on the Collective Learning platform
citation: Tatiana Íñiguez-Berrozpe, Carmen Elboj-Saso, Francesco Marcaletti, Pablo Bautista-Alcaine. (2025). Learning to deal with hate speech: An online collective intelligence experiment on the Collective Learning platform. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09460-9
title: Collective Learning platform: seven-phase AI-moderated online collective intelligence tool
description: Collective Learning is an online tool built by Zaragoza University researchers and Kampal Data Solutions "designed to yield high-quality solutions to a wide range of problems by applying collective intelligence following a model of successive digital interactions among participants". Participants work on a practical case across a 35-min, seven-phase session: individual responses, then iterative interaction with four neighbours, AI-driven swapping of network positions, forced copying for inactive participants, deletion of low-prestige answers, and final top-ten consensus phases. An AI moderator spreads ideas, applies a popularity/prestige factor and controls heterogeneity so collective intelligence can emerge in large groups.
requirements: An AI moderator is deemed "essential for collective intelligence to emerge among large groups", with participants connected simultaneously during the session.
constraints: Each participant sees only four neighbours in phases 2–5 to avoid information overload; the design addresses risks of unoriginal answers, low-quality drift and turn-taking monopoly the article states.
target_learners: Spanish adolescents in obligatory secondary education (14–16 years old)
target_learning_goals: Responding constructively to online hate speech situations
collaborative reasoning and consensus formation
examples: In this study participants read a fictional case about a 16-year-old girl confronting hate speech on social networks and answered four quantitative questions across all phases
key_sources: Tatiana Íñiguez-Berrozpe, Carmen Elboj-Saso, Francesco Marcaletti, Pablo Bautista-Alcaine. (2025). Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09460-9
title: Four-question hate speech case with a unified level-ordered scoring rubric (kappa 0.841)
description: The study used four quantitative questions on the María case, scored on level-ordered rubrics grounded in Kohlberg's moral development theory and models of empathic concern and digital citizenship. "A total of 1400 responses out of the 4508 submitted by participants were provided to each of the trained coders", coded blind to conditions and hypotheses, with Cohen's kappa of 0.841 indicating almost perfect agreement and disagreements resolved by consensus. Questions assessed perceived legitimacy of defending an influencer, awareness of who is harmed, who benefits, and prosocial action readiness on a 1–6 scale.
requirements: Coding followed a double-review and consensus protocol with rubric anchors in Appendix I
constraints: Cross-item interpretations are made "at the level of complexity (not by equating content)"; Q4 adds levels L5–L6 to differentiate interpersonal from institutional action.
target_learners: Spanish adolescents aged 14–16 in secondary education
target_learning_goals: Ethical reasoning about online hate speech
moral responsibility
empathy and prosocial action readiness
examples: Question 4 ranged from total defense of the influencer (answer 1) to reporting the account for spreading hate speech (answer 6)

Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09460-9
title: Collective intelligence as group performance exceeding mean individual performance in complex-task collaboration
description: The article adopts a construct in which "collective intelligence is defined as the performance of a large group of people collaborating on a series of complex tasks, generating responses and/or solutions in an aggregative manner, based on the idea that the mean individual performance of each member is lower than the mean performance obtained by the group". It is distinguished from group learning, defined as change within a group observable in cognition, task organisation and performance. Online environments expand the problem-solving potential by increasing participant numbers and permit an AI moderator to sustain quality, originality and interaction. The construct is used to hypothesise that CI experiments can help adolescents manage hate speech situations.
requirements: Emergence requires structured online interaction with an efficient AI moderator, conditions the article ties to large groups
constraints: The authors state conditions for emergence were met in the large group G1 but not in the small groups G2 and G3 in this study
target_learners: Adolescents collaborating in online school settings
target_learning_goals: Moral reasoning and ethical decision-making in digital contexts
collective problem-solving competencies
examples: Prior experiments applied online CI to moral dilemmas, significantly elevating groups' level of moral reasoning, as the article reports of Orejudo et al. and Bautista et al.

article_title: Advancing collaborative discourse through knowledge synthesis
citation: Xinran Zhu · Bodong Chen · David DeLiema. (2026). Advancing collaborative discourse through knowledge synthesis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09463-6
title: Knowledge synthesis in CSCL: connecting, analyzing, and integrating ideas from discourse to foster conceptual innovation
description: The article articulates knowledge synthesis (KS) as "the process of connecting, analyzing, and integrating ideas from collaborative discourse to foster conceptual innovation, generate novel knowledge, and create solutions". Unlike summarizing, synthesis-making moves beyond current explanations to create new concepts. The theory positions student-created synthesis artifacts as mediational tools that make emerging group knowledge visible and deepen ongoing discourse, situating KS relative to knowledge integration, web-mediated synthesis strategies, and Knowledge Building's "rise above".
requirements: Synthesis artifacts must be created from ideas represented in prior digital artifacts and then leveraged in new collaborative activity
Guidance outlining key components of effective synthesis, such as identifying common themes and exploring interconnections
constraints: The article notes insights about synthesis remain fragmented and underused in CSCL, with limited understanding of what makes a synthesis artifact effective
target_learners: graduate students in a teaching and learning course
target_learning_goals: advancing collaborative discourse
conceptual innovation and shared knowledge advancement
examples: In the study, students synthesized social annotation activity into individual artifacts and used them in group synthesis and application phases
key_sources: Xinran Zhu · Bodong Chen · David DeLiema. (2026). Advancing collaborative discourse through knowledge synthesis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09463-6

article_title: Advancing collaborative discourse through knowledge synthesis
citation: Xinran Zhu · Bodong Chen · David DeLiema. (2026). Advancing collaborative discourse through knowledge synthesis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09463-6
title: Synthesis Lab: a web application scaffolding annotation categorization into conceptual building blocks and synthesis development
description: The Synthesis Lab is a web application designed to interface with Hypothesis and be adaptable to other discussion environments. It "aimed to break down the complex process of knowledge synthesis into smaller, manageable steps", scaffolding two processes: categorizing peers' annotations into conceptual building blocks (CBBs) in Distill and Analyze columns, and developing a synthesis in the Synthesize column, with an "In-the-moment Notes" box for reasoning.
requirements: Integration with a social annotation tool such as Hypothesis providing annotation data to aggregate and filter
constraints: The article describes its use in a single graduate course enactment
target_learners: graduate students
target_learning_goals: knowledge synthesis from peer annotations
organizing ideas into conceptual building blocks
examples: Students filtered annotations by keywords, authors, and tags, created Annotation Groups as CBBs, merged or regrouped them, and composed syntheses in the Synthesize column

article_title: A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration
citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, Tiina Törmänen. (2026). A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09464-5
title: Provide early, targeted instructional support for group regulation rather than expecting regulation to improve with time alone
description: The article's design recommendation is that facilitators intervene early to shape groups' regulatory approaches, because its temporal analyses suggest regulation "does not naturally improve with time alone". Since most groups lock into stable patterns early, support should be targeted at the beginning of collaboration rather than delayed. This applies in online PBL and CSCL settings with small groups collaborating over multiple sessions.
requirements: Instructors or tutors must be available to provide coregulatory support within group discussion environments
constraints: The article reports that explicit regulation was infrequent and often arose only in response to challenges, questions, or disagreements, often with teacher support
target_learners: higher education students in online problem-based learning groups
target_learning_goals: effective group regulation of collaborative learning
productive collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The study tracked weekly regulation patterns across six weeks of a healthcare PBL course and found limited change over time, motivating early support rather than waiting for self-improvement
key_sources: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, Tiina Törmänen. (2026). A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09464-5

article_title: A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration
citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, Tiina Törmänen. (2026). A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09464-5
title: Temporal network analysis: combining the relational and temporal dimensions of CSCL interaction modeling
description: Temporal networks are a method that models both the relational aspects (who interacts with whom) and the temporal aspects (order, duration, concurrency) of collaborative learning. The article presents it as bringing the "best of both worlds" — combining network analysis's relational dimension with sequence methods' temporal dimension. Each node and edge carries timestamps marking start and end of activity; connections are temporary, only past interactions relate to future ones, and time-respecting paths replace static path length.
requirements: A timestamp must be attached to the start and end of each node and edge for an interaction network to count as a temporal network
constraints: The article notes centrality, connectivity, and diffusion must be reformulated for temporal dependencies, and the approach is fundamentally different from static networks rather than a straightforward generalization
target_learners: researchers of computer-supported collaborative learning
learning analytics practitioners
target_learning_goals: capturing longitudinal dynamics of collaborative learning interactions and regulation
examples: The study used temporal networks to trace tied duration of uptake among coded interaction types in PBL forum discussions
key_sources: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, Tiina Törmänen. (2026). A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09464-5

article_title: A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration
citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, Tiina Törmänen. (2026). A temporal network approach to reveal the longitudinal dynamics of CSCL group regulation and productive collaboration. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09464-5
title: Tied duration as a measure of uptake and relevance of regulatory processes
description: Tied duration is the total time an interaction process remains actively receiving responses from the group, computed from the temporal network by aggregating active intervals from first to last uptake, after trimming idle periods. The article uses it as "a temporal measure of its relevance—an improvement over simple frequency counts", feeding weekly tied durations into model-based clustering to identify regulation patterns and into growth models. It quantifies depth of thread discussion rather than treating posts as instantaneous events.
requirements: Timestamped forum data with reply structure so each edge's active interval can be derived from the replied-to and replying posts' timestamps
constraints: The article trims inactivity periods exceeding an idle threshold and treats resumed threads as new episodes unless explicitly continuous
target_learners: higher education students in online problem-based learning groups
target_learning_goals: measuring uptake and relevance of group regulatory processes in collaborative discussions
examples: In Fig. 1 the article contrasts a socioemotional response whose tied duration was limited because it did not stimulate further responses with an argument whose active uptake lasted from the first to the last reply

article_title: Collaborative knowledge construction with generative AI: Exploring argumentative co-writing processes through n-gram and cluster analysis
citation: Teresa Luther · Kate Belcher · Joachim Kimmerle · Detmar Meurers · Ulrike Cress (2026). Collaborative knowledge construction with generative AI: Exploring argumentative co-writing processes through n-gram and cluster analysis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09470-1
title: N-gram uptake analysis: mapping human–AI co-writing onto knowledge telling and knowledge transforming
description: The article proposes analyzing textual uptake in AI-supported writing via recurring n-grams between ChatGPT output and the writer's final text, extending Bereiter and Scardamalia's knowledge telling/knowledge transforming distinction to human–AI interaction. The authors write that "Overlaps in n-grams can thus serve as indicators of uptake" and that high verbatim overlap reflects adoption "analogous to knowledge-telling activities" while reformulated use points toward knowledge transforming. The three clusters are interpreted as positions on a spectrum from passive uptake to increasingly active and integrative collaboration, aligned with the ICAP framework.
requirements: Requires the writer's prompts, AI responses, and final text so overlap between AI output and final text can be computed; recurring n-grams presuppose access to both documents.
constraints: The article states the study is correlational and the design does not allow conclusions about causal mechanisms; knowledge building is used only as a conceptual backdrop, not an operationalized outcome.
target_learners: Adult writers in academic and professional contexts (participants aged 18–71 writing argumentative texts)
target_learning_goals: Argumentative writing and collaborative knowledge construction supported by generative AI
examples: Participants wrote a comment on alcohol prohibition in public with ChatGPT access; n-gram overlap classified them as reproducers, integrators, or reconstructors.

article_title: A collaboration literacy analytics framework (CLAF): Investigating students’ perspectives on collaboration quality indicators and feedback utilization
citation: Tochukwu Dominic Eze, Lucas Zurbuchen, Khalil Anderson, Marcelo Worsley. (2026). A collaboration literacy analytics framework (CLAF): Investigating students' perspectives on collaboration quality indicators and feedback utilization. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09475-w
title: Collaboration literacy as a metacognitive-behavioral construct of monitoring, interpreting, and responding to collaboration quality
description: The article defines collaboration literacy as extending beyond collaboration skills and competence: collaboration literacy emphasizes learners' ability to interpret and self-regulate collaboration using feedback and analytic representations. It is described as 'a metacognitive-behavioral construct that bridges collaboration skills, competence, and quality,' rooted in sociocultural theory (Vygotsky) and self-regulated learning theory (Zimmerman). Whereas competence describes what learners do in collaboration, collaboration literacy describes how learners understand, monitor, and act upon information about their collaboration. The study frames it as distinct from OECD-PISA performance-framed monitoring.
requirements: Learners must have access to indicators and feedback about their collaborative processes in order to interpret and self-regulate collaboration
constraints: The construct is framed as an analytic and regulatory orientation toward collaboration itself, not as a performance capacity
target_learners: University students in collaborative group activities
Undergraduate and graduate learners
target_learning_goals: Monitoring and regulating quality of collaboration
Detecting declining collaboration quality and intervening productively
examples: The article builds on Worsley and Ochoa (2020), who define collaboration literacy from a student's perspective as awareness of one's contribution and intervening when bad indicators of poor collaboration arise.
key_sources: Tochukwu Dominic Eze, Lucas Zurbuchen, Khalil Anderson, Marcelo Worsley. (2026). A collaboration literacy analytics framework (CLAF): Investigating students' perspectives on collaboration quality indicators and feedback utilization. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09475-w
title: Collaboration Literacy Analytics Framework (CLAF)
description: The CLAF is a conceptual framework 'that integrates evaluation metrics, indicator interdependencies, and feedback mechanisms.' It 'captures the dynamic relationship between process and outcome measures, connects individual- and group-level indicators, and incorporates review mechanisms as student-driven quality assurance.' The framework organizes learner-valued indicators across process, outcome, and review layers and links real-time feedback for immediate self-regulation with post hoc feedback for longer-term reflection and collaboration literacy development. It is grounded in consolidated collaboration dimensions and the student survey data.
requirements: CA systems must both represent collaborative processes and empower learners to interpret and respond to them
constraints: The framework is described as conceptual, providing an analytical basis for future CSCL research and practice rather than a validated measurement instrument
target_learners: University students collaborating in group activities
CSCL researchers and CA tool designers
target_learning_goals: Collaboration quality assessment
Self-regulation of collaboration
Collaboration literacy development
examples: The framework was developed from findings of an open-ended survey of 290 students after 12 weeks of CA tool-mediated activities across three task types: Minecraft game development, accessibility design brainstorming, and webpage accessibility implementation.

citation: Tochukwu Dominic Eze, Lucas Zurbuchen, Khalil Anderson, Marcelo Worsley. (2026). A collaboration literacy analytics framework (CLAF): Investigating students' perspectives on collaboration quality indicators and feedback utilization. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09475-w
title: Combine learner perspectives with theory-grounded CSCL constructs when defining collaboration quality indicators
description: The article advocates a strategy in which 'theory provides the validity anchors that delimit what counts as collaboration quality, while learners' experiential perspectives serve as empirically grounded probes to test, refine, and extend existing constructs.' This hybrid deductive-inductive, theory-anchored analytic approach treats convergence between learner perspectives and CSCL theory as validation and novel emergences as productive signals of under-specified constructs. It repositions learner voice as a mechanism for theory refinement rather than a threat to theoretical rigor.
requirements: Established CSCL frameworks must first be consolidated as theoretical coding frames before inductive analysis of learner responses
constraints: Learners' perceptions may be shaped by limited theoretical knowledge, social desirability bias, and reliance on salient but unreliable cues, so student-valued indicators must be examined as provisional constructs rather than adopted uncritically
target_learners: University students as primary end-users of collaboration analytics
CA tool designers and CSCL researchers
target_learning_goals: Designing interpretable, pedagogically grounded collaboration analytics indicators
Ensuring learner-aligned collaboration quality assessment
examples: The study benchmarked 290 students' survey perspectives against Worsley et al. (2021), Meier et al. (2007), OECD (2017), and Ofstedal and Dahlberg (2009) using a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis in Taguette.

article_title: Is it distracting? A further exploration of non-gameplay social interaction during collaborative digital game-based learning
citation: Jiqing Sun, Andrew Skourdoumbis. (2026). Is it distracting? A further exploration of non-gameplay social interaction during collaborative digital game-based learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09476-9
title: CSCL quality as alignment of epistemic and relational spaces, assessed through group-level flow (social flow and group flow)
description: The study conceptualises collaborative learning quality in CSCL as alignment of two interdependent spaces: an epistemic space of cognitive work such as sharing ideas and negotiating meanings, and a relational space managing interpersonal relations and emotions. Group-level flow—Walker's social flow (individual flow facilitated by group presence) and Sawyer's group flow (a collective peak state)—operationalises assessment of both spaces. The article states "high-quality collaborative learning emerges when these two spaces are well aligned and mutually supportive".
requirements: Assessment requires observable indicators: Joy–Sadness coding of behaviours and facial expressions, and synchronisation moments such as leaning towards each other, echoing gestures, and latching onto each other's words
constraints: The article states that group/social flow is not identical to high collaborative learning quality; it manifests an emergent experiential state reflecting alignment of the two spaces
target_learners: Year 7 mathematics students (aged 12–13)
target_learning_goals: Understanding pronumerals and combining like terms in early algebra
examples: The study coded students' emotions against Walker's Joy–Sadness Display Scale (kappa 0.73 and 0.80) and constructed interaction network diagrams of synchronisation per 5-min interval
key_sources: Jiqing Sun, Andrew Skourdoumbis. (2026). Is it distracting? A further exploration of non-gameplay social interaction during collaborative digital game-based learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09476-9

citation: Jiqing Sun, Andrew Skourdoumbis. (2026). Is it distracting? A further exploration of non-gameplay social interaction during collaborative digital game-based learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09476-9
title: Educators implementing collaborative DGBL in established groups can embrace NGI rather than suppress it
description: The article recommends that teachers implementing collaborative DGBL understand why and under what conditions NGI can be embraced, since in this study NGI sustained supportive epistemic and relational spaces. Rather than treating idle chat, banter and creative play with game elements as off-task distraction, NGI "seemingly functioned as a mechanism for emotional coordination and regulation, through which positive emotions are co-constructed and shared."
requirements: Groups should have pre-established basic positive collaborative relationships (mutual trust, sense of belonging, interpersonal closeness)
constraints: Findings come from one 57-min lesson, two dyads, in groups that entered the game with an already positive socio-emotional climate; scope does not extend to groups without established relationships
target_learners: Year 7 mathematics students in secondary school
target_learning_goals: Sustained collaborative engagement and cognitive investment in mathematics tasks
examples: In the study, students playfully used the card 'flip' and 'lock' functions against the opposing dyad in a 'hide and seek' game, and the teacher facilitated rather than suppressed these episodes

title: An online card-matching game for early algebra designed under Realistic Mathematics Education principles
description: The research team designed an online card-matching game in which students match equivalent mathematical structures presented in different forms, supporting understanding of algebraic symbols and expressions. It comprised "four levels of increasing challenge, with tasks progressing from arithmetic expressions to formal algebraic expressions." Students played in dyads in 2-versus-2 team competition, justifying their reasoning when matching cards to minimise random guessing.
requirements: Students must justify their reasoning when matching cards; teacher facilitates by circulating among groups
constraints: Designed for a single 57-min lesson in dyad competition; teams sat at the same table face-to-face
target_learners: Year 7 students (aged 12–13) in early algebra
target_learning_goals: Understanding pronumerals and combining like terms
examples: The game was implemented with four students in two dyads seated with their opponents, with gameplay video/audio recorded
