article_title: How gaze and proxemics shape and signal shared regulatory processes during AI-supported collaborative learning
citation: Ridwan Whitehead · Andy Nguyen · Sanna Järvelä. (2026). How gaze and proxemics shape and signal shared regulatory processes during AI-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09478-7
title: Trigger regulation framework for identifying multimodal SSRL processes
description: The trigger regulation framework (Järvelä & Hadwin, 2024) conceptualizes regulation as initiated by identifiable trigger events rather than as a continuous background process. The article states that trigger events "act as metacognitive signals that indicate when some form of regulation is needed," reflecting cognitive, motivational, emotional, or behavioral challenges. It anchors regulation cycles in discrete challenge moments, enabling examination of when regulation begins, how monitoring unfolds, and how groups coordinate responses over time, and it was designed with multimodal SSRL research in mind, allowing trigger events to be identified across synchronized data channels. In this study it guided deductive video coding of challenges and regulation processes.
requirements: Trigger events must be identifiable as discrete challenge moments (cognitive, metacognitive, socioemotional, behavioral, motivational) across synchronized data channels
constraints: The framework explains challenges as metacognitive signals inviting regulation or adaptation, not as continuous background processes
target_learners: secondary school students working in small collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: socially shared regulation of learning during collaborative inquiry
examples: The framework guided deductive ELAN coding yielding eight codes, with inter-rater agreement of mean Cohen's kappa = 0.830 for challenges and 0.844 for regulation processes
key_sources: Ridwan Whitehead · Andy Nguyen · Sanna Järvelä. (2026). How gaze and proxemics shape and signal shared regulatory processes during AI-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09478-7

article_title: How gaze and proxemics shape and signal shared regulatory processes during AI-supported collaborative learning
citation: Ridwan Whitehead · Andy Nguyen · Sanna Järvelä. (2026). How gaze and proxemics shape and signal shared regulatory processes during AI-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09478-7
title: MAI metacognitive AI agent, adaptive and static support conditions
description: Metacognitive Artificial Intelligence (MAI) (Edwards et al., 2024) is an experimental AI agent integrated into the classroom to support students' metacognitive engagement during group problem solving. In the adaptive condition it "delivered adaptive, real-time feedback contingent on the groups' ongoing activities, with prompts triggered by live transcript analysis that detected specific regulatory challenge categories." Four comparison groups received static support: "the MAI provided a fixed sequence of three prompts at predetermined intervals that were not responsive to the groups' immediate actions," scheduled at 5–8, 10–20, and 20–30 min.
requirements: Live transcript analysis capable of detecting regulatory challenge categories for adaptive triggering
constraints: Static prompts at predetermined intervals were evaluated as nonresponsive to groups' immediate actions; one static-condition episode recorded a disengaged response
target_learners: secondary school students aged 12–14 in groups of 3–4
target_learning_goals: metacognitive engagement and shared regulation during collaborative group problem solving
examples: In one adaptive-condition episode around 53 min into the task, MAI detected a cognitive challenge and asked "Do you understand all the key concepts of the task?", after which the group converged gaze and shifted closer before enacting a strategy

citation: Ridwan Whitehead · Andy Nguyen · Sanna Järvelä. (2026). How gaze and proxemics shape and signal shared regulatory processes during AI-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09478-7
title: Automated computer-vision pipeline for extracting gaze and proxemics from ordinary 2D classroom video
description: The study adapted the Sharingan gaze-estimation framework (Tafasca et al., 2024), a pretrained transformer-based model reported with AUC 0.944, to derive joint attention and mutual gaze frame by frame from standard 2D video. A separate pipeline combining YOLOv11 pose estimation, DeepOCSort tracking, and depth-based distance computation computed pairwise interpersonal distances, categorized via 33rd/66th percentile thresholds into close, neutral, and far levels. The authors present this as a nonintrusive, scalable methodological alternative to intrusive sensors, lab-only setups, and manual coding in authentic classrooms.
requirements: RGB and depth video pairs synchronized; camera geometry calibration for depth-weighted distance computation
constraints: Parameters kept constant across groups given similar camera placement; relative (percentile-based) distance categorization used because seating configurations varied across groups
target_learners: secondary school students in face-to-face collaborative group work
target_learning_goals: automated measurement of nonverbal coordination cues during collaborative learning
examples: Gaze extraction used a YOLOv5-based head detector with OCSORT tracking and the Sharingan transformer model; joint attention required predicted gaze points within 125 pixels, and mutual gaze required reciprocal gaze points within each other's head bounding box

title: A draft community-maintained CSCL taxonomy structured as a tagging system with fixed variables
description: The workshop produced an embryonic taxonomy draft (Table 1) organized as an initially structureless tagging system rather than a hierarchy. Categories span collaboration processes (goal, group size, modality, timing, temporal coordination), CSCL support (goal of support, delivery agent), CSCL context (familiarity, domain, demographics, motivation), and methods and theories (epistemological stance, method, stakeholder participation). Group members proposed "an initially structureless tagging system with a fixed set of variables to describe the variation of collaborative learning in a study".
requirements: Each variable should have a fixed and small number of potential values that are not too specific, so the taxonomy remains useful for grouping similar studies
constraints: The article states the taxonomy draft "is still in an embryonic stage" and "a provisional and community-dependent construct", not a stable or validated framework
target_learners: CSCL researchers
novice researchers navigating the CSCL field
target_learning_goals: Describing and comparing collaborative learning studies across paradigms
Scaffolding the design and preregistration of CSCL studies
examples: Table 1 lists variables such as goal type (knowledge co-construction, problem solving, design, no external goal), modality (face-to-face, video conference, chat-based, document exchange), and epistemological stance (social constructivist, critical-realist, positivist)

title: A dimensional map of CSCL theory diversity: perspective diversity and loci of collaborative learning observation
description: The workshop group described two axes of theoretical diversity in CSCL. Perspective diversity means different theories examine different aspects of the same collaborative learning situation, illustrated with Actor-Network Theory, Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, and cognitive load theory. Dimensional diversity concerns where collaborative learning can be observed: "inside the learner, focusing on individual cognition and learning processes", outside the learner in designed contexts and tools, or both stances together, with a further dimension of level of analysis ranging from the individual to communities and platforms.
requirements: The group noted the ongoing challenge of assuring that these theories complement each other rather than compete
constraints: The frameworks are presented "without claiming exhaustiveness", illustrating rather than enumerating all theoretical perspectives
target_learners: CSCL researchers
interdisciplinary learning scientists
target_learning_goals: Categorizing and connecting CSCL theories
Developing a holistic vision of collaborative learning across levels of analysis
examples: Links between internal cognition and interactional meaning-making, and bridges between micro-level group dynamics and macro-level sociocultural transformations, were cited as exemplars of connecting theories

title: Use standardized taxonomy descriptors so studies can be identified by phenomenon rather than theoretical lens
description: Because CSCL lacks shared descriptors for phenomena and analytic approaches, the article recommends standardized descriptors within a community taxonomy. These mitigate the jingle-jangle fallacy, using the same terms for different concepts or different terms for the same concept, letting researchers find relevant studies across paradigms based on the phenomenon itself. The taxonomy would also serve authors as a scaffold for articulating study aspects and as a transparent checklist supporting review processes.
requirements: Variables must describe distinct aspects of the collaboration processes and carry explanatory power for understanding the phenomenon
constraints: Details on either binary or continuous variable values were not discussed by the group
target_learners: CSCL researchers
journal and conference reviewers
target_learning_goals: Improving comparability and cross-paradigm literature navigation
Supporting preregistration of CSCL studies
examples: Group members identified descriptors such as agent and temporal scope, technological mediation (online, in-presence, hybrid), and task type (knowledge building, problem-solving, co-design) that ideal CSCL contributions should communicate

article_title: From individual annotations to shared attention: How re-annotation supports collaborative knowledge building in CSCL
citation: Yiqiu Zhou and Jina Kang. (2026). From individual annotations to shared attention: How re-annotation supports collaborative knowledge building in CSCL. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09486-7
title: Re-annotation as a construct distinguishing reciprocal annotation uptake from annotation initiation
description: The article introduces re-annotation as an analytical lens on social annotation: an annotation behavior in which a learner annotates the same referent a peer just did, signaling shared attention. It distinguishes two behavior types: "Initiating annotation denotes a learner's first act of marking or highlighting a digital object", while "Re-annotation refers to a subsequent annotation made on the same referent by another learner within a short temporal window." The concept reframes annotation as a call-and-response cycle between individual contributions and collective meaning-making.
requirements: A time threshold (120 s, informed by prior conversational-episode analysis) must be set to operationalize re-annotation as deliberate, timely engagement rather than coincidence.
constraints: Operationalized for visual highlights on constellations in a simulation where only one constellation can be highlighted per device at a time; line drawing was excluded due to infrequent use.
target_learners: undergraduate non-majors in introductory astronomy
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
shared attention and mutual awareness in group problem-solving
examples: During Task 1 (hemisphere identification), an initial annotation of Ursa Major externalized one student's hypothesis, and a peer's subsequent re-annotation reinforced it as a shared point of reference.
key_sources: Yiqiu Zhou and Jina Kang. (2026). From individual annotations to shared attention: How re-annotation supports collaborative knowledge building in CSCL. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09486-7

article_title: From individual annotations to shared attention: How re-annotation supports collaborative knowledge building in CSCL
citation: Yiqiu Zhou and Jina Kang. (2026). From individual annotations to shared attention: How re-annotation supports collaborative knowledge building in CSCL. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09486-7
title: Design CSCL environments that explicitly support timely re-annotation so annotations become dynamic resources rather than static artifacts
description: The article argues that social annotation tools and instructional strategies should actively foster re-annotation practices so that peer annotations are revisited rather than left static. In CEASAR, synchronized visual highlights across devices allowed peers to "align their attention and jointly interpret celestial data during discussion". The authors state that these insights "emphasize the importance of designing CSCL environments that explicitly support re-annotation as a tool for attention coordination and collaborative meaning-making".
requirements: Annotations must be visible synchronously across group members' devices so a peer's highlight can serve as a shared visual reference.
constraints: Evidence comes from one 16-group analysis in an immersive astronomy simulation; the authors note that peer engagement and social dynamics cannot be taken for granted even in synchronous settings.
target_learners: undergraduate non-majors in introductory astronomy
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
attention coordination and mutual awareness
examples: Students in the Lost at Sea task annotated constellations such as Ursa Major and Crux as reference points, and peers re-annotated the same objects within 120 s to signal shared attention.

title: Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning Framework: shared diagnostic spaces built via collaborative diagnostic activities
description: The Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning Framework describes how individual diagnostic content — an individual evidence space (e.g., individual observations) and an individual hypothesis space (e.g., initial hypotheses) — becomes part of shared diagnostic spaces (a shared evidence space and a shared hypothesis space) through collaborative diagnostic activities such as elicitation, sharing, and negotiation. These "shared diagnostic spaces can then be seen as the basis for generating a collaborative diagnosis", and the activities are "expected to influence the accuracy of the collaboratively generated diagnosis".
requirements: Collaborators must apply elicitation, sharing, and negotiation activities to convert individual diagnostic spaces into shared diagnostic spaces
constraints: Empirical support was recently found in a medical context; the article notes it remains ambiguous how well the framework applies to other contexts such as teacher collaboration
target_learners: pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: collaborative diagnosis of pupils' cross-domain skills such as scientific reasoning

title: Video-based simulation environment for fostering and measuring diagnosis of pupils' scientific reasoning
description: A video-based simulation environment depicting pairs of pupils conducting experiments (a biology scenario on plant growth and a physics scenario on optical lenses), built from fictional profiles of pupils' scientific reasoning sub-skills. Each case includes "a video showing the pupils while experimenting", "a so-called inquiry table" that updates automatically during the video, a note pad, and an interactive navigation area letting participants click links to "ask" pupils questions, with answered video segments inserted. Standardisation enables different pre-service teachers to diagnose the same pupils in identical situations.
requirements: Staged videos based on prepared fictional pupil skill profiles; compatible videoconferencing for dyadic collaboration phases
constraints: Not manipulated in the test phase, where each participant worked with one version whose two subject versions did not differ in sub-skills displayed
target_learners: pre-service teachers in university teacher education
target_learning_goals: observing and diagnosing pupils' scientific reasoning sub-skills
examples: Participants first practised on a shortened simulation case, then worked a full case for approximately 30 minutes in the learning phase

title: Coding scheme for collaborative diagnostic activities across 11 scientific reasoning sub-skills
description: Elicitation (asking for evidence pertinent to the diagnosed pupil's scientific reasoning skills), sharing (sharing such evidence), and negotiation (negotiating how consistent or contradictory observations affect the joint diagnosis) were coded from screen recordings at the level of the individual, for each of 11 sub-skills spanning hypothesis formulation, experimentation, and drawing conclusions. Dyad-level coverage variables counted sub-skills for which any participant performed an activity, divided by the maximum score of 11. Inter-coder agreement was acceptable to excellent (e.g., negotiation ICCabsolute = .67 in the learning phase; elicitation ICCabsolute = 1.00).
requirements: Two trained independent coders with a detailed coding manual; about 10% of recordings double-coded
constraints: Coding was independent of the accuracy or importance of the specific piece of information elicited, shared, or negotiated
target_learners: pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: measuring collaborative diagnostic activities during diagnosis of scientific reasoning skills
examples: Sample coded utterances included an elicitation of 'precision of hypotheses' and sharing about 'holding all other variables constant'

title: Hidden profiles as a special condition for the added value of collaborative diagnosis across subjects
description: The article applies the hidden-profile paradigm to teacher collaboration: "a hidden profile occurs when an optimal individually generated diagnosis differs from an optimal collaboratively generated diagnosis", because diagnostically relevant information observed by another teacher is unavailable individually and must first be shared. Naturally occurring hidden profiles arise when collaborating teachers observe the same pupils in different subjects, e.g., when some scientific reasoning sub-skills are demonstrated in biology but not physics, so complementary distributed information could boost the quality of a joint diagnosis.

constraints: The extent to which teachers' observations differ can be expected to vary considerably from situation to situation, so the relevance of collaboration differs by situation

title: Knowledge Building–Modeling (KBM): a recursive framework integrating discourse, analytics-driven reflection, and model construction
description: KBM is a proposed framework with three constructs—discourse, analytics-supported reflection, and modeling—in which 'scientific modeling is integrated within the flow of discourse and guided by knowledge building analytics to support systems thinking and knowledge advances'. Discourse informs model construction; models serve as provocations for continued discourse; analytics visualizations support meta-reflection and planning. Models function as boundary objects and improvable artifacts positioned as public goods within the knowledge building community.
requirements: Students need to engage in both collaborative discourse and ongoing modeling and reorganization of their evolving knowledge landscape
Knowledge Forum as a collaborative discourse space, Idea-Friend Map visualizations, and model-construction mediums as design embodiments
constraints: The article states that arrows in the conjecture map represent dynamic relationships 'not reducible to distinct pathways'—the constructs jointly co-mediate one another

target_learning_goals: systems thinking
domain knowledge of Earth Science
epistemic agency and collective knowledge advancement
examples: The 9-session Earth Science and Systems Thinking unit organized into three phases: introducing systems thinking, Idea-Friend Map-guided model reconstruction, and epistemic-marker-supported model-based reasoning

title: Idea-Friend Maps: student-facing visualizations of discourse word networks derived from KBDeX
description: Idea-Friend Maps are a student-facing representation based on KBDeX word networks, preserving 'the semantic co-occurrence logic of KBDeX while presenting it in a more interpretable form for students'. Concepts that frequently co-occur in student notes are grouped and visually connected as 'friendships', and color-coded concept clusters help learners identify conceptual commonalities and cross-concept connections. Teachers use the visual cues to help students notice the state of community knowledge as a basis for reflection and improvement.

article_title: How a technology-augmented inquiry approach affects teacher practice and student learning in disadvantaged science classrooms
citation: Fan Chen, Gaowei Chen. (2026). How a technology-augmented inquiry approach affects teacher practice and student learning in disadvantaged science classrooms. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09788-1
title: Technology-augmented inquiry approach (TAIA): pedagogical visibility as a mechanism to scaffold student inquiry and reduce teacher orchestration load in disadvantaged classrooms
description: TAIA is the framing model of this study: a classroom orchestration system that integrates digital tools into the inquiry workflow so that "transient student thoughts into inspectable, actionable digital artifacts" give teachers pedagogical visibility. Its utility is described as twofold — scaffolding student cognition by decomposing complex tasks, and enhancing pedagogical orchestration by externalizing student thinking for the teacher. The article evaluates a context-adapted TAIA via the WeInquiry platform in two rural classrooms, arguing prior efficacy was established only in resource-rich settings.
requirements: Digital infrastructure sufficient for simultaneous classroom use (the school's network bandwidth supported a 40-minute trial) and student groups including at least one member with high ICT competency
constraints: Prior TAIA efficacy relied on assumptions of robust infrastructure, high student ICT competency, and strong prior inquiry experience, which rarely hold in disadvantaged settings
target_learners: eighth-grade students in low-infrastructure, high-need rural science classrooms
target_learning_goals: scientific literacy through inquiry-based learning: hypothesis formulation, controlled experimentation, and evidence-based argumentation
examples: In this study, EG groups each shared one tablet to access WeInquiry, submitting hypotheses, uploading multimedia experimental recordings, and completing CER-based arguments in a shared workspace while the teacher monitored progress in real time

title: The data lifecycle: extending participatory science beyond data collection to decisions and action
description: The article describes the data lifecycle as the full arc of participatory science work, from developing expertise and defining research questions through collecting, interpreting, and sharing data to making decisions and taking action, then evaluating outcomes and reassessing goals. It holds that "data alone do not contain instructions for which actions to take" and that decisions are expressions of preference shaped by identity. The authors used it as an instructional design process for centering youth agency in their bird-monitoring CCS project.
requirements: Instructional designs must structure opportunities across all lifecycle stages, including expertise development, question definition, and data use for decisions, not only data collection
constraints: The article states the data lifecycle "does not provide instruction for how to make decisions about scientific practices or environmental decisions"

target_learning_goals: science learning through authentic data practices
environmental decision-making and agency
examples: The Ornithology Club project moved through expertise building on bird identification, designing an observation protocol, interpreting campus bird data, creating a Bird Sanctuary, submitting data to eBird, presenting to a Kindergarten class and the School District Board, and evaluating outcomes

title: Environmental science agency (ESA): youth leveraging knowledge, expertise and interests to make meaningful change
description: Environmental science agency is the concept the article uses to understand youth enactment of agency and identity within CCS contexts aimed at environmental and social action. ESA is "a means for investigating how youth enact their identities and the knowledge they value through their imagined worlds and in place." It foregrounds what youth identify as relevant, significant, and valuable as they leverage knowledge, practices, and interests to make change, and pairs with framing theory to explain how youth define environmental issues.

target_learning_goals: enacting agency and identity through science

title: Three knowledge types for environmental decision-making: systems, action-related, and effectiveness knowledge
description: The article adopts Frick et al.'s framework of three knowledge types used in environmental decision-making. Systems knowledge is "understanding of the natural states of ecosystems and the processes within them"; action-related knowledge is knowledge needed to address a particular problem, applied for direct or indirect impact; effectiveness knowledge is needed "when there are different ways to act" to evaluate and justify what "effective" means. The article uses this lens to analyze what students knew versus lacked when deciding.

constraints: The article notes having knowledge about a system still does not provide clear understanding about what action can be taken

target_learning_goals: environmental decision-making

title: Problem-posing spaces: four socio-ecological themes students pursued in a campus bird-monitoring CCS project
description: Problem-posing spaces, adapted from Freire, are figurative spaces that stimulate critical questioning and action. In this study they were "the four main themes or 'problem-posing spaces' we identified as key areas that student-ornithologists pursued through discussion and investigations": (1) predator-prey relations, (2) "who belongs" (native/non-native status and which birds "should" be present), (3) bird diets (trash, Hot Cheetos, sugar water, and the seagull named Jeff), and (4) the Bird Sanctuary. They are not bound to a single issue or location.
requirements: Educators should identify and surface student-generated socio-ecological questions as recurring investigation themes
constraints: They are not necessarily bound by a particular environmental issue or physical location

target_learning_goals: critical questioning of socio-ecological issues
environmental problem identification

description: The study's program design builds on the CCS education framework and aligns its phases with the data lifecycle: developing expertise through bird-identification lessons; defining research questions in the after-school Ornithology Club (50 min weekly); designing an observation protocol with student-chosen tools; interpreting and evaluating data; making decisions and taking action, funded by a school-garden grant for a Bird Sanctuary; submitting data to eBird and presenting to audiences; and evaluating outcomes and reassessing goals.

article_title: Linguistic demands of instructions: Effects on students’ expectancy-value beliefs
citation: Lina Wirth, Timo Ehmke, Jan Retelsdorf, Poldi Kuhl. (2026). Linguistic demands of instructions: Effects on students’ expectancy-value beliefs. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09799-y
title: Situated Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT) as a framework for treating linguistic demands as task difficulty shaping motivational beliefs
description: The article uses SEVT to argue that linguistic demands in educational contexts can be conceptualized as a form of task difficulty: "students who encounter task difficulties due to linguistic demands … may have lower expectancy and value beliefs, resulting in a lack of motivation to actively engage in these tasks". SEVT holds that expectancies of success and task value are shaped in the moment by contextual features such as task difficulty, and that the interaction between contextual and individual features is crucial, with difficulty needing to match individual abilities to promote adaptive motivation. The study operationalized this by experimentally varying linguistic difficulty and testing its main and moderated effects plus mediation into achievement.
requirements: Applied to contexts where linguistic features of instructions vary in difficulty and can be experimentally manipulated
constraints: In this study the framework's fit prediction was only partly supported; expectancies were not fostered by a good fit between demands and abilities
target_learners: pre-service teachers in higher education
target_learning_goals: statistics content comprehension (skewness and excess)
achievement motivation and engagement in academic tasks
examples: The study drew on SEVT to derive four hypotheses about linguistic conditions, language abilities, and expectancy-value beliefs measured mid-video.

title: Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning as a design framework for novice video analysis
description: The article uses the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (CTML; Mayer, 2001) as the guiding framework for designing novice-supportive video-analysis training. It states that the theory "assumes: (1) visual and auditory information is processed through separate channels; (2) each channel is limited in the amount of processing that can take place at once; and (3) learning occurs through active processing which involves information selection, organization into mental representations, and knowledge integration". The study maps two training techniques onto this framework: signaling cues for the information-selection step and principle-based self-explanation prompts for knowledge integration.
requirements: novices with limited prior knowledge whose processing capacity must be protected, per the article's statement that designers should "mitigate the challenges associated with different representations and modalities"
constraints: the article ties the framework's support techniques to transient information presentation, noting video learning "can be difficult due to the transient nature of information presentation"
target_learners: preservice teachers with limited prior knowledge and teaching experience
target_learning_goals: professional vision skill development in analyzing teaching practice
examples: The study operationalized selection support with integrated keyword cues and integration support with focused self-explanation prompts in a one-week video analysis training.

title: Professional vision conceptualized and operationalized as noticing plus reasoning components
description: The article defines professional vision, with overlap to the teacher-noticing construct, as two trainable components. title: Continuum-of-authenticity approximation tasks for training core practices
description: Following the Framework for Teaching Practice in Professional Education (Grossman et al., 2009, as cited), the article organizes novices' practice opportunities along increasing authenticity and complexity. "novices rehearse a particular element of practice on a continuum of authenticity, starting with approximation tasks that focus on a reduced set of practice components and have many low-stakes practice opportunities, and gradually work up to enacting the authentic practice itself with support". Its rationale is a moderation pattern reported in the abstract: "training with cues fostered professional vision skills for preservice teachers with low situational interest", suggesting cues "may compensate for the generative processing boost typically associated with situational interest". The second-order components are three social elements (participation, perspective taking, social regulation) and two cognitive elements (task regulation, knowledge building), which are "further divided into 19 specific sub-elements as third-order components". Because the framework "profoundly covers both social and cognitive elements" and specifies operational definitions, the authors judged it "suitable for the purposes of directed content analysis". The elements "can overlap and run parallel between the different stages of the process".

citation: Daniell DiFrancesca, Dan Spencer. (2025). The effects of competitive classroom activities on undergraduates with varied levels of competitive preference. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09741-8
title: Constructive competition within Social Interdependence Theory
description: The article frames classroom competition through Social Interdependence Theory, which defines competition as a situation in which "individuals have similar goals and each individual's performance is impacted by the actions of others." Modern views place competition and cooperation on one continuum, and treat competition as constructive to learning "when winning is relatively unimportant, in situations in which all participants have a reasonable chance to win, and under circumstances in which there are clear, specific, and fair rules, procedures, and criteria for winning." The study designed its Kahoot activities (no grade impact, immediate feedback, leaderboard with normative comparisons) to meet this definition, and examined individual-difference predispositions toward competition alongside the situational context.
requirements: Competition must be low-stakes with winning relatively unimportant, a reasonable chance for all to win, and clear, specific, and fair rules and criteria for winning
constraints: The study did not test varied competitive-activity designs; it examined one constructive implementation in a single educational psychology course without a noncompetitive control classroom
target_learners: undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: content review and comprehension monitoring in course material
examples: Eight in-class Kahoot review games worth no course credit, scored on accuracy and speed with a cumulative leaderboard rewarding monitoring accuracy

citation: Daniell DiFrancesca, Dan Spencer. (2025). The effects of competitive classroom activities on undergraduates with varied levels of competitive preference. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09741-8
title: Low-stakes constructive competitive review activities did not disadvantage low-competitive students relative to high-competitive students
description: The article reports that incorporating a constructive competitive activity (Kahoot) did not advantage highly competitive students over low-competitive students on learning outcomes, monitoring, motivation, or enjoyment, supporting the instructional use of such activities. As the authors put it, "Teachers' pedagogical decision to incorporate competitive activities to increase student engagement does not disadvantage students reporting low competitive tendencies." This holds when the activities follow constructive-competition guidelines and outcomes do not affect course grades.
requirements: Competition should follow constructive guidelines (winning relatively unimportant, reasonable chance for all, clear fair rules), and assessments should not count toward grades
constraints: No noncompetitive control classroom was included, so claims concern relative impacts on low- versus high-competitive students, not competition versus no competition; the course content covered motivational and learning theories, potentially shifting perceptions
target_learners: undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: review of course content with regular feedback and metacognitive monitoring practice
examples: A semester of eight five-item Kahoot comprehension checks in which top and bottom SIS tertiles showed similar performance, monitoring, and enjoyment outcomes

article_title: Understanding the effects of constructivist learning environments: introducing a multi-directional approach
citation: Loyens, S. M. M., & Gijbels, D. (2008). Understanding the effects of constructivist learning environments: introducing a multi-directional approach. Instructional Science, 36, 351–357. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9059-4
title: Constructivism defined by its core assumption that knowledge is actively constructed by the learner
description: The article presents a working definition of constructivism: how people create meaning is "the main concern of constructivist theories," and although definitions vary, the perspectives share one core. "In essence, constructivism is a view of learning that considers the learner as a responsible, active agent in his/her knowledge acquisition process." Learners activate prior knowledge and interpret new information against it, so understanding is a function of knowledge construction rather than mere information accumulation.
requirements: The learner must function as a responsible, active agent in his or her knowledge acquisition process
constraints: A clear, unequivocal definition of constructivism is hard to find because the concept is defined and embodied in varied ways

target_learning_goals: knowledge construction and understanding of subject matter

description: The article characterizes constructivist learning environments by several features believed to promote effective learning. These are active knowledge construction building on prior knowledge, cooperative learning in which social interactions contribute to knowledge building, self-regulated learning through goal setting and monitoring, and confronting students with "complex, ill-structured problems" similar to future professional problems. Educators applying constructivism combine these elements in learning environments.

article_title: Effects of two differently sequenced classroom scripts on common ground in collaborative inquiry learning
citation: Esther Tan (2018). Effects of two differently sequenced classroom scripts on common ground in collaborative inquiry learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9460-6
title: Grounding and testing as core regulative processes for establishing common ground in collaborative inquiry
description: The article frames collaborative inquiry learning as requiring coordination of both process and content: learners collaboratively regulate cognitive activities to establish and maintain "common ground" (mutual knowledge, beliefs and assumptions). "Grounding" is defined as "the name given to the interactive processes by which common ground (or mutual understanding) between individuals is constructed and maintained", achieved through verification questions and confirmation statements. Testing is a further regulative process in which learners summarize, check whether sufficient information has been gathered, draw conclusions and comparisons, usually in the final evaluation phase. The article applies deep-versus-surface qualifiers to code grounding and testing as high- or low-level.
requirements: Both the giver and recipient of information must mutually believe they have understood what the other meant; feedback is pivotal for grounding to count.
constraints: The article states breakdowns of common ground occur when mutual understanding cannot be reached, and common ground must be augmented or repaired over time as new information and partial or disputable claims arise.
target_learners: students in grades 6–9 collaborative science inquiry
target_learning_goals: regulative skills of grounding and checking shared understanding during collaborative inquiry
examples: The study coded every 5 seconds of 20 groups' audio-recorded discourse for high- and low-level grounding and testing using these definitions.
key_sources: Esther Tan (2018). Effects of two differently sequenced classroom scripts on common ground in collaborative inquiry learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9460-6

article_title: Effects of two differently sequenced classroom scripts on common ground in collaborative inquiry learning
citation: Esther Tan (2018). Effects of two differently sequenced classroom scripts on common ground in collaborative inquiry learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9460-6
title: Two differently sequenced classroom scripts: PISG (Plenary–Individual–Small Group) and PSGI (Plenary–Small Group–Individual)
description: Both scripts begin with the teacher modeling each inquiry skill at the plenary level, then distribute activities across social levels in opposite orders. In this study, "students in the Plenary–Individual–Small Group (PISG) classroom script first worked individually before working in small groups, whereas students in the Plenary–Small Group–Individual (PSGI) condition first worked in small groups before working individually." Both sequences ran through a pre-field trip, field trip to the Botanical Gardens and post-field trip phase on plant adaptation, with inquiry task 1 consistently used for plenary teacher modeling. The scripts are used as macro-scripts that shape interaction patterns by sequencing tasks across plenary, individual and small group levels.
requirements: Each phase began with plenary teacher modeling of the targeted inquiry skills before the script transition; the script sequence was strictly adhered to from pre- to post-field trip.
constraints: In the PSGI condition, two groups experienced dropouts in the post-field trip; implementation spanned seven lessons of approximately 45 minutes over 2–3 weeks.
target_learners: students in grades 6–9 in a collaborative science inquiry unit
target_learning_goals: inquiry processes of generating and evaluating evidence and drawing conclusions, supported by grounding and testing
examples: PISG students first worked individually on inquiry task 2 (plants in the tropical rainforest) before small-group work on inquiry task 3 (plants in the desert); PSGI students did the reverse.

article_title: Contact-2: a computer-assisted instructional strategy for promoting conceptual change
citation: Biemans, H.J.A., Simons, P.RJ. (1996). Contact-2: a computer-assisted instructional strategy for promoting conceptual change. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00120487
title: The CONTACT strategy: continuous, computer-assisted activation of individual learners' conceptions to promote conceptual change
description: The CONTACT strategy is an instructional approach premised on the idea that students need guidance to activate and correct their preconceptions in text processing. It is "characterised by continuous, computer-assisted activation of the conceptions of individual learners". The article situates it within conceptual-change instruction and demonstrates it with fifth- and sixth-graders studying physical geography texts, where it helped students construct more correct conceptions, though learners attended selectively to central concepts.
requirements: Continuous computer-assisted activation operating on the conceptions of individual learners during instruction
constraints: Original version induced selective attention: students mainly focused on the central concepts from the training texts, disregarding other information
target_learners: Fifth- and sixth-grade primary education students
target_learning_goals: Conceptual change in text processing (domain: physical geography)
examples: The original CONTACT study showed that students constructed more correct conceptions from training texts in physical geography.

article_title: Mountain rescuers’ experiences with video-assisted and verbal debriefings: a qualitative study
citation: Stefan A. Schreder, Helen Jossberger, Hans Gruber. (2025). Mountain rescuers' experiences with video-assisted and verbal debriefings: a qualitative study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09716-9
title: Implement video-assisted debriefing with careful facilitation that balances positive and negative feedback to protect psychological safety
description: The article concludes that VAD can have advantages over verbal debriefing but requires deliberate facilitator implementation. Because displayed mistakes can intimidate participants, facilitators should balance critical comments with positive visualised situations, use disclaimers ensuring confidentiality, and state that "If you use the video in the wrong way, you can hurt people." This maintains psychological safety and motivation during debriefing.
requirements: Facilitator training in VAD technology and in maintaining psychological safety
Balanced feedback including positive as well as negative video segments
constraints: Breaches of psychological safety can occur even with facilitator safeguards
Equipment unsuited to some simulation conditions (e.g., not operable inside the cooling chamber)
target_learners: volunteer rescue and healthcare professionals in simulation-based training
target_learning_goals: reflecting on team and individual performance after simulation
accepting and benefiting from feedback
examples: Facilitators added pre-debriefing disclaimers that the video was "an aid and not a tool to keep you under surveillance" and deliberately showed positive interactions alongside mistakes to avoid an overly negative impression.

citation: Avivit Arvatz, Boaz Hadas, Rotem Waitzman, Yehudit Judy Dori (2025). Putting self-regulated learning and teaching into practice: insights from two science teachers and their students. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09719-6
title: SRL-enriched online science modules with reflective prompts as instructional and research tools
description: Online modules designed by teachers after SRL&T professional development, integrating reflective questions as SRL prompts into pre-existing teaching materials. Modules served as both instruction and data sources: "each module was analysed twice—first, as an indicator of the teachers' SRL&T level, and second, as the source for the students' reflective replies." Examples include Adam's climate change module and Ben's spectrophotometry module delivered via Google Classroom.
requirements: Teachers need assessment knowledge to design reflective prompts of graded levels
Modules were adapted from teachers' pre-existing teaching materials during PD training
constraints: Reflective prompting analysis is conducted independently of student responses to keep evaluation unbiased
target_learners: 10th-12th grade secondary students in science and chemistry classes
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning skills including goal-setting, help-seeking, elaboration, and reflection

citation: Avivit Arvatz, Boaz Hadas, Rotem Waitzman, Yehudit Judy Dori (2025). Putting self-regulated learning and teaching into practice: insights from two science teachers and their students. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09719-6
title: Four-level rubric for teachers' reflective prompts adapted from Van Manen's reflective levels
description: The study adapts Van Manen's (1977) cumulative levels of reflection into a four-level rubric for classifying teachers' reflective prompts in learning modules. "Level 1 involves basic descriptive reflections" guiding students to content knowledge; "Van-Manen's practical reflection level was split in two, where Level 2 prompts reflection using limited SRL terminology" and Level 3 encourages concrete problem-solving commentary; "The highest level, Level 4, prompts critical reflections and fosters SRL." It enabled tracking teachers' SRL&T growth across a year of module design, with a parallel rubric for student reflective responses.
requirements: Prompts must be analysed independently of student responses for unbiased evaluation
Inter-rater reliability established: κ = 0.801, p < 0.001 on 15 reflective items
constraints: Rubric was developed and applied in a specific study context of two science teachers' online modules
target_learners: Science teachers in professional development programs
target_learning_goals: Teachers' assessment knowledge and SRL&T capability development
examples: Analysis of 44 reflective prompts using the rubric, with examples like Adam's low-level recall prompt and Ben's high-level insight prompt

article_title: Effects of group experience and information distribution on collaborative learning
citation: Jimmy Zambrano, Femke Kirschner, John Sweller, Paul A. Kirschner. (2019). Effects of group experience and information distribution on collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09495-0
title: Task-based collective schema account: prior collaborative experience builds a domain group schema that regulates transactional activities and optimizes collaborative cognitive load
description: The article explains its findings through cognitive load theory extended to groups. It proposes that when group members solve domain-specific tasks together they build shared schemas of joint work, and that "this group experience may be a domain group schema (i.e., a generalized domain skill at group level) that is stored in long-term memory to solve similar learning problems". Once acquired, such schemas serve as internalized guidance that regulates transactional activities — the communication and coordination specific to collaboration — and thereby optimize the collaborative cognitive load, so that working memory resources can be invested in constructing high-order schemas of the learning task rather than in unproductive inter-individual activity.
requirements: Prior collaborative experience with tasks similar to the learning tasks, so that task- or domain-based collaborative schemas can be formed and activated
constraints: The article states collaborative learning is not general knowledge applicable to any domain indiscriminately: it is better to prepare learners to collaborate according to particular characteristics of a task or domain
target_learners: Novice secondary school students learning high-complexity tasks in 3-person groups
target_learning_goals: Complex problem solving (break-even point problems) tested by individual short-term and delayed retention
examples: Experience groups trained over four sessions on quadratic equations with distributed equation values (e.g., for −15x2, each member received −5x2) before collaborating on break-even problems

citation: Lehesvuori, S., Järvinen, M., Lämsä, J., Heilala, V., Hämäläinen, R. (2026). Exploring interconnections between communicative activities, situational stress reactions and cognitive engagement in undergraduate mathematics lesson. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09786-3
title: Macro–meso–micro multimodal analysis framework combining classroom interaction coding with second-by-second cardiac stress measurement
description: The article develops a three-level analytical framework: macro-level overviews of communicative activities, meso-level visualisation of situational stress across the lesson, and micro-level second-by-second analysis of critical incidents combining discourse analysis with stress data. The authors state that "the methodological contribution of this research lies in the combination of both physiological (i.e., cardiac data) and multimodal interactional data (i.e., eye tracking, video, audio)." Stress is operationalised via the ASV derived from HRV, applying an approach from psychotherapist settings to an authentic learning environment.
requirements: Cardiac sensor data from consenting students, synchronised video/audio classroom recording, and a communicative-activity coding scheme applied in 20-second intervals
constraints: Exploratory use of second-by-second ASV beyond validated five-minute intervals; no baseline normalisation or interindividual comparison of HRV; three consenting students only

target_learning_goals: understanding how communicative activities relate to situational stress and cognitive engagement during mathematical problem-solving and presentation

title: Communicative-activity coding scheme with eight teacher-level and seven individual student-level codes for mathematics lesson interaction
description: The coding scheme maps observable communicative activities in a mathematics lesson at 20-second intervals. Teacher-level codes (N = 210 intervals) include teacher presentation, scaffolding questions, correcting/complementing, and whole-class discussion; individual student-level codes (N = 3*210 intervals) include active/passive listening, student presentation, student question, and peer discussion. article_title: Learning from interactive video: the influence of self-explanations, navigation, and cognitive load
citation: Beege, M., & Ploetzner, R. (2025). Learning from interactive video: the influence of self-explanations, navigation, and cognitive load. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09693-5
title: Do not assume interactive video features are generally beneficial: check learner use, response quality, and time-on-task boundaries
description: The article concludes that enriching instructional videos so learning shifts from receptive to active and constructive modes "is not generally beneficial", and that "the quality of the self-explanations and the control of the learning time seem to play an important role". Designers and researchers should therefore treat interactivity additions as conditional: low-quality self-explanations or unused navigation yield no gains beyond restudying. The article recommends considering moderator variables and boundary conditions rather than assuming generalizability of prior positive effects.
requirements: Interactive features must actually be used effectively by learners and elicit adequate-quality self-explanations for benefits to appear
constraints: Positive effects summarized in prior meta-analytic research may not generalize when learning time is controlled and responses are poor to moderate in quality
target_learners: university students learning from instructional video
target_learning_goals: retention and comprehension of conceptual science content such as thunderstorm formation
examples: In the experiment, navigation and prompts were each provided with strategic instructions, yet neither improved retention or comprehension with learning time fixed at 12 minutes

title: Professional development for computer-supported complex systems instruction should provide differentiated opportunities for teachers to build expertise
description: This principle holds that professional development for computer-supported complex systems instruction should vary the opportunities offered to teachers to build expertise, matching teachers' differing starting points. The article's abstract lists "providing differentiated opportunities to build expertise" among the instructional supports it demonstrates to be needed for improving implementation of such curricula. It is one of the two teacher-facing supports the 2-year study foregrounds, alongside addressing teacher beliefs.

citation: Jordan Lombard, Ivar Bråten, Cécile van de Leemput, Franck Amadieu. (2021). Performance and acceptance when using tablets as a multiple document learning tool: do application and guidance matter? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09537-6
title: MD-TRACE model of task-based multiple document processing
description: The article describes the Multiple-Document Task-based Relevance Assessment and Content Extraction model by Rouet and Britt (2011) as "a prominent framework describing the steps in working with multiple documents to complete a particular task". It consists of five steps: interpreting the task instruction and setting goals, judging which external resources are needed, selecting and processing documents, creating a task product, and evaluating its alignment with task requirements, with a cyclical return to earlier steps. The study particularly targeted the third and fourth steps: strategy guidance addressed step-three processes and effects were assessed through written task products in step four.
requirements: Working through the model's steps draws on external resources, such as a task instruction and a document set, and internal resources, such as prior knowledge and reading skills
constraints: The article applies the model to a single-issue document set on a controversial socio-scientific issue and evaluates only steps three and four empirically
target_learners: undergraduate students working with multiple documents
target_learning_goals: multiple document comprehension and integration of information across documents
examples: All participants received a task instruction, an iPad Pro, and five documents on sun exposure and health, framing the task in MD-TRACE terms

citation: Jordan Lombard, Ivar Bråten, Cécile van de Leemput, Franck Amadieu. (2021). Performance and acceptance when using tablets as a multiple document learning tool: do application and guidance matter? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09537-6
title: Select-Organize-Integrate (SOI) model of meaningful learning
description: The article builds on the SOI information-processing model of meaningful learning by Mayer, in which "strategy guidance needs to target three essential cognitive processes involved in meaningful learning: selecting relevant information, organizing the selected information, and building a coherent mental representation that can be stored in long-term memory". The authors adapted SOI to a multiple document context by guiding students to highlight content in single documents, select and extract task-relevant content, and integrate information across documents. They also note Mayer treats SOI as applicable across problem-solving types, including writing an essay on an unsettled issue.
requirements: Guidance must address all three processes: selection, organization, and integration of information
constraints: The guidance was implemented before the task with a cue card available during the task, not as embedded tutoring
target_learners: undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning and comprehension from multiple documents
examples: LiquidText Guidance participants were guided to highlight information, select and extract task-relevant information, and conceptually and spatially organize information across documents

article_title: Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl
citation: David Gijbels, Sofie M. M. Loyens. (2009). Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl. Instructional Science, 37, 499–502. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9100-2
title: Three perspectives on constructivism: theory of learning, philosophical position, and theory of instruction
description: The article argues that debates about constructivist learning environments turn on which of three perspectives one takes. Constructivism can be seen as a learning theory that is 'student-centered, since the emphasis is on students as active learners'; as a philosophical position focused on what knowledge is; or as a theory of instruction making claims at what Renkl calls the 'prescriptive level'. The authors recommend keeping theory and pedagogy apart while acknowledging that a learning theory carries implications for practice.
requirements: The perspectives must be distinguished explicitly, as Loyens and Gijbels (2008) did, to keep theory and pedagogy apart
constraints: The learning-theory perspective is descriptive, not prescriptive; the article notes that distinguishing perspectives is needed because debates misread one for another
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: understanding how constructivism is defined and applied in educational settings
examples: The article contrasts defining constructivism as a reaction to the traditional classroom (learning theory) with positions such as Colliver's that treat it as an insight into the nature of human knowledge
key_sources: David Gijbels, Sofie M. M. Loyens. (2009). Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl. Instructional Science, 37, 499–502. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9100-2

article_title: Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl
citation: David Gijbels, Sofie M. M. Loyens. (2009). Constructivist learning (environments) and how to avoid another tower of Babel: reply to Renkl. Instructional Science, 37, 499–502. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9100-2
title: Design instruction in any learning environment so students will engage in active sense-making and knowledge construction
description: The authors endorse Renkl's claim that one cannot deduce from constructivist assumptions that so-called constructivist environments are superior to traditional arrangements. Rather, 'instruction should be designed in such a way that there is a high probability students will engage in active sense-making and knowledge construction'. They extend this to recommending research on how to best induce sense-making irrespective of whether the environment is traditional or constructivist.
requirements: Instruction must be deliberately designed to make active sense-making and knowledge construction probable; the claim does not follow from constructivist assumptions alone
constraints: Traditional or constructivist labels alone do not guarantee better outcomes; the article explicitly denies that superiority can be deduced from the basic constructivist assumptions
target_learners: higher education students

active sense-making
knowledge construction
examples: The special issue encouraged research looking at a wide range of effects in a wide range of learning environments, including traditional ones designed to induce meaningful learning activities

article_title: An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom
citation: Lisa Hasenbein, Ulrich Trautwein, Jens-Uwe Hahn, Stephan Soller, Richard Göllner. (2024). An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09646-4
title: Fully preprogrammed immersive virtual reality (IVR) classroom simulating a computational thinking lesson
description: The article's IVR classroom is a 15-min simulated sixth-grade lesson on computational thinking (coding, sequences, loops), delivered via head-mounted displays to individual students in groups of up to 10. The lesson was "a fully preprogrammed simulation of a typical teaching situation based on audio recordings and motion captures stemming from a real classroom", with 24 virtual classmates whose hand-raising proportion (20/35/65/80%) was manipulated. The element works as an experimental apparatus preserving classroom authenticity while allowing strict control of social comparison information.
requirements: Requires head-mounted displays with noise-canceling headphones and technically reliable hardware; the study excluded 28 participants because of technical issues
constraints: Participants were asked to remain seated and quiet, and the lesson content assumes students have little to no prior computational thinking knowledge
target_learners: sixth-grade students (Gymnasium, southern Germany)
target_learning_goals: basic principles of computational thinking, including coding, sequences, and loops
examples: Groups of up to 10 students at their own schools each experienced the identical IVR lesson in a virtual classroom resembling a blank-slate first-day class.
key_sources: Lisa Hasenbein, Ulrich Trautwein, Jens-Uwe Hahn, Stephan Soller, Richard Göllner. (2024). An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09646-4

article_title: An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom
citation: Lisa Hasenbein, Ulrich Trautwein, Jens-Uwe Hahn, Stephan Soller, Richard Göllner. (2024). An experimental test of the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect using an immersive virtual reality classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09646-4
title: Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect (BFLPE)
description: The Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect is the theoretical account that students' academic self-concept depends on the achievement level of their reference group: higher class-average achievement depresses self-concept at fixed individual achievement. As the article puts it, "two equally able students will evaluate themselves differently depending on the performance level of their classmates, whom they use as a reference for their self-evaluation." This study experimentally reproduces the effect in an IVR classroom and identifies students' perceived class performance level as the mediating mechanism.
requirements: A reference group of classmates whose performance-related behavior is visible to the student, so that social comparison information can be perceived
constraints: In this experiment the negative effect appeared only for situational self-concept and between the extreme conditions (20% vs. 80%), not for dispositional self-concept or moderate comparison standards
target_learners: school students in classroom settings
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept, self-evaluation of one's own abilities
examples: Virtual classmates who raised their hands in response to the teacher's questions served as the manipulated reference-group performance signal.

citation: Cloude, E. B., Chapman, R., Azevedo, R., Castiglioni, A., LaRochelle, J., Hernandez, C., & Torre, D. (2025). Novice and expert self-regulated learning phase transitions in medical diagnosis: Implications for adaptive and intelligent systems. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09729-4
title: Extending Zimmerman and Moylan's socio-cognitive model of SRL to include metacognitive feelings (uncertainty) as a phase in the clinical-reasoning cycle
description: The article applies Zimmerman and Moylan's socio-cognitive model of SRL, which organizes learning processes into "forethought, performance, and self-reflection" phases, to clinical reasoning in multimedia diagnosis. The authors extend the model by adding metacognitive feelings: they state they "extend the SCT model by including metacognitive feelings as a phase in this cycle", operationalized as a Feelings of Uncertainty code drawn from the Lajoie et al. line of work. The study's sequential pattern mining treats uncertainty as a full phase whose transitions (e.g., UNC→F) cycle back into forethought and performance, framing SRL as non-linear, bidirectional, and cyclical rather than unidirectional.
requirements: Think-aloud verbalizations coded with a scheme covering the three SCT phases plus an uncertainty code
constraints: Findings are from one medical domain (common cough cases) in one multimedia system; the article notes the excluded 20% of the sample has implications including reduced generalizability.
target_learners: medical students
physicians in training and practice
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning and diagnostic accuracy
self-regulated learning competency
examples: Participants were trained to think-aloud with a 3-min video of a physician thinking aloud during an anemia case in CResME before solving the five cough cases.

title: CResME (Clinical-reasoning Mapping Exercise): a multimedia system eliciting clinical reasoning through illness-script matching across five cough cases
description: CResME is a multimedia system "built on assimilation (Ausubel, 2012) and illness script theories" that presents clinical information (history of present illness, laboratory tests/Data, physical exams) from five clinical cases with a chief complaint of a common cough. Critical findings are integrated across sources to activate illness scripts for specific diseases. Using the "drag & drop features", users must match physical exam and Data sources to the right history of present illness for each case, then write a diagnosis; identifying similarities, differences, and reconciling inconsistencies is designed to promote knowledge development and illness-script construction. The system has validity studies and was used with a diagnostic-performance rubric scoring illness script activation and diagnostic accuracy.
requirements: Users trained to think-aloud before using the system in the study workflow
A faculty-developed scoring rubric (e.g., a 0–3 scale) to quantify illness script activation and diagnostic accuracy
constraints: Assessed only five clinical cases related to the common cough in this study; electrodermal activity and eye-tracking data were collected but not analyzed.
target_learners: medical students (2nd and 3rd year)
physician faculty
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
illness script development
diagnostic accuracy
examples: Each clinical case was structured vertically (1–5) on the right-hand side of the interface with the HPI provided; correct diagnosis required integrating prototypical features of the case.

article_title: Effects of immersion in inquiry-based learning on student teachers’ educational beliefs
citation: Voet, M. & De Wever, B. (2018). Effects of immersion in inquiry-based learning on student teachers' educational beliefs. Instructional Science, 46(3), 383-403. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9439-8
title: Immersion in inquiry-based learning ('teach as you preach') as a professional development approach
description: Professional development on IBL commonly applies the teaching-as-you-preach principle: putting teachers through a substantive inquiry experience mirroring what they should do in class. The article states this roots in social learning theory, in which behaviors are "learned, either deliberately or inadvertently, through the influence of example". Rather than delivering information, immersion provides teachers with good practices they observe and potentially adopt.
requirements: Teachers work through a substantive amount of content in a way that mirrors the target pedagogical approach
constraints: Some scholars argue immersion may fail without meta-commentary making underlying ideas explicit

increasing self-efficacy for inquiry

title: Three design principles for IBL activities in professional development: authenticity, collaboration, and scaffolded inquiry
description: The IBL activity was designed around three principles. Authenticity meant a discovery-oriented approach using an ill-structured evaluative problem statement requiring students to form their own interpretations of evidence. Collaboration reflected the view that historical reasoning is a social activity in which interaction "stimulates students to elaborate their knowledge". Scaffolding sequenced key inquiry activities in a macro-script within a workflow.

sufficient guidance so learners forming their own interpretations from contradictory sources have a positive inquiry experience

conducting historical inquiries

article_title: Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners
citation: Ashlyn Pierson, D. Teo Keifert, Bethany Daniel, Sarah Lee, Tessaly Jen, Adam Bell, Heather Johnson, Rachel Askew, Andrea Henrie. (2024). Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09674-8
title: Two conceptualizations of equity: equity-as-access and equity-as-transformation
description: The article organizes its analysis around two conceptualizations of equity drawn from Grapin et al. (2023): equity-as-access, in which "learners should have access to disciplinary knowledge, practices, and career paths" (Grapin et al), and equity-as-transformation, in which "learners should transform what it means to learn and participate in disciplines" (Grapin et al). The authors use this distinction to diagnose why their initial PD design failed to disrupt deficit ideologies and to guide redesign. They cite a NASEM report arguing both are necessary, in which "equity-as-access supports short-term achievement, whereas equity-as-transformation disrupts systemic oppression in the long-term" (NASEM report).
requirements: Teachers and facilitators need explicit opportunities to distinguish and discuss both conceptions for transformative perspectives to emerge
constraints: The article reports relatively little research exists on equity-as-transformation, and notes the section is in the authors' discussion
target_learners: K-4 science teachers in professional development
target_learning_goals: Teachers' conceptualizations of equity in science teaching for multilingual learners

title: PD design pattern pairing new activities with specific facilitation moves to support equity-oriented sensemaking
description: In the redesigned Summer 2 PD, each new activity was deliberately paired with a facilitation conversation targeting a specific ideological challenge: "Language Storybook was paired with a conversation about recognizing multilingual learners' assets; Jonathan and the Sun was paired with a conversation about surfacing deficit ideologies grounded in teachers' experiences" (Design section). This pairing links immersive experiences of being a nondominant-language learner to explicit discussion of ideologies, giving facilitators structured openings to surface and challenge deficit framings rather than pivoting back to safer content-focused ground.
requirements: Activities must be paired with conversations that connect the immersive experience to teachers' own planning, teaching, and ideological assumptions
constraints: The facilitation moves examined concern multilingual learners' assets and deficit ideologies in K-4 elementary science PD

target_learning_goals: Ideological sensemaking and rearticulation toward equity-as-transformation perspectives

title: Three sustained PD features—immersive learning, student work analysis, and video club—support reflection and collaboration
description: The article describes its PD as built on three features for supporting reflection and collaboration: "(1) immersive learning, (2) student work analysis, and (3) video club" (PD design section). Immersive lessons in which teachers participate as learners build shared grounding in science teaching; student work analysis helps teachers understand and evaluate student thinking; video clubs anchor sensemaking in the realities of teachers' own classrooms. These features ran through both summer workshops and academic-year sessions and provided the substrate for ideological sensemaking about equity.

description: The article concludes that, for practice, PD must "underscore the importance of providing teachers with opportunities to explicitly connect new perspectives of equity with day-to-day experiences of classroom teaching" (Abstract, practice implications). The redesign succeeded when facilitators gave significant time for small-group discussion tying big ideas to practical, real-world stories, whereas abstract ideological debriefs alone reified deficit framings. article_title: Factors that explain simulation-based inquiry performance in physics learning
citation: Gerdesmann, D., Schwichow, M., & Koerber, S. (2026). Factors that explain simulation-based inquiry performance in physics learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09806-2
title: Extended SDDS framework: inquiry as structured search in hypothesis and experiment spaces
description: The Scientific Discovery as Dual Search framework describes inquiry as structured search in two interconnected spaces: a hypothesis space (divided by van Joolingen and de Jong into a variable space and a relation space) and an experiment space. The study maps cognitive factors onto these spaces: content knowledge constrains plausible hypotheses, CVS supports designing unconfounded experiments, and functional thinking supports reasoning about variable relations in the relation space. Seven measured inquiry facets were aligned to these spaces.

constraints: The study applies the mapping in single-task, single-user digital simulation environments; the authors limit scope to such contexts

article_title: When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains
citation: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2
title: Productive Failure: design features and three hypothesized learning mechanisms
description: Productive Failure combines two successive phases: an initial phase in which students collaboratively invent solution ideas for a complex novel problem without instructional support, and a delayed instruction phase in which the instructor builds on erroneous student solutions. The article states the design features "are expected to trigger the following three learning-related mechanisms which are hypothesized to underlie the effectiveness of PF (Loibl et al. 2017): (1) activation of prior knowledge, (2) awareness of knowledge limitations, and (3) recognition of the deep features of the targeted learning concepts." It applies this framework to design and evaluate a non-STEM instantiation of PF.
requirements: The problem must meet a sweet spot of complexity, addressing prior knowledge related to the targeted concept while students cannot solve it canonically
The delayed instruction must build on students' erroneous solution ideas, comparing and contrasting them with components of the canonical solution
constraints: The targeted concept needs a canonical solution with clearly definable components that can be compared with erroneous ideas, per the article's own argument

title: Domain-structuredness hypothesis: PF effectiveness may be restricted to structured domains
description: The article argues that PF requires a canonical solution whose components can be compared and contrasted with features of erroneous student ideas during instruction. It reports that "Loibl et al. (2017) hypothesize that the effectiveness of PF may only emerge for learning in structured domains, which \"allow for clear identification of deep features and evaluation of solution attempts\" (p. 712)". It situates social science research-methods topics on a continuum as "rather structured topics", less structured than STEM topics like standard deviation but still evaluable, making them an apt test case for transferring PF beyond STEM.
