title: Instruction that contrasts four typical erroneous solution features with components of the canonical solution
description: This instructional pattern structures the delayed instruction phase of a PF lesson: the instructor walks through ways in which typical student solutions fall short of each component of a canonical solution. For the experimental-design topic, the article's Table 3 pairs four error features (e.g. "No inclusion of a control condition") with corresponding canonical components (e.g. "Inclusion of a control condition"), presented in a step-by-step explanation based on pilot-test results, so that students can recognize their specific knowledge gaps and the deep features of the concept.

A canonical solution with clearly definable components must exist for the targeted concept

title: Definition of classical PF studies: three shared characteristics distinguishing them from PF-similar studies
description: The article defines classical PF studies (e.g. Kapur 2010-2012; Loibl and Rummel 2014a, b; Westermann and Rummel 2012) as those that focus on STEM learning and "share the following three characteristics": (a) the problem-solving condition fulfilled the crucial design features of collaboratively inventing solution ideas to a complex problem and having erroneous student solutions compared and contrasted with the canonical solution; (b) effectiveness was tested with secondary school or undergraduate students; and (c) effectiveness was examined by comparing PF to an instruction-prior-to-problem-solving control condition. article_title: Effects of short- and long-term prompting in learning journals on strategy use, self-efficacy, and learning outcomes
citation: Nadja M. Gentner, Lisa Respondek, Tina Seufert. (2024). Effects of short- and long-term prompting in learning journals on strategy use, self-efficacy, and learning outcomes. Instructional Science (2024) 52:919–950. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09671-x
title: Zimmerman's cyclical three-phase model of self-regulated learning (forethinking, performance, self-reflection)
description: The article adopts Zimmerman's (2005) model as its theoretical framework: self-regulation "refers to self-generated thoughts, feelings, and actions that are planned and cyclically adapted to the attainment of personal goals". It integrates cognitive, metacognitive, emotion-affective, and motivational components in three phases — forethought (task analysis, planning, strategy selection), performance (applying strategies, monitoring), and self-reflection (judging the process, selecting regulation strategies). Because the model treats self-regulated learning as a process unfolding over time, the authors chose it as the basis for their longitudinal design with continuous weekly measurement.
requirements: Continuous measurements over time are needed to capture the development of self-regulation components across phases.
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use and motivation in coursework
examples: The study measured cognitive and metacognitive strategy use and self-efficacy weekly at t1–t8 across two course units, following the model's process view.

description: A university international relations course built around the board game Diplomacy, with alternating "1.5-hour lectures and 2-hour game sessions" in a weekly cycle of reading, lectures with small-group discussion, game sessions, and online discussion tasks. Students played in two-player teams including a peace-mediator team, a feature added by the teacher; game performance formed one-quarter of course evaluation. Three revised win-conditions correspond to offensive realism, liberal-institutionalism and constructivism.

Negotiation success is central, making it a combination of strategy game and conflict negotiation simulation

Findings are specific to this particular game, as the authors state

title: Valence-activation classification of epistemic emotions
description: The article organises epistemic emotions — "curiosity, enjoyment, surprise, confusion, anxiety, frustration and boredom" — using a valence-activation classification (Pekrun et al., 2017). Enjoyment and curiosity are positive activating emotions; boredom is negative de-activating; surprise is neutral activating, experienced as pleasant or unpleasant; anxiety, confusion and frustration are negative activating emotions that can either drive incongruity-resolution strategies or provoke avoidance. Epistemic emotions arise from cognitive conflict between the known and unknown and are a subset of academic emotions.
requirements: Distinguishes epistemic emotions (tied to knowledge construction) from other academic emotions tied to achievement or social dynamics
constraints: Anxiety, frustration, boredom and enjoyment can also function as achievement or social emotions depending on their focus of attention
target_learners: University students in complex, knowledge-construction learning contexts
target_learning_goals: Supporting knowledge construction and cognitive processing through productive emotional experiences
examples: The study applies the framework to interpret which emotions game sessions activated and how their trajectories related to learning outcomes.

title: Use process-oriented intra-individual (time-series) analysis to capture emotion dynamics that group-level findings conceal
description: The study advocates measuring emotions repeatedly after every session and analysing them with dynamic structural equation modelling, a process-oriented, intra-individual approach "only recently applied in educational research". This distinguishes within-person processes, between-person differences and learning context. The unique individual emotional trajectories showed that group-level conclusions about emotion trends were not applicable to all individuals, since individuals with decreasing emotions learned better.
requirements: Intensive session-to-session self-report data (212 situational questionnaires across 22 students)
Bayesian estimation because of the small number of clusters
constraints: Performed at only the within level because of the small number of clusters at the between level; models assumed data missing at random

target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting emotional dynamics of learning over time
examples: Emotions were measured with single-item EES measures after each of 13 and 11 sessions across two course implementations, capturing situational fluctuation.

article_title: Significance of forms and foci of metacognitive regulation in collaborative science learning of less and more successful outcome groups in diverse contexts
citation: Iiskala, T., Volet, S., Jones, C., Koretsky, M., & Vauras, M. (2021). Significance of forms and foci of metacognitive regulation in collaborative science learning of less and more successful outcome groups in diverse contexts. Instructional Science, 49, 687–718. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09558-1
title: Forms and foci framework of metacognitive regulation in collaborative learning
description: A conceptual framework for describing metacognitive regulation (MR) in collaborative learning along two axes: forms (whose cognitive process is regulated and how the group is involved) and foci (the level of cognitive activity being regulated). Forms include VMSR ("observable evidence of a group member's MR of their own learning despite the joint effort"), IMR (a member attempting to regulate the group but being ignored), MOR ("asymmetric metacognitive interaction between partners"), and SSMR (several members' interdependent regulation of joint cognitive activity). Foci distinguish high-level (elaboration, constructing meaning) from low-level (simple acquisition, practical task aspects) cognitive activity. The article uses this framework to examine outcomes across three diverse contexts.
requirements: A shared group goal, since "the manifestation of social forms of MR, especially SSMR, presupposes the existence of a group's common goal."
constraints: Only verbalised MR is observable; most self-regulation is assumed internal and "not accessible to peers or researchers."

description: Double-content examples integrate two levels: the learning domain level (the skill being taught, here analyzing classroom videos) and the exemplifying domain level (the content illustrating it, here classroom management). title: Self-determination theory framing of motivation quality in learning environments
description: The article adopts self-determination theory (SDT) as its motivation framework. SDT "differentiates the intensity and amount of motivation from the quality or type of motivation", refining the intrinsic/extrinsic split into "a distinction between autonomous (self-determined) and controlled motivation". Autonomous motivation arises when a learning environment satisfies needs for autonomy, self-efficacy (competence), and relatedness, and is associated with positive educational outcomes. The study assumed the virtual environment would support these needs, e.g. teachers refraining from disturbing interventions to provide psychological freedom.

"The platform involves Inquiry Learning Spaces (ILSs) as learning resources that foster inquiry learning" by following "the inquiry cycle phases of orientation, hypothesis generation, experimentation, conclusion, and discussion". ILSs can include virtual/remote labs, scaffolding apps, and multimedia. In this study teachers developed nine ILSs for force and energy, each covered in about two hours over five weeks, using a hypothesis scratchpad and an experiment design tool as scaffolds.

article_title: How preparation-for-learning with a worked versus an open inventing problem affect subsequent learning processes in pre-service teachers
citation: Inga Glogger-Frey, Anne-Katrin Treier, Alexander Renkl. (2022). How preparation-for-learning with a worked versus an open inventing problem affect subsequent learning processes in pre-service teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09577-6
title: Use worked-example preparation rather than open inventing to prepare learners for subsequent instruction in complex, ill-structured domains
description: The article argues that when learning content has high element interactivity, preparing learners by having them study a worked-out solution of the invention problem deepens and focuses the subsequent learning phase. It concludes that "working through a worked example deepens future learning and thus is more beneficial for transfer than preparation with an open inventing problem" in comparable learning domains. The mechanism is more elaboration and more application of canonical criteria during future learning.

constraints: The authors state generalizations can be limited: effects may depend on learner expertise and element interactivity, and the opposite effect (inventing > worked example) was found when school students gained expertise through practice; only an immediate posttest was used

novice learners with low prior knowledge in complex domains

examples: In the experiment, the inventing group generated evaluation criteria from four contrasting learning-journal extracts while the worked-example group studied the same extracts with the criteria, ratings and notes already filled in by an experienced teacher, both for 15 minutes before learning in the CBLE

Derived via reflexive thematic analysis combining deductive coding against the FunQ model and inductive coding of focus group and observation data, then contextualized by an expert interview. It extends the FunQ model for formal primary settings.

article_title: Instructional approaches to foster third graders’ adaptive use of strategies: an experimental study on the effects of two learning environments on multi-digit addition and subtraction
citation: Aiso Heinze, Julia Arend, Meike Gruessing, Frank Lipowsky. (2018). Instructional approaches to foster third graders' adaptive use of strategies: an experimental study on the effects of two learning environments on multi-digit addition and subtraction. Instr Sci 46:869–891. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9457-1
title: Two idealized instructional approaches to fostering adaptive strategy use: explicit demonstration versus implicit generation
description: The article contrasts two idealized learning environments for fostering adaptive use of strategies. The explicit approach reduces cognitive load by demonstrating and practicing strategies with explicit efficiency criteria, building a strategy repertoire and routine execution. The implicit approach capitalizes on the generation effect: children analyze number characteristics, categorize problems as "easy problems", "smart problems" or "other problems", generate their own strategies, and compare their efficiency, with the teacher acting as a mentor who avoids presenting official strategies or preferences. Both environments used the same problems and strategy comparison from the beginning.
requirements: Students must be able to generate the target strategies correctly; the article states a necessary condition for the generation effect is that students are able to generate the target information correctly
The teacher must avoid setting socio-mathematical norms that implicitly privilege particular strategies
constraints: The generation effect does not hold for strategies too complex for students to generate, such as indirect subtraction and simplifying for third graders

target_learning_goals: adaptive use of computation strategies in multi-digit addition and subtraction
examples: In the explicit condition the five strategy types were successively demonstrated and practiced over the first three days; in the implicit condition children categorized problems and generated and compared their own strategies

article_title: Is drawing after learning effective for metacognitive monitoring only when supported by spatial scaffolds?
citation: Julia Kollmer, Katrin Schleinschok, Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Eitel. (2020). Is drawing after learning effective for metacognitive monitoring only when supported by spatial scaffolds? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09521-6
title: Generative tasks foster metacognitive monitoring by prompting situation-model reasoning that yields more diagnostic JOL cues
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that inaccurate monitoring stems from learners basing JOLs on superficial cues such as the ease-of-processing heuristic. Generative tasks like drawing "require situation-model reasoning, because they require constructing a 'new' representation in a different code", transforming verbal relations into spatial ones and giving implicit feedback about knowledge gaps. JOLs grounded in situation-model comprehension are less inflated because less forgetting occurs at that level, improving calibration. The study tests this account by comparing drawing conditions against mental reactivation.
requirements: Learners must perform the generative task after reading and directly before providing JOLs, without access to the text (closed-book conditions).
constraints: The account was tested with high visuo-spatial content; the authors state it remains open whether drawing supports monitoring for contents lower in visuo-spatial reasoning demands.
target_learners: university students learning expository text independently
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring (calibration and resolution) of expository text comprehension
examples: Students drew the crucial concepts from each aurora-text paragraph and labeled the diagram before giving a JOL on an 11-point 0-100 scale.

article_title: Self-regulation of secondary school students: self-assessments are inaccurate and insufficiently used for learning-task selection
citation: Nugteren, M. L., Jarodzka, H., Kester, L., & Van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2018). Self-regulation of secondary school students: self-assessments are inaccurate and insufficiently used for learning-task selection. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9448-2
title: SRLTS model: a normative cyclical model for self-regulated learning-task selection based on self-assessments
description: The self-regulated learning-task selection (SRLTS) model describes "a systematic way in which students could select tasks to develop their knowledge and skills". Adapted from Zimmerman's SRL cycle and Van Merriënboer and Kirschner's dynamic task-selection model, it has students self-assess via performance estimates, mental effort ratings, and JOLs, compare these to internal standards, and use the gaps to choose a next task's difficulty, support, and content. It was added to existing models with two new elements: standards and a link between JOLs and content selection.
requirements: Self-assessments need to be accurate for task selections to be based on correct information
Students must be able to compare self-assessments to internal standards for performance and cognitive load
constraints: The article states the study does not yet establish that selecting tasks according to the SRLTS model leads to higher achievement
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning-task selection
self-assessment of performance
examples: Students selected genetics tasks varying in difficulty, support (completion vs. traditional problems), and content from a 75-task database while the authors compared selections to model prescriptions

article_title: Community and citizen science in schools: nested inquiries, productive tensions, and the role of communities
citation: Ballard, H. L. (2023). Community and citizen science in schools: nested inquiries, productive tensions, and the role of communities. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09643-7
title: Nested inquiries: students pursue their own investigations intertwined with partnering scientists' projects in school-based citizen science
description: Nested inquiries are cases where educators and scientists strike a balance between students' own questions and those of partnering professional scientists, offering a solution to the tension among the multiple goals of CCS in schools. The commentary states these cases "offer evidence of students' learning and deep engagement with scientific practices, the nature of science and uncertainty, and using their science for decision-making and action." It extends earlier work on youth working with nested data situated in larger datasets, projects, and communities.
requirements: Educators and scientists must balance students' own questions alongside or intertwined with those of the partnering professional scientists, which the commentary calls a tightrope for CCS project designers
constraints: The commentary notes it is a tightrope for CCS project designers, scientists and educators to walk
target_learners: K-12 students in school-based citizen science projects
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning and practices
nature of science and uncertainty
using science for decision-making and action
identity and agency development
examples: Middle school students collected Radon Concentration Levels data and helped scientists explore the data while pursuing their own investigations, formulating questions, analyzing, and making claims
A 4th and 5th grade class investigated birds on their school campus while submitting observations to eBird and developed schoolyard planting recommendations

article_title: Examining secondary school students’ views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology
citation: Lee, S. W.-Y., Wu, H., & Chang, H. (2021). Examining secondary school students' views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology. Instructional Science, 49, 223–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09534-9
title: Integrated framework of personal epistemology for model evaluation: Kuhn's three developmental stages crossed with Kitchener's three epistemic-cognition dimensions
description: The framework interlaces Kuhn's developmental levels (absolutist, multiplist, evaluatist) with Kitchener's dimensions of epistemic cognition (limits of knowing, certainty of knowing, criteria of knowing) to form a matrix for analyzing students' epistemic views of model evaluation. As the article states, "the three epistemic levels describing the absolutist, multiplist, and evaluatist... and the three epistemic dimensions describing limits of knowing, certainty of knowing, and criteria of knowing (Kitchener 1983) are interlaced to form a new framework for analyzing students' epistemic views of model evaluation." It was operationalized in coding themes and used to interpret students' justifications.
requirements: Written justifications and forced-choice assumption responses so that epistemic levels and dimensions can be coded and triangulated
constraints: The article notes relatively fewer students referred to the limits of knowing, and the framework was applied to two non-textbook science contexts with high uncertainty
target_learners: secondary school students (eighth and 11th grade)
target_learning_goals: epistemic understanding of scientific model evaluation
examples: Students' justifications were coded into themes mapped onto the framework's dimensions and levels, and each student's assumption choice was compared with the coded written response to confirm their epistemic level
key_sources: Lee, S. W.-Y., Wu, H., & Chang, H. (2021). Examining secondary school students' views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology. Instructional Science, 49, 223–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09534-9

article_title: Examining secondary school students’ views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology
citation: Lee, S. W.-Y., Wu, H., & Chang, H. (2021). Examining secondary school students' views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology. Instructional Science, 49, 223–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09534-9
title: Contextualized model-evaluation items presenting two competing models and three epistemic assumptions
description: The study developed model-evaluation items with three design characteristics: they are "contextualized by real scientific problems," they "present at least two competing models," and they "present three epistemic positions for the students to choose from." Two item sets were built on SARS virus infection models and dinosaur-extinction models, deliberately chosen as non-textbook science contexts with high uncertainty. After reading about the two models, students chose among three epistemic assumptions and wrote justifications explaining their choice.
requirements: Item review by co-authors and by two middle school teachers and one high school teacher to ensure construct, face, and content validity
constraints: The two contexts were intentionally non-textbook and possessed high levels of uncertainty, since scientists are still attempting to understand the mechanisms or causes
target_learners: secondary school students (eighth and 11th grade)
target_learning_goals: assessing students' epistemic views of scientific model evaluation
examples: Two models of SARS virus infection and two explanatory models of dinosaur extinction were presented, and students chose among assumptions such as "one model is better than another" and "depends on the evidence"
key_sources: Lee, S. W.-Y., Wu, H., & Chang, H. (2021). Examining secondary school students' views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology. Instructional Science, 49, 223–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09534-9

article_title: Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic
citation: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w
title: Perspectival coordination framework: egocentric-to-allocentric coordination as the cognitive process of symbol grounding in embodied mathematics designs
description: The article proposes that embodied designs stage a coordination between an egocentric perspective, in which actions are experienced with respect to one's own body, and an allocentric perspective, in which objects are experienced with respect to other objects. Following Benally et al., it distinguishes "in perspectival substitution, one perspective replaces the other; in perspectival mutuality, individuals use an alternative perspective to validate their own; in perspectival synergy, a combination of two perspectives results in one that is greater than each perspective alone." The design operationalizes this as walking a body-scale number line (egocentric) then puppeteering a figurine on a desk-scale line (allocentric).
requirements: Students must experience the egocentric enaction first and then be guided to coordinate it with the allocentric normative display
constraints: Merely shifting unidirectionally from the BNL to a figurine on the SNL was often not enough, per the article's implications
target_learners: middle-school students learning integer arithmetic
target_learning_goals: understanding addition and subtraction with positive and negative integers
examples: Students walked the body-scale number line, then moved a puppy figurine on a desk-scale number line to mimic their movements
key_sources: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w

article_title: Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic
citation: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w
title: Walking number line design: body-scale number line plus desk-scale number line with figurine, using a four-step orientation-and-movement procedure
description: The design consists of a body-scale number line (a 20' × 4' paper roll displaying a number line from −5 to +5, with step-spaced marks and addition/subtraction signs at the ends) and a small number line (an 8.5″ × 11″ sheet with a scaled-down line and a puppy figurine). Students follow four steps: "start by standing on the first number in the problem"; face the addition or subtraction direction; "walk forwards if the second number (the addend or subtrahend) is positive and backwards if the second number is negative"; and walk as many steps as the absolute value of that second number. The operation is enacted as a shift in orientation and the second number's polarity as direction of movement.
requirements: Signs marking addition and subtraction at the two ends of the body-scale line
A figurine on the desk-scale line for re-enacting the walking solution
constraints: The material boundaries at −5 and +5 led some students to reject solutions outside that range, per the limitations section
target_learners: Grade 7 students in general education inclusive math classes, pre-identified as struggling with integer operations
target_learning_goals: fluency with adding and subtracting positive and negative integers
examples: A student solving −1 + 3 stands on −1, faces addition, and walks forwards three steps to arrive at 2
key_sources: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w

article_title: Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic
citation: Jacqueline Anton, Dor Abrahamson. (2025). Walking the number line: towards an enactive understanding of integer arithmetic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09707-w
title: Scaffold perspective coordination explicitly: give students multiple body-scale sessions and bidirectional switching supports before expecting desk-scale transfer
description: From the pilot's breakdowns, the authors recommend that embodied designs not shift unidirectionally from enactive to normative media. They state that "students must be given scaffolded opportunities to coordinate between perspectives when learning curricular content in an experiential situation" and that "Merely shifting unidirectionally from the BNL to a figurine on the SNL was often not enough." For the next design iteration they specify multiple body-scale sessions before advancing, a longer number line, and switching back and forth between the two lines or teaching a peer how to walk the body-scale line.
requirements: Time for multiple sessions on the body-scale number line before advancing to the desk-scale line
constraints: The pilot's limited time within a typical school day restricted participants' opportunities to train adequately with the new resources
target_learners: middle-school students learning integer arithmetic, including students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: coordinating embodied and symbolic understandings of integer operations
examples: In the pilot, students who spontaneously returned to the body-scale line when stuck used it to validate desk-scale answers; the authors propose building in such switching deliberately

article_title: Students’ voices—the dynamic interactions between learning preferences, gender, learning disabilities, and achievements in science studies
citation: Oshra Aloni, Michal Zion, Ornit Spektor-Levy. (2024). Students' voices—the dynamic interactions between learning preferences, gender, learning disabilities, and achievements in science studies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09666-8
title: Implement multi-faceted instructional strategies and an ongoing metacognitive dialogue with students about learning preferences to address student diversity in science classrooms
description: The article argues that because students favored all four learning modalities and expected variety, science instruction should be multi-faceted. The authors state that "the study results show the importance of implementing multi-faceted instructional strategies to address students' diversity and learning preferences", and that offering equal opportunities should be reflected in "an ongoing, metacognitive dialogue between the teachers and the students" about outcomes, achievements, and learning processes. Without such explicit discussion, they warn, providing learning choices may leave students confused and underachieving.
requirements: Explicit discussions with students about their learning preferences, so that offering learning choices does not end in confusion and unmet potential
constraints: The study addressed only a binary gender system and did not consider students who do not identify as male or female
Effect sizes for gender differences were low-moderate and the authors call for further examination
target_learners: Middle school (ninth-grade) science students in heterogeneous, inclusive classrooms, including students with and without learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Scientific knowledge and skills in ninth-grade science (nutrition and the digestive system, scientific inquiry, graph reading)
examples: The study asked 305 ninth-grade students about their science learning preferences via a validated Learning Preferences Questionnaire based on Fleming's VARK model and the Multi-Faceted Holistic Approach, and found all four modalities preferred above the mid-point with visual and sensorimotor highest
key_sources: Oshra Aloni, Michal Zion, Ornit Spektor-Levy. (2024). Students' voices—the dynamic interactions between learning preferences, gender, learning disabilities, and achievements in science studies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09666-8

article_title: Learning with concept maps: the effect of activity structure and the type of task
citation: Amante, C., Lucero, M., & Montanero, M. (2026). Learning with concept maps: the effect of activity structure and the type of task. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09764-1
title: Collective working memory account of why collaborative self-construction of concept maps supports learning
description: The article explains the advantage of collaborative map self-construction through a collective-working-memory account: dialogic conversation distributes the proposing and evaluating of representational alternatives across partners, so "the exchange and integration of information that characterizes dialogic conversation would generate a kind of collective working memory" that reduces the load on any single member's working memory. The authors link this to cognitive load theory, noting that individually constructing a map from a text requires producing and evaluating many alternatives, which overloads working memory. Peer help in the deep exploratory episodes of self-constructed CM pairs showed co-inference processes that offset this load.
requirements: Tasks complex enough that the intrinsic load justifies collaboration; the article states collaboration is only truly effective "when the task is sufficiently complex to justify the extra time and effort involved in collaborating with others".
constraints: Peer help showed no significant effect over individual work for relatively simple tasks such as completing a mutilated map, because the intrinsic load is much lighter.
target_learners: Undergraduate students with little or no experience using concept maps
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and delayed recall of academic text content
examples: Pairs who created complete maps showed deep exploratory episodes with co-inference, distributing the work of proposing and evaluating concept representations.
key_sources: Amante, C., Lucero, M., & Montanero, M. (2026). Learning with concept maps: the effect of activity structure and the type of task. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09764-1

article_title: Authentic evidence from the ‘SRL-AIDE’ simulative environment on explicitness and duration of in-class SRL teaching practices
citation: Orna Heaysman, Bracha Kramarski. (2026). Authentic evidence from the 'SRL-AIDE' simulative environment on explicitness and duration of in-class SRL teaching practices. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09787-2
title: SRL-AIDE: a professional development model combining direct and indirect SRL instruction through authentic, interactive, dynamic live-actor simulation experiences
description: SRL-AIDE (Authentic, Interactive, and Dynamic Experiences in SRL context) is a teacher professional development model combining explicit instruction in SRL theory and practice with simulations in which professional actors play student roles and one participant teaches. The article states it "involves live-actor simulations, where participants are highly engaged and immersed in the experience." After each simulation, participants analyze scenarios with metacognitive prompts, receive feedback from audience and actors, and take part in a guided video-based debriefing. The model addresses gaps in prior PD research that relied on pre-service teachers and self-report measures by measuring actual classroom implementation through observation.
requirements: Programs combining the model need theory–practice integration, simulations with professional actors, and materials such as video-recorded modelling, prompt cards, and reflection sessions as described in the program outline
constraints: The study examined the model with 70 elementary teachers of grades 3–5 (ages 8–10) in schools of medium–high/high socio-economic status in central Israel; the authors note future research should test impact on student outcomes and other practice types
target_learners: in-service elementary school teachers (grades 3–5)
target_learning_goals: teachers' knowledge and classroom implementation of self-regulated learning practices (MCS and KC)
examples: Over 10 three-hour sessions, the SRL-AIDE group received explicit SRL phase instruction, simulation workshops with professional actors (sessions 5 and 8), role-play, video observation, and collaborative lesson planning
key_sources: Orna Heaysman, Bracha Kramarski. (2026). Authentic evidence from the 'SRL-AIDE' simulative environment on explicitness and duration of in-class SRL teaching practices. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09787-2

article_title: Authentic evidence from the ‘SRL-AIDE’ simulative environment on explicitness and duration of in-class SRL teaching practices
citation: Orna Heaysman, Bracha Kramarski. (2026). Authentic evidence from the 'SRL-AIDE' simulative environment on explicitness and duration of in-class SRL teaching practices. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09787-2
title: Teacher PD for SRL should combine explicit theoretical instruction with authentic simulation-based practice, since promoting independence (KC) alone does not build metacognitive instruction capacity
description: The article recommends that effective SRL development for teachers requires "explicit theoretical instruction combined with authentic practice opportunities", because promoting independence through knowledge construction alone does not build teachers' capacity for explicit metacognitive instruction. PD programs should integrate direct and indirect SRL approaches with extended duration and simulation-based experiences allowing practice and reflection. The study's comparison of the SRL-AIDE group against a KC-focused comparison program provides the empirical basis for this recommendation.
requirements: PD programs need extended duration and simulation-based experiences allowing practice and reflection, per the article's implications section
constraints: The evidence comes from a quasi-experimental study of 70 elementary teachers in grades 3–5 in central Israel; the authors note student outcomes and other practice types remain untested
target_learners: in-service elementary school teachers
target_learning_goals: teachers' capacity to implement metacognitive strategic support and knowledge construction practices in class
examples: The SRL-AIDE group received explicit SRL theory instruction plus live-actor simulation workshops, while the comparison group received only KC-focused instruction; only the SRL-AIDE group's KC duration increased significantly

article_title: Inclusive pedagogy in practice within the multi-tiered systems of support framework: a design-based research in a Chinese EFL classroom
citation: Lin, T., Mullick, J., & Campbell, M. (2026). Inclusive pedagogy in practice within the multi-tiered systems of support framework: a design-based research in a Chinese EFL classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09754-3
title: Multi-Tiered System of Support (MTSS) framework with three tiers of support
description: MTSS is described as "an evidence-based framework designed to enhance academic achievement, behaviour, and social-emotional well-being through tiered levels of support". It comprises three tiers — Tier 1 universal, Tier 2 targeted, and Tier 3 intensive — and two key dimensions, Response to Intervention and Positive Behavioural Interventions and Supports. In this study MTSS guided both content teaching and classroom management in a Chinese EFL classroom, combined with TPRS to deliver inclusive pedagogy.
requirements: Tier 1 universal instruction establishing academic skills, prosocial behaviour, and emotional well-being for all students, with Tier 2 targeted and Tier 3 intensive support layered on for students needing more
constraints: The article notes MTSS's adaptation in culturally diverse contexts such as China remains underexplored, and behavioural support may be perceived as secondary to academic rigour in exam-driven systems
target_learners: elementary EFL students across low-, mid-, and high-performance levels, including students with SEN and neurodiverse conditions
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency
engagement and on-task behaviour
social-emotional well-being
examples: The first author applied MTSS as sole teacher of one class for three years, offering EFL lessons three times per week in Grade 1, four times in Grade 2, and daily in Grade 3
key_sources: Lin, T., Mullick, J., & Campbell, M. (2026). Inclusive pedagogy in practice within the multi-tiered systems of support framework: a design-based research in a Chinese EFL classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09754-3

article_title: Inclusive pedagogy in practice within the multi-tiered systems of support framework: a design-based research in a Chinese EFL classroom
citation: Lin, T., Mullick, J., & Campbell, M. (2026). Inclusive pedagogy in practice within the multi-tiered systems of support framework: a design-based research in a Chinese EFL classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09754-3
title: Teaching Proficiency through Reading and Storytelling (TPRS) method
description: TPRS, developed by Ray and Seely based on Total Physical Response, is a foreign and second language teaching approach emphasising ample clear target language input, high-frequency vocabulary, and collaborative story creation in a stress-free environment. "The method typically involves three key steps: introducing vocabulary through physical movements, collaboratively creating stories through questioning and student engagement, and reading and retelling the stories." In this study TPRS was the curricular vehicle for inclusive pedagogy within MTSS.
requirements: Pairing each vocabulary word with a corresponding physical movement so students can demonstrate comprehension kinaesthetically before being required to speak
constraints: The article notes concerns about scalability of TPRS in large, exam-driven classrooms, and that collaborative storytelling may conflict with traditional teacher-centred approaches prevalent in many Asian classrooms
target_learners: elementary EFL learners, including struggling and neurodiverse students not yet ready to speak
target_learning_goals: English listening comprehension and vocabulary
oral storytelling and communication skills
reading fluency
examples: The teacher created a recurring invisible character, Muder, that students named and voted on, which became popular in TPRS stories and student work throughout the year

citation: Lin, T., Mullick, J., & Campbell, M. (2026). Inclusive pedagogy in practice within the multi-tiered systems of support framework: a design-based research in a Chinese EFL classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09754-3
title: Design principles for inclusive pedagogy within MTSS derived from DBR iterations
description: From three iterations of planning, action, development, and reflection, the study distilled principles that "were emerged as actionable guidelines to implement inclusive pedagogy in similar contexts". The first printed principle is "Differentiation and flexibility: Instruction was tailored to meet the diverse needs of students, including those with neurodiverse conditions", operationalised through tiered tasks, random lottery participation with discreetly tailored questions, and individualised assessment alongside unified exams.
requirements: Iterative DBR cycles of planning, action, development, and reflection, refined against student performance data, teacher observations, and parent feedback
constraints: The design principles section is presented for similar contexts; the study itself was a single class in one rural boarding school

target_learning_goals: equitable access to English language learning
engagement and belonging for all performance levels
examples: Higher-performing students received more challenging tasks while lower-performing students received simpler ones, and a lottery bucket gave all students equal participation chances

article_title: Learning Theory as Teaching Resource: Enhancing Students’ Understanding of Economic Concepts
citation: Ming-fai Pang, Ference Marton. (2005). Learning Theory as Teaching Resource: Enhancing Students' Understanding of Economic Concepts. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-2811-0
title: Variation theory: for any specific object of learning there is a necessary pattern of variation and invariance learners must experience
description: The article uses a novel learning theory, grounded in phenomenography, as a resource for planning and carrying out teaching. Its central theoretical claim is that "for any specific object of learning there is a necessary pattern of variation and invariance that the learners must experience in order to appropriate the object of learning in question." By bringing out that pattern in the learning situation, the likelihood of the object of learning being appropriated is enhanced. The theory thus links what varies and what stays invariant in a lesson to what learners can discern and appropriate.
requirements: Teaching must be planned so that the necessary pattern of variation and invariance for the specific object of learning is brought out in the learning situation.
constraints: The pattern is specific to the object of learning in question; the article presents the claim as theoretical, supported by one design experiment.
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: understanding of difficult economic concepts, such as how simultaneous changes in supply and demand affect market price
examples: Experienced secondary teachers used the theory to plan and carry out three lessons on how simultaneous changes in supply and demand affect a good's market price.
key_sources: Ming-fai Pang, Ference Marton. (2005). Learning Theory as Teaching Resource: Enhancing Students' Understanding of Economic Concepts. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-2811-0

title: Three-lesson sequence on how simultaneous changes in supply and demand affect market price
description: The instructional element is a series of three lessons through which students were to come to understand "how the simultaneous change in the supply of and the demand for a certain good affects its market price." It was taught by theory-guided teachers and by comparison teachers, with mastery assessed after the series.

constraints: Demonstrated for one economic concept with secondary school students in the reported study.

target_learning_goals: understanding how simultaneous changes in supply and demand affect market price
examples: Students' mastery of the concept was compared after three lessons between theory-guided teaching and teaching without the theory.

article_title: Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld
citation: Lajoie, S. P., Lavigne, N. C., Guerrera, C., & Munsie, S. D. (2001). Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld. Instructional Science, 29(2), 155-186. http://www.jstor.org/stable/41953546
title: BioWorld computer learning environment for high school biology
description: BioWorld is a computer learning environment for high school biology students that complements the curriculum with a hospital simulation where students diagnose diseases. It embeds five features: "patient scenario, on-line library, patient chart, evidence palette, and argumentation palette", which "provide users with different learning opportunities". Students hypothesize, collect evidence to confirm or disconfirm diagnoses, adjust a belief meter, and compare their final argument to an expert argument.
requirements: A set of patient scenario problems aligned with the biology curriculum, developed with the classroom teacher
Expert benchmarks of competent performance, established by physicians and teachers, against which student actions are compared
constraints: The intent is not to make physicians out of students, but to provide opportunities to reason scientifically about data in a simulated setting
target_learners: high school biology students (grade 9)
target_learning_goals: scientific reasoning and argumentation about diseases
declarative knowledge of diseases and diagnostic procedural skill
examples: Four digestion patient scenarios (ciliacs, shigellosis, hepatitis A, cirrhosis) were solved by 20 grade-9 groups over a three-day period, each problem taking 20-45 minutes
key_sources: Lajoie, S. P., Lavigne, N. C., Guerrera, C., & Munsie, S. D. (2001). Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld. Instructional Science, 29(2), 155-186. http://www.jstor.org/stable/41953546

article_title: Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld
citation: Lajoie, S. P., Lavigne, N. C., Guerrera, C., & Munsie, S. D. (2001). Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld. Instructional Science, 29(2), 155-186. http://www.jstor.org/stable/41953546
title: Belief meter and evidence palette as memory and metacognitive scaffolds
description: The article accounts for BioWorld's support of scientific reasoning through tools that scaffold memory and metacognition. The evidence palette dynamically displays actions such as evidence selection, library searches and tests, and "Making actions and results visible in the evidence palette facilitates reasoning by supporting memory". The belief meter and evidence palette "support metacognition by providing reflection tools for learners that encourage them to assess their overall problem solving process rather than focus on a single action", externalizing and evaluating reasoning against expert arguments.
requirements: Actions and results must be made visible dynamically so learners can inspect prior plans and check how systematically they reviewed evidence
constraints: Metacognitive scaffolding in BioWorld targets the externalization and evaluation of reasoning during diagnosis, not other metacognitive activities
target_learners: high school biology students (grade 9)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness and self-evaluation during scientific problem solving
argumentation and evidence evaluation
examples: Students sort and categorize evidence, compare it to an expert argument, and receive a sequenced list of relevant information plus a narrated recap of how a physician solved the problem

article_title: Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld
citation: Lajoie, S. P., Lavigne, N. C., Guerrera, C., & Munsie, S. D. (2001). Constructing knowledge in the context of BioWorld. Instructional Science, 29(2), 155-186. http://www.jstor.org/stable/41953546
title: Allow students working alone in inquiry environments to pursue their own hypotheses, including unlikely ones
description: In the BioWorld-alone condition students generated their own hypotheses and "would pursue differential hypotheses in that they collected information on more than one hypothesis at a time", whereas coached students were sometimes thwarted from following hypotheses perceived as unlikely. The authors caution that coaches' redirections prevent wrong paths "However, there may be times that such explorations allow students to build their own conceptual understandings of the problem case". Coaches should therefore weigh closing the problem space against preserving exploratory learning.
requirements: An environment rich enough (e.g., an on-line library) that students working without a coach can find information and clarify misconceptions themselves
constraints: In the alone condition students initially spent time on insignificant details and did not use the on-line consult button; the trade-off with efficiency is stated, not resolved
target_learners: high school biology students working collaboratively
target_learning_goals: hypothesis generation and scientific inquiry
conceptual understanding built through own exploration
examples: A teacher deflected a student's cirrhosis hypothesis by noting the patient had no drinking problem, and the graduate student similarly ruled out cirrhosis for a baby, cutting off that exploration

article_title: Supporting Communication in a Collaborative Discovery Learning Environment: the Effect of Instruction
citation: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W. R. & van Hout-Wolters, B. H. A. M. (2007). Supporting Communication in a Collaborative Discovery Learning Environment: the Effect of Instruction. Instructional Science 35:73–98. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9003-4
title: RIDE rules: four principles for effective collaborative communication
description: The RIDE framework groups literature-derived characteristics of effective collaboration under four principles: Respect, Intelligent collaboration, Deciding together, and Encouraging. The article states that "The rules we extracted were grouped under four principles" and each rule carries sub-rules, such as 'everyone will have a chance to talk' for Respect and 'ask until you understand' for Encouraging. Each rule is mapped onto expected communicative activities, e.g. Intelligent collaboration onto informative responses, asking for understanding, and argumentative activities.
requirements: Instruction must be given before interaction and reminded during it, e.g. via prompts when assignments are opened
constraints: The Respect rule is represented by components not expressed in frequency of activities, so it was not analyzed via activity frequencies
target_learners: secondary school students aged 15–17 in pre-university physics education
target_learning_goals: effective collaborative communication during discovery learning in physics
examples: In the study, the rules were taught via a recorded computerized presentation with audio and visual explanation, example chats judged good or bad, and practice in a SimQuest application with prompts
key_sources: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W. R. & van Hout-Wolters, B. H. A. M. (2007). Supporting Communication in a Collaborative Discovery Learning Environment: the Effect of Instruction. Instructional Science 35:73–98. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9003-4

article_title: Supporting Communication in a Collaborative Discovery Learning Environment: the Effect of Instruction
citation: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W. R. & van Hout-Wolters, B. H. A. M. (2007). Supporting Communication in a Collaborative Discovery Learning Environment: the Effect of Instruction. Instructional Science 35:73–98. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9003-4
title: RIDE instructional program with prompts in a shared simulation discovery environment
description: A computerized instructional program that teaches the RIDE collaboration rules before learners work in a shared discovery learning environment, plus pop-up prompts reminding learners of the rules during tasks. The program "consisted of a recorded computerized presentation, where the rules were explained by both audio and visual means", followed by practice with example chats and a SimQuest logical-reasoning application, and an evaluation form. In the experimental version of Collisions, a prompt pops up whenever an assignment is opened, reminding learners of one of the RIDE rules; the control group received no pop-ups. Evaluation forms showed 83% of learners mentioned they applied the rules with ease.
requirements: Learners work in dyads on separate computers with a shared interface, communicating through a chat channel, in a simulation-based discovery learning environment
constraints: Reading prompts takes time, which the authors note can result in finishing fewer assignments in a fixed amount of time
target_learners: tenth-grade pre-university physics students aged 15–17
target_learning_goals: effective communication and collaboration during collaborative discovery learning in physics
examples: Learners practiced the rules in a SimQuest application with RIDE-rule assignments and logical reasoning problems, then filled in an evaluation form together on screen

article_title: Localizing, describing, interpreting: effects of different audio text structures on attributing meaning to digital pictures
citation: Manuela Glaser, Manuel Knoos, Stephan Schwan. (2022). Localizing, describing, interpreting: effects of different audio text structures on attributing meaning to digital pictures. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09593-6
title: Design audio explanations of complex pictures with an integrated LDI structure, presenting each element's localization, description, and interpretation in immediate succession
description: The article recommends that audio explanations of pictures localize, describe, and interpret each picture element in immediate succession rather than separating all descriptions from all interpretations. Integrated structures establish local coherence and keep visual attention on the relevant element during interpretation, enabling dual coding. The authors state that "audio explanations with LDI integrated structure as often used for audio guides (Popp, 2013) seem to be more appropriate than LDI separated structures" for educational videos, website audio texts, and museum audio guides.
requirements: Audio explanations must include localization information that directs viewers' attention to the respective picture elements before describing and interpreting them.
constraints: Evidence comes from a laboratory study with a rather homogeneous group of 55 participants; the authors call for replication in the field, e.g. with educational videos on YouTube or museum websites.
Participants with high prior knowledge (art, art history, history) were excluded, so effects for knowledgeable learners are untested.
target_learners: adult learners without domain-specific prior knowledge in art or history
viewers of educational videos, museum audio guides, and website audio explanations
target_learning_goals: attributing meaning to picture details
linking verbal interpretations to visual picture elements
picture comprehension
examples: Participants viewed history paintings with audio explanations in which each picture detail's description was immediately followed by its interpretation (LDI integrated) or with descriptions and interpretations in separate blocks (LDI separated).

article_title: Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science
citation: Rikke Magnussen, Yotam Hod. (2023). Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09641-9
title: Bridges model: professional, citizen, and student bridges connecting schools with communities outside school, linked by a learning circle
description: The article proposes a preliminary conceptual model of how community and citizen science projects connect schools with communities outside school. It defines three bridges: "The citizen bridge connects citizen communities and schools; the professional bridge connects professional communities and schools; and the student bridge connects new types of student communities and schools." A learning circle links the bridges through citizenship learning, community learning, and profession learning, with the educational design focus shifting by proximity to each bridge. The model frames the design and analysis of the two urban development projects.
requirements: CCS projects must attend to all three bridges to support the rich, cross-cutting goals they are purported to achieve
constraints: The model is preliminary and "requires further empirical work to both explicate and validate it"
target_learners: K–12 students, specifically students aged 11–15 in vulnerable residential areas
target_learning_goals: Connecting school learning to professional, citizen, and student community practices, values, and knowledge
examples: The two DBR iterations, Cities at Play and Community Drive, were designed and analyzed through the bridges model, with the second iteration strengthening the professional bridge
key_sources: Rikke Magnussen, Yotam Hod. (2023). Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09641-9

article_title: Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science
citation: Rikke Magnussen, Yotam Hod. (2023). Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09641-9
title: Five-phase design-thinking process bridging students as residents and as students in CCS urban development projects
description: The educational design used a design-thinking process comprising five phases: "discovery, definition, ideation, experimentation and model construction, and testing and presentation." In discovery, professionals present the problem and students learn the urban-developer perspective through the What Is a Place? module, interview residents, and photograph good, bad, and developable places. Definition develops problem scoping and empathy with local community members; ideation generates many ideas; model construction uses LEGO, miniature and outdoor models, and digital tools such as Minecraft; and presentation elicits feedback from urban developers and architects. The process ran over two weeks per class.
requirements: Local urban developers who set authentic challenges connected to students' local environments and participate in feedback
Teachers and researchers introducing the needs of both students and other citizen groups during discovery and evaluation
constraints: Interventions lasted one to two weeks per class; in the second iteration some classes were reduced to one week due to COVID-19 lockdown
target_learners: Students aged 11–15 in grades 5–9 in vulnerable residential areas of Copenhagen
target_learning_goals: Strengthening design-thinking skills and the ability to take part in solving complex, authentic problems derived from local expertise
examples: Students built models out of LEGO, made miniature models indoors, built large models outside, and made digital models in Minecraft before presenting to a panel of urban developers and architects
key_sources: Rikke Magnussen, Yotam Hod. (2023). Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09641-9

article_title: Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science
citation: Rikke Magnussen, Yotam Hod. (2023). Bridging communities and schools in Urban development: community and citizen science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09641-9
title: What Is a Place? introductory module teaching the urban-developer perspective on city spaces
description: The What Is a Place? module was an introductory module developed by an urban development researcher at Aalborg University and a Danish learning platform developer to bridge skills between students and the professional urban development community. "The module comprised an introduction by the teacher or urban planning researcher and a five-minute video of Tivoli," a familiar Copenhagen amusement park. Students analyzed urban spaces using three questions about what can be measured and sensed, felt and valued, and explained, with an urban development researcher participating as a co-teacher leading the discussion.
requirements: An urban development researcher participating as a co-teacher throughout the module and leading the discussion
A familiar local place, such as the Tivoli video, that students can analyze with the three professional perspectives
constraints: Designed to introduce the skilled perspective of urban developers on city space, not to substitute for the full design-thinking process
target_learners: Students aged 11–15 in grades 5–9 in Copenhagen vulnerable-area schools
target_learning_goals: Applying the perspectives of urban developers in analyzing urban spaces, including senses, feelings, and the purpose or identity of a place
examples: In a fifth-grade class, students analyzing the Tivoli video described smells of popcorn, sounds of crowds, and mixed feelings of being annoyed and happy among many people

article_title: Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning?
citation: Kirschner, P. A. (2015). Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning? Instructional Science, 43, 309–322. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9346-9
title: Five-competency professional cycle applied to teaching
description: Kirschner applies van Merriënboer and Kirschner's account of professional competence to teaching: a competency is a "combination of complex cognitive and higher-order skills, highly integrated knowledge structures, interpersonal and social skills, and attitudes and values". Professionals work through five competencies, often cyclically: gathering background/situational information, analyzing it and diagnosing, determining what steps to take, carrying out the actions, and evaluating whether results matched expectations, re-entering the cycle if not. He argues the expert teacher-designer follows the same cycle as doctors or chefs, and that the underlying competencies persist over decades while the enabling knowledge, skills, attitudes and tools change.
requirements: Teachers must be able to apply the competencies across varied situations and over an unlimited time span, as transfer and lifelong learning
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual argument, not a tested result
target_learners: teachers and teachers-in-training
target_learning_goals: professional design competence for learning experiences, including technology enhanced learning
examples: The article likens the teacher's cycle to a doctor taking a history, diagnosing, determining therapy, carrying it out and evaluating results, and to an expert chef using a broad palette of tools, techniques and ingredients
key_sources: Kirschner, P. A. (2015). Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning? Instructional Science, 43, 309–322. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9346-9

article_title: Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning?
citation: Kirschner, P. A. (2015). Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning? Instructional Science, 43, 309–322. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9346-9
title: Ecology of education: learning as a systemic interaction of learners, teachers and tools
description: The article frames education as an ecology in which effective, efficient and enjoyable learning is determined by exchanges between learners, teachers and their tools within and in interaction with the environment. Learners bring prior knowledge, skills, attitudes, dispositions and self-regulation; teacher quality strongly shapes education and educational innovation; and digital tools, virtual environments and physical spaces must integrate seamlessly, in the sense of ubiquitous computing. As a system, education is a complex whole of interconnected elements; as systemic, any change in one part affects all the rest, and the system is bounded yet influenced by its environment (policy, inspectorates, unions, economy).
requirements: Research into teachers as designers of TEL must accommodate the systems and systemic nature of the ecology of education
constraints: The article warns that too much emphasis on TEL and its technology can come at the detriment of learning in general, citing CSCL research that emphasized the computer first
target_learners: teachers
educational researchers
teacher educators
target_learning_goals: designing effective, efficient and enjoyable learning within the whole educational system
examples: The article cites CSCL research that emphasized computer support first and collaboration later, often to the detriment of learning, and the 'new learning' movement that became a goal unto itself
key_sources: Kirschner, P. A. (2015). Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning? Instructional Science, 43, 309–322. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9346-9

article_title: Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning?
citation: Kirschner, P. A. (2015). Do we need teachers as designers of technology enhanced learning? Instructional Science, 43, 309–322. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9346-9
title: Prepare teachers in three fields to become competent designers of learning
description: The article concludes that teachers need to become accomplished in three fields: the domain they teach (knowing, understanding and applying subject matter at the conceptual level), the art and science of learning and teaching (the pedagogies for achieving their goals), and the science of research and design. Only then, the author argues, will teachers be competent designers of learning, including TEL. This requires drastic rethinking of initial pre-service and continuing in-service education, with teachers functioning as professional learners and co-researchers and co-designers of the technology and tools they want and need to use.
requirements: Initial and continuing teacher training must equip teachers to learn and work as co-researchers and co-designers, with expertise developed on the shop-floor
constraints: The author frames this as requiring a drastic rethinking of both pre-service and in-service education
target_learners: preservice teachers
in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: competent design of learning, including technology enhanced learning
examples: Figure 2 visualizes the amended mapping, placing TaD of TEL motives and supports as discrete layers superimposed on the professional competencies, with customization based on student work, professional growth via collaborative design at course or lesson level, and ownership via participatory design of researchers, teachers and students

article_title: Show me your opinion. Perceptual cues in creating and reading argument diagrams
citation: Marije van Amelsvoort, Alfons Maes. (2016). Show me your opinion. Perceptual cues in creating and reading argument diagrams. Instructional Science 44:335–357. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9378-9
title: Natural cognitive resources framework: primary metaphors, Gestalt principles and cultural conventions as sources of perceptual cues in argument diagrams
description: The article frames the production and interpretation of argument-diagram perceptual cues as drawing on three "'natural' and partially overlapping cognitive resources": embodied experiences yielding metaphoric conceptualizations (primary metaphors), general visual preferences (Gestalt theory), and cultural conventions such as reading direction and color symbolism. Perceptual cues are categorized as spatial, graphical and textual elements following design guidelines on visual variables. The framework organized the coding of both studies and, in the authors' view, "enables us to shed light on what lay-people do when asked to spontaneously create a for or against argument diagram."
requirements: Learners must be untrained in formal argument-diagram conventions for the natural-resource predictions to apply; trained conventions will change visualization preferences and practices, as the article states
constraints: The framework was studied for for-against argument diagrams with simple predefined argumentative information, not complex layered argument structures or collaborative construction of a debate space
target_learners: untrained lay-people and students creating or reading argument diagrams
target_learning_goals: expressing and interpreting argumentative position in argument diagrams
structuring argumentation visually for communication and decision-making
examples: Twenty students drew for-against diagrams on a whiteboard from argument cards; their use of space, boxes, lines, arrows, color and text was coded against the framework's expectations
key_sources: Marije van Amelsvoort, Alfons Maes. (2016). Show me your opinion. Perceptual cues in creating and reading argument diagrams. Instructional Science 44:335–357. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9378-9

article_title: Productive dissent in learning communities
citation: Trninic, D., Swanson, H., & Kapur, M. (2018). Productive dissent in learning communities. Instructional Science, 46(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9466-0
title: Collins's distinction between learning communities and conserving communities
description: The article adopts Collins's (1998) distinction in which a "questioning habit of mind" demarcates two community types: learning communities, such as the science community, "aim to expand the collective knowledge of the group," while conserving communities, such as the medieval church, "aim to perpetuate and protect an established system of beliefs." The article uses this axis to argue schools should shift toward learning communities and to recharacterize seemingly dissenting groups like the alt-right as conserving communities.
requirements: A questioning habit of mind as the criterion distinguishing learning from conserving communities
constraints: The article notes, as Collins does, that conserving communities still involve a great deal of learning
target_learners: school communities
classroom learners
target_learning_goals: critical thinking as a communal habit
learning how to learn
examples: The article recasts alt-right groups as conserving communities despite their outward facade of dissent
key_sources: Trninic, D., Swanson, H., & Kapur, M. (2018). Productive dissent in learning communities. Instructional Science, 46(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9466-0

article_title: Productive dissent in learning communities
citation: Trninic, D., Swanson, H., & Kapur, M. (2018). Productive dissent in learning communities. Instructional Science, 46(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9466-0
title: Melser's account: learning is subordinate to communal belonging
description: The article highlights Melser's (2004) extension of Vygotskian scholarship, in which "the human drive to learn or to teach is better understood as a drive to act in concert with others." A child sees community members engaged in shared activity and desires to join, and in that way learning happens; thus "learning is subsumed by and subordinate to communal belonging." This predicts that even logic-like domains are subject to social approval, so individual traits like critical thinking are best developed by joining communities that value them.
requirements: Participation in a community whose valued activities make learning salient and inviting
constraints: The account predicts community values can trump individual isolated observations, so what a community does not value may not even be seen
target_learners: children joining communal activities
learners developing apparently individual traits
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
self-control
communal participation
examples: The article cites Doebel and Munakata's demonstration that self-control, typically viewed as a fixed individual trait, can be influenced through group dynamics
key_sources: Trninic, D., Swanson, H., & Kapur, M. (2018). Productive dissent in learning communities. Instructional Science, 46(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9466-0

article_title: Productive dissent in learning communities
citation: Trninic, D., Swanson, H., & Kapur, M. (2018). Productive dissent in learning communities. Instructional Science, 46(4). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9466-0
title: Revisit the beyond-the-bounds principle: learners should seek ideas that challenge their beliefs
description: The article revisits Bielaczyc and Collins's beyond-the-bounds principle, which encourages individuals to question and actively challenge the results of communal negotiation. It emphasizes that learners "should seek ideas that challenge what they believe, by soliciting diverse opinions and views on a topic" and "should not just try to find support for their current beliefs." The principle frames dissent as a guard against jumping on the bandwagon of really bad ideas.
requirements: A community whose negotiation products can be questioned and challenged in search of something better
constraints: The article acknowledges no community stands entirely free of intolerance and authoritarianism; dogmatism may need continuous vigilance rather than elimination
target_learners: members of classroom learning communities
the general public
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
a skeptical habit of mind
examples: The article points to the scientific community, which uses argumentation to reach consensus but also frequently challenges that consensus, as when one paradigm overturns another
