article_title: Facilitating small-group learning: A comparison of student and staff tutors' behavior
citation: Moust, J. C. & Schmidt, H. G. (1995). Facilitating small-group learning: a comparison of student and staff tutors' behavior. Instructional Science 22: 287-301. https://link.springer.com/journal/11251
title: Six-component framework of tutor behavior: subject-matter input versus process facilitation
description: The article organizes tutor behavior into two main components, each with three elements: the subject-matter-input component comprises use of expertise, cognitive congruence and assessment orientation, while the process-facilitation component comprises authority, role congruence and focus on cooperation. The framework was operationalized as a 39-item rating scale whose subscales were validated by generalizability study and confirmatory factor analysis. The authors state that "two main components of the tutor role were distinguished: the way a tutor handles the knowledge students must acquire, and the way a tutor establishes a personal relationship with the members of the group". It underpins the study's hypotheses about how student and staff tutors differ.
requirements: Ratings require judgements from about 11 students per tutorial group for satisfactory generalizability coefficients
constraints: Confirmatory factor analysis indicated the six-subscale model did not entirely fit the data; the six components were retained for theoretical reasons despite mixed empirical support
target_learners: first-year university law students in problem-based tutorial groups
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning of subject-matter through small-group problem discussion
examples: The six subscales were used to compare student and staff tutors in two first-year law courses, with items such as 'The tutor was able to understand problems we had with the materials' for cognitive congruence.
key_sources: Moust, J. C. & Schmidt, H. G. (1995). Facilitating small-group learning: a comparison of student and staff tutors' behavior. Instructional Science 22: 287-301. https://link.springer.com/journal/11251

article_title: Integrating dispositions in instructional design: an exploratory study in higher education
citation: Jafar Tavakoli, Marisa Exter, Ankita Kotangale. (2025). Integrating dispositions in instructional design: an exploratory study in higher education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09762-3
title: Fink's Integrated Course Design framework for aligning learning goals, teaching activities, and feedback and assessment
description: The study's organizing framework is Fink's (2013) Integrated Course Design, which "revolves around three primary components: Learning Goals, Teaching and Learning Activities, and Feedback and Assessment". The framework emphasizes creating significant learning experiences beyond simple content delivery, and holds that these three elements must be integrated and support each other; Fink warns that a course lacking this connection is a "broken course" that cannot work effectively because it is not integrated. The authors use it to structure their analysis of how dispositions are integrated across course design components.
requirements: The three components must be integrated and aligned with each other and with the desired outcomes for the course to work effectively
constraints: The article applies the framework to higher education course design and to dispositions as learning goals
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: dispositions such as attitudes, beliefs, and values alongside knowledge and skills
examples: The study analyzed instructional designers' integration of dispositions through the framework's components of learning goals, teaching and learning activities, and feedback and assessment

article_title: Fostering knowledge integration through individual competencies: the impacts of perspective taking, reflexivity, analogical reasoning and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty
citation: Olga Vogel, Marcel Hunecke. (2024). Fostering knowledge integration through individual competencies: the impacts of perspective taking, reflexivity, analogical reasoning and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09653-5
title: Knowledge integration as a super-ordinate competency of inter- and transdisciplinary work built on four individual competencies
description: The article defines knowledge integration as "the cognitive ability to combine different disciplinary insights into a common knowledge base to achieve a more comprehensive understanding of a complex ITD problem". It treats knowledge integration as a super-ordinate competency building on specific competencies, drawing on Repko and Szostak's four-step process (identifying conflicts, creating common ground, constructing and testing a more comprehensive understanding). The study empirically links four individual competencies to this construct.
requirements: Individuals must engage with multiple disciplinary perspectives whose divergent insights create the unrelated knowledge structures to be merged
constraints: The construct is measured here by self-report; the article states the postulated competencies could not be assumed to causally impact knowledge integration
target_learners: students
scientists
economic-sector professionals working in inter- and transdisciplinary contexts
target_learning_goals: integrating knowledge from multiple disciplines and fields of practice into a common knowledge base
examples: The study operationalized the construct with the German version of Claus and Wiese's three-item knowledge integration scale, α = .830

citation: Olga Vogel, Marcel Hunecke. (2024). Fostering knowledge integration through individual competencies: the impacts of perspective taking, reflexivity, analogical reasoning and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09653-5
title: Competencies of Knowledge Integration questionnaire: four newly developed self-report scales
description: A newly developed questionnaire measuring intraindividual competencies for knowledge integration, built from theoretical definitions in the ITD context with 52 initial Likert-scale items. After item reduction and residual correlations, "The resulting model contained a total of 23 items and provided an acceptable model fit (χ 2(217) = 372.408, p < 0.001, CFI = 0.913, TLI = 0.900, RMSEA = 0.045, SRMR = 0.055)". Reflexivity retained six items, perspective taking five, analogical reasoning eight, and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty seven.
requirements: Items with factor loadings λ < 0.300 and discriminative power r it < 0.300 were stepwise excluded during scale development
constraints: Perspective taking and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty had internal consistencies of α > .600, considered low but acceptable, and AVE was below .50; the authors state low reliability could have caused low beta weights and non-significant effects in the scientific sample

scientists
economic-sector professionals

article_title: When is observing failure productive? Investigating the role of solution diversity in vicarious failure
citation: Thomas C. Braas, Christian Hartmann, Vincent Hoogerheide, Nikol Rummel, Tamara van Gog. (2025). When is observing failure productive? Investigating the role of solution diversity in vicarious failure. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09706-x
title: Solution diversity defined as the number of canonical solution components present in solution attempts
description: The article proposes measuring solution diversity by counting how many of the four canonical components of the target solution (using all numbers, absolute deviations, mean as fixed reference point, division by total data points) appear in solution attempts, rather than by quantity or quality of solutions. The authors argue "utilizing the number of canonical components as measure of diversity seems more sensible", because quantity can be high with no canonical component present and quality can repeat the same components. This definition also permits experimental control in VF modeling examples.
requirements: Requires specifying the canonical solution and decomposing it into its constituent components before designing or coding solution attempts.
constraints: The article notes prior correlational evidence on RSM-diversity and conceptual knowledge has been mixed and exclusively correlational; this study's own range-based measure did not correlate with outcomes.
target_learners: secondary education mathematics students
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of statistical variability (mean absolute deviation)
examples: VF-high videos presented solutions covering all four canonical components, while VF-low videos presented only two, with total solution quality held equal across conditions.

article_title: Classifying Examples is More Effective for Learning Relational Categories Than Reading or Generating Examples
citation: Tim M. Steininger, Jörg Wittwer, Thamar Voss. (2022). Classifying Examples is More Effective for Learning Relational Categories Than Reading or Generating Examples. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09584-7
title: Use classification tasks rather than example generation in early phases of relational-category learning
description: The article recommends that when teaching concepts, learners should not generate their own examples in early phases of concept acquisition; instead, instruction should make heavier use of classification tasks in which learners reflect on which example belongs to which relational category. This rests on the finding that classifying was more effective and that generation produced overconfidence. Self-regulated learners are likewise advised to refrain from generating examples too early.
requirements: Learners must be provided with examples to classify and with the labels of the relational categories
constraints: Recommended for early phases of concept acquisition; after initial understanding, generation might be more helpful for applying concepts to real-world contexts, which the article did not test
target_learners: student teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of relational categories such as types of knowledge in lesson planning
examples: In the experiment, the classifying group selected one of four knowledge types for each provided learning objective and received feedback, while the generating group wrote their own example learning objectives
key_sources: Tim M. Steininger, Jörg Wittwer, Thamar Voss. (2022). Classifying Examples is More Effective for Learning Relational Categories Than Reading or Generating Examples. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09584-7

article_title: Classifying Examples is More Effective for Learning Relational Categories Than Reading or Generating Examples
citation: Tim M. Steininger, Jörg Wittwer, Thamar Voss. (2022). Classifying Examples is More Effective for Learning Relational Categories Than Reading or Generating Examples. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09584-7
title: Adapt the number of examples to the complexity of the relational category to be learned
description: Because learning outcomes depended on the complexity of the knowledge type, the article concludes there is no one-size-fits-all approach to learning relational categories and recommends adapting instruction to category complexity. One way it suggests is to increase the number of examples illustrating complex relational categories, for instance presenting more than two examples of knowledge about principles while two examples of facts might suffice.
requirements: Instruction must distinguish relational categories by complexity of their condition-response relationship
constraints: The article did not test varying numbers of examples; it notes two examples per knowledge type did not result in perfect classification and calls for research on the optimal number
target_learners: student teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: acquisition of relational categories of varying complexity, such as facts, concepts, principles, and procedures
examples: The article suggests that while two examples of knowledge about facts might be sufficient, more than two examples of knowledge about principles might be necessary to guarantee understanding
key_sources: Tim M. Steininger, Jörg Wittwer, Thamar Voss. (2022). Classifying Examples is More Effective for Learning Relational Categories Than Reading or Generating Examples. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09584-7

article_title: Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought
citation: de Jong, T. (2010). Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9110-0
title: Cognitive load theory: limited working memory and three types of load contribution
description: Cognitive load theory asserts that learning is hampered when working memory capacity is exceeded, and distinguishes three contributions to total load. As the article states, "Cognitive load theory distinguishes three different types of contributions to total cognitive load": intrinsic load from the content's inherent characteristics, extraneous load from the instructional material, and germane load from learning processes. The theory has had great impact on educational researchers and designers.
requirements: Working memory capacity is limited, so instructional systems must optimize its use and avoid cognitive overload
constraints: The article argues the three-type distinction itself is conceptually and empirically problematic
target_learners: learners in educational research settings generally
target_learning_goals: schema construction and automation as the main goal of learning
key_sources: de Jong, T. (2010). Cognitive load theory, educational research, and instructional design: some food for thought. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9110-0

article_title: Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant?
citation: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8
title: Sublation (Aufhebung) as a framework for integrating guidance and discovery in the discovery learning debate
description: The article proposes Hegel's concept of sublation (Aufhebung) as a way to end the one-dimensional tug of war between minimal guidance and direct instruction. Aufheben has three senses: to lift up to a higher level, to preserve elements of both sides of a tension in a new integration, and to abolish the tension. The author argues the debate should integrate "justified concerns from both opposite positions" rather than pick a winner.
requirements: The debate must move beyond dichotomized comparisons of discovery versus instruction extremes for sublation to operate.
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual proposal for the field, not an empirically tested intervention.
target_learners: All learners in instructional settings where discovery and guidance are balanced
target_learning_goals: Understanding what cannot be told but must be discovered or reinvented
examples: The author reads Trninic's martial arts case study as dissolving the dichotomies, since repetition and continued guidance coexist with student discovery.
key_sources: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8

article_title: Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant?
citation: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8
title: Inferentialism: concepts as norms governing use, with understanding as practical mastery of inferences
description: The article describes inferentialism (Brandom) as "a holistic, pragmatist, expressivist, and rationalist theory of meaning" in which a concept is not a representation of a class of referents but "the norm governing the use of the concept." Understanding a concept means having practical mastery over the inferences it is involved in, so understanding is always a matter of degree and concepts come in packages. The author applies this to argue that direct instruction cannot fully explain concepts, and that students discovering their own knowledge is equally untenable because the teacher represents disciplinary norms.
requirements: Understanding this theory takes some investment, and studying teacher-student interaction as a game of giving and asking for reasons with scorekeeping.
constraints: The article notes the inferences that can be made with concepts are boundless, so no explanation can be complete.
target_learners: Students learning disciplinary concepts such as standard deviation in statistics education
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding as practical mastery of inferential relations between concepts
examples: The author's own hours-long struggle to construct a distribution with a given mean, SD, and minimum illustrates exploring the inferential terrain of the standard deviation concept with a tool and a colleague.
key_sources: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8

article_title: Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant?
citation: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8
title: Scaffolding as a dialectic teacher-student system rather than one-directional support
description: The article argues that a source of problems in the discovery learning debate is conceptualizing teachers and students as separate systems with a one-way causal relationship. Drawing on Wood et al.'s characterization of scaffolding as "an interactive system of exchange" and Roth and Lee's subject|object ensemble, it holds that students are both subjects and objects of the pedagogical process, and teachers may be guided by their students. Within this systems view, guidance and discovery form a coordinated whole, and questions become what needs to be told, discovered, or practiced.
requirements: Researchers must stick to the original sense of scaffolding with a dynamical systems lens to avoid a one-directional view of scaffolds working on students as objects.
constraints: Answering what to tell, discover, or repeat requires professional judgment there and then, not a general rule.
target_learners: School students working with teachers in zones of proximal development
target_learning_goals: Coordinated teacher-student interaction supporting discovery of what cannot simply be told
examples: The article frames the question as what lies in the region of sensitivity to instruction or the zone of proximal development, requiring in-the-moment professional judgment.
key_sources: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8

article_title: Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant?
citation: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8
title: Design discovery tasks by deliberately covering up and constraining the problem space; more autonomy demands better task design
description: The article argues that teaching for discovery always involves deciding what to cover up and what to let students discover: "there is no teaching for discovery learning without covering up." Teachers and designers put constraints on the problem space in which students carry out tasks, and it is the designer or teacher who judges which constraints will be productive for the target knowledge or skill. The paradox is that "the more autonomy we want to give students, the better we have to design the tasks."
requirements: Designers and teachers must make professional judgments about which constraints on the problem space will be productive for the target knowledge or skill.
constraints: Some things can and should be told; discovery is appropriate only for what cannot be transmitted and must be constructed or experienced.
target_learners: Students in domain-specific didactic settings such as statistics and mathematics education
target_learning_goals: Discovering or reinventing insights that cannot simply be told
examples: Levy et al. designed constraints into the TrafficJams system to limit possible actions so as to guide and focus students on particular aspects of the system.
key_sources: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8

article_title: Half a century of Instructional Science: a bibliometric analysis
citation: Betzabe Ruiz-Morales, Víctor G. Alfaro-García, José M. Merigó, Amara Atif, Eleni A. Kyza. (2026). Half a century of Instructional Science: a bibliometric analysis. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09791-6
title: VOS viewer bibliographic mapping of Instructional Science (co-citation, bibliographic coupling, keyword co-occurrence)
description: The study uses VOS viewer software (Van Eck & Waltman, 2010) to graphically map the journal's bibliographic data. It "generates maps based on bibliographic coupling, citation, co-citation, co-authorship, and the co-occurrence of author keywords", applied to the 1,262 articles and reviews retrieved from the WoS Core Collection for 1972–2023. The mapping complements the performance analysis with visual identification of topic clusters and research profiles.
requirements: A bibliographic database export (the study used the WoS Core Collection) and the VOS viewer software to compile and generate the maps
constraints: The analysis is limited to WoS data and its language coverage, and the authors note it is not easy to compare different subfields and variables since they may have different publication and citation characteristics
target_learners: Researchers and bibliometric analysts in the learning sciences
target_learning_goals: Understanding publication, citation and topic trends in a learning-sciences journal over five decades
examples: The article applies the SPAR-4-SLR protocol (Fig. 1) to assemble, arrange and assess 1,262 documents, then maps them via co-citation, bibliographic coupling and keyword co-occurrence
key_sources: Betzabe Ruiz-Morales, Víctor G. Alfaro-García, José M. Merigó, Amara Atif, Eleni A. Kyza. (2026). Half a century of Instructional Science: a bibliometric analysis. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09791-6

article_title: Fostering pre-service teachers’ theoretical knowledge application: studying with and without text-based cases
citation: Baier, F., Maurer, C., Dignath, C., & Kunter, M. (2021). Fostering pre-service teachers' theoretical knowledge application: studying with and without text-based cases. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09560-7
title: Inert knowledge and situated cognition account of the theory-practice gap in teacher education
description: The article frames pre-service teachers' failure to apply scientific theory as the inert knowledge problem: knowledge learned at university remains purely declarative and is not used in real teaching. It draws on two explanatory families: deficits in the knowledge itself, such as insufficient conceptual knowledge and knowledge compartmentalization, and situated cognition models. As the authors put it, "situated cognition models consider inert knowledge to be a consequence of missing congruence between the context in which classroom management is studied (e.g. in university lectures) and in which it has to be applied (e.g. in the school classroom)". Case-based learning is proposed as a method to establish this congruence and thereby prevent inert knowledge.
requirements: The framework presupposes that learners study scientific theories that are meant to be applied later in real teaching situations.
constraints: The article notes that inert knowledge may also arise from deficits in the knowledge itself, such as insufficient conceptual knowledge or knowledge compartmentalization, not only from missing context congruence.
target_learners: pre-service teachers in university teacher education
target_learning_goals: application of scientific theories on classroom management to authentic teaching situations
examples: The study operationalized the framework by comparing application of the same theory to real-world text-based cases versus to abstract theoretical models in an online learning environment.
key_sources: Baier, F., Maurer, C., Dignath, C., & Kunter, M. (2021). Fostering pre-service teachers' theoretical knowledge application: studying with and without text-based cases. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09560-7

article_title: Fostering pre-service teachers’ theoretical knowledge application: studying with and without text-based cases
citation: Baier, F., Maurer, C., Dignath, C., & Kunter, M. (2021). Fostering pre-service teachers' theoretical knowledge application: studying with and without text-based cases. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09560-7
title: Use text-based cases to connect scientific theory to real-world classroom situations in teacher education, but treat them as one option rather than a panacea against inert knowledge
description: The article recommends employing text-based cases in formal teacher education because they relate theoretical input to authentic classroom situations and are economical to construct, distribute and update. It found a small advantage for case-based learning on knowledge application and higher situational interest, yet stresses that "the pre-service teachers studying without cases also substantially gained in their knowledge" and that "case-based learning may not necessarily be the only panacea to avoid inert knowledge". Designers should therefore consider the several causes of inert knowledge when designing learning environments.
requirements: Cases must be complex real-world classroom situations that learners analyse by generating courses of action grounded in the studied theory.
constraints: The measured advantage over a comparable model-based intervention was small and may not be of practical relevance; the vignette measure was of reduced complexity compared to real-life classroom situations.
target_learners: pre-service teachers in initial teacher education
target_learning_goals: productive application of scientific classroom-management theory to authentic classroom situations
examples: Pre-service teachers read theoretical input on classroom management and generated possible courses of action for two real-world text-based cases per week, with sample solutions and additional theoretical input as instructional support.
key_sources: Baier, F., Maurer, C., Dignath, C., & Kunter, M. (2021). Fostering pre-service teachers' theoretical knowledge application: studying with and without text-based cases. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09560-7

article_title: Measuring cognitive load with subjective rating scales during problem solving: differences between immediate and delayed ratings
citation: Schmeck, A., Opfermann, M., van Gog, T., Paas, F., & Leutner, D. (2015). Measuring cognitive load with subjective rating scales during problem solving: differences between immediate and delayed ratings. Instructional Science, 43, 93–114. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9328-3
title: Treat immediate (per-task) and delayed (post-sequence) subjective cognitive load ratings as distinct, non-interchangeable measures
description: When using subjective rating scales to measure cognitive load, researchers should not assume that the average of ratings given after each task equals a single rating given after the whole learning phase. Across two experiments, "the delayed ratings of both effort and difﬁculty were signiﬁcantly higher than the average of the six ratings made during problem solving", while affective ratings showed no such difference. The choice of measurement point therefore changes what the rating indicates and should be reported and justified.
requirements: Researchers must decide and report whether ratings are collected after each task or once after the whole phase, since the two yield systematically different cognitive load values.
constraints: The evidence comes from short sequences of six weekday-problems with teacher education students; the article notes it remains unclear what exactly a single delayed rating indicates (average, recency, or most complex tasks).
target_learners: university students in teacher education
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of cognitive load during learning and problem solving
examples: In both experiments, students rated mental effort, perceived difficulty, interest and motivation after each of six problems and again once after the whole sequence, allowing direct comparison of the two approaches.
key_sources: Schmeck, A., Opfermann, M., van Gog, T., Paas, F., & Leutner, D. (2015). Measuring cognitive load with subjective rating scales during problem solving: differences between immediate and delayed ratings. Instructional Science, 43, 93–114. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9328-3

article_title: Preservice elementary science teachers’ argumentation competence: impact of a training programme
citation: Daniel Cebrián-Robles; Antonio-Joaquín Franco-Mariscal; Ángel Blanco-López. (2018). Preservice Elementary Science Teachers' Argumentation Competence: Impact of a Training Programme. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9446-4
title: Toulmin's simplified argument model (evidence, justification, conclusion) as the basis for training and assessing argumentation competence
description: The article operationalises argumentation competence through a simplification of Toulmin's model suggested by Jiménez-Aleixandre (2010), reduced to three essential elements that a good argument must have: evidence (facts in Toulmin's model), justification (warrant) and conclusion (claim). PESTs must first identify these three elements in an argument and use them to design rubrics to assess arguments; only once this objective is achieved may the model consider further elements such as previous or backing ideas, and rebuttals or refutations. The three-element version was used to build the study's basic and specific assessment rubrics and its 0–100 overall argumentative quality score.
requirements: A good argument requires all three elements: conclusion, justification and evidence
constraints: The simplified three-element version omits backing ideas and rebuttals/refutations, which are introduced only as a later extension
target_learners: Preservice elementary science teachers
target_learning_goals: Argumentation competence in science
Critical thinking about science
examples: The study's specific rubrics scored each argument element in achievement levels, and example pre/post answers such as E-PEST14's and E-PEST24's bottled-water responses were scored element by element
key_sources: Daniel Cebrián-Robles; Antonio-Joaquín Franco-Mariscal; Ángel Blanco-López. (2018). Preservice Elementary Science Teachers' Argumentation Competence: Impact of a Training Programme. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9446-4

article_title: Preservice elementary science teachers’ argumentation competence: impact of a training programme
citation: Daniel Cebrián-Robles; Antonio-Joaquín Franco-Mariscal; Ángel Blanco-López. (2018). Preservice Elementary Science Teachers' Argumentation Competence: Impact of a Training Programme. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9446-4
title: CoRubric e-rubric tool for online peer assessment of arguments
description: CoRubric is an e-rubric designed by one of the authors of this research and available free of charge, used in the programme's second peer assessment so PESTs could assess and justify their scores through online rubrics. The article lists its advantages: peer assessment (formative assessment), which allows for multiple evaluations to check progress, role management using notes and comments and exporting results to other programmes for treatment. It supports a 360º assessment, i.e., peer assessment, self-assessment and teacher assessment of the questions.
requirements: Supports online rubrics for peer, self and teacher assessment of the same questions
target_learners: Preservice elementary science teachers
target_learning_goals: Peer assessment of arguments
Formative self-monitoring of argumentation competence
examples: Used in Session 2 for a second peer assessment of the tooth decay answers, this time using the specific rubric, to check whether there was any more consistency in the results when using the specific rubric
key_sources: Daniel Cebrián-Robles; Antonio-Joaquín Franco-Mariscal; Ángel Blanco-López. (2018). Preservice Elementary Science Teachers' Argumentation Competence: Impact of a Training Programme. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9446-4

article_title: The learning effects of first, second, and third order interventions in a rule-based and open simulation game
citation: Marieke de Wijse-van Heeswijk, Etienne A. J. A. Rouwette, Sander V. Meijerink. (2025). The learning effects of first, second, and third order interventions in a rule-based and open simulation game. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09715-w
title: Argyris-based framework of first-, second- and third-order interventions and learning applied to simulation-game facilitation
description: The article adapts Argyris' (1970) model, distinguishing three intervention types and three learning types. First-order interventions "aim at clarifying and applying norms", often addressing content and procedures; second-order interventions adapt a norm and change processes; third-order interventions uncover roles and behavioral patterns in an organizational context. Third-order learning is defined, based on Visser et al. (2018), as increasing insight on how to add value from a personal perspective and from one's role in the host organization. The framework grounds the study's conceptual model linking intervention type, game type, cognitive load and learning.
requirements: All three learning levels are considered necessary to achieve adaptivity because of the intricate relationships between content, processes and roles
constraints: The article notes the relations in the conceptual model are not meant to be sequential; arrows indicate the number of relations present
target_learners: professionals in organizational change contexts
new employees in in-company training
target_learning_goals: adaptivity to changes in the organization or its context
examples: Facilitators' interventions and participants' responses in two simulation games were coded with a codebook based on Argyris' levels of learning
key_sources: Marieke de Wijse-van Heeswijk, Etienne A. J. A. Rouwette, Sander V. Meijerink. (2025). The learning effects of first, second, and third order interventions in a rule-based and open simulation game. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09715-w

article_title: The learning effects of first, second, and third order interventions in a rule-based and open simulation game
citation: Marieke de Wijse-van Heeswijk, Etienne A. J. A. Rouwette, Sander V. Meijerink. (2025). The learning effects of first, second, and third order interventions in a rule-based and open simulation game. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09715-w
title: Scope and distance as new design dimensions explaining learning in simulation games
description: The article introduces scope and distance as concepts new to game science, derived from Achterbergh and Vriens' work on organizations and applied to SG design. The scope dimension "concerns the number of variables in the game on which player can make decisions (the handling space)", and includes both designed and experienced scope. The distance dimension refers to the translation of the real-world challenge to the SG and how each player perceives that distance. Together they constitute the learning environment and influence experienced cognitive load; both must be balanced, since too narrow a scope restricts autonomy while too wide a scope causes alienation, and too much or too little distance respectively alienates players or creates an unsafe learning environment.
requirements: Scope and distance need to be balanced to generate the envisioned learning environment
constraints: A too narrow scope can reduce the ability to deal with gameplay challenges, while a too wide scope can cause alienation; too much distance makes translation of learning outcomes to the real world more difficult, and too small a distance can create an unsafe learning environment
target_learners: professionals in organizational change contexts
participants in analogue simulation games
target_learning_goals: adaptivity to changes in the organization or its context
meaningful connection of game experiences to learning goals
examples: Case study 1 was a rule-based SG with narrow scope and high distance; case study 2 was an open SG with wide scope and low distance
key_sources: Marieke de Wijse-van Heeswijk, Etienne A. J. A. Rouwette, Sander V. Meijerink. (2025). The learning effects of first, second, and third order interventions in a rule-based and open simulation game. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09715-w

article_title: How design guides learning from matrix diagrams
citation: Jan van der Meij, Marije van Amelsvoort, Anjo Anjewierden. (2017). How design guides learning from matrix diagrams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9425-1
title: Eye Movement Sequence (EMS) model for identifying reading sequences from fixations
description: The EMS model is an algorithm the authors developed for an earlier study to identify reading sequences from eye-tracking fixation data over look zones. It scores a sequence after each fixation, updating with the maximum of the current score and fixation duration when the next fixation is compatible, and subtracting a constant times the fixation duration when it deviates; if the score becomes negative the sequence terminates. In this study a constant C of 2.0 was used, meaning an out-of-sequence fixation could be at most half the longest in-sequence fixation, and minimally three subsequent row or column look zones had to be present to count as a sequence.
requirements: Fixation data segmented into look zones (here 24, one per header and body cell), with a minimum of three subsequent row or column look zones to count as a sequence
constraints: The constant C was experimentally validated and set to 2.0 in this study; sequences terminate when the score becomes negative
target_learners: university students studying diagrams
target_learning_goals: reading order and processing of matrix diagrams
examples: The model classified sequences such as [5, 6, 7, 8] as strict left-to-right sequences and tolerated temporary deviations like looking at a header cell to integrate information
key_sources: Jan van der Meij, Marije van Amelsvoort, Anjo Anjewierden. (2017). How design guides learning from matrix diagrams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9425-1

article_title: How design guides learning from matrix diagrams
citation: Jan van der Meij, Marije van Amelsvoort, Anjo Anjewierden. (2017). How design guides learning from matrix diagrams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9425-1
title: Tailor perceptual cues to the processing demands of the diagram rather than grafting them on arbitrarily
description: The article recommends that cues be matched to what the visualization actually needs: "Rather than arbitrarily grafting cues onto diagrams, the use of cues should be tailored to the speciﬁc processing demands the diagram poses". In matrix diagrams, arrows as organizational cues were overruled by the conventional format and content, so their use "should be considered with care". Designers should instead focus on learners' needs and the task, designing diagrams to facilitate effective encoding strategies.
requirements: Knowledge of the specific processing demands the diagram poses and of learners' needs and the task they are to perform
constraints: In matrix diagrams, arrows as organizational cues appear futile or even detrimental, since the matrix itself already organizes relations between two variables
target_learners: designers of learning materials with diagrams
target_learning_goals: effective encoding of diagram content
examples: The experiment showed arrows did not guide initial reading behavior and had no effect on recall in four versions of a matrix diagram on personality disorders
key_sources: Jan van der Meij, Marije van Amelsvoort, Anjo Anjewierden. (2017). How design guides learning from matrix diagrams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9425-1

article_title: The Relationship Between Tutoring Mode and Learners’ use of Help Tools in Distance Education
citation: Bruno De Lièvre, Christian Depover & Pierre Dillenbourg. (2006). The relationship between tutoring mode and learners' use of help tools in distance education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-6076-4
title: Treat help tools as a set of distinct functions rather than a single concept with a single effect
description: The article's results diverge across the four help tool categories: proactivity raised metacognitive and lexical help use, left conceptual help unchanged, and HT presence reduced navigational help use. The authors conclude that "Help should therefore not be considered as a single concept having a single eﬀect, but rather as a set of distinct functions." Designers should therefore evaluate and support each help function separately.
requirements: Help tools must be categorised by function (lexical, conceptual, metacognitive, navigational) and evaluated separately
constraints: Effects of a given tutoring mode differ by help type; a mode that stimulates one function may not stimulate another
target_learners: distance education learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: effective use of integrated help resources during independent learning
examples: In the experiment, proactive tutoring stimulated metacognitive and lexical help use but not conceptual or navigational help use
key_sources: Bruno De Lièvre, Christian Depover & Pierre Dillenbourg. (2006). The relationship between tutoring mode and learners' use of help tools in distance education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-6076-4

article_title: The Relationship Between Tutoring Mode and Learners’ use of Help Tools in Distance Education
citation: Bruno De Lièvre, Christian Depover & Pierre Dillenbourg. (2006). The relationship between tutoring mode and learners' use of help tools in distance education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-6076-4
title: Proactivity intensifies the effect of a help tool's intrinsic qualities: contextualisation and ease of use matter
description: The article argues that learners are not always compliant with tutor promptings; their spontaneous use "seems to be linked to two characteristics of the tool: the contextualisation of help and its ease of use." Metacognitive help, which delivered information updated to the learner's progress, was much more contextualised than tools requiring learners to select information from an index. A given tutoring mode can only affect help use if the tools themselves have the necessary intrinsic quality.
requirements: Help tools must possess intrinsic quality — contextualisation to the learner's current difficulty and ease of access to information — for tutoring mode to influence their use
constraints: Tools requiring learners to identify relevant information on their own initiative were scarcely used without prompting
target_learners: distance education learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: spontaneous, self-initiated use of help resources
examples: Metacognitive help displayed answers given since the beginning of the session, making it more contextualised than the glossary or conceptual help, which required index or heading navigation
key_sources: Bruno De Lièvre, Christian Depover & Pierre Dillenbourg. (2006). The relationship between tutoring mode and learners' use of help tools in distance education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-6076-4

article_title: Supports for preservice teachers’ metacognitive monitoring and explanations of fraction comparisons
citation: Guba, T.-P., Barbieri, C. A., Jansen, A., & Morris, A. (2026). Supports for preservice teachers' metacognitive monitoring and explanations of fraction comparisons. Instructional Science (2026) 54:18. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09773-0
title: Three instructional supports for scaffolding preservice teachers' revision of mathematical explanations
description: The article proposes and tests three distinct supports for provoking revision of fraction comparison explanations: correct examples, defining features, and error reflection. As printed, "PSTs were randomly assigned to one of three instructional support conditions to scaffold their analysis and revision of their explanations for fraction comparisons." Correct examples provided a complete, correct explanation with a fraction-strip diagram; defining features provided "a list of steps on how to completely explain the fraction comparison" without the answer or visual; error reflection presented a fictitious student's explanation with one incorrect component and one omission. The framework links revision thinking to metacognitive monitoring and calibration.
requirements: Participants must first produce a first-draft explanation and confidence rating before encountering the condition-specific support
The supports must be presented between the first draft and the revision opportunity
constraints: The error reflection condition did not ask participants to reflect on their own errors, so the authors state they do not expect that form of reflection to impact metacognitive monitoring in particular
target_learners: elementary pre-service teachers in mathematics content courses
target_learning_goals: explaining and justifying fraction magnitude comparisons
metacognitive monitoring and calibration of one's own explanations
examples: Participants compared 7/8 and 6/7, 5/8 and 5/9, and 13/27 and 18/35, tasks chosen to evoke the distance-to-one, common numerator, and benchmark-to-one-half strategies respectively

title: Explanation completeness coding scheme with three key concepts per task
description: A paper-and-pencil coding scheme operationalizing explanation completeness as whether an explanation includes three key concepts per fraction comparison task, each with sub-components scored 0-2 and averaged into a completeness score out of 2. The article states: "We operationally defined explanation completeness as whether the explanation included three key concepts for the explanations for each task." Double-coded agreement was high, "with the average percent agreement of 98.13% on first draft and revision explanation coding," after an initial round with only 60% of codes matching.
requirements: Raters must be trained with practice rounds and discrepancy discussion; sub-components vary by task because some comparisons require more complex explanations
constraints: Only responses using the targeted strategy could be scored; strategies other than the targeted ones were not coded
target_learners: elementary pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: complete and correct mathematical explanations of fraction magnitude comparisons
examples: For Task B (5/8 vs. 5/9), the three key concepts were recognizing the common numerator strategy, comparing unit fractions, and connecting that reasoning to the final answer

title: Give preservice teachers a fully correct and complete exemplar to compare against their own mathematical explanations
description: When learners cannot receive direct instructor feedback, the article recommends providing a fully correct and complete explanation they can compare and contrast with their own draft. The authors write this "would be a proxy for getting direct feedback from their instructor on their explanation" and "is similar in design to correct examples within the worked examples literature." Their experiment found this support produced greater explanation improvement and error detection than misconception examples or a features list, informing instructional materials design for pre-service teacher mathematics content courses.

Learners need an explicit prompt to list differences between their draft and the exemplar before revising

target_learning_goals: revising explanations of fraction magnitude comparisons for correctness and completeness
examples: In the CE condition, the support was marked correct with a checkmark and included an equally partitioned rectangle (fraction strip) for visual comparison, and participants were asked to number and describe each difference before rewriting

article_title: Teachers’ subjectivities in responsive instruction: when ambitious practice encounters challenging teaching situations
citation: Ilana Seidel Horn, Yeliz Günal Aggül, Shuqin Li, Christine E. Hood. (2025). Teachers’ subjectivities in responsive instruction: when ambitious practice encounters challenging teaching situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09742-7
title: Situative framework of teachers' subjectivities: relational agency supports epistemic agency, which enables responsive practice
description: The article develops a conceptual framework in which teachers' subjectivities — their prior experiences, interpretations, agency, and emotions — are central to responsive teaching. It synthesizes two sociocultural forms of agency: epistemic agency, where teachers take responsibility for initiating and negotiating ideas to create knowledge, and relational agency, the collaborative work of expanding interpretations of problems with others. The framework holds that "in institutional environments that support practitioners' relational work in addressing challenging workplace problems, relational agency can support the development of epistemic agency," producing a virtuous cycle that sustains responsive instruction.
requirements: Institutional environments that support practitioners' relational work in addressing challenging workplace problems
constraints: The framework was built from two critical events with two teachers committed to responsive instruction in one professional development organization
target_learners: secondary mathematics teachers
target_learning_goals: sustaining responsive and culturally responsive instruction in the face of challenging teaching situations
examples: The framework was built through case analysis of two teachers, Veronica and Linda, each facing a student who challenged something core to their vision of teaching
key_sources: Ilana Seidel Horn, Yeliz Günal Aggül, Shuqin Li, Christine E. Hood. (2025). Teachers’ subjectivities in responsive instruction: when ambitious practice encounters challenging teaching situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09742-7

article_title: Teachers’ subjectivities in responsive instruction: when ambitious practice encounters challenging teaching situations
citation: Ilana Seidel Horn, Yeliz Günal Aggül, Shuqin Li, Christine E. Hood. (2025). Teachers’ subjectivities in responsive instruction: when ambitious practice encounters challenging teaching situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09742-7
title: Emotional rules of responsive teaching and the surface-acting/deep-acting account of teachers' emotional labor
description: The article argues that responsive instruction carries its own emotional rules — teachers should be welcoming, present, and attuned to students — and that meeting them requires emotional labor, the work of managing internal emotions to fit situational rules. When internal feelings misalign with these rules, teachers manage the conflict through surface acting, superficially abiding while feeling discomfort, or deep acting, where teachers "actively change their attention to and interpretations of whatever is unsettling them." Deep acting reflects epistemic agency and depends on relational agency and a supportive environment offering knowledge, psychological resources, and professional discretion.
requirements: A supportive environment offering teachers knowledge, psychological resources, and latitude for professional discretion for deep acting
constraints: Hochschild's emotional labor construct presumes a stable authentic self, which the authors replace with dynamic, negotiated subjectivities
target_learners: secondary teachers practicing responsive instruction
target_learning_goals: managing the emotional labor of maintaining empathetic, inclusive classroom environments
examples: Veronica's surface acting: swallowing fear and anxiety around Luca while presenting a pleasant demeanor; Linda's shift to deep acting after entertaining the possibility Bee was neurodivergent

article_title: Productive failure in learning from generation and invention activities
citation: Manu Kapur, Nikol Rummel. (2012). Productive failure in learning from generation and invention activities. Instr Sci 40:645-650. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9235-4
title: Productive failure: a two-phase instructional design of generation followed by consolidation
description: Productive failure designs instruction that may not maximize short-term performance but maximizes longer-term learning. It involves "a generation (or invention) phase followed by a consolidation (or instruction) phase": the generation phase lets students explore affordances and constraints of multiple representations and solution methods on novel problems, and the consolidation phase assembles student-generated RSMs into canonical ones. The special issue consolidates research on this design.
requirements: Generation tasks on novel concepts for which students possess relevant prior skills and knowledge they can apply even without canonical knowledge
constraints: The authors state PF work is still in its infancy and the concept remains largely underdetermined and under-researched
target_learners: 9th-grade mathematics students
university students
target_learning_goals: canonical concepts in mathematics and statistics, e.g. variance
conceptual understanding and transfer
examples: The four constituent studies applied PF to variance (Kapur), mathematical analysis relearning (Westermann and Rummel), uncertainty in best-fit line slopes (Roll et al.), and variance invention tasks (Wiedmann et al.)
key_sources: Manu Kapur, Nikol Rummel. (2012). Productive failure in learning from generation and invention activities. Instr Sci 40:645-650. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9235-4

article_title: Productive failure in learning from generation and invention activities
citation: Manu Kapur, Nikol Rummel. (2012). Productive failure in learning from generation and invention activities. Instr Sci 40:645-650. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9235-4
title: Provide content-general support during generation that helps without telling students the targeted content
description: Across the special issue's studies, support during the generation phase was "mainly content-general in that it does not provide speciﬁc mathematical content to students during the generation phase" — affective support, role-play support for interaction, metacognitive support, or high-ability peers. Support structures are "designed to keep students from unproductive failure experiences, while leaving a central portion of student activity unstructured, thus allowing for productive failure." This distinguishes support from direct instruction.
requirements: Support must help students without giving or telling them the targeted content knowledge directly
A central portion of student activity must remain unstructured
target_learners: 9th-grade to university students learning mathematics and statistics
target_learning_goals: generating and exploring representations and solution methods for novel concepts
examples: Kapur provided affective support and encouragement to persist; Westermann and Rummel provided the TAU role script; Roll et al. provided metacognitive prompts

article_title: Testing the testing effect with advanced materials while accounting for individual differences
citation: Redifer, J. L., Myers, S. J., Bae, C. L., Naas, A., & Scott, A. (2026). Testing the testing effect with advanced materials while accounting for individual differences. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09758-z
title: Cognitive load balance account of the testing effect with advanced materials
description: The article proposes that retrieval practice produces two opposite effects on memory: a positive effect through more effortful learning and memory-strengthening mechanisms, and a negative effect through the additional cognitive load it imposes. The authors state that "engaging in retrieval practice is most likely leading to two opposite effects", and that a testing effect occurs only when the positive effects outweigh the load costs; when mental demands interfere with retrieval's potential benefits, retrieval practice is no longer the superior strategy. This account explains why no retrieval condition beat rereading with advanced materials.
requirements: Enough cognitive resources must remain available during retrieval practice for a substantial memory search and strengthening of memory details
constraints: With materials demanding enough (e.g., a published research article), the load cost of retrieval can cancel its memorial benefits, as observed in this study
target_learners: undergraduate students learning advanced reading materials such as published research articles
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of advanced, complex educational content
examples: In the study, all retrieval conditions rated higher cognitive load than rereading, load fully mediated the strategy-to-performance relationship, and no condition outperformed rereading on the one-week delayed test.

description: DReaM (Deterministic Relativistic and Middle ground) is an integrative framework offered by the authors that organizes learners' uncertainty articulations into nine sub-categories spanning three reasoning domains. The article states: 'Based on literature from the three fields of statistics, science and nature of science education, we offer an integrative framework, Deterministic Relativistic and Middle ground (DReaM), which consists of nine sub-categories of uncertainty articulations.'

constraints: Framework elaborated through a single instrumental case study of two middle school students

The Radon Citizen Science Project learning sequence operationalized this pattern.

Designing for concurrency lets students coordinate across uncertainty types.

article_title: Micro productive failure and the acquisition of algebraic procedural knowledge
citation: Esther Ziegler, Dragan Trninic, Manu Kapur. (2021). Micro productive failure and the acquisition of algebraic procedural knowledge. Instructional Science 49, 313–336. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09544-7
title: Micro productive failure: brief, repeated problem-solving-before-instruction cycles spread across a multi-step procedure
description: This pattern adapts productive failure to procedural material by replacing the single, intense exploration phase with "multiple cycles, iterative" brief failure occasions: before each new principle is taught, students solve problems requiring that principle, generating a single solution attempt in 2–3 minutes. In the study, six units each paired a problem-solving sheet with an instructional worksheet of contrasted worked examples, example generation, practice, and an immediate learning test. The pattern targets the discrimination between structurally different yet superficially similar procedures, here algebraic addition versus multiplication.
requirements: Procedural material consisting of a series of principles that can each be attempted before formal instruction
Subsequent formal instruction, here via contrasted worked examples, immediately after each failure occasion
constraints: In the present study the pattern improved isomorphic procedural performance but showed no effects on conceptual explanation or transfer
The material required discriminating addition from multiplication, arguably more demanding than routine automated procedural skills
target_learners: sixth-graders without prior formal algebra instruction
target_learning_goals: simplifying algebraic expressions
discriminating between algebraic addition and multiplication procedures
examples: 85 Swiss sixth-graders completed six units in three 90-minute sessions, with problem-solving sheets either before (PS-I) or after (I-PS) instruction on each principle, plus posttests one day and one week later
key_sources: Esther Ziegler, Dragan Trninic, Manu Kapur. (2021). Micro productive failure and the acquisition of algebraic procedural knowledge. Instructional Science 49, 313–336. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09544-7

article_title: Micro productive failure and the acquisition of algebraic procedural knowledge
citation: Esther Ziegler, Dragan Trninic, Manu Kapur. (2021). Micro productive failure and the acquisition of algebraic procedural knowledge. Instructional Science 49, 313–336. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09544-7
title: Sequence brief problem-solving attempts before instruction when teaching multi-step algebraic procedures
description: The article recommends starting with micro productive failure occasions: have students generate a single solution attempt to a procedural problem before the relevant principle is formally taught, repeating this cycle for each new principle. The article reports this minimal intervention "impacted the development of algebraic procedural knowledge," with a stable advantage on isomorphic problems at both delays, and states that the unstable conceptual-measure interaction "does not change our recommendation of starting with micro productive failure occasions."
requirements: Failure occasions must be followed by formal instruction on the relevant principle
Students must be prompted to generate a solution even when they claim not to know how to solve the problem
constraints: The intervention showed no effects on conceptual explanation or transfer measures in this study
Caution is warranted before classroom application because procedural fluency without conceptual understanding is of limited value
target_learners: middle school students beginning algebra
target_learning_goals: acquisition of algebraic procedural skills
examples: In the study, PS-I students processed problem-solving sheets before receiving instruction in the subsequent worksheet, while I-PS students processed identical sheets after instruction as additional practice

article_title: Self-study followed by discussion enhances learning for high school students
citation: Jaeseo Lim and Jooyong Park (2026). Self-study followed by discussion enhances learning for high school students. Instructional Science (2026) 54:56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09801-7
title: Self-study and discussion model: preparatory self-study enhances learning by transforming the quality of subsequent peer discussion
description: The model, proposed by Lim and Park (2023) and extended here to high school students, holds that self-study supports individual cognitive construction while peer discussion facilitates the social construction of knowledge. The article argues its effectiveness "lies in how preparation transforms the quality of peer interaction rather than in activity level alone": self-study functions as a constructive activity that activates and reorganizes prior knowledge, enabling more substantive and co-constructive dialogue. Interpreted through the ICAP framework, discussion primarily activates and elaborates knowledge, whereas preparatory self-study establishes stable knowledge representations that persist over time.
requirements: Self-study must precede peer discussion; the article reports prior work found no difference between self-study and lecture when not followed by discussion
constraints: Prior studies were conducted with high-achieving college students; the mediating role of substantive comments did not extend to long-term outcomes in this study
target_learners: high school students
college students
target_learning_goals: retention and transfer of conceptual knowledge
examples: Seventy-three grade-12 students studied a seven-page criminal procedure text or watched an 18-minute video lecture, then discussed in triads for 15 minutes with no prompts, scripts, or guiding questions

title: When incorporating peer discussion into instruction, precede it with structured individual self-study rather than lecture-based preparation
description: The article recommends that, when peer discussion is used, students first engage in individual preparation: "allowing students to engage in self-study enables them to activate prior knowledge and set clear learning goals, thereby fostering deeper and more meaningful discussions." It further suggests encouraging individual preparation prior to class while allocating more time for discussion during instruction. The recommendation rests on the randomized experiment showing outcome and dialogue-quality advantages for self-study-prepared discussion, including at one-week delay.
requirements: A preparatory individual learning phase before discussion
Discussion time allocated after preparation
Instructional materials equivalent across preparation formats
constraints: The mediating role of substantive comments did not extend to delayed learning; discussion should not be regarded as universally superior to other active learning formats such as retrieval practice
target_learners: high school students
secondary education students
target_learning_goals: retention of conceptual knowledge
near transfer to novel scenarios
examples: Students studied written materials independently for 18 minutes (or watched an 18-minute video lecture), then engaged in a 15-minute unscripted triad discussion, with tests immediately and one week later

article_title: Interaction between the learners’ initial grasp of the object of learning and the learning resource afforded
citation: Ming Fai Pang, Ference Marton. (2013). Interaction between the learners’ initial grasp of the object of learning and the learning resource afforded. Instructional Science, 41, 1065–1082. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-013-9272-7
title: Variation Theory of Learning: the fundamental conjecture about difference and sameness
description: The Variation Theory of Learning holds that what learners discern and how they learn depends on patterns of variation and invariance in what they experience. Its fundamental conjecture, as printed in the article, is that "new meanings are acquired from experiencing differences against a background of sameness, rather than experiencing sameness against a background of differences." The article tests this conjecture empirically by building the defining patterns of variation and invariance into pedagogical tools for learning an economic principle.
requirements: Patterns of variation and invariance defining the compared conditions must be deliberately built into pedagogical tools such as text, graphs, and worksheets
target_learners: learners studying economics (the price–demand–supply principle) in the reported studies
target_learning_goals: understanding the economic principle of changes in price as a function of changes in the relative magnitude of changes in demand and supply
examples: Two studies embedded variation-consistent versus variation-inconsistent conditions in text, graphs, and worksheets about price changes
key_sources: Ming Fai Pang, Ference Marton. (2013). Interaction between the learners’ initial grasp of the object of learning and the learning resource afforded. Instructional Science, 41, 1065–1082. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-013-9272-7

As the article states, "The patterns of variation and invariance, defining the conditions compared were built into pedagogical tools (text, graphs, and worksheets)." The pattern was applied to the learning of an economic principle in two studies.

constraints: Study 2 shows the choice of tool set must match learners' initial grasp; each set was ineffective for the wrong group

article_title: Peer versus staff tutoring in problem-based learning
citation: Schmidt, H., van der Arend, A., Kokx, I. & Boon, L. (1995). Peer versus staff tutoring in problem-based learning. Instructional Science 22: 279-285.
title: Cognitive congruence framework for peer versus staff tutoring
description: The cognitive congruence framework holds that tutors are effective when there is congruence between their cognitive structures and those of the tutees, which "would qualify the student tutors to better understand the difficulties encountered by the tutees". It is balanced against a subject-matter knowledge argument, that student tutors' lesser knowledge risks a 'pooling of ignorance'. The article uses it to interpret why peer tutors were rated higher and equally effective in the first year, while staff tutors' subject-matter expertise becomes more important over the course of the years.
requirements: Tutors must display an understanding of the way in which students think and express themselves in their language for cognitive congruence to operate
constraints: Subject-matter expertise of the tutor becomes more important only over the course of the years, limiting congruence advantages to early curriculum years
target_learners: Higher education students in problem-based curricula
target_learning_goals: Facilitating learning in small-group problem-based tutorials
examples: The field experiment found no achievement difference in year 1, where students prefer tutors behaving 'cognitively congruent'
key_sources: Schmidt, H., van der Arend, A., Kokx, I. & Boon, L. (1995). Peer versus staff tutoring in problem-based learning. Instructional Science 22: 279-285. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00891781
