citation: Schmidt, H., van der Arend, A., Kokx, I. & Boon, L. (1995). Peer versus staff tutoring in problem-based learning. Instructional Science 22: 279-285.
title: In early problem-based curriculum years, peer tutors can substitute for staff tutors without achievement loss
description: Because peer tutors were rated higher on supportive behaviors in the first year and no achievement difference was found there, problem-based curricula can deploy student tutors in early years where staff are reluctant to tutor. Staff reluctance arises because lecturing "is not in high demand in tutorial groups". The advantage erodes as the curriculum advances and subject-matter expertise matters more.
requirements: Student tutors should themselves have experienced problem-based learning, so they are sensitive to tutorial groups' needs in support, information and guidance
constraints: Applicable to the first curriculum year only; staff-tutored groups achieved significantly better overall, and staff were rated higher in years 2-4
target_learners: First-year higher education students in problem-based health sciences curricula
target_learning_goals: Small-group problem explanation, self-directed learning goal setting
examples: In the field experiment, 400 tutorial groups guided by student tutors were compared with 334 guided by staff tutors across 98 courses
key_sources: Schmidt, H., van der Arend, A., Kokx, I. & Boon, L. (1995). Peer versus staff tutoring in problem-based learning. Instructional Science 22: 279-285. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00891781

article_title: Effects of person praise on students’ motivation and performance under ego-involving and task-involving feedback conditions
citation: Cheng-Hong Liu, Xian-Rui Yin. (2026). Effects of person praise on students' motivation and performance under ego-involving and task-involving feedback conditions. Instructional Science (2026) 54:34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09789-0
title: Avoid pre-task person praise for tasks with anticipated task-involving feedback; it is a strategic option only when ego-involving feedback (public comparison) is expected
description: The article offers educators a decision rule grounded in its experiment: when the anticipated feedback is ego-involving and competitive, praising students' qualities before a new task may raise participation motivation, but "if a task is likely to employ task-involving feedback, which emphasizes student learning and improvement (e.g., learning tasks in classrooms), praising students' qualities should likely be avoided" because it activates a distraction mechanism. Teachers should nonetheless prioritize task-involving feedback generally, since students were more motivated under it.
requirements: Apply only to praise given before task engagement combined with anticipated feedback structure, not to post-task praise or feedback content
constraints: Findings come from one task (subtle difference detection) with Taiwanese junior high students; the praise used targeted personality, not ability; results should not be extrapolated to praise or feedback given after task completion
target_learners: junior high school students facing a new learning task
target_learning_goals: engagement and participation motivation in a new task
task performance
examples: In the experiment, pre-task person praise before a 5-minute subtle difference detection task reduced trials attempted under expected teacher comments but increased trials under expected score-and-ranking lists
key_sources: Cheng-Hong Liu, Xian-Rui Yin. (2026). Effects of person praise on students' motivation and performance under ego-involving and task-involving feedback conditions. Instructional Science (2026) 54:34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09789-0

article_title: Effects of person praise on students’ motivation and performance under ego-involving and task-involving feedback conditions
citation: Cheng-Hong Liu, Xian-Rui Yin. (2026). Effects of person praise on students' motivation and performance under ego-involving and task-involving feedback conditions. Instructional Science (2026) 54:34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09789-0
title: Threat-conditional account of person praise: attribute affirmation mitigates threat in high-threat (ego-involving) environments but triggers self-focus distraction in low-threat (task-involving) ones
description: The article integrates self-affirmation theory and achievement goal theory into a model in which pre-task person praise functions as attribute affirmation whose effect depends on the anticipated feedback environment. Under ego-involving feedback (a high-threat, performance-goal context), the authors argue praise "may reduce the psychological threat posed by challenging learning tasks and may encourage students to approach the tasks in a positive manner"; under task-involving feedback (a low-threat, mastery context), the affirmation instead heightens self-focus and distracts from the task. Moderated serial mediation through state self-esteem supported the detrimental pathway only in the task-involving condition.
requirements: The person praise must be delivered before task engagement and paired with an anticipated feedback structure; the mechanism was tested via state self-esteem as first mediator and trials attempted as second mediator
constraints: The ego-involving condition's beneficial pathway was not mediated by state self-esteem; the article states the mechanism there remains unidentified and recommends future researchers measure other potential mediating variables. Findings apply only to pre-task affirmation with feedback expectations, not post-task praise content.
target_learners: junior high school students (aged 12–14) facing a new learning task
target_learning_goals: participation motivation in a new task
task performance
examples: In the experiment, the serial indirect effect of person praise on performance through state self-esteem and trials was negative only under task-involving feedback (−0.83, CI −2.12 to −0.06) and absent under ego-involving feedback (0.04, CI −0.19 to 0.37)
key_sources: Cheng-Hong Liu, Xian-Rui Yin. (2026). Effects of person praise on students' motivation and performance under ego-involving and task-involving feedback conditions. Instructional Science (2026) 54:34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09789-0

article_title: The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations
citation: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z
title: Teachers’ conceptions of teaching as a framework theory used to interpret and predict teaching situations
description: The article draws on the idea that conceptions of teaching — beliefs about teaching that underlie its purpose and strategies — form a coherent framework through which teachers read classroom events. As it puts it, “the conceptions the teacher holds form a framework theory the teacher can use in explaining and predicting teaching situations”. Conceptions range from teaching as knowledge transmission to teaching as learning facilitation, and they are linked to content-focused versus learning-focused approaches to teaching, which in turn relate to students’ surface versus deep approaches to learning. The study operationalises this lens by coding teachers’ written interpretations of scripted video trigger events.
requirements: Conceptions are measured indirectly through interpretations of authentic teaching situations rather than directly through self-report items
constraints: The article notes the relationship between approaches and conceptions is not exclusive: teachers “may adopt elements of both approaches in their teaching and hold conceptions that mirror elements of both conception categories”
target_learners: University teachers
Doctoral students with or without teaching duties
target_learning_goals: Developing learning-facilitation conceptions of teaching
Interpreting teaching–learning situations in terms of student learning
examples: Participants’ interpretations of a lecture interruption were coded as knowledge transmission (e.g. postponing questions to the end of the lecture) or learning facilitation (e.g. valuing interaction and activating students).
key_sources: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z

article_title: The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations
citation: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z
title: UNIPS online platform for university pedagogical support
description: UNIPS is a national Finnish online learning platform, built on WordPress, offering short one-ECTS modules in university pedagogy for self-study and guided study. It is “open to all university staff and doctoral students for self-study and one-credit guided study courses”, and guided study “utilises online discussions to create knowledge collaboratively and improve pedagogical expertise”. It was developed to give flexible access to staff, such as doctoral students not currently teaching, who traditionally could not enrol in face-to-face pedagogical training. In this study it hosted the three concurrent five-week modules whose effects were measured.
requirements: Guided study requires an online teacher who reads essays, organises the group work phase, monitors discussion and gives brief personal written feedback
constraints: At the time of the study the platform comprised around ten modules and was a collaborative project of eight Finnish universities funded from 2017 to 2019
target_learners: University teachers
Doctoral students
New faculty without prior pedagogical training
target_learning_goals: University pedagogical expertise
Shifting from content-focused to learning-focused teaching
examples: “Developed originally at the University of Turku in 2015, the guided study modules in this environment have been completed more than 500 times within a three-year period”.
key_sources: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z

article_title: The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations
citation: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z
title: Two-phase online module design combining individual reflective essays with small-group peer discussion
description: Each short online pedagogy module comprised “an individual study phase and a small-group phase”. In the individual phase, participants studied self-study materials (videos, articles, glossaries, quizzes) and wrote a reflective essay; in the small-group phase, groups of four to six shared and commented on each other’s essays in Google Docs, with experienced teachers and novices mixed in each group. The design aims to support co-construction of knowledge and conceptual change regarding educational concepts, and all tasks were designed so that doctoral students without teaching experience could complete them.
requirements: Groups composed to represent different teaching-experience levels and different faculties
A teacher role that monitors discussion and gives personal written feedback after each module
target_learners: University teachers
Doctoral students, including those without teaching duties
target_learning_goals: Conceptual development and change about teaching
Shared understanding of pedagogical concepts
examples: The three modules used were Becoming a Teacher, How to Plan My Teaching, and Lecturing and Expertise; each included essay writing followed by peer commenting.
key_sources: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z

article_title: The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations
citation: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z
title: Offer pedagogical training early in university teaching careers, including short online formats
description: Because conceptions form lenses for interpreting teaching and are hard to change once entrenched, the article recommends low-threshold, timely support before and at the start of teaching. Its stated conclusion is that “pedagogical training should be offered already at the early stages of teaching careers”, since even short online programmes changed interpretations “especially when participants are not very experienced in teaching”. This addresses the barrier that traditional lengthy face-to-face courses exclude doctoral students and new faculty who lack teaching duties.
requirements: Short online formats with guided study so that staff not currently teaching can participate
constraints: The article reports doubts about the efficacy of programmes lasting less than six months to one year, and that more experienced teachers are more likely to be reluctant to change their conceptions or practices
target_learners: Doctoral students
New university faculty in their first years of teaching
target_learning_goals: Adopting learning-facilitation conceptions of teaching before habits of teaching as taught become entrenched
examples: The UNIPS courses were five weeks long, one ECTS credit each, and open to doctoral students without teaching duties, who completed tasks such as planning an imaginary course.
key_sources: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z

article_title: Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning
citation: Lim, S., Jung, J. Y., & Kalyuga, S. (2023). Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09616-w
title: Invention-first instruction (Invention as Preparation for Future Learning / productive failure)
description: Invention-first instruction is an instructional sequence in which learners first attempt to solve or invent solutions to a novel problem and only then receive explicit instruction on the canonical solution. The article describes it as "hallmarked by two essential components—first, the solving of problems, followed by explicit instruction", and notes it is also called productive failure. Proposed mechanisms include increased awareness of knowledge gaps, heightened epistemic curiosity, and recognition of deep structure via contrast between cases. The study operationalises it against example-first instruction with gifted and non-gifted adolescents.
requirements: Learners attempt an invention or problem-solving activity prior to receiving explicit instruction on the canonical solution
Instruction follows the invention stage so the preparatory effect can operate
constraints: The article notes the specific mechanisms are not fully clarified and only a handful of studies have investigated them
target_learners: secondary school students, especially gifted adolescents in grades 6 and above
target_learning_goals: transfer of ratio/density concepts
preparation for learning new conceptual content
examples: In this study, invention-first participants spent 15 min generating a crowdedness index for clown bus companies before receiving an instructional booklet, while example-first participants studied a worked example of the same task.
key_sources: Lim, S., Jung, J. Y., & Kalyuga, S. (2023). Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09616-w

article_title: Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning
citation: Lim, S., Jung, J. Y., & Kalyuga, S. (2023). Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09616-w
title: Balanced invention-first vs example-first design with a shared additional practice stage
description: The study's instructional design gives all conditions identical stages except the first: pre-instruction (invention or worked example), problem-solving/worked example practice, recall, consolidation, and post-test. Unlike prior designs, "an additional practice stage of a problem-solving task and a worked example ... was included for all conditions prior to final consolidation", so both a problem-solving task and a worked example were given to every condition in the same order. This holds practice constant across conditions and isolates the effect of the initial activity, while responding to findings that additional problem-solving practice may increase the benefits of invention-first instruction.
requirements: All conditions must receive the same practice activities in the same order after the differing first stage
The initial stage (invention vs worked example) uses the same task materials
constraints: The article notes the low contrast conditions may not have given invention-first participants all information needed to solve the task, so high vs low contrast is a comparison of materials rather than of cases
target_learners: seventh-grade students in selective and non-selective classes
target_learning_goals: physics/ratio concepts
near and far transfer
procedural knowledge
examples: Four conditions were used: invention-first high contrast, example-first high contrast, invention-first low contrast, and example-first low contrast, each with the same five sequential stages.
key_sources: Lim, S., Jung, J. Y., & Kalyuga, S. (2023). Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09616-w

article_title: Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning
citation: Lim, S., Jung, J. Y., & Kalyuga, S. (2023). Effectiveness of invention tasks and explicit instruction in preparing intellectually gifted adolescents for learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09616-w
title: Invention-first instruction is a candidate strategy for gifted secondary students, pending confirmation
description: Based on the significant giftedness-by-instruction interaction and the theoretical fit between gifted learners' profiles and problem-solving, the article proposes invention-first instruction as a promising alternative to the conventional explicit-instruction modality in gifted education. It explicitly "puts forward the possibility of the invention-first strategy as an effective instructional strategy for gifted students". The framing is tentative: results are described with may, and the authors note prior evidence that older and higher-ability students appear more responsive to invention-first methods.
requirements: Students at secondary level (grade 6 and above), where invention-first benefits have been reported
Tasks that offer appropriate challenge and opportunities for problem-solving and creativity
constraints: Contrast materials were not found to affect performance in this study
Gifted classification relied on self-identification plus psychologist or school identification
target_learners: intellectually gifted and academically talented adolescents
target_learning_goals: transfer
creativity
engagement with novel problem-solving
examples: The study administered a crowdedness-index invention task adapted from Schwartz et al. (2011) to gifted and non-gifted seventh graders before explicit instruction.

article_title: English learners learn from worked example comparison in algebra
citation: Xiaojuan Ke · Kristie J. Newton. (2024). English learners learn from worked example comparison in algebra. Instructional Science (2024) 52:831–858. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09668-6
title: MLS-WEPs: Modified for Language Support-Worked Example Pairs supplemental algebra curriculum
description: MLS-WEPs is a supplemental curriculum for English learners adapted from Durkin and colleagues' WEP materials, in which students compare side-by-side worked examples across four types: "Which is better?", "Why does it work?", "Which is correct?", and "How do they differ?". Language supports include sentence frames, rephrased prompts of adjusted language complexity, requiring mathematical examples before conceptual answers, and allowing native-language discussion and drafting with final products in English.
requirements: Teachers received a three-hour orientation implementing the materials as if they were students, plus weekly communication with researchers
constraints: Implemented as a supplement after topics were introduced, within five unit types (Linear Equations, Functions, System Equations, Polynomials, Radicals)
target_learners: English learners in secondary sheltered algebra classes, English proficiency levels 1-5
target_learning_goals: Algebraic problem solving and calculation
Written mathematical explanation
Mathematical literacy in listening, reading, writing, and speaking
examples: Teachers implemented the Linear Equation and Function units in a crossover design, with the control group receiving the same examples with the same language supports but without comparison
key_sources: Xiaojuan Ke · Kristie J. Newton. (2024). English learners learn from worked example comparison in algebra. Instructional Science (2024) 52:831–858. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09668-6

article_title: English learners learn from worked example comparison in algebra
citation: Xiaojuan Ke · Kristie J. Newton. (2024). English learners learn from worked example comparison in algebra. Instructional Science (2024) 52:831–858. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09668-6
title: Cognitive load account of mathematics learning in a second language
description: The article frames ELs' mathematics learning through cognitive load theory: working memory handles only a very limited number of novel interacting elements and retains information for only about 30 seconds, and ELs additionally use working memory to translate or code-switch between L1 and L2. Worked examples are presented as a way to reduce cognitive load, and the authors argue the goal "is not to reduce the cognitive demands of the task, but to help ELs fully utilize their bilingual strengths to learn mathematics." This account motivates the MLS-WEPs design and its language supports.
requirements: Instructional methods that reduce ELs' cognitive load in working memory, while keeping the cognitive demands of the task themselves intact
constraints: The account applies to mathematics learned in a second-language context, where translation and code-switching add working-memory demands relative to native-speaking peers
target_learners: English learners in K-12 mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: Algebraic problem solving
Mathematical reasoning and explanation
examples: The article uses this account to justify worked examples with detailed problem-solving descriptions and to interpret why ELs benefited across proficiency levels
key_sources: Xiaojuan Ke · Kristie J. Newton. (2024). English learners learn from worked example comparison in algebra. Instructional Science (2024) 52:831–858. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09668-6

article_title: Futurising science education: students’ experiences from a course on futures thinking and quantum computing
citation: Tapio Rasa, Elina Palmgren, Antti Laherto. (2022). Futurising science education: students' experiences from a course on futures thinking and quantum computing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09572-3
title: Futures thinking connected to the projective dimension of transformative agency
description: The article frames futures thinking — the ability of "disengaging from deterministic future views, understanding the plurality of futures and identifying and questioning assumptions to develop alternative scenarios" — as deeply influencing agency, defined as the capacity for intentional transformative action. Building on Emirbayer and Mische, the projective dimension of agency links futures thinking to transformative agency because it denotes imagining alternatives free from constraining schemas. The framework maps probable, possible and preferable futures onto agentic dimensions and motivates visioning and backcasting in science education.
requirements: Teaching should engage students in building alternative scenarios and questioning assumptions for the projective dimension to be exercised
constraints: The article focuses on upper-secondary science education contexts and on individual students' takes on futures and agency, while also attending to social aspects
target_learners: upper-secondary school students
target_learning_goals: futures thinking
transformative agency
probabilistic and uncertainty-oriented thinking
examples: The course used the Futures Cone, scenario building across probable, possible and preferable futures, and backcasting from preferable futures
key_sources: Tapio Rasa, Elina Palmgren, Antti Laherto. (2022). Futurising science education: students' experiences from a course on futures thinking and quantum computing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09572-3

article_title: Futurising science education: students’ experiences from a course on futures thinking and quantum computing
citation: Tapio Rasa, Elina Palmgren, Antti Laherto. (2022). Futurising science education: students' experiences from a course on futures thinking and quantum computing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09572-3
title: Future-oriented science course combining authentic emerging technology with futures-studies methods
description: A lesson/course-level design in which a contemporary science topic (quantum computing) provides continuity from scientific knowledge to emerging technologies and their future possibilities, intertwined with futures-studies methods. "Students were guided to employ, by turns, three fundamentally different types of thinking methods commonly used in futures studies: probable, possible and preferable futures", followed by a backcasting exercise in which students imagine themselves as active participants in reaching a preferable future. Group projects on personally chosen socio-scientific problems run throughout the module, supported by the Futures Cone visualisation and systems thinking tools.
requirements: A science topic offering continuity from accessible scientific knowledge to emerging technology and future possibilities
sustained group project work on a personally relevant socio-scientific problem
constraints: The module was implemented as an extra-curricular course of about 20 hours with STEM-specialisation students
target_learners: upper-secondary school students in STEM specialisation programmes
target_learning_goals: futures thinking skills
understanding of quantum computing concepts
agentic orientation toward socio-scientific problems
examples: Two course weekends plus an evening session; students used a real publicly available IBM quantum processor; final presentations were success stories told in past tense
key_sources: Tapio Rasa, Elina Palmgren, Antti Laherto. (2022). Futurising science education: students' experiences from a course on futures thinking and quantum computing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09572-3

article_title: The effects of scaffolding in the classroom: support contingency and student independent working time in relation to student achievement, task effort and appreciation of support
citation: van de Pol, J., Volman, M., Oort, F., & Beishuizen, J. (2015). The effects of scaffolding in the classroom: support contingency and student independent working time in relation to student achievement, task effort and appreciation of support. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9351-z
title: Contingent shift framework for measuring scaffolding contingency in classroom interaction
description: The contingent shift framework, based on Wood et al. (1978), operationalizes scaffolding as the tailored adaptation of the degree of control in teacher support to a student's demonstrated understanding. The article states: "If a teacher used more control after a student’s demonstration of poor understanding and less control after a student’s demonstration of good understanding, we labelled the support contingent." Teacher turns are coded for degree of control from zero to five, student turns for demonstrated understanding, and contingency is scored as the percentage of contingent three-turn sequences per teacher. The article uses this framework as the measure of support quality in its classroom experiment.
requirements: Coding requires transcribed teacher-student interaction fragments and a three-turn-sequence unit; diagnosing or evaluating student understanding is needed before support can be contingent.
constraints: The article notes most studies, unlike this one, did not use such a dynamic operationalization; contingency scores were class-level, so all students of a class shared the same score.
target_learners: Pre-vocational secondary students (age 12-15) working in small groups
target_learning_goals: Subject-matter achievement in social studies (European Union project)
examples: Teachers' interaction fragments were coded for degree of control (0-5) and student understanding; the contingency score was the percentage of contingent three-turn sequences per teacher per measurement occasion.
key_sources: van de Pol, J., Volman, M., Oort, F., & Beishuizen, J. (2015). The effects of scaffolding in the classroom: support contingency and student independent working time in relation to student achievement, task effort and appreciation of support. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9351-z

article_title: Teacher vision: expert and novice teachers’ perception of problematic classroom management scenes
citation: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Niek van den Bogert, Henny P. A. Boshuizen. (2016). Teacher vision: expert and novice teachers' perception of problematic classroom management scenes. Instr Sci 44:243-265. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9367-z
title: Professional vision of teaching: knowledge-driven perception of classroom events underpinning withitness
description: The article frames teachers' professional vision as the skilfulness at observing, searching for, and making sense of classroom scenes, developing over time as teachers learn their profession's visual practices (Goodwin 1994; Sherin 2001). It is underpinned by Kounin's withitness: "teachers direct attention to relevant information in the classroom and continually monitor the progression of events". The account predicts that experience-built event-structured knowledge guides focused, selective attention to informative cues, whereas novices lacking such knowledge search indiscriminately and are drawn to salient but uninformative image features.
requirements: Requires event-structured classroom knowledge built through substantial teaching experience; the article notes five to seven years as a reasonable estimate for developing high-level skill
constraints: The study examined only problematic classroom situations and sheds no light on expert-novice differences in non-problematic situations
Findings concern visual processing of video scenes, not live teaching
target_learners: novice secondary school teachers
pre-service teachers in training
target_learning_goals: classroom management awareness
noticing and interpreting classroom cues and events
examples: Experts revisited AOIs showing students' trunks, shoulders, arms, hands and interactive regions between rows, while novices revisited areas void of discernible student activity such as walls and a window showing hallway activity
key_sources: Charlotte E. Wolff, Halszka Jarodzka, Niek van den Bogert, Henny P. A. Boshuizen. (2016). Teacher vision: expert and novice teachers' perception of problematic classroom management scenes. Instr Sci 44:243-265. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9367-z

article_title: Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation
citation: Mads Solberg, Charlott Sellberg. (2025). Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation. Instructional Science (2026) 54:7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09760-5
title: DCog model of debriefing as a coordination device for conversational remembering and distributed metacognition
description: The article reconceptualises the three-phase simulation debriefing through distributed cognition, arguing that the debriefing conversation itself is the major coordination device. Its model holds that "debriefing conversations function as coordination devices for two key processes: conversational remembering and distributed metacognition", coordinating a cascade of representations from private memory to public speech. A coordination device is a structure or practice that constrains participants' actions to control how representations propagate within a distributed cognitive system. The model emerged abductively from cognitive-ethnographic analysis of one exemplary debriefing case.
requirements: A facilitator-led debriefing structured through consecutive phases, in which talk-in-interaction can manage the transformation of representations between media
constraints: The model was developed from a single exemplary case of a nursing simulation debriefing, chosen for analytical richness rather than statistical typicality
target_learners: second-year nursing students
healthcare simulation participants
target_learning_goals: reflexive analysis of simulated clinical performance
professional knowledge and judgment in acute care
examples: The authors analyse a 55-minute debriefing after a hypoglycemia management simulation, showing description-phase remembering followed by analysis and application phases of distributed metacognition
key_sources: Mads Solberg, Charlott Sellberg. (2025). Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation. Instructional Science (2026) 54:7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09760-5

article_title: Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation
citation: Mads Solberg, Charlott Sellberg. (2025). Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation. Instructional Science (2026) 54:7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09760-5
title: Video review as an external cognitive artifact scaffolding memory and reasoning in debriefing
description: Before the debriefing proper, the facilitator initiates playback of a video recording of the simulation for the students who role-played, in a semi-circle arrangement. From a DCog perspective, "This video review is a common "debriefing adjunct" (Sawyer et al., 2016) and, from a DCog perspective, an external "cognitive artifact" (Hutchins, 1999) used to scaffold memory and reasoning in simulations". It anchors the description-phase questions about immediate reactions to performances seen on the TV screen.
requirements: A video recording of the simulation and playback equipment available at the debriefing site
constraints: In the analysed case, only the three role-playing students reviewed the video, while the two observing students stepped outside during playback
target_learners: nursing students in simulation training
target_learning_goals: recalling and reconstructing simulated clinical events
examples: The facilitator initiates the debriefing by inquiring about the students' reaction to their performances as seen on the TV screen

article_title: Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation
citation: Mads Solberg, Charlott Sellberg. (2025). Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation. Instructional Science (2026) 54:7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09760-5
title: Engineer the simulation environment as a safe container before the debriefing to support shared experience and epistemic outcomes
description: The article shows that debriefing outcomes depend on upstream engineering of the learning environment: briefing establishes trust, expectations, and role delegation before the scenario. "The explicit aim of this preparation is to establish the entire simulation, including the debriefing, as a "safe container" where threats to professional identity can be managed in ways conducive to learning". Observational templates also distribute the cognitive labor of observing against the learning goals.
requirements: Pre-simulation briefing covering learning targets, environment familiarisation, and role delegation; artifacts such as NEWS scorecards and ISBAR templates to distribute cognitive labor
constraints: Simulations can be highly stressful for learners, so building trust and managing expectations is crucial

healthcare trainees in high-fidelity simulation

structured acute-care assessment and communication
examples: In the analysed case, two students conducted systematic observations using template documents, and the facilitator called closed-loop dialogue the most important tool at their disposal

article_title: Collaborative design as a form of professional development
citation: Joke Voogt, Therese Laferrière, Alain Breuleux, Rebecca C. Itow, Daniel T. Hickey, Susan McKenney (2015). Collaborative design as a form of professional development. Instr Sci (2015) 43:259-282. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9340-7
title: Three key features framework for teacher learning by collaborative design: situatedness, agency, and the cyclical nature of learning and change
description: The article draws on the situative perspective of Greeno et al. (1998) and third-generation activity theory (CHAT, Engeström 1987) to propose that "three interrelated features are key to understanding learning by collaborative design in the teaching practice: the situatedness of activity, agency, and the cyclical nature of learning and educational change." Situatedness locates learning in teachers' own practice contexts; agency frames teachers as transformative agents of change, drawing on Engeström's "shared transformative agency"; the cyclical feature follows Engeström's expansive learning model of questioning, analyzing, designing, examining, implementing, and reflecting. The framework organizes the three case descriptions and the research agenda, crossed with Borko's (2004) individual, team, and system levels.
requirements: Collaborative curricular design processes must be well-scaffolded, and resulting materials must be based on up-to-date knowledge of good practice and considered usable by teachers in their contexts, per the article's introduction.
constraints: The authors state they do not establish these three characteristics as evidence-based causal factors; and the Boschman et al. (2014) study suggests that "practical concerns dominate discussion in design teams and may hinder teacher learning."
target_learners: practicing teachers
pre-service teachers
school and district leaders
target_learning_goals: teacher professional learning through collaborative curriculum design
capacity for educational change
examples: Table 1 maps the three features against the three cases (USA, Africa, Canada) across Borko's three phases of professional development research.
key_sources: Joke Voogt, Therese Laferrière, Alain Breuleux, Rebecca C. Itow, Daniel T. Hickey, Susan McKenney (2015). Collaborative design as a form of professional development. Instr Sci (2015) 43:259-282. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9340-7

article_title: Collaborative design as a form of professional development
citation: Joke Voogt, Therese Laferrière, Alain Breuleux, Rebecca C. Itow, Daniel T. Hickey, Susan McKenney (2015). Collaborative design as a form of professional development. Instr Sci (2015) 43:259-282. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9340-7
title: Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (IMPG) as used to interpret teacher learning in teacher design teams
description: In Case 2, the article uses the Interconnected Model of Professional Growth (Clarke and Hollingsworth 2002) to understand teachers' learning in each teacher design team. The model "postulates that change can take place in any of four domains: the external domain, the personal domain, the domain of practice and the domain of consequences." External-domain change means becoming acquainted with new ideas and strategies introduced by others; personal-domain change is acquiring new knowledge, skills, attitudes or beliefs; practice-domain change arises from collaborative design and enactment; and consequence-domain change concerns outcomes for teachers and students. The model holds that "Change may occur in any domain and is mediated through the processes of reflection and enactment," and the case organizes its findings under these four domains.
requirements: Interpretation requires examining change in the four domains together, with reflection and enactment as the mediating processes.
target_learners: practicing teachers
teacher design team members
target_learning_goals: understanding teacher professional growth during collaborative curriculum design
examples: In the African studies, kick-off workshops and TPACK framing served the external domain, while reflections on implemented lessons drove changes in technology integration approaches in the practice domain.

article_title: Collaborative design as a form of professional development
citation: Joke Voogt, Therese Laferrière, Alain Breuleux, Rebecca C. Itow, Daniel T. Hickey, Susan McKenney (2015). Collaborative design as a form of professional development. Instr Sci (2015) 43:259-282. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-014-9340-7
title: Situate teachers' professional development in the kinds of learning environments and communities they are encouraged to create for their students
description: From the USA case, the article proposes that professional development should "allow teachers to work and learn within the kinds of learning environments and professional learning communities they are encouraged to create for their students, and provide support throughout the implementation process." The idea is that teachers experience participatory learning first-hand during PD, so they can later foster the same participatory environment for their students; the Case 1 workshop was structured accordingly, with teachers first learning a core participatory instructional routine before designing it into their online courses.
requirements: Support throughout the implementation process; curricular designs should foster connected learning and productive disciplinary engagement while supporting conventional literacies and academic knowledge for which teachers are accountable.
constraints: The article's principle list also states the approach must "accommodate prevailing levels of student network access" and "make reasonable demands on teachers' time for designing and delivering curricula."

online high school teachers
target_learning_goals: enacting participatory and personalized learning approaches
designing technology-enhanced curricula
examples: The workshop initiated with teacher learning activities around the core participatory instructional routine, which was effective in helping teachers appreciate the central role of learner agency in participatory teaching.

article_title: Example-based learning: should learners receive closed-book or open-book self-explanation prompts?
citation: Sara Hiller · Stefan Rumann · Kirsten Berthold · Julian Roelle. (2020). Example-based learning: should learners receive closed-book or open-book self-explanation prompts? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09523-4
title: Dual theoretical lenses: generative learning theory and retrieval-based learning theory applied to self-explanation prompt format
description: The article analyzes self-explanation prompts through two theoretical frameworks. Generative learning theory predicts open-book prompts are more effective because "a closed-book format likely reduces the amount of generated self-explanations", since the number of generated self-explanations is considered crucial while retrieval amount is not. Retrieval-based learning theory instead predicts closed-book benefits, because closed-book prompts require retrieval practice, which fosters long-term retention via memory-trace consolidation. The article argues that combining both lenses, plus the imperfection of retrieval, yields time-dependent predictions.
requirements: The dual-lens account applies to generative learning tasks that can be implemented with or without access to source material during generation
constraints: The article notes the simple retrieval-practice rationale "might be too simple" because learners seldomly retrieve information perfectly
Conclusions limited to retention intervals not exceeding 1 week
target_learners: secondary school students learning from worked examples
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of science principles and examples
examples: The experiments manipulated prompt format (closed- vs. open-book) and active processing of instructional explanation prompts in a 2 × 2 factorial between-subjects design
key_sources: Sara Hiller · Stefan Rumann · Kirsten Berthold · Julian Roelle. (2020). Example-based learning: should learners receive closed-book or open-book self-explanation prompts? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09523-4

article_title: Example-based learning: should learners receive closed-book or open-book self-explanation prompts?
citation: Sara Hiller · Stefan Rumann · Kirsten Berthold · Julian Roelle. (2020). Example-based learning: should learners receive closed-book or open-book self-explanation prompts? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09523-4
title: When prompting self-explanations of examples, prefer open-book prompts or add active processing of instructional explanations before closed-book prompts
description: In example-based learning sequences where instructional explanations precede examples, self-explanation prompts should be provided in an open-book format, or learners should be prompted to actively process the main content of the instructional explanations before receiving closed-book prompts. The article concludes "closed-book self-explanation prompts do not entail an added value and can even be harmful in comparison to open-book ones" when retention does not exceed 1 week.
requirements: Learners receiving closed-book prompts should first actively process the main content items of the basic instructional explanations, e.g. by restating them in their own words
constraints: Harm from closed-book prompts was observed only when learners were not prompted to actively process beforehand
Conclusions limited to retention intervals up to 1 week
Delayed-posttest results in Experiment 1 were confounded by the immediate posttest
target_learners: secondary school students (eighth-grade chemistry)
target_learning_goals: principle-based self-explanations linking instructional explanations to examples
conceptual knowledge
examples: Both experiments assigned learners to closed- versus open-book self-explanation prompts with or without prior active processing prompts in a 2 × 2 between-subjects design

article_title: Deliberate erring improves scientific reasoning: Learning experimentation skills by intentionally designing invalid experiments
citation: Sarah Shi Hui Wong. (2026). Deliberate erring improves scientific reasoning: Learning experimentation skills by intentionally designing invalid experiments. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09819-x
title: Derring effect and deliberate erring as a guided-error learning approach within the Prevention–Permission–Promotion (3P) framework
description: The derring effect is a counterintuitive phenomenon in which "deliberate erring has been found to enhance learning", implemented by having students intentionally generate a plausible conceptual error, then strike it out and correct it. The article situates it in Wong and Lim's (2019b) 3P framework, under which "errors in learning can be observed, allowed, induced, or guided when not avoided": learning from others' invalid designs involves observing errors, whereas deliberate erring guides students into making and correcting their own errors in low-stakes contexts after correct instruction. Candidate mechanisms include failure-driven learning, development of negative knowledge, suppression of incorrect pathways, attention to correction, and structural alignment between incorrect and correct responses.
requirements: Deliberate errors must be generated after instruction on the correct principles and in low-stakes practice contexts, as in the study's open-book practice with a principles handout
constraints: The article states the benefits are specific to guiding students to commit and correct their own errors, since observing and correcting others' errors does not yield the same extent of gains
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: experimental design principles
scientific reasoning
transfer of domain-general principles
examples: Students in the derr-explain-fix condition designed a non-optimal study to test a coffee-drinking hypothesis, explained their deliberate errors, then corrected them within a 15-minute equated practice session
key_sources: Sarah Shi Hui Wong. (2026). Deliberate erring improves scientific reasoning: Learning experimentation skills by intentionally designing invalid experiments. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09819-x

article_title: Developing a ‘big picture’: Effects of collaborative construction of multimodal representations in history
citation: Maaike E. Prangsma, Carla A. M. Van Boxtel, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Developing a 'big picture': Effects of collaborative construction of multimodal representations in history. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9026-5
title: Chronological-conceptual frame of reference as the knowledge base for historical reasoning
description: The article frames history learning around a chronological frame of reference, defined as "the knowledge base that is used when reasoning about the past". It consists of three components: knowledge of historical phenomena (events, structures, themes), knowledge of temporal and causal relations between phenomena, and knowledge of concepts describing phenomena and relations. The study's multimodal tasks were designed to combine all three components, and the timeline condition additionally visualised temporal relations across tasks. The framework draws on Leinhardt's typology of historical phenomena (events, structures, themes, metasystems).
requirements: Learners must connect information represented in different formats (text, pictures, diagrams, timeline) for the frame to develop
constraints: A timeline with dates and textual descriptions only visualises temporal relationships and does not show underlying causal relationships
target_learners: lower secondary pre-vocational education pupils (aged 12–13)
target_learning_goals: acquisition of a chronological frame of reference for history
understanding of historical phenomena, temporal and causal relations, and historical concepts
examples: Dyads co-constructed storyboards, causal networks, image descriptions and cartograms about the Early Middle Ages, with Timeline-condition products linked in a large timeline (about 60 × 140 cm)
key_sources: Maaike E. Prangsma, Carla A. M. Van Boxtel, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Developing a 'big picture': Effects of collaborative construction of multimodal representations in history. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9026-5

article_title: The effects of representational format on learning combinatorics from an interactive computer simulation
citation: Bas Kolloffel, Tessa H. S. Eysink, Ton de Jong, Pascal Wilhelm. (2009). The effects of representational format on learning combinatorics from an interactive computer simulation. Instr Sci 37:503–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9056-7
title: Three-pillar schema theory with format-specific emphases and multiple-representation functions
description: The article holds that a complete schema for a domain "rests on three pillars: conceptual knowledge, procedural knowledge, and situational knowledge", acquired through selecting, organizing, and integrating information. It proposes that representational format influences which pillar is emphasized: diagrams were expected to stress conceptual knowledge, arithmetical representations procedural knowledge, and text situational knowledge. Combining formats into multiple representations is assumed to have three additional effects: formats can complement each other, one representation can constrain the interpretation of another, and integrating information from different representations supports deeper understanding.
requirements: Requires that representational formats be informationally equivalent when their effects on schema construction are compared
constraints: The study's results indicate these expected format-to-emphasis mappings are not as straightforward as expected; the data did not allow interpretation in terms of complementing, constraining, and integrating
target_learners: secondary school pupils learning combinatorics and probability theory
target_learning_goals: schema construction spanning conceptual, procedural, and situational knowledge
examples: Five SIMQUEST-built inquiry environments presented informationally equivalent representations of the same combinatorics domain in diagram, arithmetic, text, or combined formats
key_sources: Bas Kolloffel, Tessa H. S. Eysink, Ton de Jong, Pascal Wilhelm. (2009). The effects of representational format on learning combinatorics from an interactive computer simulation. Instr Sci 37:503–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9056-7

article_title: The effects of representational format on learning combinatorics from an interactive computer simulation
citation: Bas Kolloffel, Tessa H. S. Eysink, Ton de Jong, Pascal Wilhelm. (2009). The effects of representational format on learning combinatorics from an interactive computer simulation. Instr Sci 37:503–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9056-7
title: For novices facing complex, high-intrinsic-load material, prefer sequential text-plus-equation formats over tree diagrams
description: The article argues that format decisions are most critical for learners with little or no prior knowledge dealing with complex material. For combinatorics, where problem solving requires reasoning steps in a specific order, the Text + Arithmetic format "preserves the strictly sequential nature of problem solving in this domain": learners are led step-by-step through an explicit, sequential line of reasoning in everyday language, followed by an equation repeating these steps arithmetically. Tree diagrams, whose reasoning steps are implicit and require advanced diagram knowledge, are better suited to learners who already possess the relevant schemata.
requirements: Material in which problem solving requires a set of reasoning steps taken in a specific order; the text and equation components should be informationally equivalent to alternatives
constraints: The finding comes from one study with secondary pupils in one domain; the authors note the advantage of a particular format is not universal but depends on task nature, student ability, prior knowledge, and practice time
target_learners: secondary school students with little or no prior knowledge of the domain
target_learning_goals: procedural knowledge: executing action sequences to solve combinatorial problems
examples: In the experiment, pupils in the Text + Arithmetic condition read textual reasoning followed by an equation in each of five simulation sections, and outperformed the Diagram condition on procedural post-test items

article_title: What matters for students’ learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment!
citation: Jonte Bernhard. (2018). What matters for students' learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment! Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9469-x
title: Variation theory as a framework for what students can discern in laboratory learning
description: Variation theory, developed by Marton and colleagues, provides an explanatory framework for the conditions required for learning: it "holds that for learning to be brought about, the critical aspects of the object of learning must be discerned and enter the learner's focal awareness". Central concepts are discernment, simultaneity and variation: people discern aspects by experiencing variation, and the pattern of variation inherent in the learning situation fundamentally influences learning within it. The article uses it to distinguish the intended, enacted and lived objects of learning and to analyse which critical features each lab technology makes discernible.
requirements: A pattern of variation in the learning situation that makes the critical aspect of the object of learning vary while other aspects remain invariant
constraints: Results and conclusions are also consistent with conceptual conflict and cognitive conflict theories, so the framework is not uniquely required
target_learners: science and engineering students in laboratory courses
target_learning_goals: discerning critical features of physical concepts such as velocity, change of velocity and acceleration
examples: The article analyses whether motion up, down and at the turning point can be studied in each lab, since studying only downward motion gives position, velocity and acceleration the same sign, restricting discrimination between the concepts
key_sources: Jonte Bernhard. (2018). What matters for students' learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment! Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9469-x

article_title: What matters for students’ learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment!
citation: Jonte Bernhard. (2018). What matters for students' learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment! Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9469-x
title: Selective horizons model of technological mediation in laboratory inquiry
description: The article proposes a simplified model (Fig. 1) of the reductions of horizons in human inquiry using experimental technologies, in which "Amplifications & reductions, revelations & concealments, and enablements & constraints are involved in each step of the subject matter—object of study—tools for measuring and collecting data—tools for processing and (re-)presenting data chain". Mediating technologies are not neutral transmitters of information; they strongly influence figure–background relationships in experience. Human foci can be shifted through educational interventions, and what a student actually perceives depends on instructional features such as scaffolding.
requirements: Consideration of the limitations of human perception alongside the affordances of the technology
Scaffolding from the teacher and instructions to shift what students actually perceive
constraints: The categorizations in the model are solely for analytical purposes; in a real case there are no sharp boundaries between the steps
target_learners: students in science and engineering laboratories
target_learning_goals: experiencing physical phenomena through mediating technologies
examples: The model is illustrated with Galileo's telescope, which amplified perception of faint stars while reducing the visual field (magnification–reduction and revealing–concealing structures)
key_sources: Jonte Bernhard. (2018). What matters for students' learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment! Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9469-x

article_title: What matters for students’ learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment!
citation: Jonte Bernhard. (2018). What matters for students' learning in the laboratory? Do not neglect the role of experimental equipment! Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9469-x
title: Design laboratory instrumentation and tasks for the discernment of critical features, and specify the technology when drawing conclusions about lab learning
description: Because experience in labs is mediated through technologies, the possibilities for discernment and variation depend on the technology used. The article argues that "the role of experimental technologies in students' learning in labs should not be neglected" and that "crucial aspects of the technology used are not its simplicity or complexity, but the opportunities (and constraints) for discernment and (hence) learning it affords". Teachers should use these possibilities constructively by carefully designing tasks that help students discern the critical aspects of the object of learning.
requirements: Task designs based on variation theory, since probeware use alone does not necessarily lead to good learning results
Teachers who deliberately choose and exploit the affordances of the instrumentation
constraints: The use of computers and high-tech equipment is not a requirement for student learning; simple materials can work
General conclusions about learning in labs should be drawn cautiously, specifying the conditions and technology used
Belief in technological determinism is fallacious
target_learners: students in physics, science and engineering laboratory courses
target_learning_goals: discerning critical aspects of the object of learning, such as the relation between velocity and acceleration
examples: In the studied cases, photogates afforded only unsigned speed, the tape timer only downward motion, while probeware afforded study of up, down and turning-point motion; probeware tasks built on variation theory led students to discern critical aspects without prior knowledge

article_title: Accommodating heterogeneity: the interaction of instructional scaffolding with student preconditions in the learning of hypothesis-based reasoning
citation: Hanna Grimm · Peter A. Edelsbrunner · Kornelia Möller. (2023). Accommodating heterogeneity: the interaction of instructional scaffolding with student preconditions in the learning of hypothesis-based reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09601-9
title: Wooden sorting box as a static structuring scaffold for modeling hypothesis-based reasoning
description: A wooden sorting box used by teachers and student pairs to structure and visualize the conditional reasoning process: objects fulfilling the premise are tested, and outcomes are sorted into fields marked by a green smiley (verifies), a red smiley (refutes), or a yellow smiley (premise not fulfilled, no information). The article states "the wooden sorting box was aimed at helping the students to structure and visualize the complex hypothesis-based reasoning process (structuring scaffolds)" and that it was intended to relieve working memory by reducing cognitive load and supporting inhibition of irrelevant information.
requirements: Teachers received three three-hour training courses plus detailed teaching scripts and materials to implement the box and the accompanying cognitively activating questions
constraints: The box served as a static scaffold (not individually adaptive); adaptivity came from the teacher's verbal scaffolds during inquiry
target_learners: third-grade elementary students in whole science classes
target_learning_goals: hypothesis-based reasoning with conditionals: distinguishing relevant from irrelevant events and affirmative from refuting outcomes
examples: The teacher modeled the process with a table tennis ball under the hypothesis 'objects that are filled with air bounce', then pairs used one sorting box each while the teacher posed structuring and problematizing questions adaptively, fading support
key_sources: Hanna Grimm · Peter A. Edelsbrunner · Kornelia Möller. (2023). Accommodating heterogeneity: the interaction of instructional scaffolding with student preconditions in the learning of hypothesis-based reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09601-9

article_title: Accommodating heterogeneity: the interaction of instructional scaffolding with student preconditions in the learning of hypothesis-based reasoning
citation: Hanna Grimm · Peter A. Edelsbrunner · Kornelia Möller. (2023). Accommodating heterogeneity: the interaction of instructional scaffolding with student preconditions in the learning of hypothesis-based reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09601-9
title: In whole-class inquiry, combine a static structuring scaffold with teacher modeling and adaptive problematizing verbal scaffolds to serve heterogeneous student preconditions
description: The article argues that scaffolding connects two ways of dealing with heterogeneity: adapting deep structures (quality of teacher-student interaction through cognitive activation) rather than only sight structures. In the experimental condition, students received a structuring scaffold in which the teacher, supported by a visual aid, modeled the reasoning process, and — as the article states — "the teacher provides cognitively activating, problematizing verbal scaffolds during students' inquiry to react adaptively to students' difficulties with the reasoning process". This combination aimed to let a static scaffold serve students with differing prior knowledge, inhibition ability, and logical reasoning.
requirements: Teachers must be trained to deliver the modeling sequence and adaptive questions; this study supplied three three-hour courses and detailed teaching scripts
The inquiry tasks must be structured, e.g., by a predetermined order of hypotheses of increasing difficulty, which was also part of the control condition
constraints: Prototypical scaffolding takes more time than is generally available in day-to-day science instruction, so similar support is often provided for all students instead of individually tailored support
Essential scaffolding elements such as consistent diagnosis and fading of support should not be neglected
target_learners: third-graders in heterogeneous whole school classes
target_learning_goals: acquiring hypothesis-based reasoning with conditionals in inquiry-based science
examples: Within an elasticity unit on 'the bouncing ball', experimental-condition teachers modeled reasoning with the sorting box, then faded problematizing questions as student pairs no longer needed them

article_title: Testing the use of variation theory in teaching critical thinking—a field experimental study
citation: Kristoffer Larsson · Klas Andersson. (2025). Testing the use of variation theory in teaching critical thinking—a field experimental study. Instructional Science (2025) 53:1025–1046. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09721-y
title: Variation theory of learning and teaching: learning as discerning new aspects of a phenomenon through systematic patterns of variation (contrast, then generalization)
description: Variation theory is a general learning theory with an aligned teaching theory, in which learning means becoming able to handle a phenomenon in a more powerful way in novel situations by discerning a new aspect of it. The article states that "The pattern to be presented first is called contrast and is considered to be the vehicle of learning", opening up the aspect by juxtaposing values against an invariant case. Contrast is followed by the generalization pattern, where "each value, one at a time, of the aspect is kept invariant while varying the cases", so students see the aspect applies across cases. The study applied this to the aspect of alternating points of view on societal issues.
requirements: Systematic introduction of the patterns of variation in the specified order, with the case kept invariant during contrast and the value kept invariant during generalization
constraints: The theory's application to critical thinking had been theoretically developed but not extensively empirically tested before this study
target_learners: Swedish 9th grade students (15–16 years old)
target_learning_goals: Alternating between points of view when reasoning about societal issues
examples: Teachers showed four student responses to a voting-age task differing from zero to three alternations of points of view, then generalized across voting-age, referendum and wage-difference tasks value by value.
key_sources: Kristoffer Larsson · Klas Andersson. (2025). Testing the use of variation theory in teaching critical thinking—a field experimental study. Instructional Science (2025) 53:1025–1046. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09721-y

article_title: Testing the use of variation theory in teaching critical thinking—a field experimental study
citation: Kristoffer Larsson · Klas Andersson. (2025). Testing the use of variation theory in teaching critical thinking—a field experimental study. Instructional Science (2025) 53:1025–1046. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09721-y
title: Intervention teaching material: national-test tasks and scored student responses from a national database operationalizing contrast and generalization
description: The treatment material consisted of "the three tasks, i.e. the voting-age task, the referendum task and the wage-difference task, and student responses to these three tasks taken from the database" — a nationwide sample of about 600 complete Swedish national test responses per year. Student responses were pre-analysed and sorted into those showing zero to three alternations of points of view, enabling teachers to vary the aspect (number of alternations) against an invariant task for contrast, and vary tasks against an invariant value for generalization. Control teachers worked the same tasks without access to the database responses.
requirements: Access to scored student responses illustrating graded values of the target aspect, obtained from analysis of a national test database
constraints: Control teachers had no access to the student responses from the database, so the two conditions differed in materials as well as method
target_learners: Swedish 9th grade students in social studies
target_learning_goals: Alternating points of view on societal issues such as voting age, referendums and wage differences
examples: Four voting-age responses (Table 1) illustrated zero, one, two and three alternations of points of view and were used in the contrast pattern.

article_title: It matters how to recall – task differences in retrieval practice
citation: Tino Endres, Lena Kranzdorf, Vivien Schneider, Alexander Renkl. (2020). It matters how to recall – task differences in retrieval practice. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09526-1
title: Spreading activation account of task-specific retrieval practice effects
description: The article draws on elaborative retrieval theory, in which recalling specific knowledge strengthens that memory trace and search processes "spreads activation to other pieces of knowledge that are connected to the retrieved piece of knowledge". Task specificity shapes the activation pattern: specific short-answer tasks strongly activate targeted pieces, while free-recall distributes activation across many pieces. The authors argue this account has "greater explanatory value than the transfer-appropriate processing perspective" for differences among recall tasks.

constraints: The authors state their study was not designed to (dis-)confirm theories and that follow-up studies should test the spreading-activation assumption

article_title: Scrum methodology in context-based secondary chemistry classes: effects on students’ achievement and on students’ perceptions of affective and metacognitive dimensions of their learning
citation: Vogelzang, J., Admiraal, W. F., van Driel, J. H. (2021). Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09554-5
title: Scrum methodology as an educational scaffold: a project-management framework with ceremonies, roles and artefacts that structures planning, monitoring and reflection in complex context-based learning environments
description: Scrum methodology is "a project management framework" from business and industry, restyled for education. It rests on three pillars: "transparency, inspection and adaptation", enacted through ceremonies (stand-up, sprint review, retrospective), roles (product owner, scrum master) and artefacts (product backlog, scrum board with burndown chart, intermediate products). The article describes how its features scaffold three challenges of student-centred learning: sense making, process management and reflection, and it structures a thirteen-step implementation in a context-based chemistry module (Table 1).

attitude towards chemistry

article_title: Investigating construct validity of cognitive load measurement using single-item subjective rating scales
citation: Schuessler, K., Fischer, V., & Walpuski, M. (2025). Investigating construct validity of cognitive load measurement using single-item subjective rating scales. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09692-6
title: Researchers must deliberately choose between invested mental effort and perceived task difficulty items and state at which point and how frequently cognitive load is measured
description: Because the two dominant single-item cognitive load ratings capture different aspects of overall load, the article advises that "researchers should therefore discuss carefully which item they use and how this may limit the results of their study". It further advises "to precisely examine at which point and how frequently cognitive load is measured as delayed ratings are closely related to more demanding items within a set of items". The principle applies whenever single-item subjective ratings are used as an indicator of overall cognitive load.
requirements: Researchers must decide and justify which single-item rating (invested mental effort or perceived task difficulty) is used, since the two do not measure the same construct.
The timing and frequency of measurement must be specified, because delayed ratings are closely related to the more demanding items in a set.
constraints: Single-item subjective ratings provide only an impression of overall cognitive load and do not differentiate intrinsic from extraneous load.
Delayed single ratings are affected by the most demanding item, so changes in load during a task set are better captured by repeated measurement.
target_learners: secondary school students
learners in large-scale classroom or test settings
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of perceived cognitive load during task performance
examples: In the reanalyzed study, cognitive load was rated after each of 32 tasks (sets of four items) using adapted 7-point versions of the Paas (1992) mental effort item and the Marcus et al. (1996) perceived task difficulty item.

article_title: Investigating construct validity of cognitive load measurement using single-item subjective rating scales
citation: Schuessler, K., Fischer, V., & Walpuski, M. (2025). Investigating construct validity of cognitive load measurement using single-item subjective rating scales. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09692-6
title: Cognitive load as an at least two-dimensional construct with a task-difficulty component and an invested-effort component
description: Following Paas (1992), the article treats cognitive load as "an at least two-dimensional concept". One component, perceived task or item difficulty, "refers to the requirements of the task" and task-learner interactions (Paas's mental load); the other, invested mental effort, "refers to the cognitive capacity a learner invests to accomplish task demands". This definition concerns overall load and deliberately does not separate intrinsic from extraneous load. The study operationalizes the two components with the two dominant single-item rating scales and models them as two Rasch dimensions.
requirements: Measurement must distinguish which component is being rated, because the task-difficulty item pertains mainly to the task while the effort item pertains to a process involving more aspects than only the task.
constraints: The definition refers to overall load and does not differentiate between intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load.
target_learners: secondary school students
learners working on chemistry competence tasks
target_learning_goals: understanding and measuring overall cognitive load during learning and performance
examples: The study measured both components after each task with single-item 7-point rating scales adapted from Paas (1992) and Marcus et al. (1996), then estimated them as two separate Rasch dimensions.
