citation: Peretz, R., Tal, M., Akiri, E., Dori, D., & Dori, Y. J. (2023). Fostering engineering and science students' and teachers' systems thinking and conceptual modeling skills. Instructional Science, 51, 509–543. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09625-9
title: Object-Process Methodology (OPM) as the conceptual modeling language for the online assignments
description: Object-Process Methodology (OPM) is the conceptual modeling language participants used in this study: the 55 participants "performed four food-related learning assignments and created conceptual models in Object-Process Methodology". OPM models are assessed here at the level of top-level OPM diagrams, using attributes covering system function, structure, behavior, model clarity, and OPL (Object-Process Language) sentences, as detailed in the study's modified Systems Thinking Assessment Rubric (STAR*) appendix. The element therefore links modeling practice to systems thinking development.

It defines seven attributes (A1–A7) across System and Model aspects: intended purpose, main function, structural relations, level of detail, procedural relations, model readability, and OPL main-process procedural sentences, each with printed scoring scales from zero points up to two or three points. For example, A2 requires "Exactly one main process, which transforms at least one object".

article_title: The effect of contrasting cases during problem solving prior to and after instruction
citation: Loibl, K., Tillema, M., Rummel, N., & van Gog, T. (2020). The effect of contrasting cases during problem solving prior to and after instruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09504-7
title: Three-mechanism account of why problem solving before instruction can benefit conceptual understanding
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that problem solving prior to instruction (PS-I) benefits conceptual understanding through three mechanisms identified in the Loibl et al. (2017) review: "activating prior knowledge, becoming aware of knowledge gaps, and recognizing deep features of the target concept." Activating prior knowledge makes students more susceptible to subsequent instruction; incorrect attempts make knowledge gaps salient; and attention guided to deep features (functional components) prepares students to map instructed procedures onto discovered features. The study tests whether order alone (activation) versus contrasting cases (gap awareness and deep-feature discovery) trigger these mechanisms.
requirements: Each mechanism needs its own trigger; the article states the effectiveness of PS-I results from an interplay of mechanisms that each needs to be triggered.
constraints: The study found that activating prior knowledge by problem solving alone was insufficient to improve conceptual understanding, and unguided contrasting cases did not trigger the gap-awareness or deep-feature mechanisms.
target_learners: secondary education mathematics students (third year of Dutch secondary education, age 14–15)
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of the concept of variance and procedural fluency with the mean absolute deviation
examples: The experiment operationalized the mechanisms by manipulating order of phases (activation) and contrasting cases varying range, sample size, and distribution (deep-feature discovery), with no typical student solutions in instruction.

citation: W.S. de Grave, H.G. Schmidt & H.P.A. Boshuizen. (2001). Effects of problem-based discussion on studying a subsequent text: A randomized trial among first year medical students. Instructional Science 29: 33-44. https://link.springer.com/journal/11251
title: Elaboration hypothesis of the cognitive effects of problem-based learning
description: The article frames problem-based discussion as "an educational procedure, aimed at increasing the interaction between knowledge already available in the participants and the new information to be learnt". Self-generated explanations stimulated in the tutorial group promote elaboration, integrating new information into the existing knowledge base so that it is better organized, more accessible, and better recalled. The authors summarize their findings as consistent with this hypothesis as far as the analysis phase is concerned, while noting the recall patterns did not show the predicted specificity.

constraints: The article locates the demonstrated effect at the level of the analysis phase prior to individual study; effects at the course level remained to be demonstrated

title: Activate prior knowledge through small-group problem discussion before assigning a text to study
description: Because discussing a relevant problem before individual study improved recall of the text in this randomized trial, the article supports the practice of having small tutorial groups analyze and brainstorm explanations for a problem that relates to a subsequently assigned expository text. The discussion procedure used problem definition, a 30-minute brainstorming session, and tutor summaries on a flip-chart, with tutors giving no clues about correctness. The authors conclude that "it is the opportunity for problem-based elaboration on existing knowledge, prior to studying a relevant text, that is responsible for the strong effect demonstrated".

title: Three-dimensional support framework for GenAI integration: pedagogical, governance, and operational dimensions
description: The article's discussion maps its findings onto a three-dimensional framework for supporting GenAI use, which "constitutes pedagogical, governance, and operational dimensions". Pedagogically, targeted classroom strategies such as human-versus-GenAI mini-competitions and educational resources instruct students on better technology use. At the governance level, teachers and institutions offer clear guidance on GenAI implications and human translators' advantages. Operationally, the curriculum is re-evaluated and adapted for enhanced AI literacy and job-displacement concerns.

article_title: The more, the worse? The influence of the seductive detail amount on learning
citation: Lukas Wesenberg, Sebastian Jansen, Felix Krieglstein, Felicia Meusel, Sascha Schneider, Georg Valtin, Günter Daniel Rey. (2026). The more, the worse? The influence of the seductive detail amount on learning. Instructional Science (2026) 54:29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09781-8
title: Three cognitive-process accounts of the seductive details effect: distraction, disruption, and diversion theory
description: The article frames the seductive details effect within cognitive load theory and the cognitive theory of multimedia learning, which assume severely limited working memory. It details three mechanisms by which SDs exert extraneous processing: "Following distraction theory, the larger the amount of seductive content, the higher the probability that learners get distracted from the learning-relevant material." Disruption theory holds that longer interruptions impair mental organization of text segments, and diversion theory holds that thematically deviant SDs mislead learners about the overall gist. From this view SDs raise extraneous load and impair learning, predicting a dose-response relationship with SD amount.
requirements: The accounts assume limited working memory capacity, so overload likelihood rises with total cognitive load
constraints: The article notes prior evidence that SD effects can be mitigated by signaling, placement at the end rather than beginning, and marking SDs as learning-irrelevant
target_learners: students learning from texts with embedded interesting-but-irrelevant content
target_learning_goals: recall and transfer of learning-relevant text content
examples: The two experiments varied SD amount from 0% to 50% of the learning text while holding the number of interruptions constant to test the amount prediction derived from the three accounts

article_title: The more, the worse? The influence of the seductive detail amount on learning
citation: Lukas Wesenberg, Sebastian Jansen, Felix Krieglstein, Felicia Meusel, Sascha Schneider, Georg Valtin, Günter Daniel Rey. (2026). The more, the worse? The influence of the seductive detail amount on learning. Instructional Science (2026) 54:29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09781-8
title: Avoid large amounts of seductive details in learning materials; small amounts may have negligible effects
description: Because both studies showed a linear negative effect of the seductive detail amount on recall while no effect appeared for transfer, load, or motivation, the article recommends limiting the volume of interesting-but-irrelevant digressions in learning materials. As the authors state, "Especially the inclusion of large amounts of digressions should be avoided by teachers and instructional designers, while the inclusion of small amounts might have rather negligible effects." The recommendation follows from the dose-response pattern rather than from a tested optimum.
requirements: Requires keeping the amount of seductive content low relative to the learning-relevant text (conditions spanning 0%–50% SD text were tested)
constraints: The effect was observed on recall only; transfer showed no significant linear effect and a Study 2 polynomial transfer trend was unstable under cross-validation
target_learners: students in text-based learning environments, from secondary school to university
target_learning_goals: recall of learning-relevant text content
examples: Study 1 embedded 150 or 300 seductive words in a 600-word text and Study 2 embedded 120–480 seductive words in a 960-word text, holding interruptions constant across SD conditions

article_title: Teacher versus student perspectives on instructional quality in mathematics education across countries
citation: Xin Liu, Kajsa Yang Hansen, Jan De Neve, Martin Valcke. (2023). Teacher versus student perspectives on instructional quality in mathematics education across countries. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09652-6
title: Continuum for classifying instructional quality frameworks: generic, subject-specific, and hybrid
description: The article organizes frameworks for conceptualizing instructional quality along a continuum adapted from Charalambous and Praetorius (2018), in which "Senden et al. (2022) adjusted this continuum by building on three categories: generic frameworks, subject-specific frameworks, and hybrid frameworks." Generic frameworks emphasize general-level aspects without subject-specific teaching demands (e.g., the Three Basic Dimensional framework of classroom management, cognitive activation, and supportive climate); subject-specific frameworks focus on content-related interactions (e.g., MQI, M-Scan, IQA); hybrid frameworks combine both, exemplified by the Dynamic Model of Educational Effectiveness with eight key decisions. The study uses this continuum to interpret whether its identified dimensions reflect generic or mathematics-specific features.
requirements: The article applies mathematics as the specific domain to describe the primary frameworks and dimensions on the continuum (Fig. 1).
constraints: The article notes researchers consider the DMEE a generic framework without subject-specific instruction, though its own findings suggest DMEE can be seen as hybrid.
target_learners: mathematics students in primary and secondary education
target_learning_goals: conceptualizing and evaluating the quality of mathematics instruction
examples: The article situates the Three Basic Dimensional framework (classroom management, cognitive activation, supportive climate) as generic and the DMEE's eight dimensions (management of time, classroom climate, orientation, questioning, structuring, teaching-modeling, application, assessment) as hybrid.
key_sources: Xin Liu, Kajsa Yang Hansen, Jan De Neve, Martin Valcke. (2023). Teacher versus student perspectives on instructional quality in mathematics education across countries. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09652-6

article_title: Effects of related decorative pictures on learning and metacognition
citation: Demian Scherer, Annika Verkühlen, Stephan Dutke. (2023). Effects of related decorative pictures on learning and metacognition. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09618-8
title: Spreading activation account of related-picture effects: passive mutual facilitation of related concepts improves encoding into long-term memory
description: The article proposes that thematically related non-explanatory pictures improve learning through spreading activation: in semantic networks "activation can spread back and forth between related concepts", so related concepts "mutually reactivate each other", which automatically maintains related information in working memory longer and increases the probability of encoding into long-term memory (drawing on Davelaar et al., 2006, and Anderson's spreading activation theories). Because the process is passive, effects should appear mainly on retention/knowledge measures rather than transfer. The two experiments' pattern — knowledge gains in Experiment 1, metacognitive monitoring gains in Experiment 2, no transfer effects — is interpreted as consistent with this account.
requirements: Pictures must be related to the text's content without directly representing or explaining the text's main concepts, so effects cannot be attributed to explanatory power or dual coding redundancy
constraints: The effect is predicted to appear on knowledge/retention measures, not necessarily transfer, "because of the passive nature of the spreading activation process"
In Experiment 1 the monitoring effect did not appear, so the account does not predict which of the two knowledge-derived measures manifests the benefit
target_learners: university students in teacher education seminars
eighth-grade secondary school students
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition from expository text
metacognitive monitoring accuracy
examples: Experiment 1 pictures included a library photo related to study behavior and a mountain runner related to the effort assumption of self-control; the text described abstract concepts (willpower, population growth) that pictures could not directly represent
key_sources: Demian Scherer, Annika Verkühlen, Stephan Dutke. (2023). Effects of related decorative pictures on learning and metacognition. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09618-8

article_title: Effects of related decorative pictures on learning and metacognition
citation: Demian Scherer, Annika Verkühlen, Stephan Dutke. (2023). Effects of related decorative pictures on learning and metacognition. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09618-8
title: Behavioral measure of maintained situational interest based on choices of future seminar topics or take-home texts
description: The article operationalizes maintained situational interest not by verbal self-report but behaviorally: participants decided which of six described seminar topics (Experiment 1) or which of six take-home texts (Experiment 2) they wanted to engage with, and the count of yes-responses was the measure. The authors argue this is "not a merely verbal measure" but "a direct measure of whether participants want to engage further with this topic", providing a link to future interest-related behavior. The measure correlated significantly with topic interest and triggered situational interest in both experiments.
requirements: Participants must be able to choose among several genuinely related follow-up materials without inspecting them beforehand
constraints: In Experiment 2 the measure detected a reduction in maintained interest under pictures that the authors could not fully explain, calling it possibly "an incidental finding"
target_learners: university students in teacher education seminars
eighth-grade secondary school students
target_learning_goals: measuring maintained situational interest in learning research
examples: In Experiment 2, six take-home texts covered topics such as population policy in China, educational efforts in Tanzania, the carrying capacity of the earth, and world food; participants indicated yes or no for each text they wanted to take

article_title: Better self-explaining backwards or forwards? Prompting self-explanation in video-based modelling examples for learning a diagnostic strategy
citation: Meier, J., Hesse, P., Abele, S., Renkl, A., & Glogger-Frey, I. (2024). Better self-explaining backwards or forwards? Prompting self-explanation in video-based modelling examples for learning a diagnostic strategy. Instructional Science, 52, 613–638. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09651-7
title: Cognitive load theory (1998 conception) as the explanatory framework for prompt-direction and expertise effects in example-based learning
description: The article frames worked/modelling examples and self-explanation prompts through the 1998 conception of Cognitive Load Theory, which assumes limited working memory and three load types: germane, intrinsic, and extraneous. Prior knowledge reduces intrinsic load because "they already have cognitive schemas enabling them to combine multiple elements from the learning material and handle those as a single element in their working memory." The theory predicts anticipatory prompts raise both germane and intrinsic load, so only higher-prior-knowledge learners can manage them — the mechanism the study's moderation results were designed to test.
requirements: Enough working-memory capacity for germane processing, achieved by minimizing extraneous load through example study
constraints: The authors deliberately use the 1998 conception rather than the 2019 revision to GCL concepts
target_learners: automotive apprentices learning a diagnostic strategy
target_learning_goals: complex problem-solving and diagnostic strategy knowledge and skills
examples: The experiment gave all apprentices a 35-minute instruction phase on the four-step diagnostic strategy, then varied prompt direction in video-based modelling examples

article_title: Better self-explaining backwards or forwards? Prompting self-explanation in video-based modelling examples for learning a diagnostic strategy
citation: Meier, J., Hesse, P., Abele, S., Renkl, A., & Glogger-Frey, I. (2024). Better self-explaining backwards or forwards? Prompting self-explanation in video-based modelling examples for learning a diagnostic strategy. Instructional Science, 52, 613–638. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09651-7
title: Match self-explanation prompt direction in modelling examples to learners' prior knowledge — anticipatory prompts for stronger learners, retrospective prompts for weaker learners
description: The article's moderation results suggest that the direction of self-explanation prompts in example-based learning should be adapted to expertise: "anticipatory prompts are more beneficial for learners with more prior knowledge, whereas learners with less prior knowledge profit more from retrospective prompts." This follows the expertise-reversal logic: anticipatory prompts demand integration of prior and upcoming steps, which only learners with sufficient schemas can handle productively. The authors themselves caution that replication is needed before practitioners apply this.
requirements: Learners' prior knowledge must be assessed (here via a diagnosis-relevant reception competence test) before assigning prompt type
constraints: The authors state replication studies are necessary; findings rest on borderline significance (p = .05) and about 50% of prompts were answered sub-optimally
target_learners: automotive apprentices learning a complex diagnostic strategy
vocational learners with varying prior knowledge levels
target_learning_goals: diagnostic strategy knowledge and skills
self-efficacy in performing diagnoses
examples: In the experiment, apprentices with mean-centered DRC scores above 1.68 benefited from anticipatory prompts on strategy description scores, while those below −0.85 showed better self-efficacy growth with retrospective prompts

article_title: Investigating the role of an inquiry-based science lab on students’ scientific literacy
citation: Gülüzar Eymur · Pınar Seda Çetin (2024). Investigating the role of an inquiry-based science lab on students' scientific literacy. Instructional Science (2024) 52:743–760. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09672-w
title: The Argument-Driven Inquiry (ADI) instructional model with eight interrelated steps
description: ADI is an inquiry-based instructional model that gives "a more central place to argumentation and the role of argument in the social construction of scientific knowledge while promoting inquiry." It comprises eight interrelated steps, from identification of the task and research question through developing a method, generating a tentative argument with claim, evidence and justification, an argumentation session, reflective discussion, writing an investigation report, double-blind group peer review, and report revision. In this study five ADI laboratory investigations (density, germination, light, power of lamp, shade) were run over ten weeks with groups of three or four students.
requirements: Students work in groups to design their own method, generate arguments including claim, evidence and justification, and complete individual written reports that are peer reviewed and revised.
constraints: The study's teacher was experienced and taught during four months about the ADI instructional method before treatment.
target_learners: Eighth-grade students in public elementary school science classes
target_learning_goals: Scientific literacy
Scientific inquiry practices
Argumentation and scientific writing
examples: Five ADI laboratory investigations related to chemistry, biology and physics were employed through 10 weeks, exploring density, light, germination, power of lamp, and shade.
key_sources: Gülüzar Eymur · Pınar Seda Çetin (2024). Investigating the role of an inquiry-based science lab on students' scientific literacy. Instructional Science (2024) 52:743–760. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09672-w

article_title: Investigating the role of an inquiry-based science lab on students’ scientific literacy
citation: Gülüzar Eymur · Pınar Seda Çetin (2024). Investigating the role of an inquiry-based science lab on students' scientific literacy. Instructional Science (2024) 52:743–760. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09672-w
title: Use speaking and writing as literacy tools within inquiry labs to support scientific literacy
description: The article argues that engaging students in meaningful scientific practices — argumentation sessions (speaking) and writing investigation reports (writing) — supports scientific literacy, because scientific literacy has both private and public views: understanding scientific knowledge individually and discussing and criticizing ideas with peers to reach consensus. The authors conclude that "scientific practices like ADI method should be used where students learn doing science rather than only conceptual understanding to develop students' scientific literacy."
requirements: Laboratory activities must include argumentation sessions, individually written investigation reports, and peer review so both speaking and writing function as literacy tools.
constraints: In the study the implementation time may not have been enough to provide important changes in scientific literacy of students.
target_learners: Middle school / eighth-grade science students
target_learning_goals: Scientific literacy
Constructing and critiquing scientific arguments
examples: The experimental condition used five ADI laboratory investigations through 10 weeks, with argumentation sessions via a large whiteboard, individually written reports, blinded peer review, and report revision based on peer feedback.

article_title: Refuting student teachers’ misconceptions about multimedia learning
citation: Anja Prinz, Julia Kollmer, Lisa Flick, Alexander Renkl, Alexander Eitel. (2022). Refuting student teachers' misconceptions about multimedia learning. Instructional Science, 50, 89–110. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09568-z
title: Four common misconceptions about multimedia learning
description: The article organizes multimedia-learning misconceptions into four named types: the learning-styles misconception (matching material to visualizer/verbalizer styles), the hemispheric-isolation misconception (presenting text and pictures to activate both brain hemispheres), the naïve-summation misconception (more media and modalities yield better retention), and the motivation-primacy misconception (multimedia works mainly by raising motivation). It states "there are four common multimedia misconceptions" and explains the scientifically correct account for each, such as that "the extent of active processing and successful integration with prior knowledge rather than the mere number of media used to present information predicts retention".
requirements: Learners or teachers must hold the misconception for a refutation intervention targeting it to be relevant
target_learners: student teachers
in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: correct knowledge about effective multimedia material design
examples: The experiment's texts and questionnaire items each addressed one of the four misconceptions: learning styles, hemispheric isolation, naïve summation, and motivation primacy.
key_sources: Anja Prinz, Julia Kollmer, Lisa Flick, Alexander Renkl, Alexander Eitel. (2022). Refuting student teachers' misconceptions about multimedia learning. Instructional Science, 50, 89–110. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09568-z

article_title: Advances in research on composite instructional designs – investigating intermediate knowledge and preparation effects
citation: Katharina Loibl, Valentina Nachtigall, Timo Leuders. (2025). Advances in research on composite instructional designs – investigating intermediate knowledge and preparation effects. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09751-6
title: The CID framework explains preparation effects in composite instructional designs through intermediate knowledge
description: The CID framework (a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs) explains how learning in one phase affects subsequent phases by focusing on the learner's knowledge state between phases. The editorial states it analyzes "intermediate knowledge"—the knowledge between phases—and how it shapes further learning, constituting a preparation effect. It builds on Koedinger et al. (2012) by positing analysis on three levels: instructional design, learning processes, and knowledge components, supported by research designs that isolate single mechanisms.
requirements: A well-crafted research design that helps to isolate single mechanisms, and analysis on three levels—instructional design, learning processes, and knowledge components
constraints: Studying only the sequence of phases tests general effects, not single mechanisms; the framework recommends additionally manipulating one phase without altering the sequence
target_learners: learners in formal instructional settings across domains
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding and transfer in multi-phase instructional designs
examples: The editorial links all special-issue contributions to the framework, including studies altering phase sequence and studies manipulating a single phase
key_sources: Katharina Loibl, Valentina Nachtigall, Timo Leuders. (2025). Advances in research on composite instructional designs – investigating intermediate knowledge and preparation effects. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09751-6

article_title: Deficit narratives as teacher foils: how vulnerability and emotional regimes shape teacher discourse
citation: Samantha A. Marshall, Grace A. Chen. (2025). Deficit narratives as teacher foils: how vulnerability and emotional regimes shape teacher discourse. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09740-9
title: Emotional regimes as structuring conditions of teacher collegial discourse
description: Emotional regimes are socially and culturally embedded norms governing how teachers should feel and express feelings in particular situations (Zembylas, 2005), rarely explicit and enforced through social exclusion of deviators. In this study, teachers were subject to regimes that "valued positivity about themselves and their profession" and dispassionate intellectual analysis of pedagogy. The theory explains how breaches of these invisible rules precipitate discourse moves, including deficit narratives, that restore the normative emotional terrain.
requirements: Regimes operate implicitly, so analysis must attend to expressed emotions and emotions research suggests were expected
constraints: Regimes documented here arose in feminized professions like teaching and reflect gendered expectations
target_learners: mid-career mathematics teachers in collegial professional development
target_learning_goals: teacher learning of ambitious and equitable pedagogies
asset-oriented discourse about students and families
examples: Winograd's self-study identified five emotions permitted under the teacher emotional regime at his school, including love for students and avoidance of emotional extremes
key_sources: Samantha A. Marshall, Grace A. Chen. (2025). Deficit narratives as teacher foils: how vulnerability and emotional regimes shape teacher discourse. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09740-9

article_title: Deficit narratives as teacher foils: how vulnerability and emotional regimes shape teacher discourse
citation: Samantha A. Marshall, Grace A. Chen. (2025). Deficit narratives as teacher foils: how vulnerability and emotional regimes shape teacher discourse. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09740-9
title: Collective vulnerability as interactionally produced by destabilization of emotional regimes
description: Extending prior work that treated vulnerability as individual or as threats to group reputation, the article proposes that collective vulnerability can be interactionally produced when a group's normative emotional terrain is destabilized. If "affirmation and positivity are the normative way for teachers to relate to each other in a group, and a teacher breaches this norm through sustained negativity," the group's expectations of each other may be threatened. This account links vulnerability to face threats from video-based PD, where practice is on display with decreased room for plausible deniability.
requirements: Analysis must trace how a critique becomes a threat through the collective response to it
constraints: Proposed from two extreme cases of asset-oriented teachers; the authors state they do not know whether teacher vulnerability commonly precipitates deficit narratives
target_learners: teacher teams in video-based professional development
target_learning_goals: collaborative sensemaking about teaching practice
professional identity maintenance
examples: In both focal cases, the destabilization of emotional regimes by persistent negative self-critique produced collective vulnerability that colleagues resolved by blaming students and families
key_sources: Samantha A. Marshall, Grace A. Chen. (2025). Deficit narratives as teacher foils: how vulnerability and emotional regimes shape teacher discourse. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09740-9

article_title: Effects of a literary intervention on teachers’ monologic and dialogic practices and the quality of students’ contributions
citation: Dammert, Y., Gasser, L., & Murphy, P. K. (2026). Effects of a literary intervention on teachers' monologic and dialogic practices and the quality of students' contributions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09809-z
title: Quality Talk (QT): a text-based discussion approach fostering critical-analytic thinking through authentic questions, reasoning, and co-constructed responses
description: Quality Talk operationalizes dialogic pedagogy in a structured framework for language-arts discussion that fosters students' critical-analytic thinking and high-level text comprehension. The article states that "QT emphasizes three core dialogic elements: authentic questions, reasoning, and co-constructed responses (i.e., cumulative and exploratory talk)". It integrates teacher talk moves (summarizing, modeling, marking, prompting, challenging), mini-lessons, discussion rules, and literacy-journal prompts, and is designed for small groups of about four to six students in which control gradually shifts from teacher to students.
requirements: Explicit instruction in dialogic strategies via mini-lessons plus sustained teacher scaffolding and coaching
Small-group discussion format of approximately four to six students
constraints: Prior QT studies were primarily conducted in the United States with single-group designs, limiting causal inference before this study
target_learners: Fourth- and fifth-grade primary students
target_learning_goals: Critical-analytic thinking
High-level text comprehension
Dialogic discussion and reasoning skills
examples: In this study QT was adapted to Swiss fourth- and fifth-grade literary education with literary-fiction books, Character Questions and Big Questions, and video-based coaching.

article_title: Effects of a literary intervention on teachers’ monologic and dialogic practices and the quality of students’ contributions
citation: Dammert, Y., Gasser, L., & Murphy, P. K. (2026). Effects of a literary intervention on teachers' monologic and dialogic practices and the quality of students' contributions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09809-z
title: Swiss QT literary intervention package: nine mini-lessons, four literary-fiction books, literacy journals, and small-group discussions
description: The adapted intervention is a one-year language-arts program in which students were "instructed on how to identify various authentic questions, justify their claims, and collaboratively construct knowledge in discussions through nine mini-lessons". Students read and discussed four award-winning children's books in small groups across 11 literary discussions, kept literacy journals to prepare authentic questions and responses, and followed discussion rules establishing normative expectations for a dialogic culture. Teachers implemented the program with high fidelity, spending 34.07 hours versus a prescribed 32.92 hours.
requirements: Teacher professional development: two workshops plus three to four video-based coaching sessions
Heterogeneous small groups of three to seven students formed at the study's outset
constraints: The adaptation exclusively focuses on literary fiction with a moral-dilemma theme matching the assessment story
target_learners: Fourth- and fifth-grade students in German-speaking Swiss primary schools
target_learning_goals: Asking authentic questions
Justifying claims
Collaboratively constructing knowledge in discussion
examples: Books included The Very Persistent Gappers of Frip, Brown: My Alter Ego Is a Superhero, Rabbit & Bear: Attack of the Snack, and Balaclava Boy, with an average LIX score of 28.35 indicating low complexity.

citation: Dammert, Y., Gasser, L., & Murphy, P. K. (2026). Effects of a literary intervention on teachers' monologic and dialogic practices and the quality of students' contributions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09809-z
title: Scaffold dialogic discussions with talk moves and progressively fade teacher control so students assume interpretive authority
description: The article argues that simply limiting instructional control is insufficient; scaffolding—targeted, adaptive, temporary support—is crucial, and "teacher support must not only be responsive to learners' reasoning and argumentation but also be gradually withdrawn as their competence and autonomy develop". Whole-class mini-lessons model dialogic skills that are then applied and refined in small-group discussions, during which control gradually shifts from teachers to students, who increasingly manage turn-taking and assume interpretive authority over the text. This principle underpins the practice shifts the intervention produced.
requirements: Initial explicit instruction and modeling of dialogic skills before independent small-group application
Ongoing teacher scaffolding via talk moves while control is progressively faded
constraints: Even with dialogic elements present, teachers may retain underlying control through turn management and evaluation (overfacilitation), which the study's monologic codes were designed to detect
target_learners: Primary school students in language-arts/literary discussions
target_learning_goals: Student agency in discussion
Reasoning and co-construction of knowledge
examples: Students demonstrated ownership by allocating speaker turns themselves and independently posing questions and introducing new topics.

article_title: Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality
citation: Anouk ten Peze, Tanja Janssen, Gert Rijlaarsdam, Daphne van Weijen. (2024). Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09647-3
title: Dual-process (Geneplore) creative writing instruction design framework with Schacter's five creative teaching areas
description: The article grounds its creative writing unit in Finke et al.'s dual-process Geneplore model, in which "Generative and exploratory processes alternate continuously", mapped onto writing as alternation between the fictionworld (generative) and the writingrealm (explorative), following Csikszentmihalyi and Doyle. For instructional conditions it uses Schacter et al.'s Creative Teaching Framework: "Schacter et al. identified five areas that increase the likelihood of creative outcomes" — explicit teaching of creative thinking strategies, choice and discovery, intrinsic motivation, a creativity-conducive environment, and imagination and fantasy. These are restructured into a nested design of learning content embedded in learning mode and conditions.
requirements: Creative thinking strategies must be taught explicitly and be domain-specific, aligned to the task at hand, since divergent-thinking training alone did not transfer to unaligned genres in prior work the article cites (Baer)
constraints: The framework is applied to little-c creativity in fictional short-story writing in upper secondary education; Press (environmental contribution) was excluded
target_learners: Grade 10 pre-university secondary students (15-16 years)
target_learning_goals: Creative (fictional story) writing quality
Divergent thinking
Writing flow/speed
examples: The six-lesson Writing Lab operationalized the alternation: e.g., lesson 2 'Mix your story' has students generate three story ideas (divergent) then select (convergent) before drafting and peer-evaluating
key_sources: Anouk ten Peze, Tanja Janssen, Gert Rijlaarsdam, Daphne van Weijen. (2024). Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09647-3

citation: Anouk ten Peze, Tanja Janssen, Gert Rijlaarsdam, Daphne van Weijen. (2024). Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09647-3
title: Writing Lab six-lesson lesson-series pattern alternating divergent and convergent thinking with a fixed compare-contrast, generate, select, apply, evaluate activity cycle
description: A reusable lesson-series pattern for creative writing in upper secondary education: a metacognitive introductory lesson, four element-focused lessons (mindmaps/character, suspense, dialogue, perspective), and a final application lesson. "Lessons two through five followed a similar pattern: alternate divergent and convergent thinking, compare and contrast, application and evaluation." Cognitive strategy instruction follows Merrill's demonstration and application principles, using strong and weak peer models for observational learning, extensive drafting phases (about 20 of 50 minutes in four lessons), and group peer feedback with compliments and recommendations rather than competition.
requirements: Alternation must be explicitly indicated to students (icons in materials) and contextualized to the lesson's target writing task
A writer-reader community with constructive, encouraging peer feedback and a safe climate where nothing is considered crazy or stupid
constraints: Designed for a context with no existing creative writing lesson series for upper secondary education in the Netherlands; the program deliberately did not address transfer to argumentative writing explicitly
target_learners: Grade 10 pre-university secondary students in Dutch L1 education
target_learning_goals: Drafting and rewriting creative short stories
Creative thinking strategies (fluency, originality, flexibility, elaboration)
examples: Lesson 4 ('Roaring, whispering, screeching, or panting?') generates sentence variations divergently, shares them whole-class, expands with tags, drafts a dialogue-based story, and acts dialogues out in groups

citation: Anouk ten Peze, Tanja Janssen, Gert Rijlaarsdam, Daphne van Weijen. (2024). Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09647-3
title: Balance choice with structure and support through scaffolding with fading and transfer of responsibility in creative writing lessons
description: The article recommends balancing freedom and structure when teaching creative writing: tasks should be authentic, novel and exciting, and students choose between parallel open-ended assignments, while "The scaffolding principle was applied to assert the required balance between structure and freedom". Fading — the gradual withdrawal of scaffolding — provided ample idea-generation support early and removed it in later lessons until students worked independently, so that students' responsibility for task performance gradually increased. This operationalizes Van de Pol et al.'s key scaffolding characteristics cited by the article.
requirements: Open target tasks with multiple possible responses and multiple stimuli (models, examples) for compare-and-contrast discovery
Support must actually fade across the lesson series, not remain constant
constraints: The article grounds this in cited prior work (Lasky & Yoon; Liu et al.; Van de Pol et al.); the present study did not independently test the scaffolding component in isolation
target_learners: Upper secondary students with little prior creative writing experience
target_learning_goals: Creative text quality
Independent idea generation
examples: In the Writing Lab, students could choose between parallel open-ended creative assignments and among story options (e.g., three photos from nine in lesson 6), while support faded from lesson 1 to independent final drafting
