title: Creative Self-Concept questionnaire (Stubbé et al., 2015) as a moderator measure for Dutch secondary writing research
description: The study used a 44-item Creative Self-Concept questionnaire "designed and tested by Stubbé et al. (2015) for use in Dutch secondary education", with items on a 7-point Likert scale representing seven constructs: inquisitiveness, imaginativeness, focus on output, pride in own work, dare to be different, persistence, and collaborativeness. The compound average score (Cronbach's alpha ".92") was used to test whether instruction effects held irrespective of creativity (RQ3), and CSC moderated the transfer effect in panel 1.
requirements: Administered before the pretest (T1) as a self-report measure
constraints: CSC combines affective and cognitive components and is more general than task-specific creative self-efficacy; domain-specificity of creative self-beliefs remains debated in the literature the article cites
target_learners: Dutch secondary education students
target_learning_goals: Measuring students' general creative self-judgment as a moderator of writing instruction effects
examples: The questionnaire was given to the 105 participating Grade 10 students before the pretest; the compound score entered the moderation analyses
key_sources: Anouk ten Peze, Tanja Janssen, Gert Rijlaarsdam, Daphne van Weijen. (2024). Instruction in creative and argumentative writing: transfer and crossover effects on writing process and text quality. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09647-3

article_title: Scanpath analysis of expertise and culture in teacher gaze in real-world classrooms
citation: Nora A. McIntyre & Tom Foulsham. (2018). Scanpath analysis of expertise and culture in teacher gaze in real-world classrooms. Instructional Science 46, 435-455. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9445-x
title: Scanpath theory of gaze as read-out of a cognitive model applied to real-world teacher gaze
description: Scanpath theory holds that a scanpath is "a 'repetitive sequence of saccades and ﬁxations, idiosyncratic to a particular subject [person] and to a particular target pattern'" and that scanpaths reflect "the read-out of the internal representation of pictures, the so-called 'cognitive model'". The article applies this framework to real-world teaching: if expertise and culture shape teachers' cognitive models, expert and same-culture teachers should show more similar gaze sequences. Its string-edit-distance method represents gaze sequences as letter strings over coded gaze targets, preserving order information that aggregated looking-time measures discard, and the study's intra-individual similarity finding is presented as evidence that top-down cognitive models drive real-world classroom gaze.
requirements: Gaze sequences must be coded into discrete, comparable gaze targets so that sequences can be represented as strings and compared via string edit distance
constraints: Scanpaths are event- rather than duration-based, so a duration-based approach could yield a different picture
The study was limited to teacher-centred lesson segments and to attentional and communicative didactic events only
target_learners: secondary school teachers across expertise levels
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving teachers' classroom gaze behaviour and professional expertise
examples: Forty UK and Hong Kong teachers were eye-tracked with Tobii glasses during 10-minute teacher-centred lesson segments, and scanpaths of the first ten coded gaze behaviours within questioning and lecturing episodes were compared using string edit distance similarity scores
key_sources: Nora A. McIntyre & Tom Foulsham. (2018). Scanpath analysis of expertise and culture in teacher gaze in real-world classrooms. Instructional Science 46, 435-455. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9445-x

article_title: Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions
citation: Sjöblom, B., & Lymer, G. (2025). Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09717-8
title: Conceptual socialization: learning a functional professional concept through its use in reflective debriefing interaction
description: The article applies Engeström's notion of conceptual socialization and Greeno's distinction between formal and functional concepts to explain how tactical knowledge develops in debriefing. Tactics is treated as a functional concept that "has meaning in a kind of activity, in which it contributes to the way participants organize their understanding of what they are doing". Learning is framed via a participation metaphor and Goodwin's professional vision: debriefing participants parse the shared domain of scrutiny of the recent game through discursive highlighting, so the concept of tactics takes on professional significance and becomes a tool for evaluating and explaining actions.
requirements: Post-simulation reflective discussion in which the concept is explicitly used and given meaning in interaction, anchored to concrete game experiences
constraints: The concept studied is not a formal concept determined by an explicit definition; the analysis concerns its situated, functional use in military debriefing settings
target_learners: military officer cadets in professional education
target_learning_goals: professional conceptual understanding of tactics
participation in professional discourse and practical reasoning
examples: Analysis of IRE sequences in which teachers specify questions as requests for tactical considerations, ratifying student replies as tactical observations
key_sources: Sjöblom, B., & Lymer, G. (2025). Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09717-8

article_title: Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions
citation: Sjöblom, B., & Lymer, G. (2025). Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09717-8
title: Use post-game debriefing to unpack what the wargame experience does not transparently communicate about tactics
description: The article's central design implication is that knowledge of tactics requires reflective unpacking in debriefing rather than being transparently communicated through game participation. As the authors put it, "Knowledge of tactics is found to not be transparently communicated through participation in the wargame, but to require unpacking in reflective discussions". Post-simulation discussion connects concrete game experiences to generalized, conceptual understanding of the discipline, making debriefing an arena where functional concepts are put to use and anchored to shared experience.
requirements: Debriefing sessions after each game or exercise day, led by a military teacher or self-led, in which the concept of tactics is explicitly invoked
target_learners: officer students in simulation-based professional military education
target_learning_goals: connecting simulated concrete experience to conceptual disciplinary understanding
examples: Debriefings after each game in the recorded wargaming-based tactics courses, lasting from around 20 minutes to over 1.5 hours after multi-week games
key_sources: Sjöblom, B., & Lymer, G. (2025). Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09717-8

article_title: Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions
citation: Sjöblom, B., & Lymer, G. (2025). Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09717-8
title: SSM (Simple Surface Warfare Model) digital wargame platform for teaching naval tactics
description: The Simple Surface Warfare Model (SSM) is a proprietary digital wargame of the Swedish Defence University used in navy and marine tactics courses. The article describes it as "a digital map-based platform, in which a variety of scenarios can be set up", with military units maneuvered in real time and players deciding on sensors and weapons. Games are played by two opposing sides in continuous time, feature fog of war with a dynamically updated situational picture projected on a classroom wall, and range from roughly three-hour small games to multi-week exercises engaging up to 50 students in multilayered task structures.
requirements: Teams of players with computers controlling a dozen or more units, with projected situational picture for joint overview
constraints: Built on openly available data and not classified; the strategic level of warfare is not present in the game
target_learners: navy and marine cadets in the three-year Swedish officers' program
target_learning_goals: identifying and solving tactical problems of increasing complexity
examples: Coastal defense scenarios in the Baltic Sea or fictional geography with asymmetric sides modeled on Swedish and Russian materiel
key_sources: Sjöblom, B., & Lymer, G. (2025). Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09717-8

article_title: The effects of constructivist learning environments: a commentary
citation: Remy M. J. P. Rikers, Tamara van Gog, Fred Paas. (2008). The effects of constructivist learning environments: a commentary. Instr Sci (2008) 36:463–467. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9067-4
title: Effective instruction blends practices from different theoretical perspectives rather than forcing a constructivist/direct-instruction dichotomy
description: The commentary endorses the Harris, Santangelo, and Graham position that effective instruction is not a forced choice between theoretical camps. It quotes their view that instruction should be "a thoughtful, pragmatic blending of practices based on evidence gained from various perspectives and lines of research". The commentary agrees and notes SRSD may not even count as constructivist, yet its evidence base justifies its use. This mirrors the finding that deep processing does not necessarily exclude stepwise processing such as memorization and rehearsal.
requirements: Practices should be selected on evidence gained from research rather than on adherence to a single theoretical perspective.
target_learners: school and university students
target_learning_goals: writing skills
deep and meaningful learning
examples: The commentary endorses Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) as a pragmatic instructional approach with substantial empirical evidence, even though some would argue it is not a constructivist learning environment.
key_sources: Remy M. J. P. Rikers, Tamara van Gog, Fred Paas. (2008). The effects of constructivist learning environments: a commentary. Instr Sci (2008) 36:463–467. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9067-4

article_title: The effects of constructivist learning environments: a commentary
citation: Remy M. J. P. Rikers, Tamara van Gog, Fred Paas. (2008). The effects of constructivist learning environments: a commentary. Instr Sci (2008) 36:463–467. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9067-4
title: CORDTRA — Chronologically-Ordered Representations of Discourse and Tool-Related Activity
description: CORDTRA is a technique introduced in the Hmelo-Silver, Chernobilsky, and Jordan study for visually representing collaborative learning processes in a computer-supported learning (CSCL) environment. By "visually representing the chronology of discourse and tool use (such as a personal notebook, electronic whiteboard) associated with an activity", it gives a better overview of collaborative learning processes in computer-mediated problem-based learning. The commentary judges it very promising but notes its outcome measures need firmer links to a constructivist theoretical framework.
requirements: Future research must establish a firm link between outcome measures and the (constructivist) theoretical framework for the technique to be most meaningful.
constraints: Many activities in a problem-based learning environment cannot be indisputably linked to the theoretical framework.
target_learners: students in computer-mediated problem-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: understanding collaborative learning processes
examples: Hmelo-Silver, Chernobilsky, and Jordan used CORDTRA to capture the dynamic nature of collaborative learning processes, representing discourse and tool use chronologically.
key_sources: Remy M. J. P. Rikers, Tamara van Gog, Fred Paas. (2008). The effects of constructivist learning environments: a commentary. Instr Sci (2008) 36:463–467. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9067-4

article_title: Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students’ engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction
citation: Lucero, M., Montanero, M., & van Boxtel, C. (2024). Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students' engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09659-7
title: Collaborative information processing (CIP) model: externalization, divergence and convergence phases of collaborative knowledge building
description: The article invokes Jorczak's collaborative information processing model, which "distinguishes three phases of collaborative information processing that develop cyclically in the processes of negotiation and collaborative knowledge building: externalization, divergence and convergence". Externalization expresses stored knowledge to share it; in divergence learners elaborate and compare ideas to identify discrepancies; in convergence learners negotiate and resolve socio-cognitive discrepancies. The authors use CIP to interpret summary dyads as typically not going beyond externalization.
requirements: Requires processes of negotiation and collaborative knowledge building among learners
target_learners: secondary education students working in dyads
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
historical reasoning
examples: The authors conclude that pairs who jointly wrote a summary did not, in general, go beyond the initial externalization phase
key_sources: Lucero, M., Montanero, M., & van Boxtel, C. (2024). Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students' engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09659-7

article_title: Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students’ engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction
citation: Lucero, M., Montanero, M., & van Boxtel, C. (2024). Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students' engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09659-7
title: MUPEMURE model: negotiation and knowledge building are shaped by the type of external knowledge representation tool
description: The MUPEMURE (MUltiple PErspectives on MUltiple REpresentations) model of Weinberger et al. holds that "these negotiation and knowledge building processes are strongly influenced by the type of external knowledge representation tool used". It predicts a reciprocal effect between representation type and collaboration: how learners interact depends on the type and quality of the external representation. The study's finding that semiempty concept maps elicited more transactive, convergence-oriented interaction than summary writing is presented as consistent with this model.
requirements: Learners must use a shared external knowledge representation tool during collaboration
target_learners: secondary education students
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge convergence
historical reasoning
examples: The authors state their analysis of interaction in both conditions confirmed the hypothesis, finding the result consistent with what is predicted by the MUPEMURE model
key_sources: Lucero, M., Montanero, M., & van Boxtel, C. (2024). Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students' engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09659-7

article_title: Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students’ engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction
citation: Lucero, M., Montanero, M., & van Boxtel, C. (2024). Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students' engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09659-7
title: Use semiempty (moderately-directed) concept maps rather than fully student-generated maps to scaffold collaborative reasoning
description: The article argues that semiempty concept maps, which provide predetermined concepts with a limited number of blank squares to complete, scaffold collaboration by reducing cognitive cost. The authors chose them because "the research showed positive outcomes of semiempty concept maps", and the discussion states that "completing a semiempty concept map might have provided scaffolding that freed up sufficient cognitive resources to enable reasoning about the relationships between ideas". In their tasks, the incomplete map focused students on key components of historical reasoning such as causes, intentions and contexts.
requirements: Predetermined nodes must target key relations of the content; students need a training session and an individual preparation phase before collaboration
constraints: The article cautions that concept maps have no practiced reading order and impose low-level decision-making load when students are not used to working with them
target_learners: secondary education students unfamiliar with concept mapping
target_learning_goals: historical reasoning
causal explanation
collaborative knowledge construction
examples: Tasks used 3 semiempty concept maps with 19, 8 and 7 predetermined concepts and 12, 9 and 9 empty squares, completed by dyads after reading textbook texts on 19th-century Western imperialism
key_sources: Lucero, M., Montanero, M., & van Boxtel, C. (2024). Semiempty collaborative concept mapping in history education: students' engagement in historical reasoning and coconstruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09659-7

article_title: Do medium and Context Matter when learning from multiple complementary Digital texts and videos?
citation: Lucia Mason, Christian Tarchi, Angelica Ronconi, Lucia Manzione, Natalia Latini, Ivar Bråten. (2022). Do medium and Context Matter when learning from multiple complementary Digital texts and videos? Instructional Science (2022) 50:653–679. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09591-8
title: RESOLV context model: readers construct a mental model of the reading context that shapes task engagement
description: The reading as problem solving (RESOLV) model holds that readers first build a subjective mental representation of the context in which reading occurs, from cues they perceive as important, and then build a task model of the end goal and means. The article uses RESOLV to motivate its authoritativeness manipulation: "readers initially construct a mental model of the context in which reading takes place", including the requester and the digital venue. The study tested whether a professor-on-Moodle versus friend-on-Facebook context was represented in learners' context models and moderated engagement, integration, and calibration.
requirements: Context cues (requester, platform) must be perceived as relevant by readers and represented in their context model for authoritativeness to influence processing
constraints: The article notes it remained possible that authoritativeness might not be represented in participants' context models, and prior research indicates students often disregard source characteristics
target_learners: university students learning from online informational sources
target_learning_goals: integrated understanding of complex issues across multiple complementary sources
examples: Participants in the more authoritative condition read that a professor recommended two texts/videos posted on Moodle after a classroom discussion; those in the less authoritative condition read that a friend tagged them in two Facebook posts after an out-of-school discussion
key_sources: Lucia Mason, Christian Tarchi, Angelica Ronconi, Lucia Manzione, Natalia Latini, Ivar Bråten. (2022). Do medium and Context Matter when learning from multiple complementary Digital texts and videos? Instructional Science (2022) 50:653–679. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09591-8

article_title: Teaching as regulation and dealing with complexity
citation: H. P. A. Boshuizen. (2016). Teaching as regulation and dealing with complexity. Instructional Science, 44, 311–314. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9377-x
title: Teaching a class as one big regulation problem with multiple coordinated goals
description: The article frames teaching as "one big regulation problem (Cronin and Gonzalez 2007): multiple goals have to be pursued, while disturbances have to be minimised using different kinds of steering instruments." Goals vary along dimensions such as academic goals (per lesson, course, curriculum) and conducive goals (safety, quiet environment, good working relations). The goals, their hierarchy, and the quality of available instruments determine the outcome of the regulation problem.
requirements: Clear goals and valid, timely information on results for regulation
constraints: Information on results is often not available in natural practice
target_learners: teachers
target_learning_goals: classroom management
instructional regulation
key_sources: H. P. A. Boshuizen. (2016). Teaching as regulation and dealing with complexity. Instructional Science, 44, 311–314. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9377-x

article_title: Teaching as regulation and dealing with complexity
citation: H. P. A. Boshuizen. (2016). Teaching as regulation and dealing with complexity. Instructional Science, 44, 311–314. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9377-x
title: Use flexible, adaptive formative assessment during learning to provide information on results for regulation
description: The article argues regulation of teaching requires valid and timely information on results, and that end-of-term tests have minimal feedback value due to timing. Instead, "More ﬂexible, adaptive, formative (self) assessment methods applied during learning can identify the gap between goals stated and present status, and suggest resources to teachers and learners for remediation."
requirements: Valid and timely measures, preferably of process as well as outcomes
constraints: Many teachers see tests as indicators of students' success and failure, not their own
target_learners: teachers
learners
target_learning_goals: monitoring progress toward goals
remediation of learning gaps
examples: Furtak et al.'s three-year study of teachers developing formative assessment skills, in which better information on results led to better student learning
key_sources: H. P. A. Boshuizen. (2016). Teaching as regulation and dealing with complexity. Instructional Science, 44, 311–314. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9377-x

article_title: Fostering students’ motivation towards learning research skills: the role of autonomy, competence and relatedness support
citation: Louise Maddens, Fien Depaepe, Annelies Raes, Jan Elen. (2023). Fostering students' motivation towards learning research skills: the role of autonomy, competence and relatedness support. Instructional Science 51, 165–199. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09606-4
title: Need-supportive 4C/ID learning environment with 12 integrated autonomy, competence and relatedness implementations
description: An adapted version of the baseline 4C/ID-based online learning environment for research skills in which "need support consisted of 12 implementations (four implementations for each need), based on existing research on need support". Autonomy support included meaningful rationales, acknowledging negative feelings, inviting language and self-pacing; competence support included structure, informational positive feedback, progress indication and criteria-based evaluation; relatedness support included researcher-mentor messages, forum sharing and a personal welcome (Tables 1-2).
requirements: Must build on a deliberately designed 4C/ID-based environment, which the authors call an important prerequisite to provide qualitative motivational support
constraints: Ideally students work in class under teacher supervision, but COVID-19 restrictions meant some students completed modules partly at home
target_learners: 11th and 12th grade upper secondary behavioral sciences students
target_learning_goals: research skills in behavioral sciences (formulating research questions, methods, hypotheses, communication)
examples: A peer video and avatar statements stressing task value, weekly motivational messages from a researcher-mentor, and progress marking after every task class
key_sources: Louise Maddens, Fien Depaepe, Annelies Raes, Jan Elen. (2023). Fostering students' motivation towards learning research skills: the role of autonomy, competence and relatedness support. Instructional Science 51, 165–199. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09606-4

article_title: Fostering students’ motivation towards learning research skills: the role of autonomy, competence and relatedness support
citation: Louise Maddens, Fien Depaepe, Annelies Raes, Jan Elen. (2023). Fostering students' motivation towards learning research skills: the role of autonomy, competence and relatedness support. Instructional Science 51, 165–199. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09606-4
title: Self-determination theory and Basic Psychological Need Theory as a framework for motivation in complex-skill learning
description: The article adopts SDT (Deci & Ryan, 2000), which distinguishes amotivation, extrinsic (autonomous versus controlled) and intrinsic motivation, and maintains that "one should consider three innate psychological needs related to students' motivation": autonomy, competence and relatedness. Need satisfaction is hypothesized to relate to more internalized, autonomous motivation. The authors chose SDT precisely because its Basic Psychological Need Theory fits research-skills learning, where problems with both competence and autonomy feelings have been documented, and because van Merriënboer and Kirschner suggest it as the framework for motivation in 4C/ID contexts.
requirements: Operationalizations of each need drawn from existing research, as compiled in the article's overview of autonomy, competence and relatedness support
constraints: The article notes optimal circumstances for positive motivational outcomes require satisfaction of autonomy, competence and relatedness simultaneously, so single-need interventions may be insufficiently powerful
target_learners: upper secondary students learning research skills in academic contexts where learning is instrumental rather than voluntary
target_learning_goals: internalization of motivation towards learning research skills
examples: The need-supportive condition operationalized all three needs simultaneously via 12 implementations, testing the integrated-need-support hypothesis
key_sources: Louise Maddens, Fien Depaepe, Annelies Raes, Jan Elen. (2023). Fostering students' motivation towards learning research skills: the role of autonomy, competence and relatedness support. Instructional Science 51, 165–199. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09606-4

article_title: Learning from animation enabled by collaboration
citation: Rebetez, C., Betrancourt, M., Sangin, M., & Dillenbourg, P. (2010). Learning from animation enabled by collaboration. Instructional Science, 38(5), 471–485. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9117-6
title: Multimedia comprehension framework with working-memory load as the explanation for weak animation effects
description: The article frames animation effects within the multimedia comprehension framework, in which multimedia processing is constrained by human cognitive capacity. It offers a cognitive-load explanation for why intuitive expectations about animation fail: multimedia, including animated graphics, "challenges human processing capacities, and in particular imposes a substantial working memory load". The study's results are discussed within this framework "in order to propose the conditions under which animation can benefit to learning".
requirements: The account presumes that instruction design must be evaluated against learners' working-memory processing capacities, per the article's cognitive-load framing.
target_learners: Learners studying multimedia instruction explaining how natural or artificial dynamic systems work
target_learning_goals: Comprehension of dynamic systems, including retention and transfer of how such systems work
examples: The three-factor experiment crossed static versus animated graphics, snapshots versus no snapshots, and individual versus collaborative settings to test conditions for animation benefits.
key_sources: Rebetez, C., Betrancourt, M., Sangin, M., & Dillenbourg, P. (2010). Learning from animation enabled by collaboration. Instructional Science, 38(5), 471–485. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9117-6

article_title: Learning from animation enabled by collaboration
citation: Rebetez, C., Betrancourt, M., Sangin, M., & Dillenbourg, P. (2010). Learning from animation enabled by collaboration. Instructional Science, 38(5), 471–485. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9117-6
title: Collaborative learning as a design condition enabling transfer benefits from animated graphics
description: This pattern pairs animated multimedia instruction with collaborative study so that animation's potential for transfer is realised. The article notes animation "may also be used to promote interactions in computer-supported collaborative learning", and its findings show that for transfer, only dyads benefited from animated over static graphics. Collaboration thus functions as the enabling condition under which animation pays off, within the article's multimedia comprehension framework.
requirements: Learners must study in collaborative (dyad) settings for the transfer benefit of animation over static graphics to appear, per the reported findings.
constraints: Adding snapshots of critical steps was significantly detrimental for dyads, so extra static visual support should not be assumed helpful in this setting.
target_learners: Learners in computer-supported collaborative learning settings studying dynamic-system content
target_learning_goals: Transfer of understanding of how dynamic systems work
examples: The experiment assigned learners individually or in dyads to study multimedia instruction with static or animated graphics, with or without snapshots of critical steps.
key_sources: Rebetez, C., Betrancourt, M., Sangin, M., & Dillenbourg, P. (2010). Learning from animation enabled by collaboration. Instructional Science, 38(5), 471–485. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9117-6

article_title: ICT-support for grounding in the classroom
citation: Pieter J. Beers, Paul A. Kirschner, Henny P. A. Boshuizen, Wim H. Gijselaers. (2007). ICT-support for grounding in the classroom. Instructional Science 35, 535–556. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9018-5
title: Negotiation of common ground as a dual concept combining linguistic and cognitive approaches
description: The article combines the linguistic approach of Clark and Schaefer with the cognitivist approach of Bromme into one account of grounding. In this conceptualisation, "negotiation of common ground is conceived of as a dual concept": negotiation of meaning, in which unshared understanding is made public, verified, clarified and re-verified until the grounding criterion is met, and negotiation of position, in which members make their private opinions public and check they are understood. Grounding starts when team members contribute unshared knowledge, and representational differences are minimised iteratively through feedback based on one's own perspective. This framework is the design basis for the NTool formalism.
requirements: Team members must externalise their private understanding and opinions of contributions for differences to become visible and negotiable
constraints: The article's formalism is prescriptive and task-oriented, facilitating grounding related to the task at hand and disregarding other grounding activities, theoretically departing from Clark and Schaefer and Bromme
target_learners: secondary vocational education students working in multidisciplinary teams
target_learning_goals: collaborative complex problem-solving
establishing shared understanding of contributions in group discussion
key_sources: Pieter J. Beers, Paul A. Kirschner, Henny P. A. Boshuizen, Wim H. Gijselaers. (2007). ICT-support for grounding in the classroom. Instructional Science 35, 535–556. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9018-5

article_title: ICT-support for grounding in the classroom
citation: Pieter J. Beers, Paul A. Kirschner, Henny P. A. Boshuizen, Wim H. Gijselaers. (2007). ICT-support for grounding in the classroom. Instructional Science 35, 535–556. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9018-5
title: NTool: an ICT communication tool with an embedded negotiation formalism and two coercion levels
description: NTool is an online, newsgroup-reader-based communication tool for asynchronous, text-based discussion that directly supports grounding by making users externalise their private understanding of others' contributions. "The formalism consists of negotiation primitives, basic building blocks that constitute a speciﬁc dialogue model" — contribution, verification, clarification, acceptance/rejection, and position — with five rules (Table 1) prescribing their use. Two script implementations were used: the Idiosyncratic version offered primitives without coercive rules, while the Stringent version, "applied strict rules for the situations in which each message type could and could not be used," greying out unavailable options.
requirements: Participants receive a tutorial and practice case on the formalism before use (75 min practice phase)
constraints: Coercion in both implementations was aimed at the verification and clarification primitives only; no measures of actual individual learning or task performance were taken in the study
target_learners: secondary vocational education students in multidisciplinary three-person teams
target_learning_goals: negotiation of common ground during collaborative complex problem-solving
examples: 22 teams used NTool to make a functional design of floating housing as a solution for sea-level rise, in two sessions with individual pre-tests and post-tests
key_sources: Pieter J. Beers, Paul A. Kirschner, Henny P. A. Boshuizen, Wim H. Gijselaers. (2007). ICT-support for grounding in the classroom. Instructional Science 35, 535–556. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9018-5

article_title: ICT-support for grounding in the classroom
citation: Pieter J. Beers, Paul A. Kirschner, Henny P. A. Boshuizen, Wim H. Gijselaers. (2007). ICT-support for grounding in the classroom. Instructional Science 35, 535–556. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9018-5
title: Match collaboration-script coercion to learners' prior experience: when learners lack experience with collaborative complex problem-solving, coercing a formalism may be detrimental
description: The article's design recommendation is that the extent of coercion in a collaboration script must be geared toward learners' capacities: the less coercion, the more learners must themselves fulfil the prerequisites the facilitated processes require. Its conclusion from the vocational-education results is that "when learners have too little prior experience to beneﬁt from the use of a formalism, coercing such a formalism may be detrimental to the learning process." In that situation the target population may need a minimal level of prior experience with collaborative work and problem-solving before process-specific support such as NTool can be effective, and coercion would be entirely extraneous to the task.
requirements: Learners need some minimal level of prior experience with collaborative work and with problem-solving before very process-specific support can be effective
constraints: If a formalism requires unmet individual prerequisites, coercion applies it with more strength without making it easier to understand, and from a disruption-of-communication perspective may actually be detrimental
target_learners: secondary vocational education students with little prior group-work experience
target_learning_goals: effective negotiation of common ground in collaborative problem-solving
examples: Secondary vocational participants showed more regulation and 'other' communication under Stringent NTool, while university seniors in the prior study did not; the article cites Song et al. (2006) that high-school learners need more general group support
key_sources: Pieter J. Beers, Paul A. Kirschner, Henny P. A. Boshuizen, Wim H. Gijselaers. (2007). ICT-support for grounding in the classroom. Instructional Science 35, 535–556. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9018-5

article_title: Quasi-communities: rethinking learning in formal adult and vocational education
citation: Emad, G. R., & Roth, W.-M. (2016). Quasi-Communities: Rethinking Learning in Formal Adult and Vocational Education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9386-9
title: Quasi-community framework for theorizing learning in formal adult and vocational education
description: A quasi-community is an occasioned, temporally limited community within an educational context, retaining dimensions of communities of practice while abandoning others. The article defines it as "an occasioned, temporally limited community within an educational context that lacks the essentially spatiotemporal nature of relations within true communities." Unlike true communities, it has "no noticeable core and periphery": mastery is relative, dynamically distributed, and any member can act as old-timer or newcomer depending on the task at hand. The framework was developed and illustrated through a case study of mariners in formal certification training.
requirements: A common object/motive shared by members must be realized early for the community to form
constraints: The concept addresses formal adult and vocational settings where classes are administratively formed and disbanded after short periods, so collective memory is temporally limited
target_learners: Adult vocational learners returning to college for certification, e.g. mariners
target_learning_goals: Domain competency development for certification and workplace practice
examples: An eight-week Chart-work and Pilotage course for mariners seeking a watch-keeping certificate of competency
key_sources: Emad, G. R., & Roth, W.-M. (2016). Quasi-Communities: Rethinking Learning in Formal Adult and Vocational Education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9386-9

article_title: Quasi-communities: rethinking learning in formal adult and vocational education
citation: Emad, G. R., & Roth, W.-M. (2016). Quasi-Communities: Rethinking Learning in Formal Adult and Vocational Education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9386-9
title: Co-produced quasi-community pedagogy in adult certification courses
description: A lesson-to-course-level design in which instructor and students collectively co-produce the pedagogy around a shared object/motive. The article states "The pedagogy in a quasi-community is the co-production of the community members" and that "The emerging co-produced pedagogy in this course promoted students' participation and facilitated the co-development of their quasi-community." Key moves include early surfacing of motives, group activities with free group choice, storytelling, ungraded tests, turn-taking review, and shifting instructor authority toward facilitation.
requirements: A common object/motive that members recognize as shared
An instructor who aligns classroom practice with members' motives and shares hierarchical power
constraints: Evidenced in a formal adult vocational setting with an external certification authority conducting the final assessment
target_learners: Adult vocational learners preparing for certification examinations
target_learning_goals: Domain-specific competency and examination readiness through collective participation
examples: After each test the instructor read questions one at a time, a student answered, and the class discussed and evaluated the answer, including what certification examiners expected
key_sources: Emad, G. R., & Roth, W.-M. (2016). Quasi-Communities: Rethinking Learning in Formal Adult and Vocational Education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9386-9

article_title: Fostering noticing of classroom discussion features through analysis of contrasting cases
citation: Blair, K. P., Banes, L. C., & Martin, L. (2024). Fostering noticing of classroom discussion features through analysis of contrasting cases. Instructional Science, 52:417–452. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09661-z
title: Three forms of noticing required for learning to facilitate productive discussion
description: Building on Gibson's perceptual learning theory, the article proposes three forms of noticing for teachers developing discussion facilitation. "First is increased differentiation with respect to the structure and features of student talk, including both what is present and what is missing." Second, differentiation of the features and dimensions of teachers' response moves; third, identification and refinement of one's values and commitments and of alignment between a discussion and those values. The intervention was designed around these three areas.
requirements: Requires teachers to encounter varied discussion examples that make features of student talk, teacher moves, and values contrasts salient
constraints: The matching-problem analogy is acknowledged as a simplification; discussion also occurs in social and cultural contexts shaped by values and relational histories the analogy does not capture
target_learners: preservice teachers
prospective teachers (undergraduates interested in teaching)
target_learning_goals: noticing features of productive classroom discussion
differentiating talk moves such as revoicing
refining values and commitments about discussion
examples: The contrasting cases activity was designed so that ranking and principle generation engaged all three areas of development
key_sources: Blair, K. P., Banes, L. C., & Martin, L. (2024). Fostering noticing of classroom discussion features through analysis of contrasting cases. Instructional Science, 52:417–452. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09661-z

article_title: Fostering noticing of classroom discussion features through analysis of contrasting cases
citation: Blair, K. P., Banes, L. C., & Martin, L. (2024). Fostering noticing of classroom discussion features through analysis of contrasting cases. Instructional Science, 52:417–452. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09661-z
title: Contrasting cases with a synthesis (inventing principles) task to develop perceptual differentiation of discussion features
description: The instructional approach uses "juxtaposed examples that are chosen to highlight distinctive features or relationships", with most features held constant so key differences stand out. Learners synthesize across multiple cases by inventing guiding principles, in line with Schwartz and Martin's (2004) approach, so that differentiation of stimuli and of principles reinforce each other and support transfer. The activity prepares learners for an expert recap, creating "a time-for-telling".
requirements: Cases must be carefully chosen so pairwise comparisons isolate particular features; a synthesis task across the cases; a subsequent expert discussion and lecture to consolidate what was noticed
constraints: The authors used constructed transcripts rather than video because natural classroom variability makes tight video contrasts challenging; chosen features are a subset known to be important, not exhaustive
target_learners: preservice teachers
undergraduate prospective teachers
target_learning_goals: differentiating features of productive discussion
developing guiding principles for discussion
noticing present and absent discussion features
examples: Six fictitious middle school science transcripts were ranked best to least good in pairs, followed by three supplemental cases, a whole-class discussion, and a 10-minute lecture on features of classroom discourse
key_sources: Blair, K. P., Banes, L. C., & Martin, L. (2024). Fostering noticing of classroom discussion features through analysis of contrasting cases. Instructional Science, 52:417–452. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09661-z

article_title: The influence of framing on transfer: initial evidence from a tutoring experiment
citation: Randi A. Engle, Phi D. Nguyen, Adam Mendelson. (2011). The influence of framing on transfer: initial evidence from a tutoring experiment. Instr Sci 39:603–628. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9145-2
title: Expansive versus bounded framing of learning contexts as an instructional mechanism for transfer
description: This theory holds that transfer is more likely when learning and transfer contexts are framed expansively, as opportunities for students to actively contribute to "larger conversations that extend across times, places, people, and activities". It contrasts expansive framings, whose boundaries are "wide-ranging and permeable", with bounded framings having constricted, impermeable, non-overlapping boundaries. The article operationalizes framing along five aspects of context: when, where, who, what, and how learners are positioned intellectually, and tested the theory in a randomized tutoring experiment.
requirements: Framing must be initiated through meta-communicative signals in social interaction, such as the tutor's language and actions across the five aspects
Student uptake of the proposed framing must be maintained, with the tutor encouraging the favored framing until uptake is achieved
constraints: In this experiment the framing had to be established within minutes rather than the weeks available in classroom settings
No statistically reliable effects were detected for transfer of the surface area principle, so the mechanism does not guarantee transfer of all content types
target_learners: high school biology students
target_learning_goals: transfer of facts, conceptual principles, and learning strategies across body systems
examples: Tutors framed each day as one ongoing study versus separate completed studies, framed location as the university versus this room, revoiced students' self-explanations to credit authorship versus crediting the text, and framed the two days as one study about body systems versus two separate system topics
key_sources: Randi A. Engle, Phi D. Nguyen, Adam Mendelson. (2011). The influence of framing on transfer: initial evidence from a tutoring experiment. Instr Sci 39:603–628. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9145-2

article_title: The roles that students’ ethnicity and achievement levels play in teachers’ choice of learning materials in online teaching: evidence from two experimental studies
citation: Sabine Schlag, Sabine Glock. (2024). The roles that students' ethnicity and achievement levels play in teachers' choice of learning materials in online teaching: evidence from two experimental studies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09681-9
title: Stereotype-driven shortcut model of teachers' material-choice decisions
description: The article frames material choice as a decision-making process in which teachers use schemas as shortcuts that can activate stereotypes. It cites Shavelson and Stern's model in which decisions are influenced by "material and activities, teachers' beliefs about the nature of teaching, and teachers' judgments about students' abilities and behavior", and the continuum model of impression formation, under which expectation-confirming information (e.g., minority students' low achievement) triggers stereotype-based rather than individuating judgment. The two studies instantiate this by showing ethnicity and achievement cues shifting material choices.
requirements: The account presupposes student cues (names, achievement descriptions) that teachers interpret against stereotypical expectations.
constraints: The authors note they simplified the decision-making process, and preservice teachers may differ from inservice teachers, who consider more complex information.
target_learners: Ethnic minority and majority students in primary and secondary school
target_learning_goals: Understanding and improving equity in teachers' selection of learning materials
key_sources: Sabine Schlag, Sabine Glock. (2024). The roles that students' ethnicity and achievement levels play in teachers' choice of learning materials in online teaching: evidence from two experimental studies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09681-9

article_title: Do prior knowledge, model-observer similarity and social comparison influence the effectiveness of eye movement modeling examples for supporting multimedia learning?
citation: Krebs, M.-C., Schüler, A., & Scheiter, K. (2021). Do prior knowledge, model-observer similarity and social comparison influence the effectiveness of eye movement modeling examples for supporting multimedia learning? Instructional Science, 49, 607–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09552-7
title: Eye Movement Modeling Examples (EMME) as an instructional tool for multimedia learning
description: EMME are recordings of a model's eye movements performed during a task, overlaid onto the task material so that learners can see where, how long, and in what order the model looks. In this study the EMME were short videos in which "A white spotlight on the otherwise grey shaded page represented a gaze fixation", with spotlight size varying with fixation duration, and no verbal instruction. They were shown on the first four pages of an illustrated text on mitosis to demonstrate effective multimedia processing strategies such as inspecting the picture before reading and looking at corresponding picture elements during text-reading.
requirements: Learners must be informed in an introductory text that the abstract gaze cue (spotlight) represents human eye movements and that spotlight size illustrates fixation time.
constraints: In this study EMME-guidance was presented only on the first four pages of the learning material, and posttest items referred only to Part 2 to avoid direct influence of the external guidance.
target_learners: University students learning biology (mitosis) from illustrated texts
target_learning_goals: Applying effective multimedia processing strategies (selecting, organizing and integrating text and picture information)
Understanding the biological processes of mitosis
examples: An instructed female student research assistant's gaze was recorded with a remote eye tracker (RED 250, 250 Hz); the resulting videos lasted 382 s overall and were shown before learners studied the same pages again without guidance.
key_sources: Krebs, M.-C., Schüler, A., & Scheiter, K. (2021). Do prior knowledge, model-observer similarity and social comparison influence the effectiveness of eye movement modeling examples for supporting multimedia learning? Instructional Science, 49, 607–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09552-7

article_title: Do prior knowledge, model-observer similarity and social comparison influence the effectiveness of eye movement modeling examples for supporting multimedia learning?
citation: Krebs, M.-C., Schüler, A., & Scheiter, K. (2021). Do prior knowledge, model-observer similarity and social comparison influence the effectiveness of eye movement modeling examples for supporting multimedia learning? Instructional Science, 49, 607–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09552-7
title: Three complementary theoretical perspectives on why EMME foster multimedia learning (attentional, metacognitive, social-cognitive)
description: The article organizes explanations of EMME effectiveness into three perspectives that are "not mutually exclusive, but are likely to complement each other". From an attentional perspective, EMME highlight relevant information like other attention-guiding cues and may trigger synchronization processes establishing joint attention. From a (meta-)cognitive perspective, observing the model's gaze is assumed to support acquiring or regulating cognitive processing strategies, treating EMME as a particular type of video modeling example. From a social-cognitive perspective, EMME induce a social learning situation whose salience, per social agency theory, leads learners to process material more deeply.
requirements: For the social perspective to apply, learners must be able to interpret the abstract gaze cue as human gaze behavior, which the authors argue is enabled by informing learners of the cue's human origin in the introductory text.
constraints: The article states these perspectives are theoretical assumptions about mechanisms, not mutually exclusive tested alternatives.
target_learners: Novice learners studying with illustrated multimedia materials
target_learning_goals: Faster selection of relevant information
Acquisition and regulation of effective multimedia processing strategies
Deeper processing via perceived social interaction
examples: The article cites Chisari et al. (2020) showing learners with EMME-guidance looked faster at referenced information, and Grant and Spivey (2003) on attention direction improving reasoning, as supporting the attentional perspective.
key_sources: Krebs, M.-C., Schüler, A., & Scheiter, K. (2021). Do prior knowledge, model-observer similarity and social comparison influence the effectiveness of eye movement modeling examples for supporting multimedia learning? Instructional Science, 49, 607–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09552-7

article_title: Do prior knowledge, model-observer similarity and social comparison influence the effectiveness of eye movement modeling examples for supporting multimedia learning?
citation: Krebs, M.-C., Schüler, A., & Scheiter, K. (2021). Do prior knowledge, model-observer similarity and social comparison influence the effectiveness of eye movement modeling examples for supporting multimedia learning? Instructional Science, 49, 607–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09552-7
title: Illustrated mitosis learning material (11 pages, 1113 words) with EMME videos demonstrating multimedia processing strategies
description: The study's learning material is an expository illustrated text on mitosis distributed across 11 pages with an overall length of 1113 words, text on the left and a complementary picture on the right of each page. Part 1 (four pages) covered cell structures, chromosomes and DNA and carried the EMME guidance; Part 2 (seven pages) covered the phases of mitosis and was identical for all conditions, with all posttest items referring only to Part 2. The EMME videos, generated from an instructed model's recorded gaze and visualized with focus maps, had "an overall duration of 382 s and varied between 52 and 115 s per page (M = 95.5 s)" with no verbal instruction.
requirements: To build a comprehensive mental model, learners must process both the text information and the picture information, since text and picture were complementary.
constraints: Each page was displayed for a minimum of 50 s before learners could continue, and learners could not go back to previous pages during the learning phase.
target_learners: University students without biology, medicine or related fields of study
target_learning_goals: Understanding cell structures, chromosomes, DNA and the phases of mitosis from complementary text and pictures
examples: The modeled sequence included reading the page title, inspecting the picture first (pictorial scaffold), reading while looking at corresponding picture elements (integration), a final picture inspection, and in some cases rereading a text section (reaction to comprehension problems).

Do prior knowledge, model-observer similarity and social comparison influence the effectiveness of eye movement modeling examples for supporting multimedia learning? Instructional Science, 49, 607–635. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09552-7

article_title: There’s more to the multimedia effect than meets the eye: is seeing pictures believing?
citation: Ögren, M., Nyström, M., & Jarodzka, H. (2017). There's more to the multimedia effect than meets the eye: is seeing pictures believing? Instructional Science, 45, 263–287. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9397-6
title: Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning and Cognitive Load Theory as explanatory frameworks for learning with text and pictures
description: The article applies two leading theories of multimedia processing — the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning and Cognitive Load Theory — which assign a central role to a capacity-limited working memory. Active processing proceeds in three steps: information is "selected from a source by means of attention", organized into mental models, and integrated with each other and prior knowledge. Working memory load comprises germane, intrinsic, and extraneous load, and verbal and pictorial information are processed in separate channels that are later integrated into a richer mental model. The study adapts these learning-oriented principles to task performance in vector calculus and tests their predictions with eye tracking and think-aloud protocols.
requirements: Graphs must be carefully integrated with the task formulation so that students actively select, organize, and integrate information rather than process it shallowly
constraints: The article notes the study's stimuli followed the temporal contiguity principle but not the spatial contiguity principle (split attention), which may partly explain the absence of a multimedia effect

The authors state the experiment did not precisely reflect how students normally work with such problems: time was limited, no pen and paper was allowed, and the confirm/reject answer format was uncommon for these students
target_learners: university engineering-physics students in an introductory vector calculus course
target_learning_goals: interpreting and solving problems in vector calculus by integrating formulae, text, and graphical representations
examples: The study compared eight vector-calculus problems presented with or without lecturer-designed interpretational graphs, recording eye movements, think-aloud protocols, and correctness of confirm/reject decisions
key_sources: Ögren, M., Nyström, M., & Jarodzka, H. (2017). There's more to the multimedia effect than meets the eye: is seeing pictures believing? Instructional Science, 45, 263–287. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9397-6

article_title: Conceptual and procedural knowledge retention in data visualization: a longitudinal study of doctoral learning and instructional design implications
citation: Francisco José Jiménez-Hornero, Eduardo Gutiérrez de Ravé. (2026). Conceptual and procedural knowledge retention in data visualization: a longitudinal study of doctoral learning and instructional design implications. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09808-0
title: Two author-developed five-criterion rubrics operationalizing conceptual understanding and procedural execution in data visualization
description: The study implemented two scoring rubrics on a five-point scale (1 = Poor to 5 = Excellent), applied consistently across all three time points to 40 doctoral students. The conceptual rubric covered identification of plots and variables, explanation of scales and units, clarity and organization, terminology, and completeness; the technical rubric covered data accuracy and plot type, axis labeling and units, color and legend consistency, multivariate coordination, and annotations. The article states "the rubrics function not only as scoring tools, but also as an explicit operationalization of the study's central constructs", enabling comparison across graph-replication tasks that differed in content but shared underlying demands.
requirements: Raters need calibration sessions using benchmark examples before formal scoring, as the authors did
constraints: The rubrics were developed by the authors specifically for this intervention context and guided by its learning goals
target_learners: first-year doctoral students
target_learning_goals: designing, interpreting, and explaining scientific figures
examples: Applied to three multivariable graph-replication tasks: an integrated weather chart at T0, a six-panel weather figure at T1, and multi-panel time-series and pollution figures at T2
key_sources: Francisco José Jiménez-Hornero, Eduardo Gutiérrez de Ravé. (2026). Conceptual and procedural knowledge retention in data visualization: a longitudinal study of doctoral learning and instructional design implications. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09808-0

article_title: Relationships between students’ conceptions of constructivist learning and their regulation and processing strategies
citation: Loyens, S. M. M., Rikers, R. M. J. P., & Schmidt, H. G. (2008). Relationships between students' conceptions of constructivist learning and their regulation and processing strategies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9065-6
title: Three-tiered structure of student learning: conceptual, controlling, and operational levels
description: A framework, drawn from Vermunt's ILS tradition, in which students' learning aspects are organized into three levels: a conceptual level of ideas and beliefs (mental models of knowledge, learning orientations, and here conceptions of constructivist learning), a controlling level of regulation processes, and an operational-behavioural level of processing strategies. The article states that "the controlling level tunes the conceptual level to the operational level." The study tested this structure with SEM in a problem-based learning curriculum, finding it fully valid for MSLQ variables but only partially for ILS variables, where regulation strategies function on a controlling level but are not strict mediators.
requirements: Measurement instruments capturing conceptions, regulation strategies, and processing strategies so the three levels can be modelled separately
constraints: The article notes the three-level structure appeared valid for the MSLQ variables, but not entirely for those of the ILS
target_learners: higher-education psychology students in a problem-based learning curriculum
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning and study strategy use in higher education
examples: Structural equation models with ILS and MSLQ regulation and processing variables were tested in 98 psychology students
key_sources: Loyens, S. M. M., Rikers, R. M. J. P., & Schmidt, H. G. (2008). Relationships between students' conceptions of constructivist learning and their regulation and processing strategies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9065-6

article_title: Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components?
citation: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Marie Weißenfels, Lea Russer, Franziska Perels. (2021). Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09533-2
title: Three-layer model of self-regulated learning (Boekaerts): cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational regulatory layers
description: The article adopts Boekaerts' three-layer component model as its organizing framework, in which SRL comprises interacting cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational regulatory processes on three hierarchical layers. The "inner layer comprises the regulation of information processing", the second layer covers metacognitive planning, monitoring, and reflection, and the outer layer reflects regulation of the self through motivational components, beliefs, and volitional strategies. The study operationalized all three layers across its four measures.
requirements: Layer-specific strategies are needed to optimize learning processes; the model assumes the layers interact with each other
constraints: The model is described as relatively static, treating SRL as a rather stable competence with distinct components
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use across cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational components
examples: The study's strategy knowledge test and microanalytic tool were constructed based on Zimmerman's (2000) and Boekaerts' (1999) models, assessing cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational components within planning, performance, and reflection phases
key_sources: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Marie Weißenfels, Lea Russer, Franziska Perels. (2021). Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09533-2

article_title: Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components?
citation: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Marie Weißenfels, Lea Russer, Franziska Perels. (2021). Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09533-2
title: Newly developed SRL strategy knowledge test with 25 paired strategy comparisons
description: A newly developed strategy knowledge test presents an academic learning scenario (preparing an oral presentation in educational psychology) divided into forethought, performance, and self-reflection phases, where participants rate the usefulness of strategy pairs on a four-point scale. Scoring uses "the relative judgment of superiority respective of inferiority of strategies" across 25 paired comparisons, with a maximum sum score of 50. Reliabilities were 0.71 (metacognition), 0.76 (motivation), and 0.84 (cognition).
requirements: Categorization into useful and not useful strategies based on theoretical assumptions and expert evaluations; an explicit hint that the task rates general usefulness, not one's own practice
constraints: Item difficulties ranged 28%–94%, meaning some comparisons were too easy and others too difficult; discriminatory power was less consistent than the microanalytic items, revealing a starting point for further development
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: knowledge of useful cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational learning strategies
examples: In the study, the strategy knowledge test was administered first, before the learning task, and its cognition scale correlated −0.33 with GPA
key_sources: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Marie Weißenfels, Lea Russer, Franziska Perels. (2021). Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09533-2

article_title: Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components?
citation: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Marie Weißenfels, Lea Russer, Franziska Perels. (2021). Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09533-2
title: Microanalytic SRL assessment tool with open-ended and closed-ended questions across the three SRL phases
description: A microanalytic assessment instrument was constructed based on Zimmerman's and Boekaerts' models, asking forethought questions before learning, performance questions after five minutes, and self-reflection questions after the task, targeting metacognitive and motivational components. Questions were open-ended or closed-ended on four-step rating scales; open answers were coded by two independent trained raters (self-motivation ICC = 0.79, strategic planning ICC = 0.74). Closed-ended scales showed reliabilities of 0.66 (self-efficacy) and 0.71 (planning and self-monitoring).
requirements: A well-defined learning task with a clear beginning, middle, and end; a formal set of criteria to categorize open-ended answers
constraints: Open questions need clear categorization for assessment and labor-intensive coding; item difficulties of 43–64% were judged acceptable
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: situation-specific metacognitive and motivational strategy use during an actual learning task
examples: In the study, microanalytic questions accompanied a 10-minute text-learning task on catastrophe management, and the open-ended metacognitive question correlated −0.26 with GPA
key_sources: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Marie Weißenfels, Lea Russer, Franziska Perels. (2021). Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09533-2

article_title: Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components?
citation: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Marie Weißenfels, Lea Russer, Franziska Perels. (2021). Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09533-2
title: Trace data from text highlighting and notes as an objective measure of cognitive strategy use
description: Trace data were gathered from participants' text highlighting and notes while learning a catastrophe-management text, with no instruction to highlight or take notes. The authors distinguish highlighted key words (nouns and explaining verbs and adverbs) from auxiliary words (pronouns, conjunctions, modal verbs), and notes were coded by two independent raters for cognitive learning strategies (ICC = 0.91). Trace data "contain no self-report as they can be found within the learning material and therefore are not prone to subjective distortion."
requirements: A learning task producing observable materials in which cognitive strategies can be seen, e.g. making notes or underlining important text sections
constraints: Trace data only give information on observable behavioral traces, therefore not appropriate for every SRL component (e.g. motivational thoughts)
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: objective assessment of cognitive strategy use during text learning
examples: In the study, participants could use pens and highlighters by choice while preparing a text on catastrophe management, and their highlighting and notes were analyzed as trace data
key_sources: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Marie Weißenfels, Lea Russer, Franziska Perels. (2021). Multimethod assessment of self-regulated learning in college students: different methods for different components? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09533-2

article_title: Development of legal expertise
citation: Glöckner, A., Towfigh, E., & Traxler, C. (2013). Development of legal expertise. Instructional Science, 41, 989–1007. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-013-9266-5
title: Students should schedule extended breaks at roughly 8-week intervals to counteract motivational drops
description: Based on the finding of a significant motivational drop at week 8, the authors recommend that "Students might therefore consider scheduling time for somewhat more extended breaks in roughly 8-week intervals." This directly addresses the cyclic motivation decrease observed in the data, where performance drops substantially and recovers thereafter.
requirements: Students must be engaged in sustained exam practice over multiple weeks
constraints: The drop was observed in a specific German legal education context with 5-hour mock exams
target_learners: advanced law students preparing for state exams
target_learning_goals: maintaining performance during sustained practice phases
examples: The authors' recommendation follows directly from the regression estimate of a 0.24 grading-point drop at week 8

description: The authors recommend that "students with good initial performance should focus more on area-of-law speciﬁc practice exams whereas students with poor initial performance seem to proﬁt more from general exam practice in all areas of law." This differential recommendation follows from the significant interaction effects between initial performance and both general and area-specific practice experience.

article_title: Introduction: the role of affect in STEM teacher learning
citation: Chen, G. A., Vedder-Weiss, D., & Marshall, S. A. (2026). Introduction: the role of affect in STEM teacher learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09777-4
title: Four conceptualizations of emotion and affect: inside-out, outside-in, sociocultural, and what-emotions-do
description: The editorial maps how affect and emotion can be conceptualized in education research. The "inside out" model treats emotions as internal experiences individuals express; the "outside in" sociological approach emphasizes how contexts and social interactions influence individuals' emotions; sociocultural scholarship treats emotions as dynamically constructed in moment-to-moment interactions; and a fourth approach, following Ahmed, "focuses on what emotions do" rather than what they are. The authors urge scholars to consider how conceptualizing differently opens new research avenues.
requirements: Scholars must carefully consider how they are conceptualizing emotion and affect in their research designs
constraints: The what-emotions-do approach has been taken up in general teacher education but, per the authors, not yet in STEM-specific research
target_learners: STEM teachers
pre-service STEM teachers
target_learning_goals: Understanding the role of affect and emotion in teacher learning
examples: The editorial cites Chronaki's (2019) analysis of how sad affects stabilize pre-service teachers' ideas about which bodies are capable of doing mathematics

article_title: The Effects of Group differentiation by students’ learning strategies
citation: Carla Haelermans. (2022). The Effects of Group differentiation by students' learning strategies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09575-0
title: IDDI: Interactive Differentiated Directed Instruction model
description: The IDDI model is a variant of direct instruction extended with cooperative methods and convergent differentiation in groups. Lessons start with a common introduction, after which the instruction-independent group works independently while the teacher provides interactive group instruction to the rest, followed by prolonged instruction and guided practice for the instruction-dependent group. The article calls it "a variant of the direct instruction model that is found to be one of the most effective instruction methods."
requirements: Teachers trained in the model through two meetings, with additional expert support available during the intervention period
constraints: Implementation observations showed the difference between the middle and upper group was perhaps less clear than envisioned
target_learners: Secondary school students in heterogeneous classrooms
target_learning_goals: Subject-matter learning across mathematics, languages, and sciences
examples: Teachers performed the intervention minimally once a week for eight months, developing or finding materials with the option to submit them to an expert for advice

article_title: The Effects of Group differentiation by students’ learning strategies
citation: Carla Haelermans. (2022). The Effects of Group differentiation by students' learning strategies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09575-0
title: Differentiation by learning strategies grounded in self-regulated learning and metacognition
description: The article frames differentiation by learning strategies within the self-regulated learning framework of Pintrich and de Groot (1990). Learning strategies encompass metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, evaluation) and cognitive strategies (rehearsal, elaboration, organizing). The article defines metacognition as "one's ability to regulate cognitive processes" that is "strongly related to learning outcomes", explicitly distinguishing learning strategies from the concept of learning styles, which it rejects citing Kirschner (2017).
requirements: Teachers need good knowledge of how students differ on learning strategies to offer appropriate differentiated instruction
constraints: Learning strategies are subject and situation specific; there is no ground to argue students have one strategy for all subjects
target_learners: Secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation, metacognition, and subject-matter learning
examples: The intervention grouped students by five MSLQ learning strategy scales: organization, elaboration, metacognitive self-regulation, time and study environment, and effort regulation

article_title: Online peer assessment: effects of cognitive and affective feedback
citation: Jingyan Lu, Nancy Law. (2012). Online peer assessment: effects of cognitive and affective feedback. Instructional Science 40:257–275. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9177-2
title: iLAP (Interactive Learning and Assessment Platform)
description: iLAP is an online learning platform developed to support teaching and assessment of Liberal Studies in Hong Kong schools. Its functions are fourfold: "assignment submission, rubric development, assessment implementation, and performance monitoring". Its peer assessment interface comprises a rubric area, where students assign scores via drop-down menus across criteria and quality levels, and a comment area for free-text feedback; grades and comments become immediately available to assessees.

constraints: In this study assessment activities were not compulsory and students could choose which subtasks to assess
