article_title: Keeping worlds apart to put them back together: VET teachers’ instructional patterns in simulation-based training
citation: Giulia Messina Dahlberg · Susanne Gustavsson. (2025). Keeping worlds apart to put them back together: VET teachers' instructional patterns in simulation-based training. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09714-x
title: Fidelity and authenticity as interactionally accomplished, emergent properties of simulated activity rather than fixed design features.
description: Drawing on Hontvedt and Øvergård (2020), the article advocates conceptualizing fidelity as a verb rather than a noun, something that "goes beyond its connection to the simulator as a tool and the resemblance to the real work environment". Fidelity and authenticity are described as "double-edged swords" that create coherence but also confusion and stress, and as emergent processes requiring individuals' engagement rather than elements related to a task solely by design. The article applies this framework to analyze how VET teachers and students accomplish fidelity and authenticity in the moment-by-moment interaction of simulator-based training.
requirements: Analysis must attend to moment-by-moment interaction among student, teacher, and simulator rather than to the simulator's technical specifications alone.
constraints: The article notes an intrinsic conflict between the simulator and its referent regarding what knowledge is and whether it is something that is, or something that is done in interaction.
target_learners: Upper-secondary VET students (ages 16-19) in the Natural Resource Program
target_learning_goals: Vocational knowledge and skills for operating forestry and agricultural machinery
examples: The article analyzes how a student identifies the artificial dimensions of a simulated environment designed to simplify and remove complex aspects of an authentic environment.
key_sources: Giulia Messina Dahlberg · Susanne Gustavsson. (2025). Keeping worlds apart to put them back together: VET teachers' instructional patterns in simulation-based training. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09714-x

article_title: Keeping worlds apart to put them back together: VET teachers’ instructional patterns in simulation-based training
citation: Giulia Messina Dahlberg · Susanne Gustavsson. (2025). Keeping worlds apart to put them back together: VET teachers' instructional patterns in simulation-based training. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09714-x
title: Design simulation-based VET instruction to deliberately maintain and bridge the boundary between simulated and authentic work environments.
description: The article argues that the instructional work of the VET teacher deals with making sense of how simulated and authentic practices are entangled, and with "making choices that imply unravelling such entanglements and keeping the worlds apart to put them back together again". Boundary-work is described as even more emphasized in simulation-based training than in other vocational subjects because of the elements of fidelity and authenticity. Teachers and students must discern what is (ir)relevant to connect or separate the simulated activity from the authentic work practice, handled in the moment-by-moment interaction.
requirements: VET teachers with dual identity as both teachers and professional experts in the vocational field, whose previous professional experiences are constantly present in the simulator-centre.
constraints: The article notes that simulation as an instructional tool alone is not enough for the development of complex skills where learners have different levels of prior knowledge.
target_learners: Upper-secondary VET students in the Natural Resource Program
target_learning_goals: Development of vocational knowledge and skills connecting simulator-based training to future work-related activities
examples: The article illustrates this with a student who orients towards a teacher's instruction about grappling logs on uneven ground even while performing a simplified box-moving task in the simulator.

article_title: Learning the control-of-variables strategy through self-generated and vicarious errors: the mediating roles of affect, motivation, cognitive load, and error awareness
citation: Hämmerle, L., Kuhlmann, S. L., Krause-Wichmann, T., & Möller, A. (2026). Learning the control-of-variables strategy through self-generated and vicarious errors: the mediating roles of affect, motivation, cognitive load, and error awareness. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09822-2
title: Three mechanisms of learning from errors: prior-knowledge activation, motivation, and depth of cognitive processing
description: The article organizes its investigation of error-based learning around a theoretical framework, attributed to Zhang and Fiorella (2023), identifying three mechanisms that support or inhibit learning from errors. As the article states, the framework "highlights three important mechanisms: (1) activating prior knowledge, which makes existing knowledge accessible and supports its reorganization, (2) motivation, which influences the effort learners invest in engaging with errors, and (3) the depth of cognitive processing." The study operationalizes these as affect, motivation, cognitive load, and error awareness measures mediating condition effects on CVS learning, and notes the framework did not originally consider vicarious errors.
requirements: Learners must engage in deeper processing (e.g., self-explanation) rather than surface-level correction for errors to support integration into coherent knowledge structures
constraints: The article notes the framework "does not consider how these processes might be similar or different when students work with vicarious errors"
target_learners: middle school students (7th and 8th grade)
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry skills, specifically the control-of-variables strategy for designing unconfounded experiments
examples: The study measured these mechanisms via PANAS affect, Intrinsic Motivation Inventory subscales, the Klepsch cognitive load scale, and expert-student error-assessment agreement in a four-condition PS-I intervention

citation: Hämmerle, L., Kuhlmann, S. L., Krause-Wichmann, T., & Möller, A. (2026). title: PS-I error-based learning materials on thermal insulation (wool vs. down) with four condition variants
description: Worksheet-based learning materials developed by the research team, based on prior work by Schmidt (2016), in which "students worked on three experiments in total throughout the PS- and I-phases." The materials taught the CVS by "having them compare the insulating capacity of wool and down," with four PS-phase variants: planning and conducting an experiment (self-generated errors), analyzing two erroneous experiments with a checklist (vicarious errors), both (combination), or analyzing two correct experiments (no-errors). An instruction phase followed with a correct experiment, CVS explanation, and error-reflection tables. Materials were piloted with n = 65 students and provided as translated online material.
requirements: Pre-trained pre-service teacher pairs supported delivery; materials were designed to be primarily self-explanatory
A filler task was added for vicarious and no-errors groups to ensure comparable session durations
constraints: The term "error" refers exclusively to violations of the CVS; experiments with errors unrelated to CVS led to exclusion from analysis
Delayed-test data were excluded due to COVID-19 school lockdowns
target_learners: 7th- and 8th-grade middle school students in an urban region of Austria
target_learning_goals: designing unconfounded experiments by systematically manipulating the independent variable while holding other variables constant
examples: Vicarious-errors students analyzed erroneous experiments containing five CVS-errors each, informed that errors existed but not how many, using a checklist to document experimental variables

Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09822-2
title: Integrate learning from errors within a PS-I framework to retain cognitively engaging experimentation while structuring it in a resource-efficient, guided manner
description: The article proposes that teaching experimentation skills like the CVS through open hands-on work is resource-intensive, leading teachers toward structured formats that reduce planning and decision-making opportunities. It argues that "integrating learning from errors within a PS-I framework may offer a way to retain cognitively engaging elements of experimentation while structuring them in a more resource-efficient and instructionally guided manner." Learners attempt experiments before instruction, generating or analyzing errors that are then used for reflection and direct instruction on the CVS.
requirements: Openness must be carefully balanced with guidance, as both overly open and overly guided formats can hinder learning (Baur & Emden, 2020, as cited)
Error-reflection prompts and delayed direct instruction follow the problem-solving phase
constraints: In the present study, the different error types did not differentially affect CVS learning outcomes when controlling for prior knowledge, so the efficiency advantage remains to be demonstrated against error-free alternatives

target_learning_goals: experimentation competence, particularly the control-of-variables strategy
examples: In the study, all four conditions followed PS-I: a problem-solving phase with condition-specific error activities, then direct CVS instruction and re-analysis of the initial experiments with error-reflection worksheets

article_title: Constructive alignment of a mathematics methodology module
citation: Spangenberg, E. D. (2025). Constructive alignment of a mathematics methodology module. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09712-z
title: Constructive alignment (Biggs & Tang) as a student-centered framework for aligning learning outcomes, teaching-and-learning activities, and assessment tasks
description: The study is underpinned by the theory of constructive alignment coined by Biggs and Tang, derived from constructivism and advocating active involvement in creating understanding. As the article states, "CA is a student-centered model focusing on what MPTs undertake and value about learning rather than what teacher educators accomplish", with teacher educators facilitating while pre-service teachers construct knowledge through classroom activities. Aligning a module involves establishing the outcomes to achieve, the activities to engage in, and the tasks measuring achievement, so that assessment tasks mirror learning outcomes and activities and tasks inform each other.
requirements: Learning outcomes in modules must be clear for successful assessment
Teacher educators must consider LOs and ATs from both sides when designing TLAs
constraints: The article notes negative connotations persist, with CA sometimes applied top-down for quality assurance and criticized as abstract and lacking practical strategies
target_learners: mathematics pre-service teachers in higher education
target_learning_goals: specialized teaching competence in mathematics
integration of theory and practice in lesson planning and assessment
examples: The redesigned module aligned six learning outcomes with eight teaching-and-learning activities and weighted assessment tasks mirroring those outcomes

article_title: Constructive alignment of a mathematics methodology module
citation: Spangenberg, E. D. (2025). Constructive alignment of a mathematics methodology module. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09712-z
title: Weight assessment tasks so the most pertinent learning outcome carries the heaviest weighting
description: In aligning assessment tasks with learning outcomes, the article assigns weightings according to each outcome's importance, following the principle that the selection of a task and time spent on it should correspond with the outcome's importance. Because "a final summative assessment opportunity comprises a heavily weighted AT of 40% (Faculty of Education, 2019), this weighting was dedicated to the most pertinent LO" — the extended-abstract outcome on reflecting on classroom management and professional development, which amalgamates all other outcomes. Work-integrated outcomes were then weighted 30% combined, and the remaining outcomes 10% each.
requirements: Institutional assessment regulations that prescribe or permit weightings per outcome
Learning outcomes classified by kind of knowledge and level of understanding
constraints: Weightings were based on the requirements of the Faculty of Education at the university under study
target_learners: fourth-year mathematics pre-service teachers in a B.Ed. program
target_learning_goals: assessment design that mirrors the importance of learning outcomes
examples: The 40% weighting went to the reflective professional-development outcome; two practicum-based outcomes shared 30%; three remaining outcomes received 10% each

citation: Spangenberg, E. D. (2025). Constructive alignment of a mathematics methodology module. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09712-z
title: Design teaching-and-learning activities from a bilateral perspective, considering learning outcomes and assessment tasks from both sides
description: Activities should be the mediating agency that merges learning outcomes with assessment tasks, informed by outcomes and also affecting tasks. The article illustrates misalignment: an initial activity asking for a reflection on 21st-century knowledge focused on theoretical content knowledge while the outcome required integrating functioning knowledge, so "teacher educators should follow a bilateral perspective (Biggs & Tang, 2011) by considering LOs and ATs from both sides in their design of TLAs". This ensures alignment of theory with practice and attends to what pre-service teachers are expected to achieve.

constraints: A misaligned activity steers learners toward theoretical content when the outcome demands functioning knowledge in practice

teacher educators designing methodology modules

becoming competent mathematics teachers
examples: A reflection-writing activity on 21st-century knowledge was replaced in principle by a GeoGebra-based activity developing an assessment to integrate into a mathematics lesson, better matching the integrating outcome

article_title: Self-regulated learning and video annotation in a high school acting classroom
citation: Hengtao Tang, Jessica Perry Ellison. (2025). Self-regulated learning and video annotation in a high school acting classroom. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09699-z
title: Zimmerman's cyclical self-regulated learning model (forethought, performance/volition, self-reflection)
description: The study's theoretical framework is Zimmerman's (2000) model, which "illustrates self-regulated learning as a recursive cycle" in which learners prepare in the forethought phase (task analysis and self-motivation beliefs), perform and monitor in the performance/volition phase (self-control and self-observation), and reflect in the self-reflection phase (self-evaluation and causal attribution). The intervention mapped weekly goal-setting forms, rehearsal with VideoAnt annotation, and progress reports onto these three phases.

constraints: The article states the full scope of SRL strategies was not addressed due to the limited time span of the study

target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills
acting skills including physicality, vocal performance, and character analysis
examples: Weekly goal-setting forms supported forethought; filmed rehearsals annotated in VideoAnt supported self-observation; weekly progress reports supported self-evaluation

In this study, students uploaded rehearsal videos to YouTube, annotated them in VideoAnt with prompts, and used the annotations to self-evaluate progress toward weekly acting goals, facilitating metacognitive monitoring from a third-person perspective.

constraints: Some students disliked watching themselves and experienced the annotation tasks as additional workload

title: Betz et al.'s three-part model of authenticity in teaching and learning contexts
description: The article uses the model by Betz et al. (2016) as its theoretical frame, "divided into three successive parts". Part 1 covers "the characteristics of learners and of learning settings that may have an impact on students' perceived authenticity"; Part 2 covers their interaction producing perceived authenticity; Part 3 summarizes outcomes affected by perceived authenticity. The study applies the model by varying only the method feature (PF vs. DI) while holding location, instructor, content, materials and innovation constant.

constraints: The article's test varied only the learning-activity (method) feature; other setting features were identical across conditions

target_learning_goals: motivation (situational interest) and perceived authenticity of scientific inquiry practices
examples: The study operationalized the model's setting features in Table 4: method, location, instructor, content, materials, and innovation

citation: Valentina Nachtigall, Nikol Rummel. (2021). Investigating students' perceived authenticity of learning activities in an out-of-school lab for social sciences: a replication study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09556-3
title: Productive Failure problem-solving phase structured by four design principles (problem/task, activity, participation structure, social surround)
description: Drawing on Kapur and Bielaczyc (2012), the article describes four design principles for the PF problem-solving phase: the problem should be "complex and open to various solutions" (Problem/task); students explore "intuitive solution ideas to this problem by using their prior knowledge" (Activity); exploration is fostered by small-group collaboration (Participation structure) without instructional support, so students can independently explore solution ideas (Social surround). The article contrasts these with the DI phase, which fulfills none of them.
requirements: A complex, novel problem open to multiple solutions; small-group collaboration; no instructional support during problem solving
constraints: Applies to the initial problem-solving phase of PF, not to the subsequent instruction phase

target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry practices, e.g. evaluating causal versus correlational evidence
examples: Students in small groups explored a violence-in-media correlation problem before receiving instruction on the canonical solution

article_title: Investigating students’ perceived authenticity of learning activities in an out-of-school lab for social sciences: a replication study
citation: Valentina Nachtigall, Nikol Rummel. (2021). Investigating students' perceived authenticity of learning activities in an out-of-school lab for social sciences: a replication study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09556-3
title: Productive Failure as an authentic learning activity that emulates scientific inquiry
description: The article characterizes PF as highly authentic because it mirrors how scientists work: "In PF, students are asked to explore solutions to a complex problem before they have to falsify their solutions during instruction." Failure, struggle and falsifying conjectures parallel scientific practice, and PF fulfills the features of authentic learning activities (complex problem, open inquiry, collaboration, independent working). By contrast, DI is characterized as less authentic, promoting a view of scientific inquiry as an application of instructions.
requirements: An initial problem-solving phase before instruction, with collaborative exploration without instructional support
constraints: The empirical test found no effect of PF vs. DI on perceived authenticity or situational interest in this OSL context

target_learning_goals: understanding scientific practices such as evaluating causal versus correlational evidence
examples: Both conditions used the same violence-in-media problem and published studies as materials; only the sequence of problem solving and instruction differed

article_title: How are Lao teachers’ goals for teaching associated with their instructional practices?
citation: Anongsack Mahavong, József Balázs Fejes. (2026). How are Lao teachers' goals for teaching associated with their instructional practices? Instructional Science, 54, 6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09756-1
title: TARGETS framework: Ames's TARGET dimensions extended with a social component
description: The TARGETS framework organizes instructional practices that shape students' perceptions of classroom goal structures into six TARGET dimensions — task, autonomy (authority), recognition, grouping, evaluation, and time — plus a proposed seventh social dimension. The article states that "a seventh dimension—the social component—has been proposed for inclusion in the TARGET framework, expanding the acronym to TARGETS." This study measured these practices with the Bardach et al. (2019) Goal structure questionnaire plus an adapted mutual respect scale, and modeled how teachers' relational and mastery goals relate to them.
requirements: Measured via teacher self-report instruments such as the Goal structure questionnaire (Bardach et al., 2019) and an adapted classroom mutual respect scale
constraints: In this study the time subscale was excluded and one item each removed from task, autonomy, and mastery-oriented instruction subscales for psychometric reasons; the authors note the framework's application to nuanced teacher practice may require refinement
target_learners: secondary school students in Lao PDR classrooms
target_learning_goals: shaping mastery-oriented classroom goal structures through teachers' instructional practices
examples: The study administered the Goal structure questionnaire (task, autonomy, recognition, grouping, evaluation, time items) plus an adapted mutual respect scale to 207 Lao secondary teachers.

article_title: How are Lao teachers’ goals for teaching associated with their instructional practices?
citation: Anongsack Mahavong, József Balázs Fejes. (2026). How are Lao teachers' goals for teaching associated with their instructional practices? Instructional Science, 54, 6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09756-1
title: Foster teachers' relational goals alongside mastery goals to support favorable instructional practices
description: The article concludes that relational goals — teachers' aspiration to foster close and supportive student relationships — play a central role in shaping effective instructional practices, including recognition, grouping, and mutual respect. It states that "the results underscore the central role of relational goals in shaping effective instructional practices." Because relational and mastery goals were linked to distinct practices in the Lao sample, supporting both goal orientations may address complementary socioemotional and task-focused aspects of teaching.
requirements: Teachers with endorsement of relational goals alongside mastery goals; teacher self-report assessment of goals and practices
constraints: Findings are cross-sectional, so causal inferences cannot be drawn; the sample was a convenience sample from a single Lao province; fostering goals has not been tested interventionally in this study
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: classroom motivational climate, teacher–student and student–student relationships, mastery-oriented instruction
examples: In the Lao SEM models, relational goals predicted mastery-oriented instruction and the grouping, recognition, and mutual respect practices.

article_title: Relevant prior knowledge moderates the effect of elaboration during small group discussion on academic achievement
citation: Floris M. Van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. Van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2013). Relevant prior knowledge moderates the effect of elaboration during small group discussion on academic achievement. Instructional Science, 41, 729-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9252-3
title: Provide students with some relevant prior knowledge before they enter a problem-based discussion, because lacking it may be detrimental for future learning
description: The article's implication for practice is that collaborative problem-based discussions should be matched to students' prior knowledge: "it may be important to provide students with some relevant prior knowledge before they enter the discussion." The experiment showed elaboration helped only when relevant prior knowledge was present and impeded recall when it was absent. The information given beforehand should consist of loose concepts that students connect themselves during the discussion.
requirements: The pre-discussion information should only contain loose concepts, since students need to generate new connections between these concepts themselves during the discussion
constraints: Lacking some basic level of relevant prior knowledge may actually be detrimental for future learning, as the present results indicate
target_learners: undergraduate and secondary students in problem-based or small-group learning
target_learning_goals: recall of information studied after a problem-based discussion
examples: In the experiment, half the participants studied 21 thunder-and-lightning sentences before the discussion while the other half studied seismographic sentences; only the relevant sentences supported later recall

article_title: Participatory instructional redesign by students and teachers in secondary education: effects on perceptions of instruction
citation: Karin D. Könings, Saskia Brand-Gruwel, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2010). Participatory instructional redesign by students and teachers in secondary education: effects on perceptions of instruction. Instructional Science (2011) 39:737–762. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9152-3
title: Participatory design as a three-phase user-involvement approach to instructional re/design
description: Participatory design, imported from fields such as cognitive ergonomics and health promotion, aims to ensure active participation of users in design decisions that affect them. The article states that a participatory design process consists of three phases: "analysis", "design", and "implementation" — participants first analyze the current situation and its shortcomings, then generate ideas for re/design, and finally devise an implementation plan. In this study the approach was adapted for secondary students co-designing their courses with their teacher.
requirements: Participants analyze the current situation and assess its shortcomings taking their own needs and desires into account before designing changes
constraints: The article notes participatory design in school contexts is fairly new and that it found hardly any prior classroom studies of its effects
target_learners: 10th-grade pre-university secondary students
target_learning_goals: Improving the fit of instruction to students' perceptions and desires
Improving congruence between teachers' and students' interpretations of instruction
examples: Six classes each held a 50-minute participatory design meeting producing a tailor-made redesign of three to six points of improvement
key_sources: Karin D. Könings, Saskia Brand-Gruwel, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2010). Participatory instructional redesign by students and teachers in secondary education: effects on perceptions of instruction. Instructional Science (2011) 39:737–762. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9152-3

article_title: Participatory instructional redesign by students and teachers in secondary education: effects on perceptions of instruction
citation: Karin D. Könings, Saskia Brand-Gruwel, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2010). Participatory instructional redesign by students and teachers in secondary education: effects on perceptions of instruction. Instructional Science (2011) 39:737–762. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9152-3
title: IPSEE questionnaire measuring perceptions, desires, and their discrepancy across eight scales of a learning environment
description: The Inventory of Perceived Study Environment Extended (IPSEE) is a 56-item Dutch questionnaire measuring students' perceptions of a learning environment and their desires for its design, with each item answered twice on six-point scales. The "absolute difference between the scores on question A and B expresses the perceived-desired discrepancy", with small discrepancies indicating good fit. It has eight scales (fascinating contents, productive learning, integration, student autonomy, interaction, differentiation, clarity of goals, personalization); a parallel teacher version (IPSEE-T) has acceptable internal consistencies (alphas 0.68–0.87 for perception items).
requirements: Scales are sufficiently independent to warrant separate consideration, with no colinearity objections in the printed checks
constraints: Administered here only with 10th-grade pre-university students in Dutch secondary education
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Measuring the degree to which characteristics of instruction are perceived present
Measuring fit between students' perceived and desired learning environment
examples: Each item pairs a statement such as 'All students do the same work at the same moment' with perception (A) and desire (B) questions

article_title: Rigorously selected and well trained senior student tutors in problem based learning: student perceptions and study achievements
citation: Catherine De Rijdt, Janine van der Rijt, Filip Dochy, Cees van der Vleuten. (2012). Rigorously selected and well trained senior student tutors in problem based learning: student perceptions and study achievements. Instructional Science, 40, 397-411. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9173-6
title: Rigorous selection and 36-hour training programme for senior student tutors in PBL
description: The article describes a student tutor programme at Maastricht University's Faculty of Law in which students with an average final mark of seven or higher were invited to apply and "All the applicants took part in a rigorous selection procedure, based on the assessment centre method", judged on motivation, knowledge, study achievements and inherent tutor skills. The 23 selected tutors received 36 hours of intensive training in tutoring skills built around themes such as stimulating cognitive processes, scaffolding and fostering meta-cognitive strategies, using observation with reflection, peer coaching, simulations and collaborative learning, followed by further training, personal coaching and observation of experienced staff tutors.
requirements: Student tutors must be selected from high achieving students via a rigorous selection procedure and receive extensive training before and during tutoring, including observation of experienced staff tutors and weekly tutor meetings with staff tutors.
constraints: The study was conducted in one university setting with first-year PBL law courses, and the results do not warrant conclusions about the concrete impact and importance of tutor selection and training themselves.
target_learners: First-year undergraduate law students in a problem-based curriculum
Senior students serving as cross-level tutors
target_learning_goals: Effective tutorial group facilitation
Stimulating cognitive processes and active involvement
Scaffolding and meta-cognitive strategies
examples: Selected student tutors received 36 hours of intensive training during their second year and observed each of 14 tutorial sessions with an experienced staff tutor before starting; the training was similar to the obligatory 38-hour teacher training course for new staff.

article_title: A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models
citation: Namsoo Shin, Jonathan Bowers, Steve Roderick, Cynthia McIntyre, A. Lynn Stephens, Emil Eidin, Joseph Krajcik, Daniel Damelin. (2022). A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09590-9
title: Framework for Computational Systems Modeling: five cyclic modeling practices integrating ST and CT
description: The Framework for Computational Systems Modeling organizes modeling as a cyclic process of five practices: characterize a problem or phenomenon, define system boundaries, design and construct model structure, test/evaluate/debug model behavior, and use the model to explain, predict, or design solutions. The authors state it 'elucidates the synergy between modeling, ST, and CT', with each practice drawing on aspects of both types of thinking. The process is highly iterative, with involvement in one practice influencing both future and previous practices.
requirements: Learners engage in computational (not paper-pencil) modeling so that models produce output values
Curriculum, tools, scaffolds, and assessments aligned to the five practices
constraints: Focus narrowed to a computational approach rather than modeling generally
target_learners: K-12 science learners
target_learning_goals: Explaining phenomena and solving problems through modeling
Systems thinking
Computational thinking
examples: The authors illustrate each practice with example models built in SageModeler, such as dynamic time-based climate change models
key_sources: Namsoo Shin, Jonathan Bowers, Steve Roderick, Cynthia McIntyre, A. Lynn Stephens, Emil Eidin, Joseph Krajcik, Daniel Damelin. (2022). article_title: A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models
citation: Namsoo Shin, Jonathan Bowers, Steve Roderick, Cynthia McIntyre, A. Lynn Stephens, Emil Eidin, Joseph Krajcik, Daniel Damelin. (2022). A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09590-9
title: Taxonomy of five systems thinking aspects with 13 sub-aspects derived from a review of 27 manuscripts
description: From an integrative review of 27 manuscripts that defined systems thinking, the authors identified five aspects: defining a system (boundaries and structure), engaging in causal reasoning, identifying interconnections and feedback, framing problems in terms of behavior over time, and predicting system behavior based on system structure. They synthesized 13 operationalizable sub-aspects, such as identifying relevant elements within boundaries and recognizing balancing and reinforcing feedback structures. Aspects that were vague, difficult to measure, or not specific to ST were excluded by explicit filters.
requirements: Aspects must be described widely across the literature, not overly broad, and operationalizable through observable behaviors
constraints: Aspects vague or difficult to measure, such as using experiential evidence to challenge mental models, were not included
target_learners: K-12 science learners
target_learning_goals: Understanding phenomena as systems of interacting elements
Predicting system behavior from structure
examples: Table 1 summarizes how the reviewed manuscripts described each ST aspect, with counts of authors per aspect

article_title: A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models
citation: Namsoo Shin, Jonathan Bowers, Steve Roderick, Cynthia McIntyre, A. Lynn Stephens, Emil Eidin, Joseph Krajcik, Daniel Damelin. (2022). A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09590-9
title: Taxonomy of five computational thinking aspects with 13 sub-aspects derived from a review of 28 manuscripts
description: From a review of 28 manuscripts defining computational thinking, the authors identified five key CT aspects in the context of modeling: decomposing problems so they are computationally solvable, creating artifacts using algorithmic thinking, generating/organizing/interpreting data, testing and debugging, and making iterative refinements. Thirteen sub-aspects were synthesized, e.g., parameterizing relevant elements and encoding them into executable algorithmic form. Generic features like creativity and collaboration, disposition features, and overly broad features such as abstraction were deliberately excluded.
requirements: Aspects must pass the filters of wide description in the literature, specificity to CT, and operationalizability through observable behaviors
constraints: Generic, dispositional, and overly broad features (e.g., abstraction, creativity) were excluded from the taxonomy
target_learners: K-12 science learners
target_learning_goals: Computational problem solving
Building and refining computational models
examples: Table 2 summarizes how the reviewed manuscripts described each CT aspect, with counts of authors per aspect

A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09590-9
title: SageModeler: free web-based open-source computational modeling tool supporting ST and CT without coding
description: SageModeler is 'a free, web-based, open-source computational modeling tool' used by the authors to illustrate how ST and CT aspects manifest in modeling. Learners get multiple ways of building models (system diagrams, static equilibrium, and dynamic time-based models), visual and textual representations of variables, ways of defining functional relationships 'without having to write equations or computer code', and multiple pathways for visualizing model output. It takes a semiquantitative approach with slider-set initial values and word-with-graph relationship definitions.
requirements: Web access to the tool at sagemodeler.concord.org
constraints: Dynamic modeling 'may not be appropriate for all phenomena and should only be used when it is necessary to explain how the behavior of the system changes over time'
target_learners: K-12 science learners

Causal reasoning
Understanding feedback and behavior over time
examples: Learners build dynamic time-based climate models with drag-and-drop features, converting elements into measurable variables and setting relationships between them

article_title: Teaching biology with narratives: examining the impact of affective and cognitive variables on undergraduate student learning
citation: Samuel Tobler, Tanmay Sinha, Katja Köhler, Manu Kapur. (2025). Teaching biology with narratives: examining the impact of affective and cognitive variables on undergraduate student learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09723-w
title: Micro-spacing: distribution of educational content over shorter intervals interspersed with story paragraphs
description: Micro-spacing is the authors' proposed concept describing how narrative texts distribute educational content differently from expository texts. They define it as "the distribution of educational content over shorter intervals that are interspersed with story paragraphs instead of one concentrated learning session." The authors conjecture that, considering research on the spacing effect, micro-spacing might result in improved knowledge consolidation, potentially explaining part of the narrative condition's transfer advantage. The concept is offered as an interpretation, not a tested manipulation in this study.
requirements: Educational content must be interwoven with story paragraphs so that concept elements are distributed across shorter intervals rather than presented in one concentrated block.
constraints: The article presents micro-spacing as a conjecture grounded in the spacing-effect literature, not as a directly tested mechanism; the study did not manipulate spacing.
target_learners: Undergraduate natural science students
target_learning_goals: Recall, understanding, and transfer of core biological concepts such as enzyme energetics and molecular stochasticity
examples: The narrative text embedded the same biological concepts as the expository text in the historical context of the discoveries discussed, interspersing content with story paragraphs.

article_title: Seeking a science of instruction
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2010). Seeking a science of instruction. Instr Sci 38:143–145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9113-x
title: Triarchic theory of three kinds of cognitive processing during learning
description: Mayer's triarchic theory distinguishes three demands on the learner's limited cognitive capacity: "extraneous processing, which is cognitive processing that does not serve the instructional objective", "essential processing, which is cognitive processing required to mentally represent the presented material in working memory", and "generative processing, which is cognitive processing required to make sense of the material". Meaningful learning depends on selecting, organizing, and integrating material; the three kinds of processing map onto these processes in different degrees. Mayer offers it as a reconciliation of questions about the three kinds of cognitive load in cognitive load theory.
requirements: Instructional design should minimize extraneous processing while managing essential and fostering generative processing, per the theory's account
constraints: Mayer presents it as his own conceptualization within the cognitive theory of multimedia learning, offered in hopes of reconciliation rather than as settled consensus
target_learners: multimedia learners in instructional settings
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning through appropriate cognitive processing of words and pictures
examples: Mayer reports the conceptualization helped discover several research-based principles of multimedia learning (Mayer 2009)
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2010). Seeking a science of instruction. Instr Sci 38:143–145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9113-x

article_title: Seeking a science of instruction
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2010). Seeking a science of instruction. Instr Sci 38:143–145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9113-x
title: Treat boundary conditions as theory-sharpening qualifications, not immutable prescriptions
description: Mayer argues that research-based principles such as the modality principle carry boundary conditions—qualifications like pacing and learner versus system control—and that discovering them helps verify and sharpen theory. On the practical level, "research-based principles such as the modality principle should be implemented in ways that are consistent with the underlying theory rather than being seen as immutable prescriptions that must be followed in all situations". This turns apparent inconsistencies in findings into practical guidance.
requirements: Implementers need knowledge of the underlying theory to judge when a principle applies
constraints: The principle does not apply uniformly in all situations; the modality effect is not found in all studies
target_learners: instructional designers applying multimedia learning principles
target_learning_goals: effective application of multimedia design principles
examples: Mayer cites the modality principle's strongest effects under fast-paced, system-controlled presentation as an observed boundary condition
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2010). Seeking a science of instruction. Instr Sci 38:143–145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9113-x

article_title: Seeking a science of instruction
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2010). Seeking a science of instruction. Instr Sci 38:143–145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9113-x
title: Use both lab-based and school-based studies to build a complete science of instruction
description: Responding to concerns about the external validity of laboratory studies with short lessons, Mayer argues that "educational research is strengthened by multiple research methods", so both lab-based and school-based studies are useful. Each approach has its own strengths and weaknesses, and together they build a more complete science of instruction. He notes some of Sweller's cited work involved trainees in industrial training programs, and that researchers have investigated the modality principle in real school settings.
requirements: Research programs should include both lab and school venues rather than relying on one method
constraints: Lab-based work with short lessons has limited external validity, a concern Mayer says his own research reports have repeatedly recognized
target_learners: education researchers studying instructional effectiveness
target_learning_goals: building externally valid, research-based instructional theory
examples: Mayer points to Harskamp et al. (2007) investigating the modality principle in real school settings

article_title: Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers’ first- and second-order knowledge integration
citation: Lehmann, T. (2024). Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers' first- and second-order knowledge integration. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09655-3
title: Two-layer conceptualization of pre-service teachers' knowledge integration: first-order and second-order KI
description: The article adopts Lehmann's (2020b) conceptualization in which knowledge integration has two layers. First-order KI denotes "the cognitive-constructive learning processes of building and structuring an integrated knowledge base within one's memory", while second-order KI "denotes the integrated use of domain-specific knowledge" in application situations such as teaching, lesson planning, and task design. The framework connects to models of teachers' professional competence (disposition vs. situation-specific performance) and to transfer theory, and it underpins the study's mediation hypothesis.
requirements: Learning settings must involve multiple domain-specific knowledge bodies (e.g., CK, PK, PCK) that can be interrelated
constraints: The article notes empirical studies on the relation between integration in learning and in application settings are scarce and findings vary
target_learners: pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: integration of content knowledge, general pedagogical knowledge, and pedagogical-content knowledge
integrated application of professional knowledge in teaching tasks
examples: The study operationalized first-order KI via essay coding (elaborations across domains, switches) and second-order KI via an integrated knowledge application test on a lesson plan
key_sources: Lehmann, T. (2024). Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers' first- and second-order knowledge integration. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09655-3

article_title: Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers’ first- and second-order knowledge integration
citation: Lehmann, T. (2024). Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers' first- and second-order knowledge integration. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09655-3
title: Use low-threshold instructional prompts — relevance instructions and guiding questions — to foster knowledge integration when pre-service teachers read and write across domain-specific texts
description: Because curricular integration of CK-, PK-, and PCK-specific courses is organizationally costly, the article promotes "rather easy-to-implement instructional scaffolds such as prompts to promote pre-service teachers' knowledge integration within self-regulated learning scenarios" involving multiple domain-specific texts and writing to learn. Relevance instructions make the integration goal salient before learning and support task-model formation; guiding questions directly provoke integrative processing modes while answering them. Both improved first-order KI in the experiment.
requirements: A learning task involving multiple domain-specific sources (here one text each on CK, PK, and PCK) plus a writing task
Prompts are "non-standalone" means that assist learners with a task rather than replace it
constraints: The article notes guiding questions were previously found effective irrespective of CK/PCK domain, but states more empirical evidence needs to be generated for that domain-independence conclusion
target_learners: pre-service teachers in higher education
target_learning_goals: integrative processing of multiple domain-specific documents
merging CK, PK, and PCK into an integrated knowledge base
examples: The GQ group received five guiding questions such as "Can you find statements in a text that can be used to explain the content that is presented in the other texts?"; the RI group received a text explaining why integrating CK, PK, and PCK matters, linked to the upcoming writing task

citation: Lehmann, T. (2024). Bridging domains: examining the effects of relevance instructions and guiding questions on pre-service teachers' first- and second-order knowledge integration. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09655-3
title: Integrated knowledge application test: justified evaluation and improvement of a tabular lesson plan
description: The study's measure of second-order KI asks participants to evaluate how a planned third-grade spelling lesson is or is not appropriate for promoting spelling skills. Participants list positive features and suggest improvements, each with a justification, in a pre-structured template. Responses are coded for whether they apply CK, PK, PCK, prior knowledge, or incorrect knowledge, and rationales drawing on more domains score more points, yielding an overall second-order KI index. Interrater reliability was excellent (ICCs between 0.82 and 0.94).
requirements: A lesson plan containing both strengths and weaknesses identifiable from the three domain-specific text sources
Raters blind to condition and trained on the coding scheme
constraints: The scoring deducts one point per incorrect knowledge application, so the index penalizes misconceptions as well as rewarding integration
target_learners: pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: integrated simultaneous application of CK, PK, and PCK in a lesson-planning evaluation task
examples: Sample coded response: a PK application justifying more group work phases because "the cognitive activation of the pupils could probably be increased"

article_title: Minding the gender gap in advanced STEM courses: effects of student preparedness and activity level
citation: Ilana Ram, Adam Shwartz, Ido Roll. (2025). Minding the gender gap in advanced STEM courses: effects of student preparedness and activity level. Instructional Science (2025) 53:1457–1478. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09748-1
title: Multi-family explanatory framework for the STEM gender gap: learner attributes, instructional/assessment design, and motivational accounts
description: The article organizes existing explanations for the higher-STEM gender gap into three not-mutually-exclusive families. As it states, "Some focus on learner attributes such as individual level of preparation or the learner's activity level", "while others focus on instructional and assessment design", and "A third group of possible explanations look at motivational accounts" such as stereotype threat or sense of belonging. The study evaluates the first two families simultaneously using trace data, performance data on low/high-stakes assessments, and learner-attribute data, finding preparation accounts carry most explained variance.
requirements: Simultaneous modeling of multiple candidate causes (preparedness, assessment stakes, activity) to apportion explained variance
constraints: The families are not connected under a single unifying framework, possibly due to differences in epistemologies and assumptions, as the article notes
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students
target_learning_goals: understanding and reducing the gender achievement gap in advanced STEM courses
examples: The study operationalized the framework with mixed-effects models over five assessments and hierarchical regressions with theory-driven blocks in four courses

article_title: Spaced recall reduces forgetting of fundamental mathematical concepts in a post high school precalculus course
citation: Lindquist, D. S., Sparrow, B. E., & Lindquist, J. M. (2024). Spaced recall reduces forgetting of fundamental mathematical concepts in a post high school precalculus course. Instructional Science, 52, 859-878. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09680-w
title: Testing effect and desired difficulty account for durable retention through effortful spaced retrieval
description: The article frames its intervention with the testing effect: quizzing produces more durable memory than re-study because effortful retrieval strengthens memory. It states that "Memory is made more durable when effort is needed to recall information" and that testing creates new retrieval routes that increase retrieval effort. The 'desired difficulty' concept holds that increased retrieval effort leads to deeper connections and longer-lasting learning, and spacing quizzes so retrieval remains effortful is essential to the effect.
requirements: Initial retrieval attempts must be effortful; quizzing too soon after learning diminishes the effect
Spacing must balance effort against the learner's ability to still recall
constraints: The article notes mixed results in comparisons of open response versus multiple choice quiz formats
target_learners: students in mathematics courses requiring retention of foundational knowledge
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and recall of previously learned concepts
examples: The USMAPS treatment staggered and spaced quiz topics every 28 days to preserve desired difficulty and prevent students sharing quiz content.

article_title: Which events can cause iteration in instructional design? An empirical study of the design process
citation: Verstegen, D.M.L., Barnard, Y.F. & Pilot, A. (2006). Which events can cause iteration in instructional design? An empirical study of the design process. Instructional Science 34, 481–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-3346-0
title: Framework of triggers for iteration in instructional design
description: A framework listing concrete events that trigger iteration in instructional design, proposed because earlier reason-types were judged too coarse to predict when iteration should occur. Triggers 'originate from outside (new information, new opinions/arguments and acquisition procedures)' or are 'caused by, or evolve from interaction with the design process itself (discovery of missing input, need to repair errors, new insights based on work later on in the design process, and new ideas of the designers)'. It is intended as a basis for further research and for defining support measures for designers, especially novices.
requirements: Serves as a basis for further research and for the definition of measures that help designers, especially novices, deal with iteration during the design process.
constraints: Derived from one evaluation study with eight novice designers in the training-simulator domain; the article notes the limited number of subjects does not allow valid use of correlation coefficients.
target_learners: novice instructional designers
designers of training simulator specifications
target_learning_goals: managing iteration in the instructional design process
examples: In the study, scheduled design cycles and peer review most often provoked iteration, while a resources e-mail and chat sessions did so less often.

citation: Verstegen, D.M.L., Barnard, Y.F. & Pilot, A. (2006). Which events can cause iteration in instructional design? An empirical study of the design process. Instructional Science 34, 481–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-3346-0
title: MASTER-TPD prototype tool for training program design
description: A prototype tool implementing the Training Program Design phase of the MASTER method, customised from Designer's Edge (DE 2.0, 1997). It guides users through six main steps with sub-steps and Notepads, logs user actions, and 'supports iteration because intermediate results (including the subjects’ notes) remain available'. 'A small number of warnings appears automatically when an event that is a likely cause for iteration can be measured.'
requirements: Implements the middle MASTER-TPD phase of the MASTER method for specifying training simulators; guidelines provide information about relations between design activities, strategic advice, and indications for taking notes.
constraints: Subjects reported that in later steps the tool does not show all training activities but only those taking place with the simulator, and sequencing information can get lost when the tool is not used as intended.
target_learners: novice instructional designers
target_learning_goals: designing functional specifications for training simulators
training program design
examples: The tool logged time-stamped actions from which iteration counts were derived, and stored final and intermediate designs and Notepad notes.

citation: Verstegen, D.M.L., Barnard, Y.F. & Pilot, A. (2006). Which events can cause iteration in instructional design? An empirical study of the design process. Instructional Science 34, 481–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-3346-0
title: Eight characteristics of the design of training simulator specifications
description: The article characterises the design of training simulator specifications as a task with 'eight main characteristics', including complex domains requiring extensive task analysis, multiple and contradicting constraints, long time-consuming processes, incomplete and insecure information, and timing problems. The authors state these characteristics 'reﬂect the ill-structured nature of design problems and the iterative nature of the instructional design process'.
requirements: Designers of simulator specifications need extensive knowledge of the task domain, the technical systems to be used, learning, and instructional design.
constraints: The characteristics are attributed to earlier analyses of simulator specification projects (Verstegen, 2003; Verstegen & van der Hulst, 2000) rather than tested in this study.
target_learners: instructional designers specifying training simulators
domain experts and instructors tasked with simulator specification
target_learning_goals: understanding the ill-structured, iterative nature of simulator specification design
examples: The study case: designing functional specifications for a simulator to train analysts of thermal images collected with Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV).

article_title: When learning from animations is more successful than learning from static pictures: learning the specifics of change
citation: Rolf Ploetzner, Sandra Berney, Mireille Bétrancourt. (2021). When learning from animations is more successful than learning from static pictures: learning the specifics of change. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09541-w
title: Animation Process Model (APM): five interacting phases of perceptual and cognitive processing in learning from unnarrated animations
description: The Animation Process Model (APM; Lowe & Boucheix, 2008, 2011; Lowe & Schnotz, 2014) describes how learning from unnarrated animations progresses through five phases in which "perceptual bottom-up and cognitive top-down processes interact". Learners first identify confined event units, merge them into dynamic micro-chunks, combine these into relational structures such as causal chains, associate functional tasks yielding functional episodes, and finally refine the established functionality. The phases are not processed in linear order, and learners with little prior knowledge must repeatedly apply the processes. The article uses the APM to argue that perceptual-level learning is an educational objective in its own right and focused its study on perceptual processing.
requirements: Learners must sufficiently perceive and comprehend the animation for it to be educationally effective; learners with little prior knowledge need repeated processing of the phases
constraints: The article notes it remains to be described in detail how perceptual processes during learning from animations facilitate conceptual understanding and vice versa
target_learners: undergraduate pre-service teacher students learning from unnarrated animations
novice learners with little prior knowledge of the animated subject matter
target_learning_goals: constructing mental representations of displayed changes and how they unfold in time (kinematic models)
perceptual learning of motion patterns and spatial arrangements
examples: The experimental study focused on perceptual processing during learning from animation, using motion- and arrangement-identification tasks with proximity to perceptual memory tasks
key_sources: Rolf Ploetzner, Sandra Berney, Mireille Bétrancourt. (2021). When learning from animations is more successful than learning from static pictures: learning the specifics of change. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09541-w

article_title: Metacognitive scaffolding in an innovative learning arrangement
citation: Molenaar, I., van Boxtel, C. A. M., & Sleegers, P. J. C. (2010). Metacognitive scaffolding in an innovative learning arrangement. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9154-1
title: Socio-cognitive perspective on metacognitive scaffolding in collaborative learning: the why, what and how of scaffolding
description: The article organizes scaffolding research around three characteristics: the why (rationale — most students cannot perform assignments without support), the what (scaffolds directed at the object or meta level of learning), and the how (modality, static versus dynamic integration, and structuring versus problematizing form). Drawing on the socio-cognitive perspective, group members are "multiple regulating agents who co-regulate each others learning and operate as a social system", with parallel outcomes at group level (the product) and individual level (cognitive residues). Structuring scaffolds take the direct route by regulating the interpersonal plane, while problematizing scaffolds take the indirect route by eliciting individuals' metacognitive activities.
requirements: Scaffolds must be dynamically integrated into the learning process and timed to moments when metacognitive activities are generally executed
constraints: The framework was studied in triads of elementary students in an e-learning environment with scaffolds delivered during the first two lessons only
target_learners: elementary school students (Grades 4-6) working in collaborative triads
target_learning_goals: regulation of collaborative learning activities
metacognitive knowledge
domain knowledge acquisition
examples: The virtual agent showed structuring groups an exemplary plan for a mind map assignment, while problematizing groups were asked 'how can you plan a mind map assignment?' and obliged to answer in an answer box
key_sources: Molenaar, I., van Boxtel, C. A. M., & Sleegers, P. J. C. (2010). Metacognitive scaffolding in an innovative learning arrangement. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9154-1

article_title: Metacognitive scaffolding in an innovative learning arrangement
citation: Molenaar, I., van Boxtel, C. A. M., & Sleegers, P. J. C. (2010). Metacognitive scaffolding in an innovative learning arrangement. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9154-1
title: Atgentschool dynamic scaffolding system with three-dimensional virtual agent in the Ontdeknet e-learning environment
description: Atgentschool delivered metacognitive scaffolds through a three-dimensional virtual agent powered by Living Actor technology, embedded in the Ontdeknet e-learning environment where triads collaborated with an external expert on a country-study assignment. An attention management system with three levels (input, reasoning, intervention) monitored students' attention focus from keyboard strokes, mouse movements and event information to determine when to send which scaffold. For each sub-assignment, orientation, planning and monitoring scaffolds were implemented, with students receiving a minimum of 12 scaffolds shown in text balloons, spoken aloud, and accompanied by animations and emotions.
requirements: An attention management system to determine when to send which scaffold based on students' attention focus
User input via four icons (a help question mark and three emotional icons) as additional input
constraints: Scaffolds were delivered only during the first two lessons of the eight-lesson experiment
Control triads saw the same virtual agent without metacognitive support to prevent a Hawthorne effect
target_learners: elementary school students in Grades 4-6 working in heterogeneous triads
target_learning_goals: orientation, planning and monitoring of collaborative inquiry assignments
examples: Scaffolds were triggered at sub-assignment selection (orientation), just before execution (planning), and upon saving (monitoring)

article_title: Latent classes of self-reported feedback experiences: exploring students’ challenges, motivations, and action-taking behaviours in feedback processes
citation: Flora Ji-Yoon Jin, Lixiang Yan, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Dragan Gašević, Philip Wing Keung Chan, Yi-Shan Tsai. (2025). Latent classes of self-reported feedback experiences: exploring students’ challenges, motivations, and action-taking behaviours in feedback processes. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09744-5
title: Triangular framework of dialogic feedback: cognitive, social-affective, and structural dimensions
description: The article draws on a triangular framework of the dialogic feedback process proposed by Yang and Carless (2013), in which "a triangular framework has been proposed that includes three dimensions: cognitive, social-affective, and structural". The cognitive dimension concerns feedback content that enhances students' cognitive abilities; the social-affective dimension underscores trust and balanced power relationships between educators and students; the structural dimension concerns management and organisation of the feedback process by educators and institutions. The study uses this framework, together with the learner-centred feedback framework, as a deductive coding lens for qualitative analysis of feedback design themes.
requirements: Feedback conceptualised as a reciprocal, dialogic process in which students take an active role in engaging with and responding to feedback, not a one-way transmission model.
constraints: The framework is attributed to Yang and Carless (2013); the article applies it as an analytical lens rather than testing it empirically.
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: engaging with and acting on feedback
self-regulated use of feedback
examples: The study's qualitative coding scheme grouped feedback design codes using this triangular framework alongside the learner-centred feedback framework (Ryan et al., 2022).

article_title: Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling
citation: Idit Adler · Saja Rabie. (2026). Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling. Instructional Science (2026) 54:36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09785-4
title: Pragmatic constructionism: an epistemological framework for interdisciplinary understanding with four core cognitive processes
description: Boix Mansilla's pragmatic constructionism, adopted as this study's analytical framework, centers interdisciplinary learning on "purposeful, pluralist, and provisional understandings". It defines interdisciplinary learning as integrating information, data, techniques, tools, perspectives, ideas, concepts and theories from two or more disciplines to create products, explain phenomena, or solve problems in ways unlikely through single-disciplinary means. Learners engage in four dynamically interacting cognitive processes: establishing a purpose; weighing disciplinary insights; building and leveraging integrations; and maintaining a critical stance. The study used this framework to operationalize and code students' discourse.
requirements: Learners bring prior disciplinary knowledge, which informs questions, affords hypotheses, and provides an initial representation of the problem
constraints: The four processes interact dynamically and inform one another as learning progresses iteratively, so they are not sequential stages
target_learners: high school students
k-12 learners integrating two or more disciplines
target_learning_goals: interdisciplinary understanding
integration of disciplinary perspectives
examples: The study coded multidisciplinary group discourse against operationalizations of the four processes, e.g., identifying ways to connect the disciplines for establishing purpose and sharing expertise for weighing disciplinary insights
key_sources: Idit Adler · Saja Rabie. (2026). Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling. Instructional Science (2026) 54:36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09785-4

article_title: Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling
citation: Idit Adler · Saja Rabie. (2026). Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling. Instructional Science (2026) 54:36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09785-4
title: Collaborative multidisciplinary modeling task combining Jigsaw grouping with knowledge-building pedagogy
description: A unit-level design in which students first work in disciplinary groups (biology, chemistry, physics) to investigate a phenomenon and build disciplinary models, then are rearranged into multidisciplinary groups of one student per discipline who share models and develop a collaborative combined model. The Jigsaw approach "ensured symmetric knowledge advancement, as each participant acted as a disciplinary expert and was essential to the group's progress". The shared model serves as an epistemic artifact that triggers advancement of interdisciplinary knowledge in the classroom community, following knowledge-building principles such as idea improvement, diversity of perspectives, and epistemic agency.
requirements: Students with different disciplinary expertise who each contribute a disciplinary model
An authentic, real-world problem that resonates with students' lived experiences
Extended time for collaborative work (the unit comprised four learning sets and 15 lessons of 45 min each, some double periods)
constraints: Due to COVID-19 pandemic, students completed the unit online and used online tools (draw.io) to develop their models
target_learners: high school students majoring in different scientific disciplines
target_learning_goals: collaborative sense-making of a scientific phenomenon
integrating disciplinary perspectives into a shared model
examples: The unit How does alcohol consumption affect our body? had students develop disciplinary models of alcohol's effects, then combine them into multidisciplinary models and write final reports reflecting on the process
key_sources: Idit Adler · Saja Rabie. (2026). Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling. Instructional Science (2026) 54:36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09785-4

article_title: Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling
citation: Idit Adler · Saja Rabie. (2026). Towards interdisciplinarity: emerging patterns of discourses during collaborative multidisciplinary modeling. Instructional Science (2026) 54:36. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09785-4
title: The science unit 'How does alcohol consumption affect our body?'
description: A 15-lesson science unit (four learning sets, 45-minute lessons, some extended double periods) in which high-school students investigated the effect of alcohol consumption on the human body from three disciplinary perspectives: physics (reaction time, speed, acceleration), chemistry (chemical reactions in the body), and biology (effects on body systems). Students recalled prior knowledge, built disciplinary models, then developed collaborative multidisciplinary models using draw.io online software, and finally formulated reports and reflected. The unit followed project-based learning and knowledge-building design principles.
requirements: Students assigned to disciplinary groups by their major, then recombined into multidisciplinary groups of three
constraints: Implemented online due to the COVID-19 pandemic
target_learners: 11th-grade high-achieving science students
target_learning_goals: understanding effects of alcohol consumption on the body
developing and integrating scientific models
examples: Learning set 2 (7 lessons) focused on disciplinary models; learning set 3 (6 lessons) on sharing and combining them into multidisciplinary models

article_title: Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others
citation: Floris M. van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2011). Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others. Instructional Science 39, 189–204. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9124-7
title: Cognitive elaborative perspective on collaborative learning
description: One of two major theoretical perspectives on collaborative learning distinguished by O'Donnell (2006), the other being socio-behavioral. It holds that "students process information at deeper levels when they learn collaboratively", stressing elaboration and recourse to prior knowledge rather than motivation or social cohesion. Elaboration is defined as higher-order thinking that connects new information with existing knowledge, producing a richer memory structure assumed to inhibit forgetting. The present experiment was designed to test this perspective by isolating explaining as the cognitive process underlying the benefit of small-group discussion.
requirements: Learners must possess relevant prior knowledge that can be activated and elaborated during the discussion
constraints: The article notes the perspective's assumptions had not previously been tested in a controlled, experimental study
target_learners: undergraduate students in small-group or problem-based settings
target_learning_goals: deep processing and long-term retention of subject-matter knowledge
examples: The experiment compared explaining, listening and irrelevant-discussion conditions with recall of a radar text tested immediately and after one month
key_sources: Floris M. van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2011). Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others. Instructional Science 39, 189–204. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9124-7

article_title: Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others
citation: Floris M. van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2011). Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others. Instructional Science 39, 189–204. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9124-7
title: Simulated video group discussion method for isolating cognitive activities in collaborative learning
description: A laboratory research method in which participants watch a video-recorded group discussion performed by actors, so that all participants share the same prior knowledge and are exposed to the same group process. "The effects of explanation on learning could be studied by stopping the video at various points in time and instructing the participants to respond to the discussion during these 'gaps'." An edited version with the main explainer's contributions removed was used for the explanation condition and the integral version for the listening condition, allowing explaining to be compared with listening while controlling for random group dynamics.
requirements: Actors and scripts recorded in advance; participants instructed to use knowledge from a pre-experiment instruction text
constraints: The authors note it is debatable whether processes induced by watching a simulated discussion are equivalent to those in a real group discussion, which may be more dynamic and include off-topic talk
target_learners: undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: studying the cognitive processes (explaining, listening) that support learning during group discussion
examples: The radar problem discussion was performed by four drama-club students and shown to participants in isolated computer rooms
key_sources: Floris M. van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2011). Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion?
