article_title: Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others
citation: Floris M. van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2011). Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others. Instructional Science 39, 189–204. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9124-7
title: Have students actively provide explanations during small-group discussion to support long-term retention
description: When organizing small-group discussion, design activities so that students verbally explain content to others rather than only listening. The article concludes that "providing explanations as well as listening to others during a small group discussion benefit short-term recall, while producing explanations increases retention of knowledge during 1 month". The mechanism proposed is that explaining requires students to structure or restructure their knowledge before verbalizing it, which fosters elaboration and resists forgetting.
requirements: Participants need relevant prior knowledge (gained here from a pre-experiment instruction text) to draw on when explaining
constraints: The long-term advantage of explaining over listening emerged only at the one-month measurement, not immediately; the study used a simulated video discussion, and the authors call for future experiments to minimize discrepancies with real discussions
target_learners: undergraduate students in small-group or problem-based learning
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of studied subject matter
examples: In the experiment, participants in the explanation condition were instructed to explain as much as possible, answering actors' questions during gaps in the edited video

article_title: Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design
citation: Charlott Sellberg & Oskar Lindwall. (2025). Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09763-2
title: Fidelity as an interactional and instructional achievement rather than a fixed property of simulation technology
description: The editorial reconceptualises simulation fidelity, commonly defined as the extent to which a simulation reproduces physical, procedural, or functional features of a work setting, as something accomplished in practice. It argues that "fidelity emerges through participants' coordination, mutual orientation, and instructional framing, rather than from the simulator's realism alone". The educational value of a simulator depends on how it is embedded in instructional work and made relevant to learners' ongoing activity, as illustrated by forestry teachers' orchestration of simulator tasks.
requirements: Simulators must be embedded in instructional work and made relevant to learners' ongoing activity for their educational value to be realised
constraints: Applies to simulation-based education settings where participants, tools, and tasks are coordinated in instructional settings
target_learners: novices in professional education domains such as healthcare, aviation, maritime, forestry, and military training
target_learning_goals: professional skills and competencies developed through simulation-based training
examples: Messina Dahlberg and Gustavsson (2025) show fidelity in forestry-driving simulators emerges through teachers' orchestration of tasks, guidance, and links to outdoor practice
key_sources: Charlott Sellberg & Oskar Lindwall. (2025). Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09763-2

article_title: Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design
citation: Charlott Sellberg & Oskar Lindwall. (2025). Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09763-2
title: Design simulations for functional correspondence with the task elements most consequential for professional performance, matched to learner stage
description: The editorial recommends that simulation design, rather than replicating reality wholesale, focus on identifying and preserving the task elements most consequential for professional performance — motor routines, critical decisions, and forms of coordination — presented in ways appropriate to the learner's developmental stage. Functional resemblance is treated as "a design hypothesis – something to be tested, adapted, and refined in situ". Simplified or deliberately inauthentic setups may be pedagogically superior for novices.
requirements: Designers must identify which task elements — motor routines, critical decisions, forms of coordination — are most consequential for professional performance
constraints: Overly authentic environments may impede novice learning by demanding too many interacting elements before essentials are mastered; what counts as correspondence varies by domain, learner stage, and pedagogical purpose
target_learners: novices through advanced learners in professional education
target_learning_goals: professional performance skills, decision-making, and coordination
examples: Forestry teachers intentionally simplify simulator tasks to enable volume training of key manoeuvres, reconnecting them later to broader professional trajectories through discussion and fieldwork
key_sources: Charlott Sellberg & Oskar Lindwall. (2025). Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09763-2

article_title: Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design
citation: Charlott Sellberg & Oskar Lindwall. (2025). Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09763-2
title: The briefing–scenario–debriefing (BSD) cycle as a design scaffold for distributing guidance, feedback, and representational work over time
description: The editorial describes the briefing–scenario–debriefing cycle as a widely used framework for structuring simulation instruction: a prospective phase prepares learners, an in-action phase supports performance, and a retrospective phase renders experience accountable and generalisable. Conceptually, "the BSD cycle is less a fixed script than a design scaffold for distributing guidance, feedback, and representational work over time". Briefings translate curriculum goals into attentional priorities; debriefings convert concrete experiences into general principles.
requirements: Briefings must translate curriculum goals into attentional priorities and familiarise learners with the simulation environment; debriefings must convert experiences into generalisable insights
constraints: The BSD cycle is only one of many ways to embed simulations within broader instructional designs
target_learners: professional education learners across domains
target_learning_goals: converting simulation experience into general principles and actionable insights
examples: Nursing debriefings use annotated timelines, clipped video, or live-captured notes; military post-wargame debriefings use maps, gestures, and narrated fragments of play
key_sources: Charlott Sellberg & Oskar Lindwall. (2025). Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09763-2

article_title: Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design
citation: Charlott Sellberg & Oskar Lindwall. (2025). Simulation-based training in professional education: learning, participation, and instructional design. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09763-2
title: Align performance-review media such as video with instructional aims, facilitator expertise, and the emotional climate of training
description: The editorial draws the broader lesson from the video-debriefing studies that "media are not neutral – they must be aligned with instructional aims, facilitator expertise, and the emotional climate of training". Performance-review tools such as video not only extend reflection but also impose new design responsibilities, making tools instructional decisions rather than neutral add-ons.
requirements: Effective integration of multi-camera video systems requires additional pedagogical competence from facilitators
constraints: Video may risk psychological safety and narrow reflection to individual rather than team performance
target_learners: professional trainees in settings using recorded performance review, e.g., mountain rescue, healthcare
target_learning_goals: reflective team learning from simulated performance
examples: Schreder et al. (2025) demonstrate that video performance-review tools extend reflection but impose new design responsibilities in mountain rescue training

article_title: Sixth graders’ selection and integration when writing from multiple online texts
citation: Kullberg, N., Kiili, C., Bråten, I., González-Ibáñez, R., & Leppänen, P. H. T. (2023). Sixth graders' selection and integration when writing from multiple online texts. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09613-5
title: Thematic unit as a unit of analysis for observing integration in multiple-text writing
description: The study introduces the thematic unit, defined as "an idea or a chain of connected ideas", as a new unit of analysis for examining integration in written products. Unlike an idea unit containing a main verb, a thematic unit is broader and may span ideas within or across perspectives, from prior knowledge, or generated in response to the task. Ideas within a unit are connected by connective words, repetition of key concepts, organization, or elaborations. The authors claim it is better suited than idea units to reveal students' attempts to integrate content beyond single ideas.
requirements: Written products must be segmented into thematic units with identified sources of ideas (snippets, other text ideas, prior knowledge, task-generated ideas) before integration types can be coded.
constraints: The article reports this as a methodological contribution without evidence comparing its sensitivity to idea-unit analysis.
target_learners: primary school students (sixth grade)
target_learning_goals: multiple-text comprehension
integration of ideas across texts
examples: Thematic units were identified in 162 written products, yielding 578 units coded for four integration types with 80% agreement on unit boundaries.

article_title: Sixth graders’ selection and integration when writing from multiple online texts
citation: Kullberg, N., Kiili, C., Bråten, I., González-Ibáñez, R., & Leppänen, P. H. T. (2023). Sixth graders' selection and integration when writing from multiple online texts. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09613-5
title: Neurone web-based platform with snippet selection and writing tools for online inquiry
description: Neurone is a web-based platform on which students completed a four-phase online inquiry task: searching for texts, reading and selecting snippets, evaluating credibility, and composing an article. The snippet tool let students highlight and save up to two snippets per text (maximum 20 words each); the writing tool displayed selected snippets beside the writing space and let students open the source page with snippets highlighted in context. Copy-paste from snippets was blocked, and both tools were designed to save cognitive resources for integration.
requirements: Students need instruction in how to process selected information further, so the snippet tool is not used simply for copying.
constraints: The article evaluated the platform within a closed search space of three relevant and 17 irrelevant texts and time-limited phases; it did not test the tools' effects in authentic open web contexts.
target_learners: sixth-grade students (ages 11-14) in elementary school
target_learning_goals: selecting relevant ideas from multiple online texts
integrating information across texts in writing
examples: In the study, students selected six snippets across three texts and composed articles of at least 50 words with snippets visible and copy-paste disabled.

article_title: The modality effect reverses in a virtual reality learning environment and influences cognitive load
citation: Patrick Albus, Tina Seufert. (2023). The modality effect reverses in a virtual reality learning environment and influences cognitive load. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09611-7
title: Boundary-condition account of the reverse modality effect in immersive VR
description: The article explains the reversed modality effect in VRLE via boundary conditions known from classical multimedia research: the modality effect "can be reversed if, for example, when longer or more complex texts are presented or when the learning environment is self-paced". Stable visual text permits re-reading and self-regulated reading strategies, whereas transient auditory text depends on presentation speed; in VR, immersion, constant visual change, and seductive details further strain the visual channel and distract attention. The account integrates CTML, CLT, and the Colavita visual dominance effect as candidate explanations.
requirements: Applies to immersive VR learning environments with additional verbal information alongside rich visual content
constraints: The Colavita effect has primarily been studied in audio-visual discrimination tasks, not learning environments
Whether learners look around during narration is unknown without eye-tracking data
target_learners: adult students learning science content in immersive VR
target_learning_goals: recall, comprehension and transfer of science material presented in VR
examples: The study shortened texts to about 40 words on average and integrated visual text dynamically into the VRLE to remove prior boundary conditions, yet the effect still reversed

title: cellVIEW VR immersive learning unit on HIV
description: An immersive VR learning environment built on the tool cellVIEW for this study, presenting a guided tour through an HIV cell in 3D. Macromolecular structures "only became visible when the learner moved towards or into a component of the virus", and learners could move freely and observe structures from all sides. Verbal explanatory texts were presented either as integrated visual text whose rotation dynamically adapted to the learner's position, or auditorily via headset, with identical wording across conditions. The learning phase lasted on average 11 minutes and was self-paced, with no replay possible.
requirements: Head-mounted display with roomscale tracking and controllers
Text integrated into the VRLE and dynamically rotated for readability
constraints: Replaying content or returning to previous content was not possible
target_learners: adult students (aged 19-37, mostly psychology/education participants)
target_learning_goals: macromolecular biology: HIV structure and processes within the virus
examples: Used with a Vive Pro HMD in a between-subjects experiment comparing visual-only and audio-visual text modality

article_title: Teaching sourcing during online inquiry – adolescents with the weakest skills benefited the most
citation: Hämäläinen, E. K., Kiili, C., Räikkönen, E., Lakkala, M., Ilomäki, L., Toom, A., & Marttunen, M. (2023). Teaching sourcing during online inquiry – adolescents with the weakest skills benefited the most. Instructional Science, 51, 135–163. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09597-2
title: Documents Model and Online Research and Comprehension Model as the framework for sourcing throughout online inquiry
description: The study is informed by two theoretical models. The Online Research and Comprehension Model frames online inquiry as five recursive, reciprocal processes: "specifying information need and locating, critically evaluating, synthesizing, and communicating online information". The Documents Model holds that "readers can construct two types of representations when reading multiple texts: an intertext model and an integrated mental model", with source-to-content and source-to-source links connecting source information to content and across documents. The intervention and its scoring rubrics were designed around these models, treating sourcing as applicable in every inquiry phase.
requirements: Sourcing instruction should be structured to follow the phases of online inquiry so that source information is attended to in each phase
constraints: The Documents Model was initially developed in the context of interpreting historical documents, and the article applies it to online health information
target_learners: upper secondary school students
target_learning_goals: sourcing during online inquiry
critical evaluation of online information
multiple document comprehension

article_title: Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy
citation: Sam Sims, Harry Fletcher-Wood, Thomas Godfrey-Faussett, Peps Mccrea, Stefanie Meliss. (2026). Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09779-2
title: Pluralistic theoretical framework of modelling drawing on practice-based, social learning and cognitive theories
description: The article organises its hypotheses through a framework combining three traditions. Practice Based Teacher Education theorises that representations of practice help pre-service teachers notice important features of teaching; Bandura’s social learning theory holds that observation builds skills and self-efficacy; cognitive theory holds that models encode information more efficiently than verbal descriptions. The article states: “This research adopts a pluralistic theoretical approach, drawing on the practice-based, social learning and cognitive theories of modelling to develop a number of hypotheses”. The simulator experiment then tests hypotheses derived from each strand.
requirements: Models must make observable examples of the focal practice available to trainees, whether live or symbolic (video)
constraints: The skill finding supports the framework’s skill predictions, but the knowledge and self-efficacy predictions were not supported in this teacher-education domain
target_learners: pre-service (initial) teacher trainees
target_learning_goals: skill in using evidence-based teaching practices (questioning for retrieval)
knowledge of evidence-based practices
teacher self-efficacy
examples: Hypotheses 1–4 were derived respectively from cognitive/worked-example theory, feature-highlighting theory, procedural–conceptual integration, and Bandura’s vicarious modelling
key_sources: Sam Sims, Harry Fletcher-Wood, Thomas Godfrey-Faussett, Peps Mccrea, Stefanie Meliss. (2026). Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09779-2

citation: Sam Sims, Harry Fletcher-Wood, Thomas Godfrey-Faussett, Peps Mccrea, Stefanie Meliss. (2026). Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09779-2
title: Evidence-based instructional summary of five principles for questioning for retrieval
description: A written summary document given to all participants before the first simulator attempt, which “provides the basis for both our video models and the way in which we measure teacher skills within the simulator”. It sets out five evidence-based principles: signalling any student could be called on, waiting three seconds or more, framing incorrect answers as learning opportunities, telling students an answer is incorrect with elaborative feedback, and giving partial hints after ‘I don’t know’ answers. The article states: “For space reasons, we limit ourselves here to highlighting the five principles for questioning for retrieval contained in the summary”.
requirements: Trainees must read the document before practising; the simulator coding framework awards credit against these same five principles
constraints: The knowledge test covered only content included in both the summary and the annotated video, to equalise exposure across arms
target_learners: pre-service primary teacher trainees
target_learning_goals: evidence-based questioning for retrieval practice
examples: The restudy arm re-read this document for 4.5 minutes as an active control, equating training duration across arms

citation: Sam Sims, Harry Fletcher-Wood, Thomas Godfrey-Faussett, Peps Mccrea, Stefanie Meliss. (2026). Modelling evidence-based practice in initial teacher training: effects on teachers’ skills, knowledge and self-efficacy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09779-2
title: Incorporate observable video models when training early-career teachers in evidence-based teaching practices
description: Because models give trainees an observable example of the focal practice, teacher educators should build video models into initial training on evidence-based techniques rather than relying on written evidence summaries alone. The experiment found models roughly doubled simulator skill scores while restudy produced no measurable gain. The authors conclude: “Findings support the theory that incorporating models in initial teacher training can help new teachers make use of evidence-based teaching practices.”
requirements: The model should demonstrate the same evidence-based principles contained in the written guidance trainees receive
constraints: Lab simulator setting with reduced ecological validity; the skill measure has not been previously validated; benefits shown for explicit models following a written summary, not implicit models
target_learners: first-year pre-service trainee teachers
target_learning_goals: classroom skill in using evidence-based teaching techniques
examples: Participants watched a 4.5-minute video of a real primary teacher demonstrating all five evidence-based principles of questioning for retrieval before a second simulator attempt

article_title: How to assist the students while learning from text? Effects of inserting adjunct questions on text processing
citation: Alba Rubio, Eduardo Vidal-Abarca, Marian Serrano-Mendizábal. (2022). How to assist the students while learning from text? Effects of inserting adjunct questions on text processing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09592-7
title: Insert adjunct questions immediately after the question-relevant text segments when students study challenging texts with the text available
description: This principle holds that questions used as learning activities should be placed in the text right after the information needed to answer them, rather than massed after the whole text, when students study challenging, interconnected texts with the text available. The article argues that "inserting the questions would assist readers while text processing compared to post-reading questions", because the short delay keeps relevant information active and supports inference making. It is grounded in the study's finding that inserted questions produced better delayed transfer learning and more efficient processing.
requirements: Texts challenging enough that understanding sections is interconnected
Questions placed immediately after all question-relevant information has been read
Text available to students while answering the questions
constraints: Benefits may not generalize to less challenging texts or texts with relatively disconnected sections
The study cannot confirm which condition is better for retention of non-question information
No control group without questions, so comparison to just reading the text is not possible
Evidence limited to college freshmen; younger students may not benefit
target_learners: first-year college students studying challenging science texts
target_learning_goals: deep comprehension and delayed transfer of challenging conceptual text ideas
examples: In the experiment, questions were inserted immediately after reading all the information needed to answer them, and students answered with the text available on a single screen
key_sources: Alba Rubio, Eduardo Vidal-Abarca, Marian Serrano-Mendizábal. (2022). How to assist the students while learning from text? Effects of inserting adjunct questions on text processing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09592-7

citation: Alba Rubio, Eduardo Vidal-Abarca, Marian Serrano-Mendizábal. (2022). How to assist the students while learning from text? Effects of inserting adjunct questions on text processing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09592-7
title: Read&Learn web-based system for recording reading and question-answering processes
description: Read&Learn is a computer web-based system used to present texts and adjunct questions and to record students' online reading actions (Vidal-Abarca et al., 2018). Text segments and questions are masked and "To read a masked segment, students had to click on it", which lets the system register which segments are consulted, when, and for how long, classifying rereading as relevant or non-relevant per question. In this study it delivered both the inserted-question single-screen condition and the post-reading two-screen condition.
requirements: Masked segments that students unmask by clicking, enabling registration of reading actions
Segment-level classification of text as relevant or non-relevant for each question
constraints: The article notes unmasking may make scanning the text slightly more difficult, and recommends comparing question-timing effects in a more natural environment with unmasked texts
target_learners: college students reading expository science texts
target_learning_goals: measuring and supporting reading strategy use and question-answering during text study
examples: Used to record time reading the text and questions for the first time, rereading of relevant and non-relevant information, and number of segments consulted while searching

article_title: Instruction, repetition, discovery: restoring the historical educational role of practice
citation: Trninic, D. (2018). Instruction, repetition, discovery: restoring the historical educational role of practice. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9443-z
title: Bernstein's repetition-without-repetition explains how repetitive practice can be a fountainhead of discovery
description: The paper adopts Bernstein's notion of repetition-without-repetition as its explanatory framework: exercises repeat a form while varying the learner's engagement, so that repetitive practice can nonetheless generate discovery. The article states that “That repetitive practice can nonetheless be a fountainhead of discovery is explained using Bernstein's notion of repetition-without-repetition.” It uses this account to reconceptualize direct instruction, repetition, and discovery as complementary and synergistic.
requirements: Practice must be repetitive yet explorative, so that repeated exercises vary rather than merely duplicate performance.
constraints: The framework is elaborated through martial arts instruction and parallels in mathematics practice; the author notes that the trust dimension of practice while withholding information was not explored, calling it “a potentially significant limitation of present work.”
target_learners: Mathematics students
Martial arts learners
target_learning_goals: Developing proficiency through practice while making discoveries about the practiced activity
examples: The paper's empirical case is martial arts instruction in New York City and the San Francisco Bay Area, drawing on semi-structured interviews, video data, and training notes.
key_sources: Trninic, D. (2018). Instruction, repetition, discovery: restoring the historical educational role of practice. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9443-z

article_title: Instruction, repetition, discovery: restoring the historical educational role of practice
citation: Trninic, D. (2018). Instruction, repetition, discovery: restoring the historical educational role of practice. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9443-z
title: Reserve explanations for the arbitrary aspects of the discipline while learners practice and discover
description: In explorative practice, verbal explanation is withheld for aspects learners can discover through practice, and reserved for what must simply be told. The article states that “Explanations are instead reserved for conveying what Hewitt (1999) might call the ‘arbitrary’ aspects of the discipline.” This positions direct instruction as serving discovery rather than replacing it.
requirements: Learners must engage in extended repetitive practice in which discoveries can be made; the author notes this “requires trust” or that students collude with the teacher.
constraints: The trust dimension of withholding information during practice was not explored and is named a potentially significant limitation of the present work.
target_learners: Mathematics students
Martial arts students
target_learning_goals: Discovering structured aspects of a discipline while being told only its arbitrary conventions
examples: The martial arts case shows instruction in which explanations are reserved for arbitrary aspects while learners practice.

article_title: Situating collaborative disciplinary activity: creating a space for high-quality group engagement
citation: Rogat, T. K., Traynor, A., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Cheng, B. H. (2026). Situating collaborative disciplinary activity: creating a space for high-quality group engagement. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09772-1
title: Group disciplinary engagement (GDE) framework: engagement as collective, multidimensional, dynamic, and contextualized
description: The GDE framework conceptualizes engagement at the group rather than individual level, extending productive disciplinary engagement (Engle & Conant) with a situative perspective. The authors "define group's productive engagement as joint participation (behaviorally engaged) with a positive and inclusive interpersonal climate (socio-emotionally engaged), which together provide as an initial foundation to enable joint knowledge co-construction (collaborative engagement)", plus metacognitive and disciplinary engagement. Engagement is treated as co-negotiated norms unfolding dynamically over time and situated in curriculum, task, and instructional contexts.
requirements: Observational rubric ratings of group-level quality across five dimensions during collaborative activity
constraints: Developed for collaborative group activity in science, mathematics, and engineering units incorporating modeling, argumentation, and inquiry practices
target_learners: middle school students working in collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: STEM disciplinary practices such as modeling and argumentation
collaborative knowledge co-construction

article_title: Situating collaborative disciplinary activity: creating a space for high-quality group engagement
citation: Rogat, T. K., Traynor, A., Hmelo-Silver, C. E., & Cheng, B. H. (2026). Situating collaborative disciplinary activity: creating a space for high-quality group engagement. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09772-1
title: GDE observational rubric with five engagement dimensions
description: An observation rubric assessing a collaborative group's collective norms for engagement as multidimensional during shared activity. "The rubric encompasses five engagement dimensions using primarily 3-point quality rating scales, with disciplinary engagement specified using a 4-point scale (Rogat et al., 2022; Appendix A)." Ratings draw on members' behaviors, discourse, and nonverbal behaviors, with discourse as the primary data source; development included expert review and four preliminary trial rounds, and raters reached at least 0.67 Krippendorff alpha with a master rater.
requirements: Rater training with benchmark ratings and weekly coder drift checks; consensus rating by rater pairs after agreement declined
constraints: Metacognitive engagement ratings had 7% missing data due to the covert nature of metacognition; curriculum-specific indicators were developed for the disciplinary dimension
target_learners: middle school science and mathematics students
target_learning_goals: assessing quality of collaborative group engagement across behavioral, socioemotional, collaborative, metacognitive, and disciplinary dimensions

article_title: Gaming the system mediates the relationship between gender and learning outcomes in a digital learning game
citation: Baker, R. S., Richey, J. E., Zhang, J., Karumbaiah, S., Andres-Bray, J. M., Nguyen, H. A., Andres, J. M. A. L., & McLaren, B. M. (2025). Gaming the system mediates the relationship between gender and learning outcomes in a digital learning game. Instructional Science, 53, 203–238. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09679-3
title: Design digital learning games to reduce gaming-the-system behavior for male students, particularly in self-explanation activities
description: The article recommends that future design iterations of the game target disengagement behaviors among male students. As the authors state, "future design iterations of the game could focus on reducing gaming behaviors for male students, which might improve learning outcomes for female students as well." Because lower gaming mediated better learning, reducing gaming for the group that games more is a lever for improving outcomes for all students. Understanding gender-based differences in game behaviors can inform game design that promotes better learning outcomes for all students.
requirements: Detectors or behavioral measures of gaming the system must be available to identify where and for whom disengagement occurs
constraints: Simply making it more difficult to game the system leads students to find new ways to game the system, per prior work the article cites
target_learners: late elementary and middle school students
target_learning_goals: decimal number concepts and operations
behavioral engagement in digital learning games
examples: Across three Decimal Point studies, male students gamed the system significantly more than female students in the self-explanation step in the game condition, and this difference mediated gender differences in delayed posttest learning.

article_title: Unraveling the influence of domain knowledge during simulation-based inquiry learning
citation: Ard W. Lazonder, Pascal Wilhelm, Emiel van Lieburg. (2009). Unraveling the influence of domain knowledge during simulation-based inquiry learning. Instr Sci, 37, 437-451. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9055-8
title: Offer learners some information about the relations between variables in a domain to support efficient and successful inquiry learning
description: The article recommends that when relations in a domain cannot be inferred from the meaning of variables, learners should be given some information on those relations. It argues such knowledge "can bootstrap students' inquiry practices" and "can safeguard students from the adverse consequences of their quest for meaning", since learners readily induce rationales that are prone to error. This balances the inquisitory nature of learning against the need to overcome learning obstacles.
requirements: Learners are engaged in inquiry learning in a domain whose variable relations they cannot readily infer from variable meanings alone
constraints: The article notes the choice of what information to present depends upon the characteristics of the learner and domain at hand
The study was not designed to advocate tasks with unknown variables or relations; how students can be supported on a just-in-time basis is an open question for future research
target_learners: College freshmen in simulation-based inquiry tasks; the article suggests science students who have difficulty understanding material or did not prepare for class may face similar conditions
target_learning_goals: Discovering relationships between variables in an unfamiliar domain through hypothesis generation and experimentation
examples: In the experiment, only the concrete task, whose variables allowed inference of relations, produced more efficient (lower exploratory percentage) and more successful inquiry than the intermediate task

article_title: Outspoken emotions – Emotion regulation during emotional challenges in collaborative learning
citation: Piia Näykki, Tiina Törmänen, Jaana Isohätälä, Hanna Järvenoja, Sanna Järvelä. (2026). Outspoken emotions – Emotion regulation during emotional challenges in collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09815-1
title: Four observable group-level emotion regulation strategies: task structuring, encouragement, social reinforcement, and awareness raising
description: The article distinguishes four qualitatively different, socially observable emotion regulation strategies used by groups during collaborative tasks. Task structuring is "a cognitively oriented strategy" used to restore on-task behaviour when members are unfocused; encouragement involves praising or supporting a member lacking confidence; social reinforcement aims to "reinforce a stable, safe or positive socio-emotional atmosphere"; and increasing awareness involves verbalizing and addressing each other's affective states so the group can jointly explain and reduce negative feelings. The categories were developed from prior emotion regulation research and reached a Cohen's kappa of 0.79.
requirements: Coding relies on socially observable, verbal or nonverbal regulation attempts in group interaction, since purely mental self-regulatory processes are not visible in video analysis
constraints: Only social-level indicators of observable attempts at emotion regulation were categorized
target_learners: teacher education students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: managing emotional challenges during collaborative learning
maintaining a productive socioemotional climate for group work
examples: Table 1 illustrates each strategy with transcribed interaction, e.g. a member asking "Does it bother you?" to raise awareness of frustration with fraction divisions

title: Macro-script delivered on tablets prompting planning, monitoring and reflection phases of group work
description: The study used a macro-script as a discussion aid that made different parts of group work visible: the planning phase, the monitoring phase, and the reflection phase. Specific questions prompted discussion, such as "what kinds of feelings does the task evoke" in planning and "how has your work progressed" in monitoring. Questions were delivered via tablet computers, with the teacher announcing when groups could discuss them while groups decided the depth and length of discussion themselves.
requirements: Teacher instructions on tablet use at the start of each session and announcements of when to discuss script questions
constraints: The depth and length of the discussion was decided by the groups themselves
target_learners: first-year teacher education students in group work
target_learning_goals: structured collaborative discussion covering planning, monitoring and reflection
examples: In the case group's reflection phase, the script questions led members to describe obstacles related to group composition, timing and resources

article_title: Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams
citation: Cremers, P. H. M., Wals, A. E. J., Wesselink, R., & Mulder, M. (2016). Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9398-5
title: Design principles as 'ideal type' boundary objects crossing between research and educational design practice
description: The article frames a set of design principles as a boundary object of the 'ideal type' Star and Griesemer describe: "entities that are to be used and adapted flexibly in several different contexts". Because an ideal type is an abstraction without local contingencies, utilization proceeds by first decontextualizing the principles (viewing them as abstract concepts independent of their original context) and then recontextualizing them (creatively designing new features in another educational context). Brokers and reified artifacts such as a guidebook support this crossing.
requirements: The boundary object must be perceived as valuable across different contexts or perspectives
Additional information about the original context and examples of features should accompany the principles
The principles, context description and examples must be reified or materialized as a usable product
constraints: The authors note a boundary object's main function is often described as facilitating collaboration among social worlds, and a principle set traveling from research to practice facilitates potential rather than immediate ongoing collaboration
target_learners: interprofessional design teams of teachers, managers, consultants and clients designing hybrid learning configurations
target_learning_goals: utilizing research-based design principles as rationale ('know-why') for designing or redesigning educational interventions
examples: The set of seven HLC design principles was reified in a guidebook and introduced by a researcher-broker via workshops with four design teams
key_sources: Cremers, P. H. M., Wals, A. E. J., Wesselink, R., & Mulder, M. (2016). Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9398-5

article_title: Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams
citation: Cremers, P. H. M., Wals, A. E. J., Wesselink, R., & Mulder, M. (2016). Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9398-5
title: Seven design principles underpinning the design of a hybrid learning configuration
description: Generated in an educational design research project over six one-semester iterations of the 'Value in the Valley' HLC, the set comprises seven principles: fostering authenticity, inter-linking of working and learning, utilizing diversity, facilitating reflexivity, creating a learning community, enabling organization, and enabling ecology. For example, fostering authenticity means the "Working/learning environment (context, tasks, activities, roles, and communication) reflects working practice, a professional working culture and organization". The principles are abstract meta-principles that designers adapt to their context.
requirements: Designers must creatively develop context-specific features for each principle, since the principles do not prescribe how an intervention should be designed
constraints: Derived from a single case study; the authors note transposing them to another context might be considered problematic, though participants almost unanimously affirmed relevance and completeness
target_learners: students and staff in senior secondary vocational and higher education working on authentic assignments for external clients
target_learning_goals: integrating working and learning around ill-defined authentic tasks requiring transboundary, multidisciplinary learning
examples: In Value in the Valley, students collaborated in multidisciplinary teams on assignments such as a sustainability strategy for villages and rainwater storage ideas for Groningen

citation: Cremers, P. H. M., Wals, A. E. J., Wesselink, R., & Mulder, M. (2016). Utilization of design principles for hybrid learning configurations by interprofessional design teams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9398-5
title: Guidebook for Hybrid Learning Configurations
description: A written document reifying the set of design principles as a boundary object. Its final version contained three chapters: an introduction defining HLCs and their rationale; the design principles with a short description of the Value in the Valley HLC; and the context description with each principle's features, their effects, and conditions for those effects. Participants used it as preparation, common prior knowledge, and "a reference book when developing the HLC".
requirements: Should be provided before the workshop so participants can read it at their own pace and arrive with shared prior knowledge
constraints: Some participants expected an instruction guide with a working method and found practical application vague; a respondent suggested adding examples beyond Value in the Valley
target_learners: teacher-designers, educational consultants and managers in interprofessional HLC design teams
target_learning_goals: understanding and applying research-based design principles when designing or evaluating an HLC
examples: A feature of fostering authenticity—working on an authentic assignment—was reported to motivate students, conditional on a client being actively interested in the results

article_title: Enhancing students’ critical thinking skills: is comparing correct and erroneous examples beneficial?
citation: Lara M. van Peppen, Peter P. J. L. Verkoeijen, Anita E. G. Heijltjes, Eva M. Janssen, Tamara van Gog. (2021). Enhancing students' critical thinking skills: is comparing correct and erroneous examples beneficial? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09559-0
title: Contrasting examples as a generative-processing instructional method whose preconditions for critical-thinking transfer are questioned
description: The article frames contrasting examples—comparing fictitious students' correct and erroneous solutions side by side—as a method expected to induce generative processing, structural alignment, and focus on underlying principles, drawing on cognitive load theory and the temporal contiguity effect. It reasoned that "As contrasting can help learners to focus on key information and thereby induces generative processes directly relevant for learning". The study's null results led the authors to state that the findings "raise questions about the preconditions of contrasting examples effects".
requirements: Learners compare correct and erroneous solutions presented side by side and are prompted to indicate the erroneous solution and step, following explicit CT instruction
constraints: In this classroom study with elaborate instructions preceding practice, contrasting examples showed no advantage over correct examples, erroneous examples, or practice problems on learning or transfer
target_learners: first-year higher professional education students (Public Administration and Safety and Security Management)
target_learning_goals: avoiding biased reasoning (syllogistic, conjunction, confirmation-bias, and base-rate tasks)
transfer of critical-thinking skills to novel task types
examples: Participants compared fictitious students' correct and erroneous solutions to heuristics-and-biases tasks and indicated the erroneous solution step, after a 12-minute video-based CT instruction with two worked examples

citation: Macedo-Rouet, M.; Saux, G.; Potocki, A.; Dujardin, E.; Dyoniziak, Y.; Pylouster, J.; Rouet, J.F. (2024). Fostering university students' online reading: effects of teacher-led strategy training embedded in a digital literacy course. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09676-6
title: Analytical approach to strategy training: detailed step-by-step strategy presentation combined with integration of strategies across modules and practice tasks
description: The article implements and tests an analytical approach to strategy training that "combined a detailed, step-by-step presentation of each strategy with the integration of various strategies across modules and practice tasks." Rather than presenting strategies globally, each strategy is broken down and taught step by step, and learners then practice combining multiple strategies across course modules and tasks. The approach was delivered by course instructors within a digital literacy course.
requirements: Instructors received background information and instructional materials prior to the beginning of the term.
constraints: Tested with university students in the context of a digital literacy course.

target_learning_goals: online reading strategies, including searching for and evaluating the relevance and reliability of online information

article_title: Could probability be out of proportion? Self-explanation and example-based practice help students with lower proportional reasoning skills learn probability
citation: Begolli, K. N., Dai, T., McGinn, K. M., & Booth, J. L. (2021). Could probability be out of proportion? Self-explanation and example-based practice help students with lower proportional reasoning skills learn probability. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09550-9
title: Shared-root account of proportional and probabilistic reasoning schemata
description: The article frames two competing accounts of the proportion–probability connection: one in which "the conceptual schema of probabilities is separate from that of proportions" and another "where both schemata (probabilities and proportions) stem from the same root" (Fischbein & Gazit, 1984; Piaget & Inhelder, 1975). The study's findings—prior proportional reasoning predicting probabilistic learning and lower-proportion students benefiting most from example-based practice—are presented as supporting the shared-root account. Proportional reasoning is treated as integral to analyzing sample spaces, quantifying probabilities proportionally, and using correlations.
requirements: Learners must encounter probability problems whose solution requires proportional comparison and quantification for the shared schema to be exercised
constraints: The authors note the theoretical accounts on conceptual representations remain unsettled; the evidence is correlational plus one intervention
target_learners: seventh-grade mathematics students
target_learning_goals: probabilistic reasoning
proportional reasoning
examples: The study tested the account in regular seventh-grade classrooms using the Connected Mathematics Project What Do You Expect? probability unit
key_sources: Begolli, K. N., Dai, T., McGinn, K. M., & Booth, J. L. (2021). Could probability be out of proportion? title: Embed worked-example variants (correct, incorrect, and faded examples with self-explanation prompts) into practice segments of reform curricula to support lower prior knowledge learners
description: The article recommends integrating three worked-example strategies into textbook practice problems: "self-explanation prompts, incorrect examples, and fading out worked examples". Correct worked examples with self-explanation prompts reduce cognitive demands and focus processing on structural features; incorrect examples force students to confront misconceptions; fading provides an appropriate challenge as knowledge builds. In the study, 22 of the 70 core practice problems in the probability unit were replaced with these example types while lesson segments stayed identical.
requirements: Worked examples should be embedded in the existing curriculum's practice segments so treatment and control students work the same problems
Incorrect examples should be highlighted as incorrect or paired with self-explanation prompts to avoid object instantiation of wrongful solutions
Fading works best when the last solution steps are omitted
constraints: The benefit dissipates for learners with higher domain knowledge (expertise reversal effect), so fading is needed as knowledge builds
target_learners: seventh-grade mathematics students
students with lower prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: probabilistic reasoning
proportional reasoning
examples: In the study, 22 of the 70 core practice problems in the What Do You Expect? probability unit were replaced with correct worked examples (7 items), partially completed worked examples (10 items), and incorrect worked examples (5 items), with 14 self-explanation items total

article_title: External and internal smartphone distractions: Effects on phone use and learning performance in college classrooms
citation: Liao, H.-H., Liu, T.-C., & Lin, Y.-C. (2026). External and internal smartphone distractions: Effects on phone use and learning performance in college classrooms. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09794-3
title: Multistage smartphone-distraction process linking cues, vigilance, phone-use patterns, and mental effort to learning outcomes
description: The article proposes that classroom smartphone distraction unfolds as a multistage process: external notification cues and internal smartphone vigilance shape distinct phone-use patterns (checking frequency versus session duration), which raise phone-use mental effort and thereby lower learning performance. The authors state that "smartphone distraction is best conceptualized as a multistage process linking cues, vigilance, phone-use patterns, and mental effort to learning outcomes, as summarized in Fig. 6." The framework distinguishes exogenous (notification-driven) from endogenous (vigilance-driven) distraction and shows that hiding notifications changes the form of use rather than eliminating its cost.
requirements: Smartphones remain accessible to students during learning, so vigilance can translate into observable use
Measurement of both frequency and duration of phone use, since the two patterns respond differently to notification settings
constraints: The authors note that merely hiding notifications may be insufficient to prevent distractions in classrooms where smartphones remain accessible
Group-level path coefficients were weaker than the base model and should be interpreted with caution
target_learners: college and university students in device-permitted classrooms
target_learning_goals: sustaining attention and learning performance during video-based or lecture instruction despite smartphone access
examples: In the experiment, NR students checked phones frequently (many checks of one to three seconds) while NH students who did use phones engaged in longer sessions, yet both groups performed equally on the quiz

article_title: Understanding instructional design effects by differentiated measurement of intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load
citation: Melina Klepsch, Tina Seufert. (2020). Understanding instructional design effects by differentiated measurement of intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load. Instructional Science (2020) 48:45–77. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09502-9
title: Cognitive Load Questionnaire (CLQ) by Klepsch et al. (2017) for differentiated measurement of ICL, ECL, and GCL
description: The cognitive load questionnaire (CLQ) is an eight-item self-report instrument with three scales: "A scale with two items asking for perceived ICL, a scale with three items asking for perceived ECL, and finally a scale of three items asking for perceived GCL." All items are rated on 7-point Likert-type scales. The article uses it across six studies to test whether intentional variations of one load type are reflected in the corresponding scale, finding prognostic validity to be good.
requirements: Learners answer the questionnaire after the learning task; the third GCL item on "elements that helped one to understand the content" can be excluded when no such elements are present, which would otherwise decrease internal consistency
constraints: The original validation used rather short and artificial learning tasks; reliability for the GCL scale with three items was low in Study 5 (ω = .64)
target_learners: adult learners in experimental learning settings
target_learning_goals: differentiated diagnosis of intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load during learning
examples: Used after learning in all six studies, with McDonald's ω estimated per scale and GCL analyzed with two and, in Study 5, three items

article_title: Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers
citation: Frerejean, J., van Geel, M., Keuning, T., Dolmans, D., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Visscher, A. J. (2021). Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09540-x
title: 4C/ID model: four components stimulating four essential learning processes for complex learning
description: The Four-Component Instructional Design model holds that educational programs for complex skills are described using four components: learning tasks, supportive information, procedural information, and part-task practice. Each component stimulates a learning process: inductive learning, elaboration, rule formation, and strengthening. The article states that "The 4C/ID model states that educational programs can be described using four components: a backbone of learning tasks based on authentic professional tasks, supportive information describing how to approach the tasks and how the domain is organized, procedural information describing step-by-step procedures to perform routine aspects of the tasks, and part-task practice for repetition of aspects that need to be highly automated." The design team applied this model to structure a teacher PD program.
requirements: Requires analysis of the complex skill to identify nonroutine and routine aspects before components can be designed
constraints: Intended for complex skills requiring integration of knowledge, skills, and attitudes and coordination of constituent skills
target_learners: in-service primary school teachers
target_learning_goals: providing differentiated instruction in mathematics lessons
examples: The design team used 4C/ID to blueprint a five-month PD program for differentiation skills
key_sources: Frerejean, J., van Geel, M., Keuning, T., Dolmans, D., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Visscher, A. J. (2021). Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09540-x

article_title: Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers
citation: Frerejean, J., van Geel, M., Keuning, T., Dolmans, D., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Visscher, A. J. (2021). Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09540-x
title: Ten Steps approach guiding instructional designers from task analysis to training blueprint
description: The Ten Steps (Van Merriënboer & Kirschner, 2018) is a design process accompanying 4C/ID that guides designers through analysis activities (cognitive task analysis, cognitive strategy and mental model analysis, cognitive rules and prerequisite knowledge) and design steps for the four blueprint components. The article notes "The Ten Steps approach by Van Merriënboer and Kirschner (2018) lists 10 design activities that result in an educational blueprint describing the program in terms of the four components." Its strength, per the authors, lies in a comprehensive systematic approach particularly when the task is unfamiliar and few ready-made materials exist.
requirements: Requires designers familiar with 4C/ID, the Ten Steps, and cognitive task analysis approaches; requires access to expert performers for analysis
constraints: Provides guidance only for analysis and design, not for learner or context analysis, material development, implementation, motivation, or evaluation
target_learners: instructional designers and design teams
target_learning_goals: systematic design of training for complex skills
examples: Applied to design a teacher PD program for differentiation based on expert performance analysis

article_title: Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers
citation: Frerejean, J., van Geel, M., Keuning, T., Dolmans, D., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Visscher, A. J. (2021). Ten steps to 4C/ID: training differentiation skills in a professional development program for teachers. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09540-x
title: Emphasis manipulation: sequencing workplace learning tasks by shifting attentional focus across skill clusters
description: When learners practice in authentic workplace settings, designers cannot control task complexity or sequence, so simple-to-complex task classes are impossible. 4C/ID's alternative keeps tasks at natural complexity while actively allocating learner attention to one aspect or skill cluster at a time. The article explains that "4C/ID offers an alternative emphasis manipulation approach, in which learners carry out learning tasks (i.e., their daily mathematics lessons) in their natural complexity, but attention is actively allocated to just an aspect of the task or a certain skill cluster." The PD program used this across four task classes, moving the spotlight from lesson introductions and endings to monitoring, adapting instruction, and finally self-regulation.
requirements: All activities, supportive materials, and coaching must be directed at the emphasized aspect; a logical order of aspects must be determined
constraints: Errors may be expected in aspects not yet emphasized, leading to suboptimal task performance; the approach reduces but does not eliminate the need for load management
target_learners: in-service teachers learning during daily classroom practice
target_learning_goals: managing cognitive load while acquiring a complex professional skill in the workplace
examples: Task classes emphasized lesson introductions/endings, then monitoring, then monitoring plus adapting instruction, then stimulating self-regulation

title: Five-month workplace-based PD program blueprint for teacher differentiation skills
description: A professional development program designed with 4C/ID and the Ten Steps to teach primary school teachers differentiated instruction in mathematics. It combines three initial group meetings (interactive lectures, modeling examples, imitation tasks), four four-week task classes of daily classroom practice with individual coaching based on classroom recordings, cognitive feedback against 30 performance standards, and team reflection sessions. The article states "it resulted in a detailed blueprint of a five-month professional development program that strategically combines learning activities to stimulate learning processes that are essential for developing the complex skill providing differentiated instruction in a mathematics lesson."

constraints: Classroom management training was outside the program's scope; part-task practice was not included because no skills required automation

target_learning_goals: providing differentiated instruction in mathematics lessons

article_title: Fifth graders study videos faster than illustrated texts: Studying rate, review strategies, and learning implications
citation: Mikko Haavisto, Tomi Jaakkola. (2026). Fifth graders study videos faster than illustrated texts: Studying rate, review strategies, and learning implications. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09817-z
title: The modality effect grounded in cognitive load theory, with hybrid learner control as a dual-advantage design
description: The article frames its study within the modality effect: "learning from multiple sensory modalities (e.g., viewing pictures while listening to narration) produces better learning than learning from a single modality (e.g., viewing pictures and written text)". It grounds this in cognitive load theory, since speech comprehension is innate while reading requires recalling learned letter and word patterns, and in split-attention and dual working-memory capacity accounts. It also describes hybrid learner control, in which videos continue in a system-controlled manner while providing flexible navigation, as a dual advantage over pure system or pure learner control.
requirements: Materials must offer hybrid learner control, combining automatic progression with navigation options such as pause, play, rewind, and skip
constraints: The article notes meta-analyses indicate no evidence for narration outperforming written text in studies with learner-controlled narrations that did not automatically progress
target_learners: Primary school children, specifically fifth graders
target_learning_goals: Science learning from multimedia materials, including retention and transfer
examples: The experiment used learner-controlled video and illustrated text materials with identical word and picture content (1383 words, 40 pictures) segmented into slides, studied during two 45-minute science lessons with 12 minutes of learning time
key_sources: Mikko Haavisto, Tomi Jaakkola. (2026). Fifth graders study videos faster than illustrated texts: Studying rate, review strategies, and learning implications. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09817-z

article_title: Fifth graders study videos faster than illustrated texts: Studying rate, review strategies, and learning implications
citation: Mikko Haavisto, Tomi Jaakkola. (2026). Fifth graders study videos faster than illustrated texts: Studying rate, review strategies, and learning implications. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09817-z
title: Use videos with hybrid learner control for primary school multimedia learning, particularly for slower readers
description: The article's results indicate that children tend to watch and review videos linearly at their designed rate and sequence, leading to faster studying, better learning outcomes, and lower cognitive load compared to illustrated texts. Because "the videos were especially beneficial for the slower readers", and linear studying helped novices avoid skipping important content or disrupting coherence, videos with hybrid learner control are recommended for primary school science learning. The article also suggests faster videos could have even more potential, given the children hardly ever paused or rewound.
requirements: Videos should provide hybrid learner control so they progress automatically while allowing navigation
Learning time should be controlled and sufficient for an initial pass plus review, as in a school lesson context
constraints: The narration rate in this study (121 wpm) was slower than prior estimates for YouTube videos and edX courses, so optimal presentation rates for children remain an open research question
The nonsignificant picture-type effect could be due to limited statistical power, as no a priori power analysis was conducted
target_learners: Fifth graders and primary school children, especially those with weaker reading skills
target_learning_goals: Retention and transfer of expository science content from multimedia materials
examples: In the experiment, children were given 12 minutes, twice the video duration, and encouraged to review after their initial study-through; the last slide instructed participants to go back and ensure they had learned everything

article_title: Promoting Pre-Service Teachers’ Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold
citation: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar. (2025). Promoting Pre-Service Teachers' Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09745-4
title: Normative five-step model of evidence-informed reasoning about classroom situations
description: The article adopts a normative model of EIR skills (attributed to Greisel et al., 2022) in which optimal evidence-informed reasoning about classroom situations proceeds through five steps: "problem identification", "problem description", "problem explanation", "goal setting", and "select actions". The teacher first identifies a problem requiring attention, describes it, explains it by reconstructing causal relationships under consideration of scientific evidence, formulates a desired goal state, and selects an action likely to reach that goal. The study uses this model both to structure the case-analysis task and to score EIR recognition and application skills.
requirements: Learners need declarative knowledge of the five steps, e.g. via explicit teaching and an example of the five steps available throughout the task
constraints: The article focuses only on the first two skill-acquisition phases (declarative and procedural knowledge), since the fine-tuning phase extends beyond pre-service teacher education
target_learners: pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: evidence-informed reasoning about authentic classroom situations
examples: Participants analyzed a case vignette with six problems using the five steps, with an example of the steps available throughout the peer-feedback process
key_sources: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar. (2025). Promoting Pre-Service Teachers' Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09745-4

article_title: Promoting Pre-Service Teachers’ Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold
citation: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar. (2025). Promoting Pre-Service Teachers' Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09745-4
title: Skill-acquisition account: EIR skills develop from declarative knowledge (recognition) to procedural knowledge (application)
description: The article frames EIR skill acquisition with a three-phase account drawn from skill acquisition research (citing Anderson & Lebiere, 1998; Wecker & Fischer, 2014): learners first acquire declarative knowledge that helps them reproduce and identify instances of the skill (measured as EIR recognition skills), then convert it into procedural knowledge through practice (measured as EIR application skills), and finally fine-tune it through extensive application. The study targets only the first two phases and uses this account to justify teaching the steps explicitly, providing practice with authentic cases, and scaffolding during proceduralization.
requirements: Explicit teaching of the reasoning steps, opportunities to practice application on authentic classroom cases, and scaffolding during the proceduralization phase
constraints: The third phase (fine-tuning through extensive practice) extends beyond pre-service teacher education and is not addressed
target_learners: pre-service teachers
target_learning_goals: acquiring evidence-informed reasoning skills
examples: The posttest measured recognition via ranking analyses by quality and application via coding an unguided case analysis one week later

article_title: Promoting Pre-Service Teachers’ Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold
citation: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar. (2025). Promoting Pre-Service Teachers' Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09745-4
title: Feedback provision scaffold: three feed-up/feed-back/feed-forward prompts with a sample solution
description: The feedback provision scaffold is a low-threshold support given during the feedback provision phase, consisting of three prompts — "Recall the task and describe it briefly in your own words" (feed up), "Explain how well your peer completed the task" (feed back), and "Finally, make specific suggestions for how your peer can improve his or her case analysis" (feed forward) — accompanied by a sample solution illustrating how such feedback might look. Participants without it were simply asked to provide feedback on the first three problems identified by their peers. It significantly raised feedback quality in the experiment.
requirements: Integration into the learning environment at the right place in the peer-feedback process
constraints: The prompts strongly focused on structural rather than content-related aspects of feedback
target_learners: pre-service teachers in higher education
target_learning_goals: providing high-quality peer feedback
examples: In the study, scaffolded participants reached higher feedback quality (M = 0.44) than unscaffolded participants (M = 0.24)

citation: Julia Hornstein, Martin Greisel, Ingo Kollar. (2025). Promoting Pre-Service Teachers' Evidence-Informed Reasoning Through Peer-Feedback: Effects of a Feedback Provision Scaffold and a Feedback Integration Scaffold. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09745-4
title: Feedback integration scaffold: four-step color-coding prompts with a sample solution for integrating two peer-feedback messages
description: The feedback integration scaffold guides learners through integrating two peer-feedback messages via four prompts: read both messages, compare them by marking similarities in green, complementary statements in yellow, and contradictions in red, revise the case analysis using the messages, and check by marking adapted places in the same colors and verifying all criticisms are reflected. A sample solution showed how the prompts could be implemented in practice. It did not significantly improve EIR recognition or application skills, and combining it with the provision scaffold showed a negative interaction on recognition skills.
requirements: Learners must have received feedback from two peers to integrate
constraints: Showed a significant negative interaction with the feedback provision scaffold on EIR recognition skills, indicating the two scaffolds should rather be presented alone
target_learners: pre-service teachers in higher education
target_learning_goals: integrating multiple peer-feedback messages into a revised task solution
examples: Participants marked similarities in green, complementary statements in yellow, and contradictions in red, then marked their revisions in the same colors and checked whether all criticisms were reflected

article_title: Spatial supports for comparison in educational science images
citation: Benjamin D. Jee, Bryan J. Matlen, Monica Greenlaw, Nina Simms, Dedre Gentner. (2022). Spatial supports for comparison in educational science images. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09599-0
title: Structure-mapping theory: comparison as structural alignment of common relational systems
description: Structure-mapping theory holds that "comparison involves aligning two examples in terms of their common relational structure," placing elements into correspondence "according to their role in a common system of relations." The article applies this account to science images: a student viewing a forelimb diagram must align bones across animals by structural role, which highlights common structure (homology), supports inferences such as common ancestry, and also highlights differences connected to the shared relational system. Accurate alignment requires rejecting superficial perceptual matches.
requirements: Comparison is effective only if students create accurate structural alignments based on shared relationships rather than local perceptual matches
constraints: Novices may lack the domain knowledge to make accurate alignments without cognitive supports such as language, gestures, or spatial placement
target_learners: middle school science students
novice science learners
target_learning_goals: comprehending relational structure in science images
learning relational concepts such as homology, catalyst, and adaptation
key_sources: Benjamin D. Jee, Bryan J. Matlen, Monica Greenlaw, Nina Simms, Dedre Gentner. (2022). Spatial supports for comparison in educational science images. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09599-0

article_title: Spatial supports for comparison in educational science images
citation: Benjamin D. Jee, Bryan J. Matlen, Monica Greenlaw, Nina Simms, Dedre Gentner. (2022). Spatial supports for comparison in educational science images. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09599-0
title: Design educational science images so matched pairs of visual units are in direct spatial placement to support structural alignment
description: The article recommends that when student learning is the priority, image designers should place matched visual units so their correspondences are clear and unobstructed: "If student learning is the main priority, then designers of educational images should aim to support relevant cognition first and foremost." Direct placement minimizes competing matches and facilitates the intended alignment, and the authors argue it "could be applied broadly to increase the effectiveness of educational science images" at little cost to developers.
requirements: Matched pairs should be laid out so horizontal-axis units are stacked vertically and vertical-axis units are placed side by side, yielding direct placement
constraints: Designers may need to preserve realism, capture attention, follow domain visual conventions, or fit pre-specified page dimensions, which can force tradeoffs; supports may be less helpful for highly knowledgeable learners
target_learners: middle school science students
novice learners studying from textbook images
target_learning_goals: structural alignment of matched visual units
comprehension of relational scientific structure in images
examples: The study found 47 of 103 comparison images had direct placements only, while 25 of 103 contained one or more impeded placements; a horse-evolution diagram with vertical layout of vertically oriented bones exemplified impeded placement, while a comparable diagram in another textbook achieved direct placement
