article_title: Incorporating instructor presence in a multimedia language learning context
citation: Yu-Jr Lan, Emmanuel Manalo. (2026). Incorporating instructor presence in a multimedia language learning context. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09814-2
title: Before incorporating instructor presence into instructional videos, check whether the instructor's visible behaviors provide task-relevant information learners can directly use
description: The article recommends that instructional designers evaluate whether an on-screen instructor adds usable information rather than merely adding social presence. It concludes that "instructional designers should carefully consider whether the instructor's visual behaviors provide task-relevant information before incorporating instructor presence into instructional materials," because presence alone raised satisfaction and perceived learning but not performance. In this study the instructor's head gestures merely emphasized pitch diagrams already on screen, so the video was not a source of detailed articulatory guidance.
requirements: The instructor's visible behavior must convey information learners can directly use for the specific learning context and task demands
Learners may need appropriate strategies to effectively utilize the visual cues the instructor provides
constraints: In the study's tone-learning context, instructor modeling without additional cues to tone production did not improve measurable outcomes
Effectiveness may differ across domains and across content types within the same domain
target_learners: true-beginner second language learners
university students in online and distance education
target_learning_goals: second-language pronunciation and suprasegmental features such as lexical tones
multimedia learning outcomes in video-based instruction
examples: Fifty Japanese university students viewed lecture videos on the four Mandarin tones in which the only difference between versions was instructor presence, with head gestures that emphasized but did not duplicate on-screen pitch diagrams
key_sources: Yu-Jr Lan, Emmanuel Manalo. (2026). Incorporating instructor presence in a multimedia language learning context. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09814-2

article_title: Two comparative studies of computer simulations and experiments as learning tools in school and out-of-school education
citation: Krüger, J. T., Höffler, T. N., Wahl, M., Knickmeier, K., & Parchmann, I. (2022). Two comparative studies of computer simulations and experiments as learning tools in school and out-of-school education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09566-1
title: Combine computer simulations and hands-on experiments so each method compensates for the other's weaknesses when teaching complex socioscientific topics
description: The article concludes that neither method dominates: simulations produced better knowledge acquisition but higher cognitive load, while experiments better fostered epistemic and value-related interest. The authors state that "working with one method may complement and supplement the weaknesses of the other" and conclude "the most effective way to communicate complex current research topics might be a combination of both methods" in school and out-of-school settings.
requirements: Both methods must convey the same content with comparable instructional support so their effects can complement each other
constraints: The conclusion is drawn from two studies on marine ecology topics with secondary students; the authors phrase it as what "might" be most effective
target_learners: secondary school students, grades 10–13
target_learning_goals: content knowledge of complex socioscientific issues
situational interest in science
examples: In both studies the same content was taught via experiments or simulations with identical scripts, introductions and post-tests, allowing the methods' complementary strengths to be compared directly

article_title: Two comparative studies of computer simulations and experiments as learning tools in school and out-of-school education
citation: Krüger, J. T., Höffler, T. N., Wahl, M., Knickmeier, K., & Parchmann, I. (2022). Two comparative studies of computer simulations and experiments as learning tools in school and out-of-school education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09566-1
title: Support simulation-based learning with guiding scripts and supervisor help to prevent disorientation and cognitive overload
description: In both studies the simulations were used with structured instructional support: paper or digital scripts with guiding questions that students answered while working, plus supervisors for technical and content questions. The article states this was done "To avoid disorientation and cognitive overload especially by working on the simulation", and the introduction notes that simulations without support tend to cause disorientation and extraneous load.

A supervisor available for technical and content-related questions
constraints: The studies did not distinguish intrinsic from extraneous load, using a short two-item overall load measure

target_learning_goals: content knowledge of complex socioscientific issues
managing cognitive load during simulation-based learning
examples: In Study II the simulation script was digital and embedded in the simulation website with operation instructions and parameter information, while experiment scripts were paper-based with per-station instructions

article_title: Fading distributed scaffolds: the importance of complementarity between teacher and material scaffolds
citation: Martin, Nicole D., Tissenbaum, Catherine Dornfeld, Gnesdilow, Dana, Puntambekar, Sadhana. (2019). Fading distributed scaffolds: the importance of complementarity between teacher and material scaffolds. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9474-0
title: Distributed scaffolding and complementarity between material and teacher scaffolds
description: Distributed scaffolding is the framework in which support for complex project-based learning is spread across multiple tools, routines, activities, and the teacher, forming a system that simultaneously supports all students in a classroom. The article stresses that "the agents, tools, and resources must complement one another, so that they all work together in a system of scaffolding". Material scaffolds address anticipated difficulties and can be faded in printed tools, while teacher scaffolding supplies the responsive, contingent support that static materials cannot. The study tests this framework by examining how two teachers' moves complemented or merely replicated fading material scaffolds in the Scientist's Journal.
requirements: Support distributed across tools, activities, and the teacher must be integrated so the components complement rather than duplicate one another
constraints: Material scaffolds in printed tools provide a fixed set of prompts identical for all students and cannot tailor support to individual learners' needs in the moment
target_learners: sixth-grade middle school science students in mixed-ability classrooms
target_learning_goals: science practices such as hypothesis writing and data interpretation
physics concepts of forces, motion, and energy
examples: Two teachers used the same Scientist's Journal with fading High, Medium, and Low material support across nine experiments; one complemented it with responsive moves, the other largely replicated the static support
key_sources: Martin, Nicole D., Tissenbaum, Catherine Dornfeld, Gnesdilow, Dana, Puntambekar, Sadhana. (2019). Fading distributed scaffolds: the importance of complementarity between teacher and material scaffolds. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9474-0

article_title: Problem based learning: Cognitive and metacognitive processes during problem analysis
citation: de Grave, W. S., Boshuizen, H. & Schmidt, H. (1996). Problem based learning: Cognitive and metacognitive processes during problem analysis. Instructional Science: An International Journal of Learning and Cognition, 24(5), 321–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00118111
title: Stimulated recall procedure for tapping thinking processes during PBL problem analysis
description: The study used a stimulated recall procedure in which students' thinking processes during the tutorial group discussion were tapped, producing recall protocols analysed alongside verbatim transcripts of the group's verbal interaction. The article reports that "Thinking processes were tapped by means of a stimulated recall procedure." The method proved "sensitive for detecting conceptual change during problem analysis."
requirements: Requires verbatim transcripts of both the verbal interaction in the group and the recall protocols for analysis.
target_learners: students in problem-based learning tutorial groups
target_learning_goals: conceptual change
hypothesis evaluation
meta-reasoning
examples: The study analysed verbal communication among tutorial group members together with their stimulated recall protocols of thinking during problem analysis.

article_title: Problem based learning: Cognitive and metacognitive processes during problem analysis
citation: de Grave, W. S., Boshuizen, H. & Schmidt, H. (1996). Problem based learning: Cognitive and metacognitive processes during problem analysis. Instructional Science: An International Journal of Learning and Cognition, 24(5), 321–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00118111
title: Problem analysis as a key phase of problem-based learning involving cognitive and metacognitive processes
description: The article frames problem analysis as "an important phase of problem based learning in a tutorial group," during which cognitive and metacognitive processes unfold. These processes are only partially expressed in the group's verbal interaction, which concerns mainly theory building, while stimulated recall exposes hypothesis evaluation, meta-reasoning, and conceptual change when students confront anomalous data.
requirements: A tutorial group setting in which problem analysis is carried out through verbal interaction among group members.
target_learners: students in problem-based learning tutorial groups
target_learning_goals: conceptual change
theory building
metacognitive reasoning
examples: The study investigated whether PBL leads to conceptual change by analysing verbal communication and stimulated recall during problem analysis in a tutorial group.

article_title: Can we further improve tablet-based drawing to enhance learning? An empirical test of two types of support
citation: Steffen P. Schmidgall, Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Eitel. (2020). Can we further improve tablet-based drawing to enhance learning? An empirical test of two types of support. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09513-6
title: Cognitive Model of Drawing Construction (CMDC)
description: The CMDC, due to Van Meter and Firetto (2013) as described in this article, explains representational drawing when learning from text as "a set of interleaved perceptual and cognitive processes that contribute to the construction of an internal mental model of the text which is then externalized in a drawing". The drawing externalizes the mental model and provides feedback about the coherence and completeness of learners' mental models, which can be improved by reviewing the text contents. The model is based on models of learning with multiple representations such as the integrated model of text and picture comprehension. It predicts that beneficial effects of drawing appear only if the type of assessment is matched to the type of mental model constructed through the drawing activity, i.e., higher-order rather than lower-order knowledge.
requirements: Learners must actively reconsider and evaluate their drawings for the feedback function of the externalized drawing to improve mental model construction.
constraints: The article states benefits appear only when the type of assessment matches the type of mental model constructed through the drawing activity.
target_learners: university students learning expository science text
target_learning_goals: deeper comprehension and transfer of visuo-spatial science content
examples: The study tested the CMDC-aligned prediction that drawing benefits higher-order measures (transfer, drawing test) but not recognition.

article_title: The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic
citation: Tessa Eysink, Sanne Dijkstra, Jan Kuper. (2002). The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016018210897
title: Tarski's World computer-based learning environment for teaching first-order logic
description: Tarski's World is a computer-based learning environment designed for teaching first-order logic (Barwise & Etchemendy, 1992), used in this study to teach the logical connective, conditional. In the experiment, instructions for 72 first- and second-year social science students were varied within it, including "a visual representation in which geometrical objects could be manipulated". It served as the delivery setting for the guidance and manipulation variables.
requirements: Learners work on problems about the conditional within a visual representation of geometrical objects that can be manipulated or imagined to manipulate
target_learners: first- and second-year social science students
target_learning_goals: understanding the logical connective, conditional
first-order logic concepts
examples: The study varied instructions for 72 students in Tarski's World across guidance and manipulation conditions

article_title: The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic
citation: Tessa Eysink, Sanne Dijkstra, Jan Kuper. (2002). The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016018210897
title: Guidance and manipulation as complementary instructional variables in computer-based problem solving
description: The article proposes that two instructional variables play complementary roles in computer-based problem solving for concept development. Guidance leads students to see all situations relevant for developing new knowledge, benefiting performance directly after instruction; manipulation leads students to play around so that they systematically experience the results of their actions through feedback, benefiting retention. The authors state that "guidance in combination with the possibility to manipulate objects in a domain, support the acquisition of knowledge and skills in that domain".
requirements: Guidance must expose learners to all different types of basic problem situations derivable from the target concept
Manipulation requires a visual representation with objects whose manipulation yields feedback on the results of actions
constraints: Evidence concerns learning the conditional in first-order logic with social science students in Tarski's World
target_learners: first- and second-year social science students
target_learning_goals: acquisition of concepts of logic
problem-solving knowledge and skills in a domain
examples: In the experiment, guidance was operationalised via problems covering all basic problem situations, and manipulation via a manipulable visual representation
key_sources: Tessa Eysink, Sanne Dijkstra, Jan Kuper. (2002). The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016018210897

article_title: The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic
citation: Tessa Eysink, Sanne Dijkstra, Jan Kuper. (2002). The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016018210897
title: Combine guidance to all relevant problem situations with manipulable objects when designing computer-based problem-solving instruction
description: When teaching a concept through computer-based problem solving, design instruction so that guided problems lead learners to all relevant basic problem situations of the concept, while also giving them a visual representation with manipulable objects and feedback. The article's results support this combination: guidance affected immediate post-test performance and manipulation affected retention, so "guidance in combination with the possibility to manipulate objects in a domain, support the acquisition of knowledge and skills in that domain".
requirements: Problems must cover all different types of basic problem situations derivable from the target concept
The environment must give feedback so learners systematically experience the results of their actions
constraints: Demonstrated for the conditional in first-order logic with social science students; manipulation's benefit appeared on the retention test, guidance's on the post-test
target_learners: first- and second-year social science students
novice logic learners
target_learning_goals: concept development in logic
retention of problem-solving knowledge and skills
examples: Instructions in Tarski's World were varied so guided learners encountered all basic problem situations of the conditional while manipulating or imagining to manipulate geometrical objects

article_title: Go green: evaluating an XR application on biodiversity in German secondary school classrooms
citation: Mulders, M., Träg, K. H., & Kirner, L. (2025). Go green: evaluating an XR application on biodiversity in German secondary school classrooms. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09697-1
title: On Biodiversity's Tracks: greenpeace tablet-based VR application on the Amazon rainforest
description: On Biodiversity's Tracks (German: Der Artenvielfalt auf der Spur) is a virtual environment developed by greenpeace for classroom use, evaluated here in German secondary schools. It is "a virtual environment designed for classroom use that allows students to explore various places like the Amazon rainforest, the Great Barrier Reef, or a supermarket". Students scan a QR code, select South America on a globe, and freely explore a 360-degree rainforest environment with auditory and visual content and interactions with virtual agents, using touch gestures and body movements on their own tablets or smartphones.
requirements: Students need their own mobile device (tablet or smartphone) with touch input and headphones; exploration is only marginally accompanied by teachers, mainly for technical difficulties.
constraints: Teachers reported the information density in the application was too high for many students, leading to cognitive overload; the app retrieves as little personal data as possible, so no log data exists.
target_learners: German secondary school students in grades 7–9 (aged 12–19)
target_learning_goals: Knowledge about the Amazon rainforest and biodiversity
Interest in sustainability and the SDGs
Pro-environmental attitudes
examples: In the study, 108 students in eight classes explored the Amazon rainforest environment independently for approximately 20–25 minutes within a 90-minute lesson.

citation: Liu, C.-C., Wen, C.-T., Chang, H.-Y., Chang, M.-H., Lai, P.-H., Fan Chiang, S.-H., Yang, C.-W., & Hwang, F.-K. (2022). title: Engage students in critiquing problematic inquiry cases before they conduct inquiry in a virtual lab
description: This principle holds that virtual-lab inquiry is more effective when students first critique flawed or problematic inquiry cases, because students must "think and act like scientists so as to be sensitively alert to methodological flaws and various sources of error." citation: Liu, C.-C., Wen, C.-T., Chang, H.-Y., Chang, M.-H., Lai, P.-H., Fan Chiang, S.-H., Yang, C.-W., & Hwang, F.-K. (2022). Augmenting the effect of virtual labs with "teacher demonstration" and "student critique" instructional designs to scaffold the development of scientific literacy. Instructional Science, 50, 303-333. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09571-4
title: Buoyancy physics virtual lab with variable datasheet
description: A physics virtual lab demonstrating buoyancy in a liquid tank, in which students "can change values of variables in the virtual lab to observe the process and conduct experiments about Buoyancy." It exposes variables such as liquid density, cube mass and volume, volume under liquid, displaced volume, and scale readings, and was paired with a critique worksheet presenting flawed experimental designs for students to evaluate before conducting their own inquiry.
requirements: A critique worksheet with problematic inquiry scenarios accompanies the lab before students conduct their own inquiry
target_learners: middle school science students
target_learning_goals: understanding buoyancy force
experimental design and control of variables
scientific literacy
examples: The datasheet lists variables including rhoS (liquid density), M (cube mass), V (cube volume), and scale readings for weight in liquid and displaced liquid

citation: Liu, C.-C., Wen, C.-T., Chang, H.-Y., Chang, M.-H., Lai, P.-H., Fan Chiang, S.-H., Yang, C.-W., & Hwang, F.-K. (2022). Instructional Science, 50, 303-333. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09571-4
title: Critique-then-inquire sequence for virtual lab activities
description: A lesson-level sequence in which students first critique problematic inquiry cases and then conduct science inquiries with a virtual lab. The article states that before inquiry, students "were required to critique problematic inquiry cases (the critique group) or watch teachers' demonstrations (the teacher demonstration group) before taking part in the inquiry." The critique-first variant aligned with developing inquiry skills and scientific literacy, supporting a design where evaluation of flawed experiments precedes hands-on virtual experimentation.
requirements: Problematic inquiry cases matched to the virtual lab topic must be available for the critique phase
constraints: Compared in middle school science (buoyancy) with a teacher-demonstration comparison condition
target_learners: middle school science students
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry skills
scientific literacy
alertness to methodological flaws
examples: The critique worksheet presented Ann's and Hsian-Hsian's flawed experiment designs about buoyancy, which students evaluated before conducting their own virtual-lab experiments

article_title: Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process
citation: Angel Blanch. (2015). Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process. Springer Verlag. http://hdl.handle.net/10459.1/48328
title: Gf–Gc investment theory: fluid ability drives the rate of learning and feeds crystallized ability, which determines attained performance levels
description: The Cattell-Horn fluid–crystallized theory distinguishes Gf, the basic processes for resolving abstract and novel problems, from Gc, knowledge acquired through culturally transmitted language, information, and concepts. Its dynamic predictions propose that "the investment of Gf influences the course of Gc and educational outcomes during the schooling period." The article tests three investment predictions — Gf influencing Gc but not vice versa, Gc growth starting beyond a point in Gf development, and faster growth for Gf-related processes — against learning growth factors from a brief instructional intervention, finding the interplay of both factors more important for learning than either alone.
requirements: Assessment of both broad Gf and Gc factors prior to or alongside the learning process being explained
constraints: The article notes the ninth property could only be partially assessed because the dataset contained no information on educational performance in already studied areas
No data were available about motivation, interests, personality, or situational factors such as parental involvement
target_learners: High-school students (grades 10–12)
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of novel concepts and procedures in a structured instructional unit sequence
examples: The study evaluated the theory against a one-week instructional project on the imaginary science Xenograde Systems using a latent curve model with intercept and slope growth factors
key_sources: Angel Blanch. (2015). Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process. Springer Verlag. http://hdl.handle.net/10459.1/48328

article_title: Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process
citation: Angel Blanch. (2015). Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process. Springer Verlag. http://hdl.handle.net/10459.1/48328
title: Match instructional structure to learner ability: higher structured instruction benefits lower-ability students, low structured instruction benefits higher-ability students
description: Drawing on aptitude-treatment interaction (ATI) theory, the article recommends tailoring instructional structure to learner aptitude. As stated, "higher structured instruction is more beneficial for students with lower ability, while low structured instruction is more beneficial for students with higher ability." The article adds that more anxious individuals may attain optimum learning in highly structured interventions, and that novel or complex goals and inductive, unstructured organization impose higher requirements on Gf, whereas tasks requiring modification of known schemes, particularly in the language domain, impose higher requirements on Gc.
requirements: Evaluation of learners' broad cognitive abilities (Gf and Gc) to inform the choice of instructional structure
constraints: The article notes this interaction is further influenced by task and/or situational variables as suggested by ATI theory
target_learners: Students differing in cognitive aptitude, including individuals with specific learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Optimizing achievement in instructional interventions matched to learner aptitude profiles
examples: The article suggests learning goals that are novel or complex, or instruction with a more inductive or unstructured organization, may impose higher requirements on Gf
key_sources: Angel Blanch. (2015). Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process. Springer Verlag. http://hdl.handle.net/10459.1/48328

article_title: Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process
citation: Angel Blanch. (2015). Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process. Springer Verlag. http://hdl.handle.net/10459.1/48328
title: Evaluate learners' Gf and Gc before designing comprehensive instructional interventions, relying on narrower CHC abilities for more focused areas
description: The article recommends that education planners assess broad fluid and crystallized abilities prior to intervention, stating that "the evaluation of these broad intelligence factors prior to any specific intervention may allow education planners to make more informed decisions." It advises educators and curriculum designers to bear both abilities in mind when designing comprehensive interventions and curricular materials, particularly for individuals with specific learning disabilities, while noting that interventions within more focused and limited areas should probably rely on narrower abilities within the CHC taxonomy.
requirements: Cognitive ability measures capable of indexing the broad Gf and Gc factors for the target population
constraints: The article limits the recommendation to comprehensive interventions; for focused, limited areas it recommends narrower CHC abilities instead
target_learners: Students in comprehensive instructional programs, including individuals with specific learning disabilities
target_learning_goals: Improved instructional design decisions and learning performance across intervention sequences
examples: The study modeled Gf and Gc as predictors of latent intercept and slope growth factors in a one-week instructional project
key_sources: Angel Blanch. (2015). Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process. Springer Verlag. http://hdl.handle.net/10459.1/48328

article_title: Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process
citation: Angel Blanch. (2015). Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process. Springer Verlag. http://hdl.handle.net/10459.1/48328
title: Xenograde Systems instructional project (BURN11 dataset): a four-unit, one-week hierarchical learning sequence on an imaginary science
description: The instructional intervention comprised "a two-phase description of an imaginary science designated as Xenograde Systems: a lecture/discussion phase, and an individual working phase." Curricular materials spanned four hierarchical learning units delivered in booklets of four to five pages with written prose, diagrams, graphs, and tables: Unit 1 defined basic terms and operations, Unit 2 covered rules and procedures for reading graphs, Unit 3 introduced facts and concepts increasing system complexity, and Unit 4 presented the fully operating system. One multiple-choice achievement test per unit (18, 14, 16, and 16 items; reliabilities .83, .76, .80, .76) assessed knowledge, comprehension, and application.
requirements: Systematic and periodical performance assessment across the instructional sequence, as required for latent growth modeling
constraints: The article notes individual growth curves could not be modelled because raw data were not available within the BURN11 dataset, which consists of a correlation matrix
target_learners: 101 California high-school students in grades 10–12 (51 males, 50 females)
target_learning_goals: Learning novel concepts and procedures of an imaginary science system at knowledge, comprehension, and application levels
examples: The original Burns (1980) intervention found Gc related with learning throughout the intervention, whereas Gf was related with learning depending on the point in time it was measured
key_sources: Angel Blanch. (2015). Evaluating fluid and crystallized abilities in the performance of an educational process. Springer Verlag. http://hdl.handle.net/10459.1/48328

article_title: Teachers’ learning in a learning study
citation: Mona Holmqvist. (2011). Teachers' learning in a learning study. Instr Sci 39:497–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9138-1
title: Variation theory: learning as discernment, simultaneity and variation of critical aspects
description: Variation theory analyzes learning on the basis of "the concepts discernment, simultaneity and variation", all three of which the article says are required for learning to be possible. Learning is defined as a new way to experience the environment, in which the learner discerns new aspects of a phenomenon simultaneously with other aspects and combines them into a whole. In the study, teachers used this framework to identify the critical aspects of English learning objects and to organize contrasts in instruction, e.g. contrasting singular and plural forms of to be.
requirements: A variation must be offered, i.e. a number of different aspects that can be experienced, so the learner can discern new aspects of the phenomenon
constraints: Knowledge of an aspect cannot be developed if only one example has been experienced, as in the article's apple example where variation of apples is needed to discern taste
target_learners: pupils aged 9-11 in school years 4-5 learning English as a second language
target_learning_goals: discerning critical aspects of English grammar learning objects such as possessive pronouns and the verbs to be and to have
examples: Teachers planned lessons by first answering what it takes to develop knowledge about the object of learning, identifying critical aspects such as discerning that the pronoun you can be both singular and plural
key_sources: Mona Holmqvist. (2011). Teachers' learning in a learning study. Instr Sci 39:497–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9138-1

article_title: Teachers’ learning in a learning study
citation: Mona Holmqvist. (2011). Teachers' learning in a learning study. Instr Sci 39:497–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9138-1
title: Learning Study model: a fusion of lesson study and design experiment with pre-, post- and delayed post-tests
description: The Learning Study is "a fusion between lesson study and design experiment" in which teachers and a researcher jointly plan a lesson around a chosen learning object, implement it with one pupil group, and analyze pre-test, post-test and delayed post-test results together with video-recorded lessons. The knowledge gained provides the basis for a revised lesson in a new group of pupils, forming micro-cycles of three lessons. In this study six teachers ran three Learning Study cycles over three semesters, with 54, 64 and 48 participating pupils respectively.
requirements: Two to four tape-recorded planning meetings before each lesson to identify critical aspects
Video-recording and verbatim transcription of lessons, and pre-, post- and delayed post-tests for analysis
constraints: The author notes teachers may have difficulty implementing new learning studies independently because of lack of time
target_learners: pupils aged 9-11 in school years 4-5
target_learning_goals: English as a second language learning objects such as possessive pronouns, to be and to have
examples: Learning Study A focused on dependent possessive pronouns; the work sheet and lesson design were revised across lessons A1, A2 and A3 based on test results and lesson analysis
key_sources: Mona Holmqvist. (2011). Teachers' learning in a learning study. Instr Sci 39:497–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9138-1

article_title: Strategies for facilitating processing of transient information in instructional videos by using learner control mechanisms
citation: Lin, YC., Liu, TC. & Kalyuga, S. (2022). Strategies for facilitating processing of transient information in instructional videos by using learner control mechanisms. Instructional Science, 50, 863–877. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09600-w
title: Cognitive-load-based strategies for facilitating processing and integration of transient information in video learning
description: The article develops instructional strategies grounded in cognitive load theory to address the transient information effect in instructional videos, where dynamic visualizations and spoken words disappear as they play. The strategies "provid[e] learners with explicit guidance in when and how to use pausing and timeline scrollbars while watching instructional videos," so that learners can re-expose and re-process transient material and integrate it with other representations. The framework treats learner control as helpful only when supported by sufficient instructional guidance.
requirements: Videos must offer learner control mechanisms such as pause buttons and timeline scrollbars
Learners need explicit guidance in when and how to use those mechanisms
constraints: Effective learner control could be difficult to attain without sufficient instructional support
target_learners: undergraduates learning from instructional videos
target_learning_goals: comprehension and recall of spoken and dynamic visual content in instructional videos
examples: Ninety undergraduates were randomly assigned to a strategy guidance group, a learner control group, or a continuous presentation group in a single-factor between-subjects experiment
key_sources: Lin, YC., Liu, TC. & Kalyuga, S. (2022). Strategies for facilitating processing of transient information in instructional videos by using learner control mechanisms. Instructional Science, 50, 863–877. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09600-w

article_title: Strategies for facilitating processing of transient information in instructional videos by using learner control mechanisms
citation: Lin, YC., Liu, TC. & Kalyuga, S. (2022). Strategies for facilitating processing of transient information in instructional videos by using learner control mechanisms. Instructional Science, 50, 863–877. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09600-w
title: Instructional video with learner control mechanisms (pause button and timeline scrollbar)
description: The learning environment under study is an instructional video equipped with learner control mechanisms, specifically "pause buttons or timeline scrollbars," which allow learners to stop playback and return to earlier points of transient spoken and dynamic visual content. The article compares this element with and without strategy guidance and against continuous presentation, finding that the mechanisms supported learning when learners were explicitly taught how to use them.
requirements: Playback interface exposing pause and timeline scrollbar controls
constraints: Without guidance, learner control of these mechanisms was not sufficient to outperform the guided condition
target_learners: undergraduates watching instructional videos
target_learning_goals: recall and comprehension of video-presented content
examples: The learner control group was allowed to control the video but without any guidance in strategies

article_title: Online teaching in networked learning communities: A multi-method approach to studying the role of the teacher
citation: de Laat, M., Lally, V., Lipponen, L. & Simons, R.-J. (2007). Online teaching in networked learning communities: A multi-method approach to studying the role of the teacher. Instructional Science, vol. 35, no. 3, pp. 257-286. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9007-0
title: Multi-method research framework combining SNA, content analysis and contextual analysis for studying networked learning
description: The article develops a framework in which three methods answer complementary questions about networked learning: social network analysis to find out "who is talking to whom", content analysis of coded learning and tutoring activities to find out "what they are talking about", and contextual analysis (including critical event recall) to find out "why they are talking as they do". The methods triangulate and contextualise findings, using the outcomes of one method to understand the results of the next. Timeline analysis across beginning, middle and end phases adds the dimension of time, which the authors say has been largely ignored in NL research.
requirements: Methods must capture processes and outcomes of learning as well as experienced effects and individual interpretations of participation, as Hakkinen et al. suggest
constraints: Applied here to two NLCs within one workshop of an online Master's programme, with 10-day message samples per phase
target_learners: mid-career professional students in an online Master's programme in e-learning
target_learning_goals: understanding collaborative learning and tutoring processes in networked learning communities
examples: Density and centrality measures from WebCT log-files, NVivo-coded learning/tutoring activities, and CER interviews with both teachers
key_sources: de Laat, M., Lally, V., Lipponen, L. & Simons, R.-J. (2007). Online teaching in networked learning communities: A multi-method approach to studying the role of the teacher. Instructional Science, vol. 35, no. 3, pp. 257-286. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9007-0

article_title: Online teaching in networked learning communities: A multi-method approach to studying the role of the teacher
citation: de Laat, M., Lally, V., Lipponen, L. & Simons, R.-J. (2007). Online teaching in networked learning communities: A multi-method approach to studying the role of the teacher. Instructional Science, vol. 35, no. 3, pp. 257-286. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9007-0
title: Experienced online tutor's facilitation pattern: emergent group learning with subtle peripheral scaffolding
description: The experienced tutor's pattern is to let the group be emergent, letting participants seek their own rhythms and ways of working, while staying present peripherally and building a subtle support framework the group can use as it progresses. He reported: "My teaching style is to let the group be emergent in their learning and let them seek their own rhythms and ways of working and learning together." He used advanced organisers to pre-organise process and project issues, sounded notes of caution to keep the project do-able, and drew on a mental framework of pitfalls to create scaffolding he could pull back when necessary.
requirements: trust and sensitivity on the part of the teacher not to interfere immediately with learner activities
a general understanding and pedagogical framework of the course built from prior experience
constraints: the group did not take up the process organiser when offered early, being interested only in content at that stage
target_learners: mid-career professionals in online networked learning communities
target_learning_goals: collaborative course design for online learning
self- and group-regulation of learning
examples: The tutor put in an advanced organiser with two headings, one to organise the process and one to identify a project, and built an architectural framework through his messages that participants could realise themselves
key_sources: de Laat, M., Lally, V., Lipponen, L. & Simons, R.-J. (2007). Online teaching in networked learning communities: A multi-method approach to studying the role of the teacher. Instructional Science, vol. 35, no. 3, pp. 257-286. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-006-9007-0

article_title: Learning from video modeling examples: does gender matter?
citation: Vincent Hoogerheide, Sofie M. M. Loyens, Tamara van Gog. (2016). Learning from video modeling examples: does gender matter? Instructional Science, 44, 69-86. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9360-y
title: When designing video modeling examples for tasks stereotypically associated with males, create both a male and a female model version with identical content and let learners choose or allocate adaptively
description: The article recommends that because model gender does not affect test performance but does affect affective variables, designers create both a male and a female model version with identical content. It suggests distributing these "via either an adaptive system that allocates students a male or female model depending on their own gender, or by allowing students to choose the model they want to learn from", noting choice may raise feelings of autonomy, motivation and self-efficacy.
requirements: The two model versions must have identical content; in the study this was achieved with an autocue, identical scripts, matched timing, and models with comparable background and behaviour.
constraints: Findings come from a single math task (probability calculation) with novice secondary students; the authors call for replication with tasks from other domains and longer study periods before generalizing.
target_learners: novice secondary education students learning a task associated more with one gender
target_learning_goals: problem-solving skills such as probability calculation
affective outcomes: self-efficacy, perceived competence, enjoyment
examples: In the experiment, 163 students studied one video modeling example with either a male or female model; learning outcomes did not differ, but effort and enjoyment showed model-observer gender interactions.
key_sources: Vincent Hoogerheide, Sofie M. M. Loyens, Tamara van Gog. (2016). Learning from video modeling examples: does gender matter? Instructional Science, 44, 69-86. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9360-y

article_title: Problem-solving prior to instructional explanations when learning javelin throwing in primary school
citation: Christian Leukel, Katharina Loibl. (2025). Problem-solving prior to instructional explanations when learning javelin throwing in primary school. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09700-9
title: KLI framework for composite instructional designs: intermediate knowledge from the PS phase anchors processing of subsequent instruction
description: The article applies the knowledge-learning-instruction (KLI) framework, containing knowledge components, learning processes, and instructional design, as specified for composite instructional designs with two or more phases like PS-I. A key element is the intermediate knowledge after the first phase: knowledge activated during PS is incomplete and/or contains errors, but with the instructional explanation in the I phase it "can further evolve and be refined towards the target knowledge" and "serves as an anchor which supports the processing of the instructional explanations." The framework predicts PS-I benefits when declarative knowledge built during PS links to the content of I.
requirements: Students must generate intermediate knowledge during the PS phase that is pertinent to the content of the subsequent instructional explanations for integration to occur
constraints: The article reports that primary school children's limited ability to develop declarative knowledge during PS that links to the content of I may explain the absent PS-I advantage in this study
target_learners: primary school children (4th graders) learning motor skills in physical education
target_learning_goals: acquisition of complex motor skills such as javelin throwing, including execution of movement features
examples: The study applied the framework to javelin throwing, depicting the interplay of knowledge components, learning processes, and instructional design across PS and I phases (Fig. 1)
key_sources: Christian Leukel, Katharina Loibl. (2025). Problem-solving prior to instructional explanations when learning javelin throwing in primary school. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09700-9

article_title: Exploring pre-service EFL teachers’ perceptions, use cases and questioning practices of ChatGPT during practicum: a critical digital pedagogy perspective
citation: Saadet Korucu-Kış, Arif Bakla. (2026). Exploring pre-service EFL teachers’ perceptions, use cases and questioning practices of ChatGPT during practicum: a critical digital pedagogy perspective. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09783-6
title: Critical Digital Pedagogy (CDP) as a framework for examining pre-service teachers' engagement with generative AI
description: Critical Digital Pedagogy is the study's organizing theoretical lens, drawn from Morris and Stommel and aligned with Freire's vision of education as awakening critical consciousness. It advocates "the ethical, reflective, and socially responsive use of digital technologies to support learner empowerment and critical professional growth". Applied to the practicum, CDP frames technology not as inherently transformative but as a site of inquiry and intentional practice, asking whether pre-service teachers use tools like ChatGPT passively or as critical agents actively shaping their learning experiences.
requirements: Analysis of whether pre-service teachers use digital tools passively or as critical agents actively shaping their learning experiences
constraints: Within CDP, ChatGPT is treated not as a neutral aid but as a site of inquiry revealing degrees of pedagogical intentionality, reflection, and agency
target_learners: pre-service teachers
teacher educators
target_learning_goals: ethical and reflective use of digital technologies
critical professional growth
pedagogical agency
examples: The study applied CDP to analyse pre-service teachers' unscripted, self-directed ChatGPT use during practicum, foregrounding how they formulated prompts and evaluated responses
key_sources: Saadet Korucu-Kış, Arif Bakla. (2026). Exploring pre-service EFL teachers’ perceptions, use cases and questioning practices of ChatGPT during practicum: a critical digital pedagogy perspective. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09783-6

article_title: How vocal and silent forms of participation in combination relate to student achievement
citation: Sedova, K., & Sedlacek, M. (2023). How vocal and silent forms of participation in combination relate to student achievement. Instructional Science, 51, 343–361. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09609-1
title: Teachers should invite all students to participate in classroom conversation rather than assuming silent, engaged students benefit equally
description: The article derives a practical implication from its profile findings: because inequalities in student talk create uneven learning opportunities, "Teachers should invite all students to participate in classroom conversations". Teachers should not assume that silent but attentive and engaged students benefit from classroom discourse in the same way as vocal peers; the internally engaged but silent diligent students are identified as at risk, and the authors argue teachers should help such students raise their voices.
requirements: Applicable in classroom settings where whole-class discussion occurs and talk time can be distributed across students
constraints: Findings come from Czech language and language arts lessons in traditionally taught, non-dialogue-rich Czech classrooms; the article notes similar results might not be found in non-linguistic subjects
Participation was operationalized as talk quantity only, not quality
target_learners: lower secondary school students (ninth grade, ages 14–15)
target_learning_goals: reading literacy
classroom participation in subject-matter discussion
examples: In the study, teachers taught two observed Czech language and language arts lessons as they normally would; talk time per student averaged approximately 12 s per lesson, and 46 students spoke for 0 s
key_sources: Sedova, K., & Sedlacek, M. (2023). How vocal and silent forms of participation in combination relate to student achievement. Instructional Science, 51, 343–361. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09609-1

article_title: Learning to solve ill-defined statistics problems: does self-explanation quality mediate the worked example effect?
citation: Bichler, S., Stadler, M., Bühner, M., Greiff, S., & Fischer, F. (2022). Learning to solve ill-defined statistics problems: does self-explanation quality mediate the worked example effect? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09579-4
title: Justified-claims coding scheme for self-explanation quality in ill-defined statistics problems
description: The article develops a coding scheme assessing self-explanation quality as the degree to which written problem solutions include correctly applied and justified conceptual information. For each of three problems, three claims (variables and design, statistical analysis, statistical assumptions) were coded as no claim (0), incomplete (0.5), or complete (1), and separately coded for justification (visually, spatially, or verbally linked). Scores were summed to a 0–27 self-explanation quality measure (Cronbach's α = .78), with concept application coded separately to capture the inferences learners made.
requirements: Written artifacts from learners prompted to justify their answers; expert solutions used to identify the claims and justifying information per problem.
constraints: The authors argue this operationalization suits ill-defined problems, justification prompts, written artifacts, and application-oriented knowledge; whether self-explanation quality mediates may depend on how quality is conceptualized and the targeted outcome.
target_learners: university students in psychology, educational science, or school psychology
target_learning_goals: application-oriented knowledge of statistical methods for investigating research problems
examples: A learner suggesting a between-subjects design was coded 0.5 for missing details; a within-subjects suggestion was coded 0 for incorrect; verbal links such as 'consequently' or 'therefore' counted as justification.
key_sources: Bichler, S., Stadler, M., Bühner, M., Greiff, S., & Fischer, F. (2022). Learning to solve ill-defined statistics problems: does self-explanation quality mediate the worked example effect? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09579-4

article_title: SimLab: an intervention to promote expansive learning and organisational change in team-based emergency care simulation
citation: O'Hare, S., Kajamaa, A., Conn, R., & Gormley, G. (2025). SimLab: an intervention to promote expansive learning and organisational change in team-based emergency care simulation. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09734-7
title: Cultural-historical activity theory and expansive learning as a design and analysis framework for interprofessional in-situ simulation
description: The article operationalises cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) as both the design lens and analytical framework for simulation. CHAT analyses collective human activity through an activity system of six elements — subject, object, tools, rules, community, division of labour — and "enables a collaborative enquiry into systemic contradictions". Expansive learning describes how participants collectively construct a new expanded object for their activity, moving through seven learning actions from questioning to consolidation. The authors chose CHAT because it views practice and learning as inseparable and suits workplace-based interprofessional training.
requirements: Requires analysis of group discussions using the activity system model as the unit of analysis and the seven expansive learning actions
constraints: Second-generation CHAT was employed; the framework was applied in one general practice setting
target_learners: interprofessional general practice teams (GPs, nurses, trainees, pharmacists, administrative staff)
target_learning_goals: collective preparedness for paediatric emergencies
organisational change in emergency care practice
examples: The SimLab sessions were each designed to incorporate one to two expansive learning actions, with the activity system model introduced as a second stimulus

article_title: SimLab: an intervention to promote expansive learning and organisational change in team-based emergency care simulation

title: SimLab: a condensed four-session Change Laboratory pattern combining in-situ simulation with facilitated expansive learning discussions
description: SimLab adapts the Change Laboratory formative intervention — typically up to ten-plus sessions — into four sessions designed "for the demands of the general practice workplace". Each session pairs an in-situ simulation or CHAT-guided group interview with facilitation of double stimulation: video footage of the simulation and observations serve as mirror data, while the activity system model, laminated guidelines and prior-session summaries serve as second stimuli. Reflection walls and diaries capture disturbances and aha moments between sessions. The pattern is described as potentially transferable to other clinical settings.
requirements: Requires mirror data (ISS video footage, guidelines, prior-session summaries), a researcher interventionist facilitator, and flexible reflection tools between sessions
constraints: Designed and evaluated in a time-poor general practice setting; sessions ran at lunchtime when the practice was closed
target_learners: interprofessional primary care teams
target_learning_goals: expansive learning and transformative agency
team-based emergency care preparedness
examples: Session 1: anaphylaxis ISS with video playback and CHAT-guided interview; session 3: meningitis ISS testing the newly designed emergency trolley and grab bags

article_title: Do students learn more from failing alone or in groups? Insights into the effects of collaborative versus individual problem solving in productive failure
citation: Charleen Brand, Christian Hartmann, Katharina Loibl, Nikol Rummel. (2023). Do students learn more from failing alone or in groups? Insights into the effects of collaborative versus individual problem solving in productive failure. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09619-7
title: Three preparatory mechanisms account of Productive Failure
description: The article works within the account that PF's instructional effect is rooted in three preparatory mechanisms operating during the problem-solving phase prior to instruction: "prior knowledge activation, awareness of knowledge gaps, and recognition of deep features". Prior knowledge activation is operationalized as the quantity of generated solutions, deep feature recognition as solution quality, and gap awareness as self-reports linked to curiosity. The study tested whether collaboration facilitates each mechanism and thereby mediates conceptual knowledge acquisition, and found no such mediations.
requirements: A problem-solving phase before instruction on a concept students cannot yet solve, with instruction that builds on student-generated solutions
constraints: In this study the mechanisms were not associated with learning scores after instruction, and all preparatory variables showed low descriptive values in both conditions
target_learners: (mid) secondary school students
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of variance (standard deviation) in mathematics
examples: Students generated solutions to a soccer-player reliability problem for 45 minutes, reported gap awareness and curiosity, then received 45 minutes of instruction on variance
key_sources: Charleen Brand, Christian Hartmann, Katharina Loibl, Nikol Rummel. (2023). Do students learn more from failing alone or in groups? Insights into the effects of collaborative versus individual problem solving in productive failure. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09619-7

article_title: Do students learn more from failing alone or in groups? Insights into the effects of collaborative versus individual problem solving in productive failure
citation: Charleen Brand, Christian Hartmann, Katharina Loibl, Nikol Rummel. (2023). Do students learn more from failing alone or in groups? Insights into the effects of collaborative versus individual problem solving in productive failure. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09619-7
title: Collaboration is not a necessary design component of the PF problem-solving phase for conceptual learning
description: Within the traditional PF design for secondary mathematics, individual problem solving prepared students for subsequent instruction as well as collaboration: no condition differences or mediations through the preparatory mechanisms were found. The authors conclude that "collaboration does not hold a major preparatory function in itself for the design of PF", and that collaboration "does not seem to afford elaborate discussion sufficiently" to prepare learning better than individual work. Designers need not treat group work during the PF problem-solving phase as essential.
requirements: Adherence to the remaining PF fidelity criteria: a task affording multiple solution attempts, motivational scaffolds, and instruction building on student solutions
constraints: Evidence is limited to the traditional PF setting of secondary school mathematics with the variance task; prior studies in other domains, age groups, or with fidelity violations also found no collaboration advantage
target_learners: (mid) secondary school students
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge acquisition in mathematics
examples: In the experiment, 87 students worked in 35 groups of three and 50 worked individually on the same variance problem before identical instruction, with no post-test difference

title: Traditional PF variance task (soccer-player reliability problem)
description: The instructional artifact at the core of the traditional PF design: a mathematical problem on the concept of variance in which "students were asked to determine the most reliable soccer player based on a list of three players’ goal scores across ten years", with the instruction "to generate as many solutions to this problem as possible". It affords multiple solution attempts, is part of the secondary school curriculum, and has been used in studies replicating the PF effect. The study paired it with a 45-minute instruction phase highlighting typical student errors against the canonical solution.
requirements: Students must lack the knowledge to solve it correctly, so they generate incomplete or erroneous solutions before instruction

target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of variance

article_title: Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law
citation: Osman Sabancı, Nejla Yürük. (2026). Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09805-3
title: Conceptual Change Model applied to civic and political concepts
description: The article adopts the Conceptual Change Model (Posner et al., 1982) as its theoretical framework for civic education, arguing that political misconceptions are rooted in intuitive folk theories and media interpretations and resist mere informational correction. Learning occurs through interaction between new and pre-existing concepts, with change occurring through shifts in concept status. The article states: "The four essential conditions for Conceptual Change underlying the CCM are: dissatisfaction with the existing concept, intelligibility of the new concept, plausibility of the new concept, and fruitfulness of the new concept." The study's activities were designed to create cognitive conflict (dissatisfaction) and establish the new civic concepts as intelligible, plausible, and fruitful.
requirements: Instruction must deliberately create cognitive conflict highlighting shortcomings of learners' current comprehension, since deeply rooted misconceptions cannot be corrected simply by adding new information
constraints: The article notes civic-domain misconceptions are rooted in folk theories and disputed knowledge, making identification and evaluation of mistakes harder than in science domains
target_learners: 7th-grade social studies students
target_learning_goals: Understanding of republic, democracy, and the state of law
Conceptual change in civic and political concepts
examples: The study's concept cartoons were used to elicit initial alternative concepts and encourage cognitive conflict, followed by journaling, concept mapping, and poster activities addressing the remaining CCM conditions
key_sources: Osman Sabancı, Nejla Yürük. (2026). Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09805-3

article_title: Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law
citation: Osman Sabancı, Nejla Yürük. (2026). Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09805-3
title: Metaconceptual processes framework: awareness, monitoring, and evaluation
description: The article builds on Yürük's (2005) framework of metaconceptual processes, which target reflective thinking operating explicitly on learners' conceptual structures rather than cognition generally. The article states: "Three main categories are used to evaluate these processes: metaconceptual awareness, metaconceptual monitoring, and metaconceptual evaluation." Awareness is further divided into first-order (recognizing current mental representations) and second-order (recognizing previously held ideas); monitoring tracks understanding, consistency between new and existing ideas, and idea change; evaluation involves commenting, finding attractive, and defending a chosen idea among competing alternatives. Table 1 details these categories, subcategories, and their educational significance with social studies examples.
requirements: Activities must externalise students' internal conceptual structures so the three processes can be activated and observed
constraints: Framework as applied here is limited to conceptual understanding of social studies concepts over a four-week curriculum period
target_learners: 7th-grade social studies students
target_learning_goals: Conscious management of conceptual change
Correcting alternative conceptions of civic concepts
examples: The Elif and Yağız population-density episode illustrates evaluation: after hearing reasoning that density means crampedness as well as crowdedness, Elif judged her initial idea not useful
key_sources: Osman Sabancı, Nejla Yürük. (2026). Effect of metaconceptual processes on 7th-grade students’ understanding of the concepts of republic, democracy, and the state of law. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09805-3

title: Cyclical sequence of five metaconceptual activities externalising, monitoring, and evaluating civic concepts
description: The intervention organized instruction as a non-linear, cyclical sequence of five activities: analyzing concepts and their features, extracting hidden concepts from Atatürk's sayings via group posters, concept mapping with a law-making simulation, concept cartoons with concept cards, and interviews with family members. The article states: "Metaconceptual teaching activities such as poster preparation, journaling, concept maps, concept cartoons, and cards were used." Each activity was paired with group and class discussions and journal writing, and the tools were used "sequentially and cyclically to ensure continuous metacognitive engagement." Activities were mapped onto the three metaconceptual processes, e.g., cartoons maximising evaluation through cognitive conflict and role-based discussion.
requirements: Same teacher across branches; consultation with language, subject, and education specialists and the class teacher during design and implementation
constraints: "The activities were limited to the time periods specified in the curriculum (four weeks)"
target_learners: 7th-grade students in a public school in Ankara, Türkiye
target_learning_goals: Understanding republic, democracy, and the state of law
Activating metaconceptual awareness, monitoring, and evaluation
examples: In the poster activity groups of five to six students defined a concept, presented posters, voted on the best, justified revisions, and documented metacognitive processes in journals

article_title: Comparison of more effective and typical teachers’ instructional quality and implementation of engaged reader processes
citation: Fatima Zehra Allahverdi, Lynn Gelzheiser. (2025). Comparison of more effective and typical teachers' instructional quality and implementation of engaged reader processes. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09725-8
title: Instructional Quality and Implementation Coding system combining Wood's contingent teaching with Meichenbaum and Biemiller's self-direction dimension
description: A coding system the authors developed to measure explicit instruction and scaffolding of purpose setting at fine grain. It draws on Vygotsky's ZPD and the GRR model "while also incorporating research on scaffolding", operationalizing the GRR through Wood's (2003) contingent teaching (domain and instructional contingencies) and Meichenbaum and Biemiller's (1998) self-direction dimension moving students from other-directed to self-directed. Coding covers actor, content, quality of scaffold, and communication mode within instructional cycles, and uniquely includes student application, which Wood's theory does not address.
requirements: Transcribed audio/video sessions segmented into instructional cycles beginning with a purpose set for reading
Coders trained to reliability; the study reported agreement of 100% for the author, 91.4% for content, 84% for quality, and 97% for instruction communication
constraints: Applied in this study only to acquisition and early consolidation lessons related to purpose setting; no validity coefficient is available
target_learners: third- and fourth-grade students with limited reading comprehension
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension through engaged reader processes such as purpose setting
examples: Five sessions per teacher were transcribed and coded for two case-study teachers, producing Tables 9 and 10 patterns in teacher instruction and student purpose setting

article_title: Designing a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG
citation: Dillenbourg, P. (1989). The design of a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG. Instructional Science, 18(3), 193–216. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00053359
title: PROTO-TEG: a self-improving tutor for geometry
description: PROTO-TEG is a tutoring system for geometry described in this article as "a self-improving tutor in geometry". It holds a set of didactic strategies and maintains a student model; its distinctive feature is a self-improving function that discovers, from its own recorded tutoring episodes, criteria for choosing among those strategies. The system was built to test whether an ITS could acquire its own strategy-selection knowledge rather than having it fully hand-coded.
requirements: A set of didactic strategies available for selection
A student model whose states can be recorded during tutoring episodes
constraints: Domain of application described is geometry
target_learners: geometry learners
target_learning_goals: geometry learning
examples: The article reports an empirical experiment in which the system's self-improving functions were assessed and conditions were discovered for five of the nine didactic strategies

article_title: Designing a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG
citation: Dillenbourg, P. (1989). The design of a self-improving tutor: PROTO-TEG. Instructional Science, 18(3), 193–216. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00053359
title: Self-improving mechanism: learning strategy-selection criteria from student model states by concept learning from examples
description: The article's central mechanism account is that a tutor can improve itself by inducing selection criteria from its own experience. Criteria "are expressed as characteristics of the student model" and are "elaborated by comparing student model states recorded when a strategy was effective and those recorded when the same strategy was not effective". The comparison is performed by machine learning methods, "more precisely, by learning concepts from examples", so each tutoring episode contributes a labelled example of strategy success or failure.
requirements: Recorded student model states from episodes where a strategy was effective and where it was not effective
Machine learning methods able to learn concepts from examples
constraints: Criteria are limited to characteristics expressible in the student model
target_learners: geometry learners
target_learning_goals: adaptive selection of didactic strategies during tutoring
examples: The system compared student model states from effective versus ineffective uses of the same strategy to induce selection conditions

article_title: The impact of interpersonal perceptions on the process of dealing with errors while providing and processing peer-feedback on writing
citation: Jochem E. J. Aben, Mayra Mascareño Lara, Anneke C. Timmermans, Filitsa Dingyloudi, Jan-Willem Strijbos. (2024). The impact of interpersonal perceptions on the process of dealing with errors while providing and processing peer-feedback on writing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09660-0
title: Aben et al.'s model of cognitive sub-phases in dealing with errors during feedback provision and processing
description: The article builds on a theoretical model that visualizes dealing with errors during feedback provision and processing as a sequence of cognitive sub-phases. In provision, feedback providers may "identify an error", then "decode the identified error, i.e., assign meaning to the error, by labelling the error as an error of a particular kind", followed by evaluation, encoding of a feedback remark, and sending. In processing, recipients read the feedback remark, decode it, evaluate the extent to which they agree, and may encode an output such as a correction, leading to a revised performance. The study tests whether these sub-phases can be observed empirically in peer-feedback on argumentative writing.
requirements: Feedback activities that are improvement-oriented, so that errors in a performance (e.g., a written text) are the object of the provision and processing phases
constraints: The model was theorized for dyads providing and processing feedback; the article notes Timms et al.'s related model instead covers feedback from a digital learning environment and includes a feedback-identification activity in processing that Aben et al.'s model does not
target_learners: Secondary education students (grade 11, pre-university track, ages 16-18)
target_learning_goals: Improving argumentative writing through providing and processing peer-feedback
examples: Six dyads of 11th-grade students provided and processed peer-feedback on argumentative texts while thinking aloud, and the study examined whether the model's sub-phases could be empirically observed

article_title: Using heuristic worked examples to promote solving of reality-based tasks in mathematics in lower secondary school
citation: Hänze, M., & Leiss, D. (2022). Using heuristic worked examples to promote solving of reality-based tasks in mathematics in lower secondary school. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09583-8
title: Four-step heuristic worked example model for mathematical modeling with dialogical fictitious-student examples
description: The article advances a four-step account of mathematical modeling linked to Polya's steps: "(1) understand the problem, (2) mathematize it, (3) work mathematically, and (4) explain the result." Heuristic worked examples are built on this structure, presenting dialogues between two fictitious students who negotiate solutions across the four phases, make realistic attempts, "go a little wrong sometimes, discuss their detours and mistakes, but ultimately demonstrate adequate strategies." This erroneous-elements design is intended to support active processing and sensitize students to pitfalls, while the dialogue simulates expert modeling and scaffolds the problem-solving process.
requirements: Worked examples segmented into the four modeling sections with a standard strategic scheme across varying surface characteristics
Fictitious students must ultimately solve the problem adequately, since erroneous examples benefited only high-prior-knowledge learners in the cited work
constraints: The study operationalized the model on concrete content areas (basic numeracy, plane geometry, linear functions), so results must be interpreted against those domains
Intervention duration was a single 45-minute period, so effects reflect initial learning rather than comprehensive competency
target_learners: lower secondary school students in Grades 5 and 7
target_learning_goals: mathematical modeling competency for reality-based tasks
modeling-specific strategy knowledge and metacognitive self-regulation
examples: The 'Mohawk' worked example has fictitious students Paul and Sara identify the needed information, estimate the head height by measuring, and derive 125 cm for the hairdo height
key_sources: Hänze, M., & Leiss, D. (2022). Using heuristic worked examples to promote solving of reality-based tasks in mathematics in lower secondary school. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09583-8

article_title: Using heuristic worked examples to promote solving of reality-based tasks in mathematics in lower secondary school
citation: Hänze, M., & Leiss, D. (2022). Using heuristic worked examples to promote solving of reality-based tasks in mathematics in lower secondary school. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09583-8
title: Use dialogical heuristic worked examples with deliberate errors to support solving of reality-based mathematics tasks
description: The article recommends worked examples that simulate expert modeling by presenting "a dialogue between two fictitious students who discuss their ideas, go a little wrong sometimes, discuss their detours and mistakes, and ultimately demonstrate adequate strategies." The erroneous detours are meant to support active processing and sensitize students to pitfalls, while the dialogue format encourages spontaneous self-explanations without explicit prompts. The authors report this "dialogical approach" showed excellent effectiveness in their study.

Fictitious students ultimately solve the problem adequately
constraints: For fifth graders the approach improved strategy knowledge but not modeling competency, so the authors give first hints that promotion of metacognitive strategies should not be started too early
Effects were short-term, present about 1 to 3 days after treatment
target_learners: lower secondary school students, particularly seventh graders
target_learning_goals: solving reality-based mathematics tasks with adequate strategies
metacognitive self-regulation during mathematical modeling
examples: Students studied worked examples in which fictitious students Paul and Sara negotiated solutions to tasks such as the Mohawk problem for 45 minutes
