article_title: Teachers rehumanizing mathematics for students with disabilities; the role of empathy
citation: Rachel Lambert, Kara Imm. (2026). Teachers rehumanizing mathematics for students with disabilities; the role of empathy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09753-4
title: A model integrating empathy with teacher knowledge as politically situated and emergent in relationship with marginalized students
description: Building on the new uses educators made of empathy, the authors propose a model that integrates empathy with conceptualizations of teachers' knowledge as "both politically situated and emergent in relationship with marginalized students." The model links design thinking, with empathy as its central value and practice, to surrounding knowledges: political conocimiento, models of disability, UDL Math, and political knowledge for teaching mathematics to students with disability. It treats teacher knowledge as relational, emotional, and unfolding over time rather than static.
requirements: Educators engage in empathy as both a value and a repeated practice (empathy interviews) in relationship with students
constraints: The model was developed from one professional-development study conducted during the 2020–2021 pandemic year of primarily remote teaching
target_learners: Mathematics teachers and special educators of students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Rehumanizing mathematics instruction; shifting away from deficit views of disability
examples: Participants came to see empathy as the unifying concept between rethinking deficit assumptions about students and noticing and challenging unjust systems in special education and mathematics.
key_sources: Rachel Lambert, Kara Imm. (2026). Teachers rehumanizing mathematics for students with disabilities; the role of empathy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09753-4

article_title: Teachers rehumanizing mathematics for students with disabilities; the role of empathy
citation: Rachel Lambert, Kara Imm. (2026). Teachers rehumanizing mathematics for students with disabilities; the role of empathy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09753-4
title: Political/relational model of disability as the framing for rehumanizing mathematics professional development
description: The study situated disability in a political/relational model influenced by feminist and queer studies, in place of the traditional medical model focused on diagnosing and fixing individual deficits. This model "centers disability as an embodied experience that intersects with social conditions," defining disability in relation to shifting standards of normalcy and highlighting the curative imaginary. The professional development used this framing, alongside the disability rights movement and critical disability texts, to prompt educators to reassess deficit views of disabled mathematics learners.
requirements: Educators encounter political perspectives on disability rights and activism, not only individual-deficit framings
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual framing for the PD and analysis, not a tested instructional manipulation
target_learners: Mathematics and special educators teaching students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Rethinking ideas about disability; disrupting deficit thinking; analyzing oppressive systems
examples: Among the 10 survey participants who referenced political struggles related to disability, 9 specifically mentioned the Disability Rights Movement and/or the documentary Crip Camp.

article_title: Developmental relations between mathematics self-concept, interest, and achievement: A comparison of solo- and co-taught classes
citation: Lehikoinen, H., Väisänen, P., Havu-Nuutinen, S., Lappalainen, K., & Niemivirta, M. (2025). Developmental relations between mathematics self-concept, interest, and achievement: A comparison of solo- and co-taught classes. Instructional Science, 53, 239–261. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09678-4
title: Co-teaching implementation with shared planning, teaching, and evaluation supported by workshops and fidelity monitoring
description: The study implemented co-teaching as a collaborative effort of two or more educators who "share all aspects of teaching, planning, and evaluation", pairing class teachers with special education teachers in the same mathematics classes. Implementation was supported by an initial workshop for each co-teacher pair covering basics, teacher roles, and requirements for successful co-teaching, plus interviews and weekly check-list diaries. Fidelity checks showed co-teaching occurred in 70% of mathematics classes due to teacher absence, with the higher teacher-student ratio maintained via substitutes, and perceived lesson success was high (M = 4.4, SD = 0.69).
requirements: Teachers need a Master's degree in education, at least five years of teaching experience, and voluntary participation; co-teacher pairs should be formed by the teachers themselves to match interests and pedagogical views.
constraints: Co-teaching occurred in only 70% of mathematics classes due to teacher absence; joint planning and assessment were not carried out during substitute-taught lessons, and implementation is described as resource-intensive and far from straightforward.
target_learners: Sixth-grade primary school students (aged 12–13) in mathematics
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement and motivation (self-concept and individual interest)
examples: Co-teacher pairs received a researcher-led workshop, kept weekly check-list diaries, and used different co-teaching models such as team- and alternative teaching flexibly, spending around three quarters of an hour per week on planning and reflection.

article_title: Demonstration-based training (DBT) in the design of a video tutorial for software training
citation: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij. (2016). Demonstration-based training (DBT) in the design of a video tutorial for software training. Instr Sci 44:527–542. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9394-9
title: Demonstration-based training (DBT) grounded in Bandura's four-process theory of observational learning
description: DBT is a design approach for teaching procedures by observation: "DBT is a design approach in which a dynamic example of performance is complemented with instructional features." Its basis is Bandura's theory, which "posits that observational or model-based learning hinges on the four interrelated processes of attention, retention, production, and motivation." The article couples specific design measures to each process: signaling and pre-training for attention, segmentation and pauses for retention, practice for production, and simple-to-complex sequencing plus domain anchoring for motivation.
requirements: A dynamic example of performance (task demonstration) that is complemented with instructional features targeted at the four observational learning processes
constraints: During a demonstration the designer has no influence over top-down attentional processes because these depend on the user's prior knowledge; instructional measures concern bottom-up attentional processes
target_learners: novice software users, including primary and secondary school students
target_learning_goals: procedural knowledge of software task completion
examples: The tutorial in the study was developed in accordance with DBT, adding cues, segmentation, pauses, practice, reviews, simple-to-complex ordering and domain-anchored tasks to task demonstrations
key_sources: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij. (2016). Demonstration-based training (DBT) in the design of a video tutorial for software training. Instr Sci 44:527–542. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9394-9

article_title: Demonstration-based training (DBT) in the design of a video tutorial for software training
citation: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij. (2016). Demonstration-based training (DBT) in the design of a video tutorial for software training. Instr Sci 44:527–542. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9394-9
title: Follow each task demonstration with a short review recap to support retention of the procedure
description: A review is "a short recap of the main steps in a procedure" presented after a demonstration, reiterating task completion in abbreviated form to support retention. Because it comes after the demonstration, "its presence does not affect the design of the demonstration." In the reported experiment the review tutorial surpassed the demonstration-only control on practice, immediate and delayed post-tests and on post-training task relevance.
requirements: Reviews follow the demonstration automatically (in the study, after a 2-s pause) and summarize task completion in condensed format lasting between 13 and 26 seconds
constraints: The review increased presentation time by about 20 percent, so benefits may partly reflect longer exposure; the authors state this merits further research
target_learners: novice software users in primary and secondary schools
target_learning_goals: retention of software procedures; procedural knowledge development
examples: In the study, each task review followed automatically after the demonstration for that task, beginning after the 2-s pause at the end of the demonstration, introduced with the statement 'You are now done, but remember …'

article_title: Does musical training improve school performance?
citation: Olive Emil Wetter, Fritz Koerner, Adrian Schwaninger. (2009). Does musical training improve school performance? Instr Sci 37:365–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9052-y
title: Promote an early beginning of musical training for children to take advantage of a period of high brain plasticity
description: The authors recommend starting musical training early in childhood, reasoning that musical practice during brain maturation induces structural and functional brain changes with broad implications. They cite evidence that "an introduction to musical training earlier than age 7 is crucial to the development of brain structures" and conclude "it makes sense to take advantage of this period of high brain plasticity". The recommendation extends their finding that continuous musical training accompanies maintained school performance.
requirements: Musical training must be continuous over years to be associated with maintained school performance in this study's data
constraints: The study's retrospective non-randomized design does not allow causal inferences about training effects
target_learners: Children in primary school grades 3–6, with training ideally beginning before age 7
target_learning_goals: General school performance across intellectual subjects
Cognitive and intellectual development
examples: In the study, children with continuous musical training maintained high overall marks from grade 3 to 6 while controls' marks declined significantly

article_title: Team learning: building shared mental models
citation: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3
title: Team learning behavior framework: construction, co-construction, and constructive conflict building shared mental models
description: The article frames learning at team level as the development of shared cognitions, defined as "team members' overlapping mental representation of key elements of the team's task environment". Three interaction processes constitute team learning: construction of meaning (articulating personal meaning), co-construction (building meaning by refining or building on others' offers), and constructive conflict, defined as "dealing with differences in interpretation between team members by arguments and clariﬁcations". The framework hypothesizes these behaviors build shared mental models, which in turn drive team effectiveness.
requirements: Both mutual understanding and mutual agreement are necessary for shared mental model development
constraints: Divergence in opinion only benefits the team if it leads to deep-level processing of diverse viewpoints
target_learners: student teams in higher education
work teams in organizations
target_learning_goals: developing shared cognition and common ground in collaborative problem solving
examples: The framework was tested with 27 three-person student teams playing the Steer the Economy business simulation game, with behaviors measured by a nine-item questionnaire
key_sources: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3

article_title: Team learning: building shared mental models
citation: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3
title: Text-based cognitive mapping method for measuring team shared mental models
description: The study measures shared mental models using Carley's (1997) automated text-based cognitive mapping: team members' open-ended answers are coded as concept networks via filtering (delete lists and a thesaurus) and windowing (relations within a range of eight concepts), and the team's shared model is the intersection of individual maps under a lossy rule (concepts or statements identical in at least two of three maps). The article reports that "She collected evidence on the reliability and validity of the method, which showed to be satisfactory."
requirements: Researcher decisions on filtering (delete list, thesaurus) and window size
Open-ended text eliciting both declarative and procedural knowledge
constraints: The automated windowing approach based on physical proximity can be prone to accidental relation
target_learners: student teams
organizational work teams
target_learning_goals: assessing shared cognition and knowledge convergence in collaborative teams
examples: Applied to answers of 81 students in 27 teams about which game variables matter and how they influence company success
key_sources: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3

citation: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3
title: Steer the Economy business simulation game as complex interdependent team task
description: "Steer the Economy", developed by Woltjer (2005), is a business simulation game in which teams act as company management making decisions in a simulated macro-economy of four markets and five actor types, with companies interlinked through a computer network. The mission is to maximize company value (equity plus goodwill). The article chose it "because of its authenticity", requiring integration of different perspectives under information overload, making members interdependent.
requirements: Face-to-face team interaction
Computer network linking all companies' decisions
constraints: Teams in the study played the game for only two weeks
target_learners: first-year International Business Economics students
target_learning_goals: managing a company in a complex simulated economy through team decision making
examples: Teams managed their company for a simulated period of circa 8 years, with equity and goodwill in the last year taken as actual performance measures

article_title: Team learning: building shared mental models
citation: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3
title: Treat differences of opinion as windows of opportunity and manage both social and cognitive processes in teams
description: The article draws a practical implication for education and organizations: teams must "pay explicit attention to their socio-cognitive processes in order to promote team learning as an avenue to develop shared mental models". Differences of opinion "need to be seen as windows of opportunity instead of threats to progress", and an interpersonal context of psychological safety can foster these learning behaviors. Proficiency in team discussion skills — expressing ideas, asking for information and arguments, and integrating ideas — is named an important building block.
requirements: An interpersonal context characterised by psychological safety
constraints: Findings come from student teams in a two-week simulation and may not generalize directly to real project teams
target_learners: students in collaborative learning formats
professionals working in teams
target_learning_goals: developing shared mental models through constructive handling of disagreement
examples: The authors recommend training team members to monitor and strengthen their internal functioning and to build proficiency in the skills of team discussion

article_title: Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues
citation: Baruch B. Schwarz, Udi Tsemach, Mirit Israeli, Erez Nir. (2025). Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09669-5
title: Dialogic and non-dialogic networks: an ANT-based categorization of classroom talk structures
description: Applying ANT to classroom talk, the article defines networks of human and non-human actors (texts, boards, instructions) that constitute the socio-material structure of talk. A network is dialogic when no human actor is subordinated: "We call such a network, in which all the human actors have agency, and no actor, human or non-human subordinates them, as dialogic". Conversely, "We define such a network in which some human actors are subordinated as a non-dialogic network". Roles are not predetermined but translated in interactions, and networks can be blackboxed.
requirements: Tracing actors, connections, translations, shifts, outcomes, connections to other networks, and black boxes through the article's seven-step recursive ANT analysis procedure
constraints: The authors adopt ANT as a methodology rather than a theory, since they look a priori for delineating dialogic and non-dialogic networks, which would have been unacceptable for ANT as a theory
target_learners: Grade 7 students in dialogic education programs
target_learning_goals: Dialogic argumentation and collaborative reasoning across disciplines
examples: In one small-group episode, five girls subordinated themselves to the Bristol board and instructions (non-dialogic), then shifted to collaborative argumentation voicing their own opinions (dialogic), then back to card classification
key_sources: Baruch B. Schwarz, Udi Tsemach, Mirit Israeli, Erez Nir. (2025). Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09669-5

article_title: Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues
citation: Baruch B. Schwarz, Udi Tsemach, Mirit Israeli, Erez Nir. (2025). Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09669-5
title: Skidmore's dialogic sphere: three dimensions of addressivity, voicing, and semantic permeability
description: The article presents Skidmore's framework, which extends the concept of dialogic space using Bakhtin's social theory of language, as a dialogic sphere with three dimensions. "First, addressivity materializes the fact that in a speech there is always a kind of interlocutor, the quality of turning to someone". The second dimension is the voicing given to students, contrasting teacher-orchestrated homophonic plenary talk with student voice. The third, semantic permeability, varies between heteroglossic everyday speech and orthoglossic academic language, requiring enough permeability for students to cross between them.
requirements: Judging whether teacher orientation toward learners is appropriate depends on the specific context in which the talk takes place
constraints: The framework makes salient the tension between dialogism (dialogic by definition) and Dialogic Education (dialogic because appropriate educational aims are reached in situ)
target_learners: Classroom students in dialogic education settings
target_learning_goals: Participation in educational dialogues bridging everyday and academic understanding
examples: The researchers used the three dimensions while watching and listening to all recorded discussions to select episodes exemplifying (in-)appropriate orientation
key_sources: Baruch B. Schwarz, Udi Tsemach, Mirit Israeli, Erez Nir. (2025). Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09669-5

article_title: Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues
citation: Baruch B. Schwarz, Udi Tsemach, Mirit Israeli, Erez Nir. (2025). Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09669-5
title: Seven-step recursive ANT analysis procedure for classroom discourse
description: The article adapts ANT into a recursive analytic procedure for classroom talk with seven steps: recognizing actors (human and non-human), tracing connections into assemblages, identifying translations of roles, identifying shifts and changes in the network, delineating interactions' outcomes, examining connections to other networks, and revealing black boxes. Roles are translated through network dynamics: "the teacher played alternatively the role of a source of knowledge, an activity facilitator, and a referee, according to the specific dynamic in the network".
requirements: Audio- or video-recordings of discussions and ethics approvals; the steps are inter-connected and recursive, not fixed
constraints: ANT is an ethnographic methodology that describes each lesson without pretending to provide generalizable processes
target_learners: Researchers and teachers analyzing classroom dialogue
target_learning_goals: Understanding the socio-material structure and dynamics of educational dialogues
examples: Applied to episodes from two focus-day lessons on vaccination mandates and genetic engineering of embryos

citation: Baruch B. Schwarz, Udi Tsemach, Mirit Israeli, Erez Nir. (2025). Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09669-5
title: DIALOGOS focus days: interdisciplinary dialogic argumentation program for Grade 7
description: The DIALOGOS Center initiated a program in four schools in a mid-size Israeli town, with a teacher professional development program for Grade 7 in mathematics, humanities, and science. Each focus day "turned around a different societal issue; disciplinary sessions (in mathematics, science and philosophy) during which students learned about ideas relevant to the societal issue, preceded an interdisciplinary session" producing a joint product. About 130 students from four seventh grades participated, all from excellent classes.
requirements: Collaboration with the DIALOGOS team to prepare activities, conducted by regular school teachers; out-of-regular-schedule learning days rather than change to regular routines
constraints: Students were all from excellent classes, and the study focused only on the interdisciplinary sessions of the focus days
target_learners: Grade 7 students from four schools in a mid-size Israeli town
target_learning_goals: Interdisciplinary dialogic argumentation on societal issues such as vaccination mandates and genetic engineering
examples: Focus day topics included 'Would it be right for the government to mandate parents to vaccinate their children?' and 'Should the government allow parents to genetically engineer their future babies?'

article_title: Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks
citation: Ines Zeitlhofer, Joerg Zumbach. (2026). Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09807-1
title: Germane processes as a moderating account of complex desirable difficulty tasks
description: The article adopts Sweller's (2010) view of germane load as working memory resources allocated to managing intrinsic load, using the term "germane processes" to emphasize its functional, learner-driven nature. It proposes two sources of germane processes in complex desirable difficulty tasks — desirable difficulties and constantly high task complexity — which trigger metacognitive regulation and control strategies. The account holds that "germane resources are only invested if the learning task would not be solved without them", modifying CLT's stable-motivation assumption.
requirements: Learners must have sufficient prior knowledge for challenging tasks to be effective, per the article's practical implications
constraints: Findings stem from only one experiment in one domain (Italian verb conjugation), limiting generalizability as the authors state
target_learners: university students without prior Italian knowledge
target_learning_goals: grammar skill acquisition (verb conjugation) and long-term retention
examples: The 2×2 experiment crossed constantly high vs. gradually increasing complexity with interleaved vs. blocked practice schedules
key_sources: Ines Zeitlhofer, Joerg Zumbach. (2026). Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09807-1

article_title: Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks
citation: Ines Zeitlhofer, Joerg Zumbach. (2026). Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09807-1
title: Favor tasks that are cognitively demanding from the outset and include desirable difficulties such as interleaved practice
description: Based on their findings, the authors recommend that educators "incorporate tasks with consistently high complexity or desirable difficulties" to foster cognitive engagement and metacognitive strategy use. Practically, this means "favoring tasks that are cognitively demanding from the outset rather than those that progressively increase in complexity", with interleaved practice as an additional desirable difficulty, while considering learners' existing knowledge.
requirements: Educators should carefully consider learners' existing knowledge, since successful engagement with challenging tasks depends on sufficient prior knowledge
constraints: The motivational measures showed no effects, and the learning content's low personal relevance may have shaped results
target_learners: university students
learners in school contexts acquiring complex skills
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and transfer of complex problem-solving skills
metacognitive strategy use
examples: In the experiment, high-complexity conditions required assigning suffixes for all six grammatical persons in each exercise, while interleaved conditions practiced all six tenses within each round in randomized order
key_sources: Ines Zeitlhofer, Joerg Zumbach. (2026). Germane processes moderate the effectiveness of complex desirable difficulty tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09807-1

article_title: Effects of problem–example and example–problem pairs on gifted and nongifted primary school students’ learning
citation: Coppens, L. C., Hoogerheide, V., Snippe, E. M., Flunger, B., & van Gog, T. (2019). Effects of problem–example and example–problem pairs on gifted and nongifted primary school students' learning. Instructional Science, 47, 279–297. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09484-3
title: Start online learning phases with a worked example rather than a practice problem
description: The authors draw a design recommendation for online and blended learning environments from their efficiency and competence findings: "It seems solid advice to start the learning phase with an example and not a practice problem." Example–problem pairs were more efficient and beneficial for perceived competence for both gifted and nongifted primary students, even though test performance differences were not always significant.
requirements: Learning materials must include worked video modeling examples that demonstrate the solution procedure before or alongside practice problems.
constraints: Sequence effects on test performance were not always significant; the advantage lies mainly in efficiency and perceived competence, and was studied with primary school students on a puzzle-like math task.
target_learners: primary school students
gifted students
novice learners
target_learning_goals: procedural problem-solving skill acquisition
examples: Students studied two 4-minute video modeling examples and solved two isomorphic water jug practice problems in either EPEP or PEPE order before an isomorphic and near-transfer posttest.

article_title: Facilitation strategies responding to emotional displays in PD discourse: navigating relational and learning goals
citation: Dana Vedder-Weiss, Rotem Tractenberg-Maslaton, Karin Sarfati-Shaulov. (2025). Facilitation strategies responding to emotional displays in PD discourse: navigating relational and learning goals. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09737-4
title: Two-continuum framework mapping facilitation responses to emotion displays onto recognizing (relational) and exploring (learning) goals
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework in which facilitator responses to teacher emotional displays are mapped onto two continuums: recognizing the emotion, which serves relational goals (emotional support, solidarity, trust), and exploring the emotion, which serves learning goals (examining underlying beliefs, implications, and response possibilities). The authors state they "identified seven facilitation strategies (summarized in Table 3) and mapped them onto two continuums (see Fig. 2): (1) recognizing the emotion (relational goal); (2) exploring the emotion (learning goal)." The framework offers a repertoire rather than a normative ranking of strategies.
requirements: A PD group discussing problems of practice in which teachers display emotions that facilitators respond to
constraints: The authors note the location of strategies on the map is far from precise, as they do not have analytic tools to measure the extent of recognition and exploration
target_learners: PD facilitators of teacher collaborative learning groups
target_learning_goals: Navigating tensions between relational and learning goals when responding to teacher emotional displays
examples: The article maps seven strategies onto the two continuums, dividing them roughly into those that close the space to discuss emotions and those that open it
key_sources: Dana Vedder-Weiss, Rotem Tractenberg-Maslaton, Karin Sarfati-Shaulov. (2025). Facilitation strategies responding to emotional displays in PD discourse: navigating relational and learning goals. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09737-4

article_title: Facilitation strategies responding to emotional displays in PD discourse: navigating relational and learning goals
citation: Dana Vedder-Weiss, Rotem Tractenberg-Maslaton, Karin Sarfati-Shaulov. (2025). Facilitation strategies responding to emotional displays in PD discourse: navigating relational and learning goals. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09737-4
title: Seven facilitation strategies for responding to teacher emotional displays in PD discourse
description: The article identifies and defines seven facilitation strategies with their key moves: ignoring the emotion, quick transition from emotion to practice, acknowledging the emotion to prevent further discussing it, mitigating and normalizing the emotion, exploring the emotion's role in a problem of practice, normalizing and problematizing the emotion, and exploring alternative responses to the emotion. Each strategy is defined by "the discursive objectives the facilitator promotes vis-à-vis the emotion" and operationalized through specific moves such as redirecting, relabeling, revoicing, and reframing. The classification is intended to help facilitators develop awareness of their discourse patterns and open up new response possibilities.
requirements: Facilitators who lead PD groups and moderate discussions where emotions arise
constraints: Strategies were identified in one problem-based PD science program; the authors note the classification offers a repertoire rather than a manual of best practices
target_learners: PD facilitators working with in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: Managing emotional and relational dynamics in collaborative teacher learning discourse
examples: Ignoring the emotion: redirecting the discussion without referring to the emotion; Exploring the emotion's role: pressing to examine the emotional dimension by contrasting what teachers know with what they do

grain_size: lesson-level discursive moves within PD sessions

article_title: Training self-regulated learning skills with video modeling examples: Do task-selection skills transfer?
citation: Raaijmakers, S. F., Baars, M., Schaap, L., Paas, F., van Merriënboer, J., & van Gog, T. (2018). Training self-regulated learning skills with video modeling examples: Do task-selection skills transfer? Instructional Science, 46, 273–290. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9434-0
title: Task database with 75 biology problems organized by five complexity levels and three support levels
description: The learning environment contained a task database of monohybrid cross problems in biology: "The task database (cf. Kostons et al. 2012) contained 75 problems at ﬁve levels of complexity, with three levels of support within each complexity level". Complexity increased via multiple answers, reasoning type, generations, and unknowns; support faded from 4/5 worked-out steps to none, in line with the completion strategy and the 4C/ID model. Students freely selected eight tasks during the self-regulated learning phase.
requirements: Learners must be able to choose tasks themselves so that trained self-assessment and task-selection skills can be exercised

self-assessment and task-selection skills in self-regulated learning
examples: Students chose eight tasks from the 75-task database, rating mental effort on a 9-point scale and self-assessing performance on a 0-5 scale after each task

article_title: Enhancing learning of nanoscale phenomena: the role of agent-based models and embodied reasoning
citation: Polly K. Lai. (2026). Enhancing learning of nanoscale phenomena: the role of agent-based models and embodied reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09776-x
title: Embodied cognition framework of three embodied processes—perspective taking, causal inference making, and motor-supported thinking—for learning with ABMs
description: The article operationalizes embodied cognition (drawing on Clark's account of emergent patterns and Barsalou's grounded cognition) as three indicators of learning with ABMs. "These three indicators—perspective taking, causal inference making, and motor-supported thinking—operationalize how embodied cognition is enacted differently in ABMs versus visualisations and provided a coding framework for this study." Perspective taking involves shifting between agent-level (first-person) and system-level (third-person) viewpoints; causal inference making links parameter changes to system outcomes through manipulation; motor-supported thinking uses gestures and handwriting to externalise mental simulations. The framework guided both the intervention design and the reasoning-strategy coding scheme.
requirements: Learning environments must afford manipulation of agents or parameters so learners can shift perspectives, test causal inferences, and gesture; visualizations that only present pre-structured animations limit embodied exploration
constraints: The framework was developed and tested for nanoscience concepts (size-dependent properties, surface-area-to-volume ratio) with undergraduate students
target_learners: undergraduate nanotechnology students
target_learning_goals: explanatory understanding of emergent nanoscale phenomena
applying size-dependent properties concepts to novel problems
examples: The study coded post-test think-aloud protocols and bodily movements using the three indicators, adapted from Chi's (1997) method, achieving Kappa κ =.86
key_sources: Polly K. Lai. (2026). Enhancing learning of nanoscale phenomena: the role of agent-based models and embodied reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09776-x

article_title: Enhancing learning of nanoscale phenomena: the role of agent-based models and embodied reasoning
citation: Polly K. Lai. (2026). Enhancing learning of nanoscale phenomena: the role of agent-based models and embodied reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09776-x
title: Use manipulable agent-based models rather than passive visualization videos when the learning goal is explanatory and transferable understanding of invisible, emergent phenomena
description: The article recommends instructional designs that leverage embodied processes for complex scientific phenomena. Because ABMs let students "manipulate individual agents and observe system-level outcomes" while engaging perspective taking, causal inference, and motor-supported thinking, they are better suited than pre-structured videos when the goal is mechanistic explanation and transfer; videos remain adequate for declarative facts. The principle rests on the study's finding that both formats supported declarative knowledge but only ABMs fostered significant explanatory gains and transfer.
requirements: ABM environments must allow parameter manipulation and observation of emergent agent interactions
Time-on-task and informational content should be equated across formats, as the study did
constraints: Evidence comes from a single 27-participant study in nanoscience with undergraduates; declarative knowledge showed no advantage for ABMs
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students learning abstract, invisible phenomena

description: MET devices worn as glasses record the teacher's field of view and fixation point during regular lessons; teachers later watch their own footage from their own viewpoint and freely comment aloud (video-stimulated recall). The study used the ASL Mobile Eye Tracker with 37 teachers and coded commentary for noticing and alternative strategies. MET "allows teachers to 're-live' their teaching from their own viewpoint instead from the perspective of a classroom observer" and rarely shows the teachers themselves.

expert in-service teachers

article_title: Reciprocal interactions between teachers’ instructional moves and students’ social reasoning during collaborative small group discussions
citation: Nagpal, M., Lin, T.-J., Kraatz, E., Kim, S., Ha, S. Y., & Glassman, M. (2025). Reciprocal interactions between teachers' instructional moves and students' social reasoning during collaborative small group discussions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09718-7
title: Social reasoning as a multi-perspective social-cognitive capacity for justifying social decisions
description: The article defines social reasoning as "a social-cognitive capacity to consider, interpret and weigh upon multiple aspects of a complex social situation... in order to make informed social decisions." It is treated as one of the most difficult forms of reasoning because social situations contain information that is biased, fragmented, and uncertain. Reasoning about a social-moral issue requires coordinating three theory-driven perspectives — moral (obligatory virtues such as fairness and honesty), societal (authority, traditions, norms), and personal-relational (individual needs, emotions, motivations) — and justifying knowledge with reasons or evidence meeting logical integrity, clarity, credibility, and accessibility.
requirements: Speaking turns must apply or construct key social concepts meaningfully to justify a perspective; positions without supporting reasons, paraphrases, and egocentric utterances are not coded as social reasoning
constraints: Operationalized in this study within fifth-grade discussions of social-moral dilemmas drawn from stories (e.g., social exclusion, prejudice, responsibility)
target_learners: fifth-grade elementary students
target_learning_goals: social reasoning
perspective coordination
justification of social knowledge with reasons and evidence
examples: In Week-4 discussions of The Gold Cadillac, the most frequent topics were responsibility (717 turns) and social exclusion (223 turns), most often coded under the societal perspective (592 turns)
key_sources: Nagpal, M., Lin, T.-J., Kraatz, E., Kim, S., Ha, S. Y., & Glassman, M. (2025). Reciprocal interactions between teachers' instructional moves and students' social reasoning during collaborative small group discussions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09718-7

citation: Nagpal, M., Lin, T.-J., Kraatz, E., Kim, S., Ha, S. Y., & Glassman, M. (2025). Reciprocal interactions between teachers' instructional moves and students' social reasoning during collaborative small group discussions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09718-7
title: Collaborative Social Reasoning (CSR) discussions — a peer-centered, teacher-scaffolded small-group discussion approach
description: CSR discussions are a six-week dialogic inquiry intervention in which heterogeneous small groups of about five students discuss a social-moral dilemma (the "big question") arising from a story. Students generate reasons and evidence, challenge one another, and seek a collective solution, while the teacher is present throughout but "assists in the small group discussion only when needed," scaffolding reasoning or participation contingently and letting students hold more control over time. Each discussion ends with a debriefing in which students reflect and set goals. In the studied implementation, 41% of 2499 Week-4 student turns contained social reasoning.
requirements: Teacher training (a two-day workshop on argumentation principles, norms, and moves), weekly stories on social themes, and guided reading before each discussion
constraints: Teachers in the studied implementation adhered 100% to procedures except Read and Think questions (79%) and historical-context discussion (92%), mainly due to time constraints
target_learners: fifth-grade students in heterogeneous small groups
target_learning_goals: social-cognitive and social-emotional competencies
argumentation
social reasoning
examples: Week-4 groups discussed whether it was right for an African American father to drive his family to the South in the gold Cadillac during the 1960s

citation: Nagpal, M., Lin, T.-J., Kraatz, E., Kim, S., Ha, S. Y., & Glassman, M. (2025). Reciprocal interactions between teachers' instructional moves and students' social reasoning during collaborative small group discussions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09718-7
title: Seven-category teacher instructional move coding scheme for collaborative small-group discussions
description: The study adapted a coding scheme from Lin et al. (2015) classifying teacher talk into "seven research-informed teachers' instructional moves: high level prompting, low level prompting, modeling, specific praise, nonspecific praise, management, information provision," each with subcategories. High-level prompting asks for logical reasoning and perspective taking (e.g., reasons/evidence); low-level prompting asks for clarification, definitions, or repetition; modeling demonstrates good reasoning; specific praise reinforces particular cognitive or social strategy use; management regulates cognitive, participatory, and behavioral issues; information provision supplies facts or clarifications. Inter-coder reliability was Cohen's K = 0.72–0.74.
requirements: Two trained coders with reliability checks on 20% of transcripts and discussion to 100% agreement on ambiguous moves
constraints: The authors note the list of moves "is far from comprehensive"; moves were coded in a peer-led small-group context rather than teacher-centered whole-class instruction
target_learners: fifth-grade students in small-group discussion
target_learning_goals: teacher scaffolding of student reasoning and participation
examples: In Week-4 discussions, low-level prompting (221 turns) and high-level prompting (212 turns) were the most frequent moves; specific praise was rare (25 turns)

article_title: Investigating Students’ Collaborative Problem-Solving Interactions during Scaffolded and Non-Scaffolded Ill-Structured Tasks
citation: Parks, T., Shehab, S., & Mercier, E. (2026). Investigating Students' Collaborative Problem-Solving Interactions during Scaffolded and Non-Scaffolded Ill-Structured Tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09816-0
title: Include hard scaffolds in the design of ill-structured tasks for collaborative problem solving in higher education STEM classrooms
description: Hard scaffolds are static supports planned in advance (question prompts, checklists, concept maps) that direct students toward anticipated difficulties. This study shows that embedding explicit prompts for exploring, planning, and evaluating into ill-structured engineering tasks shifts group interactions toward a more balanced distribution of the four problem-solving processes and raises final solution quality. The authors conclude these findings "support the need to include hard scaffolds in the design of ill-structured tasks for collaborative problem solving in higher education STEM classrooms."
requirements: Tasks must be ill-structured and designed for face-to-face collaborative problem solving
Scaffolds must explicitly prompt underused processes (P1, P2, P4) rather than only solution attempts
constraints: Scaffold transfer to non-scaffolded tasks remains unresolved; the article notes scaffolding fading research suggests strategic removal is needed
Study did not control for perceived task difficulty or time between tasks
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in required introductory courses
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem-solving processes (exploring, planning, solving, evaluating) in ill-structured engineering tasks
examples: The scaffolded task included a marked area for constructing a free body diagram (P1), a prompt to plan the type of loading (P2), and explicit direction to evaluate the factor of safety (P4), presented on synchronized digital tablets
key_sources: Parks, T., Shehab, S., & Mercier, E. (2026). Investigating Students' Collaborative Problem-Solving Interactions during Scaffolded and Non-Scaffolded Ill-Structured Tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09816-0

article_title: Investigating Students’ Collaborative Problem-Solving Interactions during Scaffolded and Non-Scaffolded Ill-Structured Tasks
citation: Parks, T., Shehab, S., & Mercier, E. (2026). Investigating Students' Collaborative Problem-Solving Interactions during Scaffolded and Non-Scaffolded Ill-Structured Tasks. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09816-0
title: Four-process framework for collaborative problem solving in ill-structured STEM tasks (P1–P4)
description: The article operationalizes Ge and Land's four problem-solving processes for ill-structured engineering tasks: P1 (exploring and representing the problem, including joint FBD construction), P2 (planning how to solve, considering multiple approaches), P3 (attempting to solve with justifications), and P4 (evaluating the solution and considering alternatives). The framework holds that "Quality verbal interactions in collaborative problem solving can trigger these four essential processes that engage groups in more effective problem solving." An idealized distribution (0.5 P3, 0.25 P4, 0.125 each P1/P2) is proposed as a target for group engagement.
requirements: All four processes must be engaged for complete problem solving
Groups are the unit of analysis; verbal interactions are coded to identify process engagement
constraints: The optimal distribution of time across processes is unknown; the proposed ratios were iterated from prior-semester observations and literature
Novice designers tend to skip P1 and P2 and proceed directly to P3 without scaffolding
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students working in small groups on ill-structured tasks
target_learning_goals: engagement in all four collaborative problem-solving processes during ill-structured engineering tasks
examples: Turns were coded into P1–P4 categories (e.g., a P1 example: students discussing whether to account for the weight of the wood), and thematic episodes were used to construct video graphs of each group's progress

article_title: Exploring the association of student perceptions of science instruction and emotional engagement: The variance between grade level
citation: Xin Xia, Robert Tai. (2026). Exploring the association of student perceptions of science instruction and emotional engagement: The variance between grade level. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09800-8
title: Three-dimensional framework of student engagement (behavioral, emotional, cognitive)
description: The article adopts Fredricks et al.'s framework distinguishing three dimensions of engagement. "Behavioral engagement involves active participation in learning activities and extracurricular pursuits"; cognitive engagement reflects sustained mental effort toward deep understanding; and emotional engagement "encompasses feelings of connection to teachers, peers, and school, as well as a genuine interest in learning and enjoyment of problem-solving." The study focuses on the positive-affective dimension of emotional engagement, measured via enjoyment, interest, and desire to learn science, and distinguishes emotional engagement from interest as a relatively stable motivational state.
requirements: Measurement must distinguish emotional engagement from behavioral and cognitive dimensions and from the related but distinct construct of interest
constraints: The study operationalizes emotional engagement only through positive-affective indicators (enjoyment, interest, desire), excluding emotions such as frustration, confusion, or anxiety
target_learners: Students in grades 3–12 in science classes
target_learning_goals: Emotional engagement in science learning
examples: The study built a PCA composite of three positive-affective items (Desire, Favorite, Enjoy; Cronbach's alpha 0.881) to measure emotional engagement within this framework

citation: Xin Xia, Robert Tai. (2026). Exploring the association of student perceptions of science instruction and emotional engagement: The variance between grade level. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09800-8
title: Design science instruction that students perceive as interesting and understandable to foster positive emotional experiences, especially in transition grades
description: The article's findings support teachers preparing science lessons that students experience as interesting and as clear and understandable, because both perceptions are positively associated with emotional engagement. The authors state this "emphasizes the importance of advocating for teachers to prepare science classes in an interesting, organized, easy-to-understand way to foster positive emotional experiences in science classrooms." Because the grade-6 transition year shows the strongest sensitivity to perceived interestingness, targeted attention to instruction during transition grades is recommended. Understandable instruction means scaffolding complexity, not simplifying content.
requirements: Teachers' pedagogical training and practice in designing engaging, comprehensible science lessons
constraints: The study did not examine which specific instructional methods or components produce these perceptions; understandable does not imply reducing conceptual difficulty
target_learners: Students in grades 3–12, particularly students in transition grades such as grade 6
target_learning_goals: Sustaining emotional engagement and positive affect in science learning
examples: The multilevel analysis of 6,465 students found each unit increase in perceived interesting instruction associated with a 0.32 increase in emotional engagement, and the grade-6 interaction was the steepest among significant interactions

article_title: Cultivating science data literacy in K-16 science education through data practices: A systematic review
citation: Jina Kang, Chungsoo Na, Morgan Diederich, Hillary Swanson, Lili Yan. (2026). Cultivating science data literacy in K-16 science education through data practices: A systematic review. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09803-5
title: Science data literacy framework of seven core data practices with associated facets
description: The review conceptualizes science data literacy (SDL) as enacted through seven core data practices: "understanding problems, designing experiments, collecting data, cleaning data, analyzing data, and evaluating and disseminating results, along with their associated facets". Each dimension is a high-level category (e.g., Analyzing Data) with specific facets (e.g., applying statistics, visualizing data), developed via inductive and deductive coding informed by NGSS and GAISE frameworks. SDL is framed as a multifaceted, iterative process rather than a linear sequence.
requirements: Studies must involve students engaging directly with data—gathering existing data, producing their own data, or using provided datasets for analysis
constraints: Framework derived from 42 peer-reviewed empirical studies in science education published 2001–2023
target_learners: K-16 science students
target_learning_goals: science data literacy
scientific inquiry
data-driven reasoning
examples: The coding scheme clustered codes such as developing research questions under Understanding Problems and visualizing data under Analyzing Data, with inter-rater reliabilities reported per facet

title: Situate data practices in broader personal, social, and historical contexts rather than procedural tool engagement alone
description: The review argues, citing Wilkerson and Polman (2020) and Wise (2020), that science instruction should go beyond technical fluency with data tools. It reports that "instructional approaches often emphasize procedural engagement with data tools while neglecting opportunities for students to engage in deeper sense-making", and recommends situating data practices within environmental, social, political, and historical contexts and connecting them to students' personal lives to enhance engagement and agency.
requirements: Learning activities must move beyond procedural engagement with data tools to include critical interpretation of data and its broader implications
constraints: Grounded in the review's synthesis of prior scholarship rather than a tested intervention in this article

sense-making with data

citation: Dolmans, D., Schmidt, H. & Gijselaers, W. (1994). The relationship between student-generated learning issues and self-study in problem-based learning. Instructional Science: An International Journal of Learning and Cognition, 22(4), 251–267. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00891779
title: Topic Checklist (TOC) for measuring students' actual self-directed learning activities
description: The Topic Checklist is an instrument developed at the University of Limburg to measure what students actually study during self-directed learning. It "consists of a list of topics specifying the intended course content". Students rate on a five-point Likert scale how much time they spent studying each topic and their degree of mastery, allowing researchers to compare actual self-study with student-generated learning issues.
requirements: A list of topics specifying the intended course content must be available for the course being measured

target_learning_goals: Measuring self-directed learning activities and topic mastery in problem-based learning
examples: Students indicated on a five-point Likert scale how much time they had spent studying each topic and to what degree they had mastered it

article_title: Scientific reasoning abilities in kindergarten: dynamic assessment of the control of variables strategy
citation: Joep van der Graaf, Eliane Segers, Ludo Verhoeven. (2015). Scientific reasoning abilities in kindergarten: dynamic assessment of the control of variables strategy. Instr Sci 43:381–400. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9344-y
title: Dynamic hands-on ramp task for assessing kindergartners' CVS use across four variable-count levels
description: A dynamic assessment tool adapted from Chen and Klahr's ramp task in which children design hands-on experiments with two ramps, manipulating up to four variables: "ball type (i.e. weight), steepness of the slope (i.e. incline), starting gate (i.e. distance), and surface texture (i.e. friction)". Children start with one variable to set and advance one level when at least one experiment is designed correctly, up to Level 4 with all four variables. Feedback follows each experiment, and two scores are obtained: experiment correct score (max 16) and variable correct score (max 40).
requirements: An experimenter provides guidance and feedback after each experiment, explaining correct designs and demonstrating correct variable settings when the child's design is incorrect
Variables are explicitly introduced at the start, with children interacting with them and reproducing their names
constraints: Administered individually in a single session of about 45 minutes by a trained experimenter, not in ordinary classroom settings
target_learners: kindergartners aged 4 to 6 years
target_learning_goals: designing unconfounded multivariable experiments (control of variables strategy)
examples: Children designed a minimum of four experiments at Level 1 and could proceed to Level 4, where 14 of 21 children correctly designed at least one four-variable experiment

description: The article recommends that young children be given hands-on, multivariable experiments with guidance from a teacher or other students, within their zone of proximal development, before they can perform such experiments independently. citation: Mason, L., Boscolo, P., Tornatora, M. C., & Ronconi, L. (2012). Besides knowledge: a cross-sectional study on the relations between epistemic beliefs, achievement goals, self-beliefs, and achievement in science. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9210-0
title: A conceptual model integrating epistemic beliefs, achievement goals, self-beliefs, domain knowledge, and achievement in science
description: The article proposes and tests a path model in which domain-specific epistemic beliefs (development and justification of scientific knowledge) relate to achievement goals (mastery, performance-approach, performance-avoidance), which relate to self-efficacy and self-concept, which together with domain knowledge predict science achievement. The model was tested via SEM at three grade levels and showed good fit at all levels, though not all hypothesized paths were significant. The authors state that 'no causal relationships are established, which would require longitudinal or experimental designs.'

constraints: Cross-sectional design establishes no causal relationships
Not all hypothesized paths were statistically significant at any grade level

citation: Pieter Wouters, Fred Paas, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2008). Observational learning from animated models: effects of studying–practicing alternation and illusion of control on transfer. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9079-0
title: Augmented cognitive load theory incorporating learner expectations of control
description: The article builds on the augmented model of cognitive load theory proposed by Gerjets and Scheiter (2003), in which "learner goals and processing strategies moderate between the instructional design and the pattern of cognitive load". The authors argue that, if learner control is included in this augmented model, the study's results suggest that learners' expectations regarding that control should also be incorporated, since a mismatch between expected and actual control appears to impose extraneous load that wastes capacity otherwise available for genuine learning activities.
requirements: Learning environments that offer learner control must make actual control match the control learners are led to expect
constraints: The theoretical contribution is framed for situations, such as when learner expertise increases, in which a more prominent role for the learner seems appropriate

target_learning_goals: transferable problem-solving skill in probability calculation
examples: In the experiment, learners told they could choose problem order either could actually do so or received problems in a fixed order despite pressing freely named buttons

title: When providing learner control in a learning environment, ensure learners' expectations of control match the control they can actually exert
description: The article concludes that "merely providing learner control in a learning context without considering the expectations of learners regarding the control can have a negative effect on learning". Designers of responsive learning environments, which the authors note can be laborious and relatively expensive to develop, must take into account how they deal with the expectations of the learners who will use them, because a mismatch between expected and actual control wastes cognitive capacity on activities that do not contribute to learning.
requirements: The learning environment must be responsive to learner choices so that relevant changes in instruction result from learners' decisions

title: Computer-based learning environment with animated models and a dolphin pedagogical agent for probability calculation
description: A Flash MX learning environment consisting of a prior knowledge test, an instructional component and an assessment component, all user timed. Its animated models combine animations, textual explanations and a pedagogical agent implemented as a dolphin that moves across the screen to focus attention while explaining one of two problem-solving methods (individual events or counting) for eight probability problems in four categories. Each animated model lasted 120 s and was learner paced with pause and play buttons.
requirements: Learners must be given condition-specific information about the learning environment before the treatment, and all problems must be worked through
constraints: The instructional material covers probability calculation with more focus on procedural knowledge rather than cause-and-effect explanations
target_learners: pre-university secondary pupils (mean age 15.7 years)
target_learning_goals: understanding when to apply which probability procedure, including drawing order and replacement distinctions
examples: In the 'Checking mobiles' animated model the agent explains why a drawn mobile is not replaced, visualizing 'drawing without replacement'
key_sources: Pieter Wouters, Fred Paas, Jeroen J. G. van Merriënboer. (2008). Observational learning from animated models: effects of studying–practicing alternation and illusion of control on transfer. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9079-0

article_title: Learner control in animated multimedia instructions
citation: Huib K. Tabbers, Bastiaan de Koeijer. (2010). Learner control in animated multimedia instructions. Instructional Science, 38, 441–453. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9119-4
title: The interactivity principle: people learn better from multimedia instruction when they control both order and pace of the presentation
description: The interactivity principle, introduced by Mayer et al. (2003) within Mayer's theory of multimedia learning and cognitive load theory, states that "people learn better from a multimedia instruction when they are able to control both order and pace of the presentation". Its rationale is that segment-by-segment control reduces cognitive load and permits progressive mental model building, freeing resources for deeper understanding measured by transfer. This study tested the principle in its fullest form and replicated the transfer benefit, while questioning the load-reduction explanation.
requirements: Learners must be able to control both the order and the pace of the multimedia presentation, as in the Mayer et al. (2003) interactive versions.
constraints: The article argues the cognitive-load-reduction rationale is not sufficiently supported: Mayer and Chandler (2001) found no mental effort difference and system-controlled mental effort scores of 2.59 on a 1-7 scale indicated no overload.
The benefit may be confounded with increased time-on-task, which prior studies did not report.
target_learners: University students studying animated multimedia instructions
target_learning_goals: Deeper understanding (transfer) of causal-process explanations such as lightning formation
examples: The experiment gave learners stop/play buttons, a 'what happens here' narration button, and a navigation menu over 16 slides of a lightning-formation lesson.
key_sources: Huib K. Tabbers, Bastiaan de Koeijer. (2010). Learner control in animated multimedia instructions. Instructional Science, 38, 441–453. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9119-4

article_title: Do specific relevance instructions promote transfer appropriate processing?
citation: Matthew T. McCrudden. (2011). Do specific relevance instructions promote transfer appropriate processing? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9158-x
title: Give learners specific pre-reading relevance instructions to shape the quality of memory for text
description: This principle holds that telling learners, before reading, the specific questions their reading should address (e.g., what-questions or why-questions) directs processing toward those questions and improves later recall of matching information. The study found participants "did better on questions that had greater similarity to relevance instructions", consistent with transfer appropriate processing.
requirements: The relevance instruction must be given before reading as a pre-reading question or direction
constraints: The recall advantage applies to test questions similar to the instruction; control readers recalled equal amounts across question types
No reading-time differences were found on targeted sentences
target_learners: undergraduate readers
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
cued recall of text information
examples: Undergraduates were randomly assigned to what-question, why-question, or read-for-understanding pre-reading conditions before reading a text and completing cued recall
key_sources: Matthew T. McCrudden. (2011). Do specific relevance instructions promote transfer appropriate processing? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9158-x

title: Use VR-based teaching simulation to supplement or substitute for live classroom simulation in hosting participatory teaching development
description: The article recommends VR-based simulation as a complement or alternative to live classroom simulation for participatory training of student instructors. The authors state that "VR-based simulation can supplement and work as an alternative to the live classroom simulation to host participatory teaching development." The recommendation is qualified by the domain-specific knowledge results and the engagement limitation.
requirements: The VR simulation must provide domain-specific challenges and authentic environmental prompting to foster experiential and vicarious learning of teaching.
constraints: VR participants lacked mutual engagement in collaborative role-playing, so the format does not replicate the collaborative engagement of live simulation.

student instructors

class-teaching knowledge
teaching self-efficacy

In the study, 40 university teaching assistants were randomly assigned to this VR simulation or a live classroom simulation during a 4-h training session. The VR condition featured domain-specific challenges and authentic environmental prompting.

article_title: Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Jeroen Janssen, Gijsbert Erkens, Paul A. Kirschner, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9078-1
title: Representational guidance: different external representations express, make salient, and stimulate different information and cognitive processes
description: Representational guidance is the account that different external representations (ERs) afford different reasoning and learning because of what they can express and emphasize. The article states that "different ERs are capable of expressing different information (e.g., cause and effect relationships versus temporal relationships), make different information salient" and stimulate different cognitive processes. It uses this account to explain why the Graphical and Textual Debate-tools, which offer different guidance, produced different outcomes, and notes effects depend on circumstances such as the kind of task.
requirements: The representational format must be matched to the task and to the information it should make salient for the reasoning intended.
constraints: The article notes the effects of representational guidance "can differ depending on the speciﬁc circumstances (e.g., the kind of task to be performed)", so a given guidance may help one task and hurt another.
target_learners: secondary education students (eleventh grade)
target_learning_goals: argumentative reasoning and historical reasoning
constructing argumentative representations of a debate
examples: The study operationalized representational guidance as the difference between the GD-tool (distinguishing arguments, supports, refutations, visualizing support strength and progress) and the TD-tool (listwise, text-based).
key_sources: Jeroen Janssen, Gijsbert Erkens, Paul A. Kirschner, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9078-1

article_title: Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Jeroen Janssen, Gijsbert Erkens, Paul A. Kirschner, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9078-1
title: Debate-tool (Graphical and Textual versions) in the VCRI CSCL environment
description: The Debate-tool is an argumentation tool embedded in the VCRI groupware environment, used by student groups to co-construct a representation of the Martyrs-versus-Propaganda historical debate before co-authoring an essay. The article states: "Compared to the TD-tool, the GD-tool uses several visualization techniques to make information salient and to help students complete the representation more effectively and efﬁciently." The GD-tool distinguishes arguments, supports, and refutations, visualizes how well positions are supported, shows progress through the problem, and allows rating element importance; the TD-tool adds information in a listwise manner without these distinctions.
requirements: Students work in groups of two to four, each on a separate computer, with historical sources provided and a subsequent co-authored argumentative essay task.
constraints: The article notes the GD-tool's increased complexity might make it "less suited to support the linearization process that occurs when writers have to transfer the content of the ER to an essay."
target_learners: eleventh-grade secondary history students
target_learning_goals: analyzing and reconstructing a historical debate
formulating arguments, supports, and refutations
co-authoring an argumentative essay
examples: Groups used the tool during three 50-minute lessons within the VCRI environment, which also provided Chat, Sources, Cowriter, Diagrammer, Planner, and Participation tools.
key_sources: Jeroen Janssen, Gijsbert Erkens, Paul A. Kirschner, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9078-1

article_title: Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Jeroen Janssen, Gijsbert Erkens, Paul A. Kirschner, Gellof Kanselaar. (2008). Effects of representational guidance during computer-supported collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9078-1
title: Take representational guidance into account during instructional design because it affects group and individual performance
description: When designing CSCL or other activities in which learners co-construct external representations, the choice of representational format is a design variable with measurable consequences, not a neutral medium. The article concludes that "representational guidance has an impact on group and individual performance and should therefore be taken into account during instructional design." Designers should therefore deliberately select the representation (e.g., graphical versus textual argumentation formats) in light of the desired reasoning and products.
requirements: Designers must have access to or be able to create alternative representational formats so the guidance offered can be matched to task demands.
constraints: The article notes a given kind of guidance may be positive for one kind of task and negative for another, so the choice must be evaluated per task.
target_learners: secondary education students working in small groups
target_learning_goals: argumentation quality
representation construction
individual knowledge acquisition
examples: In the study, switching only the representational format of the Debate-tool while holding task, sources, and CSCL environment constant produced differences in representation quality, essay quality, and post-test performance.

article_title: Immediate and delayed effects of a modeling example on the application of principles of good feedback practice: a quasi-experimental study
citation: Floris M. van Blankenstein, Gabriela-Olivia Truțescu, Roeland M. van der Rijst, Nadira Saab. (2019). Immediate and delayed effects of a modeling example on the application of principles of good feedback practice: a quasi-experimental study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09482-5
title: Modeling example intervention: teacher demonstrates giving feed-back and feed-forward on good and bad presentation videos
description: In one lecture version, the teacher showed videos of a bad and a good presentation and, after each, demonstrated feed-back and feed-forward "first on the presentation and then on the presenter", spelled out in a script and based on the eight assessment criteria. In the comparison practice condition, students instead wrote their own feed-back and feed-forward on the same videos using a training form. Students were not instructed to give feed-back during the modeling demonstration.
requirements: A teacher script specifying the modeled feed-back and feed-forward based on the assessment criteria
Videos of a good and a bad presentation created for training purposes
constraints: Students observed the model but were not instructed to give feed-back and feed-forward at that moment
The effect on feedback skills did not persist one week later without reinforcement
target_learners: second-year bachelor students in pedagogical sciences
target_learning_goals: giving feedback on oral presentations
using assessment criteria in feedback
examples: Students observed a bad presentation (4:50 min) and a good presentation (6:59 min), after each of which the teacher presented feed-back and feed-forward from a script
