article_title: How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach
citation: Sarah von der Mühlen, Tobias Richter, Sebastian Schmid, Kirsten Berthold. (2019). How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach. Instructional Science 47:215–237. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9471-3
title: Toulmin model of argument structure
description: The article adopts Toulmin's (1958) model as the theoretical basis for its training, in which full-fledged informal arguments are deconstructed into functional components. According to the article, "full-fledged arguments contain a number of functional key components: a claim, reason(s) (or datum/data), a warrant, backing evidence, and a rebuttal". The warrant is treated as central for scientific literacy because it determines whether a conclusion is justified given the data, and warrants and backing are often implicit and hardest to identify.
requirements: Learners must be able to distinguish claim, datum, warrant, backing, and rebuttal within authentic argumentative texts
constraints: Warrants and backing evidence are often not explicitly stated in everyday arguments and must be inferred by the reader
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: comprehension of informal arguments in scientific texts
scientific literacy
examples: The article illustrates the model with an argument about eggs and cholesterol, labelling claim, datum, warrant, backing, and rebuttal sentences
key_sources: Sarah von der Mühlen, Tobias Richter, Sebastian Schmid, Kirsten Berthold. (2019). How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach. Instructional Science 47:215–237. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9471-3

article_title: How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach
citation: Sarah von der Mühlen, Tobias Richter, Sebastian Schmid, Kirsten Berthold. (2019). How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach. Instructional Science 47:215–237. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9471-3
title: Constructivist learning environment for argument structure training
description: A computerised training intervention conveying conceptual and procedural knowledge about the Toulmin model within a constructivist learning environment using Jonassen's (1999) cognitive modelling approach. It comprised a theoretical introduction with examples and learning goals, explanation prompts, two video tutorials modelling typical and atypical arguments with an expert model, twelve practice texts of varied argument types, and immediate feedback with a progress table. Participants could access theoretical information, tutorials, and notes at all stages.
requirements: Immediate feedback on each task
clear learning goals matching the task
varied argument types including atypical structures
accessible supporting information throughout
constraints: The intervention was tested with psychology students using German texts summarising empirical psychology articles
target_learners: university psychology students
target_learning_goals: identifying structural components of informal arguments and their relations
examples: Two video tutorials (03:41 and 03:58 min) in which an expert model read aloud and explained a typical and an atypical full-fledged argument stepwise, highlighting linguistic markers
key_sources: Sarah von der Mühlen, Tobias Richter, Sebastian Schmid, Kirsten Berthold. (2019). How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach. Instructional Science 47:215–237. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9471-3

article_title: How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach
citation: Sarah von der Mühlen, Tobias Richter, Sebastian Schmid, Kirsten Berthold. (2019). How to improve argumentation comprehension in university students: experimental test of a training approach. Instructional Science 47:215–237. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9471-3
title: Design argumentation interventions to match learners' ability level and include complex, atypical arguments
description: The article concludes that argumentation training should be integrated into curricula but tailored to learners' ability: benefits concentrated among high-achieving students and those with high pretest accuracy, while low performers showed no gains. It also argues interventions should use "a variety of argument types, including arguments with a more typical and arguments with a less typical structure", since training effects emerged specifically for warrants and atypical full-fledged arguments rather than for simple three-component arguments.
requirements: Training materials must include both typical and atypical, complex and less complex arguments
learners' prior ability should be assessed and matched
constraints: Effects were limited to posttest and did not persist at the 4-week follow-up; low-performing students did not benefit
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: argument structure knowledge
argument comprehension
examples: In the experiment, only students 1 SD above the mean in study performance clearly outperformed controls after argument structure training, while low performers did not differ from the speed-reading group

article_title: Sequential patterns of challenges and socially shared regulation of learning: a comparison of pre-service and in-service teachers’ collaborative learning
citation: Faisal Channa, Piia Näykki, Päivi Häkkinen, Kristóf Fenyvesi, Takumi Yada. (2026). Sequential patterns of challenges and socially shared regulation of learning: a comparison of pre-service and in-service teachers’ collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09818-y
title: Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) as an emergent, interactionally constructed group process shaped by professional trajectories
description: The study is grounded in the SSRL framework, in which "SSRL, by contrast, is a fully collaborative process in which group members jointly regulate their learning by setting shared goals, monitoring group progress and collectively managing sociocognitive, socioemotional and motivational aspects of learning". SSRL is distinguished from individual self-regulated learning and from co-regulated learning, and is treated as an emergent property of collaboration rather than a stable individual trait. The article further conceptualises professional experience as a contextual condition shaping how regulation is enacted and sequenced, explicitly not as a causal variable determining outcomes.
requirements: All group members must contribute actively to shared regulatory efforts rather than relying on a single dominant group member
constraints: The study does not assume a causal relationship between professional experience and regulatory effectiveness; differences reflect orientations, not superiority
target_learners: pre-service teachers
in-service teachers in professional development
target_learning_goals: collaborative regulation of sociocognitive, socioemotional and motivational aspects of group learning
examples: 22 triads of teachers regulated collaborative Labster simulation tasks while video-recorded, and their coded interactions were modelled as sequential process maps
key_sources: Faisal Channa, Piia Näykki, Päivi Häkkinen, Kristóf Fenyvesi, Takumi Yada. (2026). Sequential patterns of challenges and socially shared regulation of learning: a comparison of pre-service and in-service teachers’ collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09818-y

article_title: Sequential patterns of challenges and socially shared regulation of learning: a comparison of pre-service and in-service teachers’ collaborative learning
citation: Faisal Channa, Piia Näykki, Päivi Häkkinen, Kristóf Fenyvesi, Takumi Yada. (2026). Sequential patterns of challenges and socially shared regulation of learning: a comparison of pre-service and in-service teachers’ collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09818-y
title: Combined fine-grained video coding and process mining method for analysing sequential SSRL patterns
description: The article introduces a methodological contribution that combines fine-grained video analysis with process mining to study sequential patterns linking challenges and collaborative regulatory activities. Coded event logs were analysed with the BupaR package in R, producing process models in which "boxes represent challenge and regulatory categories, with numbers indicating their frequency of occurrence" and arrows depict sequential transitions. Unlike coarse-grained or aggregated measures, this method captures micro-level events as they occur in real-time collaborative interaction, offering a structured framework for analysing sequential interactional patterns in large-scale educational interaction data.
requirements: Coding restricted strictly to the interactional level and based on verbally expressed utterances, with inter-rater reliability checked via Cohen’s kappa on a subset of groups
constraints: Aggregated process models represent recurring or dominant sequential patterns rather than any single group’s complete trajectory; transitions indicate temporal proximity, not causal influence
target_learners: researchers and educators analysing collaborative learning processes
target_learning_goals: understanding how groups regulate sociocognitive, socioemotional and motivational challenges over time
examples: 25.7 h of video from 22 triads were coded into 2,047 in-service and 2,238 pre-service events and visualised as process models in Figs. 6 and 7

article_title: CID: a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs
citation: Katharina Loibl · Timo Leuders · Inga Glogger-Frey · Nikol Rummel. (2025). CID: a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09665-9
title: CID framework linking knowledge, learning, and instruction levels across phases of composite instructional designs
description: The CID framework extends the knowledge–learning–instruction approach to multi-phase designs. As the authors state, it is "a framework for conductin g cognitive analyses of composite instructional designs (CID) that links the three levels – (K) knowledge components, (L) learning processes, and (I) instructional designs". Its core element is intermediate knowledge (K1) generated by the first phase, which shapes learning processes in the second phase; modelling prior knowledge (K0) additionally allows explanation of aptitude-treatment-interactions such as expertise-reversal effects.
requirements: Specification of the framework elements (K0, K1, K2, L1, L2, I1, I2) for a concrete instructional design to derive testable predictions
constraints: The general framework is, in the authors' words citing Anderson, "insufficiently specified to enable predictions to be derived" until elements are specified per design
The analyses focus primarily on cognitive dimensions; affective-motivational states are modelled only in parallel and rarely considered so far
target_learners: All learners in multi-phase instructional settings
target_learning_goals: Understanding mechanisms of composite instructional designs across phases
examples: Applied to Rau et al. (2017), Loibl and Rummel (2014), and Glogger-Frey et al. (2015, 2017) to explain preparatory, order, and contradictory effects
key_sources: Katharina Loibl · Timo Leuders · Inga Glogger-Frey · Nikol Rummel. (2025). CID: a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09665-9

article_title: CID: a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs
citation: Katharina Loibl · Timo Leuders · Inga Glogger-Frey · Nikol Rummel. (2025). CID: a framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09665-9
title: Typology of intermediate-knowledge types and their interplay with second-phase learning processes
description: The article distinguishes types of intermediate knowledge (K1) generated in the first phase: partial or erroneous knowledge serving integration in the second phase (partial knowledge integrated into target knowledge, erroneous knowledge contributing via refutation, specific negative knowledge focusing on relevant aspects), and instrumental knowledge that supports rather than becomes target knowledge (situational knowledge as a concrete anchor, unspecific negative knowledge as global awareness of knowledge gaps generating motivation, and supportive knowledge such as strategies or fluency freeing cognitive capacity). As illustrated in Fig. 5, these types "contribute differently to the learning processes (L2) initiated by the instructional design of the second phase".
requirements: Manipulating and/or measuring the different types of intermediate knowledge separately, wherever possible, to understand composite-design mechanisms
constraints: The framework analysis focuses primarily on cognitive dimensions; affective-motivational states are treated only in parallel
target_learners: Learners in multi-phase instructional designs
target_learning_goals: Explaining how first-phase outcomes prepare learning from subsequent instruction
examples: Used to explain the contradictory Glogger-Frey et al. (2015 vs. 2017) findings via differences in the quality of intermediate knowledge

article_title: Can failure be made productive also in Bayesian reasoning? A conceptual replication study
citation: Loibl, K., & Leuders, T. (2024). Can failure be made productive also in Bayesian reasoning? A conceptual replication study. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09670-y
title: CID framework for the cognitive analysis of composite instructional designs
description: The CID framework (cognitive analyses of composite instructional designs) is presented as "a useful means to systematically describe the elements of such an instructional design and its theoretical assumptions" for multi-phase designs like PS-I. It requires theoretical specification on the levels of knowledge, learning, and instruction, and introduces the notion of intermediate knowledge acquired in the first phase, which can alter learning processes in the second phase and thereby affect outcomes. The article uses it to align the replication's materials and mechanisms with the original study.
requirements: A theoretical specification on the levels of knowledge, learning, and instruction for each phase of the composite design
constraints: Designed for composite (multi-phase) instructional designs, extending single-phase frameworks such as KLI
target_learners: students in instructional-design research, e.g., undergraduate teacher students
target_learning_goals: conceptual and procedural knowledge of a target concept such as Bayesian reasoning or variance
examples: The article analyzes PS-I and I-PS sequences with the CID framework in Fig. 1 and uses it to structure the comparison of the original and replication studies (Tables 1 and 2)

article_title: Learning about multivariable causality with interactive simulations: exploration before instruction may hurt immediate gains but benefits transfer
citation: Saba, J., Kapur, M., & Roll, I. (2025). Learning about multivariable causality with interactive simulations: exploration before instruction may hurt immediate gains but benefits transfer. Instructional Science, 53, 1603–1632. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09726-7
title: Composite Instructional Design (CID) framework: intermediate knowledge links exploration phases to subsequent instruction
description: The CID framework, introduced by Loibl et al. (2024), provides "a structured lens for interpreting how the sequence of instructional phases shapes the intermediate knowledge students acquire during exploration and impacts their cognitive processes during instruction". Its central construct is intermediate knowledge — the state of knowledge after the initial phase — which can include target-knowledge components, activated prior knowledge, erroneous knowledge requiring refutation, knowledge-gap awareness, and procedural knowledge. The framework holds that the effectiveness of subsequent direct instruction depends heavily on the intermediate knowledge and cognitive states fostered during prior exploration. This study uses CID to interpret Exploration-first versus Instruction-first sequences for MVC learning.
requirements: Instructional designs that combine multiple phases with different pedagogies and goals, so that an initial phase can foster intermediate knowledge that the subsequent phase builds on
constraints: The framework addresses designs combining multiple instructional phases; it was applied in this study to simulation-based exploration plus plenary instruction with undergraduates learning MVC
target_learners: undergraduate students in science and engineering programs
target_learning_goals: multivariable causality strategy and reasoning
scientific inquiry skills
examples: The study interpreted Exploration-first exploration as fostering intermediate knowledge (prior-knowledge activation and knowledge-gap awareness) that the subsequent instruction phase built on through structured discussion and guided reflection
key_sources: Saba, J., Kapur, M., & Roll, I. (2025). Learning about multivariable causality with interactive simulations: exploration before instruction may hurt immediate gains but benefits transfer. Instructional Science, 53, 1603–1632. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09726-7

article_title: Learning about multivariable causality with interactive simulations: exploration before instruction may hurt immediate gains but benefits transfer
citation: Saba, J., Kapur, M., & Roll, I. (2025). Learning about multivariable causality with interactive simulations: exploration before instruction may hurt immediate gains but benefits transfer. Instructional Science, 53, 1603–1632. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09726-7
title: Mechanistic reasoning as a four-component framework underlying MVC reasoning assessment
description: Drawing on Krist et al. (2019), the article treats mechanistic reasoning as "a crosscutting form of thinking across multiple scientific practices that guides students’ decision-making, evaluation, and reflection as they build and test scientific ideas". It comprises four components: considering events at a scalar level below the observed phenomenon; identifying and characterizing relevant elements at that lower level; coordinating these elements over space and/or time into chains of cause and effect; and examining how these elements give rise to the observed phenomenon. The study adapted this framework into a bottom-up coding scheme (Describing, Unpacking, Linking) for students' open-ended MVC reasoning responses.
requirements: Responses must be coded bottom-up against the Describing/Unpacking/Linking scheme, accounting for the number of factors addressed in students’ reasoning
constraints: The framework was applied in this study to open-ended written responses about virus spread and predation simulations with undergraduate participants
target_learners: undergraduate students in science and engineering programs
target_learning_goals: multivariable causality reasoning
mechanistic reasoning about complex phenomena
examples: The coding scheme scored responses from Non (no description or unpacking) through combinations such as U3L, unpacking three factors and linking them to an observed outcome

article_title: Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour
citation: Anders Bouwer, Bert Bredeweg. (2010). Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour. Instr Sci 38:173–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9083-4
title: VISIGARP: a domain-independent tool generating interactive diagrams of GARP qualitative simulations
description: VISIGARP is a tool implemented in SWI-PROLOG/XPCE that "provide[s] users (i.e. students) with automatically generated diagrams to interactively access information from GARP simulations". It generates several diagram types — state–transition graph, quantity value history, dependencies/causal model, entity–relations — built from a domain-independent visual vocabulary of shapes, arrows, indentation and meaningful vertical positioning. Users select scenarios, run or constrain simulations, and inspect states, transitions and causal dependencies interactively.
requirements: A GARP qualitative simulation (scenario plus model-fragment library) whose output VISIGARP renders as diagrams
constraints: The article notes some generated diagrams for the complex scenario were quite complex and cluttered, with graphical objects overlapping
target_learners: first-year university students without prior qualitative-reasoning experience
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of system behaviour
interpreting causal dependencies and state transitions in qualitative simulations
examples: In the evaluation, students used VISIGARP to answer 27 questions across a one-population scenario and a Cerrado Succession Hypothesis scenario, using zoom buttons on average 12 times per person

article_title: Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour
citation: Anders Bouwer, Bert Bredeweg. (2010). Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour. Instr Sci 38:173–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9083-4
title: GARP framework for qualitative reasoning and modelling: model fragments and scenarios simulated into state–transition graphs
description: GARP is a framework for qualitative reasoning and modelling in which "Given a scenario (a description of a particular situation) and a library of model fragments (the generic domain knowledge) as input, the simulation engine produces a state–transition graph as output". Model fragments come in categories (description views, assumptions, process and agent fragments, composition views), each with conditions and consequences; the engine recursively applies applicable fragments to infer states and transitions, including branches when outcomes are underdetermined. Input and output are in predicate logic (Prolog) format, which the article notes is challenging for humans to read.
requirements: A scenario describing system structure and initial quantity values
a library of model fragments encoding generic domain knowledge
constraints: The predicate logic format is challenging for humans to read and makes overview difficult for novices, motivating VISIGARP
target_learners: ecology students
future decision makers in sustainable development
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of system behaviour
explaining and predicting system behaviour qualitatively
examples: The Cerrado domain library contains 79 model fragments covering processes such as natality, mortality, immigration, emigration and interaction effects like predator–prey and amensalism

article_title: Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour
citation: Anders Bouwer, Bert Bredeweg. (2010). Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour. Instr Sci 38:173–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9083-4
title: Guiding principles for a domain-independent diagrammatic vocabulary for model inspection
description: To design VISIGARP's visualizations the authors laid down guiding principles, e.g. "Information related to a speciﬁc entity is displayed within the visual element representing that entity, using the container-metaphor as much as possible" and displaying relationships as separate connecting elements, showing context-dependent information within its context, using labelled links to distinguish multiple relationship types, and offering display toggles when multiple information types are combined. The approach deliberately avoids domain-specific symbols to remain usable across domains and drawable by hand.
requirements: Visual primitives (shapes, arrows, indentation, meaningful space) combined into views supporting specific reasoning tasks
constraints: The article notes the no-rotation rule for text can place arrows against the normal reading direction, causing readability problems such as in diagrams test question 6
target_learners: novice learners inspecting qualitative simulations
target_learning_goals: interpreting model structure, states, and causal dependencies from diagrams
examples: States are shown as numbered circles, entities as labelled boxes, quantities as round-edged boxes with vertically ordered quantity spaces, and derivatives as small black triangles or circles

article_title: Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour
citation: Anders Bouwer, Bert Bredeweg. (2010). Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour. Instr Sci 38:173–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9083-4
title: Cerrado Succession Hypothesis (CSH) qualitative model library for Brazilian Cerrado ecology
description: The CSH model is a GARP model library for the Brazilian Cerrado ecosystem, whose goal is "to provide insight in the causal mechanisms involved in the development and management of the Cerrado ecosystem". "The library for the Cerrado domain contains 79 model fragments", covering description views (population concepts), assumptions (open/closed populations, immigration flows), process fragments (natality, mortality, emigration, immigration, colonization), agent fragments (fire management), and composition views for interactions and vegetational states. Scenarios range from single-population cases to the full three-population succession simulation.
requirements: The GARP simulation engine and a scenario describing initial structure and values
constraints: Scenarios were sequenced from simple to complex, which the authors regard as a curriculum of Cerrado ecology knowledge
target_learners: ecology students
future decision makers in sustainable development
target_learning_goals: explaining vegetation succession and population dynamics in the Cerrado
understanding causal effects of fire management
examples: The evaluation used two scenarios: a simple one-population scenario (8 states, 8 quantities, 12 dependencies) and a complex Cerrado Succession Hypothesis scenario (19 states, 32 quantities, 127 dependencies)

article_title: How do higher education students regulate their learning with video modeling examples, worked examples, and practice problems?
citation: Milou van Harsel, Vincent Hoogerheide, Eva Janssen, Peter Verkoeijen, Tamara van Gog. (2022). How do higher education students regulate their learning with video modeling examples, worked examples, and practice problems? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09589-2
title: Instructional design principles for self-regulated example-based learning at multiple complexity levels
description: The article organizes its analysis around five instructional design principles for novices acquiring problem-solving skills from examples and problems: the example-based-learning-principle (studying several examples, possibly alternated with problems, is more effective and efficient than problem solving only), the example-first-principle (start with an example), the lowest-level-first-principle and simple-to-complex-principle (start at the lowest complexity level and build up gradually), and the start-each-level-with-example-principle (start each new complexity level with example study). These principles, drawn from the 4C/ID model and example-based learning research, were used as a scoring rubric against which students' spontaneous task selections were evaluated.
requirements: Learners must be novices with little prior knowledge for whom the principles prescribe optimal support and complexity
A task database offering examples and problems at multiple complexity levels so that selection behavior can be scored against the principles
constraints: The expertise reversal effect limits the example-based-learning and example-first principles: learners do not need instructional support from examples anymore when their knowledge increases, and from that point onwards they learn more from solving problems than from example study
target_learners: Novice higher education students acquiring problem-solving skills
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of well-defined problem-solving procedures, such as mathematical integration methods
examples: In the study, each participant's six self-selected tasks were scored 0, 0.5, or 1 point per principle (maximum 5 points; ICC 0.96) to quantify adherence

article_title: Successfully carrying out complex learning-tasks through guiding teams’ qualitative and quantitative reasoning
citation: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. Janssen, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2012). Successfully carrying out complex learning-tasks through guiding teams' qualitative and quantitative reasoning. Instr Sci 40:623–643. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9185-2
title: Representational scripting: sequencing part-tasks and matching each tool's ontology to part-task demands
description: Representational scripting integrates collaboration scripts with representational tools so that the problem-solving process is sequenced into part-tasks whose demands are made explicit, and each tool's representational guidance is congruent with those demands. According to the article, a script is "a set of instructions regarding to how the group members should interact, how they should collaborate and how they should solve the problem". A tool's ontology (its objects, relations and combination rules) makes certain concepts and interrelationships salient: less expressive, first-order ontologies support qualitative causal inference-making, while more expressive, second-order ontologies support quantitative inference-making. In the study, a causal tool was matched to the problem–solution phase and a simulation tool to the solution–evaluation phase.
requirements: A learning-task analysis to determine the sequence and demands of the part-tasks so that part-task congruent tools can be developed
constraints: The article states the design principles do not automatically apply to other domains, learning tasks and settings; effects depend on the characteristics of the learning task and the involved knowledge domains
target_learners: secondary-school students (novices) working on complex learning tasks in teams
target_learning_goals: acquiring a well-developed qualitative and quantitative understanding of a domain and applying it to solve complex problems
examples: In the study, teams carried out a business-economics advisory task in the VCRI CSCL environment, using a causal representational tool in the problem–solution phase and a simulation tool in the solution–evaluation phase
key_sources: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. Janssen, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2012). Successfully carrying out complex learning-tasks through guiding teams' qualitative and quantitative reasoning. Instr Sci 40:623–643. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9185-2

article_title: Successfully carrying out complex learning-tasks through guiding teams’ qualitative and quantitative reasoning
citation: B. Slof, G. Erkens, P. A. Kirschner, J. Janssen, J. G. M. Jaspers. (2012). Successfully carrying out complex learning-tasks through guiding teams' qualitative and quantitative reasoning. Instr Sci 40:623–643. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9185-2
title: Introduce qualitative representations before quantitative ones and let learners construct representations congruent with the tasks to be carried out
description: The article derives two design principles from its findings: to support acquisition of domain understanding, instruction should gradually increase complexity by "introducing qualitative representations before quantitative ones"; and to support application of that understanding, "instruction should allow for constructing representations congruent with the tasks to be carried out". Together these prescribe sequencing tools so each phase's representational guidance matches its part-task demands.
requirements: Educators and instructional designers should conduct a learning-task analysis to gain insight into the specifics of the learning tasks before designing tools or environments
constraints: The authors state there are multiple reasons to assume these design principles do not automatically apply to other domains, learning tasks and settings
target_learners: secondary-school students learning business-economics
target_learning_goals: complex learning-task performance through qualitative and quantitative domain reasoning
examples: Teams in the matched causal-simulation condition received a causal tool for defining the problem and proposing solutions, then a simulation tool for evaluating solutions, and outperformed the other conditions

article_title: Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared
citation: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4
title: Variation theory of learning: learning is discernment of critical aspects through experienced variation
description: Variation theory holds that "learning primarily involves a qualitative change in the way we experience something in the world around us", and that experiencing a phenomenon in a particular way requires that certain "critical aspects" be discerned simultaneously. Its core mechanism is that "the necessary condition for discernment is 'experienced variation' on the part of the learner": to discern an aspect such as colour, a learner must experience at least two different values of it while other aspects are kept invariant. In learning study, teachers use the theory to design patterns of variation and invariance that enable students to discern the critical aspects of the object of learning.
requirements: Teachers must identify the critical aspects of the object of learning that students must discern
The lesson must enact a pattern in which the targeted aspect varies while other aspects are kept invariant
constraints: The article notes a gap can exist between theory and practice, revealed only by carefully studying what happened in the lesson
target_learners: primary and secondary school students
target_learning_goals: discerning critical aspects of curricular objects of learning such as fractions and reaction rates
examples: In the mathematics case, the teacher varied the denominator while keeping the numerator invariant, then contrasted equal and unequal splits of a pizza
key_sources: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4

article_title: Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared
citation: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4
title: The learning study model: lesson study underpinned by an explicit learning theory, organised around intended, enacted and lived objects of learning
description: The learning study approach is "essentially a kind of lesson study with an explicit learning theory—the variation theory of learning". Groups of teachers teaching the same subject at the same level examine their own practice around the question of how an object of learning 'X' can be taught so students see 'X' in the intended way. Each study collects evidence on three questions: the intended object of learning (what students should learn, diagnosed via interviews and pre-tests), the enacted object of learning (what actually happens in the lesson, observed or videoed), and the lived object of learning (what students actually learned, via post-lesson interviews and pre/post-test comparison).
requirements: Teachers attend a course of no less than 12 h on the learning study approach and variation theory before participating
The object of learning is chosen by negotiation as worthwhile, central to the curriculum, and typically difficult for students
constraints: The article does not claim learning studies are generally superior to teachers' normal classroom teaching methods
target_learners: school teachers conducting collaborative professional development
target_learning_goals: pedagogical content knowledge about how best to teach a chosen object of learning
examples: Two Hong Kong cases: a primary four mathematics study run as a quasi-experiment, and a secondary four chemistry study run in action research cycles
key_sources: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4

article_title: Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared
citation: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4
title: Three types of variation structure learning study lesson planning: variation in students' ways of seeing, teachers' ways of seeing, and variation as a design principle
description: Learning study participants draw on three spelt-out types of variation when planning lessons. V1 is "Variation in students' ways of seeing the object of learning": teachers use phenomenographic insight that students understand a phenomenon in a limited number of qualitatively different ways, treating individual differences as a resource rather than an obstacle. V2 is "Variation in teachers' ways of seeing and dealing with the object of learning": sharing tacit professional knowledge across the group. V3 is "Using variation as a guiding principle of pedagogical design": consciously designing which aspects vary and which stay invariant so students discern the critical aspects.
requirements: A carefully defined object of learning with identified critical aspects
Diagnostic information on students' prior ways of understanding, e.g. via pre-tests and interviews
target_learners: primary and secondary school students
target_learning_goals: discernment of critical aspects of the object of learning
examples: In the mathematics case, pre-test answers were used to identify critical aspects before planning the research lesson

article_title: Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared
citation: Ming Fai Pang, Lo Mun Ling. (2011). Learning study: helping teachers to use theory, develop professionally, and produce new knowledge to be shared. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9191-4
title: Give lesson study an explicit learning theory: variation theory adds explanatory and predictive power for designing and evaluating research lessons
description: The article argues that lesson study groups lacking "a common, explicit conceptual framework" struggle to develop tasks that reveal student thinking; adding variation theory supplies guiding principles for pedagogical design, lesson analysis and evaluation. The authors claim variation theory "has both explanatory and predictive power": analysis of the enacted pattern of variation predicted the comparison group's poor equal-shares understanding and explained class 4A's failure, while guiding the cycle 2 redesign that improved outcomes.
requirements: Teachers trained in the theory (a course of no less than 12 h)
Careful study of lesson enactment to check whether the intended pattern of variation was actually experienced by students
constraints: The authors do not argue research lessons from learning studies are perfect or that learning studies are generally superior to normal classroom teaching; other theories could be used
target_learners: teachers in professional development groups
target_learning_goals: using learning theory to design, analyse and improve research lessons
examples: In the comparison group, the teacher's unguided pattern of variation led students to discern that the fraction depends on the numerator, something unintended

article_title: Problem-solving before instruction for learning linear algebra in university mathematics
citation: Baumgartner, V., Daguati, S., Trninic, D., Akveld, M., Caspar, A., Hungerbühler, N., Kapur, M. (2025). Problem-solving before instruction for learning linear algebra in university mathematics. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09709-8
title: Productive failure as a two-phase design with four core learning mechanisms, with PS-I as a subset of preparation for future learning
description: The article describes productive failure (PF) as "a two-phase learning design" comprising a problem-solving phase and an instruction phase, embodying four core learning mechanisms: activation and differentiation of prior knowledge, attention to critical features, explanation and elaboration, and organisation and assembly. It situates PS-I and PF within a family of reversed-order designs in which "PS-I learning designs are a subset of PFL and PF learning designs are in turn a subset of PS-I designs". The CID framework is used to explain how intermediate knowledge from Phase 1 serves as prior knowledge for Phase 2.
requirements: Phase 1 problems must activate and differentiate prior knowledge and allow recognition of critical features so that Phase 2 elaboration and assembly can consolidate discoveries
constraints: If the problem-solving materials fail to trigger activation and critical-feature recognition, the second-phase mechanisms do not have their desired effects
target_learners: university students in introductory mathematics and STEM courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of targeted mathematical concepts
transfer
examples: The study's ten preparatory exercise sheets were designed to trigger activation of prior knowledge and recognition of critical features, e.g. seven contrasting cases of linear systems of equations before instruction on the rank of matrices

article_title: How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language
citation: Palladino, P., Trotta, E., Bonvino, A., Carlucci, L., & Cottini, M. (2025). How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09414-4
title: MASRL and control-value theory as a joint framework for metacognition and achievement emotions in early L2 learning
description: The study grounds its design in two complementary models: Efklides' metacognitive and affective model of self-regulated learning (MASRL) for metacognitive competence, and Pekrun's control-value theory (CVT) for achievement emotions. The article states: "our study refers to the MASRL model by Efklides for metacognitive competence and the CVT by Pekrun for achievement emotions." Both models treat task characteristics via subjective experiences at the person level, with task monitoring information gaining importance at the Task × Person level. CVT holds that achievement emotions arise from perceived controllability and value, while MASRL explains how metacognitive, motivational and affective competence interact for self-regulated learning.
requirements: Both models focus on learning and evaluate task characteristics on the basis of students' subjective experiences, so tasks must be meaningful enough to trigger control and value appraisals.
constraints: The MASRL model does not explicitly explain the role of the distal environment, unlike CVT, which the authors note as a difference between the models.
target_learners: primary school children (grades 2–3, ages 6–9) learning English as a second language
target_learning_goals: second language (English) vocabulary acquisition
self-regulated learning
examples: The study measured procedural metacognition (confidence judgments, relative monitoring accuracy, withdrawal/maintenance control) alongside enjoyment, anxiety and boredom on an English vocabulary test at two time points.
key_sources: Palladino, P., Trotta, E., Bonvino, A., Carlucci, L., & Cottini, M. (2025). How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09414-4

article_title: How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language
citation: Palladino, P., Trotta, E., Bonvino, A., Carlucci, L., & Cottini, M. (2025). How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09414-4
title: AEQ-ES adapted to English as L2 for primary school children
description: An adaptation of the Italian version of the Achievement Emotion Questionnaire–Elementary School (AEQ-ES; Lichtenfeld et al., 2012; Raccanello et al., 2019) assessing enjoyment, anxiety and boredom toward learning English as L2 across lessons, homework and tests. The questionnaire "is composed of a series of 32 statements with responses on a Likert scale ranging from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very much)", accompanied by gender-adapted faces. Only mathematics-domain terms were replaced with English-language terms, preserving the original item structure; the adapted scale showed an internal reliability of α = 0.78.
requirements: Items use faces representing emotional intensity and children answer individually in class, with experimenter help available for items they do not understand.
constraints: Reliability of the original Italian mathematics version ranged between 0.61 and 0.93 in Omega values; the English adaptation was validated only in this study's sample.
target_learners: primary school children (grades 2–3)
target_learning_goals: measuring achievement emotions (enjoyment, anxiety, boredom) related to learning English as a second language
examples: Administered collectively in classrooms with no time limit at T0 and T1 in the present study.

article_title: How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language
citation: Palladino, P., Trotta, E., Bonvino, A., Carlucci, L., & Cottini, M. (2025). How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09414-4
title: Attend to metacognitive and emotional variables from the earliest stages of L2 instruction
description: Because metacognitive monitoring and control and achievement emotions predict L2 vocabulary learning from the very beginning of instruction, teachers of early L2 learning should give these variables explicit attention. The authors argue that understanding "the interplay between metacognition and emotions in learning may lead to a better perspective on school L2 learning of significant variables", and that these variables "may deserve better attention from teachers since they substantially contribute to the SRL process". The principle applies from the first stages of L2 learning in primary school.
requirements: Teachers need ways to observe or assess children's confidence judgments, control of performance, and boredom during L2 lessons.
constraints: The supporting evidence is a short-term longitudinal correlational study; the authors note longer-term studies are needed to trace developmental changes in L2 learning.
target_learners: primary school children beginning second language learning
target_learning_goals: English vocabulary acquisition
self-regulated learning in L2
examples: The study assessed 305 Italian 2nd and 3rd graders twice within one school year, showing metacognition and boredom predicted vocabulary growth from the earliest stage.

article_title: Measures of relative metacognitive accuracy are confounded with task performance in tasks that permit guessing
citation: Vuorre, M., & Metcalfe, J. (2021). Measures of relative metacognitive accuracy are confounded with task performance in tasks that permit guessing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09257-1
title: Meta-d' as a performance-normalized measure of metacognitive efficiency
description: Meta-d' is a signal detection theoretic measure of relative metacognitive accuracy, attributed in the article to Maniscalco and Lau (2012), that explicitly models the relation between primary task performance and metacognition. The article notes it "allows normalizing metacognitive performance with primary task performance", yielding a metacognitive "efficiency" measure (meta-d'/d') that is not inherently constrained by primary task performance or bias. The article presents it as an otherwise attractive measure whose general implication matches its own results: in certain tasks, resolution metrics are inherently related to performance.
requirements: The primary task must be conducted in a manner analogous to a signal detection task, such as 2AFC, as the article states.
constraints: Not suitable as a measure of metacognition in free-response tasks, or, in its current implementation, multiple-choice tasks where the number of choice alternatives exceeds 2.
target_learners: adults completing recognition or general-information tasks in laboratory or online experiments
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of metacognitive resolution independent of task performance
examples: The article discusses meta-d' in its conclusions as an existing measure whose approach aligns with its own demonstration of the guessing confound.

article_title: Analyzing multimodal data to understand medical trainees' regulation strategies and physiological responses in high- fidelity medical simulation scenarios
citation: Moreno, M., Patino Melo, L., Grewal, K., Matin, N., Azher, S., & Harley, J.M. (2024). Analyzing Multimodal Data to Understand Medical Trainees' Regulation Strategies and Physiological Responses in High-Fidelity Medical Simulation Scenarios. Metacognition and Learning, 19, 1161–1213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09403-z
title: A team regulation-based framework for high-fidelity medical simulation linking COPES phases, SSRL strategies and physiological activation across scenario segments
description: The article advances a team regulation-based framework in which the regulatory needs of individuals and teams change across the 'Beginning', 'Escalation' and 'Peak' segments of a CRM simulation, and rising physiological activation coincides with increased team-regulated learning strategies. The authors state that "the regulatory needs of individuals and teams change throughout different sections of a simulation to meet the contextual needs of simulated medical care", and that the COPES model (Winne & Hadwin, 1998) can be used with a coding scheme to describe team members' regulation strategies in theory-driven terms.
requirements: Multimodal data channels (behavioral, SRL/SSRL codes, and EDA) aligned to common time points so regulation strategies and physiological responses can be compared across segments
constraints: Findings come from ten CRM simulations with 29 residents at one North American university; simulations were 10–13 minutes long and ended at the 'Peak' without a resolution segment
target_learners: 1st to 3rd year medical residents in team-based simulation training
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning and socially-shared regulation of team-based clinical decision making and crisis resource management
examples: The authors map Execution codes to the COPES Performance phase and Facilitation codes to its monitoring and controlling facets within the coded simulation segments

article_title: Analyzing multimodal data to understand medical trainees' regulation strategies and physiological responses in high- fidelity medical simulation scenarios
citation: Moreno, M., Patino Melo, L., Grewal, K., Matin, N., Azher, S., & Harley, J.M. (2024). Analyzing Multimodal Data to Understand Medical Trainees' Regulation Strategies and Physiological Responses in High-Fidelity Medical Simulation Scenarios. Metacognition and Learning, 19, 1161–1213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09403-z
title: Multimodal medical-simulation coding scheme combining behavioral, SRL and SSRL codes
description: A composite coding scheme used to code leaders' behaviors and regulation strategies in recorded CRM simulations. As the article describes it, "Our coding scheme included codes for: 1) behaviors (posture and gestures, facial expression, and vocalics) and 2) regulation strategies, including SRL and SSRL which were then modified to fit a medically based research context." It nests subordinate codes under superordinate codes with definitions and medical-context examples, borrows established SRL and SSRL codes, and was refined with input from researchers, simulation educators and medical doctors. Three trained raters reached Cohen's Kappas of 0.71 to 0.82 before deliberation and perfect agreement after deliberation.
requirements: Trained raters and negotiated coding, with medical-doctor and simulation-educator input to clarify clinical interactions
constraints: Codes were modified for a medical context and applied to leaders' and teams' observable behavior in recorded simulations only
target_learners: Medical residents participating in team-based CRM simulations
target_learning_goals: Describing observable regulation strategies (SRL and SSRL) and team behaviors during simulated patient care
examples: Ten simulations were coded with segmentation into 'Beginning', 'Escalation' and 'Peak', with frequencies and percentages reported per segment

article_title: Analyzing multimodal data to understand medical trainees' regulation strategies and physiological responses in high- fidelity medical simulation scenarios
citation: Moreno, M., Patino Melo, L., Grewal, K., Matin, N., Azher, S., & Harley, J.M. (2024). title: Segmenting simulation scenarios into 'Beginning', 'Escalation' and 'Peak' for comparative multimodal analysis
description: A reusable analytic pattern in which a simulation scenario is divided into three scripted segments so behaviors, regulation strategies and physiological responses can be compared across critical points. The article explains: "We used the patient’s deterioration and scripted events to guide the segmentation of data, for example, we may use the “patient’s” sudden drop in pulse or the anaphylactic shock that tightens the airway to initiate the transition from the ‘‘Beginning’’ to the ‘‘Escalation’’ of a simulation." Segments were chosen for comparable length and to identify the stakes at each point, with the 'Peak' marking the convergence of medical decision-making and execution of patient care.
requirements: Scenario scripts or scripted patient-deterioration events to serve as event markers for segment boundaries
constraints: Many medical simulations lack a resolution segment, so the third segment ends at the 'Peak' rather than at a resolution
target_learners: Medical trainees working in teams in high-fidelity simulation scenarios
target_learning_goals: Understanding how team regulation strategies and physiological activation vary across phases of a simulated clinical task
examples: Raters negotiated segment boundaries jointly using each simulation's script, then compared code frequencies and APPS across the three segments

article_title: Expert example standards but not idea unit standards help learners accurately evaluate the quality of self-generated examples
citation: Linda Froese, Julian Roelle. (2022). Expert example standards but not idea unit standards help learners accurately evaluate the quality of self-generated examples. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09293-z
title: Standards must represent concrete correct responses to enhance judgment accuracy
description: The article proposes that, following Rawson and Dunlosky's (2007) original idea, standards enhance judgment accuracy only when they are "external representations of a correct answer to a task assignment" that learners can directly compare with their own products. Idea unit and full standards fail in example generation because learners must still generate an internal standard, which can be misaligned with objective standards. Expert example standards succeed because they provide objectively correct responses.
requirements: The standard must give learners access to an objectively correct response they can directly compare with their own product
constraints: The article notes expert example standards require more interpretation than standards in retrieval or problem-solving tasks, because surface features differ and learners must transfer what a good illustration looks like, which could increase cognitive load
target_learners: University students learning declarative concepts
target_learning_goals: Accurate self-evaluation of the quality of self-generated examples
examples: In the experiment, learners compared their self-generated examples with two piloted expert examples per concept that would receive full credit, which lowered bias and improved absolute accuracy

article_title: Better beware: comparing metacognition for phishing and legitimate emails
citation: Casey Inez Canfield & Baruch Fischhoff & Alex Davis. (2019). Better beware: comparing metacognition for phishing and legitimate emails. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09197-5
title: Brier-score decomposition into calibration, resolution, and knowledge as metrics of detection metacognition
description: The article uses probability judgments to reveal metacognitive states of mind, scoring them with the Brier score, which "can be decomposed into three components, calibration (or reliability), resolution, and knowledge (or uncertainty)." Calibration measures whether confidence judgments correspond to relative frequencies; resolution measures the variance of correct answers associated with different probability judgments, so high-resolution individuals "are better able to discriminate between correct and incorrect judgments by assigning them different probabilities." Judgments are binned into six confidence ranges (50–59% through 100%), with lower calibration scores and higher resolution scores indicating better metacognition; knowledge, capturing outcome uncertainty, is excluded as not an element of metacognition.
requirements: Confidence judgments elicited on a probability scale (here 50%–100%) for each detection decision, so they can be binned and scored against observed outcomes
constraints: Knowledge is not an element of metacognition and is not considered further by the article
Scores are computed per individual over a fixed set of items (N = 38 forecasts per person here)
target_learners: adults judging email legitimacy (crowdsourced adults and community-dwelling students and retirees)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring of one's own deception-detection accuracy in digital literacy tasks
examples: Applied to 40-email detection tasks in two experiments, scored separately for 19 phishing and 19 legitimate emails
key_sources: Casey Inez Canfield & Baruch Fischhoff & Alex Davis. (2019). Better beware: comparing metacognition for phishing and legitimate emails. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09197-5

article_title: Evaluating false positive rates of standard and hierarchical measures of metacognitive accuracy
citation: Manuel Rausch, Michael Zehetleitner. (2023). Evaluating false positive rates of standard and hierarchical measures of metacognitive accuracy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09353-y
title: Demonstrate an adequate false positive rate before adopting a measure of metacognitive accuracy
description: The article argues that researchers should not assume a measurement method controls its error rate; instead, each candidate measure of metacognitive accuracy should be shown via simulation or prior evidence to hold the false positive rate near the nominal alpha level. As the authors state, "we strongly recommend that only measures for which it has been demonstrated that the false positive rate is appropriate should be used." This applies to both summary-statistic and hierarchical approaches.
requirements: Simulation or empirical evidence that the measure's false positive rate is at or near the nominal alpha level for the intended design
constraints: The article notes the false-positive rate is only one consideration; validity and confounding by task performance and criteria must also be weighed
target_learners: Researchers studying metacognition in perceptual, memory, and cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of metacognitive accuracy in learning research
examples: The study itself evaluated gamma correlations, confidence slopes, type 2 ROCs, meta-d′, meta-da, HMeta-d, and logistic mixed regression via hierarchical resampling from the confidence database
key_sources: Manuel Rausch, Michael Zehetleitner. (2023). Evaluating false positive rates of standard and hierarchical measures of metacognitive accuracy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09353-y

article_title: Evaluating false positive rates of standard and hierarchical measures of metacognitive accuracy
citation: Manuel Rausch, Michael Zehetleitner. (2023). Evaluating false positive rates of standard and hierarchical measures of metacognitive accuracy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09353-y
title: Hierarchical resampling simulation framework based on the confidence database for evaluating metacognitive measures
description: A simulation methodology in which real confidence-judgment datasets are resampled hierarchically (participants with replacement, then trials within participants) to create realistic simulated experiments without committing to a mathematical model of confidence. The article states that "The 46 datasets from the confidence database were used to simulate 5000 experiments," with a continuous predictor sampled from a Gaussian distribution for each simulated participant. It enables false positive rate estimation for any measure computable from binary stimulus, binary response, and confidence data.
requirements: Datasets with binary stimulus and response categories and at least 20 participants with at least 20 trials each
constraints: Computation was capped at 200 subjects and 500 trials per subject per simulated study
target_learners: Researchers evaluating statistical methods for metacognition research
target_learning_goals: Method selection for measuring metacognitive accuracy
examples: Simulated two-group comparisons and continuous-predictor analyses were run on each simulated dataset for all included measures
key_sources: Manuel Rausch, Michael Zehetleitner. (2023). Evaluating false positive rates of standard and hierarchical measures of metacognitive accuracy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09353-y

article_title: Metacognitive awareness in relation to university students’ learning profiles
citation: Tuononen, T., Hyytinen, H., Räisänen, M., Hailikari, T., & Parpala, A. (2023). Metacognitive awareness in relation to university students' learning profiles. Metacognition and Learning, 18, 37–54. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09314-x
title: Two-component model of metacognitive awareness: knowledge about cognition and regulation of cognition
description: The article defines metacognitive awareness as "students' awareness of their own learning strategies and also of how, when and why to successfully apply them" and says it comprises two dimensions: knowledge about cognition and regulation of cognition. Knowledge about cognition covers declarative, procedural and conditional knowledge of cognition; regulation of cognition is the ability to plan, implement, monitor and evaluate learning processes across three cyclical, intertwined phases. The study's factor analyses tested and supported this two-component structure in a multidisciplinary higher education sample.
requirements: Assessment relies on self-report instruments (the shortened MAI) that ask students to reflect on their own strategies and regulation
constraints: The CFA fit indexes were only acceptable-to-modest, and the article states further development of the MAI in the multidisciplinary higher education context would be important
target_learners: Third-year bachelor's students in humanities, social sciences and theology
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive awareness of one's own learning processes
Regulation of studying
key_sources: Tuononen, T., Hyytinen, H., Räisänen, M., Hailikari, T., & Parpala, A. (2023). Metacognitive awareness in relation to university students' learning profiles. Metacognition and Learning, 18, 37–54. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09314-x

article_title: Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach
citation: Mark Feng Teng, Mei Yue. (2022). Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09328-5
title: MAWSQ: Metacognitive Academic Writing Strategies Questionnaire (43 items, eight strategies)
description: The MAWSQ is a self-report questionnaire developed and validated by Teng et al. (2022b) to measure metacognitive strategies in academic writing. It includes 43 items on a 7-point Likert scale, with 13 assessing knowledge of metacognition (declarative, procedural, conditional) and 30 assessing regulation (planning, monitoring, evaluating, information management, debugging). In this study Cronbach's alpha values "for the eight strategies ranged from 0.792 to 0.872". Validation evidence included EFA and CFA supporting an eight-factor correlated model and a one-factor second-order model, with the second-order model preferred.
requirements: Respondents must be engaged in academic writing in higher education for items to reflect their awareness and use of metacognitive strategies in writing situations
constraints: The article notes criticism that metacognitive strategy use cannot be adequately assessed by questionnaires (Veenman & Van Cleef, 2019), which the authors address by designing the instrument specifically for academic writing contexts
target_learners: EFL university students in academic writing courses
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive knowledge and regulation strategies for academic writing
examples: Applied to 644 third-year students at a Chinese university; completed online within 30 minutes during the last two lessons of the writing course
key_sources: Mark Feng Teng, Mei Yue. (2022). Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09328-5

article_title: Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach
citation: Mark Feng Teng, Mei Yue. (2022). Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09328-5
title: W-GCTA: Watson–Glaser Critical Thinking Appraisal used to assess five critical thinking subtests
description: The W-GCTA, developed by Watson and Glaser (1980), was adopted to assess learners' critical thinking skills through text-based exercises. It comprises five subtests totaling 86 items: evaluation of arguments (25 items), recognition of assumptions (16 items), deduction (25 items), inferences (20 items), and interpreting information (24 items). One point is awarded per correct answer. In this study Cronbach's alpha values "for the five sub-scales ranged from 0.792 to 0.865". Factor analytic studies are reported as supporting its construct validity and relationship with academic performance.
requirements: Administered here as a paper-and-pencil test completed within 60 minutes
constraints: Measures application of core critical thinking skills via text sentences; the article cites earlier studies for validity rather than new validation in this sample
target_learners: EFL university students
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking skills: inference, recognition of assumptions, deduction, interpretation, evaluation of arguments
examples: Completed by the same 644 participants one week before the academic writing test; instructions were in Chinese to ensure comprehension
key_sources: Mark Feng Teng, Mei Yue. (2022). Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09328-5

article_title: Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach
citation: Mark Feng Teng, Mei Yue. (2022). Metacognitive writing strategies, critical thinking skills, and academic writing performance: A structural equation modeling approach. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09328-5
title: Multi-faceted framework of metacognition: monitoring and control across knowledge, experiences, and skills
description: Drawing on Flavell, Efklides, Nelson, and Teng et al. (2022b), the article presents metacognition as a multifaceted construct spanning metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive experiences, and metacognitive skills/strategies. Learners are "consciously aware of the monitoring and control of cognition"; the monitoring function covers knowledge and experiences while control of cognition comprises skills/strategies, depicted as metacognitive regulation (planning, monitoring, evaluating) with reflection as an essential component. Metacognitive knowledge divides into declarative, procedural, and conditional types; regulation adds debugging and information management strategies. The framework frames metacognition as formed through dynamics between monitoring and control, with the three facets interacting.
requirements: Distinguishing the meta-level and object-level of cognitive processes, with acquisition, retention, and retrieval as stages between the two levels
constraints: The article notes there is not sufficient evidence showing that metacognitive deficits are solely responsible for writing performance
target_learners: EFL student writers in higher education
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated academic writing through metacognitive knowledge and regulation
examples: Operationalized in this study via the MAWSQ's eight strategy factors, all of which loaded significantly (parameter values larger than 0.50) in the SEM models
