article_title: Metacognitive judgments can potentiate new learning: The role of covert retrieval
citation: Veit Kubik, Kenneth Koslowski, Torsten Schubert, Alp Aslan. (2022). Metacognitive judgments can potentiate new learning: The role of covert retrieval. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:1057–1077. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09307-w
title: Covert retrieval account of the forward effect of metacognitive judgments
description: The article proposes that making item-based JOLs potentiates new learning to the extent that the judgment prompt elicits covert retrieval attempts before the metacognitive assessment. When only partial study information is available (word stems), "more frequent and effortful retrieval attempts and also retrieval failures are likely evoked prior to making the JOLs", engaging the same mechanisms as overt retrieval practice — retrieval-based episodic context change, list segregation, release from proactive interference, and reset of encoding. When complete study information is present, covert retrieval is unlikely and no forward benefit emerges. The account extends the forward testing effect literature to metacognitive monitoring acts.
requirements: JOLs must be delayed and based on partial cues (e.g., word stems) so that covert retrieval attempts occur prior to the judgment
constraints: Demonstrated with lists of unrelated single words; the authors note it is unclear whether JOLs with complete study information could benefit new learning with related materials
The covert-retrieval interpretation is offered speculatively: the authors write they "cannot firmly conclude" that covert retrieval was evoked
target_learners: undergraduate students in laboratory learning contexts
self-studying learners in higher education
target_learning_goals: enhancing recall of newly studied verbal material
reducing proactive interference across successive study episodes
examples: Participants who made JOLs on word stems after each of Lists 1–4 recalled more List-5 words and produced fewer prior-list intrusions than participants who restudied the lists
key_sources: Veit Kubik, Kenneth Koslowski, Torsten Schubert, Alp Aslan. (2022). Metacognitive judgments can potentiate new learning: The role of covert retrieval. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:1057–1077. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09307-w

article_title: Metacognition and motivation in creativity: examining the roles of self-efficacy and values as cues for metacognitive judgments
citation: Kamila Urban, Marek Urban. (2025). Metacognition and motivation in creativity: examining the roles of self-efficacy and values as cues for metacognitive judgments. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09421-5
title: Foster creative self-efficacy through mastery experiences with repeated practice and feedback to support accurate creative self-evaluation
description: The article argues that because creative self-efficacy acts as a direct heuristic cue for how individuals evaluate their creative performance, well-calibrated self-efficacy matters for accurate self-evaluations. It observes that interventions have enhanced self-efficacy in domains like reading and mathematics but "similar interventions targeting creative self-efficacy are notably absent." It recommends adapting the most common strategies, namely "mastery experiences through repeated practice and feedback," to foster creative self-efficacy in educational and workplace settings.
requirements: Interventions must build well-calibrated self-efficacy, since miscalibrated self-efficacy could bias metacognitive judgments
constraints: The article notes the recommendation is extrapolated from intervention evidence in other domains such as reading and mathematics, not from tested creativity-domain interventions
target_learners: university students
learners engaged in creative tasks
target_learning_goals: accurate self-evaluation of creative performance
sustained engagement in creative tasks
examples: The study measured creative self-efficacy with a 3-item scale and modeled its direct and indirect effects on expectancies and judgments across two creativity tasks
key_sources: Kamila Urban, Marek Urban. (2025). Metacognition and motivation in creativity: examining the roles of self-efficacy and values as cues for metacognitive judgments. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09421-5

article_title: The role of metacognitive experience: Can feedback training affect kindergarteners'monitoring accuracy?
citation: Kristin Kolloff, Ebru Ger, Claudia M. Roebers. (2025). The role of metacognitive experience: Can feedback training affect kindergarteners' monitoring accuracy? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09422-4
title: Cue utilization framework combined with Efklides' multilevel metacognition model as basis for monitoring training
description: The study integrates Koriat's (1997) cue utilization approach, which holds that individuals use mnemonic heuristics such as retrieval fluency as cues to inform monitoring, with Efklides' (2008) model framing metacognitive experiences and social feedback as shaping monitoring development. The article states that "retrieval fluency typically functions as a valid mnemonic cue, and its use is consistently related to monitoring accuracy." This dual framework motivated testing whether feedback and repeated experiences help children discover and use valid task-inherent cues.
requirements: Repeated metacognitive experiences across multiple task trials for children to discover valid cues
constraints: Young children's monitoring judgments tend to be inaccurate due to underdeveloped recognition and use of valid task-inherent cues, per the framework
target_learners: kindergarten-aged children (around 6 years old)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring accuracy
cue utilization in memory tasks
examples: The training app exposed children to varying retrieval fluency across 12 sessions of paired-associates memory tasks with confidence judgments after each recognition trial
key_sources: Kristin Kolloff, Ebru Ger, Claudia M. Roebers. (2025). The role of metacognitive experience: Can feedback training affect kindergarteners' monitoring accuracy? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09422-4

article_title: The role of metacognitive experience: Can feedback training affect kindergarteners'monitoring accuracy?
citation: Kristin Kolloff, Ebru Ger, Claudia M. Roebers. (2025). The role of metacognitive experience: Can feedback training affect kindergarteners' monitoring accuracy? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09422-4
title: App-based metacognitive monitoring training program with paired-associates memory tasks and feedback
description: A computerized, self-paced training program delivered on tablet computers in which children completed paired-associates memory learning tasks (learning, delay, recognition, monitoring, and feedback phases) across 12 sessions. The article describes it as "a computerized method that is modern, economical in terms of human resources, and allows upscaling." Feedback was delivered visually (green tick, red cross) and auditorily depending on condition; the active control group completed a Hearts and Flowers executive function task instead.
requirements: Some adult supervision during sessions, per the article's own note
Trained research assistants for technical setup and instructions
constraints: The active control group did not participate in any memory tasks during training sessions
target_learners: kindergarten-aged children (5.5 to 7.7 years)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring accuracy
confidence judgment calibration
examples: Children learned 12 paired associations per session (eight in session one), studied each picture pair for five seconds, completed a one-minute delay activity, took an untimed recognition test, and rated confidence on a 4-point smiley scale

article_title: Rubrics enhance accuracy and reduce cognitive load in self-assessment
citation: Rebecca Krebs, Björn Rothstein, Julian Roelle. (2022). Rubrics enhance accuracy and reduce cognitive load in self-assessment. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09302-1
title: Cue-utilization and offloading account of how rubrics support self-assessment
description: The article frames rubrics as documents that "provide learners with the assessment criteria and, based on these criteria, illustrate different levels of quality". Theoretically, transparent quality levels supply diagnostic cues on which learners base judgments, increasing accuracy per cue-utilization theory; the reduced perceived difficulty indicates rubrics also serve an offloading function, relieving learners from deciding which criteria apply to each quality level.
requirements: Learners must be introduced to the assessment criteria and quality levels the rubric covers
constraints: Under strict time constraints rubrics might induce stress and pressure and hinder task performance, per the article's citation of Panadero & Romero (2014)
target_learners: high school students self-assessing written scientific abstracts
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of complex writing performance
examples: In the experiment, rubric learners rated their abstracts on six quality levels per criterion with the rubric's aspect descriptions visible, while control learners used the same scales without guidance
key_sources: Rebecca Krebs, Björn Rothstein, Julian Roelle. (2022). Rubrics enhance accuracy and reduce cognitive load in self-assessment. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09302-1

article_title: Metacognitive experience on Raven’s matrices versus insight problems
citation: Adam Chuderski, Jan Jastrzębski, Bartłomiej Kroczek, Hanna Kucwaj, Michał Ociepka. (2021). Metacognitive experience on Raven’s matrices versus insight problems. Metacognition and Learning 16:15–35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09236-6
title: RAPM as a heterogeneous test: easy items involve fluent insight-like processing, difficult items effortful analytic combination
description: The article proposes that RAPM is not a homogeneous measure of a single reasoning process. Based on the metacognitive-rating patterns, it argues that "The easy problems involve concurrent and fluent processing, leading to insight-like, clear, and vivid outcomes," whereas difficult problems "need to be decomposed into sub-problems and require systematic analysis of the consecutive problem elements." This account contrasts with classic psychometric analyses suggesting RAPM unidimensionality, and it holds that the two experience patterns do not depend on strategy variation, since Intuition was stable across items.
requirements: Metacognitive ratings collected after each solution, with the matrix temporally separated from the response bank as in this study's administration
constraints: The interpretation of processing differences rests on subjective reports, which the authors call an imperfect method that should be validated with objective methods
The account is drawn from a variant with delayed response-bank presentation; concurrent presentation may tap fluid intelligence less validly
target_learners: adults assessed for fluid intelligence in basic, educational, and professional contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding and valid measurement of abstract inductive reasoning and fluid intelligence
examples: The study contrasted ratings across 20 RAPM items of varying difficulty against interleaved computerized insight problems and non-computerized insight and analytic problems
key_sources: Adam Chuderski, Jan Jastrzębski, Bartłomiej Kroczek, Hanna Kucwaj, Michał Ociepka. (2021). Metacognitive experience on Raven’s matrices versus insight problems. Metacognition and Learning 16:15–35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09236-6

article_title: How does monitoring set the stage for adaptive regulation or maladaptive behavior in collaborative learning?
citation: Sobocinski, M., Järvelä, S., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., Isosalo, A., & Noponen, K. (2020). How does monitoring set the stage for adaptive regulation or maladaptive behavior in collaborative learning? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09224-w
title: Three-dimensional coding framework for monitoring events (target, valence, phase) to identify adaptive regulation and maladaptive behavior in collaborative learning
description: The study contributes an empirical framework, built on the socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) framework, for identifying adaptive regulation and maladaptive behavior from process data. Monitoring events are coded on "target (cognition, motivation, emotion, behavior), valence (positive or negative), and phase in which monitoring occurs (task definition, goals and planning, task enactment, or reflection)". Combining valence with the group's reaction or lack of reaction defines on-track, adaptive, and maladaptive sequences: negative-valence monitoring followed by a reaction is adaptive, and without a reaction is maladaptive.
requirements: Monitoring events must be verbalized and observable in video data, so groups' monitoring can be identified and coded from utterances
constraints: No off-task behavior was found in the data because the task was an exam situation with a time limit
Monitoring behavior was not coded for valence due to the hands-on nature of the task
target_learners: high school students in advanced physics courses working in collaborative groups
target_learning_goals: effective socially shared regulation of learning during collaborative tasks
examples: In the coded example of an adaptive sequence, a student asked "Should we evaluate the correctness of the result?" and group members responded, keeping the group in the task enactment phase
key_sources: Sobocinski, M., Järvelä, S., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., Isosalo, A., & Noponen, K. (2020). How does monitoring set the stage for adaptive regulation or maladaptive behavior in collaborative learning? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09224-w

citation: Sobocinski, M., Järvelä, S., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., Isosalo, A., & Noponen, K. (2020). How does monitoring set the stage for adaptive regulation or maladaptive behavior in collaborative learning? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09224-w
title: Vector quantization of group heart-rate data to detect group-level physiological state transitions
description: The study treats the collaborating group as a dynamic system whose aggregated state is a three-dimensional vector of the members' heart rates, traced over the exam session. Vector quantization (VQ) discretizes the continuously varying heart-rate triplets: "This technique allowed the reduction of the number of system states and transitions between them, giving rise to delineable recurrent state patterns." Transitions occur when the heart-rate triplet changes enough to associate with another centroid in the codebook, making state pattern analysis feasible and allowing alignment of physiological state transitions with regulatory sequences.
requirements: Heart-rate data collected from all group members simultaneously (Empatica S4 bracelets were used for three of the nine groups)
constraints: Physiological analysis was available for only three groups, due to limited bracelets
target_learners: high school students collaborating face-to-face during an exam task
target_learning_goals: detecting group-level regulatory processes and physiological state changes during collaborative learning
examples: Heart-rate triplets from three group members were represented as a trajectory in a three-dimensional coordinate system, then discretized into centroid-based states with transitions between them
key_sources: Sobocinski, M., Järvelä, S., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., Isosalo, A., & Noponen, K. (2020). How does monitoring set the stage for adaptive regulation or maladaptive behavior in collaborative learning? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09224-w

article_title: Reactivity to confidence ratings in older individuals performing the latin square task
citation: Double, K. S., & Birney, D. P. (2018). Reactivity to confidence ratings in older individuals performing the latin square task. Metacognition and Learning, 13, 309–326. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-018-9186-5
title: Two-stage model of reactivity to confidence ratings
description: The article proposes a two-stage account of why eliciting confidence ratings changes performance. In the first stage, performing CR makes participants attend to confidence-related beliefs, i.e. they "rely on information-based cues"; in the second stage, participants make strategic control decisions such as speed-accuracy trade-offs based on those activated beliefs, which then affect task performance. The model explains why high-confidence participants persist longer and low-confidence participants disengage, and why CR can reinforce existing beliefs whether or not they are accurate.
requirements: Confidence ratings must direct attention to information participants would not otherwise attend to for reactivity to occur
constraints: Proposed from a single experiment with older adults; the authors state substantially more work is needed to establish robustness and generalisability
target_learners: older adult community samples performing timed problem-solving tasks
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and control during reasoning and problem solving
examples: In the experiment, high-confidence CR participants persisted longer per item while low-confidence CR participants answered more quickly, consistent with belief-driven control decisions
key_sources: Double, K. S., & Birney, D. P. (2018). Reactivity to confidence ratings in older individuals performing the latin square task. Metacognition and Learning, 13, 309–326. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-018-9186-5

article_title: Reactivity to confidence ratings in older individuals performing the latin square task
citation: Double, K. S., & Birney, D. P. (2018). Reactivity to confidence ratings in older individuals performing the latin square task. Metacognition and Learning, 13, 309–326. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-018-9186-5
title: Nelson and Narens metacognitive framework as an organizing account of reactivity
description: The article adopts the Nelson and Narens framework to conceptualise how metacognitive consequences give rise to differential reactivity effects. The framework "distinguishes between an object-level where cognitive activity occurs, and a meta-level that governs the object-level processes", linked by upward monitoring and downward control processes. The authors operationalize monitoring as retrospective appraisals of performance and control as response-time behaviour, using the framework to generate hypotheses about how CR affect each pathway.
requirements: Communicated information between levels is imperfect and may be influenced by motivation and affect
constraints: Applied here to a timed reasoning task with older adults; the article notes Bannert and Reimann's prompt findings from interactive online learning may not generalise to simpler performance strategies
target_learners: older adults solving reasoning problems
target_learning_goals: understanding metacognitive monitoring and control during problem solving
examples: The study measured monitoring via retrospective appraisal accuracy (miscalibration) and control via response-time allocation under a 15-minute time limit
key_sources: Double, K. S., & Birney, D. P. (2018). Reactivity to confidence ratings in older individuals performing the latin square task. Metacognition and Learning, 13, 309–326. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-018-9186-5

article_title: The effect of time pressure on metacognitive control: developmental changes in self-regulation and efficiency during learning
citation: Gönül, G., Tsalas, N., Paulus, M. (2021). The effect of time pressure on metacognitive control: developmental changes in self-regulation and efficiency during learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09262-y
title: Deterioration versus enhancement hypotheses of time pressure on metacognitive control
description: The article derives two competing hypotheses about how time pressure affects metacognitive control during learning. The deterioration hypothesis holds that awareness of time constraints distracts learners and reduces cognitive capacities such as working memory resources, harming self-regulation especially in children whose monitoring and control are loosely coupled. The enhancement hypothesis holds that slight time pressure improves performance because learners avoid failing courses of action and act in a more strategic and situation sensitive manner. The study frames its self-regulation and efficiency predictions around these two accounts.
requirements: A learning situation in which time constraints are made salient (e.g., a countdown) so that time pressure can influence metacognitive decisions
constraints: The article notes there were limited prior studies on study time allocation under time pressure, making developmental effects hard to predict from existing literature
target_learners: children (10-year-olds)
adolescents (14-year-olds)
adults
target_learning_goals: metacognitive self-regulation of study time
efficient allocation of study effort
examples: The study tested both hypotheses by comparing gamma-based self-regulation and efficiency rates across timed and untimed study blocks in three age groups
key_sources: Gönül, G., Tsalas, N., Paulus, M. (2021). The effect of time pressure on metacognitive control: developmental changes in self-regulation and efficiency during learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09262-y

article_title: How multiple levels of metacognitive awareness operate in collaborative problem solving
citation: Çini, A., Järvelä, S., Dindar, M., Malmberg, J. (2023). How multiple levels of metacognitive awareness operate in collaborative problem solving. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09358-7
title: Three-level framework of metacognitive awareness (individual, social, environmental)
description: The article conceptualises metacognitive awareness as operating on three interacting levels: "oneself (the individual level), one’s interplay with others (the social level), and one’s interplay with the learning environment (the environmental level)". The individual level covers conceptual systems and regulation of cognition; the social level covers interactions with group members through written and spoken language and facial expressions; the environmental level covers interaction with the learning environment such as feedback during CPS. The study uses this framework to organise measurement (MAI, situated self-reports, feedback and facial expression data) in collaborative problem solving.
requirements: Assessment at multiple time points with situated self-reports rather than trait-based measures alone, since trait-based assessment cannot sufficiently explore metacognition in action
constraints: Developed and tested in the context of a computer-based complex CPS simulation with higher education students
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive awareness in collaborative problem solving
examples: In the study, MAI measured the individual level, repeated metacognitive judgement and task difficulty self-reports measured the social level, and simulation feedback with facial expression data measured the environmental level.
key_sources: Çini, A., Järvelä, S., Dindar, M., Malmberg, J. (2023). How multiple levels of metacognitive awareness operate in collaborative problem solving. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09358-7

article_title: The pivotal role of monitoring for collaborative problem solving seen in interaction, performance, and interpersonal physiology
citation: Haataja, E., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., & Järvelä, S. (2021). The pivotal role of monitoring for collaborative problem solving seen in interaction, performance, and interpersonal physiology. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 241–268. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09279-3
title: Multilevel framework of regulation in collaborative learning across physiological, psychological, and interpersonal levels
description: The article frames regulation in collaborative learning as a multifaceted phenomenon that unfolds across multiple systemic levels. Monitoring challenges "can be seen as adjustments on different systemic levels (physiological, psychological, and interpersonal) of a collaborative group." This framework motivates simultaneously measuring interactional indicators (video-coded monitoring) and physiological indicators (EDA arousal and synchrony) to capture how regulation manifests across levels during collaboration.
requirements: Capturing the multilevel nature of regulation requires multimodal data combining video interaction coding with physiological recordings such as electrodermal activity.
constraints: The article notes that relations between interpersonal physiology and monitoring have not held true for all tasks and all groups.
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem solving
socially shared regulation of learning
key_sources: Haataja, E., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., & Järvelä, S. (2021). The pivotal role of monitoring for collaborative problem solving seen in interaction, performance, and interpersonal physiology. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 241–268. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09279-3

article_title: The pivotal role of monitoring for collaborative problem solving seen in interaction, performance, and interpersonal physiology
citation: Haataja, E., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., & Järvelä, S. (2021). The pivotal role of monitoring for collaborative problem solving seen in interaction, performance, and interpersonal physiology. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 241–268. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09279-3
title: Tailorshop business simulation for collaborative complex problem solving
description: The Tailorshop is a computer-based business simulation in which "participants were required to run a shirt production company" by adjusting variables such as employee wages, storage costs, and shirt price to maximize company value. The article used its exploration phase, consisting of six simulated months, to elicit spontaneous monitoring interactions at month transitions, with each transition followed by a one-minute monitoring episode.
requirements: The task requires a desktop computer and is designed for small groups working face-to-face on complex system dynamics.
constraints: The study concentrated on the exploration phase only, not the performance phase of the simulation.
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: complex problem solving
understanding system dynamics

article_title: The promotion of self-regulated learning in the classroom: a theoretical framework and an observation study
citation: Vosniadou, S., Bodner, E., Stephenson, H., Jeffries, D., Lawson, M. J., Darmawan, I. G. N., Kang, S., Graham, L., & Dignath, C. (2024). The promotion of self-regulated learning in the classroom: a theoretical framework and an observation study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09374-1
title: The SRL Teacher Promotion Framework (SRL-TPF) conceptualizes direct and indirect promotion of self-regulated learning in the classroom
description: The SRL-TPF brings together SRL theory and ICAP theory of cognitive engagement to analyze how teachers promote self-regulated learning. It "utilizes the ICAP theory to assess the affordances of the learning environment for the indirect promotion of SRL, proposes new variables in the investigation of the direct promotion of SRL, and examines how these two ways to promote SRL are related." Direct promotion categories include explicit and implicit strategy instruction, knowledge/beliefs promotion, metacognitive reflection, and metacognitive support, coded for capability, domain, manner, and benefit of use.
requirements: Requires analysis of lesson tasks and teacher utterances from filmed lesson transcripts, coded minute-by-minute
constraints: The ICAP theory does not investigate whether teachers give their students some independence to determine their learning activity, so student self-determination was added as a separate characteristic
target_learners: secondary school students (Year 7 to 12)
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning knowledge and strategies
metacognitive awareness
strategy use across subject areas
examples: Used to code transcripts of filmed lessons in 23 Australian classrooms via the ICAP-CG and a direct-promotion protocol derived from the ATES guide
key_sources: Vosniadou, S., Bodner, E., Stephenson, H., Jeffries, D., Lawson, M. J., Darmawan, I. G. N., Kang, S., Graham, L., & Dignath, C. (2024). The promotion of self-regulated learning in the classroom: a theoretical framework and an observation study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09374-1

article_title: The promotion of self-regulated learning in the classroom: a theoretical framework and an observation study
citation: Vosniadou, S., Bodner, E., Stephenson, H., Jeffries, D., Lawson, M. J., Darmawan, I. G. N., Kang, S., Graham, L., & Dignath, C. (2024). The promotion of self-regulated learning in the classroom: a theoretical framework and an observation study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09374-1
title: ICAP-CG: an ICAP-based coding guide for assessing indirect SRL promotion from lesson tasks
description: The ICAP-CG is an observation protocol developed in prior work (Vosniadou et al., 2023) that codes lesson tasks minute-by-minute into Passive, Active, Active/Collaborative, Constructive, and Interactive engagement modes based on the verbs teachers use in task instructions. "The ICAP-CG was used to examine the transcripts of the filmed lessons on a minute-by-minute basis and to identify the lesson tasks." An Active/Collaborative code was added for cases where teachers asked students to work together using Active rather than Constructive or Interactive verbs.
requirements: Requires filmed lesson transcripts with timestamps; coders identify lesson tasks and assign engagement codes from teacher instruction verbs and student activity
constraints: Students were assumed to engage in the tasks as described by the teachers' instructions, with student codes adjusted only when the transcript showed a discrepancy
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: assessing opportunities for indirect promotion of self-regulated learning
examples: Applied to 107 lesson tasks across 898 minutes of observation in 23 classrooms, reaching 93% agreement and Cohen's Kappa of 0.86 between coders
key_sources: Vosniadou, S., Bodner, E., Stephenson, H., Jeffries, D., Lawson, M. J., Darmawan, I. G. N., Kang, S., Graham, L., & Dignath, C. (2024). article_title: Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations
citation: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9
title: Select a self-report instrument by matching the strategies and learning task it measures to the measurement aims, not by popularity
description: The article argues that when administering a self-report instrument, practitioners and researchers should first define which learning strategies are to be measured and for which learning tasks, and then check that the chosen instrument actually measures those strategies for a representative task. It warns against simply choosing a popular questionnaire such as the MSLQ or MAI. Standard validity and reliability requirements and generalisability of the measures must also be considered.
requirements: Define the aims of measurement (which strategies, which tasks) before choosing an instrument
Check that the target task is representative of the tasks to which results will be generalised
constraints: Generalisability is an issue for all measuring methods, not only self-report questionnaires
target_learners: school learners whose strategies teachers or researchers assess
target_learning_goals: cognitive, metacognitive and affective learning strategies
examples: The article names MSLQ (Pintrich and De Groot 1990) and MAI (Schraw and Dennison 1994) as popular instruments that should not be selected merely for their popularity
key_sources: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9

article_title: Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations
citation: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9
title: Combine multiple measuring methods (triangulation) to assess learning strategies, since neither self-report surveys nor think-aloud studies alone suffice
description: Because self-report instruments have both strong and flawed points, the article reports that many researchers recommend combining measuring methods. In multi-method designs the same instruments are given to the same participants in the same learning situation, so the strengths and weaknesses of each method can be examined. The combination is said to yield a broad picture and deep insight into learners' learning strategies.
requirements: Instruments administered to the same participants in the same learning situation
Comparison should go beyond total scores and correlations, measuring the same specific strategies in a similar learning situation
constraints: Different methods may lead to a variety of results, raising the question of how to judge and combine them
Multi-method designs and interpreting combined data can be labor-intensive and cost-consuming
target_learners: school and higher-education learners studied in strategy research
target_learning_goals: cognitive and metacognitive learning strategies
examples: The article cites Dinsmore et al.'s (2008) review of 255 studies concluding that some combination of quantitative and qualitative approaches may be required to reveal self-regulated learning strategies
key_sources: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9

article_title: Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations
citation: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9
title: Tailor self-report instruments to particular tasks or contexts, since broad-brush general measures strain validity
description: The article argues that most self-report questionnaires are very broad-brush measures that generalise across multiple times, situations and domains, and questions how fairly such instruments can capture the dynamic interplay characterising self-regulated learning. It recommends that instruments be tailored to particular tasks or contexts, and that the moment of self-report collection (straight after or even during task execution) be examined. Task-specific measuring connects to evidence that learning strategies differ by task type or subject.
requirements: Instruments aimed at a specific learning task that is representative of the tasks to be generalised
constraints: The distinction between task-specific and general measures relates only indirectly to the on-line versus off-line distinction
target_learners: learners studying expository or multiple texts in school and research settings
target_learning_goals: task-specific cognitive and metacognitive reading and study strategies
examples: All five special-issue instruments described are task-specific: a history-text studying questionnaire, a multiple-text reading inventory, an on-line sentence-by-sentence reading tool, a multiple-choice strategy measure, and calibration judgments tied to specific knowledge tests
key_sources: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9

article_title: Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations
citation: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9
title: RSAT: a computer-based on-line reading assessment measuring comprehension and spontaneous reading strategies
description: RSAT is a computer-based reading assessment designed to measure readers' comprehension and spontaneous use of reading strategies while reading texts. Readers comprehend passages one sentence at a time and answer an indirect self-report question about their understanding of each target sentence, or a direct comprehension question such as "Why X?". Answers are digitally analyzed by counting target words associated with strategies or comprehension, and the resulting measures are used to predict comprehension scores on standardized tests.
requirements: Pre-selected target sentences within passages
Digital analysis counting target words associated with strategies or comprehension
constraints: It is an on-line instrument, in contrast to the retrospective off-line questionnaires used in the first two special-issue contributions
target_learners: readers of expository texts
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension and spontaneous reading strategy use
examples: Magliano, Millis, the RSAT Development Team, Levinstein and Boonthum examine this on-line instrument in the third special-issue contribution
key_sources: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9

article_title: Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations
citation: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9
title: Multiple-choice strategy use measure requiring readers to enact strategies while retaining group administration and simple scoring
description: Cromley and Azevedo developed a domain-general and domain-specific multiple-choice strategy use measure as an alternative to self-report questionnaires. The method requires readers to enact a strategy and measures whether they perform it accurately by posing multiple-choice questions. It preserves the practical advantages of questionnaires, namely group administration and simple scoring, and was examined with three samples within a series of studies testing a model of reading comprehension.
requirements: Multiple-choice items that require enacting the strategy
Correlation with standard reading comprehension and component measures such as vocabulary, word reading, inference and background knowledge
constraints: Convergent validity among the different instruments was still being searched for; commonality analysis examined the degree to which strategy use contributes to single-text comprehension
target_learners: readers assessed across three samples in reading comprehension studies
target_learning_goals: accurate enactment of reading comprehension strategies
examples: In the three studies the instrument was correlated with standard reading comprehension and component measures, and commonality analysis examined strategy use's contribution to single-text comprehension
key_sources: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9

article_title: Self-regulated learning and reflection: a tool for teachers and students
citation: Avivit Arvatz, Roee Peretz, Yehudit Judy Dori. (2025). Self-regulated learning and reflection: a tool for teachers and students. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09415-3
title: The SRL&T approach: an integrated framework of self-regulated learning and teaching
description: The SRL&T approach is the article's conceptual framework for understanding how teachers facilitate development of their own and their students' SRL by transitioning between roles. The article states it "provides a conceptual framework for understanding how teachers can facilitate the development of their own and their students' SRL by transitioning between different roles", enabling feedback aligned with three teacher perspectives: as self-regulated learners, as teachers, and as mentors. It treats teachers' SRL and SRT as intertwined processes throughout learning cycles, extending Kramarski's SRT model, and is illustrated with a desired positive feedback loop in which increased critical reflection enhances transfer of SRL skills between teachers and students.
requirements: Teachers need opportunities to reflect critically on their own and their students' SRL, since the framework links teachers' reflection skill to their ability to model and guide reflective practices
constraints: The article notes the feedback mechanism is proposed and not yet tested: further research is needed to fully understand it and its potentially positive implications
target_learners: in-service teachers
secondary school students (grades 7–12)
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning skills including goal-setting, help-seeking, elaboration, and reflection
examples: The authors used the framework to design an SRL/SRT-focused professional development course in which teachers first completed the TQsrl and were then guided to teach SRL and reflection adapted to their discipline and cohort
key_sources: Avivit Arvatz, Roee Peretz, Yehudit Judy Dori. (2025). Self-regulated learning and reflection: a tool for teachers and students. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09415-3

article_title: Self-regulated learning and reflection: a tool for teachers and students
citation: Avivit Arvatz, Roee Peretz, Yehudit Judy Dori. (2025). Self-regulated learning and reflection: a tool for teachers and students. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09415-3
title: T-SQsrl: paired teacher and student SRL questionnaires with a triangulated reflection assessment
description: The T-SQsrl is an assessment tool comprising a teacher version (TQsrl, 31 closed-ended items plus an open-ended reflective question) and a student version (SQsrl, 15 closed-ended items), both adapted from the SRLMQ and structured on Zimmerman's cyclical SRL model. It evaluates SRL sub-processes including goal-setting, task-strategy, self-efficacy, help-seeking, elaboration, and reflection. The teacher version enables triangulated assessment by correlating self-assessed reflection with expert grading of an open-ended reflective question, while teachers provided the external assessment triangulating students' self-assessments. The article describes it as innovative in its focus on reflection skills and in allowing simultaneous assessment of teachers' and students' SRL within the same classroom or school.
requirements: External assessment of the reflection skill requires open-ended items graded by experts (for teachers) or by teachers (for students) to triangulate self-reports
constraints: The study notes validity issues with self-reports, and the sampling was a convenience sample with modest sizes adequate for initial validation only
target_learners: in-service teachers
students aged 12 and above in grades 7–12
target_learning_goals: assessing SRL sub-processes and reflection skill for formative assessment and intervention design
examples: Ten teachers who participated in the PD administered the SQsrl to their students with parental consent to map baseline SRL before an SRL intervention, and policymakers may use TQsrl results as an indicator of a PD program's effectiveness
key_sources: Avivit Arvatz, Roee Peretz, Yehudit Judy Dori. (2025). Self-regulated learning and reflection: a tool for teachers and students. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09415-3

article_title: How accurate and predictive are judgments of solvability? Explorations in a two-phase anagram solving paradigm
citation: Burton, O. R., Bodner, G. E., Williamson, P., & Arnold, M. M. (2023). How accurate and predictive are judgments of solvability? Explorations in a two-phase anagram solving paradigm. Metacognition and Learning, 18, 1–35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09313-y
title: Two-phase JOS paradigm separating intuitive solvability judgments from later solving outcomes
description: The two-phase paradigm separates the JOS phase, where participants make intuitive solvability judgments for an entire set of problems, from a subsequent solving phase where solving outcomes and effort regulation are measured. This design avoids the confound of interleaved paradigms, in which "JOSs may be influenced by solving attempts, and vice versa", allowing reasoners to bootstrap their JOS intuitions. The article uses this paradigm across three experiments with anagram durations parametrically manipulated across blocks.
requirements: JOS phase must precede the solving phase so judgments capture intuitions before reasoning occurs
Participants must be able to report already-solved (AS) judgments so spontaneously solved items can be excluded from discrimination and predictiveness measures
constraints: Interleaved paradigms may inflate JOS discrimination and predictiveness relative to the two-phase approach
Spontaneous solving during the JOS phase confounds measurement if not separately reported
target_learners: adult problem solvers (MTurk participants)
target_learning_goals: accurate meta-reasoning monitoring of problem solvability
effective effort regulation during problem solving
examples: In Experiment 3 the solving phase included both solvable and unsolvable anagrams with self-regulated solving time, enabling measurement of not-solvable responses as an effort-regulation measure
key_sources: Burton, O. R., Bodner, G. E., Williamson, P., & Arnold, M. M. (2023). How accurate and predictive are judgments of solvability? Explorations in a two-phase anagram solving paradigm. Metacognition and Learning, 18, 1–35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09313-y

article_title: Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation
citation: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6
title: Collisions: a SimQuest-based collaborative inquiry learning environment on colliding particles
description: Collisions is a computer-simulation-based inquiry environment developed in SimQuest in which dyads work on two computers with a shared interface and communicate through chat. Students "had to uncover the relation between the momentum of a particle before and after it hits another particle" by varying mass and initial velocity and viewing results in graphs. Assignments with multiple-choice and open questions guide the inquiry across three content levels of increasing complexity: Uniform motion, Fixed wall, and Elastic collisions.
requirements: Dyads work synchronously from separate computers, communicating through a chat channel with a shared interface
constraints: Students were not familiar with Collisions, but were acquainted with the variables from their physics classes
target_learners: tenth-grade pre-university physics students aged 15-17
target_learning_goals: discovering underlying physics rules of colliding particles, such as momentum relations
examples: Used with 48 dyads across three support conditions for 90-minute collaborative sessions
key_sources: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6

article_title: Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation
citation: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6
title: Collaborative Hypothesis Tool (CHT): a scaffold for jointly formulating and testing hypotheses
description: The CHT provides students with a hypothesis template supporting formulation of a syntactically correct hypothesis, plus a trust indicator scaled 0 to 100%. It "provided prompting windows with instructions on how to formulate a hypothesis together, and how to plan experiments" and a conclusion window prompting students to check whether results confirmed or rejected the hypothesis, urging re-inquiry after rejection.
requirements: Used within the SimQuest simulation environment so hypotheses can be tested with planned experiments
constraints: In this study the CHT was only provided in addition to the RIDE instruction, so its standalone effect is unknown
target_learners: secondary school students working in dyads in inquiry learning
target_learning_goals: collaborative hypothesis formulation, experiment planning, and evaluation of inquiry results
examples: Presented only to the experimental group of the second study (CHT condition, N=15 dyads) alongside the RIDE rules instruction
key_sources: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6

article_title: Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation
citation: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6
title: RIDE rules: computerized instruction in effective collaboration communication
description: The RIDE instruction is a set of collaboration rules based on literature on effective collaboration, clustered under four principles: Respect, Intelligent collaboration, Deciding together, and Encouragement. It was delivered as "an introductory computerized instruction in the RIDE rules with which they could practice using the rules during collaboration", designed according to cognitive apprenticeship principles including modelling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, and reflection.
requirements: Delivered in a session prior to collaborative work, with practice using the rules in dyads in a SimQuest simulation environment
constraints: In the first study, learners instructed in the RIDE rules used more communicative activities associated especially with the rules Deciding together and Encouraging
target_learners: secondary school students working in dyads in collaborative inquiry learning
target_learning_goals: effective communication and collaboration during inquiry learning
examples: Students in the experimental groups received the RIDE instruction before working 90 minutes with Collisions, and were prompted during the experiment to use the rules
key_sources: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6

article_title: Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation
citation: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6
title: Support collaborative inquiry learning with communication instruction plus inquiry prompts to raise team regulation and improve performance
description: The article concludes that collaborative inquiry environments should provide both communication instruction and inquiry-support tools, because "different measures of support can enhance the use of team regulative activities, which in turn can lead to better learning results". Communication instruction (RIDE) raised team regulation, but only the condition that added the CHT's inquiry prompts showed team regulation relating positively to learning results. The authors also recommend building in mirroring or metacognitive tools so students learn how and when to regulate.
requirements: Support must target both the collaboration process (communication instruction) and the inquiry process (prompting tools)
constraints: The study could not attribute the learning-result relation to the CHT alone versus the combination of supports; the 90-minute session limits robust learning-outcome effects
target_learners: secondary school students in collaborative inquiry learning
target_learning_goals: regulation of collaborative learning processes and improved inquiry learning performance
examples: Dyads in the CHT condition received RIDE instruction plus the Collaborative Hypothesis Tool and showed a significant positive team-regulation–learning-result correlation
key_sources: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6

article_title: Supporting reflection to improve learning from self-generated concept maps
citation: Elise H. Eshuis, Judith ter Vrugte, Ton de Jong. (2022). Supporting reflection to improve learning from self-generated concept maps. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09299-7
title: Reflection as the joint operation of cognitive and metacognitive processing driving knowledge integration from concept maps
description: The article frames learning from concept maps as knowledge integration requiring both cognitive processing (organizing and elaborating knowledge) and metacognitive processing (monitoring and regulating one's cognitive activities). Following Davis, it treats these as unified in "reflection": "reflection can focus on goals or on one's own thinking (metacognition), or on content itself (sense-making)". Identifying weaknesses in one's knowledge is positioned as the gateway process that makes the other knowledge-integration processes likely. The study's supports (example, prompts, discussion) are designed to trigger and sustain this reflection.
requirements: Students must engage in comparing and contrasting their own knowledge against a frame of reference, such as an example concept map
constraints: Students scarcely spontaneously engage in the required (meta)cognitive processes, and often employ them suboptimally
target_learners: secondary vocational (MBO) students
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge integration in electricity and electric power transmission
examples: The study operationalized reflection support as a combined concept map with highlighted differences, reflection prompts, and a teacher-guided classroom discussion.
key_sources: Elise H. Eshuis, Judith ter Vrugte, Ton de Jong. (2022). Supporting reflection to improve learning from self-generated concept maps. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09299-7

article_title: Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations
citation: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6
title: Contextual factors as a key feature of SRL frameworks, extending beyond the immediate task to the larger learning context
description: The article defines contextual factors as encompassing "features of the learning environment, the learner, and their interaction". It chronicles how context appeared in early SRL frameworks as task, environment, or learning task, and argues that examining direct and indirect effects requires operationalizing the task and accounting for features of the task environment in research designs. The special issue extends consideration of context beyond the immediate learning task to the larger context in which the task is embedded.
requirements: The task must be operationally defined and features of the task environment accounted for and incorporated into research designs
target_learners: secondary and post-secondary students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning processes
examples: Ben-Eliyahu and Linnenbrink-Garcia (2015) and McCardle and Hadwin (2015) examine contextual factors at the course-level as well as more distal factors
key_sources: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6

article_title: Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations
citation: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6
title: Contingencies as IF–THEN relations between SRL events, examined as they unfold over time
description: The article defines contingencies as "instances where one event occurs in the context of another", formalized as IF–THEN scenarios in which a learner consciously determines that, in response to a specific SRL event (the IF), a second event or process should be initiated (the THEN). An example is a metacognitive monitoring judgment that a reading passage is dense cueing the selection of note taking as a control strategy. Contingent relations are a critical assumption of process models of SRL and the basis for research on sequential and temporal characteristics of SRL.
requirements: Fine-grained data collected in sequence so that the likelihood that one event follows another can be gauged
target_learners: learners studying with hypermedia and other structured tasks
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and control during learning
examples: Binbarasan-Tüysüzoğlu and Greene (2015) use judgments of learning made when thinking aloud to test assumptions of the COPES model and examine contingencies between monitoring and control processes
key_sources: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6

article_title: Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations
citation: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6
title: Dynamic relations: SRL as an iterative, cyclical process in which processes influence one another
description: The article defines dynamic relations as occurring "when two or more SRL processes influence one another". Because process models conceptualize SRL as iterative and cyclical, activity in one cycle can affect activities within that cycle and subsequent cycles. The article traces this idea from Zimmerman's feedback-loop formalization through Butler and Winne's recursive relations to refined accounts of motivational constructs as precursors, mediators, and outcomes of SRL processes.
requirements: Longitudinal data on two related constructs over three or more periods to examine dynamic relations with cross-lagged path analyses
target_learners: elementary school through post-secondary students
target_learning_goals: relations among motivation, metacognition, and learning behavior
examples: Bernacki et al. (2015) examine minute-to-minute relationships between self-efficacy judgments, help seeking, and problem-solving attempts; Lichtinger and Kaplan (2015) examine relations between goals, affect, and actions
key_sources: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6

article_title: Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations
citation: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6
title: The integrated Self-Regulated Learning (iSRL) model situating SRL in hierarchically nested ecological contexts with limited self-regulatory capacity
description: The iSRL model draws on social and clinical sciences to situate SRL within the broader life-context of the individual, applying "an ecological assets perspective" so that learning tasks are nested within courses, disciplines, schools, neighborhoods, and policies. It posits that self-regulatory capacity is a depleteable resource (ego depletion), so regulation of non-learning demands competes with SRL for limited resources. The model holds that "there are mutual and dynamic influences between one's ecological assets and one's ability to learn".
requirements: Researchers adopting the framework must account for unique and interactive influences of distal contextual factors on SRL in the immediate task
constraints: There is a scarcity of empirical work examining how individuals regulate learning while also accounting for additional cognitive processes unrelated to learning
target_learners: students across educational levels, including those facing unstable home environments
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting self-regulated learning within learners' broader life contexts
examples: The article illustrates depletion with a hungry child regulating hunger, addressed by school breakfast programs, and a student coping with an unstable home environment arriving at school with fewer resources to self-regulate learning
key_sources: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6

article_title: Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations
citation: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6
title: A Newell-inspired time-scale taxonomy (cognitive, rational, social bands) for aligning SRL measurement to theorized process duration
description: Adapting Newell's bands taxonomy from cognitive science, the article proposes that SRL phenomena be matched to the time scale at which they are theorized to occur: cognitive-band events over seconds observed with trace methodologies and think-alouds, rational-band events over minutes to hours including strategy changes and motivation fluctuations, and social-band contextual factors enduring over weeks and months. "Combining measures that span more than one band provides a rich account of SRL." Table 1 maps each special-issue study's measures to bands.
requirements: Researchers must consider the time scale at which an SRL process is theorized to occur and choose measurement practices that can observe such phenomena as they occur
constraints: Triangulating methods across bands, as in Lichtinger and Kaplan's qualitative study, precludes the use of large, representative samples
target_learners: SRL researchers and designers of learning research
target_learning_goals: alignment of SRL measurement methods with theoretical assumptions
examples: Lichtinger and Kaplan employ a trans-scale approach observing eight elementary students across cognitive, rational, and social bands via observation, strategy traces, and interviews
key_sources: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6

article_title: Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations
citation: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6
title: Combine multiple complementary methods to accommodate the complex structure of SRL processes
description: The article contends that while statistical methodologies for testing theorized SRL relationships have long been available, collecting sufficiently precise and comprehensive data remains a challenge. It argues that "it is often necessary to combine multiple methods in order to accommodate the complex structure of the SRL process", and intentionally includes papers demonstrating how complementary methods illuminate dynamic or contingent relations and contextual influences on SRL.
requirements: Each measurement approach must be appropriately aligned to the SRL component under investigation
target_learners: SRL researchers studying learners across contexts
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations in SRL
examples: The issue pairs think-aloud protocols with contingency analysis, embedded questionnaires with trace methodologies, and parallel context-anchored surveys with qualitative questions
key_sources: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6

article_title: Performance judgment in mathematical and reading competence in adults
citation: Maximilian Seitz, Anna Hawrot, Kathrin Lockl. (2025). Performance judgment in mathematical and reading competence in adults. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09416-2
title: Adult educators should improve learners' performance-judgment accuracy while also attending to motivational aspects and realistic learning goals
description: The article's practical implication is that adult educators face a dual task: poor judgment accuracy can lead to inadequate learning behavior, so educators should aim at improving monitoring abilities, yet grounding overly positive self-views may diminish motivation. The authors therefore recommend that teaching adults should "also focus on motivational aspects and realistic learning goals" rather than accuracy correction alone.
requirements: Educators involved in adult education who want to support self-regulated learning in settings where lifelong learning occurs.
constraints: The article notes that making judgments more accurate by grounding overly positive self-views may diminish motivation, leading to poorer learning behavior such as decreased learning time.
target_learners: Adult learners in formal and non-formal adult education, including middle-aged and older adults
target_learning_goals: Accurate self-assessment of performance
Self-regulated learning in adulthood
examples: The study provides indication that older learners' accuracy decreases or, given the sensitivity analyses, at least remains at the same level of overestimation, which the authors present as relevant for teachers and educators involved in adult education.
key_sources: Maximilian Seitz, Anna Hawrot, Kathrin Lockl. (2025). Performance judgment in mathematical and reading competence in adults. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09416-2

article_title: Reverse-correlation reveals internal error-corrections during information-seeking
citation: Lorenz Weise, Saskia D. Forster, Siegfried Gauggel. (2022). Reverse-correlation reveals internal error-corrections during information-seeking. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:321–335. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09286-4
title: Unitary confidence mechanism supporting the isomechanism view of metacognitive monitoring
description: The article advances the account that different ways of expressing confidence reflect one underlying inferential process rather than specialized processes. It states that "a unitary confidence mechanism was able to explain behavioral results in all three conditions without distinguishing between the three forms of assessing confidence", which "speaks to the isomechanism position". The mechanism is a signal-detection-style decision-and-confidence model in which low-confidence trials trigger a second internal signal sample; allowing internal error-corrections explains why info-seeking yields inverted decision weights while explicit reports and wagering do not.
requirements: Confidence is assessed on the same primary decision task across methods, with stimulus difficulty titrated by an adaptive psychometric procedure
constraints: The article notes its design does not allow correlating different judgments over the same study items because a blocked design was used, and the effects were demonstrated only in a numerical comparison task
target_learners: adult decision-makers performing perceptual-numerical judgment tasks
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring of decision confidence
examples: Fitting the signal-detection-based decision-and-confidence model to each participant's reverse-correlation decision weights from all three confidence-assessment conditions
key_sources: Lorenz Weise, Saskia D. Forster, Siegfried Gauggel. (2022). Reverse-correlation reveals internal error-corrections during information-seeking. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:321–335. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09286-4

article_title: Effects of disfluency on cognitive and metacognitive processes and outcomes
citation: Tim Kühl & Alexander Eitel. (2016). Effects of disfluency on cognitive and metacognitive processes and outcomes. Metacognition and Learning, 11, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9154-x
title: Do not implement perceptual disfluency (degraded fonts) as an instructional intervention
description: The editorial draws a direct instructional recommendation from the special issue's null results: perceptual disfluency via degraded fonts should not be implemented in educational settings, because all 13 experiments failed to show better performance and the effect appears marginal or condition-bound. The authors state: "results further question the positive impact of disfluency interventions in educational settings, and we would not recommend implementing them." This recommendation is grounded in the special issue's systematic tests of moderators and mediators.
requirements: Sound experimentation and sufficient sample size, as required for inclusion in the special issue, to establish that null effects are meaningful boundary conditions rather than methodological flaws
constraints: The recommendation concerns perceptual disfluency manipulations (fonts, blurring, greyscale); the authors note it does not necessarily generalize to stronger difficulties such as deleting words from a passage
target_learners: university students
school pupils
target_learning_goals: retention and comprehension of instructional materials
reasoning task performance
examples: The special issue assembled six manuscripts with 13 experiments and more than 1000 participants testing disfluency effects on recall, comprehension, transfer, and metacognitive monitoring
key_sources: Tim Kühl & Alexander Eitel. (2016). Effects of disfluency on cognitive and metacognitive processes and outcomes. Metacognition and Learning, 11, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9154-x

article_title: Effects of disfluency on cognitive and metacognitive processes and outcomes
citation: Tim Kühl & Alexander Eitel. (2016). Effects of disfluency on cognitive and metacognitive processes and outcomes. Metacognition and Learning, 11, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9154-x
title: Disfluency theory: perceptual difficulty as a metacognitive cue activating System 2 processing via monitoring and control
description: The editorial frames disfluency theory within dual-process considerations (System 1 quick and intuitive, System 2 slow and analytic) and the Nelson and Narens metamemory framework of monitoring and control. Perceptual disfluency is hypothesized to lower confidence, thereby initiating control processes — more mental effort, longer studying — that activate analytic processing and improve performance. The authors describe the mechanism: "lower perceptual fluency (i.e., disfluency) can influence monitoring because the contents are perceived as more difficult, leading to lower confidence (on meta-level), and in turn, control processes are initiated."
requirements: The mechanism requires learners to perceive the disfluency as a metacognitive cue about their mastery, and monitoring changes must translate into adequate control processes
constraints: The special issue's results suggest disfluency did not trigger more effective control processes such as longer and more effortful studying that fostered performance
target_learners: university students
school pupils
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognitive monitoring accuracy
examples: The editorial explains the original positive findings of Diemand-Yauman et al. (2011) via this monitoring-and-control mechanism
key_sources: Tim Kühl & Alexander Eitel. (2016). Effects of disfluency on cognitive and metacognitive processes and outcomes. Metacognition and Learning, 11, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9154-x

article_title: Reflection on exam grades to improve calibration of secondary school students: a longitudinal study
citation: Nederhand, M. L., Tabbers, H. K., Jongerling, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2020). Reflection on exam grades to improve calibration of secondary school students: a longitudinal study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09233-9
title: Ask students for grade estimates after each exam as an easy-to-implement way to improve calibration accuracy in secondary education
description: The article concludes that simply having students estimate their grade after each exam, before receiving the actual grade, improves their calibration accuracy over a school year without needing additional reflection support. As the authors state, "asking for grade estimates is an easy-to-implement way to improve calibration accuracy of students in secondary education." The practice fits existing classroom routines since grades are already collected.
requirements: Students must actually provide a grade estimate before receiving the actual grade, as part of regular exam administration.
constraints: Improvement was demonstrated in one subject (French) with objectively scored exams; calibration did not improve in non-intervention courses (German, Math).
target_learners: secondary school students, years 1–3 of Dutch pre-university education (ages 12–16)
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of exam performance; calibration accuracy; metacognitive monitoring
examples: Across a school year, students in all three conditions filled out an estimate form after each French exam, sealing it in an envelope before receiving the graded exam about a week later.
key_sources: Nederhand, M. L., Tabbers, H. K., Jongerling, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2020). Reflection on exam grades to improve calibration of secondary school students: a longitudinal study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09233-9

article_title: Reflection on exam grades to improve calibration of secondary school students: a longitudinal study
citation: Nederhand, M. L., Tabbers, H. K., Jongerling, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2020). Reflection on exam grades to improve calibration of secondary school students: a longitudinal study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09233-9
title: Three-activity framework for interventions that use grades to improve calibration accuracy
description: The article proposes that improving calibration with grades requires support on three sequential activities: making an estimate, checking the estimate against the actual grade, and reflecting on the cause of any miscalibration. As the authors put it, "First, students need to actually provide a grade estimate before receiving the actual grade. Second, students should check whether there is a mismatch between their initial estimate and their actual grade." Third, students should "reflect on the cause of their miscalibration" to improve future estimates. The study's three conditions operationalized increasing levels of support on these activities.
requirements: Interventions should provide support on all three activities: estimating, comparing estimate to grade, and reflecting on mismatch causes.
constraints: The article notes prior evidence for the third activity's benefit was mixed and dependent on performance level in university samples.
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: calibration accuracy; metacognitive awareness of performance estimates; self-regulated learning
