examples: The study's conditions mapped onto the framework: Practice-only (activity 1), Grade comparison (activities 1–2), and Reflection (all three activities, with cue checklists and an open mismatch question for deviations of at least 0.5 points).
key_sources: Nederhand, M. L., Tabbers, H. K., Jongerling, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2020). Reflection on exam grades to improve calibration of secondary school students: a longitudinal study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09233-9

article_title: Assumptions and confidence of others: the impact of socio-cognitive information on metacognitive self-regulation
citation: Schnaubert, L., Krukowski, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Assumptions and confidence of others: the impact of socio-cognitive information on metacognitive self-regulation. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09269-5
title: Socio-cognitive information as an external cue in metacognitive monitoring and control
description: The article frames other people's assumptions and confidence as external cues that learners may consult when forming metacognitive judgments, extending cue-based accounts of confidence judgments beyond internally generated information. It states that "the assumptions of other individuals might be used as an external cue validating or contradicting own initial assumptions, especially in the case of limited information requiring inductive inference". Within the Nelson-and-Narens monitoring/control cycle, such cues adjust confidence on the meta-level, which then steers control decisions such as information search. The empirical study tests this account by confronting learners with a partner's answers and confidence.
requirements: Learners must perceive socio-cognitive information such as another person's assumptions and stated confidence in the learning environment.
constraints: The studied scenario was minimalistic: an unknown, computer-generated partner with no further social cues or instructions on how to use the information.
target_learners: university students in self-regulated learning settings, especially online learning environments
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and control of learning, including confidence judgments and study decisions such as information search
examples: Participants read expository texts, judged true-false statements on a combined confidence/answer scale, viewed a computer-generated partner's answers and confidence, then re-judged and could request additional information.
key_sources: Schnaubert, L., Krukowski, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Assumptions and confidence of others: the impact of socio-cognitive information on metacognitive self-regulation. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09269-5

article_title: Introduction to special issue on facilitating self-regulated learning with scaffolds: Recent advances and future directions
citation: Joep van der Graaf, Michelle Taub, Yizhou Fan. (2023). Introduction to special issue on facilitating self-regulated learning with scaffolds: Recent advances and future directions. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09364-9
title: SMA-grid and what/when/how/by-whom-or-what frameworks for characterizing SRL scaffolds
description: The introduction uses two frameworks to compare the special-issue studies. The SMA-grid (Molenaar et al., 2023) characterizes each study by CAMM processes (Cognition, Affect, Metacognition, Motivation), data streams (physiological, behavioral, contextual), and analytical approach (unimodal, horizontal, vertical, integrated). Alongside it, the what, when, how, and by whom or what of scaffolding (Azevedo & Jacobson, 2008) distinguishes what to scaffold, when to provide a scaffold, how it is delivered, and the delivery mechanism. Together these axes organize the seven contributions' similarities and differences.
requirements: Studies must report their SRL processes, data streams, and analytical approach so they can be placed on the SMA-grid axes
constraints: The introduction notes the contributions focus on the C and M of CAMM, one data stream, and log-file data, so the grid's affect/motivation and multimodal cells are barely exercised in this issue
target_learners: university students
secondary students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognition
examples: Table 1 classifies each of the six contributions by CAMM processes, data stream(s), who, when, how, and whom or what, e.g., Dever et al.: log data and questionnaires, during learning, pedagogical agents, rule-based, log-informed
key_sources: Joep van der Graaf, Michelle Taub, Yizhou Fan. (2023). Introduction to special issue on facilitating self-regulated learning with scaffolds: Recent advances and future directions. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09364-9

article_title: The underconfidence-with-practice effect in action memory: The contribution of retrieval practice to metacognitive monitoring
citation: Kubik, V., Jemstedt, A., Mahjub Eshratabadi, H., Schwartz, B. L., & Jönsson, F. U. (2022). The underconfidence-with-practice effect in action memory: The contribution of retrieval practice to metacognitive monitoring. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09288-2
title: Three theoretical accounts of the underconfidence-with-practice effect: mnemonic debiasing, memory for past test, and anchoring-and-adjustment
description: The article organizes the UWP effect around three competing explanatory accounts. The mnemonic-debiasing account holds that "the UWP effect occurs as a function of a foresight bias, which is alleviated by self-testing during practice". The Memory-for-Past-Test (MPT) account proposes that JOLs result partly from memory for the last test, producing underconfidence when previously unrecalled items are newly learned. The anchoring-and-adjustment account maintains that people set an anchor when making JOLs from which they insufficiently depart as learning progresses. The article evaluates all three against its action-memory data and concludes no single account suffices.
requirements: Repeated study–test cycles with item-based JOLs collected at study so calibration, resolution and past-test correlations can be computed
constraints: The article concludes the UWP effect cannot be explained by any single account; evidence for the anchoring-and-adjustment account in this study is correlational because the anchor point was not experimentally manipulated
target_learners: adult learners (undergraduate students) studying verbal or enacted action material
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring of one's own learning across repeated study–test cycles
examples: The experiment tested the accounts' predictions by comparing study–test and study–study items across three cycles with enactive and verbal encoding
key_sources: Kubik, V., Jemstedt, A., Mahjub Eshratabadi, H., Schwartz, B. L., & Jönsson, F. U. (2022). The underconfidence-with-practice effect in action memory: The contribution of retrieval practice to metacognitive monitoring. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09288-2

article_title: Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning
citation: Janssen, J., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Kanselaar, G. (2010). Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9061-5
title: Four-activity framework of online collaboration: task-related activities, social activities, regulation of task-related activities, and regulation of social activities
description: The article proposes that online collaboration comprises four types of activities: task-related activities in the content space (exchanging information, asking questions), social activities in the relational space (greetings, social support, grounding via shared understanding), regulation of task-related activities (planning, monitoring, evaluating task progress), and regulation of social activities (planning, monitoring, evaluating the collaboration). The authors argue that "to gain a complete picture of the nature of online collaboration, attention should be paid to all four activities," noting researchers usually address only one or two. The framework was operationalized in a 19-category coding scheme and validated by factor analysis.
requirements: A coding scheme distinguishing the four activity types applied to logged communication, aggregated to the group level
constraints: The study examined secondary education students working on history inquiry tasks in one CSCL environment; the authors note only correlations, not cause-effect relationships, could be established
target_learners: Secondary education students in the pre-university track, aged 15–18
target_learning_goals: Collaborative historical inquiry: reading, comprehending and synthesizing historical sources into group texts
examples: The coding scheme classified chat messages into 19 categories across the four scales, coded with the MEPA program with Cohen's Kappa between .86 and .94 across the three studies
key_sources: Janssen, J., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Kanselaar, G. (2010). Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9061-5

article_title: Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning
citation: Janssen, J., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Kanselaar, G. (2010). Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9061-5
title: Virtual Collaborative Research Institute (VCRI) CSCL environment
description: VCRI is a groupware program designed to support collaborative learning on inquiry tasks and research projects, developed for students from primary to higher education. Students use it to communicate, access information sources, and co-author texts. Its shared tools support three activities of collaborative inquiry: task-related or cognitive activities (Sources-tool, Diagrammer, Debate-tool, Cowriter shared word processor), metacognitive activities (planning and evaluating the inquiry process), and social activities (monitoring the collaborative process and supporting communication, e.g., the synchronous Chat-tool).
requirements: Students work on collaborative inquiry projects over longer periods of time, with teacher access to monitor discussions and texts
constraints: In the reported studies students worked on separate computers in a computer lab and mostly communicated electronically, though they could talk face-to-face
target_learners: Students ranging from primary to higher education; in this study, fifth-year pre-university secondary students
target_learning_goals: Collaborative inquiry: exploring topics, collecting and summarizing sources, discussing, constructing argument diagrams, and co-writing essays
examples: Across the three studies, groups used VCRI for eight 50-minute lessons per inquiry task, producing chat protocols averaging 923 messages per group
key_sources: Janssen, J., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Kanselaar, G. (2010). Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9061-5

article_title: Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning
citation: Janssen, J., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Kanselaar, G. (2010). Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9061-5
title: Groups collaborating online should devote effort to regulating the collaboration itself, since social regulation supports group performance
description: The article concludes that regulating the collective activity—discussing collaboration strategies, monitoring the group process, and evaluating how the group collaborated—supports group performance, whereas regulation efforts concentrated only on the task showed no such effect. The authors state that "when groups devoted more energy to regulating the collaboration, they performed better" and that "a minimum amount of regulation of social activities is a prerequisite for successful group performance." This principle directs CSCL designers and teachers to prompt and support socially shared regulation, not merely task planning.
requirements: Group members must be interdependent on a shared group product so that coordinating the collaboration matters
constraints: The supporting evidence is correlational, from secondary students on history inquiry tasks; the authors note no causal inferences could be made, and social activities (non-regulative socializing) negatively predicted performance
target_learners: Secondary education students working in small groups in CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: Effective coordination of collaborative group processes during inquiry tasks, leading to better group products
examples: In the study, regulation of social activities included planning the collaboration (3.30% of messages), monitoring the group process (5.45%), and evaluating the group process (less than 1%)
key_sources: Janssen, J., Erkens, G., Kirschner, P. A., & Kanselaar, G. (2010). Task-related and social regulation during online collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9061-5

article_title: Introduction to special issue mind the gap between research and practice in the area of teachers’ support of metacognition and SRL
citation: Charlotte Dignath, Zemira Mevarech. (2021). Introduction to special issue mind the gap between research and practice in the area of teachers' support of metacognition and SRL. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09285-5
title: A generic model of teacher competence applied to teachers' promotion of SRL (knowledge, beliefs, self-efficacy)
description: The editorial describes applying a generic model of teacher competence (Baumert & Kunter, 2013) to the context of teachers' promotion of SRL. In the first study, profiles of teacher competence regarding SRL were "based on teachers' knowledge, beliefs, and self-efficacy about supporting SRL in the classroom" and were associated with teachers' self-reported SRL practice; a second study evaluated a professional development training on teacher and student levels.
requirements: Assessment of teachers' knowledge, beliefs, and self-efficacy about supporting SRL to identify competence profiles
constraints: Profiles were associated with teachers' self-reported SRL practice; training effects were examined in a separate second study
target_learners: in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: supporting students' self-regulated learning in the classroom
examples: The editorial describes a two-study program: profile identification from teacher characteristics, then a professional development training evaluated on both teacher and student levels, with competence profiles moderating training effects.
key_sources: Charlotte Dignath, Zemira Mevarech. (2021). Introduction to special issue mind the gap between research and practice in the area of teachers' support of metacognition and SRL. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09285-5

article_title: Is the perceptual disfluency effect moderated by working memory capacity? Direct replication of Lehmann et al. (2016)
citation: Sophia C. Weissgerber, Denia Indah Permatasari Terhorst, Ralf Rummer. (2024). Is the perceptual disfluency effect moderated by working memory capacity? Direct replication of Lehmann et al. (2016). Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09366-7
title: ATI account: WMC as a boundary condition of the perceptual disfluency effect (Lehmann et al.'s deeper-processing hypothesis)
description: Lehmann et al.'s aptitude-treatment interaction hypothesis holds that disfluent texts impose extra extraneous cognitive load on working memory, so "Only learners with a high WMC might have enough capacity for the higher ECL caused by less legible texts and could engage in deeper processing". Learners with low WMC cannot handle the increased ECL, cannot allocate germane resources, and their situational-model construction is hindered; with fluent material, high- and low-WMC learners should show similar outcomes. The present replication tested this hypothesis directly and found its data "are not indicative of WMC as a boundary condition moderating the disfluency effect on learning".
requirements: The hypothesis presupposes that perceptual disfluency increases extraneous cognitive load that competes with germane resources, per Cognitive Load Theory (Sweller et al., 2011)
constraints: The replication data do not support the hypothesis; the article questions its robustness and generalizability beyond the primary study
target_learners: learners studying expository texts, characterized by working memory capacity
target_learning_goals: retention, comprehension, and transfer of expository text material (time and date differences on earth)
examples: Lehmann et al. (2016) operationalized disfluency as a grey-scaled Haettenschweiler 12 pt font versus black Arial 12 pt, measured WMC with the Numerical Updating Memory subtest (Oberauer et al., 2000), and tested retention, comprehension, and transfer
key_sources: Sophia C. Weissgerber, Denia Indah Permatasari Terhorst, Ralf Rummer. (2024). Is the perceptual disfluency effect moderated by working memory capacity? Direct replication of Lehmann et al. (2016). Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09366-7

article_title: Towards efficient measurement of metacognition in mathematical problem solving
citation: Jacobse, A. E., & Harskamp, E. G. (2012). Towards efficient measurement of metacognition in mathematical problem solving. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-012-9088-x
title: VisA instrument (Visualization and Accuracy) for group-administered on-line metacognition assessment
description: The VisA instrument combines prediction judgments, problem visualizations, and postdiction judgments into one paper-and-pencil measure of metacognitive monitoring and regulation during word problem solving. "In the VisA instrument, four word problems are presented," each split into four booklet steps: confidence rating, sketching, solving, and postdiction. Scoring awards points for accurate judgments and for schematic versus pictorial sketches, yielding a maximum of 12 points; internal consistency was α=0.70. It can be administered to groups, unlike individual think-aloud protocols.
requirements: Students must fill in every part of the instrument; teachers or test leaders need to make sure students do not inattentively skip parts
constraints: Internal consistency of α=0.70 is modest; the authors advise adding two or three comparable word tasks to raise it toward α=0.80
The instrument only partially overlaps with the think-aloud measure, so it does not cover the full breadth of metacognitive activities
target_learners: grade 5 elementary students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and regulation in mathematical word problem solving
examples: In the study, students completed the VisA measurement in a group setting, with approximately a maximum of five minutes per word problem
key_sources: Jacobse, A. E., & Harskamp, E. G. (2012). Towards efficient measurement of metacognition in mathematical problem solving. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-012-9088-x

article_title: Connecting teachers’ classroom instructions with children’s metacognition and learning in elementary school
citation: Mariëtte H. van Loon, et al. (2021). Connecting teachers' classroom instructions with children's metacognition and learning in elementary school. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09248-2
title: Support children's metacognition through the way instructions are given, not only their content
description: The study's central design implication is that how teachers deliver instructions matters for children's procedural metacognition. Child-centered practices that give children autonomy to regulate their own learning predicted more effective restudy and more accurate self-monitoring, whereas teacher-directed delivery predicted less accurate monitoring. As the authors put it, "not only the content of the instructions itself, but particularly the way these are given, affects children's metacognition." Teachers should therefore pair strategy content with opportunities for children to practice self-regulated strategy use.
requirements: Teachers must provide opportunities for children to practice strategies during self-regulated learning activities, not only describe strategies.
constraints: Evidence comes from one standardized 30-minute secret-code lesson in second and fourth grade classrooms; relations are correlational, and the restudy benefit of child-centered instruction appeared for second graders in this sample.
target_learners: Elementary school children (second and fourth grade)
target_learning_goals: Accurate self-monitoring of performance
Effective restudy selection and regulation of study
Memory performance on paired-associate learning
examples: Teachers taught the same secret-code task in their own way for 30 minutes; classrooms varying in child-centered instruction were compared on children's restudy selections and confidence judgments.
key_sources: Mariëtte H. van Loon, et al. (2021). Connecting teachers' classroom instructions with children's metacognition and learning in elementary school. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09248-2

article_title: Relating self reports of writing behaviour and online task execution using a temporal model
citation: Tillema, M., van den Bergh, H., Rijlaarsdam, G., & Sanders, T. (2011). Relating self reports of writing behaviour and online task execution using a temporal model. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9072-x
title: Planner and reviser writing styles as temporally distinct configurations of (meta)cognitive activities
description: The article works within a temporal model of writing in which the quality of task execution depends on when (meta)cognitive activities occur, not only how often. Within it, two extreme styles are defined: "Planners are writers who generate plans before text production. Revisers use text production as a means to arrive at a content plan." The styles imply different temporal distributions of activities such as reading the assignment, planning, text production and revising, and are measured as continuous dimensions rather than categories.
requirements: Measurement of writing behaviour must capture the moments at which activities occur, since the styles are defined by temporal distribution across task execution.
constraints: The article raises doubts about the usability of the reviser dimension for less proficient writers, given its lower reliability and the extreme low frequency of revising activities in this age group.
target_learners: secondary school students (fourteen- and fifteen-year-olds) writing argumentative essays
target_learning_goals: argumentative writing processes, including planning, text production and revising
examples: Students with higher planner scores applied more planning activities at the start of task execution, fitting the planner style definition.
key_sources: Tillema, M., van den Bergh, H., Rijlaarsdam, G., & Sanders, T. (2011). Relating self reports of writing behaviour and online task execution using a temporal model. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9072-x

article_title: Relating self reports of writing behaviour and online task execution using a temporal model
citation: Tillema, M., van den Bergh, H., Rijlaarsdam, G., & Sanders, T. (2011). Relating self reports of writing behaviour and online task execution using a temporal model. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9072-x
title: Analyze writing process data temporally, taking the moments at which cognitive activities occur into account
description: The article advocates analyzing cognitive processing during writing as a function of the moment in task execution, for example by splitting protocols into equally long episodes and modelling activity occurrence per episode. As the authors put it, "analyses of cognitive processing during writing should take the moment(s) at which cognitive activities occur into account." In this study this temporal modelling is what allowed offline questionnaire scores to predict online behaviour at all.
requirements: Online process data (think-aloud protocols, keystroke logs) segmented into episodes so that start, middle and end of task execution are comparable across writers and tasks.
constraints: The article notes temporal analysis is not always needed, since frequential main effects were also found for some activities.
target_learners: researchers and designers analysing writing processes of secondary school students
target_learning_goals: understanding and predicting the temporal distribution of (meta)cognitive activities during writing
examples: Protocols were split into five equally long episodes and occurrence of each activity was modelled with multilevel polynomial regression, including score-by-episode interactions.
key_sources: Tillema, M., van den Bergh, H., Rijlaarsdam, G., & Sanders, T. (2011). Relating self reports of writing behaviour and online task execution using a temporal model. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9072-x

article_title: Curiosity can influence metacognitive processes
citation: Sunae Kim, Paul L Harris, Benjamin Néher. (2025). Curiosity can influence metacognitive processes. Metacognition and Learning (2025) 20:39. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09444-y
title: Curiosity serves a metacognitive function: a bidirectional account linking curiosity to metacognitive monitoring and control
description: The article proposes that the relationship between curiosity and metacognition is bidirectional: metacognitive experiences elicit curiosity (as prior frameworks assume), and feelings of curiosity in turn guide metacognitive monitoring and control. The authors suggest that "feelings of curiosity serve similar functions as internal heuristics, which then guide metacognitive monitoring and control", situating curiosity among internal cues such as familiarity and processing fluency. They also connect the findings to Shea and colleagues' distinction between metacognition 1 (individual level) and metacognition 2 (shared metacognitive information used to coordinate decisions), arguing that people use others' curiosity to recalibrate their own metacognitive experiences.
requirements: Curiosity must be measured or manipulated independently of information-seeking so that metacognitive functions can be distinguished from automatic curiosity-driven behavior
constraints: The exact mechanisms underlying the interplay between curiosity and metacognitive processes remain beyond the scope of the present research
Experiments 1 and 2 provide only correlational evidence; only the 3A–3B comparison directly examined the impact of curiosity on metacognitive control
Findings are from adult samples (Hungarian and UK) answering general knowledge questions
target_learners: adults answering general knowledge questions
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring of answer accuracy
metacognitive control decisions such as withholding responses
key_sources: Sunae Kim, Paul L Harris, Benjamin Néher. (2025). Curiosity can influence metacognitive processes. Metacognition and Learning (2025) 20:39. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09444-y

article_title: Metacognition, achievement goals, study strategies and academic achievement: pathways to achievement
citation: Anneke Vrugt & Frans J. Oort. (2008). Metacognition, achievement goals, study strategies and academic achievement: pathways to achievement. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-008-9022-4
title: Two-pathway model of effective self-regulated learning: a metacognitive pathway and a strategy pathway
description: The article proposes and tests a causal model in which achievement goals (mastery, performance-approach, performance-avoidance), metacognition (knowledge, regulation, experience), and four study strategy types jointly determine exam scores. As the abstract states, "effective self-regulated learning involved two pathways: a metacognitive and a strategy pathway." The metacognitive pathway runs from mastery goals through metacognition to all four strategies; the strategy pathway carries direct effects of mastery and performance-approach goals on strategies, bypassing metacognition. The model was tested with structural equation modeling controlling for intellectual ability, gender and age.
requirements: Requires measures of achievement goals, metacognition, study strategies and achievement, plus control of intellectual ability, gender and age as the article did
constraints: The fitted model required adding direct goal-to-strategy paths beyond the hypothesized indirect structure; the negative avoidance-to-metacognition path held only for effective self-regulators
target_learners: first-year university psychology students
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in an introductory course
self-regulated learning skills
examples: The model was fitted separately to 421 effective and 383 less effective self-regulators distinguished by effort expenditure on MSLQ effort regulation items
key_sources: Anneke Vrugt & Frans J. Oort. (2008). Metacognition, achievement goals, study strategies and academic achievement: pathways to achievement. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-008-9022-4

article_title: Co-regulation of learning in computer-supported collaborative learning environments: a discussion
citation: Carol K. K. Chan. (2012). Co-regulation of learning in computer-supported collaborative learning environments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 63–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-012-9086-z
title: Three-level regulation framework distinguishing self-regulation, co-regulation and shared regulation
description: A recently-advanced framework for regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning distinguishes three levels of regulation. The review reports that it "distinguishes between “self-regulation”, “co-regulation”, and “shared regulation” based on how they pertain to different processes such as monitoring, standards, control; self, task and strategy knowledge". Shared regulation emphasizes shared goals and joint understanding of the team as a whole, with regulation occurring at self, member(s) and group levels. The review treats it as a fruitful model for future co-regulation research.
requirements: Analytic schemes and instructional experiments to examine the complex nature of co-regulated learning
constraints: The review states these models of shared and collective regulation need further examination
target_learners: students working in groups in computer-supported collaborative learning environments
target_learning_goals: regulation of collaborative inquiry and learning
key_sources: Carol K. K. Chan. (2012). Co-regulation of learning in computer-supported collaborative learning environments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 63–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-012-9086-z

article_title: Co-regulation of learning in computer-supported collaborative learning environments: a discussion
citation: Carol K. K. Chan. (2012). Co-regulation of learning in computer-supported collaborative learning environments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 63–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-012-9086-z
title: Social metacognition and collective regulation account of co-regulated learning in CSCL
description: The review advances a socio-cognitive account in which regulation in collaborative learning extends self-regulation to social and collective levels. It argues that "working in groups may help students develop social metacognition and become more aware of what they do not understand", and that students must develop metacognitive awareness of their team's state of knowledge, since only when students perceive gaps in the group's knowledge do they exert regulatory strategies. It extends this to collective regulation, with students focusing on the group-team as a collective entity, moving from 'I' to 'We' perspectives.
requirements: Models of co-regulation need to include elements of metacognitive knowledge
constraints: The review notes much controversy and confusion about the regulation and metacognition constructs, and that current analyses emphasize frequencies of strategies rather than quality and depth of conceptual processing
target_learners: students in small-group collaborative inquiry
target_learning_goals: co-regulation, social metacognition, awareness of own and group knowledge gaps
key_sources: Carol K. K. Chan. (2012). Co-regulation of learning in computer-supported collaborative learning environments: a discussion. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 63–73. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-012-9086-z

article_title: Granularity matters: comparing different ways of measuring self-regulated learning
citation: Rovers, S. F. E., Clarebout, G., Savelberg, H. H. C. M., de Bruin, A. B. H., & van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2019). Granularity matters: comparing different ways of measuring self-regulated learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09188-6
title: Granularity as the organizing construct for comparing SRL measurement methods
description: Granularity is the review's central explanatory construct: it refers to the "level of detail at which self-regulatory processes are measured", distinguishing coarse-grained measurement of global SRL process phases from fine-grained measurement of students' micro-level SRL processes (Azevedo 2009). The review uses this axis to organize its 14 included studies and to explain why self-reports and behavioral measures converge at one grain size but diverge at the other. It thereby functions as a taxonomy of SRL measurement comparisons rather than a model of SRL itself.
requirements: Measurement comparisons must specify the grain size at which SRL is operationalized before calibration conclusions can be drawn
constraints: The review restricts its evidence base to students in higher education and to studies comparing offline self-reports with online measures
target_learners: students in higher education
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement and support of self-regulated learning strategy use
examples: The review separates its ten fine-grained comparison studies from its four global-level comparison studies in Tables 2 and 3 and draws different calibration conclusions for each group
key_sources: Rovers, S. F. E., Clarebout, G., Savelberg, H. H. C. M., de Bruin, A. B. H., & van Merriënboer, J. J. G. (2019). Granularity matters: comparing different ways of measuring self-regulated learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09188-6

article_title: Exploring the connection between task difficulty, task perceptions, physiological arousal and learning outcomes in collaborative learning situations
citation: Malmberg, J., Haataja, E., & Järvelä, S. (2022). Exploring the connection between task difficulty, task perceptions, physiological arousal and learning outcomes in collaborative learning situations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09320-z
title: Qridi platform with 6Q tool for situational task perception ratings
description: The Qridi® platform was used to coordinate students' collaborative learning and hosted the 6Q tool, "which was tailored to increase the students’ awareness of collaborative learning and to support their awareness of the regulation of learning". It collected single-item slider ratings (0–100) of task understanding and task difficulty before and after each collaborative task, plus quizzes, with all activities time-stamped on an external server. In this study the information was shown only to students.
requirements: Students rate task understanding and task difficulty before and after each collaborative task using single-item slider scales to minimize interference with group interaction
constraints: In this study the information was offered only to the students, not to the teacher
target_learners: upper elementary school students aged 13-14
target_learning_goals: physics content on sound, light, lenses and reflection
examples: Students rated 'How well do you understand the task?' and 'How difficult is the task?' before and after each of five collaborative physics tasks, then completed a five-to-six question multiple choice quiz
key_sources: Malmberg, J., Haataja, E., & Järvelä, S. (2022). Exploring the connection between task difficulty, task perceptions, physiological arousal and learning outcomes in collaborative learning situations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09320-z

article_title: Exploring the connection between task difficulty, task perceptions, physiological arousal and learning outcomes in collaborative learning situations
citation: Malmberg, J., Haataja, E., & Järvelä, S. (2022). Exploring the connection between task difficulty, task perceptions, physiological arousal and learning outcomes in collaborative learning situations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09320-z
title: COPES framework of self-regulated learning (Winne & Hadwin)
description: The Winne & Hadwin (1998) SRL model proposes that "regulation occurs in four loosely sequenced, recursive phases: task perceptions, goal setting, strategic enactment and adaptation". Their COPES framework (conditions, operations, products, evaluations and standards) models the conditions and identifies the facets where learners exercise SRL. External conditions (social and contextual features, task complexity, resources, time constraints) and internal cognitive conditions (metacognitive knowledge of task characteristics, judgments of task difficulty, prior domain knowledge, efficacy judgments) influence the whole process; operations create internal and external products that are compared to standards through metacognitive monitoring, and evaluations can trigger adaptations. The article uses this framework to frame how internal conditions such as task understanding and task difficulty shape regulation in collaborative learning.
requirements: Learners exercise SRL across phases in which conditions frame task perception and products are evaluated against self-set standards
constraints: The framework aims to describe how students adapt SRL to the current learning task; the article notes it provides a means to understand internal conditions in individual and collaborative learning
target_learners: students in individual and collaborative learning situations
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning across task perception, goal setting, enactment and adaptation
examples: The study operationalized internal conditions as situational ratings of task understanding and task difficulty before and after collaborative tasks
key_sources: Malmberg, J., Haataja, E., & Järvelä, S. (2022). Exploring the connection between task difficulty, task perceptions, physiological arousal and learning outcomes in collaborative learning situations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09320-z

article_title: Longitudinal associations between executive functions and metacognitive monitoring in 5- to 8-year-olds
citation: Sonja Kälin, Claudia M. Roebers. (2022). Longitudinal associations between executive functions and metacognitive monitoring in 5- to 8-year-olds. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09306-x
title: Inhibition-as-prerequisite account: inhibition enables children to hesitate and take time when monitoring, producing less overconfident judgments
description: The article proposes a mechanism account in which metacognitive monitoring requires time to accumulate evidence, and inhibition skills allow children to suppress impulsive confidence judgments and hesitate. Better inhibition is assumed to down-regulate anterior cingulate cortex activation, enabling slower, more thorough reflection on mental processes and thus more accurate, less overconfident monitoring. The account explains why inhibition, but not working memory or shifting, predicted later monitoring in this study.
requirements: Children must have sufficient inhibition skills to override the impulse to give a rushed confidence judgment so that evidence can be accumulated over time
constraints: The article states it cannot rule out an alternative direct effect in which inhibition suppresses the default of indicating high confidence independent of judgment time
The account is offered as an interpretation; the study measured associations, not the mediating process
target_learners: Children aged 5 to 8 years transitioning from kindergarten to elementary school
target_learning_goals: Accurate metacognitive monitoring of one's own performance (realistic confidence judgments)
examples: The authors draw on Espinet et al. (2013), linking reflection, slower responding and down-regulation of ACC activation to better EF skills, and on Pleskac & Busemeyer (2010) on evidence accumulation for confidence judgments
key_sources: Sonja Kälin, Claudia M. Roebers. (2022). Longitudinal associations between executive functions and metacognitive monitoring in 5- to 8-year-olds. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09306-x

article_title: Exploring the relations between teachers’ cue-utilization, monitoring and regulation of students’ text learning
citation: Janneke van de Pol, Selia N. van den Boom-Muilenburg, Tamara van Gog. (2021). Exploring the relations between teachers' cue-utilization, monitoring and regulation of students' text learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09268-6
title: Cue-utilization framework applied to teacher monitoring of student text comprehension
description: The article organizes its study around the cue-utilization framework (Koriat, 1997), in which monitoring accuracy depends on how predictive the information, or cues, used for monitoring judgments is for students' actual performance. Teachers need "bits of information (also known as 'cues') that are predictive or diagnostic of students' comprehension". The framework distinguishes performance cues, student cues, and task cues, and predicts that more diagnostic cue availability yields more accurate monitoring and, in turn, more adaptive regulation.
requirements: Teachers must have and use cues that are predictive or diagnostic of students' comprehension for monitoring judgments to be accurate.
constraints: The article notes previous studies did not find monitoring differences between student-cues-only and student-plus-performance-cues conditions, complicating the framework's simple prediction.
target_learners: secondary education teachers
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of students' text comprehension
adaptive regulation of students' learning from texts
examples: Teachers judged fifteen students under three cue-availability conditions: name-only, name + diagram, and diagram-only, with task cues always available.
key_sources: Janneke van de Pol, Selia N. van den Boom-Muilenburg, Tamara van Gog. (2021). Exploring the relations between teachers' cue-utilization, monitoring and regulation of students' text learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09268-6

article_title: Development of Children’s monitoring and control when learning from texts: effects of age and test format
citation: Steiner, M., van Loon, M. H., Bayard, N. S., & Roebers, C. M. (2020). Development of Children's monitoring and control when learning from texts: effects of age and test format. Metacognition and Learning, 15, 3–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09208-5
title: Use open-ended recall questions when test conditions should support children's accurate monitoring and control of their answers
description: The article argues that the design of a test affects students' metacognitive accuracy: recall questions elicit active retrieval, giving learners valid cues such as retrieval fluency, whereas recognition questions rely on familiarity that can produce erroneously high confidence. The authors state that understanding how test design affects monitoring may contribute to creating test conditions that support children to make accurate judgments, thereby improving performance.
requirements: Learners must answer the questions and provide confidence judgments so that monitoring cues (e.g., retrieval fluency) can inform control decisions such as maintaining or withdrawing answers.
constraints: The format advantage was demonstrated for elementary school children taking text comprehension tests; the article notes evidence on children's test-format effects was previously limited and misleading true-false formats may be unusual in school settings.
target_learners: elementary school students (second and fourth graders)
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of text comprehension during test taking
adaptive control decisions such as withdrawing incorrect answers
examples: In the study, children read six expository texts and answered twelve open-ended and twelve true-false questions, giving confidence judgments and deciding whether to maintain or withdraw each answer; monitoring and control were more accurate for the open-ended format.
key_sources: Steiner, M., van Loon, M. H., Bayard, N. S., & Roebers, C. M. (2020). Development of Children's monitoring and control when learning from texts: effects of age and test format. Metacognition and Learning, 15, 3–27. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09208-5

article_title: Payoff designs in post-decision wagering: a systematic review
citation: Lorenz Weise. (2024). Payoff designs in post-decision wagering: a systematic review. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09411-z
title: Taxonomy of PDW payoff schemes: four-cell matrices versus free-choice designs
description: The review organizes the heterogeneous payoff systems used in post-decision wagering into two broad classes: four-cell matrices, where a low and a high wager option combine with correct and incorrect responses to yield four possible outcomes, and free-choice designs with more than four cells. It reports that "A total of 78 four cell matrices (70% of all reviewed payoff schemes) were retrieved from the literature" and that "In total, 33 such free choice designs were retrieved from the literature (30% of all reviewed payoff schemes)". Within these classes it further distinguishes no-wager/safe-option variants, always-wager-high matrices, no-loss gambling, adjusted wagering, and designs matching other instruments.
requirements: A payoff scheme must be fully described in terms of wins and losses following wagers after correct and incorrect decisions to be classifiable
constraints: The review covers only original empirical studies using PDW published in English-language journals, identified via Web of Science and APA PsycNet searches in June and July of 2023
target_learners: researchers designing or evaluating metacognition studies using post-decision wagering
target_learning_goals: assessing confidence and metacognitive awareness with appropriately designed payoff schemes
key_sources: Lorenz Weise. (2024). Payoff designs in post-decision wagering: a systematic review. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09411-z

article_title: Payoff designs in post-decision wagering: a systematic review
citation: Lorenz Weise. (2024). Payoff designs in post-decision wagering: a systematic review. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09411-z
title: Design PDW payoff schemes in light of the specific research question; there is no single best practice
description: The review concludes that payoff design choices in post-decision wagering cannot follow one universal recipe: "it is clearly not the case that there is a single 'best practice' PDW procedure. Rather, the issues outlined here need to be considered in light of a specific research endeavor in order to determine the best design choices for the question at hand." Designers should weigh restriction of wager choice, safe or no-wager options, optimal-strategy analysis, loss aversion, and confidence-adjusted payoffs against their research goals.
requirements: Designers must consider the issues outlined (wager restriction, safe options, optimal strategies, loss aversion) in light of their specific research endeavor
constraints: Some difficulties can be circumvented via careful payoff design, but other issues, such as why participants deviate from optimal strategies, remain open questions
target_learners: researchers designing or evaluating PDW payoff systems
target_learning_goals: selecting payoff schemes that yield interpretable confidence or awareness measures
examples: The review documents that none of the reviewed payoff matrices follow the Schurger & Sher proposal of a low option punishing at chance via small wins and losses and a high option not punishing at chance but with large wins and losses
key_sources: Lorenz Weise. (2024). Payoff designs in post-decision wagering: a systematic review. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09411-z

article_title: Teacher involvement and self-regulation in homework: impact on secondary school students’ homework behavior
citation: Süleyman Avcı, Mustafa Özgenel, Akif Avcu. (2025). Teacher involvement and self-regulation in homework: impact on secondary school students’ homework behavior. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09431-3
title: Homework management as a five-dimension volitional self-regulation framework
description: The article frames homework management as students' use of self-regulated learning strategies during homework, grounded in volitional control — the ability to stay oriented toward goals set by another source, here the teacher. Drawing on Xu and Corno, it treats homework management as five dimensions: "environmental structuring, time management, distraction management, motivation monitoring, and emotion management", operationalized in the Homework Management Scale. In this study the framework is modeled as a latent mediator between teacher homework involvement and homework behavior in Turkish secondary students.
requirements: Students must be motivated to use the strategies; the article states students use self-regulation skills when they want to, so factors increasing motivation increase strategy use
constraints: The article notes self-regulation skill use varies by school level: acquired but little used in primary school, frequently used in secondary school, and not preferred in high school
target_learners: secondary school students in grades 5–8
target_learning_goals: completing homework independently
applying self-regulation strategies such as time management and emotion control during homework
examples: The study measured the five dimensions with the 22-item Turkish-adapted Homework Management Scale and modeled them as indicators of a latent homework management variable
key_sources: Süleyman Avcı, Mustafa Özgenel, Akif Avcu. (2025). Teacher involvement and self-regulation in homework: impact on secondary school students’ homework behavior. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09431-3

article_title: Teacher involvement and self-regulation in homework: impact on secondary school students’ homework behavior
citation: Süleyman Avcı, Mustafa Özgenel, Akif Avcu. (2025). Teacher involvement and self-regulation in homework: impact on secondary school students’ homework behavior. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09431-3
title: Teachers should invest in homework quality, feedback, and autonomy support to foster students' homework self-regulation
description: The article concludes that teachers' homework practices — planning and preparing quality homework, giving frequent and high-quality feedback, and supporting autonomy — encourage students to deploy self-regulation strategies, which in turn supports homework completion. As the authors put it, "teachers' efforts in the dimensions of homework quality, feedback quality, feedback quantity and autonomy support encourage students to use self-regulation strategies". Autonomy support means giving students choices in selection, preparation and presentation of assignments rather than pressuring them.
requirements: Homework should be matched to students' interests, needs and ability level; the article notes overly challenging homework can cause students with learning difficulties to develop negative attitudes toward homework
constraints: Findings come from a Turkish, moderately collectivist context; the authors note the strong involvement–management relationship differs from low relationships found in Chinese samples, so cultural context influences the strength of these links
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: homework completion
use of self-regulation strategies during homework
examples: In the study, students' perceptions of homework quality, feedback quality, feedback quantity and autonomy support were measured with the THIS and TFFS scales and entered as indicators of teacher homework involvement in the SEM model
key_sources: Süleyman Avcı, Mustafa Özgenel, Akif Avcu. (2025). Teacher involvement and self-regulation in homework: impact on secondary school students’ homework behavior. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09431-3

article_title: Software scaffolds to promote regulation during scientific inquiry learning
citation: Sarah Manlove, Ard W. Lazonder & Ton de Jong. (2007). Software scaffolds to promote regulation during scientific inquiry learning. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-007-9012-y
title: Cognitive regulation as a recursive three-phase process of planning, monitoring, and evaluation
description: The article frames regulation of cognition as "a recursive process which comprises three main phases: planning, monitoring, and evaluation." Planning establishes goal hierarchies that serve as strategic plans and standards for monitoring and evaluating performance; monitoring compares current knowledge or learning products to goal, task, or resource standards via self-questioning and elaboration; evaluation assesses learning processes and outcomes against whole-task goals and generalizes them to a broader context. The Process Coordinator tool was designed to scaffold exactly these three phases during inquiry learning.
requirements: Learners must be engaged in inquiry tasks whose phases (orientation, hypothesis formation, experimentation, drawing conclusions) can serve as process goals
constraints: The framework addresses regulation of cognition within self-regulated learning, not motivational or emotional aspects
target_learners: secondary school science students (aged 16–18)
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry skills
self-regulation of planning, monitoring, and evaluation during inquiry
examples: The Process Coordinator operationalized the framework with a process model, preset goal hierarchy, prompts, cues, and a report template mapped onto the three phases
key_sources: Sarah Manlove, Ard W. Lazonder & Ton de Jong. (2007). Software scaffolds to promote regulation during scientific inquiry learning. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-007-9012-y

article_title: Software scaffolds to promote regulation during scientific inquiry learning
citation: Sarah Manlove, Ard W. Lazonder & Ton de Jong. (2007). Software scaffolds to promote regulation during scientific inquiry learning. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-007-9012-y
title: Link regulative support closely to domain support so scaffolds for different purposes work in tandem
description: Because fully supported students relied on regulative support more than domain support and produced worse models, the authors argue there is "a need for scaffolds designed for different purposes to work in tandem with each other." They propose making this possible by linking regulative support more closely to domain supports and activities, and suggest future research investigate whether such integrated support yields higher use and perceived usefulness than stand-alone regulative support.
requirements: Regulative scaffolds must be connected to the domain supports and activities they should serve
constraints: In this study the PC+ hints referred students to specific helpfiles but "apparently did not go far enough in stressing that domain support would enhance their modeling work"
target_learners: secondary school science students working in dyads
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge construction through modeling
effective regulation of inquiry processes
examples: PC+ hints referred students to helpfiles, but this did not prevent PC+ dyads relying on regulative support more than domain support and producing lower-quality models
key_sources: Sarah Manlove, Ard W. Lazonder & Ton de Jong. (2007). Software scaffolds to promote regulation during scientific inquiry learning. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-007-9012-y

article_title: Sequential and temporal characteristics of self and socially regulated learning
citation: Inge Molenaar & Sanna Järvelä. (2014). Sequential and temporal characteristics of self and socially regulated learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-014-9114-2
title: Two views on temporality in S-SRL research: events in a continuous flow versus relative arrangements among multiple events
description: The editorial proposes that existing research on the temporal characteristics of S-SRL can be viewed through two distinct perspectives. The first "views events in a continuous flow", analyzing the positioning, duration and rate of individual S-SRL actions during learning. The second "analyzes relative arrangement among multiple events", focusing on the organization of actions over time, including development of sequential characteristics and transformations of sequences. The special-issue studies combine these perspectives to differing degrees.
requirements: Online measurement of S-SRL as a series of events, since all contributors used online measurement and view the construct as a series of events
constraints: The special issue constitutes only a first step towards understanding the sequential and temporal characteristics of S-SRL
target_learners: pre-school students to university students
target_learning_goals: understanding and supporting self and socially regulated learning processes
examples: Kuvalja et al. and Malmberg et al. incorporated both perspectives, showing they provide different insights into sequential and temporal characteristics of self-regulatory behaviour and strategy use
key_sources: Inge Molenaar & Sanna Järvelä. (2014). Sequential and temporal characteristics of self and socially regulated learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-014-9114-2

article_title: Sequential and temporal characteristics of self and socially regulated learning
citation: Inge Molenaar & Sanna Järvelä. (2014). Sequential and temporal characteristics of self and socially regulated learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-014-9114-2
title: Three-phase cyclical model of self-regulation: preparation, execution and reflection phases
description: The editorial describes consensus about three important phases in the process of self-regulation, drawing on Zimmerman (2002) and Winne & Hadwin (1998). In the "preparation phase students orientate on the task, activate existing knowledge and set their learning goals"; these goals guide the execution phase in which students perform the learning task; finally students reflect on their approach to optimize future process. The cyclical notion allows no strict order, as learners can jump between S-SRL actions inducing recursive sequential patterns within the cycle.
requirements: Learners' learning goals steer their learning, which entails the assumption that learners project these learning goals over time
constraints: Time window of the cycle is debated: Winne and Hadwin (2013) support a micro level COPE cycle re-occurring within one study session, whereas Zimmerman's (2002) cycle is more macro level, encapsulating one learning task possibly extending over multiple study sessions
target_learners: students across educational levels
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning of cognitive, metacognitive and motivational components
examples: Bannert et al. (2014) contributed empirical evidence of the sequential characteristics and the cyclical process in self-regulation theory via process mining of think aloud protocols
key_sources: Inge Molenaar & Sanna Järvelä. (2014). Sequential and temporal characteristics of self and socially regulated learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-014-9114-2

article_title: The meta-attention knowledge questionnaire (MAKQ): a new instrument for investigating meta-attention in a young adolescent sample
citation: Mulvihill, A., Matthews, N., Chidley, K., Macmahon, S., Armitage, K. L., Sherlock, D., Dux, P. E., & Carroll, A. (2025). The meta-attention knowledge questionnaire (MAKQ): a new instrument for investigating meta-attention in a young adolescent sample. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09433-1
title: The Meta-Attention Knowledge Questionnaire (MAKQ): a dual-component self-report instrument for adolescent meta-attention knowledge
description: The MAKQ is a self-report questionnaire measuring adolescent metacognitive knowledge in the domain of attention, built on Posner's attention network model and Efklides' metacognitive knowledge framework. It combines 20 self-knowledge Likert items with 12 open-ended strategy questions whose responses are coded and scored, so that "a comparison between student responses on these two components provides a novel means to investigate the interaction between self-perceived skill and researcher coded and quantified strategy knowledge within a simple questionnaire format."
requirements: Requires students to complete 20 Likert self-knowledge items and 12 open-ended strategy questions, completed online in a median time of 15.54 min in Study One
constraints: Designed for and validated in typically developing early adolescents (grades 7-8, ages 11-15) in Australian high schools
target_learners: young adolescents in grades 7-8 (ages 11-15)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge of attention: self-perceived attentional control and monitoring, and declarative strategies to self-regulate attention
examples: Study One administered the MAKQ online via Qualtrics to 293 students; Study Two administered it pen-and-paper to 83 students at the opening of an intervention session
key_sources: Mulvihill, A., Matthews, N., Chidley, K., Macmahon, S., Armitage, K. L., Sherlock, D., Dux, P. E., & Carroll, A. (2025). The meta-attention knowledge questionnaire (MAKQ): a new instrument for investigating meta-attention in a young adolescent sample. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09433-1

article_title: The meta-attention knowledge questionnaire (MAKQ): a new instrument for investigating meta-attention in a young adolescent sample
citation: Mulvihill, A., Matthews, N., Chidley, K., Macmahon, S., Armitage, K. L., Sherlock, D., Dux, P. E., & Carroll, A. (2025). The meta-attention knowledge questionnaire (MAKQ): a new instrument for investigating meta-attention in a young adolescent sample. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09433-1
title: Fourteen strategy types for adolescent self-regulation of attention, identified via inductive automated content analysis
description: Inductive automated content analysis (Leximancer 4.5) of student responses to the 12 MAKQ open-ended strategy questions identified "14 dominant themes" of strategies students use to self-manage alerting, orienting and executive attention, ranging from physical movement and meeting physiological needs to goal setting, planning, time management, and phone-specific management tools (reported by 6% of students). The most frequently reported was blocking distractions (87% of students). These themes inform the scoring of the strategy knowledge dimension.
requirements: Strategy responses are scored by frequency of mentioned strategies per the Table 3 taxonomy, requiring the coded strategy list as a scoring rubric
constraints: Strategy taxonomy derived from typically developing Australian grade 7-8 students; the least common strategy (phone-specific tools) was reported by only 6% of students
target_learners: young adolescents in grades 7-8 (ages 11-15)
target_learning_goals: declarative knowledge of strategies to self-regulate attention-related behaviours in daily learning contexts
examples: Sample strategies students reported include "Sit away from friends in order to have no one to distract me" and "Put it in order of priority, so I get what is most important done first"

Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09433-1

article_title: Scaffolding self-regulated learning from causal-relations texts: Diagramming and self-assessment to improve metacomprehension accuracy?
citation: Pijeira-Díaz, H. J., van de Pol, J., Channa, F., & de Bruin, A. (2023). Scaffolding self-regulated learning from causal-relations texts: Diagramming and self-assessment to improve metacomprehension accuracy? Metacognition and Learning, 18, 631–658. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09343-0
title: Cue-utilization framework for metacomprehension and the diagramming paradigm
description: The article works within the view that metacognitive judgments are inferential: students weight cues "in an analogous way to a multiple regression model" to predict performance. Metacomprehension accuracy depends on using cues whose diagnosticity (correlation with performance) is high; generative scaffolds such as completing pre-structured causal diagrams make diagnostic cues available before judgment. The diagramming paradigm sequences reading, diagram completion, comprehension judgments, restudy selection, and testing.
requirements: Students must complete a generative task (e.g., a pre-structured causal diagram) between reading and judging so diagnostic cues become available
constraints: Cue utilization is calculated with correlations, so causality cannot be asserted; the scaffold targets expository causal-relations texts rather than narrative texts or isolated facts
target_learners: secondary education students (11–17 years) reading expository texts
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of text comprehension
self-regulated restudy decisions when learning from causal-relations expository texts
examples: Students read six Dutch expository texts, completed pre-structured diagrams with four empty boxes, judged comprehension, selected texts for restudy, and took a comprehension test
key_sources: Pijeira-Díaz, H. J., van de Pol, J., Channa, F., & de Bruin, A. (2023). Scaffolding self-regulated learning from causal-relations texts: Diagramming and self-assessment to improve metacomprehension accuracy? Metacognition and Learning, 18, 631–658. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09343-0

article_title: Scaffolding self-regulated learning from causal-relations texts: Diagramming and self-assessment to improve metacomprehension accuracy?
citation: Pijeira-Díaz, H. J., van de Pol, J., Channa, F., & de Bruin, A. (2023). Scaffolding self-regulated learning from causal-relations texts: Diagramming and self-assessment to improve metacomprehension accuracy? Metacognition and Learning, 18, 631–658. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09343-0
title: Diagram self-assessment scaffold (prompting students to estimate completed and correct diagram boxes)
description: A paper-based scaffold added after diagram completion: students are prompted to "enter how many boxes you have completed in total and how many boxes you think are correct" for each diagram, without being allowed to revise the diagrams. It was designed to make the most diagnostic cue—number of correct boxes—more salient before comprehension judgments. In the experiment it required only an extra booklet page and no teacher support.
requirements: Must follow diagram completion immediately, with diagrams sealed so they cannot be changed during self-assessment
constraints: Did not increase diagnostic cue utilization or metacomprehension accuracy beyond diagramming alone; students appear to self-assess implicitly anyway
target_learners: secondary education students (11–17 years) reading expository texts
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of text comprehension
self-regulated learning from causal-relations texts
examples: In the experiment, the DC + SA group answered 12 self-assessment questions (2 per diagram) after completing six pre-structured diagrams

article_title: Metacognitive awareness as measured by second-order judgements among university and secondary school students
citation: Marloes L. Nederhand, Huib K. Tabbers, Anique B.H. De Bruin, Remy M. J. P. Rikers. (2021). Metacognitive awareness as measured by second-order judgements among university and secondary school students. Metacognition and Learning, 16, 1-14. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09228-6
title: Second-order judgements as a measure of metacognitive awareness that hinges on calibration accuracy rather than performance level
description: The article frames metacognitive awareness in calibration research as having two components: functional confidence (the performance estimate itself) and subjective confidence (the confidence assigned to that estimate), the latter measured by a second-order judgement (SOJ). On this account, students are metacognitively aware when their SOJs align with their calibration accuracy, "irrespective of students' performance level". The study's university results support the alignment account, while the secondary school results mark a developmental boundary.
requirements: Students must provide both a performance estimate and a confidence rating of that estimate (SOJ) so alignment between subjective confidence and calibration accuracy can be examined
constraints: The alignment between SOJs and calibration accuracy was found for university students but not for secondary school students, suggesting the account applies only once metacognitive awareness is more developed
target_learners: university students
secondary school students
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of exam performance
metacognitive monitoring of calibration accuracy
examples: After taking their exams, students estimated their grade on a 10-point scale and rated confidence in the estimate on a five-point scale, allowing the alignment of SOJs with absolute difference scores of calibration to be tested.
key_sources: Marloes L. Nederhand, Huib K. Tabbers, Anique B.H. De Bruin, Remy M. J. P. Rikers. (2021). Metacognitive awareness as measured by second-order judgements among university and secondary school students. Metacognition and Learning, 16, 1-14. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09228-6

article_title: Scaffolding students’ use of metacognitive activities using discipline- and topic-specific reflective prompts
citation: Sijmkens, E., De Cock, M., & De Laet, T. (2024). Scaffolding Students' Use of Metacognitive Activities Using Discipline- and Topic-Specific Reflective Prompts. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72353-1_2
title: Disciplinary Learning Companion (DLC)
description: The DLC is an online tool that scaffolds students' use of metacognitive activities during physics problem solving by offering discipline- and topic-specific reflective prompts. It consists of reflection modules, each linked to a particular physics textbook problem, where "students receive discipline- and even topic-specific reflective prompts, delivered in the form of multiple-choice reflection questions". After responding, students receive feedback tailored to their answers that addresses correctness, compares solving strategies, and offers actionable suggestions. Students can then download a model solution and write down a point of attention to stimulate transfer.
requirements: Students must first solve a standard physics textbook problem before engaging with the reflection module
Students must respond to each reflection question sequentially to access the complete model solution
constraints: Completion of reflection modules was voluntary and not included in course grading
Feedback is tailored to responses but not adjusted to other student characteristics, characterising it as a hard scaffold
target_learners: first-year university bioscience engineering students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive abilities in physics problem solving
conceptual understanding of Newtonian mechanics
examples: Integrated into an introductory Newtonian mechanics course for approximately 350 first-year bioscience engineering students at KU Leuven, with nine reflection modules corresponding to nine course topics
key_sources: Sijmkens, E., De Cock, M., & De Laet, T. (2024). Scaffolding Students' Use of Metacognitive Activities Using Discipline- and Topic-Specific Reflective Prompts. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09363-w

article_title: Scaffolding students’ use of metacognitive activities using discipline- and topic-specific reflective prompts
citation: Sijmkens, E., De Cock, M., & De Laet, T. (2024). Scaffolding Students' Use of Metacognitive Activities Using Discipline- and Topic-Specific Reflective Prompts. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72353-1_2
title: Five problem-solving dimensions structuring reflective prompts
description: The DLC's reflection questions are structured according to five problem-solving dimensions: (1) Strategy plan, (2) Concepts, (3) Mathematical model, (4) Computations, and (5) Interpretation. These align with established problem-solving models such as the logical problem-solving model of the University of Minnesota. Each dimension targets specific metacognitive activities — planning, monitoring, and evaluating — and expands students' metacognitive knowledge about strategies through tailored feedback.
requirements: Reflection questions must be crafted to align with common student difficulties for the specific problem
target_learners: first-year university science and engineering students
target_learning_goals: strategic problem solving
metacognitive planning and monitoring
self-evaluation of solutions
examples: The first reflection question asks students to recognise essential steps in their strategy plan; the final question triggers thinking about how to evaluate the validity of their own solution
key_sources: Sijmkens, E., De Cock, M., & De Laet, T. (2024). Scaffolding Students' Use of Metacognitive Activities Using Discipline- and Topic-Specific Reflective Prompts. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09363-w

article_title: Scaffolding students’ use of metacognitive activities using discipline- and topic-specific reflective prompts
citation: Sijmkens, E., De Cock, M., & De Laet, T. (2024). Scaffolding Students' Use of Metacognitive Activities Using Discipline- and Topic-Specific Reflective Prompts. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72353-1_2
title: Five characteristics of metacognitive prompt interventions
description: The article organises interventions for scaffolding metacognition around five characteristics: embedding (embedded vs non-embedded), specificity (task-specific vs generic), customisation (hard/generalised vs soft/personalised scaffolds), directness (direct instruction vs indirect guidance), and broadness (comprehensive vs narrow subset of metacognitive activities). The article reviews evidence for each: embedded prompts are more effective than non-embedded; specific prompts have a significantly larger impact than generic ones; personalised scaffolds are more effective for self-regulated skills; directness should be adapted to expertise level; and comprehensive support systems are needed for students with limited prior knowledge.
requirements: Interventions must be designed considering all five characteristics to effectively scaffold metacognition
constraints: Reflective prompts are only effective if students have a clear understanding of the task they are reflecting upon, per Kauffman et al. (2008)
target_learners: students in computer-based learning environments
students with limited prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: metacognitive abilities
self-regulated learning
transfer of knowledge to new problems
examples: The DLC is characterised as discipline-/topic-specific, non-embedded (but embedded within modules), indirect (questions) with direct (feedback suggestions), hard scaffold, and broad in scope

article_title: Individual differences in local and global metacognitive judgments
citation: Marion Händel & Anique B. H. de Bruin & Markus Dresel (2020). Individual differences in local and global metacognitive judgments. Metacognition and Learning (2020) 15:51–75. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09220-0
title: Cue-utilization approach to metacognitive judgments
description: The article adopts Koriat's cue-utilization approach as its theoretical framework for explaining the bases and accuracy of metacognitive judgments. Judgments are inferential and rest on cues: information-based (or theory-based) cues such as self-concept beliefs and prior success, and experience-based cues such as retrieval fluency and experienced task difficulty during task processing. The article uses this framework to derive hypotheses about which predictors should matter for local versus global judgments and for predictions versus postdictions, stating that "the accuracy of judgments depends on the availability of specific cues."
requirements: Judgments are inferential and depend on the cues available to the judge at the time of judging
constraints: Local judgments can more easily draw on experience-based task-specific cues, while global judgments and predictions rely more on information-based cues such as domain-familiarity or self-concept
target_learners: undergraduate teacher education students
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring of test performance
examples: Study 1 and Study 2 regressed local and global judgments and accuracy scores on performance, motivational, and personality variables interpreted as information-based versus experience-based cues
key_sources: Marion Händel & Anique B. H. de Bruin & Markus Dresel (2020). Individual differences in local and global metacognitive judgments. Metacognition and Learning (2020) 15:51–75. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09220-0

article_title: Individual differences in local and global metacognitive judgments
citation: Marion Händel & Anique B. H. de Bruin & Markus Dresel (2020). Individual differences in local and global metacognitive judgments. Metacognition and Learning (2020) 15:51–75. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09220-0
