title: Measure metacognitive judgment accuracy with more than one score, including sensitivity and specificity
description: The article argues that a single accuracy score gives an incomplete picture of metacognitive monitoring. Absolute accuracy (bias) captures over- or underconfidence, while relative measures such as sensitivity (accurately detected correct answers) and specificity (accurately detected incorrect answers) capture discrimination of correct versus incorrect items. The article states "Overall, it is suggested to measure accuracy by more than only one score" and calculated sensitivity and specificity in addition to bias in both studies.
requirements: Dichotomous local judgments and item-level performance data to build the 2 × 2 contingency table for sensitivity and specificity
constraints: Sensitivity and specificity depend on item performance and, as composite scores, their reliability is challenging to calculate and interpret; accuracy scores are statistically dependent on performance, so performance must be excluded as a predictor in accuracy analyses
target_learners: undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of test performance
examples: Both studies calculated bias, sensitivity, and specificity, revealing patterns (e.g., higher self-concept with higher sensitivity but lower specificity) that a bias score alone would not show
key_sources: Marion Händel & Anique B. H. de Bruin & Markus Dresel (2020). Individual differences in local and global metacognitive judgments. Metacognition and Learning (2020) 15:51–75. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09220-0

article_title: Unraveling the nexus among achievement goals, self-efficacy, and motivation regulation and their joint effects on L2 student writers’ writing achievement: a person-based approach
citation: Jianhua Zhang, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Unraveling the nexus among achievement goals, self-efficacy, and motivation regulation and their joint effects on L2 student writers' writing achievement: a person-based approach. Metacognition and Learning (2025) 20:29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09434-0
title: A four-profile taxonomy of L2 writing achievement goals grounded in the trichotomous achievement goal model and person-based (latent profile) analysis
description: The article organizes L2 student writers' motivation via the trichotomous achievement goal model (mastery, performance-approach, performance-avoidance) combined with a person-based latent profile approach. Latent profile analysis yielded four profiles labeled, in the article's words, "Low All Goals (LAGs)", "Mastery High (MH)", "Average All Goals (AAGs)", and "High All Goals (HAGs)". The taxonomy is used to test whether self-efficacy, motivation regulation, and writing achievement differ across learner types rather than across variables. Three profiles matched prevalent profiles in Wormington and Linnenbrink-Garcia's (2017) synthesis, which the authors take as supporting cross-contextual stability of goal adoption patterns.
requirements: Requires measures of mastery, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance writing goals (here the adapted Writing Achievement Goals Scale) and latent profile analysis with fit indices (AIC, BIC, aBIC, entropy, LMR-LRT, BLRT).
constraints: Profiles were identified in a convenience sample of tertiary EFL students in Southwest China; the authors note contextual factors in L2 writing may influence how achievement goals are endorsed.
target_learners: Tertiary EFL/L2 student writers
target_learning_goals: L2 writing achievement and motivation regulation in writing
examples: The study assigned 416 students to the four profiles and compared them on self-efficacy, motivation regulation strategies, and writing achievement in two genres.
key_sources: Jianhua Zhang, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Unraveling the nexus among achievement goals, self-efficacy, and motivation regulation and their joint effects on L2 student writers' writing achievement: a person-based approach. Metacognition and Learning (2025) 20:29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09434-0

article_title: Examining my-side bias during and after reading controversial historical accounts
citation: Iordanou, K., Kendeou, P., & Zembylas, M. (2020). Examining my-side bias during and after reading controversial historical accounts. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09240-w
title: Kuhn et al.'s developmental theory of epistemic cognition: absolutist, multiplist, and evaluativist levels
description: The article organizes individual differences in epistemic beliefs using Kuhn et al.'s (2000) theory of epistemic development, in which "epistemic cognition progresses from the absolutist level, to the multiplist level and then to the evaluativist level". At the absolutist level knowledge is objective and certain; at the multiplist level it is subjective and uncertain; at the evaluativist level a balance is achieved and the position "better supported by argument and evidence" is judged to have more merit. The study used this framework to classify participants via the Livia problem and to predict my-side bias and epistemic processing.
requirements: Assessment instrument that distinguishes responses about rightness of accounts and certainty of knowledge, such as the Livia problem used in the study
constraints: The article notes knowledge of epistemic beliefs in the domain of history is very limited and based mainly on inferences rather than direct empirical evidence
target_learners: young adults
undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of contradictory historical accounts
epistemic cognition about knowledge and knowing
examples: Participants were classified as absolutist, multiplist, or evaluativist based on their Livia problem responses; nine were evaluativists and 30 were absolutist or multiplist
key_sources: Iordanou, K., Kendeou, P., & Zembylas, M. (2020). Examining my-side bias during and after reading controversial historical accounts. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09240-w

article_title: What moderates the accuracy of ease of learning judgments?
citation: Jemstedt, A., Kubik, V., & Jönsson, F. U. (2017). What moderates the accuracy of ease of learning judgments? Metacognition and Learning, 12, 337–355. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-017-9172-3
title: Cue-utilization account of ease of learning judgments
description: The article adopts Koriat's (1997) cue-utilization approach, under which metacognitive judgments are inferential: people use available cues or heuristics, such as semantic relatedness, to infer how difficult material will be to learn. Because EOL judgments are made early, before idiosyncratic learning cues are available, accuracy "should mainly be based on the validity and discriminability of salient cues in the material". The experiments operationalize this by varying semantic relatedness within lists and measuring whether judgments track that cue.
requirements: Material must contain salient cues, such as semantic relatedness, that vary enough within the list to allow discrimination between items
constraints: EOL accuracy is capped by the predictive validity of the available cue for actual learnability
Idiosyncratic cues indicating how well material has been learned are largely unavailable at the pre-study stage
target_learners: undergraduate psychology students studying paired-associate material
target_learning_goals: accurate pre-study metacognitive monitoring of item difficulty to guide study decisions
examples: In Experiment 1, lists high versus low in semantic-relatedness variability produced gamma of .74 versus .21, supporting the cue-based account
key_sources: Jemstedt, A., Kubik, V., & Jönsson, F. U. (2017). What moderates the accuracy of ease of learning judgments? Metacognition and Learning, 12, 337–355. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-017-9172-3

article_title: Determinants of creative metacognitive monitoring: creativity, personality, and task-related predictors of self-assessed ideas and creative performance
citation: Lebuda, I., Hofer, G., & Benedek, M. (2025). Determinants of creative metacognitive monitoring: creativity, personality, and task-related predictors of self-assessed ideas and creative performance. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09432-2
title: Three-level framework of creative metacognitive monitoring (task, performance, response)
description: The article builds on a recently proposed framework of creative metacognition in which monitoring occurs pre-, during, and post-task at three levels of granularity. As printed: "metacognitive monitoring at the task level involves assessing in-real time the characteristics of the task, such as its familiarity, difficulty, or creative demands", while performance-level monitoring evaluates one's creative performance and response-level monitoring evaluates the creative quality of one's own ideas. The performance and response levels correspond to global and local monitoring, and the study uses them to evaluate the framework empirically.
requirements: Distinguishing judgments at performance level (global) from response level (local) requires separate measures of self-assessed performance and self-assessed idea creativity, as the study operationalized them.
constraints: The study focuses solely on self-assessing creative process outcomes (response and performance levels); the task level was not measured.
target_learners: University students and adults performing creative (divergent thinking) tasks
target_learning_goals: Accurate self-assessment of one's creative performance and of the creative quality of one's own ideas
examples: The study measured performance-level monitoring via two self-judgment items after divergent thinking tasks and response-level monitoring via self-ratings of up to ten of one's own ideas, comparing each against external ratings.
key_sources: Lebuda, I., Hofer, G., & Benedek, M. (2025). Determinants of creative metacognitive monitoring: creativity, personality, and task-related predictors of self-assessed ideas and creative performance. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09432-2

article_title: The many facets of metacognition: comparing multiple measures of metacognition in healthy individuals
citation: Terneusen, A., Quaedflieg, C., van Heugten, C., Ponds, R., & Winkens, I. (2024). The many facets of metacognition: comparing multiple measures of metacognition in healthy individuals. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09350-1
title: Neuropsychological model of metacognition: metacognitive knowledge and online awareness (monitoring and self-regulation)
description: The article adopts a neuropsychological model in which "Two main elements of metacognition... are metacognitive knowledge and online awareness". Metacognitive knowledge is stable knowledge and beliefs about one's cognitive processes and strategies stored in long-term memory; online awareness is flexible, task-context-dependent evaluation of performance, comprising monitoring (anticipating performance and error recognition) and self-regulation (changing strategies in response to task demands). The study uses this structure to organize its measures and test which elements predict metacognitive sensitivity.
requirements: Measures must be matched to the element being assessed: questionnaires for metacognitive knowledge, performance-based confidence and discrepancy measures for online awareness
constraints: The article notes online awareness depends on task characteristics such as complexity and familiarity, and personal factors such as motivation and meaningfulness of the task
target_learners: healthy adults
populations with metacognitive impairments such as after brain disorders (proposed application)
target_learning_goals: accurate self-monitoring of performance
self-regulation of strategies during learning tasks
examples: The study operationalized the model's elements as MAI subscales, prospective and retrospective discrepancy scores, and trial-by-trial confidence ratings yielding AUROC2
key_sources: Terneusen, A., Quaedflieg, C., van Heugten, C., Ponds, R., & Winkens, I. (2024). The many facets of metacognition: comparing multiple measures of metacognition in healthy individuals. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09350-1

article_title: The many facets of metacognition: comparing multiple measures of metacognition in healthy individuals
citation: Terneusen, A., Quaedflieg, C., van Heugten, C., Ponds, R., & Winkens, I. (2024). The many facets of metacognition: comparing multiple measures of metacognition in healthy individuals. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09350-1
title: Multi-measure metacognition assessment paradigm combining MAI, confidence judgments, and trial-by-trial AUROC2
description: An online assessment paradigm in which participants complete the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory, give prospective and retrospective confidence judgments (0-10 scales) about a word-pair memory task, and make trial-by-trial confidence ratings during a two-alternative forced-choice recognition test. The article states "The memory task was a word pair learning task consisting of two phases: an encoding phase and a recognition phase". These measures yield metacognitive knowledge, discrepancy scores, and metacognitive sensitivity (AUROC2), allowing within-person comparison of metacognitive elements.
requirements: A task with enough correct and incorrect trials for confidence judgments to be meaningful; the authors suggest an adaptive task as a solution
constraints: AUROC2 may not be meaningful under floor or ceiling effects in performance accuracy; the abstract reasoning task was disregarded because performance was at chance level
target_learners: healthy young adults (19-24 years) in the reported study
target_learning_goals: measuring metacognitive sensitivity, monitoring, and metacognitive knowledge
examples: 128 participants completed the session from home in about an hour using Qualtrics, with validity questions used to exclude inattentive responders
key_sources: Terneusen, A., Quaedflieg, C., van Heugten, C., Ponds, R., & Winkens, I. (2024). The many facets of metacognition: comparing multiple measures of metacognition in healthy individuals. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09350-1

article_title: The keyword effect: A conceptual replication, effects on bias, and an optimization
citation: Waldeyer, J., & Roelle, J. (2021). The keyword effect: A conceptual replication, effects on bias, and an optimization. Metacognition and Learning, 16, 37–56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09235-7
title: Situation model account of the keyword effect
description: According to the situation model approach to metacomprehension, "the underlying mechanism via which generating keywords after a delay fosters judgment accuracy is that it requires learners to access their situation model-level representation of the respective texts". Accessing this representation yields diagnostic cues (e.g., generation fluency, keyword quality) that learners incorporate into their judgments of learning. Immediate keyword generation does not serve this function because learners can then rely on surface- and textbase-level representations, which decay faster and are not tapped by comprehension tests; with increasing delay, access to the situation model becomes more likely.
requirements: Keyword generation must occur after a delay so that surface- and textbase-level representations have decayed and learners access their situation model-level representation
constraints: The article notes learners without external standards scarcely exploit keyword quality as a cue, and that which cues learners use to form their JOLs remains widely unclear
target_learners: university students learning from expository texts
target_learning_goals: accurate metacomprehension judgments of text comprehension
examples: In the experiment, keyword and keyword+external standard conditions generated five keywords per text after reading all four texts, before judging their comprehension
key_sources: Waldeyer, J., & Roelle, J. (2021). The keyword effect: A conceptual replication, effects on bias, and an optimization. Metacognition and Learning, 16, 37–56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09235-7

article_title: Knowing how to learn: development and validation of the strategy knowledge test for self-regulated learning (SKT-SRL) for college students
citation: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Jörn R. Sparfeldt, Franziska Perels. (2024). Knowing how to learn: development and validation of the strategy knowledge test for self-regulated learning (SKT-SRL) for college students. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09379-w
title: SKT-SRL: a scenario-based conditional strategy knowledge test for college students
description: The SKT-SRL is a scenario-based offline instrument assessing conditional SRL strategy knowledge, defined as knowledge about which strategy is most useful for a specific learning situation. It presents seven learning scenarios, each with three useful and three less useful strategies, and scores learners on how well they differentiate useful from less useful strategies. It is the first test combining cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational components within a process model viewpoint for college students.
requirements: Requires expert ratings to establish scoring standards for useful versus less useful strategies per scenario
constraints: Developed and validated with German-speaking college students in Germany
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: conditional self-regulated learning strategy knowledge across cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational components
examples: Seven scenarios covering planning, performance, and reflection phases; students rate six strategies per scenario on a four-point Likert scale
key_sources: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Jörn R. Sparfeldt, Franziska Perels. (2024). Knowing how to learn: development and validation of the strategy knowledge test for self-regulated learning (SKT-SRL) for college students. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09379-w

article_title: Knowing how to learn: development and validation of the strategy knowledge test for self-regulated learning (SKT-SRL) for college students
citation: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Jörn R. Sparfeldt, Franziska Perels. (2024). Knowing how to learn: development and validation of the strategy knowledge test for self-regulated learning (SKT-SRL) for college students. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09379-w
title: Conditional SRL strategy knowledge as a distinct competence linked to strategy maturity deficiencies
description: The article frames conditional strategy knowledge—knowledge of when and why a strategy is useful for a specific situation—as a distinct competence, drawing on Paris et al. and Karlen's position that it is a necessary prerequisite for strategy usage. It explains knowledge-usage gaps via Hasselhorn's strategy maturity deficiencies: mediation deficiency, production deficiency, and usage deficiency. The SKT-SRL operationalizes this construct as the fit between strategies and learning situations.
requirements: Assessment must distinguish conditional knowledge from strategy usage to avoid mixing the two, as questionnaires do
constraints: Studies on the relationship between conditional strategy knowledge and strategy usage are rare, with reported correlations ranging from non-significant low to moderate
target_learners: college students
target_learning_goals: conditional self-regulated learning strategy knowledge across cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational components
examples: The SKT-SRL presents scenario vignettes and scores learners on differentiating useful from less useful strategies per scenario
key_sources: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Jörn R. Sparfeldt, Franziska Perels. (2024). Knowing how to learn: development and validation of the strategy knowledge test for self-regulated learning (SKT-SRL) for college students. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09379-w

article_title: Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection
citation: Iordanou, K. (2022). Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 399–425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09289-1
title: Metacognition as competence and disposition: meta-strategic knowledge and epistemic understanding as two meta-level forms supporting strategic argument performance
description: The article frames metacognition, following Kuhn, as "a competence and as a disposition". As competence it involves meta-strategic knowledge — awareness of available strategies, their power relative to task goals, and control of their application — which is proposed to be fundamental for strategic performance. As disposition it involves epistemic understanding of the point of an intellectual task, valuing it as worth cognitive effort, connected to motivation. The study hypothesizes that reflection during dialogic argumentation develops both forms, which in turn support strategic-level argument skill.
requirements: Engagement in tasks involving the targeted strategies, so that application at the cognitive level informs meta-level knowing in a continuous cycle
constraints: The article notes understanding of how to support metacognition development is still limited, and even adults may fail to have good judgments of their own knowing
target_learners: young adolescents (11–12 years old, 6th grade)
target_learning_goals: argument skill: constructing counterarguments and using evidence to weaken opposing positions
examples: Participants in the experimental condition reflected on their own dialog transcripts using reflection sheets while waiting for the opposing pair to respond, with a same-side collaborating partner
key_sources: Iordanou, K. (2022). Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 399–425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09289-1

article_title: Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection
citation: Iordanou, K. (2022). Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 399–425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09289-1
title: Three developmental levels of epistemic understanding: Absolutism, Multiplism, and Evaluativism
description: The article describes epistemic understanding as developing through three levels across the lifespan. "The first developmental level of epistemic understanding is Absolutism", where truth is objective and disagreeing claims are dismissed as false beliefs. "Multiplism is the second developmental level", acknowledging that knowledge is subjective and multiple interpretations may exist, so disagreeing parties see no point in discussion. "The final level of development is the Evaluativist level, where the subjective and objective dimensions of knowing are coordinated": knowledge is judgment formed by evaluating alternatives against evidence, and argumentation is valued as a means of evaluating knowledge claims.
requirements: Opportunities to engage in practice in dialogic argumentation and reflection while arguing, over an extended period of time, for development toward evaluativist understanding
constraints: The article states epistemic understanding undergoes development throughout the lifespan and its roots trace to early conceptions of evidence as objective reality
target_learners: children through adults, with the levels illustrated for adolescents in argumentation contexts
target_learning_goals: epistemic understanding of the nature of knowledge and evidence; disposition to engage in argumentation
examples: The article links evaluativist understanding to a mindset of searching for more evidence and considering alternative interpretive frameworks before making a judgment
key_sources: Iordanou, K. (2022). Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 399–425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09289-1

article_title: Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection
citation: Iordanou, K. (2022). Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 399–425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09289-1
title: Reflection sheets prompting reflection on one's own dialog transcript during argumentation
description: Reflection sheets (adapted from Iordanou & Constantinou, 2015) supported experimental-condition participants in reflecting on the electronic transcript of their own dialog while waiting for the opposing pair to respond. "Own-side reflection sheets asked participants to reflect on (a) whether they had paid attention and addressed the opposing side's position, and (b) whether they had used evidence in the counterarguments they had constructed". Other-side reflection sheets asked participants to reflect on the rebuttals they used to weaken counterarguments to their own position and whether they used evidence to support their rebuttal; in both cases participants contemplated what a better counterargument or rebuttal might have been. Participants worked with a same-side collaborating partner to promote externalization of thinking.
requirements: An immediately available and permanent record of the dialog (the electronic transcript) as the basis for the reflective activity; a collaborating same-side partner
constraints: The sheets alternated across sessions and were used during Sessions 5–9 only in the experimental condition
target_learners: elementary school students, ages 11–12
target_learning_goals: meta-strategic and epistemic awareness of argumentation goals: addressing the opponent's position and using evidence
examples: During Sessions 5–9, A&R participants completed alternating own-side and other-side reflection sheets on chosen excerpts of their instant-messaging dialogs
key_sources: Iordanou, K. (2022). Supporting strategic and meta-strategic development of argument skill: the role of reflection. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 399–425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09289-1

article_title: Teachers’ judgment accuracy of students’ monitoring skills: a conceptual and methodological framework and explorative study
citation: van de Pol, J., & Oudman, S. (2024). Teachers' judgment accuracy of students' monitoring skills: a conceptual and methodological framework and explorative study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09349-8
title: Framework of teachers' judgments of students' monitoring skills with three accuracy measures
description: The article introduces a framework that integrates teachers' judgments of students' performance, teachers' judgments of students' monitoring judgments, and students' actual performance and monitoring judgments. It defines three measures: 'Teachers' judgment accuracy of students' monitoring judgments is captured with three measures' — SMA-TJ (student monitoring accuracy according to teacher judgments), TJASMJ (teacher judgment accuracy of the student's monitoring judgment), and C-SMA-TJ (correctness of student monitoring accuracy according to teacher judgments). The framework 'applies to every classroom situation, regardless of the proportion of optimists/pessimists/realists' and serves both to conceptualize the constructs and as a guideline for operationalizing them, unlike the earlier categoric approach.
requirements: Requires measuring teachers' judgments of student performance (TJSP), teachers' judgments of students' monitoring judgments (TJSMJ), students' monitoring judgments (SMJ), and students' actual performance (SP) to compute the deviation indices
constraints: The article focuses on absolute accuracy and bias measures; it defers discussion of relative accuracy measures to its Discussion section
target_learners: secondary education students whose monitoring skills are judged by their teachers
target_learning_goals: teachers' accurate judgment of students' self-monitoring of reading comprehension performance
examples: A numeric example (Fig. 2) walks through a student scoring 2 points, judging 4, with a teacher judging performance at 5 and the monitoring judgment at 2, yielding SMA-TJ, TJASMJ and C-SMA-TJ values
key_sources: van de Pol, J., & Oudman, S. (2024). Teachers' judgment accuracy of students' monitoring skills: a conceptual and methodological framework and explorative study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09349-8

article_title: Exploring the effects of a musical play intervention on young children’s self-regulation and metacognition
citation: Zachariou, A., Bonneville-Roussy, A., Hargreaves, D., & Neokleous, R. (2023). Exploring the effects of a musical play intervention on young children's self-regulation and metacognition. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09342-1
title: Whitebread et al.'s three-area model of self-regulation and metacognition
description: The study adopts Whitebread et al.'s (2009) model, which "proposes three areas of self-regulation: metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive regulation and emotional and motivational regulation". Metacognitive knowledge covers knowledge of persons, tasks and strategies; metacognitive regulation covers planning, monitoring, control and evaluation; emotional/motivational regulation covers monitoring and control of emotional and motivational experiences. The model draws on the cognitive information-processing tradition (metamemory, metacognition) and the socio-cultural tradition (self-regulation), and underpins the C.Ind.Le coding framework and CHILD checklist used to measure all outcomes in this study.
requirements: Assessment requires coding verbal and non-verbal behaviours at utterance level, since metacognitive knowledge on-task relies only on children's verbalisations
constraints: On-task identification of metacognitive knowledge relies only on children's verbalisations, which the authors note may underestimate young children's abilities
target_learners: Young children in early primary school (aged 6)
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation and metacognition across cognitive, emotional, social and motivational domains
examples: The study coded Train Track Task observations and interview responses into the model's nine facets using the C.Ind.Le scheme, with inter-rater reliability ICC = .93
key_sources: Zachariou, A., Bonneville-Roussy, A., Hargreaves, D., & Neokleous, R. (2023). Exploring the effects of a musical play intervention on young children's self-regulation and metacognition. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09342-1

article_title: The Dynamics Between Self-Regulated Learning and Learning Outcomes: an Exploratory Approach and Implications
citation: Joep van der Graaf, Lyn Lim, Yizhou Fan, Jonathan Kilgour, Johanna Moore, Dragan Gašević, Maria Bannert, Inge Molenaar. (2022). The Dynamics Between Self-Regulated Learning and Learning Outcomes: an Exploratory Approach and Implications. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09308-9
title: Two-dimensional framework of learning outcomes: structure (independent vs. connected concepts) and level (surface vs. deep knowledge)
description: The article operationalises learning outcomes along two dimensions of mental representation of knowledge drawn from de Jong and Ferguson-Hessler: structure, ranging from unconnected independent concepts to interconnected networks, and level, ranging from surface to deep knowledge. Four measures instantiate the combinations: a domain test, concept maps, a transfer test, and an essay. The article states that "learning outcomes can be characterised along two dimensions—the structure and the level of knowledge" and treats them as continuums rather than a dichotomy.
requirements: Outcomes must be measurable at identifiable points on both dimensions, as in the article's Table 1 operationalisation
constraints: The article notes the table might suggest a dichotomy, but the dimensions are continuums; outcomes are located on two continuums
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge
conceptual knowledge structure
transfer of knowledge
examples: The study placed a domain test (surface, independent), concept maps (surface, connected), transfer test (deep, independent), and essay (deep, connected) in a 2x2 operationalisation (Table 1)
key_sources: Joep van der Graaf, Lyn Lim, Yizhou Fan, Jonathan Kilgour, Johanna Moore, Dragan Gašević, Maria Bannert, Inge Molenaar. (2022). The Dynamics Between Self-Regulated Learning and Learning Outcomes: an Exploratory Approach and Implications. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09308-9

article_title: The Dynamics Between Self-Regulated Learning and Learning Outcomes: an Exploratory Approach and Implications
citation: Joep van der Graaf, Lyn Lim, Yizhou Fan, Jonathan Kilgour, Johanna Moore, Dragan Gašević, Maria Bannert, Inge Molenaar. (2022). The Dynamics Between Self-Regulated Learning and Learning Outcomes: an Exploratory Approach and Implications. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09308-9
title: Assess SRL–outcome associations against outcomes distinguished by both level and structure of knowledge
description: The article recommends that research on SRL during learning specify which kind of learning outcome is being predicted, because associations differ across outcome measures. Its conclusion states that "taking the level and structure of knowledge into account helps specify the association between SRL activities during learning and the related learning outcomes." The exploratory study demonstrated this by contrasting four outcomes varying on both dimensions.
requirements: Multiple outcome measures capturing different combinations of knowledge level and structure must be collected
constraints: Findings are exploratory due to the small number of participants and should be interpreted with caution
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
deep and surface knowledge construction
examples: The study measured domain test, concept maps, transfer test, and essay scores and related each to think-aloud-coded SRL activity frequencies in a pre-/post-test SEM
key_sources: Joep van der Graaf, Lyn Lim, Yizhou Fan, Jonathan Kilgour, Johanna Moore, Dragan Gašević, Maria Bannert, Inge Molenaar. (2022). The Dynamics Between Self-Regulated Learning and Learning Outcomes: an Exploratory Approach and Implications. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09308-9

article_title: The impact of an online tool for monitoring and regulating learning at university: overconfidence, learning strategy, and personality
citation: de Bruin, A. B. H., Kok, E. M., Lobbestael, J., & de Grip, A. (2017). The impact of an online tool for monitoring and regulating learning at university: overconfidence, learning strategy, and personality. Metacognition and Learning, 12, 21–43. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9159-5
title: Online Monitoring Exercise with feedback and 7-step Monitoring and Regulation Strategy (idea-unit self-testing technique)
description: A content-free, online intervention package for university students consisting of two separable components. The Monitoring Exercise has students read short texts with key concepts, type definitions, judge their quality, and then receive email feedback on over-, under- and correct estimations. The Monitoring and Regulation Strategy is a 7-step emailed guide that explains "how to assess their knowl- edge of key terms in textbooks by self-testing and comparing their definitions with the correct definition through counting idea-units" and emphasizes restudying unmastered concepts. In the study it was delivered via Surveymonkey and email across three faculties.
requirements: Delivered online via email and questionnaire tool; feedback email sent at most 3 days after the exercise
Strategy requires students to self-test, compare generated definitions with correct ones by counting idea units, and restudy unmastered key concepts
constraints: No guided practice with the strategy and no logging of strategy use was performed
Effects were examined in first-year undergraduate courses over 8 weeks
target_learners: first-year undergraduate university students
target_learning_goals: accurate self-monitoring of exam readiness
effective self-regulated study of textbook key concepts
examples: Students in the ME and ME-MRS conditions completed the exercise on texts titled 'Gestures' and 'Marriage', each containing four key concepts, and all but one participant overestimated their performance on at least one key concept (M = 4.95 overestimations).
key_sources: de Bruin, A. B. H., Kok, E. M., Lobbestael, J., & de Grip, A. (2017). The impact of an online tool for monitoring and regulating learning at university: overconfidence, learning strategy, and personality. Metacognition and Learning, 12, 21–43. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9159-5

article_title: Age-related differences in metacognitive reactivity in younger and older adults
citation: Murphy, D. H., Rhodes, M. G., & Castel, A. D. (2024). Age-related differences in metacognitive reactivity in younger and older adults. Metacognition and Learning, 19, 863–877. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09391-0
title: Cognitive-load / dual-task account of negative JOL reactivity
description: This account explains why making judgments of learning can impair memory: making a JOL is a secondary task alongside encoding, so "making JOLs increases learners’ cognitive load, resulting in dual-task costs (see Janes et al., 2018), leading to negative reactivity". The article applies it to aging: older adults, with reduced working memory capacity and processing speed, may be unable to engage in elaborative associative encoding while judging, whereas younger adults can manage both tasks. Preserved semantic memory may mask negative reactivity for related pairs.
requirements: JOLs must be made during encoding as an additional task concurrent with studying the material
constraints: The article states the present data cannot discern whether age differences reflect greater costs or fewer benefits of making JOLs
The account is offered as one of several mechanisms; cue-strengthening and other accounts have also received support
target_learners: younger adults
older adults
target_learning_goals: cued recall of word-pair associations
metacognitive monitoring during encoding
examples: In the experiment, older adults recalled more pairs when each pair was followed by an unfilled 7-second inter-stimulus interval than when they made a JOL, consistent with JOLs consuming resources needed for elaborative encoding
key_sources: Murphy, D. H., Rhodes, M. G., & Castel, A. D. (2024). Age-related differences in metacognitive reactivity in younger and older adults. Metacognition and Learning, 19, 863–877. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09391-0

article_title: The effect of writing script on efficiency and metacognitive monitoring in inferential word learning
citation: Polyanskaya, L., El-Dakhs, D. A. S., Tao, M., Chu, F., & Ordin, M. (2024). The effect of writing script on efficiency and metacognitive monitoring in inferential word learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09380-3
title: Writing-system account: sound-to-symbol mapping transparency and the range of monitored cognitive processes shape metacognitive monitoring of visually presented word learning
description: The article proposes that the writing system a person uses modulates metacognitive monitoring of word learning in the visual but not the auditory modality. It states that "the presence and transparency of sound-to-symbol mapping influences the success of word acquisition and the self-evaluation (metacognition) of word learning, when words are visually presented." Opaque mapping (Arabic abjad) hinders transfer of metacognitive skills from the auditory baseline to the visual modality, while the logographic Chinese script, lacking phoneme-to-symbol mapping, trains metacognition because learners must simultaneously monitor strategies for inferring both pronunciation and semantics of each character.
requirements: Learners must have literacy experience in a specific writing system, since the account rests on inculturated processing of written information
constraints: The account concerns metacognition measured via retrospective confidence ratings, i.e. processes related to conscious awareness; the authors note observed population differences may in principle be cultural rather than linguistic, though they argue the modality-specific pattern supports a linguistic origin
target_learners: University students aged 18-30 who are native speakers of Portuguese, Arabic or Mandarin Chinese learning foreign-language vocabulary
target_learning_goals: Inferential (incidental, context-based) vocabulary learning and accurate self-evaluation of word-learning success
examples: Arabic speakers showed lower metacognitive sensitivity in the visual than auditory modality; Chinese speakers showed the highest visual-modality metacognition, attributed to monitoring multiple cognitive strategies for pronunciation and semantics of logographic characters
key_sources: Polyanskaya, L., El-Dakhs, D. A. S., Tao, M., Chu, F., & Ordin, M. (2024). The effect of writing script on efficiency and metacognitive monitoring in inferential word learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09380-3

article_title: The effect of writing script on efficiency and metacognitive monitoring in inferential word learning
citation: Polyanskaya, L., El-Dakhs, D. A. S., Tao, M., Chu, F., & Ordin, M. (2024). The effect of writing script on efficiency and metacognitive monitoring in inferential word learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09380-3
title: Inferential word-learning task with retrospective confidence ratings and hierarchical Bayesian meta-d' estimation
description: A cross-modal experimental instrument in which participants learn 20 pseudoword–referent pairings through disambiguation of semantically ambiguous scenes (e.g. selecting a table with a "dax"), then select referents while rating confidence on a 4-point scale. Metacognition is quantified as meta-d' via "the signal detection theory framework", estimated with Fleming's hierarchical Bayesian HMeta-d code; metacognitive efficiency is the ratio of meta-d' to d'. The article used it to compare word-learning accuracy and metacognitive monitoring across Arabic, Chinese and Portuguese speakers in visual and auditory modalities.
requirements: Pseudowords tailored to each language's phonotactics (UniPseudo for Portuguese and Saudi Arabic; MELD-SCH non-existent characters for Chinese) and counterbalancing of modality order and referents across participants and genders
constraints: The study was not preregistered; metacognition is measured only via retrospective confidence ratings, which the authors admit cannot separate confidence judgments guided with versus without conscious awareness
target_learners: University students aged 18-30, native speakers of Arabic, Mandarin Chinese or Portuguese, with intermediate formal English knowledge
target_learning_goals: Inferential word learning from contextual cues and metacognitive monitoring of vocabulary learning success
examples: In the visual modality participants read sentences instructing them to select one of two images differing by a minor detail, learning referents implicitly across trials; in the auditory modality the same procedure used heard pseudowords and sentences
key_sources: Polyanskaya, L., El-Dakhs, D. A. S., Tao, M., Chu, F., & Ordin, M. (2024). The effect of writing script on efficiency and metacognitive monitoring in inferential word learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09380-3

article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study
citation: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2020). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09237-5
title: Task-generality account of metacognitive skills within self-regulated learning
description: The article organizes SRL components by task-specificity: cognitive strategies and motivation regulation strategies "are task-specific because they directly address particular kinds of information processing", whereas metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, evaluating) are higher-order skills that regulate cognitive or motivational strategies within all kinds of learning tasks and are therefore task-general and transferable. This account motivates the hybrid-training approach, in which metacognitive skills are trained together with a task-specific cognitive strategy so they can later regulate new strategies in new tasks.
requirements: Metacognitive skills must be trained in combination with at least one specific cognitive strategy so learners can later recognize that the skills remain the same while strategies change across tasks.
constraints: The study's evidence covers fifth-graders trained with two cognitive strategies (conducting experiments, text highlighting) over one school year; the authors call for systematic variation of tasks and domains to prove transfer more broadly.
target_learners: fifth-grade students in secondary school
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
transfer of metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, evaluating)
examples: The study trained metacognitive skills regulating either a control-of-variables experiment strategy (ME) or a three-step text-highlighting strategy (MT), then tested transfer to tasks requiring the other strategy.
key_sources: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2020). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09237-5

article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study
citation: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2020). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09237-5
title: Multi-strategy test (MST) vignette instrument for intended strategy application
description: The MST is a scenario-based test presenting "a fictitious learning situation in which students are asked to describe their intended approach to process the given learning task" in an open-response format. Two versions (MST_E for an experimentation task, MST_T for a text-highlighting task) are coded with a category system awarding up to 9 points for metacognitive skills and 9 for cognitive strategy steps. Double-coding a subsample of N = 60 (about 25% of the sample) yielded good inter-rater reliability with an average Cohen's of .91.
requirements: Requires spontaneous recall of skills and strategy steps without prompts; only conscious strategy knowledge can be named and recorded.
constraints: The MST measures intended application in a fictitious situation, not actual strategy application; the extent to which intended application reflects real application remains open, and scores may be influenced by the amount of text students produced.
target_learners: fifth-grade students in secondary school
target_learning_goals: assessment of spontaneous application of metacognitive skills and cognitive strategies
examples: MST_E asked students how they would find out what plants need to grow using an experiment; MST_T asked how they would proceed to summarize a multi-page magazine article for classmates.
key_sources: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2020). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09237-5

article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study
citation: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2020). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09237-5
title: Train metacognitive skills in combination with a specific cognitive strategy, then progress to general framing, to support transfer of metacognitive skills
description: The article's hybrid-training design follows the "principle of specific-to-general": metacognitive skills are initially trained with a cognitive strategy on a specific training task, then applied across various cognitive strategies, "finally resulting in a more general framing", ending with a transfer lesson applying metacognitive skills to everyday life situations. Teacher influence is progressively reduced so students independently solve new tasks and apply the acquired strategies. The study's results support this design for fostering near and far transfer of metacognitive skills.
requirements: Training must combine metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, evaluating) with at least one concrete cognitive strategy, include application sequences across varied tasks, and end with a general-framing transfer lesson.
constraints: Even with hybrid training, the level of metacognitive skills use remained low, and one hybrid condition's far-transfer advantage over control was not significant; the authors discuss further means to support transfer.
target_learners: fifth-grade students in secondary school
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
transfer of metacognitive skills to new learning tasks
examples: Each hybrid condition began with basics of learning and cooperative learning, moved to explicit training of metacognitive skills with the cognitive strategy, continued with application training on various experiments or expository texts, and ended with a transfer lesson on everyday situations, with a reflection questionnaire each lesson.
key_sources: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2020). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09237-5

article_title: Signaling task awareness in think-aloud protocols from students selecting relevant information from text
citation: Gonny L. M. Schellings & Hein Broekkamp. (2011). Signaling task awareness in think-aloud protocols from students selecting relevant information from text. Metacognition and Learning 6:65–82. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9067-z
title: Two-level model of task awareness in text selection (global and local task levels)
description: The article conceives task awareness as conscious task representation operating at two levels. As printed: "Task awareness runs at two levels. At the global level, selection goals and the task's instructions are represented, while at the local level, reflections about specific text parts are involved." Global representations concern major task components, selection goals, text or task difficulty, and time available; local representations are bound to specific text units such as particular words or concepts. The study operationalised these levels in a coding instrument applied to think-aloud protocols of text selection.
requirements: Task awareness can only be observed when learners verbalize about it, since it is defined as a conscious representation of the selection process
constraints: Think-aloud data capture only higher-order, non-automatized activities that consume working-memory room, per the Ericsson and Simon framework the article cites
target_learners: secondary school students (tenth-graders, age 15–16)
target_learning_goals: awareness of task demands when selecting relevant information from instructional texts
examples: Twelve tenth-graders thought aloud while performing linguistic, educational, and personal selection tasks on three biology texts; verbalizations were coded into global- and local-level categories
key_sources: Gonny L. M. Schellings & Hein Broekkamp. (2011). Signaling task awareness in think-aloud protocols from students selecting relevant information from text. Metacognition and Learning 6:65–82. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-010-9067-z

article_title: Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: an aptitude-treatment-interaction study
citation: Janina Lehmann, Christina Goussios, Tina Seufert. (2015). Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: an aptitude-treatment-interaction study. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9149-z
title: Disfluency theory as metacognitive regulation activating System 2 processing
description: Disfluency theory explains why less legible learning material can improve outcomes: the disfluency effect "can be assumed as a metacognitive regulation process during which learners assign their cognitive resources depending on the perceived difficulty of a cognitive task". Building on two processing systems, perceiving processing as difficult activates System 2, the slow, effortful, analytic and deliberate system, stimulating deeper processing and better learning outcomes. The article uses this account to motivate the WMC moderation hypothesis: only learners with sufficient capacity can absorb the extra burden and engage in deeper processing.
requirements: Learners must perceive the material as difficult and feel able to enhance effort based on their available cognitive resources
constraints: The disfluency effect has been shown only for text-based instructional material, not for spoken texts or pictures
Beneficial effects depend on learner characteristics such as sufficient working memory capacity
target_learners: University students with medium prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: Retention and comprehension of text-based instructional material
examples: The study manipulated text legibility via font (Arial vs. Haettenschweiler, grayscale) and tested whether WMC moderated outcomes on retention, comprehension and transfer tests
key_sources: Janina Lehmann, Christina Goussios, Tina Seufert. (2015). Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: an aptitude-treatment-interaction study. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9149-z

article_title: Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: an aptitude-treatment-interaction study
citation: Janina Lehmann, Christina Goussios, Tina Seufert. (2015). Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: an aptitude-treatment-interaction study. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9149-z
title: Differentiated subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaire measuring ICL, ECL and GCL
description: The study employed the paper-based Cognitive Load Questionnaire (Klepsch and Seufert 2012) to differentially assess the three types of cognitive load: three items each for intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load, rated on seven-point Likert scales after learning and after assessing learning outcomes. The authors note that "we were the first to use a differentiated measurement of the three types of CL in disfluency research". The instrument captures only subjective ratings of cognitive load, which the authors acknowledge may not coincide with objective load.
requirements: Learners must be aware of their own cognitive load for subjective ratings to be meaningful
constraints: Measures only subjectively perceived cognitive load, not objective load
Items may not cover all facets of ECL or subsemantic processes relevant to GCL
target_learners: University students learning from text-based material
target_learning_goals: Assessment of intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load during learning
examples: Items included 'For this task many things needed to be kept in mind simultaneously.' for ICL and 'The design of this task was very inappropriate to really learn something.' for ECL
key_sources: Janina Lehmann, Christina Goussios, Tina Seufert. (2015). Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: an aptitude-treatment-interaction study. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9149-z

article_title: Metacognitive control processes in question answering: help seeking and withholding answers
citation: Monika Undorf, Iris Livneh, Rakefet Ackerman. (2021). Metacognitive control processes in question answering: help seeking and withholding answers. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09259-7
title: Metacognitive monitoring-control framework for question answering, indexed by control sensitivity
description: The article frames question answering through a metacognitive monitoring-control framework: monitoring corresponds to "people's confidence in the accuracy of the knowledge they retrieve from memory", and control corresponds to strategic regulation of the answers provided, including seeking help and withholding answers. Control sensitivity — the within-participant correlation between confidence and strategy use — indexes how strongly control processes track confidence. The study extends this framework, developed mainly for withholding answers, to help seeking as a metacognitive control process.
requirements: Confidence judgments must be collected at the level of individual questions to index monitoring-control links
constraints: The framework was examined in general-knowledge question-answering tasks with numeric answers under contingency reward systems; the article notes help seeking has been largely neglected in metacognition research
target_learners: adult learners answering knowledge questions in educational and testing contexts
target_learning_goals: accurate and informative question answering
adaptive use of help seeking and answer withholding as self-regulated learning strategies
examples: Across Experiments 1-3, control sensitivity was indexed as within-participant gamma correlations between confidence and strategy use and compared across help-seeking, don't-know, combination, and no-choice conditions
key_sources: Monika Undorf, Iris Livneh, Rakefet Ackerman. (2021). Metacognitive control processes in question answering: help seeking and withholding answers. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09259-7

article_title: Using multiple, contextualized data sources to measure learners’ perceptions of their self-regulated learning
citation: McCardle, L. (2015). Self-regulated learning in and across sport and academic domains [Doctoral dissertation, University of Victoria]. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-014-9132-0
title: Winne and Hadwin's (1998) COPES model of SRL as a framework for researching SRL transfer across domains
description: The dissertation adopts Winne and Hadwin's (1998) four-phase model with the COPES architecture (conditions, operations, products, evaluations, standards) as its theoretical framework. SRL is defined as "learners' active engagement of processes to control and adapt cognition, behaviour, and motivation/affect to reach self-set goals". The model is recursive with weakly sequenced phases, allocates a central role to metacognitive monitoring and control within each phase, and its inclusion of conditions allows learning to be treated as situated. The author recommends it "serve as a framework for researching SRL transfer with a focus on conditions" because it describes regulatory processes that are similar across contexts even when tactics differ.
requirements: Research on SRL transfer should attend to conditions surrounding learning, per the model's COPES architecture
constraints: The author argues current theories of transfer have little to say about SRL because SRL is a dynamic process rather than static knowledge
target_learners: student-athletes
students in academic contexts
athletes in sport training
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning across domains
transfer of regulatory processes between sport and academics
examples: The dissertation uses the model to argue that both students and athletes define tasks, set goals, monitor and evaluate learning, and make changes when progress goes awry, even though tactics differ across contexts
key_sources: McCardle, L. (2015). Self-regulated learning in and across sport and academic domains [Doctoral dissertation, University of Victoria]. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-014-9132-0

article_title: Process mining measures students’ help-seeking transitions when completing assignments in an online learning and assessment platform
citation: Hou, C., Kuhlmann, S. L., Greene, J. A., Bernacki, M. L., & Hogan, K. A. (2025). Process mining measures students' help-seeking transitions when completing assignments in an online learning and assessment platform. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09442-0
title: Executive versus instrumental help-seeking framework
description: The article organizes help-seeking into two kinds drawn from Nelson-Le Gall (1981), distinguished by their function for learning. As the article states, "Instrumental help-seeking refers to behaviors that promote learning and improve understanding, such as the use of scaffolding. Executive help-seeking refers to behaviors that look for shortcuts to achieve the learning goal, and avoid additional work, such as accessing solutions in online learning and assessment platforms." In the platform studied, hints map onto adaptive instrumental help-seeking and requesting solutions onto maladaptive executive help-seeking. The framework underpins the study's interpretation of why lower performers' solution access signals struggling.
requirements: Help-seeking must be observable as distinct digital events (e.g., hint requests versus solution requests) so the two kinds can be distinguished in trace data
constraints: The article notes students commonly use both kinds of help-seeking to achieve a learning goal, so the categories are not mutually exclusive in practice
Common help-seeking surveys such as the MSLQ do not differentiate between executive and instrumental help-seeking
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education, particularly STEM courses using online learning and assessment platforms
target_learning_goals: effective, adaptive help-seeking as part of self-regulated learning during online formative assessment
examples: In the studied platform, hints written to guide students toward the correct answer in an increasingly specific way were treated as instrumental help, while the request-answer button, which eliminates the opportunity to receive credit for the question, was treated as executive help-seeking
key_sources: Hou, C., Kuhlmann, S. L., Greene, J. A., Bernacki, M. L., & Hogan, K. A. (2025). Process mining measures students' help-seeking transitions when completing assignments in an online learning and assessment platform. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09442-0

article_title: The limits of curiosity? New evidence for the roles of metacognitive abilities and curiosity in learning
citation: Xiaoyun Chen, Katherine E. Twomey, Miranda Hayes, Gert Westermann. (2024). The limits of curiosity? New evidence for the roles of metacognitive abilities and curiosity in learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09407-9
title: Two distinct metacognitive confidence types: Knowledge Confidence and Correctness Confidence
description: The article identifies and separates two metacognitive appraisals that relate to curiosity in distinct ways. Knowledge Confidence is the subjective estimate of one's general prior knowledge state, while Correctness Confidence is the appraisal of the likelihood that a specific guess closes the knowledge gap. As the article states, "Knowledge Confidence is different from Correctness Confidence. The former emphasises the evaluation of one's general knowledge state", whereas the latter reflects "appraisal of a specific prediction". The study uses this distinction to show the two confidence types mediate curiosity differently and play different roles in learning.
requirements: Learners must make both a general prior-knowledge judgement and a confidence rating on a specific guess for the two appraisals to be measured separately
constraints: Distinction established with blurred object images in an online young-adult sample; the authors call for extension to other age groups and paradigms
target_learners: adult learners in online experiments
educators seeking to leverage metacognitive appraisal
target_learning_goals: metacognitive appraisal of knowledge states
curiosity-driven information seeking
recall of object names
examples: Participants answered "Do you know what this is?" (Yes/No/Not Sure), gave a best guess, rated guess confidence from 1 to 6, and rated curiosity for each of 60 blurred images
key_sources: Xiaoyun Chen, Katherine E. Twomey, Miranda Hayes, Gert Westermann. (2024). The limits of curiosity? New evidence for the roles of metacognitive abilities and curiosity in learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09407-9

article_title: The process of early self-control: an observational study in two- and three-year-olds
citation: Mulder, H., van Ravenswaaij, H., Verhagen, J., Moerbeek, M., & Leseman, P. P. M. (2019). The process of early self-control: an observational study in two- and three-year-olds. Metacognition and Learning, 14, 239–264. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09199-3
title: Active hand withholding in toddlers as a rudimentary form of situation modification
description: The article interprets toddlers' active hand-withholding behaviours — holding hands under the table, crossing the arms, or holding one hand tightly with the other — as blocking the direct route to the reward, and relates this to the adult and older-child literature: "this may be seen as a form of 'situation modification'". It situates the behaviour within theoretical accounts (the hot/cool systems framework and the process model of self-control) in which self-control is facilitated by shifting attention away from the reward or making reaching more effortful. The authors note Gross's original definition of situation modification does not seem to fully cover these behaviours, since the toddlers act without changing the situation itself.
requirements: A delay-of-gratification setting in which the reward is physically present and within reach, so that blocking the direct reaching route is possible
constraints: The article notes Gross's (2015) definition of situation modification as directly altering a situation does not fully seem to cover these toddler behaviours, so the mapping is interpretive rather than exact
target_learners: two- and three-year-old children
target_learning_goals: exerting self-control and delaying gratification in the presence of an immediate reward
examples: Children were observed to hold their hands under the table, cross their arms, or hold one hand tightly with the other during 60-s snack and gift delay tasks
key_sources: Mulder, H., van Ravenswaaij, H., Verhagen, J., Moerbeek, M., & Leseman, P. P. M. (2019). The process of early self-control: an observational study in two- and three-year-olds. Metacognition and Learning, 14, 239–264. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09199-3

article_title: Integrating self-regulated learning and individual differences in the prediction of university academic achievement across a three-year-long degree
citation: Juan-Carlos Pérez-González, Gemma Filella, Anna Soldevila, Yasmine Faiad, Maria-Jose Sanchez-Ruiz. (2022). Integrating self-regulated learning and individual differences in the prediction of university academic achievement across a three-year-long degree. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:1141–1165. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09315-w
title: Integrative framework combining the SRL and individual-differences approaches to predictors of academic performance
description: The article proposes a parsimonious framework (Table 1) that organizes predictors of academic performance by crossing two research traditions: "individual differences and SRL". It maps cognitive factors (cognitive abilities, cognitive and metacognitive learning strategies) and non-cognitive factors (personality, motivation, affect, behavior, context regulation) onto Pintrich's five self-regulatory learning areas and Hilgard's three areas of psychological functioning. It is offered as a starting point for future integrative models and was partially tested via the study's regressions and SEMs.
requirements: Measured variables spanning both cognitive and non-cognitive domains, operationalized as in Table 1
constraints: The authors state there is no consensus on how to reconcile the different classifications of variables, and present the framework as tentative and parsimonious rather than established
target_learners: university undergraduates
target_learning_goals: academic performance prediction
identification of non-cognitive factors supporting self-regulated learning
examples: The framework guided selection of predictors for the three-year hierarchical regressions and the two structural equation models
key_sources: Juan-Carlos Pérez-González, Gemma Filella, Anna Soldevila, Yasmine Faiad, Maria-Jose Sanchez-Ruiz. (2022). Integrating self-regulated learning and individual differences in the prediction of university academic achievement across a three-year-long degree. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:1141–1165. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09315-w

article_title: Reading behavior as an indicator of comprehension monitoring when reading expository texts
citation: Catharina Tibken, Simon P. Tiffin-Richards. (2025). Reading behavior as an indicator of comprehension monitoring when reading expository texts. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09440-2
title: Two-Step Model of Validation: passive validation detects inconsistencies, but resolving them requires metacognitive effort
description: The Two-Step Model of Validation (Richter & Maier, 2017) assumes readers "can detect inconsistent information through non-strategic, passive validation processes, but fully processing and potentially resolving inconsistencies requires metacognitive resources and effort (strategic elaboration)". The article uses this model, alongside the Content-Source Integration Model, to motivate its hypotheses: first-pass disruptions reflect passive validation, whereas reanalysis reflects strategic, reader-initiated metacognitive regulation. The study's finding that reanalysis, not first-pass reading, predicted inconsistency identification is consistent with this account.
requirements: Readers must perceive the text as demanding or hold high standards of coherence for metacognitive effort to be engaged
constraints: The article applies the model to (short) expository texts about conceptually difficult topics read for study purposes
target_learners: university students and other experienced adult readers learning from expository texts
target_learning_goals: metacognitive comprehension monitoring and regulation during reading
construction of a coherent situation model of expository text content
examples: The study measured first-pass reading time and lookbacks as indicators of passive validation, and rereading time and revisits as indicators of strategic reanalysis, across target word, sentence-final word, and pre-target text areas
key_sources: Catharina Tibken, Simon P. Tiffin-Richards. (2025). Reading behavior as an indicator of comprehension monitoring when reading expository texts. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09440-2

article_title: Effects of a homework implementation method (MITCA) on self-regulation of learning
citation: Tania Vieites, Eleftheria Gonida, Fátima Díaz-Freire, Susana Rodríguez, Antonio Valle. (2024). Effects of a homework implementation method (MITCA) on self-regulation of learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09376-z
title: MITCA method: five conditions for homework prescription grounded in self-regulated learning phases
description: MITCA (Homework Implementation Method) is a homework prescription framework designed to turn homework into a resource for self-regulated learning. The article states that "the MITCA method we designed for homework prescription is summarized by five conditions: Varied, Specific, Worthwhile, Weekly, and Evaluated." Tasks must be diverse (post- and pre-topic revision, organization and production tasks), defined in terms of cognitive operations and content, communicated as useful and interesting, assigned weekly with student-chosen time slots, and corrected weekly with feedback indicating strengths and weaknesses. It treats homework as a learning episode with preparation, work and reflection phases, aiming to optimize the preparation phase.
requirements: Teachers must be trained in the method and receive weekly follow-up monitoring during implementation
All five conditions must be addressed simultaneously when prescribing homework tasks
constraints: The article notes the relative effectiveness of each condition separately had not yet been empirically tested
target_learners: Primary school students in the last two years of primary school (5th and 6th grade, ages 10–12)
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation of learning
planning and time management
environment management
school engagement with homework
examples: In the intervention, trained experimental-group teachers prescribed MITCA homework for twelve weeks in Spanish language, Galician language and mathematics while control teachers continued traditional homework
key_sources: Tania Vieites, Eleftheria Gonida, Fátima Díaz-Freire, Susana Rodríguez, Antonio Valle. (2024). Effects of a homework implementation method (MITCA) on self-regulation of learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09376-z

article_title: Effects of a homework implementation method (MITCA) on self-regulation of learning
citation: Tania Vieites, Eleftheria Gonida, Fátima Díaz-Freire, Susana Rodríguez, Antonio Valle. (2024). Effects of a homework implementation method (MITCA) on self-regulation of learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09376-z
title: Prescribe homework following MITCA's premises to support students' self-regulatory skills
description: The article recommends that teachers design homework as varied, specific, worthwhile, weekly and evaluated tasks rather than repetitive traditional assignments. It concludes that "if educators prescribe homework following MITCA's premises and guidelines, students will be better supported to improve their self-regulatory skills, especially those related to environmental management." Diversifying tasks and highlighting their usefulness is said to predispose learners to commit to homework, while weekly assignment with student-set time slots supports time awareness and informative correction dampens procrastination.
requirements: Teachers must be trained to prescribe homework in accordance with the framework of self-regulated learning
constraints: The study was a convenience sample in Galicia with self-report measures only and no follow-up data
target_learners: Primary school students, especially 5th and 6th graders
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation of learning
time and environment management
reduced self-regulatory deficits
examples: Trained experimental-group teachers prescribed MITCA homework weekly for twelve weeks in Spanish language, Galician language and mathematics, with weekly online monitoring of task completion and correction
key_sources: Tania Vieites, Eleftheria Gonida, Fátima Díaz-Freire, Susana Rodríguez, Antonio Valle. (2024). Effects of a homework implementation method (MITCA) on self-regulation of learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09376-z

article_title: The self-regulation for learning online (SRL-O) questionnaire
citation: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E., Lodge, J. M., & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2023). The self-regulation for learning online (SRL-O) questionnaire. Metacognition and Learning, 18, 135–163. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09319-6
title: SRL-O questionnaire: a 44-item self-report measure of online self-regulated learning
description: The SRL-O is a publicly available self-report questionnaire measuring motivated self-regulated learning in online and blended contexts. The article states that "The final questionnaire contained 44 items that make up ten subscales measured on a 7-point response scale, with higher scores indicating higher perceived motivation or strategy use." It includes scale definitions and recommendations for learners scoring under four, and is downloadable with Qualtrics versions at www.srl-o.com, which provides automatised scores to students along with academic recommendations.
requirements: Designed for undergraduate students studying in online or blended learning contexts; delivered as a 7-point end-defined response scale with radio buttons
constraints: Not tested with students with no online component to their course; some items do not refer to online at all
target_learners: Undergraduate students in online and blended higher education courses
target_learning_goals: Measuring motivational beliefs and learning strategies for self-regulated learning online
examples: The questionnaire was validated via EFA in a training sample and CFA in a hold-out sample, with items reduced from an initial pool of 82 to 44
key_sources: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E., Lodge, J. M., & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2023). The self-regulation for learning online (SRL-O) questionnaire. Metacognition and Learning, 18, 135–163. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09319-6

article_title: Commentary: Is disfluency desirable?
citation: Bjork, R. A., & Yue, C. L. (2016). Commentary: Is disfluency desirable? Metacognition Learning, 11, 133–137. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9156-8
title: Desirable difficulties framework: difficulties enhance learning only when they trigger encoding and retrieval processes the learner can engage
description: The commentary situates disfluency within the desirable-difficulties framework (Bjork 1994), arguing that the word desirable is critical: difficulties such as generation, variation, spacing, contextual interference, and testing can trigger "the very encoding and retrieval processes that support learning, comprehension, and remembering," but whether that happens depends on the learner and the materials. Difficulties become undesirable when learners lack the background knowledge or skills to respond successfully. The special issue's contribution is establishing conditions separating desirable difficulties from simply difficulties.
requirements: The learner must have the background knowledge or skills to respond to the difficulty successfully
constraints: Even proven desirable difficulties (generation, spacing, testing) can be undesirable in specific instances
