Whether a difficulty is desirable depends on learner characteristics and on the to-be-learned materials
target_learners: All learners encountering intentionally introduced difficulties during instruction
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention and transfer of learned material
examples: The commentary cites McDaniel and Einstein's material-appropriate processing framework: sentence re-arrangement helps with expository text but not familiar fairy-tale organization, while letter deletion shows the opposite pattern
key_sources: Bjork, R. A., & Yue, C. L. (2016). Commentary: Is disfluency desirable? Metacognition Learning, 11, 133–137. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9156-8

article_title: The assessment and instruction of self-regulation in computer-based environments: a discussion
citation: Veenman, M. V. J. (2007). The assessment and instruction of self-regulation in computer-based environments: a discussion. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-007-9017-6
title: Self-regulation in computer-based environments requires both valid assessment and targeted instruction, as framed in Veenman's discussion article
description: The article is framed as a discussion of how self-regulation should be assessed and instructed when learning occurs in computer-based environments. Its title states this dual focus: "The assessment and instruction of self-regulation in computer-based environments". The keyword list signals the constructs the discussion organizes around, including "Convergent Validity", "Metacognitive Skill", "Intelligent Tutor System", and "Metacognitive Activity", indicating that measurement quality and intelligent tutoring systems are central concerns of the framework.
requirements: Assessment of metacognitive skill must address convergent validity, as indicated by the article's own keyword "Convergent Validity"
constraints: The piece is a discussion article (its subtitle is "a discussion"), not a report of new empirical data
target_learners: Students learning in computer-based environments
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation of learning
Metacognitive skill
examples: The article situates its discussion within a literature on self-regulated learning with hypermedia and scientific discovery learning with computer simulations, as shown in its reference list
key_sources: Veenman, M. V. J. (2007). The assessment and instruction of self-regulation in computer-based environments: a discussion. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-007-9017-6

article_title: Self-regulated strategy development’s effectiveness: underlying cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms
citation: Jonathan Fernandez, Jessica Guilbert. (2024). Self-regulated strategy development's effectiveness: underlying cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms. Metacognition and Learning (2024) 19:1091–1135. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09398-7
title: Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD): explicit, staged strategy instruction for writing self-regulation
description: SRSD is an intervention that explicitly teaches students writing strategies and the self-regulation skills to deploy them independently, with the long-term goal that students implement strategies in new contexts without teacher prompting. Strategies are taught through staged instruction in which the teacher "first presents the strategies to students, then models their use, proposes exercises to consolidate these strategies in memory, and supports students in their first implementation until they can perform these tasks autonomously". Students also learn a self-evaluation strategy of checking whether the important parts of a narrative text were included. The present study tested a French version for story writing in real classrooms.
requirements: Teachers must present, model, and support students' implementation of the strategies through the staged sequence until autonomous use
target_learners: elementary school students (fourth and fifth graders in this study)
target_learning_goals: narrative writing quality
planning strategies
accurate self-evaluation of text quality
examples: In the story-writing lessons, students identify the important parts of a story in multiple texts, build a schema-driven planning strategy, and use a graphic-organizer planning sheet before writing their own stories.
key_sources: Jonathan Fernandez, Jessica Guilbert. (2024). Self-regulated strategy development's effectiveness: underlying cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms. Metacognition and Learning (2024) 19:1091–1135. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09398-7

article_title: Self-regulated strategy development’s effectiveness: underlying cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms
citation: Jonathan Fernandez, Jessica Guilbert. (2024). Self-regulated strategy development's effectiveness: underlying cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms. Metacognition and Learning (2024) 19:1091–1135. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09398-7
title: Schema-driven story planning with a graphic-organizer planning sheet
description: A lesson-level design pattern within SRSD for narrative writing: students are first trained to identify the important parts of a story (characters, time, place, trigger, events, denouement, resolution) across texts, then use that knowledge to build a schema-driven planning strategy for their own stories. "Students are taught to structure their planning sheets with a graphic organizer, which is expected to help them generate and organize their ideas during a planning phase to help them write higher-quality stories." The planning sheet offers a series of subgoals and supports retrieving ideas from long-term memory.
requirements: Students must first learn to identify the important parts of a story in multiple texts before building the schema-driven strategy
A planning sheet structured with a graphic organizer must be provided for idea generation and organization before writing
target_learners: upper elementary students learning narrative writing
target_learning_goals: generating and organizing story ideas before writing
writing well-structured, higher-quality stories
examples: In the study's writing task, students were offered scratch paper as a planning sheet and could keep it while writing, though they were free to return it if they felt they did not need it.
key_sources: Jonathan Fernandez, Jessica Guilbert. (2024). Self-regulated strategy development's effectiveness: underlying cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms. Metacognition and Learning (2024) 19:1091–1135. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09398-7

article_title: Self-regulated strategy development’s effectiveness: underlying cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms
citation: Jonathan Fernandez, Jessica Guilbert. (2024). Self-regulated strategy development's effectiveness: underlying cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms. Metacognition and Learning (2024) 19:1091–1135. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09398-7
title: Use knowledge of SRSD's underlying mechanisms and moderating factors to target teaching emphasis, monitor skills, and design adaptive scaffolding
description: The article argues that understanding why, how, and for whom SRSD works should directly shape classroom practice. Insight into the intervention's cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms and the factors that might hinder it "could help enhance teachers' use of SRSD by providing clear recommendations on (1) the aspect of the intervention they should emphasize to their students, (2) which skills to monitor to identify students' difficulties and adjust their teaching if needed". This supports differentiated support, such as adaptive scaffolding for students whose working memory limits strategy implementation.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of which cognitive and motivational factors moderate SRSD's effectiveness to identify students' difficulties
constraints: The article notes some students, particularly those with poor working memory, struggled to implement the taught planning strategies, indicating a need for adjusted teaching
target_learners: elementary school students receiving SRSD writing instruction
target_learning_goals: internalizing self-regulation writing skills
implementing taught planning strategies
examples: The study assessed working memory, graphomotor skills, self-efficacy, and writing motivation before the lessons to determine whether these factors moderated the intervention's effectiveness.
key_sources: Jonathan Fernandez, Jessica Guilbert. (2024). Self-regulated strategy development's effectiveness: underlying cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms. Metacognition and Learning (2024) 19:1091–1135. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09398-7

article_title: Metacognitive regulation contributes to digital text comprehension in E-learning
citation: Burin, Debora Ines; Gonzalez, Federico Martin; Barreyro, Juan Pablo; Injoque Ricle, Irene. (2020). Metacognitive regulation contributes to digital text comprehension in E-learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09226-8
title: Task-referenced metacognitive regulation in e-learning reading: Global/Monitoring and Problem Solving as two regulatory dimensions
description: The article organizes self-reported metacognitive regulation of reading in digital e-learning comprehension around two dimensions identified by factor analysis. Global/Monitoring includes "having in mind the task purpose, re-reading and paying attention to important or difficult parts", while Problem Solving covers responses "in disorientation or lack of understanding, and the use of typography and navigation elements as comprehension aids". The framework is measured with a metacognitive inventory referred to the tasks just completed.
requirements: A metacognitive inventory referred to the comprehension tasks just completed, rather than a general dispositional questionnaire
constraints: Assessed with two low previous knowledge hypertexts completed at home in an e-learning environment rather than a class or lab
target_learners: College students reading expository digital texts in e-learning settings
target_learning_goals: Expository digital text comprehension in hypertext environments
examples: 219 college students reported metacognitive activities during comprehension tasks with a metacognitive inventory referred to the tasks just completed
key_sources: Burin, Debora Ines; Gonzalez, Federico Martin; Barreyro, Juan Pablo; Injoque Ricle, Irene. (2020). Metacognitive regulation contributes to digital text comprehension in E-learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09226-8

article_title: Linking teachers’ and students’ motivation for self-regulated learning: is there a signal and how is it transmitted?
citation: Johannes Jud, Yves Karlen, Carmen Nadja Hirt. (2024). Linking teachers' and students' motivation for self-regulated learning: is there a signal and how is it transmitted? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09393-y
title: Situated Expectancy-Value Theory as a framework linking teachers' and students' SRL motivation
description: The article applies Situated Expectancy-Value Theory (SEVT) to conceptualise both teachers' motivation to promote SRL and students' motivation to use strategies. According to the article, "one's choices, effort, or persistence are influenced by a person's values and expectancies for success", with values specified as intrinsic, attainment and utility value plus perceived costs. SEVT's situated, dynamic character motivates the study's expectation that transmission from teachers to students runs indirectly through instructional behaviour (SRL promotion) rather than directly.
requirements: Motivational constructs (self-efficacy/expectancies, attainment value, utility value, cost) must be measured for both teachers and students to model transmission paths
constraints: The article notes values and expectancies are situated and change over time, so links are not static across classes and situations
target_learners: Lower secondary school students (grades 7-9)
Lower secondary class teachers
target_learning_goals: Students' motivation to apply self-regulated learning strategies
Teachers' motivation to promote self-regulated learning
examples: The study modelled teachers' self-efficacy and attainment value as predictors of SRL promotion, which in turn was modelled as predictor of students' self-efficacy, utility value, attainment value and cost
key_sources: Johannes Jud, Yves Karlen, Carmen Nadja Hirt. (2024). Linking teachers' and students' motivation for self-regulated learning: is there a signal and how is it transmitted? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09393-y

article_title: Linking teachers’ and students’ motivation for self-regulated learning: is there a signal and how is it transmitted?
citation: Johannes Jud, Yves Karlen, Carmen Nadja Hirt. (2024). Linking teachers' and students' motivation for self-regulated learning: is there a signal and how is it transmitted? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09393-y
title: Include student reports of instructional practices alongside teacher self-reports when studying links between teacher and student motivation
description: When investigating whether teacher motivation transmits to student motivation, researchers and evaluators should capture students' perceptions of the instructional practice, not only teachers' self-reports. In this study, models using only teacher-reported SRL promotion found no indirect links, whereas "including student reports of SRL promotion is especially crucial to finding indirect links". Teachers tend to overestimate their instruction, and student reports are stronger predictors of student outcomes.
requirements: Both teacher- and student-reported measures of the instructional practice must be collected
Rater-specific effects must be accounted for in the analysis
constraints: Evidence comes from a cross-sectional correlational design in Swiss lower-secondary classes; the authors call for longitudinal designs before causal conclusions
target_learners: Lower secondary school students
Class teachers
target_learning_goals: Understanding and fostering students' motivation for self-regulated learning and strategy use
examples: The authors calculated partial-perspective models with either teacher- or student-reported SRL promotion and systematically compared which perspective yielded indirect teacher-to-student motivation links
key_sources: Johannes Jud, Yves Karlen, Carmen Nadja Hirt. (2024). Linking teachers' and students' motivation for self-regulated learning: is there a signal and how is it transmitted? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09393-y

article_title: The role of achievement emotions for text comprehension and metacomprehension
citation: Prinz-Weiß, A., Lukosiute, L., Meyer, M., & Riedel, J. (2023). The role of achievement emotions for text comprehension and metacomprehension. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09331-w
title: Cue-utilization framework extended to achievement emotions as metacomprehension judgment cues
description: The cue-utilization framework holds that when providing judgments, learners infer their level of comprehension based on available information, known as cues. This study extends the framework by treating state achievement emotions experienced during reading as potential judgment cues for predictions and postdictions. The findings show learners do use these emotions as cues, but the article concludes that achievement emotions "do not necessarily represent valid cues for judging comprehension", so relying on them can produce over- or underconfidence and hinder self-regulated learning from texts.
requirements: Learners must experience and be able to report state achievement emotions during the learning activity for the emotions to function as judgment cues
constraints: The article states emotions are not regularly diagnostic of actual comprehension; positive emotions were not associated with better comprehension in this study, so emotion-based judgments can impair accuracy
target_learners: senior high school students learning from texts
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of text comprehension
effective self-regulated learning from texts
key_sources: Prinz-Weiß, A., Lukosiute, L., Meyer, M., & Riedel, J. (2023). The role of achievement emotions for text comprehension and metacomprehension. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09331-w

article_title: The role of metacognition in monitoring performance and regulating learning in early readers
citation: Ioanna Taouki, Marie Lallier, David Soto. (2022). The role of metacognition in monitoring performance and regulating learning in early readers. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09293-1
title: Procedural metacognition as object-level/meta-level monitoring and control
description: The article adopts a procedural metacognition framework in which online task performance is mediated by an interaction between an object-level process (the type-1 task, e.g., reading or perceptual decisions) and a second-order meta-level process (type-2 performance). The meta-level "monitors the first-order process" and, when cognition fails, exerts control processes to promote adaptive behaviour; these are termed metacognitive monitoring and metacognitive control. The study operationalises monitoring via trial-by-trial binary confidence judgments and signal-detection-theory estimates of metacognitive efficiency (meta-d'/d').
requirements: Trial-by-trial confidence ratings collected alongside type-1 responses, with type-1 signal accessible to the child for type-2 judgments
constraints: Metacognitive efficiency estimates can be affected by task difficulty; the M-ratio controls for type-1 performance and difficulty
Young children show overconfidence bias, motivating bias-free SDT measures
target_learners: early primary school readers (Grade 1, ages 6-7)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring of task performance
orthographic lexical processing and visual word recognition
examples: Children rated confidence on each trial of VA span, statistical learning, lexical decision and emotion recognition tasks using a two-point scale (doubtful vs sure)
key_sources: Ioanna Taouki, Marie Lallier, David Soto. (2022). The role of metacognition in monitoring performance and regulating learning in early readers. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09292-0

article_title: Applying learning strategy questionnaires: problems and possibilities
citation: Gonny Schellings. (2011). Applying learning strategy questionnaires: problems and possibilities. Metacognition and Learning, 6, 91–109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9069-5
title: Meijer et al. taxonomy of 56 metacognitive text-studying activities in four superordinate scales
description: A taxonomy for coding think-aloud protocols of secondary school students studying a history text, developed by Meijer et al. and described as "theoretically based and data driven" and tested on new protocols "in a cyclic fashion". Its revised form "discerned 56 specific metacognitive activities that adhered to four superordinate scales, orientation & planning, execution, monitoring, and elaboration & evaluation." In this article it directly formed the basis of the task-specific questionnaire, with each taxonomy category tapped by one questionnaire item.
requirements: Think-aloud protocols of text studying to code, and raters trained in the taxonomy's categories
constraints: The four-scales distinction is theoretically based; the article reports students may not perceive the items as interrelated within the expert scales
target_learners: secondary school students studying history texts
target_learning_goals: metacognitive learning activities during text studying
examples: In Study 1, 2,817 activities were coded in 16 protocols, with the maximum (541 occurrences) for the subcategory 'error detection (plus correction), keeping track'
key_sources: Gonny Schellings. (2011). Applying learning strategy questionnaires: problems and possibilities. Metacognition and Learning, 6, 91–109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9069-5

article_title: Applying learning strategy questionnaires: problems and possibilities
citation: Gonny Schellings. (2011). Applying learning strategy questionnaires: problems and possibilities. Metacognition and Learning, 6, 91–109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9069-5
title: 58-item task-specific learning strategy questionnaire scored on a three-point frequency scale
description: A questionnaire constructed "straightforwardly on the basis of a taxonomy for coding think-aloud protocols", with all items referring to the specific history text read before completion and each of the taxonomy's categories tapped by one item. Items were scored on a three-point frequency scale ('almost never'=1, 'sometimes'=2, 'often'=3), a choice the article says may "reduce the variation in the choice of a reference point amongst students." The full instrument reached α=.87 (Study 1) and α=.79 (Study 2).
requirements: Items must explicitly refer to the specific learning task, and be formulated in vocabulary fitting the target students, using real protocol fragments
constraints: Subscale reliabilities were moderate to low in both administrations; the questionnaire is tied to one specific text-studying task
target_learners: ninth-grade secondary school students
target_learning_goals: self-reported metacognitive and cognitive activities during text studying
examples: Example item: 'I tried to draw conclusions beyond the literal text', corresponding to the taxonomy category 'Inferring'
key_sources: Gonny Schellings. (2011). Applying learning strategy questionnaires: problems and possibilities. Metacognition and Learning, 6, 91–109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9069-5

article_title: Metacognitive effects of instructional visuals: the role of cue use and judgment type
citation: Jaeger, A. J., & Fiorella, L. (2024). Metacognitive effects of instructional visuals: the role of cue use and judgment type. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09370-x
title: Judgment type moderates how instructional visuals affect metacomprehension through cue utilization
description: The article proposes that the type of metacognitive judgment students are asked to make (test performance, explaining, or drawing) activates different types of cues, which in turn determines how the presence of instructional visuals affects metacomprehension accuracy. Drawing judgments uniquely prompt students to consult visual information, making them especially vulnerable to superficial visual cues when images are present. The framework builds on Koriat's cue utilization framework distinguishing representation-based cues (tied to sensemaking experiences) from heuristic cues (tied to general beliefs about self or materials). The authors state that "Prompting students to judge their ability to generate drawings may encourage students to make greater use of the provided visuals as cues to inform their judgments."
requirements: Learners must make metacognitive judgments after reading expository science texts
Judgment prompts must differ in whether they direct attention to visual representations
constraints: Tested only with undergraduate populations reading biology and chemistry texts
Diagrams were conceptual but not specifically designed to enhance text content
target_learners: undergraduate students in STEM courses
target_learning_goals: accurate metacomprehension monitoring of science text comprehension
examples: Across Studies 1a, 1b, 2, and 3, draw judgments were differentially harmed by image presence compared to test and explain judgments, and visual cues were reported only for draw judgments.
key_sources: Jaeger, A. J., & Fiorella, L. (2024). Metacognitive effects of instructional visuals: the role of cue use and judgment type. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09370-x

article_title: Examining the regulation of motivational and comprehension-related problems during collaborative learning
citation: Nadine Melzner · Markus Dresel · Ingo Kollar. (2022). Examining the regulation of motivational and comprehension-related problems during collaborative learning. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:813–836. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09316-9
title: Three social levels of regulation in collaborative learning (self, co, shared)
description: The article adopts Järvelä and Hadwin's (2013) distinction of three social levels at which groups can regulate learning. At the self-level strategies are applied "without making them visible for the other group members"; at the co-level "a student may try to support single fellow group members to improve their learning processes"; at the shared-level groups "share, negotiate, and synthetize strategies to attain joint learning goals", which the article terms an instance of shared regulation. The same strategy can operate at each level, e.g. self-explaining terms, asking one member to explain, or jointly developing shared understanding.
requirements: Groups whose members can distinguish which regulation activities are directed at their own learning, at other individual members' learning, or at the group's joint learning
constraints: Research based on this three-level model is described in the article as having a strong qualitative focus, and empirical evidence on which problems get regulated at which level was scarce
target_learners: university students in self-formed study groups
target_learning_goals: regulating motivational and comprehension-related problems during collaborative exam preparation
examples: Participants rated and described strategies at each level after every vignette; the soccer example vignette illustrated level distinctions such as 'We eat pizza together to strengthen our team spirit' as a shared-level motivational strategy

title: Four case vignettes systematically varying motivational and comprehension-related problems
description: The study's core instrument is a booklet of four case vignettes describing a study group preparing for an exam, arranged in a 2 × 2 within-subjects design: no problems ("high knowledge and high learning motivation"), only motivational problems, only comprehension-related problems, and both problems ("low knowledge and low learning motivation"). After each vignette participants indicated at three social levels whether they would "do something to ensure a high quality of learning" and wrote down open-ended strategy answers. A soccer-team example vignette familiarized participants with the level distinctions.
requirements: Participants able to imagine being a member of the described study group and to distinguish the three social levels of regulation, supported by the example vignette
constraints: The vignettes describe hypothetical rather than real group learning situations, and did not point to specific group members who might have more motivational or comprehension-related problems than others
target_learners: university students in an introductory Educational Science lecture
target_learning_goals: reporting conditional strategy knowledge for regulating motivational and comprehension-related problems at self, co and shared levels

title: Zimmerman's cyclic model of self-regulated learning: forethought, performance and self-reflection phases
description: The article presents Zimmerman's cyclic model as one of the predominant process models of SRL, grounded in social cognitive theory. It "describes SRL in terms of three cyclical phases: a forethought phase, a performance phase and a self-reflection phase", covering orienting and goal setting, strategy deployment with monitoring, and evaluation of the learning process. The article uses this model, alongside component models, as the conceptual basis for the SRL strategies addressed in iSELF and its observation instrument.

constraints: the phases do not follow a strictly linear sequence and can take place simultaneously depending on the learner, feedback and plan changes

description: The article describes Pintrich's (2004) model as combining component and process models of SRL. It "integrates cognitive, metacognitive, motivational and behavioral SRL processes, clearly categorizing the different strategies that are involved during the different phases of SRL", adding detail on how SRL operates in the classroom. Building on Pintrich and Zimmerman, the authors composed Table 1, an overview of the most stated cognitive, metacognitive, motivational and behavioral SRL strategies used to structure iSELF and its coding instrument.

description: iSELF is a professional development program for primary teachers in which "the explicit instruction of SRL strategies in their classrooms plays a central role". It combines a half-day plenary training on SRL theory and didactics with three coaching sessions in which teachers construct lesson plans using the iSELF flowchart and reflect on observed lessons with a trainer. title: Adapted ATES low-inference observation instrument for coding explicit and implicit SRL instruction
description: The study coded video-recorded lessons with an adapted version of the low-inference ATES coding system, which scores "the quantity and type of specific SRL instructions by coding teachers' utterances and observable behavior" per minute. The adapted Dutch instrument expanded the original nine codes to thirteen, distinguishing implicit from explicit instruction across cognitive, metacognitive, behavioral and motivational strategies. Interrater reliability reached κ 0.75 for the coding system, with 100% agreement on the implicit/explicit distinction.

description: The article grounds iSELF's instructional practices in research on effective teacher professional development. Citing a review of 35 PDPs, it lists characteristics of effective programs: they "incorporate active learning, (3) support teacher collaboration, (4) use models and modelling, (5) offer coaching and expert support, (6) stimulate feedback and reflection and (7) are of sustained duration". Explicit instruction means teachers clearly explain how strategies are applied, when they are most effective and what their benefits are, for example by modelling strategies through thinking out loud. iSELF trains teachers in both didactics.

article_title: Effects of availability of diagnostic and non-diagnostic cues on the accuracy of teachers’ judgments of students’ text comprehension
citation: Janneke van de Pol, Eleanor Rowan, Eva Janssen, Tamara van Gog. (2024). Effects of availability of diagnostic and non-diagnostic cues on the accuracy of teachers' judgments of students' text comprehension. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09383-0
title: Cue-utilization framework of metacognitive monitoring applied to teacher judgment accuracy
description: The cue-utilization framework (Brunswik; Koriat) holds that judgments are inferential: people use pieces of information, or cues, when making judgments, and judgment accuracy depends on how predictive, or diagnostic, those cues are of the judged outcome. For teacher judgments of student learning, cues are grouped into task cues, student cues, and performance cues, with performance cues generally correlating highest with student performance. This study experimentally tested the framework's central tenet for task-specific teacher judgments of text comprehension, manipulating cue availability and diagnosticity.
requirements: Cue diagnosticity must be determined by measuring cue values and calculating the correlation between cue value and performance on the judged task
constraints: Mnemonic cues are internal to the learner and typically not available to teachers, so the teacher-judgment variant uses task, student, and performance cues instead
target_learners: Secondary school teachers judging students' text comprehension
target_learning_goals: Accurate teacher judgment of students' text comprehension to support adaptive instruction
examples: In the experiment, diagnostic cues were the four most diagnostic performance cues from students' diagramming tasks (e.g., number of correct boxes, diagnosticity 0.63) and non-diagnostic cues included Dutch grade (0.03) and interest in the text topic (0.19)

article_title: Metacognitive Confidence Can Increase but Also Decrease Performance in Academic Settings
citation: Moreno, L., Briñol, P., & Petty, R. E. (2022). Metacognitive Confidence Can Increase but Also Decrease Performance in Academic Settings. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 139–165. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09270-y
title: Self-validation theory: perceived validity of primary cognitions determines whether they guide judgment and action
description: Self-validation theory holds that after a primary cognition forms, people generate second-order thoughts about its validity, and the perceived validity of the primary thought determines the extent to which it is used in judgment and behavior. The article defines metacognitive confidence as "a subjective belief regarding the validity of any primary cognition," independent of accuracy. Unlike accuracy-focused metacognitive research, it identifies sources of validity (e.g., head nodding, ease, recalled confidence episodes) unrelated to correctness. The theory predicts that confidence magnifies whatever valenced thought is accessible, producing opposite performance effects for positive versus negative thoughts.
requirements: Primary cognitions must be accessible and performance-relevant
Perceived validity must be measured or induced following the primary cognition
constraints: Validation processes are more likely when thinking is relatively high and the topic is of high personal relevance
The approach concerns opinion-based thoughts where there is no objectively correct answer, not accuracy judgments
target_learners: undergraduate students in academic settings
target_learning_goals: academic performance on knowledge tests and standardized assessments
self-relevant beliefs about one's abilities as a student
examples: Study 2 induced validation by framing questionnaire anchors so any answer implied high certainty, and invalidation by framing answers to imply distance from one's thoughts
Study 3 induced validation by asking participants to recall and describe a past episode of feeling confidence in their thoughts
key_sources: Moreno, L., Briñol, P., & Petty, R. E. (2022). Metacognitive Confidence Can Increase but Also Decrease Performance in Academic Settings. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 139–165. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09270-y

article_title: Metacognitive Confidence Can Increase but Also Decrease Performance in Academic Settings
citation: Moreno, L., Briñol, P., & Petty, R. E. (2022). Metacognitive Confidence Can Increase but Also Decrease Performance in Academic Settings. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 139–165. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09270-y
title: Build learner confidence only after ensuring the underlying thoughts are positive; confidence in negative self-thoughts backfires
description: This principle holds that interventions raising learners' metacognitive confidence will amplify whatever performance-relevant thoughts the learner already holds. The article shows that "when thoughts were positive, increased confidence in the primary cognitions improved performance," but the same confidence validating negative thoughts reduced performance. Educators should therefore establish positive performance-relevant cognitions (about the self, the task, or the exam) before or alongside any confidence-boosting induction, and should not assume confidence is uniformly beneficial.
requirements: The learner's dominant performance-relevant thoughts must be diagnosed before applying a confidence induction
Confidence inductions (e.g., recalling past episodes of confidence) must follow the thought-valence induction to validate the intended cognitions
constraints: Confidence in negative thoughts reduces performance, so confidence boosters can backfire
Validation processes are more likely to operate when learners are motivated to think and the topic is personally relevant
target_learners: undergraduate students
students facing exams or performance assessments
target_learning_goals: improving performance on knowledge tests and standardized assessments
fostering positive self-relevant beliefs about academic ability
examples: In Study 3, participants who listed positive thoughts about their qualities as students and then recalled a past confidence episode scored higher on GRE questions than those who recalled doubt
In Study 2, validating negative self-thoughts led participants to solve fewer geometric-shape problems than invalidating those same thoughts

article_title: To what extent can think sheets with or without reflection prompts support self-regulated learning from text?
citation: Anja Prinz-Weiß & Elisa Röhm. (2025). To what extent can think sheets with or without reflection prompts support self-regulated learning from text? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09419-z
title: Knowledge Revision Components (KReC) framework as the theoretical account for why think sheets address misconceptions
description: The article invokes the KReC framework (Kendeou & O'Brien, 2014) as the explanatory model for how think sheets foster conceptual change. It proposes that knowledge revision requires that "the misconception and correct information are simultaneously activated in a learner's memory (coactivation principle)", after which correct information is integrated and increasingly dominates the knowledge network (competing activation principle). Because think sheets require learners to extract correct information from a text and set it against the respective misconceptions, the authors argue they likely evoke coactivation and additional conceptual-change processes, and their generative character may additionally support transfer.
requirements: Learning materials must present both the misconception and the correct information so both can be coactivated in memory.
constraints: The framework is used interpretively; the article states the two methods "might have facilitated coactivation", not that coactivation was measured.
target_learners: University students with prior misconceptions about learning content
target_learning_goals: Revising misconceptions and building accurate conceptual understanding from texts
examples: The think sheet asked learners to answer central covariance questions with correct information from the text after reading a stated misconception for each question.

article_title: To what extent can think sheets with or without reflection prompts support self-regulated learning from text?
citation: Anja Prinz-Weiß & Elisa Röhm. (2025). To what extent can think sheets with or without reflection prompts support self-regulated learning from text? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09419-z
title: Use think sheets as a misconception-addressing intervention that does not require rewriting instructional texts
description: The article recommends think sheets as a practical alternative to refutation texts for addressing misconceptions during learning from text. Compared to refutation texts, "think sheets can be applied without rewriting instructional texts": the existing text stays unchanged, and a worksheet with central questions and misconceptions is added, on which learners write the correct answers using the text. The article also notes that alternating instructional methods helps keep learners motivated. In the study, this was implemented as four question-misconception blocks accompanying a statistics text.
requirements: A text providing the correct information and a worksheet listing central questions with related misconceptions.
constraints: In this study think sheets provided little benefit over having students simply read about the misconceptions and correct information, and adding reflection prompts did not improve outcomes.
target_learners: University students learning statistics content from texts
target_learning_goals: Counteracting misconceptions and supporting comprehension and transfer from text
examples: Participants in the think-sheet conditions answered four central covariance questions on a worksheet using a 539-word statistics text, with or without four reflection prompts per block.

article_title: Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts
citation: Ivar Bråten & Helge I. Strømsø. (2011). Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts. Metacognition Learning 6:111–130. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9075-7
title: Multiple-Text Strategy Inventory (MTSI)
description: The MTSI is a 15-item task-specific self-report questionnaire measuring strategic processing during multiple-text reading, with five accumulation items and ten cross-text elaboration items rated on a 10-point Likert-type scale. The authors state: "We designed the Multiple-Text Strategy Inventory (MTSI) for this purpose. This 15-item questionnaire was based on prior empirical research on students' reading of multiple texts reviewed above." Each item referred to the recently completed reading task, with verbs in the past tense. It is intended for individual assessment and large-scale investigations.

reading comprehension

Readability scores ranged from 41 to 61 with a mean of 47.6, which the authors say "suggesting that the reading material represented a sufficient challenge for the participants and was well suited for eliciting effortful, strategic processing." Source, author, credentials, and date were printed on each text.

article_title: Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts
citation: Ivar Bråten & Helge I. Strømsø. (2011). Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts. Metacognition Learning 6:111–130. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9075-7
title: Tailor strategy self-report inventories to a specific recently completed reading task
description: The article argues valid self-report measurement of strategies requires task-specific inventories rather than general ones, following four guidelines: administer a specific task the items refer to, give an instruction including reading purpose and a prompt to monitor strategies, administer the inventory immediately after task completion, and word items in the past tense without general stems. The authors note that general inventory scores "did not relate to comprehension performance, nor to the strategic processing reported on in a specific task context."
requirements: A specific task must be administered to which items refer; instruction must state purpose and direct monitoring; inventory administered immediately after task completion; items use past tense and omit general stems
constraints: Even task-specific self-reports focus on perceptions or memories of strategy use and may suffer from biased processing or reconstructive memory, with social desirability threatening validity
target_learners: higher education undergraduates
target_learning_goals: measuring reading comprehension strategies
examples: The MTSI was administered immediately after the seven-text reading task, with items in past tense referring to that task

article_title: Evaluating metacognitive self-reports: systematic reviews of the value of self-report in metacognitive research
citation: Craig, K., Hale, D., Grainger, C., & Stewart, M. E. (2020). Evaluating metacognitive self-reports: systematic reviews of the value of self-report in metacognitive research. Metacognition and Learning, 15, 155-213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09222-y
title: Competing taxonomies of metacognition: Flavell's four areas and later two-factor, self/other, and three-factor modifications
description: The article organizes metacognitive theory as a landscape of competing taxonomies. Flavell's original theory "divides metacognition into four areas: metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive experiences, goals, and actions." Later modifications include Brown's division into knowledge of cognition and regulation of cognition, Schraw and Dennison's addition of information management and debugging as regulation subcomponents, self-versus-other taxonomies, and a proposed third factor of metacognitive beliefs or attributions. The review uses this landscape to frame why so many different self-report questionnaires exist.
requirements: The article states that evaluating a generalizable structure of metacognition requires participants representing the general population, with widely applicable questionnaires.
constraints: The article states there is a lack of consensus regarding a theoretical organization of metacognition, and available self-report questionnaires reflect this lack of consensus.
target_learners: general population across primary school, secondary school, and university students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge and regulation of cognition
key_sources: Craig, K., Hale, D., Grainger, C., & Stewart, M. E. (2020). Evaluating metacognitive self-reports: systematic reviews of the value of self-report in metacognitive research. Metacognition and Learning, 15, 155-213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09222-y

article_title: Evaluating metacognitive self-reports: systematic reviews of the value of self-report in metacognitive research
citation: Craig, K., Hale, D., Grainger, C., & Stewart, M. E. (2020). Evaluating metacognitive self-reports: systematic reviews of the value of self-report in metacognitive research. Metacognition and Learning, 15, 155-213. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09222-y
title: Systematic reviews and meta-analysis of metacognitive self-report measures (24,396 articles screened; 22 factor-structure studies; 37 correlation studies)
description: This element is the article's own evidence base: two PRISMA-conducted systematic reviews and a meta-analysis of self-report in metacognitive research. Searches in seven databases located studies from 1982 through 2018, with "24,396 articles from 1982 through 2018 were screened for inclusion in the study." The first review tabulated 22 factor-structure studies; the second analyzed 37 studies, in which "the 37 articles reported 328 correlations between factors and/or subcomponents of metacognition," with instrument type and timing coded for moderator analysis.
requirements: Included articles had to statistically evaluate metacognition in the general population using widely applicable measures, or compare at least two pure metacognition measures with correlational effect sizes in a within design.
constraints: Articles were excluded when participants had a condition or disability, when questionnaires targeted a specific subset of the population, when measures included other skills such as motivation, or when articles could not be obtained in English.
target_learners: general-population learners from primary school through university and adults
target_learning_goals: measurement of metacognitive knowledge, regulation, and their subcomponents

article_title: Reflections on the field of metacognition: issues, challenges, and opportunities
citation: Roger Azevedo. (2020). Reflections on the field of metacognition: issues, challenges, and opportunities. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09231-x
title: Metacognitive instruction should embed instruction in content, inform learners of usefulness, and prolong training
description: The editorial states that the literature on metacognitive instruction clearly indicates three conditions for acquiring and instructing metacognition: "embedding metacognitive instruction in the content matter to ensure connectivity", informing learners about the usefulness of metacognitive activities so they exert initial extra effort, and prolonging training to guarantee smooth and maintained application of metacognitive activity. The author presents these as established global principles from the instruction literature.
requirements: Instruction must be embedded in subject-matter content to ensure connectivity between metacognitive activity and the content being learned.
constraints: Despite these global principles, the author notes the instruction of metacognition remains largely unexplored, with only a few notable examples in math, writing, and reading.
target_learners: Learners of all ages acquiring metacognitive knowledge and skills from parents, peers, and teachers
target_learning_goals: Acquisition and maintained application of metacognitive knowledge and skills
examples: The editorial cites notable examples of metacognitive instruction in math (Kramarski and Michalsky 2013), writing (Hacker 2018; Harris and Graham 2017), and reading (Griffin et al. 2019).
key_sources: Roger Azevedo. (2020). Reflections on the field of metacognition: issues, challenges, and opportunities. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09231-x

article_title: The Double-Edged Interactions of Prompts and Self-efficacy
citation: Nadja Gentner & Tina Seufert. (2020). The Double-Edged Interactions of Prompts and Self-efficacy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09227-7
title: Aptitude-treatment interaction perspective: state-like self-efficacy during learning as a moderator of instructional support effectiveness
description: The article applies aptitude-treatment interaction (ATI) research to motivational aptitudes, proposing that "instructional features are most effective for learners with certain characteristics" and that, unlike static aptitudes such as prior knowledge, motivational variables like self-efficacy are state-like and change over the learning process. It therefore argues learner characteristics should be assessed during learning, since learners experiencing high self-efficacy while learning might profit from prompts, whereas those experiencing low self-efficacy might need more explicit instructions. This framework motivates the study's moderation hypotheses.
requirements: Assessment of the learner characteristic (self-efficacy) during the learning process rather than only before it
constraints: The article notes motivational or emotional aptitudes were largely neglected in prior ATI research, and that classic ATI aptitudes are assumed static over the whole learning process
target_learners: undergraduate students learning with hypermedia
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use and learning outcomes in hypermedia environments
examples: The study measured self-efficacy before, 20 minutes into, and directly after a 40-minute hypermedia learning session and tested moderation of prompt effects on outcomes and strategy use
key_sources: Nadja Gentner & Tina Seufert. (2020). The Double-Edged Interactions of Prompts and Self-efficacy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09227-7

article_title: The Double-Edged Interactions of Prompts and Self-efficacy
citation: Nadja Gentner & Tina Seufert. (2020). The Double-Edged Interactions of Prompts and Self-efficacy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09227-7
title: Hypermedia environment on empirical research methods with six page-linked cognitive and metacognitive prompts
description: A hypermedia learning environment on empirical research methods containing 23 pages, of which six pages (chapters one and two on empirical methods, hypotheses, and propositional logic) were relevant for the learning session. It featured a navigation bar, forward and backward buttons, hyperlinks connecting pages non-linearly, a notepad, and a search function. The experimental group received "A combination of three cognitive and three metacognitive prompts", each linked to a specific relevant page and visible whenever the learner stayed on or revisited that page.
requirements: Learners must plan navigation, organise content, and monitor and evaluate their learning progress, since successful hypermedia learning requires self-regulation and metacognitive skills
constraints: Only the first two of four chapters were relevant and had to be learned in the 40-minute session
target_learners: first-semester undergraduate psychology students
target_learning_goals: understanding scientific hypotheses and propositional logic in empirical research methods
examples: Cognitive prompts cued organisation and elaboration (e.g., asking how to organise the structure of the learning contents); metacognitive prompts cued monitoring (e.g., which main points have not been understood)
key_sources: Nadja Gentner & Tina Seufert. (2020). The Double-Edged Interactions of Prompts and Self-efficacy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09227-7

article_title: How to design and evaluate personalized scaffolds for self-regulated learning
citation: Joep van der Graaf, Mladen Raković, Yizhou Fan, Lyn Lim, Shaveen Singh, Maria Bannert, Dragan Gašević, Inge Molenaar. (2023). How to design and evaluate personalized scaffolds for self-regulated learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09361-y
title: Personalize scaffolds based on learners' actual SRL processes detected in real time, removing options the learner has already executed.
description: The article recommends personalizing scaffold content to the self-regulated learning processes a student has actually executed, detected in real time from log data. Personalization works by removing any suggested option already performed, so scaffolds become more directive and less cognitively demanding. The authors state: "We, therefore, recommend personalizing scaffolds based on learners' SRL processes." In their study this changed learning behavior: students in the personalized condition generally showed the most monitoring and high cognition while receiving fewer suggestions than the generalized condition.
requirements: Real-time detection of SRL processes from unobtrusive log data, with rules for each scaffold option determining whether the associated process was already executed
constraints: Personalization was built on prior work in the same task and context; the article recommends first getting a thorough understanding of actual SRL in a specific context before developing a support system
target_learners: university students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning during reading and essay writing
examples: In the personalized condition, the option of checking the learning goal and instruction was not displayed when students spent at least five seconds on the instruction page
key_sources: Joep van der Graaf, Mladen Raković, Yizhou Fan, Lyn Lim, Shaveen Singh, Maria Bannert, Dragan Gašević, Inge Molenaar. (2023). How to design and evaluate personalized scaffolds for self-regulated learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09361-y

article_title: Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL
citation: Nadira Saab. (2012). Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9085-5
title: Levels of social interaction framework for regulative activities in CSCL: individual, dyadic, and group levels
description: The article organizes regulative activities during collaborative learning by the social level at which they occur. It states that "During collaborative learning, the regulation of activities can take place at different levels of social interaction: the individual level, the dyadic level, and the group level." Individual regulation is an intrapersonal process regulating one's own cognitive processes; dyadic regulation means one member regulates another member's activities; group-level regulation involves shared activities aimed at regulating the group's cognitive activities. Dyadic and group regulation are characterized as interpersonal processes. The article uses this framework to map the three special-issue studies (Fig. 1).
requirements: Regulative activities must be coded or observed in a collaborative setting so the social level at which they occur can be distinguished
constraints: The article notes the Meijer et al. coding scheme used by Lajoie and Lu was developed for individuals working alone and "it is not possible to code regulative activities at a dyadic level" with it
target_learners: collaborative learners in CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: regulation of the collaborative learning process
examples: Fig. 1 maps Saab et al.'s task and team regulation, Janssen et al.'s task-related and social regulation, and Lajoie and Lu's metacognitive activities and co-regulation onto the three levels
key_sources: Nadira Saab. (2012). Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9085-5

article_title: Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL
citation: Nadira Saab. (2012). Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9085-5
title: Taxonomy of regulation labels in CSCL: task regulation, team regulation, regulation of social activities, and co-regulation
description: The article distinguishes the labels different researchers use for forms of regulation during CSCL. Saab et al. distinguish task regulation (orientation, monitoring, and evaluation of the task) from team regulation (planning of activities and monitoring of the team process). Janssen et al. distinguish regulation of task-related activities from regulation of social activities, differentiating "activities that are performed in the content space of the collaborative learning process and activities with a social-relational function." Lajoie and Lu use co-regulation, "a form of collaboration that is needed to acquire shared understanding," involving multiple group members building shared mental models. The article argues these labels describe effective regulation of learning in CSCL.
requirements: A coding scheme or analytic distinction between task-focused and socially focused regulative activities
constraints: The labels are used inconsistently across research groups; the article's purpose is to relate them rather than standardize them
target_learners: collaborative learners in CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: regulation of task performance and of collaboration during CSCL
examples: Grounding, or establishing shared understanding, is given as an example of a social activity; asking questions as an example of a task-related activity
key_sources: Nadira Saab. (2012). Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9085-5

article_title: Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL
citation: Nadira Saab. (2012). Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9085-5
title: CSCL environments should provide scaffolding that supports regulation of the collaborative learning process
description: Because learners in CSCL usually work without a teacher present to provide regulative guidance, the article argues the learning environment itself should scaffold the learning process. It states that "the CSCL learning environment can provide scaffolding for different aspects of the learning process," for example "measures that support the regulation process," the discovery learning process, or the communication process. The special issue examines how different forms of scaffolds or technology influence the use of regulative activities during collaboration.
requirements: A CSCL environment with computer-mediated communication where no teacher is present to offer regulative guidance
constraints: The article notes CMC often implies gestures and other non-verbal signs are absent, requiring messages to be formulated and explicated more precisely
target_learners: learners working collaboratively in computer-supported environments
target_learning_goals: regulation of task performance and collaboration during complex, open-ended collaborative problem solving
examples: The special-issue studies by Saab et al. and Lajoie and Lu provide insight into how different forms of scaffolds or technology in CSCL influence the use of regulative activities
key_sources: Nadira Saab. (2012). Team regulation, regulation of social activities or co-regulation: Different labels for effective regulation of learning in CSCL. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9085-5

article_title: Comparing metacognitive monitoring between native and non-native speaking primary school students
citation: Buehler, F. J., van Loon, M. H., Bayard, N. S., Steiner, M., & Roebers, C. M. (2021). Comparing metacognitive monitoring between native and non-native speaking primary school students. Metacognition and Learning, 16, 749–768. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09261-z
title: Language competencies as a theoretical basis for metacognitive monitoring development (Ebert's account as applied by the authors)
description: The article draws on a theoretical account in which language features support children's metacognition: "A grammatical understanding may support children to represent mental states," acquiring mental words may foster conceptual understanding of unobservable cognitive processes, and language skills may facilitate verbal interactions that foster learning about the mental world. On this basis, early language competencies have been related to later metacognition, motivating the hypothesis that native and non-native speaking children might differ in monitoring. The study's null results qualify this account for procedural monitoring resolution.
requirements: The account presupposes that monitoring is typically assessed verbally, so language of assessment may matter for measurement.
constraints: The study's own results suggest procedural monitoring resolution is relatively independent of the native language and language of assessment once instructions are understood; language abilities may be more closely related to declarative than procedural metacognition.
target_learners: Primary school children (~10-year-old fourth graders), including native and non-native speaking students
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive monitoring resolution (distinguishing correct from incorrect answers)
examples: The authors hypothesized that non-native speaking children's monitoring skills might be inferior based on this account, then tested and rejected that hypothesis in two studies.
key_sources: Buehler, F. J., van Loon, M. H., Bayard, N. S., Steiner, M., & Roebers, C. M. (2021). Comparing metacognitive monitoring between native and non-native speaking primary school students. Metacognition and Learning, 16, 749–768. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09261-z

article_title: Examining metacognitive strategy use in L1 and L2 task-situated writing: effects, transferability, and cross-language facilitation
citation: Wandong Xu, Xinhua Zhu. (2024). Examining metacognitive strategy use in L1 and L2 task-situated writing: effects, transferability, and cross-language facilitation. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09387-w
title: Embed metacognitive strategy training in writing classrooms with explicit, practical guidance across task interpreting, planning, monitoring, and evaluating
description: The article recommends training metacognitive strategies as a pedagogical tool in writing classrooms, given their predictive effects on L1 and L2 writing performance and the malleability of metacognition. It specifies that "explicit guidance is needed to help students form an accurate task representation, generate logical pre-plans, execute effective monitoring linguistically and non-linguistically, and have meaningful evaluations", and that "Practical guidance appears to be more effective than vague explanations".
requirements: Training should be embedded in the writing classroom as learners sit in writing tasks and writing-related activities instead of being decontextualized
target_learners: Chinese EFL undergraduate writers
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive regulation of the writing process
L1 and L2 writing performance
examples: The study's five validated strategy subcategories (task interpreting, planning, non-linguistic monitoring, linguistic monitoring, evaluating) structure the recommended training content
key_sources: Wandong Xu, Xinhua Zhu. (2024). Examining metacognitive strategy use in L1 and L2 task-situated writing: effects, transferability, and cross-language facilitation. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09387-w

article_title: Testing pays off twice: Potentials of practice tests and feedback regarding exam performance and judgment accuracy
citation: Nick Naujoks, Bettina Harder, Marion Händel. (2022). Testing pays off twice: Potentials of practice tests and feedback regarding exam performance and judgment accuracy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09295-x
title: Meaningful classroom practice-test setting: voluntary participation, lecture-aligned content, criterial-test format, and corrective feedback
description: The article synthesizes features that prior classroom testing-effect studies share and that its own practice tests met. Such a setting in the context of a lecture is characterized by features including "voluntary participation in practice tests" and "practice tests of same format as the criterial test (multiple-choice)". In both studies, four online multiple-choice practice tests of 12 items each were offered after each thematic block, drawn from the lecture content of the previous weeks, with exam items never reused from the practice tests.
requirements: Practice-test content must reflect the material of the respective lecture/exam
Students should continue to process the content of the tests and not merely seek insight into exam difficulty and structure
constraints: Participation is voluntary, so uptake varies widely; in both studies many students took none or only the last test before the exam
target_learners: undergraduate students in regular lecture courses
target_learning_goals: course-relevant knowledge measured by a final multiple-choice exam
metacognitive monitoring of one's own performance
examples: Four online practice tests per term on a university learning platform, each available for ten days, with items saved as PDF after completion
key_sources: Nick Naujoks, Bettina Harder, Marion Händel. (2022). Testing pays off twice: Potentials of practice tests and feedback regarding exam performance and judgment accuracy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09295-x

article_title: Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing
citation: Chenghui Chen, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09435-z
title: MRIM scale: a 19-item instrument for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing
description: The MRIM scale is a 6-point Likert questionnaire measuring L2 learners' metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse in argumentative writing. Items were generated through literature review and unstructured interviews with nine students, then piloted with PhD reviewers, two content experts, and a 117-student pretest. The finalized 19-item scale comprises three subscales: planning of interactive metadiscourse (PIM), monitoring of interactive metadiscourse (MIM), and evaluating of interactive metadiscourse (EIM).
requirements: Items were generated through literature review and unstructured interviews with target participants, which the authors say can increase the credibility and quality of items
constraints: The scale was developed and validated with first-year non-English major students at two Chinese universities, so its validated scope is that population
target_learners: first-year non-English major university students learning English as a foreign language
target_learning_goals: metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing
examples: Sample One (1417 cases) completed the original version for EFA; Sample Two (1078 cases) wrote a timed argumentative essay and completed the revised version for CFA and regression
key_sources: Chenghui Chen, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09435-z

article_title: Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing
citation: Chenghui Chen, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09435-z
title: Hyponymic relationship between metacognition and metadiscourse: metadiscourse as linguistic expression of metacognition
description: The article proposes that metacognition and metadiscourse stand in a hyponymic relationship, with metacognition as superordinate and metadiscourse as hyponym. As the authors state, "metadiscourse is the linguistic expression of metacognition, and metacognition regulates and monitors the cognitive activity through metadiscourse to some extent". The scale development was designed to corroborate this theoretical rationale combining metacognition and metadiscourse with empirical data, extending metacognition to the specific domain of interactive metadiscourse use in L2 writing.
requirements: The framework applies metacognitive regulation (planning, monitoring, evaluating) to a specific domain, here interactive metadiscourse use in L2 argumentative writing
constraints: The study focuses only on metacognitive regulation, not metacognitive knowledge or experiences, in the L2 writing context
target_learners: L2 writers in higher education
target_learning_goals: metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse use in argumentative writing
examples: The MRIM scale operationalizes the framework using Wenden's (1998) tripartite model of planning, monitoring, and evaluating applied to interactive metadiscourse
key_sources: Chenghui Chen, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09435-z

article_title: Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing
citation: Chenghui Chen, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Development and validation of a scale for metacognitive regulation of interactive metadiscourse strategies in L2 argumentative writing. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09435-z
title: Attend to monitoring of interactive metadiscourse during writing, since it is the strongest predictor of L2 argumentative writing performance
description: Because monitoring of interactive metadiscourse showed the strongest predictive power for L2 argumentative writing performance, writing instruction should give particular attention to real-time monitoring of metadiscourse use, guiding students to check how interactive metadiscourse devices guide readers through the text while writing. The authors note students "are not fully aware of the importance of pre-writing planning and post-writing revisions/reflection", suggesting instruction should also strengthen planning and evaluating.
requirements: Instruction must address all three regulation strategies, since PIM and EIM were also significant positive predictors
constraints: The predictive hierarchy comes from one regression study with Chinese first-year university students; the authors' explanation for the difference is speculative, drawn from teaching experience
target_learners: Chinese EFL university student writers
target_learning_goals: L2 argumentative writing performance
examples: The regression showed MIM (β = 0.344) predicting writing performance more strongly than PIM (β = 0.115) and EIM (β = 0.179)

article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition
citation: Stebner, F., Schuster, C., Weber, X.-L., Greiff, S., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2022). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x
title: Structure-mapping theory of analogical transfer applied to metacognitive skill transfer in self-regulated learning
description: The article applies Gentner's structure-mapping theory of analogical transfer to self-regulated learning, distinguishing the source problem from the target problem and four steps of analogical transfer including retrieval and mapping. It states that "Retrieval is primarily influenced by surface similarity" while "Deep structure similarity is determined during the mapping process," and uses this distinction to define near versus far transfer of metacognitive skills between learning tasks.
requirements: A source task and a target task whose surface and deep structure similarity can be distinguished, so that transfer distance can be classified
constraints: The article notes the term transfer is inconsistently defined and that it specifically adopts the analogical transfer perspective rather than actor-oriented or situated perspectives
target_learners: fifth-grade students in secondary school
target_learning_goals: transfer of metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, evaluating, regulating) across learning tasks and domains
examples: The article illustrates near transfer with a chemistry text and a history text both processed by text highlighting, and far transfer with a chemistry reading task versus a chemistry experiment
key_sources: Stebner, F., Schuster, C., Weber, X.-L., Greiff, S., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2022). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x

article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition
citation: Stebner, F., Schuster, C., Weber, X.-L., Greiff, S., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2022). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x
title: Hybrid-training approach: metacognitive skills trained in combination with a cognitive strategy to regulate its application
description: Within the hybrid-training approach (Schuster et al., 2020), students learn to use metacognitive skills to regulate the application of a cognitive strategy, learning both the criteria of high-quality strategy application and their use in planning, monitoring, evaluating, and regulating. The article argues that "the repeated and consistent use of the same quality criteria by metacognitive skills support the automatization of metacognitive skill execution," so that metacognitive skills "require less working memory capacity and leave more capacity for direct information processing, that is content knowledge acquisition."
requirements: A series of training tasks requiring repeated and consistent application of a certain cognitive strategy, so the same quality criteria are practiced repeatedly
constraints: Implementation of hybrid metacognitive skill training costs much more effort than the implementation of a non-hybrid training, and pays off only if transfer to different domains is demonstrated
target_learners: fifth-grade students at the end of primary / beginning of secondary school who do not yet possess developed metacognitive skills
target_learning_goals: high-quality application of cognitive learning strategies and content knowledge acquisition
examples: In the article's example, hybrid reading training consists of six steps combining the three-step reading strategy with planning, monitoring, and evaluating and regulating, whereas non-hybrid training consists only of the three-step reading strategy

Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x

article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition
citation: Stebner, F., Schuster, C., Weber, X.-L., Greiff, S., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2022). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x
title: Year-long hybrid versus non-hybrid metacognitive skill training design with strategy crossover
description: The study trained 243 fifth-grade students from two German secondary schools across one full school year. For the first 15 weeks of 90-minute training, students were randomly assigned to two hybrid conditions (metacognitive skills with conducting experiments, or with text highlighting) or one non-hybrid condition; in the second 15 weeks all groups received non-hybrid training in the cognitive strategy not trained before, so "the cognitive strategy of the second half of the school year represented a new strategy for all participants." Transfer was tested at T2 and T3.
requirements: Random assignment to conditions and a second-half strategy crossover so that transfer of metacognitive skills to a new cognitive strategy could be observed
constraints: Not all students were present at all times of measurement; 159 participants provided complete data for RQ 1 and 183 for RQ 2
target_learners: fifth-grade students in German secondary schools
target_learning_goals: spontaneous transfer of metacognitive skills and content knowledge acquisition in science learning tasks
examples: Group 1 (ME, N = 40) received hybrid training on conducting experiments with the control-of-variables strategy; Group 2 (MT, N = 42) received hybrid training on text highlighting; Group 3 (0 M, N = 161) received non-hybrid training
