article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition
citation: Stebner, F., Schuster, C., Weber, X.-L., Greiff, S., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2022). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x
title: Multi-Strategy Test (MST) scenario-based vignette measure with a new seven-category quality-focused coding manual
description: The Multi-Strategy Test (MST; Stebner et al., 2015) presents fictitious learning scenarios in which students describe their intended approach in open-response format, coded for metacognitive skills. The new coding manual covers "Goal setting, planning, monitoring (observing), monitoring (assessing), reacting, reflecting, and evaluating," awarding zero to two points per category (maximum 14). Three versions were used: MST_E (experimenting), MST_T (text highlighting), and MST_P (preparing for a class exam), serving as near- or far-transfer tasks depending on group.
requirements: Trained raters applying the category system; inter-rater reliability was checked with 25 doubly coded answers
constraints: MST_P was not practiced in the training but represented a familiar everyday scenario; the measure captures intended, not actual, strategy application
target_learners: fifth-grade students
target_learning_goals: assessment of spontaneous recall and intended application of metacognitive skills across transfer distances
examples: Two raters coded 25 answers with average Cohen's κ = 0.98 (0.89 ≤ κ ≤ 1.0; n = 25) before answers were randomly assigned to one rater
key_sources: Stebner, F., Schuster, C., Weber, X.-L., Greiff, S., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2022). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x

citation: Stebner, F., Schuster, C., Weber, X.-L., Greiff, S., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2022). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: effects on strategy application and content knowledge acquisition. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 715-744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09322-x
title: MicroDYN computer-based learning scenario with control-of-variables strategy scoring and knowledge-map knowledge acquisition scoring
description: MicroDYN (Greiff et al., 2012; Schweizer et al., 2013) is an established, validated computer-based learning scenario in which students acquire content knowledge by conducting experiments on simulated dynamic systems, manipulating input variables with a digital lever to infer the system's underlying structure. Two measures were derived: a process measure scoring consistent application of the control-of-variables strategy from log files (up to eight points) and a knowledge acquisition measure scored via arrows drawn in a knowledge map (up to nine points).
requirements: Scenarios designed so they could be solved without relying on prior declarative knowledge about the cover stories
constraints: MicroDYN was administered at T2 only; it represented a near-transfer task for the experiments group and a far-transfer task for the text-highlighting group
target_learners: fifth-grade students
target_learning_goals: exploration behavior and content knowledge acquisition in complex dynamic systems
examples: In the complex experiment, students received four points if CVS was used consistently for all three variables in each round, down to zero points if CVS was not used at all

article_title: Reactivity to confidence ratings: evidence of impaired rule-learning
citation: Kit S. Double, Micah B. Goldwater, Damian P. Birney. (2025). Reactivity to confidence ratings: evidence of impaired rule-learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09413-5
title: Conservatism Hypothesis of reactivity to confidence ratings
description: The Conservatism Hypothesis holds that when confidence ratings are elicited, participants "become more conservative in their approach to a task", prioritizing immediate performance over mastery. Drift Diffusion Modelling evidence shows confidence ratings increase response thresholds, and participants given limited time attempt fewer items and spend longer on each. The current study interprets impaired rule-learning as support: ratings push participants toward memorization, "the strategy that maximizes short-term performance".
requirements: Confidence ratings elicited online, after each response on a primary task
constraints: The authors state the current study "is not a direct test of this hypothesis" and does not tell us why confidence ratings impede rule learning
target_learners: adult learners in cognitive tasks
first-year university students
target_learning_goals: rule-based category learning
metacognitive monitoring accuracy
examples: Participants who made confidence ratings were more likely to respond to ambiguous transfer items in ways indicating greater use of memorization strategies
key_sources: Kit S. Double, Micah B. Goldwater, Damian P. Birney. (2025). Reactivity to confidence ratings: evidence of impaired rule-learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09413-5

article_title: Reactivity to confidence ratings: evidence of impaired rule-learning
citation: Kit S. Double, Micah B. Goldwater, Damian P. Birney. (2025). Reactivity to confidence ratings: evidence of impaired rule-learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09413-5
title: Little and McDaniel category learning paradigm distinguishing memorization from rule learning
description: A shape categorization task in which participants learn to sort 12 stimuli into two categories ('blickets' and 'daxes') defined by a disjunctive rule about inner and outer shape form or color. Success is possible "either by learning the underlying rule or by simply memorizing the category membership of each stimulus". Ambiguous transfer items, visually similar to trained items but with rule-based membership contradicting their visual match, behaviorally distinguish the strategies. In this study, strategies were inferred solely from responses to ambiguous transfer items.
requirements: Transfer test including ambiguous items whose rule-based and similarity-based classifications oppose each other
constraints: The authors did not collect self-reported strategy use data, leaving open whether participants were aware of their strategy changes
target_learners: adult learners in cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: rule-based category learning
distinguishing memorization from rule-abstraction strategies
examples: Little and McDaniel (2015) showed self-reported strategies strongly predict classification of ambiguous transfer items (r =.76)
key_sources: Kit S. Double, Micah B. Goldwater, Damian P. Birney. (2025). Reactivity to confidence ratings: evidence of impaired rule-learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09413-5

article_title: How undergraduate students learn: uncovering interrelationships between factors that support self-regulated learning and strategy use
citation: Rebecca Hey · Mark McDaniel · Flaviu A. Hodis. (2024). How undergraduate students learn: uncovering interrelationships between factors that support self-regulated learning and strategy use. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09389-8
title: Self-regulation factor framework predicting learning strategy use: eagerness, vigilance, MCSR, self-control, attention control, effort regulation, and engagement
description: The article draws on a review of influential SRL models (Panadero, 2017) to propose a set of self-regulation factors that might predict individual differences in students' use of learning strategies. It states: "our overview of pivotal SRL models enabled us to propose a set of self-regulation factors (eagerness, vigilance, MCSR, self- control, attention control, effort regulation, and engagement) that might predict individual differences in students' use of learning strategies". Each factor is grounded in a major SRL model: goal-related processes appear in all major models, MCSR in Zimmerman's, Efklides', Pintrich's and Winne and Hadwin's models, and effort regulation in Efklides' and Pintrich's models. Engagement is added as a factor not explicitly considered in leading SRL models but overlapping with many aspects of SRL.
requirements: Measurement of the factors via validated self-report scales (MSLQ, RGSQ, and adapted scales as used in the article)
constraints: The article states the set of predictors is not exhaustive: "we do not propose an exhaustive set of predictors"
The lack of existing research connecting these factors to specific learning strategies constrained predictions about specific strategies
target_learners: Undergraduate university students
target_learning_goals: Effective self-regulated learning and use of effective learning strategies across academic domains
examples: The article tested the framework by regressing seven learning strategies and self-reported achievement on self-control, student engagement, effort regulation, and MCSR in a survey of NZ undergraduates
key_sources: Rebecca Hey · Mark McDaniel · Flaviu A. Hodis. (2024). How undergraduate students learn: uncovering interrelationships between factors that support self-regulated learning and strategy use. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09389-8

article_title: Confidence in COVID problem solving: What factors predict adults’ item-level metacognitive judgments on health-related math problems before and after an educational intervention?
citation: Scheibe, D. A., Fitzsimmons, C. J., Mielicki, M. K., Taber, J. M., Sidney, P. G., Coifman, K., & Thompson, C. A. (2022). Confidence in COVID problem solving: What factors predict adults’ item-level metacognitive judgments on health-related math problems before and after an educational intervention? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09300-3
title: Cue-utilization theory of metacognitive monitoring
description: The article frames monitoring judgments via cue-utilization theory (Koriat), in which confidence judgments are informed by information-based cues (beliefs about the self, cognition, and the task) and experience-based cues (e.g., solving speed, familiarity, feedback). The authors state that "The accuracy of judgments is dependent upon the validity of the cues that are used". The study applies this framework to health-related math problems, testing math self-efficacy and anxiety as information-based cues and worked-example training and accuracy as experience-based cues.
requirements: Monitoring judgments must be measurable item-by-item so cue influences can be modeled
constraints: Judgment accuracy depends on cue validity, so invalid cues can produce misaligned confidence
target_learners: adults solving health-related math problems
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring of math problem-solving
examples: The study tested whether math self-efficacy, math anxiety, gender, worked-example condition, and problem accuracy predicted item-by-item confidence judgments on COVID-19 fatality and infection-rate problems
key_sources: Scheibe, D. A., Fitzsimmons, C. J., Mielicki, M. K., Taber, J. M., Sidney, P. G., Coifman, K., & Thompson, C. A. (2022). Confidence in COVID problem solving: What factors predict adults’ item-level metacognitive judgments on health-related math problems before and after an educational intervention? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09300-3

article_title: Confidence in COVID problem solving: What factors predict adults’ item-level metacognitive judgments on health-related math problems before and after an educational intervention?
citation: Scheibe, D. A., Fitzsimmons, C. J., Mielicki, M. K., Taber, J. M., Sidney, P. G., Coifman, K., & Thompson, C. A. (2022). Confidence in COVID problem solving: What factors predict adults’ item-level metacognitive judgments on health-related math problems before and after an educational intervention? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09300-3
title: Worked-example educational intervention with apple-orchard analogy for case-fatality-rate problems
description: The intervention was a step-by-step worked example designed to combat whole number bias in ratio comparison. It used "an analogy to a familiar context–an apple orchard" illustrating procedural steps for calculating a case-fatality rate, emphasizing number lines and relational reasoning, then asked participants to map the analogy to a health-context worked example comparing COVID-19 and flu case-fatality rates. In the parent study it improved problem-solving accuracy relative to business-as-usual control, and in this analysis it raised monitoring judgments.
requirements: Participants must engage with the worked example before solving target problems; the parent study randomly assigned participants to intervention or business-as-usual control
constraints: The intervention did not include feedback or practice problems, which the authors note may artificially increase monitoring judgments without improving monitoring accuracy
target_learners: adults in a Qualtrics panel solving health statistics problems
target_learning_goals: correct comparison of case-fatality and infection rates (rational-number reasoning)
examples: Participants saw an apple-orchard worked example, drew an analogy to a health worked example, then solved three posttest problems with strategy reports and confidence sliders

article_title: Association and dissociation between judgments of learning and memory: A Meta-analysis of the font size effect
citation: Chang, M., Brainerd, C.J. (2022). Association and dissociation between judgments of learning and memory: A Meta-analysis of the font size effect. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09287-3
title: Fluency-based account: font size memory effects are tied to (dis)fluency but JOL effects are not
description: The article's working explanation separates the two font size effects mechanistically. Memory effects of font size are attributed to perceptual (dis)fluency, whereas JOL effects arise through other bases (e.g., beliefs), so the two can diverge in some font-size ranges. The authors state: "Our working explanation is that the memory effects of font size are tied to (dis)fluency, but its JOL effects are not." This account organizes the meta-analytic moderator pattern, including the restricted range of dissociation.
requirements: A range of font sizes spanning fluent and disfluent categories so that fluency-based memory effects and non-fluency-based JOL effects can be distinguished
constraints: The article labels this a working explanation, not a tested mechanism
target_learners: Adult learners in laboratory memory experiments studying word lists
target_learning_goals: Calibration of self-monitoring judgments (JOLs) with actual memory performance
examples: The meta-analysis classified font sizes against a 17–161 pt. fluent range established with a fixed 85 cm viewing distance, and found the quadratic font size–fluency relation remained robust when viewing distance was not fixed
key_sources: Chang, M., Brainerd, C.J. (2022). Association and dissociation between judgments of learning and memory: A Meta-analysis of the font size effect. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09287-3

article_title: Are children’s judgments of another’s accuracy linked to their metacognitive confidence judgments?
citation: Carolyn Baer, Puja Malik, & Darko Odic. (2021). Are children's judgments of another's accuracy linked to their metacognitive confidence judgments? Metacognition and Learning (2021) 16:485–516. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09263-x
title: SDT/Simulation Theory account of self- and other-oriented accuracy reasoning
description: The article tests a combined account in which Signal Detection Theory supplies the mechanism for confidence and Simulation Theory extends it to social reasoning. SDT holds that "confidence should be directly proportional to the degree of variability" of a decision, while Simulation Theory holds that "interpreting others’ mental states occurs through a simulation process, metaphorically putting oneself in another’s shoes." Together they predict strong self–other correlations when representations are shared, and that controlling for decision imprecision should eliminate those correlations.
requirements: Both judgments must be computed from the same, dimension-specific decision imprecision for correlations to appear
constraints: The account's predictions were not consistently supported: correlations appeared in only one of the first three experiments, and area accuracy did not predict social judgments
target_learners: children aged 4–8
target_learning_goals: evaluating the reliability of one's own knowledge
evaluating the reliability of informants' knowledge
examples: Four experiments used area-discrimination tasks in which imprecision was experimentally manipulated by making shapes close in size (harder) or disparate (easier)
key_sources: Carolyn Baer, Puja Malik, & Darko Odic. (2021). Are children's judgments of another's accuracy linked to their metacognitive confidence judgments? Metacognition and Learning (2021) 16:485–516. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09263-x

article_title: The impact of retrieval processes, age, general achievement level, and test scoring scheme for children’s metacognitive monitoring and controlling
citation: Krebs, S.S., Roebers, C.M. (2012). The impact of retrieval processes, age, general achievement level, and test scoring scheme for children's metacognitive monitoring and controlling. Metacognition and Learning 7, 75–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9079-3
title: Metacognitive development is fueled by both cognitive resources (achievement level) and mnemonic experience (age)
description: The article offers a two-factor explanatory account of children's metacognitive development: "Results suggest that both cognitive resources (operationalized through achievement level) and mnemonic experience (assessed through age) fuel metacognitive development." Cognitive resources are indexed by general achievement level, while mnemonic experience is indexed by age, and the account explains why both high achievers and older children showed more accurate monitoring and control. The account also carries a scope qualification: under higher retrieval demands, experience appears to take the more important role.
requirements: Both an index of cognitive resources (achievement level) and an index of mnemonic experience (age) must be available to disentangle their contributions.
constraints: When facing higher demands regarding retrieval processes, experience seems to play the more important role, qualifying the equal-weight reading of the two factors.
target_learners: Primary school children aged 9/10 and 11/12 years
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive monitoring accuracy
Metacognitive control (strategic regulation of answers)
key_sources: Krebs, S.S., Roebers, C.M. (2012). The impact of retrieval processes, age, general achievement level, and test scoring scheme for children's metacognitive monitoring and controlling. Metacognition and Learning 7, 75–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9079-3

article_title: The impact of retrieval processes, age, general achievement level, and test scoring scheme for children’s metacognitive monitoring and controlling
citation: Krebs, S.S., Roebers, C.M. (2012). The impact of retrieval processes, age, general achievement level, and test scoring scheme for children's metacognitive monitoring and controlling. Metacognition and Learning 7, 75–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9079-3
title: Film-plus-cloze metacognitive assessment paradigm with confidence judgments and answer withdrawal
description: A multi-phase assessment paradigm for children's metacognitive monitoring and control. Children "watched an educational film and predicted their test performance," then "solved a cloze test regarding the film content including answerable and unanswerable items and gave confidence judgments to every answer." Finally, "children withdrew answers that they believed to be incorrect," allowing monitoring accuracy and control behavior to be measured before and during test taking across answerable and unanswerable items.
requirements: An educational film establishing the content to be tested
A cloze test containing both answerable and unanswerable items
Confidence judgments collected for every answer
target_learners: Primary school children aged 9/10 and 11/12 years
target_learning_goals: Assessment of metacognitive monitoring and control processes during test taking
examples: Applied with N = 150 high and low achievers who watched an educational film, predicted performance, took the cloze test, and withdrew answers they believed incorrect.
key_sources: Krebs, S.S., Roebers, C.M. (2012). The impact of retrieval processes, age, general achievement level, and test scoring scheme for children's metacognitive monitoring and controlling. Metacognition and Learning 7, 75–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9079-3

article_title: How social challenges affect children’s regulation and assignment quality in hypermedia: a process mining study
citation: Cindy Paans & Erdem Onan & Inge Molenaar & Ludo Verhoeven & Eliane Segers. (2019). How social challenges affect children's regulation and assignment quality in hypermedia: a process mining study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09204-9
title: Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) and three types of regulation in collaborative settings
description: The article frames collaborative learning through socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL), defined as "the collective and interdependently sharing of regulatory processes, beliefs, and knowledge, in order to arrive at a shared and co-constructed product or learning outcome". Drawing on Järvelä and Hadwin, it distinguishes three types of regulation: self-regulated learning, in which learners regulate independently; co-regulation, in which peers provide temporary support to each other's self-regulation; and SSRL, characterized by "a shared task understanding and by collective goals and strategies". The study uses this framework to interpret how dyads' cognitive, metacognitive, and relational activities jointly regulate group learning in hypermedia.
requirements: Collaborative settings in which dyad members must coordinate cognitive, metacognitive, and relational activities toward a shared product
constraints: The study coded activities at the level of individual turns, so it "could distinguish between cognitive and metacognitive activities, but not between self-regulation, co-regulation, or shared regulation of learning"
target_learners: Primary school children (5th and 6th grade, ages 10–12) working in dyads
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge construction and writing in a hypermedia inquiry task (heart and healthy living)
examples: The study applied the framework to 30 dyads writing a 300-word text in a WebQuest environment, coding verbal interactions for cognitive, metacognitive, relational, and off-task activities
key_sources: Cindy Paans & Erdem Onan & Inge Molenaar & Ludo Verhoeven & Eliane Segers. (2019). How social challenges affect children's regulation and assignment quality in hypermedia: a process mining study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09204-9

article_title: The effects of meta-creative pedagogy on elementary school students’ creative thinking
citation: Nurit Paz-Baruch, Guy Grovas, Zemira R. Mevarech. (2025). The effects of meta-creative pedagogy on elementary school students' creative thinking. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09412-6
title: CREATE: a six-strategy meta-creative pedagogy for fostering creative thinking
description: CREATE is an explicit, theory-grounded meta-creative pedagogy whose acronym names six strategies: comprehending the core problem and subproblems, reconstructing connections, exploring and experimenting, adding more ideas, thinking over constraints and reservations ("True but…"), and evaluating. It combines regulation of cognition, creative self-regulation, and metacognitive pedagogy, training students "to be aware of their creative thinking process, while also fostering fluency, flexibility, and the generation of original ideas." The article presents it as suitable for natural classroom settings.
requirements: Explicit instruction with clear, specific guidance on approaching tasks creatively
Tasks that are complex, unfamiliar, and non-routine (CUN tasks) so meta-creative strategies are needed
constraints: The article reports the flexibility component responded less to the pedagogy on the immediate assessment
target_learners: elementary school students (sixth grade, aged 11–12)
target_learning_goals: creative thinking: fluency, flexibility, and originality of ideas
meta-creative self-regulation during creative problem-solving
examples: In the study, teachers introduced CREATE through a Valentine's Day mug-design task, gave students index cards bearing the six strategies, and led reflection on how CREATE helped them think of more and different ideas over about two months of science lessons
key_sources: Nurit Paz-Baruch, Guy Grovas, Zemira R. Mevarech. (2025). The effects of meta-creative pedagogy on elementary school students' creative thinking. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09412-6

article_title: Relations between undergraduates’ self-regulated learning skill mastery during digital training and biology performance
citation: Matthew L. Bernacki, Megan Claire Cogliano, Shelbi L. Kuhlmann, Jenifer Utz, Christy Strong, Jonathan C. Hilpert, Jeffrey A. Greene. (2023). Relations between undergraduates’ self-regulated learning skill mastery during digital training and biology performance. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09356-9
title: Skill-training design model: introduce surface declarative knowledge, consolidate to conceptual understanding, then prepare transfer to applied settings
description: The article organizes its training design and analyses around models of learning-skill development, chiefly Hattie and Donoghue's (2016) framework and Efklides' (2011) MASRL model. These hold that trainings "should introduce surface-level declarative knowledge about a skill and consolidate that knowledge to a conceptual level of understanding," and should include "activities that promote transfer" so learners can apply skills in authentic settings. Metacognitive knowledge of skills accrues from metacognitive experiences. The studies test whether mastery at each depth predicts later course performance.
requirements: Training must provide exposure and opportunities to engage in SRL so learners develop metacognitive knowledge of skills
Activities must assess declarative, conceptual, and applied knowledge of the skills
constraints: The article notes meta-analyses' moderator analyses "provide little information as to why such programs are effective"
target_learners: Undergraduate students in high-enrollment STEM gateway courses
target_learning_goals: Declarative, conceptual, and applied biology learning objectives
Self-regulated learning skills including cognitive strategies and regulation of behavior and environment
examples: The Science of Learning to Learn training introduced skills via direct instruction (definitions, theory, evidence), then had students rehearse and demonstrate declarative and conceptual knowledge and complete hypothetical planning activities applying skills to their course
key_sources: Matthew L. Bernacki, Megan Claire Cogliano, Shelbi L. Kuhlmann, Jenifer Utz, Christy Strong, Jonathan C. Hilpert, Jeffrey A. Greene. (2023). Relations between undergraduates’ self-regulated learning skill mastery during digital training and biology performance. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09356-9

article_title: Relations between undergraduates’ self-regulated learning skill mastery during digital training and biology performance
citation: Matthew L. Bernacki, Megan Claire Cogliano, Shelbi L. Kuhlmann, Jenifer Utz, Christy Strong, Jonathan C. Hilpert, Jeffrey A. Greene. (2023). Relations between undergraduates’ self-regulated learning skill mastery during digital training and biology performance. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09356-9
title: Science of Learning to Learn: a three-module digital SRL skill training embedded in undergraduate biology courses
description: A brief digital training program delivered within high-enrollment STEM courses. "Students completed three modules that trained students on enacting cognitive strategies (e.g., self-testing, spacing, self-explanation), improving self-regulated learning (e.g., defining the task, identifying resources, setting goals, monitoring progress), and engaging in behavioral and environmental regulation." Modules were completed at students' own pace over weeks 2–4, took roughly 90–120 minutes, and earned credit amounting to less than 1% of the course grade. Embedded activities doubled as assessments of skill mastery.
requirements: Completion of all three modules and activities for full-fidelity exposure
Delivery within the course's learning management system with completion indicators
constraints: In the original text-based edition, completion rates were low, which the authors cite as motivation for the multimedia redesign
target_learners: Undergraduate biology students, largely first-generation, at a Minority-Serving Institution
target_learning_goals: Cognitive strategy use (self-testing, spacing, self-explanation)
Task definition, goal setting, planning, and monitoring
Behavioral and environmental regulation including implementation intentions, mental contrasting, and distraction management
examples: In Study 1 the text-and-static-image edition was administered in weeks 2–4 of an anatomy and physiology course; in Study 2 a video-based multimedia edition replaced textual content to improve learning efficiency
key_sources: Matthew L. Bernacki, Megan Claire Cogliano, Shelbi L. Kuhlmann, Jenifer Utz, Christy Strong, Jonathan C. Hilpert, Jeffrey A. Greene. (2023). Relations between undergraduates’ self-regulated learning skill mastery during digital training and biology performance. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09356-9

article_title: Are metacognition interventions in young children effective? Evidence from a series of meta-analyses
citation: Janina Eberhart, Franziska Ingendahl, Donna Bryce. (2024). Are metacognition interventions in young children effective? Evidence from a series of meta-analyses. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09405-x
title: Coding framework of metacognition intervention components and instructional methods
description: The article develops a fine-grained coding framework for metacognition interventions, distinguishing intervention focus (primary vs. secondary focus on metacognition), four metacognition components, and six instructional methods. Components are defined temporally: "Before starting a task, children are encouraged to think about how they could approach a task or set goals for themselves" (planning), monitoring during tasks, control during tasks, and reflection after tasks. Instructional methods include informed instruction, modelling, prompts, practice, feedback, and peer activities. This framework enabled the first meta-analytic tests of which components and methods drive effectiveness.
requirements: Interventions must include aspects of metacognition such as planning, monitoring, control, or reflection, and consist of more than one session with a control group
constraints: The article notes the motivational-orientations outcome category is rather heterogenous and groups concepts from different theoretical traditions
target_learners: typically developing pre- and elementary school children up to 12 years of age
target_learning_goals: metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, control, reflection) and related self-regulated learning and academic outcomes
examples: Studies were coded with Cohen's Kappa of .84 (89.5% agreement) between two coders for intervention focus; Fuchs et al. (2003) is given as a primary-focus example and Artuso et al. (2019) as a secondary-focus example
key_sources: Janina Eberhart, Franziska Ingendahl, Donna Bryce. (2024). Are metacognition interventions in young children effective? Evidence from a series of meta-analyses. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09405-x

article_title: Are metacognition interventions in young children effective? Evidence from a series of meta-analyses
citation: Janina Eberhart, Franziska Ingendahl, Donna Bryce. (2024). Are metacognition interventions in young children effective? Evidence from a series of meta-analyses. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09405-x
title: Deliver metacognition interventions for young children through teachers or task materials rather than researchers
description: This principle recommends that metacognition interventions for young children be delivered predominantly by teachers, task materials (computer programs or workbooks), or a combination, rather than by researchers. It rests on the meta-analytic moderator finding that "interventions that were delivered by teachers or task materials were more effective than interventions that were delivered by researchers for two outcomes related to self-regulated learning". The authors attribute this to recent improvements in how teachers and researchers collaborate to develop intervention programs.
requirements: Teachers or task materials must actually implement the metacognitive components (planning, monitoring, control, reflection) as designed
constraints: The finding applies to two outcomes related to self-regulated learning; the article does not claim delivery-mode superiority for all outcomes
target_learners: typically developing pre- and elementary school children up to 12 years of age
target_learning_goals: metacognitive skills and self-regulated learning outcomes
examples: The meta-analysis coded mode of delivery as teacher, researcher, task materials (computer program or workbooks), or a combination of teacher and task materials across 67 studies

article_title: Improving the measurement of self-regulated learning using multi-channel data
citation: Yizhou Fan, Lyn Lim, Joep van der Graaf, Jonathan Kilgour, Mladen Raković, Johanna Moore, Inge Molenaar, Maria Bannert, Maria Bannert, Dragan Gašević. (2022). Improving the measurement of self-regulated learning using multi-channel data. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09304-z
title: Trace parser with action library and process library for measuring SRL from multi-channel data
description: A trace-based measurement protocol that converts raw multi-channel trace data into SRL processes. Its trace parser has two components: "the action library and the process library" — the action library labels raw log data with 12 learning actions, and the process library detects SRL processes from action sequences. The study examined "the eight groups of SRL processes: four groups of metacognitive and four groups of cognitive processes, including Orientation, Planning, Monitoring, Evaluation, First-reading, Re-reading, Elaborating and Organising", grounded in Bannert's (2007) theoretical framework and validated through theory-driven and data-driven perspectives.

A theoretical framework and coding scheme defining rules for identification of SRL processes

article_title: Motivating children to (pre)monitor: positive effects on monitoring accuracy?
citation: Sophie Wacker, Claudia M. Roebers. (2024). Motivating children to (pre)monitor: positive effects on monitoring accuracy? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09351-0
title: Memory-metamemory interplay account of children's overconfidence
description: The article organizes its manipulation and interpretation around frameworks in which "memory and metamemory are no longer considered separated, independent constructs, but rather to be closely intertwined". Monitoring and control processes rely on retrieval from long-term memory, and early retrieval coupled with early monitoring regulates later monitoring. The unexpected overconfidence increase after pre-monitoring is interpreted through this coupling, confirmation bias, and cue-based heuristics such as ease of accessibility.
requirements: Interpretation assumes monitoring judgments are entangled with memory retrieval processes rather than isolated confidence reports
constraints: The article questions whether a confidence judgment can be considered an isolated, memory-independent process at all
target_learners: kindergartners (5-6 years)
second graders (7-8 years)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring accuracy
calibration of confidence in memory recognition
examples: The paired associates task with a pre-monitoring phase was designed to weaken the influence of a single prepotently selected memory trace before recognition

article_title: Teachers’ Humour Use in the Classroom: A Scoping Review
citation: Hannah Robinson, Sarah E. Rose, Jade M. Elliott, Romina A. Vivaldi. (2024). Teachers' Humour Use in the Classroom: A Scoping Review. https://osf.io
title: Taxonomy of seven teacher humour styles and three affiliative sub-styles in adolescent classrooms
description: The review organises teachers' classroom humour into seven styles drawn from the included literature: course-related, course-unrelated, affiliative, aggressive, self-enhancing, self-defeating, and festive humour. It defines each, e.g. course-related humour is "humour used to explain or display information related to the class", and notes styles overlap and can be positive or negative in nature. Şahin's (2021) three affiliative sub-styles (shy, passive, partial) are included, with classroom observations identifying students as the most common trigger for teachers' humour.
requirements: Humour styles are identified via teacher and student self-report surveys, interviews, and classroom observations; existing scales do not capture all seven styles
constraints: The styles outlined in prior scales focused on higher education classrooms, so it is not known if all apply to adolescent classrooms
Styles are not distinct and may overlap when used in the classroom

target_learning_goals: Understanding how teachers' humour use shapes classroom environment, learning processes, motivation and wellbeing
examples: Şeďová (2015) identified festive humour such as teachers playing April Fool's Day pranks by pretending to assign a surprise test

article_title: Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice
citation: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5
title: Intersectional Ecological Belonging Model (IEBM)
description: The IEBM is a framework combining intersectionality theory and ecological systems theory to explain how belonging in higher education is shaped by both identity and structure. The article states it 'draws on foundational insights from intersectionality theory (Crenshaw, 1989, 1991; Collins, 1990; Comabehee River Collective, 1982) and ecological systems theory (Bronfenbrenner, 1977, 1995) to explain how students' experiences of belonging in higher education are shaped by both identity and structure.' It maps nested levels—individual, microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem, chronosystem—with intersectionality embedded across all levels rather than treated as a separate layer.
requirements: Analysis must attend to proximal and distal factors, including institutional and structural conditions often neglected in belonging research
constraints: The article presents it as a conceptual framework for research, policy, and practice, not a tested intervention
target_learners: higher education students, especially racially minoritized, first-generation, LGBTQ+, and disabled students
target_learning_goals: understanding and fostering students' sense of belonging in higher education
examples: The model is illustrated with Table 3 scenarios showing how a Black first-gen woman in STEM, an Indigenous student at a land-grant university, and a queer commuter student experience belonging across ecological levels
key_sources: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5

article_title: Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice
citation: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5
title: Six core assumptions of the IEBM
description: The article enumerates six starting-point assumptions for understanding belonging: it is personal and political; structured by multi-level systems; not assimilation ('Students may appear to belong when they conform to dominant norms, but this is a false belonging, premised on erasure of difference'); a shared responsibility with institutions bearing the primary burden; requiring intersectional analysis; and involving agency as well as structure. These assumptions frame how the ecological levels are interpreted and emphasize that institutions, not students alone, are responsible for creating belonging conditions.
requirements: Researchers and practitioners should treat these as starting points rather than fixed truths
constraints: The article notes these are 'not prescriptions or fixed truths but rather starting points'
target_learners: higher education students, particularly marginalized student populations
target_learning_goals: equity-minded understanding of how belonging is produced and constrained
examples: The assumptions are presented as a numbered list preceding the model's visual overview in Fig. 1

article_title: Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice
citation: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5
title: Mesosystem linkages shaping belonging (Table 1)
description: Table 1 maps common mesosystem linkages in higher education—such as advising-financial aid coordination, faculty-counseling referrals, disability services-academic department consistency, and Title IX responses to harm—alongside their mechanisms and potential impacts on belonging. The article states 'mesosystem connections are not just the sum of individual settings but the infrastructure that links them, shaping whether students experience campus as coherent or fragmented.' When systems reinforce one another they create coherent opportunities for belonging; when siloed, students face contradictory messages.
requirements: Cross-unit coordination and alignment for coherent belonging opportunities
constraints: The article notes meso-level connections remain underexplored in higher education research compared with microsystem factors
target_learners: higher education students, including low-income, disabled, racially minoritized, and international students
target_learning_goals: institutional coordination that supports students' sense of belonging
examples: When academic advising works closely with financial aid, low-income students can stay on track; uneven accommodation implementation signals weak institutional commitment

citation: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5
title: Exosystem policies and practices shaping belonging (Table 2)
description: Table 2 catalogs exosystem factors—financial aid rules, faculty hiring and promotion standards, accreditation mandates, student conduct policies, campus policing, institutional responses to harm, housing allocation rules, and budget allocations—with their mechanisms and potential impacts on belonging. The article states 'exosystem factors organize the conditions under which belonging is made possible or foreclosed.' It notes some levers (accreditation, budget allocations, conduct policies) have received little to no empirical attention in relation to belonging.
requirements: Research extending beyond micro- and meso-level interactions to structural policies
constraints: The article flags that empirical work linking accreditation mandates, conduct policies, and budget allocations directly to belonging is limited

citation: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5
title: Structural belonging: institutions embed belonging or its absence in policies and routine practices
description: Structural belonging is the author's term for how institutions embed belonging—or its absence—into policies, rules, and routine practices. The article states: 'Structural belonging is the term I use to capture how institutions embed belonging—or its absence—into their policies, rules, and routine practices. It draws attention to the fact that campuses script inclusion and exclusion through their design, making clear that belonging isn't just emotional or interpersonal but tied to institutional structure.' It operates at the exosystem level through institutional rules and at the macrosystem level through cultural logics determining whose identities are recognized as legitimate.
requirements: Analysis of supposedly neutral policies (credit hour requirements, dependency definitions, promotion standards) for differential advantage
constraints: Concept introduced in this essay as an extension of Johnson (2022); empirical operationalization is not provided in the text
target_learners: higher education students, particularly those marginalized by institutional policy design
target_learning_goals: recognizing how institutional structure, not only interpersonal climate, produces inclusion and exclusion
examples: Grading practices, financial aid rules, and codes of conduct encode macrosystem ideologies such as meritocracy and neutrality

citation: Jiang, Y., Zhang, Y., Brown Campbell, K.-A., Zhong, T., Zehner, T., James, V., Devlin, B., Geer, E., Shire, S., & Schmitt, S. (2025). Untangling Conceptual Clutter: A Systematic Review of Adult-Reported Self-Regulation Measurement in Children Aged 0–8 Years. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10066-8
title: Three-tiered classification system of self-regulation: categories, domains, and facets
description: The review establishes a hierarchical taxonomy for organizing the variety of self-regulation terms found in early-childhood measures. As the authors state, "a three-tiered classification system was established, starting with the most detailed processes (facets), which form the domains that, in turn, contribute to the broader categories." Facets are specific processes or skills (e.g., adaptability, attention shifting), which group into domains such as cognitive flexibility, which belong to the broader categories of cognitive, emotion, or behavior regulation. The system was built by open-coding terms from measure manuals and mapping facets to established constructs.
requirements: Facets must be rated for alignment with conceptual models of self-regulation before domain and category assignment
constraints: Built from adult-reported measures only; self-reported measures were excluded from the review
target_learners: children aged 0-8 years
target_learning_goals: self-regulation (cognitive, emotional, and behavioral regulation skills)
examples: Adaptability, attention shifting, and shifting were grouped under the domain cognitive flexibility within cognitive regulation

description: The review recommends grounding observational tool development in analysis of adult-reported measures because such tools emphasize overt behaviors across diverse daily contexts and informants. As the authors argue, "adult-reported tools emphasize overt and observable behaviors. This makes them a valuable source for identifying candidate behaviors to serve as coding items in observational tools." Item wording overlap and variation across measures can also inform operational definitions of target behaviors.

article_title: Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation
citation: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x
title: Effort Monitoring and Regulation (EMR) framework for metacognitive regulation of investing mental effort
description: The article describes the EMR framework, proposed by de Bruin et al. (2020) and building on Nelson and Narens' (1990) model, as one that "describe[s] the processes of metacognitive regulation of investing mental effort." Monitoring relies on perceiving and interpreting cues (e.g., perceived demand characteristics, speed and fluency of performance) to form effort appraisals of both required and invested mental effort; because learners cannot directly evaluate learning at the object level, they infer from cues and may use invalid cues or misinterpret them. Control can be data-driven (experienced required effort triggers more invested effort) or goal-driven (learners instead adapt goals, reducing required effort). The article applies EMR to define goal-setting, planning, monitoring, and controlling specifically for mental effort regulation.
requirements: Learners need good metacognitive knowledge to decide which cues to look for, which the article says results from previous experience with the task type and reflection on it
constraints: Cue perception and interpretation are easier for familiar than unfamiliar learning tasks; the meta-level model may represent the object level imperfectly, so subjective and actual effort can diverge
target_learners: school students (5th and 6th grade in the study)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive regulation of investing mental effort during learning tasks
examples: The study operationalized EMR-style regulation as an effort regulation score subtracting required from invested mental effort ratings after each task
key_sources: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x

article_title: Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation
citation: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x
title: Distinction between required mental effort (mental load) and invested mental effort as the basis for effort regulation
description: Following Paas and van Merriënboer (1994), the article distinguishes mental load, renamed "required mental effort," imposed by the task and learner characteristics, from mental effort, renamed "invested mental effort," the mental capacity learners actually invest. Required effort "is passively experienced by learners" and is hardly modifiable within a task, whereas invested effort "results from the active allocation of germane resources in learning" and is a strategic decision, making investing mental effort a learning strategy. The article incorporates Grund et al.'s (2024) decomposition into effort-by-complexity, effort-by-need frustration, and effort-by-allocation, and argues there is no direct link between required and invested effort, citing Arslan-Ari's (2013) opposite-pattern finding.
requirements: Regulation requires learners to evaluate whether invested effort corresponds to required effort, using cues, since neither can be directly evaluated at the object level
constraints: Required mental effort is determined by relatively stable task and learner characteristics and cannot be lowered within a task except by adapting learning goals
target_learners: school learners
target_learning_goals: strategic allocation of mental effort to learning tasks
key_sources: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x

article_title: Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation
citation: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x
title: Effort regulation score: bias measure of metacognitive regulation of mental effort
description: The article's measure of metacognitive regulation of mental effort: after each Multi-Strategy Test version, learners retrospectively rated required mental effort ("How hard would you have had to work on this assignment to get a very good grade?") and invested mental effort ("How much effort did you actually make at the task right now?") on 9-point Likert-type scales. The authors "computed an effort regulation score by subtracting the required mental effort rating from the invested mental effort rating"; negative values indicate deficient regulation, values around zero or positive indicate optimal regulation. Extreme difference scores of +8 or -8 were treated as missing values. The measure deliberately references effort for the task's intended goals to relate regulation to task performance.
requirements: Ratings are administered retrospectively after task completion, because continuous monitoring during learning changes effort estimates and retrospective measures are argued to be more valid
constraints: Learners can score high even if their subjective experience of required effort differs from the objective effort actually required
target_learners: students aged about 10 years (5th and 6th grade)
target_learning_goals: measuring metacognitive regulation of investing mental effort
examples: Administered after both the MST Experimentation and MST Exam Preparation versions at pretest and posttest

citation: Wirth, J., Weber-Reuter, X.-L., Schuster, C., Fleischer, J., Leutner, D., & Stebner, F. (2025). Far Transfer of Metacognitive Regulation: From Cognitive Learning Strategy Use to Mental Effort Regulation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09983-x
title: Learning Buddy: structure-promoting tool supporting planning, monitoring, and control of learning
description: A structure-promoting tool developed for the direct training component that integrates goal-setting, planning, monitoring, controlling, and reflection. "With the help of this so-called 'Learning Buddy,' students have the opportunity to plan, monitor, and control their learning process when they have been assigned a learning task." Before learning, students decide what to learn and choose a cognitive learning strategy and think of possible distractions; during learning, a generated checklist helps monitor whether the cognitive strategy is used properly; after learning, students are prompted to reflect on what went well and badly. In the experiments phase of training it supported metacognitive regulation of the experiment strategy, especially in the performance phase.
requirements: Delivered by teachers who had received specialized training in facilitating learning-strategy knowledge and metacognitive regulation skills, with standardized materials
target_learners: 5th and 6th grade students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive regulation (goal setting, planning, monitoring, controlling) of learning strategies
examples: Used in every class session of the 8-week experiments phase to systematize repeated metacognitive regulation aimed at reducing metacognitive load

article_title: Using DNA to Predict Education: a Meta-analytic Review
citation: Wilding, K., Wright, M., & von Stumm, S. (2024). Using DNA to Predict Education: a Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09928-4
title: Teaching should be personalized to respond to children's individual learning needs rather than one-size-fits-all
description: The article argues that acknowledging genetic influences on learning differences supports teaching that recognizes children's inherent heterogeneity in abilities, skills, and interests. It states that effective teaching must be "personalized" to respond to and remediate children's vastly different, individual learning needs, rather than applying "one-size-fits-all" pedagogical approaches. Existing differentiated practices such as individual education plans for students with SEND are cited as partial implementations.
requirements: Teaching must respond to and remediate children's vastly different, individual learning needs, recognizing inherent heterogeneity in abilities, skills, and interests
constraints: While teachers strongly and unanimously endorse the principles of personalized learning, the practical implementation of corresponding pedagogies within current schools and education settings remains difficult
target_learners: school pupils, including students with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND)
target_learning_goals: improved learning outcomes through instruction tailored to individual learning needs
examples: The article cites individual education plans supporting students with SEND to monitor their learning progress, and notes that in 2022, 17% of UK pupils received support for SEND, including 4% taught according to personalized education, health, and care plans.
key_sources: Wilding, K., Wright, M., & von Stumm, S. (2024). Using DNA to Predict Education: a Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09928-4

article_title: Using DNA to Predict Education: a Meta-analytic Review
citation: Wilding, K., Wright, M., & von Stumm, S. (2024). Using DNA to Predict Education: a Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09928-4
title: Polygenic scores as probabilistic, non-causal predictors of educational outcomes
description: Polygenic scores are person-specific aggregates of inherited DNA differences, computed by aggregating SNPs identified in GWAS weighted by their effect size. The article defines them as indexing "person-specific estimates of genetic propensities for a given target phenotype", while also capturing environmental variances due to gene-environment correlations, assortative mating, and population stratification. They are stable across the lifespan, unaffected by self-report biases, normally distributed, and modeled as continuous variables. Crucially, they are probabilistic rather than deterministic or causal predictors of phenotypic outcomes.
requirements: Genotype data in independent samples and GWAS summary statistics identifying SNPs associated with the target phenotype
constraints: They are probabilistic rather than deterministic or causal predictors of phenotypic outcomes, and they also capture environmental influences
Polygenic scores based on GWAS in European ancestry populations have limited prediction in populations of other ancestries
target_learners: children and adolescents in education systems whose learning differences may be predicted from DNA
target_learning_goals: prediction of individual differences in educational attainment and achievement to inform personalized learning and early intervention
examples: The article describes how GWAS summary statistics enable computing polygenic scores in independent samples by aggregating SNPs weighted by their effect size, and how scores from the Lee et al. (2018) GWAS were used across the 18 retained studies.

article_title: Interventions to Teacher Well-Being and Burnout A Scoping Review
citation: Pauliina Avola, Tiina Soini-Ikonen, Anne Jyrkiäinen, Viivi Pentikäinen. (2025). Interventions to Teacher Well-Being and Burnout A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09986-2
title: PERMA-H model of positive psychology as a unifying framework for teacher well-being intervention research
description: The PERMA-H model is Seligman's multidimensional well-being theory, "later expanded to include physical health (H) by Norrish et al. (2013)", comprising positive emotions (P), engagement (E), relationships (R), meaning (M), accomplishment (A) and health (H). The review applies it to unify the heterogeneous field of teacher well-being intervention research, mapping 43 of 46 interventions' contents onto its elements. Alignment was broadest for engagement, positive emotions, relationships and health, with no intervention content identified for meaning or accomplishment.
requirements: Interventions must have describable content activities that can be interpreted as similar to one or more PERMA-H elements; the review created an O (other) category for interventions without clear connections to the model
constraints: The review found no intervention contents related to meaning (M) or accomplishment (A), and three studies showed no PERMA-H alignment at all
Alignment was the reviewers' interpretation of similarity, not the original studies' deliberate use of the framework
target_learners: Teachers across educational domains from early childhood education to higher academia
target_learning_goals: Teacher well-being and flourishing
Prevention of teacher burnout and ill-being
examples: The review classified interventions aligned with P as focused on emotional skills, E on mindfulness, R on interaction or classroom management, A on goal setting or self-leadership, and H on physical well-being

article_title: How is the Impact of Responsible Conduct of Research Education Evaluated? A Review of Measures Used and a Content Analysis of Outcome Measures with Reported Validation Evidence
citation: M. van Loon, D. Crean, M. van den Hoven, J. Katsarov, N. Evans. (2026). How is the Impact of Responsible Conduct of Research Education Evaluated? A Review of Measures Used and a Content Analysis of Outcome Measures with Reported Validation Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10187-8
title: Framework of reliability and validity evidence categories for classifying RCR outcome-measure validation
description: The review develops a coding framework distinguishing forms of reliability evidence (test–retest, parallel forms, split-half, internal consistency via Cronbach's alpha or Kuder–Richardson formulas) and validity evidence (content validity including cognitive interviews and S-CVIs, face validity, criterion validity, construct validity). It extends the framework of Fenn et al. (2020) with additional categories such as "Global Content Validity Indices (S-CVIs)". The framework was applied so that each measure was coded independently by one reviewer and checked by a second, documenting only explicitly reported evidence.
requirements: Requires retrieving all associated measure materials, including supplementary files, user manuals and earlier development papers, to determine what validation was undertaken
constraints: The protocol focused on documenting only forms of evidence authors explicitly reported; validation was not inferred from statements of intent or general descriptions of test development
target_learners: RCR course educators and evaluators
measure developers in research-integrity education
target_learning_goals: evaluating the impact of Responsible Conduct of Research education on participants
examples: Applied to classify the 15 identified measures in Table 5, e.g. PDR with Cronbach's alpha 0.84 and parallel-forms correlation 0.70, and REKASA with face and content validity from expert review of 74 draft items

article_title: Does Burnout Affect Academic Achievement? A Meta-Analysis of over 100,000 Students
citation: Madigan, D. J. & Curran, T. (2020). Does burnout affect academic achievement? A meta-analysis of over 100,000 students. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09533-1
title: Academic burnout as a three-symptom syndrome (exhaustion, cynicism, reduced efficacy)
description: The article defines academic burnout as "a multidimensional syndrome of exhaustion from studying, cynicism directed to one's study, and reduced efficacy in relation to academic work", adapting the original occupational burnout construct to students on the grounds that student activities can be considered "work". The framework treats the three symptoms as separable but related predictors, each hypothesised to undermine achievement via reduced effort, disengagement, and absenteeism. The meta-analysis tests and confirms negative relationships for the total score and each symptom separately.
requirements: Measurement via validated instruments capturing the three symptoms, such as the SBI or MBI-SS
constraints: The construct was examined only in secondary and tertiary education; the authors note there is currently no understanding of its effects in primary education
target_learners: secondary and tertiary students
target_learning_goals: sustaining effort and engagement in academic study
protecting academic achievement from ill-being
examples: The meta-analysis coded each study's burnout instrument (SBI or MBI variants) and estimated separate pooled correlations for total burnout and each of the three symptoms

article_title: Attention and Long-Term Memory in System and Process Theories of Working Memory: A Reply to Soemer’s (2015) Comment on Schweppe and Rummer (2014)
citation: Judith Schweppe & Ralf Rummer. (2015). Attention and Long-Term Memory in System and Process Theories of Working Memory: A Reply to Soemer's (2015) Comment on Schweppe and Rummer (2014). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9336-0
title: The embedded-processes model as a unitary framework for attention, working memory, and long-term memory in multimedia learning
description: The article advocates Cowan's (1999) embedded-processes model as the working-memory framework for multimedia learning theory. Unlike the multicomponent model, it conceives of working memory as the interplay of attentional processes and long-term memory, allowing multimedia principles to be explained in a unitary manner. The authors state it "provides an integrated account of the cognitive processes that are most relevant for learning with text and pictures (attention and long-term memory) and their interaction."
requirements: A framework must already provide a unified account of attention, working memory, and long-term memory to serve multimedia learning theory
constraints: The authors do not claim the multicomponent model should be rejected; they argue the embedded-processes model is the more productive focus for multimedia research
target_learners: learners with multimedia learning materials (text and pictures)
target_learning_goals: explaining cognitive constraints on learning with text and pictures

description: The article recommends that multimedia learning theory adopt a basic framework that already provides a unified account of attention, working memory, and long-term memory, rather than layering principles onto a model that treats these separately. The authors argue such a framework "provides the opportunity to explain the theoretically almost disintegrated effects in an integrally connected way."

constraints: The authors state this does not mean the multicomponent model should be rejected; the recommendation concerns theoretical focus for multimedia research

article_title: The Other Side of the Coin – A Call to Investigate the Influence of Reduced Levels of Physical Activity on Children’s Cognition
citation: Herold, F., Ludyga, S., Mavilidi, M. F., Benzing, V., Vazou, S., Tomporowski, P. D., & Pesce, C. (2025). The Other Side of the Coin – A Call to Investigate the Influence of Reduced Levels of Physical Activity on Children's Cognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10031-5
title: Structured day hypothesis
description: The structured day hypothesis proposes that in children, days that are preplanned, segmented, and supervised by an adult are associated with healthier movement behaviors, whereas unstructured days are not. As the article states, it "proposes that, in children, a less structured day that is not preplanned, segmented, and supervised by an adult is often associated with unhealthy behaviors such as less physical activity, and more sedentary behavior including screen time". The authors use it to explain why the loosely structured summer break produces reduced physical activity, and propose it as a framework for studying cognitive and academic outcomes during that period.
requirements: Predictions apply to children's days that vary in adult-imposed structure, segmentation, and supervision
constraints: The article notes the hypothesis's predictions have not been tested using cognitive and academic outcomes
target_learners: school-aged children
target_learning_goals: understanding how day structure relates to physical activity, sedentary behavior, and academic performance
examples: The article applies the hypothesis to the summer break, where days are loosely structured and children show less physical activity and more sedentary behavior

citation: Herold, F., Ludyga, S., Mavilidi, M. F., Benzing, V., Vazou, S., Tomporowski, P. D., & Pesce, C. (2025). The Other Side of the Coin – A Call to Investigate the Influence of Reduced Levels of Physical Activity on Children's Cognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10031-5
title: Displacement hypothesis within the 24-hour movement behavior framework
description: Within the 24-h movement behavior framework, time spent on movement behaviors is mutually exclusive, so changing time in one behavior changes time available for others. The article describes the displacement hypothesis, "which postulates that one behavior (e.g., sedentary behavior) can displace another behavior (e.g., physical activity)". The authors use this framework to argue that reducing physical activity is, assuming fixed sleep duration, identical to increasing sedentary behavior, and that studying reduced activity can clarify the causal role of specific behaviors in the 24-h cycle for cognitive development.
requirements: Assumes a fixed sleep duration so that time reallocations between waking behaviors are interpretable
constraints: The article notes the supporting systematic reviews are based on observational studies, which do not allow robust causal conclusions
target_learners: school-aged children
target_learning_goals: understanding how the composition of the 24-h activity cycle relates to cognitive and academic development
examples: The article cites an isotemporal substitution analysis in preschoolers showing replacing mentally passive sedentary behavior with structured physical activity or mentally active sedentary behavior was associated with improved academic performance

title: Ambulatory assessment with intensive longitudinal data for physical activity-cognition research
description: Ambulatory assessment is a measurement approach in which intensive longitudinal data are captured in real-life settings with repeated within-subject assessments of physical activity (e.g., via accelerometry) and cognitive performance (e.g., via a smartphone app) at high measurement density, such as sub-daily or daily. The article proposes it to complement between-subjects analyses with within-subject analyses of "the differences between days with less or more physical activity", and recommends continuous monitoring of activity level and context across intervals of at least 7 days before, during, and after the summer break.
requirements: Repeated assessments of both the independent variable (physical activity level) and dependent variable (cognitive performance) at high measurement density
constraints: The article notes the approach's frequent within-subject active assessments for gathering contextual information can be demanding for participating children and caregivers
target_learners: school-aged children
target_learning_goals: capturing real-life dynamic relationships between daily physical activity and cognitive performance
examples: The article describes device-initiated prompts triggered after a child spends a specific amount of time being sedentary to query the child or caregiver about the type of sedentary behavior

article_title: Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Loyens, S. M. M., Magda, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2008). Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9082-7
title: Candy's four-dimension model of self-directed learning
description: Candy's framework, drawn from adult education and frequently used to study SDL in PBL, treats SDL as both a goal and a process and "defines four dimensions of SDL: personal autonomy, self-management in learning, the independent pursuit of learning, and the learner control of instruction". Personal autonomy is a dispositional attribute; self-management is its exercise in learning; learner control concerns the instructional situation; independent pursuit concerns autodidaxy outside formal settings. Blumberg applied it to PBL learning processes, strategies, and outcomes.
requirements: The framework is applied by analyzing the learning process, learning strategies, and performance outcomes separately, as Blumberg did for PBL
constraints: Stems from adult education, so its independent-pursuit dimension concerns learning outside formal educational settings
target_learners: higher education and medical students in PBL
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning skills
deep-level processing strategies
examples: Blumberg (2000) used the model to evaluate whether problem-based learners are self-directed learners, organized along learning process, strategies, and outcomes

article_title: Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Loyens, S. M. M., Magda, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2008). Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9082-7
title: SDL encompasses SRL: SDL is both learner characteristic and environment design feature, with learner control at task initiation
description: The article argues SDL and SRL share active engagement, goal-directed behavior, metacognition, and intrinsic motivation, yet cannot be used synonymously. SRL is usually a learner characteristic, while SDL is both a learner characteristic and a design feature of the learning environment. The decisive difference is control at task definition: "In SDL, the learning task is always defined by the learner", whereas in SRL the task can be teacher-generated. Hence "SDL can encompass SRL, but the opposite does not hold".
requirements: Conceptual clarity about what SDL entails so the terms are not used synonymously in research and practice
constraints: The distinction rests on the degree of learner control specifically at the beginning of the learning process when the task is defined
target_learners: higher education students
medical students
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning
self-regulated learning
examples: In PBL, students formulate learning issues collaboratively after problem analysis, making the learner the initiator of the learning task

article_title: Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Loyens, S. M. M., Magda, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2008). Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9082-7
title: Provide conceptual clarity and guidance to teachers and students so PBL can produce self-directed learners
description: The review concludes that PBL only brings forth self-directed learners when everyone understands what SDL means and receives support. When faculty fear content will not be covered, they supply core literature, which "completely undermined" freedom to select materials and makes SDL impossible. The article recommends "Conceptual clarity of what SDL entails and guidance for both teachers and students can help PBL to bring forth self-directed learners". Students themselves reported needing teacher support to become self-directed.
requirements: Teachers and students share a clear conception of SDL
Guidance and support are provided rather than SDL being equated with lack of support
constraints: If students or faculty interpret SDL as do-it-yourself education or lack of support, SDL becomes impossible
target_learners: PBL students including medical and higher education students
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning skills
selection and critical evaluation of learning materials
examples: Dornan et al. found students indicated they needed support by teachers to become self-directed, and when guidance was given they were motivated to plan their learning needs
