article_title: Conditions for Effective Learning from Erroneous Examples: A Systematic Review
citation: Sonja Dieterich, Stefan Rumann, Marc Rodemer. (2025). Conditions for Effective Learning from Erroneous Examples: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10071-x
title: Theory of negative knowledge as the review's conceptual framework for learning from errors
description: The review adopts the theory of negative knowledge by Oser et al. (1999, 2012) as its conceptual framework because it directly addresses how learning is supported by engaging with errors. According to the review, "encountering errors fosters negative knowledge, i.e., an understanding of what is wrong, which complements positive knowledge, i.e., how to do something correctly". The theory attributes a preventive function to negative knowledge: recognizing incorrect procedures helps reinforce correct approaches and avoid future mistakes without personally making the errors. Several included studies drew on this theory to explain their results.
requirements: Errors must be intentionally embedded in instructional materials for learners to retrace and often correct
constraints: The review notes cascade theory focuses on learners' own errors, whereas this framework addresses errors of others embedded in instruction
target_learners: school students in grades two to eleven
university students in the first to sixth semesters
vocational education and training students
target_learning_goals: negative knowledge about what is wrong
positive knowledge of correct principles and procedures
examples: Several studies included in this review draw on the theory of negative knowledge to explain their results on (contrasting) erroneous examples, including Barbieri et al. (2021), Heemsoth and Heinze (2014), Loibl and Leuders (2018), and Wernecke et al. (2018)
key_sources: Sonja Dieterich, Stefan Rumann, Marc Rodemer. (2025). Conditions for Effective Learning from Erroneous Examples: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10071-x

article_title: Conditions for Effective Learning from Erroneous Examples: A Systematic Review
citation: Sonja Dieterich, Stefan Rumann, Marc Rodemer. (2025). Conditions for Effective Learning from Erroneous Examples: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10071-x
title: Use contrasting erroneous examples rather than erroneous examples alone when the goal is comparing incorrect and correct solutions
description: The review's synthesis indicates that contrasting erroneous examples, which pair incorrect with correct solutions, were more often the beneficial condition than correct examples or problem-solving, and sometimes equally or more effective than erroneous examples alone. It states that "contrasting erroneous examples are more often effective than correct exam- ples and problem-solving and are sometimes equally or even more effective than erroneous examples". Designers should therefore prefer explicit contrasts when learners are not expected to correct errors unaided.
requirements: Errors must be explicitly paired with correct solutions, either of the same problem or a different one
constraints: Evidence on the comparison between contrasting erroneous examples and erroneous examples is contradictory, especially regarding prior knowledge, cognitive load, and long-term effects
target_learners: school students in grades two to eleven
university students
target_learning_goals: distinguishing correct from incorrect solution approaches
conceptual and procedural knowledge
examples: In Corral and Carpenter (2020), Con-ErrEx learned significantly more than CorrEx and ErrEx for classification questions, while for application questions ErrEx and Con-ErrEx enhanced learning equally

article_title: Issues of Constructs, Contexts, and Continuity: Commentary on Learning in Higher Education
citation: Patricia A. Alexander. (2017). Issues of Constructs, Contexts, and Continuity: Commentary on Learning in Higher Education. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 345–351. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9409-3
title: Constructs, context, and continuity as three barriers to an integrated theory of learning in higher education
description: Alexander's organizing framework holds that integration of models of higher-education learning is blocked by three issues: constructs (lack of explicit, shared definitions of core terms), context (insufficient characterization of what is unique about higher education as a learning environment), and continuity (neglect of learners' prior and subsequent academic development). She states the common threads across the reviews "do not forge the framework for the type of meta-theory of learning in higher education" until these questions "can be resolved," and offers ways over, around, and through these barriers.
requirements: Researchers must explicate their working definitions of key constructs in their writings and presentations for integration to proceed
constraints: The framework is argued from a commentary on five reviews, not tested empirically; the author acknowledges the developmental perspective was not the focus of the special issue
target_learners: tertiary (higher education) students
target_learning_goals: academic development and learning within higher education
examples: The commentary applies the triad to the five reviews: construct ambiguity in engagement definitions, NSSE benchmarks shared with K-12 as a context example, and unidimensional treatment of higher education without disentangling required from optional courses

article_title: Confounded or Controlled? A Systematic Review of Media Comparison Studies Involving Immersive Virtual Reality for STEM Education
citation: Lawson, A. P., Martella, A. M., LaBonte, K., Delgado, C. Y., Zhao, F., Gluck, J. A., Munns, M. E., LeRoy, A. W., & Mayer, R. E. (2024). Confounded or Controlled? A Systematic Review of Media Comparison Studies Involving Immersive Virtual Reality for STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09908-8
title: Five control criteria framework for judging degree of control in media comparison studies
description: The review proposes that a media comparison is adequately controlled when five criteria are met: matched activities, matched non-IVR activities, matched practice with the dependent measure, matched time spent learning (within 20% difference), and matched content. The article states "To determine the degree to which the IVR and conventional conditions were controlled on instructional method and content in each article, five control criteria were assessed." Comparisons are then graded from fully controlled to fully not controlled, with a second approach flagging comparisons whose control is difficult to determine due to missing information.
requirements: Each condition must be operationally defined well enough for coders to judge whether activities, practice, time, and content were matched between conditions.
constraints: When information for any criterion is missing, the comparison's degree of control is labeled difficult to determine rather than counted as met.
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students in STEM courses
target_learning_goals: STEM content learning outcomes such as retention and transfer
examples: The review applied the criteria to 50 comparisons, e.g., coding a comparison as confounded when the IVR condition received a paper-based worksheet the conventional condition did not.
key_sources: Lawson, A. P., Martella, A. M., LaBonte, K., Delgado, C. Y., Zhao, F., Gluck, J. A., Munns, M. E., LeRoy, A. W., & Mayer, R. E. (2024). Confounded or Controlled? A Systematic Review of Media Comparison Studies Involving Immersive Virtual Reality for STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09908-8

article_title: Confounded or Controlled? A Systematic Review of Media Comparison Studies Involving Immersive Virtual Reality for STEM Education
citation: Lawson, A. P., Martella, A. M., LaBonte, K., Delgado, C. Y., Zhao, F., Gluck, J. A., Munns, M. E., LeRoy, A. W., & Mayer, R. E. (2024). Confounded or Controlled? A Systematic Review of Media Comparison Studies Involving Immersive Virtual Reality for STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09908-8
title: IVR comparison studies should control instructional methods and content between conditions before attributing learning gains to the medium
description: Building on the media methods debate, the review argues that media comparison conditions must be equivalent on instructional methods and content so that only the medium differs. It notes that active learning techniques "are not necessarily unique to the VR device and can be used in conventional media, thus potentially conflating the usefulness of VR itself." Researchers should therefore match activities, non-IVR activities, practice, time, and content, and provide complete operational definitions of both conditions.
requirements: Complete operational definitions allowing replication of both conditions; matching of activities, practice with the dependent measure, time spent learning, and content across conditions.
constraints: Active learning benefits found in meta-analyses were for methods embedded in VR, which may conflate the usefulness of VR itself rather than reflect the medium.
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students learning STEM content
target_learning_goals: Valid causal attribution of learning outcomes to instructional media
examples: The review coded 50 comparisons against its five criteria and found only 26% fully controlled, illustrating how rarely current studies meet this standard.

article_title: Gender Disparity in Computational Thinking Pedagogy and Assessment: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
citation: Suya Liu · Yun Dai · Oi Lam Ng · Zhihui Cai. (2025). Gender Disparity in Computational Thinking Pedagogy and Assessment: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10095-3
title: Brennan and Resnick's three-dimensional CT framework (concepts, practices, perspectives) as the study's organizing scaffold
description: The article adopts Brennan and Resnick (2012)'s framework as its theoretical scaffold for understanding CT learning and assessment. It classifies CT into three dimensions: "concepts, practices, and perspectives" — concepts are foundational programming ideas (sequences, loops, conditionals, events), practices are how learners apply concepts in problem-solving (testing, debugging, decomposition), and perspectives address how learners view themselves in relation to computing. The framework integrates cognitive, procedural, and dispositional dimensions and directly informed the coding of the learning-outcome moderator.
requirements: Assessment tools must be aligned with the specific CT dimension being measured for the framework to support meaningful synthesis of evaluation results
constraints: The meta-analysis is constrained to male/female comparisons because most quantitative primary studies report only binary gender data
target_learners: K-12 students
higher education students
target_learning_goals: computational thinking concepts, practices, and perspectives
examples: The coding scheme classified learning outcomes as CT performance, self-perceived CT skill, or CT attitude, mapped onto the framework's three dimensions

article_title: Learning Mathematics Problem Solving through Test Practice: a Randomized Field Experiment on a Global Scale
citation: Avvisati, F., & Borgonovi, F. (2020). Learning Mathematics Problem Solving through Test Practice: a Randomized Field Experiment on a Global Scale. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 791–814. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09520-6
title: Elaborative retrieval theory and transfer-appropriate processing as complementary accounts of why testing effects occur
description: The article presents two theoretical mechanisms for the testing effect. Elaborative-retrieval theory (Carpenter, 2009) holds that "two factors determine the testing effect: spreading activation and semantic elaboration," predicting stronger effects with greater retrieval effort. Transfer-appropriate processing instead emphasizes "the match between the cognitive processes involved during the learning phase (the retrieval test) and those required during the criterial test," predicting stronger effects with greater similarity between practice and criterial tests. The authors used both frameworks to motivate their two studies: varying the amount of content-relevant material (study 1) and varying content match (study 2).
requirements: Retrieval practice must involve effortful retrieval of previously encoded material for elaborative-retrieval mechanisms to operate
constraints: The article notes theoretical work explaining testing effects "lagged somewhat behind" the empirical literature; the theory of disuse (Bjork & Bjork, 1992) is presented as a broader framework subsuming both accounts
target_learners: 15-year-old secondary school students
target_learning_goals: Mathematics problem solving
Transfer of learned principles and procedures to new situations
examples: Study 1 varied the amount of mathematics content in an otherwise equal-length practice test; study 2 held practice constant but changed the criterial test to non-curricular problem-solving tasks
key_sources: Avvisati, F., & Borgonovi, F. (2020). Learning Mathematics Problem Solving through Test Practice: a Randomized Field Experiment on a Global Scale. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 791–814. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09520-6

article_title: Learning Mathematics Problem Solving through Test Practice: a Randomized Field Experiment on a Global Scale
citation: Avvisati, F., & Borgonovi, F. (2020). Learning Mathematics Problem Solving through Test Practice: a Randomized Field Experiment on a Global Scale. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 791–814. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09520-6
title: Use content-relevant practice tests to produce small domain-specific learning gains, without expecting improvements in general reasoning
description: The article's findings support designing practice tests that emphasize the target content domain: "the greater the proportion of mathematics problems included in the practice session, the better students performed on the target test." However, the gains are subject-specific — mathematics practice did not improve domain-general problem solving — and are small in magnitude (~2% of a standard deviation per hour of practice). Educators should therefore expect practice testing to consolidate domain-specific skills rather than to build transferable general reasoning.
requirements: Practice tasks must relate to the same content domain as the target assessment
Adequate exposure time within the practice session (effects observed across 0.5–1.5 hours of domain-relevant content)
constraints: Effects are small in magnitude
No corrective feedback was provided in this study, so gains may differ with feedback
No improvement in domain-general problem-solving ability was found
target_learners: 15-year-old secondary school students across diverse countries and educational systems
target_learning_goals: Mathematics problem solving
examples: In the PISA 2012 field experiment, students randomly assigned to forms with 1.5 hours of mathematics content outperformed those with 0.5 hours on a subsequent computer-based mathematics test covering the same content areas
key_sources: Avvisati, F., & Borgonovi, F. (2020). Learning Mathematics Problem Solving through Test Practice: a Randomized Field Experiment on a Global Scale. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 791–814. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09520-6

article_title: To What Extent Do Situation-Model-Approach Interventions Improve Relative Metacomprehension Accuracy? Meta-Analytic Insights
citation: Anja Prinz & Stefanie Golke & Jörg Wittwer. (2020). To What Extent Do Situation-Model-Approach Interventions Improve Relative Metacomprehension Accuracy? Meta-Analytic Insights. Educational Psychology Review (2020) 32:917–949. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09558-6
title: Situation-model approach to metacomprehension within the cue-utilization framework
description: The cue-utilization framework holds that learners lack direct access to their cognitive states and must infer comprehension from cues, with accuracy depending on how strongly cues tie to the mental text representation determining test performance. The situation-model approach specifies that judgments are accurate when cues tap the situation-model level of representation, since "The situation model represents a learner's deep understanding and what is typically referred to as text comprehension." Interventions are designed to help learners "generate, attend to, or select situation-model cues."
requirements: Comprehension tests must assess the situation model, requiring inferences or application rather than recall of specific textual information
constraints: Learners tend to default to heuristic or memory-based cues rather than situation-model cues, per self-report studies cited
target_learners: school students
university students learning from expository texts
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of text comprehension
self-regulated learning from texts
key_sources: Anja Prinz & Stefanie Golke & Jörg Wittwer. (2020). To What Extent Do Situation-Model-Approach Interventions Improve Relative Metacomprehension Accuracy? Meta-Analytic Insights. Educational Psychology Review (2020) 32:917–949. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09558-6

article_title: To What Extent Do Situation-Model-Approach Interventions Improve Relative Metacomprehension Accuracy? Meta-Analytic Insights
citation: Anja Prinz & Stefanie Golke & Jörg Wittwer. (2020). To What Extent Do Situation-Model-Approach Interventions Improve Relative Metacomprehension Accuracy? Meta-Analytic Insights. Educational Psychology Review (2020) 32:917–949. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09558-6
title: Taxonomy of situation-model interventions by cue-generation (encoding- vs retrieval-based), cue-attention, and cue-selection mechanisms
description: The article classifies the seven interventions by mechanism: self-explaining and concept mapping are encoding-based cue-generation interventions; delayed-summary writing, delayed-keywords listing, and delayed-diagram completion are retrieval-based cue-generation interventions; rereading is a cue-attention intervention; and comprehension-test expectancy is a cue-selection intervention. The distinction is empirically supported because effects of self-explaining were "nonoverlapping" with those of rereading and test expectancy. Delayed-generation tasks work because "performing a generation task after a delay allows for the surface and textbase representations to decay, forcing learners to access and use their situation model."
requirements: Delayed-generation tasks must be performed after a delay, after all texts are read, to be effective
Concept mapping requires extensive instruction and training before learners benefit
constraints: Delayed-generation benefits may not consistently occur for primary- and secondary-school students, depending on generation quality and cognitive capacity
target_learners: school students
university students
target_learning_goals: improved relative metacomprehension accuracy
use of situation-model cues in self-assessment
key_sources: Anja Prinz & Stefanie Golke & Jörg Wittwer. (2020). To What Extent Do Situation-Model-Approach Interventions Improve Relative Metacomprehension Accuracy? Meta-Analytic Insights. Educational Psychology Review (2020) 32:917–949. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09558-6

article_title: An International Review of Assessment Tools for Teachers’ Professional Competence in Teaching Autistic Children
citation: Nick Gerrit Hasche, Charlotte Dignath, Sumeja Mustafi, Mareike Kunter. (2026). An International Review of Assessment Tools for Teachers' Professional Competence in Teaching Autistic Children. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10176-x
title: Kunter et al. (2013) model of teachers' professional competence adapted to autism-sensitive inclusive teaching
description: The review adopts the multidimensional model of teachers' professional competence by Kunter et al. (2013), which distinguishes psychologically distinct constructs — knowledge, beliefs, and motivation — as personal prerequisites for effective professional behavior, separate from observable practices. As adapted by Hasche et al. (2025), it specifies autism-relevant knowledge facets (knowledge about autism and about specific evidence-based practices) alongside inclusion-related beliefs and motivational orientations such as self-efficacy. The review states: "Due to its multidimensionality, this model provides a suitable framework to systematically describe the professional characteristics that enable teachers to successfully include autistic children in mainstream classrooms." The three aspects are treated as equally relevant and mutually influencing.
requirements: Instruments must distinguish the psychologically distinct constructs of knowledge, beliefs, and motivation, since interventions targeting each operate through different mechanisms
The model requires separating observable practices from the personal prerequisites that enable competent professional action
constraints: The self-regulation component of the original model could not be incorporated because no operationalizations linking it to inclusive teaching of autistic students were found
The three competence aspects influence each other as well as inclusion outcomes, so they are not independent
target_learners: Mainstream (regular education) teachers of autistic children
Special education teachers and other educational professionals included in some instrument samples
target_learning_goals: Teachers' professional competence for the inclusion of autistic children in mainstream classrooms: knowledge about autism and evidence-based practices, beliefs/attitudes toward inclusion, and motivational orientations such as self-efficacy
examples: The review classified all 52 included instruments by whether they assessed knowledge, beliefs, or motivation within this framework
key_sources: Nick Gerrit Hasche, Charlotte Dignath, Sumeja Mustafi, Mareike Kunter. (2026). An International Review of Assessment Tools for Teachers' Professional Competence in Teaching Autistic Children. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10176-x

article_title: Relation Between the Essential Components of Reading and Reading Comprehension in Monolingual Spanish-Speaking Children: a Meta-analysis
citation: Baker, D.L., Alberto, P.C., Macaya, M.M., García, I., & Gutiérrez-Ortega, M. (2022). Relation Between the Essential Components of Reading and Reading Comprehension in Monolingual Spanish-Speaking Children: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09694-1
title: Essential components of reading framework applied to Spanish-speaking children's comprehension
description: The article organizes its synthesis around a framework of essential components of reading, which it enumerates as follows: "The essential components included phonological awareness, morphological awareness, alphabetic principle, fluency, vocabulary, and oral comprehension." The framework functions as the coding scheme for the meta-analysis: each component's relation to reading comprehension is estimated separately, allowing the review to compare which components are most studied and which show the largest relations in monolingual Spanish-speaking children.
requirements: Studies must measure one or more of the six essential components and a reading comprehension outcome in Spanish-speaking children to be codable within the framework.
constraints: The framework as applied covers monolingual Spanish-speaking children in studies published 2000–2021; the available text does not extend it to bilingual learners.
target_learners: Monolingual Spanish-speaking children learning to read in Spanish
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Foundational reading skills (decoding, fluency, vocabulary, oral language)
examples: The meta-analysis coded 33 studies against the six components and pooled 146 component–comprehension effect sizes with a random effects model using Fisher's z.
key_sources: Baker, D.L., Alberto, P.C., Macaya, M.M., García, I., & Gutiérrez-Ortega, M. (2022). Relation Between the Essential Components of Reading and Reading Comprehension in Monolingual Spanish-Speaking Children: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09694-1

article_title: Relation Between the Essential Components of Reading and Reading Comprehension in Monolingual Spanish-Speaking Children: a Meta-analysis
citation: Baker, D.L., Alberto, P.C., Macaya, M.M., García, I., & Gutiérrez-Ortega, M. (2022). Relation Between the Essential Components of Reading and Reading Comprehension in Monolingual Spanish-Speaking Children: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09694-1
title: Meta-analytic dataset of component–comprehension correlations in Spanish-speaking children
description: A synthesized evidence base of correlations between the essential components of reading and reading comprehension in monolingual Spanish-speaking children. The authors state: "We found 33 studies involving 146 effect sizes between the essential components of reading and reading comprehension." The dataset was assembled through searches of WOS, Scopus, and ERIC covering 2000 to 2021 and pooled with "a random effects model" using "Fisher's z as an index of effect size."
requirements: Access to the 33 primary studies' component and comprehension measures; searches restricted to WOS, Scopus, and ERIC, 2000–2021.
constraints: Limited to monolingual Spanish-speaking children and to literature published between 2000 and 2021 in the three databases searched.
target_learners: Monolingual Spanish-speaking school-age children
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension development
Early literacy and foundational reading skills
examples: The authors pooled Fisher's z effect sizes across the 146 component–comprehension correlations under a random effects model.

Relation Between the Essential Components of Reading and Reading Comprehension in Monolingual Spanish-Speaking Children: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09694-1

article_title: Are Mathematics and Writing Skills Related? Evidence from Meta-Analysis
citation: Young-Suk Grace Kim, Dandan Yang, Jinkyung Hwang. (2024). Are Mathematics and Writing Skills Related? Evidence from Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09960-4
title: Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): dynamic relations of skills to writing by development and measurement
description: The direct and indirect effects model of writing (DIEW; Kim & Graham, 2022; Kim & Park, 2019) is the explanatory framework this article uses to generate its moderation hypotheses. It "recognizes subskills of writing and associated skills and knowledge that contribute to different subskills," holding that "lower order writing skills are necessary but not sufficient for higher order writing skills." DIEW posits "dynamic relations as a function of development" — transcription skills constrain writing early, while oral language and higher order cognition play increased roles later — and "dynamic relations as a function of measurement." The article uses these hypotheses to predict stronger mathematics–writing relations in earlier developmental phases and variation by assessment characteristics.
requirements: The model presupposes that writing comprises distinguishable lower order transcription skills (spelling, handwriting/keyboarding) and higher order discourse-level composition skills
constraints: The article notes it is not aware of theoretical models of mathematics that explicitly state a similar dynamic-relations hypothesis
target_learners: students from pre-kindergarten through adulthood
target_learning_goals: writing composition, spelling, and handwriting skills and their contributing language and cognitive skills
examples: The meta-analysis tested DIEW-derived predictions that the mathematics–writing relation would be stronger in primary grades and would vary with assessment reliability and standardization
key_sources: Young-Suk Grace Kim, Dandan Yang, Jinkyung Hwang. (2024). Are Mathematics and Writing Skills Related? Evidence from Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09960-4

article_title: Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners’ Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
citation: Yijia Yuan & Yiran Du. (2026). Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners' Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10227-3
title: Functional framework of technology-supported metacognitive scaffolding across four regulatory processes
description: The article frames technology-supported metacognitive interventions functionally: scaffolds embedded in prompts, dashboards, portfolios, diaries, adaptive feedback, and conversational tools support four regulatory processes — planning, monitoring, evaluation/reflection, and strategic control. It argues "the relevant distinction is therefore not only the technology used but the regulatory activity its features are intended to support", so technological category alone may not fully explain intervention effectiveness. AI systems extend this repertoire by making support more adaptive, with roles ranging from directing learning to augmenting learner decision-making.
requirements: A process is coded as supported only when the intervention explicitly supports it, not merely from outcome instruments, theoretical framing, or automated system adaptivity
constraints: The article notes extensive system control may reduce opportunities for learners to practise independent regulation, and that capable systems can perform regulatory work on learners' behalf, raising questions about learner agency
target_learners: K–12 and post-secondary students in formal educational settings
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive planning, monitoring, evaluation/reflection, and strategic control during learning
examples: The review coded each of the 33 included interventions for which of the four regulatory-support processes its features explicitly represented, producing a study-level evidence map (Table 1)
key_sources: Yijia Yuan & Yiran Du. (2026). Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners' Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10227-3

article_title: Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners’ Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
citation: Yijia Yuan & Yiran Du. (2026). Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners' Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10227-3
title: Interpret claims of metacognitive improvement in light of the regulatory process targeted and the measurement format used
description: Because metacognition is a multicomponent construct measured in different ways, the article recommends that conclusions about metacognitive improvement take account of both the metacognitive domain assessed and the measurement format. Self-reported awareness or strategy use is conceptually different from demonstrated monitoring or control during performance. The meta-analysis itself illustrates this: 95.7% of effect sizes relied on self-report, so the pooled association primarily reflects self-reported metacognitive regulation.
requirements: Studies should report which metacognitive domain (knowledge, regulation, composite) and which measurement format (self-report, performance/calibration, trace/log, researcher-rated) underlies each effect
constraints: The article states the validity of process-oriented indicators depends on whether observed behaviour can be linked convincingly to the regulatory construct of interest
target_learners: K–12 and post-secondary students
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of metacognitive outcome evidence in technology-supported learning research
examples: The meta-analysis used measurement format as a descriptive construct-validity audit rather than as an additional moderator, because non-self-report formats were sparse
key_sources: Yijia Yuan & Yiran Du. (2026). Technology-Supported Interventions and Learners' Metacognition: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10227-3

article_title: How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
citation: Christy M. Byrd, Alisa Sas, Renata Halls-Gordon, Jacqueline Cerda-Smith, Stella Jackman-Ryan, Jaylene Patterson. (2026). How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10078-4
title: Meta-analytic corpus of 77 studies and 276 effect sizes on school racial climate and belonging
description: The article assembles a corpus for meta-analysis: a search yielding 6396 citations produced "a final sample of 77 studies and 276 effect sizes." Studies spanned primary, secondary, and postsecondary settings, with most US-based (83.1%) and most peer-reviewed (72.7%). Sample sizes ranged from 67 to 4708, plus one PISA study with 445,534 participants; 48.2% of effect sizes came from marginalized-group samples. Datasets were deduplicated so each dataset was represented once.
requirements: Studies had to report at least one correlation, regression coefficient, or SEM direct effect between continuous quantitative measures of perceptions of racial climate and belonging tied to a specific educational institution
constraints: Objective measures such as school racial composition, observational measures, own intergroup contact, and discrimination distress/stress scales were excluded
Discrimination measures had to be school-specific in items or instructions
target_learners: students in primary and secondary schools
postsecondary students
target_learning_goals: understanding how school racial climate relates to students' sense of belonging
examples: Searches were run on October 6, 2023 across EBSCOhost, Proquest, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, managed in Covidence
key_sources: Christy M. Byrd, Alisa Sas, Renata Halls-Gordon, Jacqueline Cerda-Smith, Stella Jackman-Ryan, Jaylene Patterson. (2026). How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10078-4

article_title: How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
citation: Christy M. Byrd, Alisa Sas, Renata Halls-Gordon, Jacqueline Cerda-Smith, Stella Jackman-Ryan, Jaylene Patterson. (2026). How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10078-4
title: Multidimensional framework of school racial climate: intergroup interactions and ethnic-racial socialization domains
description: The article conceptualizes school racial climate as a multidimensional construct organized in two domains: "Intergroup interactions, which covers dimensions relating to interactions and relationships; and ethnic-racial socialization, which includes dimensions relating to norms, values, policies, and practices." The intergroup interactions domain includes discrimination (personally experienced and general), equal status, and frequency of interactions. The ethnic-racial socialization domain comprises seven content areas: cultural, intercultural competence, critical consciousness, mainstream, color-evasive, and positive interaction socialization, plus commitment to diversity/diversity messaging. The framework centers racialization and systems of oppression rather than treating climate as unidimensionally positive or negative.
requirements: Measurement at the level of student perceptions of school climate rather than objective institutional features
constraints: The dimensions are based on existing literature on student perceptions; scholars note other salient perceptions such as monocentric identity enforcement, silence about race, ethnic-racial composition, and historical context are not covered
target_learners: students in primary, secondary, and postsecondary settings
target_learning_goals: understanding how racialized school environments shape belonging
examples: Figure 1 illustrates how the two domains are hypothesized to relate to belonging through interpersonal, instructional, and institutional opportunity structures
key_sources: Christy M. Byrd, Alisa Sas, Renata Halls-Gordon, Jacqueline Cerda-Smith, Stella Jackman-Ryan, Jaylene Patterson. (2026). How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10078-4

article_title: How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
citation: Christy M. Byrd, Alisa Sas, Renata Halls-Gordon, Jacqueline Cerda-Smith, Stella Jackman-Ryan, Jaylene Patterson. (2026). How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10078-4
title: Opportunity structures for belonging: interpersonal, instructional, and institutional pathways from racial climate to belonging
description: The article adopts Gray et al.'s (2018, 2020) construct of opportunity structures for belonging, defined as "aspects of a school or classroom environment that fulfill or thwart students' needs to belong." Interpersonal opportunity structures involve promoting positive peer and student–staff interactions; instructional opportunity structures involve alignment between course content and students' cultural values and identities; institutional opportunity structures involve joint student–staff efforts to dismantle structural barriers, such as developing critical awareness about racism. School racial climate dimensions are mapped onto these structures, with intergroup interactions most influencing interpersonal structures and socialization dimensions creating all three.
requirements: Belonging is treated as a subjective, perception-based inference students make from experiences, messages, and relationship quality
constraints: The framework is applied to racialized societies where cultural group membership makes belonging questions salient; marginalized students tend to experience greater uncertainty about belonging
target_learners: marginalized and dominant group students across school levels
teachers and staff
target_learning_goals: fostering school belonging through equitable climate design
examples: Examples include Mix It Up at Lunch Days for intergroup interaction, ethnic studies curricula, and clear diversity mission statements
key_sources: Christy M. Byrd, Alisa Sas, Renata Halls-Gordon, Jacqueline Cerda-Smith, Stella Jackman-Ryan, Jaylene Patterson. (2026). How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10078-4

article_title: How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
citation: Christy M. Byrd, Alisa Sas, Renata Halls-Gordon, Jacqueline Cerda-Smith, Stella Jackman-Ryan, Jaylene Patterson. (2026). How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10078-4
title: School diversity models: clustering climate dimensions into multicultural/pluralist versus colorblind/assimilationist approaches
description: The article groups racial climate dimensions into clusters characterizing how schools approach cultural difference, called school diversity models (SDMs) or diversity approaches. "More multicultural or pluralist approaches characterize schools that celebrate diversity, actively incorporate different cultural groups into the curriculum, and encourage positive interactions across groups," while colorblind or assimilationist approaches de-emphasize, ignore, or punish cultural differences. Culturally relevant pedagogy is treated as another diversity model emphasizing cultural competence, equal status, and critical understanding of power differences. Figure 2 shows a hypothetical clustering of dimensions for three example SDMs.
requirements: SDMs are inferred from patterns across multiple climate dimensions, particularly in policies
constraints: The clustering shown is explicitly hypothetical, illustrating how average dimension values might vary across school types
target_learners: whole school communities including students, teachers, and staff
target_learning_goals: revealing the ideologies that inform a school's policies, practices, and interactions around cultural difference
examples: An assimilationist school might ban ethnic studies courses or prevent students from speaking a non-dominant language; a culturally relevant school would value ethnic studies, home languages, and engagement in cultural communities
key_sources: Christy M. Byrd, Alisa Sas, Renata Halls-Gordon, Jacqueline Cerda-Smith, Stella Jackman-Ryan, Jaylene Patterson. (2026). How School Racial Climate Creates Opportunity Structures for Belonging: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10078-4

article_title: Editor’s Note
citation: Dan Robinson. (2011). Editor's Note. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9167-6
title: Reserve prescriptive recommendations for scholarly outlets that synthesize efficacy studies, not empirical research articles
description: This principle holds that empirical research articles should report only what the study found — causal, correlational, or descriptive conclusions — while prescriptive recommendations for practice belong in outlets that "synthesize the efficacy studies for a particular intervention." The editorial argues this separation protects the field from building recommendations on "anecdotes, observations, and self-report data."
requirements: A synthesis of efficacy studies for the particular intervention must exist or be conducted before prescriptions are issued
constraints: The editorial states prescriptive statements are rarely appropriate in empirical research articles
target_learners: educational researchers, authors, reviewers, and editors
target_learning_goals: standards for causal claims and evidence-based prescriptive recommendations in educational research
examples: The journal EDPR's 'Research into Practice' article category, defined as articles "written for practitioners that summarize research on educationally relevant topics and prescribe implications for practice," is cited as the intended outlet for such prescriptions
key_sources: Dan Robinson. (2011). Editor's Note. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9167-6

article_title: Editor’s Note
citation: Dan Robinson. (2011). Editor's Note. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9167-6
title: EDPR 'Research into Practice' article category for practitioner-oriented synthesis articles
description: An article category in Educational Psychology Review created about 10 years before the editorial, intended to serve educational practitioners by having researchers describe how a well-supported intervention could be implemented. The editorial reports the idea "has never really taken flight" because authors instead submit original empirical research manuscripts, which are rejected outright.
requirements: Manuscripts must summarize research on educationally relevant topics and prescribe implications for practice rather than report original empirical research
constraints: The editorial states the category has never really taken flight due to misinformed submissions
target_learners: educational practitioners
target_learning_goals: implementing well-supported educational interventions in practice
examples: The category was defined in Kiewra's 2001 editorial as articles written for practitioners that summarize research and prescribe implications for practice
key_sources: Dan Robinson. (2011). Editor's Note. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-011-9167-6

article_title: Children’s Theory of Mind and Academic Achievement: a Meta-analysis on Reading Comprehension and Math Skills
citation: Lecce, S., Stagnitto, S. M., Mascheretti, S., Lampis, V., & Devine, R. T. (2026). Children's Theory of Mind and Academic Achievement: a Meta-analysis on Reading Comprehension and Math Skills. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10185-w
title: Individual-differences account of theory of mind as a cognitive resource for academic learning
description: The article adopts an individual-differences account of ToM, contrasting with earlier views of ToM as an innate, modular capacity. On this view, "there is an important variation in the children’s ability to put standard ToM concepts into use", these differences "reflect a stable trait rather than measurement error", and ToM may serve "as a cognitive resource that supports children’s learning and school achievement". The meta-analysis tests this account by estimating the ToM–achievement association and its independence from covariates.
requirements: Studies must measure ToM with behavioral tasks and correlate performance with academic achievement measures
constraints: The account concerns variability in using standard ToM concepts among school-aged children and adolescents, not the presence or absence of ToM itself
target_learners: children and adolescents aged approximately 2.5 to 17 years in formal schooling
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
mathematics skills
general academic achievement
examples: The meta-analysis operationalizes the account by pooling zero-order and partial correlations between behavioral ToM tasks and reading, math, and general achievement measures across 53 studies
key_sources: Lecce, S., Stagnitto, S. M., Mascheretti, S., Lampis, V., & Devine, R. T. (2026). Children's Theory of Mind and Academic Achievement: a Meta-analysis on Reading Comprehension and Math Skills. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10185-w

article_title: Primary School Learning Topics Involving Inhibitory Control: A Scoping Review
citation: Élisabeth Bélanger, Marine Moyon, Lorie-Marlène Brault Foisy, Steve Masson. (2026). Primary School Learning Topics Involving Inhibitory Control: A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10198-5
title: Four recurring characteristics of competing automatisms in learning topics requiring inhibitory control
description: The review proposes four recurring characteristics of the automatisms that compete with correct responses in learning topics requiring inhibitory control: "strong perceptual salience, reliance on the “more A–more B” intuitive rule, susceptibility to whole-number bias, and frequent reinforcement through instruction and experience." These characteristics serve as initial conceptual landmarks intended to help identify other learning topics likely to involve similar automatisms and thus require inhibitory control, moving beyond a binary view of whether a topic requires inhibition.
requirements: Automatisms are rapidly and automatically activated, often without conscious awareness, and can interfere with task-relevant processing when not adequately inhibited
constraints: The characteristics are proposed as initial conceptual landmarks, not validated diagnostic criteria

article_title: Primary School Learning Topics Involving Inhibitory Control: A Scoping Review
citation: Élisabeth Bélanger, Marine Moyon, Lorie-Marlène Brault Foisy, Steve Masson. (2026). Primary School Learning Topics Involving Inhibitory Control: A Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10198-5
title: Dual-process theory with an added inhibition system as a framework for inhibitory control in learning
description: The review presents dual-process theory as a prominent framework bridging research traditions: System 1 encompasses fast, automatic, intuitive processes, while System 2 involves slower, deliberate, effortful processes. Building on this, Houdé and colleagues proposed a third system, the inhibition system: "This system enables individuals to suppress intuitive or dominant responses, facilitating the shift to the more controlled reasoning associated with System 2." In this framework, inhibitory control is the key mechanism allowing learners to move from heuristic to algorithmic reasoning, applied to both Piagetian tasks and school subjects.
requirements: Learners must suppress automatically activated automatisms before analytical (System 2) reasoning can operate
constraints: Alternative interpretations related to conflict processing or strategy adjustment cannot be entirely ruled out for negative priming effects

secondary students and adults reasoning about earlier-grade topics
target_learning_goals: overriding intuitive responses in favor of analytical reasoning across school subjects

article_title: Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources
citation: Kyong Mi Choi, Jin Mun, Brian Hand. (2026). Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10115-2
title: Utilization of resources: reasoning as selectively activated intellectual resource rather than transferred skill
description: This framework reconceptualizes cross-domain reasoning not as direct transfer of skills but as utilization—the active deployment of intellectual resources across contextual boundaries. Drawing on diSessa's knowledge in pieces, Hammer et al.'s resources framework, Bailin's reasoning-as-practice, and situated learning theory, the article treats procedural knowledge in the applying domain as an assemblage of cognitive resources that learners "strategically mobilized and adapted" for reasoning tasks. It guides the study's hypothesis that applying components are foundational resources selectively activated during reasoning.
requirements: Reasoning is treated as domain-embedded practice coordinated with background knowledge, standards of inquiry, heuristic strategies, and habits of mind rather than isolated technical competencies
constraints: The article distinguishes this lens from transfer frameworks, noting transfer attempts predicated on superficial similarity can precipitate negative transfer
target_learners: K-12 mathematics and science students assessed in TIMSS
target_learning_goals: Cross-domain reasoning in mathematics and science
examples: The study analyzes TIMSS applying and reasoning components as candidate intellectual resources supporting reasoning across mathematics and science

citation: Kyong Mi Choi, Jin Mun, Brian Hand. (2026). Bridging Reasoning in Mathematics and Science: a Document Analysis of Applying and Reasoning in the TIMSS Assessment Framework and the Case for Utilization of Resources. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10115-2
title: Three-layer hierarchical framework: Pellegrino's assessment triangle, Webb's Depth of Knowledge, and the TIMSS cognitive domains
description: The article organizes its analysis through three complementary frameworks in a hierarchical relationship: Pellegrino et al.'s assessment triangle (cognition, observation, interpretation) as meta-theory, Webb's Depth of Knowledge as taxonomic theory, and the TIMSS framework as the operational layer. The mapping holds that "DoK Level 1 corresponds to the knowing domain in TIMSS, DoK Level 2 to the applying domain, and DoK Levels 3–4 to the reasoning domain." This structure justifies analyzing TIMSS documents as evidence about cognitive structure and predicts that applying functions as a prerequisite foundation for reasoning.
requirements: Effective assessment design requires a clear theory of cognition as its foundation, with cognition, observation, and interpretation in synchrony
constraints: The knowing domains (MK, SK) were excluded from the analysis as involving reproduction and recognition of facts and terms
target_learners: Assessment developers and researchers in mathematics and science education
target_learning_goals: Understanding cognitive demand levels in mathematics and science assessment
examples: The study extracted MA, MR, SA, and SR constituent elements from TIMSS 2011, 2015, 2019, and 2023 frameworks as analytical units under this hierarchy

description: The authors constructed an integrated list of cognitive components from the MR, MA, SR, and SA domains across the 2011, 2015, 2019, and 2023 TIMSS cycles, presented in Tables 2 and 3. The integration documented three revision types: new additions (e.g., Evaluate added to MR in 2015), component combinations (e.g., Represent and Model combined as Represent–Model), and name changes with unchanged descriptions (e.g., Select renamed Determine, later Formulate; Use Models changed to Interpret Models). This list served as the data corpus for identifying commonality and subset relationships between components.

title: Design instruction that strengthens reasoning through discipline-specific procedural engagement
description: The article proposes that instruction can strengthen reasoning by engaging students in discipline-specific procedural tasks—the applying domain—rather than treating reasoning as a decontextualized general skill. The authors state their insight "offers a conceptual foundation for designing instruction that strengthens reasoning through discipline-specific procedural engagement." Because procedural knowledge is conceptualized as a mobilizable resource, rich applying experiences are positioned as the foundation learners draw on when reasoning within and across mathematics and science.

article_title: Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7
title: Five principles of natural information processing systems underpinning the evolutionary approach in cognitive load theory
description: The evolutionary approach in cognitive load theory describes human cognitive architecture as a natural information processing system analogous to biological evolution by natural selection, characterized by five principles: randomness as genesis, borrowing and reorganizing, narrow limits of change, information store, and environmental organizing and linking. The paper states these principles explain "the operation of these two natural information processing systems", with the first two relating to acquisition of information, the next two to processing and storing, and the last to using stored information. Working memory is analogous to the epigenetic system and long-term memory to the genetic system.
requirements: The analogy was established to substantiate the main characteristics of human cognitive architecture relevant to cognitive load theory
target_learners: learners acquiring biologically secondary knowledge in formal education
target_learning_goals: acquisition of domain-specific knowledge in educational institutions
examples: The paper maps random mutations to trial-and-error problem solving, genome to long-term memory, and the epigenetic system to working memory
key_sources: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7

article_title: Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7
title: Biologically primary versus biologically secondary knowledge distinction in evolutionary educational psychology
description: Evolutionary educational psychology distinguishes two types of human knowledge based on evolutionary origins. Biologically primary knowledge is acquired "early in life, implicitly and unintentionally", requires no working memory resources, and is encoded directly into long-term memory. Biologically secondary knowledge is culture-specific, slow to acquire, heavily dependent on conscious effortful working memory processing, and not naturally motivating. The paper notes that instructional design principles and cognitive load theory recommendations "are mostly related to learning of biologically secondary/explicit types of knowledge".
requirements: Secondary knowledge acquisition requires conscious, explicit, and effortful processes in working memory
constraints: The paper notes primary knowledge and type 1 dual-process mechanisms could not be equated, since reading skills represent type 1 mechanisms for many adults even though they belong to secondary knowledge
target_learners: students in organized educational institutions
target_learning_goals: acquisition of scientific knowledge, literacy and numeracy as biologically secondary knowledge
examples: Listening to and speaking a native language are cited as primary knowledge; writing, reading skills and scientific knowledge as secondary
key_sources: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7

article_title: Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7
title: Dynamic emerging-principle view: natural information processing systems gain new principles with increasing complexity
description: The paper's first proposed modification views natural information processing systems as dynamically evolving, with new principles added at higher levels of complexity. A downward extrapolation suggests three principles (information store, randomness as genesis, environmental organizing and linking) could apply even to simple non-organic systems such as atoms, while all five apply to complex organic and biological systems. The paper concludes that "the basic information processing principles used by cognitive load theory apply in attenuated form even to non-organic systems associated with physics and chemistry".
requirements: Information is treated as an attribute of objects of any nature representing stable patterns in their organization
constraints: The paper states such specification of applicability is not critical to the theory, as the analogy's purpose was to substantiate human cognitive architecture
target_learners: human learners as intelligent natural information processing systems
target_learning_goals: understanding the evolutionary origins of human cognitive architecture
examples: Atomic shells preserving stable electron energy levels illustrate the information store principle in non-organic systems

article_title: Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7
title: Explicit intention to learn: a proposed sixth principle of intelligent natural information processing systems
description: The paper proposes adding a sixth principle at the level of human cognition: the explicit intention to learn secondary knowledge, defined as "the explicit intention to acquire new secondary information into the information store to effectively act in the changing future environment". This principle addresses the emergence of controlled, conscious processing in working memory for biologically secondary information and the role of learner motivation, postulating the fundamental interconnectedness of cognition and motivation. It parallels Woolcott's preparedness for learning principle and implies that every learning task needs activities aimed at setting learners' explicit intention to learn.
requirements: Specific learner cognitive activities aimed at externally motivating and cognitively engaging learners prior to acquiring biologically secondary knowledge
constraints: The paper notes the principle could be suppressed in experts acting in their area of expertise, and this form of expertise reversal needs experimental investigation
target_learners: novice learners acquiring biologically secondary knowledge in formal instruction
target_learning_goals: motivated, cognitively engaged acquisition of secondary knowledge
examples: Activities may trigger curiosity, establish gaps in the knowledge base, or activate relevant available knowledge
key_sources: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7

article_title: Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2023). Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture in Cognitive Load Theory: a Dynamic, Emerging Principle Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09812-7
title: Design pre-instructional activities that motivate and engage learners before secondary-knowledge instruction
description: Because formal learning focuses on biologically secondary knowledge requiring conscious working memory processing, the explicit intention to learn principle implies that "every learning task needs to be associated with specific activities aimed at setting the learner's explicit intention to acquire this secondary information". These pre-instructional activities aim to externally motivate and engage learners, trigger curiosity, establish knowledge gaps, or activate relevant knowledge, preparing learners for the following instructional goals.
requirements: Learner activities intentionally designed to get learners motivated for and engaged in learning prior to acquiring the targeted secondary knowledge
constraints: For experts, additional activities designed to foster motivation and engagement could inhibit performance, per the paper's predicted expertise reversal
target_learners: novice learners in formal educational settings
target_learning_goals: preparation and motivation for acquiring biologically secondary knowledge
examples: The paper notes motivating the learner was considered the first step of any instruction by Gagné (1965), and cites productive failure and invention approaches as empirical evidence for exploratory activities achieving pre-instructional goals

citation: Daniel H. Robinson. (2012). Editor's Note: Introducing Intervention Studies as a New Article Category. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9209-8
title: Intervention studies: a new Educational Psychology Review article category for quality intervention research
description: A new article category introduced by the editor of Educational Psychology Review in 2012 for studies in which "the researcher manipulates one or more independent variables and measures the effect on one or more dependent variables". Its stated purpose is "to provide an outlet for quality intervention studies that are not finding their way into educational psychology journals". It replaced the retired research-into-practice category.
requirements: Reports original empirical intervention research in which independent variables are manipulated and effects on dependent variables are measured
constraints: The editor states it is not intended to encroach on the turf of existing empirical educational psychology journals, which rarely publish intervention studies
target_learners: Educational psychology researchers and journal authors
target_learning_goals: Publishing and disseminating classroom-relevant intervention research
examples: The editor introduced the category in a 2012 editorial after descriptive investigations showed randomized experiments declining to 23% of articles by 2010

citation: Daniel H. Robinson. (2012). Editor's Note: Introducing Intervention Studies as a New Article Category. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9209-8
title: Demonstrate the stability of potentially useful interventions through independent replication before trusting them
description: The editor argues, quoting Wainer, that replicability is the principal epistemological tenet of modern science: small initial studies tolerate false positives, and other investigators should rush to replicate so anomalous results are brushed aside. He suggests educational psychology should "demonstrate the stability of potentially useful interventions through independent replication" and states that EDPR encourages such replications.
requirements: Independent investigators replicating others' intervention studies rather than only producing novel studies
constraints: In educational psychology, the field generally does not attempt to replicate others' work, so it is unknown whether its literature is littered with anomalous findings
target_learners: Educational psychology researchers
target_learning_goals: Establishing which interventions have stable, replicable effects
examples: EDPR retains its replication article category despite receiving few replication studies, in the hope that replications will be valued in the field

article_title: Does Instruction-First or Problem-Solving-First Depend on Learners’ Prior Knowledge?
citation: Cheng-Wen He, Logan Fiorella, Paula P. Lemons. (2025). Does Instruction-First or Problem-Solving-First Depend on Learners' Prior Knowledge? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09993-3
title: Competing theoretical accounts: cognitive load theory versus productive failure for instructional sequencing
description: The article frames the instructional-sequence debate through two named accounts. Cognitive load theory posits that "instruction should avoid overloading the capacity of students' limited working memory", predicting I-PS benefits novices and weakens as expertise grows (the expertise reversal effect). Productive failure is "a specific form of PS-I in which the experience of failure during an initial problem-solving phase prepares students to benefit more from subsequent instruction", activating prior knowledge and revealing knowledge gaps. The two experiments were designed to test these competing hypotheses.
requirements: The problem-solving phase in PS-I must be followed by explicit instruction that consolidates learning, per the productive failure guidelines the article cites
constraints: The article notes existing evidence for the moderation is limited and based largely on cross-study comparisons rather than controlled experiments using the same materials
target_learners: undergraduate introductory biology students
upper-level undergraduate biochemistry students
target_learning_goals: understanding the causal mechanisms of noncovalent interactions
near- and far-transfer problem-solving in biochemistry
examples: Experiment 1 tested the productive failure hypothesis with introductory biology students; Experiment 2 tested the cognitive load hypothesis with biochemistry students using identical materials

article_title: The Brilliance–Belonging Model: How Cultural Beliefs About Intellectual Ability Undermine Educational Equity
citation: Christina A. Bauer, Aashna Poddar, Eddie Brummelman, & Andrei Cimpian. (2025). The Brilliance–Belonging Model: How Cultural Beliefs About Intellectual Ability Undermine Educational Equity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10034-2
title: The Brilliance–Belonging Model: brilliance-oriented FABs and brilliance stereotypes undermine belonging through self-related and other-related pathways
description: The Brilliance–Belonging Model is a theoretical framework proposing that brilliance-oriented FABs (beliefs that a field requires exceptional intellectual ability) and brilliance stereotypes (associations of brilliance with certain groups) jointly reduce educational equity. As the article states, "students from groups targeted by negative brilliance stereotypes are perceived—by themselves and others—as not belonging in contexts where brilliance-oriented FABs are common." These perceptions compromise psychological safety and invite disempowering treatment, producing gaps in achievement and representation. The model specifies a self-related pathway (self- and meta-perceptions of low belonging lowering safety, self-efficacy, and motivation) and an other-related pathway (others' low-belonging perceptions producing bias), which mutually reinforce each other in a self-perpetuating cycle.
requirements: Both belief types must operate jointly: a field perceived to require brilliance and brilliance stereotypically associated with certain groups
constraints: The model remains agnostic on whether exceptional intellectual ability is actually necessary for success in any given context
The model remains agnostic about the nature of brilliance itself (fixed vs. malleable, universal vs. non-universal)
target_learners: students from groups facing negative brilliance stereotypes: women, people from lower-SES backgrounds, and people from historically marginalized racial/ethnic groups
target_learning_goals: sustained sense of belonging in academic contexts
equitable achievement and representation across academic fields

article_title: Why Growth Mindset Training Alone may not Improve Academic Outcomes: A Call for Research on Bundling Growth Mindset and Retrieval Practice Interventions
citation: Anne M. Cleary, Daniel H. Robinson. (2026). Why Growth Mindset Training Alone may not Improve Academic Outcomes: A Call for Research on Bundling Growth Mindset and Retrieval Practice Interventions. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10188-7
title: KBCP framework: knowledge, belief, commitment, and planning as sequential requirements for students' adoption of study strategies
description: The review describes the knowledge, belief, commitment, and planning (KBCP) framework of McDaniel et al. (2021), which "holds that students must first have the knowledge that a particular study strategy will work, believe that it will work, commit to using it, and then make a plan for using it." The article positions GMT within this framework as potentially serving the purpose of instilling a belief that learning can be improved with adherence to the right strategies, making it a stepping-stone rather than a standalone treatment.

constraints: The review notes more research is needed to further explore the suggestion of combining science of learning and socio-motivational interventions

K-12 and higher education students targeted by study-strategy interventions
target_learning_goals: adoption and persistent use of effective, science-backed learning strategies such as retrieval practice and spacing

article_title: Effects of Rubrics on Academic Performance, Self-Regulated Learning, and self-Efficacy: a Meta-analytic Review
citation: Panadero, Ernesto; Jonsson, Anders; Pinedo, Leire; Fernández-Castilla, Belén. (2023). Effects of Rubrics on Academic Performance, Self-Regulated Learning, and self-Efficacy: a Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09823-4
title: Empirical-quality rubric instrument for evaluating rubric studies
description: The authors designed an instrument to rate the empirical quality of rubric intervention studies, consisting of "a rubric with the following categories: research design, quality of the measurement tools, quality of the intervention (three subcategories: training, practice, length of the intervention), quality of dependent variables, and quality of the sample." Each study was scored on all categories to compute a summary quality score, used as a moderator. They also provide it "to be filled out for rubric scholars in forthcoming studies" to improve reporting quality. Data and coding are shared via an OSF link printed in the article.
requirements: Studies must be codable on research design, measurement tools, intervention quality, dependent variables, and sample quality
target_learners: rubric researchers
target_learning_goals: improving quality and reporting of rubric intervention research
examples: Applied to the 24 included studies to compute an empirical quality score used in moderator analyses

article_title: When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective
citation: Axel Grund, Stefan Fries, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl, Julian Roelle. (2024). When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09852-7
title: Three-fold conception of mental effort: effort-by-complexity, effort-by-need frustration, and effort-by-allocation
description: The article proposes that the term effort carries three fundamentally different meanings that should be clearly separated: effort-by-complexity (object-level processing demands), effort-by-need frustration (negatively valenced affective-emotional processing demands), and effort-by-allocation (self-initiated effort as an outcome of motivation). The authors state: "we plea for a three-fold conception of effort that clearly distinguishes the different psychological sources of experiencing and allocating effort in learning environments." Each conception has different operationalizations, theoretical roots (CLT, SDT, SEVT), and practical implications, summarized in the article's Table 1.
requirements: Researchers and instructional designers must use measurement items that distinguish the three conceptions rather than ambivalent general effort items; the article recommends a multi-facet, multimodal assessment of effort, ideally in real-time
constraints: The conceptions can be confounded in school settings where tasks are both complex and aversive; the article notes effort-by-complexity and effort-by-need frustration may often be confounded when learning at school but must not be for all learning settings
target_learners: students in formal learning settings such as school and college
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of effort and cognitive load appraisals in learning research and instructional design
examples: Table 1 pairs each conception with an ambivalent item (e.g., "How much effort do/did you have to invest in order to solve the task?") and a more specific item (e.g., "How strenuous is/was working on that task for you?")
key_sources: Axel Grund, Stefan Fries, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl, Julian Roelle. (2024). When is Learning “Effortful”? article_title: When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective
citation: Axel Grund, Stefan Fries, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl, Julian Roelle. (2024). When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09852-7
title: Self-Determination Theory account of effort-by-need frustration: aversive effort arises from frustrated needs for competence, autonomy, and relatedness
description: Within the article's framework, effort-by-need frustration is the negatively valenced affective-emotional experience of task execution, explained through Self-Determination Theory. SDT assumes three basic psychological needs — competence, autonomy, and social relatedness — whose satisfaction or frustration determines how attractive or aversive learning feels. The article states: "learning contexts can both foster and frustrate need satisfaction and consequently, can contribute to how attractive or aversive learning is experienced." For example, materials too easy or difficult for prior knowledge frustrate the need for competence, manifesting in aversion such as boredom, overload, or anxiety.
requirements: Learning environments must satisfy the needs for competence, autonomy, and relatedness to avoid aversive effort experience
constraints: Effort-by-need frustration is data-driven (arising from task execution) but is of a different kind than object-level processing requirements, with different psychological conditions of origin
target_learners: students in formal learning settings
target_learning_goals: reducing aversive learning experience and supporting autonomous motivation
examples: The article's homework vignette: a student reframed homework as a game, removing autonomy frustration while object-level requirements stayed the same
