article_title: When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective
citation: Axel Grund, Stefan Fries, Matthias Nückles, Alexander Renkl, Julian Roelle. (2024). When is Learning “Effortful”? Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09852-7
title: Situated Expectancy-Value Theory account of effort-by-allocation: self-initiated effort as outcome of expectancy and value appraisals
description: Effort-by-allocation refers to the initiation, intensity, and persistence of learning behavior as a direct outcome of momentary motivation. From SEVT, "effort-by-allocation is the out- come of future-directed expectancy and value appraisals concerning a specific task or activity": the more likely a person deems solving a task and the higher its judged incentives, the more willing they are to start and persist. SEVT also considers three motivational costs — effort cost, opportunity cost, and emotional cost — as negative valences weighed before task execution. The article links opportunity cost to motivational interference, where students miss valued leisure when deciding to learn.
requirements: Expectancy and value beliefs need to be high to support learning and effort allocation
constraints: Effort-by-allocation does not refer to task characteristics but to students' self-initiated allocation; metacognitive information alone may not raise it when task values are low
target_learners: students in formal learning settings including homework contexts
target_learning_goals: initiation, intensity, and persistence of effective learning behavior
examples: The article cites interventions offering compensation to top-50% performers or performance feedback after strategy use as attempts to change expectancy and value beliefs

Scrutinizing the Concept of Mental Effort in Cognitively Oriented Research from a Motivational Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09852-7

article_title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout
citation: Lisa E. Kim, Verena Jörg & Robert M. Klassen. (2019). A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9458-2
title: Big Five framework as the organizing taxonomy for teacher personality research
description: The article adopts the Big Five as the dominant personality framework, underpinned by the lexical hypothesis, and organizes its meta-analysis around five replicated domains: "openness(creative, curious, cultured), conscientiousness (organized, responsible, reliable), extraversion (sociable, assertive, energetic), agreeableness (kind, cooperative, trustful), and emotional stability (calm, secure, unemotional)". It treats the closely similar five-factor model (FFM) as combinable with Big Five domains, as prior meta-analyses do, and argues teacher personality research should use such established frameworks rather than ad hoc trait lists.
requirements: Personality measures used must be classifiable within the Big Five framework empirically or theoretically, as the article's own exclusion criteria state
constraints: The Big Five and FFM differ slightly, e.g., the FFM's broader definition of openness including unconventionality and behavioral flexibility
target_learners: teachers across elementary, secondary, and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: understanding which teacher personal characteristics relate to teacher effectiveness and burnout
examples: The meta-analysis classified 25 studies' personality measures (e.g., BFI, NEO-PI-R, 16PF) into Big Five domains and pooled their correlations with effectiveness and burnout
key_sources: Lisa E. Kim, Verena Jörg & Robert M. Klassen. (2019). A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9458-2

article_title: Pictures in Mathematical Word Problems: A Systematic Review on the Role of Task and Student Characteristics
citation: Terhi Vessonen, Heidi Hellstrand, Pirjo Aunio, Anu Laine. (2026). Pictures in Mathematical Word Problems: A Systematic Review on the Role of Task and Student Characteristics. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10112-5
title: Three-function taxonomy of provided pictures in word problems: representational, decorative, and informative
description: The review adopts a three-category taxonomy of provided pictures following Schewior and Lindner: "pictures are divided into three categories: representational, decorative, and informative". Representational pictures present the task situation or its mathematical structures (pictorial or schematic, static or dynamic); decorative pictures bear little to no relation to the specific task; informative pictures provide essential information additional to the text. The taxonomy organizes the review's coding and findings about when each picture type helps or harms performance.
requirements: Pictures must be provided rather than self-generated for this taxonomy to apply as coded in the review
constraints: Separating representational from organizational pictures is described as theoretically and practically challenging, so they are collapsed
target_learners: elementary school students in grades 1 to 6
target_learning_goals: mathematical word problem-solving skills
examples: The review coded each included study's pictures into these categories, additionally coding pictorial versus schematic and static versus dynamic dimensions
key_sources: Terhi Vessonen, Heidi Hellstrand, Pirjo Aunio, Anu Laine. (2026). Pictures in Mathematical Word Problems: A Systematic Review on the Role of Task and Student Characteristics. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10112-5

article_title: A Systematic Review on Student Engagement in Undergraduate Mathematics: Conceptualization, Measurement, and Learning Outcomes
citation: Elissavet Papageorgiou · Jacqueline Wong · Qinyi Liu · Mohammad Khalil · Annoesjka J. Cabo. (2025). A Systematic Review on Student Engagement in Undergraduate Mathematics: Conceptualization, Measurement, and Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:66. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10046-y
title: Multidimensional, activity-specific conceptualization of student engagement (affective, behavioral, cognitive)
description: The review organizes SE as a multifaceted construct comprising affective, behavioral, and cognitive components, always tied to a specific learning activity. It defines affective engagement as "positive (interest, alertness) or negative feelings of activation (tiredness, boredom)", behavioral engagement as "the effort students intentionally exert", and cognitive engagement as the degree to which students concentrate and think strategically. It also notes extensions: social-affective/behavioral/cognitive engagement, agentic engagement, and productive disciplinary engagement, and a dynamic perspective treating SE as changing over time.
requirements: A clear and explicit definition of the term engagement in each study to support conceptual coherence and cumulative understanding
constraints: The review adopts the learning-engagement perspective (active involvement in learning) rather than school engagement, given its undergraduate mathematics focus
target_learners: undergraduate mathematics students
target_learning_goals: engagement in mathematics learning activities such as problem-solving, self-study, and lectures
examples: The review used Wong and Liem's (2022) comprehensive definitions to infer the appropriate SE dimension when papers did not align indicators to dimensions
key_sources: Elissavet Papageorgiou · Jacqueline Wong · Qinyi Liu · Mohammad Khalil · Annoesjka J. Cabo. (2025). A Systematic Review on Student Engagement in Undergraduate Mathematics: Conceptualization, Measurement, and Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:66. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10046-y

article_title: A Systematic Review on Student Engagement in Undergraduate Mathematics: Conceptualization, Measurement, and Learning Outcomes
citation: Elissavet Papageorgiou · Jacqueline Wong · Qinyi Liu · Mohammad Khalil · Annoesjka J. Cabo. (2025). A Systematic Review on Student Engagement in Undergraduate Mathematics: Conceptualization, Measurement, and Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review (2025) 37:66. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10046-y
title: Corpus of 48 peer-selected empirical studies of SE in undergraduate mathematics (2009–2024)
description: The review's evidence base: 48 papers identified via PRISMA-guided searching of SCOPUS, Science Direct, Web of Science, and ERIC in September 2024, screened with PICo-based inclusion criteria and a 7-item quality appraisal checklist adapted from Liu and Khalil (2023). Publication years "ranged from 2009 to 2024", with most (n = 30, 63%) published after 2019; 85% were journal articles. Studies were mainly quantitative (n = 35, 73%) and set in 23 different countries, with first-year students well represented (n = 20).
requirements: Papers must explicitly use the term engagement and state the specific mathematics learning activity in which SE was observed
constraints: Studies referring only to related terms such as participation, involvement, or interest without referencing engagement were excluded
target_learners: undergraduate mathematics students across STEM, social sciences/humanities, and business/finance programmes
target_learning_goals: engagement in mathematics subjects including statistics (16 papers), algebra (10), and calculus (10)
examples: Four papers from additional sources supplemented the 1,579 database records; 52 papers passed full-text screening and 48 met quality criteria

article_title: The Cronbach’s Alpha of Domain-Specific Knowledge Tests Before and After Learning: A Meta-Analysis of Published Studies
citation: Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Bianca A. Simonsmeier, Michael Schneider. (2025). The Cronbach’s Alpha of Domain‑Specific Knowledge Tests Before and After Learning: A Meta‑Analysis of Published Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09982-y
title: Judge knowledge test internal consistency against empirically based expectations rather than fixed Alpha cut-offs
description: The article argues that fixed cut-off values (e.g., 0.70) for knowledge test Alphas lack theoretical or empirical basis and bias research by suppressing publication of heterogeneous knowledge tests. Instead, researchers should compare their test's Alpha against empirically derived prediction intervals that account for test length. The authors note "dropping guidelines altogether may be a better way forward."
requirements: Researchers need the expected Alpha range for their test length, derivable from the Spearman–Brown prophecy formula applied to the meta-analytic estimate.
constraints: The proposed prediction interval guideline applies to knowledge tests with about 20 items; the article provides separate guidelines for shorter and longer tests.
target_learners: Educational researchers developing and evaluating domain-specific knowledge tests
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of domain-specific knowledge before and after learning
examples: The meta-analysis derived a 90% prediction interval of [0.35, 0.96] as a guideline for Alphas of knowledge tests with 20 items, with guidelines for shorter and longer tests.
key_sources: Peter A. Edelsbrunner, Bianca A. Simonsmeier, Michael Schneider. (2025). The Cronbach’s Alpha of Domain‑Specific Knowledge Tests Before and After Learning: A Meta‑Analysis of Published Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09982-y

article_title: Cognitive Profiles of Children with Isolated and Comorbid Learning Difficulties in Reading and Math: a Meta-analysis
citation: Nurit Viesel-Nordmeyer, Julia Reuber, Jörg-Tobias Kuhn, Kristina Moll, Heinz Holling, Christian Dobel. (2023). Cognitive Profiles of Children with Isolated and Comorbid Learning Difficulties in Reading and Math: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09735-3
title: Multi-deficit model versus three independent disorders model of comorbid reading and math difficulties
description: The article frames two competing explanatory models for comorbid RDMD. Under the "multi-deficit model", the RDMD profile is "characterized by the sum of domain-specific core deficits of RD and MD (additivity)" plus shared domain-general risk factors producing less severe EF deficits than expected (under-additivity). The "three independent disorders model" instead treats RDMD as a distinct disorder with "distinct and/or more severe deficits, compared to the sum of RD's and MD's profiles (over-additivity)". The meta-analysis was designed to adjudicate between them.
requirements: Studies must include groups of children with isolated RD, isolated MD, and comorbid RDMD plus a control group, so that the linear additivity hypothesis g1 + g2 − g3 can be tested
constraints: The article limits the age span to 6–12 years, the age span where LD mostly become visible
Detecting a small interaction effect would require screening around 10,000 children, which the authors note requires large multicenter studies
target_learners: children aged 6–12 with isolated or comorbid reading and math learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: reading skills
math skills
executive function skills
examples: The meta-analysis translated additivity into the linear hypothesis gAdd = g1 + g2 − g3 = 0 and tested it across math, reading, and EF outcomes in 74 studies
key_sources: Nurit Viesel-Nordmeyer, Julia Reuber, Jörg-Tobias Kuhn, Kristina Moll, Heinz Holling, Christian Dobel. (2023). Cognitive Profiles of Children with Isolated and Comorbid Learning Difficulties in Reading and Math: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09735-3

article_title: Self-Regulated Learning, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid: Where Are We Now and Where Are We Going?
citation: Joni Lämsä, Susanne de Mooij, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar, Sanna Järvelä. (2026). Self-Regulated Learning, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid: Where Are We Now and Where Are We Going? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10113-4
title: The SMA grid as a framework for mapping SRL measurement across CAMM processes, data streams, and analytical approaches
description: The self-regulated learning, multimodal data, and analysis grid (SMA grid) organizes how studies measure SRL by relating CAMM processes to data streams and analysis approaches. The article states that "The self-regulated learning, multimodal data, and analysis grid (SMA) is used as a framework for mapping and analyzing these processes across diverse data streams." It distinguishes unimodal, horizontal, vertical, and integrated approaches to combining data streams, and reveals that affective and motivational processes receive less attention than cognitive and metacognitive ones.
requirements: Reliable and valid measurement of CAMM processes, which the article calls the basis for providing personalized support
constraints: The grid shows temporal aspects of affective and motivational processes have gained little attention in LA and AI measurement of SRL
target_learners: Learners in digital and technology-enhanced learning environments
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning across cognitive, affective, metacognitive, and motivational processes
examples: The special issue's five contributions map their studies onto the SMA grid, including reviews of motivation and mind wandering and two empirical studies.
key_sources: Joni Lämsä, Susanne de Mooij, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar, Sanna Järvelä. (2026). Self-Regulated Learning, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid: Where Are We Now and Where Are We Going? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10113-4

article_title: Self-Regulated Learning, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid: Where Are We Now and Where Are We Going?
citation: Joni Lämsä, Susanne de Mooij, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar, Sanna Järvelä. (2026). Self-Regulated Learning, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid: Where Are We Now and Where Are We Going? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10113-4
title: Human-AI interaction as shared regulation: offloading metacognitive monitoring to AI and onloading metacognitive control to learners
description: The article frames human-AI interactions in SRL support as a form of shared regulation in which AI and learners reciprocally adapt. As the authors write, "these invitations to self-regulate can include offloading metacognitive monitoring from learners to AI, after which controlling one's learning is onloaded from AI to learners." AI augments decision-making about learning while learners develop the capacity to enact those decisions, supporting a transition to empowered, agentic learners in digital environments.
requirements: Learners must critically evaluate and act upon AI's invitations rather than offload their regulatory practices wholesale
constraints: The dynamic benefits both learners and AI only when learners do not offload their regulatory practices to AI
target_learners: Learners using AI-supported learning technologies
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive monitoring and control of one's own learning
examples: A learner consults a learning-analytics dashboard indicating they are off-track, gains metacognitive awareness, and revises learning goals or adapts cognitive strategies.
key_sources: Joni Lämsä, Susanne de Mooij, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar, Sanna Järvelä. (2026). Self-Regulated Learning, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid: Where Are We Now and Where Are We Going? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10113-4

article_title: Investigating Visual Perception in Teaching and Learning with Advanced Eye-Tracking Methodologies: Rewards and Challenges of an Innovative Research Paradigm
citation: Nückles, M. (2021). Investigating Visual Perception in Teaching and Learning with Advanced Eye-Tracking Methodologies: Rewards and Challenges of an Innovative Research Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09567-5
title: An emerging research paradigm joining four originally separated research strands on visual perception in teaching and learning
description: The article characterizes an emerging research paradigm in which eye-tracking methodologies are used to study professional vision and teacher expertise. It argues the paradigm brings together "different and originally separated strands of research": professional vision in teacher education, expertise structure and development in cognitive science, eye-tracking study of cognitive processes in psychology, and educational effectiveness and instructional quality research. The seven special-issue contributions instantiate this paradigm.
requirements: Advanced eye-tracking technologies, including mobile eye-tracking glasses, to study gaze in naturalistic classroom settings
constraints: The paradigm is at an early stage; the author identifies theoretical assumptions in it that he considers controversial
target_learners: teachers and teacher students in professional development
target_learning_goals: professional vision
teacher expertise
instructional quality
examples: The seven contributions of the special issue each combine at least two of the four strands, e.g., expert-novice comparisons using mobile eye-tracking during real lessons
key_sources: Nückles, M. (2021). Investigating Visual Perception in Teaching and Learning with Advanced Eye-Tracking Methodologies: Rewards and Challenges of an Innovative Research Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09567-5

article_title: Investigating Visual Perception in Teaching and Learning with Advanced Eye-Tracking Methodologies: Rewards and Challenges of an Innovative Research Paradigm
citation: Nückles, M. (2021). Investigating Visual Perception in Teaching and Learning with Advanced Eye-Tracking Methodologies: Rewards and Challenges of an Innovative Research Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09567-5
title: Classroom management script model of expert-novice differences in classroom management
description: Wolff et al.'s theoretical model explains the cognitive differences between expert and novice teachers in classroom management via the notion of a "classroom management script": knowledge structures allowing proficient teachers to establish a productive work climate by preventing and managing off-task or disruptive behavior. Scripts comprise enabling conditions specifying classroom-situation factors, pedagogical consequences such as proliferation of off-task behavior, and possible alternative courses of action. Experienced teachers' scripts are argued to be more numerous, richer, and more integrated, enabling faster anticipation of critical events.
requirements: Scripts evolve through exposure to numerous and varied experiences in the classroom, blended with formal professional knowledge
constraints: The author questions whether expertise development can be taken for granted, since teacher education programs offer sparse opportunities for deep learning of scientific pedagogical knowledge
target_learners: novice and experienced teachers
target_learning_goals: classroom management expertise
examples: The author cites experimental studies showing experienced mathematics teachers displayed the same procedural bias in instructional explanations as teacher students, questioning experience-based expertise development

article_title: A Half Century of Progress in US Student Achievement: Agency and Flynn Effects, Ethnic and SES Differences
citation: M. Danish Shakeel · Paul E. Peterson. (2022). A Half Century of Progress in US Student Achievement: Agency and Flynn Effects, Ethnic and SES Differences. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09657-y
title: Principal-agent framework for interpreting variation in student achievement trend estimates
description: The article applies the principal-agent model from political economy to educational measurement: policymakers (principals) lacking technical expertise delegate trend measurement to survey organizations (agents), risking adverse selection and moral hazard. Because principals hold "ambiguous and not always consistent objectives", agents interpret them distinctively, generating varied trend estimates. The authors use this framework to explain why four agents administering 160 waves of 17 linked surveys produce divergent estimates, and to justify using median rather than mean estimates across surveys.
requirements: Multiple survey agents administering psychometrically linked tests to national probability samples, so medians can be taken across agents
constraints: The framework applies where principals' objectives are unranked or ambiguous, as in a federal system with boundary organizations such as NCES and NAGB
target_learners: US school-age students in cohorts born between 1954 and 2007
target_learning_goals: Tracking cohort progress in mathematics and reading achievement over half a century
examples: The four agents — LTT NAEP, main NAEP, TIMSS-PIRLS, and PISA — each interpret principals' objectives differently: LTT tracks national trends only, NAEP adjusts to changing curricula, TIMSS-PIRLS measures performance against an international curriculum, and PISA measures "preparation for life".
key_sources: M. Danish Shakeel · Paul E. Peterson. (2022). A Half Century of Progress in US Student Achievement: Agency and Flynn Effects, Ethnic and SES Differences. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09657-y

article_title: A Half Century of Progress in US Student Achievement: Agency and Flynn Effects, Ethnic and SES Differences
citation: M. Danish Shakeel · Paul E. Peterson. (2022). A Half Century of Progress in US Student Achievement: Agency and Flynn Effects, Ethnic and SES Differences. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09657-y
title: NCES restricted-use individual-level dataset of seven million US student observations across 160 survey waves
description: The study's empirical base is individual-student data from the NCES restricted-use dataset, covering "Approximately seven million student-level observations of US students and approximately four and a half million observations of non-US students". The data span 160 waves of 17 psychometrically linked surveys in math and reading administered to national probability samples of cohorts born between 1954 and 2007, with survey weights applied and the second plausible value used per wave.
requirements: Access restricted to qualified research centers; parental education and possession-index measures are unavailable in some survey waves
constraints: Ethnicity information is missing for PIRLS 2001 and 2016; NAEP 12th-grade math trends are included only for students born after 1987 because earlier tests were not psychometrically linked
target_learners: US students aged 9, 13, 15, and 17 and in grades 4, 8, and 12
target_learning_goals: Measuring change over time in math and reading achievement
examples: The SES index is extracted as the first principal component of the household possession index and parental education categories, available for 15 surveys.
key_sources: M. Danish Shakeel · Paul E. Peterson. (2022). A Half Century of Progress in US Student Achievement: Agency and Flynn Effects, Ethnic and SES Differences. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09657-y

article_title: Evermore Wellbeing for Teens: A Scoping Review of Stand-alone and Brief Positive Psychology Interventions for Potential Use in Educational Settings
citation: Lucciarini, E., Carr, A., Bressoud, N., Boniwell, I., Audrin, C., Gay, P., & Burel, N. (2025). Evermore Wellbeing for Teens: A Scoping Review of Stand-alone and Brief Positive Psychology Interventions for Potential Use in Educational Settings. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10033-3
title: PoETA: a toolbox approach of short, stand-alone, flexible positive psychology interventions for classroom integration
description: PoETA (Lucciarini & Boniwell, 2023) is a framework for integrating wellbeing practices into schools through a curated toolbox of brief interventions. The article states that "The PoETA aims at providing short (5 to 10 min), stand-alone, explicit, and flexible interventions that require minimal or no specialised training." It complements rather than replaces CASEL and SAFE, targeting implementation barriers of time, training, and curricular flexibility, and lets teachers and students select activities. The authors stress that effectiveness in real classrooms still requires dedicated validation studies.
requirements: Interventions must be validated through meta-analyses and implementable without specialised expertise or technological platforms
constraints: Pending further validation in real-world educational settings; substantial research is still needed to confirm its effectiveness
target_learners: adolescents in mainstream educational settings
target_learning_goals: psychological wellbeing
psychosocial skills
academic engagement
examples: The review screened Carr et al.'s (2023) mega-analysis and retained 64 interventions meeting PoETA's brevity, stand-alone, and evidence criteria

citation: Lucciarini, E., Carr, A., Bressoud, N., Boniwell, I., Audrin, C., Gay, P., & Burel, N. (2025). Evermore Wellbeing for Teens: A Scoping Review of Stand-alone and Brief Positive Psychology Interventions for Potential Use in Educational Settings. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10033-3
title: ACTIONS framework: seven categories for classifying positive psychology interventions
description: The ACTIONS framework (Boniwell, 2017) organises PPIs into seven categories: Activity, Calming, Thinking, Identity, Optimising, Nourishing, and Social. The review states that "Through systematic analysis, Boniwell developed seven distinct categories that better reflected the diversity of the PPIs as detailed in Table 2." Each category carries key elements, e.g. Activity covers movement and sport, Calming covers mindfulness and breathing, Identity covers character strengths and values, and Social covers positive relationships and prosocial behaviour. The review uses ACTIONS to structure consideration of the 64 selected interventions for future implementation.
requirements: Derived from a review of 12 meta-analyses encompassing over 60 distinct PPIs
target_learners: adolescents in educational settings
target_learning_goals: wellbeing
psychosocial skills
examples: The review evaluated its 64 selected PPIs using the ACTIONS framework to support implementation decisions

article_title: Evolution of Self-Awareness and the Cultural Emergence of Academic and Non-academic Self-Concepts
citation: Geary, D., Xu, K.M. (2022). Evolution of Self-Awareness and the Cultural Emergence of Academic and Non-academic Self-Concepts. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09669-2
title: Biologically primary versus biologically secondary abilities framework for academic development
description: The article proposes an evolutionary framework distinguishing evolved, biological primary abilities such as spoken language from evolutionarily novel, biologically secondary academic competencies such as reading. Instruction is the mechanism that converts one into the other: "instructional practices modify evolved or biological primary abilities (e.g., spoken language) to create evolutionarily novel or biologically secondary academic competencies (e.g., reading)". The framework grounds the article's account of why academic development requires schooling.
requirements: Formal instruction is needed to build biologically secondary academic competencies from primary abilities
constraints: The framework is a theoretical proposal about evolutionary recency of schooling, not a tested empirical result in this article
target_learners: school-age students in formal schooling
target_learning_goals: academic competencies such as reading built from evolved primary abilities
examples: The article contrasts spoken language as a primary ability with reading as a secondary academic competency created by instruction
key_sources: Geary, D., Xu, K.M. (2022). Evolution of Self-Awareness and the Cultural Emergence of Academic and Non-academic Self-Concepts. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09669-2

article_title: Evolution of Self-Awareness and the Cultural Emergence of Academic and Non-academic Self-Concepts
citation: Geary, D., Xu, K.M. (2022). Evolution of Self-Awareness and the Cultural Emergence of Academic and Non-academic Self-Concepts. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09669-2
title: Attend to cultural supports for valuing academic competencies when interpreting variation in students' academic motivation
description: Because the article argues that academic self-concepts are culturally contingent, educators and researchers should consider whether explicit social and cultural supports for valuing academic competencies are present when explaining students' motivation. The article states these self-concepts' importance is "dependent on explicit social and cultural supports for their valuation", with "implications for understanding variation students’ relative valuation of academic competencies and their motivations to engage in academic learning".
requirements: Explicit social and cultural supports for the valuation of academic competencies must exist for academic self-concepts to become centrally important to students
constraints: The article offers this as a theoretical implication, not a tested intervention recommendation
target_learners: students in formal schooling across cultures
target_learning_goals: academic motivation and engagement in academic learning
examples: The article contrasts culturally contingent academic self-concepts with universal social and physical self-concepts to explain variation in motivation
key_sources: Geary, D., Xu, K.M. (2022). Evolution of Self-Awareness and the Cultural Emergence of Academic and Non-academic Self-Concepts. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09669-2

article_title: Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition
citation: Michael W. Asher & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10103-6
title: Theory of practice-centered learning: feedback can deliver lecture-equivalent instruction, while upfront practice prepares learners to encode it
description: The article proposes "a theory of practice-centered learning that integrates theoretical insights from research on problem-solving before instruction", including productive failure, pre-questioning, and replacing lecture with practice and feedback. Its premise is that effective learning requires both clear instruction and preparation to encode it; well-designed feedback can deliver the same key information as lecture, but pairing feedback with upfront practice engages attention and sharpens metacognitive monitoring. The theory predicts memory benefits from any feedback, but generalization only when feedback explains underlying principles and learners have sufficient prior knowledge.
requirements: Feedback must deliver the instructional content a lecture would provide, including facts and the rules and principles required to generalize.
For generalization, feedback must explain underlying principles and learners must have sufficient prior knowledge to engage productively with these explanations.
constraints: When the two ingredients for generalization are absent, practice may enhance retention without supporting the deeper understanding needed to apply knowledge flexibly.
Challenge from practice may feel frustrating or discouraging, particularly for learners with lower confidence or less prior knowledge.
target_learners: Adult online learners (Prolific participants) learning introductory statistics
target_learning_goals: Memory for factual statistical content
Generalization of regression concepts to novel problems
Metacognitive calibration
examples: Across two experiments, practice conditions used problem sets matched to the lecture's worked example, with feedback that either gave correct answers or explained why answers were correct.
key_sources: Michael W. Asher & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10103-6

article_title: Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition
citation: Michael W. Asher & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10103-6
title: GPT-4o-generated personalized explanatory feedback for open-ended practice
description: In Study 2, the explanatory feedback condition used GPT-4o to "provide immediate, tailored explanatory feedback after each practice item", evaluating open-ended responses in real time. The prompt instructed the model to state "Correct!" or "Incorrect", explain why incorrect answers were wrong, and edit the student's exact wording with the smallest possible changes into a corrected version. Manual review of all 309 AI-generated responses found the AI correctly scored 90% of correct answers and 98% of incorrect answers, with appropriate corrections 98% of the time and no hallucinations.
requirements: GPT-4o must be given a written explanation of the problem, the criteria expected in a correct answer, and sample correct and incorrect responses based on pilot work to ensure feedback accuracy.
constraints: Accuracy was validated for this study's three regression questions and judged "sufficiently accurate for our research purposes", not as a general-purpose tutoring guarantee.
target_learners: Adult online learners practicing open-ended statistics questions
target_learning_goals: Interpreting slope and intercept of a regression line
Generating correct open-ended explanations of statistical concepts
examples: For a student who wrote only that the intercept intersects the Y axis at 5.58, the AI identified the missing interpretation and supplied a corrected version stating the predicted murder rate when temperature equals zero.
key_sources: Michael W. Asher & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10103-6

article_title: Specialized Purpose of Each Type of Student Engagement: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Johnmarshall Reeve, Geetanjali Basarkod, Hye-Ryen Jang, Rafael Gargurevich, Hyungshim Jang, Sung Hyeon Cheon. (2025). Specialized Purpose of Each Type of Student Engagement: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09989-z
title: Specialized purpose hypothesis: each type of engagement has its own specialized function targeted toward a specific purpose
description: The article proposes and tests the specialized purpose hypothesis, namely that each type of engagement has its own specialized function targeted toward a specific purpose, such as to boost achievement, social support, motivation, or well-being. As illustrated in Fig. 1, it assigns behavioral engagement primarily to achievement, agentic engagement to recruiting social support, cognitive engagement to achievement and cognition-based motivations, and emotional engagement to well-being and need-based motivations. The four meta-analyses were designed to test whether one type of engagement predicts each correlate more strongly than the others.
requirements: Studies must measure all four types of engagement so relative strengths can be compared
constraints: The article notes the findings raise challenging questions about how to better conceptualize and measure each type of engagement
target_learners: P-16 students in K-16 classroom settings
target_learning_goals: achievement
social support
motivation
well-being
examples: Four multilevel random effects meta-analyses tested whether engagement type moderated the relation with each correlate
key_sources: Johnmarshall Reeve, Geetanjali Basarkod, Hye-Ryen Jang, Rafael Gargurevich, Hyungshim Jang, Sung Hyeon Cheon. (2025). Specialized Purpose of Each Type of Student Engagement: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09989-z

article_title: Specialized Purpose of Each Type of Student Engagement: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Johnmarshall Reeve, Geetanjali Basarkod, Hye-Ryen Jang, Rafael Gargurevich, Hyungshim Jang, Sung Hyeon Cheon. (2025). Specialized Purpose of Each Type of Student Engagement: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09989-z
title: Four-dimensional model of learning engagement: behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and agentic engagement
description: The article conceptualizes learning engagement as a multidimensional phenomenon in which students involve themselves in learning activities behaviorally, cognitively, emotionally, and agentically. It defines behavioral engagement as exert effort, cognitive engagement as absorbed in thought, emotional engagement as feel activated, and agentic engagement as the student's constructive contribution into the flow of instruction they receive, with operational indicators such as offering input, asking questions, and making suggestions. The paper argues agentic engagement is a fourth strategic approach a student might use to optimize and advance their learning, not just another way of involving oneself.
requirements: Measurement of each dimension separately, as in Table 1's conceptual and operational definitions
constraints: The article focuses narrowly on learning engagement in academic work, nested within the broader school engagement literature
target_learners: P-16 students
target_learning_goals: active involvement in learning activities
examples: Table 1 provides conceptual and operational definitions for each type of engagement and each correlate
key_sources: Johnmarshall Reeve, Geetanjali Basarkod, Hye-Ryen Jang, Rafael Gargurevich, Hyungshim Jang, Sung Hyeon Cheon. (2025). Specialized Purpose of Each Type of Student Engagement: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09989-z

article_title: The Big-fish–little-pond-effect Stands Up to Critical Scrutiny: Implications for Theory, Methodology, and Future Research
citation: Marsh, H. W., Seaton, M., Trautwein, U., Lüdtke, O., Hau, K. T., O'Mara, A. J., & Craven, R. G. (2008). The Big-fish–little-pond-effect Stands Up to Critical Scrutiny: Implications for Theory, Methodology, and Future Research. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9075-6
title: The BFLPE theoretical model: frame-of-reference effects on academic self-concept
description: The BFLPE model holds that students evaluate their academic accomplishments against the average ability level of others in their school, so the same objective ability produces different academic self-concepts depending on the school's average ability. Marsh formulated this as an educational application of frame-of-reference and psychophysical judgment research. The model generates seven predictions, including that "school-average ability will be negatively related to ASC after controlling for individual student ability" and that all students in a high-ability school would have lower ASCs than they would in a low-ability school, with small or non-significant interactions between school-average and individual ability.
requirements: Testing requires a multilevel design with many schools, an objective achievement measure comparable across schools, an appropriate ASC measure, and tests of school-average achievement effects controlling for individual achievement
constraints: The model operationalizes the standard of comparison as school-average ability and makes no predictions about the relative importance of school versus class frames of reference
target_learners: school students (K-12 and secondary)
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept formation
examples: Marsh (1984a) operationalized the standard of comparison as school-average ability; the model predicts a below-average ASC for an average-ability student attending a high-ability school
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Seaton, M., Trautwein, U., Lüdtke, O., Hau, K. T., O'Mara, A. J., & Craven, R. G. (2008). The Big-fish–little-pond-effect Stands Up to Critical Scrutiny: Implications for Theory, Methodology, and Future Research. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9075-6

article_title: The Big-fish–little-pond-effect Stands Up to Critical Scrutiny: Implications for Theory, Methodology, and Future Research
citation: Marsh, H. W., Seaton, M., Trautwein, U., Lüdtke, O., Hau, K. T., O'Mara, A. J., & Craven, R. G. (2008). The Big-fish–little-pond-effect Stands Up to Critical Scrutiny: Implications for Theory, Methodology, and Future Research. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9075-6
title: School organization policies (tracking, ability grouping, selective schools, gifted programs) should account for the negative BFLPE on academic self-concept
description: Because academic self-concept predicts future achievement, coursework selection, and educational attainment, the BFLPE carries policy implications for how schools are organized. The article states the results "have important implications for the way in which schools are organized (e.g., tracking, ability grouping, academically selective schools, and gifted education programs)" — grouping high-ability students together imposes a more demanding frame of reference that lowers each student's academic self-concept. Planners should weigh these self-concept costs against any achievement benefits of such arrangements.
requirements: Decisions about ability grouping or selective schooling should be evaluated with the BFLPE evidence on academic self-concept in view, since ASC predicts future achievement and educational attainment
constraints: The article notes the achievement effects of tracking itself are near zero (Hattie's meta-analytic average effect size = 0.05), and it treats gifted programs as distinct from high-ability tracks
target_learners: school students, particularly those in or being considered for tracked, selective, or gifted education settings
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept, coursework selection, educational attainment
examples: The article cites the BFLPE's robustness across countries and long-term follow-ups as the basis for its policy relevance to tracking, ability grouping, selective schools, and gifted education programs
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Seaton, M., Trautwein, U., Lüdtke, O., Hau, K. T., O'Mara, A. J., & Craven, R. G. (2008). The Big-fish–little-pond-effect Stands Up to Critical Scrutiny: Implications for Theory, Methodology, and Future Research. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9075-6

article_title: Reply to Sana et al.’s (2022) Commentary on Rest-from-Deliberate-Learning as a Mechanism for the Spacing Effect
citation: Ouhao Chen, Fred Paas, John Sweller. (2022). Reply to Sana et al.'s (2022) Commentary on Rest-from-Deliberate-Learning as a Mechanism for the Spacing Effect. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 1851–1858. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09678-1
title: Rest-from-deliberate-learning framework: working memory resources deplete with cognitive effort and replenish with rest, explaining part of the spacing effect
description: The framework assumes that "working memory resources diminish with cognitive effort and replenish with rest", providing an explanation of the spacing effect that is distinct from the interleaving effect. It was proposed to resolve mixed results of spacing and interleaving rather than as a theory of everything. The authors state its scope covers learning tasks, not simple processing tasks unrelated to learning.
requirements: Rest must involve no intentional learning, since without intentional learning there is no reason to assume a working memory load
constraints: Cannot account for lag effects (spacing effects found when shorter and longer intervals between repetitions are compared)
Does not apply to processing tasks unrelated to learning, such as digit shadowing tasks that did not require any learning
Whether rest and its effect on working memory are important for the spacing effect must ultimately be determined empirically
target_learners: students in all stages
target_learning_goals: retention of learned material under spaced versus massed practice
examples: Chen et al. (2018) is cited as the only published study the authors know that specifically tested the hypothesis, providing evidence for it
key_sources: Ouhao Chen, Fred Paas, John Sweller. (2022). Reply to Sana et al.'s (2022) Commentary on Rest-from-Deliberate-Learning as a Mechanism for the Spacing Effect. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 1851–1858. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09678-1

article_title: Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt
citation: Tina Seufert. (2020). Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 1151–1162. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09574-6
title: Effort Monitoring and Regulation (EMR) framework linking self-regulated learning with mental effort and cognitive load
description: The EMR-framework, introduced by the special-issue editors (de Bruin, Roelle, Baars, and the EARLI Emerging Field Group), builds a bridge from self-regulation to cognitive load by linking self-regulated learning with mental effort. The review states that "mental effort is crucial for dealing with the task as well as for self-regulation," and that awareness of invested resources "can serve as a cue to inform processes both on the object-level and on the meta-level." At its center is the CLT differentiation of intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load, though most papers measure effort with a one-item rating. The framework frames all nine papers, which stimulate learning on the object level, for effort utilization, or on the meta-level.
requirements: Learners must be aware of their invested resources so these can serve as cues for monitoring and regulation
constraints: Effort appraisals in the framed papers are mostly measured with a one-item rating and are not differentiated into intrinsic, extraneous, and germane categories
target_learners: Learners in self-regulated learning settings, including learners studying on their own
target_learning_goals: Improved monitoring accuracy and regulation of learning through use of effort cues
examples: The special-issue papers apply the framework via generative tasks, effort-utilization training, and meta-level journal writing
key_sources: Tina Seufert. (2020). Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 1151–1162. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09574-6

article_title: Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt
citation: Tina Seufert. (2020). Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 1151–1162. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09574-6
title: Self-regulation as a function of resources and imposed cognitive load: an inverted-u relationship with task difficulty
description: The review proposes that the relation between self-regulation and cognitive load depends on learners' resources—cognitive, motivational, and affective—drawing on the INVO-model of individual prerequisites for successful learning (Hasselhorn & Gold, 2006). Task difficulty comprises affordances of accomplishing the task on both object and meta levels. Two forces moderate a reverse u-shaped relationship between task difficulty and required self-regulation: available resources decrease with increasing difficulty, and imposed load increases with it. As the review states, "Only with medium task difficulty, resources and load are balanced to allow for effective self- regulation: learners have sufficient resources to deal with the task, and regulation can help to use these resources more effectively."
requirements: Learners must have sufficient cognitive, motivational, and affective resources (prior knowledge, strategy skills, interest, willingness) relative to task difficulty
constraints: At very low difficulty learners have no need to regulate; at very high difficulty resources are insufficient and imposed load too high, so regulation fails
target_learners: Learners across task-difficulty levels whose available resources vary
target_learning_goals: Effective self-regulation of learning under varying cognitive load
examples: Fig. 1 depicts self-regulation as low at easy and difficult tasks and highest at medium task difficulty
key_sources: Tina Seufert. (2020). Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 1151–1162. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09574-6

article_title: Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt
citation: Tina Seufert. (2020). Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 1151–1162. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09574-6
title: Unconscious self-regulation via resonant states in sensory memory that trigger automatized strategy use without working-memory resources
description: Citing Wirth, Stebner, Trypke, Schuster, and Leutner, the review presents a new perspective in which self-regulation can be not only conscious but unconscious. "They introduce the so-called resonant states in sensory memory which trigger a bottom-up and top-down interaction, where external stimuli are aligned with expectations." A material feature, such as text without subsections, can match an expectation of a difficult text and automatically start a strategy like underlining and note taking without reaching consciousness, so it does not require working-memory resources. This account implies the cognitive costs of self-regulation can be eliminated when learning strategies are highly automatized.
requirements: Learners need substantial self-regulation knowledge and expertise: they must know which text features indicate complexity and which strategy is functional, and be able to apply the strategy without attentional control from working memory
constraints: The trigger needs a fruitful ground for resonance, so the account applies to learners with automatized strategies rather than novices
target_learners: Learners with highly automatized learning strategies and substantial self-regulation expertise
target_learning_goals: Automatic initiation of appropriate learning strategies without consuming working-memory resources
examples: A text without subsections or paragraphs matching the expectation of a difficult text automatically triggers underlining and note taking
key_sources: Tina Seufert. (2020). Building Bridges Between Self-Regulation and Cognitive Load—an Invitation for a Broad and Differentiated Attempt. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 1151–1162. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09574-6

article_title: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis to Support Power Analyses for Randomized Intervention Studies in Preschool: Cognitive and Socio-Emotional Learning Outcomes
citation: Martin Brunner, Sophie E. Stallasch, Cordula Artelt, Oliver Lüdtke. (2025). An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis to Support Power Analyses for Randomized Intervention Studies in Preschool: Cognitive and Socio-Emotional Learning Outcomes. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09981-z
title: Match design parameters to the key characteristics of the planned intervention study when conducting a priori power analyses
description: This principle holds that a priori power analyses should strive for an ideal match between the selected design parameters and the planned study's characteristics: the clustering structure (single-, two-, or three-level), the target outcome domain, the assessment method, and the target age group. The article urges selecting "design parameters that offer the best match to the assumptions of how the data of the planned study will be clustered" and, given heterogeneity, using estimates from the same or a very similar target measure and age group.
requirements: Design parameters must be available for the target population, outcome, and assessment method of the planned study
constraints: Suitable estimates may be unavailable for a specific data structure, measure, age group, or covariate set
target_learners: preschool children aged two to six attending daycare centers
target_learning_goals: cognitive outcomes (math/science, verbal, general cognitive, psychomotor skills)
socio-emotional learning outcomes (self-, other-, and task-orientation)
examples: The article illustrates matching two-level parameters (ρCenter, R2Child, R2Center) to a two-level CRT and notes that when ρGroup and R2Group are missing, relevant two-level parameters can be used because between-group differences were often smaller than between-center differences
key_sources: Martin Brunner, Sophie E. Stallasch, Cordula Artelt, Oliver Lüdtke. (2025). An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis to Support Power Analyses for Randomized Intervention Studies in Preschool: Cognitive and Socio-Emotional Learning Outcomes. The materials support researchers applying the parameters in a priori power analyses.

examples: OSM B provides detailed interactive tables of design parameters required for sample size planning; OSM A documents the systematic search that identified NUBBEK, BIKS, and NEPS

article_title: Instructional Implications of Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture as an Intelligent Natural Information Processing System
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2026). Instructional Implications of Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture as an Intelligent Natural Information Processing System. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 33. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10135-6
title: Human cognition as an intelligent natural information processing system integrating primary and secondary processes
description: The article characterizes human cognitive architecture as a higher-level natural information processing system that, unlike other such systems, integrates evolved implicit (biologically primary) abilities with controlled explicit (biologically secondary) processes. It builds on five principles of natural information processing systems and a provisionally added explicit intention to learn principle. The article states that intelligent systems "are capable to intentionally, willingly switch to the controlled, explicit mode of operation" and generate biologically secondary knowledge in novel situations.
requirements: The framework presupposes the five established principles of natural information processing systems (information store, borrowing and reorganizing, randomness as genesis, narrow limits of change, environmental organizing and linking) as its base.
constraints: The article notes the explicit intention to learn principle "remains in need of direct empirical testing before it becomes a settled principle."
target_learners: learners acquiring biologically secondary knowledge
target_learning_goals: generating and learning biologically secondary knowledge
key_sources: Kalyuga, S. (2026). Instructional Implications of Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture as an Intelligent Natural Information Processing System. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 33. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10135-6

article_title: Instructional Implications of Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture as an Intelligent Natural Information Processing System
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2026). Instructional Implications of Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture as an Intelligent Natural Information Processing System. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 33. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10135-6
title: Select instructional methods based on the specific instructional goal to be achieved (goal-driven approach)
description: The article proposes extending cognitive load theory with a goal-driven approach in which methods are matched to pre-instructional goals (motivating, engaging, altering affective states), instructional goals (schema acquisition), and post-instructional goals (novel problem solving and far transfer). It argues that "specific instructional approaches and methods need to be selected based on exact instructional goals to be achieved," so a single method cannot serve all goals.
requirements: Instructional designers must first specify which goal level (pre-instructional, instructional, or post-instructional) a method is meant to serve.
constraints: The article frames this as a theoretical proposal whose proposed approaches "need to be compared with traditional approaches in controlled experimental studies."
target_learners: novice and experienced learners acquiring biologically secondary knowledge
target_learning_goals: schema acquisition, learner motivation and engagement, affective states, novel problem-solving ability
examples: Exploratory activities such as productive failure or invention learning are cited as serving motivational goals prior to explicit learning; emotional design techniques are cited for modifying learner emotional states before schema instruction.
key_sources: Kalyuga, S. (2026). Instructional Implications of Evolutionary Perspective on Human Cognitive Architecture as an Intelligent Natural Information Processing System. Educational Psychology Review, 38, 33. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10135-6

article_title: Single- and Multilevel Perspectives on Covariate Selection in Randomized Intervention Studies on Student Achievement
citation: Stallasch, S. E., Lüdtke, O., Artelt, C., Hedges, L. V., & Brunner, M. (2024). Single- and Multilevel Perspectives on Covariate Selection in Randomized Intervention Studies on Student Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09898-7
title: Compiled single- and multilevel design parameter database and OSF repository with R scripts and interactive Excel workbooks for RT study planning
description: The article releases an extensive compilation of empirical and meta-analytic single- and multilevel design parameters (R2 and intraclass correlations) for covariate sets varying type, combination, and 1-7 year time lag, estimated from six German probability samples totaling N = 68,502 students in grades 1-12. The repository includes "all R scripts, and instructions for accessing the analyzed data" at https://osf.io/nhx4w, with OSM A-G and interactive Excel workbooks compiling empirical, meta-analytic, and simulation results. It is accompanied by the multides R package (Stallasch, 2024).
requirements: Access to the German large-scale assessment datasets via the documented research data centers
constraints: Estimates stem from German samples whose school-system characteristics, such as early ability-based school-type-tracking, deviate markedly from those of the United States
target_learners: Students in grades 1-12 in elementary, lower secondary, and upper secondary school
target_learning_goals: Design sensitivity and statistical power of randomized trials measuring student achievement outcomes
examples: The article applies the compiled design parameters in illustrative scenarios of study planning and precision simulations conceding ρ and R2 uncertainties via a Bayesian rationale

article_title: Evaluating the Dynamics of Learning Approaches: A Systematic Review Investigating the Nexus Between Teaching Methods and Academic Performance in Medical and Dental Education
citation: Marlen A. Roehe, Carmen Trost, Julia S. Grundnig, Anahit Anvari-Pirsch, Anita Holzinger. (2024). Evaluating the Dynamics of Learning Approaches: A Systematic Review Investigating the Nexus Between Teaching Methods and Academic Performance in Medical and Dental Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09952-4
title: Three learning approaches framework: deep, surface, and strategic approaches that are malleable rather than fixed traits
description: The review organises its synthesis around the learning approaches construct originating with Marton and Säljö and developed by Biggs and Entwistle, in which students' traits are "categorised into three distinct, yet complementary, learning approaches: a deep, surface, or strategic approach to learning." A deep approach involves intrinsic motivation to understand and relate ideas; a surface approach relies on rote learning driven by fear of failure; the strategic approach combines good time management with flexible shifting between understanding and memorisation. The review stresses these are not fixed: "students can shift between these approaches to adapt to educational circumstances."
requirements: Measurement via questionnaire inventories based on the established approaches constructs (e.g., SPQ, ASI, ASSIST)
constraints: Approaches are context-dependent and shift with workload, performance, motivation, and personal factors, so they are not stable learner traits
target_learners: undergraduate medical and dental students
target_learning_goals: long-term knowledge retention and application of knowledge in clinical contexts
examples: The review used this three-approach framework to code 470 co-occurrences between teaching methods, learning approaches, and academic performance across 49 studies
key_sources: Marlen A. Roehe, Carmen Trost, Julia S. Grundnig, Anahit Anvari-Pirsch, Anita Holzinger. (2024). Evaluating the Dynamics of Learning Approaches: A Systematic Review Investigating the Nexus Between Teaching Methods and Academic Performance in Medical and Dental Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09952-4

article_title: Evaluating the Dynamics of Learning Approaches: A Systematic Review Investigating the Nexus Between Teaching Methods and Academic Performance in Medical and Dental Education
citation: Marlen A. Roehe, Carmen Trost, Julia S. Grundnig, Anahit Anvari-Pirsch, Anita Holzinger. (2024). Evaluating the Dynamics of Learning Approaches: A Systematic Review Investigating the Nexus Between Teaching Methods and Academic Performance in Medical and Dental Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09952-4
title: Taxonomy of learning-approaches measurement inventories (SPQ, R-SPQ-2F, ASI, ALSI, ASSIST)
description: The review describes the family of questionnaires used to measure learning approaches: Biggs' Study Process Questionnaire (SPQ), whose strategic approach is termed the achieving approach; its revision, the R-SPQ-2F, which "uses fewer items to narrow in on solely the deep and surface approaches"; Entwistle and Ramsden's ASI with meaning, reproducing, achieving, and non-academic orientations; the ALSI, which "splits the strategic approach into organised studying and effort management"; and the ASSIST. The review notes "the ASSIST, alongside the R-SPQ-2F, is the most commonly used inventory for studying learning approaches."
requirements: Studies must use a questionnaire based on these existing inventories for the approaches to be measured comparably
constraints: The R-SPQ-2F predominantly focuses on deep and surface approaches, so the strategic approach is examined less extensively in studies using it
target_learners: higher education students, particularly medical and dental students
target_learning_goals: measuring students' deep, surface, and strategic approaches to learning
examples: In the review's sample, ASSIST and R-SPQ-2F were each used in 38.8% of the 49 studies

title: Systematic review evidence corpus: 49 studies of learning approaches and academic performance in medical and dental education (2000–2023)
description: A PRISMA 2020-guided, PROSPERO-registered (CRD42023474280) systematic review corpus of empirical, peer-reviewed studies published 2000–2023 on learning approaches and academic performance in medical and dental education. "This systematic search yielded a total of 859 publications" across eight databases, screened down to "Records included in systematic review (n = 49)". The corpus spans 26 countries, with the UK most represented (16.3%), and yielded "470 co-occurrences were observed between teaching methods, learning approaches, and academic performance". Quantitative studies were quality-appraised with an adapted MERSQI and qualitative studies with QualSyst.
