article_title: How Future Goals Enhance Motivation and Learning in Multicultural Classrooms
citation: Phalet, K., Andriessen, I., & Lens, W. (2004). How Future Goals Enhance Motivation and Learning in Multicultural Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review, Vol. 16, No. 1. https://hdl.handle.net/1874/23520
title: Foster internal regulation along with positive perceptions of instrumentality to make future goals motivate achievement in multicultural classrooms
description: The review's central design principle is that future goals motivate school achievement only under two conditions: students must perceive a clear positive connection between doing well in school and later success, and they must experience future goals as internally driven rather than externally imposed. As the authors state, "future goals will motivate achievement in multicultural classrooms, provided that schools and families succeed in fostering internal regulation along with positive perceptions of instrumentality." Schools and families are jointly addressed as the agents fostering these conditions.
requirements: Students must perceive a clear positive connection between doing well in school and success later in life
Future goals must be experienced as internally driven or self-set rather than externally controlled or imposed
constraints: The principle is derived from a review of largely correlational cross-cultural evidence, not from an intervention test
target_learners: minority and migrant students in multicultural classrooms
target_learning_goals: school engagement and achievement motivation
examples: The review draws on questionnaire studies measuring future goals, perceived instrumentality, and regulation among Turkish, Moroccan, and native students in Dutch high schools
key_sources: Phalet, K., Andriessen, I., & Lens, W. (2004). How Future Goals Enhance Motivation and Learning in Multicultural Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review, Vol. 16, No. 1. https://hdl.handle.net/1874/23520

article_title: How Future Goals Enhance Motivation and Learning in Multicultural Classrooms
citation: Phalet, K., Andriessen, I., & Lens, W. (2004). How Future Goals Enhance Motivation and Learning in Multicultural Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review, Vol. 16, No. 1. https://hdl.handle.net/1874/23520
title: Future time perspective theory: cognitive (instrumentality) and dynamic (incentive value) aspects connecting present task goals to distant future goals
description: The review's organizing motivational framework, drawn from Nuttin and Lens (1985) and De Volder and Lens (1982), holds that formulating goals in the distant future creates an extended future time perspective (FTP) that strengthens goal striving. The theory distinguishes two aspects: "the cognitive aspect of FTP refers to the instrumentality or utility value of immediate task goals to reach distant future goals, the dynamic aspect concerns the incentive value of more or less distant future goals." A longer FTP raises perceived utility of schoolwork and reduces the steepness of incentive discounting of delayed rewards. The review applies this framework to explain when future goals motivate minority students.
requirements: Distinguishing immediate task goals from delayed future goals
Perceived positive connections between present tasks and future goals
constraints: The effect of FTP extension on incentive value is curvilinear, smaller for goals in the very near or very distant future than for goals in the intermediate future
target_learners: secondary and vocational school students, including minority students in multicultural classrooms
target_learning_goals: achievement motivation, learning strategy use, and school performance
examples: De Volder and Lens (1982) found a positive correlation between Grade 11 students' total motivation and the length of their FTP; Creten et al. (2001) found positive correlations between perceived instrumentality of theoretical and practical courses and motivation in vocational schools
key_sources: Phalet, K., Andriessen, I., & Lens, W. (2004). How Future Goals Enhance Motivation and Learning in Multicultural Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review, Vol. 16, No. 1. https://hdl.handle.net/1874/23520

article_title: Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging
citation: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3
title: Productive disciplinary engagement: a situative framework and four design principles for fostering deep engagement
description: Productive disciplinary engagement (PDE), introduced by Engle and Conant, is both a situative framework for understanding engagement and a set of design principles. Engagement is characterized as "socially rich intellectual discourse, where students make substantive contributions, build on each other's ideas, attend to one another, and work toward advancing shared understanding of disciplinary content." Engagement is productive when students' ideas advance, generate new questions, and reveal confusion. The article treats PDE as central to redefining motivation as socially situated.
requirements: Disciplinary engagement must be both productive (problem-driven inquiry, epistemic agency) and accountable to disciplinary norms
constraints: Few studies have examined these frameworks with systematic attention to motivation
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students in disciplinary classrooms
target_learning_goals: Deep disciplinary engagement and productive discourse
examples: Engle and Conant's analysis of an extended fifth-grade discussion of whether orcas were whales or dolphins, drawn from the Fostering Communities of Learners curriculum
key_sources: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3

article_title: Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging
citation: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3
title: Four guiding principles for fostering productive disciplinary engagement
description: Engle and Conant proposed four guiding principles for fostering productive disciplinary engagement: "(1) problematizing content from each student's own viewpoint, (2) giving students authority to address these problems, (3) holding students accountable to each other and disciplinary norms, and (4) providing appropriate resources for accomplishing the first three." The article reports these have become among the most influential instructional strategies to emerge from situative perspectives, and that studies embodying the principles most strongly showed the strongest PDE outcomes.
requirements: All four principles must operate together; authority must be balanced with accountability
constraints: Too much authority and too little accountability leads students away from participation in the discipline
target_learners: Students in discussion-based disciplinary classrooms
target_learning_goals: Productive, disciplinary, and sustained engagement with content
examples: Engle's 2012 retrospective review of 23 PDE studies rated each study's embodiment of the four principles and associated outcomes
key_sources: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3

article_title: Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging
citation: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3
title: Expansive framing: a situative model of learning transfer built on authorship and intercontextuality
description: Expansive framing, advanced by Engle, is a situative model of learning transfer holding that transfer depends on how teachers and learners frame the boundaries of participation, not only on physical affordances and constraints. Engle argued that "when students were positioned as authors whose ideas were relevant beyond the immediate classroom, they perceived more affordances for applying their knowledge in future settings." The framework reframes transfer as social accountability and identity-building, with design principles concerning authorship, connections across time, place, and roles, accountability, and generalizing authorship across settings.
requirements: Teachers must invite students to author their own contributions rather than reproduce an authority's answers
constraints: Transfer depends on the relation between prior learning and the opportunities and constraints present in a new situation
target_learners: Classroom learners across grade levels
target_learning_goals: Generative learning that transfers readily and widely across contexts
examples: Engle's 2006 reanalysis of the PDE study recordings, examining student performance on a challenging far-transfer performance task after significant delays and interruptions
key_sources: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3

article_title: Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging
citation: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3
title: Introduce accountability gradually along an inside-out continuum from self to recognized authorities
description: The article describes an "inside-out" approach to accountability, drawing on Lampert's continuum of justification, as essential to motivating productive disciplinary engagement. "Learners begin by explaining why their ideas make sense to themselves, then share their reasoning with trusted peers, proceed to peers who offer greater intellectual challenge, and eventually present their ideas to recognized authorities within and beyond the immediate learning community." At each stage students strengthen and refine their thinking while maintaining ownership of their ideas.
requirements: The progression must be carefully timed so learners can compare their ideas with authoritative perspectives and revise
constraints: Accountability should be introduced gradually rather than imposed at full rigor from the start
target_learners: Students in discussion-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: Maintaining ownership of ideas while refining thinking against disciplinary standards
examples: The article's progressive accountability structure: self, then safe peers, then challenging peers, then recognized authorities across contexts
key_sources: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3

article_title: Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging
citation: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3
title: Situative synthesis: motivation as primarily a social phenomenon with individual accounts as special cases
description: The article contrasts aggregative reconciliation (exemplified by Bandura's collective efficacy as aggregated individual judgments) with Greeno's situative synthesis. Under the situative synthesis, "motivation is primarily a social phenomenon; individual experiences, theories, and measures are presumed to be secondary 'special cases' of activity that resides in social, cultural, and material contexts beyond individual participants." Organized activity, not individual beliefs, is the primary unit of analysis. The authors adopt this as an interventionist design argument rather than a naturalistic claim about the nature of motivation.
requirements: Study of individuals must include analysis of the meaning systems in which those individuals exist
constraints: The authors frame this as an interventionist argument about educational practice, not a naturalistic claim about the nature of motivation
target_learners: All learners studied through situative accounts of motivation
target_learning_goals: Understanding how goals and values emerge in learning environments and sociocultural contexts
examples: Greeno's 1997 response to Anderson, Reder, and Simon arguing the situative perspective can provide a broader framework that includes individual cognitive functioning but goes beyond it
key_sources: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3

article_title: Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging
citation: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3
title: Race-reimaged motivation research reconceptualizes belongingness around racial identity affirmation and cultural validation
description: The article reviews a strand of motivation research sparked by DeCuir-Gunby and Schutz that is race-focused and race-reimaged. In race-reimaged research, "belongingness is reconceptualized to account for racial identity affirmation, representation, and cultural validation." This recognizes that motivation is strengthened when students feel valued as members of racial, gender, and cultural communities whose histories and voices are respected. Critical race mixed methodology centers the lived experiences of racially minoritized students and integrates quantitative motivational measures with qualitative narratives.
requirements: Research must center lived experiences of racially minoritized students rather than deficit perspectives
target_learners: Racially minoritized students
target_learning_goals: Sustaining engagement and motivation through cultural validation and identity affirmation
examples: Gray et al.'s reconceptualization of belongingness cited by the article as an example of race-reimaged research
key_sources: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3

article_title: Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach
citation: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1
title: Motivation regulation as conscious, deliberate control of one's motivation, distinguished from motivational monitoring and from automatic underlying motivational processes
description: The review organizes the field around Wolters' (2003) definition of motivation regulation as "activities through which individuals purposefully act to initiate, maintain, or supplement their willingness to start, to provide work toward, or to complete a particular activity or goal". It distinguishes motivation(al) control (maintaining or changing motivation) from motivational monitoring (observing and becoming aware of one's motivational states and needs), and separates deliberate regulation from underlying processes such as causal attributions and value appraisals that occur more or less automatically. Recent definitions add a qualitative dimension: learners may lack not enough motivation but the right type of motivation, where task-motivation misfit can produce less efficient approaches and poorer performance.
requirements: Applies to learners' consciously and deliberately implemented thoughts and behaviors targeting underlying motivational processes, not automatic motivational states themselves.
constraints: The review notes the term is often used for the full monitoring-plus-control sequence but sometimes synonymously with motivational control only.
target_learners: school and university students studying in formal and informal learning contexts
target_learning_goals: initiating, maintaining, and supplementing motivation for studying and goal completion
examples: The review includes studies on interest regulation when defined as conscious action or thought to change one's own motivation, and excludes studies of motivation regulation styles from self-determination theory's organismic integration theory.
key_sources: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1

article_title: Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach
citation: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1
title: Motivation regulation strategies span interest enhancement, goal-based self-talk, proximal goal setting, self-consequating, environmental control, and use of social resources
description: The review enumerates the families of motivation regulation strategies documented in the literature: enhancing situational interest or personal significance (e.g., turning a task into a game), goal-based self-talk (mastery, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance self-talk), proximal goal setting (splitting large tasks into smaller, more easily reachable tasks), self-consequating (promising oneself rewards), environmental control (excluding distractions), and using social resources (joining fellow students for group studying). Strategies target different motivational experiences such as task value or success expectancy; for example, self-consequating targets extrinsic aspects of task completion while situational interest enhancement aims at intrinsic motivation.
requirements: Effective use requires procedural and conditional strategy knowledge about how strategies work and when they apply, and strategies must match the respective motivational problem.
constraints: Strategies need to be applied thoroughly in a qualitatively good manner, not merely frequently.
target_learners: school and university students regulating their own motivation for studying
target_learning_goals: enhancing, maintaining, or changing motivation for tedious or difficult learning tasks
examples: The review cites Schwinger et al. (2009) reporting correlations with effort expenditure for eight different motivational strategies, with a positive relationship for six strategies and no significant relationship for two.
key_sources: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1

article_title: Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach
citation: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1
title: Five research traditions overlap conceptually with motivation regulation: self-regulated learning, metacognition, emotion regulation, resource management, and volitional control
description: The review maps the conceptual neighborhood of motivation regulation, stating that "several broader research areas share conceptual overlap with motivation regulation—namely self-regulated learning, emotion regulation, volitional control, resource management, and metacognition". Within self-regulated learning, motivation regulation is one regulated domain alongside cognition, behavior, and context; metacognition covers motivation regulation when the object of monitoring and control is motivation; emotion regulation operates in parallel and in service of motivation regulation, with metamotivational feelings such as boredom or frustration linking the two; resource management includes motivation as an internal resource; and volitional control shields set intentions from competing desires. The review includes studies from these traditions when they explicitly reference motivational processes.
requirements: Inclusion requires an explicit reference to motivational processes when studies come from the intersecting traditions.
constraints: The review explicitly does not draw clear theoretical boundaries between motivation and emotion regulation, noting research has mainly been conducted in a siloed fashion.
target_learners: learners in formal and informal academic settings studied across these traditions
target_learning_goals: regulating motivation, emotion, cognition, resources, and intentions during learning
examples: The review excludes volitional strategies such as implementation intentions unless they clearly aim at building and maintaining intentions and goals for studying rather than shielding them.
key_sources: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1

article_title: Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach
citation: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1
title: Interactive evidence and gap maps of motivation regulation research, built with EPPI-Mapper, with the underlying dataset released on OSF
description: The review's central artifact is a pair of interactive evidence and gap maps built with the EPPI-Mapper tool. The maps are matrices in which "Larger 'bubbles' in cells represent larger numbers of studies available, while smaller or non-existent bubbles indicate absence of evidence", with bubble color indicating how motivation regulation was operationalized and clickable cells exporting the references of the studies concerned. One map plots educational settings, study designs, and motivation regulation contexts against variables examined, split by reported relation direction; the second maps the sources of knowledge (settings, designs, operationalizations) against contexts. Maps can be filtered by analogue versus digital settings, questionnaire type, and level of analysis.
requirements: The dataset for creating the maps is obtainable from the project's OSF page together with a tutorial on how to create one's own map.
constraints: Relation directions in the maps are summaries of relations reported in studies, not statistical aggregations of effect sizes.
target_learners: researchers, university and school teachers seeking overviews of motivation regulation evidence
target_learning_goals: rapid identification of existing evidence, gaps, and studies relevant to specific samples, methods, or contexts
examples: The preregistered search covered EBSCO, PubPsych, BASE, Web of Science, ProQuest, Scopus, Science Direct, Google Scholar, ERIC, dissertation databases, conference programs, and manual reference searches, yielding N = 289 included studies.
key_sources: Maike Trautner, Carola Grunschel, Malte Schwinger. (2025). Motivating Motivation Regulation Research—An Evidence and Gap Map Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10019-1

article_title: A Motivational Perspective on (Anticipated) Mental Effort Investment: The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat
citation: Tamara van Gog, Eva Janssen, Florence Lucas, Maaike Taheij (2024). A Motivational Perspective on (Anticipated) Mental Effort Investment: The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat. Educational Psychology Review (2024) 36:54. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09861-6
title: The biopsychosocial model of challenge and threat explains motivational antecedents of (anticipated) mental effort investment
description: The biopsychosocial model of challenge and threat (Blascovich, 2008) describes how challenge and threat motivational states arise in goal-relevant motivated performance situations. As the article states, "These resource/demand evaluations result in a challenge motivational state when the evaluation of resources matches or exceeds the evaluation of demands, and in a threat motivational state when demands outweigh resources". The authors propose it as a lens for cognitive load theory to explain why, in similar instructional conditions, some students invest effort while others do not, and they test it in four feedback-valence experiments.
requirements: A motivated performance situation: a goal-relevant situation requiring instrumental cognitive responses, leading to task engagement
Measurement of challenge and threat states, via self-reports or physiological measures
constraints: The model was, at the time of writing, not yet widely applied in educational research
target_learners: students in self-regulated learning contexts
target_learning_goals: understanding and explaining individual differences in mental effort investment
examples: Four experiments manipulated predominantly positive vs. negative (and no) feedback on CRT or weekday problems and measured challenge/threat, self-efficacy, and effort ratings
key_sources: Tamara van Gog, Eva Janssen, Florence Lucas, Maaike Taheij (2024). A Motivational Perspective on (Anticipated) Mental Effort Investment: The Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat. Educational Psychology Review (2024) 36:54. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09861-6

article_title: The Impact of Writing Instruction for English Language Learners in the United States: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Aitken, A. A., Graham, S., Cao, Y., & Nusrat, A. (2026). The Impact of Writing Instruction for English Language Learners in the United States: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10197-6
title: Writers-within-community (WWC) model of writing
description: The writers-within-community model holds that "writing takes place because of the reciprocal relationship between the writer's cognitive resources and the sociocultural context in which writing occurs". It positions the writer, with cognitive and linguistic resources such as attention, working memory, knowledge, and beliefs, as embedded in a layered system of community influences from immediate goals and tools to classroom norms and broader institutional forces. The model served as the theoretical foundation of this meta-analysis and guided how outcomes were grouped into constructs (transcription, translation, output, writing beliefs) and how treatments were coded as writer-focused, community-focused, or both.
requirements: Writing is understood as situated in a community context; analysis of writing instruction must account for both writer-side cognitive and linguistic resources and community-side influences such as classroom norms and institutional factors.
constraints: The article notes that practices found effective in other countries or contexts may not yield the same outcomes in U.S. classrooms, so evidence must be situated within the social, cultural, and institutional features of U.S. schools.
target_learners: K-12 English language learners in the United States
target_learning_goals: Writing performance, including writing quality, transcription, translation, output, and writing beliefs
examples: The meta-analysis grouped narrow measures (e.g., spelling, grammar errors, words written) into WWC-aligned constructs and coded interventions as targeting writer-focused processes, community-focused supports, or both.
key_sources: Aitken, A. A., Graham, S., Cao, Y., & Nusrat, A. (2026). The Impact of Writing Instruction for English Language Learners in the United States: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10197-6

article_title: Playful Study Design: A Novel Approach to Enhancing Student Well-Being and Academic Performance
citation: Costantini, A., Bakker, A. B., & Scharp, Y. S. (2025). Playful Study Design: A Novel Approach to Enhancing Student Well-Being and Academic Performance. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10022-6
title: Playful study design: a student-driven, two-dimensional construct of ludic (fun) and agonistic (competitive) play applied to academic tasks
description: The article defines PSD as "a proactive cognitive-behavioral approach that students use to infuse their academic tasks with enjoyment and challenge," positioning the student as the designer who creates the study experience. It comprises two dimensions mapped onto play theory: ludic play, involving "lightheartedness, humor, and imagination," and agonistic play, focused on "challenge, competition, and personal achievement." Unlike top-down gamification, PSD emphasizes self-initiated play integrated into study routines, and is distinguished from deliberate practice because it treats play as an approach to activities rather than an activity itself.
requirements: Students must have discretion over how they approach their study tasks, since PSD is defined as self-initiated and student-driven rather than instructor-imposed.
constraints: The article develops and tests PSD in university settings; the authors note structured, top-down play approaches can even backfire, citing a gamified course in which students felt less motivated over time.
target_learners: university students in higher education
target_learning_goals: study engagement
academic performance
student well-being
social integration
examples: Students may introduce fun by using humor, creating imaginative study tools, or developing engaging narratives, and may incorporate competition by setting personal goals, engaging in friendly competition with peers, or striving to surpass previous performance.
key_sources: Costantini, A., Bakker, A. B., & Scharp, Y. S. (2025). Playful Study Design: A Novel Approach to Enhancing Student Well-Being and Academic Performance. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10022-6

article_title: The Value of Using Tests in Education as Tools for Learning—Not Just for Assessment
citation: Dillon H. Murphy, Jeri L. Little, Elizabeth L. Bjork. (2023). The Value of Using Tests in Education as Tools for Learning—Not Just for Assessment. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09808-3
title: Desirable difficulties framework: challenges that slow apparent performance gains can produce long-lasting, transferable learning
description: The commentary organizes its argument around the desirable difficulties framework (Bjork & Bjork), under which learning strategies that "create challenges for learners" and initially slow apparent performance can ultimately produce "learning that is both long-lasting and transferable." It names four examples: spaced practice, contextual variation, interleaving, and testing/retrieval practice. Crucially, difficulty alone is not sufficient—what matters is whether the challenge induces the cognitive processes that enhance retention and understanding. The framework explains why learners and instructors are often tricked into preferring easier methods whose gains are superficial.
requirements: The difficulty must induce the type of cognitive processing that enhances learning, not merely make the task harder
constraints: Desirable difficulties can slow apparent performance gains and be misinterpreted as impairing learning
Students with prior academic success without desirable difficulties may resist changing their study approach
target_learners: students in high school and college courses
target_learning_goals: long-term retention and transfer of course content
examples: The commentary lists spaced practice, contextual variation, interleaving, and testing/retrieval practice as examples of desirable difficulties
key_sources: Dillon H. Murphy, Jeri L. Little, Elizabeth L. Bjork. (2023). The Value of Using Tests in Education as Tools for Learning—Not Just for Assessment. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09808-3

article_title: Still No Convincing Evidence for a Causal Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Reply to Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2025
citation: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Still No Convincing Evidence for a Causal Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Reply to Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2025. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10083-7
title: Reciprocal effects model (REM) of academic self-concept and achievement, including its extended RI-CCLPM-C operationalization
description: The REM consists of two claims: achievement affects self-concept (skill-development) and self-concept affects achievement (self-enhancement). Marsh et al. concluded both occur at different rates, with the achievement effect more or less instantaneous and the self-concept effect slower; this temporal dynamic is captured statistically by the constrained random-intercept contemporaneous and cross-lagged panel model (RI-CCLPM-C), which Núñez-Regueiro et al. call the "extended REM". This commentary challenges the empirical support for the self-enhancement component.
requirements: Longitudinal data on self-concept and achievement across multiple waves
A specified timescale structure matching the RI-CCLPM-C, which the authors argue was endorsed after evaluating only a limited set of models
constraints: The authors argue support for the REM appears sensitive to specific modeling choices, so the hypothesis should probably not be seen as corroborated

target_learning_goals: understanding the relationship between academic self-concept and achievement over time

citation: Kimmo Sorjonen, Bo Melin, Gustav Nilsonne. (2025). Still No Convincing Evidence for a Causal Effect of Academic Self-Concept on Achievement: A Reply to Núñez-Regueiro et al., 2025. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10083-7
title: Do not treat statistically significant cross-lagged effects with good model fit in observational SEM data as strong evidence of causality
description: The article argues that structural equation models reproduce covariances and correlations, and well-fitting models minimize the difference between reproduced and empirical correlations, but correlations do not prove causality. Statistically significant parameter values in SEMs fitted to observational data do not prove causality, not even if the model has good fit; the question of causality is more about how data were generated than about the structure of overlapping variance.
requirements: Causal questions should be addressed by how data were generated, e.g. observational versus randomized controlled trial designs
constraints: This inability to prove true causal effects from correlations in observational data is stated to be general to all structural equation models
target_learners: researchers analyzing longitudinal observational educational data
target_learning_goals: drawing valid causal inferences about self-concept and achievement relationships
examples: The authors note Núñez-Regueiro et al. partly agree, writing that causal directionality cannot easily be assessed

title: True causal hypotheses should survive testing with a broad set of different analyses; model-choice-sensitive support warrants suspended judgement
description: The authors report that the RI-CLPM and the LCSM (with a covariance between X at time T and subsequent change in X), as well as corresponding multilevel models fitted to person-mean centered scores, reached the same conclusion when applied to data with a known causal effect by construction. They argue that if support for a hypothesis is sensitive to specific modeling choices, as the REM appears to be, the hypothesis should probably not be seen as corroborated.

constraints: The article's robustness demonstration rests on data with a known causal effect by construction (adding stones in a container on the weight of the container), not on the self-concept data itself

target_learning_goals: judging when cross-lagged findings corroborate a causal hypothesis

article_title: Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model
citation: Elena Savina, Caroline Fulton, Christina Beaton. (2025). Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10018-2
title: Teacher emotional competence model of eight competencies in two groups (teacher-oriented and students-oriented)
description: The article proposes a conceptual model of teacher emotional competence organized into two groups of competencies: those related to teachers' own emotions and those related to students' emotions. As the abstract states, the eight competencies include "(1) understanding teachers' own emotions; (2) effective emotion regulation; (3) effective emotional communication; (4) maintaining teachers' emotional well-being; (5) understanding and responding to students' emotions; (6) utilizing emotions to promote learning; (7) utilizing emotions to foster positive relationships and emotional climate in the classroom; and (8) promoting students' social-emotional learning." Each competency is further delineated into discrete emotional skills, and the skills are described as building on and working in conjunction with each other, e.g., awareness of one's emotions supports regulation, which supports responding to students' emotions.
requirements: The model is grounded in integration of emotion, developmental, educational, and clinical research and in the identified emotional demands of the teaching profession
constraints: The model is a conceptual proposal intended as a springboard for training programs and assessment, not itself an empirically tested intervention
target_learners: pre-service and in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: using emotions for instructional and relational purposes
managing teachers' own and students' emotions
preventing emotional burnout
examples: Table 1 organizes the eight competencies into teacher-oriented and students-oriented columns

article_title: Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model
citation: Elena Savina, Caroline Fulton, Christina Beaton. (2025). Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10018-2
title: Distinction between emotional demands of teaching and demands for emotional skills, with teacher emotional work as an others-oriented construct
description: The review differentiates the emotional demands of teaching (job aspects requiring sustained emotional effort, such as emotional labor, dealing with anger, and disturbing situations) from the demands for emotional skills, which reflect the need to use those skills to achieve instructional, relational, and behavioral goals. A unique feature is that teacher emotional skills "serve not only teachers but students as well." Drawing on Strazdins's construct of emotional work, the authors state: "We conceptualize teacher emotional work as an intentional use of emotions to facilitate students' learning, enact effective behavior management, and promote positive relationships in the classroom." This distinction grounds the model's two-group structure.
requirements: Conceptualizing teacher emotional skills must capture the transactional and contextual nature of emotions in the classroom, per the Ecological Dynamic Systems framework
constraints: The distinction is a conceptual proposal by the authors, adapted from the Job Demands-Resources model and Strazdins's family-interaction construct
target_learners: pre-service and in-service teachers
target_learning_goals: understanding the emotional requirements of the teaching profession
examples: Emotional labor is discussed via Hochschild's definition as effort to conceal or fabricate emotions according to professional display rules

article_title: Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model
citation: Elena Savina, Caroline Fulton, Christina Beaton. (2025). Teacher Emotional Competence: A Conceptual Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10018-2
title: Use the teacher emotional competence model as a springboard for developing emotional training programs and guiding assessment of teachers' emotional skills
description: The article's forward-looking recommendation is that its conceptual model should drive the design of teacher emotional training and assessment. Because existing training targeted generic emotional skills without delineating how they meet the profession's emotional demands, the authors argue training should be calibrated to the eight profession-specific competencies and their discrete skills. As the abstract states, "The proposed model of teacher emotional competence can be used as a springboard to develop emotional training programs and guide assessment practices aimed at the evaluation of teachers' emotional skills." The model can inform teacher preparation, professional development, and evaluation of teachers' preparedness for the emotional demands of teaching.
requirements: Training should target the specific emotional skills pertinent to the teaching profession rather than generic emotional skills
constraints: The model itself has not been empirically validated as a training framework in this article
target_learners: pre-service teachers in teacher education programs
in-service teachers in professional development
target_learning_goals: developing teachers' emotional competence for instruction, classroom management, and well-being
examples: The review documents existing training studies of emotion identification, empathy, regulation, coping, and mindfulness as the evidence base the model would refine

article_title: The Role of Individual Differences in Sourcing: a Systematic Review
citation: Anmarkrud, Ø., Bråten, I., Florit, E., & Mason, L. (2022). The Role of Individual Differences in Sourcing: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09640-7
title: Documents model framework: source-content and source-source links constitute the intertext model
description: The documents model framework (Perfetti et al., 1999), built on Kintsch's construction-integration model, holds that readers of multiple documents represent both an integrated situations model of content and source information. The review explains that "the source-content links and the source-source links described above constitute the intertext model within the documents model framework", which is required to judge content in light of its source and understand relationships between sources. The framework grounds the review's expectation that disciplinary expertise influences intertext model construction.
requirements: A complete documents model requires the situations model to be supplemented and integrated with an intertext model
constraints: The framework was originally focused on reconciling accounts of historical events, later extended to other domains
target_learners: readers of multiple documents across educational levels
target_learning_goals: multiple document literacy
sourcing
critical reading
examples: The review traces the framework's origin to Wineburg's (1991) observation that expert historians attended to author, document type, and date before judging evidentiary value

article_title: The Role of Individual Differences in Sourcing: a Systematic Review
citation: Anmarkrud, Ø., Bråten, I., Florit, E., & Mason, L. (2022). The Role of Individual Differences in Sourcing: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09640-7
title: Integrated framework of multiple texts: four stance profiles differing in sourcing behavior
description: List and Alexander's integrated framework of multiple texts (IF-MT) describes preparation, execution, and production stages of multiple document use, with the preparation stage most important for individual differences. Readers adopt one of four stance profiles combining individual interest, attitudes, and multiple document proficiency: disengaged, affectively engaged, evaluative, and critical analytic. The review notes that "these four stance profiles are also assumed to differ in terms of their sourcing behavior", with evaluative and critical analytic readers sourcing frequently and only critical analytic readers using source information to reconcile conflicts. The review stresses these assumptions remain loosely grounded in evidence.
requirements: Stance adoption depends on combinations of individual interest, attitudes, and multiple document proficiency
constraints: The review states these assumptions "must be regarded as hypotheses that are fairly loosely grounded in empirical evidence"
target_learners: readers working with multiple documents
target_learning_goals: sourcing
source evaluation
content integration across documents
examples: Readers with high interest, strong attitudes, and low proficiency are assumed to adopt an affectively engaged stance and source infrequently

article_title: The Role of Individual Differences in Sourcing: a Systematic Review
citation: Anmarkrud, Ø., Bråten, I., Florit, E., & Mason, L. (2022). The Role of Individual Differences in Sourcing: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09640-7
title: Conflict-driven accounts of sourcing: D-ISC and CSI models
description: The review describes two specialized models of sourcing under conflicting information. The discrepancy-induced source comprehension (D-ISC) model proposes that "when readers encounter conflicting information about a particular topic or issue and thereby experience a break in situational coherence, they may strategically pay attention to source information". The content-source integration (CSI) model adds that readers lacking prior knowledge shift from asking "what is true?" to evaluating who presents claims. Both models imply individual difference roles for topic beliefs and prior knowledge, though the review notes their opposing predictions about knowledge remain to be clarified empirically.
requirements: Conflicting information or belief-content conflict that breaks situational coherence triggers strategic source attention
constraints: The review states that whether belief-content conflicts influence sourcing "is an issue for further research"
target_learners: readers of multiple conflicting documents
target_learning_goals: sourcing
evaluating conflicting information
restoring coherent understanding
examples: The CSI model implies less prior knowledge may be associated with more sourcing, whereas the IF-MT implies more knowledge increases sourcing

article_title: The Relation Between Students’ Effort and Monitoring Judgments During Learning: A Meta-analysis
citation: Martine Baars & Lisette Wijnia & Anique de Bruin & Fred Paas. (2020). The Relation Between Students' Effort and Monitoring Judgments During Learning: A Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09569-3
title: Cue utilization perspective with data-driven versus goal-driven self-regulation as an account of effort-based monitoring
description: The article organizes its synthesis around the cue utilization perspective (Koriat 1997), in which monitoring judgments are inferential and learners use cues such as perceived invested effort. Under the memorizing effort heuristic, data-driven self-regulation in self-paced learning produces a negative effort–monitoring correlation, whereas goal-driven self-regulation (incentives, time pressure, self-agency) can reverse or nullify it. The meta-analysis provides evidence for both processes: "learners tend to focus on data-driven self-regulation in which monitoring judgments are based on the amoun t of effort that was needed to learn the study material".
requirements: Effort and monitoring must be measured in the same trial for the same item or criterion task for the association to be observed
constraints: A significant positive correlation under goal-driven regulation was not obtained in the moderator analyses
Some studies report an inverted U-shaped curvilinear relationship that neither data-driven nor goal-driven accounts alone explain
target_learners: learners across grades 1–6, grades 7–12, and higher education
target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive monitoring during self-regulated learning
examples: The meta-analysis tested Hypothesis 1 (negative association) and Hypotheses 3a/3b (goal-driven manipulations) derived from this framework

article_title: A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research
citation: Felix Krieglstein, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Paul Ginns, Moritz Krell, Sascha Schneider. (2022). A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09683-4
title: Three-factor model of cognitive load: intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load additively contributing to overall load
description: Cognitive load theory stipulates three additive types of cognitive load: intrinsic cognitive load (the learning task's inherent complexity, determined by element interactivity and prior knowledge), extraneous cognitive load (determined by how learning materials are presented and organized), and germane cognitive load (working memory resources devoted to schema construction, a productive load). The article states that "Perhaps the best-known version of CLT stipulates three additive types of cognitive load" and that the three-factor model "was then developed by Sweller et al. (1998) in the mid- to late 1990s." The meta-analysis used this model because the most commonly used questionnaires measure the three types separately. Recent approaches suggest intrinsic and germane loads share the same theoretical foundation and can be classified as one type.
requirements: Questionnaires must measure the three load types separately with multiple items to assess the model empirically
constraints: The additivity assumption only applies if the capacity of working memory is not exceeded; recent approaches (Kalyuga, 2011; Sweller, 2010) propose an intrinsic-extraneous two-factor alternative
target_learners: learners in multimedia learning experiments across school and adult education
target_learning_goals: managing working memory load during multimedia learning
instructional design of learning materials
examples: The meta-analysis collected Cronbach's alpha values separately for ICL, ECL, and GCL following the three-factor model

Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09683-4

article_title: A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research
citation: Felix Krieglstein, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Paul Ginns, Moritz Krell, Sascha Schneider. (2022). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09683-4
title: Four frequently used multidimensional subjective cognitive load questionnaires (Eysink 2009; Leppink 2013; Leppink 2014; Klepsch 2017)
description: The meta-analysis examines four subjective cognitive load questionnaires that measure the cognitive load types separately with multiple items: the Eysink et al. (2009) six-item instrument (which also includes one item on perceived overall load), the Leppink et al. (2013) ten-item scale (three ICL, three ECL, four GCL items), the revised Leppink et al. (2014) version with added mental-effort items, and the Klepsch et al. (2017) instrument with ICL (two items), ECL (three items), and GCL (three items), which "is not specific to the learning topic and can therefore be easily adapted to the material used in a specific study." Across the meta-analysis sample, the Leppink (2013) questionnaire was used in 33 experiments, Leppink (2014) in seven, Klepsch (2017) in 20, and Eysink (2009) in 10.
requirements: Multiple items per load type so internal consistency can be calculated
For the Klepsch naïve rating, the authors recommend conducting a reliability test
constraints: The Klepsch GCL items "should be used with caution because of varying levels of under standings on the part of respondents"; the Leppink (2014) added mental effort items increased reliability of intrinsic and extraneous load factors, but not for germane load
target_learners: participants in experimental multimedia learning studies (mean age 20.4 years, 63.5% women)
target_learning_goals: measuring intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load during multimedia learning
examples: Klepsch et al. validated their instrument with an informed rating (students trained on CLT) and a naïve rating; the naïve rating is frequently used in experimental studies

citation: Felix Krieglstein, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey, Paul Ginns, Moritz Krell, Sascha Schneider. (2022). A Systematic Meta-analysis of the Reliability and Validity of Subjective Cognitive Load Questionnaires in Experimental Multimedia Learning Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09683-4
title: Use multi-item multidimensional cognitive load scales rather than single-item measures to enable reliability estimation and differentiation of load types
description: The article argues that measuring cognitive load with a single item, as in the popular Paas (1992) nine-point mental-effort scale, is psychometrically questionable because "a measuring instrument consisting of only one item makes it impossible to calculate internal consistency, an important indicator for an instrument's reliability." It further reports that measuring cognitive load without differentiating between the individual cognitive load types "seems to be insufficient when evaluating the effectiveness of multimedia learning environments or interventions." The principle therefore recommends multi-item scales targeting the load types separately.
requirements: Scales must include multiple items per cognitive load type so internal consistency can be calculated
constraints: Test-retest reliability is only valid for constructs stable over time, and cognitive load is dynamic in nature
target_learners: researchers and instructional designers evaluating multimedia learning environments
target_learning_goals: reliable and valid measurement of cognitive load types in experimental research
examples: The meta-analysis restricted inclusion to studies using the four multi-item questionnaires measuring all cognitive load types with multiple items

article_title: Socioeconomic Status and Student Learning: Insights from an Umbrella Review
citation: Tan, C. Y. (2024). Socioeconomic Status and Student Learning: Insights from an Umbrella Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09929-3
title: Expanded conceptualization of SES: objective and subjective, individual and collective, capital mobilization, asset-based
description: The umbrella review argues that researchers need to expand the conceptualization of SES from an objective, individual attribute measuring hierarchical differences in access to resources to a construct incorporating "objective and subjective evaluations of individual and collective SES attributes", emphasizing students' mobilization of capital, and adopting a diverse, asset-based perspective. It traces four shifts: adding subjective to objective indicators; recognizing collective attributes (school, neighborhood SES); shifting from access to resources to mobilization of capital (economic, cultural, social); and moving from a hierarchical, deficit perspective to an asset-based one (community cultural wealth).
requirements: Researchers should consider both objective and subjective SES indicators and both individual and collective attributes
constraints: The review notes subjective measures may be invalid due to mood, reference groups, or tendency to identify as middle class
target_learners: students from pre-K to university
target_learning_goals: understanding how socioeconomic status relates to student achievement and learning outcomes

article_title: Learning-by-Teaching Without Audience Presence or Interaction: When and Why Does it Work?
citation: Lachner, A., Hoogerheide, V., van Gog, T., & Renkl, A. (2022). Learning-by-Teaching Without Audience Presence or Interaction: When and Why Does it Work? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09643-4
title: Three proposed mechanism views of learning by non-interactive teaching: retrieval practice, generative processing, and social presence
description: The review organizes its account of why non-interactive teaching works around three not mutually exclusive explanatory views. The retrieval practice view treats explaining as a special case of retrieval; the generative processing view holds that explaining additionally triggers inference-making, organization, and elaboration; and the social presence view argues that the actual, implied, or imagined audience shapes the extent of generative processing. As the review states: "There are three (not mutually exclusive) main views that aim to explain the beneficial effects of learning by non-interactive teaching: (1) retrieval practice, (2) generative processing, and (3) social presence (of an actual/implied/imagined audience)." The social presence view is further decomposed into discourse pragmatics, affective (arousal), and motivational perspectives.
requirements: Empirical studies that experimentally compare non-interactive teaching with retrieval, self-explaining, or restudy conditions to test the mechanisms
constraints: The review notes most research did not explicitly or systematically test these different assumptions, so the evidence for each view is preliminary
target_learners: University students
Primary and secondary students
target_learning_goals: Deep comprehension and transfer of studied content through explaining it to an audience

title: Preliminary theoretical model of when and why learning by non-interactive teaching is effective
description: The review synthesizes its evidence on processes and boundary conditions into a preliminary theoretical model of when and why non-interactive teaching works. As the authors state: "We then synthesize the available empirical evidence on processes and boundary conditions to provide a preliminary theoretical model of when and why non-interactive teaching is effective." The model integrates the generative processing and social presence mechanisms with boundary conditions of modality, induced social presence, timing, teaching expectancy, prior knowledge, and ability beliefs, and is used to derive future research directions and recommendations for educational practice.
requirements: Studies implementing non-interactive teaching as an intervention with an experimental design and a peer-reviewed journal publication, per the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: The model is explicitly preliminary; the review states the available boundary-condition evidence should be considered preliminary because most studies did not explicitly test boundary conditions
target_learners: Students across age groups using non-interactive teaching as an individual study activity
target_learning_goals: Understanding and transfer of previously studied material through explaining it to an actual, remote, or imaginary audience

article_title: Contemplative Education: A Systematic, Evidence-Based Review of the effect of Meditation Interventions in Schools
citation: Lea Waters, Adam Barsky, Amanda Ridd, Kelly Allen. (2015). Contemplative Education: A Systematic, Evidence-Based Review of the effect of Meditation Interventions in Schools. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9258-2
title: School-Based Meditation Model
description: The School-Based Meditation Model is the review's conceptual framework linking school meditation programmes to three student success outcomes (well-being, social competence, academic achievement) through two mediating mechanisms: improved cognitive functioning and improved emotional regulation. It was built from three research strands: education research linking cognitive function and emotional regulation to outcomes, adult neuroscience linking meditation to relevant brain areas, and contemplative education studies showing students gain these functions. The authors state "The pathways in the School-Based Meditation Model are hypothetical", and it gives rise to two propositions about meditation increasing cognitive functioning and emotional regulation.
requirements: Future youth meditation research including neuroscience measures to test whether meditation affects students' brains as shown in adults
constraints: The pathways are hypothetical; no neuroscience research has been conducted in youth meditation samples, so the adult neuroscience link is described as an educated guess
target_learners: school students across junior, middle and senior schools
target_learning_goals: well-being
social competence
academic achievement
cognitive functioning
emotional regulation

article_title: The Need to Belong: a Deep Dive into the Origins, Implications, and Future of a Foundational Construct
citation: Allen, KA., Gray, D.L., Baumeister, R.F., & Leary, M.R. (2022). The Need to Belong: a Deep Dive into the Origins, Implications, and Future of a Foundational Construct. Educational Psychology Review, 34, 1133–1156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09633-6
title: The need to belong: desire for interpersonal attachments as a fundamental human motivation
description: The need-to-belong construct, originating in Baumeister and Leary's influential 1995 paper titled "The need to belong: Desire for interpersonal attachments as a fundamental human motivation," posits that the desire for interpersonal attachments is a fundamental human motivation. The article revisits this foundational construct through an interview with its originators to "explore the value and relevance of belonging for understanding human behavior and promoting well-being." It serves as the explanatory framework underpinning the article's review of belonging research in educational psychology.
requirements: Belonging research is interpreted through the construct of a fundamental motivation for interpersonal attachments
target_learners: students across educational settings
target_learning_goals: understanding motivation and interpersonal connection as bases of student well-being and academic outcomes
examples: The article interviews Emeritus Professors Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary, foundational pioneers in belonging research, reflecting on their 1995 paper

It functions as a primary reflective source on the origins, implications, and future of the belonging construct for educational psychology audiences.

article_title: School Belonging: Evidence, Experts, and Everyday Gaps
citation: Kelly-Ann Allen. (2025). School Belonging: Evidence, Experts, and Everyday Gaps. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10055-x
title: Integrative Framework of Belonging, extended for school contexts
description: The Integrative Framework of Belonging (Allen et al., 2021) organizes belonging around "four primary antecedents—perceptions, competencies, motivations, and opportunities—shaped by both systemic features and individual experiences". It was designed as a practical, non-prescriptive guide to address the how of fostering belonging for leaders, psychologists, and educators. This study extends it by showing school belonging is an ongoing, negotiated process also shaped by social hierarchies, variation in the need to belong, intersecting identities, and interpersonal, instructional, and institutional opportunities.
requirements: Requires synthesis of empirical, conceptual, and theoretical work on belonging within a unified structure, with flexibility to evolve as new knowledge emerges
constraints: The framework was never intended to be a prescriptive model; interviewees noted it gives limited attention to cultural and political contexts, historically colonized settings, structural and compositional aspects of schools, and social networks
target_learners: school students across primary, secondary, and higher education
target_learning_goals: fostering students' sense of school belonging to support motivation, wellbeing, and persistence
examples: Semi-structured interviews with ten internationally recognized scholars were organized around the framework's four antecedents and contextual, temporal, structural, and individual factors

article_title: A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity
citation: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9
title: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity (DSMRI): a two-level CDS model of motivated action
description: The DSMRI is a Complex Dynamic Systems model of identity, motivation, and action whose unit-of-analysis is the individual's situated role identity. It answers the question of why a particular person acts a particular way in a particular situation through two integrated levels: a sociocultural level, in which "a person generally acts according to the sociocultural role they occupy in a particular cultural activity system," and an individual level, in which different people in the same role construct idiosyncratic role identities as non-deterministic dynamic systems. Culture and individual are treated as two facets of a single emergent motivational phenomenon rather than independent construct sets. The model draws its sociocultural framing from Cultural-Historical Activity Theory and its individual-level content from Personal Investment Theory.
requirements: Requires conceptualizing the unit-of-analysis as the agent-within-her-sociocultural-situation rather than isolated individual constructs or activity structure alone
constraints: The article states the model's contribution is clarification of its conception of culture, not a comprehensive review of complexity theory or a catalog of motivational constructs
target_learners: Students in classrooms
Participants in professional-development programs
target_learning_goals: Understanding and explaining situated motivated action
Designing motivationally supportive educational environments
examples: The article uses the case of Maya, a high-achieving student who remains silent during a whole-class discussion of a contested historical event, to illustrate how the two levels integrate
key_sources: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9

article_title: A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity
citation: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9
title: Complex Dynamic Systems assumptions for an integrative motivation perspective
description: The article specifies CDS assumptions that allow motivational phenomena to be conceptualized as simultaneously individual and sociocultural: interdependence, irreducibility, and nonlinearity; dynamism, self-organization, emergence, and agency; attractor and repellor states; and control parameters, hierarchy, and self-similarity. The approach emerged "as an alternative to reductionist, deterministic, and linear cause-effect explanations, and which conceptualizes phenomena as holistic systems composed of interdependent, interacting elements." Agency is treated as a top-down process that co-acts with bottom-up self-organization, dissolving the dichotomy of automatic-unconscious versus agentic-conscious processes.
requirements: Research must identify the system's landscape of possible states and attend to behavior over time rather than averaging across diverse cases
constraints: The article cautions that because control parameters co-act interdependently, their influence cannot be understood by isolating or experimentally fixing them one at a time
Studies may foreground some system levels and background others while remaining cautious of conclusions of primacy
target_learners: All learners in culturally situated activity systems
target_learning_goals: Explaining situated motivated action
Reconciling stability and change in motivation
examples: The article illustrates nonlinearity with a minor change in task difficulty triggering sudden total disengagement, while an intensive program might yield only minimal effect
key_sources: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9

article_title: A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity
citation: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9
title: Culture in the DSMRI as a complex, dynamic, symbolically mediated cultural activity system integrating four perspectives
description: The DSMRI conceptualizes the sociocultural facet of motivated action as a complex, dynamic, symbolically mediated cultural activity system that frames the emergence of individuals' role identities, motivation, and action. It integrates four complementary perspectives: Maehr's conception of culture as collective meaning-making in context, symbolic interactionism's symbolic social structures and role identities, conceptions of culture as itself a CDS reflecting self-organization, nonlinearity, and micro–macro influences, and Cultural-Historical Activity Theory as the framing structure. The article states the four perspectives "converge on culture as a shared, hierarchically structured, dynamic system of meanings." CHAT's third-generation model contributes the six interrelated elements—subject, object, tools, community, rules, and division of labor.
requirements: Requires treating culture as a comprehensive system of shared meanings rather than reducing it to variables, artifacts, or behavioral scripts
constraints: The article notes the culture concept has a long history of jingle-jangle ambiguity, with the same term used for different phenomena
target_learners: Participants in culturally situated educational activity systems
target_learning_goals: Explaining how cultural activity systems frame role identity emergence
examples: The article draws on Serpell's three metaphors of culture—Womb, Language, and Forum—arguing cultures manifest all three simultaneously
key_sources: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9

article_title: A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity
citation: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9
title: Role identity content comprises four interdependent, partially overlapping conceptual categories
description: Building on Personal Investment Theory, the content of the role identity system comprises interdependent elements from four conceptual categories: ontological and epistemological beliefs, purpose and goals, self-perceptions and self-definitions, and perceived action possibilities, each with tied emotions. The article states that established motivational constructs are posited "as dynamic, situated and interdependent elements within this CDS rather than as independent predictors." The categories are not mutually exclusive—constructs such as self-efficacy lie at the intersection of multiple categories—and the particular construct salient within a component ebbs and flows across time, situations, and persons.
requirements: Each component comprises both role-related knowledge and the associated affect; emotion is the affect tied to all four components and their relations
constraints: The article notes the components' partial overlap means some established constructs are located at their intersections rather than within a single category
target_learners: Students
Teachers
Any agent occupying a sociocultural role
target_learning_goals: Explaining why a particular person acts a particular way in a particular situation
examples: Table 1 maps illustrative established constructs to each component, e.g., causal attributions and implicit theories under ontological and epistemological beliefs, achievement goal orientations under purpose and goals
key_sources: Avi Kaplan · Joanna K. Garner. (2026). A Complexity Perspective on Culture, Identity, and Motivation: The Dynamic Systems Model of Role Identity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10221-9

article_title: From Body to Word: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Embodied Vocabulary Learning
citation: Xiaoxuan Li · Julia Chatain · Fan Wang · Manu Kapur. (2026). From Body to Word: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis of Embodied Vocabulary Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10194-9
title: Design embodied vocabulary activities so learners' movements meaningfully align with target word meanings
description: The meta-analysis identifies movement-meaning congruency as the most robust moderator of embodied vocabulary learning: movements that transparently represent the semantic meaning of the target word (e.g., miming jumping when learning the verb jump) yield larger effects than arbitrary movements in both between- and within-subject designs. The authors conclude that "semantic alignment between movement and target word meanings is a key design feature of embodied vocabulary learning" and that congruency "should be considered as a key factor when developing embodied learning interventions."
requirements: Bodily actions must be physically performed by the learners themselves, not by teachers, robots, or pedagogical agents
constraints: The pooled effects may overestimate the true magnitude due to detected publication bias
target_learners: preschool children
primary school students
high school students
college students
adult language learners
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning
second and foreign language word learning
examples: In the included studies, congruent conditions included producing iconic gestures (Tellier, 2008) and acting out word meanings with full-body movements (Toumpaniari et al., 2015), whereas non-congruent conditions involved arbitrary hand movements or repetitive tapping patterns

article_title: Effective Strategies for Research Integrity Training—a Meta-analysis
citation: Johannes Katsarov, Roberto Andorno, André Krom, Mariëtte van den Hoven. (2021). Effective Strategies for Research Integrity Training—a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:935–955. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09630-9
title: Five-type taxonomy of research-integrity learning outcomes
description: The article organizes RCR training effects into five distinct learning outcome types: knowledge, attitude, sensitivity, judgment, and behavior. Its core methodological claim is that "approaches that support the achievement of one type of learning outcome of RCR may not be as helpful in achieving other learning outcomes", so effect sizes must be analyzed separately per outcome rather than pooled. The taxonomy draws on prior taxonomies of moral-domain learning outcomes and RCR learning objectives, and structures the entire moderator and meta-regression analysis.
requirements: Outcome measures must be classifiable into one of the five types, and effect sizes calculated separately per outcome type
constraints: Two originally planned categories (basic skills, bias awareness) were dropped for lack of instances; attitude, behavior, and sensitivity were pooled as orientational outcomes where heterogeneity was low
target_learners: high school students
university students and professionals below doctoral level
researchers and doctoral candidates
target_learning_goals: responsible conduct of research
ethical decision-making
research integrity knowledge and attitudes
examples: The meta-analysis calculated separate effect sizes for knowledge, judgment, and pooled orientation outcomes, finding large deviations between these outcome groups
key_sources: Johannes Katsarov, Roberto Andorno, André Krom, Mariëtte van den Hoven. (2021). Effective Strategies for Research Integrity Training—a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:935–955. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09630-9

article_title: Incoming Editor’s Editorial
citation: Fred Paas. (2015). Incoming Editor's Editorial. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9347-x
title: Journal articles in educational psychology should be clear and accessible for educational practice as well as rigorous
description: The incoming editor states a quality expectation for contributions to EDPR: articles should not stop at rigor but should also communicate in terms usable by practitioners. He writes that it is important that articles "not only emphasize theoretical and methodological rigor but also are clear and accessible for educational practice." This principle applies across all the article types the journal accepts.
requirements: Articles must meet theoretical and methodological rigor standards while remaining clear and accessible for educational practice.
target_learners: Educational psychology researchers and education practitioners reading journal articles
target_learning_goals: Communicating research findings so they can inform educational practice
examples: The editor applies this expectation to all submissions to the EDPR portal, whether reviews, meta-analyses, intervention studies, replications, essays, interviews, commentaries, or reflections.
