article_title: Strengthening Conscientiousness by Means of Interventions: A Systematic Review
citation: Melanie Turner, Flaviu A. Hodis. (2025). Strengthening Conscientiousness by Means of Interventions: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10016-4
title: Three-level personality hierarchy with bottom-up (and optionally top-down) change frameworks guiding conscientiousness interventions
description: The review organizes personality change around a hierarchy of trait, habit/habit-building, and state levels, noting that "Change can manifest at any of the three levels of personality hierarchy: trait, habit/habit-building, and states". Bottom-up frameworks (TESSERA; Sociogenomic theory) hold that accumulated changes in state expressions become habitual and integrated into self-concept, producing trait change; the General (Common) Change Factors model adds top-down processes via four mechanisms: discrepancy awareness, strengths orientation, insight, and practice. All 11 reviewed interventions used a bottom-up approach, and 55% also theorized top-down processes.
requirements: Interventions require theoretical grounding to identify specific targets (e.g., trait-relevant behaviors, habits, or state expressions) and to explain how state-level change leads to trait change
constraints: The review states that not all short-term changes in personality states lead to changes in the corresponding trait; only habitualized, integrated changes do
target_learners: general adults
university students
target_learning_goals: strengthening conscientiousness (industriousness, orderliness, impulse control) to support learning, achievement, and well-being
examples: The reviewed digital coaching interventions were guided by the General (Common) Change Factors framework; behavior activation interventions by Behavior Activation theory; in-person coaching by the Stepwise process, GROW model, and Intentional Change theory
key_sources: Melanie Turner, Flaviu A. Hodis. (2025). Strengthening Conscientiousness by Means of Interventions: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10016-4

article_title: The Transfer of Teacher Training to Inclusive Classroom Practice: A Meta-Analytic SEM Approach
citation: Donath, J. L., Lüke, T., Tran, U. S., Botes, E., & Goetz, T. (2025). The Transfer of Teacher Training to Inclusive Classroom Practice: A Meta-Analytic SEM Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10081-9
title: Five competing models of learning transfer from teacher training to classroom practice
description: The article synthesizes overlapping theories of teachers' learning in in-service training into five models of the transfer process: Knowledge-to-Practice, Knowledge-Skills-Beliefs, Reaction-to-Training, Practice-to-Belief, and Willingness-to-Change. Each model specifies a different central aspect and sequence — for example, Knowledge-to-Practice "assumes a serial succession from knowledge acquisition to improved classroom practices and student outcomes", while Willingness-to-Change models "assume that teacher training can enhance teachers’ willingness to change and professional knowledge by provoking ‘aha’ moments". The taxonomy served as the framework tested against pooled empirical data in the MASEM analyses.
requirements: Testing a model requires primary studies reporting correlations among at least two of the seven transfer variables (knowledge, skills, practices, beliefs, willingness to change, satisfaction, student outcomes).
constraints: The models were tested in the context of teacher training for inclusive education, with influencing factors such as training design and school context deliberately omitted to focus on the steps of the transfer process.
target_learners: in-service teachers participating in professional development on inclusive education
target_learning_goals: transfer of training content to inclusive classroom practice and improved student outcomes
examples: The article illustrates each model with a vignette, e.g. a teacher whose provocative training questions prompted willingness to try a new classroom-management approach
key_sources: Donath, J. L., Lüke, T., Tran, U. S., Botes, E., & Goetz, T. (2025). The Transfer of Teacher Training to Inclusive Classroom Practice: A Meta-Analytic SEM Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10081-9

article_title: Revisiting the Role of Worries in Explaining the Link Between Test Anxiety and Test Performance
citation: Schillinger, F. L., Mosbacher, J. A., Brunner, C., Vogel, S. E., & Grabner, R. H. (2021). Revisiting the Role of Worries in Explaining the Link Between Test Anxiety and Test Performance. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09601-0
title: German Test Anxiety Inventory (PAF) four-facet model of test anxiety
description: The PAF conceptualizes test anxiety as comprising three cognitive facets and one emotional facet. As the article states, "The PAF differentiates between worry, interference, and lack of confidence as cognitive facets and arousal as an emotional facet of test anxiety." Worry refers to concerns about a test and the consequences of failing; interference captures test-irrelevant thoughts experienced as distracting; lack of confidence refers to low confidence of performing well, similar to academic self-efficacy but specific to the test situation; arousal refers to bodily reactions such as a pounding heart. The 20-item questionnaire uses five items per subscale rated on a 4-point Likert scale.
requirements: Assessed via the 20-item PAF questionnaire with five items per subscale on a 4-point Likert scale, sum scores ranging 5 to 20
constraints: Lack of confidence items are positively formulated and item scores are inverted before scoring
target_learners: university students
secondary school students
target_learning_goals: assessment of test anxiety facets to identify students at risk of underperforming on tests
examples: In the present study, internal consistency was good for all subscales (arousal α = .85; worry α = .81; interference α = .84; lack of confidence α = .87), and low-to-medium correlations between the cognitive subscales confirmed they are distinct facets.

article_title: A Learning Patterns Perspective on Student Learning in Higher Education: State of the Art and Moving Forward
citation: Jan D. Vermunt & Vincent Donche. (2017). A Learning Patterns Perspective on Student Learning in Higher Education: State of the Art and Moving Forward. Educ Psychol Rev 29:269–299. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9414-6
title: The learning patterns framework: four components of student learning forming coherent patterns
description: The learning patterns perspective conceptualizes a learning pattern as "a coherent whole of learning activities that learners usually employ, their beliefs about learning and their learning motivation". The framework discerns four components: cognitive processing strategies, metacognitive regulation strategies, conceptions of learning, and learning motivations or orientations. Processing strategies lead directly to knowledge and skill; regulation strategies plan, monitor, steer and evaluate learning; conceptions are metacognitive views about learning; orientations encompass aims, goals, motives and worries. Four qualitative patterns recur: reproduction-directed, meaning-directed, application-directed, and undirected learning. The model is dynamic, with bidirectional relations between personal and contextual factors, learning patterns, and outcomes.
requirements: Measurement via an instrument operationalizing the four components, such as the ILS inventory with its processing, regulation, conception, and orientation scales
constraints: Learning patterns are conceived not as hard-to-change traits but as the result of interplay between personal and contextual influences; patterns are prototypical dimensions and not mutually exclusive
target_learners: students in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding and describing students' characteristic ways of learning (strategies, conceptions, motivations)
examples: The ILS scales define each pattern: e.g., the meaning-directed pattern combines deep processing, self-regulation, construction of knowledge conception, and personal interest orientation
key_sources: Jan D. Vermunt & Vincent Donche. (2017). A Learning Patterns Perspective on Student Learning in Higher Education: State of the Art and Moving Forward. Educ Psychol Rev 29:269–299. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9414-6

article_title: A Learning Patterns Perspective on Student Learning in Higher Education: State of the Art and Moving Forward
citation: Jan D. Vermunt & Vincent Donche. (2017). A Learning Patterns Perspective on Student Learning in Higher Education: State of the Art and Moving Forward. Educ Psychol Rev 29:269–299. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9414-6
title: Inventory of Learning Styles (ILS) measuring four components of student learning patterns
description: The ILS is the self-report instrument developed by Vermunt (1996, 1998) to measure the four components of student learning patterns on a larger scale: processing strategies (deep, stepwise, concrete), regulation strategies (self-regulation, external regulation, lack of regulation), conceptions of learning, and learning orientations. Its name was kept after the 2004 renaming of 'style' to 'pattern' to avoid confusion, though the authors note Inventory of Learning Patterns would have been a better name. A strong point is that "it was grounded in interview research with the target student population about their learning in natural, real-life settings".
requirements: Used with populations whose learning in natural, real-life settings informed its development; self-report instruments have limitations that should be matched to the purpose of measurement
constraints: As a self-report instrument it has limitations shared with other methods; the name retains 'styles' although the concept was renamed 'learning pattern'
target_learners: university and higher education students
target_learning_goals: measuring students' processing strategies, regulation strategies, conceptions of learning, and learning orientations
examples: The review's systematic search retained 44 learning pattern studies in which the ILS was used between 2004 and 2016

article_title: How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? Contrasting Traditional and New Methods to Investigate the Reciprocal Effects Model of Self-Concept and Achievement
citation: Hübner, N., Wagner, W., Zitzmann, S., & Nagengast, B. (2023). How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? Contrasting Traditional and New Methods to Investigate the Reciprocal Effects Model of Self-Concept and Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09724-6
title: Three assumptions for causal interpretation of cross-lagged panel models: consistency, strong ignorability, and positivity
description: Drawing on the Rubin causal model and potential outcomes, the article specifies the assumptions under which cross-lagged coefficients may be read causally. It states that "Usami et al. (2019a) outlined three assumptions that need to be satisfied in order for CLPMs to identify causal effects: (a) consistency, (b) strong ignorability/no unobserved confounding, and (c) positivity". Consistency ties observed outcomes to potential outcomes, strong ignorability requires all confounders to be measured, and positivity requires covariate overlap across treatment values. The article argues these are often unrealistic in REM research.
requirements: All potential confounding variables must be measured and adequately considered in the model for strong ignorability to hold.
constraints: The article notes positivity checks become increasingly difficult with continuous treatments and many covariates, and some authors argue the assumption might be very strong in practice.
target_learners: lower secondary school students
target_learning_goals: understanding causal relations between academic self-concept and achievement
key_sources: Hübner, N., Wagner, W., Zitzmann, S., & Nagengast, B. (2023). How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? Contrasting Traditional and New Methods to Investigate the Reciprocal Effects Model of Self-Concept and Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09724-6

article_title: How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? Contrasting Traditional and New Methods to Investigate the Reciprocal Effects Model of Self-Concept and Achievement
citation: Hübner, N., Wagner, W., Zitzmann, S., & Nagengast, B. (2023). How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? Contrasting Traditional and New Methods to Investigate the Reciprocal Effects Model of Self-Concept and Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09724-6
title: Three structural causal models of the self-concept–achievement reciprocal relationship, differing in lag-2 paths and confounders
description: The article derives a taxonomy of three structural causal models for the reciprocal effects model: "(a) a model with prior scores predicting post scores; (b) a model with additional lag-2 effects ... also referred to as a full-forward model; and (c) a model with lag-2 effects and additional confounders". Model (a) assumes no hidden confounders or carry-over effects and is judged unrealistic; model (c), including time-invariant and time-varying confounders such as gender or school track, "seems to be most realistic". The taxonomy determines which statistical model can identify causal effects.
requirements: If model (c) holds, confounders must be controlled for; otherwise CLPM and FF-CLPM coefficients are biased due to unconsidered confounders.
constraints: The article states model (a) is very (and probably overly) restrictive and seems unrealistic in the context of the REM.
target_learners: lower secondary school students
target_learning_goals: causal modeling of self-concept and achievement
key_sources: Hübner, N., Wagner, W., Zitzmann, S., & Nagengast, B. (2023). How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? citation: Hübner, N., Wagner, W., Zitzmann, S., & Nagengast, B. (2023). How Strong Is the Evidence for a Causal Reciprocal Effect? Contrasting Traditional and New Methods to Investigate the Reciprocal Effects Model of Self-Concept and Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09724-6
title: RI-CLPM separates within-person processes from time-stable between-person differences, relaxing strong ignorability for time-invariant confounders
description: The random intercept cross-lagged panel model, introduced by Hamaker et al. (2015), adds random intercepts to the CLPM from a multilevel perspective in which repeated observations are nested within individuals. Its advantage is that "it separates processes that take place within individuals from time-stable observed and unobserved differences between individuals". The article notes the RI-CLPM requires strong ignorability and positivity to hold only after controlling for time-invariant differences between individuals, but cites simulation work questioning whether it controls unobserved confounding.
requirements: Covariates must be assessed prior to the repeated measures when RI-CLPMs are specified with covariates.
constraints: The article reports simulation evidence that RI-CLPMs are not necessarily able to control for unobserved confounding and yield biased estimates if the true model includes lag-2 effects.

target_learning_goals: estimating within-person reciprocal effects of self-concept and achievement

citation: Gehlbach, Hunter. (2004). A New Perspective on Perspective Taking: A Multidimensional Approach to Conceptualizing an Aptitude. Educational Psychology Review 16 (3). https://doi.org/10.1023/B:EDPR.0000034021.12899.11
title: SPT as a multidimensional, situated aptitude with commitment and performance pathways
description: The article applies Snow's situated aptitude theory to social perspective taking, defining aptitude as the "degree of readiness to learn and to perform well in a particular situation or in a fixed domain". SPT aptitude has two pathways: a commitment pathway whose outcome is SPT propensity (how frequently students attempt perspective taking) and a performance pathway whose outcome is SPT ability (accuracy of inferring others' thoughts and feelings). Aptitudes develop through these pathways coalescing into an aptitude complex, and interact with a layered problem space of task and context.
requirements: Assessment of both propensity and ability simultaneously, since each pathway has a distinct measurable outcome
constraints: The article divides the situation into task-level and contextual-level factors only, omitting Snow's treatment layer because SPT is rarely taught in schools
target_learners: adolescents

conflict resolution

description: The article organizes research and hypotheses into a taxonomy summarized in Tables 1 and 2, structured so that moving left to right, perspective taking should be facilitated by increasing propensity and/or accuracy. Person-level factors include motivation and emotion regulation (commitment pathway) and cognitive level, strategy, and cognitive style (performance pathway). As the article states, "Students' SPT propensity and accuracy will vary according to seven aspects of these tasks: locus, decipherability, familiarity, temporality, reality, duration, and morality", plus two contextual features, cooperativeness and distractions.

constraints: Many cells of the taxonomy are explicitly hypothetical; the article notes no research has examined several associations, such as familiarity's effect on propensity

article_title: Prediction Versus Explanation in Educational Psychology: a Cross-Theoretical Approach to Using Teacher Behaviour to Predict Student Engagement in Physical Education
citation: Michael Noetel, Philip Parker, Theresa Dicke, Mark R. Beauchamp, Nikos Ntoumanis, Ryan M. Hulteen, et al. (2023). Prediction Versus Explanation in Educational Psychology: a Cross-Theoretical Approach to Using Teacher Behaviour to Predict Student Engagement in Physical Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09786-6
title: Prediction versus explanation as two cultures of statistical modelling in educational psychology
description: The article articulates a framework distinguishing explanatory from predictive statistical modelling. Explanatory approaches build parsimonious, theory-derived models to understand mechanisms, assessing fit on the same data used to build them; by contrast, "the predictive culture does not prioritise explaining the mechanisms underpinning a phenomenon: it instead optimises directly for accuracy on future data". The framework centres on overfitting — where a model predicts training data but fails to generalise — and holds that both approaches are needed, since prediction errors can point to gaps in explanatory models.
requirements: Assessing predictive validity requires data withheld from model building, so studies must reserve held-out test data
constraints: The article notes the approach is arduous if done prospectively, so a pragmatic alternative is quarantining retrospective test data
target_learners: educational psychology researchers
target_learning_goals: improving the predictive validity of models of student outcomes
examples: The authors applied the framework by training elastic-net models on 70% of their data and testing once on the held-out 30%

title: Test predictive models on held-out data not used in training, checking them only once
description: The article recommends that educational psychologists evaluate predictive accuracy on data never used to build the model. It states that "the least biased assessment of predictive models involves testing those models on new data, not used to train the model", and warns that checking test data more than once means learning from it and overfitting again. Researchers may use cross-validation or AIC to choose among competing models, then check the chosen model on unseen data once.
requirements: Reserve a portion of the data (the article used a 70% training to 30% testing split) that is never used for model building or tuning
constraints: More data held out for testing means less data for building models, so models themselves may fit the general population more poorly
target_learners: educational psychology researchers
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of how well models generalise to new data
examples: In this study, elastic-net hyperparameters were tuned on training data and predictive validity was assessed once on the held-out 30%

description: A reproducible list of teacher behaviours hypothesised by four motivational theories, created through a systematic binning and winnowing protocol. From 111 papers the authors sourced 49 unique scales containing 1151 candidate items, binned them into 61 categories, and winnowed to exemplars, ending with 69 unique behaviours plus two idealised-influence perception items. The article reports "our final list included 71 unique behaviours, 68 related to a psychological need in self-determination theory, 47 of which were characteristic of a leadership style in transformational leadership theory".

title: Cross-theoretical integration of four motivational theories of teacher influence on engagement
description: The article synthesises four theories of how teachers improve student engagement: self-determination theory, achievement goal theory, growth mindset theory, and transformational leadership theory. SDT hypothesises three basic psychological needs — competence, autonomy, and relatedness — whose fulfilment leads to optimal motivation and engagement. Achievement goal theory holds that "students with mastery goals... will be more engaged than those who have performance goals". Growth mindset theory recommends praising effort and improvement rather than ability, and transformational leadership theory describes leaders who empower followers beyond their own self-interests. The framework treats these as overlapping and competing sources of behavioural predictions to be assessed simultaneously.
requirements: A mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive list of theory-recommended behaviours so each theory's predictions can be assessed simultaneously
constraints: The theories overlap — all four emphasise improvement-oriented specific feedback — creating empirical redundancy and jingle-jangle problems the integration must manage

description: The article describes Zimmerman's cyclical phase model of SRL as his most enduring theoretical contribution. It articulates three interrelated phases that "operate recursively as learners plan, execute, and evaluate their actions": forethought, performance, and self-reflection. The model gave researchers a structured lens for investigating SRL mechanisms and gave educators a basis for designing interventions that foster strategic, motivated, independent learners, framing SRL as central to academic success and lifelong learning.

citation: Alexander S. Browman. (2025). Centering Social Fit, Self-Concept Fit, Goal Fit, and Resource Fit as Core Elements of Students' Experiences of Belonging at School. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10009-3
title: Four-fit model of students' experiences of belonging in school (social, self-concept, goal, and resource fit)
description: The article proposes that when students report feeling they do or do not belong at school, their experience hinges on four forms of person-environment fit: "social fit", "goal fit", "self-concept fit", and "resource fit". The model extends Schmader and Sedikides' State Authenticity as Fit to Environment (SAFE) model, adding resource fit as a fourth form. Belonging is framed as the cumulative result of whether students currently experience the four associated fluencies in that environment, and the model is illustrated in Figure 1.
requirements: The model presupposes students have a clear sense of their true self-concept, since the article notes a metacognitive prerequisite of authentic self-awareness for experiencing fit or non-fit
constraints: The article states the model focuses on state (versus trait) authenticity, and does not extensively explore the distinction between social fit with peers versus with teachers
target_learners: students at all levels of education, especially those from historically under-researched or marginalized backgrounds
target_learning_goals: students' sense of belonging at school and its relation to academic motivation and performance

title: Four fluency experiences (interpersonal, motivational, being-cognition, need-cognition) as precursors of belonging
description: Building on the SAFE model, the article proposes that each form of fit promotes its own unique experience of fluency: social fit yields interpersonal fluency, goal fit yields motivational fluency, self-concept fit yields being-cognition fluency, and the newly proposed resource fit yields need-cognition fluency, in which students can devote mental and temporal bandwidth to schoolwork without tending to unmet needs. These fluencies are proposed to be "precursors to a more gestalt sense of being authentic", and the article argues they cumulatively constitute students' phenomenological experience of belonging.
requirements: Each fluency is proposed to arise only when the corresponding form of fit is experienced in the academic environment
constraints: The fluency mechanisms are proposed theoretically; the article notes psychological research on belonging has generally not examined the majority of these proposed factors
target_learners: students in academic environments
target_learning_goals: academic motivation, effort investment, and performance

title: Classroom ecological model of ECEC quality as co-created by educator, child, and collective of children
description: The article proposes a classroom ecological model (Fig. 1) in which ECEC quality is the product of a reciprocal, bidirectional relationship: educators, each child, and the collective of children co-create quality. In contrast to ecological models treating community and family as distal influences, the authors propose these experiences "enter the classroom with the two key players in the educational relation -ship", so the differing social circumstances and learning experiences of child and educator determine both child requirements and educator capacity to respond. The model reframes quality as relational rather than a property of educator inputs alone.
requirements: Measurement and research designs must be capable of capturing both child requirements and educator capacity, rather than educator actions alone
constraints: The model is presented as a hypothesis about contextual factors determining quality, depicted in Fig. 1 and adapted from Thorpe et al. (2021), not as a tested model in this article

target_learning_goals: Interactional quality supporting constrained curriculum content and unconstrained skills such as emotion regulation, getting on with others, and learning to learn
examples: The article contrasts the model with standard measures: in CLASS-PreK's Instructional Support domain, three of four dimension descriptors commence with the phrase "the teacher (action)…" while only one focuses on educator-child interaction

title: Proportionate universalism: universal ECEC access with greater intensity of resourcing for services experiencing higher complexity and educator demand
description: The article proposes proportionate universalism (citing Marmot, 2025) as a policy mechanism for equitable ECEC: all children receive access to ECEC services, but services experiencing higher levels of complexity and educator demand receive greater intensity of resourcing. article_title: Enhancing the Peer-Feedback Process Through Instructional Support: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Hornstein, J., Keller, M. V., Greisel, M., Dresel, M., & Kollar, I. (2025). Enhancing the Peer-Feedback Process Through Instructional Support: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10017-3
title: Two-dimensional framework for classifying instructional support in peer-feedback: phase (provision vs. reception) and specificity (content-specific vs. generic)
description: The article proposes two orthogonal ways to differentiate instructional support in peer-feedback scenarios. The first distinguishes support by the phase in which it is presented — feedback provision vs. feedback reception — within the five-phase peer-feedback process (design, task performance, provision, reception, evaluation). The second distinguishes support by specificity: content-specific support focuses on "the application of specific knowledge in a selected subject area", whereas generic support assists students independently of content, e.g. prompting feed up, feed back, and feed forward. The meta-analysis applies both categorizations to estimate differential effects.
requirements: Peer-feedback scenarios in which a control condition receives peer-feedback without the instructional support being evaluated, so effects can be attributed to the support alone
constraints: The two categorizations are orthogonal: the same presentation mode (rubrics, questions, sentence starters) can be either content-specific or generic
target_learners: School students
University students
target_learning_goals: Providing high-quality peer-feedback
Processing and using received peer-feedback
Acquiring subject-matter-related knowledge
examples: The meta-analysis coded each included study's support by phase and by specificity, then pooled effects separately for each cell, e.g. generic support during feedback provision on subject-matter-related knowledge.
key_sources: Hornstein, J., Keller, M. V., Greisel, M., Dresel, M., & Kollar, I. (2025). Enhancing the Peer-Feedback Process Through Instructional Support: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10017-3

article_title: Enhancing the Peer-Feedback Process Through Instructional Support: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Hornstein, J., Keller, M. V., Greisel, M., Dresel, M., & Kollar, I. (2025). Enhancing the Peer-Feedback Process Through Instructional Support: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10017-3
title: Integrate instructional support into peer-feedback scenarios, prioritizing the feedback provision phase
description: Based on the meta-analytic findings, the authors recommend that practitioners integrate instructional support into peer-feedback processes, with the strongest and most consistent evidence for support presented during the feedback provision phase. They state that "increasing its effectiveness by almost one half of a standard deviation through the integration of instructional support is definitely notable and strongly suggests that it is worthwhile for practitioners to ponder about including further instructional support in the peer-feedback process". Generic provision support is the only type that also improved subject-matter-related knowledge.
requirements: A peer-feedback activity in which learners exchange task-related feedback on each other's task solutions, with a condition receiving the support and a comparable condition not receiving it
constraints: Evidence for supporting the feedback reception phase is too limited to interpret; effects on subject-matter-related knowledge were significant only for generic provision support
target_learners: School students
University students
target_learning_goals: Quality of peer-feedback messages
Use of received feedback in revisions
Subject-matter-related knowledge
examples: Across the 32 included studies, support during feedback provision (e.g. rubrics, sentence starters, guiding questions, preparatory activities) was compared against unsupported peer-feedback, yielding g = 0.51 overall for provision support.

article_title: Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education
citation: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y
title: AI-GLM framework for generative learning in AI-mediated mathematics education
description: The AI-Enhanced Generative Learning in Mathematics (AI-GLM) framework is a conceptual framework specifying how generative AI reshapes the conditions of Wittrock's generative learning theory in mathematics. The article states: "I propose the AI-Enhanced Generative Learning in Mathematics (AI-GLM) framework, which identifies three roles AI can occupy in relation to learners' generative processes". It comprises a three-role typology, a role determination mechanism combining tool design, task design, learner orientation, and teacher mediation, and five design principles, with propositions stated with operationalizations and falsification conditions.
requirements: Propositions require operationalizations and falsification conditions for empirical testing, as the article states
constraints: The framework is developed for mathematics learning specifically, addressing its representational, symbolic, and justificatory demands
target_learners: mathematics learners in AI-mediated learning environments
target_learning_goals: generative learning and deep mathematical understanding
examples: The framework was derived by coding each of the eight generative learning strategies for the cognitive process affected, the direction of change, and the condition of dependence, retaining themes supported by more than one form of generative work
key_sources: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y

article_title: Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education
citation: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y
title: Three roles of AI in generative learning: Generation Partner, Generation Substitute, Generation Catalyst
description: A typology of three roles AI can occupy relative to learners' generative processes. Partner and Substitute occupy the poles of a scaffolding–substitution continuum, while Catalyst is defined functionally: "When AI serves as a Generation Catalyst, it neither performs the learner's generative work, as in the Substitute role, nor supports the learner in performing it, as in the Partner role. It supplies an output that becomes the object of further generative work by the learner". Roles are properties of episodes, not tools, determined by tool design, task design, learner orientation, and teacher mediation.
requirements: Catalyst episodes require three jointly necessary conditions: an AI artifact the task does not treat as the answer, learner activity directed at that artifact, and activity required only because the artifact is present
constraints: Within an episode the three roles are mutually exclusive; extended interactions move among roles as trajectories
target_learners: mathematics learners using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: sustaining learner generative cognitive engagement under AI mediation
examples: Catalyst configurations include teaching a concept to an AI and evaluating its performance, instructing the AI to find counterexamples to a learner-generated claim, and co-constructing problems by iteratively refining conditions and constraints
key_sources: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y

article_title: Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education
citation: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y
title: Scaffolding–substitution continuum as the principal analytical axis of AI-mediated generative activity
description: The continuum locates any AI use that supports or replaces an existing generative activity between two poles: "AI use falls along a continuum from scaffolding (supporting the learner's own generative activity) to substitution (performing that activity in place of the learner)". Where a use falls is not a fixed property of the tool but a function of task design, instructional context, and teacher guidance, placing the teacher's pedagogical reasoning at the center of whether AI enhances or undermines generative learning. The continuum defines the Partner and Substitute roles but does not encompass the Catalyst role.
requirements: Position on the continuum should be analyzed as a continuous variable, with any descriptive cut point preregistered and accompanied by a sensitivity analysis
constraints: Does not encompass the Catalyst role, which is distinguished by a functional criterion rather than position on the continuum
target_learners: mathematics learners and teachers designing AI-integrated instruction
target_learning_goals: preserving learner generative cognitive engagement
examples: Role assignment is coded from the task specification and interaction record: a prior learner attempt plus a high learner share of submitted work places an episode near the Partner pole; absence of both places it near the Substitute pole
key_sources: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y

article_title: Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education
citation: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y
title: Role determination mechanism: task design, tool design, learner orientation, and teacher mediation
description: The mechanism specifies how four factors combine to determine which AI role obtains in a given episode. "Task design is logically prior: it designates which generative work is the target and thereby fixes the referent against which a role is defined". Tool and task design jointly establish an opportunity structure; learner orientation is the proximal determinant selecting among permitted assignments; teacher mediation is distal, operating through the other three. Learner expertise and instructional context moderate the weights.
requirements: Role assignment must be identifiable independently of the learning outcome, from the task specification and the interaction record, for the framework's predictions to be falsifiable
constraints: In unsupervised settings such as homework, tool defaults and learner orientation dominate; where activity is supervised and teacher-designed, task design and teacher mediation dominate
target_learners: mathematics learners across expertise levels; teachers mediating AI use
target_learning_goals: predicting and steering AI role assignment in instructional episodes
examples: A task asking students to explain why the quadratic formula works and then test that explanation against AI output makes the explanation the target and the AI output an object of evaluation, a Catalyst assignment
key_sources: Hoyun Cho. (2026). Relocating the Locus of Generation: The AI-GLM Framework for Generative Learning in AI-Mediated Mathematics Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10210-y

article_title: Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data
citation: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7
title: Large-scale assessments reverse the individual-measurement logic: population distributions are modeled first and student scores generated from them
description: The article articulates an epistemic framework contrasting two measurement traditions. In the psychoeducational tradition, individual students' minds are 'upstream from all other patterns we observe', with population inferences extrapolated from reliable individual scores. Large-scale assessments reverse this: 'modeling population distributions as conditioned on student background variables first and then generating student test scores'. The framework organizes the paper's comparison of what each data type can validly support.
requirements: Analysts must understand which measurement tradition a dataset comes from before choosing analytic procedures
constraints: The framework applies to performance-assessment aspects of large-scale assessments; self-report questionnaires are less affected by planned missingness at the item level
target_learners: educational researchers and secondary analysts of assessment data
target_learning_goals: understanding valid inference from large-scale assessment data
examples: Table 1 of the article contrasts individual measures and large-scale assessments across dimensions such as construct coverage, score type, and level of valid inference
key_sources: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7

article_title: Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data
citation: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7
title: Matrix sampling with planned missingness in large-scale assessments (e.g., PISA testlets counterbalanced across students)
description: Large-scale assessments organize items into testlets counterbalanced across students within a sampling frame, so that 'no student ever takes the entire battery of assessments, or even all the items on any one test'. In PISA, 'each student participates for 2 h, seeing only a fraction of the total set of test items', and for optional domains many students see no items yet still receive PVs. This design makes individual-level scoring from item responses impossible and necessitates the PV methodology.
requirements: A scoring methodology that models population distributions rather than individual item-response-based scores
constraints: Planned missingness primarily affects performance testing; background questionnaires are typically more completely responded to, though PISA has begun incorporating planned missingness there too
target_learners: students participating in population-level educational monitoring
target_learning_goals: monitoring educational systems at the population level
examples: PISA 2022 used a balanced incomplete block design; a full battery would take up to 15 hours, so students respond for 2 hours
key_sources: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7

article_title: Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data
citation: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7
title: Account for both sampling and imputation error when analyzing plausible values, using weights and Rubin's rules
description: The article recommends that secondary analysts of PVs weight student observations to restore population representativeness, repeat each analysis separately across all PVs (usually 5 to 10), and aggregate results using Rubin's rules with replicate-weight variance estimation. Without these steps, analysts 'risk underestimating the amount of uncertainty in their findings', which can lead to overstated claims.
requirements: Use the representation weights provided in publicly available datasets; perform each analysis separately per PV and aggregate with Rubin's rules; include replicate weights for sampling uncertainty
constraints: PVs cannot simply be averaged to produce an overall score for a student, a common misconception the article identifies
target_learners: educational researchers conducting secondary analysis of large-scale assessment data
target_learning_goals: valid population-level statistical inference from PV data
examples: TIMSS and PIRLS use Jackknife Repeated Replication methods and PISA uses Fay-adjusted Balanced Repeated Replication to produce replicate weights included in public datasets
key_sources: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7

article_title: Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data
citation: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7
title: Make inferences from plausible values only at the population level, conditional on the assessment design
description: The article's central recommendation: with large-scale assessment data, 'inferences are only possible at the population-level—and then only when framed as conditional on the assessment design and assumptions—not at the level of individual students'. Findings can inform system-level policy decisions but not classroom-level instructional decisions about individual students.
requirements: Analyses must correctly incorporate the sampling design and the multiple-imputation logic for PVs before any population-level inference is valid
constraints: Reporting percentages of students above or below a threshold is invalid because a student having low PVs does not necessarily imply they even took the assessment in question
target_learners: educational psychologists and policy researchers using secondary assessment data
target_learning_goals: drawing valid inferences about population distributions of academic abilities
examples: It is valid to say a population average is higher or lower from one wave to the next or across countries, but not to extrapolate that a different percentage of students scored poorly
key_sources: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7

article_title: Theories of Motivation in Education: an Integrative Framework
citation: Detlef Urhahne · Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Theories of Motivation in Education: an Integrative Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09767-9
title: Integrative action-model framework with six stages of motivated action
description: The article proposes an integrative framework for six major motivation theories grounded in the Heckhausen and Heckhausen action model. The basic model is "deliberately parsimonious, consisting of six stages of action: the situation, the self, the goal, the action, the outcome, and the consequences." Motivational constructs from expectancy-value, social cognitive, self-determination, interest, achievement goal, and attribution theory are mapped onto these stages, revealing "differences and to a lesser extent commonalities." The model builds on the Rubicon model of action phases and treats motivated behavior as arising from person-environment interaction.
requirements: The framework requires mapping each theory's constructs onto the six action stages to compare theories against a common background
constraints: The article states the model is intentionally parsimonious and that the situation, though the overarching context, is depicted by only one box
target_learners: students in educational settings
target_learning_goals: understanding and predicting the direction, initiation, intensity, and persistence of learning behaviors
examples: The article maps situated expectancy-value theory, social cognitive theory, self-determination theory, interest theory, and the 3x2 achievement goal model onto the six-stage model in separate figures
key_sources: Detlef Urhahne · Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Theories of Motivation in Education: an Integrative Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09767-9

article_title: Theories of Motivation in Education: an Integrative Framework
citation: Detlef Urhahne · Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Theories of Motivation in Education: an Integrative Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09767-9
title: Situated expectancy-value theory with three value beliefs and three costs
description: The review describes situated expectancy-value theory (Eccles & Wigfield) as a modern framework in which expectancy of success and subjective task values are proximal explanatory factors shaped by goals, self-schemas, and sociocultural background. The article states that "The value component of the situated model is divided into three types of value beliefs and three types of costs that contribute to approaching or avoiding certain tasks." Value beliefs are attainment, intrinsic, and utility value; costs are opportunity, effort, and emotional costs. In the action model, expectation of success links self to outcome, and the values and costs attach to different stages.
requirements: Expectancy and value beliefs are assumed to jointly predict achievement-related choices and performance
constraints: The article notes the earlier Atkinson assumption of an inverse relation between expectancy and value was not tenable
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students
target_learning_goals: explaining and predicting achievement-related choices and behavior
examples: The article locates opportunity costs at the goal, effort costs at the action, and emotional costs at the anticipated consequences within the action model
key_sources: Detlef Urhahne · Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Theories of Motivation in Education: an Integrative Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09767-9

article_title: Shunned and Admired: Montessori, Self-Determination, and a Case for Radical School Reform
citation: Angeline S. Lillard. (2019). Shunned and Admired: Montessori, Self-Determination, and a Case for Radical School Reform. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09483-3
title: Self-determination as Montessori's central premise, with evidence-based corollaries
description: This framework holds that Montessori's central premise is independence or self-determination, from which several research-aligned features follow as natural corollaries: free choice, interesting work (aided by embodied cognition and interconnection), deep concentrated attention developing executive function, intrinsic rather than extrinsic rewards, warm teacher–child relationships, and natural peer engagement in an orderly environment. The article states that "self-determination requires that children choose their own activities" and maps these prerequisites and consequences in Fig. 2, arguing each is supported by educational psychology research.
requirements: Children must be able to choose their own activities in a prepared environment for self-determined learning to occur
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretive alignment framework, not a directly tested causal model
target_learners: children from birth to 18
target_learning_goals: intrinsic motivation
executive function
academic and social–emotional development
examples: The article maps the corollaries in Fig. 2: interesting work, embodied cognition, interconnected work, intrinsic rewards, work with peers in 3-year age groups, teacher warmth and direction, and order and organization
key_sources: Angeline S. Lillard. (2019). Shunned and Admired: Montessori, Self-Determination, and a Case for Radical School Reform. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09483-3

article_title: Shunned and Admired: Montessori, Self-Determination, and a Case for Radical School Reform
citation: Angeline S. Lillard. (2019). Shunned and Admired: Montessori, Self-Determination, and a Case for Radical School Reform. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09483-3
title: The Montessori education system (birth to 18)
description: Montessori is a system of education for children from birth to 18, developed by an Italian physician through observations between 1890 and 1952. It involves "3-year age groupings (0 –3, 3 –6, and so on)" with carefully developed apparatus for each age group, an interconnected network of materials across all curriculum areas, and a teacher whose role is not to impart information but to connect children to an environment where self-guided learning occurs. Its central premise is that children are active learners with intrinsic motivation who develop themselves when adults do not interfere and they can concentrate on meaningful work.
requirements: AMI-recognized implementations require AMI-trained teachers, a full set of approved materials, specific age divisions, 3-hour morning and 2–3-hour afternoon work periods, and one trained teacher with 24–35 children per class
constraints: Implementation quality varies significantly (Daoust 2004), particularly outside stricter AMI-recognized implementations
target_learners: children from birth to age 18, including atypically developing children and children of low-income families
target_learning_goals: independence and self-determination
academic achievement across language, math, geometry, science, geography, music, art, and practical life skills
social–emotional development
examples: The article describes the system's 3-year age groupings, interconnected apparatus across curriculum areas, and teachers presenting individual lessons meeting successive developmental needs
key_sources: Angeline S. Lillard. (2019). Shunned and Admired: Montessori, Self-Determination, and a Case for Radical School Reform. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09483-3

article_title: Long-Term Effects of an Intervention Targeting Dimensional and Temporal Comparisons on Students’ Math and English Academic Self-Concepts: A Waiting-List Replication and Extension Study
citation: Hörsch, H., Schumacher, J., & Wolff, F. (2026). Long-Term Effects of an Intervention Targeting Dimensional and Temporal Comparisons on Students' Math and English Academic Self-Concepts: A Waiting-List Replication and Extension Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10137-4
title: COMPASS: a theory-driven intervention addressing dimensional and temporal comparison processes and their associated beliefs
description: COMPASS (comparison processes in students' self-concept formation) is an intervention framework that enhances subject-specific academic self-concepts by educating students about dimensional comparisons (comparisons of one's own performance across subjects) and temporal comparisons (comparisons with one's own past performance) and the beliefs moderating them. The article states that "COMPASS represents a coherent, theory-driven application of comparison theories that jointly addresses dimensional and temporal comparison processes and their associated beliefs." Its modules work with psychoeducation, exercises, and discussions, delivered in roughly 120 minutes with lectures, class discussions, group exercises, and mnemonic posters.
requirements: Delivery in regular school lessons by trained intervention leaders with group sizes limited to a maximum of 20 students to ensure active discussion engagement
constraints: The social comparison module was excluded because it did not change the targeted belief and led to an unintended decrease in students' German self-concept, and the cohort-comparison idea is not applicable in nonacademic track schools
target_learners: Students in Grades 9 to 11 at German secondary schools of the academic track
target_learning_goals: Subject-specific academic self-concepts in math or English
Belief in the positive interdependence of mathematical and verbal abilities
Belief in the changeability of abilities
examples: Students imagined performing the same in the intervention subject while performing worse in all other subjects, and reflected on how this would affect their self-concept
Students wrote down three key learnings from the past year and discussed them to emphasize their actual learning gains
key_sources: Hörsch, H., Schumacher, J., & Wolff, F. (2026). Long-Term Effects of an Intervention Targeting Dimensional and Temporal Comparisons on Students' Math and English Academic Self-Concepts: A Waiting-List Replication and Extension Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10137-4

article_title: Long-Term Effects of an Intervention Targeting Dimensional and Temporal Comparisons on Students’ Math and English Academic Self-Concepts: A Waiting-List Replication and Extension Study
citation: Hörsch, H., Schumacher, J., & Wolff, F. (2026). Long-Term Effects of an Intervention Targeting Dimensional and Temporal Comparisons on Students' Math and English Academic Self-Concepts: A Waiting-List Replication and Extension Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10137-4
title: Foster beliefs in the positive interdependence of mathematical and verbal abilities and in the changeability of abilities to mitigate dimensional contrast effects and support balanced self-concept development
description: The article recommends targeting the beliefs that moderate comparison effects rather than the comparisons alone. As the authors put it, "fostering a belief in the positive interdependence of mathematical and verbal abilities as well as a growth mindset may help mitigate dimensional contrast effects and support more balanced self-concept development across domains." The COMPASS intervention operationalizes this by educating students that mathematical and verbal abilities are not mutually exclusive and that abilities are changeable, pairing belief change with reflection exercises.
requirements: Students receive education about comparison effects plus exercises and discussions that let them apply the beliefs to their own performance histories
constraints: Effects were demonstrated in math and, per the abstract, English in academic-track secondary schools; the pilot study's modules did not enhance German self-concept
target_learners: Secondary school students in subjects where they perform relatively worse
target_learning_goals: Balanced academic self-concept development across domains
Sustainable belief change about ability interdependence and changeability
examples: In the COMPASS intervention, students reflected on whether they were a math or a language type and chose behaviors they could transfer from other subjects to the intervention subject

article_title: Text Generation Benefits Learning: a Meta-Analytic Review
citation: Julia Schindler · Tobias Richter. (2023). Text Generation Benefits Learning: a Meta-Analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09758-w
title: Material appropriate processing / contextual framework of desirable difficulties
description: The contextual framework by McDaniel and Butler, incorporating material appropriate processing (MAP) and transfer appropriate processing (TAP), describes desirable difficulties such as text generation as "the result of a complex interaction of learning material, difficulty intervention, learning assessment tasks, and learner characteristics." It predicts generation benefits learning only when the generation task stimulates cognitive processes relevant to the learning test that are not already stimulated by the material. It distinguishes individual-item (propositional) processing from relational (integrative) processing and holds that narratives foster relational processing while expository texts draw attention to individual propositions, so letter completion should complement narratives and sentence unscrambling should complement expository texts.
requirements: The generation task must stimulate cognitive processes relevant for the specific learning test that are not already stimulated by the learning material or initiated by the learners themselves
constraints: The article reports the framework's genre-by-task predictions received only partial support in the meta-analysis: the expository-text contrast was significant but the narrative-text contrast was not
target_learners: learners studying narrative or expository texts, including university students and other populations such as high-school students
target_learning_goals: text comprehension and memory for text content at text-base and situation-model levels
examples: The meta-analysis tested the framework's predicted genre-by-generation-task interaction across 129 effect sizes, finding sentence unscrambling (g = 0.77) significantly stronger than letter completion (g = 0.23) in expository texts
key_sources: Julia Schindler · Tobias Richter. (2023). Text Generation Benefits Learning: a Meta-Analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09758-w

article_title: Stimulating Elementary School Students’ Self-Regulated Learning Through High-Quality Interactions and Relationships: A Narrative Review
citation: Niels J. de Ruig, Peter F. de Jong, Marjolein Zee. (2023). Stimulating Elementary School Students' Self-Regulated Learning Through High-Quality Interactions and Relationships: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09795-5
title: Teaching Through Interactions framework: three domains of classroom-level teacher-student interaction quality
description: The review adopts the Teaching Through Interactions (TTI) framework as its organizing model for classroom-level interaction quality, integrating attachment theory and self-determination theory. As the review states, "The TTI-framework includes three broad domains; instructional support, classroom organization, and emotional support (Hamre et al., 2013)." Instructional support covers promoting inquiry, learning formats, quality feedback, and instructional dialogue; classroom organization covers behavior management, routines, and maximizing learning time; emotional support covers positive climate, sensitivity, and regard for student perspectives. The review uses these domains to structure its synthesis of interaction-SRL associations.
requirements: Studies must measure at least one TTI domain of teacher-student interaction quality, typically via the CLASS observation instrument
constraints: The framework addresses classroom-level interactions; dyadic relationship quality is conceptualized separately via closeness, conflict, and dependency
target_learners: elementary school students (grades 1-6, ages 4-13)
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning components: metacognition, regulation of cognition, motivation, behavior, and emotions

article_title: Stimulating Elementary School Students’ Self-Regulated Learning Through High-Quality Interactions and Relationships: A Narrative Review
citation: Niels J. de Ruig, Peter F. de Jong, Marjolein Zee. (2023). Stimulating Elementary School Students' Self-Regulated Learning Through High-Quality Interactions and Relationships: A Narrative Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09795-5
title: Five-component model of self-regulated learning embedded in a cyclic process
description: The review conceptualizes SRL as a process in which students "systematically attempt to monitor, regulate, and control" five components: cognition, metacognition, motivation, emotions, and behaviors. It draws primarily on social-cognitive models (Pintrich, Boekaerts) and organizes the components within a preparatory, performance, and appraisal phase cycle. The review uses this five-component structure as its outcome taxonomy, coding each included study's SRL measures against it (Table 1), and structures its results sections by component rather than by phase because the phases may occur dynamically rather than sequentially.
requirements: Measurement instruments must distinguish the SRL components being targeted; the review notes most self-report instruments capture only a narrow subset of components
constraints: The review notes theoretical debate about whether the phases are clearly distinguishable, so it structures its synthesis by component rather than phase
target_learners: elementary school students (grades 1-6, ages 4-13)
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning across cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, emotional, and behavioral components
examples: The review's Table 1 maps subcomponents such as target goal setting, planning, monitoring, help-seeking, and emotion regulation strategies onto the three phases

article_title: Do Pedagogical Agents Enhance Student Motivation? Unraveling the Evidence Through Meta-Analysis
citation: Gladstone, J. R., Schroeder, N. L., Heidig, S., Zhang, S., Palaguachi, C., & Pitera, M. (2025). Do Pedagogical Agents Enhance Student Motivation? Unraveling the Evidence Through Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10050-2
title: Theory-driven taxonomy of six motivation constructs for pedagogical agent research
description: The article organizes PA motivation research around four prominent theories — social cognitive theory, situated expectancy-value theory, interest theory, and self-determination theory — arguing that lumping motivation into one meta-construct is "theoretically unstable." From these theories it derives six discrete constructs: "self-efficacy expectancies (SCT, SEVT), subjective task values or task relevance (SEVT), utility value (SEVT), engagement (SEVT), interest (interest theory), and intrinsic motivation (SDT)," plus a broad "motivation" category for unspecified measures. The taxonomy structures the seven meta-analyses and is offered as categories future PA researchers can use for theory-driven measurement.
requirements: Studies must measure motivation outcomes with sufficient detail to classify them into one of the theoretical construct categories
constraints: Motivational measures in the PA literature were often not described in sufficient detail to be classified into one of the six categories, necessitating the broad 'motivation' category
target_learners: learners across grade levels using digital learning environments with pedagogical agents
target_learning_goals: motivation outcomes: self-efficacy, value beliefs, utility value, engagement, interest, intrinsic motivation
examples: The authors ran seven separate 3LMAs, one per construct, rather than pooling all motivation measures into one outcome

Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09662-9
title: Reciprocal Effects Model (REM) of academic self-concept and achievement
description: The REM is a causal theoretical model holding that academic self-concept and achievement each cause the other over time, integrating the earlier skill-development model (achievement → self-concept) and self-enhancement model (self-concept → achievement). The article states the hypothesis "is clearly causal" and that "the REM generated a substantial research literature that treats these reciprocal effects as causal." It is tested with longitudinal cross-lagged panel data and underpins the study's a priori hypotheses.
requirements: At least two, preferably three or more, waves of longitudinal data measuring both self-concept and achievement
Structural equation modeling to test directional ordering
constraints: The article prefers the term directionality to causality, noting interpretation is compromised by potential unmeasured covariates

target_learning_goals: academic self-concept in mathematics
mathematics achievement
examples: The study tests REM hypotheses with tripartite RI-CLPMs and CLPMs on five waves of PALMA data

title: Within-person (RI-CLPM) versus between-person (CLPM) perspectives on longitudinal panel data
description: A methodological framework distinguishing two ways of analyzing cross-lagged panel data. RI-CLPMs add stable trait factors and evaluate how "within-person deviations in one construct are related to subsequent within-person deviations in another construct," whereas "CLPMs confound the within- and between-person processes." The article argues the two models address different research questions, produce different interpretations, and should be juxtaposed rather than one treated as the default, with model choice resting on theoretical grounds as well as fit.
requirements: At least three waves of data for basic RI-CLPMs
Understanding that RI-CLPMs are person-centered/residualized statistical models, not tests of within-person mechanisms
constraints: Neither model provides good controls for unmeasured time-varying covariates
RI-CLPMs sometimes fail to converge to proper solutions even when the RI-CLPM structure generated the data

target_learning_goals: longitudinal analysis of self-concept and achievement relations

article_title: Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play
citation: Wynberg, E. R., Boland, A., Raijmakers, M. E. J., & van der Veen, C. (2021). Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09608-7
title: Unified theoretical framework of object-oriented play synthesizing genetic epistemology, cultural historical psychology, and evolutionary psychology
description: The review synthesizes three independently developed theoretical perspectives on children's exploration and/or manipulation of objects and materials into one comprehensive framework. The authors state they "aim to synthesize these existing theories into a unified theoretical framework", arguing that assessing the behavior from only one perspective yields an incomplete view of its features, trajectory, and developmental value. The framework organizes each perspective by defining labels and features, developmental trajectory, and developmental value, and is offered as "a starting point for future research on OOP in early childhood (education)".
requirements: Integrates the three perspectives by comparing similarities that enhance each other and differences that complement each other, rather than replacing any single perspective
constraints: The authors note that no comprehensive theoretical framework existed previously despite the behavior's universality, and the framework is proposed as a starting point rather than a validated model
target_learners: children in early childhood (approximately 18 months to 3.5 years)
target_learning_goals: cognitive development
motor development
social cognition
symbolic thought and speech
examples: The paper reviews each perspective against the same three research questions (defining labels/features, developmental trajectory, developmental value) and compares them in a synthesis section, with Table 1 providing an overview of main concepts per perspective.

article_title: Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play
citation: Wynberg, E. R., Boland, A., Raijmakers, M. E. J., & van der Veen, C. (2021). Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09608-7
title: Genetic epistemological account of object-oriented play as practice/functional play serving scheme construction
description: Within genetic epistemology, children's exploration and/or manipulation of objects is labeled practice play (Piaget) or functional play (Smilansky), defined as "the repetition of already acquired behavior, detached from its function, purely for the joy of practicing and mastering it". Casby subdivides this play into exploratory sensorimotor, relational-nonfunctional, and functional-conventional levels, with constructive play as a separate later term. The perspective holds that cognitive development is rooted in sensorimotor interactions with objects, with schemes built through assimilation and accommodation, and play progressing through Piaget's six sensorimotor substages toward early symbolic thought.
requirements: Progression through the play levels relies on imitation and repetition as the main features of practice and functional play
constraints: The authors note Piaget's stages of cognitive development and accompanying stages of play received some criticism early on, though the theory is still used, for example in prescriptive play therapy
target_learners: children from infancy through early childhood (sensorimotor stage, around 0 to 2 years)
target_learning_goals: cognitive development
sensorimotor development
scheme formation
examples: The introductory example of Bobby twisting a bottle top is classified as practice play, with his spoon-in-bottle behavior as constructive play and his functional use of the bottle as functional-conventional play.

article_title: Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play
citation: Wynberg, E. R., Boland, A., Raijmakers, M. E. J., & van der Veen, C. (2021). Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09608-7
title: Cultural historical psychological account of object-oriented play as mediated, socially embedded manipulative play
description: In cultural historical psychology, children's object manipulation is understood as child-caregiver joint object-centered activity and manipulative play, whose defining features are its associative nature and repetition. Development proceeds through leading activities: emotional interaction with caregivers in the first year, then manipulative play as the leading activity of the second and third years, followed by object substitution and sociodramatic play. The perspective emphasizes mediation: adults model procedures with psychological tools, which the child internalizes, and play "has the potential to create a zone of proximal development".
requirements: Children depend on their surroundings and caregiver mediation to discover the social meanings of objects
Adults must first model the procedure of object substitution for the child to acquire, master, and internalize it
constraints: The two types of manipulative thought (exploring characteristics without a practical goal and manipulating toward a practical goal) are described as not separable in their pure forms but closely interrelated
target_learners: children aged 1 to 3 years in joint activity with caregivers
target_learning_goals: speech development
symbolic thought
social-emotional stability
motor skills
communication skills
examples: In the bottle example, the educator models twisting off the top, involves Bobby by directing his attention, then withdraws until the procedure mediates his mental process.

article_title: Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play
citation: Wynberg, E. R., Boland, A., Raijmakers, M. E. J., & van der Veen, C. (2021). Towards a Comprehensive View of Object-Oriented Play. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09608-7
title: Evolutionary psychological taxonomy distinguishing exploration, object play, and tool use by physiological features and developmental timing
description: The evolutionary psychology perspective distinguishes object-oriented behaviors "based on their difference in physiological features, developmental histories, and developmental consequences". Exploration is defined by elevated heart rate, low distractibility, and negative/flat affect; object play by lower heart rate, high distractibility, and positive affect, with purposelessness, repetition, segmentation, sequential variation, and exaggeration as features; tool use is the instrumental use of an object toward a goal. Construction is a later, accommodative behavior concerned with the end product, occurring between 3 and 5 years.
requirements: Distinguishing the behaviors relies on observable physiological markers such as heart rate, distractibility, and affect
constraints: The age range for tool use is described as less rigid, developing somewhere during infancy-childhood
target_learners: children in early childhood
cross-species comparison including primates
target_learning_goals: tool use
social cognition
adaptation
examples: In the bottle example, squeezing the nipple is exploration, presenting the bottle for pretend drinking is object play, and drinking from the bottle is tool use.
