article_title: Student Learning in Higher Education: a Commentary
citation: John T. E. Richardson. (2017). Student Learning in Higher Education: a Commentary. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 353–362. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9410-x
title: The presage–process–product (3P) model of student learning and its elaborations
description: Biggs' 3P model distinguishes presage variables (characteristics of students and institutional context), process variables (motives and strategies), and product variables (performance outcomes). The commentary notes Biggs (1991) added feedback loops and Biggs (1993a) adopted a systems approach allowing interactions among all components, and that Richardson (2000) argued the process component actually measures predispositions, warranting elaboration into four stages: presage, predisposition, process, and product. The commentary judges these elaborations introduce flexibility but may render the models unfalsifiable.
requirements: Requires measures of the process component, which in practice are questionnaire instruments such as the Study Process Questionnaire that capture predispositions rather than actual task processes
constraints: The commentary states that systems-style models with feedback loops and interactions seem to render these models unfalsifiable because they can accommodate virtually any pattern of empirical results
The commentary finds the assumption that personal characteristics influence learning implausible for characteristics like ethnicity, which is more likely a proxy for other characteristics
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: understanding and explaining individual differences in student learning approaches and outcomes
examples: Fryer critiqued the 3P model and suggested perceived control as an organizing principle for a system approach; Biggs based his account on Dunkin and Biddle's (1974) presage–process–product model of classroom teaching

article_title: Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning?
citation: Katharina Scheiter. (2025). Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10037-z
title: Taxonomy of effort constructs distinguishing task-imposed from voluntarily allocated effort
description: The commentary organizes the proliferating effort terminology along one axis: whether effort is imposed by the task or voluntarily allocated by the learner. Mental load, data-driven effort, and effort-by-complexity can be modelled purely cognitively, whereas mental effort, goal-driven effort, effort-by-allocation, and effort-by-need frustration — defined as "how strenuous or aversive a person experiences task execution" — all carry a motivational component. The article uses this taxonomy to diagnose where CLT and SRL accounts diverge.
requirements: Distinguishing task-imposed from learner-allocated constructs when measuring or discussing effort
constraints: The commentary notes there are no precise scientific definitions of effort; research traditions each use their own understanding of the construct
target_learners: learners in educational settings studying with instructional materials
target_learning_goals: understanding and regulating effort during learning and problem solving
examples: The commentary maps CLT's mental load/mental effort distinction onto Koriat et al.'s data-driven/goal-driven effort and Grund et al.'s effort-by-complexity/effort-by-allocation distinctions

article_title: Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning?
citation: Katharina Scheiter. (2025). Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10037-z
title: Avoid jangle fallacies: use precise definitions, require added explanatory power for new constructs, and reach measurement consensus
description: The commentary recommends that researchers linking fields be parsimonious with constructs: define constructs precisely, show that allegedly novel constructs have additional explanatory power before introducing them, and reach consensus on measurement. As the article puts it, "Simply inventing new names for the same constructs should be avoided, as it creates unnecessary redundancy (i.e., jangle fallacies)." It cites renamed constructs in the special issue (effort-by-complexity vs. data-driven effort; required mental effort vs. mental load; cognitive demand vs. cognitive load) as examples.
requirements: New constructs must demonstrate additional explanatory power, such as resolving conflicts in empirical data or explaining previously unexplained observations
Community consensus on how key constructs like cognitive load and effort are measured, including critical test scenarios and multiple measures within one paradigm
constraints: Researchers must be aware of the type of appraisals they prompt learners to make, since appraisal wording can affect results; David et al. found no evidence that the formulation of effort appraisals moderated their mediation model
target_learners: education and psychology researchers studying effort and cognitive load
target_learning_goals: accurate conceptualization and measurement of effort and cognitive load constructs
examples: The commentary questions the added benefit of renaming monitoring accuracy as self-assessment accuracy, and of shifting from mental load to required mental effort

citation: Katharina Scheiter. (2025). Commentary: How can We Come to Terms when Discussing the Role of Effort from the Perspective of Cognitive Load Theory and Theories of Self-regulated Learning? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10037-z
title: Move beyond fragmented mapping toward integrated theories of cognition and motivation linking CLT and SRL
description: The commentary argues that borrowing isolated assumptions, constructs, and measures across CLT and SRL — as the EMR framework research has done — has been empirically productive but has not produced a coherent theoretical integration. It recommends that "there is a necessity to formulate integrated theories of cognition and motivation by defining intertheoretical connections between existing theories and evaluating their congruence," either via a rigorous structuralist mapping or by inserting each account's missing assumptions into the other (e.g., a central executive in CLT; information-processing detail in SRL).
requirements: Identifying matches, contradictions, and non-correspondences between the two theories' assumption networks, ensuring no contradictions between networks
constraints: The structuralist integration approach is described as very rigorous but also very demanding; De Bruin and van Merriënboer (2017) estimated at least 25 years to develop a combined approach
target_learners: learners in complex, longer-duration self-regulated learning scenarios
target_learning_goals: comprehensive explanation of how effort is monitored and regulated at the meta-level and implemented at the object level of information processing
examples: The commentary notes van Merriënboer and Sluijsmans (2009) used CLT to derive instructional support recommendations for SRL without unifying the theories

title: Extended reciprocal effects model (REM): contemporaneous skill-development effects of achievement on self-concept and lagged self-enhancement effects of self-concept on achievement
description: The extended reciprocal effects model (REM) is a longitudinal model of reciprocal processes between academic self-concept (ASC) and achievement (ACH). The article describes it as positing "contemporaneous skill-development effects (of ACH on ASC) and lagged self-enhancement effects (of ASC on ACH)", so achievement and self-concept influence each other through two temporally distinct pathways. The article uses this model as the target structure its reanalyses test against alternative specifications proposed by Sorjonen et al. (2025).

target_learning_goals: Understanding reciprocal relations between academic self-concept and achievement over time
examples: The article reanalyzed the original PALMA dataset used in Marsh et al. (2024) to test the extended REM against alternative models.

article_title: Why We Might Still be Concerned About Low Cronbach’s Alphas in Domain-specific Knowledge Tests
citation: Steffen Zitzmann, Gabe A. Orona. (2025). Why We Might Still be Concerned About Low Cronbach's Alphas in Domain-specific Knowledge Tests. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10015-5
title: Report confidence or Bayesian credible intervals around estimated alpha rather than comparing a point estimate to a threshold
description: The authors propose complementing the usual reporting practice with intervals for alpha, because the real problem with thresholds is that comparing an estimated alpha to a threshold "does not properly account for sampling error." Placing a confidence interval or, preferably, a Bayesian variant around the estimate conveys the uncertainty of the value; only when the upper bound does not exceed the threshold can one reasonably infer alpha is too low. They argue this practice may counteract the inflation of seemingly high alphas in educational psychology.
requirements: Intervals for alpha might not be readily available in software; the article states they can be obtained via factor analytic methodology or resampling techniques.
target_learners: Educational psychology researchers
Test developers
Practitioners assessing individual students
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement and reporting of the reliability of domain-specific knowledge test scores
examples: The article showcases the procedure with an estimated alpha of .61 below the 0.70 threshold whose calculated interval [0.48, 0.74] includes the threshold, suggesting a fair chance the true alpha is acceptably high.

article_title: Why We Might Still be Concerned About Low Cronbach’s Alphas in Domain-specific Knowledge Tests
citation: Steffen Zitzmann, Gabe A. Orona. (2025). Why We Might Still be Concerned About Low Cronbach's Alphas in Domain-specific Knowledge Tests. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10015-5
title: Keep well justified alpha thresholds as rough guidelines rather than abandoning them, and view a low alpha as a threat rather than a sign of validity
description: Against the recommendation to drop alpha thresholds, the authors argue that "a well justified threshold can be a valuable means if it is understood as a rough guideline to achieve a level of reliability that is high enough to prevent most of the discussed adverse effects on results." They contend that interpreting a low alpha as indicating content validity could be exploited to legitimate low reliability, and that a high alpha remains an important prerequisite for research and individual diagnostics. Developers should opt for a balanced strategy rather than playing reliability off against validity.
requirements: Thresholds must be well justified and understood as rough guidelines, and interval estimates should accompany the point estimate when applying them.
constraints: The authors acknowledge a threshold can be misused in ways that increase the file drawer problem or reduce the content validity of tests.
target_learners: Educational psychology researchers
Journal reviewers and editors
Test developers
target_learning_goals: Maintaining reliability of domain-specific knowledge test scores for research and individual assessment
examples: The commentary argues that viewing a low alpha as a feature of knowledge tests unintentionally provides an argument other authors could exploit to play down or legitimate a low alpha.
key_sources: Steffen Zitzmann, Gabe A. Orona. (2025). Why We Might Still be Concerned About Low Cronbach's Alphas in Domain-specific Knowledge Tests. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10015-5

article_title: The Distorting Influence of Primacy Effects on Reporting Cognitive Load in Learning Materials of Varying Complexity
citation: Krieglstein, F., Beege, M., Wesenberg, L., Rey, G. D., & Schneider, S. (2025). The Distorting Influence of Primacy Effects on Reporting Cognitive Load in Learning Materials of Varying Complexity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09980-0
title: When measuring cognitive load in learning materials of varying complexity, measure during learning rather than relying solely on a single post-learning self-report
description: The article shows that a single delayed self-report of cognitive load can be biased: in learning contexts the first impression of complexity is the strongest predictor of the overall assessment, and when complexity decreases the delayed rating significantly exceeds the during-learning average. The authors argue that "measuring cognitive load multiple times during problem-solving (i.e., after each individual problem-solving task) is more accurate than a single measurement after all problem-solving tasks have been completed" and extend this concern to explicit learning contexts.
requirements: Learning materials must contain varying levels of complexity for the bias to arise; the delayed assessment must be a retrospective self-report.
constraints: The bias toward the first impression appeared in learning contexts; delayed group-level assessments did not differ between increasing and decreasing complexity sequences.
target_learners: university students studying multimedia learning units
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of experienced cognitive load during learning
examples: In the main study, learners studied three learning units in increasing or decreasing complexity sequences and rated ICL, ECL, and GCL after each unit and once after learning; the delayed ICL assessment anchored on the first impression.
key_sources: Krieglstein, F., Beege, M., Wesenberg, L., Rey, G. D., & Schneider, S. (2025). The Distorting Influence of Primacy Effects on Reporting Cognitive Load in Learning Materials of Varying Complexity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09980-0

article_title: Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape
citation: Julia Chatain, Charlotte Müller, Keny Chatain, Leon Calabrese, Manu Kapur. (2025). Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10073-9
title: A data-driven taxonomy organizing the meanings of concrete and abstract along a learner–representation–concept dimension
description: The article proposes a taxonomy of the semantic landscape of concreteness and abstraction in mathematics education, built from qualitative coding of a corpus of 368 papers. It models learning as follows: "To learn a concept ( C ), a learner ( L ) interacts with a representation ( R) of C , designed through mapping." Axes are placed at the interaction level (learner–representation) or the mapping level (representation–concept), each running between a concrete and an abstract end, and each paired with a design question to make the taxonomy usable in research and practice.
requirements: Axes must be defined according to the representation, as it is the only element that can be acted upon when designing interventions or studies
constraints: For two axes, only codes for one end of the spectrum were found in the data; the other end was added during analysis and is indicated by dotted lines
The authors do not claim objectivity, as they offer a specific perspective
target_learners: Mathematics education researchers and designers of mathematics learning interventions
target_learning_goals: Precise use of the terms concrete and abstract in mathematics education research and intervention design
examples: The taxonomy was built by two researchers through reflexive thematic analysis, iteratively grouping codes until both agreed every code was assigned a group
key_sources: Julia Chatain, Charlotte Müller, Keny Chatain, Leon Calabrese, Manu Kapur. (2025). Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10073-9

article_title: Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape
citation: Julia Chatain, Charlotte Müller, Keny Chatain, Leon Calabrese, Manu Kapur. (2025). Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10073-9
title: Interaction-level axes of concreteness are subjective, depending on the learner's perception of the representation
description: The taxonomy distinguishes five interaction-level axes relating to how the learner perceives the representation: familiarity, interest, simplicity, relevance, and sensoriality. The article states that "all axes at the interaction level depend on the representation and on the learners and are therefore related to the subjective experience of the learners." Designing along these axes requires knowing the targeted learners, and only actual measurement with target learners can ensure the desired effect occurred.
requirements: Designing according to these axes requires knowing who the targeted learners are
Only actual measurement with target learners can ensure that the desired effect indeed happened
constraints: Whether a designed effect occurs depends on learners' sensory abilities and on how and whether they choose to engage with the representation
target_learners: Mathematics learners in high school and higher education
target_learning_goals: Selecting representations whose perceived familiarity, interest, simplicity, relevance and sensoriality support learning
examples: A designer might create a physical and interactive object to increase engagement, but whether it increases interest depends on the learner
key_sources: Julia Chatain, Charlotte Müller, Keny Chatain, Leon Calabrese, Manu Kapur. (2025). Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10073-9

article_title: Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape
citation: Julia Chatain, Charlotte Müller, Keny Chatain, Leon Calabrese, Manu Kapur. (2025). Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10073-9
title: Mapping-level axes of concreteness are objective properties of how a representation maps to a concept
description: The taxonomy identifies six mapping-level axes between representation and concept: "situatedness between idealized and real life, experientiality between symbolic and enacted, speciﬁcity between universal and speciﬁc, informality between formal and informal, approximation between rigorous and approximate, and physicality between virtual and physical." These axes are objective because they depend only on the designer's decisions about how the representation is defined in relation to the concept, not on the learner.
requirements: Axes at the mapping level depend only on the representation and the represented concept, so they are fully under the designer's control
constraints: Mapping-level axes may relate to interaction-level axes: making certain design decisions along one axis may impact another
target_learners: Mathematics learners in high school and higher education
target_learning_goals: Making deliberate design choices about how representations map to mathematical concepts
examples: A designer may decide to use real-world examples (situatedness) or to design an experiential representation of the concept, independent of the learner
key_sources: Julia Chatain, Charlotte Müller, Keny Chatain, Leon Calabrese, Manu Kapur. (2025). Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10073-9

article_title: Editor’s Note
citation: Daniel Robinson. (2009). Editor's Note. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9103-1
title: Replication studies in educational psychology should use a multi-experiment structure that first replicates the original method and then extends it to identify boundary conditions of the effect
description: The editorial sets out the journal's expectation for replication manuscripts: a successful replication article requires at least three experiments, the first reproducing the original study's method with only participants changed, later ones extending the method. The stated aim is that 'we can begin to identify the boundary conditions of the effect'.
requirements: The first experiment must follow the method used in the original study, with participants as the only difference
Extensions must change one aspect of the method besides participants, such as materials, exposure, or delay between acquisition and testing
constraints: Applies to replication manuscripts submitted to Educational Psychology Review, which does not publish primary empirical reports but does publish replications
target_learners: educational psychology researchers
target_learning_goals: establishing the generality and boundary conditions of empirical learning effects
examples: A failed replication should be followed by a second replication attempt, and if results still cannot be replicated, a third experiment containing an extension the authors believe would allow replication of the original results
key_sources: Daniel Robinson. (2009). Editor's Note. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9103-1

article_title: What Does Research Say About the Science of Reading for K-5 Multilingual Learners? A Systematic Review of Systematic Reviews
citation: Kittle, J. M., Amendum, S. J., & Budde, C. M. (2024). What Does Research Say About the Science of Reading for K-5 Multilingual Learners? A Systematic Review of Systematic Reviews. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09942-6
title: Four-cluster evidence-based component model of the science of reading for K-5 multilingual learners
description: This review of reviews organizes the science of reading for K-5 multilingual learners into four broad clusters of components related to English reading comprehension: "oral language, phonological awareness (PA), decoding and oral reading fluency, and reading comprehension." Each cluster includes components in both MLs' first language and English, and the review grounds the framework in the Simple View of Reading (RC = D × LC) and Scarborough's Reading Rope, extended by multilingual theories such as Bernhardt's compensatory model in which knowledge sources interact synergistically, not additively.
requirements: Components must be directly related to English reading comprehension outcomes, in accordance with the SVR, as the review's inclusion criterion required
constraints: The review notes reading comprehension is widely considered multidimensional rather than a unitary construct and is likely less componential
Evidence is drawn from reviews of studies conducted primarily in U.S. K-5 classrooms, with at least 50% of studies in that setting
target_learners: K-5 multilingual learners, with and without disabilities
target_learning_goals: English reading comprehension and its component skills (oral language, phonological awareness, decoding, fluency, comprehension strategies) in L1 and L2
examples: The review synthesized 30 systematic reviews published 2000–2023, coding components significantly related to English reading comprehension with 0.88 inter-rater percent agreement across major extracted categories
key_sources: Kittle, J. M., Amendum, S. J., & Budde, C. M. (2024). What Does Research Say About the Science of Reading for K-5 Multilingual Learners? A Systematic Review of Systematic Reviews. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09942-6

article_title: Classroom Active Breaks as a Physical-Educational Intervention for Executive Functions and Mathematical Outcomes: a Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
citation: Melguizo-Ibáñez, E., Zurita-Ortega, F., Tadeu, P., Ubago-Jiménez, J. L., & Alonso Vargas, J. M. (2026). Classroom Active Breaks as a Physical-Educational Intervention for Executive Functions and Mathematical Outcomes: a Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10146-3
title: Cognitive load theory as an interpretive framework for how active-break modality relates to executive function and learning outcomes
description: The article uses cognitive load theory, with its distinction between intrinsic, extraneous and germane load, to interpret why different active-break modalities may relate differently to cognitive and academic outcomes. It distinguishes a motor-only modality of "simple physical movements that do not require decision-making", a cognitive-motor light modality with "simple rules or basic cognitive demands alongside physical movement", and a cognitive-motor high modality involving "complex decision-making, dual-task coordination or problem-solving during movement". Each modality is theorised to carry a distinct profile of element interactivity and working-memory demand.
requirements: Effects depend on how the movement modifies cognitive demands relevant to schema construction; benefits require alignment with instructional goals and control of extraneous load
constraints: Cognitive load and its components were not directly assessed in the primary studies; the framework is interpretive, not an empirically tested causal mechanism
The theory does not model physiological arousal, attentional set-shifting, or fatigue
target_learners: Primary and secondary school students aged 6–16
target_learning_goals: Executive functions (attention, inhibitory control, working memory) and mathematical achievement and fluency
examples: The meta-analysis coded each included study's active break as motor-only, cognitive-motor light, or cognitive-motor high and used these categories as prespecified moderators in exploratory RVE meta-regressions.
key_sources: Melguizo-Ibáñez, E., Zurita-Ortega, F., Tadeu, P., Ubago-Jiménez, J. L., & Alonso Vargas, J. M. (2026). Classroom Active Breaks as a Physical-Educational Intervention for Executive Functions and Mathematical Outcomes: a Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10146-3

article_title: How Eye Read: A Social Network Approach
citation: Catrysse, L., van Daal, T., Jarodzka, H., Kaakinen, J. K., Donche, V., & Gijbels, D. (2025). How Eye Read: A Social Network Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10000-y
title: Microscopic network measures as indicators of sentence-level integration during reading
description: The article frames reading networks with sentences as nodes and transitions between sentences as weighted edges, and proposes four microscopic measures of integration. "Strength refers to the number of edges connected to a node" and reflects how much a sentence has been visited; betweenness identifies sentences lying on shortest paths between others; harmonic centrality (a form of closeness centrality) quantifies proximity to all other sentences; and the local clustering coefficient captures interconnection among a sentence's neighbors. The approach aligns with construction-integration accounts of mental representation building.
requirements: Eye-tracking data segmented into sentence-level AOIs with transition matrices convertible to weighted network objects
constraints: The study examined short expository texts read by higher education freshmen; suitability for other genres and longer texts is untested
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: understanding integration processes during expository text reading
examples: Hypothetical example networks in Fig. 1 contrast a linear reading pattern (TI strength 1) with an integrated pattern (TI strength 4)
key_sources: Catrysse, L., van Daal, T., Jarodzka, H., Kaakinen, J. K., Donche, V., & Gijbels, D. (2025). How Eye Read: A Social Network Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10000-y

article_title: How Eye Read: A Social Network Approach
citation: Catrysse, L., van Daal, T., Jarodzka, H., Kaakinen, J. K., Donche, V., & Gijbels, D. (2025). How Eye Read: A Social Network Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10000-y
title: Sentence-level social network analysis pipeline for eye-tracking reading data (OSF dataset and scripts)
description: A reusable analytic pipeline in which fixations are filtered (Tobii I-VT), sentence AOIs are classified as topic-introducing, topic-medial or topic-ending, AOI strings are converted to transition matrices, and weighted networks are built in R with igraph to compute strength, betweenness, harmonic centrality and local clustering coefficient. The authors state "The dataset and scripts are available at osf.io (https:// osf. io/ qbctd/)", supporting reuse and replication of the approach.
requirements: Eye-tracking fixation data exportable per AOI; R packages igraph and DirectedClustering for metric computation
constraints: Applied here to three short Dutch expository texts read by 31 participants; generalization to other texts and populations is not demonstrated
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: measuring moment-to-moment integration processes during reading
examples: 31 networks per text were constructed from the eye-tracking data of the reused Catrysse et al. (2018) dataset

article_title: Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review
citation: Sofie M. M. Loyens, Julianne E. van Meerten, Lydia Schaap, Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09757-x
title: Barrows' six core characteristics and three-phase process model of problem-based learning
description: The review characterizes PBL through Barrows' (1996) six core characteristics — student-centered learning, small groups with a tutor, the tutor as facilitator, authentic problems encountered before study, problems as triggers for prior knowledge activation revealing knowledge gaps, and self-directed learning to close those gaps. It adds that "PBL as a process consists of three separate stages: an initial discussion phase, a self-study phase, and a reporting stage." These criteria also served as inclusion criteria for judging whether studies genuinely implemented PBL.
requirements: Implementation must include authentic problems as the start of learning, collaborative small groups, a facilitating tutor, and ample time for self-directed self-study
constraints: Studies whose learning process started with a lecture instead of a problem, or that did not contain the three process phases, were excluded as not meeting the defining criteria
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students
target_learning_goals: Domain knowledge acquisition through self-directed learning on authentic problems
examples: The review's inclusion coding assessed studies' definitions and implementations against these characteristics (Barrows, 1996; Hmelo-Silver, 2004; Schmidt et al., 2009)
key_sources: Sofie M. M. Loyens, Julianne E. van Meerten, Lydia Schaap, Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09757-x

article_title: Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review
citation: Sofie M. M. Loyens, Julianne E. van Meerten, Lydia Schaap, Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09757-x
title: Schraw et al.'s four-component framework of higher-order thinking, with CT as a subcomponent
description: The review presents HOT as an overarching concept of "skills that enhance the construction of deeper, conceptually-driven understanding," aligned with Bloom's taxonomy levels above remembering. It reports that "HOT has been put forward as having four components (Schraw et al., 2011): (a) reasoning (i.e., induction and deduction), (b) argumentation (i.e., generating and evaluating evidence and arguments), (c) metacognition (i.e., thinking about and regulating one's thinking), and (d) problem solving and critical thinking (CT)." In this framework CT is treated as a subcomponent of HOT, and alternative characterizations add creative thinking as a possible further component.
requirements: Knowledge remains essential: the framework holds that knowledge is needed and related to thinking processes
constraints: The review acknowledges its definitions are selective, focusing on those relevant to student-centered learning environments rather than all philosophical, psychological, and educational traditions
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students
target_learning_goals: Reasoning, argumentation, metacognition, problem solving, and critical thinking
examples: The two included HOT studies (Sasson et al., 2018; Sugeng & Suryani, 2020) operationalized HOT via Bloom's taxonomy levels of application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation
key_sources: Sofie M. M. Loyens, Julianne E. van Meerten, Lydia Schaap, Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09757-x

article_title: Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review
citation: Sofie M. M. Loyens, Julianne E. van Meerten, Lydia Schaap, Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Situating Higher-Order, Critical, and Critical-Analytic Thinking in Problem- and Project-Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09757-x
title: Critical-analytic thinking as evidence-weighing across four consecutive steps
description: The review defines CAT as the processes used "when we question or at least do not simply passively accept the accuracy of claims as givens," distinguishing it from CT by its focus on justification and on whether credible evidence supports a claim. It reports that "Alexander (2014) describes the process of CAT in four consecutive steps": starting with a claim or task for which one collects data or evidence, evaluating or judging that evidence, and integrating it with one's knowledge and beliefs. Unlike CT, the CAT literature does not consider dispositions, though prior knowledge and goals can act as moderators.
requirements: Instructionally, students should pose unanswered questions requiring data collection, gather evidence with appropriate methodologies, and discuss or debate how anticipated, unanticipated, and missing evidence should be interpreted
constraints: Dispositions are not considered in the CAT literature the review describes, although individual differences such as prior knowledge and goals can act as moderators
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students
target_learning_goals: Weighing evidence and justifying claims rather than passively accepting them
examples: The review draws parallels between these CAT-facilitating approaches and PBL and PjBL, in which a problem or question is the starting point for learning activities

article_title: Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025)
citation: Eitel, A., Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Schöne, C. (2026). Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025). Educational Psychology Review, 38, 65. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10163-2
title: The FoRe-Squares model: effective instruction requires both focus support and reward
description: The FoRe-Squares model is a 2×2 framework in which instruction is characterized by two predictor constructs: focus support (cognitive guidance and stimulation) and reward (motivational support). The model postulates that effective instruction requires both factors to enable and energize active goal-directed processing: "we expect instruction to be effective when it provides at least medium levels of both focus support and reward." Only the top-right square (both medium-to-high) is expected to yield good learning outcomes; the other three squares, where either factor or both are lacking, are expected to yield lower outcomes. The model builds on CTML and CLT for its cognitive techniques and on SEVT for its value facets.
requirements: Instruction must provide at least medium levels of both focus support and reward simultaneously for active goal-directed processing to occur
constraints: The model does not (yet) address the dynamic interactions between instructional design and individual learner characteristics, unlike CLT and CTML
target_learners: students in technology-augmented and multimedia instruction
target_learning_goals: learning outcomes from instruction
examples: The model's main prediction is illustrated in a 2×2 figure where the combination of medium to high focus support and reward is hypothesized to stimulate active goal-directed processing and good learning outcomes
key_sources: Eitel, A., Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Schöne, C. (2026). Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025). Educational Psychology Review, 38, 65. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10163-2

article_title: Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025)
citation: Eitel, A., Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Schöne, C. (2026). Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025). Educational Psychology Review, 38, 65. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10163-2
title: Assess overall instructional quality at the level of broad predictor constructs rather than individual techniques
description: The predictor-constructs approach evaluates whether instruction is likely 'good enough' by rating overall levels of focus support and reward, rather than tallying individual techniques. The authors argue it is difficult to determine "how many techniques, which combinations, and at what magnitude they need to be applied" because technique effects may interact rather than add up. Experienced researchers, designers, or teachers can expert-rate the two constructs, yielding a testable prediction and a practical heuristic for planning, designing, and evaluating instruction.
requirements: Raters must be familiar with the constructs of focus support and reward and their instantiations such as techniques, effects, and value facets
constraints: The approach complements rather than replaces the technique-focused approach; techniques map to constructs not in a one-to-one fashion
target_learners: most students in (technology-augmented) instruction
target_learning_goals: overall instructional effectiveness for learning
examples: Expert ratings of instruction with medium-to-high focus support and reward yield the testable prediction of better learning outcomes than instruction rated low on either construct
key_sources: Eitel, A., Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Schöne, C. (2026). Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025). Educational Psychology Review, 38, 65. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10163-2

article_title: Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025)
citation: Eitel, A., Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Schöne, C. (2026). Advocating the FoRe-Squares Model of Technology-Augmented Instruction: a Reply to Mayer (2025). Educational Psychology Review, 38, 65. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10163-2
title: Focus support as an instruction-level predictor construct
description: Focus support is defined in the FoRe-Squares model as "the overall degree of (meta-)cognitive guidance and stimulation for students to focus their processing on the crucial elements of instruction." It is a construct at the level of instruction, distinct from CLT's cognitive loads and CTML's processing types, which are mediator-level consequences of instruction. Cognitive techniques such as signaling, coherence, and testing are concrete instantiations of focus support, and the construct builds on CTML and CLT assumptions about stimulating active processing and reducing unnecessary processing in limited working memory.
requirements: Element interactivity should not be excessive for the target learner group for focus support to be high
target_learners: students in multimedia and technology-augmented instruction
target_learning_goals: focusing cognitive processing on the crucial elements of instruction
examples: Signaling, coherence, and testing are named as cognitive techniques that instantiate focus support in instruction

article_title: A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education
citation: Jeffrey Buckley, Niall Seery, Donal Canty. (2018). A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9432-z
title: Extended heuristic framework of spatial ability uniting CHC factors with contemporary spatial factors
description: The article synthesises the spatial factors contained in the CHC theory with factors emerging from contemporary factor-analytic research into a single extended framework, presented as a conceptual diagram. It argues that "the remit of spatial ability could theoretically contain 25 factors", some known to be more powerful representations than others. The framework deliberately emphasises narrow factors (a splitter perspective) so that a greater variety of factors can be explored across STEM education contexts.
requirements: Empirical validation of the framework as a whole after its presentation; many factors within it may not exist as individual factors and may instead represent, in whole or part, currently well-established spatial factors
constraints: The framework is heuristic and not recognised as an absolute model; newly included factors are hypothetical or tentatively defined pending investigation
target_learners: STEM learners across disciplines and educational levels
target_learning_goals: Understanding and developing the spatial factors underlying STEM educational performance
examples: The article presents Table 2 listing factors not represented in the CHC theory (e.g. spatial orientation, spatial relations, imagery quality, dynamic factors, directional and speed judgement) and Figure 2 as a conceptual diagram of the extended framework.
key_sources: Jeffrey Buckley, Niall Seery, Donal Canty. (2018). A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9432-z

article_title: A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education
citation: Jeffrey Buckley, Niall Seery, Donal Canty. (2018). A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9432-z
title: CHC theory definition of spatial ability as visual processing (Gv) with eleven first-order spatial factors in three categories
description: Within the CHC theory, spatial ability is the second-order Gv (visual processing) factor, defined as the ability to make use of simulated mental imagery to solve problems, with the empirical definition being the first-order factors that load on it. The article reports that "In total, 11 first-order factors are shown to load on spatial ability in the CHC theory", grouped into spatial skills (e.g. visualisation, speeded rotation), perceptual factors (e.g. perceptual alternations), and memory factors (e.g. visual memory). Table 1 prints definitions for each factor.
requirements: Adoption of the CHC theory as the contemporary framework of cognitive factors, acknowledging it is not an absolute model and further factors may be underrepresented
constraints: The printed definition acts more as a description; the empirical definition is the set of loading first-order factors
target_learners: STEM learners across disciplines and educational levels
target_learning_goals: Defining and measuring spatial ability relative to empirical factor structure
examples: Table 1 of the article lists the eleven CHC spatial factors with definitions, including visualisation (Vz), speeded rotation (SR), closure speed (CS), flexibility of closure (CF), visual memory (MV), spatial scanning (SS) and imagery (IM).
key_sources: Jeffrey Buckley, Niall Seery, Donal Canty. (2018). A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9432-z

article_title: A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education
citation: Jeffrey Buckley, Niall Seery, Donal Canty. (2018). A Heuristic Framework of Spatial Ability: a Review and Synthesis of Spatial Factor Literature to Support its Translation into STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9432-z
title: Classify a spatial factor only if it concerns visual stimuli, is uninfluenced by semantic knowledge, and is theoretically separable from existing factors
description: The article establishes inclusion and exclusion criteria for calling a factor a spatial factor, because factor names do not always align across studies and knowledge-laden factors have been misclassified. It states that "the criteria used to identify factors as spatial factors are that they are mental abilities concerned specifically with visual stimuli and which are not influenced by semantic knowledge", and that newly identified factors must at minimum be theoretically separable from existing factors. This guards against misrepresenting knowledge-dependent performance as spatial cognition.
requirements: Test instruments may require contextual adaptations, but their capacity to validly identify a unique factor should not be compromised; semantic knowledge must not dictate access to the cognitive resources
constraints: Factors describing feelings, fixation periods, or knowledge-reliant tasks (e.g. geographic knowledge in the Spatial Thinking Ability Test) do not qualify as spatial factors
target_learners: STEM education researchers designing studies of spatial factors
target_learning_goals: Accurate identification and measurement of spatial factors in educational research
examples: The article excludes Roff's maintenance-of-contact and effect-of-uncertainty factors and flags Lee and Bednarz's spatial thinking components as relying on geographic knowledge rather than qualifying as spatial factors.

article_title: Basic Psychological Needs Under Constrained Autonomy: A Substantive–Methodological Reflection and Analysis of School Leaders’ Needs from a Self-Determination Theory Perspective
citation: Marsh, H. W., Ryan, R. M., Dicke, T., Pekrun, R., Guo, J., Bradshaw, E. L., Reeve, J., Lüdtke, O., Clarke, T., & Waterschoot, J. (2025). Basic Psychological Needs Under Constrained Autonomy: A Substantive–Methodological Reflection and Analysis of School Leaders' Needs from a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10079-3
title: SDT dual-process model of need satisfaction and frustration applied to constrained-autonomy leadership roles
description: The article applies Self-Determination Theory's dual-process model, in which need satisfaction and need frustration "are not merely opposite ends of a continuum; instead, they represent distinct processes", to school leaders operating under constrained autonomy—formal authority paired with limited discretion. Job resources are expected to feed primarily into need satisfaction and positive outcomes, whereas job demands feed primarily into need frustration and negative outcomes. School leaders are theorized as a boundary case that both crafts and experiences the climates they lead, making them a novel test of the model's generalizability.
requirements: Measurement must distinguish satisfaction from frustration as separate valence facets (e.g., the BPNSFS two-facet operationalization) rather than collapsing them into one continuum.
constraints: The article treats time methodologically (replicability across occasions), not as a basis for temporal or causal inference; findings are interpreted within the Australian school-leadership context.
target_learners: school leaders (principals and deputy/associate leadership team members)
target_learning_goals: understanding how workplace demands and resources shape leaders' motivation, well-being, and burnout through basic psychological need processes
examples: The study tested the model with 1,950 Australian school leaders using a two-wave survey and a nomological network of 64 workplace variables organized by the Job Demands–Resources framework.
