article_title: Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review
citation: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7
title: Two-dimensional taxonomy of embodied learning environments for graphing motion based on bodily involvement and immediacy
description: The review proposes categorizing embodied learning environments for graphing motion on two dimensions: bodily involvement (own motion vs. observing/influencing others' or objects' motion, ranging from "motor execution" to "motor mirroring") and immediacy (immediate vs. non-immediate, from "direct enactment" to "reactivated enactment"). Crossing these dimensions yields four classes: Class I — Immediate Own Motion, Class II — Immediate Others/Objects' Motion, Class III — Non-immediate Own Motion, and Class IV — Non-immediate Others/Objects' Motion. The authors state: "we propose to categorize embodied learning environments supporting students ' understanding of graphing motion on two dimensions: bodily involvement and immediacy". Immediacy concerns whether the graphical representation is constructed in parallel with the motion or at a later stage.
requirements: Learning environments must contain task-relevant bodily experiences that can be coded on bodily involvement and immediacy; environments with multiple degrees are assigned to the highest degree
constraints: The authors note task integration is a less informative dimension for graphing motion because "the congruency between a motion event (either experienced or observed) and the graph of that motion is already an essential element of the learning environment"
target_learners: Students from primary education to higher education in mathematics and physics
target_learning_goals: Understanding graphical representations of motion (distance–time, velocity–time, acceleration–time graphs)
examples: The 62 reviewed learning environments were classified into the four classes; Class I contained 34 environments, Class II and IV 12 each, and Class III 4
key_sources: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7

article_title: Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review
citation: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7
title: Moderate embodiment view: bodily experiences constitute the fundament of knowledge while allowing off-line simulation and links to a-modal conceptual knowledge
description: The review frames embodied learning environments within a moderate view of embodied cognition, positioned between simple and radical readings. It acknowledges "the critical importance of bodily experiences as part of the meaning of both concrete and abstract concepts, thus as constituting the fundament of all human knowledge, but allows for two additional resources": off-line grounding through mental simulation re-using sensorimotor circuits, and Hebbian-associative connection of multimodal sensorimotor cognition to a-modal verbal conceptual knowledge. Under this view, both making one's own movements and observing others' or objects' movements (via mirroring mechanisms) count as embodied, and embodied simulation supplies previously acquired sensorimotor experiences when immediate interaction is unavailable.
requirements: Perceptual-motor experiences must be task-relevant for the learning content for embodiment to support learning
constraints: The radical view is noted to have difficulty explaining cognition in the absence of direct environmental stimuli, such as symbolic language and mental arithmetic
target_learners: Learners across education levels, from primary education to higher education
target_learning_goals: Grounding abstract formal mathematical and scientific concepts in concrete bodily experiences
examples: The review cites studies where task-relevant whole bodily motion conditions outperformed non-motion conditions in learning two-digit numbers, and where observing a teacher demonstrating a geometry concept improved understanding
key_sources: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7

article_title: Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review
citation: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7
title: Review corpus of 44 peer-reviewed articles comprising 62 embodied learning environments for graphing motion
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 44 empirical, peer-reviewed journal articles in English, identified through searches in Web of Science, ERIC, PsycINFO, and Scopus (initial 1953 articles, 1651 after deduplication) plus snowballing. "The 44 articles contained a total of 62 different embodied learning environments", some used as control and some as experimental conditions. Each environment was coded on bodily involvement and immediacy; an independent second rater coded a subsample of 12 articles containing 20 learning environments, with Cohen's Kappa = 1.00 for bodily involvement and 0.74 for immediacy. All articles addressed mathematics, physics, or both, with graphs representing motion data.
requirements: Included articles needed a clear description of tools and tasks and task-relevant bodily experiences
constraints: The number of bodily actions and their duration was not coded due to lacking information in most articles
target_learners: Students from primary education to higher education
target_learning_goals: Learning graphing of change and motion in mathematics and physics
examples: The search flowchart reports 1953 initial articles reduced to 36 relevant articles, with 13 added by snowballing and 5 excluded for lacking description of the embodied learning environment
key_sources: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7

article_title: Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review
citation: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7
title: Design embodied graphing environments with real-world elements so students can link personal experiences and physical actions to formal mathematics or physics concepts
description: Among the mediating factors the review uncovered, real-world context is the most frequently mentioned (15 articles). The review reports that "through a learning environment containing real-world elements, links can be made between students ' personal experiences, physical actions, and formal mathematics or physics concepts". Real-world contexts also draw on students' prior knowledge and experiences and present the environment as a natural venue for scientific exploration, for example microcomputer-based laboratories providing genuine scientific experiences.
requirements: Learning environment elements must be recognizable from or connected to students' real-world experiences, such as authentic graphs or real objects in motion
constraints: Some reviewed environments use simplified worlds; Solomon et al. use the term micro world for a learning environment less complex than the real world
target_learners: Primary through higher education students in mathematics and physics
target_learning_goals: Connecting bodily and real-world motion experiences to formal graphing concepts such as distance–time and velocity–time relations
examples: Mitnik et al. let students study the motion of a real robot in an explorative, immersive environment; Holbert and Wilensky used authentic player-created graphs resembling typical velocity–time graphs
key_sources: Carolien Duijzer, Marja Van den Heuvel-Panhuizen, Michiel Veldhuis, Michiel Doorman, & Paul Leseman. (2019). Embodied Learning Environments for Graphing Motion: a Systematic Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09471-7

article_title: How do Students Regulate Their Use of Multiple Choice Practice Tests?
citation: Badali, S., Rawson, K.A. & Dunlosky, J. (2023). How do Students Regulate Their Use of Multiple Choice Practice Tests?. Educational Psychology Review 35, 43. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09761-1
title: Self-regulated practice task with restudy, practice-test, and item-removal options
description: This task environment let undergraduate learners control their own practice of German-English word pairs. After an initial study trial for each pair, "they had the options to restudy an item, take a practice test, or remove it from further practice." One self-regulated group used multiple-choice practice questions and a comparison self-regulated group used cued-recall questions, allowing the authors to observe how students regulate testing with different question formats and to compare their outcomes with experimenter-controlled criterion groups.
requirements: Learners must have options to restudy an item, take a practice test, or remove it from further practice after an initial study trial.
constraints: The article evaluates the task with German-English word pairs and undergraduate participants.
target_learners: undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: learning and retaining German-English vocabulary translations
examples: Participants practiced word pairs across sessions, choosing restudy, multiple-choice or cued-recall testing, or dropping items, with experimenter-controlled groups practicing to a higher number of correct answers for comparison.
key_sources: Badali, S., Rawson, K.A. & Dunlosky, J. (2023). How do Students Regulate Their Use of Multiple Choice Practice Tests?. Educational Psychology Review 35, 43. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09761-1

article_title: A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Defining and Measuring Task Complexity Through Element Interactivity
citation: Ouhao Chen · Fred Paas · John Sweller. (2023). A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Defining and Measuring Task Complexity Through Element Interactivity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09782-w
title: Element interactivity as a cognitive load theory-based measure of task complexity
description: The article proposes that the complexity learners experience is determined by element interactivity: "An element is defined as a concept or procedure that needs to be learned, which can be decomposed based on a learner's level of expertise." High element interactivity "occurs when more elements than can be handled by working memory must be processed concurrently." The measure is an amalgam of information structure and long-term memory knowledge, so the same task is complex for novices but simple for experts. It underpins both intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load.
requirements: Estimating element interactivity requires instructors to know learners' knowledge levels and the characteristics of the information under different instructional procedures
constraints: Element interactivity is an estimate rather than a precise measure because learners' long-term knowledge cannot be measured exactly
The emphasis has primarily been on well-structured tasks such as mathematics, with fewer examples for expository materials
target_learners: All learners of biologically secondary information, from novices to experts
target_learning_goals: Determining and managing the complexity of learning tasks across domains
key_sources: Ouhao Chen · Fred Paas · John Sweller. (2023). A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Defining and Measuring Task Complexity Through Element Interactivity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09782-w

article_title: A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Defining and Measuring Task Complexity Through Element Interactivity
citation: Ouhao Chen · Fred Paas · John Sweller. (2023). A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Defining and Measuring Task Complexity Through Element Interactivity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09782-w
title: Instructional design must account for element interactivity because cognitive load effects shrink or reverse as it decreases
description: The article recommends that instructional procedures be chosen according to the element interactivity of the material and the learners' expertise: "As element interactivity decreases, the size of effects decreases and may reverse." Because "most cognitive load theory effects disappear or even reverse when students study low element interactivity information", the same information may suit one knowledge level and be unsuitable for another. Element interactivity or a similar architecture-aware complexity measure is described as "an essential ingredient of a viable instructional design science."
requirements: Instructors must estimate learners' prior knowledge and the element interactivity of materials and procedures
constraints: Element interactivity estimates are not precise; effects of small differences in interactivity are unlikely to be visible in experiments, whereas very large differences are readily demonstrated
target_learners: Learners at differing expertise levels studying biologically secondary information
target_learning_goals: Selecting instructional procedures appropriate to task complexity and learner expertise
examples: The review notes experiments typically study only very large differences in element interactivity, such as memorising periodic table symbols versus balancing chemical equations
key_sources: Ouhao Chen · Fred Paas · John Sweller. (2023). A Cognitive Load Theory Approach to Defining and Measuring Task Complexity Through Element Interactivity. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09782-w

article_title: Beyond the “Wow” Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making
citation: Guido Makransky, Ban M. Shiwalia, Tue Herlau, Steven Blurton. (2025). Beyond the "Wow" Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10039-x
title: Framework for student-focused GenAI educational applications that prompt generative learning activities and use GLA products as formative assessment
description: The article proposes a framework for developing student-focused GenAI educational applications grounded in generative learning theory and the select-integrate-organize framework, in which "interaction is initiated by a) the learner, b) the AIEd system, and c) the instructor." Because many learners do not spontaneously engage in sense-making, the system can systematically prompt generative learning activities and "use the quality of these products as formative assessments to inform further adjustments of learning materials and GLA support." The framework adopts an augmentation perspective in which AI complements human intelligence, and it distinguishes GenAI tools designed for students from tools merely used by students, following the Holmes and Tuomi taxonomy.
requirements: The GenAI system must be able to prompt learners who do not automatically initiate sense-making and to assess the quality of their GLA products to adapt subsequent support
constraints: The article states it is not proposing that GenAI is necessary or, in its current technological iteration, optimal for progressing from explicit instruction through scaffolded practice to independent practice
target_learners: university students in an authentic cognitive psychology course
high school psychology students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of course content
generative sense-making during lessons
examples: ChatTutor operationalizes the framework by prompting students to engage in the GLA of teaching with scaffolded feedback and by referencing course slides when generating replies
key_sources: Guido Makransky, Ban M. Shiwalia, Tue Herlau, Steven Blurton. (2025). Beyond the "Wow" Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10039-x

article_title: Beyond the “Wow” Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making
citation: Guido Makransky, Ban M. Shiwalia, Tue Herlau, Steven Blurton. (2025). Beyond the "Wow" Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10039-x
title: ChatTutor: a theory-informed GenAI chatbot that scaffolds the generative learning activity of teaching
description: ChatTutor is a student-focused GenAI chatbot built on generative learning theory, in which "The ChatTutor chatbot engages students in personalized written conversations based on the course slides and texts and responds to address the specific answers provided by students and correcting any misconceptions or gaps in knowledge." Its interface presents self-explanation prompts developed in a workshop with instructors one at a time, lets students respond and ask follow-up questions, and displays specific feedback helping students evaluate and improve their responses, while a side panel shows targeted course knowledge the chatbot references. It simulates a student-tutor interaction, intervening when misconceptions are evident or help is requested, and allows escalating questions to a human instructor.
requirements: A targeted knowledge bank linked to the course slides and texts so the chatbot's prompts and feedback reference the taught content
constraints: In the studies the generative activity lasted approximately 15 minutes in Study 1 and at least 25 minutes in Study 2, and the tool was evaluated within authentic course lessons rather than as standalone study support
target_learners: university psychology students
high school psychology students
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of the Sternberg memory scanning experiment
self-explaining and teaching as generative learning activities
examples: In Study 1, two exercise classes used ChatTutor, two used an identical interface linked to ChatGPT-4, and three received teaching-as-usual; in Study 2 the design was replicated with 234 high school students and a re-studying control
key_sources: Guido Makransky, Ban M. Shiwalia, Tue Herlau, Steven Blurton. (2025). Beyond the "Wow" Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10039-x

article_title: Beyond the “Wow” Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making
citation: Guido Makransky, Ban M. Shiwalia, Tue Herlau, Steven Blurton. (2025). Beyond the "Wow" Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10039-x
title: Use theoretically informed GenAI chatbots to scale personalized scaffolding of generative learning activities where instructor formative assessment is not feasible
description: The principle is that GenAI chatbots should be designed to prompt and guide generative learning activities with personalized, formative feedback, because assessing knowledge gaps and giving targeted feedback is time-consuming for instructors. The authors propose that "GenAI can be used to scale this process when resources to formatively assess students and provide personalized support are not possible." Support should progress through explicit instruction, scaffolded practice, and independent practice, with specific rather than generic prompts, since specific prompting and scaffolding have been shown to be more effective in explaining, visualizing, or enacting concepts.
requirements: Guided rather than discovery-only use, since complete discovery without guidance is ineffective for novices; the chatbot needs targeted prompts and a knowledge bank aligned with the curriculum
constraints: The authors state they are not proposing GenAI is necessary or currently optimal for progressing from explicit instruction to independent practice, and independent practice was not investigated in this study
target_learners: novice learners who do not spontaneously engage in sense-making
students in authentic course settings
target_learning_goals: generative sense-making through teaching and self-explanation
durable conceptual knowledge
examples: ChatTutor prompts students to explain specific content, provides scaffolded feedback correcting misconceptions, and was tested against generic ChatGPT and control conditions in two between-subjects experiments
key_sources: Guido Makransky, Ban M. Shiwalia, Tue Herlau, Steven Blurton. (2025). Beyond the "Wow" Factor: Using Generative AI for Increasing Generative Sense-Making. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10039-x

article_title: Placing Social and Emotional Support at the Center of School Climate: A Scoping Review of Measures for Middle and Secondary Schools
citation: Castro, C., Barata, M. C., Alexandre, J., & Santos, R. (2026). Placing Social and Emotional Support at the Center of School Climate: A Scoping Review of Measures for Middle and Secondary Schools. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10192-x
title: Integrative model of the social and emotional domain permeating all school climate dimensions
description: The review proposes that the social-emotional domain should not be treated as an additional school climate dimension but as a domain that permeates all dimensions. Relationships, safety, teaching practices and leadership all have inherent social and emotional aspects, operationalized as behavioral, relational, or policy-oriented forms of SEL support that affect students' social and emotional development. The article states the domain "is not to be framed as an additional dimension of school climate, but rather as a domain that permeates all school climate dimensions", illustrated by Figure 4 revisiting the study's conceptual framework.
requirements: Researchers and practitioners measuring school climate should critically assess the extent to which available instruments embed SEL support across dimensions
constraints: The model was developed from a scoping review of measures for upper middle and secondary school settings
target_learners: Upper middle and secondary school students (grades 7-12)
target_learning_goals: Support for students' social and emotional learning within school climate measurement and practice
examples: The review illustrates the model with students collaborating to solve a disagreement, a teacher motivating a struggling student, and a SEL-focused instruction hour led by the principal as part of the curriculum.
key_sources: Castro, C., Barata, M. C., Alexandre, J., & Santos, R. (2026). Placing Social and Emotional Support at the Center of School Climate: A Scoping Review of Measures for Middle and Secondary Schools. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10192-x

article_title: The Effects of Problem-Based, Project-Based, and Case-Based Learning on Students’ Motivation: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Wijnia, L., Noordzij, G., Arends, L. R. A., Rikers, R. M. J. P., & Loyens, S. M. M. (2024). The Effects of Problem-Based, Project-Based, and Case-Based Learning on Students' Motivation: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09864-3
title: Three-question taxonomy of motivation constructs: beliefs, task value, and reasons for engaging
description: The article organizes motivation constructs using Graham and Weiner's three basic questions — "Can I do it?", "Do I want to do it?" and "Why am I doing this task?" — mapping them onto competence and control beliefs, feelings-related and importance-related task value, and intrinsic versus extrinsic reasons for studying, plus attitudes toward school subjects including a future-interest subcategory. Figure 1 provides "a visual overview of the motivation categories used in our meta-analysis". The taxonomy structures which motivation measures were coded and how moderator analyses were run per construct.
requirements: Motivation measures must be mappable onto the constructs in Fig. 1 (competence beliefs, importance, feelings-related values such as interest/enjoyment) on Likert-type or continuous scales
constraints: Intrinsic motivation within self-determination theory is distinguished from interest value: it concerns the origin of engagement, whereas interest value concerns the source of the activity's value
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students
target_learning_goals: Student motivation in problem-driven learning contexts
examples: The meta-analysis coded 288 effect sizes into these categories, treating reasons for studying as a dichotomous intrinsic-versus-extrinsic construct because most primary studies did so
key_sources: Wijnia, L., Noordzij, G., Arends, L. R. A., Rikers, R. M. J. P., & Loyens, S. M. M. (2024). The Effects of Problem-Based, Project-Based, and Case-Based Learning on Students' Motivation: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09864-3

article_title: Writing Self-Efficacy in Postsecondary Students: a Scoping Review
citation: Kim M. Mitchell, Sharon Zumbrunn, Danielle N. Berry, Lisa Demczuk. (2023). Writing Self-Efficacy in Postsecondary Students: a Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09798-2
title: Writing self-efficacy as beliefs about writing ability within Bandura's social cognitive framework of triadic reciprocality
description: The review organizes writing self-efficacy research within Bandura's social cognitive framework, defining writing self-efficacy as "a learner's beliefs about their ability to write" and situating it in triadic reciprocality, where learning depends on reciprocal interactions among thoughts, behaviors, and environment. On this view, writing self-efficacy beliefs influence perseverance, academic choices, and performance, while social and contextual factors such as feedback and instructional conditions shape the beliefs in turn. The review uses this framework to justify its focus on writing contexts and pedagogy.
requirements: Studies must employ a self-efficacy measure specific to writing rather than a general academic self-efficacy measure
constraints: The review excluded reflective, blog, and creative writing contexts, focusing only on academic writing in postsecondary English-language settings
target_learners: postsecondary undergraduate and graduate students
target_learning_goals: writing ability and writing success in academic contexts
key_sources: Kim M. Mitchell, Sharon Zumbrunn, Danielle N. Berry, Lisa Demczuk. (2023). Writing Self-Efficacy in Postsecondary Students: a Scoping Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09798-2

article_title: Perfectionism in Academically Gifted Students: A Systematic Review
citation: Grugan, M. C., Hill, A. P., Madigan, D. J., Donachie, T. C., Olsson, L. F., & Etherson, M. E. (2021). Perfectionism and Academically Gifted Students: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09597-7
title: Two-factor higher-order model of perfectionism (PS vs PC) as the review's organising framework
description: The review organises all evidence using the two-factor higher-order model of perfectionism (Stoeber & Otto, 2006), which integrates different perfectionism measures into two dimensions. Perfectionistic strivings subsume "aspects of perfectionism associated with self-oriented striving for perfection and the setting of very high personal performance standards". Perfectionistic concerns subsume concerns about mistakes, fear of negative evaluation, and negative reactions to imperfection. The review classifies subscales from F-MPS, HF-MPS, CAPS, APS-R and PNPS as PS or PC indicators.
requirements: Studies must use multidimensional perfectionism measures whose subscales can be classified as PS or PC indicators
constraints: Some indicators such as organisation and order subscales are peripheral facets that may load on a third factor independent of PS and PC
target_learners: young students identified as academically gifted
target_learning_goals: understanding personality correlates of academic achievement and well-being in gifted learners
examples: The review categorised the personal standards subscale of the F-MPS and socially prescribed perfectionism subscales of the HF-MPS and CAPS as PS and PC indicators respectively
key_sources: Grugan, M. C., Hill, A. P., Madigan, D. J., Donachie, T. C., Olsson, L. F., & Etherson, M. E. (2021). Perfectionism and Academically Gifted Students: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09597-7

article_title: Perfectionism in Academically Gifted Students: A Systematic Review
citation: Grugan, M. C., Hill, A. P., Madigan, D. J., Donachie, T. C., Olsson, L. F., & Etherson, M. E. (2021). Perfectionism and Academically Gifted Students: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09597-7
title: Evidence base of 36 studies (N = 10,737) on perfectionism in academically gifted students, 1994–2018
description: The review assembles and catalogues the full empirical evidence base on perfectionism in young academically gifted students: "We identified a total of 36 studies (N = 10,737 students) published over 24 years (1994–2018)". Each study is coded for gifted-identification method, perfectionism measure, design, and outcomes, and appraised with a methodological quality score. Twenty-four studies used a variable-based approach and twelve a group-based approach, organised into achievement, personality, motivation, emotion and well-being, and interpersonal domains.
requirements: Studies must include an empirical examination of perfectionism in students identified as gifted within an educational context, aged under 18, with criterion variables or group comparisons
constraints: Studies vary considerably in how giftedness is operationalised and measured, so the review cautions that "some caution is required when comparing and aggregating findings across the studies"
target_learners: young students identified as academically gifted
target_learning_goals: mapping correlates and consequences of perfectionism in gifted education research
examples: The included studies span the USA, China, Czech Republic, Australia, Canada, the Philippines, and one Japan–USA cross-national study
key_sources: Grugan, M. C., Hill, A. P., Madigan, D. J., Donachie, T. C., Olsson, L. F., & Etherson, M. E. (2021). Perfectionism and Academically Gifted Students: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09597-7

article_title: The Caring Professor: A Meta-Analysis of Associations between Faculty-Student Relationships and Postsecondary Student Success
citation: Fathi, Z., Zarei, P., Fong, C. J., Saha, A. K., & Sharmeen, S. (2026). The Caring Professor: A Meta-Analysis of Associations between Faculty-Student Relationships and Postsecondary Student Success. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10100-9
title: Integrated theoretical framework: FSRs support success by meeting psychological needs, providing emotional security, affirming identities, and enabling campus integration
description: The article organizes its review around psychological models (self-determination theory, relationship motivation theory, attachment theory) and higher education models (the culturally engaging campus environment framework, and Tinto's and Astin's integration theories). It argues that "satisfaction of three basic psychological needs of relatedness, autonomy, and competence is essential for triggering human motivation and psychological thriving", and that attachment theory frames faculty as "secure bases" and "safe havens". Integration theories add that FSRs contribute to both academic and social integration, which together shape persistence.
requirements: The framework applies to postsecondary settings where students perceive relational closeness with faculty, not merely frequent interaction
constraints: The article acknowledges that frequent interaction does not necessarily mean students are perceiving relational closeness
target_learners: postsecondary/college students
target_learning_goals: academic achievement (GPA, grades)
persistence and retention
examples: The framework guided the meta-analysis's hypotheses that care-characterized dimensions and demographic/institutional factors would moderate associations
key_sources: Fathi, Z., Zarei, P., Fong, C. J., Saha, A. K., & Sharmeen, S. (2026). The Caring Professor: A Meta-Analysis of Associations between Faculty-Student Relationships and Postsecondary Student Success. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10100-9

article_title: The Caring Professor: A Meta-Analysis of Associations between Faculty-Student Relationships and Postsecondary Student Success
citation: Fathi, Z., Zarei, P., Fong, C. J., Saha, A. K., & Sharmeen, S. (2026). The Caring Professor: A Meta-Analysis of Associations between Faculty-Student Relationships and Postsecondary Student Success. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10100-9
title: Six-dimension taxonomy of faculty-student relationships extracted from over a dozen measures
description: To handle heterogeneity across FSR measures, the authors inductively reviewed more than a dozen survey instruments and derived a categorical coding scheme. As they state, "we extracted the following six dimensions: caring attitude, approachability and accessibility, personal connection and bonding, inclusivity, mutual respect, and encouragement and engagement." Each dimension has an operational definition and sample items (Table 2), and each effect size was flagged via a checklist approach for which dimensions its measure contained, enabling dimension-based moderator analysis.
requirements: Coding requires examining original scale items to determine which relational dimensions a measure captures, since not all surveys consistently contain items tapping these dimensions
constraints: The dimensions were coded qualitatively from measures, and a single scale could capture multiple dimensions, so dimension flags are not mutually exclusive
target_learners: postsecondary/college students
target_learning_goals: conceptualizing and measuring perceived relational closeness with faculty
examples: Table 2 lists operational definitions and sample items, e.g., caring attitude: "My professor cares about students' well-being"

article_title: Citizenship in the Elementary Classroom Through the Lens of Peer Relations
citation: Krijnen, M. A., Wansink, B. G. J., van den Berg, Y. H. M., van Tartwijk, J., & Mainhard, T. (2024). Citizenship in the Elementary Classroom Through the Lens of Peer Relations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09870-5
title: Lived citizenship: children enact citizenship through everyday peer behaviors and relationships in the classroom
description: The review adopts the concept of lived citizenship, in which "children are citizens already in their own ways" and enact citizenship in relation to others within their contexts. Common classroom behaviors and relationships are thus viewed as expressions of children's citizenship, making the classroom a practice ground where enacting and learning citizenship are intertwined. The review connects this to peer relations research, which views children as active agents shaped by the social classroom context.
requirements: A classroom context in which children interact and build interpersonal relationships with peers and teachers
constraints: The constructs used (prosociality, aggression, acceptance, rejection) do not exhaustively cover all citizenship competences, as the review itself notes
target_learners: Elementary school students
target_learning_goals: Social citizenship competences such as solidarity, peace, and social cohesion
key_sources: Krijnen, M. A., Wansink, B. G. J., van den Berg, Y. H. M., van Tartwijk, J., & Mainhard, T. (2024). Citizenship in the Elementary Classroom Through the Lens of Peer Relations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09870-5

article_title: Citizenship in the Elementary Classroom Through the Lens of Peer Relations
citation: Krijnen, M. A., Wansink, B. G. J., van den Berg, Y. H. M., van Tartwijk, J., & Mainhard, T. (2024). Citizenship in the Elementary Classroom Through the Lens of Peer Relations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09870-5
title: Peer nomination (sociometric) methodology for assessing classroom citizenship behaviors and relationships
description: Peer nomination methods ask children to nominate classmates on behavioral and affective items, so that "children act as multiple observers of classmates' typical behaviors and of their relationships with others." Behavioral items describe interpersonal behavior (e.g., who helps others) and affective items capture relationships (e.g., whom classmates like most). The review proposes this approach as a systematic, quantitative complement to self-report measures in citizenship research, mapping classroom social dynamics into a social network.
requirements: Peer group of classmates who observe each other regularly; nomination items for behaviors and affective relationships
constraints: The review notes equating low aggression with peace is arguably too simplistic, and nominations may reflect perceivers' biases
target_learners: Elementary school students
target_learning_goals: Assessing enacted solidarity, peace, and social cohesion in the classroom
examples: The review's Fig. 1 example: child A nominated by 11 classmates for helping, child B by 1, with a classroom density of 0.32

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Jere Brophy
citation: Daniel Robinson. (2009). Editor's Note: Remembering Jere Brophy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9115-x
title: Improve education through research-based principles and strategies rather than criticism — less heat, more light
description: Carolyn Evertson's tribute presents Brophy's guiding stance for research on teaching: educational problems are not solved by heaping criticism but by finding research-based principles and strategies that enable teachers and schools to be effective. In the preface to Learning from Teaching he wrote that education needs less heat and more light, and Evertson says he dedicated his career to showing what worked.
requirements: Research must be directed at finding solutions that enable teachers and schools to be effective, as the tribute describes Brophy's commitment
target_learners: teachers and schools as improvement targets, K-12 classrooms
target_learning_goals: improving educational practice and teaching effectiveness
examples: Evertson cites Brophy's preface line education needs less heat and more light and his career-spanning work from effective praise to motivating students to learn and helping teachers deal with problem students
key_sources: Daniel Robinson. (2009). Editor's Note: Remembering Jere Brophy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9115-x

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Jere Brophy
citation: Daniel Robinson. (2009). Editor's Note: Remembering Jere Brophy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9115-x
title: Looking in Classrooms — Brophy and Good's long-running textbook
description: Looking in Classrooms is the Brophy–Good book referenced in Tom Good's tribute. Good recalls their final exchange was the every-two-year discussion of whether to revise it again, and that they had decided to rest on their laurels and not do a new edition. The book is presented as the product of their long collaboration on teaching research.
requirements: Periodic revision decisions by the authors, as described in the tribute
constraints: As of the tribute, the authors had decided not to produce a new edition
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in education
target_learning_goals: understanding effective teaching and classroom observation
examples: Good recalls introducing Brophy as the winner of the APA Division 15 Thorndike Award and their decision to stop revising the book

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Jere Brophy
citation: Daniel Robinson. (2009). Editor's Note: Remembering Jere Brophy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-009-9115-x
title: Brophy and Good's chapter in the Third Handbook of Research on Teaching — the definitive archival summary of process-outcome research, 1973–1983
description: Rosenshine's tribute identifies the chapter by Jere and Tom Good in the Third Handbook of Research on Teaching as containing a summary of each process-outcome study Brophy and colleagues conducted. He calls it a detailed, accessible account of the process-outcome research studies from 1973 to 1983 and the definitive archival summary of that research program.
requirements: Serves as an archival record; readers seeking the underlying studies are directed to this chapter
target_learners: education researchers and graduate students
target_learning_goals: understanding the process-outcome research tradition on teaching effectiveness
examples: Rosenshine states the chapter summarizes each of the process-outcome studies Brophy and his colleagues conducted

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: The practicing connections framework: instructional design organized around three connection types and three design principles
description: The practicing connections framework holds that deep understanding in complex domains develops when students repeatedly practice making connections among a domain's contexts and practices, its core concepts, and its key representations. The article states: "we propose three types of connections that should be the focus of instructional design: the world (including practices and contexts); core concepts, which organize the domain; and key representations used for communication and thinking within a domain." It pairs these with three pedagogical principles: making connections explicit, productive struggle, and deliberate practice over time. The framework was developed while designing an online introductory statistics textbook and is offered as a complement to skill-focused frameworks such as 4C/ID.
requirements: Instruction must be designed over long periods such as a semester-long course, since understanding in complex domains develops slowly
A detailed analysis of what expert practice in the domain looks like must precede design decisions
constraints: The authors position the framework as a complement to frameworks such as 4C/ID, which they say apply especially well to complex skills; the framework targets domains requiring reasoning with abstract conceptual structure
target_learners: Novice students in complex academic domains such as statistics, mathematics, and science
target_learning_goals: Deep understanding and transferable knowledge in a complex domain
Adaptive expertise: flexibly applying knowledge in novel contexts
examples: The authors organized their online introductory statistics textbook around three core practices (explore variation, model variation, evaluate and compare models) and three core concepts, repeatedly asking students to translate across five key representations.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: Three core concepts organizing introductory statistics: statistical model, distribution, and randomness
description: In their introductory statistics textbook the authors selected three core concepts to organize the domain: statistical model (captured as DATA = MODEL + ERROR), distribution (following Wild, "the pattern of variation in a variable", including the sample data, data generating process, and sampling distributions of the distribution triad), and randomness as a data generating process. They state: "we chose to focus our textbook around three core concepts: statistical model, distribution, and randomness." Concepts were chosen for being connectable throughout the course, accessible to novices, not needing later unlearning, and jointly supporting coherent understanding.
requirements: Core concepts must be accessible to novices within their zone of proximal development
Concepts must not need to be unlearned later and must form a coherent whole without introducing misconceptions
constraints: Concepts introduced to novices are almost always simplified in complex domains, and the authors warn against simplification that yields a collection of concepts failing to form a coherent whole
target_learners: Novice students in introductory statistics at the college level
target_learning_goals: Coherent conceptual understanding of statistics that transfers to advanced courses and data analysis practice
examples: The mean is introduced as the simplest statistical model; standard deviation quantifies error around model predictions; ANOVA and regression are both taught as examples of linear models.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: Five key representations for introductory statistics: verbal descriptions, visualizations, word equations, GLM notation, and R code
description: The textbook asks students to repeatedly translate and connect among five representations: "verbal descriptions, visualizations, word equations, GLM (general linear model) notation, and R code." Students describe models in words, write word equations (e.g., Thumb Length = Height + other stuff), map them to DATA = MODEL + ERROR, write R code, and learn GLM notation, which the authors value for its generalizability, alignability with other representations, and ecological validity. Algebra was deliberately excluded because students do not find it accessible or useful.
requirements: Selected representations must be accessible to novices, important for the field, and productive for making connections
Learning a representational system requires an investment of time and effort, so the set must be limited
constraints: GLM notation is described as a difficult representational system for students to learn
target_learners: Novice college students in introductory statistics
target_learning_goals: Using and connecting multiple representations of statistical models
Participating in computational, reproducible data analysis practices
examples: Students fit a regression model in R, save predictions into the data frame, plot predictions against the explanatory variable, and explain why predictions coincide with a regression line while data points do not.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: Make domain connections explicit for students rather than relying on self-discovery
description: This principle holds that the connections among core concepts, key representations, and the world must be explicitly pointed out during instruction, because learners often fail to recognize structural relatedness on their own. The authors implement it in two ways: structuring the textbook so connections are visible and stated (e.g., every concept tied to DATA = MODEL + ERROR), and repeatedly asking questions whose answers are the target connections. They also use R to reduce extraneous load, leaving resources for reflection on connections, consistent with cognitive load theory's distinction of intrinsic, germane, and extraneous load.
requirements: Instructional materials must be structured so the targeted connections recur and are named in the text
Questions must repeatedly ask students to articulate the connections themselves
constraints: The article notes effort alone is usually not enough; explicitness must be combined with productive struggle rather than replacing learner effort
target_learners: Novice learners in complex academic domains, especially those who get stuck on surface features
target_learning_goals: Recognizing structural relatedness across problems and contexts
Building coherent domain knowledge
examples: When the mean is introduced, the text explicitly identifies it as a function that fills the MODEL slot in DATA = MODEL + ERROR; residuals, sum of squares, variance, and standard deviation are explicitly connected to ERROR.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: Engage students in productive struggle before presenting explicit connections and solutions
description: The principle holds that connections must be earned through hard work: simply making them explicit is insufficient for deep understanding. The authors design each textbook page with a "struggle first" pedagogy, asking students open-response questions before presenting the information needed for a well-formulated answer. They also remove calculation opportunities, delaying formulas until chapter 5 and using number-free problems so students grapple with concepts rather than rushing to compute, thereby reserving attention for conceptual connections.
requirements: Tasks must be challenging enough that learners work to connect problem features with prior knowledge
Struggle must precede, not follow, the explicit presentation of connections
constraints: The article notes students may resist the sequence, sometimes pointing out that the authors have mistakenly gotten the order wrong
target_learners: US college students in introductory statistics
target_learning_goals: Developing intuitive ideas about models and model comparison
Retaining learning through effortful engagement
examples: Before discussing mean and median, students see a five-point distribution and are asked in what sense each might be the better model; in chapter 4 they compare faceted histograms of restaurant tips across smiley-face conditions without calculating group means.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: Provide repeated, deliberately practiced opportunities to make connections over sustained time, with continually varying contexts
description: The third principle extends deliberate practice from skill acquisition to conceptual understanding: instructional materials must maintain a high level of challenge as abilities develop, raising the difficulty of the connections practiced along a learning trajectory. The authors state that "Deliberate practice requires that instructional materials maintain a constant (and high) level of challenge as abilities develop." Varying contexts, such as introducing new data sets nearly every class session, forces learners to adapt their conceptual understanding and stretches the range of situations a concept covers. The authors stress deliberate practice must be combined with the first two principles, since skill progression alone can occur without attention to conceptual connections.
requirements: Practice opportunities must recur over long periods as knowledge deepens
Task difficulty must be raised to match growing capability, targeting specific weaknesses
constraints: Repetitive practice aimed at automaticity produces a feeling of fluency that signals plateau, not deepening understanding; deliberate practice alone risks skill learning without conceptual connection
target_learners: Students developing expertise in a complex academic domain over a semester or longer
target_learning_goals: Strengthening and robustness of connections across contexts, concepts, and representations
Applying domain knowledge flexibly across varied contexts
examples: Although the online book uses a limited number of data sets, the authors introduce new data at almost every class session so students connect data analysis to the contexts they care about.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains
citation: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x
title: Online interactive introductory statistics textbook implementing the practicing connections framework
description: The article's design artifact is an online interactive textbook for introductory statistics developed by the authors, in which the framework's connection types and principles are instantiated. The book is organized around the practice of data analysis (explore variation, model variation, evaluate and compare models), three core concepts, and five key representations, with each page using a "struggle first" pedagogy asking students to answer questions before the relevant information is presented. R is interleaved throughout to reduce extraneous load and free resources for reflecting on connections.
requirements: A description of the world outside the classroom (the practice of data analysis) must be made explicit for textbook authors, students, and instructors
constraints: The article presents the textbook as an illustration of design decisions justified by learning sciences research, not as an evaluated intervention with outcome data
target_learners: College students in introductory statistics courses across multiple academic departments
target_learning_goals: Explaining variation in data through statistical modeling
Developing transferable statistical understanding connected to data science practice
examples: Students are told from the beginning that the goal of statistics is to explain variation in the world, and the textbook continually reminds them where specific skills connect to data scientists' work.
key_sources: Fries, L., Son, J. Y., Givvin, K. B., & Stigler, J. W. (2020). Practicing Connections: A Framework to Guide Instructional Design for Developing Understanding in Complex Domains. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09561-x

article_title: Mapping Mind Wandering to the “Self-Regulated Learning Process, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid”: A Systematic Review
citation: Bühler, B., Fütterer, T., von Keyserlingk, L., Bozkir, E., Kasneci, E., Gerjets, P., & Trautwein, U. (2025). Mapping Mind Wandering to the “Self-Regulated Learning Process, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid”: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10041-3
title: Adapted SMA grid adding a mind-wandering column to map mind-wandering research onto SRL processes, data streams, and analytical approaches
description: The SMA grid (Molenaar et al., 2023) organizes SRL research along axes of multimodal data streams, CAMM SRL processes (cognition, affect, metacognition, motivation), and analytical approaches. The review extends it by adding a mind-wandering column and redefining the analytical approaches: "our adaptation modifies the horizontal approach to specifically include analyses that assess mind wandering alongside at least one other CAMM process." Unimodal approaches cover only mind wandering with one modality; vertical approaches cover only mind wandering with multiple streams; integrated approaches combine mind wandering, at least one CAMM process, and multiple streams.
requirements: Studies must report the CAMM processes and data streams they assess so reports can be located in the grid
constraints: The adaptation applies to mind-wandering research in learning contexts, not to the original SRL-only grid
target_learners: university students
school students
target_learning_goals: sustained attention during learning
self-regulated learning processes
examples: The review situated 134 studies in the adapted grid, distinguishing unimodal, horizontal, vertical, and integrated analytical approaches.

article_title: Mapping Mind Wandering to the “Self-Regulated Learning Process, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid”: A Systematic Review
citation: Bühler, B., Fütterer, T., von Keyserlingk, L., Bozkir, E., Kasneci, E., Gerjets, P., & Trautwein, U. (2025). Mapping Mind Wandering to the “Self-Regulated Learning Process, Multimodal Data, and Analysis Grid”: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10041-3
title: Conceptual integration of mind wandering into SRL: subtypes defined by meta-awareness and intentionality may serve regulatory functions rather than only signaling attentional failure
description: The review conceptually integrates mind wandering with SRL frameworks (COPES; MASRL), arguing that "mind wandering should not be viewed merely as a disruption of SRL but rather as an integral process that interacts with cognitive, metacognitive, motivational, and affective regulation." It distinguishes subtypes by meta-awareness — "one without awareness (zone-outs) and one with awareness (tune-outs)" — and by intentionality. Unaware mind wandering signals a lapse in metacognitive monitoring, whereas aware, intentional mind wandering may function as an affective or motivational regulation strategy, e.g., managing frustration or sustaining engagement.
requirements: Researchers must precisely specify which subtype of mind wandering (by meta-awareness and intentionality) they study
constraints: The review focuses on the performance phase of SRL models, where most mind-wandering studies examine task-unrelated thoughts
target_learners: university students
school students
general population learners
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring
affect and motivation regulation during learning
examples: The review describes learners deliberately allowing their minds to wander to manage heightened frustration, reflecting on pleasant or rewarding thoughts to stabilize their emotional state.

citation: Moreno, M., Grewal, K., Cutumisu, M., & Harley, J.M. (2025). Employing Machine Learning to Predict Medical Trainees’ Psychophysiological Responses, Self- and Socially-Shared Regulated Learning Strategies While Completing Medical Simulations. Education Psychology Review, 37 (70), 1-29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10044-0
title: COPES model of self-regulated learning (Winne & Hadwin)
description: The article describes COPES as a model of self-regulated learning consisting of five interconnected facets: conditions, operations, products, evaluations, and standards. Conditions include internal factors (prior knowledge, motivation, emotions) and external factors (task instructions, learning environment); operations are the cognitive and metacognitive strategies learners employ; products are outcomes such as comprehension and performance; evaluations involve assessing progress against goals or gold standards; and standards are benchmarks used to judge success. The article notes the facets are "interconnected, with feedback from one facet (e.g., evaluation) influencing earlier facets (e.g., conditions), making the model cyclical and adaptive in nature."
requirements: Learners establish goals, engage in metacognitive monitoring, and have a self-reflection mechanism to make adaptations throughout the learning process
target_learners: medical trainees
post-secondary learners
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognitive monitoring and self-reflection

Education Psychology Review, 37 (70), 1-29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10044-0
title: Mapping medical simulation phases onto SRL phases: beginning, escalation, and peak
description: The article proposes mapping the three segmented phases of a medical simulation onto the phases of an SRL model. The "beginning" maps onto task definition and goal setting and planning, where trainees establish a goal and collect information on the patient's condition; the "escalation" maps onto enacting study tactics and strategies, where trainees execute a developed course of treatment; and the "peak" maps onto adaptation, where trainees analyze how to adjust their plan to meet new demands and ensure patient survival. The article states these phases "could be interpreted as having a gradual increase in requirements," potentially coinciding with increases in arousal.
requirements: Segmentation of simulation videos into beginning, escalation, and peak phases, guided by simulation scripts and patient deterioration events
constraints: Medical simulations may not have a resolution and can end abruptly after the script is completed
target_learners: medical residents in team-based simulation training
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning during clinical simulation
team regulation under escalating task demands

citation: Moreno, M., Grewal, K., Cutumisu, M., & Harley, J.M. (2025). Education Psychology Review, 37 (70), 1-29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10044-0
title: Simulation video coding scheme for behaviors and SRL/SSRL strategies
description: The research team developed a coding scheme for (1) behaviors (posture and gestures, facial expressions, and vocalics) and (2) regulation strategies including SRL codes (C.2.1–C.2.6) and SSRL codes (C.3.1–C.3.2), plus social climate and participation codes (C.3.3–C.3.6), adapted from prior literature to fit a medical context. Each code was structured as "a superordinate code, a definition to that code, followed by an example of the code in a medical context," with nested subordinate codes. Four raters were trained; inter-rater agreement after the first negotiation ranged from 0.62 to 0.83 Cohen's kappa, described as "substantial" agreement, with perfect agreement reached after deliberation.
requirements: Rater training with expert evaluation and negotiation of coded events; codes made explicit to minimize rater inferences
constraints: Coding emotion regulation from video is difficult unless the learner verbalizes, which may require non-replicable rater inferences
target_learners: medical residents in team-based simulations
target_learning_goals: observable indicators of SRL and SSRL during clinical simulation

Education Psychology Review, 37 (70), 1-29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10044-0
title: Multimodal EDA collection and SCR extraction protocol for simulation research
description: The study collected electrodermal activity with Empatica E4 wristbands worn on participants' non-dominant hand throughout simulations. Raw EDA was preprocessed in MATLAB's Ledalab package using a 30 Hz Butterworth low-pass filter, with artifacts removed via linear interpolation. Skin conductance responses were extracted using continuous decomposition analysis with "a threshold of 0.05 μS to identify SCRs," a 3-second delay to account for perception-to-response latency, and quantification with a 5-second moving window and 1-second step. The final physiological measure was average peaks per segment (APPS) computed per participant per simulation phase.
requirements: Signal-quality screening (sensor disconnection, flat-lines, noise, square-angled waves); no baseline assessment was collected due to ecological and time constraints
constraints: Approximately a 48% loss of physiological data; EDA alone cannot distinguish stress responses from emotion
target_learners: medical residents in simulation training
target_learning_goals: measuring sympathetic arousal during collaborative clinical learning

article_title: Situational Motivation in Academic Learning: A Systematic Review
citation: Törmänen, T., Ketonen, E., Lehtoaho, E., Turunen, M., Zabolotna, K., Shubina, T., & Järvenoja, H. (2025). Situational Motivation in Academic Learning: A Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10036-0
title: Five major motivation theories as a comprehensive framework for situational motivation
description: The review organizes situational motivation research through five theories — attributional theory, expectancy-value theory (including its situated extension SEVT), social cognitive theory, achievement goal theory, and self-determination theory. The authors state these "provide a comprehensive framework to understand the multifaceted nature of motivation," collectively covering constructs such as intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, goal orientations, and attributions, and each explicitly considering situational and contextual factors in different ways. The framework structures which constructs were measured situationally and how studies approach situatedness theoretically and methodologically.
requirements: Each included study must measure at least one construct from the five theories or another situational motivational construct as defined by the study authors
constraints: The review notes evidence on a situational level is still limited for theories other than SDT, EVT, and SCT's self-efficacy construct
target_learners: Learners across all ages and educational levels in academic contexts
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting students' situational motivation during academic learning
examples: The review coded all 80 included studies by motivation theory (SDT, EVT, SCT, AGT, ATT, or other) and summarized measured constructs and instruments for each wave

article_title: The Evolution of Race-Focused and Race-Reimaged Approaches in Educational Psychology: Future Directions for the Field
citation: Jessica T. DeCuir-Gunby · Paul A. Schutz. (2024). The Evolution of Race-Focused and Race-Reimaged Approaches in Educational Psychology: Future Directions for the Field. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09873-2
title: Race-focused and race-reimaged approaches as a metatheory for centering race in educational psychology inquiry
description: The article presents race-focusing and reimaging as a metatheory, defined as a "fundamental set of ideas about how phenomena of interest in a particular field should be thought about and researched". As a metatheoretical lens, it guides how theories should be refined and reconstructed, allowing educational psychologists to critique and expand their theories to include race-focused constructs. Race-focused research centers race within data collection and analysis; race-reimaging critiques and expands traditional theories using a critical social-cultural-historical lens.
requirements: Race must be centered during all stages of the research process, from research questions through data collection, analysis, and interpretation
constraints: The approach is centered within the U.S. context, though the authors state it can be applied to international contexts
target_learners: Educational psychology researchers
Doctoral students in educational psychology
target_learning_goals: Theory building that centers race
Critiquing and expanding race-neutral educational psychology theories
examples: The authors describe how reimagining self-concept using a Chicana feminist epistemological framework ends in the development of a race-focused construct
key_sources: Jessica T. DeCuir-Gunby · Paul A. Schutz. (2024). The Evolution of Race-Focused and Race-Reimaged Approaches in Educational Psychology: Future Directions for the Field. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09873-2

article_title: The Evolution of Race-Focused and Race-Reimaged Approaches in Educational Psychology: Future Directions for the Field
citation: Jessica T. DeCuir-Gunby · Paul A. Schutz. (2024). The Evolution of Race-Focused and Race-Reimaged Approaches in Educational Psychology: Future Directions for the Field. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09873-2
title: Common design features of exemplary race-reimaging studies
description: From three exemplar race-reimaging studies (López et al. 2022 on SDT; Fong et al. 2019 on belonging; Gray et al. 2020 on utility value), the article identifies shared design features: scholars "foregrounded a variety of social-cultural-historical theories as they centered race in their inquiry", and participant selection and methods honored the POC who participated, with no White control group and mixed methods used to share participants' voices as counterstories.
requirements: Foreground critical social-cultural-historical theories when centering race
Select participants and methods that honor the POC studied, without defaulting to a White control group
constraints: The article states that although the exemplars used mixed methods, doing so is not required; qualitative methods or critical quantitative methods such as QuantCrit are viable options
target_learners: Educational psychology researchers
target_learning_goals: Designing race-reimaged empirical studies
Reconceptualizing race-less constructs to consider race
examples: Fong et al. (2019) used CRT and TribalCrit to reconceptualize belonging for Indigenous community college students, distinguishing institutional support for Indigenous identities from belonging as assimilation

citation: Theobald, M., Kerner auch Koerner, J., Breitwieser, J., Buhr, L., Karbach, J., Könönen, T., Nobbe, L., Reinelt, T., Schaaf, M., Schmiedek, F., Wieland, L. M., & Blume, F. (2026). Executive Functions, Metacognition, Self-Regulation, and Self-Regulated Learning – What are We Talking About? A Review and Introduction of the EMERGE Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10157-0
title: The EMERGE model positions EF, MC, SR and SRL along a continuum from biologically grounded mechanics to culturally shaped pragmatics
description: The EMERGE model is a conceptual framework introduced by this review to integrate four research traditions that have been examined in isolation. It positions EF, MC, SR and SRL along a continuum, "ranging from more biologically grounded mechanics (e.g., EF) to more culturally shaped pragmatics (e.g., strategy knowledge in SRL)", and conceptualises SR in learning situations as an integrative construct. The model highlights both shared mechanisms and distinct functions of the four constructs in learning processes.
requirements: The model is intended to bridge fragmented research traditions that have examined EF, MC, SR and SRL in isolation due to disciplinary and methodological divides
constraints: The review's focus is on school-aged children, as the four constructs demonstrate significant development during this stage of life
target_learners: school-aged children
target_learning_goals: self-regulated and adaptive learning
goal-directed learning behaviour

article_title: “Valued” Thinking in Education: Liberating the Narrative
citation: Murphy, P. Karen, Ogata, Tyler, & Schoute, Eric C. (2023). “Valued” thinking in education: Liberating the narrative. Educational Psychology Review, 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09754-0
title: Valued thinking in education as a narrative manifested as higher-order, critical, and critical-analytic thinking
description: The article frames valued thinking in education as a historical narrative whose contemporary manifestations are higher-order thinking (HOT), critical thinking (CT), and critical-analytic thinking (CAT). The authors state their purpose is "to forward a narrative of valued thinking in education—manifested as higher-order (HOT), critical thinking (CT), and critical-analytic thinking (CAT)—by overviewing its past and present, possible future." The framework organizes the review across philosophy, psychology, and future-oriented theory.
requirements: The narrative is traced through the philosophical tradition spanning from Socrates to present analytic philosophy, as the article states
constraints: The authors state that "Tracing an exact lineage of valued thinking in the history of philosophy is beyond the current scope and virtually impossible in relation to specific manifestations such as HOT, CT, or CAT"
target_learners: educational psychology researchers and theorists
target_learning_goals: understanding the conceptual history and future directions of valued forms of thinking
key_sources: Murphy, P. Karen, Ogata, Tyler, & Schoute, Eric C. (2023). “Valued” thinking in education: Liberating the narrative. Educational Psychology Review, 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09754-0

article_title: “Valued” Thinking in Education: Liberating the Narrative
citation: Murphy, P. Karen, Ogata, Tyler, & Schoute, Eric C. (2023). “Valued” thinking in education: Liberating the narrative. Educational Psychology Review, 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09754-0
title: Philosophical forebears of valued thinking: rationalism, empiricism, and pragmatism as schools emphasizing methods for finding knowledge
description: The article organizes the philosophical past of valued thinking around three named schools of thought. It states: "we begin by examining the philosophical forebearers of valued thinking, including theories such as rationalism, empiricism, and pragmatism." In reviewing these schools, the authors "underscore the value placed upon the nature of methods for finding knowledge," positioning epistemological method as the axis along which philosophy investigated thought in pursuit of knowledge and knowing.
requirements: Understanding this axis requires reading the schools as investigations of methods for finding knowledge, as the article frames them
constraints: The article presents this as a narrative history rather than an exact lineage, noting an exact lineage is "virtually impossible"
target_learners: educational psychology researchers and theorists
target_learning_goals: understanding the philosophical foundations of valued thinking
