article_title: “Valued” Thinking in Education: Liberating the Narrative
citation: Murphy, P. Karen, Ogata, Tyler, & Schoute, Eric C. (2023). “Valued” thinking in education: Liberating the narrative. Educational Psychology Review, 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09754-0
title: Standpoint epistemology: knowledge stems from socially situated positions and meaning making is value-laden and subjective
description: Standpoint epistemology is one of two theoretical perspectives the article overviews as liberating prevailing epistemic notions of valued thinking. Its unifying premise, as the article states, is that "knowledge stems from socially situated positions and that the process of meaning making is value-laden and subjective." The perspective centers the social and political realms in meaning making and liberates non-traditional epistemic notions within the narrative of valued thinking.
requirements: Within this perspective, scientists collaborate with local knowers who have firsthand, often minoritized, experiences
constraints: The article presents it as a theoretical perspective overviewed humbly, not as an empirically tested model
target_learners: educational psychology researchers and theorists
target_learning_goals: broadening conceptions of knowing and reasoning beyond narrow epistemological justification
key_sources: Murphy, P. Karen, Ogata, Tyler, & Schoute, Eric C. (2023). “Valued” thinking in education: Liberating the narrative. Educational Psychology Review, 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09754-0

article_title: “Valued” Thinking in Education: Liberating the Narrative
citation: Murphy, P. Karen, Ogata, Tyler, & Schoute, Eric C. (2023). “Valued” thinking in education: Liberating the narrative. Educational Psychology Review, 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09754-0
title: Critical pragmatism: experience and discourse as ways of coming to know and verifying knowledge
description: Critical pragmatism is the second liberating theoretical perspective the article overviews. The article states: "Critical pragmatism draws on critical theory as well as pragmatism to emphasize the importance of experience and discourse as ways of coming to know and verifying knowledge." Like standpoint epistemology, it underscores the ways that the social and political realms bear on meaning making, and it centers concrete problems and community-based validation of interpretations.
requirements: Knowledge verification occurs through community-based discourse where all voices are heard, per the article's description
constraints: The article presents it as a forward-looking theoretical perspective, not a tested instructional model
target_learners: educational psychology researchers and theorists
target_learning_goals: verifying knowledge through experience and discourse rather than narrow epistemic criteria

article_title: Racializing Motivation: A Race-Reimaged Framework of Belonging, Emoting, and Achieving Within STEM Higher Education Contexts
citation: Jessica T. DeCuir-Gunby, Paul A. Schutz, Saba L. Modaressi. (2026). Racializing Motivation: A Race-Reimaged Framework of Belonging, Emoting, and Achieving Within STEM Higher Education Contexts. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10220-w
title: The Race-Reimaged Systems Model of Belonging, Emoting, and Achieving organizes motivation inquiry across three nested system levels
description: The article proposes a metatheoretical, race-focused framework for studying motivation among racially marginalized students in U.S. STEM higher education. Building on Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory, PVEST, and Johnson's Intersectional Ecological Belonging Model, it examines "how race and racism influence marginalized STEM students' experiences from matriculation through graduation" across "three system levels": Self-Systems, Immediate Contexts, and Social-Cultural-Historical Contexts. Interactional episodes in activity settings serve as the unit of analysis for developing counterstories.
requirements: Inquiry must center race-focused constructs (race-evasive ideologies, white STEM spaces) and race-reimagined constructs (racialized belonging, emoting, achieving) within social-cultural-historical contexts
constraints: The framework is developed for the U.S. STEM higher education context and focuses on a selected set of constructs (belonging, emoting, achieving), not the full range of motivational processes
target_learners: Racially marginalized students in U.S. STEM higher education
target_learning_goals: Understanding how race and racism shape belonging, emotions, and achievement in STEM programs
examples: The authors analyze Katherine's advising-meeting counterstory, in which white advisors discouraged her biomedical engineering application despite her 3.5 GPA, across all three system levels
key_sources: Jessica T. DeCuir-Gunby, Paul A. Schutz, Saba L. Modaressi. (2026). Racializing Motivation: A Race-Reimaged Framework of Belonging, Emoting, and Achieving Within STEM Higher Education Contexts. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10220-w

article_title: Racializing Motivation: A Race-Reimaged Framework of Belonging, Emoting, and Achieving Within STEM Higher Education Contexts
citation: Jessica T. DeCuir-Gunby, Paul A. Schutz, Saba L. Modaressi. (2026). Racializing Motivation: A Race-Reimaged Framework of Belonging, Emoting, and Achieving Within STEM Higher Education Contexts. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10220-w
title: Race-focused and race-reimaged metatheoretical approaches for studying motivation constructs
description: The article distinguishes two metatheoretical approaches for educational research: race-focused approaches, which "center on issues of race and are grounded in racial or cultural theories and constructs" such as racial identity and stereotype threat, and race-reimaged approaches, which reconceptualize traditional motivational constructs by integrating racial theories through critical social-cultural-historical lenses. The authors extend these approaches from single constructs to interactions among multiple interrelated constructs (belonging, emoting, achieving) contextualized in STEM education.
requirements: Research must move beyond using race merely to describe demographics, explain variance, or compare groups
constraints: The approaches are grounded in the U.S. context, described as a race-centric nation; the authors note international contexts often focus on ethnicity, immigration, or nationality rather than race
target_learners: People of Color in U.S. educational contexts
Racially marginalized STEM students
target_learning_goals: Critically understanding racialized motivational experiences of students of color
examples: Byrd (2017) employed a race-focused approach to assess school racial climate using intergroup interaction and racial socialization frameworks

article_title: Racializing Motivation: A Race-Reimaged Framework of Belonging, Emoting, and Achieving Within STEM Higher Education Contexts
citation: Jessica T. DeCuir-Gunby, Paul A. Schutz, Saba L. Modaressi. (2026). Racializing Motivation: A Race-Reimaged Framework of Belonging, Emoting, and Achieving Within STEM Higher Education Contexts. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10220-w
title: Race-evasive ideologies as a race-focused construct maintaining structural racism in STEM
description: Race-evasive ideologies are defined as "a tendency to overlook or dismiss the role of race and racism in the experiences and achievements of racially marginalized students, contributing to the maintenance of structural racism within society and STEM." They include narratives claiming racial progress, meritocratic explanations dismissing structural analysis, and claims that focusing on race is discriminatory. The article treats them as a societal belief system within the Social-Cultural-Historical Contexts level of its framework, obscuring racial inequalities and leaving racism in STEM spaces unaddressed.
requirements: Researchers and practitioners must recognize and contradict race-evasive narratives to address racial inequalities in STEM
constraints: The construct is situated in U.S. STEM higher education contexts
target_learners: Racially marginalized students in U.S. STEM higher education
target_learning_goals: Recognizing how race-evasive ideologies shape motivational experiences and institutional climates
examples: The article notes white STEM spaces "tend to be saturated and maintained by race-evasive ideologies"

citation: Jessica T. DeCuir-Gunby, Paul A. Schutz, Saba L. Modaressi. (2026). Racializing Motivation: A Race-Reimaged Framework of Belonging, Emoting, and Achieving Within STEM Higher Education Contexts. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10220-w
title: White STEM spaces as racially hierarchical educational contexts that question minoritized students' belonging and competence
description: White STEM spaces emerge when racially minoritized students pursue STEM goals in white educational spaces whose "history, symbols, and traditions... replicate whiteness and white supremacy ideologies." For most white students these spaces seem normal, but for racially minoritized students, "white STEM spaces promote and make salient the presumed deficit ideological questions about whether racially minoritized students belong, are competent, and can be autonomous in those spaces." The construct is a core contextual element of the article's systems framework.
requirements: Analysis of minoritized students' experiences must account for the white-space character of STEM academic and work settings
constraints: The construct is developed for U.S. higher education STEM contexts
target_learners: Racially minoritized STEM students in predominantly white institutions
target_learning_goals: Understanding racialized barriers to belonging, competence beliefs, and autonomy in STEM spaces
examples: The article cites Anderson's observation that Black people are required to navigate white space as a condition of their existence

article_title: How Rigorous is Active Learning Research in STEM Education? An Examination of Key Internal Validity Controls in Intervention Studies
citation: Amedee Marchand Martella, Ronald C. Martella, Jane K. Yatcilla, Alexandra Newson, Eric N. Shannon, Charissa Voorhis. (2023). How Rigorous is Active Learning Research in STEM Education? An Examination of Key Internal Validity Controls in Intervention Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09826-1
title: Active learning intervention studies should incorporate internal validity controls such as randomization, group equivalence checks, matched instructors, dosage matching, and implementation fidelity assessment
description: The review recommends that active learning researchers apply a set of internal validity controls—randomized designs, group equivalence measures, attrition equivalency, matched sample size and instructor, operational definitions, dosage matching, matched time frame and content, equal dependent measures, and implementation fidelity—so that cause-and-effect claims about active learning interventions are warranted. It coded studies against these 12 controls and found "high percentages of articles that did not meet each internal validity control."
requirements: Studies must report group equivalence measures, operational definitions of both conditions, dosage, and implementation fidelity for the controls to be evaluable
constraints: The review examined undergraduate STEM/STEMM face-to-face courses comparing active learning with lecture or other active learning, so its recommendations are scoped to that literature
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students
target_learning_goals: academic performance in STEM courses
examples: The authors coded 176 Freeman et al. (2014) articles and a random sample of 84 post-2015 articles against the 12 controls and found no article met all of them

article_title: What Works for Teaching Word Reading to Adolescents? A Meta-Analytic Investigation
citation: Julia J. Yi, A. Angelique Aitken, Emily Sharp, Adiba Nusrat, Micheal Sandbank. (2026). What Works for Teaching Word Reading to Adolescents? A Meta-Analytic Investigation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10124-9
title: Simple View of Reading: word reading and language comprehension as the two critical elements of reading comprehension
description: The article adopts the Simple View of Reading (SVR) as its organizing framework for defining and selecting word-reading interventions. The SVR is described as "a well-validated reading framework that identified word reading as one of two critical elements of reading comprehension, with the other being language comprehension" (Gough & Tunmer, 1986; Hoover & Gough, 1990). The meta-analysis uses this model to justify narrowing its analytic lens to interventions with a primary focus on word-reading instruction, defining multi-component interventions as those combining word reading with language comprehension components.
requirements: Interventions are classified by whether their word-level reading component comprises at least 50% of instructional time, following the SVR distinction between word reading and language comprehension.
constraints: The article applies the framework to English, characterized as a morphophonemic language with deep orthography; findings are not assumed generalizable to other orthographic systems.
target_learners: Adolescents in middle school and high school (grades 6-12, ages 11-21)
target_learning_goals: Word reading, decoding, and related foundational literacy skills
examples: The inclusion criteria required the word-level reading intervention to comprise at least 50% of instructional time, and non-language-based interventions (e.g., color overlays, medical treatments) were excluded.
key_sources: Julia J. Yi, A. Angelique Aitken, Emily Sharp, Adiba Nusrat, Micheal Sandbank. (2026). What Works for Teaching Word Reading to Adolescents? A Meta-Analytic Investigation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10124-9

article_title: AI-Related Threats to Information Sovereignty and Challenges for Research Ethics
citation: Skulmowski, A. (2024). AI-Related Threats to Information Sovereignty and Challenges for Research Ethics. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09939-1
title: Expand informed consent with AI- and cloud-related privacy warnings to restore consent validity
description: The article recommends incorporating additional information into informed consent forms so participants understand how their devices may collect and transfer data. For sensitive studies, it would be "recommendable to include a brief warning concerning the threats that AI-related and cloud-based data collection poses to privacy and anonymity", ideally with suggestions for changing settings or software. The author argues this restores informed consent, while cautioning that many participants do not read consent forms, so other security measures remain necessary.
requirements: Consent forms must describe device-related data-transfer risks and practical mitigations such as disabling cloud-based features.
constraints: A large part of participants do not read informed consent forms, so this measure alone is insufficient.
target_learners: remote study participants in educational research
target_learning_goals: protecting participant privacy and information sovereignty during data collection
examples: For studies involving sensitive data such as health data or learning impairments, the author recommends a warning notice with suggestions on avoiding the issues by changing settings or using different software.

article_title: AI-Related Threats to Information Sovereignty and Challenges for Research Ethics
citation: Skulmowski, A. (2024). AI-Related Threats to Information Sovereignty and Challenges for Research Ethics. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09939-1
title: Table of AI-related and cloud-based functionalities, participant risks, and solutions
description: Table 1 of the article enumerates concrete functionalities that threaten participant privacy during research: browser spell checking using cloud services, malware scanners using cloud databases, word processors using AI assistants, and user tracking in operating systems. For each it names the risk, such as "Transfer of user input to clouds and AI training databases", and a solution or workaround, such as recommending participants disable spell checking or AI assistants, or boot alternative operating systems for high-risk studies.
requirements: Researchers must communicate the recommended workarounds to participants, e.g., in informed consent forms.
constraints: The listed workarounds depend on participants changing settings or software on their own devices, which may not be feasible in every context.
target_learners: educational researchers collecting data remotely
study participants using personal devices
target_learning_goals: mitigating AI- and cloud-related privacy risks during data collection
examples: One row recommends disabling cloud-based malware scanners during the time of diary studies, since scanners may transfer user files containing identifiable information.

article_title: Foreign Language Attainment of Children/Adolescents with Poor Literacy Skills: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
citation: von Hagen, A., Kohnen, S., & Stadie, N. (2021). Foreign Language Attainment of Children/Adolescents with Poor Literacy Skills: a Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09566-6
title: Evidence corpus of 16 studies (968 participants) on foreign language attainment in poor readers/spellers, with datasets and code on the Open Science Framework
description: The review assembled a corpus of 16 group-comparison studies with 968 participants (404 poor readers/spellers, 564 controls), all assessing English as a foreign language, identified via a PRISMA-guided search across Ovid databases, PubMed, ProQuest, Web of Science and gray-literature sources. The authors state that "the datasets and code used to compute the analyses can be accessed on the Open Science Framework at https://osf.io/np97f/". The corpus supported meta-analyses on 10 of 15 foreign language outcome measures.
requirements: Studies must compare poor readers/spellers with control participants with typical literacy skills on a foreign language outcome measure, with literacy status confirmed by test rather than self- or teacher report
constraints: Only studies of English as a foreign language were available
Participants had little or no access to the foreign language outside classroom instruction
target_learners: children and adolescents in primary and secondary education with poor literacy skills
target_learning_goals: foreign language attainment subskills such as phonological awareness, word reading, spelling, and reading comprehension
examples: Round 1 of the search screened 1370 references after duplicate removal and ended with 16 included studies; a second round of reference checking added none

article_title: Assessing Writing Motivation: a Systematic Review of K-5 Students' Self-Reports
citation: Alves‑Wold, A., Walgermo, B. R., McTigue, E., & Uppstad, P. H. (2023). Assessing Writing Motivation: a Systematic Review of K‑5 Students’ Self‑Reports. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09732-6
title: Four‑component framework of writing motivation (self‑efficacy, goal orientations, interest/value, outcome attributions)
description: The review adopts Troia et al.’s (2012) account that writing motivation comprises four broad components: self‑efficacy beliefs, goal orientations, task interest and value, and outcome attributions, with associated constructs such as domain self‑concept and task utility. The review uses this schema to systematize the 32 motivational constructs identified across the 56 studies (Table 4). The review notes that some links, such as the causal pathways between self‑efficacy, interest, and value, remain unclear, and that the schema’s authors invite combining methods such as classroom observation and students’ self‑reports to test these connections.
requirements: Motivation constructs must be clearly defined for the framework to guide accurate measurement of students’ voices
constraints: Some causal pathways between components (self‑efficacy, interest, value) are stated by the source review to remain unclear
target_learners: K‑5 elementary students in mainstream classrooms
target_learning_goals: Assessing and understanding students’ motivation to write
examples: The review categorized the 32 identified constructs into the four theorized components plus associated constructs, with interest and value (n = 39) and self‑beliefs (n = 28) most frequent

article_title: The Effects of Educational Technology Interventions on Literacy in Elementary School: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Rebecca D. Silverman, Kristin Keane, Elena Hammond, S. Khanna. (2025). The Effects of Educational Technology Interventions on Literacy in Elementary School: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 95(5), 972-1012. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241261073
title: Four-outcome literacy framework: constrained and unconstrained skills underlie reading comprehension and writing proficiency
description: The meta-analysis organizes literacy outcomes along two levels: two broad constructs, reading comprehension and writing proficiency, and the underlying skills that support them. It distinguishes "the constrained and unconstrained skills that underlie these two literacy constructs," allowing effects of educational technology interventions to be estimated separately for each of the four outcome categories. This framework structures both the synthesis and the moderator analyses of intervention and participant characteristics.
requirements: Studies in the corpus must measure one or more of the four literacy outcome categories so effects can be assigned within the framework.
target_learners: elementary school students
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
writing proficiency
constrained literacy skills
unconstrained literacy skills
examples: The meta-analysis estimated effects separately for constrained skills, unconstrained skills, reading comprehension, and writing proficiency.

article_title: Effects of Family Literacy Programs on the Emergent Literacy Skills of Children From Low-SES Families: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Suzanne Fikrat-Wevers, Roel van Steensel, Lidia Arends. (2021). Effects of Family Literacy Programs on the Emergent Literacy Skills of Children From Low-SES Families: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654321998075
title: Design family literacy programs for low-SES children as targeted programs focused on a limited set of activities and skills, restricted to one (training) context
description: The meta-analysis concludes that low-SES children benefit most from family literacy programs that are targeted rather than comprehensive: "children benefit from targeted programs that focus on a limited set of activities and skills and that are restricted to one (training) context." The authors describe this as a "less is more" pattern emerging from several moderator effects. It applies to program developers designing interventions for families with low socioeconomic status.
requirements: Programs should focus on a limited set of activities and skills rather than a comprehensive mix.
constraints: Effects on follow-up measures were marginal (d = 0.16), so the principle rests mainly on immediate posttest results; the formal-activities and L2-training comparisons were based on only one study.
target_learners: Children aged 0–6 from low-SES families
target_learning_goals: Comprehension-related emergent literacy skills
Code-related emergent literacy skills
examples: The meta-analysis found shared-reading-only programs averaged d = 0.75 on comprehension-related skills, while programs combining all three activity types showed d = 0.13.

article_title: Leveraging What Students Know to Make Sense of Texts: What the Research Says About Prior Knowledge Activation
citation: Courtney Hattan, Patricia A. Alexander, and Sarah M. Lupo. (2023). Leveraging What Students Know to Make Sense of Texts: What the Research Says About Prior Knowledge Activation. Review of Educational Research. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Leveraging+What+Students+Know+to+Make+Sense+of+Texts+Prior+Knowledge+Activation
title: Eight-category taxonomy of prior knowledge activation techniques
description: The review inductively grouped 30 unique activation techniques into eight categories: "open-ended prompts, procedural or strategic supports during reading, visual representation, analogical reasoning, text alteration, augmented activation, extra-textual activities, and spontaneous activation." Categories were derived from shared attributes such as mode of activation (e.g., questioning, altering the text), with no explicit hierarchy; some techniques belonged to more than one category. Open-ended prompts were the largest category, investigated in 23 of 54 articles, while spontaneous activation has the least empirical evidence and requires less explicit prompting.
requirements: Techniques must involve an explicit, intended activation of students' prior knowledge during a connected-text learning task to fall within the taxonomy's scope
constraints: Derived from 54 peer-reviewed articles on K-16 text-based learning, mostly expository texts, so narrative-text activation is underrepresented
target_learners: K-16 students reading connected expository or narrative texts
target_learning_goals: Text comprehension and learning from text
examples: The review describes visual representations as concept maps helping students see relations between concepts and sub-concepts, and text alteration as manipulating texts so a known concept (e.g., tire pressure) supports learning a new one (e.g., wind flow patterns)
key_sources: Courtney Hattan, Patricia A. Alexander, and Sarah M. Lupo. (2023). Leveraging What Students Know to Make Sense of Texts: What the Research Says About Prior Knowledge Activation. article_title: Leveraging What Students Know to Make Sense of Texts: What the Research Says About Prior Knowledge Activation
citation: Courtney Hattan, Patricia A. Alexander, and Sarah M. Lupo. (2023). Leveraging What Students Know to Make Sense of Texts: What the Research Says About Prior Knowledge Activation. Review of Educational Research. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Leveraging+What+Students+Know+to+Make+Sense+of+Texts+Prior+Knowledge+Activation
title: Multidimensional Knowledge in Text Comprehension framework
description: Introduced by McCarthy and McNamara (2021) and used by the review as a lens on definitional adequacy, this framework "posits that researchers should consider the amount, accuracy, specificity, and coherence of readers' academic knowledge, including topic and domain knowledge, before reading." The review uses it to judge whether researchers' definitions captured the multidimensionality of knowledge, finding only a few articles' implicit conceptual definitions encompassed it. The review also discusses extending activation beyond academic knowledge to personal knowledge and funds of knowledge drawn from students' life experiences and sociocultural resources.
requirements: Researchers should characterize readers' knowledge on amount, accuracy, specificity, and coherence before judging activation effectiveness
constraints: The framework addresses academic knowledge before reading; the review notes some researchers contend activating only academic knowledge undervalues other forms of background knowledge
target_learners: K-16 students reading academic texts
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension grounded in relevant prior knowledge
examples: The review illustrates with a middle school teacher preparing students to read a book on the Great Migration, where students could activate social studies content, expository text structure knowledge, or personal and sociocultural knowledge

article_title: Pathways to Student Motivation: A Meta-Analysis of Antecedents of Autonomous and Controlled Motivations
citation: Bureau, J. S., Howard, J. L., Chong, J. X. Y., & Guay, F. (2022). Pathways to Student Motivation: A Meta-Analysis of Antecedents of Autonomous and Controlled Motivations. Review of Educational Research, 92(1), 46–72. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211042426
title: Self-determination theory's motivational sequence: autonomy support → psychological need satisfaction → motivation quality
description: Self-determination theory explains student motivation along a continuum of motivation quality, from intrinsic motivation and identified regulation (autonomous motivation) through introjected and external regulation (controlled motivation) to amotivation. Its central premise asserts "a causal sequence that links autonomy support with enhanced psychological need satisfaction, which in turn fosters high-quality motivation, which in turn fosters adaptive outcomes." This meta-analysis systematically tested that sequence for the first time in education.
requirements: Need-supportive behaviors from notable others such as teachers and parents, namely "empathy, providing information, and supporting active participation", to satisfy students' psychological needs
constraints: The theory "makes no proposition about whether each need contributes equally or whether some will be more relevant than others"
target_learners: students from primary school to university
target_learning_goals: fostering self-determined (autonomous) academic motivation and reducing amotivation
examples: The meta-analysis tested the sequence with meta-analytic correlations, relative weight analysis, and W-COV GLS structural equation modeling across 144 samples
key_sources: Bureau, J. S., Howard, J. L., Chong, J. X. Y., & Guay, F. (2022). Pathways to Student Motivation: A Meta-Analysis of Antecedents of Autonomous and Controlled Motivations. Review of Educational Research, 92(1), 46–72. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211042426

article_title: The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development
citation: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. http://rer.aera.net
title: Vygotsky's zone of proximal development as a genetic-method account of a socially mediated, elastic and unbounded mind
description: The article elaborates Vygotsky's ZPD as "each person's range of potential for learning, where that learning is culturally shaped by the social environment in which it takes place." Development proceeds through a genetic (developmental) method in which mental processes are mediated by tools and signs, so knowledge passes from the intermental to the intramental plane via assisted performance. The mind is elastic (its direction depends on the sociocultural environment) and unbounded (theoretically limitless in potential, and spatially distributed through tools: Wertsch's point that the mind "extends beyond the skin"). The article uses this framework to critique research methodology.
requirements: The learner must be consonant with the cultural tools mediating development: tools work when they are sanctioned by the cultural environment, recognized by the learner as tools, and used volitionally.
constraints: The article notes the ZPD has been interpreted in three completely different ways and invoked for theoretically incompatible pedagogies, so any neo-Vygotskian claim is one social construction among competing readings.
target_learners: learners in culturally shaped social environments
school students and research participants
target_learning_goals: development of culturally mediated higher mental processes
appropriation of cultural knowledge through assisted performance
examples: The article cites Vygotsky's illustration of a child performing at a more advanced level with adult or peer assistance than alone, and internalizing the knowledge transacted through that assisted performance.
key_sources: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543065003191

article_title: The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development
citation: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. http://rer.aera.net
title: Research results are valid only when the learner is consonant with and can appropriate the mediational means of the research as useful cultural tools
description: The article proposes that "Research results, I propose, are only valid when the learner is consonant with and can appropriate the mediational means of the research as useful cultural tools." Under this conception, valid research is inherently instructional, because the congruence of learner and learning materials affords development; conversely, valid teaching represents inquiry. The principle treats researcher and teacher as parallel mediators, each needing the learner's shared sense of telos and intersubjective agreement on task and tool use.
requirements: The learner must share the researcher's or teacher's sense of telos, and the mediational means must build on the learner's prior culturally fostered tool use; instruction fails when there is little or no congruence and no reciprocal relationship regarding appropriate tool use.
constraints: The article states this conception of validity holds only under the particular conception of Vygotsky's ZPD outlined in the essay, which is itself one selective reading among competing appropriations.
target_learners: school students
research participants in learning studies
target_learning_goals: development through the zone of proximal development
appropriation of cultural tools for thinking
examples: The article cites Moll and Greenberg's (1990) finding that instruction failed when formal schooling was incongruent with students' prior culturally fostered tool use, and Heath's (1991) point that school mediational means must be congruent with students' prior learning experiences.
key_sources: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543065003191

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Three positions on knowledge specificity in literacy: general, task-specific, and community-specific knowledge
description: The review organizes debates in composition and literary understanding around three positions on knowledge transfer. The general knowledge position holds that writers and readers can transfer knowledge across situations; the task-specific position holds that different tasks require different knowledge; and the community-specific position holds that even similar tasks demand knowledge of particular communities, which Colomb calls specialized areas "with all the ideological, economic, political, material, linguistic, moral, and other determinants of communal life." Each position carries assumptions about learning and transfer with clear implications for curriculum and instruction.
requirements: Researchers and teachers must articulate their assumptions about knowledge and transfer to establish a coherent relationship between theory and practice
constraints: The discussion is circumscribed to extended written discourse and the reading of imaginative literature, and excludes grammatical knowledge because both readers and writers unquestionably transfer such basic knowledge
target_learners: students in school and professional writing and reading contexts
target_learning_goals: composition
literary understanding
transfer of knowledge across tasks and contexts
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543062003279

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Typology of knowledge: content, form, declarative, procedural, and conditional knowledge
description: The authors define knowledge as used in cognitive psychology, encompassing the what, how, and when of learning. Knowledge of content includes factual and personal-experience knowledge one can name; knowledge of form enables distinguishing one thing from another by features. Each type includes declarative knowledge (what) and procedural knowledge (how), and the typology adds conditional knowledge, "the knowledge of when to apply knowledge of content or form," such as knowing not to exaggerate when reporting research results.
requirements: Distinguishing these knowledge types is needed to analyze what particular writing and reading tasks demand
constraints: The typology is applied to extended written discourse and imaginative literature, not to grammatical knowledge
target_learners: students learning to compose and interpret texts
target_learning_goals: knowing what, how, and when to apply knowledge in writing and reading tasks
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543062003279

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Community-specific knowledge position: discourse conventions and community knowledge shape writing within tasks
description: The third position holds that even given task-specific skills, writers in different communities produce similar texts in quite different ways. Using Toulmin's argument elements, the review shows that literary criticism employs its own repertoire of persuasive tactics and topoi that "invoke the shared assumptions of the community of literary scholars, and at the same time create that community," while legal brief writing requires knowledge of the unique rhetorical demands structuring appellant-appellee relationships. The position requires conventional knowledge of the social or situational understandings governing behavior in particular circumstances.
requirements: Instruction must address conventional knowledge—tone, sources of evidence, voice—specific to the community being written for
constraints: Teachers adopting this position face the daunting problem of either instructing students to differentiate writing in seemingly unlimited ways or accepting limited influence on student writing
target_learners: students learning discipline-specific and professional writing
target_learning_goals: adapting argumentation and composing to the conventions of specific discourse communities
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543062003279

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Foster mindful attention to transfer by systematically saturating instruction with attention to transfer
description: Drawing on Perkins and Salomon, the review recommends that teachers who want knowledge to transfer across domains make transfer an explicit, conscious object of instruction. Teachers who "persistently and systematically . . . saturate the context of education with attention to transfer" improve the likelihood that students will reapply knowledge when they shift domains. This saturation must be integral to class structure rather than a tag at the end of a lesson.
requirements: Consistent mindfulness must be fostered in students adapting knowledge to new situations
constraints: Salomon found most students are decidedly unmindful unless specifically and vigorously cued
target_learners: students in composition and literary understanding instruction
target_learning_goals: applying knowledge in contexts other than the one originally studied
examples: The review presents this as hope for teachers adopting the community-specific knowledge position who aspire to retain influence on student writing
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543062003279

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Cognitive view of reading: active readers flexibly use general comprehension strategies
description: The review describes the cognitive view of reading offered by Dole, Duffy, Roehler, and Pearson, which contrasts with the traditional subskills view that "assumes a passive reader who has mastered a large number of subskills and automatically applies them to all texts." The cognitive view "assumes an active reader who constructs meaning through the integration of existing and new knowledge and the flexible use of strategies to foster, monitor, regulate, and maintain comprehension." The five strategies named—determining importance, summarizing, drawing inferences, generating questions, monitoring comprehension—reflect faith in general procedural knowledge at the center of the reading curriculum.
requirements: Instruction should help students gain conscious control over strategies they can adapt to any text
constraints: The review notes these researchers emphasize that good readers adapt strategies based on purpose, task and text demands, and situational context
target_learners: students learning to read across text types
target_learning_goals: comprehension monitoring and flexible strategy use in reading

article_title: A Systematic Review of the Impact of the Multilevel Digital Divide in Technology-Integrated Family–School Partnerships
citation: Badiuzzaman, Md; Lee, Jung-Sook; Cumming, Terry. (2025). A Systematic Review of the Impact of the Multilevel Digital Divide in Technology-Integrated Family–School Partnerships. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251400771
title: Multilevel digital divide framework applied to technology-integrated family–school partnerships
description: The review organizes its analysis around a multilevel digital divide framework, in which barriers to technology-integrated family–school partnerships occur at different levels. Its most emphasized level is "the second-level digital divide, which relates to skills and usage gaps," beyond first-level access barriers such as having technology at all. The framework explains why access alone does not ensure that parents benefit from technology-integrated partnership practices, and it grounds the review's recommendation that schools address parental socioeconomic differences, information provision, and training.
requirements: Schools must account for multiple divide levels, including skills and usage gaps, not only physical access to technology.
constraints: The framework is applied here to parents in technology-integrated family–school partnerships, based on 10 included studies.
target_learners: parents in technology-integrated family–school partnerships
target_learning_goals: effective participation in technology-integrated family–school partnership practices
examples: The review analyzed 10 high-quality studies of technology-integrated family–school partnership practices through this multilevel lens.

article_title: Educational Responses Toward Community Violence: A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions
citation: van Dijk, A, de Haan, M & de Winter, M 2026, 'Educational Responses Toward Community Violence : A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions', Review of Educational Research, vol. 96, no. 3, pp. 829-869. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251324491
title: Multidisciplinary taxonomy of educational approaches to counter community violence
description: The review establishes a multidisciplinary taxonomy that organizes the broad range of educational interventions to counter community violence into distinguishable approaches. It was built, in the authors' words, by a "critical analysis of distinctions in perspectives, objectives, and strategies", so approaches are differentiated by what they take the causes of violence to be, what objectives they pursue, and what strategies they deploy. The taxonomy serves as the organizing framework for the paper's coherent overview of current educational responses and for identifying which kinds of approaches are underrepresented.
requirements: Requires critical analysis of distinctions in perspectives, objectives, and strategies across theory and research on educational interventions
constraints: The review reports that strategies for transformation of social systems are underrepresented among the approaches captured by the taxonomy
target_learners: youth affected by community violence
target_learning_goals: violence prevention
conflict resolution
promotion of peace
examples: The review uses the taxonomy to show that most interventions focus on either individual behavior or group interaction while systems-transformation strategies are underrepresented
key_sources: van Dijk, A, de Haan, M & de Winter, M 2026, 'Educational Responses Toward Community Violence : A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions', Review of Educational Research, vol. 96, no. 3, pp. 829-869. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251324491

article_title: Educational Responses Toward Community Violence: A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions
citation: van Dijk, A, de Haan, M & de Winter, M 2026, 'Educational Responses Toward Community Violence : A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions', Review of Educational Research, vol. 96, no. 3, pp. 829-869. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251324491
title: Conceptual reorientation of community violence including structural mechanisms and multilevel targeting
description: Based on imbalances in theoretical orientations among existing interventions, the paper suggests a conceptual reorientation of community violence. In the authors' words, this reorientation "includes structural mechanisms and enables a targeted approach of the many levels through which youth and communities are affected." It reframes community violence as not only a matter of individual behavior or group interaction but also of social-system structures, so that educational responses can be targeted to the multiple levels at which violence affects youth and communities.
requirements: Requires moving beyond the individual-behavior and group-interaction orientations that dominate current interventions
constraints: The paper presents this as a suggested reorientation based on the review, not as a tested intervention
target_learners: youth affected by community violence
target_learning_goals: violence prevention
equity
promotion of peace
examples: The reorientation is offered to policymakers and practitioners as a basis for integrating multiple strategies in a context-based and community-involved approach

citation: van Dijk, A, de Haan, M & de Winter, M 2026, 'Educational Responses Toward Community Violence : A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions', Review of Educational Research, vol. 96, no. 3, pp. 829-869. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251324491
title: Integrative review of theory and research on educational interventions to counter community violence
description: The article itself is an integrative review: it states "This paper presents an integrative review of theory and research on the broad range of educational interventions to counter community violence." Motivated by "alarming rates of community violence and the detrimental impact on youth and communities", the review spans multiple disciplines, critically analyzes distinctions in perspectives, objectives, and strategies, and yields the multidisciplinary taxonomy and the coherent overview of current educational responses that structure the paper's contributions.
requirements: Requires theory and research on the broad range of educational interventions to counter community violence
constraints: The review notes strategies for transformation of social systems are underrepresented in the literature it covers
target_learners: youth affected by community violence
target_learning_goals: violence prevention
conflict resolution
examples: The review establishes a multidisciplinary taxonomy of distinguishable approaches based on critical analysis of perspectives, objectives, and strategies

article_title: Educational Responses Toward Community Violence: A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions
citation: van Dijk, A, de Haan, M & de Winter, M 2026, 'Educational Responses Toward Community Violence : A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions', Review of Educational Research, vol. 96, no. 3, pp. 829-869. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251324491
title: Educational responses to community violence should be well-founded and address the many levels through which youth and communities are affected
description: Because community violence affects youth and communities at many levels, educational responses should be well-founded in theory and research rather than ad hoc. The paper argues that a conceptual reorientation that includes structural mechanisms "enables a targeted approach of the many levels through which youth and communities are affected," and presents its coherent overview of current responses to help design such well-founded interventions. The principle follows from the review's finding that single-level, individual- or group-focused responses dominate the field.
requirements: Requires grounding in an integrative analysis of theory and research on educational interventions
constraints: The review reports that systems-transformation strategies are currently underrepresented, limiting ready-made multilevel responses
target_learners: youth affected by community violence
target_learning_goals: violence prevention
promotion of peace
examples: The paper suggests a conceptual reorientation that includes structural mechanisms and enables targeted approaches across the many levels affecting youth and communities

article_title: Hunter-Gatherer Children at School: A View From the Global South
citation: Ninkova, V., Hays, J., Lavi, N., Ali, A., Lopes da Silva Macedo, S., Davis, H. E., & Lew-Levy, S. (2025). Hunter-Gatherer Children at School: A View From the Global South. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241255614
title: A three-part framework of autonomy, access barriers, and impacts organizes hunter-gatherer children's experiences with formal schooling
description: The review synthesizes 82 publications from 23 countries into a framework of interwoven dynamics: childhood autonomy at odds with school hierarchy, multiple barriers to access, and long-term impacts of participation. It reports that hunter-gatherer communities "prioritize different sets of values and learning goals than those set by schools, creating conflicting expectations for children," and that these dynamics are interwoven rather than separable. The framework underpins the review's argument that education is locally negotiated rather than universally deliverable.
requirements: Requires ethnographic literature on hunter-gatherer communities' school experiences, coded and synthesized across study community, geography, years, and methods as the review describes.
constraints: The review states the dynamics are interwoven and "it is not easy to tease out a single 'barrier to' or 'effect of' formal schooling for hunter-gatherer children."
The term hunter-gatherer glosses over localized beliefs, values, and practices, as the authors acknowledge.
target_learners: Hunter-gatherer children in formal education systems in the Global South
target_learning_goals: Culturally responsive education for marginalized Indigenous communities
examples: The review's coding of 82 publications from 23 countries, with themes synthesized through group discussion into the framework.
key_sources: Ninkova, V., Hays, J., Lavi, N., Ali, A., Lopes da Silva Macedo, S., Davis, H. E., & Lew-Levy, S. (2025). Hunter-Gatherer Children at School: A View From the Global South. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241255614

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Three positions on knowledge specificity in literacy: general, task-specific, and community-specific knowledge
description: The review organizes literacy debates around three positions on the nature of composing and reading knowledge. The general knowledge position holds that "general knowledge is sufficient and that writers can transfer it spontaneously from situation to situation with relative ease." The task-specific position holds that different types of tasks require different types of knowledge, and the community-specific position holds that even similar tasks require knowledge of the conventions of particular discourse communities. Each position carries assumptions about learning and transfer with distinct instructional consequences.
requirements: Researchers and teachers must articulate which position they hold, since "Whenever teachers instruct, they implicitly convey their beliefs about knowledge transfer."
constraints: The discussion is circumscribed to extended written discourse and the reading of imaginative literature, and excludes grammatical knowledge because both readers and writers unquestionably transfer such basic knowledge.
target_learners: students learning composition and literary reading in secondary and higher education
target_learning_goals: writing competence across tasks and contexts
literary understanding
examples: The review illustrates the community-specific position with Pauline Kael's film criticism and Antonin Scalia's courtroom defining, both using task-specific defining skills within vastly different communities.
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.2307/1170740

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Typology of knowledge: content, form, declarative, procedural, and conditional knowledge
description: The authors define knowledge as used in cognitive psychology to encompass the what, how, and when of learning. Knowledge of content is "not merely one's factual knowledge of information" but also knowledge of personal experiences; knowledge of form "enables one to distinguish one thing from another according to their features." Each type can be declarative (what) or procedural (how), and conditional knowledge is "the knowledge of when to apply knowledge of content or form."
requirements: Distinguishing these knowledge types is needed to analyze what particular writing and reading tasks demand of learners.
target_learners: students in composition and literature instruction
target_learning_goals: knowing what, how, and when to apply knowledge in composing and reading
examples: The authors illustrate conditional knowledge: one might know how to exaggerate for humorous effect, but conditional knowledge should inform one not to exaggerate when reporting research results.
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.2307/1170740

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Community-specific argumentation: literary criticism and legal brief writing employ distinct argumentative conventions
description: The review argues that even shared task-specific skills operate differently across discourse communities. Fahnestock and Secor show literary criticism employs "a definable repertoire of persuasive tactics to achieve communication in its well-defined environment," including special topoi such as paradox and metaphor. Stratman's analysis of legal brief writing shows appellate brief writers must anticipate how judges and opponents read and integrate briefs, knowledge the review says is almost absent in law school instruction despite law schools' belief in transferable general critical reasoning.
requirements: Effective argumentation within a community requires "knowledge that gives background and definition to [each discipline]—not only 'facts' but the terms of art, operational concepts, canons of relevance, patterns of association, characteristic argumentative gestures."
constraints: The community-specific position creates a daunting instructional problem: teachers must either instruct students to differentiate their writing in seemingly unlimited ways or accept limited influence on student writing.
target_learners: students learning discipline-specific writing such as literary criticism or legal brief writing
target_learning_goals: argumentation adapted to the conventions of a discourse community
examples: The review contrasts Kael's film reviews and Scalia's flag-burning-case deliberations: both use defining skills of generating criteria through problematic examples, yet each requires community-specific knowledge the other lacks.
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.2307/1170740

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Cognitive view of reading: five general comprehension strategies at the center of the reading curriculum
description: The review describes the cognitive view offered by Dole, Duffy, Roehler, and Pearson, which "assumes an active reader who constructs meaning through the integration of existing and new knowledge and the flexible use of strategies to foster, monitor, regulate, and maintain comprehension," in contrast to the traditional view of a passive reader applying subskills automatically. They identify five strategies—determining importance, summarizing information, drawing inferences, generating questions, and monitoring comprehension—that ought to stand at the center of the reading curriculum.
requirements: Instruction should help students gain conscious control over strategies they can adapt to any text, with good readers adapting strategies based on purpose, task and text demands, and situational context.
constraints: The review classifies this position as reflecting faith in general procedural knowledge, since the researchers name strategies meant to apply across texts.
target_learners: students learning reading comprehension across text types
target_learning_goals: strategic, flexible reading comprehension
examples: The review contrasts this cognitive view with traditional skill instruction, which Dole et al. criticize for connoting consistency, if not rigidity.
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.2307/1170740

article_title: Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review
citation: Ray Breed, Riki Lindsay, Aden Kittel, Michael Spittle. (2025). Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241227236
title: Tactical game-centered approaches as a family of game-centered pedagogies grounded in constructivist and situated learning
description: TGAs are a family of PE teaching approaches, originating with the Teaching Games for Understanding (TGfU) model proposed in 1982, in which structured, modified small-sided games are the central context through which learners develop tactical, technical and strategic skills. The review states the variants "share common elements related to cognitive, constructivist, and situated learning theories", with learners generating their own solutions through problem-solving and responding to teacher questioning. Variants named include play practice, tactical games approach, tactical-decision learning model, and game sense. The review situates TGAs within an ecological dynamics, constraints-led perspective of skill acquisition.
requirements: A TGA unit of at least four consecutive lessons, per the review's eligibility criteria
Modified games with manipulated task constraints (rules, aims, scoring, playing area, number of players) creating tactical problems
constraints: The review notes there is only a little evidence showing transfer of knowledge and skills across different games within a category
TGAs are suggested as more suitable from upper primary school years, aged 9 onwards
target_learners: Primary and secondary school physical education students
target_learning_goals: Tactical skill and decision-making
Procedural knowledge and game understanding
Technical skill development through game contexts
examples: Included interventions used terminology TGfU (n = 11), TGA (n = 6), tactical games model (n = 4), and game-centered approach (n = 3)
key_sources: Ray Breed, Riki Lindsay, Aden Kittel, Michael Spittle. (2025). Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241227236

article_title: Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review
citation: Ray Breed, Riki Lindsay, Aden Kittel, Michael Spittle. (2025). Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241227236
title: Game Performance Assessment Instrument (GPAI) as the most utilized in-game performance tool in PE
description: The GPAI is an observational tool developed and validated in 1998 specifically for PE settings, used to assess in-game performance variables such as skill execution and tactical variables (e.g., decision-making with the ball and off-ball support), with observations coded as successful/effective or unsuccessful/ineffective, typically during a game or from postgame video. The review reports that "the GPAI has become the most utilized tool to assess in-game performance (e.g., skill execution and tactical variables) in PE and sport school settings". Related tools named are the Team Sport Assessment Procedure (TSAP) and Game Performance Evaluation Tool (GPET).
requirements: Observation during a game or postgame recording, often via video
Trained coding of observed behaviours as successful or unsuccessful
constraints: The review notes some studies used modified versions without reporting reliability or validation, or used tools in settings different from those they were validated in
target_learners: Primary and secondary school physical education students
target_learning_goals: Assessing in-game skill execution and tactical decision-making
examples: Included studies applied the GPAI in small-sided games such as 3v3, 4v4, and 5v5 formats with postgame video
key_sources: Ray Breed, Riki Lindsay, Aden Kittel, Michael Spittle. (2025). Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241227236

article_title: Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review
citation: Ray Breed, Riki Lindsay, Aden Kittel, Michael Spittle. (2025). Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241227236
title: Align the chosen PE teaching model with the curriculum's intended student outcomes
description: The review endorses the suggestion that specific teaching models should be selected to emphasize particular student outcomes depending on curriculum aims: "specific models should be used to emphasize certain student outcomes, depending on the aims and objectives of the PE curriculum". Tactical skill, procedural knowledge and affective domains are accentuated in TGAs, while technical skill and declarative knowledge are emphasized more in TAs. The review notes it seems commonplace that PE teachers do not align appropriate models to curriculum goals, with most still featuring traditional teacher-centered models.
requirements: Clarity about the aims and objectives of the PE curriculum before selecting a model
Teacher capacity to deliver the chosen model as intended
constraints: The review also reports complexity thinking suggests no one correct teaching model, indicating teachers adopt a range of pedagogical models
target_learners: Primary and secondary school physical education students
target_learning_goals: Matching pedagogy to intended outcomes across tactical, technical, cognitive and affective domains
examples: The review classifies outcomes into seven categories (tactical skill, skill execution, technical skill, affective, declarative knowledge, procedural knowledge, physical activity) that different approaches emphasize differently
key_sources: Ray Breed, Riki Lindsay, Aden Kittel, Michael Spittle. (2025). Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241227236

article_title: The Effects of Co-Teaching and Related Collaborative Models of Instruction on Student Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Vembye, M. H., Weiss, F., & Bhat, B. H. (2022). The Effects of Co-Teaching and Related Collaborative Models of Instruction on Student Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. https://osf.io/ur2bs
title: Three-category taxonomy of collaborative instruction models with distinct causal mechanisms
description: The review organizes two-teacher in-class interventions into three categories studied largely separately: co-teaching (general plus special education professionals), teacher assistants/aides (collaboration with adults without formal teaching qualifications), and team teaching (two general education teachers). It "broadly define[s] collaborative instruction as the simultaneous presence of two or more educators/adults working together and sharing responsibilities in instructional and/or behavioral interventions." Mechanisms include improved student-teacher ratio, freed teacher time, scaffolding, feedback, and behavior management.
requirements: Both educators at least 18 years old teaching in-class in the same physical space
At least two weeks (ten school days) of treatment
constraints: Excludes peer teaching, tutoring, and out-of-classroom two-teacher arrangements
General education setting focus; special education school settings excluded
target_learners: Students in grades one to twelve in primary and secondary schools
General education and special needs students
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in arts, social science, and STEM subjects
examples: The review's data extraction scheme was developed in line with co-teaching literature to test these theoretical hypotheses empirically
key_sources: Vembye, M. H., Weiss, F., & Bhat, B. H. (2022). The Effects of Co-Teaching and Related Collaborative Models of Instruction on Student Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. https://osf.io/ur2bs

article_title: The Effects of Co-Teaching and Related Collaborative Models of Instruction on Student Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Vembye, M. H., Weiss, F., & Bhat, B. H. (2022). The Effects of Co-Teaching and Related Collaborative Models of Instruction on Student Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. https://osf.io/ur2bs
title: Expand collaborative instruction using assistants without teaching qualifications, given similar effects at lower cost
description: Because effects were mostly the same size whether interventions involved trained teachers or unqualified assistants, the review concludes there is "a potential for the expansion of such interventions at lower costs than otherwise expected." This principle recommends deploying paraprofessionals, pedagogues, or parent volunteers in in-class supporting roles as a cost-effective alternative to fully qualified co-teachers for raising achievement.
requirements: In-class collaboration in the same physical space with a general education teacher
At least two weeks of treatment
constraints: Based on largely non-randomized studies; the article calls for more rigorous experimental research, especially on co-teaching interventions
target_learners: Primary and secondary students in grades one to twelve
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement across STEM and arts/social science subjects
examples: The meta-analysis compared interventions staffed by trained teachers against those using assistants with no teaching qualifications and found mostly equal effects
