article_title: World Bank Influence on Policy Formation in Education: A Systematic Review of the Literature
citation: Edwards Jr., D. Brent; Caravaca Hernández, Alejandro; Rappeport, Annie; et al. (2023). World Bank influence on policy formation in education: A systematic review of the literature. Review of Educational Research, Vol. 94, Núm. 4. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231194725
title: Eleven-pathway typology of World Bank influence on national education policy formation
description: The review proposes a typology of 11 'pathways' of World Bank influence, defined as 'those observable avenues through which the World Bank exercises its influence (Samoff, 2009)'. The framework draws on the work of Roger Dale and Joel Samoff on forms of influence of international organizations, combining, retaining and separating pathways relevant to the World Bank. The pathways range from issuing loans to producing research, offering technical assistance, and guiding the work and investments of other international organizations, and each is illustrated with examples from the retained literature.
requirements: Studies must shed light on World Bank involvement and influence in policymaking processes at the national level, where policy means decisions taken by political actors on behalf of the state
constraints: The review is not exhaustive of all World Bank literature; it covers studies providing insight on policy formation rather than the effects of World Bank projects in practice, and books were not included
target_learners: Education policymakers and researchers studying international organizations in education
target_learning_goals: Understanding the specific avenues through which international organizations influence national education policy formation
examples: The review's results section discusses each pathway in turn, including loans, conditionalities, pilot projects, and technical assistance, with country examples such as Nepal, Tanzania, Egypt, El Salvador, and China
key_sources: Edwards Jr., D. Brent; Caravaca Hernández, Alejandro; Rappeport, Annie; et al. (2023). World Bank influence on policy formation in education: A systematic review of the literature. Review of Educational Research, Vol. 94, Núm. 4. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231194725

article_title: World Bank Influence on Policy Formation in Education: A Systematic Review of the Literature
citation: Edwards Jr., D. Brent; Caravaca Hernández, Alejandro; Rappeport, Annie; et al. (2023). World Bank influence on policy formation in education: A systematic review of the literature. Review of Educational Research, Vol. 94, Núm. 4. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231194725
title: Lukes' three dimensions of power as an analytic lens for international-organization influence
description: The review analyzes its 11 pathways through Lukes' (2005) three dimensions of power: influencing formal decision-making by advancing one's interests; shaping others' preferences or preventing decisions; and using 'social forces and institutional practices' to keep unfavorable issues out of politics and policy. Dale's summary describes the dimensions as the 'naked' use of superior power, the politics of non-decisionmaking such as agenda setting, and control of the 'rules of the game'. The review's key insight is that many pathways contribute to multiple dimensions of power at once, which shows the value of combining Lukes' abstract dimensions with a concrete typology of influence strategies.
requirements: A nuanced typology of concrete influence pathways is needed alongside the power dimensions, since the dimensions alone operate at more abstract levels
constraints: The framework is applied to one international development bank's actions at the national level, not to policy diffusion generally
target_learners: Education policy scholars and researchers of global governance
target_learning_goals: Analyzing how international organizations exercise overt and less overt forms of power in policymaking
examples: The discussion section classifies pathways such as loans, conditionalities, and knowledge production according to the dimension(s) of power they engage
key_sources: Edwards Jr., D. Brent; Caravaca Hernández, Alejandro; Rappeport, Annie; et al. (2023). World Bank influence on policy formation in education: A systematic review of the literature. Review of Educational Research, Vol. 94, Núm. 4. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231194725

article_title: Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature
citation: Surr CA, Gates C, Irving D et al (2017) Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Review of Educational Research. 87(5): 966-1002. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723305
title: Deliver dementia education with a total duration of at least 8 hours and individual sessions of 90 minutes or more
description: This principle holds that workforce education on dementia should be long enough to allow depth and consolidation: the review's synthesis found more efficacious programs "have a total duration of at least 8 hours with individual sessions of 90 minutes or more." It applies to designing training schedules for health and social care staff learning dementia knowledge and skills.
requirements: Programs must be planned so total contact time reaches at least 8 hours and individual sessions run 90 minutes or more, as the synthesis identified as a feature of more efficacious programs.
constraints: The duration thresholds come from a critical interpretive synthesis of papers of variable quality; the review itself calls for further robust research to develop the evidence base.
target_learners: Health and social care workforce staff receiving dementia education and training
target_learning_goals: Dementia knowledge, skills, and care practice for the health and social care workforce
examples: The synthesis of 152 papers identified the 8-hour total and 90-minute-plus session thresholds as common features of more efficacious educational programs.
key_sources: Surr CA, Gates C, Irving D et al (2017) Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Review of Educational Research. 87(5): 966-1002. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723305

article_title: Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature
citation: Surr CA, Gates C, Irving D et al (2017) Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Review of Educational Research. 87(5): 966-1002. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723305
title: Underpin practice-based dementia learning with theory and support application of learning in practice
description: This principle states that dementia education for care staff should connect workplace learning to underlying theory and help learners transfer it into daily care. The synthesis found efficacious programs "underpin practice-based learning with theory" and "support application of learning in practice," linking conceptual grounding to on-the-job use for the health and social care workforce.
requirements: Education must combine practice-based learning with theoretical underpinning and include mechanisms that support applying the learning in practice.
constraints: The feature was identified in a synthesis of studies of variable quality; no effect sizes are printed in the available text.
target_learners: Health and social care workforce staff receiving dementia education and training
target_learning_goals: Applying dementia care knowledge and skills in day-to-day practice
examples: The critical interpretive synthesis listed theory-underpinned practice-based learning and support for application in practice among the common features of more efficacious programs.
key_sources: Surr CA, Gates C, Irving D et al (2017) Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Review of Educational Research. 87(5): 966-1002. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723305

article_title: Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature
citation: Surr CA, Gates C, Irving D et al (2017) Effective Dementia Education and Training for the Health and Social Care Workforce: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Review of Educational Research. 87(5): 966-1002. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723305
title: Critical interpretive synthesis underpinned by Kirkpatrick's return on investment model for reviewing workforce education effectiveness
description: This is the review's methodological framework: a "Critical interpretive synthesis underpinned by Kirkpatrick's return on investment model" applied to identify features of effective dementia educational programs. The approach integrates interpretive synthesis of heterogeneous studies with Kirkpatrick's evaluation framework, allowing the authors to judge program efficacy across training outcomes for the workforce.
requirements: Requires a corpus of studies on the educational interventions of interest, synthesised interpretively and evaluated against Kirkpatrick's return on investment model.
constraints: The authors note there remains limited understanding of how an informed and effective dementia workforce can be achieved, and that further robust research is required to develop the evidence base.
target_learners: Health and social care workforce staff receiving dementia education and training
target_learning_goals: Identifying features of effective dementia education and training programs
examples: The review applied this synthesis approach to 152 included papers of variable quality to derive the common features of more efficacious programs.

article_title: The Evolution of “Loaded Moments” Toward Escalation or De-Escalation in Student–Teacher Interactions
citation: Kennedy, B L & Junker, R (2024). The Evolution of “Loaded Moments” Toward Escalation or De-Escalation in Student–Teacher Interactions. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231202509
title: Loaded moments framework for the co-construction of escalation and de-escalation in student–teacher interactions
description: The review defines loaded moments as “points in time when two or more parties realize that their needs differ and that they must confront that difference.” It synthesizes 30 studies (2000–2020) into a staged process account: macro contexts set the scene, instigating circumstances co-construct incompatibilities, moment-by-moment co-construction drives (de)escalation, and outcomes feed long-term relationship and bond development. The framework organizes classroom conflict research around co-construction rather than individual blame.
requirements: Studies must describe the evolution of loaded moments between teachers and students during classroom interactions
constraints: Synthesis limited to 30 studies published from 2000 to 2020
target_learners: K-12 and school students in classroom settings
target_learning_goals: Successful negotiation of loaded moments to minimize negative interactions and their impacts
key_sources: Kennedy, B L & Junker, R (2024). The Evolution of “Loaded Moments” Toward Escalation or De-Escalation in Student–Teacher Interactions. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231202509

article_title: The Teacher’s Invisible Hand: A Meta-Analysis of the Relevance of Teacher–Student Relationship Quality for Peer Relationships and the Contribution of Student Behavior
citation: Endedijk, H. M., Breeman, L. D., van Lissa, C. J., Hendrickx, M. M. H. G., den Boer, L., & Mainhard, T. (2022). The Teacher's Invisible Hand: A Meta-Analysis of the Relevance of Teacher–Student Relationship Quality for Peer Relationships and the Contribution of Student Behavior. Review of Educational Research, 92(3), 370–412. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211051428
title: Three-mechanism framework linking teacher–student relationships to peer relationships: attachment, social learning, and social referencing
description: The article organizes explanations of how teacher–student relationship quality affects peer relationships around three theoretical mechanisms. It states that "The most prominent mechanisms that have been put forward in previous research are rooted in attachment theory, social learning theory, and social referencing theory." Attachment theory treats the teacher as a secure base and safe haven; social learning theory casts the teacher as a model whose behavior students copy with peers; social referencing theory holds that peers read teacher–student interactions as information for evaluating the student. The article notes the first two locate learning in the student, whereas social referencing locates the effect in peers' perceptions.
requirements: A teacher occupying a central social position in the classroom whose interactions with individual students are observable to peers
constraints: The framework is a theoretical account; the meta-analysis tests associations, not the mechanisms themselves
target_learners: students in preschool, primary, and secondary education (ages 3–18)
target_learning_goals: social skill development and peer relationship formation
examples: The article's Figure 1 depicts the theoretical model of the association between teacher–student and peer relationships, with student behavior as a contributing factor

citation: Eva Vives, Céline Poletti, Anaïs Robert, Fabrizio Butera, Pascal Huguet, et al.. (2024). Learning With Jigsaw: A Systematic Review Gathering All the Pieces of the Puzzle More Than 40 Years Later. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241230064
title: The jigsaw classroom as a cooperative learning method designed to improve minority children's performance by reducing intergroup conflict and increasing self-evaluations
description: The jigsaw classroom is a cooperative learning method originating in the late 1970s. According to the review, it was "designed in the late 1970s to improve the academic performance of minority children by reducing intergroup conflict and increasing self-evaluations." The method rests on social interdependence and collaboration, and its intended mechanisms are simultaneously academic (performance) and psychosocial (intergroup relationships, self-evaluations). This review is the first systematic synthesis of the evidence base for the method across more than 40 years of research.
requirements: Implementation as a cooperative learning activity structured to reduce intergroup conflict and raise self-evaluations, per the method's original design aims
constraints: The review notes that despite high popularity, the available evidence for effectiveness seems scant and mixed

Intergroup relationships
Self-evaluations

Sixty-nine studies met the inclusion criteria, making this the first systematic review of the method — prior to it there was "neither meta-analysis nor systematic review." The corpus underpins the review's conclusions about overall positive effects and their variation across subjects and outcome variables.

article_title: The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education
citation: Hagger, M. S., & Chatzisarantis, N. L. D. (2016). The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education: Conceptual and Empirical Issues and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315585005
title: The trans-contextual model of autonomous motivation explains transfer of autonomous motivation from educational to out-of-school contexts
description: The trans-contextual model is a multitheory framework integrating self-determination theory, Vallerand's hierarchical model, and the theory of planned behavior to explain how motivation transfers across contexts. As the authors state, it "outlines the processes by which autonomous motivation toward activities in a physical education context predicts autonomous motivation toward physical activity outside of school, and beliefs about, intentions toward, and actual engagement in, out-of-school physical activity." The model comprises three propositions linking perceived autonomy support, autonomous motivation in educational contexts, autonomous motivation in out-of-school contexts, belief-based antecedents, intentions, and behavior.
requirements: Empirical support for the three model propositions and their fundamental hypotheses (H1-H5, H15) is required for the model to be accepted
constraints: Originally developed and predominantly tested in the physical education and leisure-time physical activity context, with generalizability to other domains proposed but not yet extensively tested
target_learners: school students aged 12 to 16 years in physical education
target_learning_goals: transfer of autonomous motivation from classroom activities to out-of-school engagement in related activities

article_title: The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education
citation: Hagger, M. S., & Chatzisarantis, N. L. D. (2016). The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education: Conceptual and Empirical Issues and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315585005
title: Self-determination theory differentiates qualities of motivation, with autonomous forms most adaptive for persistence
description: Self-determination theory serves as the leading explanatory system in the model and distinguishes types rather than amounts of motivation: "The defining characteristic of the theory is that it differentiates between qualities or types of motivation experienced by individuals toward the activities and behaviors in which they engage rather than the quantity of motivation alone." Autonomous motivation (intrinsic, identified, integrated regulation) reflects acting with choice and volition, while controlled motivation (external, introjected regulation) reflects externally referenced contingencies. Basic psychological need satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness) and internalization are the mechanisms by which autonomous motivation develops and persists.
requirements: Satisfaction of the three basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness) underpins optimal functioning and autonomous motivation
target_learners: students in educational contexts
target_learning_goals: self-regulated participation in and persistence with educational activities

article_title: The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education
citation: Hagger, M. S., & Chatzisarantis, N. L. D. (2016). The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education: Conceptual and Empirical Issues and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315585005
title: Teachers foster autonomous motivation and persistence by providing choice, rationale, and self-directed learning support
description: The article identifies autonomy support as the key means by which social agents foster students' autonomous motivation: "teachers are able to foster higher levels of autonomous motivation and greater behavioral persistence by providing instruction and feedback that focuses on self-directed learning and by giving students choice over, and a rationale for, their actions." Specific autonomy-supportive behaviors include providing choice and meaningful rationale, offering encouragement and positive feedback, avoiding controlling directives, acknowledging students' perspectives, and promoting an exploratory approach toward tasks. This principle grounds Proposition 1 of the trans-contextual model and points to autonomy-supportive programs as an intervention route.
requirements: Teachers must display autonomy-supportive behaviors so that students perceive autonomy support, which correlates with actual teacher support
target_learners: school students in classroom contexts
target_learning_goals: autonomous motivation and self-directed persistence with learning activities
examples: Research mapped specific teacher behaviors supporting autonomy, including providing choice, offering hints, and avoiding controlling commands

article_title: The Trans-Contextual Model of Autonomous Motivation in Education

title: Fundamental-versus-peripheral hypothesis taxonomy specifies criteria for rejecting or failing to replicate the model
description: To answer criticisms that social-cognitive models are unfalsifiable, the authors classify each of the model's 23 hypotheses as fundamental or peripheral. Fundamental hypotheses test the three core propositions (H1-H5 and H15); peripheral hypotheses cover the belief-mediated pathways. The authors state that "Support for Hypotheses 1 to 5 is fundamental for the test of model to be accepted and a null finding for any of these hypotheses in an overall test of the model will render it rejected as a failed replication." Failure of peripheral hypotheses does not invalidate the core pathways, since mediation through any one belief-based construct suffices.
requirements: Any test must provide unequivocal support for the three model propositions and acceptance of all fundamental hypotheses
constraints: Component paths of indirect effects (e.g., H6-H8, H12-H14) need not all be supported for the indirect effects to be valid
target_learners: researchers testing motivational models in educational settings
target_learning_goals: evaluation of replication and falsification criteria for motivational theories
examples: Table 1 outlines the status of each hypothesis as fundamental or peripheral to supporting or rejecting the model

title: Meta-analytic corpus of 42 U.S. causal studies yielding 73 effect estimates of grant aid on persistence and degree attainment
description: This element is the analytic corpus the review assembled: 42 primary U.S. studies (plus 5 international studies analyzed separately) providing linear probability estimates of grant aid effects on persistence and degree completion, yielding 73 effect estimates. The authors state they "provide the first such study by incorporating 73 effect estimates from 42 primary U.S. studies." Studies were screened from over 21,000 records via a three-phase PRISMA-guided process, coded by multiple coders with 96% cell agreement, and rated 1-5 for risk of bias; 83 percent were rated high quality and 60 percent were RCTs or regression discontinuity designs.

article_title: A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis to Synthesize the Influence of                     Contexts of Scaffolding Use on Cognitive Outcomes in STEM                     Education
citation: Belland Brian R., Walker Andrew E., Kim Nam Ju. (2017). A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis to Synthesize the Influence of Contexts of Scaffolding Use on Cognitive Outcomes in STEM Education. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723009
title: Scaffolding as contingent support characterized by contingency, intersubjectivity, and transfer of responsibility
description: The article defines scaffolding as "contingent support that structures and highlights the complexity inherent in problem solving, thereby supporting current performance and promoting skill gain." Three key attributes characterize it: contingency, intersubjectivity, and transfer of responsibility. Scaffolding is contingent on dynamic assessment indicating students' current abilities, so support can be faded or added as skill changes; students must recognize successful performance; and scaffolding must engender independent task completion. The review uses this definition to frame its synthesis of scaffolding across problem-centered instructional models in STEM.

Scaffolding needs to engender independent task completion

citation: Belland Brian R., Walker Andrew E., Kim Nam Ju. (2017). A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis to Synthesize the Influence of Contexts of Scaffolding Use on Cognitive Outcomes in STEM Education. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723009
title: Taxonomy of computer-based scaffolding types: conceptual, strategic, metacognitive, and motivational
description: The article presents a four-part taxonomy of computer-based scaffolding functions: scaffolding is often designed to (a) help students with what to consider when addressing a problem (conceptual scaffolding), (b) bootstrap a strategy for addressing a problem (strategic scaffolding), (c) invite students to question their own understanding (metacognitive scaffolding), and (d) enhance interest, autonomy, self-efficacy, and other motivational variables (motivational scaffolding). Specific embedded strategies include highlighting critical problem features, modeling expert processes and demonstration, and motivational support such as recruitment, direction maintenance, and controlling frustration. This taxonomy organizes the scaffolding interventions synthesized in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Computer-based scaffolding must support students addressing an ill-structured problem

title: Six-code thematic framework for knowledge claims in ITE-diversity research: content, teaching-to-diversity, program approaches, ITE-student challenges, teacher-educator challenges, and transformative commitment
description: The review developed an inductive, iterative coding framework to classify knowledge claims about preparing teachers for diverse learners. It began with two broad issues — "Issues of ITE diversity content" and "Issues of ITE delivery relevant to diversity" — and expanded these into six codes, including arguments about knowledge needed, specific program approaches such as specialist courses and partnerships, challenges relating to ITE students' beliefs, challenges relating to teacher educators' context, beliefs and skills, and a final code for "Papers marked by an overt commitment to social justice and social transformation through education". The framework was tested for inter-coder agreement and applied to all 209 papers.

citation: Michael Brown, Rachel Smith, Jennifer Tipton, Gabrielle Leitner. (2026). The Threads of Campus Life: A Review of the Literature on the Use of Social Network Analysis in Research Articles on Undergraduate Students. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543261438444
title: Campus Ecological Networks Model with bonding and exploring mechanisms for campus community formation
description: The review organizes its analysis with the Campus Ecological Networks Model (M. G. Brown & Smith, 2024), which builds on Renn and Arnold's campus ecological perspective to connect students' individual characteristics, interaction contents, institutional social structure, and educational outcomes. It incorporates Smith and Vonhoff's (2019) mechanisms: "social mechanisms that help students bond with one another, such as balance, exchange, homophily, and proximity, as well as those that help students explore broadly, such as self-interest and contagion" (Table 1). The framework hypothesizes mechanisms may compete in shaping community structure and that networks can have negative as well as beneficial educational outcomes.
requirements: Institutional personnel should intentionally choose which theoretical mechanism(s) to draw on to help students form community, make program and policy decisions accordingly, and then measure resulting networks and outcomes
constraints: The review observes the field lacks a theory for how relational structure emerges, is maintained, or abandoned on campus, in classrooms, and across a student's academic career
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding how campus community structures form, persist, and dissolve and how they relate to learning, development, and persistence
examples: Table 1 maps each mechanism to measures: homophily to shared characteristics predicting ties, proximity to physical closeness, self-interest to betweenness centrality, contagion to longitudinal tracking of behavior spread

title: Provide opportunities for students to observe short fragments of peer-expert models interspersed with instructional guidance to increase IPS performance
description: Design principle 3 advises providing "opportunities for students to observe short fragments of peer-expert models, interspersed with instructional guidance, to increase IPS performance." It is theoretically grounded in social cognitive theory (observational learning reveals underlying cognitive processes and strengthens self-efficacy) and cognitive load theory (modeling examples reduce cognitive load and support schema construction).
requirements: Model fragments should be short, show each IPS process step, be interspersed with reflective prompts or explicit instruction, and be followed by practice
constraints: Evidence for non-expert (peer) models is mixed and based on varied operationalizations with unvalidated outcome measures
target_learners: (under)graduate students, particularly first-year contexts
target_learning_goals: IPS performance and self-efficacy
examples: Peer-expert videos showing short fragments of each IPS process step, interspersed with reflective prompts or explicit instruction and followed by practice, outperformed practice-only groups on IPS performance

citation: Boetje, J., Sichterman, B., Van Ginkel, S., Smakman, M., & Versendaal, J. (2026). Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251338057
title: Provide opportunities for students to practice IPS in preparation for or following instruction or modeling
description: Design principle 4 states: "Provide opportunities for students to practice IPS in preparation for or following instruction or modeling to develop IPS knowledge, skills, and performance." Fifty-three of the reviewed publications adopted practice as a crucial learning environment characteristic, and theoretical arguments drew on social constructivist theory, collaborative practice principles, and the 4C/ID model's emphasis on part-task practice and repetition.
requirements: Practice should be scheduled in preparation for or following instruction or modeling; the literature suggests combining deliberate practice with instruction or modeling examples to enhance skill retention and knowledge acquisition
target_learners: (under)graduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: IPS knowledge, skills, and performance
examples: Fifty-three of the reviewed publications adopted the opportunity to practice IPS as a crucial learning environment characteristic to improve IPS knowledge, skills, and performance

citation: Boetje, J., Sichterman, B., Van Ginkel, S., Smakman, M., & Versendaal, J. (2026). Design Principles for Developing Information Problem Solving Competence in Higher Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251338057
title: IPS-EDP model: seven educational design principles for developing information problem solving competence organized by constructive alignment
description: The IPS educational design principles (IPS-EDP) model integrates seven design principles—"encompassing (1) learning task, (2) instruction, (3) modeling, (4) practice, (5) learning activities, (6) support, and (7) feedback"—derived from a systematic review of 69 peer-reviewed articles. Sequenced according to Biggs's constructive alignment, the principles move from intended learning outcomes (principle 1) through teaching and learning activities (principles 2–6) to assessment strategies (principle 7), providing a theoretical foundation for designing IPS learning environments in higher education.
requirements: It is recommended to apply at least one principle from each component of constructive alignment within the learning environment; comprehensive application of each principle is not imperative
constraints: Empirical evidence predominantly addressed information search and selection, potentially limiting generalizability to broader IPS competence
target_learners: (under)graduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: IPS competence: knowledge, skills, attitudes, performance, and self-efficacy
examples: The model summarizes how the seven principles address learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities, and assessment strategies, mirroring the stages of course development

article_title: The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development
citation: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. http://rer.aera.net
title: Smagorinsky's neo-Vygotskian account of the ZPD as an elastic and unbounded mind
description: The article develops an account of Vygotsky's zone of proximal development in which the mind is 'both elastic in that cognitive growth may take different directions depending on the sociocultural environment in which it occurs, and unbounded in terms of its extent and potential for growth'. Elasticity means higher mental processes have no fixed operations but embody culture-specific ways of thinking; unboundedness means the zone's upper reaches continually evolve and the mind extends beyond the skull through mediational tools. The article uses this account to ground its critique of research methodology.
requirements: Development requires the learner's consonance with, and volitional use of, the cultural tools that mediate it
constraints: The account assumes development is socially mediated; unadulterated development could only take place in vacuo, a state not possible in human society
target_learners: learners in culturally diverse educational settings
target_learning_goals: development of culturally shaped higher mental processes
examples: The article contrasts this view with Piagetian conceptions in which direct instruction can inhibit a child's own exploration
key_sources: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. https://doi.org/10.2307/1170682

article_title: The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development
citation: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. http://rer.aera.net
title: Vygotsky's genetic method: development as tool- and sign-mediated social process
description: The article describes Vygotsky's genetic method, 'a term translated from the Russian word geneticheskii and referring to development rather than genes or genetic codes'. It rests on three themes the article attributes to Wertsch: a developmental method, the social origins of consciousness, and mediation of mental processes by tools and signs. Signs such as speech genres, art, dance, and physical space structure the developmental environment and mediate internalization of cultural values. The article uses this framework to argue that data are social constructs.
requirements: Analysis of development must use goal-directed, tool-mediated activity as the unit of analysis, per Wertsch's position the article endorses
constraints: The article notes Vygotsky's work has been translated three times under two titles and interpreted in incompatible ways, so any neo-Vygotskian claim is itself a social practice of knowledge construction
target_learners: learners across cultures participating in tool-mediated activity
target_learning_goals: internalization of culturally valued ways of thinking through mediational tools
examples: The article cites Tulviste's heterogeneity principle: overlapping social networks present learners with varied problems, allowing several frameworks for thinking to develop simultaneously
key_sources: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. https://doi.org/10.2307/1170682

article_title: The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development
citation: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. http://rer.aera.net
title: Valid research on learning requires learner consonance with the mediational means of the research
description: The article proposes that 'Research results, I propose, are only valid when the learner is consonant with and can appropriate the mediational means of the research as useful cultural tools'. Researchers must therefore take account of the learner's appropriation of research tools when finding evidence for a claim, and recognize that any assessment vehicle carries a telos. On this view valid research is inherently instructional, since congruence of learner and learning materials affords development.
requirements: The learner must share the researcher's sense of telos and be able to appropriate the research's mediational means as useful cultural tools
constraints: Validity as defined here depends on the particular conception of the ZPD the article outlines; the article acknowledges its reading of Vygotsky is one selective appropriation among competing ones
target_learners: research participants and students in culturally diverse settings
target_learning_goals: valid documentation and support of development in the ZPD
examples: The article argues that by choosing a means of assessment the researcher enters the learning environment with assumptions that it can determine learning
key_sources: Peter Smagorinsky. (1995). The Social Construction of Data: Methodological Problems of Investigating Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development. Review of Educational Research, 65(3), 191-212. https://doi.org/10.2307/1170682

article_title: Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics
citation: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Dragan Gašević, Omid Noroozi, Halszka Jarodzka, Desiree Joosten-ten Brinke, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251370753
title: Black and Wiliam's (2009) model of formative assessment as the review's organizing framework: three agents crossing three key processes
description: The review adopts Black and Wiliam's (2009) model, in which formative assessment is 'assessment for learning' undertaken by three agents — teachers, peers, and learners — across three processes: where the learner is going, where the learner is now, and how to get there. The authors state that "formative assessment is conceptualized by five key strategies: (1) articulating and disseminating learning goals and success criteria, (2) orchestrating productive classroom discussions and activities to uncover student understanding, (3) providing feedback that facilitates student progression, (4) encouraging peers as instructional resources, and (5) fostering student autonomy in their learning process." The model supplied the study's coding scheme and research questions.
requirements: Evidence collected in the 'where the learner is now' phase must actually be used to adapt teaching to meet student needs for assessment to be formative
constraints: The review restricts application of the model to higher education contexts, excluding K–12 and MOOC settings
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: formative assessment practices by teachers, peers, and self-assessors
examples: The coding scheme in Table 1 codes actors (teacher, peer, self and combinations) and processes (B1–B7) drawn from this model
key_sources: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Dragan Gašević, Omid Noroozi, Halszka Jarodzka, Desiree Joosten-ten Brinke, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251370753

article_title: Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics
citation: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Dragan Gašević, Omid Noroozi, Halszka Jarodzka, Desiree Joosten-ten Brinke, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251370753
title: Four levels of learning analytics (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive) map onto the three stages of formative assessment
description: The review organizes learning analytics into four levels — descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive — and argues they align with formative assessment's three processes. It states: "These levels of analytics seem to be well-aligned with formative assessment practices as they provide insights into the main three stages of formative assessment (Black & Wiliam, 2009), including where the learner is going (for this purpose, learning analytics at the predictive level could serve), where the learner is now (descriptive and diagnostic analytics tend to be appropriate learning analytics levels for supporting this stage of formative assessment), and how to get there (prescriptive analytics could serve this stage)." This mapping structured the review's coding scheme (levels C1–C7).
requirements: A combined coding category was added because several studies used learning analytics at multiple levels rather than in a unimodal way
constraints: The alignment is the authors' conceptual mapping, not an empirically tested result
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: connecting analytics outputs to formative assessment stages
examples: Descriptive analytics answers 'What has happened?' via dashboards; predictive analytics provides early warnings for at-risk students; prescriptive analytics suggests task-specific strategies
key_sources: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Dragan Gašević, Omid Noroozi, Halszka Jarodzka, Desiree Joosten-ten Brinke, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251370753

article_title: Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics
citation: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Dragan Gašević, Omid Noroozi, Halszka Jarodzka, Desiree Joosten-ten Brinke, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251370753
title: Use learning analytics to deliver scaled, real-time, personalized feedback that relieves teacher workload constraints on formative assessment
description: Because effective formative feedback must be timely and of sufficient quality, yet teachers face high workloads and large student populations, the review recommends leveraging learning analytics to scale feedback. It states: "This is also where learning analytics can significantly contribute to formative assessment by offering scaled, real-time, and personalized feedback." The review adds that learning analytics can make feedback manageable for busy teachers and provide real-time personalized reflections to both teachers and learners.
requirements: Feedback must remain well-designed, timely, ongoing, formatively useful, and easy to understand to be adequately valid
constraints: Automated tools may lack the nuance needed to assess complex thinking, potentially undermining educational intentions, as the review notes citing Bearman et al. (2023)
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: timely, personalized formative feedback
examples: The review cites studies where learning analytics monitored learning activities and provided real-time reflections and feedback to teachers and learners

article_title: Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics
citation: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Dragan Gašević, Omid Noroozi, Halszka Jarodzka, Desiree Joosten-ten Brinke, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251370753
title: Four characteristics underpin the validity of formative assessment, which learning analytics can strengthen through rich multimodal evidence
description: The review presents validity as a matter of degree and identifies characteristics that underpin valid formative assessment. It states: "According to Gikandi et al. (2011), four characteristics underpin the validity of formative assessment: (1) authenticity of assessment activities, (2) effective formative feedback, (3) inclusion of multidimensional perspectives, and (4) robust learner support." It further argues that learning analytics strengthens the validity argument by "capturing, analyzing, and reporting rich, multimodal evidence of student learning progress," and cites Divjak et al. (2023) on using analytics to compare ideal learning-objective priorities, assessment weights, and achievement data.
requirements: Valid formative assessment must provide sufficient evidence that inferences about student learning are accurate and aligned with intended learning outcomes
constraints: The validity framework is attributed to Gikandi et al. (2011) and Divjak et al. (2023); the review does not empirically test it
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: valid evidence-based formative assessment
examples: Divjak et al.'s model uses clustering and trace data analysis to support constructive alignment between learning outcomes and assessment

article_title: Principal Burnout: A Systematic Review
citation: Rogers, L. K., Nguyen, T. D., Timmer, M., & Samson, J. (2025). Principal Burnout: A Systematic Review. Working paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED666666
title: Three-category taxonomy of principal burnout antecedents: environmental, job/organizational, and personal factors
description: The review organizes antecedents of principal burnout into three categories derived from inductive coding of 99 studies: environmental conditions ("pressures and stressors relating to external or societal context, e.g., accountability, the pandemic"), job/organizational conditions (pressures from the particular school, e.g., workload, teacher interactions, parent demands), and personal factors (traits and characteristics such as gender, age, personality, and coping strategies). The authors initially proposed four categories but combined professional and organizational conditions due to difficulty delineating them.
requirements: Studies must empirically examine or hypothesize burnout in relation to at least one antecedent category
constraints: The taxonomy is descriptive and derived from a literature with no causal frameworks; category boundaries between professional and organizational conditions are acknowledged as difficult to delineate
target_learners: school principals
education researchers
target_learning_goals: understanding causes of principal burnout
informing policies and practices to address principal burnout
examples: The review coded 99 studies and found 67% addressed job/organizational conditions, 12% environmental conditions, and personal factors as the most studied category overall

article_title: Democratic Education: A Theoretical Review (2006–2017)
citation: Edda Sant. (2019). Democratic Education: A Theoretical Review (2006–2017). Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654319862493
title: Democratic education as a floating signifier constructed by eight competing political discourses
description: The review theorizes democratic education as a nodal point or floating signifier in education scholarship: a contested term that rival political discourses struggle to invest with their own meaning. Discourse analysis of 377 articles yielded eight versions: two against (elitist, neoliberal) and six pro (liberal, deliberative, multiculturalist, participatory, critical, agonistic). Each version is distinguished by ontological and epistemological assumptions, normative approaches to democracy, and conceptions of the education–politics relationship. The review states that "Democratic education functions as a privileged nodal point of different political discourses."
requirements: Articles must explicitly discuss the term democratic education and aim to invest it with meaning, since the term is treated as a floating signifier
constraints: Findings are limited to theory and research published in English language peer-reviewed journal articles between 2006 and 2017; dissertations, books, and other languages were excluded
target_learners: students in formal education, particularly primary and secondary institutions
target_learning_goals: education for democratic citizenship and participation in democratic life
examples: The review maps each version's key principles, educational implications for policy and practice, and the debates and critiques raised against it
key_sources: Edda Sant. (2019). Democratic Education: A Theoretical Review (2006–2017). Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654319862493

title: Evolution of the PIL knowledge base as parallel to broader evolution of leadership perspectives and models in education
description: The article offers an explanatory account in which the thematic evolution of principal instructional leadership research mirrors developments in the wider educational leadership field. It states that "This evolution parallels the evolution of leadership perspectives and models in the educational field broadly, and the increasing focus on leadership as key to school effectiveness and improvement." On this account, the shift from directive to integrated PIL conceptions is part of a field-wide movement, driven by growing attention to leadership for school effectiveness and improvement.
requirements: Interpretation rests on the bibliometric and thematic analysis of the 695-article PIL corpus across the three analysis periods
constraints: The article presents this parallelism as an interpretive claim about the literature, not a tested causal relationship

educational leadership researchers
target_learning_goals: understanding how conceptions of principal instructional leadership have developed over time
examples: The SciMAT thematic analysis traced PIL themes across three periods between 1941 and 2024

article_title: Do New Forms of Reading Pay Off? A Meta-Analysis on the Relationship Between Leisure Digital Reading Habits and Text Comprehension
citation: Altamura, L., Vargas, C., & Salmerón, L. (2023). Do New Forms of Reading Pay Off? A Meta-Analysis on the Relationship Between Leisure Digital Reading Habits and Text Comprehension. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231216463
title: Shallowing versus displacement hypotheses as competing accounts of digital reading habits' comprehension payoff
description: The article frames two competing explanatory accounts for how leisure digital reading habits relate to comprehension. The displacement hypothesis holds that "time previously devoted to print reading may just be replaced by time devoted to digital reading", predicting a positive association comparable to print. The shallowing hypothesis holds that frequent use of ultra-brief social media promotes rapid, relatively shallow thought, so short-length, fast-paced, low linguistic-quality digital texts foster scanning and skimming rather than deep processing. The authors state their results do not support displacement and tentatively favor shallowing as an explanation for the small pooled effect.
requirements: The account applies to leisure (not academic or work-related) digital reading habits measured via self-report frequency questionnaires in correlational studies.
constraints: The authors state they can only speculate about the divergent patterns, since the primary studies are correlational and cannot establish causal mechanisms.
target_learners: readers across the lifespan, from primary school students to university students and adults
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension development
examples: The meta-analysis tested the displacement prediction of a positive association and the shallowing prediction of negative-to-null effect sizes against the pooled r = .055 and the stage moderation pattern.

article_title: Statistical Practices of Educational Researchers: An Analysis of Their ANOVA, MANOVA, and ANCOVA Analyses
citation: Keselman, H.J., Huberty, C.J., Lix, L.M., Olejnik, S., Cribbie, R.A., Donahue, B., Kowalchuk, R.K., Lowman, L.L., Petoskey, M.D., Keselman, J.C., & Levin, J.R. (1998). Statistical Practises of Educational Researchers: An Analysis of Their ANOVA, MANOVA and ANCOVA Analyses.
title: Use robust test procedures, focused hypothesis tests, and routine effect size reporting when analyzing between-subjects designs
description: The article's central recommendation for improving between-subjects univariate analysis practice: researchers should adopt procedures designed for use under variance heterogeneity and/or nonnormality, prefer focused tests over general omnibus tests, and routinely report measures of effect. The authors state, "We strongly encourage: (a) selecting robust methods for conducting omnibus tests and contrasts, (b) conducting focused tests of hypotheses, and (c) routinely reporting measures of effect." They point to research reviews documenting conditions under which robust procedures such as the Welch and James tests exhibit optimal results.
requirements: Analysts must consider the distributional assumptions of their procedures and consult research reviews documenting when robust procedures are optimal
constraints: The recommendation addresses between-subjects univariate designs as reviewed in this content analysis
target_learners: educational researchers
graduate students in methodological courses
target_learning_goals: selecting valid inferential procedures
interpreting published research
reporting research results
examples: The content analysis found the ANOVA F test used in more than 90% of between-subjects univariate articles while effect sizes arose in only 10 articles (16.1%), motivating the recommendation.

article_title: Social Robots for Language Learning: A Review
citation: van den Berghe, R., Verhagen, J., Oudgenoeg-Paz, O., van der Ven, S., & Leseman, P. (2019). Social Robots for Language Learning: A Review. Review of Educational Research, 89(2), 259-295. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318821286
title: Robot-assisted language learning (RALL) as a rapidly developing research field spanning languages, age groups, language aspects, robots, and methodologies
description: The review organizes the field of robot-assisted language learning (RALL), which it describes as developing rapidly, along several axes: the languages targeted, the age groups studied, the aspects of language taught, and the robots and methodologies used. It states that "Studies have been published targeting different languages, age groups, and aspects of language and using different robots and methodologies." The review uses this organizing scheme to present "an overview of the results obtained so far in RALL research" and to discuss current possibilities and limitations of social robots for first- and second-language learning.
requirements: A corpus of RALL studies targeting different languages, age groups, language aspects, robots, and methodologies is needed to map the field as the review does.
constraints: The review's overview is limited to studies in which vocabulary, reading skills, speaking skills, grammar, and sign language were taught.

target_learning_goals: vocabulary
reading skills
speaking skills
grammar
sign language
examples: The review discusses thirty-three RALL studies as the basis of its overview of the field.

article_title: Inclusive Strategies for Children With Developmental Disabilities in Mainstream Classrooms in African Countries: A Systematic Review of Stakeholder Experiences, Attitudes, and Perspectives
citation: Genovesi Elisa, Gaches Akhina, McKenzie Judith, Hanlon Charlotte, Hoekstra Rosa A. (2024). Inclusive Strategies for Children With Developmental Disabilities in Mainstream Classrooms in African Countries: A Systematic Review of Stakeholder Experiences, Attitudes, and Perspectives. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241288247
title: Six interrelated themes organize stakeholder perspectives on inclusive strategies for children with DD in African mainstream classrooms
description: The review's reflexive thematic analysis of extracts from 28 qualitative African studies developed a thematic map of six interdependent themes with subthemes: meeting learners' needs, targeted support and feedback, whole-class approach, inclusive environment, engaging teaching, and fit with the evidence base. The authors state that "Our interpretation of the data lead to the development of six interdependent themes, each with subthemes, as shown in the thematic map in Figure 1." Subthemes were closely interrelated across themes.
requirements: Studies must be qualitative reports of stakeholder experiences of inclusive education for children with DD in mainstream African classrooms
constraints: Synthesis focused on approaches, drivers, and aims of strategies rather than technical details such as specific tasks, needs assessment or timings
Not all studies are equally represented in the synthesis; five contributed only one or two short relevant extracts
target_learners: children with developmental disabilities in mainstream primary and secondary schools in non-Arab African countries
target_learning_goals: inclusive education for learners with developmental disabilities
examples: The thematic map in Figure 1 exemplifies subthemes with extracts and participant quotes from 13 synthesized papers
key_sources: Genovesi Elisa, Gaches Akhina, McKenzie Judith, Hanlon Charlotte, Hoekstra Rosa A. (2024). Inclusive Strategies for Children With Developmental Disabilities in Mainstream Classrooms in African Countries: A Systematic Review of Stakeholder Experiences, Attitudes, and Perspectives. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241288247

article_title: Navigating an Academic Career in Marketized Universities: Mapping the International Literature
citation: Oliveira, T., Nada, C., & Magalhães, A. (2024). Navigating an Academic Career in Marketized Universities: Mapping the International Literature. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231226336
title: Four-theme framework of academic careers under marketization: individual project, surviving the game, emotionality, and inclusion/exclusion
description: The review organizes its answer to how marketization affects academic careers into four inductively derived themes: "academic careers as an individual project," "surviving the academic career “game,”" "academic careers influenced by emotionality," and "academic environments as places of inclusion and exclusion." The framework maps how neoliberal dynamics individualize career projects, frame careers as competitive games governed by audit metrics, embed emotional narratives that normalize exploitation, and produce inclusion and exclusion in academic environments. It was derived via thematic analysis of 54 documents in NVivo.
requirements: A corpus of literature on academic careers amenable to inductive thematic analysis, as the review conducted with NVivo-supported coding
constraints: The review states it is a partial expression located geographically, overrepresented by English-language countries, with no article from Scielo remaining after selection
target_learners: Academics and early career academics in higher education
target_learning_goals: Understanding how marketization shapes academic career development and professional pathways
examples: The review's findings section presents the four themes in sequence, each supported by documents from the 54-article corpus marked with an asterisk in the reference list.
key_sources: Oliveira, T., Nada, C., & Magalhães, A. (2024). Navigating an Academic Career in Marketized Universities: Mapping the International Literature. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231226336

article_title: Navigating an Academic Career in Marketized Universities: Mapping the International Literature
citation: Oliveira, T., Nada, C., & Magalhães, A. (2024). Navigating an Academic Career in Marketized Universities: Mapping the International Literature. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231226336
title: Systematic literature review corpus of 54 documents on academic careers from 21 national contexts (Scopus and Scielo, 2000–2021)
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 54 selected documents assembled from searches of Scopus (475 results) and Scielo (39 results) in February 2022, screened in two levels from an initial pool of 509 entries after duplicate removal. The corpus "included both theoretical contributions and empirical findings from 21 different national contexts," published between 2000 and 2021 in English or Portuguese. Most documents came from English-primary-language countries (n = 33), and most employed qualitative designs, with interviews the largest data-collection technique (n = 24).
requirements: Access to Scopus and Scielo databases and the review's Boolean search string on academic careers
constraints: No article from Scielo remained after applying the selection criteria, and the corpus was overrepresented by research from English-primary-language countries
target_learners: Researchers studying academic careers and higher education work
target_learning_goals: Mapping the international literature on academic careers under marketization
examples: Searches in February 2022 yielded 475 Scopus and 39 Scielo entries; after screening, 54 documents were thematically analyzed.

article_title: A Systematic Review of Early Childhood Exclusionary Discipline
citation: Katherine M. Zinsser, H. Callie Silver, Elyse R. Shenberger, and Velisha Jackson. (2022). A Systematic Review of Early Childhood Exclusionary Discipline. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211070047
title: Ecological systems theory as the organizing framework for factors associated with early childhood exclusion
description: The review uses Bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory to structure its synthesis of factors associated with ECCE exclusion, organizing predictors into micro- (child and family characteristics), meso- (teachers and classrooms), and exo-system (program administration, policies, resources) levels. The authors state that "Children's exclusions are the result of a series of adult decisions that themselves are informed by context." They deliberately exclude the macrosystem and chronosystem because those involve contextual factors evolving over extended periods. The framework is used to identify gaps in the literature as blind spots in understanding the phenomenon.
requirements: Studies must report predictors that can be assigned to ecological levels (child, teacher/classroom, program) for the framework to organize findings
constraints: The review does not anticipate identifying research capturing macrosystem or chronosystem phenomena because these evolve over generations
target_learners: children birth to age 5 in early care and education settings
target_learning_goals: reducing exclusionary discipline (suspension and expulsion) of young children from early care and education settings
examples: Table 3 of the review assigns each included study's predictors to micro-, meso-, and exo-system columns, with disagreements resolved by lead-author third coding until consensus
key_sources: Katherine M. Zinsser, H. Callie Silver, Elyse R. Shenberger, and Velisha Jackson. (2022). A Systematic Review of Early Childhood Exclusionary Discipline. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211070047

article_title: Statistical Practices of Educational Researchers: An Analysis of their ANOVA, MANOVA, and ANCOVA Analyses
citation: Keselman, H. J., Huberty, C. J., Lix, L. M., Olejnik, S., Cribbie, R. A., Donahue, B., Kowalchuk, R. K., Lowman, L. L., Petoskey, M. D., Keselman, J. C., & Levin, J. R. (1998). Statistical Practises of Educational Researchers: An Analysis of Their ANOVA, MANOVA and ANCOVA Analyses. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Statistical+Practises+of+Educational+Researchers
title: Adopt robust statistical test procedures and routinely report effect sizes when analyzing group differences
description: The article recommends that behavioral science researchers replace routine use of the conventional ANOVA F test with procedures designed for heterogeneous variances and nonnormality, and that they report measures of effect size alongside p-values. It states: "It is strongly recommended that test procedures that have been designed specifically for use in the presence of variance heterogeneity and/or nonnormality be adopted on a routine basis." It also encourages focused tests of hypotheses rather than preliminary omnibus tests, citing the omnibus F test's limitation that it "typically does not address an interesting substantive question."
requirements: Access to robust procedures (e.g., Welch and James tests) and the computer programs and research reviews that document their use
constraints: The article notes nonparametric procedures are not good practice when variance homogeneity is suspect, since the Kruskal-Wallis test is highly sensitive to unequal variances
target_learners: educational researchers
graduate students in methodological courses
target_learning_goals: conducting valid inferential analyses of group differences
interpreting published educational research
examples: The content analysis found fewer than 20% of between-subjects articles mentioned assumption violations, and effect sizes were almost never reported despite APA Publication Manual encouragement

article_title: Teacher Self-Efficacy and Its Effects on Classroom Processes, Student Academic Adjustment, and Teacher Well-Being
citation: M. Zee, H.M.Y. Koomen. (2016). Teacher self-efficacy and its effects on classroom processes, student academic adjustment, and teacher well-being: A synthesis of 40 years of research. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315626801
title: Teacher self-efficacy as an organizing framework for classroom processes, student adjustment, and teacher well-being
description: Teacher self-efficacy (TSE) serves as this review's organizing framework: the authors integrate "40 years of teacher self-efficacy (TSE) research" to map the consequences of TSE for three outcome domains — the quality of classroom processes, students' academic adjustment, and teachers' psychological well-being. Within the framework, TSE is positioned as a teacher-level belief variable positively linked to classroom quality practices and well-being factors and negatively linked to burnout, with indirect paths through instructional support and classroom organization.
constraints: The review discusses "gaps in the measurement and analysis of TSE in the educational literature".
target_learners: teachers
target_learning_goals: quality of classroom processes
students' academic adjustment
teachers' psychological well-being
examples: A criteria-based review of 165 eligible articles integrating 40 years of TSE research
key_sources: M. Zee, H.M.Y. Koomen. (2016). Teacher self-efficacy and its effects on classroom processes, student academic adjustment, and teacher well-being: A synthesis of 40 years of research. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315626801

article_title: Teacher Self-Efficacy and Its Effects on Classroom Processes, Student Academic Adjustment, and Teacher Well-Being
citation: M. Zee, H.M.Y. Koomen. (2016). Teacher self-efficacy and its effects on classroom processes, student academic adjustment, and teacher well-being: A synthesis of 40 years of research. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654315626801
title: Criteria-based review corpus of 165 teacher self-efficacy articles
description: The evidence base for this synthesis is a corpus of 165 eligible articles on teacher self-efficacy, selected through a "criteria-based review approach". The corpus spans 40 years of TSE research and underpins the review's conclusions about links between TSE and classroom processes, students' academic adjustment, and teachers' psychological well-being, including the burnout findings and the small set of indirect-effect studies.
requirements: Articles had to meet the review's inclusion criteria to be counted as eligible for analysis
target_learners: teachers
target_learning_goals: teacher self-efficacy and its consequences for classroom processes, student adjustment, and teacher well-being
examples: 165 eligible articles included for analysis via a criteria-based review approach
