article_title: The Association Between School Discipline and Self-Control From Preschoolers to High School Students: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
citation: Li, J. B., Bi, S. S., Willems, Y. E., & Finkenauer, C. (2021). The Association Between School Discipline and Self-Control From Preschoolers to High School Students: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 91(1), 73-111. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320979160
title: Three-component taxonomy of school discipline: structure, support, and teacher-student relationship
description: The meta-analysis organizes school discipline into three components: "structure, support, and teacher-student relationship". This taxonomy frames how facets of the school environment are hypothesized to relate to individual differences in students' self-control, and it served as the organizing moderator dimension across the 68 synthesized studies, with effect sizes found similar across the three components.
requirements: Studies must operationalize school discipline through one of the three components to be synthesized under the taxonomy
constraints: The taxonomy concerns school discipline as an environmental factor, not disciplinary techniques such as authoritarian or authoritative styles the keywords mention
target_learners: students from preschool to high school
target_learning_goals: self-control and self-regulation development
key_sources: Li, J. B., Bi, S. S., Willems, Y. E., & Finkenauer, C. (2021). The Association Between School Discipline and Self-Control From Preschoolers to High School Students: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 91(1), 73-111. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320979160

article_title: The Association Between School Discipline and Self-Control From Preschoolers to High School Students: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis
citation: Li, J. B., Bi, S. S., Willems, Y. E., & Finkenauer, C. (2021). The Association Between School Discipline and Self-Control From Preschoolers to High School Students: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 91(1), 73-111. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320979160
title: Attend to school discipline — structure, support, and teacher-student relationships — when aiming to develop students' self-control
description: Because school discipline is consistently associated with self-control across ages and measures, schools seeking to develop students' self-control should treat discipline practices — structure, support, and teacher-student relationships — as a relevant design lever. The article concludes these "findings point to the importance of school discipline associated with individual differences in self-control in students from preschool to high school".
requirements: Discipline practices must be measurable across the three components for schools to monitor their association with self-control
constraints: The evidence is correlational; the article does not establish that changing discipline causally develops self-control
target_learners: students from preschool to high school
target_learning_goals: self-control and self-regulation development
examples: The meta-analysis synthesized 68 studies of school discipline and self-control spanning preschool to high school students
key_sources: Li, J. B., Bi, S. S., Willems, Y. E., & Finkenauer, C. (2021). The Association Between School Discipline and Self-Control From Preschoolers to High School Students: A Three-Level Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 91(1), 73-111. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320979160

article_title: A Systematic Mapping Literature Review on Two-Eyed Seeing in P-20 Education
citation: Gardner-Vandy, K., Utley, J., Just, A., Hathcock, S., & Stansberry, S. (2025). A Systematic Mapping Literature Review on Two-Eyed Seeing in P-20 Education. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251329570
title: Two-Eyed Seeing (Etuaptmumk) as a pedagogical approach interweaving Indigenous and Western ways of knowing
description: Two-Eyed Seeing (TES), in Mi'kmaq Etuaptmumk, was originally presented by Mi'kmaq Elder Albert Marshall in 2004. It "refers to learning to see from one eye with the strengths of Indigenous ways of knowing and from the other eye with the strengths of western ways of knowing and to using both of these eyes together" (Hatcher et al., 2009a, p. 146). A TES approach weaves Indigenous and Western knowledges, implies "responsibilities for reciprocity, mutual accountability, and co-learning" (Hogue & Bartlett, 2014), seeks commonalities between the two sciences while respecting differences, and aims to eliminate conflicts between them. Elder Marshall described TES as "a guiding principle that covers all aspects of our lives," applicable beyond science education.
requirements: Requires interweaving rather than side-by-side introduction of the two knowledge systems, with Indigenous knowledge holders included as part of the process
constraints: The review limits its scope to TES specifically, excluding other frameworks that merge Indigenous knowledges with Western science
target_learners: P-20 students, including Indigenous students in formal educational settings
target_learning_goals: Interweaving Indigenous ways of knowing with Western science to increase Indigenous students' engagement with content
examples: TES was first used at Cape Breton University in Nova Scotia in an integrative science program devised to encourage Mi'kmaw students to pursue science and science-related programs
key_sources: Gardner-Vandy, K., Utley, J., Just, A., Hathcock, S., & Stansberry, S. (2025). A Systematic Mapping Literature Review on Two-Eyed Seeing in P-20 Education. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251329570

article_title: A Systematic Mapping Literature Review on Two-Eyed Seeing in P-20 Education
citation: Gardner-Vandy, K., Utley, J., Just, A., Hathcock, S., & Stansberry, S. (2025). A Systematic Mapping Literature Review on Two-Eyed Seeing in P-20 Education. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251329570
title: Five-theme guideline set for incorporating Two-Eyed Seeing into P-20 classrooms
description: Twelve of the 13 reviewed articles suggested recommendations or guidelines for incorporating TES into the classroom, which the review compiled and organized into five themes, each divided into categories (Figure 7). "These included guidelines that dealt with philosophical framework, teacher supports, generation of curriculum, the teacher's role in the learning process, and the classroom environment." The philosophical framework theme includes inclusive science, holistic approaches, identity-building and self-reflection, and acknowledgment of settler-colonialism; the curriculum-generation theme includes experiential, inquiry-based, and land-based learning, interweaving knowledges, lesson planning, storytelling, and respectful inclusion of Indigenous knowledges.
requirements: Educators must develop relationships within the Indigenous community first, holding elders and knowledge holders as experts and trusted consultants and instructors
constraints: Guidelines were compiled from only 13 peer-reviewed articles, nearly all from Canada, and one article offered no specific guidelines
target_learners: P-20 educators and their students, including Indigenous students
target_learning_goals: Incorporating Two-Eyed Seeing into classroom curriculum and instruction
examples: Slightly more than half of the articles (n = 7) noted that educators and administrators must acknowledge that Indigenous knowledge and Western science are equally significant, valid, and complimentary
key_sources: Gardner-Vandy, K., Utley, J., Just, A., Hathcock, S., & Stansberry, S. (2025). A Systematic Mapping Literature Review on Two-Eyed Seeing in P-20 Education. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251329570

article_title: Team-Based Professional Development Interventions in Higher Education: A Systematic Review
citation: Gast, Inken; Schildkamp, Kim; van der Veen, Jan T. (2017). Team-Based Professional Development Interventions in Higher Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317704306
title: Three-level framework of conditions for successful team-based professional development in higher education
description: The review organizes the conditions for successful team-based professional development into three levels: "conditions at the individual teacher level, conditions at the team level, and conditions at the organizational level." Six individual conditions were identified (attitudes, motivation, commitment, self-efficacy, professional identity, availability), five team conditions (team interaction, goals and objectives, team composition, team leadership, small group work), and four organizational conditions (organizational support, rewards, research focus, finances and resources). Only conditions mentioned in at least two articles were included.
requirements: Conditions must be mentioned in at least two of the reviewed articles to be included in the framework
constraints: The framework was derived from 18 studies in higher education, a field the review describes as fairly new, using mostly qualitative methods
target_learners: higher education faculty members who teach and/or design courses
target_learning_goals: teacher learning of new knowledge and skills for curriculum innovation and teaching practice
examples: The review's Table 3 maps each theme and condition to the supporting studies, e.g., organizational support was supported by 12 of the 18 studies
key_sources: Gast, Inken; Schildkamp, Kim; van der Veen, Jan T. (2017). Team-Based Professional Development Interventions in Higher Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317704306

article_title: Impact of In-Service Professional Development Programs for Early Childhood Teachers on Quality Ratings and Child Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
citation: F. Egert, R.G. Fukkink, A.G. Eckhardt. (2018). Impact of In-Service Professional Development Programs for Early Childhood Teachers on Quality Ratings and Child Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317751918
title: Quality improvement as the key mechanism linking teacher professional development to child development
description: The article proposes that improving pedagogical process quality is the pathway through which in-service training affects young children's development. It states that "quality improvement is a key mechanism to accelerate the development of young children," grounded in its finding that child-level effect variance was significantly related to effects on quality ratings (53% explained variance). The framework positions external quality ratings as the proximal outcome and child development as the distal outcome of professional development.
requirements: Programs must produce measurable improvements in externally rated process quality for child-level benefits to follow
constraints: Evidence base limited to (quasi)-experimental ECEC in-service training studies; the mechanism relation is meta-analytic and correlational across studies
target_learners: young children in early childhood education and care settings
target_learning_goals: developmental outcomes in young children supported by improved pedagogical process quality
examples: The meta-analysis tested the mechanism by relating child-level effect sizes to quality-rating effect sizes across the nine-study subset
key_sources: F. Egert, R.G. Fukkink, A.G. Eckhardt. (2018). Impact of In-Service Professional Development Programs for Early Childhood Teachers on Quality Ratings and Child Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317751918

article_title: Impact of In-Service Professional Development Programs for Early Childhood Teachers on Quality Ratings and Child Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis
citation: F. Egert, R.G. Fukkink, A.G. Eckhardt. (2018). Impact of In-Service Professional Development Programs for Early Childhood Teachers on Quality Ratings and Child Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317751918
title: Invest in in-service professional development for ECEC professionals as a lever for raising process quality and child outcomes
description: The article supports investing in in-service training for early childhood professionals because its synthesis shows such training reliably raises externally rated process quality and, through quality improvement, child development. It concludes that "quality improvement is a key mechanism to accelerate the development of young children," with a medium teacher-level effect (ES = 0.68) and a small but significant child-level effect (ES = 0.14).
requirements: Training should target improvements in pedagogical process quality as rated by external observers
Programs should be evaluated with (quasi)-experimental designs to verify quality and child outcomes
constraints: Child-level effects are small and depend on the training also improving quality ratings
target_learners: in-service early childhood education and care professionals and the young children they teach
target_learning_goals: improving pedagogical process quality and accelerating young children's development
examples: The meta-analysis aggregated 36 studies with 2,891 teachers on quality ratings and nine studies with 4,504 children on child development
key_sources: F. Egert, R.G. Fukkink, A.G. Eckhardt. (2018). Impact of In-Service Professional Development Programs for Early Childhood Teachers on Quality Ratings and Child Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317751918
